## Front Matter of the Volume

### Title Page of the Series

**The Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, and Economical Library**, containing all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age down to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reissue of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived through the first twelve centuries of the Church, prepared from the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with several manuscript codices, and corrected with the greatest diligence; continuously elucidated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all the works discovered after the extensive editions owed to the last three centuries had been completed; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume and each author of any importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with headings distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter treated; expanded by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and by works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a single glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it is immediately evident to the reader which Fathers, and in which places in their works, have commented on the individual texts of the individual books of Scripture.

A most accurate edition, and one easily to be preferred to all others, if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the works reprinted, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, the low price, and above all this collection, which is the first unified, systematic, and chronological gathering of six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, but now assembled for the first time in our library from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.

### First Series

In this series appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church, from Tertullian to Gregory the Great.

Prepared by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Complete Courses in the individual branches of ecclesiastical scholarship.

# The Works of John Cassian

## John Cassian, Presbyter of Massilia, Seven Books on the Incarnation of Christ against the Heretic Nestorius

[Col. 0009]

### Note

It may be inferred from the old and accepted judgment of Gennadius that Cassian’s preface to the books on the Incarnation of Christ was prefixed to them and sent and dedicated, in the manner of a dedicatory letter, to Leo, then archdeacon of the Roman Church and afterward made supreme pontiff, who had been the instigator and adviser of his writing this work. Gennadius says of Cassian in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 61:

“At the end, when requested by Leo, archdeacon of the city of Rome, afterward its bishop, he wrote seven books against Nestorius on the Incarnation of the Lord; and while writing these books at Massilia, he brought his life to an end, during the reigns of Theodosius and Valentinian.”

It will be worthwhile, however, to hear the author of the *Ecclesiastical Annals* discuss these matters more fully and accurately, and in no words other than his own. In volume V he writes:

“In this very year—that is, the seventh year of Pope Celestine, the year of Christ 430—John Cassian, at the urging of Leo, archdeacon of the Roman Church, published seven splendid books against Nestorius on the Incarnation of the Word.

Since it is certain that he wrote them while Nestorius was still seated at Constantinople, and since it is clear that Nestorius was deposed from his see in the council of Ephesus in the following year, with Maximus substituted in his place; and since, moreover, these books contain no mention of the Council of Ephesus, which necessarily would have been remembered, it must plainly be said that Cassian composed them before the Council of Ephesus and before Nestorius’s condemnation—indeed, in that very year when, as we have seen, Nestorius’s heresy became fully known to the Western Church. Before that time, only certain rumors concerning it had reached the Western shores.

“But why,” someone might ask, “did the archdeacon Leo have these things undertaken by Cassian, when Leo himself was extremely learned and could have presented the matter most successfully, especially since Cassian had become known, through the published books of the *Conferences*, as holding an incorrect view of free will and as sharing something with the Pelagians?”

Cassian himself testifies in the preface to the work that, after writing the *Conferences*, he composed this commentary against Nestorius at Leo’s urging:

“First of all, it must be said that Cassian and the others who at this time criticized the writings of Saint Augustine did not profess that they supported the errors of Pelagius. Rather, as Prosper frequently says, and as the letters of Celestine, Roman pontiff, to the Gauls indicate, they behaved as Catholics among Catholics; they professed to condemn the errors of Pelagius and made a show of declaiming against them. We see this done by Cassian himself in these very books that he wrote on the Incarnation of the Word against Nestorius, where he frequently exclaims that Nestorius himself borrowed his error from the Pelagians.

“Leo’s intention, therefore, in this respect seems to have been that the Easterners should not suppose that the Nestorian heresy had defenders in the West who were in any way suspected of the Pelagian error; and so he wished Nestorius to be attacked with the greatest force by one of those men.

“Again, lest any in the West who had until then defended in published writings the Pelagian position concerning free will should, because of the affinity of the doctrines, rise up in defense of Nestorius, the deacon Leo prudently wished to bind Cassian—who surpassed them all—in the first place by his writing, and with him all those who among the Catholics appeared to favor the Pelagian error.

“Cassian willingly fulfilled this task and devoted himself with every effort to the work, so that he might present himself as an exceedingly fierce enemy both of the Pelagian and of the Nestorian error. The most notorious of all the Pelagians, Leporius, had already expressed his abhorrence of the latter in public letters.

“Moreover, Leo may also have had this purpose in the matter: that through John Cassian, formerly a deacon of the Church of Constantinople, the Church of Constantinople might be admonished to avoid Nestorius. The apostrophe placed by the author at the end of the work easily persuades us that this too may be believed. After attacking Nestorius with other such invective, Cassian writes:

“‘You, most impious and most shameless defiler of that glorious city, grievous and deadly contagion of the Catholic and holy people: you dare to stand in the Church of God and to speak, and with your blasphemous and frenzied words to defame priests of unshaken faith and Catholic confession, making the people of the city of Constantinople err through the fault of their earlier teachers!’ (*On the Incarnation of the Word*, book VII).

“And the other passages found at the end of the seventh book, which Baronius also quotes in full.”

From this we have learned by what means and on what occasion Cassian was prompted by Leo to write these books.

---

## Preface to Leo, Bishop of the City of Rome

[Col. 0009A]

### Note

It is sufficiently evident from this passage that John Cassian, before applying his hand to the composition of these books, had long since completed the books of the *Conferences*. Baronius rightly infers this from the words of Cassian cited in support:

“From these words,” he says, “we may understand that he completed the *Conferences* in the preceding year, 429, or in the year before that—unless perhaps he completed those same *Conferences* in this very year.”

This work, therefore, must be called Cassian’s final work and the last product of his intellect, as Gennadius also testifies when he says that, while writing these books at Massilia, Cassian brought his life to an end.

After I had long since completed the little books of the *Spiritual Conferences*, distinguished more by their meaning than by their language—for our language was unequal to the profound meaning of holy men—I had considered, and had almost decided, that after the shame of the ignorance I had displayed I should place myself in the harbor of silence, so that, insofar as possible, I might excuse by the modesty of silence the audacity of speech.

### Note

Thus he himself had professed at the end of the twenty-fourth Conference:

“It remains that I, tossed until now upon a most dangerous storm, may now be accompanied by the breeze of your spiritual prayers into the safest harbor of silence.”

But you have overcome my purpose and my judgment by your praiseworthy zeal and most commanding affection, my venerable Leo [in the Leipzig edition, “venerable” is feminine], and—[the text continues with an uncertain reading]—you, the esteem-worthy splendor of the Roman Church and the ornament of the divine ministry, draw me from that retreat of deliberate silence into the public and dreaded tribunal, and compel me to undertake new trials while I am still ashamed of what has gone before. Though I have been unequal even to lesser things, you force me to be equal to greater ones.

### Note

There appears to be an error in these words, which agree neither with what precedes nor with what follows; still more so in the Lyons edition, where the text reads: “My charity for the Roman Church must be undertaken,” and so forth. For what could “my charity for the Roman Church” mean? I would believe that the passage should be corrected so that *claritas*—“splendor”—rather than *charitas*—“charity”—is read, and that *mea*—“my”—should be deleted, as follows:

“My venerable and esteemed Leo, the splendor of the Roman Church worthy of esteem, and the ornament of the divine ministry …”

The words should thus be understood as referring to Leo himself, whom Cassian adorns with these honorary titles, calling him the splendor, or light, of the Roman Church and the ornament of the ecclesiastical order, or ministry, as he truly was.

For I would not even have attempted to undertake or claim anything in those little works by which, through the small offering of our intellect, we sacrificed to the Lord, had I not been drawn on by episcopal authority.

Through you, therefore, the dignity of our mouth and pen has increased. For whereas previously, when ordered, we spoke of the Lord’s studies, now you require us to speak of the Incarnation and majesty of the Lord himself. Thus, after we were first led into the holy temple, as it were by a priestly hand, we now, under your guidance and with your assistance, enter as though into the Holy of Holies.

It is a great honor, but a perilous advance [in the Leipzig margin: “undertaking”], because the prize of attaining the inner sanctuaries and the divine reward cannot be won unless the enemy has been overcome.

You therefore require and command me to bring my weak hands against a recent heresy and a new enemy of the faith, and to stand, as they say, with open mouth against the dreadful jaws of the poisonous serpent.

### Note

That is, Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople, who in the year of the Lord 428 or 429 began to teach that the blessed Virgin Mary was not *Theotokos*—θεοτόκος, “God-bearer,” or mother of God—but *Christotokos*—χριστοτόκος, as he called her, that is, the mother not of God but of Christ, that is, of a man. He also taught that there were two persons in Christ, one divine and the other human.

Thus Prosper writes in his *Chronicle*:

“Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople, attempted to introduce a new error into the Churches, preaching that Christ was born from Mary as man only and not as God, and that divinity had been bestowed upon him as a reward for merit. The authority of Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, and of Pope Celestine opposed this impiety above all.”

This is what Prosper says. But who Nestorius was, and what sort of man he was, will be explained more fully below.

The prophetic power and divine force of evangelical speech may therefore burst upon the dragon that rises against the Churches of God with winding coils, using me as though I were an enchanter.

I obey your entreaty; I obey your command. For I prefer to trust you about myself rather than myself, especially because the love of Jesus Christ, my Lord, commands this together with you—and commands the same thing in you.

It remains that you should ask from him by whom you commanded that the task you have commanded may be brought to completion. For the matter now concerns your cause more than mine; your judgment, rather than my service, is endangered.

Whether I am equal to your command or not, the very principle of obedience and humility excuses me to some extent—except that there is greater merit in my obedience if there is less ability to accomplish it.

We easily satisfy anyone’s command out of abundance; but great and admirable is the service of the one who has in his will even what he does not have in his strength.

This, therefore, is your affair, your task, the work of your honor. Pray and entreat that your choice not be endangered by my incompetence; and that, since I do well to obey through the pardon granted by obedience, you may nevertheless appear to have commanded badly through an inconsiderate judgment if we fail to correspond to so great an opinion of us.

# Book One

[Col. 0011]

## Chapter One. Heresy Is Compared with the Poetic Hydra

[Col. 0011C]

### Note

Thus Saint Jerome writes in the preface to book I of his *Commentary on Jeremiah*:

“Stories tell that the Lernaean serpent produced many snakes from its middle head.”

And in the preface to book VI on Ezekiel, speaking of the successors of the deceased Rufinus in impiety, he says:

“I thought that, after the serpent in the middle had been pierced, the young shoots of the hydra would not revive; and, according to the fable of the poets, once Scylla had died, the dogs of Scylla, which never cease barking, would not rage against me.”

The poets imagined the hydra as a beast with many heads, devastating everything in the marsh of Lerna. When one of its heads was cut off, several more were born in its place; at last Hercules overcame it with sword and torches. On this subject see Hesiod in the *Theogony* and Plato in the *Sophist*.

The Fathers commonly compare heresies and heretics with this monster. Thus Irenaeus, reproaching the Gnostics, writes in book I, chapter 34:

“Such, according to them, are their opinions, from which, as from the Lernaean hydra, the many-headed beast generated from the school of Valentinus has arisen.”

Athanasius writes against the Arians:

“The heretic, as the matter itself shows, possesses a mind wholly and everywhere depraved and corrupted toward impiety. For behold, although the Arians have been refuted everywhere, they nevertheless cannot be ashamed. Rather, just as in the tales of the pagans the celebrated hydra, after its former serpents had been removed and others had sprouted forth, stubbornly persisted, always presenting a new brood of serpents against the one who removed its serpents, so these accursed men, with a pagan mind, when cast down from the objections they had raised, discover others and invent Jewish and foolish controversies, thereby showing themselves still more plainly to be traitors to Christ and his opponents.”

Basil the Great also gives an elegant adaptation of this same fable at the end of his book *On True Virginity*.

The poets’ fables relate that when the hydra’s heads had once been cut off, it grew larger through its own losses, multiplying more abundantly, so that, by a new and unheard-of marvel, the monster gained through its deaths and its loss became a source of profit. Whatever the cutting sword severed, its prodigious fertility doubled; until the industrious pursuer of that first beheading, laboring and burning with effort, repeatedly finding his strength nullified by ineffective work, armed the courage of warfare with the art of strategy.

Then, when fires had been applied, as they say, he severed with a blazing sword the multiplied offspring of the monstrous body. Thus, as he burned its inward marrow and consumed the rebellious veins of its wicked fertility, at last the monstrous birth ceased.

So, too, heresies in the Churches bear the likeness of the hydra invented by the poets. They hiss at us with savage tongues; they cast forth deadly venom; and when their heads have been cut off, they are born again.

But because medicine must not cease when disease returns, and because the more serious the illness, the more persistent the treatment must be, our Lord God is powerful enough to accomplish in the battles of the Churches what pagan falsehood imagined concerning the death of that hydra. May the fiery sword of the Holy Spirit so burn away the innermost marrow of pernicious generation in extinguishing the newly arisen heresy that, at last, its prodigious fertility may cease to give birth as its veins die.

---

## Chapter Two. He Describes the Various Monsters of Heresy Sprouting from One Another

### Note

At the beginning of this work it is first necessary to know that, concerning the mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation, various errors and heresies once arose and were condemned by the Church, most of which the author reviews here in summary. Some of these may rightly be called parents and others their offspring. They may be reduced to three principal heads.

The Catholic faith chiefly professes three things concerning Christ, insofar as his person is concerned. First is his divinity, or the reality of the divine nature; second is his humanity, or the reality of human nature; third is the union of these natures, through which it comes about that he is truly and properly both God and man.

Accordingly, three kinds of heresy are also found to have gone astray concerning Christ’s person. For, as Saint Augustine says in book I of the *Questions on the Gospels*, at the end:

“They are mistaken either about his divinity, or about his humanity, or about both, that is, about the union of the two.”

And Saint Leo, in sermon 8 on the Nativity of the Lord, composing a catalogue of these heresies concerning Christ much like Cassian’s, says:

“Some”—the Manichaeans—“ascribed to the Lord humanity alone, others divinity alone. Others said that he certainly possessed true divinity, but that his flesh was only apparent. Others professed that he had assumed true flesh, but denied that he possessed the nature of God the Father; and, assigning to his divinity the things that belonged to human substance, they imagined for themselves a greater God and a lesser one, although there can be no degrees in true Divinity. For whatever is less than God is not God.

“Others”—the Sabellians and Patripassians—“recognizing no distinction between the Father and the Son, because they could not understand the unity of divinity except as unity of person, asserted that the Father was the same as the Son. They held that birth and nourishment, suffering and death, burial and resurrection belonged to the same one, who in every respect fulfilled both the person of a man and that of the Word.

“Some thought that the Lord Jesus Christ did not possess a body of our substance, but one taken from the higher and more subtle elements.

“Others”—the Valentinians, Apollinarists, and Eunomians—“believed that a human soul neither dwelt nor existed in Christ’s flesh, and that the divinity of the Word itself filled the functions of the soul.

“Their shamelessness went so far that, while admitting that a soul was indeed present in the Lord, they said that it lacked a mind, since the man’s divinity was sufficient for every function of reason.

“Finally, these same people dared to assert that some portion of the Word had been changed into flesh, so that, amid the manifold variety of a single doctrine, not only the nature of the flesh and soul but also the very essence of the Word would be dissolved.”

This is Saint Leo. See also his sermon 4 on the Nativity of the Lord. The matters that follow will make these things clearer.

For these are not new shoots of monstrous seed in the Churches. The harvest of the Lord’s field has always endured thistles and thorns, and the choking growth of weeds has continually emerged within it.

From this source came the Hebionites; from this source the Sabellians; from this source the Arians; finally from this source the Eunomians and Macedonians; from this source the Photinians and Apollinarists; and from this source sprang the other brambles of the Churches, choking the crop of sound faith.

### Note on Hebion

Ebion, or Hebion—from whom the Ebionites, or Hebionites, take their name—was the first heresiarch after Simon Magus, as Saint Ignatius testifies in his Letter to the Philadelphians. See Baronius, volume I, under the year 74.

Saint Jerome called him half-Christian and half-Jewish. He asserted that Christ was a mere man, or man only, and not also God; and therefore blasphemously denied that he had existed before his mother.

See Irenaeus, book I *Against Heresies*, chapter 26; Epiphanius, heresy 50; and Augustine, *On Heresies*.

### Note on Sabellius

Sabellius, a disciple and heresiarch of Noetus—from whom the Sabellians, also called Patripassians, derive their name—confused the persons in the Holy Trinity. See Baronius under the year 260.

He asserted that God, according to his will, was either the Father, or the Son, or the Holy Spirit; consequently, that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit were one person and three names.

Against him a synod was assembled at Alexandria, which decreed that three subsistent persons in one substance of God must be confessed. See Baronius, volume III; Epiphanius, heresy 57; and Augustine, in the place cited above.

### Note on Arius

Arius, or Arrius, who has also been discussed elsewhere, was an Alexandrian presbyter during the reign of the Emperor Constantine the Great. He denied that Christ was God, asserted that he was a creature, and refused to acknowledge that the Son was coeternal and *homoousios*—ὁμοούσιος, that is, consubstantial and of the same essence—with the Father.

For this reason he was condemned by the great Council of Nicaea and died an infamous death in the public latrines, expelling his life together with his intestines.

See Epiphanius, heresy 69; Augustine, heresy 49; Theodoret, *On Heretical Fables*; and Socrates, book I of his *History*, chapter 25.

### Note on the Eunomians

Eunomius, a disciple of Aetius, equal to him in impiety and a most disgraceful heresiarch—as is clear from Epiphanius, from the letter of the Council of Constantinople to Damasus, and also from Suidas and others—not only maintained the same position as Arius, asserting that the Son of God was a creature, and the same position as Macedonius, discussed below, denying that the Holy Spirit was God and placing him among creatures; he further added, on the basis of the filthy and diabolical teaching of his teacher Aetius, that the Holy Spirit was the creature of the created Son.

For this reason Saint Jerome said in his Letter to the Ephesians, chapter IV:

“Arius, Macedonius, and Eunomius, in discord agreeing in impiety, drew diverse streams of heresy from one fountain.”

See Saint Basil, books I and II against Eunomius; Augustine, heresy 54; and Sozomen, book VI, chapter 26. See also Baronius, volume III, under the year 360.

### Note on the Macedonians

Macedonius, bishop of Constantinople, taught around the year of the Lord 358 that the Son of God was in every respect like the Father, but that the Holy Spirit was a creature.

The Council of Constantinople, assembled at the command of Pope Damasus, condemned him. See the year 381; Epiphanius, heresy 78; Augustine, heresy 52; Socrates, book I, chapter 35; and Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, book II, chapter 6.

### Note on Photinus

Photinus, or Photius, bishop of Sirmium, arose as a heresiarch during the reign of the Emperor Constantius. Saint Epiphanius writes the following about him in heresy 71; see also Baronius, volume III, under the years 347 and 357:

“Photinus—from whom the Photinians derive their name—lived at this time and was bishop of the holy Catholic Church. Inflated by no small notoriety and becoming more insane than all those before him, he held opinions about the Son of God similar to those taught by Paul of Samosata, and poured forth words of abuse that could not stand.

“He originated at Sirmium. When he introduced the tares into the world, which happened during the time of Constantius, he survived in this life until the present, having been overthrown by the Western synod assembled at Sardica because of the blasphemy he had uttered.

“He asserted that Christ did not exist from the beginning, but came into existence from Mary and continued to exist from the time when, as he says, the Holy Spirit came upon him and he was begotten from the Holy Spirit.”

This is what Epiphanius says.

Sozomen adds, in book IV, chapter 5, that Photinus attempted to restore and revive not only the condemned heresy of Paul of Samosata but also those of Cerinthus and Ebion.

Blessed Jerome likewise confirms this insofar as Ebion’s heresy is concerned, in his *Book on Ecclesiastical Writers* under Photinus and in his Letter to the Galatians, chapter I. From these passages it is clear that Photinus, together with Ebion and the other heresiarchs, taught that Christ was a mere man and had not existed before Mary.

Theodoret also reports that, concerning the divine persons, Photinus taught the same thing as Paul of Samosata and Sabellius, and that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit possessed only one operation. Socrates confirms this in book I of his *History*, chapter 25, and writes that Photinus was condemned for this reason at the Council of Sirmium.

### Note on the Apollinarists

Apollinaris, or Apollinarius—from whom the Apollinarists, or Apollinarians, derive their name—was a grammarian of Laodicea, at first a Catholic and a man of great authority among Catholics. See Baronius, volume IV, under the year 373 and following.

Later he became a heretic and was condemned because he taught that the Word of God had assumed human flesh without a rational soul, and that the divine persons were unequal: the Holy Spirit, he said, was great, the Son greater, and the Father greatest.

See Epiphanius, heresy 77; Augustine, heresy 55; and the Saint Leo cited above.

The first of them, Hebion, while asserting the Lord’s Incarnation too strongly, stripped it of the union with divinity. After him, the heresy of Sabellius—

### Note on the Origin of Sabellius’s Heresy

He says that the heresy and schism of Sabellius burst forth from the dissimilarity, or opposition, of the preceding heresy, namely that of the Ebionites—that is, that it emerged or arose from it.

Since the Ebionites asserted that Christ was a mere man, Sabellius and his followers, so that they would not appear to admit that divinity had suffered in Christ, acknowledged, in opposition to them and in order to distance themselves from them as far as possible, one person of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

The consequence was that, just as the Son was said by them to have become incarnate and suffered, so too were the Father and the Holy Spirit—an unspeakable crime!

Thus most heresies are said to have arisen from an imprudent flight from and attack upon another heresy. This is evident in the case of Arius, who, out of hatred for Sabellius, who confused the persons, fell into a distinction of nature; and in the case of Eutyches, who, fleeing Nestorius’s error, fell into a confusion of the natures, establishing one nature in Christ formed from two.

Of such a matter one may rightly say:

He fell into Scylla while wishing to avoid Charybdis. Hence it follows that the Fathers proclaim the conflicts and dissensions among heretics to be glorious victories and trophies of the Catholic Church. Thus Justin Martyr, in Question 4 to the Orthodox:

> Now, he says, when heretics condemn one another on account of disagreements in their opinions, it is evident that all their heresies originated in the ambition and mutual envy of the leaders of the heresies. For this reason they are called “grievous wolves” by the Apostle (Acts 20); indeed, while opposing one another, they confirm our faith.

And Hilary, Book VII on the Trinity:

> The discordant opinions of the impious harmonize into one pattern of right faith; and their empty conflicts produce the trophy of our victory.

“For the impiety of Sabellius condemns the error of Arius, while, conversely, the error of the Arian doctrine excludes the wickedness of Sabellius,” says the martyr Vigilius, who treats this argument at length (Books II and IV Against Eutyches). And if they should ever agree among themselves, the result is only what Athanasius observes against the Arians, Oration 2: that they agree, like Herod and Pilate, in blasphemies against Christ.

[Col. 0016A] A schism arising from the dissimilarity of the preceding heresy then followed Sabellius: while he insisted that there was no distinction at all between the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, he mixed together the sacred and ineffable Trinity in a blasphemous confusion, as far as lay within his power.

[Note: [Col. 0016B] Here it is pleasing to append another, similar catalogue of heresies composed by Saint Leo, so that this entire passage may be more fully elucidated by comparing the two. For, comparing and contrasting the other Christological heresies with the single heresy of the Manichees, he says: “Other heresies, although all deservedly condemned for their perversity, nevertheless each have something true in some respect. Arius, by defining the Son of God as less than the Father and a creature, and by thinking that the Holy Spirit was created by him among all created things, destroyed himself by great impiety; yet he did not deny in the Father’s essence the eternal and immutable deity which he failed to see in the unity of the Trinity. Macedonius, estranged from the light of truth, did not receive the divinity of the Holy Spirit; yet he confessed one power and the same nature in the Father and the Son. Sabellius, confused by an inexplicable error, perceiving the inseparable power of substance in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, gave to singularity what he ought to have attributed to equality; and, unable to understand the true Trinity, believed one and the same Person to exist under a threefold designation. Photinus, deceived by blindness of mind, confessed in Christ a true human being of our substance, but did not believe that the same one was God, begotten of God before all ages. Apollinaris, deprived of firmness in the faith, believed that the Son of God had assumed the true nature of human flesh in such a way that he said there was no soul in that flesh, because the divinity itself had fulfilled its function. Thus, if all the errors condemned by the Catholic faith are reviewed, in one and another of them something is found that may be separated from what is damnable. But in the most wicked doctrine of the Manichees there is absolutely nothing that can be judged tolerable in any respect.” Thus far Saint Leo.]

The impiety of the Arian perversity followed this man whom we have mentioned. To avoid appearing to confuse the sacred Persons, it declared that the substances in the Trinity were different and unlike.

After him came Eunomius, indeed, but of very similar depravity. [Note: [Col. 0016D] Saint Augustine’s words appear to conflict with this statement, unless the similarity is understood together with great dissimilarity. Thus he says concerning heresy 54: “Eunomius, powerful in dialectic, defended this heresy more sharply and swiftly, asserting that the Son was unlike the Father in every respect, and the Holy Spirit unlike the Son.”]

Although Eunomius asserted that the divine Trinity was like itself, he nevertheless maintained that it was different from itself: he admitted likeness but excluded equality.

Macedonius too, blaspheming against the Holy Spirit with irreparable impiety, although he said that the Father and the Son were of the same substance, nevertheless called the Holy Spirit a creature and thereby became guilty of an offense against the whole Godhead, because nothing can be injured in the Trinity without injury to the entire Trinity.

Although Photinus called Jesus, who was born from the Virgin, God, he nevertheless falsely constructed the beginning of God from the beginning of the human being. [Note: [Col. 0016D] It does not appear from Epiphanius, Jerome, and others that Photinus confessed Jesus to be God; rather, the opposite appears from what has been said, unless he called him God improperly and equivocally, as did other heretics.]

[Col. 0017A] The obscure phrase means that Christ was not regarded merely as a human being, born in time, but also as God—since Photinus believed that the divinity communicated to Christ by God came not through eternal generation but through the anointing of grace and indwelling. Christ could therefore be called God, but a God made and temporal, not eternal. Nestorius likewise taught this according to Theodoret, Book IV of the Heretical Fables.

But Apollinaris, imprudently understanding a human being united to God, wrongly believed that Christ had no human soul, because it is no less an error to add improper things to the Lord Jesus Christ than to take away what properly belongs to him. Whatever is not said of him as it truly is, even if it appears to be an honor, is an injury.

Thus each, by producing one heresy from the similarity of another, held opinions that were all different from one another, yet all opposed to the faith.

Recently also—that is, in our own days—a poisonous heresy emerged. [Note: [Col. 0017A] Although he does not name it, I believe that he clearly designates the Pelagian heresy, which he attacks more vigorously in the following chapter. Just as this heresy drew its origin from the error of the Ebionites, so it passed over to Nestorius and the Nestorians, standing between the two in time, as he says below. It could therefore be called their offspring and daughter, and the parent and progenitress of the others, as will be shown more fully below.

Cassianus says that this heresy—namely, the Pelagian—had emerged recently, that is, in his own time, around the year of the Lord 410, according to Baronius. Hence Jerome repeatedly calls it “a new heresy from an old one” and calls the Pelagians “new heretics from ancient ones” (Jerome, Commentary on Jeremiah, chapters 2, 25, and 30).

Augustine likewise says in his book On Heresies: “The heresy of the Pelagians is at this time the most recent of all, having arisen from the monk Pelagius.” He calls it uncertain in name but certain in error, because its author was not yet known.

Jerome indicates clearly enough that Pelagius had remained hidden among the Catholics for a very long time and had secretly sown his heresies before he was exposed as a heretic and his name became known. In the preface to Book IV on Jeremiah he says:

> Suddenly the heresy of Pythagoras and Zeno—of ἀπάθεια (*apatheia*, “impassibility”) and ἀναμαρτησία (*anamartēsia*, “impeccability”)—which was once slain in Origen and, not long ago, in his disciples, the Egyptian and Pontic Evagrius, and Jovinian, began to revive. It began to hiss not only in the regions of the West, but also in those of the East, and to defile many in certain islands, especially Sicily and Rhodes, increasing day by day while its adherents teach secretly and deny publicly. I, who had long kept silent and swallowed my grief in silence, was compelled by the repeated complaints of the brothers to respond; yet I have not gone so far as to name the authors, preferring that they be corrected rather than disgraced. For I am not an enemy of persons but of error, and so forth.

That Jerome is referring here to the Pelagians is clear from his letter to Ctesiphon and from his dialogues Against the Pelagians, in which, among the other errors of the Pelagians, he especially attacks that *apatheia* and *anamartēsia*, that is, impassibility and impeccability.

Jerome further adds, in the same work, while attacking the Pelagians who lay hidden and taught secretly:

> Either what you teach is good, or it is evil. If it is good, defend it openly; if it is evil, why do you secretly slaughter the wretched with error and throw out an exposition of the right faith to deceive the simple? If it is true, why is it concealed? If it is false, why is it written? I ask: what madness is this? The Apostle commands us to be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks us for a reason concerning the hope that is in us (1 Peter 3), while the Prophet cries out: “I spoke of your testimonies before kings, and I was not ashamed” (Psalm 118). These men avoid the public sphere and whisper in the corners of the lost; they grieve as though over their own teachings, which they fear to confess as their own.

Thus Jerome.]

We saw this poisonous heresy, of certain error but uncertain name, emerging recently from the great city of Beligars. [Note: [Col. 0017D] This is the reading of the Basel manuscript, followed by Plantin. Others, as noted in the margin, read: “from the greatest city of Veligars.” That reading is equally acceptable.

But what city is this of Beligars or Veligars? Could it perhaps stand for Belgians? I do not think so, for Cassianus is reported by Gennadius, Trithemius, and other authors to have lived and written not in Belgium, or Belgic Gaul, but in Narbonese Gaul, presumably near Massilia.

In this uncertainty, nothing occurs to me before the possibility that the homeland of Pelagius—namely Britain, or a city of Britain—from which that plague emerged is here being designated. Saint Jerome implies in his letter to Ctesiphon (chapter 4) that Pelagius, the author of the Pelagian heresy, was British by nationality, when, attacking him and his companion Coelestius, he mentions “Britain, fertile in tyrants,” and the Scottish people—for it should be read *Scoticae*, not *Stoicae*, as in the reading of Marianus.

Again, elsewhere (in the preface to Book III on Jeremiah), he says the following about the same man, while suppressing his name:

> For he has the offspring of the Scottish people, from the neighborhood of the Britons; according to the tales of the poets, he must be struck down by a spiritual club like Cerberus, so that with his teacher Pluto he may fall silent in eternal silence.

This is found there. “By these unmistakable signs,” says Baronius (Volume V, under the year 410), “you may see Pelagius described as British by nationality, at that time a pleasure-loving monk.” Finally, Saint Augustine, in Letter 105, asserts that Pelagius was surnamed the Briton.

Nor does it follow from this that Cassianus was in Britain or in the city of Beligars. He does not say that he saw Britain or the city of Beligars with his own eyes; rather, he says that he saw that poisonous heresy—namely, in its adherents—recently emerging and advancing from that place under an uncertain name.

If anyone dislikes this explanation concerning the city of Beligars, I offer another, no less probable, which he may follow if it pleases him more: namely, that by the city of Veligars—not Beligars—Velia is meant, that is, Rome, “the city of the Veligars,” that is, the city of the Romans, and indeed the greatest city, as the other reading has it here.

For authorities who write about the antiquities of the city of Rome and of the Romans state that Rome was called Velia in the ancient vocabulary, or, in the plural, Veliae, after the higher hill of Rome called Velia—almost as though it were *Vellia*—because shepherds once used to shear wool there (see Ortelius, *Synonyma*, under “Roma”).

This conjecture and whatever explanation may accompany it appears the more plausible because it is certain that when Pelagius moved from the East, where he had first been condemned, into the West, he initially spread the poison of his heresies in the city of Rome under the pretext of discussing certain questions. Augustine testifies to this (On Original Sin, chapter 21), saying that Pelagius lived in Rome for a very long time and was occupied there in disputations and controversies, seeking everywhere an opportunity to disseminate and defend his heresy.

During that interval it is highly credible that John Cassianus was living in Rome and serving as envoy to the supreme pontiff on behalf of Chrysostom, who had been driven into exile. At that time this poisonous heresy, like a dreadful serpent slowly emerging from its hiding place, began to infect that great city with its pestilential breath. Thus the Author could rightly say that he had recently seen it emerging from the greatest city of the Veligars, using an ancient and less familiar name so that he would not appear deliberately to disparage or defame the city of Rome.

But when the mind still found no rest even in this explanation, another opportunity arose for forming a different opinion about Velia, or the city of the Veligars, from a passage of Aulus Gellius (*Attic Nights*, Book X, chapter 19). There he introduces a certain philosopher criticizing these verses of Virgil (*Aeneid* VI):

> Rescue me from these evils, unconquered one, or cast  
> the earth upon me—for you can—and seek the Velian harbors.

[Col. 0019B] “How,” he said, “could Palinurus have known or named the Velian harbors, and Aeneas have found the place from that name, when the town of Velia, from which the harbor located there was called Velian, was founded in Lucanian territory under Servius Tullius, who was ruling at Rome more than six hundred years after Aeneas came to Italy, and was given that name? For those who were driven from Phocis by Harpalus, the prefect of King Cyrus, founded some Velia and others Massilia.”

This is found there.

Ambrosius Calepinus, following Stephanus, agrees:

> Velia, he says, is a town of Lucania founded in the Gulf of Paestum by the Phocaeans. It was formerly called Ἐλέα (*Elea*), and its inhabitants were called Eleatae.

There is also Lake Velinus, mentioned by Pliny in Book II, chapter 12, and by Columella in Book VI, chapter 16. From these references one may conjecture that this Velia—after which the Velian harbor was named—was perhaps far removed from and distinct from Rome, and that Cassianus designated it here because it was comparable to Massilia, where he himself lived, both in name and antiquity, and even related and nearby in its foundation, well known to him and frequently visited. It may have been there that the Pelagian heresy had already begun to sprout or to spread its poisons.

You have here, reader, three opinions or conjectures concerning Velia and the city of the Veligars, not an assertion. It will be for you to judge or decide which you prefer to embrace, or to offer graciously whatever better explanation may occur to you.

[Col. 0019A] Because it had recently arisen from the ancient stock of the Ebionites, it is exceedingly doubtful whether it should be called ancient or recent. [Note: [Col. 0019C] The following explains the extent to which the Pelagian heresy arose from the ancient Ebionite stock and drew some origin from it: namely, insofar as, together with the Ebionites, who denied Christ’s divinity, it asserted that he was a solitary or merely human being. Yet Jerome and Augustine do not expressly list this error among the errors of the Pelagians, unless it is included under Augustine’s words. After listing the distinctive doctrines of the Pelagians, he says:

> “Other things are also alleged against them, but these are the principal ones, from which those other things, or nearly all of them, are understood to follow” (On Heresies, chapter 88).

Baronius had this passage in view when, discussing the origin and source of the Nestorian heresy (Volume V, under the year 428), he says:

> Cassianus traces it from the filthy Dionaean springs and leads it through their muddy channels—those who denied Christ’s divinity—and finally reports that it was conducted through the sewers of the Pelagians.

These words of Baronius shed some light on this passage and support our interpretation.]

It was new to its advocates, but ancient in its errors. For, blasphemously asserting that our Lord Jesus Christ was born as a solitary human being, it maintained that the fact that he later attained honor and power with God belonged to human merit, not to a divine nature. Consequently, it asserted that he had not always possessed divinity itself by reason of the divinity united to him as its proper possession, but that he later earned it as a reward for the labor and suffering he had undergone. It therefore blasphemously declared that our Lord and Savior was not born God but was assumed by God. [Note: [Col. 0019D] The Pelagian heresy is closely related to the Nestorian heresy, standing between the Ebionites and the Nestorians, as has been said.]

This heresy, which now exists, was therefore its neighbor—so to speak, its sister and blood-relative—agreeing both with the Ebionites and with these recent heretics. It stood between the two in time, yet was joined to both in perversity.

Although it has certain other points resembling those we have already mentioned, it would take too long to recall them all. For we have undertaken this task not now to recount past events, but to refute recent ones.

## Chapter III. The poisonous error of the Pelagians is marked out.

[Note: [Col. 0019D] Cardinal Baronius likewise illuminates this passage and plainly demonstrates from it that Nestorius not only favored the Pelagians—as he had previously shown both from the edict of the Emperor Theodosius and from the letters of Pope Coelestine to Nestorius—but also shared some of their opinions.

“For,” he says, “just as a trunk grows from a root, so it is clear that Nestorian blasphemies proceeded from Pelagian impiety. Thus it should not surprise you when you see Nestorius receive in Constantinople the Pelagian heretics, who had certainly been condemned as bishops, cherish them as his fellow countrymen with every kind of service, and write on their behalf once again to the Roman pontiff himself, Coelestine.

Cassianus, who was thoroughly aware of the hidden doctrines of the Pelagians, clearly reveals that there was a kinship between the Pelagian and Nestorian heresies in his books to Leo, deacon of the Roman Church, On the Incarnation of the Word. At the beginning he says:

‘We certainly do not think that we should omit this one point: it was peculiar and proper to that heresy mentioned above, which had descended from the Pelagian error, that although they said that the solitary man Jesus Christ lived without any contagion of sin, they went so far as to assert that human beings, if they wished, could be without sin.’

And below:

‘Thus the new author of a heresy that is not new—namely, Nestorius—who now contends that our Lord and Savior was born a solitary man, has realized that he is saying precisely what the Pelagianists said before him,’ and so forth.

A little later he adds:

‘Nor is there any doubt of this, since the reality itself makes it entirely clear. For this is the source of the fact that by his intercessions—namely, Nestorius fosters the complaints of the Pelagianists, and by his writings asserts their cause. He subtly, or, more accurately, craftily, acts as their advocate and, with wicked affection, gives wicked support to a depravity akin to his own, knowing that he is of the same mind and the same spirit. He therefore grieves that a heresy known to him has been separated from the Church, although he knows that it is joined to him in perversity.’

Thus Cassianus speaks of the protection and fellowship of Nestorius with the Pelagians. Later he repeats and intensifies the same points and, as is fitting, attacks Nestorius, the wicked leader of the heresy, with the utmost sharpness.

But all these matters have been demonstrated with sufficient clarity in the example of Leporius the Pelagian (Book V On the Incarnation), who expressly professed in the West the very doctrines that Nestorius later preached in the East after becoming a bishop, although Leporius, in repentance, later sang a recantation.

You should know, however, that Nestorius’s excuse to Coelestine was as deceptive as it was entirely empty. In it, to deny that he was in any way a Pelagian, he demonstrated that he held correct views concerning original sin and human free will. For even if you do not see in him all the heads of the Pelagian Hydra, at least one—and a particularly savage one—was clearly stretched out against the Son of God and his Mother.

Thus far Baronius. Drawing especially on this passage of Cassianus, he shows what communion and agreement of mind and opinion Nestorius had with the Pelagians. From these matters we understand that Nestorius did not agree with the Pelagians in every respect, but especially on two points: Christ’s divinity, or the one Person of Christ subsisting in two natures through the hypostatic union, whereby he is the same God and man; and the true designation of the Virgin as Θεοτόκος (*Theotokos*), or God-bearer, because the Virgin bore God and man—a proposition Nestorius, adhering to Pelagian doctrines, utterly denied. Pelagius, however, denied original sin in infants and preferred human free choice to God’s grace; Nestorius did not do so, as Baronius infers from Nestorius’s own letters to Pope Coelestine.]

We do not think that we should omit this one point, which was peculiar and proper to that aforementioned heresy that had descended from the Pelagian error: although they said that the solitary man Jesus Christ had lived without any contagion of sin, they proceeded so far as to assert that, if they wished, human beings could be without sin. [Note: [Col. 0021B] Understand this as meaning “without God’s help,” that is, without supernatural assistance from God.

The Author here attributes four errors to the Pelagians.

The first error was that the Lord Jesus Christ was a solitary man, that is, merely human and not God. Many other heretics had taught this before Pelagius.

The second error was that each human being, if willing, could be without sin, and could be so without the assistance of divine grace, as has been said. He calls this error proper and peculiar to the Pelagian heresy—not because Pelagius was the first or the only person to teach it. Saint Jerome says the contrary in his letter to Ctesiphon, where he lists Manichaeus, Priscillian, Origen, and others as authors and proponents of the same heresy. Rebuking the Pelagians, he says:

‘Let them therefore be ashamed of their leaders and companions, who say that a human being can be without sin, if he wishes—what the Greeks call ἀναμάρτητον (*anamartēton*, “without sin”).’

But because this was one of the principal doctrines of the Pelagian heresy, a doctrine almost peculiar to Pelagius and promulgated by him with particular zeal and insistence—as is evident both from that letter of Saint Jerome and from the books Against the Pelagians—the Catholic, under the name Atticus, begins his first dialogue with the Pelagian Critobulus as follows:

“Tell me, Critobulus: is it true that I hear you have written that a human being can be without sin, if he wishes?”

Critobulus answers that it is true.

Saint Augustine likewise testifies to the same point, writing the following about the Pelagians (Heresy 88):

‘They also proceed so far as to say that the lives of the righteous in this age have absolutely no sin, and that from such people the Church of Christ is perfected in this mortal life, so that it is entirely without stain or wrinkle—as though it were not the Church of Christ that throughout the whole world cries out to God: “Forgive us our debts.”’

Finally, at a certain council in Palestine, Pelagius was compelled to condemn this proposition: “The children of God cannot be called such unless they have been made entirely free from every sin” (see Baronius, Volume V, no. 415).

The third error noted here is that Christ the Lord came into this world not to redeem the human race but merely to provide an example of virtue: namely, to teach human beings humility, charity, and so forth. Saint Leo piously and prudently warned against this error, observing that two things must be considered in Christ’s death: example and sacrament.

“Our Savior,” he says (Sermons 14 and 16 on the Passion of the Lord), “established both a sacrament and an example for all who believe in him, so that they might grasp the one by being reborn and follow the other by imitation.”

Here observe that the sacrament, or mystery, of human redemption is designated first as the primary cause of Christ’s coming, while his example, proposed for imitation, is secondary.

Elsewhere he says:

> An all-powerful physician has prepared a twofold remedy for us. One part of it is in the sacrament, the other in the example, so that through the one divine things may be bestowed and through the other human things may be raised up.

Saint Bernard likewise, writing Against Peter Abelard, who preached the same error, says:

> What else do the Law, the Prophets, the Apostles, and apostolic men evangelize to us, he asks (Letter 190), except what you alone deny: namely, that God became human in order to free humanity? And if an angel from heaven should evangelize anything else to us, let him be accursed.

And below:

> What does it profit if he instructed us, if he did not restore us? Or are we instructed in vain if the body of sin is not destroyed in us, so that we may no longer serve sin? If everything Christ accomplished was only the display of virtues, it remains to be said that Adam too harmed us only by displaying sin, since the remedy was brought according to the character of the wound. For just as all die in Adam, so all will be made alive in Christ. Therefore, as with one, so also with the other. If the life Christ gives is nothing other than his instruction, then the death Adam gave will likewise be nothing other than his instruction: Adam instructing human beings toward sin by his example, while Christ instructed them by example and word toward living well and loving him.

> If, accepting the Christian faith rather than the Pelagian heresy, we confess that Adam’s sin was transmitted to us by generation, not by instruction, and death through sin, then we must also confess that Christ restored righteousness to us by regeneration, not by instruction, and life through righteousness. Thus, just as through one trespass condemnation came upon all human beings, so through one act of righteousness justification leading to life came upon all human beings.

This is Saint Bernard’s argument, followed by further points in the same sense.

The fourth error of the Pelagians noted here is that Christ attained divinity not by nature but finally through his own merits: that he became Christ through baptism in his twentieth year, and after his passion and resurrection became God through his own merits; and that other human beings could likewise live well by their own strength and attain blessedness and a kind of divinity, just as Christ attained it.

The Author indicates that Nestorius followed all these errors, except perhaps the second, so that he deserved to be called not merely Pelagius’s associate but his disciple.

It should be observed here that Nestorius posited two persons in Christ in such a way that he even said that, temporally, Christ was a human being before being assumed by the Word. Through zeal, will, and the merits of his virtues, he had finally attained such honor that he was joined to the Son of God by a singular friendship—or even that he was called the Son of God and God.

Hence the blasphemous boast attributed to Nestorius is remembered:

> I do not envy Christ, who was made God from a human being, because, if I wish, I too can become so.

For this reason Prosper, in his epitaph on the Nestorian and Pelagian heresies, introduces them speaking as follows (Book On the Ungrateful):

> Into what abysses has insane pride plunged us,  
> stripped of gifts and swollen with merits?  
> For while wishing Christ to be God through the piety of his works  
> and the reward he earned, we did not remain in the covenant of the Head.]

For they thought it followed that, if the solitary man Jesus Christ had been without sin, all human beings too could be without sin without God’s help—whatever that solitary man, without communion with God, had been able to accomplish. Thus they would make no distinction at all between any human being and our Lord Jesus Christ, since the same human being could earn by effort and diligence what Christ had earned through zeal and labor.

As a result, bursting into an even greater and more monstrous madness, they said that our Lord Jesus Christ came into this world not to provide redemption for the human race but merely to offer examples of good works. [Col. 0023A] He came, they said, so that human beings, by following his discipline and walking along the same path of virtue, might arrive at the same rewards of virtue.

[Note: [Col. 0023C] Thus Saint Bernard rebukes Peter Abelard, who held opinions similar to those of Pelagius (Letter 190):

> If this is what he thinks, he is thinking foolishly with Pelagius. Whatever he thinks about these matters, it is clear how much, as far as lies within him, he empties the great dispensation of the mystery: he attributes everything concerning salvation to devotion and nothing to generation; he places the glory of our redemption and the sum of salvation not in the power of the cross, not in the price of blood, but in the progress of our way of life. “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Galatians 6), in whom are our salvation, life, and resurrection.

> In this work of our salvation I discern three chief things: the form of humility, in which God emptied himself; the measure of charity, which he extended even to death, and death on the cross; and the sacrament of redemption, which overcame the very death he endured. The first two of these are like painting upon emptiness. They are a great and wholly necessary example of humility, and a great example of charity, worthy of every acceptance; but they have no foundation and consequently no stability if redemption is absent.]

Thus, as far as lay within them, they emptied the entire gift of the sacred coming and all the grace of divine redemption, since they said that human beings could obtain through living what God had accomplished for human salvation by dying.

They also added that our Lord and Savior became Christ after baptism and God after the resurrection: assigning the first to the mystery of anointing and the second to the merit of his passion.

Thus the new author of a heresy that is not new—who now contends that our Lord and Savior was born a solitary man—recognized that he was saying precisely what the Pelagianists had said before him. [Col. 0023B] It follows from his error that whoever asserts that the solitary man Jesus Christ lived without sin must also blasphemously assert that human beings can, by themselves, be without sin. Nor do they say that the Lord’s redemption was necessary even as an example, since human beings can reach the heavenly kingdom by their own effort alone, as they claim.

Nor is there any doubt of this, since reality itself makes it completely clear. [Note: [Col. 0023D] How Nestorius fostered the complaints of the Pelagians by his intercessions and defended their cause in his writings is evident from his letters to Pope Coelestine, which Baronius cites (Volume V, under the year 430).]

For this is the source of the fact that by his intercessions he fosters the complaints of the Pelagianists and by his writings asserts their cause. He subtly—or, to speak more accurately, craftily—acts as their advocate and, with wicked affection, gives wicked support to a depravity akin to his own, knowing that he is of the same mind and the same spirit. He therefore grieves that a heresy known to him [Lipsius, in the margin: “related to him”] has been separated from the Church, although he knows that it is joined to him in perversity.

## Chapter IV. Leporius, together with several others, recants Pelagianism.

Yet, because those who had descended from that pestilent stock of thorns [Col. 0024A] [Note: [Col. 0023D] He indicates rather obscurely that certain Pelagians had been recalled to a sounder mind and to the catholic faith; among them was Leporius, of whom below.] have now been healed by divine assistance and mercy, our Lord God must also now be entreated that, since that former heresy and this new one agree with each other in certain respects [Note: [Col. 0024C] The former Pelagian heresy, that is, the earlier one; the new Nestorian heresy, that is, the later one, as stated above.], He may grant them a similar outcome of good things through similar beginnings of evil.

[Note: [Col. 0024C] Concerning him Gennadius writes as follows (On Illustrious Men, chapter 59): “Leporius, still a monk and later a presbyter, relying on the purity of life which he believed he had obtained solely by his own will and effort, and not through God’s assistance, had begun to follow the Pelagian doctrine. But, admonished by the Gallican teachers and corrected in Africa by Augustine, he wrote a short account of his correction, in which he both gave satisfaction for his error and offered thanks for his correction. At the same time, correcting his mistaken opinion concerning the Incarnation of Christ, he expressed the catholic position, saying: ‘While two natures remain in Christ in their own substance, one person of the Son of God must be believed.’” Thus far Gennadius. Cassian likewise asserts that this man was the originator of Nestorius’s own heresy, in Book VII of On the Incarnation, where, among other things, addressing Nestorius, he says: “Thus, then, you too, thorny offspring of the Pelagian heresy, show in the shoot what your father is said to have possessed at the root. For that Leporius (as Leporius himself, his disciple, said) maintained that our Lord Christ had been made through baptism; whereas you say that in baptism the temple was made through the Spirit. The words are not entirely the same, but the perversity is entirely one,” and so forth. Baronius notes (under the year 420) that another Leporius is likewise found, a man of illustrious birth who professed in the monastery of Saint Augustine; Augustine himself mentions him in Sermon 50, On Various Subjects.]

For Leporius—then a monk, now a presbyter—who, as we said above, had descended from Pelagius’s instruction, or rather from his depravity, and who in Gaul had been one of the foremost, or among the greatest, advocates of that heresy, was admonished by us and corrected by God. He condemned his badly conceived opinion with such magnificence that his correction is scarcely less worthy of admiration than the unblemished faith of many; for the first achievement is never to fall wholly into error, while the second is to reject it well.

Having therefore come to his senses, he not only confessed his error with grief but without shame in Africa, where he then was and still is [Col. 0024B], but also sent letters of tearful confession and lamentation to all the cities of Gaul, so that where his deviation had previously become known, his correction might also be known, and those who had formerly been witnesses of his error might afterward become witnesses of his correction.

## CHAPTER V. He confirms by Leporius’s example that public sin must be expiated by public confession, while at the same time teaching from Leporius’s judgment what must be believed concerning the Incarnation of the Word.

From his confession—or rather, his lamentation—we have thought that certain passages should be inserted, for two reasons: so that the correction of such men might serve as testimony for us and as an example for those who waver; and so that those who had not been ashamed to follow their error might not be ashamed to follow their correction. Just as they had been weakened by a similar illness, so they might be healed by a similar remedy.

Having recognized the perversity of his opinion and looked upon the light of faith, Leporius wrote to the Gallican bishops and began as follows:

> “I do not know what I should first accuse in myself, my venerable and most blessed lords and priests, nor can I find what I should first excuse in myself. Thus ignorance and pride, thus foolish simplicity together with a harmful persuasion, thus fervor together with lack of restraint, thus—in order to speak more truly—a feeble faith together with self-impoverishment, all at once received strength in me, so that it is both a source of confusion that I obeyed so many and such great things all at once, and a matter of astonishing rejoicing for me that these same things could withdraw from my mind.”

A little later he adds:

> “If, therefore, failing utterly to perceive this power of God, and deeming ourselves wise by our own judgment and reasoning, we should say that God appears to have reduced Himself to inferior things, and should say that man was born together with God in such a way that we attribute separately what belongs to God to God alone, and separately what belongs to man to man alone, [Note: [Col. 0025B] Thus Augustine writes in his Tractate 78 on John: “Let us acknowledge,” he says, “a twofold substance: the divine, by which He is equal to the Father, and the human, by which He is less than the Father. Yet both together are not two but one Christ, lest God be a quaternity rather than a Trinity.” Vincent of Lérins likewise (Commonitory I, chapters 18 and 22), among other heretics, pronounces an anathema against Nestorius, who denied that God was born from the Virgin and, having rejected faith in the Trinity, introduced a quaternity among us.] we most clearly introduce a fourth person into the Trinity, [Col. 0025B] and from the one Son of God begin to make not one but two Christs. May the Lord and God Christ Himself avert this from us!

> “Therefore we confess our Lord and God Jesus Christ, the only Son of God, who before the ages was born for Himself from the Father, and who for us, in time, was made man from the Holy Spirit and Mary, ever Virgin—God born. And while confessing both substances, of the flesh and of the Word, we receive in pious faith one and the same God and man, inseparable forever. From the time when He assumed flesh, we say that all the things which were God’s passed into man, [Note: [Col. 0025B] Through that communication of properties resulting from the unity of person in Christ, to be discussed below, it comes about that the properties of man are truly attributed to God and the properties of God to man (Euthymius, on John, chapter IV), and are reciprocally predicated of the one person of Christ, since He is numerically the same God and man, and, as the Greeks happily say, θεάνθρωπος, “God-man.” “Though He is God and man, He is not two, but one Christ,” says Blessed Athanasius in the Creed.] so that all the things which were man’s might come into God.

> [Note: [Col. 0025C] One substance is said to become another in three ways (Euthymius, on John, chapter 1). First, by change, conversion, or transition of one nature into another, so that one substance is changed into the nature of the other, as when water becomes wine (John 2), or a staff becomes a serpent (Exodus 6). Second, by succession, as when day arises from night, a creature from nothing, or Christ’s body in the Eucharist from bread, and in other cases in which one substance plainly takes the place of another that has perished. Third, by assumption or accession of another substance or nature, so that from both, remaining unharmed, preserved, and entire, one subject comes into existence; this is called a hypostasis. Thus iron becomes fire when it is so transformed into it that the iron is not called fire but fiery iron, because it preserves the nature and property of both iron and fire. So—as the holy Fathers use this comparison—the Word became flesh because He assumed flesh, or human nature, into Himself, not because He was converted into it or succeeded to the place of something that had perished. Just as the first man is said to have been made into a living soul (Genesis 1), or a living soul, because he received a living soul divinely breathed into him and joined into one hypostasis, so the Word became flesh, that is, He assumed flesh into the unity of the divine person. Saint Athanasius explained this in two lines in the Creed: “One, not by conversion of divinity into flesh, but by assumption of humanity into God; altogether one, not by confusion of substance, but by unity of person.”]

> “By this understanding, therefore, the Word became flesh—not as though through some conversion or mutability He began to be what He was not, but so that, by the power of the divine dispensation, the Word of the Father, never departing from the Father, deigned properly to become man and to be incarnate through that secret mystery which He alone knows. It is our part to believe; His to know. Thus God the Word Himself, receiving the whole of what belongs to man, is man; and man, having received the whole of what belongs to God, cannot be anything other than God.

> [Note: [Col. 0025D] Thus in Book II, chapter 3: “Man united to God.” The Fathers sometimes used this expression, although improperly (Augustine, On the Christian Contest, book I, chapter 11, and Sermon 8 on the Word of the Lord), especially those who preceded the time of Nestorius; by “man” they understood human nature. Yet whenever they wished to speak more carefully and precisely, they said not that man but that humanity had been assumed by the Word and united to Him. Later theologians, especially the scholastics, spoke in this way more frequently and readily. “For in matters concerning religion, we are permitted to speak according to a definite rule, lest freedom in words generate an impious opinion concerning the things signified by them,” says Saint Augustine (The City of God, Book X, chapter 23).]

> “Yet because He is said to be incarnate and mingled, this must not be understood as a diminution of His substance. For God knows how to mingle without corruption of Himself, and yet truly to mingle; He knows how to receive into Himself in such a way that nothing is added to Him, just as He knows how wholly to pour Himself out so that no loss occurs.

> [Note: [Col. 0026B] Several terms should be noted which the Fathers use as synonyms to signify the mystery of the Incarnation [Col. 0026C]. The first is the very term ‘Incarnation.’ Although it is not expressed in Scripture, it was suitably coined and used by the Fathers, both Latin and Greek, after the Council of Nicaea, since it is plainly derived from John’s words: ‘The Word became flesh’ (John 1). For ‘the Word became flesh’ and ‘was incarnate’ mean the same thing. Here, by synecdoche, ‘flesh’ is put for man, the part for the whole; this is extremely common in Scripture, as blessed Augustine shows in the Enchiridion, chapter 34. Familiar examples are: ‘All flesh shall see the salvation of God’ (Isaiah 40); ‘I will not fear what flesh can do to me’ (Psalm 117); ‘By the works of the law no flesh shall be justified’ (Romans 3). Therefore, since the term ‘Incarnation’ is derived from John’s oracle, it most aptly denotes the mystery by which God the Son became not merely flesh but man, who is signified by the name ‘flesh.’ The Word is called incarnate not because He was enclosed in flesh or joined to flesh—as Augustine speaks of the incarnation of souls in Letter 28 [Col. 0026D]—and still less because He was changed into flesh, but because the Word became flesh, that is, God became man, with the property of each nature preserved.

> “Accordingly, the term ‘Incarnation’ embraces more than the terms ‘union’ and ‘mixture,’ although the ancients are also found to have used these terms in this matter. We may rightly say that a soul is united to flesh, but not that it is incarnated in the sense of being made flesh; for the soul did not become flesh or man, but man is formed from soul and flesh.

> “Moreover, Erasmus rejects the term ‘union’ in one place as novel and scholastic, failing to observe that the most authoritative writers frequently used it. Leo, in Sermon 1 on the Nativity, says: ‘The inviolable nature has been united to the passible nature.’ The Council of Chalcedon says that a union of natures was effected in Christ. Other Fathers speak in the same way throughout.

> “The term ‘mixture,’ likewise, although it may seem somewhat harsh, is nevertheless used from time to time by the Fathers. Tertullian, in the Apology, says: ‘Man is born mingled with God.’ Cyprian, in On the Vanity of Idols: ‘God is mingled with man.’ Vigilius the martyr, in Book I Against Eutyches: ‘The Son of God wished to display the nature of our race through the indivisible unity of mixture.’ Augustine, in his third letter, addressed to Volusianus, says that God is ‘mixed with man.’ Leo, in Sermon 3 on the Nativity, says: ‘The creature was not taken into fellowship with its Creator in such a way that He was the inhabitant and it the dwelling, but in such a way that one nature was mingled with the other.’

> “Finally, Cassian—or rather Leporius—here speaks of God as incarnate and ‘mingled,’ not negatively, as though He were unmixed, but positively and affirmatively, as though He were within the mixture or mingled. Hence he later adds: ‘For God knows how to mingle without corruption of Himself.’

> “Augustine, however, wisely warns in the aforementioned letter to Volusianus that the catholic hearer must here depart from the customary analogy of bodies, according to which two liquids are usually mixed so that neither preserves its integrity, although, he says, even among bodies incorruptible light is mixed with air. Therefore, according to Augustine’s warning, when this word ‘mixture’ is heard or read, one must not look to the mixture of liquids, but rather to that by which light, penetrating the whole of the air, is mingled with it. Hence Cyril, in the book called the Golia, denies that the divine nature underwent mixture in humanity. And in the ecclesiastical office it is sung of Christ: ‘He suffered neither mixture nor division.’

> “There remains a fourth related and no less customary term, ‘assumption.’ The Fathers commonly use it (Saint Leo, Letter 97, chapter 11), and theologians [Col. 0027D] teach that in Christ it was not nature assumed from nature, nor person from person, but human nature assumed by the divine person. See the Master of the Sentences, Book III, distinction 5, and the doctors there. This verb ‘to assume’ is very well suited to this mystery, and Scripture often uses it and similar terms. Paul says to the Hebrews 2: ‘He does not take hold of angels, but he takes hold of the seed of Abraham’—ἐπιλαμβάνεται, he apprehends, receives, assumes. To the Philippians 2: ‘He took the form of a servant’—ἔλαβεν, he received, assumed.”

> “Therefore, not making conjectures about God and man being mixed on the basis of the visible evidence of our experiences, as though equal creatures entered into one another, let us not suppose that God and man were mingled and that by such a confusion of flesh and Word some sort of body was produced. [Note: [Col. 0027D] This was the heresy of Eutyches, abbot of Constantinople, who, in opposition to Nestorius, asserted that in Christ there was only one nature, formed and confused from two natures in the very Incarnation. The Council of Chalcedon condemned him together with Dioscorus of Alexandria in the year of the Lord 451. Hence Saint Leo, in Sermon 8 on the Nativity, says: “After the various impieties which are connected with one another by the kinship of manifold blasphemies, I urge your devotion to be watchful especially against those errors from which you must turn: one of them attempted long ago, under Nestorius as its author, to arise with impunity; the other recently broke forth, with equal execration, under Eutyches as its advocate. For the former dared to proclaim blessed Mary the virgin merely the mother of a man, so that no union of the Word and flesh was believed to have occurred in her conception and childbirth, because the Son of God had not Himself become the son of man, but had merely joined Himself to the man created by Him through condescension. Catholic ears could in no way tolerate this, for they are so imbued with the Gospel of truth [Col. 0028C] that they know most firmly that there is no hope of salvation for the human race unless He Himself was the Son of the Virgin who is the Creator of His mother. But this profane advocate of the more recent sacrilege confessed indeed a union of two natures in Christ, but said that the result of that union was that one nature remained from the two, with the substance of the other entirely absent—something that could occur only through either destruction or separation.” Thus Saint Leo, describing and refuting both heresies at once. See the same author, Letter 97; also Flavian’s letter to Leo and Theodoret, Book IV of On the Fables of Heretics.]

> “Far be it from us to believe this, as though we should suppose that, by some kind of fused composition, two natures had been reduced to one substance; for such a mixture is the corruption of both parts.

> “For God, who contains yet cannot be contained, who penetrates yet cannot be penetrated, who fills yet cannot be filled, who is wholly everywhere at once and is diffused everywhere, was mercifully mingled with human nature through the infusion of His power.

> “A little later he says: ‘Therefore Jesus Christ, God-man, the Son of God, is born for us properly from the Holy Spirit and Mary, ever Virgin. Thus the Word and flesh become one in mutual relation, so that, while each substance remains naturally in its perfection, without injury to itself, the divine may share in humanity and the human in divinity. It is not one God and another man, but the same one who is both God and man; and conversely, the man who is also God, Jesus Christ, is named and truly is the one Son of God.

> “‘Therefore we must always do and believe this: that our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, true God, whom we confess to have always been with the Father and equal to the Father before the ages, is the same one whom we do not deny to have become God-man from the time of His assumed flesh. Nor should we believe that, progressing toward God by stages and through time, He had one state before the resurrection and another after the resurrection, but rather that He always possessed the same fullness and power.’
