> “And shortly afterward: ‘Since the Word, God, graciously descended into man by assuming man, and through the assumption of God man ascended into the Word, [Note: [Col. 0028C] Damascene explains this as follows (Orthodox Faith, Book III, chapter 7): “Christ is *totus* (‘whole,’ referring to the person), perfect God, but not *totum* God, since He is also man; and He is *totus* man, perfect, but not *totum* man, since He is not merely man but also God. For *totum* signifies nature, whereas *totus* signifies hypostasis; just as nature is one thing and hypostasis another.” Commenting on this, John Cochlaeus says: “In setting forth the mystery of the most holy Trinity and likewise of the Incarnation, *totus*, *alius*, and similar masculine terms designate hypostasis and person, whereas the neuter terms designate nature and its properties. Therefore, in the Trinity it is admitted that the Father is *alius* and the Son *alius*. But the Father is not *aliud* and the Son *aliud*, because the person of Father and Son differs, but the substance of the one and the other is not different. Conversely, in the interchange involved in assuming human nature, God is *aliud* and man *aliud*, but God is not *alius* and man *alius*, because the natures of God and man differ, but not the persons. Thus we rightly say that Christ is *totus* perfect God and *totus* perfect man, since He lacks nothing of divinity or humanity; nevertheless, He is not *totum* God, since He possesses not only the divine nature but also the human, nor *totum* man, since He also shares the divine nature.” Thus far Cochlaeus.]

> “‘the whole God the Word became whole man. For God the Father did not become man, nor the Holy Spirit, but the Father’s Only-Begotten. Therefore one person of flesh and Word must be understood, so that in faithful and unwavering belief we may believe that the one and same Son of God, inseparable forever, [Note: [Col. 0029B] Thus the Church sings in the hymn for the Nativity:

> *A giant of twofold substance,*
>
> *eagerly running along the way;*

> alluding to Psalm 18: ‘He rejoiced as a giant to run his course.’]

> “‘was also called a giant in the days of His flesh (Psalm 18), and that He truly always accomplished everything that belongs to man and truly always possessed everything that belongs to God. For He was crucified indeed in weakness, but He lives through the power of God (2 Corinthians 13).’”

## CHAPTER VI. The harmonious teaching of the Catholics must be embraced as the orthodox faith.

This confession of his [Note: [Col. 0029B] That is, Leporius’s confession, which he continued to the end of the preceding chapter. It is truly remarkable, as Baronius also observed (under the year 420), that before Nestorius’s heresy had been promulgated, Leporius is found to have thoroughly refuted it in his own little book and to have sincerely asserted the catholic faith concerning this matter: that Christ the Lord is true God and man in one person, and that the most holy Virgin Mary is rightly affirmed to be the Mother of God and *Deipara*. It happened by a great miracle that the former heresiarch himself, in so sincere and true a confession, condemned what he had previously been accustomed to defend in contentious disputation.]—that is, the faith of all Catholics—was approved both by all the African bishops, from whose region he was writing, and by all the Gallican bishops, to whom he was writing.

No one has yet appeared to whom this faith was displeasing without the crime of unbelief, because it is a profession of impiety to deny a piety that has been approved. The agreement of all ought therefore now by itself to suffice for refuting the heresy, since the authority of all is the manifestation of undeniable truth, and the argument is complete where no one has dissented [Lips. in the margin: “dissents”].

Thus, anyone who attempts to think contrary to this should at once be judged not so much worthy of hearing as worthy of condemnation: for he who attacks the judgment of all has brought the prejudice of condemnation upon himself, and he has no place in the hearing who tries to overturn what has been established by everyone. Once the truth has been confirmed by all, whatever comes against it must immediately be recognized as false precisely because it disagrees with the truth. Accordingly, the fact that it differs from the judgment of truth ought by itself to suffice to bring upon it a sentence of condemnation.

Yet, because a rational discourse does not harm reason, and truth always shines more brightly when it has been examined, and because it is better to correct those who err through the healing of disputation than to condemn them with the severity of a sentence, the ancient heresy must, insofar as it lies within our power and through divine assistance, be treated in the new heretics. Once they have recovered health through sacred mercy, their cure should provide a testimony to holy faith rather than their condemnation provide an example of just severity.

Let Truth itself be present in the disputation and discourse concerning it, and may He who deigned in such piety to come to human beings assist human errors—He who chiefly wished for this reason to be born on earth and in man, so that there might no longer be any place for falsehood.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0029]

## CHAPTER I. The errors of later heretics have been condemned and refuted in their authors and inventors.

Since in the first little book we prefaced certain matters by which we established that a new heretic had sprouted from the ancient roots of heresy [Note: That is, Nestorius, who arose during Cassian’s lifetime and was his contemporary; in the preface Cassian also calls him “the new enemy of the faith.”], the just condemnation of the earlier heretics ought to suffice for him to receive a just sentence of condemnation.

For since he has the same roots and emerges from the same errors [Lips. in the margin: “pits”], he has already been condemned in his own authors—especially since those who immediately preceded these men and followed the same assertions badly nevertheless condemned them rightly. Thus the examples of their own kind ought already to suffice abundantly for them, whether the examples of those who were corrected or of those who were condemned.

If they can be corrected, they possess a remedy in the corrections of their own people; if they cannot be corrected, they possess a sentence in their condemnation. Nevertheless, lest we appear to wish to use prejudice against them more than judgment, let us bring into the open their own destructive proposition—or rather, their blasphemous madness:

> “Taking up in every respect the shield of faith and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Ephesians 6),

so that the same sword of the divine word which once cut off the head of the ancient dragon, now risen again, may also cut off the heads of the new serpents. For since the error of these men is the same as that of those others, the cutting down of the former must be regarded as the cutting down of the latter. And because these reborn poisonous snakes breathe their pestilential airs within the Lord’s Church and cause some to waste away through their hissing, a new remedy must be joined to the ancient cures because of these new illnesses, so that, even if what was done previously does not avail for the condemnation of the disease [Lips. in the margin: “cure”], what we are now doing may nevertheless contribute to the health of those who are sick.

## CHAPTER II. He demonstrates that the Virgin is not merely *Christotokos* but also *Theotokos*, and that Christ is truly God.

[Col. 0031A]

You say, then—whoever you are, heretic—that God was not born from a Virgin, and that Mary cannot be called Θεοτόκος (Theotokos), that is, “Mother of God,” but only Χριστοτόκος (Christotokos), that is, “Mother of Christ,” and of Christ alone, not of God—for, you say, no one gives birth to one older than himself.

[Col. 0032A]

[Note: [Col. 0031A] Heretics who have denied that Mary, the most blessed Virgin, is truly and properly Θεοτόκος, that is, Deipara, or Mother of God, are found in two distinct categories. The Valentinians, who attributed a heavenly body to Christ and asserted that he had descended from heaven and flowed through Mary as through a channel, as well as the Manichaeans, who imagined for him a phantom body, and others who devised similar theories, consequently denied that she was Christ’s mother, since they claimed that Christ had received no substance from Mary. Others, however, acknowledged her as Christ’s mother but denied that she was the Mother of God, or Θεοτόκος—that is, Deipara—such as Photinus and Nestorius, although on different grounds.

Photinus, following the Ebionites, whose error was discussed above, denied that Mary was the Mother of God because he believed Christ to be not God but a mere human being, who nevertheless eventually progressed through his virtues to the point of being called the Son of God. Nestorius refused to acknowledge her as the Mother of God because he divided the persons in Christ, saying that the one eternally begotten from God the Father was different from the man born in time from the Virgin mother—namely, that there were two sons, one of God the Father and the other of the Virgin mother. He made the former God and Son of God, and the latter man and son of man.

These are two chief doctrines of Nestorianism, so interconnected and mutually dependent that, once one is admitted or denied, the other must likewise be admitted or denied; and when one is destroyed, the other is similarly destroyed, as is self-evident. For if Christ, the son of Mary, is true God, it necessarily follows that Mary is his mother, Θεοτόκος, Deipara. Conversely, from the opposition of the consequent follows the opposition of the antecedent: if Mary is not Deipara, then Christ, her son, is certainly not God.

Whoever, therefore, denies that God was born from a Virgin—as the Author says here—consequently denies that Mary is Θεοτόκος, that is, Mother of God, and vice versa. Accordingly, everything that serves to prove either Christ’s divinity or the communication of properties, whether advanced for this purpose by other Fathers or by Cassian, likewise serves to prove that the blessed Virgin is truly and absolutely the Mother of God, Θεοτόκος and Deipara, and therefore must be so named by all without reservation.

Hence Saint Cyril, in his first letter, expresses great astonishment at those who doubt whether the blessed Virgin should be called Deipara. “For if,” he says, “our God and Lord is Jesus Christ, how is the Virgin who bore him not Deipara?” In the same place he discusses the name Deipara at greater length and declares it to be the teaching of the apostles, taking it for granted, as a matter universally known, that according to the faith Christ the man is God.

But in order that what we have said about Nestorius and his errors may be made clearer and more certain, reason requires that it be confirmed by the authority of the ancients. Thus Evagrius, following Socrates (Book VII, chapter 32) and others, describes Nestorius and the origins of his heresy (Book I, chapter 2):

“Nestorius, who attacked God with his tongue; who, together with Caiaphas, convened another council against the Son of God; who established a workshop of blasphemy in which Christ was again slaughtered and sold; who divided and tore apart his natures—although, on the cross itself, not even a bone of him was broken, as it is written, nor was his seamless garment entirely torn apart by the parricides—rejected and utterly cast aside this title, Θεοτόκος, which had been fashioned by many distinguished and approved Fathers, and opposed to it the title Χριστοτόκος, craftily invented and fabricated by himself. He filled the Church with countless seditions and filled it with internal and civil bloodshed.”

And shortly afterward:

“The conflict that arose in the Churches had this as its beginning. A certain presbyter named Anastasius, imbued with a perverse opinion, and a zealous supporter of the Judaic doctrines that Nestorius held, accompanied him when he was going to assume the episcopate. When Nestorius met Theodore in the city of Mopsuestia and, after hearing his teaching, departed from true piety, Anastasius—as Theodulus wrote in a certain letter concerning these matters—dared openly to say in a public disputation held in the Church of Constantinople before a people devoted to the worship of Christ: ‘Let no one call Mary Deipara.’ For, he said, ‘she was a human being, and God cannot be born from a human being.’

“When the people consecrated to Christ received these words with profound indignation and bitterness, and not without reason regarded that disputation as blasphemous, Nestorius, the author and leader of this blasphemy, not only did not prevent it or defend sound and orthodox doctrine, but even strove especially to reinforce those words and persisted more aggressively in defending them. Adding and, so to speak, attaching his own opinion to them, and pouring out and ejecting the poison of his mind into the Church, he attempted to teach a much greater blasphemy, to such an extent that, to his own destruction, he did not hesitate to utter this impious statement: ‘I certainly shall not call him God who grew through periods of months—that is, through a second month, a third month, and so on.’”

This is what Evagrius relates. Further below (chapter 7 of the same book), he writes that this same Nestorius, condemned by the Council of Ephesus and transported by decree of the Emperor Theodosius to Oasis, the most notorious place of exile, was consumed by a punishment worthy of him for diminishing the dignity of Deipara: his tongue was eaten away by worms, and his entire body rotted.

(See Baronius, volume V, under the year 430.)

Theodoret also agrees with this in *Haereticarum Fabularum Compendium*, chapter 4, where, among other things, he says of Nestorius:

“His first innovation was the claim that the holy Virgin, who bore the Word of God, which had assumed flesh from her, ought not to be confessed as Deipara, but only as Christipara, although the earliest preachers of the orthodox faith, following apostolic tradition, taught that she should be named and believed to be the Mother of the Lord.”

And at the end of the chapter he says the following concerning Nestorius’s unhappy end:

“Since the wicked are destined to perish by a most shameful and disgraceful death, he was expelled from the episcopate by the holy men assembled at Ephesus through divine judgment, and was condemned by imperial command to live in Oasis. There the beginning of the future punishment of the impious commenced for him, so that, consumed by his own madness, he fulfilled in himself the Apostle’s saying: ‘The sins of some people are manifest, going before them to judgment’ (1 Tim. V).”

Such is Theodoret’s account. Although he had once been devoted to and a supporter of Nestorius, he later came to his senses and attacked him severely.

To this must finally be added Vincent of Lérins, a contemporary of our Cassian and likewise a most vigorous opponent of heretics. He says (*Commonitorium* I, chapter 17):

“Nestorius, by a disease contrary to that of Apollinaris, while pretending to distinguish two substances in Christ, suddenly introduces two persons and, in unheard-of wickedness, wants there to be two sons of God, two Christs: one God and the other man; one from the Father, the other generated from the Mother. For this reason he asserts that holy Mary should be called not Θεοτόκος but Χριστοτόκος, since, according to him, the Christ who was born from her was not the one who is God, but the one who was man.”

This is what he says, together with what follows to the same effect.

As stated, the universal Council of Ephesus was assembled against Nestorius. It was the third of the four earliest and most holy councils, held under Pope Celestine, with Cyril of Alexandria acting as his representative. It condemned the errors mentioned above together with their author and issued there this decree:

“If anyone does not confess that Emmanuel is truly God, and therefore that the blessed Virgin is Mother of God—for she gave birth in the flesh to the Word of God made flesh, according to what is written, ‘The Word was made flesh’—let him be anathema.”

[Col. 0033A]

Again, at the Council of Chalcedon and afterward at the second Council of Constantinople, both of which were also universal councils, the name Θεοτόκος, or Deipara, was approved and commended by the unanimous agreement of all the Fathers as proper and especially honorable for the blessed Virgin.

Thus, in canon six of the Council of Constantinople, which rests upon the authority of the earlier council, we read that it was defined:

“If anyone abusively and not truly calls the blessed Virgin Mother of God, whether by reference—as though a mere human being had been born—or if anyone calls her the mother of a human being, or the mother of Christ on the supposition that Christ is not God, and does not specifically, properly, and truly confess her to be Mother of God because God the Word, begotten before the ages, was incarnate and born from her in the last days, and thus refuses, in accordance with the holy Council of Chalcedon, to confess her to be Mother of God, let him be anathema.”

Finally, the Lateran Council under Martin V, consultation 5, canon 3:

“If anyone, in accordance with the holy Fathers, does not properly and truly confess the holy, ever-Virgin and immaculate Mary to be Mother of God, and so forth, let him be condemned.”

This is what the texts say.

It should be observed here that the holy Fathers deliberately and with great care added those adverbs—“truly,” “properly,” “specifically,” and similar expressions—so that no one might suppose that Mary could be called Mother of God improperly, abusively, or metaphorically. This would be in the sense in which anyone who generates God in his own mind or in the mind of others through faith working by charity is called in Scripture, by a kind of mystical and spiritual bond of kinship, the Mother of God. Thus, when someone said to Christ, “Behold, your mother and your brothers are standing outside, seeking you,” the Lord, stretching out his hand toward his disciples, replied: “Behold my mother and my brothers. For whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother, sister, and mother” (Matt. XII).

But the most holy Virgin is not merely the Mother of God in that spiritual sense; she is so in another, much more proper and genuine sense, since she truly gave birth to God bodily from herself, according to the reality of the matter itself, with every metaphor and ambiguity of expression excluded. She is not only Mother of God and so called because, by her most blessed childbirth, she produced and bore God, but also because she conceived God—not a mere human being, but true God and true man—as the preceding arguments also make clear.

For this is the fullest and most perfect basis for the maternal title: she is truly called Mother of God because she both conceived and gave birth to the true God. If she had conceived a mere and pure human being, subsisting in himself and sustained for some time in a human hypostasis, and if he had then been assumed by the Son of God before the time of birth, she would indeed have brought forth in childbirth true God and man; nevertheless, she would not for that reason be called so truly and absolutely the Mother of God, since the consideration underlying the maternal designation is drawn chiefly from conception, and that would then be lacking.

Vincent of Lérins makes the same point no less clearly than piously in these words:

“Far be it from anyone to attempt to deprive holy Mary of the privileges of divine grace and her distinctive glory” (*Commentary* I, chapter 2). “By a singular gift of the Lord and our God, who is also her Son, she must most truly and most blessedly be confessed as Θεοτόκος. But she is not Θεοτόκος in the manner imagined by a certain impious heresy, which asserts that she should be called Mother of God merely by designation, because she bore a human being who afterward became God—just as we speak of the mother of a presbyter or the mother of a bishop, not because she gave birth to a presbyter or bishop, but because she generated a human being who afterward became a presbyter or bishop.

“Holy Mary is not Θεοτόκος in that way. Rather, she is so because, as was said above, that most sacred mystery was already accomplished in her consecrated womb: by reason of the singular and unique unity of person, just as the Word in the flesh is flesh, so man in God is God.”

This is what he says.

It should be noted secondly that when the Fathers say that the blessed Virgin should not be called Christipara but Deipara, they do not mean that she should not be understood to be Christ’s Mother, nor do they simply advise abstaining from that word. Rather, they do so because Nestorius asserted her to be Christipara in such a way as to deny that she was Deipara, implying that the Christ born from her was a mere human being, not God. Since, by introducing the term Christipara, he attempted to eliminate and expel the name Deipara entirely from the speech and usage of the faithful, the wisest Fathers of that period rightly rejected the term Christipara as one devised and employed by heretics and therefore suspect.

Thus Damascenus says in Book VII of *The Orthodox Faith*, chapter 12:

“We by no means call the holy Virgin Christipara, because the wicked, detestable Nestorius, who thinks as the Jews do, invented that term in order to reject the title Θεοτόκος—that is, Deipara and Mother of God.”

But in later centuries, once the Nestorian heresy had been extinguished and eradicated and the danger of error and false interpretation had been removed, nothing prevents the faithful—as is now commonly done—from calling the blessed Virgin indiscriminately both Χριστοτόκος and Θεοτόκος, that is, both Mother of Christ and Mother of God. It is like kinds of food from which one must abstain during an illness: once the illness has been removed, they may safely be eaten.

Finally, it should be noted that the name Θεοτόκος, Deipara, or Mother and Genetrix of God, is the noblest and most august of all the titles that can be attributed to the blessed Virgin, surpassing every dignity of a created being. Whatever excellence or distinction is contained in the other titles of that consecrated Virgin is also contained in this unique title, Deipara.

For this reason blessed Thomas observes (*Summa theologiae* III, question 28, article 3, reply to objection b) that she is not ordinarily named in the Gospel without the designation of this dignity, namely, that she is the mother of Jesus:

“Joseph, the husband of Mary, from whom Jesus was born” (Matt. I);

“Mary, the mother of Jesus” (ibid.);

“They found the child with Mary his mother” (Matt. II);

“From where is this granted to me, that the Mother of my Lord should come to me?” (Luke II);

“And the Mother of Jesus was there” (John II);

“They stood beside the cross of Jesus, his mother” (John XIX);

“And when Jesus saw his mother, he said to his mother…”

The holy Fathers likewise commend and proclaim the prerogative of this dignity and title in many praises, of which I shall offer only a few here.

Saint Augustine says in Book III of *On the Creed for Catechumens*:

“So great is the Virgin’s dignity, because she is Mother of God, that it plainly surpasses not only the dignity of all human beings but even that of the angels, since it is far more excellent and glorious to be the mother of a prince than to be his servant. For each thing is called more perfect in proportion as it is more closely united and joined to God, who is supreme perfection.”

Saint John Damascene, in the place cited above (see here the commentary of Johannes Cochlaeus), says:

“With the utmost justice and in accordance with the truth we call Mary, the undefiled one, Deipara. For this name commends the entire mystery of the divine dispensation. If she who gave birth is Deipara, then the one begotten from her is truly God, and truly also man. For how could God, who possesses a hypostasis before the ages, be born and generated from a woman unless he had become man?”

And Saint Bernard of Siena says in sermon 52, *On the Angelic Salutation*:

“The blessed Virgin is greeted by the faithful when she is called Mother of God. Such praise do we assign to her when we say ‘Mother of God’ that this unimaginable dignity is not found even among the uncreated persons, except in one person, who is the Father and has the Son of God, and in one human person, who is the Mother.

“Moreover, it is a greater gift to be Mother of God than to be mistress of God’s creatures, because the latter depends upon the former as a branch depends upon its root. Therefore we call her Mother of God rather than mistress of the world or of the universe.”

Saint Thomas further compares the blessed Virgin with Christ’s humanity (*Summa theologiae* I, question 25, article 6), assigning to both a certain infinite dignity derived from the infinite good, which is God, to whom they are immediately united:

“Christ’s humanity, because it is united to God; created blessedness, because it is the enjoyment of God; and the blessed Virgin, because she is Mother of God, possess a certain infinite dignity derived from the infinite good, which is God. In this respect nothing can be made better than they, just as nothing can be better than God.”

And Peter Canisius says in Book III, chapter 13, *On the Virgin*:

“If, the higher the son, the more worthy the mother must be considered, who could rightly doubt that the authority and dignity of the infinite Son redound upon the mother herself and procure for her immense honor? She alone, together with the Father, can say to the eternal Son: ‘You are my Son; I have begotten you.’”]

You say, therefore, that she cannot be called Θεοτόκος—that is, Mother of God—but Χριστοτόκος, that is, only Mother of Christ, not of God, since no one, you say, gives birth to one older than himself.

[Col. 0035A]

[Note: [Col. 0035D] This was Nestorius’s argument: “No one can beget one older than himself. God is older than Mary; therefore Mary could not beget God. Consequently, she should not be called the Mother of God, or Θεοτόκος, but Χριστοτόκος, that is, mother of Christ, merely a man and not God.” Cassianus refutes this argument at length in Book VII. But it can be answered briefly that no one can beget another older or earlier than himself according to that respect in which the other is older. Thus Mary gave birth to Christ God not according to his divinity, in which he was earlier than she, but according to his humanity, in which he was later than she. Nor is it surprising that we have no other examples, since this mystery is unique. “If a reason is sought, it will not be astonishing; if an example is sought, it will not be unique,” says Saint Augustine in Letter 3.]

For this foolish argument, by which you think God’s birth should be assessed according to carnal understanding, and believe that the mystery of majesty must be judged by human reasoning, we shall discuss later, if God permits. For the present, let us establish by divine witnesses both that Christ is God and that Mary is the Mother of God.

Hear, then, the angel of God speaking to the shepherds about God’s birth:

“Today a Savior has been born for you, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David” (Luke II).

He added the names “Lord” and “Savior” so that you would not understand merely a human being in Christ, but would recognize that the one whom you acknowledged as Savior could in no way be doubted to be God. Since the power of saving belongs only to divine authority, you would not doubt that he possessed divine power in whom you had learned that the power to save resided.

But perhaps this seems insufficient to your unbelief, because the angel called him “Lord” and “Savior” rather than “God” or “Son of God,” even though you most impiously deny him to be God while confessing him to be Savior.

Hear also the archangel Gabriel proclaiming to the Virgin Mary:

“The Holy Spirit,” he says, “will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born in you will be called the Son of God” (Luke I).

Do you see how, intending to indicate God’s birth, he first set forth the works of divinity? “The Holy Spirit,” he says, “will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.”

The angel spoke most beautifully: through the divinity of his words he explained the majesty of the divine work. For the Holy Spirit, sanctifying the Virgin’s inward parts and breathing into them the power of his divinity, inserted and mingled himself with human nature, and by his own power and majesty made his own what had previously been alien to him.

And lest human weakness perhaps fail to endure the entrance of divinity, the power of the Most High strengthened the Virgin whom all must revere, supporting bodily weakness by the protection of the shadow spread over her, so that human frailty might not fail in bringing to completion the unspeakable sacrament of the holy conception, sustained as it was by the divine overshadowing.

“The Holy Spirit,” he says, “will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.”

If, then, the man who was to be born from the sound Virgin was merely an isolated human being, what was the purpose of such a solemn announcement of his sacred coming? What was the purpose of such a display of divinity itself? If merely a human being was being born from a human being, and merely flesh from flesh, a command or simple divine will would surely have been sufficient for this.

For if, in making the heavens, founding the earth, creating the sea, and finally creating thrones and seats, angels and archangels, principalities and powers; if, in creating at last the entire heavenly host and those countless myriads upon myriads of divine armies, God’s will and command alone were sufficient—“He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. XXXII)—why did you think that insufficient for the conception, as you say, of a single human being, when it was sufficient for the generation of all divine things? Why did you believe that God’s power and majesty were insufficient for the birth of a little infant, when they had sufficed for the creation of all things earthly and heavenly?

But the point is this: all those works were accomplished by God’s command, whereas this birth could take place only through his coming. God could neither be conceived by a human being unless he gave himself, nor be born unless he entered into the Virgin. Therefore the archangel announced the sacred majesty that was to come upon the Virgin, namely, that since so great a thing could not be accomplished through human agency, it was fitting that his own majesty should be present in the conception—he whose presence would be manifested in the birth. [Lipsius, in the margin: “should speak” (diceret).]

And so the Word, the Son, descended; the majesty of the Holy Spirit was present; the power of the Father overshadowed her—all so that, in the sacrament of the sacred conception, the cooperation of the entire Trinity might be present.

Therefore he says: “And the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God.”

He aptly added the word “therefore,” showing that these things would follow because those others had preceded, and that because God had come upon her in the conception, God would be present in the birth.

He therefore explained the reason for so great a mystery to the girl who did not understand it, saying: “Because the Holy Spirit will come upon you, and because the power of the Most High will overshadow you, therefore the holy one who will be born will be called the Son of God.”

This is to say: “Do not fail to understand this preparation for so great a thing, this sacrament of so great a mystery. The entire majesty of God will come upon you for this reason: because the Son of God will be born from you.”

What more can be doubted here, or what more can be said? He said that God would come upon her and that the Son of God would be born. Ask now, if you wish, how the Son of God is not God, or how she who brought forth God cannot be Theotokos, that is, Mother of God.

These things alone ought to suffice for you—indeed, these supreme things ought to have sufficed.

## CHAPTER III

The same argument is continued with testimonies from the Old Scripture.

Since testimonies to the sacred birth are abundantly available—inasmuch as all these things were written for the very purpose of being witnesses to it—let us examine a small portion of them, including the announcement concerning God in the Old Testament, so that you may understand that God’s birth from a Virgin was not announced only when it took place, but was foretold from the very beginning of the world. Indeed, since an ineffable work was to be accomplished, the prior announcement of future events would eventually remove disbelief concerning present realities.

The prophet Isaiah therefore says:

> [Note: [Col. 0037B] St. Jerome, on Matthew 1: “In place of what the evangelist Matthew says, ‘She will have in her womb,’ the prophet has written, ‘She will receive in her womb.’ But because the prophet indicates future events—what will happen—and writes ‘she will receive,’ whereas the Evangelist, because he narrates a past event rather than a future one, changed ‘she will receive’ and put ‘she will have.’ For whoever has something will certainly not be about to receive it.”]

“Behold, a virgin will conceive and bear a son, and they will call his name Emmanuel,”

> [Note: [Col. 0037B] Matthew thus cites and interprets this passage of Isaiah (chapter 1), although Isaiah himself has only: “And you will call his name Emmanuel.” Lest anyone wonder at this, St. Jerome observes concerning that passage: “In many testimonies which the evangelists or apostles took from the books of old, they did not follow the order of the words, but the meaning. Hence, in the present passage, instead of ‘she will conceive in the womb,’ Matthew put ‘she will have in the womb,’ and instead of ‘you will call,’ ‘they will call.’”]

which is interpreted, “God with us” (Isaiah 7).

> [Note: [Col. 0037C] Cyril of Alexandria, *On the Incarnation of the Only-Begotten* (chapter 2, and on Hebrews 2): “Emmanuel” is the name given to God the Word, because he took hold of Abraham’s seed and, like us, shared in flesh and blood. Emmanuel is interpreted as “God with us.” We confess that the Word of God was with us, not locally. For in what place is God not present, since he fills all things? Nor is this said of his being with us in the sense of assistance—for this was said in such a manner to Jesus (that is, Joshua): “As I was with Moses, so I will also be with you”—but because he came to be among us, that is, in humanity, without abandoning his own nature. Therefore we say that God the Word came to be with us at the time of which Baruch says: “He was seen on earth and lived among human beings.” Thus far Cyril. From this we understand that Jesus and Emmanuel are, as far as the matter is concerned, the same, although they appear to be different names. Jesus means “Savior”; Emmanuel, “God with us.” God was with us in order to save us. Therefore “God is with us” signifies nothing other than “God is our Savior.”]

What place for incredulous hesitation is left here? The prophet said that a virgin would conceive; the virgin conceived. He said that a son would be born; the son was born. He said that he would be called God; he is called God. For he is called by the name that corresponds to his nature. Accordingly, when the Spirit of God said that he would be called God, the person who excludes himself from sharing in the divine designation proves himself devoid of the Spirit of God.

“Behold,” he says, “a virgin will conceive and bear a son, and they will call his name Emmanuel,” which is interpreted, “God with us.”

But perhaps unbelieving evasiveness may turn to this argument: the prophet’s statement that he would be called God, it may say, pertains not so much to the majesty of divinity as to the designation of a name. But what are we to do when Christ is nowhere at all called by this name in the Gospels, and yet the Spirit of God cannot be said to have lied through the prophet?

What, then, does this mean? We must understand that the prophecy foretold the name of divinity, not of the flesh.

> [Note: [Col. 0037D] This concerns an objection that could be raised about the name Emmanuel: how Isaiah could say that he would be called Emmanuel when Christ is nowhere found in the Gospels to have been called by this name. The distinguished doctor Maldonado also raises and resolves this question in these words (*On Matthew*, chapter 1): “Someone may wonder how the angel could command that Jesus be called by this name, when Isaiah said that he would be called Emmanuel. The Jews commonly raise this objection against us to prove that the prophecy does not apply to Christ. But the ancient authorities have long since answered them sufficiently and abundantly. Justin [Col. 0038B], *Questions to the Orthodox* 131; Tertullian, *Against the Jews* and book 3 *Against Marcion*; Lactantius, book 4 *On True Wisdom*, chapter 12; and Chrysostom, *On the Incarnation*, chapter 2, wished to show that the prophet declared not the name by which Christ would be called, but what he would be; and that the evangelist declared both what he would be called and what he would be. For the prophet did not wish to say that Emmanuel would be Christ’s proper name, but that the reality signified by that name would belong to him, and therefore that he could rightly be called Emmanuel. In the same way, Isaiah himself had foretold concerning Jerusalem in chapter 1: ‘After this you will be called the city of the righteous, the faithful city.’ This does not mean that it would ever be called by that name, but that it would become such that it could rightly be so called. And concerning Christ himself, the same Isaiah said in chapter 9 that his name would be called ‘Wonderful, Counselor, God, Mighty, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace’—not because he would have so many names, but because he would possess so many realities. And Jeremiah, chapter 23: ‘This is the name by which they will call him: The Lord our righteous one.’ Truly Christ was the Lord our righteous one, and truly Emmanuel, which means ‘God with us.’ That the evangelist understood Isaiah’s passage in this way is clear from the fact that, after saying, ‘You will call his name Jesus,’ as though to prove that he ought to be called by that name, he added Isaiah’s passage: ‘And his name will be called Emmanuel’ (Isaiah 7). Jesus and Emmanuel are therefore the same, not in sound, as Tertullian says (*Against the Jews*, chapter 9), but in meaning. For ‘God with us,’ which is expressed by Emmanuel, means that he is our saving God, which is signified by the name Jesus.” Thus far Maldonado, with a few omissions.]

> [Note: [Cols. 0038C–D] Namely, the name Jesus, which was given by the angel before he was conceived in the womb. This designation must necessarily have belonged to the human being—that is, have been attributed to Christ as man—whereas the other, Emmanuel, belongs to divinity, that is, is fitting for Christ as God, as its very sound indicates. Accordingly, Christ is both true man and true God, because the person of the Word is not one and that of the human being another, but he is one and the same person, subsisting in two natures, divine and human. This unity of person necessarily entails the communication of the properties of both natures: whatever is truly and properly said of Christ as God is truly and properly said of the same Christ as man, and conversely. Hence, just as we confess in accordance with Catholic faith that he is one and the same God and man, Son of God and son of man, so we must confess that he is the same Emmanuel foretold by the prophet and Jesus named in the Gospel.]

For since, in the Gospel, the man united to God received another name, this name must necessarily have belonged to the human being, and the other to divinity. But let us proceed further and summon other testimonies of the truth to establish the truth. For when the subject is God, divinity is approved by nothing more effectively than by its own witnesses.

The same prophet says elsewhere:

> “A son has been born for us, a child has been given to us; his sovereignty is upon his shoulder, and his name will be called the messenger of great counsel, God, Mighty, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace” (Isaiah 9).

> [Note: [Col. 0039D] These two expressions should be read separately, with a comma between them, since they are two distinct designations or epithets of that child whom the prophet says was born for us, both of which are names of God among the Hebrews. St. Jerome teaches this in his discussion of the passage.]

Just as above the prophet said that he would be called Emmanuel, so here he says that he would be called the messenger of great counsel, God, Mighty, Father of the age to come, and Prince of Peace, although nowhere in the Gospels do we read that he was called by these names. We must therefore understand that these names belong not to the flesh but to divinity.

> [Note: [Col. 0039D] Nevertheless, on account of the hypostatic union of divinity and flesh, these names equally belong to one and the same person and divine subject.]

And that name in the Gospels is the name of the assumed human being,

> [Note: [Col. 0039D] The name Jesus, the name of the assumed human being—that is, of the humanity taken on—or of Christ according to his humanity, according to which the office of Savior and Redeemer belongs to him, is denoted by this name. “There is one mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2).]

whereas this is the name of innate power.

> [Note: [Col. 0040D] That is, of divine and eternal majesty.]

> [Note: [Col. 0040D] That is, in humanity, as above, not in the person of a human being.]

And because God was to be born in a human being, the names themselves were thus divided through the sacred dispensation, so that one name might be assigned to the human flesh and another to divinity. “He will be called,” he says, “the messenger of great counsel, God, Mighty, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace.”

Not here, whoever you are, O heretic—not here did that prophet, filled with the divine Spirit, in accordance with the example of your assertion, compare the one who was born with a cast statue and an insensible image. “A son,” he says, “has been born for us; a child has been given to us; his sovereignty is upon his shoulder, and his name will be called the messenger of great counsel, God, Mighty.”

Lest you understand the one he announced to be someone other than the one born in the flesh, he added the designation of birth, saying: “A child has been born for us; a son has been given to us.” Do you see how many titles the prophet used to demonstrate the reality of a bodily birth? He called him both born and a child, clearly expressing, through the name “child,” the meaning of offspring that had been born. Without doubt the divine Spirit foresaw this perversity of blaspheming heretics and, through these designations of the realities themselves, demonstrated to the whole world the God who was being born, so that even if a heretic sought to blaspheme, he would be completely unable to find an opportunity for blasphemy.

“A son,” he says, “has been born for us; a child has been given to us; his sovereignty is upon his shoulder, and his name will be called the messenger of great counsel, God, Mighty, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace.”

He taught that this child who was born was the Prince of Peace, the Father of the age to come, and God, Mighty. What room for evasion remains? This child who was born cannot be separated from the God who was born in him. For the one whom he called born, he named the Father of the age to come; the one whom he called a child, he declared to be God, Mighty.

What is there, heretic, to which you can retreat?

> [Col. 0040A]

Everything is enclosed and confined; there is absolutely no place of escape anywhere. It remains only that the error which the will refused to understand may at last begin to confess under compulsion.

But since we are not satisfied with these things, which are sufficient, let us also inquire what the Holy Spirit said through another prophet:

> [Note: [Col. 0040D] Jerome follows the Hebrew here, and this is the Vulgate version. The Septuagint, as he himself notes in the same place, translated: εἰ πτερνιήσει—that is, “if he will trip up”—instead of which Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion put μὴ ἀποστερήσει, that is, “if he will defraud,” yielding the sense: “If a human being defrauds God, because you have defrauded me?”]

“Will a human being fasten his God?” he says, “Because you fasten me?” (Malachi 3).

Thus the things foretold would become clearer: concerning the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, the prophet sang as though he were predicting it in the very voice of the one about whom he spoke:

> “Will a human being fasten his God? Because you fasten me?”

Does not our Lord God seem to you to have said this, as though led to the cross?

Why, I ask, do you not acknowledge me as your Redeemer? Why do you not recognize God clothed in flesh for your sake? Are you preparing death for your Savior? Are you leading the author of life to death?

I am your God, whom you hang; I am your God, whom you crucify.

What error, I ask, or what madness is this?

> “Will a human being fasten his God? Because you fasten me?”

Do you see how this voice is, in a certain sense, the voice of the very events that took place? Could you seek anything more explicit or clearer? Do you see how the sacred testimonies have followed the Lord Jesus Christ, born in the flesh, from his very swaddling clothes, so to speak, all the way to the cross that he endured? Although elsewhere you read that God was born in the flesh, here you see God fastened to the cross.

Therefore the prophet calls him God both where he was born and, most unmistakably, where he was crucified, lest the assumption of flesh prejudice the dignity of divinity in any respect, or the honor of majesty be diminished either by the lowliness of the body or by the disgrace of the passion. Indeed, the condescension of so humble a birth and the compassion of one who suffered with such kindness ought to increase in us affection for him and reverence toward him, since it is the greatest and most monstrous crime that he should receive less honor from us precisely because he bestowed greater love.

## CHAPTER IV. He adduces testimonies from the apostle Paul in support of the same doctrine.

But leaving aside these matters, which cannot in any way be fully explained because, just as the immensity of his benefits has no limit, so their narration has no limit, it is time that we consult his strongest and clearest witness concerning him, the apostle Paul. For he can speak to us most faithfully about God, from whose heart God has always spoken.

He therefore testifies in this manner concerning the grace and coming of our Lord God, having been sent as the chosen teacher of the nations to destroy the error of pagan superstition:

> [Note: [Col. 0041D] St. Jerome also presses this passage against heretics who deny Christ’s divinity (*Commentary*): “Where is the serpent Arius? Where is the snake Eunomius? Jesus Christ is called the great God—not ‘the firstborn of all creation,’ not ‘the Word and Wisdom’ (that is, not insofar as he is God and the Son of God), but Jesus Christ. These are names of the assumed human being—that is, of the assumed humanity. We do not say one Jesus Christ and another Word, as the new heresy—that is, the Nestorian heresy—calumniously alleges, but we call the same one, both before the ages and after the ages, both before the world and after Mary, indeed from Mary, our Savior Jesus Christ, the great God.”]

> “The grace of God our Savior has appeared to all human beings, training us to renounce impiety and worldly desires and to live soberly, piously, and justly in this present world, awaiting the blessed hope and the appearance of the glory of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ” (Titus 2).

“The grace of God our Savior,” he says, “has appeared.”

He aptly used language suited to display the coming of a new grace and a new birth. By saying “has appeared,” he expressed the origin of a new grace and birth, because the gift of the new grace began to appear from the time when God appeared born in the world.

He therefore pointed out this light of the new grace with a word whose propriety was fitting and almost indicated it with a finger. For that is most correctly said to have “appeared” which is displayed through the sudden light, as when we read in the Gospels that a star appeared to the eastern Magi (Matthew 2), and in Exodus: “The angel of the Lord appeared to Moses in a flame of fire from the bush” (Exodus 3).

In all these and other sacred visions, Scripture considered the verb “appear” especially appropriate, saying that those things had appeared which shone with an extraordinary brightness. Thus the Apostle, knowing that the heavenly grace had appeared through the birth of the sacred child, expressed it with the word “appearance,” saying that what shone with the splendor of a new light had appeared.

“The grace of God our Savior has appeared.”

Can you here raise any objection based on an ambiguity of names, saying that Christ is one thing and God another? Can you separate the Savior from the majesty of his name, and distinguish the Lord from divinity?

Behold, here the man of God speaks from God and bears witness, in the clearest proclamation, that the grace of God appeared from Mary. And lest you perhaps say that God did not appear from Mary, he immediately added the name “Savior,” so that you would believe him who was born from Mary to be God, since you cannot deny that the one born as Savior was born.

This agrees with the saying:

> “For today a Savior has been born for you” (Luke 2).

O admirable teacher of the nations, truly given by God! He knew that this future madness of heretical perversity would turn the names of God into a quarrel and would not fear to slander God on account of his own names. Therefore, lest a heretic separate the title “Savior” from divinity, he placed the name “God” first, so that the preceding name “God” would claim for itself all the names that followed, and no one would believe Christ to be a solitary human being when he had immediately learned from the first title that he was God.

“The same Apostle says,”

> “Awaiting the blessed hope and the appearance of the glory of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ.”

That teacher of divine wisdom clearly saw that simple instruction alone was insufficient against the treacherous cunning of the devil’s deception unless he armed the sacred proclamation of faith with the protection of caution. Therefore, after he had previously joined the names “God” and “Savior,” he added here “Jesus Christ,” lest you perhaps think that the single name “Savior” was insufficient to signify the Lord Jesus Christ, and fail to understand that the same Jesus Christ was God whom you had recognized as God the Savior.

What does he say?

> “Awaiting the blessed hope and the appearance of the glory of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ.”

Nothing is lacking here among the names of our Lord. Here you see God, Savior, Jesus, and Christ. Yet when you see all these things, you perceive that all are in God.

You heard “God,” but also “Savior.” You heard “God,” but also “Jesus.” You heard that he is God, but also “Christ.” What divinity joined together in unity cannot be separated by a diversity of designations.

Whatever you wish to inquire about among these, you will find the same reality. The Savior is God, Jesus is God, Christ is God. All this that you hear is plural in designation but one in power.

> [Note: [Col. 0042D] That is, distinct in designation, as is explained below, because the appellations and names are different, although they belong to one and the same person.]

Since the Savior is God, Jesus is God, and Christ is God, it is clear that all these terms are distinguished by designation but joined in majesty. And when you hear most clearly that one God is named in each case, you can plainly understand that there is one God in them all.

Thus you may no longer seek a difference of power from the dissimilarity of the Lord’s designations, nor make a difference of person out of the variety of names. You may not say: “Christ was born from Mary, but not God,” for the Apostle proclaims: “God.” You may not say: “Jesus was born from Mary, but not God,” for the Apostle testifies: “God.” You may not say: “The Savior was born, but not God,” for the Apostle confirms: “God.”

There is nowhere for you to turn. Whatever you take from the names of the Lord, what you name is God.

> [Note: [Col. 0042D] That is: whatever you name, Christ is God; whatever is said about him, whatever is said about the human being, is said about God.]

There is nothing you can say, nothing you can bring forward, nothing you can fabricate through wicked falsehood. In your impious disbelief you may have something that you do not believe; you have nothing, as an occasion for slander, that you can deny.

## CHAPTER V. From the gifts of divine grace that we receive through Christ, he concludes that Christ is truly God.

> [Col. 0042D]

Although we began a little earlier to speak of this divine grace of our Lord and Savior, I wish us to say something further about the same matter from the sacred readings.

In the Acts of the Apostles we read that the apostle Peter rebuked those who, while accepting the Gospel, nevertheless maintained that the yoke of the ancient law had to be borne:

> “Why,” he says, “do you test God by placing upon the necks of the disciples a yoke which neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? But we believe that we are saved through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, just as they are” (Acts 15).

The Apostle says that this gift of grace was given through Jesus Christ. Now answer me, if you please: do you think that this grace, which was given for the salvation of all, was given by a human being or by God?

If by a human being, Paul, the vessel of God, contradicts you when he says:

> “The grace of God our Savior has appeared” (Titus 2).

He teaches that this grace belongs to a divine gift, not to human weakness.

Indeed, even if sacred testimony were unavailable, the truth of the matter itself would provide testimony, because fragile and earthly things cannot bestow an enduring and immortal good, nor can anyone give another what he himself needs, or grant an abundance of something whose lack he admits that he suffers.

Therefore you cannot deny that grace was given by God. God, then, is the one who gave it; but it was given through our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore the Lord Jesus Christ is God.

But if he is God—as he certainly is—then she who bore God is *Theotokos*, that is, the mother of God.

Unless perhaps you wish to pursue so ridiculous a contradiction in blasphemy as to deny that she from whom God was born is the mother of God, although you cannot deny that the one who was born is God.

Let us nevertheless see what the Gospel of God has also understood concerning this same grace of our Lord.

> “Grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1).

If Christ is a solitary human being, how did these things come through Christ? From where was divine power in him, if, as you say, there was in him only human condition? From where was heavenly generosity, if there was earthly poverty? No one can give what he does not possess.

Therefore, in giving divine grace, Christ possessed what he gave. For no one can sustain a distinction between such utterly different realities that he simultaneously suffers the neediness of one who lacks and possesses the generosity of one who gives.

And therefore, knowing that all the treasures of heavenly riches are in Christ, the apostle Paul rightly writes to the churches:

> [Col. 0043D] “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you” (1 Corinthians 16).

Since he had already taught repeatedly that the one who is Christ is also God, that the entire majesty of divinity is in him, and that the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily in him, he now rightly prays for the grace of Christ alone, without adding the name “God.” For having repeatedly taught that the grace of God is the grace of Christ, he now prays most fully for the grace of Christ alone, because he knows that all the grace of God is contained in the grace of Christ.

> “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.”

I ask you, whoever you are, O heretic: when Paul wrote this to the churches, what was he praying for those to whom he wrote?

> “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.”

If Jesus Christ is a solitary human being,

> [Note: [Col. 0043] That is, separated from divinity, or merely human, as above and very often elsewhere in this treatise; this one reminder should suffice.]

then, by wishing the grace of Christ to be given to the churches, he was wishing that the grace of a human being be given. And by saying, “The grace of Christ be with you,” he was saying: “May the grace of a human being be with you; the grace of flesh; the grace of bodily weakness; the grace of human frailty.”

Or why would he mention the name of Christ’s grace at all if he were wishing for human grace? The purpose of the prayer would not stand where there was nothing to be desired, nor should he pray that Christ’s grace come upon those who, as you claim, did not possess the substance of the grace that was being desired.

Therefore you see that these ideas are utterly foolish and ridiculous—or rather, not ridiculous but to be mourned. For what is ridiculous to some who find certain matters easier to grasp must be mourned by the devout and faithful, because in the folly of your unbelief they pour out tears of charity, and in the ignorance of another’s impiety they possess tears of their own piety.

Let us therefore come to our senses at last and recover our breath, because this view lacks not only wisdom but also the Spirit: it is empty of spiritual wisdom and estranged from the Spirit of salvation.

## CHAPTER VI. The capacity to bestow divine grace did not come to Christ in the course of time, but was congenitally his from his very birth.

But perhaps you will say that this grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, about which the Apostle writes, was not born with him, but was afterward infused into him through a divine act; [Col. 0044C] for you also say that our Lord Jesus Christ himself, whom you call solitary—being a man, as you hold, and not born with God but afterward assumed by God—was taken up by God later; and therefore, at what point were both divinity and grace given to that man?

We say nothing other than that divine grace descended together with divinity, since divine grace belongs to God and is, in a certain sense, the generosity and gift of divinity itself. Thus, the difference between us may perhaps be thought to concern time more than substance, since you say that divinity was afterward infused into the Lord Jesus Christ, whereas we say that it was born with him. But this is the point: by denying that divinity was born with the Lord, you cannot afterward confess it faithfully either, because one and the same thing cannot be impious in one respect and approved as pious in another, nor be part faith and part unbelief.

[Col. 0044D] First, therefore, I ask you this: do you say that our Lord Jesus Christ, who was born of the Virgin Mary, is only the Son of man, or also the Son of God? For we—that is, the faith of all Catholics—we, I say, both believe, understand, know, and confess both: that he is the son of man because he was born from a human being, and the Son of God because he was conceived through Divinity. Do you therefore assert both—that he is the Son of God and the son of man—or only that he is the son of man?

If only the son of man, the apostles protest against you; the prophets protest against you; finally, [Col. 0045A] he himself protests—

[Note: [Col. 0045A] This refers to Christ’s conception, which is said to have taken place through the Holy Spirit, because that body which was conceived and formed in the Virgin’s womb was conceived and formed not by human agency but by the power and operation of the Holy Spirit, and in the very act of its formation and conception was assumed, together with a rational soul, by the Word, or Son of God. In this sense the Evangelist signifies that Christ was conceived from the Holy Spirit when he says: “Before they came together”—that is, Mary and Joseph for the act of marriage—she was found to have conceived in the womb from the Holy Spirit (Matt. I). And the angel said to Joseph: “For that which is born in her is from the Holy Spirit.” And to the Virgin herself: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy thing that will be born [of you],” and so forth. Hence in the Creed we profess that the Son of God was conceived from the Holy Spirit.

For a fuller explanation of this matter, several things should be noted here. First, the work of the Lord’s Incarnation must be attributed to the whole Trinity as its efficient cause, in accordance with the familiar rule of Catholic faith that the works of the Trinity are indivisible. For, as St. Augustine says in Book I of *On the Trinity* (chapter 4): “Those divine Persons are inseparable, and therefore they also operate inseparably.” And St. Leo says (Sermon 3 on Pentecost): “Nothing there is divided in action where nothing is different in will.”

Therefore, although the Son is said to have been conceived from the Holy Spirit, this does not mean from him as begetter—for the Holy Spirit did not communicate his own substance to the Son, which belongs to the notion of a parent or begetter—but from him as the maker and fashioner of the human body assumed by Christ. It follows that the same operation proceeded equally from the Father and from the Son. Thus, when the Holy Spirit is named in this work, the other Persons must also be understood; just as, when the Father alone or the Son alone is named in some work, the Holy Spirit must not be excluded.

Second, although the Incarnation, considered as an action and operation, is common to the three Persons, Catholic faith maintains that only the Son of God was incarnate. Hence the Sabellian heretics were rightly condemned long ago: they asserted that the Father too had become incarnate and suffered in the flesh no less than the Son, and were consequently called Patripassians, or Patropaschites, because they did not distinguish the Persons in God.

The reason and explanation of this truth is that the union of human nature with the divine nature, which we call the Incarnation, was made and terminated in the Person of the Son alone. Therefore, although the three Persons cooperated in the same union, only the Son is said to have become incarnate and to have assumed flesh. This is partly illustrated by a familiar example: if three men should join together to clothe one of them, that one alone puts on the garment and is consequently clothed, although the others also cooperate in the act of clothing. So, in the work of the Incarnation and the assumption of human nature, the three divine Persons cooperated together, but only the Person of the Son assumed flesh and united it to himself.

Third, the Fathers assign two principal reasons why the Incarnation, or conception, of the Son is specially attributed to the Holy Spirit, since he is said to have been conceived from the Holy Spirit. The first is that, when the name of the Holy Spirit is heard, the purity and holiness of this conception, free from every stain of sin, may be understood. For whatever is holy in creatures is specially attributed to the Holy Spirit. Hence he is called “the Spirit of sanctification” in Romans I. The angel also seems to have suggested this reason (Luke II) when, after the words “The Holy Spirit will come upon you,” and so forth, he added: “Therefore the holy thing that will be born of you,” and so forth.

“Holy,” he says, “will be born of you,” because it was conceived when the Holy Spirit came upon you, with no impurity of lust arising through sexual union whatsoever. Therefore what will be born will not be impure, because it will not be conceived from impure seed, but through the power of the Holy Spirit.

The second reason is that a twofold benefit—each part of it supreme—is signified as having been bestowed upon us by God through the Incarnation. One benefit was bestowed upon Christ as man, or according to his human nature: human nature, without any preceding merits of its own, was raised to such honor that it was joined to the Son of God in the unity of Person and was rendered wholly free from every contagion. The other benefit was bestowed upon the whole human race, namely, the benefit of redemption, procured through the Incarnation and the ministry of the Mediator. For in Scripture gifts of grace and everything pertaining to the sanctification of human beings are ordinarily attributed to the Holy Spirit. Since no grace is greater and no gift more excellent than what is contained in the mystery of the Incarnation, this supreme benefit is most appropriately attributed to the Holy Spirit.

See St. Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 36.]

through whom the conception took place: the Holy Spirit.

Your utterly shameless mouth is overwhelmed by all the testimonies of the divine writings; it is overwhelmed by the sacred books and holy witnesses; finally, it is overwhelmed by the very Gospel of God, as though by a divine hand. And that great Gabriel, who by the power of his word restrained the incredulous voice of Zechariah, condemned your blasphemous and impious speech all the more by his own mouth, saying to Mary, the virgin and Mother of God: “The Spirit,” he says, “will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Therefore the holy thing that will be born of you will be called the Son of God” (Luke I).

Do you see that, before Jesus Christ became the son of man according to the flesh, he was proclaimed the Son of God? For the Virgin Mary, about to bear the Lord, conceived when the Holy Spirit descended upon her and the power of the Most High cooperated. And from this you understand—

[Note: [Col. 0046C] I confess that I struggled for a long time with the elucidation of this passage and did not sufficiently grasp the author’s meaning according to my own wishes until I came upon the commentary of the most learned Father Maldonado (*On Luke*, chapter I). I have therefore thought it worthwhile to reproduce his entire opinion here and compare it with this passage of Cassian; the reader, I trust, will not find it unwelcome.

Thus he explains the angel’s words to the Virgin: “Therefore the holy thing that will be born of you will be called the Son of God.” After refuting Euthymius’s opinion, who understands only that Christ would be called the Son of God by human beings because of the wondrous and divine works he was to perform, he says:

“All the others whom I have seen interpret the passage as though the angel were speaking of Christ as God, or at least as man assumed into one Person with God; for in either respect Christ is the true and natural Son of God: as God, because he was produced by eternal generation from God; as man, because, although begotten in time, he was nevertheless united with God the Son in one Person. Therefore there are not two sons, just as there are not two persons, but one Son, just as there is one Person.

“For this reason the ancient authors refuted from this passage the heresy of Nestorius, who imagined two Sons in Christ just as he imagined two Persons, including Gregory in Book XIX of the *Moralia*, chapter 37, and Bede in his commentary on this passage.

“Yet I myself think the meaning is different: that this should be understood neither of Christ as God, nor of Christ as man united to the divine Person, but only of his conception and human generation, as though the angel were saying: ‘He will be called’—that is, ‘He will be the Son of God,’ because he will be generated not by a man but by God, through the power of the Holy Spirit.

“For the angel was speaking not of Christ’s nature but of the mode of his generation. The reason he gives for why he will be the Son of God—that the Holy Spirit will come upon the Virgin and the power of the Most High will overshadow her—would not be adequate to prove, in that sense, that Christ would be the Son of God insofar as he was God or insofar as he was man assumed into one Person with God. For a mere man too could have been conceived when the Holy Spirit came upon the Virgin and the power of the Most High overshadowed her, and yet he would not in either of those respects have been the Son of God, since he would neither be God nor united to the divine Person.

“But to prove that what was to be born from the Virgin would be the Son of God in the sense I have explained, the angel’s reason is entirely fitting, because he was to be conceived not from a man but from God alone. Thus, even if Christ had not been God, nevertheless, if he had been generated in the manner in which he was generated, he would rightly have been called the Son of God—not merely in the same way as the other holy men of whom it is said, ‘I have said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High’ (Ps. LXXXI; John II), but in a singular and proper way, because he would have no father other than God and would have been generated by no one other than him.

“This is precisely the way Luke below, in chapter III, calls Adam the Son of God, because he was not begotten by a man but by God: ‘who was of Cainan, who was of Enos, who was of Seth, who was of Adam, who was of God.’ The word ‘son’ is understood here as in all the preceding cases.

“What then? Will this passage be lost to us and useless against the Nestorians? It is not lost. We do not lack Scriptural testimonies by which to refute Nestorius’s error, and Gregory refuted it more effectively from this very passage and the words immediately following, in Book IX of his *Register*, Letter 61.

“For when the angel says here, ‘That which will be born of you,’ Elizabeth says in verse 63: ‘And from where is this granted to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?’ From this Gregory concludes that the same virgin was both mother of the man of whom the angel speaks and Mother of God, of whom Elizabeth speaks. Therefore there were not two Sons, but one; for Nestorius denied that the blessed Virgin was θεοτόκος (*theotokos*), that is, Mother and Begetter of God, for no other reason than that he posited two Sons in Christ.

“Thus far Maldonado.”

From his opinion, this otherwise sufficiently obscure and intricate passage may apparently be clarified as follows: The origin of our Savior is from the same source as his conception—namely, according to his human nature, from the Holy Spirit, indeed from the whole Trinity, or from the fullness of the entire Godhead, as is said here. The word “conceived” may be a substantive, meaning “conception,” or an adjective referring to Christ, who was conceived and born from the Holy Spirit.

And he could not be the son of man unless he had first been the Son of God, because the Son of God himself made himself the son of man. Therefore he was the Son of God before he was the son of man; for being is prior—at least by nature—to acting, according to the Philosopher.

And although from the angel’s words it could not be established with certainty that he was the natural Son of God, but only in that special respect that he was generated not by a man but by God alone and had no father other than God—just as Adam too is called the son of God—nevertheless, when other passages of Scripture are considered together, this is sufficiently and plainly established.]

that the origin of our Lord and Savior is from the same source as his conception; and since he was born when the fullness of the entire Godhead descended upon the Virgin, he could not be the son of man unless he had first been the Son of God. Therefore the angel of God, sent to announce the birth of the sacred offspring, having first spoken of the mystery of the conception, gave a name to the birth itself, saying:

[Note: [Col. 0047D] The venerable Bede says concerning this passage:

“To distinguish it from our birth, Jesus is affirmed to be about to be born holy. For although we are made holy, we are not born holy, because we are constrained by the very condition of corruptible nature, so that each of us rightly says with the Prophet in lamentation: ‘For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me’ (Ps. L). But he alone is truly holy who, in order to overcome the condition of corruptible nature itself, was not conceived through the union of carnal intercourse.

“‘He will be called the Son of God.’ What do you say to this, O Nestorian? By denying that blessed Mary is the Mother of God, you openly strive to attack the truth. Behold, he said that God would come upon her and that the Son of God would be born. How, then, is he not the Son of God? Or how can she who gave birth to God not be θεοτόκος (*theotokos*), that is, the Mother of God?”

This is Bede; Gregory says nearly the same in the passage cited above (*Moralia*, Book XVIII, chapter 37).

Moreover, “to be called” is used here for “to be,” according to the idiom of the Hebrews. Thus “he will be called the Son of God,” or “the Son of the Most High,” means “he will truly be the Son of God Most High,” so that he rightly ought to be called this. Thus in Isaiah, chapter I: “After this you will be called the city of the just, the faithful city,” that is, “you will be the city of the just.” And in Isaiah IV: “And everyone who has been left in Zion and remains in Jerusalem will be called holy,” that is, “will be holy.”

Nor should anyone stumble here, as the Arians do, over the future-tense verb “will be called,” as though before he was born he were not the Son of God. It should be observed that the passage concerns the man whom the Virgin was to conceive and bear. Before he was conceived, he was not merely not the Son of God, but was not even a man. For the Virgin was to conceive not a bare God but a God-man; the God-man did not exist before he was conceived. But once conceived, the man became God, because at the very moment of conception he was assumed by God into the same hypostasis.]

“Therefore the holy thing that will be born of you will be called the Son of God”—that is, he will be named the Son of the one by whom he was generated.

[Note: [Col. 0048C] That is, by whose operation and production he was brought forth. For this passage does not concern the divine and eternal generation from the Father, but Christ’s human conception and birth, as has been said.]

Therefore Jesus Christ is the Son of God, because he was both generated by divinity and conceived through divinity.

[Note: [Col. 0048D] That is, by God, or through divine operation; for divinity properly neither begets nor is begotten, as St. Thomas teaches (*Summa*, Part I, question 39, article 5), following the Master (*Sentences*, Book I, distinction 5). For begetting and being begotten belong to a person, not to a nature.]

[Note: [Col. 0048D] In the sense, namely, that he is God insofar as he is understood to be the Son of God. For if “Son of God” is taken in the sense explained by Maldonado, he is not properly and essentially God but only nominally so, since he is called the Son of God because he was conceived in that manner—that is, not from a man but from the Holy Spirit. But if he is understood in the sense transmitted by the other authors as the natural Son of God, then he is consubstantial with the Father and cannot be anything but God. Therefore, if he is the Son of God, he is unquestionably God.]

But if he is the Son of God, then he is unquestionably God; and if he is God, then he is not without the grace of God, for he was never without that which he himself made. “For grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.”

## CHAPTER VII. That Christ’s divinity, majesty, power, virtue, and so forth were, are, and will be perfect from eternity

[Col. 0048A]

Therefore, all grace in him, all virtue, all power, all divinity, and finally the entire fullness of his divinity and majesty, were always with him and in him, whether in heaven, on earth, in the womb, or at his birth. Nothing of God was ever lacking to God: deity was always with God, never separated from him by place or by time. For God is everywhere wholly present, everywhere perfect, neither divided, changed, nor diminished, since nothing can ever be added to God or taken away from him. Thus he has no diminution of deity, just as he has no increase.

He was therefore the same on earth as in heaven; the same in lowliness as in exaltation; the same in the smallness of human condition as in the majesty of God. Accordingly, when the Apostle names the grace of Christ (1 Cor. XVI), he rightly names the grace of God, because Christ was everything that God is. At the very conception of the man, all the power of God and the entire fullness of divinity came to him. His entire perfection of divinity came from the same source as his origin.

For that man had never been without God, since he had received from God the very thing that he was. This, therefore, you cannot deny, whether you wish to or not: that the Lord Jesus Christ is the Son of God. The Archangel cries this out in the Gospels: “The holy thing that will be born of you will be called the Son of God” (Luke I).

Once this has been established, know that whatever you read about Christ, you read about the Son of God; whatever you read about the Lord or Jesus, they name the Son of God. All these names of his proclaim the Son of God. Therefore, whenever you hear any of these things, recognizing the name of divinity and seeing that in every case you must understand the Son of God, argue—if you please—how you can separate God from the Son of God.

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 0049]

## CHAPTER I. That Christ, the same man and God according to the flesh, was born from Israel and the Virgin Mary

[Col. 0049B]

That divine teacher of the churches, writing to the Romans and reproving—or rather mourning—the unbelief of the Jews, that is, of his own brothers, used these words:

[Note: [Col. 0049D] Joan. Gagnaeus has excellently explained this passage in the following brief commentary:

“If we understand the words as referring to separation from Christ’s glory, the expression is hyperbolic, intended to indicate his affection for the Jews. For the man who shortly before said, ‘I know that no creature can separate me from the love of God, which is in Christ’ (Rom. VIII), would not really wish immediately to be torn away from him. It is hyperbolic speech, like that of Moses in Exodus XXXII: ‘Either forgive them this offense, or, if you do not, blot me out of your book.’
