“Yet it seems to me that the passage can be read without hyperbole. Among the Greeks, *anathema* refers to sacred and accursed persons who were sacrificed to the divine spirits and the infernal powers for the purification of a city, whenever some plague or disaster arose. People thought that such calamity would be brought to an end by the destruction of these persons and the appeasement of the gods. Alluding to sacrifices of this kind, Paul says: ‘So deeply do I grieve over the rejection of the Jews that, if I could appease God’s anger against them by any misfortune of my own, I would wish to be anathema—and, in the Greek expression, ἀναθεματίζεσθαι (*anathematizesthai*), that is, to be utterly ruined and exterminated—from Christ, provided that I might benefit them even in this way.’

“Certainly Jerome understands *anathema* as bodily death.”

Thus far Gagnaeus. See other remarks to the same effect elsewhere (*Conferences*, 9.18 and 13.6), and more on *anathema* and its various meanings in Baronius, Book I of the *Annals*.]

“I myself was wishing to be anathema from Christ for the sake of my brothers, who are my kinsmen according to the flesh, who are Israelites, to whom belong the adoption as sons, and the glory, and the covenants, and the giving of the law, and the worship, and the promises;”

[Note: [Col. 0050D] “Whose fathers”—that is, from whose people the fathers and patriarchs came, from whom Christ was descended according to the flesh. Origen, Ambrose, Chrysostom, and others also understand the passage in this way, so that Christ is called true God, since nothing is “over all” except the supreme God.]

“whose fathers, and from whom Christ is according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever” (Rom. IX).

O what affection—of the most faithful apostle and most devoted kinsman—he who wishes to die out of immeasurable love, for his kinsmen as their relative, and for his disciples as their teacher! And what was the reason he wished to die? Certainly only this: that they might live.

And in what did their life consist? In this, clearly, as he himself says: that they should recognize Christ God, born according to the flesh from their own flesh. Therefore the Apostle grieved all the more because they did not understand that he was born from Israel, whom they ought to have loved more because he had been born from their own people.

“From whom Christ is according to the flesh,” he says, “who is God over all, blessed forever” (Rom. IX). He says that Christ born from them according to the flesh is God over all, blessed forever. You do not deny that Christ was born from them according to the flesh; but the same one who was born from them is God.

Why do you go around in circles? Why do you evade the issue? The Apostle says that Christ, born according to the flesh from Israel, is God. You must show when he was not God. “From whom Christ is according to the flesh, who is God over all,” he says.

You see that the Apostle has joined these matters together in unity, and that God cannot in any way be separated from Christ. For just as the Apostle proclaims Christ to be from them, so he confirms that God is in Christ. Either you must deny both, or confess both. Christ is said to have been born according to the flesh from them, but the Apostle proclaims that the same Christ is God. Hence elsewhere also: “For God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. V). These things cannot in any way be divided from one another.

Either deny that Christ was born from them, or confess that God was born from the Virgin in Christ: “who is,” he says, “God over all, blessed forever.”

## CHAPTER II. The title “God” is attributed to Christ in one way and to human beings in another

For the faithful, the name “God” by itself might have been fully sufficient to indicate the majesty of divinity. But by adding “God over all, blessed,” he excluded the blasphemy of the impious assertion, lest any of the wicked should take the title “God,” which is sometimes temporarily granted even to human beings as a gift of divine dispensation, and apply it insultingly to the supreme divinity by making God subject to comparison.

Thus there is the passage in which God says to Moses:

[Note: [Col. 0050D] The Vulgate text reads: “Behold, I have appointed you god of Pharaoh” (Exod. VII). Moses was called “the god of Pharaoh” because of the power granted to him by God for crushing Pharaoh’s pride, so that Pharaoh, who refused to submit to God, might submit to a human minister of God.

In Sacred Scripture, says St. Gregory (*Homily 8 on Ezekiel*), God is sometimes spoken of nominally and sometimes essentially. He is spoken of nominally, for example, where it is written: “Behold, I have appointed you god of Pharaoh.” Likewise Moses says: “If anyone does this or that, bring him to the gods” (Exod. XXII), meaning to the priests. Again he says: “You shall not insult the gods,” that is, the priests. And the Psalmist says: “God stood in the assembly of gods; in their midst he judges the gods” (Ps. XXXII).

But God is spoken of essentially where he says to Moses: “I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob” (Exod. III). Therefore the Apostle Paul, wishing to distinguish the nominal title “God” from the essential one, speaks of our Redeemer, saying: “Whose fathers, and from whom Christ is according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever” (Rom. IX).

He who is called god nominally is god among all; but he who is God essentially is God over all. Thus, to show that Christ is God by nature, Paul did not merely call him God but remembered that he is God over all. For, as we have said, any chosen person, because he is placed before others as an example by his excellence in righteousness, may be called god, but only among all, because he is god nominally. Christ, however, is God over all, God by nature.

Thus far St. Gregory.]

“I have appointed you god of Pharaoh” (Exod. VII), or the passage, “I have said, You are gods” (Ps. LXXXI), since these clearly express the meaning of a title bestowed.

For when he says, “I have said,” it is not so much the name of power as the statement of the one who speaks. Likewise, when he says, “I have appointed you god of Pharaoh,” he explains not the divinity of the one receiving but the power of the one giving. For when he says “I have appointed,” the power of God who gave is signified in that expression, not the nature of divinity in the one who received it.

But when it is said of God and our Lord Jesus Christ, “who is God over all, blessed forever,” the matter is immediately proved in the verb, and the reality of the verb is demonstrated in the name, because the name “God” in the Son of God—

[Note: [Col. 0051C] Christ is called God and Son of God not by adoption but by nature; nor can he in any way be called the adoptive Son of God, since according to the divine nature he is the natural, or true, Son of God, as Scripture says in the final chapter of 1 John: “We know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know the true God and may be in his true Son. This is the true God and eternal life.”

The Father’s voice from heaven also confirms this, as does Peter’s confession, by which Christ is asserted to be the Son of God in such a way that he is distinguished from all other just and holy men, who are acknowledged to have been sons of God by adoption (the Master, *Sentences*, distinctions 3 and 10).

Nor should Christ be called an adoptive son according to his human nature, or insofar as he is man, since it is incompatible for the same person to be both a natural son and an adoptive son. “Filiation,” says St. Thomas (*Summa*, Part III, question 13, article 3), “like adoption, properly belongs to a hypostasis, not to a nature; for sonship is a personal property.”

In Christ there is no person or hypostasis other than the uncreated one, to which it belongs to be Son by nature. This excludes every notion of adoption. For he becomes an adoptive son who, since he was not, or certainly could not have been, a son, is made a son by this benefit. In this way we say that the angels and the first human beings were sons of God from the beginning of their creation by the grace of adoption: although they were never separated from this grace and the right of eternal inheritance, they could nevertheless have been created in a purely natural condition, without that grace.

But the Person in Christ, since it is none other than the divine Person, and since it is naturally and eternally related to God the Father, could never have been a stranger to the right of sonship that belonged to it by reason of its origin. Therefore it cannot in any way be called an adoptive son unless, according to Nestorius’s opinion, a plurality of persons is established in Christ, one of whom bears the name of natural son and the other that of adoptive son.

The support of the holy Fathers agrees with this doctrine. St. Ambrose, commenting on chapter I of the Epistle to the Romans, says: “I have read and reread the Scriptures, and nowhere have I found Jesus to be the Son of God by adoption.” St. Hilary, in Book III of *On the Trinity*, says: “When the Lord says, ‘Glorify your Son,’ he testified not merely by name that he is the Son, but also by proper sonship. We are sons of God, but this Son is not such as we are. He is the true and proper Son by origin, not by adoption; by reality, not by designation; by birth, not by creation.” St. Jerome, commenting on chapter I of the Epistle to the Ephesians, says: “It is written of Christ Jesus that he was always with the Father, and that the Father’s will never preceded him in order that he might exist; he is the Son by nature, whereas we are sons by adoption. He was never not the Son; we were predestined before we existed, and received the spirit of adoption when we believed in the Son of God.”]

is not an indication of an adoption granted, but the truth and proper character of nature.

## CHAPTER III. He explains the Apostle’s statement: “From this point onward we know no one according to the flesh,” and so forth
Therefore, says the same Apostle:

> “From this time onward we know no one according to the flesh.”  

[Note: That is, from the time when, through faith, we learned that we must live for Christ alone, who died for us, we neither regard nor revere anyone’s fleshly affinity or kinship. We desire to benefit everyone equally; we recognize no one according to the flesh, whether he be a relative or someone formerly associated with us, for whose sake I might wish to live. For the Apostle had in view the preceding words: “So that those who live may no longer live for themselves, but for him who died and rose again for them” (II Cor. V).]

[Note: That is, not as a human being like ourselves living on earth. But “now we no longer know him” means that we do not recognize him as such; rather, we recognize him as true God and man, and, after his resurrection, as immortal, impassible, and glorified even in his body. Thus we no longer know Christ “according to the flesh,” that is, according to a fleshly understanding, as the Jews did, or according to the condition of passible flesh.

The meaning may therefore be twofold. First, Paul may be speaking of himself concerning the time when he was persecuting Christ, saying: “Although at one time”—namely, when we were in Judaism—“we had an unworthy opinion of Christ, judging according to the flesh,” that is, carnally, “as though he were merely a human being subject to death, we no longer know or regard him in this way.”

Or, secondly, these words may refer to different periods, not in Paul’s life but in Christ’s: first, to the period of mortal flesh, when he himself was subject to our sufferings, of which he says to the Hebrews V, “In the days of his flesh,” that is, of his passibility; and, second, to the period of the resurrection, when Christ, rising from the dead, “dies no more” (Rom. VI), which is beyond the condition of flesh.

Thus, he says, although in that first period—so that he may be speaking more in the person of the apostles than in his own—we knew Christ “according to the flesh,” that is, as passible, which belongs properly to flesh, now, in the period after his resurrection, when he did not lose flesh itself but the condition proper to flesh, we no longer know him as passible. See St. Thomas in his Commentary.

This exposition is transmitted in the Seventh Synod toward its conclusion; it is found in the Acts of the Council of Ephesus, volume V. Yet Cassian here had the former meaning more in view, as the fuller one, using it to prove Christ’s divinity, as is clear from the text.

St. Cyril of Alexandria agrees, explaining the same passage as follows:

> “What does Paul mean here? Does he deny Christ’s resurrection? Did he not know that he had been raised according to the flesh, and that he had gone up into heaven in that same flesh? Who would dare say that he was ignorant of this? For he knew that he existed in the same form in which he had ascended into heaven and would one day return from there. How, then, does he deny that he knows the Son according to the flesh? Because, as soon as he had risen from the dead, it was better to know and confess him from the eminence of his divinity than from the weakness of his flesh. For, while the mystery of the dispensation had not yet been completed, he was proclaimed according to the flesh, so that it might be believed that the Only-Begotten had become flesh. But once this sacrament had been completed, it was preferable to recognize and confess him according to his divinity rather than according to the lowliness and self-emptying of his flesh. There is therefore one Christ, one Son, and one Lord.”  

Thus Cyril.]

“And although we once knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him” (II Cor. V).

All the writings of sacred discourse harmonize beautifully with one another. Throughout every part of themselves, even where they do not agree in the appearance of their words, they nevertheless agree in the force of the realities they express. So it is here: “Although we once knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him.” This statement confirms the preceding testimony, in which he said: “From them is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever” (Rom. IX).

There he said, “from them is Christ according to the flesh”; here, “although we once knew Christ according to the flesh.” There, “who is God over all”; here, “we no longer know Christ according to the flesh.” The outward form of the words is different, but the force of the matter is one. For the very one whom he there proclaims as God over all, born according to the flesh, he here confirms that he no longer knows according to the flesh.

This is because he confesses as God forever the same one whom he knew as born in the flesh; and for that reason he says that he no longer knows him according to the flesh, since he is God blessed forever. Thus the statement there, “who is God over all,” says the same as this statement here: “We no longer know Christ according to the flesh,” because he is God blessed forever.

The preaching of apostolic doctrine therefore rises, as it were, to a higher level. Although the meaning agrees in both places, it nevertheless confirms the mystery of perfect faith with a more explicit statement, saying:

> “And although we once knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him.”

[Note: This does not mean that he ceased to be human, but that after his resurrection he retained nothing human—that is, nothing weak or mortal—and laid aside all the weakness of human mortality, as is explained below.]

That is, formerly we knew him as both man and God; now we know him as God alone.

[Col. 0053C] For when the weakness of the flesh had ceased, we no longer know anything in him except the power of divinity. Everything in him is now the power of divine majesty, since the weakness of human frailty has ceased to exist in him.

Thus, through this testimony, he has explained the entire mystery both of the flesh assumed and of the perfect divinity.

When he says, “Although we once knew Christ according to the flesh,” he speaks of the mystery of God born in the flesh. When he adds, “Yet now we no longer know him,” he explains the force of the weakness that has been laid aside.

Accordingly, the former knowledge of flesh refers to the meaning of humanity, while the subsequent not-knowing refers to the honor of divinity. For this is what he means: “We knew Christ according to the flesh as long as there remained something in him to be recognized according to the flesh; now we no longer know him in that way, since he has ceased to be such.”

[Note: This does not mean that his true and bodily flesh ceased to exist in itself, but that it became spiritual—that is, incorruptible, glorious, and free from every weakness—as the Apostle says in I Corinthians XV: “It is sown an animal body; it will rise a spiritual body.”

The resurrection of the Lord, says St. Leo the Supreme Pontiff (Sermon 1, On the Resurrection of the Lord), was not the end of the flesh but its transformation; nor was its substance destroyed through an increase of power. Its quality passed away, but its nature did not fail. The body became impassible, although it had been capable of crucifixion; it became immortal, although it had been capable of death; it became incorruptible, although it had been capable of being wounded.

And rightly it is said that the flesh of Christ, in whatever condition it may have been known, became unknown, because nothing passible and nothing weak remained in it, so that it is itself in essence, but is no longer itself in glory.

What is remarkable, however, if the Apostle confesses this concerning Christ’s body, when he says of all spiritual Christians: “Therefore, from this time onward, we know no one according to the flesh”? “From this time,” he says, the beginning of our resurrection in Christ was made, since in him who died for all the form of our entire hope went before us, and so forth.]

For the nature of the flesh has been transferred into a spiritual substance, and that which once belonged to humanity has become wholly God’s. Therefore we no longer know Christ according to the flesh, because bodily weakness has been swallowed up by divine majesty, and nothing remains in the sacred body from which the weakness of flesh could be recognized.

Accordingly, whatever had previously been of a twofold substance has become a single power. For there can be no doubt that Christ, who was crucified through our weakness, now lives wholly through divine majesty.

## CHAPTER IV. From the Epistle to the Galatians he adduces a testimony proving that the weakness of the flesh in Christ has been swallowed up by divinity.

The Apostle, proclaiming this throughout the whole body of his writings, writes well also to the Galatians:

> “Paul, an apostle, not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father” (Gal. I).

You see how well this agrees with what was said earlier and with what is now being said. There he says, “Now we no longer know Christ according to the flesh”; here he says, “Not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ.”

[Col. 0054C] It is clear how he teaches here the same thing as in the preceding passage. For when he says that he was sent not through man, he means: “We no longer know Christ according to the flesh.” Therefore:

[Note: “Through man” means through a mere mortal human being, but “through Jesus Christ” means through the true God. Cyril uses the same argument for the same purpose as Cassian, namely, to prove Christ’s divinity:

> “Does the Apostle not make known to us through these words the incarnate God, and the one Son and Lord in both respects? For what could be said more plainly than that he was sent neither from man nor through man, but through Jesus Christ? What then? Was he ignorant that the one whom he proclaimed to the whole world was a human being? Certainly not. He knew that he was human, but not human alone: he was the Word of God made human. When he therefore says that he was sent not from man but through Jesus, who could doubt that he establishes Jesus Christ as true God?”  

And St. Jerome likewise, commenting on this passage of the Apostle, says:

> “From this it is proved that the heresy of Ebion and Photinus must also be refuted on this point: our Lord Jesus Christ is God, since the Apostle, who was sent by Christ to preach the Gospel, denies that he was sent from man.”]

“I was not sent through men, but through Jesus”; because, having been sent through Christ, I was not sent through man but through God. For the name “man” no longer applies to him in whom divinity has claimed everything for itself.

Therefore, after saying that he had been sent neither from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ, he rightly added, “and God the Father,” thereby indicating that he had been sent by God the Father and by God the Son.

Although, because of the mystery of sacred and ineffable generation, there are two persons—the one generating and the one begotten—there is nevertheless one power of the God who sends.

Thus, by saying that he had been sent by God the Father and by God the Son, he shows a dual number in the persons, but teaches one authority in the sending.

## CHAPTER V. Just as it is blasphemous to take divinity away from Christ, so it is also blasphemous to deny that he is truly human.

[Col. 0055B]

“But through Christ,” he says, “Jesus, and God the Father, who raised him from the dead.”

A distinguished and admirable teacher, knowing that the Lord Jesus Christ must be proclaimed as true God and also as true man, always proclaims his divine majesty in such a way that he does not abandon the confession of the Incarnation at all. He excludes both the phantom of Marcion through the reality of the Incarnation and—

[Note: The heresiarchs Cerdon and Marcion, and after them Manichaeus, taught that Christ had assumed not a true body or true flesh but a phantom body, because they imagined that flesh was evil by nature and derived from an evil principle. Tertullian expressly refutes this error in his book On the Flesh of Christ; Irenaeus, in Book I, chapter 29; and Augustine argues against the Manichaeans in almost innumerable passages.]

—and the poverty of Ebion through perfect divinity.

[Note: This alludes to the name Ebion, which in Hebrew signifies “poor” or “needy.” Thus Blessed Ignatius, bishop and martyr, says in his Letter to the Philadelphians:

> “If anyone says that there is one God and confesses Jesus Christ, but thinks that he is merely a naked human being, such a person is a serpent, proclaiming deceit and error to the destruction of human beings; he is needy in understanding, and is called Ebion.”

And St. Jerome, commenting on Isaiah I, says:

> “Ebion plows with an ox and an ass,” deserving this name because of the humility of his understanding and the poverty of his name; for he accepts the Gospel in such a way that he does not abandon the ceremonies of Jewish superstitions, which preceded in shadow and image.

And again, on Isaiah LXVI:

> “The Jews, and the Ebionites, heirs of Jewish error, received their name from the poverty of their understanding.”

The Author therefore calls Ebion’s “poverty” his foolish opinion of Christ as a mere human being—an opinion arising from poverty of understanding and lack of judgment, but even more from a deficiency of sound doctrine, of which he spoke above.]

This was so that, through neither of the two perverse forms of blasphemy, the Lord Jesus Christ might be believed either to be wholly man without God or God without man.

The Apostle therefore rightly proclaims that he was sent both by God the Father and by God the Son, and immediately adds the confession of the Lord’s Incarnation, saying:

> “Who raised him from the dead.”

By this he teaches that the true body of the incarnate God was raised from the dead, in accordance with the statement:

> “Although we once knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him.”

He says that he knows him according to the flesh in that he was raised from the dead. But he says that he no longer knows him according to the flesh because, once the frailty of the flesh had ceased, he knows him only in the power of God.

He is therefore a faithful and wholly suitable witness to the divinity of the Lord that must be proclaimed. At the beginning of his calling, he was corrected from heaven; and he approved the majesty of our Lord Jesus Christ, raised from the dead, not merely by the faith of his mind but—

[Note: That Paul also saw with bodily eyes the majesty—that is, the glorious flesh of Christ, or Christ present in the flesh and near to him—may be gathered from Acts IX.

First, this is evident from the light that surrounded him and from the blindness he suffered because of its excessive brilliance. Second, it is evident from the words of Ananias: “Brother Saul, the Lord Jesus, who appeared to you on the road.” If he appeared to Saul, he certainly presented himself as visible in his own flesh and form.

This is stated still more plainly in the Greek, where we read:

> ὁ ὀφθείς σοι  
> “The one who was seen by you.”

The same passage says that Barnabas took Paul and led him to the apostles, “and told them how he had seen the Lord.”

Third, Paul himself says in I Corinthians IX: “Am I not an apostle? Have I not seen Jesus Christ our Lord?”

Finally, the same Apostle testifies in I Corinthians XV that Christ appeared after his resurrection to many people—that is, he was seen in visible and perceptible flesh, at one time by these disciples and at another time by others:

> “Last of all,” he says, “as to one untimely born, he appeared also to me.”

This can be understood only of bodily sight and appearance. For here he enumerates the witnesses of the resurrection who had seen the Lord with bodily eyes, and he places himself among them. Whether Paul had other visions and appearances of Christ—imaginary or intellectual—is not for this place to examine.]

—he also confirmed it with his bodily eyes.

## CHAPTER VI. From Christ’s appearance to the Apostle while he was persecuting the Church, he demonstrates that both natures were in Christ.

Therefore, while he was speaking before King Agrippa and the other judges of the world, he also said:

[Note: Three Agrippas are recorded as having reigned among the Jews. The first was the son of Aristobulus and grandson of Herod the Great of Ascalon—the first foreigner to hold the sceptre of the Jewish kingdom. Tiberius Caesar cast him into prison; Gaius Caligula released him and made him king of the Jews. See Josephus, *Antiquities*, Book XVIII, chapters 14 and 15, and Eusebius, Book II, chapter 4.

The second was Herod Agrippa, son of the first Herod, king of the Jews. He received the Jewish kingdom from the emperor Claudius; he killed the apostle James, imprisoned Peter, and finally, because he accepted without rejecting the divine honor bestowed on him by the people, was struck by an angel, consumed by worms, and died. See Acts XII; Josephus, *Jewish Antiquities*, Book XIX, chapter 7; and Eusebius, Book II, chapter 9.

The third, finally, was his son, called Agrippa the Younger, of whom this passage speaks. Before him and Festus, governor of Judaea, with Bernice, Agrippa’s sister, also present, Paul—accused by the Jews—made his speech and pleaded his cause (Acts XXIV and XXV). He held the kingdom of Judaea until the destruction of Jerusalem, always a friend of the Romans, says Bede in his commentary on this passage.]



> “As I was going to Damascus with authority and permission from the chief priests, at midday on the road I saw, O king, a light from heaven, brighter than the sun, shining around me and all those who were traveling with me. When we had all fallen to the ground, I heard a voice saying to me in the Hebrew language: ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goad.’ But I said: ‘Who are you, Lord?’ And the Lord said to me: ‘I am Jesus the Nazarene, whom you are persecuting’” (Acts XXVI).

You see that the Apostle rightly said that he no longer knew according to the flesh the one whom he had seen in such a great splendor of majesty.

For when he had seen that radiance of divine light, which he could not endure, in the very moment of his prostration, this voice followed:

> “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?”

When he asked who he was, the Lord answered with such a clear indication of his person:

> “I am Jesus the Nazarene, whom you are persecuting.”

You, you, I say, heretic, I now question; you I address: do you believe the Apostle concerning himself, or do you not? Or, if you attach little weight to that, do you believe the Lord concerning himself, or do you not? If you believe, the question is finished. You must believe what we believe.

For we, in accordance with the Apostle, say:

> “Although we once knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him.”

We do not heap insults upon Christ; we do not separate the flesh from God; and we believe that everything Christ is exists in God.

If, then, you believe what we believe, you must confess the same mysteries of faith. But if you disagree with us—if you believe neither the Churches, nor the Apostle, nor finally God himself speaking about himself—show us in what the Apostle saw what is flesh and what is God.

I can distinguish nothing here. I see an ineffable illumination; I see an incomprehensible brightness; I see a splendor intolerable to human frailty; and, above what mortal eyes can bear, I see an immeasurable majesty shining with the light of God.

What separation is there here? What distinction? In the voice we hear Jesus; in the majesty we behold God. What else does this mean but that we should believe God and Jesus to exist in one and the same substance?

Yet I wish to speak with you further about this same matter. Tell me, I ask: if, while you were now persecuting the Catholic faith, the same thing appeared to you that appeared then to the Apostle in his ignorance—if that radiance surrounded you unexpectedly and while you were secure, and the splendor of immense light struck and terrified you, throwing you down in the darkness of your eyes and errors—what immeasurable and unspeakable anguish would the terror of your mind increase for you?

Tell me, I beseech you: when fear of imminent death pressed upon you, and terror of the majesty threatening from above weighed upon you, and, amid such confusion of mind, you heard a name worthy of your perfidy:

> “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?”

and, when you asked who he was, a voice from heaven answered:

> “I am Jesus the Nazarene, whom you are persecuting,”

what would you say?

“‘I do not know; I do not yet fully believe. I want to deliberate further with myself about whom I should think you to be, you who speak from heaven, who overwhelm me with the radiance of your divinity, whose voice I hear and whose majesty I cannot endure. I must consider this matter: whether I ought to believe you or not; whether you are Christ or God; whether, if you are God alone, you are in Christ, or, if you are Christ alone, you are in God. I want this distinction to be carefully observed and diligently considered: what you ought to be believed to be, and what you ought to be judged to be.

For I do not wish to neglect any part of my duty, so that, while I despise you as a human being, I may nevertheless render you some divine honor.’”

If, therefore, as the Apostle Paul then lay prostrate, you were lying on the ground, overcome by the splendor of divine light and breathing out your last breath, perhaps you would say such things and mutter them in this idle chatter of loquaciousness.

But what are we to do? What else was then shown to the Apostle? When he had fallen trembling and half-dead, he did not think that anything could be concealed any longer; he did not think that further deliberation was necessary. It was enough for him that, through ineffable experiences, he was warned and recognized as God the one whom, in his ignorance, he had believed to be a man.

He did not conceal or delay the matter. He did not suspend a badly conceived error through further unfaithful deliberation. Rather, having heard from heaven the name of Jesus his Lord, he answered with a voice submissive as a servant, trembling as one scourged, and devoted as one converted:

> “What shall I do, Lord?”

Thus, through faith that was ready and wholly devoted, he immediately merited this: that he should never be deprived of the one whom he had faithfully believed; and that the one to whom he had passed over in heart should himself pass into his heart, as the Apostle himself says concerning him:

> “Do you seek proof of the Christ who speaks in me?” (II Cor. XIII).

[Note: That is, “Do you wish to test how great is the judicial authority conferred upon me by Christ, who speaks in me and through me, as through his minister and instrument? Just as a king is said to speak and decree in his council and senate, and through the senate, whatever the senate says and decrees by the king’s authority.”

St. Ambrose reads: “How do you seek proof of him who speaks in me, Christ?” and adds: “They seek proof of Christ speaking in the Apostle because they do not obey his commands; they wish to test whether he dares to exercise punishment, so that they may understand that he possesses authoritative power and may thereafter fear him.”]

## CHAPTER VII. In further testimonies of the Apostle he declares that Christ is God.

At this point, heretic, I want you to explain to me whether this one whom the Apostle says speaks within him is man or God.

If he is man, how could the body of another speak in his heart? If he is God, then Christ is no longer man but God; for since Christ has spoken in the Apostle, he could not speak in him except as God. Therefore Christ God has spoken in him.

[Note: You may object: “How could he have spoken in him only as God, since angels too have spoken in prophets, as in Zechariah II: ‘The angel who spoke in me,’ and demons very often speak in the possessed?”

I answer that the Author argues from assumptions. For he assumes what must also be assumed: that the Christ who spoke in the Apostle was not an angel, still less a devil—something that did not occur to Nestorius.

Given this assumption, Christ, who spoke in the Apostle, had to be either God or a mere human being, as Nestorius wished. But if he had been merely human, he could not have spoken in the Apostle, since he would have had to penetrate the Apostle’s body with his own body; and this cannot occur according to nature or by human power.

Christ, therefore, was God, speaking in Paul, and not a mere human being.]

You see, then, that nothing can now be said here, nor can any separation or division be made between Christ and God, because God is wholly in Christ and Christ wholly in God.

No separation can be admitted here, no division or tearing apart. There is only one simple, one pious, one sound confession: to adore, love, and worship Christ God.

If you still wish to know more fully and abundantly that there is no distance between God and Christ, and that the God who is to be understood is entirely the same as Christ, listen to the Apostle speaking to the Corinthians:

> “For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive what is due for what he has done in the body, whether good or evil” (II Cor. V).

But elsewhere, writing to the Church at Rome, he says:

> “We shall all stand before the judgment seat of God” (Rom. XIV).

For it is written:

> “As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess to God” (Isaiah XLIX).

You see, then, that the judgment seat of God is to be the very same as Christ’s.

Understand, therefore, without hesitation that Christ is God; and wherever you see that Christ’s and God’s substance are entirely inseparable, recognize also that their person is inseparable.

Unless, perhaps, because the Apostle says in one epistle that we shall appear before the judgment seat of Christ and in another that we shall appear before the judgment seat of God, you should construct two judgment seats and maintain that some will be judged by Christ and others by God.

But such notions are frivolous and insane—more insane than those who are themselves raving.

Recognize, then, the Lord of all; recognize the God of the universe; recognize in the tribunal of Christ the tribunal of God.

Love life; love your salvation; love the one by whom you were created; fear the one by whom you will be judged.

Whether you wish it or not, you will be brought before the judgment seat of Christ. Once the impiety of blasphemy and the song of unfaithful words have been set aside, if you think that God’s judgment seat is something other than Christ’s, you will come before Christ’s judgment seat and will discover, by an inexplicable proof, that Christ’s judgment seat is itself God’s judgment seat, and that the whole majesty of the Son of God and the power of God the Father are present in God’s Son, Christ.

For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father (John V).

> “Whoever denies the Father also denies the Son; everyone who denies the Son does not have the Father. Whoever confesses the Son has the Father” (I John II).

[Note: See this statement explained below.]

Learn, therefore, that the honor of the Father and the Son is inseparable, and their dignity inseparable; neither can the Son be honored without the Father, nor the Father without the Son.

No one can honor God and the Son of God except in Christ, the only-begotten Son of God; for no one can possess the Spirit by which God is honored except in the Spirit of Christ, as the Apostle says:

> “You, however, are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you. But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him” (Rom. VIII).

And again:

> “Who will bring an accusation against God’s elect? God, who justifies. Who is the one who condemns? Christ Jesus, who died—indeed, who was raised” (ibid.).

You see, then, whether you wish it or not, that there is absolutely no distinction either between the Spirit of God and the Spirit of Christ or between the judgment of God and the judgment of Christ.

Choose, therefore, which you prefer; one of the two must necessarily follow: either you understand by faith that Christ is God, or you will come to know, through condemnation, that God is in Christ.

## CHAPTER VIII. In confessing Christ’s divinity, the confession of the cross must not be suppressed in silence.

But let us nevertheless examine the remaining passages that follow. Writing to the Church of the Corinthians, the same Paul whom we discussed above, the teacher of all the Churches, spoke as follows: “The Jews demand signs, and the Greeks seek wisdom; but we preach Christ crucified,” [Note: Hence he is called by Isaiah and by the chief of the Apostles “a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense” (Isaiah 8; 1 Peter 2). For the Jews, not believing in him and scandalized by his Passion and disgrace, made him for themselves, through their own fault and blindness, a stone of stumbling [an occasion and object of their condemnation and destruction] and a rock of offense. Hence that righteous Simeon also said to Mary his mother: “Behold, this child is appointed for the fall and resurrection of many in Israel, and for a sign that will be opposed” (Luke 2). And Christ himself says in Matthew 11: “Blessed is the one who is not scandalized by me.”] “a stumbling block to the Jews,” [Note: For, as Blessed Gregory says (Homily 6 on the Gospels), it seemed foolish to human beings that the Author of life should die for human beings. Thus humanity took offense at him precisely where it ought to have become more deeply indebted to him. For God is to be honored by human beings with greater reverence the more unworthy things he undertook for their sake.] “and foolishness to the Gentiles, but to those who are being saved, both Jews and Greeks,” [Note: These words can be understood in two ways, namely of Christ as God and of the same Christ as man—that is, either according to his divinity or according to his humanity. If they are understood according to his divinity, Christ is called “the power of God” and “the wisdom of God” by a certain appropriation, as Saint Thomas says. He is called power insofar as through him the Father accomplishes all things. “All things were made through him” (John 1). He is called wisdom insofar as the Word himself, who is the Son, is nothing other than Wisdom begotten from the Father. “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High, the firstborn before every creature” (Ecclesiasticus 24).

This must not, however, be understood to mean that God the Father is strong and wise by means of a power or wisdom begotten by him, for, as Augustine proves in Book 6 of On the Trinity (chapter 2), it would follow that the Father derived his being from the Son, since for God “to be” is the same as “to be strong and wise.” Thus Saint Thomas in his commentary. And in the First Part, question 39, article 7, he says: “The Father is not wise by the Wisdom whom he begot, as though the Son alone were Wisdom, and thus the Father and the Son together could be called wisdom, but the Father could not be called wisdom without the Son. Rather, the Son is called the Wisdom of the Father because he is Wisdom from the Father, who is Wisdom. Each, therefore, is wisdom in himself, and together they are one wisdom. Hence the Father is not wise by the Wisdom whom he begot, but by the wisdom that is his essence.” Thus far Saint Thomas.

The Apostle, however, seems here to have had Christ’s humanity specifically in view when he says: “We preach Jesus crucified, a stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the Gentiles,” and yet calls this same Christ “the power of God and the wisdom of God” to Jews and Greeks—that is, to those who are converted from the Jews and the Gentiles to faith in Christ, who recognize in Christ’s flesh, as Saint Thomas himself says, “the power of God, by which demons are overcome, sins are forgiven, and human beings are saved.” He therefore calls Christ “the power of God and the wisdom of God” even according to his humanity, because in him and through him, crucified upon the cross, the power and wisdom of God were most clearly manifested. For, he says, “what is foolishness of God is wiser than human beings, and what is weakness of God is stronger than human beings.” That is, what people regard as ridiculous and weak in God and man, Christ crucified, is wiser and stronger than every human wisdom and power.] “Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1).

O most powerful teacher of the faith! Even here, while teaching the Churches, he considered it insufficient to say that Christ is God unless he added “crucified”—namely, so that, in setting forth the most penetrating and powerful doctrine of faith, he might proclaim the very one who was crucified as the wisdom of God. He therefore did not employ any subtlety or circumlocution of words, nor, in preaching the Lord’s Gospel, did he blush to name Christ’s cross.

And although this was a stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the Gentiles, [Note: That the Jews thought it scandalous to hear God spoken of as born, corporeal, suffering, dead, and so forth, while the Gentiles regarded it as foolishness, arose solely from the fact that they neither recognized nor wished to recognize the mystery of the Incarnation. For whoever acknowledges Christ as both God and man cannot doubt that he is corporeal as man and incorporeal as God.

Since the Jews and Gentiles did not understand this, and the heretics called Nestorians expressly denied it, it is not surprising that they could not accept God as corporeal, suffering, and dead—something that Scripture openly testifies and that Catholics profess not only in the Creed but also in their daily speech. For this is required by that communion of idioms, so frequently celebrated by theologians, which necessarily follows from the unity of person in Christ. By it, the properties of both natures—called ἰδιώματα in Greek—are simply and truly predicated of one another and of Christ’s one and the same hypostasis or person.

Whoever understands this believes no less that God is corporeal, crucified, and dead than that God is man, the Word made flesh, and the Son of God made of a woman, and so forth (see Damascene, Book 3 of The Orthodox Faith, chapter 4). For if he is man, he is certainly corporeal and passible; if he is God, he is certainly incorporeal and impassible. Therefore he is both corporeal and incorporeal, passible and impassible—something that would not be true if there were several persons in Christ. For nature is so constituted that what belongs properly to one nature is never attributed to another unless both have a common person or common subject; all those properties that are predicated of one and the same individual thing must converge upon one subject.

Thus we do not say, among accidents, that “sweet is white” unless the two natures of sweetness and whiteness have the same subject and suppositum, as we see in milk. Yet no other suppositum and no other person can be posited in Christ except the eternal person of the Son of God. For if you say that there is a human person in him, it follows—something utterly absurd—that the person of the Son of God is not in Christ, either extinguished in the very Incarnation of the Word or completely alien to it.

Therefore, just as communion of idioms is proved in Christ a priori, as the dialecticians say, or as proceeding from its cause, from the unity of his one hypostasis, so conversely the unity of person is demonstrated a posteriori, as proceeding from its effect, through the communion of idioms. Upon this, accordingly, are founded all the arguments used by Cassian and the other Fathers to prove Christ’s divinity. It was therefore appropriate to treat the matter at greater length here, since the whole hinge of the discussion turns upon it.

From these considerations it is sufficiently clear that this communion of idioms consists in two things. Either divine properties are attributed to the man and Son of man, as when it is said: “That man Jesus is the creator of heaven and earth, King of kings and Lord of lords, eternal, almighty,” and so forth; or human properties are attributed to God and the Son of God, as when we say that the Son of God was born of a Virgin, crucified, dead, and so forth.

In both classes, however, two points must be observed. First, one must examine in what respect something is said, lest absurdity, impossibility, or contradiction be imagined in the language. Human properties are said of God, but according to his human nature; divine properties also are attributed to the man, but by reason of the divine nature. Therefore no opposition or contradiction need be feared here, as though contrary predicates were being asserted of the same thing, because they are not understood of the same thing in the same respect.

Second, attention must be paid to whether the subject to which the attribution is made is expressed abstractly or concretely. Thus, just as we truly say that “that man is almighty,” so it is false to say that “humanity is almighty.” Likewise, although you may truly say that God suffered, was crucified, and died, you may not truly say that divinity suffered, was crucified, and died. For suffering, being crucified, and dying pertain to the person, which is expressed concretely, not to the nature, which is expressed abstractly and as a form.

Third, it must be noted that there are three kinds of idioms: some proper to the divine nature, some to the human nature, and others to the person composed of both natures. To create, to be almighty, to be omniscient, and other things of this kind are predicated by reason of the divine nature alone. To suffer, hunger, thirst, and similar things are predicated by reason of the human nature alone. But to make satisfaction, redeem, and be mediator are attributed to Christ because of both natures. For these involve both an action and a passion. To make satisfaction includes both death and the efficacy of death: the former falls within the human nature, while the latter depends upon the divine nature.

Thus these attributes, by reason of both natures, are conferred upon one hypostasis; the others, however, by reason of one nature alone. The same distinction applies to what is said of a human being: some things are said by reason of the soul alone, such as that he understands and knows; some by reason of the body alone, such as that he is fat or thin; and some by reason of both, such as that he speaks and writes. These points concerning the communion of idioms in Christ the Lord may suffice, briefly stated for the explanation of this passage and the needs of the argument.]

to hear that God was born, to hear that God was corporeal, to hear that God suffered, to hear that God was crucified—nevertheless, because of the impiety of the Jewish scandal he did not weaken the power of his piety, nor, because of the unbelief arising from another’s foolishness, diminish the strength of his faith. Rather, openly, steadfastly, and courageously he proclaimed as the power and wisdom of God the one whom the flesh had brought forth, human beings had killed, the lance had pierced, and the cross had stretched out—as a stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the Gentiles. Yet what was a stumbling block and foolishness to some was the power and wisdom of God to others. For according to the diversity of persons there was a diversity of perceptions; and what foolish disbelief, deprived of sound understanding and incapable of the true good, had denied, wise faith recognized within the innermost recesses of the soul as sacred and saving.

## CHAPTER IX. That the apostolic preaching was rejected by Jews and Gentiles because it confessed Christ crucified to be God

Tell me, then, heretic—an enemy of all, but especially your own enemy—for the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ is both a stumbling block with the Jews and foolishness with the Gentiles: why was the preaching of the Apostle Paul foolishness to the pagans or a stumbling block to the Jews? Could it have offended people if he too had taught, as you assert, that Christ was merely an isolated human being? To whom could his birth, his suffering, his cross, or his death have seemed incredible or grievous? Or what new or unheard-of element would Paul’s preaching have contained if he had said that Christ was merely a man who suffered what the human condition endures daily in ordinary people?

But this was precisely what pagan foolishness could not accept, what Jewish unbelief rejected: the Apostle said that Christ—whom they, like you, regarded as merely an isolated human being—was God. This was what the minds of the impious rejected, what the ears of the faithless could not bear: to preach in the man Jesus Christ the birth of God, to assert the suffering of God, and to announce the cross of God. This was grievous; this was incredible, because it was beyond human hearing that such a thing should have happened to the divine nature.

You are therefore safe in such an assertion and teaching: your preaching will never be foolishness to the Gentiles or a stumbling block to the Jews. You will never be crucified with Peter by Jews and Gentiles, nor be stoned with James, nor beheaded with Paul. [Note: Someone might suspect that “James” has been put here in place of Stephen, the first martyr, who is known to have been stoned, whereas it is not equally clear that this happened to the Apostle James. But this suspicion is opposed, indeed entirely excluded, by the fact that it would be most incongruous for the Author to place Stephen between the two Apostles and princes of the Apostles, Peter and Paul, with the order of dignity confused.

Accordingly, no one other than the Apostle James is to be understood here. He was called the brother of the Lord, the Just, and also the Younger, and was appointed the first bishop of Jerusalem by Blessed Peter. The Apostle Paul writes of him to the Galatians (chapter 1): “I saw no other apostle except James, the brother of the Lord.” His is also the one epistle counted among the seven canonical epistles, according to Saint Jerome as well (Book on Illustrious Men, under James).

There is, however, some difficulty in explaining how he is here implied or assumed to have been stoned, since the Roman Martyrology says that he died after being thrown from the pinnacle of the Temple, breaking his legs, and being struck on the head with a fuller’s club. Eusebius likewise reports this from Clement of Alexandria in Book 2 of his Ecclesiastical History, chapter 22.

Eusebius himself removed this difficulty by showing that the history of his martyrdom was more fully and accurately described by Hegesippus, who lived close to the age of the Apostles, and that what Clement omitted was supplied and expressed by Hegesippus. For Hegesippus relates that James was first thrown from the pinnacle of the Temple. “And because,” he says, “when cast headlong he did not immediately die, but, raising his face upward and bending his knees, said: ‘I beg you, Lord God the Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing,’ they began to throw stones at him. As they continued to crush him with their stones, one of the priests, from the sons of Rechab—who are commended in the testimony of Jeremiah—cried out more loudly: ‘What are you doing? The Just One is praying to God for you.’ Nevertheless, one of them, who was a fuller, seized the club with which they used to press clothes and struck it against the head of the Just One. Thus, afflicted and tormented by the blessed and happy suffering of martyrdom, he lost his life.” Thus Hegesippus.

Saint Jerome also confirms the same account by the testimony of Josephus, which can be found in Josephus himself. See also Baronius’s notes on the Martyrology under May 1.]

For your preaching does not contain their offense. You assert that a solitary man was born and that a solitary man suffered. You cannot fear that their persecution will harm you, since by your preaching you confirm them.

## CHAPTER X. How the Apostle asserts Christ to be the power of God and the wisdom of God

[Col. 0063C]

But let us nevertheless consider something further concerning this very matter. According to the Apostle, then, Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God. What do you have to answer? Where can you turn? You can go nowhere and advance no further from here. Christ is the wisdom of God and the power of God. [Col. 0064A] He whom the Jews persecuted, whom the Gentiles mocked, whom you yourself, together with them, persecute—he, I say, who is foolishness to the pagans, a stumbling block to the Jews, and both to you—he, I say, is the power of God and the wisdom of God.

What can you do? Perhaps you will close your ears so as not to hear. The Jews did the same when the Apostle preached. Whatever you do, Christ is in heaven and in God, and with him and in him in the heights, just as he was in the depths; you can no longer persecute him there together with the Jews. Yet you do one thing that you can do: you persecute him in the faith, you persecute him in the Church, you persecute him with the weapon of an impious opinion, you persecute him with the sword of a perverse doctrine.

Perhaps you do something worse than some of the Jews of old: you now persecute Christ after even those who had persecuted him came to believe. But perhaps you think the crime less serious because you can no longer lay hands upon him. It is no less—no less grievous to him—is that persecution in which the impious persecute him in his own people.

The name of the Lord’s cross offends you; this has always offended the Jews as well. You shudder to hear that God suffered; pagan error also mocked this. I ask, then, in what respect you differ from them, since in this perversion you agree with them?

But I not only do not diminish this preaching of the sacred cross, this preaching of the Lord’s Passion; insofar as my desire and substance permit, I increase it. For I shall proclaim this one who was crucified not merely as the power and wisdom of God, than which nothing is greater, but also as the Lord of the whole divinity and majesty.

All the more so because this discourse of mine is the doctrine of God, as the Apostle says: [Note: The Author interprets “wisdom” either as Christ himself, true God and man, or as the same Christ together with the doctrine of his Incarnation, which the Apostle calls “the wisdom of God hidden in a mystery,” because it cannot be known by natural reason.] “We speak wisdom among the perfect; yet not the wisdom of this age, nor of the rulers of this age, who are being destroyed; but we speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, the wisdom hidden, which God predestined before the ages for our glory,” [Note: Chrysostom interprets “the rulers of this age” as Herod, Pilate, and the Jews. Although they had some knowledge of Christ, they never knew that he was God, for if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Corinthians 2). Thus Peter says in Acts: “I know that you did it through ignorance, as did your rulers” (Acts 3).

Ambrose interprets the passage as referring to demons, who, if they had truly known God and the Redeemer, would never have brought about his death. Saint Thomas, in his Commentary, teaches that it can be understood of three kinds of rulers: “Secular rulers did not know this wisdom because it exceeds the reason of human government. Philosophers did not know it because it exceeds human reason. Hence it is said in Baruch 3: ‘The seekers after prudence and knowledge did not know the way of wisdom.’ Demons also do not know it because it exceeds all created wisdom.”] “which none of the rulers of this age has known. For if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2).

But, as it is written: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, what God has prepared for those who love him” (the same passage and Isaiah 64).

Do you see how much the Apostle’s discourse has said in such few words? He says that he speaks wisdom, but wisdom that only the perfect know and the wise of this age do not know. He says that this is the wisdom of God, covered by a divine mystery and predestined before all ages for the glory of the saints; and therefore that it is known only to those who have the wisdom of God, while it is entirely unknown to the rulers of this age.

He then added the reason by which he proved both statements, saying: “For if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.” But it is written: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, what God has prepared for those who love him.”

Do you see, then, that the wisdom of God, hidden in a mystery and predestined before the ages, was unknown to those who crucified the Lord of glory, but known to those who received him? He rightly says that the wisdom of God was hidden in a mystery, because no human eye could ever see, no ear hear, and no heart conceive that the Lord of glory would be born of a Virgin, come in the flesh, and be subjected to every suffering and humiliation.

But just as no one, while these gifts of God were hidden in a mystery, could ever know them by himself, so blessed is the one who has recognized them once they have been revealed. Hence all who did not recognize it must be counted among the rulers of this age, while those who did recognize it belong among God’s wise.

Therefore the one who denies that God was born in the flesh does not recognize God; and you too do not recognize him, because you deny it. But whatever you do, however impiously you deny it, we believe the Apostle more. And why do I say “the Apostle”? We believe God more. For through the Apostle we believe the one whom we are certain spoke through the Apostle.

The divine word says that the Lord of glory was crucified by the rulers of this age; you deny it, and those who crucified him denied that they were crucifying God. [Col. 0066A] Those who confess together with the confessing Apostle therefore have a share with him; you must have your portion with the persecutors.

What, then, can now be said? The Apostle says that the Lord of glory was crucified. Change this, if you can; separate Jesus from God, if you are able. You certainly cannot deny that Christ was crucified by the Jews. But the one who was crucified is the Lord of glory. Therefore you must either deny that Christ was fastened to the cross or confess that God was fastened to the cross.

## CHAPTER XI. He corroborates the same doctrine with Gospel testimonies

But perhaps you are offended because I have spoken for so long chiefly on the testimony of the one Apostle Paul. He whom God chose is sufficiently authoritative for me; nor am I ashamed to have as a witness of my faith the one whom God willed to be the teacher of the whole world.

Nevertheless, to accommodate your wishes, since perhaps you do not think that I have other witnesses whose testimony I can use, hear Martha proclaiming in the Gospel the perfect mystery of human salvation and eternal blessedness. What does she say? “Yes, Lord,” [Note: In these words Martha briefly confessed everything that could be confessed about Christ (see Maldonado on this passage), namely, his divinity and humanity. For Peter confessed nothing more in Matthew 16, when Christ called him blessed and promised to build his Church upon him. Indeed, Martha added this to Peter’s confession: “who have come into this world,” as Rupert observes. By these words she noted the work and mystery of our redemption, which was the purpose and goal of the Lord’s coming and Incarnation. For the Son of man came for this purpose, “to seek and to save what was lost” (Luke 19).] “I have believed that you are the Christ, the Son of the living God, who has come into this world” (John 11).

Learn true faith from a woman; learn the confession of eternal hope. Yet you have great consolation: do not be ashamed to acknowledge the mystery of salvation from one from whom God did not refuse to receive testimony.

## CHAPTER XII. From the most glorious confession of Blessed Peter he proves that Christ is God

[Col. 0066C]

But if the authority of a more eminent person perhaps pleases you—although neither the person nor the sex of anyone ought to displease one whose confession gives authority to the mystery, since however humble someone’s condition or station may be, the power of faith is not diminished—let us nevertheless question not some inexperienced child whose instruction is unformed, nor a woman whose faith might perhaps seem to be only beginning, but that supreme man, the disciple among disciples and the teacher among teachers, [Note: Eusebius, Book 2 of his Ecclesiastical History, chapter 14, speaking of Peter: “By the word of his saving preaching, he was the first in the city of Rome to open the gate of the heavenly kingdom with the keys of his Gospel.”

Leo, Sermon 1 on the Nativity of the Apostles: “When the Apostles, having divided the regions of the earth among themselves, undertook to imbue the world with the Gospel, the most blessed Peter, prince of the apostolic order, was sent to the citadel of the Roman empire, so that the law of truth, which was revealed for the salvation of all nations, might spread more effectively from the very head throughout the body of the world.”

And Prosper, in his book On the Ungrateful:

> The seat of Peter, Rome, which was made  
> The head of the world in pastoral honor,  
> Holds by religion whatever it does not possess by arms.”] who, governing the Roman Church, [Note: Saint Leo, Sermon 3 on the Anniversary: “From the whole world one Peter is chosen, and he is set over the calling of all nations, over all the Apostles, and over all the Fathers of the Church. Thus, although there are many priests and many shepherds among the people of God, Peter alone properly governs them all, just as Christ principally governs them all.

The divine condescension granted this man a great and wondrous partnership in its power. And if it wished the other leaders to have anything in common with him, it never gave anything through anyone else except through him whatever it did not deny to the others.

Finally, the Lord asks all the Apostles what people think about him, and the speech of the respondents remains common as long as the uncertainty of human understanding is being clarified. But when he demands what the disciples themselves understand, the first in the confession of the Lord is the one who is first in apostolic dignity.”] possessed the primacy of the priesthood just as he possessed the primacy of faith.

Tell us, then—tell us, we beg you—Peter, prince of the Apostles; tell us how the Church ought to believe God. For it is right that you, taught by the Lord, should teach us and open for us the door whose key you received. Shut out all who dig beneath the heavenly house, and repel those who attempt to enter through adulterous breaches and unlawful passages, because it is certain that no one will be able to enter the gate of the kingdom unless a key placed by you in the Churches has opened it for him. [Note: This passage is obscure and, unless I am mistaken, corrupt. I think that “to you” should be corrected and restored in place of “by you”; “in the Church” in place of “in the Churches”; and “entrusted” in place of “placed.” For who does not know that the keys of the kingdom of heaven were entrusted to Peter not by Peter but by Christ, and were entrusted, not placed? Unless perhaps it is explained in this way: the key—that is, the power of binding and loosing, interpreting Scripture, and defining controversies of faith—was placed and left in the Church by Peter as Christ’s first vicar, or through Peter.]

Tell us, then, how we ought to believe and confess Jesus Christ as the common Lord. You will certainly reply without hesitation: “Why do you ask me how the Lord should be confessed, when you have the manner in which I myself confessed him? Read the Gospel, and you will not need to inquire about my person, since you have my confession. Indeed, there you have my person where you have my confession, because since my person has no authority without my confession, the confession itself is the authority of my person.”

Tell us, then, Evangelist; tell us the confession. Tell us the faith of the supreme Apostle: did he confess Jesus to be merely a man or God? Did he say that there was merely flesh in him, or did he proclaim him to be the Son of God?

When the Lord Jesus Christ asked whom the disciples believed and confessed him to be, Peter, the first of the Apostles, answered on behalf of all; his was the response of one, but it contained the faith of all. It was fitting that he should answer first, so that the order of the response might correspond to the order of honor; and that he should lead the confession, [Note: The Author seems to imply that Peter was older than the other Apostles, or at least preceded them in age, as Bede also holds in his commentary on John 1. There were also some who said that the primacy of the Church was conferred upon Peter because of his age. Baronius refutes them (Volume 1 of the Annals, under the year 31): “From this it is evident how shamefully those err who think that primacy was conferred upon Peter because he was older than the others. For as far as this matter is concerned, even if no one else, certainly Andrew surpassed Peter in age, in priority of calling, and in the choice of a more perfect life—namely, celibacy. But if it is sometimes permitted to the human mind to investigate the reason of the divine counsel, the cause we have mentioned seems to have preceded in Peter, so that he was established as prince of all the Apostles: he excelled the others in his profession of faith.” Thus Baronius.

And in his notes on the Martyrology under November 30, he reports these words of John Chrysostom in his sermon on Saint Andrew: “Andrew entered life after Peter, but led Peter to the Gospel before him,” and so forth. “Some,” he says, “misunderstanding these words, wrongly said that Peter was older than Andrew. But Saint Epiphanius testifies that Andrew was older than Peter.”

Thus far Baronius. As for the Author’s words, however, if we interpret him suitably, insofar as possible, they do not seem to be taken so strictly as meaning that Peter preceded all the other Apostles in age, but rather that he preceded most, or nearly all, of them.] being the one who preceded the others in age.

What, then, does he say? [Note: First, it should be noted that this confession of Peter was made to Peter alone through a special revelation from God, and that it was simultaneously approved by the three divine persons, as the Author observes in the following chapter. This revelation is rightly numbered among Peter’s other prerogatives; concerning it, see Bellarmine, Book 1 On the Roman Pontiff, chapter 19.

Second, it should be noted that Christ asked whom people said the Son of man was—that is, what they thought about him and who they believed him to be. He used to call himself “the Son of man” out of humility and to speak of himself in the third person. Peter, however, answered in the second person: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” It is as though he said: “Although you are the son of man and call yourself the Son of man, you are nevertheless also the Son of God. The son of man and the Son of God in you are not two different sons, but one and the same Son of man and Son of God.”

This is especially effective against Nestorius, who separated the son of man in Christ from the Son of God—that is, who posited two persons in him.

Third, a beautiful antithesis is to be observed here. Christ asks: “Whom do people say the Son of man is?” Peter answers: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” As much as Christ humbles himself, Peter exalts him: “For everyone who humbles himself will be exalted.”

Finally, it should be noted that Christ is truly and properly called the Son of God here—that is, not by adoption or grace but by nature. The most certain proof of this is that when Peter calls Christ the Son of God, he contrasts him with John, Elijah, Jeremiah, and the other prophets, whom no one denies to have been sons of God by the grace of adoption. Peter therefore called Christ not an adoptive but a natural Son of God, just as the Apostle Paul does in Hebrews 1, where he compares him with the angels in such a way that he alone is called the natural Son of God, while the angels are called servants and ministers, although otherwise they too are adoptive sons of God, and indeed eminent ones.]

“You are,” he says, “the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16).

I must use a simple and rustic question to refute you, heretic. Tell me, please, who was the one to whom Peter replied these words? You cannot deny that he was Christ. I ask, then: which Christ do you mean? A man or God? A man, certainly, without a doubt; for this is the source of your entire heresy, that you deny Christ to be the Son of God.

For this reason you also say that Mary is Christotokos, “mother of Christ,” not Theotokos, “Mother of God,” because she is the mother of Christ, not of God. You therefore assert that Christ is merely a man, not God, and for that reason that he is the son of man, not the Son of God.

What, then, did Peter answer to this? “You are,” he says, “the Christ, the Son of the living God.” The Christ whom you assert to be merely the son of man is testified by Peter to be the Son of God. Whom do you want us to believe—you or Peter? I suppose that you are not so shameless as to dare to place yourself before the first of the Apostles. Yet what is there that you would not dare? Or how could you refrain from despising an Apostle when you have been able to deny God?

“You are,” he says, “the Christ, the Son of the living God.” Does this contain anything ambiguous or obscure? It is simply and openly a confession that proclaims Christ to be the Son of God. Perhaps you deny that this was said, but the Evangelist bears witness to it. Do you accuse the Apostle of lying? That would be detestable falsehood, accusing the Apostle of falsehood. Or do you maintain that this was perhaps said of some other Christ? That would be a new form of monstrous invention.

What, then, remains? Only this: when what is written is read and what is read is true, you are finally compelled, whether by force or necessity, since you cannot establish falsehood, to cease attacking the truth.

## CHAPTER XIII. Blessed Peter’s confession received from Christ himself the testimony of truth
Nevertheless, since I have used the testimony of the chief of the apostles, by which he himself confessed the Lord Jesus Christ before God, let us see how the one whom he confessed approved his confession, since it is much more than what the apostle said if God himself praised his statement. When the apostle therefore said, “You are [Col. 0069B] Christ, the Son of the living God,” what answer did the Lord and Savior give?

[Note: That is, “Therefore you are blessed,” says Saint Leo (Sermon 3, *On the Anniversary*, and Sermon 2, *On the Nativity of the Apostle*), “because my Father taught you, and no earthly opinion deceived you, but heavenly inspiration instructed you; and it was not flesh and blood, but he who is my only-begotten Son, who revealed me to you. And I,” he says, “tell you this”: just as my Father manifested my divinity to you, so I also make your excellence known to you: “For you are Peter”—that is, although I am the unassailable rock, the cornerstone who makes the two one, the foundation besides which no one can lay another, yet you too are a rock, because you are made firm by my power, so that what belongs properly to me by authority may be shared with you through participation with me. “And upon this rock I will build my Church.” Upon this strength, he says, I will construct an eternal temple, and the exalted grandeur of my Church, to be brought into heaven, will rise upon the firmness of this faith. The gates of hell will not hold this confession, nor will the bonds of death bind it; for this voice is the voice of Life, and so forth. This is Saint Leo, together with what follows.]

“You are blessed,” he says, “Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood did not reveal this to you, but my Father’s Spirit who is in heaven.” If you dislike using the apostle’s testimony, use God’s: for by praising what was said, God added his own authority to the apostolic statement, so that although that statement proceeded from the apostle’s mouth, God nevertheless made it his own by approving it.

“You are blessed,” he says, “Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood did not reveal this to you, but my Father’s Spirit who is in heaven.” Thus, in the apostle’s statement, you see the testimony of the Holy Spirit, of the Son who was present, and of God the Father. What more, then, or what similar testimony do you seek? The Son praised it, the Father was present, and the Holy Spirit revealed it. The apostle’s statement is therefore the testimony of the entire Divinity, because that statement must possess the authority of the one by whose authority it proceeded.

“You are blessed,” he says, “Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood did not reveal this to you, but my Father’s Spirit who is in heaven.” Therefore, if it was not flesh and blood that revealed and inspired these things to Peter, you now understand who inspired you. If the Spirit of God taught the man who confessed that Christ is God, you see that you have been taught by the spirit of the devil, since you were able to deny it.

## CHAPTER XIV. Peter’s confession is the faith of the whole Church.

Nevertheless, after that statement of the Lord by which he highly praised Peter, what other statements follow?

“And I,” he says, “tell you: You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church.” Do you see that Peter’s statement is the faith of the Church? Therefore the person who does not hold the faith of the Church must necessarily be outside the Church.

“And to you,” the Lord says, “I will give the keys of the kingdom of heaven.”

[Note: Saint Leo expresses the same thought (*Sermon 1, On the Anniversary*):

“This was achieved by that confession which, inspired by God the Father in the apostolic heart, transcended all the uncertainties of human opinions and received the firmness of a rock that no assaults could shake. For throughout the universal Church Peter says daily, ‘You are Christ, the Son of the living God,’ and every tongue that confesses the Lord is instructed by the teaching of this utterance. This faith conquers the devil and dissolves the bonds of his captives; it removes those rescued from the world and joins them to heaven, and the gates of hell cannot prevail against it. For it has been fortified by such divine solidity that neither has heretical depravity ever been able to corrupt it, nor pagan unbelief to overcome it.”]

This faith earned heaven; this faith received the keys of the heavenly kingdom. Understand what awaits you. You will not be able to enter through the door opened by this key, since you have denied the faith of this key.

“And the gates,” he says, “of hell will not prevail against you.” The gates of hell are the faith of heretics—indeed, unbelief. For as far as hell is distant from heaven, so far is the person who denies from the one who has confessed Christ to be God.

“Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose upon earth will be loosed also in heaven.” The apostle’s perfect faith received, in a certain sense, the power of the Divinity, so that whatever it had bound or loosed on earth would be bound or loosed in heaven. You, therefore, who come against the apostle’s faith, when you see that you are already bound on earth, have only to recognize that you are also bound in heaven.

But it would take too long to go through each point, which by its number would make an extremely long and abundant discussion, even if mentioned briefly and summarily.

## CHAPTER XV. Saint Thomas also professed Peter’s same faith after the Lord’s resurrection.

Nevertheless, I still wish to add one testimony of the apostle, so that you may understand that what occurred before the Lord’s passion agrees with what followed after the passion. When the Lord entered the assembly of his disciples through closed doors, wishing to make the truth of his body known to the apostles, and the apostle Thomas had touched his flesh, handled his side, and examined his wounds, having thoroughly established the reality of the manifested body, what did he proclaim?

“My Lord,” he says, “and my God” (John XX).

Did he say what you say—that Christ is man and not God, and that there is no Divinity? He touched the body of his Lord and answered that he was God. Did he introduce any distinction between the man and God?
