[Note: Because of the similarity of the words, an error had even entered the Plantinian edition, so that *Theodochon*, or in Greek Θεοδόχον, was read as *Theotocon*. Since among the Greeks this word can be understood in two ways according to the difference of accent, neither form or meaning can suit this passage. For Θεοτόκος, with the accent on the penultimate syllable, means “parent of God,” or “God-bearer” (*Deipara*), as stated above—thus Nestorius did not want Mary to be called Θεοτόκον, but Χριστοτόκον, that is, “mother of Christ,” not “of God.” Θεότοκος, with the accent on the antepenultimate syllable, means “begotten by God.” It is obvious in itself that neither meaning can be applied to Christ’s flesh, nor was either one used by Nestorius.

Rather, Θεουδόχος, or Θεοδόχος, means “one who receives God,” from the verb δέχομαι, “I receive” or “I take in.” Hence it is immediately and most properly explained as follows: *the flesh Theodochon*, that is, “the receiver of Divinity.” For that impious Nestorius called the flesh—that is, Christ’s humanity, or Christ as man—not Θεότοκον, “begotten by God,” but Θεοδόχον, “receiver of God,” or, as it were, “host” of God, or Θεοφόρον, “God-bearing.” He did this as though Christ the man were someone other than God, having received and carried God within himself, joined to him not by hypostatic union but by some privilege of dignity and friendship.

Against this heresy, canons were issued and sanctioned under anathema at the general council of Ephesus. The third of them reads: “If anyone divides the hypostases in the one Christ after the union, joining them only by a connection according to dignity or authority, and not rather by a union according to nature, let him be anathema.” The fifth canon reads: “If anyone dares to call Christ a God-bearing man, and not rather God according to the truth, let him be anathema.”

Nestorius misused the name Θεοφόρος, just as he did Θεοδόχος, to indicate the distinction between the persons from which he wanted Christ to be composed. For a “God-bearer” is a man who is God not by nature but through participation in divinity, because he has God as an inhabitant and intimate guest of his heart, as the Lord promises in John XIV: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him.” Whoever is such a person is nevertheless only a solitary and naked man, receiving the designation “God” solely by reason of participation.

But Christ is God not by participation but by nature, and the natural Son of God, God begotten from God. He must not therefore be called “God-bearer” or “receiver of God,” as Nestorius argued, wishing under cover of such an appellation to deny Christ’s true divinity and assert only his humanity. Both positions are impious and blasphemous.

From these considerations it is clear that the word “image” was rightly and not arbitrarily deleted as superfluous, inserted—I do not know by what reasoning, negligence, or incompetence. For what has flesh in common with an image? And who would interpret Christ’s flesh, *Theodochon*, “receiver of Divinity,” as an image, when *Theodochos* signifies nothing other than “receiver of God,” whether masculine or feminine? See more on this in Book V, chapter 2.]

Did he call that flesh *Theodochon*, as you say—that is, “receiver of Divinity”? Or, in accordance with your impiety, did he remember that the one whom he encountered was to be venerated not for his own sake but because of the one whom he had received within himself?

Perhaps the apostle of God did not know this subtle distinction of your reasoning, nor possess the refinement and discrimination of your judgment—a man, naturally, rustic and uneducated, ignorant of dialectical method and inexperienced in philosophical disputation, for whom the instruction of his Lord was sufficient, and who knew absolutely nothing except what he had learned from his Lord’s teaching.

And so that rustic and uneducated man, as you perhaps think, now traps you with a brief answer and crushes you with a few words of his speech.

What, then, did the apostle Thomas touch when he approached to touch God? Christ, certainly and without doubt. What did he proclaim?

“My Lord,” he says, “and my God.”

Now, if you can, separate Christ from God and alter this statement, if you are able. Produce your dialectic; produce worldly prudence and that foolish wisdom characterized by verbal cunning. Turn yourself every which way and twist yourself about. Whatever you possess in mind or skill, whatever you say or do, you can get nowhere from this point unless you confess that the one whom the apostle touched is God.

Indeed, if you could somehow alter the proclamation of the Gospel narrative, you might perhaps wish it to be read neither that the apostle Thomas touched the Lord’s body nor that he called Christ the Lord God. But what is written in God’s Gospel cannot be altered in any way. “Heaven and earth will pass away, but the words of God will not pass away” (Matthew XXIV).

For even now that apostle Thomas, who then bore witness, cries out to you: “Jesus whom I touched is God; the one whose limbs I handled is God. I did not grasp an incorporeal being, nor handle something untouchable. I did not touch a spirit with my hand, so that I might be thought to have said only of him, ‘He is God’; for, according to the statement of my Lord, a spirit does not have flesh and bones” (Luke XXIV).

“I touched the body of my Lord; I handled flesh and bones; I placed my fingers in the place of the wounds; and concerning Christ my Lord, whom I had touched, I proclaimed: ‘My Lord and my God.’ For I do not know how to make a distinction between Christ and God. I do not wish to insert sacrilegious opinions between Jesus and God. I do not know how to tear my Lord away from himself. Let anyone who thinks otherwise depart from me; let anyone who speaks otherwise depart from me.”

[Note: I would prefer *alius* (“another”) to *aliud* (“another thing”). *Alius* properly denotes a person, whereas *aliud* denotes a nature, as shown above. Thus in divine matters we say that the Son is *alius* than the Father—that is, another person—not *aliud*, which would mean of another nature, as Saint Thomas teaches (Part I, question 31, article 22).

Moreover, Nestorius asserted that Christ was other than God because he recognized him as a mere man, not as God. The Author, contradicting him, demonstrates from the words of the apostle Thomas that Christ is not another person but one and the same with God, and is himself God. For according to his human nature, it cannot be denied that Christ is *aliud* than God—that is, another thing, namely a man—but not *alius*, that is, another person.]

I do not know Christ as something other than God. With my fellow apostles I held this; I handed this on to the Churches; I preached this to the nations; and I proclaim this to you as well: Christ is God, Christ is God. My sound mind does not think otherwise; sound faith does not speak otherwise. Divinity cannot be torn away from him. And since whatever Christ is, he is God, nothing other than God can be found in God.

## CHAPTER XVI. The testimony of God the Father concerning the divinity of the Son.

What do you say now, heretic? Are these testimonies of the faith sufficient even for the greatest unbelief, or must something more still be added? And what can be added after the prophets or after the apostles, unless perhaps, as the Jews once demanded, you too request a sign from heaven?

But if you ask this, the answer once given to them must be given to you: “An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and no sign will be given to it except the sign of the prophet Jonah.”

Indeed, this sign could have sufficed for you even together with the Jews who crucified him, so that you might believe that our Lord is God by this one fact alone—a fact by which even those who had persecuted him came to believe.

Nevertheless, since we have mentioned a sign from heaven, I will show you a sign from heaven—and one such that demons themselves have never contradicted it. Compelled by the very necessity of the truth, although they saw Jesus to be corporeal, they nevertheless proclaimed him to be God, which he was.

What, then, does the Evangelist say about the Lord Jesus Christ?

“When he had been baptized,” he says, “he immediately went up from the water. And behold, the heavens were opened to him, and he saw the Spirit descending like a dove and coming upon him. And behold, a voice from heaven said:”

[Note: Ὁ υἱός μου ὁ ἀγαπητὸς, as if to say, “That Son of mine—the one, I mean, who is most beloved.” The double article shows that he is speaking not of just any son, but of the natural, unique, eternal Son equal to himself; the others are sons only by adoption. Thus Maldonado.

Saint Leo the pontiff explains this more fully in his sermon on the Lord’s Transfiguration:

“It was a broad and manifold testimony, and more was heard in the force of the words than in the sound of the voice. For when the Father said, ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him,’ was it not clearly heard: ‘This is my Son, whose being from me and with me is without time’? For the begetter is not earlier than the begotten, nor is the begotten later than the begetter.

“This is my Son, whom divinity does not separate from me, power does not divide, and eternity does not distinguish. This is my Son, not adopted but proper; not created elsewhere but begotten from me; not made comparable to me from another nature, but born equal to me from my essence.

“This is my Son, through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made; for everything I do, he does together with me, and whatever I accomplish, he accomplishes inseparably and without distinction with me. The Son is in the Father, and the Father in the Son, and our unity is never divided. Although I, who begot, am one person and he whom I begot another, it is nevertheless not permitted you to think anything about him other than what it is possible to think about me.”]

“This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew III).

What do you say to this now, heretic? Does the statement displease you, or the person who spoke it? The meaning of the address certainly needs no interpretation, nor does the dignity of the speaker need the commendation of words. God the Father is the one who spoke. What was said is evident.

Will you be able to utter a voice so impudent or sacrilegious as to say that God the Father himself must not be believed concerning the only-begotten Son of God?

“This, therefore,” he says, “is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”

But perhaps, in your madness, you will try to say that this was spoken about the Word, not about Christ.

[Note: To remove the ambiguity, the syntax should be construed as follows: “This was spoken about the Word, not about Christ.” The reference is to the Father’s oracle, “This is my beloved Son.” The Word is understood as the person of the Son, whom Nestorius separated from Christ, or from the person of Christ. Thus, when pressed by the orthodox Fathers, that crafty man tried to evade their arguments. For since he distinguished two persons in Christ, whatever passages from Scripture were brought forward to prove Christ’s divinity he interpreted as referring not to Christ but to the Word dwelling in Christ.

This escape route is blocked when Scripture most clearly shows that Christ and the Word are the same, as the Author demonstrates here and as other Fathers also demonstrated. Consequently, the statements made about the Word were made about Christ, as Nestorius himself admitted.]

Tell me, then: who was being baptized—the Word or Christ? Flesh or spirit? You cannot deny that it was Christ. That man, therefore, born from a human being and from God, conceived when the Holy Spirit descended upon the Virgin and the power of the Most High overshadowed her, and thus the Son of man and the Son of God—that man, certainly, as you cannot deny, was baptized.

Therefore, if he was baptized, he was also named; for the one who was named was plainly the one who was baptized.

“This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” Can anything be said more significantly or explicitly?

Christ was baptized; Christ went up from the water; when Christ was baptized, the heavens were opened; because of Christ, the dove descended upon Christ; the Holy Spirit stood present in bodily form; the Father addressed Christ.

If you dare deny that this was said about Christ, it remains for you to assert that Christ was not baptized, that the Spirit did not descend, and that the Father did not speak.

But the truth itself presses and overwhelms you, so that even if you refuse to confess it, you cannot deny it. What does the Evangelist say?

“When he had been baptized, he immediately went up from the water.” Who was baptized? Christ, certainly.

“And behold,” he says, “the heavens were opened to him.” To whom, unless to the one who was baptized? To Christ, certainly.

“And he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming upon him.” Who saw? Christ, of course. Upon whom did it descend? Upon Christ, certainly.

“And a voice came from heaven, saying.” Concerning whom? Concerning Christ, certainly.

What follows? “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”

So that everything might be shown to have happened on account of the one for whom it happened, the voice followed, saying: “This is my beloved Son”—that is, “This is the one for whom all these things happened. This is my Son: because of him the heavens were opened; because of him my Spirit came; because of him my voice was heard. This is my Son.”

When he said, “This is my Son,” whom was he identifying? The one whom the dove touched, certainly. Whom, then, did the dove touch? Christ, of course. Therefore Christ is the Son of God.

I think my promise has been fulfilled. You see, then, heretic, that a sign from heaven has been given to you—and not one sign only, but many and extraordinary ones. You have one in the opening of heaven, another in the descent of the Spirit, and a third in the Father’s voice.

All these things most clearly declare that Christ is God: the opening of the heavens indicates that he is God; the descent of the Holy Spirit upon him confirms that he is God; and the Father’s address confirms that he is God. For neither would heaven have opened except in honor of its Lord, nor would the Spirit have descended in bodily form except upon the Son of God, nor would the Father have declared the Son unless he were truly the Son—especially since these signs of divine birth not only confirm the truth of the pious faith but also exclude the perversity of impious opinion.

For in the ineffable majesty of the divine utterance, after the Father had expressly and significantly said, “This is my beloved Son,” he added also what followed: “in whom I am well pleased.” Just as through the prophet he had already proclaimed “the strong God” and “the great God” (Isaiah IX), so here, saying “my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased,” he further added the name of his proper Son, so that the addition of the names might signify the property of the divine nature and might belong peculiarly to the honor of the Son of God—something that had happened to no human being at all.

Thus, just as those distinctive and particular features belonged to the person of our Lord Jesus Christ: that the heavens were opened; that God the Father, in the sight of all, touched him in a manner resembling the action of his hand through the approaching and hovering dove, and pointed him out, as it were, with a finger, saying, “This is my Son”; so too this was distinctive and unique to him: that he was named specially “beloved” and specially pleasing to the Father.

These peculiar additions therefore revealed the special character of his nature, and the special character of the titles confirmed the distinctiveness of the only-begotten Son, which the honor of the preceding signs had already established.

But let this little book now come to an end. For this statement of God the Father can neither be increased nor equaled by human words. Concerning our Lord Jesus Christ, his Son, God the Father himself is a sufficient witness, saying, “This is my Son.” If you think that these words of God the Father must be contradicted, then you must contradict the one who caused the whole world to acknowledge him as his Son through the clearest declaration.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0075]

## CHAPTER I. Christ was God from eternity before assuming flesh.

Having completed three books, as it were most faithful and richly furnished witnesses—since their truth has been enriched not only by human but also by divine testimonies—they could certainly have sufficed for the proof of our case through divine authority, since the divine authority of the case itself is fully sufficient.

Nevertheless, because the sequence of the sacred books is full of such testimonies, where there are as many witnesses as there are statements—or rather, where Holy Scripture itself is in a certain sense one testimony from the divine mouth—we have thought it appropriate to accumulate still more, not out of necessity for proof but in view of the abundance and scope of the material, so that everything not necessary for the defense might nevertheless contribute to its adornment.

Therefore, since in the preceding books we proved by prophetic, apostolic, evangelical, and angelic testimonies that the Lord Jesus Christ was God while he was in the flesh and on earth, we shall now show that the one who was born in the flesh had always been God even before assuming flesh.

Thus you may understand, from the agreeing and almost unanimous testimonies of the divine books, that the same one whom at his bodily birth you must believe to be both man and God—who before his bodily birth was God alone, and who after being brought forth from the Virgin was God in the body—was the same one who before the Virgin’s delivery was the divine Word, God.

Learn first, therefore, from the apostle, the teacher of the whole world, that the one who is God without beginning, the Son of God, was made the Son of man at the end of the world, that is, in the fullness of time.

For he says: “When the fullness of time had come, [Note: In Greek, ἐξαπέστειλε properly means “sent out,” or rather “dispatched.” He sent the Son, I say, not separated from himself, but through the fact that he assumed human nature, while nevertheless not departing from the Father’s bosom, as the Evangelist bears witness when he says, “The only-begotten Son who is in the bosom of the Father” (John I)—eternally, says Saint Thomas.

And in John III: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of man who is in heaven,” because although he descended through the assumption of flesh, he nevertheless remained in heaven through the presence of his divinity.

Likewise, he dispatched or sent him into the world not so that he might begin to be there, where previously he had not been, but so that he might be there in a new manner in which he had not previously been—namely, so that he might appear visibly to the world, clothed in mortal flesh.

Explaining this, the Apostle adds: “made from a woman,” that is, from the Virgin Mary. For in Holy Scripture “woman” does not always denote corruption, but merely the natural sex, as is clear from Genesis III: “The Lord built the rib into a woman.” And again: “The woman whom you gave me,” where the reference is to Eve while she was still whole and untouched by man.

Nor did Christ hesitate to call his mother “woman” (John II): “What is there between me and you, woman?”

Through this phrase, Saint Thomas also says, two errors are destroyed: the error of Valentinus, who said that Christ did not assume a body from the Virgin but brought it from heaven and passed through the blessed Virgin as through a pipe or channel. If this were true, he would not have been “made from a woman,” as the Apostle says; for the preposition “from” designates material cause.

The error of Nestorius is also destroyed: he said that the blessed Virgin was not the mother of the Son of God but of the son of man. This is shown to be false by the Apostle’s statement: “God sent his Son, made from a woman.” For whoever is made from a woman is her son. Therefore, if the Son of God was made from a woman, namely from the blessed Virgin, it is evident that the blessed Virgin is the Mother of the Son of God.

This is Saint Thomas (in his Commentary), who also adds the reason why the Apostle said “made from a woman,” just as in Romans I Christ is said to have been made from the seed of David: namely, to signify that Christ was not brought forth by the customary manner of generation, but was incarnated in the virgin womb by a unique work of divinity and made man.]

God sent his Son, made from a woman, made under the Law” (Galatians IV).

Tell me, then: before the Lord Jesus Christ was born from his mother Mary, did God have a Son or did he not? You cannot deny that he had one. For there was never either a son without a father or a father without a son, since just as the son is named from the father, so the father is named from the son.

## CHAPTER II. From his statements he concludes that the Virgin Mary gave birth to a Son older and greater than herself.

You see, then, that when the Apostle says, “God sent his Son,” he means his own Son. To use the Apostle’s own words: God sent his own Son. For he did not send some son belonging to another, since he is said to have sent his own; nor could he have sent him at all if there were no one to be sent.

“He sent,” he says, “his Son, made from a woman.”

Therefore, because he sent him, he sent one who already was; and because he sent his own, he sent not another’s but his own.

Where, then, is that argument of your earthly cunning: “No one gives birth to one older than himself”?

Is the Lord not older than Mary? Is the Son of God not older than the daughter of man? Is God not older, finally, than man himself, since no human being exists who is not from God?

You see, then, that Mary gave birth not only to one older than herself—as I say—but not only to one older than herself: she gave birth to her own author, and, producing her creator, became the parent of her parent. For just as it was easy for God to grant birth to a human being, so it was easy for him to be born from a human being; just as it was easy for him to make a human being be born, so it was easy for him himself to be born from a human being.

For God’s power is not confined within his own person, so that what is permitted to him in all things would not be permitted to him in himself, and so that he who possesses in the nature of his divinity the power to do all things would lack in his own person the power to be God in man.

Once the frivolous and fleeting stupidities of earthly arguments have been set aside and rejected, we must believe only simple testimony and bare truth, and faith must be given only to those witnesses concerning God whom God sent and in whom he himself, so to speak, proclaimed himself.

For it is right that we believe those concerning the knowledge of him who alone is the source of everything we know about him. God could not be known by man unless he himself had granted the knowledge of himself. Therefore it is just that we believe everything we know about him, since everything we know belongs to him. For if we do not believe the one from whom we know, it follows that we know nothing at all, since we do not believe the one through whom we know.

## CHAPTER III. From the Epistle to the Romans he proves Christ’s divinity from eternity.

Therefore, since it was made clear by the preceding testimony that God sent his Son, and that this Son—who had always been the Son of God—became the Son of man, let us see whether the same Apostle elsewhere said something similar in his testimony, so that the truth, already shining by itself, may shine more brightly through the doubled light of the testimonies.

The same Apostle therefore says: “God sent his Son in the likeness [Col. 0078D] of sinful flesh” (Romans VIII).

[Note: The Latins commonly have it this way, and it is the wording of the Vulgate; the Greeks, however, have ἐν ὁμοιώματι, “in the likeness.” Augustine, Sermon 6 on the Words of the Apostle, reads it both ways, as does Cassian in this chapter. See the other observations made elsewhere on this subject.]

You surely see that the Apostle did not say something by chance or with an unconsidered expression, as though he would then pass over what he had once said; for chance or carelessness could not occur in one in whom the fullness of divine counsel and speech dwelt. Thus, when he says, “God sent [Col. 0079A] his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh,” he repeats and reinforces the same point by saying, “God sent his Son.”

What an outstanding and admirable teacher! Knowing that the whole mystery of the Catholic faith is entirely contained in this—that the Lord, born in the flesh, should be believed to have been sent into this world as the Son of God—he repeatedly proclaims this, saying: “God sent his Son.” Nor is it surprising that, having been sent in a special way to announce the coming of God, he preached in this manner, since the Lawgiver himself had proclaimed the same thing even before the Law, saying:

[Note: In this manner Saint Jerome explains Isaiah, chapter VI: “Moses,” he says, “to whom the Lord had said, ‘Come, I will send you to Pharaoh, king of Egypt,’ replied, ‘I beg you, Lord, I am not worthy. Provide another whom you may send’; or, as it is read in Hebrew, ‘Send whom you are going to send.’ He replied not out of contempt, but out of humility.”

These, then, are the words of Moses, whom the present Author calls the lawgiver, when he was being sent by the Lord to the Hebrew people and to King Pharaoh and was excusing himself from undertaking this office and mission—as though he were saying: “Send whom you are going to send,” that is, the one whom you know to be suitable for this mission and whom you have in fact decided to send.

But the Author interprets these words allegorically of the Messiah, who was to be sent for the redemption of the human race. The Church likewise applies the same words in the ecclesiastical office to the coming of Christ, whom the holy patriarchs and prophets ardently desired. Such are those prayers and sighs: “Send forth the Lamb, O Lord, the ruler of the earth” (Isaiah IX); “Would that you would tear open the heavens and descend” (Isaiah LXIV); “Visit us with your salvation” (Psalm CXV); “Show us, O Lord, your face,” and so forth (Psalm LXXXIV).]

“I beg you, Lord, provide another whom you may send” (Exodus IV). In the Hebrew books this is read much more clearly: “I beg you, Lord, send whom you are going to send.”

The pious prophet, bearing within himself the longing of the entire human race, was asking God the Father, as though with the voice of all human flesh, that the one who was to be sent by the Father for the redemption and salvation of all might be sent as quickly as possible, saying: “I beg you, Lord, send whom you are going to send.”

“God therefore,” he says, “sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh.” Well did he exclude sin from him when he said that he had been sent in the flesh. For he says: “God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh”—that is, so that, while the reality of his assumption of flesh was recognized, it might also be recognized that there was no sin in him; and that, insofar as the body was concerned, there was reality, while, insofar as sin was concerned, there was only the likeness of sin.

For since all flesh is sinful, while he possessed flesh without sin, he had in himself the likeness of sinful flesh, since he was in the flesh; but he lacked the reality of sin, because he was without sin. “God therefore,” he says, “sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh.”

## CHAPTER IV. He adduces testimonies of the same doctrine from elsewhere.

Do you wish to know how well the Apostle proclaimed this? Listen to how it flowed into the Apostle’s mouth, as though from the very mouth of God himself, when the Lord said: “For God did not send his Son into the world to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him” (John V).

Behold, as you see, the Lord himself declares that he was sent by God the Father for the salvation of the human race. But if you think it should be shown more clearly which Son God sent to save human beings—although there is only one proper and only-begotten Son of God, and when God is said to have sent his Son, he is plainly shown to have sent his only-begotten Son—listen nevertheless to the prophet David, who most clearly identifies the one sent for human salvation.

“He sent,” he says,

[Note: Here the Author takes “Word” personally, that is, as referring to the person of the Son, whose proper name is Word, as Saint Thomas teaches (I, q. 34, art. 2). This Word was sent through the Incarnation to heal human beings. For “there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved,” as it is said in Acts III.

In the same way Saint Basil, explaining the same verse, says: “He teaches the manner of salvation: for God the Word, having become man and having been sent as man—for as God he is uncircumscribed—healed the wounds of souls of every kind and restored corrupted minds to soundness.”

Saint Jerome likewise interprets “Word” as the Son himself, who “in the beginning was the Word” and who in the Gospel heals every disease and every infirmity among the people (John I).

Others understand “Word” to mean God’s command or will, by which, as the principal cause, the Psalmist signifies that the Hebrews were healed in the wilderness from the bites of serpents—not by the bronze serpent that Moses raised up, nor by any other created thing.]

“his Word and healed them” (Psalm CVI).

Can you turn this toward the flesh, so as to say that merely a man was sent by God to heal the human race? You certainly cannot. For the prophet David, together with all the sacred Scriptures, cries out against you, saying: “He sent his Word and healed them.”

You see, therefore, that the Word was sent to heal human beings. For although healing was given through Christ, it was nevertheless the Word of God in Christ that healed all things through Christ; and thus, through the sacramental union of Christ and the Word of God, Christ and the Word of God, united in one, became the one Son of God from both realities.

The Apostle John, wishing to make this clear, says: “God sent his Son as the Savior of the world” (1 John IV). Do you understand how he joined God and man by an inseparable connection? Christ, who was born from Mary, is undoubtedly called Savior, in accordance with the saying: “Today a Savior has been born for you, who is Christ the Lord” (Luke II). But here he calls the very Word of God who was sent the Savior, saying: “God sent his Son as the Savior of the world.”

## CHAPTER V. Because of the hypostatic union of the two natures in Christ, the Word is rightly called Savior, and the incarnate man the Son of God.

[Col. 0080C]

It is therefore clear that, through the sacramental union of the Word of God with man, the Word who was sent to save is called Savior; and that the Savior born in the flesh is, through the fellowship of the Word, called the Son of God. Thus, because the majesty of both names is undivided, since God has been united with man, whatever is man and God is wholly called [Col. 0081A] God.

[Note: This is by virtue of the communication of properties, which follows from the union of the two natures in one and the same suppositum, as has often been said (see Book II, chapter 9).]

And therefore the same Apostle rightly adds: “Whoever believes that Jesus is the Son of God, God remains in him, and the love of God is perfected in him” (1 John IV). He truly proclaims that person to believe, and asserts that person to be full of divine love, who believes Jesus to be the Son of God.

He testifies that the Son of God is the Word of God; and consequently he wishes the only-begotten Word of God and Jesus Christ the Son of God to be understood as entirely one and the same.

But do you wish to know more fully that, although Christ was truly born from a human being as a human being according to the flesh, nevertheless, because of the ineffable unity of the mystery by which man has been united with God,

[Note: As regards the person, which is one and indivisible in Christ, and in which there can therefore be no separation—that is, no disjunction or distinction—between the man and God, or the Word. “For Christ is one, not by confusion of substance, but by unity of person,” says Blessed Athanasius.]

there is absolutely no separation between Christ and the Word? Listen to the Lord’s Gospel; or rather, listen to God himself descending. “This is eternal life,” he says,

[Note: The Arians abused this passage, and from it inferred that the Son was not true God, because here the Father alone is called the true God. The Fathers answered them in various ways.

First, they said that the words “the only true God” are not restricted to the Father but extend also to the Son through the coordinating conjunction, when it continues, “and Jesus Christ whom you sent.” The order of the words, they maintained, is: “This is eternal life, that they may know you and Jesus Christ whom you sent as the true God.” Thus Chrysostom and Cyril explain the passage.

A simpler response is that “only” does not exclude the Son or the Holy Spirit, who are persons of the same nature as the Father; it excludes only idols and creatures, which are not true gods.

As for what follows—“and Jesus Christ whom you sent”—this is said of Christ as man, so that the meaning is: “This is eternal life,” that is, the way and means of attaining eternal life, if people know through faith that you, the Father, are the only true God—that is, that besides you there is no other true God—and also know the one Mediator between God and human beings, whom you sent, Jesus Christ.

Thus Hilary, Book IX, On the Trinity. This explanation presupposes what is most true: that the particle “only” is not the subject but the attribute, or, as dialecticians say, that it belongs not to the subject but to the predicate. In other words, it does not refer to the Father but to God.

The meaning is not: “that they may know you, the Father, who alone are the true God,” but rather: “that they may know you, who are that God who alone is true God.” This is expressed more clearly in the Greek text: ἵνα γιγνώσκωσι σε τὸν μόνον ἀληθινὸν Θεόν, “that they may know you, the only true God.”]

“that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John XVII, 3).

Earlier you heard that the Word of God was sent to heal human beings; here you hear that the one who was sent is Jesus Christ. Separate these, if you can, when you see that the unity of Christ and the Word is so great that not only is the Word said to be united with Christ, but, because of that very unity, Christ himself is now called the Word.

## CHAPTER VI. There is one hypostasis in Christ.

But perhaps you think this is not sufficiently clear—not because it shines too little, but because dark unbelief always creates darkness for itself even in the light. Listen, then, to the Apostle comprehending the whole mystery of the Lord’s unity in a few words:

“One,” he says, “is our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things” (1 Corinthians VIII).

O Jesus, how great is the authority in your words! For what is spoken by your own people through you is yours. Behold how much this saying of the Apostle contains in so few words: “One,” he says, “is the Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things.”

Did he use any elaborate circumlocution to proclaim the mystery of so great a sacrament? Or did he develop what he wished us to understand in a long discourse? “One,” he says, “is our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things.”

By a simple and brief expression he taught the secret of such great majesty, with the confidence that he knew his speech, in God’s cause, needed no lengthy arguments, and that divinity gives authority to his words. For the demonstration of realities alone is sufficient to confirm what has been said, when proof rests upon the authority of the speaker.

“One,” therefore, he says, “is the Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things.” Consider where you have read this concerning the Father’s Word, which you read here concerning Christ. “All things,” says the Gospel, “were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John I).

The Apostle says: “Through Christ are all things.” The Gospel says: “Through the Word are all things.” Do the sacred statements contradict one another? Certainly not. The Apostle also wished Christ to be understood as the one through whom all things were created, while the Evangelist remembered the Word as the one through whom all things were made.

Listen, I say, to what the Word of God, God himself, declared about himself.

[Note: It should be noted here that both verbs, “ascended” and “descended,” are in the past tense, not the present, as is clear from the Greek forms ἀναβέβηκεν and καταβάς. Hence a twofold difficulty arises: one concerning the ascent and another concerning the descent.

As for the ascent, how can the Son of man—that is, Christ—be said already to have ascended into heaven when he was speaking these words to Nicodemus, since he did not ascend into heaven until the fortieth day after his resurrection?

As for the descent, how can he be said to have descended from heaven who, as God, fills all things and is wholly everywhere, and who, as man, was not in heaven before his conception?

These difficulties cannot be resolved unless we acknowledge that the same person is both the Son of man and the Son of God. He is said to have ascended into heaven before he spoke these words because, through the Incarnation and hypostatic union, that man, Christ, began to be in heaven, where he had not been before his conception.

This is required by the communication of properties and by a certain mutual interchange, as Damascene says (Book III, chapter 4, *On the Orthodox Faith*), which results from the hypostatic union, as has been said.

Therefore, because that man Christ was not in heaven before he was conceived, but after his conception was in heaven because of the hypostatic union, he is said to have ascended into heaven. For, speaking in human terms, whatever was previously on earth and then began to be in heaven is said to have ascended into heaven.

Conversely, he is said to have descended from heaven because the one who was previously in heaven, although he was also on earth, was not visible there; having assumed human nature, he suddenly began to be seen on earth, as though he had descended from heaven.

Thus his descent and ascent are nothing other than the Incarnation, through which the Son of God became the Son of man. Through the communication of properties, therefore, the Son of man ascended into heaven and descended from heaven.

He ascended through the exaltation of his humanity; he descended through the humiliation of his divinity, because, as the Apostle testifies, the Son of God “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings, and being found in appearance as a man” (Philippians II).

By this statement Christ indicates three things that must be believed: the reality of the assumed human nature, when he calls himself the Son of man, that is, a human being; the reality of the divine nature, when he asserts that he descended from heaven and was in heaven while he was speaking these words on earth; and the union of these natures in one person, when he says that the Son of man is in heaven.

For because of this unity it necessarily follows that whatever is truly said of the Son of God is also truly said of the Son of man, and conversely.]

“No one,” he says, “has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of man who is in heaven” (John III). And again: “When you see,” he says, “the Son of man ascending where he was before” (John VI).

He said that the Son of man had been in heaven; he stated that the Son of man had descended from heaven. What is this? Why do you mutter? Deny it, if you can. But you seek the reason for what was said? I will not provide it—for now God said this; God spoke this to me. His word is the highest reason.

I remove arguments; I remove disputations. The person who speaks is alone sufficient for my belief. I may not doubt the truth of what has been said in faith; I may not deliberate about it. Why should I ask how what God has said is true, when I ought not to doubt that what God has said is true?

“No one,” he says, “has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of man who is in heaven.”

The Father’s Word was always in heaven. How, then, did he state that the Son of man had always been in heaven? Understand, therefore, that he taught him to be the Son of man who had always been the Son of God, since he confirms that the one who recently became the Son of man had always been in heaven.

There is something even greater than this: he says that the same Son of man—that is, the Word of God whom he said had descended from heaven—was also in heaven at the very time when he was speaking on earth.

For he says: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of man who is in heaven.”

Who, I ask, is the one speaking this? Christ, certainly. And where was he at that time, when he was speaking? On earth, obviously.

How, then, does he testify both that he descended from heaven when he was born and that, while speaking, he is in heaven? How does he say that he himself is the Son of man, when clearly no one except God could have descended from heaven, and when, while speaking on earth, no one except through God’s infinity could be in heaven?

Understand, then, at last, and perceive that the Son of man is the same as the Word of God: he is the Son of man because he was truly born from a human being, and he is the Word of God because the same one who speaks on earth remains always in heaven.

Thus his being truly the Son of man belongs to his human birth, while his never departing from heaven belongs to his divine infinity.

And therefore the Apostle, teaching in the manner of divine words, rightly says: “The one who descended is the same one who ascended above all the heavens, in order to fill all things” (Ephesians IV). He says that the one who ascended is the same one who descended. But no one could have descended from heaven except the Word of God.

[Col. 0083D]

This Word of God, though he was in the form of God, “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings, and being found in appearance as a man; he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Philippians II).

The Word of God therefore descended from heaven [Col. 0084A]; the Son of man, however, ascended. Yet he says that the one who ascended is the same one who descended. Thus you see that the Son of man is the same as the Word of God.

## CHAPTER VII. He returns to the preceding consideration, showing that, against the Nestorians, things belonging to the divine nature are said of the man as though of the hypostasis of the divine nature, and things belonging to the human nature are said of God as though of the hypostasis of the human nature, because the hypostasis in Christ is one and simple.

And therefore, in accordance with the teaching of the divine Word, we must now say fearlessly and without hesitation both that the Son of man descended from heaven and that the Lord of majesty was crucified. For, according to the mystery of the assumed body, the Son of God became the Son of man, [Col. 0084B] and in the Son of man the Lord of majesty was crucified.

And what more? It would take too long to say many things about each point. For my day would fail me if I attempted to gather together or explain everything that can be brought forward on this subject.

The whole of sacred Scripture must be revisited and read by anyone wishing to do this. For what does not pertain to this matter, when everything was written for this purpose? It is therefore necessary to say a few things briefly and concisely, so that they can be said; and certain matters must be enumerated rather than explained, and, so to speak, losses must be redeemed by losses. Since it is appropriate to pass over some matters for this reason, nearly everything must necessarily be left unspoken.

“Therefore,” says the Savior in the Gospel, “the Son of man came to save what had perished” (Luke XIX). And the Apostle says: “The saying is trustworthy and worthy of all acceptance: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the first” (1 Timothy I).

But the Evangelist John also says: “He came to his own, and his own did not receive him” (John I).

Do you see, therefore, that Scripture proclaims in one place that the Son of man came into the world, in another that Jesus Christ came, and in another that the Word of God came?

Understand, then,

[Note: That is, of persons, as Nestorius taught.]

that there is a difference in the designations, not in the realities; and that under the different form of the names there is one power.

[Note: What the Greeks call *hypostasis*, the Latins call *suppositum* or *person*. Above, the Author uses the related term “majesty,” that is, divinity or the divine person.]

For although the one who came into the world is now called the Son of man and now the Son of God, that is, the Word, one and the same person is nevertheless designated under both names.

## CHAPTER VIII. This variety of designations in no way prejudices the divine power.

[Col. 0084D]

For since, according to the Evangelist, the one through whom the world itself was made came into the world, and he who is God, the Creator of the world, was made the Son of man, it makes no difference what he is called in each instance, since God is understood in all of them.

For condescension does not prejudice divinity, nor does his own will; rather, it most fully confirms divinity itself, because whatever he willed, that he was.

Therefore, because he willed it, he came into the world; because he willed it, he was born a man; because he willed it, he was called the Son of man.

For all things are, just as they are names, likewise powers of God. The difference of the name does not diminish the force of his power. Whatever he may be called, he is one and the same in all things. There is some diversity in the form of the designations, but in the power of the names there is only one majesty.

## CHAPTER IX. He confirms this doctrine by the authority of the ancient prophets.

But because up to this point we have used chiefly the evangelical and apostolic writings as though they were new witnesses, let us now bring forward the ancient prophetic witnesses

[Note: [Col. 0085B] He sets the old witnesses, that is, the prophets, against the new witnesses, namely the apostles. The alternative reading noted here comes to the same thing: “from the ancient prophets”; for “witnesses” is understood, and it seems to allude to the Gospel saying: “Every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven is like a man who brings forth from his treasure things new and old” (Matthew 13).]

[Lipsius in the margin: “from the prophets, the ancient ones”], occasionally mingling new testimonies with the ancient, so that all may understand that Sacred Scripture, as it were through its whole body and with one mouth, cried out that the Lord was to come in the flesh.

Thus speaks that eminent and admirable man, rich both in God’s gift and in testimony,

[Note: Scripture explicitly teaches that Jeremiah was sanctified in his mother’s womb before he was born, when the Lord says: “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you; and before you came out of the womb I sanctified you” (Jeremiah 1). But whether this means that Jeremiah was sanctified in his mother’s womb—that is, justified by the infusion of grace and cleansing from original sin, as is certainly believed concerning John the Baptist—is not so clear and established. On this matter one should consult the interpreters of that passage. Certainly Saint Jerome seems to understand by the term “sanctification” nothing other than predestination and God’s special providence, and the decree by which Jeremiah was foreordained to prophesy, just as Paul was foreordained to evangelize. For he explains the words “Before I formed you,” and so forth, as follows: “Not,” he says, “that Jeremiah existed before conception, as the heresy supposes, but that the Lord foreknew that he would exist; for to Him things not yet made are already made, according to what the Apostle says: ‘Who calls those things which are not as though they were’” (Romans 4). What is said of being sanctified in the womb, according to the Apostle, should be understood in the sense: “When it pleased Him who separated me from my mother’s womb and called me through His grace, to reveal His Son in me, so that I might preach Him among the Gentiles” (Galatians 1). Thus Jerome indicates that Jeremiah was sanctified in the same manner as Paul, that is, foreknown and foreordained by God for prophetic work. No one would say that Paul was sanctified within his mother’s womb—that is, justified through the grace of the Holy Spirit. Likewise Saint Augustine, in Letter 57 to Dardanus, says: “That sanctification of Jeremiah before he came forth from the womb, although some understand it as a type of the Savior, who had no need of regeneration, can nevertheless, even if it is understood of the prophet himself, suitably be taken according to predestination; just as the Gospel calls those who are regenerated children of God when Caiaphas, speaking about the Lord, had said: ‘It is expedient for you that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation should not perish.’ The Gospel immediately adds: ‘He did not say this of himself; but, being high priest that year, he prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation, and not for the nation only, but also to gather into one the children of God who were scattered abroad.’ He called ‘children of God’ those established not only among the Hebrew people but also among all the other nations—though they were not yet believers or baptized. How, then, could they be children of God except according to predestination, according to which the Apostle also says that God chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1)? That gathering into one was destined to make them children of God.” Thus Augustine. [Col. 0086B] I cannot adequately explain how what the Author says here can be true—namely, that it happened to Jeremiah alone to be sanctified before he was born—and I suspect that perhaps the word “alone” has slipped in, unless he is speaking only of the saints of the Old Testament. For if he understands sanctification as predestination and divine calling, as we have just explained, it was certainly common to all the prophets. But if he means internal sanctification through the grace of God infused into the soul, as he seems to suggest, it is also certain that John the Baptist was sanctified in that manner before he was born, as the angel says: “He will be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb” (Luke 1). Nothing need be said here of the Blessed Virgin or of the other saints. How, then, did it happen to one person—that is, to Jeremiah alone—to be sanctified before he was born?]

the prophet Jeremiah, to whom alone it happened in a very special way to be sanctified before he was born,

[Note: He is one of the four prophets who are called “greater” κατ’ ἐξοχήν—that is, “by eminence.” Apart from what is read in the Sacred Scriptures, Josephus writes about him in *Antiquities*, Book 10, chapters 6, 7, 10, and 11; Epiphanius, *On the Life and Death of the Prophets*, chapter 8; Jerome, commentary on Jeremiah, chapter 1; and Augustine, *City of God*, Book 18, chapter 33. It should be noted that the prophecy cited here under Jeremiah’s name is nevertheless taken from the Book of Baruch. This is indicated because Baruch was Jeremiah’s secretary and scribe, as is evident from Jeremiah 36. For this reason the ancient councils and Fathers did not place Baruch’s name in the canon, although the Fathers of the Council of Trent received him among the sacred authors (Session 4): they judged, namely, that this book formed part of Jeremiah’s prophecies. Thus Clement of Alexandria, *Paedagogus*, Book 1, chapter 10, cites under Jeremiah’s name the words of Baruch 3: “Hear, O Israel, the commandments of life.” He likewise cites Baruch 4: “We are blessed, O Israel, because what is pleasing to God has been made known to us.” Saint Basil, Book 4 *Against Eunomius*, and Saint John Chrysostom, in his sermon that Christ is God, bring forward this passage of Baruch 3 under Jeremiah’s name: “This is our God.” Saint Augustine, *City of God*, Book 18, chapter 33, citing the same passage, adds: “Some attribute this testimony not to Jeremiah but to his secretary, who was called Baruch. Nevertheless, it is more commonly regarded as Jeremiah’s.” Thus Augustine.]

He says: “This is our Lord; no other shall be accounted beside Him, who discovered every way of instruction and gave it to Jacob His servant and to Israel His beloved” (Baruch 3). “After this He appeared on earth and lived among human beings.”

“This, then,” he says, “is our God.” Do you see how the prophet points out God as though with a directing hand, and displays Him as though with a signifying finger? “This,” he says, “is our God.” Tell me, then: which God was the prophet at that time indicating by these signs and tokens? Was it perhaps the Father? And what need was there to point out Him whom everyone was believed to know? The Jews did not then fail to know God, for they lived under God’s law. Rather, the purpose was that they should recognize the Son of God as God. Therefore the prophet rightly said that the One who had discovered all instruction—that is, who had given the law—was to be seen on earth, that is, was to come in the flesh. Since the Jews had no doubt that the One who had given the law was God, they were to recognize as God the One who was to come in the flesh. They would hear that the One whom they believed to be God the Lawgiver was to be seen among human beings through the assumption of human flesh, while He Himself also promised through the prophet His own coming: “For I myself, who was speaking—behold, I am here” (Isaiah 52).

“Therefore,” he says, “no other shall be accounted by Sacred Scripture beside Him.” Beautifully, this prophet, foreseeing perverse doctrines, excluded every sense of heretical perversity when he said: “No other shall be accounted beside Him.” For He is the one who was born from God into God,

[Note: That is, God born from God. Hence in the Creed we say: “God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God.”]

at whose command the work of the universe came into being; whose will was the origin of created things; whose command is the structure of the world; who spoke all things, and they came to be; who commanded all things, and they were created.

This, then, is the one who spoke to the patriarchs, remained in the prophets, was conceived by the Spirit, was born from the Virgin Mary, appeared in the world,

lived among human beings,

[Note: He alludes to the Apostle’s words in Colossians 2: “Blotting out the handwriting of the decree that was against us, which was contrary to us, and He took it out of the way, fastening it to the cross,” and so forth. There the “handwriting” means the debt or guilt by which Adam, through eating the forbidden tree, had made himself and his descendants liable to eternal death, according to God’s decree: “At whatever hour you eat of it, you shall die” (Genesis 2).]

fastening to the wood of the cross the record of sins, triumphing in Himself, killing by death the powers hostile and opposed to us, granting to all the faith of resurrection, and destroying by the glory of His body the corruption of human flesh.

You see, therefore, that these things belong peculiarly to the Lord Jesus Christ. For this reason no other shall be accounted beside Him, since one God from God was born in this singular glory and blessedness.

The purpose of prophetic teaching at that time, therefore, was that the Only-Begotten should be recognized by all as the Son of God the Father [Lipsius in the margin: “should be said”]; and when they heard that no other God was to be accounted beside the Son, they would recognize that there is one God in the Father and the Son.

“After this,” he says, “He appeared on earth and lived among human beings.” Do you see that the Lord’s advent and birth are clearly indicated here? For did the Father ever—of whom it is written that He is visible only to the Son—appear on earth, or come forth in the flesh, or live among human beings? Certainly not. You understand, then, that all these things are said of the Son of God.

For when the prophet said that God was to be seen on earth, and no one other than the Son was seen on earth, the prophet undoubtedly spoke of the One whom subsequent events proved this statement to concern. Since he said that God was to be seen, he could truly have spoken of no other than the One who was afterward truly seen.

But enough of this for now; let us proceed to other matters.

[Note: These are the words of the eternal Father concerning the Son who was to come in the flesh and become the true Messiah, by which His divinity is plainly confirmed. Saint Jerome writes that there is no escape from the snares of this testimony. Although the preceding passage speaks of Cyrus, king of the Persians, what follows here in the same continuous context makes clear that these words refer not to Cyrus but to Christ. For, as Saint Jerome says, how could the words “Truly you are God, the hidden God, God of Israel, the Savior” suit the person of Cyrus? Therefore “God, in whom God is,” is more correctly and truly understood as our Lord Jesus Christ, who says in the Gospel: “I and the Father are one,” and “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 10; 14). He is called the hidden God because of the mystery of the body He assumed, and “God of Israel, the Savior,” which is interpreted as “Jesus.” Thus Jerome.]

The prophet Isaiah says: “The labor of Egypt and the commerce of Ethiopia, and the Sabaeans, men of stature, shall pass over to you, and they shall be yours. They shall walk behind you; bound with handcuffs they shall proceed, and they shall worship you and entreat you, because God is in you, and there is no God besides you.”

[Note: Thus Saint Jerome follows the Septuagint. From the Hebrew, however, the Vulgate reads: “Truly you are a hidden God, God of Israel, the Savior.” Because some, excessively devoted to Latin eloquence, translate this in such a way that instead of *Salvator* (“Savior”) they say *Servator* (“Preserver”), recoiling from the word *Salvator* as less Latin, I have thought it worthwhile to transcribe here the serious and useful judgment on this matter of the very learned John Molanus. He writes as follows in his annotations on Usuard, under the fifth day before the Kalends of March: “I am greatly astonished that certain writers and interpreters always avoid the noun *Salvator*, because Cicero says in the fourth speech against Verres: ‘And so I saw inscribed at Syracuse not only “patron” of this island but also “soter.”’ How significant is this? It is so great that it cannot be expressed in a single Latin word. A *soter*, of course, is one who gives salvation. Thus Cicero. But since being a *Servator* is one thing and being a *Salvator* another—for this is clear from Cicero’s passage, where he says that the one who gives salvation cannot be expressed in a single Latin word—we should prefer to use the word *Salvator*, which is much more common among ecclesiastical writers and expresses the office of our Savior Jesus Christ far more meaningfully than the word *Servator*. Nor should we attach much importance to Robert Estienne’s statement that learned men religiously avoid the word *Salvator* as insufficiently correct, just as they avoid the verb *salvo*, which they likewise judge not to be sufficiently Latin.” Thus far Molanus. Baronius approves and commends his opinion in his notes on the Martyrology under 9 November, and adds other observations agreeing with the same doctrine, which I leave the reader to consult, lest I become too lengthy.]

“For you are our God, and we did not know it, God of Israel, the Savior” (Isaiah 45).

How well the divine writings always agree with one another! The earlier prophet said: “This is our God”; this prophet says: “You are our God.” In the one there is divine instruction; in the other, human confession. The one expressed the role of a teacher instructing; the other, the role of a people confessing [or: confirming].

Imagine, then, the prophet Jeremiah teaching every day in the Church, as he does, and saying concerning the Lord Jesus Christ: “This is our God” (Baruch 3). What else would the whole Church answer, as it does, than what the other prophet said to the Lord Jesus: “You are our God”? Thus the former ignorance can rightly be joined to the present confession, when the people say: “You are our God, and we did not know it.”

Those who previously, occupied by demonic superstitions, did not know God can rightly say after turning to the faith: “You are our God, and we did not know it.”

## CHAPTER X. He proves Christ’s divinity both from the perfidy of the Judaizing Jews and from the confession of those who convert to faith in Christ.

[Col. 0089B] If you wish this same point to be proved for you especially from the person of the Jews, consider the peoples of the Jews after that wretched ignorance and impious persecution: turning to the faith and openly recognizing God; and see whether they can rightly say: “You are our God, and we did not know it.”

But I add something else, so that I may prove the point for you not only from Jews who confess, but also from those who deny. Ask those Jews who still persist in sacrilege whether they know or believe in God. They will certainly confess that they know and believe. But then ask whether they believe in the Son of God: they will assuredly deny and blaspheme.

You see, therefore, that the prophet spoke of the One whom the Jews have always failed to know and still fail to know—not of the One whom they think they believe in and confess. Therefore those who come from the Jews to the faith after their ignorance can rightly say: “You are our God, and we did not know it.”

[Note: That is, Jews who have converted to the faith and, having laid aside ignorance—that is, unbelief—recognize Christ as their God, whom previously they did not know or recognize.]

For those who believe after their ignorance rightly say that they did not know the One whom those who still do not believe insist that they do not know.

It is plain that those who confess after their ignorance say that previously they did not know Him whom those who deny Him still say they do not know.

## CHAPTER XI. He returns to Isaiah’s prophecy.

[Note: Saint Jerome, in his commentary on this passage, says: “That Egypt, the Ethiopians, and Saba, men of stature and height, served Him—no one doubts this, when he sees that the world has been subjected to Him and recognizes that, under the names of a few nations dwelling at the ends of the earth, all the regions of heaven and all the shores of the earth would believe in Him. Hence, beautifully, as though speaking of those laboring in the error of idolatry, the labor of Egypt is said to cease. For no nation was so devoted to idolatry and worshipped so many monstrous images as Egypt, of which we read above: ‘Behold, the Lord will ascend upon a swift cloud and will enter Egypt, and the idols of Egypt will be shaken at His presence, and the heart of Egypt will melt within it’ (Isaiah 19).”]

“The labor of Egypt and the commerce of Ethiopia, and the Sabaeans, men of stature, shall pass over to you” (Isaiah 45).

No one doubts that under these names of different nations the coming of the nations that would believe is signified. You cannot deny that the nations have passed over to Christ, since, having acquired [*indepto* for *adepto*, a frequent form in Cassian] the name “Christianity,” they passed over to the Lord Jesus Christ not only in faith but also in name itself.

For when they are called by the same name as what they are, what was a work of faith became the sacrament of a name.

[Note: That is, through faith in Christ they obtained the name “Christians,” which is the sign and sacrament of faith and religion. Saint Luke records in Acts that believers were first called by this name at Antioch (Acts 11). Saint Athanasius explains how this came about in his discourse against Arius as follows: “All who believed in our Lord Jesus Christ were called not Christians but merely disciples. And because many founders of new doctrines arose, opposing apostolic teaching, each called his followers disciples. There was no distinction of name between true and false disciples, whether they were followers of Christ, Dositheus, a certain Judas, or John—though they professed themselves to belong to the Church of Christ; rather, they were all counted under the single name ‘disciples.’ Then the apostles assembled, as the Acts narrated by Luke testifies, and called all the disciples by the single name ‘Christians,’ distinguishing them from the common designation ‘disciples’; and thus the word of the divine oracle through Isaiah was fulfilled, where it says in chapter 62: ‘My servants shall be called by a new name,’ and so forth.” Thus Athanasius.]

“To you,” he says, “they shall pass over, and they shall be yours; behind you they shall walk, bound with handcuffs they shall proceed.”

Just as there are bonds of constraint, so there are bonds of charity, according to what the Lord says:

[Note: The Vulgate edition reads: “With cords of Adam I will draw them, with bonds of charity” (Hosea 11). Instead of *Adam*, Aquila, Symmachus, the Septuagint, and Theodotion translated “human beings,” so that they read: “With cords of human beings I will draw them, with bonds of charity,” says Saint Jerome.]

“I drew them with bonds of charity” (Hosea 11).

Truly these bonds are great and ineffable bonds of charity; those who are bound by them rejoice in their chains. Do you wish to know that this is true? Hear the Apostle Paul rejoicing and exulting in his bonds when he says: “I beseech you, I who am bound in the Lord” (Ephesians 4). And again: “I beseech you, being such a one as Paul the old man, and now also a prisoner of Jesus Christ” (Philemon).

You see how greatly he rejoiced in the merit of his bonds,

[Note: Previously the words “and by their example God also provoked others” were read unnecessarily. For what place would “God” have here, when these things are said about the Apostle—as the syntax and connection of the words themselves show—who both rejoiced in the merit of his own bonds and by their example provoked others, namely, to endurance and to undertaking martyrdom for Christ? In the Basel edition the same error appears: “and by their example God also provoked us.” There, too, one word is omitted from the preceding phrase: “in which there is one love of the Lord.”]

by whose example he also provoked others.

There is no doubt that where the love of the Lord is one, the affection of the Lord’s binding is also one, according to the saying: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul” (Acts 4).

“They shall worship you and entreat you, because God is in you, and there is no God besides you.”

The Apostle clearly explained the prophet’s statement when he said: “For God was in Christ, reconciling the world to Himself”

[Note: “How?” asks Ambrose in his commentary on this passage. “As in a vicar or ambassador, as He was in the prophets, or in some other way?” It cannot be understood that He was in the Son in the same way as He was in the prophets, for the Son is naturally the Son of God the Father. Hence He says: “The Father is in me, and I am in the Father.” The Father is understood to be in the Son because they have one substance. For there is unity where there is no difference; and consequently they are in one another, since their image and likeness are one, so that whoever sees the Son is said to have seen the Father, just as the Lord Himself says: “Whoever sees me sees the Father.” Therefore it is rightly said: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to Himself,” and so forth (John 14). Thus Ambrose understands God the Father to be in Christ—that is, in the Son—and through Him to have reconciled the world, that is, the human race, to Himself. This also agrees with what precedes, where it says: “But all things are from God, who reconciled us to Himself through Christ.” There the person of the heavenly Father is plainly distinguished from the person of the Son, that is, Christ; the Father is designated as the one reconciled, and the Son as the reconciler.

Others, however, explain the passage differently, in this way: “God was in Christ,” that is, the Son of God was hypostatically united to the humanity of Christ. Accordingly, “God was in Christ” is equivalent to saying: “God was Christ, reconciling the world to Himself as God, and therefore to the whole most holy Trinity—but through Himself, that is, through His humanity.” By virtue of the communication of properties, the reconciliation of the world, which is the work of Christ the mediator, is attributed to God Himself. Likewise elsewhere it is said that God acquired the Church with His own blood (Acts 20), because of the communication of properties by which things proper to one nature are attributed to the other on account of the hypostatic union, as has often been stated.

The Author appears to have intended this interpretation, as is evident from the text; and Saint Leo explicitly conveys it in these words (*Sermon 18 on the Passion of the Lord*): “With the veil of flesh interposed, God was read as reconciling the world to Himself in Christ.” This can be understood only of the person of the Son.]

(2 Corinthians 5).

“In you, then, is God,” he says, “and there is no God besides you.”

The prophet rightly said, “In you is God,” and indicated not only the One who was present but also the One who was in the present one, showing the indweller as distinct from the One in whom He dwelt,

[Note: That is, not only the One who appeared visibly as a human being but also the One who was present in Him—God hidden within humanity. For the humanity was, as it were, the temple of divinity.]

distinguishing the natures without denying the unity.

[Note: That is, distinguishing the natures in Christ, not the persons. For when he addresses Christ as a human being and says, “In you is God,” he signifies that in Christ there is one nature of divinity and another of humanity, yet one person subsisting in both; the Word dwells in the flesh, and the flesh is inhabited by the Word.]

## CHAPTER XII. The title “Savior” is attributed to Christ in one way and to human beings in another.

You, he says, are God, and we did not know you, God of Israel, Savior. [Col. 0092A] Although Scripture had already indicated through many passages and evident signs whom he was speaking about, nevertheless he expressed the name of Christ most unmistakably in the title “Savior,” because the Savior is certainly the same as Christ, as the angel says: “For today a Savior has been born for you, who is Christ the Lord” (Luke II).

[Note: [Col. 0091C] St. Jerome, in his commentary on Matthew I: “Jesus” is called “Savior” in the Hebrew language. Thus the Evangelist indicated the etymology of his name when he said: “You shall call his name [Col. 0091D] Jesus,” because “he himself will save his people.” Cyril, in Catechesis 10: “Jesus,” he says, “is truly called by this name because he derives his designation from saving medicine.” Thus, among the Hebrews, Jesus means “savior”; in the Greek language it signifies “physician,” since he is both physician of bodies and healer of souls. Finally, St. Augustine, in his Meditations (chapter 39), repeatedly inculcates the same etymology in these words: “For what is Jesus except Savior? Therefore, for your own sake, Jesus, be Jesus to me.” Yet St. Peter, prince of the apostles, taught this more explicitly and sublimely when he said (Acts IV): “Let it be known to all of you that there is salvation in no one else except in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ; for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved.”

Moreover, concerning this most holy name of Jesus, several other considerations suited to this passage are available. First, it must be presupposed, following the teaching of St. Thomas (III, q. 37, a. 2), that the names commonly imposed upon individual human beings derive either from some property of the person receiving the name; or from the time of naming, as certain saints’ names are given to those born on their feasts; or from relationship, as when a son is given his father’s name; or from someone in the family, as when the relatives of John the Baptist wished to call him by the name of his father, Zechariah, rather than John, because no one in his family was called by that name, as Luke I relates; or even from an event, as when Joseph named his firstborn Manasseh, saying: “God has made me forget all my labors”; or from some quality of the person receiving the name, as Genesis XXV says that, because the first one to emerge from his mother’s womb was red and entirely hairy like a hide, his name was called Esau, which is interpreted as “red.”

Names, however, that are divinely imposed upon people always signify some gratuitous gift divinely bestowed upon them. Thus in Genesis XVII it was said to Abraham: “You shall be called Abraham, because I have made you the father of many nations.” And in Matthew XVI it was said to Peter: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church.” Since, therefore, this gift of grace had been conferred upon Christ—that through him all should be saved—his name was suitably called Jesus, that is, “Savior.” The angel foretold this name not only to his mother, but also to Joseph, who was to be his foster-father. Thus St. Thomas.

Second, it must be noted that this name Jesus was imposed upon the Lord Christ as a proper and personal name, and that it is the new and singular name of which Isaiah had prophesied (chapter LXII): “You shall be called by a new name, which the mouth of the Lord will name.” Although we read that many others before him were called by this name—among whom the principal ones are Jesus son of Nun, Joshua XI; Jesus son of Jehozadak the priest, Haggai I; and Jesus son of Sirach, whose book is called Ecclesiasticus—nevertheless, if we attend to what this name signifies, it is certain that the name belongs to the Lord Christ alone, and was attributed to him by a proper and singular right and reason. He alone was to bring salvation by himself, through his own power and merit—not only to bodies but also to souls, and not merely temporary salvation but, above all, eternal salvation—and not to one or two nations and peoples alone, but to all. The angel disclosed this reason and meaning when he said: “For he himself will save his people from their sins” (Matthew I). [Col. 0092D]

Interpreting that passage of Isaiah, Cyril says: “The new name for the divine Word is Jesus, and it coincides with the birth according to the flesh. For to others the name was in a certain sense common, and certainly ordinary; but to Christ it was proper, and, as the prophet foretold (Isaiah LXII), new and singular, because, in the sense in which it is spoken of Christ, it belongs to no one else, since there is salvation in no one else.”

Explaining the same etymology of the name, divinely delivered by the angel and proper and particular to Christ, St. Jerome, cited above, says: “He saves not unbelievers, but his own people—that is, those who believe in him. And he saves not so much from visible enemies as from invisible ones: he saves from sins, not by fighting with weapons, but by forgiving sins.” St. Chrysostom likewise comments on the same passage: “For he himself will save,” and so forth. “The angel,” he says, “announces that the people will be delivered not from visible war, nor from the sword of barbarians, but from their sin—which is far greater. This was never possible for any human being to accomplish.” St. Anselm likewise says in *Cur Deus Homo*: “He will save not from bodily enemies, as Joshua and David did, but from sins; and this belongs not to human beings, but to God alone.” Hence Hosea says: “I will save them in the Lord their God, and I will not save them by bow, or sword, or war, or horses, or horsemen.”

Finally, St. Thomas, who habitually gathers together the very marrow of all the Fathers, says: “It must be said that, for those who lived before Christ, the name Jesus could be fitting according to some other reason—for example, because they brought some particular and temporal salvation. But according to the reason of spiritual and universal salvation, this name is proper to Christ; and in this respect it is called a new name” (III, q. 37, a. 2). Thus he.

This, therefore, is Christ’s proper name, by which both the divine and human nature and the supreme office of the Redeemer are declared. This is the name given to him which is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth (Philippians II). Accordingly, some have rightly observed that, when the Evangelists wish to call our Savior by his proper name, they call him not Christ but Jesus, as in Matthew I, Luke I, II, III, and elsewhere. For “Christ” is the name of his office, while “Jesus” is the name of his nature and person. Thus Jesus is the name, and Christ the surname.

Third, it must be noted that in this name the remaining names—both proper and metaphorical—that are attributed to the Messiah in Scripture are contained by virtue. For it contains the properties and powers of all the names; hence it is rightly called by some the epitome of all Christ’s works and benefits.

St. Thomas explains this theologically and in his customary manner (*in the place cited above*) in these words:

“In all those names [placed in the argument], this name Jesus, which signifies salvation, is signified in a certain way. For in the name ‘Emmanuel,’ which is interpreted ‘God with us’ (Isaiah VII), the cause of salvation is designated: the union of the divine and human natures in the person of the Son of God, through which it came about that God was with us, as a sharer in our nature.

“By the words ‘Call his name, hasten; strip off the spoil,’ and so forth (Isaiah VIII), the one from whom he saved us is designated—namely, the devil, whose spoils he stripped away, according to the passage in Colossians II: ‘Stripping principalities and powers, he led them openly in triumph,’ and so forth.
