“But by the words ‘His name shall be called Wonderful,’ and so forth, the way and goal of our salvation are designated: namely, that by the wonderful counsel and power of the divinity we are led to the inheritance of the age to come, in which there will be the perfect peace of the children of God under God as their ruler.

“Furthermore, what is said, ‘Behold, a man; the East is his name’ (Zechariah VI), refers to the same thing as the first expression—namely, to the mystery of the Incarnation, according to which light has risen in the darkness for the upright of heart (Psalm CXI).”

Thus far St. Thomas.

More concerning the glorious name of Jesus may be seen in the same author’s *Opusculum* 60, and in St. Bernard’s sermons 14 and 15 on the *Song of Songs*, and in the Abulensis on Exodus XX, question 7. Among more recent authors, see Salmeron, volume III, *On the Infancy of the Savior*, treatise 37, and Serrarius, book I on Joshua, chapter II.]

“For Jesus,” there can be no doubt, “is interpreted ‘Savior’ in Hebrew,” just as the angel declares to the holy Virgin Mary, saying: “And you shall call his name Jesus; for he himself will save his people from their [Col. 0093A] sins” (Luke I and Matthew I).

[Note: [Col. 0093D] From these words the Fathers rightly conclude against the Arians and Nestorians that Christ is true God, because it belongs to God alone to forgive sins, or to free people from sins, by his own authority and power, according to Isaiah XLIII: “I am, I am he who blots out iniquities.” Thus Severianus, bishop of Gabala, in his commentary on Matthew I, as quoted by St. Thomas in the *Catena*: “Let those who ask who he is whom Mary bore come and hear: ‘For he himself will save his people.’ From what? From their sins. He is God, who forgives sins. If you do not believe Christians, believe unbelievers, or Jews, who say: ‘No one can forgive sins except God alone’ (Luke V).”

Origen, *Homily 39 on Various Subjects*: “‘For he himself will save his people from their sins.’ Through this word two things are clearly indicated: that he is true God and true man, and that his people are to be saved by him. Therefore it was said: ‘For he himself will save his people from their sins,’ as true God. For it belongs to divine power to save from sin or to forgive sins.”

Theophylact likewise briefly concludes: “He will save his people from their sins. Hence it is clear that the one who will be born is God, for it belongs to God alone to pardon sins.” We have noted similar passages from Chrysostom and Anselm above. Finally, let St. Thomas be added, who was accustomed to gather together the essence of all the Fathers: “Observe,” he says (on Matthew I), “that Nestorius is confuted here. He said that those things which belong to God—such as existing from eternity, being omnipotent, and the like—do not belong to that man. Behold, that very man who was born of the Virgin and is called Jesus will himself save his people from their sins. Since no one except God alone can forgive sins, it must be said that this man is God, and that the things belonging to God truly belong to him.”]

And lest you should perhaps call him “Savior” in the same manner in which that title was applied to others: “The Lord raised up for them a savior” [Note: [Col. 0094C] There are similar passages in which the name “Savior” is attributed to human beings. 4 Kings XIII: “The Lord saw the distress of Israel, and the Lord gave Israel a savior.” Likewise Ezra IX: “They cried to you, and you heard from heaven, and according to your many mercies you gave them a savior who saved them from the hand of their enemies.” From these passages we must conclude—and this bears on the interpretation of the present passage—that there are two kinds of saviors. One is supreme and primary, namely God; the others are secondary, being servants and cooperators of that supreme Savior. Jesus, therefore, insofar as he is God, is the primary Savior, dependent on no one; insofar as he is man, he is indeed secondary, but in that category he surpasses all others both in effectiveness and in dignity. Concerning the terms “Savior” and “Preserver,” see what was said above (chapter 9).]—“and he raised up for them Othniel son of Kenaz” [Note: [Col. 0094D] This was the first of the twelve Judges who governed the people of Israel after Joshua’s death; their history is contained in the sacred Book of Judges. He is called the brother of Caleb, or rather Caleb’s nephew through his brother.] (Judges III). And again: “The Lord raised up for them a savior” [Note: [Col. 0094D] This concerns Ehud, who is named as the second among the same judges and is discussed elsewhere.]—“Ehud son of Gera” (ibid.). He added: “For he himself will save his people from their sins” (Matthew I).

It is not within human power to redeem a people from captivity to sin; this is possible only for him of whom it was said: “Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who takes away the sins [Col. 0094A] of the world” (John I). For the others saved not their own people but God’s, and not from sins but from enemies.

## CHAPTER XIII. The persons whom the prophet Isaiah represented in the words, “You are our God, and we did not know you,” are explained.

“You are therefore,” he says, “our God, and we did not know you, God of Israel, Savior” (Isaiah XLV).

[Note: [Col. 0094D] This is correct according to the Greek version, which the author follows and strongly presses; it is not so according to the Latin, which has: “Truly you are a hidden God,” whereas they translated the phrase as “and we did not know it,” referring it to Jews and Gentiles. In our text, however, the words are attributed to God the Father and directed by him to the Son, as stated above. In either form the passage is clear and effective for proving Christ’s divinity; yet it appears more effective in the Vulgate edition, which St. Jerome and the other Fathers followed.]

Whom do you think is more likely to say this? To whom do you think it was more appropriate? To the Jews, or to the Gentiles?

If to the Jews: the Jews certainly did not know Christ, according to the words: “But Israel did not know me, and my people did not understand” (Isaiah I), and also: “The world was made through him, and the world did not know him; he came to his own, and his own did not receive him” (John I).

But if to the Gentiles: it is obvious that the Gentile world, occupied with idols, did not know Christ, although it did not know the Father either. Yet even if it now knows him, it knows him only through Christ.

You see, therefore, that whether the believing people is from the Gentiles or from the Jews, each rightly says on its own behalf: “You are our God, and we did not know you, God of Israel, Savior.” For the Gentiles, who previously worshiped idols, were ignorant of God; and the Jews, who denied the Lord, [Col. 0095B] were ignorant of the Son of God. Accordingly, both groups rightly say of Christ: “You are our God, and we did not know you.” For both those who did not believe were ignorant of God, and those who denied the Son of God were ignorant of him.

Thus Christ must be believed as the truth speaks, as the divinity bears witness, and as Christ himself, who is both, finally proclaims. Why, unhappy madness, do you attempt to insert something between God and Christ? Why do you seek to separate his body from the Son of God, and attempt to divide God himself from himself? You tear apart what has been united and distinguish what has been joined.

Believe concerning God from the Word of God. For you will be able to confess God’s divinity in no way better than by confessing with your own voice those very things concerning him that the Divinity has taught.

[Note: [Col. 0095B] Thus corrected from the Basel edition, where the conjunction “if,” which is entirely necessary, is nevertheless lacking. For the author refers to the preceding words, namely “united” and “joined”—that is, God and man in Christ—which Nestorius nevertheless divided and separated.]

Know, then, according to the prophet, that the Lord himself is God, who discovered every path of knowledge; he was also seen on earth and lived among human beings. He brought the light of faith into the world; he displayed the light of salvation. For God the Lord has shone upon us. Believe in him, then; love him; confess him.

For [Note: [Col. 0095B] This refers, namely, to the universal judgment, when we shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive according to what he has done, whether good or evil (2 Corinthians V). Those words signify both the manifestation of Christ’s divinity—which will then become especially and openly known to all, when every knee shall bow before him, as in Isaiah XLV, to which passage the Apostle alluded in Romans XIV—and the judicial authority given to Christ as man by the Father, by whom he was appointed judge of the living and the dead (Acts X). For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father (John V). “And he gave him authority to execute judgment because he is the Son of Man,” that is, insofar as he is man, as St. Augustine explains; for, he says, insofar as he is the Son of God, he has always possessed it (Tractate 9 on John and Sermon 64 on the Words of the Lord). See St. Thomas, III, questions 58 and 59, article 2.]

When, as it is written, every knee shall bow before him—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—and every tongue shall confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father (Philippians II), whether you wish it or not, you will not be able to deny that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father.

For this is the perfect power of a perfect confession: always to confess God and the Lord Jesus Christ in the glory of God the Father. Amen.

# BOOK FIVE

[Col. 0095]

## CHAPTER I. He vehemently attacks the error of the Pelagianists, who affirmed that Christ was a solitary man.

[Col. 0095C]

We said in the First Book [Note: [Col. 0095D] This means the Nestorian heresy, which he also shows to be a disciple and imitator of the Pelagian heresy in Book I, chapter 2, where he says that Nestorius teaches precisely what the Pelagianists had previously taught, and therefore is not the author of a new heresy but the restorer of an old one. Hence it is also said below that the heresy of Nestorius, newly arisen in the time of Cassian, revived, as it were, the ashes of Pelagian depravity. St. Prosper likewise says in his *Chronicle*, concerning the conspiracy of the Pelagians with Nestorius and the similar condemnation that followed:

“When a synod of more than two hundred bishops had assembled at Ephesus, Nestorius was condemned together with the entire heresy bearing his name and with many Pelagians who were supporting a doctrine akin to his.”

The same is attested by an elegant epitaph on the condemned Pelagian heresy, buried together with the Nestorian heresy, published by Prosper himself (*Book On the Ungrateful*), which begins as follows:

“The Nestorian plague succeeded the Pelagian,

which was nevertheless begotten in my womb.

Unhappy mother of a wretched daughter,

I sprang from the very seed that I bore.”

We have said more about the affinity and kinship of these two heresies above. The author also repeats the point in the following chapter.]

that heresy, the disciple and imitator of the Pelagian heresy, had attempted and struggled by every means to make the Son of God, the Lord Jesus Christ, born of a virgin, be believed to be merely a solitary man; and that afterward, having taken the path of virtue, he had obtained this by living piously and religiously, so that through this holiness of life he became worthy for the divine majesty to be joined to him. Thus, with the dignity of his sacred origin entirely excluded from him, only the choice based on merits would remain for him.

Since they were striving and laboring to assert this, they said that whatever he had merited by living well could be merited by all human beings, as though he had been sent down [Note: [Col. 0096D] That is, reduced to the common lot and condition of human beings, with divinity removed from him as though it were a title of nobility. The author alludes to the Roman custom, according to which many plebeians were made from patricians, and conversely patricians from plebeians. The former were said to be “sent into the plebs,” that is, relegated to the common people or the dregs of the population, because of cowardice or disgrace.] into the plebeian mass of all people, and as though he had been incorporated into the crowd of the human race.

This was a pestilential and deadly assertion which, detracting from the true God and making a false promise to human beings, was condemnable as a wicked lie in both respects: it injured God by sacrilegious insult and led human beings into the hope of false presumption.

It was a most perverse and impious assertion [Note: [Col. 0097C] That is, attributing to mortal man what does not belong to him—namely, the ability to attain divinity through his own merits.] granting to mortality what it did not possess and taking away from God what he did possess.

This recent heresy, therefore, which has now arisen from that destructive and deadly perversity, reviving its ashes as it were, kindled a new fire from ancient embers. For it asserts that the Lord Jesus Christ was born as a solitary man.

Why, then, should we need to inquire whether the same perversity that exists at the head of this one crime is also found in what follows? It is pointless to await the later portions to discover what a thing is when, at the beginning, it has left no reason at all for waiting. What purpose is there in investigating whether it makes the same promise to man as the earlier heresy—which is a monstrous crime—while taking the same thing away from God? Thus, when we see what has preceded, it is almost impious to ask what follows, as though some reason could be brought forward later by which one who denied God might prove himself not to be impious.

Therefore, as we have often already said, the new heresy claims that the Lord Jesus Christ was merely a solitary man, born from a virgin; and therefore [Note: [Col. 0097C] St. Leo, in Letter 97 to the emperor Leo: “Let Nestorius be anathematized, who believed that blessed Mary was the mother not of God but only of a man, thereby making one person of the flesh and another of the divinity.” Gregory of Nazianzus likewise says in his first letter to Cledonius: “If anyone does not believe that the Virgin Mary is truly the Mother of God, let him also be separated from the divinity.” Finally, at the general Council of Ephesus, these two points above all were defined against Nestorius: first, that Christ is one person, not two; second, that the Virgin Mary should truly and properly be called Θεοτόκος and not Χριστοτόκος—that is, “God-bearer” and not “Christ-bearer”—not because she was not Christ-bearer, but lest she be thought to be only Christ-bearer and not God-bearer, which was Nestorius’s position.

Concerning the terms θεοτόκος and χριστοτόκος we have treated above. It should be noted, however, that although blessed Mary is the true and natural Mother of God, because she gave birth to Christ, who is not only man but also God, she nevertheless is not, and cannot be called, the mother of divinity, nor can she be said to have given birth to divinity or deity, as St. Thomas teaches in these words:

“Although Deity and God do not differ in reality, they differ according to their mode of signification. For ‘Deity’ signifies the divine nature in the abstract, and therefore cannot stand for a person. But ‘God,’ because it signifies the divine nature in a concrete manner—that is, as possessing divinity—can make a statement true of a suppositum. Therefore, because the blessed Virgin is the mother of the Son of God, she can be called the mother of God, but not the mother of divinity.”

Thus St. Thomas (III, distinction 4, question 2, article 2).]

it says that Mary ought to be called Christotocon, not Theotocon, because she is the mother of Christ, not of God.

Moreover, it adds to its sacrilegious assertion arguments as perverse as they are frivolous, saying: “No one gives birth to one who existed before him.” As though the birth of the only-begotten God, foretold by the prophets and announced from the ages, were to be handled or assessed by human reasoning!

Or as though Mary the Virgin herself—whoever you are, heretical accuser—had accomplished and completed by her own powers what took place in her childbirth, so that human weakness could be brought forward against her in so great a matter and so great a work.

If, therefore, something in this matter was accomplished through human activity, seek human explanations. But if everything that took place was the work of God’s power, why do you consider human impossibility where you see divine efficacy?

But we shall speak more fully about this later. For now, let us complete what we began to say a little earlier, so that all may know that you seek fires among the Pelagian ashes [Note: [Col. 0097D] The reading does not mean “to seek,” as it was printed previously. Nestorius is being addressed here, and the words refer to what precedes: “reviving the ashes,” and so forth. These are elegant metaphors and synonymous phrases: “to revive ashes,” “to kindle a new fire from ancient embers,” “to seek fires among the Pelagian ashes,” and “to stir up ancient embers with new gusts of sacrilege.” Related expressions occur in the following chapter: “to spew out Pelagian poison” and “to hiss with the Pelagian spirit.”] and stir up ancient embers with new gusts of sacrilege.

## CHAPTER II. The doctrine of Nestorius is connected and closely allied with the Pelagian error.

You therefore say that Christ was born merely as a solitary man. This is precisely what the heresy of Pelagian impiety, which we clearly exposed in the First Book, also preached: that Christ was born merely as a solitary man.

Moreover, you add that the Lord himself, Jesus of all [Note: [Col. 0098C] I do not know whether the reader will tolerate the word “image” here, and again below in the next chapter, since it is sufficiently clear from what has been said and from the text itself that it is superfluous and was inserted into the text through ignorance of the Greek word θεοδόχον or through the incompetence of copyists. For Theodochon must be read, not Theotocon, as I demonstrated above. This word—namely, Theodochos—means nothing other than “receiver of God,” or one who receives or accepts God, just as above he called Christ’s flesh Theodochon, that is, the receiver of divinity.

And again below: “And through this all are Theodochi,” with no consideration or mention of “image,” because it has nothing to do with the matter—unless one interprets “Christ theodochon image” as “Christ, the image who receives God,” called by Nestorius. Yet I have not read this expression in any other author, nor can I easily persuade myself that it was used by him, since no question concerning an image was raised, but rather concerning divinity.

Nevertheless, because both the Basel and Plantin editions have it in this form, I did not wish to delete it here or below. I have been content to warn the reader about the matter, leaving everyone free to judge for himself.

Furthermore, lest anyone rashly suppose that Theodochon was changed into Theotocon, the distinction indicated above among these three closely related words should be recalled: Theotocos, Theotocos, and Theodochos. Some authorities must be brought forward concerning each.

It should therefore be noted that compounds or derivatives from τίκτω or τόκος, when used passively, are proparoxytones—that is, they are accented on the antepenultimate syllable; when used actively, they are accented on the penultimate syllable. This is undisputed among all grammarians.

Thus “Theotocos” (Θεοτόκος), a word extremely common among the Greek Fathers, signifies “parent of God”; it is also written “Theotocos” and “Theoutocos” (see Damascene, Book III of the *Orthodox Faith*, chapter 12). Poets often use these latter two forms for the sake of meter. Thus Nonnus, in his commentary on John, chapter 1:

> Παρθενίκη Χριστοῖο θεουτόκος ἵκετο μήτηρ.

“A virgin, the God-bearing mother of Christ, came.”

And again, chapter 2:

> Παρθένος ὡμάρτησε θεουτόκος υἱεῖ μήτηρ.

“The Virgin followed her son, the God-bearing mother.”

“Theotocos” (Θεότοκος), however, is understood as “begotten by God,” as Henry Stephanus teaches from other similar compounds. The same distinction applies to Prototocos [read πρωτότοκος] and Prototocos [read πρωτοτόκος] (Isidore of Pelusium, Letter I, letter 31).

For Prototocos means “firstborn.” Luke II has ἔτεκε τὸν υἱὸν αὐτῆς τὸν πρωτότοκον: “She gave birth to her firstborn son.” And in Colossians I, πρωτότοκος πάσης κτίσεως: “the firstborn of all creation”—that is, begotten before every creature, or he whom God the Father begot before he made anything, from the beginning, as Scripture explains (Proverbs VIII).

The same word occurs there and in Revelation I, Ὁ πρωτότοκος ἐκ τῶν νεκρῶν, “the firstborn from the dead”; for this our translator renders in the latter passage “the firstborn of the dead”—that is, the one who first of all rose from death by his own power, or the first of those rising to immortal life, that is, to a resurrection not followed by death.

Prototocos, however, means “the one who first gave birth.” From Homer’s *Iliad*, book P:

> Πρωτοτόκος, κινύρη, οὐ πρὶν εἰδυῖα τόκοιο

“Firstborn, lamenting, though previously unacquainted with childbirth.”

Hence πρωτοτοκέω, “to give birth for the first time.”

Theodochos, moreover, is one who receives or accepts God, as has been said; it is also written Theodocos. For compounds from δέχομαι admit both κ and χ. Thus we have Xenodochos, “host,” or Xenodocos, and ξενοδοχεῖν, “to receive,” from which *xenodochium* is derived; and θεουδόκος occurs poetically, as above when Nonnus speaks of Mary Magdalene in his commentary on John, chapter 11:

[Col. 0099C]

> Χριστοῦ καλλιέθειρα θεουδόχος, ἣ πόδας αὐτοῦ  
> Ἀμφοτέρους ἤλειψε.

“Christ’s beautiful-haired guest of God, who anointed both his feet.”

[The supplied source ends here, with the sentence and the surrounding discussion incomplete.]

He anointed both. These grammatical remarks concerning these three words, made grammatically for the occasion of this passage and set out for the less learned—or, if I may say so, the foolish—to whom, just as to the wise, we are debtors according to the Apostle’s saying, will, I hope, be received with fairness and goodwill by fair-minded readers.

They think, then, that Christ should be called a θεοδόχος (*Theodochos*), “an image,” that is, not God but one who receives God—namely, that he should be honored not on his own account, because he is God, but because he receives God within himself. This, indeed, was also asserted by that heresy of which I spoke earlier:

> [Col. 0099C] The question of Christ’s adoration, or the worship to be offered to him, was also raised by the Nestorians themselves. For those who posited two persons in Christ, establishing God and man as one and another, likewise maintained that a twofold adoration, or veneration, was to be offered: one, as to a man; the other separately, as to God. This, as contrary to the Catholic faith, was rightly condemned by the decrees of the general councils. For thus runs the eighth canon of the Council of Ephesus, held against Nestorius: “If anyone dares to say that the assumed man is to be co-adored with God the Word and co-glorified, as though one were another, and does not rather worship Emmanuel with one adoration and offer him one glorification, according to the fact that the Word became flesh, let him be anathema.”
>
> Again, the ninth canon of the Council of Constantinople decreed as follows: “If anyone says that Christ is to be adored in two natures, thereby introducing two adorations, separately for God the Word and separately for the man, and does not adore God the Word incarnate with one adoration together with his flesh, according to what has been handed down from the beginning to the holy Church of God, let him be anathema.”
>
> The Fathers likewise present this doctrine as Catholic against the Nestorians. Among them Cyril, in his letter to Nestorius, says: “Thus we confess Christ to be one God and man, not adoring the man together with the Word, lest a kind of division be introduced, but adoring one and the same, because the body is not alien to the Word, with which he himself also sits beside the Father.”
>
> These were his words against Nestorius, whose statements were commonly reported as follows: “Because of him who put on the man, I venerate him who was clothed; because of the invisible one, I adore the visible one.” Similar statements are found elsewhere in Cyril (Letters 10 and 29): “Because of the one who was hidden, I adore him who appeared. God is inseparable from him who appeared; therefore I do not separate the honor of him who is not separated. I separate the natures, but I unite the adoration.” This was Nestorius.
>
> In these words there is a sufficiently evident indication of two hypostases, or persons, when he says that, because of the hidden one, he adores him who appeared—as though one person in Christ were hidden and another manifest: that is, one person of the hidden God and another of the appearing man. Yet that cunning man most artfully pretended a certain unity of adoration—not because he considered the one adoration to belong to one person, but because he did not wish the adoration of one to be distinguished from the adoration of the other. Thus, while one was adored, the other too would be adored, because of the closest conjunction, as he said, of one with the other, though not a hypostatic and substantial conjunction.
>
> This is what the Author indicates was asserted by Nestorius in this passage: that Christ should not be worshiped on his own account—as if he were saying that Christ the man should not be worshiped on his own account, but because of the God dwelling within him, personally distinct from him though most closely joined to him.
>
> For a fuller elucidation of this passage, it should first be known that the whole doctrine concerning Christ’s adoration consists in two points. The first is that Christ, or the person of Christ subsisting in the divine and human natures, is to be adored with that most perfect adoration of *latria* with which the whole Trinity and the individual divine persons are adored.
>
> [Col. 0100C] That this must be held with certain faith is clear from Scripture. For Christ, speaking of himself, says in John 5: “That all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father.” And Paul, in Romans 4, explains concerning Christ that saying of Isaiah 45: “Every knee shall bow to me”—which, no one doubts, was spoken of the adoration due to God alone. In the same sense he says in Philippians 2: “At the name of Jesus every knee should bow.” And the Apostle Thomas, adoring Christ, said: “My Lord and my God” (John 20). In the same faith the blind man, illuminated by Christ, fell down and adored him (John 9). So too did the centurion, whose faith Christ so greatly commended (Matthew 9).
>
> In Hebrews 1 the Apostle cites those words from Psalm 95: “And let all his angels adore him.” It is certain there that the adoration proper to God alone is meant. For the preceding words are: “Let all who adore graven images be confounded, and those who glory in their idols.” There idolatry is set against the worship of God. The Fathers understand the adoration offered to Christ by the Magi in the same way, as they sufficiently professed by their gifts (Matthew 2).
>
> Finally, in Revelation 5 and 22, all the saints adore the slain Lamb in this manner; and to him and to the one seated on the throne all sing together: “Blessing, and honor, and power, forever and ever.” In short, whatever proves Christ the man also to be true God proves consequently that he is to be adored by reason of the hypostatic union and the communication of properties of both natures, as was said. Hence Athanasius, Augustine, and other Fathers writing against the Arians conclude from this adoration—which Scripture establishes as due to Christ the Lord—as from a sign, or *a posteriori*, that he is true God.
>
> The second point is that Christ’s humanity is to be adored simultaneously and with the same adoration as the Word. That is, Christ’s human nature and its parts, body and soul, are not to be worshiped with an adoration different from that due to the Word, as the Nestorians taught, but with exactly the same adoration as is offered to God. Thus teach Thomas (Part III, question 25, articles 1 and 2) and other Doctors after the Master (Book III, distinction 9).
>
> Two reasons are assigned for this doctrine. The first is the unity of the person in Christ. Honor is properly offered to the whole subsisting reality, that is, to the hypostasis or person; and since there is only one person in Christ, one honor or adoration is likewise due to the whole Christ—namely, that which they call *latria*. Thus Augustine judges that the worship due to God alone should be expressed in a single formula (Book X of *The City of God*, chapter 1).
>
> We must not, then, venerate the human nature in Christ separately, but insofar as it has become the nature of the Word. When we offer honor to it, we thereby venerate the Word whose nature it is. Thus Augustine says in Sermon 58 on the Words of the Lord: “I adore the Lord’s flesh, indeed the perfect humanity in Christ, for this reason: it was assumed by the divinity and united to the Godhead, so that I may confess not one God and another, but one and the same God and man, the Son of God,” and so forth.
>
> In his exposition of Psalm 98, he explains those words concerning Christ, “Adore his footstool,” understanding the footstool to mean Christ’s humanity; Cassiodorus follows him there. Likewise Damascene (*Orthodox Faith*, Book IV, chapter 3) says that Christ’s flesh is in itself not to be adored, but that, as joined to the Word, it is to be worshiped with the same adoration. “For,” he says, “we do not adore bare flesh, but the flesh of God—that is, the incarnate Word.”
>
> To this may be added the Council of Trent (session 13, chapter 5 and canon 5), which defined that the sacrament of the Eucharist is to be adored with *latria* because of Christ’s divine and human presence:

> “No room for doubt remains that all Christ’s faithful, according to the custom received in the Catholic Church, should offer to this most holy sacrament in veneration the worship of *latria*, which is due to the true God. Nor is it to be adored any less for having been instituted by Christ the Lord to be received. For we believe that the same God is present in it whom the eternal Father, when introducing him into the world, says: ‘And let all the angels of God adore him’ (Psalm 96; Hebrews 1). He is the one whom the Magi, falling down, adored; and finally, Scripture testifies that he was adored by the Apostles in Galilee (Matthew 2; Matthew 28; Luke 24).”

> [Col. 0101D] From this we understand that, in the sacrament of the altar, not Christ’s divinity alone but also his humanity is adored, and that adoration is directly exercised with respect to the humanity. For the priest handles the Lord’s body not merely as the body of a man, but as what it truly is, the body of God himself; and all that adoration must be judged to belong not to *dulia* but to *latria*. Hence the Apostle says that whoever receives this sacrament unworthily is guilty of the body and blood of the Lord (1 Corinthians 11)—that is, guilty of having violated the divine majesty, whose worship and reverence he profanes by sacrilegious contact with and use of the Lord’s body and blood.

> The other reason is that, in the offering of honors, the dignity of the person is considered; and this is assessed according to what is nobler and more excellent. Since, therefore, the dignity of Christ’s person consists above all in his being God, this must be considered in honoring him, rather than only what is less noble. Accordingly, someone who honored Christ merely as a man, disregarding his divine majesty, would inflict an injury upon the dignity of the person rather than honor it—just as if someone venerated a bishop only as a teacher of the arts.
>
> It also follows that, although Christ intercedes for us with the Father, since invocation by which we implore his help is an act of honor, and honor regards what is more excellent in the person, it is not properly said to Christ, “Pray for us,” but, “Son of God, have mercy on us.”
>
> It should further be noted that the proposition “Christ is not to be worshiped on his own account” is amphibological and can have two meanings. One is Nestorian and heretical: Christ is not to be worshiped on his own account with the adoration of *latria*, which is due to God alone, because he is not himself God but a mere man, other than God though closely joined to him. By reason of this conjunction—which is not substantial but accidental—the man himself would be worshiped together with God and would share in a kind of similar veneration.
>
> The Fathers condemned the proposition in this sense because it would divide Christ and separate him from God, as is clear from what has been said. The other sense is Catholic and true: Christ the man is not to be worshiped and adored on his own account, that is, by reason of his humanity, but by reason of the divine hypostasis in which the human nature subsists, or because he is the same true God and man. Thus the whole basis of the adoration due to Christ is to be regarded as arising not from the humanity itself but from the divinity united to it. By virtue of that union, the adoration offered to Christ overflows upon and likewise embraces his humanity.
>
> This is what the Fathers mean when they say that Christ’s humanity or flesh is to be adored not considered separately, but as united to the Word, and so forth. Therefore, when we pray in the Church’s prayer, “Soul of Christ, sanctify me,” we do not ask sanctification—which is God’s work—from the soul alone as its author, but from Christ himself, through the merit of his soul. Similarly, from his blood we ask that he wash us: that is, from Christ himself, through the merit of his Passion, in which he shed his blood, or through the sacrament of the altar, under which his soul, blood, and flesh are contained (Gabriel Vásquez, *On the First Part*, disputation 96, article 5). But enough of this.

[Col. 0101A] Christ should not be worshiped on his own account, namely because he was God, but because by good and pious actions he had merited having God within himself. You see, therefore, that you are spewing forth Pelagian poison and hissing with a Pelagian spirit. Accordingly, it is fitting that, as regards you, he should be regarded not so much as awaiting judgment as already judged; for since you share the same error, you must necessarily be believed to share the same condemnation. Not to mention, meanwhile, that by comparing the Lord with an imperial statue, you have burst into such sacrilegious impiety and blasphemy that you seem quite rightly to have surpassed even Pelagius himself—who nearly surpassed everyone in impiety—in this madness.

## CHAPTER III. The participation in divinity that the Pelagians and Nestorians attribute to Christ is common to all holy men

[Col. 0101B]

[Col. 0102A] You say, then, that Christ should be called a Θεοδόχος (*Theodochos*), “an image”—that is, that he should be honored not on his own account because he is God, but because he has received God within himself. In this way, therefore, you assert that there is no difference between him and all holy human beings, because all holy men certainly had God within themselves.

For we know that God was in the patriarchs and that God spoke in the prophets. Finally, we believe that not only the Apostles and martyrs, but all the saints and servants of God, have the Spirit of God within them, according to the saying: “You are the temple of the living God; as God said, ‘I will dwell in them’” (2 Corinthians 6). And again: “Do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” (1 Corinthians 3).

[Col. 0102B] And by this reasoning all are Theodochi, and in this way you declare them all altogether like Christ and equal to God.

> [Col. 0102D] The context itself indicates that *Theodochi*, rather than *Theotoci*, should be read here. For he explains who the Θεοδόχοι, *Theodochi*, are: those who receive God, namely those in whom, according to the Apostle, the Spirit of God dwells as in his temple. Thus above (Book III, chapter 15) he said that Christ was called *Theodochos* by Nestorius because he had received God within himself. In the same way, that impious man asserted that all the saints were Θεοδόχοι, and therefore like—or even equal to—Christ.

But far be from us the impiety of this detestable error: that the maker should be compared with his own work, the Lord with his servants, God with earthly weakness, and God with things earthly and heavenly; and that this should become an injury to him on account of his benefits, so that because he deigns to dwell in a human being, he should therefore be said to be the same as a human being.

## CHAPTER IV. The difference between Christ and the saints

Indeed, the difference between him and all the saints is the difference between a dwelling and its inhabitant. Insofar as it is inhabited, the dwelling belongs not to the dwelling but to the inhabitant, whose choice determines both the building of the dwelling and its use—that is, whether he wishes to make the dwelling itself, when he wills, or, once he has made it, deigns to inhabit it.

“Do you seek,” says the Apostle, “proof of the Christ who speaks in me?” (2 Corinthians 13). And elsewhere: “Do you not know that Jesus Christ is in you? Unless, perhaps, you are reprobate” (ibid.). And again: “That Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts in the inner man” (Ephesians 3).

You see the difference between the Apostle’s teaching and your blasphemy. You say that God dwells in Christ as in a human being; the Apostle testifies that Christ himself dwells in human beings. This plainly proves, as you say, that flesh and blood cannot accomplish such a thing—namely, that from the very fact that you deny him to be God, he is proved to be God. For since you do not deny that the one who dwells in human beings is God, we must necessarily believe that the one whom we know to dwell in human beings is most evidently God.

All, therefore—whether patriarchs, prophets, Apostles, martyrs, or finally all the saints—had God within themselves; and all became children of God; and all were Theotoci.

> [Col. 0103C] Whether *Theodochi* or *Theotoci* should be read here, I find the matter ambiguous. The reading *Theodochi* seems to be supported by the fact that the Author used the same words above: “All are Theodochi,” where we noted that *Theodochi* should rather be read. Nevertheless, the Plantinian reading is more persuasive, as is the Basel reading: *Theotoci* may here be used passively of righteous human beings, generated spiritually by God, or born from God, and made children of God through adoption, just as the Author immediately explains. In the same way Saint John says that human beings become children of God who are “born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God” (John 1). And again elsewhere: “Everyone who loves his brother is born of God” (John 4).
>
> But Christ is *Theotocos*, just as he is *Prototocos*: begotten and firstborn from God, not by adoption or participation, but by nature and the fullness of divinity, as was said. We thus have from Cassianus those three words mentioned above and frequently used in this argument: *Theotocon*, that is, “God-bearer” (*Deiparam*), which is the more customary term; *Theotocon* with the accent on the antepenult, that is, “begotten by God,” or “born from God” and “son of God”; and *Theodochon*, that is, “one who receives God,” whether masculine or feminine.
>
> Nor does it matter that in the preceding chapter the holy men are called *Theodochi*, but here *Theotoci*. Nestorius admitted both descriptions of them: namely, that they were Τεοδόχοι and Θεοτόκοι, because they were both receivers of God—that is, dwellings of God—and children of God, namely adopted children. In both names he compared them with Christ, reserving for him no distinctive or peculiar feature except a certain superiority and prerogative of dignity above the others.

All who believe are children of God by adoption; but the Only-Begotten is Son by nature. He was not begotten by the Father from some material substance, because every thing and every material substance of things exists through the Only-Begotten Son of God; nor from nothing, because he is from the Father; nor as a birth, because there is nothing empty or mutable in God. Rather, ineffably and incomprehensibly, God the Father begot his Only-Begotten in those things that were unbegotten in himself. Thus, from the unbegotten, supreme, and eternal Father, the Only-Begotten is supreme and eternal Son.

He who is regarded in the flesh is the same as he who is regarded in the spirit; he is the same to be believed in majesty, because he was to be born in the flesh.

[Col. 0104B] [Lipsius in the margin: “He must be believed in the body as he is believed in majesty, because he was to be born in the flesh.”]

He did not divide or sever himself, so that one part of him, which was not born, might be born separately, or so that something of divinity might later come upon him which had not been born in him from the Virgin. For, according to the Apostle, all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily in Christ (Colossians 2).

> [Col. 0104C] “Bodily” means substantially, and according to substance, not merely according to energy and operation. Or “bodily” means truly, and not merely according to shadow and figure, as in the angels of the Old Testament who represented the person of God. Or “bodily” means in the body, through the hypostatic union, and not in the soul alone as in the other saints, because the divine nature was united not only to Christ’s soul but also to his body; and from the divine Word and the human nature there exists one corporeal and visible substance.
>
> In this sense Saint Augustine says that “bodily” signifies the same as the words “the Word became flesh” (John 1). Theophylact says: “He dwelt in him in embodied form, and was one substance with what he assumed.” Pope Leo says: “All the fullness of divinity dwells bodily in Christ. The whole divinity therefore fills the whole body; and just as nothing is lacking of that majesty by whose dwelling the dwelling is filled, so nothing is lacking in the body that is not filled by its inhabitant.” Elsewhere he says: “Since God’s substance is incorporeal, how does he dwell bodily in Christ, unless it is because the flesh of our race became the flesh of the Godhead?” and so forth.

It is not that he once dwelt there and at another time did not dwell there, nor that he came to be afterward when previously he had not been. Otherwise we would fall into the impiety of the Pelagian heresy:

> [Col. 0104D] Concerning this, see Book I, chapter 3, where he reviews the errors of the Pelagians: “They also added,” he says, “that the Lord and our Savior became Christ after his baptism, and God after his resurrection, assigning one event to the mystery of anointing and the other to the merit of his Passion.” This is what he says there.
>
> The same error belonged to the earlier heresiarch Photinus, from whom the Pelagians received it, as was noted in the preceding chapter of this same book from Epiphanius and others.

Thus we would say that God came to dwell in Christ from a definite point in time, and that he came upon him afterward, when by his life and conduct he had merited that the power of divinity should dwell within him.

These things belong to men, then, not to God: insofar as human weakness permits, they humble themselves before God, submit themselves to God, make themselves a dwelling for God, and by faith and piety merit having God as guest and inhabitant. For divine grace rewards each person according to the degree to which he has become fit by God’s gift. As someone is judged worthy of God, so he enjoys God’s coming, according to the Lord’s promise: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word; and my Father and I will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14).

The matter and condition of Christ are altogether different. In him all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily, and he possesses the fullness of divinity within himself in such a way that he gives to all from his fullness. While the fullness of divinity dwells within him, he himself dwells in each of the saints insofar as he has judged them worthy of being his dwelling; and he gives to all from his fullness in such a way that he himself continually remains in his fullness.

Even while he was on earth in his body, he was present in the souls of all the saints; he filled the heavens, the earth, the sea, and indeed the entire universe by the infinity of his power and majesty. He was wholly within himself, yet the entire universe could not contain him. For however great and ineffable the things that have been made may be, none is so capacious and immense that it can contain its maker.

## CHAPTER V. That Christ was always called God by the prophets before his temporal birth

[Col. 0106A]

Therefore this is the one of whom the prophet says: “For in you is God, and there is no God besides you. For you are our God, and we did not know you, God of Israel, Savior” (Isaiah XLV). He was afterward seen on earth and lived among human beings (Baruch III). Of him the prophet David also says, speaking in Christ’s person: “From my mother’s womb you are my God” (Psalm XXI), thereby showing that that “Lordly man” never existed without union with God, since the fullness of divinity dwelt in him from the very womb of the Virgin.

[Note: Concerning the “Lordly man,” and whether Christ ought to be called a “Lordly man,” see what was said elsewhere (*Against the Collations*, book 11, chapter 13). It is sufficiently astonishing that Cassian, although he is expressly opposing Nestorius in these books, did not refrain from using this phrase, which appears to favor Nestorius and to suggest two hypostases, two *supposita*, in Christ. And although other Fathers, especially Saint Augustine, are also occasionally found to have used this expression, Augustine himself, later retracting it, declares that it displeased him, as we have shown in its proper place. Following his retraction, Saint Thomas (Part III, question 16, article 3) simply denies that this expression should be used, because *Dominicus* (“Lordly”) is denominatively derived from *Dominus* (“Lord”) and presupposes a distinction from the Lord. Since Christ himself is the Lord, therefore, he ought not to be called a “Lordly man.” For this indicates the Nestorian error and a distinction of persons. Hence Saint Gregory Nazianzen, in Oration 51, reports that the Apollinarists habitually used that expression; but he himself adds: “Lest these men deceive others and at the same time deceive themselves, while asserting that the ‘Lordly man,’ as they put it—or rather, our Lord and God—is without a mind.” For we do not separate the man from the divinity, but confess one and the same person. Here Elias of Crete says: “Very cautiously”—as though, evidently, calling him “Lordly” were not free from error and might introduce suspicion of division—“he added these words, ‘as they put it,’ and likewise this correction, or, to speak more accurately, ‘our Lord and God.’ For Christ is wholly Lord and God, not a Lordly man. This is what the Apollinarists babbled, as though there were one person and another—namely, the Lord and that visible man.” Thus far he. Nevertheless, as to how this expression may be excused and in what sense it is occasionally used by the Fathers, an explanation is given elsewhere in the notes (see Suárez, in Part III, at the place cited above). If you wish, see Rufinus, *Apology for Origen*, near the end.]

As elsewhere the same prophet says: “Truth has sprung up from the earth, and righteousness has looked down from heaven” (Psalm LXXXIV), so that we might understand that, when the Son of God looked down from heaven—that is, when he came and descended—righteousness was born from the Virgin’s flesh, not an apparition of a body, but a reality. For he himself is the truth, according to his own testimony, the testimony of Truth: “I am the truth and the life” (John XIV).

Therefore, since in the preceding books we proved that this truth—that is, the Lord Jesus Christ, born from the Virgin—is God, let us now, as we undertook in the little book immediately preceding this one, show that the one who was to be born from the Virgin was always foretold as God. The prophet Isaiah therefore says:

[Note: The passage in Isaiah is difficult and obscure. It should first be noted that the Septuagint interpreters—as Jerome reports—omitted this statement altogether; Basil, writing on this passage, also attests to this. From this we learn that the Greek edition now in circulation is not the edition of the Septuagint interpreters, or at least is not pure, but has been enlarged or altered in some places (see Bellarmine, Book II, *On the Word of God*, chapter 6). Justin, in his dialogue with Trypho, and Jerome, in the preface to Chronicles and elsewhere, likewise affirm this. For in all copies, both Greek and Latin, this statement is found intact, and the other translators, apart from the Septuagint, rendered it, although differently from our translator.

Aquila, who translated the Old Testament from Hebrew into Greek, rendered the latter part as follows: “For in what is he reckoned?”—as if to say, “In nothing.” Pagninus, who translated from Greek into Latin, published it as: “For what reckoning is he?” The heretical translator Münster rendered it: “For what is he reckoned?” Saint Jerome alone interpreted it in the manner found in the Latin and Vulgate version. Cassian approves and commends that version here as the more accurate and clearer, although elsewhere he frequently follows the Greek version of the Septuagint, as may be seen in the index of the passages he cites from it.

Second, it should also be noted, following Jerome, that the Hebrew word *Bama* is ambiguous. Sometimes it means “high place” or “exalted”; at other times, “in which.” Hector Pintus, commenting on this passage, says: “This word, *Bamah*, means ‘high place’; it is taken in this sense in 1 Kings IX: ‘Before he goes up to the high place,’ and in the Psalms: ‘And setting me upon high places’ (Psalm XVII), as well as in other passages. Saint Jerome followed this meaning here, and rightly so, translating it as it appears in the Vulgate edition. But because *mah* means ‘what’ and *ba* means ‘in,’ Aquila supposed that there were two words here and, guided by this reasoning, translated it ‘in which,’ saying: ‘For in which is he reckoned?’” Thus Pintus.

Third, Saint Jerome vigorously rejects Aquila’s interpretation as Jewish and malicious—an interpretation akin to those of Pagninus and Münster—and at the same time explains his own view in these words: “Since the Jews understood the prophecy to concern Christ, they interpreted the ambiguous word in the worse sense, so that they might appear not to praise Christ but to regard him as worthless. For what continuity of words, what order of reasoning and meaning, would there be if we said: ‘Since these things are so, and the day of the Lord is to come, on which the whole condition of Judea is to be overturned and everything crushed, I warn and command you to desist from a man who breathes and lives as we human beings do, because he is to be counted as nothing’? Would anyone praise someone in such a way as to say: ‘Beware of offending one who is absolutely nothing’?

“On the contrary, it must be understood as follows: Since all these things are to come upon you and are proclaimed in the prophetic Spirit, I warn and command you to desist from one who, according to the flesh, is indeed a man and possesses a soul, breathing and drawing breath through his nostrils as we human beings breathe and live; but according to the divine majesty he is, and is reckoned and believed to be, exalted.

“Reflecting silently within myself, I cannot discover why the Septuagint did not wish to translate into Greek so evident a prophecy concerning Christ. As for the others who did translate it but drew the ambiguous expression toward an impious meaning, it is not surprising that they interpreted it badly and did not wish to say anything glorious about Christ, in whom they did not believe—namely, the Jews or semi-Jews, the Ebionites.”

Thus far Saint Jerome. This is the first explanation of these words, which Cassian follows here, as is evident throughout this chapter.

Others explain them somewhat differently: “Beware of offending or injuring that man, namely, the coming Messiah, because there is spirit in his nostrils”—that is, because he will manifest his anger against you and rage against you with a mighty breath, as angry people commonly emit great breaths and blasts from their mouths and nostrils. Hence it is said of the raging devil: “Smoke proceeds from his nostrils, like a pot that is heated and boiling” (Job XLI). Thus Pintus says: “To have spirit in one’s nostrils is to be angry. By saying, ‘Cease from the man,’ he shows Christ’s humanity. By saying, ‘For he is reckoned exalted,’ he shows Christ’s most holy name. It is as though he said: ‘See that you do not despise Christ, true God and true man, who, when angry, can easily destroy you, undermine your entire state, and utterly extinguish it.’” This is Pintus’s interpretation, although he also offers the explanation of Saint Jerome given above.

A third explanation is that of Saint Gregory, Book XXXI of the *Moralia*, chapter 21: “The nostrils also signify foreknowledge, as it is said through the prophet: ‘Cease from the man whose spirit is in his nostrils, because he is reckoned exalted.’ For often we apprehend by smell what we do not see; thus, even when certain things lie far away, their fragrance makes the nature of their quality known to us, and while we draw breath through our nostrils, we often perceive things that are unseen. Therefore the spirit of our Redeemer is said to be in his nostrils, so that his knowledge may be signified as foreknowledge; for whatever he made known that he knew in the nature of his humanity, this he certainly foreknew from eternity through his divinity. And he immediately explains how he had spirit in his nostrils, saying through the prophet: ‘Because he is reckoned exalted.’ It is as though he said: ‘He foreknew what was to come in the lower regions, because he came down from the heavenly realms.’” Thus Gregory.]

“Cease from the man whose spirit is in his nostrils, because in what is he reckoned?” or, as it is more accurately and clearly expressed in Hebrew, “because he is reckoned exalted” (Isaiah II).

By beautifully saying “cease,” he expressed, through a word prohibiting action, the force of the persecution’s unrest. “Cease,” he says, “from the man whose spirit is in his nostrils, because he is reckoned exalted.” Does not this one and the same statement speak both of the assumption of a human body and of the truth of God? “Cease,” he says, “from the man whose spirit is in his nostrils, because he is reckoned exalted.” Does he not seem to be speaking openly to the Lord’s persecutors, saying: “Cease from persecuting the man, because this man is God”? Although he appears in the lowliness of human flesh, he nevertheless remains in the loftiness of divine majesty.

The prophet rightly demonstrated that he was a man by the most certain sign of a human body when he said: “Cease from the man whose spirit is in his nostrils.” He did so fearlessly and confidently, since he asserted the truth of the man as steadfastly as the truth of God. For this is the true and catholic faith: to believe that the Lord Jesus Christ possessed the substance of a true body just as he possessed the reality of perfect divinity.

Unless perhaps you think that there is something ambiguous in this because he used “the Exalted” for God, although it is certainly the custom of Sacred Scripture to call God “the Exalted,” as in the prophet’s words: “The Exalted gave forth his voice, and the earth was shaken” (Psalm XLV), and: “You alone are Exalted over all the earth” (Psalm LXXXII). Isaiah likewise says: “The Exalted and Sublime, dwelling in eternity” (Isaiah LVII). From this it must plainly be understood that, since in that passage he used “the Exalted” without adding “God,” here too he named God by the title “the Exalted.”

[Note: “The Exalted,” elsewhere “the Most High,” is a proper name of the one true God alone, as Saint Jerome maintains in Epistle 136 to Marcella. In the Psalms cited here by the Author, the Vulgate reads not “the Exalted” but “the Most High.” This name is applied to Christ by David in Psalm LXXXVI, as was just said. Hence Jerome, in the same place, attacking the Arians just as Cassian here attacks the Nestorians, says: “Let the Arians answer, who say that the Father alone is the Most High. Behold, here it is said of the Son: ‘And the Most High himself founded her.’ He did not say, ‘The Son of God, who was in the beginning with the Father’; but what did he say? ‘A man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her.’ But if he is the Most High, how much more is he the Word of God?” Thus Jerome. Zacharias also applies the same name to Christ in Luke I, according to Bede in his commentary; the words themselves make this sufficiently clear: “And you, child, shall be called the prophet of the Most High; for you shall go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways.” John is called the prophet of the Most High because he would go before him to prepare his ways; and, as is well known, he went before Christ, not before anyone else.]

Therefore, since the divine word through the prophet clearly foretold the Lord Jesus Christ as both man and God, let us see whether the testimonies of the ancients also now agree and correspond with those of the New Testament.

## CHAPTER VI. He illustrates the same doctrine by testimonies from the New Testament.

[Note: The opening of the First Epistle of Blessed John the Apostle, on which there is a particular treatise or commentary by Saint Augustine in volume IX of his works. Saint Thomas aptly asks why John did not, as the other apostles who wrote epistles did, and as he himself did in his other two epistles, place a greeting before this one. He answers that John wished the beginning of his epistle to correspond with the beginning of his Gospel, where it says, “In the beginning was the Word,” and so to make it apparent that the same person wrote both the Gospel and the epistle, and that this work was, as it were, a continuation of the preceding Gospel. Thus Saint Thomas.

He then explains that the construction of this passage should be arranged as follows: “We apostles heard, saw, bore witness to, and announced to you what was from the beginning”—that is, eternally—“namely, the Word of God.” He adds: “There are three times: past, present, and future. Of these, what belongs to perfection is applicable to God; what belongs to imperfection is not. The past is spoken of God on account of perfection, the present on account of actuality, and the future on account of duration. Otherwise no tense can properly be said of God: not the past, because it is no longer; not the present, because it passes; and not the future, because it does not yet exist.” Thus Saint Thomas.]

The Apostle John says: “That which was from the beginning, which we heard, which we saw with our eyes, which we looked upon, and our hands touched, concerning the Word of life—and the life was manifested, and we saw and bear witness and announce to you the eternal life, which was with the Father and appeared to us.”

Do you see how ancient things are strengthened by recent ones, and how the confirmation of the new proclamation follows upon the ancient prediction?

Isaiah said: “Cease from the man whose spirit is in his nostrils, because he is reckoned exalted” (Isaiah II). John himself, however, says: “That which was from the beginning, which we heard, which we saw with our eyes, which we looked upon, and our hands touched.” Isaiah said that the man was to be persecuted by the Jews; John proclaimed that the man had been touched by human hands. Isaiah foretold that the same one whom he had announced as a man was exalted God; John recalled that the one whom he had taught to have been touched by human beings had always been God in the beginning. It is therefore perfectly clear that both revealed the Lord Jesus Christ as man and as God: the same one who was afterward man had always been God, and thus was man and God, because that very man was God.

“That which was,” he says, “in the beginning” [Lipsius, in the margin: “from the beginning”], “which we heard, which we saw with our eyes, which we looked upon, and our hands touched, concerning the Word of life—and the life was manifested, and we saw and bear witness and announce to you the eternal life, which was with the Father and appeared to us.”

[Note: Saint Augustine, commenting on this passage: “Who is there who touches the Word with his hands, unless it is because the Word became flesh and dwelt among us? The Word that became flesh and could be touched with the hands began to be flesh from the Virgin Mary, but the Word did not begin then, because he said that he was from the beginning.” Saint Thomas derives from this the argument that not only the Apostle Thomas touched Christ’s side and wounds, but that the other apostles did so as well, according to the Gloss. The Author also indicates this below, where he says that he was touched—that is, handled and felt—with the hands both of his own apostles and of the others.]

Do you see by how many indications, in how many ways—so varied and manifold—that beloved apostle, so devoted to God, intimates the mystery of the divine incarnation? First of all, he testifies that the one who had always existed in the beginning was seen in the flesh. Then, lest what he had said was heard and seen appear insufficient to those who were slow to believe, he also confirmed that he had been touched—that is, felt and handled—not only by his own hands but by the hands of the others as well.

[Note: This matter was treated above. It was an ancient heresy that arose near the time of the apostles: the Son of God had appeared not in a true body but in a phantasmal and shadowy one. That is, he had not assumed flesh like ours, but only a phantasm, presenting to human sight nothing but an empty apparition. Tertullian reports Cerdon as the first author of this error in Book *On the Prescription of Heretics*, chapter 51; Augustine does likewise in *On Heresies*, heresy 21.

Marcion, his disciple, later taught the same doctrine, against whom Tertullian wrote at length in *On the Flesh of Christ* and Book IV *Against Marcion*. Irenaeus likewise treats it in Book I *Against Heresies*, chapter 29; Epiphanius, heresy 42; Ambrose, *On the Mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation*; and Augustine, heresy 22 and elsewhere repeatedly.

Apelles, Marcion’s disciple, succeeded him. As regards Christ’s flesh, Apelles did not entirely agree with his teacher: he admitted that Christ had true flesh, but asserted that it had been taken from the elements rather than from the Virgin, and therefore that Christ, in his Passion, had returned it to the elements. This is reported by Philaster in *On Heresies* and by Augustine in *On Heresies*, chapter 28.

The Manichaean heretics agreed with Marcion and others. They were so called from a certain Manes, a Persian by nationality, or from “Manin,” as Saint Augustine says in *On Heresies*, chapter 25.

Later, Priscillian, bishop of Ávila, and his disciples, called Priscillianists, taught the same error in Spain, in the time of Pope Leo I, who condemned that error in them in Epistle 93 to Turibius. The same error was condemned at the Lateran Council under Innocent III (chapters 4 and 17), and is reported in the chapter “Firmiter” (Book I of the *Decretals*, *On the Supreme Trinity and the Catholic Faith*), as well as in all councils in which the two natures in the one person of Christ are defined. Concerning these matters, see what was said above. See also Alfonso de Castro, under “Christ,” heresy 2.]

By manifesting the flesh he had assumed, he excluded the opinion of the Marcionites and the error of the Manichaeans, lest anyone believe that what human beings saw was merely a phantasm, since the apostle proclaimed that the reality of the body had been touched.

Then he adds “the Word of life” and “the life manifested,” saying that he had seen this, announced this, and testified to this—at once carrying out the duty of faith and striking terror into unbelief, so that, since he openly testified that he was preaching, the one who refused to listen might recognize that the danger was his own.

“We announce to you,” he says, “the eternal life, which was with the Father and appeared to us”: that which had always been with the Father appeared to human beings; that which had always been in the beginning was seen by human beings; that which had existed without beginning as the Word of life was shown to have been touched by human hands.

Do you see in how many ways, so varied, manifold, indivisible, and clear, he explained the mystery of flesh united with God, so that no one could speak of one without necessarily mentioning the other?

As the Apostle himself says elsewhere, most plainly:

[Note: Cyril of Alexandria: “We discover that the Word begotten from God then received the name Jesus Christ, when he became man from a woman. But how is he the same yesterday, today, and forever? It is certainly not for any other reason than the union of the flesh he assumed with the Word of God and their relation to one Son. For by this consideration, even if he is conceived in thought as clothed with flesh, he nevertheless always retains his own natural stability intact.”

Many other explanations of this statement may be found in F. Ribera; they differ somewhat from the one supplied here. Nevertheless, Saint Anselm’s explanation is consistent with it, and the same author reports it in these words, in his commentary on the Epistle to the Hebrews: “‘Yesterday’ signifies all past time and the whole span of eternity that existed before the origin of the world; ‘today’ signifies all present time; and ‘he himself and forever’ signifies the whole span of time and infinity that is to come. Thus Jesus Christ was yesterday, because ‘in the beginning was the Word,’ and from eternity until our own time he is the same. He is also today, that is, he exists in our time; and he will be forever, because he will remain eternally. Hence in the Apocalypse it is said of him: ‘The one who was, and who is, and who is to come’—that is, who will be throughout all ages.” Thus Anselm, whose interpretation Saint Thomas appears to have adopted, since in his commentary on this passage he concludes: “In this, therefore, the Apostle demonstrates the eternity of Christ.”

Gagneus, on the same passage: “Jesus Christ, yesterday and today, will remain the very same forever; that is, he is the one who existed from eternity, signified by ‘yesterday’; the one who exists now, signified by ‘today’; and the one who will remain eternally.”

Bellarmine gives a somewhat shorter explanation (Book I, *On Christ*, chapter 8): “Jesus Christ yesterday, today, and forever—that is, he always was, always is, and always will be.” A similar passage occurs in Hebrews VII: “Having neither beginning of days nor end of life.” So too in John V: “This is the true God and eternal life.” For if Christ is eternal life, he cannot fail to have been and to be himself eternal, and consequently the true God, which is what the Author intends.]

“For Jesus Christ,” he says, “is the same yesterday and today, and forever” (Hebrews XIII). This is precisely what he said in the preceding testimony: “What was from the beginning, this our hands touched.” Not because a spirit can of itself be touched, but because the Word, having become flesh, was in some way touched in the man to whom it had been united.

Therefore the same Jesus is yesterday and today: the same before the world’s beginning as in the flesh; the same in the past as in the present; the same also forever, because he is the same in all things as he is before all things. And this whole reality is the Lord Jesus Christ.

## CHAPTER VII. Again he shows that, from the conjunction of the two natures in Christ into one person, what belongs to the divine nature may rightly be attributed to the man, and what belongs to the human nature to God.

And how is he the same before the world’s birth, who was born only recently [Col. 0112A]? Clearly, because he who was recently born as man is the same as he who was God before the birth of all things. And therefore Christ is wholly called God, because the unity of Christ and God is so great that no one can now say “Christ” without entirely naming God in the name of Christ, nor say “God” without naming Christ in the name of God. And thus, through the complete union of both substances in himself by the majesty of the sacred birth, whatever he was—namely, man and God—became wholly God.

Accordingly, the Apostle Paul, seeing with the unveiled eyes of faith the entire mystery of the ineffable majesty in Christ, spoke in this way, inviting peoples to give thanks to God as they acknowledged God’s benefits:

> Giving thanks, he says, to the Father, who has made us worthy to share in the inheritance of the saints in light; who has rescued us [Col. 0112B] from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of his beloved Son, in whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins;

[Note: [Col. 0111D] Chrysostom says that, because of the complete likeness and equality, he calls the Son “the image.” For Christ, as the Son of God, is called the image of the Father because he is in every respect like the Father and represents the Father most perfectly, as he himself says: “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John XIV). The word *invisibilis* (“invisible”) is here in the genitive case and refers not to “image” but to God the Father, as is clear from the Greek ἀοράτου. Thus the Arians abused this passage, saying that the term “invisible” applies to God the Father alone, not to the Son, and consequently that the Son is not true God, since “invisible,” among other things, is a proper name of God, according to the Apostle’s statement: “To the immortal, invisible, only God, be honor and glory” (I Timothy I).

But the Fathers replied that the Son is called, and is, the most perfect image of the invisible God because the image itself is also invisible: for it is wholly like its exemplar, and therefore entirely such as the exemplar itself. Hence Hebrews I calls him “the radiance of his glory and the figure of his substance,” that is, of the Father—complete likeness and exact representation, not accidental but substantial, not imitative but natural. For an imitative image does not share the same essence as its exemplar. Thus Christ is the image of the invisible God in such a way that he himself is also invisible, like the Father, as Saint Thomas says.

That “invisible” also applies to the Son, just as to the Father, because he cannot be seen according to his divinity unless he himself reveals himself—a prerogative belonging to God alone—is evident from Matthew XI, where it is said: “No one knows the Son except the Father; nor does anyone know the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son wishes to reveal him.” And Revelation XIX says: “He has a name written which no one knows except himself, and his name is the Word of God.” From this it follows that the Word of God is something invisible, since only he who is the Word of God knows what this is; yet the Father and the Holy Spirit are not thereby excluded, since they possess the same essence and knowledge as the Word.

Saint Thomas further observes (in his Commentary on Colossians I) that in the Apostle’s words quoted here Christ’s dignity and excellence are commended and proclaimed from three perspectives, or by three comparisons; and this also bears upon the present passage and the Author’s purpose.

First, in relation to the Father, or by comparison with the Father, whose most perfect image he is, so livingly expressed that he possesses in number the same whole essence and nature. Second, in relation to creatures generally, when he is called “the firstborn of every creature,” that is, begotten before every creature, as Chrysostom interprets it—not because he is the first creature, as Arius maintained, nor because the Father later begot a creature from himself, but just as, according to his humanity, Mary’s firstborn is so called, not because the Virgin later bore other children from herself, but because she bore no one before him; and because Scripture customarily uses “first” for “one,” so that “firstborn” and “only-begotten” have the same meaning. This matter will be treated more fully below (Book VI, chapter 18).

Or, according to Saint Thomas, he is called “the firstborn of every creature” because he was begotten by the Father in such a way that, as the Word conceived in the mind, he represents every creature and is the principle of every creature. Hence, explaining what he had said, the Apostle immediately adds: “For in him all things were created,” and so forth. “In him,” that is, through him, as it is said in John I: “All things were made through him”; or “in him” as in the exemplar, archetype, and prototype.

Third, by comparison with the whole Church, when it is said: “And he is the head of the body, the Church; he is the beginning,” and so forth. Thus Ephesians I says: “He gave him as head over the whole Church, which is his body and his fullness.” “Over the whole Church,” namely, the Church militant on earth [Col. 0113D] and the Church triumphant in heaven, which, according to Augustine (*Enchiridion*), also includes the angels. Hence the Apostle concludes that Christ holds primacy in all things, whether he is considered as God or as man.]

> who is [Col. 0113A] the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation; for in him all things were created in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or powers: all things were created through him and in him, and he is before all things, and all things hold together in him. And he is the head of the body, the Church; he is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, so that he himself might hold first place in all things; because in him it was pleasing that all fullness should dwell, and through him to reconcile all things to himself, making peace through the blood of his cross, whether the things in heaven or the things on earth (Colossians I).

Does this require any addition by way of interpretation, when it has been expressed so fully and clearly that it contains within itself not only the truth of the matters but also the clarity of their exposition?

For he commands us to give thanks to the Father, [Col. 0113B] adding an entirely sufficient reason for giving thanks: because he has made us worthy to share in the inheritance of the saints, and, having rescued us from the power of darkness, has transferred us into the kingdom of his beloved Son, in whom we have redemption and forgiveness of sins; who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation; because in him and through him all things were created, and, as he himself is their maker, so also is he their governor.

And what follows? “He is,” he says, “the head of the body, the Church; he is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead.” Scripture calls resurrection a kind of generation: for just as generation creates life, so resurrection generates for life.

[Note: [Col. 0113D] Scripture expresses two kinds of regeneration. One is baptism, concerning which John III says: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit,” and so forth; Titus III: “He saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit”; and I Peter I: “He regenerated us unto a living hope.”

The other is the resurrection of the dead at the end of the age, concerning which Matthew says: “In the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits”—in Greek, ἐν τῇ παλιγγενεσίᾳ. This resurrection will be, as it were, a generation according to the body, just as baptism is a second generation of the human being according to the soul (Maldonado on Matthew XIX).

Two reasons are given for why the resurrection itself, or the final judgment, is called regeneration. First, because the whole world will then be renewed and, in a certain sense, regenerated, as John says in Revelation XXI: “I saw a new heaven and a new earth”; and verse 5: “Behold, I make all things new.” Saint Peter likewise says in his Second Epistle, chapter III: “We await new heavens and a new earth according to his promises.” And Isaiah LXV:17: “Behold, I create new heavens and a new earth.” And chapter LXVI: “As the new heavens and the new earth which I will make shall stand before me, says the Lord, so shall your descendants and your name stand.” And Saint Paul says to the Romans VIII: “Creation itself will be set free from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God.”

The second reason is that, once stripped of mortality and clothed with immortality, we human beings will in a certain sense be regenerated, as Saint Paul says in II Corinthians V: “For we who are in this dwelling groan, being burdened, because we do not wish to be unclothed but clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life.” And Philippians III:21: “He will refashion our lowly body, configured to his glorious body.” So teach Saint Augustine, Book III *Against the Two Letters of the Pelagians*, chapter 3; Saint Gregory, Book IV of the *Moralia*, chapter 26; and Saint Bernard in the declamation he wrote on these words: “Behold, we have left everything.”]

Therefore resurrection itself is called regeneration, according to the Lord’s testimony:

> Amen, I say to you, that you who have followed me, in the regeneration, [Col. 0113C] when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel (Matthew XIX).

Thus he calls him “the firstborn from the dead” whom above he proclaimed to be the invisible Son and image of God. But who is the image of the invisible God if not the Only-Begotten, the Word of God? And how is he said to have risen from the dead who is called the invisible image and Word of God?

And what is nevertheless added? “So that,” he says, “he himself might hold first place,” [Col. 0114A] because in him it was pleasing that all fullness should dwell, and through him to reconcile all things to himself, making peace through the blood of his cross, whether the things in heaven or the things on earth.
