Does the Creator of all things require primacy over all things? Or does he who made them require primacy over the things made by him? Or can it be said of the Word that it pleased him who is the firstborn from the dead that all fullness should dwell in him, when he is certainly the Only-Begotten Son of God, the Word of God before the beginning of all things, possessing the invisible Father in himself, and therefore possessing all fullness in himself from the beginning, so that he himself was the fullness of all things?

And finally, what follows? “Making peace,” he says, “through the blood of his cross, whether the things on earth or the things in heaven.” He has made entirely clear whom he meant when he called him [Col. 0114B] “the firstborn from the dead.” For were all things reconciled and pacified through the blood of the Word or of the Spirit? Certainly not. No thing could undergo passion in an impassible nature; blood could be shed only from a human being; and no one other than a human being could die. Yet the same one who is said in what follows to have died is proclaimed above as the invisible image of God.

How, then, is this so? Clearly, because the Apostles took every possible precaution lest any division should appear to exist in Christ, and lest the Son of God, united in the Son of Man, should begin through misguided interpretations to have two persons, and lest, through perverse and impious opinions, the one who was in himself one should become two in our understanding.

And therefore the apostolic proclamation descends beautifully and wonderfully from the Only-Begotten Son of God himself to the Son of Man, united to the Son of God, so that, just as the order of events proceeds, so also the discourse of doctrine might proceed. In this way it connects everything by an inseparable bond and, as it were, by a bridge, so that without any division or interval whatsoever you might find at the end of time the one whom you read of at the beginning of the world, and, with no impious separation admitted, would not believe the Son of God to be one in the flesh and another in the spirit.

For apostolic teaching so united God and man through the mystery of bodily birth that it showed you the same one reconciling all things on the cross whom it had proclaimed before the beginning of the world to be the image of the invisible God.

## CHAPTER VIII

He corroborates the apostolic statement by the authority of the Lord.

Although this was said by the Apostle, it is nevertheless the teaching of the Lord. For the same thing was spoken by the Apostle to Christians which he himself had spoken in the Gospel to the Jews, saying:

> But now you seek to kill me, a man who has spoken to you [Col. 0115B] the truth which I heard from God. For I did not come from myself, but he sent me (John VIII).

[Note: [Col. 0115B] Chrysostom says that this truth is that he is equal to the Father; for this reason the Jews sought to kill him. And to show that this is not contrary to the Father, he adds: “Which I heard from God.”]

And he indicates that he is both God and man. He is man insofar as he proclaims himself to be man; he is God insofar as he confirms that he was sent. For he necessarily existed with the one from whom he had come, and he had come from the one by whom he said he had been sent.

Hence, when the Jews said to him, “You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?” he replied with the most fitting expression of his eternity and majesty:

> Amen, amen, I say to you, [Col. 0115B] before Abraham came to be, I am (ibid.).

[Note: [Col. 0115B] “Weigh the words,” says Augustine (*Tractate 43 on John*), “and recognize the mystery. ‘Before Abraham came to be’: understand ‘came to be’ as belonging to human nature, while ‘I am’ belongs to the divine substance. ‘Came to be,’ because Abraham was a creature. He did not say, ‘Before Abraham existed, I was,’ but, ‘Before Abraham came to be’—he who could not come to be except through me—‘I am.’ Nor did he say, ‘Before Abraham came to be, I came to be.’ In the beginning God made heaven and earth; for ‘in the beginning was the Word.’ Before Abraham came to be, I am. Recognize the Creator; distinguish the creature.”

So Augustine.

Saint Gregory (*Homily 18 on the Gospels*) says: “‘Before’ belongs to past time; ‘I am’ to the present. And because divinity has neither past nor future time but always possesses being, he did not say, ‘Before Abraham I was,’ but, ‘Before Abraham I am.’ Hence it is also said to Moses: ‘I am who I am’; and, ‘You shall say to the children of Israel: He who is has sent me to you.’ Abraham had a before and an after, since he could approach through the presentation of his presence and depart through the course of life. Truth, however, always possesses being, because nothing in it begins at an earlier time or ends at a later one.”

These statements of the holy Fathers are entirely consonant with Cassian’s words in this chapter.]

Whose statement, then, do you wish this to be? Clearly Christ’s, beyond all doubt. And how could one who had been born only recently say that he existed before Abraham? Through that with which he had been completely united: the Word of God. Thus everyone might understand how great the unity of Christ and God was, since whatever God said in Christ, [Col. 0115C] the unity of divinity now claimed wholly for itself.

[Note: [Col. 0115C] I would rather believe that the reading should be: “The divinity united to him claimed everything for itself.” The meaning would be: Whatever God spoke in Christ, the human Christ spoke wholly, on account of the unity of person in Christ. “The man united” means humanity united to divinity in the unity of person. As stated elsewhere, “the divinity of the one united” and “the man united to God” are therefore the same.]

He was rightly conscious of his eternity when, in the body, he then replied to the Jews with the voice in which he had once spoken to Moses [Col. 0115C] in the spirit.

Here he says: “Before Abraham came to be, I am.” But to Moses: “I [Col. 0116B] am who I am.”

[Note: [Col. 0115D] First, it should be noted that in Hebrew the reading is: “I will be who I will be.” For the Hebrews use the future tense for the present, since the Hebrew verb lacks a present tense. In Greek, however, it is: ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ὤν. Here the participle is ὢν, as if he were saying: “I am the one who is.”

Second, it should be noted that Christ alluded to these words when he repeatedly said in the Gospel, “I am,” thereby signifying his divinity. John VIII: “Before Abraham came to be, I am.” In the same chapter: “If you do not believe that I am, you will die in your sins.” John XVII: “Where I am, they also may be with me.” And many similar passages. The Fathers did not overlook this point.

Cyril of Alexandria, commenting on the words “If you do not believe that I am,” says (*Commentary on John*, Book VI, chapter 23): “Our Lord uses among them that verb which designates essence, taken absolutely and without any addition, by which he might more surely signify his divinity to them, since he speaks of himself with the word recognized as belonging to God alone and previously spoken of God to Moses. When Moses, being sent to free the people of Israel from Egyptian slavery, asked about the name of the one who was sending him, the Lord replied: ‘I am who I am.’ And again: ‘Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: He who is has sent me to you’ (Exodus III). By this word, therefore, he recalls to their memory himself, who had previously testified to Moses that he was called by this name.”

Augustine, in *Tractate 38 on John*, says: “It is a great thing that he says, ‘I am,’ because the Lord had said to Moses: ‘I am who I am.’ Who can worthily express what ‘I am’ means? God was sending his servant Moses through his angel to free his people from Egypt; he was sending one who trembled, made excuses, but obeyed. When he was making his excuses, he said to God, whom he understood to be speaking through the angel: ‘If the people say to me, “Who is the God who sent you?” what shall I say to them?’ And the Lord said to him: ‘I am who I am.’ And he repeated: ‘You shall say to the children of Israel: He who is has sent me to you.’

“He did not say there: ‘I am God,’ or ‘I am the maker of the world,’ or ‘I am the creator of all things,’ or ‘I am the defender of the people to be liberated’; but only this: ‘I am who I am,’ and, ‘You shall say to the children of Israel: He who is.’ He did not add: ‘He who is your God,’ or ‘He who is the God of your fathers’; he said only this: ‘He who is has sent me to you.’”

Third, it should be noted that from these very words it can be inferred that the name “He who is,” or ὤν, is one of God’s proper—and most proper—names. The Fathers affirm this unanimously.

Dionysius the Areopagite (*On the Divine Names*, chapter 15) says: “It is not without reason that God himself is celebrated more principally and preferably by the designation ‘He who is’ than by all the other names, as by a gift older, prior, and more ancient—namely, by nature—than the other gifts of his that have been distributed among creatures. Indeed, God, existing before all creatures and transcending existence, and doing so supremely, made being itself, through itself, surpass and excel all his other gifts communicated to created things; and by this very being he caused whatever exists in any mode of existence to subsist.”

Gregory Nazianzen, in Oration 36, says that among all the names of God, “Being” and “God” are the most proper, and that between these two the name “Being” is the more proper: “For,” he says, “we seek a nature that possesses being through itself; and this is signified by the name ‘Is,’ or ‘He who is.’”

Eusebius of Caesarea interprets it in the same way in Book XI of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, chapters 6 and 7: “He who is,” that is, “he who necessarily and always exists in the same manner.” There he also reports the view of Pythagoras and Plato, who taught that God should be called by this name. From Plutarch he reports an explanation of the Greek word written in the temple at Delphi, so that those entering might greet God or confess him by that word, saying: εἶ, “you are.”

Ambrose, explaining the same name in Letter 63, says: “This is the true name of God: to be always.”

Jerome, in Letter 136 to Marcella, places among the ten Hebrew names customarily used for God, in sixth place, *Eser cheie*, which, he says, is read in Exodus as: “He who is has sent me.”

Augustine, in Book III *Against Maximus*, chapter 26, and in Book II, chapter 1, *On the Morals of the Manichaeans*, as well as elsewhere, says that this is the name of immutability, because everything that changes ceases in some way to be; and the name of eternity, because “I am” and “He who is” mean the same as “I am eternal”—in whom nothing was and nothing will be, but only is.

Rupert of Deutz, Book I on Exodus, chapter 14, says that in Exodus III God imposed two names upon himself: one of nature, namely “He who is”; the other of gracious condescension and favor, namely “God of Abraham and God of Isaac,” and so forth.

John of Damascus, Book I, chapter 12, *On the Orthodox Faith*, says: “The name ‘He who is’ seems to be the most principal of all the names spoken of God; just as he himself, answering Moses on the mountain, says: ‘Say to the children of Israel: He who is has sent me.’ For, comprehending everything in himself, he possesses being itself, as an infinite and boundless sea of substance.”

Bernard, Book V *On Consideration*, says: “Nothing is more fitting to eternity, which is God, than this name ‘He who is.’ If you say of him ‘good,’ ‘great,’ or anything else of that kind, it is restored in this word: ‘That which is.’”

Finally, Saint Thomas (I, q. 13, a. 11) proves from this that the name “He who is” is most proper to God, because it formally signifies being itself, which is God’s very essence. He also offers two further reasons for the same assertion, which I leave to be consulted in his work.

This name, then, is essential and intimate to God, signifying the three persons insofar as they are one God, who is the source and origin of all being and whose essence is being itself; and, since he does not receive being from another, he gives all things their being.

Closely related to this are two other names: “God,” and the tetragrammaton, which the Greeks call ἀνεκφώνητον, “ineffable.” These too are derived from “that which is.” The distinction is that the name “God” signifies God’s own being as though in a specific form, whereas “He who is” signifies being itself generically, or absolutely and without determination. The tetragrammaton, however, signifies God’s own essence existing in three persons (Jerome, Letter 136 to Marcella). But let this be said only in passing and by way of occasion.]

> “I am who I am” (Exodus III).

He proclaimed the eternity of the divine nature with truly admirable magnificence of expression, because [Col. 0117A] nothing can be said so fittingly of God as that he is said always to be, since being has neither a beginning in the past nor an end in the future.

[Note: [Col. 0117C] There are many excellent praises of the holy Fathers expressing the same judgment, beyond those just mentioned concerning the name “He who is.” It will be useful for explaining this passage to select a few of them here.

Hilary, Book I *On the Trinity*, commenting on “I am who I am,” says: “I have been utterly astonished at so absolute a designation of God, which expressed the incomprehensible condition of the divine nature in language most suitable to human understanding; for nothing is understood to be more proper to God than being.”

Jerome, Letter 57 to Damasus, says: “There is one nature of God, and that nature alone truly is—that is, it has being from itself, and possesses it unchangeably and eternally.” He adds below: “God alone is the one who truly bears the name of essence.”

Augustine, in that same Tractate 38 on John, addresses God in this way: “O Lord our God, what is this that you say? Is the earth not real? Are the things that are in the earth and in heaven not real? Is the human being to whom you speak not real? Is the angel whom you send not real? If all these things are real, since they were made through you, what is this distinctive thing that you retained for yourself—being itself—which you did not give to others, so that you alone might be?

“For how do I hear: ‘I am who I am,’ as though other things did not exist? And shortly afterward he answers himself: Any thing whatsoever, however excellent, if it is changeable, does not truly exist. For there is no true being where there is both being and not-being. Whatever can be changed has already become something other than what it was; if it is no longer what it was, a kind of death has occurred in it; something that was has been destroyed, and is no longer.

“O truth, which truly are! In all our actions and movements, and in every activity of creation, I find two times, past and future; I seek the present, but nothing stands still. What I have said is no longer; what I am going to say is not yet. I find past and future in every movement of things; in the truth that remains, I find neither past nor future, but only the present—and this incorruptibly, something that does not exist in creation.”

Cyril of Alexandria, Book VI, chapter 23, on John, says: “If we investigate the nature of all things, we shall discover that being belongs above all to God alone, since he does not subsist from another but is the primary source of the existence of all things, from whom, through whom, and in whom all things are.

“Nothing else can attain the perfection of the divine essence; rather, everything falls short of it beyond all proportion and in a certain way slips toward non-being. For in comparison with him who truly is, who is unchangeable and has no beginning and receives being from no other but possesses it from himself, mutable things, which have the beginning of their being from another and receive that same being from another, are as though they were not. For what is said to have been is not; and what is said to be will be is not yet. God alone is, and he knows what has been and what will be.”

Gregory, Book XVIII of the *Moralia*, chapter 33, says: “He alone truly is, because he alone is unchangeable. Therefore, if we are to be something through participation in that essence, let us recognize ourselves, because in our own proper nature we are nothing.”

I omit many other passages, lest I burden the reader.]

Thus this is said most openly of the nature of the eternal God, because it corresponds perfectly to eternity. The Lord Jesus Christ himself showed this when speaking of Abraham, using a different form of expression:

> Before Abraham came to be, I am.

He said “before Abraham came to be” of Abraham; but of himself, “I am,” clearly because coming to be belongs to temporality, while being belongs to eternity.

[Note: [Col. 0118C] I find this passage and a large part of the following chapter expressed in nearly the same words in that sermon or treatise *On the Assumption of Blessed Mary*, falsely attributed under Saint Jerome’s name to Paula and Eustochium and circulated among his works (Volume IX, Letter 10). Some believe it to be by that Sophronius whom Saint Jerome mentions in his *On Illustrious Men*. Since that author added a number of things which Cassian or his copyists or printers may perhaps through negligence have omitted here, although they can provide considerable assistance and supplementation for clarifying this passage, it did not seem inappropriate to transcribe the words of that same author here, so that, when compared with Cassian, his meaning might be more fully illuminated and, insofar as possible, restored in its entirety.

Thus, after saying much about the praises of the Virgin Mother of God and the mystery of the Incarnation, he says:

“It is evident that time did not prejudice the mystery of the man united to God, so that the one who did not yet exist—born of the Virgin Mary—was already in him through the unity of person from the beginning of the age. This is declared by many indications in Scripture. Hence the Lord says to the Jews: ‘Before Abraham came to be, I am.’ For ‘before Abraham came to be’ expresses the brevity of humanity. But ‘I am’ declares the eternity of nature, in which eternity he who was speaking indicated that he had already existed through the mystery of his incarnation.

“When the Apostle Jude wished to make this clearer, he said: ‘Jesus, saving the people from Egypt, later destroyed those who did not believe’ (Jude 5). And elsewhere Paul says: ‘Let us not tempt Christ, as some of them tempted him’ (I Corinthians X). This is not because Jesus or Christ, born of Mary, already existed, but because in that one Son of God the unity of person was already being commended, though it was hidden in mystery.

“And elsewhere he says plainly: ‘He chose us in him before the foundation of the world’ (Ephesians I), because whatever God did from the beginning, Christ did entirely through the unity of the mystery. Therefore Jesus was already in the Son who led the people out, and Christ was in the one who was tempted, since it cannot be doubted that he had always existed in God through the unity of the mystery.

“Otherwise, unless you believe this, either Christ will not be God at all, or, contrary to the prophet, God will appear to be recent. But lest we be shaken by such accusations, the Scriptures must be examined, in which the unity of person in Christ is commended, since time does not prevent one and the same person from always being so called.

“Blessed Peter also, speaking of the Fathers, says: ‘Through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ we believe that we are saved, just as they were’ (Acts XV). For the Lord alone led them, and their God was not another. Hence God is not recent for us either, because he is one and the same: he was both their leader and our redeemer through the suffering of his flesh—one in his flesh, one in the mystery, one in the spirit. Reason does not permit us to understand one Son of Man and another Son of God: he is limited neither by time nor separated by suffering. Rather, God entirely passed into Christ, and Christ into God, so that whatever the Son of God is may be called Christ, and whatever Christ endured in the flesh may rightly be believed to have been endured by God.

“Otherwise, if we attend to reason and human senses, divinity and human condition could never have been brought together in this way. Yet they were brought together in Christ, and one Emmanuel arose from both.”

So far that author. His words and those that follow agree with Cassian’s statements not merely in meaning but also in wording, arrangement, and style so closely that anyone comparing the two could hardly doubt that one was borrowed from the other.

As for who that author was, learned men do not agree. Erasmus certainly placed that letter, as spurious, with others of the same kind in the fourth volume, and thought it should rather be attributed to Sophronius. Marianus Victorius, however, included it in the ninth volume of his edition, though he prefaced it with this judgment of his own:

“The sermon on the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary to Paul and Eustochium is rather the work of a Greek than of a Latin author, since its writer was not practiced in writing Latin and one can see a Greek speaking Latin in it. Yet it is considered certain that it belongs to Sophronius, the friend of Saint Jerome—namely, the Sophronius who rendered Jerome’s catalogue of ecclesiastical writers from Greek.”

Thus Marianus wrote, perhaps reporting the judgment of others more than his own.

Cardinal Baronius disagrees with them, both in the *Annals* (Volume I, year of Christ 48) and in his notes on the Roman Martyrology. In the former place, discussing the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin, he writes among other things:

“As for that little book or letter to Paula and Eustochium on the Assumption of Blessed Mary, bearing Jerome’s name as its heading: I appeal to the judgment of all learned men that it is not only not Jerome’s, but not Sophronius’s either, as some have thought. For it is clear that the author of that commentary is wholly engaged in attacking and refuting the doctrine of Nestorius, who indisputably lived long after the times of Jerome and Sophronius.”

A little later he accuses the same author of falsehood because no heresy concerning the incarnation of Christ is known to have arisen in Jerome’s time. “Here,” he says, “you can see the man’s manifest imposture, since in that work he traded upon the names of Jerome, Paula, and Eustochium in order to obtain credibility.”

So Baronius (August 15).

In his notes on the Martyrology he likewise says:

“There exists a sermon written under the title of Saint Jerome to Paula and Eustochium, which some have thought to be by that Sophronius whom Saint Jerome mentions in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. But I think it belongs to neither of them. Rather, it is certainly by an author who lived around or after the time of the Council of Ephesus or Chalcedon; for he is deeply occupied with destroying the doctrines of Nestorius and Eutyches, which invaded the Church long after the times of Jerome and Sophronius.”

Thus far Baronius.

I do not know whether his argument from chronology is sufficiently strong and effective to suppress the widespread opinion that Sophronius was the author of that little book or sermon, since it has been demonstrated above from Cassian that the doctrine or heresy of Nestorius was not first invented and devised by Nestorius himself, but had been introduced much earlier by Pelagius and other ancient heresiarchs. The author, therefore—whether Sophronius or someone else—could have attacked it before Nestorius when the occasion arose, just as we earlier discussed Leporius, the Pelagian converted to the faith.

Since, then, nothing certain can be known about this matter, and Baronius himself had no fully established knowledge of it, it is better to leave the question uncertain and unresolved than to affirm anything without due consideration.]

And therefore [Col. 0119A] he attributed the former event to the brevity of human nature, but the latter—“I am”—to his own nature. And all this was Christ, who, through the mystery of the man united to God, said that he had already existed in the one who had always been.

## CHAPTER IX

Since those miraculous works performed for the children of Israel from the time of Moses onward are attributed to Christ, it is likewise established that he existed long ago, before his temporal birth.

[Col. 0120A]

[Note: [Col. 0120B] The Apostle Jude—not Judas the betrayer, but the other, who is also called Thaddaeus, whose Epistle survives and is received by the Church as canonical and cited by the Holy Fathers as canonical (Dionysius the Areopagite, *On the Divine Names*, ch. 4; Jerome, ch. 1 to Titus; Council of Trent, session 4)—from whom the testimony that follows is taken. Moreover, since the author cited above expressly names the apostle Jude here, and later, when adding another testimony from Paul, distinctly says, “And elsewhere Paul,” whereas Cassianus, without any distinction, adds “But also elsewhere,” as though speaking of the same apostle, it is quite evident that this passage of Cassianus is corrupt and mutilated, and must be supplemented or explained from that author.]

When the apostle also wished to clarify and make this manifest to all, he spoke as follows:

[Note: [Col. 0120C] In these words it should first be noted that where the Latin has *Jesus*, the Greek has Κύριος, that is, “Lord,” which militates against those who interpret these words as referring to Jesus Nave, or Joshua son of Nun, the successor of Moses. Second: “saving the people from Egypt.” In Greek this is a participle of the past tense, σώσας, that is, “when he had saved”; here the salvation and deliverance of the Israelite people from Egyptian bondage is plainly attributed to Christ, by reason of the divine person who is one in Christ, God and man. This passage indeed refers to Deuteronomy 20: “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt,” and to Deuteronomy 32: “The Lord alone was his guide, and no foreign god was with him.” These statements are unquestionably made concerning the true and supreme God whom the Jews worshipped. Yet the apostle Jude says: “Jesus, saving the people from Egypt, afterward destroyed those who did not believe.” Therefore Jesus is that true and supreme God. The Venerable Bede also noted this argument in his commentary on the passage. Third, it should be observed that the word “second,” which follows in Jude’s sentence, is used for “then” or “afterward,” as the Gloss explains. Fourth, “those who did not believe” means those who did not persevere in faith and in the worship of the true God, but joined Korah and the others. Fifth, “he destroyed”—by fiery serpents, Numbers 21, and in other ways, says Saint Thomas: “For they perished in many ways: some by fire, Numbers 11 and 16; some by the swallowing up of the earth, Numbers 16; and some by an ordinary death, namely, all those from twenty years old and upward, except Joshua and Caleb, Numbers 14.” [Col. 0121A] He therefore first saved his people through mercy, but afterward punished them through justice, because the Lord is more ready to show mercy than to punish. Thus Saint Thomas.]

For Jesus, when he had saved the people from the land of Egypt, afterward destroyed those who did not believe. But also elsewhere:

[Note: [Col. 0121B] They tempt Christ who distrust his power, providence, or mercy, as the Jews did in the wilderness when they said, “Why did you bring us out of Egypt?” and so forth (Numbers 21). And again: “Can God prepare a table in the wilderness?” (Psalm 78). They were tempting Christ their God, who was their guide in Moses. For whoever wishes to test someone’s power or goodness thereby shows that he distrusts him, and is rightly said to tempt him. Therefore they perished from the serpents, until the bronze serpent was raised, at the sight of which they were healed. From this passage, compared with Moses’ words, an argument similar to the preceding one is formed to prove Christ’s divinity. For in Numbers 21 it is said: “And the people spoke against God and Moses, saying, ‘Why have you brought us up from Egypt, that we might die in the wilderness?’” and so forth. “Therefore the Lord sent fiery serpents among the people,” and so forth. There is no doubt that this concerns the one true God of Israel. Yet the Apostle says that this very God was Christ: “Let us not tempt Christ,” he says, “as some of them tempted him, and were destroyed by serpents” (1 Corinthians 10). Therefore Christ must be the true God, and altogether one God with the Father. It should further be observed that in the two passages just explained—an observation also made by that author concerning the Assumption of Blessed Mary—our Lord and Savior was called both Jesus and Christ before the ineffable union with flesh. For there it is said, in the Epistle of Jude, that Jesus, under Moses’ leadership, saved the people from Egypt; here, in 1 Corinthians 10, that the children of Israel tempted Christ in the wilderness. Both events plainly occurred long before the Lord’s Incarnation. Furthermore, Ecclesiasticus, chapter 47, says in praise of King David: “Christ cleansed his sins and exalted his horn forever” (for this is how the older Bibles read). It is manifest, however, that David’s sins were cleansed by God long before the assumption of flesh (2 Samuel 12). Again, the Apostle says to the Ephesians 1: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places, in Christ, and chose us in him before the foundation of the world,” and so forth. Paul says here that we were chosen by God the Father before the foundation of the world, “in Christ” (Acts 4), that is, through Christ or on account of Christ’s merits. We also read in several places in the Psalms that Christ was so called, as in Psalm 2: “The kings of the earth stood forth, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ.” Psalm 88: “But you have rejected and despised; you have delayed your Christ.” Psalm 131: “For the sake of David your servant, do not turn away the face of your Christ.” Likewise Habakkuk 3: “You went forth for the salvation of your people, for salvation with your Christ.” [Col. 0122A] Here above all the error of Origen must be avoided. He maintained that human souls were created in heaven a long time before they were united to bodies; from which it would follow that Christ’s most holy soul was united to the Divinity before it was united to the body, and was then called Christ. John Damascene refutes this error in these words: “It was not, as some falsely maintain, before the Incarnation from the Virgin, that the soul was united to God the Word and Christ was from that time called Christ. For this is the absurd declaration of Origen’s ravings, which dogmatizes the pre-existence of souls. But we say that the Son and Word of God was begotten and called Christ from the time when he was conceived in the womb of the holy Virgin, became flesh without change, and the flesh was united to the divinity. For the anointing itself pertains to the humanity, as Gregory the Theologian says, and the most holy bishop of Alexandria, Cyril, writing to Theodosius. For he says: ‘I declare that neither the Word which is from God without humanity, nor the man born of a woman, nor the temple not united to the Word, ought to be called Jesus Christ. For the Word which is from God, ineffably joined to humanity according to the dispensatory union, is understood to be Christ.’ And below, from Athanasius: ‘The God who existed before his coming in the flesh was not man, but was God, existing with God the Father, invisible and impassible. [Col. 0122C] But when he became man, the name Christ was assumed, together with the suffering and death that follow the name. For divine Scripture affirms: “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness” (Psalm 44).’ It should be known, moreover, that divine Scripture very often uses the past tense for the future, as: ‘After this he was seen upon earth and conversed with men’ (Baruch 3). For he had not yet been seen or conversed with men when these words were spoken. And: ‘By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept, when we remembered you, Zion’ (Psalm 136). These things had not yet occurred. Thus Damascene; from his words two reasons are drawn why Scripture named Christ before his coming in the flesh. First, to signify the unity and identity of the person, or hypostasis, of the Word before and after the assumption of flesh. From this unity would follow that κοινωνία ἰδιωμάτων, the communication of properties, by which the properties of both natures are truly and absolutely attributed to Christ, as has often been said; consequently, whatever the Son of God is read to have done, or to have been done to him, before the Incarnation is said also to have been done by Christ or to have happened to him. [Col. 0122D] Second, to suggest that, although before Christ’s coming in the flesh the anointing of the humanity assumed by the Divinity had not actually been effected—whence the name Christ was derived and bestowed—it had nevertheless been pre-defined, predetermined, and preordained by God, and was no less certainly to come to pass than if it had already then been completed. Thus, in order to commend the mystery of this union—future indeed in its actual realization, but foreseen by God—sacred Scripture named him Christ before the assumption of flesh. So the oracles of the prophets announcing a future event were very often written in the past tense, to indicate the infallible certainty of the future event, just as if it were past.]

“Let us not tempt Christ,” he says, “as some of them tempted him, and were destroyed by serpents” (1 Cor. 10). The outstanding apostle Peter also says:

“And now why are you tempting God by placing upon the necks of the disciples a yoke which neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? But through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ we believe that we are saved, just as they also are.”

We know without any doubt that the people of God, liberated from Egypt, led with dry feet through immense channels of water, and preserved through the vast solitudes of the wilderness, were delivered by God alone, in accordance with the words: “The Lord alone led them, and there was no foreign god with them” (Deut. 32). How, then, does the Apostle, on the basis of so many and such evident testimonies, proclaim both that the Jewish people were liberated from Egypt by Jesus and that Christ was tempted by the Jews at that time in the wilderness, saying, “Let us not tempt Christ, as some of them tempted him, and were destroyed by serpents”? And how does the blessed Apostle Peter proclaim that all the saints who lived under the law of the Old Testament were saved through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ?

Come forth, then; flee from here, if you can, whoever you are who, raging with a savage mouth and blasphemous spirit, think there is scarcely any difference between Adam and Christ, and who deny that he was God even after the Virgin’s childbirth. Show fully how you can prove that he was not God even before the birth of his body. For behold, the Apostle cries out that the people were saved from the land of Egypt by Jesus, that Christ was tempted in the wilderness by the unbelieving, and that our fathers—that is, the patriarchs and prophets—were saved through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ. Deny these things, if you can. Nor shall I be surprised if you do so, since you have denied what we all read, just as you denied what we all believe.

Understand at last, therefore, that even then Christ, as God, led the people out of Egypt; that Christ, as God, was tempted by the tempting people; and that Christ, as God, saved all the righteous through the generosity of his grace. For through the unity of the mystery, God passed into Christ and Christ into God in such a way that whatever God did is said to have been accomplished by Christ, and whatever Christ afterward endured is said to have been endured by God.

And therefore, when the Prophet says:

[Note: [Col. 0123B] “A recent god,” that is, a god whom your fathers did not worship. This is how the statement is explained in the Song of Moses, Deuteronomy 32. Saint Augustine nevertheless writes that all false gods are “recent gods,” because they are not eternal and lack a beginningless existence, but were recently fashioned in a sculptor’s workshop or in the mind of human vanity; hence they are called graven images and idols. “These things also,” says Saint Basil (in his *Scholia on the Psalms*), “refute the madness of Arius and Eunomius. For if the Only-Begotten is not consubstantial with the Father, he will rightly be called foreign. And if there was a time when he was not, then he is recent and not eternal.” Basil would certainly have named Nestorius together with Arius and Eunomius, had Nestorius not lived later.]

“There shall be no recent god among you, and you shall not worship a foreign god,”

he was preaching in this sense and with this spirit when the Apostle said that Christ was the leader of the Israelite people out of Egypt. He intended that the one who was born from the Virgin as man should nevertheless always have been in God through the unity of the mystery. Otherwise, unless this is believed, either Christ is, with the heretics, not God, or else, contrary to the Prophet, he is believed to be recent.

But far be this from the Catholic people of God: that they should appear either to dissent from the Prophet or to agree with the heretics. Perhaps that people of blessing might fall under the curse that says it has placed its hope in man. For whoever asserts that our Lord Jesus Christ was born as a solitary man must necessarily be subject to a twofold curse, whether he believes in him or does not believe in him. If he believes:

[Note: [Col. 0123C] Saint Jerome likewise argues from this passage: “If cursed is the man who trusts in man, while Paul of Samosata and Photinus, although they proclaim the Savior as holy and exalted in every virtue, nevertheless confess him to be a man, then those who place their hope in a man will be cursed.” Jerome would similarly have included Nestorius here, had he known him.]

“Cursed is he who places his hope in man” (Jer. 17).

But if he does not believe, he is nonetheless cursed, because, although he has not believed in a man, he has altogether denied God.

## CHAPTER X. He explains what it means to confess Jesus and what it means to dissolve him.

For this is what that beloved John of God, foreseeing it when the Lord revealed it to him, spoke concerning the very one who was speaking in him. “Every spirit,” he says, “that confesses Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God; and”

[Note: [Col. 0123C] Properly, he “dissolves Jesus” who divides the Savior into two, or who posits two persons in Christ, as Cerinthus, Nestorius, and others did. More broadly, as Bede explains: “He dissolves Jesus who denies either his divinity, as Arius did, or his rational soul, as Apollinaris did, or his flesh, as Manichaeus did”—all of which Catholic faith teaches that he truly possessed. He also dissolves Jesus who corrupts Jesus’ commandments and words either by living perversely or by interpreting them more perversely. Likewise, he who disturbs the unity of the holy Church, which Jesus came to gather, attempts, so far as he is able, to dissolve Jesus. Nor is it surprising that such people are not from God, since they sever God’s works, words, or sacraments. Indeed, they are so far from being from God that some of them, who wished by an evil doctrine to separate Christ’s divinity from the dispensation of his humanity, even erased from this Epistle the verse that says, “Every spirit that dissolves Jesus is not from God,” lest they be convicted of their error by the authority of blessed John. Finally, Nestorius revealed that he did not know that this sentence had been included in the authoritative copies, and therefore he did not fear dissolving Jesus, saying that blessed Mary the Virgin was not the mother of God but only the mother of a man, thereby making one person for the man and another for the divinity, and so forth. This is the Venerable Bede. What he says about the heretics’ presumed erasure of this sentence and about Nestorius’ ignorance he seems to have taken from Socrates, who records the same matters more fully in these words (Book 7 of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 32): “Moreover, Nestorius did not know that it was written in the ancient copies of the Catholic Epistle of Saint John: ‘Every spirit that dissolves Jesus is not from God.’ Indeed, all who sought to separate divinity from Christ’s humanity did not hesitate to erase and remove this sentence from the ancient copies. For this reason the ancient interpreters indicated that certain people had corrupted that Epistle in order to separate the man in Christ from God. But his humanity is joined with his divinity, and they are not two but one. Relying on this, the ancients did not hesitate to call Mary *Theotokos*, ‘Mother of God.’ Thus also Eusebius Pamphilus speaks in Book 3, chapter 42, of the *Life of Constantine*: ‘God with us consented to be born for our sake, and the place of his birth is called Bethlehem by its proper name among the Hebrews. Therefore the most holy empress Helena adorned the childbirth of the Mother of God with magnificent monuments and illuminated that sacred cave with insignia of every kind.’ Origen, too, in the first volume of his commentaries on Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, discusses this matter at length when he explains why Mary was called *Theotokos*. Thus Nestorius seems to have been entirely ignorant of the writings of the ancients, and for that reason attacks the term *Theotokos*. Thus far Socrates, whose account agrees well with Cassianus’ argument.]

“and everyone who dissolves Jesus is not from God.”

[Note: [Col. 0124D] Thus in the Greek text: καὶ τοῦτο ἔστι τοῦ Ἀντιχρίστου ὁ ἀκηκόατε, “and this is of the Antichrist, which you have heard.” The Latin and Vulgate version, however, has: “And this is the Antichrist, of whom you have heard,” and so forth. “Antichrist” is not meant as a person but figuratively, just as John is called Elijah, Matthew 12. “Antichrist,” that is, the forerunner of Antichrist, says Saint Thomas in his commentary.]

“And this is of the Antichrist, which you have heard because it is coming, and now it is already in the world” (1 John 4).

O admirable and singular piety of God, who, like the most vigilant and prudent physician, foretold beforehand the diseases that would one day come into his Church! And when he announced the illness, he provided a remedy through the very announcement, so that all, recognizing the approaching sickness, might begin from far away to avoid what they had learned was imminent.

And therefore Saint John says: “Everyone who dissolves Jesus is not from God, and this is of the Antichrist.” Do you recognize him, heretic? Do you recognize that he has already spoken openly and specifically about you? For no one dissolves Jesus in this way except one who does not confess him to be God. Since the whole faith and worship of the Church consist in confessing Jesus as true God, who could more completely dissolve his veneration and worship than one who denied in him the very thing that we all worship?

Beware, I beg you, beware lest anyone also be able to call you Antichrist. Do you think that I am insulting or cursing you? What I say is not my own; behold, the Evangelist says: “Everyone who dissolves Jesus is not from God, and this is the Antichrist.” If you do not dissolve Jesus and do not deny that he is God, no one can call you Antichrist. But if you deny it, why do you object when someone calls you Antichrist? You yourself have said this about yourself—you, I say, by your denial.

Do you wish to know that this is true? Tell me: when Jesus was born from the Virgin, what do you wish him to have been, man or God? If only God, then you certainly dissolve Jesus, since you deny that a man was united to God in him. But if man, you likewise dissolve him, since, as you do, you blaspheme that he was born only and solely as a man. Unless perhaps you think that you do not dissolve Jesus by denying that he was God, although you would certainly dissolve him even if you denied that the man born was united with God.

But perhaps you would like this to be made clearer by examples. Receive an example of each kind.

[Note: [Col. 0125D] Manichaeus denied that Christ assumed true flesh, namely human flesh, and claimed that he merely presented to human eyes a phantom or empty apparition; consequently, he acknowledged Christ as God only and not also as man. Conversely, Ebion, Cerinthus, and their follower Nestorius clamored that he was man only, as has often been said. Hence Saint Jerome, in his commentary on Galatians 1, says: “The faith of the Church, established amid the shipwrecks of false doctrines, if it confesses Christ as man, is assailed by Ebion and Photinus. If it maintains that he is God, Manichaeus and Marcion, and the author of the novel doctrine, arise.” Saint Augustine likewise says in his book *On Heresies*: “The Ebionites say that Christ was only a man.”]

Manichaeus is outside the Church because he asserts that Jesus was God only; Ebion, because he asserts that he was man. Each denied and dissolved Jesus: the one by saying that he was merely man, the other by saying that he was merely God. Although they said different things, the impiety of their difference was equal.

Except that, if any distinction can be made among the magnitude of evils, your blasphemy is more injurious—the blasphemy that asserts him to be only a man—than that which asserts him to be only God. For although both are evil, it is nevertheless more insulting to rob the Lord of what is divine than of what is human.

This, therefore, and this alone is the Catholic faith; this, and this alone, is true: to believe the Lord Jesus Christ to be God just as he is man, and man just as he is God. “Everyone who dissolves Jesus is not from God.”

To dissolve him means to wish to tear apart what has been united in Jesus and to separate what is indivisible. But what has been united and made indivisible in Jesus? Man, certainly, and God. Therefore he dissolves Jesus who separates and tears these apart. Otherwise, if he does not tear them apart and separate them, he does not dissolve him. But if he separates and tears them apart, then he certainly dissolves him.

## CHAPTER XI. The mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation clearly proves Christ’s divinity.

And therefore, to every person who breaks out into this blasphemy and madness, the Lord Jesus himself, in the Gospel, cries out and solemnly declares on his own behalf what he said to the Pharisees:

> “What God has joined, let no human being separate” (Matthew 19).

[Note: What the Lord said literally about the union of husband and wife, the Author allegorically applies to the mystery of the Incarnation, by which divinity and humanity were so joined in one hypostasis that they can in no way be separated or divided. It should also be noted that the Lord did not say, “Those whom God has joined,” but “What God has joined,” so that he might seem to speak not of two, but of one body, since shortly before he had said: “Therefore they are no longer two, but one flesh.” This also fits the mystery of the Incarnation, in which God and man are not two, but one Christ, one hypostasis, one subsistent being, which cannot be dissolved or separated.]

Although, where it was spoken by God, this may seem to have been an answer concerning another matter,

[Note: Namely, in response to the Pharisees’ question about the carnal marriage of man and woman and the reasons for dismissing a wife.]

nevertheless the depth of God, which was speaking no less about spiritual than about carnal things, intended this to be understood not only of that matter but still more of this one. For when the Jews at that time believed what you say—that Jesus was merely a man without God—and the Lord was questioned about the marital union, he instructed them not only about that matter but also about this one; and, when consulted about lesser matters, he answered concerning higher and greater ones, saying: “What God has joined, let no human being separate.”

That is: “Do not separate what God has joined in me; let human impiety not separate what divine majesty has united in me.”

But if you wish to know more fully that this is so, listen to the Apostle discussing these very matters about which the Savior then taught. As a teacher sent by God, he explained those same things that God had proclaimed mystically, insofar as the weakness of his hearers at that time was able to grasp them.

When he was discussing carnal marriage, about which the Savior had been questioned in the Gospel, he repeated the testimonies of the ancient law that the Savior himself had used, so that it might be understood that the one who used the same testimonies was explaining the same matter. Moreover, so that nothing might seem to be lacking from the argument, he also introduced carnal marriage and the names of woman and man, whom he urged toward mutual affection, in this way:

> “Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ also loved the Church” (Ephesians 5).

And again:

> “So husbands ought to love their wives as their own bodies. He who loves his wife loves himself. No one has ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the Church, because we are members of his body” (Ephesians 5).

You see how, joining the names of Christ and the Church to the names of man and woman, he drew everyone from carnal hearing toward spiritual understanding.

When he had said all these things, he added the testimonies that the Lord had used in the Gospel, saying:

[Note: These are the words not of the Apostle but of Adam in Genesis (chapter 2). Yet, although they were spoken by Adam, they were spoken under God’s breath and inspiration; therefore the Lord recalls them in the Gospel as spoken by God (Matthew 19), because God uttered them through Adam, or by Adam’s mouth, just as he spoke through the mouth of the prophets (Luke 1). The Fathers infer from these words that, during the sleep or ecstasy divinely sent upon Adam, the mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation was revealed to him, and that, awakened from that sleep, he burst into these words: “This now is bone of my bones” (Genesis 2), and what follows. By these words he signified Christ’s most intimate union with the Church—or with human nature—which was to occur through the Incarnation. Thus, from the beginning of the human race, it was announced to human beings that Christ would come in the flesh.

The principal foundation used by the Fathers to establish this view is the testimony of the Apostle cited here, where, explaining Adam’s words, he says: “This mystery is great; but I speak concerning Christ and the Church” (Ephesians 5). That is, in Adam’s words there lies hidden the great mystery of Christ’s union with the Church.

Thus Tertullian, *On the Soul* (chapters 11 and 21): “Adam immediately prophesied that great mystery concerning Christ and the Church: ‘This now is bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh; for this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh.’ He experienced a displacement of the spirit, for ecstasy fell upon him; the operative power of the Holy Spirit was at work in prophecy.”

Saint Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* 48, says that Adam prophesied in those words concerning future events.

Jerome, on the same passage in Ephesians, says: “Adam, the first man and the first prophet, prophesied this concerning Christ and the Church: that our Lord and Savior would leave his Father, God, and his heavenly mother, Jerusalem; that he would come to earthly regions for the sake of his body, the Church; that he would fashion her from his side; and that for her sake the Word would become flesh.”

Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book 9, chapter 19: “That ecstasy which God sent upon Adam, so that he fell asleep in a trance, is rightly understood to have been sent for this purpose: that his mind, through ecstasy, might become a participant, as it were, in the angelic court and, entering into the sanctuary of God, might understand the last things. Finally, awakening as though filled with prophecy, when he saw the woman brought to him together with the rib, he immediately uttered what the Apostle commends as a great mystery: ‘This now is bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh; she shall be called woman, because she was taken from man; and for this reason a man shall leave his father and mother, cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh.’ Although Scripture testifies that these words belonged to the first man, the Lord nevertheless declared in the Gospel that God had spoken them. For he says: ‘For this reason a man shall leave father and mother,’ etc. (Matthew 19), so that from this we might understand that, because of the ecstasy that had preceded in Adam, he was able to say this divinely, as a prophecy.”

Leo the Pope, letter 23: “From the very beginning of the human race, Christ was announced to humanity as one who would come in the flesh. In that flesh, as it was said, ‘the two shall be one flesh’: God and man, Christ and the Church. The Church came forth from the bridegroom’s flesh when, from the side of the crucified, blood and water flowed, and she received the sacrament of redemption and regeneration.”

Prosper, *On the Predestination and Promise of God*, book 1, chapter 1: “That this was done both as a reality and as a figure, the Apostle Paul is witness. Explaining this passage in the Epistle to the Ephesians, he says: ‘This mystery is great; but I speak concerning Christ and the Church.’ The great mystery, therefore, looked toward what had been promised. Adam saw beside him the one whom he believed to be his wife. For us, by the faith of those who live, he signified the future Church. He called her the mother of all living, for this reason: just as Eve was formed from the side of the sleeping Adam, so he foresaw that the Church would be formed—as indeed she was—from the side of Christ hanging on the cross. She is the mother of all living. For she is that woman who is protected from the serpent’s sight for a time, times, and half a time, as is said in the Apocalypse concerning the Church (Revelation 12).”

Bernard, sermon 6 on the Vigil of the Nativity of the Lord: “The first man, the father of all living, uttering the great mystery that the Apostle later commended more clearly in Christ and the Church, said: ‘A man shall leave father and mother, cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh.’”

And in sermon 2 on Septuagesima: “What kind of sleep should that be called, or believed to have been, which the Lord sent upon Adam, during which, without any sensation of pain whatsoever, a rib was taken from the side of the sleeping man to build a woman? For my part, I do not think that he fell asleep except through contemplation of immutable truth and of the abyss of divine wisdom, rising above bodily senses. This can be inferred especially from his words. On returning, he indicates what he had left, coming as if drunk from a wine cellar and uttering that great mystery which the Apostle much later commended in Christ and the Church: ‘This now is bone of my bones.’ And again: ‘For this reason a man shall leave father and mother,’ etc. Does he seem to you to have been completely asleep, when he awoke and burst into this utterance? Would he not rather have been able to say: ‘I sleep, but my heart is awake’ (Song of Songs 5)?”

These are Bernard and the other Fathers cited in the same sense.]

> “For this reason a man shall leave his father and his mother and be joined to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Matthew 19).

After this, indeed, as though with a great and emphatic proclamation, he added:

[Note: The Apostle calls this “mystery” (*τὸ μυστήριον*), which our translator renders as *sacramentum*, “sacrament.” In the previous Epistle to the Corinthians (chapter 10) he calls it *τύπον*, “figure,” and in the Epistle to the Galatians (chapter 4) an “allegory.” Nazianzen used the word in this sense, as can be seen in Budaeus’s commentary on the Greek language.

Hence Saint Ambrose says: “‘This mystery is great; but I speak concerning Christ and the Church.’ He signifies that the sacrament of the mystery is great in the union of man and woman.”

And Jerome: “He interprets the same thing allegorically concerning Christ and the Church, so that Adam might prefigure Christ and Eve the Church. For the last Adam became a life-giving spirit” (1 Corinthians 15). Just as the entire human race is born from Adam and his wife, so the whole multitude of believers is generated from Christ and the Church. Having become one body of the Church, it is once more placed in Christ’s side, fills the place of the rib, and becomes one body with the man, as the Lord himself requested in the Gospel: “Father, grant that, just as you and I are one, so they too may be one in us” (John 10).

Saint Thomas, in his Commentary, interprets *sacramentum* as “the sign of a sacred reality,” namely, the union of Christ and the Church.

The meaning of the Apostle handed down by the Fathers is therefore this: although, literally and historically, Adam spoke these words about the mutual union and love of man and wife, nevertheless this is a great sacrament and mystery—that is, beneath these same words and beneath the original institution of marriage there lies mystically hidden and signified the harmonious and indissoluble union of Christ and the Church.

For just as a man leaves father and mother in order to cling to his wife, so, in a certain sense, Christ, having become man, left the Father, as he himself says: “I came forth from the Father and came into the world” (John 16)—not by abandoning his divinity, but by assuming humanity. He also left his mother, the synagogue, to which, insofar as he was a Jew, he had been subject, in order to cling to his wife or bride, that is, the Church of the Gentiles.

The Author diverges somewhat from this interpretation of the ancient Fathers in the following chapter, adapting and applying the Apostle’s passage to his own purpose. For what they understand as the union of Christ with the Church, as the Apostle’s words plainly indicate and require, he interprets as the union of divinity with the soul in Christ’s flesh, as will become clearer in the following chapter.

This passage is also commonly cited by the Fathers in confirmation of the Church’s doctrine that marriage is a sacrament. They understood the Apostle’s words in such a way that the pronoun “this” refers not only to the mystery hidden in Adam’s words—namely, the betrothal and union of Christ with the Church, as stated above—but also to the reality first signified by those same words, namely, the closest marital bond and conjugal union between husband and wife.

Although, both under the law of nature and under the Mosaic law, this union was nothing more than a natural contract—a function of nature before sin, but a remedy for concupiscence after sin—nevertheless, now, that is, in Christ or under Christ and in the Church, it is a great sacrament: a true and properly so-called sacrament of the New Law, an efficacious sign of invisible grace instituted by the Lord Christ (Master of the Sentences, book 4, distinction 26; Saint Thomas; Soto and others in the same place).

This is evident from the Council of Florence, in the decree given to the Armenians, where marriage is numbered among the seven sacraments of the New Law. It is stated still more explicitly by the Council of Trent, in the chapter *Ad abolendam* concerning heretics, session 24, in the doctrine on the sacrament of marriage, where this is defined in these words:

“Moreover, the grace that would perfect that natural love, confirm the indissoluble unity, and sanctify the spouses, Christ himself, the institutor and perfecter of the venerable sacraments, merited for us by his passion. The Apostle Paul indicates this when he says: ‘Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the Church and gave himself for her’; and he immediately adds: ‘This is a great sacrament; but I speak concerning Christ and the Church.’ Since, therefore, in the evangelical law Christ has bestowed grace upon ancient marriages, the holy Fathers, councils, and the universal tradition of the Church have always rightly taught that marriage must be numbered among the sacraments of the New Law,” and so forth.

And in canon 1, issued on the same subject:

“If anyone says that marriage is not truly and properly one of the seven sacraments of the evangelical law, instituted by Christ the Lord, but was invented by human beings in the Church, and that it does not confer grace, let him be anathema.”

This is what was stated there.

Finally, it should not be omitted that Saint Thomas also notes in his Commentary that there are four sacraments called “great,” but for different reasons:

“Baptism,” he says, “because of its effect, since it removes all guilt and opens the gate of paradise. Confirmation, because of its minister, since it is conferred only by bishops and not by others. The Eucharist, because of what it contains, since it contains the whole Christ. And marriage,”

[Col. 0130B]

“because of its signification, since it signifies the union of Christ and the Church.]

> “This mystery is great,”

[Col. 0129A]

he says.

He entirely removed and cut off the carnal interpretation of this matter when he declared the sacrament to be wholly divine. And what did he add after this?

[Note: Saint Jerome, and before him Gregory Nazianzen, observed that the clause “But I speak” was added by the Apostle as an expression of modesty and humility.

“His humility,” says Gregory, “is shown when he adds: ‘But I speak concerning Christ and the Church.’ Gregory Nazianzen, a highly eloquent man and exceptionally learned in the Scriptures, used to say to me, when he discussed this passage with me: ‘See how great the mystery of this chapter is, since the Apostle, interpreting it concerning Christ and the Church, does not assert it explicitly in the manner required by the dignity of the testimony, but says, in a certain sense: I know that this passage is full of ineffable mysteries and requires a divine heart for its interpretation. But, in view of the smallness of my understanding, for the present I think that it should be understood as referring to Christ and the Church—not because anything greater than Christ and the Church is involved, but because it is difficult to interpret everything said about Adam and Eve as referring to Christ and the Church.’”]

> “But I speak concerning Christ and the Church.”

When he had said, “This mystery is great,” he did not say, “This is the explanation of the mystery.” Rather, what did he say? “But I speak concerning Christ and the Church.”

This is what he means: “That is indeed a great mystery, but I speak of it as concerning Christ and the Church.” That is,

[Note: This is an obscure and ambiguous passage. For what difference is there between what perhaps everyone cannot grasp at present and what they can grasp more easily? It seems to me to refer to the preceding words: “This mystery is great”; he did not say, “This is the explanation of the mystery.”

He therefore calls “mystery” what, from the very sound of the words, is immediately understood to be that great mystery of piety mentioned by the Apostle, which was manifested in the flesh—that is, the Word of God incarnate—which he sets forth from the Apostle at the beginning of the following chapter and later calls the “more accessible understanding.”

By the explanation of the mystery, however, he seems to understand the deeper and more hidden allegory concerning Christ’s union with the Church, like that of the head with the body and the bridegroom with the bride. This is not grasped so easily or immediately upon hearing of that mystery, although both refer to Christ, as he says below, and are related to Christ.

For, as is also prior by nature, one more easily conceives that Christ is God incarnate than that he is the head and bridegroom of the Church; and it is precisely this that the Apostle’s words in Ephesians 5 concern.]

because perhaps not everyone can grasp that at present, let them at least grasp this—which nevertheless does not differ from or depart from that, since both concern Christ.

But if some cannot grasp those deeper things, let them at least recognize these easier ones, so that, once they have begun to grasp the more accessible understanding, they may be able to reach the higher one, and so that attaining the clearer matter now may afterward become the path to the deeper matter.

## CHAPTER XII. He explains more fully what that mystery is which is signified under the names of husband and wife.

What, then, is that great mystery which is signified under the name of husband and wife? Let us question the Apostle himself, who, elsewhere, in order to teach the same matter, used words referring to the reality itself, saying:

[Note: Clearly, *ὁμολογουμένως*, which sounds as though one were to say “confessedly” or “it is confessed.” Hence Ambrose rendered it by a circumlocution: “And indeed,” he says, “by the confession of all, the mystery of piety is great,” and so forth.

Cyril, citing this same passage against Nestorius, says: “Who, I ask, is the one who was manifested in the flesh? Is it not clear in every respect that he is none other than God the Word himself? From this the great mystery of piety is perceived. He was seen by angels when he was received into heaven. He was then preached among the Gentiles through the holy Apostles. He was believed on in the world. But was this merely as a man absolutely like us? By no means; rather, as God made man and given an origin like ours. Finally, he was taken up into glory, so that he might hear the Father saying: ‘Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet’ (Psalm 109).”]

> “And confessedly great is the mystery of piety: he was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, appeared to angels, preached among the Gentiles, believed on in the world, taken up in glory” (1 Timothy 3).

What, then, is that great mystery which was manifested in the flesh? God, plainly, born from flesh; God seen in a body. Just as he was openly manifested in the flesh, so he was openly taken up in glory.

This, then, is the great mystery of which he himself says:

> “For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Matthew 19).

Who, then, were the two in one flesh? God, plainly, and the soul.

[Note: Cassianus seems unique in this interpretation of his, since none of the ancient writers thought of it, as is clear from what has been said; nor does it sufficiently fit the Apostle’s words. He does not say, “This mystery is great; but I speak concerning Christ alone,” but “concerning Christ and the Church.” Why would he add “and the Church” if he were considering Christ alone—that is, the union of the Word with the soul in Christ’s flesh, as this Author explains? Although what he says about this union is true.

Moreover, the interpretation added here—“That man of whom the prophet says, ‘A brother does not redeem,’ etc.; that man, I say, clung to human flesh as to his wife”—is plainly harsh and foreign to the sense of Scripture, although he later attempts to excuse and defend it. Still, he may be permitted here to abound in his own meaning, since he abounds and labors in defense of the faith, not against it.]

For in the one flesh that has been united to God, there are God and soul together with human flesh, according to the Lord’s own saying:

> “No one can take my soul from me, but I lay it down of myself. I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up again” (John 10).

Thus you now see three things here: God, flesh, and soul. God is the one who speaks; flesh is that in which he speaks; soul is that about which he speaks.

Therefore that man of whom the prophet says:

[Note: This verse is variously explained by the Fathers.

Saint Ambrose agrees with Cassian in this commentary: “The brother whom one human being, poured forth into the light from the same mother’s womb, cannot redeem, because he is held back by the weakness of a similar nature; a man will redeem—but that man of whom it is written: ‘The Lord will send them a man who will save them’ (Isaiah 19), and who said of himself: ‘You seek to kill me, a man who has told you the truth’ (John 8).’ And below: ‘The only redeemer is understood, who could not be subject to ancient sin. Therefore, by “man” let us understand the Lord Jesus, who assumed the condition of man in order to crucify the sin of all in his flesh and erase the bond of everyone by his blood.’” Thus Ambrose.

Jerome reads the passage interrogatively in this way: “A brother does not redeem; will a man redeem?” He suggests two interpretations:

“If Christ did not redeem,” he says, “those who trust in their own strength, and who called himself the brother of the Apostles and, by rising again, became the firstborn of the risen—will he not redeem Adam, since the first man died and did not rise again? For our brother is Christ, God and man, who redeemed us. Or, what Moses did not redeem, Christ redeemed.”

This is Jerome—or the author of his Commentary.

As to the first interpretation and that question, Augustine agrees in these words: “Do you expect a man to redeem you from the coming wrath? If your brother does not redeem you, will a man redeem you? Who is the brother who, if he does not redeem, leaves no human being able to redeem? He who, after his resurrection, said: ‘Go, tell my brothers’ (Matthew 28; John 20). He wished to be our brother; and when we say, ‘Our Father,’ this is manifested in us. For whoever says to God, ‘Our Father,’ says to Christ, ‘Brother.’ Therefore, if he himself does not redeem, will a man redeem? Will some human being redeem if the Son of Man does not redeem? If Christ does not redeem, will Adam redeem?” Thus Augustine.

Chrysostom and others, however, interpret the entire passage as referring to Christ, in this way: “Christ will not redeem”—the world, that is—“as a brother,” that is, as a Jew, or through the Jewish law, “but as one made man.” Nor will he offer himself for his own redemption or give God his own propitiation and the price of redemption for his own soul, but for all others. For Christ died not for his own sake but for ours.]

> “A brother does not redeem; will a man redeem?” (Psalm 48).

He who, as was said, ascended to where he was before (John 6), and of whom we read:

> “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3).

For this reason, I say, the man left his father and mother—that is, God from whom he was born, and that Jerusalem which is the mother of us all—and clung to human flesh as to his wife.

And for this reason he expressly said of the father, “a man shall leave his father,”

[Note: An ingenious observation, as though “his” were not understood, just as “his” is expressed above. Certainly Saint Jerome, in his Commentary on the Epistle to the Ephesians, has both *patrem suum* (“his father”) and *matrem suam* (“his mother”), although there he omits *suam*. Indeed, Cassian himself earlier, in chapter 12, quoted the passage in this way: “For this reason a man shall leave his father and his mother,” which it is surprising that he forgot, unless the text has been corrupted.]

but, concerning the mother, he did not say “his,” but merely said “mother,” because she was not so much his mother as the mother of all believers, that is, of all of us.

And he was joined to his wife, because just as man and woman are one body, so the majesty of divinity and human flesh are united, and the two became one flesh—that is, God and soul in one flesh.

For just as that flesh had God dwelling within it, so it also had a soul dwelling together with God within it.

This, then, is that great mystery to the investigation of which the Apostle’s astonishment calls and the exhortation of the Divinity invites us. It is certainly not alien to Christ and the Church, as he himself says: “But I speak concerning Christ and the Church.”

For the flesh of the Church is also the flesh of Christ, and in Christ’s flesh there are God and soul. Thus what is in Christ is also in the Church, because the mystery believed in Christ’s flesh is likewise contained by faith in the Church.

## CHAPTER XIII. With what longing the ancient patriarchs desired to see the revelation of this mystery.

This mystery, which was manifested in the flesh, appeared in the world, and is preached among the Gentiles,

[Note: In agreement with this passage is blessed Irenaeus, book 4 *Against Heresies*, chapter 34:

“Since not only the prophets but also many righteous people, foreseeing through the Spirit his coming, prayed to arrive at that time when they would see their Lord face to face and hear his words, the Lord made this clear to the disciples, saying: ‘Many prophets and righteous people desired to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it’ (Matthew 13; Luke 10). How, then, could they have desired both to hear and to see unless they had foreknown that his coming would take place? And how could they have foreknown it unless they had first received foreknowledge from him?” and so forth.

It should be observed in those words of the Lord that Matthew names “prophets and righteous people,” whereas Luke names “prophets and kings.” Maldonado considers it credible (on Matthew 13) that Christ named the three most distinguished classes of persons—prophets, kings, and righteous people—but that Matthew omitted kings and Luke omitted righteous people.]

many of the ancient saints, just as they foresaw it in spirit, also wished to see it in the flesh.

“For truly,” says the Lord,

> “I tell you, many prophets and righteous people desired to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it” (Matthew 13).

And therefore the prophet Isaiah said:

[Note: To show the ardent nature of their desire, the prophet did not say, “Would that you would come now,” but, “Would that you would tear open the heavens and descend.” As though he were saying: “Would that you would come so quickly and with such force that you would not seek an entrance, but would suddenly tear open the heavens and descend.” This does not mean that God needed to tear or break the heavens in order to come; rather, the prophet speaks in human fashion to display the fervor of the desire with which the ancient Fathers longed for Christ’s coming.

In the same way David says: “Lord, bow down the heavens and descend” (Psalm 143). Here the great desire of the eminent prophet is expressed, when he asks that God not delay at the gates of the opening heaven but bend the heaven and descend.]

> “Would that you would tear open the heavens, Lord, and descend” (Isaiah 64).

David also says:

> “Lord, bow down the heavens and descend” (Psalm 143).

Moses likewise:

[Note: Saint Jerome, on Isaiah 65:

“This,” he says, “Moses was seeking when he spoke to God: ‘If I have found favor with you, show yourself to me plainly.’ He awaited Christ’s reproach as greater riches than the treasures of Egypt, while desiring the future recompense; and, as though he saw the invisible God, he contemplated him in his mind. Concerning him we also read in the Psalms: ‘The hope of all the ends of the earth and of the distant seas’ (Psalm 64). And in Genesis: ‘He himself will be the expectation of the nations’ (Genesis 49).”

Thus Jerome indicates that Moses, in those words, sought the coming of the Messiah in the flesh, in which he would be visibly seen. Saint Augustine, however (*Questions on Exodus* 151), and others thought that Moses was earnestly requesting a vision of the divine essence.]

> “Show yourself to me, that I may see you plainly” (Exodus 33).

No one came closer than Moses to receiving the law, hearing God speak from the clouds, and approaching the very presence of his majesty.

And yet, although no one saw more immediate things concerning God than he did, why did he still ask for things more manifest, saying:

> “Show yourself to me, that I may see you plainly”?

He did so because he was asking that what the Apostle said had been accomplished should take place in the very same words: namely, that the Lord should be openly manifested in the flesh, openly appear to the world, openly be taken up in glory, and that the saints should finally see with bodily eyes everything they had foreseen with spiritual eyes.

## CHAPTER XIV. He refutes the impious and blasphemous opinion of the heretics who said that God dwelt and spoke in Christ as in an instrument or statue.

Otherwise, if, as the heretic says, God was to dwell in the Lord Jesus Christ,

[Note: Just as demons dwelt in statues and idols, then spoke and delivered their oracles, so the impious Nestorius blasphemed that God had dwelt in the man Christ and had spoken through that man’s mouth—just as he also spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets, who have existed from the beginning of the world (Luke 1)—and that he had no hypostatic union with him.

He said that God spoke as though in an instrument, as wind or spirit produces a sound in an instrument and through an instrument, namely, a musical instrument; or “in an instrument” in general, that is, as in a tool. For *ὄργανον* means any instrument.

Now, being God’s dwelling and God’s instrument is something shared with other holy human beings. That God dwells in his saints as in temples, the Apostle testifies in 1 Corinthians 3: “Do you not know that you are God’s temple?” And in 1 Corinthians 6: “Do you not know that your bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit, who is in you? Glorify and carry God in your body.”

That God works through human beings as through his organs and instruments, the same Apostle repeatedly teaches in Romans 15: “I would not dare to speak of anything that Christ did not accomplish through me, in word and deed, through the power of signs and wonders, through the power of the Holy Spirit.” And in 1 Corinthians 12: “There are varieties of works, but the same God who works all things in all.”

These things, therefore, and others like them, which Nestorius attributed to Christ, are also found in the other saints. Yet it is certain that the incarnate Word dwelt in man—that is, in humanity—and spoke to us through humanity in a very different way from that in which he dwelt in the other saints, since the Apostle says that it is a great mystery and sacrament of piety that God appeared in the flesh (1 Timothy 3).

For what is great and singular about something shared by all others?]
