as though in a statue or an instrument—that is, so that he merely dwelt as if in a man and spoke as if through a man, rather than being himself the one who dwelt there and who, from himself and from his own body, spoke as God—

then he had already dwelt in the saints in the same way and had spoken through the saints.

He was also present and spoke in those very people whom I mentioned above, who were praying for his coming.

And what need was there for all of them to ask for something they already possessed, if they were asking for what they had already received?

Or why would they desire to see with their eyes what they held in their hearts, especially since it is more to possess the same thing within oneself than to see it outside oneself?

Or, if God was to dwell in Christ as he dwelt in all the saints, why would all the saints desire to see Christ more than themselves?

And if they were to see in the Lord Jesus the same thing they possessed in themselves, why would they not much rather consider it preferable to possess that same thing in themselves than to see it in another?

But you are mistaken, wretched madness, not understanding, as the Apostle says, either what you are saying or about what you are making assertions (1 Timothy 1).

For all the prophets and all the saints received from God a certain portion of the divine Spirit, according to what they were able to receive.

But in Christ “all the fullness of divinity dwelt and dwells bodily” (Colossians 2).

And therefore all are far beneath his fullness, since they receive something from his fullness (John 1). Their fulfillment is Christ’s gift, because all were empty unless he were the fullness of all.

## CHAPTER XV. What the prayers of the saints concerning the coming of the Messiah contained, and what kind of desire it was.

All the saints, therefore, desired this, prayed for this, and longed to see with their eyes what they understood with their soul and mind. And therefore the prophet Isaiah says: “Would that you would rend the heavens and descend” (Isaiah 64).

[Col. 0134C] Habakkuk likewise, announcing the same thing that Isaiah desired, says: “When the years draw near, you will be shown; at the coming of the appointed times you will be manifested: God will come from Theman,” or, as the passage may read, “God will come from the South” (Habakkuk 3).

[Note: [Col. 0134D] That is, “you will be manifested.” The Vulgate edition reads: “In the midst of the years you will make it known.” Saint Jerome, translating from the Septuagint, has: “When the years draw near, you will be known”; and: [Col. 0135B] “When the time comes, you will be shown.” “Apart from the Septuagint,” he says, “this is found neither in the Hebrew nor in any of the other interpreters.” Elsewhere (Vol. II), Jerome, referring to this passage, says: “The two years of which, in the song of Habakkuk, we read according to the Hebrew are: ‘In the midst of two periods you will be known.’ It is written in the Gospel according to John that the Lord came to Jerusalem through three Passovers, which make two years.” Thus Jerome.]

David also says: “God will come manifestly” (Psalm 49). And again: “You who sit upon the cherubim, appear” (Psalm 79).

Some announced his advent, which he granted to the world; others requested it. Several, with differing expressions but equal devotion, understanding to some extent what a great thing they were praying for—that God dwelling in God, remaining in the form and bosom of God, should empty himself, take the form of a servant, and humble himself even to accepting all the bitterness and insults of suffering; that he should undergo punishment in return for benefits and, what is most intolerable and most unworthy, receive death from those for whom he himself would die—understanding this, then, to some extent, all the saints, understanding it, I say, to some extent, [Col. 0136A] since no one understands how great it is, unanimously requested the advent of God with one voice and, as it were, in mutual harmony.

They knew that in this lay the hope of all and that in this the salvation of all was contained, because no one can release the bound unless he is free from bonds; no one can rescue sinners unless he is without sin. For no one can free another from anything unless he himself is free from that thing by which the other is freed. And since death had passed into all, all needed life, so that, dying in Adam, they might live in Christ.

For although many saints, many chosen persons, and many who were very close and dear to God existed, nevertheless none could be completely saved by himself unless he had been saved through the Lord’s advent and redemption.

# BOOK SIX

[Col. 0135]

## CHAPTER ONE  
He demonstrates the immensity of divine power through the miracle of the multitude’s being fed with five barley loaves and two fish.

[Col. 0135B]

[Note: [Col. 0135C] We read twice in the Gospel that a miracle of this kind occurred. In the first instance—which all four Evangelists report—the Lord fed five thousand men, *ἀνδρῶν*, that is, males, apart from children and women, with five barley loaves and two fish (Matthew 14; Mark 6; Luke 9; John 6). In the later instance—which only Matthew and Mark mention—he is said to have fed four thousand people with seven loaves and a few small fish (Matthew 15; Mark 8).

That these were two different miracles is also clear from the Lord’s words to the disciples, who were anxious about the shortage of bread, in Matthew 16, where he distinctly recalls and emphasizes both events: “Why are you thinking among yourselves, you of little faith, because you have no bread? Do you not yet understand, nor remember the five loaves and the five thousand men, and how many baskets you took up?”

Accordingly, Augustine says in Book 2, chapter 50, *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*: “It will certainly not be out of place to point out, concerning the miracle of the seven loaves that the two Evangelists Matthew and Mark have reported, that if one of them had mentioned it without mentioning the five loaves, he would have been thought contrary to the others. For who would not have supposed that one and the same event had occurred? But because those who narrated the miracle of the seven loaves did not remain silent about the five loaves either, no one is troubled, and everyone understands that both events occurred. We have said this so that whenever something similar is found to have been done by the Lord, which appears in some respect to conflict with another Evangelist so that it cannot be resolved at all, nothing else should be understood than that both events occurred and that one was reported by one Evangelist and the other by another, just as we have mentioned the groups reclining by hundreds and by fifties. For if we did not also find both events in one writer, we would think that the individual writers had made contradictory statements.” Thus Augustine.

Saint Jerome explains the varying and different circumstances of both miracles in the following words (*Commentary on Matthew*, chapter 15):

“Let us dwell only on the points in which they differ. Above, we read: ‘When evening had come, the disciples approached him, saying: The place is deserted,’ and so forth; here, after the disciples have been summoned, the Lord himself says: ‘I have compassion on the crowd, because they have already remained with me for three days.’ There were five loaves there and two fish; here, seven loaves and a few small fish. There they recline upon grass; here, upon the ground. There the number of those who eat is five thousand; here, four thousand. There twelve baskets are filled with the remnants of the fragments; here, seven hampers,” and so forth.]

We read in the Gospel that, when five loaves had been set before the people at the Lord’s command, an innumerable multitude of God’s people was fed (John 6). Yet how this happened, neither speech can recount, nor calculation gather, nor understanding conceive.

So great and so incomprehensible is the force of divine power that, although we possess within ourselves an awareness of the event itself, [Note: [Col. 0136C] I think that “impossible” is used here in the sense of “very difficult,” as it often is in Scripture. Although we cannot comprehend God’s omnipotence, whether in this multiplication and distribution of the loaves or in other miracles, nevertheless, from other similar examples and miracles we can understand to some extent the means or manner of this miracle.

In this breaking and distribution, the multiplication of the loaves must be understood as having occurred miraculously, in the manner by which, through the multiplication or addition of foreign matter, Eve was formed from Adam’s single rib (Genesis 2); and by which the jar of flour did not fail and the jug of oil was not diminished in the house of the woman of Zarephath, according to Elijah’s word (1 Kings 17); and by which a small amount of oil, at Elisha’s prayer, filled many vessels (2 Kings 4).

Hugh of Saint Victor treats the first example in Book 1 of *On the Sacraments*; the Master of the Sentences, in Book 2, distinction 18; and Saint Thomas, Part 1, question 92, article 3. Tertullian cites the second and third examples in Book 4, chapter 21, *Against Marcion*. He also adds a fourth similar example concerning Elisha, who fed one hundred men with twenty barley loaves (2 Kings 4).

“If you review”—that is, reread—“the fourth book” of Kings, he says, “you will find the whole of this sequence concerning that man of God. When he had ordered the twenty barley loaves that had been offered to be distributed among the people, his servant, considering the size of the crowd and the smallness of the food, replied: ‘What? Shall I set this before one hundred thousand men?’ ‘Give it to them,’ he said, ‘and they will eat, for thus says the Lord.’ And they ate and left some over, according to the word of the Lord.” Thus Tertullian.

Where, instead of “one hundred thousand,” the Septuagint renders *ἑκατόν* and our translator “one hundred”—as it should be read, with “thousand” omitted—as Pamelius notes.

Saint Ambrose also compares this same miracle with the miracle of the water changed into wine at Cana of Galilee (John 2), in his commentary on Luke, chapter 9:

“Thus at the wedding, wines are colored from fountains while the servants perform the work; and those who had filled the jars with water drew out wine that they had not brought. Grasp, if you can, such great miracles of things. Here, while the crowds eat, the fragments increase according to their desire, and from five loaves more remains is gathered than the total quantity. There, elements are changed into another form; nature neither suffers its usual deficiencies nor recognizes its customary origins, yet the things made still recognize their proper uses. Indeed, the nature of the changed wine is better than that of wine produced naturally, because it lies within the Creator’s power both to assign whatever uses he wills to natures and to impart whatever natures he wills to things being generated.”]

[Col. 0137A] nevertheless it is impossible for us to know the process by which the event occurred. For who, first of all, could comprehend how so small a number of loaves could suffice—not merely for eating and satisfaction, but even for the very division and distribution—when there were many thousands more people than there were loaves, [Note: [Col. 0137C] This refers to Luke 9: “Make them recline in groups of fifty.” In Mark the corresponding passage reads: “Command them to make everyone recline by groups upon the green grass. And they reclined in groups, by hundreds and by fifties” (Mark 6).

Theophylact explains: “By this it is understood that they reclined in separated groups, in groups and groups. For in the Greek, what is here said as ‘by groups’ is repeated, as though it said, ‘by groups, groups.’”

Jansenius explains this more clearly (*Harmony of the Gospels*, chapter 57): “What we have as ‘by groups’ is in Greek *συμπόσια συμπόσια*, that is, ‘banquets, banquets.’ It is a Hebraism by which words are doubled to express a distributive number, so that the sense is: ‘by individual banquets,’ or ‘by distributed banquets.’ Likewise, when we later have in Mark ‘by groups’ (Mark 6), the Greek is *πρασίαι πρασίαι*, that is, ‘garden plots, garden plots,’ in place of ‘by individual garden plots.’

“The Lord ordered the crowds to recline in this way, in groups of one hundred or fifty, both so that everything might be done orderly and without confusion and so that, through this arrangement, the number of those eating might quickly be perceived by the apostles, whose ministry he also used for this purpose; and so that those who were eating might themselves better notice the greatness and reality of the miracle.” Thus Jansenius.]

Could there almost be more banquets than fragments could possibly come from so many loaves? [Note: [Col. 0138B] Saint Hilary, Book 5, *On the Trinity*: “Five loaves are offered to the crowd and broken; in the hands of those breaking them, certain productions of fragments begin to appear. That from which it is broken is not diminished, and fragments occupy the hand of the one breaking it. Neither understanding nor sight can comprehend the progress of so visible an operation. What was not there exists; what is not understood is seen. The only thing left is to believe that God can do all things.

“Ambrose, in his commentary on Luke: ‘Visibly, this bread, by an incredible process, while it is broken, divided, and eaten, is increased without any discernible loss. Nor should you doubt that the food increases in the hands of those serving or in the mouths of those eating, when everywhere the testimony of our work is added to strengthen belief.’

“Jerome, in his commentary: ‘When the Lord breaks it, a seedbed of food is made. For if the loaves had remained whole, and had not been torn into pieces and divided into a multiplied harvest, they could not have fed the crowds, the boys, the women, and so great a multitude.’ He then adds the allegorical sense: ‘The Law, therefore, is broken together with the Prophets and torn into pieces, and its mysteries are brought forth into the midst, so that what, whole and remaining in its original state, did not feed them, when divided into parts may feed the multitude of the nations.’

“These are the statements of the holy Fathers that seemed relevant to the explanation of this passage.

“Furthermore, as to where the loaves were multiplied—whether in Christ’s hands, in the apostles’ hands, or in the hands or mouths of those receiving them—Hilary is uncertain. Jerome thinks they were multiplied in Christ’s hands; Chrysostom and Euthymius, in the apostles’ hands. Ambrose, however, appears to suggest that this also occurred in the hands and mouths of those eating. But what has been said on this occasion concerning the passage is sufficient.”]

Thus an abundance of things arose from the Lord’s word. The work grew in its execution. And when what was seen appeared insufficient, what was given became immeasurable. Therefore there is no place here for conjecture, nor for human estimation or reasoning. The one thing that the minds of the faithful and wise may rightly know in such a matter is this: however great and immeasurable the things done by God may be—and even if the senses cannot grasp them—they should recognize that nothing is impossible for God.

[Col. 0137B] But concerning these ineffable acts of divine power, since the subject requires it, and since they most rightly correspond to the ineffable miracles of sacred birth, more will be said later.

## CHAPTER TWO  
The author adapts the mystery of the number seven—the five loaves and the two fish—to his own work.

Since, meanwhile, we have mentioned the five loaves, it seems, I think, not inappropriate to compare them with the five books that we are now unfolding. For just as they are equal in number, so they are not unlike in character.

[Note: [Col. 0138D] Many expositions, both allegorical and moral, of the barley loaves and the entire sequence of this miracle may be found among the holy Fathers: Hilary, canon 14 on Matthew; Jerome, Ambrose, and Bede in their commentaries; Cyril, Book on John, chapter 17; Augustine, Book 83 of the *Questions*, question 61; and the ordinary Gloss on the passage “Seven loaves,” and so forth, which Saint Thomas also cites in the *Catena*.]

For since those loaves were made of barley, these books too, insofar as our intellectual ability is concerned, may be called barley loaves, although enriched with sacred testimonies and concealing saving treasures beneath contemptible wrappings.

They do not differ from those loaves in this respect either: just as those loaves, poor in appearance, became rich through blessing, so these books, though base in our own intellectual composition, are nevertheless precious through their sacred admixture. And although they display in themselves, through our discourse, the lowliness of barley, they nevertheless contain within them, through the Lord’s testimonies, the savor of living bread.

It remains for them, after the example of those loaves, through the grace of the divine gift, to provide saving food from innumerable seeds; and just as those loaves gave bodily strength to those who ate, so may these grant spiritual health to those who read.

The Lord is powerful—and this gift, too, is his, just as that one was—so that he who, through that food, caused those who had been filled not to grow faint on the way may also, through this food, cause those who have been filled not to go astray.

But since, in that event where the innumerable people of God were fed with little food but a great gift, two fish are also said to have been added to the five loaves, it is fitting that we, who desire to offer through ourselves to all peoples who follow God [Note: [Col. 0139B] Up to this point the text had been printed, I do not know through what error, as follows: “We desire the nourishment of a spiritual meal,” and so forth. It is certain that something is missing in order to complete the sense. Therefore we have judged that the word *alimoniam*—“nourishment”—which is proper and suitable to this passage, must be added. If anyone judges otherwise, I do not object, provided that he suggests something better.] the nourishment of a spiritual meal, should add to those five books, as to five loaves, two further little books, as two fish.

We pray to you, Lord; we entreat you: seeing the effort of our service and prayer, grant effective accomplishment to our devout endeavor. And since, in accordance with our devotion and affection, we desire to make the number of our little books equal to that number of loaves and fish, transfer the power of that blessing to these books. You who count our little writing according to the Gospel number, complete that number also with Gospel fruit, and grant that these writings may become a holy and health-giving food for all the peoples of your Church, for every age and both sexes.

And if some have already been breathed upon by the venomous spirit of that deadly serpent and, their souls and minds corrupted, are dragging pestilential diseases through their languishing veins, grant all the vigor of sound understanding; grant the full health of faith. As, through these writings of our work—which is your gift—you grant saving care to all, so command that, in the likeness of food wholly sanctified by you in the Gospel, just as you strengthened the hungry through that eating, so through this food you may heal those who are wasting away.

## CHAPTER THREE  
He refutes the adversary by the testimony of the Council of Antioch.

Therefore, since, as I think, we have already answered the heretic who denies God sufficiently, in all the preceding writings, by the authority of the divine testimonies, let us now come to the faith and power of the Antiochene Creed.

> **[Note: [Col. 0139B] First, it should be noted that two most famous cities called Antioch are also mentioned in Scripture. One is the metropolis of Syria and the capital of the whole region, situated on the river Orontes; it was formerly called Reblatha, where Nebuchadnezzar, after having the sons of Zedekiah killed before their father, ordered Zedekiah’s eyes to be put out (2 Kings 26 and Jeremiah 39). It was also called Coele and Great Hamath, as Saint Jerome states (in his commentary on Isaiah 4 and in the immediately following commentary on Amos). In this city the disciples first began to be called Christians (Acts 11). Here Paul and Barnabas were appointed and commissioned by the Holy Spirit for the work and preaching of the Gospel (Acts 13). Here too the dispute between Peter and Paul concerning the observance of the legal prescriptions arose (Galatians 2). Finally, the first bishop of this Church of Antioch was the apostle Peter, who governed it for seven years before departing for Rome. Luke entirely omitted this, says Saint Jerome, following Eusebius in the *Chronicle*. This same city, restored by the emperor Justinian, was called Theopolis, that is, “city of God,” according to Nicephorus, book 17, chapter 2, and Cedrenus, in the second year of the reign of the emperor Justinian.**

> **The other is Antioch, the metropolis of Pisidia, concerning which see Pliny, book 5, chapter 27, and Strabo, book 12. Pisidia is a region of Asia Minor, whose inhabitants were formerly called Solymi, as the same Pliny relates. Paul and Barnabas also preached in this Antioch (Acts 13), which is not called simply Antioch but, to distinguish it from the other, Antioch of Pisidia.**

> **Second, it must be noted that the Antiochene Creed mentioned here is to be referred to the former Antioch, which was better known to writers and more celebrated and illustrious because of its patriarchal see and because Peter’s see was established there; for this reason it was accustomed to be called simply by this name. It is therefore understood that this creed was issued in that Antioch of Syria and is called Antiochene from that place—that is, it is the formula or profession of faith expressed and approved in the council held there.**

> **Third, leaving aside the many councils—or rather, councils of heretics—which took place at Antioch at various times, three Antiochene councils in particular are enumerated as having been held by the orthodox, or Catholics, and approved by the Church. They were provincial, not general, councils.**

> **The first was convened in the year of the Lord 266, the sixth year of Pope Dionysius and the twelfth year of the emperor Gallienus, against Paul of Samosata. Eusebius of Caesarea mentions it in book 7, chapter 22 of his *Ecclesiastical History*. In this council the bishops who had assembled, at their very first meeting and above all else, declared in writing the catholic faith concerning the Son of God which they had received from their ancestors and preserved whole and undefiled, as it had been handed down by the apostles themselves; they sent it from the synod to Paul, bishop of Samosata. Baronio reproduced it in full in the second volume of his *Annals*, after Francisco Turriano had rescued it from obscurity and translated it into Latin. Here it will suffice to give its beginning, adapted to the present passage, as follows:**

> **“We have decided to publish and set forth in writing the faith which we received and possess from the beginning, handed down and preserved in the catholic and holy Church to this present day by the blessed apostles, who themselves saw and were ministers of the Word, and which was preached from the Law and the Prophets and from the New Testament: There is one unbegotten God, without beginning, invisible and unchangeable, whom no human being has seen or can see; whose glory and greatness, as they truly are in reality, human nature cannot adequately understand or proclaim. We should be content if we possess some moderate knowledge of him, however limited, revealed by his Son, as he says: ‘No one knows the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son reveals him.’**

> **“We confess and preach that this Son is begotten, the only-begotten, the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation, the Wisdom, Word, and Power of God before the ages—not God by foreknowledge, but in substance and hypostasis, God, the Son of God, as we have come to know him in both the Old and New Testaments,” and so forth.”**

> **Confronted by this confession, Paul recanted his error and promised that he would preserve the catholic faith. But afterward, when, like a dog returning to its vomit, he attempted to restore the heresy which he had once renounced and which had been condemned by the earlier council of Antioch, the bishops again assembled at Antioch for this reason, and he was condemned by the unanimous judgment of all and deprived of his episcopate.**

> **This was the second Antiochene council, held under the same Pope Dionysius in the year of the Lord 272, concerning which Eusebius speaks in book 7, chapters 23 and 24. At it another profession of faith was issued, likewise reproduced by Baronio in the fourth volume of his *Annals*, and incorporated into the proceedings of the Council of Ephesus. It begins:**

> **“We confess our Lord Jesus Christ, before the ages indeed from the Father, but in recent times born from a virgin according to the flesh through the Holy Spirit: one person only, subsisting as a union formed from heavenly divinity and human flesh,” and so forth.**

> **The third Antiochene council was held in the year 363, under Pope Liberius and the emperor Jovian. No new formula or creed of faith is recorded as having been issued there; rather, the faith of the Council of Nicaea was simply confirmed and established. Saint Jerome attests to this in the *Chronicle* in these words: “A synod was held at Antioch by Meletius and his followers, in which, after rejecting *homiusion* and *homeusion*, they accepted the intermediate *homoousion* and rejected the Macedonian doctrine.”**

> **From these statements we conclude that the Antiochene Creed discussed here must refer either to the first or the second Antiochene council; or, what I consider more likely, the Antiochene Creed here means the creed received from the Council of Nicaea and confirmed and approved in that final Antiochene council (Baronius, volume 3, under the year 325).**

> **For this is the sacred formula of faith composed at the great Council of Nicaea, which the faithful customarily call the Nicene Creed. Since it is found in different writers with somewhat different wording, Saint Athanasius expresses it in his letter to the emperor Jovian as follows:**

> **“We believe in God the Father, creator of all things visible and invisible; and in the Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, born from the Father and only-begotten—that is, from the substance of the Father—God from God, light from light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, and consubstantial with the Father, through whom all things were made, both in heaven and on earth.**

> **“He came down for us human beings and for our salvation, and was incarnate and became human; he suffered, rose on the third day, and ascended into heaven; from there he will come to judge the living and the dead. And in the Holy Spirit.**

> **“But those who say, ‘There was when he was not,’ and ‘Before he was made he did not exist,’ or who say that the Son of God came into existence from things that did not exist, or from another substance and subsistence, or who call him created, changeable, or alterable—these the catholic and apostolic faith strikes with anathema.”**

> **Thus far the Nicene Creed. In the various translations made into Latin it is sometimes written with somewhat different words, as in the Council of Chalcedon (Act 2), in Saint Basil (Letter 78), and elsewhere. From this creed the Author quoted what served his purpose, omitting the rest, which will be discussed below. “And the rest,” he says—that is, the remainder which he himself omitted.]

Let us therefore come to the faith and power of the Antiochene Creed.

> **[Note: [Col. 0141C] *In qua*, namely—not *in quo*, as was printed previously. Note carefully that in former times it was customary to observe in which church each person had been baptized. Hence Cassian presses Nestorius very strongly here because he attacked the faith of the Church of Antioch, in which he had been baptized and brought up, and because, like a viper, he tore apart his mother’s womb. Socrates relates that Nestorius was an Antiochene by birth, had first been a presbyter from the Antiochene monastery, and was later made bishop of Constantinople (book 8, chapter 24); this will be shown more fully below.**

> **Nor, I think, does Cassian call it the Antiochene Creed for any other reason—although it ought rather to have been called the Nicene Creed—than that by mentioning the Antiochene Creed he might more sharply sting and reproach Nestorius himself, as a citizen of Antioch and therefore a traitor to and deserter from the religion and faith of his native city.**

> **For this reason it is also recorded as having been established anciently in Gratian that, when adults were baptized, they should submit their name and vow in writing, to be entered in a special book (*Decretum*, II, question 1, chapter “Legum”; and *De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter “Baptizandi”). In the Council of Trent priests are likewise instructed to record the names of the baptized in a book (session 24, chapter 2, *On the Reform of Marriage*).**

> **Following this example, Saint Benedict establishes in chapter 58 of the Rule that the brother who is to be received—namely, for profession, which the Fathers call a second baptism—should promise in the oratory before everyone, before God and the saints, stability, conversion of his manner of life, and obedience, so that, if he should ever act otherwise, he may know that he will be condemned by the one whom he mocks. Concerning this promise he is to make a petition which he writes with his own hand; or, if he does not know letters, another person, asked by him, shall write it, and the novice shall make his mark and place it upon the altar with his own hand. Thus far Saint Benedict.**

> **It is also worthy of observation that it was once likewise customary for Catholics, when dealing with heretics or defining something against them, to present and oppose to them the faith in which they had been baptized, so that, protected as though by a shield, they might attack or repel them more forcefully. Thus, in the Council of Chalcedon (Act 2), after the exposition of the Nicene Creed, the Fathers are recorded as acclaiming: “This is the faith of the Catholics; we all believe this; in this we were baptized and baptize; this is the true faith, this is the sound faith, this is the eternal faith; in this we were baptized, in this we baptize.”**

> **This is relevant to the custom that those approaching baptism, if adults, were accustomed to recite the Apostles’ Creed aloud with their own mouths; but if they were infants, the priest asked the child: “Do you believe in God the almighty Father?” The godparents or sponsors answered in the child’s name: “I believe.”**

> **The most ancient witnesses to this very ancient observance include Saint Dionysius the Areopagite, in the final chapter of *The Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, where he rebukes those who mocked this rite, saying that those who present infants renounce Satan and profess the mysteries of the faith on their behalf. Saint Ambrose writes in book 2, chapter 7, *On the Sacraments*: “You were asked: ‘Do you believe in God the almighty Father?’ You said: ‘I believe,’ and you were immersed,” and so forth. Saint Jerome—or rather, whoever wrote the commentary on Proverbs 2—says that those to be baptized profess that they will believe the Creed. And in the *Dialogue against the Luciferians*: “Moreover,” he says, “since it is customary in the font, after the confession of the Trinity, to ask: ‘Do you believe in the holy catholic Church? Do you believe in the forgiveness of sins?’”**

> **Saint Augustine, *On Faith and Works*, chapter 11: “Why, then, do we either hand over the Creed to those who are to be baptized, or demand that it be returned?” And in Letter 13 to Boniface, near the end: “Thus, although the infant does not yet possess that faith which consists in the will of believers, the sacrament of faith itself already makes him faithful; for just as ‘I believe’ is answered, so he is also called faithful—not by mentally assenting to the thing itself, but by receiving the sacrament of the thing itself. Whoever does not believe this and thinks that it cannot happen is certainly an unbeliever.”]

Since he himself was baptized and reborn in this faith, he must be convicted by his own professions and, so to speak, crushed by his own weapons. For this is the order of the argument: having already been defeated by the sacred testimonies, he must also be defeated, so to speak, by himself as a witness. There will be no need to proceed against him by other means, since he himself will have openly and unmistakably convicted himself.

> **[Note: [Col. 0142C] It is likely that Cassian received this formula of faith, written in Greek and preserved in the Church of Antioch, from that final council held at Antioch, and translated it into Latin in these words. For the other Antiochene creeds that survive, although they agree in substance, differ considerably in wording, as is clear from what has been said.]**

The text and faith of the Antiochene Creed, therefore, are as follows:

> “I believe in one and only true God, the almighty Father, creator of all visible and invisible creatures; and in our Lord Jesus Christ, his only-begotten Son and firstborn of all creation, born from him before all the ages and not made, true God from true God,

> **[Note: [Col. 0142C] Concerning *homoousion*, whether written *homousion* or *homusion*, three things must be said: first, what it signifies and how it differs from other similar terms; second, why this word was placed in the Nicene and Constantinopolitan Creeds and, as it appears here, also in the Antiochene Creed; third, in how many ways it may be understood.**

> **The Fathers of the Council of Chalcedon explained what *homoousios* is in Act 2, where, in the exposition of the Nicene Creed, after the words “consubstantial with the Father,” they added: “that is, of the same substance as the Father”—the same, I say, and one substance, not merely in species but in number and individuality. For this, in the Constantinopolitan Creed sung in the Church, we have “consubstantial with the Father.”**

> **The word *homoousios* is derived from ὁμὸς (*homos*), meaning “the same,” and οὐσία (*ousia*), meaning “substance”; or from ὁμοῦ (*homou*), meaning “together,” as Marius Victorinus explains in his booklet *On Homoousion*.**

> **There are two other terms very closely related to this one, derived from the same source, namely οὐσία (*ousia*): *synousios* and *homoiousios*. Both might be admitted and predicated of the divine persons in some sound sense, yet both were suspect to the Fathers and rightly rejected. The former seemed to favor Sabellius and the Sabellians, who confused the divine persons; the latter seemed to favor the Arians, who denied Christ’s divinity, and appeared to have been cunningly devised and introduced by them to suppress the faith in τὸ ὁμοούσιον (*to homoousion*).**

> **For although *synousios* sounds almost the same as “consubstantial,” it seems to imply some confusion, union, or commixture. *Synousion* signifies unity without distinction; *homoousion*, however, signifies unity with distinction and the procession of one from another. Thus Epiphanius writes in the *Ancoratus*:**

> **“The Son is *homoousios* with the Father, not *synousios*, but *homoousios*; that is, he was not begotten outside the Father, as some, speaking ironically, claim, wishing the Son to exist by position or adoption and not in truth. To say ‘homoousios’ is the bond of faith. For if you say ‘homoousios,’ you have dissolved the power of Sabellius; for *homoousios* does not signify one hypostasis, but indicates the Father as subsisting in himself, the Son as subsisting in himself, and the Holy Spirit as subsisting in himself.**

> **“Again, *homoousios* does not signify something alien to the same divinity, but the Son as God from God and the Holy Spirit as God of the same divinity—not three Gods.”**

> **The Son, he says, is *homoousios* with the Father, not *synousios*, that is, “having essence together,” but *homoousios*, that is, begotten not outside the Father, as some ironically assert, wishing the Son to exist by position or adoption and not in truth. To say *homoousion*, that is, “of the same essence,” is the agreement of the faith. If you say *homoousion*, that is, “coessential,” you have dissolved the force of Sabellius. For this word does not signify one hypostasis, but the Father subsisting in himself, the Son subsisting in himself, and the Holy Spirit subsisting in himself. Moreover, it does not signify something alien to the same divinity, but the Son as God from God and the Holy Spirit as God of the same divinity—not three Gods.”**

> **Thus Epiphanius. Caesarius, the brother of Nazianzen, agrees with him in his book of *Questions* (question 12): “Believe,” he says, “that the Son is of the same essence as the Father, not ‘with one essence,’ according to the drunkenness of Sabellius. The former term (*homoousion*) declares a hypostasis, or subsistence. The latter (*synousion*) is blasphemy, mingling the Son and the Holy Spirit with the Father and dissolving the Trinity into unity; this is utterly foreign to the divine laws.” Thus he writes, according to the translation of Genebrard.**

> **Furthermore, *homoiousios* means “of similar nature” (book 1, *On the Trinity*), or “similar in nature, essence, or substance”—for these are synonyms. But “similar in substance” is very different from “consubstantial,” which includes both being from the substance of the Father and being similar to him in substance.**

> **For Athanasius says in his book *On the Councils of Ariminum and Seleucia*: “It is not at all sufficient to say that the Son is like the Father according to substance, since tin is like silver, a wolf like a dog, and gleaming bronze like true gold; yet tin is not silver and is not from silver, nor is a wolf’s cub considered a dog.”**

> **From this it is evident that the term *homoousios* appears to have been divinely devised, and not without a great miracle, in order simultaneously to destroy the opposing heresies of Arius and Sabellius. Sabellius indeed acknowledged that the Father and the Son have the same essence, but denied that one proceeds from the other. The Arians, on the other hand, acknowledged that the Son is from the Father, but denied that he is of the same substance. Hence Athanasius says in his book *On the Decrees of the Council of Nicaea* that the Arians accepted every other expression except this one, because they could twist all the others to their own meaning. Therefore, after the Nicene council had said that the Son is true God from true God, begotten, not made, and born from the substance of the Father, it recognized that the Arians could evade all these statements and therefore added, “consubstantial with the Father.”**

> **Saint Ambrose likewise says in book 3, chapter 7, *On the Faith*: “Rightly do we call the Son consubstantial with the Father, because by this word both the distinction of the persons and the unity of nature are signified.”**

> **Finally, the Marius cited above says in book 2 *Against Arius*: “By this one word, *homoousios*, all the poison of the Arian doctrine is destroyed. O learned bishops, O holy men, confirming the faith by the Spirit! O Word, truly the Word of God, by whom God and the Logos are shown to be from eternity, always, and of the same substance.”**

> **Thus the term was said in Latin as *homoousion*; consequently it must also be set forth and discussed in Greek. This is what he himself says.**

> **As for the occasion that moved the Nicene Fathers to employ such a word in establishing the doctrine of faith concerning Christ’s divinity, Saint Ambrose explains it as follows (book 3, final chapter, *On the Faith*). Remarkably, he suggests that the Arians themselves handed the Catholics the sword by which their error was strangled and overthrown. He writes:**

> **“What other reason is there why they do not want the Son to be called consubstantial with the Father, except that they do not want to confess him as the Son of God? Their own leader, Eusebius of Nicomedia, revealed this in his letter, saying: ‘If we call him the true and uncreated Son of God, we begin to confess him consubstantial with the Father.’ When this letter was read in the Council of Nicaea, the Fathers inserted this word into the definition, since they saw that it terrified their opponents, so that, as though with a sword drawn by the Arians themselves, they might cut off the head of their wicked heresy.”**

> **Thus Ambrose indicates that the Fathers of the Nicene council took the occasion for using this name from the words of the Arian bishop Eusebius of Nicomedia, recited in the synod.**

> **It is well known from ecclesiastical history with what intense struggle the Arians labored to introduce *homoiousion* in place of *homoousion*, and, by bringing into use among the faithful this almost identical word differing by only one added letter, to banish from the Church not merely the reality signified by *homoousion* but the word itself. Yet they could achieve this neither by force nor by fraud.**

> **The orthodox Fathers remained firm in this truth and held steadfastly to the word which had triumphed over the impious Arian doctrine at the Council of Nicaea. They even considered the name *homoousiast*, which the Arians used reproachfully against them for this reason, honorable and distinguished, as Saint Basil testifies (Letter 73).**

> **When the Arians accused the word of being foreign and novel, and of not being found in sacred Scripture, the Fathers first replied that it was not indeed the word itself but the reality, or the meaning of the word, that was found in the sacred writings—especially in the Lord’s words in John 10: “I and the Father are one.” This means nothing other than, “We are of one and the same substance.”**

> **Thus Augustine says in his book *Against Maximinus*, chapter 14: “The Father and the Son are of one and the same substance. This is the *homoousion* which, in the Council of Nicaea, was established against the Arian heretics by the Catholics through the authority of truth and by the truth of authority. Later, at the Council of Ariminum, because of its novelty in wording, it was understood less adequately than it ought to have been, although the ancient faith had produced it; and heretical impiety, under the heretical emperor Constantius, attempted to weaken it, with many deceived by the fraud of a few. But after not a long time, when the freedom of the catholic faith prevailed and the force of the word was understood as it ought to be, that *homoousion* was defended far and wide with the soundness of the catholic faith [another reading: ‘was spread abroad’]. For what is *homoousion* except ‘of one and the same substance’? What, I ask, is *homoousion* except ‘I and the Father are one’?”**

> **Thus far Saint Augustine. Peter Lombard, citing these same words in book 1, distinction 34 of the *Sentences*, adds: “Therefore this term must not be avoided as a profane novelty of words.”**

> **Second, the Fathers replied that this word was not new or recently invented, but had been used by earlier Fathers before the Council of Nicaea, namely by Dionysius, the Roman pontiff, and Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, and by others, as may be seen in Saint Athanasius and Theodoret (Athanasius, in the letter concerning the decree of the Council of Nicaea against the Arians; Theodoret, book 2, chapter 21 and following).**

> **Now, concerning the third question—namely, in how many ways this term *homoousion* can be understood—the answer is that after the great Council of Nicaea Catholics accepted and used it only in the sense in which those Fathers had established and explained it, as we have just explained. Before that, however, namely at the council assembled against Paul of Samosata at Antioch, it was understood somewhat differently.**

> **There the Fathers explicitly denied that the Son was *homoousios* with the Father, but they did so according to the mind of Samosata, who said that the Son was consubstantial with the Father in the same way that one human being is consubstantial with another—so that there are two substances, but of the same species.**

> **Saint Athanasius mentions this controversy in his book *On the Councils*, when he argues against the Arians, who criticized the Nicene council because the Antiochene council had understood the word “consubstantial” differently. He demonstrates that both councils held the same view concerning Christ’s divinity. He writes:**

> **“If anyone criticizes the Nicene Fathers because they did not say everything that their predecessors had approved, he should likewise rightly criticize the seventy bishops who condemned Paul of Samosata because they did not preserve everything that had belonged to their predecessors. Their predecessors were those two Dionysii and the others who were then assembled at Rome. Yet it is not lawful to criticize either them or the others. For all cared for Christ and directed their efforts against the heretics: these condemned Samosata, while those condemned the Arian heresy. Both groups wrote rightly according to the matter before them.”**

> **A little farther on he says: “Although the Fathers of the two councils spoke differently about consubstantiality, we must not therefore disagree with them, but examine their intentions. If we do so, we shall certainly find that both synods agree with one another. For those who overthrew Samosata understood the word ‘consubstantial’ in a bodily sense, since Paul attempted to argue sophistically and said: ‘If Christ was not made God from a human being, then he is consubstantial with the Father, and it necessarily follows that there are three substances: one prior, as the source, and the other two arising from it.’**

> **“Therefore, rightly avoiding Paul’s sophism, they said that Christ was not consubstantial; for the Son does not stand in relation to the Father as Paul imagined.”**

> **These words of Athanasius have seemed worth quoting at greater length here so that we may understand in what sense the Author says that the Antiochene Creed contains “consubstantial with the Father,” when, on the contrary, it is clear that this word was rejected there. For it does not seem that he means the first or second Antiochene creed and council, which took place before the rise of Arius’s heresy, but the third, where the creed of the Council of Nicaea was received and approved, and where those words are contained, as was shown above (see Baronius, volume 3, under the year 325; Bellarmine, book 2, *On Christ*, chapter 3).**

> **But enough concerning *homoousion*. Whoever desires more should consult Baronius in the *Annals* and Bellarmine in the *Controversies*.]

> “consubstantial with the Father; through whom the ages were joined together and all things were made; who came for us; and was born from the Virgin Mary; and was crucified under Pontius Pilate and buried; and on the third day rose again according to the Scriptures; and ascended into heaven; and will come again to judge the living and the dead. And the rest.”

In the Creed, which speaks the faith of all the Churches, I wish to know what you will choose to follow: human authority or God’s? Although I shall not deal with you censoriously or severely, as though I were merely giving you the option of choosing one of the two alternatives, so that, by determining one, I might deny the other—

> **[Note: [Col. 0145D] Thus in the Basel edition. The Plantin edition nevertheless suggests in the margin that *permittens* should be read instead of *perimens*. The result is the same. For *perimens* here means “defining,” “determining,” or “concluding.” Thus among jurists a case is said to be *perempta*, that is, defined or terminated; a *peremptory exception* is one that terminates a lawsuit if it is proved; a *peremptory term* is a fixed or definitive term. In games, too, that which is yielded by right or voluntarily is said to be “destroyed” or “eliminated.”]

—you deny one [reading in Lipsius’s margin: “permit one”] and reject the other: for I grant and concede you both.

> **[Col. 0146A] “Both,” namely, the authority of God and of human beings. See above.]

And what do I concede? I draw you to both, even if you do not wish it. For if you wish the Creed to contain both, you must understand this willingly; if you do not wish it, you must be compelled unwillingly. For the Creed, as you know, received its name from “bringing together.”

> **[Note: [Col. 0146A] Among the various and manifold meanings and senses of *symbolum* recorded by the learned Budaeus in his *Thesaurus*, there are three principal ones that can be applied to the Creed. The first, touched upon here, explains *symbolum* as “a contribution,” from the verb συμβάλλομαι (*symballomai*), “I contribute” or “I bring together.”**

> **Paschymere, the translator of Dionysius, therefore writes in chapter 3 of *The Ecclesiastical Hierarchy* that *symbolum* means τὸν ἐρανὸν (*ton eranon*), “a collection,” and τὸ διδόμενον εἰς δεῖπνον (*to didomenon eis deipnon*), “what was contributed toward a dinner,” as in Terence’s *Andria*: “He contributed his share,” and, “Are you not ashamed to come anointed to the contribution-dinner?” Hence someone who had dined without contributing was called ἀσύμβολος (*asymbolos*).**

> **From this meaning, many of the Fathers judged that the brief collection of the articles of faith was called a *symbolum* because each of the apostles contributed something in common to a fixed rule of faith, as though preparing a table for believers.**

> **Thus, besides Cassian in this passage, Clement of Rome writes in his first letter to James, the brother of the Lord: “When Christ had risen and ascended into heaven and the Holy Spirit had been sent, and knowledge of languages had been imparted to the apostles, while they were still together, they composed the Creed which the faithful Church now holds, each stating what he believed, so that, when they departed from one another, they might preach this rule throughout all nations.”**

> **“Thus, reviewing the summary of the whole catholic faith—in which the integrity of belief is shown, the equality of the one almighty God, that is, of the Holy Trinity, is declared, and the mystery of the incarnation of the Son of God is set forth: how, for the salvation of the human race, he came down from the Father in heaven and deigned to be born from a Virgin; in what order and at what time he suffered death; how he was buried and rose again; how in that same flesh he ascended into heaven and sat at the right hand of the Father; how he will come as Judge; how he bestowed the remission of sins through holy baptism on those reborn; and how the resurrection of the human race in the same flesh will occur unto eternal life—they taught in this way.”**

> **“For *symbolum* in Greek is called *collatio* in Latin. And these holy apostles, as has been said, composed it beneficially among themselves through the Holy Spirit.”**

> **Thus writes the pontiff.**

> **Saint Ambrose expresses the same view in sermon 38: “I believe,” he says, “that the apostolic faith was fashioned by the work of twelve craftsmen.”**

> **Saint Jerome—or rather Bede—in his commentary on Proverbs 23, referring to the same etymology, says: “*Symbolum* is a Greek word and is interpreted as ‘a contribution.’” And farther on: “To give one’s contribution means that, just as each person customarily contributes food for eating, so in a conversation of detraction one contributes words.”**

> **Saint Augustine, sermon 2 on Palm Sunday: “The Creed,” he says, “is the comprehension and perfection of our faith.” Cassian seems to have borrowed these words in this passage. Augustine then describes the contribution of the individual articles of this Creed by the individual apostles in this way:**

> **Peter said: “I believe in God the almighty Father.”**

> **John said: “Creator of heaven and earth.”**

> **James said: “And in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord.”**

> **Andrew said: “Who was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born from the Virgin Mary.”**

> **Philip said: “Who suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died, and was buried.”**

> **Thomas said: “He descended into hell; on the third day he rose from the dead.”**

> **Bartholomew said: “He ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of God the almighty Father.”**

> **Matthew said: “From there he will come to judge the living and the dead.”**

> **James, son of Alphaeus, said: “And in the Holy Spirit, the holy catholic Church.”**

> **Simon the Zealot said: “The communion of saints and the forgiveness of sins.”**

> **Judas, son of James, said: “The resurrection of the flesh.”**

> **Matthias completed it: “Eternal life. Amen.”**

> **Thus Augustine. Whether this sermon is genuinely Augustine’s is uncertain, as Baronius noted (volume 1 of the *Annals*, under the year 44). “But,” he says, “it makes no difference whose it is, since testimonies of others are also available concerning the distinct statements of each of the twelve apostles.”**

> **For concerning the same statements of the individual apostles, Pope Leo also writes to the empress Pulcheria (Letter 13): “The brief and perfect confession of the catholic Creed, marked by twelve statements corresponding to the twelve apostles, is so fortified with heavenly defenses that all the opinions of the heretics can be cut down by its sword alone.”**

> **Venantius Fortunatus and others likewise transmit this account (Venantius, preface to the exposition of the Creed; Alcuin, *On the Offices of the Church*, chapter 22; Rabanus, *On the Instruction of Clergy*, book 2, chapter 56; Budaeus, cited above; Genebrard, book 3, *On the Trinity*). Thus Baronius.**

> **Furthermore, because *symbolum* also signifies “a sign,” “indication,” or “token,” others preferred to call the Creed of faith a *symbolum*, deriving the name from the military token given to soldiers so that they might recognize one another. It was as though it were an indication and sign by which the soldiers of Christ might be distinguished from false brothers serving Satan.**

> **The Greeks also customarily used certain tokens in agreements and contracts, which took the place of written instruments and signed documents and by which legal judgments were made; these tokens were likewise called *symbola*.**

> **In this manner, therefore, the summary of the faith, expressed in a brief collection of words—whether by the apostles or by the Church—is truly called a *symbolum*, because, having been set forth as an indication of the Church, it declares that the truth of religion belongs to the one who contributes it as proof of his faith.**

> **Thus Clement, in the passage cited, whose words are quoted in session 21 of the Council of Florence: “It is also called an indication, because by means of it the one who believes rightly is identified.”**

> **Rufinus of Aquileia explains both senses and the origin of the Creed at greater length in the following manner:**

> **“Our ancestors relate that after the Lord’s ascension, when, through the coming of the Holy Spirit, tongues like fire had rested upon each of the apostles, no barbarian language seemed inaccessible or impassable to them, and the Lord’s command had been given that each should go to the various nations to preach the word of God.**

> **“As they were therefore about to depart from one another, they first established together a rule for their future preaching, lest, being separated from one another, they should present something different to those whom they invited to the faith of Christ.**

> **“Thus, all assembled in one place and filled with the Holy Spirit, they composed this brief indication of the preaching that was to be theirs, as we have said, by bringing together into one what each person thought; and they established it as a rule to be given to believers.**

> **“They wished to call it the *symbolum* for many and very just reasons. For *symbolum* in Greek can mean ‘indication’ and ‘contribution,’ that is, something which many people bring together into one. This is what the apostles did in these statements, bringing together into one what each of them believed.**

> **“It is called an indication or sign for this reason: at that time, as the apostle Paul says (1 Corinthians 11) and as is related in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 15), many from among the circumcised Jews pretended to be apostles of Christ and went out to preach for the sake of profit or their bellies. They named Christ, but did not announce him according to the complete line of the traditions.**

> **“They therefore established this indication, by which the one who truly preached Christ according to the apostolic rules might be recognized.**

> **“Finally, it is said that this was also observed in civil wars, because the armor was alike, the sound of the voice the same, the custom one, and the methods of warfare identical; lest some deception be introduced, each person used distinct tokens—”**
[The commander] gives these to his soldiers, and in Latin they are called either *signa* (“signs”) or *indicia* (“tokens”), so that, if someone should happen to appear [Col. 0148A] about whom there is doubt, when asked for the *symbolum* (password) he may disclose whether he is an enemy or an ally.

Thus far Rufinus. Saint Maximus, bishop of Turin, also agrees in his homily *On the Tradition of the Creed*:

> “The blessed apostles,” he says, “following Christ’s example, entrusted to the Church of God—which they were arming against the malice of the devil’s fury—the mystery in the Creed, so that, since under the one name of Christ there was to be a diversity among believers, the seal of the Creed might distinguish the faithful person from the traitor, and thus a person alien to the faith and an enemy might be made known to the Church.””

In the third place, as Budaeus reports, *σύμβολον* signifies “likeness” and a certain commonality of nature. For this reason Aristotle beautifully said (*On Generation*, Book II) that elements which share one quality with one another “symbolize”: “From water [comes] earth, and from earth there will be fire; for each has symbols in relation to the other.” Yet this explanation also properly suits our Creed, by which the faithful, as though through the whole religion and faith taken together and shared in common, unite and agree with one another, and, as though bound by a certain rule, are held together so that they do not deviate from the truth even by the breadth of a fingernail [Col. 0148B].

The Apostle also seems to indicate this in these words:

> “Eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace: one body and one Spirit, just as you were called in one hope of your calling. One Lord, one faith, one baptism” (Ephesians 4).

And elsewhere:

> “For in one Spirit we were all baptized, whether Jews or gentiles, whether slaves or free, and we were all given to drink of one Spirit” (Romans 12).

That is, we were imbued with one faith and doctrine.

Likewise Saint Augustine, in Sermon 1 for the Vigil of Pentecost:

> “The holy apostles,” he says, “handed down a certain rule of faith which, because it was comprised in twelve statements according to the apostolic number, they called the Creed. Through it, believers were to maintain catholic unity and convict heretical perversity.”

For this reason, then, the Creed is so called as a kind of union and composition of the faithful; yet this explanation nearly coincides with the first. But enough has now been said about the name and etymology of the Creed [Col. 0148C].

*Σύμβολον* is called *collatio* in Latin [Col. 0147A]. It is called *collatio* because, having been brought together into one by the apostles of the Lord, the entire faith of the catholic law—whatever is poured forth in immense [Col. 0148A] abundance throughout the whole body of the divine books—is collected into the perfect brevity of the Creed, in accordance with the Apostle’s statement:

> “For he is bringing the word to completion and shortening it in righteousness [Col. 0149A]; for the Lord will make a shortened word upon the earth” (Romans 9).

[Note: [Col. 0148C] The Apostle quotes the passage from Isaiah with a few alterations; according to the Vulgate version it reads as follows: “A consummation, shortened, will overflow with righteousness. For the Lord God of hosts will make a consummation and an abbreviation in the midst of all the earth.” Here, however, the word is in the accusative case, as is clear from the Greek, *λόγον συντελῶν*, and the sense is: “For, bringing the word and discourse to completion, he is”—that is, “the Lord completes and shortens, or will complete and shorten, the discourse.” Hence Tertullian, *Against Marcion* (Book IV, chapter 1), reads and explains it in this way: “Because the Lord will make a curtailed discourse upon the earth”; for “the New Testament has been abridged and freed from the burdensome fringes of the Law.” Saint Jerome himself, following Tertullian, says in his commentary on Isaiah concerning the same passage: “The Gospel discourse, shortened and perfected, which, in place of all the burdensome ceremonies of the Law, gave the very brief commandment of love and faith.” There Rhenanus, commenting on Tertullian, says: “He calls them burdensome fringes [Col. 0148D] because they are manifold and kept people occupied, just as a fringed garment impedes one’s entrance.” Saint Basil likewise says in his commentary on the same passage: “The Apostle, in the Epistle which is addressed to the Romans, used this saying of the prophet, altering only a very few expressions. But if anyone should inquire why the Apostle omitted some things and altered others, let him know first that, since he was a Hebrew, he did not wish to use slavishly the editions which we Greeks use, but interpreted and expounded the meaning of Scripture as it stands. For the Hebrews seem to approach more closely and to agree more fully with the Apostle’s exposition.” Thus Basil.]

“Bringing the word to completion and shortening it in righteousness,” he says, “for the Lord will make a shortened word upon the earth” (Romans 9).

This, then, is the shortened word which the Lord made: namely, gathering into a few words the faith of his twofold Testament, and condensing the meaning of all the Scriptures into a brief form, making a compact whole of his own from his own materials, and completing the force of the entire Law with the briefest possible concision.

[Note: [Col. 0149C] Saint Cyprian, *On the Lord’s Prayer*: “When our Lord Jesus Christ, gathering together the learned and the unlearned alike, gave the precepts of salvation to every sex and age, he made a great compendium of his commandments, so that the memory of those learning the heavenly discipline would not be burdened, but that they might quickly [Col. 0149D] learn what was necessary for simple faith.” Saint Jerome, in his letter to Pammachius (Letter 61): “In the Creed of our faith and hope, which was handed down by the apostles and is written not on paper and ink but on the fleshy tablets of the heart, after the confession of the Trinity and the unity of the Church, the whole mystery of Christian doctrine is concluded with the resurrection of the flesh.” Saint Augustine, Sermon 1 for the Vigil of Pentecost: “The Creed is brief in words but great in mysteries. For whatever was prefigured in the patriarchs, whatever was announced in the Scriptures, whatever was foretold by the Prophets—whether concerning God unbegotten, or concerning him born from God into God, or concerning the Holy Spirit, or concerning the reception of every sacrament, or concerning the Lord’s death and the mystery of his resurrection—the whole of this the Creed briefly contains; by containing it, it possesses it and confesses it.” And in another sermon (*Sermon 3 for Monday after Palm Sunday*): “The Creed is a rule of faith briefly comprehended, so that it may instruct the mind without burdening the memory [Col. 0150C]; it is spoken in few words, from which much is gained.” Isidore (*On Ecclesiastical Offices*, Book II, chapter 23), Rabanus (*On the Instruction of Clergy*, Book II, chapter 56), and others have similar statements.]

He did this, clearly, like a most devoted father, taking account either of the negligence of some of his children or of their lack of understanding, so that even a simple and uneducated mind would not struggle to grasp what could also be easily retained in memory.

# CHAPTER IV. The Creed of Faith Possesses Divine and Human Authority

You see, therefore, that the authority of God is present in the Creed: “For the Lord will make a shortened word upon the earth” (Romans 9).

[Note: Supply “authority in the Creed,” concerning which he said above: “In the Creed, which speaks the faith of all the churches, I wish to know what you prefer to follow: the authority of men [Col. 0150D], or that of God?” Here, however, he seems to confuse the Apostolic Creed with the Antiochene Creed, which he discussed above (chap. 3), and to pass from one to the other. Both may truly be called an abbreviated word—that is, a brief compendium of the whole Catholic doctrine—and the faith and meaning of both are the same, although something may be stated more explicitly in one which is implicit in the other.]

But perhaps you ask for the authority of men. Even that is not lacking, for God accomplished this through men. Just as he established that immense [Lipsius, in the margin: “whole”] abundance of the sacred Scriptures chiefly through his patriarchs and prophets, so he established the Creed through his apostles and priests. Whatever he expanded there through his own agents in generous and overflowing abundance, he here likewise gathered together through his own agents in the fullest brevity.

Nothing, therefore, is lacking in the Creed. Since it was composed by God’s apostles from the writings of God, it contains within itself, insofar as authority is concerned, everything that belongs either to men or to God. Indeed, whatever was done through men should also be considered God’s, because it should be believed to belong not so much to those through whom it was done as to the one who did it.

“I believe,” says the Creed, “in one true and only God, the almighty Father, creator of all visible and invisible creatures; and in our Lord Jesus Christ, his only-begotten Son and firstborn of all creation, born from him before all ages and not made, true God from true God, homoousios with the Father, through whom the ages were joined together and all things were made. He came for our sake and was born of the Virgin Mary, and was crucified under Pontius Pilate and buried. And on the third day he rose again according to the Scriptures, and ascended into heaven. And he will come again to judge the living and the dead.” And so forth.

# CHAPTER V. He Argues against His Adversary with the Most Carefully Chosen Arguments and Shows that the Religion Received from the Ancestors Must Be Held Fast

[Note: The Arian and Sabellian heresies, and their authors, have been treated elsewhere on many occasions.]

If you were an advocate of the Arian or Sabellian heresy, and I were not using your own Creed against you, I would nevertheless convict you by the authority of the sacred testimonies; I would convict you by the voice of the Law itself; and finally I would convict you by the truth of the Creed approved throughout the whole world.

I would tell you that, even if you were devoid of understanding and sense, you ought at least to follow the consensus of the human race, and that you should not value the perversity of a few wicked men more highly than the faith of all the churches. That faith, founded by Christ and handed down by the apostles, ought certainly to be considered nothing other than the voice and authority of God, possessing within itself both the voice and the meaning of God.

And what, finally, if I dealt with you in this way—what would you say? What would you answer? Would you not, I ask, say something like this?

“You have not been instructed in that way; you have not been trained in that way. Something else was handed down to you by your parents, something else by your teachers and authorities. You did not hear this in that assembly of your ancestral doctrine, nor in the church of your confession. Finally, the very text and discourse of the Creed handed down and imparted to you contain something else. In it you were baptized; in it you were reborn. You hold what you received, and you would say that you live in that in which you learned that you had been regenerated.”

Would you not, I ask, while saying these things, think that you were using even against the truth a very strong shield? And in a matter, however blameworthy, this would indeed be a defense that was not inappropriate, and one that could not absurdly be called the cause of the error, if obstinacy had not joined itself to the error.

For when you held what you had received from childhood—

[Note: That is, greater effort would have to be devoted to correcting the present error than to punishing the past fault.]

—correction would have had more to amend in you concerning your present error than severity would have to punish concerning your past offense.

[Note: That is, the city of Antioch. He again presses and sharply stings Nestorius as a deserter of his native and ancestral religion, as one who had abandoned the faith in which he had been baptized and which he had received from his ancestors. On this matter, see above (chap. 3).]

But now, since you were born in a Catholic city, instructed in the Catholic faith, and regenerated by Catholic baptism, can I deal with you as though you were an Arian or a Sabellian? Would that you had been one! I would grieve less that you had been born into evils than that you had fallen away from good; less that you had never possessed the faith than that you had lost it; less that you were an ancient heretic than a new apostate. For you would have brought less defilement or pestilence upon the whole Church; finally, you would have been less bitter to grieve over and less burdensome as an example,

[Note: If he had been a commoner—that is, a layman, as the term is commonly used—or anyone from the people. A layman attacking the Church would have caused less scandal than a priest, indeed a bishop, the spouse and shepherd of the Church, as Nestorius was. How grave a scandal Nestorius himself brought upon the Church is forcefully assessed and lamented by Vincent of Lérins, a writer of that period, in these words (*Against the Profane Novelty of Heresies*, chap. 16):

“What sort of temptation do we think there was recently, when that unhappy Nestorius, suddenly changed from a sheep into a wolf, began to tear apart Christ’s flock? Those very people who were being gnawed still, for the most part, believed him to be a sheep, and for that reason they were more vulnerable to his bites. For who would readily have thought that he could err whom he saw being followed with such devotion by the priests? When he was celebrated with great love by the holy and with the highest favor of the people, he handled the divine Scriptures publicly every day and refuted even the harmful errors of Jews and gentiles. In what fair way, then, would he not persuade everyone that he taught, preached, and thought correctly, when, in order to open a way for his one heresy, he attacked the blasphemies of all heresies?” And so forth.

No less aptly and appropriately to this passage does Saint Augustine say in Book 21 of *The City of God* (chap. 25):

“It is intolerable and exceedingly far from sound doctrine that many, indeed almost all, who founded impious heresies—departing from the Catholic Church and becoming leaders of heresy—should have better grounds than those who had never been Catholics, when they fell into the snares of those heresiarchs. If the fact that they were baptized in the Catholic Church and first received the sacrament of Christ’s body in the true body of Christ frees those heresiarchs from eternal punishment, then surely the deserter of the faith, who has consequently become its assailant, is worse than the one who did not desert what he had never held.”]

if you could have attacked the Church as a commoner rather than as a priest.

Therefore, as I said above, if you were a disciple and advocate of the Sabellian, Arian, or any other heresy, and wished to defend yourself by the example of your parents, the instruction of your teachers, the fellowship of the people, and the faith of the Creed, I would not be asking anything unjust, heretic—not anything unjust or burdensome. Do, as one born into the Catholic faith, what you would have been prepared to do on behalf of perversity.

[Col. 0151B] Hold fast to the instruction of your parents; hold fast to the faith of the Church; hold fast to the truth of the Creed; hold fast to the salvation of baptism.

What sort of prodigy, what sort of monster are you?

[Note: In place of “for yourself,” I think “for the truth” should be read. For here truth is being set against error, so that the sense is: “You do not defend the Catholic faith and truth which you received from your ancestors and parents, whereas others, in the opposite way, cling tenaciously to and defend an error received from their ancestors, relying upon paternal instruction and example.”]

On your own behalf, you do not do what others have done even on behalf of error.

But we have advanced sufficiently far into the depths. And,

[Note: That is, the city of Constantinople, where Cassian had stayed with Saint Chrysostom and had been honorably received. For this reason he calls it related to him—that is, friendly, familiar, and closely connected by a great bond. He rightly and affectionately grieves that such a shepherd should have fallen to it, one who would be changed into a wolf and tear it apart. Or, alternatively, “the related city” means Antioch, which was related to Nestorius—that is, his nurturer and educator—and which likewise had good reason to mourn that such a pupil and citizen had fallen to it. Cassian also recalls this city and Church at the beginning of the following chapter: “In which,” he says, “you were born, in which you were instructed, in which you were reborn.”]

because of our affection for the related city, while we were eager to pursue the rush of our grief as though it were a hot wind, we have gone far beyond the course of a very straight journey.

# CHAPTER VI. Again He Challenges Him with the Profession of the Antiochene Creed

The Creed, then, heretic, whose text we gave above, although it belongs to all the churches—because the faith of all is one—nevertheless belongs especially to the city and Church of Antioch, that is, to the one in which you were born, in which you were instructed, and in which you were reborn.

The faith of this Creed brought you to the fountain of life,

[Note: Through the sacrament of baptism, or regeneration, he immediately adds the Eucharist, apparently having in view the ancient custom of the primitive Church, by which the Eucharist was ordinarily given immediately after baptism to those who had been baptized, whether infants or adults. Blessed Dionysius the Areopagite reports this in two places.

First, in *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, chap. 2, after recalling the rites and ceremonies customarily used in baptism, he concludes:

“At the end of all these things, the bishop calls the one who has been perfected to the most sacred Eucharist and bestows upon him the divine communion of the sacraments that bring perfection.”

Regarding this passage, Stapulensis, an expert in antiquity, says (*Sotus on Book 4, distinction 12, question 1, article 9*):

“It was the custom of the primitive Church, after those cleansed by the holy bath of regeneration had been illuminated through baptism, to call them to the consummating communion of the most holy body and blood of our Redeemer, and to make them participants in that highest mystery which completes all things.”

The same is still found in the ancient books of the mysteries concerning infants:

“If a bishop is present, the infant ought immediately to be confirmed and afterward admitted to communion. If the bishop is not present, before the infant is suckled or tastes anything, the priest should give him communion from the body and blood of the Lord, even before Mass, if necessity requires it.”

Thus far he.

Again, the same Dionysius says in chapter 7 of the same work:

“The bishop gives the holy mysteries to the child, so that the child may be nourished by them and have no other life than this one, which always contemplates divine things and advances through such holy communion.”

The same practice concerning infants may also be inferred from Saint Cyprian’s sermon *On the Lapsed*. Speaking of certain Christians who, during the persecution, sacrificed to idols, he says that their infants, who were carried to the idols, did not lose the righteousness they had received in baptism:

“Therefore, when the day of judgment comes, they will be able to say to God: ‘We did nothing, nor did we, after abandoning the food and cup of the Lord, voluntarily hasten to profane contagions.’”

Saint Augustine, quoting these words of Saint Cyprian in Epistle 23 to Boniface, adds another story reported by Cyprian himself. It concerns a little girl whose parents, he says, had fled in confusion and had left her with a nurse. The nurse brought her into the sacrileges of idols. Later, when the Eucharist that had been brought to her was given to her in church, she rejected it with extraordinary movements and gestures because, Cyprian says, “the Eucharist could not remain in a body and mouth that had been violated.”

Saint Augustine himself testifies that the same custom of giving communion to little children still existed in his own time, in Epistle 107 to Vitalis.

Finally, Gennadius—or whoever was the author of *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, chap. 52, cited by Gratian in *On Consecration*, distinction 4, chapter “If There Are Any”—says:

“If they are little children, or mentally deficient persons who cannot understand instruction, those who present them should answer on their behalf, according to the custom of baptism; and thus, after being communicated through the laying on of hands with chrism, they should be admitted to the mysteries of the Eucharist.”

So much for that passage.

Since, however, other authors make no mention, or only very rare mention, of this custom, the most learned Pammelius rightly suspects (*On the passage of Cyprian cited above*) that it was neither universal nor long continued after Saint Augustine.
