It is reasonable to believe that this was done—or rather, permitted by the Church—in certain places, especially during the period of persecution, so that people might be drawn more effectively away from the sacrifices of idols, in which something offered to idols was sometimes placed even in the mouths of infants. Once the storm of persecutions had ceased, and the baptism of adults had fallen into disuse, that custom was rightly abolished, along with other rites formerly practiced concerning the baptized, which Durandus discusses (*On the Rites of the Church*, book 1, chap. 19). Reason teaches that infants are unable to distinguish the Eucharist from other foods, or to bring to its reception that devotion of mind and self-examination which the Apostle requires (1 Corinthians 11).

For the rest, it is not entirely certain at what age Nestorius was baptized in the Church of Antioch—whether as an infant or as an adult. But if conjecture may be used, I would rather believe that he was baptized when already an adult.

For the following words of the Author seem to suggest this:

“In which you were born, in which you were instructed, and in which you were reborn.”

That is, in which you were born, catechized, and finally baptized. If he was instructed and catechized before being baptized, then he was certainly capable of reason and instruction—not an infant, but an adult in possession of his faculties. Otherwise this attack upon Nestorius would appear weaker and less effective. It reproaches and taunts him for having defected from the faith that he had publicly professed in baptism; but if, while still an infant and ignorant, he had professed it not personally but only through his parents or sponsors, as infants do today when they are baptized, the force of the reproach would be diminished.

This may be inferred much more clearly from Theodoret if he is compared with Cassian. In his letter to Sporadius, Theodoret writes the following about the birth of Nestorius, his arrival in Antioch, his education, character, studies, priesthood, and the pastoral care he assumed there before being elevated to the episcopate of Constantinople (*Heretical Fables*, book 4):

“He became known to everyone. This man was born in the city of Germanicia—Suidas [under ‘Nestorius’] explains this as a city of Syria called Germanicia, lest anyone here think of Germany. I do not know at first to what occupation he devoted himself. Traveling from one region to another, he finally reached the Egyptian district and then the great city of Antioch. There, moderately instructed and trained in the liberal arts and endowed with a most beautiful and powerful voice, he entered the Church of God, to its certain ruin. Enrolled among the priests and having undertaken responsibility for governing God’s people, he showed from the very beginning what he would be throughout his life.

“For he did not imitate that noble and fruitful style of speaking which could nourish the minds of men. Instead, by turning toward popular favor and, like anyone else, courting the empty applause of the people, he stirred up the unstable and base crowd to desire him. Wearing a filthy garment, gloomy and entering with a sorrowful appearance, avoiding public disturbances, pretending abstinence through bodily pallor and emaciation, for the most part applying himself attentively to books at home and living quietly for himself—by these practices and pretenses he attracted many to admire him, until he reached a more advanced age, striving to appear rather than to be a Christian and seeking his own glory more than Christ’s.”

Theodoret says this and other things about Nestorius, which are quoted elsewhere.

[Col. 0154D] It should be observed that Theodoret says that he traveled from one region to another and finally arrived at Antioch, where he was instructed and trained in the liberal arts and eventually attained the priesthood, which is the matter mentioned here.

If Nestorius was baptized in the city and Church of Antioch, as Cassian repeatedly asserts, although Theodoret says nothing of it, it follows that Nestorius must have arrived in Antioch at least during childhood or adolescence, after traveling through other regions, and that he received baptism there.

For how could he, while still an infant, have traveled through various regions before coming to Antioch?]

—to the regeneration of salvation, to the grace of the Eucharist, and to communion with the Lord. And what more need be said? O grievous and mournful complaint! It brought you even to the office of ministry, to the summit of the presbyterate, and to the dignity of the priesthood.

Do you think this easy, unhappy madness, or something insignificant? Do you not see what you have done? Into what abyss you are hurling yourself?

By destroying the faith of the Creed,

[Note: This does not mean that he altogether lost the indelible characters of baptism, confirmation, or priestly and episcopal ordination. Rather, by losing the faith that is the symbol and foundation of all Christianity, he made himself unworthy and empty of every Christian merit and of the honor and office of the ecclesiastical order.]

you have lost everything that you had been. For the sacraments of your priesthood and salvation rested upon the truth of the Creed.

Do you think that you are merely denying that? You have denied yourself, I say. But perhaps you do not think that you are denying it. Let us examine the text of the Creed, so that if you say what you said earlier, you may not be accused; but if you say something very different and contrary, do not expect me now to refute you, since you have condemned yourself.

For if you now assert something different from what is in the Creed and different from what you yourself formerly said, what remains except that you attribute your punishment to no one but yourself, since you see that the judgment of everyone against you is the same as your own?

The Creed says:

“I believe in one God, the almighty Father, creator of all visible and invisible creatures; and in the Lord Jesus Christ, his only-begotten Son, firstborn of all creation, born from him before all ages and not made.”

You ought first to answer concerning this: do you confess this about Jesus Christ, the Son of God, or do you deny it? If you confess it, everything is sound. If not, how do you now deny what you previously confessed yourself?

Choose, then, which you prefer. One of two things must necessarily happen: either your own confession, if it remains unchanged, will alone free you, or, if you deny it, your first confession will condemn you.

For you said in the Creed:

“I believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, his only-begotten Son and firstborn of all creation.”

If the Lord Jesus Christ is the only-begotten Son and firstborn of all creation, then by your own confession he is undoubtedly God. For there is no other only-begotten firstborn of all creation except the only-begotten Son of God. As he is the firstborn of creatures, so also is he God, the creator of all.

And how do you assert that he was merely a man born from the Virgin, when you confessed that he existed as God before the ages?

Then, says the Creed:

“Born from the Father before all ages and not made.”

The Creed has spoken through you, and you through the Creed: Jesus Christ was born from God the Father before the ages and was not made.

Does the Creed say anything about these fantasies with which you now rave?

Did you yourself say anything of the kind?

[Note: This refers to what he said above (Book 5, chap. 14): “If, as the heretic says, God was to become present in the Lord Jesus Christ as though in a statue or an instrument—that is, so that he merely dwelt in him as in a man and spoke as through a man,” and so forth.

As for whether Nestorius actually used these very words and called Christ the statue and instrument of God, I find no evidence in another author. But as far as the matter itself is concerned, it is plainly inferred from Nestorius’s teaching. Cassian therefore concluded that Nestorius truly thought this, even if he may not have expressed it in precisely these words. For whoever asserted that Jesus was a mere man, not God but merely God-bearing, deified, or simply God’s dwelling-place, lodging, image, *θεοδοχον* (*theodochon*)—that is, one who receives God—God’s co-worker, and the Lord’s man, and who held that he should be honored and adored not for his own sake but because of the God dwelling within him: what else, in reality, did he fashion him to be than a statue, image, or instrument of God?

The words are Nestorius’s own, collected from his writings and reported at the end of Cyril’s works:

“I adore the one who said, ‘My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?’—the one who remained in death for three days—with the divinity, as a co-worker of divine authority.”

And again:

“Because of him who bears, I honor him who is borne; because of the hidden one, I adore the one who appeared.”

Thus he constructed his statue and instrument.

Against this statue—or rather, against the Nestorian idol and the fantastic or Satanic instrument—Saint Cyril hurled the following decisive anathemas:

“If anyone says that Jesus was acted upon and impelled by the Word of God as though by a man, and that the glory of the Only-Begotten accrued to him as to someone other than and distinct from the Word, let him be anathema.

“Again: If anyone dares to say that the assumed man should be worshiped and glorified together with God the Word, and that one God should be called with the other—for the particle ‘with,’ whenever it is added, continually compels us to understand this—and does not rather honor Emmanuel with one worship and apply one glorification to him, as the Word became flesh, let him be anathema.

“Again: If anyone says that the one Lord Jesus Christ was glorified by the Spirit as by an alien power, which he used through him, and that he received from the Spirit the works he performed against unclean spirits and the signs of divinity he displayed among men, and does not rather say that the Spirit was his own, through whom he performed the signs of divinity, let him be anathema.”

Thus Cyril.]

Where is your statue here? Where is your instrument, I ask? For surely it cannot be anyone else’s rather than yours.

Where is that doctrine according to which you assert that the Lord Jesus Christ is like a statue and think that he should be worshiped not because he is God but because he is the image of God? Where is that blasphemy by which, making the Lord of majesty an instrument, you say that he should be honored not for his own sake but because of the one who supposedly breathes and resounds through him?

You said in the Creed that the Lord Jesus Christ was born from God the Father before all ages and was not made—a statement that certainly applies only to the only-begotten Son of God—

[Note: Among scholastic theologians this question is debated (Peter Lombard, *Sentences*, book 3, distinction 11, and the doctors there): whether Christ may be called a creature, or a made thing. For some clarification, which this passage seems to require, the following should first be noted.

It is not disputed among the teachers that Christ, insofar as he is man, is a creature. The human nature in Christ is a creature, just as it is in all other human beings. Therefore, insofar as Christ is considered as man, it can neither be denied nor even doubted that he is a creature.

The question, however, is whether this proposition should be admitted simply and without qualification: “Christ is a creature,” or “Christ is made,” or “Christ is created.”

Second, it should be noted that the holy Fathers express different judgments on this matter, and that they may appear opposed to one another. In favor of the affirmative position, besides Scripture—which says that Christ was made from a woman and was created according to God (Galatians 4; Ephesians 4)—the Greek Fathers speak plainly. Cyril of Alexandria says in Book 10 of the *Treasury*:

“Although by nature he is uncreated and Lord and creator of all, he is also found to have become a creature, first among men whom the nature he assumed restored.”

John of Damascus likewise says in Book 3 of *The Faith*, chap. 4:

“Christ possesses this: that he is called both God and man at the same time, created and uncreated, passible and impassible.”

Among the Latin Fathers, Saint Ambrose teaches the same no less clearly in Sermon 5 on Psalm 118:

“I do not fear that anyone will say: ‘Then you assert that Christ was created?’ I will answer: ‘Yes. I call him created in the way in which I read that he was made’—that is, made from a woman, made under the Law. He was created in order to redeem creatures.”

Saint Jerome says similarly in his commentary on Ephesians 2:

“We freely proclaim that there is no danger in calling him a creature whom, with the whole confidence of our hope, we confess to be a worm, a man, crucified, and a curse.”

He denies that there is danger of error or falsehood because, evidently, one need not fear that a person departs from the truth by calling Christ a creature.

Saint Leo’s statement in Sermon 3 on Pentecost is equally clear:

“If man, made in the image and likeness of God, had remained in the honor of his nature and had not, deceived by the devil’s fraud, deviated through desire from the law imposed upon him, the Creator of the world would not have become a creature. Since man did not remain in the honor of his nature, Leo confesses that the Creator of the world became a creature.”

Finally, Saint Augustine says in his book *On Faith and the Creed* (chap. 4):

“The same Wisdom that was begotten from God deigned also to be created among men.”

And in Sermon 12 *On the Time*:

“For our sake the Creator was created.”

To these authorities must be added an equally manifest reason: it is the most certain rule and axiom of theologians that the properties of both natures may truly be predicated of Christ’s hypostasis by reason of the hypostatic union, as was said above.

Therefore, just as he is and is called creator by reason of his divinity, so he is a creature by reason of his humanity. Just as he is incorporeal and incomprehensible according to his divinity, so he is corporeal and comprehensible according to his humanity.

Accordingly, just as Christ truly said, without qualification, “The Father is greater than I” (John 14), because the Father is greater according to divinity, so it may also truly be said, without qualification, “Christ is less than the Father,” as Athanasius said in the Creed, because he is less according to his humanity.

The addition “according to this nature” or “according to that nature” is not a restriction or necessary qualification imposed upon speech so that it may be true; rather, it explains what is to be understood according to what. Hence one may say simply and without qualification that God was born, suffered, and died, and that Christ the man is creator, almighty, eternal, and so forth.

Against this, and on the negative side, are set the words of Saint Ambrose in his book *On the Faith*:

“Let us prove that the Son of God is not a creature. For we have heard in the Gospel that the Lord commanded his disciples: ‘Preach the Gospel to every creature’ (Mark 16). He who says ‘every creature’ excludes none. Where, then, are those who call Christ a creature? For if he were a creature, he would command the Gospel to be preached to himself and would be subject to vanity, since, as the Apostle testifies, ‘Every creature is subject to vanity’ (Romans 8). Christ, therefore, is not a creature but the creator, who assigns the disciples the duty of teaching the creature.”

Likewise Augustine says in Book 1 of *On the Trinity*, chap. 6:

“All things were made through him” (John 1). He does not say “all things” except those that were made—that is, the whole creature. Hence it is clearly evident that he himself was not made, through whom all things were made; and if he was not made, he is not a creature.

Again, elsewhere (Book 83, question 67):

“Whatever God the Father made through the Son is called a creature. The Son himself cannot be called a creature, because all things were made through him.”

Thus Augustine.

Finally, in the Nicene, Constantinopolitan—or, as Cassian calls it, Antiochene—and Athanasian Creeds, we simply confess that the Son of God was begotten, not made.

From these statements the Author also concludes in this passage that Christ’s birth was not a making, and that the one born should be called born only, not made, and so forth.

Third, one should note and embrace Saint Augustine’s rule (Book 1 of *On the Trinity*, chap. 12), where he says:

“When we speak about Christ, the prudent, diligent, and devout reader ought to understand what is said according to what and for what reason.”

“According to what” means according to which nature—divine or human.

With these points established, the question may be answered as follows. There are two ways of considering the Son of God: one in relation to his incarnation, and the other considering him in himself, with this mystery set aside, just as he existed before all ages as the only-begotten Son of God.

In this latter sense Arius maintained that the Son of God was created, because he was not begotten from the substance of the Father but was created from nothing by the Father’s almighty will. This is the point at which the holy Fathers most steadfastly resisted that heretic. They taught that the Son of God was not created by the Father but begotten from God, and that he must not be numbered among creatures, since he is the one through whom all things were made.

But when they considered the mystery of the incarnation, through which God became man and therefore the creator became a creature, they did not absurdly judge that the Son of God could be called a creature. For he is not asserted to be merely a creature or a pure creature, as by Arius, but both creator and creature.

Nevertheless, because when “creature” is said without qualification the circumstance often does not appear that would indicate what is being considered, it is customary to understand “creature” as excluding the creator—that is, as referring to something that is purely a creature. Consequently, it is neither useful nor fitting to call Christ a creature indiscriminately and ordinarily. Rather, because of his excellence, by which he is equal to the Father, he should be honored with the title “creator.”

The doctors therefore rightly judge that one should abstain from such language because of the danger of error and perverse interpretation, lest we seem to agree with the Arians, or at least to share their language, when they called Christ a creature and understood this not according to his humanity but according to the proper nature of the Son of God. According to that interpretation, the proposition was rightly condemned long ago by the Fathers as belonging to Arian doctrine.

Or at least, in propositions of this kind, concerning whose interpretation heresy once arose, such caution should be used that we state the nature according to which they are to be understood. The Fathers did this whenever they wished to speak more carefully. Jerome and Ambrose, in the passages cited at the beginning, explain themselves by testifying that they were speaking of Christ according to the assumed nature.

Finally, it should be noted that Cassian did not use the term “made” in this passage carelessly or by chance rather than “creature.” When he says that the Son of God was not made, he attacks and stings certain crafty Arians and their Nestorian followers.

For, regarding the word “creature” as too hateful and detested by the whole world, they did not use it, since they could scarcely endure without horror any such diminution of the majesty of their Redeemer, upon whom the whole hope of salvation depended. Instead, covering their poison with honey, they repeatedly confessed that the Son of God was not created and was not a creature, but proclaimed that he was “made.” Under this specious title they intended to signify that Christ was not the natural Son of God and true God, but deified and “essentiated,” and raised by the gift of grace to such majesty that he could be called God.

With this also in view, Athanasius, in the Creed, said distinctly and without tautology that the Son of God was neither made nor created, but begotten.]

so that his birth is not a making and he is said to be born only, not made. For it is contrary to reason and to the honor of the thing itself to believe that the maker of all things is a making, and thus that the author of all beginnings himself began in the same way that all things began from him.

Therefore he is said to be born, not made, because his birth is singular, not the common making of all things. And since he is God born from God, the divinity of the one begotten must necessarily possess everything that belongs to the greatness of the one who begets.

# CHAPTER VII. He Persists in the Same Argument Drawn from the Antiochene Creed
It continues in the Creed: “True God from true God, of one substance with the Father, through whom the ages were joined together and all things were made.” And when you have said all this,

[Note: For what does the relative pronoun *who* or *whom* refer, unless to “true God from true God,” just mentioned immediately before? Even grammarians—and indeed uneducated people—understand this. Why, then, does Nestorius separate Jesus and divide him into two, assigning one part of the Creed’s sentence to one and another part to the other, although they plainly refer to one and the same Son of God?]

remember that you have said everything concerning the Lord Jesus Christ. For this is what you have in the Creed: that you believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God and firstborn of all creation. And after this, among other things: “True God from true God, of one substance with the Father, through whom the ages were joined together.” How, then, is the same one God and not God; the same one God and the same one statue; the same one God and the same one instrument? These statements, heretic, do not agree or fit together in any respect, so that you may call him God whenever you wish and whenever you wish regard him as a fabrication. You said in the Creed that he is true God; now you call him a solitary man. How can these things correspond and be reconciled, so that the same one is supreme power and the same one mere weakness; the same one supreme majesty and the same one mere mortality? These things do not belong together in one and the same Lord, when, dividing the same one between worship and insult, you honor him in whatever aspect you prefer and injure him in whatever aspect you prefer.

You said in the Creed, when you received the mystery of true salvation: “The Lord Jesus Christ, true God from true God, of one substance with the Father, creator of the ages, maker of all things.” Where are you, O grief? Where is that man you then were? Where is that faith? Where is that confession? Now you have fallen back into monstrosities and marvels [Lipsius has *recessisti* in the margin, “you have retreated”]. What folly, what madness has destroyed you? You have transferred the God of all power and majesty to lifeless matter and insensible fabrications:

[Note: “A little one,” though not, in my opinion, an infant, but an adolescent or a boy possessing reason, when he was baptized and professed the faith, as was shown above (on chapter 6 of this work).]

Your faith has evidently advanced with time, advanced with age, advanced with the priesthood; yet you have become a worse old man than you once were a little boy, now a worse veteran than a recruit, a worse bishop than a beginner—and after you began to be a teacher, you were no longer a disciple.

## CHAPTER VIII. How Christ is said to have come and to have been born of the Virgin

But let us examine what follows. Thus, when the Creed says: “The Lord Jesus Christ, true God from true God, of one substance with the Father, through whom the ages were joined together and all things were made,” it immediately adds, in an inseparable connection:

“He who for our sake came and was born of the Virgin Mary.”

Therefore he who was true God, who was of one substance with the Father, who was creator of the ages and maker of all things—he, I say, came into the world and was born of the Virgin Mary, in accordance, of course, with the statement of the Apostle Paul: “But when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the law” (Galatians 4).

Do you see how the mysteries of the Creed agree with the sacred Scriptures? The Apostle proclaims that the Son of God was sent by the Father; the Creed confirms that he came. For it was surely the necessary consequence that the one whom the Apostle had taught was sent should be confessed by our faith to have come.

Next the Apostle says, “made of a woman”; the Creed, however, says, “begotten from Mary.” You therefore perceive that Scripture itself speaks in the Creed, and that the Creed testifies that it descended from Scripture.

The Apostle appropriately said “made,” rather than “born,” of a woman, according to the customary usage of divine language, in which “made” is used for “born,” as in the statement:

[Note: Thus Saint Jerome also interprets “made” as used in place of “born” (in his commentary on this passage). “Pay close attention,” he says, “to the fact that he did not say ‘made through a woman,’ as Marcion and the other heresies wish, which fabricate a merely apparent flesh of Christ, but ‘of a woman,’ so that he may be believed to have been born not through her but from her.” Saint Thomas, commenting on the same passage of the Apostle (on Galatians 4), says: “Although one could say ‘born of a woman,’ he nevertheless expressly says ‘made,’ and not ‘born.’ For something is born when it is produced solely from a joined principle; but it is made when it is produced from a separate principle. An ark, for example, is made by an artisan, whereas fruit is born from a tree. The principle of human creation, however, is twofold: material and active. With regard to the material principle, Christ proceeded from a joined principle, since he took the material of his body from the Virgin. Accordingly, he is said to have been born from her, as in Matthew 1: ‘from whom Jesus was born.’ The other principle is the active principle, which in Christ, insofar as it had a role in his origin—that is, in the formation of his body—was not joined but separate, because the power of the Holy Spirit formed it. With regard to this, he is not said to have been born of a woman but to have been made, as from an external principle.” Saint Thomas.]

[Note: So too from the Greek ἐγεννήθησαν, from the verb γίνομαι, “I become” or “am made.” But the Vulgate translation is better: “In place of your fathers, sons have been born to you” (Psalm 44). For we say more properly that children are begotten or born than that they are made; for “to be made” has a broader application. The verb γίνεσθαι is frequently used even by pagan authors in the sense “to be born,” as in Plato, Epistle 8, γίνεσθαι αὐτῷ, “to be born for himself,” and Epistle 9, ἕκαστος ἡμῶν οὐκ αὐτῷ μόνον γέγονε, “each of us has not been born for himself alone.”]

“Instead of your fathers, sons have been made for you” (Psalm 44).

Or this:

[Note: Likewise in Greek: “before Abraham came into being” (*prin Abraam genesthai*). “To come into being” and “to be” are here set against each other as though diametrically opposed. Coming into being belongs to human beings and every creature; being is proper to God, of whom it is said: “I am who I am” (Exodus 3). See what was noted above on this subject.]

“Before Abraham came into being, I am” (John 8).

In this statement he is plainly recognized as having said: “Before he was born, I am,” indicating the reality of birth by the word “made,”

[Note: That is, the reality and meaning itself; this is equivalent to saying that he is truly made—he who, once born, begins to exist, whereas previously he did not exist. Cassian likewise uses “made” elsewhere in the sense of coming into being.]

because whatever does not require being made possesses the efficacy of having been made. “He who for our sake,” he says, “came and was born of the Virgin Mary.”

If a solitary man was born of Mary, why is he said to have come? For no one comes unless he possesses in his essence the very capacity to come.

[Note: That is, according to Nestorius, if he did not exist before he was born of the Virgin, how could he have come? Yet it is established that he came; therefore he existed before he came.]

But he who had not yet received existence, how could he possess the capacity to come? Do you therefore see how, by the word “coming,” his prior existence is designated in the one who comes?

[Note: “Had possessed” is used for “possessed,” namely, the capacity to come in the flesh and to be born in the flesh, if he had not existed before his coming.]

For no one could have possessed that capacity unless it could proceed from the very fact that he existed. But a man did not exist at all before conception; therefore he did not possess in himself the capacity to come. It is therefore certain that God came,

[Note: That is, the one to whom both belong: eternal existence and the perpetual capacity to come.]

for in both respects he possesses what was proposed—existence and the capacity to come. He came because he existed; and because he could always come, he always existed.

## CHAPTER IX. He again refutes his opponent from the latter’s own confession of his destructive error

But why do we argue from words when the facts are clear? Why do we seek the judgments of realities in the text of the Creed, when the very speech contained in it concerns realities? Let us repeat the confession of the Creed—and yours, since you made its confession your own by confessing what it confessed—so that you may understand that you have transgressed not only against the Creed but also against yourself.

The Creed says: “I believe in one sole true God, the almighty Father, creator of all visible and invisible creatures; and in the Lord Jesus Christ, his only-begotten Son and firstborn of all creation, born from him before all the ages and not made; true God from true God, of one substance with the Father, through whom the ages were joined together and all things were made; who for our sake came and was born of the Virgin Mary.”

“For our sake,” the Creed says, “our Lord Jesus Christ came and was born of the Virgin Mary, was crucified under Pontius Pilate, was buried, and rose again according to the Scriptures.”

The Churches are not ashamed to confess this; the apostles were not ashamed to preach it. You yourself—you, I say, yourself—whose every utterance is now sacrilege, who leave absolutely nothing undenied, have nevertheless denied all these things: that God was born, that God suffered, that God rose again.

And what happened after this? To what depths have you sunk? What have you become? Into what have you been reduced? What do you say? What do you vomit forth?

[Note: “Not sane,” that is, “insane.” This is a proverbial expression used by Juvenal and others for mad and deranged people who blurt out anything, swear and perjure themselves, and do not know what they are saying, like Orestes, whom the poets imagine to have been seized with madness and deprived of his reason because of the murder of his mother. Hence Virgil, *Aeneid* 3: “Orestes driven by the furies of his crimes”; and Statius, *Thebaid* 1: “Orestes bereft of mind.” A similar proverb occurs in Junius (*Centuries* 5): “The madness of Orestes—go mad.” The author therefore compares Nestorius with Orestes, a madman with a madman, since Nestorius sometimes affirms and sometimes denies, assuming various faces like Proteus; indeed, he declares him even more insane than mad Orestes, since he vomits forth things that not even Orestes in his madness would have blurted out.]

—things which, as someone says, not even mad Orestes would swear were the words of a sane man.

What do you mean? You say:

[Note: This passage, previously manifestly corrupt, we conjectured should be restored in this way from what follows, where the same words are repeated with superfluous material removed. These are the words of Nestorius himself, whom the author introduces as speaking. They should, if I am not mistaken, be explained as follows: “What does it mean that the Son of God was born from the Christ-bearer?” That is, how absurd and paradoxical it is to believe that the Son of God was born from the Christ-bearer—that is, from the Virgin who bore Christ—as though we were to say: “I believe in God the Word, the Son of God.” Does not the hearer immediately receive a blow? That is, when this is heard, are not the ears immediately struck, horrified, and unable to endure it? “And God died”—that is, if we were to say that God died, would not the hearer likewise recoil and be grievously wounded by hearing it?]

“What does it mean that the Son of God was born from the Christ-bearer?” Suppose that we were to say: “I believe in God the Word, the Son of God, the only-begotten, born from the Father, of one substance with the Father, who descended and was buried”—would not the hearer immediately receive a blow? “God dead?” And again:

[Note: *Nae* is written with a diphthong from the Greek *nai*, an adverb of affirmation; or perhaps it is an exclamation of astonishment, as in Cicero’s *Against Catiline*: “Indeed, they are seriously mistaken,” that is, “certainly.” Perhaps, however, the word was reversed through the carelessness of scribes or printers, so that instead of *fieri potest* (“it can happen”) one should read *ne fieri potest*, and so forth. These are again the words of Nestorius, who recoils from and regards as absurd Christ’s two births, divine and human.]

“Can it indeed happen,” you say, “that the one who was born before all the ages should be born a second time—and that he should be God?”

[Note: Thus Nestorius, arguing from what he regarded as impossible, attacked Christ’s twofold generation and birth, almost like Nicodemus, who uses a similar argument in a similar matter in John 3. For while Nicodemus, still inexperienced, said: “Can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter his mother’s womb a second time and be born again?” so Nestorius asked: “Could the Son of God be born a second time from the Virgin, when he had already been born before all the ages and from eternity?” By claiming this to be impossible, he wished it to follow that the Son of God had neither been born of the Virgin nor that she should be believed to be *Theotokos*—“God-bearer”—but merely *hominipara*, “bearer of a human being.” This was the aim and end of the entire Nestorian tragedy: to deprive Christ of his divinity and Mary of the maternal dignity of being the parent of God. The Catholic Church, however, recognizing Christ as true God and man, confesses and believes that God had an eternal generation and man a temporal generation, without confusion of the natures, and likewise confesses two births in Christ: one by which the Son of God was born from the Father before the ages, and the other by which he was born from his mother as man and the son of man in time. Hence John of Damascus, book 3 of *The Orthodox Faith*, chapter 7: “We confess,” he says, “two births of Christ, one eternal, from the Father, and one temporal, from his mother.” This doctrine is also plainly gathered from the Apostles’ Creed itself. When we say, “I believe in Jesus Christ, his only Son,” we acknowledge the first generation and birth, namely, the eternal and divine one; but when we say of the same Son of God, Jesus Christ, “who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary,” we openly profess the other and second birth, namely, the human and temporal one. Accordingly, in canon 2 of the Council of Constantinople, an anathema is pronounced against anyone who does not confess that the Word of God has two births: one before the ages and outside time, incorporeally from the Father; the other, in the last days, when the same one descended from heaven and was incarnate from the holy and glorious Mother of God. The same point had earlier been declared at the Council of Ephesus and at that of Chalcedon, in Cyril’s letter to Nestorius, in these words: “He who was born from the Father before all the ages was also physically brought forth from a woman in time—not because his divine nature took its beginning from the Virgin, nor because it needed to be born a second time after the birth it had from the Father. For it is foolish and senseless to say that he who existed before all the ages and is coeternal with the Father needed a second generation in order to begin to exist. Rather, because for our salvation he united a human nature to himself and proceeded from a woman, he is therefore said to have been born physically. For the common man was not first born from the holy Virgin and only afterward did the Word dwell in him; instead, in the very virgin womb and uterus he united flesh to himself and underwent physical generation, making the birth of his flesh his own birth.” Thus far Cyril. According to the Catholic faith, then, one and the same person of Christ must be acknowledged to have a twofold generation and a double birth; consequently, it must be confessed that Christ was born twice, generated twice: once from eternity and again in time, as a certain poet expressed no less elegantly than truthfully (see the beginning of the *Christiad*):

> Life-giving Spirit, by your divine power may I be permitted to sing of the King  
> twice born.

In each of Christ’s births there is both something similar and something unique. In the first, Christ had a Father without a mother; in the second, he had a mother without a father. To this Saint Ambrose referred what is written in Hebrews 7 about Melchizedek as a figure of Christ: “Without father, without mother.” “Without a mother,” he says, “the Son of God was born by a heavenly generation, because he was born from God the Father alone; and again he was born without a father when he was born of the Virgin. For he was not generated from male seed, but was brought forth by the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary’s virginal womb.” Nor is it necessary for that reason to speak of two sons or two offspring, since a twofold generation must be acknowledged; there is only one Son of God and man, because of the unity of the person upon whom both births fall. It should not seem impossible that he existed before he was born from his mother, because in one respect—namely, according to his divinity—he always existed, while in another—namely, according to his humanity—he began to exist by being born.]

“If all these things could not happen at all, how do you say that they were accomplished in the Creed of the Churches? How did you yourself say them?”

Let us compare what you said earlier with what you are saying now. Earlier you said: “I believe in God the Father and in Jesus Christ his Son, true God from true God, of one substance with the Father, who for our sake came and was born of the Virgin Mary, was crucified under Pontius Pilate, and was buried.”

[Note: This passage confirms the correction of the text introduced above. He repeats and reinforces what was said once, not only here but also in chapter 11, in order to convict Nestorius of forgetting himself and contradicting himself, since he repudiated and denied what he had professed in the Creed.]

But now what do you say? “If we were to say: ‘I believe in God the Word, the only-begotten Son of God, born from the Father, of one substance with the Father, who descended and was buried,’ would not the hearer immediately receive a blow?”

The bitterness and impiety of your statement can compel us to an excessive and passionate rush of response, but the restraints of pious grief must for a little while be held back.

## CHAPTER X. He attacks him because, although he had deserted the Catholic religion, he nevertheless dared to teach, offer sacrifice, and administer justice in the Church
I mean you, then—you yourself I address: tell me, I beg you, if some Jew or pagan were to deny the creed of the Catholic faith, would you think he ought to be heard? Certainly not. What if it were a heretic or an apostate? Much less, surely, because it is more intolerable to abandon a truth once known than to deny one that was unknown.

[Note: This follows the judgment of the chief of the apostles, who says (2 Peter 2): “For if, having escaped the pollutions of the world through the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, they are again entangled in them and overcome, the latter state has become worse for them than the former. For it would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness than, after knowing it, to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them” (2 Peter 2:20–21). For what happened to them is expressed in the true proverb: “The dog has returned to its own vomit, and the washed sow to wallowing in the mire” (Proverbs 26:11). See Saint Thomas in his Commentary.]

We therefore see two persons in you: a Catholic and an apostate—first a Catholic, and afterward an apostate.

[Note: Nestorius, of course, became a heretic and apostate—that is, a deserter of the faith—from being a Catholic. On this occasion something must be said briefly about heresy and apostasy, and about the distinction between them.

First, as regards the name and concept of heresy, it is commonly said that *heresy* derives from choice, from the Greek ἀπὸ τοῦ αἱρέομαι, “I choose” (Alphonsus de Castro, *Against Heresies*, book I, chapter 9; Melchior Cano, *Theological Places*, book XII, chapter 9). Hence Tertullian says in *On the Prescription against Heretics*: “Heresies are so called from the Greek word, according to the interpretation of choice, which one uses either to establish or to accept them. Therefore the Apostle also declared that the heretic is condemned by himself (Titus 3), because he has chosen for himself the very thing by which he is condemned.” And in book I *Against Marcion*: “From this point the heretic may already be designated: he is one who, having abandoned what previously existed, afterward chose for himself what had not previously existed.”

The same idea appears in Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, book III, chapter 2: “Each of them says that this is the wisdom he himself has discovered”—that is, a fabrication—“for each of them, utterly perverse, is not ashamed to proclaim himself as the rule of truth.”

Saint Jerome says on Galatians 5: “Heresy is called so in Greek from choice, because each person chooses for himself the discipline he thinks best. Whoever, therefore, understands Scripture otherwise than the sense of the Holy Spirit, by whom it was written, demands, even if he has not withdrawn from the Church, may nevertheless be called a heretic, and belongs among the works of the flesh, choosing what is worse.” Likewise, in his commentary on Titus 3: “Heresy is called so in Greek from choice, because each person chooses for himself what seems better to him. Philosophers too—the Stoics, Peripatetics, Academics, and Epicureans—are called adherents of this or that heresy.” Thus Jerome.

Isidore says much the same in *Etymologies*, book VIII, chapter 3, as does Rabanus in *On the Instruction of Clerics*, book II, chapter 58. The Latin translator of the New Testament sometimes preserves the Greek word (1 Corinthians 11), but sometimes renders it as “sect,” as in Galatians 5, where the Latin version lists “sects” among the works of the flesh, while the Greek has αἱρέσεις, “heresies.” In Acts 28 the Jews say to Paul: “For concerning this sect we know that everywhere it is opposed.” Luke has αἵρεσις in Greek.

Thus “sect” and “heresy” refer to the same thing; but just as *sect* derives from following, so *heresy* derives from choosing. Since, therefore, heresy means nothing other than a private choice by which someone selects something according to his own judgment and adheres to it, the word is in itself common and indifferent, and can designate any sect. Hence among the pagans the various schools of philosophers were called by the Greeks *heresies* and by the Latins *sects*, without any insult or reproach, because different people chose and followed different kinds of discipline and way of life. Four in particular were famous at Athens: the Academic, Peripatetic, Stoic, and Epicurean schools, mentioned above by Saint Jerome.

Cicero too used the Greek word, both in the *Paradoxes* (*To Atticus*, book XIV, letter 15; *To Friends*, book XIV, letter 16) and elsewhere. Philo the Jew likewise, in *On the Life of Supplicants*, preserved by Eusebius (*Ecclesiastical History*, book II, chapter 17), calls our religion a *heresy*, not in an evil sense, but speaking according to the usage of his age. Galen also wrote and entitled a book Περὶ αἱρέσεων, that is, *On the Sects or Opinions of Physicians*. Finally, the Latin expression is not improper: “I belong to that heresy,” meaning “that opinion.”

In the Holy Scriptures, too, the word is sometimes used indifferently. Acts 15: “Certain men rose up from the sect of the Pharisees.” Acts 24: “But this I confess to you, that according to the sect which they call a heresy, so I serve the Father and my God.” Again, chapter 26: “According to the strictest sect of our religion I lived as a Pharisee.” In Greek: κατὰ τὴν αἵρεσιν, “according to the heresy.”

More often and customarily, however, it is taken in a bad sense, as in 1 Corinthians 11: “There must be heresies.” Galatians 5: “The works of the flesh are heresies, envies, murders,” and so forth. Titus 3: “Avoid a heretical person after one or two admonitions.” 2 Peter 2: “They will introduce destructive heresies.”

In this way Christian writers, using the term in a restricted sense, call *heresy* a sect and division by which someone separates himself from the common faith of the Church, choosing a private opinion and departing from Catholic instruction and the rule of truth.

It follows, as something known to all but nevertheless worth mentioning, that evangelical and Catholic doctrine should properly be called neither a heresy nor a sect. First, because we do not follow it by our own choice but by divine instruction; and second, because, as Tertullian says (*On the Prescription against Heretics*, chapter 6), “We are permitted to introduce nothing from our own judgment, nor to choose what someone has introduced from his own judgment. We have as our authorities the apostles of the Lord, who themselves chose nothing from their own judgment to introduce, but faithfully assigned to the nations the discipline they had received from Christ. Therefore, even if an angel from heaven were to preach another gospel, we would call him accursed” (Galatians 1). So Tertullian himself.

Theophylact agrees with him in his commentary on chapter 2 of the Epistle to the Colossians. Origen (*On Titus 3*) depicts a heretic in this way: “Anyone is to be regarded as a heretic who professes to believe in Christ but believes something about the truth of the Christian faith other than what the definition of ecclesiastical tradition contains.”

Saint Augustine puts it somewhat differently in book 1 of *On the Usefulness of Believing*: “A heretic is one who, for the sake of some temporal advantage—especially empty glory and the desire for power—either invents or follows false and novel opinions.” And in book XVIII of *The City of God*, chapter 51, he says: “Seeing the temples of demons abandoned and the human race running to the name of the liberating Mediator, the devil stirred up heretics who, under the Christian name, would resist Catholic doctrine—as though they could be tolerated without correction in the city of God in the same way that the city of confusion tolerated philosophers who held opinions diverse and opposed to one another. Therefore, those who in the Church of Christ hold sick and perverse opinions, and, when corrected so that they may hold what is sound and right, stubbornly resist, refusing to amend their poisonous and deadly doctrines but presuming to defend them, become heretics,” and so forth. Thus Augustine.

More clearly and precisely, the scholastics ordinarily define it as follows: “Heresy is the obstinate error of one who has professed the faith, contrary to Catholic truth.” Properly speaking, a heretic is one who, while professing the Christian name, errs against the Catholic faith with a firm judgment of the will, or embraces a contrary doctrine.

Here the clause “while professing the Christian name” must be noted especially. By this clause heresy is distinguished from apostasy in the strict sense, as will later be shown.

The name *apostasy* itself means nothing other than desertion, defection, or retreat. Hence canonists distinguish three kinds of apostasy: first, apostasy from the faith; second, apostasy from religion, or monastic life; and third, apostasy from an order, or from the clerical state.

Apostasy from the faith, which is at issue here, may be defined as the renunciation and denial of the whole of Christianity, or of the Christian faith and religion. It therefore becomes clear in what way apostasy differs from heresy. Although they agree in this, that both depart from the faith, they differ in the manner of departure: apostasy from the faith departs from it absolutely and entirely, whereas heresy departs only in some respect. Moreover, heresy retains for itself the name and profession of the Christian religion, while apostasy completely rejects and renounces them (Gregory of Valencia, *Disputation* 22, question 1, chapter 11).

Properly, therefore, an apostate is one who, after once embracing the Catholic faith, afterward entirely abandons it, ridiculing and attacking the teaching of the Word of God as foolish, as the emperor Julian is said to have done; hence he acquired the name “the Apostate.” Thus the ancient Christians called those apostates by an infamous name who, having abandoned not only the faith but also the name of Christianity, defected to paganism or Judaism.

From this it is clear that, if *apostate* is taken properly and strictly, neither is a heretic an apostate nor an apostate a heretic, since they differ even by the profession and renunciation of the Christian name alone. But if *apostate* is taken less properly and more broadly, for any deserter of the faith—as the author takes it here when he calls Nestorius both a heretic and an apostate—then every heretic can be called an apostate, though not the reverse, because the term extends more broadly, as is evident.

Thus the ancient and famous apostates—Aquila, who became a Christian from Judaism and a Jew from Christianity; likewise Lucian, Julian, Porphyry, and others who became atheists or pagans—are nowhere, as far as we read, called heretics. And rightly so. For, as Saint Thomas says, one who rejects the whole doctrine of Christ seems to choose nothing but to depart entirely from the faith. Such a person is therefore called an apostate from departure, not a heretic from choice, as the words themselves indicate.]

Which of these two, then, do you think we ought to follow? You yourself must decide; for you cannot prefer one in yourself without condemning the other in yourself. Do you therefore say that the person you formerly were is condemned by you, that the Catholic creed is condemned by you, that the confession of all is condemned, that the faith is condemned? And what follows, then? O disgraceful crime! O intolerable grief!

[Note: In nearly the same way Pope Celestine, in his letters to Nestorius, which were also read at the Council of Ephesus (Baronius, volume V, year 430), severely reproves and rebukes him in these words: “Who would have thought that a ravening wolf was hidden within the sheepfold?” And below: “You have wickedly taken up the weapons of despair against the one who had previously appointed you over his household as though you were faithful and prudent. The blessedness promised in place of this office has perished for you. You not only fail to give food at the proper time, but kill with poison those whom he acquired by his own blood and death. For there is poison beneath your lips, which we see to be full of cursing and bitterness, when you strive to argue against him who is sweet. Where is pastoral care? The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep; but the hireling leaves and hands them over to wolves (John 10). What kind of shepherd will you act as here, when you yourself scatter the Lord’s flock before the wolves? To what enclosure will the Lord’s flock flee if it is wounded within the sheepfolds of the Church? By what protection will one be defended who suffers a robber to be his guardian? And elsewhere the Lord says: ‘I have other sheep that are not of this fold, and I must bring them also.’ He promises to bring others; those you had are perishing. Yet it is certain that whenever such things occur, it is not the sheep who perish because of the shepherds, but rather the shepherds who perish because of the sheep. ‘And they will hear my voice,’ he says. Why? ‘So that there may be one flock.’ At his voice the flock becomes one; at your voice it is either infected or driven away. It is grievous that the words of blessed Paul in the Acts of the Apostles should apply to you: ‘I know that after my departure fierce wolves will enter among you, not sparing the flock; and from among your own selves men will arise speaking perverse things, to draw the disciples after them’ (Acts 20). Would that these things had been spoken by you to others rather than to you. They ought to have been taught to you, not learned by you. Who could endure teaching a bishop how he ought to be a Christian? Carefully consider to what condition you are called, summoned, and rebuked. Which of these things is fitting for a priest?” and so forth.]

What are you doing in the Catholic Church, you traitor to Catholics? Why do you pollute the assembly of the people, having denied the faith of the people? Moreover, you have dared to stand at the altar, ascend the tribunal, and offer your most shameless and treacherous mouth to the people of God? To occupy the chair, presume upon the priesthood, and claim to be a teacher?

Why do you teach Christians while not believing in Christ, when you deny that he is God in whose temple they stand? And after all this—O madness! O frenzy!—you think yourself a teacher and bishop, while, O wretched blindness, you deny that very one whom you claim to be the priest of: that very God, I mean? But grief carries us away.

What, then, does the creed say? Or what did you yourself say in the creed? It says, of course, that the Lord Jesus Christ is true God from true God, consubstantial with the Father, through whom the ages were created and all things made; that this same one came for our sake and was born of the Virgin Mary.

Since, then, you said that God was born of Mary, how do you deny that Mary is the Mother of God? Since you said that God came, how do you now deny that the one who came is God?

You said in the creed: “I believe in Jesus Christ, the Son of God. I believe in true God from true God, consubstantial with the Father, who came for our sake and was born of the Virgin Mary, and was crucified under Pontius Pilate and buried.”

But now you say: “If we say, ‘I believe in God the Word, the only-begotten Son of God, born from the Father, consubstantial with the Father, who descended and was buried,’ does not the one who hears it immediately receive a blow?”

You see, then, that you utterly destroy and uproot the entire faith of the Catholic creed and the entire faith of the Catholic sacrament. O crime!

[Note: Cicero, *Against Verres*, speech 4.]

O portent, as he says, to be carried away to the ends of the earth!

[Note: It seems that Cassian here acted as a prophet or seer and foretold what was to happen: namely, that the impious Nestorius would be transported to the Oasis—or Oasene—desert, the most remote and vastest of the Egyptian deserts, after the Council of Ephesus had pronounced sentence of condemnation and deposition against him and the emperor Theodosius had issued the order. There, as is said here, he would be unable to find anyone whom he could destroy or infect with his heresy.

Theodoretus reports in his letter to Sporadius that Nestorius was banished and transported into exile at the Oasis: “Nestorius was not only expelled from the priesthood; by divine judgment, through the decree of the holy Fathers assembled at Ephesus, but by imperial command he was condemned to inhabit the Oasis, and began to taste in advance the punishments awaiting the impious.” Socrates also affirms the same (*History*, book VII, chapter 33).

Finally, Evagrius derives the account from letters of Nestorius himself, writing as follows (*History*, book I, chapter 7): “But how Nestorius was driven into exile, what afterward happened to him, what end of life he met, and what punishments he suffered on account of his blasphemy, has not at all been handed down by those who recorded his deeds in writing. All these matters would plainly have perished and, through the passage of time, would have been erased and buried so completely that nothing about them could ever have been heard, had I not by chance come upon a book published by Nestorius himself, containing an account of these events.” And below, quoting other letters of the same Nestorius, he reports these words: “By the emperor’s edict we were compelled to depart for the Oasis, otherwise called Ibin.” This is found in Evagrius.

As for what that Oasis desert was like, and what kind of place it was, into which the most criminal men were accustomed to be banished, Baronius explains it fully in his notes on the *Martyrology* (under June 12), so that there is no need to seek information elsewhere.]

For this is more properly said of you, so that you may pass into that desert where you will be unable to find anyone whom you can destroy.

You regard the faith of our salvation, the sacrament of ecclesiastical hope, as a blow to your hearing and a wound to your ears. And how, then, once, when you ran to baptism, did you hear these sacraments with sound ears? How, when the teachers of the Churches instructed you, were your ears not wounded? At that time, certainly, without any wound, you performed the double function of mouth and ears: you both repeated what you had heard from others and heard yourself speaking as the speaker.

Where were those wounds of your ears then? Where was that blow to your hearing? Why did you not contradict and protest? But evidently, according to your own will and desire, you are a disciple when you wish, an enemy of the Church when you wish, a Catholic when you wish, an apostate when you wish.

Surely you are a worthy authority: whichever direction you turn, you drag the Churches after you; your will is to be the law of our life; by your fickleness you transform the human race. And because you do not wish to be what all are—[text defective]—what you wish.

[Note: This passage is evidently mutilated and incomplete, although it was printed in this form both in the Basel and Plantin editions. The sense absolutely requires supplementation along these lines: “Because you do not wish to be what all are”—supply “Catholics,” that is, all who think correctly—“you want all to be what you are,” namely, Nestorian heretics. Or, if the wording seems more harmonious: “Because you do not wish to be what all are, you want all to be what you are”—that is, heretics, as has just been explained.

In this way he wished all to be like himself, to think and judge alike, just as Paul, though in another sense and spirit, said: “I wish that all of you were as I myself am” (1 Corinthians 7). And elsewhere, to Agrippa: “I would to God that, both in little and in great, not only you but also all who hear me today might become such as I am” (Acts 26).]

A splendid authority indeed: because you are no longer what you were, you want the world to cease to be what it was.

## CHAPTER XI  
He refutes the unspoken objection of the heretics who wish to retract the profession of their faith made in childhood.

[Note: “When you were reborn,” that is, when you were baptized—which is to be reborn from water and the Holy Spirit, according to John 3. This was another escape or quibble by which Nestorius might evade the accusation brought against him: he could say that a foreign faith had wrongly been attributed to him when he was an infant, and that an infant could neither understand what was being done nor protest.

But we have already demonstrated above, by comparing the statements of Theodoretus and Cassian, that this quibble is false and deceitful, and we have shown that he was baptized as an adult, not as an infant, which the author has consistently maintained up to this point.

Nevertheless, here he may seem to have hesitated somewhat and to have treated the matter as unexamined. For although he has so far assumed as certain that Nestorius was baptized and reborn as an adult, he now, granting him the contrary hypothesis, nevertheless rebukes him because he did not later retract, when he had grown older and his rational judgment had matured, the faith that he had once professed, at least through those who presented him for baptism. Rather, while serving in ecclesiastical and priestly office, for so long a time and even into old age, he knowingly and deliberately retained it. Hence he cannot, even on this account, escape the stain of treachery as a stubborn recanter.]

Perhaps you say that you were a little child when you were reborn, and therefore at that time you could neither understand nor protest. It is true: infancy prevented you from contradicting, although, had you contradicted as a grown man, you might have been put to death.

[Note: That is, you would have incurred the danger of death if you had contradicted as an adult.]

For if, in that most faithful and devout Church of Christ—

[Note: The Antiochene Church, in which Nestorius was baptized, as stated above. In it the apostle Peter both planted the faith and established his see (Acts 11), and in it the disciples were first called Christians. Because of its faith and devotion it was later called Theopolis, that is, “City of God” (Nicephorus, book XIV, chapter 34).]

—when the priest delivered the creed to the people of God, who were responding and acclaiming it, you had attempted to mutter something or protest, would you perhaps have been heard?

[Note: This was a solemn rite and ancient ceremony observed in administering baptism from apostolic times: if those being baptized were adults and catechumens, they recited the Apostles’ Creed themselves, with their own mouths and publicly; but if they were infants, the priest asked, “Do you believe in God the almighty Father?” and the sponsors or presenters answered on behalf of the infant, “I believe.”

Saint Dionysius the Areopagite is a witness to this practice in *The Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, chapter 2, where he says that the person being baptized professes Christ three times and assents to all the divinely delivered articles of faith—something accomplished through the profession of the creed.

Saint Ambrose likewise says in book II of *On the Sacraments*, chapter 7: “You were asked, ‘Do you believe in God the almighty Father?’ You said, ‘I believe.’ And you were immersed,” and so forth.

Saint Jerome writes *Against the Luciferians*: “Since it is customary in the font, after the confession of the Trinity, to ask, ‘Do you believe in the holy Catholic Church? Do you believe in the forgiveness of sins?’” And in his commentary on Proverbs 2 he says that those being baptized profess that they will believe the creed.

Saint Augustine says in *On Faith and Works*, chapter 11: “Why, then, do we either hand over the creed to those being baptized or require them to recite it?” And in book IV of *On the Creed for Catechumens*: “You have received the creed, a protection against the poisons of the serpent that gives birth.” And in book III, chapter 1: “Know that the sacrament of the creed, which you have received and committed to memory and retain for your salvation, is the foundation of the Catholic faith, upon which the building of the Church was constructed by the hands of the apostles and prophets.” See also the many passages cited above concerning this rite.]

You might have been heard, perhaps, rather than immediately sent away for destruction as some new kind of prodigy or monster.

Not because that most devout and religious people of God would wish to be polluted by the blood of even the most impious person, but because in great cities a people fervent in the love of God, whenever it sees someone rise up against its God, often does not know how to restrain the ardor of its faith.

But let us grant it: if you were an infant, assuming that this is so, you could not contradict or protest against the creed. Why, then, when you had grown older and stronger, did you remain silent? You certainly grew, became a man, and were incorporated into the ecclesiastical ministry. Through so many ages, through so many grades of office and dignity, did you never understand the faith that you had taught for so long?

You knew, surely, that you had been its deacon and priest. If the rule of salvation displeased you, why did you accept the honor of an office whose faith you did not approve? But evidently, as a prudent and simple religious man, you wished to balance yourself between the two, retaining both the treachery of sacrilege and the dignity of a Catholic.

## CHAPTER XII  
Christ crucified is a stumbling block and folly to those who assert that he was a mere man.

[Note: Above, in chapter 5, Nestorius said: “Does not the one who hears it immediately receive a blow?”—namely, by hearing that God was born, that God suffered, that God died, and so forth.]

The blow to your hearing, then, and the wound to your ears, is God born and God who suffered. Where, then, is your statement, O apostle Paul: “We preach Christ crucified, to the Jews a stumbling block and to the Gentiles foolishness, but to those who are called, Jews and Greeks alike, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1)?

What is the wisdom and power of God? God, of course. Yet he preaches Christ, who was crucified, as the power and wisdom of God. Therefore, if Christ is unquestionably the wisdom of God, Christ is unquestionably God.

“We preach,” he says, “Christ crucified, to the Jews a stumbling block and to the Gentiles foolishness.” The Lord’s cross, then, which was foolishness to the Gentiles and a stumbling block to the Jews, is both to you. For there is no greater foolishness than refusing to believe, and no greater stumbling block than refusing to hear.

Their ears, therefore, were wounded by the preaching and suffering of God, just as yours are now wounded. They thought this was a blow to their hearing, just as you do. Thus, when the apostle preached Christ as God, at the name of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ they closed the ears of their heads, just as you close those of your mind.

[Note: Nowhere do I find it explicitly stated that the Jews or Gentiles closed their ears while Paul was preaching, unless one understands the following passage from Acts in this way: “When the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy and contradicted what was spoken by Paul, blaspheming. Then Paul and Barnabas spoke boldly: ‘It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you first; but since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life,’” and so forth (Acts 13). Again: “When some were hardened and did not believe, speaking evil of the way of the Lord before the multitude,” and similar passages in Acts 22 and 28.

Scripture frequently mentions people of this kind, who close the ears either of their head or of their mind to the preaching of God’s word. Isaiah 6: “Make the heart of this people dull, and make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes, lest they see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, and be converted and I heal them.” Matthew repeats this passage in chapter 13: “Hearing you will hear and not understand; seeing you will see and not perceive. For the heart of this people has become dull, and they have heard heavily with their ears and closed their eyes, lest they ever see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, be converted, and I heal them.” The other Evangelists and Paul express the same thought with some words changed or omitted (Mark 4; Luke 8; John 12; Acts 28).

Likewise Jeremiah 5: “They have eyes and do not see; they have ears and do not hear.” And chapter 6: “Their ears are uncircumcised, and they cannot hear.” Micah 7: “Their ears will be deaf.” Zechariah 7: “They made their ears heavy, so that they would not hear.” Acts 7: “Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears.” And again: “They stopped their ears and rushed upon him with one accord.”]

The impiety of both of you might seem equal in this respect, except that your crime is greater: they denied him in whom his suffering still displayed humanity, whereas you deny him whom the resurrection has already proved to be God.

Accordingly, they persecuted him on earth, while you persecute him even in heaven. Not only that, but this is more cruel and criminal: they denied him through ignorance, whereas you deny him after faith; they did not know the Lord, whereas you confessed him as God; they acted under zeal for the Law, whereas you act under the profession of a bishop; they denied one from whom they thought themselves separated, whereas you deny the one whose priest you are.

O disgraceful and unheard-of crime! You persecute the very one by whose dignity you still make use of your own.

## CHAPTER XIII  
He answers the objection that the birth ought to be consubstantial with the one who gives birth.

But evidently you use this as a great argument of your treachery and impiety for denying and persecuting the Lord God, when you say:

[Note: That is, the son must be consubstantial with his mother, or of the same nature as his mother. Here an abstract noun is used for a concrete one: “birth” for “the one born.”

Nestorius’s argument, which is indicated somewhat obscurely, may be stated more clearly as follows: “The son must be consubstantial with his parents; but Christ is not consubstantial with Mary, since he is eternal and omnipotent God, qualities that in no way belong to Mary; therefore,” and so forth.

Cassian answers this argument and objection in two ways. First, he denies the premise when it is taken universally. Even if this axiom were true and constant in natural things—although its contrary is established by many examples in the following book, chapters 3 and 5—it would not follow that it applies to the birth of the Son of God, which is supernatural. He who established nature itself could be born above the common law of nature, as he willed, and did not bind himself to the laws of nature.

Second, Cassian grants the premise and shows that it also applies to Christ, provided it is understood and explained correctly. The proper meaning of the axiom is that a son must be consubstantial with his parents according to the nature he received from them, or in that respect in which he is their son. Christ, as God, did not receive the divine nature from Mary but the human nature; nor is he her son except insofar as he is human. It is therefore sufficient that, insofar as he is human, he be consubstantial with his mother, just as, insofar as he is God, he is consubstantial with the Father.

This solution is not only easier but also much more solid than the first.]

“The birth must be consubstantial with the parent.”

I do not yet state or assert fully that this principle should not be observed in the birth of God, because the birth itself did not belong to the one who gave birth but to the one born; and he was born as he willed, since it was his will that he be born.

[Note: That is, the birth of the Son of God should not be attributed so much to the mother from whom he was born as to the one who was born, who was born in the manner and at the time he willed, and brought about his birth from a Virgin. As Saint Leo says (*Sermon 2 on the Nativity*): “Here let not the condition of the one giving birth be considered, but the will of the one being born, who was born human as he wished and as he was able. If you seek the truth, recognize the material of human nature; if you investigate the reason for the origin, confess the divine power.”]

In the meantime, although you say that the birth must be consubstantial with the parent, I say that the Lord Jesus Christ was consubstantial both with the Father and with the mother.

[Note: It is inferred from what follows that *parent* rather than *the one giving birth* should be read here and above, since the subsequent explanation says “with both Father and mother,” and shortly afterward “of both parents.” Nevertheless, the statement would be more general if *the one giving birth* were read and “birth” were understood of every offspring.]

For, according to the distinction between the persons, he rendered to each parent his own likeness. According to his divinity, he was consubstantial with the Father; according to the flesh, he was consubstantial with his mother.

It was not that there was one who was consubstantial with the Father and another who was consubstantial with the mother. Rather, the same Lord Jesus Christ, both human and God, possessed in himself the property of both parents: in that in which he is human, he rendered the likeness of his human mother; and in that in which he is God, he possessed the truth of God the Father.

## CHAPTER XIV  
He compares this error with the doctrine of the Pelagians.

[Col. 0171B]

Otherwise, if it is not the same Christ who is from Mary as the one who was born from God, you unquestionably make two Christs, in accordance with that crime of Pelagian impiety which, asserting that a solitary man was born from the Virgin, [Note: The Pelagians, denying original sin and the necessity of grace, consequently denied that Christ had redeemed us or made satisfaction for us; rather, they said that he had come only to instruct human beings by his teaching and example and to summon them to the pursuit of virtue. Hence they acknowledged him as an instructor and teacher, not as redeemer and mediator, as was shown above. Peter Abelard partly followed this error (Book I, chapter 3, letter 190), in the time of St. Bernard, who vigorously opposed him. For although Abelard did not deny original sin, he nevertheless denied that Christ had redeemed us and freed us from the power of the devil. The same error was condemned by Innocent II in his rescript to Bernard, which is preserved among Bernard’s letters (Letter 194).] declared him to have been a teacher of the human race rather than a redeemer, because he had given human beings not redemption of life but an example of how to live—that is, so that people, by following him and doing similar things, might attain similar results. Your impiety, then, has one and the same origin, one and the same root of error. They assert that a solitary man was born from Mary, and so do you. They separate the Son of Man from the Son of God, and so do you. [Note: The first authors of this heresy were Ebion and Cerinthus, in apostolic times, as Irenaeus teaches in Book I, chapter 25, Against Heresies, and Tertullian in On the Flesh of Christ. They separated Christ from Jesus and wanted Jesus to be merely a man, born from Mary and Joseph; but they held that Christ, the eternal Son of God, descended upon Jesus in the form of a dove in the thirtieth year, when he was baptized, and dwelt in him. In this way, Jesus was united with Christ through a kind of association and indwelling.

The Pelagians later revived this heresy. Their claim was that a mere man had been born, and that only later, in the thirtieth year, he had become Christ through his own merits; after the Passion, he had likewise become God through his own merits. They maintained that other human beings could similarly attain blessedness by their own powers through living well, just as Christ had attained it. Thus Cassian, recounting the errors of the Pelagians in Book I, chapter 3, says: “They added that, after his baptism, our Lord and Savior became Christ; after his resurrection, God—assigning one status to the mystery of anointing, and the other to the merit of his Passion.” This is his statement.

Nestorius later followed them, adding this further point: he denied that Christ was God even after his ascension and asserted that he was a mere man, as is explained here. The heralds and leaders of the same error were Theodore of Mopsuestia, a certain Anastasius, and other followers and defenders of Nestorius, as Theodoret reports in Book IV, On Heresies.] They say that the Savior was made Christ through baptism; you say that he was made the temple of God in baptism. They do not deny that he was made God after the Passion; you deny that he was God even after the ascension. Your perversity differs from theirs, then, in only one respect: they seem to blaspheme the Lord on earth, while you do so also in heaven. You have surpassed and gone beyond those whom you imitate—we do not deny it. They at least cease at some point to deny that he is God; you never do. Yet even their confession cannot be regarded as fully true, since they grant the Savior the honor of divinity only after the Passion: having denied that he was God before, they confess it afterward. For, as it seems to me, whoever denies a part of God denies the whole; and whoever does not confess that he has always existed as God denies him always. Likewise, even if today you were to say that the Lord Jesus Christ, who was born from the Virgin Mary, is true God in heaven, unless you said that he has always been God, you would not truly confess him. But plainly you do not wish to alter or vary your position in any respect: since you call him a solitary man when he was born, you insist that even today he is not God. O new and singular impiety! Although you assert with the heretics that he is a man, you do not confess with the heretics even that he is God.

## CHAPTER XV. He shows that those who defend this error acknowledge two Christs.

Nevertheless, as I was beginning to say, it must be clarified that you unquestionably make two Christs. Tell me, please: you who separate Christ from the Son of God, how do you confess in the Creed that Christ was born from God? For you say: “I believe in God the Father, and in Christ Jesus, the Son of God.” Here, then, you have Jesus Christ, the Son of God. Yet you say that the same Son of God was not born from Mary. Therefore one Christ is from God and another from Mary. There are consequently two Christs in your position.

Although in the Creed you do not deny Christ, you assert as Christ from Mary someone other than the one whom you confess in the Creed. But perhaps you will say that Christ was not born from God. And how, then, do you say in the Creed, “I believe in Jesus Christ, the Son of God”? You must either deny the Creed or confess Christ as the Son of God. If you confess in the Creed that Christ is the Son of God, you must necessarily confess that the one born from Mary is Christ, the Son of God.
