Or, if you assert that the Christ from Mary is another, you plainly blaspheme by making two Christs [Lipsius in the margin: “blaspheme”].

## CHAPTER XVI. He further shows that this teaching overturns the confession of the Trinity.

Nevertheless, even if your perversity and infidelity are not refuted by this faith of the Creed, are you not, I ask, overwhelmed by reason itself and by the light of truth? Tell me, whoever you are, heretic. There is certainly a Trinity whom we believe and confess: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. There is no dispute concerning the majesty of the Father and the Spirit. You slander the Son because you say that the one brought forth from Mary is not the same as the one begotten from God the Father. Tell me, then: since you do not deny that the only-begotten Son of God was born from God, who do you want this one born from Mary to be? [Note: In the preceding edition, the negative “not” had wrongly been omitted, wholly overturning the sense. Nestorius did not deny, as is well known and as the text makes clear, that the Son of God was born from God the Father.]

You call him a solitary man, in accordance with what he himself said: [Note: Nestorius also abused this passage, reasoning as follows: “What is born from flesh is flesh: Christ was born from flesh; therefore Christ is flesh.” This is entirely true, but it does nothing to support Nestorius. For who denies that Christ is flesh, since the Word became flesh (John 1), and the whole mystery of the Incarnation consists in this? But it does not follow that Christ is only flesh and therefore a solitary man—that is, a mere man and not God—or that one is the son of flesh, or of man, and another the son of the Spirit, as Nestorius wanted. Rather, he is both flesh and Spirit. The passage continues: “What is born from the Spirit is spirit.” From this, by a similar argument against Nestorius, one concludes: “What is born from the Spirit is spirit; Christ was born from the Spirit—that is, from God, for God is Spirit (John 4); therefore Christ is Spirit.” He is therefore not merely flesh, but flesh and Spirit—that is, man and God: flesh from flesh, Spirit from Spirit. For if the first statement applies to Christ, why should the second not also apply?

Tertullian touches on this argument in On the Flesh of Christ, chapter 18: “The Lord,” he says, “pronounced decisively and definitively: ‘What is born in flesh is flesh,’ because it is born from flesh. But if he spoke only about a human being and not about himself, plainly deny that Christ is man, and thus maintain that the statement does not apply to him. Yet he adds: ‘And what is born from the Spirit is spirit,’ because he is Spirit and was born from God.” And in Against Praxeas, chapter 27: “From these two elements Jesus was constituted: from flesh, man; from Spirit, Spirit.” Thus he speaks.

Therefore, just as the later statement and syllogism do not rightly conclude that Christ is only Spirit, so neither does the earlier statement rightly imply that he is only flesh and not Spirit. For, as Tertullian says in the same place, “From these two elements Jesus was constituted,” and so forth.

The learned Maldonado proposes and explains another meaning of Christ’s words, entirely different from Nestorius’s interpretation. Since his words are especially useful for elucidating this passage, I have thought it worthwhile to quote them here. “Theophylact,” he says (Commentary on John 3), “properly observed that ‘flesh’ in this passage means a carnal human being, and ‘spirit’ a spiritual human being—that is, substantives used in place of adjectives. For the whole human being is said to be born from flesh and to be flesh, although the soul, which is another part of him, is neither born from flesh nor is flesh; because he is born from blood, from the will of the flesh, and from the will of a man—that is, in a carnal and human manner—and those who are born in that way are born sinners, that is, carnal, while the soul itself, although a spiritual substance, is carnal because it has been stained by sin.

“By contrast, flesh that is free from sin and united to God is called spirit: ‘He who is joined to the Lord,’ he says, ‘is one spirit’ (1 Corinthians 6). This readily resolves the question raised by Chrysostom and Euthymius, though in my judgment they did not explain it sufficiently: if what is born from the Spirit is spirit, Christ, who was born from the Holy Spirit, ought to be spirit. They answer that he was also born from the flesh of the Virgin and therefore possessed true flesh. It is as though they were reluctant to concede that Christ is spirit and not flesh, and that he was born from spirit and not from flesh. In the sense in which Christ himself speaks here, however, there was no reason for such reluctance.

“For although Christ possesses true flesh and was truly born from flesh, in the sense in which he speaks here he was neither born from flesh nor is he flesh. To be born from flesh in this passage means to be born in the human manner: to be born a sinner from a sinful human being; and this is precisely what it means to be flesh. Christ, however, was neither a sinner nor born from a sinful human being. Thus he possesses flesh, but is not flesh.

“Conversely, to be spirit and to be born from spirit means to be like God and to receive his Spirit. Since both are supremely present in Christ, he above all was born from the Spirit and is Spirit.” Thus far Maldonado.] “What is born from flesh is flesh” (John 3). But one cannot call him a solitary man who was not generated solely according to the law of human creation. “The one who is conceived in her,” the angel says, “is from the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 1).

Yet even you, who deny virtually all the mysteries of salvation, do not dare deny this. Since, then, he was born from the Holy Spirit, and a man conceived through God’s inspiration cannot be called solitary, if he is not the one who, according to the Apostle, “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2), and “the Word became flesh” (John 1), and “humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death” (2 Corinthians 8), and who “became poor for our sake, although he was rich” (Philippians 2), tell me, then, who is this one who was brought forth from the Holy Spirit and conceived through God’s overshadowing?

You plainly say that he is another. Therefore there are two: the one begotten from God the Father in heaven, and the one conceived from Mary through God’s inspiration. [Note: This is Nestorius’s distinctive and well-known doctrine: that there was one Jesus, or one person, born from the Virgin, and another Son of God, born from the Father, as is clear from this entire treatise and from other sources. It follows from this—although Nestorius did not expressly state it—that there are two Sons in Christ, two supposita, and two distinct persons.

This gives rise among the scholastics to two questions (Peter Lombard, Sentences, Book III, distinction 6, and the commentators thereon). The first is whether Christ may be called “one and another,” “the one and the other,” or “several” or “two,” in the masculine form. Although these matters are subtle, they seem relevant to understanding this passage and therefore should not be entirely passed over.

With regard to the first question, the true and Catholic position is that Christ cannot be called “one and another” or “the one and the other,” nor can he be called two or several; rather, he must absolutely be called one and the same. This is a position well known among the Fathers and confirmed by sound reasoning, because just as unus, “one,” in the masculine properly refers to the unity of person, so alius, “another,” alter, “the other,” and duo or plures, “two” or “several,” refer to a distinction of persons. Thus, in speaking of the divine persons, we say that the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another, because the person of the Father is one, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another, as Saint Athanasius says.

Since there is only one person in Christ, it follows that he must in no way be called “one and another.” This doctrine is shown to be a matter of faith by all the testimonies of Scripture that can establish it. Cassian has both previously shown and will later show that Christ is one and the same God and man. It was also expressly defined at the Council of Alexandria, in the letter to Nestorius that is the tenth among Cyril’s letters; confirmed at the Council of Ephesus in the confession of faith and in canons 2 and 3, where those who divide Christ into two are condemned; and at Chalcedon, in the first session, where Christ is defined as one. The third canon condemns the one who suffered. At the Sixth Council, session 4, the letter of Pope Agatho expressly states that Christ is not one and another, nor is one in another Christ. Finally, at the Lateran Council under Martin I, consultation 5, canon 6, Christ is defined as one and the same.

The Fathers, both Greek and Latin, teach the same. Athanasius, speaking of Christ in the Creed: “Although he is God and man, yet he is not two, but one Christ.” Leo the Great, Letter 95, chapter 1, condemns anyone who says that Christ is one and another. Hilary, On the Trinity, Book IX: “Since the Son of Man is not one, and the Son of God another,” and so forth. Augustine, Enchiridion, chapter 38: “Both together, namely God and man, are not two but one Christ.” Likewise Anselm, On the Incarnation, chapter 5, and Damascene, Book II, chapters 5 and 7.

As for the second question, this must be held above all: although there is in Christ one thing and another—that is, one divine nature and another human nature—it cannot properly or ordinarily be said, “Christ is one thing and another,” and still less should he be said to be several or two.

Saint Thomas explains the reason very clearly in these words (Part III, question 17, article 1): “It must be said that a nature considered in itself, insofar as it is signified abstractly, cannot truly be predicated of a suppositum or person, except in God, in whom what he is and by which he is do not differ, as was explained in the First Part. In Christ, however, since there are two natures, divine and human, one of them—the divine—can be predicated of him both abstractly and concretely. For we say that the Son of God, who is the suppositum signified by the name ‘Christ,’ is the divine nature and is God.

“But human nature cannot be predicated of Christ in itself and abstractly, but only concretely, insofar as it is signified in the suppositum. For it cannot truly be said that Christ is human nature, since human nature is not suited to be predicated of its suppositum.”

And below: “The Nestorians, positing two persons in Christ, said that Christ was not only two in the neuter but also two in the masculine. Since we, however, posit one person and one suppositum in Christ, as is clear from what has been said, it follows that we should say not only that Christ is one in the masculine, but also that he is one in the neuter.”

In the solution to the fifth argument he adds that, in the mystery of the divine Trinity, the divine nature is predicated abstractly even of the three persons; therefore it can simply be said that the three persons are one. In the mystery of the Incarnation, however, neither nature is predicated abstractly of Christ; therefore it cannot simply be said that Christ is two.” Thus far Saint Thomas.

Accordingly, what is sometimes read among the Fathers—that Christ is one thing and another because there are two natures in him, as in Hilary, On the Trinity, Book IX, where he says that Christ is one thing from the Father and another from the mother, and in Augustine, On the Trinity, Book I, chapter 7, and Enchiridion, chapter 35, where he says that Christ is one thing because of the Word and another because of the man—these and similar statements must be judged improper and require a suitable interpretation. Their meaning is that in Christ there is, or that Christ possesses within himself, one thing and another: that is, one nature and another.

Augustine explains himself in this way when writing Against Felicianus. After saying, “In the mediator between God and human beings, one thing is the Son of God and another the son of man,” he adds (chapter 11): “I say ‘one thing’ to distinguish substance, not ‘another’ to distinguish person.”

Gregory of Nazianzus, in his First Letter to Cledonius, spoke more properly and accurately: “One thing and another,” he says, “are the elements from which the Savior is constituted, but not one person and another. Far from it. Both are one through their conjunction.” And below: “According to one thing and another, he is firstborn according to his humanity, only-begotten according to his divinity.”]

Consequently, you introduce a fourth person. [Note: That is, Christ is the natural son according to Nestorius, as though he had been in some way added and associated with the three divine persons and were an adopted or honorary god—just as the pagans called their adopted gods in Greek παρεγγράπτους (parengraptous), “registered” or “enrolled gods,” minor deities who had been admitted from among human beings into the order of the gods (Cicero, On the Laws; Lucian, Jupiter the Tragic; Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 51).

Although Nestorius called Christ a solitary man—that is, separated from the person of the Word and from divinity—he nevertheless held that Christ should be honored and adored with equal honor because of his exceedingly close union with the Word. This union, however, was not hypostatic or personal, but merely accidental and precarious, as was explained above. Hence below he calls Christ a fourth person in the Trinity.

Augustine addressed this error in Tractate 78 on John, where he says: “Let us acknowledge the twofold substance of Christ: divine, by which he is equal to the Father, and human, by which he is less than the Father. Both together, however, are not two but one Christ, lest God be a quaternity rather than a Trinity. For just as a human being is one person consisting of rational soul and flesh, so Christ is one, God and man; and therefore Christ is God, rational soul, and flesh.” Thus Augustine.

A different quaternity in the divine nature was proposed by a certain abbot named Joachim. Innocent III refutes and condemns it in Extra, On the Supreme Trinity and the Catholic Faith, chapter 2 (Book I of the Decretals, title 1).] Although in words you call him a solitary man, in reality you confirm that he was not solitary, since you confess that he is honorable, venerable, and worthy of adoration—even if not in the manner you ought. Therefore, since the Son of God who was born from the Father must certainly be adored, and the one brought forth from Mary through the Holy Spirit must also be adored, you make two honorable and venerable beings for yourself. You divide them from each other so completely that you venerate each with his own particular honor. Thus you understand that, by denying and separating the Son of God from himself, you overturn, as far as lies within you, the entire mystery of divinity. For while you attempt to insert a fourth person into the Trinity, you see that you have utterly denied the whole Trinity.

## CHAPTER XVII. He shows that one who errs in a single article of the Catholic religion destroys the whole faith and the merit of faith.

Since these things are so, [Note: This assertion, although it may be understood not absolutely of every article of faith but, as the matter requires and according to the author’s intention, of those alone that pertain to the mystery of the Incarnation and depend upon and cohere with one another—as the following discussion makes clear—nevertheless is also generally asserted by Saint Thomas: faith in one article cannot be possessed without faith in another, and whoever loses faith in one also loses faith in the others.

Saint Thomas proves this in the following way (2a2ae, question 5, article 3): “It must be said that in a heretic who disbelieves one article of faith, faith remains neither formed nor unformed. The reason is that the species of any habit depends upon the formal nature of its object; once this is removed, the species of the habit cannot remain. The formal object of faith is the First Truth, insofar as it is manifested in the sacred Scriptures and in the teaching of the Church, which proceeds from the First Truth.

“Therefore, whoever does not adhere to this infallible divine rule—the doctrine of the Church, which proceeds from the First Truth manifested in the sacred Scriptures—does not possess the habit of faith. Rather, he holds the matters of faith in some other way, not by faith. It is as if someone held a conclusion in his mind without knowing the middle term of its demonstration: it is clear that he would not possess knowledge of it, but only an opinion.

“It is clear that the person who adheres to the doctrine of the Church as to an infallible rule assents to everything the Church teaches. Otherwise, if among the things taught by the Church he accepts what he wishes and rejects what he does not wish, he no longer adheres to the doctrine of the Church as to an infallible rule, but to his own will.

“Thus it is clear that a heretic who obstinately disbelieves one article of faith is not prepared to follow the Church’s teaching in all things. If he is not obstinate, he is no longer a heretic but merely someone in error. It is therefore clear that such a heretic does not possess faith concerning the other articles, but only an opinion formed according to his own will.”

Thus Saint Thomas.

Scripture also appears to support this position. The Apostle considers heretics of every kind to suffer shipwreck in the faith and thereby to fall away from it, although it is certain that they do not deny every article of faith. He urges us to “hold faith and a good conscience,” which, he says, “some have rejected and suffered shipwreck concerning the faith” (1 Timothy 1). And in Ephesians 4 he declares that there is only one true faith—that is, the faith by which all believe the same divinely revealed truths proposed by the Church.

The Council of Trent also supports this position, session 6, chapter 15, where it simply asserts that faith is lost through unbelief, of which heresy is a form. “It must be affirmed,” it says, “not only that through unbelief faith itself is lost, but also that, although faith is not lost, the grace of justification once received is lost through any mortal sin.” Although this is not expressly defined there, the truth is presupposed as certain and beyond dispute.

Nevertheless, there are also numerous arguments on the contrary side, and they are not implausible. For reasons of brevity, however, I refrain from presenting them, content merely to have cited those arguments that confirm the opinion of our author.] Therefore, by denying one Jesus Christ, the Son of God, you have denied everything. For this is also the rule of the Church’s sacrament and of the Catholic faith: whoever denies one part of the divine sacrament cannot confess the rest. Everything is so interconnected and joined together that one thing cannot stand without another, and whoever denies one element of the whole gains nothing by having believed the others.

Thus, if you deny that the Lord Jesus Christ is God, then, by denying the Son of God, you must also deny the Father. For, according to John’s words: [Note: These are the words of the Apostle John in the First Epistle: “Who is the liar except the one who denies that Jesus is the Christ? This is the Antichrist, who denies the Father and the Son. Everyone who denies the Son does not have the Father; whoever confesses the Son also has the Father” (1 John 2)—that is, acknowledges him.

It is unclear how the phrase “according to the voice of John” came previously to be printed as “according to the voice of the Father himself,” as though these were the words of God the Father, unless someone prefers to read “according to the voice of the pious father,” understanding this as referring to the Apostle John.] “Whoever does not have the Son does not have the Father; whoever has the Son also has the Father” (John 2). Therefore, by denying the one begotten, you also deny the one who begot him.

Likewise, by denying the Son of God born in the flesh, you necessarily deny that he was born in the Spirit, because the same one who was born in the flesh was first born in the Spirit. [Note: That is, in divinity, in accordance with John 4: “God is Spirit.” Hence in the following chapter he says: “Born in divinity, born bodily,” referring here to the flesh.] Therefore, by not believing that he was brought forth in the flesh, you must also refuse to believe that he suffered. And if you do not believe in his Passion, what remains except that you also deny the resurrection? For faith in the one raised arises from faith in the one who died. The account of the resurrection cannot stand unless faith in the death has preceded it.

Therefore, by denying that he suffered and died, you also deny that he rose from the dead. It follows that you must deny that he ascended, since the ascension could not have occurred without the resurrection. And whoever is not believed to have risen must also not be believed to have ascended, as the Apostle says: “The one who descended is the one who also ascended” (Ephesians 4). Therefore, as far as lies within you, the Lord Jesus Christ neither rose from the dead nor ascended into heaven, nor sits at the right hand of God the Father, nor will come on that final day of judgment which is awaited, nor will judge the living and the dead.

## CHAPTER XVIII. He turns his speech to the very opponent against whom he is arguing and invites him to repent. The sacrament of reconciliation is necessary for the salvation of those who have fallen.

You understand, then, O unhappy and frenzied perversity, that you have utterly emptied out all the faith of the Creed, all the power of hope and of the sacrament. And yet you have dared to stand in the Church and think yourself a priest, although you have denied all those things through which you began to be a priest. Return, then, to the right path; recover your former understanding; come at last to your senses, if you ever possessed understanding. Return to yourself, if indeed you once had within you something to which you might now return. Recognize the sacraments of your salvation, through which you were renewed and through which you were reborn. You need them now no less than you needed them then, so that they may now regenerate you through repentance,

[Note: That is, may repair and restore you. Properly speaking, regeneration belongs to baptism, which is “the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit” (Acts III). Yet because repentance is here compared with baptism, as with the first spiritual generation, repentance itself may reasonably be called regeneration, that is, a second or renewed spiritual generation. Thus it is frequently described by the Fathers (Tertullian, *On Repentance*; Jerome, on Isaiah III; Gratian, *On Repentance*, distinction I; Council of Trent, session 14, chapter 2) as “the second plank after shipwreck”: second, namely, after baptism; after the shipwreck, namely, of sin. Baptism, however, is called regeneration without qualification, since it follows upon carnal generation, according to John III: “Unless someone is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.” Explaining this later, he adds: “Unless someone is born of water and the Holy Spirit,” etc.]

which previously regenerated you through the font.

[Note: Through the baptismal font, that is. “They generated” applies if one has in view the second renewal and a kind of spiritual regeneration that takes place through repentance; but “they regenerated” is more accurate if one considers the first, carnal generation, as stated above. This is a kind of synecdoche, in which the genus is put for the species: “the sacraments of our salvation” stands for repentance and baptism, which are signified by “the font” and “the fonts.” Psalm VI: “Bless the Lord from the fountains of Israel.” Isaiah XII: “You shall draw water with joy from the fountains of the Savior.” Zechariah XIII: “There shall be an open fountain for the house of David and for the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for the washing of the sinner and of the menstruous woman.”]

Hold fast the full order of the Creed; hold fast the perfect truth of the faith. Believe in God the Father; believe in the Son, God: in one begetter and one begotten—and yet the same Lord,

[Note: Christ is “firstborn” according to his humanity and “only-begotten” according to his divinity, says the blessed Gregory of Nazianzus, cited above (on chapter XVI). But someone may ask why he is not also firstborn according to his divinity and only-begotten according to his humanity; why he is not firstborn of the Father just as he is firstborn of his mother, just as he is the only-begotten of both Father and mother. I hope that this objection will later be answered from the Fathers, if I first make a few preliminary remarks.

First, I believe that Gregory of Nazianzus had in view two very well-known Gospel passages. In the first, namely Matthew II, Mary is said to have given birth to “her firstborn son,” which refers to his humanity. In the second, namely John I, we read: “No one has ever seen God; the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has made him known to us.” This certainly refers to his divinity. From these two passages of the respective Gospels, as it were their initial and widely known statements, Nazianzus inferred, as I think, the proposition that Christ is “only-begotten according to his divinity and firstborn according to his humanity.” This does not mean that he is not also the only-begotten of his mother according to his humanity, or the firstborn of the Father according to his divinity; rather, the Gospel distinguished the two titles in such a way that it initially assigned one to his divinity and the other to his humanity.

That Christ must also be called firstborn according to his divinity is made clear by Scripture, when it calls him “the firstborn of all creation” and “the firstborn among many brothers” (Colossians I; Romans VIII). For if he is firstborn, then he is begotten—and by no one other than God the Father; therefore he is the Father’s firstborn. The Apostle states the same thing even more explicitly in Hebrews I, when he says: “And when he again brings the firstborn into the inhabited world” (the heavenly Father).

Thus, although the word and concept are different, in reality “firstborn” and “only-begotten” mean the same thing in Christ. He is both only-begotten and firstborn: of the Father according to his divinity and of his mother according to his humanity. He is firstborn because he is first; only-begotten because he is the sole and unique Son.

But how, you ask, can he be firstborn if he is only-begotten, since these seem opposed? Where there is no second-born, there can be no firstborn either; “first” has reference to “second” and to what follows. Helvidius used this argument against Saint Jerome, as did other heretics who held erroneous views about Mary’s perpetual virginity. Because the Evangelists call Christ Mary’s “firstborn,” they attempted to establish that after Christ’s birth she had other children by Joseph; in relation to these, they thought, our Lord would be called firstborn, believing that only the one followed by others could properly be called firstborn.

Hence Saint Jerome, commenting on Matthew I—“Joseph took his wife, and he did not know her until she had given birth to her firstborn son”—says: “From this passage some most perversely infer that Mary had other sons, saying that no one is called firstborn unless he has brothers; whereas it is the custom of the divine Scriptures not to call firstborn the one whom brothers follow, but the one who was born first.” See the aforementioned treatise against Helvidius.

From Jerome’s position we conclude that “firstborn” has two meanings, affirmative and negative. In the first sense, the firstborn is the one born first among brothers of the same parents, after whom others are born; thus Reuben is called Jacob’s firstborn (Genesis XXX). In this sense, the same person cannot be both firstborn and only-begotten. But this meaning of “firstborn” is much narrower and more restricted than the other, according to which someone is called firstborn if no one was born before him—whether others were born after him, as other sons of Jacob were born after Reuben, or no one was born and born after him, as no one was born after our Lord from the most holy Virgin Mary. According to this meaning of “firstborn,” every only-begotten child is also firstborn, though not every firstborn is only-begotten, as is evident.

In this sense Saint Jerome and the other Fathers cited below teach that Christ is called firstborn—not because another son was born after him, as Helvidius maintained, but because no one was begotten before him. This, they say, is the most common usage of Scripture: even only-begotten children are called firstborn, because whoever is only-begotten necessarily comes before all others; that is, no one was begotten before him, which is what it means to be firstborn.

Thus in Exodus IV God calls the people of Israel his firstborn, although he had no other worshiper. In chapter XII he is said to have struck all the firstborn of the land of Egypt; among them, there is no doubt that some were only-begotten. In chapter XIII he commands that every firstborn be consecrated to him. The custom of the law, which interprets it, also teaches that only-begotten children are to be understood; otherwise one would have to wait until later-born children came into existence.

Since, then, according to the more usual scriptural usage, “firstborn” denotes the one who is begotten first, before whom no one else has been begotten by the same parents, and after whom no one is required to be begotten, it is clear that both titles—only-begotten and firstborn—most properly apply to Christ the Lord, whether he is considered as begotten of the Father or of the mother. For he alone is, from eternity, the natural Son of God, and he is called by the Apostle the firstborn of all creation, because he was begotten before all things and nothing was before him (Colossians I). When he chose to become human, he likewise became Mary’s firstborn, and also her only-begotten, because he was the first and only one born from her, with no brother naturally begotten of the same mother.

But so that these matters may become clearer and more apparent, let us now hear the Fathers discussing, in more than one way, the two titles just mentioned as belonging to Christ the Lord.

Athanasius, in *Against the Arians*, discourse 3, having in view the two passages of the Apostle (Colossians I and Romans VIII) in which Christ is called firstborn with respect to creatures, says: “The same person cannot be both only-begotten and firstborn unless the reference differs in each case: he is considered only-begotten because of his generation from the Father, but firstborn because of his condescension toward creatures and the kinship with many brothers that thereby results. Since these two things are contrary to one another, one may rightly say that the proper force of the word ‘only-begotten’ prevails above all, because there is no other Word or other Wisdom besides him, who alone is the true and unique Son of his Father; and he is called the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, not with an added explanatory cause, but simply. He is called firstborn with an added cause: he is firstborn for the sake of creatures.” Thus Athanasius.

Observe that he does not absolutely deny that Christ should be called firstborn with respect to the Father; rather, he teaches that, on this side, the proper force of “only-begotten” applies to him more than that of “firstborn.” With respect to creatures, however, the proper force of “firstborn” applies to him more than that of “only-begotten.” In this same sense Gregory of Nazianzus earlier said that Christ is only-begotten according to his divinity but firstborn according to his humanity.

Likewise Cyril of Alexandria, in his book *On the Faith to Theodosius*, says: “He is both the only-begotten and the firstborn. Only-begotten, indeed, as God; firstborn, insofar as, according to the union of the divine dispensation, he lived among us and among many brothers, so that we too might become, in him and through him, sons of God according to nature and according to grace. According to nature, or naturally, as his members; but by participation and according to grace, through him in the Spirit. Just as it became the proper effect of Christ’s humanity, because it was joined to the Word according to the bond of the dispensation, that it should be and be called only-begotten, so it became peculiar to the Word, because he was united to flesh, that he should be and be called firstborn among many brothers.”

Saint Jerome, in *Against Helvidius*, further demonstrates that Christ is truly called and is truly the only-begotten and firstborn even according to his human nature. “From this passage,” he says—that is, from the passage of Matthew cited above—“Helvidius attempts to prove that no one can be called firstborn unless he has brothers, just as the one who is the sole son of his parents is called only-begotten. But we define the matter thus: every only-begotten child is also firstborn; not every firstborn is only-begotten. The firstborn is not merely the one after whom others are born, but the one before whom no one was born. Otherwise, if only the one followed by brothers is firstborn, firstborn offerings would not be owed to priests until others had been born, lest, if no birth followed, the child should turn out to be only-begotten and not firstborn.”

And further: “Finally, I ask about John, who is known to have been only-begotten: was he also firstborn? Was he himself, according to the law, subject to the whole of that law? There can be no doubt. Certainly Scripture speaks of the Savior as follows: ‘When the days of their purification had been completed according to the law of Moses, they brought him to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord, as it is written in the law of the Lord: Every male opening the womb shall be called holy to the Lord,’ etc. (Luke II). If this law applies only to firstborn children, and if subsequent children make someone firstborn, then the one who knew nothing of later brothers ought not to have been bound by the law concerning the firstborn. But since even the one not followed by brothers is bound by the law of the firstborn, it follows that the firstborn is the one who opens the womb and before whom no one exists—not the one whom a brother born afterward follows.” This is Saint Jerome, together with what follows in the same vein.

Damascene also agrees. In book IV of *The Orthodox Faith*, chapter 8, he writes: “The firstborn is the one who is born first, whether he is only-begotten or born before other brothers.”

Thus, if the Son of God were called firstborn but not also called only-begotten, we might suspect that he was firstborn of creatures, as though he himself were a creature. But since he is called both firstborn and only-begotten, we must preserve both meanings in him (see Billius’s commentary there). We call him the firstborn of all creation because he is from God, and creatures are from God; but he alone is begotten timelessly from the substance of God the Father, and therefore is rightly called only-begotten. He is firstborn, not first-created, for a creature does not come from the substance of the Father but is brought from nothing into existence by his will.

He is also firstborn among many brothers. For he exists as the only-begotten from his mother. After he shared in flesh and blood, as we do, and became human, we too became through him sons of God, adopted through baptism. He himself is Son of God by nature; he became firstborn among us through adoption and grace, when we were made sons of God and became his brothers, etc.

See also Isidore of Pelusium, book III of the letters, letter 31; Isidore of Seville, *On Differences*, question 5; and finally Saint Thomas, part III, question 28, article 3.]

the Lord of all, Jesus Christ, of one substance with the Father; born in divinity, born in the body: of a twofold birth, indeed, but of one majesty. He who is the creator of all creatures was the same one born from the Father, and afterward born from the Virgin.

## CHAPTER XIX. Temporal birth took nothing away from Christ’s divinity, either in honor or in power

For this fact—that he came from flesh and in flesh—was his origin, not a diminution; he was born, and was not changed. For although, while remaining in the form of God, he assumed the form of a servant, the weakness of his human condition did not weaken the nature of God. Rather, while the power of divinity remained wholly unharmed and intact, everything accomplished in human flesh was the advancement of humanity,

[Note: Pope Leo, in sermon 11 *On the Passion of the Lord*: “This is the rule of faith that, at the very beginning of the Creed, we received through the authority of apostolic instruction. We confess our Lord Jesus Christ to be the only Son of God the almighty Father; we likewise confess him to have been born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary. Nor do we depart from his majesty when we believe that he was crucified, died, and on the third day was raised. For all that belongs to God and all that belongs to humanity are fulfilled together by both humanity and divinity, so that while the impassible is present in the passible, neither can power be affected by weakness nor weakness overcome by power.”

And in sermon 8 *On the Nativity*: “God the Son of God, the only-begotten of the eternal and unbegotten Father, remaining eternal in the form of God and possessing unchangeably and timelessly an existence no different from that of the Father, assumed the form of a servant without any loss to his majesty, so that he might raise us up into what is his, not himself fall short into what is ours. Hence, while each nature remains in its own properties, such a communion of unity has been effected that whatever is there of God is not separated from humanity, and whatever is of humanity is not divided from divinity.” See the same author, sermons 1 and 2 *On the Nativity*.]

not a diminution of majesty. For when God was brought forth in human flesh, he was born in flesh not so that God would cease to remain in him, but so that, with God remaining in him, the human would be God.

[Note: That is, he was not born in flesh in such a way that God did not remain in him.]

And therefore Martha, although she saw a human being with bodily eyes, nevertheless confessed God with spiritual eyes, saying: “Yes, Lord, I have believed that you are the Christ, the Son of the living God, who has come into the world” (John XI). Therefore Peter, when by the revelation of the Holy Spirit he saw externally the Son of Man, nevertheless proclaimed him the Son of God, saying: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew XVI). Therefore Thomas, when he touched flesh, believed that he had touched God, saying: “My Lord and my God” (John XX). All confessed one Christ, lest they make two.

Believe in this one, then; and believe thus in the Lord of all, Jesus Christ, the only-begotten and firstborn, the same creator of all things and preserver of humanity; the same one who first fashioned the whole world and afterward redeemed the human race. While remaining with the Father and in the Father, of one substance with the Father, according to the Apostle, he assumed the form of a servant and humbled himself to death, even death on a cross. And according to the Creed: “He was born of the Virgin Mary, crucified under Pontius Pilate, and buried; and on the third day he rose again, according to the Scriptures; and he ascended into heaven; and he will come again to judge the living and the dead.”

For this is our faith; this is our salvation: to believe that Jesus Christ, God and Lord, is the same one both before all things and after all things. For, as it is written: “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today, and forever” (Hebrews XIII).

[Note: This sentence was cited and explained above.]

By “yesterday” he indicates all past time, in which he was begotten by the Father before the beginning. By “today” he indicates the periods of this present age, in which he was again born from the Virgin, suffered, and rose again. But by the statement that he is “the same forever,”

[Note: Other manuscripts read: “All the immensity and boundlessness of the future eternity is signified.”]

the whole immensity of the future eternity is signified.

## CHAPTER XX. He teaches from the foregoing that it does not follow that God was mortal or corporeal before the ages, although Christ is the same one who was God from eternity and became human in time

But perhaps you say: If I call the same one born from the Virgin at the end of time who was born from God the Father before all things, I am also calling God corporeal before the beginnings of the world; I, who call him afterward a human being whom I call always God, am consequently saying that the human being who was born afterward had always existed. I do not want you to be confused by this blindness of ignorance and this night of errors, so that you think I am asserting that the human being born from Mary existed before the beginnings of created things, and that I am also proclaiming God to have been corporeal before the foundations of the world.

[Note: “The human being,” namely, insofar as he is human, or according to his human nature. Otherwise, stated simply and absolutely, this proposition is true when Christ is indicated: “This human being born from Mary existed before the beginnings of the universe and before the ages,” because “human being” stands for the person, and in Christ that person is none other than the person of the Son of God, who always existed and was from eternity (Saint Thomas, part III, question 16, article 9; the Master of the Sentences, beginning of distinction 12).

Hence he himself says in the Gospel of John VIII: “Before Abraham came to be, I am.” He could no less truly have said: “Before the world came to be, I am.” For elsewhere he says: “Father, glorify me with the glory that I had with you before the world existed” (John XVII).

Long ago Paul of Samosata was condemned as a heretic because he said that Christ had not always existed but had his beginning from Mary, as Saint Augustine reports (heresy 44; Eusebius, book VII of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 24). And the statement of Arius concerning Christ—“There was when he was not, and he was not before he was born”—was condemned by the Fathers of the Council of Nicaea with an anathema (Rufinus, book I of the *Ecclesiastical History*).

Thus, just as the Son of Man is everywhere, both in heaven and on earth, as he himself says: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven” (John III)—not because he was then in heaven insofar as he was the Son of Man, but because he was the same Son of God and Son of Man—so that human being is truly said always to have existed, by reason of his person, not by reason of his human nature, as Nestorius dreamed or quibbled. In the same way, from the fact that through the incarnation the Son of God became corporeal, Nestorius inferred that he had been corporeal from eternity, as foolishly as deceitfully.]

I am not saying, I repeat, that the human being existed in God before he was born, but that God was afterward born in the human being. For that flesh which was born from the flesh of the Virgin did not always exist; rather, God, who always existed, came from the flesh of the Virgin in human flesh. “The Word became flesh,”

[Note: Flesh that already existed, or that was received from elsewhere—such as Apollinaris claimed, saying that Christ had drawn his body from heaven and passed through the Virgin’s womb as through a conduit, as Epiphanius and Augustine report in their books *On Heresies*. Or as others said, claiming that Christ’s flesh was conceived before it was assumed by the Word.

Against this error Augustine writes in *On Faith to Peter*, chapter 18: “Believe most firmly, and in no way doubt, that it was not Christ’s flesh, without divinity, that was conceived in the Virgin’s womb before it was assumed by the Word; rather, the Word himself, God, was conceived through the taking of his flesh, and that flesh itself was conceived through the incarnation of the Word.”

And in letter 3 to Volusianus: “For when the Word of God was joined to a soul possessing a body, he assumed both soul and body at once.”

Athanasius, in *On the Incarnation of the Word*: “The union of flesh with the divinity of the Word took its origin from the womb. There the Word, when he came from heaven, established it, since it did not exist before the Word came from heaven.”

Damascene, book III of *The Orthodox Faith*, chapter 2: “Thus flesh, flesh of the Word of God, and animated flesh possessing reason and understanding were formed at the same time. Therefore we do not say that a human being was deified, but that God was made human.”

The same author, chapter 12: “Conception and subsistence were wonderfully accomplished at the same time: the conception of the Word, and the subsistence of the flesh in the Word.”]

not that he brought flesh with him, but that by the gracious condescension of divinity he united himself to human flesh.

Tell me, then, when or where the Word became flesh, or where he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, or where he became poor, though he was rich—unless it was in that sacred womb of the Virgin, where, when he was incarnate, the Word of God is said to have become flesh; when he was brought forth, he truly assumed the form of a servant; and when, in human condition, he was fastened to the cross, he became poor and was made needy by bodily suffering, although he was rich in divine majesty?

Otherwise, if, as you say, divinity came into him afterward, as into one of the prophets and saints, then the Word also became flesh in those in whom he deigned to dwell. Therefore, through each of them he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant. Consequently, nothing new or extraordinary occurred in Christ; nothing unique or marvelous belonged either to his conception, his birth, or his death.

## CHAPTER XXI. The authority of the divine Scriptures teaches that Christ existed from eternity

And yet, to return to what was said earlier: since all these things are as we have stated, how is Jesus Christ—whom you assert to be merely human, even before he was born from the Virgin—read of as having always existed, and proclaimed by the prophets and Apostles as God even before the ages?

Paul says: “One Lord Jesus, through whom are all things” (1 Corinthians VIII). And elsewhere: “For in Christ,” he says, “all things were created in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible” (Colossians I).

The Creed also, composed equally from human and divine authority, says: “I believe in God the Father, and in God

[Lips. in the margin: “the Lord”]

Jesus Christ, his only-begotten Son and the firstborn of all creation.” And afterward: “True God from true God, through whom the ages were joined together,”

[Note: Some manuscripts read here, as also in the preceding passages: “the ages were created.” In that reading, “ages” means worldly things, that is, things created in the world or in time.]

## CHAPTER XXII. The hypostatic union causes those things that belong to the flesh in Christ to be attributed to God
[Col. 0184C] How, then, when by our confession the Lordly man [Note: [Col. 0184D] Namely, the confession by which above (Chapter 20) he excluded Nestorius’s error and false interpretation, saying: “I do not say—no, not so—that, before he was born, the man existed in God, but that afterward God was born in the man.” For that flesh, which was born from the Virgin’s flesh, did not always exist, etc. Here it is clear that “man” is understood as human nature itself, or the flesh of a man, as he immediately explains: “how the Fathers often speak,” although less precisely, as has been said elsewhere, when they say that the man was assumed by the Word, or that God was born in man—understanding by “man” not a person but human nature.] did not exist at all before the Virgin’s birth and conception [Note: [Col. 0185B] Here again he runs into that expression, disapproved by most of the Fathers and more favorable to Nestorius, concerning which see above (Book V, chapter 5). There, however, it was indicated in what sense it can be tolerated to some extent—namely, among other possible interpretations, if by “man” we understand humanity itself, as has just been said, and consequently by “the Lordly man,” the Lord’s humanity itself, or the Lord’s flesh and humanity; this interpretation is plainly required here. Although Christ as man, since he is not distinguished from the divine suppositum, which is the Lord, cannot be called “Lordly,” because that expression suggests Nestorius’s error and a distinction of persons in Christ (Suárez, *In III partem*, question 16, article 3), nevertheless there is nothing to prevent Christ’s humanity from truly being called “Lordly,” since it is distinct from the suppositum, just as one says “the Lord’s cross” or “the Lord’s Passion.” Perhaps the Fathers, both Greek and Latin, spoke in this manner when they called him “the Lordly man”: Athanasius in the *Exposition of the Faith*, Chrysostom in his homily *On the Lord’s Cross*, Epiphanius in *Heresy* 69, Augustine in *Tractate* 28 on John, and frequently elsewhere. That the present passage demands this interpretation is evident from the fact that it says—and the Author repeatedly asserts—that before his conception and birth the Lordly man did not exist at all. If this proposition is referred to Christ’s person, as the words sound and require, it is absolutely false, as is clear from what has been said. It must therefore be understood of his humanity, or of Christ insofar as he is man.] is nevertheless Christ—whom you call merely a man—proclaimed in the holy Scriptures as God without beginning? And such unity of man and God is read of [Note: [Col. 0185C] That is, Christ the man is eternal, because he is the same one who is and always was God.] that the man also appears to have been eternally coeternal with God, [Note: [Col. 0185C] That is, God suffered together with the man, because the same one is both God and man, and suffered. From this identity and unity follows that communication of properties (*communicatio idiomatum*) discussed several times above (Book III, chapter 8). St. Thomas, treating this article (Part III, question 16, article 4), asks: “Can things that belong to the Son of man be predicated of the Son of God, and conversely?” In agreement with this passage, he writes: “It should be said that, apart from this question, there was a disagreement between the Nestorians and the Catholics. For the Nestorians wished to divide the expressions said of Christ in this manner: things belonging to the human nature were to be said of the man. Hence Nestorius said: ‘If anyone attempts to attribute sufferings to the Word of God, let him be anathema.’ But if there were names that could belong to either nature, they predicated of such names what belonged to both natures, as with the name ‘Christ’ or ‘Lord.’ Thus they conceded that Christ was born of the Virgin, or that the man had existed from eternity. The Catholics, however, maintained that such things said of Christ—whether according to the divine nature or according to the human nature—could be said both of God and of man. Hence Cyril says (at the First Council of Ephesus, canon 4): ‘If anyone divides between two persons, or substances—that is, hypostases—the expressions contained in the evangelical and apostolic writings, or the things said about Christ by the saints, or by Christ himself about himself, and believes that some of these should be applied to the man while others should be assigned to the Word alone, let him be anathema.’ The reason is that, since there is one and the same hypostasis of both natures, the same hypostasis is signified by the name of either nature. Therefore, whether one says ‘man’ or ‘God,’ the hypostasis of the divine and human nature is signified. Consequently, things belonging to the divine nature can be said of the man, as of the hypostasis of the divine nature; and things belonging to the human nature can be said of God, as of the hypostasis of the human nature.” And below, in the solution to the first objection, he says: “It should be said that it is impossible for opposites to be predicated of the same thing according to the same aspect; but according to different aspects nothing prevents it. In this way opposites are predicated of Christ—not according to the same aspect, but according to different natures.” These words of St. Thomas seem necessary for understanding this chapter and for fully and profoundly grasping the whole controversy between the Nestorians and the Catholics, which provided the occasion and subject for the composition of these books; they therefore ought by no means to be omitted. It will be useful to compare them with what has been noted elsewhere concerning the communication of properties.] and afterward God appears to have suffered together with the man? For certainly neither [Note: [Col. 0186C] That is, without beginning; in Greek, ἄναρχος (*anarchos*). Moreover, although neither man in himself is without beginning, nor God in himself subject to suffering (Damascene, *On the Faith*, Book I, chapter 4), nevertheless Christ, because he is God and man, is without beginning insofar as he is God—that is, having neither beginning of days nor end of life (Hebrews 7), as the Apostle explains—and is truly and absolutely proclaimed subject to suffering insofar as he is man. Hence it also follows that these same predicates can be predicated reciprocally of one another. For just as it is truly said, “Man is God,” so it is no less truly said, “The servant is Lord,” “the finite is infinite,” “the temporal is eternal,” “the lesser is equal,” and conversely. Such expressions may be found in Leo’s *Sermon* 2 on the Nativity, in Vigilius of Trent, Book V, and in other Fathers. For this interchange and reciprocal predication is nothing other than the communication of properties, as Damascene teaches in Book III of *On the Orthodox Faith*, chapter 4.] a man without beginning nor God subject to suffering should be believed to be. This is precisely what we have already attested in the preceding writings: that God, united to the man—that is, to his own body—does not permit any separation between man and God to be made according to human opinion. Nor did he in any way wish it to be admitted that one person should be believed by anyone to be the Son of man and another the Son of God. Rather, throughout all the sacred writings he joins and incorporates the Lordly man with God [Col. 0186A] in such a way that, whether one considers time or the Passion, no one can altogether distinguish the man from God or God from the man. For if you look to time, you will always find the Son of man with the Son of God. If you look to the Passion, you will always find the Son of God with the Son of man: Christ, the Son of man and Son of God, being so united and indivisible in himself that, insofar as the wording of divine Scripture is concerned, the man cannot be separated from God in time, nor God from the man in the Passion. Hence the saying: [Note: [Col. 0186D] If Christ—for he calls himself the Son of man—was in heaven when he spoke on earth, then he was simultaneously in heaven and on earth. Yet he was not then in heaven bodily, since he said that he would ascend into heaven; therefore there was another nature in Christ besides that human nature which was visible to the eyes—namely, the divine nature, which is immeasurable and fills heaven and earth at once (Bellarmine, *On Christ*, chapter 8). See the other matters noted above in this connection (On Book IV, chapter 6).] “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of man who is in heaven” (John 3). There, while the Son of God was speaking on earth, he testified that the Son of man was in heaven; and he likewise testified that the same Son of man whom he said would ascend into heaven had previously descended from heaven. Or consider this: [Note: [Col. 0187B] Augustine, commenting on this passage (*Tractate* 7 on John 7), writes: “Christ the Son of man, from the Virgin Mary, began to exist here on earth, where he assumed flesh from the earth. What, then, does he mean when he says, ‘When you see the Son of man ascending,’ except that we should understand Christ to be one person, God and man, not two, lest our faith be a quaternity rather than a Trinity? Thus the Son of man was in heaven in the same way that the Son of God was on earth: the Son of God on earth in the flesh he assumed; the Son of man in heaven in the unity of person.”] “If you see the Son of man ascending to where he was before” (John 6). Although he names him who was born from man, he nevertheless testifies that he had always been in the heavenly regions.

But the Apostle too, if one considers time, proclaims that all things were made through Christ: “For there is one Lord Jesus Christ,” he says, “through whom are all things” (1 Corinthians 8). But if one considers the Passion of his majesty, he declares that the Lord was crucified. “For if they had known,” he says, “they would never have crucified the Lord of majesty” (1 Corinthians 2). And therefore the Creed too, calling the only-begotten and firstborn Lord Jesus Christ true God from true God, *homoousios*—“of the same substance”—with the Father and creator of all things, testifies that he was born of the Virgin, crucified, and afterward buried.

Thus it incorporates the Son of God and the Son of man [Col. 0187B] and unites man and God in such a way that no division can arise either in time or in the Passion. For the same Lord Jesus Christ is taught to be God through the eternity of time and man through the endurance of suffering. And although neither man should be called without beginning nor God subject to suffering, nevertheless in the one Lord Jesus Christ the man is proclaimed everlasting before all things and God is proclaimed dead. You see [Col. 0188A] therefore that Christ is everything, and that his name signifies both natures: for he was born both man and God. Thus he embraces all things in himself, so that nothing is understood to be lacking in his name. Therefore, before the Virgin’s birth, man did not possess the same eternity in the past as God; but because God was united to man in the Virgin’s womb, it came about that in Christ one could not at all be named without the other.

## CHAPTER XXIII. This synecdochic manner of speaking, by which the whole is understood from a part, is exceedingly familiar in the divine Scriptures.

[Note: [Col. 0187C] That is, you say the same thing about the same person: whatever is predicated of Christ is predicated both of the Son of God and of the Son of Man through the communication of properties, because Christ is one and the same Son of God and Son of Man.]

Therefore, whatever you say about the Lord Jesus Christ, you say it in its entirety: in the Son of God you will name the Son of Man, and in the Son of Man you will name the Son of God; [Col. 0188B]

[Note: [Col. 0187C] On this, see Quintilian, Book VIII, chapter 6, and Book IX, chapter 3. On the frequent use of synecdoche in the sacred writings, see St. Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 51, or his Letter to Cledonius, where he gives several examples of the matter. St. Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, Book III, chapter 35, says: “The trope synecdoche makes either the whole understood from a part or the part from the whole. Thus one Evangelist says that something happened after eight days, while another says after six days, when, with only three disciples present on the mountain, the face of the Lord shone like the sun and his garments became like snow” (Luke 9; Matthew 17). For both statements concerning the number of days could not be true unless the one who said “after eight days” is understood to have counted, as the whole of two complete days, the final part of the day on which this was shown and the night belonging to it; while the one who said “after six days” counted all the complete days, but only those lying between them. By this manner of speaking, in which the whole is signified by a part, the difficulty concerning Christ’s resurrection is likewise resolved. For the final part of the day on which he suffered, unless it is taken for the whole day—that is, with the preceding night included—and the night during whose final part he rose, unless it is taken for the whole day, with the dawning Sunday included, cannot amount to the three days and three nights during which he foretold that he would be in the heart of the earth. Thus far Augustine; and elsewhere he says more in the same sense, to be quoted below.

The present Author indicates that four kinds of synecdoche are used in Scripture: first, in days, or the number of days and nights; second, in any kinds of things, when a part is put for the whole or the whole for a part; third, specifically in human beings; fourth, in periods of time. He presents the first example, in reverse order, in the designation of periods or spans of time, as will subsequently be explained.]

—namely, the trope synecdoche, by which the whole is understood from a part and a portion is named from the whole. The sacred writings also teach this, for in them the Lord often uses this trope and, while teaching in this way about others, wished the same manner of speech to be understood of himself. For in the divine books days, things, persons, and periods of time are not otherwise sometimes designated.

[Note: [Col. 0188B] A considerable difficulty arose among interpreters and commentators of Scripture from two or three passages that seem to contradict one another. The first is the passage cited here from Genesis 15, where God foretold that Abraham’s offspring—that is, the Israelite people—would serve in Egypt (as the text seems to imply) for four hundred years. A corresponding passage is Acts 7, where St. Stephen says: “God spoke to him, saying that his offspring would be an alien in a foreign land, and they would enslave them and mistreat them for four hundred years.” A third passage is Exodus 12: “The dwelling of the children of Israel, during which they dwelt in Egypt, was four hundred and thirty years. When these were completed, on that very day the whole army of the Lord went out,” and so forth. A fourth is the Apostle’s statement in Galatians 3: “This I say: the covenant confirmed by God, the law which came into being after four hundred and thirty years, does not invalidate it.” These words should be construed as follows: the Mosaic Law, which was made and given after 430 years, does not invalidate—that is, abolish or weaken—the covenant, namely, the pact or promise made to Abraham concerning the blessing of the nations in his offspring.

The whole difficulty consists in two matters: first, over what length of time, or for how many years, the Israelites remained or served in Egypt; second, from what point in time those years are to be reckoned. For the partial and summary explanation required here—for a fuller and more exact treatment must be sought from the interpreters themselves, such as the ordinary Gloss, Abulensis, Pererius, and others—it will be sufficient to bring forward several testimonies of the ancients.

First, Eusebius of Caesarea says the following in his *Chronicle*: “When Abraham was seventy-five years old, he was judged worthy of divine address and of the promise made to him. From Abraham’s seventy-fifth year until Moses and the departure of the Hebrew nation from Egypt, 430 years are reckoned; Paul refers to these when he says: ‘The covenant confirmed by God, the law which was made after 430 years,’ and so forth. Moses himself likewise speaks in agreement with this in Exodus: ‘The dwelling of the children of Israel, in which they dwelt in Egypt and in the land of Canaan, they and their fathers, was 430 years.’” Thus Eusebius.

Jerome, however, merely indicating the difficulty of the question, left it undecided. For he writes in his *Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians* (see also St. Thomas’s Commentary there): “In this passage it must be determined whether the years are to be reckoned from the time when the Lord spoke to Abraham, saying, ‘And in your offspring all nations shall be blessed’ (Genesis 22), up to Moses the lawgiver, and whether they amount to 430; or how, in Genesis, the Lord promises Abraham himself that after four hundred years his children will depart from the land of slavery. For this is no small matter, and has been investigated by many; I do not know whether it has been discovered by anyone.” Here it should be noted that Jerome did not doubt the truth of that reckoning, as Pererius rightly observes (*Commentary on Genesis*, Book III), but rather the manner of reconciling Paul’s passage with the other passages of Scripture that seem discrepant, as stated above.

The same Jerome mentions this difficulty in his Letter to Damasus (Letter 125), question 2. Augustine, *City of God*, Book XVI, chapter 24, says:

“What was said to Abraham—‘Know for certain that your offspring will be an alien in a land not their own, and they will enslave them and afflict them for four hundred years’—was most clearly prophesied of the people of Israel who were destined to serve in Egypt. It was not that they would spend four hundred years in that slavery under the Egyptians who afflicted them; rather, within those four hundred years it was foretold that this would happen.

“For just as it is written concerning Terah, Abraham’s father, ‘The days of Terah in Harran were two hundred and five years,’ not because all of them were spent there, but because they were completed there, so here too the words ‘They will enslave them and afflict them for four hundred years’ were inserted because that number was completed in the same affliction, not because the whole period was spent there.

“Four hundred years are mentioned because of the fullness of the number, although the actual period is somewhat longer, whether the reckoning begins from the time when these things were promised to Abraham or from the time when Isaac was born, on account of Abraham’s offspring of whom these things are predicted. For, as we have already said above (Book XVI, chapter 16), 430 years are reckoned from Abraham’s seventy-fifth year, when the first promise was made to him, to Israel’s departure from Egypt, which is the period mentioned by the Apostle.

“These 430 years could therefore be called four hundred, since they are not much more; all the more so because some of those years had already passed when these things were shown and spoken to Abraham in a vision, or when Isaac was born to his hundred-year-old father. At that point, twenty-five years after the first promise, 405 years remained of the 430; and God wished these to be called four hundred.”

Thus far Augustine.

The same author, in Book I of volume IV, treating the same question more fully in his *Questions on Exodus*, question 47, says:

“If we take the four hundred years in such a way that they are understood as years spent in slavery under the Egyptians, it was not a short period during which the people could have multiplied in this way. But Scripture gives unmistakable evidence that they did not spend so many years there.

“Some think that the 430 years should be reckoned from the time Jacob entered Egypt until the people were liberated from there by Moses, because Exodus says: ‘The sojourning of the children of Israel, during which they sojourned in the land of Egypt and in the land of Canaan, they and their fathers, was 430 years.’ But they think that the years of their slavery amounted to four hundred, because Genesis says: ‘Know for certain that your offspring will be an alien in a land not their own, and they will enslave them and harm them for four hundred years.’ Yet since their years of slavery are reckoned after Joseph’s death—for while he was alive they not only were not enslaved there but actually ruled—there is no way that the 430 years can all be counted as having been spent in Egypt,” and so forth.

And further:

“Therefore that reckoning which Eusebius followed in his chronological history is founded upon evident truth. For he reckons the 430 years from the promise by which God called Abraham to leave his land and go into the land of Canaan. The Apostle, too, when praising and commending faith, had in mind that promise in which he wishes Christ to be understood as having been foretold: namely, the promise in which God promised Abraham that all the tribes of the earth would be blessed in him. ‘This I say,’ he writes, ‘because the covenant confirmed by God, the law which came four hundred and thirty years afterward, does not annul the promises.’

“Thus Paul says that the law was made 430 years after that calling by which Abraham was called and believed God, not from the time when Jacob entered Egypt.

“Moreover, Scripture itself sufficiently indicates this in Exodus. It does not say, ‘The sojourning of the children of Israel, during which they sojourned in the land of Egypt, was 430 years’; rather, it plainly says, ‘During which they sojourned in the land of Egypt and in the land of Canaan, they and their fathers.’ From this it is clear that the time of the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob must also be included in the reckoning, from the time when Abraham began to live as an alien in the land of Canaan—that is, from the promise in which the Apostle praises his faith—until the time when Israel entered Egypt.

“Throughout this entire period the fathers lived as aliens in the land of Canaan, and thereafter Israel lived in Egypt until the law was given on Mount Sinai,” and so forth.

Finally, he concludes:

“What God therefore said to Abraham—‘Know for certain that your offspring will be an alien in a land not their own, and they will enslave them and harm them for four hundred years’—must not be understood as though the people of God endured that harsh slavery for four hundred years. Rather, since it is written, ‘In Isaac shall your offspring be called,’ the years from Isaac’s birth to the year of the departure from Egypt amount to 405.

“When, therefore, you subtract from the 430 years the twenty-five years between the promise and Isaac’s birth, it is not surprising that Scripture wished to call the total of 405 years four hundred, since Scripture customarily designates periods in such a way that what slightly exceeds or falls short of a complete number is not counted.

“Accordingly, the words ‘They will enslave them and harm them’ are not to be referred to the four hundred years, as though they had held them in slavery for that entire period. Rather, the four hundred years belong to the words, ‘Your offspring will be an alien in a land not their own.’ The intervening words, ‘They will enslave them and harm them,’ should be understood as inserted in such a way that they do not belong to the four hundred years. For it was only toward the end of this whole period—that is, after Joseph’s death—that the people of God came to endure harsh slavery in Egypt.”

Thus far St. Augustine.

In his words the following should first be observed: he says that Exodus contains, according to the translation of the Septuagint, the statement that the dwelling, or sojourning and pilgrimage, of the children of Israel in Egypt and Canaan lasted 430 years. Venerable Bede likewise teaches, from the truth of the Hebrew text, that this reading must be followed, in his book *On the Six Ages of the World*; and all chronographers, both Greek and Latin, have followed it.

Accordingly, in accordance with this interpretation, the passage of Exodus must be understood as referring to the dwelling of the children of Israel in Egypt and Canaan, whereas in the Vulgate edition it says only: “The dwelling of the children of Israel in Egypt,” and so forth (Exodus 12). For it is certain that the children of Israel did not dwell in Egypt for 400 years, but for much less, as will become clear below.

Therefore, when Genesis 15 says that Abraham’s offspring would be aliens for 400 years in a land not their own, the land not their own must be understood to include not only the land of Egypt but also the land of Canaan, in which Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob lived as aliens until Jacob’s descent into Egypt. Both periods of alien residence are included within that span of 400 years.

Second, four periods must be distinguished here.

The first extends from the promise made to Abraham until the departure from Egypt and the giving of the law to Moses on Mount Sinai. According to the Apostle’s statement in Galatians, this period lasted 430 years.

The second is the period of pilgrimage, or sojourning, during which Abraham’s offspring lived partly in the land of Canaan and partly in Egypt. It must be reckoned from the birth of Isaac, who was the first offspring of Abraham given according to the promise. Since Isaac was born when his father was one hundred years old, this period lasted 405 years—that is, with the twenty-five years from Abraham’s seventy-fifth year to his hundredth year deducted.

This is the period meant in Genesis 15 and Acts 7, where Abraham’s offspring are said to serve for 400 years. Scripture names only 400 years because of its customary manner of reckoning periods and things by stating merely the cardinal number, even when something remains over or falls short. For just as, in law, the praetor does not concern himself with trifles, so it is not surprising that Scripture, naming the great and complete number of 400 years, did not trouble to express the small excess of five years.

The third is the period of the pilgrimage or dwelling of the children of Israel in the land of Egypt. It began with Jacob’s descent into Egypt and lasted only 215 years, according to Josephus, Eusebius, Augustine, and others.

This follows from the Apostle’s words in Galatians 3. If the law was given 430 years after the promise made to Abraham, at the time when he was seventy-five years old, as Genesis 12 records, and if 215 years elapsed from that time until Jacob entered Egypt—namely, twenty-five years until Isaac’s birth (Genesis 21), sixty years from Isaac’s birth until Jacob’s birth (Genesis 25), and 130 years from Jacob’s birth until his entry into Egypt (Genesis 47)—then only 215 years remained until the law was given. These, together with the equal number already mentioned, make the 430 years of which the Apostle speaks.

The fourth is the period of the Hebrews’ slavery and affliction in Egypt. It began shortly after the death of Joseph and his brothers, as Exodus 1 says, and lasted approximately 120 years.

For from the 215 years during which the Hebrews dwelt in Egypt, one must subtract the seventy-one years Joseph lived after his father’s arrival in Egypt—for during all that time they were not enslaved but rather ruled in Egypt, as St. Augustine says above—and one must also subtract the twenty-two years by which Levi outlived his brother Joseph. These amounts total ninety-three years. Subtracting them from the 215 years leaves only 122 years to be assigned to the Jews’ slavery and affliction.

Pererius explains these matters at greater length.

From this material, then, the text of our Author must be explained when he says: If the entire period from the time when God spoke—that is, the period preceding the words “Know for certain that your offspring will be an alien,” and so forth—is considered, it amounts to more than four hundred years, because 430 years are reckoned from that time until the departure from Egypt and the end of Egyptian slavery. But if only the period during which they served is considered, it is less, and certainly much less, as the foregoing shows.

Thus either a part is understood from the whole or the whole from a part; that is, either the whole is put for a part or a part for the whole, namely, by synecdoche, which is frequent and familiar in sacred Scripture. A part is understood as standing for the whole if the number is more than four hundred; the whole is put for a part if it is fewer. The former is the case if the entire period from God’s speaking to Abraham until the giving of the law is considered; the latter if only the period during which the Hebrews served in Egypt is considered. But enough on this subject.]

—God predicts that Israel will serve the Egyptians for four hundred years, saying to Abraham: “Know for certain [Col. 0189A] that your offspring will be an alien in a land not their own, and they will subject them to slavery and afflict them for four hundred years” (Genesis 15). If the entire period from the time when God spoke is considered, it is more than four hundred; but if only the period during which they served is considered, it is less.

Unless that period is understood through this trope, the word of God might seem to have lied—which is far from Christian understanding. But since, [Col. 0192A]

[Note: [Col. 0192A] That is, the promise made to Abraham concerning the blessing of the nations in his offspring, who is Christ (Galatians 3). The Apostle calls this promise the covenant confirmed by God. Jerome says here: “If anyone carefully compares the Hebrew books and the other editions with the translation of the Septuagint, he will find that where ‘covenant’ is written, the term does not mean ‘testament’ but ‘pact,’ which in Hebrew is called *berit*.” And further, explaining the Apostle’s meaning: “The simple sense woven into this passage has the force of teaching that the Apostle says the promises previously made to Abraham cannot be destroyed by the law subsequently given, nor can later things prejudice earlier ones. The promises were given to Abraham 430 years beforehand, namely, that all nations would be blessed in him; but the observance of the law—according to which the one who performed it would live by it—was given to Moses on Mount Sinai after 430 years.” Thus Jerome.]

the entire period from the time of the divine utterance contains more than four hundred years, while the period of slavery contains considerably fewer, it follows that either a part may be understood from the whole or a whole from a part.

A similar meaning is sometimes found with days and nights. When one day is understood as including both periods, the whole time is indicated through one portion of it. In this way the difficulty that seems obscure concerning the time of the Lord’s Passion is also clarified.
