[Note: [Col. 0193B] In what sense the Son of Man, that is, Christ, is said to have been for three days and three nights in the heart of the earth—that is, either in the tomb or rather in the underworld [Col. 0193C] (hence the article of faith concerning Christ’s descent into hell)—since he was buried on Friday and rose on Sunday, which was called the first day of the week, is explained in different ways by the Fathers.

Isidore of Pelusium, Letter 114 of Book I, gives several explanations, two of them especially important, in these words: “At the sixth hour of the Preparation the Lord was led to the cross. From that hour until the ninth darkness prevailed. Understand this as night. Again, from the ninth hour there was light. Count this again as day. Then again the night of the Preparation, followed by the day of the Sabbath, the night of the Sabbath, and the dawn of the Lord’s Day, in accordance with the Evangelist who says, ‘In the evening of the Sabbath, as the first day of the week was dawning.’

“If you ask me for a third explanation, it is as follows: On the day of the Preparation the Lord gave up his spirit. That is one day. He spent the whole Sabbath in the tomb, and afterward its night. At dawn on Sunday he rose from the tomb; that too is a day. For, as you know, the whole is understood from a part.

“Indeed, when we celebrate the memory of those who die, if someone exchanges life for death at any hour of the day, we observe his third day only on the following day, with the intervening day having passed.” This is Isidore’s account.

But Sts. Jerome and Augustine reject that earlier interpretation with equal care and in agreement. Jerome writes as follows in his commentary on Jonah 2:

“The Lord explains the mystery of this passage in the Gospel (Matthew 12), and it is superfluous to say either the same thing or something else. We ask only this: When did he spend three days and three nights in the heart of the earth?

“Some divide the *paraskeuē* (παρασκευή), when, as the sun withdrew, night followed day from the sixth hour to the ninth, into two days and nights; then, adding the Sabbath, they calculate three days and three nights. But we understand the whole from a part *synecdocheally*—that is, we understand the whole from a part—so that, because he died on the *paraskeuē*, we count one day and its night, and another night, that of the Sabbath; but we assign the third night, which belongs to the Lord’s Day, to the beginning of the following day. For in Genesis, too, the night does not belong to the preceding day but to the following one: it is the beginning of the future, not the end of the past.

“To make this intelligible, I shall put it more simply. Suppose someone left one lodging at the ninth hour and arrived at another lodging at the third hour of the following day. If I say that he made the journey quickly, I would not immediately be accused of lying, because the traveler did not spend all the hours of both days on the journey, but only a portion of them.”

And in his Commentary on Matthew 12 he says:

“We have discussed this passage more fully in the commentaries on the prophet Jonah; we therefore refer the reader’s diligence to that work. For now we are content briefly to say that, by synecdoche, the whole is understood from a part—not that the Lord remained in the underworld for all three days and three nights, but that three days and as many nights are understood in the portions of the Preparation, the Lord’s Day, and the whole day of the Sabbath.” Thus Jerome.

Augustine, *Harmony of the Gospels*, Book III, chapter 24, says:

“It is the customary manner of speaking in divine Scripture to signify the whole by a part. For even the three-day period during which the Lord died and rose again cannot be properly understood except by this manner of speaking, in which the whole is customarily expressed by a part.

“Thus the Lord’s saying is given its full meaning. He said to them: ‘As Jonah was in the belly of the sea-monster for three days and three nights, so the Son of Man will be in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights.’

“Some, however, being ignorant of this manner of speech in Scripture, wished to count as a night the three hours from the sixth to the ninth during which the sun was darkened, and as a day the other three hours during which light was restored to the earth, namely, from the ninth hour until sunset. Then follows the night of the coming Sabbath, which, counted together with its day, makes two nights and two days. After the Sabbath follows the night of the first day of the week—that is, the night preceding the dawning Lord’s Day—during which the Lord rose.

“There will therefore be two nights and two days and one night, even if the whole could be understood, without our showing that the dawn was its final part. Consequently, even when those six hours are counted—three during which the sun was darkened and three during which it shone again—the reckoning of three days and three nights will not be complete.

“We must therefore employ that most customary manner of speaking in Scripture by which the whole is understood from a part. We take the final day, the day of the Preparation on which the Lord was crucified and buried, from its final portion, and from that final portion we understand the whole day together with its night, which had already elapsed. The middle day, the Sabbath, is not taken from a part but in its entirety. The third day is again taken from its first part, namely, from the night, and is understood together with its daytime. Thus there will be three days, just as there were eight days after which he ascended the mountain: Matthew and Mark, attending to the complete middle days, say ‘after six days’ (Matthew 17; Mark 9), while Luke says ‘after eight days’ (Luke 9).”

Thus far Augustine in that passage.

Elsewhere, in Book IV of *On the Trinity*, chapter 6, he explains the same matter somewhat more clearly:

“Scripture itself bears witness that the three-day period was not whole and complete. The first day was counted in its entirety from its final portion; the third day likewise in its entirety from its first portion; but the day between them, the second day, was wholly complete, with its twenty-four hours, twelve of night and twelve of day. For the night up to the dawn at which the Lord’s resurrection was revealed belongs to the third day.

“Just as the first days, because of humanity’s future fall, are reckoned from light to darkness, so these days, because of humanity’s restoration, are reckoned from darkness to light.”

Thus far the holy Fathers on the three-day period of the Lord’s death and burial.]

For when, under the example of the prophet Jonah, the Lord foretold that the Son of Man would be in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights (Matthew 12), and when, after the sixth day of the week, on which he was crucified, he was in the underworld for only one day and two nights, how is the truth of the divine utterance preserved?

It is preserved through the trope synecdoche: the night preceding the day on which he was crucified is assigned to that day, and the day following the night on which he rose is assigned to that night. Thus, when the preceding night is added to its day and the day following is added to its night, no part of the complete period is lacking; the whole is fulfilled through its parts.

Scripture abounds in examples of these arguments, but it would be tedious to recall them all. Thus the Psalm says:

[Note: [Col. 0195B] Two examples of synecdoche concerning human beings: the first, in which a part is put for the whole, namely, one individual human being for the entire human race; the second, in which the whole is put for a part, namely, the people for a portion of the people. The Author gives no example from other things belonging to the second category stated above, since such examples are extremely frequent and everywhere apparent, especially the use of “flesh” or “soul” for the whole human being (Genesis 46; Romans 3 and 13; and John 1).]

“What is man, that you are mindful of him?” (Psalm 8)

The whole is understood from a part, since by naming one human being the fullness of the human race is indicated.

Likewise, in the passage [Col. 0195B]

[Note: [Col. 0195B] Ahab was the seventh king of Israel—that is, of the ten tribes. He married Jezebel, the daughter of the king of the Sidonians, and, driven mad by her, introduced the idols of the nations, built a shrine in Samaria, dedicated an altar to Baal, and consecrated a sacred grove to the idols. Finally, he was the first to introduce new superstitions. Hence the familiar statement in Scripture: “He sinned and caused Israel to sin” (3 Kings 14 and 16). This does not mean that the entire Israelite people sinned after his example and abandoned the worship of the true God, but rather the greater part, as the Author indicates here. For in Elijah’s time the Lord had left seven thousand men in Israel whose knees had not bowed before Baal (4 Kings 19). In this example, therefore, a portion is designated by the whole: the whole is put for a part.]

where Ahab sinned, the people are said to have sinned. By naming the whole, a portion is designated from the whole.

[Note: [Col. 0195C] Here he now shows how that synecdochical manner of speech, examples of which he previously brought forward from Scripture, also applies in discourse about Christ. What belongs to Christ according to his divine nature is attributed to the man when, with Christ being indicated, we say that this man is the Son of God, eternal, omnipotent, and so forth. Conversely, whatever belongs to that man according to his proper nature is also attributed to God when we say that the same Christ is the Son of Man, born of the Virgin, subject to suffering, and dead. For this reason the same Christ is truly said to be both before John and after John.]

John, the Lord’s forerunner, likewise says: “After me comes a man who was made before me, because he was before me” (John 1).

How, then, does he indicate that the one who is to come after him existed before him? If this is understood of the man who was born later, how did he exist before John? If it is understood of the Word, how was he a man?

[Note: [Col. 0196B] “Who came after me.” Some explain this as referring to Christ’s coming into the world through his birth, as though he were said to have come after John because he was born six months after him. So Epiphanius, *Against Heresies*, 69; Ambrose, *On the Faith*, Book III, chapter 5; Gregory, Homily 7 on the Gospels. Cassianus also seems to suggest this interpretation here when he says, “of the man who was born later.” But the participle *erchomenos* (ἐρχόμενος), “who comes,” though a present-tense form used for the future, “who is to come,” does not seem to permit this meaning. Christ had already been born when John said these words, yet John speaks of the future, just as Matthew 17 says of Elijah, “Elijah has come,” meaning “he is to come,” as our translator also renders it.

It is therefore better understood as referring to Christ’s preaching and manifestation, as Chrysostom and Euthymius explain. Christ is said to have come after John because, after John, he manifested himself to the world through preaching and miracles.

By the words “He was made before me,” the Fathers teach that Christ is not said to have been produced before John, but to have been preferred and placed before him, as though John had said: “He who comes after me is greater than I,” or, as Matthew has it: “He who comes after me is mightier than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry” (Matthew 3). This is gathered from the text. For it says: “He was made before me, because he was before me”—that is, he preceded me in dignity, because he preceded...
eternity, for he himself is eternal, whereas I am temporal. Thus Augustine, in Tractate 4 on John: “He was made before me,” he says, “because he was placed above me. He was before me, because ‘in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.’”] came after me? [Col. 0196A] Except that in the one Lord Jesus Christ both the later appearance of the man and the antiquity of the Word are demonstrated. And so it comes about that one and the same Lord existed before him and came after him, because in the flesh he is later than John, but according to his divinity he is prior to all. And therefore, by naming only the man (vir), he indicated both the human being (homo) and the Word; for since the Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, was made complete both by humanity and by the Word, by saying one thing about him he indicated all things. And why say more? As I think, my day would fail me if I attempted to gather together or explain everything that can be said about this. And what we have now said is sufficient, at least for this part of the discussion, both for the exposition of the Creed, for the requirements of the case, and for the scope of the book.

# BOOK SEVEN

## Chapter One. He invokes the help of the divine majesty in answer to the calumnies of his adversaries, so that he may teach that prayer ought to precede those who approach disputation with heretics.

What commonly happens to those who, having already escaped the open sea, fear either the sandbanks stretched across the harbor entrances or the rocks near the shores happens to me in a remarkable way: having reserved certain calumnies of the heretics for the end, when I have already reached the limit of the labor undertaken, I begin to fear that very end which I had desired to reach.

But, as the Prophet says, “The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what man can do to me” (Psalm 117). Let us therefore not fear the snares of the heretics who lie in wait, nor the paths everywhere bristling with enclosing thorns. Since these roughen the roads more than they close them, our concern should be rather with cleansing than with fear of whether the journey is possible. For when, as we proceed along the right path, they weakly oppose themselves to us, and tremble more at those walking in the Lord’s way than they hinder them,[^c0029-1] [Note: That is, they are shaken with horror and fear; with *ambulantibus* (“as we walk”) an ablative absolute.] our task and duty have more to do with purification than with fear of the difficulty.

Therefore, stretching out our hand toward that monstrous head of the deadly serpent, and desiring to handle all the tightly knotted limbs of its twisting body, we pray to you again and again, Lord Jesus, whom we have always besought: “Grant us speech in the opening of our mouth” (Ephesians 6), for the destruction of strongholds, “destroying arguments and every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and taking every thought captive in obedience to you” (2 Corinthians 10). For truly free is the one who has begun to be your captive.

Come, then, to your work through your ministry, to those striving for you beyond the measure of their strength.[^c0029-2] [Note: *Officio* seems superfluous unless it is understood as the benefit or efficacy of grace, so that it is ablative: “by your efficacy.” Donatus considers *officium* to derive from *efficiendo*, “bringing about,” because it is what each person ought to do according to his station. Hence Ambrose, *On Duties* I: “We think *officium* is named from *efficiendo*, as though *efficium*; but, for elegance of speech, with one letter changed, it is called *officium*.” Perhaps, however, “to your efficacy and work” would be better, with the conjunction supplied. The author appears to refer to his earlier words, “Our task and work have more …,” where he joins *officium* with *opus*; but what there he called his own, here he acknowledges as God’s gift and ascribes to God.] Grant us to crush the gaping jaws and swollen necks of the new serpent, filled with deadly poisons; you who make the feet of believers pass unharmed over serpents and scorpions, and walk upon the asp and basilisk, trampling down the lion and the dragon (Luke 10; Psalm 90).

Grant also, through the fearless boldness of steadfast innocence,[^c0029-3] [Note: Thus Tertullian, *Against Marcion* IV, though in another rendering: “The Creator also promised this power through Isaiah even to little children: to put their hand into the asp’s cavern and into the lair of the asp’s young, and not to be harmed at all. And indeed we know—without prejudice to the plain sense of Scripture, for even the beasts themselves will be unable to harm where faith is—that spiritual wickedness is figuratively signified by scorpions and serpents; their prince himself is designated by the name of serpent, dragon, and every most eminent beast,” etc.] “that the infant may delight himself at the hole of the asp, and that the weaned child may put his hand into the den of the basilisk” (Isaiah 11). Grant us, then, to put innocent hands into the dens of this most savage and wicked basilisk.

And if, in certain holes—that is, in the hiding places of the human mind—this serpent has already made its dwelling, or has had its lair, or has laid its eggs, or has left behind a path marked by its scaly trail, remove from all people the filthy and deadly contagion of this most pernicious snake. Draw out the impurities of faithlessness that have been introduced, and cleanse souls occupied by foul-smelling mire with the winnowing fan of sacred purification,[^c0029-4] [Note: He also alludes to Malachi 3, where the Messiah is said to be “like a refiner’s fire and like fullers’ soap; he shall sit refining and cleansing silver, and shall purify the sons of Levi and strain them like gold and silver.” And Luke 3: “Whose winnowing fan is in his hand, and he shall cleanse his threshing-floor and gather the wheat into his barn,” etc.] so that dens of thieves may become houses of prayer.

And in those places where, as it is written, the haunts of the hedgehog and the onocentaur, the hairy creatures, and monsters of various prodigies now dwell (Isaiah 34), may the gifts of your Holy Spirit—that is, the ornaments of faith and religion—shine forth.[^c0029-5] [Note: This concerns Isaiah 34, where Jerusalem and Judaea are said to be occupied by the pelican and hedgehog, ibis and raven, and to become a den of dragons and ostriches; demons will meet onocentaurs, the hairy one will call to the other, and there Lilith will rest and find repose; there the hedgehog will have its hole and rear its young, etc. Jerome, in Isaiah 21, Ezekiel 16 and 18, Hosea 12, and elsewhere, says: “Those who follow the tropological interpretation maintain that, after the Jewish people have been driven out, idolaters—such as heretics also are, since heresy too is a form of idolatry, according to the same author—and those serving diverse superstitions will dwell in Jerusalem under the names of beasts and portents. These are the pelicans and hedgehogs, ibis and raven, dragons and ostriches, onocentaurs, demons, hairy ones, and Lilith, called *lilith* in Hebrew and translated ‘Lamia’ only by Symmachus; some Hebrews suppose her to be *Erinys* (ἐρύννη), that is, a Fury.” Thus Jerome. The author therefore compares Nestorius and like heretics to such monsters and portents, as Jerome likewise, using the same allusion, wrote most elegantly against Vigilantius, a heresiarch who had arisen like a new monster in Gaul: “Many monsters have been generated in the world. In Isaiah we read of centaurs and sirens, owls and pelicans. Job describes Leviathan and Behemoth in mystical speech. Poets’ fables tell of Cerberus and the Stymphalian birds, the Erymanthian boar, the Nemean lion, the Chimaera, and the many-headed Hydra. Virgil describes Cacus; Spain has handed down the three-formed Geryon; Gaul alone had no monsters, but always abounded in men most brave and eloquent. Suddenly Vigilantius has arisen—or rather Dormitantius—who, with an unclean spirit, fights against the Spirit of Christ,” etc. Thus Jerome, portraying in the one Vigilantius all heresiarchs and likening them to monsters. Other Fathers compare them with foul and savage beasts: Ignatius, in his letter to the Smyrnaeans, with rabid dogs, serpents, basilisks, and scaly dragons; blessed Cyprian (*Letter* 52) with wolves and dogs, as Scripture also confirms; Ambrose (*Sermon* 43) with owls and foxes; Jerome, again, in Habakkuk 2, with beetles; Vincent of Lérins, in the *Commonitorium*, with frogs and dying flies; Augustine with bedbugs, which bite while alive but stink when dead (*On Psalm* 80).]

And just as, once the worship of idols had been expelled and the images destroyed, you made temples of virtues out of the shrines of demons, inserting rays of shining light into the dens of serpents and scorpions and transforming the dwellings of error and disgrace into houses of ornament and beauty, so pour the light of your mercy and truth into all whose eyes have been darkened by the blindness of heretical perversity. Thus, when at last they behold with unveiled and pure light the great and saving mystery of your Incarnation, may they understand that you, born into the world from that most holy and immaculate womb of the Virgin, are truly man, while recognizing that you have nevertheless always been true God.

## Chapter Two. He dissolves the objection drawn from the words, “No one gives birth to one older than himself.”

Before I begin to speak about matters that I have not yet touched upon in the earlier books, I think it right to strive to discharge what I previously promised. Once my pledge has been completely fulfilled, I shall begin more freely to speak about what remains untouched, since I shall have satisfied what I promised.

Thus, hissing in the Church of God like a new serpent, he says this in order to destroy faith in the sacred birth:[^c0029-6] [Note: We have dealt several times in the preceding books with this axiom of Nestorius.] “No one gives birth to one older than himself.”

First, then, I think that you do not know not only what you are saying, but also from where you are saying it. If you knew or understood the basis of your statement, you would never judge the birth of the only-begotten God by the reasoning of a mortal little opinion. Nor would you attempt to prejudice the one born outside the conception of human origin by human definitions. Nor would you bring earthly impossibilities against divine omnipotence, if you had known that nothing is impossible for God.

“No one,” you say, “gives birth to one older than himself.” Tell me, I ask, concerning what kinds of things you are speaking, and concerning the natures of what living creatures you think you are laying down a definition. Do you suppose that you are imposing a law upon human beings or wild animals, birds or cattle? These are the things—and others of this sort—about which such statements can be made.

For none of these can bring forth one older than itself, because things that have already arisen cannot return again to the condition from which they came in order to be generated by a new creation. Therefore no one gives birth to one older than himself, since no one can generate one older than himself; for the cause of giving birth arises only from the possibility of generation.

Do you therefore apply to the birth of almighty God what you think must be observed in the origin of earthly animals? Do you impose the nature of human limitation upon the one who himself is the author of nature?

You see, then, as I said above, that you do not know the basis or subject of your statement, since you compare created things with their Creator and use, in assessing God’s omnipotence, examples of things that themselves would not exist unless they had from God the very fact that they are what they are.

God therefore came as he willed, when he willed, and from whatever source he willed. Neither time, nor person, nor human custom, nor the examples of created things prejudiced him, because the law of creatures could not resist the one who himself is the Creator of all. And it was easy for him to accomplish what he willed, because power was present with his will.

Do you wish to know, to some extent, how great God’s omnipotence is? I believe that God can even do with his creatures what you do not believe he could have done with himself. All living creatures that give birth to things later than themselves could, if God should command it, give birth to things much older than themselves. For food and drink themselves, if such were the will of the divine power, could be changed into conceptions and offspring. Even the waters themselves, which flowed from the beginning of creation and which all living creatures use so extensively, could, if God commanded it, be embodied and generated within the womb.[^c0029-7] [Note: It would indeed be a great miracle, if what is nowhere recorded as having occurred did occur: that one animal should newly generate and produce another animal which had existed earlier—which, in Nestorius’s terms, would be to give birth to one older than itself. Yet this would not be impossible for God, nor as wonderful and supernatural as the mystery of the Incarnation. God can restore the same body numerically, even after its death and dissolution into its first elements, as we certainly believe concerning the resurrection of human beings. He can raise up children of Abraham from stones, and produce a human being or any animal from water, food, or drink; thus food and drink themselves would be changed into conceptions and offspring. Even without miracle they are naturally changed into the substance of the nourished person and into seminal matter, from which offspring arise. In this respect a human being or any animal may in some fashion seem to generate and give birth to one older than itself, since what existed first emerges in another substance. By the same reasoning waters, which existed before humankind and are therefore older than humankind, can be embodied—that is, formed into an animate body—in a human body. But how water or a human being can then be said to give birth to one older than itself, as the author seems to indicate, I certainly do not see, unless “waters” is taken as the whole species created before humankind; the same may be said of food and drink. It is sufficiently clear that these examples do not press the point very strongly and were offered by Cassian only to illustrate the matter somewhat and incidentally to show that divine power can make what is later give birth to what is earlier, contrary to Nestorius’s axiom. It is therefore not impossible for God that Mary should have borne the Son of God, older than herself, as the angel attests: “No word shall be impossible with God” (Luke 1); and as the Savior himself says: “Father, all things are possible to you” (Mark 14)—that is, things possible absolutely, those not involving a contradiction, as Thomas Aquinas explains (*Summa Theologiae* I, question 25, article 3), after Augustine, *City of God* V.10.]

Who, then, could set a limit to sacred works or restrict divine providence? Or who, as it is written, says to him, “What have you done?” (Isaiah 45)? If you deny that God can do all things, deny also that the one older than Mary could have been born from Mary, with God himself being born. But if nothing is impossible for God, why do you impose impossibility upon him in his own coming, when you acknowledge that nothing is impossible for him in all things?

## Chapter Three. He answers the words, “The birth must be of the same substance as the one giving birth.”

Your second statement is either a blasphemous calumny arising from perversity, or a calumnious blasphemy, when you say:[^c0029-8] [Note: This is Nestorius’s other axiom, treated in the preceding book, chapter 13; there *parenti* (“to the parent”) was approved rather than *parienti* (“to the one giving birth”).] “The birth must be *homoousios* with the one giving birth.” It is not unlike the preceding statement; it differs more in words than in substance or kind.

Since the discussion concerns the birth of God, you are saying the same thing: that a being more powerful than Mary could not have been born from her, just as earlier you said that one older than her could not have been generated. Therefore either consider what was said above as an answer to this statement also (see Book VI, chapter 13), or consider what is now to be said as an answer to the former statement as well.

You say, then, “The birth must be *homoousios* with the one giving birth.” If this refers to earthly creations, it happens very often in that way. But if it refers to the origin of God, why do you consider examples from created nature in his birth? For constitutions are subject to the one who constitutes them, not the one who constitutes them to constitutions.

Do you wish to know more fully how not only impious but also foolish are these calumnies of yours, this monotonous refrain that shows complete blindness to the omnipotence of God? Tell me, I ask you, since you think that only like things are born from like things: from where did that once innumerable multitude of quails suddenly arise in the wilderness as food for the Israelite people (Numbers 11)? For we do not read that they had previously been produced by their mothers in some place, but that they were brought in by a sudden arrival.[^c0029-9] [Note: It would indeed be a great miracle if an animal newly generated and produced another animal which had existed earlier; nevertheless it would not be impossible for God. Concerning the divinely sent multitude of quails, Numbers says: “A wind went forth from the Lord, swept quails over from the sea, and dropped them around the camp, a day’s journey on every side of the camp, flying two cubits high above the earth. The people rose up all that day and night and the following day and gathered quails; he who gathered least gathered ten *cors*” (Numbers 11). A *cor* contains thirty bushels according to Jerome, *On Ezekiel* 4. Thus one may estimate how immeasurable that multitude was, since even the person gathering least filled ten *cors*. Psalm 77 compares that immense abundance to the dust of the earth and the sand of the sea, which cannot be counted: “He rained flesh upon them like dust, and winged birds like the sand of the sea; they fell in the midst of their camp, around their tents. They ate and were exceedingly filled.” God gave the Hebrews meat twice: once with manna, Exodus 16, “In the evening quails came up and covered the camp; in the morning dew lay around the camp”; and again meat alone, Numbers 11. Manna with meat was given before water was brought from the rock, but meat alone after that bringing forth of water. Pliny, *Natural History* X.23, records many noteworthy facts about quails and their characteristics.]

What of the manna, which was called by that name from the astonishment of the Israelite people? Seeing the earth covered with that new food, they exclaimed, “Man hu!”—which means, “What is this?” The Seventy translators therefore, passing over the name itself, gave only the interpretation of the name: “What is this?” (*Τί ἐστι τοῦτο;*). Flavius Josephus followed them in Book III of the *Jewish Antiquities*, chapter 1: “The Hebrews,” he says, “call this food manna. For *man*, in our vernacular speech, is an interrogative particle asking, ‘What is this?’” Thus he speaks.

Manna is called food or heavenly bread because it rained down from the lower heaven; and the bread of angels because it came about through the work and ministry of angels. Concerning it Sedulius sang beautifully and suitably to this passage in Book II:

> What shall I say of the countless throngs  
> Who took angelic food in heavenly bread,  
> And, nourished by the sweetness of the upper air,  
> By showers of heavenly nectar,  
> Had banquets in the rain and food in the downpour?

When Christ says in John 6, “Moses did not give you bread from heaven,” this must be understood of the ethereal heaven, which is properly called heaven. That is properly said to be from heaven which descends from heaven itself, as Christ, the true bread, descended from heaven and therefore was truly heavenly bread.

But that manna had rained down not from heaven, but from the air; it was improperly called bread from heaven, just as the birds are called “birds of heaven,” either because the air itself is called heaven by *catachresis*, or because something falling from high in the air seems to fall from heaven. So Chrysostom and Augustine explain it in their writings on John (Chrysostom, Homily 44; Augustine, Tractate 25).

Did that heavenly food, then, which flowed down into the camps of the Hebrews for forty years, generate manna from manna (Exodus 16)?

But these are ancient miracles of creation. What of newer ones?[^c0029-10] [Note: This miracle was also discussed in the preceding book, Book VI, chapter 1. Sedulius compares it with those ancient miracles and thus illustrates the Gospel narrative:

> When, like the typological Moses and the true Prophet, he saw the people following him into the wilderness feel their ancient hunger, he displayed the ancient help by greater deeds. Then Moses gave rich flesh by many birds; now Christ increased it by two little fish. Then sufficient manna rained down; now, with five loaves, he gave abundant food to five thousand men. The remaining crowd is hidden, nor is it bounded by any number—the vast company of little children and of mothers. And, that you may marvel the more, the leftovers filled twelve baskets: the fragments increased while the people ate, and from every table there returned an abundance not set out at all.

And below, of the other similar miracle:

> With a few little fish and seven loaves he fed an enormous throng of men, and besides the weaker sex and age, satisfied four thousand who ate there. Marvel further and learn that the provisions were increased: the crowd nourished the meal by eating, and the food worn away by bites increased.] 

The Lord Jesus Christ fed innumerable crowds of people following him in the wilderness more than once with a few loaves and fish (Matthew 14 and 15). The explanation of their satisfaction did not lie in the food, since an invisible and hidden cause satisfied the hungry—especially since far more remained over after they were satisfied than had been set out for their hunger.

How, then, did the whole thing happen, so that as those who ate received satisfaction, the food itself also grew rich through ineffable increase?

The Church hymn says this elegantly:[^c0029-11]

> A new kind of power:  
> The waters blush with wine,  
> And the water, commanded to pour forth wine,  
> Changed its nature.

Nor can I pass over Sedulius’s elegant verses on this subject (*Carmen*, Book III):

> The Lord, deeming himself worthy to be present  
> At the first wedding, gave signs of his power.  
> Present as a guest, he came to feed,  
> Not to be fed—a wonder—and changed  
> The poured-out waters into wine.  
> The liquid rejoiced to lay aside its pallor;  
> The wounded water changed its taste,  
> Giving forth unmixed wine,  
> And sweet cups, though no new wine had been born,  
> Blushed across every table.  
> Thus Christ filled six jars with this nectar:  
> For he was a fruitful vine,  
> Making all things bear fruit by his power,  
> Beneath whose gentle shelter  
> The mild vine nourishes grapes that do not die—  
> That is, immortal or everlasting grapes.

We read that wine was made from water at Cana in Galilee (John 2). Tell me: how did a nature unlike its own produce a substance different from its own quality? Especially since what most closely corresponds to the Lord’s birth is that the origin of a much nobler thing proceeded from something inferior.

Tell me, then, how from the simplicity of that water there arose the excellent and marvelous flavor of wine. How was one thing drawn and another poured in? Did that cistern or well possess the nature of changing water taken from it into the finest wines? Or did the quality of the vessels accomplish this, or the skill of the servants? Certainly none of these things did.

And how can the process of what happened not be grasped by the mind, when the truth of what happened is nevertheless preserved with the firm conviction of conscience?

Clay was placed over the eyes of the man born blind in the Gospel (John 9), and when it had been washed away, his eyes were born anew.[^c0029-12] [Note: Most interpreters hold that Christ put clay upon the eyes of the man born blind in order that the power and greatness of the miracle might appear more clearly. Had he cured him by something less opposed to sight (John 9), it might have seemed that he had healed by some natural and hidden medicinal power rather than by divine power (Maldonado, *Commentary*). But because he healed with clay, than which nothing is more contrary to the eyes, it could not be believed that the cure had been accomplished by a natural power of clay rather than Christ’s divine power. For this reason God is accustomed to use the most contrary things in working miracles. Nothing makes water more bitter and undrinkable than salt—who could drink seawater? Yet Elisha, putting salt into bitter waters, made them sweet and drinkable (4 Kings 2). What is more contrary to drawing iron from water than wood, which itself must be drawn out by another thing? Yet Elisha, throwing wood into the river, made the axe-head that had fallen into it float (4 Kings 6). Thus Jerome, on Isaiah 38, where Hezekiah is commanded to apply a mass of figs to his sores: “The Hebrews say that the word *sehin*, omitted by the Septuagint, means an ulcer, not a wound. Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion also render it *helkos* (ἔλκος), by which they wish a royal disease to be understood; anything sweet, whether eaten or applied to the body, is thought contrary to it. Therefore health was restored through harmful and adverse things, that God’s power might be shown.” Thus Jerome.] Did the water possess the nature of producing eyes, or the clay the nature of creating light? Certainly neither, especially since water contributes nothing to a blind man, while clay can even harm those who see.

How, then, did a thing possessing the power to cause harm perform the function of a remedy and salvation? How did that which ordinarily harms the healthy then serve as an agent of health?

You therefore say that God bestowed this power, that God provided the medicine, and that all the things we have mentioned were accomplished entirely by divine omnipotence. God is indeed powerful enough to create new things from what is unusual, to establish remedies from opposites, and to transform what lies among impossibilities and non-productive causes into possibilities and effective results.

## Chapter Four. God, in his temporal birth, displayed his omnipotence just as in all other things.

Acknowledge, then, the same concerning the Lord’s origin as concerning all things. Believe that God was born as he willed, since you do not deny that he could do what he willed—unless perhaps you think that the power which was present for all other things was lacking to him in his own case, and that in his own birth he lacked the omnipotence which, proceeding from him, penetrated the universe.

You object to me concerning the Lord’s birth, “No one gives birth to one older than himself”; and concerning the birth in which almighty God was born, you say, “The birth must be *homoousios* with the one giving birth,” as though you were dealing with an ordinary human being and could impose upon him his own impossibility, enclosing him within earthly weakness.

You say that the condition of being born is common to all, and that the law of generation is the same; that it could not happen to one person alone within the entire human race, when God had forbidden it from happening to all.

You do not understand of whom you are speaking, nor do you see about whom your words are spoken. For he is the author of every condition and the law of all natures: through him exists whatever man can do and whatever he cannot do. He himself has established the limit of both things completely—how far ability may advance and where weakness must go no farther.

How foolishly, then, do you impose human impossibility upon the one to whom possibility itself is owed?

If you assess the Lord’s person by earthly weaknesses and measure God’s omnipotence by human reasoning, you will certainly find nothing that seems compatible with God according to the bodily sufferings of Christ himself.

For if it can seem probable that Mary was unable to give birth to God, who was older than she, how will it be probable that God was crucified by human beings? Yet the same one who was crucified, God himself, foretold this: “If a man will crucify his God, because you crucify me” (Malachi 5).[^c0029-13] [Note: See this saying explained above, Book II, chapter 3.]

If the Lord born of a Virgin is not to be believed because he was older than the one who gave birth to him, how is God believed to have had blood? Yet it is said to the presbyters of Ephesus: “Tend the Church of God, which he acquired with his own blood” (Acts 20).

Finally, how can the author of life be considered deprived of life? Yet Peter says, “You killed the Author of life” (Acts 3).

No one situated on earth can be in heaven. How, then, does the Lord himself say, “The Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3)?

Finally, if you do not believe that God was born of a Virgin because “the birth must be *homoousios* with the one giving birth,” how will you believe that dissimilar things have been brought forth from dissimilar natures?

According to you, then, neither did the wind suddenly bring in the quails, nor did the manna fall, nor did wine come forth from water, nor were many thousands of people fed with a small amount of food, nor did sight appear in the blind man after the clay.

But if all these things seem incredible and contrary to reason unless they are believed to have been done by God, why do you deny in his birth what you confess in his works? Or was he unable to grant to his own origin and coming what he did not refuse to human remedies and needs?

## Chapter Five. From arguments drawn from nature itself, he shows that the adversaries’ rule—that the birth must be *homoousios* with the one giving birth—fails in many cases.

It would be lengthy, and almost fabulous, to say more on this subject. Nevertheless, to refute your folly and madness—in claiming that a birth must be *homoousios* with the one who gives birth, that is, that nothing can give birth to anything unlike itself—I shall also produce examples from earthly things, by which I shall prove that many things are born from unlike things. I do not do this because any comparison can or ought to be made in such a matter, but so that you may not doubt that, in the sacred birth, it could exist which you see also occurring in these earthly and transitory things.

> **[Note: Col. 0205B]** It will be useful here to gather a few encomia concerning bees, their skill, and their industry, both from sacred and from other authors. First of all, two notable passages of Scripture should be observed. The first is from Proverbs, chapter VI: “Go to the bee, and learn how industrious she is; and learn also the work which she performs, worthy of honor; whose labors kings and ordinary people use for the restoration of health. She is desirable to all and illustrious, although weak in strength; honoring wisdom, she has been raised up” (Prov. VI according to the Septuagint). Although this passage is found neither in the Hebrew text nor in the Vulgate edition, the Fathers nevertheless cite it as a saying of Scripture, just as they do the other passage concerning the ant found in the same place in Scripture.
>
> Among others, Saint Basil, in Homily 8 on the *Hexaemeron*, after listing several properties of bees, says: “Let Christians hear this, for whom it has been ordained by law never to repay evil to anyone with evil, but to overcome and conquer evil with good. Imitate the characteristic ways of the bee, which, harming absolutely no one and destroying no one else’s fruits, builds and joins together its own honeycombs. For it openly gathers wax from the flowers; but honey—the moisture resembling dew, scattered over the flowers—which it has tasted and drawn in with its mouth, it places in the hollow recesses of the honeycombs.” And further: “The bee has been proclaimed by the author of Proverbs with beautiful and becoming praise, being called a wise and industrious worker, so diligently and carefully gathering its food. ‘Its labors,’ he says, ‘are consumed both by kings and by private persons for the preservation of health.’ So wisely, so exactly, and with such marvelous skill it constructs and shapes its honey-stores,” and so forth.
>
> Likewise Saint Ambrose, book V of the *Hexaemeron*, chapter 21: “The Scriptures rightly praise the bee as a good worker, saying: ‘Go to the bee, and see how industrious she is. She performs work that is worthy of honor; kings and common people take her labor for their health. For she is desirable to all and illustrious.’ Do you hear what the prophet says? He sends you to follow the example of that little bee and imitate her work. You see how laborious and how pleasing she is. Her fruit is desired and sought by all, and it is not distinguished according to the differences of persons; rather, by her impartial graciousness she sweetens kings and ordinary people alike with equal sweetness. She is useful not only for pleasure but also for health: she sweetens the throat, heals wounds, and pours medicine even into inward ulcers. Thus, although the bee is weak in strength, she is powerful in the vigor of wisdom and virtue.”
>
> At the beginning of the same chapter Ambrose also says: “This is the use of the commonwealth: that laws be common to all and observed through common devotion; that all be bound by one bond; that one person should not have the right to do what another understands he may not do; but that what is permitted should be permitted to all, and what is not permitted should be permitted to none. There should also be a common reverence for the fathers, by whose counsel the commonwealth is governed; a common dwelling-place in the city; a common duty of social life; one rule prescribed for all; and one counsel for all. These are great things. But how much greater are those found among bees! They alone, among all kinds of living creatures, have offspring common to all; all inhabit one dwelling; all are enclosed within the boundary of one homeland; labor, food, work, use and fruit, and flight are common to all,” and so forth.
>
> Saint Ambrose says these and many other things, citing the foregoing saying not only from Solomon’s Proverbs but also explaining it excellently and in detail. Saint Jerome, on chapter III of Ezekiel, says: “In Proverbs it is also said of the bee—although the Hebrew copies do not contain this: ‘Go to the bee, and learn how she is industrious and makes her work chaste, whose labors kings and unlearned people use for their health.’” And in Letter 4 to Rusticus the monk, referring to the same saying: “Build beehives, to which Solomon’s Proverbs send you, and learn the order of monasteries and royal discipline from these small bodies.”
>
> The Church also seems to allude to the same passage when, in the blessing of the paschal candle, it solemnly praises the little bee in these words: “Receive, holy Father, the evening sacrifice of this incense, which the Church offers to you through the hands of her ministers in this solemn offering of the candle, from the works of bees.” Later, after the candle has been lit, it adds: “Although it is divided into parts, it knows no loss of the light it has borrowed. For it is nourished by the liquefying waxes which the mother bee has produced as the substance of this precious lamp.” Finally, the same subject is intended by what is sung in the office of Blessed Cecilia: “The virgin Cecilia served the Lord like a resourceful bee.”
>
> The other passage is Ecclesiasticus XI: “The bee is small among flying creatures, and the beginning of sweetness is its fruit.” Here the translator rendered the word as “beginning” instead of “primacy,” because the Greek word ἀρχή means both. For honey has primacy among liquids in sweetness. Hence sacred Scripture is accustomed to express the highest sweetness by the name of honey: “Sweeter than honey and the honeycomb” (Psalm XVIII); “How sweet are your words to my palate, more than honey to my mouth!” (Psalm CXVIII); “My spirit is sweeter than honey, and my inheritance sweeter than honey and the honeycomb” (Ecclesiasticus XXIV); “In your mouth it will be sweet as honey” (Revelation X). Finally, it places honey above all things, however sweet, when it says in Judges XIV: “What is sweeter than honey?” More concerning the sweetness and usefulness of honey may be found in Basil and Ambrose at the passages cited above.

Bees, although very small, are exceedingly prudent and skillful animals; they are born from entirely different elements and emerge from different natures. Since they are creatures of marvelous intelligence, abounding not only in sensation but also in prudence, they are produced from selected flowers of certain plants. What greater example do you think should be offered or adopted?

> **[Note: Col. 0206D]** Although another reading, perhaps more probable, may have been written in the margin, this reading too should not be despised or rejected. It is supported both by the Basel and Plantin editions and likewise by the truth. For bees truly are generated from atoms—that is, from the very small and delicate juices or tufts of flowers. An atom is an indivisible little body, which cannot be divided or cut any further. Hence Lucretius said that atoms are smaller than those little bodies which we see floating through the rays of the sun entering through a window; and Epicurus believed that the world was made from its atoms, that is, indivisible little bodies, as Aristotle reports in his book *On Coming-to-be*. Nevertheless, the other reading, as I have said, appears more probable and more genuine, because it is more suited to the Author’s purpose and expresses more directly the matter under discussion.

Animals are born from atoms [Lipsius in the margin: “animals from inanimate things, living things from insensible things”]. Who is the craftsman there, who is the maker, who is the shaper of bodies, who is the giver of souls? Who, finally, gave them the very sound by which they speak, as it were, with one another? Who fashioned and arranged these harmonies of their feet, the art of their mouths [Lipsius in the margin: “of their intellects”], and the elegance of their wings [Lipsius in the margin: “feathers”]?

> **[Note: Col. 0207B]** Whoever wishes to have these matters handed down and explained at greater length should read Aristotle, book III of *On the Generation of Animals*, chapter 10, and book IX of *The History of Animals*, chapter 40; Varro, book III of *On Agriculture*, chapter 16; Pliny, book XI, chapter 5 and the following chapters; and finally Virgil, book IV of the *Georgics*, where he describes the nature and properties of bees with the greatest elegance.
>
> I shall nevertheless add a few things from the Fathers, not only useful but also pleasant. Gregory Nazianzen, in Oration 43, says: “Now the industrious bees, with wings unfurled and their hives abandoned, offer a lesson in their wisdom and fly together to the meadows, plundering the flowers. Some work at their cells, hexagonal and set opposite one another, weaving tubes together and alternating straight ones with angular ones, no less for the elegance of the work than for security. Others store honey in their granaries and bring forth for their guest a sweet and uncultivated fruit. Would that we too, who are Christ’s apiary and have received such an example partly of wisdom and partly of industry and labor, might do likewise!” Nicetas also has a beautiful and extensive discussion of the same subject.
>
> Saint Ephrem, in a certain ascetical sermon on the religious life, addresses a monk as follows: “Imitate the bee, dearest one, and contemplate its wonderful mystery: how it gathers its work from the various flowers scattered over the earth. Consider great skill in this small and insignificant creature. For if all the wise men of the earth and all the philosophers of the world were gathered together, they could never explain its wisdom,” and so forth.
>
> Saint Ambrose, at the passage cited above, says: “The work itself is pleasant: its first foundations are laid from flowers and sweet herbs. For what else is the honeycomb but a kind of camp? What camp could possess as much art and grace as the latticework of the honeycombs, in which small and round cells support one another by their interlocking? What architect taught them to arrange those hexagonal cells with their sides equally and continuously joined, to suspend delicate wax between the partitions of the chambers, to pack in the honey, and to fill granaries woven from flowers with a kind of nectar? You may see them all competing in their duties: some keeping watch while searching for food; others anxiously providing guard for the camp; others investigating future rains and observing the courses of the clouds; others shaping wax from flowers; others gathering in their mouths the dew poured over the flowers. Yet none lies in wait for another’s labors or seeks life by robbery. Would that they did not have to fear the plots of robbers! Nevertheless, they have their own stings, and if provoked they pour poison among the honey and lay down their lives in the wound, burning with the heat of vengeance.” Thus far Ambrose, in many phrases borrowed from Virgil. See the rest in the same author. Saint Chrysostom has similar remarks in Homily 15 on chapter IV of the Epistle to the Ephesians; I omit them for fear of excessive length.

Who gave them their intelligence, anger, foresight, movement, gentleness, concord, disagreement, wars, peace, order, arrangement, duties, authorities—in short, all the things that they possess as though in common with the human race? By whose instruction, or by whose gift, through whom did they receive and learn these things? Did they acquire them from paternal seed? Or did they learn them in the generative womb and in the mother’s flesh?

> **[Note: Col. 0207D]** Aristotle, book V of *On Animals* (chapter XXI), says that it is not established how bees reproduce, some denying that they mate and claiming that they bring their offspring from elsewhere. Pliny likewise writes about the generation of bees with uncertainty (book XI, chapter 19): “How they produce offspring was a great and subtle question among learned men. For the mating of bees has never been seen.” Many thought that they must be produced from flowers collected and suitably prepared. Others thought they were produced through the mating of the one called the king in each swarm. Thus far Pliny.
>
> Others, however, take it as certain that bees produce and are produced without mating, and therefore remain virgins; this Cassianus here affirms as a known and common fact. Thus Virgil says in book IV of the *Georgics*:
>
> “You will marvel that this custom has pleased the bees:
>
> > They neither give themselves to mating, nor sluggishly
> > Unloose their bodies for love, nor bring forth offspring in travail;
> > Rather, they themselves gather their offspring from leaves
> > And sweet herbs with their mouths; they themselves provide
> > Their king and their little citizens, and restore
> > Their halls and waxen realms.”
>
> Saint Ambrose, clearly imitating Virgil, says: “Generation is common to all; bodily virginity is common to all, and childbirth also, since they do not mingle in any mating. They are not loosened by lust, nor are their births shaken by pains; suddenly they send forth a vast swarm of offspring, gathering their progeny with their mouths from leaves and herbs” (at the passage cited above).
>
> Rufinus of Aquileia, in his *Exposition of the Apostles’ Creed*, using similar examples and arguments from nature with Cassianus, proves that it is not incredible that a virgin gave birth: “For what seems astonishing,” he says, “if a virgin conceived, when it is established that the bird of the East, which they call the phoenix, is born or reborn without a mate to such a degree that it is always one and the same and always succeeds itself through birth or rebirth? It is plain to all that bees know nothing of marriage and do not produce offspring through labor pains. Yet several other creatures are also found to be born in this manner. Will this, then, seem incredible if it was accomplished by divine power for the renewal of the whole world, when examples of it are also seen in the birth of animals?” Thus Rufinus, appropriately applying the point to this passage.
>
> Saint Augustine, book XV of *The City of God*, chapter 27, speaking of small animals, says: “There are some creatures which are born from various things without mating, and afterward mate and produce offspring, such as flies; but there are others in which there is neither male nor female, such as bees.”
>
> Peter Damian, cardinal and bishop of Ostia, Letter 18 of book II of his *Letters*: “As bees are free from mating, so they are in no way corrupted in childbirth; and just as in conception one sex is not mingled with another, so in producing offspring virgin integrity is not violated. For they do not produce offspring from a womb but, so to speak, from their mouth, and remain wholly undefiled and intact from every taint of corruption. For with their mouths they gather their children from leaves, and thus send forth a swarm of successive posterity.” Thus he.
>
> Moreover, it is commonly said that bees are also born from the flesh and dung of cattle. Hence Virgil, at the end of book IV of the *Georgics*, invents a certain shepherd named Aristaeus, who restored his lost bees after slaughtering several pairs of oxen. And Pliny says: “There are those who think that bees, when entirely lost, can be restored from the bellies of fresh cattle buried with dung; Virgil says from the dead body of young oxen.” More concerning bees may be found in Thomas of Cantimpré, in his *Apiarium*.

They know neither womb nor seed. Only flowers, having been eaten, are gathered into the hives; from them bees emerge through a work beyond estimation. The entrails of mothers contribute nothing there to their offspring; nor are bees born from bees. They are workers only, not procreators. Living creatures come forth from little flowers of plants. What resemblance is there between plants and living creatures? Therefore, I believe you understand who the maker of these things is. Go now and doubt whether the Lord could grant to his own birth what you see him grant even to the smallest of his works. Perhaps after this it would be superfluous to add anything else; nevertheless, let even things unnecessary to the example be added to the accumulation.

> **[Note: Col. 0208D]** The locust is a sufficiently familiar little animal of the insect kind, generally flying low and by leaps; hence it also has its French name *sauterelle*. In Africa and greater Syria they are born larger in body and with stronger wings, and in such abundance that they either eat away or scorch by their touch all the grasses and crops. They are even said to fly across the seas and, after consuming everything domestic, to seek foreign pastures—not without an evil omen for those whom they reach.
>
> The Greeks call them ἀκρίδες (*akrides*), either because they feed upon the summits of crops and trees or, as Isidore wishes (*Etymologies*, book XII, final chapter), because they have long legs, as though furnished with spears; hence they are also called “spearbearers.”
>
> Saint Basil, Homily 5 on the *Hexaemeron*: “How shall I describe to you the terrifying campaigns and armies of locusts, which, as though formed into battle order, rise all together into the air under one standard, laying out their camps across the whole countryside, and do not consume the fruit until it has been permitted and commanded to them by God,” and so forth.
>
> Saint Ambrose, book V of the *Hexaemeron*, chapter 23: “Divine grace has penetrated even to the locust, which, after occupying the breadth of a region in a formed swarm, is said first to approach a harmless dwelling and not to consume its fruit by an unwelcome invasion unless it has received a sign of divine command. For, as we read in Exodus (Exodus X), it too carries out the vengeance of heavenly offense, a pious minister of punishment. A bird also devours it, the *seleucis*—for this is the Greek name of the bird—given as a remedy for the evils that the locust customarily inflicts. The Creator gave it an insatiable appetite for devouring, so that by its voracious feeding it might extinguish the plague mentioned above.” Thus Ambrose.
>
> That passage of Exodus is chapter X, where the eighth plague of Egypt, the plague of locusts, is listed in these words: “Moses stretched out his staff over the land of Egypt, and the Lord brought a scorching wind throughout that entire day and night. When morning came, the scorching wind lifted the locusts, which rose over the whole land of Egypt and settled in all the territories of the Egyptians, countless, such as had not existed before that time and would never exist afterward. They covered the entire surface of the earth, devastating everything,” and so forth.
>
> Saint Jerome, on chapter II of Joel: “Even in our own times,” he says, “we saw swarms of locusts cover the land of Judea. Afterwards, when the priests and peoples entreated the Lord and said, ‘Spare your people,’ between the vestibule and the altar—that is, between the place of the cross and the place of the resurrection—they were driven by a rising wind into the first and the last sea. When the shores of both seas were filled with heaps of dead locusts vomited forth by the waters, their rotting and stench were so harmful that they even corrupted the air, and a pestilence arose among both beasts and human beings.”
>
> Finally, Augustine, book III of *The City of God*, chapter 31: “They have recorded in writing that the multitude of locusts in Africa was like a prodigy, when the province was already subject to the Roman people. For after the fruits and leaves of the trees had been consumed, they say that the locusts were cast into the sea in an enormous and immeasurable cloud. When they died and were returned to the shores, and the air was corrupted by them, they say that so great a pestilence arose that in the kingdom of Massinissa alone eight hundred thousand people are reported to have perished, and many more in the neighboring lands and along the neighboring shores.” Thus Augustine.
>
> Livy, book IX; Orosius, book V, chapter 11; and Eutropius, book V, also report this disaster inflicted by locusts.

We see the air suddenly covered with locusts and the lands filled with them.

> **[Note: Col. 0209D]** Aristotle reports this in book V of *The History of Animals*, chapter 19, and in book VI of *The Generation of Animals*, chapter 16, where he says this concerning insects: “Insects are produced either from animals of the same kind, as spiders and spiderlings from spiders and spiderlings, or as caterpillars, locusts, and cicadas.” In the same book, chapter 17, he discusses locusts and their offspring at greater length.
>
> Pliny also reports it in book XI, chapter 29, discussing locusts: “They lay their eggs in the earth, lowering the stalk of their spine and depositing their eggs in a compact mass, at the time of autumn,” and so forth. Later he says: “The mating of locusts, as of all insects that mate, consists in the female carrying the male.” Thus Pliny.
>
> But the subject here is not ordinary and natural generation, but extraordinary—and, if not supernatural and miraculous, certainly prodigious—generation of locusts, such as was undoubtedly that of the Egyptian locusts, and such as was the other instance mentioned by Saint Jerome, as well as other examples of the same kind. Their seeds, origins, and mothers—who can report them, who can reveal and make them known in these creatures? How can one show that in them birth is *homoousios* with the one who gives birth? This is what the Author intended.

Reveal their seeds; reveal their origins; reveal their mothers. For, as you see, they emerge from the place from which they are born. Impose upon all these things the rule that their birth must be *homoousios* with the one who gives birth. By such prescriptions you will find yourself as ridiculous as you are now mad in denying the Lord’s birth.

And what follows? Do you yourself think that we ought to proceed any further? Nevertheless, we shall add something more:

> **[Note: Col. 0210B]** Something similar is read in Isaiah LIX, to which the Author seems to have looked: “They have broken the eggs of asps and woven spiders’ webs. Whoever eats from their eggs will die, and what has been warmed will break forth as a basilisk.” Saint Jerome translates the words both from the Hebrew and from the Greek as “the eggs of asps,” as do the other translators, together with the Chaldean paraphrast.
>
> In what follows he offers various interpretations: “Whoever eats from their eggs”—that is, whoever assents to their counsels, just as Abel assented to Cain when he said, “Let us go into the field,” and was immediately killed; or, as the Septuagint translated it: “Whoever wishes to eat from their eggs, when he breaks one, will find something rotten, and within it a basilisk.” For anyone deceived at first glance who thinks that they are hens’ eggs or the eggs of other birds, whose consumption is harmless, will discover, if he breaks one before eating it, an extremely foul rottenness and stench; and what has been warmed will be found to be a basilisk. Or, according to Symmachus and Theodotion, an asp. Aquila, however, rendered it “viper.” Thus Jerome.
>
> What is said there of the asp and its eggs Cassianus attributes here to the ibis and its eggs. Hence it may be thought—and there is no slight suspicion—that, instead of “the eggs of asps,” he read, or heard from someone else, “the eggs of ibises,” an error very easily arising from the great similarity of the words. Alternatively, it must be said that this same property is naturally present in the ibis as well, or that a basilisk emerges from its eggs when they have been warmed and incubated. Cassianus asserts this so confidently that he appears to have learned it either from the authority of sacred Scripture or from the tested and confirmed testimony and experience of human beings.
>
> The ibis discussed here is a bird peculiar to Egypt, which feeds on serpents. Cicero, book II of *On the Nature of the Gods*, says of it: “Ibises destroy a very great number of serpents. They are tall birds, with hard legs and a long, horny beak. They avert pestilence from Egypt when they kill and consume the flying serpents carried in by the south wind from the desolation of Libya; thus those serpents, while alive, do no harm by their bite, nor, when dead, by their odor.” He says again in the *Tusculan Disputations* (book V): “Who does not know the custom of the Egyptians? Their minds, steeped in errors of depravity, would rather undergo execution than do violence to an ibis, asp, or crocodile.”
>
> Pliny likewise says in book X, chapter 28: “The Egyptians invoke their ibises against the approach of serpents.” And in chapter 30: “The ibis is black only around Pelusium; in all other places it is white,” which is taken from Aristotle (book IX of *Animals*, chapter 27). Finally, Isidore, *Etymologies*, book XII, chapter 7: “The ibis is a bird of the Nile River which cleanses itself by pouring water into its belly with its beak. It feeds on the eggs of serpents, carrying from them very agreeable food to its nests.” These are the facts concerning the ibis and its properties.
>
> The basilisk, however, is a serpent called in Latin *regulus* (“little king”), which kills human beings by its mere appearance. Jerome says of it, on Isaiah XIV: “The *regulus*, which the Greeks call the basilisk, is a creature whose gaze no bird can pass unharmed; even if it is far away, the bird is sucked in by its mouth—that is, killed by its breath.”
>
> In this example of such extraordinary generation, two wonders of nature appear, contrary to the Nestorian axiom: an innocent, poisonless bird, the ibis, produces and gives birth from its own eggs to the most poisonous and harmful basilisk serpent, as is asserted here. The appropriate venom of its food—that is, of the serpents on which it feeds—flows into its seed-material, as may be inferred from Cicero’s statement. It is therefore reasonable that a venomous animal should sometimes emerge.
>
> Here the offspring is so far from being *homoousios* with the one who gives birth, as Nestorius maintained, that it differs from her entirely in kind. For who does not know that flying creatures belong to one genus and reptiles to another?
>
> A similar saying is also read in Isaiah XIV concerning the root—that is, the seed, as the Septuagint translated it—or, which amounts to the same thing, concerning the egg of a serpent: “From the serpent’s root will come forth a basilisk, and its seed will swallow the flying creature.” If this is understood according to the proper meaning of the words and the truth of nature, it likewise supplies an example of generation across different kinds. For the serpent and the basilisk are undoubtedly of different substance and differ in species.
>
> Nevertheless, no attentive reader fails to notice that these examples have little or nothing to do with the matter, and were rather brought forward against Nestorius as a reply to him. Since he used his axiom to prove that Christ is not the Son of God and therefore that Mary should be called *Christ-bearer*, not *God-bearer*, because a human being cannot be *homoousios* with God, nor God with a human being, Cassianus opposed examples of this sort to show that unlike kinds and unlike substances are also generated from unlike kinds and unlike substances. His foundation was therefore false, and nothing could be concluded from it.
>
> In reality, no one denies that Christ, as a human being, is *homoousios* with his human mother, just as, as God, he is consubstantial with God the eternal Father, except Arius, Nestorius, and heretics of that sort. Accordingly, Nestorius’s axiom may also be admitted here without danger, as was shown above; yet it suffers exceptions in certain cases, as is clear from the examples produced by Cassianus.

It is certain that basilisk serpents are generated from the eggs of birds which in Egypt are called ibises. What kinship or likeness is there between a bird and a serpent? Why, then, is its birth not *homoousios* with the one who gives birth? Yet none of these creatures brings about or understands either the generation or the birth; rather, they come to be through hidden causes and through a certain inexplicable and manifold law of the nature that generates them.

And you bring against his birth the little prescriptions of earthly opinions, although you cannot even give an account of the births of those creatures which come into being at the nod and command of the one whose will governs everything and whose command accomplishes everything; against whom nothing could prevail or resist, and for whom willing was sufficient for everything that could be accomplished.

## CHAPTER VI. He refutes another argument of Nestorius, by which Nestorius attempted to make Christ equal to Adam in every respect.

But at last it is time to expose your other, still more hidden and more treacherous blasphemies, since—contrary to what we would have preferred—we can no longer remain ignorant of them, at least lest they capture others through their ignorance.

> **[Note: Col. 0211C]** It is uncertain which work is meant. Nestorius published many treatises and books of this kind, filled with blasphemies. Concerning them Gennadius of Marseille writes as follows (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 53, or in the *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*):
>
> “Nestorius—also called Nestor—the arch-heretic, when he was a presbyter in the Church of Antioch and was regarded as an outstanding preacher and extemporaneous speaker, composed countless treatises on various forms of exposition. In them, even then, he subtly and wickedly infused the poisons of the impiety that later appeared, which he sometimes concealed beneath moral exhortation. After his eloquence and abstinence had commended him and he had been appointed bishop of the Church of Constantinople, he revealed himself openly as the enemy of the Church whom he had long concealed. He wrote a book on the Lord’s Incarnation constructed from sixty-two testimonies of divine Scripture according to his perverse interpretation; what he asserted in it is shown in the catalogue of heretics.”
>
> Thus Gennadius. But which “catalogue of heretics” he means here I do not see, unless it is the one he himself identifies and lists among his works at the end of his book *On Illustrious Men*, where he says: “I, Gennadius, a presbyter of Marseille, wrote eight books against all heresies, six books against Nestorius, and three against Pelagius,” and so forth. Some judge, however, that these words are not Gennadius’s but were added by someone else (Possevinus, in the *Apparatus*). Nor does this catalogue now seem to exist.
>
> Baronius, discussing such writings of Nestorius and their pernicious dissemination in his *Annals* (year 420), says: “After Nestorius had proclaimed his heresy at Constantinople, wishing to spread it throughout the whole world over wider spaces, he devoted all the strength at his disposal to accomplishing this. For he considered it insufficient to have proclaimed the new heresy in that chief city alone. To spread it more widely, he sent his writings to various people, including the monks of Egypt. In order to deceive them, he pretended that he was nothing other than a confessor of the faith of Nicaea and fraudulently represented in his letters that he taught nothing except what had been prescribed by the Council of Nicaea. As a result, some of the Egyptian monks agreed with his error. Cyril himself bears witness to all this (Letter 1).”
>
> Nestorius did not merely distribute letters to various people; he also gave books defending the same heresy to them. He sent these books, through Antiochus, an illustrious man, to Pope Celestine, as Celestine himself, who received them, testifies (Letter 5). What they were like is shown by what was later revealed in a vision to a most holy anchorite concerning those same books of Nestorius. We shall here set forth the account from Sophronius, who describes the event as it occurred (*Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 66):
>
> “We approached Abbot Cyriacus, a presbyter of the Laura of Caelamon near the holy Jordan, and he told us the following: ‘One day I saw in a dream a woman of dignified appearance, dressed in purple, and with her two men, likewise of venerable bearing and splendid appearance. I supposed that the woman was our Lady, the holy Mother of God, and that the two men with her were Saint John the Baptist and Saint John the Theologian and Evangelist.
>
> “‘I went out of my cell and asked her to enter, but she did not come near. I therefore continued for a long time praying and entreating her, saying: “May the humble man who has become ashamed not, I beg you, be turned away,” and many other things of this sort. When she saw me persisting in prayer and repeating the same request, she answered me more sternly: “You have my enemy inside your cell, and you want me to enter?” After saying this, she departed.
>
> “‘When I awoke, I began to be distressed, and I wondered whether I had committed some sin against her; for there was no one else in my cell except me. After examining myself for a long time, I found nothing by which I had sinned against her. When I saw myself overwhelmed by excessive sorrow, I rose and took a book to read, so that by reading I might drive away my grief and thoughts. I had borrowed the book from the blessed Esychius, a presbyter of the Church of Jerusalem.
>
> “‘As I opened the book, I found two books of Nestorius written at the end of the volume, and at once recognized that this was the enemy of our holy Lady, the Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary. Then I rose, went away, and returned the book to the man who had lent it to me, saying: “Take back your book, brother; for I have received from it not as much benefit as harm.”
>
> “‘When he asked me the cause of the harm, I related the entire sequence of events. Inflamed with zeal, he immediately cut those two books of Nestorius out of the volume and consigned them to the fire, saying: “The enemy of our Lady, the holy Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary, shall not remain in my cell.”’”
>
> Such, then, were those books which Nestorius, as we have said, disseminated through various parts of the world. Cyril, the same author mentioned above, separately collected and refuted their blasphemies.

Thus far from Baronius and the authors whom he cites.

You have written in a certain pernicious treatise of yours, saying:

> “Since the human being is the image of the divine nature, and the devil cast this image into corruption, God grieved over it as an emperor grieves over his statue, and he restores the corrupted image. He formed from the Virgin a nature without seed, after the likeness of him who was born without seed, Adam; and through a human being he raises up human nature, since, as death came through a human being, so also the resurrection of the dead came through a human being” (1 Corinthians XV).

It is the custom of certain poisoners, as they say, to mix honey into the cups which they prepare with poisons, so that what is harmful may be concealed by sweetness; and while someone is captivated by the sweetness of honey, he may be destroyed by the plague of poison.

So you too, when you say, “The human being is the image of the divine nature; the devil cast this image into corruption; God grieved over it as an emperor grieves over his statue,”—

> **[Note: Col. 0213C]** Perhaps *oras* should more correctly be read here, in accordance with the following passage of Lucretius, cited by Saint Jerome in his letter to Ctesiphon:
>
> **[Col. 0213D]**
>
> “And just as physicians, when they try to give children
>
> > The bitter wormwood, first smear the rims
> > Around the cup …”

They touch the edges of the cup with the sweet, yellow liquid of honey. With these verses Saint Jerome reproaches Rufinus, who, having employed this device, inserted many Origenists into the book he wrote about the monks. He immediately adds:

“Thus he placed one John at the beginning of that very book—one whom there is no doubt was Catholic and holy—in order that, through the opportunity afforded by him, he might introduce into the Church the other men he had presented as heretics.”

In the same sense Gregory Nazianzen writes (*Book on the Faith*, or *Oration* 49):

“As it is customary to kill with a deadly cup tempered by the sweetness of honey, deceiving through pleasantness, so this evil—heresy—also, contaminating the hearers’ minds by a certain defilement through the allurements of the ears, infects them with a clinging contagion.”

[Col. 0214C]

Theodoret likewise uses the same comparison (*Preface to Book I of the Heretical Fables*):
