“When the devil had chosen men worthy of his operation, he smeared the mouth of the cup, as it were, with honey of some kind, and offered men the deadly poison of falsehood.”

But Vincent of Lérins expresses the point much more explicitly in the *Commonitory* (chapter 35):

“Heretics must be avoided and feared all the more because they lurk more secretly beneath the shadows of divine law. For they know that their foul odors would perhaps quickly please no one if they were exhaled naked and undisguised; [Col. 0214D] and therefore they sprinkle it, as it were, with the fragrance of heavenly eloquence, so that one who would readily reject human error may not readily despise the divine utterances. Thus they do what those do who prepare certain bitter potions for children: they first smear the rims of the cups with honey, so that the unwary age, when it has sensed the sweetness, will not recoil from the bitterness. The same concern is shown by those who disguise harmful grasses and poisonous medicinal juices in advance with the names of remedies, so that scarcely anyone, when he has read the word ‘remedy’ written above them, suspects poison.”

See the same author in the following chapter of the same book, and Irenaeus, Book III *Against Heresies*, chapter 19.

Thus, in a certain manner, you smear the rim of a deadly cup with a certain sweetness and, as it were, with honey, so that men, while drinking the administered cup and tasting what is alluring, may not perceive what is destructive. You put forward the name of God so that you may lie under the name of religion; you place holy things first so that you may persuade of perverse things; and by confessing God you bring it about that you deny the very one whom you confess. For who does not see where you are going and what you are attempting?

You say, then:

“God grieved as over his image, just as an emperor grieves over his statue, and he repairs the corrupted image; and without seed he formed nature from the Virgin, according to that Adam who was born without seed, and through a man he raises up human nature; for since death came through a man, therefore also the resurrection of the dead comes through a man.”

[Col. 0213C]

With such great zeal and such effort, through flattering preliminary speeches, you—the deceitful schemer—acted in this way: after naming God in what preceded, you arrived at man in what followed, and afterward inflicted the insult of a solitary man upon the very one whom, through the service of deceptive humility, you had previously honored with the honor due to God.

You therefore say that the divine mercy repaired the image of God which the devil had cast into corruption: [Col. 0214A]

“For,” you say, “he repairs the corrupted image.”

How subtly you say this—“he repairs the corrupted image”—namely, so that you may persuade us that there was nothing more in the one in whom the image was repaired than there had been in that very image to which the repair was given. Hence you wish the Lord to be nothing other than Adam, and the repairer of the image to be no greater than the fallen image itself.

Finally, what you are doing and attempting you prove by what follows, saying:

“Without seed he formed nature according to that Adam who was born without seed, and through a man he raises up human nature.”

[Col. 0214D]

Another heresy of Nestorius, who attributed nothing more to Christ the Lord than to Adam and made the two equal—although this is included within that primary and principal heresy by which he asserted that Christ was nothing but a pure and solitary man.

You assert that the Lord Jesus was in every respect like and equal to Adam: Adam, certainly, without seed, and Christ without seed; Adam a man alone, and Christ a solitary man.

[Col. 0214B]

And thus you can see that you carefully guarded and provided against the possibility that the Lord Jesus Christ might be thought greater than Adam in any respect, or perhaps better, since you compared them with such equal measures that you would in a certain way have considered yourself to detract something from Adam if you had preferred anything to him.

## CHAPTER VII. Heretics customarily conceal their doctrines beneath the cloak of divine Scripture.

“For since death came through a man, therefore also the resurrection of the dead comes through a man.”

Do you even attempt to prove your perversity and crime by apostolic testimony? And do you dishonor the Vessel of Election through the contagion of your impiety? Apparently, because the author of your salvation is not understood by you, the Apostle must therefore also appear to have denied God. [Col. 0214C]

Yet if you wished to use apostolic testimonies, why, satisfied with one of them, did you suppress all the rest and not immediately add this:

“Paul, an apostle, not from men nor through a man, but through Jesus Christ” (Galatians 1)?

Or this:

“We speak wisdom among the perfect” (1 Corinthians 2);

and afterward:

“Which none of the rulers of this age knew; for if they had known, [Col. 0215A] they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (ibid.)?

Or this:

“For in him dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily” (Colossians 2);

and:

“One Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things” (1 Corinthians 8)?

[Col. 0215C]

Observe in Nestorius the common disposition of heretics and the ancient practice—often noted by the Fathers—of perverting, mutilating, and twisting the Scriptures to their own meanings.

Tertullian writes in *On the Prescription Against Heretics*:

“Heresy does not receive certain Scriptures; and if it receives any, it alters them by additions and omissions according to the arrangement of its own system. And if it receives them, it does not receive them whole; and if it presents them as whole to some extent, nevertheless, having devised different interpretations, it turns them to another meaning” (chapter 17).

Saint Cyprian writes in *On the Unity of the Church*:

“Corruptors of the Gospel and false interpreters place the latter parts first and pass over the earlier ones, remembering one portion and craftily suppressing another. As they themselves have been torn away from the Church, so they tear apart the meaning of a single passage.”

See Pamelius’s note there.

Saint Augustine writes of the Manichaeans, heresy 46:

“They read the Scriptures of the New Testament in such a way that they take from them whatever they wish and reject whatever they do not wish.”

And concerning heresy 70 he writes:

“The Priscillianists are more cunning than the Manichaeans in this respect: they reject none of the canonical Scriptures, but read everything together with the apocryphal books and accept everything as authoritative; nevertheless, by allegorizing, they turn whatever is in the sacred books that opposes their error toward their own meanings.”

Epiphanius discusses this same fraud of heretics at greater length, *Heresy* 42.

Do you accept the Apostle in part while rejecting him in part, receiving him only where, in accordance with the economy, he names Christ a man, but rejecting him where he calls him God? For Paul does not deny that Jesus is a man; nevertheless, he confesses that this same man is God. Thus he proclaims that the resurrection came to the human race through a man, while at the same time confirming that God himself rose in that man.

Consider, then, whether, when he proclaims as God the one who rose, he does not also testify that the one who was crucified is the God of majesty.

## CHAPTER VIII. Heretics attribute to Christ only the image of deity and therefore assert that he is to be honored with God, not as God.

[Col. 0215B]

Nevertheless, lest you should think of the Lord Jesus as merely one of the common people, you granted him something of dignity, assigning him honor as a holy man, but not divinity as man and true God.

For what do you say?

“God formed the Lord’s Incarnation. Let us honor the form of the *theotoci*—that is, of those begotten by God—together with God, as one form of deity, as the inseparable statue of the divine will, as the image of the hidden God.”

[Col. 0215D]

*Theotoci*, that is, “begotten by God,” from θεότοκος (*theótokos*), not θεοτόκος (*theotókos*). We have discussed their difference elsewhere (*On Book V*, chapter 2).

For the impious Nestorius, whose words these are, established two persons in Christ and consequently two sons, one man and the other God. He accordingly called that man *theotoci*, that is, “the form, statue, image, organ,” and similar things, of the Son of God, as is clear from what precedes. Hence he immediately explains it here as “the image of the hidden God.” [Col. 0216C] Although elsewhere he also called the same man *theodocos*, that is, “the recipient and host of God,” he proclaimed for both reasons that the form of the *theotoci* was to be honored and adored together with God.

Therefore it may rightly be questioned whether *theodoci* or rather *theodochi* should be read. For he also attributed to Christ the form and image of the *theodochi*—that is, Christ himself bore and displayed one who was *theodocos*, the recipient and host of God, whose God, as he wished it, was an inhabitant and indweller.

Above, you said that Adam was the image of God; here you call Christ an image: Adam a statue, and Christ a statue. But evidently we must give you thanks for the honor you show to God, since you concede that the form of the *theotoci* is to be honored together with God. In this there is not so much honor as insult.

For even in this you do not grant the Lord Jesus Christ the honor of divinity, but deny it. By the subtle art of impiety, you say that he is to be honored with God, so that you may not confess him to be God; and by the very act through which you appear deceitfully to have joined him, you separate him.

For when you blasphemously say that he is not to be worshiped as God but is to be honored as if he were with God, you assign him a conjunction with divine proximity in order to remove from him the truth of deity. Most impiously and cunningly, enemy of God, you wish to carry out the crime of one who denies under the name of one who confesses.

“Let us honor him,” you say, “as the inseparable statue of the divine will, as the image of the hidden God.”

Evidently, through his benefits, the honor due to the Creator and our Redeemer, the Lord Jesus Christ, has advanced among us. If we were redeemed by him from eternal destruction [Col. 0216B] for the purpose of calling our Redeemer a statue, then we strive to respond with worthy obedience and worthy worship to his kindness and mercy if we also attempt to take away the majesty which he did not refuse to humble for our sake.

[Col. 0216A]

## CHAPTER IX. They are mistaken who said that Christ’s birth was hidden, since he was also manifestly revealed to the patriarch Jacob.

But you excuse, of course, the insult inflicted upon the Lord by the service of the honor offered to him, saying: “as the image of the hidden God.” In calling him an image, you compare him with the human condition. In calling him the image of the hidden God, you detract from his most certain dignity.

[Note: [Col. 0216C] Although this passage is plainly to be understood of Christ’s second coming, namely, for judgment, as the following verses of the same psalm show and the Fathers interpret it, the Author nevertheless refers it to his first coming in the flesh. He says that Christ also came manifestly—not because he was then known and revealed to everyone, but because he could become known through sufficient signs, both from heaven and on earth, and because he did become known to many, gradually becoming more and more renowned. In this same way St. Jerome also seems to interpret the same passage of the Psalmist as referring to Christ’s first coming. He writes in chapter 30 of Isaiah, where he compares other passages of Scripture with it, especially that passage in Luke 12: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and how I wish that it were burning!”—so he himself cites it—which undoubtedly refers to the first coming.

But why Christ’s coming and human birth ought not to have been immediately manifest to everyone, St. Thomas gives three reasons (III, q. 36, art. 1): “It must be said,” he says, “that Christ’s birth ought not to have been commonly manifest to everyone. First, because human redemption, which was accomplished through his cross, would thereby have been impeded; for, as it is said in 1 Corinthians 2: ‘If they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.’ Second, because this would have diminished the merit of faith, through which he had come to justify human beings, according to Romans 3: ‘The righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ.’ For if, at Christ’s birth, his birth had appeared to everyone through manifest indications, the basis of faith would already have been removed, since faith is ‘the evidence of things not seen,’ as Hebrews 11 says. Third, because this would have cast doubt upon the truth of his humanity. Thus Augustine says in his letter to Volusianus: ‘If from infancy to youth he had undergone no changes of age, had taken no food, had accepted no sleep, would he not have confirmed the opinion of error? Would he not have been believed in no way to have assumed true humanity, and, while doing everything miraculously, would he not have taken away what he mercifully accomplished?’]

For, David says, “God will come manifestly, our God, and he will not be silent” (Psalm 49). And indeed he came and was not silent: before he himself had said anything after his birth, he declared his coming through earthly as well as heavenly witnesses—when the star gave its sign, when the Magi worshiped, when the angels announced it. What more do you seek? His voice was still silent on earth, yet his honor was already proclaiming him in heaven. Do you therefore say that God was and is hidden in him? But did not the prophets, the patriarchs, and, finally, the whole Law foretell this? They did not say that he would remain hidden, when they foretold to everyone that he would come.

You err, unhappy blindness, seeking causes for blasphemy and finding none. You say that he remained hidden even after his coming; I affirm that he was not hidden even beforehand, before he came. For did that eminent patriarch, whose name was given by the vision of the God who was present—through which he passed from the name of “supplanter” [Jacob] into the name of Israel—did he not know the mystery of God’s future birth from a virgin?

[Note: [Col. 0217B] Namely, Jacob, who was first called Jacob, that is, “supplanter,” either because at birth he seized the heel of his brother who was being born, or because afterward he overthrew and overcame that same brother by craft, having taken from him his birthright and his father’s blessing. Hence Esau said to his father: “Justly has his name been called Jacob, for he has supplanted me these two times” (Genesis 27).]

[Note: [Col. 0217B] That is, he received the more dignified and holier name of Israel—or, in the Author’s expression, he acquired it after wrestling with the angel (Genesis 32). I find among ancient writers three interpretations of this name, and these deserve some discussion here.

The first and common interpretation is that Israel is explained as “a man seeing God.” Thus Cassian here says of Jacob: “He to whom was given the name ‘vision of the God who is present.’” And in the first Preface to the Conferences, considering the tropological significance of both names, he says: “Whoever has earned the name of that intelligible Jacob through the supplanting of carnal vices, now also, receiving not so much my institutions as those of the Fathers, and passing through the contemplation of divine purity to the attainment—and, so to speak, the dignity—of Israel, should likewise be instructed in what he ought to observe at this summit of perfection.”

So too St. Jerome says in chapter 31 of Jeremiah: “He is Israel who beholds God with the mind.” And on Psalm 113: “We too,” he says, “must first be Jacob, that is, supplanters of vices, so that afterward we may become Israel, that is, souls seeing God and contemplating God with the eyes of the heart, according to the saying: ‘Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God’” (Matthew 5).

Similarly, Augustine says in The City of God, book 16, chapter 40: “Israel is interpreted as ‘seeing God,’ which will be the final reward of all the righteous.” Gregory Nazianzen also suggests the same in these words (Oration 34): “Jacob received a change of name as the reward of his piety; instead of Jacob, he was called by that great and eminent name, Israel.”

But elsewhere St. Jerome approves this interpretation less (Questions on Genesis), and calls it forced, citing the angel’s words to Jacob: “Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but your name shall be Israel, because you have prevailed with God, and with men you shall prevail” (Genesis 32).

Josephus, in the first book of the Antiquities (chapter 27), thinks that Israel was so called because he stood against the Angel; but, after carefully examining the matter, I have been unable to find this at all in the Hebrew. Why should I need to seek the opinions of individuals, when the one who imposed the name himself explains its etymology? “Your name shall not be called Jacob,” he says, “but Israel shall be your name.” Accordingly Aquila interprets it: ὅτι ἤρξας μετὰ Θεοῦ, “because you have ruled with God.” Symmachus: ὅτι ἤρξω ἰσχύϊ πρὸς Θεόν, “because you have prevailed in strength against God.” The Septuagint and Theodotion: ὅτι ἐνίσχυσας μετὰ Θεοῦ, “because you have grown strong with God.”

For *Sarith*, which is derived from the name Israel, signifies “prince.” The meaning, therefore, is this: “Your name shall not be called ‘supplanter,’ that is, Jacob, but your name shall be ‘prince with God,’ that is, Israel.” For just as I am a prince, so also you, who were able to wrestle with me, shall be called a prince. And if you were able to fight with me, who am God—or with an angel, since many interpret the passage differently—how much more will you prevail with human beings, that is, with Esau, whom you need not fear?

But the interpretation found in books of names, according to which Israel means “a man seeing God,” or “a mind seeing God,” has been worn away by nearly everyone’s usage, and seems to me to have been interpreted not so much truly as forcibly. Jerome proves this from the Hebrew letters in which the two expressions—namely, “Israel” and “seeing God”—are written. Then he adds:

“Although they possess great authority and eloquence, and their shadow overwhelms us—those who have translated Israel as ‘a man’ or ‘a mind seeing God’—we are guided more by the authority of Scripture and of the angel, or of God, who himself called him Israel, than by the eloquence of anyone.”

Thus Jerome.

The second etymology of Israel, according to Jerome, is the one gathered from the angel’s words: “Jacob shall no longer be called your name, but Israel; for if you have been strong against God, how much more shall you prevail against men” (Genesis 37?). By these words he plainly declares the etymology of the name he himself imposed, as St. Jerome repeatedly emphasizes.

This interpretation is also supported by Tertullian, book 4 Against Marcion, chapter 39, where he says: “Prevailing with God, which is the interpretation of Israel.” According to this interpretation, then, Israel means “prince with God,” as Jerome wishes; or “prevailing,” “ruling with God,” or “growing strong against God,” as Tertullian has it.

There is, however, a third interpretation related to this, according to which Israel is εὐθύτατος Θεοῦ, that is, “most upright of God,” or “directed by God.” Thus St. Jerome combines the two interpretations in the passage cited: “Israel is interpreted as ‘prince of God,’ or ‘directed by God,’ that is, εὐθύτατος Θεοῦ.” Elsewhere, however, he separates and distinguishes them (on Isaiah 44):

“Properly, according to the Hebrews and the evidence of the letters, Israel is called ‘upright of God’; but ‘a man seeing God’ is found not in the elements of the word but in the sound of the voice.” Hence the book of Genesis is also called εὐθείων, that is, “of the righteous”—Abraham, Isaac, and Israel.

And in chapter 12 of Hosea he says: “Jacob was made upright in strength with the angel, when at the ford Jacob wrestled against the angel throughout the night. And because he was made upright with the angel, he therefore received the name εὐθυτάτου, which in Hebrew is called *iasar*, that is, ‘directing’ or ‘directed.’”

Cassian also seems to have had this etymology in view. In Conference 12, chapter 11, he says: “Whoever, therefore, has passed beyond the degree of that intellectual Jacob, that is, of the supplanter, from that struggle and supplanting of vices, with the sinew of the thigh struck numb, will ascend to the attainment of Israel through perpetual direction of heart.”]

—the very one who, having recognized the mystery of the future Incarnation in the struggle of the man wrestling with him, said:

[Note: [Col. 0218D] The allegorical interpretation of Jacob’s wrestling with the Angel is relevant here. Eusebius of Caesarea writes concerning it in book 1, chapter 2 of his Ecclesiastical History, where he proves that Christ was seen, worshiped, and invoked by the fathers of the Old Testament under human form:

“He”—Christ—“appeared again to Jacob in the form of a man and addressed him thus: ‘Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name, because you have prevailed with God.’ Divine Scripture calls him God. At that time Jacob also called the name of that place ‘vision of God,’ for he spoke as follows: ‘I have seen God face to face, and my soul has been saved’” (Genesis 32).

Eusebius is entirely consistent with this passage. Cyril of Alexandria likewise, in book 9 Against Julian, after recalling the same history of Jacob, adds:

“O great miracle, and power that enables one to understand clearly, with perceptive mind, the mystery of Christ! For while wrestling with a man, he says that he saw God face to face, and calls him the appearance of God. For he truly was God, and is the Word, although he became flesh. That the man wrestling with Jacob was the only-begotten Word of God, who in his proper time was to come in our form, having already shown this beforehand to the holy Fathers, anyone may easily perceive from what Moses wrote. For he says: ‘And the Lord said to Jacob,’ and so forth.”

St. Ambrose likewise, in book 2 On Jacob and the Blessed Life, says:

“Because Jacob’s faith and devotion were unconquerable, the Lord revealed secret mysteries to him, touching the breadth of his thigh, since the Lord Jesus was to arise from his descendants, born of a virgin, neither inferior nor unequal to God. The breadth of the thigh, struck with astonishment, signified his cross, because the remission of sin, diffused throughout the whole world, would be salvific for all, and because, through the amazement of his body and his sweat, he would grant resurrection to the dead. Hence the sun arose, not without reason, upon holy Jacob, for the saving cross of the Lord shone upon his race; and likewise the Sun of righteousness arose for him (Malachi 4), who sees God, because he himself is the eternal light.”

So Ambrose.

St. Augustine, however, somewhat differently, though under the same allegory, teaches in book 16 of The City of God, chapter 39, that not the Son of God or a divine person, but an angel bearing the role and type of Christ, appeared to Jacob in human form and wrestled with him. He writes:

“This name”—Israel—“was imposed upon him by the angel who wrestled with him as he was returning from Mesopotamia, most clearly bearing the type of Christ. For the fact that Jacob prevailed over him, since the angel willed it, signifies, so that the mystery might be represented, the passion of Christ, in which the Jews appeared to prevail against him. Yet Jacob obtained a blessing from the same angel whom he had overcome; and thus the imposition of this name was itself a blessing.”

And elsewhere Augustine says (Sermon 40 on the Words of the Lord according to John):

“When Jacob was returning from Mesopotamia, an angel wrestled with him on the way. What strength can be compared between an angel and a man? Therefore it is a mystery, therefore it is a sacrament, therefore it is prophecy: when the victor was blessed by the vanquished, Christ was being represented.”

Again, elsewhere (Sermon 80 on Time):

“In that wrestling Jacob represented the people of the Jews, while the angel who wrestled with him bore the type of the Lord and Savior. Jacob wrestled with the angel because the Jewish people were going to wrestle with Christ. Jacob overcame the angel because the Jewish people were going to persecute Christ even unto death. And because not the entire Jewish people proved unbelieving toward Christ, but a considerable multitude is recorded to have believed in his name, therefore the angel touched Jacob’s thigh, and he began to limp. The foot with which he limped represented those Jews who did not believe in Christ; but the foot that remained sound bore the type of those who received Christ the Lord,” and so forth.

This is what concerns the allegorical sense of that wrestling, which relates to the mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation. Anyone seeking moral or tropological interpretations should consult Ambrose in the passage cited, Jerome on chapter 6 of the Letter to the Ephesians, Augustine on Psalm 77, Gregory in Homily 14 on Ezekiel, and others who comment upon that passage of Genesis.

That Jacob is here said to have recognized the mystery of the future Incarnation during the wrestling is consistent with Christ’s words in John 8: “Abraham your father rejoiced that he might see my day; he saw it, and was glad.” For what he said of Abraham he could likewise have said of Isaac, Jacob, and the other prophets: namely, that they had “seen”—that is, foreseen and recognized by faith and prophetic revelation—“his day,” meaning his coming in the flesh and the time of his dispensation and dwelling among human beings on earth, as the holy Fathers explain (Irenaeus, book 4, chapters 11 and 12; Hilary, book 15 On the Trinity; Leo, Sermon on the Epiphany; Bernard, Sermon 6 on the Vigil of the Nativity, chapter 28).]

“I have seen God face to face,” he says, “and my soul has been saved” (Genesis 32).

[Note: [Col. 0220A] How Jacob saw God face to face is no small question. Omitting other authorities, it will be sufficient to clarify it from Gregory alone. He writes as follows in book 18 of the Morals, chapter 37, commenting on the words of the book of Job: “Wisdom, which is God, is hidden from the eyes of all the living”:

“If it were hidden from the eyes of all the living, unquestionably none of the saints would have seen it. Yet I hear John agreeing with this statement when he says: ‘No one has ever seen God’ (John 1 and 1 John 5). But when I look again at the fathers of the Old Testament, I recognize that many of them, as the history of sacred reading itself testifies, saw God.

“Jacob saw the Lord, saying: ‘I have seen the Lord face to face, and my soul has been saved’ (Genesis 32). Moses saw God, of whom it is written: ‘The Lord spoke to Moses face to face, as a man is accustomed to speak with his friend’ (Exodus 33). Job likewise saw the Lord, saying: ‘I have heard you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you’ (Job 42). Isaiah saw the Lord, saying: ‘In the year in which King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and lofty throne’ (Isaiah 6). Micaiah saw the Lord, saying: ‘I saw the Lord sitting upon his throne, and all the host of heaven standing beside him on his right and on his left’ (2 Chronicles 18).

“What, then, does it mean that so many fathers of the Old Testament testified that they had seen God, while it is nevertheless said of this Wisdom, which is God, ‘It is hidden from the eyes of all the living,’ and John says, ‘No one has ever seen God,’ unless this is plainly to be understood: as long as one lives here in mortal existence, God can be seen through certain images, but he cannot be seen through the appearance of his very nature. Thus the soul, breathed upon by grace through the Spirit, sees God through certain figures, but does not reach the very power of his essence.

“Hence Jacob, who testifies that he saw God, saw him only in an angel. Hence Moses, who spoke face to face with God, as a man speaks with his friend, says to him in the very course of their conversation: ‘If I have found favor in your sight, show yourself to me plainly, so that I may see you’ (Exodus 33). Certainly, if he was not God with whom Moses was speaking, he would have said, ‘Show me God,’ and not, ‘Show yourself to me.’ But if he was God with whom he spoke face to face, why did he ask to see God whom he already saw?

“From this request of his it is inferred that he thirsted to behold him in the unbounded splendor of his nature, whom he had already begun to see through certain images; so that the heavenly essence might be present to the eyes of his mind, in such a way that no created image, existing in time, would intervene before the vision of eternity.

“Thus the fathers of the Old Testament saw the Lord, and yet, according to the statement of blessed Job, ‘Wisdom, which is God, is hidden from the eyes of all the living,’ because, for those existing in mortal flesh, he could both be seen through certain bounded images and could not be seen through the unbounded light of eternity.”

Thus far St. Gregory.

St. Thomas, summarizing his teaching (Part I, q. 12, art. 11), says:

“It must be said that, according to Dionysius, chapter 4 of the Celestial Hierarchy, Scripture says that someone has seen God insofar as certain figures, either sensible or imaginary, have been formed which represent something divine according to a certain likeness. Therefore, what Jacob says—‘I have seen God face to face’—must be referred not to the divine essence itself, but to the figure in which God was represented.”]

What, I ask, had he seen, that he believed he had seen God? Did God present himself to him amid flashes of lightning and thunder? Or, with heaven opened within, did the face of the divine nature display itself to him in a blaze of light? None of these things occurred. Rather, on the contrary, he saw a man and recognized God.

[Note: [Col. 0221A] *Indepto* is used for *adepto* and should be noted repeatedly in Cassian, in connection with the name Israel, that is, “seeing God.” The meaning is that Jacob, who recognized God with his inner eyes in human form, affirmed that he had seen God and called the name of that place “vision of God.”]

O truly worthy of the name he had acquired—and one who deserved, more through inward than outward eyes, the dignity of the name given by God! He saw a human form wrestling with him, and declared that he saw God. He certainly knew that that human form was the reality of God, because in the form in which God was then seen, he was afterward to come in the reality of that form.

[Col. 0222A] Yet why should we marvel if so great a patriarch believed without hesitation what God himself so clearly showed him, when he himself said: “I have seen God face to face, and my soul has been saved”? What so great a manifestation of the present divinity had God shown him that Jacob would say that the face of God had been shown to him? A man, as it appeared, had merely appeared to him, and he had even overcome him in the contest.

But God was accomplishing this through indications provided beforehand by the events:

[Note: [Col. 0221A] St. Leo also suggests this reason, in his Letter 13 to Pulcheria, for why God appeared to the ancient fathers and patriarchs under human form:

“The omnipotence of the Son of God,” he says, “could have appeared for the instruction and justification of human beings in the same way in which he appeared to the patriarchs and prophets in the appearance of flesh—when he entered into a wrestling match, or engaged in conversation, when he did not refuse the duties of hospitality, or even when he accepted food that had been set before him. But those images were signs of this man, whose reality the mystical indications, drawn from the preceding fathers, announced.

“Moreover, it must be observed that there can be no doubt that God frequently appeared in visible form in the Old Testament, as Scripture most clearly testifies. The question, however, is whether God appeared by himself and personally; whether he himself assumed a body and visible form and displayed himself visibly in it; or whether he arranged for these things to be done through angels. For there are ancient opinions supporting both sides.

“Cassian, in this passage, seems to hold that the Son of God appeared by himself and in his own person both to Jacob and to the other fathers, especially a little earlier, where he says: ‘He knew that that human form was the reality of God,’ and so forth. If it was the reality of God, then it was God, not an angel, who appeared.

“Again, from the very reason he adds—‘so that no one would fail to believe that God had been born from a human being’—it seems to follow that, since God himself and personally was born in the flesh from a virgin, he must likewise have formerly manifested himself in human form by himself.

“In addition to Ambrose, cited above, not a few other distinguished authors support this opinion.

“St. Clement, in book 5 of the Apostolic Constitutions, chapter 21, speaks as follows: ‘Jacob saw this Christ as a man and said: “I have seen God face to face, and my soul has been saved.” Abraham received him as a guest and confessed him to be his judge and his Lord. Moses saw him in the bush. Jesus son of Nun saw him armed, the commander of the Lord’s army, fighting at the same time at Jericho.’

“Origen, in Homily 1 on Isaiah 6: ‘Who is this one of the Seraphim? My Lord Jesus Christ. He was sent according to the dispensation of the flesh, holding a coal in his hand and saying: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth.”’

“Tertullian, in his book Against the Jews, says: ‘The one who spoke to Moses was the Son himself, who was always seen. For no one has ever seen God the Father and lived. Therefore it is established that the Son of God himself spoke to Moses and said to the people: “Behold, I send my angel before your face.”’

“Eusebius of Caesarea adds the following in the passage cited above: ‘It is not even permissible to suspect that those visions representing God—such as those made to Abraham and Jacob—which are recorded in the sacred writings, should be attributed to angels serving God’s will and diligently carrying out his ministries. For whenever one of these angels was seen by human beings, Scripture does not conceal the fact but expressly names him an angel, not God; nor does it assert that the Lord spoke to human beings, as is very easily proved by countless testimonies of Scripture.’

“So much for them.

“On the other side stand other very ancient and holy Fathers.

“Dionysius the Areopagite, whose words these are, says in book 4 of the Celestial Hierarchy:

“‘The Law, as divine Scripture testifies, was bestowed upon us through angels; and those illustrious fathers of ours, both those who lived before the Law and those who lived after the Law, were borne up to God by angels. The angels either admonished them concerning what ought to be done and led them away from sacrilegious error and profane life onto the straight path of truth, or, by teaching them, disclosed sacred institutions, hidden visions of heavenly mysteries, and certain divine predictions.’

“And below he adds:

“‘Those divine appearances occurred to holy men through signs most suitable to God, in certain sacred forms adapted to the manner and capacities of those who beheld them. Through the ministry of heavenly powers, those celebrated fathers of ours learned such divine visions.’

“St. Jerome, commenting on Galatians 3—‘The Law was ordained through angels’—says:

“‘He wishes this to be understood: throughout the whole Old Testament, wherever an angel is first reported to have appeared and afterward is introduced as speaking almost as God, an angel truly appeared, one of the many ministering spirits, whoever he may have been; but in him the Mediator speaks, saying: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” Nor is it surprising that God speaks in angels, since God also speaks through angels who are in human beings, namely, through the prophets, as Zechariah says: “And the angel who spoke in me said”; and thereafter he introduces the words: “Thus says the Lord Almighty.” For the angel who was said to be in the prophet did not dare to speak in his own person: “Thus says the Lord Almighty.”’

“Augustine, in book 9 Against Adimantus, says:

“‘The Son himself, who is the Word of God, not only in the last times, when he deigned to appear in the flesh, but also earlier, from the foundation of the world, announced the Father to whomever he wished, whether by speaking, appearing, through some angelic power, or through any creature; for he himself is the truth in all things, all things subsist in him, and all things serve him and are subject to him at his command, so that he may also appear to the eyes, through a visible creature, to whomever he wishes and whenever he deigns to do so. Yet, according to his divinity and according to what he is as the Word of the Father—coeternal with the Father and unchangeable, through whom all things were made—he is seen only by a heart that has been most purified and made simple.

“‘Therefore in certain passages Scripture itself also testifies that an angel was seen where it says that God was seen, as in the wrestling of Jacob, where the one who appeared was called an angel, and in the bush where he appeared to Moses (Genesis 32), and again in the wilderness, after he had led the people out of the land of Egypt, when God spoke to him as he received the Law (Exodus 3). But whether in the bush, when he sent him, or afterward, when he gave the Law, Stephen says in the Acts of the Apostles that an angel appeared to him.

“‘We say this so that no one may suppose that the Word of God, through whom all things were made, can be confined to places or appear visibly to anyone except through some visible creature. Just as the prophet is the word of God, and it is rightly said, “The Lord said,” because the Word of God, who is Christ, speaks the truth in the prophet, so he also speaks in an angel when the angel announces the truth; and it is rightly said, “God spoke,” and “God appeared.” Likewise it is rightly said, “The angel spoke,” and “the angel appeared,” when the former is said in the person of the one who indwells and the latter in the person of the serving creature.

“‘According to this rule the Apostle also says: “Do you seek proof of Christ speaking in me?” (2 Corinthians 12).’

“The same Augustine, in book 3 of On the Trinity, chapter 11, says:

“‘It is manifest that all the things which appeared to the fathers, when God presented himself to them according to his dispensation suited to the times, were accomplished through a creature.’

“And, answering the objection ‘Why, then, is it written, “The Lord spoke to Moses,” and not rather, “The angel spoke to Moses”?’ he says:

“‘Because when the herald pronounces the words of a judge, it is not written in the records, “The herald said,” but, “The judge said.” So too, when a holy prophet speaks, even if we say, “The prophet said,” we wish nothing other than that the Lord said it to be understood. And if we say, “The Lord said,” we do not remove the prophet, but indicate who spoke through him.’

“Finally, at the end of that book he concludes:

“‘But now, I think, enough has been argued and established according to our capacity, and according to the probability of reason, insofar as a human being—or rather, insofar as I—was able, and according to the firmness of authority, insofar as the divine utterances of Scripture have disclosed it: that, before the Savior’s Incarnation, when God was said to appear to our ancient fathers, those voices and bodily forms were produced through angels, whether the angels themselves spoke or acted in the person of God, or assumed from creation something that was not themselves, by which God was figuratively shown to human beings.’

“Thus far Augustine.

“Finally, Gregory, in book 28 of the Morals, chapter 2, teaches that every speech of God not produced solely by the internal power of inspiration takes place through angels:

“‘It must be known,’ he says, ‘that divine speech is distinguished in two ways. The Lord either speaks through himself, or his words are formed for us through an angelic creature. When he speaks through himself, only the inner power of inspiration is disclosed to us. When he speaks through himself, the heart is taught concerning his word without words and syllables, because his power is recognized through a certain inward elevation,’ and so forth.

“You have, reader, what the ancient Fathers think concerning this disputed matter.”

“From these I conclude, first, that this question is not among those in which one side must be held by faith and the other rejected as contrary to faith; rather, it must be counted among disputed questions, upon which, without prejudice to faith, one may hold either view, since neither side has been defined or condemned by the judgment of the Church. Hence one may say without fear of heresy that God immediately and in himself assumed some bodily form in which he was formerly seen by mortals, as the Fathers cited for the first opinion taught.

“Second, I conclude nevertheless that the opinion of the other Fathers, which teaches that those divine appearances were produced through the work and ministry of angels, is much more probable: both because it rests on stronger arguments and reasons—the chief of which is that suggested by the divine Dionysius (Celestial Hierarchy, chapter 4), namely, that God administers this world and all things in it not by himself alone but through secondary causes, especially through angels—and because it is more commonly received in the schools and approved by the common agreement of theologians; see the Master of the Sentences, book 2, distinction 28, and the Doctors there.

“Third, from the same authorities produced for this opinion it is easy to answer the principal foundation of the first opinion, drawn from Scripture, which records that God appeared to many in the Old Testament. For the Fathers have already answered that such appearances are attributed to God because the appearing angels acted in God’s stead and exercised his authority and commission. See more in Peter Thyraeus, book 1, On Visions and Apparitions, chapter 23.”]

so that no one would fail to believe that God had been born from a human being, since the patriarch had already seen God in human form.

## CHAPTER X. He gathers further testimonies to the same matter.

But why should I linger so long over one example, as though many others were lacking? Could it already then have been possible for human beings not to know that God would come in the flesh, when the prophet openly proclaimed him, as it were, to the whole human race: “Behold your God” (Isaiah 40); and elsewhere, “Behold our God” (Isaiah 25); and: “God, the mighty one, the Father of the age to come, the Prince of peace; and there will be no end of his kingdom” (Isaiah 9)?

But when he had already come, could it have been hidden from those who openly confessed that he had come? Did Peter not know of God’s coming when he said: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16)? Did Martha not know what she was saying, or whom she believed? “Indeed, Lord,” she said, “I have believed that you are the Christ, the Son of the living God, who has come into this world” (John 11).

Finally, all those who sought from him remedies for diseases, restoration of limbs, or life for the dead—were they asking these things from the weakness of a human being or from the omnipotence of God?

## CHAPTER XI. That the devil was impelled by many reasons to suppose that Christ was God.

[Col. 0224A]

Finally, when the devil tested him with every enticement and every art of his wickedness, what was he either suspecting without knowing, or desiring to discover by testing? Or what had moved him so greatly that he sought God in the humility of a human being? Had he learned this from earlier signs? Or whom had he recognized as having come in a human body as God?

Certainly not. Rather, through great indications of signs, through great experiences of events, and through the very voices of truth, he was driven toward suspicion and investigation of this matter. For he had already once heard from John:

[Note: [Col. 0224C] The Greek manuscripts and many Latin copies read in the singular: “the sin of the world.” Theophylact explains the reason as follows: “Why did he not say ‘the sins of the world’? So that, by saying ‘sin,’ he might seem to indicate sin universally, just as we are accustomed to say that a human being was expelled from paradise, meaning the whole human race.” So he.

The Hebrews also often use the singular number, as Lyranus correctly notes, to signify the whole nature of a thing and a great multitude. “A very grievous fly came,” it says (Exodus 8)—that is, a great multitude of flies, or every kind of fly, as it is explained in that same passage.]

“Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sin of the world.” And again from the same man: “I ought to be baptized by you, and you come to me?” (John 1).

Moreover, the dove, descending from heaven and standing above the Lord’s head, had given a clear indication of God’s glory being made manifest [Lipsius in the margin: “a manifest sign of the glory being declared”] (Matthew 3).

The voice also sent by God had moved him—not through riddles or figures—saying: “You are my beloved Son; in you I am well pleased” (Matthew 1).

And therefore, although outwardly he saw a human being in Jesus, …

A very perplexing and ambiguous question is whether, and when, the devil came to know Christ’s divinity and the mystery of the Incarnation. For Scripture contains various passages that seem, at first sight, to contradict one another. For it appears that the devil recognized Christ as the true God even before his passion and resurrection, as can be gathered from Matthew 8, where the demons cried out: “What have we to do with you, Jesus, Son of God? Have you come here to torment us before the time?” And in Mark 1: “What have we to do with you, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are: the Holy One of God.” The Greek has ὁ ἅγιος, with the article added for emphasis, as Euthymius and Theophylact note; by this expression God himself is called holy, as by his proper name. And in Luke 8: “What have I to do with you, Jesus, Son of the Most High God?”

Nor do the demons alone—whom we might readily suppose to have been lying, or to have spoken flatteringly in order to avoid being tormented by Christ—claim to know Christ; the evangelists themselves, who certainly could not have lied while moved by the Holy Spirit, teach that they truly knew him. Mark, in the same chapter, says: “He cast out many demons and did not allow them to speak, because they knew him.” And Luke, chapter 4: “Demons went out from many, crying out and saying, ‘You are the Son of God’; and rebuking them, he did not allow them to speak, because they knew that he was the Christ.”

To this may be added a most certain demonstration by which the demon could have concluded that Christ was God, reasoning as follows: Whatever God confirms by miracles must be true; otherwise he would be a witness to falsehood and deceit. But Christ proved by many miracles that he was truly God and the Son of God. Therefore this must necessarily be true. The demon could not have been unaware that Christ’s miracles surpassed the entire power of nature and were genuine miracles; nor could he have slandered them in the manner of the Jews, who said: “He casts out demons by Beelzebub” (Matthew 12). Christ performed other miracles as well, even though the demons knew that nothing of this kind had been granted to them; therefore they could not in any way have doubted this truth.

On the other hand, however, there is Paul’s statement, in which he expressly testifies that the wisdom hidden in the mystery which he preached—that is, the mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation and passion—had remained hidden even from the demons, whom he calls “the rulers of this age”: “We speak God’s wisdom in a mystery, which has been hidden, which God predestined before the ages for our glory, which none of the rulers of this age has known; for if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2). Ambrose interprets this passage as referring to demons, as does Jerome in chapter 10 of Daniel, along with other Fathers.

The Apostle, however, is not speaking about the time when he wrote these words. At that time the demons knew this wisdom, just as no one now doubts that they recognize and believe Christ to be God. The Apostle James says: “The demons believe, and tremble”; they believe, I say, not with infused and supernatural faith, but with acquired and experiential knowledge. Rather, the Apostle is speaking about the time before Christ’s passion and the preaching of the Gospel. At that time, if the demons had known Christ to be the true God and the Redeemer of the world, they would never have brought about his death, but would instead have tried to prevent it.

Yet they did not prevent it; they brought it about. For they put it into Judas’s heart to betray him (John 13). They also incited the Jews to kill him, as Christ himself testifies when he says: “You are of your father the devil, and you wish to carry out your father’s desires”—that is, to kill me, as he himself explains in John 8.

The same conclusion may be drawn from the devil’s temptations: first, because if the demon had known Christ to be the true Son of God and the true Messiah, he would not have tested him by temptation; and second, because he tempted him precisely in order to discover this. “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become loaves of bread.” And again: “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down” (Matthew 4).

Among the other reasons which the Fathers give for Christ’s having wished to be born of a betrothed and truly married virgin, this too is mentioned: that the mystery of the Incarnation might be concealed from the devil, since the devil would suppose that Christ had been born not of a virgin but of a wife. Thus Saint Ignatius says in his fifth letter to the Philippians. Saint Jerome also reports this in his commentary on the first chapter of Matthew.

In this question, ancient and recent authors hold differing opinions. To explain and reconcile them briefly, I say first that the demon approached Christ to tempt him chiefly in order to investigate his divinity. Therefore, up to that time, on the basis of what he had heard and seen both at Christ’s birth and afterward, and at his baptism and afterward, the demon was still doubtful and anxious as to whether Christ was the Son of God, and had not yet acquired certain knowledge of the matter. Nevertheless, he did not suppose that it was impossible for Christ to be the Son of God. Cassian rightly makes this point when he plays upon the matter here: no one doubts or investigates by testing something which he knows with certainty to be false or impossible. Thus Nestorius is shown to be worse than the devil, since he asserted to be altogether false and impossible what the devil suspected to be true.

This is also the opinion of the blessed Ignatius, a most ancient Father, in his eighth letter to the Philippians:

> “The angelic salutation astonished you, O demon; the worship of the Magi, the rising of the star. Again you return to ignorance because of what you see as lowly. For the exile, the cradle, the hardships, the circumcision, and the nursing seem to you unworthy of God,” and so forth.

Again:

> “You saw a man persist for forty days and nights without tasting human food, with angels ministering to him. At first you had seen him baptized like an ordinary man; then, after the fast, you saw him hungry. You recovered your confidence and again tempted him as though he were an ordinary man, ignorant of who he was; for you said, ‘If you are the Son of God.’ This is the mark of ignorance.”

Thus far the blessed Ignatius.

Other Fathers teach the same. Among the Greeks, Chrysostom, in Homily 13 on Matthew, writes:

> “Not knowing clearly the mystery of the humanity he had assumed, and who Christ was, he attempts to cast out his nets, by which he supposes that he may learn this secret.”

Among the Latins, Saint Ambrose, in his commentary on Luke, chapter 4, writes:

> “The demon knew that the Son of God would come, but he did not suppose that he had come through this weakness of the body. Thus he tempts in order to investigate; thus he investigates in order to tempt. Conversely, the Lord deceives in order to conquer, and by conquering he continues to deceive. For if he had transformed nature, he would have proved the Creator.”

Saint Jerome, on Matthew 4:

> “In all the temptations the devil acts in order to determine whether he is the Son of God. But the Lord so moderates his response that he leaves him in uncertainty.”

Saint Augustine, book 9 of *The City of God*, chapter 21:

> “The prince of demons doubted concerning him and tempted him, investigating whether he was the Christ, insofar as he himself allowed himself to be tempted, so that he might adapt the humanity which he bore as an example for our imitation.”

Ludovicus Vives explains this as follows:

> “He did this so that Christ would not appear exempt from the ancient condition of human beings, as though he alone were to go away untempted; and so that others who revered him would not resent being tempted, knowing that that most envious and confident enemy of the human race had not refrained even from Christ.”

Thus far Vives.

Saint Maximus, in Homily 2 on the Lenten Fast:

> “The devil, as I suppose, thought to himself and said: ‘If this is he’—that is, God or the Son of God—‘at whose command manna flowed for hungry peoples through the deserts, he will now be able to transform stones into bread, even if not at my request, nevertheless because of his own need, since he is hungry. If he does so, I shall prove him to be God; if he cannot, I shall discover him to be a man,’” and so forth.

Finally, Saint Leo the pontiff, in Sermon 4 on Lent, says:

> “The devil, astonished by Christ’s fasting for forty days and nights, craftily wished to investigate whether he possessed this self-restraint as something granted to him or as something proper to himself, so that he would not fear that the works of his deceptions would be undone if Christ were of the same condition as his body. First, therefore, he examined by deceit whether Christ was the Creator of substances, who could change the natures of corporeal things into whatever he wished. Second, he examined whether divinity was concealed beneath the appearance of human flesh, to which it would be easy to make the air passable and to balance earthly limbs through the void. But when the Lord chose to oppose the justice of the true man rather than reveal the power of his divinity, the devil turned the ingenuity of his third deception toward tempting him, in whom the signs of divine power had ceased, with the desire to rule, and toward leading him astray by promising him the kingdoms of the world. But the wisdom of God made the devil’s wisdom foolish, so that the proud enemy, seeing a man whom he had once overcome—namely, in Adam—would not fear to attack him who had to be slain for all.”

Thus Saint Leo indicates a twofold temptation by the devil, or a twofold intention in tempting: the first and primary, which we have mentioned, was to investigate what he desired to know and suspected—whether Christ was God; the second was to entice him into some kind of sin. Cassian discusses this latter kind of temptation elsewhere, as do the Fathers cited in our notes at that place.

But someone may ask how it could have happened that the devil did not understand from the divine predictions and prophecies, from the angelic annunciation, from the Virgin’s undefiled childbirth and unimpaired virginity, from the angels’ rejoicing, the Magi’s worship, Simeon’s testimony, John’s words, the Father’s voice sent from heaven at the baptism, and the other astonishing signs, that Christ was God—even before he approached him to tempt him.

Cajetan answers in his commentary on Luke, chapter 4, that the demon’s understanding was restrained by God so that he would not understand this. Cajetan learned this from his teacher. For Saint Thomas says the following:

> “It must be said that, as Augustine says in book 3 of *On the Trinity*, chapters 7 and 8, the devil can do many things by the power of his nature, from which he is nevertheless restrained by divine power. In this way it may be said that, by the power of his nature, the devil could know that the mother of God had not been violated but was a virgin; yet he was prevented by God from knowing the manner of the divine birth. That the devil later came in some way to know that he was the Son of God is no objection, because the time had already come for Christ to display his power against the devil and to suffer the persecution stirred up by him. But in infancy the devil’s malice had to be restrained, so that he would not persecute Christ more fiercely, when Christ had neither decided to suffer nor to display his power,” and so forth.

Thus Saint Thomas. What he asserts concerning the intact virginity of the Mother of God must also be understood concerning the many other signs and indications from which the demon, by natural ability and intellectual acuity, could have concluded that Christ was the true Messiah and the true Son of God, unless he had been restrained by God.

Saint Hilary supports this opinion, writing as follows in Canon 3 on Matthew:

> “It was fitting for the devil’s wickedness that he should be conquered in the very man whose sufferings he gloried in, and that he who had envied human beings the benefits of God should not, before the temptation, have been able to recognize God in the man,” and so forth.

And Saint Augustine, book 9 of *The City of God*, chapter 21:

> “Christ became known to the demons only insofar as he wished; but he wished only insofar as was necessary,” and so forth.

Hence, Cajetan says, it is evident that the demons’ understanding was bound or restrained by God as a punishment for sin: not only was their power bound, but their intellectual faculty also, so that they could not know what they would have been able to know by the force of natural illumination. For from the fact that, after Gabriel’s words to the Virgin, after the angel’s words to the shepherds, and after the words spoken from heaven at the baptism, the devil did not know that Jesus was the Son of God, it follows that he did not understand those testimonies.

Thus Cajetan. Abulensis holds the same opinion in question 22 on Matthew 4.

Second, I say—not on my own authority, but following the Fathers—that even after the devil’s temptations had been nullified, that is, overcome and rendered fruitless, as will be said below, Christ the Lord became increasingly known to the demons through his works and miracles, and was at least with moral certainty regarded as God, the Son of God, and the true Messiah. Yet they did not possess a wholly stable and firm assent or conviction, without any doubt or fear concerning the contrary, as dialecticians speak.

The reason is that the devil saw in Christ many signs of human weakness, which he did not think could be present in God; nor did he see that Christ’s humanity was hypostatically united with the person of the Word. For this is supernatural; and whatever is above nature the demon cannot grasp by his own intelligence. Christ’s miracles, moreover, were not so clear and evident that they were sufficient by themselves to produce certain faith in his divinity, or to make one believe that Christ was the natural Son of God, without inward inspiration, illumination, and divine motion—which the demons certainly did not possess.

Therefore, although they knew that the miracles were genuine, yet, blinded by their own malice, they perhaps suspected—or at least partly doubted—that these miracles were performed by God not to prove Christ’s divinity, but to demonstrate an exceptional holiness and prerogative of dignity. From this they concluded that Christ was indeed the Son of God, specially adopted and uniquely loved, but not the natural, genuine, and proper Son.

This is how the demonstration made above is answered.

The Fathers attribute to the demons a certain and moral knowledge of Christ’s divinity, but not a complete and undoubting conviction. Besides Cassian, in this and the following chapter, Saint Jerome says in his commentary on Matthew 8, concerning the words “What have we to do with you, Jesus, Son of God?”:

> “The demons, as well as the devil—that is, the prince of the demons—must be understood to have suspected rather than known that he was the Son of God.”

Augustine, or whoever was the author of the *Questions on the New and Old Testaments*, cited by Saint Thomas in the *Catena*, says:

> “When the demons cried out, ‘What have we to do with you, Jesus, Son of God?’, we should believe that they spoke more from suspicion than from knowledge. For if they had known, they would never have allowed the Lord of glory to be crucified.”

And elsewhere, in book 9 of *The City of God*, chapter 21:

> “The demons themselves knew this in such a way that, when the same Lord was clothed in the weakness of flesh, they said to him: ‘What have we to do with you, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us before the time?’ It is clear from these words that they possessed great knowledge, but not charity. They feared their punishment from him; they did not love justice in him.”

And below:

> “After that temptation, when angels, as it is written, ministered to him—good and holy angels, and therefore objects of fear and trembling to unclean spirits—it became increasingly clear to the demons how great he was. Thus, although the weakness of the flesh in him appeared contemptible, no one dared resist him when he gave a command.”

Remigius, cited by the same Saint Thomas:

> “Whenever they were tormented by his power, and saw him performing signs and miracles, they thought that he was the Son of God. After they saw him hungry, thirsty, and suffering such things, they doubted and believed him to be merely a man.”

Gregory, on Job 2; see also book 33 of his *Morals*, chapter 7:

> “When the evil spirit sees our Redeemer shining with miracles, he cries out: ‘We know that you are the Holy One of God.’ By saying this, he fears the Son of God because he recognizes him. Yet, because he does not know the force of heavenly mercy, when he sees him capable of suffering, he thinks him a mere man,” and so forth.

Bede, on Luke 4:

> “The devil had recognized him, exhausted by forty days of fasting, as a man, but by tempting him he could not ascertain whether he was also the Son of God. Now, through the power of his signs, he either understood—or rather suspected—that he was the Son of God.”

Finally, Saint Thomas says:

> “When the demon saw the miracles, he conjectured from a certain suspicion that he was the Son of God” (Third Part, question 44, article 1).

From this it is clear how the statement found in the Gospel—“He did not allow them to speak, because they knew him” or “because they knew that he was the Christ” (Mark 1 and Luke 4)—is to be understood. They knew not by certain and evident knowledge, but by probable conjecture and strong suspicion, as has been said.

Some, however, explain the passage differently. They take *quoniam* or *quia* as standing for *quod*, so that the meaning is: the Lord did not allow the demons to say this—namely, that they knew him to be the Messiah. He did not permit them to speak these words: “We know who you are, the Holy One of God,” that is, the Messiah sent by God, because they were lying when they said that they knew what they did not know, and Christ did not wish to receive testimony from the father of lies. Thus Cajetan, Jansenius, and others.

Accordingly, the evangelists do not assert that the demons knew this; they assert only that the demons said that they knew it and were forbidden by Christ to speak. A similar passage occurs in Matthew 16: “He commanded his disciples to tell no one that he was the Christ.” There it is clear that *quia* is used for *quod*.

Third, I say likewise, following the opinion of the Fathers: the demons did not know the mystery of human redemption through Christ’s death and resurrection before it had actually been accomplished. For this is the wisdom hidden in the mystery—that is, the secret or mystery which was also hidden from the demons—which, as the Apostle says, none of the rulers of this age knew; for if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Corinthians 2), since they would have understood that through him they themselves were to be conquered and stripped of their power.

Thus Saint Leo, in Sermon 9 on the Passion of the Lord:

> “The devil himself did not understand that, by raging against his Christ, he was destroying his own dominion; he would not have lost the rights of his ancient deceit if he had kept himself from the blood of the Lord Jesus. But, eager to cause harm, while he rushed upon him, he fell; while he seized him, he was seized; while he persecuted a mortal, he encountered the Savior.”

And in Sermon 11:

> “In order to release the human race from the bonds of deadly transgression, Christ both concealed the power of his majesty from the raging devil and set before him the weakness of our lowliness. For if the cruel and proud enemy had been able to know the plan of God’s mercy, he would have sought to temper the minds of the Jews with gentleness rather than inflame them with unjust hatred, lest he lose the servitude of all the captives while persecuting the freedom of one who owed him nothing. His own malice therefore deceived him: he inflicted punishment on the Son of God, which would become a remedy for all the sons of human beings; he shed righteous blood, which would be both the price and the drink by which the world was reconciled.”

And again, in Sermon 18:

> “This mystery of great mercy, beloved, was unknown to the devil’s pride just as it was unknown to Jewish impiety. For if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory. But because the plan of God’s mercy was hidden from the enemy of the human race, and because God, reconciling the world to himself in Christ, was concealed beneath the veil of flesh, he persisted in raging against the one in whom he could find nothing that belonged to him.”

Saint Gregory, commenting on the words of Job 40, “Will you play with him as with a bird?”:

> “In his passion the Lord mocked the bird, that is, the devil, when he showed him the bait of his only-begotten Son but concealed the snare. For the devil saw what he might take with his mouth, but he did not see what he would hold in his throat. Although he himself had confessed Christ to be the Son of God, nevertheless he believed him to die as a mere man, and stirred up the minds of the Jews to bring about his death.”

Saint Isidore, book 1 of *On the Supreme Good*, chapter 16:

> “By displaying the mortality of his flesh, which the devil desired to destroy, Christ concealed his divinity, so that he might set a snare in which to entangle the devil, as an unsuspecting bird,” and so forth.

Finally, Saint Thomas, in the First Part, question 64, article 1, reply to objection 4:

> “The mystery of the kingdom of God, which was accomplished through Christ, was known in some way by all the angels from the beginning, especially from the time when they were blessed by the vision of the Word—a vision the demons never possessed. Yet not all the angels knew it perfectly or equally. Hence the demons knew the mystery of the Incarnation much less perfectly while Christ was in the world. It was not made known to them as it was to the holy angels, who enjoy the participated eternity of the Word, but in the manner in which it was necessary for it to be made known to them through certain temporal effects, for their terror. If they had known perfectly and with certainty that he was the Son of God, and the effect of his passion, they would never have brought about the crucifixion of the Lord of glory.”

Thus the holy Fathers.

Enough has now been said about the question proposed. May the reader forgive us if, in a matter so ambiguous and perplexing, we have exceeded the limits of our notes to some extent; Cassian himself devotes three entire chapters to it.

He was investigating whether Christ was the Son of God, saying: “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become loaves of bread” (Luke 4). Did the devil’s contemplation of Christ’s humanity remove his suspicion of divinity, so that, because he saw him as a man, he believed that he could not be God? Certainly not. What, then, does he say? “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become loaves of bread.” He certainly did not doubt that it was possible; he was investigating whether it was so. He was concerned about the truth, not secure in the impossibility of the matter.

## CHAPTER XII. How he compares this opinion and plausible suspicion of the demon with the obstinate and unyielding opinion of the adversaries, and demonstrates that the latter is worse and more blasphemous than the former.

[Col. 0229A]

Yet he certainly knew that the Lord Jesus Christ had been born of Mary; he knew that he had been wrapped in swaddling clothes and laid in a manger; he knew that during the beginnings of his human life he had been poor and small, and that even his infancy had been needy of the ordinary services of a cradle.

[Note: Saint Leo uses similar words in Sermon 4 on the Epiphany: “The Magi saw and worshiped the child, small in size, dependent upon another’s help, unable to speak, and in no respect unlike the general condition of human infancy.”]

He also had no doubt that Christ possessed true flesh and had truly been born a man. Why, then, did this seem insufficient to reassure him? Why did he believe that the one whom he knew to be truly a man could also be God?

Learn, then, unhappy madness; learn, insanity and cruel impiety; learn at last that you are less faithful than the devil. If he said, “You are the Son of God,” while you say, “You are not the Son of God,” then what he asked, you deny.

[Note: This is hyperbole. For others older than Nestorius, who were likewise injurious to Christ and may be said to have surpassed him no less than he did in diabolical impiety in this respect, include Cerinthus, Ebion, Arius, Manichaeus, and other heresiarchs.]

No one has yet been found, apart from you, who surpassed the devil’s impiety. What he confessed could be true of the Lord, you do not believe could have been true.

## CHAPTER XIII. How he shows that the demon retained this opinion of Christ’s divinity, because of the hidden operation which he perceived in Christ, all the way to Christ’s very cross and death.

But perhaps afterward he ceased and grew calm; and, once his temptations had been frustrated, he abandoned his suspicion because he did not find the expected result.

[Note: Some think that after the devil’s temptations in the desert had been frustrated and overcome, not only did a suspicion or opinion accompanied by fear of the contrary remain among the demons, but a certain faith and conviction of Christ’s divinity arose in them; and thus what the Apostle James says was true even then: “The demons believe, and tremble” (James 2). This is the opinion of Maldonatus in his commentary on Matthew 8. We have set against this opinion above many statements of the holy Fathers, by which we showed that the demons did not know with certainty and clear understanding either Christ’s divinity or the mystery of our redemption before his death, when they learned it through actual and certain experience.]

On the contrary, it remained in him continually, and his suspicion of Christ, intensified by his own fears, persisted all the way to the Lord’s very cross. What more need be said? Even then he did not cease to regard him as the Son of God, after he had learned that the persecutors were able to do so much against him.

But the cunning enemy, seeing signs of divinity even amid Christ’s bodily sufferings, was compelled to suspect him to be God, although he preferred him to be a man. For although he preferred to believe what he wanted, he was nevertheless compelled, by the certain indications of events, to believe what he feared.

Nor is this surprising. For although he saw Christ spat upon, scourged, insulted, and driven to the cross, he nevertheless perceived, amid those very indignities, divine powers abundantly manifest: the veil of the Temple was torn, the sun withdrew, the day was darkened, and all things felt the power of the passion. Even those things that do not know God recognized the work of divinity.

Therefore, seeing and trembling at this, the devil was driven entirely toward recognizing God even in the very consummation of Christ’s humanity. He attempted this through those who had crucified Christ, saying:

[Note: Chrysostom, in a sermon on the Passion of the Lord, says: “Consider the voice of the devil’s sons, how they imitate their father’s voice. The devil said, ‘Throw yourself down, if you are the Son of God.’ And the Jews say, ‘If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross.’” Jerome, in his Commentary: “Their promise is deceitful when they add, ‘and we will believe him.’ For what is greater: to descend alive from the cross, or to rise from the tomb after death? He rose, and you did not believe; therefore, even if he had descended from the cross, you would not have believed. But it seems to me that the demons prompted this. For as soon as the Lord was crucified, they felt the power of the cross and understood that their strength had been broken; and they did this to make him come down from the cross. But the Lord, knowing the plots of his adversaries, remained on the gibbet in order to destroy the devil.”

“‘If he is the Son of God, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him’” (Matthew 27).

Pope Leo, rebuking both the blindness of the Jews and the malice of the demons, says in Sermon 4 on the Lord’s Passion:

> “From what source of error, Jews, and from what pool of envy did you drink the poison of such blasphemies? Who was your teacher? What doctrine persuaded you that you ought to believe that man to be the king of Israel and the Son of God who would either not allow himself to be crucified or would tear his body free from the nails? The mysteries of the Law and the mouths of the prophets did not sing this to you. Rather, you truly read: ‘I did not turn my face away from the shame of spitting’ (Isaiah 53). And again: ‘They pierced my hands and my feet, and they counted all my bones’ (Psalm 21). Did you read: ‘The Lord came down from the cross’? But you read: ‘The Lord reigned from the wood’ (Numbers 21).”

Gregory has similar words in Homily 21 on the Gospels, as does Bernard in Sermon 1 on the Resurrection:

> “This is what pains the cunning of the poisonous serpent: the bronze serpent lifted up in the desert, by looking upon which the wounds he inflicted are healed. Otherwise, under whose prompting do we believe that Pilate’s wife sent to him, saying: ‘Have nothing to do with that righteous man, for I have suffered many things today in a dream because of him’? The enemy already feared then, but now especially, feeling himself weakened by the power of the cross. Late repentance follows; and those whom he incited to crucify him, he incites to persuade him to come down. Finally, they say: ‘If he is the king of Israel, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him.’ This is plainly the serpent’s cunning, this is the invention of spiritual wickedness,” and so forth.]

He sensed that the Lord our God was accomplishing the redemption of human salvation through the suffering of his body, and at the same time that by this suffering the devil himself was being destroyed and subjected, while we were being redeemed and saved. Therefore the enemy of the human race sought by every means and every deception to frustrate what he knew was being carried out for the redemption of all.

“If he is the Son,” he says, “let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him”—namely, so that, provoked by the insult of their words, the Lord might abandon the mystery while avenging the injury.

You see, then, that even while the Lord was hanging on the cross he was called the Son of God; you see that those who named him suspected what they named him to be. Learn, therefore, as I said above, to believe the Son of God either from the persecutors themselves or from the devil.

Who has ever equaled demonic unbelief? Who has surpassed it? He suspected that Christ was the Son of God even while Christ endured death; you deny it even after he has risen. He suspected him to be God, though Christ concealed himself from him; you deny him, though he has proved himself to you.

## CHAPTER XIV. How he shows that heretics corrupt Sacred Scripture, responding to the argument drawn from the Apostle’s words, “without father, without mother,” and so forth, in Hebrews 7.

You therefore use the Sacred Scriptures against God and try to make his own testimonies witnesses against him. But how? In such a way, certainly, that you become not only a transgressor against God but also a violator of the testimonies themselves.

Nor is this surprising. Since you cannot do what you want, you do only what you can. You cannot turn the sacred testimonies against God, so you turn the testimonies themselves upside down.

For you say: “Then Paul also lies when he says of Christ:

[Note: More elegantly in Greek, with compound words, the passage reads: ἀπάτωρ, ἀμήτωρ, ἀγενεαλόγητος—“without father, without mother, without genealogy.” These words are spoken by the Apostle (Hebrews 7) of King Melchizedek, insofar as he bore the type and likeness of Christ, just as do the words that follow in the same passage: “Having neither beginning of days nor end of life.” Therefore the statements must correspond to both in their respective ways and must truly be declared of both.

But Nestorius craftily suppressed the first part of the statement, since it appeared to contradict his position. Having truncated the passage in this way, he concluded that Mary was not Θεοτόκος, “Mother of God,” because the Apostle called Christ ἀμήτωρ, “without mother.” He deceitfully concealed the fact that, by the same reasoning, one could also conclude that Christ, as God, had no Father, since the same apostolic statement also calls him ἀπάτωρ, “without father,” as is explained more fully here.

Melchizedek was called “without father, without mother, without genealogy,” not because he had no father or mother, but because Scripture makes no mention of them.
