For this reason he was a type of Christ: just as his father is not found in Scripture, so Christ has no father according to the flesh; and just as his mother is not mentioned, so Christ has no mother according to his divinity—indeed, he did not have one in reality either.

Hence the verse also cited by Saint Thomas in his commentary on Hebrews 7:

> “God is without mother; flesh is without father.”

Another similar verse is:

> “God from a father; a child from a mother.”

That is: God is without mother, and the child is without father. And just as Melchizedek is found in Scripture as ἀγενεαλόγητος, “without genealogy,” because his genealogy is not named, so neither can the origin and manner of Christ’s divine generation be comprehended.]

“Without mother, without genealogy.”

I ask you: of whom do you wish Paul to have said this? Of the Son and Word of God, or of Christ, whom you separate from the Son of God and blasphemously assert to be merely a man?

If he said it of Christ, whom you call a solitary man, how could a man be born without a mother and without a genealogy on his mother’s side? But if he said it of the Word of God and the Son of God, what are we to do with the fact that the same Apostle—whom you sacrilegiously regard as your witness—says in the same place and in the same testimony that the one whom you assert to be without a mother is also without a father, saying: “without father, without mother, without genealogy”?

It therefore remains that, by using the Apostle’s testimony to assert that the Son of God is without a mother, you also blasphemously assert that he is without a father.

You see into what a precipice of impiety you have cast yourself through your zeal for perversity and wickedness: by saying that the Son of God had no mother, you deny him a father as well—something which no one throughout the ages has yet said, except perhaps a madman.

And this, I do not know whether it is greater in impiety or in folly. For what is more foolish, what more absurd, than to introduce the name of a son while wishing to suppress the name of a father?

But you say: “I do not suppress it; I do not deny it.”

Then what madness compelled you to cite that testimony in which, by saying that he had no mother, you appear also to have denied his father? For since the same testimony says that he is without a father just as he is without a mother, it is necessary that, if “without mother” can be understood there in the same way in which it is said that he is without a mother, then “without father” must also be believed in the same way.

But that headlong insanity bent on denying God did not understand this. By presenting in truncated form what is written in full, it failed to see that the sequence of the sacred text, once opened up, rebukes the shameless and manifest lie.

O foolish blasphemy and madness! While it does not see what must follow, it has not even understood what may be read—as though, because it deprived itself of understanding, it could deprive everyone else of the ability to read; or as though everyone would lose the eyes in their heads for reading because it had already lost the eyes of its mind.

[Note: That is, he did not wish to understand what he was reading. Concerning this the Psalmist says: “He did not wish to understand, lest he do good.” More specifically, with reference to Nestorius: “lest he think and speak rightly.”]

Listen, then, heretic, to what you stole; listen to the complete and intact passage which you presented in weakened and truncated form.

The Apostle, wishing to indicate to everyone Christ’s twofold birth, so as to show that the Lord was born both in divinity and in the flesh, says: “without father, without mother.” One of these belongs properly to the birth of divinity, the other to the birth of the flesh. For just as he was generated in divinity without a mother, so in the body he was born without a father.

Thus, since he is neither without a father nor without a mother, he must nevertheless be believed to be without a father and without a mother. For if, when you consider that he is born from the Father, you look to his being without a mother; and if, when you consider that he is born from his mother, you look to his being without a father, then in each birth he has one of these and does not have the other in that birth. The birth of divinity had no need of a mother, and for the birth of his body he was himself sufficient without a father.

Therefore, says the Apostle, “without mother, without genealogy.”

## CHAPTER XV. How Christ is said by the Apostle to have been without genealogy

How does he say that the Lord was without genealogy, when Matthew’s Gospel began the Gospel with the genealogy of the Savior, saying: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham”? Therefore, according to the Evangelist he has a genealogy, and according to the Apostle he does not: according to the Gospel, he has one from his mother; according to the Apostle, he has none from his father. And therefore the Apostle rightly says, “Without father, without mother, without genealogy”: where he stated that He was begotten without a mother, there he also recalled that He was without genealogy.

Thus, in both births of the Lord, the evangelical and apostolic writings agree with one another. According to the Evangelist, He has a genealogy, having been born in the flesh without a father; according to the Apostle, He has none, the Lord having been begotten in the Godhead without a mother. Isaiah says:

> “Who shall declare His generation?” (Isaiah 53)

[Note: [Col. 0233C] Saint Jerome also interprets these words of Isaiah as referring to Christ’s divine and eternal generation from the Father. Writing on Matthew 1, he says: “In Isaiah we read, ‘Who shall declare His generation?’ Let us not therefore suppose that the Evangelist contradicts the prophet, as though the one should begin to narrate what the other declared impossible to express. For in Isaiah it is spoken of the generation of the Godhead, while here it is spoken of the Incarnation.” This is said by Matthew, who began his Gospel in this way: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David” (Matthew 1), and so forth.

Other Fathers, however, explain the same passage also of Christ’s human and temporal generation and birth from the Virgin: Tertullian, *Against the Jews*, chapter 13; Cyril, book 5 on John, chapter 2; Chrysostom, in his homily on Saint John the Baptist; and Ambrose, book 1 of *On the Faith*, addressed to Gratian, chapter 5. Ambrose, after first speaking of the eternal generation, says: “For me, it is impossible to know the secret of the generation: the mind fails, the voice is silent—not mine only, but that of the angels also.” He adds below: “It is not only Christ’s generation from the Father that is wondrous; His generation from the Virgin is wondrous also.”

Jerome himself, in his commentaries on Isaiah, admits that the same words may be understood in two ways: either of the Godhead or of the Virgin’s childbirth. Saint Leo, most explicitly, says in sermon 3 on the Nativity: “For we believe that what was said, ‘Who shall declare His generation?’ pertains not only to that mystery by which the Son is co-eternal with the Father, but also to that birth by which the Word became flesh.” And in sermon 10: “The birth of our Savior, not only according to His Godhead from the Father, but also according to the flesh from His mother, so exceeds the capacity of human speech that what was said, ‘Who shall declare His generation?’ is rightly referred to both,” and so forth.

Saint Thomas, explaining and reconciling both interpretations (*Summa theologica*, III, question 31, article 3), says: “It must be said that, as Jerome says on Matthew, Isaiah speaks of the generation of the Godhead, whereas Matthew recounts Christ’s generation according to His humanity—not, indeed, explaining the manner of the Incarnation, since that too is ineffable, but enumerating the fathers from whom Christ proceeded according to the flesh.”]

## CHAPTER XVI. After the example of the demon tempting Christ, he shows that heretics mutilate and pervert Sacred Scripture

Why, then, heretic, did you not present in this way what you had read, complete and uncorrupted? You see, therefore, that the Apostle used the same reasoning by which he stated that the Lord was born without a father to state also that He was without a mother, so that by the same reasoning by which He was understood to be without a father He might be recognized as being without a mother. And just as He certainly cannot be believed to be without a father, so also He cannot be understood to be without a mother.

Why, then, heretic, did you not present in this way what you had read in the Apostle, unharmed and inviolate? Instead, you insert one part and withdraw another; and, in order that you may establish falsehood through crime, you steal the words of truth.

[Note: [Col. 0234D] This perversity of heretics in mutilating and tearing apart the Scriptures was discussed above.]

I see from whom you learned this. For you must be thought to possess the instruction of the one whose example you follow. Thus the devil, tempting God in the Gospel, says: “If You are the Son of God, throw Yourself down. For it is written that He has commanded His angels concerning You, that they should guard You in all Your ways” (Luke 4; Psalm 90). And when he had said this, he omitted the connected words that follow, namely: “You shall walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and you shall trample upon the lion and the dragon.”

He cunningly set forth the preceding words and withdrew those that followed; for he stated the former in order to ensnare Him,

[Note: [Col. 0235C] Saint Chrysostom aptly says (*Homily 5 of the Imperfect Work*): “O devil, you read that the Son of God is carried in the hands, but you did not read that He treads upon the asp and the basilisk. You produce the former example as a proud being, but you conceal the latter as a cunning one.” Saint Jerome writes in his commentary: “We read this in Psalm 90; yet there the prophecy concerns not Christ but a holy man. The devil therefore interprets the Scriptures wrongly. Certainly, if he truly knew that it was written about the Savior, he ought also to have stated what follows in the same psalm against himself: ‘You shall walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and you shall trample upon the lion and the dragon.’ He speaks of the angels’ assistance as though to a weak man, but as a deceiver he is silent about his own trampling. Saint Bernard likewise says in sermon 14 on the same psalm: ‘Observe and see how the wicked and deceitful one kept silent about what would dissolve the fabrications of his wickedness. What did He command? Clearly, what follows in the psalm: “That they should guard You in all Your ways.” Surely not on precipices? What sort of way is it to throw oneself down from the pinnacle of the temple? This is not a way but a ruin; and if it is a way, it is yours, not His. Why, moreover, are you silent about what follows: “You shall walk upon the asp and the basilisk,” and so forth? For this parable concerns you. Your monstrous wickedness is signified as something to be trampled underfoot by monstrous names,’ and so forth.]

He concealed the latter so that he might not condemn himself. For he knew that by the prophetic voice he himself was signified as the asp and the basilisk, the lion and the dragon.

So you too, putting forward one part and withdrawing another, present the former in order to deceive, but withdraw the latter lest, if you presented the whole, the very whole should condemn your deception. But it is now time to pass on to what follows; for by lingering too long over individual points, while we are carried along by the affection that prompts an abundant reply, we exceed even the limits of a longer book.

## CHAPTER XVII. Christ’s glory and dignity must not be attributed to the Holy Spirit in such a way that they are denied to have proceeded from Christ Himself, as though all excellence that was in Him were foreign and derived from elsewhere

[Col. 0235B]

You say, then, in another disputation—or rather, in another blasphemy of yours—while separating from the divine nature the Spirit who created Christ’s humanity.

[Note: [Col. 0235D] Here the words of Nestorius are again brought forward. He attempted to prove from the Sacred Scriptures that Christ possessed nothing from Himself, but had received everything from the Holy Spirit as from another and gratuitous giver and bestower: humanity itself, generation, justification, sanctification, power, exaltation, and glory. Consequently, he held that Christ was not true God but a mere and solitary man, as he called Him. Each of these statements contains an equal number of blasphemies against Christ’s divinity.

Here, therefore, and in what follows, the reading should be “He says”—that is, Scripture says—not “you say,” as at the beginning of the chapter, a distinction not observed in the previous edition. For in each of his statements Nestorius employed individual scriptural authorities, wrongly understood, as may be seen here.]

For Scripture says: “That which was born from Mary is from the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 1). He also filled with righteousness that which was created. For Scripture says: “He appeared in the flesh, He was justified in the Spirit” (1 Timothy 3). He also made Him feared by demons. “For I,” He says, “cast out demons by the Spirit of God” (Luke 11). He also made His flesh a temple. “For I saw His Spirit descending like a dove and remaining upon Him” (John 1). He also granted Him elevation into heaven. For Scripture says: “Giving a command to the apostles whom He chose, He was taken up through the Holy Spirit” (Acts 1). Finally, it was this Spirit who bestowed such great glory upon Christ.

Your entire blasphemy in all these claims is this: that Christ possessed nothing through Himself; and that even the solitary man, as you call Him, received nothing from the Word—that is, from the Son of God—but that everything in Him was the gift of the Spirit.

If, therefore, we demonstrate that everything you attribute to the Spirit belongs to Christ Himself, what remains except that, whereas you wish Him to be understood as man because, as you say, He possessed everything alien to Him, we should prove Him to be God precisely because He possessed everything as His own?

We have proved this not merely by disputations or arguments, but by the voice of the Godhead itself, since nothing bears more correct witness concerning God than the divine things themselves. And since nothing knows itself better than God’s own Majesty, no testimony concerning God is thought more worthy of belief than that in which God Himself is His own witness.

First, then, when you say that the Spirit created His humanity, we could understand this simply if we recognized that you had not stated it impiously. For we do not deny that the Lord’s flesh was conceived from the Holy Spirit; but we say that, although the body was conceived through the Spirit’s cooperation, it was nevertheless created for Himself by the Son of God, and that it is His own man.

[Note: [Col. 0236C] “His own man,” that is, His own humanity—an expression the Fathers often use, as was stated elsewhere. I say that the Son of God Himself created His own humanity, because at the very moment of conception He fashioned for Himself a body from the most pure blood of the immaculate Virgin, infused His most blessed soul into it, and certainly hypostatically united and joined His Godhead to it. Saint Athanasius expressed this very clearly in his creed.]

The Holy Spirit Himself says and bears witness in the Sacred Scriptures: “Wisdom built herself a house” (Proverbs 9).

[Note: [Col. 0236C] Jerome—or rather Bede—on this passage says: “Wisdom built herself a house,” because the Son of God Himself created the man whom He was to assume into the unity of His person. Here, too, “man” is used for the assumed humanity.]

You see, therefore, that what was conceived from the Holy Spirit was built and perfected by the Son of God. This is not because the work of the Son of God is one thing and the work of the Holy Spirit another, but because, through the unity of the Godhead and Majesty, the Spirit’s work is the Son of God’s building, and the Son of God’s building is the Spirit’s cooperation.

And therefore Scripture records not only that the Holy Spirit came upon the Virgin,

[Col. 0237A]

but also that the power of the Most High overshadowed the Virgin. Since Wisdom itself is the fullness of the Godhead, no one could doubt that the whole fullness of the Godhead was present with Wisdom as she built herself a house.

[Note: [Col. 0236D] Chrysostom likewise interprets this passage (*Homily 49 on Genesis 4*), distinguishing the Power of the Most High from the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit and calling Christ Himself the Power of the Most High: “And the Power of the Most High will overshadow you.” The Power of the Most High King is Christ, who is formed in the Virgin through the coming of the Holy Spirit.

Gregory, too, says in *Moralia* 18, chapter 2: “Because of the refreshment of mind given from heaven, it is said to Mary: ‘The Power of the Most High will overshadow you.’” Yet in this matter both natures of the incarnate God could be signified by the word “overshadowing.” A shadow is formed by light and body; the Lord, however, is light through His divinity and, through the mediation of the soul, graciously became a body in her womb through His humanity. Since incorporeal light was to be embodied in her womb, she who conceived the incorporeal for embodiment was told: “The Power of the Most High will overshadow you”—that is, the incorporeal light of divinity will receive in you a body of humanity.

Damascene likewise says so in book 3, chapter 2, as do Bede and Theophylact in their commentaries. Saint Thomas summarizes these authorities, in his usual manner, in a way that suitably clarifies this passage. He says (*Summa theologica*, III, question 32, article 1):

“It must be said that the work of the conception is common to the whole Trinity, but according to a certain mode it is attributed to the individual persons. Authority concerning the person of the Son is attributed to the Father, since through this conception the Son assumed human nature for Himself. The assumption of the flesh itself is attributed to the Son. But the formation of the body assumed by the Son is attributed to the Holy Spirit. For the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of the Son, according to Galatians 4: ‘God sent the Spirit of His Son.’

“Just as the power of the soul, which is in the seed, forms the body in the generation of other human beings through the spirit contained in the seed, so the power of God, which is the Son Himself—according to 1 Corinthians 1, ‘Christ the power of God’—formed through the Holy Spirit the body that He assumed.

“The angel’s words also show this, when he says: ‘The Holy Spirit will come upon you,’ as though to prepare and form the material of Christ’s body; ‘and the Power of the Most High will overshadow you,’ that is, Christ will receive in you a body of humanity, while the incorporeal light of divinity remains. For a shadow is formed from light and body, as Gregory says in *Moralia* 18. The Most High is understood as the Father, whose Power is the Son.”

Thus far Saint Thomas.

Furthermore, Euthymius and others take the statements that the Holy Spirit came upon the Virgin and that the Power of the Most High overshadowed her as referring to the same thing. The second statement is therefore a repetition of the same meaning in different words, a form of repetition frequently found in Scripture. The Holy Spirit is also commonly called the finger of God, and likewise the power of God, by the same analogy. Thus Luke 24 says: “But remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high.” And Acts 1: “You will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you.”]

But this unhappy madness of blasphemy, while attempting to separate Christ from the Son of God, does not see that it is itself utterly tearing apart the nature of the Godhead.

Unless, perhaps, he believes that the house was therefore built for Christ by the Holy Spirit because He Himself was not capable or powerful enough to build a house for Himself. But this is as insane as it is ridiculous: that He who is believed to have created the whole universe of heavenly and earthly things by a mere nod should be believed unable to build a body for Himself—especially since the power of the Holy Spirit is His power.

[Note: [Col. 0238C] Saint Leo says (*Sermon 3 on Pentecost*): “The Majesty of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit has never been separated from the Father’s omnipotence; and whatever divine governance does in the ordering of all things proceeds from the providence of the whole Trinity. There is one goodness of mercy, one judgment of justice; nor is anything divided in action where nothing is different in will,” and so forth.]

The divinity and Majesty of the Trinity are so united to one another and inseparable that nothing whatsoever can be understood in one person of the Godhead that can be separated from the fullness of the Godhead.

Once this has been established and understood—that, according to the faith of Sacred Scripture, when the Holy Spirit came upon her and the Power of the Most High overshadowed her, Wisdom built herself a house—all the remaining blasphemous accusations amount to nothing.

For there is no doubt that He Himself, through Himself and in Himself, made all things, in whose name and faith no faith of believers could exist otherwise. He did not need the assistance of another, since not even those who believed in His power needed such assistance.

Therefore, what you say—that He was justified by the Spirit, that the Spirit made Him feared by demons, that His flesh was made a temple by the Spirit, and that He was raised by the Spirit into heaven—all of this is sacrilegious and furious. This is not because one should believe that, in all these things which He Himself did, the unity and cooperation of the Spirit were absent, since the Godhead is never absent from itself and the power of the Trinity was always present in the works of the Savior. Rather, it is because you wish the Holy Spirit to have assisted the Lord Jesus Christ as though He were needy and weak, granting Him what He could not provide for Himself.

Learn, then, from the sacred testimonies to believe that He is God and not to mix falsehood with truth, since reality does not allow it and reason recoils from it: that the understanding of a demonic spirit should be mixed with divine testimonies.

## CHAPTER XVIII. How the Apostle’s statement should be understood: “He appeared in the flesh, He was justified in the Spirit,” and so forth

[Col. 0238B]

First, you say that the Spirit filled what was created with righteousness; and you wish to prove this by the Apostolic testimony, which says: “He appeared in the flesh, He was justified in the Spirit.” You speak both statements with an insane understanding and a mad spirit.

For you state that He was filled with righteousness by the Spirit in order to show His emptiness, since you assert that the fulfillment of righteousness was supplied to Him. And, in using the Apostolic testimony concerning this matter, you steal the order and meaning of the divine testimony. For the Apostle did not set it down in the way you have mutilated and corrupted it.

What does the Apostle say? “And manifestly”—or, more fully:

[Note: [Col. 0238C] In Greek it reads: **Καὶ ὁμολογουμένως** (*kai homologoumenōs*), that is, “by the confession of all,” as Ambrose renders it, or “beyond controversy,” as others translate it: **μέγα ἐστὶ τὸ τῆς εὐσεβείας μυστήριον** (*mega esti to tēs eusebeias mystērion*), “great is the mystery of piety,” followed by **Θεὸς ἐφανερώθη ἐν σαρκί, ἐδικαιώθη ἐν Πνεύματι** (*Theos ephanerōthē en sarki, edikaiōthē en Pneumati*), “God was manifested in the flesh, He was justified in the Spirit.”

It is evident here that the reading is not “which,” as in our text, but instead **Θεὸς**, that is, “God,” as Gagneius aptly observed. The meaning is therefore that Christ God is understood as the great mystery—or sacrament—of piety and religion: He was manifested in the flesh. The One who had previously been hidden from human beings in His divinity became known to them in His humanity through the assumption of flesh.

“He was justified in the Spirit” must unquestionably be understood according to His humanity, according to which He is said to have been justified, just as He is said to have been sanctified in John 10: “Him whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world.” He was justified by the Spirit—that is, through the Holy Spirit and the fullness of grace—or “He was justified” means that He appeared to be righteous.

For although the Jews called Him a glutton, a drinker of wine, and one who had a demon, He was nevertheless recognized by all as righteous, and He will be recognized even more fully when He appears as Judge of all. Thus in Psalm 18 the judgments of the Lord are said to be “justified in themselves,” that is, perfected, so that no one can detract from them. And in Matthew 11: “Wisdom is justified by her children,” that is, approved and vindicated from every accusation.]

Thus, from both the Greek text and the Latin, Nestorius’s wickedness and cunning are clearly refuted.

From the Greek, because he suppressed the name **Θεός** (*Theos*, “God”), which condemned him, and so quoted the Apostle’s words: “He appeared in the flesh, He was justified in the Spirit,” when he ought to have said: “God appeared in the flesh, He was justified in the Spirit,” as the Greek text reads. This is the complete and true meaning.

This is how the Greek Fathers quote the passage. Athanasius, at the beginning of his book *On the Incarnation*, says: “Paul declared that, beyond controversy, the mystery of piety is great: that God was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, seen by angels, preached among the nations,” and so forth.

Cyril, in his explanation of the second anathema against Nestorius, writes: “The divine Paul writes: ‘It is confessed that the mystery of piety is great. God appeared in the flesh, He was justified in the Spirit, He was seen by angels, He was preached among the nations, faith was placed in Him in the world, He was taken up in glory.’

“What, then, does it mean that he says, ‘God appeared in the flesh’? It means that the Word from God the Father became flesh—not that He was changed or converted into flesh, but rather that the one and same Son made the flesh taken from the Virgin His own, and was called one and the same Son: before the Incarnation, without flesh and Word alone; after the Incarnation, the same existing in a body,” and so forth.

Nestorius is also refuted from the Latin interpreter and the Vulgate version, which Cassian, writing in Latin among Latins, followed. This is so first because, although “God” is not expressed, it is understood when the text says: “The great sacrament of piety, which was manifested in the flesh,” and so forth. For what other great mystery of piety and Christian religion could be imagined, manifested in the flesh, except Christ God and man, the Word made flesh?

He is refuted also because Nestorius interpreted Christ as justified by the Holy Spirit as by someone external to Him, as though He were empty of righteousness in Himself, deprived of all grace, and in need of assistance from another. Yet He must be said to have been justified not by the Holy Spirit alone but equally by the Father and by Himself—that is, by the whole Trinity, whose works are undivided, as has been said.

Therefore, to answer the fool—namely Nestorius—in accordance with his folly: the Holy Spirit filled with righteousness the man Christ whom He had created, as Nestorius says; but He did not do so alone. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit did so. Consequently, Christ Himself, as God, filled Himself, as man—that is, His humanity—with righteousness and holiness.]

“Great is the mystery of piety, which was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit.”

You see, therefore, that the Apostle proclaimed the mystery, or sacrament, of piety to have been justified. He was not so forgetful of his own statements and teaching as to say that He needed righteousness whom he had always proclaimed to be righteousness, saying: “He was made for us righteousness, sanctification, and redemption” (1 Corinthians 1). Elsewhere also he says: “But you were washed, but you were justified, but you were sanctified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 6).

How far, then, is it from the truth that He needed the fulfillment of righteousness, when He fulfilled all righteousness; or that His Majesty did not possess righteousness, when even His name justifies all things?

You see, therefore, how foolish or insane your blasphemy is, since you attempt to take away from our Lord what is always poured forth abundantly by Him upon all believers, yet is never diminished by that continual generosity.

## CHAPTER XIX. That Christ, no less than the Holy Spirit, made Himself feared by demons

You also say that the Spirit made Him feared by demons. To reject and refute this claim, although the very horror of the statement should be sufficient, we shall nevertheless bring forward examples.

Tell me, please: you say that the fact that demons feared Him was not His own but another’s, and that this was not an exercise of power but a gift. How, then, did His name possess the power by which He Himself, as you say, was in need? How were demons cast out in His name, the weak healed, and the dead raised?

The Apostle Peter said to the lame man sitting at the Beautiful Gate of the temple: “In the name of Jesus Christ, rise and walk” (Acts 3). Again, in the city of Joppa, he said to Aeneas, who had lain paralyzed in bed for eight years: “Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you; rise and make your bed” (Acts 9).

Paul likewise says: “I command you, in the name of Jesus Christ, to come out of her,” addressing the pythonic spirit (Acts 16). And the demon came out of her.

[Note: [Col. 0240D] Christ Himself established the form and method of casting out demons by invoking His name when He said: “In My name they will cast out demons” (Mark 16). Hence the apostles, boasting of this gift bestowed upon them, say: “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in Your name” (Luke 10). John likewise speaks of the Jewish exorcists: “We saw someone casting out demons in Your name, and he does not follow us” (Luke 9).

The first Christians and holy men in every age likewise used this method in expelling demons, as Justin testifies in his dispute with Trypho: “By the name of the Son of God Himself and the firstborn of creation, every demon, when adjured, is conquered and brought under control.” A little earlier he says: “The demons tremble at and fear the power of that name, and even today, when adjured in the name of Jesus Christ who was crucified under Pontius Pilate, they obey us.”

Athanasius likewise writes in his book *On the Incarnation of the Word*: “Where Christ or His faith is named, all idolatry is driven away and the demons’ plots are exposed. The demons, however many there are, cannot even endure His name; as soon as they hear it, even if only once, they flee.”

Prudentius, in his *Apotheosis*, against the Jews:

> Apollo is tormented,  
> Struck by the name of Christ; nor can he endure  
> The thunderbolts of the Word. So many blows  
> Agitate the wretched one as the tongue resounds  
> With the praised miracles of God’s Christ.

And, to cite one example from the centuries, Sozomen reports concerning Arsacius (*Ecclesiastical History*, book 4, chapter 15) that when a man possessed by a demon ran through the marketplace with a drawn sword and everyone fled from him, while turmoil seized the city, Arsacius went to meet him, named Christ, struck the man down by his word, and immediately cleansed him of the demon.]

But how far removed this weakness was from our Lord, understand from this: I do not even call those weak whom He made powerful through His name. For we know that after the Lord’s resurrection no apostle was ever obstructed by a demon or by any illness.

How, then, did the Spirit make Him feared who made others feared? Or was He Himself weak whose faith, even through others, ruled over all things?

Finally, those who received power from God never used that power as their own, but referred the power itself back to Him from whom they had received it. For that power could never have possessed any force except through the name of the One who gave it. Therefore the apostles and all God’s ministers did nothing in their own name, but everything in Christ’s name and invocation. The power received its force from the source from which it had its beginning; and it could by no means be given through ministers unless it had come from its author.

You, then, who say that the Lord was the same as one of His servants—for just as the apostles possessed nothing unless they had received it from their Lord, so you wish the Lord Himself to have possessed nothing except what He received from the Spirit—and therefore you wish Him to have possessed what He had not as Lord but received as a servant: tell me, then, how He used that power as His own rather than as something received.

What do we read about Him? “Rise,” He says to the paralytic, “take up your bed and go to your house” (Matthew 9). Again, to the father pleading for his son: “Go,” He says, “your son lives” (John 4). And when the only son of a mother was being carried to the grave:

[Note: [Col. 0241D] Observe here the distinction between Christ and the apostles and other saints in the performance of miracles. Peter did say to the dead girl, “Tabitha, arise” (Acts 9), but he did not say, “I say to you, arise,” because he spoke not by his own authority but by Christ’s authority and in His name.

Hence elsewhere Christ is said to have manifested His glory through miracles (John 2), that is, His divinity. We are therefore to understand that Christ performed miracles in one way and the prophets and others in another. Many prophets indeed performed miracles, but of none of them is it said that he manifested his own glory. They performed miracles in created things not as lords of creatures but as ministers of the Creator, and thus manifested not their own glory but God’s. Christ, however, manifested His own glory because He Himself was the Creator and Lord, the first author and performer of miracles.]

“Young man,” He says, “I say to you, arise” (Luke 7).

Did He, then, in the manner of those who received power from God, ask that power also be given to Him so that He might act by invoking the divine name? Why did He not work in the name of the Spirit, just as the apostles worked in His name?

Finally, what does the Gospel testify about Him? “He was teaching them as one having authority, and not as the scribes and Pharisees” (Matthew 7).

Or do you perhaps wish Him to have been proud and arrogant, attributing to His own power the authority which, as you say, He had received from God? But what shall we do with the fact that power never obeyed servants except through the name of its author, nor could it have effectiveness if someone attributed any part of it to himself?

## CHAPTER XX. He attempts to invalidate that opinion by weightier and more compelling arguments

But why do we spend so long bringing arguments against this frenzied blasphemy—arguments that are indeed evident, but nevertheless lesser ones? Let us hear God Himself speaking to the disciples:

> “Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons” (Matthew 10).

And again:

[Note: [Col. 0241D] Two things should be noted in these words. First, the phrase “in My name” is understood in various ways in Scripture, for the meaning of the name is not always the same.

Sometimes it is taken to mean command or authority. I do not see why Thyraeus distinguishes these two meanings (*On Demons*, chapter 42), since when Christ says that He came in the name of the Father (John 5), this means according to the Father’s decree, authority, or will.

Sometimes it means merits, as when He promises all things to those who ask and petition the Father in His name (John 14). To ask in Christ’s name means to ask through Christ’s merits, as the usage of the Church interprets it.

Finally, it is taken to mean power and authority, as when Christ says: “The works that I do in My Father’s name bear witness about Me” (John 10).

Although demons may be said to be expelled by Christ’s command, Christ’s merits, or Christ’s authority when they are expelled through the invocation of His name, we properly understand His power—namely, His divine power—so that “to cast out demons in Christ’s name” means the same as “to cast them out by Christ’s power.”

The Author confirms this when he says: “Did He who made His very name His power need another’s name in order to exercise power?”]

“In My name,” He says, “they will cast out demons” (Mark 16).

Did He who made His very name a power need another’s name in order to exercise power?

But what is added afterward? “Behold,” He says, “I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy” (Luke 10).

He certainly says that He is gentle, as He truly was, and humble of heart (Matthew 11). How, then, as possessing supreme power, does He command others to act in His name, if He Himself acted in another’s name? Or how did He give to others as their own what He Himself, as you say, did not possess unless He had received it from another?

Tell me, which of the saints who received power from God acted in this way? Would Peter have been considered insane, or John mad, or Paul senseless, if they had said to the sick: “Rise in our name”; to the lame: “Walk in our name”; to the dead: “Live in our name”; or to certain people: “We give you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy”?

You understand, therefore, your own madness from this: just as these words would be insane if they arose from human presumption, so you are most insane not to understand that they express divine power.

For you must confess one of two things: either that a human being can possess and give divine power, or else, if no human being can do this, that He who could do it was God. No one can bestow divine power as a gift unless he possesses it by nature.

## CHAPTER XXI. That Christ, equally with the Holy Spirit, must be credited with making His flesh and humanity the temple of God

[Col. 0242C]

It follows in your blasphemy that his flesh was made a temple by the Spirit, because John said: “For I saw the Spirit descending from heaven and remaining upon him” (John 1). Since you try to confirm your mad assertion even by divine testimonies, let us see whether the sacred testimony has said what you claim.

[Note: [Col. 0242D] St. Gregory teaches at the end of Book II of the *Moralia* that the Holy Spirit remains in Christ in one way and in holy men in another. “How,” he says, “is it a unique sign that the Holy Spirit remains in Christ? In those gifts without which life cannot be attained, the Holy Spirit always remains, whether in his preachers or in all the elect. But in those gifts by whose manifestation our life is not preserved, but that of others is sought, he does not always remain in his preachers: for he always presides in their hearts so that they may live well, yet he does not always display signs of power through them, but sometimes withdraws from them the manifestation of signs. Christ, however, has the Spirit present in all things, always and continually, because the same Spirit is brought forth from him according to substance. Therefore, although he remains in the holy preachers, he is said to remain uniquely in Christ: because in them he remains by grace for a particular purpose, whereas in him he remains by substance for all things.” Thus Gregory.]

“For I saw,” he says, “the Spirit descending like a dove and remaining upon him.” Distinguish here, if you can, who is more powerful, who is greater, who is more honored: the one who was descending, or the one upon whom he descended? The one who bestowed honor, or the one upon whom honor was bestowed? Where does the testimony here say that he made his flesh a temple of the Spirit? Or in what way did he diminish God’s honor, if God himself descended in order to reveal God to the human race? Certainly, the one whose dignity is indicated must not be understood to be less than the one who indicates that dignity.

But far be it from us to believe that any distinction exists or comes to be within the Godhead: for the one same divinity and equal power entirely exclude the notion of impious inequality. And therefore, in this matter, since the persons of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are all present, and since the Son of God is the one upon whom the descent takes place, the Spirit is the one who descends, and the Father is the one who bears witness, no one received greater honor, and no one suffered any injury. Rather, everything flows equally toward the fullness of the Godhead, because every person in the Trinity contains within himself the honor of the entire Trinity.

And therefore there is no need to say anything further about this, except merely to reveal the cause and origin of your impiety.

[Note: [Col. 0243C] This seems to refer to Luke 6: “For there is no good tree that produces bad fruit, nor is there a bad tree producing good fruit. For each tree is known by its fruit. For they do not gather figs from thorns, nor do they gather grapes from a bramble.”]

For thorns and thistles, springing from their roots, plainly reveal their stock by their own quality; by what they are, they indicate from where they have grown. Thus you too—

[Note: [Col. 0243C] He calls Nestorius the offspring and shoot of the Pelagian heresy for the reason already given: Nestorius was not merely an heir and follower of the Pelagian heresy, but also its champion and supporter, as was shown above (Book I, chapter 3). Others, however (the Basil edition), read: “You display in the shoot the thorny faith of the Pelagian heresy in the offspring which your father is said to have possessed in the root.” Following this reading, Baronius (*Annals*, vol. V, year 420) concludes that the Pelagian Leporius, mentioned below, was the source from whom Nestorius derived his own heresy. But the earlier reading, as easier and clearer, pleased Dr. Cuychius more in the Plantin edition, and I willingly follow it. For it is difficult to explain what those words—“You display the thorny offspring of the Pelagian heresy in the shoot”—mean and how they fit together. According to our reading, the meaning seems to be this: “You, Nestorius, display yourself as the thorny offspring of the Pelagian heresy—which produced nothing but thorns and thistles, like a cursed land—in the shoot, that is, in yourself, who are the shoot of that which your father, that is, your predecessor (namely Pelagius or the Pelagian Leporius), is said to have possessed in the root. For your heresy sprang from his error as from a root; that is, you teach and assert in reality the same things that they taught before you.”]

“You, the thorny offspring of the Pelagian heresy, display in the shoot the same thing which your father is said [Col. 0244A] to have had in the root.”

For that Leporius—for so his disciple Leporius said—asserted that our Lord Christ was made so through baptism; whereas you say that in baptism the temple of God was made through the Spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0244C] Similarly, in Book I, chapter 3: “They added that our Lord and Savior, after baptism, was made Christ, and after the resurrection, God, assigning the one to the mystery of anointing and the other to the merit of his passion.” Hence the new author of an old heresy, Nestorius, observes that by contending that our Lord and Savior—

[Col. 0244D]—was born a solitary man, he says exactly what the Pelagianists had said before, and so forth.]

The words are not indeed identical in full, but the perversity is identical in full.

## CHAPTER XXII  
### Christ’s elevation into heaven is not to be ascribed to the Spirit alone

You add this also to your preceding impieties: that the Spirit granted the Lord elevation into heaven. You thus show, in your sacrilegious understanding, that you believe the Lord Jesus Christ to have been so weak and so destitute that, unless the Spirit had lifted him into heaven, you would perhaps think that he would still today be remaining on earth.

For confirmation of your statement you also produce a sacred testimony. You say: “After giving commands to the apostles whom he had chosen, he was lifted up through the Holy Spirit” (Acts 1). What should I call you? What should I think of you, who by corrupting the divine writings strive to prevent the sacred testimonies from possessing the force of testimonies? This is a new kind of audacity: by arguments born of wickedness, you strive to make falsehood appear to be confirmed by truth.

For it is not said in the Acts of the Apostles as you claim. What does Scripture say? “The things that Jesus began to do and to teach—

[Note: [Col. 0244D] The Author rebukes Nestorius because in these words he perverted and confused not only the meaning of Scripture but also the order of the words. The words “through the Holy Spirit,” which ought to be referred to the choosing of the apostles, he himself referred to Christ’s assumption or ascension, quoting and arranging the passage in this way: “After giving commands to the apostles whom he chose, he was lifted up through the Holy Spirit.” But other authors judge that the phrase διὰ Πνεύματος ἁγίου, “through the Holy Spirit,” can be joined with Christ’s command, with the choice of the apostles, or with Christ’s assumption.

First, it can be referred most immediately to Christ’s command, according to Chrysostom, because Christ gave the apostles spiritual commands under the guidance and inspiration of the Holy Spirit, not human commands, as Chrysostom himself says. The meaning would then be: “Until the day on which he was taken up, after giving, through the Holy Spirit, a command to the apostles whom he had chosen.” He seems to allude to the command reported by Mark in the final chapter:

[Col. 0245B] “Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you.” And immediately afterward he adds: “And the Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, was taken up,” and so forth. Christ therefore commanded the apostles through the Holy Spirit because he delivered to them a command conceived not by a human spirit but by the divine Spirit (so Gagneius).

Second, διὰ Πνεύματος ἁγίου, “through the Holy Spirit,” can be referred to the choosing of the apostles (Salmeron and Lorinus). In order to designate and choose them, Christ is first said to have spent the night in prayer to God, thereby showing that the choice of the apostles made on the following day proceeded not from a human spirit but from the divine Spirit. After his resurrection he breathed the Holy Spirit upon them, after saying: “As the Father sent me, I also send you” (John 20). In this sense the Syriac translator renders the passage: “Until the day on which he was taken up, after he had given commands to those apostles whom he had chosen through the Spirit of holiness.” Thus he.

Christ chose the apostles through the Holy Spirit, not as through another or foreign agent or minister, as Nestorius wished, but through the author of the same inspiration, calling, choosing, and sending that he himself possessed: through his own Spirit, naturally united to him and cooperating with him in all things. For nothing is divided in action where nothing is different in will, as St. Leo says (*Sermon 3 on Pentecost*): “What the Father illuminates, the Son illuminates; the Holy Spirit illuminates,” and so forth.

Finally, “through the Holy Spirit” can be joined—though less suitably—to the verb ἀνελήφθη, “he was taken up,” although Cassian seems to understand the passage otherwise: “Until the day on which he was taken up through the Holy Spirit.” For just as he is said to have been conceived and born of the Holy Spirit (Matthew 1 and Luke 1), justified—that is, sanctified—by the Holy Spirit (1 Timothy 3), anointed and sent to evangelize (Isaiah 61 and Luke 4), and to have cast out demons and performed other miracles in the Spirit of God (Matthew 8), and, according to the Apostle, to have offered himself spotless to God through the Holy Spirit (Hebrews 9), and finally, just as the whole work of our redemption is in a particular way attributed to the Holy Spirit, so he is truly and rightly said to have been taken up into heaven as man through the Holy Spirit, because his ascension and assumption were the completion and consummation of our redemption.

But the words inserted in between—οὓς ἐξελέξατο, “whom he chose”—seem somewhat to hinder this interpretation. For if Luke had wished to join τὸ διὰ Πνεύματος ἁγίου, “through the Holy Spirit,” to the final verb ἀνελήφθη, “he was taken up,” why would he have inserted οὓς ἐξελέξατο, “whom he chose,” when the relative pronoun can refer to no one other than the apostles?

Nestorius therefore is rightly rebuked: he deliberately or rather maliciously chose this interpretation, confused and perplexed by so great a hyperbaton, instead of the two earlier and more convenient interpretations, in order to cast a veil over his error. Yet he accomplished nothing, since Christ was taken up “through the Holy Spirit” and “by the Holy Spirit” in no other way than by the Father and by himself—that is, by the whole Trinity, whose works are undivided, as was said above.

For he was taken up by himself insofar as he was man: that is, by his divinity, or by his divine person, and by his soul, which communicated to his body the gift of agility, one of the gifts assigned to glorified bodies, according to Isaiah 40: “They shall take wings like eagles; they shall fly and shall not faint.”]

“—until the day on which, giving commands to the apostles whom he chose through the Holy Spirit, he was taken up.” [Col. 0245A]

[Note: [Col. 0246B] The Venerable Bede likewise says in his commentaries (Book VIII, chapters 2 and 6): “It must be read by hyperbaton: ‘Until the day on which he was taken up, giving commands concerning the assumption,’ that is, giving commands to the apostles,” and so forth. Among rhetoricians, a hyperbaton is a disturbed order of words and construction. Quintilian interprets it as the transposition of words, which the demands of comparison or elegance frequently require. Niccolò Perotti (*Cornucopia*): “A hyperbaton,” he says, “is wholly confused, as in Virgil (*Aeneid* III):

> The south wind whirls three vessels swept away upon hidden rocks,

> Rocks which the Italians call altars amid the waves.

Thus in Luke’s words there is a hyperbaton, that is, a certain confusion and transposition of the words. For it ought to have been said: “Until the day on which he was taken up,” and so forth. The intervening words make the speech disjointed and less elegant, as in the verse of Psalm 44: “Your arrows are sharp; peoples shall fall beneath you, into the hearts of the king’s enemies.” It would have been more smoothly said and without hyperbaton: “Your arrows are sharp in the hearts of the king’s enemies. And afterward: Peoples shall fall beneath you.” So here: “Until the day on which Jesus was taken up, giving commands,” that is, after he had given commands to the apostles whom he had chosen through the Holy Spirit.]

This is indeed a hyperbaton, and it must be understood as follows: “The things that Jesus began to do and to teach until the day on which he was taken up, giving commands to the apostles whom he had chosen through the Holy Spirit.” Thus, in this matter, perhaps no further answer should be given to you than the testimony itself: for the integrity of a testimony ought fully to suffice for the truth, if correction could suffice for falsehood.

But you, who think that our Lord Jesus Christ could not ascend into heaven unless he were lifted up by the Spirit, tell me—

[Col. 0246A]—how he himself says:

[Note: [Col. 0246C] In addition to what has been noted elsewhere on this subject (Book IV, chapter 6, and Book VI, chapter 22), St. Augustine says in Sermon 14 on the words of the Apostle: “He was on earth and said that he was in heaven; and, what is greater, he spoke of the Son of Man as being in heaven, in order to demonstrate one person in both natures,” and so forth. Theophylact likewise says concerning John: “When you hear the Son of Man descending from heaven” (John 3), “do not think that flesh descended from heaven. Apollinarius taught this: that Christ had a body from heaven, which passed through the Virgin as through a channel. But because Christ is one hypostasis—that is, one person—constituted from two natures, the things that belong to man are spoken of the Word, and the things that belong to the Word are attributed to man. Thus also in this passage the Son of Man is said to descend from heaven, because there is one person, one hypostasis,” and so forth.]

“No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3).

Recognize, then, how ridiculously and foolishly you think that he could not ascend into heaven who, although he had descended to earth, is said never to have been absent from heaven. And consider whether it could have been possible for him, having left the lower regions, to ascend into heaven, when it was also easy for him, while situated on earth, always to remain in the heavenly places.

What of the statement that he himself makes: “I am ascending to my Father” (John 20)?

[Note: [Col. 0246D] St. Gregory speaks very beautifully of Christ’s ascension in Homily 29 on the Gospels, and his words are highly suitable for illustrating this passage: “In the Old Testament we know that Elijah was carried up into heaven” (2 Kings 2), “but the airy heaven is different from the ethereal heaven. The airy heaven is close to the earth; hence we speak of the birds of heaven, because we see them flying in the air. Elijah was therefore lifted up into the airy heaven, so that he might suddenly be brought to a certain hidden region of the earth, where he would live in great repose of flesh and spirit until he should return at the end of the world and pay the debt of death. He postponed death; he did not escape it. But because our Redeemer did not postpone death, he conquered it, consumed it by rising again, and made the glory of his resurrection manifest by ascending.

“It should also be noted that Elijah is said to have ascended in a chariot, in order plainly to show that a mere human being needed assistance from another. Those events and manifestations were accomplished through angels as helpers, because he whom the weakness of his nature weighed down could not even ascend into the airy heaven by himself.

“But our Redeemer is not said to have been lifted up by a chariot or by angels, because he who had made all things was carried above all things by his own power. He returned to where he was and went back from where he remained, because when he ascended into heaven through his humanity, through his divinity he continued to contain both earth and heaven.” Thus Gregory.]

Did he indicate that assistance from another would intervene in this ascension, when in the very statement by which he said that he would ascend he displayed the power of his own authority?

[Note: [Col. 0247B] The reading formerly had *indiguit*, “he needed.” This is not entirely wrong, but the accusative should have been changed to the ablative, which the verb *indigere* requires. Our reading, however, seems easier and more suitable. The verb *indicavit*, “he indicated,” corresponds to the words that follow, *dixit*, “he said,” and *ostendit*, “he showed,” and looks back to the preceding words, “I am ascending to my Father.” By these words Christ did not indicate or signify that he would need the intervention of another in his ascension, but showed that he would ascend by his own power.]

David also spoke of the Lord’s own ascension: “God has ascended with a shout; the Lord with the sound of a trumpet” (Psalm 46). He plainly explained the majesty of the one ascending through the power of the ascension.

## CHAPTER XXIII  
### He persists in the same argument, showing that Christ did not need another’s glory but possessed his own

But let us see how, finally, you conclude your preceding blasphemies by adding this statement: “He nevertheless granted glory to Christ.”

You name glory in order to inflict an insult. For by asserting that glory was granted to the Lord, and by saying that he received it, you blasphemously claim that he was in need. This is what his impious reasoning says: that the generosity of the giver reveals the neediness of the recipient. O wretched impiety of yours! And what becomes of the prophecy by which divinity itself once foretold the Lord Jesus Christ’s ascent into heaven?

[Note: [Col. 0247B] Various and manifold interpretations of this verse and those that follow are found.

The first, and most obvious and literal, is that these are the words of the Psalmist, who, foreseeing through the prophetic Spirit and contemplating in his mind Christ’s glorious ascent into heaven after conquering death, is seized by immense wonder. He addresses and calls upon the princes of the heavenly court in this way: that they should open the heavenly gates to the arriving King of glory and Lord of hosts, that is, to Christ the true God, and should joyfully receive him in triumph. In poetic fashion he introduces the angels asking in turn who this King of glory is—not because the angels were ignorant during the Lord’s ascension that Christ was the King of glory, but to express the immense astonishment produced by the novelty of seeing a true human being in bodily form ascending above all the heavens, not as a guest but as Lord and King of the glorious and eternal city.

The Prophet answers that the King of glory is Christ the Lord, most strong and most powerful, who displayed his power in battle against the prince of darkness, whom he conquered, stripped, and bound. So Bellarmine. The Author seems to understand the passage in this way when he adds: “And when he himself, as divine speech ordinarily does—that is, prophetic speech—had answered himself in the guise of the one asking,” and so forth.

The second interpretation is that there is a dialogue and conversation among the good angels, namely, between the higher and lower angels, discussing among themselves the astonishing ascension of Christ. This is common among almost all the holy Fathers.

Thus Blessed Dionysius the Areopagite says in chapter 7 of *The Celestial Hierarchy*: “The theologians”—that is, the writers on divine things—“indicate this more clearly: namely, that the lower orders of the heavenly spirits most reverently learn from the higher orders the knowledge of divine works, while those who are higher than all the others are taught more sacredly and separately by the Godhead itself, as is fitting. For they introduce some of them as learning the mysteries from those who preceded them, and as coming to know through others that the Lord of the heavenly powers and the King of glory, having assumed human form, had been taken up into heaven. They also introduce others as hesitating at the sight of Jesus himself and desiring to learn the knowledge of that divine work and of the flesh assumed for our sake, while Jesus himself teaches them directly and first implants in them his supreme goodness: ‘For I speak of righteousness and of a judgment of salvation’” (Isaiah 63).

“It is worthy of wonder why even those first angelic powers”—which surpass the others by such an honor of elevation—“should reverently desire to learn the understanding of divine things from God as though they were not among the highest but among the middle ranks. For they do not immediately address words to him, asking: ‘Why are your garments red?’ Rather, they first hesitate among themselves and inquire, showing that they are eager to learn and desire knowledge of the divine work, but do not presume to appropriate it for themselves before the grace of divine illumination has proceeded to them in its proper order.”

Thus the divine Dionysius, combining and joining together the two passages of Scripture as similar and closely related.

St. Jerome says in Letter 142 to Damasus: “The powers that ministered to the ascending Lord called out to the other heavenly powers, so that they might open the gate to the returning Lord: ‘Lift up your gates, O princes,’ or, as Aquila translates it, ‘Raise your heads, O gates, and the King of glory shall enter.’ Again, those powers, astonished by the new mystery when they saw him clothed in flesh, ask: ‘Who is this King of glory?’ They receive the answer: ‘The Lord of hosts himself is the King of glory.’ What is written in Hebrew is ‘the Lord Sabaoth.’ It should be known that wherever the Seventy Translators expressed ‘Lord of hosts’ and ‘Lord Almighty,’ the Hebrew has ‘the Lord Sabaoth,’ and so forth.”

And in chapter 63 of Isaiah, where he similarly compares this passage with that one, he says: “This is the one whom the angelic powers, seeing him ascend to the Father covered in blood, command the other angels: ‘Lift up your gates, O princes, and the King of glory shall enter,’ and so forth.” The angels therefore ask, terrified by the novelty of the event—for the mystery of Christ’s passion and resurrection had been unknown to all former generations, according to the Apostle Paul (2 Corinthians 2): “Who is this who comes from the earth covered in blood?” and so forth.

Finally, in commenting on Psalm 23, he says: “As the Lord ascended, those who went before or accompanied him called out to the other princes among them: ‘Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, O eternal gates.’ That is: open the heavenly entrances; let the eternal entryway stand open.”

St. Augustine says in Sermon 5 on the Lord’s Ascension: “All the heavenly beings saw Christ, beautiful in his wounds, carrying back spoils taken from the tyrant’s camp. Astonished at the shining standards of divine power, they resounded with such hymns and joyfully escorted him: ‘Who is this King of glory?’ And they answered: ‘The Lord of hosts himself is the King of glory.’ This is the one who is white and rose-colored, pierced by the multitude. This is the one who had neither beauty nor comeliness” (Isaiah 53), “weak in the snare, strong in the spoil, lowly in his little body, armed in battle, disfigured in death, beautiful in resurrection, white from the Virgin, red upon the cross, darkened in disgrace, radiant in heaven.”

The third interpretation is that this is a mutual conversation and response between good and evil angels. Thus St. Jerome says in his commentary on the same psalm: “The voice is that of the good angels addressed to the evil angels, whose prince is the devil.” And below: “‘Who is this King of glory?’ The voice of the greater demons, as if they were saying: ‘We have our own king, the devil; who is this King of glory?’ The voice of the good angels: ‘He is strong, who bound your mighty prince; strong when he accepted death, powerful when he conquered hell. In battle, after stripping Tartarus, he led back with him a multitude of captives.’” Thus Jerome.

In the same sense St. Thomas speaks (Part III, question 52, article 2), when he gives reasons why it was fitting for Christ to descend into hell. He assigns this third reason: “So that, just as he showed his power on earth by living and dying, he might also show his power in hell by visiting and illuminating it.” Hence it is said in Psalm 23: “Lift up your gates, O princes.” The Gloss explains: “That is, princes of hell, remove your power by which until now you detained human beings in hell.” And thus “at the name of Jesus every knee should bow,” not only of those in heaven but also of those in hell, as it is said in Philippians 2. Thus St. Thomas.

The same Jerome offers several other interpretations in the same place, which I omit for the sake of brevity.

Moreover, since from the Fathers mentioned above, especially Dionysius and Jerome, it might seem that both angels and demons were ignorant—even during the very Ascension—that Christ was true God, St. Thomas’s notable teaching on this matter should be noted (Part I, question 57, article 5, reply to objection 1):

“Of the mystery of the Incarnation it is possible to speak in two ways. In one way, in general terms; and in this sense it was revealed to all from the beginning of their blessedness. The reason is that this is a certain general principle to which all their offices are ordered. For they are all ministering spirits, as it says in Hebrews 1, sent to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation, which takes place through the mystery of the Incarnation. Hence it was necessary that all should be commonly instructed concerning this mystery from the beginning.

“In another way, we can speak of the mystery of the Incarnation with regard to its particular conditions. In this sense, not all the angels were instructed from the beginning about everything. Indeed, some of the higher angels learned these things only afterward, as is clear from the authority of Dionysius cited above.” Thus St. Thomas.

Lyranus adds that the angels came to know the mystery of the Incarnation through the Church by intuitive knowledge, whereas previously they had known it by abstract knowledge. “The mystery of Christ,” he says, “and especially the calling of the Gentiles, was hidden not only from human beings; the holy angels also did not know it fully until it was accomplished through the preaching of the apostles. Previously they possessed only a simple knowledge, which may be called abstract, insofar as it concerns a thing that is not present. But when it was accomplished, they possessed experimental or intuitive knowledge,” and so forth.

According to this understanding, therefore, the words of Dionysius and Jerome—which seem to attribute ignorance both of the Incarnation and of Christ’s divinity to the blessed angels, even during his Ascension—should be interpreted to mean that they did not fully and clearly know all its circumstances, conditions, and effects. These they learned afterward through divine revelation, the preaching of the apostles, and experience itself.

To this also pertains the statement of St. Paul (Ephesians 3): “To me, the least of all the saints, this grace was given: to evangelize among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ and to enlighten all concerning the dispensation of the mystery hidden from the ages in God, who created all things, so that through the Church the manifold wisdom of God might be made known to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places,” and so forth.]

“Lift up your gates,” he says, “and the King of glory shall enter” (Psalm XXIII). [Col. 0249A]

And when he himself, as divine speech ordinarily does, had answered himself in the guise of one asking, “Who is this King of glory?” he immediately added: “The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle,” showing under the name of a battle fought the victory of the triumphant Lord.

Then, to complete the exposition of the matter, when he had repeated the text of the foregoing speech, he displayed the majesty of the Lord entering heaven in this conclusion, saying: “The Lord of hosts—he himself is the King of glory.” Clearly, lest the assumption of a body diminish the honor of the supreme divinity, he taught that the same Lord of hosts and King of heavenly glory was the one whom above he had proclaimed victorious in the battle against hell.

Now say that glory was granted to the Lord, since both prophecy said that he was the King of glory and he himself bore witness concerning himself: “When the Son of Man comes in his glory” (Matthew 25). Contradict this, if you can, and oppose it, so that while he testifies that he possesses his own glory, you may say that he received another’s.

Although we say that he possesses glory proper to himself, we nevertheless do not deny that this very property of glory is shared by him with the Spirit and the Father. For whatever God possesses belongs to the Godhead; and the kingdom of glory is so proper to the Son of God that it is nevertheless not divided from the property of the whole Godhead.

## CHAPTER XXIV  
### He confirms this teaching by the authority of Blessed Hilary
But at last it is time to bring this book—or rather, the entire work—to a conclusion, provided that I add the statements of a few holy men and distinguished priests, so that what we have already established by the authority of sacred testimonies may also be strengthened by the faith of the present age.

[Note: [Col. 0250C] Saint Hilary, bishop of Poitiers and a contemporary of Saint Athanasius, although he became a Christian only at an advanced age, nevertheless made such rapid progress in ecclesiastical doctrine that he was deservedly regarded as a great teacher and a pillar of the Catholic Church (Bellarmine, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*). Concerning him the Roman Martyrology says (13 January): “At Poitiers in Gaul, the feast of Saint Hilary, bishop and confessor, who, because of the Catholic faith which he vigorously defended, was exiled to Phrygia for four years and, among other miracles, raised a dead man.” As Baronius notes there, Saint Jerome writes about him especially in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, in the *Apology against Rufinus*, in Letter 6 to Florentius, Letter 7 to Laeta, Letter 84 to Magnus, *Against the Luciferians*, [Col. 0250D] and elsewhere; Sulpicius Severus in Book II of his *Sacred History*; Rufinus in Book II of his *History*, chapters 30 and 31; Socrates, Book III, chapter 8; Sozomen, Book III, chapter 13, and Book V, chapter 12; and Cassiodorus in the preface to *Divine Readings*. Fortunatus wrote Hilary’s deeds in two books, but touched on only a few of them out of many. Venantius Fortunatus also has an epigram about him in Book XII, *On His Miracles*, and Gregory of Tours writes about him in *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 2.]

Hilary was a man adorned with every virtue and distinction, remarkable in life as well as in eloquence; [Col. 0250B] he became both a teacher of the Churches and a priest, growing not only through his own merits but also through the advancement of others. Amid the storms of persecution he stood so immovable that, through the strength of his unconquered faith, [Note: [Col. 0250D] At this point one must not pass over the distinguished and noteworthy observation of Cardinal Baronius concerning the term “confessor” (*Notes on the Martyrology*, 2 January): “It should be understood,” he says, “that our predecessors used this word with a meaning very different from that of the present age. They called no one by this name unless, when challenged, he had confessed the faith of Christ openly before its enemies. If he had undergone some form of torture but had not succumbed to martyrdom, he was then called both a martyr and, at times, also a confessor, since he had not yet completed his martyrdom. Although, if the force of these words is considered, they are identical, nevertheless it is sufficiently established that both Tertullian (*To the Martyrs*) and Cyprian, as well as most of the ancients, customarily understood them in the sense just described. If you wish to know these matters more precisely, consult especially Cyprian’s Letters 7, 9, 10, 15, 30, 31, 52, and 81 in Pamelius’s edition; he made the same observation in his scholia on Letter 9 (Notes on Letters 9, 30, and 83).”

Thus far Baronius; shortly afterward he adds: “According to the judgment of that same Cyprian, one who thrust himself into martyrdom without having been challenged was called a *professor*. If someone, still seized by fear lest he betray the faith, abandoned his own people and possessions and lived in voluntary exile far from his homeland, he was called an *extorris*—an exile—whose condition was not to be despised; indeed, he was to be counted among the martyrs if he had suffered death for that reason. All these expressions belong to the custom of the ancestors and to the ancient manner of speaking. Later, usage prevailed whereby all who had lived a holy and praiseworthy life and had finally rested in the Lord with a holy and approved end were called confessors.” Thus far Baronius. Consult the same author in volumes III and IV of the *Annals*.

From this it is easy to understand in what sense Hilary is said to have gained or received the dignity even of a confessor: by the steadfastness of his faith he overcame not only the Arian bishops but also the emperor Constantius, likewise an Arian. In view of the persecutions and exile endured for the faith, he deserved, according to ancient usage, to be called not merely a confessor but also a martyr. In this sense the Church sings of Saint Martin of Tours: “O most holy soul, whom, although the sword of the persecutor did not take away, nevertheless did not lose the palm of martyrdom” (Sulpicius Severus, Letter on the Death of Saint Martin; Baronius, volume IV, under the year 369).]

he also gained [Col. 0251A] the dignity of a confessor. [Note: [Col. 0251C] By “the books of the faith” he means the books on the Trinity composed by Hilary. Concerning them Saint Jerome says in his *Catalogue*: “Exiled from the synod of Béziers to Phrygia, he composed twelve books against the Arians,” and so forth. He commends them when writing to Laeta (Letter 7) in these words: “Let her read the letters of Athanasius and the books of Hilary without stumbling; let her delight in the intellects of those whose books do not allow the piety of faith to falter.” This concerns their sound doctrine of the Trinity, about which controversies existed between Catholics and Arians.

Sozomen says of the same works (Book III, chapter 1): “They report that Hilary’s books on the faith were highly commended even by those who defended an opinion contrary to the Catholic faith.” Cassiodorus, moreover (*On Divine Readings*, chapter 16), mentions thirteen books of Hilary written on the Trinity—unless this is perhaps an error—writing as follows: “For the confirmation of our faith and the prevention of the heretics’ snares, the thirteen books of blessed Hilary should be read, which he composed on the holy Trinity in language exceedingly profound and eloquent.”]

In the first book of *The Faith* [*On the Trinity*, Book I], he testifies that the Lord Jesus Christ is true God from true God, born before the ages and afterward born as man. Likewise, in the second book: [Note: [Col. 0251D] These and other words of Hilary are quoted by Pope Leo the Great in Letter 97, addressed to Emperor Leo, chapter 3.]

“One only-begotten God, inserted into the form of a little human body in the womb of the holy Virgin, grows; he who contains all things, and within whom all things are, is brought forth according to the law of human birth.”

Likewise, in the same book: “The angel is witness: God is with us, he who is born.”

Likewise, in Book X: “We have also taught the mystery of God born as man from the Virgin’s childbirth.”

Likewise, in the same work: “For although God was born as man, he was not born for that reason so that he might cease to remain God.”

Likewise, in the preface to his *Commentary on the Gospel according to Matthew*: [Note: [Col. 0252B] Saint Jerome also mentions this work in his catalogue of Hilary’s writings.]

“For it was first necessary for us that the only-begotten God, for our sake becoming man, should be born as what he then was not.”

The same author says in the same work: “Next, it was fitting that, since God was born as man in the world, and so forth.”

These are only a few examples from a great many. Nevertheless, you can see from what we have said that he openly and plainly proclaims God to have been born of Mary. And where is that statement of yours: “A creature could not give birth to the Creator; what is born of flesh is flesh”? It would be a long task to produce corresponding testimonies from each individual author. What should be done is rather an enumeration than a full exposition of the statements, since they themselves are sufficient for their own exposition.

## CHAPTER XXV. He shows that Ambrose agrees with the foregoing testimony of Hilary

[Note: [Col. 0252B] Saint Ambrose, bishop of Milan, a most holy and learned doctor of the Church, flourished under the emperors Gratian and Theodosius. Concerning him the Roman Martyrology says (4 April): “The deposition of Saint Ambrose, bishop and confessor, through whose zeal, among other distinctions of doctrine and miracles, almost all Italy was converted to the Catholic faith during the time of the Arian perfidy.” Baronius should be consulted in his notes.

A *Life of Saint Ambrose* exists, written with the greatest fidelity by a certain Paulinus—not Paulinus, bishop of Nola, as Baronius himself shows in the *Annals* (Volume V, under the year 397), but a cleric of the Church of Milan and Ambrose’s own secretary. He wrote it at the urging and encouragement of Saint Augustine, as he himself testifies at its beginning, writing as follows: “You urge me, venerable Father Augustine, to pursue with my pen the life of blessed Ambrose, bishop of the Church of Milan, just as the blessed men Athanasius and the presbyter Jerome pursued in writing the lives of Saints Paul and Antony, who lived in the desert; and just as Severus, servant of God, composed in words the life of Martin, venerable bishop of the Church of Tours,” and so forth.

So he writes. Baronius nevertheless says that he did so more briefly than was appropriate, and that, to the great loss of posterity, he omitted very many things. We wrote a fuller life of that most holy Father, which Pope Sixtus, the supreme pontiff—at whose command I undertook the task—had prefixed to his edition of the works of Saint Ambrose. When you find anything different in it from what is written about him in the *Annals*—for later reflections are usually better—you will understand that it was composed to confirm that account. Thus Baronius. He says nearly the same in his notes on the Martyrology for 7 December, the day on which the ordination of Saint Ambrose, bishop and doctor of the Church, is commemorated; there he acknowledges that his life was also published by John Costerus, namely in the Basel edition of 1555.]

Ambrose, an outstanding priest of God, who, never departing from the hand of the Lord, shone continually as a jewel on God’s finger, [Note: [Col. 0252D] He alludes to the custom of the great, who, if they possess a gem more precious than others and especially brilliant and radiant, set it in gold and wear it not so much for the finger as for the eyes; they guard it with the utmost care, scarcely ever remove it, and sometimes use it as a seal. Hence it is called a signet or seal ring.
