To this may be added the familiar proverb among us: “Guard your faithful servant as a pearl upon the fingernail.” The following passage from Ecclesiasticus 33 may also be referred to this: “If you have a faithful servant, let him be to you as your own soul.” Likewise Exodus 13: “And it shall be as a sign upon your hand, and as a memorial before your eyes, and so that the law of the Lord may always be in your mouth.”]

mentions in the book addressed to Virgins, as follows (Book I): [Note: [Col. 0253C] Four books—or rather treatises—of nearly the same subject were published by Saint Ambrose, all of which were contained in the first volume of the old Paris edition and of several other earlier editions. In a later Paris edition of 1586, however, they were placed, in a different order, in the fifth and final volume.

The first treatise is *On Virgins*, addressed to his sister Marcellina and consisting of three books; the second is *Exhortation to Virgins*, in one book; the third, entitled *Institution of a Virgin*, addressed to Eusebius, in one book; and the fourth, *To a Devoted Virgin*, in one book. Another book, *To a Fallen Virgin*, follows. In Bellarmine’s judgment (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*), however, this does not appear to be by Saint Ambrose, for the reason he gives.

The words of Ambrose quoted here are not found in the book commonly entitled *To Virgins*, but in the first book *On Virgins*. They are also read somewhat differently in that author, as follows: “My brother is white and red. For it is fitting that you should know fully, O virgin, whom you love, and recognize in him both the mystery of innate divinity and that of the assumed embodiment. He is rightly white, because he is the splendor of the Father; red, because he is the offspring of the Virgin. For in him the color of both natures shines and gleams. Remember, nevertheless, that the signs of divinity in him are older than the mysteries of the body, because he did not begin from the Virgin; rather, he who already was came into the Virgin.” Thus Ambrose.

Cassian altered a few words from this passage and omitted a few that were unnecessary. According to the title now commonly used, he should have said “in the first book *On Virgins*,” rather than “in the book *To Virgins*.” But this may perhaps be an error of the period rather than of the author.]

“My brother is white and red. He is white because he is the splendor of the Father; red because he is the offspring of the Virgin. Remember, nevertheless, that the signs of divinity in him are older than the mysteries of the body. For he did not begin from the Virgin; rather, he who already was came into the Virgin.”

Likewise, in his work [Note: [Col. 0254B] These words are found not in any of the sermons now circulated under Saint Ambrose’s name, but, for the most part, in Saint Augustine’s sixth sermon on the Nativity of the Lord. Many sermons attributed to Ambrose are found among Augustine’s sermons; others likewise among the sermons of Saint Maximus, as Bellarmine shows (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*): “So that it cannot plainly be judged,” he says, “whether they should be attributed to Ambrose or Maximus.” It is also certain that very many sermons of Ambrose have been lost, as Baronius teaches (*Annals*, Volume V, under the year 397). They may still have existed in Cassian’s time, including that sermon on the Nativity of the Lord from which the words quoted here may have been taken.]

*On the Nativity of the Lord*: “Behold the miracle [Note: [Col. 0254C] In that sermon as found in Augustine, the reading is: ‘of the body of the Lord’s mother.’] of the Lord’s mother: a virgin conceived, a virgin gave birth, a virgin while giving birth, a virgin pregnant, a virgin after childbirth. As it is said in Ezekiel: ‘The gate was closed, and it was not opened, because the Lord passed through it’ (Ezekiel 44). Glorious virginity and splendid fecundity! The Lord of the world is born, and there is no groan of the woman in labor; the womb is emptied and the true infant is received, yet virginity is not violated. It was fitting that, when God was born, the merit of chastity should increase, and that by his coming forth the intact state should not be violated—he who had come to heal what was corrupt.”

Likewise, in his *Commentary on the Gospel according to Luke*: [Note: [Col. 0254C] Ambrose, whose authorship of this exposition no one doubts, begins the second book as follows: “The divine mysteries are indeed hidden, and, according to the prophetic statement (Isaiah 41), no human being can easily know the counsel of God. Nevertheless, from the other deeds and commands of the Lord our Savior we can understand that it was also a matter of a more deliberate counsel that the woman chosen above all others to give birth to the Lord was one who had been betrothed to a man. But why was she not made pregnant before she was betrothed?” and so forth.

The words that follow—“He certainly proclaims God to have been born of the Virgin,” and so on—are not the words of Ambrose but of Cassian, arguing from Ambrose against Nestorius. Ambrose does proclaim God born of the Virgin and calls Mary the Mother of God, when he asserts that she was chosen by God to give birth to God. For what else does it mean to be the Mother of God, or *Theotokos* (θεοτόκος), than to have given birth to God?]

“For this very reason she was chosen to give birth to God: she had been betrothed to a man” (Book II). “He certainly proclaims God to have been born of the Virgin and calls Mary the Mother of God.”

And where is that monstrous and execrable statement of yours, in which you say, [Note: [Col. 0254D] This is what Nestorius said above in different words (Book VI, chapter 13, and Book VII, chapter 3): “Birth must be consubstantial with the parent.” It was refuted there at greater length.]

“How can a mother be the mother of one alien to her nature? If she is called mother by them, what was born is humanity, not God.” [Col. 0255A] Behold the outstanding teacher of the faith: he says that the one who gave birth was a human being, and that the one who was born was God; nevertheless, he does not regard this as a cause of unbelief but as a miracle of faith.

## CHAPTER XXVI. He adds the testimony of Saint Jerome to the foregoing

[Col. 0256A]

[Note: [Col. 0255A] Saint Jerome, presbyter and eminent doctor of the Church, who, as the Roman Martyrology says, “having attained mastery of every branch of literature and become an imitator of approved monks, pierced many monstrous heresies with the sword of his teaching; finally, having lived to extreme old age, he rested in peace and was buried at the Lord’s manger.” Thus far the Martyrology.

He deservedly and rightly received the title “doctor of the Church” for his outstanding learning, admired in every age—not only after his death but while he was still living—as Baronius gathers from this very passage of Cassian (*Notes on the Martyrology*, 30 September), where he is called by the most exalted title “teacher of the Catholics.”

No less distinguished and illustrious are the testimonies handed down by Saint Augustine and other Fathers concerning Saint Jerome’s remarkable learning and his writings, which, as is said here, shine throughout the world like lamps. It is enough to quote a few of them, all agreeing with this passage.

Augustine, who compares him with John the Baptist, acknowledges that he neither possessed nor could ever possess as much knowledge of the divine Scriptures as he saw in Jerome (Letter 113). In another letter (Letter 15) he says: “Although, according to the titles of honor that ecclesiastical usage has now established, the episcopate is greater than the presbyterate, nevertheless in many matters Augustine is less than Jerome.”

Writing against Julian (Book I, chapter 7), he says: “Do not despise holy Jerome because he was a presbyter. He was learned in Greek, Latin, and also Hebrew eloquence; passing from the Western Church to the Eastern, he lived to extreme old age amid the holy places and sacred writings. His eloquence shone for us from East to West like a lamp.”

Likewise, in Book XVIII of *The City of God* (chapter 43): “In our own times there was the presbyter Jerome, a most learned man and skilled in three languages, who translated the Scriptures into Latin not from Greek but from Hebrew.”

Following Augustine, Prosper expressed the same thought in verse, writing the following about Jerome in his *Book against the Ungrateful*:

“Graceful in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin speech,  
An example of character and teacher of the world,” and so forth.

Cassian likewise, in the preface to the *Institutes*, mentions Basil together with Jerome: “Another”—namely Jerome—“not only published books worked out by his own intellect, but also rendered works composed in the Greek language into Latin eloquence.”

Cassiodorus expresses the same judgment (*On Divine Readings*, chapter 21), adding, after very high praise of the man: “I do not think that he lived idly at Bethlehem except so that, in that land of miracles, his eloquence too might shine for us from the East like the sun.” [Col. 0255D] [“*Lampare*,” meaning “to shine,” from the Greek verb λάμπω, *lampo*.]

Marcellinus Comes likewise writes in his *Chronicle*: “He ended his life at a very advanced age and was buried there”—namely at Bethlehem—“an unconquerable tower to the Catholics but an indefatigable enemy to the heretics, fighting both by the discipline of his life and by the assertions of the books he published.”

Finally, Marianus Victorius adorns the life of Saint Jerome that he himself wrote—which Baronius also commends (*Annals*, Volume V, under the year 420)—with this notable eulogy, which must not be omitted:

“Jerome is a man for whom neither the Greeks nor the Latins have anyone whom they can compare with him. For all learning and virtues came together in him in such abundance that, after him, the Church finds no one whom the nations could envy him in any particular. Although we have had many outstanding and learned men in the Church, we find no one who knew so many and such great things in every branch of learning, or who possessed knowledge of so many languages. If he is surpassed by someone in one respect, there always remain other respects in which Jerome, finally excelling that person, departs as victor.”

Thus he writes.]

Jerome, the teacher of the Catholics, whose writings shine throughout the world like divine lamps, [Note: [Col. 0256A] Here he calls the book addressed to Eustochium the twenty-second letter of Saint Jerome, concerning the preservation of virginity. It was addressed to Eustochium, the noble Roman daughter of Paula and a virgin devoted to God, about whom we have said more elsewhere. At its conclusion, according to the edition of Marianus (*Notes on the Rule of Saint Pachomius*), these words are found: [Col. 0256B] “The Son of God, for our salvation, became the Son of man; he awaits birth for ten months in the womb; he endures the discomforts of pregnancy; he emerges bloody; he is wrapped in cloths and soothed by caresses; and he who encloses the world in the hollow of his hand is confined within the narrowness of a manger.” Thus there.

It is plausible, however, that Cassian read *ten months* in ancient copies of Jerome rather than *nine months*, which explains why he repeats and emphasizes the same words twice in this chapter. It seemed preferable to retain this reading as both more ancient and more authentic rather than alter it. There is no difficulty in saying that Christ awaited birth for ten months—that is, remained hidden in the Virgin’s womb before being born—not for ten complete months, but after nine had been completed and the tenth begun. This is an entirely customary ecclesiastical manner of speaking.

Indeed, the statement “he awaited ten months” has greater force and emphasis than “nine,” as is clear in itself. It is highly credible that Saint Jerome had this in mind, with Scripture supporting it, where Solomon says: “I too am mortal,” and so forth: “For ten months I was formed, compacted in blood, from the seed of a man” (Wisdom 7).

It is established both by ecclesiastical tradition and by the authority of the holy Fathers—Athanasius in *Questions to Antiochus*, Chrysostom in his first homily on Luke, and Augustine in Sermon 18 on the Nativity of the Lord and in Book IV of *On the Trinity*, chapter 5—that the Lord Christ was conceived on 25 March and born on 25 December. Augustine explains this judgment most beautifully as follows:

“Not without reason, in the building of the Lord’s body, whose figure was the temple which he said he would raise again in three days when the Jews had built it, the number six itself is understood as representing a year. For they said: ‘This temple was built in forty-six years’ (John 2), and forty-six times six makes 276. That number of days completes nine months and six days, which, as though they were ten months, are reckoned for women giving birth. This is not because all women reach the sixth day after the ninth month, but because the perfection of the Lord’s body is found to have been brought to birth after so many days, as the authority of the Church, receiving the tradition handed down by the ancients, preserves.

He is believed to have been conceived on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, the day on which he also suffered. Thus the new tomb in which he was buried, where no dead person had been placed either before or afterward, corresponds to the Virgin’s womb in which he was conceived, where no mortal seed had been sown. He is traditionally said to have been born on the eighth day before the Kalends of January.

From that day to this day, when counted, 276 days are found; that number contains forty-six groups of six. The temple was built in that number of years because, through that number of sixes, the Lord’s body was perfected; destroyed by the suffering of death, it was raised again in three days. For he was speaking of the temple of his body, as the Gospel’s clearest and strongest testimony declares when it says: ‘Just as Jonah was in the belly of the sea monster for three days and three nights, so the Son of man will be in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights’ (Matthew 12).

Scripture bears witness that this three-day period was not complete and entire: the first day was counted in full from its latter part, while the third day was counted in full from its beginning; the day between them, the second day, was wholly complete in its twenty-four hours, twelve of night and twelve of day.”

Thus far Saint Augustine. He says similar things in *Eighty-Three Questions*, question 56, and in his *Tractate on Psalm 132*.

From these statements we understand that nine months and six days intervened between Christ’s conception and birth, a period containing 276 days. If, according to ancient custom, thirty days are assigned to each of the nine months, the total is 270 days, leaving six days belonging to the tenth month and counted as part of it (see Orosius, Book VII, chapter 2, and Peter Damian, *Letters*, Book II, Letter 21).

Therefore what John of Damascus handed down in Book IV of *The Orthodox Faith*, chapter 15, is entirely true: Christ completed nine months in his mother’s womb and had already entered the tenth when he came into the light. His words are: “For since he is born at the customary time—for he is born after completing nine months and reaching the tenth—this occurs according to the law of childbirth; but birth without pain is beyond the law of childbirth.”

The same conclusion is drawn from the letter of Volusianus to Saint Augustine and Augustine’s reply to him (Letters 2 and 3 among Augustine’s letters), where these words likewise appear, as though taken from Jerome: “But the Lord and ruler of the world filled the body of an undefiled woman; the mother endured the discomforts of ten months, and yet she gave birth as a virgin,” and so forth.

Both statements, therefore, are true: Christ may be said to have awaited birth for nine months or for ten, provided the preceding explanation is understood. To avoid this ambiguity, the Roman Martyrology expresses the matter more clearly in these words, full of majesty and holiness (8 days before the Kalends of January): “Jesus Christ, eternal God and Son of the eternal Father, wishing to consecrate the world by his most holy coming, conceived by the Holy Spirit and, after nine months had elapsed from his conception, is born at Bethlehem in Judah from the Virgin Mary, having become man.”]

says in his book addressed to Eustochium: “The Son of God, for our salvation, became the Son of man; he awaits birth for ten months in the womb; and he whose hand encloses the world is confined within the narrowness of a manger.”

Likewise, in his commentary on Isaiah (on Isaiah 7): “For the Lord of hosts, who is the King of glory, descended into the Virgin’s womb and entered and departed through the eastern gate, which always remains closed” (Ezekiel 44). “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born in you will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1).

[Note: [Col. 0257D] Up to this point these are Jerome’s words in that commentary on Isaiah. What follows, however, belongs to Cassian, with an apostrophe addressed to Nestorius, as in the preceding passages.]

And in Proverbs: “Wisdom built herself a house” (Proverbs 9).

Compare this, if you please, with your doctrine—or rather, your blasphemy—in which you say: “For God is the creator of months, not the offspring of months.” [Note: [Col. 0257D] Evagrius expressed this blasphemy of Nestorius, and its origin, more clearly in Book I, chapter 2, where he recounts what happened. We have already related the same matters above, and there is no reason to repeat them here.

Cyril likewise writes the following about Nestorius in Letter 20: “We marveled at the man’s stubbornness. For he did not repent, nor did he weep over what he had dared to say against Christ our Savior before all of us; rather, while present at Ephesus, he used the same expressions and again showed that he held perverse opinions. Thus, when distinguished and most devout metropolitan bishops spoke to him and established and proved from divine Scripture that God was the one born according to the flesh from the holy Virgin, he used this impious expression: ‘I do not call a two- or three-month-old God,’ along with other statements by which he removed the Incarnation of the Only-Begotten.”

[Col. 0258B] The wicked Nestorius uttered these things when he conferred with Theodotus, bishop of Ancyra, and Acacius of Melitene. These men afterward reported the same matters to the Fathers assembled at the Council of Ephesus, as the acts of that council record.]

Behold, then, Jerome: a man of the greatest learning and of the most approved and pure doctrine. In nearly the same words by which you deny that the Son of God is an offspring of months, he testifies that he is an offspring of months. ‘For he awaits birth,’ he says, ‘for ten months in the womb.’ But perhaps the authority of this man seems small to you. Consider everyone to say the same thing, and in the same words; for whoever does not deny that the Son of God is the offspring of the Virgin confesses that he is the offspring of months.

## CHAPTER XXVII. He adds Rufinus and blessed Augustine to the foregoing testimony
[Note: [Col. 0258B] Rufinus, or Ruffinus, a presbyter of Aquileia, was once a very close friend of Saint Jerome, as the holy Jerome himself writes in Letter 5 to Florentius: “Brother Rufinus,” he says, “is joined to me by an indivisible affection of brotherhood. Do not judge us by his merits: in him you will behold the clearly expressed traces of holiness,” and so forth. Likewise, in writing to Rufinus himself in Letter 41, he expresses his love for him as follows: “O if the Lord Jesus Christ would now suddenly grant me either Philip’s translation to the eunuch (Acts 18), or Habakkuk’s to Daniel (Dan. 15), how I would now clasp your neck tightly in my embrace; how I would fix upon my lips that mouth which has sometimes erred or spoken wisely with me.” And below: “Believe me, Brother, no sailor tossed by a storm so looks for a harbor, no thirsty fields so long for rain, no anxious mother sitting on a curved shore so awaits her son, as I have longed since a sudden whirlwind tore me from your side, since an impious separation ripped me away from one joined to me by the bond of charity,” and so forth.

Later, however, Rufinus became his bitterest enemy, as Rufinus’s attacks against the holy Jerome abundantly testify. Among other works, he wrote an exposition of the Apostles’ Creed, explaining each of its articles at great length and confirming them from the Scriptures of both Testaments. This work, long ago published under Rufinus’s name among the works of the holy Jerome, now appears among the works of Saint Cyprian, in the edition of Pamelius.

Concerning Rufinus, Gennadius of Marseille gives the following remarks, agreeing with Cassian’s statements, in his book *On Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 17: “Rufinus, a presbyter of the Church of Aquileia, was no small part of the Church’s teachers, and in translating from Greek into Latin he possessed an elegant talent. Finally, for the most part he presented the Greeks’ library to the Latins.” And below: “By his own labor—or rather by the grace and gift of God—the same Rufinus expounded the Creed, so that compared with him others may seem not to have expounded it at all.”

Thus far Gennadius may be tolerated; but toward the end of the same chapter he deserves correction, since he is not an entirely trustworthy author. While he so exalts Rufinus that he diminishes the holy Jerome and gravely accuses him as though he were Rufinus’s rival and detractor, he acts with the same rashness (chapters 38, 84, 19, 32, and 42) with which he disparages Saint Augustine, another light of the Church, for excessive speech—or rather for error; condemns Prosper’s book *Against the Collator*; commends Pelagius’s *Eulogies*, which the holy Jerome, in Book 1 *Against the Pelagians*, chapter 85, declares to be full of heresies; extols with extraordinary praise the two books of Faustus the Semi-Pelagian, *On Grace and Free Will*, which Peter the Deacon and all the Easterners anathematize; praises Severus’s *Dialogue*, which the holy Jerome, in his commentary on Ezekiel 36, and after him Pope Gelasius, in the chapter “Sancta Romana,” distinction 15, reject; and, finally, makes many other similar statements, by which he left considerable suspicion that his faith was not sound. So says Cardinal Bellarmine.

But where Rufinus should be ranked among ecclesiastical writers, and how inferior he was in authority, holiness, and learning to Jerome, was declared by Pope Gelasius in the Roman council of seventy bishops, in a solemn decree issued in these words (D., chapter “Sancta Romana,” in Gratian): “We receive with every honor the Lives of the Fathers, of Paul, Antony, Hilarion, and all the hermits, which the most blessed Jerome nevertheless wrote.” And below: “Rufinus, a religious man, published many books of ecclesiastical works and also interpreted certain Scriptures; but because blessed Jerome censured him on some points concerning freedom of choice, we hold those views which we know the aforesaid blessed Jerome to have held. And this applies not only to Rufinus, but also to all whom the man so often mentioned criticized out of zeal for God and reverence for the faith.” Thus Gelasius. Let Gennadius now go and compare Rufinus with Saint Jerome—or, more impudently, prefer him to Jerome.]

Rufinus too, a man of Christian philosophy, [Col. 0259A] no negligible portion of the teachers of the Church, bears this testimony concerning the Lord’s birth in his exposition of the Creed: “For the Son of God,” he says, “is born from a Virgin, not joined principally to the flesh alone, but generated with the soul intervening between the flesh and God.”

[Note: [Col. 0259B] To make Rufinus’s meaning in these words clearer, his complete sentence should apparently be quoted. It reads as follows: “The substance of God, which is incorporeal in every respect, cannot in itself be inserted into bodies or be received by them unless there is some intermediate spiritual substance capable of receiving the divine spirit. For example, we may say that light can illuminate all the members of the body, but can be received by none of them except the eye alone; for the eye alone is capable of light. Thus, then, the Son of God is born from a Virgin, not joined principally to the flesh alone, but generated with the soul intervening between the flesh and God. Therefore, with the soul intervening, and with the Word of God received in the secret citadel of the rational spirit, God was born from the Virgin without any of the injury you imagine. Consequently, nothing shameful is to be supposed there, where the sanctification of the spirit was present, and where the soul, which was capable of God, also became a participant in the flesh.”

So Rufinus. Similar statements are found in Augustine and Damascene. Augustine, in Book *On Christian Combat*, chapter 18, says: “The invisible and unchangeable Truth, receiving flesh through the soul and the soul through the spirit, having assumed the whole human being, freed him from every weakness without any contamination of itself.” Damascene, in Book 3 of *The Orthodox Faith*, chapter 6, says: “The Word of God was united to the flesh through the mind as an intermediary, the mind intervening between God’s purity and the grossness of the flesh. For the mind holds primacy over the soul and the flesh, while God is the purest reality of the mind.”

To understand what the Fathers intend by such statements, it should first be noted that the two terms “spirit” and “soul” do not signify different entities, but different functions of one and the same entity, namely the rational soul. For “spirit,” or “mind,” means the soul’s higher part, which contemplates divine and human realities; whereas the soul’s lower part is directed toward human and temporal matters. Augustine repeatedly distinguishes them in this way.

Second, this doctrine signifies no temporal order, but only an order of nature, derived from the various degrees of excellence belonging to those parts of which our nature consists. As far as temporal order is concerned, it must be held as certain and definite that the soul was not assumed earlier in time than the flesh, nor the flesh joined to the Word earlier in time than the soul; rather, all the parts of human nature were assumed simultaneously and at the same moment by the Son of God. Emphasizing this, Saint Augustine writes in Letter 3 to Volusianus: “When the Word of God was mingled with a soul possessing a body, he assumed both soul and body simultaneously.” And in the *Enchiridion*, chapter 34: “We must understand ‘flesh’ as the whole human being wherever it is said, ‘The Word became flesh.’ For it is not permissible to say that anything belonging to human nature was lacking in that assumption.”

There are also, in Nicephorus (Book 17, chapter 28), canons of the Council of Constantinople expressing this doctrine: “If anyone says or thinks that the Lord’s soul pre-existed and was united to God the Word before the Incarnation and birth from the Virgin, let him be anathema.” And: “If anyone says or thinks that the body of our Lord Jesus Christ was first formed in the Virgin’s womb and afterward God the Word and the soul—which had previously existed—were united to it, let him be anathema.”

Third, one must also take care not to conceive of Christ’s flesh as united through the soul in such a way that it is understood not to be united proximately and immediately, but with the soul interposed, as though it were binding and joining the flesh to the Word, just as adhesive bodies are said to lie between things that we want to adhere to one another. The divinity is joined proximately and intimately both to the flesh and to the soul; nor can the soul be understood as nearer than the flesh by some arrangement or order of position, which has a place only in the conjunction of bodies.

Fourth, therefore, it remains that we should consider here only an order of nature and dignity. Since, by order of nature and excellence, the soul surpasses the body, and the mind or spirit surpasses the soul, and since the soul therefore approaches more closely than the body, and the spirit more closely than the soul, to the perfection and purity of the divine nature, an order of this kind is rightly established in the assumption of these parts, so that the soul is said to be assumed through the spirit, and the body through the soul, or through the mediation of the soul. See the Master of the Sentences, Book 3, distinction 2, and Saint Thomas (Part 3, question 6, articles 1 and 2).]

“Was he not clearly testifying that God was born from a human being?”

[Note: [Col. 0260C] The Roman Martyrology, on the fifth day before the Kalends of September: “At Hippo Regius in Africa, the birth into heaven of Saint Augustine, bishop and outstanding doctor of the Church. Converted to the Catholic faith through the work of blessed Bishop Ambrose and baptized, he defended it most vigorously against the Manichaeans and other heretics, and after undertaking many other labors for the Church of God, he departed to heavenly rewards,” and so forth.

Baronius adds in his notes a point that also concerns our present purpose: Augustine departed this life during the consulship of Theodosius XIII and Valentinian, when he was being summoned by an imperial delegation of Theodosius to the Ecumenical Council of Ephesus—namely, the council convened against Nestorius, at which Nestorius was also condemned. The year was 430 after the Lord’s birth. See Baronius there in the *Annals*.

Possidius, bishop of Calama, writes in his *Life of Augustine*: “Through Ambrose, the priest most pleasing to God and most distinguished among excellent men, a most frequent preacher of the Word of God, by the gracious assistance of divine aid, he received both salutary teaching and the divine sacraments. Soon, from the deepest marrow of his heart, he abandoned every hope that he had placed in the world. It then came about that, after some time, while the holy bishop Valerius arranged it, and while everyone rejoiced, he was compelled to accept the episcopate while his bishop was still alive. This occurred so that, as bishop, he might preach the word of eternal salvation with much greater urgency and fervor, and with greater authority, joyfully, to the Lord’s Church, which was springing up and growing.”

And below: “So many things were dictated and published by him, and so many things were discussed, received, and corrected in the Church, or written against various heretics, or expounded from the canonical books for the edification of the holy children of the Church, that scarcely anyone devoted to study could learn and read them all.” Again below: “He preached the Word of God in the Church without interruption until his final illness, eagerly and courageously, with sound mind and sound judgment.” So far Possidius himself.

There is also, among other things, a noble encomium of Saint Augustine in Letter 8 of Pope Celestine to the bishops of Gaul. In it he gravely rebukes certain Gallic presbyters who opposed Augustine’s writings and everywhere dragged them under suspicion of heresy. Among other statements, he says: “We have always held Augustine, a man of holy memory, in our communion on account of his life and merits, nor has even a rumor of false suspicion ever touched him. We remember that he once possessed such great learning that even before my predecessors he was counted among the best teachers.” Therefore, he concludes, everyone rightly formed a common judgment about him, since everywhere he was both loved and honored by all. So the pope.

There are further praises of blessed Augustine in Saint Jerome’s Letter 94 to the same man. There Jerome commends two books on the Origin of Souls, which Augustine had dedicated to him, in these words: “Certainly, whatever could be said, and whatever could be drawn by a lofty intellect from the fountains of the sacred Scriptures, you have set forth and explained.” And below: “For my part, I have resolved to love you, esteem you, honor you, admire you, and defend your statements as though they were my own.”

And in Book 3 *Against the Pelagians*, where he boasts that he has as a very powerful fellow soldier in the battle against those same heretics the most holy and learned Augustine—who had already unsheathed the sword of the Spirit against that heresy—after listing Augustine’s commentaries written on this subject to Marcellinus, he adds: “It is said that he is also forging others specifically under your name, which have not yet come into our hands. I therefore think this labor should be set aside, lest Horace’s words be applied to me: ‘Do not carry wood into the forest.’ For either we would say the same things superfluously, or, if we wished to say something new, better things have already been occupied by that most illustrious intellect.” So Jerome.

To these testimonies may be added Saint Prosper, who was most attentive to Augustine. He writes of him in his *Chronicle*: “Augustine, bishop, outstanding in every respect, died on the fifth day before the Kalends of September, answering Julian’s books amid the attacks of the Vandals who were besieging him, at the very end of his days, and gloriously persevering in confession of Christian grace” (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 38).

But let us also hear Gennadius’s judgment concerning Augustine, so that, according to the proverb, things placed side by side may shine more clearly by contrast. “Augustine,” he says, “an African and bishop of Hippo, a man renowned throughout the world for divine and human learning, sound in faith and pure in life, wrote more than can be found anywhere. Who, then, can boast of possessing all his works? Or who can read with as much diligence as he wrote?” Thus far Gennadius speaks honorably of Augustine.

[Col. 0261D] But it is characteristic of detractors to attach some fault after praising a person, so that the whole praise may be obscured. Thus Gennadius thoroughly tarnished the praises bestowed on Augustine when he added: “Therefore, as happens to one who speaks much, what the Holy Spirit said through Solomon also happened to him: ‘You will not escape sin in much speaking’” (Proverbs 10). And below: “Nevertheless he remained Catholic, and his error, contracted—as I have said—through much speech and magnified by the struggle with his opponents, has not yet given rise to a question of heresy.”

So he branded Augustine with the notable marks of excessive speech and error, and in a certain way retracted or diminished the praise he had earlier given him. “His error,” he says, “has not yet given rise to a question of heresy,” as though he meant: Although it has not yet provided the occasion for heresy, it will nevertheless easily do so in the future.

Thus this man, stained with Pelagian soot and, among the other clergy of Marseille, a rival of Augustine, subtly bit the most vigorous enemy of the Pelagians, whom he could not openly injure, as though by flattering him. Yet “better are the wounds of a lover than the deceitful kisses of an enemy,” says the Wise Man (Proverbs 27).

The pope Celestine cited above judged and felt very differently. Following his predecessors, he cleared Augustine of every suspicion of error and imposed silence on his detractors. Pope Gelasius likewise approved the works of blessed Augustine—he himself calls them “little works,” as he does the writings of the other Fathers—with the same apostolic authority, and decreed that they were to be retained in the Catholic Church (D., chapter “Sancta Romana,” distinction 15).

As for Hippo Regius—or, as it is written here, Hippona Regiensis—two cities in Africa are remembered by this name. One, closer to Utica, is called Hippo Regius; the other, farther from the coast and situated in a marshy place, is called Diarrythum, that is, “diluted,” on account of its abundant waters, as Pliny writes in Book 5, chapter 4.

The former was called Hippo Regius because it was inhabited by kings. Hence Silius Italicus writes:

> Hippo, beloved by ancient kings.

Saint Augustine was bishop of this Hippo Regius, or Hipponensis Church, not of the other, as Ludovicus Vives incorrectly noted (*On the City of God*, Book 16, chapter 8), contrary to everyone’s judgment. While Valerius, the bishop of the same city, was still alive and arranging for Augustine to act in his place, Augustine was consecrated and appointed his successor, although unwilling. After he had served in this office for approximately thirty-five years, while the city of Hippo was under siege by the Vandals, he died in the third month of the siege—for Possidius testifies that the siege lasted fourteen months. At that time African affairs were in such a state that, except for three cities—Carthage, Cirta, and Hippo—all the others had been captured by the Vandals. After Augustine’s death, however, the city of Hippo itself, abandoned by its inhabitants, was burned by the enemy, as the same Possidius testifies (Baronius, year 430).

Ambrosius Calepinus further notes that the name “Hippo” is sometimes masculine and sometimes feminine. Thus we read “Hippo Diluted” in Pliny, in the passage cited above, and “both Hippos” in the same author, Book 6, chapter 34. Solinus likewise states that both of these towns were founded by Greek horsemen and received their name from that fact. So he writes. As for “Hippona Regiensis,” or “the town of Regiense,” as it appears here, I do not find it used in this sense by any other author.]

Augustine, the great priest of the town of Hippo Regius (*Treatise 2 on John*), says: “But in order that human beings might be born from God, God was first born from human beings. Christ is God, and Christ was born from human beings: he sought only a mother on earth, since he already had a Father in heaven. He was born from God, through whom we are made; and born from a woman, through whom we are restored.”

[Note: [Col. 0262D] It appears that something is missing here in the Basel edition, which reads as follows: “‘But in order that human beings might be born from God,’ he says, ‘God was first born from human beings. For Christ is God, and Christ was born from human beings. He sought only a mother on earth, since he already had a Father in heaven. He was born from God, through whom we are made; and born from a woman, through whom we are restored.’ So there. In Augustine himself I read the final words as follows: ‘Born from God, through whom we might be made; born from a woman, through whom we might be restored’; in other editions: ‘Through whom we might be restored’ (*Treatise 2 on John*, toward the end).]

Again, in the same work: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. Why, then, do you marvel that human beings are born from God? Consider that God himself was born from human beings.”

Again, in his Letter to Volusianus (Letter 3): “Moses himself and the other prophets most truly prophesied the Lord Christ and bestowed great glory upon him. They foretold that he would come not as their equal, nor as one superior to them in the same power of miracles, but plainly as the Lord God of all, and as one made human for the sake of human beings. For this reason he himself also wished to perform such deeds, lest it be absurd that he should not do what he had done through them. Yet he also had to do something proper to himself: to be born from a Virgin, to rise from the dead, and to ascend into heaven. If anyone thinks this too little for God, I do not know what more he could expect.”

## CHAPTER XXVIII

He is about to produce the testimonies of Greek, or Eastern, bishops, and first brings forward Saint Gregory of Nazianzus.

[Col. 0263A]

“But perhaps, because the men we have listed lived in different parts of the world, their authority may seem less convincing to you. This is ridiculous, since faith is not diminished by place; one must consider what a person is, not where he is, especially since religion unites everyone, and those who share one faith are also known to be in one body. Nevertheless, we shall also bring forward some men from the East whom you will not despise.”

[Note: [Col. 0263B] Gregory was called Nazianzenus from Nazianzus, a town of the second Cappadocia (*Martyrology*, 9 May). He was a contemporary and intimate friend and companion of Saint Basil. Because of his singular knowledge of divine matters, he was given the title “Theologian.” He restored the Catholic faith, which had collapsed at Constantinople, and suppressed the heresies that were arising.

Saint Jerome frequently mentions him elsewhere and also writes in his *Catalogue*: “Gregory, first bishop of Sasima and then of Nazianzus, a man of the greatest eloquence and my teacher, from whom I learned the explanation of the Scriptures, composed all his works in thirty thousand lines.” Saint Jerome and others say this.

Baronius teaches that Jerome’s statement that Gregory of Nazianzus was a bishop should be understood in this way (Volume 4, year 371): not that Gregory was ever ordained bishop of Nazianzus, but that, while Gregory the Elder, the bishop of that see, was alive and requested it, Gregory assumed the care and administration of that Church and for a short time carried out its spiritual functions as vicar and coadjutor, namely until his father’s death. On this matter there is a public discourse that Gregory delivered before his father (Oration 8, Bill’s edition), as well as his explicit testimony in a letter to Gregory of Nyssa, in these words: “It is universally acknowledged that I was not appointed bishop of Nazianzus, but overseer of Sasima; although, out of reverence for my father and for those who earnestly pleaded this request with me, we accepted the office for a short time, as though receiving guests.”

Let these remarks be understood as incidental to Jerome’s statement (Letter 42).

Rufinus of Aquileia: “Gregory was a man incomparable in every respect. Famous in word and deed, he provided the Churches with a most brilliant light of the knowledge of Christ, teaching what he practiced and not condemning himself by doing the opposite of what he taught.”

After several intervening remarks: “No one can be found whose life was more commendable and holy, whose eloquence clearer and more distinguished, whose faith purer and more upright, or whose knowledge fuller and more perfect than his. He alone was such that even parties and factions disagreeing among themselves—as commonly happens—could not dispute his faith; rather, he obtained such merit before God and the Churches of God that anyone who dared to oppose his teaching in any respect would by that very fact be proved the more heretical. For it is a manifest indication that anyone who does not agree with Gregory in the faith does not possess the right faith.”

Saint Augustine, in Book 1 *Against Julian the Pelagian*, after citing the bishops of the West, speaks of Gregory of Nazianzus—whom he names first among the Eastern bishops, as Cassian does here—in this way: “You will not lack a bishop of great name and most celebrated fame, from the regions of the East, whose eloquence, deserving of immense grace, has shone everywhere after being translated into the Latin language.” And below: “Does the authority of one Gregory seem to you too little among the Eastern bishops? He is indeed so eminent a person that he would not have said this unless he had derived it from the Christian faith, nor would they have held him so distinguished and venerable as to recognize what he said according to the rule of well-known truth.”

Gregory the presbyter, in the *Life* of that same Bishop Gregory, writes: “He excelled so greatly in the sublimity of dogma and theology that, although very many men renowned for learning in different ages devoted themselves to theological matters, he alone, after John the Evangelist, was distinguished by the name ‘Theologian,’ and this title was attributed to him as though it were his own and peculiar designation. Indeed, just as he possessed all other praises and virtues in the embrace of his character, so he was not deprived even of the gift of prophecy.” So he writes.

See the many other eulogies in praise of Gregory of Nazianzus collected by Jacobus Billius and annotated in the preface to his works.]

Gregory was a most brilliant beacon of knowledge and learning. Although he died long ago, he still lives in authority and faith; and although he has long been absent from the Churches in body, he has not departed from them in voice and teaching.

He therefore says—in his Oration on the Nativity of the Savior—that when God had come forth from the Virgin in the human nature he had assumed, being made one from two mutually opposed things, flesh and spirit, one of which was assumed into God, while the other was endowed with the grace of divinity. “O new and unheard-of mixture! O marvelous and unsearched joining! He who was becomes what he was not, and the Creator is created; he who is boundless is contained through the mediation of the soul, between God and flesh; and he who makes all the rich rich becomes poor.”

[Note: [Col. 0264B] Pope Leo the Great cites these same words from Nazianzus in Letter 97, chapter 9, to Leo Augustus, against the blasphemies of Nestorius and Eutyches, following the same translation as Cassian. This is Oration 38, entitled *On the Nativity of Christ*, according to the edition of Jacobus Billius, who translates these same words somewhat differently as follows: “When God came forth with humanity, one of two mutually opposed things—namely, flesh and spirit—was deified, while the other was deified. O new mixture! O marvelous blending! One deified, the other was deified; he who was not created is created; he who can be contained in no place is contained through the intervention of the intellectual soul between divinity and the grossness of the flesh; he who enriches others is afflicted with poverty,” and so forth.]

Again, concerning the Epiphany: “But what happens? What is done concerning us, or for us? A new and unheard-of exchange of natures takes place, and God becomes human.”

Again there: “The Son of God also began to be the son of man, not by being changed from what he was—for he is unchangeable—but by assuming what he was not. He is merciful, so that he who could not be contained might be contained.”

[Note: [Col. 0264C] This is Oration 39 in the same edition of Billius, the companion and related discourse to the preceding one, entitled *On the Holy Lights*, or *On the Feast of the Holy Lights*. It concerns Christ’s baptism, which is also called “illumination” by the Fathers and is celebrated on the day of Epiphany by both Greeks and Latins. It does not concern the purification or presentation of the Lord in the Temple, which the Greeks call ὑπαπαντή (*hypapantē*), as some have thought.

Billius’s translation and edition of this passage read as follows: “What, then, occurs, and what great mystery is signified concerning us? Natures are renewed, and God becomes human; and he who ascended above the heaven of heaven to the East of his glory and splendor is celebrated in the setting of our lowliness and humility. The Son of God also accepts being and being called the son of man—not changing what he was (for change cannot be attributed to God), but, out of his love for human beings, assuming what he was not, so that he who by nature cannot be comprehended might be comprehended,” and so forth. See the commentary of Nicetas.]

Do you see how splendidly and magnificently he proclaims the majesty of the divinity while indicating the condescension of the Incarnation and enfleshment? This admirable teacher of the faith surely knew that all the things God bestowed upon us by coming into the world constitute an accumulation of benefits, not a diminution of honor, because whatever God has granted to humanity should increase his affection for us, not diminish his dignity.

## CHAPTER XXIX

Next he places the authority of blessed Athanasius.

[Note: [Col. 0265B] “Priest” is used by meiosis in place of “bishop” (as above in the case of Augustine); according to an old manner of speaking, a bishop is also called the high priest or chief presbyter. Thus Augustine writes in Question 4 (Volume 4), combining both terms: “That a presbyter is to be understood as a bishop is proved by the Apostle Paul, when he instructs Timothy—whom he ordained a presbyter—regarding the kind of person he ought to appoint as bishop (1 Tim. 3). For what is a bishop except the chief presbyter, that is, the high priest? Finally, he calls them not otherwise than fellow presbyters here, and his fellow priests.” So Augustine.

Concerning Saint Athanasius, bishop or archbishop of Alexandria, the following is recorded in the *Martyrology*, May 2: “At Alexandria, the birth into heaven of Saint Athanasius, bishop of that city, most distinguished in holiness and doctrine. Almost the entire world conspired in his persecution; nevertheless, from the time of Constantine to that of Valens, he vigorously defended the Catholic faith against emperors, governors, and countless Arian bishops. He suffered many plots from them and, driven as an exile throughout the whole world, found no place safe for hiding. At length he returned to his own Church and, after many struggles and many crowns of patience, departed to the Lord in the forty-sixth year of his priesthood, during the reigns of the emperors Valentinian and Valens.” So it is recorded there.

Saint Gregory of Nazianzus delivered a splendid oration in his praise (Oration 21, Billius’s edition), beginning with this distinguished exordium: “In praising Athanasius, I shall praise virtue. For to say ‘Athanasius’ is the same as to extol virtue with praise, since he held all virtues gathered together in himself—or, to speak more truly, still holds them.”

Again, in the oration he wrote in praise of Heron, after other praises he calls Athanasius “the eye of the world,” “the chief of priests,” “a sublime voice,” “a pillar of the faith,” “the lamp of Christ,” and “a second forerunner” (Oration 23).

Saint Basil also wrote many and very distinguished things about him. Several letters of Basil to Athanasius are extant, especially Letter 48, where, imploring his assistance for the Church of Antioch, he writes: “Who could surpass your prudence in accomplishing these things? Who could more sharply consider what must be done? Who could be more effective in carrying out what is useful? Who could possess a more compassionate disposition for considering the needs of the brethren? Who could be more venerable to the whole of the West than your honorable gray hair?” and so forth.

There is also that distinguished statement of Cosmas the abbot, preserved by Sophronius, concerning the eager search for Athanasius’s writings and the reverent care with which they should be treated: “Whenever you find something among the works of Saint Athanasius,” he says, “and have no paper on which to write it, write it on your garments.”]

Athanasius too, priest of the city of Alexandria, was an outstanding example of steadfastness and virtue. The storm of heretical persecution did not crush him but proved him. His life was always like a shining mirror; he almost obtained the merit of a martyr before he received the dignity of a confessor.

[Note: [Col. 0265D] Concerning the use and meaning among Christians of the terms “confessor” and “martyr,” see what was said above (chapter 24). It is therefore easy to understand why Saint Athanasius is said here to have almost first acquired the merit of a martyr before he assumed the dignity of a confessor. Having suffered the gravest persecutions, calumnies, and exiles both from pagans and from the Arians, and having often even been sought for execution, he obtained the praise and merit of a martyr not only before God, but also among Catholics he earned the name of martyr—according to the manner of speaking by which, in former times, one who had endured some kind of torture in defense of the faith was called a martyr, even though he had not actually died a martyr’s death. See above, chapter 24. Tertullian and Cyprian commonly use “martyr” in this way.

“Before he assumed the dignity of a confessor” means before he had professed the Catholic faith when questioned before the enemies of the faith, and thereby deserved to be honored in the Church with the title and dignity of confessor.]

Let us see what he thought concerning the Lord Jesus Christ and the Lord’s mother. “This, then,” he says, “is the character and purpose of sacred Scripture, as we have often said: that there is a twofold signification in the same Savior—namely, that he always was and is God, Son, Word, light, and wisdom of the Father; and that afterward, for our sake, he took flesh from the Virgin Mary, the *theotokos*, and became human.”

Again, after other statements: “Many saints, therefore, were holy and free from sin. Jeremiah was sanctified even from the womb; and John, while still in the womb, leapt for joy at the voice of Mary the *theotokos*.”

[Note: [Col. 0266B] Not *theolocae*, as it was formerly printed. The word is θεοτόκος (*theotokos*), common in gender, as is well known. Nor is *theotoca* found among the Fathers, but only *theotocus*. We have noted enough elsewhere concerning this word.]

He says that the Virgin Mary is called *theotokos* because she is the mother of God—the God who is the Son of God and, to use his own words concerning the faith of all, is “the Word, the light, and the wisdom of the Father,” and who for our sake took flesh (*Book On the Incarnation of the Word*).

## CHAPTER XXX

He also adds Saint John Chrysostom.

[Note: St. John, archbishop of Constantinople, was surnamed Chrysostom on account of the golden stream of his eloquence. Through word and example he greatly benefited the Christian religion, and after many labors ended his life in exile (from the Roman Martyrology, January 27). Baronius gathered his deeds and his entire life, including his death endured in exile, from ecclesiastical history and inserted them into his Annals (vol. V of the Annals). There also exists a distinguished eulogy of John by Pope Celestine, addressed to the clergy and people of Constantinople, in which he places before their eyes the memory and example of him and of the other pastors of that Church, and seriously urges them—just as Cassian does here—to persevere steadfastly in the faith and religion of their ancestors, in these words:

“Above all, I think you must remain steadfast in those things which you have drawn from the teaching of your former pastors, being firmly persuaded that the priests who have served you until now were outstanding in holiness and learning. Without departing even a little from the traditions of their fathers, they ruled the Church of God in the greatest peace and tranquility. For, to begin with the dead, what did the learning of John, the bishop of blessed memory, not instill in your minds? His discourse, building up and confirming the Catholic faith, spread throughout the whole world. He was so never lacking in his duty of teaching that even now, wherever I happen to read him, he seems to preach. His precise wisdom was followed by a widely celebrated steadfastness and severity. For the bishop Atticus, of holy memory, governing the Christian people according to the example of his predecessor, attacked the sacrilegious madness of the heretics with the utmost vigor,” and so forth.

As for the writings of Chrysostom, Cassiodorus says the following (in the preface to *Divine Readings*): “They say that Clement of Alexandria, surnamed Stromateus, Cyril, bishop of the same city, and John Chrysostom explained the divine Scriptures of the Old and New Testament in Greek from beginning to end,” and so forth. Suidas likewise says, in the same vein (in his article on John Chrysostom): “He so illuminated the whole Jewish and Christian Scripture with commentaries that no one before him had done so.” A little later he adds: “As for the works written by him, it is not for a human being to count them by numbering them, but only for God, to whom all things are known.” This is Suidas.

Sophronius also writes the following about his writings and character: “John was justly and most deservedly surnamed Chrysostom on account of the purity of his doctrine and the splendor of his most graceful eloquence. From the time he received saving baptism, he never swore,” and so forth. I think it superfluous to bring in further material in his praise from elsewhere, since in this chapter and the next there is available so ample and brilliant an encomium of John Chrysostom by Cassian, his disciple, left to posterity for his immortal memory.]

John, the glory of the bishops of Constantinople, [Note: For he did not suffer persecution from gentiles, or pagans, but was unjustly condemned and deposed by Christians—namely, by Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, who was exceedingly hostile to him—and was twice driven into exile by the emperor Arcadius and the empress Eudoxia, who raged against him like another Herodias. He was transported by soldiers to the most distant regions and treated with the utmost indignity; exhausted by hunger, cold, illness, and other hardships, he finally ended this life in exile, as has been said, in order to find a better one. He may rightly be called blessed and a martyr, not only in the broader sense discussed above, but also in the stricter sense in which a martyr is properly one who suffers persecution and death for the faith or for justice. That this happened to John Chrysostom is well known from ecclesiastical history (Socrates, book VI, chapter 19).] whose holiness attained the merits of martyrdom without any storm of pagan persecution—listen to what he thought and proclaimed concerning the incarnation of the Son of God:

“And him whom, if he had come in bare divinity, neither heaven, nor earth, nor the seas, nor any creature could have sustained, the untouched womb of the Virgin carried.”

Therefore, even if you had been ignorant of the faith and teaching of others, you ought to have followed and retained his. [Note: Concerning the election of Nestorius, Baronius writes (under the year 428): “Under the same consuls, Felix and Taurus, on the fourth day before the Ides of April, Nestorius, a presbyter from Antioch and formerly a monk, was substituted for Sisinnius as bishop of Constantinople.” Socrates reports this in book VII, chapter 29. Because the Church of Constantinople had formerly received from that same Church of Antioch the most holy and learned bishop St. John Chrysostom, it chose Nestorius, after an interval of several years, with extraordinary unanimity, hoping to receive another like him. Cassian, a writer of that period, testifies that this was their intention when he says to Nestorius: “Since the Church of Constantinople chose you for itself as priest from the Church of Antioch, from which it had previously selected him—that is, John—it believed that in you it would receive whatever it had ceased to possess in him.” Baronius says that this was done especially at the urging of the emperor Theodosius.

But let us hear Socrates on how and when Nestorius was elected (book VII, chapter 29): “After the death of Sisinnius, the emperor, because of men eager for empty distinctions, decided that no one from that Church should be elected to that episcopate—although many desired Philip and many others Proclus to be designated—but that a stranger should be summoned from Antioch” (Nicephorus, book XIV, chapter 31; *Tripartite History*, book XII, chapter 4). “For Nestorius was there, a native of Germania, distinguished especially by a powerful voice and eloquent speech. For this reason, as someone highly suitable for teaching the people, he was summoned with their approval.” Thus far Baronius from Socrates. See above for other remarks to the same effect.]

It was because of his love and longing for him that the devout people chose you as their bishop: “Since the Church of Constantinople chose you for itself as priest from the Church of Antioch, from which it had earlier selected him, it believed that in you it would receive whatever it had ceased to possess in him.”

I ask you, did not all these men, as though once inspired by a prophetic spirit, say everything in order to confound [Lipsius, in the margin: “refute”] your blasphemies? You proclaim that Christ our Lord and Savior is not God; but they proclaim Christ the Lord to be true God. You blasphemously assert that Mary is *Christotokos*—“Christ-bearer”—not *Theotokos*—“God-bearer”; [Note: In what sense and for what reason the holy Fathers did or did not deny that Blessed Mary should be called *Christotokos*, “Christ-bearer,” has been explained at length above (book II, chapter 2). Since Nestorius, blaspheming against the Blessed Virgin, called her *Christotokos* in order by that name to signify that she had given birth to a bare and merely human being who was called Christ—that is, anointed with the oil of the Holy Spirit and endowed abundantly with his charism, in the same way that priests, kings, prophets, and just men have been called “Christs” on account of bodily or spiritual anointing—the most discerning and perceptive Fathers, observing that poison lay beneath the honey and a serpent in the grass, refused to admit the title “Christ-bearer.” They did not absolutely deny that the Blessed Virgin was *Christotokos*, that is, that she had conceived and borne Christ; rather, they wished to distance themselves as far as possible from Nestorius’s impious assertion and to appear not to communicate with it even in a word or in that single title.

Indeed, if the name “Christ” is understood—as it ought to be understood—as designating the two natures, divine and human, united in the one hypostasis of the Son of God, according to which meaning it is proper and peculiar to our Lord Jesus Christ alone, it follows that the most blessed Virgin may no less truly and properly be called *Christotokos* and *Theotokos*. Indeed, it makes no difference whether one says “Christ-bearer” or “God-bearer.” For Christ is our God; therefore the mother of Christ is also the God-bearer.

In the present age and for many centuries past, this word has rightly been used without any danger of a wicked opinion or heretical association, since the impiety of Nestorius was long ago rejected and condemned and no longer troubles the Church. Thus the holy Fathers did not deny that Mary was *Christotokos*, “Christ-bearer,” because they recognized and proclaimed Christ himself to be God and therefore his mother also to be *Theotokos*, “God-bearer.”]

They do not deny her to be *Christotokos* in such a way that they fail to recognize her as *Theotokos*. Not only were realities opposed to your blasphemies, but words as well, so that we may plainly understand that an impregnable defense had long ago been prepared by God against your blasphemies, a wall of truth ready to break the force of the heretical attack whenever it should come.

And you, most impious and most shameless defiler of a distinguished city, grievous and deadly contagion of a Catholic and holy people, dare to stand in the Church of God and speak? With your blasphemous and frenzied words you slander priests of unfailing faith and Catholic confession, claiming that the people of the city of Constantinople have gone astray through the fault of their earlier teachers. [Note: He names three bishops of the see of Constantinople, then especially famous and celebrated in recent memory, the predecessors of Nestorius and his immediate successors: Gregory of Nazianzus, mentioned above, who was first bishop of Sasima and, as has been said, was elevated to the episcopate of Constantinople in 381 through the efforts of the emperor Theodosius. After a short time, for the sake of peace and to calm the envy of certain bishops, he voluntarily resigned. Nectarius succeeded Gregory and held that see for several years; he died in 397 and had John Chrysostom as his successor, who is named here in third place and likewise opposed to Nestorius. John had been summoned from the desert and monastic life to the clergy and ordained presbyter of Antioch in the eleventh year of Valentinian the Younger and the eighth of Theodosius the Elder. In the fourth year of Arcadius and Honorius he became bishop of Constantinople; finally, in the thirteenth year of those emperors and the ninth of his episcopate, he died, around the year of the Lord 407.]

So you are the corrector of earlier bishops, the condemner of ancient priests, superior to Gregory, more approved than Nectarius, greater than John, and greater than all the priests of the Eastern cities—even though, if they did not bear the same name as those whom I have mentioned, they possessed the same faith. For insofar as this matter is concerned, that is enough: when faith is at issue, all are equal in that respect in which they share the excellence of the best.

## CHAPTER XXXI. He laments the unhappy fall of the city of Constantinople because of the defeat inflicted upon it by this heretic; at the same time he urges the citizens to persevere in their ancient Catholic and ancestral religion.

Therefore I too, humble and obscure in name, as I am also in merit, although I cannot presume to claim among the eminent bishops of the city of Constantinople the position of a teacher, nevertheless presume the devotion and affection of a disciple. [Note: From this chapter Baronius clearly refutes, under the year 404, certain men who fell into error by claiming that Cassian was ordained deacon by John Chrysostom and, after several years, was expelled by him and withdrew to Marseille. We have discussed this matter more fully elsewhere (in the preface to the reader) and refuted that opinion. For how or when could he have been expelled by John, when he is known to have remained in his service even after John’s exile and to have undertaken an embassy on his behalf to Pope Innocent? Cassian also praises the memory of John after his death before the people of Constantinople with such high commendation, and addresses them as men who in everything displayed a model of John’s most loving and devoted disciple. He had striven to merit so well even after John’s exile, indeed even after his death, that no trace of any alleged hostility could be discerned in him. Thus Baronius.]

For I was adopted by Bishop John, of most blessed memory, into the sacred ministry and offered to God; although I am absent in body, I am present there in affection. And although I am not now joined in bodily presence to that beloved and most venerable people of God, I am nevertheless united with them in mind. Hence, grieving and sympathizing with them, I have now burst into an expression of common sadness and sorrow, and in the only way I could, through the tearful complaint of my little works, I have cried out as though on behalf of the weakness of my own limbs and joints.

For if, according to the Apostle (1 Corinthians 12), when a lesser part of the body suffers, the greater part grieves and suffers with it, how much more ought the lesser part to sympathize when the greater part suffers? It is utterly inhuman that, in one and the same body, the lesser members should not feel the weakness of the greater, when the greater members suffer the pains of the lesser.

Therefore I beseech and implore all of you who dwell within the bounds of the city of Constantinople—who are my fellow citizens by affection and my brothers by the unity of faith—to separate yourselves from that ravening wolf who, as it is written, devours God’s people as though they were bread (Psalm 52). Do not touch or taste anything of his, for all his things lead to destruction (2 Corinthians 6). Come out from among them and separate yourselves, and do not touch what is unclean (Colossians 2).

Remember your former teachers and priests: Gregory, renowned throughout the world; Nectarius, distinguished for holiness; John, marvelous for faith and purity. John, I say—John who, truly in the likeness of John the Evangelist, was both a disciple and an apostle of Jesus, as though he had always reclined upon the Lord’s breast and rested in his affection.

Remember him, I say; follow him. Consider his purity, his faith, his teaching, and his holiness. Always remember that teacher and nourisher of yours, in whose lap, as it were, and embrace you grew. He was a common teacher to me and to you; we are his disciples and his formation. Read his writings; hold fast to his instruction; embrace his faith and merit.

Although it is great and difficult to attain to him, it is beautiful and sublime to follow him. For, in the sum of things, not only attainment but imitation itself is to be praised, since scarcely anyone is wholly without some share of the thing toward which he has striven to climb and attain.

Let him therefore always be present in your understanding and, as it were, before your eyes; let him occupy your heart and your thoughts. Finally, let him himself commend to you these things written by me. For what I have written, he taught me, and therefore believe that these things are not so much mine as his, since a stream depends upon its source, and whatever is thought to belong to the disciple ought entirely to be referred to the honor of the teacher.

But above all and beyond all else, I earnestly beseech you, God, Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, with voice and mind alike humble, that you impress upon us, by the gift of your love, these things which we have written through the generosity of your grace.

And because, as our Lord God, your only-begotten Son, himself taught us, you loved this world so greatly that you sent your only-begotten Son for the salvation of the world, grant this to your people whom you redeemed: that, in the incarnation of your only-begotten Son, they may recognize both your gift and his affection; and that all may understand and love what your only-begotten Son, our Lord and God, endured for us—his birth, his suffering, and his resurrection—in such a way that the condescension of his [Lipsius, in the margin: “sacred”] majesty may become the advancement of our love.

Let his humility not diminish the honor owed to him in the hearts of all, but always produce an increase of love. May we all understand the benefits of sacred mercy with such piety and wisdom that we recognize ourselves to be so much more indebted to our God the more humbly God became because of us.

[APPENDICES]

## FIRST APPENDIX

[Note: As I have decided to append at the end of this volume the Rule of St. Pachomius the Abbot, translated into Latin, as is believed, by St. Jerome, friendly reader, two reasons moved me. First, Peter Ciaconius, a priest of Toledo, in his Roman edition, judged that this Rule—nearly obliterated by the passage of time and hitherto lying in obscurity, but diligently sought out, purged of errors, and restored, at least for the greater part—should, as a distinguished monument of antiquity most recently recovered, be attached in the manner of an appendix to Cassian’s works. I thought it useful to imitate his plan and example for the public benefit.

Second, our Cassian frequently mentions and scatters through his writings much concerning the Pachomian, or Tabennesian, monks and their customs and institutions, especially in the fourth book of the *Institutes*. This Rule, therefore, restored here in full insofar as possible and preserved for posterity, seems likely to shed no little light upon those matters.

A considerable difficulty nevertheless arises: whether this Rule should be regarded as the same one mentioned by Palladius in the *Lausiac History* and by others (Palladius, *Lausiac History* 38; Gennadius, *On Illustrious Men* 7; Martyrology, May 14; Sozomen, book III, chapter 13; Nicephorus, book IX, chapter 14), or as a different one. For from many arguments it certainly seems possible to conclude that at least two, if not more, Rules of monks proceeded from St. Pachomius.

One Rule was received from an angel, either dictated by him, as Gennadius reports, with the Roman Martyrology also supporting this account, or divinely delivered on a bronze tablet, as that uncertain Greek author, Palladius, Sozomen, Nicephorus, and others relate. The other was composed not by Pachomius alone but by the three Fathers named below and published jointly; St. Jerome rendered it into Latin.

That they are not one and the same Rule is proved first by this: the former is attributed to Pachomius alone, whereas the latter is attributed to three Fathers—Pachomius, Theodore, and Orsiesius. Hence the Rule begins in this fashion: “These are the life-giving precepts delivered to the three by the elders.”

Second, the two have almost nothing in common, as is clear to anyone who examines them. This Rule contains many more precepts, and they differ greatly from the precepts and regulations of the other Rule. To make this more certain and evident, I have decided to place immediately after this Rule that very one, in the same words in which it was set out by Palladius, so that their differences may be recognized by comparing the two.

Finally, Jerome himself testifies in the preface placed before it that he translated this Rule of the three Fathers—or rather, these precepts—first written in Egyptian and afterward translated into Greek, into Latin. The one described by Palladius, however, is said to have been translated from Greek into Latin by Gentianus Hervetus, its translator, as may be seen in the third edition of the *Library of the Holy Fathers*, volume VII.

On the other hand, there are also arguments that reasonably permit the suspicion that only one Rule of Pachomius should be recognized: the one delivered to St. Pachomius by an angel, whether the angel dictated it or brought it to him, and eventually translated into Latin by St. Jerome. Palladius and others may have reported only a part of it briefly and cursorily; that part is to be joined, inserted, and continued with this Rule so as to form one whole.

First, Palladius himself—and Sozomen and Nicephorus followed him—plainly suggests that he did not describe the whole Rule of Pachomius, in the words with which he says that, while Pachomius was sitting in a cave, an angel appeared to him and said: “Pachomius, you have rightly and virtuously performed the things that concern you; therefore you sit here needlessly. Come, then, go out, gather all the younger monks, live with them, and, following the form that I shall give you, establish laws for them.” And he gave him a bronze tablet [Lipomanus reads “wax tablets”] on which these things were written: “Allow each one to eat and drink according to his strength, and assign them works proportionate and appropriate to them,” and so forth.

Who would believe that the angelic and heavenly Rule began with so abrupt an opening, without many other precepts being omitted—precepts more spiritual, more salutary, and more worthy of monks? Such precepts are both those that follow there and those expressed in this fuller and more extensive Rule.

Moreover, no author of any reputation makes any mention of the distinction described above or acknowledges that several different Rules were handed down by St. Pachomius. Rather, all agree that the Rule was brought to Pachomius or dictated to him by an angel, so that he might form monks according to its standard.

Therefore, if St. Jerome translated any Rule and monastic institution of Pachomius, as he himself professes here, it ought to be that very Rule and not another. Nevertheless, it is plausible that it was expanded, enlarged, and completed with additional precepts both by Pachomius himself and by other Fathers who were his disciples—Theodore and Orsiesius—so that in this respect it could be called a plurality of Rules, or a Rule established by the three Fathers.

Finally, Baronius appears to support this view. Both in his *Annals* and in his notes on the Martyrology, he explicitly and without distinction asserts that the Rules of St. Pachomius, which Pachomius himself received while an angel dictated them, were rendered into Latin by St. Jerome (Baronius, volume V, under the year 404, and Martyrology, May 14).

The Reverend Father Heribert Rosweyde agrees with this opinion in his preliminary essays to the *Life of St. Pachomius*, where he adds: “Here in chapter 32 of the *Life of Pachomius* you have a certain abridgment of this Rule. The first person, so far as I know, to publish it in full was Achilles Statius of Portugal, printed in Rome in the year of the Lord 1575. Then, in 1588, Peter Ciaconius published it in a more accurate form, also in Roman type, and appended it to his edition of Cassian.”

Thus he understands the “abridgment”—that is, a short summary or fragment—to be only a portion of the Rule, not the whole Rule of St. Pachomius described by that uncertain Greek author whom Palladius and others followed and whose account they expressed in other words. The complete Rule that we are considering, however, was translated by St. Jerome and in our own times first published in Roman type, then repeatedly issued in later editions, and rescued from the injury of oblivion.

You have, reader, the question concerning the Rule of St. Pachomius examined from both sides. It will be your judgment and diligence to discern and determine toward which side you should incline.]

## THE RULE OF ST. PACHOMIUS, TRANSLATED INTO LATIN BY ST. JEROME

## JEROME’S PREFACE

[Col. 0271A] Although a sharp and polished sword, if it is kept concealed in its sheath for a long time, becomes dirty with rust and loses the brilliance of its former beauty, therefore I, [Note: Thus St. Jerome frequently uses *sleep* for departure from this life (Letter 29). He also gives the reason for this usage in these words: “Against the harshness and most cruel necessity of death we raise ourselves by this consolation, that in a short time we shall see those whom we grieve to be absent. For it is called not death but sleeping and slumber. Hence the blessed Apostle forbids us to grieve over those who sleep (1 Thessalonians 4), so that, knowing them to sleep, we may believe that they can be raised and, after their sleep has been completed, awaken with the saints,” and so forth. Elsewhere again (Against Vigilantius, chapter 3): “The saints are not called dead but sleeping; hence Lazarus, who was to be raised, is said to have slept (John 11), and the Apostle forbids the Thessalonians to grieve over those who sleep.”] grieving over the sleep [Note: This was Paula, that most noble and holy Roman matron, the mother of Eustochium, celebrated everywhere by St. Jerome with so many praises (Letter 27). She supported Jerome from her resources and, having built two monasteries at Bethlehem—one in which men served God and another in which women virgins did so—and a third for receiving pilgrims who came from everywhere to visit the holy places, provided Jerome with a permanent home there (see book III of the *Institutes*, chapter 4).

In gratitude for these benefits, he enclosed her life, death, and deeds in a distinguished epitaph.
