He testifies that she died (Baronius, in the Martyrology, January 26) while Honorius was consul for the sixth time and Aristenetus was consul, a year which, according to Onuphrius, is reckoned from Christ as 404, with St. Innocent presiding over the Roman Church.

There was also another Paula, called the younger, a granddaughter through the son of the elder Paula, Toxetius. Jerome wrote his seventh letter to her mother, Laeta, concerning her education, at a time when St. Paula had long since departed this life, as Baronius demonstrates in his *Annals* (volume V).] of the holy and venerable Paula—not as though I were acting against [Note: The Apostle’s command in the First Letter to the Thessalonians, chapter 4, where he says: “We do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who sleep, so that you may not grieve like the rest, who have no hope.” The Apostle does not absolutely forbid grieving over the death of friends, but forbids grieving in a disordered or excessive manner, after the fashion of the pagans, who have no faith or hope in the resurrection. Hence Ecclesiasticus 22 says: “Weep moderately over the dead, for he has found rest.”] [the Apostle’s command] (1 Thessalonians), but because the sources of comfort of many were cut off by her death, [Note: *Refreshment* (*refrigerium*) is also used for almsgiving, assistance, or provision by Tertullian in the *Apology* (chapter 39). Speaking there about Christian love-feasts, he says: “However great the expense, it is gain to incur expense in the name of piety. For by this refreshment we assist the needy.” Likewise, in Tertullian (*Against Praxeas*, chapter 16), *to refresh* means to help, console, and restore, which in Greek, according to Gellius (*Attic Nights*, book XIII, final chapter), is called *anapsyxai* (ἀναψῦξαι), as though meaning “to restore life” or “to give back the soul.”

The translator also renders the Apostle’s words in this way in 2 Timothy 1: “He often refreshed me.” And later in this preface St. Jerome says (Letter 27): “Refreshing the soul of the holy woman.”

How the sources of comfort of many were cut off—that is, removed and diminished—by Paula’s death is explained by Jerome himself in her epitaph. He says that she left not even a single coin to her daughter, but rather debts and responsibility for the brothers and sisters, namely the monks and nuns, for whom she had built monasteries and to whom she had distributed everything with such faith and devotion that she nearly reached utter poverty. The whole multitude of the poor cried out that they had lost their mother and provider.

Again, in his letter to Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, Jerome excuses himself for having translated Theophilus’s Paschal book into Latin only after a delay, on account of St. Paula’s death: “I beg you to forgive my slowness. For I have been so exhausted by the sleep of the holy and venerable Paula that until the present I have written no other work of God besides the translation of this book. For we have suddenly lost—as you yourself know—the support which, as the Lord is witness to our conscience, we do not speak of as serving our own needs but as serving the refreshment of the saints, for whom she diligently cared.”] I received books sent to me by Silvanus, a priest and man of God, which he had received after they had been sent to me from [Note: That is, Egyptian Alexandria. There are several Alexandrias founded by Alexander the Great, but this one is by far the most celebrated. It was called *No* by the Hebrews and lay between Egypt, Africa, and the sea, situated like a barrier beside Lake Mareotis. See Pliny, book I, chapter 10.] Alexandria [Col. 0274A] so that he might commission me to translate them.

For he said that in the Thebaid, and in the monastery of [Note: *Metanoea* means “penitence” in Latin. The monastery was therefore called Metanoea because the monks there practiced the most severe penitence; for this reason its name was changed, since it had previously been called Tanobus. John Climacus writes remarkable things about this kind of monastery of penitents, which was also called a prison, and about the monks confined there and doing penance, in the fifth step of his *Ladder*.] Metanoea, which had been changed from Tanobus into “penitence” by a fortunate alteration of name, many Latins lived who did not know the Egyptian or Greek language, in which the precepts of [Note: Pachomius, also called Pachumius, became a highly esteemed monk after having been a pagan soldier. He was a contemporary, and perhaps a disciple, of St. Antony. The Roman Martyrology says the following about him (May 14): “In Egypt, St. Pachomius, abbot, who established many monasteries in that region and wrote a Rule for monks, which he learned while an angel dictated it.”

An anonymous Greek author first described his life, and Dionysius Exiguus translated it into Latin; it is found in book I of the *Lives of the Fathers* in the new edition. Sozomen (book III, chapter 13), Palladius in the *Lausiac History* (chapter 38), Cassiodorus in the *Tripartite History* (book VIII, chapter 11), Nicephorus (book IX, chapter 14), and finally Gennadius in his *Catalogue* (chapter 7) also discuss him. Gennadius further testifies that Pachomius wrote several letters, whose titles he lists. Trithemius (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*) says that Pachomius flourished under the emperors Valentinian and Theodosius, in the year 390.

This Pachomius was different from Abbot Pachon, who was also called Pachomius and is discussed by Palladius in *Lausiac History* 29.] Pachomius and [Note: Cassian discusses Abbot Theodore, Pachomius’s successor in the monastery at Tabennisi, in book V of the *Institutes*, chapter 33, and in the sixth Conference, which bears Theodore’s name. We have added further notes about him in those places. See Gennadius above (chapter 8).] Theodore and [Note: Orsiesius, also written Oriesis or Oresiesis—for the name is written in various ways—was a contemporary of Pachomius and flourished in the year 340, according to Cardinal Bellarmine (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*).

Gennadius writes the following about him in his *Catalogue*: “Oriensis, a monk and colleague of both Pachumius and Theodore, a man perfectly instructed in the Holy Scriptures, composed a book wholly seasoned with divine salt and entirely constructed from the instruments of monastic discipline. To put it simply, it contains an exposition of almost the whole Old and New Testament in concise discussions, solely according to the needs of monks. Shortly before his death, he presented it to the brothers in place of a testament.” Thus Gennadius.

Suffridus Petrus adds: “In printed copies, as also in Honorius and Trithemius, this writer is called Oriesis; in our manuscripts, Orestesis.” Thus he. This book exists in volume IV of the second edition of the *Library of the Holy Fathers*.] Orsiesius [Col. 0275A] had been written the precepts of those who first laid the foundations of communities throughout the Thebaid and Egypt, according to the command of God and of the angel who had been sent by God for this very institution.

Therefore, because I had remained silent for a long time and had swallowed my grief in silence, while Leontius the priest and the other brothers with him, who had been sent to me for this very reason, were pressing me, I summoned a [Note: Among the ancients, notaries were those who received and recorded what was dictated by another in letters or symbols (see Baronius, volume II, under the year 220). They did this so quickly and readily that by abbreviation they matched the speaker’s speed; as St. Jerome says (Letters 34 and 140), “the swift hand rapidly followed the words spoken,” and “the signs seized the speed of the tongue.” Hence Martial, *Epigrams*, book IV:

[Col. 0275C] “Though words may race, the hand is swifter than they.”]

The tongue had not yet completed its work; the hand had completed its own. These were also called scribes and amanuenses. Librarians, however, were those who transcribed distinctly and fully in books what the notaries had taken down.] I dictated to a notary, as they had been translated from Egyptian into Greek, in our own language, so that I might obey such eminent men commanding—indeed, I should say, asking—and under a favorable omen, as they say, break a long silence, returning to my former studies and [Col. 0275C] refreshing the soul of the holy woman [Note: Paula, namely, who was mentioned above. By this writing he teaches that her blessed soul, already in heaven, was refreshed—that is, cheered and affected and enriched by a certain additional or accidental joy, as theologians call it—and that he undertook this labor on her account and in her memory, for the benefit and advantage of the monks whom she had cherished and supported so greatly during her life. On this matter see St. Jerome’s Letter 27.] who had always burned with love for monasteries and who had meditated on earth what she would see in heaven.

The venerable virgin of Christ, Eustochium [Col. 0275B] [Note: The daughter of the aforementioned Paula. She was brought up with her mother at the Lord’s manger—that is, in the Bethlehem monastery—together with other virgins, and, long surviving her mother, shone forth through outstanding examples of virtue. She was also called Julia because she traced her origin from Julius and the Julian family, [Col. 0275D] as St. Jerome relates in Paula’s epitaph. He also dedicated complete Commentaries on Isaiah and Ezekiel, along with others, specifically and by name to her; and, writing to Pammachius, he commends her with this sort of eulogy: “What was stronger than Eustochium, who broke through the gates of nobility and the arrogance of consular birth by her virginal purpose, and subjected the first family in the first city to chastity?”], might have something to give the sisters to read, and our brothers might follow the examples of the Egyptians—that is, of the monks of Tabennesis [Note: Concerning the island of Tabenna and the monks of Tabennesis, see the notes on Book IV, chapter 1.]—who have in each monastery fathers, administrators, weekly servants, and ministers, as well as superiors of the individual houses [Note: Two matters here deserve attention and concern monastic antiquities. First, four or five distinct offices, or orders of officials, among those Egyptian monks are designated here. The first were called Fathers, or abbots, archimandrites, and coenobiarchs—that is, the governors and presidents of the individual monasteries. In Pachomius’s Rule they are also called the leaders of the monastery. The second were called administrators, or, in Greek, oikonomoi; they supplied and distributed what the brothers needed. The third were ministers, and these were of various kinds: some were weekly servants, who took turns serving the brothers at table each week; others were ministers of guests, of the sick, of the kitchen, and so forth. Fourth were the superiors of the houses. Houses were distinguished from monasteries: in each monastery there were thirty or forty houses subject to individual superiors, who, under one common Father or leader of the monastery, or of the entire congregation, [Col. 0276C] administered the houses entrusted to them, like superintendencies or conventual priories. In each house at least thirty, or as many as forty, monks lived. From this one may gather how great the number of monks was in each monastery. For if there were thirty houses, and thirty monks in each, the number would be 1,200 monks, which is the minimum stated here; but if there were forty houses, and forty monks in each, the number would be 1,600 monks, which is the maximum indicated here. The intermediate numbers would have been 1,300, 1,400, and 1,500.] so that in one house approximately forty brothers might live, obeying the superior; and according to the number of brothers there might be thirty or forty houses in one monastery, while three or four houses were joined into one tribe, either to go together to their work or to succeed one another in turn in the weekly service.

[Note: St. Benedict imitated this arrangement in his Rule, likewise establishing that, according to the ranks appointed by the abbot or possessed by the brothers themselves, they should approach for the kiss of peace, for communion, for the assignment of a psalm, for standing in the choir, and in every place whatsoever. Age should not determine the order or prejudice anyone, because Samuel and Daniel, though boys, judged priests. [Col. 0276D] Therefore, except for those whom the abbot, after higher deliberation, has advanced or degraded for specific reasons, all the rest should remain as they are when they enter religious life [that is, when they enter or profess religion]. For example, whoever comes to the monastery at the second hour of the day should know himself to be junior to anyone who came at the first hour of the day, whatever that person’s age or rank. This is St. Benedict’s teaching.]

Whoever first enters the monastery sits first, walks first, says the psalm first, first stretches out his hand at table, and receives communion first in the church. No question is asked about age among them, but about profession. They have nothing in their cells [Note: Concerning the cells and small rooms of the monks, see the notes on Book V, chapter 57.] except a mat and two lebitonaria [Note: The mat has been discussed in Book IV, chapter 13, and elsewhere in Book I, chapter 7. The Rule of Pachomius calls it a reclining stool in article 50. Concerning the lebitonarium, see Book I, chapter 5.]—a kind of sleeveless garment among the Egyptian monks—and one worn garment for sleeping or working; and a linen wrap [Note: Cassianus there calls it a small, narrow cloak, with which they covered both their necks and shoulders.], two hoods [Note: All these items are treated individually and distinctly in several chapters of Book I.], a goatskin, which they call a melote [Col. 0276B], a linen belt, sandals, and a staff as a companion for travel.

The sick are supported by extraordinary services and by food prepared in abundant measure; the healthy display greater abstinence. Twice a week, on the fourth and sixth days of the week, all fast, except during Pentecost. On the other days those who wish eat after midday; and in the evening a meal is likewise provided for laborers, the elderly, children, and times of extreme heat. Some eat a little at the second meal; others are content with only one food at lunch or dinner; some, after tasting a little bread, go out. All eat together. Whoever does not wish to go to table receives only bread, water, and salt in his cell, whether he wishes this for one day or for two.

When the senior, or the one who stands first in rank, gives a stroke with his hand, reciting something from Scripture from memory, as the prayer ends no one rises later than the others, but all rise together. No one looks at another who is working; rather, with their eyes fixed downward, each is intent on his own work, etc.

## HERE BEGINS THE RULE OF ST. PACHOMIUS

[Col. 0277]

These are the life-giving precepts [Note: Spiritual precepts, namely, those by which the spiritual and religious life is lived here and eternal life is obtained. Cassianus, Conference 23, chapter 4.] handed down by three elders [Note: Namely, Pachomius, Theodore, and Orsiesius, mentioned above in the preface]:

### I.

[Note: Silence to be observed in the oratory or church. On this see Cassianus, Book II of the Institutes, chapter 10, and St. Benedict, chapter 52.]

If it should happen that, during the time of psalmody, prayer, or the reading, anyone speaks or laughs, he shall loosen his belt and, with his neck bowed and his hands lowered toward the ground, stand before the altar; and he shall be rebuked by the head of the monastery [Note: Elsewhere called the Father of the monastery, or abbot]. He shall do the same in the assembly of the brothers when they have gathered together for food.

### II.

When the trumpet has sounded during the day for the assembly [Note: That is, for the gathering or congregation of the monks in the church, either for prayer or to hear the word of God. Cassianus commonly calls it “the Mass” and synaxis. Likewise St. Jerome, Letter 60: “When the assembly was being celebrated in the church,” he says. And below in the same place: “So that I might celebrate the assembly with you according to ecclesiastical custom.”] [Note: The trumpet was, I suppose, made of horn, used instead of a bell, or campana, formerly among hermit monks, who lacked bronze and every kind of metal. On this occasion it should be noted that the faithful, especially monks, were usually summoned to church by three instruments: a trumpet, as here; a wooden board; and a little bell or campana. I have so far encountered no other example of a trumpet used among Christians. Among the Hebrews, Josephus, Jewish War, Book V, chapter 9, relates that a priest used to announce the appointed hours of the day and the Sabbaths to the people from a high tower by the sound of a trumpet; and it is well known from Scripture that the use of trumpets in sacred rites was customary. As for the wooden board [Col. 0277D], the Church now uses it only during the final three days of Holy Week, when the bells are silent, as a sign of mourning. Yet monks formerly also used it at times as a sign of festivity and joy. Thus we read in the Second Council of Nicaea, article 4: “When the holy relics had approached the holy city, they suddenly rose, striking the sacred wood, and went out to meet them in the venerable church of the Virgin Mother of God,” etc. So much for that passage. They used two methods for summoning monks to church: either all were summoned equally by one striking, or the doors of each individual were struck separately. An example occurs in Palladius, Lausiac History 104, where he says: “When he had completed the customary time in this manner, striking with the mallet’s signal, by which he awakened the other brothers, he knocked on the doors of all the cells and gathered them for the oratory.” See the notes on Book III of the Institutes, chapter 2, and Book IV, chapter 12. Hence, perhaps, the striking of a mallet or board at the individual doors and workshops of the cloister, as though at the monks’ cells, even at the funerals of deceased brothers, became customary in certain places and monasteries. The use of little bells, moreover, was introduced after peace had been restored to the Church following the persecutions of the tyrants. If they were larger, they were called campanae, after Campania, the region of Italy where they were first made; if smaller, they were called nolae, after Nola, a city of the same Campania, as Durandus notes, Book I of the Rationale, chapter 4. It seems especially remarkable that St. Jerome reports in Letter 27 that, in St. Paula’s monastery, all the nuns were accustomed to be summoned to the synaxis by one voice singing more loudly, namely, “Alleluia.” He says: “After the Alleluia had been sung, by which signal they were summoned to the assembly, no one was permitted to remain seated; but the first to come, or one of the first, waited for the arrival of the others.” So much for that passage.]

Whoever comes one prayer later shall be rebuked according to the order of the earlier correction and shall stand in the place of the meal. At night, however, because somewhat more allowance is made for bodily weakness, whoever comes after three prayers shall be corrected in the same order, both in the assembly [Note: Ciaconius placed in the margin: “or two.”] and in the place of eating [Note: Above, “the place of the meal,” commonly called the refectory. This term was also used by Pope Innocent III in the chapter “Cum ad monasterium,” concerning the status of monks; by the Council of Tours, chapter 23; by the Council of Aachen, chapter 117; and by Leo IX in Gratian, 12, question 1, chapter “Necessaria.”].

### III.

When the brothers are praying in the assembly, no one shall leave [Note: All the elders were called seniors. St. Benedict likewise calls them priors and deans, chapters 21 and 70.] without the command of the seniors, unless he has asked and has been granted permission to leave for a natural necessity.

### IV.

[Note: This article should be compared with articles 26 and 80, where it is explained what things had to be memorized and learned.]

All shall recite from memory whatever has been commanded them. If anyone has forgotten anything or hesitates while speaking, he shall be rebuked for negligence and forgetfulness.

### V.

[Note: The solemn sacrifice on Sundays. We call it the solemn and conventual Mass, at which all the monks received communion. Cassianus, Book III of the Institutes, chapter 11, and frequently elsewhere.]

On Sunday, at the assembly in which the offering is to be presented [Col. 0278B], no one except the superior of the house and the notable seniors of the monastery shall have the authority to sing the psalms. If one of the seniors is singing—that is, reciting the responsory—and anyone is absent, he shall immediately undergo before the altar the prescribed penalty of penitence and rebuke.

### VI.

At the assembly in which the offering is to be presented, whoever leaves without the command of a senior shall immediately be rebuked.

### VII.

In the morning, in each house, after the prayers have ended, they shall not immediately return to their cells. Rather, they shall discuss among themselves what they heard the superiors disputing, and then enter their rooms.

[Note: Monastic disputations, formerly frequent in monasteries, were also called conferences by Cassianus. St. Jerome likewise reports the following in Letter 22: “After the ninth hour they come together in common; psalms resound, the Scriptures are read according to custom, and when the prayers have been completed and all have taken their seats, the one whom they call the Father begins to speak. While he is speaking, such silence prevails that no one looks at another, and no one dares even to clear his throat. The speaker’s praise is found in the tears of his hearers; silent tears roll down their faces, and grief does not even break out into sobs. But when he begins to announce the kingdom of Christ, future blessedness, and the glory that is to come [Col. 0279C], you may see everyone, with measured sighs and eyes raised to heaven, saying: ‘Who will give me wings like a dove, and I shall fly away and rest?’ Afterwards the council is dismissed, and each decury goes with its father to the table,” etc. St. Augustine has similar material in Book I, On the Morals of the Catholic Church, chapter 31.]

The disputation shall be held by the superiors of the houses three times each week. During the disputation, whether sitting or standing, the brothers shall not change their order, either according to the order of the houses or according to that of the individual men.

### VIII.

If anyone should fall asleep while sitting, while the superior of the house or the head of the monastery is speaking, he shall immediately be compelled to stand, and shall stand until the superior sees fit for him to sit.

### IX.

When the signal sounds for them to gather and hear the commands of the seniors, no one shall remain behind. Nor shall the common fire [Note: The common fire in the monastery: while sitting there during the time of silence, they were to be silent and devote themselves to reading or spiritual conversation, not to idle and worldly chatter. Thus in the Constitutions of the Cassinese monks, on chapter 52 of the Rule: “Silence shall be observed at the brothers’ common fire.” See also below, article 67.] be lit before the disputation is completed. Whoever neglects one of these commands shall be subject to the aforementioned correction.

### X.

After the assembly has been dismissed, each person, as he leaves and goes to his cell and to the place of eating, shall meditate on something from Scripture; and no one shall have his head covered during the time of meditation [Note: The exercise of meditation, or mental prayer, was extremely common among the ancient Fathers and especially characteristic of monks. From it they were chiefly called ἀσκηταί, that is, “exercisers,” by Eusebius, Book II of the Ecclesiastical History, chapter 16. Hence the frequent mention of spiritual exercises in both their histories and writings, so that nothing is more often impressed upon them or more earnestly commended. [Col. 0279D] The same matter is treated below in articles 16, 35, and 65, and by Cassianus, Book II of the Institutes, chapter 14, where he teaches that the Egyptian monks devoted themselves continually, both by night and by day, equally to manual labor and meditation. “For,” he says, “just as scarcely any time of leisure is allowed them, so no end is placed upon spiritual meditation. For by exercising equally the virtues of body and soul, they make the wages of the outward person equal to the benefits of the inward, so that no one can easily discern which depends upon which: whether they perform unceasing manual labor because of spiritual meditation, or whether, because of the continuity of their work, they acquire such notable spiritual progress and the light of knowledge.” He repeats the same teaching in Book III, chapter 2, and Book IV, chapter 12, and elsewhere teaches, following the opinion of Abbot Theodore, that knowledge of Scripture is acquired more through prayer and meditation than through extensive study and reading of commentaries. See also Conference 14, chapter 10. St. Benedict likewise imposed the same rule and practice of meditation on his coenobites in two places. In chapter 48 he establishes that the hours of the day not occupied with the work of God, or divine office, should be distributed so that some are devoted to prayer, whether mental or vocal, others to reading, and others to manual labor. In this threefold kind of occupation, Turrecrematus teaches in the same place, the monastic life consists. And in chapter 58, treating of the initial formation of a newly admitted novice, he says: “Afterwards he shall eat and sleep in the novices’ cell, where he shall also meditate.” From these things it is clear how far from the character of their institution and ancestral piety are those monks who, although by the rule of their order they profess the contemplative life, think of nothing less than contemplation or meditation and devote not even a quarter of an hour each day to this pious and healthful exercise of meditation, being wholly occupied with external matters and duties.]

### XI.

When they have come to eat, they shall sit in order in the appointed places and cover their heads. As soon as a senior commands you to move from one table to another, you must go, offering no resistance whatsoever. Nor shall you stretch out your hand at table before the superior of your house, nor look around at the others who are eating. Each superior shall teach in his house how they are to eat with discipline and gentleness.

[Note: Silence at table, or in the refectory. On this matter see St. Jerome above: “There is no noise during eating; no one speaks while eating,” Cassianus, Book IV, chapter 17. Among the Egyptians, and especially the monks of Tabennesis, such silence is observed by all that, although so great a multitude of brothers sits together for refreshment, no one dares even to mutter, except the one who presides over his decury. Such discipline of silence is maintained among the diners that, with their hoods lowered beyond their eyelids, so that their eyes may not have unrestricted opportunity to wander curiously, they look at nothing beyond the table and the foods placed upon it or taken from it. Thus no one observes how or how much another is refreshed. Cassianus says this, plainly in agreement with this article of the Pachomian Rule. See our notes on the same passage.]

If anyone either speaks or laughs during the meal, he shall do penance, shall immediately be rebuked in the same place, and shall stand until the others rise from eating.

### XII.

If anyone comes late to eat [Col. 0280B] [Note: These words are ambiguous. They may refer to the preceding sentence, as follows: “If anyone comes late, unless by command of a senior or otherwise lawfully prevented,” etc.; or to the following sentence, so that he is to do penance unless he is absolved or exempted from it by the judgment or command of a senior or superior. The former meaning is preferable, as is clear from article 72, where it is said: “No one shall go outside except by command of a senior,” that is, unless he does so by the senior’s command.], except by command of a senior, he shall likewise do penance or return fasting to his house.

### XIII.

If anything necessary is needed at table, no one shall dare to speak, but he shall give a sound as a signal to those serving.

[Note: The antiquity and institution of monastic signs for preserving silence. Cassianus says in the same place: “If the dean sees that anything needs to be brought to or removed from the table, he should indicate it by a sound rather than by his voice.” Nicephorus, Book IX, chapter 14, likewise says: “By certain signs, by movements of the hands or nods, they would indicate and request what was necessary from those appointed to provide for the table.” More about these signs is recorded at the same place in Cassianus. See also article 65 below.]

### XIV.

If you leave after eating, do not speak on the way back until you have reached your place.

### XV.

The ministers shall eat nothing besides what has been prepared in common for the brothers, nor shall they dare to prepare altered foods for themselves [Note: That is, foods different from the common foods, or even the same foods changed in some respect, prepared or seasoned differently.].

### XVI.

[Note: That is, the person who gives or strikes the signal for the meal. The instrument struck is variously called by some a board, by others a little bell or nola, by others a small bell, a cymbal, or a scilla or squilla—namely, a round bronze vessel resembling at its upper part the sea onion, or scilla, which is properly called scilla. Durandus, Book I of the Rationale, chapter 4, says: “The squilla is struck in the refectory, the cymbal in the cloister, the nola in the choir,” etc. Peter of Cluny, Book I of the Miracles, chapter 12, says: “According to custom, the scilla was struck once by the prior; when he heard the sound, the demon who was trying to lead the monk away from the cloister is then reported to have fled.”]

The one who strikes the signal for eating, while the brothers are gathering, shall meditate on something as he strikes.

### XVII.

The one who distributes sweetmeats to the brothers leaving before the doors of the refectory [Note: Perhaps some honey or fruit; elsewhere, confectionery or dessert.] shall meditate on something from Scripture while distributing them.

### XVIII.

[Note: From this we learn that those monks lived not only from the work of their hands but also from alms, whether begged or spontaneously offered and donated [Col. 0281D]. The mendicant orders therefore took their example from them.]

The one who receives what is given shall receive it not in his hood but in a skin, and shall not taste anything he has received until he reaches the house. The person who distributes it to the others shall receive his own portion from the superior. The other ministers shall do the same, receiving from another and claiming nothing for themselves at their own discretion. No one shall give one person more than another has received. But if illness is alleged, the superior of the house shall go to the ministers of the sick and receive from them what is necessary.

[Note: A superior, formerly so called, who is now called a prior, as also in St. Benedict’s Rule, chapter 65. St. Jerome says in his preface: “They have superiors of the individual houses, so that in one house approximately forty brothers live, who obey the superior,” etc. Gennadius says of Pachomius that he wrote one letter to the superiors of all the monasteries. Likewise, for the day of remission, which is observed in August, he wrote one letter so that the superiors might gather together. So much for that.]

### XIX.

If one of these ministers becomes ill [Note: Concerning the various ministers among those monks, see above, column 275, note e.], he shall not have permission to enter the kitchen or storeroom and take anything for himself. Rather, the other ministers shall give him whatever they judge necessary. Nor shall he be permitted to cook for himself whatever he desires; instead, the superiors of the houses shall receive from the other ministers whatever they see to be necessary for him.

### XX.

No one who is not sick shall enter the place of the sick [Note: The nosocomium, or infirmary, and the care of the sick among the ancient monks, concerning which St. Jerome says in his preface: “The sick are supported by extraordinary services and by food prepared in abundant measure.” And in Letter 22 to Eustochium: “If anyone begins to fall ill, he is transferred to a larger room and is comforted by the service of so many elders that he does not long for the luxuries of cities or a mother’s affection.” St. Augustine, Rule for Clerics, chapter 8; St. Benedict, chapter 36.]. Whoever becomes ill shall be led by the superior of the house into the refectory of the sick. If he needs a small cloak, tunic, or anything else necessary for covering himself or eating, the superior himself shall obtain it from the ministers and give it to the sick man. The invalid may not enter the dining room and eat whatever he desires unless he is led to eat by the minister appointed for this purpose. He shall not be permitted to carry to his cell any of what he received in the place of the sick, not even a piece of fruit.

### XXI.

[Note: We have made some observations concerning stews or dishes in Conference 15, chapter 1; St. Benedict also treats them in chapter 39 of his Rule.]

Those who cook the dishes shall eat nothing themselves but shall serve those who are eating.

### XXII.

[Note: St. Jerome, Letter 22, speaking of these same Egyptian monks, says: “Only the elderly receive wine; children are also often given it, so that the wearied age of some may be supported and the beginning age of others not broken.” St. Augustine, Book I, On the Morals of the Catholic Church, chapter 31, says: “They abstain not only from meat and wine, as sufficient for subduing lust, but also from those things which provoke the appetite of the belly and throat more vigorously the cleaner they seem to some,” etc. Hence, I think, St. Benedict took what he says in chapter 40: “Although we read that wine is altogether unsuitable for monks, because in our times monks cannot be persuaded of this, let us at least agree to this: that we should not drink to satiety, but more sparingly, because wine makes even the wise apostatize.” But the saying is found more explicitly in the Lives of the Fathers, Book V, in these words, Book IV, number 31: “Some told Abba Pastor about a monk who did not drink wine, and he said to them: ‘For wine is altogether not for monks.’” So it is written there. Hence it is likely that this saying passed into a proverb. St. Benedict had evidently read it somewhere when he says: “Although we read that wine,” etc.]

No one shall touch wine or fish sauce except in the place of the sick [Note: Liquamen was a liquid pressed from fish, as is clear from the following article, where it says “fish sauce.” Isidore, Book XX of the Etymologies, chapter 3, says: “It is called liquamen because the little fish dissolved in brine liquefy the same moisture.” This liquid is called salsugo or muria. See Conference 8, chapter 1.].

### XXIII.

If one of those who are sent abroad becomes ill on the journey or along the road, and has a need or desire to eat fish sauce or something else that they are not accustomed to eat, he shall not eat with the other brothers. Rather, he shall be separated, and the ministers shall give him an abundant supply, so that the sick brother may be distressed in no respect.

### XXIV.

No one shall dare to visit a sick person without the permission of a senior. Not even a relative or brother shall have authority to minister to him without the command of the superior of the house.

### XXV.

If anyone neglects and omits one of these provisions, he shall be corrected by the customary rebuke.

### XXVI.

[Note: The manner of receiving novices, or, as St. Benedict puts it, the discipline for receiving brothers. Cassianus discusses this at length in Book IV of the Institutes. See also article 80 below.]

If anyone comes to the door of the monastery wishing to renounce the world and join the number of the brothers, he shall not have permission to enter. Instead, the matter shall first be announced to the Father of the monastery, and he shall remain outside before the gate for a few days. He shall be taught the Lord’s Prayer and as many psalms as he can learn, and he shall carefully prove himself, lest perhaps he do something and, disturbed, depart after a short time [Note: For example, if he is a slave, a boy, or a minor. Such persons cannot enter or be admitted into religious life without the consent of their masters or parents, as is expressly stated in the sacred canons.], or lest he be under some authority, and whether he is able to renounce his parents and despise his own property.

If they see that he is suitable for everything, he shall then be taught the remaining disciplines of the monastery: what he must do and what duties he must perform, whether in the assembly of all the brothers, in the house to which he is assigned, or in the order of eating. Once instructed and perfected in every good work, he shall be joined to the brothers.

[Note: The change of habit and other ancient rites of monastic profession, concerning which see Cassianus, Book IV, chapter 3 and following. St. Benedict also received these practices from the same authors.]

Then they shall strip him of his secular clothing and dress him in the monks’ habit. He shall be handed over to the doorkeeper, who shall bring him before all the brothers at the time of prayer. He shall sit in the place commanded him. Those appointed for this matter shall receive the clothing he brought with him, carry it into the storeroom, and place it under the authority of the head of the monastery.

### XXVII.

No one remaining in the monastery shall have authority to receive anyone for eating. Rather, he shall send him to the door of the hospice, and those appointed for this purpose shall receive him.

[Note: The reception of guests and those responsible for it are discussed by Cassianus in Book V, chapters 23 and following, and in Conference 2, chapters 25 and 26. St. Benedict also imitated this institution in chapter 43, “On Receiving Guests.”]

### XXVIII.

When clerics or monks come to the door of the monastery, they shall be received with greater honor. They shall wash their feet, observe the commands of the Gospel, and lead them to the hospice. They shall provide everything suitable for the use of monks. If they wish to come to the assembly of the brothers at the time of prayer and the gathering, then, provided they are of the same faith, the minister of the hospice shall inform the Father of the monastery, and they shall thus be led to pray.

### XXIX.

If secular persons, the weak, or “weaker vessels,” that is, women [Note: Scripture commonly calls a woman a vessel. 1 Thessalonians 4: “That each of you may possess his vessel”—that is, his wife—in sanctification and honor; 1 Peter 3: “Showing honor to the female vessel as the weaker one.”], come to the door, they shall receive each separately in different places according to the order of the superior and according to their sex. They shall care especially for the women with greater honor and diligence, in complete fear of God, and shall give them a place separated from all proximity to men [Col. 0284A], so that there may be no occasion for blasphemy.

[Note: This is explained in other words at the end of the same article: “Let no one be given an occasion for slander.”]

If they come at evening [Note: “At vespers” is used for “in the evening.”], it is not right to cast them out. Rather, as we have said, they shall be given a separate and enclosed place, with every discipline and precaution, so that the flock of the brothers may freely perform its duty and no one be given an occasion for slander.

### XXX.

If someone stands before the door of the monastery saying that he wishes to see his brother or relative, the doorkeeper shall inform the Father of the monastery. He shall summon the superior of the house and ask whether the brother or relative is with him; and, with the superior’s permission, the monk shall take as a companion for his departure someone whose faith has been tested. He shall then be sent to see his brother or relative.

If he happens to have brought food that is permitted to be eaten in the monastery, he himself may not receive it. Rather, he shall call the doorkeeper, and the doorkeeper shall receive what has been brought. If it is food to be eaten with bread, those for whom it was brought shall receive none of it; everything shall be taken to the place of the sick.

### XXXI.

If it is announced that one of someone’s relatives is ill, the doorkeeper shall first inform the Father of the monastery. He shall summon the superior of the house and ask him. They shall select a man whose faith and discipline have been tested and send him with the monk to see the sick person. He shall receive only as much travel provision as the superior of his house decides.

### XXXII.

If necessity compels him to remain outside and eat in the house of his parents or relatives, he shall not do this. Rather, he shall remain in a church or in a monastery [Col. 0284C] of the same faith [Note: That is, of the Catholic and orthodox faith and communion. In those times there were many heretical or schismatic monks whom Catholics had to avoid; Cassianus discusses them in Conference 1, chapter 20. Hence St. Jerome writes in Book III of his Apology against Rufinus that, while living in the Bethlehem monastery, he received all guests except heretics.].

If his relatives or kindred prepare food and set it before him, he shall neither receive nor eat it at all, except those things which he is accustomed to eat in the monastery. He shall not taste fish sauce, drink wine, or consume anything else that he is not accustomed to eat. If he receives something from his parents, he shall eat only as much as is sufficient for the journey. The remainder shall be given to the superior of his house, who shall carry it to the cell of the sick.

### XXXIII.

If someone’s relative or blood relation dies, he shall not have permission to accompany the funeral unless the Father of the monastery commands it.

[Col. 0285A] **XXXIV.** [Note: [Col. 0285C] This custom—that monks should go out not singly but in pairs, that is, one with a companion and associate—first arose from the example of Christ, who sent his disciples not singly but two by two before him into every city and place where he himself was about to come (Luke 10), and to prepare the Passover (Luke 22), as also to visit his tomb (John 20); and into the city of Samaria Peter and John, that is, two together, went (Acts 8). Secondly, it arose from the institution of the holy Fathers: Pachomius in this passage, Basil in Sermon 1, *On the Institution of Monks*, Dorotheus in Sermon 20, and Augustine in the Rule; it will suffice to quote the words of the last alone. “When you go out,” he says, “walk together; when you arrive where you are going, stand together.” Thirdly, it arose from the example of those same men. The first abbot, as reported by Sozomenus in Book 6, chapter 29, would not go to his sister except with a companion. Saint Thomas Aquinas called a religious who went out alone “a solitary devil.” And when he was summoned by a steward who did not recognize him to accompany him to the market, he willingly and promptly followed, as related in the *Chronicle of the Dominicans*. See Cassian, Book 5, chapter 40, and Saint Gregory in the *Register*, Book 10, letter 22, where he rejected and judged unworthy of the abbacy a certain monk named Constantine, whom the brothers had requested, for this reason: he had presumed to go alone, without any of his brothers, to a certain monastery. “From his action,” he says, “we learn that if he walks without a witness, he does not live rightly. But how can he keep a rule for others which he does not know how to keep for himself?” Thus Gregory. Finally, it arose from what is honorable and useful: the honor of religion and monastic life demands that monks not walk alone, like gyrovagues and undisciplined men. Ecclesiasticus commends the usefulness of this in the words: “Woe to the one who is alone; when he falls, he has no one to raise him up” (chapter 4).] No one shall be sent outside alone on any business unless another has been joined to him. When they have returned to the monastery, if they see someone at the entrance asking for one of his relatives who lives in the monastery, they shall not dare go to him, report to him, or call him; and whatever they have done or heard outside, they shall not be able to relate in the monastery at all. [Note: [Col. 0285D] Saint Benedict, chapter 67: “Let no one presume,” he says, “to tell others whatever he has seen or heard outside the monastery, because this causes the greatest destruction. If anyone presumes to do so, let him be subject to the regular punishment.” The same is repeated below, article 49.]

**XXXV.** [Note: [Col. 0286C] The manner of going outside to perform manual labor—that is, to cultivate fields or gardens, reap grain, gather crops or fruits, and so forth. Cassian treats this at length in Book 10 of the *Institutes*, chapter 22 and following. Saint Jerome, referring to this institution, writes to Rusticus the monk in Letter 4: “The monasteries of the Egyptians,” he says, “observe this custom, that they admit no one without the labor of work.” Augustine likewise discusses it in *On the Customs of the Catholic Church*, in the passage cited above. Cassian also treats it in Book 2, chapter 3, and Saint Benedict in chapters 48 and 57.] When the signal has been given for them to go out to work, the superior shall go before them, and no one shall remain in the monastery except the one whom the Father has ordered to remain, and those who go shall not ask where they are going; rather, each one shall meditate on something from Scripture. If someone should happen to meet them or wish to speak with one of them, the superior appointed for this shall answer those who meet them. While working, they shall say nothing secular, but shall either meditate on holy things or remain silent. No one shall take a small cloak with him when going to work unless the superior permits it. A worker shall not sit without the superior’s command. After the work, all tools shall be carried back to the house.

**XXXVI.** Without the superior’s command, none of the brothers may send someone anywhere, even if he has need to do so. If the one who is superior is himself compelled by necessity to go somewhere, he shall delegate his office to the one next after him in rank.

**XXXVII.** If anyone wishes to wash a garment, he shall inform his superior, and the superior shall send another with him; when the garment has been washed, they shall return to the house, and the one charged with this shall put it away once it is dry.

**XXXVIII.** No one shall take vegetables from the garden unless he has received them from the gardener.

**XXXIX.** [Note: [Col. 0286C] We discussed the palm tree and its many uses among the monks of antiquity in Book 10, chapter 24.] No one shall take palm leaves, from which baskets are woven, on his own authority, except the one to whom the palms have been entrusted.

**XL.** [Note: [Col. 0286C] Cassian, Book 4, chapter 18, referring to this passage: “Before or after they receive the lawful common meal,” he says, “the greatest care is taken that no one presume to indulge his mouth in any food outside the table. Thus, when they walk through gardens and orchards, where fruits hang attractively and abundantly from the trees, and not only present themselves to the breasts of those passing by but also lie scattered on the ground, offering themselves to be trampled underfoot and ready to be gathered, they can easily entice those who look at them to consent to desire; and by their opportunity or abundance provoke even those who are strict and most abstinent to desire them. It is called sacrilege not only to taste any of these things, but even to touch them with the hand, unless they are openly provided for all who are eating in common and publicly distributed for consumption by the steward through the service of the brothers.” Thus far Cassian; this also applies to the following article, 42.] No one shall dare eat grapes or ears of grain that are still unripe, contrary to the order of discipline; and, in general, no one shall eat separately from anything in the field or orchard before the Father has offered it to all the brothers.

**XLI.** Those who cook shall not dare eat before the brothers have eaten. [Note: [Col. 0286D] The same rule is given above, article 21.]

**XLII.** Those who are in the fruit trees and among the vines shall not eat of their fruits until the brothers have eaten first. If they have been ordered to gather the fruits of the orchards or vineyards, the superior of those gathering shall give each person a small amount to eat at the same place; and when they have come to the monastery, they shall receive their portions among the other brothers. If they find apples fallen beneath the trees, they shall not dare eat them, but shall place what they have found in passing beside the roots of the trees. The very man who distributes the fruit among the others who are gathering shall not be able to taste it either; he shall carry it to the steward, who shall give it out with the rest and assign him his portion.

**XLIII.** [Note: [Col. 0286D] The same rule is given below, article 63. See the example of Serapion in *Conference* 2, chapter 11.] No one shall store anything in his cell for eating [Col. 0287A] except what he has received from the steward.

**XLIV.** [Note: [Col. 0287C] Saint Jerome, toward the end of his preface: “Let all eat together. Whoever does not wish to go to the table shall receive only bread, water, and salt in his cell, whether he wishes this for one day or for two.”] Those who do not wish to eat in common with the others, as though claiming greater abstinence for themselves, shall receive only enough bread and salt for one day when they are due to eat. Outside the monastery kitchen, no one shall have authority to cook food.

**XLV.** [Note: [Col. 0287C] Cassian, Book 4 of the *Institutes*, chapters 13 and following; Saint Benedict, chapter 33. See below, article 63.] No one shall have in his cell anything except what is prescribed by the law of the monastery; neither a few coins nor anything of his own. If you find anything besides his habit, you shall take it away without objection.

**XLVI.** If anyone is transferred from one house to another, [Note: [Col. 0287C] *Excepto* here means “with the exception of,” since *excepto* is an adverb meaning “apart from” or “besides.”] he shall not be able to transfer anything with him except those things necessary for daily use and clothing.

[Col. 0287B] **XLVII.** No one shall have permission either to walk about in the monastery [Note: [Col. 0287C] Monastic enclosure requires that no one leave the monastery without permission. The Fathers valued this permission—which they regarded as a principal sign of obedience and submission—so highly that Saint Basil says in the *Institution of Monks*: “If anyone leaves the monastery without receiving a blessing or without being dismissed by the Father and the prefect of the monastery, let him be excommunicated.” That this was strictly observed by monks is clear from Gregory the Great, Book 2 of the *Dialogues*; Saint Dorotheus, Sermon 9; John Climacus, step 4; Saint Benedict, chapter 67; and others. (On monastic enclosure, see the note on *Conference* 24, chapter 4.)] or to proceed beyond the monastery wall unless he has asked the superior and the superior has granted permission.

**XLVIII.** Care must be taken that no one carries words from one house to another, or from monastery to monastery, or from monastery to field, or from field to monastery.

**XLIX.** If anyone has walked on the road, sailed, or worked outside, he shall not speak in the monastery about what he saw being done there.

**L.** [Note: [Col. 0287D] That is, outside the *psiathium*, discussed by Saint Jerome in the preface and by Cassian in Book 4, chapter 13, *Conference* 1, final chapter, and elsewhere. He says *sellula*, not *cellula*. The former is a diminutive of *sella*, which derives from sitting. A *reclina* is a chair inclined backward or reclining, so that those lying upon it could sleep. In Palladius’s *Rule of Pachomius* it is written: “Let them sleep not reclining, but after constructing seats for themselves that are somewhat more tilted backward, let them sleep there sitting, with their coverings placed upon them.”] No one shall sleep except in a reclining chair. When he has settled down to sleep, he shall not speak to another. After he has fallen asleep, if he wakes during the night after sleeping, he shall pray.

[Col. 0288A] **LI.** If a day of fasting is at hand and he begins to thirst, he shall not dare drink.

**LII.** No one shall wash or anoint another unless he has been ordered to do so.

**LIII.** [Note: [Col. 0287D] Cassian, Book 2, chapter 15, and Book 4, chapter 16.] No one shall speak to another in the darkness. No one shall sleep with another; no one shall hold another’s hand. Whether walking, sitting, or standing, each shall remain one cubit from the other.

**LIV.** No one shall cut his hair without the superior’s decision.

**LV.** [Note: [Col. 0287D] The exchange or barter of anything of value—such as books, clothing, and so forth—without the consent of the superior is just as unlawful for monks as a gift, because it is an act of ownership contrary to the vow of poverty.] No one shall dare exchange with another anything he has received from the superior. He shall neither take something better and give something worse, nor, conversely, give something better and receive something worse; and in his clothing and habit he shall find nothing new, for the sake of adornment, beyond what the others have.

[Col. 0288B] **LVI.** No one going to the assembly for eating shall leave an unbound codex. [Note: [Col. 0288C] The care of the library was extremely ancient in monasteries, where all the manuscript codices were stored and preserved with the greatest diligence. Saint Augustine likewise says in the Rule, chapter 22: “Those appointed over the codices shall serve their brothers without murmuring.” And in chapter 23: “Let codices be requested at a fixed hour each day; whoever asks outside that hour shall not receive one.” Saint Benedict says in chapter 48: “During the days of Lent, let all receive individual codices from the library and read them through in order. These codices are to be distributed at the beginning of Lent.” See Cassiodorus, *Institutions of Divine Reading*, chapter 8. Related are the observations we made concerning the writing of books in monasteries, especially Benedictine monasteries, in Book 5, chapter 39.] After None, the codices shall be attended to by the one to whom this belongs.

**LVII.** [Note: [Col. 0288C] This article also concerns care of the sick, discussed above in article 20.] If one of the brothers has been injured or struck but is not confined to bed, rather walking about in weakness, and needs something—a garment, a small cloak, or other articles—the superior shall receive the request and provide it. When he has recovered, he shall return it without any delay.

**LVIII.** No one shall receive anything from another unless the superior has ordered it.

**LIX.** No one shall go to the village unless sent. Two people shall not sit together on the bare back of a donkey, nor upon the pole of a wagon.

**LX.** [Note: [Col. 0288D] Monasteries contained workshops for nearly all the crafts that seemed necessary for the use of the monks and the monastery. Thus Palladius, speaking of the Pachomian monks in Aphthonius, says: “They practice every craft: one works at cultivating the field, another in the garden, another in the bakery, another in the bronze workshop, another in carpentry, another in sewing shoes, another in beautiful writing.” Thus far Palladius. To prevent anyone from entering the workshops of the craftsmen uninvited or without orders, Saint Basil also enacted in these words: “If anyone intrudes into the kitchen or storeroom, except those designated or those who care for the discipline of good order, let him be deprived of the blessing.” See Cassian, Book 4, chapter 16.] Only the superiors shall go to the workshops of the various crafts, in order to receive what is necessary.

[Col. 0289A] **LXI.** [Note: [Col. 0289C] Saint Benedict expresses the same rule in other words in chapter 48: “Nor shall a brother be joined to a brother at inappropriate hours.”] No one shall dare enter another’s cell.

**LXII.** No one shall receive anything entrusted to him, even by his own brother.

**LXIII.** [Note: [Col. 0289C] The same rule is given above, article 43.] No one shall store anything in his cell without the superior’s command—not even apples.

**LXIV.** If the superior has departed, another superior, or the one who is second, shall take charge of the one who has departed, or the superior shall choose one of the brothers and entrust his own responsibility to him.

**LXV.** [Note: [Col. 0289C] This agrees with what was said above about the workshops of craftsmen, in which silence was maintained.] When they mix flour with water and knead the dough, no one shall speak to another. When they carry the loaves on boards to the oven, they shall observe the same silence; they shall meditate only on psalms or on something from [Note: [Col. 0289C] You see that the exercise of meditation, discussed above, was extremely frequent and familiar to the ancient monks—indeed, almost constant—so that they occupied themselves with it not only in the oratory or privately in their cells, but in nearly every place and at nearly every time, and in almost all activities and duties. By this means they withdrew themselves from vain thoughts and conversations and kept the soul sighing and uplifted toward heavenly and salutary things. See articles 16 and 17.] Scripture until they complete the work. If anything necessary is needed, they shall not speak, but shall give a sign to those who can bring what is required. When they have been summoned to mix the flour, no one shall remain in the place where the bread is baked except those sufficient for the baking and those who have been ordered to do so.

**LXVI.** There is a similar discipline on ships. No one shall untie the ship’s rope from the shore or move the ship without the Father’s command. In the inner part of the ship, while the other brothers are resting upon the crossbeams and decking, no one shall sleep; and no one shall permit secular persons to sleep with them. [Note: [Col. 0289C] That is, women, as above in article 29.] The weaker vessels shall not sail with them unless the Father of the monastery happens to command it.

**LXVII.** No one shall dare kindle a fire in his own house unless one is lit in common for everyone.

[Col. 0289C] **LXVIII.** [Note: [Col. 0289C] Cassian, Book 4, chapter 16; Saint Benedict, chapter 43.] Whoever comes late to one prayer, or mutters or speaks to another, or laughs during the remaining prayers, shall do penance according to the established order.

**LXIX.** When they are sitting at home, [Note: [Col. 0289D] Conversations about vain, profane, and secular matters are to be avoided. Evil conversations corrupt good morals (1 Corinthians 15). Cassian, Book 5, chapter 9: “We saw,” he says, “an old man named Machetes obtain this grace from the Lord through prolonged prayers: however many days and nights a spiritual conversation lasted, he was never completely relaxed by the torpor of sleep. If anyone attempted to introduce a word of slander or idleness, he immediately fell asleep; thus the poison of malicious speech could not reach even his ears and pollute them. In the *Lives of the Fathers* (Book 3, no. 36; and Book 6, booklet 1, no. 3), we read that a certain great man obtained from God this grace: in the pious conversations of the brothers, which concerned the sacred Scriptures, he saw holy angels standing by and taking great delight in their conversations. “But,” he says, “when they spoke about anything else, the holy angels immediately withdrew farther away; exceedingly filthy pigs came instead and wallowed among them. For demons, in the form of animals, delighted in their vain talk.” The blessed old man, seeing this, warned the brothers throughout the monasteries, saying: “Restrain yourselves from much speaking, and your tongue from idle conversations, through which the soul’s evil destruction is generated.”] they shall not be permitted to speak about anything secular. But if a superior teaches something from Scripture, they shall meditate on it among themselves in turn and repeat what they have heard or what they remember by heart.

**LXX.** [Note: [Col. 0290C] Cassian, Book 4 of the *Institutes*, chapter 16; Saint Benedict, chapters 32 and 46.] Whoever breaks an earthen vessel or any useful object intended for the monastery’s use shall do penance.

**LXXI.** [Note: [Col. 0290C] If a brother “sleeps,” that is, dies, the whole brotherhood—that is, the congregation of the brothers—shall accompany him, namely, to the tomb, and bury him honorably. Saint Chrysostom, describing the death and funeral of monks in Homily 1 on Job, says: “When they have a brother laboring with his final breath, they sit around him and hear his last words; they deliberately offer exhortations and admonitions, kiss his mouth with a final kiss; then, when he has given up his soul, they arrange his hands and close his eyes,” and so forth. See Saint Jerome in the *Epitaph for Paula*, Sulpicius in the *Life of Saint Martin*, and the most ancient Dionysius the Areopagite, *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, chapter 7.] If a brother dies, the whole brotherhood shall accompany him.

**LXXII.** No one shall go outside, no one shall speak, and no one shall remain behind, except by the superior’s command.

**LXXIII.** When the signal calling them to rise has been heard, or the voice of the one chanting, let all rise and run to the prayers. [Col. 0290B] No one shall chant beforehand unless he has been ordered to do so; nor, when one psalm has been completed, shall anyone dare join another without the superior’s command.

**LXXIV.** No one shall walk before his superior and leader. [Note: [Col. 0290D] That is, no one shall stray from his proper place while they are walking together.] No one shall remain behind his rank.

**LXXV.** If anyone loses something, he shall be publicly reproved before the altar. If what was lost belonged to his own clothing, he shall receive nothing for three weeks; in the fourth week, after doing penance, what he lost shall be given back to him.

**LXXVI.** Whoever finds something shall hang it up for three days [Note: [Col. 0290D] That is, before the doors of the church or oratory.] before the gathering of the brothers, so that the person who recognizes it may take it.

**LXXVII.** [Note: [Col. 0290D] Washing clothing, or the house itself and its vessels.] No one shall do washing in the house without the superior; and everything new shall be arranged according to his judgment.

**LXXVIII.** [Note: [Col. 0290D] See above, article 50, and what we noted in Book 2, chapter 16, on regular correction and discipline.] Every correction shall be carried out in such a way that those being corrected are unbelted [Col. 0291A], with their hands lowered and their heads bowed; promising that they will amend the vices of which they are accused, they shall beg pardon.

**LXXIX.** [Note: [Col. 0291B] That is, apart from or contrary to the order and law of regular obedience.] Whoever has departed without the order of the brothers and later returns after doing penance [Note: [Col. 0291B] That is, he shall not retain his place but shall occupy the last place in the congregation. Thus Saint Benedict, chapter 29: “A brother who leaves through his own fault or is expelled from the monastery, if he wishes to return, shall first promise every correction of the fault for which he left, and thus shall be received in the last rank, so that his humility may thereby be proved.” The same punishment, in addition to others, is imposed in canon law upon monks who leave their monasteries to study medicine or civil law and do not return within two months: chapter *Non magnopere*, *Nec clerici vel monachi*, and so forth. The same punishment is prescribed below for the furious and the angry in article 85.] shall not be in his proper rank without the superior’s command.

**LXXX.** Whoever enters the monastery uneducated shall first be taught what he must observe. When, having been instructed, he has consented to everything, they shall give him twenty psalms, or two Apostolic Epistles, or a portion of another Scripture. If he does not know letters, at the first, third, and sixth hours he shall go to the one who can teach and has been assigned to him; he shall stand before him and learn with the greatest diligence and complete thanksgiving. Afterwards the letters, syllables, words, and names shall be written for him; and even if unwilling, he shall be compelled to read. No one at all shall be in the monastery who does not learn letters and retain something from Scripture, at least as far as the New Testament and the Psalter. [Note: [Col. 0291B] This passage is obscure and, unless I am mistaken, corrupt. What does “as far as the New Testament and the Psalter” mean? I think it can nevertheless be explained as follows. “What is least,” that is, what is easiest to understand; “as far as the New Testament and the Psalter,” that is, apart from the New Testament and the Psalter, which all or most of the monks learned by heart. As for the phrasing, lest it seem absurd to anyone, Ambrosius Calepinus reports an elegant expression in Pliny: “All the consuls agreed, except Pompey”—that is, apart from Pompey or besides Pompey. This agrees with our vernacular usage as well. The sense, therefore, is: No one shall be in the monastery who does not retain something from Scripture—that is, from the Old Testament—which can easily be understood by everyone, such as most sayings in Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and Ecclesiasticus, and the easier and more familiar histories. But everyone shall learn the New Testament and the Psalter. Concerning committing the Gospel and the New Testament to memory as far as possible, Saint Jerome writes to Laeta in Letter 7, on the education of her daughter, a virgin to be dedicated to God, where he prescribes this order for reading Scripture: “Let her first learn the Psalter; let these songs draw her away from other things; let her be instructed for life in Solomon’s Proverbs; in Ecclesiastes let her become accustomed to trampling underfoot the things of the world; in Job let her follow examples of virtue and patience. Let her pass to the Gospels, never laying them down from her hands; let her absorb the Acts of the Apostles and the Epistles with all her heart’s desire. When she has enriched the storehouse of her heart with these treasures, let her commit the Prophets to memory,” and so forth. Saint Chrysostom, Sermon 3 on Lazarus, Saint Basil, and others advise that those things belonging to the New Testament should be read and memorized especially and first, because they are more useful, clearer, more necessary, and proper to us. Cassian likewise reports in Book 2, chapter 6, that the ancient monks added one reading from the Old Testament and another from the New Testament to the Psalms on the other days of the week: “But on the Sabbath and Sunday,” he says, “they use both readings from the New Testament.” Those who care about reading or memorizing Scripture do this throughout all the days of Pentecost. Thus far Cassian. I infer that monks also customarily learned the Psalter word for word and retained it by heart, first from the words of Saint Jerome just quoted, and then from another passage of his letter to Rusticus the monk (Letter 4): “Let the book”—supply, “of the Psalms”—“never leave his hand or eyes,” for he continues, “let the Psalter be learned word for word,” and so forth. And on Psalm 133: “We read the Scriptures, learn the Psalms by heart, retain the Gospels, and expound the Prophets.” Monks customarily competed among themselves to learn more Scripture, and thought themselves better insofar as they had learned more. Finally, Cassiodorus, in the preface to the *Institutions of Divine Reading*, urges Christ’s novices first to learn the Psalms. Another interpretation of the sentence has also recently occurred to me—more subtle, though not implausible—in this sense: “Let him retain something from Scripture, what is least, up to the New Testament and the Psalter.” That is: Let him retain at least the New Testament and the Psalter; or, let him retain something up to knowledge of the New Testament or Psalter. Here *up to* is not exclusive but rather conjunctive or inclusive. It is used in nearly this sense in Scripture: in Genesis, “from human beings up to animals”; “to your offspring forever”; “to the present day.” In the Psalms: “There is not one”; “until night my kidneys chastised me”; “from human being to beast.” And in very many similar passages, what is attached to this little word is not excluded but included and comprehended. Yet, on careful inspection, this interpretation nearly coincides with the first. For when it is explained as “up to the New Testament and Psalter,” that is, “apart from the New Testament and Psalter,” the New Testament and Psalter are not excluded as though they need not be learned; rather, they are included and commended above all and before the rest for memorization.] Whatever they have heard discussed in the assembly of the brothers, they shall be compelled to recall among themselves.

**LXXXI.** For chanting and praying, no one shall find excuses by which he claims to be occupied, as though he could not go—whether he is on a ship, in the field, on a journey, or detained in the monastery by any duty—and he shall not omit the appointed times for prayer and chanting.

[Note: [Col. 0292D] Namely, of nuns, consecrated women, or female monks. Palladius reports in the *Life of Abbot Aphthonius* that across the Nile, opposite the monastery of Tabennesis, or the Pachomian monastery, there was another monastery of four hundred girls following the same institutions of Pachomius, to whom no one crossed over except the priest. Saint Jerome writes in Letter 16 that Saint Marcella learned from the Alexandrian priests and Saint Athanasius the life of Saint Antony, as well as the discipline of the monasteries of Pachomius in the Thebaid and of the virgins and widows instituted by him, and was not ashamed to profess what she had learned to please Christ. Concerning these and other nuns, he writes in Letter 48: “It is the custom in the monasteries of Egypt and Syria that every virgin and widow who has consecrated herself to God, renouncing the world and trampling underfoot all worldly pleasures, offers her hair to the mothers of the monasteries to be cut off, and thereafter does not walk with her head uncovered, contrary to the Apostle’s command (1 Corinthians 11), but with it bound and veiled alike,” and so forth. See also his *Epitaph for Paula*, where he describes the discipline of the nuns, their manner of chanting, and other institutions. Saint Augustine likewise, in the often-cited passage of *On the Customs of the Church*, after discussing the life of monks and coenobites, then adds what concerns nuns and virgins, who lived under the same laws and institutions: “This is also the life of women who serve God carefully and chastely. Separated in their dwellings and removed from men as far as is fitting, they are joined to them only by pious love and imitation of virtue. No young man has access to them, nor even old men, however serious and powerful, except as far as the vestibule, for the purpose of supplying what they need. They exercise and sustain their bodies by wool-working, and hand over the garments themselves to the brothers, receiving from them in return what is needed for food,” and so forth.] **On the discipline of the girls.**

**LXXXII.** [Note: [Col. 0292D] That is, to visit and greet them. This does not concern the visitation of nuns carried out by superiors, according to the chapter *Attendentes* in *On the Status of Monks*, but familiar visiting, greeting, conversation, and association, which are also forbidden by the sacred canons, particularly to monks. See the chapter *Monasteries* in *On the Life and Honesty of Clerics* (Book 1 of the *Decretals*).] No one shall go to visit them unless he has there a mother, sister, relative, cousin, or the mother of his children. If an inheritance from their father is owed to them from before his conversion, or if there is some evident cause, they shall send with him a man of proven age and conduct; they shall see them and return together. No one shall go to them except those mentioned above, and they shall first have the matter announced to the father of the monastery. He shall send to the elders assigned to the monastery of the virgins [Note: [Col. 0294C] From this it may be inferred that even at that time nuns had certain elders or spiritual fathers living nearby, by whom they were instructed and directed, commonly called confessors.], who shall meet them and, with them, see those whom it is necessary for them to see, with complete discipline and fear of God. They shall not speak to them about secular matters.

**LXXXIII.** Whoever transgresses any of these commands shall, without any doubt, do penance for negligence and contempt, so that we may be able to possess the kingdoms of heaven.

[Col. 0293B] [Note: [Col. 0294C] Something else seems to need to be added here, so that this may be a new section and part of the Rule concerning the correction of vices.] The precepts and institutions of our father Pachomius, the man of God, who at the beginning founded the communion of holy life according to the command of God. The fullness of the law is love. Knowing the time, that the hour has come for us to rise from sleep, and that our salvation is nearer than when we believed: the night has passed, and the day has drawn near. Let us put aside the works of darkness, which are quarrels, slanders, hatreds, and the pride of a swollen spirit.

**LXXXIV.** Whoever is quick to slander and declares that he has not been caught in this sin shall be warned a second time; if he scorns to listen, they shall separate him outside the assembly of the brothers for seven days, and [Note: [Col. 0294C] Fasting on bread and water in the case of more serious offenses. The same is mentioned below in articles 87 and 121.] he shall receive only bread and water until he promises and affirms that he will withdraw from this vice; then he shall be released.

**LXXXV.** If anyone is angry and furious, becoming angry frequently without cause and over some empty and trivial matter, he shall be warned six times. On the seventh, they shall make him rise from the place of his rank in the seating order and place him among the last; they shall teach him to cleanse himself of this disturbance of mind. When he has brought three witnesses worthy of belief who will promise on his behalf that he will never do anything similar, he shall recover his place. Otherwise, if he persists in the vice, he shall remain [Note: [Col. 0294C] The same rule is given above in article 62 and below in articles 92 and 94.] among the last, having lost his former place.

**LXXXVI.** Whoever desires to prove a false charge against another in order to oppress an innocent man shall be warned three times; afterwards [Note: [Col. 0294C] He shall be subject to the punishment established for slander, or false accusation, and for slanderers. Two decrees concerning this are found in Book 5 of the *Decretals*, title 2, *On Slanderers*.] he shall be guilty of iniquity, whether he held a former rank or a lower one.

**LXXXVII.** [Note: [Col. 0294C] Whisperers and disturbers of the community were formerly restrained by beatings. See the Rule of Saint Benedict, chapters 23 and 28, following Cassian, Book 4, chapter 16.] Whoever has the very bad habit of provoking the brothers by his speech and corrupting the minds of the simpler ones shall be warned three times. If he scorns the warning [Col. 0294B] and persists with a stubborn spirit in his hardness, they shall separate him outside the monastery and beat him before the gate thirty-nine times, [Note: [Col. 0294C] I think *triginta novem* is ablative rather than nominative, with *verberibus* or *plagis* understood. They seem to have had in mind the Apostle’s example: he states that he received from the Jews five times forty lashes less one—that is, thirty-nine lashes (2 Corinthians 11). For why would thirty-nine monks come together to beat one man? The same punishment is prescribed below in article 121.] and they shall give him only bread and water to eat until he has been cleansed of his filth.

**LXXXVIII.** [Note: [Col. 0294D] The vice of murmuring was formerly punished severely among the monks. Cassian discusses it in Book 4, chapter 6, and Saint Benedict frequently elsewhere, but especially in chapter 34: “Above all,” he says, “care must be taken that the evil of murmuring does not appear for any reason, in any word or sign whatsoever.”] Whoever has the very bad habit of murmuring and complains that he is being crushed by excessively hard labor shall be instructed five times that he murmurs without cause, and the truth shall be clearly demonstrated to him. If after this he is disobedient, and is of mature age, they shall treat him as one of the sick; he shall be placed in the infirmary and fed there in idleness until he returns to the truth. But if his complaint is just and he is being unjustly oppressed by a superior, the one who caused his scandal shall be subjected to the same sentence.

[Col. 0294C] **LXXXIX.** [Note: [Col. 0294D] Saint Benedict, chapters 23 and 28.] If anyone is disobedient, contentious, argumentative, or a liar, and is of mature age, he shall be warned ten times to cease from his vices. If he does not wish to listen, he shall be reproved according to the laws of the monastery. But if another person’s fault has led him into these vices, and this has been proved, the one who was the cause shall be liable to punishment.

XC.
