If any of the brothers is caught willingly laughing and playing with boys, and forming friendships with those of immature age [Note: This was forbidden by the Fathers with great caution and severity because of the danger of sexual impropriety, to which childhood is especially exposed.], he shall be admonished three times to withdraw from their company and to remember propriety and the fear of God. If he does not cease, he shall be corrected, as he deserves, with the severest correction.

XCI. Those who despise the commands of their superiors and the rules of the monastery, which have been established by God’s command, and who make light of the counsels of the elders, shall be corrected according to the established order until they are reformed.

XCII. [Note: That is, a priest, or a superior appointed as judge over the consciences of his subjects.] Whoever is judge in all matters of sin and, through perversity of mind and negligence, abandons the truth, twenty holy men who fear God—or ten, or as few as five—of whom all shall bear witness, shall sit and judge him; and they shall degrade him to the lowest rank until he is corrected.

XCIII. Whoever disturbs the minds of the brothers, is quick to slander, and sows quarrels and disputes, shall be admonished ten times; and if he is not reformed, he shall be corrected according to the order of the monastery until he is corrected.

XCIV. [Note: The phrasing is obscure and should be explained in this way: Whoever among the superiors or overseers sees a brother in tribulation or distress and refuses to help and comfort him, indeed judges against him unjustly, deserves to be degraded. Therefore I do not think that “tribulation” should be understood as contention, tumult, or altercation, as I rendered it in the earlier edition, but rather as genuine distress and grief, though arising from some contention with the superior; hence below, in article 112, it is called “sadness.”] Whoever among the superiors and overseers sees one of his brothers in tribulation and refuses to investigate the cause of the tribulation, and disregards it, shall have the matter investigated by the judges mentioned above between the brother and the superior. If they discover that the brother has been distressed by the superior’s negligence or pride, and that he judged him not according to the truth but according to his personal status, he shall be degraded from his seat until he is corrected and cleansed from the filth of injustice, because he did not consider the truth but persons, and served the perversity of his own soul rather than God’s judgment.

XCV. If anyone has promised to observe the rules of the monastery and has begun to do so, but then abandoned them, and afterward returns and performs penance, alleging bodily weakness by which he cannot fulfill what he had said, they shall make him remain among the sick, and he shall be fed among the idle [Note: That is, those released from manual labor because of weakness, or those placed in the infirmary.], until, having performed penance, he fulfills what he promised.

XCVI. [Note: The instruction and discipline of boys, concerning which see St. Benedict, chapter 30.] If the boys in the house are devoted to games and idleness and cannot be reformed by correction, the overseer himself ought to admonish and correct them for up to thirty days. If he sees them persisting in wickedness and does not report this to the Father of the monastery, and some sin is discovered in them, he himself shall be subjected to the penalty corresponding to the sin that has been found.

XCVII. All boys who do not fear being mocked on account of sin, and who through shamelessness do not consider God’s judgment, and who are not reformed by verbal correction, shall be beaten for as long as is necessary for them to receive discipline and fear.

XCVIII. Whoever judges unjustly shall justly be condemned by others.

XCIX. [Note: This saying is attributed to Isidore by Gratian, 1, q. 3. The same saying occurs in Smaragdus, *Exposition of the Rule*, chapter 69.] Whoever consents to sinners and defends another who has committed an offense shall be accursed before God and men, and shall be corrected with the severest rebuke. But if he was deceived through ignorance and did not think the matter to be as it truly was, he shall be forgiven; and everyone who sins through ignorance shall readily receive pardon. Whoever sins knowingly, however, shall endure correction according to the measure and deed of his sin.

C. [Note: This is another division; to designate it, the word “another” appears to have to be supplied here, as above.] The commands and laws of Pachomius. [Note: The same is explicitly stated in the Rule of St. Pachomius according to Palladius, Sozomen, and Nicephorus, in the passages cited above. So too St. Benedict, chapter 48: “Let all things be done moderately for the sake of the fainthearted.”] The brothers shall not be compelled to do more; rather, moderate labor shall encourage everyone to work. Let there be peace and harmony among them, and let them willingly submit to their superiors. Sitting, walking, and standing, let them compete with one another in humility.

CI. [Note: Supply “public.” For correction of this kind of monks belongs especially to the abbot, or Father of the monastery. See the Council of Trent, decree of session 25, chapter 14, concerning religious.] If anyone commits a sin, the Fathers of the monasteries shall be able to correct him and determine what course ought to be followed.

CII. [Note: Many laws and duties are imposed here upon the overseer, or cloister prior.] The overseer of the house, and the one who is second to him, shall have only this authority: to compel the brothers, at each point or at the house assembly, or at the greater assembly—that is, the assembly of all the brothers—to submit to penance.

CIII. But if the overseer is away on a journey, the one who is second shall take his place, both in receiving the brothers’ penance and in every other matter necessary in the house.

CIV. If anyone goes to another house without the knowledge of two persons, or asks a brother of another house to lend him a codex for reading, or does anything else of the kind, he shall be rebuked according to the monastery’s order. [Note: That is, unless two persons know of it and serve as witnesses: namely, the overseer and the companion with whom he is to be sent. This appears intended to prevent anyone from leaving secretly or alone, as above, articles 34, 47, and elsewhere.]

CV. Whoever wishes to live without blemish and without contempt in the house to which he has been assigned must observe before God everything that has been commanded.

CVI. Whatever is necessary, whether in the field or in the monastery, the overseer shall carry out even without being asked.

CVII. [Note: There is great diversity of wording among authors and interpreters concerning this article of the Rule of Pachomius. Palladius reports it thus: “He appointed that throughout the whole day they should make twelve prayers, and twelve during the night vigils, and twelve at Matins, and three at the ninth hour.” Sozomen says: “That they should pray twelve times each day, and likewise toward evening; so many times during the night, and three times at the ninth hour.” Nicephorus says: “That they should always pray twelve times during the day; likewise toward evening; similarly during the night; and also three times at the ninth hour.”] They shall perform six evening prayers, according to the example of the greater assembly, at which all the brothers gather together.

CVIII. It is the height of love, even if it is difficult, that they bear no burden and that weariness not arise from the burden. [Note: The Lyons edition read: “Even if it is easy,” reversing the meaning and making no sense. The intended meaning is that for one who loves and truly obeys nothing is difficult or burdensome, because perfect obedience, which is joined to charity, knows no law and is not confined by limits. Not content with the narrowness of profession, it is carried by a more expansive will into the breadth of charity; and, without considering the measure of a vigorous spirit, it extends itself into infinite freedom. So says St. Bernard in *On Precept and Dispensation*. See chapter 68 of St. Benedict’s Rule, entitled “If impossible tasks are enjoined upon a brother.”]

CIX. If anyone comes from outside and is exhausted by the heat, while the other brothers are celebrating the prayer, he shall not be compelled to go if he cannot.

CX. [Note: No one was permitted to be absent from the superior’s sermon or exhortation.] When the overseers of the houses teach the brothers about conversion to a holy life, no one shall be absent except on account of the gravest illness.

CXI. [Note: I believe the reading should be: “Those superiors who are sent outside with the brothers,” and so forth. For elders were accustomed to be sent with the younger men to care for and guard them.] Whatever superiors are sent out from among the brothers shall have the authority of overseers for as long as they are there. Everything shall be done according to their decision. On the appointed days they shall teach the brothers; and if some dispute should arise among them, those superiors shall hear the matter, judge it, and rebuke the one deserving blame. At their command they shall immediately consent wholeheartedly to peace.

CXII. [Note: The Fathers acted with great prudence and moderation in judging and settling the brothers’ cases and controversies. See above, article 94.] If one of the brothers has some sadness against the overseer of his house, or the overseer himself has some complaint against a brother, brothers of approved conduct and faith shall hear them and judge between them. If, however, the Father of the monastery is absent or has gone somewhere, they shall first wait for him; but if they see that he will remain away for a longer time, they shall then hear the case between the overseer and the brother, lest greater sadness arise from a judgment being suspended. Both the one who is overseer and the one who is subject, and those who hear the case, shall do everything according to the fear of God and shall give no occasion at all [Note: Supply: “for complaining or murmuring.”].

## Concerning the Clothing of Monks

CXIII. [Note: See above, article 45. Cassian, Book IV, chapter 15; St. Benedict’s Rule, chapters 33 and 55.] If anyone has more than what has been commanded, without the permission of his superior, the items shall be taken to the keeper of the clothing. He shall have no authority to enter there or to ask for them; rather, they shall remain under the decision of the overseer, or of the one who is second to him.

[Note: Another division and regulation concerning summoning and gathering the brothers, either for a sermon or for the public synaxis, which was called the greater assembly and is discussed below.] The commands of Pachomius concerning the assembly of the brothers: how the assembly ought to be held, and how the brothers are to be gathered to hear the word of God, according to the commands of the elders and the teaching of the holy Scriptures, so that those converted may be freed from the error of the soul and glorify God in the light of the living; so that they may know how they ought to conduct themselves in the house of God without ruin or scandal, and may not be intoxicated by any passion, but stand within the measure of truth and the traditions of the Apostles and Prophets, and observe the order of the feasts, imitating their conduct in the house of God, and completing fasts and prayers according to custom. For those who minister well follow the rule of the Scriptures.

CXIV. This, therefore, is the ministry which the ministers of the Church ought to fulfill. Let them gather the brothers at the time of prayer, and let them do everything that must properly be completed, so that they give no occasion for slander and do not allow anyone to walk contrary to the practice of discipline. If they ask for a codex, let them bring it to them.

CXV. If anyone comes from outside in the evening and does not arrive in time to receive the work he is to do on the following day, let it be assigned to him in the morning. If the work he had in hand has run out, let him refer the matter to the superior’s decision [Note: That is, let him consult the superior.], and let him do what the superior commands.

CXVI. [Note: The office of the minister, or superintendent, of the works, and so forth.] Whoever is minister shall be diligent lest any work be lost in the monastery, in any craft whatsoever practiced by the brothers. If something is lost and has been wasted through negligence, the minister of the individual works shall be rebuked by the Father, and he himself shall rebuke the other who lost the work, but only [Note: That is, according to the will and decision of the head, the Father of the monastery.] according to the will and decision of the head; without that authority no one shall have power to rebuke a brother.

CXVII. If a garment spread out in the sun is found there on the third day, the owner of the garment shall be rebuked for it and shall perform public penance in the assembly; he shall stand in the place where food is eaten. [Note: “Owner” is used improperly for the user, since a monk has ownership of nothing—not even the garment with which he is clothed or the bread on which he feeds—but only a simple use dependent upon the superior’s will.] [Note: This is a form of monastic correction and mortification: standing in the refectory during the time of the meal. See the notable example in Climacus, Step 4.]

CXVIII. If one of the brothers is found acting contentiously or contradicting the command of his superior, he shall be rebuked according to the measure of his sin.

CXIX. Whoever lies, or is discovered to hate someone, or is disobedient, or is more devoted to joking than is proper, or is idle, or answers harshly, or has the habit of slandering the brothers or those who are outside, and, in general, whoever does anything contrary to the rule of the Scriptures and the discipline of the monastery, shall be heard by the Father of the monastery and punished according to the measure and deed of his sin.

CXX. [Note: This was called among them the *melotes*, concerning which see Cassian, Book I, chapter 8.] If a sheepskin, footwear, a belt, or anything else is lost, the one who lost it shall be rebuked.

CXXI. If anyone takes something that is not his, it shall be placed upon his shoulders, and he shall perform public penance in the assembly and stand in the place where food is eaten. But if he is caught in theft, thirty-nine shall beat him, and outside they shall give him only bread and water to eat and drink; clothed in sackcloth and ashes, they shall compel him to perform penance at each time of prayer. [Note: The use of sackcloth among monks is ancient; see the note on Book I, chapter 3.] [Note: Fugitives and apostates were also punished with beatings and scourging. See John Climacus, Step 5.] The same law shall be observed in the case of fugitives.

CXXII. The overseer of the house shall be subject to rebuke if he does not report to the Father within three days anything lost, whether on the road, in the field, or in the monastery; and he shall perform penance according to the established order.

CXXIII. But if it is a person and he does not report him to the Father within three hours, he shall be guilty of the person’s loss, unless he finds him again.

CXXIV. This is the punishment for one who has lost a brother from the house: he shall perform public penance for three days. But if he does not report to the Father in the very hour in which the brother fled, he shall be guilty of sin.

CXXV. If the overseer sees an offender in his house and does not report him to the Father of the monastery, he himself shall be subjected to the order of correction.

CXXVI. [Note: So also above, article 83. But perhaps, because six psalms were joined to the six prayers, Palladius and the others therefore said that twelve prayers were prescribed for them.] In each house they shall complete six prayers and psalms in the evening, according to the order of the greater assembly, which is celebrated collectively by all the brothers. [Note: The greater assembly was so called when all the brothers of the same monastery or congregation gathered in the church—namely, on Saturdays and Sundays and on other solemn occasions—to celebrate and receive the divine mysteries and hear the word of God. The lesser assemblies and private meetings, however, took place daily in each house at fixed hours and times, where only thirty or forty gathered, as is clear from the statements above. See article 102.] Each week the arrangements [Note: That is, the ordinances, constitutions, and laws of each house.] shall be completed by the overseers. No one in the house shall do anything except what the overseer has ordered.

CXXVII. If all the brothers who are in the house see that the overseer is excessively negligent, exceeding the monastery’s measure, they shall report it to the Father, and he shall be rebuked by him. The overseer himself shall do nothing except what the Father commands, especially in a new matter; [Note: That is, in customary and familiar matters he shall observe the rules of the monastery. A “new matter” is contrasted with customary matters, which derive from practice and occur frequently.] for in matters arising from custom he shall observe the rules of the monastery.

CXXVIII. [Note: The customs and qualities of the overseer, or prior, are described at length here.] The overseer shall not become drunk, [Note: I cannot adequately explain this, unless perhaps it means that he is not to frequent the storerooms where wine was kept, at least for the sick and the elderly. See above, article 22.] nor sit in the lower places beside the monastery’s vessels, [Note: I think this means the brothers’ vows or the statutes of the elders.] lest he break the bonds that God established in heaven to be observed on earth; [Note: That is, lest he fast on Sunday, as Ciaconius correctly noted. Whether this is permitted or not is explained by Cassian, Book II, final chapter; Conference 21, chapter 19 and following.] let him not mourn on the feast day of the Lord Savior. Let him rule his flesh according to the measure of the saints. [Note: In my view this refers to what he said above, article 43: no one is to sleep outside his reclining little seat—that is, his low bed, or rather his curved seat, as explained there. He therefore wishes overseers, or priors, like the other monks, to use no beds other than their own mats or little seats, lest, he says, they imitate the custom of gentiles or secular men, who, the more honored or powerful they are, use higher and more splendid couches and beds.] Let him not be found in lofty beds, imitating the custom of the gentiles. Let him not be double-minded. Let him not follow the thoughts of his heart, and let him not resist the higher authorities with an inflated spirit. Let him not rage or attack those beneath him. Let him not move boundary markers. Let him not be fraudulent, nor devise deceit in his thoughts. Let him not neglect to uproot the sin of his soul, nor be overcome by the lust of the flesh. Let him not walk carelessly. Let him not quickly utter an idle word. Let him not place a stumbling-block before the feet of the blind. Let him not teach his soul pleasures. Let him not be loosened by the laughter and joking of fools. Let his heart not be carried away by those who speak foolishly or sweetly. Let him not be overcome by gifts. Let him not be led by the speech of children. Let him not be distressed in tribulation. Let him not fear death, but God, lest through overwhelming fear he become a transgressor. [Note: Another reading has: “Nor let him abandon the true river for little streams.” This alludes to Jeremiah 2: “They have abandoned me, the fountain of living water, and dug for themselves cisterns, broken cisterns that cannot hold water.”] Let him not abandon the true light for small portions of food. Let him not waver or fluctuate in his works. Let him not change a true judgment, but let him be firm and steadfast in his decision, considering and judging everything justly in truth, without desire for glory, manifest before God and men, and keeping away from deceit. Let him not be ignorant of the conduct of the saints, nor blind to their knowledge. Let him harm no one through pride, lest he follow the desires of his eyes. Let the incitements of vice not overcome him. Let him never pass over the truth. Let him hate injustice, and never judge a person for gifts. Let him not condemn the innocent through pride. Let him not laugh among children. Let him not abandon the truth because he is overcome by fear. Let him not eat the bread of deceit. Let him not desire another’s land. Let him not oppress a soul for the sake of another’s spoils. Let him not despise those who need mercy, nor give false testimony seduced by profit. Let him not lie through pride, nor contend against the truth because of arrogance. Let him not abandon justice because of weariness, nor destroy his soul because of shame. Let him not look toward the dishes of a richer table, nor desire beautiful clothing. Let him not neglect the elderly. Let him always examine his thoughts. Let him not become drunk with wine, but, when he judges, let him join humility to truth.

Let him follow the commands of the elders and the law of God, which has been proclaimed throughout the world. If he transgresses any of these things, a measure shall be returned to him according to the measure with which he measured, and he shall receive according to his works, because he committed adultery with wood and stone, and because of the glitter of gold and its splendor he abandoned the judgment of his mind, and clothed himself in the snares of the wicked through temporal desires for profit. [Note: When Eli heard that the ark of God had been captured by the Philistines, he fell backward from his seat and died with his neck broken. Let superiors note here the great punishments to which they make themselves liable if they fail in their office or act negligently in it, especially in correcting the excesses of their subjects. A notable passage suited to this place occurs in canon law under the title “On Simony,” in these words: “Although Eli, the high priest, was good in himself, nevertheless, because he did not effectively rebuke the excesses of his sons, he received in himself and in them the vengeance of divine punishment; when his sons had been killed in battle, he fell from his seat and died with his neck broken. Therefore a prelate ought to rise up all the more diligently to correct the excesses of his subjects, the more damnably he would leave their offenses uncorrected.” This is the passage.] The destruction of Eli and his sons shall come upon him (1 Samuel 4), and the curse of God which Cain invoked (Genesis 4); the destruction by which the earth’s opening swallowed sinners (Numbers 16); the destruction of the Canaanites; and the breaking of the pitcher at the fountain (Ecclesiastes 12); [Note: Ecclesiastes 12: “Before the pitcher is broken over the fountain.” St. Jerome says: “The breaking of the pitcher over the fountain and the breaking of the wheel over the cistern are symbols of death,” and so forth.] and the breaking of the sands on the shores beaten by salty waves; and [Note: This refers to Jeremiah 48: “How the strong rod is broken, the glorious staff!”] the breaking of the glorious rod (Jeremiah 48); [Note: Deuteronomy 28: “You shall grope at noon as a blind man gropes in darkness.” And Isaiah 59: “We grope like the blind along a wall, and like those without eyes we feel our way; we stumble at noon as in darkness, in gloomy places like the dead.”] so that he is like a blind man groping with his hand along a wall (Isaiah 59). All these things shall come upon him because he did not preserve the truth in judgment and acted unjustly in everything entrusted to him.

## The Rule of the Same Saint Pachomius as Reported by Palladius

[Col. 0301]

Tabennesis is a place so called in the Thebaid, where Pachomius the monk lived, a man among those who lived according to the highest and most perfect discipline of life, so much so that he was deemed worthy of predictions concerning the future and of angelic visions. He was greatly devoted to the poor [Col. 0301D] and possessed great charity toward human beings. While he was sitting in this cave, an angel of the Lord appeared to him and said: “Pachomius, you have rightly and virtuously carried out the matters that concern you; therefore you are sitting in this place needlessly. Come, then, go out, gather together all the younger monks, live with them, and, following the form that I shall give you, establish laws for them.” And he gave him a bronze tablet on which the following things had been written.

I. Grant each person permission to eat and drink according to the strength of those who eat. Also assign them tasks that are proportionate and suitable; do not forbid them either to rest or to eat. Thus assign strong tasks to the strong, but weak and light tasks to those who exert themselves more and are weaker.

II. Make separate cells in the same courtyard, and let three remain in each cell.

III. Let everyone take food in one house.

IV. Let them sleep not lying down, but sitting on seats constructed for themselves, somewhat reclined, with blankets placed upon them. Let them sleep sitting. [Note: That is, on *psiathia*, mats.]

V. At night let them wear linen *lebitones* [Note: That is, linen tunics], girded.

VI. Let each person have a worked white sheepskin. [Note: That is, a *melotes*.] Without it, let them neither eat nor sleep.

VII. When they enter for communion with Christ on Saturday and Sunday, let them loosen their belts, lay aside the sheepskin, and enter wearing only the hooded garment.

VIII. He made soft hoods for them, like those of children, and commanded that a purple cross be placed upon them.

IX. [Note: Nicephorus expressed this passage more clearly in Book IX, chapter 14, in these words: “Moreover, he divided the assembly of monks living together into twenty-four orders, according to the number of the Greek letters, and assigned each order a name corresponding to the disposition, life, and character of its members: the simpler ones were called iota and omicron, while those who were wicked and less upright were called zeta and xi; and similarly the others, assigning to each a suitable name according to each one’s discipline and the character of the letter itself.”] He commanded that there be twenty-four orders of brothers, according to the number of the twenty-four letters. He ordered that each order be assigned a Greek-letter name, beginning with α, β, and those that follow, up to ω, so that when the archimandrite asked about someone in so great a multitude, he might inquire how order A was doing, or how order B was doing. Again, “Greet R,” following a particular name of the letters. He assigned I as the name of the simpler and more sincere, but Ξ to the more difficult, fitting to each order a letter corresponding to its discipline, life, and character; these significations being understood by spiritual persons alone.

X. If a guest from another monastery comes, one that has another form—that is, another manner of life—he shall neither eat nor drink with them nor enter the monastery, unless he has been found on the road.

XI. They shall not admit one who enters once but cannot endure the contest with them for three years. [Note: That is, the austerity of the religious life.] But after he has performed more difficult tasks, let him enter the arena after three years. [Note: A three-year probation before profession.]

XII. While eating, let them cover their heads with their hoods, so that one brother does not see another chewing.

XIII. A person who is eating may not speak or turn his eyes from his dish and table anywhere else. [Note: Nicephorus adds: “They were to ask for what was necessary by certain signs, by movements of the hands or by nods, indicating what they needed.”]

XIV. He ordained that throughout the day they should make twelve prayers, twelve during the night vigils, twelve at Matins, and three at the ninth hour. [Note: This was so that, when food was to be taken, each prayer would be preceded by a psalm. Sozomen, Book III, chapter 13; Nicephorus, Book IV, chapter 14.] When it seemed time for the multitude to eat, he ordained that each order should first sing a psalm at each prayer.

Thus far extends the Rule, or part of the Rule, of St. Pachomius drawn from Palladius, which Sozomen and Nicephorus expressed in various other words.

## SECOND APPENDIX. SELECTIONS FROM JOHN CASSIAN, OR CERTAIN MORE NOTABLE AND BRIEFER SAYINGS EXCERPTED FROM HIS WORKS

[Col. 0303]

*(Book I of the Institutes, chapter 3.)* Whatever is presumed by one or a few among the servants of God, and is not held universally by the whole body of the brotherhood, is either superfluous or arrogant; and for this reason it must be judged harmful, displaying more the appearance of vanity than of virtue.

*(Ibid.)* The judgment of a few ought not to be preferred to, or prejudice, the general constitution of all.

*(Book II of the Institutes, chapter 3.)* They declare that governing well, or being governed well, is characteristic of the wise, and define it as the highest gift and grace of the Holy Spirit. For no one can prescribe salutary commands to those who obey unless he has first been instructed in every discipline of the virtues; nor can anyone obey an elder unless he is perfected in the fear of God and in the virtue of humility.

*(Book III of the Institutes, chapter 8.)* In no way can fragile flesh be deprived of the rest of the entire night in such a manner that, throughout the following day, it can preserve an unshaken watchfulness without drowsiness and torpor of mind and spirit.

*(Chapter 11.)* Every fatigue is always endured more calmly, and labor is undertaken without disgust, if some alternation or change of work follows it.

*(Book IV of the Institutes, chapter 8.)* Taught by many experiments, they hand down that a monk, and especially a younger monk, cannot restrain even the pleasure of his desire unless he first learns through obedience to mortify his own wills.

*(Chapter 9.)* The most subtle devil cannot deceive or cast down a younger monk in any other way than by enticing him, whether through arrogance or shame, into concealing his thoughts. For they declare it to be a general and evident sign of a diabolical thought if one is ashamed to reveal it to an elder.

*(Chapter 12.)* They place the virtue of obedience not only before manual labor, reading, silence, and the quiet of the cell, but also before all virtues, judging that everything must be subordinated to it. They are content to undergo every loss, provided that they do not appear in any way to violate this good.

*(Chapter 20.)* They believe that they themselves do not belong to themselves, but also that everything belonging to them has been consecrated to the Lord. Therefore, if anything has once been brought into the monastery, they decree that it must be treated with every reverence, as something most sacred.

*(Chapter 33.)* Just as immense glory is promised in the future to those who serve faithfully and adhere to it according to the institution of the Rule, so the gravest punishments are prepared for those who have carried it out sluggishly and negligently, and who have failed, in accordance with what they professed or what people believe them to be, to offer it the corresponding fruits of holiness.

*(Chapter 34.)* Renunciation is nothing other than a sign of the cross and of mortification—that is, a representation of them.

*(Chapter 37.)* It will do no good to have begun well or to have undertaken the beginnings of renunciation with full fervor if a suitable end does not likewise commend and complete it.

*(Chapter 41.)* You must observe these three things necessarily in the community: namely, that according to the Psalmist’s saying you proceed as though deaf, mute, and blind, so that whatever you see that has little edifying value, you do not see, as though blind, and so forth. But cultivate this fourth matter above all: according to the Apostle’s saying, make yourself foolish in this world, so that you may be wise, discerning and judging nothing among the things that have been commanded to you, and so forth.

*(Book V of the Institutes, chapter 4.)* A monk who desires to store up spiritual honey, like a most prudent bee, ought to pluck each virtue from those who possess it most familiarly and store it in the vessel of his own breast. He should not investigate what anyone possesses less of, but should contemplate only what virtue he possesses and diligently gather it.

*(Chapter 6.)* A belly filled with any kind of food produces the seeds of lust, and the mind, weighed down by the burden of food, cannot prevail in directing the reins of discernment.

The Fathers’ saying is most true and most approved: the measure of fasting and continence consists solely in the measure of moderation and restraint; and the common end of perfect virtue for all is that, while still desiring the foods which bodily necessity compels us to take for sustenance, we nevertheless practice self-control in relation to them.

*(Chapter 11.)* No one will ever be able to restrain the impulses of burning desire if he has not been able to curb the cravings of the palate.

*(Chapter 21.)* Whatever is presumed beyond custom and common usage, the most ancient tradition of the Fathers marks as defiled by the disease of vainglory and display.

*(Chapter 41.)* A monk ought to devote himself to fasts as though he were going to remain in the body for a hundred years; and so to restrain the movements of his soul, forget injuries, reject sorrows, and despise pains and losses, as though he were going to die every day.

*(Book VI of the Institutes, chapter 6.)* Carnal human beings are never so properly made equal to spiritual angels by imitation of their manner of life as by the merit and grace of chastity. Through it, while still dwelling on earth, they possess, according to the Apostle, citizenship in heaven; what they are promised they will possess in the future after the corruption of the flesh has been laid aside, they already possess here in fragile flesh.

*(Chapter 23.)* Just as purity and the guarding of the day prepare nocturnal chastity, so nocturnal vigils promise the heart and the observance of the day a most steadfast stability and strength.

(Lib. VII Instit.---Cap. 19.) The saying of Saint Basil is reported as having been addressed to a certain *syncleticus*, that is, a senator, who, after retaining part of his property for himself, had professed the monastic life: “You have lost your position as senator,” he said, “and you have not become a monk.”

(Cap. 21.) It is not only the possession of money that must be avoided; the very desire for possession must also be driven completely from the soul. For it is not so much the affection for *philargyria* (that is, proprietorship) that must be avoided as the affection for possession itself that must be cut out by the roots. It will do no good not to have money if the desire to possess remains in us.

(Cap. 27.) There is no one who does not have something to renounce. Whoever has cut out by the roots the desire to possess the world’s goods has renounced all its resources.

[Col. 0306A] (Inst. l. VIII.---Cap. 16.) The height of our amendment and tranquility must not be placed in another’s power, since it is in no way subject to our control; rather, it rests in our own authority.

(Cap. 17.) Just as solitude knows how to open the purest contemplation and reveal, through the most sincere vision, knowledge of spiritual mysteries to those whose morals have been amended, so it is accustomed not only to preserve but even to aggravate the vices of those who are less reformed.

(Ibid.) For when human exercise and practice cease, our vices become more savage if they have not first been cleansed.

(Inst. l. IX.---Cap. 8.) Therefore we must hasten rather to amend our vices and correct our conduct. If these have undoubtedly been corrected, we shall find it easy to live in harmony not only with human beings but even with wild animals and beasts.

(Inst. l. X.---Cap. 6.) An idle mind knows how to think of nothing other than food and the belly.

[Col. 0306B] (Cap. 23.) This is the judgment sanctioned in Egypt by the ancient Fathers: a working monk is harassed by one demon, but an idle monk is ravaged by countless spirits.

(Cap. 24.) Experience has proved that the assault of acedia is not to be avoided by fleeing from it, but overcome by resisting it.

(Inst. l. XI.---Cap. 7.) This is the subtle stratagem of the enemy: to make Christ’s soldier fall by his own weapons, when he was unable to overcome him with hostile arms.

(Cap. 11.) Thus you see how harmful the outcomes of prosperity generally are: those who could not be broken by adversity are struck down more severely by prosperity if they are heedless; and those who escaped the dangers of death in conflict and battle succumb to their own trophies and triumphs.

(Inst. l. XII.---Cap. 3.) There is no other vice that so drains away all virtues and strips and deprives a person of every kind of justice and holiness as the evil of pride.

[Col. 0306C] (Cap. 27.) Whoever has been seized by the disease of pride not only does not deign to observe any rule of submission or obedience, but does not even allow the teaching of perfection to enter his ears.

(Cap. 32.) In no way can the structure of the virtues rise within our soul unless the foundations of true humility have first been laid in our heart; once firmly established, these foundations can support the summit of perfection and charity.

(Collat. 1.---Cap. 4.) The end of our profession is indeed the kingdom of God, or the kingdom of heaven; its appointed goal, that is, its aim, is purity of heart, without which no one can reach that end.

(Cap. 7.) Fasts, vigils, meditation on the Scriptures, nakedness, and deprivation of all possessions are not perfection but instruments of perfection, because the end of this discipline does not consist in them; rather, through them one reaches the end. Therefore whoever is content with these exercises as though they were the highest good, fixes the intention of his heart on them, and does not stretch himself with every effort toward attaining the end for which these practices are to be desired, will labor at them in vain.

[Col. 0306D] (Cap. 8.) This must be our principal effort, this the heart’s immovable aim that we must continually desire: that the mind always cling to divine things and to God. Whatever differs from this, however great it may be, must nevertheless be judged secondary, or even of the lowest importance, or certainly harmful.

(Cap. 17.) It is impossible for the mind not to be assailed by thoughts; but it is possible for everyone who strives either to accept or to reject them.

(Collat. 2.---Cap. 4.) Discernment is the mother, guardian, and guide of all the virtues.

(Cap. 10.) True discernment is acquired only through true humility. The first proof of this humility will be that all things—not only what must be done but also what is being thought—are disclosed for the examination of the elders, so that no one, trusting his own judgment, may fail to assent in every respect to their decisions, and may learn from their tradition what ought to be judged good or evil.

[Col. 0307A] No one can be deceived if he lives not by his own judgment but by the example of his superiors. The cunning enemy will not be able to mock his ignorance when he does not know how to conceal from harmful shame any of the thoughts arising in his heart, but either rejects or admits them after the elders’ mature examination. For as soon as an evil thought has been exposed, it withers; and before the judgment of discernment is pronounced, the most hideous serpent, as though dragged into the light from a dark and subterranean cave by the power of confession, and in a manner exposed and disgraced, departs. His harmful suggestions dominate us only so long as they are concealed in the heart.

(Cap. 11.) The devil drags and drives a monk headlong to death through no other vice so precipitously as when, after he has neglected the counsel of the elders, he persuades him to trust his own judgment and decision.

[Col. 0307B] (Ibid.) Therefore the footsteps of the elders must always be followed with the utmost care, and everything that arises in our hearts must be brought to them, the veil of shame having been removed.

(Cap. 12.) No one could withstand the enemy’s ambushes, or extinguish or restrain the carnal passions blazing with a kind of natural fire, unless God’s grace either helped our weakness or protected and fortified us.

(Cap. 22.) This is the general rule of continence (that is, abstinence): according to the capacity of his strength or age, each person should allow himself as much food as the sustenance of the flesh requires, not as much as the desire for satiety demands.

(Collat. 3.---Cap. 3.) It will do us no good to have begun nobly if we do not display a similar quality at the end.

(Cap. 10.) Just as, moved by the Lord’s inspiration, we run to the way of salvation, so also, led by his instruction and illumination, let us reach the perfection of supreme blessedness.

[Col. 0307C] (Cap. 11.) None of the righteous is sufficient for himself to obtain righteousness unless divine mercy continually places its hand beneath him when he stumbles and falls, lest, having collapsed through the weakness of free will, he perish utterly when prostrate.

(Collat. 4.---Cap. 20.) It is one and the same kind of disobedience to violate an elder’s command either because of eagerness for work or because of a desire for idleness; and it is no less destructive to overturn the regulations of the monastery for the sake of sleep than for the sake of wakefulness.

(Collat. 5.---Cap. 14.) Let each person examine the vice by which he is most severely harassed and take up his principal struggle against it, fixing all the care and concern of his mind upon attacking and watching it; directing against it the daily arrows of fasting; against it, at every moment, hurling the sighs of his heart and frequent missiles of groaning; devoting against it the labors of vigils and the meditations of his heart; continually pouring out before the Lord the tears of his prayers; and specifically and unceasingly asking him to extinguish the assault.

[Col. 0307D] (Cap. 26.) The soul that boasts of having renounced this world, while vices rule over it, will be more shameful and unclean and will be punished with a heavier penalty than it was formerly in the world, when it had neither professed the discipline nor borne the name of a monk.

(Ibid.) No one can ever obtain the purity of perfection if he hopes to acquire it solely through continence, that is, bodily fasting, unless he understands that he must practice it for this reason: so that, with the flesh humbled by fasting, he may more easily enter into battle against the other vices, rather than allowing the flesh to grow insolent through the excess of satiety.

(Collat. 6.---Cap. 10.) A person can be struck down more easily by prosperity than by adversity. For adversity sometimes restrains and humbles even those unwilling to be restrained, through a most salutary contrition; it either makes them sin less or corrects them. Prosperity, however, raises the mind through soft and harmful flatteries and, by the success of their happiness, casts the secure down into a greater ruin.

[Col. 0308A] (Cap. 16.) No virtue can be possessed immovably by a human being. To retain it once acquired, it must always be guarded by the same diligence and effort through which it was gained—and, what is more truly the case, by the aid of sustaining grace.

(Collat. 9.---Cap. 1.) The whole purpose of the monk and the perfection of his heart tend toward continual and uninterrupted perseverance in prayer and, insofar as human weakness permits, strive toward immovable tranquility of mind and perpetual purity.

(Cap. 3.) Whatever our soul has conceived before the hour of prayer must necessarily confront us during prayer through the intrusion of memory. Therefore, if we wish to be found in a certain condition while praying, we must prepare ourselves beforehand in the same condition.

(Collat. 10.---Cap. 13.) There are three things that make a wandering mind stable: vigils, meditation, and prayer. Their constancy and continual concentration give the soul firm stability.

(Collat. 11.---Cap. 13.) There are three things that make people abstain from vices: fear of Gehenna or of present laws; hope for and desire of the kingdom of heaven; or affection for the good itself and love of the virtues.

(Cap. 10.) It is clear evidence that the soul has not yet been refined of the dregs of vice if, in the sins of others, it does not grieve out of compassion but maintains the harsh severity of a judge.

(Collat. 12.---Cap. 5.) If we desire to drive carnal desires from our hearts, let us immediately plant spiritual pleasures in their place, so that our mind, always bound to these, may have objects on which it can continually dwell and may reject the allurements of present and temporal joys.

[Col. 0308C] (Cap. 61.) To the extent that a person progresses in gentleness and patience of heart, he will progress in purity of body; and the farther he has driven away the passion of anger, the more firmly he will possess chastity. For no one will avoid the heat of the body unless he has first restrained the movements of the soul.

(Cap. 16.) For each one of us who labors with all his strength against the spirit of fornication, there is a singular victory in not expecting the remedy to come from the merit of his own effort. Although this faith may seem easy and straightforward to everyone, beginners possess it with no less difficulty than they attain the perfection of chastity itself. For when even a small measure of purity has smiled upon them, they immediately flatter themselves in the secret places of their conscience, as a certain subtle elation slips in; believing that they have obtained it through their own diligent effort, they must be stripped of that heavenly protection, so that they may be oppressed by those passions that divine power had extinguished until experience teaches them that they cannot obtain the good of purity by their own strength and effort.

(Collat. 13.---Cap. 3.) The beginning not only of good actions but also of good thoughts comes from God, who inspires in us the beginnings of a holy will and grants us the power and opportunity to carry out what we rightly desire.

(Collat. 14.---Cap. 6.) It is impossible for one and the same person to shine simultaneously with every virtue. If someone wishes to pursue them all at once, he must fall into this situation: while following all of them, he achieves none completely and suffers greater loss than progress from this change and variety.

(Ibid.) There are many roads by which one advances toward God. Therefore each person should complete the path he has once undertaken with an unchanging determination to continue on it, so that he may be perfect in whatever profession he has chosen.

(Cap. 9.) It is impossible for someone who applies himself to reading with the aim of acquiring human praise to earn the gift of true knowledge.

(Cap. 10.) If you desire to reach true knowledge of the Scriptures, you must hasten first to acquire humility of heart. Through the perfection of charity, this humility will lead you not to the knowledge that puffs up but to the knowledge that gives illumination.

[Col. 0309A] For it is impossible for an unclean mind to obtain the gift of spiritual knowledge (1 Cor. 8).

(Ibid.) Therefore, with every precaution, avoid allowing your study of reading to produce in you—not the light of knowledge, nor that everlasting glory promised through the illumination of teaching—but instruments of destruction born from the vanity of arrogance.

(Cap. 13.) The human mind cannot be free from all thoughts. Therefore, so long as it has not been occupied with spiritual pursuits, it must become entangled in those things that it learned previously.

(Ibid.) It is clear evidence of a lukewarm and proud mind if it receives disdainfully and negligently the medicine of salutary words, even when it has been taken in through the effort of excessive diligence.

[Col. 0309B] (Cap. 16.) No one in whom the desire for carnal passions—and especially for fornication—still rules can possess spiritual knowledge.

(Cap. 18.) The teaching of spiritual matters is evidently rendered ineffective for two reasons. Either the teacher, commending things he has not experienced, attempts to instruct his listener through a varied sound of words; or else the listener, wicked and filled with vices, does not receive with a hardened heart the holy and salutary teaching of a spiritual man.

(Collat. 15.---Cap. 7.) Humility is the teacher of all the virtues, the firmest foundation of the heavenly building, and the distinctive and magnificent gift of our Savior.

(Cap. 8.) It is a greater miracle to uproot from one’s own flesh the fuel of lust than to expel unclean spirits from the bodies of others; and it is a more magnificent sign, through the power of patience, to restrain the savage movements of anger than to command the powers of the air. It is greater to drive the most voracious diseases of sadness from one’s own heart than to expel the bodily illnesses and fevers of another.

[Col. 0309C] (Ibid.) In many ways it is a more glorious virtue and a loftier achievement to care for the illnesses of one’s own soul than for the body of another. For the more sublime the soul is than the flesh, the more excellent is its health; and the more precious and superior its substance, the more serious and harmful is its ruin.

(Cap. 10.) It is a greater virtue and a loftier grace to extinguish the inward lust of the flesh than to subdue, by the Lord’s sign and the power of the Most High, the wickedness of demons attacking from outside, or to drive them from possessed bodies by invoking the divine name.

(Collat. 16.---Cap. 3.) This is the faithful and indissoluble bond of friendship, which is founded solely upon equality of virtue. “The Lord makes those of one way of life dwell in a house” (Ps. 67). Therefore undivided love can remain only among those in whom one purpose and one will consist in willing and refusing the same things.

(Ibid.) It is the sharing of character before God, not dwelling together in the same place, that joins brothers together. The integrity of peace can never be preserved where diversity of wills is found.

[Col. 0309D] (Cap. 6.) How could one who believes that he will depart from this world every day, indeed continually, retain even a slight resentment against a brother?

(Cap. 7.) Just as nothing must be preferred to charity, so, conversely, nothing must be postponed to fury or anger. For everything, however useful and necessary it may appear, must nevertheless be despised in order to avoid the disturbance of anger; and everything even that is thought adverse must be accepted and endured so that the serenity of love and peace may be preserved unimpaired. For nothing is to be considered more harmful than anger and hatred, nor anything more useful than charity.

(Cap. 12.) Let no one, however endowed with knowledge, persuade himself through empty swelling that he has no need of another’s conference. For even if the devil’s deception does not mislead his judgment, he will nevertheless not escape the more serious snares of self-exaltation and pride.

[Col. 0310A] (Cap. 28.) That saying of the wisest men is entirely certain: true concord and undivided fellowship cannot exist except among men of amended character and of the same virtue and purpose.

(Collat. 18.---Cap. 10.) Although some customarily use the terms monasteries and coenobia interchangeably, there is nevertheless this difference: *monastery* is the name of a lodging, signifying nothing more than the place, that is, the dwelling of monks; *coenobium*, however, also designates the quality and discipline of the profession itself. The dwelling of a single monk may be called a monastery; but it cannot be called a coenobium unless there is an united community of many inhabitants living there.

(Cap. 11.) True humility of heart must be retained. It does not arise from an affected posture of body or from words, but from the innermost humiliation of the mind. It will then shine with the clearest signs of its patience when a person does not himself boast of crimes that others would not believe, but despises accusations arrogantly brought against him by others and patiently tolerates injuries inflicted upon him with a gentle evenness of heart.

(Cap. 13.) Patience would not be praiseworthy or admirable if, attacked by no arrows of enemies, it merely maintained its resolve of tranquility. Its excellence and glory lie in remaining immovable when storms of temptation rush against it. For in the very thing in which it is thought to be harassed and broken by adversity, it is strengthened; and in the very thing in which it is thought to be blunted, it is sharpened.

(Ibid.) No one is unaware that patience receives its name from suffering and endurance. Therefore it is clear that no one can be called patient except one who has endured without indignation everything inflicted upon him.

[Col. 0310C] (Ibid.) A holy man does not differ from a sinner because he is not likewise tempted, but because, even under a great assault, he is not conquered, whereas the other is overcome even by a small temptation.

(Cap. 16.) We should not be surprised that perverse and detestable people are sometimes found concealed among the number of holy men. For while we are trampled and crushed in the threshing floor of this world, it is necessary that chaff destined for everlasting fire also be mixed among the choicest grain.

(Cap. 17.) It must certainly be understood that the disease of envy is more difficult to bring to a cure than the other vices. For the one whom it has once corrupted with the plague of its poison, I might almost say, is without a remedy.

(Ibid.) It is therefore clear that envy is more harmful than all the vices and more difficult to cleanse, since it is inflamed by the very remedies through which the others are extinguished.

(Collat. 19.---Cap. 3.) It is better to be found devoted in lesser professions than undevoted in greater ones.

[Col. 0310D] (Cap. 5.) It is miserable for someone to profess the discipline of any art or study and not reach its perfection.

(Cap. 8.) The end of the coenobite is to mortify and crucify all his own wills and, according to the salutary command of evangelical perfection, to think of nothing concerning tomorrow.

(Ibid.) The perfection of the hermit, however, is to have a mind stripped of all earthly things and, as far as human weakness permits, to unite it with Christ.

(Cap. 13.) In communities the beginning of salvation is acquired, and those who have not first been healed by the medicine of coenobia cannot be healthy in solitude.

(Cap. 14.) A salutary remedy cannot be lacking to those who are concerned about the cure of their diseases. Therefore, just as the symptoms of each vice are identified, remedies must also be sought.

[Col. 0311A] (Collat. 20.---Cap. 10.) For each sin to be extinguished, the cause and occasion through which it was committed must first be cut off.

(Collat. 21.---Cap. 5.) It is not so praiseworthy to abstain from what is unlawful as to abstain even from what is lawful and, out of reverence for the one who permitted us to use these things because of our weakness, not to use them.

(Cap. 14.) Whatever is decreed as a command imposes death if it is not fulfilled; but whatever is rather advised than commanded is beneficial when done and does not punish when left undone.

(Cap. 26.) We must take every precaution to preserve all the senses of our body, especially in the morning hours, unimpaired and untouched in every respect, as sacred holocausts of the Lord.

The gain from fasting is not so great as the loss caused by anger; nor is the benefit obtained from reading as great as the harm incurred through contempt of a brother.

We must believe two things: first, that no one is tempted at all without God’s permission; second, that everything inflicted upon us by God—whether it presently appears sad or joyful—is imposed for our benefit by a most loving Father and a most merciful physician.

(Collat. 22.---Cap. 1.) The dispenser of spiritual things gathers a double profit. For he gains not only from the progress of the one who listens but also from his own discussion, kindling himself no less than the desire for perfection while instructing his hearer.

(Collat. 2.---Cap. 3.) There is one and only one theory, that is, contemplation of God, to which all the merits of justification and every pursuit of the virtues are rightly subordinated.

[Col. 0312A] (Cap. 20.) The more the human mind advances and reaches a purer sincerity of contemplation, the more unclean it will see itself to be, as though in the mirror of its own purity. For when the soul extends itself toward a loftier vision and longs to behold greater things than those it is accomplishing, it must despise as inferior and always more worthless the things in which it now remains.

(Collat. 24.---Cap. 2.) It is little for a monk to have renounced once—that is, at the beginning of his conversion, to have despised present things—unless he persists in renouncing them every day.

(Cap. 8.) Each of us ought carefully to weigh the measure of his strength beforehand and undertake whatever discipline he wishes according to that measure. For although all disciplines are useful, not all can be suitable for everyone.

(Cap. 25.) If you wish to compare the fragrant flower of virginity and the tender purity of chastity with the foul and fetid mire of lust; the peace and security of monks with the dangers and hardships in which the people of this world are entangled; the repose of our poverty with the devouring sorrows and sleepless cares of the rich, by which they are consumed day and night not without the greatest danger to their lives—you will very easily find proved the most sweet yoke of Christ and his exceedingly light burden.

[Col. 0312B] (Cap. 26.) Monks alone retain the unity of perpetual fellowship and possess all things without distinction: they believe that everything belonging to the brothers is their own, and that everything their own is the brothers’.

# APPENDIX THREE

[Col. 0311]

## H. CUYCHIUS’S ANNOTATIONS OR CENSORIAL NOTES ON THE BOOKS OF J. CASSIAN

[Col. 0311C] Pope Gelasius, in distinction 15, chapter *Sancta Romana*, counts the works of John Cassian among the apocrypha. And Blessed Prosper expressly condemns the discussion of Abbot Chaeremon on Grace and Free Will, which is contained in the thirteenth Conference, having published against it a short work entitled *Against the Collator*. Therefore, lest an incautious reader, persuaded by the authority of this Chaeremon and of the other abbots whose opinions Cassian reports in the Conferences, should fall into some error, we have deliberately appended these censures to the end of the work itself.

### Book VI of the Institutes, chapter 18

There are different gifts, and the grace of the Holy Spirit is not granted to all in one form, but according to what each person has shown himself worthy and capable of receiving through his zeal or effort. Finally, although the virtue of integrity is believed to have been perfect in all the holy Apostles, the gift of knowledge nevertheless overflowed more abundantly in Paul, because he prepared himself for it by diligent zeal and effort.

(Annot. 1.) The opinion of the Pelagians was that God distributes his gifts not entirely gratuitously but according to human merits. Catholic and orthodox faith, however, teaches something else. Those who make themselves suitable and capable of these virtues do not thereby become wise, just, and temperate; rather, God, in his generous and gratuitous goodness, deigns to adorn with these virtues those whom he wills. For God is free in his gifts and bound to no one. Nevertheless, it must not altogether be denied that it is also our task to strive, to will, and to labor so that we may become capable of receiving divine benevolence and his gifts—provided that we nevertheless ascribe this very preparation of the soul also to him from whom every good gift and every perfect gift descends (James 1).

But faith and the first movement of a good will are given by God alone, without any merit of ours. Christ indicates this in the words recorded by John: “No one comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6). For although those who live honestly and laudably according to the law of nature may present themselves as less unsuited and less unworthy of God’s grace and gifts, they cannot make themselves suitable, capable, or worthy apart from divine assistance.

[Col. 0312C] Yet because God never fails the person who has once been justified through baptism and, insofar as lies within him, acts through the indwelling Spirit in those things necessary both for remaining in righteousness and for salvation—for the Apostle says, “The Spirit helps our weakness” (Rom. 8), and God himself says through the same Apostle, “I will not abandon you or forsake you” (Heb. 13)—Cassian was right to say that each of us excels especially in the virtue in which he has exercised himself through zeal and unremitting labor, and that the gift of knowledge overflowed in the Apostle Paul because he prepared himself for it by diligent zeal and effort.

### Book XII of the Institutes, chapter 14

For just as we say that human efforts cannot grasp perfection by themselves without God’s assistance, so we declare that God’s mercy and grace are bestowed upon those who labor and toil, and, to use the Apostle’s words, are imparted to those who will and run, and so forth. And again: “For he is ready, when only the opportunity of a good will has been offered to him by us, to bestow all these things.”

(Annot. 2.) These words also seem to carry the scent of the Pelagian heresy, since the Author asserts that God grants his grace only to those who labor, while it is our task to offer God the opportunity of a good will, by which he is moved to pour out his gifts upon us. But the matter is otherwise. He is not speaking of pagans, unbelievers, or impious people, but of those who have been made sons by adoption and in whom the Spirit dwells. Thus he does not exclude divine assistance from this preparation, as though a person could labor by his own spontaneous power and dispose himself to receive God’s grace. Rather, in these words he rouses our sluggishness, so that we who receive the Spirit of God, who have once been enlightened, who have tasted the heavenly gift, may devote all our intelligence and strength to those things that advance our eternal salvation. This is precisely what divine majesty demands of all who have been reborn in Christ and through the Holy Spirit.

That Cassian intended in these words to detract nothing from divine grace can be seen clearly from the five chapters that follow, in which he develops his judgment concerning the necessity of grace at great length and confirms it both by reason and by the authority of divine Scripture. He teaches that all our efforts, labors, and attempts are empty and futile unless we are both anticipated in goodness by divine assistance and supported and sustained by it at every moment.

[Col. 0313B] He pursues this judgment here so fully and clearly that I am convinced that what he wrote in these chapters from his own position should be accepted as a kind of apology against those who have mistakenly thought that he held an opinion about the assistance of divine grace contrary to the doctrine of the Catholic and orthodox faith. For in these twelve books of the Monastic Constitutions, as also in the books *On the Incarnation of the Word*, he presents his own position. In the Conferences, however, he reports the opinions of those whom he introduces as speaking. If some errors that conflict with true and Catholic doctrine are occasionally found among them, they must be ascribed to the speakers themselves, not to Cassian.

### Book I of the Conferences, chapter 17

It is impossible for the mind not to be assailed by thoughts, but it is possible for everyone who strives either to accept or to reject them. Therefore, just as their arising does not depend entirely upon us, so their approval or selection rests with us. Yet from what we have said—that it is impossible for the mind not to be approached by thoughts—it does not follow that everything must be attributed either to their assault or to the evil spirits who try to impose them. Otherwise, free will would not remain in human beings, nor would the effort of our correction lie within us.

[Col. 0313D] (Annot. 3.) These abbots whom John Cassian introduces as speaking in the Conferences often seem to speak as though, together with Pelagius, they were hostile to the grace of Christ. Yet most of them can easily be defended from this error if we observe that they are not speaking about people entirely deprived of God’s grace and governed solely by the judgment of free will, but about Christians and those who have made great progress toward the perfection of the monastic life—those who, made sons through the Spirit of adoption, persevere, grow, and advance in what they once received.

Abbot Pinufius also spoke of such people in Book IV of the Institutes, chapter 42, when he said that we ought not to expect the virtue of patience from the uprightness and moderation of others—that is, that we should possess it only when no one has irritated us. Since that cannot fail to happen, it does not lie within our power. Rather, we must expect it from our own humility and endurance, which depend upon our will.

[Col. 0314A] For he did not exclude the assistance of God’s grace; he denied that patience could be acquired merely through the moderation of other people, while affirming that our own zeal and labor are necessary for acquiring it. Without doubt he was speaking of those in whom the divine Spirit dwells and whom he continually urges and invites to attain the summit of perfection.

Thus, because of what theologians call habitual grace, since they are continually moved by the Spirit of God, it is no more difficult for them to reach the highest summit of patience through constant practice and endurance of evils than it is to repel and reject impure thoughts suggested by unclean spirits or arising from ourselves. Nevertheless, there can be no doubt that, just as these thoughts are partly suggested by evil spirits and partly arise from within us, so their rejection and repudiation must likewise be attributed jointly to our free will and to God’s grace.

I omit the fact that some manuscript copies read: “But it is possible for everyone who strives either to accept or to reject them through the grace of God.” This reading does not appear to be genuine and is found only in a very few, and those more recent, copies.

### Conference 1, chapter 19

Thoughts arise from within us when we naturally remember things that we are doing, have done, or have heard. Concerning these Blessed David says: “I considered the days of old, and I held the eternal years in my mind; and I meditated at night with my heart, and I was exercised, and I swept my spirit.”

(Annot. 4.) Blessed David, in the seventy-sixth Psalm, from which this verse is taken, speaks of the remembrance of ancient days and eternal years that contributes to true and Christian repentance. Through it we weep over committed sins by considering eternal and infernal punishment, and by exercising ourselves in this way we cleanse and sweep our spirit.

Saint Hezekiah likewise, in the Canticle, recalls all his days in the bitterness of his soul. This sort of remembrance, however, does not arise in us through the powers of free will alone. The rock of our breast must be struck from heaven by the Lord, so that waters and springs of tears may flow abundantly from our eyes, with which we may lament our former sins.

Nevertheless, it can happen that sinners sometimes demand an account from themselves of the time they have spent badly and remember the eternal years, while still deciding nothing about a true conversion of heart or a resolve for a better life. Such remembrance can arise in us from things we have naturally done or heard, even when divine assistance is excluded. This appears to be the judgment of Abbot Moses.

### Conference 3, chapter 12

Just as we recognize that God works in different ways through opportunities for salvation, so it is our task to serve more zealously or more sluggishly according to the opportunities granted by the Divinity. For just as the offer, “Go out from your land,” belonged to God who called, so the obedience of Abraham who went out belonged to Abraham, and so forth.

(Annot. 5.) In the work of our justification, some things are accomplished by God alone, while others must be ascribed jointly to our free will and to God. For he first inspires the spirit of salvation in us, while we are still under his anger and undeserving, and makes us willing to will the good; then, after our corrupt will has been stirred, he works together with us to will and to accomplish according to good will (Phil. 2); finally, he completes the work and adds the finishing touch.

Abbot Paphnutius means nothing else in this passage, as can be clearly seen from what is set forth both in this chapter and in the following chapters up to the end of the Conference, especially chapters 19 and 22. “By what we have brought forward,” he says, “we do not wish to remove human free will, but to demonstrate that the assistance and grace of God are necessary to it every day and at every moment.”

## Col. 4, chapter 7

[Col. 0315A]

We read of this struggle, profitably implanted also in our own members, in the Apostle as follows:

> “For the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh. These are opposed to one another, so that you do not do whatever you wish.”

Here too you have a struggle somehow embedded in our body, brought about by the Lord’s providential arrangement. For whatever is generally present in everyone, without exception, what else can it be believed to belong to than human nature itself? What else can it be believed to be than something attributed, as it were naturally, to human substance after the fall of the first man? And when something is found to be innate and fused into everyone, how could it not be believed to have been implanted by the Lord’s decision—not to harm, but to provide for us?

### (Annot. 6.)

[Col. 0315B]

Abbot Daniel attributes to God as its author the desire which, from the very beginning, has been implanted and born in our members on account of the fault of the first human beings, and through which the flesh continually resists the spirit. If this is understood of the natural appetite by which we desire and seek things wholly consonant with our nature, his opinion is entirely true, since God is the author both of nature and of all its faculties and natural powers.

But if, in desire itself, we consider that excess and deviation from the rectitude of reason by which the flesh continually struggles against the spirit, this should not equally be attributed to God—unless perhaps for the following reason: after the fall of our first parents, God withdrew from human beings the bridle of original righteousness, by which reason kept all the lower powers within the limits it had prescribed. Once that bridle had been removed, it necessarily followed that those powers of sensation, like untamed horses released from every halter and barrier, should rush in every direction.

Peter Lombard expresses the matter more or less in this way in the second book of the *Sentences*, distinction 31. Having raised the question whether desire comes from God or from elsewhere, he replies that, insofar as it is a punishment inflicted on account of sin, it has God as its author; but insofar as it is guilt, it has the devil or the reprobate human being as its author.

[Col. 0315C]

In those who have been initiated and regenerated through the sacrament of baptism, when reason no longer obeys desire but resists and opposes it, desire is not sin. The Apostle says in Romans 8 that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the spirit. Nevertheless, desire remains in them as a punishment and so that it may serve the regenerate as material for the exercise of virtue. Abbot Daniel affirms that this has been brought about here by the Lord’s providential arrangement and decision—not to harm, but to provide for us. Blessed Augustine develops the same opinion at great length in Book 5 of *Against Julian*, chapters 3 and 7.

## Coll. 7, chapter 4

The quality of these things depends upon us, for, he says, “good thought approaches those who know it, and the prudent man will find it.” Whatever is subject to our prudence and diligence so that it may be found, [Col. 0315D] if it is not found, must without doubt be attributed to our laziness or imprudence, not to a defect of nature.

The Psalmist also agrees with this meaning when he says:

> “Blessed is the man whose help is from you; he has arranged ascents in his heart.”

You see, therefore, that it lies within our power to arrange in our hearts either ascents—that is, thoughts reaching toward God—or descents, namely, thoughts falling toward earthly and carnal things, and so forth.

### (Annot. 7.)

The discussion concerned the instability of the human mind and the wanderings to which our spirit is accustomed to descend from contemplation of spiritual and divine things: whether these wanderings should be attributed to a defect of nature or to human beings themselves.

Since the mind wanders at every moment through slippery thoughts, and even when it applies itself to the fear of God or to spiritual contemplation, to such a degree that it seems unable to prevent itself—[Col. 0316A] even with our greatest effort and the most tenacious concentration of the heart—from slipping away toward other and external things, some were therefore persuaded that these wanderings of the soul were implanted in the human race not through our fault but through a defect of nature.

Abbot Serenus answers this question by asserting that the human mind is indeed always and greatly mobile and can never remain idle, just as the authority of the Wise Man teaches when he says that “this earthly dwelling weighs down the mind occupied with many thoughts” (Wisdom 9). Yet he maintains that it remains our responsibility to bend the mind continually and through prolonged exercise in one direction or the other, so that, once habituated through long practice, it may direct its tireless flights around good or evil—for that is how he puts it—and acquire strength to remain in one place.

We must not, therefore, attribute this wandering of our mind either to God the Creator or to human nature. For true is the saying of Scripture:

> “The Lord made man upright, but they themselves sought out many devices” (Ecclesiastes 7).

[Col. 0316B]

When Abbot Serenus consequently adds that the quality of our thoughts depends upon us, this should not be understood as though it lay solely within the powers of free choice for our mind to devote itself exclusively to spiritual pursuits. Rather, he wishes to deny that the mobility and wandering of our mind should be attributed to God or to nature, since it lies within our power—with the assistance of divine grace, through long habituation—to incline the mind only toward honorable, holy, and chaste pursuits and thoughts.

This is the clear and evident meaning of this fourth chapter. Expressions of this kind are found everywhere in Chrysostom, Nazianzen, and other ancient writers, indeed even in Augustine himself, that vigorous defender of divine grace. For in Sermon 36 of the *Sermons on Various Subjects* he speaks as follows:

> “What you ought to fear is much greater”—he is speaking of the punishments of Gehenna and eternal death—“and it lies within your power that what you fear should not come upon you. What you ought to fear is greater—far greater, incomparably greater—and it lies within your power that it should not come upon you. For whether you live well or badly, [Col. 0316C] you are going to die. You cannot escape death, whether you live well or live badly. But if you choose to live well here, you will not be sent into eternal punishments.”

## Col. 7, chapter 8

Just as the demons possess abundant opportunity for instigation, so in us has been granted the power to reject, or the freedom to consent.

### (Annot. 8.)

This agrees with what we said in the preceding note: namely, that the slipperiness and volatility of our mind, by which it so often wanders from holy contemplation toward external things utterly irrelevant to the matter at hand, should not be attributed to the demons, as Abbot Germanus wished, but rather to our own negligence and slowness, because we do not habituate ourselves to holy and spiritual exercises.

Although those hostile powers are always lying in wait for our progress, Abbot Serenus rightly denies that they are the instigators of evil. For, he says, if that were so, no human being [Col. 0316D] could avoid any sin whatsoever that they wished to implant in our hearts, if they possessed the power to compel us violently just as they possess the power to suggest.

Therefore, just as they have the opportunity to instigate, so in us has been granted the power to reject, or the freedom to consent. Yet this must by no means be understood as excluding divine assistance, as is clear from the words that follow. He adds:

> “If, however, we fear their power and attacks, let us set against them, in return, the protections and helps of God. For it is said: ‘Greater is he who is in us than he who is in the world.’ His aids fight for us with a much more powerful strength than the multitude of those others contends against us. For God is not only the suggester of good things but also their supporter and impeller, so that at times he even draws us to salvation against our will and without our knowledge.”

Thus far Abbot Serenus.

## Col. 7, chapter 13

[Col. 0317A]

Although we affirm that there are certain spiritual natures—such as angels, archangels, and the other powers, as well as our own soul, or at least this subtle air—we must nevertheless not regard them as altogether incorporeal. For, according to their own nature, they have a body by which they subsist, although one much more subtle than ours.

For they are bodies, according to the Apostle’s statement:

> “There are celestial bodies and terrestrial bodies.”

And again:

> “It is sown a natural body; it rises a spiritual body.”

From these words it is plainly gathered that nothing is incorporeal except God alone.

### (Annot. 9.)
