The question of angelic bodies has long been debated among philosophers and theologians. Some attribute bodies to angels and maintain that God alone is spirit and purely incorporeal; others deny this.

The more commonly received and more firmly established opinion is the one that makes angels free from bodies. Thus teaches Blessed Dionysius in chapter 2 of *The Celestial Hierarchy* and in chapter 4 of *The Divine Names*; Athanasius in his book *On the Common [Col. 0317B] Essence of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit*; Gregory of Nazianzus in Oration 2, *On Theology*; Chrysostom in Homily 22 on Genesis; Cyril in Book 4 on John, chapter 10; Theodoret in Book 3 *Against the Greeks*, near the end; Sophronius in his letter to the bishops of Constantinople, which was read at the Sixth Council, session 11; Damascene in Book 2 of *The Orthodox Faith*, chapter 3; Gregory the Great in Book 4 of the *Moralia*, chapter 9; Bede in Book 1 *On Philosophical Elements*; and finally Blessed Thomas Aquinas in *On Spiritual Creatures*, article 5, in Book 2 *Against the Gentiles*, chapter 91, and in Part 1 of the *Summa Theologiae*, questions 50 and 51.

The scholastic doctors who write on the eighth distinction of the second book of the *Sentences* likewise support this position.

The same opinion can also be established by arguments. Angels are repeatedly called “spirits” in the divine writings, and “spirit” is the term for an incorporeal substance. Again, in Mark 5 and Luke 6 Scripture relates that an entire legion of demons entered one man. By the name “legion”—as Blessed Jerome states in Book 4 of his commentary on Matthew—six thousand demons are understood. [Col. 0317C] If they were corporeal, they could by no means have entered one man.

Finally, the first chapter of the Lateran Council held under Innocent III clearly indicates that the angelic nature is free from corporeal substance. [Col. 0317D] For the words of that council are as follows:

> “God, from the beginning of time, created both creatures from nothing: the corporeal and the spiritual, namely the angelic and the worldly; and afterward the human creature, as a common creature, constituted from spirit and body.”

## Col. 7, chapter 30

We have never heard that our elders forbade the holy Communion to the possessed; indeed, they judged that, if possible, it should even be administered to them every day.

### (Annot. 10.)

By the example of a certain Abbot Andronicus and other possessed persons who were freed from demons through Eucharistic Communion, Abbot Serenus shows that the possessed should by no means be excluded from receiving this saving food.

Nevertheless, because of the discharges, vomiting, and other inconveniences of this kind to which those afflicted by demons are ordinarily subject, they should be admitted to these fearful and most holy mysteries only after mature judgment and a careful examination of all the circumstances.

This should not seem surprising, since even to those who suffer only from bodily illness holy Communion is often denied for legitimate reasons, lest any irreverence be shown toward the most holy and august sacrament.

## Col. 7, chapter 32

That there are as many dispositions among unclean spirits as among human beings is clearly established beyond doubt. For it is evident that some of them—those whom the common people also call Fauns—are such deceivers and jesters that, continually occupying certain places or roads, they take no pleasure in [Col. 0318A] tormenting those whom they have been able to deceive as they pass by, but, content merely with laughter and mockery, seek rather to weary them than to harm them. Others, however, merely spend the night with human beings through harmless hauntings.

### (Annot. 11.)

Blessed Antony, speaking in Athanasius about the diversity of dispositions that exists among demons, says that some reach the highest degree of harmfulness, while others, by comparison with them, appear almost harmless; and that each, according to the extent of its powers, has undertaken different conflicts against different causes. Yet all possess a hostile hatred toward Christians, and especially toward monks and virgins of Christ.

What Abbot Serenus says here—that some have such a disposition that they prefer to jest rather than to harm—should therefore be understood in this way: through divine power they have been deprived of the ability to harm. Thus they content themselves with playful deception because they are not permitted to inflict injury or damage. They would certainly do so [Col. 0318B] if they were not divinely restrained.

For all of them possess the will to harm. Saint Antony therefore rightly warns us to regard with suspicion all their schemes, jokes, applause, laughter, and everything else they do around us, because, when they cannot harm us with fury and savagery, they seek to circumvent us by these tricks and devices.

> “Their rebukes and admonitions to fast are to be despised, as is their deceitful suggestion of vigils. For this reason they assume familiar forms among us: so that, while harming us through the resemblance of virtues, they may more easily insert their poison and strike down the innocent under the appearance of goodness.”

And a little later:

> “For this reason also the Lord commanded them to be silent when they spoke from the Scriptures. For God says to the sinner: ‘Why do you recount my judgments and take up my covenant in your mouth?’ The demons imitate everything. They often converse with the brothers and often trouble them; often they raise disordered noises, seize their hands, hiss, and laugh foolishly, so that they may enter the Christian heart even for a [Col. 0318C] moment of sin. When they have been driven back by everyone, at last they reveal their weakness by lamentation.”

The Lord, as God and conscious of his own majesty, commanded them to be silent. We, following the footsteps of the saints, should walk the same path. Perceiving their aforementioned subtle deceptions, they sang:

> “When the sinner stood against me, I was silent, was humbled, and kept silence from good things.”

And again:

> “But I was like a deaf man and did not hear, and like a mute who does not open his mouth; I became like a man who does not hear.”

Christ, as Lord, commanded silence so that we might believe nothing the devil says—and we shall conquer.

If they compel us to pray, or advise us to fast, let us do these things not because of their admonitions but according to our own practice. Finally, even if they appear to rush upon us and threaten us with death, they should be laughed at rather than feared, because, being weak, they threaten everything but accomplish nothing.

Thus far from Blessed Antony.

From these words it is clear that everything the demons do around us—so that through jokes, laughter, and similar [Col. 0318D] absurdities they may draw us into familiarity with them—is directed toward enticing us to sin. Their companionship must therefore be avoided cautiously and wisely, so that we consent to them in nothing and place no trust, in any matter whatsoever, in their words or counsels.

The Apostle accordingly warns the Corinthians in the tenth chapter of his First Letter:

> “I do not want you to become companions of demons.”

And in Ephesians, chapter 6:

> “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against rulers and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world.”

Again, Blessed Peter says in the fifth chapter of his First Letter:

> “Your adversary the devil,” he says, “prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour.”

From the time when, in baptism, we renounced the devil and professed him to be our enemy, a deadly hatred has existed between us and him. So great is it that he never wishes to benefit anyone in one respect without harming another person much more bitterly, destructively, and grievously.

Clear testimony and an example of this can be found in [Col. 0319A] Blessed Gregory, Book 1 of the *Moralia*, chapter 9. There he writes that a certain possessed virgin was freed from a single demon through magicians and fortune-tellers, but that six or seven thousand demons succeeded it in her place.

Blessed Leo, in Sermon 19 *On the Passion of the Lord*, also affirms that the demon, if not in the body, nevertheless always harms and injures the soul. Blessed Augustine likewise confirms this in Book 83 of the *Questions*, question 78.

## Coll. 8, chapter 7

No believer doubts that, before the creation of this visible creation, God made the spiritual and heavenly powers. Because they knew that they had been brought forth from nothing by the Creator’s favor for the very purpose of attaining such a great glory of blessedness, they continually gave him thanks and clung to his praises, and so forth.

### (Annot. 12.)

[Col. 0319B]

It was once an accepted opinion among ancient Christians that spiritual substances existed long before the creation of heaven and earth and that they had praised God for many ages, as Abbot Serenus asserts here.

Blessed Basil likewise supports this view in Homily 1 of the *Hexaemeron*, explaining the words of Genesis, “In the beginning God created heaven and earth,” and in Homily 2, on the words, “The earth was formless and empty.”

Origen also teaches this in the books *On First Principles* (*περὶ ἀρχῶν*), especially Book 3, chapter 3, and in Homily 4 on Isaiah; Gregory of Nazianzus in his Oration on the Nativity of Christ; Ambrose in Book 1 of the *Hexaemeron*, chapter 5, and in the preface to the first Psalm; Hilary in Book 12 *On the Trinity*, somewhat beyond the middle of the book, and in his *Against Auxentius*, shortly before the end; Jerome in chapter 1 of his letter to Titus; Isidore of Seville in Book 1 *On the Supreme Good*, chapter 12; Damascene in Book 2 of *The Orthodox Faith*, chapter 3; and many others, both Greek and Latin.

Blessed Augustine, although he prefers the opinion of those who assert that the angels were created at the same time as heaven and earth, nevertheless permits each person, in Book 11 of *The City of God*, chapter 32, to hold whatever opinion he wishes on this controversy, provided that he does not make spiritual substances coeternal with God, but acknowledges [Col. 0319C] that all visible and invisible things were created in time.

Theodoret likewise, in Question 3 on Genesis, after arguing at length against Blessed Basil, finally concludes as follows:

> “It is necessary to know that everything that exists, except the holy Trinity, possesses a nature subject to corruption. Once this has been granted, if someone says that the hosts of angels were created before heaven and earth, he will not offend the word of piety.”

What the Lateran Council held at Rome under Innocent III in chapter 1—that the Creator of all visible and invisible, spiritual and corporeal things, by his omnipotent power created both natures simultaneously from nothing at the beginning, namely the spiritual and the corporeal, the angelic and the earthly—should not be understood as though, in these words, the former opinion were rejected as false.

The council’s purpose was to refute the error of Origen and others who said that spiritual substances were first produced by God so that they might possess spiritual dignity, and that, after they had sinned, [Col. 0319D] all bodies were created as prisons in which they might suffer punishment for their crimes. Saint Thomas understood this passage in this way in his exposition of the first decretal.

That the later opinion is more consonant with the truth is demonstrated by the authority of the divine writings and of many ancient authors. For Moses writes in Exodus 20 that God created heaven, earth, the sea, and all that is in them over the course of six days. No one doubts that the angels are in heaven and are therefore called the heavenly host. Consequently, we must confess that they too were created within those six days.

Ecclesiasticus, chapter 18, also says:

> “He who lives forever created all things together,”

namely, within the first six days of the world.

And Blessed John says in the third chapter of his First Letter that the devil sinned from the beginning. It is certain that he was in heaven when he sinned, for this is signified by Christ’s words in Luke 10:

> “I saw [Col. 0320A] Satan falling from heaven like lightning.”

It therefore becomes clear that he was created together with heaven.

To this may be added the opening words of Genesis:

> “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.”

That is, as Philo and many others explain them, heaven and earth were created before all other things, though in such a way that by “heaven” the angels also are understood, and by “earth” corporeal and living things.

The preceding view is also supported by Blessed Epiphanius in his treatment of the heresy of Paul of Samosata, which is heresy 65 in Augustine; by Augustine in Book 11 of *The City of God*, chapters 6 and 9, and Book 12, chapter 15; by Theodoret in Question 3 on Genesis; and by Gregory the Great in Book 32 of the *Moralia*, chapter 10.

For the time being, let us omit the many authors whom we previously brought forward in support of the first opinion, since, if examined carefully, they do not detract from ours. Most of them do not so much assert one position as express doubt, presenting both opinions for consideration. Others merely report the opinion commonly accepted in their own time, as Abbot Serenus did here.

Finally, the Master of the *Sentences*, together with the whole company of scholastic writers, subscribes to the later opinion in Book 2 of the *Sentences*, [Col. 0320B] distinction 2.

For this reason we too prefer the opinion which, with Augustine and those whom we have mentioned, says that angels are signified by the name “heavens” when Moses says that God created heaven and earth in the beginning, and that they were therefore created on the first day together with heaven itself.

Hence Blessed Gregory, in Book 28 of the *Moralia*, chapter 14, commenting on the words, “When the morning stars praised me,” says that the angels are called morning stars because they were created at the first dawn.

Nor should we be moved by the argument brought forward by Abbot Serenus from the words of Job:

> “When the stars were made together, all my angels praised me together.”

Theodoret and Epiphanius answer this objection in the passages cited by saying that the stars were created only on the fourth day, and that the angels could therefore already have been praising the Lord at that time—as indeed they were praising him.

As for the objection that, if the angels had not been created before the world, it would follow that God had at some time lacked those who praised him, Theodoret resolves it by saying that God had no need of [Col. 0320C] praisers, just as even now he has no need of them.

Moreover, even those who hold that the angels were created earlier cannot deny that God was always much older than they were. Accordingly, there was always some time during which God lacked praisers, although he never needed them.

## Coll. 8, chapter 10

The devil’s first fall, by which he was brought down through pride and by which he also deserved to be called a serpent, was followed by a second fall through envy. This second fall found him still possessing something upright within himself, so that he could even have fellowship with human beings in a certain kind of conversation and counsel. The Lord’s sentence therefore rightly cast him down into the depths, so that he would no longer walk erect, gazing upon something exalted as before, but, clinging to the ground, would crawl and, humbled upon his belly, feed upon earthly foods and deeds of vice.

(Annot. 13.) In these words Abbot Serenus attributes a twofold fall to the devil: the first, through pride, by which [Col. 0320D] he wished to ascend into heaven, exalt his throne above the stars of God, and be like the Most High; the second, through envy, by which he led the first fathers of our race into sin. He also adds that, before this second fall through envy, there still remained in the demon something upright which he lost through that later transgression—namely, when the Lord said to him: “You shall walk upon your breast, and you shall eat earth all the days of your life” (Gen. III).

Both matters must here be examined. First, as regards the demon’s fall, it is generally acknowledged that, since he is spiritual and incorporeal, he could not sin by his own action except through those two kinds of sin—namely, pride and envy—because the object, as they call it, of each is spiritual: in the case of pride, one’s own excellence; in the case of envy, another’s excellence when it obstructs our own. The objects of other sins are money, food, drink, the pleasures of touch and [Col. 0321A] taste, sluggishness, and similar things. Therefore demons cannot commit sins concerning such matters by their own action, but only through counsel, exhortation, suggestion, consent, and similar means.

Whether one of those two sins—pride or envy—was first committed by the demon is disputed. For Blessed Augustine, in Book XI of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 14, writes that some held the demon to have sinned only when he saw that man had been created in the image of God and envied him this glory, fearing that man might be exalted above him into the immortal life from which he himself had fallen; only afterward, they thought, did the guilt of pride arise, by which he wished to be equal to the Most High. This was the view of St. Cyprian in his sermon *On Jealousy and Envy*, and of St. Basil in his homily *On Envy*.

Against this, Blessed Augustine, in the passage mentioned, demonstrates by many arguments that envy followed pride. “The beginning of every sin is pride,” says Ecclesiasticus (ch. X). And St. Job writes of the devil that he is “king over all the sons of pride” (Job [Col. 0321B] XLI). Tobias likewise says in chapter IV: “Never allow pride to rule in your mind or in your speech; for in it every ruin began.”

This opinion is supported by St. Athanasius, *Questions to Antiochus*, question 6; Gregory of Nazianzus, *Oration on the Nativity of Christ*; Chrysostom, Book I *On Compunction of Heart*; Theodoret, in the *Epitome of Divine Decrees*, the chapter *On Demons*, and Book III *Against the Greeks*; Ambrose, on Psalm XXXVI, at the words “I saw the wicked man exalted,” and in Letter 84 to Demetrias, which many attribute to Prosper; St. Jerome, on chapter XIV of Luke; Augustine, Book XII of *The City of God*, chapter 6, and Book XIV, chapter 13; Leo, Letter to Tubius, chapter 6; Gregory, Book XXXIV of the *Moralia*, chapters 14–17; Damascene, Book II *On the Orthodox Faith*, chapter 4; Anselm, *On the Devil’s Fall*, chapter 4; and Bernard, Sermon 22 *On the Song of Songs*.

Reason also supports it. The demon tempted the first human beings to pride; it is therefore plausible that he himself first fell through pride. Thus St. Augustine reasons in Book XIV of *The City of God*, chapter 13. [Col. 0321C] Moreover, the king of the City of God was especially distinguished and renowned for the virtue of humility and moderation. Conversely, therefore, the prince of darkness and king of the diabolical city fell chiefly and first through pride.

Again, the archangel Michael, prince of the heavenly army, once fought against the devil and is especially opposed to him. He received his name from humility, for *Michael* means the same as “Who is like God?” and signifies a rebuke of pride: no one should wish to be equal or similar to God. This is opposed to that satanic pride through which Lucifer sinned.

Finally, envy is by its nature later than pride and proceeds from it, as St. Bonaventure learnedly explains in Book II of the *Sentences*, distinction 21. He writes:

> The proud man loves excellence and therefore admits no equal to himself; rather, he desires excellence to be possessed uniquely and by himself alone. Thus he immediately envies, either in act or in disposition, since he does not wish the good he possesses to be shared with another.

So Bonaventure.

It is therefore credible that the demon [Col. 0321D] fell through pride—by which he attempted to ascend into heaven—before the first human beings had been created by God. They were formed from the clay of the earth only on the sixth day. It is plausible that he remained in the truth for a very brief time and fell through pride shortly after his creation, namely, on the first day.

After man had been created, the devil noticed that man had been placed in a condition in which he could be surrounded by the devil’s deceptions and guile and brought under his power—or in which, if he obeyed the divine command, he could ascend to the everlasting happiness from which the demon himself had fallen. Inflamed by pride and envy, he began to tempt man, attempting to subject him, together with all his offspring and descendants, to his tyranny and to cast him down from hope of heavenly reward.

Pride urged him on insofar as he wished to subject man to himself, to rule over him, and to command him. Envy urged him on insofar as he sought to prevent man from attaining [Col. 0322A] everlasting blessedness.

Nor may we suppose that, as Abbot Serenus writes here, after his first fall through pride, by which he had wished to be equal to God, the demon retained something upright and was stripped of it through the subsequent sin of envy, by divine permission and justice. For just as the angels, after their first act and merit of good will, were so confirmed in goodness that they can never fall away from it, so in precisely the same way the evil spirits, through their first sin of pride, were hardened in evil so completely that they could never turn back to goodness. Having been removed from the state of meriting, they lost all their uprightness and integrity.

Hence St. Damascene, in Book II of *The Orthodox Faith*, chapter 4, says that what death is for human beings, that first fall was for the demons. For just as death closes to us every path of merit and demerit, so the demons’ first fall, before the creation of man, likewise deprived them of every possibility of meriting.

[Col. 0322B] God appointed the entire period of mortal life for human beings as a state of pilgrimage; but for the demons, immediately from the beginning of their creation, he granted a very brief period in which they might merit either everlasting blessedness or perpetual, dreadful, and perfectly just abandonment by God.

Nor should we be moved by the fact that Abbot Serenus attempts to establish his opinion on the ground that, before the demon’s sin of envy by which he enticed man into sin, he had not yet been denied association and conversation with human beings. This does not prove that anything upright remained in him, since even now that power has been left to him: he can transform himself into human form, or even into an angel of light, present himself to our eyes, insinuate himself into our intimacy through the allurements of speech, and strive to plunge the unwary into the pit of sin.

As for the words spoken by the Lord to the serpent—“Because you have done this, you are cursed above all the beasts of the earth; upon your breast you shall walk, [Col. 0322C]” and so forth (Gen. III)—the difficulty is greater. For through this sentence it appears that the demon was deprived of some uprightness, freedom, and ability, and that he was not stripped of all the adornment in which he had been created until after that second transgression by which he seduced man through envy.

Although, according to Blessed Chrysostom’s interpretation, those words were first addressed to the physical serpent, Blessed Augustine nevertheless contends, in Book XI of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 36, that they are to be understood either exclusively of the demon or at least principally of him.

After the demon, inflamed by pride and envy, had tempted man—not only to close to him the way to the heavenly blessedness which he envied him, but also, through pride, to subject him to himself and his tyranny—and had already drawn him into consent to sin, divine justice required that he increase his own condemnation. Because he had wished to bind and subject the entire human race to himself, the Lord pronounced him cursed above all the beasts of the earth, [Col. 0322D] as though he were saying:

> You wished to usurp dominion over human beings; you shall be regarded by all as accursed, and you shall be most wretched and contemptible, not only among sinners but even above all the beasts and animals of the earth.

“You shall walk upon your breast, and you shall eat earth all the days of your life”—that is:

> Trusting in your own craftiness, you hoped that you would rule over all human beings, with a proud and haughty breast raised above them. But the opposite of what you hoped will occur: you shall eat nothing but earth—that is, earthly, carnal, and contemptible human beings, whom the Lord casts out and vomits from his mouth.

“For man,” says Augustine, “was made the devil’s food as punishment for sin. For when it was said to the serpent, ‘You shall eat earth,’ it was also said to man, ‘You are dust.’ If, then, sinful man is dust, and dust is the serpent’s food, sinful man is therefore the serpent’s food.” So Augustine (*On the Christian Contest*, chapter 2, and Book III of *Genesis Against the Manichaeans*, chapter 17).

[Col. 0323A] This, then, is the punishment most worthy of that diabolical pride by which he wished to rule over all human beings: that he can and must consume only those who are earthly, dusty, and stained with the filth of sin, and rule over them; while those who strive to strip off the image of the earthly man—those whom divine Scripture frequently calls heavenly and celestial—might be freed through Christ from his tyranny.

This is signified by the words that immediately follow:

> “I will place enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed. She shall crush your head, and you shall lie in wait for her heel.”

In this sentence, St. Irenaeus, Book III *Against Heresies*, chapter 38; St. Leo, Sermon 2 *On the Nativity of the Lord*; and Blessed Rupert, Book III *On Genesis*, chapter 19, teach that “the seed of the serpent” means Antichrist and “the seed of the woman” means Christ.

For, says Leo:

> God foreshadowed, from the very beginnings of the world, the remedies of his mercy destined to renew mortals, announcing to the serpent the future seed of the woman who, by his power, would crush the uplifted arrogance of that guilty head: namely, Christ, God [Col. 0323B] and man, destined to come in the flesh, signifying that, born of a Virgin, he would condemn the violator of human descent through an undefiled birth.

So Leo.

Christ, then, is that blessed seed of the woman who crushed the head—that is, the arrogance and pride—of the most cunning serpent, and prevented him from extending the boundaries of his dominion farther, so that he would rule only over the impious, earthly, and sinful, who, wrapped in the foulness and filth of this world, have a taste for nothing but earth and flesh.

From this it can now be clearly understood that the sentence by which the Lord cursed the serpent deprived the devil of none of his uprightness. Nor do the words “You shall walk upon your breast” signify that he had previously been upright, as Abbot Serenus seems to have understood. Rather, because he had wished to raise himself above all human beings and rule over them, he was thrown down and cast upon the earth; and it was said to him:

> “You shall walk upon your breast, and, like those animals that feed and live upon the earth, you too [Col. 0323C] shall eat nothing but earth all the days of your life.”

## Coll. 8, chapter 17, and Coll. 13, chapter 12

“That two angels—that is, a good one and an evil one—are attached to each of us, Scripture testifies,” and so forth.

(Annot. 14.) This opinion concerning the two angels assigned to each of us, one for protection and the other for exercise, is taken from a very ancient book called *The Shepherd*, which they assert was dictated by Hermas, the disciple whom the Apostle Paul mentions on one occasion. Origen also defended the same opinion in Homily 35 on Luke.

As for the authority of that book entitled *The Shepherd*, although it is sometimes cited as canonical by Athanasius, Theodoret, and others, St. Jerome nevertheless rejected it among the apocrypha in the *Galeate Prologue*, as did Pope Gelasius at a council of seventy bishops. Nor should Origen’s authority influence us, since he was frequently mistaken in many matters.

St. Prosper likewise rejects as false this very opinion concerning two angels, one evil and the other good, in his work published [Col. 0323D] against the Thirteenth Collation. Nor is this surprising. It was neither necessary nor fitting that two angels be assigned to us. Demons do not need any incitement in order to trouble us or incite us to sin, since they are themselves inclined to do so by the inclination of their perverted nature.

If God had also assigned an evil angel to us for exercise, he would plainly seem to be the author of sin, supplying us with the author, fuel, or cause of sin.

Moreover, that Satan who is said to have tempted St. Job was not specially assigned to him by God for exercise, as Abbot Serenus supposes. Rather, it is credible that he was that dragon and ancient serpent of whom John speaks in the Apocalypse, who is called the devil and Satan, who deceives the whole world, who walks about and traverses the four [Col. 0324A] corners of the earth (Rev. XII), who once, together with his angels, fought in heaven against Michael and the angels at the very beginning of his creation, but did not prevail; instead, he was cast down and thrown to the earth with his angels.

In the same way, the statement in Psalm CVIII, “Let the devil stand at his right hand,” does not mean that some particular evil spirit was assigned to Judas the betrayer and was continually at his right hand. It means that the demon—whom the preceding half-verse had called “the sinner” in the words “Appoint a sinner over him”—would prevail over Judas.

Thus “a sinner,” or Satan, was appointed over him, because he was handed over to the author of all crimes, and that author received power and dominion over him.

The meaning of the second half-verse is therefore the same: “Let the devil stand at his right hand.” The Chaldean Paraphrase reads, “Let the devil stand over his right hand,” a translation also admitted by the Hebrew truth. That is:

> The demon will prevail against him by force and will dominate him, because he will prevail over his right hand.

[Col. 0324B] For it is common in divine Scripture to understand by the right hand a person’s supreme power and strength.

God therefore gave us one guardian angel, as it were a nurse and tutor. But evil spirits, often many and various, trouble us; the ancient Satan and serpent uses them as satellites to attack us. Once they have overcome us, he is said to have been appointed over us and to stand at our right hand—that is, over our right hand.

## Coll. 8, chapter 12

“By no means should we believe that spiritual beings can have carnal intercourse with women. For if this could ever literally happen, how would it be that it does not also happen now, either frequently or rarely, and that we do not likewise see some persons born of women through the conception of demons, without the seed or intercourse of a man—especially since it is clear that demons take great pleasure in the filth of lust, which they would undoubtedly prefer to practice through themselves rather than through human beings, [Col. 0324C] if this could in any way be accomplished?””

(Annot. 15.) St. Augustine, in Book XV of *The City of God*, chapter 23, holds an opinion concerning the intercourse of unclean spirits with human beings contrary to what Abbot Serenus says here:

> Sacred Scripture most truly testifies that angels appeared to human beings in bodies that could not only be seen but also touched. Since it is widely reported—and many affirm that they have experienced it themselves or heard it from those who experienced it, whose testimony ought not to be doubted—that Silvans and Fauns, commonly called Incubi, have often behaved wickedly toward women and desired and accomplished intercourse with them, and that certain demons, whom the Gauls call *Dusii*, continually attempt and accomplish this impurity, they assert that there are so many such cases that to deny it seems shameless.

There also exists a decretal letter of Innocent VIII against the heresy of women who practice sorcery, in which these words are read:

> It has come to our ears, not without great distress, that many persons of both [Col. 0324D] sexes, forgetful of their own salvation and straying from the Catholic faith, have intercourse with demons, incubi, and succubi. Therefore, wishing to prevent the stain of this heretical depravity from spreading its poisons to the ruin of souls, and desiring to provide suitable remedies as our office requires, we decree that the inquisitors appointed by us carry out the proper duty of inquiring into such persons.

Some excuse Abbot Serenus by saying that he did not wish to deny that demons can have intercourse with human beings, but only that this cannot occur naturally and in the ordinary manner of animals—that is, by communicating semen from their own substance.

For, according to Augustine’s testimony, demons can not only have intercourse with women but also beget offspring and truly generate human beings. Yet they do not do so by the power of their own semen, since they have none of their own, being incorporeal; rather, they do so by means of another’s semen, which they shamefully receive by acting as succubi toward men and, after receiving it, [Col. 0325A] infuse into women by acting as incubi. Thus, according to Blessed Augustine’s opinion in Book III *On the Trinity*, chapter 8, the one born from such a generation is not the son of a demon but of a man.

Those who excuse Abbot Serenus in this way seem to have read *carnaliter* (“carnally”) as *naturaliter* (“naturally”), although all the manuscript codices that we have so far been able to see read *carnaliter*.

He then adds that demons take the greatest pleasure in the filth of lust and that they would prefer to practice it through themselves rather than through human beings, if this could in any way happen. This also does not seem acceptable to us.

Demons do not delight in bodily pleasures and allurements for their own sake, as though these were suited to their nature, but because experience and long familiarity with human affairs have taught them that our nature is so perverse and filthy that, once entangled in such desires, it cannot escape.

No vice makes human beings so effeminate and soft as luxury; none equally dulls, clouds, and obscures the sharpness of the mind. Reason is absorbed by [Col. 0325B] sexual pleasures, understanding is darkened, the senses are perverted, and all the powers of body and soul are bound, weakened, and broken. Thus a person perceives nothing further of the things that belong to God. For that blindness and dullness of mind removes not only all taste, sweetness, and delight in spiritual things, but even their knowledge.

Abbot Serenus rightly reproves those who asserted that women were loved by us and by the blessed angels and violated through shameful unions, referring to the statement in Genesis, chapter VI: “When the sons of God saw that the daughters of men were beautiful,” and so forth.

For it is impossible that those carnal minds, having despised the divine love in which they had once been confirmed through God’s grace, should have lowered themselves to the impure lust of women, changing their angelic nature into human form according to the stories of the poets’ *Metamorphoses*.

This is expressly demonstrated by Blessed Chrysostom, Homily 22 on Genesis; Augustine, Book XV of *The City of God*, chapter 23, and *Questions on Genesis*, question 3; and Philastrius, [Col. 0325C] bishop of Brescia, chapter 108 of his *Catalogue Against Heresies*.

## Col. 9, chapter 19

“The second petition of the purest mind eagerly desires the kingdom of its Father to come at once—namely, that kingdom which, at the appointed time, has been generally promised to all the perfect and to the sons of God, in which Christ says to them: ‘Come, you blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.’ Desiring and awaiting it with eyes, as it were, fixed and intent upon it, the mind says to him: ‘Your kingdom come.’ For by the testimony of its conscience it knows that, when it appears, it will immediately become a sharer in it.”

(Annot. 16.) “The Spirit himself,” says the Apostle in Romans, chapter VIII, “bears witness to our spirit that we are children of God; and if children, then heirs—heirs indeed of God, and joint heirs with Christ.” And St. John says in his First Letter, chapter V: “Whoever believes has the testimony of God within himself.”

Although this testimony is not so certain or evident [Col. 0325D] that one may not doubt it—for none of us, unless through divine revelation, can know with certainty whether he is worthy of love or hatred, and no one can determine with certainty that he will become an heir of heavenly and everlasting reward—the divine Spirit nevertheless suggests such testimony to us that we ought to trust confidently in God’s goodness, and that our own conscience, on account of our fellowship in faith, our common bond of charity, and the communication of Christ’s merits applied to us in the sacraments, may dare to expect the blessings of salvation and eternal life with firm confidence.

Thus Christian hope is commonly defined by theologians: it is a virtue infused by God, through which the blessings of our salvation and eternal life are awaited with firm confidence.

We have noted these matters so that no one may suppose that Abbot Isaac, in these words, intended to affirm with the sectarians of our own time that each of us ought [Col. 0326A] to determine with certainty and infallibly within himself that he will attain eternal life.

For sacred Scripture frequently protests against this opinion. Ecclesiasticus warns us not to call anyone blessed before death (Eccles. III). The Apostle Paul wants us to fear lest we fall away from the olive tree (Rom. II), and says, “Let him who stands take heed lest he fall” (1 Cor. X). He therefore also exhorts us to work out our salvation with fear and trembling (Phil. II).

For who knows whether he will persevere in the progress of righteousness to the end? Unless he is made certain of this by revelation from the one who, through a just and hidden judgment, does not instruct everyone concerning it, says Augustine in Book II *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 13, and *On Rebuke and Grace*, chapter 13, and again in Book II of *The City of God*, chapter 11.

## Col. 9, chapter 24

“You see, therefore, what kind of pattern and form of prayer has been proposed to us by the one who is to be entreated through it: it contains no petition for riches, no remembrance of dignities, no request for power or strength, [Col. 0326B] no mention of bodily health or temporal life. For the creator of eternal things does not wish anything perishable, worthless, or temporal to be implored from him.”

(Annot. 17.) Abbot Isaac reproves those who put higher and spiritual goods in a secondary place and, neglecting them, ask God for temporal things.

Although temporal and perishable goods should also be expected and requested from God, our concern for them ought to be minimal. For Christ does not warn us without reason to seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, promising that the other things will then be added to us.

That this was the opinion of this abbot can be clearly observed from the words that follow. He adds:

> Therefore, whoever, having neglected these everlasting petitions, prefers to ask him for something transitory and perishable, inflicts the greatest injury upon his magnificence and generosity and, through the worthlessness of his prayer, incurs the displeasure [Col. 0326C] rather than the favor of his judge.

## Col. 9, chapter 34

“If all grounds for being heard fail us completely, at least let the persistence of importunity encourage us; and this lies within the power of anyone who wishes, without any difficulty of merit or labor.”

(Annot. 18.) The assistance of divine grace is not excluded. For just as without it we cannot pray, so neither can we be constant or importunate in prayer. Therefore, when Abbot Isaac says that this persistence of importunity lies within the power of anyone who wishes, this must be understood of those whom the indwelling Holy Spirit continually governs and leads, and in whom the will to act and pray well has been strengthened through long practice. Let the reader consult the third annotation.

## Col. 10, chapter 2

“Within the region of Egypt this custom is preserved by ancient tradition: after the day of Epiphany has been completed—which the priests of that [Col. 0326D] province define as the day both of the Lord’s baptism and of his birth according to the flesh, and for that reason celebrate the solemnity of this mystery not in two separate observances, as in the western provinces, but under a single festival of this day—the letters of the Alexandrian pontiff,” and so forth.

(Annot. 19.) The statement enclosed in this parenthesis is doubtful, obscure, and difficult to explain. Its obscurity is caused chiefly by the disjunctive conjunction *vel* (“or”), which seems here to have to be understood as copulative (“and”). The meaning would then be that the Egyptian priests appear to have accepted the opinion that Christ our Redeemer was born and baptized on the same day on which he was manifested to the Magi who came from Persia.

For ancient opinions differ on this matter. Although the view has by now gained sufficient acceptance among Christians that the Lord was worshiped by the Magi on the same day and was baptized after completing the thirtieth [Col. 0327A] year of his age, opinions concerning his Nativity are uncertain and varied (Epiphanius, heresy 51; Origen, Homily 8 *On Various Matters*, vol. II; Ambrose, Sermon 22; and Jansenius, *Evangelical Harmony*). We leave their examination to others.

As for the celebration of these festivals, it is clear from the Council of Florence that there was once controversy in the Church, on the occasion of the Armenians, concerning the time at which they ought chiefly to be celebrated. Pope Eugenius IV settled this controversy in the decree appended to the Council of Florence.

For in chapter 8 of that constitution, by apostolic authority, he commands the Armenians to adopt and follow the custom of the Roman Church, which agrees with the testimonies of the holy Fathers and with the custom of all the other Churches, both Greek and Latin; and to celebrate with festive and solemn remembrance:

- the feast of the Annunciation of the Virgin Mother of God on March 25;
- the Nativity of St. John the Baptist on June 24;
- the Nativity of Christ on December 25;
- the Circumcision [Col. 0327B] on January 1;
- the Epiphany on January 6; and
- the Purification on February 2.

## Col. 13, chapter 8

“When God observes in us the beginning of some good will, he immediately enlightens and strengthens it and urges it toward salvation, granting it increase—whether he himself planted it or saw it emerge through our effort,” and so forth.

### (Annot. 20.)

This opinion of Abbot Chaeremon is wholly heretical; for that reason, the prudent reader should pass it over through to the end of the conference. For much is brought forward here to exalt the powers of free choice and to diminish the necessity of divine assistance. Dionysius Carthusianus therefore deliberately omitted these points in his *Paraphrase* and substituted in their place the correct, orthodox, and catholic doctrine concerning grace and human free choice.

To state the whole matter briefly, this is Abbot Chaeremon’s [Col. 0327C] opinion: some things are rightly accomplished by human beings through the prior intervention and prompting of divine grace; others, however, arise solely from the direction of nature, with God’s assistance excluded—although God himself completes what has been begun and initiated. After presenting this opinion near the end of the eighth chapter in the words annotated here, he then continues and confirms it in chapter nine; afterward, in chapters eleven, twelve, thirteen, fourteen, fifteen, and seventeen, he strengthens it with arguments drawn from Sacred Scripture, various examples, and finally reason itself.

But Blessed Prosper, bishop of Riez, refuted this error in a work of his own, entitled *Against the Collator*. The dispute concerning grace and free choice is intricate and difficult because of the conflicting and opposed heresies, one of which is more unjust toward free choice and the other toward the grace of Christ. It is therefore extremely difficult to attain the middle ground and the truth itself. [Col. 0327D] To this is added the fact that divine Scripture itself sometimes so exalts the powers of free choice that it seems to detract greatly from grace, while at other times it appears to refer everything to grace, excluding free choice. Yet the matter is otherwise. For the Holy Spirit, foreseeing both heresies—the one concerning grace, arising among the Pelagians, and the other concerning nature, arising among the Manichaeans—willed to temper his speech in the divine writings in such a way that, because of both errors, he might appear in one place to refer everything to grace and in another to free choice: namely, so that we might thereby understand that we are **συνεργούς** (*synergous*), that is, cooperators with the grace of God.

For grace and free choice act together, and those passages of Sacred Scripture that appear to conflict with one another are easily brought into harmony if we join the act and effort of our will to God’s assistance—yet in such a way that we attribute the first and more important parts to God himself. For he first anticipates every movement of a good will within us [Col. 0328A] and makes willing people out of those who are unwilling, resistant, and rebellious—something that does not lie within our own powers.

Our will, by which we choose and reject, has been so corrupted by the sin and disobedience of the first human beings that, relying on its natural resources, it cannot will anything, much less accomplish anything, that contributes to salvation unless it has first been aroused and assisted by God’s gratuitous gift. Then, once it has been freed and healed through grace, it cannot persist and advance in what is good and right unless it is supported at every moment by the resources of divine grace. For it is God who works in us both to will and to accomplish according to his good pleasure (Philippians 1).

The royal prophet David likewise acknowledges this in Psalm 29, when he says: “In my prosperity I said, ‘I shall never be moved.’ Lord, by your favor you had established strength for my honor; you hid your face from me, and I was troubled.”

What we ourselves do in the work of our justification is therefore very little, so that almost everything must be ascribed to God. For he first calls and moves us; then [Col. 0328B] he brings it about that we will; and finally he completes and perfects our will.

In the first and third stages, therefore, nothing can be attributed to our freedom, because just as God’s grace first invites us to what is good, so too it alone perfects our will. But in the middle stage—namely, in consent, or, so to speak, in the act of willing—our will cooperates with grace. Even here, however, grace holds the most important and primary role, while our will has a secondary one. For this reason, divine grace is praised more frequently and more extensively in the divine writings than our will, since from grace come the principal strength and the power to accomplish; and since it was advantageous for this to happen for our sake, namely, to remove all arrogance from our minds.

“For who makes you different, O human being? And what do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Corinthians 4). And elsewhere: “No one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Corinthians 11). Again, in 2 Corinthians 3: “We are not sufficient [Col. 0328C] to think anything from ourselves, as though from ourselves, but all our sufficiency is from God.”

No one, therefore, can in any way prepare himself for grace or for any good by means of a good thought, without the singular gift and grace of God himself. For Blessed Augustine, in Book I, chapter 19, of *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, rightly observes that Christ did not say that no one can come to him unless the Father “led” him, but unless he “drew” him (Canon 15). He thereby shows that, before God’s prevenient action, no one wishes to go; and consequently no one prepares himself. For whoever prepares himself certainly wishes to go.

Hence David also says in Psalm 76: “And I said, ‘Now I have begun; this is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High.’” Likewise Isaiah, in chapter 65, speaking in the person of God: “I was found by those who were not seeking me; I openly appeared to those who were not asking about me.” Thus Jeremiah says in Lamentations, chapter 5: “Turn us back to you, Lord, and we shall be converted.” To be converted is undoubtedly to be prepared for salvation and grace; and by these words the prophet intimates that this preparation must be expected from God.

[Col. 0328D] Finally, Saint Ezekiel says in chapter 36: “It is not for your sake that I will act, house of Israel, but for the sake of my name.”

God therefore finds nothing in any mortal by which he is moved to call that person to salvation, as Abbot Chaeremon holds concerning Zacchaeus and the thief. Rather, whatever he does concerning a human being, he grants out of his sheer mercy and grace to those who are undeserving and unworthy.

This can be demonstrated as clearly as daylight not only from the divine writings but also from the constant teaching of the ancient and orthodox Fathers. For at the Council of Arausio, which was convened and celebrated somewhat later, in the time of Cassian, and which Pope Leo convened on account of this error, the Fathers deny that anyone can invoke the grace of God without grace:

“If anyone says that the grace of God can be conferred through human invocation, but does not acknowledge that grace itself causes us to invoke it, he contradicts the prophet Isaiah and the Apostle, who says the same thing: ‘I was found by those who were not seeking me; [Col. 0329A] I openly appeared to those who were not asking about me’” (Canon 3).

Again, in canon 4 of that council and in the following canons, the opposing position is expressly condemned as heretical and false, as it were expressly, in Augustine’s own words.

After the teaching of Pelagius had been rejected by the Church—according to which he held that human beings could will and perform every good work without the grace of God, unless by the name “grace” one understood free choice, the law, teaching, correction, and similar external aids—certain others arose in Gaul, especially around Massilia. They are called the remnants of the Pelagians. Attempting to pursue a kind of middle path between the orthodox doctrine of the Church and the Pelagian error, they taught that human beings could not indeed attain true righteousness without God’s assistance; nevertheless, they said that God offered and proposed salvation and faith to everyone, requiring and awaiting nothing else than the readiness of our will.

They held that each person could, by the powers of free choice, will to believe and will to be healed, although it belonged to God to [Col. 0329B] complete and perfect this will.

These people therefore compared God’s grace to a public fountain, from which anyone who wished could draw; or to the sun, which illuminates everyone, provided that they open their eyes and offer no other obstruction; or to a most generous physician, prepared to heal all who wished, free of charge.

Thus taught a certain Faustus, bishop of Gaul, and many others, among whom this Abbot Chaeremon must also be numbered.

Against this error Blessed Prosper wrote in Book I, chapter 5, of *On the Calling of the Nations*. He also wrote against it in his *Works Against the Collator*, in his responses to the Vincentian objections, in his *Replies to the Chapters of the Gauls*, and elsewhere. He wrote on this subject as well in a letter to Augustine that is found in volume VII of Augustine’s works; attached to it is a letter of the same subject by Saint Hilary of Arles to that same Augustine.

On account of this same error, Gelasius, the Pope, appears to have listed the works of John Cassian among the apocrypha at the council of seventy bishops, as he did the books of Faustus, bishop of Gaul. He praises the writings of Blessed [Col. 0329C] Augustine and Prosper, in which this error was refuted.

To these should be added Saint Fulgentius, *On the Incarnation and the Grace of Christ*, chapters 13, 17, 18, and following; Gregory, *Homily 9 on Ezekiel*; Bernard, *On Grace and Free Choice*; Innocent I, the letter to the Council of Carthage, which is Letter 91 among Augustine’s letters; Celestine I, in his letter to the bishops of Gaul, where he says that those who thought or wrote contrary to Blessed Augustine’s opinion on this matter ought to be restrained; Saint Jerome, writing against Pelagius; and finally Blessed Augustine, in very many passages, especially in *On Grace and Free Choice*, chapters 14 and 17; Book I of *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, the final chapter; Book II, chapters 8–10; Book IV of *Against Julian*, chapter 8; Letter 107 to Vitalis; and in the two books addressed to Prosper and Hilary—one *On the Predestination of the Saints*, the other *On the Gift of Perseverance*.

Also relevant here are those comparisons in Sacred Scripture by which our soul is described as resembling either mud or dry, waterless ground. Thus, after the royal Prophet had said that no one would be justified in God’s sight, [Col. 0329D] he added shortly afterward: “I stretched out my hands to you; my soul is like land without water before you” (Psalm 142).

If our soul is without water, that is, dry, then it can produce nothing. Again, if Jeremiah in chapter 18 and the Apostle in Romans 9 rightly compare the human soul to clay, then it can do nothing of itself; rather, it must await from the Lord not only the ability to act but also the preparation for action. Clay is not merely shaped by the potter into a clay vessel; it is also prepared, softened, and made ready by him.

What we have said briefly, insofar as the purpose of our undertaking requires, is sufficient. For the refutations of the arguments brought forward by this Chaeremon to weaken the necessity of divine assistance may be found in Saint Prosper, who treats and criticizes each of them at considerable length in his work *Against the Collator*.

### Column 17, chapter 8

**[Col. 0330A]**

It is better for you to bear the loss of this lie, or of a promise left unfulfilled—a loss which, once past, can neither itself be repeated nor of its own accord generate further sins—than to fall into that loss by which, as you say, the state of a more tepid life brings you a daily and unending loss.

### (Annotation 21)

It was not without reason that Dionysius the Carthusian omitted from his paraphrase what Abbot Joseph teaches in this eighth chapter and onward to the end of the Collation concerning the permissibility of lying. For Blessed Augustine, in his books *On Lying* and *Against Lying*, and elsewhere throughout his works, demonstrates with the strongest arguments that lying is permissible for no reason whatsoever; and all the other orthodox writers likewise adopt his opinion.

Origen, however, in his *Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians* and in Book VI of the *Stromata*, asserts that simulations and lies are permissible for Christians:

> “A man upon whom the necessity of lying has fallen should take care to use a lie occasionally [Col. 0330B] as a seasoning and medicine, so as to preserve its measure, and not exceed the limits within which Judith acted against Holofernes and conquered him by prudent simulation. Let him imitate Esther, who, after remaining silent for a long time, corrected the judgment of Artaxerxes concerning her people by revealing the truth; and above all the patriarch Jacob, whom we read to have obtained his father’s blessing by an artful lie.”

From this it is evident that, unless we have lied in such a way that some great benefit is sought for us from it, we must be judged as enemies of him who said, “I am the truth.” In the same book he approves Plato’s opinion in Book III of *The Republic*, where Plato says that a lie is unfitting and useless for God, but at times useful and necessary for human beings, so that they may use it like a medicine to procure great benefits or avoid great evils.

Again, in Book X of the *Stromata*, he adds that Peter and Paul engaged in a dispute at Antioch not in earnest but by simulation, so that by this kind of pretense they might bring Jews and Gentiles, who were divided among themselves over legal observances, back to concord [Col. 0330C].

This was also the opinion of Blessed Jerome in his letter to Saint Augustine and in his *Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians*. He teaches that hypocrisy may at times be necessary for good men, in imitation of many distinguished persons: among them Jehu, king of Israel, who, under the deceptive promise of worshiping Baal, killed the priests of Baal; David, who escaped danger to his life by feigning madness; Paul, who, by a simulated rebuke, reproached Peter, who was guilty of no fault, to terrify those who were inclined toward Judaism; and who circumcised Timothy in order to win Jews for Christ, and himself shaved his head at Cenchreae and presented an offering in Jerusalem.

Saint Chrysostom also appears to have shared Jerome’s view. At the end of the first book *On the Priesthood*, he asserts that frauds, tricks, and deceptions undertaken not from a desire to injure but for the sake of some great benefit are sometimes so necessary that certain people have suffered punishment because they did not employ them. He confirms this not only by the example of soldiers who deceive their enemies in war by various kinds of stratagems, and of physicians who use many devices to get the sick to take bitter medicines [Col. 0330D], but also by the authority of the Apostle Paul, whom he writes to have frequently employed this kind of simulation and by this means to have drawn many thousands of Jews to himself.

> “The power of deception is great, provided that it is not done with a deceitful intention. Moreover, whoever always proceeds along a straight road, never turning aside from it, often becomes the cause of very many evils and troubles even for one against whom he has constructed no stratagem.”

Likewise, in his *Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians*, he agrees with Blessed Jerome that Peter and Paul engaged in a simulated dispute, not a real one, for the benefit of the disciples and believers who were present, although they contended with complete harmony of mind. While Peter was reproved by Paul through a simulated rebuke because of the observance of legal requirements, Peter did not contradict him but, as though acknowledging his fault, remained silent. In this way the Jews and those who thought that the legal requirements had to be maintained might come to their senses and abstain from observing them [Col. 0331A].

The same opinion is supported by Theodoret, bishop of Heraclea; Eusebius, bishop of Emesa; Didymus of Alexandria; Apollinarius, bishop of Laodicea; Theodoret, bishop of Cyrus; Theophylact; and Oecumenius, in their commentaries on the Epistle to the Galatians. They further add that neither of the two apostles sinned by simulation, since it is permissible—indeed, sometimes necessary—to employ simulation from a pious desire to help.

Blessed Augustine, however, expressly condemns these assertions in his two books addressed to Consentius, one entitled *On Lying*, the other *Against Lying*. In his letter to Saint Jerome he grieves that Jerome had at some time defended this position (*Epistle* 8, chapter 3). He speaks as follows in that letter:

> “I have read certain writings said to be yours on the Epistles of Paul. When you wished to explain one of them, the Epistle to the Galatians, that passage came into your hands where the Apostle Peter is recalled from a pernicious simulation. There I am not a little grieved that you, such a man, undertook the defense of a lie. For it seems to me most disastrous to believe that those men through whom divine Scripture was delivered and written for us told any lies [Col. 0331B].
>
> “One question is whether a good man may at some time lie; another is whether the writer of the sacred Scriptures ought to have lied. Indeed, it is not another question, but no question at all. For if we once admit into so great a height of truth some well-intentioned lie, no part of those books will remain which, according to anyone’s judgment, could not by that most destructive rule be referred to the author’s purpose and office as a liar—whether the passage seemed difficult for morality or incredible for faith.
>
> “If the Apostle Paul was lying when, rebuking the Apostle Peter, he said, ‘If you, though a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how can you compel the Gentiles to Judaize?’—and if it seemed right to Paul that Peter had done what he himself said and wrote that Peter had not done rightly—what shall we answer when perverse men arise?” and so forth.

Augustine continues this discussion in his ninth letter to the same Jerome, chapters 3 and 4. Peter, therefore, was reproved by Paul not fictitiously or by simulation, but truly and justly, because that simulation [Col. 0331C], undertaken for the salvation of the Jews, was turning into the scandal and ruin of the Gentiles and was leading them into the error of supposing that the legal rites had to be observed by everyone.

Nevertheless, one must admit that Saint Augustine sometimes wrote more harshly about Peter, when he said that Peter wished, through a superstitious and perverse simulation, to impose the burdens of the law upon the Gentiles, and when he included that very simulation among Peter’s serious crimes, as may be seen in his *Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians* and in *On Christian Combat*, chapter 30.

Furthermore, that lies are neither permissible nor have ever been permissible, not even in the time of the Old Testament—as Abbot Germanus appears to have thought in chapter 18 of this Collation—the Scriptures plainly teach in Exodus 23:

> “You shall not accept a lying report,” says the Lord, “nor shall you join your hand with the wicked to give false testimony.”

A little later:

> “You shall flee from lying.”

Again, the royal prophet says in Psalm 5:

> “You hate all who work iniquity; you will destroy all who speak lies.”

[Col. 0331D] The Wise Man likewise says in Proverbs, chapter 20:

> “The bread of lying is sweet to a man, but afterward his mouth will be filled with gravel.”

And in the Book of Wisdom, chapter 1:

> “The mouth that lies kills the soul.”

Finally, Ecclesiasticus, chapter 17:

> “Do not desire to utter any lie.”

Blessed Augustine discusses this opinion at greatest length in those two books addressed to Consentius. There he shows that lying is impermissible against the Priscillianists—not for the preservation of chastity, not for the protection of temporal life, and not for any reason whatsoever. Their maxim was: “Swear, perjure yourself, but do not reveal the secret.”

Blessed John the Anchorite, that great prophet mentioned by Palladius in chapter 43 of the *Lausiac History*, likewise teaches that neither a small nor a great lie is to be fabricated, even to preserve one’s humility—which Abbot Joseph permits in chapters 21 and 22 of this Collation—because every lie is from the evil one, as is said in John 8.

Saint Justin also says in his *Second Apology* that Christians would rather die than lie even once. Ambrose, in Book II of his *Commentary on Luke*, [Col. 0332A] near the beginning, says:

> “The mouth of the righteous knows no lie.”

Blessed Jerome, in his *First Apology against Rufinus*, rebukes the Origenists because of the passage cited above from Book VI of the *Stromata*. To this may be added Blessed Gregory, *Moralia* XVIII, chapter 2, where he says that even the lightest lies are sins. Blessed Isidore, in his *Synonyms*, likewise declares that every kind of lying must be avoided.

Pope Innocent III, in the *Decretals*, title *On Usury*, chapter *Super eo*, firmly asserts that the words of the divine commandment prohibit anyone from lying even to preserve another person’s life. All the schools of theologians subscribe to this papal ruling, writing in Book III of the *Sentences*, distinctions 37 and 38, that every lie is a sin, and that every simulation and deception—whether harmful or well-intentioned—is a vice contrary to truth and belongs to the crime of lying. For whether a person lies by speech or by any other act, from a desire either to injure or to help, he is a liar, and every lie is a sin.

Aristotle likewise says in Book IV of the *Ethics*, chapter 7 [Col. 0332B]:

> “A lie is in itself something small and to be avoided, whereas truth is wholly good and praiseworthy.”

If a lie is evil and blameworthy in itself, then no purpose and no circumstance can make it good—not even when it is undertaken for the sake of humility, chastity, or safety. Theft, robbery, and similar sins do not cease to be sins merely because they are directed toward helping one’s neighbors or toward an honorable and useful end, since they contain wickedness in their very nature and, as the philosophers say, have wickedness folded into them.

As for what Cassian wrote in this Collation according to the opinion of Abbot Joseph, we may resolve the whole matter briefly by answering, in accordance with Saint Augustine’s judgment, that the large number of lies which seem to be contained in the divine Scriptures can be divided into two classes. In the first class are those who did not in fact lie, although they may appear to have done so.

Abbot Joseph first errs [Col. 0332C] in confusing a change of pledge or promise with lying. His position is that, just as it is permissible to change one’s plan and intention when something better and sounder occurs to us or is suggested to us, so it is also permissible to lie.

A pledge—even one confirmed by an oath—may indeed be changed and corrected without danger of lying, especially when it was made rashly and imprudently. Hence Blessed Isidore rightly advises that faith in evil promises should be withdrawn, as is stated in *Gratian*, 22, question 4, chapter *In malis*.

Accordingly, Abbot Joseph rightly says in chapter 8 of this Collation:

> “A rash decision may be changed, honorably and even praiseworthily, if it passes over to the more salutary side. Nor should it be considered a violation of constancy whenever a faulty promise is corrected; rather, it is a correction of rashness.”

He confirms this afterward by arguments and examples drawn from divine Scripture and elsewhere, in chapters 9, 14, and 27.

Yet the correction of a pledge or agreement is not a lie, as he himself supposed. Whoever promises something, if he has the intention [Col. 0332D] of carrying out what he promises, does not lie when he makes the promise, because he says nothing other than what he intends to do. If he does not fulfill what he promised, he does indeed seem to violate faith, because he has changed his plan and undertaking; nevertheless, this correction and change may be excused for two reasons.

First, if he promised something impermissible, or something whose execution is contrary to divine law. Whoever sins by making a promise does well to correct that promise. Thus David, after rashly swearing that he would kill Nabal, withdrew his decision and oath when his wife pleaded with and rebuked him. He understood that he ought not to have sworn to do what he later saw that he ought not to do. Blessed Augustine properly notes this in *Against Lying*, chapter 9.

Second, the correction may be excused if the circumstances and conditions of the matter itself have changed. As Seneca rightly says in Book IV of *On Benefits*, chapters 34 and 35, a person is bound to do what he promised if everything remains unchanged. Otherwise, he was not a liar in making the promise, because he promised what he had in mind [Col. 0333A]; nor was he unfaithful in failing to fulfill it, because the same conditions no longer exist.

In this way the Apostle Paul must be defended against the charge of lying because he did not go to Corinth, although he had promised that he would go there; he was prevented from going by obstacles that arose afterward, as he says in 2 Corinthians 1.

The threats by which God in Scripture threatened Hezekiah with death, the Ninevites with overthrow and destruction, and sinners with various punishments must be understood in the same way. We read that he relaxed and withdrew these threats in view of the repentance that followed. Abbot Joseph cites all these examples in chapter 15 of this Collation to support his opinion and establish that lies are permissible—as though God, who is the first and infallible truth, could be believed to have lied at some time without enormous blasphemy.

The author therefore failed to distinguish between a threat and an assertion, and likewise between a lie and a change of intention. An example of the latter is found in the angels whom Moses says at first refused to enter Lot’s house, but afterward, moved by his prayers, changed their decision [Col. 0333B] (Genesis 19).

Moreover, when in chapter 8 he considers all simulations and fictions to be lies, and asserts that the apostles themselves sometimes used lies, this too is false. Although Blessed Peter, as we said above, used simulation when, for the sake of the Jews, he distinguished foods and observed certain similar legal precepts, he must not for that reason be thought to have lied.

> “We do not lie unless we intend something false,” says Augustine (*Book II, Questions on the Gospels*, chapter 51), “nor is everything that we fashion a lie, but only when we fashion something that signifies nothing. When our fiction refers to some true meaning, it is not a lie but a figure of truth.”

He offers a similar argument from figurative expressions such as metaphors, irony, hyperbole, and antiphrasis. In these, something is fashioned not in order to assert it as true, but to present it as a figure of something else that we wish to assert.

In this way [Col. 0333C] Christ in the Gospel pretended that he was going farther, because he shaped his movement as though he intended to travel farther. This was either to signify that he was still far from their faith, as Gregory holds (*Homily 23 on the Gospels*), or because, although he was about to depart from them and go up into heaven, he was in a certain manner detained on earth by their hospitality, as Augustine explains in Book II, the final chapter, of his *Questions on the Gospels*, and in chapter 13 of *Against Lying*.

Peter’s simulation was of the same kind: he acted as a Jew in those Jewish observances, not because he wished to be or to be regarded as a Jew, but so that the Jews would not be offended if he had disregarded the burdens of the law together with the Gentiles.

The Apostle Paul likewise adopted a similar simulation when he became a Jew to the Jews, weak to the weak, and to those without the law as though without the law, becoming all things to all people in order to win them all. According to Blessed Augustine (*Letter 9 to Jerome*), these words were spoken from compassionate mercy, not from deceptive simulation.

> “It is like a sick person ministering to the sick—not by falsely claiming to have a fever, but by compassionately considering [Col. 0333D] how he would wish to be ministered to if he himself were sick.”

Paul had indeed been a Jew, but after becoming a Christian he had not abandoned the sacraments of the Jews, which that people had received appropriately and at the lawful time. Therefore, although he was already Christ’s apostle, he undertook to celebrate them, so as to teach that it was not harmful for those who wished to preserve them—as they had received them from their parents through the law—even after they had believed in Christ. They were not, however, to place their hope of salvation in them, since through the Lord Jesus the salvation signified by those sacraments had arrived.

Peter was therefore not corrected because he observed the traditions of his fathers. If he wished to do so, he would act neither deceitfully nor improperly. He was corrected because he was compelling the Gentiles to Judaize. That could not have happened unless he acted as though those observances were still necessary for salvation even after the Lord’s coming, a position from which the truth had vigorously dissuaded through the Apostle Paul.

Peter himself was not ignorant of this [Col. 0334A]; he acted as he did because he feared those who belonged to the circumcision.

Thus far Augustine.

He develops the same opinion further in chapters 12 and 13 of *Against Lying*, explaining many similar Gospel passages that appear to support lying. Among these must be counted the action of the Apostle Paul which Abbot Joseph emphasizes in chapter 20 of this Collation: Paul was ordered by the Apostle James and the elders of the Church to observe the Mosaic rites in Jerusalem, lest he appear to despise or reject the law.

In this action the Apostle did not employ a wicked simulation. Rather, he wished to show that he was genuinely zealous for the law, and that he did not hold an erroneous or harmful opinion about it. He intended to show that its observance was free for those who had converted from Judaism, but was by no means to be imposed upon the Gentiles.

For this reason Blessed Augustine, in *On Lying*, chapter 5, excuses the same Apostle from the suspicion of simulation that might be imputed to him because of Timothy’s circumcision and certain other Jewish rites which he observed. He asserts that Paul [Col. 0334B] did this from the freedom of his own judgment, by which he preached that circumcision benefited neither Gentiles nor harmed Jews:

> “Therefore Timothy, although he had been called while uncircumcised, nevertheless, because he was born of a Jewish mother and ought to show his relatives, in order to win them, that he had not adopted the Christian discipline so as to detest those sacraments belonging to the old law, was circumcised by the Apostle. In this way Paul demonstrated to the Jews that the Gentiles did not reject those rites because they were evil or because their fathers had observed them wickedly, but because they were no longer necessary for salvation after the coming of so great a sacrament, which the whole of that ancient Scripture had been bringing forth through prophetic expressions for so many ages.”

The matters brought forward there from chapter 17 of the Acts of the Apostles, or from the Epistles to the Romans and Corinthians, are of less importance. Although the Apostle says and concedes many things from an impulse of mercy, there is nothing in them for which he can rightly be charged with deceptive simulation or lying.

[Col. 0334C] All military stratagems, military ambushes, and the other simulations employed by physicians and judges may be referred to the same category. Once every charge of falsehood has been removed, they consist solely in concealing the truth.

In the judgment of Solomon in 1 Kings 3, which Abbot Joseph cites in chapter 25 to establish the permission to lie, there is no lie. Nor is there any lie in the words spoken by Joseph the patriarch to his brothers in Genesis 42: he spoke not so much by asserting as by investigating and testing.

Nor did those who are described as speaking figuratively, mystically, and prophetically lie. We have an example of this kind of speech in the patriarch Jacob, in the words, “I am Esau, your firstborn.”

> “This is not a lie,” says Augustine in chapter 50 of *Against Lying*, “but a mystery. If we call these things lies, then all parables and all figures used to signify whatever things—expressions that are not to be taken literally, but in which one thing is understood through another—will also be called lies. God forbid that this should ever happen.”

Augustine develops the same point [Col. 0334D] in *Questions on Genesis*, question 74; Ambrose in Book II of *On Jacob*, chapter 2; and Innocent in the chapter *Gaudemus*, title *On Divorce*.

It is also probable that Jacob himself was not unaware that, according to divine providence—which had chosen him for the birthright—he was truly the firstborn and had rightly been placed before his brother. He could have learned this from his mother, who had received a divine revelation of the mystery.

Abbot Joseph therefore speaks incorrectly in chapters 12 and 17 of this Collation when he asserts that the patriarch Jacob not only incurred no condemnation or reproach for his lie, but was even enriched with the inheritance of perpetual blessing.

As for David, who feigned madness in 1 Samuel 21, there is no doubt that here too, as elsewhere, he expressed a type and figure of Christ.

Those who affirm something true while also keeping silent about something else that is true through a useful silence likewise belong to this first class of those who did not lie [Col. 0335A]. Blessed Augustine clearly teaches this in his commentary on Psalm 5, when explaining the words, “You will destroy all who speak lies”:

> “Let no one suppose that a perfect and spiritual person ought to lie for the sake of this temporal life, in whose death the soul—whether his own or another’s—is not killed. But because lying is one thing and concealing the truth another, and because saying what is false is one thing and remaining silent about what is true another, if someone does not wish to betray a person to visible death, he ought to be prepared to conceal the truth, not to speak falsely, so that he may neither betray nor lie and thus kill his own soul for another’s body.”

In this way the patriarch Abraham, in Genesis 12, did not lie when he said that Sarah was his sister; he spoke the truth, but concealed a certain other truth. For she was his sister not by the same mother but by the same father, as Scripture says.

Some more recent writers, including Cajetan in his commentary on Genesis and Dominic Soto, Book II *On Justice and Law*, question [Col. 0335B] 3, article 8, understand this literally, as though Sarah were not Abraham’s uterine sister, born of the same mother, but had been born of the same father.
