This interpretation, however, is opposed by Josephus, Book I of the *Antiquities*, chapter 14; Saint Jerome in his *Questions on Genesis*, where he explains chapter 11; and Augustine in Book XVI of *The City of God*, chapter 19, and Book XXII of *Against Faustus*, chapter 35. They say that Sarah was not Abraham’s sister in the strict sense, but the daughter of his brother.

For in Genesis 11, after Moses had said that Abraham and Nahor took wives—Abraham Sarai and Nahor Milcah—he immediately adds that Milcah and Jeschah were daughters of Aram, the brother of Abraham and Nahor. Saint Jerome asserts that Jeschah was Sarah; for it is not credible that Scripture would give the name of Milcah’s father but not Sarah’s. Saint Augustine holds this view in Book XVI of *The City of God*, chapter 12.

Moreover, nature utterly rejects taking one’s own sister as a wife, to such an extent that in Leviticus 20 the Lord commanded that the man who took as wife a sister, whether by father or by mother, should be put to death.

It is familiar in divine [Col. 0335C] Scripture to call grandfathers “fathers,” grandchildren “sons,” and blood relatives “brothers.” Thus, in Daniel 5, Nebuchadnezzar is called the father of Belshazzar, although he was his grandfather, as Saint Jerome writes in his commentary on that passage. Likewise, in Genesis 13 Lot is called Abraham’s brother, although chapter 11 establishes that he was Abraham’s brother’s son.

Again, in the eighth chapter of the younger Tobias, the Book of Tobit says that Tobias took his sister as a wife, although she was not literally his sister.

Sarah must therefore be understood in the same sense to have been Abraham’s sister: she was his relative and the daughter of his brother.

> “Abraham concealed some truth,” says Augustine, “but he did not say something false, when he concealed that she was his wife and called her his sister.”

His son Isaac did the same, for we know that he too took a female relative as his wife.

As for what Abraham said in Genesis 22, when he was about to sacrifice his son:

> “Wait here with the donkey; I and the boy will go over there. After we have worshiped, we will return to you,”

Saint Ambrose [Col. 0335D], in Book I of *On Abraham*, chapter 8, explains this as an admission that Abraham lied by concealment, while also prophesying, as Caiaphas did when he prophesied without knowing it. Thus Ambrose thinks that the same words were a lie insofar as Abraham uttered them, but a prophecy insofar as they were directed by God.

In my judgment, however, Blessed Augustine is more correct. In Sermon 72 *On the Seasons* and in Book II of the *Retractions*, chapter 22, he denies that Abraham lied in these words:

> “He believed that God would immediately raise Isaac from the dead if he sacrificed him, and that he would therefore return with him to the servants, in accordance with what the Apostle says of him in the Epistle to the Hebrews: ‘By faith Abraham offered Isaac, considering that God was able to raise him even from the dead.’”

### The second class

In the second class, chapter 11, we place those about whom there can be no doubt that they lied: David before Achimelech the priest in 1 Samuel 21 [Col. 0336A]; King Hieu, or Jehu, before the priests of Baal in 2 Kings 10; Rahab on behalf of the Jewish spies in Joshua 1; Chusi before Absalom for the safety of King David in 2 Samuel 17; Judith before Holofernes in Judith 11; the Hebrew midwives in Exodus 1; Tamar in Genesis 38; and many others.

But their action and lie by no means establish that lies are permissible. Augustine says in Book II of *Against Lying*, chapter 9:

> “We must not transfer into our conduct everything we read that holy or righteous men did. Rather, from this too we must learn how far-reaching and how extensive is what the Apostle says: ‘Brothers, if someone is overtaken in any transgression, you who are spiritual should restore such a person.’”

These are instances in which people were overtaken and sinned because, for the moment, they did not see what ought to be done, or because the person who did see it was overcome. Sin is committed when the truth is hidden or weakness compels.

Although divine Scripture records these lies [Col. 0336B], it nowhere praises or approves them. We do indeed read that those who lied were sometimes praised and enriched by God with temporal goods. Nevertheless, it is in no way permissible to suppose that their deception or lie was rewarded or praised. Rather, what was rewarded was the piety, charity, and faith with which they embraced those for whom they were not afraid to lie. Blessed Augustine explains this at length and learnedly in *Against Lying*, chapters 14–17.

Therefore this Collator is wrong in chapter 17 to suppose that Rahab the prostitute was counted among the people of God or inserted into Christ’s genealogy because of the merit of her lie, or that the patriarch Jacob was enriched by the Lord’s blessing because of his lie, as Augustine discusses at greatest length in the chapters cited.

Besides the testimonies and examples from divine Scripture which the author adduces to establish that lying is permissible, several harmful propositions occurring in this very Collation must be avoided. We shall set them out in order [Col. 0336C].

1. A lie may be used like hellebore when some deadly illness is imminent (chapters 7 and 19).

The body’s safety and life may sometimes be preserved by a lie. But because the lie is evil in itself, it has no power to heal the soul. Whatever the reason for which it is employed, it harms the soul, as Scripture says: “The mouth that lies kills the soul.”

2. When serious danger threatens in confessing the truth, one may take refuge in lies, provided that one is salutarily pricked by the guilt of a humble conscience (chapter 17).

This amounts to saying that evil must be done so that good may come.

3. God does not regard or evaluate the vocal or external confession of truth, but only the inward piety of the heart (the same chapter and elsewhere).

The Apostle contradicts this when he says: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness [Col. 0336D], but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.” The royal prophet likewise requires both of a righteous person in Psalm 14: that he speak truth in his heart and not act deceitfully with his tongue.

4. Some people could have been justified through lying (the same chapter).

Far be it from Christian minds to believe that righteousness can be acquired by lying. There is no righteousness where deceit or falsehood reigns.

5. Charity excuses a lie if it is undertaken to preserve another person’s life, one’s own or another’s chastity, or some great good.

The Wise Man says that those being led to death must be rescued. The Apostle says: “Let no one seek his own advantage, but that of another” (chapter 19).

Blessed Augustine teaches more correctly in his books *On Lying* and *Against Lying* that we should strive for another’s salvation without putting our own salvation second:

> “If someone should flee to you who could be freed from death by your lie, you will not lie; for the mouth that lies kills the soul [Col. 0337A],”

and so forth.

Those who are being led to death must indeed be rescued, but not by crooked paths—not by theft, fornication, lying, or any other sins. These things do not advance charity; they violate it.

6. Truth harmed some people, while lying benefited them.

Doeg the Idumean, when he reported to Saul what the priest Achimelech had done, deserved on account of this truth to be rooted out of the land of the living, as is said in Psalm 51; whereas in that land Rahab the prostitute was planted, together with her relatives, because of her lie. Samson likewise suffered just punishment for revealing the truth (chapter 20).

We have already said that Rahab’s lie was not rewarded, but her piety and faith toward the spies and toward the city and land of Jericho. Nor does it matter that a confession of truth, if made carelessly and imprudently, has turned out badly for some people. It was not so much the truth or its confession as the imprudence with which they acted that brought them into danger.

As for the martyrs, although their confession of truth caused them temporal [Col. 0337B] harm, they should not therefore be considered unhappy. It became for them a source of glory and of eternal victory and salvation.

7. Those who used to present the wonders of their virtues or their own actions—which had to be brought forward in a Collation for the instruction of the younger brethren—under the names of other persons: what else can we judge this to be than an open lie? The Teacher of the Gentiles clearly instructed us in this practice. He preferred to recount the greatness of his revelations in the person of another, saying, “I know a man in Christ, whether in the body…” (chapter 24).

This is plainly a frivolous argument. A person who speaks of himself in the third person does not thereby lie. He asserts nothing false, although he conceals something true. To suppress the truth by silence is not to lie, as was said above, unless some falsehood is mixed into it.

8. One must lie for the sake of humility, so that, even when questioned, one will not reveal one’s own virtues to others and, by revealing them, fall into the harmful vanity of boasting (chapters 21, 23, and 24) [Col. 0337C].

Blessed Augustine condemns this opinion in these words:

> “When you lie for the sake of humility, if you were not a sinner before you lied, by lying you become what you had avoided. Truth itself is not in you unless you call yourself a sinner in such a way that you also recognize yourself to be one. Truth itself consists in saying what you are. For how can humility exist where falsehood reigns?”

More may be found in Gratian, 22, question 2, chapter *Cum humilitatis*, which is canon 9, and the following chapters.

Nor does Abbot Joseph’s argument in chapter 21 of this Collation move us. He brings forward Gospel testimonies in which the Lord forbids us to wish to appear to be fasting:

> “Let not your left hand know what your right hand is doing.”

Blessed Gregory properly resolves this objection in Homily 11 on the Gospels:

> “A treasure that has been found is hidden so that it may be kept, because the zeal for heavenly desire is not sufficiently protected from evil spirits if it is not also concealed from human praise.”

In the present life we are like travelers on a road by which [Col. 0337D] we are journeying toward our homeland. Evil spirits, like bandits, lie in wait along our path. Whoever carries his treasure openly on the road desires to be robbed.

I say this not so that our neighbors should not see our good works, since it is written, “Let your good works be seen, and let them glorify your Father who is in heaven,” but so that by what we do we do not seek external praise.

The work should therefore be done publicly in such a way that the intention remains hidden: we should offer our neighbors an example through our good work, while in the intention by which we seek to please God alone we should always desire secrecy.

Thus far Gregory.

Therefore, if someone is questioned about a virtue he possesses or some good work he has performed, and confesses the truth without taking pleasure in himself but attributing it to God and ascribing all glory to him, he does not violate the command, “Let not your left hand know what your right hand is doing.” That command concerns and governs only the intention and purpose of our mind.

John [Col. 0338A] Cassian appears to have recalled these opinions of Abbot Joseph in such a way that he also gave us reasonable grounds for suspecting him of them. Near the end of the Collation he says:

> “Confirmed by this blessed Joseph’s instruction and teaching as by a divine oracle, we preferred to remain in Egypt,”

and so forth.

More relevant still is what he writes in Book VI of the *Institutes* about Abbot Archebius, chapter 37: he says that Archebius used religious circumvention and a charitable lie among the brothers.

This expression seems to mean nothing other than that lies may rightly be employed for the sake of preserving charity and helping others. We have shown above that this is not permissible.

Indeed, there is no such thing as a charitable lie. Charity and truth are not opposed to one another; rather, charity is the enemy of lying and falsehood.

Finally, in the last chapter of the seventeenth Conference, Abbot Joseph forbids a monk to define or establish anything certain concerning the observance of bodily disciplines—such as an unrelaxed strictness of fasting, perpetual abstinence from wine, oil, or meat [Col. 0338B], the complete restriction of leaving one’s cell, or uninterrupted persistence in reading or meditation. This is not to be understood of those things that are sometimes promised by a solemn vow in religious orders, for that is permitted in an approved religious order; rather, it concerns what each monk, through a kind of private rashness, pledges to himself. Such a practice is as full of danger as it is of imprudence.

### Conference 20, chapter 8

Who is there who could not humbly say, “I made my sin known to you, and I did not conceal my iniquity,” so that through this confession he might also confidently add, “And you forgave the wickedness of my heart”? But if, held back by shame, you blush to reveal your sins before men, do not cease to confess them with continual supplication to him from whom they cannot be hidden, and to say: “I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is always before me; against you alone have I sinned, and I have done evil before you”—for he is accustomed both to heal without any public exposure that would cause shame and to forgive without reproach [Col. 0338C].

**(Note 22.)** Several similar passages may be found in St. John Chrysostom, the teacher of John Cassian: Homily 2 on Psalm 50; Homily 4 on Lazarus, on Luke 6; the homily on the Publican, on Luke 18; Homily 1 on Hebrews 12; the homily on penance and confession; Homily 8 on penance; and Homily 5 on the incomprehensible nature of God. The Lutherans, together with Calvin in chapter 9 of the *Institutes*, cite these passages against the necessity of sacramental confession.

But they do so incorrectly and ineptly. For Chrysostom and Cassian are not speaking of secret and auricular confession made to priests, which is part of the sacrament of penance. They mean only that the theatrical and public confession that formerly took place during public penance was not necessary for salvation. At that time a penitent, as though on a stage, confessed some grave offense before the bishop, the priests, and a multitude of the people [Col. 0338D].

Accordingly, St. John Chrysostom did not wish to compel those who had sinned secretly to make this confession, both because he did not judge that every hidden sin ought to be made public and because, around this very time, public confession had been abolished by Nectarius, bishop of Constantinople and Chrysostom’s predecessor, out of fear of the raging populace. This happened because a certain matron had been violated by a deacon under the pretext of confession, as Zozomenus reports in book 9, chapter 35, of the *Tripartite History*.

### Conference 21, chapter 4

Thus we know that David surpassed the precepts of the Law. Although Moses had commanded that enemies be repaid in kind, David not only failed to do this but embraced those who persecuted him with love, devoutly praying to the Lord for them; he even mourned bitterly and avenged the slain.

**(Note 23.)** He seems to allude to chapter 1 of the Second Book of Kings [2 Samuel], where Sacred Scripture relates that, after Saul, Jonathan, and many others had been killed in battle with the Philistines, and the news had been brought to David, David tore his garments, and all the men who were with him mourned, wept, and fasted that day until evening for Saul, Jonathan his son, the people of the Lord, and the house of Israel, because they had fallen by the sword. But he ordered the Amalekite youth who had reported these things to be killed, because he had laid his hand upon the Lord’s Anointed.

This was an outstanding instance of David’s piety toward Saul, his enemy. David had always spared him, prayed to the Lord for him, and, after his death, wept and fasted for him.

But when Abbot Theonas says that Moses commanded the law of retaliation, do not understand him to mean that this command applied to everyone, so that anyone who had been injured was permitted to inflict as much harm upon the person who had injured him as he himself had suffered. Rather, that law concerned judges, who in the commonwealth, according to Aristotle’s view (*Ethics*, book 5, chapter 4), are like a certain living and impartial medium of justice, reducing unequal things to equality. For in Exodus 21, where this law is established, a definite rule is prescribed for judges to follow in punishing offenses. The chapter begins: “These are the judgments that you shall set before them,” and so forth.

Likewise, in Leviticus 24, shortly after repeating the law of retaliation, the Lord God adds: “Let there be equal judgment among you, whether a resident alien or a citizen has sinned.” Finally, in Deuteronomy 19, the Lord commands that the determination of this punishment belong to the judges and priests. When they discover that someone has given false testimony against his brother, they are to do to him as he intended to do to his brother.

But the Jews, and especially the school of the scribes and Pharisees, extended this law even to all private individuals, as though any one of them could exact this punishment of retaliation from his neighbor if he had been injured by him.

To counter this corrupt opinion, Christ in Matthew 5 exhorts us not to seek any vengeance from our brothers, but to be ready, when struck on the right cheek, to offer the other as well, if necessary. “You have heard,” he says, “that it was said, ‘An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth’; but I say to you, do not resist evil.”

In these two statements, Augustine says (*Against Adimantus*, chapter 8), “the difference between the two Testaments is demonstrated, although both were established by the one God.” Since carnal people at first were burning with a desire to avenge themselves far more greatly than the injury about which they complained, a first degree of gentleness was established for them: the pain of the avenger was not in any way to exceed the measure of the injury received. In this way, someone who had first learned not to surpass an injury might at some point also be able to forgive it.

Therefore, the Lord, now leading the people through the grace of the Gospel toward complete peace, built another degree upon this one, so that the person who had learned not to return a greater vengeance than the injury he had suffered might, with a pacified mind, rejoice in forgiving everything.

The same thing is proclaimed by the Prophet in those ancient books, who says: “Lord my God, if I have done this, if there is iniquity in my hands, if I have repaid those who repaid me evil” (Psalm 7). Another Prophet speaks of a man who patiently suffers injuries and endures them with great gentleness: “He shall give his cheek to the one who strikes him; he shall be filled with reproaches” (Lamentations 3).

From this it is understood both that a measure of vengeance was rightly established for carnal people and that complete forgiveness of injury was not commanded only in the New Testament but had been foretold long before in the Old.

Augustine pursues the same argument in book 19, chapter 25, of *Against Faustus*:

“Who is easily content to return only as much vengeance as he has received injury? Do we not see people who have been lightly wounded plotting murder, thirsting for blood, and scarcely finding in the misfortunes of their enemy anything with which they can be satisfied? Against this immoderate and unjust revenge, therefore, the law, setting a proper limit, established the punishment of retaliation: that each person should receive a penalty corresponding to the injury he inflicted. This is not fuel but a boundary for fury—not so that what had been quiet might be kindled by it, but so that what was already burning might not spread farther. A just vengeance was imposed, and it is justly owed to the person who has suffered injury. What is owed may indeed be generously remitted, but it is not unjustly demanded.”

Thus, since the person who wishes to avenge himself immoderately sins, but not the person who wishes to be avenged justly, the person who does not wish to be avenged at all is farther removed from sin. For this reason he adds: “But I say to you, do not resist evil.”

St. Jerome, explaining this passage of St. Matthew, writes:

“Our Lord, removing retaliation, cuts off the beginnings of sins. Under the Law, guilt is corrected; here, the beginnings of sins are removed.”

So much for him.

That law which commanded retaliation was therefore given to judges, so that a just compensation might be made according to its prescription. The injured person was not permitted to return retaliation to the one by whom he had been injured; rather, the judge who decreed this penalty was also the one who exacted it.

### Conference 21, chapter 5

[Col. 0340B] Christ, therefore, does not constrain anyone by the necessity of a precept to the lofty heights of virtue; rather, he appeals to the power of free will and, by the salutary benefit of counsel, kindles him with the desire for perfection.

**(Note 24.)** Christ does indeed call upon the powers of free will; but we neither follow nor obey when called except through the gift of God himself. For he touches our hearts, moves, arouses, and inclines them, and makes us walk in his commandments. This applies not only to commandments or orders but also to the acceptance of the evangelical counsels. The higher and more exalted these are, the greater the grace of God that they require in order to be fulfilled.

We have discussed these matters at length in the thirteenth note; therefore, here we shall strive for brevity and refer the reader to that passage. Many passages of this kind will occur throughout the work, of which we shall indicate only some. In all of them I want the reader always to remember what we said in the third note: these abbots are not speaking of people wholly deprived of divine grace, but of those whom the Spirit dwelling within them governs and continually invites to what is good, never allowing them to remain idle. Thus the grace of God is neither excluded nor injured; it must always be understood to cooperate.

A similar passage occurs at the beginning of chapter 7, in these words: “It lies within our power whether we wish to remain under the grace of the Gospel or under the terror of the Law.” This is heretical and false if God’s help is excluded.

### Conference 21, chapter 9

“If I,” said blessed Theonas, addressing his wife, “cannot draw you away from death, neither will you separate me from Christ. It is safer for me to be divorced from a human being than from God.” With the grace of God inspiring him, he therefore immediately undertook to carry out his decision, and he did not allow the ardor of his desire to grow cold through any delay. For he immediately stripped himself of all worldly possessions and hastened to the monastery.

**(Note 25.)** Although the action of Abbot Theonas—who, after his fall, had lived in marriage with his wife for five years and fled to a monastery despite her protest—was not criticized by the Egyptian Fathers, and although he himself was even preferred in the office of deacon to many other eminent and most exalted men because of his various qualities of mind and the signs of apostolic virtues and miracles, as Cassian writes in chapter 10 of this Conference, it must nevertheless in no way be taken as an example. All the canons oppose it. For a foolish and deceptive promise cannot be acceptable to God when someone offers not what belongs to him but what lies in another person’s power.

Therefore, if a husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does, according to the Apostle’s statement—and conversely, if the wife does not have free authority over her own body, but the husband does—the marriage bond, which has been consummated and perfected through the subsequent union of the flesh and the mutual surrender of bodies, cannot be dissolved except by the death of the body alone. Nor can either spouse make a vow of continence to God to the detriment of the other.

For this reason the Apostle again says to the Romans (chapter 7): “The woman who is under a husband, while her husband is alive, is bound by the law”—that is, the law of marriage—“but if her husband has died, she is released from the law, so that she is not an adulteress if she lives with another man.”

But if a marriage has indeed been contracted by mutual consent and by all the other things that the Council of Trent defined as necessary for the perfection of this sacrament, yet the carnal union through which each spouse transfers authority over his or her body to the other has not yet taken place, that freedom remains: either spouse may pass to more sacred vows even against the will of the other. Erasmus of Rotterdam held the contrary opinion. In explaining chapter 7 of the First Epistle to the Corinthians, he thinks that a bridegroom should not be deprived of his bride because he enters an approved religious order.

But the sacred canons have determined otherwise, as may be seen in the chapter *Verum* on the conversion of married persons, in the chapter *Ex publico*, and in canon 27, question 2, from Eusebius, and from Nicholas, canon *Scripsit*—to omit the examples of Macarius, Alexius, and others whom we read bound themselves by a vow of chastity after their weddings but before the consummation of their marriages.

Some have held the same concerning St. John the Evangelist, asserting that Christ called and raised him from the midst of his wedding celebrations to the honor of the apostolate.

But if, after consent, sexual union and the mutual surrender of bodies have followed, this freedom is removed, so that neither spouse can enter or profess religious life without the other’s consent. For just as that spiritual and prior union, which is effected through mutual consent in the reception of the sacrament itself, is dissolved by entry into religious life, which is a kind of spiritual death, so the carnal union and mingling of bodies can be dissolved only by bodily death—unless, perhaps, both spouses mutually consent to profess religious life.

Accordingly, blessed Augustine says rightly in his exposition of Psalm 149:

“If the husband says, ‘I now wish to live in continence,’ but the wife does not, he cannot do so. What you want, she does not want. Must she become a prostitute because of your continence? If she marries another while you are alive, she will be an adulteress. God does not wish such a loss to be compensated by such a gain. Pay what is owed; and if you do not demand it, still pay it. God will reckon it to you as perfect sanctification if you do not demand what is owed to you but return what you owe your wife” (33, question 5, canon *Si dicat vir*).

Again, in Letter 199 to Ecdicia (canon *Secundum verba*):

“According to the Apostle’s words, even if the husband had wished to live in continence and you had not, he would be compelled to render you the debt.”

And in Letter 43 (canon *Una sola*):

“There can be only one reason why we would not merely fail to encourage you to fulfill what you have vowed but would even forbid you to do so: if your spouse should refuse to undertake it with you because of weakness of mind or body. For such vows ought not to be made by married persons except with mutual consent and agreement. If something has been done rashly, the rashness should be corrected rather than the promise fulfilled. For God does not demand something that someone has vowed from what belongs to another; rather, he forbids the usurpation of what belongs to another.”

So much for Augustine. Elsewhere as well, in book 1, chapter 2, *On Adulterous Marriages*, he confirms this judgment by the authority of the Apostle Paul. For in 1 Corinthians 7 he does not want spouses to defraud one another of the marital debt, except for a time, so that they may devote themselves to prayer—and this by mutual consent. Then he says: “Return again, lest Satan tempt you because of your lack of self-control.”

The authority of the Council of Reims also supports what has been said (33, question 5). It decreed that a man who had allowed his wife to receive the veil should not take another wife but should likewise enter religious life.

St. Gregory likewise writes in book 5, Letter 49, to Abbot Urbicus:

“Since Agatho, the bearer of this letter, desires to enter the monastery of your love, we exhort you to receive him with all gentleness and affection. Yet understand that he should be received only if his wife also wishes to enter religious life. Since the two of them have become one body through the union of marriage, it is unfitting for one part to enter religious life while the other remains in the world.”

Furthermore, Alexander III, writing to the bishop of Exeter about the conversion of married persons, chapter 4 (see also the same work, chapter 8, *Uxoratus*, and chapter 13, *Ad apostolicam*), says:

“Although you are endowed with literary knowledge, you ought not to be unaware that it is contrary to the constitution of the holy Fathers for a husband to enter religious life without his wife assuming the religious habit, or a wife without her husband doing so. A man who desires to enter a monastery must not be received unless his wife likewise enters. Since the two have become one body through the union of marriage, it is unfitting for one part to enter religious life while the other remains in the world. Therefore, by apostolic authority, we prohibit you from permitting a husband or wife in your diocese to enter religious life unless both have transferred themselves to it.

“However, if the wife is so old and sterile that she can remain in the world without suspicion, you may overlook the matter, so that, while she remains in the world and promises chastity, her husband may enter religious life.”

Nor does it matter that these canons were issued long after the time of Abbot Theonas and Cassian, since a consummated marriage has, by its own condition and nature—not by pontifical authority—the quality that makes it incapable of dissolution.

There are three principal reasons for this bond. First, the nature of the sacrament prevents it from being dissolved in any way. Thus Pope Eugenius says at the Council of Florence:

“The third good is the indissolubility of marriage, because it signifies the indivisible union of Christ and the Church. Although separation from the marriage bed is permitted on account of fornication, it is not lawful to contract another marriage, since the bond of a lawfully contracted marriage is perpetual.”

The Apostle says the same in Ephesians 5: “This is a great sacrament; but I speak of Christ and the Church.” Blessed Augustine repeatedly presses this same argument: in *The Good of Marriage*, chapter 7; book 5, chapter 9, *Against Julian*; and book 1, chapters 10 and 21, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*.

The second reason is taken from the law that God prescribed for the first human beings in paradise (Genesis 2), and that Christ repeats and confirms in Matthew 19 when he says:

“For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh. Therefore they are no longer two but one flesh. What God has joined, let no human being separate” [Col. 0342C].

The Apostle had this law in mind in 1 Corinthians 7: “To those who are joined in marriage I command—not I, but the Lord—that a wife should not depart from her husband; but if she departs, let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband.”

Blessed Augustine also insists upon this law in his books to Pollentius *On Adulterous Marriages* and in chapter 7 of *The Good of Marriage*, where he calls it the divine rule.

Finally, marriage is indissoluble by the very law of nature. This seems to be suggested by Christ’s question in Matthew:

“Have you not read,” he says, “that he who made them from the beginning made them male and female?” It is as though he were saying that God established nature in those two sexes in such a way that, from the constitution of nature itself, it would be understood that marriage cannot by any means be broken or dissolved.

Hence blessed Jerome, explaining this passage of Matthew, says that Christ brought forward the natural law as a witness [Col. 0342D]. For if this bond had not been implanted in human nature by the law of nature itself and by the original creation, but had arisen only from some later institution, then it would not bind pagans and unbelievers. But that is false. For Innocent, in the chapter *Gaudemus*, under the title *On Divorce*, affirms that divorce is unlawful even for pagans and that they ought to remain with their first wife.

For this reason, among the nations, and especially among the Romans, it was considered a fault if someone repudiated his spouse. When Spurius Carvilius repudiated his wife 523 years after the founding of the City, this was held against him, as Aulus Gellius records in book 4, chapter 3, and Valerius Maximus in book 2, chapter 1. Following the example of this Spurius, many other Romans repudiated their wives for very slight reasons, as Plutarch writes in his *Roman Questions*.

Nor is it credible that divorce was ever truly lawful for the Jews, as Theonas asserts here in confirmation and excuse of his own decision [Col. 0343A] (chapter 9). Because of the hardness of their hearts, they had merely been permitted, without punishment, to repudiate their wives after giving them a bill of divorce.

It was an error of the scribes and Pharisees, as can be seen in Matthew, that they believed divorce had been lawful during the time of the Law. This was also the view of Durandus, Peter of Palude, and Scotus in their writings on the *Sentences* of the Master, as well as of Alfonso Tostatus, bishop of Ávila, in his exposition of Matthew.

But Christ himself contradicts this opinion in Matthew. “It was said,” he says (chapter 5), “‘Whoever divorces his wife must give her a bill of divorce’” (Deuteronomy 24). “But I say to you that everyone who divorces his wife, except on account of fornication, makes her commit adultery; and whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery.”

If the man who marries a divorced woman commits adultery, then the divorce itself is not lawful in such a way that the marriage is dissolved through it.

Again, when the Pharisees tested the Lord in Matthew and asked whether it was lawful to divorce one’s wife for any reason, he answered:

“Have you not read that he who made them from the beginning made them male and female? And he said, ‘For this reason a man shall leave father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh.’ Therefore they are no longer two but one flesh. What God has joined, let no human being separate.”

They asked again: “Why, then, did Moses command a bill of divorce to be given and the wife to be dismissed?” He said to them: “Moses permitted you to divorce your wives because of the hardness of your hearts; but from the beginning it was not so” (Matthew 19).

It is as though he were saying: Moses indeed commanded that a bill be given before the dismissal, in which the accusation against the wife to be dismissed was written; but he did not command the dismissal and divorce itself, although he did not punish it because of your hardness of heart. “From the beginning it was not so,” because God’s will and the institution in paradise were different, and that original arrangement ought rather to have remained inviolate.

The Mosaic Law itself, which is found in Deuteronomy 24, plainly shows that Moses did not command divorce. It even acknowledges that the woman who had been repudiated was not free or released from the law of her husband but would be defiled if she joined herself to another:

“If a man takes a wife and has her, and she does not find favor in his eyes because of some indecency, he shall write a bill of divorce, place it in her hand, and dismiss her from his house. And when she has gone out and married another husband, and he too has hated her, given her a bill of divorce, and dismissed her from his house—or if he has died—the former husband may not take her again as his wife, because she has been defiled and made abominable before the Lord.”

St. Jeremiah likewise says in chapter 3:

“It is commonly said, ‘If a man divorces his wife, and she departs from him and marries another man, will he return to her again? Will that woman not be polluted and defiled?’”

If such a woman is polluted, defiled, and abominable, then she was not released from the law and bond of her former husband, nor was the second marriage that she contracted after receiving a bill of divorce legitimate.

This judgment is embraced by St. Augustine in book 19, chapter 26, *Against Faustus*; by Chrysostom in his homilies on Matthew 5 and 19; and by St. Jerome in his exposition of Matthew 19.

The other arguments that this Theonas adduces have less force. For the words by which the Lord promises a hundredfold in this age and eternal life in the next to those who leave father, mother, wife, children, or fields (Matthew 19) are not to be understood, says Chrysostom in explaining this passage, as though marriages were to be torn apart or dissolved—unless, perhaps, this occurs with the consent of both spouses.

Blessed Augustine likewise says (Letter 89, question 4):

“Among those things that the Lord commanded to be abandoned, a wife is also mentioned. No human law permits a man to sell her, while the laws of Christ do not permit him to dismiss her, except on account of fornication. What, then, do these commandments mean? They cannot be contradictory unless a moment of necessity sometimes arises in which either the wife must be dismissed or Christ. To omit other cases, suppose that the husband is a Christian but his wife dislikes him for this reason and offers him either a divorce from herself or a divorce from Christ. What can he choose except Christ, and what can he do except laudably dismiss his wife for Christ’s sake?

“To two Christian spouses the Lord commands that neither should dismiss the other, except on account of fornication. But where one of them is an unbeliever, the Apostle’s counsel should be followed: if the unbeliever consents to live with the believing spouse, the believer should not dismiss the unbelieving spouse. Likewise, a believing wife should not dismiss her husband if he consents to live with her. But if the unbeliever departs, let him depart; for in such a matter the brother or sister is not enslaved. That is, if the unbeliever does not wish to remain with the believing spouse, the believer should recognize his or her freedom and not consider himself or herself so subject to slavery as to abandon the faith in order not to lose the unbelieving spouse.

“The same is to be understood of children and parents, brothers and sisters: for Christ’s sake all are to be abandoned when the condition is presented that one must abandon Christ if one wishes to have them remain with oneself.”

So much for Augustine in that passage. In these words he clearly explains how those passages of Scripture are to be understood in which we are admonished to hate parents, brothers, relatives, wives, and even our own life. From this explanation it becomes clear how frivolous and weak is the argument that Abbot Theonas derives from those passages to excuse his divorce and repudiation.

For the Lord did not say in Matthew that whoever dismisses a wife, father, or mother will receive a hundredfold. Rather, he says that whoever abandons these things “for my name,” that is, for the name of Christ or of the Christian, will receive it—namely, when the condition is presented that either Christ’s name or those persons must be abandoned.

In exactly the same way, it is foolish to add that he had to pass to more sacred vows in order to escape the punishment of Gehenna. The same is true of what he says next: “If I cannot draw you away from death, neither will you separate me from Christ.”

In these words he seems to condemn the sacrament of marriage, although the Apostle says that it is a great sacrament in Christ and the Church (Ephesians 5). Writing to the Hebrews (chapter 13), he says: “Let marriage be honorable among all, and the marriage bed undefiled.”

For this reason blessed Augustine also says rightly (Letter 89, question 4):

“Let these people cease speaking against the Scriptures. In their exhortations to greater things, let them encourage people in such a way that they do not condemn lesser things. Surely they cannot persuade people to pursue holy virginity in any other way than by condemning the bonds of marriage, when, according to the Apostle’s teaching, ‘each person has his own gift from God, one in this way and another in that’?” And so forth.

It is therefore not right to condemn the state of married people or the laws of marriage, instituted by God himself in paradise, implanted in human nature, and again praised by Christ in the new law and enriched with the dignity of a sacrament. Nor is it lawful to dissolve the marriage bond under the pretext of a more sacred vow, as this Theonas did when his wife protested—although it can legitimately be done by mutual consent if both spouses wish to enter an approved religious order.

If someone objects that Theonas had been preferred to all the members of his community by the vote of the entire group, and therefore had been adorned by God himself with the gift of performing miracles, we shall answer that what was rewarded in him was his zeal and desire for perfection and chastity, not the divorce. We made the same point in the twenty-first note concerning those who sometimes lied: God never praised the lie in them, but rather their good piety and their zeal to help those for whom they are said to have lied.

It seems, however, that Theonas perceived in himself the gift of chastity and recognized that he had undertaken the obligations of marriage less by his own will than by the command of his parents, as is stated in the first chapter of this Conference. For that reason he hastened with greater confidence to the monastery after dismissing his wife.

### Conference 21, chapter 29

A person who is just and perfect is not bound by the law of Lent, nor is he content with subjection to this minor canon, which the leaders of the Churches established for those who are entangled throughout the year in pleasures or worldly business, and so forth.

And shortly afterward:

But the just, for whom no law has been established and who devote not merely that small portion—that is, the tenth part—but all the time of their lives to spiritual duties, are free from the obligation of legal tithes. Therefore, if an honorable and holy necessity should overtake and constrain them, they dare to relax the station of fasting without any dispute.

**(Note 26.)** When the Apostle Paul says in 1 Timothy 1 that the law was not established for the just but for the unjust, the disobedient, the ungodly, and sinners, he must be understood to mean the Old Law, which includes fear, coercion, and punishment. For shortly before this he had urged Timothy to charge certain people not to teach differently or devote themselves to myths, and so forth. Then he adds:

“From these some have gone astray and turned aside to empty talk, desiring to be teachers of the law, although they understand neither what they say nor the things about which they make assertions. We know that the law is good, if one uses it lawfully.”

It is as though he were saying: The old law had its usefulness among the people of God, whom it pressed through fear, and it was like a tutor leading them to Christ. But insofar as it includes fear, compels, and coerces, it does not pertain to the just and the willing—those who, through the grace of the New Testament and the indwelling Holy Spirit, keep the law. They do not need to be driven to observe the law by fear or punishments, although it is otherwise also commanded to the just that they should not kill, commit fornication, or steal.

The word “law” in this passage is understood as the Old Law, and in such fullness that it includes all the terrors, threats, punishments, and burdens imposed by Moses upon the ancient people. These had to cease when people, reborn through the grace of the New Testament, were no longer driven by fear but freely and willingly cultivated righteousness and observed the commandments of charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith.

Blessed Augustine clearly indicates that this is the meaning of the passage in Sermon 10 on Psalm 118, explaining the verse: “Establish your law for me, Lord, the way of your statutes” [Col. 0345C]:

“Was that person like those of whom the blessed Apostle says that the law was established, when he says, ‘Establish your law for me, Lord’? Certainly not. For if he had been such a person, he would not have said earlier, ‘I ran in the way of your commandments.’

“What, then, does it mean that he prays for the law to be established for him by the Lord, if the law is not established for the just? Is it not established for the just in a manner different from that in which it was established for the rebellious people on tablets of stone rather than on tablets of fleshly hearts, according to the Old Testament on Mount Sinai, producing slavery? Rather, according to the New Testament, of which it is written through the prophet Jeremiah: ‘After those days, says the Lord, I will place my laws in their minds and write them on their hearts.’

“See how he wished the law to be established for him by the Lord: not as it was established for the unjust and disobedient belonging to the Old Testament, but as it is given to the holy, the children of the free woman—that is, of the heavenly Jerusalem—the children of promise, the children of the eternal inheritance. It is given to them by the Holy Spirit as by the finger of God in their minds, and written upon their hearts, not so that they may retain it in memory while neglecting it in life.”

So much for Augustine.

Theonas is therefore mistaken when he thinks that the Apostle was speaking about every kind of law and that, for this reason, just and religious people are not bound by the law of the Church concerning fasting, but may relax and set it aside because of some honorable and holy necessity.

“For every soul must be subject to the higher authorities.” It would not be subject to a superior authority unless it were also subject to that authority’s laws. Nor can anyone, however just and upright, be exempted from the obligation of those laws prescribed for the whole Christian commonwealth, unless the law itself or the legislator grants a dispensation for a just reason.

Even if someone should contend that the Apostle Paul was speaking about every precept and law, it would still not follow that the just are not bound to observe the fast of Lent, as Abbot Theonas wishes. The Apostle denies that the just are under the law because no law has coercive force over them, as it does over the unjust. Thus the law is not established for the just because, as the Apostle says, they are a law to themselves, since they show that the work of the law is written in their hearts (Romans 2).

All, therefore—the just and the unjust alike—are subject to the law. They differ in this respect: the just obey willingly and freely, whereas the unjust are compelled against their will; and every law seems harsh, bitter, and difficult to observe to the latter.

This was the common error of Abbot Theonas, the Begards, and the Beguines. They said that Christians were not bound by ecclesiastical fasts once they had reached the state of perfection. This error was condemned at the Council of Vienne under Clement V.

### Conference 21, chapter 30

It must certainly be understood that this observance of Lent did not exist at all as long as the perfection of that primitive Church remained inviolate. Those who were enclosed throughout the whole period of the year by an equal fast were not confined within the narrow limits of fasts by the necessity of a precept or as though by a legal sanction.

### (Annot. 27.)

That the observance of the Lenten fast is an apostolic ordinance and tradition, Blessed Jerome clearly indicates [Col. 0346B] in his letter to Marcella against the errors of Montanus, in these words:

> “We fast one Lent, according to the tradition of the apostles, at the season appropriate to us; but they make three Lents in the year, as though there had been three Saviors who suffered.”

The sixty-ninth canon among the Apostolic Canons supports this; so does Saint Clement of Rome, *Apostolic Constitutions*, Book V, chapter 12; Saint Ignatius, *Letter to the Philippians*, chapter 4, where he calls the Lenten fast an imitation of God and of man; and Basil the Great, in his sermon *On Drunkenness* and in both sermons *On Fasting*. In one of these he says that angels are described as fasting throughout all the churches during Lent, and that there is less danger if a soldier, having cast aside his shield, passes through the enemy’s battle line and camp than if a Christian is found outside the ranks of those who fast.

In the same sense Blessed Ambrose, sermon 2, asserts that it is no slight sin to violate the Lent commanded by the Lord [Col. 0346C], because “whoever says that he remains in Christ ought himself to walk as he walked.” Epiphanius, Leo, Jerome, Theophilus, Eusebius, Chrysostom, and many other ancient Fathers agree with them. With one accord they teach that, from the beginning of the nascent Church, there existed an apostolic doctrine and institution concerning the undertaking of this fast, because it contains a commemoration of Christ’s life and of evangelical legislation.

For the Lord, when he was about to preach the Gospel, first fasted for forty days and forty nights. Those who deny that this fast was imposed upon us, as the Protestants do, would also have to deny that the memory of Christ’s life should be retained—just as one does not wish to retain the memory of Christ’s Passion if one does not wish to follow his footsteps and suffer with him, so as to be glorified together with him. For just as Christ suffered so that we might also follow his footsteps, so likewise he fasted for forty days so that we might imitate him by fasting, praying, abstaining, and following his footsteps in all things.

For this is to remember Christ’s life ἐνεργῶς—that is, effectively and with the very disposition of the heart: to imitate it and, according to the measure of our nature and as each person is able to bear it, to express it in conduct and life [Col. 0346D].

### Col. 23, chapter 2

Let us investigate more carefully what the principal good was that the Apostle could not accomplish when he wished to do so. For we know many goods that we cannot deny the blessed Apostle and all men of similar merit both possessed by nature and sharpened through grace.

### (Annot. 28.)

“Good” is said in two ways: namely, good according to duty, or according to the substance of the act, as the scholastics speak, and the good of true virtue, which is meritorious of eternal life.

The former can be performed by human beings through the powers of nature alone. Thus many philosophers, and many celebrated men among the Romans and Greeks, performed many things that were morally and dutifully good. After sin, a certain general inclination toward the virtues remained in human beings [Col. 0347A], or certain remnants of the virtues. Because of these remnants, the man in the evangelical parable is described, after his fall, as having been left half-dead. Such remnants include these dispositions: that it is good to love God, that gratitude should be returned to benefactors, that parents should be honored, and that injury should be done to no one.

Through these remnants, Blessed Augustine asserts in Book II of *On the Sermon on the Mount* that God speaks every day even in the most perverse human beings. For they are never entirely erased or extinguished; rather, as long as nature itself endures, some inclination toward the good also remains. Augustine demonstrates this in *On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapters 25 and 27, and in Book II of *On Free Will*, chapter 10; Basil, in the *Longer Rules*, chapters 2 and 3; Cyril, in his commentary on the words of John, “He enlightens every person coming into this world”; Saint Thomas, *Summa Theologiae* I–II, question 63, article 1, and question 85, articles 1, 2, and 3.

The more recent theologians agree with these views: Master Turnhout, Ruard, Latomus, Dominic de Soto, and many others.

But the good of true virtue, which makes us pleasing to God [Col. 0347B] and contributes toward meriting the attainment of eternal salvation, is not placed within our own powers; it must be given by God. For God, by his gratuitous goodness, must raise us up when we are weighed down under the burden of sin, enlighten us, and lift us up through Christ. For it is he, as the Apostle says, who works in us both to will and to accomplish, according to his good pleasure (Philippians 2).

Hence Saint Jeremiah rightly confesses:

> “I know, Lord,” he says, “that a person’s way is not his own, nor is it in man to walk and direct his steps” (chapter 10).

And elsewhere:

> “Just as an Ethiopian cannot change his skin, so neither can you do good when you are evil” (chapter 13).

The Lord himself says in the Gospel:

> “No one comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him.”

Again, in another place:

> “Without me you can do nothing.”

The Apostle Paul likewise speaks, rebuking our pride:

> “What do you have, O man, that you have not received? But if you have received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it? For we are not sufficient of ourselves to think anything as though from ourselves; rather, our sufficiency is from God.”

Many other passages could be brought forward [Col. 0347C], but we refer the reader to the twentieth annotation, where we discussed this matter at length.

Therefore, when Theonas says here that the Apostle Paul and other men of similar merit possessed many goods by nature and acquired many through grace, if he is speaking of those goods that are truly good, and which he himself shortly afterward enumerates—namely, chastity, mercy, temperance, and justice—his statement is erroneous and approaches the Pelagian heresy. But if he is understood to mean certain gifts of nature, it can be tolerated, since it is not contrary to truth that the Apostle possessed certain inclinations from nature itself, whether toward kindness, mercy, prudence, or similar virtues. God himself is accustomed to implant different inclinations in different human natures.

### Col. 23, chapter 4

Just as our goodness, when compared with the goodness above, is turned into evil, so also our justice, when set beside divine justice [Col. 0347D], is reckoned like a menstrual cloth, as Isaiah says:

> “All our justice is like a menstrual cloth.”

### (Annot. 29.)

John Sotteau, licentiate in sacred theology, in the preface to the works of Blessed Prosper, on the occasion of what Abbot Theonas says in this fourth chapter of the twenty-third Collation about human justice through a certain ταπείνωσις—that is, humiliation or depreciation—charges Cassian with that most pestilential error of Martin Luther, by which Luther taught that our justice is more truly injustice, and indeed that no one is just in this life except externally and through the imputation of Christ’s justice. But he does so rashly and falsely.

For Theonas does not deny that justice exists in us; rather, he says that, in comparison with the excellent justice that exists in God, it is obscured [Col. 0348A], so that it does not appear to be justice. In this sense the Psalmist says in Psalm 142 that “no living person shall be justified in your sight.” This means, as Euthymius, Hilary, Arnobius, and the commentary attributed to Saint Jerome explain, that if human justice is compared with that extraordinary justice of God and examined according to it, no one will be justified in his sight, nor will it appear to be justice.

For can a human being be justified in comparison with God, as Saint Job says in chapter 25, or can one born of a woman appear clean?

> “Behold, the moon does not shine, and the stars are not pure in his sight; how much more man, who is rottenness, and the son of man, who is a worm?”

And in chapter 4:

> “Can a human being be justified in comparison with God?”

God’s justice is therefore so sublime that all human and angelic justice, when compared with it, seems to be injustice. The stars are indeed exceedingly bright in themselves; but if they are compared with the sun or placed before it, they appear to possess no light at all.

Saint Bernard, sermon 5 on the words of Isaiah, extends the Prophet’s statement, “No living person shall be justified in your sight,” even to the angels.

> “The angels are just,” he says, “but just from him, not before him; by his gift, not by comparison with him. For he is justice to himself, whose will is as equitable as equity itself. The angels live all the more truly the nearer they stand before him with whom is the fountain of life. Therefore, when their justice is compared with God’s most exact justice and its rule, it does not appear to be justice.”

If this is so, then a human being will be even less able to be justified in his sight, since, as Hilary says, anger, grief, desire, ignorance, forgetfulness, accident, and necessity are always mingled in him, whether through the nature of the body or through the movement of the constantly fluctuating soul.

Consequently, the justice that exists in us, although it is justice in the true sense of the word, nevertheless appears in a certain way to be unclean because of hidden stains, creeping thoughts of pride, and venial sins, which we frequently commit even when we are acting rightly, and by which our good works themselves are at least venially defiled. It therefore appears like a cloth contaminated by the filth of menstruation.

More concerning this discussion may be found in Saint Augustine, throughout Book II of *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*; Saint Jerome, *To Ctesiphon*; and Blessed Gregory, Book IX of the *Morals*, chapter 1, and his commentary on Psalm 142.

Moreover, the prophet Isaiah, whose authority Abbot Theonas cites here from chapter 64 in the words “Like a menstrual cloth,” assumes the person of the impious, whose acts of justice had been contaminated by many defilements of idolatry and similar crimes. For although they seemed to worship the one God, they repeatedly contaminated this justice through frequent worship of idols. Blessed Augustine, in *On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapter 36, treats this passage of Isaiah most learnedly against the heretics of our own time.

### Col. 18, chapter 16

Although some maintain that this Nicolas was not the one who was chosen by the apostles for the work of the ministry, nevertheless they cannot deny that he belonged to the number of those disciples [Col. 0348D]. It is clear that all of them were at that time such and so perfect as we now scarcely find even a few in monasteries.

### (Annot. 30.)

We add this thirtieth and final annotation out of order because of the opinion here reported by some concerning the heretics called Nicolaitans. Certain people have supposed that they received their name and designation from another Nicolas, rather than from that one deacon among the seven who is described in the Acts of the Apostles as having been chosen by the apostles for ecclesiastical ministry.

This opinion is improbable and contrary to the view commonly received by all. For Saint Ignatius, writing to the Trallians, thinks that the Nicolaitans were named after Nicolas the deacon:

> “Flee the utterly impure Nicolaitans,” he says, “lovers of lust and wicked slanderers.”

For such was Nicolas, the minister of the apostles. Blessed Irenaeus, Book I against the Heresies, chapter 27; Epiphanius, heresy 25; Augustine, heresy 5; Jerome, *To Sabinus*; and many others support this opinion.

### [Col. 0349]

## Observations of P. Ciaconius on John Cassian

### [Col. 0349A]

Since Pope Gelasius the Great, in a council of seventy bishops, judged the works of John Cassian to be apocryphal, chiefly because in the thirteenth Collation and in other places he spoke about grace and human free will in the manner of the Pelagians, and since Prosper of Aquitaine convicted him in a book written against him, it must be examined what in his writings ought to be rejected and what can receive a pious interpretation.

I shall therefore include in eleven propositions all the passages that could generate suspicion of Pelagianism.

## The First Proposition of Cassian

Before I set down the first proposition here, the following should be noted. Human free will, in order to merit glory or to increase grace, is entirely in need of the abiding grace of the Holy Spirit. It cannot fulfill the whole law of God by its own powers, nor prepare itself proximately for grace unless it is raised up by the movement of the Holy Spirit. Finally, it cannot of itself will or do anything that pertains to eternal salvation [Col. 0349B]. For this reason the Lord said:

> “Without me you can do nothing.”

On the other hand, when fortified by God’s grace, it can accomplish all these things.

Thus holy actions and rightly performed deeds are neither the work of grace alone nor of free will alone, but of both—just as a journey along the right road is completed both by the labor of the horse that walks and by the skill of the rider who directs it.

Besides these inward works of true justice, there are other works that free will cannot perform, although it can perform some things; otherwise it would differ in no respect from a dead person.

Among the scholastics, Saint Thomas, *Summa Theologiae* I–II, question 109, article 2, and II–II, question 10, article 4, and in both places Cajetan; Alexander of Hales, Part III, question 69, membrane 3, article 3, toward the end; Bonaventure, Book II of the *Sentences*, distinction 28, article 2; and nearly all the others defend this view.

Most of the Fathers favor their teaching, especially Saint Jerome, Book III against the Pelagians:

> “This is what I told you at the beginning: it lies within our power either to sin or not to sin, and to extend our hand either toward good or toward evil, so that free will may be preserved. But this is according to the measure, time, and condition of human weakness. Perpetual freedom from sin is reserved for God alone, and for him who, having become flesh, did not endure the weaknesses and sins of the flesh. Nor, because I can do something for a short time, will you compel me to be able to do it continually. I can fast, keep vigil, walk, read, sing psalms, sit, and sleep—but can I do these things forever?”

A little earlier [Col. 0349C] he says:

> “We also say that a person can avoid sinning, if he wishes, for a time, in a place, and according to bodily weakness, as long as the mind is attentive and as long as no defect slackens the string on the lyre. But if he relaxes even a little, then, just as one who is pulling a small boat against the current will immediately drift backward if he relaxes his hands, and will be carried by the flowing waters wherever he does not wish to go, so the human condition, if it relaxes even a little, learns its own weakness and recognizes that it cannot do many things.”

Origen says much to the same effect [Col. 0349D] in Book II of his *Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans*, chapter 11, and in Homilies 6 and 14 on Genesis; Basil, in the *Questions Explained at Greater Length*, question 2; Prosper, Book I of *The Call of All Nations*, chapter 2; and Oecumenius, in chapter 9 of the Epistle to the Romans.

The Fathers also commonly praise the most honorable actions of certain philosophers, performed through the powers of nature—for example, Basil in his *Letter to Young Men*; Jerome, Book II against Jovinian; Clement of Alexandria, in the *Stromata*; Augustine, in the book *Hypognosticon*, in *On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapter 28, in *The City of God*, chapter 25, and Book XXI, chapter 16, and in Book IV against Julian the Pelagian, chapter 3.

In these passages Augustine grants that philosophers could, without the grace of the Holy Spirit, perform actions that are honorable according to their own kind, by following the prescription of right reason. Nevertheless, he does not wish to adorn them with the name of virtue, because they did not refer them to the true and supreme good, namely God.

In accordance with this teaching of the holy Fathers [Col. 0350A], Cassian’s first proposition can apparently be understood as referring only to moral good:

> “We can will and do something good through the powers of nature.”

For he asserts this in the twenty-third Collation, chapter 2, and in the thirteenth Collation, chapters 4, 5, and 12. It is clear from these passages that he is speaking of moral good, because elsewhere he repeatedly denies that we can accomplish, begin, or will anything from ourselves unless God assists us.

These statements do not fit together unless the latter passages are understood of the good that is intrinsic to Christian justice, while the former concern what is honorable and morally praiseworthy.

Nevertheless, I would not deny that, although Cassian thought correctly about this matter, he nevertheless somewhat improperly used, in the thirteenth Collation, chapter 12, the example of David contemplating the building of the Temple as though he had conceived the idea from himself. More probably, he conceived it not from himself but from God’s grace, on account of the religious character of the work itself.

## The Second Proposition of Cassian

### [Col. 0350B]

By some rightly performed deed and good will, we can in some way prepare ourselves for grace, so that our will sometimes precedes the movement of the Holy Spirit.

This is what he seems to teach in Book XII of the *Institutes*, chapter 14; the seventh Collation, chapter 7; and the thirteenth Collation, chapters 7, 9, 11, 12, and 13.

For this second proposition to be understood in a Catholic sense, the following must first be stated. Theologians distinguish two kinds of disposition or preparation for grace.

One is remote preparation, which is ordinarily produced through certain morally good works, as a kind of beginning of returning to God and obeying him. In performing some good action, a person begins to heed natural reason, which is the light of the divine countenance marked upon us. Through this, he becomes in some measure suited to receive God’s assistance in attaining his grace, since he makes himself in some degree teachable and tractable.

The other is what they call proximate disposition. This consists in our mind, supported by divine aid, believing in, hoping in, and loving God as it ought [Col. 0350C], and detesting every sin for his sake.

The Council of Trent describes this kind of preparation in session 6, chapter 6, and adds in chapter 7:

> “Justification itself follows this disposition or preparation. It is not merely the remission of sins, but also sanctification and the interior renewal of the human being through the voluntary reception of grace and gifts. Through these, a person is transformed from unjust to just, and from an enemy to a friend, so that he may be an heir according to the hope of eternal life.”

So far the Council.

We certainly believe with assured faith that we can attain proximate preparation only with God’s help. It is also clear that, even when remote disposition is present, it is not sufficient for grace, nor is it necessary that it always be present, since sometimes one arrives at proximate preparation without it.

Theologians also agree [Col. 0350D] that at times an impious person may be so badly disposed and so weighed down by the burden of sins that he cannot even remotely prepare himself for grace, even if he might otherwise be able to do so, unless he is stirred by the prompting of the Holy Spirit.

On the other hand, it often happens that some people whose minds have been less dulled by vices can perform, by the sole power of nature, many things required by duty and moral propriety. Through these actions they remotely prepare themselves to receive the gift of grace, doing in some measure what lies within them.

Many scholastic theologians have embraced this opinion.

Nor is this view contradicted by canon 8 of the Council of Orange, which regards as alien from the faith anyone who thinks that one person can attain mercy and another the grace of baptism through free will. I say that it is not contradicted, because one does not attain the grace of baptism without proximate disposition, which does not belong to the person who runs or wills, but to God who shows mercy.

Many of the Fathers [Col. 0351A] sometimes favor this doctrine when they teach that God is at times preceded by us, or that he does not bestow the assistance of grace except upon those who have made themselves worthy, or that he comes to our aid when we have done what lies within us, or that God awaits some good affection or effort of our will before he assists us.

To confirm all these points, I shall bring forward certain testimonies of the Fathers.

First, Chrysostom, in his homily *On the Conversion of Paul* and in Book I *On Compunction of Heart*, says:

> “The grace of God comes to everyone; but among those who worthily accomplish what lies within them, it remains. From those who act less worthily, it quickly departs. But to those who do not even begin to turn to the Lord, it does not come at all. For it loves upright minds and an unfeigned purpose. Regarding Paul as well, although he still seemed to be traveling on another road, because he was doing this with an upright purpose and zeal for God, the Lord says of him: ‘This man is a vessel of election for me.’”

The same author says in Homily 19 on the Acts of the Apostles:

> “It is certainly worthy of wonder that eunuch of Queen Candace. He had not seen Jesus Christ; he had not seen a sign. He had gone farther than that: he had learned what the situation was in Jerusalem, and he believed Philip. How, then, did he become such a person? His soul was earnest; he attended to the Scriptures and devoted himself to reading.”

He teaches the same thing in many other places.

At the beginning of Book III against the Pelagians, Jerome says:

> “Know that baptism grants forgiveness for past sins, but does not preserve future justice. That justice is guarded by labor, effort, diligence, and above all by the mercy of God, so that it is ours to ask and his to grant what is asked; ours to begin and his to complete; ours to offer what we can and his to fulfill what we cannot.”

Augustine writes several things in this direction in Book XXXVIII of the *Questions*, question 68; Ambrose, Book II of *On Abraham*, chapter 10, and in his tenth sermon on Psalm 118; Hilary, in his commentary on Psalm 118, on the words “Incline my heart, O God, to your testimonies”; Clement of Alexandria, Book VII of the *Stromata*; Cyril of Alexandria, *Apology against Julian*, Book III; and Origen, Book VII on chapter 8 of the Epistle to the Romans, on the words “Those who are called according to the purpose.”

These are the statements of those Fathers, which seem to support Cassian’s position.

Yet, if we can approach God somewhat through an effort of our own, divine attraction is not thereby removed. For it is this attraction that properly completes the approach; the effort does not, since it is neither sufficient by itself nor always necessary, and is worthy of so great an approach only in an improper sense.

Nor does it follow from this that some portion of believers is justified by Christ’s grace and the remainder by the powers of nature. That is foreign to Cassian, who everywhere in his seven books *On the Incarnation* attributes the redemption of all to Christ.

For all justification is of grace, although not all preparation for it is. Proximate preparation is always the work of the Holy Spirit; in some people remote preparation is the fruit of grace, and in others it is of nature.

Nor are certain passages of Scripture, councils, and the Fathers opposed to Cassian—passages that frequently insist that we can neither do, begin, nor even think anything good from ourselves. Cassian himself repeatedly teaches this.

The reconciliation of all these statements is therefore as follows: whenever some good is attributed to our faculty, it should be understood of the goodness of works and wills that is considered according to moral propriety and duty and disposes a person remotely toward grace. But whenever every effort and power for good is denied to our nature, the statement should be understood of that good which either merits glory or prepares a person proximately for grace, and which is intrinsic to true piety, Christian justice, and the ordering of life according to God.

Augustine, who at first held a very restrained view of the powers of nature, eventually explains himself in this way in Book IV against the Two Letters of the Pelagians, chapter 6; Book II of *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 13; Book IV against Julian the Pelagian, chapter 3; Tractate 45 on John; and *On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapter 28.

With this in view, the Council of Trent, session 6, canon 3, decrees:

> “If anyone says that, without the prevenient inspiration of the Holy Spirit and his help, a person can believe, hope, love, or repent as he ought, so that the grace of justification may be granted to him, let him be anathema.”

## The Third Proposition of Cassian

### [Col. 0352A]

Some beginning of repentance, or a purpose of changing one’s life, or a plan of returning to God, can arise from ourselves.

This is what he seems to think in the thirteenth Collation, chapters 11, 13, and 15.

The repentance or conversion of which Cassian speaks is a certain beginning of attrition, which most theologians place within the power of nature—for example, Saint Thomas, Book IV of the *Sentences*, distinction 17, question 2, article 1, question 3; Bonaventure, Book II of the *Sentences*, distinction 28, article 2, question 1, toward the end; and others.

They hold this because, just as a natural love of self is implanted in every nature, so too is there a natural fear of things conceived as harmful.

Now sin causes great harm: to a person’s dignity because of its disgracefulness; to reputation and honor if it becomes known to others; to property if it is squandered; and to the body if it produces illnesses. Moreover, every guilt gives rise to liability to punishments decreed either by human or divine law. It is therefore not wholly beyond nature to hate sin, which makes nature itself subject to so many evils and injuries.

This, then, is a certain beginning of repentance and return to God.

Accordingly, once this has been established, the distinction that Cassian gives in the thirteenth Collation, chapter 17, can be tolerated, although it is somewhat harsh:

> “Of some,” he says, “God is the receiver; of others, the savior.”

He does not seem to be speaking there of justifying grace. According to that grace, he is the savior of all, because all who are justified are justified by this Savior. Rather, he is speaking of remote effort and approach toward justification. In this sense he calls God the Savior of those whom he saves entirely from idleness and negligence, but the receiver of those whose good concern he kindly receives and mercifully advances.

Finally, what Cassian says in the thirteenth Collation, chapter 19—that it was an act of divine condescension that David was rebuked through the Prophet, but that it was the work of his own free will that he recognized his sin—can be explained according to what he himself had written in the preceding chapter: that it lies within human freedom and choice to neglect or love God’s grace, and either to obey or resist it, as the Council of Trent decrees in session 6, chapter 4.

This must nevertheless be understood in such a way that the special movement of God is never excluded—the movement by which a person obeys the one who calls and effectively detests sin.

Therefore, when Cassian had first stated that God’s grace, which rebuked David not only inwardly but also outwardly, was involved, he adds that the recognition of his sin was the work of his own free will.

## The Fourth Proposition of Cassian

Some movement of faith can begin from ourselves.

This is indicated in the thirteenth Collation, chapters 11 and 13, but more clearly in chapter 15, where he writes that Christ performed healings according to the measure of faith in which he found each person, or according to the measure that he himself distributed to each—almost as though he were saying that we possess some faith from ourselves, while God imparts another kind.

He had expressed himself much more correctly in the third Collation, chapter 16, where he says that faith is given and increased by God—unless this and similar passages are understood of human faith or persuasion. In response to what God reveals through the Church [Col. 0352D], we begin at least probably to assent on account of certain reasons, arguments, miracles, and the holiness of the person preaching Christ.

The authors who hold that such faith can be acquired naturally are Soto, Book III of the *Sentences*, distinction 27, single question; Durand, Book II of the *Sentences*, distinction 28, question 1; Alexander of Hales, Part III, question 68, membrane 2; Bonaventure, Book III of the *Sentences*, distinction 23, article 2, question 2; Cajetan, I–II, question 109, article 1, note 3; and Capreolus, Book III of the *Sentences*, distinction 24, single question, article 3, in response to the arguments of Scotus, conclusion 2. In that place he also brings forward many passages of Saint Thomas in support of this position.

Saint Thomas himself does not appear to reject it. In II–II, question 6, article 1, he grants that there can be a human persuasion leading to belief, although it is insufficient—namely, insufficient for Catholic faith. He would not deny that it is sufficient for human faith, since every human persuasion is naturally suited to produce at least some opinion and slight assent.

Thus, in the same place, question 6, article 3 [Col. 0353A], he denies Catholic faith to a heretic who does not believe one article, even with respect to the other articles that he does believe. Yet he grants that the heretic can possess a human belief arising from his own judgment and will. Such a thing could happen to a heretic even before he acquired the habit of human faith: he might believe at one hour and afterward cease to believe.

This is also highly consistent with reason.
