Things that move us externally toward faith—such as miracles, holiness of life, prophecies, and other matters of this kind—do not produce evidence of truth, but they do provide evidence of credibility. That is, they show that it is not rash or imprudent to believe. Nature can therefore spontaneously break forth into some assent; but this assent is not Catholic faith unless it is illumined by the light of the Holy Spirit.

Whatever Cassian’s view may have been, it is certain that Prosper’s interpretation deserves much stronger approval. Prosper maintains that the faith of Andrew, Peter, Paul, and the other apostles, as well as the calling of Zacchaeus, Cornelius, the Centurion, and the Thief [Col. 0353B], must be attributed to grace.

Not only did the apostles lack any movement of faith before they were preceded by grace; neither did those others possess one. For although the Holy Spirit did not draw them outwardly, he drew them inwardly, and he draws his own to salvation in various ways.

Prosper says:

> “It must not be thought that the power of grace draws to the Son only those whom it has rebuked with a voice, crushed with punishment, or made to tremble with terror, while it applies none of its power to the minds of others through tranquil exhortation.”

So Prosper.

Certainly, this passage, among others, seems to have given Pope Gelasius cause to number Cassian’s works among the apocryphal writings.

## The Fifth Proposition of Cassian
Our prayers sometimes precede the grace of God, in accordance with the saying: “And in the morning my prayer will come before you.” —This is transmitted in *Conference* 3, chapter 19, and *Conference* 13, chapters 9 and 12. This opinion seems to contain nothing absurd. For although the very inclination to pray to God is a gift of God, nothing prevents someone [Col. 0353C] from drawing some effort toward prayer from the good of nature and, through it, becoming to some extent worthy of God’s assistance. The following words of the Fathers signify this in a certain manner.

Chrysostom, *Homily 2 on the Second Epistle to the Corinthians*: “Consider this also with me: even if God grants something out of mercy, nevertheless entreaty contributes greatly to the matter. At first he attributed his salvation to the mercies of God: ‘The God of mercies himself will rescue us’; but here he attributes it also to their prayers. For when the man who owed so many talents had fallen on his knees, the master took pity on him; for it is written: ‘Moved with compassion, he dismissed him.’ Moreover, after much persistence and importunate cries, he finally granted the Canaanite woman the salvation of her daughter, and yet he saved her out of mercy. From this, then, we learn that although we are to experience mercy, we must first present ourselves as worthy of mercy.”

Jerome, *Book III against [Col. 0353D] the Pelagians*: “Know,” he says, “that baptism forgives past sins, but does not preserve future righteousness, which is guarded by labor, effort, diligence, and always above all by the clemency of God; so that it is ours to ask, but his to grant what is asked; ours to begin, but his to complete.” And below: “The entire speech of the saints is prayer to God; every prayer and supplication wrests the Savior’s clemency, so that we, who cannot be saved by our own strength and effort, may be preserved by his mercy. But where there is mercy and grace, free will ceases in part; it consists only in this, that we wish and desire, and give assent to what is pleasing. It is now in the Lord’s power that, by his aid and assistance, we may be able to fulfill what we desire, labor for, and strive toward.”

Hilary, on Psalm 118: “The beginning is ours,” he says, “when we pray, so that the gift may be from God.”

Nor does Saint Thomas seem alien to this doctrine. For in *Summa theologiae* II, question 83, article 10, he grants that prayer can proceed from sinners out of a good desire arising from nature [Col. 0354A] and that it is heard by God—not by a debt of justice, but out of pure mercy—if people perseveringly and devoutly ask for what is necessary for salvation. Cajetan explains this last point as referring to an intention by which even a sinner can love God in some action for God’s own sake. If someone should argue that this piety, necessary for obtaining what is asked, cannot exist without some special assistance—as article 15, reply 1, there seems to indicate—certainly he could not deny that, according to Saint Thomas, some prayer can arise from the good of nature, even though it will not obtain what is asked unless some piety is joined to it through divine assistance.

Nor should anyone be troubled by canon 3 of the Council of Orange, which states: “If anyone says that the grace of God is conferred in response to human invocation, but does not say that grace itself causes us to invoke it, he contradicts the prophet Isaiah or the Apostle, who says the same thing: ‘I was found by those who were not seeking me; I appeared openly to those who did not ask about me.’” For the council itself [Col. 0354B] explains this in canon 6, when it affirms that without the grace of God it is impossible to pray as one ought; and this cannot be done as it ought without faith and hope.

Augustine, on Psalm 87: “I cried out to the Lord,” he says; that is, “I called upon the Lord so that I might be saved. But how could I call upon him unless I believed? How could I believe unless I heard? But in order that I might believe what I had heard, he himself drew me.” Hence it follows that the council correctly establishes that grace causes us to pray, since we do not pray except from faith, which is a gift of grace.

And whoever thinks that faith alone, without new assistance, is sufficient for addressing some kind of prayer to God will not depart from the opinions of the saints just cited, provided that he does not also deny that, even in those who already believe, the perfect disposition for prayer proceeds only from the Holy Spirit, who intercedes for us with unspeakable groanings. At the same time, if we accept that divine Providence can naturally be recognized, there is nothing absurd in supposing that, apart from any divine faith, an inclination to pray can arise from the powers of nature—not an effective and fervent inclination, perhaps, but at least some inclination—since the nations themselves [Col. 0354C] dedicated temples and altars to those whom they thought to be gods, and established sacrifices, hymns, and priests.

That Cassian understood God to be preceded by us only through some small effort and inclination toward prayer, while full and perfect prayer proceeds from the Lord who precedes us, seems to be indicated in *Conference* 13, chapter 12, toward the end:

“The mercy of the Lord,” he says, “precedes the human will, of which it is said: ‘My God, his mercy will precede me.’ And again, our will precedes the Lord when he delays and, in a certain useful manner, holds back, so that he may test our free will, as it is said: ‘And in the morning my prayer will come before you’; and again: ‘I came before the dawn and cried out’; and: ‘My eyes anticipated you at dawn.’”

“He also calls and invites us when he says: ‘All day long I stretched out my hands to a people who did not believe in me and contradicted me.’ And he is invited by us when we say to him: ‘All day long I stretched out my hands to you.’

“He waits for us when it is said through the prophet: ‘Therefore the Lord waits, that he may have mercy on you.’ And he is awaited by us when we say: ‘Waiting, I waited for the Lord, and he inclined toward me’; and: [Col. 0354D] ‘I awaited your salvation, O Lord.’

“He strengthens us when he says: ‘And I instructed and strengthened their arms, yet they devised evil against me.’ And he urges us to strengthen ourselves when he says: ‘Strengthen the hands that are weak, and make firm the feeble knees.’

“Jesus cries out: ‘If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink.’ The prophet also cries out to him: ‘I have labored in crying out; my throat has become hoarse; my eyes have failed while I hope in my God.’

“The Lord seeks us, saying: ‘I sought a man, and there was none; I called, and there was no one who answered.’ And he himself is sought by the bride, who mournfully complains: ‘In my bed at night I sought him whom my soul loved; I sought him and did not find him; I called him, and he did not answer me.’

“And in chapter 7 he says: ‘When divine kindness perceives that even the smallest spark of good will has begun to shine in us, or that he himself has struck it from the hard flint of our heart, he cherishes and kindles it, and strengthens it by his inspiration.’”

[Col. 0355A]

You see in these passages not only that we are sometimes preceded, and sometimes precede, but also that it belongs to us to make some small beginning; and, in order that we may complete it, we are preceded by God.

## SIXTH PROPOSITION OF CASSIAN

Even after the fall of transgression, the knowledge of good remained in Adam, since the natural law itself, together with certain seeds of the virtues, has been implanted in every soul by the Creator’s beneficence.

He left this written verbatim in *Conference* 13, chapter 12. But lest anyone think that knowledge of good could not coexist with the stain of sin, nearly all the holy Fathers acknowledge in us some natural knowledge of good—although less clear than that which innocent Adam had possessed—as well as certain seeds of the virtues and inclinations toward what is right.

Thus Basil does so in the *Questions Explained at Length*, question 2; Ambrose in Letter 71; Saint Jerome in Letter 151 to Algasius, question 8; Cyril of Alexandria in Book III against Julian; Chrysostom in Homily 9 on Repentance; and nearly all interpreters, in their exposition [Col. 0355B] of Romans 2, on the words: “The Gentiles, who do not have the law,” including Chrysostom, Jerome, Oecumenius, and others.

Moreover, with respect to the knowledge of truth and goodness, Augustine openly retracts what he seemed to have written in Book II of the *Soliloquies* against this opinion: “I do not approve,” he says in Book I of the *Retractions*, chapter 4, “what I said in the prayer: ‘O God, who did not wish anyone except the pure to know the truth’; for it can be answered that many who are not pure nevertheless know many truths.”

Concerning the seeds of the virtues, he writes in *On Free Choice of the Will*, chapter 10: “For you see sufficiently with me, and you grant that it is most certain, that these things are present to all who are capable of contemplating them by their own reason and mind, as rules and as certain lights of the virtues—true and unchangeable—whether individually or all together, and commonly available for contemplation.”

## SEVENTH PROPOSITION OF CASSIAN

We must take care not to refer all [Col. 0355C] the merits of the saints to the Lord in such a way that we attribute to human nature nothing except what is evil and perverse.

These are Cassian’s words in *Conference* 13, chapter 12. But do not infer from them that some people are saved by the merits of nature and others by divine grace. Cassian did not teach that. Rather, he wished to teach not that, just as all evils come from us, so all merits come from God alone, since everything belongs both to God and to us: our will cooperates with grace in meriting.

Cassian writes this repeatedly, as in Book XII of *The Institutes*, chapter 12; *Conference* 3, chapters 11, 12, 15, and 19; *Conference* 5, chapters 16 and 24; and *Conference* 13, chapters 9, 10, 11, and the final chapter.

Nor is Cassian alone in this, but all the Fathers teach that the power of free will consists not only in this: that someone can do what is right of himself, and can resist God when he calls and moves him; it also consists in this: that a good and meritorious work is completed not by God alone, but by God and our will—wholly by him and wholly by it.

Nearly all the Fathers teach this: Saint Jerome in his letter to Demetrias, *On the Preservation of Virginity*, and in Books II and III against the Pelagians; Augustine in *On Nature and Grace*, chapters 16 and 29, and in *On Grace [Col. 0355D] and Free Will*, chapters 4 and 5, and Book III of the *Hypognosticon*; Chrysostom in Homily 2 on the Second Epistle to the Corinthians; Anselm in his exposition of 1 Corinthians 15, on the words: “Not I, but the grace of God with me”; Saint Gregory in Homily 9 on Ezekiel; Bernard in *On Grace and Free Will*; and the Council of Trent, session 6, canon 32.

## EIGHTH PROPOSITION OF CASSIAN

The quality of our thoughts or recollections lies within our power.

He affirms this in *Conference* 1, chapters 17 and 19, and *Conference* 7, chapter 4. Here we should note what Anselm writes in *On the Harmony of Foreknowledge and Predestination with Grace and Free Will*, chapter 3:

“If the things that have been said are properly considered,” he says, “it is clearly understood that when Scripture says something in favor of grace, it does not remove free will altogether; nor, when it speaks in favor [Col. 0356A] of free will, does it exclude grace, as though grace alone or free will alone were sufficient to save a person.”

This is correct, because when something depends on many causes, it can be attributed now to one of them and now to another, provided that the others are not excluded. Hence those statements of Scripture: “You have been saved by hope”; “The righteous person lives by faith”; “Charity covers a multitude of sins”; “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near”; “Your faith has saved you”; “Almsgiving extinguishes sin.”

Certainly none of these, taken alone, perfected Christian righteousness, yet righteousness is attributed now to one and now to another separately, because true piety rests upon all of them.

The holy Fathers speak in the same way, and from them we obtain great assistance for understanding Cassian. With regard to the quality of thoughts, Augustine writes in Book III of *On Free Choice of the Will*:

“Since nothing attracts the will to do anything unless something has been perceived, and since it lies within a person’s power either to accept or reject what has been perceived, while there is no power over what perception touches him, it must be acknowledged, both from what has been said above [Col. 0356B] and from what follows, that the mind is touched by perceptions arising from above and from below, so that the rational substance may take from either what it wills, and that misery or blessedness may follow from the merit of choosing.”

Basil teaches the same in his homily “Pay Attention to Yourself.”

Cassian follows Augustine and Basil, teaching that the quality of our thoughts depends upon us. But neither of them attributes this to us alone. Rather, they wished to indicate that, with God’s assistance, it also lies within our power to reject or approve the perceptions by which we are touched, and thus to accustom ourselves to devout meditations so that access may be barred to shameful perceptions.

## NINTH PROPOSITION OF CASSIAN

After the recent fall of humanity, the light of reason was clearer, so that people then needed God’s illumination less than they did afterward.

This is found in *Conference* 8, chapter 23. It should not be judged a novelty, since Jerome had taught it before Cassian in explicit words in Letter 8, *On Virginity*, to Demetrias. The following reason can be assigned for it. [Col. 0356C]

It is well known to philosophers that the passions which disturb the sentient mind are not aroused without some change in the body. For the blood now grows hot, now cools; it flows and ebbs, advances and returns. The heart, too, is variously contracted or expanded.

The bodies of parents are variously affected by these conditions of the heart and blood, as are their reproductive faculties. What they have drawn in as a defect from the source, they transmit to their children as to streams flowing from it. And while children themselves add, through their own habits, corruption to the corrupted nature they received from their parents, the result is that, the longer the passage of time, the more the good seeds of nature are buried, and the greater the need of illuminating grace becomes for descendants than it was for their ancestors.

## TENTH PROPOSITION OF CASSIAN

The Holy Spirit distributes different degrees of grace according to the differing capacity, labor, diligence, and effort of human beings.

This is signified in Book VI of *The Institutes of Renunciation*, chapter 18; *Conference* 3, chapters 11 and 12; and *Conference* 13, chapters 15 and 16.

For this to be understood in a Catholic manner [Col. 0356D], it must be held that this capacity and effort of ours, to which God is said to adapt the measure of his grace, can be referred to three things.

First, it can refer to remote preparation. Since this preparation can in some measure come from us, and since God mercifully regards it and grants his gifts in accordance with it, our effort may in some manner be called the measure of grace.

I say “in some manner,” because it is not properly and perfectly so: partly because this preparation scarcely enters the boundaries of congruent merit, and partly because the greatness of divine generosity frequently exceeds its measure. Cassian explicitly affirms this in *Conference* 13, chapter 16. He adds in chapters 11 and 15 that there are some whom God, by the spontaneous favor of his grace, has chosen beforehand for salvation even though they were thinking nothing about the remedy of their salvation and were not preparing themselves for it.

Second, our effort and capacity can refer to proximate disposition. Since God is the author of this disposition, and God measures justifying grace according to its degree, our will cannot [Col. 0357A] be called the measure of grace; the measure is divine. He infuses only as much grace by which we are justified as the grace preceding it had prepared for, although even here an effort of our will is required. Joined with divine motion, this effort possesses the quality of condign merit for attaining righteousness, as the Council of Trent decrees in session 6, chapter 8.

Finally, our capacity and effort can be considered in one who is already righteous through indwelling grace. It cannot be denied that this capacity is a measure proportionate, by condignity, to the increase of grace and charity.

“Charity,” Augustine says in Tractate 5 on the First Epistle of John, “merits increase, so that when increased it may merit perfection.” The Council of Trent teaches the same in session 6, chapter 10.

Although a righteous person, possessing only the habit of infused grace and virtues, is not sufficiently equipped to perform all works of piety, or to perform them always, theologians nevertheless judge that indwelling grace and the virtues are sufficient for some works and for some period of time without the need for a new assistance. Cajetan teaches this in I–II, question 109, article 8; Dominic Soto in Book III of *On Nature and Grace*, chapter 4; and the Dean of Leuven in article 7 [Col. 0357B] of *On Free Will*.

And just as it lies within the power of one who possesses grace to make no use of it for action—for which reason the Apostle says, “Let us not receive the grace of God in vain,” and says of himself, “His grace toward me was not in vain”—so also every righteous person is free either to work as much as he can from grace or to work less. Thus the ability to do this much or that much comes from grace; but whether one acts more sluggishly or more energetically, within the measure and breadth of the grace received, and whether through the grace one possesses one gains more or less grace, depends upon our freedom, as Cassian says. Nor is a new assistance always required for this.

There are many testimonies of the holy Fathers in support of this opinion, especially Jerome in Book II against Jovinian and Book I against the Pelagians; Dionysius the Areopagite in Book 9 of *The Celestial Hierarchy* and Book 5 of *The Divine Names*; Origen in Book VII on Romans 8; Chrysostom in Homily 9, “No One Is Harmed Except by Himself.” Indeed, this same most holy teacher indicates in Homily 19 on the Acts of the Apostles what [Col. 0357C] Cassian teaches in Book IX, chapter 18, concerning Saint Paul’s particular progress in knowledge through his vehement study of Scripture.

## ELEVENTH PROPOSITION OF CASSIAN

Those whose faith and virtue God tests, either directly or through another tempter, are for a short time left by divine grace so that they may be tested and conquer by their own strength, not by God’s.

He asserts this in exactly these words in *Conference* 13, chapter 14. In this way he considers the endurance of Job, who was handed over into Satan’s power; the obedience of Abraham when he was about to sacrifice his son; and the faith of the centurion to whom the Lord offered his presence, saying: “I will come and heal him.”

Someone may wonder how so glorious a victory over the most terrible enemy could have come to the exceptionally strong Job without grace, so that it would seem that even martyrs in their struggles would have had no need of the power of grace, if Job, without God’s help, struck down so formidable an adversary.

This passage can be interpreted in two ways.

The first is that Cassian uses the word “grace” according to its very broadest [Col. 0357D] meaning. In that meaning it includes not only the interior motions of the Holy Spirit and infused habits, but also every gratuitous care of God and every protection of the righteous applied externally. In this sense, those whom God does not preserve or deliver from troubles, labors, afflictions, and injuries are said to be deprived of divine grace.

Hence the groans and complaints of the righteous: “God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”; “They say, ‘God has forsaken him; pursue and seize him, for there is no one to deliver him’”; and: “Zion said, ‘The Lord has forsaken me, and the Lord has forgotten me,’” and so forth.

This abandonment of the saints signifies affliction and torment, not the removal of interior strength. For it is principally of the latter that these promises are made: “I will not abandon you, nor forsake you”; “I am with him in tribulation”; “I have not seen the righteous forsaken”; “Wisdom did not abandon the righteous man who had been sold,” and so forth.

That Cassian is not speaking of an interior abandonment but an exterior [Col. 0358A] one, and not of grace assisting us to endure but of grace protecting us from evils, is clear from the words he writes concerning Job:

“Although it must not be believed that the grace of God was entirely absent from him—for that grace gave the tempter as much power to tempt as it knew him to possess strength to resist—it did not protect him from the enemy’s assault in such a way as to leave no place for human virtue. It merely ensured that the most violent enemy, by making his soul senseless and bereft of understanding, would not weigh him down with an unequal and unjust burden of battle.”

And below, concerning Abraham, he says:

“Thus the constancy of his faith is rightly approved, and it is said that the grace of God, which had left him for a short time in order to test him, came to his assistance: ‘Do not lay your hand upon the boy, nor do anything to him; for now I know that you fear God, and you have not spared your beloved son for my sake.’”

He therefore wished to teach only that the righteous are deprived of the grace that protects them from adversity, not of the grace that sustains and supports them in adversity so that they do not succumb. He says that they fight not by God’s [Col. 0358B] strength but by their own. They fight by God’s strength when God acts to preserve them unharmed; they fight by their own when, though injured, they endure the things that injure them.

He said “by their own,” not “by their own alone,” to indicate that the struggle and effort of our will must be brought into play, and that we must not rely upon grace alone. Thus he had said of Job that he engaged the enemy by his own virtue, with grace not alone protecting him; he was not supported solely by divine assistance without any virtue of his own endurance.

And below he says:

“When God permits this prophet or dreamer to arise, is one to believe that he will protect those whose faith he intends to test in such a way that he leaves their free will no place at all in which they may fight the tempter by their own strength?”

I shall add a second interpretation. Even if grace is understood properly as a gift that assists or even dwells within us, we may nevertheless understand ourselves to be deprived of it in two ways.

First, when the ability necessary for endurance is not supplied. [Col. 0358C] Second, when enough is supplied, but nothing further is added to make what we are able to endure less laborious and burdensome through grace.

In the first way, God never abandons those who seek him; in the second, he frequently does. For he wishes his athletes to exercise the virtues he has bestowed upon them, not to seek to be touched by no sense of pain or hardship, as though they were lulled to sleep by intoxication with divine sweetness, but to experience the full power of the grace they have received, applying it in practice and action through endurance, even though this will bring them much sadness and anguish.

Thus those words apply to them: “Going, they went and wept, casting their seeds”; “Every creature groans and labors in birth until now”; “And not only it, but we ourselves, who have the first fruits of the Spirit”; “When a woman gives birth, she has sorrow, because her hour has come,” and so forth.

God therefore abandons his own when he does not supply new grace, but requires the use of the grace already granted.

Origen splendidly illuminates this entire passage in Book III of *On First Principles*:

“Just as those who preside over contests do not allow those who come to [Col. 0358D] compete to enter into combat with one another indiscriminately or by chance, but, after careful examination, match them by the fairest comparison according as they observe their bodies or ages—boys with boys, men with men, those who are similar in age or strength being joined together—so we must also understand divine Providence. It distributes with the most just moderation all who descend into these contests of human life, according to the measure of each person’s virtue, which is known only by him who alone sees human hearts.

“Thus one person fights against such flesh, another for so long a time, another for so long; one attacks the flesh in this matter or that, another in something else. Again, one resists this or that hostile power, while another resists two or three at once; sometimes one hostile power, and sometimes another, and for a definite period [Col. 0359A] against a particular one. Consider also after what deeds they fight against what enemies, and after what deeds against what vices.

“For perhaps something of this kind is indicated by what the Apostle says: ‘God is faithful, and he will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you can bear’; that is, each person is tempted according to the measure of his virtue and capacity.

“Yet, because we have said that each person is tempted according to the measure of his virtue, it must not therefore be thought that it is fitting for the one who is tempted to conquer in every respect. One who competes in a contest, although he has been fairly matched with his opponent, will not necessarily be able to conquer in every respect.

“But unless the strength of the competitors is equal, the victor’s crown will not be just, nor will the defeated person be justly blamed. God permits us to be tempted, but not beyond what we can bear; we are tempted according to our strength. Whether we use what he himself has given us the ability to do energetically or sluggishly, however, lies within us.

“For there is no doubt that in every temptation we possess the power of endurance, provided that we make proper [Col. 0359B] use of the power granted to us. For possessing the power to conquer is not the same as conquering, as the Apostle himself carefully indicated when he said: ‘God will provide a way out, so that you may be able to endure,’ not ‘so that you will endure.’ Many endure, but are defeated in temptation.

“God grants the power not so that we will endure—for otherwise there would no longer seem to be any contest—but so that we may be able to endure. By the power given to us so that we may be able to conquer, according to the capacity of free will, we either use it diligently and conquer, or use it sluggishly and are overcome.

“For if the whole matter were given to us so that we would conquer in every respect and never be defeated, what reason for fighting would remain for one who cannot be defeated? Or what merit would there be in victory when the ability to resist and to conquer had been removed?

“But if the possibility of conquering is equally offered to all of us, while it is left to our power how we should use this possibility—that is, diligently or sluggishly—then the blame of the defeated person or the victor’s [Col. 0359C] crown will be just.”

This is Origen. Saint Gregory writes similar things, but more briefly, in Book II of the *Moralia*, chapter 11.

That Cassian thought the same as Origen can be understood from *Conference* 13, chapter 13. He writes:

“Although the Teacher of the Gentiles testifies that he received the rank of apostle by the grace of God, saying, ‘By the grace of God I am what I am,’ he nevertheless declares that he also responded to divine grace, saying: ‘His grace toward me was not in vain, but I labored more abundantly than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God with me.’

“When he says, ‘I labored,’ he signifies the effort of his own free will. When he says, ‘Not I, but the grace of God,’ he shows the power of divine protection. When he says, ‘With me,’ he declares that grace cooperated not with someone idle or secure, but with one who was laboring and sweating.”

This is Cassian. Immediately, at the beginning of chapter 14, he adds:

“We read that divine justice made provision for the same thing in Job, its most approved athlete, when the devil demanded him for single combat.”

You see that what he had said about Paul he transfers also to Job: Job certainly labored, but not [Col. 0359D] alone; the grace of God was with him, and the grace of God toward him was not in vain. He confirms this in the words that follow:

“If he had engaged the enemy not by his own strength but with God’s grace alone protecting him, and had been supported solely by divine assistance without any virtue of his own endurance” (observe that grace is not excluded, but is denied to have been alone, since Job himself employed the grace he had received, and Cassian calls this fighting by his own strength), “and if he had endured those numerous masses of temptations, how could the slanderous enemy not have more justly repeated, after the struggle, the accusation he had earlier brought against him: ‘Does Job worship God for nothing? Have you not surrounded him, his house, and all his possessions? But take away your hand—that is, let him contend with me by his own strength—and surely he will bless you to your face’?

“But since the slanderous enemy did not dare to repeat any such complaint after the conflict, he confessed that he had been conquered not by God’s strength but by Job’s.” [Col. 0360A]

“By his strength,” he says, because Job used his own strength, bringing grace to bear against all hardship and not waiting for such an abundance of grace to be poured into him that it would absorb every hardship. Rather, he brought forth whatever was in him to cooperate with grace, which was undoubtedly equal to the battle, although the battle was most terrible.

For he would not have reached such holiness without abundant grace, as that divine proclamation declares: “Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on earth—a simple and upright man, fearing God and turning away from evil?”

That this was also Cassian’s opinion is shown by what he adds there concerning Abraham:

“Divine justice likewise arranged the testing of Abraham’s faith, when it is said: ‘After these words, God tested Abraham.’ For divine justice did not wish to test the faith that the Lord inspired in him, but the faith that, once called and illuminated by the Lord, he was able to exhibit through the freedom of his will.”

You see that only the increase of grace is removed during the time [Col. 0360B] of testing, not the grace previously bestowed, whose use he was able to exhibit in the testing.

The same interpretation can be applied both to what he adds about God testing us through a false prophet or dreamer and to what he writes about the nations left around the Hebrews so that Israel might be trained for battle.

The same applies to what he asserts concerning the centurion’s faith, of which the Lord says in the Gospel: “I have not found such faith in Israel.” Cassian, who often taught that faith is a gift of God, does not deny that the centurion’s faith descended from the Father of lights. Rather, he argues that, in addition to the faith by which the centurion already believed in Christ, some further grace was added, so that he might break forth into that magnificent confession: “Lord, I am not worthy,” and so forth. He maintains that the centurion could exhibit this confession from the faith he already possessed.

Some arguments seem to support this interpretation. First, Cassian writes that when the Lord offered the centurion his presence, he offered it in order to test his faith; in this testing of faith he makes the centurion like Abraham. Yet he does not attribute faith to Abraham, but its [Col. 0360C] use.

Second, he adds these words:

“The same applies to what the Apostle says: ‘Therefore let the one who thinks he stands take care lest he fall. No temptation has overtaken you except a human one. But God is faithful, and he will not [Col. 0360D] permit you to be tempted beyond what you can bear, but with the temptation he will also provide a way out, so that you may be able to endure.’

“When he says, ‘Let the one who stands take care lest he fall,’ he makes free will vigilant; for he knew that, once grace had been received, it could stand through diligence or fall through negligence.

“When he adds, ‘No temptation has overtaken you except a human one,’ he reproves their weakness and inconstancy, since their minds were not yet strong enough to be attacked by the storms of spiritual wickedness. He knew that he and those who were perfect fought daily against such powers; concerning them he says to the Ephesians: ‘Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this age, against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places.’

“When he further says, ‘God is faithful, and he will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you can bear,’ he certainly does not wish the Lord to prevent them from being tempted, but only that they not be tempted beyond what they could endure.

“The first statement indicates the capacity of human free will; the second shows the grace of the Lord, who regulates the struggles of temptation.”

In all these matters, therefore, it is approved that divine grace always incites human free will in such a way that it does not always protect and defend it so completely that it does not also make it confront spiritual enemies through its own efforts. In these struggles the victor learns the grace of God, while the defeated person learns his own weakness. Thus he learns not to hope in his own strength, but always in divine assistance, and continually to return to his protector.

Nor should anyone be troubled by what Cassian had said shortly before concerning the centurion’s faith:

“It would have possessed no praise or merit if Christ had preferred in him what he himself had given; otherwise he would have said, ‘He did not give such faith in Israel.’”

For, as we have shown, he is not speaking about the habit of faith, but about its use and act, which it lies within our power to exhibit. [Col. 0361A] In this consists the basis of merit arising from the work of the one who acts, which was the subject under discussion here.

These two interpretations seem capable [Col. 0362A] of applying to this chapter. Unless a cautious reader adopts one of them, he will easily judge that Cassian agreed with the Pelagians on this matter.

[Col. 0361]

## SOME OF CASSIAN’S OPINIONS REQUIRING A PIOUS INTERPRETATION

Col. 8, chapter 17, and *Conference* 13, chapter 12.

[Col. 0361A]

Each of us has two angels attached to us, namely a good one and an evil one, as the *Book of the Shepherd* teaches.

Concerning this *Book of the Shepherd*, Jerome writes in the *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*:

“Hermas, whom the Apostle Paul mentions when writing to the Romans, is said to be the author of the book called the *Shepherd*, and it is even read publicly in certain churches of Greece. In truth, it is a useful book, and many ancient writers have made use of its testimonies; but it is unknown among the Latins.” [Col. 0361B]

This is Jerome.

Yet long before that, Tertullian, in his book *On Modesty*, asserts that this writing had been judged by the entire council of the churches to be among the apocryphal and false books. Finally, Pope Gelasius rejected it as apocryphal in chapter “Sancta Romana,” distinction 15.

Therefore, what that *Book of the Shepherd* asserts concerning an evil angel is false, although Origen also wrote it in Homily 35 on Luke—unless perhaps, figuratively speaking, the name “evil angel” is understood as the very tinder of sin that is attached to us and that took its origin from the suggestion of the evil angel.

*Conference* 9, chapter 19.

He who possesses the purest mind knows, by the testimony of his conscience, that when Christ appears he will immediately become his companion. — To this belongs Paul’s statement in Romans, chapter VIII: “The Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit that we are children of God,” and that in II Corinthians, chapter I: “Our glory is this: the testimony of our conscience.” From this testimony Cassian says that the righteous know they will become Christ’s companions; but he does not assert that they know this with certainty, since this knowledge may be more or less certain according as the Holy Spirit bears witness to our salvation through clearer or more obscure signs. Such signs include inward sweetness, illumination of the mind, purity of life, and other things of that kind. Yet nothing in these is beyond doubt unless a most certain revelation is added, for the human mind needs this in order not to be deceived in recognizing the presence of the Holy Spirit, and much more in order to become certain of its perseverance in the good. Therefore, when Cassian posits the testimony of conscience concerning the attainment of fellowship with Christ, this cannot be certain either with respect to persevering righteousness or with respect to present righteousness; it is either probably true of one or probably true of both.

Column 9, chapter 23, or 24.

[Col. 0361D] In the Lord’s Prayer Christ, the founder of eternal things, does not wish anything perishable, worthless, or temporal to be sought from him. — This does not mean that Cassian thinks temporal things should not be requested, but that the petition for spiritual things should not be postponed on their account. He adds: “Whoever, after setting aside these petitions for eternal things, prefers to ask him for something transitory and perishable will inflict the greatest injury upon the majesty and generosity of God.”

Conference 17, chapter 15 and following; and Book V of the Institutes of Renunciation, chapters 37 and 39.

By a certain economy and dispensation it is permissible to tell an officious lie. It is preferable to incur this blemish, or a kind of cloud, rather than to profess the truth when doing so would harm others. This is demonstrated by the many lies of the patriarchs and prophets, who became all things to all people and, by lying, relaxed something of the strictness of perfection. — This opinion is not safe, as Augustine proves at length in his two books Against Lying, addressed to Consent­ius, and condemns it among the heretics called Priscillianists. Hence Innocent III, in chapter *Super eo* of *De Usuris*, decrees that the command of God’s word protects the principle that no one may lie even to preserve another’s life. Before this truth was defined by the Church, however, some Fathers, following Plato in Book V of the *Republic*, held that a prudent man could use a beneficial lie just as he might use medicine. Thus Origen, in Books VI and X of the *Stromata*; Chrysostom, at the end of Book I *On the Priesthood*, and in Homilies 32 and 53 on Genesis, and in his letter to Olympias; and Saint Jerome, in his commentary on chapter II of the Epistle to the Galatians—a position which Augustine reproaches him for in a letter. Cassian therefore followed the opinion of these men before the Church decreed the contrary.

Conference 20, chapter 8.

Who is unable humbly to say: “I have made my sin known to you, and I have not concealed my iniquity,” so that through this confession he may confidently add: “And you forgave the wickedness of my heart”? But if, held back by shame, you are embarrassed to reveal these things before human beings, do not cease to confess them through continual supplication to him from whom they cannot be hidden, and to say: “I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is always before me; against you alone have I sinned, and I have done evil before you,” for he is accustomed both to heal without exposing anyone to shame and to forgive sins without reproach. — He does not appear to deny the necessity of secret repentance and confession, but of public repentance and confession, which Cassian himself mentions in Book II of the *Institutes of Renunciation*, chapters 15 and 16; Book III, chapter 7; Book IV, chapters 16 and 20; and Book I *On the Incarnation*, chapter 4. Certainly, if anyone carefully examines his words, he will notice that they suit public penance for secret sins. “If,” he says, “you are embarrassed to reveal your sins before human beings”—he did not say “before a human being” or “before a priest”—and he adds: “God is accustomed to forgive without anyone’s exposure to shame and without reproach.” For both exposure and reproach are far removed from secret confession. That he was not speaking of secret confession is indicated by the fact that no ancient or modern writer ever charged him with this error. He therefore seems to have followed his teacher Chrysostom, who speaks in this way throughout; yet neither Chrysostom nor his predecessor Nectarius ever abolished secret confession, but only public confession, as the Dean of Louvain proves at length against Calvin in Article 5, *On Confession*.

Conference 21, chapter 4.

[Col. 0362D]

Thus we understand David’s knowledge of the precepts of the law. Although Moses commanded that retaliation be exacted from enemies, David not only did not do this but also embraced his persecutors with love, piously praying to the Lord on their behalf, lamenting and weeping, and avenging the slain. — “He commanded,” he says, and rightly so: a command is indeed given in Exodus XXI, Leviticus XXIV, and Deuteronomy XIX. But it is given to judges, who are God’s ministers for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good. It is not commanded to private persons; rather, it is forbidden to them, as is said in Deuteronomy XXXII: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay.” The Apostle Paul cites this in the Epistle to the Romans, chapter XII, in these words: “It is written: ‘Vengeance is mine, I will repay.’” Nevertheless, neither Moses nor any law prohibited private persons, once hatred had been laid aside and scandal removed, from seeking punishment from judges out of zeal for justice or the common good, or for the correction of the sinner, as Saint Thomas explains at length in II–II, question 108. For Augustine explains the Gospel’s teachings concerning enduring injuries and forgiving them, in Book *On the Sermon on the Mount*, chapter 34, not always according to the outward performance of the act but according to the disposition of the mind. David is said to have gone beyond this concession of the law because he was unwilling to use the law that commanded judges to exact retaliation, especially when those who had been injured demanded it.

In the same place, chapter 10.

Cassian narrates the deed of Theonas, who, after completing his marriage, abandoned his wife and professed the monastic life—not, perhaps, with the zeal of a panegyrist, but with the fidelity of a narrator—and adds: “I think that the judgment pronounced by so many spiritual men under God’s authority did not err; and this was also confirmed by the great admiration for the signs, as has already been said above.” — These words indicate that a special impulse of the Holy Spirit intervened, either impelling him to act or confirming the deed through the power of miracles. This occurred beyond the ordinary order and law, so that we would have something to admire, not something to imitate.

In the same place, chapter 29.

For understanding chapter 29 of column 21, it should first be noted that theologians distinguish two forms of force and authority belonging to both divine and human law. One serves as a rule directing human actions and binding transgressors by the bond of sin; the other compels subjects to observe the law by restraining them with threats and punishments. All Catholics agree that, with respect to its directive force, everyone is subject to the law—unjust and just, imperfect and perfect alike—so that those who knowingly and willingly violate it, even if they had previously been most holy, incur both guilt and liability to punishment. But with respect to the power of compulsion and punishment, the Apostle Paul exempts perfect men from the law when he says: “The law is not laid down for the righteous,” because they obey the law not under compulsion and fear of punishment but out of charity, which, if it is perfect, “casts out fear.” Augustine holds this view in Sermon 10 on Psalm CXVIII; so also Cassian in Book IV of the *Institutes of Renunciation*, chapter 39, and Conference 21, chapter 13.

Once this has been explained, what Cassian writes about Lent in the same conference, chapter 29, can easily be interpreted in a Catholic manner. He says:

“Therefore, the just and perfect man is not bound by this law of Lent, nor is he satisfied with submission to this small canon, which the leaders of the Churches certainly established for those who are entangled throughout the entire year in pleasures or secular business, so that, compelled by this kind of legal necessity, they would at least on these days be forced to devote themselves to the Lord and dedicate to him a tenth of the days of their life—days which they would otherwise consume altogether, as it were, like fruits. But the righteous, for whom the law is not laid down, and who devote not a small portion—that is, a tenth—but the whole of their life to spiritual matters, are free from the obligation of legal tithes. Therefore, if an honorable and holy necessity overtakes and constrains them, they dare to relax their station of fasting without argument.”

Rabanus proves this same point in Book II of *The Institution of Clergy*, chapter 20, and Isidore in Book I of *Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 36; both confirm it by Cassian’s testimony. Nevertheless, some suspect that Cassian here favors the Begards and Beguines, whose heresies were condemned under Clement V at the Council of Vienne and recorded among the Clementines in *Clementine Ad nostrum*, *On Heretics*. Concerning their second and third errors, the council writes:

“Second, they assert that a person need neither fast nor pray after attaining this degree of perfection, because sensuality is then so perfectly subject to the spirit and reason that a person may freely grant the body whatever it desires. Third, they assert that those who are in the aforesaid degree of perfection and in the spirit of freedom are not subject to human obedience and are bound by no precepts of the Church, because, as they say, ‘Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.’”

Cassian displays neither error. In Conference 10, chapter 10, he says that the perfect fast throughout the whole year, while they pray at every moment and in every action. In addition to the very frequent praises of obedience with which he filled all his *Institutes* and *Conferences*, he adds in Conference 19, chapter 6, among the advantages of communal life in the monastery, this statement by Abbot John:

“Subject to the abbot until the end, I seem in some measure to imitate him of whom it is said: ‘He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death’; and may I deserve humbly to say his words: ‘I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me, the Father.’”

Cassian therefore does not exempt the perfect from the law of Lent either in the name of perfection or under the pretext of that empty freedom on which the Begards and Beguines relied when they said: “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.” Rather, he does so for three reasons that can be gathered from his words. First, because the Apostle says in I Timothy I: “The law is not laid down for the righteous.” Second, because those who devote their entire life to spiritual duties are free from the obligation of legal tithes, and he says that Lent is such a tithe, by which a kind of tenth of the year’s days is rendered to God. Finally, it is permitted if an honorable and holy necessity overtakes and constrains them.

These three reasons are true if properly understood. As to the first, it is well known that just and perfect men are indeed bound by the law and become liable to guilt and punishment if they do not follow it as a guide to right living. Nevertheless, they are called free from the law insofar as it compels people to worship and obey through terrors and punishments. Just men do not need this fear of severity, because the grace and charity of the Holy Spirit have enlarged their hearts so that they may run in the way of God’s commandments. Cassian explains himself in this sense in the present conference, chapter 13, and in Book IV of the *Institutes of Renunciation*, chapter 39.

The second reason has force among those who hold that such persons are not bound by the law, especially human law, when the law’s purpose and rationale no longer apply. For if the forty-day fast was instituted so that a kind of tenth of the year’s time might be paid to the Author of time, those who offer their entire life and themselves wholly to God as a kind of holocaust abundantly pay it—in great endurance, afflictions, necessities, distresses, labors, vigils, fastings, chastity, and so forth. Certainly, if the authority of a law rests upon the law’s purpose, they cannot fail to approve, according to Cassian’s reasoning, those who derive the obligation of the law from its purpose.

Although the Church has nowhere condemned this opinion—in fact, many very learned men defend it—it does not entirely satisfy me unless Cassian’s third reason is added: an honorable and holy necessity. If this necessity is evident, and access to the prelates, who possess the authority to dispense from such ecclesiastical sanctions, is not readily available, each person may of himself suspend the fast, as Thomas teaches in II–II, question 147, article 4.

Conference 21, chapter 30.

It should certainly be understood that this observance of Lent did not exist at all as long as the perfection of that primitive Church remained inviolate. Those who enclosed the whole year within an equal fast were not confined within the narrow limits of fasts by the necessity of this precept or as though constrained by a legal sanction. But when the multitude of believers, departing from that apostolic devotion, began day by day to cling to their possessions and did not divide them for the use of all according to the apostles’ institutions, but, privately providing for their own expenses, strove not merely to preserve them but also to increase them—content not merely to follow the example of Ananias and Sapphira—it pleased all the priests at that time to recall people bound by secular cares and almost, so to speak, ignorant of self-restraint or compunction, to the holy work through the canonical imposition of fasts, and to compel them, as it were, by the necessity of legal tithes. This could indeed benefit the weak, but it could not prejudice the perfect, who, living under the grace of the Gospel, surpass the law voluntarily through devotion.

This passage does not entirely conflict with the very consistent opinion of the Fathers, who trace Lent back to the tradition of the apostles. Although the rationale for instituting the Lenten fast was consecrated both by the fasts of Moses, Elijah, and Christ and by the Lord’s general command concerning fasting, when he says in Luke V: “The days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they will fast,” and so forth, as well as by the many benefits that arise from fasting, it could nevertheless have happened that during the earliest years of the nascent Church almost everyone fasted daily and that there was no command concerning Lent. The command may have been added later, by the decision of all the priests—that is, the apostles and elders—to restrain the license that had already begun to spread among certain people. Luke testifies in Acts XV that the apostles were accustomed to summon the elders also to council.

It is therefore certain that Lent was instituted by the apostles; it is also probable that the Church began with it. Yet this is not so certain that Cassian could not, in a Catholic manner, have held that it was instituted after some years—namely, ten or twelve—and instituted in such a way that it did not prejudice the perfect, as Cassian says, in the manner explained in the preceding chapter, while recalling the incontinent to the duty from which they had departed, since they were the principal reason for its institution. Saint Leo indicates this not obscurely in Sermon 4 on Lent:

“Such uninterrupted devotion and continued reverence were indeed owed to these great mysteries, so that we should remain in God’s sight such as it is fitting for us to be found at the very feast of Easter. But because this strength belongs to few, and because more rigorous observance is relaxed through the weakness of the flesh, while the cares of this life stretch us in various directions, it is necessary that even religious hearts become soiled by the dust of the world. Therefore, by the great and salutary providence of divine institution, a forty-day exercise was provided to restore purity of mind, during which the sins of other times might be redeemed by pious works and dissolved through chaste fasting.”

Book V of the *Institutes of Renunciation*, chapter 40.

[Col. 0365C] He praises two young men who preferred to lose their lives rather than eat figs contrary to the command of their elders, when they had nothing else available. — He rightly praises their obedience and simplicity, on account of which the act was not counted as a fault against them, although in itself it was not done wisely, since they could have interpreted the elder’s command in their own favor in an extreme necessity—unless their inexperience due to age prevented them—if doing so would have been sufficient to preserve their lives.

Book XII of the *Institutes of Renunciation*, chapters 4 and 5.

The devil lost the blessedness that he enjoyed as God’s gift. — Understand this as the blessedness of the way, not of the homeland. The former consists in faith, hope, love, and contemplation of the absent good; the latter in seeing God face to face and knowing him as we have been known.

Book III of the *Institutes of Renunciation*, chapter 2.

A voluntary gift is more pleasing than offerings rendered under canonical compulsion. — “More pleasing,” supply: to us; for God, not in the same way, except incidentally, since sadness arising from a command greatly diminishes the cheerfulness of the soul, and such an affection is more suited to the growth of spiritual gifts than sadness arising from necessity. “For God loves a cheerful giver.”

In the same place, chapters 9 and 10.

He thinks that the reason for the former Roman practice of fasting on Saturday was that the Romans asserted that the Apostle Peter had fasted on that day in preparation for his conflict with Simon Magus, whereas previously there had been no Saturday fast. — But Innocent I, in Letter 1 to the Bishop of Eugubium, chapter 4, teaches that one should fast on Friday and Saturday because on those two days they fasted in mourning for the death of Christ the Lord. If both reasons cannot be true, Cassian was mistaken in his historical account. Since he was far from Rome, he reported it as he had received it from certain Romans, who, Augustine reports in Letter 86 to Casulanus, held this opinion, although he adds that most Romans judged it false.

Cassian also adds that throughout the East people fast on five days of the week by apostolic tradition, while the fast is relaxed on Saturday and Sunday so that the body may not waste away from hunger. Augustine testifies that this was observed by many, especially monks. At Rome, too, very few clerics or monks fasted for six days, relaxing the fast only on Sunday.

Cassian also agrees with Augustine that Saturday was not a fast day either in the East or in many parts of the West. From this they rightly conclude that this practice did not depart from the tradition of the apostles. Nor does Innocent say that the Saturday fast was instituted by an apostolic command, but by apostolic example—namely, because the apostles fasted when Christ suffered.

Augustine nevertheless held that Wednesday and Friday had been assigned to fasting by the apostles: Wednesday because they then took counsel about killing the Lord, and Friday because he died on that day. On Saturday, because he rested in the tomb after completing the work of redemption, just as God rested after completing the work of creation, Augustine says that [Col. 0366B] the variation arose whereby some—especially the peoples of the East—preferred to relax the fast in order to signify rest, while others fasted because of the humility of the Lord’s death, as did the Roman Church and certain Western Churches, including the African Church. Augustine’s mother came from that Church to Milan and, finding that people there did not fast on Saturday, received this response from Ambrose: “When I am at Rome, I fast on Saturday; when I am here, I do not fast,” as Augustine relates in the same work and in Letter 128 to Januarius.

Indeed, concerning the annual fast on Wednesday and Friday, as a practice received throughout the Church and handed down by the apostles, Clement of Alexandria in Book VII of the *Stromata*, Epiphanius in Heresy 75, Origen in Homily 10 on Leviticus, and Damascene in his *Book on Heresies*, under the heading “The Aerianists,” write the same as Augustine.

Book V of the *Institutes of Renunciation*, chapter 34.

Abbot Theodore advises the monk who wishes to attain knowledge of the Scriptures that he should devote his effort and diligence more to purifying his mind than to the books of commentators. Certainly he teaches nothing other than what all the Fathers teach: that the principal support for understanding the Scriptures lies in purity of heart. Yet he does not condemn the books of commentators, especially those of the saints. Otherwise he would condemn himself, since in the final book *On the Incarnation of the Lord* he draws from the books of the Fathers the clearest testimonies against Nestorius; and he could not have drawn them out unless he had read those books carefully.

Conference 1, chapter 20.

Those who, after professing the monastic life, were captivated by the polish of speech and by certain doctrines of philosophers were deceived in the same way. When they heard these doctrines at first glance, they seemed to accord with certain pious sentiments and with religion; but, like the glitter of gold, they deceived those whom they had once attracted by their surface, and, like people deceived by bronze and counterfeit coins, left them perpetually naked and wretched—either recalling them to the noise of the world or dragging them into heretical errors and arrogant presumptions. We also read that Achar suffered the same fate in the Book of Joshua: desiring and stealing a golden bar from the camp of the foreigners, he deserved to be struck with an anathema and condemned to eternal death.

Cassian does not condemn the study of eloquence or philosophy, by which we are aided both in understanding the invisible things of God through the things that have been made and in explaining, defending, and adorning the truth of divine doctrines. Rather, he reproves the unwary, who are captured by certain empty inventions of the philosophers instead of extracting gold from their dung, and who contaminate themselves with Egyptian superstition instead of taking vessels from them as from unjust possessors and transferring them to the worship of the true God. Augustine teaches that this should be done in Book II of *Christian Doctrine*, chapter 4, when one occupies oneself with pagan books. Those who have not used this discernment and discrimination have found in philosophy the seedbed and nourishment of many heresies, as Tertullian writes in his book *On the Prescription Against Heretics* and in his book *Against Hermogenes*.

Book VIII of the *Institutes of Renunciation*, chapter 20.

It should nevertheless be understood that in the wording found in certain copies—“Whoever is angry with his brother without cause will be liable to judgment”—the words “without cause” are superfluous and were added by those who did not think anger should be removed even when there were just causes. For no one who has been moved to anger, however unreasonable the provocation, will say that he is angry without cause. It is therefore apparent that these words were added by those who did not understand the intention of Scripture, which wishes to remove the fuel of anger altogether and to leave no occasion for indignation at all. Otherwise, when we are commanded to be angry with cause, an opportunity for being angry without cause is introduced to us.

The end of patience consists not in becoming justly angry but in not becoming angry at all. I know, however, that some interpret the words “without cause” in this way: namely, that the person is angry without cause when, while angry, he is not permitted to seek vengeance. It is nevertheless better to retain the wording as it is found in many new copies and in all the ancient ones.

Jerome had said the same before Cassian in commenting on Matthew V: “Whoever is angry with his brother.” “In some manuscripts,” he says, “there is added ‘without cause’; but in the true and definitive wording the sentence is complete, and anger is entirely removed.” And against the Pelagians: “Whoever is angry with his brother without cause will be liable to judgment,” although in many ancient copies “without cause” is not added, so that we understand that we ought not to become angry even with cause. Augustine says the same in Book I of the *Retractions*, chapter 19.

Nevertheless, we should not think that these teachers wished to commend the Stoic ἀπάθεια (*apatheia*), which Augustine rightly refutes in Book IX of *The City of God*, chapter 4. For if anger is not present when there is cause, as Chrysostom says in Homily 11 on Matthew, neither does instruction make progress, nor do judgments stand, nor are crimes restrained.

By the word “anger,” therefore, Jerome and Cassian understood a certain emotion that precedes reason. Even if it arises from a just cause, it cannot preserve due measure; for this reason they advise that one should not become angry at all. Others sometimes allow anger because they understand by it the emotion that awakens and is governed by the authority of reason. Hence Saint Gregory says in Book I of the *Moralia*, chapter 33:

“One must take the greatest care that anger, which is assumed as an instrument of virtue, not dominate the mind. It should not go before the mind as a mistress, but should never depart from behind reason as a servant prepared to obey.”

Although Cassian, in the same book, chapters 6, 7, and 8, suggests that the ministry of anger has been implanted in us solely so that we may be angry at the unruly impulses and vices of our own soul, he nevertheless indicates clearly in Conference 16, chapter 26, that for the same reason anger may sometimes be expressed toward others when reason requires it. He writes:

“I did not say that the virtue and endurance of one who is strong and robust must be overcome, but that the grievous sickness of one who is weak, nourished by the support of one who is healthy and daily slipping into a worse condition, will generate reasons why he should no longer be supported.”

Conference 11, chapter 13.

[Col. 0368B] Cassian calls Christ *homo Dominicus*, “the Lordly man,” just as many ancient Fathers had previously done, as had Augustine in Book LXXXIII of the *Questions*, question 36. Augustine later corrected this expression in Book I of the *Retractions*, chapter 19, because, since Christ is Lord, it would be improper to call him *Dominicus*. The expression would imply that the man was not God and Lord but merely “Lordly”—that is, a human supposit united to the Lord, or to the Lord’s supposit. Thus two supposits would be posited in Christ, which is Nestorian.

Since it is certain that Cassian not only did not agree with Nestorius but wrote seven books against him, in which he proves that Christ has not two persons but one, the expression *homo Dominicus* must be excused in his case in the manner proposed by Saint Thomas in Part III, question 16, article 3:

“‘The Lordly man’ could be defended in a certain respect, because one might say that the expression ‘the Lordly man’ is used on account of the human nature signified by the term ‘man,’ but not on account of the supposit.”

See Rufinus in his *Apology for Origen*, near the end.

[Col. 0367]

ANNOTATION ON CASSIAN’S DOCTRINE BY DIDACUS ALVAREZ. From Book I, disputation 2, section 3, *On the Divine Helps of Grace and the Powers of Free Will*. Cassian’s error concerning the necessity of grace and the natural powers of our free will.

[Col. 0367C] Before presenting Cassian’s statements, it should be observed that in Conference 13 of Abbot Chaeremon, he disclosed the same abbot’s mind concerning grace and free will. Since he does not reject that opinion, he appears to follow it; for this reason Saint Prosper vigorously attacks him in the book he composed against the *Collator*, and demonstrates with the clearest arguments, drawn from Sacred Scripture and Augustine’s writings, that he does not depart from the paths of the Pelagians. Hence Pope Gelasius, in distinction 15, chapter *Sancta Romana*, also numbers John Cassian’s book called the *Pastor* among the apocrypha. The doctors of Louvain, who are highly learned in Augustine’s doctrine, likewise appended certain annotations and a censure concerning various statements of Cassian at the end of the Antwerp edition of 1578.

Cassian’s first statement is therefore this: In fallen nature, man possesses a natural judgment by which to know good and evil, and a natural capacity to embrace either one. His words are as follows (Conference 13, chapter 12, at the beginning):

“For one must not believe that God made man in such a way that he can neither ever will nor ever be able to do good. Otherwise he would not have left him free will, if he had granted him only the ability and will to choose evil, while not granting him the ability or will to choose good from himself.”

A little later he proves that the human race did not lose the knowledge of good after Adam’s transgression, citing Romans II: “For when the Gentiles, who do not have the law, do by nature the things of the law,” and so forth. He says:

“Adam therefore acquired, after his transgression, the knowledge of evil, which he had not possessed; but he did not lose the knowledge of good, which he had received.”

Finally, the Apostle’s statement most clearly declares that the human race did not lose the knowledge of good after the transgression: “For when the Gentiles, who do not have the law, do by nature the things of the law” (Romans II). A little farther on he adds:

“Finally, to indicate that they possess the ability, when rebuking the Pharisees he says: ‘Why do you not even judge for yourselves what is right?’ (Luke XII). He certainly would not have said this to them unless he knew that by natural judgment they were able to distinguish what is equitable.”

We must therefore beware lest we refer all the merits of the saints to God in such a way that we attribute to human nature nothing except what is evil and perverse. A little later he says:

“Free will always remains in man, by which he can either neglect or love the grace of God.”

Second, he says that man naturally possesses certain seeds of virtue, which nevertheless cannot reach perfection except through grace:

“There can therefore be no doubt,” he says (the chapter cited above), “that the seeds of virtue are naturally present in every soul, implanted by the Creator’s gift. But unless they are aroused by God’s assistance, they cannot advance toward perfection, because, according to the Apostle: ‘Neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the growth’” (I Corinthians III).

And in chapter 8:

“When God perceives in us a certain beginning of good will, he immediately illuminates, strengthens, and urges it toward salvation, granting growth to what he himself has planted or has seen emerge through our effort.”

Third, he says that man can possess charity by the mere power of free will. This assertion is gathered from his statements in Conference 13, chapter 14, where, explaining Deuteronomy XIII according to the Septuagint—“The Lord your God tests you so that it may become evident whether you love him with all your heart and with all your soul, or not”—he says:

“Certainly, he would not have permitted them to be tested by the Lord’s justice unless he knew that an equal power of resisting was present in them, by which, according to the judgment of equity, they could be judged either guilty or praiseworthy in either respect.”

The same conclusion is drawn from chapter 10, where he acknowledges that the seeds of virtue are naturally present in every soul. He includes charity among them, since he speaks absolutely about the virtues. Hence Saint Prosper attributes this statement to Cassian when he says (Book *Against the Collator*, chapter 30):

“And according to this man, such is the soundness or capacity of free will that he possesses charity, which stands at the summit of all the virtues, not as a gift from God but from the will alone.”

Fourth, he says that man in fallen nature possesses sufficient strength to resist even the more serious temptations and to overcome every difficulty. Thus he says in Conference 13, chapter 14, speaking of Job’s temptations, which were extremely severe:

“But since the slanderous enemy, after the conflict, dared not repeat any complaint of this kind against him, he confessed that he had been overcome not by God’s strength but by Job’s. Yet we must not believe that God’s grace was entirely absent from him, since it granted the tempter as much power to tempt as it knew Job possessed strength to resist, not protecting him from the enemy’s assault in such a way as to leave no place for human virtue.”

A little later he says:

“Why would it be necessary for those to be tested whom he knows to be so weak and fragile that they are entirely unable by their own virtue to resist the tempter? Certainly the Lord’s justice would not have permitted them to be tested unless he knew that an equal power of resisting was present in them, by which, according to the judgment of equity, they could be judged either guilty or praiseworthy in either respect.”

And in Conference 7, chapter 7, when Germanus says: “We would believe that resisting them”—that is, the terrible temptations of the adversaries—“was impossible for this especially fragile flesh, unless your statements, like heavenly oracles, encouraged us to this conviction,” he replies in chapter 8 of the same conference:

“Therefore, just as they possess an abundance of means for instigation, so freedom has been granted to us as the power either to reject or to consent.”

In chapter 14 he explains the statement: “God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond what you can bear” (I Corinthians X), as referring to the power to resist temptations through the capacity of nature. He says:

“‘God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond what you can bear, but with the temptation he will also provide a way out, so that you may be able to endure.’ When he says, ‘Let the one who stands take heed lest he fall,’ he makes free will vigilant. He certainly knew that, after receiving grace, it could stand through diligence or fall through negligence.”

A little later:

“‘God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond what you can bear.’ The Lord does not wish that they should not be permitted to be tempted, but that they should not be tempted beyond what they were able to endure. The former indicates the capacity of human free will; the latter demonstrates the grace of the Lord, who moderates the struggles of temptation.”

Fifth, he says that God awaits our efforts and that at times he goes before us. Cassian explicitly presents the first part of this statement in Conference 13, chapter 13, when he says:

“Thus the grace of God always cooperates with our will for what is good and assists, protects, and defends it in everything, so that at times it even demands or awaits from it certain efforts of good will. Otherwise it might seem to bestow its gifts upon one who is completely asleep or dissolved in idle inactivity, seeking, as it were, occasions through which, once the sluggishness of human indolence has been shaken off, the generosity of its munificence may not appear unreasonable.”

And in chapter 12 he says:

“He awaits us, as it is said through the Prophet: ‘Therefore the Lord waits, that he may have mercy on us’” (Isaiah XXX).

But that God does not always precede [human willing], he affirms in the same chapter 12, when he says:

> “The mercy of the Lord therefore precedes the will of man,”

of which it is said:

> “My God, his mercy will precede me” (Psalm 58).

And again, while the Lord delays and, in a certain useful sense, holds back in order to test our free choice, our will precedes him, when it is said:

> “And in the morning my prayer will precede you” (Psalm 87).

And in chapter 17 he teaches that God sometimes stimulates the course of some who are willing and thirsting to a greater ardor, but compels others even when unwilling and resisting. He repeats the same point in chapter 18, where he says:

> “To receive some who are willing and running, but to drag others who are unwilling and resisting, and to compel them to a good will.”

He says, sixth, that everything must not be attributed to grace in such a way that no praise or effort remains to free choice. For he says (Conference 13, chapter 14):

> “For there would be no praise or merit if Christ had preferred in him that which he himself had bestowed; otherwise he would have said: ‘I have not found such faith in Israel.’” [Col. 0370B]

Saint Prosper also attributes this assertion to Cassian (Book Against the Collations, definition 11), when he says:

> “It is an impious opinion that considers the person to whom God has given nothing happier than the one to whom he has granted everything.”

He says, seventh, that by the capacity of nature a person can seek a physician and desire health:

> “For,” he says (the same Conference, chapter 9, at the end), “when someone wishes to enjoy health, or to be freed from the disease of sickness according to the desire of his free choice, [this does not occur simply by his willing it]. What benefit is there, however, in having desired the grace of health, unless the Lord, who grants the use of life itself, also bestows the strength of soundness?”

Saint Prosper, attacking these words (Saint Prosper, Book Against the Collations, chapter 8), says:

> “You therefore teach that a person cannot obtain health by himself, but that he has from himself the desire for health and comes to the physician solely by his own will; yet you do not also acknowledge that it belongs to the physician himself that he comes.”

He says, eighth, that when a person, relying on the resources of nature, strives to do what lies within him, grace is given by which God directs and strengthens nature’s good efforts and stimulates the will toward salvation. But lest he appear to agree with Pelagius, he qualifies this assertion by saying that those efforts are neither meritorious of grace nor always necessary.

That grace is given to a person striving by the powers of nature, he affirms in Conference 13, chapter 8, when he says:

> “When he has perceived in us some beginning of a good will, he immediately enlightens it, strengthens it, and stimulates it toward salvation, granting it growth—whether he himself planted it or saw it arise through our effort.”

And in chapter 11:

> “For when God sees us turning our will toward the good, he meets us, directs us, and strengthens us: ‘As soon as he hears the voice of your cry, he will answer you’” (Isaiah 30).

That those efforts are not meritorious of grace, he asserts at the very beginning of chapter 16 of the same Conference, when he says:

> “Let no one suppose that these things have been stated by us in order to assert that the whole of salvation rests within the control of our faith, according to the profane opinion of certain people who, assigning everything to free choice, define God’s grace as distributed according to each person’s merit.” [Col. 0370D]

And in chapter 13, after he had said that God sometimes demands or awaits certain efforts of good will, he adds:

> “Nevertheless, the grace of God always remains free, since by certain small and slight efforts it bestows, with immeasurable generosity, such great glory of immortality and such great gifts of everlasting blessedness.”

And shortly afterward:

> “However much human frailty may have exerted itself, it cannot be equal to the recompense that is to come; nor does it diminish divine grace by its labors in such a way that grace does not always remain.”

That these efforts are not always necessary, he affirms in the chapter cited above, chapter 13, saying:

> “Thus the grace of God always cooperates with our free choice for the good, and in everything assists, protects, and defends it, so that it sometimes even demands or awaits from it certain efforts of good will.” [Col. 0371A]

“Sometimes,” he says, not “always.” And in chapter 17:
