> “By these examples, therefore, which we have brought forward from the Gospel records, we shall be able to perceive most clearly that God provides for the salvation of the human race in diverse and innumerable ways and by inscrutable paths; that he invites the course of some who are willing and thirsting to a greater ardor, but compels others even when unwilling and resisting. At one time, in order that those things may be fulfilled which he has usefully perceived to be desired by us, he assists them; at another, he even inspires the beginnings of that holy desire, or grants the beginning of a good work or perseverance.”

By saying, plainly, that he “invites the course of some who are willing and thirsting to a greater ardor” but “compels others who are unwilling,” he sufficiently indicates that preceding efforts of good will are not always necessary for the assistance of grace to be conferred upon a person.

He says, ninth, that prevenient grace depends upon the works of nature, and that this is the true causal relationship: because a person supplies the beginning of a good will, God therefore has mercy on him. This is clear from Conference 13, chapter 11, at the beginning, where he says:

> “These matters are in some fashion so indiscriminately mixed and confused that among many people the question of what depends upon what is debated at great length: namely, whether God has mercy on us because we have supplied the beginning of a good will, or whether, because God has mercy, we attain the beginning of a good will. For many, believing one or the other of these points and asserting it too strongly, have become entangled in various errors that contradict one another.”

In the course of the same Conference he teaches that sometimes God has mercy on us because we supply the beginning of a good will, while at other times, because God has mercy, we attain the beginning of a good will. He thus indicates quite openly that the assistance of prevenient grace is given on account of that good use of our will.

The same conclusion is drawn from the same Conference, chapter 9, where he understands the Apostle’s words—“God will repay each person according to his works” (Romans 2)—as referring to works of nature preceding grace. Hence Saint Prosper attributes this assertion to Cassian, when he says (Book Against the Collations, chapter 6):

> “How, then, do you fail to notice that you fall into the condemnation which, whether you wish it or not, you are convicted of expressing—namely, that the grace of God is given according to our merits—when you assert that some good work proceeds from human beings themselves, on account of which they obtain grace?”

Cassian, however, qualifies this statement, as he does the preceding one, by saying that grace is not given because of those good works as though they were merits, but as though they were merely an occasion. This is evident from Book 12 of the Institutes, chapter 14, where he says:

> “For [God] stands ready, with only the occasion supplied to him by us through a good will, to bestow all these things.”

By these words he excludes all merit from the works of nature, both merit *de condigno*—merit of worthiness—and merit *de congruo*—merit of fittingness—since he says that those works are merely the occasion by which God, once they have been received, bestows the prior helps of prevenient grace.

And in the same chapter he explicitly excludes merit *de condigno*. For among other things he says:

> “For according to the Savior’s statement, we say that what is given is given to those who ask, that what is opened is opened to those who knock, and that what is found is found by those who seek; but our asking and knocking are not worthy unless the mercy of God gives what we ask.”

Hilary appears to have understood the error of the Semipelagians in this sense in his letter to Augustine, when he reports that they asserted:

> “Grace is not denied if it is said that a will may precede which seeks only a physician, although it is not itself yet capable of anything.”

The Council of Orange speaks in the same sense, canon 6:

> “If anyone says that, without the grace of God, mercy is bestowed upon us who believe, will, desire, and knock.”

“Mercy,” it says. For the Massilians admitted that the aids of prevenient and assisting grace were given out of mercy, not as a debt of justice, to those who, by the capacity of nature, asked, sought, and knocked, although they held that God bestowed them on the occasion of these efforts of nature. [Col. 0372A]

Some more recent theologians, among those who deny that God, by assisting actual grace, effectively moves, applies, or predetermines the created will to consent, acknowledge that this was likewise the Semipelagian position. They confirm this by the authority of the holy Fathers, especially Augustine, Book *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 2, where he says:

> “See whether anything else is being done in this manner except that grace is given in some way according to our merits, and thus grace is no longer grace.”

There they emphasize the expression “in some way,” since it extends merit to every possible form of merit.

Finally, he says that God’s predestination is general with respect to everyone and not gratuitous with respect to some. This is clear from Conference 13, chapter 7, where he says:

> “When his goodness has perceived that even the smallest spark of a good will has flashed forth—or one which he himself has struck from the hard flint of our body—he cherishes and revives it, strengthening it by his inspiration; and he wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.”

And shortly afterward:

> “For how can he who does not will that even one of the little ones should perish be thought, without grave sacrilege, to will that, in place of all without exception, only some should be saved?”

Let these remarks, stated in general terms, suffice concerning the error of the Pelagians and Semipelagians. From them each person will easily be able to gather in what respects the Semipelagians differ from the Pelagians and in what respects they agree with them.

At the conclusion of this discussion, one point must be noted: although Faustus and Cassian admitted some kind or other of prevenient grace, in practice they ultimately denied it when they asserted that grace is given to us according to the merit of faith. Hence Maxentius, speaking against Faustus, who in his book had promised to prove against Pelagius that grace is not given according to our merits, says:

> “Afterward, however, forgetting his promise, he is clearly shown to have emptied grace entirely.”

# In the Year of Our Lord 430. Vigilius the Deacon

[Col. 0373]

## Prolegomena

[Col. 0373A] “Vigilius the Deacon,” says Gennadius in chapter 51, “compiled, from the tradition of the Fathers, a Rule for Monks which is read in the coenobium, in the assembly, for the advancement of the brothers. It contains within itself the discipline of the entire monastic profession, expressed in concise and clear language.”

The following is found in Trithemius’s *Commentaries*:

> “Vigilius the Deacon and monk, a man devoted to and learned in the Holy Scriptures, guardian and director of monastic discipline, is said to have composed certain brief works for the edification of monks, but the distance of places and times prevented them from reaching our knowledge. The presbyter Gennadius says that he wrote, in a single book, a very useful Rule concerning the conduct of monks. He says nothing about the other works. He flourished under the emperors Honorius and Theodosius, in the year 420.” [Col. 0373B]

Nevertheless, this Rule exists under the title *The Eastern Rule*, compiled from the Rules of the Eastern Fathers by Vigilius the Deacon, in the *Codex of Rules* published at Rome in 1661 in quarto by Lucas Holstenius; in the Paris edition of 1663, in quarto, part 1, pages 88–95; and in the new edition prepared by Marianus Brockie and published after his death by his associates at Augsburg in 1759, in six folio volumes, volume 1, pages 60–64.

[Col. 0374A] Thus Schoenemannus. Earlier, the editor himself, Marianus Brockie, had said the following about Vigilius’s Rule:

> “Up to this point, eight Rules of the Eastern Fathers have been presented in this *Codex* of Lucas Holstenius. From these Vigilius the Deacon composed this Rule for Monks, which may therefore rightly be called Eastern, although it appears to have been written in the West. Gennadius praises this Rule and asserts that it contains, in concise and clear language, the discipline of the entire monastic profession. Accordingly, Saint Benedict, abbot of Aniane, inserted much from it into his *Concordance of Rules*, as did Smaragdus, abbot of Saint Michael in Lorraine, in his *Exposition of the Benedictine Rule*.

> “This Rule consists of forty-seven chapters, containing everything that pertains to the good governance of any monastery; it is for the most part drawn from the Rule of Saint Pachomius, since the actual sayings of Saint Pachomius are often found in it. Vigilius the Deacon certainly lived in the fifth century, but it is unknown to which Church he was a deacon, although it may be supposed that he flourished among the Gauls, since some maintain that this Eastern Rule, composed by him, was observed in the monastery of Saint Maximinus at Trier during the same century.” [Col. 0374B]

[Col. 0373]

# The Rule of Vigilius the Deacon for Monks, Commonly Called the Eastern Rule

(*Codex of Rules*, Marianus Brockie, volume 1.) (C, S)

[Col. 0373C]

## I

So that the elders may not labor uselessly in governing the brothers, and so that the discipline of the juniors may not waver but remain firm, established by the abbot’s conduct, the abbot must be blameless, strict, patient, given to fasting, devout, and humble, so that he may fulfill the role of teacher and father, presenting himself as a model of good works. All the brothers shall look to his direction and do nothing without his counsel and authority. Bearing the needs of the monastery, he shall judge freely concerning everything in the monastery, showing favoritism toward no one and granting special favor to no one, but judging each person truthfully according to the merits of his daily conduct. He shall admonish, encourage, chastise, condemn, or receive those who come to the monastery, if this seems useful; or expel those who live badly, if necessity requires.

## II

There shall be two elders in the monastery, to whom, whether the abbot is present or absent, the discipline of all the brothers and the entire care of the monastery shall belong. They shall alternate by days and divide between them the burden and needs of the monastery. One of them shall always be present in the monastery during his period of service, to provide assistance to the abbot, to attend to visiting brothers, to go out when common necessity requires, and to exercise care concerning everything that pertains to the monastery’s daily custody and conduct, so that whatever must be done for the service and use of the monastery may be done without negligence or complaint.

The other shall remain with the brothers during his period of service and go out with them for every task and need, taking care that they do nothing contrary to discipline. Observing all the actions of individuals, if he sees anything done contrary to reason, he shall either correct it himself or report it to the abbot.

## III

The man who, according to the order of discipline and by the appointment of the abbot, with the counsel and consent of all the brothers, has been placed over the brothers shall gather to himself all care for the brothers’ discipline and diligence in the monastery. In the abbot’s absence, he shall have the power to do everything that the abbot does when present.

He shall preserve patience, gentleness, humility, charity, and equity, without favoritism, acting so that he neither causes annoyance to the abbot nor makes the brothers suffer through his intemperance. The elder of the monastery who has been placed over the brothers shall observe these things and report everything to the abbot, especially matters that he does not wish to settle himself.

## IV

No one shall accept a deposit, even from his own brother. No one shall have anything in his cell without the order of the superior—not even the most worthless fruit or anything of that kind.

## V

While working, the brothers shall speak of nothing worldly. They shall either meditate upon holy things or remain silent.

## VI

The person who cooks shall taste nothing before the brothers have been refreshed by food.

[Col. 0375C]

## VII

No one shall have in his cell or house anything except what has been prescribed by the common rule of the monastery.

## VIII

When they have settled down to sleep, they shall not speak to one another. No one shall dare enter another’s cell unless he first knocks at the door.

## IX

No one shall dare exchange with another anything that he has received from the superior. Nor shall anyone accept something better and give something worse, or conversely give something better and receive something worse. No one shall accept anything from another unless the superior has ordered it.

## X

No one shall sleep in a locked cell, nor have a bedroom that can be locked, unless perhaps the father of the monastery has granted this because of someone’s age or illness.

## XI

No one shall remove a cord from the ground without the father’s permission. Whoever finds anything in the monastery belonging to the brothers shall hang it up, so that the person who recognizes it may take it.

## XII

No one shall invent excuses to avoid the assembly or psalmody, claiming to be occupied and unable to go. If someone is in the monastery, in the fields, on a journey, or engaged in any service, he shall not omit the time for prayer and psalmody.

## XIII

The official shall take care that no work is lost in the monastery. In absolutely any craft practiced by the brothers, if something is lost and has been wasted through negligence, the steward of the works shall be rebuked by the father; and he shall in turn rebuke the one who lost the work, but only according to the will and foreknowledge of the superior, without whose authority no one shall have the power to rebuke a brother.

## XIV

If one of the brothers is found to be doing something contentious or contradicting the command of a superior, he shall be rebuked according to the measure of his offense.

## XV

If the father of the monastery hears that someone lies, is found to hate anyone, is disobedient, is excessively devoted to joking, is idle, answers harshly, has a habit of slandering the brothers or outsiders, or in any way does what is contrary to the Rule of Scripture and the discipline of the monastery, he shall punish him according to the measure and nature of the offense.

## XVI

If all the brothers see that the superior is excessively negligent, harsh in rebuking the brothers, or exceeding the measure of the monastery, they shall report this to the father, and he shall rebuke him. The superior himself shall do nothing except what the father orders, especially in a new matter. In matters handed down by custom, he shall observe the Rule of the monastery.

## XVII

The superior shall not become drunk, nor sit in low places. He shall not break the bonds that God established in heaven to be observed on earth. He shall not mourn on the feast day of the Lord and Savior. He shall rule his flesh according to the measure of the saints. He shall not be found in lofty beds, imitating the custom of the pagans. He shall not be double-minded. He shall not follow the thoughts of his own heart, but the law of God. He shall not resist higher authorities with a swollen spirit. He shall not roar or snarl angrily at those beneath him, nor move the boundaries of the Rule.

He shall not be deceitful, nor devise frauds in his thoughts. He shall not neglect the sin of his soul, nor be overcome by the lust of the flesh. He shall not walk carelessly. He shall not speak an idle word. He shall not place a stumbling-block before the feet of the blind. He shall not teach his soul its own will. He shall not be undone by the laughter and jokes of fools. His heart shall not be captured by those who speak foolish and flattering words. He shall not be overcome by gifts, nor be led by the speech of children. He shall not fail in tribulation.

He shall fear not death but God. He shall not become a transgressor because of impending fear. He shall not abandon the true light for the sake of small amounts of food. He shall not waver or vacillate in his works. He shall not change his judgment, but remain firm and steadfast in his decision; just, considering everything; judging truthfully, without desire for glory; open before God and human beings, and far from fraud.

He shall not be ignorant of the conduct of his people, nor blind to their condition. He shall harm no one through pride, nor follow the desires of his eyes. He shall never pass over the truth; he shall hate injustice. He shall never judge according to a person’s status for the sake of gifts, nor condemn an innocent soul through pride. He shall not laugh among children. He shall not abandon the truth because he has been overcome by fear. He shall not despise those who need mercy. He shall not abandon justice because of weariness, nor lose his soul because of shame. He shall not look toward the dishes of a more sumptuous table, nor desire beautiful clothing. He shall not neglect himself, but shall always discern his thoughts.

He shall not become drunk with wine, but shall join truth to humility. [Col. 0377A] When he judges, he shall follow the precepts of his superiors and the law of God, which has been proclaimed throughout the whole world.

## XVIII

If one of the brothers is discovered willingly laughing and playing with children, and maintaining friendships with those of immature age, he shall be warned three times to withdraw from their company and remember propriety and the fear of God. If he does not stop, he shall be corrected as one deserving the severest correction.

## XIX

Those who despise the precepts of their superiors and the Rules of the monastery, which have been established by God’s command, and who make light of the counsel of the elders, shall be corrected according to the established order until they are reformed.

## XX

The elders who are sent outside with the brothers shall have the authority of superiors for as long as they are there, and the brothers shall be governed by their judgment. They shall instruct the brothers for the appointed days. If some disagreement should arise among them, the elders themselves shall hear the matter, judge the case, and rebuke the person at fault; or, at their command, they shall immediately restore peace with a full heart.

## XXI

If a brother has a grievance against his superior, or the superior has some complaint against a brother, brothers of proven conduct and faith shall hear them and judge between them. If the father of the monastery is absent or has gone somewhere, they shall first wait for him. But if they see that he is remaining away for a longer time, they shall then hear the matter between the superior and the brother, lest a greater sadness arise from a judgment long suspended. Both the superior and the subordinate, as well as those who hear the case, shall do everything according to the fear of God and shall give no occasion for discord in anything.

## XXII

No one shall be sent outside alone on any business. Those who are sent shall travel not singly but in pairs or groups of three, so that, while they watch over and console one another, their elders may be secure concerning their honorable conduct and they themselves may not be endangered. They shall nevertheless observe this rule: they must not destroy one another through empty talk or give negligence an opportunity for ruin; each person must be attentive to his own task, according to the time.

## XXIII

When they have returned to the monastery, if before the door they see someone seeking one of his relatives who lives in the monastery, they shall not go to him to report the matter or summon the relative. In general, they shall not presume to recount in the monastery anything they have done outside.

## XXIV

Everyone shall have permission to read until the third hour, unless some circumstance arises that makes it necessary to do something else as well. After the third hour, if anyone fails to observe the established rules, as they are written, because of pride, negligence, or laziness, he shall know that, when he is caught in this error, he is to be judged culpable; for through his error he also leads others into vice.

## XXV

The cellarer shall take care, diligently and faithfully, to preserve with abstinence and sobriety whatever has been brought into the monastery for the brothers’ provisions. He shall receive or distribute nothing without the authority or counsel of the elders.

He shall also guard all the utensils in the monastery—that is, clothing, vessels, tools, and whatever is necessary for daily use—and, whenever something is needed, he shall bring it out and afterward receive it back for storage from the person to whom he entrusted it for use.

For the brothers’ food he shall bring out and distribute what is needed to the weekly servers. For seasoning the food he shall provide what is necessary according to the custom of daily expenditure, neither lavishly nor sparingly, lest through his fault the substance of the monastery be burdened or the brothers suffer injustice.

Considering also the needs and labor of sick brothers, he shall deny them nothing from what he has, insofar as they require it. He shall prepare food for visiting brothers. This shall be the care of the keeper of the cellar, who shall always have recourse to the counsel of the elders and inquire about everything, especially matters that he is unable to carry out by his own understanding.

## XXVI

The doorkeeper shall take care to receive all who arrive within the doors, giving them a proper reply with humility and reverence, and immediately reporting to the abbot or the elders who has come and what he has requested. He shall allow no outsider to suffer injury, nor shall he permit any outsider to speak or transact business with one of the brothers without the abbot’s knowledge or the presence of the elders.

If anything has been sent or entrusted to any of the brothers, nothing shall reach him before it has been reported to the abbot or the elders. Above all, the monastery’s doorkeeper shall observe this: he shall not permit any of the brothers to go outside the door.

## XXVII

If someone approaches the door wishing to renounce the world and join the number of the brothers, he shall not have permission to enter. First the matter shall be reported to the father of the monastery. He shall remain outside the door for a few days and shall be taught the Lord’s Prayer and as many psalms as he can learn. He shall carefully be put to the test, lest perhaps he has done something evil and, disturbed by fear for the moment, should depart, or lest he be under some authority. It shall also be determined whether he can renounce his parents and despise his own property.

If they see that he is suited to everything, he shall then be taught the remaining disciplines of the monastery: what he must do, whom he must serve, whether in the assembly of all the brothers, in the house to which he is assigned, or in the order of eating. Thus, instructed and perfected in every good work, he shall be joined to the brothers.

The guardian of the door shall observe these matters, reporting everything as written above and announcing it to the elders.

## XXVIII

The weekly servers assigned to prepare food, arrange the lamps, perform cleaning, and carry out whatever pertains to the service and use of the monastery shall always be ready. No other necessity shall occupy them; they shall devote themselves to this task, so that they may fulfill what they have undertaken usefully and diligently. If they do not know something concerning what they ought to do, they shall always ask their elders without concealment.

## XXIX

Those to whom the discipline, usefulness, reputation, or service of the monastery is entrusted shall faithfully guard and fulfill the duties assigned to them. For those who have been appointed to correct all errors ought not to err themselves. If through pride, negligence, or laziness they omit anything contained in the Rule, and destruction begins to arise through those by whom edification ought to increase, they shall be subject to all the condemnations contained in the Rule.

## XXX

Among all the brothers the following shall be observed: while obeying their elders and showing deference to one another, they shall have patience, moderation, humility, charity, and peace without deceit or falsehood, cursing, excessive talk, or the habit of swearing. No one shall claim anything as his own, and no one shall appropriate anything individually; rather, they shall have everything in common.

## XXXI

Without the word and authority of the elders, none of the brothers shall do anything, whether accept anything, give anything, or go anywhere at all.

## XXXII

When a fault has been discovered, the person found culpable shall be rebuked by the abbot privately. If this is not sufficient for correction, he shall be rebuked by a few elders. If he is not corrected even then, he shall be excommunicated and shall eat nothing.

If this too does him no good, wherever he may be, he shall be placed last of all in the order of psalmody. If he persists in wickedness, he shall even be deprived of the opportunity to take part in psalmody.

If this disgrace does not move him, he shall be excluded from the assembly of the brothers, so that he shall attend neither the table nor Mass, and no younger brother shall speak with him.

He shall remain excluded for as long as the seriousness of the fault requires, according to the judgment of the abbot and elders, or until he humbles himself from the heart in repentance for his fault and asks forgiveness for his error before everyone present. If he has sinned against a brother, he shall also ask forgiveness from the brother whom he injured.

## XXXIII

If anyone consents to his error and, in accordance with his harshness, gives him counsel that causes him to humble himself more slowly, he shall know that, when caught in this error, he is likewise to be judged culpable.

## XXXIV

This too must be added: a brother who is accused or rebuked for any fault shall have patience and shall not answer the person rebuking him. He shall humble himself in everything and make amends.

## XXXV

If someone is so harsh and so alien to the fear of the Lord that he is not corrected by so many chastisements and so many remissions, he shall be expelled from the monastery and regarded as an outsider, lest others be endangered by his fault.

## XXXVI

If anyone speaks or laughs while eating, he shall be rebuked and shall do penance.

## XXXVII

If anyone comes late to eat without the command of his superior, he shall likewise do penance or return fasting to his cell.

## XXXVIII

If something necessary is wanted at the table, no one shall dare speak; he shall give a signal by sound to those serving. The servers shall eat nothing except what has been prepared in common for the brothers, nor shall they dare prepare different food for themselves.

## XXXIX

No one shall give one person more than another has received. If illness is alleged, the superior of the house shall go to the attendants of the sick and receive from them what is necessary.

## XL

When some people arrive at the monastery door, if they are clerics or monks, they shall be received with greater honor. Their feet shall be washed according to the command of the Gospel, and everything suitable for the use of monks shall be provided to them.

## XLI

If someone comes to the monastery door saying that he wishes to see his brother or relative, the doorkeeper shall inform the abbot. With the abbot’s permission, he shall take as a companion someone whose faith has been tested, and he shall then be sent to see the brother or relative.

## XLII

If someone’s relative has died, he shall not have permission to accompany the funeral unless the father of the monastery has ordered it.

## XLIII

No one shall take vegetables from the garden unless he has received them from the gardener.

## XLIV

No one shall speak to another in the darkness. No one shall sleep with another on a mat. No one shall hold another’s hand. Whether standing, walking, or sitting, each shall remain one cubit from the other.

## XLV

If anyone takes something that is not his, it shall be placed upon his shoulders, and he shall do public penance in the assembly.

## XLVI

If the superior judges unjustly, he shall be condemned by the others for injustice.

## XLVII

Whoever consents to sins and defends another who has committed an offense shall be accursed before God and human beings and shall be rebuked with the severest correction.

# In the Year of Our Lord 430. Fastidius, Bishop of the Britons

## Prolegomena

[Col. 0379]

## Gallandi’s Historical-Literary Notice on Fastidius

(*Bibliotheca Veterum Patrum* of Gallandius, volume 9.)

[Col. 0379C]

### 1

From Gennadius we understand that Fastidius, bishop of the Britons, flourished at the time when Cyril of Alexandria and Theodotus of Ancyra were prominent; Gennadius places this writer between them. [Note: [Col. 0381D] Gennadius, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 56.]

The most learned men deprive Fastidius of the title of bishop, [Note: [Col. 0381D] The Benedictines, in the Appendix to volume 6 of the works of Saint Augustine, page 183.] and Pagius followed them in this. [Note: [Col. 0381D] Pagius, on the year 420, section 29.]

They were evidently influenced by the authority of the ancient Corbie manuscript of Gennadius, in which only “Fastidius the Briton” is read; the title is not written by the first hand, but was added after the word “Briton” by a more recent hand.

Yet, with the exception of the Corbie manuscript, the other manuscripts—including the far superior Verona manuscript, as learned men prove at length [Note: [Col. 0381D] The Ballerini, *Observations on the Works of Noris*, volume 4, pages 884 and 923–926.]—and two other very ancient manuscripts of the Lambeth library cited by Warthon [Note: [Col. 0381D] Warthon, *History of the Bishops and Deans of London*, page 6.] present the reading found in the common text of Gennadius.

Nor is it otherwise found in the manuscript of Honorius of Autun, who copied Gennadius. [Note: [Col. 0381D] Honorius of Autun, Book 2, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 55.] Therefore, in addition to the Ballerini mentioned above and Warthon, Usserius [Note: [Col. 0381D] Usserius, *Ancient History of the British Church*, chapter 11, page 171 of the second London edition, 1687.] and Norisius [Note: [Col. 0381D] Norisius, *History of Pelagianism*, book 1, chapter 19, works, volume 1, page 194.] also acknowledge Fastidius’s episcopate; Tillemontius too appears to join them. [Note: [Col. 0381D] Tillemontius, volume 15, pages 16 and 18 at the beginning, and page 837, note 4, on Saint Germain.] His episcopal see, however, is considered uncertain.

## 2.

Gennadius testifies [Note: [Col. 0381D] Gennad. loc. cit.] that Fastidius wrote a book to Fatalis, *On the Christian Life*, and another, *On Maintaining Widowhood*, containing sound and worthy teaching—as the Corbie manuscript reports. In the printed editions of Gennadius it reads “to a certain Fatalis,” perhaps through an error either of Gennadius himself or, more probably, of a copyist. For the book about which we shall speak presently is said to have been sent to a certain widow, whom the author calls his most beloved sister [Note: [Col. 0381D] Fastid. preface, *On the Christian Life*, below.]. Hence Pagius [Note: [Col. 0381D] Pagi. loc. cit.] wrongly took the opportunity to deny Fastidius authorship of the book, as the learned men whom we have just praised rightly argue [Note: [Col. 0381D] Baller. loc. cit.]. Possinus [Col. 0381C] likewise maintains [Note: [Col. 0381D] Possin. in the note to Fastidius, Roman edition.], along with others, that Gennadius was mistaken in making two books out of one: what the author discusses at the end of the little work concerning three kinds of widowhood [Note: [Col. 0382D] Fastid. loc. cit., chap. 15 below.] is not a new treatise, but the conclusion of the book *On the Christian Life*.

This little book, which had long appeared repeatedly among the works falsely attributed to Saint Augustine, has at last been restored to its author through the efforts of Lucas Holstenius. For that learned man, having found an ancient copy in the monastery of Monte Cassino bearing the name of Fastidius, transcribed the work and left it prepared for publication. Peter Possinus subsequently published it, together with two other little works from the Holstenian collection, at Rome in 1663. The most distinguished Parisian editors of Augustine’s works later issued the work anew, revised and collated with the ancient Corbie, Remi, [Col. 0382A] Michaeline, Victorine, and two Sorbonne manuscripts, as well as with Holstenius’s Roman edition [Note: [Col. 0382D] In the appendix to vol. VI of Augustine’s works, pp. 183–192.]. We have had this excellent exemplar set in type. Yet, lest we seem entirely to have neglected our duty, we compared it once more with Holstenius’s published text. From this collation we discovered some readings that may perhaps make the author’s text clearer, and therefore we have wished to record them below.

## 3.

Yet what the most learned men long ago pointed out must by no means be passed over: namely, that Fastidius was attached to the heresy of his fellow countryman Pelagius. It is therefore not surprising that Gennadius reported that he was imbued with sound and worthy doctrine; for no one is unaware that that presbyter of Massilia favored the enemies of divine grace. On this matter I would especially urge you to consult the very distinguished historian of Pelagianism [Note: [Col. 0382D] Noris. *History of Pelagianism*, book II, chap. 16, works, vol. I, pp. 462 ff.], those who arranged for his works to be published together [Note: [Col. 0382D] Baller. in Noris’s works, vol. IV, pp. 923 ff.], and the authors of the *Literary History of France* [Note: [Col. 0382D] *Literary History of France*, vol. II, pp. 633 ff.].

But, to return to our subject, Fastidius says the following about Adam [Note: [Col. 0382D] Fastid. *On the Christian Life*, chap. 13 below.]:

> In him I find nothing that was unbelief except disobedience alone, on account of which he was condemned, and by whose EXAMPLE all are condemned.

This is precisely the heresy of Pelagius, who taught as Saint Prosper says [Note: [Col. 0382D] Prosp. *Poem Against the Ungrateful*, near the beginning, works, vol. I, p. 71, new edition.]:

> Thus those born drew no guilt  
> from their fathers, nor are those now born unlike  
> that first birth, when the first parents, having misused  
> their freedom, sinned: the harmful pattern, not the seed,  
> was the source of injury to their offspring.

And still more clearly the unknown author of the letter to Demetrias [Col. 0382C] [Note: [Col. 0382D] The same, in the appendix, *Letter to Demetrias*, chap. 10, p. 527.]:

> Hence, he says, Adam’s sin was asserted to have harmed posterity by EXAMPLE, NOT BY TRANSMISSION.

Saint Augustine frequently attacks this Pelagian error [Note: [Col. 0382D] Augustine, *On Nature and Grace*, chap. 9, works, vol. X, p. 131, and elsewhere.].

Moreover, our author offers the following advice to his widow [Note: [Col. 0382D] Fastid. loc. cit., chap. 11 below.]:

> He rightly lifts his hands to God, and pours out his prayers with a good conscience, who can say: “You know, Lord, how holy, how innocent, how pure from every deceit, injustice, and robbery are the hands that I stretch out to you; how just, how immaculate, and free from every lie are the lips with which I pour out prayers to you, that you may have mercy on me.”

These are the very words of Pelagius by which he taught the widow Juliana, the mother of Demetrias, how the holy ought to pray. Saint Augustine quotes them [Note: [Col. 0382D] Augustine, *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, chap. 6, no. 16, works, vol. X, p. 200.] and says that they were brought as an accusation against Pelagius at the synod of Diospolis. Saint Jerome also reports the same words [Note: [Col. 0383A] Jerome, *Dialogue Against the Pelagians*, book III, no. 14, works, vol. II, p. 784, Verona edition.]; and, after producing them, he immediately exclaims: “Is this the prayer of a Christian, or of a proud Pharisee?”

Tillemontius further notes other statements in this work of Fastidius that were not correctly expressed [Note: [Col. 0383A] Tillem. vol. XV, p. 17.].

> “Therefore,” to speak with Norisius [Note: [Col. 0384A] Noris. *History of Pelagianism*, book I, chap. 19, works, vol. I, p. 195.], “since this Fastidius inserted into the said book *On the Christian Life* impious Pelagian opinions copied out, I do not doubt that he was sprinkled with Pelagian darnel. My suspicion is increased by the fact that Pelagius infected Britain, and that this plague spread widely throughout the whole island. Hence, in the year 429, envoys were sent by a Gallican council against the Pelagians in Britain.”

[Col. 0383]

# ONE BOOK OF FASTIDIUS, BISHOP OF THE BRITONS, ON THE CHRISTIAN LIFE (C, G, S)*

## Preface

[Col. 0383B] Although I am a sinner [Note: [Col. 0383D] The printed editions add *primus* (“first”), which is absent from the manuscripts and Holstenius’s edition.] and the last, more foolish than others and more inexperienced than everyone, I dare to admonish you through repeated letters to pursue the way of holiness and righteousness—not because I trust in my own righteousness, nor because of knowledge of wisdom, nor because of the glory of learning, but because I am compelled solely by the reason of the love for you that I have conceived in soul and mind according to God. That love urges and impels me, a sinner and ignorant man, to speak in such a way that, although I do not know how to speak, I cannot remain silent.

I would therefore gladly and willingly wish you to have the acquaintance of those whose wisdom is richer, whose eloquence is greater, whose knowledge is fuller, and whose conscience is freer from every contagion of sins—people who could instruct you rightly both by their words and by their examples. For, apart from the fact that the darkness of foolishness and ignorance has so blinded our mind that it cannot perceive or utter anything divine, the consciousness of all our sins also reproves us, so that even if it could possess some light, it hides it. Thus it comes about that, besides having nothing to say, we are also unable to offer confidently what we do possess, because conscience forbids it.

Nevertheless, while someone more learned and better may appear to you, be content for the present with our unpolished admonitions, and pardon our love. Love does not consider what it offers, nor does it seek what it does not have; rather, it gladly imparts everything it possesses [Col. 0384B]. Look not so much at the appearance of the gift as at the will of the heart, and carefully consider what that love could refuse you which was able to give everything it had [Note: [Col. 0383D] The printed editions read *voluit* (“wished”).]. It would also have offered what it did not have, if it had been able; for it was able to offer everything it possessed [Note: [Col. 0384D] Thus the manuscripts. Holstenius has: “It gave everything it was able to offer.” Other printed editions have: “It was offering everything it was able to offer.”].

That man thirsts, though only a little, who cannot meanwhile be content with the water of a running stream until he reaches a fuller and purer spring. Nor do I think that he hungers sufficiently who, although he has ordinary bread, waits for bread that is fine and white. So you too, most beloved sister, whom I am certain hungers exceedingly and thirsts for heavenly things, eat ordinary bread for the present until you find bread shining white with fine flour; drink the water of a small and turbid stream until you draw the purer water of a more abundant one.

Meanwhile, may our bread not displease you, although it may seem rustic [Col. 0384C]. Rustic bread appears rougher and less cultivated, but it is stronger and satisfies the hungry stomach more quickly, strengthening the weary more than bread that appears to be made of fine flour and polished.

Now, therefore, I shall speak as I am able, and I shall explain, as best I can, what is fitting for a Christian to do. I find no more appropriate starting point for this matter than first to discuss the very word “Christian” and explain why someone is called a Christian.

# THE BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 0383]

## CHAPTER I. The Name and Dignity of Christians

[Col. 0383D]

No wise or faithful person is unaware that “Christ” means “anointed.” It is evident that the anointed have always been holy men and men sufficiently worthy of God, and no others than prophets, priests, or kings. So great was the mystery of anointing itself that among the Jewish people not everyone, but only a very few among the many, deserved to receive it. This continued until the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, whom God anointed with the oil of gladness—that is, with the Holy Spirit—above his companions (Ps. XLIV, 8).

From that time, those who believe in him and have been cleansed by the sanctification of his baptism are anointed not merely as some were formerly under the Law, but all as prophets, priests, and kings. By the example of this anointing we are admonished about what we ought to be, so that in those who possess such holy anointing there may be conduct no less holy.

From the sacrament of this anointing comes the designation and name both of Christ and of all Christians—that is, of those who believe in Christ. Yet that person assumes the name in vain who in no way imitates Christ. For what benefit is it to you to be called what you are not, and to appropriate a name that does not belong to you? But if you are pleased to be a Christian, do what belongs to Christ, and rightly take upon yourself the name “Christian.”

Or perhaps you do not wish to be one, but only to be called one? It is deeply shameful and wretched for you to wish to be called what you are not. No one passes over to Christ in such a way that he is called a Christian without being one. Whoever is called a Christian professes that he has Christ as his Lord. And he truly has him if he obeys and serves him in all things. Otherwise, he is not Christ’s servant but his mocker and derider: he calls himself the servant of one whom he pretends not to serve.

Thus a twofold judgment is reserved: one for mocking God, whom he called Lord without cause, and another according to the nature of his sin.

## CHAPTER II. God Does Not Immediately Punish Sinners for Two Reasons

But God’s long-suffering mercy makes most unbelieving, shameless, and treacherous people sin without fear, so that from the fact that he does not immediately wish to punish sinners they do not regard God as the avenger of their sins [Note: [Col. 0385D] The printed editions have *sinit* (“allows”), which is absent from the manuscripts.]. Wretched and ungrateful, careless of their salvation, they even charge God with delaying their destruction [Note: [Col. 0385D] Holstenius has *qui* (“who”).]. They do not understand that by God’s providence they are preserved for two reasons [Col. 0385C]: so that his long-suffering may benefit the human race, and so that he may not be judged impatient if he should immediately wish to condemn sinners. For if he were not so patient, the human race would have perished long ago; nor would we have any righteous people among sinners if God wished to punish those who sin at once.

For we know and read of some who had previously been held captive by many and various kinds of sin—deceived either by the blindness of ignorance, or by the cause of their unbelief, or by the frivolity of youth—and who afterward, through the most merciful patience of the sustaining God, were converted from error and performed works of righteousness greater than the sins they had previously committed [Note: [Col. 0385D] The printed editions have *opera* (“works”), against the manuscripts.].

For God does not pardon sins, but delays punishment. He does not free the persevering sinner from death, but patiently waits for him to turn, even at the last moment, and live, as the blessed apostle Peter says:

> The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise, but is patient for your sake, not wishing any to perish, but all to turn to repentance (II Pet. III, 9).

For, as though he were pious, kind, and merciful, he does not strike you immediately in order that you may recognize how great is his piety toward you and how great his mercy: he prefers to await you as a sinner and ungodly person and to save you when converted rather than punish you while sinning. Thus the Lord himself speaks through the prophet, expressing by the kindness of his own voice how greatly he wishes to bestow mercy and compassion upon a human being:

> But if the wicked person turns away from all his wickednesses that he has committed, and keeps my commandments, and practices judgment, justice, and mercy, he shall surely live and shall not die. None of his offenses that he has committed shall be remembered; in his righteousness that he has practiced, he shall live (Ezek. XVIII, 21–22).

And again:

> Do I desire the death of the unjust person, says Adonai the Lord, rather than that he should turn from his evil way and I should make him live? (Ibid., 23.)

And elsewhere:

> The wickedness of the wicked shall not harm him on whatever day he turns away from his wickedness (Ezek. XXXIII, 12).

And again:

> Turn back, you children who are turning back, and I shall heal your brokenness (Jer. III, 22).

See how God admonishes and urges you to turn from your sins, even at the last moment, so that you may be saved. See how he urges one already subject to death to live; how gently and mercifully he invites him, refusing even to deny a father’s compassion to sinners. He still calls them “children,” although by sinning they have lost God the Father. In another passage he himself testifies, with a sorrowful voice and a certain miserable lamentation, that sinners have lost themselves, saying:

> I have become childless; I have lost my people because of their sins (Jer. XV, 7).

From this, then, recognize how God loves you: he prefers you to live rather than perish. And you despise and scorn him—him who loves you more than you yourself do, who wishes you to live when you desire to die?

> I do not desire, says the Lord, the death of sinners, but that they should turn and live (Ezek. XVIII, 32).

You, then, wished to die by sinning; he wishes to give you life by your conversion [Col. 0386C] [Note: [Col. 0386D] The manuscripts have *vivificare* (“to give life”).]. O foolish, irreverent, and ungrateful person, who do not even agree with God in this: he wishes to have mercy on you and prefers to save you by his compassion rather than let you perish through your sin!

## CHAPTER III. Those Who Abuse God’s Mercy Are Also Punished in This Life

Let no one, therefore, flatter himself; let no one deceive himself with a foolish and empty suspicion; let no one sin carelessly and freely because God’s anger and judgment do not immediately come upon sinners, imagining from this that he has sinned with impunity because he is not instantly destroyed. Rather, let him recognize that God delays punishment rather than overlooks sin, and that his anger will come suddenly and unexpectedly upon sinners, however delayed, rather than his pardon [Note: [Col. 0386D] The printed editions have: “however late, suddenly.”], as it is written:

> Do not say, “I have sinned, and what sad thing has happened to me?” For the Most High is a patient retributor (Ecclus. V, 4).

And elsewhere:

> Do not delay turning to the Lord, nor postpone it from day to day; for his anger will come suddenly (Ibid., 8–9).

This is fulfilled in many people: because of their excessive sins, God’s anger overtakes them even in the present, and it is also reserved for them in the future. But no one understands or recognizes this. When someone suffers adversity, he does not consider it inflicted because of his evils; rather, he thinks that what he has endured belongs to the ordinary course of things rather than to punishment for his crime.

For this reason God does not appear to punish sinners in the present [Col. 0387A]: when he punishes them, they do not recognize it. There are many whom no one understands, who, because of the multitude of their sins, are judged even now before the day of judgment.

Or let someone say whether, in the present time, he has been able to see any person who is sacrilegious, bloodthirsty, rapacious, deceitful, homicidal, thieving, fraudulent, adulterous, or guilty of other crimes living to an advanced age. We see many examples by which we can sufficiently prove that the wicked and ungodly, once the course of their sins has run its full length, are judged even in the present time, and are deprived of their present life no less than of the future one.

But this can more easily be understood by one who has awaited the death of various impious and criminal rulers at different times [Note: [Col. 0387D] *Pro.* has *spectavit* (“has observed”).]. The higher their power, the greater their audacity in sinning: whatever they can do, they believe they are permitted to do. And because those who judge others do not fear another’s judgment, they rush headlong into sin.

Thus those who do not fear human judgment when committing offenses come to feel God as judge and avenger. Among them, some who had frequently shed the blood of innocent souls experienced God’s anger and judgment so fully that afterward they themselves were forced to shed their own blood, although they had willingly shed that of others. Others who had committed similar acts were struck down by God’s indignation in such a way that they lay unburied and became food for wild beasts and the birds of heaven.

Still others who had unjustly killed an innumerable multitude of people were cut to pieces, limb by limb, so that the number of their severed limbs was no less than the number of those whom they had caused to be killed. By their judgment, many wives had been made widows through the unjust killing of their husbands, and many children had been left orphans through the murder of their fathers; in addition to bereavement, they were reduced to begging and nakedness [for the perpetrators added to their impiety and cruelty what was still lacking: they stripped the possessions from those whom they had caused to be killed, along with their children]. Now, however, the wives of those very perpetrators are widows, and their children orphans, daily dependent on the bread of others.

Does it not seem to you that this testimony has been fulfilled in them—the threatening word of God:

> You shall not mistreat a widow or an orphan. If you do mistreat them, and they cry out to me, I shall surely hear their cry; my anger will be kindled, and I shall kill you with the sword, and your wives shall be widows and your children orphans (Exod. XXII, 22–24)?

O shameful wickedness! O criminal deed! O excessive and intolerable cruelty! Two savage and atrocious crimes are perpetrated at one time: murder is committed so that robbery may follow. Husbands are killed, and fathers are killed, so that widows may more easily be stripped and orphans despoiled. Thus each person rejoices in another’s death, as though he himself were not someday going to die.

God is therefore rightly moved by such cruelties and impieties. He rightly reveals his judgment in some even before the appointed time. Life is rightly granted to such people neither in the present nor in the future. We are warned by their example, lest we suppose that the criminal and ungodly can escape God’s judgment even in the present.

[Col. 0388A] Rather, we ought to understand that each person is sustained by God’s patience only so long as he has not yet filled up and completed the limit and end of his sins. Once that has been completed, he is struck immediately, and no pardon remains reserved for him.

## CHAPTER IV. God Punishes the Sinner When a Definite Number of Sins Has Been Completed

That there is a definite measure and limit of sins is declared by God’s own testimony. It is also demonstrated most clearly that each person is judged sooner or later according as he has filled up the measure of his sins. Thus, speaking of the destruction and burning of Sodom and Gomorrah, which had already filled up their sins, God says to Abraham:

> The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah has been filled up, and their sins have become exceedingly great and have been filled up (Gen. XVIII, 20).

But what does he say about the Amorites, whose sins had not yet reached their end, although it is known that they were destroyed many years after the cities mentioned above had been burned?

> The sins of the Amorites have not yet been filled up, even to this point (Gen. XV, 16).

By this example we are most clearly instructed and taught that each person is brought to completion according to the fullness of his sins, and is sustained in order that he may turn for as long as he has not yet reached the accumulation of his offenses.

Let no one, I say, deceive himself; let no one delude himself. God does not love the wicked; he does not love sinners, the unjust, the rapacious, the cruel, or the ungodly. But he loves the good, the just, the pious, the humble, the innocent [Col. 0388C], and the gentle, as it is written:

> For you are not a God who desires iniquity. The wicked shall not dwell beside you, nor shall the unjust remain before your eyes. You hate all who practice iniquity; you will destroy all who speak falsehood (Ps. V, 5–7).

## CHAPTER V. A Swift Death Is Punishment for the Wicked and Security for the Good

But someone says: “Why do we see the good perish along with the wicked?”

They do not perish; rather, those who are freed from the company and persecutions of the wicked and transferred to rest escape. They truly die and perish whom, after departing from this world, a punishment and penalty of still greater judgment await.

The good are called away before their time lest they be harassed any longer by the harmful; the wicked and ungodly are removed lest they persecute the good any longer. The righteous are summoned from pressures, tribulations, and distress to rest; the ungodly are snatched from luxury, wealth, and pleasures to punishment.

For the former go to judge, the latter to be judged; the former to be vindicated, the latter so that vengeance may be carried out against them, as it is written:

> But if the righteous person is overtaken by death, he will be in refreshment (Wis. IV, 7).

And again:

> While he lived among sinners, he was transferred (Ibid., 10).

And again:

> For his soul was pleasing to God; therefore he hastened to remove him from the midst of iniquity (Ibid., 14).

And again:

> The way to death is with the ungodly; but they are in peace (Wis. III, 3).

You see, therefore, that for the righteous and worshipers of God this dissolution of the body is rest, not punishment; and that when they are dissolved, they are liberated rather than destroyed. For this reason the faithful neither fear nor dread that dissolution; rather, they desire and long for it to come [Note: [Col. 0389D] Three manuscripts have *exspectant* (“await”).], because they understand that through it rest, not punishment, is being provided for them.

But the unjust and ungodly, conscious of their crimes, rightly dread it by natural foresight, because they know that they will be judged by it. Therefore, once this reasoning has been given and accepted, we ought not to sin at all, especially since we know that judgment is reserved for sinners both in the present and in the future.

## CHAPTER VI. It Is Shameful for a Christian to Claim the Name Without the Reality

[Col. 0389B] Let us not flatter ourselves merely because we are called Christians; rather, let us believe that for this very reason we shall be judged if we falsely claim for ourselves a name that does not belong to us.

Or if anyone is so unbelieving, so faithless, so stubborn, so obstinate, and so bold that he does not fear the anger and indignation of God the judge, which will come at the appointed time [Note: [Col. 0389D] The word “of God” is absent from the manuscripts.], let him at least be ashamed before ordinary human custom. Let him see how that person is judged even by the Gentiles—how brutish, foolish, and senseless he is—whose vanity and madness are so great that he acquires for himself a name that does not belong to him.

Who is so vain and wretched that he would dare to profess himself a lawyer when he does not know letters? Who is so insane and senseless as to profess himself a soldier when he does not know how to bear arms?

No one assumes any name without a reason. A person must make shoes in order to be called a shoemaker; skill in an art makes someone a smith or craftsman; someone is called a merchant when he sells at a higher price what he bought more cheaply. From such examples we understand that no name exists without an action, but every name arises from an action.

How, then, are you called a Christian, when there is no Christian action in you? “Christian” is the name of justice, goodness, integrity, patience, chastity, prudence, [Note: [Col. 0389D] The word “humility” is absent from the manuscripts.] humility, kindness, innocence, and piety. How do you defend and claim that name for yourself when, among so many things, scarcely any of them remain in you?

A Christian is one who is a Christian not in name only but in deed; one who imitates and follows Christ in all things; who is holy, innocent, undefiled, and untouched; in whose heart there is no place for malice [Col. 0389D], but in whose heart piety and goodness alone abide; one who knows how to harm or injure no one, but to bring help to everyone.

A Christian is one who, following Christ’s example, knows not how to hate even his enemies, but rather to do good to those who oppose him and to pray for his persecutors and enemies. For whoever is prepared to injure or harm someone is lying when he says that he is a Christian.

A Christian is one who can say in a just voice:

> I have harmed no human being; I have lived justly with everyone.

## CHAPTER VII. God Has Always Been Pleased by Righteousness and Offended by Injustice

[Col. 0390A]

Lest anyone think or believe that I am speaking from my own opinion, or suppose that he can easily disregard what I say because I speak by my own will rather than by the authority of the Law, I shall now begin to produce examples from the Law itself, whose precepts open the way to life for us—examples from both the Old and the New Law. I shall show what God commanded the human race to observe from the beginning [Note: [Col. 0389D] Thus the better manuscripts. The printed editions have *statim* (“immediately”).] of the world, and in what he has always been pleased or offended.

For I read that after Adam, who was first formed by God (Gen. I, 27)—the reason for whom need not now be discussed—at the beginning of the world Cain and Abel were brothers, born of the same parents (Gen. IV, 1 ff.). One of them pleased God because he was innocent and just; the other, because he was unjust and guilty, could not please God.

Then, as time passed, Scripture indicates that Enoch was exceedingly just (Gen. V, 22 ff.). Righteousness bestowed so much upon him that he did not even experience present death, but was uniquely snatched away from the midst of all mortals to immortality. His example shows that one just person is dearer to God than many sinners.

We likewise know what the merit of righteousness accomplished for Noah, who was also just (Gen. VI, 8): because of it, life was granted to him and his alone, while the whole world was condemned through the Flood.

Scripture testifies what Abraham obtained through the merit of faith and righteousness (Gen. XV, 5–6): at that time he alone was God’s friend on earth because he alone had been found righteous.

What else was it than the merit of righteousness that caused Lot (Gen. XIX, 12) to be rescued from the fire of the Sodomites while all the others perished?

It would take too long to go through each person and recount the merits of all.

## CHAPTER VIII. God Afflicted the Israelites with Many Miseries in Order to Instruct Them in Works of Piety

It is fitting for us to know how God educated the Jewish people, whom he first chose from the seed of Abraham to belong to him above all other nations; what he commanded them to do and observe in order to please him.

First, I do not think it happened without cause or without God’s providence that he made them leave the land in which they had always wished to dwell, abandon their homeland, and migrate to a foreign province, namely Egypt [Note: [Col. 0390D] The better manuscripts omit *migrare* (“to migrate”); the Sorbonne manuscript has *ire* (“to go”), and Holstenius has *iter* (“journey”).].

I think the reason was this: God wished to educate his chosen people in mercy, compassion, justice, and the other good works. He therefore wanted them for a time to be strangers and captives in a foreign land, so that they might learn the misery and hardship of captivity and exile. In this way they would more easily learn afterward to have mercy on exiles and laborers, if they had first learned the miseries of exile themselves.

No one shows mercy to a stranger and foreigner so willingly as one who knows the outcome of exile. No one receives a guest without lodging into his own home as readily as one who has previously needed another’s shelter. No one feeds the hungry so readily, or gives drink to the thirsty, except one who has suffered thirst and hunger. No one covers the naked with his own garments so readily as one who knows the hardship of nakedness and cold. No one comes to the aid of the afflicted, miserable, and laboring so readily as one who has experienced tribulation, misery, and toil.

Rightly, therefore, God—the teacher of mercy and compassion, who was later to give the Law through which he would hand down to his people precepts of mercy, compassion, and every good work—wished them first to endure every pressure, tribulation, and distress in a foreign land. Thus afterward they could more easily pity those suffering such things and obey his commandments.

You may imagine him to have been a good farmer who, before sowing the seed, long tames the earth with plows and harrows, lest the seed entrusted to it perish. So too God first long disciplines and subdues his people before imparting to them the seed of saving commandments.

Finally, to make it clearer that they endured these things for this reason, let us consider the commandments of the Lord himself:

> You shall not mistreat or oppress a stranger, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt (Exod. XXII, 21).

And again we read:

> The great God, who does not show partiality and does not accept gifts, executing judgment for the proselyte, the orphan, and the widow. Love giving bread and clothing, because you too were strangers in the land of Egypt (Deut. X, 17–19).

And elsewhere he says:

> When you reap your harvest in your field and forget a sheaf [Col. 0391C] [Note: [Col. 0391D] Other copies have *manipulum* (“sheaf”), against the manuscripts.], you shall not return to take it; it shall belong to the proselyte, the orphan, and the widow, so that God may bless you in the works of your hands. You shall remember that you were a servant in the land of Egypt; therefore I command you to do this thing (Deut. XXIV, 19–22).

From this it is easily seen and recognized that God afflicted that people with all these miseries for this reason: so that, by their own example, they might be taught to have mercy on others, as it is written:

> You have taught your people through such works that the righteous ought to be just and humane (Wis. XII, 19).

What kind of people God wishes his people to be is, I think, sufficiently clear, and the works by which they can win his favor are proved by numerous examples.

But lest what we have said seem insufficient to reveal his will, let us join to it the precepts of the Law and the Prophets, and let us establish by testimonies from both the Old and the New Law what pleases God and has always pleased him, and what he has most frequently commanded to be done and observed. [Note: [Col. 0391D] Most manuscripts have: “I shall begin to produce examples from the New Law also. You shall love …”]

> You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your mind, and with all your strength (Deut. VI, 5); and you shall love your neighbor as yourself (Lev. XIX, 18).

That this is the principal commandment of the Law and the Prophets is confirmed by the testimony of our Lord and Savior, who says:

> On these two commandments the whole Law and the Prophets depend (Matt. XXII, 40).

This cannot be abolished or changed: the entire commandment of both the Law [Col. 0392A] and the Prophets consists in these two commandments, and the person who can fulfill them has fulfilled the Law. For nothing else is sought in the Old Law than that one should love God and one’s neighbor.

And truly, the fulfiller and doer of the Law is the person who sins neither against God nor against his neighbor.

## CHAPTER IX. Who Loves God

But I must by no means pass over or conceal what it means to love God and what it means to love one’s neighbor.

He loves God who obeys all his commandments in everything. He loves God who keeps his laws and precepts. He loves God who sanctifies himself, just as God is holy, as it is written:

> Be holy, because I, the Lord your God, am holy (Lev. XIX, 2).

[Col. 0392B] He loves God who fulfills the word of the Prophet:

> You who love the Lord, hate evil (Ps. XCVI, 10).

He loves God who thinks of nothing other than heavenly and divine things. For God is a lover of nothing except holiness, justice, and piety; and he loves God who does not do anything other than what God appears to love.

What it means to love God is declared by the teaching of our Lord and Savior:

> Whoever hears my words and does them is the one who loves me (John XIV, 21).

If, therefore, the person who does what God commands loves God, the person who does not do so does not love him. Everyone who does not love hates. Hence it is clear and evident that those who do not keep God’s commandments hate him. I think the Prophet spoke of them:

> Do I not hate those who hate you, Lord, and waste away because of your enemies? I hate them with perfect hatred; they have become my enemies (Ps. CXXXVIII, 21–22) [Note: [Col. 0392D] We have restored the text in this way with Holstenius and from the context. The printed edition BB has: “of whom, through the Prophet …”].

The righteous Prophet hates sinners, adulterers, and the unjust, and those who scorn God’s commandments, as he says elsewhere:

> I saw the transgressors, and I wasted away (Ps. CXVIII, 158).

And again:

> I have hated the unjust, and I have loved your law (Ibid., 113).

See, therefore, how just, how upright, and how holy we ought to be: not only is it forbidden us to live badly, but we are not even to acknowledge those who live badly.

The blessed Apostle also clearly demonstrates this. He did not command us even to break bread with sinners, saying:

> If someone who is called a brother among you is a fornicator, or greedy, or a worshiper of idols, or a slanderer, or a drunkard, or rapacious, with such a person you are not even to eat (I Cor. V, 11).

[Col. 0392D] God willed his people to be holy and free from every contamination of injustice and iniquity. He willed them to be such—so just, devout, pure, undefiled, and simple—that the nations would find nothing in them to condemn, but rather something to admire, and would say: “Blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord, the people whom he chose as his inheritance” (Ps. XXXII, 12). Such ought the worshipers and servants of God to be: gentle, serious, prudent, devout, blameless, untouched, and undefiled, so that whoever sees them may be astonished and admire them and say, [Col. 0393A] “Truly, these are men of God; such is their conduct.”

A man of God ought to present and conduct himself in such a way that there is no one who would not wish to see him or desire to hear him; that everyone who sees him may believe him to be a son of God; so that the prophetic saying may truly be fulfilled in him: “His palate is sweetness itself, and he is altogether desirable” (Song V, 16).

For if a Christian presents himself in such a way, if a servant of God presents himself in such a way that, by his conduct, he becomes like those who serve demons and idols, God will begin to be blasphemed through him, and people will say: “What a Christian servant of God! His actions are so evil, his deeds so shameful, his conduct so wicked; his life so impious, criminal, dissolute, and sordid.” And he will be guilty of that prophecy: “For the name of God is blasphemed among the nations because of you” (Isa. LII, [Col. 0393B] 5; Rom. II, 24).

But woe to those through whom the name of the Lord is blasphemed. For God desires and requires nothing more from us than that his name be magnified by all through our actions, as it is written: [Note: [Col. 0393D] Thus in the manuscripts. Elsewhere: “He honored me with a sacrifice of praise.”] “Offer a sacrifice of praise” (Ps. XLIX, 14). This is the sacrifice that God seeks and loves above all sacrifices: that his name be praised everywhere through the works of our righteousness, and that by the actions and deeds of his servants God be shown to be truly God. Those, however, love God who do nothing except what glorifies his name.

## CHAPTER X. Love of Neighbor

We have explained, as best we could, how God ought to be loved. [Col. 0393C] Now let us explain, as best we can, what it means to love one’s neighbor as oneself, although the reason for this command is briefly discussed elsewhere, where it is said: “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another” (Tob. IV, 1).

Our Lord and Savior likewise says: “Everything that you wish people to do to you, you also do to them in the same way” (Matt. VII, 12). No one wishes evil to be done to him by anyone. Therefore, he loves his neighbor as himself who does not wish any evil to be done to him, since he does not wish it for himself; but if there is anything good, he gladly bestows it, just as he himself wishes and hopes to receive and obtain it from everyone. For it is not enough to ask of a Christian merely that he avoid evil; he must also practice good.

Even if someone has done neither evil nor good, he is not admitted to the reward of eternal life, but is consigned to the fires of Gehenna, as we read that the Lord said in the Gospel concerning those who do no evil, yet perform no good deed: “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire, [Note: [Col. 0393D] Holstenius here and below in chapter 13: ‘which my Father prepared for the devil and his angels.’] which my Father prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry, and you did not give me food; I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink; I was a stranger, and you did not welcome me; I was naked, and you did not clothe me; I was sick, and you did not visit me; I was in prison, and you did not come to me” (Matt. XXV, 41–43).

They are condemned not because they did evil, but because [Col. 0394A] they did not do good. From this every prudent and wise person should recognize what hope those engaged in evil can have, when even those who have done no evil are denied life unless they have also done some good. For God asks of us not merely that we not be evil, but that we become good.

People are called evil because of evil deeds; conversely, they are called good because of good deeds. There are two whom both the good and the evil appear to serve [Note: Holstenius and the manuscripts read: “be instructed”]: the good God, whom all who conduct themselves well serve; and the evil devil, whose servant is everyone who acts badly. We are not merely required to cease being servants of the devil by living badly no longer; by living well, we must also be seen to serve God.

For [Note: [Col. 0394D] Thus we read with Holstenius. The Benedictine edition, however, reads: “everyone who neither seems to do evil nor good.”] I do not know whose servant anyone may be seen to be who appears to do neither evil nor good; nor how he can hope for everlasting life from God, which he has not earned by doing good. Let no one, I say, deceive or mock himself by his own judgment; let no one mislead himself by a vain opinion.

Whoever is not good does not possess life. Whoever has not performed works of righteousness and mercy cannot reign with Christ. Whoever is not humane, devout, hospitable, kind, and merciful will not escape the fire of Gehenna. God does not love the wicked; he does not love sinners. Whoever does evil is an enemy of God. Whoever is not free from deceit cannot have a share with Christ.

A Christian must seek and desire nothing more, and strive with all his strength for nothing more, than to drive wickedness from his heart, [Col. 0394C] not to admit evil into the conscience of his breast, to hold fast to goodness, preserve righteousness, and guard the purity of his mind.

Be innocent if you wish to live with God. Be simple if you wish to reign with Christ. What benefit is wickedness, which drags one to death? What benefit is evil, which prevents one from reigning with Christ and destroys the person who possesses it? As it is written: “For a wicked soul destroys the one who possesses it” (Eccli. VI, 4).

If you wish to live, hear what the Prophet says; if you love Christ’s kingdom, hear how you may deserve to attain it. “Who is the person,” he says, “who desires life and wishes to see good days? Restrain your tongue from evil, and let your lips not speak deceit. Turn away from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it” (Ps. XXXIII, 13–15).

For God honors and loves such people: those who know no evil, who do not know how to lie, whose lips speak no deceit, in whom nothing but goodness and purity is seen.

Innocence is what commends us to God; simplicity is what makes us reign with Christ. That God loves only the innocent and wishes them to be united with him is declared by many testimonies, as it is written in the Psalms: “The innocent and upright have clung to me” (Ps. XXIV, 21).

And elsewhere it is commanded and said: “Guard innocence and observe equity, for there are survivors for the peaceful person” (Ps. XXXVI, 37). How much innocence benefits and assists a person, even when it is preserved late in life, is confirmed by the testimony of the prophet David. Although he had previously sinned gravely, he afterward did not fear being judged, once he had begun to know innocence, as he himself says: “Judge me, O God, for I have walked in my innocence” (Ps. XXV, 1).

He therefore knew that he no longer needed to fear judgment, because, even if late, he had come to know innocence. And elsewhere he says: “But as for me, you received me because of my innocence” (Ps. XL, 13). God afterward received on account of innocence the one whom earlier he had rejected on account of wickedness.

That the innocent cannot be put to shame before God is clear from the saying: “As long as the innocent preserve righteousness, they will not be put to shame” (Prov. XIII, 6). Nothing can be more worthy or dearer to God than that innocence be preserved with complete observance.

Although someone may appear devout in other works, if he does not possess innocence, he flatters himself in vain about his devotion. If innocence was commanded even to the Jews living under the old law, when they were still permitted to hate their enemy, what ought you now to do as a Christian, who are commanded to love your enemy (Matt. V, 44)?

For when will you not be innocent—or to whom could you be evil—when you are commanded to be good even to your enemies? Yet perhaps you hate even your neighbor, although you are not permitted to hate an outsider; and you persecute your brother, although you are commanded to love your enemy; and you believe yourself to be a Christian, although you observe neither the commands of the New nor those of the Old Testament.

But so that you may not consider yourself a Christian without cause and flatter yourself merely because of the name, hear the Apostle saying what you ought to be: “Let the one who stole steal no longer; rather, let him labor, working with his hands at what is good, so that he may have something to give to one in need. Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth, but only what is good for building up the faith, so that it may give grace to those who hear. And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption. Let all bitterness, anger, indignation, shouting, and blasphemy be removed from you, along with all malice. Be kind and merciful to one another, forgiving one another, just as God in Christ forgave you” (Eph. IV, 28–32).

“Be imitators of God, [Note: [Col. 0395D] The manuscripts, except Michael, read ‘of me.’] as beloved children, and walk in love, just as Christ loved us and gave himself for us as an offering and sacrifice to God, for a pleasing aroma. But let fornication, every impurity, and greed not even be named among you, as is fitting for saints; nor obscenity, foolish talk, or coarse joking, which is inappropriate, but rather thanksgiving. For know this: no fornicator, impure person, or greedy person—for greed is the service of idols—has any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God” (Eph. V, 1–5).

Let the one who observes these commands rightly consider himself a Christian: one who is holy, humble, chaste, and just, and whose life is occupied with works of mercy and righteousness.

It is innocence that commends us to God, and simplicity that enables us to reign with Christ. That God loves none but the innocent and wishes them to be joined to him is made clear by many testimonies, as it is written in the Psalms: “The innocent and upright have clung to me” (Ps. XXIV, 21).

And elsewhere it is commanded and said: “Guard innocence and observe equity, for there are survivors for the peaceful man” (Ps. XXXVI, 37). How much innocence benefits and assists a person, even when it is preserved late in life, is confirmed by the testimony of the prophet David. Although he had previously sinned gravely, he afterward did not fear judgment, once he had begun to know innocence, as he himself says: “Judge me, O God, for I have walked in my innocence” (Ps. XXV, 1).

He therefore knew that he no longer needed to fear judgment, because, even if late, he had come to know innocence. And elsewhere he says: “But as for me, you received me because of my innocence” (Ps.
