XL, 13). God afterward received on account of innocence the one whom earlier he had rejected because of wickedness.

That the innocent cannot be put to shame before God is clear from the saying: “As long as the innocent preserve righteousness, they will not be put to shame” (Prov. XIII, 6). Nothing can be more worthy or dearer to God than that innocence be preserved with complete observance.

Although someone may appear devout in other works, if he does not possess innocence, he flatters himself in vain about his devotion. If innocence was commanded even to the Jews living under the old law, when they were still permitted to hate their enemy, what ought you now to do as a Christian, who are commanded to love your enemy (Matt. V, 44)?

For when will you not be innocent—or to whom could you be evil—when you are commanded to be good even to your enemies? Yet perhaps you hate even your neighbor, although you are not permitted to hate an outsider; and you persecute your brother, although you are commanded to love your enemy; and you believe yourself to be a Christian, although you observe neither the commands of the New nor those of the Old Testament.

But so that you may not consider yourself a Christian without cause and flatter yourself merely because of the name, hear the Apostle saying what you ought to be: “Let the one who stole steal no longer; rather, let him labor, working with his hands at what is good, so that he may have something to give to one in need. Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth, but only what is good for building up the faith, so that it may give grace to those who hear. And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption. Let all bitterness, anger, indignation, shouting, and blasphemy be removed from you, along with all malice. Be kind and merciful to one another, forgiving one another, just as God in Christ forgave you” (Eph. IV, 28–32).

“Be imitators of God, [Note: [Col. 0395D] The manuscripts, except Michael, read ‘of me.’] as beloved children, and walk in love, just as Christ loved us and gave himself for us as an offering and sacrifice to God, for a pleasing aroma. But let fornication, every impurity, and greed not even be named among you, as is fitting for saints; nor obscenity, foolish talk, or coarse joking, which is inappropriate, but rather thanksgiving. For know this: no fornicator, impure person, or greedy person—for greed is the service of idols—has any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God” (Eph. V, 1–5).

Let the one who observes these commands rightly consider himself a Christian: one who is holy, humble, chaste, and just, and whose life is occupied with works of mercy and righteousness.

## CHAPTER XI. Whose Prayers God Does Not Hear

[Col. 0396A]

For [Note: [Col. 0395D] Thus Holstenius and the Benedictine edition. Perhaps: “Now.”] do you consider him a Christian in whom there is no Christian action, in whom there is no conduct of righteousness, but only wickedness, impiety, and crime? Do you consider him a Christian who oppresses the wretched, burdens the poor, covets what belongs to others, makes many needy in order to make himself rich, rejoices in unjust profits, feeds on the tears of others, grows wealthy through the destruction of the miserable, whose mouth is continually polluted by lies, whose lips speak nothing but what is unworthy, obscene, criminal, and shameful, and who, although commanded to distribute what is his own, seizes what belongs to others?

Such a man nevertheless boldly approaches the church and rashly and presumptuously spreads out impious hands, polluted by unlawful seizure and the blood of the innocent. With that polluted and sacrilegious mouth, with which shortly before he had spoken either falsehoods or obscenities, he pours out prayers to the Lord as though he were conscious of no evil.

What are you doing, shameless and wretched man? Why do you burden yourself with the weight of still greater sins? Why do you inflict an injury upon God beyond mere contempt? Why, to provoke his anger more swiftly and call down punishment upon yourself, do you stretch out criminal hands toward God—hands upon which he does not look, since he commanded that only holy and undefiled hands be offered to him?

With what mouth do you ask God, when shortly before you spoke evil with it, and when he abhors your prayers, however much you multiply them, as it is written: “When you stretch out your hands, I will turn my face away from you; and when you multiply your prayers, I will not hear you, for your hands are full of blood. Wash yourselves, be clean; remove your wickedness from your souls” (Isa. I, 15–16).

The person who stretches and raises his hands to God ought to be fully conscious and certain of his innocence and confident in it, since the Apostle says: “I wish men to pray in every place, lifting up pure hands” (I Tim. II, 8).

[Note: [Col. 0395D] These are the words of Pelagius in Jerome, near the end of Dialogue 3.] That man rightly raises his hands to God, that man pours out prayers with a good conscience, who can say: “You know, Lord, how holy, innocent, and pure from every deceit, injustice, and theft are the hands that I stretch out to you; how just and undefiled, and free from every lie, are the lips with which I pour out prayers to you, asking that you have mercy on me.”

[Note: [Col. 0396D] For these words the manuscripts have only the single word “this one,” and Holstenius has “he.”] Such a person quickly deserves to be heard, and before he has fully poured out his prayers, he can obtain what he asks.

For I know that some have been so blinded by the deep darkness of wickedness and greed that, when things have gone well for them—whether they have bound a poor person by their power, overwhelmed an innocent person with false testimony, overcome a weak person by force, committed theft, or carried out robbery—they give thanks to God, believing that, with his help, they have committed such acts, and judge God to be so unjust that they suppose him to have been their accomplice in their crimes.

## CHAPTER XII. Almsgiving from Unjust Profits

Foolish and wretched people are so blinded by their iniquities [Col. 0397A] that they do not understand that what God forbids cannot please him; and, as though one crime were not enough, they add another by forming an evil opinion of God.

Some think that they are justified because they give a small alms from the substance of the poor; and from what they have taken away from many, they give a tiny portion to one person. One person is fed from what leaves many hungry, and from the spoils of many scarcely a few are clothed.

God does not seek such an alms, nor does he wish piety to be shown to one person through another’s cruelty. It is better for you not to give alms than to make many naked from the very source by which you clothe a few; and, in order to clothe one person, to strip several who are already clothed.

God approves that alms which is supplied from just labor, as it is written: “Honor God from your just labors, and offer him the first fruits of the products of your righteousness” (Prov. III, 9). But he abhors and rejects alms that is provided from the tears of others.

For what benefit is it to you if one person blesses you while many curse you? Or what advantage does that alms bring you which is provided from another person’s substance? It must truly be feared that God should have no means by which to feed his poor unless you seize what belongs to others.

## CHAPTER XIII. Faith without Works Is of No Benefit

I know others whom the dark ignorance of folly and lack of understanding so deceives and misleads that they consider the faith they pretend to possess capable of benefiting them before God without works of righteousness. Through this kind of error they commit unspeakable crimes without fear, believing that God punishes not crimes but only faithlessness.

Such people are not content merely to perish themselves; they also attempt to entangle in their snares others who possess no light of divine knowledge. In them the saying of our Savior is fulfilled: “If the blind lead the blind, both fall into a pit” (Matt. XV, 14).

For if only faithlessness is condemned, and no crime, then we sin safely and freely. And God gave his commandments of righteousness without purpose if faith alone, without works of righteousness, is beneficial.

We cannot know from where this impious, criminal, and faithless error of ignorance has crept in, unless perhaps it comes from those who, by this example, were seducing the people under the old law and handing themselves and others over to eternal death and perpetual destruction. Concerning them it is written: “Do not listen to the words of the prophets who prophesy to you, for they are vain; they speak visions from their own heart and not from the mouth of the Lord. For they say to those who reject the words of the Lord, ‘There will be peace for you’; and to everyone who walks according to his own desires, to everyone who walks in the error of his heart, they say, ‘Evils will not come upon you’” (Jer. XXIII, 16–17).

We had many testimonies—indeed, the testimonies of the whole law—by which we could destroy and bury so destructive an error; but, so as not to weary the reader by continuing too long, let a few of the many suffice.

Let the person whose opinion is such answer me: Was Adam, the first man made by God at the beginning of the world, condemned because of faithlessness or because of sin (Gen. III, 17)? I find no unbelief in him except disobedience, on account of which he was condemned, and on whose example all are condemned.

Cain likewise was condemned not because of faithlessness, but because he had killed his brother (Gen. IV, 11). Why say more? I read that the whole world perished in the flood not because of faithlessness, but because of crimes (Gen. VI, 13).

I find no reason why Sodom and Gomorrah were suddenly consumed by fire except sins and crimes (Gen. XVIII, 20), as Scripture most clearly demonstrates when it says: “The men of Sodom were evil and great sinners before God” (Gen. XIII, 13).

Did that Jewish people not repeatedly seem to perish and be punished because of sins (Acts V, 4–9)? [Note: [Col. 0397D] Most manuscripts read: “did it not perish so frequently?”]

But someone may say: “I accept only the testimonies of the Old Law unless you bring me examples from the New Testament.” Consider Ananias and Sapphira, whom the apostolic judgment condemned not for the crime of faithlessness, but on account of theft and lying.

Perhaps you will say to me: “What, then, does the Apostle mean when he says: ‘For we hold that a person is justified by faith without the works of the law’” (Rom. III, 28)? I read that the very man who says this also condemned an absent man because he had taken his father’s wife (I Cor. V, 1).

Scripture must be understood in a way that appears consistent in all respects to those who understand it, and discordant only to those who understand it least. The Apostle says that a person is justified by faith without the works of the law [Col. 0398C] (Rom. III, 28), but not without those works concerning which I hear another apostle saying: “Faith without works is dead” (Jas. II, 20).

The apostle Paul was speaking of the works of the law—that is, physical circumcision, the new moon, the Sabbath, and other things of this sort, which the law had previously commanded to be done but which were no longer necessary in the time of Christ. The other apostle, however, is speaking of works of righteousness; whoever does not perform them is dead, even if he pretends to be faithful.

But someone cites that saying of the Apostle: “For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. X, 10). Foolish person, this is fulfilled at the time of baptism, when, in order for someone to be baptized, only confession and faith are required.

For what benefit does the washing of baptism itself bring you if faith alone, without righteousness, is sought? Everyone holds that sins are washed away in baptism. If one is afterward to continue sinning, what benefit is there in having been washed?

Hear what the Lord says to the man who has once been healed: “Behold, you have been made well; [Note: [Col. 0398D] Some manuscripts: “Do not sin any longer.”] now sin no more, lest something worse happen to you” (John V, 14).

The blessed apostle Peter also teaches this most clearly: something worse happens to the person who sins after acknowledging the way of righteousness, when he says: “For if, after escaping the pollutions of the world through the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, they are again entangled in them and overcome, their latter condition has become worse than the former. For it would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness than, after knowing it, to turn back from the holy commandment handed down to them. What has happened to them accords with the truth of the proverb: ‘The dog has returned to its own vomit,’ and, ‘The washed sow to wallowing in the mud’” (II Pet. II, 20–22).

The blessed apostle Paul also bears witness and says that a person who sins in his former error after the sanctification of baptism is not preserved without profound repentance: “For it is impossible for those who have once been enlightened, who have tasted the heavenly gift, who have become participants in the Holy Spirit, who have tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come, and then have fallen away, to be renewed again to repentance, crucifying again for themselves the Son of God and holding him up to contempt” (Heb. VI, 4–6).

The evangelist bears witness that someone approached the Savior and asked what he should do to receive eternal life. The Lord answered him: “If you wish to have life, keep the commandments” (Matt. XIX, 17).

He did not say, “Keep faith alone.” For if faith alone is sought, the command to keep the commandments is superfluous. But far be it from me to say that my Lord commanded anything superfluous.

Yet those who have already become sons of perdition through sinning say this, and they believe that they have this one consolation: if they can consign others to everlasting death along with themselves.

For if God does not punish the sinner, where is the prophetic saying: “If the righteous person is scarcely saved, where will the sinner and the impious appear?” (Prov. XI, 31; I Pet. IV, 18). And elsewhere: “For sinners will perish” (Ps. XXXVI, 20). And again: “Let sinners vanish from the earth, and the wicked, so that they may be no more” (Ps. CIII, 35). And again: “As smoke vanishes, so let them vanish; as wax melts before the fire, so let sinners perish before the face of God” (Ps. LXVII, 3).

Here I hear not merely the unbelieving and faithless being condemned, but sinners. And I read that our Savior said in one place: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. VII, 21).

Certainly they believed in Christ, since they even called him Lord; yet the door of the heavenly kingdom is not opened to them for this reason, because they confess with their mouths the one whom they deny by their deeds.

The Apostle says that God can be denied by deeds no less than by words: “They profess to know God, but by their deeds they deny him” (Tit. I, 16).

And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Many will say to me on that day: ‘Lord, Lord, did we not cast out demons in your name, [Col. 0399D] and perform many miracles in your name?’ And I will say to them: ‘I never knew you. Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity’” (Matt. VII, 22).

They are said to have believed to such an extent that they even performed miracles in the Lord’s name; yet their faith will not benefit them, because they did not perform works of righteousness.

Therefore, if faith alone is beneficial, why are those who are judged not because of faithlessness but because they had done no good consigned with the angels of Satan to the fires of Gehenna forever, as it is written: “And the King will say to those on his left: ‘Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal Gehenna, which my Father prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry, and you did not give me food,’” and so forth (Matt. XXV, 41–42).

He certainly did not say, “Because you did not believe in me.” From this it may be understood that they will be condemned not because of unbelief, but because of the barrenness of their good works.

## CHAPTER XIV. Who Is Truly a Christian

Let no one, therefore, deceive another; let no one mislead another. Unless someone is righteous, he does not have life. Unless someone has kept Christ’s commandments in all things, he cannot have a share with him. Unless someone has despised earthly things, he will not possess divine things; unless he has scorned human things, he cannot possess heavenly things.

Let no one consider himself a Christian unless he both follows Christ’s teaching and imitates his example. But do you consider him a Christian whose bread has never filled any hungry person, whose drink has refreshed no thirsty person, whose table no one knows, beneath whose roof neither a stranger nor a traveler has ever found lodging, whose clothing has covered no naked person, whose assistance has sheltered no poor person, whose goodness no one experiences, whose mercy no one knows; a person who imitates the good in nothing, but rather mocks and derides them, and never ceases to persecute the poor?

Far be this from the minds of all Christians. Far be it that such a person should be called a Christian; far be it that one who is such should be called a son of God.

That person is a Christian who follows Christ’s way and imitates Christ in all things, as it is written: “Whoever says that he abides in Christ ought himself to walk just as he walked” (I John II, 6).

A Christian is one who shows mercy to everyone, who is not moved at all by injury, who does not allow a poor person to be oppressed in his presence, who helps the wretched, assists those in need, grieves with those who grieve, feels another’s pain as his own, and is moved to tears by the tears of others.

His house is open to all; his door is closed to no one; no poor person is unaware of his table; his food is offered to everyone; everyone knows his goodness, and no one experiences injury from him.

He serves God day and night; he continually meditates upon and considers his commandments; he becomes poor to the world so that he may become rich toward God; he is held in dishonor among human beings so that he may appear glorious before God and the angels; nothing false or feigned seems to be in his heart.

His soul is simple and undefiled; his conscience is faithful and pure; his whole mind is directed toward God, and all his hope is in Christ. He desires heavenly things rather than earthly things; he despises human things so that he may possess divine things.

For those who love this world and glory and take pleasure in the present age, hear what is said: “Do you not know that friendship with this world is enmity with God? Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world is made an enemy of God” (Jas. IV, 4).

## CHAPTER XV. The Three Classes of Widows

I have explained to you, dearest sister, as best I could, what it is fitting for a Christian to do. If, then, all who are generally called Christians ought to be such, it is now for your prudence to consider what kind of widow you ought to show yourself to be, since you ought to be an example to all who conduct themselves well.

I believe you are not unaware that there are three classes of widows. One is the most perfect and destined for a heavenly reward: following the example of that widow in the Gospel (Luke II, 37), she serves God with prayers and fasts day and night.

Another is said to have the care of children and of the household. She is not as worthy as the first, but is nevertheless not subject to sins.

The third class is devoted to banquets and pleasures; it is reserved for eternal death and punishment, as it is written: “Honor widows who are truly widows” (I Tim. V, 3).

These are the first, who are called both true widows and those whom so great a priest—that is, Timothy—is commanded to honor. The second are those whom he no longer commands to be honored, but to whom life is nevertheless not denied. Concerning them it is said: “But if any widow has children or grandchildren, let them first learn to manage their own household devoutly [Note: [Col. 0401C] In most manuscripts: “well.”] and to repay their parents an equivalent kindness” (ibid., 4).

The third are those concerning whom it is written: “But the widow who lives in pleasure is dead while she lives” (ibid., 6). From this it may be understood that not all widows are equal, and that those who are widows only in body, not in conduct, do not please God.

The Apostle says what Christ’s widow ought to be: “But she who is truly a widow hopes in the Lord and persists in prayers day and night” (ibid., 5).

Nor do I wish you to overlook the fact that when the Apostle speaks of true widows, he shows that there are false ones as well—that is, widows who are such in action, mind, and conduct, but not in body.

Elsewhere the same Apostle describes the conduct and way of life of true and chosen widows, saying: “Let a widow be chosen who has a testimony of good works: if she has raised children”—understand, for God—“if she has shown hospitality, if she has washed the feet of the saints, if she has supplied the needs of those suffering tribulation, if she has pursued every good work” (ibid., 10).

He judged that woman to be a true widow whose works are such. But how can that woman call herself Christ’s widow who has never done anything of this kind?

There are, however, some women who are rich, noble, and powerful. Perhaps they consider it beneath their dignity either to raise children for God rather than for the world, to welcome a stranger as a guest, or to wash the weary, muddy, and filthy feet of the saints and touch them with their delicate and clean hands.

But such women will not be worthy in the future to share in the company of the saints, whom they despised in the present; nor will they be able to have a share with Christ, whom they refused to receive and whose feet they shrank from touching with their hands. For whoever despises Christ’s servants despises Christ, as he himself says: “Whoever despises you despises me” (Luke X, 16).

Mary had an abundance of tears with which to wash Christ’s feet; [Note: [Col. 0401C] See St. Augustine, Sermon 145, no. 1, in the appendix to volume V.] but among the women of our time even the water with which they might wash the feet of travelers is lacking.

Therefore, you most holy and prudent woman, do not wish to imitate such women, who, although they have boldly done evil, are ashamed to do good; who are embarrassed to live justly, though they were not ashamed to sin; who have voluntarily offered themselves to death and, although invited, do not return to life; who fear the laughter, mockery, and gossip of human beings more than God’s judgment; and for whom it is dearer to please wretched people than Christ.

But be such as the Lord commanded you to be, such as the Apostle commands [Note: [Col. 0402C] Thus we read with Holstenius. The reading in the Benedictine edition is not satisfactory: “He commands her to be shown as Christ’s widow; be, and so forth.”] you to present yourself to Christ.

Be a holy, humble, and quiet widow; practice works of mercy and righteousness without ceasing. Let everyone hold you in reproach; let everyone mock and ridicule you—only please God and perform what belongs to Christ.

Above all, meditate incessantly on the commandments of your Lord; devote yourself earnestly to prayers and psalms, so that, if possible, no one may ever find you doing anything except reading or praying.

And when you have become such a woman, remember us, who love you so dearly that, although we cannot give you what we would if present, we bestow it while absent.

## In the Year of Our Lord 430. Possidius, Bishop of Calama

## PROLEGOMENA

### Schoenemann’s Historical-Literary Notice on Possidius

*(Schoen., Historical-Literary Library of the Latin Fathers, vol. II.)*

### § I. Life

[Col. 0401]

An African, a disciple and intimate friend of Augustine, than whom Augustine scarcely had anyone dearer or more devoted to him. For Possidius himself relates that he lived with Augustine for approximately eleven years in close and affectionate fellowship, without any bitter disagreement. No less honorable is the testimony that the bishop of Hippo gave concerning his friend and disciple in a letter to Memor, bishop of Capua and father of Julian of Eclanum, when he says:

“It would have been excessively ungrateful and hard-hearted if this holy brother and colleague of ours, Possidius, in whom you will find no small part of our presence, had either not learned that you love us so much or had learned it without our letters. For through our ministry he has been nourished not by those liberal arts which the slaves of various passions call liberal, but by the Lord’s bread, insofar as it could be distributed to him through our own straitened circumstances.”

These words sufficiently show how close and how long-lasting their bond was. Hence, and not without reason, they judge—on the basis also of the corresponding mark of affection—that Possidius was enrolled in that community of clerics whom Augustine, while a presbyter at Hippo, had gathered together and bound by monastic rules.

Nor does it seem at all improbable that he was promoted from that same monastery [Col. 0403B] to the episcopate of Calama, a town of Numidia not far from Hippo Regius. This occurred in the year 397, after the death of Megalius.

In that place a broad field was opened for him to develop those gifts that the training and companionship of the bishop of Hippo had formed and shaped in him. Many matters also presented themselves that had to be managed by the united counsel of the two friends and in which he needed Augustine’s authority or assistance.

Such, for the most part, were the hardships that he himself and his Church suffered from the pagans of Calama at the beginning of his office, and soon afterward the struggles he undertook against the Donatists.

Since this cause was no less common to the Church of all Africa than it was Augustine’s own, Possidius could not take it up with only slight zeal. Accordingly, as early as 404 he urged Crispinus, the Donatist bishop among the people of Calama, to enter into a conference with him; although unwilling, Crispinus was compelled to do so, and Possidius overcame him by his resourcefulness.

In 410 he was sent, together with three other bishops, as an envoy by the African bishops assembled at Carthage to the Emperor Honorius, seeking the abrogation of the law enacted in favor of the Donatists and the securing of a conference with them.

He was subsequently chosen, in 411, among the seven representatives of the Catholic party at the conference with the Donatists, and he signed its proceedings.

He also took part in the African councils held because of the heresy of Caelestius and Pelagius, and, together with the other bishops of Numidia, sent a letter from the council of Milevis to Innocent, bishop of Rome.

Finally, when the savage army of the Vandals invaded all the provinces of Africa in 430 and Calama was overwhelmed by them, Possidius, moved—as though by a divine prompting—went to Hippo.

He had scarcely arrived there when that city too was enclosed by siege, while Augustine lay ill with fever and, a few days later, in the presence of his friend, fell asleep.

After Augustine’s death, Possidius is mentioned less frequently, except that Prosper relates in his Chronicle, under the consulship of Aetius II and Sigisvult (A.D. 437), that Possidius, together with the Catholic bishops Novatus and Severianus, courageously resisted Genseric, who sought to overthrow the Catholic faith by Arian impiety; but that he thereby deserved to be deprived of his churches and expelled from his cities.

From this they infer that, after Genseric captured Carthage in 439 and a huge multitude of clergy was expelled from all Africa, Possidius was proscribed, exposed to shipwreck, and reached Naples, thus ending his final days in Italy.

### § II. Writings
Two writings of Possidius survive, worthy memorials of his friendship and affection for Augustine: the *Life of Augustine* and the *Catalogue of His Writings*.

## § III. Editions, translations, and manuscripts

### Editions

From the beginnings of the printing art, the *Life* was customarily prefixed to nearly all collections of Augustine’s works and minor writings. In this form it was corrected by the Maurist Fathers through the notable abundance of manuscript readings, and finally revised separately with the aid of a new supply of variant readings and furnished with not unlearned notes by Giovanni Salinas, a Roman theologian, in 1731. The *Catalogue of Augustine’s Writings* was first published by Johann Vlimmerius in 1564. From that time it likewise passed into various editions of Augustine’s works, and was corrected from ancient parchment manuscripts in the Benedictine edition. But a much fuller and more accurate edition, based on a manuscript from Verona, appeared at Venice in 1735 [lacuna]. In the following catalogue nothing has been omitted that contributes to a more accurate knowledge of the notable editions; no one, however, should expect a textual recension of each individual work of Augustine.

### Sixteenth century

**1564.** Louvain, at the press of Hieronymus Wellaeus; quarto. *The Life and Catalogue of the Works of the Lord Augustine by Possidius, Bishop of Calama*, from the edition of Johann Vlimmerius and with his marginal scholia; together with several sermons of Augustine [Col. 0404C] recently brought to light and edited by the same man. This entire work of Vlimmerius was transferred into the Basel edition of Augustine’s works of 1569.

**1573.** Cologne; folio. *The Life of Augustine, Bishop … published by Possidius, first his disciple and later Bishop of Calama*, in Laurentius Surius’s *Approved Lives of the Saints* for 28 August, vol. IV, pp. 933–947. In the latest Cologne edition of 1618, for this month, pp. 302–309.

### Seventeenth century

**1690.** Paris, at the press of François Muguet; folio. *The Life of Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, by the Bishop of Calama, his disciple. Also the Catalogue of the Books, Treatises, and Letters of Saint Augustine, Bishop of Hippo*, edited by Possidius, E. C., corrected from various manuscript codices and with variant readings, in part III of the appendix to volume X of Augustine’s works, from the Benedictine edition. In the Antwerp edition, pp. 164–200. The observations of Clericus on Possidius are not of such importance that they need trouble anyone. Nor should Salinasius boast of the victory he won, since his entire defense, not only by him but also by others, failed in the mere attempt.

### Eighteenth century

**1731.** Rome, printed by Joannes Zempel; octavo. *The Life of Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo*, by Saint Possidius, Bishop of Calama, revised according to manuscript codices and illustrated with notes, prepared and edited by Don Giovanni Salinas of Naples, Canon Regular of the Lateran Congregation and lecturer in Sacred Theology [Col. 0405A], dedicated to the most reverend Father Don Ascanio Varesio, Canon Regular of the Lateran, General Abbot.

2. In the same place and year: *A Dissertation on the Life and Deeds of Saint Possidius, Bishop of Calama*, compiled from the writings of Father Augustine and ecclesiastical monuments, prepared and edited by Don Giovanni Salinas, etc.

The editor revised the text according to the readings proposed by the Maurist Fathers from manuscript codices and from ancient Vatican exemplars previously used by no one; he carefully recorded the variants and added notes and observations abundantly enriched with the resources of the Benedictines and other learned men. It was certainly not difficult, amid such a wealth of Augustine’s writings and writings about Augustine, and after so many and such varied studies concerning the matters he accomplished and the events of that age—especially after the most learned [Col. 0405B] commentary of the Parisian editors on his life—to pour out notes on Possidius that were not wholly inept. Without doubt these guides greatly supported Giovanni Salinas, who otherwise was less energetic on his own resources, as we shall show by the example of Vincent of Lérins, published by him in the same year and in the same format and dedicated to Clement XII. In the preface he had promised to append to Augustine’s *Life* the short work of Hugh of Saint Victor, *On the Instruction of Novices*, together with the author’s history. Later, however, he changed his plan and instead had a substantial and not unlearned *Dissertation on the Life and Deeds of Possidius* printed separately. It is therefore all the more surprising that the author was led to this idea so late. See the *New Acts of the Learned of Leipzig*, 1734, pp. 18–21.

**1735.** Venice [lacuna]. *The Catalogue of the Writings of Saint Augustine* [lacuna], enlarged beyond the common version from a very ancient manuscript codex of Verona; with two letters of Augustine recently discovered in the Gottweig Abbey in Austria. Mansi, in his additions to Fabricius’s *Bibliotheca Latina Mediae et Infimae Aetatis*. I have found it praised nowhere else, and thus am wholly unaware what in this edition is earlier or later.

**1743.** Antwerp, at the press of Bernard Albert van der Plasche; folio. *The Second Part of the Life of Saint Augustine*, especially from the thirty-third year of his age until his death, by Saint Possidius, the holy Doctor’s disciple and his companion for nearly forty years. From the Roman edition of 1731, collated with an ancient manuscript codex. The *Catalogue of Augustine’s Writings* by the same author is also included; in the Antwerp *Acts of the Saints*, August, vol. VI, pp. 427–460. The second part of the *Life* is called Possidius’s work here because the Augustinian *Confessions* are prefixed to it; the Bollandists gave those the title of the first part of Augustine’s *Life*. Each section is accompanied by learned and soberly written annotations.

**1768.** Augsburg, at the press of the Veith Brothers; octavo. *The Life of Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo*, by Saint Possidius, Bishop of Calama, revised according to manuscript codices and illustrated with notes, prepared and edited by Don Giovanni Salinas of Naples, Canon Regular of the Lateran Congregation. Added is Michael III’s, prelate of the Exempt Wengen Islands of the Canons Regular at Ulm in Swabia, Imperial and Catholic Majesty’s counselor and perpetual chaplain, *Critical Inquiry into Various Deeds, Sayings, and Visions Falsely or Insufficiently Attributed to Saint Augustine*. In the latter dissertation the origin of many stories about Augustine is shown learnedly and sagaciously.

### Translations

**1742.** Venice, printed by Pietro Bassaglia and Francesco Hertzhauser; quarto. *The Life of Saint Aurelius Augustine … written by Saint Possidius, Bishop of Calama*, translated into Italian by an anonymous author, with the Latin text; at the beginning of Augustine’s *City of God*, published here in two volumes in Latin and Italian, the Italian being based on the ancient translation of an anonymous author commonly thought to be Jacob Passavanti.

**1764.** Milan, at the press of Antonio Agnelli; octavo. *The Life of Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo and Doctor of the Holy Church, written by Saint Possidius, Bishop of Calama*, translated into Italian by an anonymous author. In this second edition it has been adapted to the Latin text of the best manuscript codices, enlarged with several notes, and dedicated to the most illustrious Don Antonio Fissiraga, doctor of the Collegium, decurion, and emeritus orator of the city of Lodi.

The editor, F. Romualdo Maria de Saint Cajetan, a Discalced Augustinian of Milan, had the translation of the preceding edition printed, but recast according to the text of the latest recension and with the Latin text omitted. He candidly admits that the notes he scattered through it are not his own, but were selected from the notes or commentaries of the Benedictines, Salinasius, Cesare Benvenuti, and Lorenzo Berti, the author of an Augustinian life.

### Manuscripts

1. **The *Life of Augustine*.** The Benedictine manuscripts: six, namely two from Fleury, the Germanensis, Vedastinus, Fossatensis, and Cisterciensis. From these comes a large supply of variant readings. Nor are there fewer readings from the five manuscripts which Salinasius used: two of them were formerly preserved in the library of Queen Christina of Sweden under nos. 541 and 1025, while he obtained three others from the Vatican, marked 1188, 1190, and 1191. Finally, the manuscript copy of the Museum of the Society of Jesus at Antwerp must be added to all these; the Bollandists note that it was marked P. MS. 5 and call it very ancient.

2. **The *Catalogue of Augustine’s Works*.** The manuscript of the library of Villers Abbey used for the first edition, from which Vlimmerius was the first to print it. The Benedictines used the same codices as for the *Life of Augustine*. Finally, the latest edition is based on the Verona manuscript.

[Col. 0407]

## POSSIDIUS, BISHOP OF CALAMA, ONE BOOK ON THE LIFE OF SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, AND THE CATALOGUE OF THE WORKS OF THAT SAME SAINT AUGUSTINE

We have already published these two distinguished works in volume I of the works of Saint Augustine, which is volume thirty-two of our *Patrology*. It is enough, therefore, to remind the kindly reader to consult the cited place.

## A.D. 422–432. POPE CELESTINE I

[Col. 0407]

# PROLEGOMENA

[Col. 0407]

## NOTICE FROM THE *BOOK OF THE POPES*

*(From Mansi, New Collection of the Councils, vol. IV, col. 453.)*

[Col. 0407A] Celestine [Note: Since the see had been vacant for nine days after the death of Boniface, on the third day before the Nones of November, in the year of Christ 423 and the sixteenth year of the Emperor Theodosius, Celestine, as Augustine says in Letter 161, was made pope without any division among his people, although those who belonged to the faction of Eulalius persisted in schism and were unwilling by any means to communicate with Celestine.

Theodosius, an emperor most devoted to piety and religion, was, because of his opposition to heresies and defense of the Catholic faith, freed by God’s singular favor from the fear and danger of all tyrants.

Africa, most obstinate in its Arian treachery and the bitterest persecutor of Catholics, was, by God’s hidden judgment, burned, plundered, and devastated by the Vandals and other barbarians, and thereafter remained for a hundred years under the barbarian yoke.

By the authority of this pope, Britain, Scotland, and Italy were purged of the Pelagian heresy, the Eastern Churches of the Nestorian heresy, and the Burgundians and Irish were converted to the faith of Christ. Thus everyone can understand how absurdly Laurentius Valla, a grammarian wholly ignorant of ecclesiastical affairs, asserted that Pope Celestine—who was the first of all to condemn Nestorius at Rome and, through legates sent by the ecumenical Council of Ephesus, likewise arranged for his expulsion—had been infected with the heresies of that same Nestorius.

These statements are taken from Prosper, Bede, and Baronius under the years 423 and following.

Severinus Binius.] a Roman by nationality [another reading: Campanian], son of Priscus, occupied the see for eight years, ten months, and seventeen days [Note: He died on 8 April 432. From the beginning of his pontificate until the day of his death, he could have held the see for only five months and three days beyond the completion of eight years. Baronius at the place cited. Severinus Binius.]. He made many decrees, and decreed that the 150 psalms of David should be sung before the sacrifice, antiphonally by all, which had not been done previously; only the Epistles of blessed Paul [another reading: the Epistle was recited] and the holy Gospel had been read. He made a decree concerning the whole Church, especially concerning religious communities, which is kept deposited to this day in the archives of the Church.

He dedicated the Basilica of Julius, in which he presented: a *postigem zeticum* [another reading: *postignegeticum*; perhaps *postem sethicum*]; a silver paten weighing 26 pounds [another reading: 25]; two silver cups, each weighing 8 pounds; two silver vessels, each weighing 10 pounds; five smaller silver chalices [another reading: “smaller” is absent], each weighing 3 pounds; silver water vessels weighing 10 pounds [another reading: 20]; two silver candelabra, each weighing 30 pounds; twenty-four bronze or brass candle-bearing vessels [another reading: “or brass” is absent], each weighing 30 pounds [another reading: 20]; likewise ten silver crowns, each weighing 10 pounds [another reading: the entire phrase “likewise … 10 pounds” is absent].

For blessed Peter the apostle [another reading: Paul], a large silver candle-bearing vessel weighing 25 pounds [another reading: 15], made of the purest silver [another reading: the phrase is absent]; twenty-four silver candle-bearing vessels [another reading: “silver” is absent] in the basilica [another reading: “in the basilica” is absent], each weighing 20 pounds; for blessed Paul the apostle, a large silver candle-bearing vessel weighing 25 pounds; twenty-four candle-bearing vessels, each weighing 20 pounds [another reading: all of this from “for blessed Paul” onward is absent].

[Col. 0409A] He held three ordinations in the city of Rome during the month of December: thirty-two priests, twelve deacons, and forty-six bishops for various places. He was also buried in the cemetery of Priscilla on the Salarian Way, on 8 April. The episcopate in the city of Rome then ceased for twenty days [another reading: twenty-one days].

[Col. 0409]

## NOTICE OF GALLANDIUS

*(Bibliotheca of the Ancient Fathers, vol. IX.)*

[Col. 0409A] 1. Since we are going to speak of Saint Celestine, we have thought it preferable to copy here, rather than our own words, what the learned Coustant has explained—though briefly, yet sufficiently and appropriately for our purpose. Thus he writes [Note: Coustant, *Epistles of the Roman Pontiffs*, p. 1051.]:

“When Boniface departed this life on 4 September 422, the Lord God, as Augustine testifies [Note: Augustine, Letter 209, no. 1.], immediately established Celestine in the Roman see without any division among his people. The learned man observes that it was then the custom of the Roman Church, unless some obstacle intervened, to appoint a successor immediately after the death of its bishop; and therefore that Celestine, since the votes of the entire people had united in his favor, was ordained without delay on the Sunday immediately following Boniface’s death, which fell on 10 September.

2. “His episcopate was distinguished by many achievements. In particular, he was the first to pronounce a judgment against Nestorius; he appointed Cyril as his representative to carry it out and prescribed a rule and form which the Fathers of the Council of Ephesus freely professed that they would follow as canonical. Moreover, he confirmed the acts of that council; he saw to it that the Pelagians were driven from the whole of Italy; he deprived the Novatians of the several churches they possessed at Rome [Col. 0409C]; he restrained the emerging Semi-Pelagian heresy and defended Augustine against its new critics.

3. “That he ended so glorious a pontificate in the very year 432, in which he approved the ordination of Maximian, appointed in place of Nestorius, as the crowning sign of the overthrown Nestorian heresy, is confirmed by the chronicles of Prosper and Marcellinus. On what day this occurred is not so certain. The papal books and martyrologies report that he was buried on 6 or 9 April. Yet the papal books are inconsistent with themselves, since, like the ancient catalogues, they assign nine years, ten months, and several days to Celestine’s pontificate. Antonius Pagius says [Note: Pagius, under the year 432, § 5.] that it must be certain that he sat for nine years, ten months, and nine days, and therefore died on 18 or 19 July. In the Corbie manuscript, however, written in the time of Pope Vigilius, with which at least some copies of Prosper’s *Chronicle* agree, he is said to have sat for nine years, ten months, and seventeen days. Hence Sebastian Tillemont thinks it permissible to assign Celestine’s death to 26 July 432 [Note: Tillemont, vol. XIV, p. 738].”

Thus far the learned author.

4. We now present the edition of Celestine’s letters prepared by Coustant himself, revised in several places; from his annotations it is therefore easy to draw what bears on the fuller elucidation of this pontiff’s notable achievements. For the rest, if anything should be added to them, I think the inquiry arranged in ten chapters on Celestine’s Letter 21 to the bishops of Gaul should be read; learned men composed it [Note: Ballerini, book II, chapter 6, *Observations on the Works of Noris*, vol. IV, pp. 909 ff.], where, following Coustant himself, they explain with the greatest precision what should be judged concerning these matters.

On the occasion of this letter of Celestine to the Gauls, it may be noted that Vincent of Lérins highly valued the judgment of that same pontiff contained in the letter to the bishops of Gaul, in these words [Note: Celestine, Letter 21, § 2.]: “If matters stand thus, let novelty cease to attack antiquity.” After reporting these words, Vincent adds [Note: Vincent of Lérins, *Commonitorium*, chapter 32.]: “This, then, was the blessed judgment of blessed Celestine: not that antiquity should cease to overwhelm novelty, but rather that novelty should cease to attack antiquity.”

I am certainly not unaware that the most learned Cardinal Noris twisted Vincent’s words of this kind into a meaning different from the one they appear to convey [Note: Noris, *History of Pelagianism*, book II, chapter 11, Works, vol. I, pp. 391 ff.]. Yet his opinion is in no way approved by the learned Coustant [Note: Coustant, note 3 on Celestine’s Letter 21, below, p. 333].

Nor should Prosper’s distinguished testimony concerning Celestine be omitted here [Note: Prosper, *Against the Collator*, chapter 21, elsewhere 41, no. 2.]: “To him,” he says, “the Lord granted many gifts of his grace for the protection of the Catholic Church.”

[Col. 0409]

## NOTICE OF SCHOENEMANN

*(Historical-Literary Library, vol. II.)*

### § I. Life of Pope Celestine

[Col. 0409D]

A Campanian by birth and the son of a certain Priscus, he was ordained bishop immediately on the Sunday following the death of Boniface, that is, on 10 September 423.

The authority of the Roman see in African judgments still endured, having been granted by the African bishops themselves until they had consulted the most authentic copies of the Council of Nicaea and become certain whether the canons praised by Zosimus were actually found in them. On this basis, at the very beginning of his new office, Celestine undertook the case of Antonius, Bishop of Fussala, and somewhat later that of Apiarius, who had been removed because of new crimes and appealed to Celestine.

Augustine overturned the complaints of the former as deceitful and unjust, and, by his account of the matter to Celestine, prevailed upon him to ratify the sentence passed against Antonius by the Africans; his own confession of crimes condemned him. When they reported this to Celestine, they at the same time completely abolished whatever right concerning appeals they had meanwhile permitted to the Roman see, begging that in the future bishops, priests, lower clergy, or even laymen coming from Africa should not be so readily admitted or restored prematurely to communion under threat of excommunication.

For they said that this provision, no more than the claim formerly made by Faustinus concerning the right of the Roman bishop to send legates from his side into Africa, was found written in the Nicene councils which had been sent to them from an authentic copy by Atticus, Bishop of Constantinople. Therefore they declared that in future they would accept no overseas judgment at all, much less Roman clergy sent to them as executors.

But whatever seemed to be lost from the authority of the Roman see on this side was in a certain way restored on the other by the alliance Celestine entered into with Cyril of Alexandria against Nestorius. Celestine used this so skillfully that whatever was done in the case appeared no less attributable to the vigilance of the Roman bishop than to Cyril’s zeal.

For as soon as he felt sufficiently instructed by Cyril concerning what was to be regarded as heresy, he hastened to strike it first with an anathema and to deprive its author of communion unless he renounced his errors. Soon afterward he sent legates to the synod summoned by the Emperor Theodosius at Ephesus, with this general instruction: they were to press for the condemnation of Nestorius [Note: He arranged for the judgment pronounced against Nestorius at the Roman council to be sent through Cyril first to Nestorius and, if Nestorius would not submit, to the other bishops of the East. This is what he meant when he said that Cyril was acting in his place, so that his decision might be made known either to Nestorius or to all the brethren. Letter to Nestorius, 13, in Coustant, p. 1130, and again in the Letter to the Clergy and People of Constantinople. Coustant, p. 1201.] and his deposition from his see. In the remaining matters that circumstances or the order of debate might bring forward, they had been instructed to do whatever they saw Cyril deciding.

Accordingly, he fully approved everything done by Cyril at that synod, congratulating him and all who had stood with him there as though they had won a victory over the enemies of Christ—and even congratulating the emperor himself, though an unwilling victor. He immediately greeted Maximian as the bishop appointed in place of the deposed Nestorius, restricting only this point in the instructions issued to them: that all hope of pardon and restoration should not be entirely cut off from Nestorius’s followers who repented [Note: Letter to the Council of Ephesus after Nestorius’s condemnation, in Coustant, no. 22, p. 1146.].

Indeed, these actions against Nestorius constitute the more illustrious part of Celestine’s life, but they do not contain all his services to the Catholic faith and Church. He was also the one who suppressed the flourishing heresy in Gaul later called Semi-Pelagian, and, on reports brought by Prosper of Aquitaine and Hilary, a layman, severely rebuked the bishops of Gaul because they indulged their priests so far that, calling undisciplined questions into public discussion, they preached things contrary to the truth and dared to oppose Augustine, whom he praises enthusiastically [Note: Letter 21 in Coustant, to which, because of this subject, the authorities of earlier bishops of the Apostolic See concerning the grace of God and free will are customarily appended in most codices.].

In addition, the Prosper just mentioned praises his efforts to expel the Pelagians not only from all Italy but also from Britain; for this purpose Saint Germanus of Auxerre was sent by him together with Lupus, Bishop of Troyes. Finally, Prosper’s testimony supports the claim that Palladius was ordained by him and sent as the first bishop to the Scots who believed in Christ. Celestine died in July 432.

### § II. Writings of Pope Celestine

[Col. 0412B]

Eighteen letters of Celestine remain, with the following addresses:

I. To the bishops of Illyricum. Assigned to the year 425.

II. To all bishops established throughout the provinces of Vienne and Narbonne, written on 25 July 428.

III. To all bishops established throughout Apulia and Calabria, written in 429.

IV. To Cyril, Bishop of Alexandria, written on 2 August 430, as were the following three.

V. To the bishops John, Juvenal, Rufus, and Flavian throughout the East, of equal rank.

VI. To Nestorius.

VII. To the clergy and people of Constantinople.

There can be no doubt that these four letters were written in Latin; but Coustant suspects that they were immediately translated into Greek and sent to Cyril together with the Greek translation. At the same time, he proved that the text we possess is the original.

VIII. To Cyril of Alexandria, written on 7 May 431. Coustant thought he had detected, from various indications, that this was translated from Greek and not copied from an authentic Latin original.

IX. *Commonitorium* to bishops and priests traveling to the East, written on 8 May 431.

X. To the holy synod assembled at Ephesus, written in 431. It was first read in Latin at the Council of Ephesus and inserted into its acts, and then, for the benefit of those who did not know Latin, recited in Greek as well.

XI. To the Emperor Theodosius Augustus, written in the same year.

XII. To the bishops of Gaul, written in the same year.

XIII. To the holy synod convened at Ephesus, as were the following letters, in 432, after the condemnation of Nestorius.

XIV. To Theodosius Augustus, after the synod.

XV. To Maximian, Bishop of Constantinople.

XVI. To the clergy and populace residing in Constantinople.

In addition, Arnobius preserved, in book II of *The Conflict with Serapion*, a fragment of a sermon which Celestine delivered at the Roman council in August 430 against the heresy of Nestorius.

The *Authorities of Earlier Bishops of the Apostolic See concerning the Grace of God* are more rightly excluded from Celestine and attributed to Celestius. [Col. 0413A] Coustant indicates what works were falsely attributed to Celestine or have been lost.

### § III. Editions of Celestine’s works

Of these letters of Celestine, IV, V, VI, and VII were preserved in the acts of the Council of Ephesus; II, III, and XII in the collections of Dionysius Exiguus, the Hadriana, the Hispana, and the collection of Isidore; and they were published both in those collections and from them through various editions of the councils.

Their number first began to increase through Petrus Crabbe’s fragment of Letter X, which Antonius de Aquino later published in full in the *Collection of Pontifical Letters of Cardinal Antonius Carafa*. The same Antonius intended subsequently to publish several more letters of Celestine, recovered from Vatican papers, in an *Auctuarium* which he had decided to add to the aforementioned collection. But he died before his time, and of all that he had prepared for publication with tireless zeal, nothing escaped the darkness except the letters which he had once given to Baronius.

As a result, six new letters of Celestine—namely VIII, XI, XIII, XIV, XV, and XVI—appeared in the *Annals* under the years 431 and 432. To these fourteen letters, which Binius and the Royal Collection of the Councils meanwhile presented together, and which Philippe Labbe soon repeatedly reproduced in more accurate form, Letter I was finally added by Holstenius in the two-part Roman Collection, and Letter IX by Étienne Baluze in the *New Collection of the Councils*.

Peter Coustant received the entire group for correction and illustration; Andreas Gallandi recently reproduced his edition. Mansi, however, follows Labbe’s footsteps.

### Sixteenth century

[Col. 0413C]

**1525.** Mainz; folio. *Twenty-two Decrees of Pope Celestine*, that is, three letters:

1. To the bishops of Gaul, with the *Authorities of Earlier Bishops of the Apostolic See concerning the Grace of God* appended;

2. To the bishops throughout the provinces of Vienne and Narbonne;

3. To the bishops established throughout Apulia and Calabria;

in Johann Wendelstinus’s edition of the collection of Dionysius’s canons.

**1530.** Cologne; folio. The same works, in Jacques Merlin’s *Collection of the Councils*, vol. I, fols. CLXXXIII–CLXXXVI. The first edition was made in 1523. A third appeared in 1535 at Paris, octavo, where Celestine’s letters appear on fols. CXCVII–CC.

**1536.** Basel; folio. *The Decrees of Pope Celestine*, that is, the letter to all the bishops of Gaul, with chapters or a catalogue of the constitutions of the holy Fathers concerning the grace of God appended; among the selected letters of the most ancient prelates added to Clement’s *Recognitions*, from the edition of Johann Sichard, pp. 302–306.

**1538.** Cologne, at the press of Peter Quentel; folio. *The Decrees of Pope Celestine*, by which title the three aforementioned letters are included; *Decrees from Gratian* and a fragment of the Letter to the Synod of Ephesus; in Peter Crabbe’s *Councils*, vol. I, fols. CCCIX–CCCXIII.

**1570.** Cologne, at the press of Johann Brinckmann; folio. *The Decrees of Celestine, or the Letter to All the Bishops of Gaul*, etc., among the letters of the Roman pontiffs appended to the works of Clement, from Lambert Gruter’s edition, pp. 561–563.

[Col. 0414A] **1576.** Ingolstadt, from the printing house of David Sartorius; quarto. *Various Letters of Celestine Written on the Occasion of the Council of Ephesus*, among *The Complete Acts of the Sacred, Great, and Ecumenical Council of Ephesus*, edited by Theodore Peltanus of the Society of Jesus, chapters 16, 17, 18, 19, and 64, pp. 248–274 and 388.

These are letters to Cyril, Nestorius, the clergy and people of Constantinople, John of Antioch, and the Council of Ephesus.

**1591.** Rome; folio. *The Letters of Pope Celestine*, in volume I of the *Collection of Decretal Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, begun by Cardinal Antonius Carafa and completed by Antonius de Aquino.

There are eight: four among the acts of the Council of Ephesus and three transmitted to us by Dionysius Exiguus. One, whose fragment Peter Crabbe had previously published, now appears in full, supposedly excerpted from the Cresconian collection, as Coustant says.

**1594.** Rome, from the Vatican Press; folio. *The Letters of Celestine* (fourteen), in volume V of Baronius’s *Annals*, under the years 430–432. Six previously unpublished letters appear under 431, nos. 6 and 19, and under 432, nos. 4, 12, 17, and 20. This volume was reprinted at Rome in 1607. The fifth volume of the Cologne edition of 1624 and the seventh volume of Mansi’s Lucca edition of 1741 cover the same period. Baronius hoped that Antonius de Aquino, from whom he had received those unpublished letters, would identify in the supplement to the *Pontifical Letters* that he was planning the sources from which he had drawn them. But his hope was disappointed.

### Seventeenth century

**1606.** Cologne, at the press of Johann Gymnich and Antonius Hierat; folio. *The Life, Letters, and Decrees of Pope Celestine I*, in Severinus Binius’s *Councils*, vol. I, pp. 622–632.

Of the fourteen letters which Binius collected partly from Antonius de Aquino and partly from Baronius, not all are presented in a single sequence; some occupy a place among the acts of the Council of Ephesus, indicated only by their respective numbers. Bini’s notes are added to some of them.

**1609.** Paris; octavo. *The Decrees of Pope Celestine I*—three letters—in the *Code of the Ancient Roman Church*, pp. 404–426.

**1629.** Paris, at the expense of Sebastian Cramoisy; folio. Two letters of Pope Celestine I to the bishops of the provinces of Vienne and Narbonne and to all the bishops of Gaul; in volume I of Jacques Sirmond’s *Councils of Gaul*.

[Col. 0414D] **1644.** Paris, from the Royal Press; folio. *The Life, Letters, and Decrees of Pope Celestine I*, in volume IV of the Luparian collection of councils, pp. 469–510. The *Authorities concerning the Grace of God* precede the letters.

**1661.** Paris, at the press of Louis Billaine; folio. *The Decrees of Pope Celestine*—three letters with the *Authorities*—in the codex of Dionysius Exiguus, published by Guillaume Voël and Henri Justel in the *Bibliotheca of Canon Law*, pp. 215–222.

**1662.** Rome; octavo. *The Letter of Celestine to the Bishops throughout Illyricum*, now published for the first time from Vatican papers, among the acts of the Roman synod under Boniface II; in part I of Luke Holstenius’s two-part Roman Collection, pp. 85–88.

[Col. 0415A] **1671.** Paris; folio. *The Life, Letters, and Decrees of Pope Celestine I*, with the notes of Severinus Binius, Jacques Sirmond, and the observations of Philippe Labbe; in volume II of the *Councils* edited by Philippe Labbe and Gabriel Cossart, pp. 1610–1638.

Several letters in this series are represented only by their titles. The letters themselves appear among the acts of the Council of Ephesus, vol. III, pp. 345, 346, 353, 376, and 614. Labbe follows Binius and the editor of the Royal Collection more closely. This adherence led him to have some letters printed twice. For the letters numbered IX to Theodosius, X to Cyril, XI to the Council of Ephesus, XII to the younger Theodosius, XIII to Maximian, and XIV to the Constantinopolitans are again given in full in volume III, pp. 619, 621, 1069, and 1072; volume IV, pp. 1074 and 1075. In the appendix to this second volume, pp. 1817–1819, are added Sirmond’s posthumous notes on two letters to the bishops of Gaul and on the *Authorities of the Apostolic See*.

**1675.** Paris, at the press of Jean-Baptiste Coignard; quarto. *The Letter of Pope Celestine to the Bishops of Vienne and Narbonne, and His Letter to the Bishops of Apulia and Calabria*, in the *Code of the Canons of the Roman Church* published by Paschasius Quesnell in volume II of the works of Leo the Great, chapters 35 and 36, pp. 133–137; in the Lyon edition of 1700, pp. 71–73.

**1682.** Louvain, printed by Hieronymus Nempaeus; quarto. *The Commonitorium of Pope Celestine to the Bishops and Priests Traveling to the East*, now published for the first time from a manuscript of the Vatican Library by F. Christian Lupus of Ypres, in *Letters of Various Fathers to the Council of Ephesus*, taken and published by him from a manuscript of the Cassine Library, chapter 226, fol. CCCCLXX. This work was reprinted in volume VII of the works of Christian Lupus (Venice, at the press of Giovanni Battista Albritius, Quirinus Hieronymus and Sebastian Coleti, 1726; folio), where Celestine’s *Commonitorium* appears on pp. 385–386.

**1683.** Paris, from the printing office of François Muguet; folio. *The Commonitorium of Pope Celestine Given to the Bishops and Priests Traveling to the East. Various Letters of the Same Man Written on the Occasion of the Council of Ephesus*, in Étienne Baluze’s *New Collection of the Councils*, vol. I, pp. 381, 424, 431, 436, 438, and 489–493.

Baluze first found the *Commonitorium* in the very ancient and excellently written codex no. 1865 of the Colbert Library. Jerome Cardinal Casanata later sent him another, more recent copy from the Vatican, no. 1320, written during the pontificate of Nicholas V. But the Colbert copy was more accurate than the Vatican one. Baluze did not know that Lupus had already published it the previous year.

The remaining letters, distributed among the acts of the Council of Ephesus, are:

1. The letter to Nestorius;

2. The letter to the clergy and people of Constantinople;

3. The letter to Cyril;

4. The letter to John of Antioch;

5. The letter to the Council of Ephesus;

6. The letter to the Emperor Theodosius;

7. The second letter to Cyril of Alexandria.

**1687.** Paris, from the Royal Press; folio. *The Decrees of Pope Celestine*—three letters—in the *Code of Canons of Dionysius Exiguus*, from the edition of François Pithou, reprinted here and now, pp. 219–228.

### Eighteenth century

**1715.** Paris, from the Royal Press; folio. *The Decrees of Pope Celestine*—three letters; also the letters distributed through the acts of the Council of Ephesus: to Nestorius; to the clergy and people of Constantinople; to Cyril; to John of Antioch; the *Commonitorium* to the legates; to the Council of Ephesus; to Theodosius; the second letter to Cyril; to the synod after the condemnation of Nestorius; to the younger Theodosius; to Maximian; and the second letter to the clergy and people of Constantinople; in Jean Hardouin’s *Acts of the Councils*, vol. I, pp. 1251–1262, 1299, 1311, 1321, 1323, 1347, and 1467–1474, 1671–1682.

**1721.** Paris; folio. *The Letters and Decrees of Saint Pope Celestine, Restored to the Correct Chronological Order, Revised and Corrected According to the Evidence of Ancient Codices, with Preliminary Admonitions, Critical Notes, and Dissertations*, by Pierre Coustant; in the *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, vol. I, pp. 1051–1228.

Letters of others to Celestine, or concerning matters handled by him, have been inserted—namely, at the beginning of the whole collection: 1. Augustine’s letter to Celestine, written around the beginning of 423, numbered 209 among the Augustinian letters; 2. the letter of Aurelius and the others who attended the universal African Council of Carthage, from the code of canons of the African Church, written, according to Coustant’s judgment, either toward the end of 425 or at the beginning of 426. Then, after III: 3 and 4, two letters of Nestorius to Celestine, in Greek and Latin; 5. Cyril’s letter to Celestine, written in 430, in Greek and Latin; 6. Cyril’s memorandum given to Posidonius when he was sending him to Rome, in Greek and Latin. After XIV: 7. a letter of Nestorius to Celestine, written in 430, in Greek and Latin. After XIX: 8. the letter of the Council of Ephesus to Celestine, in Greek and Latin. In the tenth place there is a fragment of a sermon delivered by Celestine. A Notice of the Letters pertaining to Pope Celestine is appended.

1757. Venice, at the press of Simon Occhi; in folio. Celestine’s letter to the bishops of Vienne and Narbonne, likewise to the bishops of Apulia and Calabria, with variant readings from both printed and manuscript copies; in Paschasius Quesnel’s *Code of the Ancient Canons and Constitutions of the Apostolic See*, reprinted by the Ballerini brothers, volume III of the works of Leo the Great, chapters 35 and 36, pages 270–277.

1760. Florence; in folio. *The Life, Letters, and Decrees of Saint Celestine I, Pope*, with the notes of Binius and Sirmond, together with several excerpts from manuscript copies of letters and titles of certain ancient letters of Celestine; in volume IV of the very extensive collection of Councils by John Dominic Mansi, pages 453–474.

He did not reproduce in full in this series the letters reported among the Acts of the Council of Ephesus contained in this same volume. Coletus too had done this after Labbe—although Mansi otherwise rarely departs from Coletus—but Mansi preferred to follow Binius and, after reciting their titles and opening words, refers readers to them.

1773. Venice, from the press of Giovanni Battista Albritius; in folio. *The Letters and Decrees of Saint Celestine, Pope*, with several items inserted that pertain to the same holy pontiff. From the edition of the distinguished Peter Coustant; in volume IX of Andrew Gallandi’s *Library of the Fathers and Saints of the Ancient Church*, pages 287–346.

He cut out the admonitions that Coustant had prefixed to some of the letters and frequently abridged their sentences in the notes. He discusses Celestine in the preliminary essays, chapter 8, pages XIX–XX.

1789. Paris, at the expense of Peter Didot the eldest son; in folio. Celestine’s letter to the bishops of the province of Vienne and Narbonne. Also his letter to the bishops of Gaul on behalf of Saint Augustine, with the decrees and titles of the decrees, as well as excerpts from the notes and variant readings of Sirmond, Quesnel, and Coustant; in the newest collection of the Councils of Gaul recently begun by the Maurist Fathers, volume I, pages 384 and 426.

## THE LETTERS AND DECREES OF SAINT CELESTINE I, POPE

(From Coustant’s edition in Gallandi’s *Library of the Ancient Fathers*, volume IX.) (S)

[Note: Written around the beginning of the year 423. It is found among Augustine’s letters. As soon as Celestine’s election and ordination had been announced in Africa—and therefore around the beginning of 423—Augustine himself plainly declares from the outset that it was written. His scruples concerning the case of Antony of Fussala would not allow him either to delay or to remain at rest until he had found an immediate remedy for them.]

## LETTER I. AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, TO POPE CELESTINE (S)

The case of Antony, bishop of Fussala, who had been deprived of the administration of his church because of his crimes and had appealed to the Apostolic See, having been explained, Augustine begs that the sentence pronounced against him be allowed to remain in force.

To the most blessed lord and holy pope Celestine, worthy of veneration in due charity, Augustine sends greetings in the Lord.

### 1

First, I offer congratulations appropriate to your merits, because our Lord God has appointed you to that See without, as we have heard, any division among his people.

[Note: Although the schismatics had not yet withdrawn from the faction of Eulalius, Baronius thinks that against them the law was given at Aquileia on 16 July 425, in the consulship of Theodosius Augustus for the eleventh time and Valentinian Caesar, namely, book XVI, title 5, law 62 of the Theodosian Code. It provides: “Against these above all a vigorous action must be undertaken who, through wicked persuasions, withdraw themselves from communion with the venerable pope, by whose schism the rest of the people too are corrupted. After prior summons, we grant them a respite of twenty days, within which, unless they return to the unity of communion, they shall be expelled to the hundredth milestone and waste away in the solitude they have chosen.”]

Then I bring to your holiness’s attention what is taking place around us, so that you may assist us not only by praying for us but also by giving advice and help. For, being placed in great tribulation, I have directed this letter to your blessedness, because, wishing to benefit certain members of Christ in our neighborhood, I have, through lack of foresight and caution, inflicted a great calamity upon them.

### 2

Fussala is said to be a fortified town bordering the territory of Hippo. Previously it had never had a bishop, but, together with the adjoining region, belonged to the parish of the Church of Hippo. That land had few Catholics; the Donatist error had miserably taken possession of the remaining populations settled there in great numbers, so that there was not a single Catholic at all in the town itself.

By God’s mercy it came about that all those places adhered to the unity of the Church. It would take too long to explain through how many labors and dangers of ours this happened, so that the priests whom we first appointed to gather them together were stripped, beaten, maimed, blinded, and killed.

[Note: That is, the schismatics were to be brought back to unity.]

Nevertheless, their sufferings were not useless or fruitless, since the security of unity was completed there. But because the town mentioned, Fussala, is separated from Hippo by forty miles, and because, while governing them and gathering their remnants—even though small—which were wandering in both sexes, I found myself extending my reach farther than was proper, since they were no longer threatening but fleeing, and I saw that the diligence that ought, for the most certain reasons, to be applied was beyond my capacity, I arranged that a bishop should be ordained and appointed there.

### 3

To accomplish this I sought someone suitable and appropriate for that place, who was also equipped with the Punic language. I had a priest ready whom I had in mind. For his ordination I obtained by letter that the holy old man who then held the primacy of Numidia should come from a distant place.

[Note: That is, Silvanus, who in Augustine’s Letter 128 subscribes as “elder of the church of Summis,” and in Letter 129 as “bishop of the first see of the province of Numidia.”]

When he was already present, and everyone’s attention was anxiously fixed upon so important a matter, the man whom I had thought ready for the purpose withdrew by resisting me in every possible way at the very moment. But I, who, as the outcome showed, ought certainly rather to have postponed than rashly hastened the dangerous undertaking, did not wish the venerable and exceedingly holy old man, worn out by coming all the way to us, to return home without accomplishing the purpose for which he had traveled so far. Therefore I offered to those who had not requested him a certain young man, Antony, who was then with me. He had indeed been raised by us in the monastery from early childhood, but apart from the office of reader was unfamiliar with any clerical rank or labor.

[Note: Zosimus, in Letter 9, section 5, decrees that anyone who has devoted himself to ecclesiastical ministries from infancy should, with uninterrupted observance, remain among the readers until the twentieth year of his age. In this he followed the decree of Pope Siricius, Letter 1, section 13. Accordingly, it is reasonable to believe that Antony, having been initiated as a reader from early childhood and immediately entrusted to Augustine, was an instance of a practice then customary; we have demonstrated this by several examples in the passage of Siricius cited above. To this we add the case of Chrysostom, concerning whom Palladius writes in his *Dialogue*, page 227: “At the age of eighteen he withdrew from the rhetor Libanius, was baptized by Meletius, archbishop of Antioch, and was ordained a reader.” It may nevertheless be inferred from this that Antony continued in the office of reader beyond his twentieth year.]

Those unfortunate people, not knowing what was to happen, accepted him whom I offered to them with complete obedience. What more is there to say? He began to be their bishop.

### 4

What am I to do? I do not wish to burden your veneration with one whom I gathered in order to nurture; I do not wish to abandon those whom I brought forth amid fears and griefs so that they might be gathered in. And I cannot discover how to do both.

The matter has indeed reached such a degree of scandal that here among us they brought charges against him who had obeyed us, as though we were giving them good counsel, when they accepted his bishopric. In the course of that trial, the capital crimes of sexual misconduct—which had been alleged not by the people over whom he was bishop but by certain others—could by no means be proved, and he appeared to have been cleared of the matters most maliciously spread abroad.

He became so pitiable both to us and to others that whatever the townspeople and inhabitants of that region alleged concerning intolerable domination, robberies, and various acts of oppression and abuse did not appear to us to be of such a nature that we should deprive him of the episcopate either on that account or because all the accusations had been piled together. Rather, we thought that whatever could be proved to have been taken away should be restored.

### 5

Finally, we tempered our judgments in such a way that, while his episcopate was preserved, the actions that ought not thereafter to be repeated by him or imitated by others were not left wholly unpunished. We therefore preserved the young man’s honor intact for the sake of correction, but reduced his power for the sake of discipline. He was not to preside any longer over those with whom he had acted in such a way that, in their justified grief, they could not endure him presiding over them at all, and might, through the danger threatening both themselves and him, allow their impatience and resentment to burst into some crime.

Their disposition had already clearly appeared when the bishops dealt with him before them, even though the distinguished man Celer—of whose powerful administration against them he complained—now held no authority either in Africa or anywhere else.

### 6

But why delay over many details? Work together with us, I beg you, most blessed lord, venerable for your piety and holy pope, worthy of veneration in due charity, and order that everything sent to you be read aloud. See how he administered the episcopate; how he agreed so completely with our judgment that, having been deprived of communion, he was not to be restored unless everything was first returned to the people of Fussala; and how, after the matter had been completed and the goods assessed, he set aside solidi so that communion might be restored to him.

See by what crafty persuasion he induced our primate, that most serious and distinguished old man, to believe everything he said, so that he might commend him to the venerable Pope Boniface as a man entirely blameless.

[Note: Namely, Valentinus Baianus, who at the beginning of Letter 2 to Boniface is styled “bishop of the first see of the province of Numidia.” It may be inferred from this that he did not sit among Antony’s judges. Yet what follows indicates that, after the proceedings had been communicated to him, he not only abandoned his error but also sent Celestine, together with this letter of Augustine, a truer account of the whole matter.]

And why do I need to review the remaining matters, when the venerable old man just mentioned has reported everything to your holiness?

### 7

In those numerous proceedings containing our judgment concerning him, I ought rather to fear that we may appear to you to have judged less severely than we should have done, were I not aware that you are so inclined toward mercy that you think mercy ought to be shown not only to us, because we spared him, but also to him himself.

But he is trying to turn what we did either kindly or leniently into a legal claim and to seize it as a right. He cries out: “Either I ought to have sat in my own chair, or I ought not to have been a bishop,” as though he now sits anywhere except in his own.

For this reason those places were left and entrusted to him in which he had previously been bishop, so that he would not be said to have been illicitly transferred to another’s chair, contrary to the statutes of the Fathers.

[Note: The Africans were then unaware of the Sardican decrees, as will become clear from the following letter, section 3. Augustine therefore has only one matter in mind here, and Antony’s judges proposed to observe for themselves canon 15 of the Council of Nicaea, which decrees that no bishop, priest, or deacon may be transferred from one city to another. It would be desirable if this rule were observed in our own age as well, especially with regard to priests whose life is disgraceful and harmful and brings scandal and ruin upon the people. They would not so readily be allowed, after harming the Church first entrusted to them, to move far away to administer another church, to which they bring harm all the more certainly because precautions are taken less carefully against their crimes. The only exception would be when men accused of serious crimes, though not fully convicted, were judged less useful to their own people because of the stain cast upon their reputation.
