The Africans seem to have acted in this way toward Apiarius, when he shamelessly denied the crimes brought against him and there was no clear means by which he could be convicted.]

Or must anyone be so exacting either in severity or in leniency that those who are not thought worthy of being deprived of the honor of the episcopate may in no way be punished, while those whom it is thought necessary to punish in some respect must be deprived of episcopal honor?

### 8

There are examples—some judged by the Apostolic See itself, others judged elsewhere and confirmed by it—of men who, for certain offenses, were neither stripped of episcopal honor nor left entirely unpunished.

[Note: Here the authority of the Apostolic See in the judgments of the Africans is openly proclaimed. But an erudite man observes that this was said during the interval in which the Africans permitted appeals to Rome, until, after consulting the most accurate copies of the Council of Nicaea, they had become certain whether the canons praised by Zosimus were found in them. Certainly, Laurence, who was to be appealed against below, subscribes in chapter 133 of the Code of the Canons of the African Church, in the year 419, to the Council of Carthage not merely as bishop of Icosium but as legate of the province of Caesarea. Therefore, in that year the sentence against him that Augustine soon mentions had not yet been pronounced.]

To avoid seeking examples from times far removed from our own, I shall mention recent ones.

Let Priscus, bishop of the province of Caesarea, cry out: “Either the place at the primacy ought to have been open to me, as it was to the others, or the episcopate ought not to have remained to me.”

Let another bishop of the same province, Victor, cry out. He was left under the same penalty as Priscus and nowhere receives communion from any bishop except in his own diocese. Let him cry out, I say: “Either I ought to have received communion everywhere, or I ought not to have received it even in my own places.”

Let a third bishop of the same province, Laurence, cry out—and let him cry out in precisely these words: “Either I ought to have sat in the chair to which I was ordained, or I ought not to have been a bishop.”

[Note: It would have been easy to add the example of Apiarius, concerning whom the African Council writes in its second letter to Pope Boniface that it had decreed that he should be removed from the Church of Sicca, while retaining the honor of his rank, and that, once he had received a letter of authorization, he might exercise the honor of the presbyterate wherever else he wished and was able. But when Augustine brings forward examples of judgments confirmed by the Apostolic See, the example of Apiarius was less appropriate, since he was only a priest and since the Africans judged him in such a way that there is no record of their judgment having been confirmed by the Apostolic See. Nevertheless, it serves to prove Antony’s injustice, insofar as it shows that a cleric can be punished for crimes without being entirely removed from his rank of honor.]

But who would criticize such arrangements except one who pays little attention to the fact that not everything should be left unpunished and that not everything should be punished in the same way?

### 9

Therefore, since the most blessed Pope Boniface, with pastoral and watchful caution, wrote in his letter, speaking of Antony the bishop, “If he has faithfully reported the order of events to us,” now receive the order of events that he omitted in his own little book, and then learn what was done after the letters of that holy man of blessed memory had been read in Africa.

[Note: These letters do not survive.]

Come to the aid of these people, in the mercy of Christ, much more eagerly than he asks, for they desire to be freed from his disturbance. For he himself, or frequent rumors, threatens them with judges, public authorities, and military attacks as though they were to carry out the sentence of the Apostolic See.

[Note: We shall discuss the office of the enforcement agents more conveniently in the notes to Letter 2. It has been observed in the new edition of Augustine that Antony was never restored to the administration of the Church of Fussala, since Augustine himself exercised its care toward the end of his life; and therefore Celestine did nothing of the sort that that pious bishop feared so greatly.]

Thus these wretched Christian Catholics fear worse things from a Catholic bishop than, when they were heretics, they feared from the laws of Catholic emperors.

Do not allow this to happen, I beg you, by the blood of Christ and by the memory of the apostle Peter, who warned the leaders of Christian peoples not to domineer violently over their brothers (1 Peter 5:3).

I commend to the kindness of your charity and holiness both the Catholics of Fussala, my children in Christ, and Antony the bishop, my child in Christ, because I love them both and commend them both to you.

I do not resent the people of Fussala because they bring a just complaint against me to your ears, namely, that I inflicted upon them a man whom I had not yet tested and who was not even yet established in age, from whom they were to suffer such affliction.

Nor do I wish harm to this man. The more sincerely I love him, the more strongly I resist his perverse desire.

May your mercy be shown to both: to them, so that they may not suffer evil; to him, so that he may not do evil. May they not hate the Catholic Church if Catholics, and especially the Apostolic See itself, do not come to their aid against a Catholic bishop. And may he not bind himself by so great a crime that, while he tries to make those whom he wishes into his unwilling subjects, he makes them strangers to Christ.

### 10

As for me, I confess to your blessedness that such fear and sorrow torture me amid the danger threatening both sides that I am thinking of withdrawing from the duty of governing the episcopate and surrendering myself to lamentations suited to my error, if I should see the Church of God laid waste through him whose episcopate I imprudently supported, and—God forbid—see him perish together with the one who lays it waste.

For, recalling what the Apostle says, “If we judged ourselves, we would not be judged by the Lord” (1 Corinthians 11:31), I shall judge myself, so that he who will judge the living and the dead may spare me.

But if you restore the members of Christ who are in that region from their destructive fear and sorrow, and console my old age by this merciful justice, he who through you comes to our aid in this tribulation, and who has established you in that See, will repay you with good for good, both in the present life and in the life to come.

[Note: This letter closes the code of the canons of the African Church. It is also found in the same manuscripts and collections in which we said that the second letter of those same Africans to Boniface is found. It was written on the occasion of Apiarius, who, having been removed from the Church of Sicca by the judgment of the Council of Carthage in 419, withdrew to Thabraca, a prominent city in the proconsular province. But after being accused again by the citizens of that city of abominable crimes, and therefore deprived of communion by another Council of Carthage, he fled to Rome and falsely claimed that he had appealed from this sentence. Celestine restored him to communion and sent Faustinus to Africa so that communion might also be restored to him there.

Tillemont observes, volume XIII, page 860, that the disturbances arising from the death of Honorius and the usurpation of John in the West did not permit free communication between Rome and Africa from August 423 until July 425. Accordingly, this letter must be assigned either to the end of 425 or to the year 426. Its opening does not allow it to be believed that it was written before August 423, since it contains no congratulation on the happy auspices of the new pontificate, a customary form of greeting that would not ordinarily have been omitted.]

## LETTER II. OF THE AFRICAN COUNCIL TO POPE CELESTINE, BISHOP OF THE CITY OF ROME (C)*

They inform him that Apiarius was compelled to confess his crimes. Then they ask: 1. that he not restore those whom they have excommunicated to communion too hastily; 2. that he reject the improper refuges or appeals of priests and other clerics; 3. that he not send anyone from his side to investigate the case of an appellant; 4. that he not grant enforcement agents to those who request them; and finally, that he not send Faustinus back to Africa.

To their beloved and honorable lord and brother Celestine, Aurelius, Palatinus, Antonius, Tutus, Servant of God, Terentius, Fortunatus, Martinus, Januarius,

[Note: Some manuscripts of inferior quality read “Palastinus.” In one manuscript of Harleian type, as in Merlin, “Palestinus.” In Labbe, in the margin, “Palentinus” and “Palatinus”; but in the text, “Valentinus”—a reading we would readily adopt if the more reliable manuscripts, Reginensis, Colbertinus, two Harleian manuscripts, and others, did not prefer “Palatinus,” as it is also read by the Greek translator.]

Optatus,

[Note: In printed editions, “Celtitius” or “Celticius.” In some manuscripts, “Celsitius.” In the better ones, “Celticus.” Augustine mentions this bishop in *On Eight Questions to Dulcitius*, question 7, section 3, although the name is represented in no uniform way in the manuscripts.]

Celticus, Donatus, Theasius, Vincentius, Fortunatianus, and the rest who were present at the universal African Council of Carthage.

[Note: The Colbertine manuscript reads: “We are present at Carthage.”]

### 1

We would have wished that, just as your holiness informed us by a letter sent through our fellow presbyter Leo that you had rejoiced at the arrival of Apiarius, so we too might send this letter with joy concerning his acquittal.

[Note: The manuscripts agree almost unanimously on “siquidem admodum,” except that one Harleian manuscript has “siquidem quemadmodum,” and the Coislinian manuscript, in a second revision, has “si quemadmodum,” which Merlin and Crabbe adopted. That the Leo mentioned shortly afterward is a different man from the one who succeeded Pope Xystus is shown by the fact that Prosper, in his *Chronicle*, calls this Leo a deacon even under Xystus.]

Certainly, our rejoicing—and yours—would now be more secure and would not seem premature, since it had preceded the hearing rather than followed it.

When our holy brother and fellow bishop Faustinus arrived among us, we convened a council and believed that he had been sent for this reason: just as through his efforts Apiarius had previously been restored to the presbyterate, so now, through his efforts, he might be cleared of the many crimes alleged against him by the people of Thabraca.

But the ongoing examination of our council found his crimes so great and monstrous that they outweighed the advocacy rather than the judgment of the man mentioned, and the service of a defender rather than the justice of an examiner.

[Note: That is, Faustinus, whose manner of proceeding is criticized here: whereas he ought to have fulfilled the role of a just judge and impartial examiner, he was acting as patron and defender. But Apiarius’s vices surpassed Faustinus’s efforts, so that he was wholly unable either to defend or to clear them.]

[Note: That is, the justice of one who acts as examiner and therefore gives a fair sentence. The Greek translator renders both the examiner here and the “examiners” below, in section 3, by the single term τοῦ διαγνωστοῦ and τῶν διαγνωστῶν. An examiner is one who presides as judge and arbiter over the investigation of a case. Marcellinus Comes is repeatedly honored by this title in the conference at Carthage over which he presided. This is relevant to what Habetdeus said in that same conference, chapter 258: “The great mark of a just examiner is that what he grants to one party he does not deny to the other”; and also to what the emperor Honorius decrees in the Theodosian Code, book XVI, title 5, law 45: “For public confidence ought not to perish through the death of the examiner.”]

For first, consider how much he opposed the entire assembly by bringing forward various insults, as though asserting the privileges of the Roman Church, and as though we wished to receive into communion the man whom your holiness, believing that he had appealed, had restored to communion, although he could not prove the appeal.

[Note: The Greek translator has πρῶτον γὰρ ἀντέστη, that is, “for first he opposed—or resisted—strenuously”; this is clearer if the question mark is removed.]

This was not permissible, as you will learn more clearly by reading the proceedings. Nevertheless, after a most laborious trial lasting three days, while we were searching in extreme distress through the various charges brought against him, and while our fellow bishop Faustinus delayed and Apiarius himself employed evasions by which he tried to conceal his unspeakable disgraces, God, the judge, strong and long-suffering, cut the matter short with great dispatch.

For when his filthy and more than foul obstinacy was crushed—the impudence of his denial having attempted to bury so great a mass of lustful filth—and when our God constrained his conscience and made public to human beings the hidden things that he had already condemned in his heart as though in a sewer of crimes, the cunning denier suddenly burst into a confession of all the crimes alleged.

At last, he voluntarily convicted himself of all the incredible disgraces, and changed into groans the very hope we had held and desired: that he might be cleansed of such shameful stains.

Yet our sorrow was mitigated by this one consolation: his confession freed us from the labor of a more prolonged investigation and provided some sort of remedy for his wounds, although it was made unwillingly and against the resistance of his own conscience, my lord and brother.

[Note: All our manuscripts agree with Justellus, except that one Colbertine manuscript reads: “and, although unwilling, with his conscience resisting, he disclosed it by his confession.” But the edition of the councils reads: “although his will and conscience resisted, he revealed it by confession.” In later editions, however, “by confession” was removed. God compels the guilty to make such unwilling confessions by that power through which he can do all things. Augustine relates elsewhere, in Letter 137, now numbered 78, section 3: “At Milan, at the memorial of the saints, where demons confess in a wondrous and terrifying manner, a certain thief who had come to that place to deceive him by swearing falsely was compelled to confess the theft.” He likewise testifies that the same thing regularly occurred at Nola, at the place where the body of blessed Felix is buried; for this reason he sent two of his clerics, who were accusing one another, there so that the truth of the matter might be disclosed.]

### 2

After offering the greeting due to you, we earnestly beg you henceforth not to admit too readily to your ears those who come from here, nor to wish any longer to receive into communion those whom we have excommunicated.

[Note: Isidore Mercator, in the letter he forged in the name of Easterners writing to Pope Julius, substitutes *propter beati Petri honorem impenso* (“earnestly, for the honor of blessed Peter”) for *impendio* when copying this passage.] Your venerableness should readily recognize that this too was defined by the Council of Nicaea.

[Note: Council of Nicaea, canon 5.]

[Note: Thus the Colbertine manuscript. Merlin has *advertit*, and the other books have *advertet*.]

For if it appears that provision was made there concerning lower-ranking clerics or laymen, how much more did it wish this to be observed concerning bishops, so that those suspended from communion in their own province may not appear to be restored to communion by your holiness too hastily or improperly?

### 3

May your holiness, as is fitting for you, reject the improper appeals of priests and of the clerics below them, because this has not been derogated from the African Church by any definition of the Fathers, and because the decrees of Nicaea most plainly entrusted both clerics of lower rank and the bishops themselves to their metropolitans.

[Note: The Second Council of Milevis, canon 22, decrees: “If priests, deacons, or other lower-ranking clerics, in cases that concern them, complain about the judgments of their bishops, let the neighboring bishops hear them, and, appointed by them with the consent of their own bishops, let them settle whatever exists between them. But if they think they ought to appeal from them as well, let them appeal only to the African councils or to the primates of their own provinces. Anyone who thinks he ought to appeal overseas shall be received into communion by no one within Africa.” This canon is inserted in the same words into the Code of the Canons of the African Church, chapter 125. If we adhere to its wording, only priests and lower clerics, not bishops, are forbidden to appeal overseas—that is, to the Apostolic See.

Yet although the Africans now adapt their words to that same decree and ask Celestine to reject the improper appeals of priests and lower clerics, they by no means indicate that they allow bishops to appeal overseas. Indeed, they soon reveal what their judgment on this matter is when they praise the decrees of Nicaea, which most clearly entrusted both clerics of lower rank and the bishops themselves to their metropolitans.

In the Code of the Canons of the African Church, chapter 28, this canon is presented in such a way as to teach that appeals overseas were forbidden to bishops no less than to other clerics. Its concluding clause is given there as follows: “But if they think they ought to appeal from them, let them not appeal to overseas tribunals, but to the primates of their provinces or to the universal council, as has often been established concerning BISHOPS ALSO.”

Hence the mention of bishops seems to have been omitted from the canon of the Council of Milevis because the same matter had already often been decreed concerning them. Moreover, this addition—“as has often been established concerning bishops”—which Dionysius Exiguus also preserved, gave rise to great controversies, too extensive to be settled in the narrow space of a marginal note.

If, however, we consider these words of Cyprian near the end of Letter 55: “Since it has been established for all of us, and is equally fair and just, that each person’s case should be heard there where the crime was committed”; and if we compare the other things that the same holy man adds with what the Africans now assert, we shall easily discover in them the same disposition and attitude, equally hostile to appeals overseas.]

For they very wisely and justly understood that all cases ought to be concluded in the places where they arose, and that the grace of the Holy Spirit would not be lacking to anyone’s prudence, so that equity might be both wisely discerned and most steadfastly maintained by Christ’s priests.

[Note: They provided for this in canon 5 by ordering—not merely by advising—that councils be held twice each year in every province, so that, with all the bishops of the province gathered together, such questions as had arisen might be examined collectively. By the same canon they also understood that bishops were forbidden to be judged outside the boundaries of their own province, as we observed in the note to page 775 of Innocent’s Letter 4. The Africans are not wrong to say that bishops and clerics of lower rank were entrusted by this canon to their metropolitans, because, although the metropolitan is not explicitly mentioned, what the council of the province over which he presides decrees and judges is rightly attributed to him.]

For it has been granted to everyone, if he has been offended by the judgment of the examiners, to appeal to the councils of his own province or even to a universal council.

[Note: For this reason the Third Council of Carthage, canon 2, established—as the statute is recorded in the Code of the Canons of the African Church—that, in accordance with the decrees of Nicaea, because of ecclesiastical cases that grow old to the destruction of the peoples, a council should be convened every year. To it, all the provinces that have first sees should send from their councils two bishops, or as many as they might choose, so that, when the assembly had been gathered, its authority might be complete.

From this one may understand what the Africans here simply call a “universal council,” what the Third Council of Carthage, canon 7, calls an “annual universal council,” and what Augustine calls in various places a “plenary council.” A council is called universal because it is assembled from all the provinces; it is also called plenary because it possesses complete authority.]

Unless perhaps someone believes that our God can inspire the justice of examination in any one person and deny it to countless priests gathered in council.

Or how will that overseas judgment be valid when the necessary witnesses cannot be brought there, whether because of their sex, the weakness of old age,

[Note: To avoid this inconvenience, Cyprian decreed in Letter 55: “It is certainly necessary that those over whom we preside should plead their case there where they can have both their accusers and witnesses to their crime.” For this reason the Africans also provided in the Code of the Canons of the African Church, chapter 30, that if an accused person or accuser fears some violence from a reckless crowd, he should choose for himself a nearby place from which the accused comes, where it will not be difficult to produce witnesses and conclude the case.]

or because of many other obstacles?

4. For we find nothing established in any synod of the Fathers to the effect that some persons should be sent as though from the side of Your Holiness [Note: If they had discovered that this had been decreed at the Synod of Sardica, at which Gratian, bishop of Carthage, was present, they would apparently have accepted it without difficulty. But they were also greatly deterred from accepting this decree by Faustinus’s certain arrogance throughout the whole affair and by his not entirely equitable manner of proceeding.]—because, in the more authoritative councils, the document which you previously sent through our fellow bishop Faustinus, as though it came from the Council of Nicaea, is not found among those authentic copies of the Council of Nicaea which we received from our fellow bishop Saint Cyril of the Church of Alexandria and from the venerable bishop Atticus of Constantinople. These copies were sent from the original, and we ourselves had already sent them, through the presbyter Innocent and the subdeacon Marcellus, by whom they were directed to us from those bishops, to Boniface, your predecessor, of venerable memory; yet in them we could find nothing of the sort.

5. Do not send even your clerical executors to any who request them, nor grant them [Note: According to the preceding letter, no. 9, “executors” were those who were sent as though to execute the sentence of the Apostolic See. Their duty was to summon the interested parties and warn and inform them of the sentence pronounced, so that, if they refused to abide by the judgment within the prescribed number of days, they might be treated and separated as rebels. Hence the act by which they were summoned was likewise called a “summoning” or an “execution.” Thus Celestine, in Letter 10, no. 4, addresses Cyril as his legate and executor of his sentence against Nestorius: “Therefore, having enlisted with you the authority of our see, and acting in our place, you shall EXECUTE this sentence with strict force, so that either within ten days reckoned from the day of this SUMMONS he may condemn his perverse teachings by a written profession,” etc. And at the end of Letter 11, he warns Nestorius, regarding the formula sent by him, with which Cyril was to summon him, in these words according to the ancient translator: “Acknowledge openly, therefore, that this is our sentence: for unless you separate this impious novelty from the adored and venerable Scripture, and condemn it openly and in writing within ten days reckoned from the first day on which this EXECUTION became known to you, you shall be excommunicated from the whole Catholic Church.” This also clarifies what we read in chapter 96 of the Code of the African Church: “It was furthermore decided that five EXECUTORS should be requested for all the Church’s needs, to be assigned in the various provinces,” namely, to carry out the decree concerning the summoning of the Donatists, which had been set forth earlier in chapter 91 of the same Code. Accordingly, chapter 123 subsequently provides that, if a bishop has been negligent in converting the Donatists, he is to be summoned by the neighboring bishops; and, after three months from that time, if he persists in his negligence, communion is not to be extended to him, provided that execution has been assigned in his province. Otherwise it is prescribed that, if the executor has not come to the places concerned, this is not to be charged against the bishop. Augustine also indicates in the preceding letter, no. 4, that those clerical executors sent by the Roman bishop sometimes employed the support of the public authorities and military force in order to execute the sentence of the Apostolic See. But here the Africans accuse them of arrogance, not violence. Leo, in Letter 12, openly reproves both faults in Anastasius: the first, in no. 2, in these words: “When it pleases one to rule rather than to care for one’s subjects, honor inflates pride, and what was provided for harmony tends toward harm”; the second, in no. 3, as follows: “That has been exposed—namely, the prefecture of Illyricum, and the most exalted power among worldly offices, roused for the production of an innocent bishop, so that a TERRIBLE EXECUTION might be sent, one that would attach all public offices to itself,” etc. Yet the same pope asserts at the end of no. 2 that executions of this kind had never been approved by the Apostolic See in any writing of his own or of his predecessors. He himself uses the word “execute” more simply in Letter 73: “After the venerable day we shall send our men, who … shall execute what has been established by us”; and in Letter 76, when he writes that he has sent Lucentius and Basil, “who,” he says, “shall execute my arrangements according to the rules they have received.” The same word, however, has a harsher sound in Gregory, Book XII, Indiction 5, Letter 31, where John, bishop of Justiniana Prima, is ordered to have a certain contumacious bishop named Paul compelled by strict execution.]

lest we appear to be introducing the smoke-filled arrogance of the world into the Church of Christ, which displays the daylight of simplicity and humility to those who desire to see God.

6. As for our brother Faustinus (with Apiarius now, to our sorrow, removed from the Church of Christ because of his unspeakable wickedness [Note: In the Colbert manuscript the words “separated from himself” are added here; this could be accepted if “who is” had preceded them. At the conclusion of the preceding letter it is determined that the person who separates himself is to be segregated.]—we are confident that Africa, in view of the integrity and moderation of Your Holiness, will no longer endure him, while fraternal charity remains unharmed.

And in another hand: May our God preserve Your Holiness, as you pray for us for a longer life, my lord and brother.

[Note: We have transcribed this letter from the two-part Roman collection published through the efforts of Lucas Holstenius. Although its year cannot be determined with certainty, it may nevertheless be asserted that this appears to be the first letter by which Celestine informed the bishops of Illyricum that Rufus had been entrusted with his representation throughout their provinces. He was moved to entrust this to him as quickly as possible both by the examples of his predecessors and by the new efforts of certain persons who had attempted to annul the rights of the Roman See over Illyricum and transfer them to the bishop of Constantinople. We therefore readily believe this letter to be earlier than those that follow. Moreover, the profound silence concerning Nestorius’s affairs is no slight indication that, when this letter was written, that heretic had not yet caused any disturbance in the Church.]

## LETTER III OF POPE CELESTINE I TO THE BISHOPS OF ILLYRICUM

How great his concern for the province of Illyricum. How he prevented Felix, bishop of the province of Dyrrhachium, from being oppressed by a certain faction. That he had entrusted his representation to Rufus. What authority Rufus possessed.

To his most beloved brothers Perigenes, Dynatus, Basil, Sapius, Paul, Aeternalis, Sabatius, Julian, and Senecion, bishops throughout Illyricum, Celestine.

[Note: At the Council of Ephesus, act 6, Perigenes is listed as bishop of Corinth, well known from the letters of Boniface; likewise Dynatus, or Dinatus or Donatus, bishop of Nicopolis in Old Epirus, and Senecion, bishop of the Scodrenses. Furthermore, Henricus Noris, *History of Pelagianism*, Book II, chapter 9, pp. 232–233, proves that Basil of Larissa in Thessaly and Julian of Sardica or Serdica—corruptly written as Eridica in some manuscripts—in Mediterranean Dacia were metropolitans.]

Among the many concerns and varied affairs that continually come to us from all the Churches, you will learn from the force of our decrees, and you will be able to perceive from the nature of the cases themselves, that we nevertheless take a more attentive concern for you. Now, however, the case of the province of Dyrrhachium has warned us [Note: Perhaps “moved us”], where our brother and fellow bishop Felix would have been oppressed by the faction of certain accusers, had our diligence not intervened.

Nor is this concern for you something new to the Apostolic See. You know [Note: Perhaps “you have often learned by experience”] that this arrangement, which we are now carrying out, has repeatedly been established: the Church of Thessalonica has always been entrusted with watching over you. One who embraces discipline as is fitting readily submits to discipline. For the whole ordering of things is arranged so that those who are taught to be under greater authorities obey them, and all things turn upon this order of rules.

We, above all, are bound by concern for all those to whom Christ, through the holy apostle Peter, granted the responsibility of dealing with everything when he gave him the keys of opening and closing; and among his apostles he chose not one who was inferior to the others, but the one who was especially first.

Let rules rule us; let us not rule the rules. Let us be subject to the canons while we observe the canons’ commands. There are certain grave faults born in those provinces which, although we are far away, cannot reach us; or, once everything has been removed, they are not reported as they occurred because of the intervening passage of time. We wish all these faults to be cut away through the intervention of our brother and fellow bishop Rufus, whose tested experience in every case and in all the actions of his life is evident. Know that our representative authority has been entrusted to him throughout your province, so that, dearest brothers, whatever is being dealt with concerning cases may be referred to him.

Let no one be ordained without his advice; let no one, without his knowledge, usurp the province entrusted to him [Note: A learned writer observes that what the Council of Nicaea assigns to each metropolitan in his province and to their councils, which were to be assembled twice a year, is here and elsewhere attributed to the bishop of Thessalonica; and he therefore judges that this cannot be reconciled with the preceding statements, in which Celestine professes that he does not rule the rules but is subject to them. Yet the same council, in canon 6, decrees that the privileges of the Churches are to be preserved. No one will deny that Celestine attributes nothing here to the bishop of Thessalonica except what had at least been consistently granted to him by Damasus and his successors. Celestine therefore decreed nothing against the council when he wished a privilege confirmed by the authority of so many predecessors to be preserved. Moreover, he does not deny the metropolitans of Illyricum unrestricted power either to ordain or to assemble bishops; he merely takes care that they undertake neither action without the knowledge of the bishop of Thessalonica. Leo explains how both the privilege of the bishop of Thessalonica and the rights of the metropolitans are to be preserved in Letter 14, nos. 8–10.]. Let them not presume to assemble bishops except with his consent; and through him let anything that arises be referred to us.

By this command they will also learn that the person who thinks he ought to resist our authority or his order is to be separated from the fellowship of the brothers, if he himself separates himself [Note: We supply the little word “himself,” which the scribes may easily have omitted once when it was repeated three times. By this conclusion Celestine, as also below in Letter 12, no. 4, places the odium of segregation or excommunication upon the guilty party himself. The final note to Letter 2 has likewise shown that, after Apiarius was removed, the Africans imposed the same penalty upon that presbyter.]

[Note: In the editions of the Councils this is numbered 11; what was formerly 4 is now 11. It is found in nearly all the ancient collections, for example those of Dionysius Exiguus, Hadrian, the Code published by Quesnel, the Hispana, and Isidore Mercator, as well as in the very old copies represented by the Corbie manuscript and the Colbert manuscript written in Lombard script. Cresconius cites it in his *Breviary of Canons* and elsewhere.]

## LETTER IV OF POPE CELESTINE I TO THE BISHOPS OF THE PROVINCE OF VIENNE AND NARBONNE

[Note: In Quesnel, as in one Colbert manuscript, the title reads “To the Bishops of Vienne and Narbonne,” followed by no heading. In the oldest Corbie manuscript the whole letter is divided into these eight chapters: I. On priests serving superstitious worship; II. On not denying penance to the dying; III. On ordaining inexperienced bishops; IV. On the ordination of priests; V. On the accusation of virgin-monks; VI. On the privilege reserved to the Apostolic See; VII. On preserving the right of all metropolitans; VIII. On the appointment of those who are to be admitted to the priesthood. Dionysius Exiguus, however, divided the whole letter into five headings, numbered XIV, XV, and so forth, because he prefixed to it two other letters of Celestine, which he divided into thirteen headings. We reproduce those headings as transcribed from his work.]

[Col. 0429B]

I. That priests or clerics should not minister in church wrapped in cloaks or girded about the loins.  
II. That final penance must be denied to no one.  
III. That the office of the episcopate must be reached through the ecclesiastical ranks.  
IV. That each province should be content with its own metropolitan.  
V. That no bishop should be ordained against the unwilling (Isidore adds: “clerics or people”).  
VI. That unlawful ordinations must be avoided.

[Col. 0430A] Celestine to all the bishops established throughout the provinces of Vienne and Narbonne [Note: Dionysius and Isidore add “greeting in the Lord,” which is absent from the better manuscripts.]

1. We should indeed wish to rejoice in the ordering of your Churches in such a way that we would congratulate you on your progress rather than grieve over something committed against ecclesiastical discipline. For both good deeds reach us as a source of joy, and deeds done badly sting us with the goads of sorrow. Nor can we be silent [Note: The Roman edition and the councils after Crabbe read “to this end.” We remove the preposition “to” on the authority of Merlinius and all the manuscripts. Quesnel alone presents the passage as follows: “That we should recall some from unlawful practices and, by the prompting of our office, urge them toward good.”], since the prompting of our office impels us to call certain persons back from unlawful practices: we have been established by God as watchmen, so that, proving the diligence of our vigilance, we may cut away what must be restrained and establish what must be observed.

Although spiritual care extends over distant places, it does not fail but reaches everywhere that the name of God is proclaimed; nor do the things escape our knowledge which, through the authority of novel presumption, are attempted for the overthrow of the rules [Note: The printed editions, together with Dionysius and Isidore, read: “And although spiritual care extends over distant places.” Five of the best manuscripts correct this.]

### CHAPTER I

2. For we have learned that certain priests of the Lord serve superstitious worship rather than purity of mind or faith. But it is not surprising that those who did not grow up in the Church act against ecclesiastical custom, but, coming from elsewhere [Note: The printed editions and several manuscripts read “on a journey” or “while on the journey.” The reading is corrected through the Corbie manuscript, written in the sixth century, and one Colbert manuscript, which read *e ritu*—“a norm and manner of life”—instead of *itinere*. In another manuscript, immediately after “grew up,” there follows: “For those who are in another way of life.” The phrase “did not grow up in the Church” is not to be understood as though they matured outside the Church in heresy or schism; rather, “Church” here means the ecclesiastical order, in contrast with the monastic order. It is clear that those are being indicated whom the cities of Narbonne and other neighboring provinces were accustomed to summon from monasteries to govern their Churches. For some time, however, this custom of seeking bishops for various cities from monasteries—especially from Lérins—continued to the considerable benefit of the Church.] from another manner of life [Note: That is, “in another kind of way of life.” For this reason the reading found in two manuscripts, “conversion,” is not acceptable. Our Mabillon observes in the preface to the second part of the fourth-century Benedictine Acts, no. 179, that as early as the fifth century bishops who had previously professed monasticism considered it a religious duty to lay aside the monastic habit completely. From this passage he argues—though I would not wish to affirm it as entirely certain and evident, although it may appear probable—that some bishops, even though they had not lived a monastic life, adopted the monastic habit after the example of others. At least, this passage is speaking of those who had been taken from a profession of monastic life to the episcopate: “wrapped in a cloak.” Ennodius notes in Letter 130 that Caesarius of Arles wore such a cloak when he came after being summoned to the episcopate. Accordingly, in the words that follow we should understand a monastic cloak more correctly than, with Holstenius in his notes on the letter of Damasus to Acholius and his companions, a philosophical cloak—the garment which Damasus calls in that same letter the “habit of an idol,” and from which philosophers are called *palliati* by Augustine, *City of God*, Book XIII, chapter 16. It should not be left unmentioned that Cresconius, under the same heading as this passage of Celestine, also joins to it canon 12 of the Council of Gangra: “If any man, on account of the continence that is supposed to exist, uses a cloak as his garment, believing that by this he possesses righteousness, and despises those who wear with reverence the ordinary and customary garments, such as cloaks and other common clothing, let him be anathema.” Hence it appears that the special cloak was a distinguishing sign of professed continence.], they brought these things with them into the Church from a different way of life: wrapped in a cloak and girded about the loins, believing that they would fulfill the faith of Scripture not through the spirit but through the letter.

For if these commands are meant to be observed in such a manner, why are the things that follow not likewise done—why are burning lamps not held in the hands together with a staff [Note: These words, together with “a staff,” are absent from one Colbert manuscript and another from Laon. That they should not be omitted is clear from what follows. Did Celestine then read in the Gospel of Luke words that now appear in no copy? Perhaps the pope intended nothing more than to show how inconvenient it would be if bishops, in addition to the staff they customarily carried according to ecclesiastical usage, also held burning lamps in their hands in accordance with the Gospel text.]?

These things have their own mystery, and they are so clear to those who understand that they should be observed according to the meaning appropriate to them. For the girding of the loins signifies chastity; the staff, pastoral governance; and the burning lamps, the brilliance of good works, of which it is said: “Let your works shine” (Matthew 5:16).

Nevertheless, perhaps those who live in more remote places and dwell far from other people may retain this form of dress, following custom rather than reason [Note: The Roman edition and the councils, together with the copies of the Hadrian collection, read *habeant*, “let them have.” Other books more correctly read *habeat*, “let him have.” Celestine allows that distinctive dress to inhabitants of remote places, that is, to monks who lived far from other people, such as the inhabitants of the islands of Lérins. By this time, therefore, the custom had become established that monks should be distinguished from the common people by their clothing.].

Why, then, should this habit be introduced into the Gallican Churches, so that the custom of so many years and so many bishops should be changed into another form of dress? We are distinguished from the common people and from others by teaching, not by clothing; by our manner of life, not by our dress; by purity of mind, not by outward adornment.

For if we begin to pursue novelty, we shall trample upon the order handed down to us by the Fathers and make room for unnecessary superstitions. We must not therefore lead the inexperienced minds of the faithful into such things. They should be taught rather than mocked [Note: Merlinius, Crabbe, and the Roman edition, together with Isidore, read “mocked.”]. Nor should things be imposed upon their eyes; rather, the precepts should be poured into their minds.

There were indeed many things which, in the interest of ecclesiastical discipline or by the reasoning proper to the matter itself, we could say; but we are called away from these to other subjects.

### CHAPTER II

3. We have learned that penance is denied to the dying, and that the wishes of those who desire this remedy for their souls at the time of death are not granted. I confess that we shudder to find anyone guilty of such impiety as to despair of God’s mercy—as though He could not come to the aid of one who turns to Him at any moment, and free a man endangered beneath the burden of sins from the weight from which he longs to be released.

What else, I ask, is this than to add death to one who is dying, and by cruelty to kill his soul so that it cannot be absolved? God is fully prepared to help, inviting people to repentance, and thus promises: “On whatever day the sinner turns, his sins shall not be counted against him” (Ezekiel 33:15). And again: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” (ibid., 18, 23) [Note: The oldest Corbie manuscript reads “the death of the dying man”; and afterward, “provided only that he turn,” where Quesnel has “but rather that he turn.”].

Whoever denies repentance for past sins to a person at the time of death therefore takes salvation away from him [Note: The printed editions, together with the Pithoean manuscript, read: “whoever has denied repentance hoped for at the time of death.” None of the other manuscripts, nor Ivo, has “hoped for.” The old Corbie manuscript, together with one Colbert manuscript, has “has passed over by denying repentance at the time”; some others have “has denied repentance at a time beyond this.” The remaining manuscripts more correctly read “of the past,” etc.; the clearer sense would be: “whoever has denied repentance for the past at the time of death.” The same expression occurs in Letter 22, no. 5: “Now, because we rejoice over the correction of the past.”]. And he has despaired of God’s clemency who did not believe that God could suffice to help the dying even in a moment.

The thief hanging on the cross at Christ’s right hand would have lost his reward (Luke 23:42) if repentance during a single hour had not helped him. While he was in punishment, he repented, and by the confession of a single utterance he obtained, with God’s promise, the dwelling-place of paradise.

True conversion to God in those placed at the end of life must therefore be judged by the mind rather than by the time, as the prophet asserts in these words: “When you have turned and groaned, then you shall be saved” (Ezekiel 18:33).

Since the Lord is an examiner of the heart, repentance must not be denied at any time to one who asks for it, since that person binds himself to the Judge to whom he knows that all hidden things will be revealed.

[Col. 0433A] ### CHAPTER III

4. We have learned, dearest brothers, that certain men have been ordained bishops who had not been trained in any ecclesiastical orders before reaching the summit of such dignity, contrary to the decrees of the Fathers [Note: Namely, the fifth letter of Siricius, no. 5; the thirty-seventh letter of Innocent, no. 4; and the ninth letter of Zosimus, no. 2. The scholiast in the Harleian manuscript adds decrees 11 and 12 of Silvester, taken from the *Constitutum*, which we have consigned to the appendix of volume II.]. This was done by the usurpation of one who acknowledges that he himself did it, although the episcopate ought to be reached through those stages which have most often been carefully prescribed, so that those initiated into lesser offices may be strengthened for greater ones.

Whoever desires to be a teacher must first be a student, so that he may teach what he has learned. Every institution of life confirms itself in this way for the goal toward which it tends. One who has given no attention to letters cannot be a teacher of letters. One who has not advanced through each successive service cannot reach the rank appropriate to a higher service. Is the priesthood alone, I ask, cheaper than all these things, when it is more difficult to fulfill but more easily bestowed?

5. But it is no longer enough to ordain laymen, whom no order permits to be ordained; even those whose crimes are known far and wide through nearly every province are being ordained.

Daniel, after a report was recently sent to us from the eastern regions, was accused by the entire monastery of virgins that he had governed of unspeakable charges. Many disgraceful acts were alleged against many persons [Note: The Roman edition and Labbe read “many alleged many disgraceful acts.” One manuscript has “acts which many alleged.”]. He was sought out in whatever part of the world he might be hiding, so that, if he trusted in his innocence, he would not avoid the trial demanded against him.

A written mandate was sent to the bishop of Arles through our subdeacon Fortunatus, so that Daniel might be sent for judgment [Note: The old Corbie manuscript, together with the Colbert manuscript, reads *epistolium*—“a letter”—except that the latter has “episcopal” and the former “episcopal” in place of the word *epistolium*. The same reading is confirmed by another Colbert manuscript written in Lombard script, which reads: “Letters sent to the bishop of Arles through our subdeacon Fortunatus, so that he might be sent for judgment.” The royal copy of the original collection of Dionysius differs from this only in that it incorrectly adds *praeceptiones*, “instructions,” before “so that he might be sent for judgment.” Hence the copies of the Hadrian collection have: “Letters sent … instructions, so that he might be sent for episcopal judgment.” From this the old editions of the councils and the Roman edition obtained, as in the manuscripts: “Instructions have been sent … so that he might be sent for episcopal judgment”; Sirmond has: “Letters have been sent … so that he might be sent for episcopal judgment”; Quesnel, together with a third Colbert manuscript and Labbe, has: “A letter has been sent so that he might be sent for episcopal judgment.” All these readings are defective, either because they contain the added word “instructions” or because, from the corrupted word *epistolium*, they retain both “episcopal” and the word “letter.” The passage is not speaking of an episcopal judgment in the province of Arles, but of the judgment of the Apostolic See, to which Daniel’s name had been referred; this is indicated by the word “sent” and by the whole sequence of the sentence. Misled by the addition of the word “episcopal,” a learned man thought that Daniel had been sought so that he might be sent to the eastern bishops, to be judged by them as his own bishops. But Celestine himself, below, no. 9, leaves no doubt about his meaning, where he says of the same Daniel that “he must submit himself to our judgment,” not that of the eastern bishops. Moreover, *epistolium* is equivalent to a written mandate or official written notice. Hence the man who is now said to have been summoned by a letter sent later is the same person who is said shortly afterward to have been summoned by letters sent by us. The bishop to whom this letter was sent was Honoratus, who succeeded Patroclus after Patroclus was killed in 426, as Prosper records in his Chronicle.].

Burdened with so many testimonies and assailed by accusations of so many crimes, polluted, as it is said, by incest with sacred virgins, he is asserted to have been ordained bishop. The documents are preserved in our papal archives [Note: The Roman edition reads “is contained”; Merlinius and Crabbe, after Isidore, read “as is contained in the archive of our documents”; Quesnel reads “and as is contained in the documents of our archive.” The text is corrected from other books. Celestine says that the originals of the documents sent to him by the entire monastery of virgins against Daniel, copies of which he sends, are kept in the archives of the Apostolic See.], copies of which we have also sent to you. At the very time when he was being summoned to answer the charge by letters sent from us, he slipped into the dignity of the episcopate.

May no injury be done to the sacred name. It is more likely that the ordainer himself lost this dignity by giving it to such a man than that the ordained man should possess it [Note: Zosimus, Letter 7, no. 2, likewise wishes the ordainer of such a person to suffer the same penalty as the ordained person.]. Once he has been convicted, the man who thought him worthy to receive the episcopate by bestowing it upon him will be joined to him in punishment. For whoever ordains such men reveals what kind of person he himself is.

Having now brought these matters forward, and since many of you have come to know the statutes of the Apostolic See and have spent some time with us, let your fraternity hasten to restore everything to the norm of discipline, in accordance with the admonitions we have addressed to you.

### CHAPTER IV

6. First, in accordance with the decrees of the canons, let each province be content with its own metropolitan, as the decrees contained in the letter of our predecessor to the bishop of Narbonne state [Note: The twelfth letter of Boniface.]. Let no priest be allowed scope for usurpation to the injury of another [Note: The published editions, as well as the Pithoean manuscript, read “of usurpation”; the copies of the Hadrian collection and Isidore read “by usurpation.” Celestine seems, after citing Zosimus’s letter to Hilary of Narbonne, to criticize and identify as usurpation the privilege that Patroclus had obtained over the two provinces of Narbonne. Leo, in Letter 11, no. 7, holds the same view of this privilege. It must nevertheless be admitted that Celestine here prescribes—or rather confirms—a general rule concerning all provinces.].

Let each person be content with the limits granted to him; let no one presume anything in another’s province.

7. Nor should foreign, outsider, and formerly unknown clerics be placed over those who have earned the good testimony of their fellow citizens, to the exclusion of clergy who have served honorably in their own Churches, lest a certain new institution appear to have been established as a college from which bishops are made.

### CHAPTER V

No bishop is to be given against the will of the people. The consent and desire of the clergy, the people, and the order must be sought.

Only then may someone be chosen from another Church if no worthy man can be found among the clergy of the very city for which a bishop is to be ordained—something we do not believe can happen. For those men must first be rejected, so that persons from foreign Churches may rightly be preferred.

Let each person possess the fruit of his service in the Church in which he has spent his whole life through all the offices [Note: The Roman edition and later editions add “of the clergy” here. The devout writer observes that the episcopal office, which the greatest and holiest men have always shunned as something to be feared, should not be regarded by the clergy themselves as the fruit of their military service, but should be conferred by others.]. Let no one intrude upon another’s service, nor dare to claim for himself the reward owed to someone else.

Let the clergy be free to resist if they see themselves being burdened; and when they recognize that persons are being thrust upon them from elsewhere, let them not be afraid to reject them. If they do not receive the reward they deserve, they must at least have free judgment concerning the person who is to govern them.

### CHAPTER VI

8. Let unlawful ordinations be avoided. Let no layman, no married man who has had two wives, and no man who is or has been the husband of a widow be ordained; rather, let the person ordained be blameless and of the kind chosen by the Apostle.

Through Moses the Lord commanded: “Let the priest take a virgin as his wife” (Leviticus 21:13). The Apostle, speaking in the same Spirit, follows and completes this instruction: the bishop must be consecrated as “the husband of one wife” (1 Timothy 3:2).

Let priests therefore be chosen according to this standard; and if any unlawful ordinations have occurred, let them be removed, because they cannot stand and will not be able to evade our investigation, even though those who have attained office in another manner think that they can remain hidden [Note: Quesnel, together with an old Capuchin manuscript from Rouen, reads “who attained it in this way”; other editions, with one Colbert manuscript and another Harleian manuscript, read “who attained it in such a way.” The remaining manuscripts read “in whatever manner.”].

Let no religious dignity be darkened by obscurity. Let those who are bishops follow the episcopal custom. Let there be no empty boasting among those wrapped in cloaks.

9. Daniel, as we said [Note: One Colbert manuscript, together with the Corbie manuscript, spells the name “Danihel”; it has been observed in a new edition of Hilary, p. 343 note b, p. 379 note a, and p. 403 note c, that this form was customary with Hilary.], who thought that he could evade the accusation by means of pontifical honor and reached only the summit of office by fleeing his accusers [Note: The royal copy of the Dionysian collection reads “by grieving”; the copies of the Hadrian and Isidorean collections, as well as the printed books except Quesnel, read “by hiding”; one Colbert manuscript, together with the old Corbie manuscript, reads “by acting.” Two other Colbert manuscripts and the Pithoean manuscript, with Quesnel, more correctly read “by fleeing.”], must know that for the present he has been separated from the assembly of Your Holiness. He must submit himself to our judgment, if he knows that he possesses confidence in his conscience.

10. [Note: [Col. 0435D] The Corbie manuscript has *Marsiliensis*. In the copies collated by Hadrian, *Maxiliensis*. This bishop is thought to have been Venerius.] But the priest of the Church of Massilia is said—shameful even to say—to have rejoiced at his brother’s death [Note: [Col. 0435D] The Roman edition and later councils have *his brother*. *His* is absent from Merl., Crab., Quesn., and the manuscripts. The death of Patroclus, bishop of Arles, seems to be intended here. As Prosper says in his *Chronicle* under the year 425, he was torn by wounds by a certain barbarian tribune; but this crime was attributed to the secret command of Felix, master of the soldiers. Therefore the Massilian bishop who was killed should be regarded as his brother in rank, not by blood. Nor is it surprising that enmity and certain quarrels arose between Proculus’s successor, to whom the Council of Turin, canon 1, had granted the primatial prerogative in those provinces, and Patroclus, who, with Zosimus’s permission, was then arrogating that dignity to himself.]—and to have welcomed him in such a fashion that he might meet this man, who had arrived stained with his blood, as one who would share a portion with him [Note: [Col. 0436C] The particle *et*, used in the sense of *etiam* (“also”), is restored from the Colbertine manuscript, supported by the other witnesses, together with Merl. and Crab., in which *ex* is read in its place. Quesnel subsequently deleted *et* as well. It cannot be denied that this little word is redundant, but it appears in all the manuscripts.]; and we delegate him to your council to be heard. Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of August [Note: [Col. 0436C] July 25, 428. Sirmond had already restored the praenomen *Flaviis* from the Corbie manuscript. It is also found in one Colbertine manuscript and in Pithoeus; no one should be troubled by the fact that the same consuls are recorded in the Theodosian Code, book IV, title 6, law 2, and book VI, title 2, law 15, etc., without this praenomen. In that manuscript such praenomina are commonly omitted. Earlier, the Pithoeus manuscript reads *Given on the eighth day before the Kalends*.] in the consulship of the most illustrious men Flavius Felix and Taurus.

[Note: [Col. 0436D] Written in the year 429. In the edition of the Councils it is number 3; what was formerly number 5 is now number 14. It occurs in the same manuscripts in which we previously noted the existence of the preceding letter. The division of the titles, however, is not the same in all copies. Dionysius divided it into three sections, which he called XX, XXI, and XXII. Four titles precede these in the Corbie manuscript, the first being the same as Dionysius’s; II. How laymen are to be admitted to the clergy; III. Likewise, that laymen are not to be placed before clerics in ordinations; IV. Let these statutes be made known to all Churches. One Colbertine copy of Quesnel’s manuscript has this title: Let no layman be admitted to the priestly order.]

## EPISTLE V

I. That no priest may be ignorant of the canons.—II. That bishops ought not to be ordained from among laymen, with the clerics of the Churches disregarded.—III. That the people are to be taught, not followed.

**COELESTINE, bishop, to all the bishops established throughout Apulia and Calabria.**

### 1

No priest is permitted to be ignorant of his canons [Note: [Col. 0436D] So also Siricius, *Epistle* 1, no. 21, Distinction 38, chapter 4], or to do anything that could conflict with the regulations of the Fathers. For what worthy institution will be preserved by us if the standard of the decretal statutes is broken at the whim of certain persons, with license granted to the people?

### 2

We have heard that certain cities, deprived of their own rulers, wish to request bishops from among laymen [Note: [Col. 0436D] See the Council of Nicaea, chapter 2], and consider so exalted an office so cheaply that they think we can confer it upon those who have served not God but the world. In doing so, they judge badly not only of their own clerics, in contempt of whom they act thus, but also most badly of us, believing that we are capable of doing this. They would never dare such a thing if the favorable judgment of certain persons there did not wink at it.

Thus the decrees so frequently issued accomplish nothing, since this matter is ignored as though nothing had ever been written about it. What benefit is there in clerics having served through the successive stages of service and spent their whole lives in the Lord’s camp, if those who are to preside over them are sought from among laymen—men occupied with the world, ignorant of the entire ecclesiastical order, and, in reckless haste, eager to cross over into an alien honor through immoderate ambition, passing into another kind of life while trampling upon the reverence due to ecclesiastical discipline?

Therefore, dearest brothers, since we guard the helm of our law—that is, of the canons—we must oppose such men. By this letter we admonish your fraternity that no one admit a layman to the clerical order or allow something to be done that both deceives him and generates for himself grounds on which he may be held guilty under the established decrees.

### 3

The people are to be taught, not followed. We, too, if they do not know what is permitted and what is not, ought to admonish them [Note: [Col. 0437D] See Gelasius, *Epistle* 2, no. 15], not offer them our assent. Whoever attempts what has been forbidden will find that the censure of the Apostolic See will by no means be lacking. For what we do not correct by the authority of admonition alone, we must punish with a severity appropriate to the regulations.

We wish this to be made known throughout all the Churches that lack their own rulers, so that no one, perhaps flattering himself with some hope, may deceive himself. Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August [Note: [Col. 0437D] July 21, 429. In one Colbertine manuscript: *Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August*; in another, as in the Corbie manuscript: *Given on the Kalends of August*. Another Corbie manuscript adds *the illustrious men Florentinus*, and Pithoeus has *the illustrious men Florentius and Dionysius*. Just as notaries customarily write *aug.* and *augg.* for *Augustus* and *Augusti*, doubling the letter *g* for the plural, so, since they commonly write *Fl.* for *Flavius*, they wrote *F Fll.* for *Flaviis*. For this reason the reading in Quesnel’s old copy—*Flavius, Florentinus, and Dionysius*—is not satisfactory; we prefer, with one Colbertine and the Corbie manuscript, *Flaviis Florentinus and Dionysius*. *Flaviis* is absent from other books. Dionysius entirely omitted the chronological note. In the Theodosian Code, book XVI, title 8, law 29, the law is dated to the same consuls.]

in the consulship of the most illustrious men Flavius Florentius and Dionysius.

## NOTICE ON THE TWO FOLLOWING EPISTLES (S)

### 1

Those two letters were first published by Baronius under the year 430 from the papers of Antonio Agustín; then by Labbe, volume III of the *Councils*, page 349, from a manuscript of the old Latin edition of the Council of Ephesus; and finally by Stephanus Baluzius, *New Collection of the Councils*, page 428, from three manuscripts.

John Garnerius inserted both in the first part of the works of Marius Mercator, page 66, applying such care and diligence as he used to correct them according to conjectures of his own invention. Their Greek text, which Nestorius had sent without a Latin translation, has perished. At least the first of them, while an interpreter was awaited, long remained unanswered.

In both letters, as also in the others sent either from Constantinople to Rome in Greek or from Rome to Constantinople in Latin, the translation is repeatedly obscure and involved. This indicates that at that time few people in either city were thoroughly skilled in both the Latin and Greek languages. Accordingly, in the time of Pope Coelestine, one might have said of both cities what Gregory wrote in his own age concerning Constantinople, in book VII, letter 30, to Narses: “For today in the city of Constantinople there are no people who can properly transfer dictated matter from Latin into Greek; for while they preserve the words and pay no attention at all to the meaning, they neither make the words intelligible nor preserve the meaning.”

Nor was the age of Leo more fortunate in this respect, as the earlier translation of Flavian’s letter to that same Leo, letter 37, provides an example.

### 2

The authenticity of those letters is confirmed not only by Coelestine but also by Cassian and Cyril. Cyril, indeed, in writing to John of Antioch, does not hesitate to quote and reproduce the very words of the earlier letter; but why he called that letter lengthy (*makran*, μακράν) is less clear.

Nor should another letter be sought, nor should the one that has reached us be thought mutilated. It was perhaps called lengthy—or rather long—because it is by no means of that class of shorter letters in which someone, fearing to disclose his thoughts, barely reveals them in a few words. In that letter Nestorius asserts his heresy at sufficient length and in considerable detail, so that it can no longer remain hidden or appear ambiguous.

### 3

Cassian’s reproach of Nestorius applies to both letters: that Nestorius fostered the complaints of the Pelagianists through his intercessions and supported their causes in his writings (*On the Incarnation*, book I, chapter 3). From this one may reasonably infer that at least the first letter was written in the year 429. For in that year Julian and his associates certainly disturbed the city of Constantinople with their agitation. It was precisely to remedy this evil that Marius Mercator, during the consulship of Florentius and Dionysius—that is, in the year 429—made the heresy of Julian and his associates, and their just condemnation, known to all by presenting his *Commonitorium* to the Church of Constantinople and to others.

Nor does the conjecture conflict with the fact that Coelestine replied to Nestorius only in August of the year 430. The pope himself excuses the delay in answering on the ground that a person who could render Nestorius’s letters into Latin had long been awaited. Perhaps, too, when he detected clear signs of heresy in the translation, he was afraid to reply sooner, until he had become better informed and more fully instructed concerning the entire matter.

## EPISTLE VI: NESTORIUS TO COELESTINE, POPE OF THE CITY OF ROME (S)

To inform him how he ought to deal with certain Western bishops who complained that they were suffering injustice. He also exposes as heretics those who asserted that God the Word was born, died, and was buried, and that Mary was *Theotokos* (θεοτόκος, “God-bearer”).

### 1

We owe one another fraternal conversations, so that together, in accordance with the concord that prevails among us, we may fight against the devil, the enemy of peace [Note: [Col. 0438D] So Baluzius. Baronius and Labbe have *with concord prevailing among us according to the Scriptures*. Labbe noted in the margin, *with unanimous concord prevailing among us, as we prepare to fight the Devil*. Garnerius composed the text itself as follows: “as though we were to fight against the Devil, with true concord prevailing among us according to the Scriptures.”]

Why this preface? A certain Julian, Florus, Orontius, and Fabius, [Note: [Col. 0438D] These are leaders of the Pelagian sect. Julian, bishop of Eclanum, became especially famous for his writings against Augustine. He dedicated those writings to Florus, whom he also calls “most pious father” in Augustine, *Unfinished Work*, book I, chapter 2. One of Pelagius’s principal disciples, named Annianus, dedicated to Orontius his labor in translating Chrysostom’s homilies into Latin. See below, epistle 19, no. 6.] claiming to be bishops of the Western regions, have often approached both the most pious and most renowned emperor and lamented their cases, as though, in orthodox times, they had suffered persecution as orthodox men. They have often made the same complaints to us, and, though often rejected, have not ceased to do the same; rather, every day they persist, filling everyone’s ears with tearful cries.

We addressed them as we ought in such speeches, since we did not know the truth concerning their case. But because we need more precise knowledge of their affairs, lest our most pious and Christian emperor suffer repeated annoyance from them, and lest, being ignorant of their case, we be divided in defending it, deign to grant us information about them. Otherwise, some, through ignorance of the justice of the truth, may be disturbed by an inopportune compassion, or may think that the canonical indignation of your Blessedness—which has perhaps been rightly directed against them on account of their religious sects [Note: [Col. 0439B] It would perhaps be more agreeable to read *the indignation*, that is, “the indignation of your Blessedness.” Thus Nestorius seems to express some doubt whether the expulsion of the aforesaid followers of Pelagius had any cause other than religion.]—was directed against them for some other reason. For the novelty of sects deserves much vigilance from true shepherds [Note: [Col. 0439B] Baronius and Labbe have *much*; in the margin, *none*, a conjecture which Garnerius transferred into the text. Baluzius rightly observed that this is alien to Nestorius’s meaning. Nestorius means only that whenever new sects arise, much vigilance is required from pastors so that they may defend the sheep from wolves.]

### 2

Accordingly, finding no small corruption of orthodoxy among certain people here, we employ both anger and gentleness toward the sick every day. For the illness is not slight but akin to the rottenness of Apollinaris and Arius [Note: [Col. 0439B–C] If those whom Nestorius accused had actually held the Catholic belief he attributed to them—namely, that the human and divine natures in Christ had been confused—their opinion would indeed have been very close to the error of Apollinaris and Arius. For from the corrupt opinion of Arius and Apollinaris, who maintain that the Word took the place of the soul, it follows that sorrow, pain, and other affections belonging solely to the soul entered the nature of the Word; similarly, the same perversity follows from the alleged confusion of the natures. But Catholics, while defending the unity of the person in such a way that they do not cease to distinguish the natures, are far removed from the inventions of Arius and Apollinaris. See Cyril, *Epistle* 1 to Succensus, page 131.]

They commonly mingle the Lord’s union in man into a confusion resembling a mixture, so that certain clerics among us—some through ignorance, others through a heretical fraud formerly concealed within them, such as occurred repeatedly even in the times of the Apostles—are sick as heretics and openly blaspheme God the Word, consubstantial with the Father, as though he had taken the beginning of his origin from the Virgin Christotokos. They say that, as though he had been built together with his temple, he was buried with the flesh [Note: [Col. 0439C] Supply *as though*. Therefore Garnerius’s reading is not satisfactory: “that he was built together with his temple and buried with the flesh.”]

They say that after his resurrection the flesh did not remain flesh but passed into the nature of the Godhead [Note: [Col. 0439C–D] Baronius and Labbe read: “They say that after his resurrection he mingled the same flesh, but…” Garnerius: “They say that after his resurrection the same flesh did not remain, but…” Baluzius: “They say that after his resurrection the flesh did not remain flesh, but…” This last reading is entirely sound once the error by which *mingled* was substituted for *remained* has been removed. The unusual expressions of the Fathers that gave occasion for this calumny are explained in the general preface to the new edition of Hilary, beginning at no. 182.]

In short, to state the matter briefly, they blasphemously assert that the Godhead of the Only-Begotten is referred both to the origin of the flesh joined to it and to its dying together with the flesh [Note: [Col. 0439D–0440A] By suppressing the conjunction *and*, which is superfluous here, the entire obscurity of the passage disappears. Since Catholics profess that the Only-Begotten God was both born and died, Nestorius accuses them of referring both birth from the Virgin and death to the divine nature, as though they believed that the Godhead was born and died together with the flesh united to it. He usually conceals the distinction between “God being born” and “the Godhead being born,” although in Baluzius’s *New Collection of the Councils*, page 695, he himself acknowledges some distinction between the two expressions and complains that, after he had said that Mary did not give birth to the Godhead, his statement had been altered so that the word “God” was substituted for “Godhead”.]

They blaspheme that the flesh joined to the Godhead passed into the Godhead by the very word *deification* [Note: [Col. 0439D–0440C] Nestorius attempted by this use of the word to bring Catholics into disrepute, as though they proclaimed that Christ’s human nature had been changed into the divine. For this reason he composed a treatise entitled *Against Those Who, Because of the Union, Either Diminish the Godhead of the Only-Begotten or Deify His Humanity*. Cyril refutes this treatise in his letter to the clergy of Constantinople, in Labbe, volume III of the *Councils*, page 333. Yet the word “deification” does not imply that the flesh’s nature in Christ perished; indeed, the holy Fathers do not hesitate to use the same word for the transformation that other human beings hope for after the resurrection. Bernard, in *On Loving God*, chapter 10, after speaking of perfect charity—which he later declares to exist only in the blessed—explains its power as follows: “To be affected in this way is to be deified.” Augustine explains this form of deification in the final words of Sermon 166: “Therefore, putting away falsehood, speak the truth, so that this mortal flesh which you still possess from Adam, when the renewal of the spirit has gone before, may itself also receive renewal and transformation at the time of its resurrection; and thus the whole deified human being may cleave to the perpetual and unchangeable Truth.” Just as the spirit is said to become fleshly by cleaving to flesh, and the flesh spiritual by obeying the spirit in all things, so after the resurrection a human being, possessing nothing of human weakness and clothed with a certain divine power, is proclaimed deified. Indeed, even before the resurrection, the body assumed by God the Word, as the Fathers of the Council of Antioch say in their letter to Paul of Samosata, in Labbe, volume I, page 847, “has been deified” (*tetheopoiētai*, τεθεοποίηται).]

This is nothing other than corrupting both natures.

### 3

They have even dared to call the Virgin *Christotokos* (“Christ-bearer”) while also, in a certain fashion, calling her *Theotokos* (“God-bearer”). For they do not shrink from calling her *Theotokos* [Note: [Col. 0440C–D] Cyril explicitly notes this passage in his letter to John of Antioch, part I of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 21. Concerning Nestorius he writes: “In the lengthy letter sent to my lord Coelestine, most pious bishop of the Roman Church, among other things he added this against those who disagreed with him: ‘They do not shrink from calling the holy Virgin God-bearer,’” followed by the Greek: “They do not shudder when they call the holy Virgin Theotokos” (ὅτι τὴν ἁγίαν παρθένον Θεοτόκον λέγοντες οὐ φρίττουσιν). Cassianus, apparently summarizing the same point, says in book II of *On the Incarnation*, chapter 2: “You say, then, whoever you are, heretic, who deny that God was born from the Virgin, that Mary, mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, may be called Theotokos, that is, Mother of God, but say that she should be called Christotokos, that is, CHRIST’S MOTHER ONLY, NOT GOD’S.”]

when those holy and surpassingly authoritative Fathers at Nicaea said nothing more concerning the holy Virgin than that our Lord Jesus Christ was incarnate from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary. I say nothing of the Scriptures, which everywhere proclaim through angels and Apostles that the Virgin is the mother of Christ, not of God the Word.

In consequence of these matters, we have endured how many struggles! I think that the report preceding this letter has already informed your Blessedness of them, and also that you have observed that we did not struggle in vain, since, by the grace of the Lord, many who had been perverse were corrected and departed from us.

For a birth that is *consubstantial* with the one giving birth is proper to the one who gives birth to offspring entrusted with life [Note: [Col. 0440D–0441C] Baronius and Labbe read: “For a birth that is consubstantial with the one giving birth is proper to her who gives birth to offspring to whom life has been entrusted; that union in man is the creature of the Lord’s humanity joined to God from the Virgin through the Spirit.” Baluzius’s reading appears more carefully corrected, except that where he has “the vision is the creature,” we prefer “the union is the creature.” Garnerius attempted to correct this passage by changing and reversing the words so extensively that no one could say he was presenting the original text.

Nestorius’s meaning may be explained as follows: “It is proper to the one giving birth to beget consubstantially offspring to whom life has been imparted” (in Greek, *to zēn*, τὸ ζῆν, rather than *hē zōē*, ἡ ζωή). “That union in man of the Lord’s humanity, joined to God from the Virgin through the Spirit, is a creature, not God.” The heretic states this more plainly in Marius Mercator, Baluzius edition, page 55 and following: “Mary did not give birth to God; for what is born from flesh is flesh. She did not give birth to the uncreated from a creature, but she gave birth to a man, the instrument of the Godhead. The Holy Spirit did not create God the Word—for what was incarnate is from the Holy Spirit—but fashioned for God the Word a temple in which he might dwell, from the Virgin.”]

That union in man is a creature: the Lord’s humanity, joined to God from the Virgin through the Spirit.

If someone proposes the name *Theotokos* on account of the humanity that was born and joined to God the Word, and not on account of the parent [Note: [Col. 0441C] Perhaps read *the one giving birth*], we say that this term is not properly applicable to the woman who gave birth.
