For a true mother must be of the same essence as that which is born from her [Note: [Col. 0441C] We supply the conjunction *and*, which could easily have dropped out because of the preceding word ending in *a*. In Baluzius, immediately after the word “appropriate,” the following is added: “It can nevertheless be tolerated on account of the inseparable temple of God,” with several words omitted.]

Nevertheless, the term can be tolerated on account of this very consideration, and because this word alone is applied to the Virgin on account of the inseparable temple of God the Word that derives from her [Note: [Col. 0441C–D] Instead of *and because*, we would prefer *because*. The Greek phrase *to ex autēs* (τοῦ ἐξ αὐτῆς) should not simply be translated “from her,” but “that which derives its origin from her.” The point is that Mary may tolerably be called Mother of God for one reason only: she gave birth to the body that is the inseparable temple of God the Word.

Thus, in sermon 4, delivered after he had received Coelestine’s letters, Marius Mercator, page 78, allows Mary to be called Mother of God on account of the Word united to the temple: “Mother of God, not on account of the bare humanity’s divinity, but on account of God the Word united to the temple.” At the same time, he wishes her also to be called mother of a man—that is, *anthropotokos* (ἀνθρωποτόκος)—on account of the temple that is naturally substantial (read: consubstantial) with the Virgin. Or, as he has it in Sermon 5, page 89: “Mother of God, indeed, because the temple created in her by the Holy Spirit was united to the Godhead; but mother of a man, on account of the first-fruits of our nature assumed by the divine nature.”

Thus he admitted that Mary was Mother of God in such a way that he appeared to deny the personal unity and divide Christ into two: a man, that is, and God. He did not deny that the nature assumed by the Word was the inseparable temple of God, or, as he says at the end of Sermon 5, “the garment of the Godhead that cannot be stripped away”; but, as Cyril remarks in his second letter to Succensus, he wished that the man in whom the Word dwelt should be undivided according to equality of honor, authority, and the same will—not according to the unity of person.]

not because she herself is the mother of God the Word. For no one gives birth to one older than oneself [Note: [Col. 0441C] This seems to refer to Cassianus, *On the Incarnation*, book VII, chapter 7: “To destroy belief in the sacred birth, a new serpent hisses in the Church of God: ‘No one gives birth to one older than oneself.’” Nestorius repeats the same thought in sermon 3, in Marius Mercator, page 71: “For no one who is older than himself gives birth.” It is not certain which writing Cassianus had in view. Cyril likewise, in his *Protestation*, articles 5 and 6, in which he asserts that Nestorius was a follower of Paul of Samosata, proves their agreement on this specific statement: “Paul said, ‘Mary received the Word, and she is not older than the Word’; Nestorius said, ‘How, then, did Mary give birth to one older than herself?’”]

### 4

I think the preceding report has indicated these matters; but we also explain what happened. By the facts themselves we show that we desire to know the case of the men mentioned above with fraternal concern, not from an inopportune desire for curiosity. We recount our own affairs as brothers to brothers, publishing the truth about the sects to one another, so that this may be the most genuine beginning of my letter.

For when I began this letter I said that we owe one another fraternal conversations. I and those with me greet all the fraternity that is with you in Christ.

## EPISTLE VII: NESTORIUS TO COELESTINE, POPE—SECOND EPISTLE

[Col. 0442A]

Again he asks that he be informed as soon as possible how he should deal with Julian and others of the same sect; and he boasts of his own labors against those whom he pretends confuse Christ’s two natures.

### 1

[Note: [Col. 0442D] This word “often” indicates that certain letters of Nestorius are missing. Cyril, in the letter which he appended to Coelestine’s reply, mentions a letter of Nestorius to Coelestine in which he indicated that he had excluded laypeople from communion and punished clerics with deposition because they had contradicted him; yet neither this letter nor the preceding one contains any word at all about such depositions or excommunications.] I have often written to your Blessedness concerning Julian, Orontius, and the others, who usurp episcopal dignity and make frequent approaches to the most pious and most renowned emperor, cutting us down with repeated lamentations, as though they had been expelled from the West during orthodox times. But up to now we have received no letters from your Veneration about them. If I had them, I could answer them and give a brief response to their lamentations [Note: [Col. 0442D] Garnerius substituted *sorrows*, but *lamentations* fits the rest of the sentence better.]

For now, from their uncertain statements, one does not know where to turn: some call them heretics [Note: [Col. 0442D] Marius Mercator, when presenting his *Commonitorium* to the Church of Constantinople, not only called them heretics but also demonstrated that they were not free from the stain of heresy. The *Tractoria* of Zosimus proved the same thing; according to Marius Mercator, page 138, it had recently been sent to Constantinople.] and say that they were expelled from the Western regions, while they themselves swear that they have suffered calumny and endured danger because of the orthodox faith through false accusation. Whichever of the two is certain, our ignorance is grievous.

For if they are truly heretics, it is a crime to sympathize with them; and, again, if they are suffering calumny, not to sympathize with them is harsh and impious. Therefore may your soul, most beloved of God, deign to instruct us, who have until now been divided between both impulses toward them—that is, hatred and compassion. We wish to be taught what judgment we should hold concerning them.

We defer dealing with these same men day after day, concealing our action in the hope and expectation of your Blessedness [Note: [Col. 0443B] Baronius has *we detain them*. Labbe relegated that word to the margin and has *we have failed*, doubtless for *we defer*, which Baluzius restored from the manuscripts. The sequence of the sentence requires *we defer*, which Garnerius also preferred.] For, most venerable one, as you know, the examination of a pious sect is not a trivial matter, nor is the testing of those who undertake it a small thing.

### 2

A great labor is also being carried on here by us, as we strive to extract from the Church of God the most filthy impiety of the worst opinion of Apollinaris and Arius. For I do not know how certain ecclesiastics, taking from the Godhead and humanity of the Only-Begotten an image of a kind of mixture, are afflicted with the sickness of those heretics. They dare to pour the passions of the body over the Godhead of the Only-Begotten and falsely imagine that the unchangeableness of the Godhead has passed into the nature of the body [Note: [Col. 0443B–C] The following passage from Cyril’s letter to Nestorius, part I of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 8, page 320, is sufficient to refute this calumny: “The Word of God, united to flesh in the womb itself, is said to have been born according to the flesh, since he claims as his own the generation of his own flesh. In the same way we say that he suffered and was raised—not because the Word of God received wounds, the piercing of nails, or anything of that sort into his own nature—for, just as the divine nature is without a body, so it cannot suffer—but because the body which he had assumed experienced these things. For that reason he is said to have suffered them on our behalf. THE WORD, INCAPABLE OF SUFFERING, EXISTED IN A BODY CAPABLE OF SUFFERING.” It is therefore false that the defenders of this doctrine attribute either passibility to the divine nature of the Only-Begotten or impassibility and unchangeableness to the nature of his body.]

and confuse the two natures—which are worshiped in the one person of the Only-Begotten through their supreme and unconfused union—by the mutability of a mixture [Note: [Col. 0443C–D] Nestorius would seem here openly to profess the Catholic faith, unless Vincent of Lérins had wished to warn us concerning passages of this kind, in chapter 17: “If anyone thinks that Nestorius, in his letters, says that there is one Christ and proclaims one person of Christ, let him not believe it rashly. Either he contrived this by an artifice of deception, so that through good things he might more easily persuade people of evil things… or else, after the Virgin’s childbirth, he says that two persons came together into one Christ, while nevertheless maintaining that at the time of the virginal conception or childbirth, and for some time afterward, there were two Christs.

But if he denied one person of Christ at the Virgin’s childbirth so that Mary would not be called Mother of God and God would not be said to have been born, still less should we believe that he later admitted the unity of person in Christ. He prohibited the proclamation of God suffering or God dying with no less zeal than that of God being conceived or born.”]

Blind men, who remember neither the exposition of those holy Fathers, who openly cry out against them [Note: [Col. 0443D] Read *reclamantium*.]: “We believe in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, incarnate from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary” [Note: [Col. 0443D–0444C] Garnerius reads: “The word ‘in the Lord’ signifies both natures, for Christ belongs to the Godhead.” Baluzius rightly rejects this reading. The phrase “in the Lord” does not in itself signify both natures of Christ, but one divine nature; hence, when the Word assumed human nature, the Apostle says that he assumed the form of a servant, not of a lord.

The passage would be clearer if arranged as follows: “For this word—that is, ‘Christ,’ insofar as this name signifies both natures—is consubstantial with the Godhead of the Father.” Nestorius himself explains the thought more plainly in fragments excerpted by Cyril and published by Marius Mercator, Baluzius edition, page 109: “I now recall the Council of Nicaea, which nowhere dared to say that God the Word was born from the Virgin Mary. It says: ‘We believe in one almighty Father, and in one Lord Jesus Christ.’ Observe that, after it had first used ‘Christ,’ a name that indicates the two natures, it did not say ‘in one God the Word,’ but took a name that signified both.

He repeats similar statements in his letter to Cyril, Labbe, volume III of the *Councils*, page 324, adding: ‘In this matter they followed the authority of Paul. For when he had mentioned the incarnation of God and was then about to mention the things belonging to the Passion, he first used the name “Christ,” as I said shortly before, as a name common to both natures.’ Nothing is repeated more frequently in Nestorius’s speeches and letters than this assertion of his: that the name “Christ” is a significant designation of two natures.”]

For this word—“Christ”—in the name that signifies both natures is consubstantial with the Godhead of the Father. But the humanity, born in later times from the holy Virgin [Note: [Col. 0444D] The relative pronoun refers not to the Virgin but to the humanity; therefore Garnerius suppressed it, together with the preceding verb, to remove the ambiguity.], is worshiped together by angels and human beings because of its union with the Godhead.

### 3

I consider, then, what I myself, worn out here by so many labors on account of the perversity of sects, must suffer again if I do not know the case of the men mentioned above and greatly fear lest, stationed here, I should through ignorance add to the number of heretics [Note: [Col. 0444D] Baluzius has *they make through those imposed*. The reading *he makes through those placed here* is preferable.] I therefore ask that your holy soul be diligent in every way to grant information about the men mentioned above, especially since the most faithful intermediary, the chamberlain Valerius, can personally explain their troubles to your Blessedness.

I and those with me send abundant greetings in Christ to all the fraternity that is with you.

## NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING EPISTLE (S)

1. Liberatus mentions this letter in these words (Chapter 4): “But Cyril, through his deacon Posidonius, reported concerning him (Nestorius) to Pope Celestine, and by his letter set forth what was happening at Constantinople.” It is found in Cyril (Letter 9) and in Labbe, *Councils*, Part I, Council of Ephesus, chapter 14. In Greek and Latin it appears there, whereas in the Roman edition of the papal letters it is given only in Latin. Although this translation is deficient in many respects, the same version has nevertheless been preserved in the passages cited. [Col. 0445A] Indeed, it can scarcely be doubted that Cyril took care to have it translated into Latin before sending it, since at the end of the letter itself he expressly indicates that he did this with regard to the tomes appended to it. But the following circumstance shows that this translation was unknown to Liberatus: whenever he mentions Cyril’s other letters, he usually indicates them by the opening words with which they begin, but he does not follow this practice in the case of this letter. Nor does it appear in the ancient translation of the Council of Ephesus, which Stephen Baluzius observes to have been in the possession of Gregory I and Liberatus himself (*New Collection of the Councils*, p. 383). Since, therefore, that old and genuine version has perished, and the version now extant is not approved in every respect, we have had to prepare a new one.

2. If we are to trust Nicephorus Callistus (*Book XIV*, chapter 33), this letter was sent to Rome along with the acts of the synod of the province of Alexandria. Yet Cyril himself below, no. 2, testifies that he had indeed intended to admonish Nestorius by a synodical letter, but that he had by no means done so. He did not even wish Celestine to be informed of the matter except with the greatest caution. For he had been compelled by necessity to defend both the catholic faith against heretical innovation and himself against the accusations of Nestorius, but he feared to forestall Nestorius himself. Accordingly, when he sent Posidonius to Rome with this letter—in which he spares the name of the aforementioned heretic so carefully that he scarcely names him even once—he gave him the instruction not at all to deliver the letter entrusted to him to Celestine, but rather to report back if he discovered that Nestorius’s writings against Cyril had not been delivered to the pope. This is related in the Ephesine material (*New Collection of the Councils*, Baluzius, p. 453) as follows:

> When the same most reverend Cyril learned that letters and books containing his expositions had been sent by him (Nestorius) to Rome, he too wrote to the most reverend Celestine, bishop of Rome, through his own deacon Posidonius, instructing him: “If it should be discovered that his books of expositions and letters have been delivered to him (Celestine), deliver my letters as well; but if not, bring them here [Col. 0445C] without delivering them.” When he found that the expositions and letters had been delivered to him, he too necessarily delivered his own. And the writings appropriate to the matter were composed by the most holy and most reverend Celestine, bishop of the Roman Church, containing a definite ruling.

3. From the time when these writings of Celestine were sent, the date of Cyril’s letter can be inferred. It is not likely that Celestine would have long delayed replying in so serious a matter, which admitted of no delay, especially since Cyril had taken care to attach a Latin translation to his letter. Nevertheless, this pope must be thought to have hastened in such a way that he did nothing precipitately. For, as Cyril teaches in his letter to John of Antioch, Celestine first wished to investigate the matter after holding many sessions and consultations, before writing back anything. Celestine, however, replied on 10 August of the year 430. There is therefore no reason to suppose that Cyril wrote this letter either much earlier or long after the middle of the year 430.

4. When Posidonius was traveling to Rome with this letter, [Col. 0445D] Cyril gave him a memorandum which, left among the papers of Jacques Sirmond and published by Stephen Baluzius in the *New Collection of the Councils*, p. 337, we append to the end of the letter. Finally, Cyril indicates that through the same Posidonius he was sending Celestine both copies of two letters that he had written to Nestorius and tomes containing certain extracted chapters, by which Celestine might distinguish what belonged to Nestorius and what belonged to the Fathers. Thus, although Cyril calls the chapters in which he summarizes Nestorius’s teaching in the memorandum “tomes” at the end of that memorandum, those tomes are nevertheless very different from the tomes that he mentions near the end of his letter to Celestine.

5. Nestorius himself seems to indicate those tomes in Christianus Lupus, volume I, chapter 6, and in Stephen Baluzius, *New Collection of the Councils*, p. 694, where he reproaches Cyril in the following manner:

> But he (Cyril), omitting to make clear to me by letter whether anything seemed to him deserving of condemnation as blasphemous or impious, having been driven by fear of refutation and seeking disturbances as aids for this purpose, turned to the Roman Celestine, on the assumption that he was simpler than one who could penetrate more subtly into the force of doctrines. And having discovered that man’s simplicity, he childishly deceived his ears with the tricks of his writings, sending writings that had long ago been composed by **us**, as though for the demonstration of charges to which no contradiction could be offered—as though I defined Christ as a mere human being. For I certainly enacted the law [namely, *Theodosian Code* 16.5.65] against those who say that Christ is a mere human being, and against the remaining heresies, at the very beginning of my ordination.
>
> But weaving in excerpts, he composed a compilation of written discourses, so that the calumny introduced might not be detected through the joining together of the passages. Adding some things from **our addresses**, breaking off portions of others, and interweaving with them what we had said about the Lord’s becoming human, as though we had said these things about a mere human being, while cutting out in every possible way certain praises of the divinity that we had written, and leaving others out of their proper order, he skillfully contrived a plausible deception.
>
> And in order to expose briefly what his wickedness is also in other matters, we said somewhere, while speaking against the pagans, that they said we proclaim that the substance of God had recently been created from the Virgin: “**Mary did not give birth, excellent men, to divinity, but she gave birth to a human being, the inseparable instrument of divinity**.” But he altered the word “divinity” and made it read: “**Mary did not give birth, excellent men, to God**.”
>
> Then he adds another example, sufficiently lengthy, similar to what is brought forward in the Council of Ephesus, session 1, as though from Nestorius’s twenty-seventh notebook. From this he attempts to prove that Cyril, by cutting up his own words, permitted himself many things contrary to the faith. Finally he concludes:
>
> “By using many such devices, both robberies and additions, as it seemed good to him, Cyril immediately carried away by his deceptions both the others and also Celestine.”

Baluzius certainly thinks that Nestorius is marking here, in his annotations on this passage, Cyril’s work that is prefixed to the beginning of volume VI of the works of this holy teacher. The designation “tomes” does fit that writing. For it is divided into five books, each of which is called a tome. Moreover, it is evident from Nestorius’s words that Cyril intersperses his own material with passages from Nestorius in the interest of catholic doctrine. It also agrees with Cyril’s letter, which was sent to Celestine together with the tomes, in that both writings are equally sparing of Nestorius’s name. In this work, however, we do not encounter the very words that Nestorius complains Cyril excerpted from him contrary to the faith, but only similar ones, on p. 40. In any event, it is beyond doubt that by the name of the tomes sent by Cyril to Celestine we are to understand passages excerpted from Nestorius’s writings, and perhaps also from the works of the catholic Fathers, such as those found in session 1 of the Council of Ephesus, in order to prove that Nestorius’s assertions differed from the faith of the Fathers.

[Col. 0446D] 6. What, then, should be thought concerning Nestorius’s recently mentioned reproach, whether directed against Cyril or against Celestine? Since we cannot remain entirely silent on the matter, a brief explanation must be given.

First, concerning the passage in which Nestorius, claiming to have said “Mary did not give birth to divinity,” complains that Cyril changed the word “divinity” and made it “Mary did not give birth to God”: we observe that the same passage is reported in the same words by Marius in Baluzius, p. 55 (*Councils*, Part I, Council of Ephesus, chapter 13). We do not deny, however, that the clergy of Constantinople preserved the word “divinity” in the public protest that was presented, and that they are recorded as having said: “**Mary gave birth, excellent man, to divinity**” (*ἔτεκεν, ὦ βέλτιστε, Μαρία τὴν Θεότητα*). Nevertheless, those same clergy criticized this statement, doubtless because of what accompanied it, and on that basis proved that Nestorius agreed with Paul of Samosata.

In fact, Arnobius reports the same passage in Book II of *The Conflict with Serapion* as follows:

> Most holy Mary did not give birth to Deity; for what was born from flesh is flesh. [Col. 0447A] The creature did not give birth to the Creator, but she gave birth to a human being, the minister of Deity.

It is therefore clear that Nestorius indiscriminately denied Mary to be the mother not only of Deity but also of God and the Creator. Certainly, if he himself had not deliberately confused the terms “God” and “Deity,” there would have been no reason for him to attribute the inventions of Arius and Apollinaris so persistently to Cyril.

But in saying that Cyril ought to have declared to him by letter whether he had found anything impious in Nestorius’s writings or statements, and in asserting that Cyril had omitted to do so, Nestorius is plainly convicted of falsehood. For Cyril warned him about this not in one letter only, but in two, to such an extent that Celestine wished those two letters to be regarded as equivalent to two canonical admonitions. Accordingly, what Nestorius adds—namely, that Cyril wickedly removed or added many things to his own writings, by which both others and Celestine were immediately carried away—deserves no greater credence (*Letter 13*, no. 5).

Certainly, he makes a futile claim that Celestine was deceived and carried away by Cyril’s robberies and additions (*Letter 13*, no. 2), since that pope, writing to Cyril, testifies that he had learned of Nestorius’s heresy from no source more than from Nestorius’s own letters sent to him. Nor do the remaining writings or acts of this pontiff give any support to what that heretic poured forth about Celestine’s ignorant simplicity (*see Council of Ephesus*, Part I, chapter 26). Besides, it is established that Celestine did nothing in this matter without the Roman synod; and no one but a slanderer could say that this synod, especially in matters concerning the faith, lacked knowledge.

Here one should recall how rare it is for the leaders of heretics to find men for whom it is a matter of conscience either to defend a friendly error by lies or to slander those who oppose them.

7. Cyril’s attitude toward Celestine was very different. We believe that the writings he then sent to him contained the following testimony of the highest respect, which Arnobius recorded in Book II of *The Conflict with Serapion* in these words:

> Saint Cyril, bishop of the Alexandrian Church, having learned that the Nestorian doctrine was springing up contrary to the faith, wrote throughout Egypt and sent word to the holy Celestine, bishop of apostolic memory, saying that it would belong to his praise if something were corrected by him who held the citadel of the episcopate.

That is, Cyril submitted his writings to Celestine’s judgment and decision, declaring that he would regard it as a credit to himself if anything were corrected by him.

[Note: [Col. 0447D] Around the middle of the year 430.]

# Letter VIII

[Note: [Col. 0447] The following Latin and Greek texts are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0447]

Cyril explains how pestilential Nestorius’s doctrine is and what he has so far done, in order to recall him to the right faith. He states that he has not yet openly withdrawn from communion with him, until he learns from Celestine what action he should take. He asks Celestine to make his judgment on the matter known as soon as possible by letters sent to the bishops of the East and of Macedonia. At the end are appended certain chapters in which the whole of Nestorius’s doctrine is explained.

[Col. 0447B] **Cyril to the most holy and God-loving father Celestine: greetings in the Lord.**

1. If it were permissible to remain silent and, without blame or fear of an unfavorable suspicion, not to inform your piety by letter about all that is taking place—especially in matters so necessary, in which the right faith is also endangered by some people’s corruption—I would say to myself: “Silence is good and free from danger, and it is better to lead a quiet life than a troubled one.” But [Col. 0447C] since God requires vigilance from us in these matters, and [Note: [Col. 0447D] Labbe prints *vetus* (“ancient”). The Greek text should be followed, since it commends a custom that is not only ancient but also established by a long succession of time.] the long-standing custom of the Churches urges that such affairs be communicated to your holiness, I write under compulsion of necessity and plainly declare that Satan is now throwing everything into confusion, raging against the Churches of God, and plotting the subversion of all peoples everywhere who walk in the right faith. For that most wicked and unrestrained beast never ceases from its zeal for impiety.

Until now I have maintained a deep silence and have written nothing at all either to your piety or to any of our fellow priests concerning the man who now administers the Church of Constantinople, believing that rash haste in matters of this kind is not free from fault. But since we have reached almost the extreme point of evils, I have judged it necessary, breaking my silence, to recount everything that has happened.

2. As soon as the man mentioned above was ordained, he ought to have encouraged the peoples—both the local inhabitants and the foreigners residing there, of whom a very great multitude regularly gathers there from practically every city and region—to virtue by his exhortations. Instead, he made it his aim to proclaim certain absurdities alien to reason, far removed from the apostolic and evangelical faith, which the Fathers have always preserved with the greatest steadfastness and handed down to us like a precious pearl.

I sent your piety his homilies, which he has frequently delivered in church and has not ceased to deliver, as clear evidence of his teaching. I confess that I had intended to warn him by a synodical letter that we cannot communicate with one who says and thinks such things, but I did not do so. Believing, however, that one must extend a hand to those who have fallen and raise them as brothers when they have been brought low, I exhorted him by letter to withdraw from such perverse teaching.

[Note: [Col. 0449D] Cyril recalls in the just-mentioned letter to John of Antioch that he sent copies of those letters together with this letter to Celestine. They are extant in Part I of the *Council of Ephesus*, chapter 6, and in Baluzius, *New Collection of the Councils*, p. 400, in an ancient translation different from the one which Liberatus the deacon, chapter 4, indicates that he had seen by citing their opening words.]

[Note: [Col. 0449D] Nestorius himself had already sent his notebooks of expositions to Celestine, as Cyril writes in his letter to John of Antioch (*Council of Ephesus*, Part I, chapter 21). “For this reason,” Cyril says there, “I too was compelled to disclose to the same pope everything that had taken place between him and me.” Celestine testifies below, in Letter 11, that these notebooks of Nestorius had been delivered to him by the distinguished man Antiochus.]

But we accomplished nothing. Indeed, when he learned that we were so far from sharing his views that we even rebuked him and admonished him to abandon his inventions—for I would not call them doctrines—he attempted every possible means of laying ambushes, and has not ceased to attempt them to this day. While we waited for him to come to his senses and abstain from what he had taught against Christ, we discovered that our hope had been disappointed when the following event occurred.

3. There was a bishop in Constantinople [Note: namely, of Marcianopolis in Moesia, who also subscribed to the deposition of Cyril and Memnon at the Robber Council of Ephesus. Cyril again explains this bishop’s impiety in Part I of the *Council of Ephesus*, chapter 10, and immediately adds: “What prevented us also from writing against his words and saying: ‘Let him be anathema who denies that Mary is the Mother of God’? But until now I did not wish to do this because of Nestorius, lest there be those who said that the Alexandrian bishop or the Egyptian synod had pronounced the sentence of anathema against Nestorius. In this he used moderation, both to avoid schism and lest he appear to imitate the injustice of his uncle Theophilus toward John Chrysostom.] named Dorotheus, holding the same opinions as Nestorius, a man devoted to flattery for the sake of gain and, as it is written, with a tongue ready for rashness.

In a public assembly, while the most reverend Nestorius was seated on the chair of the Constantinopolitan Church, Dorotheus rose and dared to shout in a loud voice: “If anyone says that Mary is the Mother of God, let him be anathema.” Then there followed a great outcry and departure of the entire people. For they did not wish to have communion any longer with those who held such opinions. Indeed, even now the Constantinopolitan people, except for a few who are more frivolous and those who flatter him, abstain from the assembly; and almost all the monasteries, their archimandrites, and many members of the senate do not gather with them, fearing that they might suffer some loss in the faith, since both he and all those whom he brought with him when he left Antioch proclaim perverse teachings.

[Note: [Col. 0450D] Among those perverse preachers whom Nestorius brought with him from Antioch, Liberatus, chapter 4, following Socrates, Book VII, chapter 32, notes the presbyter Anastasius, who, while teaching in church, broke out, according to Socrates, with these words: “Let no one call Mary the Mother of God. For Mary was a human being, and God cannot be born from a human being.”]

4. When I learned that, after his homilies had been brought to Egypt, certain less discerning people had been led into error and were asking one another whether he spoke correctly or was mistaken, I feared that the contagion of the disease might take deeper root in the minds of the simple. I therefore wrote a general letter to the monasteries of Egypt [Note: this is found in Part I of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 2] in order to strengthen their monks in the right faith.

Copies of this letter were carried to Constantinople by some people and read there. They were so helpful that many members of the magistracy wrote to thank me for it. [Note: [Col. 0451D] That is, Nestorius, whose name the common translation expresses here and below; but because Cyril consistently and for good reason suppresses it in Greek, we have judged that it should be suppressed in Latin also.]

But this supplied further fuel to the anger that he had conceived against me. He attacks me as an enemy, having nothing else with which to reproach me except that I abhor what he believes and, seriously persuading people to embrace the faith that we received from the Fathers and learned from the divine Scriptures, have brought many back to sound judgment.

I paid no attention to what he plotted against me, entrusted everything to God, who knows and is able to do all things, and sent the aforementioned man another letter [Note: this letter also appears in Part I of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 8; Stephen Baluzius presents its ancient translation in the *New Collection of the Councils*, p. 404], containing a brief exposition of the right faith, while exhorting and beseeching him not to think or speak otherwise. Again, however, I accomplished nothing. [Col. 0451B] For he obstinately clings to the inventions he devised at the beginning and does not cease teaching perverse doctrines.

5. [Note: [Col. 0451D] The common translation departs from the Greek text in the following manner. Nevertheless, your holiness should know this also: namely, that the Easterners do not approve his inventions, but are offended and grieve.] Let your piety know this also: the things being said are opposed by all the bishops of the East; all are offended and grieve, especially the most reverend bishops of Macedonia.

Yet, knowing this, he considers himself wiser than everyone and thinks that he alone has grasped the meaning of divinely inspired Scripture and understood the mystery of Christ. But how ought he not rather to be convinced that, since all orthodox bishops and laypeople throughout the whole world confess that Christ is God and that the Virgin who gave birth to him is the Mother of God, he alone is in error by denying this? Instead, swollen with pride and abusing the power of his see in order to lay ambushes for everyone, he thinks that he will cause both us and all the others to subscribe to his own opinion.

[Note: [Col. 0451D] Socrates, Book VII, chapter 32, censures the same fault in these words: “For, puffed up with arrogance because of his skill in speaking, he did not deign to read the books even of the ancient interpreters, but considered himself superior to all the others.” The words reported in the preceding admonition, in which he describes Celestine as so simple and dull that he could not penetrate the force and meaning of doctrines, likewise reveal this disease of arrogance. Socrates proves Nestorius’s own ignorance from the fact that he refused to call Mary the Mother of God, although the ancients, relying on the Scriptures—especially Origen in volume I of his commentary on Paul’s Letter to the Romans, and Eusebius in Book III of *The Life of Constantine*—did not hesitate to call her by this name. Nestorius’s example warns those who take pleasure in a similar eloquence that this one gift is not sufficient for handling matters of faith. Others, too, whose intellectual sharpness or natural charm pleases them more than is fitting, should learn not to allow themselves to be rashly led astray by it. Matters of faith belong not so much to ingenuity as to tradition; they are supported not by the sharp and subtle inventions of the human mind, but by the constant and faithful tradition of the Fathers transmitted to us through the word of God. In imitation of what Cyril relates here about Nestorius, the following words of Vincent of Lérins are expressed at the end of chapter 42: “We have also inveighed against the wicked presumption of Nestorius, because he boasted that he alone and first understood sacred Scripture and that all who before him had handled the divine words in the office of teaching had been ignorant.”]

6. What, then, shall we do? We cannot persuade him either to come to his senses or to stop such discourses, while the Constantinopolitan people are being corrupted more and more each day, even though they are indignant at this and await assistance from orthodox teachers. We are not speaking about ordinary matters, and our silence would not be free from danger. If Christ is attacked with insults, how shall we remain silent? Especially since Paul writes: “For if I do this willingly, I have a reward; but if unwillingly, I have been entrusted with a stewardship” (1 Cor. 9:17). What, then, shall we to whom the stewardship of the word and the guardianship of the faith have been entrusted say on the day of judgment, if we remain silent about these things?

7. Nevertheless, we have not openly and publicly withdrawn ourselves from communion with him before informing your piety of these matters. Therefore, deign to declare to us what seems good to you, and whether it is appropriate at some point to communicate with him or whether we should freely announce that no one may communicate with one who thinks and teaches such things.

It is necessary that the judgment of your piety on this matter be made known by letter both to the most devout and God-loving bishops of Macedonia and to all the bishops of the East. For they desire this, and we shall give them an opportunity to remain united in one mind and one judgment and to assist the right faith that is under attack.

8. So far as he was concerned, both our great, admirable, and approved Fathers, who said that the holy Virgin is the Mother of God, and we who are still alive were struck with anathema together with them. [Note: Nestorius is considered to have anathematized both the Fathers who had died and the catholic Fathers who were still alive in the same manner as Hilary, in *On the Synods*, no. 91, proves from the decree issued at Ancyra. In that decree, those who proclaimed the *homoousion* were anathematized, so that it would follow that the Nicene Fathers and the other holy priests who rested in Christ were included in the anathema.]

Since he did not wish to do this with his own voice, he appointed another, namely the aforementioned Dorotheus, and induced him to say it while Nestorius himself was present and listening. He immediately descended from the chair, celebrated the divine mysteries, and communicated with Dorotheus.

9. In order that your holiness might know clearly what Nestorius himself says and thinks, and what our blessed and great Fathers say and think, I sent tomes containing excerpts of certain chapters. I took care to have them translated into Latin, insofar as this could be done by those living in Alexandria.

[Note: namely, the three letters mentioned above, if I am not mistaken, in nos. 3 and 4: one written to the monks of Egypt and the other two to Nestorius himself.]

I also entrusted to my beloved Posidonius the letters that I had written, instructing him to present them to your holiness.

**To the most holy and most God-loving father Celestine, Cyril sends greetings in the Lord.**

If it were possible to remain silent, and without blame not to write to your godliness about everything that is taking place, and to avoid what appears distressing—especially in matters so necessary, in which the correctness of the faith is being shaken by certain people—I would say within myself: “Silence is good and free from danger, and being at rest is better than being disturbed.”

But since God also requires sobriety from us in these matters [Col. 0448C], and the long-standing customs of the Churches persuade us to communicate such things to your holiness, I write again under compulsion of necessity, declaring that Satan is now throwing everything into confusion, raging [F. read *κατὰ*, “against”] against the Churches of God, and attempting to lead astray all peoples everywhere who walk uprightly in the faith. For that utterly wicked beast does not rest, being most ready—or perhaps, according to the variant reading, “unbearable”—in impiety.

Until now I remained silent about what had happened. I wrote nothing at all either to your godliness or to any other of my fellow ministers concerning the man who is now in Constantinople and governs the Church there, believing that rashness in such matters is not free from blame. But since, as it were, we have reached the crisis of the evil, I judged it necessary to release my tongue at last and recount everything that has taken place.

[Col. 0448D] The man mentioned above had scarcely been ordained when, instead of benefiting by exhortations toward the good both the local people and the foreign visitors—of whom there are very many, coming, so to speak, from every city and region—he made it his aim to speak certain extraordinary things, outside reason, and far removed from the apostolic and evangelical faith, which the Fathers have preserved to the end and handed down to us like a precious pearl.

I sent to your godliness the homilies that he delivered in church, and has delivered very frequently, and does not cease to deliver, as an exact account. I confess that, although I wished to make clear to him by a synodical letter that we cannot communicate with one who says and thinks such things, I did not do this. But, reasoning that one must extend a hand to those who have stumbled and raise those who have fallen as brothers, I exhorted him by letter to abstain from such false teaching.

But we accomplished nothing. When he learned that we were so far from thinking the same things that we even rebuked him and admonished him to abandon his own inventions—for I would not call them doctrines—he set every kind of plot in motion and has not ceased to stir up such plots even now. When we were expecting him to be healed and to abstain from the doctrines he had taught against Christ, we realized that our hope had been mistaken when such an event occurred.

There was a bishop in Constantinople named Dorotheus, holding the same opinions as Nestorius, a man devoted to gain and rash with his lips, as it is written. While Nestorius, the most reverend bishop of Constantinople, was seated on the throne of the Church at an assembly, Dorotheus rose and dared to say in a loud voice: “If anyone says that Mary is the Mother of God, let him be anathema.”

There was a great outcry from all the people, and they departed. For they no longer wished to communicate with those who held such opinions. Thus even now the people of Constantinople are excluded from the assemblies, except for a few who are more frivolous and those who flatter him. Almost all the monasteries, their archimandrites, and many members of the senate do not assemble with them, fearing that they might suffer injury in the faith, since he and all those who came with him from Antioch proclaim perverse doctrines.

When I learned that, after his homilies had been brought to Egypt, certain less discerning people had been carried away and thereafter said to one another in doubt, “Does he speak correctly? Has he gone astray?”—fearing that the disease might take root in the souls of the simple—I wrote a catholic letter to the monasteries throughout Egypt, confirming them in the right faith.

Some people then carried copies of it to Constantinople, and many benefited from reading them, so much so that many of the officials wrote to give thanks. This too became nourishment for his resentment against me. He fights against me as an enemy, having nothing else with which to reproach me except that I alone cannot endure thinking the same things as he does. Yet I also corrected many people, persuading them to accept the faith that we received from the Fathers and learned from the divine Scripture.

Nevertheless, without concerning myself with what he had done against me, but entrusting everything to God, who knows and is able to do all things, I again wrote another letter to the man mentioned above, containing an exposition, in brief, of the right faith, while exhorting and protesting that he should think and speak accordingly. Again I accomplished nothing. He continues to cling to what he held from the beginning and does not cease proclaiming perverse doctrines.

[Col. 0452B] Let your godliness know this also: what is being said is opposed by all the bishops of the East. All are displeased and grieve, especially the most reverend bishops of Macedonia. Yet, knowing this, he thinks that he is wiser than everyone, that he alone knows the meaning of divinely inspired Scripture and the mystery of Christ.

But how ought he not rather to be convinced that, since all orthodox bishops and laypeople throughout the inhabited world confess that Christ was God and that the Virgin who gave birth to him is the Mother of God, he alone is in error by denying this? Instead, he raises his brow and thinks that, by the power of his throne and by plotting against everyone, he will persuade both us and all the others to think as he does.

What, then, shall we do? We can neither persuade him nor make him cease from such discourses, while the people of Constantinople are being corrupted day by day, grieving at this but awaiting assistance from orthodox teachers. We are not speaking about trivial matters, and silence is not free from danger. If Christ is reviled, how shall we remain silent? Yet Paul writes: “For if I do this willingly, I have a reward; but if unwillingly, I have been entrusted with a stewardship.” What, then, shall we to whom the stewardship of the word and the security of the faith have been entrusted say on the day of judgment, when we remain silent about these things?

We do not openly withdraw ourselves from communion with him before communicating these matters to your godliness. Therefore deign to set forth what seems good, and whether at any time we ought to communicate with him, or whether we should henceforth declare openly that no one communicates with one who thinks and teaches such things. The judgment of your godliness on these matters must be made clearly known by letter both to the most devout and God-loving bishops of Macedonia and to all the bishops of the East.

For we shall thereby give them the opportunity, which they desire, to stand with one soul and one mind and to fight on behalf of the right faith that is under attack.

So far as he was concerned, our great, admirable, and approved Fathers, who said that the holy Virgin is the Mother of God, were anathematized, and we who are still alive were anathematized with them. Since he did not wish to do this with his own voice, he appointed another, the aforementioned Dorotheus, and arranged for him to say it while Nestorius himself was seated and listening. Immediately afterward Nestorius descended from the throne and communicated with him after celebrating the divine mysteries.

In order that your holiness might know clearly what Nestorius himself says and thinks, and what our blessed and great Fathers say and think, I sent tomes containing excerpts of chapters. I had them translated as far as was possible by those in Alexandria, and I gave the letters written by me to my beloved Posidonius, instructing him to present them also to your holiness.

# Letter IX

[Note: [Col. 0453] The following Latin and Greek texts are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0453]

[Col. 0453C] Or, the memorandum of the most holy bishop Cyril, which he gave to Posidonius when he sent him to Rome on account of the affair of Nestorius.

1. Nestorius’s faith, or rather his perverse opinion, is as follows. He says that the Word of God, foreknowing that the one who would be born from the holy Virgin would be holy and great, therefore chose him and caused him to be born from a virgin without a man, and bestowed on him the grace of being called by God’s own names; [Note: The translator who lent his services to Baluzius added these words from his own hand, so that the sentence would read: “and thus he would be called Son, Lord, and Christ.” He also caused him to die for us, unless perhaps the corresponding words were omitted from the Greek through a copyist’s carelessness.] finally, he raised him from the dead.

Accordingly, when the only-begotten Word of God is said to have become incarnate, he is said to have become incarnate because he was always with that holy man who was born from the Virgin. Just as he was with the prophets, he says, so he was with this man according to a greater conjunction.

[Note: For this reason Christ alone, having the pre-eminent conjunction with the Word of God, is proclaimed in the Nestorian creed published by Marius Mercator in Baluzius, p. 191.]

Thus he everywhere avoids saying “union” and instead calls it “conjunction,” such as that by which one who is external is connected, and of which God says to Joshua: “As I was with Moses, so I will be with you” (Joshua 1:5).

[Note: Rather, he attached certain particles to this word by which the mind was diverted from the thought of the closest conjunction. Certainly Marius Mercator, p. 206, cites from his fifteenth notebook: “We call the man co-worshipful with Almighty God **by a certain divine conjunction**.” Related to this is the following from the Nestorian creed in the same Marius Mercator, p. 191: “We introduce also the Son who was assumed from Nazareth, whom God anointed with Spirit and power, **as though by a conjunction with the Word of God**.” Accordingly, Cyril also rejected the term “conjunction,” or *synapheia*, which Nestorius used: “Rather, we reject the name of conjunction, as not sufficiently capable of signifying union,” he says in his letter to Nestorius, volume V, Part II, p. 71. That is: “Rather, we avoid the name of conjunction, as not being suitable to signify the mystery of unity.”]

To conceal his impiety, he says that the Word was with him from the womb.

[Note: Even the Nestorian creed, cited by Marius Mercator, p. 190, does not express this without ambiguity. It says that “God the Word joined to himself, in an immeasurable manner, a man like us in nature, fashioned in the Virgin’s womb by the power of the Holy Spirit.” It is not clear whether “in the Virgin’s womb” belongs with “fashioned” or with “joined to himself.”]

2. For this reason he does not say that the man himself is the true God, but that he was given that name as if through God’s beneficence.

[Note: Nestorius gives this reason for the designation in notebook 16, apud Mercator, p. 207: “Because God is in the man who was assumed, the one who was assumed is recognized as being God, as though joined to God, from the one who assumed him.” Likewise, in the Nestorian creed, p. 191, one reads: “The Lord is by substance the Word of God, and this man, joined to him, shares in his honor.” Yet Nestorius complained, as can be seen in Christianus Lupus, volume I, chapter 6, that Cyril had slanderously accused him of proclaiming Christ to be a mere human being.]

Although he has been called Lord, he likewise wants him to be Lord for the same reason: because the Word of God gave him this title so that he might be called so.

3. Nor does he say what we say, that the Son of God died for us and rose again. Rather, he says that the man died and the man rose, and that nothing of this kind pertains to the Word of God.

[Note: “If you search through the whole of the New Testament,” he says in notebook 16 apud Mercator, p. 210, “you will nowhere find death assigned to God, but either to Christ, or to the Son, or to the Lord.” But if Christ is Lord and Son only in the manner in which he is called God, as we have just seen and as the Nestorian creed explains on p. 191, then, since the New Testament attributes death to the Lord and the Son, he permits it also to be assigned to God. Since it is God who died, although not according to the divine nature, God is nevertheless truly said to have died.]

4. We confess that the Word, God, is immortal and life itself; but we also believe that he became flesh—that is, that when he had united flesh with a rational soul to himself, he suffered in the flesh according to the Scriptures. Since his body endured suffering, he himself is said to have suffered, although by nature he is incapable of suffering. Again, since his body rose—for his flesh did not see corruption (Ps. 15:10)—he himself is said to have risen from the dead.

Nestorius, however, does not think in this way. He says that the suffering belonged to the man and the resurrection belonged to the man; and he proclaims that what is set forth in the mysteries is the body of a man.

[Note: What Nestorius simply calls *prokeimenon*, and Marius Mercator renders in Latin as *procimenum*, Nestorius himself, in the same Mercator, p. 209, and in Cyril, volume VI, p. 108c–d, affirms to be not Deity but humanity. Nor did the heretic see that in Christ’s words, “As the living Father sent me,” and “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him,” the words “me” and “I” signify not humanity but the divine person. Cyril refutes his perverse interpretation both in the cited passage of volume VI and in anathema 11. In this controversy, however, Cyril and Nestorius agree that the true body of Christ is eaten by us in the sacrament of the Eucharist.]

We believe that the flesh of the Word therefore possesses the power of giving life because it has become the flesh and blood of the Word, who gives life to all.

[Note: In Baluzius, “therefore made alive” appears here, apparently through a copyist’s carelessness, the copyist having substituted *made alive* for the word *giving life* or *life-giving*.]

### 5

Since he could not bear to say these things, he arranged for Coelestius to submit written accusations against the presbyter Philip, who was rebuking him and no longer wished to associate with him because of the heresy. [Note: This was Philip who, as we learn from Socrates, Book VII, chapters 26, 27, and 29, while still a deacon, was accustomed to associate chiefly with John Chrysostom. Later, in the suburb of Constantinople called Aelea, after attaining the rank of presbyter, following the death of Atticus and of his successor Sisinnius, he was chosen by many to replace them, but was passed over in favor first of Sisinnius and later of Nestorius. The Coelestius who accused Philip is thought to have been that disciple of Pelagius who, as Marcellinus Mercator reports on p. 113, had been expelled from Constantinople under Bishop Atticus. A letter of Nestorius to this Coelestius is preserved in Marcellinus Mercator, p. 131; in it Nestorius consoles him as one enduring undeserved treatment and unjust condemnation and tells him to remain of good courage. It was customary for the Pelagians to call Catholics “Manichaeans,” as though they were destroyers of free will.] One of these accusations was that he was a Manichaean. Then he summoned the man to a council. He came, conducting himself according to the canons, in order to answer the charge. But since Coelestius could prove nothing, he secretly withdrew and did not come to the council.

### 6

When that opportunity had failed, he devised another. For he said: “Why have you held private gatherings and celebrated the oblation in a house?” [Note: Philip undoubtedly began holding these gatherings when the Constantinopolitans, after hearing Dorotheus’s impious sermon, ceased to assemble with Nestorius, as is related in the preceding letter, section 4.] And when almost the whole clergy said, “Each of us does this whenever circumstances and necessity require it,” he pronounced a sentence of deposition against the man.

Here you have the volumes containing the principal charges of Nestorius’s blasphemies. [Note: That is, the principal statements excerpted in summary from Nestorius’s writings.]

[Col. 0454C] **Memorandum of the most holy Bishop Cyril, prepared for Posidonius, whom he had sent to Rome, concerning the proceedings against Nestorius.**

Nestorius’s faith—or rather, his false doctrine—has this substance. He says that the Word of God, foreknowing that the one born from the holy Virgin would be holy and great, chose him for this purpose; he arranged that he should be born from the Virgin without a man, and granted him that he should be called by the Word’s own names and raised him up. [Note: In Coustant there is no conjunction; shortly before this he also has προσεγνωκὼς, incorrectly. We have compared this memorandum with the edition in Garner’s *Auctarium of Theodoret*, pp. 51 ff. GALLAND.]

Thus, even if the only-begotten Word of God is said to have become incarnate, he is said to have become incarnate because he was always present with the holy man who came from the Virgin, as with a man. And just as he was present with the prophets, so, he says, he was present with this man in a greater conjunction. For this reason he everywhere avoids saying “union,” but calls it “conjunction,” as though it were something external; and as if he were saying to Jesus: “As I was with Moses, so I will be with you.” But while concealing his impiety, he says that the Word was present with him from the womb.

For this reason he does not say that he is truly God, but that he was called so by the good pleasure of God. And although he was called “Lord,” he again wishes him to be Lord in the sense that the Word of God granted him the privilege of being called so.

He does not say what we say: that the Son of God died for us and rose again. Rather, he says that the man died and the man rose, and that none of this pertains to the Word of God. [Note: Perhaps, “anything of this sort.”]

For we indeed confess that the Word of God is immortal and is life; but we believe that he became flesh—that is, that he united to himself flesh together with a rational soul—and that, according to the Scriptures, he suffered in the flesh. Since his body suffered, he himself is said to have suffered, although by nature he is impassible. And since his body rose—his flesh did not see corruption—he is said himself to have risen from the dead.

But that man does not think this way. Rather, he says that the passion belonged to a man, that the resurrection belonged to a man, and that in the mysteries what is set before us is the body of a man. We, however, believe that the flesh of the Word possesses the power to give life because it became the flesh and blood of the Word who gives life to all things.

Since he could not bear to say these things, he arranged for Coelestius to submit written accusations against the presbyter Philip, who was rebuking him [Note: Read ἐλέγχοντος, “rebuking,”] and no longer wished to associate with him because of the heresy [Note: Below, read θελήσαντος, “who wished.”]. In the accusations there was also the charge that he was a Manichaean. Then he summoned the man to a council. The man came, acting in a canonical manner and prepared to defend himself. But since Coelestius had nothing to demonstrate, he made himself disappear and did not go to the council.

When he found no opening in that matter, he proceeded to another. For he said: “Why did you hold an unauthorized gathering and celebrate the oblation in a house?” When nearly the whole clergy said, “Each of us does this in times of need and necessity,” he issued a sentence of deposition against the man.

“Here you have volumes containing the principal charges of Nestorius’s blasphemies.”

[Note: Arnobius, Book II of *The Conflict with Serapion*, transmitted this document to us. He introduces it there as follows: “Saint Coelestine so praised him [Cyril] that, in condemning Nestorius, he pronounced judgment, while proclaiming Cyril’s praise both in the sight of God and of all, asserting that Cyril’s doctrine was strengthened by the preaching of the distinguished bishops of our province, and that this had also been the teaching of Damasus, Ambrose, and Hilary. For he says in the council itself, ‘I remember,’ and so forth.” It is not obscure that this was said in the council in which, after receiving the letters of Nestorius and Cyril, Coelestine composed his judgment against that heretic and the letters that followed—thus, in August of the year 430.]

## Fragment of a Sermon Delivered by Coelestine in the Roman Council against the Heresy of Nestorius (C)

[Col. 0457]

### 1

I remember that Ambrose, of blessed memory, caused the whole people, on the day of the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ, to sing to God with one voice:

> Come, Redeemer of the nations, show forth the Virgin’s birth;  
> let every age marvel: such a birth befits God.

Did he say, “Such a birth befits a man”? Therefore our brother Cyril’s understanding, when he calls Mary *Theotokos*—“God-bearer”—agrees entirely with the words, “Such a birth befits God.” In her childbirth the Virgin brought forth God, by the power of the one who is full of omnipotence.

### 2

Hilary also, a man of keen intellect, writing to the emperor Constantius, says the following about the Lord’s Incarnation: [Note: In the new edition of Hilary, p. 1215, it has been observed that the words quoted here belong to that part of Book I *To Constantius* which is manifestly mutilated. The sense in which Hilary uttered them is explained there on p. 1367, note b, and in the general preface, no. 190. From that explanation it will become clear that they are suitable for illustrating and confirming what Cyril asserted concerning the deification of human nature after Christ’s resurrection.]

> “The Son,” he says, “having become man, is God. And, reversing the expression, he repeats: God the Son became the son of man—for man became God, not God became man—and the son of man became the Son of God. For the Lord’s greatness surpassed the lowliness of the servant’s form, so that the very servant’s form which he assumed ceased to be servile through the Lord who assumed it. If those who by nature are not sons of God are made sons of God through him, how much more did he who by nature is the Son of God so exalt into God the one with whom, by his own will, he was conceived and born in a virgin womb, that at his name every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father” (Philippians 2:10).

### 3

My predecessor Damasus also, writing to Paulinus, bishop of the Church of Antioch, says among other things: [Note: Letter 5, section 3.]

> “We anathematize those who assert two sons of God: one begotten from the Father before the ages, and another born from the Virgin through the assumption of flesh.”

Again, that man of apostolic memory, Damasus, says in another letter to Paulinus [Note: That is, in the exposition of the Catholic faith appended to Letter 5, cited immediately above, section 1]:

> “We anathematize those who confess two sons in the Savior: one before the Incarnation and another after the assumption of flesh from the Virgin, and who do not confess that the same one is the Son of God both before and afterward—the same Christ, the Lord, the Son of God, who was born from the Virgin.”

## Notice Concerning the Following Four Letters (S)

[Col. 0457]

### 1

There is no room for doubt concerning their authenticity, since they are supported not only by the authority of ancient manuscripts but also by the testimonies of Pope Nicholas I, the deacon Liberatus, Cyril of Alexandria, John of Antioch, and others.

### 2

Liberatus the deacon, chapter 5, and Cyril in his letters to John of Antioch and to Juvenal report that they were written at the Roman council presided over by Coelestine, at which those bishops who were then found in the City had assembled, after many sessions had been held. For this reason Cyril himself attributes them to Coelestine in his letter to John, in his letter to Juvenal, and elsewhere; and in all the copies they are attributed to Coelestine alone (Council of Ephesus I, parts 21 and 24). The ancient manuscripts disagree about the day on which they were issued: some date them to the third day before the Ides of August, others to the fourth.

### 3

Those four letters were sent to Cyril by Posidonius, a deacon of the Alexandrian Church who had carried Cyril’s letters and writings to Rome, so that Cyril might transmit them, through his own agency, to those to whom they were addressed. Coelestine explicitly testifies to this concerning Letters 13 and 14 (Letter 14, section 8), and Cyril concerning Letter 11 in his letter to Juvenal. John of Antioch likewise informs Nestorius that he had received from the Alexandrian clergy a copy of the letter sent to him by Coelestine (Council of Ephesus I, part 25).

As for Rufus and Flavian, since they were closer to the City, there was no need for them to receive from Cyril another copy of the same letter. Nevertheless, because the very letter sent to John is addressed equally to Rufus and Flavian, it is probable that they too received the letter from the same person from whom John received it.

### 4

It is worth noting what Coelestine writes: namely, that Nestorius’s case was one that required Coelestine’s personal presence; but because the great distance between the places did not permit this, Coelestine delegated his place and authority to Cyril in the whole matter.

Cyril obeyed this mandate; the others likewise complied with it, and John of Antioch did not oppose it (ibid.). Indeed, after receiving Coelestine’s letters, he urged Nestorius to obey them in these words:

> “Although my lord Coelestine, the bishop most devoted to God, has inserted in his letter only an interval of ten days, a very short period fixed as the limit for your reply, nevertheless the matter is of such a kind that it can be completed not merely in ten days but in one day—or rather, in a few hours.”

John did not write this alone, but together with many bishops whom he lists at the end of the letter.

### 5

Someone may perhaps ask in what language Coelestine wrote at that time: in Greek, in Latin, or in both. As far as we are concerned, we are persuaded that he wrote in Latin, first because, as he himself states in Letter 13, he did not know Greek; and second because it was customary for the Roman bishops to write in Latin to the Greeks, and even in the Greek councils their letters were first read in Latin, as we learn from Act 2 of the Council of Ephesus, p. 111.

Nevertheless, we suppose that he took care not to send his letters, like Nestorius, in the vernacular alone and without a suitable translation. Otherwise Nestorius would have had an opportunity to refuse obedience to those letters within the prescribed period. Rather, he imitated Cyril, who had arranged for the writings sent to him to be translated first into Latin.

Thus he should be thought to have done on that occasion what he later did when writing to the Ephesian synod, where the legates of the Apostolic See presented his letters, written in Latin, together with a Greek translation. Certainly the manuscripts present the following letters in both languages as well. We found two Greek copies in the Royal Library and one Latin copy in the Navarre Library. Earlier, Stephen Baluze had published them in Latin, from three other manuscripts: the Tours, Beauvais, and Colbert manuscripts.

### 6

This gives rise to a new question: namely, whether their original text has reached us. The manuscripts just mentioned testify that the text we still possess is ancient. Indeed, it is not different from the text circulating in the time of Liberatus—that is, in the sixth century—for Liberatus indicates the beginnings of Letters 11 and 13 in the very words in which they have reached us.

Nevertheless, some expressions in these letters, especially in Letter 14, are improper; this proves that they flow not from a Latin source but from Greek streams. Therefore, wherever such less appropriate expressions occur, or sentences arising from the ambiguous idiom of one language or the other, we have generally taken care either to note or to explain them. We thought this especially necessary in the last letter, which is less faithful than the others to the original Latin text.

We further observe that, although the last letter repeats the judgment which Coelestine pronounces against Nestorius in the preceding letter, in neither letter is it stated in the same words—not only in Latin but also in Greek.

## Letter XI: Pope Coelestine I to Cyril, Bishop of Alexandria

[Note: The following Latin and Greek texts are printed in parallel in Migne.]

Coelestine praises Cyril’s zeal in defending the faith, condemns Nestorius’s heresy, and orders Cyril, acting in his place, to remove him from communion with the Church and provide another pastor for his Church unless he is corrected.

[Col. 0459C] **Coelestine to his dearest brother Cyril.** [Note: The Greek requires that “brother” be added here.]

### 1

The letters of Your Holiness, sent through our son Posidonius the deacon, restored joy to our sorrow, and we exchanged gladness for grief. For when we looked back and considered what had been said by the man who is attempting to disturb the Church of Constantinople with perverse teachings, our spirit, struck by no small grief, was tormented by various stings of thought as we considered how the peoples might be helped to remain steadfast in the faith.

But when we turned our mind to the writings of your brotherhood [Note: That is, those which Cyril had recently sent together with the preceding Letter 8: namely, two letters to Nestorius and one to the monks, together with the volumes in which he made clear which opinions belonged to Nestorius and which to the Fathers. This does not refer to Cyril’s further writings or to that notable approval by Coelestine in which he testifies that what Posidonius had delivered to him agreed completely with his own faith. Nor, therefore, does this refer to Cyril’s anathemas.] we found at once a ready remedy by which the pestilential disease might be driven away with a healing medicine: namely, the liquid of a pure spring flowing from the speech of your charity, which would wash away all the mud of the foully flowing stream and disclose to everyone what they ought to think concerning our faith.

Therefore, just as we reproved and marked him, so we have embraced Your Holiness in your letters with the Lord’s charity, as though you were present, since we saw that we held one and the same view concerning the Lord. Nor is it surprising that the Lord’s most provident priest should fight with such courage for the love of the faith [Note: In Baluze: “by love and courage.” The Greek wording requires “by love, by this (or such) courage.”], so as to resist the wicked audacity of his opponents and strengthen by this admonition those entrusted to him. As bitter as those things were to us, so sweet are these; as muddy as those were, so pure are these.

We rejoice that such vigilance is present in Your Holiness, so that you have already surpassed the examples of your predecessors, who themselves had always been defenders of orthodox doctrine. Truly the evangelical testimony applies to you:

> “The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep” (John 10:11).

But just as you are a good shepherd, so he cannot even be accused as a bad hireling who is charged not with abandoning the sheep but with being found slaughtering them himself. [Note: Baluze has “slaughters them”; the Greek text requires: “He is worthy to be accused, not as a bad hireling, since he is not accused because he abandoned the sheep, but because he was found slaughtering them himself.”]

### 2

We would add something, dearest brother, if we did not see that you share all the same convictions as we do and had not proved you, in the very defense of the faith, to be an exceedingly strong champion. Everything that Your Holiness has written about this matter was reported to us in order by our son Posidonius the deacon.

You have exposed all the snares of his crafty teaching and fortified the faith in such a way that the hearts of those who believe in Christ our God cannot be drawn to the other side. This is a great triumph of our faith: to have asserted our position so forcefully and to have defeated the opposing arguments so thoroughly by the testimonies of the Holy Scriptures.

What will he do now? Where will he turn, this man who, having become a lover of impious novelty, wished to serve his own ingenuity rather than Christ and sought to infect with the poison of his teaching the people entrusted to him, although he ought both to read and to hold fast that perverse questions, which do not advance salvation but strive toward the destruction of souls, should be avoided rather than pursued (Titus 3:9)?

### 3

But we must recall him, if we can, as he hastens toward precipices—or rather, now stands on the precipice from which he may fall—lest, if we do not come to his aid, we press him toward his ruin. [Note: In the Greek Royal manuscripts, after βοηθεῖν, “to help,” there is the addition ἢ μὴ, “or not,” undoubtedly taken from a marginal note in which a corrector indicated that the particle μὴ, “not,” was missing before the aforementioned verb. For this ἢ, “or,” corresponds to our “perhaps”; ancient correctors used that particle to mark readings which they preferred to the common text and regarded as better. Thus the corrector judged that the Greek should read τῷ μὴ βοηθεῖν, “by not helping,” and the Latin reading “if we do not come to his aid” confirms the correction.]

Christ our God, whose birth is being made the subject of dispute, taught us to labor for one sheep (Luke 15:5), wishing it to be brought back even upon his own shoulders, lest it be exposed to the ravenous wolf as prey. And he who taught us to run for the salvation of one sheep—how does he wish us to labor for the shepherd of the sheep himself, who, forgetting his office and his title, has himself changed into the rapacity of a wolf, desiring to destroy the flock which he ought to have guarded?

We must remove him from the sheepfolds if we cannot correct him as we wish. Let there be hope of pardon for one who corrects himself; for we prefer that he return and live, provided he does not himself destroy the life of those entrusted to him. [Note: The printed Greek has: “If there is still hope of pardon for one who would correct himself, he will be able to remain”; the words “we wish” are corrected from the manuscripts, which agree with the Latin reading and the sequence of the sentence.]

But let there be an open sentence against one who persists. [Note: The common editions have “let there be a certain sentence.” The Greek text requires “let there be an open sentence,” that is, let the sentence be pronounced openly and plainly, condemning him if he persists in error. This corresponds to Coelestine’s response and fully satisfies Cyril’s request. In Letter 8, section 7, Cyril had indicated that he had not yet openly withdrawn from communion with Nestorius but earnestly asked Coelestine to instruct him what he should do next.] For such a wound must be cut away, by which not one member is harmed but the whole body of the Church is wounded.

For what can he do with those who agree together, when he alone, thinking himself wise, disagrees with our faith? [Note: That is, with those who agree in the one faith. Coelestine alludes to Cyril’s words in Letter 8, section 5, from which he had learned that Nestorius departed from the common judgment of all the orthodox and considered himself wiser than everyone.]

Let those whom he himself removed from communion as resisting him remain in communion; and let him know that he cannot have our communion if he persists in this path of perversity, contrary to apostolic teaching.

### 4

Having therefore joined to you the authority of our see and acting in our place, you shall execute this sentence with strict firmness: either [Note: Thus the Navarre manuscript, supported by the Greek; Baluze reads “below.”], within ten days counted from the day of this summons, he shall condemn his perverse teachings in a written profession and affirm that he holds this faith concerning the birth of Christ our God which the Roman Church, the Church of Your Holiness, and the universal devotion hold; or, if he does not do this, Your Holiness, having immediately provided another shepherd for that Church, must know that he is to be removed in every way from our body. He refused to admit the care of those who were trying to heal him, and hastened wickedly toward the destruction both of himself and of all entrusted to him. [Note: It is therefore clear that the Greek should read κακῶς, “wickedly,” not κἀθως, as the Royal manuscripts report. This error seems to have occasioned the gloss found in the common Greek copies: “Like a pestilential disease, invading the whole body of the Church, it hastened to spread while being driven through it.”]

### 5

We have written the same things to our holy brothers and fellow bishops John, Rufus, Juvenal, and Flavian, so that our judgment concerning him—or rather, the divine judgment of our Christ—may be known. Given on the third day before the Ides of August [Note: August 11, in the year 430], in the consulship of Theodosius XIII and Valentinian III [Note: The manuscripts have “Valentinian VI.”].

[Col. 0460C] **Coelestine to his beloved brother Cyril.**

The letters sent by Your Holiness through our son Posidonius the deacon restored cheerfulness to our gloom, and we exchanged gladness for sorrow. For as we looked upon and considered what had been said by the man attempting to disturb the Church in Constantinople with distorted teachings, we were, in our very soul, struck with no small pain and tormented by various goads of thought, considering how help might be given so that the people would remain in the faith. [Note: The Royal manuscripts read βοηθηθῇς, “that you may be helped.” Perhaps the reading should be βοηθῇ τις, “that someone may help.”]

But when we turned our mind to what had been written by your brotherhood, there appeared to us immediately a most ready remedy by which the pestilential disease might be expelled through a wholesome medicine: namely, the outflow of a pure spring flowing from the speech of your charity, by which all the mud of the foully spreading stream would be cleansed [Note: One manuscript has καθαρεῖται, “is cleansed.” Perhaps καθαιρεῖται, “is removed,” should be read], and the manner of the proper understanding of our faith would be opened to all.

Therefore, just as we mark and reproach him, so we embrace Your Holiness with the Lord’s charity, as though you were present in your own letters, seeing that we hold one and the same opinion concerning the Master. [Note: The manuscripts read thus; the printed edition has εἰδότες, “knowing.”] Nor is it surprising that the Lord’s most provident priest should fight with such courage for love of the faith [Note: In Baluze: “by love and courage.” The Greek wording requires “by love, by this (or such) courage.”], so as to resist the senseless boldness of his opponents [Note: The printed editions add δύνασθαι, “being able”; the manuscripts do not] and strengthen those entrusted to him by such admonitions.
