As those things were bitter to us, so these are sweet; as those were muddy, so these are pure. And we rejoice to see such vigilance present in your reverence that you have already surpassed the examples of your predecessors, who themselves had always been champions of orthodox doctrine.

Truly the evangelical testimony applies to you, which says:

> “The good shepherd lays down his life for his own sheep.”

But just as you are a good shepherd, so he is not even worthy to be accused as a bad hireling: he is not accused because he abandoned his own sheep, but because he himself was found scattering them.

We also intended to add something, beloved brother, if we had not seen you holding all the same opinions as we do and had not tested you in the affirmation of the faith as its strongest champion. For everything that Your Holiness has written concerning this matter was reported to us in order through our son Posidonius the deacon.

You stripped bare all the nets of deceitful teaching and so fortified the faith that the heart of those who believe in Christ our God could not be drawn to another side. This is the great triumph of our faith: to have demonstrated our position so strongly and to have overcome the opposing arguments through the testimony of the divine Scriptures.

What, then, will he accomplish? Or where will he turn himself, this man who became a lover of impious innovation and, wishing rather to serve his own ideas than Christ, desired to injure the people entrusted to him with the poison of his own teaching? He ought both to read and to hold fast this principle: that vain inquiries, which do not advance toward health but proceed toward the destruction of souls, must be avoided rather than pursued. [Note: The manuscripts lack ἀσεβοῦς, “impious.”] [Note: The printed edition has “he was seen serving himself rather than following Christ”; this is corrected from the manuscripts.]

Nevertheless, as he hastens toward precipices—or rather, lives already on the very precipice from which he will fall—we ought, if we can, to call him back, lest by failing to help we push him toward his fall.

Christ our God, whose own birth is being made the subject of dispute, taught us to labor for one sheep, wishing to recall it even upon his own shoulders, lest it be exposed to the wolf for prey. Then how does he who taught us to run for the salvation of one sheep wish us to labor for the shepherd of the sheep himself? Having forgotten this title and office, he has transformed himself into the rapacity of a wolf [Note: The manuscripts read “into the rapacity of a wolf”; the printed editions read “into a ravening wolf.”], desiring to destroy the flock which he ought himself to have preserved.

We therefore ought to drive this man away from the enclosure of the lambs if we cannot correct him as we wish. Let there still be hope of pardon for one who corrects himself; for we wish him to return and live, provided he does not himself destroy the life of those entrusted to him. But let there be a clear sentence against the one who persists.

Such a wound must be cut away, by which not one member is harmed but the whole body of the Church is pierced. For what does he do among those who agree with one another, when he alone, thinking himself wise [Note: The common editions add ἄριστα, “most wisely”], disagrees with our faith? Therefore let those whom he himself removed from communion as opposing him remain in communion. And let him know that he cannot have our communion if he remains on this path of perversity, opposing apostolic teaching.

Since, then, the authority of our throne has been joined to you, and you are acting in the capacity of our representative [Note: The manuscripts have δοχῇ, “reception” or “acceptance”], you shall carry out this sentence with exact firmness: either, within ten days counted from the day of this memorandum, he shall reject his evil proclamations in a written profession and affirm that he holds this faith concerning the birth of Christ our God which the Church of the Romans, the Church of Your Holiness, and the universal devotion hold; or, if he does not do this, Your Holiness, having immediately provided for that Church, shall know that he must by every means be removed from our body. He refused to accept the healing of those who were treating him, and hastened wickedly toward the destruction both of himself and of all entrusted to him.

We have written the same things to our holy brothers and fellow bishops John, Rufus, Juvenal, and Flavian, so that our judgment concerning him—or rather, the divine judgment of our Christ—may be manifest.

## Letter XII

Coelestine explains how destructive Nestorius’s doctrine is. He states that he has excluded Nestorius and his supporters from communion with him, while admitting again to communion those whom Nestorius had most recently expelled. He urges the bishops named below to fight courageously for the Church and warns that Nestorius must be removed from communion with the Church unless, after being admonished, he condemns within ten days what he had preached.

[Note: The following Latin and Greek texts are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0465A] **Coelestine, bishop, to John, Juvenal, Rufus, and Flavian, bishops throughout the East, on equal terms (*a pari*).**

[Note: There appears to be a discrepancy between the Greek and Latin inscriptions of this letter, since the Greek is addressed to John alone, while the Latin is addressed to several others. The Latin is supported both by the deacon Liberatus, chapter 5, who identifies this letter of Coelestine as follows—“On the same matter [concerning Cyril] he likewise wrote to John of Antioch, Rufus of Thessalonica, Juvenal of Jerusalem, and Flavian, archbishop of Philippi”—and by Coelestine himself in Letter 11, section 5, where he says, “We also wrote to our holy brothers and fellow bishops John, Rufus, Juvenal, and Flavian.” Pope Nicholas I also supports this in Letter 8 to Michael, where he mentions this letter as having been written to the Eastern bishops.

Nevertheless, the whole context of the letter favors the Greek: Coelestine nowhere addresses several people but always directs his speech to one, and he uses “dearest brother,” not “dearest brothers,” and “your holiness,” not “your holinesses.”

There is also another disagreement between Cyril and the inscriptions of the two texts. Both texts attribute this letter to Coelestine, whereas Cyril attributes it to the synod. Cyril reconciles and resolves the first discrepancy in his letter to John of Antioch, where he addresses him as follows: “The Roman synod wrote also to your piety. It wrote likewise, *a pari* (τὰ ἴσα), to the most devout Rufus, bishop of Thessalonica, and to several other most religious bishops of Macedonia, who are accustomed always to support it. It nevertheless wrote to Juvenal, bishop of Jerusalem.”

For letters addressed equally to several persons were sent separately to each of those whose names they bore, in a similar copy inscribed with each individual’s own name. Hence the popes speak in them as though they were writing to one person; and when one such individual copy is found, it ought to bear the name of the one for whom it was intended. Therefore the fact that the Greek text of this letter is addressed to John alone indicates that only the copy sent to John was found and published.

Letters written by the Roman pontiffs after a synod had first been held could be attributed to the synod itself, although common custom and usage generally attributed them to the pontiffs personally. Accordingly, this letter is attributed both by Cyril to the Roman synod and by others to Coelestine.

It is also clear that Coelestine is now complying with Cyril’s wishes. In Letter 8, section 7, Cyril had entreated that Coelestine clearly explain his judgment concerning Nestorius’s doctrine both to the bishops of Macedonia and to the bishops of the East.

Moreover, the following statement of Gennadius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, properly refers to this letter of Coelestine: “Coelestine, bishop of the city of Rome, sent the decree of the synod [the Roman synod] to the Churches of the East and West, affirming that, while two natures remain perfectly in Christ, one person of the Son must be believed.” He affirmed this not indeed in these precise words, but insofar as he condemned Nestorius, who, as Gennadius immediately explains, was shown to oppose this doctrine.

As for the Latin text of this letter, we present the text which Stephen Baluze revised from four manuscripts and which we revised from the Navarre manuscript; Nicholas I consistently follows it.]

[Note: The expression *a pari* is omitted in the Navarre manuscript. Baluze supplied it from his manuscripts. He also notes that the expression signifies what Liberatus calls *pariter*, what Cyril in his letter to John of Antioch calls τὰ ἴσα, and what Marcellinus Mercator calls “similar and identical copies” in *Memorandum*, chapter 3. Therefore, Theodosius I’s statement in part 32 of the Council of Ephesus, γέγραπται γὰρ τὰ ἴσα παρὰ τῆς ἡμετέρας γαλήνης, was not badly translated by the ancient interpreter of the Council of Ephesus, published by Baluze in the new collection of councils, p. 454: “For it has been written *a pari* by our majesty.” From this, he also observes that the conjecture of Christian Lupus collapses: Lupus inferred that the bishop of Thessalonica had no authority over the bishop of Philippi, as though the expression *a pari* meant that one was the equal and peer of the other. The same conjecture is further refuted because, if it were valid, the bishop of Philippi would have to be regarded as no less the equal and peer of the bishop of Antioch than of the bishop of Thessalonica.]

### 1

We would wish that, just as the essence of God is one, so all people everywhere might hold one truth of the right faith. Nevertheless, our lament is lessened if those who separate themselves outside the Lord’s flock and hide in corners and secluded places persuade themselves, or a few who think with them, of their hidden error. [Note: The Greek text does not know the word “others.” The Latin would be clearer if rendered: “persuade themselves or the few who agree with them to accept a hidden error.” In the Greek of Labbe one reads: “They conceal themselves and advise one another, through certain foolish arguments, to agree with one another.” Our reading is that of the Royal manuscripts, except that one has ὁμονοεῖν, “to agree,” instead of ὁμονοοῦσιν, “who agree,” and it is more consistent with the old Latin text.]

But when someone set over the holy Church of God under the title of priest turns Christ’s own people away from the path of truth into the abyss of misguided persuasion [Note: The construction would be neater as “set over ... under the title of priest.” Further on, instead of “of misguided persuasion,” the Greek translator reads “by misguided persuasion.”]—and does so in a most distinguished city, to which, because of the reverence owed to the empire dwelling there, a multitude flows from the whole world—then our lament must plainly be doubled, and greater vigilance must be employed lest the rapacity of the approaching wolf prevail. [Note: Add “of the approaching wolf.”]

For there is less concern when an enemy besieges the wall than when he rages within the walls; and a wolf wandering outside the sheepfolds troubles and torments the mind less severely than one invading the place of the shepherd among the flock. [Note: Or: “There is less concern when the enemy besieges the wall than when he rages within it; and the wolf troubles and torments the mind less severely when wandering outside than when within.”]

For the war is more than civil when, within the Church—that is, within Christ’s own bridal chamber—the weapons of an impious sect are hurled. [Note: The Greek interpreter reads, “within the very house of God.”]

Hence our inmost being was deeply grieved because the man who appears to hold the Church of Constantinople is pouring into peoples most devoted to Christ certain perverse teachings against reverence for the Virgin’s childbirth and against the hope of our salvation.

These matters reached us through the pain of the faithful; they were published in the books which he himself had sent; and, what provides still greater proof, they were presented to us in letters bearing the author’s own signature [Note: Above, Letters 6 and 7], so that there can no longer be any doubt.

### 2

Since in matters of this kind prolonged inaction is not safe—for it is almost as much a crime to connive at such things as it is a wickedness to preach such sacrilege—we have excluded Bishop Nestorius, and anyone else who follows him in preaching these things, from our communion, until he condemns in a written profession the perversity which he began to teach and declares that he holds this faith concerning the Virgin’s childbirth—that is, concerning the salvation of the human race—which, according to apostolic teaching, the Roman, Alexandrian, and universal Catholic Church holds, venerates, and proclaims.

But if anyone, whether by Bishop Nestorius or by those who follow him, has been excommunicated or stripped of the dignity of bishop or cleric since they began to preach such things, it is clear that he both has remained and continues to remain in our communion; nor do we judge him removed. For no one could be removed by the sentence of one who had already shown himself to be deserving of removal. [Note: The Greek interpreter omits the word “bishop,” and shortly afterward, instead of “they began to preach,” reads “he began to preach.” Nevertheless, Nicholas I preserves the very words of the Latin reading in Letter 8 to Michael.]

### 3

We have judged it necessary to write these things to Your Holiness, dearest brother, so that, strengthened in the Lord and clothed with the breastplate of Christ, familiar to your heart, together with the shield of Catholic proclamation [Note: The Greek interpreter incorrectly reads “hope” instead of “shield”], you may defend the flocks of our Lord Jesus Christ from the wickedness of the most evil persuasion.

He was born and suffered for us; with the realms of the dead opened and death conquered, he rose again for us on the third day.

4. But just as we wrote to our holy brother and fellow bishop Cyril, the good defender of the catholic faith, let Your Holiness know that this sentence concerning the same Nestorius has been issued by us—or rather by Christ God—that either, within ten days reckoned from the day of this meeting, he condemn in a written declaration his sacrilegious teachings concerning Christ’s birth and profess that he follows the faith which the Roman, Alexandrian, and universal Church preserves; or, removed from the assembly of the bishops, he should understand that he has brought ruin upon himself.

[Note: [Col. 0469C] More plainly, in accordance with the Greek text: that he has himself been the author of his own destruction. Thus below, Epistle 15, Nestorius is said to perish through his own agency if he rejects the remedy for correction offered to him. Celestine transfers the entire odium of the excommunication to the accused.] 

But so that these decrees of ours might be carried out with greater diligence,

[Note: [Col. 0469C] Or, more exactly, “more earnestly.” The Greek interpreter seems to have read *studiosius perficerentur*, “might be carried out more diligently.”]

we wished our letters to Your Beloved to be conveyed with greater fidelity through our son Posidonius, deacon of the Alexandrian Church.

[Note: [Col. 0469C] The printed editions, with three manuscripts, read “to commend”; this is corrected from the Bellovac manuscript. Then it would be permissible to supply from the Greek: “May God keep you safe and sound.” Soon afterward, the manuscripts have “on the fourth Ides,” and, against the printed editions, “in the fourth consulship of Valentinian.”]

Written on the Ides of August.

[Note: [Col. 0469C] August 11, 430.]

In the consulship of Theodosius for the thirteenth time and Valentinian for the third.

[Col. 0466A] To the beloved brother John, Celestine.

We pray that, just as the essence of the Godhead is one, so among all human beings wherever they may be there might likewise be one truth of the right faith. Yet the groaning is less if certain people, separating themselves from the Lord’s flock and hiding in corners and shadowy places, advise themselves or even a few others and agree among themselves in their concealed error. But when, in the holy Church of God, the man appointed under the name of its priest turns Christ’s people away from the way of truth and toward precipices by unsound counsel—and does so in the greatest city, to which, out of reverence for the royal resident, a multitude gathers from the whole world—

[Note: [Col. 0466D] Thus the manuscripts and Labbe: “of the emperor” (*basileus*).]

then the mourning must plainly be doubled and the concern increased, lest the wolf’s seizure, once it has arrived, should prevail.

[Col. 0468A] For concern is less when the enemy is besieging from without than when he is raging within the walls; and the wolf wandering outside the flocks causes less trouble than when, having seized a shepherd’s place, he is inside the very flock. For it is worse than civil war when, inside the Church—that is, inside the very house of God—the spears of an impious religion are hurled. Hence our inward parts are deeply troubled, because this man, who appears to hold the Church of Constantinople, pours out distorted teachings upon Christ’s consecrated people, contrary both to the honor and reverence due to the birth of the holy Virgin and to the hope of our salvation.

These things came to light through the pain of the faithful, as became known from the books which he himself sent; and what provided still greater proof was that letters sent to us were fortified by the signature of their very author, so that it was impossible for others to cast doubt upon them.

[Note: [Col. 0467D] Read “further.”]

Therefore, since in matters of this kind prolonged delay is not safe—for to delay such things is almost as great a crime as it is an abomination to utter such sacrilegious statements—we separate Bishop Nestorius, and anyone else who follows him and speaks in this manner, from our communion until, by a written confession, he condemns the distortion which he began to teach and confesses that he himself holds the faith concerning the Virgin Birth—that is, concerning the salvation of the human race—which, according to apostolic teaching, the Roman, Alexandrian, and catholic Church everywhere holds,

[Note: [Col. 0467D] Read: “and worships and confesses.”]

worships, and confesses.

If anyone, whether from Nestorius or from those who followed him, has, since he began to speak such things, either been excluded from communion or stripped of the dignity of priest or cleric, it is acknowledged that this person both has remained in our communion and will remain in it henceforth; nor do we say that he has been removed, since the sentence of one who had already made himself liable to removal could not remove anyone.

Dearest brother, we have written these things to Your Holiness so that, strengthened in the Lord and clothed with the breastplate proper to your breast and with the hope of catholic confession, you may draw the flock of our Lord Jesus Christ away from the wicked and most shameful teaching—he who was born and suffered for us, and who, when the regions below had been opened and death conquered, rose again for us on the third day.

[Note: [Col. 0468D] In the Greek, “of the Church and of the faith.”]

Just as we also wrote to our most holy brother and fellow bishop Cyril, the exact defender of the catholic Church and faith, so let Your Holiness know that this sentence concerning the same Nestorius has been issued by us—or rather by Christ the Lord and God himself—that either, within ten days reckoned from the day on which he was admonished, he condemn in a written confession his sacrilegious teachings concerning Christ’s birth and confess that he follows that faith which the Roman, Alexandrian, and catholic Church preserves; or, removed from the council of bishops, he should understand that he has been harmed by a ruin of his own making.

[Col. 0470A] But so that these decisions pronounced by us might be carried out more earnestly, we wished our letters to be conveyed more faithfully to Your Disposition through our son Posidonius, deacon of the Alexandrian Church. May God preserve you in health, dearest brother.

[Note: [Col. 0469C] In the Roman edition, the Latin context is identified as having been copied from Cresconius. Navarreus and three other manuscripts mentioned by Baluzius present the same text. Liberatus, chapter 5, indicates its beginning as follows: “Pope Celestine of Rome wrote to Nestorius a letter of rebuke with exhortation and censure, because he ought not to have gone astray in the matter of whose ordination he had rejoiced.” Its beginning is: “For some days of our life.” The same letter is praised by Evagrius, book I, chapter 4, and by Photius, codex 15; according to what we shall see below, it was received by Nestorius on November 30. It was read in its entirety at the Council of Ephesus. Indeed, in act 1, when Juvenal of Jerusalem requested that the letters of the most holy and most reverend archbishop of the Romans, Celestine, which he had sent concerning the faith, should be read, the chief notary read them, as reported by Baluzius, p. 462: “Letter of the lord Celestine, bishop of Rome, to Nestorius. Celestine to his dearest brother Nestorius. For some days of our life, after the infamous and repeatedly condemned doctrine of Pelagius, etc.” We have established the Greek text according to the authority of the royal manuscripts.]

# LETTER XIII OF POPE CELESTINE I TO NESTORIUS

[Col. 0469]

He proves him guilty of impious innovation and deserving of anathema. He announces that, unless he recalls those whom he had unjustly expelled from the imperial city and openly condemns what he had impiously believed, he is to be separated from the communion of the Church after ten days.

[Note: [Col. 0469B] The following Latin and Greek texts are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0469B] Celestine to his dearest brother Nestorius.

## 1.

For some days of our life, after the infamous and repeatedly condemned doctrine of Pelagius and Coelestius, the catholic faith enjoyed peace, when East and West struck them and their followers with the weapon of a united judgment.

[Note: [Col. 0470C] The printed editions, agreeing with the Greek, read “the catholic faith had peace”; but the manuscripts of both this letter and the ancient interpretation of the Council of Ephesus oppose this reading.]

[Note: [Col. 0470C] The printed editions read “with weapons,” and Baron[ius], following the Roman edition, “of unity”; these readings are corrected from the manuscripts. The event now recalled occurred especially when the letter of Bishop Zosimus—which, to use the words of Marius Mercator, p. 138, is called the “Tractoria,” by which Coelestius and Pelagius were condemned and which was sent to Constantinople and throughout the world—was confirmed by the signatures of the holy Fathers.]

Finally, Atticus of holy memory, teacher of the catholic faith and successor, even to the blessed John, in these matters, pursued them in this way on behalf of the common king, so that they were not even allowed an opportunity to remain there.

[Note: [Col. 0470C] The Roman edition and Baronius read “for the common cause,” while the other books and the Greek oppose this. The common king is Christ, king of all, whose grace the Pelagians, to use the Apostle’s expression, were trying to nullify. Marius Mercator recounts Atticus’s resistance to them in the Commonitorium as follows: “Under Atticus, bishop of holy memory, Coelestius came to the city of Constantinople; when he was exposed in similar matters, by the great zeal of that holy man he was expelled from the aforesaid blessed city, with letters concerning his name sent to the bishops in Asia, Thessalonica, and Carthage.” For this reason Prosper also deserved to praise him in his poem Against the Ungrateful:

“What should I say, and why recount the care which in the great city

Constantinople the good priest Atticus, with learned speech,

undertook, refuting by the ancient faith the envoys

of the heretics, etc.”]

After his departure, our anxiety remained very great, as we wondered whether his successor would also succeed him in the faith, since it is difficult to maintain what is good, for opposites often follow one another in alternation. Nevertheless, after him we had holy Sisinnius, whom we had continuously [Note: [Col. 0470D] Since, as Socrates reports in book VII, chapter 28, he had not yet completed two years; Socrates also testifies in chapter 26 that he was everywhere highly renowned both for his piety and because he devoted himself to assisting the poor even beyond his means.] to fear losing, a colleague celebrated for simplicity and holiness, preaching the faith which he had found.

Simple holiness and holy simplicity had surely read that one must fear rather than be wise in one’s own eyes (Romans 11:20); and elsewhere, that one must not pursue things too lofty (Sirach 3:22); and again: “If anyone preaches anything other than what we have preached, let him be anathema” (Galatians 1:8–9).

But when he too was departing from the world, and our concern had extended as far as the Lord permitted it, the report of messengers who came gladdened our spirit; and it was soon confirmed by the report of the colleagues who had attended your ordination. They gave you as much testimony as was due to one who appeared to have been elected from elsewhere.

[Note: [Col. 0471D] That is, from another Church, namely Antioch. One should recall what Celestine himself prescribes concerning this matter in Epistle 4, section 7.]

You had lived with so great a reputation beforehand that a foreign city envied your own city for possessing you; now you are avoided with such horror that your own people see in others how they have been delivered.

[Note: [Col. 0471D] The Roman edition reads “in error,” Baronius “in terror,” while the other Latin books read “in horror.” The testimony to this horror is found in Cyril’s preceding letter, section 3. Moreover, the Greek interpreter appears to have read “you made yourself to be avoided” instead of “you made yourself to be avoided with horror.”]

## 2.

A short while ago we received your letters, to which we were able to give no reply immediately; for the message had to be translated into Latin.

[Note: [Col. 0471D] That is, more quickly, with only a brief interval.]

[Note: [Col. 0471D] The Greek text requires: “Although we did this late because of necessity”—that is, because an interpreter had previously been unavailable.]

Although we do so late, we have now received, through my son Posidonius the deacon, writings concerning you from my holy brother and fellow bishop Cyril, a most approved priest. They were such that we grieved that the testimony of those who had reported on your ordination had perished.

[Note: [Col. 0471D] The Greek text says more precisely that we were greatly grieved because the testimony of those who had reported concerning your ordination had been lost and vanished. It was not the testimony given by them that had perished, but the testimony given to Nestorius.]

For your good beginnings have, as far as we see, been followed by an evil outcome—good beginnings, I say, which had been so celebrated among us that, in replying to the report of the brethren, we made ourselves participants in their rejoicing.

[Note: [Col. 0472D] Or, as the Greek text says, “we showed ourselves to be participants.” Celestine’s reply, as well as the synodal report of the bishops concerning Nestorius’s ordination, is missing.]

But now, considering both the complaint of the aforesaid brother against you and, at last, your translated letters, which contain open blasphemy, we see that we must say what the Apostle said: “I wish that I could change my tone, because I am ashamed of you” (Galatians 4:20).

Indeed, I have changed it—unless the impious disputant recalls himself from his headlong course. For it is necessary that we remove the evil from among ourselves, as we are commanded.

We have therefore read the text of your letters, and those books which we received when my illustrious son Antiochus returned them. In these books you have been examined, caught, and held fast by us, because you were slipping through a certain excess of speech, while you wrapped truths in obscurities.

[Note: [Col. 0472D] Literally according to the Greek: “and again you confuse both things, either confessing what you denied or striving to deny what you confessed.” In his letters Nestorius first denies that Mary is the Mother of God; then he appears to confess what he had denied; and afterward he confuses both positions, arguing that since a created thing could not give birth to the uncreated Godhead, Mary did not give birth to God by giving birth to the Word made flesh.]

You again confuse both positions, either confessing what you denied or trying to deny what you confessed. But in your letters you have rendered an open judgment—not so much against our faith as against yourself—wishing to discuss the Word of God otherwise than the faith of all holds.

## 3.

Behold now to what judgment concerning you we are summoned; behold the benefits produced by your innovations. Since you were elected while unknown and are accused now that you are known, we must say with that teacher of the nations: “For we do not know what we ought to pray for as we should” (Romans 8:26).

Do not these words suit that Church which, following not personal knowledge of you but your reputation, passed over men whom it had proved for itself? The confidence of those who believed well of you has been imposed upon.

[Note: [Col. 0473D] The Greek more aptly has “for itself,” that is, men trained in its own bosom and service. Of such men the same pope says in Epistle 4, section 7: “Those must first be rejected, so that some from other Churches may deservedly be preferred”; and immediately adds: “Let each person enjoy the fruit of his own service in the Church in which he has spent his lifetime through every office.” Nestorius’s example seemed to commend the necessity of this decree; but that heretic displayed such an appearance of piety joined with eloquence that he might no less have deceived the Antiochene Church itself, in which he had served.] 

For who would have thought that a rapacious wolf was hidden inside the fold?

[Note: [Col. 0473D] The Greek reads: “inside the sheep’s skin, a rapacious wolf.”]

The same Apostle says: “There must even be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest” (1 Corinthians 11:19). Open your ears and listen to the words spoken by the same Apostle to Timothy (1 Timothy 6:20) or Titus (Titus 3:9). What else does he command in these passages than that they avoid profane novelties of speech? Such things advance toward impiety, and they have always produced thorns and thistles.

He says that he also asked Timothy (1 Timothy 1:3), while remaining at Ephesus, to charge certain people not to preach otherwise. The words of the prophet Jeremiah stand before my eyes: “Horrible things have been done upon the earth: the prophets prophesy iniquity” (Jeremiah 5:30).

Do you say that these matters pass you by as though unknown, or that, as though known, you despise them? If they pass you by as unknown, let it not be shameful to learn what is right, since it was not fearful for you to teach what is wrong. If you despise them as known, understand that you will be without excuse when he who always expects his profit from this holy investment through us demands an account from you for the talent entrusted to you (Matthew 25:26).

Consider what punishment awaits the man who hid what he had received, although he certainly restored intact what he had received.

[Note: [Col. 0474D] It would be clearer, and the Greek has it, “and yet the one who restored the whole.” The sequence of the sentence certainly rejects the particle “not.” This sentence, because of the repeated verb “had received,” has dropped out of the Royal manuscripts.]

From this clearly understand what and how great the danger is: that one may fail to return even what one has received. Will you say to our Lord, “Those whom you gave me, I guarded” (John 17:12), when we hear that his Church is being split into factions in this way?

With what conscience do you live, almost abandoned by everyone in this city? I had wished that they had been as cautious then as they are now, when they desire assistance. How did you come to direct words toward questions which it was blasphemous even to think?

[Note: [Col. 0474D] The Roman edition and Baronius read “what the blasphemy is,” against the manuscripts and the Greek. Earlier, instead of “I had wished that they,” we would prefer: “Would that they had then, when they elected you, been as cautious as they are now,” and so forth.]

Why should you, as bishop, preach these things to peoples whose reverence for the Virgin Birth is wounded by them? The purity of the ancient faith must not be disturbed by blasphemous words against God.

## 4.

Who has ever been judged undeserving of anathema if he adds to or subtracts from the faith? For what was fully and clearly handed down to us by the Apostles requires neither increase nor diminution.

We read in our books (Revelation 22:18) that nothing should be added and nothing taken away; for a great punishment binds both the one who adds and the one who subtracts. Hence we prepare the cautery and the knife, since wounds that deserve to be cut away must no longer be nursed.

We know certainly that greater vices are always healed by greater pain. Among the many things impiously preached by you which the universal Church rejects, we lament that words were removed from the creed handed down by the Apostles—words that promise us the hope of the whole of life and salvation.

[Note: [Col. 0475C] The words “handed down by the Apostles” escaped the Greek interpreter. From their side, the Roman editor noted that “Nestorius mutilated the Apostles’ Creed,” apparently without fully grasping Celestine’s meaning. The pope is complaining that Nestorius removed words which promise the hope of salvation by suppressing their natural meaning, not by literally erasing particular letters. The Apostles’ Creed first says, “And in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord,” and then adds, “Who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary.” Whoever denies that Mary is the Mother of God removes the latter words completely. For if she is not the Mother of God, neither can the Son of God, our Lord, be said to have been born from Mary; by these words we profess that he has God as Father and Mary as mother. Celestine’s successor Sixtus likewise writes in Epistle 5, section 3, that Nestorius’s inventions detract from the creed first handed down among the Apostles; and in Epistle 6, section 4, he sets out and explains his own view and that of his predecessor in these words: “For Nestorius preached that Christ was merely a man who had been born, removing the mystery of the Incarnation and emptying it—or rather attacking it—from which, according to the creed, both our faith and our salvation subsist.” This may be confirmed by the words of Acacius, bishop of Melitene, in act 1 of the Council of Ephesus, p. 493. He first speaks of Nestorius as one who had corrupted the divine Scriptures and adulterated even the teachings of the saints; then, to prove this, he adds: “For his letter, which was read shortly before, most clearly indicates that, after removing the expressions used in their creed concerning the only-begotten Son of God by the 318 Fathers and divine bishops, and attributing to the flesh alone what belongs to the mystery of that saving dispensation, he preached that a mere temple of God endured birth and death.” Thus he also falsely attributed this opinion to the divine Scriptures. In the letter cited, in which he asserts that this corruption of the Nicene Creed and of Sacred Scripture is most evident, it is clear that not the syllables of the words but their genuine meaning was removed, whether from the Nicene Creed or from divine Scripture. Acacius himself sufficiently explains his view of the matter in the words quoted.]

Why this happens is explained by your letters, about which there can be no doubt, since you yourself sent them—letters which we had not wished to reach our hands, lest we be compelled to judge concerning so great a kind of crime.

The brief statement of these letters has brought all the paths of your arguments to a close. You extended yourself more widely, went around through many winding paths, and nevertheless arrived by a different route, though late, at an impious conclusion.

We know what the man commanded who taught that disputes and quarrels about the law must be avoided, for he says that they are “useless and futile” (Titus 3:9). Therefore, no one doubts that what is judged futile and useless is in no way beneficial.

## 5.

Therefore, although our brother Cyril has already stated in his second letter that he has confronted you, I want you to understand that, after his first and second letter and after this correction of ours—which is plainly already the third—you are completely separated from the whole company and assembly of Christians, unless the things wrongly said are immediately corrected, unless you return to that way which Christ testifies that he himself is (John 14:6).

[Note: [Col. 0476C] Cyril complied with this and appended to Celestine’s letter his own letter, which is found in the Council of Ephesus, part I, chapter 26. He confronts and addresses Nestorius in these words: “Behold, therefore, together with the holy synod which assembled in the great city of Rome under the presidency of our most holy and most reverend brother and fellow minister, Bishop Celestine, we now admonish and beseech you for the third time by this letter,” and so forth. This practice rests upon the Lord’s command in Matthew 18:15, which prescribes how a brother is to be rebuked, as Celestine himself explains in Epistle 24, section 9. Julius Paulus explains the civil law concerning this matter in book V, title 5: “If, after being summoned by three letters or edicts, or by one serving for all, or by three notices, he does not come to the judge to whom notice was given, or by whose letter or edict he was summoned, the sentence pronounced against him as contumacious has the force of a judgment. Indeed, no appeal may be made from it.” The apostolic canon 73 concerning this matter is well known; it orders that an accused bishop who does not appear for judgment must first be summoned three times before sentence is pronounced against him. Celestine followed this legal prescription in such a way that he wished Cyril’s two letters to Nestorius—even though they had been written before Nestorius was referred to the Roman bishop—to count as the two admonitions. The urgency of the illness, as he says below in section 9, permitted no delay. Indeed, in accordance with the Lord’s prescription in Matthew 18:15, Celestine conducted himself in this matter.]

You have turned your weapons wickedly against the one who had previously allowed you to be established over his household as a faithful and prudent servant (Matthew 24:45). The blessedness promised to you for such an office has perished.

[Note: [Col. 0477D] Baluzius, together with the manuscripts, reads “the blessedness of this office”; other printed editions read “the blessedness in place of this office.” The Greek letter should simply be rendered: “The blessedness promised to you for such a ministry has perished.” Immediately afterward, instead of “he sought,” the Greek interpretation suggests reading “he acquired,” especially since the reference to Paul’s words in Acts 20:28 is clear. Hence below, in section 7, “sought” is suspected to stand for “acquired,” and this suspicion is confirmed by what follows, “to acquire the reward of confession.” Certainly, in all three places the Greek interpreter used the same word, κερδαίνειν, “to gain” or “acquire.”]

Not only do you fail to give food at the proper time, but you also kill with poison those whom he acquired by his own blood and death (Acts 20:29).

For poison is under your lips: we see that they are full of curse and bitterness, while you strive to argue against him who is sweet.

[Note: [Col. 0478D] Literally according to the Greek: “For those things which we see to be full of curse and bitterness are under your lips.”]

Where is pastoral diligence? “The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep,” but “the hireling abandons and hands them over to the wolves” (John 10:11).

[Note: [Col. 0478D] The manuscripts have this reading. The printed editions read, “the hireling is one who abandons them”; and below they read “you scatter” instead of “you tear apart.” Earlier, we would prefer “like wolves” rather than “for wolves.”]

What will you do here as a shepherd, when you yourself tear apart the Lord’s flock for the wolves? To what enclosures will the Lord’s flock flee if it is wounded within the sheepfolds of the Church? By what protection will the one who suffers you as a guardian, though you are a predator, be defended?

And elsewhere the Lord says: “I have other sheep which are not of this fold, and I must bring them also” (John 10:16). He promises to bring other sheep; but the sheep you had are perishing.

[Note: [Col. 0478D] The common editions have in Greek, “but you destroy those which he had.” The Greek found in the Royal manuscripts agrees with the Latin reading, except that it mistakenly has σὺ δέ instead of σοὶ δέ. The correction proposed here is confirmed by what follows.]

Yet it is certain that whenever such things occur, it is not the sheep who perish for the shepherds, but rather the shepherds who perish for the sheep. “And they will hear my voice,” he says (John 10:16). Why? “So that there may be one flock.” At his voice the flock becomes one; at yours it is either corrupted or driven away.

## 6.

It is grievous that the words of blessed Paul from the Acts of the Apostles should apply to you: “I know that after my departure savage wolves will enter among you, not sparing the flock. And from among your own selves men will arise speaking perverse things, to draw the disciples after themselves” (Acts 20:29–30).

We would wish these words had been spoken by you to others rather than applying to you. For you ought to have taught, not learned, the things we are saying. Who could endure teaching a bishop how he ought to be a Christian?

Look carefully at the condition to which you are summoned. You are attacked, reproved, accused; which of these is appropriate to a priest? To harsh words, a harsh reply—if indeed it is a reciprocal exchange—to avenge blasphemy with words.

Do you think that we ought to spare you, when you yourself do not spare your own soul, but wish to take away from everyone—past, present, and future—the benefit of salvation?

I shall certainly pursue the enemies of my good Lord as his faithful servant, since the Prophet declares that he hates them with perfect hatred (Psalm 138:22).

[Note: [Col. 0479D] The printed editions read “Remembering again”; this is corrected from the manuscripts and the Greek.]

Again I am warned, while another speaks, not to spare (1 Samuel 15:3). Whom shall I respect here? For whom shall I preserve any honor, when the issue is that the cause of all my hope is to be taken from me?

The Lord himself says in the Gospel that one must not prefer father, mother, children, or any other relationship to him (Matthew 10:37). For there is often a kind of piety from which impiety arises, when, with bodily affection prevailing, human affection is placed before that love which is God; because of it we often show deference to certain people.

[Note: [Col. 0479D] Baronius, following the Roman edition, reads “but when he comes to him.” The manuscripts more correctly read “but when one strives against him,” that is, when someone opposes him who is love itself; then, according to the Greek, those affections whose author is being called into question must also necessarily be rejected.]

But when the effort is directed against him who is love itself, it is necessary that even those affections whose author is being called into question be preserved no longer.

## 7.

Awaken at last, for these are not vigils that ought to be spoken of when you do not offer watchfulness but plunder. We would wish you to sleep in what you preach and keep watch in what you attack.

[Note: [Col. 0479D] The Greek supplies here: “But what am I saying?”]

We would certainly bear it more lightly if you slept in both.

No one would be lost to you, no one gained; the Church would grieve over no loss of souls and rejoice over no gain. It would be better for her if you surrendered her to her Bridegroom just as you had received her.

[Note: [Col. 0480D] Or, literally according to the Greek: “You would lose no one, you would acquire or gain no one”; the Church would grieve over the loss of no soul and rejoice over the gain of none; it would be enough for her if you surrendered her to her Bridegroom, etc. Celestine writes this because, as he will acknowledge below in Epistle 25, section 8, he knew that Nestorius was not idle or negligent in his pastoral office, but a man constant in speech. For this reason, in the same place he calls him a watchful destroyer.]

But why do I dwell on much? While the architect Paul speaks, I seek in vain for anything built up by you when I find no foundation (1 Corinthians 3:11).

I hear that clerics who think catholically and with whom we are in communion are enduring very great force, so much so that the city is even said to have been forbidden to them.

[Note: [Col. 0480D] The speech would be smoother in this order: “I hear that the clerics who think catholically and with whom we are in communion are enduring and suffering very great force.”]

We rejoice that they are acquiring the reward of confession, but we grieve that this is happening while the bishop persecutes them.

Blessed Paul changed from a persecutor into a preacher; it is the greatest impiety for a preacher to have been changed into a persecutor.

[Note: [Col. 0480D] The Greek reads: “He was changed from a persecutor into a preacher; but now it is the greatest impiety for one who was a preacher to have been changed into a persecutor.”]

List the heretics who have brought such questions into the Churches in their order.

[Note: [Col. 0480D] The Bellovac manuscript has “heretics.” “Heretics” should be retained; earlier we would prefer “review” or “enumerate” rather than “arrange in order.” Immediately afterward, Baluzius, together with the manuscripts, preferred “Churches” instead of “Church.”]

Who has ever returned victorious from such a contest? You certainly have an example in your own city. Paul of Samosata, having seized the Church of Antioch, gathered the harvest of his own seeds when he preached certain doctrines. The other inventors of evils, after occupying the Churches, were always expelled by the censure of a similar judgment.

## 8.

These heretics also, concerning whom you wished to consult us as though ignorant of what had happened, were expelled from their sees by a just condemnation because they spoke unjustly; we do not think it surprising that they found rest there, for they encountered an impious preaching by comparison with which they might consider themselves innocent.

Here, since the opportunity of the subject demands it, we cannot remain silent about what astonishes us. We read how well you hold the doctrine of original sin, how you assert that nature itself is indebted, and that the one who descends from the race of the debtor rightly pays the debt.

What, then, have those who were condemned for denying these things to do with you?

[Note: [Col. 0481C] The Greek reads: “Those who were condemned because they denied these things.”]

Things opposed to one another never come together without suspicion. They would have been expelled if they had likewise displeased you.

Why, then, are the actions once taken against these men now being investigated, when it is certain that what was done there was sent to us by Atticus, then the catholic bishop?

[Note: [Col. 0481C] Marius Mercator says in the Commonitorium that, after Coelestius had been expelled from the imperial city, Atticus immediately sent letters concerning his name to the bishops in Asia and Thessalonica, but he had said nothing about the fact that what had then taken place was also transmitted to Rome; Celestine now supplies this information.]

Why did Sisinnius of holy memory not investigate these matters? Because, under his predecessor, he had certainly approved that they had been justly condemned.

Let the wretched men mourn that they had been deceived by the hope placed in human beings,

[Note: [Col. 0481C] This alludes to the hope which Nestorius had given them. Although that heretic, as Marius Mercator explains in the preface to his edition of Nestorius’s treatises, Baluzius, p. 119, disagreed with the Pelagian opinions, he nevertheless decided to receive Julian, who had once been deprived of office and deposed by an apostolic sentence, into friendship for the time being, together with his associates. By promising the hope of acquittal, he also consoled Coelestius in his letters. The same author admits that he is uncertain with what intention Nestorius thought they should be encouraged and fed by the hope of a vain promise. When the aforementioned Mercator saw that this dissimulation of Nestorius threatened the faith with danger, in the year 429 he presented a Commonitorium to the emperor Theodosius. Once the disastrous error had been recognized, Julian, his follower, together with Coelestius’s other associates and participants, and afterward Coelestius himself, were expelled from Constantinople by imperial order and later condemned in the Council of Ephesus by the judgment of 275 bishops. These words plainly establish that they had been driven from Constantinople before the Council of Ephesus was held. Relying on the same evidence, Henry Noris, History of Pelagianism, book II, chapter 7, p. 204, thinks that they had been expelled before this letter of Celestine’s reached Constantinople. Yet this does not necessarily follow from Mercator’s statements, since he does not say that they were expelled from the imperial city immediately after he presented the Commonitorium. Indeed, it is certain that they had not yet been expelled when Nestorius sent Celestine his second letter, which was written long after the first. Nor is it obscure that Celestine did not know they had been expelled when he wrote this letter to Nestorius. For when he now says, “Let the wretched men mourn that they were deceived by the hope placed in human beings,” he does not say this because he knew that the Pelagians had been expelled from the imperial city by imperial order, but because he judged that the grace of acquittal, the hope of which Nestorius had given them, must be entirely denied them. Therefore, whether the emperor Theodosius ordered the Pelagians to be expelled from the imperial city before this letter of Celestine’s reached the East cannot be established with certainty from Mercator’s words.]

to whom only penance could now provide help for communion.

[Note: [Col. 0482C] The Greek reads: “They could be helped with regard to communion only through penance.” This is not unsuitable if understood to mean that, since they had lost both communion and dignity, only communion—not dignity—could be restored to them after repentance. Yet the Latin reading has no other meaning, and it is supported by Prosper, Against the Collator, chapter 21, section 58: “Celestine, knowing that for the condemned not the investigation of judgment but only the remedy of penance was to be offered,” and so forth. For ecclesiastical law had established that no one from among the penitents should be admitted to the clergy. The judgment of Innocent and Zosimus concerning Pelagius and Coelestius had already preceded this, as Augustine testifies in On Original Sin, chapter 22, and Epistle 190, section 22.]

Behold, you are beginning to learn about these matters, if previously you knew nothing of them.

9. Take care of your own case more than that of others, with Catholic and prompt deliberation, because we appropriately say, “Physician, heal yourself” (Luke 4:23), since you desire to help others. The nature of your illness neither accepts nor permits delay. We have approved, and do approve, the faith of the priest of the Alexandrian Church; and you, admonished by him, think again with us, if you wish to be with us. If you give your assent to this brother, condemning everything you have thought up to now, we wish you immediately to proclaim what you see him proclaiming.

[Note: [Col. 0482D] In Greek: “Your wound,” which fits better with what follows.]

[Note: [Col. 0482D] Thus Baluze, with the manuscripts. The Roman edition, however, reads: “You ought to think the same things again that we do”; and then: “If you wish, brother, to be with us.” If understanding is granted you, “having condemned” should be read; the latter agrees with the Greek.]

We even wish priests to be corrected contrary to what is proper; and just as we care for them through the preliminary admonition, so, if they abuse our salutary warning, it is necessary for us to confirm against them the sentence of condemnation. Yet this will be a full indication of correction, after the condemnation of the wicked doctrine:

[Note: [Col. 0483D] Greek: “After you have condemned the wicked doctrine.”]

if all those who plainly appear to have been excluded because of Christ, its head, are recalled to the Church; let them all be recalled.

[Note: [Col. 0483D] The words “let them all be recalled” seem superfluous; therefore they have been suppressed in Labbe’s Greek and Latin texts. Nevertheless they occur in the Roman edition and in ancient manuscripts of both languages, and they have a certain emphasis, by which Celestine indicates that he especially wishes what he commands. Earlier the Greek has: “whom it is manifest to have been excluded because of Christ.” Then, in the same Greek, “unless this is done” is more elegant than “which.” Soon afterward the Roman edition has “you will be recognized” instead of “it is recognized,” with the support of the Greek ὤφθης.]

If this which we say is not done, let the one who expelled them be expelled, even though those against whom he is recognized to have acted thus are in communion with us.

10. We have also sent letters to the clergy of the Church of Constantinople, and to all who are called by the Christian name, as necessity requires:

[Note: [Col. 0483D] Letter 14.]

so that, if you persist in perverse disputation and do not proclaim what our brother Cyril proclaims together with us, they may understand that you are separated from our fellowship, with whom you cannot have communion. They will know, having already been warned by this example, how they ought to provide for their souls with judgment that has been thoroughly considered and brought to maturity.

11. Know plainly, therefore, that this is our sentence: unless you proclaim concerning Christ our God what the Roman, Alexandrian, and universal Catholic Church maintains—as the most holy Church of the city of Constantinople also maintained perfectly up to your time—and unless, within ten days counted from the first day on which this warning becomes known to you, you condemn by an open and written confession this impious novelty which attempts to separate what Holy Scripture joins together, you are expelled from communion with the universal Catholic Church.

[Note: [Col. 0484C] The words “to you” are absent from the Roman edition.]

We have sent the form of our judgment to you, through my aforesaid son, the deacon Posidonius, together with all the documents, to my holy fellow-bishop, the bishop of the aforesaid city of Alexandria, who has reported to us more fully concerning this very matter, so that he may act in our place and make known to you and to all the brethren what we have determined; for all ought to know what is being done whenever the cause of all is under consideration.

And in another hand: May God keep you safe and sound, dearest brother.

[Note: [Col. 0484C] August 11, in the year 430.]

Given on the third day before the Ides of August, in the consulship of Theodosius XIII and Valentinian III, august emperors.

[Note: [Col. 0484C] Thus the Navarre manuscript, together with the Roman, Baronius’s, and Labbe’s editions. Baluze, however, with three manuscripts, prefers “the fourth day before the Ides.” The Roman edition then incorrectly has “in the fourteenth consulship of Theodosius.” Henry Noris, *History of Pelagianism*, book II, chapter 7, p. 204, observes that in the Palatine-Vatican codex there is a sermon of Nestorius with this heading: “Likewise, a sermon delivered in the church after he had received the letter of Celestine, bishop of Rome, and the denunciation of Cyril of Alexandria, on the eighth day before the Ides of December, in the consulship of Theodosius XIII and Valentinian III, august emperors, on the sixth day after he received the same letters.” When Stephen Baluze had this codex examined and found it to agree with the Bellovacense copy of Mercator, *New Collection of Councils*, p. 422, he pointed out that Garnerius, part 2, p. 84, should correct the heading of the same sermon, which reads: “A sermon delivered in the church in which he received Celestine’s letter on the seventh day before the Ides of December,” whereas it ought to retain: “after he received Celestine’s letter on the eighth day before the Ides.” From this note just mentioned we learn that this letter of Celestine to Nestorius was sent first to Cyril and then to Nestorius, and that Nestorius received it through Cyril’s agency, together with other letters of Cyril, on the last day of November in the year 430. Noris, in the place cited, joining “the eighth day before the Ides of December” with the following word “received,” rather than with the preceding “a sermon delivered in the church,” judged that the letter was received on December 6. But both the natural order of the sentence and, above all, the synodical letter of Cyril to Nestorius, which was received at the same time, suggest that the sermon itself was delivered there on December 6. That letter is marked in all manuscripts as having been dated on November 30, in the fourteenth indiction, as Stephen Baluze observed, *New Collection of Councils*, p. 422. There the word “dated,” as the same learned man remarked, designates not the time at which the letter was written but the time at which it was delivered to Nestorius, from which the ten days of delay were to be counted.]

[Col. 0470B] To the beloved brother Nestorius, Celestine.

After the impious and repeatedly condemned doctrine of Pelagius and Celestius, the Catholic faith enjoyed peace for some days of our life, when both East and West struck those men and their followers with a sentence of agreement, as with a spear. At once Atticus, of holy memory, teacher of the Catholic faith and truly the successor in this matter of the blessed John, persecuted them on behalf of the common emperor so thoroughly that they were not allowed any respite to remain there.

After his departure, we were deeply concerned, wondering whether the one who succeeded him would also be his successor in the faith.

[Note: [Col. 0470D] The Regius manuscripts omit ἐκδεχομένους, “expecting.”]

For it is difficult for good things to continue: often opposing forces succeed one another in turn. But after him we had the holy Sisinnius, who was soon to leave us, distinguished for his simplicity and associated with it, proclaiming the very faith that he had received. That simple reverence and reverent simplicity had learned that one ought rather to fear than to seek the depths of one’s own understanding; and elsewhere, that one ought not to investigate deeper matters; and again: “If anyone should proclaim and establish anything other than what we have proclaimed, let him be anathema.”

But when he too was taken from this world, and our concern had extended itself as far as the Lord permitted, the account brought by the angels who came to us gladdened our soul. It was immediately confirmed by the report of our fellow believers who had attended your ordination. They bore witness about you to the extent that was fitting for one chosen from another place.

You lived previously with such a reputation that even a foreign city envied your virtues. Now, however, you have prepared yourself to be avoided because of such grave impropriety that you may see your own people among strangers, and see how they have been driven away.

Recently we received your letters, to which we could not reply promptly, since the message had to be translated into Latin. While we were delayed in doing this because of necessity, we received from our holy brother and fellow-bishop Cyril, that most approved priest, through my son the deacon Posidonius, such letters concerning you that we were deeply grieved to find lost those who had brought us a favorable report about you. For, as we see, a bad outcome has followed your good beginnings. I call them good beginnings because they had been so highly praised among us that, in our reply to the report of the brethren, we showed how we shared their joy.

But now, considering both the criticism of you by the brother mentioned above and your letters once they had been translated—letters containing manifest blasphemies—we see that we must say what the Apostle said: “I would change my voice, because I am ashamed of you.” Rather, I would have changed it, unless the impious speaker should recall himself from the precipice; for it is necessary that, as we were commanded, we remove the evil from our midst.

We therefore read the style of your letters, and accepted the books as they were presented by my son, the most illustrious man Antiochus. In these matters, after you had been investigated, discovered, and apprehended, you slipped into a certain loquacity, concealing the truth with obscure expressions and again confusing both sides by acknowledging what had been denied while attempting to deny what had been acknowledged.

In your letters you made an open declaration, not so much concerning our faith as concerning yourself, wishing to proclaim something different about the Word of God from what the faith of all holds.

Behold now to what kind of judgment concerning you we are summoned. Behold the benefits produced by your innovations: when you were unknown, you were chosen; once known, you were accused.

[Note: [Col. 0473D] One Regius manuscript reads ἐπελέχθης, “you were chosen”; another has ὑπελέχθης, “you were selected.”]

Henceforth we must say with the teacher of the Gentiles: “For we do not know what we should pray for as we ought.”

Do not these words suit that Church which, despising men tested within it, followed your reputation rather than knowledge? The expectation of those who believed good things about you was deceived.

For who would think that a ravenous wolf lay hidden beneath a sheep’s wool? It is the voice of the Apostle himself that there must be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest. Open your ears, and hear this man’s words to Timothy and Titus. What else does he command except that they turn away from profane novelties of speech? For such things advance toward impiety and always produce thorns and thistles.

[Note: [Col. 0473D] The manuscripts have ἂν instead of ἀεί, “perhaps” instead of “always”; and shortly afterward ποιῇ, “produces,” not ποιεῖ, “produces.”]

He also says that he urged Timothy, so that, while remaining at Ephesus, he might command certain persons not to proclaim anything else.

The words of Jeremiah the prophet are before my eyes: “Fearful things have appeared upon the earth; the prophets prophesy injustice.” Tell me: do these things pass you by as though unknown to you, or do you despise them as though known? If they pass you by as unknown, do not be ashamed to learn what is right, since you were not afraid to teach what is distorted.

[Note: [Col. 0474D] The printed editions add μαθεῖν, “to learn,” here and καί, “also,” before διδάξαι, “to teach”; the manuscripts disagree.]

But if you despise them as things known, understand that you will have no defense when he demands an account from you for the talent entrusted to you—the one who, through us, continually expects to gain profit for himself from this holy loan.

See what punishment awaits the one who hid what he had received, and even more the one who did not restore in full what he had received. Therefore pay clear attention to how great and serious the danger is, lest you fail to return what you received.

Will you say to our Lord, “Those whom you gave me I guarded,” when we hear that his Church is being divided into parts in this way? With what conscience do you live, having been abandoned by nearly everyone in this city? I wished that they had then been made more secure than they are now, when they seek help for themselves.

From where did you obtain the right to direct speeches toward such questions—questions that it is blasphemous even to conceive? From where did a bishop obtain the right to proclaim such things to the people, through which reverence for the virgin birth is wounded? Blasphemous words ought not to disturb the purity of the ancient faith concerning God the Word.

[Col. 0476A] Who has ever been judged unworthy of anathema, whether by taking something away from the faith or by adding something to it? What the Apostles handed down to us fully and openly accepts neither addition nor diminution. We have read in our books that one must neither add nor subtract; for the greatest punishment binds both the one who adds and the one who takes away.

Therefore we prepare cautery and iron, since otherwise the wounds cannot be drained—wounds which now deserve amputation. For we know that the greatest defects are always healed with greater pain.

But among the many things which the universal Church rejects as impiously proclaimed by you, we especially mourn that you have spoken these words about the Creed, which promises us the hope of all life and salvation. Why this has happened is stated by your letters, about which there is no doubt, since you yourself sent them—letters which we would not have wished to come into our hands, lest we be compelled to judge concerning the form of so great an outrage.

The brief statement of those letters enclosed the paths of all your discussions. You spread yourself out more broadly and wandered through many turns; yet at last, by different routes, you reached the impious conclusion.

[Note: [Col. 0476C] One Regius manuscript has στροφαῖς προῆλθες, “you proceeded through turns”; another, στροφαῖς διῆλθες, “you passed through turns.”]

We know what that one commanded who ordered people to avoid disputes and quarrels about the Law: “They are useless and futile.” Therefore no one doubts that what is judged useless and futile is far from beneficial.

Therefore, even if brother Cyril says that he has already admonished you by a second letter, wishing you to understand this, after his first and second letters, and after this admonition of ours—which is plainly a third—you have been completely excluded from our assembly and from the council of Christians.

[Note: [Col. 0476C] Read: “I want you to understand this.”] Unless you immediately correct what you have wrongly said, unless you return to this path, which Christ testifies that he himself is, you will remain excluded.

You have wrongly taken up weapons against him in unexpected hostility, although he had previously appointed you over his servants as a faithful and prudent slave. The blessedness promised for such service has been lost to you. For you not only fail to provide food at the proper time, but destroy with poison those whom he won for himself by his own blood and his own death.

These things are poison beneath your lips; we see them filled with curses and bitterness whenever you attempt to speak against the one who is truly sweet.

Where is pastoral care? “The good shepherd lays down his life for his own sheep”; but he is a hireling who abandons and hands them over to wolves.

What will you do here, shepherd, since you yourself are scattering the Lord’s flock in place of wolves? To what enclosures can the Lord’s flock now flee, if it is wounded within the ecclesiastical boundaries?

[Note: [Col. 0478D] The printed editions read “within the courtyards,” corrected from the manuscripts.]

Or by what vigilance will it be safe, when you suffer yourself to be a ravager instead of a guardian? “I have other sheep,” says the Lord, “which are not from this fold; those too I must bring in.” He promises to bring in other sheep, while those whom you had are being destroyed.

Although it is especially clear that whenever these things happen, it is not the sheep who destroy the shepherds, but rather the shepherds who destroy the sheep. “They will hear my voice,” he says. Why? “So that there may be one flock.” At his voice one flock is formed; at yours it is harmed or driven away.

It is harsh that the words of blessed Paul from the Acts of the Apostles should fit you: “I know that after my departure fierce wolves will enter among you, not sparing the flock. From among you men will arise speaking perverse things, to draw the disciples after them.” We wished these things to have been spoken by you to others, rather than to you by us; for you ought to have taught them, not learned them from us.

Who can endure teaching a bishop how he ought to be a Christian? Pay careful attention to what kind of heresy you have been called to. You provoke, slander, and accuse. Which of these is fitting for a priest? To the harsh, a harsh reply is appropriate, if there is any defense at all: to punish blasphemous things with words.

Do you suppose that we will spare you, when you yourself do not spare your own soul, since you wish to deprive everyone—those who have gone before, those who are present, and those who are to come—of the benefit of salvation?

I persecute, as a faithful servant, the enemies of my good Lord, since the prophet says that they are to be hated with perfect hatred. I am reminded again of another speaker, so that I may not spare you. To whom should I pay attention here? To whom should I preserve honor, when I see this being done so that the foundation of all hope may be removed from me?

These are the words of the Lord himself in the Gospel: neither father, nor mother, nor children, nor any relation ought to be preferred to him. For there is often a kind of piety from which impiety is born, when, with affection according to the flesh prevailing, bodily love is preferred to that love which is God. Through the former we often honor certain people. But when it is directed against him who is love itself, it is necessary to cast out those thoughts whose originator is summoned to judgment.

[Note: [Col. 0479D] Read εὐνοίας, “goodwill” or “affection,” instead of ἐννοίας, “thoughts.”]

Wake up, at last. We should not call these “watchings” which you devote not to guarding but to ravaging. We wanted you to sleep in what you proclaim and to remain awake concerning what you attack.

But what am I saying? It would have been more bearable for us if you had slept in both matters. You would have destroyed no one and gained no one; the Church would have grieved over no loss of souls and rejoiced over no gain. It would have been enough for her if you had preserved and handed her over to her own Bridegroom just as you had received her.

But why do I delay over many matters? When the master-builder Paul says, I seek in vain something built up through you, since I see no foundation in you.

I hear that the clergy who hold Catholic views, with whom we are in communion, are enduring the greatest violence, so that they are said even to have been shut out from the city. We rejoice that they have gained the reward of their confession; but we grieve that a bishop is the persecutor.

The blessed Apostle Paul was changed from a persecutor into a preacher. But now it is the greatest impiety for someone to have been changed from a preacher into a persecutor.

Count the heretics of former times who brought such disputes upon the Church. Who ever withdrew victorious from such a quarrel? You have an example in your own city. Paul of Samosata, having taken possession of the Church of Antioch, gathered in the harvest of his own seeds while he proclaimed his doctrine. The same firmness of judgment always overthrew the other inventors of evils when they seized the churches.

But these heretics too, about whom you wished to question us as though we were ignorant of their deeds, were expelled by a just condemnation from their own thrones as men speaking unjustly. We do not wonder that they found rest there; they found an impious proclamation when, by comparing themselves with others, they thought themselves free from guilt.

Since the occasion for speaking demanded it, we cannot be silent about what amazes us. We have read how correctly you believe concerning sin according to descent, and how you show that nature itself is burdened with debt, and that he who descends from the race of the debtor should justly pay the debt.

What do those who were condemned do with you, since they denied these things? Opposing claims never agree securely with one another.

[Note: [Col. 0481C] The Regius manuscripts omit ἀνυπόπτως, “without suspicion” or “securely.”]

Yet they were expelled, even if they displeased you in the same way. Nevertheless, why do you now seek the proceedings carried out against them, when it is clear that the records were sent from there to us by Atticus, then bishop of the Catholic Church? Why did the holy Sisinnius not seek them? Clearly because he judged that they had been rightly condemned by his predecessor.

[Note: [Col. 0482C] The manuscripts read κεκρίσθαι, “to have been judged.”]

Let the wretched men who have fallen from human hope weep; they were able to receive help only for communion through repentance. Behold, you are beginning to learn about them, if previously you knew nothing.

But care for your own wound more than that of others, with Catholic and prompt deliberation, because we appropriately say, “Physician, heal yourself,” since you are considering how to help others. The nature of your illness neither accepts nor permits delay.

[Note: [Col. 0482D] In Greek: “Your wound,” which fits better with what follows.]

We have held, and continue to hold, the faith of the priest of the Alexandrian Church to be approved. And you, reminded through him, think again the same things as we do, if you wish to be with us, brother. If understanding has been granted to you, condemn everything you have thought until now and immediately proclaim what you see him himself proclaiming.

We even tolerate priests being corrected contrary to what is proper; but just as we first take care of them through admonition, so, if they abuse our sound warning, it is necessary for us to confirm against them the sentence of condemnation.

[Note: [Col. 0483D] One Regius manuscript has “ourselves.”]

But this will be a full testimony of correction, after you have condemned the evil teaching, if all those whom it is evident were excluded because of Christ, who is the head of the Church, are recalled to the Church. Let them all be recalled. If what we say is not done, the one who expelled them must be expelled, even though those against whom he was shown to have acted thus are in our communion.

[Note: [Col. 0483D] The manuscripts read “of consciousness” instead of “of testimony.”]

We also sent letters to the clergy of the Church in Constantinople and to all who bear the name of Christ, as necessity demanded, so that, if you continue in your adherence to perverse disputation and do not proclaim what brother Cyril proclaims with us, they may learn that you have been separated from our assembly, with whom you cannot have communion. They will also know this and, being henceforth made secure by the example, will understand how they ought to care for their own souls with judgment that has been thoroughly considered and brought to maturity.

[Note: [Col. 0483D] The manuscripts read “which” instead of “and, being.”]

Know plainly, therefore, that this is our judgment: unless you proclaim concerning Christ our God what the Roman, Alexandrian, and entire Catholic Church holds—as the holy Church of the great city of Constantinople also held perfectly up to your time—and unless you reject, by an open and written confession within ten days counted from the day of this warning, this unbelieving novelty which attempts to separate what Holy Scripture joins together, you are expelled from all communion with the Catholic Church.

[Note: [Col. 0483D] The manuscripts do not contain “from all.”]

We have sent this form of our judgment concerning you, through our aforesaid son, the deacon Posidonius, together with all the documents, to my holy fellow-bishop, the priest of the aforesaid Alexandria, who reported this very matter to us in greater detail, so that he might carry this out in our place and make known to you and to all the brethren what has been determined by us; for all ought to know what is being done whenever the matter under consideration is a common one.

[Note: [Col. 0484C] The manuscripts read “as our representative.”]

[Note: [Col. 0485D] In the Roman edition this is noted as having been copied from Cresconius in Latin. That Latin text, now published after being cleansed of very many errors, was established by Stephen Baluze from three manuscripts and most recently by us from the Navarre manuscript. Nicholas I used the same text in letters 8, 40, and 43. We have revised the Greek copied from part I, chapter 19, of the Council of Ephesus against two royal manuscripts. The deacon Liberatus summarizes the whole letter in chapter 5 as follows: “He also wrote to the clergy of Constantinople, admonishing them to stand firmly against the teaching of Nestorius and to endure his persecutions patiently, for these bring the fruits of crowns; and to know that those excommunicated or expelled by him remain in communion with the Apostolic See.”]

EPISTLE XIV OF POPE CELESTINE I TO THE CLERGY AND PEOPLE OF CONSTANTINOPLE

[Col. 0485]

[Col. 0485] He exhorts the people to persevere steadfastly in the doctrine handed down to them by their ancestors and to reject the new impieties of Nestorius; and he exhorts the clergy to fight bravely for the faith against him, to bear hardships patiently, and not to fear exile. He declares invalid the sentence by which Nestorius had expelled certain persons either from their office or from communion. He announces that he has entrusted his authority to Cyril. At the end he appends the form of the sentence issued against Nestorius.

[Note: [Col. 0485A] The following Latin and Greek texts are printed in parallel in Migne.]
