[Col. 0485A] Celestine, bishop, sends greetings in the Lord to the priests, deacons, clerics, servants of God, and Catholic people residing in Constantinople, his most beloved brothers.

1. Since I am about to speak to those who constitute the Church of God, let the apostolic utterance provide the beginning of my speech, so that the holy disciples may first hear the words of that teacher who preached to the Gentiles: “Besides those things which are external,” he says, “there is my daily pressure, the concern for all the churches” (2 Corinthians 11:28). And again: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not burning?” (ibid., 29).

Thus we too, although far away, when we learned that our members were being torn apart by the perversity of false teaching, burned with a fire not our own, while paternal concern was consuming us on your behalf. Yet among the churches of God, which everywhere are understood as united in the one bridal chamber of Christ, nothing is far away and nothing is considered foreign.

Since, therefore, you are our very inward parts, we rightly trembled, lest the insinuation of an evil teacher turn your faith—which is proclaimed everywhere—from the path of truth. For Nestorius, the bishop, as though he had forgotten the reverence due to Christ and the common salvation of all, proclaims, concerning the virgin birth and the divinity of Christ, God our Savior, abominable teachings that must be shunned. This has been disclosed both by his writings, sent to us by him with his own signature, and by the report of our holy brother and fellow-bishop Cyril, sent to me through my son, the deacon Posidonius.

After examining all these things, we found a great and avoidable perversity in his impious preaching. For he investigates the human and divine nature in our Christ, sometimes assigning to him merely humanity and sometimes associating him with God, whenever he deigns to do so.

[Note: [Col. 0486D] Since the Greek verb ἀνακρίνει properly means “to investigate” or “to conduct an inquiry,” this passage could appropriately be rendered in Latin as: “For he investigates the human and divine nature in Christ, now asserting him to be merely human, now joining him to God whenever he deigns to do so.” This interpretation is supported by section 2: “Your faith ought to reject impious disputation,” and by section 3: “Whoever disputes otherwise concerning our God.” The same verb, however, is used in the same way below, in section 4. Nor should it be denied that, when speaking of the impiety of Nestorius, Celestine is very familiar with the verb “to investigate”; in particular, in letter 18, section 3, he reproaches him because his rashness investigates the one who will investigate all.]

But we cannot, as Jeremiah says, listen to the empty speeches of such prophets (Jeremiah 23:16). Let him also hear Ezekiel and recognize what threatens him: “I will stretch out my hand against the prophets who see falsehoods and speak vanities; they shall not be in the discipline of my people, nor shall they be written in the writing of the house of Israel, nor shall they enter the land of Israel, because they have deceived my people” (Ezekiel 13:9–10).

Where is the shepherd’s proper care for the holy flock? Where is concern for the Lord’s enclosures? What hope can the flock have when the shepherd himself shows himself to be a wolf and attacks the sheep so that he may rage against each one? They are torn by the very mouth from which impious words are uttered. Food is supplied that does not restore but harms.

[Note: [Col. 0487D] Greek: “Not food that fattens and makes them strong, but food that weakens them.”]

Yet blessed is the flock to which the Lord has granted the ability to judge its pastures.

[Col. 0487B] 2. Therefore, just as we do not doubt that you are acting, your faith ought to reject impious disputation, so that, while you keep watch in Christ, there may be a clear distinction among you between food and poison. Remain in the things which you have learned through the teaching of your earlier shepherds, knowing that until now you have had priests distinguished by instruction and holiness, who, never departing from the traditions of their fathers, governed the Lord’s Church in the greatest peace.

[Note: [Col. 0487D] This passage reveals a translator clinging too closely to the Greek. He would have avoided ambiguity and obscurity by rendering it: “while you keep watch in Christ.”]

To begin with the more recent ones, what did the instruction of the bishop John, of holy memory, not pour into your minds? His discourse, establishing the Catholic faith, has spread throughout the world. He was never absent through his teaching, because wherever he was read, he preached.

[Col. 0488D] His successor Atticus was celebrated for the constancy of his diligent prudence.

[Note: [Col. 0488D] That is, the successor received this man, commended by diligence and devotion, with distinguished constancy.]

For Bishop Atticus, of holy memory, governed the Christian people according to the example of his predecessor and persecuted the sacrilegious madness of the heretics. When he died, we had as our colleague Sisinnius, of blessed memory, who knew what glory would remain for him if he preserved whole and undefiled the ornaments of the Catholic faith that had come down to him.

[Note: [Col. 0488D] Greek: “How much glory would remain for him.”]

We understood that he lacked neither the simplicity of the dove nor the prudence of the serpent.

[Note: [Col. 0488D] The Roman edition has “cunning” instead of “prudence.”]

We wept, dearest brothers, as though foreseeing the future, because we were soon deprived of his protection.

3. For in this man, who disputes otherwise concerning our God than God himself spoke concerning himself and than the Apostles handed down concerning him, I do not know what hope we can find. He does not merely fail to bind up the crushed but crushes those who have been bound; he not only fails to lift up those who have fallen but attempts to strike down those who stand; he not only fails to gather what has been scattered but scatters what has been gathered.

Yet a mind devoted to God cannot be crushed, nor can one who stands by heavenly strength be struck down, nor can the holy multitude be scattered.

We therefore announce openly to your love what we cannot say without tears. Your disputant has stirred up battle against the truth; he has laid hands upon the ancient faith. He attacks the Apostles, rejects the prophets, and does not follow the words of our Lord himself, who spoke concerning himself.

By what religious principle, or by what laws, does he call himself a bishop while abusing both the Old and the New Testament? He rejects the meaning of the figure and does not accept the truth that has lived among us. Finally, he treats the mystery of Christ our God otherwise than the sacrament of our faith permits—a mystery which every Catholic teacher has followed with reverence.

No one truly devoted to religion thinks anything about Christ other than what Christ himself wished to be thought about him.

Paul of Samosata once stirred up a sacrilegious question when he presided over the holy Church at Antioch; but the united judgment of Catholic priests cast him down from the throne over which he presided so disastrously.

Such men must always be cut off: by disturbing the minds of the Christian people and overturning the Gospels according to their own will, they cannot bear fruit for God. The vineyard must be cultivated which acknowledges the right of its owner.

4. It is certain, however, that such novelties of speech arise from a love of empty glory. When some wish to appear clever, perceptive, and wise, they seek something new to put forward, by which they may gain among inexperienced minds a temporary reputation for acumen.

But who has ever obtained true glory while appearing wise to himself? For our God chose the weak things of the world against the strong, and by the foolish things of the world he confounds the wise (1 Corinthians 1:27).

[Note: [Col. 0490D] The Roman edition reads, “to confound the strong,” against Labbe, Baluze, and the manuscripts. According to the Greek it should read, “and from opposites he confounds the strong.” But the Greek translator, against Celestine’s meaning, rendered the Latin verb “confundit”—which in Latin is ambiguous and can mean either “mixes together” or “covers with shame”—not by the Apostle’s own word καταισχύνει, “covers with shame,” but by συγχέει, “mixes together.”]

Who would glory in the wisdom of the world except one who admits that he belongs to the world, except one who denies that he is a disciple of him who says that he is not of the world (John 17:16)? There is one glory: as the Apostle says, “Let the one who glories, glory in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 1:31).

Do we not see this judgment applying to your bishop—but still your bishop, unless he believes what we believe?—“He became foolish when he said he was wise” (Romans 1:22). For it is avowed foolishness not to know him whom we know to be the wisdom and power of God (1 Corinthians 1:24). By investigating these things, he confesses that he does not know them.

[Note: [Col. 0490D] Or: “the things which he calls into question.”]

Nor should your love be surprised that he has strayed from the way of truth, since he has lost Christ, who is our way (John 14:6).

We sometimes detect him exposing himself through an erroneous argument, and sometimes hiding in certain tunnels while concealing his poisons. Although we ought, following the judgment of the most prudent Solomon, to give no answer to his folly, lest we become like him (Proverbs 26:4), nevertheless we urge him to follow the Apostles and the prophets with us, lest, when he alone opposes all, he alone be rejected by all.

But you must keep more vigilant watch, so that you may resist the enemy’s preaching. Your concern is greater when things contrary to the Church are spoken within the Church. Let those whom the adversary attacks from outside have some respite from labor, since they are dispersed around the fortifications and protect themselves by the defense of the walls.

[Note: [Col. 0491D] Greek: “Around the fortifications.” The Roman edition then reads, “They rely on the defense of the walls.” It does not understand the breaks available to those who have an enemy within, and is corrupt.]

But they do not know any rest when the enemy is inside. In this internal war, in this domestic battle, let faith be your wall, and let it defend itself against impiety with spiritual weapons. Let us preserve it, because, when preserved, it guards us. Through it God is our strength and refuge (Psalm 70:3–4).

[Note: [Col. 0491D] Labbe, following the Roman edition, has “refuge from the hand,” omitting the verb “he snatches away,” which is restored from the manuscripts and the Greek. A more polished order of words would be: “He snatches him from the hand of the sinner.”]

To you, placed amid the waves, it is fitting to say: “Lord, save us; we are perishing” (Matthew 8:25).

5. Now our speech must turn to you, clergy, and to all who are devoted to the Lord. Someone may perhaps say that the order has not been preserved. We too first wished to speak with you about what reason demanded, but greater concern for those whom we wished to preserve together prevailed.

For we ought not to doubt you, since we believe that, as leaders, you stand for the faith on behalf of those others.

[Note: [Col. 0491D] Greek: “In the faith.” This passage deserves notice: although Celestine, prudence dictating, addressed the people before the clergy, he wished to excuse this, openly admitting that the dignity of the clergy would have required another order, unless the pious necessity of circumstances had compelled him to alter it.]

The report of my holy and God-beloved brother and fellow-bishop Cyril, sent to me through my son, the deacon Posidonius, says that things are being done against you which one who did not spare the head of the Church could do against its members.

[Note: [Col. 0492D] Baluze, with the manuscripts, reads “what is being done concerning you.” It would be more pleasing to follow the Greek here and read “he has informed us” rather than “he speaks.”]

Do not let these things torment you. The greater the labor, the greater the glory, because the quality of the contest determines the quality of the reward. For you read with us that “the one who competes lawfully will be crowned” (2 Timothy 2:5).

Therefore our exhortation is owed to you, and it is necessary both for the fainthearted and for those who resist manfully: so that those who cannot endure the trials may be enabled to bear them, and those who are fighting may be able to stand more firmly.

[Note: [Col. 0492D] We would prefer: “those who cannot, because of the weakness of their souls.”]

The weapons of our King are never defeated. Every trial is a test for the Christian, since, as we read, it produces endurance (Romans 5:4–5). From endurance arises hope, which, as Scripture promises, puts no one to shame.

Therefore, dearest brothers, since your consolation is from God, to whom you present your bodies—that is, yourselves—as sacrifices, as the Apostle says (Romans 12:1), do not cease resisting.

[Note: [Col. 0492D] That is: “Do not cease resisting and standing firm.” This passage reflects the Greek phrase somewhat too closely.]

He gives strength—the one who, admonishing us through the Apostle (Romans 6:13), wishes our members to be weapons of his righteousness.

[Col. 0493A] You have the examples of the saints, who once sowed in tears and will later reap in joy (Psalm 125:5). Our Lord does not love a servant unless he has been tested by experience.

[Note: [Col. 0493D] From the Greek one might translate: “tested in trial,” which is more appropriate here.]

The Christian soul is always exercised in the arena of life. Run, so that you may pass one another along the ways of the Lord. I do not want you to be seized by adversaries.

[Note: [Col. 0493D] Labbe has “to be seized,” although the Apostle says that it ought to be so, as we see. The reading of the other manuscripts should be retained. Celestine refers to the Apostle’s statement, also recalled in the preceding letter to Nestorius, section 3: “There must also be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest.”]

The Apostle says that what we see must exist (1 Corinthians 11:19). The field reveals strength and faith. It is difficult to be crowned in idleness; rewards are awarded only for labors. I do not want you to lay aside the helmet of salvation from your heads; I do not want one who professes to be a worthy soldier of Christ to strip off the breastplate of faith.

[Col. 0493B] 6. Our own people have made war against us—if they are to be called our own, whom we see to have crossed over to the enemy after breaking the bond of friendship.

It is your part to have steady feet in the courts of Jerusalem (Psalm 121:2). We want your steps to be perfect, so that no one’s footsteps may ever move according to a similar example. Let those follow the devil along with evil who recognize that they belong to him.

[Note: [Col. 0493D] Baluze has “the devil” here, as in the manuscripts, but the Greek text shows that the word was rashly added.]

But you, who appear to be sons of God by your works, since he wishes each person to be known by his fruits (Matthew 7:16, 20), console one another and support the weak, strengthening them. Do not let impiety deceive you; according to the nature of good and evil, hold to a judgment, avoiding what is perverse and praising what is right.

For, as Solomon says, whoever regards the just as unjust or the unjust as just is an abomination to God (Proverbs 17:15).

No temporal tribulation exists if an eternal reward stands before one’s eyes—a reward to which nothing ought to be preferred.

[Note: [Col. 0494D] From Baluze and the manuscripts the particle “if,” omitted in other books, is restored. Therefore we prefer the Greek ἂν, “if,” with one royal manuscript, rather than ἀλλά, “but,” with the others. Earlier the Greek has “there is nothing,” that is, “it is counted as nothing,” instead of “there is no tribulation.”]

Our hymn-singer cries out that, even if camps should encamp against him, he need not fear at all because of hope in that illumination (Psalm 26:3).

If you were engaged in battle with foreign peoples, it would certainly be a great victory to overcome those whom you had always held as enemies.

[Note: [Col. 0494D] Read “whom you had,” rather than “whom you always had.”]

How great a victory must be declared when a priest, having changed his preaching, has become the persecutor of Catholics! Paul, in particular, thought in every respect against this man: he had previously persecuted the Lord’s Gospel but afterward became its preacher.

The impious disputant was abandoned by the Holy Spirit after he adopted a position contrary to the Spirit himself.

[Note: [Col. 0494D] The Roman edition has “abandoned by the holy Spirit,” without the preposition. The Greek has “by the divine Spirit.” The same edition soon afterward reads “against the Spirit himself.” Other books more correctly have “into the Spirit himself.” From this, and from the Greek κατ’ αὐτοῦ rather than καὶ αὐτοῦ, it may be conjectured that the meaning is: “after he himself too adopted a position contrary to the divine Spirit.”]

Rightly, if he persists, he will hear from us the words of Samuel, which the priest himself once spoke to Saul: “The Lord rejects you, so that you may not reign over Israel” (1 Samuel 15:23).

If Saul deserved this because, in carrying out his affairs, he merely despised God’s commands, what punishment will be owed to this man, who has risen up against the Lord of majesty himself?

[Note: [Col. 0495D] In the standard Greek reading: εἰ ἐκεῖνος ἀνάξιος, “if he was unworthy,” which can be accepted by supplying the honor of kingship. But, preferring ἄξιος, “worthy,” with the royal manuscripts, since the Latin text agrees with them, we understand that the words “to be rejected by God” are implied.]

It is now your task to care for whatever wound he has inflicted and to provide medicine for those wounded by his words. Stand firmly in the footsteps of the one whom, as his speech shows, we see to have already fallen.

Whatever he has brought upon you, endure patiently. Has he imposed insults? Has he imposed exiles? The one whom he refuses to acknowledge as having taken humanity for our sake endured these things among his own people.

[Note: [Col. 0495D] Baluze, with the manuscripts, reads “wisely.” The Roman edition has “he introduced insults.”]

Therefore let no one lament whatever he has attempted to do against some of you.

### 7

Let Stephen, the first witness of Christ, be for you a model of patience and steadfastness. The crowd of unbelievers roared against him as he preached; yet Christ’s worthy companion did not remain silent about what he saw. He cried out among the maddened, among the enemies of religion, declaring that he saw the heavens opened and the Son of Man—for whose sake he was suffering such things—standing at the right hand of God.

It would take too long to proceed through all those who purchased life either by death or by confession. You who have been expelled from the Church have, almost within our own times, the example of Athanasius, of blessed memory, that most discerning priest of the Church of Alexandria. Whom would his endurance not console? Whom would his courage not instruct? In whom would his eagerly desired return not kindle hope?

[Note: In Epistle 43 of Nicholas I to the people of Soissons, where this entire passage is copied, the unexpected reading is found; but an older Colbert manuscript of the same letter also has the expected reading. The Greek word properly means “most greatly desired.” There is, however, reason to suspect that, in the old manner, *exspectata* was written for *spectata*, that is, “distinguished and glorious.”]

He was expelled while Arius pursued him, but was to be recalled while the Lord advanced his cause. He endured imprisonment; he endured hardships.

[Note: Athanasius is not recorded as having endured any prison, unless one calls a prison the hiding-place in which he concealed himself while fleeing Valens’s persecution.]

And is it surprising that an apostolic man endured the things by which the Apostle boasts that he was trained? Yet in all these things he followed him who testifies that he is well pleased with himself in tribulations. After being driven from there, he was restored in our regions.

[Note: Thus the manuscripts, with Baluzius. This reading corresponds to the Greek word *anektisato* (ἀνεκτίσατο), or, in the common editions, *anektesato* (ἀνεκτήσατο). But the Roman and Labbe editions, as also Nicholas I, read “he was strengthened.” Baluzius then preferred “Finally, from here,” although the Colbert, Tours, and Navarre manuscripts oppose it. Yet both the preceding “in our regions,” rather than “from our regions,” and the following “in this see,” rather than “from this see,” recommend “here,” rather than “from here.” No one is ignorant how Pope Julius aided Athanasius.]

Finally, his position was reestablished here, and in this see he found the rest of communion, from which assistance is always born for Catholics.

[Note: Nicholas I cites this passage in Epistle 40.]

Yet he did not feel weariness in tribulations, he who became a confessor during persecution. Therefore no Christian ought to mourn the temporary exile inflicted upon him, because none of them is exiled from God. Rather, let us fear that we may be exiled from the land of the living—that is, from the place which we wish to be our homeland. That is what is ours; that is perpetual; that is eternal. For that is not ours which is merely passed through; but those things are truly ours which the most certain hope promises.

The Apostle says that these are the things “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the human heart—those things which God has prepared for those who love him” (I Cor. II, 9).

Yet, so that the sentence of the man who had already provoked the divine judgment against himself might not seem effective even for a time, the authority of our see openly decreed that no bishop, cleric, or Christian of any profession who, from the time when Nestorius or those like him began to preach such things, had been removed from his own place or from communion, should be regarded as removed or excommunicated. All these persons both have been and remain in our communion to this day, because no one could depose or remove a person who, while preaching such things, was himself wavering.

[Note: Greek: “who, by firmly preaching such things, himself had not stood”—that is, had not stood firm in the teaching and faith of the Church. Nicholas I, Epistle 8 to Michael, copies the preceding words as far as this point and nowhere departs from the Latin reading.]

### 8

The present discourse therefore embraces everyone together, so that, strengthened more and more and made confident in the Lord, you may not be shaken, but rather may heal one another’s weaknesses.

For already we commend the sick to you there, where we see the physician himself seeming to be sick, although we nevertheless wish, if we still can, to help him. When we sent suitable replies to our holy brother and fellow bishop Cyril, we also transmitted to you, through his deacon Posidonius, our dearest son, the writings which we sent from that same brother of mine to the man in question.

[Note: The words “to you,” and subsequently “these things,” and “to the man in question,” are absent from the Roman edition. By means of them Coelestine indicates that he sent both this letter and the preceding one to Cyril, so that through Cyril’s agency this letter might be transmitted to the Constantinopolitans and the other to Nestorius.]

And because in so great a matter our personal presence seemed almost necessary, on account of the distances by sea and land we delegated our place to my holy brother Cyril, lest this disease should worsen through the delay occasioned by distance.

[Note: That is: the long distances by sea and land prevent me from easily going there myself.]

Keep the apostolic writings before your eyes, and be perfected in the same understanding and in the same judgment (I Cor. I, 10), so that, as we read, by persevering to the end you may be able to be saved (Matt. X, 22).

But so that you may know under what definition we sent the letter, we have appended to this letter the very sentence which we pronounced against him, so that you may recognize the formula issued concerning him.

[Note: Greek: “We sent to the man about whom we are speaking the very sentence which we pronounced against Nestorius and appended it to this letter,” and so forth.]

May God preserve you unharmed, dearest brothers.

Given on the third day before the Ides of August, in the consulship of Theodosius XIII and Valentinian III.

[Note: August 11, A.D. 430. Baluzius reads “the fourth day before the Ides”; the Roman edition lacks this chronological note.]

### 9

Recognize clearly, therefore, that this is our sentence: unless you explain concerning Christ our God those things which the Roman, Alexandrian, and universal Church hold, just as the holy Church of Constantinople also understood them up to you, dearest brother, in accordance with the faith set forth at the Council of Nicaea; and unless you separate this faithless innovation from the adored and venerable Scripture, and condemn it in an open and written profession within ten days counted from the day on which notice of this proceeding is made known to you, know that you have been excommunicated from the whole Catholic Church.

[Note: In the Roman and Labbe editions the same formula is expressed differently: “Recognize openly, therefore, that this is our sentence: unless you preach concerning Christ our God what the Roman, Alexandrian, and universal Church, and the holy Church of Constantinople, has held most rightly up to your time, in accordance with the faith set forth at the Council of Nicaea; and unless, within ten days counted from the first day on which this summons becomes known to you, you renounce and condemn in an open written profession this faithless novelty by which you endeavor to separate what venerable Scripture joins, know that you have been cast out of the communion of the universal Catholic Church and are wholly unfit for anything belonging to priestly authority.” This version was taken not from the manuscripts from which the preceding text was copied, but from Epistle 13, with a later clause added. Yet, although the Greek and Latin texts have here been printed on the authority of ancient manuscripts, both must be acknowledged to be purer in the preceding letter.]

[Note: The sense requires: “Know that you have been excommunicated.” If nothing has been rashly added to the Greek text, one should supply here: “and incapable of every function belonging to priestly authority.” This supplement is lacking not only in Latin but also in Greek in the preceding letter. It is nevertheless supported by Cyril’s declaration of Coelestine’s sentence to Nestorius, where he addresses him as follows: “If your Reverence does not do this within the fixed period stated in the letter of the most holy and reverend bishop and fellow minister of the Romans, Coelestine, know that you yourself have no share with us, nor any place among the priests and bishops of God.”]

## Coelestine, Bishop, to the Priests, Deacons, Clergy, Servants of God, and All the Catholic People Residing in Constantinople, Beloved Brothers in the Lord, Greeting

When I speak to those who constitute the Church of God, may the apostolic word provide an introduction, so that the devout disciples may first hear the words of that teacher who preached to the nations: “Apart from the things that are outside, my daily burden is the concern for all the churches.” And again: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I am not on fire?”

So also we, although we are far away, since we have learned that our members here are being scattered by a perversion of teaching, have been set aflame by another’s fire, our paternal concern burning for you. Yet what could be far away or regarded as foreign among the churches of God, which everywhere are referred to one bridal chamber of Christ? Since you are therefore our members, we were rightly anxious, lest the persistence of the one who teaches wrongly should turn your faith, proclaimed everywhere, away from the path of truth.

For Bishop Nestorius, having forgotten the virgin birth, the divinity of Christ our God and Savior, his worship, and the common salvation of all, preaches things contrary to law and advises things that must be avoided. This was shown both by his writings sent to us under his own signature and by the report of my holy brother and fellow bishop Cyril, sent to me through my son Posidonius the deacon. When all these writings had been read, we found a most serious and reprehensible perversion in his impious preaching.

For he distinguishes the human nature and the divine nature in Christ, at one time attaching to him only the designation “man,” and at another attributing to him a participation in God whenever he deems this appropriate. But we, as Jeremiah says, cannot listen to the empty words of such prophets.

Let him hear Ezekiel and recognize what threatens him: “I will stretch out my hand against the prophets who see false visions and speak empty things. They shall not be among the deliberations of my people, nor shall they be written in the record of the house of Israel; they shall not enter the land of Israel, because they deceived my people.”

[Note: One of the Regius manuscripts reads *machaira* (μάχαιρα), “sword.” Read *cheira* (χεῖρα), “hand.”]

Where is the shepherd’s required care for the sacred flock? Where is his providence for the Lord’s fold? What hope will the flock have when the shepherd shows himself to be a wolf and thus attacks the sheep, raging against each one? They are scattered by the very mouth from which impious things are uttered. Foods are set before them—not those which make them fat, but those which make them thin. Yet blessed is the flock to which the Lord has granted judgment concerning its own pasture.

Therefore your faith, which we do not doubt is doing so, ought to reject the impious discourse, so that among you, who are watchful in Christ, the difference between food and poison may be evident, and so that you may remain with those teachings which you have learned from the words of the earlier shepherds.

You know that until the present you have had priests distinguished both in teaching and in holiness, men who, never departing from the traditions of the fathers, governed the Church of the Lord with the greatest tranquillity. To begin with those of more recent times: what did the instruction of John, the bishop of holy memory, not instill in your souls? His word spread throughout the whole world, building up the Catholic faith. He was nowhere absent from teaching; wherever he was read, he preached.

His diligent understanding was succeeded by a renowned steadfastness. The bishop Atticus, also of holy memory, governed the Christian people according to the example of his predecessor and drove away the sacrilegious madness of the heretics. After Atticus had passed away, we received as his associate Sisinnius, of holy memory, who knew how much glory would remain to him if he preserved whole and unharmed the ornaments of the Catholic faith that had endured up to that time.

We perceived that he possessed both the simplicity of a dove and the prudence of a serpent. We wept, beloved brothers, as though foreseeing what was to come: that we would soon be deprived of his assistance.

For in this man, who understands our God differently from what he himself has handed down concerning himself or what the apostles have handed down concerning him, I do not know what hope we shall find. He not only does not bind up the broken, but also breaks those who have been bound; he not only does not raise the fallen, but attempts to cast down those who are standing; he not only does not gather what has been scattered, but divides what has been gathered.

Yet a mind devoted to God cannot be broken; one standing by heavenly power cannot be cast down; nor can the sacred multitude be divided. Nevertheless, we plainly announce to your love what we cannot say without tears.

Your dialectician has stirred up war against the truth; he has raised his hands against the ancient faith; he wars against the apostles; he expels the prophets; and he does not follow the words by which our Lord himself spoke concerning himself.

By what religion, or by what laws, does he call himself a bishop, after making the New and Old Testaments of no account? He casts out the spiritual meaning of the form and refuses to accept the truth that circulates among us. In short, he speaks of the mystery of Christ our God differently from what the holiness of our faith tolerates—the faith which everyone who speaks as a Catholic has followed with reverence.

For no one properly devoted to religion has ever thought differently about Christ from what Christ himself wished to be thought about him.

[Note: The Regius manuscripts read *ekdedemenos* (ἐκδεδεμένος), “bound” or “devoted,” at “properly devoted to religion.”]

Paul of Samosata once stirred up a sacrilegious controversy when he presided over the holy Church at Antioch. But a united judgment of the Catholic priests deposed him from the throne on which he had wickedly sat.

For such men must always be cut off decisively: they disturb the soul of the Christian people and twist the Gospels according to their own opinion, and therefore cannot bear fruit for God. The vine that acknowledges the justice of its owner must be cultivated.

It is clear that such innovations in speech arise from a vain love of glory. Some people wish to seem, in their own eyes, acute, perceptive, and wise. They search for something novel to offer, so that among uneducated minds they may carry away a temporary reputation for cleverness.

But which of them ever gained true glory by thinking himself wise? For our God chooses the weak things of the world and, by means of opposites, confounds the strong; he confounds the wise through the foolish things of the world.

Who boasts in the wisdom of the world unless he acknowledges himself to be of the world? Who does so unless he denies that he is a disciple of the one who said that he himself was not of the world? There is one glory: as the Apostle says, “Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord.”

Does this judgment not seem especially suited to your bishop—for the moment still your bishop, if he does not believe what we believe? He has become a fool who calls himself wise. For it is acknowledged folly to be ignorant of the one whom we know to be the wisdom and power of God. He admits that he does not know the very things which he judges.

[Note: At “Does this judgment not seem,” the Regius manuscripts read *oun* (οὖν), “therefore.”]

Nor should your love be surprised that he has wandered from the path of truth, seeing that he has lost Christ, who is our way.

[Note: At “Nor should your love be surprised,” the Regius manuscripts read *thrausē* (θραύσῃ), “be broken.”]

At times we have caught him betraying Christ through a crooked argument; at times hiding him along certain concealed paths and sheltering his own poisons. Yet we ought to follow the judgment of the wisest Solomon and give no answer to his folly, lest we become like him. We advise him to follow with us the apostles and prophets, lest, by resisting everyone alone, he be expelled by everyone alone.

You, however, must keep watch with even greater care, so that you may resist the enemy’s preaching. Your concern is greater when, within the Church, things are said that attack the Church.

Let those who are provoked by the adversary living outside enjoy a respite from their labors; scattered around the outer defenses, they protect themselves by the support of the walls. But those who have the battle within know no rest.

Nevertheless, in this civil war, in this domestic conflict, let your faith be a wall for you; and against unbelief let faith itself avenge its cause with spiritual spears.

[Note: At “this domestic conflict,” the Regius manuscripts read *oikeiakē* (οἰκειάκῃ), “household.”]

Let us guard it, because when guarded it guards us. Through it God is our security and our refuge. He snatches us from the hand of the sinner.

[Note: Perhaps the text should read: “He to whom we ought to say,” removing the preceding stop.]

To him, while we lie amid the storm, it is fitting for us to say: “Lord, save us; we are perishing.”

Now our discourse must turn to you, clergy and all who are consecrated to God. Someone may perhaps say that the proper order has not been observed. We too wished earlier to speak to you, as the sequence required; but the greater concern for those whom we wished to save together prevailed.

For we ought not to doubt concerning you, under whose leadership we believe that those others are standing firm in the faith. The report of my holy and beloved brother and fellow bishop Cyril, which he sent to me through our son Posidonius, his deacon, has taught us that things have been done against you which one who does not spare even the head itself can do against the members of the Church.

But do not let these things distress you. Greater glory exists in greater labor, because the quality of the struggle produces the quality of the reward. Read with us that “the one who competes lawfully is crowned.”

Therefore our exhortation is owed to you, and it is necessary both for the fainthearted and for those who resist bravely: so that those who are unable may be able to endure trials, and those who resist may stand more firmly.

[Note: At “our exhortation,” one Regius manuscript reads *tropē* (τροπή), “turning,” and another *rhopē* (ῥοπή), “inclination.”]

The weapons of our King are never defeated. Every trial is a test for the Christian; for, as we have read, trial produces endurance.

[Note: At “trial produces endurance,” read: *houtos* (οὗτος), “this,” [lacuna], *hypomonēn* (ὑπομονήν), “endurance.”]

From endurance hope is born, and hope has deceived no one, as Scripture promises.

Therefore, beloved brothers, since your consolation comes from God, to whom you offer your bodies—that is, yourselves—as living sacrifices, as the Apostle says, do not grow weary in resisting.

He will provide strength who, through the Apostle, teaches us that our members are to be weapons of his own righteousness.

You have examples among the saints—those who once sowed in tears but later reaped in joy. Our Lord does not love a servant unless he has been tested in trial. The arena of events continually trains Christian souls.

Run, so that you may surpass one another on the roads of the Lord. I do not want you to be overtaken by your adversaries.

[Note: One of the Regius manuscripts adds *tou Kyriou* (τοῦ Κυρίου), “of the Lord,” after “adversaries.”]

The Apostle also says that what we see had to happen. Strength and faith are not tested unless there is a place for combat.

[Note: At “Strength and faith,” one manuscript reads *kai kopon* (καὶ κόπον), “and labor,” and another *kai topon* (καὶ τόπον), “and place.”]

It is difficult to be crowned in tranquillity; prizes are not given without labors. Let your heads not lay aside the helmet of salvation; let the soldier of Christ who claims to be worthy not remove the breastplate of faith.

### [Col. 0494B]

Our own people have begun war against us—if indeed those whom we have learned to have defected to the enemy, after the law of friendship was broken, ought still to be called our own.

[Note: The manuscripts read *philanthropias* (φιλανθρωπίας), “human kindness” or “benevolence,” at “the law of friendship.”]

It is your task to keep the feet of those who stand firm at the gates of Jerusalem. We want your steps to be sound, lest anyone’s footsteps ever be shaken by an equal example, and those who recognize themselves as belonging to that one follow the devil together with evil.

You, who show by your works that you are sons of God—for he wishes each person to be recognized by his fruits—console the minds of the fainthearted in turn, and receive each of the weak, confirming them.

[Note: One Regius manuscript adds *kai* (καί), “and,” after “sons of God”; Labbe reads *hekastos* (ἕκαστος), “each person.”]

Do not let impiety deceive you. Rather, retain judgment concerning good and evil according to the quality of each, fleeing what is distorted and praising what is upright. For the one who accepts the righteous in place of the unrighteous, or the unrighteous in place of the righteous, is to be rejected by God, as Solomon says.

Temporary affliction is nothing if the eternal reward is before our eyes, and nothing should be preferred to it. Our psalmist cries out that, even if war is arrayed against him, he will not be afraid at all because of his hope in that illumination.

If you had a struggle against the nations, it would clearly be a great victory to conquer those who have always been your enemies. But how great must that victory be called when a priest, after changing his preaching, has become a persecutor of the Catholics, thinking in every respect like Paul, who later became a herald of the Lord’s Gospel, though formerly he had persecuted it?

The impious dialectician has been abandoned by the divine Spirit, since he has thought contrary even to the divine Spirit itself. If he persists, he will rightly hear from us the words of Samuel that were then spoken by the priest himself to Saul: “The Lord will despise you, so that you shall not reign over Israel.”

If Saul deserved this because, only in the matters he carried out, he despised God’s commandments, what punishment will be owed to this man, who has raised himself against the Lord of divinity?

It is now your task to heal whatever wound he inflicted and to cure those who have been wounded by his words. Stand with firm steps against the one whom, as his own speech shows, we see already fallen. Whatever he has brought upon you, bear patiently.

Has he devised insults? Has he devised expulsions? He himself has suffered these things in his own case, though he denies that the one whom he refuses to acknowledge as having assumed humanity for our sake did so.

[Note: The reading “those things” is preferable.]

Therefore let no one mourn what he has contrived against any of you.

Our psalmist cries out that, even if war is arrayed against him, he will not be afraid at all because of his hope in that illumination.

If you had a struggle against the nations, it would clearly be a great victory to conquer those who have always been your enemies. But how great must that victory be called when a priest, after changing his preaching, has become a persecutor of the Catholics, thinking in every respect like Paul, who later became a herald of the Lord’s Gospel, though formerly he had persecuted it?

The impious dialectician has been abandoned by the divine Spirit, since he has thought contrary even to the divine Spirit itself. If he persists, he will rightly hear from us the words of Samuel that were then spoken by the priest himself to Saul: “The Lord will despise you, so that you shall not reign over Israel.”

If Saul deserved this because, only in the matters he carried out, he despised God’s commandments, what punishment will be owed to this man, who has raised himself against the Lord of divinity?

It is now your task to heal whatever wound he inflicted and to cure those who have been wounded by his words. Stand with firm steps against the one whom, as his own speech shows, we see already fallen. Whatever he has brought upon you, bear patiently.

Has he devised insults? Has he devised expulsions? He himself has suffered these things in his own case, though he denies that the one whom he refuses to acknowledge as having assumed humanity for our sake did so. Therefore let no one mourn what he has contrived against any of you.

Let Stephen, the first martyr of Christ, be a model of patience and endurance. The crowd of unbelievers roared against him; yet Christ’s companion did not remain silent about what he saw. He cried out among the madmen, among the enemies of religion, declaring that he saw the heavens opened and the Son of Man—for whose sake he was suffering such things—standing at the right hand of God.

It would take too long to proceed through each of those who purchased life either by death or by confession. You who have been expelled from the Church have, almost within our own times, the example of Athanasius, of blessed memory, that most learned priest of the Church of the Alexandrians.

Whom would his endurance not console? Whom would his courage not instruct? In whom would his greatly desired return not kindle hope?

He was expelled while Arius pursued him, but was to be recalled while the Lord advanced his cause. He endured imprisonment; he endured hardships. And is it surprising that an apostolic man endured the things by which the Apostle boasts that he was trained?

In all these things he followed him who testifies that he is well pleased with himself in tribulations. He was driven from there and was restored in our regions. Here his position was renewed, and in this throne he found the rest of communion, from which assistance is always born for Catholics.

Yet he did not feel pain in tribulations, he who became a confessor during persecution. Therefore no Christian ought to mourn the temporary exile inflicted upon him, because none of them is exiled from God.

Rather, let us fear that we may be exiled from the land of the living—that is, from the place which we wish to be our homeland. That is what is ours; that is perpetual; that is eternal. For that is not ours through which there is only passage; but these things are truly ours which the most secure hope promises.

The Apostle says: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart—these things God has prepared for those who love him.”

And so that this decision, which had already summoned divine judgment against himself, might not appear to be effective even temporarily, the authority of our see openly decreed that no bishop, cleric, or Christian of any profession who, from the time when Nestorius or those like him began to preach such things, had been removed either from his own place or from communion, should be regarded as having been removed or excommunicated.

All these persons both have been and remain in our communion to this day, because no one could depose or remove a person who, while preaching such things, had not stood firm.

The present discourse therefore embraces everyone together, so that, strengthened more and more and made confident in the Lord, you may not be shaken, but rather may heal one another’s weaknesses.

For already we commend the sick to you there, where we see the physician himself seeming to be sick, although we nevertheless wish, if we still can, to help him.

When we sent suitable replies to our holy brother and fellow bishop Cyril, we also sent to you through his deacon, the most beloved Posidonius, the writings which were to be sent by that same brother of mine to the man in question.

And because in so great a matter our personal presence seemed almost necessary, on account of the distances by sea and land we assigned our place to my holy brother Cyril, lest this disease should worsen through the delay occasioned by distance.

Keep the apostolic writings before your eyes, and become perfect in the same understanding and judgment, so that, as we have read, by persevering to the end you may be able to be saved.

But so that you may know under what condition we sent the written materials to the man about whom we are speaking, we appended to this letter the very sentence which we pronounced against Nestorius, so that you may know the formula issued concerning him.

May God preserve you in health, dearest brothers.

## The Sentence That Follows

Recognize clearly, therefore, that this is our sentence: unless you explain concerning Christ our God those things which the Roman, Alexandrian, and universal Church understand, just as the most blessed Church of Constantinople also understood them up to you, dearest one, in accordance with the faith set forth at the Council of Nicaea; and unless you separate this faithless innovation from the venerable and revered Scripture, and condemn it openly and in writing within ten days counted from the day on which these writings of this proceeding are made known to you, know that you yourself are excommunicated from the whole Catholic Church and rendered incapable of every function belonging to priestly authority.

[Note: The Regius manuscripts read “that you yourself are excommunicated.” The passage is expressed more clearly above in Epistle 13, section 11.]

[Note: Written in A.D. 430, toward the end of November. It was transmitted to us by Marius Mercator and is reproduced here from the editions prepared by Stephen Baluzius and John Garnerius, with both compared. He observed that a general synod is indeed mentioned in it, but that no mention is made of Coelestine’s letters sent through Cyril; consequently, those letters had not yet been delivered to Nestorius. Unless Nestorius concealed this fact, it follows that the letter was written between November 19 and November 30. The imperial decree of Theodosius convening the ecumenical synod is dated November 19; Nestorius received Coelestine’s letters on November 30 of the same month.]

## EPISTLE XV. NESTORIUS TO POPE COELESTINE

What Cyril, and what Nestorius himself, thinks concerning the terms *Theotokos* and *Christotokos*.

### Nestorius, Bishop of Constantinople, to Pope Coelestine

#### 1

I have learned that the most honorable Cyril, bishop of the city of Alexandria, terrified by the libels presented against him and seeking hiding places for himself in order to avoid the sacred synod that was to be held because of those very writings, has meanwhile devised other verbal arguments and embraced the term *Theotokos* and *Christotokos*. He admits the former, but at one time excludes the latter from the Gospels and at another again admits it—that is, *Christotokos*—according, I suppose, to a certain excess of prudence.

[Note: Baluzius reads this on the authority of the manuscripts. Garnerius reads “the words which are.”]

#### 2

As for the term *Theotokos*, unless it is uttered, according to the madness of Apollinaris and Arius, for the confusion of the natures, I do not resist those who wish to use it. Nevertheless, I do not doubt that the term *Theotokos* must yield to the term *Christotokos*, as terms delivered by angels and by the Evangelists.

[Note: Supply “as far as this term is concerned.” Otherwise, with Garnerius, one might read “and this term.”]

If I were not saying this to your Reverence, who already knows the matter, I would have to speak at length and in great detail about the subject itself.

#### 3

Even apart from this, it is in every way known to your Blessedness that, if we imagine two sects standing opposed to each other—one of which utters only the term *Theotokos*, while the other utters only *anthropotokos*—and if each sect draws the other toward its own confession, or, failing to achieve this, risks falling away from the Church, then the person appointed to deal with this disputed matter, caring for both sects, must heal the danger threatening both parties by means of the term handed down by the Gospels, a term that signifies both natures.

For, as I have said, the term *Christotokos* removes the assertion of those who maintain that Christ is merely a man, since it removes the blasphemy of Paul of Samosata; and it also drives away the wickedness of Arius and Apollinaris.

[Note: Garnerius supplies “to moderate” here and earlier reads “of those sects” instead of “of these.” By “these” one may understand those who belong to the sect asserting that Christ is merely a man. The passage will be complete if, after “the term,” we reject the word “removes” and read “as a mere man.” Garnerius unnecessarily supplies “blasphemy,” although he later retains the existing wording, even though grammar would require “which has been spoken.” Nestorius vainly claims that the term *Christotokos* removes the blasphemy of Paul of Samosata. Samosata did not deny that Mary gave birth to Christ; he was blasphemous because the Christ whom he confessed was, in his view, merely a man and not also God. John of Antioch, a friend of Nestorius, discusses the name *Theotokos* in a letter to Nestorius as follows: “If we do not accept what is offered by the meaning of this name, it remains that we fall into the gravest error, or rather that we deny the incomprehensible economy of the Only-Begotten God; for once this name has been removed, or rather once the meaning of this name has been rejected, it immediately follows that he is not God who undertook that wondrous dispensation for the sake of our salvation. Therefore the term cannot be rejected without immediately favoring the heresy of Samosata.” A little earlier the same John had written: “No ecclesiastical teacher ever rejected the name *Theotokos*. Those who used it are numerous and highly celebrated. Nor does the term *Christotokos* more effectively drive away the impiety of Arius or Apollinaris than that of Samosata, since neither of them denies that Mary is the mother of Christ.”]

#### 4

I have also written these very things to the most honorable bishop of the Alexandrians, as your Blessedness can learn from the copies which I have appended to this letter, or from those which he wrote to us.

It pleased God, with his help, also to summon an unavoidable synod of the whole world for the investigation of other ecclesiastical matters.

[Note: Garnerius adds “the most pious emperors.” Their decree summoning the bishops to the Council of Ephesus is found in Part I of the Acts of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 32.]

For I do not think that the investigation will have any difficulty because of uncertainty about the words, nor that this will be an impediment to the discussion of the divinity of the Lord Christ.

[Note: Garnerius attempted to repair the passage as follows: “The uncertainty … will not make the investigation difficult or impede the discussion.” Nestorius confirms what he had stated earlier, namely that the question of the two terms—whether *Christotokos* or *Theotokos* should be preferred—would present no difficulty and would not prevent Christ’s divinity from being discussed and affirmed.]

[Note: Written May 7, A.D. 431. Baron first published this letter, together with the following one, under the year 431. He had received them from Antonio de Aquino, who was then planning a supplement to the collection of papal letters. He would certainly have indicated where he had found them had he been able to complete the work. Since he died before doing so, the matter has remained unknown. Nevertheless, there seems little reason to doubt that they were extracted from some Latin copy of the Council of Ephesus, such as one preserved in the library of the Church of Beauvais. Among the documents collected by Lucas Holstenius, either as new materials or as collations with ancient codices, and judged worthy of publication, autograph copies are also found in the celebrated Barberini Library. Stephen Baluzius had both letters reprinted in his new collection of councils, pages 492 and 494, on the authority of the Beauvais manuscript. In this first letter there are notes that lead us to suspect that it was translated from Greek rather than copied from the authentic Latin.]

## EPISTLE XVI. COELESTINE I TO CYRIL, BISHOP OF ALEXANDRIA

Indulgence is to be offered to the sentence pronounced against Nestorius if he corrects himself; but if he remains obstinate, he is to be judged the author of his own destruction. Coelestine will treat with the greatest caution those whom Cyril regards with suspicion.

### Coelestine, Bishop, to Cyril, Bishop of Alexandria

#### 1

I understand that the judgment of the wisest Solomon has been fulfilled. For, no differently from one who thirsts for cold water, I have received from a distant land repeated news through the letters of your affection, which unite us by sharing our counsels.

The tranquillity of the churches and of the Catholic faith may confidently be hoped for when we see Christian princes laboring for it in this way. Royal concern is not ineffective, especially in divine matters; it concerns God, who faithfully holds the hearts of kings (Prov. XXI, 1).

Therefore we briefly return a reply to your Holiness.

#### 2

For you ask whether the holy synod ought to receive the man who condemns the things he previously preached, or whether, since the period of delay has elapsed, the sentence formerly issued should remain in force.

[Note: That is, whether it should receive Nestorius, provided that he condemns what he previously preached impiously. The phrasing has the odor of an interpreter clinging too closely to the Greek. The same is true of the unidiomatic “not with difficulty” above.]

Concerning both matters that you ask about, let us together consult our common Lord. Does he not immediately answer us through the prophet that he does not desire the death of the one who dies (Ezek. XVIII, 32), and through the Apostle Paul that he wishes everyone to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (I Tim. II, 4)?

Correction, whenever it occurs, is never displeasing to God when it is hastened. Let this be the task of your Holiness, together with the venerable counsel of the brothers: to suppress the disturbances that have arisen in the Church and, with God’s help, to learn that the matter has been concluded by a correction that fulfills our hopes.

#### 3

We do not say that we are absent from the assembly. For we cannot be absent from those whom, wherever they may be, one faith nevertheless joins to us.

I do not wish us to be judged by this bodily presence, whose weakness the Apostle identifies (II Cor. X, 10). We are there, in that we contemplate what is being done there on behalf of all; spiritually we do what we seem unable to do bodily.

[Note: Baron reads “Whatever is done there.” Baluzius’s reading is preferable: “because what is being done there.” Since the mind is the principal part of a human being and is distinguished from bodily things, a person is considered more truly to be where he is in mind than where he is bodily present.]

I am devoted to the tranquillity of the Catholic Church; I am devoted to the salvation of the one who is perishing, if only he is willing to confess his sickness. We say this so that we may not seem to be lacking, should he wish to correct himself.

For if, while we await the fruit, he adds thorns to himself, let the earlier decrees remain in force and let him be judged by the fruit of his own judgment. Let him gather what he sowed in a devilish furrow—not by our counsel, but as the author of his own destruction.

[Note: Coelestine continues to place the odium of excommunication upon those who are excommunicated, since they themselves are the authors of their destruction.]

Let him prove that we do not have feet swift to shed blood (Ps. XIII, 3), when he recognizes that a remedy has also been offered to him.

#### 4

As for those whom your Fraternity says you regard with suspicion concerning the Catholic faith, if they send writings, we must answer them according to the nature of the matters involved.

In this affair no one will secretly intervene so as to prevent the matter from being handled with complete caution.

[Note: Baron reads, “because the whole matter is handled with caution.” Baluzius’s reading is better: “indeed, it will be handled with complete caution.” That is, no one will succeed through secret intervention in preventing the matter from being handled with complete caution. This was said especially with John of Antioch and the other Syrian bishops in mind. They had taken offense at the twelve anathemas which Cyril had appended to his letter to Nestorius and had consequently suspected Cyril of Apollinarian heresy. In turn, Cyril himself had become suspect to them as a supporter and partisan of Nestorius. See Liberatus, chapter 4. John’s abhorrence of Nestorius’s arguments is made very clear in the letter he wrote to Nestorius.]

Given on the Nones of May, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Bassus and Antiochus.

## EPISTLE XVII, OR COMMONITORIUM OF POPE COELESTINE TO THE BISHOPS AND PRIESTS GOING TO THE EAST

[Col. 0503A]

### How They Are to Conduct Themselves at the Council of Ephesus, Whether It Has Not Yet Been Dissolved or Has Already Been Concluded

#### 1

When, as we believe and hope, with our God as author, your affection has reached the places assigned to you, direct all your counsel to our brother and fellow bishop Cyril, and whatever you see him decide, do it. We command that the authority of the apostolic see be preserved.

[Note: The same Veronese codex omits the conjunction “and” and punctuates the passage as follows: “Whatever you see in his judgment, you shall do. We command that the authority of the apostolic see be preserved.” This is preferable. Lupus likewise reads this, though he has “since the instructions.”]

For if the instructions delivered to you indicate that you ought to attend the assembly, then, if the matter proceeds to a debate, you should judge their opinions rather than enter into the contest.

[Note: The Veronese codex reads “you ought to judge,” which appears more correct.]

But if you see that the synod has been concluded and that all the bishops have returned, you must inquire how the matter was brought to an end.

[Note: Theodosius had ordered the metropolitans by letters to assemble at Ephesus on Pentecost itself, which in that year, 431, fell on May 7. Therefore, if the bishops had assembled on the appointed day, the synod could have been convened on the day before this Commonitorium was delivered and could have been dissolved before the legates arrived.]

If the matter was conducted in accordance with the ancient Catholic faith, and you learn that my holy brother Cyril has gone to Constantinople, you must go there so that you may present our letters to the emperor.

But if the matter was handled otherwise and the situation is one of dissension, you will be able to infer from the facts themselves what you ought to do with the counsel of the brother mentioned above.

[Note: A.D. 431, May 8.]

Given on the eighth day before the Ides of May, in the consulship of Bassus and Antiochus.

## NOTE ON THE FOLLOWING LETTER

#### 1

This letter was written in Latin. At the Council of Ephesus (Act 2, p. 611), in accordance with the custom that letters of the apostolic see should first be read in Latin, it was first read in Latin on the sixth day before the Ides of July and was then inserted into the official acts. At the insistence of the synod it was also recited in Greek, for the benefit of those who did not know Latin.

For this reason the legates had brought it translated into Greek. Peter Crabbe was the first to publish the first part of the Latin text. Subsequently the complete letter appeared in the Roman edition of papal letters, as though extracted from Cresconius—that is, from the Cresconian collection.

When Baron copied the whole letter from that source under the year 431, he prefaced it with the following criticism:

“It should be observed that these letters of Coelestine were written, according to Latin custom, in the Latin language, but are found translated into Greek and then restored from the Greek into Latin, not without serious damage to their genuine authenticity, as can sufficiently be understood from their divergence. Moreover, everyone sees that the older Latin copies must be followed; the oldest of all is supplied to us by the Cresconian collection, so that no suspicion of falsification can arise.”

It must indeed be admitted that the Greek wording of the same letter, as it has reached us, differs in many places very substantially from the authenticity of the Latin discourse. If this is the Greek translation which the legates presented to the Council of Ephesus, one may infer how rare at that time were people who possessed even a moderate command of both languages.

Nevertheless, it cannot be granted that the Latin copy which Baron had reprinted according to the Roman edition is altogether genuine. It is more like a stream that has here and there carried along with it some Greek corruptions than a pure spring.

The text published by Stephen Baluzius in his new collection of councils, page 490, is considerably purer and much sounder. It is preserved in the ancient manuscripts of Colbert, Tours, Beauvais, and Navarre, inserted into the ancient interpretation of the Council of Ephesus.

There seems no doubt that this is the very text which was recited before the synod and, by order of the synod itself, inserted into its acts.

[Additional textual apparatus for the Greek version: At “properly devoted to religion,” the Regius manuscripts read *ekdedemenos* (ἐκδεδεμένος), “bound” or “devoted.” At “Does this judgment not seem,” they read *oun* (οὖν), “therefore”; at “Nor should your love be surprised,” they read *thrausē* (θραύσῃ), “be broken.” At “this domestic conflict,” the Regius manuscripts read *oikeiakē* (οἰκειάκῃ), “household.” At “He snatches us from the hand of the sinner,” perhaps read: “He to whom we ought to say,” removing the preceding stop.]

[At “our exhortation,” one Regius manuscript reads *tropē* (τροπή), “turning,” and another *rhopē* (ῥοπή), “inclination.” At “trial produces endurance,” read: *houtos* (οὗτος), “this,” [lacuna], *hypomonēn* (ὑπομονήν), “endurance.” One Regius manuscript adds *tou Kyriou* (τοῦ Κυρίου), “of the Lord,” after “adversaries.” At “Strength and faith,” one manuscript reads *kai kopon* (καὶ κόπον), “and labor,” and another *kai topon* (καὶ τόπον), “and place.”]

[At “the law of friendship,” the manuscripts read *philanthropias* (φιλανθρωπίας), “human kindness” or “benevolence.” One Regius manuscript adds *kai* (καί), “and,” after “sons of God”; Labbe reads *hekastos* (ἕκαστος), “each person.” At “heal one another’s weaknesses,” read *tōn allōn* (τῶν ἄλλων), “the weaknesses of others.” At “even temporarily,” the edition reads *proschairos* (πρόσκαιρος), “temporary.” In the concluding sentence, the Regius manuscripts read *hēmetēran* (ἡμετέραν), “our,” and the passage is expressed more clearly above in Epistle 13, section 11.]

## 2

These letters of Celestine were received at Ephesus with the greatest veneration and with the loudest acclamation of the entire synod. For when they had been read aloud (Act 2, p. 618), all the most reverend bishops together acclaimed:

“This is a just judgment. The synod gives thanks to the new Paul, Celestine; to the new Paul, Cyril; to Celestine, guardian of the faith; to Celestine, in agreement with the synod; to Celestine, the universal synod gives thanks.”

Then, when Projectus, the legate of the Apostolic See, requested that the matters which Celestine had long ago determined and had now graciously recalled to their memory should be carried by order of the synod to a fully completed conclusion, Firmus, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, said:

“The Apostolic and holy See of the most holy bishop Celestine, by letters which it sent to the most religious bishops Cyril of Alexandria, Juvenal of Jerusalem, and Rufus of Thessalonica, and likewise to the holy Churches of Constantinople and Antioch, prescribed even earlier a judgment and rule concerning the present matter. Following this also, we have carried that form into execution, bringing against him a canonical and apostolic judgment.”

Here, however, instead of *bringing forward*, the Greek has **κατανοήσαντες**, that is, “having considered and recognized that the judgment pronounced against Nestorius was canonical and apostolic.”

Of the letters mentioned by Firmus, we still possess those written to Cyril and to the Church of Constantinople. Nor need we regret the loss of those said to have been sent to Rufus and Juvenal, since Letter 12 to John of Antioch had merely sent equivalent and similar copies to those two bishops together. At most, the letter to the Church of Antioch has been lost, if a different letter is meant there from the one written to John, bishop of that city.

# LETTER XVIII. OF THE BLESSED POPE CELESTINE I TO THE SYNOD OF EPHESUS

[Col. 0505]

That they should faithfully preserve what had been handed down by the apostles; that they should fight bravely for Christ’s cause; that with one mind and one faith they should support both the peace of the Churches and the faith; and that he had sent legates to attend the proceedings of the synod and carry out what it decreed.

[Col. 0505A] **CELESTINE, bishop, to the holy synod assembled at Ephesus,**

**Note [Col. 0505C]:** The Bellovacensis manuscript alone, despite the Greek, reads *constitutae* (“established”). The Greek translator then added: “to those beloved in the Lord, greetings.”

1. The assembly of priests testifies to the presence of the Holy Spirit. For it is certain what we read—for truth cannot lie, and this saying is found in the Gospel:

> “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them” (Matthew 18:20).

Since this is so, if the Holy Spirit is not absent even from so small a number, how much more should we believe that he is now present, when so great a multitude of holy men has gathered together? For the assembly is holy, as its due reverence requires; and in it we must behold the reverence of that very great gathering of the apostles which we read about in Acts 15.

The one whom they had received to be proclaimed was never absent from them. The Lord and Teacher was always present with them, and those who were being taught were never abandoned by their own Teacher. He who had sent them taught; he who had told them what they should teach taught. He taught who confirms that he himself is heard in his apostles (Luke 10:16).

This concern for the preaching entrusted to all the Lord’s priests reaches all of us together. For by hereditary right we are bound to this responsibility, whoever throughout the various regions of the earth preaches the Lord’s name in their place, since it was said to them:

> “Go, teach all nations” (Matthew 28:20).

### 2

Your Fraternity understands that we have received a general command. He also wished all of us to do what he had thus commonly commanded them all. It is necessary that we follow appropriately the example of our predecessors.

Let us all undertake the labors of those whose honor we have inherited. Let us show diligence toward what they preached; after that, as the Apostle warns (Galatians 1:8–9), we are commanded to admit no preaching.

**Note:** The Roman edition has *adducere* (“to bring forward”), and Baronius, following the Greek, has *adjicere* (“to add”). The reading *admittere* (“to admit”), found with Baluze and the manuscripts, is preferable. The reference is clearly to Paul’s words in Galatians 1:9: “If anyone preaches to you a gospel contrary to what you received, let him be accursed.” Accordingly, the reading *admittere*, found in Baluze and the manuscripts, is preferred.

The guardianship of what has been handed down is not less than the office of the one who handed it down.

**Note:** That is, guarding what has been handed down is not something inferior to the office of the one who handed it down. Therefore the work of pastors, whose task is to preserve what has been handed down, is no less necessary than the work of the apostles, whose task was to transmit what must be believed. The Greek interpreter rendered Celestine’s words as though he had read: “It is no less honorable to obey the teacher than to preserve what has been handed down,” and thus did not fully grasp his meaning.

Let them sow the seeds of faith; let this concern of ours guard them, so that our Master’s arrival may find an incorruptible and abundant fruit, to whom alone the harvest is assigned.

**Note:** Baluze, with the manuscripts, reads *semen* (“seed”), but the pronoun that follows cannot agree with it. The manuscripts soon afterward read *patrisfamiliae* (“of the master of the household”).

For when the Vessel of Election speaks, planting and watering are not enough unless God gives the increase (1 Corinthians 3:7).

Therefore we must now labor together, so that we may preserve what has been entrusted to us and held fast until now through apostolic succession.

**Note:** Three manuscripts read *ut commissa* (“so that what has been entrusted”), with no difference in meaning. Shortly afterward, *retenta* (“held fast”) is preferable to *detenta* (“held”).

What is being challenged in us is that by which we walk according to the Apostle.

**Note:** Baluze and the manuscripts have this reading. Other editions, following the Greek, add *apostolorum* (“of the apostles”), contrary to Celestine’s intention. The Greek text also departs from his meaning in what follows.

For it is not some external appearance, but our faith, that is now summoned to judgment.

**Note:** The Greek interpreter, rendering **πρόσωπόν τι** (“some person” or “some appearance”), appears to have understood the word as referring to a particular person. Yet the earthly substance—which commonly becomes the source and origin of disputes—is more suitably understood here.

### 3

Spiritual weapons must be taken up, because the battles are battles of minds and the missiles are words, so that we may persevere in the covenant of our King.

**Note:** Literally, the Greek has “in the faith.” The manuscripts resist this reading. The word *covenant* suits Celestine’s allegorical expression.

The blessed Apostle Paul now exhorts all those who are present there, where he commanded Timothy to remain (1 Timothy 1:3). Therefore the same place and the same cause now require the very same duty.

Let us also now do what he then undertook to do: let no one think otherwise, and let no one devote himself to questions that are chiefly concerned with outstanding fables, as he himself commanded (1 Timothy 1:4; 4:7).

Let us be of one mind, thinking one thing, because this is expedient. Let us desire to do nothing through contentiousness and nothing through empty vainglory. Let one soul and one heart belong to all (Philippians 2:2–3).

Since the one faith is being assaulted, let this entire assembly suffer—indeed, let it mourn—with us as a common body.

He who will judge the world is summoned before judgment; he who will examine everyone is himself examined; and he who redeemed us suffers accusation.

Let your Fraternity put on the armor of God (Ephesians 6:17).

You know what helmet protects our head and what breastplate encloses our chest. You have not only now taken up the command of the Church’s camp.

**Note:** The Greek interpreter reads “now for the first time,” which is also more attractive, as though he were saying: “You are not recruits in the Church’s army.” Baluze has *rectoris* (“of the ruler”), but *rectores* (“rulers”) should be retained, as is clear both from the Greek and from the sequence of the argument.

Let no one doubt that, with the Lord’s favor—he who makes both one (Ephesians 2:14)—once the weapons have been laid aside, peace will follow, since the cause itself defends itself.

### 4

Let us again recall those words of our Teacher which he addressed especially to bishops when he foretold these things:

> “Take heed to yourselves and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as bishops, to govern the Church of God, which he acquired with his own blood” (Acts 20:28).

**Note:** This is Baluze’s reading with the manuscripts, except that the Navarre manuscript has *inde adhuc vocatos* (“called still from there”). Other printed editions have *inde advocatos* (“summoned from there”). Celestine refers to Acts 20:17: “From Miletus Paul sent to Ephesus and summoned the elders of the Church,” to whom he said: “Take heed to yourselves,” and so forth. The Greek interpreter should have rendered **ἐκεῖθεν** (“from there”), not **ὅθεν** (“whence”); **πρὸς τοῦτο** (“to this”), not **τοιούτους** (“such”); and **ἀκούσοντας** (“those who would hear”), not **ἀκούσαντας** (“those who heard”). Then, after omitting **Ἐφεσίους** (“Ephesians”), he should have added **Ἐφεσίοις** after **τοιγαροῦν**.

From this, we read, those who were called to hear this were the Ephesians, among whom your holiness has now assembled.

Therefore, for the Ephesians, who know the preaching of the faith, let our defense of it also now be known.

Let us show them, with the reverence of our mind, firmness in those things which are worthy, which are great, and which enduring tranquility has preserved with devout understanding; let those things reign inviolate.

**Note:** Baluze, with the Bellovacensis manuscript, has: “The things preached by the apostles have reigned among us inviolate, because never…” Labbe has: “Let what was preached by the apostles be announced to you inviolate, because never…” Other editions have: “Let what was preached by the apostles be announced to you, because never…” The Greek reading has been explained in the preceding note. The reading *quae*, apart from the conjunction, is found in the Colbertine, Tours, and Navarre manuscripts and appears less likely to be a gloss.

Never have words of tyrannical domination been admitted against the King of kings, nor could the cause of truth be oppressed by falsehood.

I urge you, dearest brothers: let that love be regarded in which we must remain, according to the word of the Apostle John (1 John 3:17; 4:16), whose relics you presently venerate.

**Note:** Hilary and Jerome had earlier expressed, by the word *venerari* (“to venerate”), the reverence owed to sacred relics. Both call them “venerable bones”: Hilary in *Against Constantius*, section 8, and Jerome in *Against Vigilantius*. In the same way, Eusebius Gallicanus, in the homily on Saint Blandina—which is more probably Eucherius’—rebukes the impious judges because they reduced venerable bones to ashes. Indeed, the same writer also uses the word *adorare* (“to adore”). Thus he addresses Blandina’s judge: “You consign relics worthy of adoration to the Rhône.” A little earlier, having observed how even the beasts and flames preserved the bodies of the saints unharmed and inviolate, he turns his speech against those who despise sacred relics:

> “Where are those who say that reverence should not be offered to the bodies of the holy martyrs? Behold the savagery of bloody ferocity, which does not admit the meaning of religion yet offers the service of reverence … and, while showing respect to piety, gives silent judgment against impiety.”

Let our prayer to the Lord be common.

We know what power that divine presence will have, when so great a multitude of priests supplicates in harmony. The place was shaken where we read that the twelve prayed with one accord (Acts 4:31).
