**Note:** The Roman edition has *movere poterit* (“will be able to move”), and the Greek has *movere potest* (“is able to move”). The manuscripts provide the correction, supported by the words of Acts: “When they had prayed, the place in which they were gathered was shaken.”

But what was the Apostles’ petition as they prayed? Clearly, that they might receive the word of God and speak it with boldness (Acts 4:29–30), and perform mighty works by his hands, powers which they had received through the favor of Christ our God.

**Note:** Baluze has: “And by his hands to perform powers, of which…” The Roman edition has: “And by his hand to perform power, of which…” Labbe, following the Greek, has: “And by his power to perform, of which…” At first the reading of the Navarre manuscript seemed preferable: “And through him to perform powers, of which.” But after considering the words of Acts—“Grant to your servants to speak your word with all boldness, while you stretch out your hand to heal, and signs and wonders are performed through the name of your holy servant Jesus”—we have become convinced that the reading followed with Baronius is the more authentic.

And what else should your holy assembly now ask, except that you speak the Lord’s word with boldness? That he may grant you to preserve what he has permitted you to preach? That, filled with the Holy Spirit, as it is written (Acts 4:31), although with different mouths, you may proclaim one thing, which the Spirit himself has taught?

**Note:** Printed editions, except Baluze, have *quam ea servare* (“which you may preserve together with those things”); the manuscripts restore the reading.

Strengthened briefly by all these exhortations—for, as the Apostle says, “I speak to those who know the law,” and “I speak wisdom among the mature” (Romans 7:1; 1 Corinthians 2:6)—support the Catholic faith and the peace of the Churches.

**Note:** Labbe has *quietem* (“peace”), and then, with the Roman edition, *defendite* (“defend”), since this is what was said.

Support them, as must be said, past, present, and future, asking for and preserving the things that make for the peace of Jerusalem (Psalm 122:6).

### 5

Out of our pastoral concern we have sent holy brothers and fellow priests of ours, men of one mind with us and thoroughly approved: the bishops Arcadius and Projectus, and our presbyter Philip. They are to attend what is being done and carry out what we previously decreed.

**Note:** Perhaps *exsequantur* (“carry out”) is intended.

We do not doubt that your holiness will grant them assent, since what is being undertaken appears to have been decreed for the security of the universal Church.

**Note:** The manuscripts, together with Labbe and Baluze, have this reading. Baronius has *legitis* (“you read”), while the Roman edition has the same. Hence the Greek interpreter seems to have read **ἀνέγνωτε** (“you read”), although the text now has **ἂν γνῶτε** (“whatever you may recognize”).

Given on 8 May, in the consulship of Bassus and Antiochus.

**Note:** 8 May, A.D. 431. This chronological note is absent from the Roman edition.

---

### Additional editorial notes to Letter XVIII

**Note [Col. 0505C]:** Baronius, with the Roman edition, reads *veritas nostra* (“our truth”). More correctly, *nostra* is absent from the other books. The Greek translator rendered the passage as if he had read: “For what is written is true, since truth cannot lie, because such a saying occurs in the Gospel.” This alone shows that neither our Latin text nor the one inserted by Baronius in his *Annals* was translated from Greek; many similar places confirm it.

**Note [Col. 0505C]:** In place of *si* (“if”), the Roman edition has *nam* (“for”) and Baronius *ut* (“as”); but the Navarre manuscript simply reads: *Quod si* (“But if”), and does not have *nec huic*.

**Note [Col. 0505C–D]:** The Roman edition and the councils printed by Baronius read *concilium* (“council”), against the manuscripts. For Celestine, *collegium* (“assembly”) is a familiar designation for a gathering of bishops.

**Note [Col. 0505D]:** The word *magister* (“Teacher”), and shortly afterward the particle *sed* (“but”) before *nec docentes*, printed in the same editions through erroneous repetition from the Greek, are removed on the authority of the manuscripts.

**Note [Col. 0505D]:** The Roman edition and Baronius read *eorum voce* (“by their voice”); this is corrected from the manuscripts and the Greek.

**Note [Col. 0506C]:** The printed texts have *qui* (“who”); the Navarre manuscript more suitably has *quod* (“what”). Baronius and the Roman edition then read: “He thus gave them all a common duty”; the Greek has: “He gave commands concerning faith and ministry.” The Latin text is corrected from the manuscripts, partly in conformity with the Greek: “He wished all of us also to do what he had thus commanded them all in common; it is necessary that we follow our predecessors.”

**Note [Col. 0506C]:** The printed texts repeat *omnes* (“all”) here; it is better absent from the Navarre manuscript and the Greek.

**Note [Col. 0506C–D]:** Baronius reads *praedicantes* (“preaching”); the Roman edition, *praedicationis* (“of preaching”). The other books more truly read *praedicatis*: that is, we are to give diligence to what they preached, or, as the Greek rendering has it, to their teachings.

**Note [Col. 0507D]:** The Roman edition reads *adducere* (“to bring forward”); Baronius and Labbe, following the Greek, *adjicere* (“to add”). The reference is plainly to Galatians 1:9; therefore *admittere* (“to admit”), supported by Baluze and the manuscripts, is preferable.

**Note [Col. 0507D]:** The Greek translator rendered Celestine as though he had read: “It is no less honorable to obey the teacher than to preserve what has been handed down,” and did not adequately grasp his meaning.

**Note [Col. 0507D]:** Baluze and the manuscripts read *semina* (“seeds”); Baluze has *semen* (“seed”), with which the following pronoun *haec* cannot agree. Shortly afterward the manuscripts read *patrisfamiliae* (“master of the household”).

**Note [Col. 0507D]:** Baluze, with the manuscripts, reads *ubertas* (“fruitfulness”). Other editions add *apostolorum* (“of the apostles”) from the Greek, contrary to Celestine’s meaning; the Greek likewise departs from him in what follows.

**Note [Col. 0508D]:** The manuscripts omit *ipsa etiam modo* (“the same also now”). The Greek reading calls for: “the same cause now requires the same duty,” which would be neater.

**Note [Col. 0508D]:** The Greek text has *fide* (“faith”) in a literal rendering, against the manuscripts; *foedere* (“covenant”) is more fitting to Celestine’s allegorical expression.

**Note [Col. 0508D]:** The Greek translator reads *nunc primum* (“now for the first time”), which is also more appealing: as though Celestine were saying, “You are not novices in the Church’s army.” Baluze has *rectoris* (“of the ruler”), but *rectores* (“rulers”) must be retained, as is clear both from the Greek and the course of the argument.

**Note [Col. 0509C]:** Baluze and the manuscripts read *huic* (“to this”), which can refer to the faith; other books have *his* (“to these people”).

**Note [Col. 0509C]:** Labbe after Baronius reads: “Let the things that are great be worthy of what is fitting, and let what perpetual tranquility has preserved by devout understanding remain untainted.” The Roman edition has a different corrupt wording. The Greek translator rendered it as though he had read: “Let those things which are worthy remain above slander, which perpetual tranquility has preserved with devout understanding. Let those things proclaimed by the apostles be announced by you, because never…”

**Note [Col. 0509C–D]:** Baluze, with the Bellovacensis manuscript, reads: “The things that were preached by the apostles have reigned among us inviolate, because never…” Labbe reads: “Let the things that have reigned inviolate, preached by the apostles, be announced to you, because never…” Other editions read: “Let the things preached by the apostles be announced to you, because never…” The Greek reading was explained above. The reading *nostra, quae*—apart from the particle *et*—is found in the Colbertine, Tours, and Navarre manuscripts and seems less suspect as a gloss.

**Note [Col. 0510C]:** The Roman edition reads *movere poterit* (“will be able to be moved”); the Greek has *movere potest* (“can be moved”). The other books correct the text, as Acts says: “When they had prayed, the place was shaken.”

**Note [Col. 0510D]:** The printed editions except Baluze read *quam ea servare*; the manuscripts restore *quam ut det servare* (“that he may grant [you] to preserve”).

### Additional editorial notes to Letter XX

**Note [Col. 0514D]:** The manuscripts variously read *definitivis*, *definitivum*, and *definitivus*; the Greek makes clear that *definientibus* (“fixing”) must be restored. The imperial decree, or sacred rescript, establishing this is found in Part I of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 32, p. 437.

**Note [Col. 0514D]:** That is, after the appointed period of postponement.

**Note [Col. 0514D]:** More clearly: once it had become evident, both from this deliberate delay and from what he had communicated, that he was refusing the council.

**Note [Col. 0515D]:** Add *Cyrillum* (“Cyril”).

**Note [Col. 0515D]:** Baluze and three manuscripts read *recognitione*; the Navarre and Campensis manuscripts have *recogitationis*. Neither is satisfactory, since the Greek properly means “to come to one’s senses” or “repent.” A more apt Latin rendering would be: “So far was he from repenting and, coming to his senses, retracting what he had blasphemously uttered while he still held the Church of Constantinople, that…”

## Greek Text

[Col. 0506A] **Celestine to the holy synod assembled at Ephesus, to those beloved and most dearly cherished in the Lord: greetings.**

The assembly of priests manifests the presence of the Holy Spirit. For what is written is true, since truth cannot lie, and in the Gospel there is such a saying:

> “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them.”

Since this is so, if the Holy Spirit does not abandon even such a small number, how much more should we believe that he now acts among us, where so great a multitude of holy men has gathered? For the assembly is holy, according to the reverence proper to it; and in it one may behold the reverence of that greatest assembly of the apostles, as we have read.

The Teacher proclaimed by them has never abandoned them. The Lord and Teacher was always present with them; nor were those being taught ever abandoned by their own Teacher.

He who sent them taught; he who told them what they should teach taught; he who manifested himself in his own apostles, confirming that he was heard, taught.

**Note:** Read **διδάσκοντες** (“teaching”).

**Note:** Add **ἐν** (“in”).

**Note:** Read **προσβεβαιῶν ἀκούεσθαι** (“confirming that he is heard”). The whole passage should read: “The concern for the teaching entrusted to all the priests of the Lord has reached them in common. By a rightful inheritance we are bound in this concern, we who everywhere and throughout the inhabited world proclaim the Lord’s name through their succession, as they were commanded: ‘Go and make disciples of all the nations.’”

Let these things be heard by all together, lords and brothers: the responsibility for the teaching entrusted to us has followed them. By rightful inheritance we are bound to this concern, we who everywhere and throughout the whole inhabited world proclaim the Lord’s name through their succession, as they were commanded:

> “Go and make disciples of all the nations.”

Your Fraternity ought to understand that it has received a general command. He wished all of us ourselves to carry this out, he who gave all those men commandments concerning faith and ministry. It is necessary that we follow our fathers appropriately, all undertaking their labor, we who have succeeded to their honor.

**Note:** Read **ὑπεισελθῶμεν** (“let us enter into”); delete the following **καὶ** (“and”).

Let us provide care for their teachings. After these things, with the Apostle reminding us, we are commanded to add no teaching.

**Note [Col. 0506C]:** Read **ὑπομιμνήσκοντος** (“with the Apostle reminding us”).

The guarding of what has been handed down is not an honor inferior to service rendered to the teacher.

They sowed the seeds of faith; let our concern secure them, so that our Master’s presence may find fruit incorruptible and multiplied. To him alone the fruitfulness is attributed.

**Note:** Read: “Fruitfulness is attributed to him.”

For Paul, speaking to his chosen ones, said that planting and watering himself were not enough unless God granted growth and increase.

Therefore we must be very diligent and must act so that, through common labor, we may preserve what has been entrusted to us and held fast until now through apostolic succession.

For this is what is demanded of us: that we walk according to the Apostle.

For it is not now some person or external appearance, but our faith, that is summoned to judgment.

Spiritual weapons must be put on, since wars are stirred up against souls and the weapons are words, so that we may remain in the faith of our King.

The blessed Paul reminds all those who are now present there, where he commanded Timothy to remain. Therefore the same place and the same matter now require the same ministry.

Let us now act and strive toward what he was commanded to do: let no one think otherwise, and let no one extend himself into inquiries amid the present abundance of words, as he himself commanded.

**Note:** Read: “Let no one pay attention to inquiries, especially to fables.”

Let us remain united in soul, thinking one and the same thing, since this is expedient. Let us desire to do nothing through contentiousness and nothing through empty vainglory. Let there be one soul and one heart among all.

When the one faith is disturbed, let the entire assembly suffer this with us in common—indeed, let it mourn.

He who judges the whole inhabited world is summoned before judgment; he who governs the whole earth is held accountable; and the Redeemer suffers accusation.

**Note:** Read **εὐθύνων** (“governing” or “directing”).

Let your Fraternity put on the whole armor of God.

You know the helmet that secures our head and the breastplate that fortifies our chest. The ecclesiastical enclosures have not received you as teachers for the first time.

Let no one doubt, with God cooperating—he who makes both one—that when the weapons have been laid aside, peace follows, since the cause itself vindicates itself.

Let us recall again those words of our Master and Teacher which he used specifically for the bishops, giving this command:

> “Take heed to yourselves and to all the flock, over which the Holy Spirit has appointed you bishops, to govern the Church of God, which he acquired with his own blood.”

From there we read that the Ephesians were called to hear these things, where your holiness has now assembled.

Therefore, since the teaching of the faith is known to them, let our defense also be known.

Let us give them, through the disposition of our mind, the strength of that reverence which they deserve. Let those things remain higher than slander which enduring peace has preserved with devout understanding.

Let what was proclaimed beforehand by the apostles be announced by you, because never have tyrannical words prevailed against the King of kings, nor could the power of truth be weakened by fabricated speech.

**Note:** Add **κατά** (“against”).

I exhort you, dearest brothers: let that love alone be observed in which we ought to remain, according to the word of John the Evangelist, whose relics you have honored in your presence.

**Note:** Read **προτρέπω** (“I exhort”).

**Note:** Read: “Love, in which we ought to remain according to…”

Let prayer to the Lord be common.

We know what power his divine presence, which is to come, will have, when so great a multitude of priests calls upon him with one accord. For that place can be moved in which we have read that the twelve prayed unanimously.

What was the petition of the twelve as they prayed? Clearly, that they might receive the word of God and speak with boldness, and act through his power in those things for which, by the gift of Christ our God, they had received authority.

And what else is there for your holy synod now to ask except that you speak the word of Christ with boldness? And that he grant you to preserve what he has granted you to proclaim?

**Note:** Read **διδῷ** (“may he grant”).

And, filled with the Holy Spirit, as it is written, although with different mouths, may you offer one thing—the very thing which the Spirit himself has taught and approves.

**Note:** Read **προσοίσητε** (“you may offer”).

Strengthened by all these things, because, as the Apostle says, “I speak to those who know,” and “I speak understanding among the mature,” strive for the Catholic faith and the peace of the Churches.

Support them, since thus it has been said, both those of former times, those now living, and those who are to come, exhorting and preserving the things that make for the peace of Jerusalem.

We have sent men who undertake our concern: our holy brothers and fellow ministers, Arcadius and Projectus, bishops who are of one mind with us and approved, and Philip, our presbyter. They are to be present at what is being done and carry out what was formerly decreed by us.

We do not doubt that your holiness will grant them assent, since whatever you recognize appears to have been decided for the security of all the Churches.

---

**Note:** From the same sources from which Letter 17 came to us.

# LETTER XIX. OF POPE CELESTINE TO THE EMPEROR THEODOSIUS

[Col. 0511]

That he should permit nothing to the authors of turbulent innovation; that he ought to have greater concern for the faith than for the kingdom.

[Col. 0511B] **CELESTINE, bishop, to Theodosius Augustus.**

### 1

Although your Clemency’s concern for the defense of the Catholic faith—toward which, for love of Christ our God, who governs your empire, you hasten by every means to be present—would itself be sufficient, since you preserve it whole and undefiled by condemning the error of perverse doctrines, and since you always establish the security of your empire in this protection, knowing that your kingdom will endure more firmly when fortified by observance of holy religion; nevertheless, each of us, in accordance with our priestly office, contributes to this heavenly concern and glory whatever service we are able to provide.

To this synod, which you commanded to assemble, we offer our presence through those whom we have sent. Under an earnest appeal to the divine judgment, we beseech your piety that your gentleness permit no license to turbulent innovation, and that no opportunity be granted to those who strive to confine the power of the divine Majesty within the terms of human disputation, thereby disturbing ecclesiastical peace.

### 2

The cause of the faith ought to be greater for you than that of the kingdom; and your Clemency ought to be more concerned for the peace of the Churches than for the security of the whole world.

All prosperity follows if those things which are dearer to God are preserved first.

Abraham flourished through faith and filled the whole world with the glory of his posterity.

**Note:** Printed editions have: “He filled the whole world with the glory of his prosperity … and armed himself with the zeal of the Lord against those, if any…” The Holstenius manuscripts more correctly have: “He filled the whole world with the glory of his posterity … with zeal…” Hence it has been established that *se* (“himself”), not *si* (“if”), should be read: “Moses … armed himself with zeal against them.”

Moses, deliverer of the people, armed himself with the zeal of the Lord against those whom he found to have departed from the true worship of God.

The Lord guarded David, a king who observed his commandments in his kingdom, so that he might subject his enemies to him.

I ask you, fortified by the protection of these examples—by faith, observance, and courage—to guard the universal Church’s most devout worship of our God, lest dissension claim anything for itself.

**Note:** The Archetype has *fidei* (“of faith”), and *observ.* (“of observance”).

For whatever is undertaken for the peace of the Church or the reverence of holy religion is undertaken for the sake of your empire.

**Note:** Holstenius has this reading. Other books have: “for the safety of your empire.”

### 3

These things, most glorious, tranquil, and august Emperor, which we know to be in your heart—and, since God is present there, of this we have no doubt—we make known even to your august ears through my brothers and fellow bishops Arcadius and Projectus and my fellow presbyter Philip, whom we have sent.

We humbly ask this of your piety, believing that you possess it within yourself: that what you ask of God, you may grant in the cause of his faith.

**Note:** 25 May, A.D. 431.

Given on the Ides of May, in the consulship of Bassus and Antiochus.

---

**Note:** This letter appears among the proceedings of the Council of Ephesus, in the acts of Session 5, recorded as having been held on 17 July in the year 431. It was written in Greek and received a Latin translator who adhered very closely to the wording and therefore sometimes departed from clarity of meaning, not to say from the truth. Nicholas I followed this translation in Letter 8 to Michael and thereby gave us information about its authority. For this reason we have judged it preferable to retain it, while not hesitating to suggest a more convenient rendering where appropriate. We present it transcribed from Baluze’s new collection and the four manuscripts frequently mentioned. In these, the copy of the letter is addressed from the holy synod to Celestine, archbishop of Rome. Such Latin copies were not unknown to Labbe.

# LETTER XX, OR THE REPORT WHICH THE HOLY SYNOD OF EPHESUS SENT TO POPE CELESTINE,

[Col. 0511]

in which the proceedings of the holy and great synod itself are explained.

[Note: The following Latin and Greek texts are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0511C] **To the most holy and most reverend fellow minister Celestine, the holy synod, which by God’s grace has assembled in the metropolis of the Ephesians, sends greetings in the Lord.**

**Note:** Labbe has in Latin “to Celestine, bishop,” and in Greek repeats **Κελεστίνῳ ἐπισκόπῳ** (“to Celestine, bishop”). But these two words are found neither in the Latin manuscripts nor in the two ancient Greek copies of the royal library. Therefore one should not read **Ἀναφορὰ τῷ ἁγιωτάτῳ** (“a report to the most holy”), but, with the punctuation changed: **Ἀναφορά. Τῷ ἁγιωτάτῳ**, “A report. To the most holy…” This deserved notice because certain Roman pontiffs, especially Nicholas I, complained in letters—both to Solomon, king of Britain, and to Festinianus, bishop of Dol, in a letter dated 26 May 866—that the names of those who write were placed before the apostolic name.

### 1

Your holiness’s zeal for piety, and your God-loving or God-pleasing concern for the right faith of the Savior of us all, was worthy of every admiration. It is your custom, being great in all things, to be well approved in everything and to make all the concerns of the Churches your own.

**Note:** Literally: “And to make your efforts the strengthening of the Churches,” or, “to make it your concern that the Churches be strengthened” in the faith.

Since, however, everything that followed had to be reported to the knowledge of your holiness, we necessarily write. In accordance with the will of all of us, and in accordance with the decrees of the most devout and Christ-loving emperors, we assembled in the metropolis of the Ephesians, numbering more than two hundred bishops from many different provinces.

Then, when the most devout decrees of the Christ-loving emperors—which had summoned us—had fixed the day of the holy synod’s session as the day of holy Pentecost, all assembled, especially since the emperors’ letters stipulated that, if anyone did not appear, he would be absent without a good conscience after the appointed postponement and would be inexcusable before both God and human beings.

The most reverend John, bishop of the Antiochenes, was absent—not from simple choice, nor because the length of the journey created an obstacle, but because he concealed in his mind a plan and intention opposed to God, which he later demonstrated when he came to Ephesus.

Accordingly, after the appointed day of holy Pentecost, we postponed the council for sixteen full days. Many bishops and clerics had been seized by illness and worn down by the expense, and some had even died. As your holiness perceives, what was happening was rather an insult against the holy synod.

For he had perversely taken advantage of such a long delay, although many had preceded him from much greater distances.

Nevertheless, after the sixteenth day, two of the bishops who had been with him arrived before the others: Alexander, metropolitan of Apamea, and another Alexander, metropolitan of Hierapolis.

Then, when we complained about the tardiness of the arrival of the most reverend bishop John, they said not once but repeatedly:

“He instructed us to announce to your Reverence that, if he should happen to remain delayed any longer, the synod should not be postponed, but that you should do what is necessary.”

When this had been reported, and it had become clear both from the delay and from what had been announced on his behalf that he was refusing the council—whether because he was favoring Nestorius out of friendship, or because he had previously been a cleric of the Church subject to him, or because he was yielding to the petitions of certain people on his behalf—the holy synod assembled at Ephesus in the larger church called Mary.

**Note:** The Bellovacensis manuscript has *commodans*, perhaps for *concedens*, with the object understood: “acting thus either to oblige the friendship that existed between him and Nestorius, or because he had been a cleric of the Antiochene Church,” and so forth.

### 2

When everyone was eagerly assembling and Nestorius alone was absent from the council, the holy synod summoned him canonically through the bishops on the first, second, and third summons.

But he surrounded his house with soldiers and acted arrogantly against the laws of the Churches. He did not permit himself to appear openly, nor to give an account of his wicked blasphemies.

**Note:** These words are absent from the royal manuscripts: **καὶ οὐκ ἠνέσχετο ἑαυτὸν ἐμφανῆ καταστῆσαι, οὔτε … αὐτοῦ δυσφημιῶν**. In Latin they would read: “Nor did he deign to appear in person or to give an account of his impious blasphemies.”

Afterward the letter written to him by the most holy and most reverend bishop Cyril of the Alexandrian Church was reread. The holy synod judged it to be correct and irreproachable, and in no way at variance either with the divinely inspired Scriptures or with the faith handed down and expounded in the great synod of the holy Fathers who had assembled at Nicaea in earlier times. Your holiness also rightly testified to this by approving it.

The letter of Nestorius, written to the aforesaid most holy and most reverend brother and fellow minister of ours—Cyril—was likewise read. The holy synod judged the doctrines contained in it to be entirely alien to the apostolic and evangelical faith, afflicted by many new blasphemies.

**Note:** Or: “and suffering from numerous new blasphemies.”

His most impious doctrinal statements were then read as well, together with the letter written to him by your holiness, by which he was most reasonably condemned, since he had written blasphemies and inserted irreligious expressions into his doctrinal statements.

A just sentence of deposition was therefore pronounced against him, especially because he was so far from repentance or from retracting the things over which he had blasphemed while still possessing the Church of Constantinople that, even in the metropolis of the Ephesians, he addressed certain metropolitan bishops—men who were not ignorant but learned and most reverend—and dared to say:

“I do not confess a God who is two or three months old,”

and he also uttered other statements still more bitter.

**Note:** Some might prefer *bimestrem et trimestrem* (“two and three months old”), but the manuscripts resist this. Liberatus, in chapter 5, reports these same words as follows: “Although many confessed Jesus Christ as God, Nestorius said: ‘I never confess a God who is two or three months old. For this reason I am clean from your blood, and I do not come to you now.’” Liberatus adds that Nestorius withdrew with his supporters and thereafter refused to meet with the other Fathers of the council.

### Report to Celestine

[Col. 0512C] **Report.** To the most holy and God-fearing fellow-minister Celestine, the holy synod assembled by God’s grace in the metropolitan city of Ephesus, greeting in the Lord.

Your holiness’s zeal for piety, and its care for the right faith, beloved of and pleasing to God, the Savior of us all, have become worthy of every admiration. For it is your custom, eminent as you are in all things, to make your labors a support for the churches.

[Col. 0514A] Since it was necessary that all the events which followed should be reported to your holiness, we write that, according to the will of Christ, the Savior of us all, and by decree of the most pious and Christ-loving emperors, we assembled in the metropolitan city of Ephesus from many and diverse provinces, more than two hundred bishops in number.

The pious decrees of the Christ-loving emperors by which we were summoned had fixed the day of holy Pentecost for the session of the holy synod. Everyone had gathered, especially because of the force of the imperial injunctions: anyone failing to appear by the appointed deadline was regarded as remaining behind with no good conscience and as without excuse before God and men. Yet the most reverend John, bishop of Antioch, delayed—not from any simple purpose, nor because the length of the journey hindered him—but while concealing a plan and design displeasing to God, which he soon revealed upon arriving at Ephesus.

We therefore postponed the session for a full sixteen days after the appointed day of holy Pentecost, although many bishops and clergy were burdened by illness, distressed by expenses, and some had even died. As your holiness sees, this conduct was rather an affront to the holy synod. For he made perverse use of so great a delay, although those travelling from still greater distances had arrived.

[Col. 0514C] Nevertheless, on the sixteenth day certain bishops who were with him arrived in advance: two metropolitans, Alexander of Apamea and another Alexander of Hierapolis. When we complained of the tardy arrival of the most reverend Bishop John, they said repeatedly that he had instructed them to report to your God-fearing holiness that, should he be delayed still longer, the synod was not to be postponed, but should do what was necessary. Once this had been reported, and it had become evident both from his delay and from their message that he was declining the session—whether from favoring his friendship with Nestorius, because he had become a cleric of the church subject to him, or from yielding to certain entreaties on Nestorius’s behalf—the holy synod convened in the great church at Ephesus called Mary.

[Col. 0516A] Since, though all had eagerly assembled, Nestorius alone remained absent from the session, the holy synod canonically summoned him by bishops a first, second, and third time. But after barricading his house with soldiers, he devised a course contrary to the ordinances of the Church and would neither present himself nor defend himself concerning his impious blasphemies.

Then the letter written to him by Cyril, the most holy and God-beloved bishop of the Church of Alexandria, was read. The holy synod judged it to be right and irreproachable, and in no way discordant either with the divinely inspired Scriptures—that is, with the tradition of the faith—or with the faith set forth in the great synod of the holy fathers assembled at Nicaea, as your holiness, having rightly approved it, also testified.

[Col. 0516B] When Nestorius’s letter to the aforesaid most holy and God-fearing brother and fellow-minister Cyril had likewise been read, the holy synod judged its doctrines wholly alien to the apostolic and evangelical faith and infected with the gravest and most foreign blasphemy. When his most impious expositions had similarly been read, together with the letter written to him by your holiness, through which he was rightly condemned for having written blasphemies and inserted impious utterances in his own expositions, a just sentence of deposition was pronounced against him. This was especially so because, far from repenting or changing his mind concerning the blasphemies he had uttered, while he still held the Church of Constantinople, he even dared in the metropolitan city of Ephesus to say to certain holy metropolitan bishops—men not obscure but distinguished and most devout, “For I do not confess a God two months old or three months old.” He also said other things still more grievous.

### 3

Thus, as we have already said, we deposed an irreligious and utterly abominable heresy, one that overturns our most holy religion and removes from its foundations the whole economy of the mystery.

[Note: In place of the Greek word εὐαγέστατην, restored from the royal manuscripts, while the printed editions had εὐσεβεστάτην, our translator read εὐαγγελικήν. Nor did he make sufficiently clear that the particle ὡς has an explanatory, not comparative, force. It should have been translated: “Accordingly, we overthrew the heresy as an irreligious movement that perverted our most holy religion and wholly destroyed the entire dispensation of the mystery.” What is here called “the dispensation of the mystery,” and by Hilary in *On the Trinity*, book V, §17, “the mystery of the evangelical dispensation,” is to be understood as the mystery of the Incarnation. In reality, the whole of this mystery, and with it our religion, collapses if one holds that the Word of God dwelt in Christ only in the manner in which he existed in the prophets.]

But it could not happen, it seems, that those who possessed sincere love for Christ and zeal for the Lord would not undergo many difficulties.

[Note: Add “sincere,” and shortly afterward read “for the Lord.”]

For we expected the most reverend John, bishop of the Antiochenes, to praise the diligence and piety of the synod, and perhaps even to blame the delay in issuing the deposition.

[Note: In Baluzius, as in the manuscripts, the reading is *subtilitatem* (“subtlety”); the Greek word requires *sedulitatem* (“diligence”). The remainder would more elegantly be translated: “For we expected that he would praise … and perhaps blame the delay in pronouncing the sentence of deposition.”]

Everything that happened to us, however, turned out contrary to our expectation.

[Note: Supply “to them” (*iis*).] For he was found to be an enemy and most hostile both to so holy a synod and to the orthodox faith of the churches, as the facts themselves show.

As soon as he entered Ephesus, before he had shaken off the dust of the journey or removed his traveling garments, he gathered certain men who had seceded with Nestorius, who spoke blasphemously against their own head and all but mocked the glory of Christ.

[Note: The Colbertine and Tours manuscripts read *exutis mentis*, a mutilated reading restored from the Navarre, Beauvais, and Campanian manuscripts. The Greek *ἱμάτιον*, which in early writers means a cloak or outer garment covering the tunic, is suitably rendered by our author as a travelling garment.]

[Note: Here *non solum* is wrongly used for “all but.” More aptly: “They spoke against their own head—that is, Christ, the head of the Church—and all but made Christ’s glory a mockery.”] He collected for himself, as though forming a guild, about thirty men bearing the name of bishops. Some of them were without cities, being at leisure and possessing no churches; others had been deposed many years earlier by their own metropolitans on grave charges. Along with them were Pelagians and Coelestians, including some who had been expelled from Thessaly.

[Note: The more recent translation in the Roman edition and in the common editions of the councils renders the word ἀπόλιδες as *exsules* (“exiles”). Our translator, whom Nicholas I also followed when citing this passage, expressed more suitably the force and meaning of the Greek word. By that term are understood bishops who are vacant and possess no churches, either because they have not been admitted by the people or because they have been expelled.]

He dared to undertake an impious act such as none of his predecessors had ever attempted.

[Note: Supply “dared.”]

For, acting alone, he composed a document under the title of a deposition and insulted the most holy and most reverend bishop of the city of Alexandria, Cyril, as well as our most reverend fellow bishop, Memnon of Ephesus.

[Note: Although he composed it alone, the conventicle over which he presided had decided that Cyril and Memnon should be deposed and the others excommunicated. Therefore he dictated it in the name of the entire gathering, which also subscribed it. It is printed in Labbe, vol. III, p. 597.] None of us knew what was being done, nor did those who suffered the insult understand what was happening or for what reason they had dared to do this.

But as though God were not angered by these acts, as though there were no ecclesiastical canons, or as though they themselves would not be endangered because of this audacity, they also insulted the entire synod under the name of excommunication.

[Note: Read *injurioso* (“insulting”) here.]

Then, having inserted these matters into a public document, they displayed it for anyone who wished to read it, fastening it to the walls of the theater, so that they might make a spectacle of their impiety.

[Note: Baluzius reads “so that they might make a spectacle”; *spectaculo facerent*, or “so that they might make it manifest to everyone in the theaters,” would be preferable.]

Nor did their audacity stop there. They even took the confidence to write something as though it were canonical and to report matters of this kind to the ears of the most pious and Christ-loving emperors.

[Note: From the Greek, read: “They dared, as though they had done something canonical, even to bring such matters to the ears …”]

### 4

When these things had been done, the most holy and most reverend bishop of Alexandria, Cyril, and likewise the most reverend bishop of the city of Ephesus, Memnon, presented written statements composed by themselves, in which they accused both the most reverend bishop John himself and those who had carried out this act with him. They implored our holy synod canonically to summon John himself and those who were with him, so that they might give an account of what they had dared to do; and, if they had any accusation to make, that they should state it, if they could, and prove it.

[Note: In place of the words of the ancient translator, we have judged that the words “in which they accused them” should be substituted from the Greek, lest the sentence remain unintelligible or appear to say something contrary to the synod’s decision.]

For in the document they had written concerning the deposition—or rather, the insulting document—they put forward this as a pretext:

[Note: More correctly, “they put this forward as a pretext.”] “Because they are Apollinarists, Arians, and Eunomians, and for this reason they have been deposed by us.”

Since, therefore, those who had suffered the insult at their hands were pressing the matter, we again necessarily assembled in the great church—more than two hundred bishops in number—and over the course of two days summoned John himself and those who were with him to the council, by a first, second, and third summons. They were to prove the charge against those who had suffered the insult, give an account of themselves, and state the reasons for which they had drawn up the document of deposition. But they did not dare to come.

[Note: The Greek marginal correction reads *ἐθάρσησεν* (“he did not dare”), rather than the printed plural *ἐθάρσησαν*. The Greek verb also requires *praesumpserunt* (“they dared”) in the Latin translation; the sequence of the Latin translation shows that the text should be corrected accordingly.]

He ought, however, if he was truly able to prove that the holy men mentioned above were heretics, to have appeared and shown this to be true, and, accepting it as a serious and incontrovertible charge, to have pronounced his rash sentence against them. But, because of a guilty conscience, he did not appear.

[Note: Alternatively: “Deterred by a bad conscience, he declined to appear.”]

The scheme he had in mind was this: he thought that, when this foolish and unlawful insult had been set aside, the just sentence of the synod pronounced against the heretic Nestorius would likewise be overturned.

Therefore, rightly indignant, we resolved to pronounce lawfully an equal sentence against him and the others, such as he had unlawfully pronounced against men convicted of no offense.

[Note: The translator’s difficulty obscures the council’s sentence and does not explain it sufficiently. Its meaning is: “Moved by the disgracefulness of the deed, we rightly considered issuing against him and the others a sentence according to the laws, of the kind that he himself had unlawfully pronounced against men convicted of no crime.”]

But, in order that patience might overcome his rashness, although he would justly and lawfully have deserved this treatment, we left this matter to the judgment of your reverence. For the present, we have excluded them from communion and deprived them of all priestly authority, so that they may be unable to harm anyone by their judgments.

For those who habitually rush so savagely, cruelly, and contrary to the canons into actions so wicked and atrocious—how could it not have been necessary to deprive them, even against their will, of the power to cause harm?

[Note: If we follow the common Greek reading, the text should mean “or to deprive them even against their will.” But our translator read οὐκ ἔχοντας, “not having,” rather than οὐχ ἑκόντας, “against their will”; one royal manuscript supports him, in which the same reading appeared in the first hand. The surrounding material confirms this reading, since it again attacks their unrestrained license to pronounce judgments against those over whom they had no authority.]

### 5

As for our brothers and fellow ministers, Cyril and Memnon, who suffered insult at their hands, we are all in communion with them; and after their rash act we have ministered with them and continue to minister with them, all celebrating the assemblies together, having annulled in writing their farce and declared it invalid, ineffective, utterly without force, and null.

[Note: Supply “whom they dared to depose.” After the word “ministered,” understand “in the church.” The passage could be stated more clearly and without ambiguity as follows: “We have celebrated the sacred rites with them and continue to do so, all of us jointly holding the assemblies—those gatherings customarily convened for prayer and the offering of sacrifice to God—while we have annulled their laughable documents and declared them invalid, ineffective, wholly void, and null. The proceedings that the synod of Ephesus here calls a farce are called ‘trifling’ in its letter to the emperors, since it was convinced that bishops could not have undertaken them seriously.”]

For it was nothing but an insult. Thirty men in all—some marked by the stain of heresy, others without cities and expelled—what standing as a synod do they possess, or what power against a synod assembled from the whole world beneath heaven?

[Note: Read “power” rather than “virtue.”]

The most reverend bishops Arcadius and Projectus, sent by your holiness, also sat with us, together with the most holy presbyter Philip. Through them you graciously granted us your presence and they filled the place of the apostolic see.

Your reverence should therefore be suitably indignant at what has happened.

[Note: Nicholas, who cites this passage in Letter 8, reads *religio* (“your holiness”); otherwise there is no difference in the remaining text.]

For if permission is granted to those who wish to insult the greater sees and to pronounce judgments—or rather insults—so unlawfully and contrary to the canons against those over whom they have no authority, matters in the Church will proceed toward the utmost disorder, even against those who have endured so many struggles for the sake of piety, through whose efforts piety has now shone forth through the prayers of your reverence.

[Note: This is the reading of the Beauvais manuscript; four others read *quorum causa* (“on whose account”).]

[Note: Perhaps: “to inflict insults.”]

[Note: Read “against those over whom.”]

[Note: Read “to pronounce judgments,” or rather “insults.”]

But once those who dare such things have been corrected in the appropriate manner, all disturbance will cease, and the reverence required by the canons will be preserved by everyone.

### 6

When the records of the proceedings held concerning the deposition of the impious Pelagians and Coelestians—Coelestius, Pelagius, Julianus, Praesidius (Greek *Περσίδιος*, “Persidius”), Florus, Marcellianus, Orontius, and those who held the same opinions as they—had been read in the holy synod, we too judged that the decisions made concerning them by your reverence should remain valid and firm. We all agree in the judgment, holding them to be deposed.

[Note: Our manuscripts read *Laurentii* (“Laurentius”). Other books, following the Greek text, read *Orentii*. It is certain that the reading should be *Orontii*. Nestorius writes of him above, in Letter 6, §1: “Julianus, Florus, Orontius, and Fabius, claiming to be bishops of the Western provinces”; and in Letter 7: “I have often written to your blessedness concerning Julianus, Orontius, and the others.” The letter prefixed by Annianus, the distinguished follower of Pelagius, to the homilies of John Chrysostom on Matthew is addressed to this Orontius.]

[Note: “Those who held the same opinions” should be read, unless one prefers “those who shared their views.”]

So that you may know accurately all that took place, we have sent the records and the synod’s subscriptions.

[Note: What proceedings concerning the Pelagians are meant here—proceedings said to have been read in the synod and confirmed by it—is a matter of inquiry. Henricus Norisius, *History of Pelagianism*, book II, chapter 9, infers that Coelestine published certain proceedings which were later lost through the misfortunes of the times. Yet Coelestine nowhere mentions such proceedings or decrees, even when it seemed necessary for him to do so. For when Nestorius asked him once, twice, indeed repeatedly, what should be thought concerning the Pelagians, Coelestine answered his repeated requests in Letter 13, §8, only this: “These heretics also, concerning whom you wished to consult us as though we were ignorant of their proceedings, were justly expelled from their sees by a condemnation that declared their claims unjust.” Here, as also in what follows, he mentions no new action or decree of his own against the Pelagians, but is content to recall old proceedings that Nestorius could not have been unaware of, proceedings about which his predecessor Sisinnius had no need to inquire, and which Atticus, agreeing with them earlier, had sent to Rome concerning the Pelagians he had condemned. Therefore, the proceedings against the Pelagians read at the synod of Ephesus seem, with good reason, to have been none other than those mentioned by Coelestine in the aforesaid Letter 13. The same point is made by Prosper, *Against the Collator*, chapter 21, §58: “Through this man [Coelestine] the Eastern churches also were cleansed of a twofold plague, when he most gloriously assisted Cyril, bishop of Alexandria and defender of the Catholic faith, with the apostolic sword for the cutting down of Nestorian impiety; and through that same sword the Pelagians, while they allied themselves with kindred errors, were again overthrown.” At that same time Coelestine wrote both the letter to Cyril condemning the errors of Nestorius and the letter to this heresiarch confirming the condemnation of the Pelagians. Tillemont, volume XIII, page 752, thinks that no proceedings were read at Ephesus other than those of the Roman synod held under Zosimus, at which Pelagius and Coelestius were condemned again, together with Julianus and their associates, and expelled from their sees.]

And the subscription: “We pray that you may be in good health and remember us in the Lord, most beloved and most desired.” Thereafter all the bishops signed, each according to his name.

## Notice concerning the following letter and the authorities appended to it (S)

[Col. 0521]

### 1

There is no controversy concerning the authenticity of the letter. It survives not only in the collections of Dionysius Exiguus, Hadrian I, the Hispana, and Isidore, but is also cited by Prosper in *Against the Collator*, chapter 21, §§58–59; by Vincent of Lérins in the *Commonitorium*, chapter 43; by Cresconius in the *Canonical Breviary*, chapter 288; and by Photius in codices 53 and 54.

As Vincent says, Coelestine sent it to the priests of Gaul, censuring their connivance because, while abandoning the ancient faith to silence, they allowed profane novelties to arise. “He clearly declared,” says Prosper in the passage cited, “how displeasing to him was the presumption of this novelty, by which certain men dared to rise up against the ancient teachers and, through undisciplined slander, obstruct the preaching of the truth.”

On the basis of these words of Prosper, learned men think that those chiefly denounced were the men who, at Marseille, under Cassian as their teacher and master, began to oppose Augustine and preach a new doctrine. For this reason the name of Venerius, then head of the Church of Marseille, is placed before the others in the inscription of this letter. Prosper’s opinion is substantially confirmed both at the beginning and at the end of his book *Against the Collator*.

Vincent of Lérins acknowledges that such preachers, so far as his words indicate, were rightly charged with error and therefore deserved correction and prohibition from freely preaching their novelties. If they did not desist, they ought to be understood as insulting the memory of Blessed Coelestine. He praises the saying of that pope: “The matter rightly concerns us if we foster error by silence.”

After a short interval he adds: “This, then, was the blessed judgment of Blessed Coelestine: not that antiquity should cease to overwhelm novelty, but rather that novelty should cease to attack antiquity.”

Finally, he immediately adds: “Whoever resists these apostolic and catholic decrees must first of all insult the memory of Saint Coelestine, who decreed that novelty should cease to attack antiquity.”

Accordingly, either Vincent should not be counted among those innovators whom Coelestine is here rebuking, and must be regarded as a different person from the Vincent whose objections Prosper refuted in the book entitled *Against the Objections of Vincent*; or, if we should accept the contrary position defended by Cardinal Norisius in book II of his *History of Pelagianism*, pages 257 and following, we must concede that Vincent employed great skill in that passage and spoke with unworthy dissimulation.

### 2

Scholars generally assign this letter of Coelestine to the year 431. It is certainly established that it was not written until after the death of Augustine—which occurred on 28 August 430—had become widely known in Italy and Gaul.

Indeed, it is conjectured that the letter was not delivered to the Gauls long before Coelestine’s death. For Augustine’s detractors would have tried in vain to evade the commendation by which Coelestine praised him, and to claim that this praise had been offered for the merits of his earlier writings rather than for his latest works, which they considered worthy of criticism, if Coelestine had still been alive and available for consultation, so that he could have stated his judgment on the matter more clearly.

### 3

With regard to the authorities of the apostolic see appended to the letter, there is disagreement as to whether they were written and sent at the same time by Coelestine himself, or whether they belong to another author or another period. Nor has the judgment of all scholars on this matter always been the same.

If we choose to follow the older writers, from the beginning of the sixth century almost down to our own time, they must be attributed to Coelestine. For the deacon Peter and his associates, in a letter written around the year 520 to the bishops exiled in Africa, insert many words from chapters 11 and 12 of the appended material and praise them as words of the most blessed Coelestine in his letter to the Gauls.

As though they wished to anticipate the doubts of later generations, they carefully marked where the letter they had cited ended, writing as follows: “The same teacher Coelestine ends and concludes this very letter in these words: ‘Because for confessing the grace of God … [lacuna] … so that we may by no means think Catholic anything that appears contrary to the foregoing propositions.’”

Dionysius Exiguus agrees with Peter and his associates. For when he divides Coelestine’s decrees into twenty-two titles, he lists the letter to the Gauls together with the authorities of the apostolic see appended to it among the first thirteen titles or decrees of this pope, in the following form:

1. Concerning Prosper and Hilary.  
2. A remarkable statement in praise of Saint Augustine.  
3. Authorities of earlier bishops of the apostolic see concerning the grace of God.  
4. That Adam injured everyone, and so forth, as below.

Cresconius follows Dionysius, as is his custom, in the *Canonical Breviary*. From chapter 288 through chapter 298, he praises individually as decrees of Pope Coelestine the thirteen titles into which Dionysius divided the letter to the Gauls and the appended authorities, omitting only the third.

The compiler of the Hispana collection and Isidore the Merchant likewise place these thirteen titles at the beginning of the same letter.

Moreover, many serious writers, mentioned by Henricus Norisius and Paschasius Quesnellus, attribute the appended chapters to Coelestine: the deacon Florus, in the work he composed in the name of the Church of Lyons against John Scotus Eriugena; Hincmar of Reims, in *On Predestination*, chapters 21 and 22, and elsewhere; Lupus of Ferrières, abbot, in the *Collections*, question 2; Remigius, bishop of Lyons, together with his Church, in *On the Three Letters*, chapter 23, and in his short treatise *On the Absolution of the Question*; Ivo of Chartres; and others.

### 4

Later, however, many more recent scholars did not hesitate to depart from the judgment of so many eminent men. Among them were John Wendelstinus, who published at Mainz in 1525 a *Code of Canons and Papal Decrees*; the editors of the councils after Merlin—Crabbe, Surius, Nicolinus, and Labbe; Cardinal Carafa, or rather the person who, after his death, prepared the edition of the papal letters in Rome; Baronius, under the year 431; Francisco Suárez, *Prolegomena on Grace*, section 6, chapter 1, §11; Jacques Sirmond, in his notes to volume I of the *Gallican Councils*; Gerardus Vossius, book I of his *History of Pelagianism*, chapter 30; Elias du Pin, in the *Bibliotheca*; and Jacques Hyacinthe Serry, in the work entitled *Augustine Vindicated*.

Paschasius Quesnellus devoted a special dissertation to this matter, dissertation 3 in his edition of the works of Leo. Henricus Norisius treats the same question no less carefully in *Augustine Vindicated*, chapter 8, page 208.

### 5

The principal arguments that moved these learned men to deny the aforesaid chapters to Coelestine are the following.

First, their author and originator speaks of the Roman see as something foreign, not as his own. When he praises the Roman rulers, he does not call them his predecessors, contrary to the custom of other popes and even to Coelestine’s practice in this very letter to the Gauls.

Furthermore, in the preceding letter Coelestine says nothing about appending those chapters, although Roman pontiffs, whenever they attach certain writings to their letters, ordinarily give advance notice of them in the letters themselves.

In addition, when Prosper, in book 10 of *Against the Collator*, wishes to prove that the beginnings of good intentions are generated by God’s inspiration, he adduces the testimonies of Innocent and Zosimus and addresses his opponent as follows:

“Do you see your rules shattered by the solidity of invincible constitutions …? When the question between our people and the Pelagians concerned the origin of holy intentions and the beginnings of faith and love, the contest was settled by no uncertain victory and no doubtful conclusion, so that we should still have to debate the unjust peace of your agreement.”

But why would Prosper need to seek in the writings of Innocent and Zosimus against the Pelagians the means of showing that the controversy revived by Cassian had already been settled, if Coelestine had most recently ended the new controversy in explicit terms by sending these chapters to Gaul?

This argument is all the stronger because, in the same book, chapter 21, Prosper praises Coelestine for many admirable actions against the Pelagians and specifically for defending Augustine in his letter to the Gauls.

Norisius proposes another kind of argument, which he declares he has always preferred to the others. If those chapters had proceeded from Coelestine, and therefore from the apostolic see, he says that he cannot understand how Faustus of Riez, Hilary of Arles, and other bishops of Gaul could be cleared of heretical taint.

It is admitted that even after Coelestine’s death they taught certain things contrary to the rules transmitted in these chapters. The compiler of the chapters himself testifies to this in the final words of his work, stating that one must ensure “that we in no way think that what appears to be contrary to the preceding statements is Catholic.”

### 6

Paschasius Quesnellus, defending for Leo the same work that he calls the *Indiculus*, explains his view in these words:

“I consider it altogether certain that this concise *Indiculus* was compiled by Leo—not after he became pope, but during the period when, while serving only in the office of deacon, he acted as minister of ecclesiastical affairs for Pope Coelestine.”

But if the matter were so, what would prevent the same *Indiculus* from being attributed to Coelestine? It certainly happens that when a minister performs something by the authority of the person whom he serves, the work is attributed not to the minister but to the person who gave the order.

Accordingly, a secretary who writes letters at someone’s command subscribes them not in his own name but in the name of the person he serves. Thus, if Leo undertook the aforesaid *Indiculus* as Coelestine’s minister in ecclesiastical affairs, it ought to be attributed to this pope.

The earlier arguments therefore return against this position: they show that the work fits neither Coelestine nor his period. We shall confirm this same point from the material appended to it.

### 7

Many others attribute the same work to Prosper. First, they observe in it a certain agreement of language and thought with his other writings.

Second, the very testimonies of Innocent, Zosimus, and the African councils on which the propositions of the aforesaid *Indiculus* depend are brought forward by Prosper in his book *Against the Collator*. Indeed, he seems to have wished to summarize briefly in this *Indiculus* what he had explained at greater length in that book.

Moreover, this *Indiculus* was collected with the purpose of defending the memory of so great a teacher against those who persisted in opposing Augustine. That Prosper undertook this task of defending Augustine against his newer critics in a special way is shown by his book *Against the Collator*, as well as by his responses to the chapters of the Gauls, to the extracts of the Genoese, and to the objections of Vincent.

He himself indicates in the preface to the final work that this task had been entrusted and assigned to him by the Roman pontiff, where he testifies that he is defending the faith against the Pelagians on the authority of the apostolic see.

Thus Hincmar of Reims, in the letter prefixed to his first work *On Predestination*, writes to King Charles shortly after the beginning:

“After his [Augustine’s] death, certain envious men undertook to collect, chapter by chapter, passages from his writings … These lies of his rivals Saint Prosper, by delegation of the Roman see through Pope Coelestine, demonstrated in a Catholic and prudent style to be false and recklessly alleged.”

### 8

While Coelestine was still alive, Prosper went to Rome with his associate Hilary and obtained a letter to the Gauls (Letter 21, §2). In it the praised pontiff sharply rebuked Augustine’s critics and testified that this teacher had never been touched even by the rumor of an unfavorable suspicion, but had everywhere been held in both love and honor by everyone. He therefore seemed to have left his rivals nothing that they could allege against him.

“But,” says Prosper in *Against the Collator*, chapter 21, §59, “against the trumpet of this most illustrious praise, against the dignity of this most sacred testimony, can anyone dare to utter the murmur of a malicious interpretation and cast a cloud of oblique ambiguity over a clear and most sincere judgment, so that, because the title of the books under discussion is not expressly given in the pope’s letter [that of Coelestine], it may appear that those books [the books being called into question] were not approved, and that this praise of Augustine was bestowed for the merits of his earlier writings?”

Prosper was not content merely to demonstrate from the fullest agreement of Augustine’s latest books with his earlier writings how unjust and foolish this sinister interpretation was. To leave his opponents no avenue of escape, he thought he should also arrange for Augustine’s teaching to be approved by Pope Xystus.

Hence he adds (§60):

“Lest this be secured by the plots of hypocrites”—that is, lest Augustine’s latest books be thought not to have been approved by the apostolic see—“we trust that, through the Lord’s protection, what he accomplished through Innocent, Zosimus, Boniface, and Coelestine, he will also accomplish through Xystus; and that, in guarding the Lord’s flock, this portion of glory has been reserved for that pontiff: just as those others drove away the manifest wolves, so may he drive away the hidden ones.”

Thus, in order more easily to induce Xystus to do this, Prosper may reasonably be thought to have composed the *Indiculus*. In it he demonstrated that the doctrine criticized by his opponents in Augustine’s latest books agreed with the definitions of the earlier bishops of the apostolic see.

The fact that Xystus confirmed this *Indiculus*, so that what it teaches in explicit chapters concerning grace and free will thereafter became the proper doctrine of the Roman Church, may indicate that Prosper successfully achieved what he had hoped for from that pontiff.

For Hormisdas writes to Possessor in Letter 122:

“Although what the Roman—that is, Catholic—Church follows and preserves concerning free will and the grace of God can be learned from various books of Blessed Augustine, and especially from those addressed to Hilary and Prosper, nevertheless explicit chapters are also contained in the ecclesiastical archives.”

Learned men understand no other chapters to be designated here than those expressly set out in our *Indiculus*.

That the matter for whose settlement our *Indiculus* was composed had not been brought to an end by Coelestine is clearly taught by Prosper in the cited book *Against the Collator*, chapter 22. Speaking of Augustine’s critics, he adds:

“Since they have not yet been separated from fraternal fellowship, their intention should rather be tolerated than their correction despaired of, until the Lord, through the leaders of the Church and the legitimate ministers of his judgments, settles these matters which have been disturbed by the pride of a few and the ignorance of certain others. With God’s help, it should be our endeavor to repay hatred with love through quiet and moderate patience.”

But if Coelestine, as leader of the Church and legitimate minister of God’s judgments, had already pronounced judgment on the disputed matter and explicitly declared that he in no way considered Catholic whatever appeared contrary to the statements prefixed in the *Indiculus*, and if this had been promulgated in Gaul, there would have been no reason for Prosper to hope so well for those who persisted in defending positions contrary to those statements, or to deal with them so moderately.

Certainly, once this had been established, there would have been no reason for Augustine’s rivals to claim that only his earlier books, and not his latest ones, had been approved by Coelestine.

Thus it is plainly confirmed that the frequently mentioned *Indiculus*, though already completed, was by no means compiled with Coelestine’s authority or at his command.

### 9

Gerardus Vossius holds that, in preparing this work, Prosper joined to himself not only Hilary but also other defenders of Augustine.

He offers no other reason for this opinion than that Prosper uses the plural number and says, “we should join,” “we demonstrate in a concise *Indiculus*,” and so forth, rather than “I should join” or “I demonstrate.”

But if this argument is valid, it must likewise be said that Prosper did not answer the objections of Vincent alone but together with associates, since in the preface to that book he consistently speaks in the plural: “let us unfold,” “let us judge,” “we defend,” and similar expressions. We should therefore judge such matters, in our view, to be of the kind contained in the diabolical *Indiculus*.

### 10

Although it is clear that Pope Celestine’s letter and the appended *Indiculus* belong to different years, we have nowhere found either document published separately. As we stated earlier, from the beginning of the sixth century the African bishops, followed by Dionysius Exiguus and innumerable others, treated both documents as one writing of Celestine. Hence it may reasonably be inferred that Prosper fused them into a single whole, so that a full and integral defense of Augustine’s books and of the doctrine affirmed in them might at once be supported both by Celestine’s judgment and by the consensus of the earlier bishops of the Apostolic See. For this reason we considered it irreverent to separate what we have always read joined together, and what we believe was combined with the approval and consent of the Apostolic See itself. Nor did we think that the titles prefixed to it by Dionysius Exiguus should be removed, so that the reliability of the ancients who used them might be established.

### 11

Henricus Norisius observed (*Vindicatio Augustiniana*, p. 213) that the same chapters had been inserted, beginning with chapter 22, in the book *On the Dogmas of the Church*, which is attributed to Gennadius of Marseilles. But our scholars, who prepared the latest edition of Augustine [*Appendix*, vol. VIII of Augustine], noted that this had been done contrary to the evidence of the ancient manuscripts and therefore suppressed those chapters. The aforementioned cardinal also pointed out that the final chapters—namely, from chapter 11 to the end—had been copied word for word, together with forty other verses from book 3, chapter 3, of Augustine’s *Against Julian*, in the homily of St. John Chrysostom on Adam and Eve, vol. II of the Basel edition. Hence it is clear that that homily is a cento.

### 12

This concluding clause discusses what are called the “deeper and more difficult parts” of the questions that arise. Some think that this passage leaves to theological debate those points concerning grace and the predestination of the saints which Augustine defends as belonging to the faith. But how far the Roman Church is from their opinion is shown adequately by Hormisdas alone. In the passage cited above, he teaches that what the Roman—that is, Catholic—Church follows and maintains concerning free choice and the grace of God can be learned from various books of blessed Augustine, especially those addressed to Hilary and Prosper.

The learned Norisius, however, in the *Vindications* mentioned above, p. 216, thinks that the “deeper questions” are those in which original sin and the manner of its transmission are discussed, along with concupiscence and the other miseries that are punishments of original sin. He believes that the author of the *Indiculus* omitted an assertion of these matters, not because he regarded them as *ἀδιαφορὰν*—“indifferent matters”—or as left open to party debate, but because he judged them unnecessary for the time and for the purpose then in view.

“The author,” he says, “of those chapters intends to teach the Massilians how weak are the powers of free choice and how necessary grace is. But since there was no controversy between Augustine and the Massilians concerning original sin, the manner of its transmission, or the miseries that follow it, he therefore said, ‘WE DO NOT NEED TO ESTABLISH’ these things. That means that he did not wish to formulate canons concerning them, because they did not bear upon the controversy then being conducted with the Massilians—not that he wished to leave them to the free assent or dissent of disputants, which is the foolish interpretation of recent writers.”

If, however, we examine the force of the words “the deeper and more difficult parts of the questions that arise,” we must admit that they suggest something further. It is appropriate to understand by “questions that arise” questions treated not primarily in themselves, but, as it were, incidentally and therefore not necessarily. When we hear of the “deeper and more difficult parts” of those questions, everyone understands that the reference is to matters less obvious to each person than those already explained.

Paschasius Quesnellus, discussing this passage at length and in detail at the end of his edition of Leo’s works (*Dissertation* 3, part II, chapter 2), thinks that the deeper questions designated here can be recognized from these words of Augustine, *To Boniface*, book III, chapter 8:

“When, therefore, the Pelagians are pressed by these and similar testimonies and declarations of the truth . . . they introduce the clouds of other questions . . . concerning the praise of creation, the praise of marriage, the praise of the law, the praise of free choice, and the praise of the saints.”

And in chapter 10:

“The Pelagians certainly add to the clouds of their hiding places an unnecessary question concerning the origin of the soul . . . For they say that we maintain the transmission of souls along with the transmission of sin.”

Concerning this last question, the bishops exiled in Sardinia explain their position to Fulgentius, *Letter* 15, no. 10, as follows:

“We ought either to leave the question of souls unspoken, or to discuss it without contention . . . especially since the faithful may remain ignorant of it without harm to the faith.”

Fulgentius himself adds, *On Predestination and Grace*, book III, chapter 8:

“Seeing that the depth of this question was inscrutable to him, blessed Augustine wished to offer no definite judgment concerning it.”

There can be no doubt that the same and similar matters are indicated there.

---

## LETTER XXI. OF BLESSED POPE CELESTINE I TO THE BISHOPS OF GAUL

I. On Prosper and Hilary, who accuse certain presbyters of Gaul as followers of Pelagius.  
II. A remarkable affirmation in praise of Saint Augustine.  
III. Authorities of former bishops of the Apostolic See concerning the grace of God.  
IV. That Adam injured everyone, and that no one can be saved except by the grace of Christ.  
V. That no one is good by his own powers, except through participation in him who alone is good.  
VI. That unless we are continually aided by the grace of God, we cannot avoid the devil’s snares.  
VII. That through Christ we make good use of free choice.  
VIII. That all the merits of the saints are gifts of God.  
IX. That every holy thought and movement of a devout will comes from God.  
X. That grace not only forgives sins but also assists us not to commit them, and enables the law to be fulfilled—not, as Pelagius says, “easily,” as though without God’s grace it could be fulfilled only with greater difficulty.  
XI. That, besides the decrees of the Apostolic See, all the prayers of the Church proclaim the grace of Christ, by which the human race is restored and brought back from eternal condemnation [addition of Isidore Mercator].  
XII. That the prescribed purification of those being baptized also bears witness to God’s grace, since unclean spirits are driven out of them by exorcisms and insufflations.  
XIII. That deeper questions should neither be despised nor asserted categorically.

To our most beloved brothers Venerius, Marinus, Leontius, Auxonius, Arcadius, and Fillucius, and to the other bishops of Gaul, Celestine.

### Chapter I

#### 1

The words of the apostolic command are that we must be without offense among Jews and Gentiles (1 Corinthians 10:32). Every Christian guards this with the whole strength of his soul. Since this is so, a person who refuses even to display it toward the faithful may face no small danger before God. For the Lord’s word in the Gospel testifies how such things grieve us—things that, when done by Christian leaders, strike Christian hearts. The Savior himself says that it is better for the one who causes one of the little ones to stumble to be cast into the depths of the sea (Matthew 18:6). Let us therefore ask what punishment awaits the person for whom we read that such a penalty is better.

#### 2

Our sons Prosper and Hilary are present with us; their concern for our God is deserving of praise. They have reported against certain presbyters there—who, I do not know by what permission, are allowed to promote dissension within the Churches—that, bringing undisciplined questions into public discussion, they stubbornly preach things opposed to the truth. We more justly lay this to your charge, since they have the opportunity to dispute before you.

We read that “a disciple is not above his teacher” (Luke 6:40)—that is, no one ought to claim a teaching for himself as an insult to his teachers. For we know that these teachers themselves have been appointed by our God for instruction, since, as the Apostle says, the third place within the Church is assigned to teachers (1 Corinthians 12:28).

What hope is there where, while the teachers are silent, those speak who, if this is so, were not their disciples? I fear that silence here amounts to connivance. I fear that the very people who permit them to speak in this way are speaking through them. In such cases silence is not free from suspicion, because truth would come forward if falsehood were displeasing. The matter rightly concerns us if by our silence we encourage error.

Therefore, let such men be corrected. They should not be allowed to speak freely according to their will.

Let novelty cease, if this is how matters stand, to attack antiquity; let unrest cease to disturb the peace of the Churches. They often attempt to plunge into shipwreck those whom a secure station keeps safe within the harbor. Secure indeed is the station of all whose footprints remain unmoved in steady steps.

The persons mentioned above have appealed to the Apostolic See, complaining to us about this very disturbance that it is attempting to cause. Understand, dearest brothers, that this matter has been taken up for the peace of the Catholic people. Let them know—if indeed they are regarded as presbyters—that in dignity they are subject to you. Let them know that all who teach wrongly ought rather to learn more and more than to teach.

For what are you doing in the Churches if they possess the chief authority to preach? Unless perhaps this consideration stands in the way: that it has not yet been established by authority or reason that some of the brethren, recently admitted, perhaps, from the company of the laity into our college, know what they ought to claim for themselves.

Much has already been said about these matters at the time when we sent a written reply to our brother Tuentius. Even now, however, repeating our admonition, we say again and again: such men must be avoided—men who strive throughout the world to sow something other than what that farmer of ours commanded.

Nor can we be surprised that they now dare to attempt such things against the living, since they also strive to scatter the memory of brothers who have fallen asleep.

### Chapter II

#### 3

We have always regarded Augustine, a man of holy memory, as belonging to our communion on account of his life and merits, and never did even a rumor of sinister suspicion touch him. We remember that he was once a man of such learning that, even before our time, he was always counted by my predecessors among the best teachers.

All therefore formed a good judgment of him in common, since everywhere he was held in love and honor by everyone. How then can such people be resisted—people whom we see growing wickedly? It is impious for religious souls to endure these things. Since they are our members, their affliction ought also to make us suffer, although blessedness remains promised to all who are proved to endure persecution for righteousness’ sake (Matthew 5:10).

What the Lord promises them in the future is declared by what follows. The matter at issue is not that of those alone who are acting; the universal Church is shaken by any novelty. Let us understand that you too are displeased by these things, which displease us. We shall be able to prove this only if, after imposing silence upon the wicked, complaints about such a matter cease in the future.

May God keep you safe, dearest brothers.

---

## Authorities of Former Bishops of the Apostolic See Concerning the Grace of God

### Chapter III

#### 4
