Since no one who boasts of the Catholic name, while lingering in the condemned opinions or perversity or ignorance of heretics, dares to oppose devout teachers—and since, although they do not hesitate to anathematize Pelagius and Coelestius, they nevertheless contradict our teachers as though they had exceeded what was necessary, while professing that they follow and approve only what the most sacred See of blessed Peter, through the ministry of its bishops, decreed and taught against the enemies of God’s grace—it was necessary to inquire carefully what the rulers of the Roman Church had judged concerning the heresy that had arisen in their time, and what they had held should be believed concerning God’s grace against the most harmful defenders of free choice.

We therefore joined to these certain statements of the African councils, which the apostolic bishops made their own when they approved them. So that those who are uncertain about any point may be more fully instructed, we set forth in a concise summary the constitutions of the holy Fathers. Anyone who is not excessively contentious may recognize that the coherence of all the disputations depends upon the brevity of the authorities set out below, and that no ground for contradiction remains if one believes and speaks together with Catholics.

### Chapter IV

#### 5

Pope Innocent of blessed memory declares that, through Adam’s transgression, all human beings lost their natural ability and innocence, and that no one can rise by free choice from the depth of his ruin unless the grace of the merciful God raises him up. He says in his letter to the Council of Carthage:

“For that man, who had once possessed free choice, used his own goods too heedlessly; falling, he was plunged into the depths of transgression, and found no means by which he could rise from it. Deceived forever in his own freedom, he would have lain crushed beneath the ruin of this fall, unless the coming of Christ had restored him by his grace. Through the cleansing of the new birth, Christ washed away every former fault in the bath of his baptism.”

### Chapter V

#### 6

No one is good by himself, unless he who alone is good grants him participation in himself. This is affirmed by the judgment of the same pontiff in the same writings, where he says:

“Can we henceforth judge that anything right is present in the minds of those who think that they themselves are owed what makes them good, and do not consider him whose grace they receive every day, while they trust that they can attain so much without him?”

### Chapter VI

#### 7

Even a person renewed by the grace of baptism is not capable of overcoming the devil’s snares and conquering the desires of the flesh unless, through God’s daily assistance, he has received perseverance in a good way of life. The teaching of the same bishop confirms this in the same writings:

“For although he had redeemed man from his former sins, yet, knowing that he could sin again, he preserved many remedies for his restoration, so that he might correct him even after these things, providing him with daily cures. Unless we rely upon and trust in these, we shall in no way be able to conquer human errors. For it is necessary that, by whose help we conquer, without that same help we should again be conquered.”

### Chapter VII

#### 8

No one uses free choice well except through Christ. The same teacher proclaims this in the letter sent to the Council of Milevis, saying:

“Recognize at last, O perverse doctrine of the most depraved minds, that freedom itself so deceived the first man that, while he used its reins too indulgently, he fell through presumption into transgression. He could not be rescued from it unless the coming of Christ the Lord, through the providence of regeneration, restored the condition of his original freedom.”

### Chapter VIII

#### 9

All the endeavors, works, and merits of the saints must be referred to the glory and praise of God, because no one pleases him from any other source than what he himself has given. The authoritative teaching of Pope Zosimus, of blessed memory, directs us to this judgment. Writing to the bishops of the whole world, he says:

“We, however, by God’s prompting—for all good things must be referred to their author, from whom they arise—reported everything to the conscience of our brothers and fellow bishops.”

The African bishops revered this speech, radiant with the purest light of truth, with such honor that they wrote to the same man:

“But what you placed in the letter that you arranged to be sent to all the provinces, saying, ‘Nevertheless, by God’s prompting,’ and so forth, we understood as having been said in such a way that, passing swiftly as though with a sword of truth, you cut off those who exalt the freedom of human choice against God’s assistance.

“For what have you done more by free choice than to refer everything to the conscience of our humility? Yet you rightly and wisely saw that this was done by God’s prompting, and you truthfully and confidently said so. This is because the will is prepared by the Lord (Proverbs 8:25, according to the Septuagint), and, so that they may do something good, he himself touches the hearts of his children with paternal inspirations. For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God (Romans 8:14). Thus we recognize that our free choice is not absent, yet we do not doubt that in every movement of the human will toward what is good, his assistance is more powerful.”

### Chapter IX

#### 10

God works in the hearts of human beings and in free choice itself in such a way that holy thought, devout counsel, and every movement of a good will come from God, because through him we can do something good, while without him we can do nothing.

The same teacher instructed us to make this profession when, speaking to the bishops of the whole world concerning the assistance of divine grace, he said:

“What time, then, intervenes in which we do not need his assistance? In all actions, affairs, thoughts, and movements, the helper and protector must be entreated. For it is arrogant for human nature to presume anything for itself, while the Apostle cries out: ‘Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the principalities and powers of this air, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places’ (Ephesians 6:12).

“And as he himself says again: ‘Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God, through Jesus Christ our Lord’ (Romans 7:24).

“And again: ‘By the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me was not empty; but I labored more than all of them—not I, however, but the grace of God with me’ (1 Corinthians 15:10).”

### Chapter X

#### 11

“Also, what was established within the decrees of the Council of Carthage, we embrace as proper to the Apostolic See—namely, what was defined in the third chapter:

‘If anyone says that the grace of God by which we are justified through Jesus Christ our Lord is effective only for the remission of sins already committed, and not also as assistance to prevent their commission, let him be anathema.’

“And again, in the fourth chapter:

‘If anyone says that the grace of God assists us through Jesus Christ only because through it the understanding of the commandments is revealed and opened to us, so that we know what we ought to seek and what we ought to avoid, but does not grant us that, once we have recognized what ought to be done, we may also love and be able to do it, let him be anathema.’

“For when the Apostle says, ‘Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up’ (1 Corinthians 8:1), it is exceedingly impious to believe that we have Christ’s grace for the knowledge that puffs us up, but not for the love that builds us up, since both are gifts of God: knowing what we ought to do, and loving so that we may do it. Thus, when love builds up, knowledge cannot puff up.

“Just as it is written of God, ‘He teaches human beings knowledge’ (Psalm 93:10), so it is also written: ‘Love is from God’ (1 John 4:7).

“Likewise, in the fifth chapter:

‘If anyone says that the grace of justification is given to us for this reason: so that, through grace, we may more easily fulfill what we are commanded to do by free choice—as though, even if grace were not given, we could indeed fulfill the divine commandments without it, not easily but nevertheless could do so—let him be anathema.

“For the Lord was speaking of the fruits of the commandments when he did not say, “Without me you can do it with greater difficulty,” but said, “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).’”

### Chapter XI

#### 12

Besides these inviolable decrees of the most blessed Apostolic See, by which our most devout Fathers, rejecting the pestilential choice of novelty, taught us to refer to the grace of Christ both the beginnings of a good will, the growth of worthy endeavors, and perseverance in them to the end, let us also consider the solemn prayers of the priests. These prayers, handed down by the Apostles, are celebrated uniformly throughout the whole world and in every Catholic Church, so that the law of prayer establishes the law of belief.

For when the bishops of holy peoples carry out the commission entrusted to them, they plead the cause of the human race before the divine mercy. With the whole Church groaning together with them, they ask and pray that faith may be granted to unbelievers; that idolaters may be freed from the errors of their impiety; that, once the veil of their hearts has been removed, the light of truth may appear to the Jews; that heretics may recover through reception of the Catholic faith; that schismatics may receive the spirit of renewed charity; that remedies of repentance may be granted to the fallen; and, finally, that the heavenly court of mercy may be opened to catechumens brought to the sacraments of regeneration.

That these things are not requested from the Lord superficially or in vain is shown by the effects of the things themselves. For God deigns to draw very many people from every kind of error, transferring them, once rescued from the power of darkness, into the kingdom of the Son of his love (Colossians 1:13), and making them vessels of mercy out of vessels of wrath (Romans 9:22). This is so clearly perceived to be wholly the work of God that thanksgiving and a confession of praise are always offered to God, who brings it about, for the illumination or correction of such people.

### Chapter XII

#### 13

We do not contemplate without serious attention what the holy Church uniformly does throughout the world concerning those who are to be baptized. Whether infants or young adults come to the sacrament of regeneration, they do not first approach the font of life before the unclean spirit has been driven out from them by the exorcisms and insufflations of the clergy. Then it truly becomes apparent how “the ruler of this world” is cast out (John 12:31), how “the strong man” is first bound (Matthew 12:29), and how his vessels are afterward plundered (Mark 3:27)—transferred into the possession of the victor, who “leads captivity captive” (Ephesians 4:8) and “gives gifts to human beings” (Psalm 67:19).

---

### Editorial and textual notes

- **Address, [Col. 0527D, 0528D].** The editions of Merlin, Crabbe, and Rome read *Sillucius*. The later editions, with the Hadrian collection, read *Filtanius*. We retain *Fillucius* with the uncorrupted royal exemplar of the Dionysian collection and with the manuscripts of the Spanish and Isidorian collections.

- **§1, [Col. 0528D].** Labbe reads “we ought” (*debere*), against the other books.

- **§2, third place for teachers, [Col. 0529C].** The passage is missing in the royal manuscript. Celestine refers to Paul’s words: “And God has appointed some in the Church, first apostles, second prophets, third teachers.”

- **§2, encouraging error, [Col. 0529C].** This is the reading of the royal Dionysian exemplar; Vincent of Lérins reads no differently. In the Hadrian collection “we encourage error” (*faveamus errori*) was substituted; the author of the Spanish and Isidorian collection, and consequently the editors of this letter, adopted that reading.

- **§2, “They should not be allowed to speak freely according to their will,” [Col. 0529C–0530C].** On these words Vincent of Lérins raises this question: “Perhaps someone may doubt who those are whom he forbids to have freedom of speech at will: the preachers of antiquity or the inventors of novelty.” He immediately adds: “Let him himself [Celestine] speak and himself resolve his readers’ doubt.” For what follows is: “Let novelty, if this is how matters stand, cease to attack antiquity.” That is, “if it is so that, as certain persons accuse your cities and provinces before me, you permit them by harmful dissimulation to agree with certain novelties, let novelty cease, if this is so, to attack antiquity.” Henry Noris (*History of Pelagianism*, book II, pp. 429 and 250) maintains that Vincent ingeniously twists Celestine’s words against Augustine’s teaching and its defenders. Yet it is plain that Celestine adds “if this is how matters stand” not because he doubted which party—the opponents of Augustine’s doctrine or its defenders—were to be considered innovators, but because prudence dictated that he should not condemn the presbyters whom Prosper and Hilary had reported as fostering dissension in the Churches unless the report proved true. It is no less evident that Celestine ascribes to Augustine the praise of defending ancient doctrine, since, he says, “we remember that he was once of such learning that even before our time he was always counted by my predecessors among the best teachers.” Otherwise he would concede that a teacher of novelty had been counted by his predecessors among the best teachers. Nor should we readily believe that Vincent was so blind as to miss so clear a fact, or so deceitful as to try to persuade readers otherwise, or so ill-disposed toward others as to suppose that he could persuade them of this against manifest truth.

- **§2, presbyterial dignity, [Col. 0530C].** The printed editions read “let them be considered in presbyterial dignity”; this is corrected from the manuscripts.

- **§2, reply to Tuentius, [Col. 0530C–0530D].** Whether the reply to Tuentius’s writings was given concerning those whom Celestine had just complained were admitted from the laity into the episcopal college, or concerning those whom he had learned were preaching novelties; and whether this Tuentius was the man whom Zosimus, in Letter 4, no. 4, forbids to be received in any ecclesiastical rank because Proculus, bishop of Marseilles, had ordained him unlawfully—these matters are left to others’ judgment. It is nevertheless probable that this Tuentius was not different from that man, and that the reply to his writings concerned those who introduced undisciplined questions into public discussion. That reply is no longer extant. Further, it is clearer than daylight that by those who attempt to introduce new doctrines into the Church Celestine means not Hilary or Prosper, but those who strive to dissipate and defame even the memory of brethren at rest, specifically Augustine.

- **§3, “always,” [Col. 0530D].** *Always* is restored from Merlin and the manuscripts; Crabbe and subsequent editions had omitted it.

- **§3, “not the case of those acting alone,” [Col. 0530D].** In the manuscripts of the Isidorian collection the reading is *sola* (“alone”); Merlin has *solarum* (“of those alone”). The other printed editions then add *quando* (“when”). That word is absent from the manuscripts, but in one of them *sola cum* entered in place of *solorum*; *quando* probably arose from this *cum*. Celestine’s meaning is clearer in this syllogism: every novelty assails the universal Church; the case under consideration has the flavor of novelty; therefore it is not the case of persons acting or litigating alone, but of the whole Church.

- **Heading before the *Indiculus*, [Col. 0531C–0531D].** The word “They begin,” marking the following writing as distinct from the preceding letter, occurs in every exemplar of the Dionysian or Hadrian collections. It was deleted by the compiler of the Spanish collection, whom Isidore followed. In the old editions of the councils and in the Roman edition this whole title was omitted. Quesnel and Labbe, following Sirmond, add here “and concerning free choice of the will,” but this is absent from the manuscripts both here and in the general index of titles. At the end of this *Indiculus* those same manuscripts do read: “The authorities of former bishops of the Apostolic See concerning the grace of God and free choice are completed.” But the title prefixed at the beginning is more authentic, as is shown by the collector himself: he declares that he undertook this work in order to make known, against the most harmful defenders of free choice, what the rulers of the Roman Church had judged concerning the grace of God—not adding “and concerning free choice.”

- **§4, [Col. 0531D].** The early editions, like the manuscripts, read “our teachers” (*magistris tamen nostris*).

- **§5, citation, [Col. 0531D].** Innocent, Letter 29, no. 6.

- **§5, “free choice,” [Col. 0531D].** The word *olim* (“formerly”) is missing in Merlin and the manuscripts. Quesnel, as in Innocent’s letter, substitutes: “For that man, formerly perverted through free choice” (*Libero enim arbitrio olim ille perversus*), and retains that same reading here, despite manuscripts which oppose it no less here than in Innocent’s letter. If the editor were permitted to alter the text on his own authority, he would prefer, as stated, “For that man, formerly permitted through free choice” (*Libero enim arbitrio . . . permissus*).

- **§5, “could rise,” [Col. 0531D–0532C].** Sirmond, Labbe, and Quesnel, after the old council and Roman editions, read “could rise again” (*resurgere*), against the manuscripts, with which Prosper, *Against Cassian*, chapter 5, no. 15; Augustine, *To Boniface*, book II, chapter 4, no. 6; and Innocent agree.

- **§5, “would have lain crushed,” [Col. 0532C].** Thus the manuscripts, except that they read *latuisset* (“would have remained hidden”), as does Prosper in the Corbie manuscript of *Against Cassian*, and, as has been observed, as Augustine in *To Boniface*, book II, in several manuscripts. Merlin reads *hujus ruina latuisset oppressis*; Crabbe, *hujus ruina jacuisset oppressus*; the Roman edition, *huic ruinae jacuisset oppressus*; Sirmond, Labbe, and Quesnel, *huic ruinae subjacuisset oppressus*.

- **§5, Christ’s grace, [Col. 0532C–0532D].** The manuscripts consistently read “after Christ’s coming had raised him by his own grace,” whether here, in the passages of Augustine and Prosper where the same words are quoted, or in Innocent’s letter itself. Sirmond and Quesnel, with the council and Roman editions, read “through his grace.”

- **§6, [Col. 0532D].** The council, Roman, and Sirmond editions read “Can we?” (*Numquid*); this is corrected from the uncorrupted royal Dionysian exemplar, which agrees with the cited letter of Innocent. Further, the Coislin manuscript, with one Harleian manuscript, reads “who think that what makes them good is owed to them.” The verb *deberi* (“to be owed”) is also found in the early council and Roman editions, as in most manuscripts.

- **§6, omitted words, [Col. 0532D].** Some words of Innocent are here omitted, whether deliberately for brevity or through scribal error because of the repeated word *consequuntur* (“they receive”).

- **§7, citation and reading, [Col. 0532D].** Innocent, Letter 29, no. 6. Merlin and Crabbe, like the manuscripts, read *redimeret* (“had redeemed”).

- **§8, [Col. 0532D].** The Roman edition, following Merlin and Crabbe, reads “by grace, [one] makes good use of free choice”; the text here reads “through Christ.”

- **§9, [Col. 0533C–0533D].** Peter the deacon and his companions, in their letter to the African exiles in Sardinia, preserved in Fulgentius, Letter 16, chapter 8, no. 26, take these words as though they referred to the immediately preceding passage from Innocent and quote them thus: “Likewise Innocent, bishop of the Apostolic See, in his letter to the Council of Milevis: ‘All endeavors and all works and merits . . . except from what he himself has given.’” They then add: “The African councils explain this more carefully and clearly in their letter to Pope Zosimus, repeating the pope’s own judgment: ‘But what you placed in the letter,’ and so forth, as below.”

- **§9, African letter, [Col. 0533D].** Thus the manuscripts read; the printed editions read “they wrote back.” The cited writings of Zosimus and of the Africans have not come down to us.

- **§9, “the hearts of his children,” [Col. 0533D].** The printed editions read “the hearts of the faithful.” The manuscripts more aptly read “the hearts of his children,” as does Prosper, *Against Cassian*, chapter 5, no. 17.

- **§11, [Col. 0533D–0534D].** The editor of the Roman edition observed that this decree and those following occur in the Council of Milevis. In editions of the councils they are indeed printed under the name of the Second Council of Milevis, held in 416, canons 3, 4, and 5. But they belong to the Council of Carthage held on the Kalends of May 418, as is clear both from chapters 111, 112, and 113 of the *Code of Canons of the African Church* and from chapter 13 of the old exemplars of the code published by Quesnel, as well as from these words of Zosimus. Prosper, *Against Cassian*, chapter 5, praises the middle of the three decrees in rhetorical form: “The African councils erred when by their decrees they established that both are gifts of God: knowing what we should do, and loving in order that we may do it.” Moreover, the words “Also, what was established within the decrees of the Council of Carthage,” and what follows, must be understood as spoken and continued by Zosimus himself, not by the collector of these authorities. The words “we embrace as proper to the Apostolic See” suit not the collector but the bishop of the Apostolic See. The three chapters called here 3, 4, and 5 by Zosimus are called 4, 5, and 6 in Quesnel’s code.

- **§11, “through it,” [Col. 0534D].** In the exemplars of the Hadrian collection, as in Quesnel’s code, the reading is “through him” (*per ipsum*). But in the *Code of Canons of the African Church*, both Latin and Greek, it is “through it” (*per ipsam*), as Dionysius reads and as still appears in the royal exemplar of his collection.

- **§12, apostolic prayers, [Col. 0535C–0535D].** These prayers were handed down specifically by Paul in 1 Timothy 2:1. After citing the words, the author of the books *On the Calling of the Gentiles*, book I, chapter 12, adds: “Therefore the Apostle commanded—or rather, the Lord speaking in the Apostle commanded—that supplications, petitions, and thanksgivings be made for all human beings, for kings, and for those in high position. The devotion of all priests and all faithful so observes this law of supplication that there is no part of the world in which prayers of this kind are not celebrated by Christian peoples. Thus the Church everywhere entreats God not only for the saints and those already regenerated in Christ, but also for all unbelievers . . . for Jews, heretics, and schismatics. Clearly the just Lord wishes prayers to be made to him for all human beings, so that, when we see countless people rescued from such profound evils, we may not doubt that God has granted what he was asked to grant.” Augustine uses the same argument more than once. It is enough to cite his words from Letter 107, formerly 207, to Vitalis: “Bring your disputations against the prayers of the Church. And when you hear God’s priest at the altar exhorting God’s people to pray for unbelievers, that he may convert them to the faith; for catechumens, that he may inspire in them the desire for regeneration; and for the faithful, that by his gift they may persevere in what they have begun to be—mock these devout utterances.” And in no. 26: “Will you forbid the Church to pray for unbelievers, that they may become believers; for those who are unwilling to believe, that they may be willing to believe; and so forth?” These passages attest the antiquity of the rite which the Church still observes on Good Friday.

- **§12, “reception,” [Col. 0535D].** The manuscripts of the Hadrian collection read *perfectione* (“perfection”); the royal Dionysian manuscript more correctly reads *perceptione* (“reception”).

- **§12, repentance, [Col. 0535D].** All the manuscripts read “that remedies of repentance may be granted”; the printed editions read “that a remedy may be conferred.”

14. Therefore, strengthened by these ecclesiastical rules and by testimonies drawn from divine authority [Note: In one manuscript, Remigius, and in the Coislin manuscript, as in the printed editions, *confortati* (“strengthened”). In others, *conformati* (“formed according to”). With the Regius manuscript, we prefer *confirmati* (“confirmed”). This passage has a certain affinity with the passage with which Augustine closes his book *On the Gift of Perseverance*, where he recalls the aim of his work in these words: “I think I have taught sufficiently—or rather, more than sufficiently—that it is God’s gift both to begin believing in the Lord and to remain in the Lord to the end. They also concede that the other goods belonging to a devout life, by which God is rightly worshiped, are God’s gifts, even those for whose sake we undertake this work.”], with the Lord’s help, we have been confirmed, so that we profess God to be the author of every good disposition and action, and of all the endeavors and virtues by which one strives toward God from the beginning of faith; and so that we do not doubt that all human merits are preceded by his grace [Note: In Sirmond and Labbe, *omnia* (“all”) is lacking; all our manuscripts, together with the other editions, contain it. In Fulgentius, *Letter* 16 of Peter the Deacon and his companions to the Africans, chapter 8, one reads *hominis omnis merito* (“by every human merit”), a reading that could be accepted insofar as it expresses a view primarily contrary to Cassian’s comment. For Cassian, as Prosper testifies in book 5 of his work *Against Cassian*, wanted both groups to be equally in error: those who wished to say that good will arises from grace, and those who thought that grace depended on good will. He decided that both positions should be accepted, so that sometimes grace precedes good will—as in Paul and Matthew—and sometimes depends upon good will—as in Zacchaeus and the Thief. The present statement plainly opposes that view, since it teaches that not the merits of this or that person, but the merits of every human being, are preceded by God’s grace. Nevertheless, as I have said, all the manuscripts read *omnia* (“all”). Prosper also notes, in Augustine’s *Letter* 225, those who do not think rightly because they refuse to admit that all good merits are preceded by grace and bestowed by it so that they may exist.], through whom it comes about that we both begin to will and to do something good (Philippians 2:13).

By this help and gift of God free will is not taken away but set free, so that what was dark becomes bright, what was crooked becomes straight, what was weak becomes sound, and what was imprudent becomes prudent. For God’s goodness toward all human beings is so great that he wishes the merits that are his gifts to be ours, and for the things he has bestowed he will give eternal rewards. He acts within us so that we may both will and do what he wills, and he does not allow the gifts he has granted us to remain idle within us, but requires them to be exercised and not neglected [Note: In the Regius manuscript, *non negligenda* (“not to be neglected”) is absent.], so that we may be fellow-workers with God’s grace [Note: Labbe, following Sirmond: *operatores* (“workers”). The reading *cooperatores* (“fellow-workers”), found in the other books, should be retained. First the text speaks of grace: “He acts within us”; then, concerning his gifts, it says that they are not to remain idle within us, but are to be exercised and not neglected. From this it appropriately follows that we are fellow-workers with God’s grace. How this happens is explained by the bishops exiled in Sardinia in their response to Augustine, in the appendix to volume 10, page 154, and by Fulgentius, *Letter* 15, no. 11, to John and his companions: namely, that God’s mercy alone confers the beginning of salvation, and that thereafter the human will becomes a fellow-worker in its own salvation; that preceding mercy directs the course of the human will, and that the obedient human will, with the same mercy following after it, runs toward the prize according to its intention.].

If we see anything within us growing weak through our own negligence, let us earnestly return to him who heals all our diseases and redeems our life from destruction (Psalm 102:3–4), and to whom we say daily: “Lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil” (Matthew 6:13).

### CHAPTER XIII

15. As for the deeper and more difficult aspects of the questions that arise [Note: The Roman edition and the ancient councils read *occurrentium* (“that arise”). Other books, as well as Crabbe in the margin, read *incurrentium* (“that intrude” or “that occur”).], which those who resisted the heretics have treated at greater length, we neither dare to disregard them nor have need to establish them, because we believe that, for confessing the grace of God—whose work and favor must in no way be diminished—whatever the writings of the apostolic see have taught us according to the rules stated above is sufficient [Col. 0537B]; so that we may in no way regard as Catholic anything that appears contrary to the judgments set forth [Note: Labbe and Sirmond, after Crabbe and the Roman edition, read *quod apparuit* (“what appeared”). The examples collected by Hadrian read *quod oportuerit* (“what ought to have appeared”). The Regius manuscript and the others read *quod apparuerit* (“what may appear”). In all copies, the following is added at the end: “Here end the authorities of the preceding bishops of the apostolic see concerning grace and free will.”].

[Note: Baronius first published this letter and the three following ones, which he had received from Antonius of Aquino, in the *Annals* under the year 432. Labbe had them reprinted more accurately, both in volume 2 among the letters of Celestine, following Binius and Baronius, and in volume 3, part 3, of the Council of Ephesus, chapters 20, 21, and 22. We compared and corrected them, as far as we could, against the very ancient Colbert manuscript, whose upper leaves have been eaten away by the damage of time. In Labbe, this letter is entitled “of holy memory Celestine,” doubtless because it was copied from some record in which it had been issued or praised after he had already died.]

## LETTER XXII OF POPE CELESTINE, WRITTEN AFTER THE CONDEMNATION OF NESTORIUS TO THE HOLY SYNOD OF EPHESUS

He praises and approves the ordination of Maximian in the place of Nestorius. He advises that Nestorius be sent far away from Antioch. Concerning those associated with him, and especially concerning John of Antioch, he determines what is to be decided and what course is to be followed.

**CELESTINE, bishop, to the holy synod constituted at Ephesus** [Note: That is, “which had been constituted”; for the synod had already been dissolved. For this reason the three following letters, although issued on the same day, are also entitled “after the synod” in the manuscripts. Celestine addresses this letter to the Ephesian synod because the bishops who had ordained Maximian represented that synod as envoys to the imperial city, since they were carrying out its decrees.]

1. At last we should rejoice in the end of our troubles; at last we should all say together: “Your right hand, Lord, has been glorified in power; your right hand has shattered your enemies” (Exodus 15:6). For they were truly shattered when, as David says, we see the mouth of those who speak wickedness stopped up (Psalm 72:12).

Yet we see that you were executors with us of this deed, so faithfully accomplished [Note: Baronius reads *defensores* (“defenders”). Labbe, more correctly, following the Colbert manuscript, reads *exsecutores* (“executors”). In the Ephesian synod itself, Labbe, volume 3, page 618, Firmus, bishop of Caesarea, had said that Celestine prescribed the form and rule by his letters, and that they had followed it and carried that form into execution.], priests of God [Note: Labbe reads “defenders of the faith.” Baronius and the Colbert manuscript read “priests of the faith.” We were persuaded that the reading should be “priests of God” (or “O priests of God”) by the words in section 3: “He will have thought with those whom he knows to be priests of God.”]; for, gathering together and, according to the Apostle, seeking not your own interests but those of Christ Jesus (Philippians 2:21), you carried out the business of the common Lord.

Therefore, among you we speak of your holiness, whose sound we rejoice to have gone out into all the earth, since the words of the aforesaid truth have come from you even to the ends of the world (Psalm 18:5). Our God does not permit what he has granted to remain hidden, because heavenly benefits are never concealed. Thus, when such a heavenly gift becomes known, it comes about, according to the divine will, as it is written, that every person is saved and comes to the knowledge of the truth (1 Timothy 2:3).

I speak, then, to victors—to those who carried into battle against the enemy nothing but faith, which, as the Apostle John says, conquered the world (1 John 5:4). I write especially to you in the words of that same Apostle, who, according to the divine Scripture, says that as fathers you have known him who is from the beginning, and that as young men, because you are strong and the word of God remains in you, you have conquered the evil one (1 John 2:13–14).

Rejoicing in such companions, we had no doubt at all concerning the outcome. Our heart possessed confidence of victory [Note: Baronius reads *sperandi* (“of hoping”). Labbe, more correctly, reads *superandi* (“of overcoming”). Since Celestine is speaking to victors, to whom he has just said “you have conquered the evil one,” he explains why he himself had not been doubtful of the outcome.], because we saw the weight of the divine cause resting upon you; and we knew you very well to hate, in accordance with the prophetic saying, the assembly of the wicked and not to sit with the impious (Psalm 25:5). [Note: Baronius: “Therefore I believed most confidently.”]

Thus I obtained what I believed, because, against the guilty and perverse, as the same Psalmist says: “The innocent and upright have adhered to me” (Psalm 24:21).

2. Therefore, in one and the same report, conveyed by our sons, religious and beloved of God, the presbyter John and the deacon Epictetus, we learned of the just deposition and the still more just exaltation of the righteous. We approve what we read in the Gospel: that our God exalts the humble and brings down the powerful from their thrones (Luke 1:52).

Our most wise predecessor did not depart from this judgment when he said that our God preserves the memory of the humble and destroys that of the proud (Ecclesiasticus 10:21). When could this appear more fully accomplished than now, when our Savior, preparing to honor those who deserved well, scattered the bones of those who pleased themselves (Psalm 52:6), and, having provided a most worthy shepherd, drove the savage wolf from his folds—the spotless Lamb?

We have read the praises of him that were written by your fraternity [Note: The reading “the first praises that were written” found in Baronius is not satisfactory. Here the praises by which the synodical report adorned Maximian, who had been substituted in the place of Nestorius, are being mentioned.]; and none of us could wonder, since you said what was known. Assertion is needed for uncertain matters; testimony is not sought for things already known.

The arena of good works has always exercised him. We learned that he was such as we found him in your letter—such, certainly, to put it briefly, as our Teacher commanded a priest to be, so that by the judgment of all he deserved to hear: “Behold, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit” (John 1:47).

Do these things not fit your praises of him? In the end, you heard such a man as you described. The blessed simplicity of Sisinnius, of holy memory, was seeking such a successor, so that no one but his equal might occupy his place. Indeed, we act more appropriately if, now refraining from the name of that sacrilegious man, we say that the see was vacant.

By divine judgment it came about that the Church deserved to receive him as its remedy. Finally, when he was ordained, he removed discord and restored concord [Note: The Colbert manuscript reads *ornatus* (“adorned”).]. What will he not be able to accomplish over time, whose beginning has accomplished this? These things we say together concerning him whom the restoration of peace was seeking.

We were present—and let us not say that we were absent—when mystical words were spoken over his head, while divine, saving joy was being restored to all [Note: Edmund Martene, *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, volume 2, page 340, gives from a Pontifical written more than nine hundred years ago the following rite for the ordination of a bishop: “When a bishop is ordained, two bishops are to place and hold the book of the Gospels upon his neck, and one is to pronounce a blessing over him; afterward all the bishops who are present are to recite these three prayers, while the others touch his head with their hands.” Referring to this, Celestine here means: “We too were present at Maximian’s ordination and recited the prayers that all bishops who are present are required to recite when the Gospel is held over the head of the one being ordained.” This proves the antiquity of the custom.]. Finally, no Catholic was absent there, where all conquered together.

3. We also rejoiced in the testimony of this most merciful and Christian prince, when we saw that his judgment agreed with the letters of your affection. Nor is it surprising that the heart of a king, which is in the hand of God (Proverbs 21:1), should think with those whom he knows to be God’s priests.

Accordingly, the royal speech, in carrying out divine affairs, served the emperor [Note: Baronius reads *multiplicat in Augusto* (“increases in Augustus”), with the marginal reading *militat Aug.* (“serves Augustus”). We would prefer *exsecuturo militavit* (“served the one who was to carry it out”). We suspect that something has been omitted; otherwise we would be taught that the king served the priest, and the priest the emperor. The following should therefore be understood thus: “Blessed is the empire, or the emperor, whom he serves whose task is to carry out divine things; and no less blessed is the bishop whom he praises who rules over worldly matters.”]. Blessed is the empire to which the execution of divine things gives service, and no less blessed is he whom the dominion over worldly matters praises.

He is worthy of this testimony—worthy to be approved when he was to be ordained, not to be rejected after he had been ordained [Note: Nestorius is tacitly indicated, since after his ordination he began to be rejected.].

4. We know by what road our holy brother and fellow bishop Maximianus, and by what successive services, reached the summit of the priesthood. He was not lifted up by the glory of riches, nor, as though he were powerful, by the ambition [Note: Someone might perhaps prefer *tumidum* (“puffed up”) here. But from what follows it is clear that *cupidum* (“ambitious”) must be retained, even if the desire was for the episcopate. Where the expression *saltus evexit* (“raised by a leap”) occurs, we have judged that *saltus* should be restored [Col. 0540C]. Celestine is testifying that Maximian was far removed from the vices of those whom he had blamed in Letter 5, section 2—men who, being occupied with the world and knowing nothing of the entire ecclesiastical order, seek, with rash haste and immoderate ambition, to leap across into another’s honor. This also confirms that *cupidum* should not be changed.] that usually belongs to those who seek offices. Instead, as a faithful and prudent servant, he gave food at the proper time and was set over all his master’s goods (Matthew 24:45, 47) [Note: This appears to be said because he had been steward of the Church of Constantinople. Socrates, book 7, chapter 35, praises him as having acquired a reputation for holiness because he had built, at his own expense, monuments where religious men might be buried after death. From what follows, however, it is clear that in the office entrusted to him he excelled not only in caring for the bodies of the dead but also in caring for the bodies of the living. In this he showed himself a worthy successor of Sisinnius, whom Socrates, book 7, chapter 26, says was chosen for the same see by the votes of the whole people chiefly because he devoted himself to supporting the poor even beyond his means.].

And yet, even if he desired the episcopate, he desired it only for the sake of the good work, as the Apostle says (1 Timothy 3:1). Thus our God takes account both of what we wish and of why we wish it. Who could doubt that one who presides can accomplish more than he was able to exercise while subordinate?

The hated and blasphemous man, Nestorius, could not hold this office—that is, the care of bodies—because he was striving to wound souls. His fall was great, as great as his perverse doctrine.

5. Now that we rejoice in the correction of what is past, it is fitting that we take precautions for the future, lest what has been cut off be able to sprout again more and more. For wherever this plague may be located, it is necessary that the members of our body be afflicted, and that, through our patience, things worse than before appear to have been nourished.

We have written to the imperial clemency that the sickness be removed farther from the midst of health. For we have learned that this man has returned to Antioch [Note: Nestorius himself reports in Evagrius, book 1, chapter 7, that when he requested it, he was permitted to return to his monastery situated before the gates of Antioch; and that after he had stayed there for four years and had been treated with every honor, he was banished by an edict of the emperor Theodosius to a place called Oasis. Evagrius thinks that this was the monastery called Euprepius, although Nestorius does not state its name. As for Nestorius’s assertion that he was treated there with every honor, Celestine confirms it shortly afterward. We shall show in Letter 6 of Sixtus III that he did not remain there even for two complete years. From that point onward he experienced changing fortunes.] and has been granted the opportunity to live there, in the place from which he came. This exile is a harmless punishment.

Let us look more carefully at what those things might produce which were conceived there. It is not difficult for us to make our position known. Before our eyes is the Church of that same city, which through this man lost its bishop [Note: Baronius reads *periit* (“perished”), a reading that Labbe, volume 3, page 1070, also says he prefers. Nevertheless, *perdidit* (“lost”) should be retained. The Church of Antioch is said to have lost its bishop, John, through Nestorius because John adhered too stubbornly to Nestorius. John had not yet been deposed, but had been removed from communion with the Church, and certainly would be deposed unless, by abandoning the condemned Nestorius, he showed that he had been deceived.], although we are laboring to determine who was the cause of whose sin—unless perhaps, for the sake of the peace of the churches, which is what we are saying, he demonstrates that he has been deceived by abandoning the condemned man.

But who could hope that anyone there might be corrected, when he sees the author of perversity holding the citadel, and sees an exiled man honored by everyone? Great there is the despair of recovery—we say this with mourning—where, as Isaiah says, “Every head is in pain, and every heart in sorrow, from the sole of the foot even to the head” (Isaiah 1:5–6).

When could any member there have hope of salvation, when the body’s entire structure is in danger? Work, dearest brothers, work, I beg you, so that the one who did this deed may truly be removed from your midst (1 Corinthians 5:2). Solitude alone is fitting for such men. For where should this man find consolation, who treated in this way the one who reigns everywhere?

6. You have completed the whole substance of the matter; now what remains and presses upon us must be undertaken, lest our labor have been in vain. We are placed at a distance, certainly, but through our concern we see everything as though nearby. The care of blessed Peter the Apostle makes everyone present to us, and before our God we cannot excuse ourselves concerning what we know.

For although your holiness has kept silent about the things we are discussing, we have nevertheless learned everything by investigating with the greatest diligence. Therefore, I ask that the conclusion of this great matter that remains may correspond to your actions, because we do not wish you to fall short in a small matter, after accomplishing the greatest things.

Be helpers before the kings of the earth in the matters about which we have written. They themselves know what they ought to provide for their times [Note: Celestine refers to the imperial letter by which the bishops had been summoned to the Ephesian synod. It began with these words: “The condition of our state depends upon the religion by which God is worshiped,” and shortly afterward continued: “Above all, we strive to ensure that the condition of the Church is such as becomes God and is most suitable to our times, and that it obtain its tranquility from the agreement and consensus of all.”]. They know that their kingdoms rest upon the foundation of the Catholic faith.

The pure stream of their fathers’ and ancestors’ belief is preserved by holy heirs; it flows incorrupt through their descendants, and no one has ever sullied it with mud. The faithful course of its fountain guards its source [Note: Baronius and Labbe, volume 2, read: “The strong one, whose course is faithful.” Labbe, volume 3, restored *sui* (“of its own”), which should be retained. Likewise, earlier, where *fortis* (“strong”) occurs, we were persuaded that *fontis* (“of the fountain”) should be read, for this reason: “The faithful course guards the beginning of its own fountain.”], since what was received at its origin is seen in its offspring.

7. Let us pursue the dog and the wicked worker alike. Do while present what we urge while absent. For although we owe this care to everyone generally, it is especially fitting that we assist the Antiochians who are in danger [Note: The printed editions read *praecipitantibus* (“falling headlong”); this is corrected from the Colbert manuscript.], whom a pestilential disease has besieged.

Let us free the city by such means [Note: Labbe reads *modis omnibus* (“by every means”). With Baronius and the Colbert manuscript, *modis talibus* (“by such means”) is preferable—that is, by sending Nestorius, the head of all the evil, far away. The importance of the Church of Antioch, and the source of its commendation, are explained by Innocent in Letter 24, section 1.], in which, as the Acts of the Apostles say, we first read that the disciples were called Christians (Acts 11:26). [Note: Perhaps *hominibus* (“to the people” or “for the people”).]

Therefore, let us render aid to all those to whom, in accordance with the religion by which we are called, we know that we owe it. Our present concern was approved by the present, beloved sons of God, dearest and most cherished in our hearts, John the presbyter and Epictetus the deacon. We hastily sent them back to you after their return, taking particular care that those whom we received during the days of the Lord’s Nativity might be restored to you at the time of the Lord’s Resurrection [Note: The time consumed in completing the journey is evidently included in the calculation.].

8. Concerning those who appear to have thought with Nestorius [Note: Baronius, and Labbe, volume 2, following him, read “who consented with insufficient piety.” Shortly afterward, Labbe alone, in volume 3, substitutes *sceleris* (“of the crime”) for *sceleribus* (“crimes”). Scholars dispute what these words refer to. Some think that the fourth canon of the Council of Ephesus is being indicated, where it is decreed: “If any clerics should defect and dare, either privately or publicly, to hold the opinions of Nestorius or Caelestius, it is decreed by the holy synod that these too be deposed.” Tillemont, volume 14, page 498, believes that Celestine’s words may refer to the synod in which Himerius of Nicomedia, Helladius of Tarsus, Eutherius of Tyana, and Dorotheus of Marcianopolis were deposed. Garnerius, in Marcellinus Mercator, part 2, page 357, regards it as certain that those four bishops were deposed at the synod in which Maximian was substituted for Nestorius, in the manner briefly narrated by Baluze, *New Collection of Councils*, page 581. But, says the cited Tillemont, page 497, the synodical letter of Maximian’s ordination is reported by Baluze, *New Collection of Councils*, chapters 48 and 49, pages 752–753, to have been sent to Helladius; and it is inconsistent that Maximian should have sought communion with a bishop whom he knew had been deposed by his own ordainers. Yet one may ask in turn whether he sought communion with a bishop whom he knew had been deprived of ecclesiastical communion and all priestly authority by the judgment of the Council of Ephesus, issued in act 5 and repeated in act 7. Or perhaps Maximian’s synodical letter was brought to Helladius and the others who had assembled with John, bishop of Antioch, so that if they received it, they would be judged to approve and accept the deposition of Nestorius and the other acts performed at Ephesus? If Helladius was subsequently removed from the episcopate because he refused to receive Maximian’s synodical letter, Celestine could not yet have known this when he wrote the present letter, since it was delivered to the very men who had brought that synodical letter. Nothing therefore remains except to suppose that those who had assembled at Constantinople to ordain Maximian, dissatisfied with the moderation of the Ephesian synod, issued a stricter judgment against the associates and supporters of Nestorius, by which even those who repented were deprived of the hope of pardon; and that Celestine now disapproves this. His moderation is consistent with the decree of Theodosius on peace, sent to John of Antioch, which may be read in part 3 of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 30.], and have joined themselves to his crimes, although your judgment concerning them is recorded, we too decree what seems right.

Many things must be considered in such cases—things that the apostolic see has always examined. What we say is shown by the examples of the Caelestians [Note: The printed editions read: “The examples show that they have maintained hope from the synod up to this point.” We thought the reading should first be restored by conjecture; the Colbert manuscript confirmed it. The meaning is: “Those who have maintained until now the hope of pardon that the synod offered to those who repented still have the opportunity to return under the same condition.”].

If they have maintained hope from the synod until now, they have the opportunity to return if they repent. This remedy of repentance, however, is granted only to those who are not themselves the leaders of the heresy, since it is established by the subscription of all the brothers that the leaders of the heresy were condemned together with its authors. [Note: This does not mean that every entrance into the Church was denied to them, but that it was permitted more cautiously, and that sometimes their rank was preserved when others returned. Augustine repeatedly asserts that the only remedy left to Pelagius and Caelestius was this. Celestine, however, considers it necessary to adhere to the decree that Hilary first issued against the Arians in the year 355, as he recounts in his *Against Constantius*, section 2, and which afterward the whole Church, especially the Roman Church, continually upheld in practice against the remaining heretics: namely, that the heads of heresy, who might advance their cause to the ruin of others, should be cut off, while the other associates should be granted the opportunity to repent.].

By the mercy of God, we rejoice that some of their number have already returned to us [Note: This *some* can appropriately be referred to the Caelestians, so that Celestine begins to explain what their examples show. Certainly Marcellinus Mercator, in the *Commonitorium* he wrote in 429, after recounting that Caelestius and Pelagius had been condemned by the letter of Zosimus, that their condemnation had been confirmed by the subscriptions of the Fathers throughout the world, and that Julian and his companions who refused to subscribe had been deposed, adds: “Many of them, repenting and corrected from the aforesaid error, returned as suppliants to the apostolic see and, being received, recovered their churches”—first, as is added at the end of the same *Commonitorium*, submitting themselves to the apostolic see after Pelagius had been condemned and confessing repentance for what they had wrongly believed. It is therefore clear that Celestine, keeping in view what had occurred concerning the Pelagians after Zosimus condemned them, prescribes what should be done with the supporters of Nestorius.].

This was done with the purpose that those whom a divided conscience could not separate might at least be separated by a judgment. I urge your fraternity to follow this example. Let the head of the crime be condemned together with those whom the synodical decrees declare condemned [Note: These are the men listed in the judgment issued in act 5 of the Council of Ephesus and repeated before the canons in act 7.]; let the others, whom we do not have in ecclesiastical communion because they think with him, be expelled from their cities, and let them know that they will not be members of our college unless, in accordance with the decree of the Church and of the Christian princes, they condemn the condemned doctrine [Note: That is, “the things that have been condemned.” Baronius altered the wording to: “condemning the condemned heresy together with its authors and associates.” The decree of the Christian princes mentioned immediately above appears to be none other than the one issued by the emperor Theodosius in part 3 of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 47, in another imperial letter given in April of the year 433: “We decree also that whoever imitates the impious opinion of Nestorius or follows his wicked teaching, if they are bishops or clerics, are to be expelled from the holy churches; but if they are laymen, they are to be anathematized, as has already been provided by law through our sacred majesty.”] together with its authors and associates, and profess themselves Catholic priests.

We also wish this procedure to be observed concerning those who believed that Christian princes should be deceived in ecclesiastical matters [Note: Baronius reads: “who believed that the princes should be drawn into ecclesiastical cases.” Holstenius likewise reads *causas* (“cases”).] and again occupied the churches by another arrangement.

As for the Antiochian, if he has hope of correction, we wish your fraternity to summon him by letters [Note: The same editor substitutes *episcopum* (“the bishop”) for *epistolis* (“by letters”).], so that, unless he adopts what we think, condemning the novel blasphemy by a written profession in the same manner, he may understand that the Church too, as the regard for our faith requires, will make an arrangement concerning him.

Nevertheless, we must trust in divine mercy that all may return to the way of truth, if the evil head and cause of these things [Note: Namely, Nestorius, who was eventually deported into exile through the agency of John of Antioch.] is removed from the aforesaid place. [Note: March 15, 432.]

Given on the Ides of March, in the consulship of Aetius and Valerius [Note: The Colbert manuscript is inconsistent in recording these consuls. Here it gives Aetius and Valerius; in the following letter, Flavius Aetius and Valerius; in the next, Flavius and Valerius; and in the last, Flavius Aetius and Valerius.].

## LETTER XXIII OF POPE CELESTINE I TO THEODOSIUS THE YOUNGER AUGUSTUS, AFTER THE SYNOD

That victory over the enemies of Christ was achieved through him. How great his glory is on this account. That he rightly supported Maximian’s ordination. That he should remove Nestorius from every association. That he received the envoys with the imperial letters. He commends to him the Church’s properties in Asia left by Proba.

**CELESTINE, bishop, to THEODOSIUS Augustus**

1. We have recognized that divine providence has granted what we hoped for in our affairs. For while you reign, the minds of the faithful could expect nothing else than what we rejoice has happened: that the impious preaching against God should fall, and that the condemned perversity of the new doctrine should perish together with its author.

Wars were indeed waged against the faith, and the birth of the eternal King was attacked with the sacrilegious arrows of words. But while you reign, with Christ our God as your author, you have conquered the impious enemies by the strength of your faith, restoring the heavenly triumph, through which you provide perpetual protection for the devout empire.

Truly the prophetic voice of your glory applies to you, and your kingdom may be called “the kingdom of all ages” (Psalm 149:13), since it is extended by the merits of the faith you have defended. As observance of holy religion increases, what has been implanted in Christian reverence is continually enlarged, most glorious and most tranquil Emperor Augustus.

Behold, now the house of the Lord is free for prayer, and throughout all the churches your empire is commended in sacrifices offered to our God. Once the attempt of the disturber has been removed, scandals have no license; no longer does a pestilential speech wound human souls. While you care for the universal Church, you have restored salvation to all their souls.

This is the clemency by which you proclaim your reign: through it not lands, not provinces, but the souls of all have been defended. In every way you will count this as a victory that you won not by wars or swords but solely by the devotion with which you are dedicated to God.

2. This title of glory remains yours and will remain, so that no age and no antiquity may erase it. For the things accomplished through love of the eternal King are eternal.

Thus Abraham’s faith endures through the ages. The zeal of David the king made his merit perpetual, when he regarded God’s enemies as his own enemies and hated those whom he had approved as hateful to God (Psalm 138:21–22).

The prophet Elijah, too, was not content merely to refute those who prophesied falsely; he also wished to take vengeance upon them, so that by pursuing he might destroy those whom he saw striving for the destruction of his people (1 Kings 18).

Your glory is equal to his. He resisted those who prophesied falsely; you resist those who teach falsely. He pursued prophets who lied against God; you drive away priests who preach impiously about Christ our God. He was intent only upon vengeance; your piety takes vengeance on impiety in such a way as to defend what is religious.

3. For it would not be enough to drive away diseases and repel the plague unless you also restored healthy air and supplied infected people with a life-giving substance, by appointing to that Church a pontiff who had long before proved himself worthy of this rank to all who knew him.

The Roman Church bears witness on his behalf, as though he were a member of its own body, since it has always held and counted him among its own; the merits of his predecessors, to whom he had adhered in holiness, support him. For he was so united in mind and service to Atticus, a man of most reverend memory and a most courageous defender of the Catholic faith, that even then the marks of his future episcopate shone forth.

But let this be left to the secret judgment of the divine majesty, so that whatever is better may be preserved for the future and that through the disturbances of certain disturbers we may arrive at peace. It was due to the glory of my brother, Bishop Maximian, that the city should regret having had someone placed over it in what he endured; and now, having chosen the same man, it should recognize that it owes him the integrity of the faith.

[Note: The statement that the Roman Church always counted Maximian among its own may be understood in the sense in which Celestine says in Letter 22, section 3, against the Massilians who were disturbing Gaul: “It is impious that religious souls should endure these things; and because they are our members, we too ought to be afflicted by their distress.” Maximian therefore never ceased to belong to the communion of faith of the Roman Church. Moreover, the Greek *Menaea* testify that he was Roman by birth; this is confirmed by the name Maximian, which is certainly not Greek. Nevertheless, he should not have seemed foreign to the Church of Constantinople, since the following makes clear that he had grown old in its bosom.]

### 4

But to this priest of that Church, elected in such a manner in accordance with his great merit and ordained with the consent of the holy assembly that was present, in order to restore the Church’s condition and uproot entirely every wound inflicted by perverse heresy, lest what has been cut away dare sprout again, we beseech and ask you, under the invocation of the one whom you worship, to furnish, as is your custom, the weapons of your faith.

For now every guard must be set in place, lest, when the ravenous wolf has raged against the sheepfolds of the Lord’s flock, excluded from them, he should once again reach the death of souls by a serpentine glide, digging tunnels wherever he can. Nor can he rest, since in his greed he longs to settle upon his prey. Provide protection for the healthy and remedies for those needing healing. Surround the truth of the Catholic faith with the walls of your faith, so that believers may be defended by them and the followers of so great an error may not dare enter. For this is the complete fruit of your victory: to leave nothing that the Church of God ought again to fear.

Therefore, let him whom the judgment of all the priests expelled while he persisted in sacrilegious preaching be removed by your clemency from every association, so that he may have no opportunity to destroy anyone.

**Note:** [Col. 0545D] Labbe reads *nostrae* (“our”). *Vestrae* (“your”), found with Baronius and in the Colbertine manuscript, is preferable. Thus below: “Surround with the walls of your faith,” not “our faith.” Here *fidei vestrae arma* (“the weapons of your faith”) is expressed in the manner in which we would simply say *fidem vestram* (“your faith”) or *vestra arma* (“your weapons”).

### 5

We received my religious sons, the priest John and the deacon Epictetus, messengers of so great an affair, with the rejoicing of the entire Church; and, after your pious letters had been read in the assembly of the whole Christian people before the most blessed Apostle Peter, we offered prayers to our God on your behalf.

For they reached you by the Lord’s direction in such a way that they arrived on the very day on which we were celebrating the birth according to the flesh of Christ our God, concerning whom the dispute had arisen, and the entire assembly together refuted the impiety.

**Note:** [Col. 0546D] Baronius, with the Colbertine manuscript, reads “in the assembly of the whole congregation of the Christian people.” The Labbe edition has “in the entire assembly of the Christian people.” We have departed from a manuscript as little as possible. This confirms the ancient custom of bishops, especially the Roman bishops, whereby they arranged for letters concerning the Church to be read in church before the people. Above, [see vol. VIII of our *Patrologia*], we heard Liberius testify that he had made known the letters of the Eastern bishops, had read in the church the judgment of the Egyptian bishops concerning Athanasius, and had likewise had it recited.

### 6

A matter concerning the faith is appropriately followed by one concerning the Church and the welfare of the poor: since you have upheld the integrity of the faith, you should also provide for the interests of the poor.

Proba, illustrious and holy in memory, left estates situated in Asia in such a condition, through the long-standing custom inherited from her ancestors, that each year she ordered a larger sum of the revenues to be distributed to the clergy, the poor, and the monasteries.

But these estates situated there were managed, to the detriment of the poor—and, not to speak more severely, through the negligence of the person who had charge of them—in such a way that they not only failed to pay what was customary, but even, by a fraudulent petition, violated their rightful ownership and legal title.

We ask your piety to grant this, in your clemency, to the religious and illustrious household and to the Church: that every disturbance caused by those lying in wait may withdraw from them, and that the possession may be secure both for the Church and for its rightful owners; so that whatever provision for the poor is acquired from it may be regarded as belonging to you.

**Note:** [Col. 0546D] Baronius has “rightful ownership.”

**Note:** [Col. 0547D] March 15, in the year 432.

Given on the Ides of March, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Flavius Aetius and Valerius.

---

## Letter XXIV: Pope Celestine I to Maximian, Bishop of Constantinople, after the Synod

He confirms Maximian’s election by his own vote and urges him to repair the losses suffered by the Church entrusted to him and to resist the Celestinian error with vigilance.

**Celestine, bishop, to Maximian, bishop of Constantinople.**

### 1

We saw and embraced your fraternity in your letters, and recognized in you the holiness that we had known: glorious in its simple purity and made conspicuous more by the radiance of the mind than by eloquence.

**Note:** [Col. 0547D] Baronius reads “than by honor.” The reading of the Colbertine manuscript and Labbe is supported by Socrates, Book VII, chapter 35, and by Liberatus the deacon, chapter 7. They describe Maximian as uncultivated and unpolished in speech, perhaps because, when compared with Nestorius, who excelled in eloquence, he appeared inexperienced in expression. His letter to Cyril—the one letter of his that has reached us, preserved in Part III of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 17—certainly conveys a man not highly polished in human eloquence, but well instructed in Christian understanding.

But that Church, whose faith we have always celebrated, returns to itself and to its proper condition, now that by divine judgment it has received you as its bishop after expelling the man who had occupied it. Take up the helm of the ship known to you, and govern it, as we know you learned from your predecessors.

Resist the waves that the wind stirred up—the wind that had driven the passengers from the ship and was hostile to everyone, desiring to break it apart in all its timbers so that it might devour it in the rushing whirlpools—while falsely claiming the office of helmsman. For what does iniquity not claim? He wished to appear to govern those whom he was striving to destroy.

**Note:** [Col. 0547D] Baronius reads “which he possessed in himself,” against the manuscripts. The reading is complete if *redit* (“returns”) is restored in place of *sedit* (“sat”); we have therefore, after considering Labbe’s conjecture on the matter, judged that it should be corrected in this way.

### 2

Even now the waves stirred up by that man roar around you, and the raised waters or storms trouble you. Resist with sleepless vigilance, and, as master of the ship entrusted to you, assist the safety of those entrusted to you with all the care you can.

Make the sea on which you sail calm; by your skill make safe the ship you govern after the storms it has endured. Follow that fisherman who trod upon the waters of the sea so that he might reach Christ our Lord, whom he had seen walking upon the sea (Matt. 14:29).

Follow the examples of the bishops who preceded you, by whom you were instructed and nourished: the most blessed John’s knowledge in preaching; Saint Atticus’s vigilance in purifying heresies; and the simple purity of your predecessor Sisinnius, whose successor we believe you to be, so that we may rejoice over that Church as we used to.

Gather the scattered, and exercise upon those whom the disturber had dispersed the pious disposition that we know you possess. Gather your people to the breasts of their mother; recall those whom the enemy had drawn away by the taste of forbidden food.

**Note:** [Col. 0548D] Labbe has *invitos* (“unwillingly”). From Baronius we restore *inhibito* (“forbidden”), although we would prefer *imbibito* (“imbibed”), which Labbe also noted in the margin.

Strengthen in the faith those whom you see attacked; care for those whom you find wounded; remove those who do not accept the remedy. For sometimes illness is removed by pain, and when harmful things are cut away, health is prepared for what remains.

**Note:** [Col. 0548D] Baronius prefers *dolor* (“pain”). Perhaps the reading should be: “For illness is removed by pain,” with *aegritudo* (“illness”) substituted for the particle *interdum* (“sometimes”).

A broad field lies before you, dearest brother, in which you may exercise both the glory of a watchful shepherd and the kindness of a compassionate priest, and pour in the flavor of Christian healing.

**Note:** [Col. 0548D] The same author has “and pour the flavor into their minds.”

Thus it may become clear that you were more powerful in restoring than he was in injuring—he who preferred to be an imitator of the devil rather than of Christ, disturbing the peace of all the Churches. We now owe it to him to labor together so that all may have one faith and the priests one mind.

Let your hand hold the Lord’s winnowing-fan, and cleanse the threshing floor entrusted to you, so that the chaff may be separated from the grain (Luke 3:17), and, in accordance with the command of Christ our God, the wheat may all be gathered into the granaries (Matt. 13:30).

### 3

Let the recent impiety have no place, and let your vigilance resist the Celestinian error, formerly condemned and marked throughout the whole world by its condemnation.

**Note:** [Col. 0548D] That is, the *tractoria* of Zosimus, sent to all the Churches.

Let all who follow this doctrine be excluded from every human association. May the Holy Spirit, through you, oppose them in every respect—those who endeavor to reach any of these provinces—lest their impious preaching rise again.

Resist them. For they become known wherever they go so that they may be condemned; and, as though a sentence repeated so many times were not sufficient for them, they disturb distant lands and remote provinces.

But the one whose faith they were striving to persecute by their perversity pursues them; wherever they flee, they cannot hide from him, exposing themselves by their own impiety.

**Note:** [Col. 0548D] The printed editions have: “and where they may hide themselves, to whatever hiding places they may flee.” The reading is repaired with the help of the Colbertine manuscript, which nevertheless has *ad quesvis* in place of *ad quasvis*. In manuscripts, *at* frequently occurs for *ad*, and the change of *a* to *e* is easy.

We received our religious sons, the priest John and the deacon Epictetus, with great joy, and sent them back with even greater rejoicing.

**Note:** [Col. 0548D] March 15, in the year 432.

Given on the Ides of March, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Flavius Aetius and Valerius.

---

## Letter XXV: Pope Celestine I to the Clergy and People Established at Constantinople, after the Synod

He attacks Nestorius’s perverse doctrine, stubbornness, and pride, and then demonstrates that his condemnation was just. Again and again he commends both his own devotion toward the Constantinopolitans and their steadfastness in the faith. At the end he briefly praises Maximian, who had been placed over them.

**Celestine, bishop, to the clergy and people residing at Constantinople.**

### 1

A mother’s joy is the gathering of her children. Thus the Church rejoices that she has gathered again the children whom the devil had scattered, so that among them no one has been lost except the son of perdition, because the father did not acknowledge him as his son at all.

For, imitating the one from whom he came, as we read (John 8:44), he was trying to take away the inheritance from you, the legitimate sons of God, whom, as the Apostle says (Rom. 8:17), we believe will be heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ our Lord on account of your faith.

Therefore he was not permitted to carry away the prize from these people, who instead triumphed over him by the weapons of faith. The expelled tyrant speaks of you as victors—or rather, of the victory of the common King over the enemy. He conquered in you, the one whose divinity was thought to have been rendered uncertain.

Let the birth be set apart—I mean the question—which every true believer ought simply and rightly to make clear to himself. For who would dare summon God to examination and investigate how he came to bring help? It was not difficult for God to do what he willed, since he graciously undertook to save those whom he was able to save.

But how could that sinner, in his great darkness, fail to see the light? How could he gather by earthly arguments the truth placed above? Those who do not know the word of that lamp cannot see these things in their darkness—the word which the prophet David testifies to be a light for his paths (Ps. 119:105).

With that psalm-scribe, as we said above, it is pleasing to sing of the rejoicing mother receiving her children back into her womb, which their ridiculous and blasphemous dispersion had until now disturbed: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity” (Ps. 133:1).

**Note:** [Col. 0549D] In the common editions, *psalmographo* (“psalm-writer”) appears. From the manuscripts we restore *psalmigrapho*, formed in the same way as below the same prophet is called *hymnidicus*, not *hymnodicus*.

I may appropriately borrow these words here. For, with the help of the venerable Trinity, I claim for myself in very large measure the peace of the universal Church and the fullness of the present joys: those who were scandalized had until now burned me (2 Cor. 11:29), and the weakness of some had made me weak.

**Note:** [Col. 0549C] Labbe prefers *pravitas* (“depravity”), moving *nativitas* (“birth”) to the margin. This word occurs in the manuscripts. It signifies the question concerning the Lord’s birth from Mary. The meaning is: “Let the birth—not the question, which every believer ought to hold clearly and simply—detain us.”

**Note:** [Col. 0549D] It seems that *non* (“not”) should be deleted.

### 2

Your charity remembers that long ago I spoke to you about patience.

**Note:** [Col. 0549D] Letter 14, sections 5 and following.

As a priest, I sowed in a Christian mind the seeds that I ought to have sown, and the harvest I expected did not disappoint me in you (Matt. 13:24–25). For what the harvest of your patience produced is demonstrated by its very fruits.

The farmer who was destined to perish, jealous of these things, sowed destructive weeds within the minds of some: he sowed something quite different from what he had received to sow, or from what he had found already sown.

Certainly we possess the seeds of our faith, scattered by the Lord’s own word or by the teaching of the apostles. Whenever such things occur, it is not the soil that received them but other things scattered over it that corrupt them.

**Note:** [Col. 0549D] Labbe reads *non ea qua terra*; Baronius, *non ea terra quae*. From the manuscripts we restore *non ea terrae*, which may be referred to the things spread over it. A more polished reading would be: “It is not the soil that received them, but other things spread over it, that corrupt them.”

He cannot attribute anything to the harvest of your simple faith who, in the Gospel, showed the originator of the weeds when he was asked about them. They said to him then, “From where, in the good seed, did the weeds come?” (Matt. 13:27). Let us say: “In so great a kingdom of faith, from where did faithlessness come?”

Nevertheless, we answer you with the words of Christ: “An enemy has done this” (Matt. 13:28).

The strength of your mind has shown how the training-ground of your earlier teachers exercised you. To them you owe your recognition of this error; he was unworthy of the praises by which they were honored.

**Note:** [Col. 0549D–0550D] This refers evidently to John, Atticus, and Sisinnius, whose unworthy successor Nestorius was, and unworthy even of the praises with which they were celebrated. Nevertheless, that hierarch does not hesitate to accuse them, in Marcellus Mercator’s edition by Baluze, p. 210, and Garnier’s edition, Part II, pp. 8–9, as though they had been negligent and inactive in instructing the people. He says:

“I see our people slipping into ignorance of the doctrine of divine knowledge; but this is not the people’s fault; rather, to speak honestly, they did not previously have teachers who carefully demonstrated the doctrines to you.”

Cyril appropriately responds in Letter 8:

“Is he more eloquent than John? Is he equal or wiser than blessed Atticus? Why, indeed, does he not honestly acknowledge that he has discovered a doctrine that is entirely foreign and wholly unusual, which, because of its absurdity, was known or approved in none of the Churches or assemblies of the faithful by our forefathers?”

He who despised such glorious goods devoted himself not partly to the dove’s simplicity (Matt. 10:16), but entirely to the serpent’s cunning.

**Note:** [Col. 0550D] We have judged that this should be corrected, since the other reading would mean that he “held a part.”

### 3

Nor is it surprising that, preparing to kill simple minds, he followed by persuasion the one who first killed by persuasion. We read that the latter deceived him by words; this man attempted to inflict death only through words.

Yet he did not follow his author with impunity, since another received his episcopate, as Matthias received Judas’s place (Acts 1:20).
