**Note:** [Col. 0550D] Baronius suppresses *ejus* (“his”). It should rather be added, perhaps in the form *instar*, before *Judae*: just as Matthias received Judas’s place, so Maximian received Nestorius’s episcopate.

One judgment rightly holds both, since, as we read, both sinned in the same respect.

Although each is before our eyes as a slanderer of our Savior and a betrayer, it is difficult to decide between the investigator of the birth and the author of death.

Judas, clearly, immediately repented of his deed; the punishment of the betrayer anticipated the death of the one who had been betrayed.

**Note:** [Col. 0550D] Baronius has “the destruction of his mouth.” Labbe has “the end of the betrayer,” as the Colbertine manuscript initially had. In that manuscript, however, the reading was rightly restored on a second correction as “the end of the betrayed one,” that is, the death of Christ who had been betrayed.

Judas immediately chose the noose, confessing his sin; this man glories in the stubbornness of his impiety.

Nor will I call this faithlessness an error, for not every impiety is an error. Indeed, whenever the devil, jealous of the Church or of its peace, has arisen, conflict born within it has preserved the cause of the struggle itself.

What did this conflict accomplish? For what were we laboring—not that someone might conquer through religion, but that religion itself might be conquered?

Certainly you remember him—for it is necessary to remember—because of his blasphemy.

**Note:** [Col. 0551D] The Colbertine manuscript reads *pro quo fiebat iste* (“for whom this was being done”).

**Note:** [Col. 0551D] The same manuscript has *blasphemii* (“of blasphemy”) and below *blasphemiorum suorum* (“of his blasphemies”).

### 4

But now I wish oblivion concerning so many evils to be imposed upon holy minds. Let the man who has been removed from your eyes also be removed from your thoughts. Let him, I say, be removed who was called the forerunner of hell.

That sinister preacher had frequent snares; he often bent his bow and, as we read, hurled poisoned arrows from his mouth (Ps. 10:3). Yet among your number he found no one whom he could strike. His weapons rebounded upon him after he was unable to shoot at the upright in heart in darkness (ibid.); and the son of darkness was allowed nothing against the sons of light.

What care and concern did we then have for you, placed in an internal war? We counted nights as though they were days, because in such matters all time is too short; we did not turn our troubled eyes toward sleep. For who could be carried away by the love of sleep while the robber was so awake? We did not know.

**Note:** [Col. 0551D] In the same manuscript, the reading is *sciamus quis intra* (“let us know who [is] within”).

What fear was within the folds, what dread within the enclosures, whenever the wolves’ neighboring hunger circled by many approaches, seeking prey, raging and threatening destruction even in the absence of its victims?

**Note:** [Col. 0551D] The printed editions have: “A great, fasting hunger circles around, seeking prey; then Baronius: ‘It rages, and destruction not yet completed threatens those who are absent.’ These readings are corrected on the authority of the Colbertine manuscript, except that it has *minata pernicie* (“having threatened destruction”) rather than the printed reading.

How greatly this flock deserves praise for its vigilance, since the robber enclosed with it did not touch it!

### 5

The cause of this protection is evident; it is clear who resisted the enemy. Let us all understand and confess that you were protected by that shepherd who says in the Gospel that he is the shepherd (John 10:11): he was present and did not abandon you who was suffering in you.

For against him the blasphemous interpreter sharpened his tongue daily; against him the impious expositor armed his teeth. Yet he was always foiled by an empty bite, since the rod and staff of that same shepherd comforted you (Ps. 23:4), the shepherd to whom, as he was going up to heaven, he entrusted his flock to be fed as well (John 21:15).

### 6

Your pastures have remained unchanged until now; you have been filled with the same food, and apostolic teachers have always fed you with pious speech.

But harmful food had been substituted for wholesome nourishment when the adversary presented thorns mixed with flowers to hungry souls.

**Note:** [Col. 0551D] Celestine alludes to the flowers of eloquence with which Nestorius mixed the thorns of heresy.

Yet this deception did not mislead you, for you are the sweet fragrance of Christ in the Lord (2 Cor. 2:15), since what he gave off to you smelled entirely different from what it once had.

You recoiled from the grass of deadly weeds; you hedged your ears with thorns (Sirach 28:28), and you could not listen to the wicked tongue.

**Note:** [Col. 0551D] Baronius has: “lest you should wish the wicked tongue.” The reading *nec voluistis* (“nor did you wish”) would not be objectionable, although *nec potuistis* (“nor could you”) is not bad in place of *nec sustinuistis* (“nor did you endure”).

Therefore what offended the ear did not reach the understanding, and what the exterior did not receive could not wound the interior. You avoided him, and, as we have learned, you even resisted him to his face.

You avoided the man whom the holy Alexandrian Church, worthy of remembrance, had already recognized, in accordance with the Apostle Paul’s sentence (Titus 3:10), as corrected.

**Note:** [Col. 0551D–0552D] The common editions have *correctum* (“corrected”). The more harmonious reading in the Colbertine manuscript is *correptum* (“rebuked”), namely, by the Alexandrian Church. Celestine now attributes to that Church the deed by which Cyril, its bishop, convened a synod and wrote against the rising heresy of Nestorius; for this reason the Church is proclaimed worthy of remembrance and praise.

### 7

For you have read, and now hold firmly in memory, the writings of a priest—that is, a Catholic teacher—addressed to him; by them that teacher strove to rebuke him so that he might be willing to be corrected.

He attempted to recall his wavering colleague; he extended the right hand of his teaching, wishing to help many through one.

The old priest was troubled by the thought that a bishop was wavering toward the ruin of many.

**Note:** [Col. 0552D] The Colbertine manuscript has: “That the bishop changes the ruin.” Perhaps: “That the bishop is wavering toward ruin.” Cyril, made bishop in 412 and writing to Nestorius in 429, could be called an old priest, especially in comparison with Nestorius.

He carried out, as it is written, the blessed work of the Lord diligently.

**Note:** [Col. 0552D] The printed editions have *benedicam* (“I shall bless”); the Colbertine manuscript’s *benedictum* (“blessed”) is better. These words are expressed by a kind of irony from Jeremiah 48:10, where, according to the ancient translation, we read: “Cursed is he who does the work of the Lord negligently.”

In no apostolic duty did this apostolic man fail him: he entreated, admonished, and rebuked (2 Tim. 4:2).

But the man who was being submerged beneath the weight of his blasphemies, rejecting the teaching of so great a man and abusing his exhortation, refused to be teachable when he could not be a teacher.

The defender of perversity assailed with insults the man who was steadfast in what was right. The former boasts of this; the brother was not saddened, reflecting that he rightly spared no fellow servant who disparaged his own master.

Through diligence, that prudent servant and fruitful son from the Gospel was found (Matt. 25). For he both preserved his father’s property and increased the number of talents.

I should not say that he merely doubled his portion, but multiplied it, since we see that he even helped those who were far away by pious interest.

O interest of holy preaching! What favor will this trader in faith find before the common Lord, who practiced his business for the profit of souls even where another had received the task?

**Note:** [Col. 0552D] Baronius has “where he had the talents.” Labbe, as in the Colbertine manuscript, more correctly has “where the other received”—namely, Nestorius, who, having become bishop of Constantinople, accepted responsibility for caring for that Church, while Cyril cared for it by sending various writings and letters to it.

Will he not rightly hear from the master of the household: “Well done, good and faithful servant; enter into the joy of your lord” (Matt. 25:21, 23)?

These words apply to the man who preserved even those things that had been entrusted to others.

### 8

What will that man hear, or what will he say, when an account is demanded from him of the matter entrusted to him—he who is certainly entangled in guilt, even if he himself had been preserved while others destroyed you?

You know perfectly well, in accordance with your instruction, what punishment awaits negligent priests, since the Apostle commands them also to preside carefully over their own households (1 Tim. 3:4).

Thus the priest Eli, blameless in himself, incurred divine displeasure through his sons (1 Sam. 4). The priest offended; authority and piety offended.

If, then, that man incurred guilt because he did not restrain the presumption of his sons, how much more does this man offend the Lord, since he does not spare even himself?

**Note:** [Col. 0553D] Supply: “guilt” (*offensam*).

I would not call him inactive, nor would I call him negligent. You had a man constant in speech and—as I speak before those who know—an alert destroyer.

### 9

Yet blessed Peter the Apostle did not abandon those who were laboring under so grave a burden. When the rottenness of such a sore had persuaded everyone that it was dreadful to separate it from the ecclesiastical body, we brought both the knife and the soothing remedy.

But he, abusing our care—by which we follow the one who does not wish any of the little ones to perish—chose death, though his salvation was desired.

**Note:** [Col. 0553D] Baronius has *desperatus* (“despairing”). The Colbertine manuscript is obliterated here; since Labbe has *desideratur* (“is lacking”), we restore *desideratus* (“desired”), which expresses how ardently Celestine sought Nestorius’s salvation.

Indeed, rejecting the medicine, he chose to be cut off. He accepted upon himself the apostolic judgment that he should be cut off, perhaps agreeing with us in this much: that the man who grieved us and wished to pervert the Gospel of Christ should be cut off (Gal. 5:12; 1:7).

We failed the sick man, as we said, in none of the physician’s duties. Our sentence was not so hasty that he became to us as a tax collector or a pagan (Matt. 18:17).

We know how and how often Scripture commands that those who tend toward such things be admonished (ibid. 15), and it now appears that this was fulfilled.

It must be said once more. First a brother admonished his brother; then, when he remained stubborn, he was summoned once and again—indeed, with many witnesses—and finally rebuked by the whole Church, including by our own speech.

**Note:** [Col. 0553D] The printed editions have *et multis testibus* (“and with many witnesses”). The Colbertine manuscript’s *et multo teste* (“and with a single great witness”) is more elegant. Here Celestine shows that the rules of correction prescribed by the Lord were observed toward Nestorius. Therefore below, instead of *diuturnae constitutionis* (“of a long-standing arrangement”), we would prefer *divinae constitutionis* (“of a divine ordinance”), although here Celestine is responding to those who kept saying that Nestorius had been condemned too hastily.

We did nothing premature or immature in this matter; the order of a long-standing process, having been observed, condemned him.

We could not delay any longer, lest, as it is written, we appear to run with the thief and to share our portion with the adulterer (Ps. 50:18), especially when the offending eye is commanded to be removed (Matt. 5:29).

At this point he demanded, as a shortcut, a field for combat after remedies had so often been offered; he demanded a priestly examination that he would not attend. He went forth to war as a commander of the camp, professing himself the enemy; as a teacher of the faith, he carried weapons of faithlessness against the faith, since he appears not so much to have advanced as to have been expelled.

### 10

I do not ask what vows you then poured out to our Lord, since the outcome teaches what you were able to desire.

Do not think us ignorant of the events that took place; the report of our holy brother Cyril disclosed their order to us.

He admonished the man whom a customary summons would now make inexcusable; the man scorned to attend.

Who would have believed that the man who had demanded a synod would be absent from the synod?

**Note:** [Col. 0553D–0554D] This is how the word appears in the Colbertine manuscript, not *abfuturum* (“would be absent”), as in the common editions. Likewise, below the same manuscript reads *afuit* (“was absent”), not *abfuit*. The common editions have *perculsa est* (“was struck”), whereas the cited manuscript more fittingly has *pressa est* (“was pressed down”), since pressing is proper to weight.

There the lightness of falsehood was pressed down by the weight of truth, and the darkness of hidden faithlessness did not dare mingle with the radiance of shining priests. Darkness fled from the light, because we read that there can be no fellowship between them (2 Cor. 6:14). Opposites always offend one another.

Where is what was said to him: that what he spoke in the light and above the rooftops, and what he heard in the ear, he should proclaim (Matt. 10:27)?

But perhaps he wished to remain hidden while present so that, with his conscience acting as judge, shame might anticipate the sentence that had to be borne.

**Note:** [Col. 0554D] Baronius has: “But if for this reason.” The sentence would be more complete as follows: “Unless he wished to remain hidden while present for this reason, so that shame, with conscience judging, might anticipate the sentence that had to be borne; why, then, did he wish to keep his lamp under a bushel?”

Why did he wish to keep his lamp under a bushel (Matt. 5:15), if he thought it had been lit properly? It ought to have shone before the entire holy assembly, so that it might be proved to possess light by the light of all.

The divine sentence does not deceive, since those who are in darkness cannot see the light (John 12:35). He remained hidden so that, by avoiding the college of priests, he might in some way renounce his own dignity.

Thus the first man, Adam, conscious of his sin, hid himself naked before the face of the Lord (Gen. 3:8). Though he had sinned not against him but against his commandments, he feared the voice he had despised and, deceived, fell into fear after losing the confidence of simplicity through the fault of transgression.

**Note:** [Col. 0554D] The printed editions have *nam facit* (“for he does”); this is corrected on the authority of the Colbertine manuscript.

A confession of hiding places gives no reason to doubt the crime; no one innocently hides himself in serious cases.

Thus, following the example of that author of our death, who had lost the garment of honor and glory, he rightly did this together with the first man Adam—he who in this way denied the divinity of the new Adam.

The harassment of so many priests was not before his eyes; nor was the council assembled from almost every part of the world. He was absent from those with whom he did not know how to be present.

### 11

What did avoiding this profit him? He wished to flee those whom he could not escape. For by what means could he evade the one from whom no one can hide?

Or did he, because he had used such associates, consider himself without sin and deign to deny what the Prophet cried out:

“Where shall I go from your face, and where shall I flee from your Spirit? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present” (Ps. 139:7–8).

**Note:** [Col. 0554D] Thus the Colbertine manuscript reads. The printed editions have *indignatus est* (“he was indignant”), and shortly afterward *ab aspectu* (“from the sight”) instead of *ab Spiritu* (“from the Spirit”).

The prophet declares that his sins have no hiding place and that he cannot be concealed from God. He confesses that God is present everywhere, while this man attempts to assert that God was absent within the womb of the one he assumed.

### 12

At last the Holy Spirit, living in his priests as always and one in all, established what would help everyone.

He received nothing from the rottenness or the wound that had arisen, because what the hand of such a Spirit cut away had been carefully amputated.

Solomon says: “Cast the contentious man out of the council, and discord will go out with him” (Prov. 22:10).

He cut off the scandal he had introduced together with himself, because he left with you what he had found there.

**Note:** [Col. 0555D] That is, the Catholic doctrine with which his predecessors had instructed the Constantinopolitans, which he could not remove from their minds.

For, when the Lord speaks (Matt. 15:13), the planting that the Father had planted could not be uprooted—planting that was shown to bear abundant fruit in him.

The Lord preserved his vineyard, Israel—for the house of Israel is the Lord’s vineyard (Isa. 5:7). Therefore it is not surprising that the vineyard escaped its thief, whose guardian we read neither sleeps nor slumbers (Ps. 121:4).

### 13

What will the stubborn impious man do? What hope remains for him, what help?

He has no place for pardon, since it is written that he cannot be forgiven either in this age or in the age to come (Matt. 12:32).

Every arrogant person is brought low. By contrast, Christian humility produces exaltation, because the one who rests above him himself exalts the humble (Isa. 66:2).

These are the words of the Lord through the prophet: “He who acts proudly shall not dwell in the midst of my house” (Ps. 101:7). Through the Apostle he promises that he will destroy the wisdom of the world, foolish though it is (1 Cor. 1:19).

Let him now hear from us what Paul heard then while preaching: “Your great learning is driving you to madness” (Acts 26:24).

Yet may this example be far from him. For an unlearned man is not worthy to hear what was said about a teacher.

Moreover, why should we bring forward the vessel of election against the vessel of dishonor, when the thief alone suffices to reproach this man—the thief whom the Lord, hanging on the cross with Christ after such great crimes, made to confess him through the benefit of punishment (Luke 23:42)?

He asks that Christ remember him in his kingdom. By this brief speech he wipes away whatever he had committed, assisting crimes accumulated over time in a single moment.

The reward does not delay for the one who confesses: immediately came his recompense and return. The one who gladly receives whoever turns to him at any hour answered:

“You will be with me in paradise” (ibid. 43).

He promises future fellowship to the man who was suffering with him in the present. Belief in the heart was made for righteousness, and confession with the mouth for salvation (Rom. 10:10).

Here, amid such a contrast of circumstances, we must cry out and weep together: it is outrageous that a bishop should have lost what a robber was able to find.

**Note:** [Col. 0555D] The printed editions have: “that a bishop should not have found what the robber could.” The Colbertine manuscript restores the reading. Nestorius lost paradise through stubbornness, whereas the robber found it through repentance. Celestine, marveling at God’s judgments, acknowledges that the justice of these two cases is not so hidden that it cannot be perceived: Nestorius faithlessly denies what the robber faithfully professes.

O reward of faith and faithlessness! O judgments of God, a great abyss (Ps. 36:6)! The robber earned paradise, and the priest exile.

Nevertheless, let us have interpreters to explain this matter.

**Note:** [Col. 0555D] Thus the Colbertine manuscript reads. The printed editions have: “Nevertheless, we have true interpreters of this matter.” Our reading may conveniently be understood in this way: nor should we lack an explanation to offer those seeking the interpretation of this matter.

The robber, placed amid torments, recognized the one whom the priest, placed in honor, failed to recognize.

### 14

Is this not the meaning of the words: “And man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts” (Ps. 49:13)?

What else are understanding and judgment except knowing wisdom and discipline and understanding the words of prudence (Prov. 1:3)?

**Note:** [Col. 0556D] The Colbertine manuscript reads *intellectus in judicium* (“understanding unto judgment”).

That is true wisdom which, as Solomon himself says, takes its beginning from fear of the Lord (ibid. 7). The blessed Apostle affirms that he speaks this wisdom among the mature (1 Cor. 2:6).

It is not so serious that the world then scarcely recognized this wisdom as that a bishop has now failed to recognize it.

Here I shall use the words of our Lord through Jeremiah:

“The keepers of my law did not know me, and the priests applauded with their hands the prophets who prophesied iniquity” (Jer. 2:8).

And elsewhere through the same prophet:

“My priests sacrificed to me deceitfully.”

### 15.

Nevertheless, he made use of the defense and praise of the pagans, who testified that such a bishop had never existed. They were speaking truthfully and, in all likelihood, correctly. For when could a bishop ever be found who did not know how to be a Christian? Yet he was thereby proved to be an enemy, because traitors are never displeasing to their enemies.

[Note: It seems that *inimicis iste probatus est* should be restored. Thus Celestine sharply mocks the empty glory that Nestorius may perhaps have acquired among the pagans through his facility in speaking: it is surely no wonder if a betrayer of the Christian religion pleases his enemies and is approved by them.]

### 16.

We have heard what consolations followed this man, who was acting against the law and unjustly (Psalm 70:4). Among others, the Celestinians were present and did not abandon him—workers of iniquity, whom the clear sentence of our hymn-singer pursues: “Long ago, indeed, the enemies of God are scattered, and those who practice iniquity perish” (Psalm 91:10); and, as the same writer says, “they devoured the Lord’s people as though they were eating bread” (Psalm 13:4).

Thus he had with him teachers of his own exile, experienced instructors in this matter. For it is difficult to separate those whom crimes alone have joined, since alliances of vices are bound by a stronger glue. What, however, is the end of such men? Precisely the end that we read of: “The Lord provoked him, and thereafter they shall fall, without honor, in disgrace among the dead forever” (Wisdom 4:19).

But why do we linger longer? Perhaps a more extended discourse will cause weariness. Let us leave “the dead to bury their own dead” (Matthew 8:22).

### 17.

Now hear and understand the words of a simple teacher [Note: Maximian, recently elected, whose teaching was above suspicion and whose life was praiseworthy]. Hear from him what, when he was with us, he frequently heard from our predecessors; hear, certainly, things always heard, not discovered through any desire for novelty.

Our colleague speaks to you with our own mouth, because one faith must necessarily be preached with one accord. Here he does not borrow someone else’s testimony in his own person; he has been given by us, having been elected from among our own number. He is not unknown, nor brought in from elsewhere; you have his own praiseworthy judgment concerning the present matter [Note: That is, the judgment formed concerning him by his presence among you, through which he was known to you—not, as in the case of Nestorius, a judgment formed concerning someone never seen and known only by reputation].

Reputation long deceived those who were absent. Caution prevents us from saying more about him, since it is superfluous to praise what is known. Nevertheless, it is fitting that you now take heed, having been admonished by our own words.

### 18.

Let no one among you shake that foundation which the firm rock and cornerstone established. Build upon it, as Catholics customarily do. You have learned what it means to build upon it with material destined to burn (1 Corinthians 3:11 ff.); this loss will be weighed when the fire’s testing begins to prove the work of each person.

I rejoice that upon this foundation you have laid neither straw, nor wood, nor hay, but those riches which the precepts of wise architects commanded to be laid upon it. You will remain secure, because you are building with such care. Such expenditure promises a great dwelling: with gold, silver, and precious stones you are constructing for yourselves a dwelling-place that cannot be valued.

Eternal things are assessed at no price, since they are not destroyed by injury or age; indeed, the Lord prepared them for the righteous from the foundation of the world.

Let the hands of the faithful, wearied by labor, be strengthened; let their failing knees, at the prophet’s exhortation, be made firm; let those who are fainthearted recover their strength (Isaiah 35:4). Our Savior has appeared. God has shown falsehood what it means to strike at and attack the truth, after controversy arose against the very source from which help comes.

Therefore, dearest sons, remain in him who is, so that you may conquer within yourselves. Be perfected in the same understanding and in the same judgment (1 Corinthians 1:10), so that when the Son of Man comes in his majesty, you may not hear from him, “Depart from me, accursed ones,” but may be able to hear, “Come, blessed ones” (Matthew 25:34, 41).

Let the goats who are to be rejected remain outside. We wish you to be found such that, while those rejected on the left stand in the fire, he may invite you on the right to the kingdom. You will not wait for what has long been waiting for you, so that you may reign. Enter hastily through the narrow gate (Matthew 7:13), which receives those whom the wide gate has never found.

### 19.

Let these words, spoken for the joy of Catholics, suffice for your charity. We wish you to review them frequently, so that, rejoicing in the triumph of the faith, you may understand that the God of love and peace is with us (Philippians 4:9).

Given on the Ides of March, in the consulship of Flavius Aetius and Valerius, men of illustrious rank.

[Note: March 15, A.D. 432.]

[Column 0557]

## APPENDIX. INFORMATION CONCERNING THE REMAINING WRITINGS RELATING TO POPE CELESTINE I

### § I. Letters Relating to Celestine

[Column 0557C]

#### 1.

A certain Antonius, a bishop appointed by Augustine over Fussala, was later accused by the inhabitants of the district and by the people of the surrounding villages of intolerable domination, plunder, and various forms of oppression (Celestine, Letter 1, no. 4). By episcopal judgment he was condemned in such a way that the honor of the episcopate was preserved for him, but its governance and administration were denied him; moreover, he was deprived of communion until he had restored what he had taken (ibid., no. 6).

At first he appeared to consent to this judgment, even to the extent that, after estimating the damage he had inflicted upon the people of Fussala, he set aside a sum of solidi so that communion might be restored to him. But soon he induced Valentinus Baianus, primate of Numidia, by whom he had been ordained, to commend him to Pope Boniface as though he were in every respect blameless (ibid., no. 9).

Boniface then sent a letter to Africa and absolved Antonius, but on the condition that he had given a faithful account of the sequence of events (ibid., no. 4). Soon afterward Boniface departed this life. The bishops of Numidia, however, after receiving his letters, assembled in larger numbers. Then the primate Valentinus himself, having examined the records by which Antonius had been justly condemned, did not hesitate to change his judgment and gave Celestine, Boniface’s successor, a more faithful account of the facts.

This report of Valentinus to Celestine was undoubtedly sent together with Augustine’s letter to the same pope.

#### 2.

At the same time, the people of Fussala complained to Celestine, together with Augustine, because Augustine had rashly placed over them a young man who had not been sufficiently tested; they earnestly implored Celestine’s assistance so that they might be freed from his oppression.

Confirming that their complaint was just, Augustine addressed Celestine as follows: “Nor am I angry with the people of Fussala, because they bring a just complaint against me to your ears: I inflicted upon them a man whom I had not yet tested, and who was not even yet established in age, by whom they were so grievously afflicted” (ibid., no. 9).

For this reason that pious father added his own prayers to theirs and said: “Come to the aid of these people, who ask for your help in the mercy of Christ far more eagerly than he does, and who desire to be freed from his oppression.”

We believe that this petition was presented to Celestine together with the letters of Valentinus and Augustine.

#### 3.

By the example of Antonius, a bishop condemned in Africa who appealed to the Roman pontiff—and by the fact that the Africans did not regard his appeal as invalid—the same bishops demonstrated how sincerely they intended to observe what had been established in the decrees sent by Zosimus concerning episcopal appeals, until it had become clear to them that those decrees were not Nicene (Boniface, Letter 3, no. 5).

The case of Antonius had indeed begun under Pope Boniface. The Africans, however, received authentic copies of the Nicene canons only after that pontiff had died.

#### 4.

About the same time, Caelestius, seized by the hope of deceiving the new pontiff, presented a petition to Celestine in which he requested a hearing. But the prudent pontiff disdained to hear the shameless and obstinate heretic and ordered him to be expelled from the entire territory of Italy.

Prosper preserved this in his *Against the Collator*, chapter 21, no. 58, in these words:

“Celestine, pontiff of venerable memory, to whom the Lord had granted many gifts of his grace for the protection of the Catholic Church, knowing that those condemned are to be offered not an examination of judgment but only the remedy of repentance, ordered Caelestius, who was requesting a hearing as though the matter had not been examined, to be expelled from the whole territory of Italy.

“He judged that the statutes of his predecessors and the synodal decrees were to be observed inviolate, so that he would in no way permit what someone had once deserved to be cut off to be reconsidered.”

#### 5.

Celestine was supported not only by the statutes of his predecessors and of the councils, but also by imperial commands, so that he could deal with Caelestius with such severity (Baronius, under the year 420, nos. 2–3).

For already in the year 481 the emperor Constantius had expressly commanded the prefect Volusianus to drive Caelestius from the City. He was immediately removed by an edict of the praetorian prefects. Yet, after Boniface’s death, he did not hesitate to return to Rome and consequently deserved to be excluded from the whole territory of Italy as well.

He then hastened to Constantinople, where he found an easier opportunity to insinuate himself into the favor and friendship of Nestorius. From Nestorius, indeed, he obtained a consolatory letter as though he were a defender of the truth; Marius Mercator translated it into Latin (Marius Mercator, Baluze’s edition, p. 131).

#### 6.

Apiarius, a presbyter of the Church of Sicca, had been removed from that Church under Pope Boniface at an African council in such a way that, through the agency of Faustinus, the legate of the Apostolic See, the honor of the presbyterate was preserved for him, and he was permitted to exercise the function of his rank elsewhere, wherever he wished or was able.

Later, after being accused by the people of Thabraca of monstrous crimes and therefore deprived of communion, he fled to Rome. Because Celestine somewhat too readily believed his false claim that he had appealed to the Apostolic See, he restored him to communion without hearing the other side.

Nevertheless, unwilling that the Africans should remain ignorant of what had occurred, the pope sent them a letter through the presbyter Leo. In it he declared that he had been exceedingly pleased by Apiarius’s arrival and indicated that he had restored him to communion.

Thereafter Apiarius joined Faustinus, bishop of Potentia and legate of the Apostolic See, on his return to Africa and submitted to a new judgment by the Africans. Celestine’s letter just mentioned was delivered to the Africans shortly before they themselves wrote to that pope concerning Apiarius’s case, and therefore toward the end of the year 425.

#### 7.

Celestine also received from the East a report or petitions from nuns against Daniel, who had governed their monastery (Letter 4, nos. 1 and 9). In these petitions Daniel was accused of unspeakable crimes, specifically of having defiled sacred virgins through incest.

The reason why the virgins, who were situated in the Eastern regions, sought the judgment of the Roman pontiff against him seems to have been no other than that they had heard that Daniel had fled to Gaul. Celestine had recently received those petitions when, in a letter dated July 25, 428, he stated that he had ordered Daniel to be brought to Rome and that Daniel had not yet obeyed the order.

From this it may be inferred that those petitions were written neither much before nor long after the beginning of the year 428. Celestine sent copies of them, together with his fourth letter, to the bishops established throughout the provinces of Vienne and Narbonensis in Gaul, and ordered the originals to be deposited in the archives of the Apostolic See.

#### 8.

Before Celestine wrote to the bishops just mentioned concerning this matter, he had sent a letter to Patroclus, bishop of Arles, through the subdeacon Fortunatus (Letter 4, no. 5). In it he ordered Daniel to be sent to Rome, where, if he trusted his own conscience, he could clear himself of the charges brought against him and not evade the judgment of the Apostolic See demanded by his accusers.

Daniel, however, happened to be ordained bishop during the interval that the subdeacon Fortunatus took to deliver the letter summoning him to give an account of his case. Hence it is clear that this letter to Patroclus, Letter 4, which is dated July 428 and mentions Daniel’s ordination, was written somewhat earlier.

#### 9.

In the same year, 428, in the month of April—according to Liberatus on the first day, but according to Socrates on the tenth—Nestorius, a presbyter of the Church of Antioch, was chosen and ordained bishop of Constantinople.

A report of his ordination was sent to Celestine by the bishops who had attended it. In that report they attributed to Nestorius only as much testimony, Celestine says, as “was required for one summoned from elsewhere to govern another Church” (Letter 13, no. 1).

#### 10.

Celestine immediately replied to the bishops who had written to congratulate him on the newly elected Nestorius (Letter 13, no. 2). He showed himself to be a participant in their mutual joy, while nevertheless hinting that the election of a presbyter from another church ought not to be approved unless this breach of discipline were compensated by the merit of the one elected.

#### 11.

Here the mission of Saint Germanus, bishop of Auxerre, to Britain must not be passed over in silence. Prosper recorded the following in his *Chronicle* under the year 429:

“Agricola the Pelagian, son of the Pelagian Severianus, corrupted the churches of Ireland by introducing his teaching. But through the action of the deacon Palladius, Pope Celestine sent Germanus, bishop of Auxerre, in his place, so that, after the heretics had been driven out, he might direct the Britons to the Catholic faith.”

For who could persuade himself that Celestine entrusted his authority to Germanus without a written commission, or that Germanus went to Britain without his letters? Nor did Celestine stop there. After Palladius had been ordained bishop for the Scots, he ensured that in those islands the faith was not merely cleansed of heresy but also spread more widely.

Prosper praises his zeal in this matter in *Against the Collator*, chapter 21, no. 58, in these words:

“Nor did he free Britain from this same disease”—the Pelagian one—“with less care: for he not only excluded certain enemies of grace, who occupied only the place of their origin, even from that secluded part of the Ocean; but, after ordaining Palladius bishop for the Scots, while striving to preserve the Roman island as Catholic, he also made the barbarian island Christian.”

#### 12.

When Nestorius began to publish a new and perverse doctrine, he offended many, both clergy and laity, who contradicted him. He deprived the laity of communion and the clergy of their rank. He then hastened to inform Celestine of this by letter.

Cyril mentions this letter in the document by which he announced to Nestorius the sentence that Celestine had issued against him. He begins there as follows:

“We communicate with all those who have been separated from you, O Nestorius, because of the faith, or who have been deposed, both laity and clergy.”

He immediately adds:

“For it is not right that those who know how to think correctly should be condemned by your judgments, BECAUSE THEY DID WHAT WAS RIGHT AND CONTRADICTED YOU; for this you indicated in the letter that you wrote to our most holy fellow bishop Celestine of great Rome.”

Yet of the letters sent by Nestorius to Celestine before Cyril wrote this, we possess only two, and in neither does that heretic make any mention of those who contradicted him and had been removed either from communion or from the clerical order. Moreover, in the second of them Nestorius recalls that he had already written to Celestine many times from the beginning.

Accordingly, the letter of which Cyril speaks should rightly be considered to have been written between the first and second letters that have come down to us, and therefore around the end of the year 429.

#### 13.

After the sentence issued against Nestorius had been announced to him, and after the period of respite granted him had long since elapsed, he did not in the least withdraw from his heresy. While the synod summoned at Ephesus was being prepared, Cyril consulted Celestine (Letter 16) as to whether Nestorius should be received at the synod even if he abandoned his error, or whether the sentence of deposition into which he had fallen by despising the respite should not be remitted to him.

Cyril also warned Celestine not to allow himself to be caught unwarily by those whose faith was suspect. Celestine replied to this letter of Cyril on May 7, 431. It follows that Cyril’s letter was written not long after the beginning of that year, especially since it mentions the synod to be held at Ephesus, which the emperor Theodosius had first begun to summon on November 19, 430.

#### 14.

In the same year, certain presbyters in Gaul brought forward various questions concerning free will, which were disturbing the Church by their novelty. Tuentius, a bishop, then decided that Celestine should be consulted concerning them, and deserved to receive a response from him (Letter 21, no. 2).

Later, when writing to the bishops of Gaul for the same reason, Celestine recalls both Tuentius’s letter and his own reply in these words:

“Much has already been said concerning these matters at the time when we sent a written response to our brother Tuentius.”

Since this Tuentius appears to be none other than the man whom Zosimus indicates was ordained by Proculus, bishop of Marseilles (Letter 4, no. 4), we should rightly consider those presbyters whom Celestine was consulted about by Tuentius to have been from Marseilles. They were the men who at that time began openly to disapprove of Augustine’s teaching concerning grace.

Accordingly, we believe that both what Tuentius wrote and what Celestine wrote in reply belong to the same year, 431.

#### 15.

While the synod at Ephesus was being held, Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, sent a letter to Leo, then archdeacon, to be delivered by him to Celestine. In it Cyril stated that Juvenal, bishop of the Church of Jerusalem, had sought primacy over the province of Palestine at the aforesaid synod and had attempted to support his insolent ambitions with fictitious documents. At the same time he earnestly begged that no assent be given in Rome to such unlawful efforts.

The reason why this letter was addressed to the archdeacon, so that it might be delivered to the pope himself, and the fact that it actually was delivered to him, are demonstrated by the circumstance that an authentic copy of it was preserved in the archives of the Apostolic See.

Accordingly, when a copy of it happened to be sent by Maximus, bishop of Antioch, to Leo, now pope, Leo himself replied to Maximus (Letter 110, no. 4):

“You should know that we sought out in our archives and found the authentic original of the letter of Cyril of holy memory, a copy of which you sent to us.”

#### 16.

After four months had elapsed from the deposition of Nestorius, on October 15, 431, the bishops whom the synod of Ephesus had delegated to the emperor Theodosius ordained Maximian, a presbyter of the Church of Constantinople, in the place of the aforementioned heretic. They immediately sent letters announcing his ordination to Celestine through John the presbyter and Epictetus the deacon.

Celestine states that these letters, which contained a commendation of Maximian, were delivered to him shortly before Christmas (Letter 22, no. 4).

#### 17.

The emperor Theodosius added a personal letter to the bishops’ aforementioned letter, in which he testified that he approved Maximian’s ordination. When Celestine saw that the emperor’s judgment agreed with the testimony of the bishops, he was so filled with joy that he wished those sacred letters of imperial piety to be read on Christmas Day itself before the gathering of the entire Christian people in the basilica of Saint Peter, so that the people might share in his joy and more willingly offer public prayers to God for the emperor (Letter 23).

#### 18.

Maximian himself, having been raised to the see of the royal city, also informed Celestine by letter of his ordination (Letter 24, no. 1). Those letters, written in simple language, revealed the sincere purity of his mind and faith.

#### 19.

Socrates, in Book VII, chapter 40, mentions certain famous letters of Celestine which, he says, he had sent to Cyril of Alexandria, John of Antioch, and Rufus of Thessalonica [Valesius adds this in connection with the matter, although it is absent from the Greek]. In them Celestine allegedly taught that nothing prevented someone who had been designated for a particular Church, or who actually existed as its bishop, from being transferred to another Church.

In this matter, however, we regard Socrates’s account as highly suspect.

#### 20.

The learned Tillemont, in volume XIV, pages 149–150, without doubting the authenticity of those letters, thinks that they were perhaps written when Nestorius was appointed in the place of Sisinnius after the latter’s death and when many who had chosen Proclus suffered rejection.

But if Celestine had written such a letter on that occasion—that is, in the year 428—and had then decided the question whether bishops ordained for one Church could be transferred to another, there would have been no reason why Proclus, after Nestorius was deposed in 431 and after many more had supported him, should not have been appointed to the throne of the Church of Constantinople.

Socrates testifies that the only obstacle preventing the victory of the opinion of those who sought this was that some opposed his election, saying that ecclesiastical canon prohibited the transfer of a man designated bishop of one city to another city.

#### 21.

Indeed, Socrates shows that Celestine’s letters by which this matter was decided were written after Maximian’s ordination and were first produced only after the death of that bishop.

After relating that Maximian died after administering his Church for two years and five months, Socrates says that the emperor Theodosius, without any hesitation and before Maximian’s body had even been buried, ordered the bishops who were present to place Proclus on the episcopal throne. This, he says, was also confirmed by letters of Celestine, bishop of Rome, then produced, which Celestine had sent to John of Antioch and Rufus of Thessalonica, teaching that nothing prevented this, and so forth, as above.

But this too cannot easily be reconciled with historical truth. In the year following Maximian’s ordination, Celestine died; and John of Antioch, who had previously been removed from communion by the judgment of the synod of Ephesus, remained separated from it until Celestine’s death.

Who could believe that this pope gave letters of peace and communion to a bishop who had been separated by the judgment of a synod that Celestine himself had confirmed?

#### 22.

I will readily grant that Celestine could have written that nothing prevented Proclus, ordained at Cyzicus but never admitted there, from being placed over the Church of Constantinople.

But I will never persuade myself that the Roman pontiff—whose writings everywhere breathe the greatest zeal for the inviolate preservation of the statutes of his predecessors—could, contrary to the discipline carefully commended by his predecessors and consistently preserved by his successors for many centuries, have written, without any necessity requiring it, that not only a man who had been designated but not admitted, but even one who actually existed as a bishop, could be transferred to another Church.

Celestine was not unaware that this latter practice had been expressly forbidden, not only by the Council of Nicaea, canon 16; the Council of Sardica, canons 1 and 2; and the Council of Carthage, held at Capua, canon 38, which is cited, but also by his predecessors: Julius I, Letter 1, no. 5; Damasus, Letter 5, no. 4, and Letter 6, no. 3; and Siricius, Letter 10, no. 16.

Nor was he the sort of man who, knowing this, would either prescribe or permit the opposite.

#### 23.

Nevertheless, Socrates’s account should not be rejected entirely. Nor can it be denied that letters of Celestine could have been produced before Theodosius showing that nothing prevented Proclus from being appointed to the see of the Church of Constantinople.

Perigenes, once ordained for the people of Patras but rejected by them, was later chosen bishop by the Corinthians and was granted to them by the authority of the Apostolic See. Thereafter Celestine’s predecessor Boniface allowed no one to reopen or reconsider the case of Perigenes, since he regarded it as settled by the judgment of the Apostolic See.

Celestine himself addressed the third of his letters to Perigenes by name, as one who held a place among the principal bishops of Illyricum.

Therefore, when the election of Proclus was under discussion, and so that no one might be troubled by the canon once brought against him, a copy of this letter could appropriately have been brought forward. It would demonstrate that Proclus could lawfully be transferred to the episcopate of the Church of Constantinople, since Celestine—whose decrees the synod of Ephesus had treated with such reverence—had clearly approved such a transfer.

Socrates, however, hearing this from another person and, in a manner not unusual for him, combining and confusing entirely different events, persuaded himself that Celestine had taught this in those famous letters (Celestine, Letter 12) which he sent to Cyril, John, and Rufus and which we still possess, although we read nothing similar in them.

He adopted this view all the more readily because it favored the opinion concerning the transfer of bishops that he had already formed and deliberately defended in Book VII, chapter 36.

#### 24.

The same writer seems more worthy of belief in what he reports in Book VII, chapter 10:

“Celestine also took away from the Novatians the churches that they had in Rome and compelled Rusticulus, their bishop, to gather the people secretly in private houses.”

He adds:

“For until that time the Novatians had flourished greatly at Rome, possessing many churches there and gathering a very large multitude of the people in them.”

Yet earlier, as Socrates himself testifies in the same place, chapter 9, Innocent had already begun to persecute those same heretics and had taken many churches away from them.

### § II. Decrees Ascribed to Celestine

[Column 0564D]

#### 25.

In the *Pontifical Book* Celestine is said to have established that the 150 psalms of David should be sung before the sacrifice, whereas previously this had not been done and only Paul’s Epistles and the holy Gospel had been read.

Yet we still possess homilies and sermons in which Fathers older than Celestine explain the psalms and other Scriptures apart from the Gospels and Paul’s Epistles—Scriptures that had been read to the people when they assembled for the celebration of the sacrifice.

#### 26.

Four other decrees were published in editions of the councils beginning with Crabbé’s, as though they had been excerpted from Gratian.

The first of them is expressed as follows: “No primate, no metropolitan, and none of the other bishops shall enter the city of another,” and so forth. It is identified as having been issued by Gratian in Celestine’s name, in Distinction 9, Question 2, chapter 3.

But the other editors of the councils rashly followed Crabbé, who had been deceived by some false edition of Gratian. For in Gratian himself, at the cited place, as also in Ivo, Part V, chapter 102, and in Burchard, Book I, chapter 66, and in other compilers of canons, the passage is not attributed to Celestine but to Callistus. It is in fact read in Callistus’s second letter, fabricated by Pseudo-Isidore.

#### 27.

The second is reported from Gratian, Distinction 30, Question 1, chapter 9, in this form:

“If any priest has fornicated with his spiritual daughter, let him know that he has committed serious adultery. Therefore, if the woman is a laywoman, she must abandon everything, give her possessions to the poor, and, having entered a monastery, serve God until death.

“But the priest who has given a bad example to the people must be deposed from every office and do penance for twelve years while living as a pilgrim. Thereafter he must go to a monastery and serve God there for all the days of his life.”

#### 28.

Related to this is the third decree, which Gratian immediately adds under the same name in these terms:

“A bishop or presbyter ought not to associate with women who have confessed their sins to him. If, God forbid, this should happen, let him do penance in the same manner as in the case of a spiritual daughter: a bishop for fifteen years, a presbyter for twelve; and let him be deposed, if the matter should nevertheless come to the knowledge of the people.”

#### 29.

Concerning those two decrees, it seems beyond doubt that they were issued together and by the same author. Nor is it less clear to anyone who has acquired some knowledge of ecclesiastical discipline that decrees of this kind do not at all belong to the age of our Celestine.

At that time fallen bishops or presbyters were indeed removed from their rank, but public penance was not imposed upon them to be completed over a fixed number of years. Much less had the practice yet arisen of completing such penance by living as a pilgrim. This custom corresponds much more closely to the age of Celestine III than to that of Celestine I.

#### 30.

The final decree determines which woman is the true wife of a man who has married twice and establishes that parents, brothers, and relatives may be called as witnesses when a marriage is contracted or dissolved. Gratian, Distinction 35, Question 6, chapter 2, describes it as attributed by the *Palea* to Celestine in this form:

“It seems to us that the second woman whom he married contrary to the prohibition of the Church is not his wife, even if he had not had the first one betrothed,” and so forth.

But in Gregory IX’s *Decretals*, Book IV, Title 18, chapter 3, it is restored to Clement III, and a marginal note indicates that it had formerly been attributed to Celestine III.

# In the Year of Our Lord 438. Antoninus Honoratus, Bishop of Constantine

## Prolegomena

[Column 0565]

## Schoenemann’s Historical and Literary Account of Antoninus

*(Schoenemann, Historical and Literary Library, volume II.)*

### § I. Life

[Column 0565C]

Antoninus Honoratus, or, as he is called elsewhere, Honoratus Antoninus, bishop of Constantine in Africa, lived during the persecution that Genseric, king of the Vandals, had stirred up against the Catholics. He consoled by letter a certain Arcadius, a Spaniard who had been driven into exile on account of his faith, and encouraged him to endure still greater hardships.

### § II. Writings

There remains today that Letter exhorting its recipient to endure labors for Christ—a serious and elegant work—which Baronius rightly says breathes the character of an ancient apostolic writing. It was composed approximately between the years 437 and 440.

### § III. Editions

It was first published by Sichard in 1528, and after being reproduced in various editions of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, it was made more accurate and illuminated by Theodoric Ruinart, as the following record demonstrates.

## The Sixteenth Century

**1528. Basel,** at the press of Heinrich Petri; folio. *A Consolatory Letter of Antoninus, Bishop of Constantine, to Arcadius the Exile*, in Johann Sichard’s *Antidote against All Heresies*, fols. 241–242.

**1556. Basel,** at the same press; folio. *A Consolatory Letter of Antoninus to Arcadius, Sent into Exile by Genseric, King of the Vandals*, in Johann Herold’s *Hæresiologia*, pp. 702–704.

**1575. Paris,** at the press of Michel Sonnius; folio. The same work in the Bigne edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, volume I.

**1589. Paris;** folio. *The Consolatory Letter of Antoninus, Bishop of Constantine, to Arcadius, Sent into Exile by Genseric, King of the Vandals*, in the second edition of the Bigne *Bibliotheca Patrum*, volume III.

**1595. Rome,** from the Vatican press; folio. *The Letter of Antoninus, Bishop of Constantina, to Arcadius*, in Cardinal Baronius’s *Annals*, under the year 437, first edition, volume IV, pp. 659–661 (the whole volume was accurately reprinted in the same press in 1607); in the Cologne edition of 1624, volume V, pp. 743–745; and in the Mansian edition, volume VII (Lucca, 1741), pp. 499–501.

## The Seventeenth Century

**1618. Cologne,** Agrippina; folio. *The Consolatory Letter of Antoninus to a Certain Arcadius, Sent into Exile by Genseric, King of the Goths*, in *The Larger Bibliotheca Patrum*, volume V, part III.

[Column 0568A]

**1644 and 1654. Paris;** folio. *The Consolatory Letter of Antoninus to Arcadius the Exile*, in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, volume III.

**1677. Lyon,** at the press of the Anissons; folio. *The Consolatory Letter of Antoninus Honoratus, Bishop of Constantine, and His Exhortation to Endure Labors for Christ*, in the *Maxima Bibliotheca Patrum*, volume VIII, p. 665 ff.

**1694. Paris,** from the press of Théodore Muguet; octavo. *The Exhortatory Letter of Honoratus Antoninus, Bishop of Constantia in Africa, to Arcadius, an Exile for the Faith under Genseric, the Arian King of the Vandals*, in Theodoric Ruinart’s *History of the Vandal Persecution*, part II, chapter 4, pp. 433–439.

[Column 0567]

# A Consolatory Letter of Antoninus Honoratus, Bishop of Constantine, to Arcadius, Sent into Exile by Genseric, King of the Vandals

*(The Larger Bigne Bibliotheca Patrum, volume VIII.)* (C)

[Column 0567B]

Go forward, faithful soul, go forward; and, as a confessor of unity, rejoice, because you have been worthy to suffer disgrace for the name of Christ, just as the apostles did when they were scourged.

Behold, that serpent now lies beneath your feet. He was able to fight, but he fell because he could not crush you. I beg you, press upon his head. Let him not rise again in this contest of martyrdom; let no one move you.

Behold, Christ rejoices and watches you; the angels rejoice and help you. The throng of demons watches your heel. Do not fail, lest the demons who now mourn should rejoice.

With you is the entire choir of the martyrs who preceded you. The martyrs await and defend you, and they extend the crown to you. I beg you, hold fast what you hold, lest another receive your crown (Revelation 31).

How short is the time during which you will be fighting! And how long will be the time during which you will live victorious forever!

You have already begun; complete the work. Today it is revealed why you suffer. Nothing is hidden from the Lord. Let the devil not deceive you in this matter when he brings a cloud upon you; this is what he wants: that you, beloved brother, may not suffer.

But, brother, you have a contest before you. This confession is unimpaired: if you die, be certain that you will be a martyr.

Job paid no attention to his wife, and therefore he conquered; he paid no attention to his household, his wealth, or his friends, and rightly overcame. Adam loved his wife more than was proper, and therefore fell so lamentably. Thus says the Lord: “Whoever does not leave father, or mother, or wife, or sons, or daughters for my sake is not my disciple” (Mark X). What if, under the condition of this life, you had died—would your wife or household have been able to call you back? For hold fast to the one whom you have grasped; cling to him; hold him firmly and do not let him go. [Col. 0567D] Do not look back at your wife or household. [Col. 0568B]

Lift up your heart: you have begun a perfect battle. The very archangel who fell is fighting; he himself is wrestling with you. But the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are with you. See that you do not fear: he helps you so that he may crown you. The mother of the seven Maccabean sons sent them to death for Christ. They were tortured before her, and she herself encouraged them all the more to die; and after her sons had been killed, behold, she now rejoices, crowned together with her sons. Consider that God formed you in your mother’s womb; he himself gave you spirit and soul; he himself adorned you with reason and wisdom. He himself made heaven and earth and everything in them. Thus he wishes to receive you dying for the faith, so that he may display his full majesty to you. Consider the world: it is destined to perish. Consider the sun, moon, and stars: they too are destined to be dissolved. Fight bravely for your soul, which either lives forever or perishes forever. [Col. 0568C] Behold, your sins have been forgiven you, and for this struggle God will erase all your iniquities—whatever you may have been able to commit up to this day.

Hear the prophet Ezekiel speaking on this matter: “On whatever day the wicked person turns away from his wickedness and does justice, I will no longer remember any of his iniquities, says the Lord” (Ezekiel III). Your justice, your faith—for “the righteous person lives by faith” (Romans I; Hebrews X)—your tribulation, stripping, and exile have brought you forgiveness of sins; but death opens the kingdoms of heaven to you. What will you be like when you see yourself with Saint Stephen? What will you be like when you have Peter and Paul, whom you used to ask to be your patrons, as friends? Your soul will soon see Christ; and your body will be in the refreshment [Col. 0568D] of the resurrection, so that the flesh itself may see what your [Col. 0569A] soul will see immediately when it departs. The devil rages; Christ rejoices. Pray, weep, ask for help; and soon you will receive consolation in your mind. Fear the eternal punishments, where there is everlasting burning, where both body and soul are perpetually tortured in darkness, where soul and body are eternally burned together with the devil. Dread Gehenna, and now hold fast to Christ. Now is the moment when you either live or perish. No one will recover you if you fail in this struggle. And what benefit is it to you if you consent to the devil and soon lose your body? Or do you not know that the life of your body is in the power of your God, who can immediately take your flesh away from you if you abandon the faith?

A certain Christian, while being tortured on the rack for the faith, reported that an angel of radiant appearance had stood beside him, carrying a linen cloth soaked with water, and that the angel sprinkled water on his face [Col. 0569B] and wiped it with the cloth. As long as this man was being tortured, the angel did not depart, consoling and refreshing him. Yet the confessor of Christ felt none of the punishments he was enduring. Torments are felt less when one fights for Christ, because the strength of the spirit overcomes the pains of the world; and when the divinity is invoked, the harshness of the tortures is mitigated. Behold, you are detained for a man; and though afflicted, you will not lose the faith, even if you lose your flesh. Offer this perseverance to God, and do not fear the punishment too greatly; for either it will be severe and quickly end, or it will be light and the soul will not be greatly tortured. Nevertheless, continue to pray, because you have begun to wrestle and have not failed; you have begun martyrdom—guard your soul. I adjure you by the unity of the Trinity, for which you suffer death: preserve your heart, and strengthen it through the Holy Spirit [Col. 0569C] whom you wished to breathe forth upon yourself and whom you honored within yourself. Fight bravely through the purity of baptism, which you were unwilling to despise. Be confident of the crown; fight confidently until the Lord wishes to bring your victory to an end. God is now testing your spirit; there is the eye of God: hour by hour he observes you—what you do, what you think, how you fight, how you stand. If he sees you firm, he rejoices and helps you; if weak, he comes to your aid and lifts you up.

Fight, nevertheless, for the truth unto death, and you will be a means of salvation not only for yourself but also for others; otherwise God will demand from you both your own soul and the souls of others. You are Christ’s standard-bearer; you walk first in the battle line. If you fall, you will not be free from responsibility for the death of others. Fear this; for if you conquer, you have fought for the salvation of many, [Col. 0569D] and you have received a manifold crown. God is one; God cannot be lesser; God cannot be changed. You know these things: hold the truth firmly.

But hear briefly what I stated above. God is one: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; and yet flesh belongs to Christ alone. Certainly, soul is one thing and reason another, and yet reason is in the soul. The soul is one; but the soul does one thing and reason another: the soul lives, reason understands. Life belongs to the soul; wisdom belongs to reason; and yet neither is the soul without reason nor reason without the soul. Although they are one, the soul alone receives life, and reason alone receives wisdom. Thus the Father and the Son, although they are one and there is one God, nevertheless flesh belongs to Christ alone, just as wisdom belongs to reason alone, although it does not depart from the soul. [Col. 0570A]

Consider, then, how in the sun heat and brightness are present together in a single ray; yet heat dries and brightness illuminates. Heat receives one thing, brightness another, although heat and brightness cannot be separated from one another. Brightness therefore receives illumination, not heat; heat receives warmth, not illumination.

Thus they act individually, yet do not depart from one another. So too the Son alone received flesh, yet he did not abandon the Father or separate himself from the Father. The Son therefore received flesh in his own distinct property, and yet neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit was absent in majesty. There is equality in divinity and distinct property in the Son’s flesh; nevertheless the divinity of the Father or of the Holy Spirit did not depart from him. Christ assumed flesh—did he, then, [Col. 0570B] depart from the Father or from the Holy Spirit? Therefore the unity is real.

Both the Father and the Holy Spirit filled Christ’s flesh, but in majesty, not by assuming it. Do you wish to know that the Father was in him? “I am not alone,” Christ says, “but the Father is with me also” (John XVI). Hear concerning the Holy Spirit, because the evangelist reports that he was with him: “Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned to the Jordan” (Luke IV). Behold, Christ alone assumed flesh, yet the Father and the Holy Spirit were not absent in majesty. If they fill heaven and earth, they could not abandon Christ’s flesh while remaining in the unity of divinity.

For this purpose, consider a lyre, so that it may produce a musical melody in sweet sounds: three things appear to be present together—skill, hand, and string. Skill directs, the hand touches, and the string resounds. Three things work together, but only the string produces the sound that is heard. Neither skill nor hand produces the sound, but they work together with the string to produce it. So neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit assumes flesh, yet they work together with the Son. Only the string receives the sound; Christ alone received flesh. The operation consists in three, but just as the production of sound belongs to the string alone, so the assumption of human flesh belongs to Christ alone.

These are words from a little one set amid great grief, so that whatever has been said could scarcely come to my heart. This is the right rule of faith. If anything happens to you for this faith, you have completed your martyrdom. Christ received slaps; Christ endured the spittle of others; Christ was given gall and vinegar to drink; Christ was crowned with thorns; Christ was crucified; and, though righteous, was counted among wicked [Col. 0570D] robbers. Christ was pierced with a spear. Christ endured these things for your sin: how much more firmly must you stand for your soul, so that no one may take your crown. You are already in the stadium; tread firmly and do not fear. Be afraid of nothing, fear nothing at all, because the whole Church prays for you to conquer. The Catholic Church awaits you as its martyr, so that it may honor you as it honors its Stephen. See that you do not shame us in this world. See that you do not humiliate us before our adversaries. The Lord Christ sustains you; the Church sustains you. Be utterly confident of the crown; do not fear at all whatever past sins you may have been able to commit.

# In the Year of Our Lord 432–440. Saint Sixtus III, Pope.

# Prolegomena

[Col. 0571]

## Notice on the *Liber Pontificalis*

*(From D. Mansi’s New and Most Ample Collection of the Councils, vol. V.)*

[Col. 0571A] Sixtus, [Note: [Col. 0571B] After an interregnum of twenty days, Sixtus, a Roman by birth, was made pope in the year of Christ 432, the twenty-fifth year of Theodosius and the eighth of Valentinian. To preserve the right faith intact throughout the world, at the beginning of his pontificate he confirmed the Council of Ephesus and its decrees by apostolic authority. He restored John of Antioch and other bishops of the East, who had been divided from the Church by schism, to its unity and communion. Through a revelation from God and at the prompting of Saints Peter and Apollinaris, the first bishops of the see of Ravenna, he learned that, in place of the deceased John, bishop of that see, the deacon Peter, surnamed Chrysologus, ought to be placed over the people of Ravenna. He restored Brictius, bishop of Tours, to his see after seven years, although Brictius had miraculously refuted the accusations of his adversaries and had been removed from office. Nestorius, sent beyond the Roman world and, through the clemency of the emperor Theodosius, permitted to live freely among the Catholics at Antioch in the monastery of Saint Euprepius, appears—according to Saint Prosper and Marcellinus in their chronicles—to have brought about the three-day fire of the city of Constantinople by the just judgment of God the avenger. For this reason the emperor, incited against Nestorius—presumably by Melania, who was burning with zeal for the Catholic faith—forbade that his books be kept and ordered them burned under penalty of confiscation of property. Finally, he ordered the same man, as the author of all the evils of the present time, to be sent into exile. Evagrius writes that, while he was living in exile, his tongue was consumed by worms. Theodorus in his *Collections*, Cedrenus in his *Compendium*, and Nicephorus, book XIV, chapter 26, write that, together with his tongue, his entire body was consumed by putrefaction. Genseric, the Arian king of the Vandals, wishing to overthrow the Catholic faith by Arian impiety, renewed the persecution of Catholics in Africa. He deprived orthodox bishops of their basilicas and expelled them even from the cities, and inflicted martyrdom on many other faithful. After Carthage had been seized by treachery under the pretext of peace, the churches of the Catholics plundered, the remains of the pagans removed, and the famous idol of Caelestis overthrown in Africa, he accomplished in approximately a single day what many councils, the efforts of bishops, and imperial rescripts had been unable to accomplish. Saint Prosper, in his *Chronicle*. See Baronius, from the year 432 through the year 440. SEV. BINIUS.] a Roman by nationality and the son of Sixtus [Ballerini: Xistus], held the see for eight years and nineteen days. [Note: [Col. 0572B] Having held office for eight years less thirty days, he departed this life on the fifth day before the Kalends of April in the year of Christ 440, which was the thirty-third year of Theodosius and the sixteenth of the emperor Valentinian. Saint Prosper, in his *Chronicle*. Baronius, year 440. SEV. BINIUS.] After one year and eight months he was accused by a certain Bassus. [Note: [Col. 0572B] On this matter, see what we shall say below in the notes on the Roman council under Sixtus. SEV. BINIUS.] At that time, when the emperor Valentinian Augustus heard of this, he ordered a council and holy synod to be assembled. When the assembly had taken place, he was cleared by synodal judgment after a thorough examination by fifty-six bishops. Bassus, however, was condemned by the synod, though it was decreed that the viaticum should not be denied him on the final day, out of the Church’s humane compassion [In the Lucensis manuscript, *propter humanitatem* is absent]. When the emperor Valentinian Augustus heard this, he and his mother, the empress Placidia, moved by holy zeal, condemned Bassus by proscription and transferred all his estates and property to the Catholic Church [Ballerini: “they transferred”]. Bassus, by divine will, died within three months. [Col. 0571B] Bishop Sixtus handled his body with his own hands, using linen cloths and aromatics, placed it in a tomb, and buried it at Saint Peter the Apostle, in the chamber of his parents. [Col. 0572A]

He built the Basilica of Saint Mary, Mother of the Lord, which the ancients called Liberius’s, near the Macellum of Libya, where he offered the following:

[Note: Perhaps he merely restored it to a larger form and adorned it with more ample ornaments, in praise and honor of Mary Mother of God; to her, triumphant over Nestorius’s blasphemies, he wished to erect so great a triumphal arch. Pope Hadrian mentions this church in writing to the emperor Charlemagne, in these words: “Moreover, Celestine’s successor Pope Sixtus made the basilica of holy Mary Mother of God, called the Greater, which is also said to be at the Manger. In the same way he himself adorned it with sacred images in golden mosaic, although representing different histories.” These images, having suffered some damage through age, Cardinal Domenico Pinelli, most worthy archpriest of that basilica, took care, with the utmost diligence of craftsmen, to have them restored and preserved when already collapsing; and, following the example of his predecessors, added other venerable images representing the history of Mary Mother of God. Baronius, year 440, no. 2. SEV. BINIUS.]

A very pure silver altar, weighing 300 pounds; three silver patens, weighing 60 pounds; four silver vessels, weighing 60 pounds; a very pure gold bowl, weighing 12 pounds; five silver bowls, weighing 50 pounds; two gold ministerial chalices [Ballerini: three], each weighing one pound; ten silver ministerial chalices, each weighing three pounds; silver water vessels, weighing eight pounds; a silver lamp-crown before the altar, weighing 30 pounds; thirty-four silver lamp-crowns, each weighing ten pounds; four silver candelabra, each weighing twenty pounds; a silver censer, weighing five pounds; twenty-four bronze-gilt *canthara*, each weighing fifteen pounds; the Scavirian estate [Lucensis manuscript: Scaurian] in the territory of Caieta [Lucensis: Geta], yielding, with all its adjoining properties, 312 solidi and a tremissis; the Marmoratian estate in the territory of Praeneste, yielding 92 solidi; the estate of Celer in the territory of Asilinum [Lucensis: Filianum], yielding 111 solidi and a tremissis; the house of Palmatius within the city, near the basilica there, with a bath and a press, yielding 154 solidi and three siliquae; the houses of Claudius at Siciminum [Lucensis: Sicinum], yielding 104 solidi; a silver stag pouring water into the baptistery fountain, weighing twenty pounds; all the silver sacred vessels for baptism, weighing fifteen pounds; the upper rooms of the *aregia* of the steps adjoining the basilica [the phrase is obscure], or whatever appears to be inside it. [Col. 0573B]

He had the shrine of blessed Peter the Apostle made of silver; it weighs 400 pounds. At his request, the emperor Valentinian Augustus offered a golden image with twelve gates and the twelve apostles, together with the Savior adorned with very precious gems, above the shrine of blessed Peter the Apostle [Lucensis: “the Savior adorned above the shrine by the grace of his vow,” sic].

The emperor Valentinian Augustus also made, at the request of Bishop Sixtus, a silver canopy in the Constantinian basilica, which had been taken away by the barbarians, [Note: [Col. 0573C] From this it is perfectly clear that, when the Goths occupied the city, they did not refrain from stripping the ornaments of all the churches, but only those which they knew belonged to the basilicas of the holy apostles Peter and Paul. This is how the plundering and despoiling of the City mentioned above under Innocent must necessarily be understood. SEV. BINIUS.] weighing 1,610 pounds [Lucensis: 11]. During his time the emperor Valentinian Augustus also made the shrine of blessed Paul the Apostle [Col. 0573C] out of silver, weighing 200 pounds [Ballerini: “which”].

Likewise Bishop Sixtus made the shrine of blessed Laurence the martyr with porphyry columns, and adorned the screen [Lucensis: “Plato adorned the screen”; Ballerini: “the exedra”; others: “the platform”], the altar, and the shrine of Saint Laurence the martyr with the purest silver. He made an altar weighing fifty pounds; silver grilles above the porphyry platforms, weighing 300 pounds; and an apse above the grilles, with a silver statue of blessed Laurence the martyr, weighing 200 pounds.

He built a basilica for blessed Laurence, which the emperor Valentinian Augustus granted [Ballerini: consented]. [Note: [Col. 0573C] After these words the Lucensis Codex continues as follows: “He built a monastery in the catacombs. He also made a baptistery fountain at Saint Mary and adorned it with porphyry columns. He set up in the baptistery of the Constantinian basilica eight columns of porphyry which had been assembled since the time of the emperor Constantine; he raised them and adorned them with his letters and verses; and he made a marble panel in the cemetery of Callistus, where he commemorated the names of the bishops. He made three golden bowls: one for Saint Peter, weighing six pounds; one for Saint Paul, weighing six pounds; and one for blessed Laurence, weighing three pounds; and fifteen gold ministerial chalices, each weighing one pound. In this period he held three ordinations in the month of December: twenty-eight priests, twelve deacons, and fifty-two bishops in various places. During his time Bishop Peter made in the city of Rome the Basilica of Saint Sabina, where he also constructed a fountain. He too was buried on the Tiburtine Way, and so forth, as in the printed editions.” MANSI.] There he offered the following: three silver patens, each weighing fifteen pounds [Ballerini: twenty]; three silver vessels, each weighing fifteen pounds; four silver bowls, each weighing eight pounds; a single gold bowl decorated with pearls, weighing ten pounds; a golden lamp of ten wicks [Ballerini: “lamps”], weighing ten pounds; twelve silver ministerial chalices, each weighing [Col. 0574B] two pounds; silver water vessels, weighing eight pounds; a silver service for baptism or penance, weighing five pounds; a gold-and-bronze basin, weighing twenty pounds; thirty silver lamp-crowns, each weighing six pounds; three silver lamp-vessels, each weighing fifteen pounds; two silver candelabra, each weighing thirty pounds; twenty-four bronze *canthara* in the body of the basilica; sixty bronze processional vessels.

In the Constantinian basilica he made an ornament over the fountain which had not previously existed—that is, marble architraves—and erected porphyry columns which the emperor Constantine had assembled and left behind, ordering that they be erected; he also adorned them with verses. [Note: [Col. 0573D] He inscribed two of these verses on each architrave in the octagonal structure. Since they contain a Catholic affirmation concerning original sin against the Pelagian heresy, it seemed appropriate to reproduce them here, so that what is usefully proclaimed throughout the whole world might be preserved for all eternity.

A people destined for heaven is here born from blessed seed,

which the Spirit brings forth from the fertilized waters.

The virginal mother, the Church, conceives her children

as God breathes upon them, and gives them birth in the stream.

Hope for the kingdom of heaven, reborn in this fountain.

The blessed life does not receive those born only once.

This fountain is life, and it washes the whole world,

taking its beginning from Christ’s wound.

Immerse yourself, sinner, in the sacred stream that purifies;

the water will receive the old person and bring forth the new.

If you wish to be innocent, cleanse yourself in this washing,
