whether you are weighed down by ancestral sin or by your own.

There is no difference among those reborn, whom

one fountain, one Spirit, and one faith make one.

Let neither the number of anyone’s sins nor their character

frighten him. Born in this stream, you will be holy.

These verses are from Baronius, year of the Lord 440, no. 5. SEV. BINIUS.] He made a marble panel in the cemetery of Callistus on the Appian Way, where he wrote and commemorated the names of bishops and martyrs [Ballerini: “with memorials”]. He held an ordination in the city of Rome during the month of December: twenty-eight priests, twelve deacons, and fifty-two bishops in various places. He too was buried [Note: [Col. 0574D] The injuries which, in the notes above on the first letter of Sixtus I, we said the first Sixtus, Roman pontiff and martyr, suffered after his death at the hands of Jerome, were also suffered—and indeed to a greater extent—by Sixtus III, whom we are discussing here. For just as a book of the Pythagorean Sixtus or Sextus was circulated by the Origenists under his name, so under the name of this Sixtus three volumes were written by the Pelagians: the first on wealth; the second on evil teachers, works of faith, and the future judgment; and the third on chastity. Baronius demonstrates that these works are full of Pelagianism, years 440, nos. 7–11: the first volume contains the Pelagian claim that a rich person cannot be saved unless he distributes all his possessions to the poor; the second attributes everything to free will and nothing to divine grace; and the third mocks those who maintain that the good of chastity comes from God’s grace. Reader, recognize the book clearly painted in these colors—a book not long ago published under Sixtus’s name, with grave danger to the faithful—lest you drink from the golden cup of Babylon poisons made respectable by an illustrious name. SEV. BINIUS.] on the Tiburtine Way [Col. 0575A] in a crypt near the body of blessed Laurence [Ballerini: “at Saint Laurence”], on the fifth day before the Kalends of April. And the episcopate remained vacant for twenty-two days. [Note: [Col. 0576A] More correctly, forty-two days. For Saint Prosper writes in his *Chronicle*, under the year 440: “When the pontiff Sixtus died on the Kalends of April, the Roman Church remained without a bishop for more than forty days, awaiting with remarkable peace and patience the arrival of the deacon Leo; at that time the latter was being detained in Gaul between Aetius and Albinus, commanders of the Roman army, for the purpose of restoring friendship,” and so forth. There is therefore no doubt that an error entered this passage of Anastasius. Baronius, vol. VI, year 440, nos. 1–2. SEV. BINIUS.]

## Notice by Gallandius

*(From Gallandius, *Bibliotheca Veterum Patrum*, vol. IX.)*

[Col. 0575B] 1. After Celestine, who departed this life at the end of July in the year 432, Xistus was appointed shortly afterward and raised to the Roman see. Since he was made pope during the consulship of Aetius and Valerius, and after exercising the pontificate for eight years and eighteen days departed this life in the year 440, during the consulship of the emperor Valentinian Augustus for the fifth time and Anatolius, we learn from Prosper’s *Chronicle*. [Note: [Col. 0575D] Prosper, *Chronicle*, in the new edition of his works, pp. 432, 434.]

The learned are not in agreement, however, about the day and month on which he was either ordained or died. Some think that his ordination should be assigned to July 31, which fell on a Sunday, and his death to August 18. [Note: [Col. 0575D] Tillemont, vol. XIV, pp. 260, 265, and vol. XV, p. 889, note 2, on Saint Leo.] Others date them somewhat differently.

“In the *Liber Pontificalis*,” says a learned man, [Note: [Col. 0575D] Coutant, *Epistles of the Roman Pontiffs*, p. 1227.] “with which a very ancient Corbie copy and other old catalogues of the Roman pontiffs agree, as does Prosper, at least in the latest edition, the same pontiff is said to have presided over the Church for eight years and eighteen days. Accordingly Antonius Pagius places his ordination on July 24 of the year 432, which was a Sunday, and his death on August 11 of the year 440, [Note: [Col. 0575D] Pagi, on the year 432, § 6, and on the year 440, § 2.] relying especially on the words of Prosper, who records that after his death he was awaited for more than forty days so that someone might be appointed in his place. There would nevertheless be greater agreement with the words of Prosper cited above if Xistus were taken to have died around the end of July.” Thus far the learned author.

2. “The supreme bishop entered upon the pontificate,” says Prosper, [Note: [Col. 0576D] Prosper, cited work, p. 432.] “amid the peace and remarkable unanimity of the entire City.” We have a particularly authoritative witness to this fact in Xistus himself. For, writing to Cyril of Alexandria, [Col. 0575D] [Note: [Col. 0576D] Xistus, Letter 1, no. 1, below.] he says:

“When your Holiness learns, both from our letters and from the report of the brethren, with what unanimity of all, through the dispensation of divine Providence, this ordination of ours took place, you will certainly give thanks to the Lord who grants grace on our behalf, dearest brother, that as guardian of his own gift he may deign to preserve ecclesiastical peace.”

Moreover, the following notable circumstance also occurred at that time: the whole East was in a certain sense present at his ordination, since it was carried out in the presence of Hermogenes and Lampetius, envoys of the Eastern bishops. Thus the holy pontiff speaks in the same letter to Cyril: [Note: [Col. 0576D] Same work, same place.]

“We give thanks to the humanity of our God toward us, because at the time when he deigned to call us to the highest summit of the priesthood, he granted us, in accordance with your devotion, the presence of our holy brothers and fellow bishops Hermogenes and Lampetius. Through them we necessarily sent this letter to your fraternity, as witnesses of our ordination. For we believed that all of you, by whom they had been sent, were present in them, since those whom spiritual grace joins together are in no way separated by distance.”

3. Xistus achieved great renown for his name while he was still serving as a priest. For he was the first to pronounce an anathema against the Pelagians before a very large gathering, as Augustine says in his reply to the priest Xistus: [Note: [Col. 0576D] Augustine, Letter 194, no. 1, works, vol. II.] He also testifies elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0576D] Same author, Letter 191, no. 1, same place.] that Xistus’s letters on this matter, although brief, which had been sent through the acolyte Leo to the blessed elder Aurelius, were copied by him with exultant eagerness and read with great zeal to anyone he could reach. “For what,” he adds, “could be more pleasing to read or hear than so pure a defense of God’s grace against its enemies, from the mouth of one who had previously been portrayed as a powerful patron of those same enemies?”

Shortly afterward, having received on this same subject a longer letter from the priest Xistus, filled with the sincerity of his faith, the holy Doctor was filled with great joy of heart. He immediately wrote a most learned letter to Xistus [Note: [Col. 0576D] Same author, Letter 194, cited.] [Col. 0577A] in which he presented the chief points of the Catholic doctrine asserted against the Pelagians, adding the following at the beginning: [Note: [Col. 0577B] Augustine, Letter 194, no. 2.]

“Therefore, dearest brother, although we do not see you with the eyes of the flesh, in spirit we hold you, embrace you, and kiss you in the faith of Christ, in the grace of Christ, and among the members of Christ.”

4. Prosper quotes a fragment of this Augustinian letter. In praising Xistus’s pastoral vigilance, he prefaces it with these words: [Note: [Col. 0577B] Prosper, *Against the Collator*, chapter 21, elsewhere 44, no. 4.]

“We trust that, by the Lord’s protection, what he accomplished in Innocent, Zosimus, Boniface, and Celestine he will accomplish in Xistus; and that, in guarding the Lord’s flock, this share of glory has been reserved for this shepherd: just as those men openly drove away wolves, so may he drive away hidden ones.”

Then Prosper quotes the speech of the most learned elder Augustine, who urged Xistus to labor with him, saying: [Note: [Col. 0577B] Augustine, Letter 194, cited, no. 2.]

“Some people think that impieties justly condemned ought still to be defended with greater freedom. Others enter houses more secretly and do not cease sowing in private what they already fear to proclaim openly. There are also those who have become completely silent, restrained by great fear, but who still retain in their hearts what they do not dare to utter with their mouths; yet they may be well known to the brethren from their earlier defense of that same doctrine. Accordingly, some must be restrained more severely, others investigated more vigilantly, and others treated more gently but taught no less diligently: so that, if they are not feared, they may not be lost; yet they must not be neglected, lest they perish.”

5. Xistus, once established in Peter’s chair, confirmed Prosper’s hopes by his distinguished deeds. His letters, which we have again published following Coutant, abundantly attest this. Quoting a passage from one of them, Vincent of Lérins writes as follows: [Note: [Col. 0578B] Vincent of Lérins, *Commonitory*, chapter 32 of book 2.]

“At last we added … the authority of the Apostolic See … namely, that of the holy Pope Xistus, who now venerably illumines the Roman Church … . Thus the holy Pope Xistus says in the letter which he sent to the bishop of Antioch concerning the case of Nestorius: [Note: [Col. 0578B] Xistus, Letter 6, no. 7, below.]

“‘Therefore,’ he says, ‘since, as the Apostle says, there is one faith which has clearly prevailed [another reading: “and conquered”], let us believe what must be said, and say what must be held.’”

What, then, are the things that must be believed and said? He continues:

“‘Let nothing further be permitted to novelty, because nothing ought to be added to antiquity. Let the clear faith and belief of our ancestors not be disturbed by any admixture of mire.’”

Entirely apostolic: he adorned the belief of the ancestors with the light of clarity, while describing novel profanities as an admixture of mire.

## Notice by Schoenemann

*(From Schoenemann, *Bibliotheca Historico-Litteraria*, vol. II.)*

### § I. Life of Pope Xistus

[Col. 0577C]

A Roman by birth, he succeeded Celestine in the year 432. According to Baronius, he was ordained on April 26; according to Pagius, on July 24. While he was still a priest, he made his name famous through his opposition to Pelagius and Caelestius. For when, somehow or other, a rumor had arisen that Xistus not only favored the teaching of Pelagius but was also a friend and patron of the Pelagians themselves, he became so inflamed with zeal to dispel this calumny that he was the first, at the council held concerning Caelestius in the year 418, to pronounce an anathema against him.

Soon afterward, in letters written to Augustine and Alypius, he explained his doctrine of grace so clearly that Augustine indicated, in letters still preserved, that he greatly approved and welcomed it. [Col. 0577D] All this could not fail to help him attain the highest summit of ecclesiastical dignity.

It happened that, at his very ordination, envoys of Cyril of Alexandria and of other bishops, who had been sent to his predecessor to establish peace in the East, were present. For this reason he expresses exceptional joy in the letter concerning his ordination which he sent to Cyril.

Following Celestine’s example, he firmly adhered to Cyril and to the decisions of the Council of Ephesus. Eutherius of Tyana and Helladius of Tarsus, bishops, unsuccessfully attempted to alienate him from them, although they had written to him with no less truth than seriousness, maintaining that Nestorius, like the other bishops, had been unjustly condemned; that Cyril’s Twelve Chapters were a blasphemous novelty contrary to all Scripture and anathematizing the legitimate and ancient traditions of the holy Fathers; and that the acts of that council had been rejected without reason or legal basis, even by the emperor himself, with Cyril’s conduct in them being altogether unrestrained.

His joy was therefore all the greater at the change of John of Antioch, who, finally, at the emperor’s urging, declared that he assented to the sentence passed against Nestorius and recognized Maximian as bishop of Constantinople.

Among his greatest praises they usually include what we have learned from Prosper: that by his vigilance he frustrated the schemes of Julian, who had attempted once again to insinuate himself into communion with the Catholic Church.

According to Baronius’s calculation, he died on March 28; according to Pagius, on August 11; but according to Coutant, toward the end of July in the year 440.

### § II. Writings of Pope Xistus

[Col. 0578D]

The letters of his that survive are these:

I and II, to Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, written in the middle of the year 432. They have been transmitted to us only through a Greek translation; Cotelerius translated them into Latin, and he also observes that the first, although addressed only to Cyril, was in reality an encyclical.

III, to the same recipient, written in the year 433.

IV, to John, bishop of Antioch, written in the same year.

V, to Perigenes, bishop of Corinth, written in the year 435.

VI, to the synod to be assembled at Thessalonica, written, like the following letter, in the year 435.

VII, to Proclus, bishop of Constantinople, written, together with the following letter, in the year 437.

VIII, to the bishops of all Illyricum.

[Col. 0579A] Coustantius provides information about those works now lost that Xystus wrote both before and during his pontificate [Note: [Col. 0579D] See this information below. EDIT.]. To this Xystus, Jacobus Salonius first attributed—and later Joannes Garnerius also assigned—the three books *On Wealth*, *On Evil Teachers and Works of Faith*, and *On Chastity*; but it must be acknowledged that they rest more on conjecture than on any probable argument. The same Joannes Garnerius, in a very lengthy dissertation prefixed to the works of Marius Mercator, attempted [Note: [Col. 0579D] This dissertation of Garnerius is found in our volume XLVIII above, among the works of Marius Mercator. EDIT.] to attribute to this Xystus the books of the *Hypomnesticon* published by the Benedictines in the appendix to volume X of Augustine’s works. Natalis Alexander, however, refutes him in century V, pp. 49 ff. The *Acts concerning the Purging of Xystus and the Accusation of Polychronius, Bishop of Jerusalem*, collected at Xystus’s own command and first published by Petrus Crabbius in the councils edited by him, reveal their author as not only an impostor infected with a harsh and barbarous style but also guilty of countless offenses against historical truth. Coustantius suspects that they came from the same workshop in which the acts of the Synod of Sinuessa under Marcellinus, and of the Roman synods under Sylvester and Liberius, were forged—works about which he discussed their proper places with exceptional acumen and learning—namely, during the time of Pope Symmachus and for the benefit of the judgment delivered by the Roman synod at the beginning of the sixth century concerning that pontiff’s case. This fraud is therefore far older than the forgeries of Isidore Mercator, although Isidore himself was by no means idle: he fabricated a letter of Xystus III to the Easterners, into which he inserted the tale of Bassus’s accusation and Xystus’s purgation. Coustantius observes, however, that everything he says there was borrowed from the single published *Anastasius*, or *Pontifical Book* [Col. 0579C].

## § III. Editions of the Writings of Xystus

Before Baronius, no genuine writing of Xystus was available. Merlinus had published the offspring of Isidore, and Crabbius published it again; it may perhaps also have been received into the Roman collection of the *Decretal Letters*. After completing that work, Antonius de Aquino finally obtained two letters—III and IV—from manuscript copies in the Vatican and communicated them to Baronius, who published them in the *Annals* under the year 433. After a sufficiently long interval, Lucas Holstenius discovered four new letters—V, VI, VII, and VIII—in the same library’s codices; Cardinal Barberini brought them to light in the *Roman Bipartite Collection*, published after Holstenius’s death from his papers [Col. 0579D]. Finally, Cotelerius discovered the remaining two, but only in Greek. He therefore translated them into Latin himself and had them printed in the *Monuments of the Greek Church*; Baluzius and Harduinus reproduced them. Coustantius eventually undertook to correct and elucidate all of them, and Gallandius follows him.

**1523.** Paris; folio. *Decrees of Pope Sixtus*, that is, the *Letter to the Easterners* fabricated by Isidore Mercator, in Jac. Merlinus’s *Councils*, vol. I; in the second edition (Cologne [Col. 0580A], 1530, folio), fols. CXLVI–CLXXVII; and in the third edition (Paris, 1535, octavo), fols. CC–CCI.

**1538.** Cologne, at the press of Petrus Quentel; folio. *Decrees of Pope Sixtus III, or Letter to the Easterners*, in Petrus Crabbe’s *Councils*, vol. I, fols. CCCXVIII–CCCXX. Also, *Pope Sixtus’s Collections concerning His Purgation*, which he compiled when accused by Marinianus and Bassus, fols. CCCXXI–CCCXXV.

This is the first edition of that purgation of Xystus and Polychronius which Petrus Crabbius discovered in two very old, highly faulty, and corrupted copies. Although these agreed with one another in a certain harsh barbarism, they differed greatly in the variation of individual words and sentences. Crabbius therefore thought it not unworthy to reproduce the text of each, without alteration, in two columns [Col. 0580B]; he also attempted, by conjecture, to reconcile their discrepancies and restore the text to a sounder meaning and more polished expression. The narrative that he himself composed occupies the middle position between the two columns.

**1589.** Paris; folio. *Pope Sixtus III’s Book on Wealth*; his *Letter on Evil Teachers, Works of Faith, and Future Judgment*; and his *Book on Chastity, addressed to a Certain Truly Christian Man*, in the second edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. V.

**1591.** Rome; folio. *Pope Sixtus III’s Letter to the Easterners*, in the *Collection of the Decretal Letters of the Ancient Roman Pontiffs* of Cardinal Carafa, vol. I.

**1594.** Rome, from the Vatican press; folio. Two letters of Pope Sixtus III, namely: (1) to Cyril of Alexandria, congratulating him on the removal of Nestorius and the condemnation of his heresies; (2) to John of Antioch, on the same subject; published from a Vatican codex in Baronius’s *Annals* under the year 433, nos. 12–21, vol. V; reprinted in 1607, pp. 635–637; Cologne, 1624, pp. 718–719; and in the Mansian edition, vol. VII, pp. 451–455. **1721.** Paris; folio. *The Letters and Decrees of Saint Xystus III, Collected from Every Source and Arranged Chronologically, Further Illustrated with Critical and Historical Notes and Admonitions*, by Petrus Coustantius, in *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, vol. I, pp. 1229–1272. Included are: (1) after the second letter, a letter of John of Antioch to Xystus, in Greek and Latin, written around 433, and found in the same place; (2) a letter of Eutherius, bishop of Tyana, and Helladius, bishop of Tarsus, to the same Xystus, written in the same year. From pp. 1273 to 1280 there follows a notice of the remaining writings relating to Xystus; and in the appendix to this volume, the *Acts of Xystus’s Purgation*, with notes and an admonition, pp. 111–124. With these, all this outstanding work of Coustantius comes to an end. From the preface we learn that a large part of it still lay hidden in the autograph manuscripts of the blessed author. We hoped that, if one of the Maurist congregation did not publish the whole work of that distinguished man, nevertheless, in the progress of the splendid work which those Fathers had recently begun—a collection, I mean, of all the councils of Gaul, greatly enlarged and improved beyond Sirmondus’s edition—at least those monuments of the Roman pontiffs that concern the Gallican Church, which are certainly neither few nor insignificant, might emerge polished by Coustantius’s hand. But the most turbulent circumstances into which Gaul has now fallen have deceived, indeed destroyed, that most welcome hope.

**1761.** Florence; folio. *The Life, Letters, and Decrees of Pope Sixtus III*, in Mansi’s *Very Large Collection of Councils*, vol. V, pp. 1150–1156. The first two letters, however, are not transcribed here but among the *Acts of the Council of Ephesus*. The *Acts of the Purgation*, etc., follow here from p. 1162.

**1773.** Venice; folio. *The Letters and Decrees of Saint Xystus III, Pope*, with several interpolated items concerning the same holy pontiff, from the edition of the distinguished Petrus Coustantius, in Andrea Gallandius’s *Bibliotheca of the Fathers and Holy Writers of the Ancient Church*, vol. IX, pp. 518–532. Notes selected from Coustantius were added, and chapter 19 of the *Prolegomena* contains a dissertation on Xystus.

[Col. 0581]

# LETTERS AND DECREES OF POPE XYSTUS III

With certain items concerning the same pontiff interwoven.

(From the edition of the *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs* by Petrus Coustantius, in Gallandius, *Library of the Ancient Fathers*, vol. IX.) (C, S)

## NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING TWO LETTERS

[Col. 0581D]

1. These letters were first recovered from a Greek copy in the Royal Library by Joannes Baptista Cotelerius, translated into Latin, and published in volume I of the *Greek Monuments*. Stephanus Baluzius subsequently had both reprinted in his new collection of councils, p. 658. Both were certainly written in Latin, according to the custom of the Roman pontiffs, although only their Greek translation has come down to us [Col. 0582D]. It is clear that both were written immediately after Xystus’s ordination, and therefore in the year 432—either around the beginning of May, if the commonly accepted date for this pope’s ordination is not mistaken, or around the end of July, if Paghius’s opinion is to be preferred. Each letter attempts to respond to the letters that Cyril and the other Eastern bishops had sent through legates to his predecessor Coelestinus, for the restoration of peace in the East. Perhaps for this reason the first is addressed not simply in Xystus’s name but in the name of “Xystus, successor of Coelestinus,” with Coelestinus mentioned contrary to normal usage. It may nevertheless have happened through the care of a single ancient copyist, so that our Xystus might be distinguished from other Xystuses.

2. The first letter was written not only to Cyril but also, equally, to the other bishops of the East by whom the legates had been appointed and to whom the legates themselves had asked that letters be written, although it bears only Cyril’s name. No doubt this is because the copy specifically addressed to him is the one that has reached us. Cyril’s praises should therefore trouble no one: unless this letter had also concerned the others, Xystus would have had either to omit them or to express them differently. We think that the same letter was sent to Acacius, bishop of Beroea, and that no other letter of his is indicated in the *Synodicon* which Baluzius reprinted after Christianus Lupus in the new collection of councils, chapter 55, p. 757, where it says: “The bishop who is in Rome wrote one letter to me.” Acacius was in fact the chief among those who stood with John or opposed Cyril. Hence John himself, together with his synod, writes to the emperor Theodosius in the same Baluzius, chapter 17, p. 711:

“These chapters of Cyril, as your imperial authority has recognized, our most God-loving and holy father and bishop Acacius also informed the holy synod by letter, saying that they agree with the impiety of Apollinarius.”

The man who had completed 110 years of life knew these matters clearly, and he had spent his whole life laboring in evangelical struggles and had taken part in many synods. Xystus also had another reason for writing to Acacius: when Acacius was summoned to Ephesus but could not attend because of his advanced age, he sent, in his own place, the letter mentioned above to Theodosius, so that it might be communicated to the synod; the emperor in fact arranged for it to be brought to Ephesus (Labbe, vol. III of the *Councils*, p. 722). Theodosius himself mentions this letter of Acacius in the official letter that he wrote to the synod after the deposition of Nestorius, Cyril, and Memnon. Since Xystus therefore observed that Acacius possessed great influence not only with John and his associates but also with the emperor, he judged it of the highest importance that Acacius should first be brought over by suitable conditions for restoring peace. Finally, Gennadius seems to have intended to identify this first letter of Xystus when he says in *On Illustrious Men*: “Xystus, successor of Coelestinus, sent judgments concerning the same matter both to Nestorius himself and to the bishops of the East, in order to cut down his error.” If this is so, Gennadius was seriously mistaken when he said that the letter was addressed to Nestorius himself, since Xystus expressly pronounces against him in section 4: “Let him alone, therefore, be the shipwrecked man whom the waves of impiety, seeing nothing amid such darkness of his own doctrines, have dashed against the rock of deposition.”

[Note: [Col. 0583D] Written around the middle of the year 432.]

# LETTER I

[Col. 0583]

He announces to the bishops of the East that his ordination was carried out with unanimous consent, and congratulates them on having been present through their legates. Cyril’s pious petition on behalf of Nestorius’s followers is praised and confirmed.

[Note: [Col. 0583B] The following Latin and Greek texts are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0583B] **XYSTUS III, MOST BLESSED POPE OF ROME, SUCCESSOR OF COELESTINUS, TO CYRIL**

### 1

Giving thanks for the kindness of our God toward us, because at the time when he deigned to call us to the highest summit of the priesthood, he granted us, in accordance with his own piety, the presence of our holy brothers and fellow bishops Hermogenes and Lampetius, we have necessarily sent these letters through them to your fraternity [Note: [Col. 0583D] Cotelerius observes that the word “witnesses” refers to the letters, not to the legates; accordingly, the Greek should read μαρτυροῦντα rather than μαρτυρούντων. For although the legates were witnesses of Xystus’s ordination, if the Greek translator had intended to say this, he would have used the noun μαρτύρων rather than the verb μαρτυρούντων. This observation is confirmed by the opening words of section 3.], as witnesses of our ordination. In them we believed that all of you by whom they were sent were present, since those whom spiritual grace binds together are in no way separated by distance. When your holiness has learned, both from our letters and from the report of the brothers, with what unanimity, through the dispensation of divine Providence, this ordination of ours took place, you will certainly give thanks for us to the Lord who bestows grace, dearest brother, that, as guardian of his own gift, he may deign to preserve ecclesiastical peace. Our God, who so orders everything belonging to him that he does not permit even one thing to fail, has given me a benefit through this occasion of brotherhood. For through our holy fellow priests Hermogenes and Lampetius, who were present at our ordination, I thought it right to send these letters to your piety—letters of the kind we sent to the holy synod [Note: [Col. 0583D] If Xystus is referring here to Coelestinus’s Letter 22, addressed to the synod at Ephesus, in which Nestorius’s followers are discussed and what should be done concerning them is determined, he uses “we sent” either because a successor is regarded as acting in the person of his predecessor, or because Coelestinus sent that letter by the decision of the council in which Xystus himself played a leading role. More probably, however, he means that he is sending Cyril letters of the same kind as, or copies similar to, those which he was sending at the same time to the other bishops of the East, in whose name Lampetius and Hermogenes had come to Rome.]—concerning the deceivers who follow Nestorius.

### 2

I confess that we rejoiced greatly, because it happened that on one and the same occasion we could communicate both matters relating to the faith and matters relating to ourselves. Our ordination had all the brothers present. For who did not seem to be present when the East came through its legates [Note: [Col. 0585D] Cotelerius, following the Greek letter, translates “through its presbyters”; but anyone who notices both section 1 above and the present passage will readily acknowledge that a corruption has entered the Greek text and that πρεσβευτῶν should be restored in place of πρεσβυτέρων. The Eastern bishops are said to have been present at Xystus’s ordination under no other designation than that their legates Hermogenes and Lampetius were there. These legates were not presbyters but bishops: Lampetius of Casium and Hermogenes of Rhinocura, both in the province of Augustamnica.], who beheld one heart among all and recognized one soul in everyone, and the harmonious voice of the divine multitude? Thus the Roman Church preserved a single vote in the appointment of the herald of the faith, just as in the very proclamation of the faith it has always maintained a single judgment.

### 3

Since it is enough to have indicated my ordination in a few words, we must now speak about the matters requested by our holy brother Cyril, who has forgotten his own insult and labors. What my predecessor of blessed memory has already written about the faith is sufficient—the faith over which we rejoice and triumph through the help of Christ our God, against whom the controversy was raised. Nevertheless, since we must not shrink from repeating what has been soundly defined, I judged it necessary, now writing to your fraternity through our holy brothers and fellow bishops Hermogenes and Lampetius, to declare briefly what the judgment of the apostolic see established long ago in an already lengthy discourse. Let the hearer not grow weary, but listen willingly, because he has conquered. If Nestorius [Note: [Col. 0585D] In Cotelerius and Baluzius, “teacher of an impious school.” We read that Nestorius was the teacher of no school, but that, after being transferred from the Church of Antioch to the episcopal see of the imperial city, he immediately began to stir up and promote impious disputes against the birth of Christ and the dignity of his mother.] the teacher of impious disputations published books preaching what had to be overturned, how much more ought we to appear as guardians of the ancestral faith, utterly removing what has been overturned? [Note: [Col. 0586D] Baluzius, with Cotelerius, has “what must be overturned,” as though the matter had not yet been dealt with. The preferable reading is the one required by the Greek letter: what Nestorius had preached had already been overturned, first by Coelestinus’s authority and then by that of the Council of Ephesus.]

### 4

Our holy brother and fellow bishop, the presiding bishop of the Church of Alexandria, showing how great and careful is his concern for the faith, and disregarding the insults which, gloriously and according to the Apostle, he has suffered (2 Cor. 12:9), desires the Churches to be put in order rather than himself to be vindicated. At once he asks that a harbor be opened for those struggling in shipwreck: satisfied with the death of the one man who, although he seemed to be a teacher in ignorance, claimed for himself the rudder of the Lord’s [Note: [Col. 0586D] The Greek letter should perhaps be translated “of the Lord’s fear” or “terror.” Cotelerius, judging both expressions less suited to Xystus’s purpose, substituted “of the Lord’s religion.” It is not obscure, however, that the Greek translator was deceived by the similarity of the words and, in the Latin exemplar, read “of fear” or “terror” in place of “rudder.” A related reading is found in Coelestinus’s Letter 24 to Maximianus, section 1: “Take up the helm of the ship known to you.”] helm; but he could not remain in the see, since he did not know how to teach. Let him alone, therefore, be the shipwrecked man whom the waves of impiety, seeing nothing amid such darkness of his own doctrines, have dashed against the rock of deposition. One storm indeed afflicted them all; but once the man who devised these things has been sunk, Cyril wishes the others to be healed. We therefore share the same judgment. It is better to act piously toward those who have ceased to act impiously toward God. Let those who wish to return to the right path therefore be received. There is no need to say much about them, since these few words suffice. Let them know that care will be taken for the Churches occupied by them if they do not take care of themselves and become willing to hold the same opinions as we do. [Note: [Col. 0587D] Cotelerius translates, “Concerning the Churches abandoned by them,” although he read and retained the Greek καταληφθείσας, not καταλειφθείσας. There seems to be no reason to depart from the Greek text. I do not think, however, that the passage concerns those who, as Coelestinus says in Letter 22, section 8, “believed that Christian rulers should be secretly drawn into ecclesiastical affairs, and occupied the Churches again by another order,” but those who, although they had obtained their Churches by legitimate order, subsequently showed themselves unworthy of this honor through the favor they extended to heresy. Xystus threatens that, unless they repent, provision will be made for their Churches by substituting better shepherds. Coelestinus speaks in the same way of Nestorius in Letter 11 to Cyril, section 4: unless he does what was commanded, “your holiness must immediately provide for that Church”—the one he occupied or held—and know that he must be removed from our body by every means.]

### 5

Concerning John of Antioch, we define that the provisions prescribed in the letters sent earlier must be observed [Note: [Col. 0588D] Namely, Coelestinus’s Letter 22.], so that he may know that he will be one of the Catholics if, by overturning everything overturned by the synod, he shows himself to be a Catholic priest. Hold firmly, therefore, dearest brother, both what has been defined by the synod and what has been defined by us. [Note: [Col. 0588D] Or, as Coelestinus says in the letter just cited, Letter 22, section 8: let him “profess himself a Catholic priest by condemning, together with its authors and associates, what has been condemned.”] For the brother [Note: [Col. 0588D] Cyril.] forgives the insults that are useful to him before our common Lord. Such an insult is victory. Therefore he bore calmly the blows of all the goads; nor did those things grieve him in which he now rejoices, remembering that he struggled for a crown. He knows what rewards await those who have conquered such things. Let everyone who returns and agrees in mind with the same judgment rejoice in sharing this kind of triumph. [Note: [Col. 0588D] Cotelerius: “everyone who is present and agrees in mind.”]

### 6

I wish these matters to be sent through your piety for the knowledge of the neighboring brothers, so that they may learn that, even if everything in so great a matter was long ago fully defined, the apostolic see nevertheless does not cease or grow sluggish; for the concern of all the Churches does not allow us to remain at rest from such cares.

[Col. 0584B] **LETTER OF XYSTUS, MOST BLESSED, SUCCESSOR OF COELESTINUS AS BISHOP OF ROME, TO CYRIL**

Giving thanks for the kindness of our God toward us, because at the time when he deigned to call us to the highest summit of the priesthood, he granted us, in accordance with his own piety, the presence of our holy brothers and fellow bishops Hermogenes and Lampetius, we have necessarily sent these letters through them to your fraternity, as witnesses of our ordination. In them we believed that all of you by whom they were sent were present, since those whom spiritual grace binds together are in no way separated by distance. When your holiness has learned, both from our letters and from the report of the brothers, with what unanimity, through the dispensation of divine Providence, this ordination of ours took place, you will certainly acknowledge the gift to the Lord who bestowed it, dearest brother, so that, as guardian of his own gift, he may deign to preserve ecclesiastical peace. Our God, who so orders everything belonging to him that he does not permit even one thing to fail, has given me a benefit through this occasion of brotherhood. For through our holy fellow priests Hermogenes and Lampetius, who were present at our ordination, I thought it right to send these letters to your piety, letters of the kind we sent to the holy synod concerning those who follow Nestorius.

[Col. 0586A] I confess, therefore, that we rejoiced exceedingly, because it happened that on one and the same occasion we could communicate both matters relating to the faith and matters relating to ourselves. Our ordination had all the brothers present. For who would seem not to have been present when the East came through its own [Note: [Col. 0585D] Read πρεσβευτῶν, “legates.”] legates, and they beheld one heart among all, recognized one soul in everyone, and heard the harmonious voice of the divine multitude? Thus the Church in Rome preserved a single vote in the appointment of the herald of the faith, just as in the proclamation of the faith itself it has always maintained a single judgment. [Note: [Col. 0585D] Read ἐτήρησεν, “maintained.”]

Since it is enough to have indicated my ordination in a few words, we must now speak about the matters requested by our holy brother Cyril, who has forgotten his own insult and labors. What my predecessor of blessed memory has already written about the faith is sufficient—the faith over which we rejoice and triumph through the help of Christ our God, against whom the controversy was raised. Nevertheless, since we must not shrink from repeating what has been soundly defined, I judged it necessary, now writing to your fraternity through our holy brothers and fellow bishops Hermogenes and Lampetius, to declare briefly what the judgment of the apostolic see established long ago in an already lengthy discourse. Let the hearer not grow weary, but listen willingly, because he has conquered. If Nestorius, the teacher of impious disputations, published books preaching what had to be overturned, how much more ought we to appear as guardians of the ancestral faith, utterly removing what has been overturned?

[Col. 0586C] Our holy brother and fellow bishop, the presiding bishop of the Church of Alexandria, showing how great and careful is his concern for the faith [Note: [Col. 0586D] Perhaps φροντίζει, “is concerned.”], and disregarding the insults which, gloriously and according to the Apostle, he has suffered, desires the Churches to be put in order rather than himself to be vindicated. At once he asks that a harbor be opened for those struggling in shipwreck: satisfied with the death of the one man who, although he seemed to be a teacher in ignorance, claimed for himself the rudders of the Lord’s fear, but could not remain in the see, since he did not know how to teach. Let him alone, therefore, be the shipwrecked man whom the waves of impiety, seeing nothing amid such darkness of his own teachings, have dashed against the rock of deposition. One storm indeed afflicted them all; but once the man who devised these things has been sunk, he wishes the others to be healed. We therefore share the same judgment. It is better to act piously toward those who have ceased to act impiously toward God. Let those who wish to return to the right path therefore be received. There is no need to say much about them, since these few words suffice. Let them know that care will be taken for the Churches occupied by them if they do not take care of themselves and become willing to hold the same opinions as we do.

Concerning John of Antioch, we define that the provisions contained in the letters sent earlier must be observed, so that he may know that he will become one of the Catholics if, by overturning everything overturned by the synod, he shows himself to be a Catholic priest. Hold firmly, therefore, dearest brother, both what belongs to the synod and what has been defined by us. For the brother forgives the insults that are useful to him before our common Lord. Such an insult is victory. Therefore he bore calmly the blows of all the goads; nor did those things grieve him in which he now rejoices, remembering that he struggled for a crown. He knows what victor’s rewards await those who conquer such things. Let everyone who is present and agrees in mind rejoice in sharing this kind of triumph.

I wish these matters to be sent through your piety for the knowledge of the neighboring brothers, so that they may learn that, even if everything in so great a matter was long ago fully defined, the apostolic see nevertheless does not remain idle. For the concern of all the Churches does not permit us to rest from such cares.

[Note: [Col. 0588D] This letter, which was common with the preceding one to the bishops of the East, was sent privately and specifically to Cyril.]

# LETTER II

[Col. 0587]

He sends him letters as witnesses of his ordination, at which he rejoiced that Cyril had been present through his legates. He explains what had been decreed concerning John of Antioch and the other associates of Nestorius.

[Note: [Col. 0587B] The following Latin and Greek texts are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0587B] **LETTER OF POPE XYSTUS III TO CYRIL**

### 1

I rejoiced at what your holiness informed me by letter concerning my holy brothers and fellow bishops [Note: [Col. 0588D] Hermogenes and Lampetius, the legates.], whom a brief acquaintance and meeting revealed to be men of such character and worth. Perhaps we would have believed less readily the letters you wrote about them, had not the testimony of their own presence prevailed, bearing witness to itself. We truly saw the priests of the Lord; we saw men filled with spiritual grace, which is granted first of all by God himself. Indeed, God’s judgment concerning us made them still more pleasing to us. Our ordination had them present. Adorned with everything that makes a priest complete, they displayed to us the very presence of your holiness, whom we embrace with brotherly affection, not without great appreciation. For the Church throughout the world owes you as much as all those who are subject to you owe you; and you have surely conquered them all everywhere.

### 2

Since our son Themisone, the archdeacon, persisted and offered every sound suggestion, we gave appropriate letters to our brothers and fellow bishops to whom our aforesaid fellow priests had asked that they be sent. Those letters would indeed have been sufficient—the ones that I had previously sent, through the clerics of the Church of Constantinople [Note: [Col. 0589D] The four later letters of Coelestinus were sent through the clerics of the Church of Constantinople, namely the presbyter John and the deacon Epictetus; and later I sent them, full of everything necessary, through the deacons of your holiness. No other letters can be meant here, since Xystus wrote this immediately after his ordination, before he could have sent any letters himself. He says that he sent these because Coelestinus, at his command, first sent them through the clerics of the Constantinopolitan Church, and afterward, through the intervention of Cyril’s deacons, sent copies of them to the same recipients. “We sent” would be more satisfactory, referring to the Roman synod in which Xystus had taken part.], and afterward through the deacons of your holiness, full of everything necessary. But now, obeying both the expectation of your holiness and our custom, I have not failed to do what was soundly suggested to me: giving thanks and counting among my benefits this, which I am persuaded was granted to me from heaven, that we should join the same words concerning my ordination and the faith to your unanimity. [Note: [Col. 0589D] Cotelerius translates the Greek as follows: “Now, following both the patience of your holiness and our custom, I have not neglected,” etc. This does not sufficiently express Xystus’s meaning: he is saying that it is the Roman custom to reply in writing to those from whom greetings have been received, and that, if he failed in this duty, he would undoubtedly disappoint Cyril’s expectation.]

### 3

Concerning the Antiochene and the others who wished to become followers of Nestorius with him, and concerning all who establish Churches contrary to ecclesiastical discipline, we have already defined what must be observed [Note: [Col. 0590D] Literally, “We have occupied ourselves in defining this for observance.” The Greek verb κατειληφότες does not here mean, as Cotelerius translates it, “receiving,” but “occupying ourselves with” or “anticipating.” The matter had already been taken up by Coelestinus and his synod in Letter 22, section 8; Xystus refers to it more clearly in the preceding letter, section 5, with the words: “Concerning John of Antioch, we have defined that the provisions prescribed in the letters sent earlier must be observed.”]: if they repent and, together with their leader, reject everything that the holy synod rejected with our confirmation, let them return to the assembly of priests. For just as, by persisting in their former position, they could not be in communion with us, so we wish to receive them—once they have made satisfaction as we said—for the unity and peace of the Churches. They will themselves be found to have pronounced an equal judgment against themselves if, by remaining outside, they show themselves associates and participants in such impiety together with him [Note: [Col. 0590D] Nestorius.] who has been deposed and expelled.

[Col. 0588B] **LETTER OF POPE XYSTUS TO CYRIL**

I rejoiced at what your holiness informed me by letter concerning my holy brothers and fellow bishops, whom a brief acquaintance and meeting revealed to be men of such character and worth. Perhaps we would have believed less readily the letters you wrote about them, had not the testimony of their own presence prevailed, bearing witness to itself. We truly saw the priests of the Lord; we saw men filled with spiritual grace, which is granted first of all by God himself. Indeed, God’s judgment concerning us made them still more pleasing to us. Our ordination had them present. Adorned with everything that makes a priest complete, they displayed to us the very presence of your holiness, whom we embrace with brotherly affection, not without great appreciation. For the Church throughout the world owes you as much as all those who are subject to you owe you; and you have surely conquered them all everywhere.

Since our son Themisone, the archdeacon, persisted and offered every sound suggestion, we gave appropriate letters to our brothers and fellow bishops, to whom our aforesaid fellow priests had asked that they be sent. Those letters would indeed have been sufficient: the ones that I had previously sent through the clerics of the Church of Constantinople and afterward through the deacons of your holiness, full of everything necessary [Note: [Col. 0589D] Perhaps ἀπεστείλαμεν, “we sent.”]. But now, following both the patience of your fraternity and our custom, I have not neglected the sound matters suggested to me: giving thanks and counting among my benefits this, which I am persuaded was granted to me from heaven, that concerning my ordination and the faith we should join the same words to your unanimity.

Concerning the Antiochene and the others who wished to become followers of Nestorius with him, and concerning all who govern Churches contrary to ecclesiastical knowledge, we have already defined what must be observed: if they repent and, together with their leader, reject everything that the holy synod rejected with our confirmation, let them return to the assembly of priests. For just as, by persisting in their former position, they could not be in our communion, so we wish to receive them, for the unity and peace of the Churches, once they have made satisfaction as we said. But they will themselves be found to have pronounced an equal judgment against themselves if, by remaining outside, they show themselves associates and participants in such impiety with him who has been deposed and expelled.

## NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING LETTER

[Col. 0589]

[Col. 0589C] 1. This letter, which we bring here from part III, chapter 27, of the Council of Ephesus, is assigned by Baronius and others to the year 432, but Tillemont postpones it to March of the year 433. It certainly preceded the sermon that Cyril delivered to his people on the twenty-eighth day of the month Pharmuthi, that is, 23 April, after peace had already been confirmed. The comings and goings by which this peace was reached do not allow us to think that it occurred earlier in the year 433. It will also be useful not to ignore how that peace was initiated and concluded, and therefore to retrace the matter somewhat further.

2. Maximianus, bishop of the imperial city, inspired by these words of Celestine (Epistle 24), “Display the glory both of a vigilant shepherd and of a kindly priest, and pour forth the savor of Christian healing, so that it may become clear that you have been more capable in restoring than he [Nestorius] was in injuring,” convened, for the sake of restoring peace, the bishops whom he discovered to be in Constantinople, together with the entire clergy. With their agreement he first resolved that the emperor, at their request, should send a letter to John, bishop of Antioch, promising that every cause of dispute would be removed if he subscribed to the deposition of Nestorius and anathematized his teaching (Council of Ephesus, Part III, chapter 24). Theodosius agreed and, in a letter sent through the tribune Archelaus to John—while he still believed Celestine to be alive—proposed the aforesaid conditions of peace (ibid.). Moved by these, John did not yield immediately but delayed for some time, as we learn from Cyril’s letter to Donatus (ibid., chapter 38), where the whole sequence of events is recounted. At first, certain men who were with him themselves persuaded him to write to Cyril through Acacius, bishop of Beroea, asking that all Cyril’s writings against Nestorius be suppressed and treated as null. This was done; but Cyril refused to consent to so absurd a request and replied that it would be far more equitable for John himself, together with his supporters, to anathematize the blasphemies of Nestorius, subscribe to his deposition, and approve the ordination of Maximianus.

John and his associates then sent Paul, bishop of Emesa, to Alexandria to deliver a letter to Cyril (it is extant in Baluzius, *Synodicon*, chapter 80). The letters were indeed tokens of communion, but because Cyril had received several complaints against himself, he judged that they should not be accepted until Paul had sworn that they had been written in complete sincerity. Finally, Paul, in the name of those who had sent him, presented Cyril with a petition (it is found in the Council of Ephesus, Part III, chapter 28), in which he granted everything that had been demanded concerning the agreed conditions of peace.

Even then Cyril was not satisfied. He sent two of his clergy, Cassius and Ammonius, together with the tribune Aristolaus, to Antioch, and they demanded that John confirm the same conditions by his subscription. When John and the more distinguished men who were with him had complied, they immediately sent Cyril the letter that had been awaited for the completion of peace, which may be seen in Part III of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 30. “They sent,” says Cyril (ibid., chapter 38), “that same letter which they wrote to me also to the most devout and most holy Xystus, bishop of great Rome, and Maximianus, bishop of the holy Church of Constantinople.”

3. From what Cyril relates both in the aforesaid letter to Donatus and in another to Acacius of Melitene, it follows that, after John had received the emperor’s *sacra* from Archelaus, he held a council and then sent someone to Beroea to induce Acacius to write to Cyril. Acacius did send a letter to Alexandria; but when Cyril rejected it, Paul of Emesa, delegated by John and his associates as an intermediary for peace, hastened to Alexandria, delivered to Cyril new letters from John, as well as a petition in the name of John and his associates, and only then did Cyril’s clergy travel from Alexandria to Constantinople, entrusted with our letter.

There is also a plausible conjecture that the two homilies of Paul of Emesa addressed to the Alexandrian people—one dated December 25 and the other January 1—were delivered during the delay while the return of the aforementioned legates was being awaited (Council of Ephesus, Part III, chapters 31 and 32). If this is so, it must be admitted that this letter was written around the beginning of the year 433. Certainly, the sequence of events from the beginning of the peace negotiations does not permit us to believe that it was written earlier.

Baronius’s opinion therefore cannot stand, whether he thinks that this letter was written by the council which John convened at Antioch after receiving Theodosius’s *sacra*, or whether he denies that it was given to Cyril. Its heading expressly states that it was addressed to Cyril no less than to Xystus and Maximianus, and Cyril’s own words quoted above clearly confirm this. Another letter belonging to the same period, in Part III of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 30, is addressed to Cyril alone. But in such circumstances there is nothing to prevent us from admitting that two letters were written simultaneously to one and the same bishop, one jointly with others and the other privately. Examples need not be sought far away, since the two preceding letters of Xystus sent to the same Cyril bear witness to this practice.

[Note: [Col. 0591D] Around the beginning of the year 433.]

## LETTER III. (C, S)

[Col. 0591]

They declare that they approve the sentence of deposition pronounced by the holy synod against Nestorius, anathematize his blasphemous doctrines, and assent to the ordination of Maximianus.

[Note: [Col. 0591] The following Latin and Greek texts are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0591B] **JOHN, BISHOP OF ANTIOCH, AND THE OTHER MEN WHO WERE WITH HIM, TO XYSTUS, BISHOP OF ROME, CYRIL, BISHOP OF ALEXANDRIA, AND MAXIMIANUS, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE.**

[Col. 0591C] To the most holy and most beloved of God brothers and fellow priests, Xystus, Cyril, and Maximianus, John and all the others who are with me send greetings in the Lord.

### 1

All who have received the priesthood and to whom the divine ministry of the episcopate has been entrusted by Christ, the Savior of us all, ought to make it their concern and aim to excel in the true faith and to teach it to the peoples entrusted to them. Since, then, this is the case, in the past year, by decree of the most devout and Christ-loving emperors, a holy synod of bishops most beloved of God assembled in the metropolis of the Ephesians on account of the teaching of Nestorius. When they had assembled together with the legates sent by the blessed Celestine, formerly bishop of the city of Rome, they pronounced a sentence of deposition and expelled the aforementioned Nestorius, as one who used profane teaching, scandalized many, and did not walk rightly in matters of faith.

[Note: [Col. 0591D] The Council of Ephesus first assembled on June 22, 431. It follows that, if the year mentioned here is understood to be the immediately preceding year, this letter belongs to the year 432.]

[Note: [Col. 0591D] Or, literally, “defenders.” Those who were sent by Celestine to the Council of Ephesus are nowhere called ἔκδικοι in the Greek acts of the council itself, but by the Latin term adapted to Greek, λήγατοι, “legates.” Nevertheless, since they were sent to defend and vindicate the sentence pronounced by Celestine against Nestorius, they are not improperly called ἔκδικοι.]

But when we too had hastened there and found that the matter had already been completed, we were distressed. For this reason, when a dispute had arisen between us and the holy synod, and many things had been said and done on both sides, we returned to our own Churches and cities. During that period we did not agree with the holy synod to the extent of subscribing to the sentence of deposition pronounced against Nestorius.

### 2

When the Churches had fallen into serious discord, at a time when everyone ought above all to have been concerned with how, after every dissension of spirit had been removed, they might be brought into harmony, and when the most devout and God-loving emperors had commanded that this be done—

[Note: [Col. 0593C] Namely, the *sacra* found in Part III of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 24, followed by two others, one to Simeon and the other to Acacius of Beroea, in which Theodosius asks for their prayers and assistance in bringing John and his associates back to harmony.]

—and had sent for this purpose the distinguished tribune and notary Aristolaus, we ourselves also, so that every contention might be removed and peace restored to the Churches of God, resolved to assent to the sentence of the holy synod pronounced against Nestorius, to regard him as deposed, and to anathematize his blasphemous doctrines. For our Churches, just as your Holiness, have always possessed and preserved the true and sincere faith and have handed it on to the peoples.

[Note: [Col. 0593C] How truthfully John makes this claim is shown by his own letter to Nestorius, written before the Council of Ephesus, in which he strongly urges him not to be ashamed to correct what he had rashly said and not to refuse to call the holy Virgin *Theotokos*, “Mother of God,” since no ecclesiastical teacher had ever rejected that name. This letter is extant in Part I of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 25.]

We also assent to the ordination of Maximianus, the most holy and devout bishop of the holy Church of Constantinople, and we are in communion with all the most devout bishops throughout the world who possess and preserve the orthodox and undefiled faith.

[Col. 0592B] **LETTER OF JOHN, BISHOP OF ANTIOCH, AND THE OTHER MEN WHO WERE WITH HIM, TO XYSTUS, BISHOP OF ROME, AND TO CYRIL, BISHOP OF ALEXANDRIA, AND TO MAXIMIANUS, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE.**

[Col. 0592C] To the most holy and most beloved of God brothers and fellow ministers, Xystus, Cyril, and Maximianus, John and all the others who are with me send greetings in the Lord.

The concern and aim of all who have been called to the priesthood and entrusted by Christ, the Savior of us all, with the divine ministry of the episcopate, must be to excel in the true faith and accordingly to teach the peoples under their care. Since the matter therefore stands thus, in the past year, by decree of the most devout and Christ-loving emperors, a holy synod of bishops beloved of God assembled in the metropolis of the Ephesians on account of the affair concerning Nestorius. When they had assembled together with the legates sent by the blessed Celestine, formerly bishop of the holy Church of the Romans, they subjected the aforementioned Nestorius to a sentence of deposition, as one who used profane teaching, scandalized many, and did not walk rightly in matters of faith.

[Col. 0592D] But when we too had gathered and then found that this had taken place, we were distressed. For this reason, when a disagreement had arisen between us and the holy synod, and many things had been done and said in the interval, we returned to our own Churches and cities, not having at that time joined the holy synod by subscription to the sentence of deposition pronounced against Nestorius.

When the Churches had been divided toward schism, although everyone ought above all to have taken thought for how they might be brought together once every dissension had been removed, and when the most God-fearing and Christ-loving emperors had decreed precisely this and had sent the distinguished tribune and notary Aristolaus for that purpose, it pleased us also, for the removal of every dispute and so that peace might be awarded to the Churches of God, to agree with this sentence of the holy synod, pronounced against Nestorius, to regard him as deposed, and to anathematize his infamous doctrines. For the Churches among us, just as our Holiness, have always possessed the true and undefiled faith, have always preserved it, and have handed it on to the peoples.

[Col. 0594B] We also agree to the ordination of Maximianus, the most holy and God-fearing bishop of the holy Church of the Constantinopolitans, and we are in communion with all the most God-fearing throughout the world who possess and preserve the faith.

[Note: [Col. 0593C] This is among the letters which Christian Lupus extracted from the Codex Casinensis and which Stephanus Baluzius subsequently published in the new collection of the Councils under the title of the *Synodicon*, chapter 117. It was sent in the name of numerous bishops from both Cilicia, Second Cappadocia, Bithynia, Thessaly, and Thrace, as chapter 12 states, through clergy and monks. Before it was delivered to Xystus, Helladius and Eutherius, as we learn from another letter of Eutherius reported in the same *Synodicon*, chapter 116, arranged for it to be sent to Alexander, bishop of Hierapolis, and Theodoret, bishop of Cyrus, for their approval, at the same time asking them to append their own letters to it. They thought it necessary to hurry lest the Roman bishop be forestalled by John’s letters.

John’s change of position therefore occasioned this letter. They foresaw that John himself would inform Xystus of it as soon as possible, which he in fact did in the preceding letters. Consequently, it is clear that this letter of Eutherius and Helladius was written not long after John’s letters.

Here one may note the eagerness of the parties throughout the whole affair of Nestorius: Nestorius himself, Cyril, John and his associates, Eutherius and the other bishops who agreed with them—that is, heretics, Catholics, schismatics or those departing from schism, or those persisting in it—all sought to anticipate and win over the bishop of the Apostolic See. Something similar occurred in the case of John Chrysostom, as is shown by what we have gathered in the *Notice of the Non-extant Letters of Innocent*.]

## LETTER IV, MOST BELOVED OF GOD

[Note: [Col. 0594C] According to Cyril, as he himself writes in his letter to Donatus, Paul of Emesa, acting as intermediary for peace, had strongly pressed on behalf of Eutherius, Helladius, Himerius, and Dorotheus that the decrees issued against them should be rescinded, arguing that peace among the Churches could not otherwise be completed. But when Cyril replied that Paul was attempting something impossible, he abandoned the proposal, and no mention of them was made in the agreed conditions of peace. Garnerius asserts in his notes on Marius Mercator, p. 357, that these metropolitans were deposed by the synod that ordained Maximianus bishop of Constantinople, and even considers it probable that others were substituted in their places.

In the *Synodicon*, however, in Christian Lupus and Baluzius, chapter 48, there is a letter of John, bishop of Antioch, to Helladius, bishop of Tarsus, at the time when Helladius, having received Maximianus’s synodical letter concerning his ordination, refused to admit his name into the diptychs. Then, in chapter 49, there follows another letter of the same John to the clergy and people of the Church of Tarsus, at the time when it had been reported that the emperor had ordered Helladius to be expelled because he had not accepted the synodical letter of Maximianus, bishop of Constantinople.

This proves that Helladius, at least, was not deposed by the synod that ordained Maximianus, but somewhat later, when he refused to accept the ordination of that bishop; or at any rate that for this reason he was judged liable to the sentence pronounced by the Council of Ephesus against the heretics, and therefore worthy to be expelled from his see by order of the emperor.

Here, incidentally, one should note the ancient custom of the Church by which the name of a newly appointed bishop, once his synodical letters had been received, was ordinarily entered in the diptychs as a sign of communion. In this way Bassianus, bishop of Ephesus, proved in the Council of Chalcedon, act 11, p. 693, that he had communicated with Proclus, when the clergy of the Church of Constantinople testified: “For blessed Proclus truly received him, communicated with him, issued synodical letters, and placed him in the diptychs.”]

**EUTHERIUS, BISHOP OF TYANA, AND HELLADIUS, BISHOP OF TARSUS, TO XYSTUS, BISHOP OF ROME, OF GREAT RENOWN.** (C, S)

[Note: [Col. 0594D] In the *Synodicon*, “Sixtus.”]

[Col. 0593]

Astonished at the change of John of Antioch, they ask Xystus, in the name of several provinces, not to delay in coming to the aid of the world, both the part that is in error and the part that suffers tyranny.

[Col. 0593B] ### 1

The Lord Christ, exercising great providence over the human race through successive ages, has at one time prepared one set of luminaries and at another another, for the guidance of those who are well disposed, for the refutation of opponents, for the destruction of falsehood, and for the confirmation of truth.

[Note: [Col. 0595C] That is, to refute those who oppose people of good will.]

[Note: [Col. 0595C–D] Lupus, warning that he had encountered *amore* in the archetype, prints in the larger text a reading as though it implied that Cyril, here compared with Pharaoh, should be called a lesser Pharaoh. Yet, not standing by this conjecture either, he thinks that perhaps *Achori* should be substituted for *amore*—a name by which, according to some, Pharaoh, the persecutor of the Hebrews, was called. Baluzius restored the archetype’s reading, although he admits that it is devoid of all sense. Our reading is simpler and subject to no error.]

Thus, under the bitter Pharaoh, he raised up the blessed Moses against Jannes and Jambres (2 Timothy 3:8), and, through Simon Magus, Peter, who conquered him well. So also, against those who have now risen up, he has brought forth your Holiness, through whom we too have good hope that the whole world may be delivered from Egyptian error.

[Note: [Col. 0595D] Namely, Cyril.]

For, being a new Moses, you will strike down every Egyptian heretic, but you will save every orthodox Israelite. Therefore, when the truth has been assailed by many thousands and the most pure pearl of orthodoxy—

[Note: [Col. 0595D] That is, Nestorius.]

—has encountered countless hostilities, such as no history has ever recorded, from those who have devised these novel expressions against the apostolic faith of the Fathers—

[Note: [Col. 0595D] Lupus reads *pepererunt*, “gave birth to.” The twelve anathemas of Cyril are being criticized here.]

—it is our task, as we suffer triple and manifold storms and have almost fallen among pirates, to cry out to him whom God has produced as helmsman and to inform him, as far as possible, of everything concerning the love of truth. It belongs to your grace and wisdom not to despise or pass over casually so great a question and so great a cause, but to investigate it with the loving care of good labor and to impose a correction with complete firmness and confidence beloved of God.

### 2

In former times, whenever such heretical tares arose from Alexandria, your apostolic see repeatedly sufficed throughout that whole period to convict falsehood, suppress impiety, correct what required correction, and fortify the world for the glory of Christ, both under that bishop who was thrice blessed and to be counted among the saints, Damasus, and under several other glorious and admirable men.

[Note: [Col. 0595D] They could have named Julius, who did not cease defending the case of Athanasius, who had fled to him, until Athanasius was restored to his see. They preferred to mention Damasus because he condemned the heresy of Apollinarius, which they wished to represent as having been revived by Cyril.

Accordingly, Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History* V.3, records that Meletius said to Apollinarius, who boasted that he was in communion with Damasus: “I am astonished, my friend, that you so shamelessly resist the truth, especially since you know perfectly well that Damasus asserts that a complete man was assumed by God, while you do not cease to affirm the contrary . . . . If what we say is false, at least now renounce your novelty and embrace the teaching of Damasus.”

Theodoret then adds: “From this root [of Apollinarius] there sprang up in the Churches that opinion that there is one nature of flesh and divinity, and that opinion which attributes suffering to the divinity of the Only-begotten.” Perhaps by these words he intended to point to Cyril, to whom Theodoret and his associates falsely attributed such an opinion because, in his first letter to Succensus, he happened to speak of “one incarnate nature of God the Word.”

Thus Damasus is to be understood as mentioned here not merely, as Lupus interprets it, because of the Arian bishop Lucius or Maximus the Cynic, whom he condemned, but especially because of the errors of Apollinarius, which Damasus proscribed in his fifth letter to Paulinus.]

For this reason we too presume to offer these petitions, so that you may assist the world, both the part that is in error and the part that suffers tyranny and is attacked for this purpose: that it may assent to things that are unsuitable, because it neither wishes nor judges it expedient to receive the various novel expressions of the Egyptian chapters.

### 3

For Cyril of Alexandria, writing blasphemous novelty of expression in twice six chapters contrary to the whole divinely inspired Scripture, and anathematizing the lawful and ancient traditions of the holy Fathers—especially those who ascribe exalted things to Christ’s divinity and humble things to his humanity, without ever severing their union—proposed these chapters to Nestorius, who at that time governed the holy see of the city of great renown.

[Note: [Col. 0596D] Constantinople.]

Nestorius had from the beginning been approved and known for his faith, his life, his doctrine concerning the Word, and everything else. Cyril demanded that he either agree with Cyril’s chapters, subscribe to them, and remain bishop, or else suffer danger to his rank and be expelled from the holy Church. But Nestorius, placing the fear of God before the wicked proposal, chose rather to surrender himself to many thousands of dangers unjustly inflicted upon him than to give assent to heretical deceit and confirm the error of the whole world.

### 4

After this the synod assembled at Ephesus. Without being convicted of anything, and without being asked to give an account before all those whose arrival was being awaited—

[Note: [Col. 0596D] The Greek word here expected has been rendered more suitably by the Latin. Everyone can easily see that this refers to John of Antioch and the others who were with him. But Nestorius is falsely said earlier not to have been asked to give an account.]

—he was subjected to punishment because he had opposed the blasphemies of those chapters, and was subjected to the condemnation so called, and to certain other measures, on the basis of every sort of credulity. Yet Cyril certainly did not possess the authority of a judge, but rather the standing of one who was himself to be judged, since they had brought charges against one another.

The accused was presiding, and the prince who was being awaited was issuing judgment—

[Note: [Col. 0596D] It would again have been preferable to read *exspectabatur*, “was being awaited,” that is, the man whom we expected would be subjected, as a defendant, to multiple judgments; he himself is issuing sentence as judge.]

—although he himself was expected to be subjected to many judgments.

### 5

After these events, some regarded everything that had happened as worthy of tears, while others considered it ridiculous. Thus the man who held the Church of God at Antioch, arriving afterward, subjected Cyril and Memnon to condemnation by the common decree of the most holy and God-beloved bishops, numbering as many as twenty-two metropolitans and the others who were present with them. These judged them leaders of heresy and sedition and rivals of ecclesiastical ordinances.

[Note: [Col. 0597C] This decree, with the subscriptions of forty-three bishops, is extant in the Ephesine conciliabulum, Labbe, vol. III, p. 598. Shortly afterward one should perhaps read “and twenty-two.”]

[Note: [Col. 0597C] That is, “their adversaries.” In the decree just cited they are addressed as follows: “You, Cyril of Alexandria, and you, Memnon, bishop of this city, know that you have been deposed . . . because you were responsible for the trampling underfoot of the canons of the Fathers and the contempt of the imperial decrees.”

[Col. 0597D] It should be observed that what is there called “the canons of the Fathers” is here called “ecclesiastical ordinances.” John himself also, in the preface to the sentence pronounced against Cyril and Memnon, uses these expressions interchangeably.]

They separated the others who had been accomplices with them in every improper act from communion. But those eminent men, indulging themselves in a relaxation of the rules both against the truth and against the regulations, immediately and irreverently presumed to share in the dread mysteries, and dangerously caused others to communicate with them. Thus all were subjected to the decree of the divine rule, which utterly condemns those who govern in this way.

[Note: [Col. 0597D] Namely, the rule of the Council of Antioch, whose fourth canon states: “If any bishop has been deposed by a synod . . . and presumes to perform any act of priesthood or sacred ministry, he may no longer have hope of restoration, either in another synod . . . and those who communicate with him are also to be cast out of the Church.” Hence below we restore *perdamnat*, “condemns,” where the text had *perdamnant*, “they condemn.”

The sentence would be clearer if it read: “so that all may be subject to the decree of the divine rule, which . . .” But this canon can easily be turned back against those who cite it, since they themselves had not ceased to communicate with Nestorius, whom they knew to have been deposed by the sentence of Celestine and his council, confirmed by so many Fathers of the Council of Ephesus. We have observed that John’s opponents in the case of John Chrysostom also abused the same decree.]

### 6

When the most God-beloved and victorious emperor, a good prince, learned of these things, he immediately decreed that the actions so disorderly and inconsistent, carried out against one who had been convicted of nothing but had been abruptly and furiously condemned, should be declared void. He further decreed that the question of doctrine should again be examined with love of truth, through question, answer, and demonstration—an examination that would persuade everyone, rather than one that would command by tyrannical authority.

[Note: [Col. 0598C] This decree of Theodosius is found among the acts of the Ephesine conciliabulum, p. 703.]

### 7

But they added this also to their violation of the canons: they refused to obey even these devout letters. Agreeing henceforth neither to say nor to hear anything concerning the faith, they all turned solely to obstinacy. They began to obtain agreement with the unjust judgment, some by fraud, others by violence, and others by rewards.

### 8

Astonished at these things, we pleaded and entreated for a long time, and appealed with complete confidence that nothing irrational should be done or maintained. We asked that a common discussion and council be proposed concerning the questions of doctrine and Cyril’s chapters, and that whatever pleased everyone should be confirmed by a single judgment.

We further asked that a true and lawful judgment be rendered concerning the man who had so openly suffered tyranny—

[Note: [Col. 0598C] Nestorius.]

—so that, if he were convicted of corrupting the truth, he might appropriately endure condemnation at the hands of all; but if he were proved altogether innocent, he might, in writing and together with us, renounce whatever unsuitable statements certain people, whether in his own name or in the name of others, had alleged through suspicion or accusation.

[Note: [Col. 0598C] They do not dare deny that the unsuitable things, because of which Nestorius was condemned, ought to be renounced in writing.]

### 9

But these proposals displeased those who wished to overcome by authority alone and neither to persuade nor to be persuaded. They commanded everyone abruptly to anathematize and subscribe to the condemnation. Whoever reserved himself for more careful deliberation was condemned, deposed by them, subjected to accusations, and called a teacher of evil doctrine.

[Note: [Col. 0598C] The sequence of the sentence requires *abdicabatur*, or “was renounced” or “was deposed by them,” or something similar.]

Others were ordained in place of such men because they did not wish to agree with them in praising chapters worthy of condemnation while condemning the man who, as far as we know, said nothing other than what had plainly been handed down by the holy prophets, evangelists, and apostles through the Holy Spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0598C] The sentence would be clearer as follows: “because they did not wish to agree with them in this: that they should praise chapters worthy of condemnation but condemn him.” The immediately preceding statement, “Others were ordained in place of such men,” refers chiefly to Nestorius, in whose place Maximianus was ordained. Whether others were similarly substituted in the places of other men, we do not know. We are clearly taught in chapters 11 and 12 only that many were driven from their sees.]

### 10

For they wished even to bring accusations against the apostles, when they gratuitously condemned the man who proclaimed what belonged to the apostles. They therefore composed such a record of the proceedings that discordant and uncertain charges were brought against that man and often irreproachable statements were censured.

“Why,” they ask, “did Nestorius say that suffering affected not the deity but the humanity of Christ?”
