[Note: [Col. 0598D] He was not deserving of censure because, distinguishing the two natures of Christ, he attributed suffering to the humanity rather than to the deity. He was censured because, refusing to admit the unity of person, he denied that God had suffered, just as he denied that God had been born. For this reason he was unwilling to apply the name *Theotokos*, “Mother of God,” to Mary. This alone was demanded of him: that, on account of the unity of the natures in the one person of the Word, he should confess that God had suffered.]

At other times they wrote false things, attributing to him words that no unbeliever, indeed not even a rustic demon, would have presumed to utter—namely, that Christ was “the Lord’s Christ,” like Saul, like David, like the unbelieving Cyrus.

[Note: [Col. 0598D] Lupus reads *Christi Dominus*, “Christ the Lord,” but Baluzius has rightly corrected it. Neither Saul nor David nor Cyrus nor anyone else has ever been called, or could be called, “Christ the Lord.” As for Helladius and Eutherius’s denial that Nestorius said this, it has been proved that he did say it in the Council of Ephesus, act 1, p. 524, from his twenty-seventh quire.

Nestorius himself, in Baluzius, *Synodicon*, chapter 6, p. 693, admits that he said this: “Just as Saul is called Christ and David Christ, and again Cyrus Christ, and then the Babylonian, although David certainly was not like them in piety, so we indeed call Christ, or even the Son, the Lord. Nevertheless, the sharing of names does not create equality of dignity.”

For this one point he protests against those who produced these words of his, namely, that they had omitted the qualification, “Nevertheless, the sharing of names does not create equality of dignity.” But here too fraud was rightly to be feared, when one recalled that formerly Valens and Ursacius had loudly declared at the Council of Ariminum: “If anyone says that the Son of God is a creature, as the other creatures are, let him be anathema.” Since by these words they appeared sincerely to deny that the Son was a creature, they later began openly, as Jerome testifies in his *Dialogue Against the Luciferians*, to boast that they had not denied the Son to be a creature, but only that he was like the other creatures.

Nestorius’s qualification was much more open to fraud than the words of Ursacius and Valens.]

In these matters it is easy for anyone who wishes to do so to expose the calumny.

### 11

As for what was done concerning John of Antioch, we would prefer, if possible, to remain silent. His fickleness has thus become irrational in our eyes, and his manifest betrayal of the truth was suddenly completed—or rather, carried through. For before we came to Ephesus, he had discovered the heretical fraud of the Chapters and indicated it to many by letter, through First and Second Cappadocia and various other places, warning them to guard themselves against them, as being in agreement with Eunomius, Arius, and Apollinarius. #### Note

Perhaps: “and keenly.”

He who had leapt forward sharply and fervently to condemn Cyril, and had urged everyone to do the same, even went to the imperial city itself to resist this impiety. He also wrote to us, while we were still at Ephesus, first saying:

“Since, on learning that he—that is, Nestorius—had been dismissed from Ephesus, our souls were greatly grieved, because those things which had been done without judgment and unjustly seemed meanwhile to be receiving confirmation.”

Then he wrote:

“Even if Cyril has rejected those blasphemous Chapters, we nevertheless promised under oath that we would not then receive him, because he himself has become the leader of an unjust heresy.”

How, then, after receiving another heart, we do not know why, he opposed him in all his actions and became Cyril’s communicant, without rejecting what he had wrongly written—although he had sworn that he would never receive him, even if he rejected those things in writing—and alone dissolved the bond which he had consequently imposed upon Cyril and Memnon together with so many others who had been hostile to them and had subscribed to their condemnation.

#### Note

That is, together with so many—namely, forty-two—bishops who opposed Cyril and Memnon and had subscribed to their condemnation. He provided no security for those who had been offended on behalf of piety.

#### Note

They tacitly accuse John of neglecting them and of taking no care for their restoration to their sees. Yet Cyril’s letter to Donatus, as we have already explained, bears witness that he did not fail in this duty. Moreover, John himself writes to the emperor on their behalf in *Synodicon*, chapter 91, page 798:

“We beseech your piety to grant the world a complete festival, so that no city may be excluded from the celebration of this common feast, and to order that the bishops most beloved of God, who amid the earlier tumults seemed to have been driven from their churches, be restored to their former condition.” He himself was reconciled with the man whom he had previously marked out as unworthy of such love, yet he permitted the Churches to be disturbed and allowed certain bishops to remain deposed while others were still driven out in various ways.

#### Note

Those Chapters, before Cyril published his explanation of them, John strongly disapproved. In his letter to Firmus, bishop of Caesarea, preserved by Baluze, *Synodicon*, chapter 4, page 691, he even writes that he cannot believe them to be Cyril’s:

“For they agree—or rather, they are identical—with those things on account of which Apollinarius was expelled from the Church of Christ.”

In the Ephesian assembly, page 595, and elsewhere, he explicitly calls them heretical. Hence, in *Synodicon*, chapter 32, page 731, he adjures the emperor by the dread judgment of God to order that those heretical Chapters, which have been introduced into the faith, be expelled, because they are entirely alien to sound doctrine and consonant with heretical madness. For he had persuaded himself, as he says in the aforementioned letter to Firmus, that those Chapters intended the body which God the Word assumed from the holy Virgin to be believed to be of the same nature as his divinity.

Yet even Theodorettus, before withdrawing from the society of the schismatics, did not deny that Cyril’s explanation of them, subsequently published, was consonant with the orthodox faith. Thus many disputes could have been laid to rest if he who thought correctly but was wrongly understood had not disdained to issue a clearer explanation of his words; and those who had previously suspected him of thinking wrongly would not have refused, once he had finally supplied a Catholic explanation of his words, to praise and accept it as orthodox. By this course of action Cyril first brought John, and somewhat later Theodorettus and others, to peace and unity.

Worth noting in this connection is the heading, or summary, of John’s letter to the emperor Theodosius in chapter 17 of the *Synodicon*. There, as the text says, the confession of the Catholic faith is also contained which Cyril later praised in his peaceful letter. Yet at the end of that same letter John writes that the Chapters introduced by the aforementioned Cyril against the orthodox faith, for the subversion of the Churches, ought to be condemned by all bishops. Cyril was not deterred by these reproaches from openly praising John’s faith, which he approved as right and complete; by this conduct he more easily led John to form a fairer opinion of him.

John also wrote remarkable letters in which he said that he held Nestorius condemned and anathematized whatever he had said or thought impiously. In this way he failed both in accusation and in clarity: he did not say, “I anathematize this, or that, or the other proposition,” but said:

“Whatever he has said impiously”—although he ought clearly to have said this in order that everyone might be made more cautious concerning that doctrine.

Just as, on the other hand, “we clearly abominate Cyril’s Chapters and ask everyone to guard himself against his innate malignity, demonstrating the blasphemies contained in them and publishing them openly to all.””

#### Note

Perhaps the phrase should be rendered more clearly: “But we do not know from where—or for what reason—he received another heart.”

#### Note

It was probably at that very time when John and the envoys with him wrote from Constantinople to the Orientals who had remained at Ephesus. We read in Baluze, *Synodicon*, chapter 26:

“From the report we have learned that eight days before our arrival it pleased our most pious emperor to dismiss the lord Nestorius from Ephesus, to go wherever he wished; and our soul was greatly grieved.”

They indicate that they wrote this letter on the eleventh day of the month Gorpiaeus—that is, according to Baronius, on September 11, or, according to Lupus, on September 4. The letter of the prefects by which Nestorius was dismissed from Ephesus is presented in the frequently mentioned *Synodicon*, chapter 24.

As for John’s letters, he said that he condemned Nestorius and anathematized everything he had said or thought impiously. Yet he should have clearly specified the particular doctrine, so that everyone might be made more cautious concerning it. He said:

“Whatever he has said impiously.”

#### Note

In the preceding letter to Xystus, number 2, John professes that he anathematizes Nestorius’s blasphemous doctrines. He repeats the same words in his letter to Cyril, *Ephesian Council*, part III, chapter 30. They agree with the statement in the memorandum which Paul of Emesa delivered to Cyril in John’s name:

“We anathematize the things spoken by him impiously in the sphere of teaching” (*ἀναθεματίζομεν τὰ ἐν διδασκαλίας μέρει ἀσεβῶς αὐτῷ εἰρημένα*).

But closer to the words just cited is what John says in his letter to Theodosius, *Synodicon*, chapter 91, page 798:

“We hold Nestorius deposed, or condemned … subjecting to anathema whatever he has said alienly and foreignly, against apostolic doctrine.”

### 12

We have written these few things out of many, with considerable abbreviation, knowing that the excess of these evils deserves not only the lamentations of Jeremiah but surpasses the whole tragedy. We beseech you, and prostrate ourselves at the feet of your religious holiness, that you extend a saving hand, remove the shipwreck of the world, order an investigation of all these matters, and cause heavenly correction to be imposed upon these unlawful proceedings. Let the holy shepherds who have been unjustly driven away from their sheep be recalled; let order and the ancient concord be restored to the flocks; and let lamentation and bleating no longer be offered as vows and psalms while many are scattered. Let no one be endangered in matters of primary importance while avoiding, because of heretics, either the laver of regeneration or mystical communion—things which they are by no means permitted to receive from the orthodox for salvation.

### 13

Seeing some of these things ourselves and hearing others, we who come from different regions would long ago have hastened to your holiness—namely, from Euphratesia, both Cilicias, Second Cappadocia, Bithynia, Thessaly, and Moesia—to pour out fountains of tears and publicly mourn the foreign and unfamiliar evils of this life, had not the terror of wolves lying in wait for the flocks, for plunder, error, and every kind of adversity, restrained us. Therefore we have been compelled, in our place, to send most religious clergy and monks to fill our place.

### 14

We ask you, therefore, to rise without delay and, with fervent zeal, erect the great trophy of victory against the ranks of your rivals, keeping before your eyes the diligence and care of the Good Shepherd concerning the sheep that had gone astray (Luke 15:4). Do not consider it without danger if anything is done contemptuously concerning so many shepherds and sheep—while the sheep are wandering and the shepherds are enduring tyrannical violence.

Rather, imitate the great herald of piety, Paul, the eye of the world, whom we believe to be a pledge of our familiarity with your holiness. For he was our fellow citizen,

#### Note

Since he was born at Tarsus, whose bishop Helladius was when he wrote this.

he became, after the error of the whole world had been extinguished, the ornament of that apostolic see and received from blessed Peter the right hand of fellowship (Galatians 2:9), so that it might be evident that both guarded an equal precision of doctrine.

### 15

We also ask that you not despise us, whom so many evils surround. For we are not contending over money, glory, or any other temporal matter, but for the common possession of piety, for the ancestral treasure of faith, for the common hope of the faithful, for the good confession of the apostles, for the immortal struggle of the martyrs, and especially for the Lord’s coming and clemency. Invoking his unconquerable power, we cry out without ceasing:

“Spare, O Lord, your people, and do not give your inheritance over to reproach” (Joel 2:17).

Eutherius, bishop of the metropolis of the Tyanenses, have subscribed, and I ask that you pray for my safety, most God-loving and holy father.

Helladius, bishop of the metropolis of Tarsus, have subscribed, and I ask that you pray for my safety, most God-loving and holy father.

#### Note

Cyril, as Rusticus, deacon of Pope Vigilius, observes somewhat after the beginning of his *Dialogue against the Acephali*, diligently sought to have his letters and those of the Orientals concerning the peace confirmed by the Roman Church’s see through the most holy Xystus. After those letters had been read in the synod of priests who had assembled to celebrate the day of Xystus’s ordination, Xystus replied from that same synod—as he testifies below, in number 7—that Cyril’s labors were approved and confirmed in every respect both by himself and by the whole brotherhood.

Rusticus also praised this reply in the dialogue cited, and from it he excerpted not, as the editor of the *Bibliotheca Patrum* thought, the very words, but certain statements summarized and selected from them. Baronius arranged for this precious monument, copied from a Vatican manuscript by Antonio de Aquino, to be printed in the *Annals* under the year 433. Labbe later appended it, somewhat more accurately, to the acts of the Council of Ephesus, part III, chapter 41, page 1173.

## Letter V: Saint Xystus, Pope, to Cyril of Alexandria, after Peace Had Been Made between Cyril and John

An account of this matter was made known in the assembly of bishops. The great joy of the Church that followed. The happy outcome of Cyril’s labors, which were approved by Xystus and his council in every respect.

### Xystus, bishop, to Cyril, bishop of Alexandria

#### 1

We have been filled with great and joyful gladness since, as we read, the Orient from on high has visited us (Luke 1:78).

Behold, while we were anxious because we wish no one to perish, your holiness has announced by your letters that the body of the Church has been restored.

#### Note

This alludes to John, who presided over the East and whose letters, together with the other documents concerning the peace which Cyril had sent, Xystus had already received. As its members return to their proper joints, we now see no one wandering outside, because one faith bears witness that all are placed within.

We rejoice that the one who accomplished this work has been removed from our midst, for he now understands that he alone, not believing what he had perceived, suffered harm by striving against him whom we confess to have benefited all.

#### Note

Here Cyril seems to be set against Nestorius: Cyril resisted him and benefited everyone. Yet it is more fitting to understand the reference as Christ, whose dignity Nestorius attacked. The whole passage is seriously corrupt in Baronius.

### 2

But it is fitting for us to pass from sorrowful things to joyful ones, because he against whom the dispute had been raised, after removing universal grief from the Church, has granted us a season of rejoicing. Finally, Christ our God showed how truly this was his cause when he deigned to govern events in such a way that he preserved the evidence of so great and such a matter for the assembly of his priests.

#### Note

Here too, and below in “we present an indication of heavenly joy,” *indicium* (“indication” or “evidence”) should be read rather than *judicium* (“judgment”), although the latter is found in the printed texts. The matter is not one to be judged, but to be made known and received; it calls the assessors not to examine the case, but to share the joy arising from its happy conclusion. In ancient books, moreover, *judicium* and *indicium* are written alike.

#### Note

Baronius reads, “how true it is”; Labbe reads, “how true it may be.”

The apostles often discussed the faith when gathered together in one place; now the apostolic men, assembling together, rejoice over its victory. O report worthy of its sender, worthy of the assembly! Such witnesses were needed for an indication of heavenly joy. And since the matter and the cause demand it, it is fitting that the place also not be left unmentioned.

#### Note

Baronius reads: “It is fitting also to contemplate the place.”

### 3

The whole brotherhood assembled at the blessed apostle Peter: behold, an audience suited to its hearers and appropriate to what was to be heard. Our fellow bishops had as a witness to their congratulation the one from whom we derive the beginning of our honor.

#### Note

This passage resembles the opening of Siricius’s Letter 4: “When very many of us had assembled together at the relics of the holy apostle Peter, through whom both the apostolate and the episcopate in Christ took their beginning.” For he presided over the holy and venerable synod which my anniversary day, by the Lord’s favor, had gathered, since we must believe that he himself was present, neither absent in spirit nor in body.

#### Note

This was not the day on which he was born on earth, but the day on which he was ordained bishop of the Roman Church. Anastasius I likewise called this day his “birthday,” and, as though by an already established custom, many bishops were accustomed to be invited to it. Xystus’s successor Leo delivered several sermons at the same celebration. In the first, chapter 3, he notes that many bishops regularly assembled there:

“When I see this most splendid gathering of venerable fellow priests, I feel that an angelic assembly is present among so many saints.”

Then, referring that celebration, after the manner of Xystus, to the glory of blessed Peter, he added:

“Nor, as I trust, is the gracious presence and faithful devotion of the blessed apostle Peter absent from this assembly; nor does he abandon your devotion, whose reverence has gathered us.”

Accordingly, he closes Sermon 3:

“To him, therefore, let us ascribe this anniversary day of our service; to him let us attribute this festival, by whose protection we have deserved to share in that very see.”

Pope Hilary speaks of this festival in the same way in Letter 8.

He was present at the victory, who had not been absent from the struggle; he aided the prayers of our hearts, who sees the symbol first delivered among the apostles being disparaged. He did not permit the impious head to rejoice in consolations, nor did he allow the purity of that clear fountain to remain long disturbed by a muddy whirlpool. The brothers have returned to us—to us, I say, who, by common effort, pursued the disease and cared for the health of souls.

#### Note

Baronius reads, “who would see it.” See the note on letter 13 of Nestorius, number 4, concerning the corruption of the Nicene Creed.

#### Note

Since Xystus calls Nestorius first the infamous head, then your exile, later the inventor of evils, and afterward the deserter of the camp, along with other such expressions, he seems to have wished to spare his name, for he does not mention it even once.

### 4

Our holy brother John did not add himself to your exile, nor was he deceived by your blasphemous preaching. For, as the outcome of events shows, he suspended his judgment; he did not deny it. What else could he have judged concerning the inventor of evils except what Christ himself, whose cause was at issue, is shown to have judged through his priests assembled in the Ephesian synod?

#### Note

That is, except what Christ, whose cause was being defended, is shown to have judged through his priests gathered at Ephesus.

He had determined this concerning the deserter of our camp: that he should be judged as his perfidy deserved, as the leaders of the faith advised.

#### Note

Labbe would prefer *sua deberet*. The reading should be retained in the sense that John had determined concerning Nestorius what his perfidy advised should be judged concerning him by the leaders of the faith.

He would never have separated himself from our number, to which he was able to return.

#### Note

Rusticus, the deacon, shortly after the beginning of the *Dialogue against the Acephali*, renders this passage in his own style as follows:

“Because our most holy brother John never held opinions like those of Nestorius, but was orthodox from the beginning, although formerly he suspended his judgment so as not to condemn Nestorius together with us. If John was orthodox from the beginning and did not hesitate to rebuke Nestorius in an excellent letter before he was condemned, why afterward did he refrain from condemning this heretic? The reason was certainly that, after receiving John’s letter, Nestorius replied that he avoided the title ‘Mother of God’ only so that the followers of the heretic Apollinarius might not reproach us on that account. Hence John writes concerning Nestorius to Firmus, in *Synodicon*, chapter 4:

‘Since he had previously held the same opinion as we do concerning the Mother of God, it is thereby proved that he quickly yielded to our admonitions, as one does to his own people; he accepted the name itself and sent us, in two discourses, a sound and irreproachable exposition of the faith.’

Yet that heretic, even if he sometimes changed his tongue, never changed his mind, according to the judgment of prudent men.”

### 5

Rejoice, dearest brother, and rejoice as victor with the brothers who have been restored to us. The Church was seeking those whom she has received. If we wish no one, even one of the little ones, to perish, how much more ought we to rejoice at the recovery of the leaders? We read how much joy the one sheep, when brought back, produced (Luke 15:6); and therefore we must understand how much praise belongs to the restoration of so many shepherds.

Flocks are seen in each individual; this is not the case of one alone whenever the health of many is at issue.

#### Note

Labbe’s conjecture that *rectorum* (“leaders”) should perhaps be read is not unacceptable. Yet, since the multitude of the people is reckoned in its leaders, the health of each leader is the health of many. We rejoice that we did nothing prematurely, now that we celebrate the fruit of our judgment.

We endured the brothers, certain that they would produce not thorns but grapes (Matthew 7:17).

#### Note

Baronius reads, “who would gather.” Labbe, in the margin, reads, “who would bear”; but the text’s “who would produce” is more correct. Xystus is alluding to Matthew: “Do they gather grapes from thorns?” Yet he proves that they are not thorns because he was certain that they would produce grapes, whereas Christ says: “A bad tree cannot produce good fruit.” In that passage, verses 17–19, the consistent usage is *facere*, “to make or produce,” not *ferre*, “to bear.”

The harvest of our joy is evident; it has filled the holy synod with abundant rejoicing. That guardian cared for his vineyard whom the prophet David testifies neither to slumber nor to sleep while guarding the house of Israel (Psalm 120:4). The flame received that barren shoot, which bore no fruit for our Christ (John 15:6).

But just as this is fittingly said of the condemned man, so concerning the brothers who have returned to us it is fitting to say that the planting which the Father planted could not be uprooted by the devil (Matthew 15:13). Eternal fire therefore claimed him for itself, while the vineyard of the eternal owner claimed these men, to such an extent that we may now rejoice that your holiness calls the priest of the Antiochene Church a venerable man and *domnus*.

#### Note

In the heading of the letter Cyril sent to John after peace had been made, *Ephesian Council*, part III, chapter 34, Cyril calls him *dominus*, but does not add “venerable man.” We therefore suppose that a letter from Cyril to Xystus, now lost, is indicated here. If there is no corruption in the archetype, Quesnellus is mistaken in note 43 on Leo’s Letter 34, where he denies that the use of *domnus* was established before Leo’s time.

His opinion is likewise contradicted by what we read in Augustine, at the end of Sermon 111 in the new edition:

“Your Charity knows what we suggest: tomorrow the anniversary of the ordination of the aged *domnus* Aurelius will dawn.”

The same usage is confirmed in Act 10 of the Council of Chalcedon, page 657d:

“Now *domnus* Samuel was unwell.”

The distinction and usage of *dominus* and *domnus* are explained by this ancient verse, cited by Pagius under the year 433, number 4:

“Call the heavenly one *Dominus*, the earthly one *domnus*.”

The Greeks likewise call the heavenly Lord *Κύριον* (*Kyrion*) and the earthly lord *κύρον* (*kyron*). Accordingly, in the passage from the Council of Chalcedon just cited, Samuel is called *κύρος* (*kyros*), not *κύριος* (*kyrios*).

Pagius notes the following concerning this passage of Xystus:

“Moreover, those who had been deposed were no longer called *domni*, nor were they adorned with any title of honor.”

He then concludes:

“Xystus rejoices that John is now called by Cyril a venerable *domnus*; from this he infers that John’s honor had been completely restored.”

But from Xystus’s words it follows only that Cyril, adorning John with honorific titles, openly testified that he recognized him as a participant in the same communion. It does not follow equally that Cyril had previously injured John’s honor or regarded him as punished by deposition. Certainly Coelestine had advised Cyril to deal with him with the greatest prudence and moderation.

He is rightly called *domnus*, who acknowledged the common Lord and, with us, confesses in Catholic speech the mystery of his incarnation.

### 6

Your fraternity has briefly and well narrated for us what was done concerning this same affair. Yet we were not surprised to read that the injury of your deposition had been contrived against you by dissenters (Matthew 5:11).

#### Note

Baronius and Labbe place *dictionis* in the margin, but rightly prefer *dejectionis*. The reference is not to some speech or insult against Cyril, but to the sentence of deposition pronounced against him at Ephesus by those who followed John of Antioch and posted on the walls. The Ephesian synod complains of this in Letter 20 to Coelestine, number 3.

We know that truth is FREQUENTLY EXPOSED TO CALUMNY, yet can never be overcome by falsehood. Troubles are always a source of blessing for one who proclaims the faith. For those who endure curses, persecutions, and every evil for the sake of righteousness, abundant reward is prepared in heaven (Matthew 5:12). You suffered falsehood in order to make truth victorious; therefore falsehood must now be mocked, because no one could be lost to the truth.

### 7

We therefore await the clergy of our aforementioned brother John, and we desire them to come. We know that they will give a response both for your honor and for your labor. You yourself are not reluctant to open the door to those returning, as we have often written to our brother and fellow bishop Maximian.

#### Note

The common texts read, “He is not”; but this would have to be said of John, and it cannot refer to him, since before peace was established there was nothing that would have led Xystus to write to Maximian about John’s readiness to open the door to those returning. We have therefore restored *Non es*, “You are not,” so that it may be said of Cyril himself. In the first letter, also sent to Maximian, Xystus commends Cyril’s zeal for peace because, despising his own insults, he preferred the Churches to be restored rather than himself avenged; immediately afterward he asks that the harbor be opened to those laboring in the shipwreck.

Thus, truly, no one is lost except the son of perdition (John 17:12); and the greater reason for him to mourn is that he alone deserved to be excluded.

This brotherhood writes these things with me to your veneration, approving and confirming your labors in every respect. Yet those labors could not have been burdensome or bitter, because they were devoted to him whose burden we carry as light and whose yoke is easy (Matthew 11:30).

#### Note

September 15, 433. Pagius suspects this chronological note of being false because the letter was written by the council of bishops whom the anniversary of Xystus’s ordination had gathered, whereas the note cannot be reconciled with the day on which he assumes Xystus was consecrated.

Tillemont also observes that John’s clergy, whose arrival was expected in order to deliver his letters to Xystus, had not yet reached the city when this letter was written. Consequently, this letter and the following one, which was issued after John’s clergy arrived, ought not to have the same date.

He does not deny, however, that although one letter was written earlier and the other later, both could have been issued together and dated on the same day. But on that assumption he thinks that the passage in number 7 should be altered, where Xystus says that he is awaiting John’s clergy.

Yet it is not prudent to reject or alter certain chronological notes on the basis of conjectures of this kind, especially when an ancient copy is otherwise faithful in preserving them. Xystus himself, who above, in number 2, says that Cyril’s letters were read and approved by all the bishops assembled for the anniversary of his ordination, indicates in the following letter, number 3, that the same bishops also heard the reading of John’s letters.

It follows that Xystus judged that the bishops who had assembled for the celebration of his anniversary should be detained until John’s clergy arrived. Those who had already been refreshed by Cyril’s letters concerning peace in the East would then, after hearing John’s writings on the same matter, be filled with complete joy.

There is no doubt that those who had come from Cyril were detained along with the others and were dismissed only with John’s clergy. The letters were then delivered to both parties on the same day. Although one letter, written shortly before the arrival of John’s clergy, indicates that they were being awaited, this statement ought not to be altered, since those through whom it was sent were competent to describe the order of events.

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the consulship of Theodosius XIII and Maximus.

## Letter VI: Saint Xystus III, Pope, to John of Antioch

#### Note

Recovered, together with the preceding letter, by Antonio de Aquino from a Vatican manuscript, it was published through the efforts of Baronius. It is praised by Vincent of Lérins, *Commonitorium*, chapter 4. It is not a reply to John’s preceding letter 3, but to another letter that is no longer extant and which John began with praise of Xystus.

The Church’s joy at John’s return. The justice of the sentence pronounced against Nestorius. The constancy of the Roman Church in preserving the faith, and the emperors’ zeal in the same cause of faith. How suitable Maximian is to heal the evils inflicted by Nestorius.

### Xystus, bishop, to John, bishop of Antioch

#### 1

If your affection would deign to consider the glory and integrity of the ecclesiastical body, you would certainly not seek an interpreter for our joy. The facts themselves speak most clearly: our sorrow has been changed into joy by the sudden message of our holy brother Cyril.

We are delighted to have escaped so great an anxiety, since your soundness of faith has become a punishment to the one accused of subverting our faith.

#### Note

Labbe reads, “your holiness has become the fullness”; this reading would not be unworthy of consideration if it could be attached to the preceding words, *rebus fidei nostrae*. We therefore restore the reading expressed faithfully by Baronius from the Vatican manuscript and understand it as meaning that John’s recovery was grievous and distressing to Nestorius, who was accused of subverting our faith. Xystus clearly continues speaking about Nestorius.

### 2

Now, truly, Nestorius feels himself an exile; now he recognizes that he is cast out.

#### Note

This was accomplished through John himself. Evagrius, book I, chapter 7, relates that when John saw Nestorius living in a suburb of Antioch and not ceasing from his blasphemies, he reported the matter to the emperor and brought about his condemnation to perpetual exile.

The decree of his perpetual exile may be read in part III of the Council of Ephesus, chapters 14 and 15. Therefore, when Nestorius tells the same Evagrius that he spent four years in the monastery to which he had been sent from Ephesus, he is either lying or the four years must be understood otherwise than his words, as reported by Evagrius, appear to mean.

As we observed in the preceding Letter 4, Nestorius was dismissed from Ephesus in 431, eight days before the eleventh day of Gorpiaeus—that is, either at the end of August or the beginning of September—and went into exile in his monastery. From this letter it is clear that before September 433 he had been sent from the populous city into a deserted place, where there was no one whom he could corrupt. Thus, from his first exile to this second one, he did not spend even two complete years in his monastery.

He has thorns in the desert (Matthew 7:16), because he lacks a grape to gather. Such are the fruits of the man who refused to cultivate the vineyard of our Lord. I believe that the course and sequence of events have reached your affection: how we sought to help him by our admonition.

#### Note

This passage seems to agree with the words of Gennadius in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, where he says that Xystus sent judgments to Nestorius and to the bishops of the East to cut down his error.

But from the first letter which Xystus wrote upon entering the episcopate, he speaks of Nestorius as utterly hopeless and approves Cyril’s judgment, by which he is content with Nestorius’s death alone. He immediately declares concerning this heresiarch:

“Let him alone be shipwrecked who, seeing nothing amid the great darkness of his own doctrines, has been dashed by the waves of impiety against the rock of deposition.”

It should be remembered that Xystus often speaks of what his predecessor Coelestine did in this matter as though he himself had done it. Coelestine, however, after granting Nestorius a period of delay, urged him to accept the sounder faith. Later, when Cyril asked whether, after the period of delay had expired, the sentence against Nestorius should not remain in force, Coelestine replied paternally in Letter 16, number 3:

“I desire the salvation of the one who is perishing, provided that he is willing to confess his sickness.”

We restrained him as he rushed headlong, when he was about to be plunged into the depths under the weight of his blasphemies. If we weigh the nature of the matter in a just balance, everyone will think that Nestorius was condemned too late.

#### Note

Baronius reads, “from which nothing profited him”; Labbe rejects that reading to the margin and restores, “Here the due statement has passed away.” We would prefer *deletus* in place of *debitus*, as though Xystus were saying:

“Let the speech in which John and his companions complained that Nestorius had been condemned by a rash judgment now be erased by oblivion and no longer remembered; let those sad things have completely passed away.”

Let us now enjoy the blessings of the present and not linger long over the sorrows from which the Lord has allowed us to emerge into joy.

### 3

All the brotherhood assembled for my anniversary heard how, for the good of the human race, with me presiding over the apostolic see, …

#### Note

Labbe observes that something is missing here. Baronius attempted to supply it by adding the word “may they rejoice.” Yet the passage would be more suitably restored according to Xystus’s intention as follows:

“May you rejoice that I preside over the apostolic see for the good of the human race.”

It appears that John, at the beginning of his letter, had praised Xystus by declaring that he presided over the apostolic see for the good of the human race. With a certain modest ingenuity, Xystus turns this praise from himself toward Christ, who was truly born for the good of the human race. Later, when John called him a light-bringer and one shining everywhere, Xystus with the same skill shares this praise with all who participate in and proclaim the same faith.

Although these words exceed my merit, and I recognize that they lie beyond me, I gratefully accept the beginning of your speech, because you have no dispute to endure when you confess Christ our Lord, for the good of the human race, as he was born.

Next you add that the Church is a light-bringer and shines everywhere. But now we confess you—or rather, all of us who bear upon our foreheads the sign of that light—as light-bringers. Let all the priests who proclaim the Lord’s faith therefore be light-bringers and shine everywhere.

#### Note

Baronius reads, “which you bear.”

4. Let that Lucifer also be Nestorius, of whom it is written: “Lucifer fell, who was rising at dawn” (Isaiah 14:12). He fell, but he fell in his pride; he was cast down when he resolved to ascend into heaven, set his throne above the stars of heaven, and promise that he would be like the Most High. The former was fashioning himself in the likeness of the Most High; the latter was calling the Most High into his own likeness. For he proclaimed Him to be merely a man who had been born, removing the mystery of the Incarnation, indeed attacking it—that mystery upon which, according to the Creed, both our faith and our salvation rest. It is no longer time for combat, now that the enemy has been struck down; we must pass beyond the matters that provoked the wars. At the time of victory it is still untimely to debate the battles.

5. What clearer proof of the matter, what stronger argument, can there be than the palm of victory [Note: “The palm” is understood to mean the palm won over the adversaries of the faith. Xystus’s argument rests on 1 John 5:4: “This is the victory that conquers the world, your faith,” as though he were saying: “If it is characteristic of faith to conquer, what greater indication could there be that the true faith is with us than that the palm and victory are with us?” For this reason, Baronius’s reading is not acceptable: “so that we may enjoy the palm, with the Lord as its author and with goodness.”]? Let us enjoy it, with the Lord as its author, as a good and delightful thing, because we have begun once again to dwell together as brothers (Psalm 132:1). This is the holiness of your character that we wish to proclaim in what you write. By the outcome of the present affair you have learned what it means to share our convictions [Note: That is, to share the convictions of the apostolic see, to which Christ entrusted the deposit of the faith chiefly in Peter, and which Peter handed down and transmitted to his successors.].

The blessed apostle Peter, in his successors, handed down what he received. Who would wish to separate himself from the teaching of the one whom the Teacher Himself instructed first among the apostles? He was not instructed by hearing it through another, nor by reading a discourse; he was taught, together with the others, by the mouth of the Teacher. He did not have to undergo examination concerning Scripture or the writings; he received an unqualified and simple faith, one that admitted no controversy. We must always meditate upon it and remain in it, so that, following the Apostles with a pure understanding, we may deserve to be numbered among the apostolic faithful [Note: “At Vincent of Lérins: ‘faith and belief.’]. It is no small burden, no small labor, that rests upon us, so that the Church of the Lord may be without stain or wrinkle (Ephesians 5:27).

6. How continually solicitous we ought to be about this is demonstrated by the care of our most merciful and Christian kings. Look, dearest brother, how vigilantly they have devoted themselves to this heavenly affair. They knew no respite from their thoughts [Note: Pope Simplicius uses the same expression; he begins Letter 19 in this way: “We have no respite from our thoughts, for the matter does not permit us to rest.”]; nor did they deign to concern themselves with earthly affairs unless they had first submitted to heavenly ones. How often did their words move the apostolic see, and how often did they move various brothers? They devoted themselves to the cause of the one who never refused to submit Himself to their authority. They know that they lend their solicitude at interest to the One who repays it with great usury.

In this we ought rightly to glory, because we see the heavenly King possessing earthly kings as His allies. “Understand, therefore,” as David says, “and be instructed, you who judge the earth” (Psalm 2:10), since, as he says elsewhere, they and all peoples praise the name of the Lord (Psalm 148:12).

7. Therefore, since, as the Apostle says, there is one faith (Ephesians 4:5), which has prevailed victoriously [Note: Baronius and Labbe read: “It is one and has obtained the victory.” In the commonly printed text of Vincent of Lérins, *Commonitorium*, chapter 43, where this sentence is quoted, the reading is: “It is one that has evidently prevailed.” Instead of *evidenter*, an extremely ancient manuscript of the same *Commonitorium*, Corbie, has *vincenter*, which amounts to “with the palm of victory.” Here again Xystus is adapting the words of 1 John 5:4.], let us believe that it is to be proclaimed, and say that it is to be maintained. Let novelty have no further license, since nothing should be added to antiquity. Let the lucid and transparent faith of our forebears [Note: Vincent of Lérins has: “faith and belief.”] not be clouded by any admixture of mire.

We have in our brother and fellow bishop Maximian, priest of the Church of Constantinople, a man approved by us, consecrated there by divine judgment, so that the disease which the poisons of cunning alone had infused might be overcome, as the sweetness of simplicity took its place [Note: Baronius reads “having been lulled to sleep.” The simplicity of Maximian’s preaching is set against the empty eloquence of Nestorius, which, supported only by cunning, poured in the poison of heresy; Maximian delivered a certain faith received from the apostolic see, and did so with the sweetness that truth produces.]. He will be able to preach there nothing other than what we believe—namely, what he frequently heard when he was present with my predecessors and us.

[Note: September 15, in the year 433.] Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the consulship of Theodosius for the fourteenth time and Maximus.

[Note: This letter, together with the following three, was inserted into the Roman Council under Boniface II, which Lucas Holstenius published. The chronological notice lacking here must be supplied from the following letter. For it is not obscure that both were written for the same reason and on the same occasion.]

## LETTER VII OF POPE XYSTUS III TO PERIGENES, BISHOP OF CORINTH

That he should respect the dignity of Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica, whom Xystus had granted authority as the apostolic see’s vicar according to ancient custom, and should not attempt to withdraw himself from his authority.

**Xystus to his dearest brother Perigenes.**

1. We ought to rejoice rather than complain about the actions of your fraternity, since the authority of the apostolic see was present to you from the very beginning of your ordination—a fact you must always remember [Note: Letters 4, 5, and 15 of Boniface I provide evidence of this.]. But just as it is our duty not to reopen these matters, so it is appropriate to your faith to retain them. We have learned that you recently wished to stir up certain matters; but since these matters have been quieted through the presence of our representatives, whom we sent to those regions in our place for this very reason, we pass them over.

For you may believe that our holy brothers, the presbyter Martianinus [Note: Perhaps “also.”] and the deacon Lollianus, acted in a manner consistent both with your interests and with the authority of the apostolic see. For that reason we have now written nothing of this kind to your fraternity that might cause you sorrow, since we prefer that what had been attempted should be abolished by peaceful correction.

2. Therefore now, dearest brother, admonished by our letters through our brother and fellow bishop Lucas, who came to you moved solely by charity, preserve toward our holy brother and fellow bishop Anastasius, bishop of the city of Thessalonica, the reverence that the other bishops established throughout Illyricum likewise do not refuse to preserve toward the dignity mentioned above. We know that nothing new was granted to him by us, but that what our predecessors had conferred upon his predecessors was established after due consideration of ecclesiastical discipline.

It is especially in your interest to show the greatest deference to the Church that conferred so great an honor upon you [Note: Perigenes owed much to the Roman Church, since its bishop Boniface had appointed him over the Corinthians and had secured his retention of that see despite unwilling rivals. He also owed something to the Church of Thessalonica, especially since Boniface had refused to establish him as bishop of the Corinthians without the testimony and assistance of Rufus, bishop of Thessalonica. Yet Perigenes, if our conjecture is not mistaken—and it can be supported by Leo’s Letter 13—was reluctant to attend synods summoned by the bishop of Thessalonica or to submit to him in any matter.], so that it opposed those who at that time were your rivals on your behalf.

[Note: It was produced in the acts of the Roman council published by Lucas Holstenius only in a greatly curtailed form. No other manuscript has come to hand from which it may be restored. Certainly nothing was omitted that contributed to establishing the right of the apostolic see over the provinces of Illyricum, since it was produced for that reason alone.]

## LETTER VIII OF POPE XYSTUS III TO THE SYNOD TO BE CONVENED AT THESSALONICA

That he has, according to custom, granted Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica, the dignity of vicar throughout Illyricum. What his authority and duties are. That Perigenes, bishop of Corinth, is to be subject to him.

**Xystus to all his dearest brothers, the bishops who are to assemble in synod at Thessalonica.**

1. If we rendered as much obedience to the divine and eternal laws [Col. 0611B] and commands as is rendered to the laws and decrees of rulers—which are temporal, subject to change, and very often abolished—we would certainly possess the highest blessedness and avoid the troubles of worldly affliction, under that Ruler or Shepherd who, wishing continually to come to our aid, cries out in daily appeals: “Turn to me, and I will turn to you” (Zechariah 1:3) [lacuna].

Among other things, and at this point: We grant to our brother and fellow bishop Anastasius as much as our predecessors granted to his predecessors. We follow the judgment of those who came before us by establishing what we know they established, since we also approve him as possessing the merit of those who deserved such authority. Let no one obstruct these salutary provisions; let no one resist these commands.

Let the metropolitans of each province have their proper honor [Note: Supply: “of the provinces.”], without prejudice to the privilege of the one whom those already honored ought to honor more greatly. Let them have the right to ordain in their province; but no one may dare to ordain without the knowledge or consent of the one whom we wish to be consulted concerning all ordinations. Let the more important cases be referred to the bishop of Thessalonica. Let the greater responsibility rest upon him of carefully examining and testing those who are called to the episcopate. Let him choose the best and most diligent from among your number to join him as assessors in matters of business; or let him appoint, without being present himself, persons who may settle matters submitted for adjudication.

2. Let the bishop of Corinth know that he is by no means to be granted unrestricted freedom of authority if he wishes to resist this Church [Note: The Church of Thessalonica.], which he must acknowledge has benefited him. We too must oppose him if he attempts anything, since we remember what was formerly granted to him through us and always oppose unlawful usurpations.

3. As for all other matters, whatever they may be, we wish them to be settled in the presence of our representatives, since their good faith with us is complete: whatever they approve, we believe that we have likewise judged and approved.

[Note: Read “so great” rather than “whole.” Here Xystus commends the trustworthiness of the legates whom he was sending to the synod.]

[Note: July 8, in the year 435.] Given on the eighth day before the Ides of July, in the consulship of the Augusti Theodosius for the fifteenth time and Valentinian for the fourth time.

## LETTER IX OF POPE XYSTUS III TO PROCLUS, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE

That he should receive no priest coming to him from those provinces belonging to the bishop of Thessalonica without a *formata* issued by the bishop of Thessalonica.

**Xystus to his dearest brother Proclus.**

1. Although we know that your fraternity, instructed in ecclesiastical discipline, carefully observes everything pertaining to the observance of rules and canons, and although we have established by clear evidence that you neither do anything yourself nor allow other priests, with your connivance [Note: Holstenius reads *cohibente*, “restraining.” We have no hesitation in restoring *connivente*, “with your connivance,” since we have found nothing more common in old books than for *connivere* and *conniventia* to be written as *conhibere* and *conhibentia*.], to do anything that overturns the ancient decrees of the Fathers—for this is proper and worthy of a priest most pleasing to God: to guard with every possible care what belongs to him and in no way to disturb or violate what is owed to his brothers, preserving his moderate and honorable dignity with greater glory if he permits nothing to be attempted against the custom of the ancients—nevertheless, by our exhortation and through the grace of charity, this special duty must be added to your fraternity: that your vigilant holiness should not provide an opportunity for the improper will of certain persons, who desire of themselves to generate scandal and discord among the Churches, wishing to increase through the disturbance of the Churches and to make a place for themselves through the administration of priests.

2. We therefore wish your fraternity to observe what we also observe and know you will do according to your customary practice [Note: Namely, the practice by which he usually observes matters belonging to ecclesiastical discipline. To show that he was not demanding anything harsh or unworthy of Proclus, Xystus immediately testifies that he himself observed this same rule toward the bishops of Illyricum.]. That is: if a priest from any of these provinces, which belong to our brother and fellow bishop Anastasius, bishop of the city of Thessalonica, comes to you without his knowledge and attempts to come without his letters and *formata*, let him be regarded as a despiser of ecclesiastical discipline and a contemptuous violator of the canons, which we do not permit to be violated in any respect.

Your common reverence is preserved if each of you safeguards the honor owed to the other, anticipating one another through the grace of charity. We wish this to be done, as we read [Note: It appears that *volumus* should be restored, as we have read it; Paul gives the relevant command in Romans 12:10: “Outdo one another in showing honor.”]. Let all the priests of that province learn that your fraternity exercises such authority that you do not permit a priest to attempt what is unlawful.

3. We would say more if we did not know that your fraternity understands greater things in this matter than we can convey in these letters that we send to you. You have the most recent example in the action recently held concerning our brother Idduas [Note: At the Council of Ephesus, page 544, column E, Idduas, bishop of Smyrna, subscribes to the sentence deposing Nestorius. Hence Holstenius thinks that Proclus acted toward this bishop by patriarchal right, that Idduas appealed from Proclus’s judgment to the apostolic see, and that Xystus ordered Proclus’s sentence to be upheld. It would follow that Xystus recognized Proclus’s patriarchal authority over the Asian diocese—an authority that not even the synod of Constantinople had assigned to that see. For canon 2 of that synod decrees that the bishops of the Asian diocese should administer only what lies within Asia, and that the bishops of Thrace should govern Thrace alone. Although this authority was first granted to him by canon 28 of the Council of Chalcedon, the archdeacon Aetius, at that same synod, session 15, page 796, claims it as though it had already been assigned to that see by the synod of Constantinople. Indeed, unless we grant that the bishop of Constantinople possessed this authority over the Asian provinces even before the Council of Chalcedon, Philip the presbyter cannot be cleared of falsehood. At the Council of Chalcedon, session 15, when Leontius, bishop of the Asian provinces, claimed the privilege and said, “From Saint Timothy until now twenty-seven bishops have been made, all of them ordained at Ephesus,” Philip replied: “John, of holy memory, bishop of Constantinople, deposed fifteen bishops after going into Asia and ordained others; and Memnon here was ordained.” However the bishops of the royal city interpreted canons 2 and 3 of the Council of Constantinople, it is certain that Xystus’s successors, at least until Hormisdas, did not accept them—much less did Xystus himself—for they did not acknowledge this authority in the bishops of Constantinople.].

With regard to him we have decreed that your fraternity’s judgment should be observed. We do not wish to do an injustice to your investigation, since by your innocence you uphold his entirely just purpose. The ignorant must be admonished; but if you wish to instruct at greater length someone who knows and observes such matters, you would appear not so much to admonish him as to reproach him for ignorance [Note: This should not be connected with what was just said about Idduas, whose example Xystus touched upon only in passing, but with what came before. Xystus, having said that he would not say more, now gives the reason: those who are ignorant must be taught at greater length, but not someone like Proclus, who knows his duty very well.].

Let what we have written suffice, dearest brother, since we are confident that your disposition and judgment agree with ours in correcting and preserving these matters. For we believe—and ought to believe—that, as Scripture says, we have one heart and one soul (Acts 4:32) in observing religion, guarding the canons, and maintaining ecclesiastical discipline.

[Note: December 18, in the year 437.] Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January, in the consulship of Aetius for the second time and Segisvultus.

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING LETTER

1. To understand the purpose of this letter, it is important to know what Xystus means by these words in section 3: “Nor should you, dearest brothers, believe yourselves bound by those decrees that the Eastern synod wished to enact contrary to our instructions, except for what it judged concerning the faith with our agreement.” The question is which Eastern synod this was, and what its decrees were by which the Churches of Illyricum were not bound.

2. Lucas Holstenius, in his notes on this passage, thinks that the words refer to the affair of Juvenal, bishop of Jerusalem, who sought at the Council of Ephesus to obtain primacy over the province of Palestine. On this matter he advises consulting Leo’s letter to Bishop Maximianus, where we read: “It is difficult for the desire of wicked men not to attempt to grasp something beyond measure, as Bishop Juvenal also believed at the Council of Ephesus that he could succeed in obtaining primacy over the province of Palestine, and sought to strengthen his insolent attempts by fabricated documents” (Leo, Letter 110, chapter 6).

But we are convinced that Xystus is not referring to this matter. First, because, through Cyril’s intervention against Juvenal’s ambition, his attempts were rendered void, so that no decree on the matter—and indeed not even a word—appears in the Council of Ephesus. Yet Xystus here speaks of decrees enacted not by one bishop but by a synod. Furthermore, even if Juvenal had obtained what he sought and had secured its confirmation by some decree, what had the usurped primacy of Palestine to do with the bishops of Illyricum? And why would Xystus have needed to summon them to a synod where they would be warned that they were not at all bound by such a decree?

3. Tillemont writes that he does not know to what else the same words could refer (volume 14, page 264), unless the decree meant is the decree of the Council of Ephesus, session 7. In that decree not only is the freedom of the Churches of Cyprus asserted, but the rights of the other Churches are also preserved, and it is declared:

“It was therefore decided by the holy and ecumenical synod that each province should preserve pure and inviolate the rights it has had from the beginning, according to the ancient custom, and that every metropolitan should be free to obtain copies of the acts for his own security.”

At the same time, however, this most modest scholar admits that the decree was enacted after the legates of the apostolic see had arrived at Ephesus, though nowhere does he find anything from which we can infer that the legates objected to it. Xystus, however, speaks of decrees that the apostolic see had never approved.

Moreover, who could believe that Xystus rejected the decrees of a synod that showed the apostolic see the highest reverence, or wished to diminish its authority? He would surely have designated an ecumenical council not by the vague title “Eastern synod,” but at least by the proper name “Council of Ephesus.”

4. At first sight the words of this pope seem more readily to accord with the synod held at Constantinople in the year 381. The Roman pontiffs accepted its decrees concerning the faith, yet for a very long time after Xystus’s era they utterly refused to approve its other enactments. Accordingly, when Anatolius repeatedly boasted of such decrees, Leo, writing back to Anatolius himself, argued that they were entirely without force, in these words: “For the written decision of certain bishops made, as you claim, sixty years ago, and never transmitted by your predecessors to the knowledge of the apostolic see, provides absolutely no support for your position” (Leo, Letter 97, section 6).

The matters concerning the faith that had then been defined were sent by the same synod to Damasus, as can be gathered from the synod’s Letter 13, section 4, to that pope; nor do we read that any Catholic subsequently rejected them. Certainly the creed of this synod was recited with universal approval at the Council of Chalcedon, session 2, and was inserted in its entirety, together with the Nicene Creed, into the definition of that Council in session 5. Yet it is almost certain that Xystus is here concerned with certain decrees enacted more recently.

5. We therefore think that the synod meant by this pope was held in his own time, and that in it certain provisions were enacted against the rights of the Churches, especially the Church of Thessalonica, at the instigation of Proclus—or, to use Xystus’s milder expression, with his connivance.

Accordingly, in the preceding letter Xystus rebukes Proclus with the utmost moderation and prudence, devoting himself entirely to exhorting him both to preserve the ancient decrees of the Fathers and to maintain the honor owed to the bishop of Thessalonica.

From Theodoret’s Letter 86 to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, we learn that a synod was held under Proclus in which certain measures were enacted—undoubtedly for the benefit of the bishop of Constantinople—against the rights of the other Churches. Theodoretus addresses Flavian as follows:

“Know, my lord, that he”—Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria—“has shown this weakness toward me ever since we agreed to the synodical decisions made under Proclus, of blessed memory, adhering to the regulations of the holy Fathers; and he has reproached us once and again, as though, in his words, we had betrayed the rights both of the Antiochenes and of the Alexandrians.”

Clearly, there is nothing in these words of Theodoret that does not fit perfectly with what Xystus says about the Eastern synod.

6. If this is so, we may affirm the following concerning the council that Theodoret mentions as having been held under Proclus. First, it was held no later than the year 437; and in it some matters concerning the faith were established with the agreement of the apostolic see, while other matters outside the faith and concerning discipline were established contrary to the instructions of that same see.

Furthermore, Xystus plainly teaches that by those decrees issued contrary to his instructions the rights of the bishop of Thessalonica were injured. It is no less clear from Theodoret that, in Dioscorus’s judgment at least, the privileges of the Alexandrians and Antiochenes were likewise violated. Thus Dioscorus regarded Theodoret as a traitor to the rights of the Alexandrians and Antiochenes because he had approved those decrees by his agreement, and for this reason considered himself justified in pursuing him with hatred.

It is therefore reasonable to conjecture that those decrees confirmed, or even enlarged, the privileges already attributed to the bishop of the royal city in the Council of Constantinople in the year 381. If Theodoret did not attend the synod under Proclus but subsequently agreed to its decrees, it follows that those enactments were sent throughout the provinces to be confirmed by the agreement and subscription of the bishops.

7. Baronius and the editors of the councils who followed him must therefore be corrected. They assign that council under Proclus to the year 439 and, relying solely on Theodoret’s words, imagine many things wholly foreign to his meaning.

They suppose that Dioscorus, still a deacon and acting as apocrisarius of the Alexandrian Church at Constantinople, disputed with the bishop of Antioch over primacy. They further suppose that, for this reason, a synod was convened and decreed that whatever had formerly been established concerning the matter at Nicaea and at other councils should remain ratified and firm (Baronius, toward the end of the year 439; Labbe, volume 3, page 1284). Finally, they suppose that Theodoret, bishop of Cyrus, took the side of the bishop of Antioch in order to defend him, and thereby incurred Dioscorus’s bitter hatred.

But in the letter just mentioned Theodoret does not say that Dioscorus’s hatred was aroused because he had vigorously defended the rights of the bishop of Antioch. He says rather that, by agreeing to the decrees enacted under Proclus, he was judged to have betrayed the rights of the Antiochene bishop no less than those of the Alexandrian bishop. Nor were the Nicene decrees confirmed at that synod; rather, as is established from Xystus, they were derogated from. There is no trace at all in Theodoret’s words of a dispute between the deacon Dioscorus and the bishop of Antioch; the story has the character of a mere fabrication.

8. Accordingly, Joan. Garnerius, in the *Auctarium* to Theodoret, in chapter 7, section 7 of his history, and, following him, Anton. Pagius under the year 439, section 13, rightly departed from Baronius’s opinion.

Yet they too do not seem to have understood Theodoret’s meaning much more successfully, since they think that this writer refers to a synodical letter which Proclus wrote to Domnus, bishop of Antioch, on behalf of Athanasius, bishop of the Pyrrhenians, and which was inserted into session 14 of the Council of Chalcedon.

To make this clearer, it should be observed that Theodoret wrote the letter whose meaning we are seeking in order to secure Flavian’s help and support against Dioscorus’s accusations. For this purpose he urges Flavian to defend the decrees sanctioned in the general Council of Constantinople and to restrain Dioscorus’s arrogance, by which he refuses to remain within the limits assigned to him.

He then says that he incurred the bishop’s hatred because he had agreed to the synodical letter made under Proclus, as though by this agreement he had betrayed the rights of the Alexandrians and Antiochenes.

But what connection is there between Proclus’s letter written on behalf of Athanasius and the synodical letter to which Theodoret agreed? Clearly, if Theodoret had merely subscribed to a letter written on behalf of a bishop of the Pyrrhenians, there would have been no reason for him to be regarded by Dioscorus as a traitor to the rights of the Antiochenes, much less to those of the Alexandrians.

First, that letter is merely commendatory, and Proclus claims no right for himself in it. Indeed, he expressly declares that the rights of the Church of Antioch remain safe and unharmed throughout the entire affair, when he addresses its bishop Domnus as follows:

“Let not your religious reverence therefore suppose that the aforesaid most God-loving bishop Athanasius has come here as though to inflict an injury upon the see of Antioch, the greatest of cities,” and so forth.

Moreover, he testifies that the letter was written not only in his own name but also in Cyril’s, saying:

“By this present letter we consoled him—Athanasius—and ordered him to be confident: I together with the most holy bishop and fellow priest Cyril.”

Could Cyril be thought at that time to have been ignorant of, or to have betrayed, the rights of his own Church?

It is far more reasonable to believe that the synodical letter of Proclus mentioned by Theodoret in Letter 86 to Flavian was entirely different from the one produced by the Council of Chalcedon in session 15.

But when we compare Xystus’s letter with the aforementioned letter of Theodoret, we easily perceive, from the mutual light they shed upon one another, that both speak of one and the same synod and of the same decrees.

## LETTER X OF POPE XYSTUS III TO ALL THE BISHOPS OF ILLYRICUM

[Note: Xystus addresses them at the beginning as gathered together in one synod. From the preceding letter and from this one itself it may be inferred that the synod was convened so that the rights of the Church of Thessalonica, which Proclus was attempting to usurp or diminish, might be vindicated intact.]

He indicates that, according to custom, he has entrusted his authority throughout Illyricum to Anastasius. What his authority is. That they should show him reverence.

**Xystus to all his dearest brothers, the bishops established throughout Illyricum.**

1. The Teacher of the Gentiles, the vessel of election, the firmest foundation of our religion, bears witness in all the letters that he writes to the Churches of the individual cities to his rejoicing in the Lord when he sees those whom he addresses obeying the commands of the law and living in the fear of our God.

If, then, the Apostle, so learned and holy, possesses such joy of mind that he addresses so many at once [Note: That is, so many people together.], knowing that this benefits both those to whom he writes and religion itself, how great do you think our joy must be, since we are permitted to address the council of your holiness collectively and to join our discourse, which contains the testimony of our devoted affection toward you, to your holiness?

He visits the individual Churches by his letters, as we have said; we believe that we are addressing by our letters as many Churches at once as there are of you who are assembling for the holy synod [Note: The first occurrence of *nos* is in the nominative; the second is in the accusative.]. His discourse was with the uneducated and with disciples; ours is with colleagues and learned men.

And, so that we may not depart from the example of the blessed Paul, whose commands you ought especially to obey, let it not be burdensome for you to be admonished, as though we were present, about matters that come to our knowledge for the preservation of ecclesiastical discipline.

Therefore, with you, we communicate what we know contributes to the observance of the rules and canons, according to our solicitude, through our son Artemius, the presbyter, whose effectiveness in action, moderation, and devotion have alike pleased us. In this way the path handed down by the Fathers may be held by the firm footsteps of your affection, and what has been preserved by us for the peace of the Churches may continue to be preserved [Note: Holstenius prefers “what has been established.” Yet *custodite*, “preserve,” is not foreign to Xystus’s purpose. He established nothing new, but preserves what had been established by the forebears.].

2. All the Churches of Illyricum, as we received from our predecessors and as we too have done, now belong to the care of the bishop of Thessalonica. He is to distinguish and settle, through his solicitude, whatever proceedings arise among the brothers, as they commonly do, and whatever is done by the individual priests is to be referred to him.

Let there be a council whenever cases arise, whenever he determines that one is needed because of emerging necessities, so that the apostolic see, properly informed by his report, may confirm what has been done. Let no one summoned refuse to come, nor deny himself to the holy assembly to which he ought to hasten. Let no excuse based on defiance be sought, so that, when you have assembled together, a common decision may be made that preserves the peace of the Churches and holds the peoples to salvation.

3. Nor should you, dearest brothers, believe yourselves bound by those decrees that the Eastern synod wished to enact contrary to our instructions, except for what it judged concerning the faith with our agreement. Let none of you depart from the commands of the canons or deviate from those decrees that the frequent authority of the apostolic see has sent to you in accordance with the order of the rules.

If anything should arise among the brothers, or if some proceeding should be brought against any brother, let the matter be settled there before our brother and fellow bishop Anastasius, who is known to exercise the authority of the apostolic see, as did his predecessor Rufus of blessed memory, by our will. Or, if it cannot be concluded there, let the examination come to us, while he nevertheless pursues the entire case in his letters.

4. There is no body that is not governed by a head. You are indeed, as we know, holy members; but it is fitting for you to look to and honor your head, because the honor shown to the head contributes to the hope of the entire body’s holiness. The head itself, with watchful eyes, protects the body that appears suited to it and fitted by its worthy functions for each task.

But just as every body is governed by its head, so the head itself, unless it is supported by its body, loses its firmness and strength and does not retain the dignity it had possessed.

Therefore be, as is fitting, priests of the Lord, bishops of the Churches, and teachers of our religion. Preserve for our brother and fellow bishop the reverence that you owe him, and maintain peace and harmony among yourselves. Let there be among you, as we believe there is, one heart and one soul (Acts 4:32).

Do not think that anything is diminished from your reverence if the honor owed to the one to whom both our forebears and we have wished the Churches of Illyricum to belong according to the established custom is preserved and paid by your affection.

[Note: December 18, in the year 437.] Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January, in the consulship of Aetius for the second time and Segisvultus.

[Col. 0617]

# APPENDIX. INFORMATION ABOUT THE REMAINING WRITINGS THAT CONCERN XYSTUS III

## § I. What Xystus wrote while still a presbyter

[Col. 0617D]

1. Under Pope Zosimus, Xystus was a presbyter of the Roman Church of such great reputation that, when rumor falsely proclaimed him favorable to the Pelagians, the enemies of Christian grace were greatly elated, while the defenders of that same grace were nevertheless saddened (Augustine, Letter 194, no. 1). But, in order to dispel the sinister rumor as quickly as possible, he first of all, in a very large gathering of the people, pronounced an anathema against the enemies of Christian grace [Col. 0618D]; and afterward, through the agency of Leo, then an acolyte, he sent a letter to the elder Aurelius. It was very brief, but in it he sufficiently explained what he thought both about the most pernicious doctrine and about the grace of God; nor did he conceal how vigorously he had acted so that the supporters of the recent error might be restrained (the same author, Letter 191, no. 1). Finally, not long afterward, he sent another, more extended letter to Augustine and Alypius, delivered by the presbyter Firmus, in which he explained more fully and clearly what he had asserted [Col. 0619A] in the earlier letter. Those two letters have been lost.

2. Augustine in turn replied to these with two letters, namely Letters 191 and 194. Alypius also sent a separate reply, but that writing too has not reached us.

3. In the *Library of the Fathers*, under the sixth century, there are three books: the first *On Riches*, the second *On Evil Teachers and on the Works of Faith*, and the last *On Chastity*. They were first attributed to Pope Xystus III by Jacobus Salonius, but almost all learned scholars have denied that they belong to him. Salonius indeed attributed them to our Xystus on the sole authority of his exemplar; yet he admits that, first, the title had been prefixed to these books in his copy by a later hand, and, second, the copy bore not the name of Pope Xystus III but that of Pope Xystus and martyr. Finally, [Col. 0619B] he admits that the books could not belong to Pope Xystus and martyr, since it is established that they were written later than his time. But if the title was false, why, on the basis of its authority, should they have been attributed to Pope Xystus III, who certainly was not a martyr? Furthermore, all learned scholars agree that these books are filled with Pelagian errors, and that they explicitly defend this statement of Pelagius: “A rich man who remains in his riches cannot enter the kingdom of God.” Augustine refutes this at length in Letter 157 to Hilary, chapter 4.

4. John Garnerius uses this very argument—by which others deny that the work belongs to Xystus—to attribute it to him. “For,” he says, “it is established that Xystus once favored the Pelagians and for some time offered them his patronage” (Garnerius, in Mercator, part I, p. 362). But what the learned man, apparently relying on Augustine’s words in Letters 191 and 194, treats as certain is by no means certain. Augustine does not say that Xystus favored them, but that rumor proclaimed him favorable to the enemies of Christian grace. Or if from such a rumor it is inferred that he was infected with Pelagian error and favored those heretics, then it must also be conceded that he was a Nestorian. For a similar rumor was later spread about him, namely, that he favored Nestorius. Accordingly, Cyril writes at the end of his letter to Acacius of Melitene:

“If some people bring a letter as though written by Philip, the most reverend presbyter of the Roman Church, with wording suggesting that the most holy bishop took the deposition of Nestorius badly and came to his aid, let not your holiness believe this” (Council, vol. III, p. 1229).

[Col. 0619D] Cyril then adds:

“For he wrote everything in agreement with the holy synod (of Ephesus), confirmed all its proceedings, and shares our view. The letters themselves are witnesses to this.”

Xystus, then, had always possessed an entirely sound faith; nevertheless, he was of such a disposition that, in condemning heretics, he wished nothing to be done rashly, but first desired everything to be attempted, in case they might perhaps be brought to the truth by some measure of moderation. This gave occasion to men who were less patient to regard his faith with suspicion and rashly to sow the aforementioned rumors. But it is one thing to display a certain kindness toward heretics and another to teach or defend their errors.

5. The strongest indication that Xystus did not defend that singular and perverse [Col. 0620A] opinion of Pelagius by which the rich are excluded from the kingdom of heaven is that, when Augustine sets out everything concerning Xystus in Letter 194 and at the same time refutes the arguments of the Pelagians, which he thought Xystus should be warned about, he is completely silent about this particular opinion of Pelagius concerning the rich. Thus it is proved that the first book, *On Riches*, is in no way appropriate to Xystus. Once it has been denied to him, no one will deny that the other two must likewise be denied to him. Moreover, if those books had really been written by Xystus, and if it were established that he had thought and taught wrongly in them, he should have been regarded as a supporter of heretics not merely on the basis of suspicions and false rumors but on the basis of definite arguments. Nor would it then have been enough for him to clear himself of the rumor brought against him merely by pronouncing an anathema against the Pelagians; at the same time those books and the perverse doctrines of Pelagius inserted in them would have had to be condemned and suppressed, and the contrary faith publicly professed. Since, therefore, attributing those books to Xystus conflicts with historical truth in more than one way, it is astonishing that a plainly false title, added by a later hand, could have been given so much weight that a heretical work was attributed to a Catholic presbyter later distinguished by the dignity of supreme pontiff.
