If it had belonged to our Xystus, it ought to have been inscribed not under the name of Pope Sixtus and martyr but under the name of Xystus the presbyter.

6. Having laid down this foundation—that Xystus had for some time been a supporter of Pelagian errors and had transmitted them in published books—the aforementioned scholar proceeds to other conjectures. He consequently thinks that the books of the *Hypomnesticon*, published by Augustine in the appendix to volume X, may also be attributed to Xystus [Col. 0620C]. But once this foundation has been demolished, the conjectures resting solely upon it must necessarily collapse. Indeed, in the latest edition of Augustine, the critical judgment prefixed to those books demonstrates that they belong to Marius Mercator rather than to Xystus.

7. There are arguments from which we may conclude that, while still a presbyter, Xystus wrote to Nestorius, to John of Antioch, and to Cyril of Alexandria. Gennadius, in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, mentions a letter of Xystus to Nestorius. Xystus himself, in Letter 6, no. 2, recalls to John, bishop of Antioch, how—speaking of Nestorius—“we wished to come to his aid by our admonition.” It is clear that he is there speaking of letters written before his pontificate, from his own Letters 1 and 2. While Celestine was still alive, Cyril had sent legates to Rome and had consulted him about how one ought to deal with John of Antioch. Then Xystus, succeeding Celestine and having been ordained while the legates were present, replied:

“Those letters were indeed sufficient, which I had previously sent, full of everything necessary, both through the clerics of the Church of Constantinople and through the deacons of your holiness”—that is, of Cyril.

In these passages we suspect that the letters written and sent in Celestine’s name are being recalled. We think that Xystus speaks of them as though they were his own, not only because a successor may attribute to himself his predecessor’s writings and actions in such cases, or because he may have shared in the letters written by Celestine from the synod, but also because he may have assisted Celestine in writing his letters. Indeed, Celestine’s and Xystus’s letters bear the same style and the same character, fond of frequent maxims.

## § II. On the writings that concern Xystus now that he was pope

8. The legates of the East, Hermogenes, bishop of Rhinocorura, and Lampetius, bishop of Cassium, had in fact been sent to Celestine; but the letter of Cyril that had been entrusted to them was delivered to Xystus (Letter 2, no. 1). The legates were praised in that letter with such an encomium that, as Xystus says, he might perhaps have believed less readily in the letters that Cyril had written about them, unless their presence, bearing witness to itself, had overcome the testimony of the letters [Col. 0621B]. Cyril then explained at length the disposition with which he regarded the Easterners who dissented from him. In order to open an easier path to peace in the East, he declared that he willingly disregarded his own insults and preferred that the Churches be set in order rather than that he himself be vindicated. Therefore, content with the exile of Nestorius alone, he asked that a hand be extended to the others who were struggling in the same shipwreck, and at the same time requested advice about how he should conduct himself toward John of Antioch.

9. In replying to this letter of Cyril, Xystus indicates that he had also sent copies of the reply to the other Eastern bishops to whom the legates had asked that it be sent. This shows that those legates had come in the name of the Eastern bishops, though they carried only Cyril’s letters. Otherwise there would have been no need for Xystus to learn from the legates to whom he ought to write, especially since it had been customary for Roman pontiffs to reply to those who wrote to them. It is probable, however, that this legation was appointed only after the letters of Celestine, dated March 15 of the year 432, had reached the East; hence the opinion that Xystus was ordained in April of that same year 432 becomes less probable. Nor does Pagius postpone this ordination without reason if the aforementioned letters were received before the legates departed from the East—legates whom Xystus congratulates for having been present at his ordination.

10. When the legates were returning, Xystus gave them two letters to be delivered to Cyril, one private and the other shared with others. Acacius, bishop of Beroea, testifies that a copy of the latter had been sent to him, writing these words to Alexander of Hierapolis:

“The bishop who is in Rome wrote one letter to me” (Baluzius, *New Collection*, p. 757).

But because Acacius immediately adds, “At Alexandria, however, three or four, of which I have sent the reply of one to your holiness,” Tillemont (vol. IV, p. 521) interprets this as though he had read *Alexandriam* (“to Alexandria”) instead of *Alexandriae* (“at Alexandria”), and therefore supposes that Xystus, at the time when he wrote to Acacius, also sent three or four letters to Alexandria. Baluzius’s interpretation is preferable: he understands *Alexandriae vero* as though the text read, “But the bishop who is at Alexandria.” Thus Acacius is simply indicating in the quoted passage that one letter from Xystus and three or four from Cyril had been written to him [Col. 0622A]. He confirms this himself when, having announced that he was sending Alexander a copy of one of Cyril’s letters, he hopes that Alexander’s foot pain would be relieved when he examined what Cyril had carefully and accurately explained in that copy. “But if,” he says, “as you wrote, your feet still hurt, examine the letter of the bishop Cyril, most beloved of God, and learn how much precision (*akribeia*, ἀκρίβεια) he has employed in the matter of the faith,” and so forth. There is therefore no reason, on account of Acacius’s celebrated words, to look for any letters of Xystus to Alexander, bishop of Hierapolis.

11. Although Xystus, in Letter 5, no. 7, dated September 15 of the year 433, frequently recalls that he had written to Maximian about the readiness with which Cyril ardently desired those returning to the Church to be received [Col. 0622B], only one of those letters survives, namely the first. It is addressed to Cyril, but a copy of it was also given to Maximian. It follows that at least one letter written to Maximian has been lost.

12. As soon as John of Antioch, together with the other Eastern bishops, returned to the unity of the Church after peace had been settled, he sent a legation to Rome to testify that he was united with Xystus. Cyril then hastened to inform Xystus by letter both about the peace that had been concluded and about John’s legation (Letter 5, no. 6). Xystus had those letters read aloud in an assembly of bishops who had gathered for the anniversary of his ordination (Council of Ephesus III, part, chapter 32). Since the peace of the East was established at the beginning of the year 433, as is clear from the homily of Paul of Emesa delivered on the first day of that year, it may reasonably be inferred that Cyril’s letters were written after the beginning of 433 and received before the anniversary of Xystus’s ordination.

13. A few days later, the legates of John, whom Cyril had announced beforehand, arrived in Rome and delivered letters whose opening was filled with praises of Xystus (Letter 6, no. 3). John expressly proclaimed that Xystus presided over the apostolic see for the good of the human race and called him a light-bearing star shining everywhere. These letters had been written so that John might solemnly testify both that he approved the deposition of Nestorius and that he approved the ordination of Maximian in his place. Xystus also judged them worthy to be read at the assembly of the same bishops who had come to the City to celebrate his anniversary [Col. 0622D]. Nor did he think that those who had brought the letters announcing John’s legation should be dismissed before they had become witnesses to the legation itself.

14. At the very time when John and Cyril were preparing their legation, the Eastern bishops who were displeased with the peace made by John thought they must hurry so that the agreements reached would not be confirmed by Xystus. For this reason Eutherius, bishop of Tyana, and Helladius, bishop of Tarsus, not only composed the letter that we still possess to Xystus, but also took care to share it, before it was sent, with Alexander, bishop of Hierapolis, and Theodoret, bishop of Cyrus. Eutherius was not content with this; he also sent private letters at the same time, exhorting both men to send representatives themselves to the West, that is, to Rome (Baluzius, *New Collection*, p. 817). “For there is fear,” he said, “that, when the letters of others”—namely, of Cyril and John—“arrive first, it may appear that union has been achieved, and, when everyone agrees to incongruous matters”—that is, when everyone has agreed to incongruous matters—“that they [the Romans] will seem slower to correct what has been badly done.”

Following these admonitions, Alexander sent legates to the City, accusing those impious agreements—which Cyril and John had made—“that, in addition to other incongruities, increased the discord in matters of faith” (ibid., pp. 821–822), as Irenaeus, that is, the fiercest defender of Nestorius, was pleased to say. Theodoret and the other bishops also obeyed the same admonitions; their names are given to us by Meletius, bishop of Mopsuestia [Col. 0623B].

15. When their clerics, traveling to Rome, had turned aside to Mopsuestia, Meletius wrote back concerning them to Alexander, Theodoret, Abibus, Heliadius, Maris, David, and Acilinus as follows (ibid., p. 822):

“We received the clerics sent to the West, most devoted to God, as was fitting, as our own”—read “your own”—“and as men sent for such a cause”; that is, “we received your clerics as it was fitting to receive them, especially since they had been sent for such an important cause.”

He then added:

“We too are hastening, if the Lord grants the prayers of your holiness, to do something similar, because it is altogether necessary that we also offer what we believe to be expedient.”

Whether Meletius fulfilled what he promised there, or in what manner Alexander’s [Col. 0623C] and the other legates were received by Xystus, we know from no record. Nevertheless, it is indisputable and clear from his own letters that this pope was always steadfast in defending the faith. Nor does it seem doubtful that, at the same time, he customarily showed himself pious and kind toward those who were in error, supporting them and, insofar as he could, bringing them back to unity.

16. Although they could not induce him to write anything in favor of their party, the shamelessness of some nevertheless advanced so far that they fabricated a letter concerning an alleged change of mind on his part and arranged for it to be circulated throughout the provinces. Cyril warned Succensus about this matter at the end of Letter 2, which he wrote to that bishop, in these words:

“If some people circulate a letter as though it had been written by Philip, the most religious presbyter of the Roman Church, suggesting that the most holy bishop had taken the deposition of Nestorius badly and had come to his aid, let your holiness place no credence in this. For he wrote in agreement with the holy synod, confirmed everything done there, and shares the same view as we do.”

The same warning is repeated at the end of Cyril’s Letter 1 to Acacius, bishop of Melitene. In both letters alike Cyril then adds:

“If a letter is brought by some people as though written by me, suggesting that we regret what we did at Ephesus, let that too be received with laughter.”

It may therefore be conjectured that, when Cyril published his explanation of his *Chapters*, which was approved by all fair-minded men and even by Theodoret himself, his opponents seized this opportunity to fabricate that double letter.

17. The fortunes of Saint Britius, bishop of the city of Tours, who had succeeded blessed Martin, were varied. Formerly accused by Lazarus, he deserved to be acquitted by Proculus at the Synod of Turin (Zosimus, Letter 3, no. 3). Later, however, expelled by his own people in the year 430, he was forced to flee to Rome, as Gregory of Tours relates in Book II, chapter 1, of his *History of the Franks*. “But,” says the same Gregory, in Book X, chapter 31, “in his seventh year he decided to return to Tours with the authority of that pope.” This can be understood in two ways.

Either the phrase “with the authority” means that Britius returned to his Church not by his own authority but at the command of Xystus. This interpretation is supported by the same Gregory’s statement in the same passage:

“Britius, having spent seven years with the Pope of the City, was found free of the charge”—perhaps “innocent”—“and was ordered to return to his own city.”

Or, with Tillemont (vol. XIV, p. 264), the word “authority” may be interpreted as referring to a letter given by Xystus, by which he vouched for Britius’s innocence and ordered that he be received without dispute. Pope Zosimus uses the same term “authority” for his first letter, where he says (Letter 1, no. 1):

“It is clear that we have sent this authority everywhere.”

This usage is familiar not only to Roman pontiffs but also to other writers, and it applies especially in this testimony of Gregory. No one will think it probable that, after such a long retirement in the City, Britius was sent back from there to the people who had expelled him without a commendatory letter from the pope.

18. Prosper commended another splendid deed of Xystus to memory in his *Chronicle* under the year 439, in these words:

“At this time Julian of Athela”—read “of Eclanum”—“the most boastful defender of the Pelagian error, whom an immoderate desire for the bishopric he had long since lost was tormenting, attempted by many deceptive devices to insinuate himself into communion with the Church, holding out hope of correction”—the Augustinian manuscript reads “an appearance”—“of correction. But Pope Sixtus, watchfully countering these intrigues at the urging of the deacon Leo, allowed no access to the pernicious attempts; and thus he caused all Catholics to rejoice at the defection”—the same manuscript reads “at the disclosure,” perhaps “at the overthrow”—“of the deceitful beast, as though the apostolic sword had then for the first time cut down that most arrogant heresy.”

Thus he placed an excellent final crown upon his deeds and showed himself worthy to succeed Innocent, Zosimus, Boniface, and Celestine, all of whom, with one mind, vigilantly and diligently labored to restrain the various efforts of Pelagius and his disciples.

# IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 440. VINCENT OF LÉRINS

## PROLEGOMENA

[Col. 0625]

## INFORMATION FROM GALLANDIUS

(From Gallandius, *Bibliotheca Veterum Patrum*, vol. X, Prolegomena)

[Col. 0625A]

1. Vincent, a Gaul by nationality, called Lirinensis—that is, of Lérins—in order to distinguish him from two others of the same name who flourished at the same time, professes that for some time he had been tossed about by various and grievous storms of secular service [Note: [Col. 0625C] Vincent of Lérins, *Commonitorium*, § 1, below]. But at last, entering the harbor of religion with Christ’s help, he there sought to appease God by the sacrifice of Christian humility, having laid aside the blasts of vanity and pride [Note: [Col. 0625C] The same, ibid.]. From these words our Baronius was led to the opinion [Note: [Col. 0625C] Baronius, under the year 434, § 20] that the author under discussion was that Vincent whom Sulpicius Severus mentions [Note: [Col. 0625C] Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogue* 1, chapter 26], an outstanding man distinguished by every kind of virtue, who is known to have been elevated to the prefecture of Gaul while Saint Martin was bishop of Tours. But this conjecture concerning such a great man [Col. 0625B] is less pleasing to Papebrochius [Note: [Col. 0625C] Papebrochius, *Acta Sanctorum*, May, vol. V, p. 284, no. 4], Tillemont [Note: [Col. 0625C] Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical Memoirs*, vol. XV, p. 143], and other learned writers [Note: [Col. 0625C] *Literary History of France*, vol. II, p. 305]. Moreover, others infer from a letter of Saint Eucherius to Hilary, *On the Praise of the Desert* [Note: [Col. 0625C] Eucherius, letter to Hilary, p. 562, Paris edition of 1579], that our Vincent was the biological brother of Saint Lupus, bishop of Troyes. But this opinion likewise is not approved by the learned men just mentioned—Papebrochius, I mean [Note: [Col. 0625C] Papebrochius, loc. cit., no. 2], Tillemont [Note: [Col. 0625C] Tillemont, loc. cit., p. 859, note 1, “On Vincent of Lérins”], and the authors of the literary history of Gaul [Note: [Col. 0626C] *Literary History of France*, loc. cit.]. To these must be added the editors of the works of Noris [Note: [Col. 0626C] Ballerini, in vol. IV of Noris’s works, p. 913], and above all Noris himself, who discusses the matter learnedly at length [Note: [Col. 0626C] Noris, *History of Pelagianism*, Book II, chapter 11, Works, vol. I, p. 395].

2. Accordingly, after renouncing the concerns of the world and choosing the monastic life, Vincent withdrew to the island of Lérins [Note: [Col. 0626C] Vincent of Lérins, loc. cit.]. “The place,” he says, “is that where, avoiding the crowds and disturbances of the cities, we inhabit the dwelling-place of a monastery in a more remote little estate and in its solitude” [Col. 0625C]. From these words Noris infers [Note: [Col. 0626C] Noris, loc. cit., p. 396] that Vincent was indeed a monk when he wrote his *Commonitorium*, but not a monk of Lérins, because he says that he inhabited “the dwelling-place of a monastery in a more remote little estate”; for, says the very learned man, there was no little estate on Lérins, but only monks’ cells scattered throughout the island. He therefore conjectures that Vincent lived in some monastery at Marseille, although, later moved by the authority of Gennadius, he agrees that Vincent died among the people of Lérins.

The distinguished Antelmius, however, adopted a position different from that of Noris—a position that Tillemont overlooks [Note: [Col. 0626C] Tillemont, loc. cit., p. 860, note 2]. Antelmius agrees with Noris in thinking that our author composed the *Commonitorium* outside the monastery of Lérins; but, unlike Noris, he holds that Vincent was already a monk of Lérins. For he writes as follows [Note: [Col. 0626C] Antelmius, *On the True Works of Saints Leo and Prosper*, Dissertation 9, chapter 15, p. 419]:

“Vincent, withdrawing from the monastery of Lérins into the secluded places of Capo-Fulvi Mountain”—Cap Roux, which is a promontory on the coast of Fréjus, opposite Lérins—“with great zeal for religion and the solitary life, there conceived the plan of writing and arranging the *Commonitorium*.”

So writes this learned man, and other things besides. Tillemont allows the two most learned men, Noris and Antelmius, to hold their own opinions [Note: [Col. 0626C] Tillemont, loc. cit., pp. 144 and 860]; meanwhile, himself adhering to Gennadius, he thinks that Vincent lived and wrote as a monk in the island of Lérins. The writers of the literary history of Gaul hold the same view [Note: [Col. 0626C] *Literary History of France*, vol. II, p. 306].

3. In truth, Gennadius gives the following account of our author [Note: [Col. 0626C] Gennadius, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 64]:

“Vincent, a presbyter at the monastery of the island of Lérins, a man learned in the Scriptures and sufficiently instructed in knowledge of ecclesiastical doctrines, composed, for avoiding the associations of heretics, a very powerful disputation in a sufficiently polished and clear style, which he titled under an assumed name, *Peregrinus against the Heretics*.”

This is the celebrated *Commonitorium*. As Baronius says [Note: [Col. 0626C] Baronius, under the year 434, § 20], it plainly shows how remarkable the writer’s learning was, “so that it would scarcely be possible to find anyone who enclosed greater matters in fewer pages and in a more successful treatment.” Its author therefore [Note: [Col. 0627D] Baronius, in the notes on the Martyrology, May 24] left a great reputation for his name in the Catholic Church.

Thus far the great Baronius, who elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0627D] The same, under the year 431, § 188] calls that work, written against heresies, certainly “golden.” And with excellent justice other very learned men have increased such an outstanding little book with the highest praises, as may be seen in Noris, who gathers together in a few words not only the praises of Catholics [Note: [Col. 0627D] Noris, *History of Pelagianism*, Book II, chapter 11, Works, vol. I, p. 387] but also those of non-Catholics [Note: [Col. 0627D] The same, vol. III, pp. 993 ff.]. They have called the *Commonitorium* an exceptional, golden, golden-hued, divine work—one that no Christian should ever put down from his hands, as an expression of honor.

4. Vincent himself testifies to the time when he wrote this work, when he mentions [Note: [Col. 0627D] Vincent of Lérins, *Commonitorium* 2, § 29, below] “the holy council that was held almost three years ago in Asia at Ephesus, when the illustrious men Bassus and Antiochus were consuls” [Col. 0627B]. Everyone knows that the ecumenical Synod of Ephesus was convened in the year 431; accordingly, Vincent wrote his little book in the year 434. Nor is it permissible to think that he committed this work to writing anywhere other than on the island of Lérins, as we have just learned from Gennadius. I would also like to add the testimony of Eucherius, bishop of Lyons, who addresses his son Salonius as follows [Note: [Col. 0627D] Eucherius, preface to *On the Excellence of the Old and New Testament*]:

“Scarcely ten years old, you entered the desert; among those sacred hands you were not only instructed but also nourished under that father Honoratus—first father of the islands, and afterward teacher also of the Churches—while there the teaching of the most blessed Hilary, then a novice of the island but now supreme pontiff, formed you in every discipline of spiritual matters; and afterward holy men, Salvianus and Vincent, outstanding alike in eloquence and knowledge, brought you to completion.”

There you have Vincent in the desert, that is, at Lérins, where Honoratus and Hilary were instructing Salonius in the sacred disciplines. At last this excellent man died, according to Gennadius [Note: [Col. 0627D] Gennadius, loc. cit.], while Theodosius the Younger and Valentinian III were reigning. Thus his death occurred around the year 450, when Theodosius died on July 28, in the third indiction, as Theodore the Lector records [Note: [Col. 0627D] Theodore the Lector, Book II, no. 64]. His memory is commemorated in the ecclesiastical calendars on May 24; his relics, placed in an honored location, are preserved in the monastery of Lérins [Note: [Col. 0627D] Noris, *History of Pelagianism*, Book II, chapter 11, Works, vol. I, p. 397].

5. In addition to the *Commonitorium*, many learned men also believe that our author wrote the *Vincentian Objections*, which we know Saint Prosper refuted. For this reason they maintain that Vincent was subject to a legitimate suspicion of Semi-Pelagianism; indeed, they do not regard even his *Commonitorium* as free from this stain. Among these men, to pass over others, the leading figures are Noris [Note: [Col. 0627D] The same, ibid., pp. 387 ff. and elsewhere throughout, both in the *Refutation of the Palinode* and in the Dissertation entitled *The Scruples of an Anonymous Author*, etc.], Antelmius [Note: [Col. 0627D] Antelmius, loc. cit., § 17, pp. 419 ff.], Natalis Alexander [Note: [Col. 0628D] Natalis Alexander, *Ecclesiastical History*, fifth century, part I, chapter 3, article 2 and following], Pagius [Note: [Col. 0628D] Pagius, under the year 434, §§ 16 ff.], and the editors of Noris’s works [Note: [Col. 0628D] Ballerini, *Observations*, Book I, chapter 6, no. 3, in vol. IV of Noris’s works, p. 912].

On the other hand, Baronius above all vindicates Vincent from this charge [Note: [Col. 0628D] Baronius, under the year 431, § 188, and in the notes on the Martyrology, May 24], as do Labbeus [Note: [Col. 0628D] Labbeus, *Dissertation on Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. II, p. 489], Papebrochius [Note: [Col. 0628D] Papebrochius, *Acta Sanctorum*, May, vol. V, p. 285, nos. 6 ff.], and the writers of the literary history of Gaul [Note: [Col. 0628D] *Literary History of France*, vol. II, p. 309]. Tillemont is not far from their position [Note: [Col. 0628D] Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical Memoirs*, vol. XV, p. 860, note 3].

Whatever the case may be, “we do no injury,” says Noris [Note: [Col. 0628D] Noris, loc. cit., vol. I, pp. 397 ff.], “either to Vincent’s learning or to his holiness when we reckon him among those men of Marseille who are commonly called Semi-Pelagians. For at that time they were not heretics, but very learned and very holy men, whom Saint Augustine called ‘his brothers and beloved ones’ [Note: [Col. 0628D] Augustine, *On the Gift of Perseverance*, at the end, and *On the Predestination of the Saints*, beginning and chapter 14]; while Prosper, although otherwise their enemy, called them holy men, distinguished by honors and merits, and outstanding in the pursuit of every virtue, as a mark of respect [Note: [Col. 0628D] Prosper, letter to Augustine]. Who does not know that Hilary of Arles, John Cassian, and Faustus of Riez were still held in great esteem throughout Gaul while alive, and, after their deaths, were venerated as saints at Arles, Marseille, and Riez, although they were nevertheless teachers of the Semi-Pelagian school? At that time they departed from Augustine’s position in the controversy over predestination, when it was permissible to dispute that matter on either side. Only a hundred years after Augustine’s death was the opinion of the holy doctor included among the canons of the Synod of Orange … Therefore, since in the opinion of almost everyone Augustine’s teaching concerning effective election to initial grace was thought contrary to the opinion of the Fathers and to ecclesiastical understanding, as Prosper testifies in his letter to that same holy doctor, and since, apart from a few, the rest conspired against him with one accord, what wonder if Vincent—who throughout that most learned and elegant volume presses only this point, namely, that the common opinion should be preferred to private little opinions, to use his own words—thought that in the controversy common among the doctors of Gaul one ought to adhere to the common judgment, abandoning the opinion of the African Augustine, which was thought new and contrary to the opinion of the Fathers and to ecclesiastical understanding?

“I have pursued these matters at greater length in order to satisfy the complaints of certain people [Col. 0629A] who think that the man who places Vincent of Lérins, a father of exceptional learning and holiness, in the ranks of the men of Marseille is bound by a grave offense, as though the Semi-Pelagians of that time had been heretics rather than men who, above all others in Gaul, were most learned and most holy.”

Thus far this outstanding man, who elsewhere also argues most effectively against Blondel [Note: [Col. 0629B] Blondel, *On Primacy in the Church*, section 6, p. 52, edition of 1641] [Note: [Col. 0629B] Noris, works, vol. III, pp. 1010 ff.] that Vincent was rightly entered by the Church in the rolls of the saints.

6. Not only did the critical scholars mentioned above attribute the *Vincentian Objections* to our author; the distinguished Antelmius also attempted, by various arguments, to assert that the *Quicumque* Creed belonged to him. Among these arguments, one of some weight seems to be that the learned man derives from certain formulas of speech a great similarity to some passages of the Creed [Col. 0629B], which he collected from Vincent’s *Commonitorium*. The distinguished Montfaucon reports and examines these [Note: [Col. 0630B] Montfaucon, *Dissertation on the Quicumque Creed*, in the works of Athanasius, vol. II, p. 724 ff.], and says that the arguments of learned men establish quite satisfactorily that nothing prevents the Creed from being a work of Vincent of Lérins, provided that some definite evidence from a manuscript or from a writer could otherwise be supplied in Vincent’s favor.

But enough of this. Nothing further remains for us to add concerning our author except a notice about the edition that we used in printing his *Commonitorium*. We used the edition that Étienne Baluze published for the third time at Paris in 1684, superior to the others. He first compared the little work with two manuscript codices of the Royal Library; afterward he examined it again against two others, both extremely ancient. One of these, now preserved in the Colbert Library, formerly belonged to Pierre Pithou; the other belonged to the celebrated monastery of Corbie. We added Baluze’s notes, whose principal purpose is to indicate variant readings, to the text, placing a few notes, as is our custom, at the foot of the pages.

[Col. 0629]

## INFORMATION FROM SCHOENEMANN

(From Schoenemann, *Bibliotheca Historica-Litteraria Patrum*, vol. II)

### § I. Life of Vincent of Lérins

[Col. 0629B]

Lirinensis was given as his cognomen so that he might be distinguished from other writers of the same name and period, after the island in which he devoted the greater part of his life to monastic studies. Few and insufficiently certain details about his origin and status have been handed down [Col. 0629C]. He was born in Celtic or Belgic Gaul; and if that Lupus of Troyes was truly his brother—which, however, the most learned historians of both men deny [Note: *Hist. Litt. de la France*, vol. II, p. 305]—he had Toul in the territory of the Leuci as his homeland. We do not know when he first renounced the world and withdrew to the island, or when and where he attained the dignity of the presbyterate. It must nevertheless have happened early, since Eucherius says of him that together with Salvianus he completed the education of his son Salonius, who had begun to be instructed by the abbot Honoratus; his death is assigned to the year 450.

## II. The Writings of Vincent of Lérins

“He composed, to overthrow the schools of heretics, a very powerful disputation in polished and lucid language, which he entitled, concealing his own name, *Peregrinus, Against the Heretics*. Since certain persons stole and he lost the greater part of the second book of this work in written sheets, he summarized its meaning in a few words and compiled it into a single book, which he published.” Thus Gennadius, chapter 64.

This little work survives, entitled *Commonitorium*, or *Two Commonitories Concerning the Antiquity and Universality of the Catholic Faith against the Profane Innovations of All Heretics*. It is certain, however, that neither the name *Peregrinus* nor the title *Commonitorium* originated with the author himself, but was taken from the preface to the book.

Much has been debated by modern writers, beginning with Vossius and Norisius, concerning Vincent’s Semi-Pelagianism and his alleged endeavor to represent Augustine’s doctrine of grace as heretical [Col. 0629C]. Some have even thought that they could discern in him the specific purpose of this work, and have carefully marked all the passages consonant with Semi-Pelagianism. For these passages, as well as for the arguments advanced by others against that interpretation, it is preferable to consult Oudinus [Note: *Dissertatio de Vincentio*, chapters 2, 3, and following, vol. I, pp. 1234–45. Compare the authors of *Hist. litt. Galliae*, vol. II, p. [Col. 0630D] 309, who by no means agree with those who detect the odor of Pelagianism].

For nearly the same reason, those *Vincentian Objections* against Augustine’s doctrine began to be attributed to Vincent. Prosper attacked them with particular vigor in his book *Response to the Chapters of the Vincentian Objections*; for nearly the same reason the work *Praedestinatus*, which Jacques Sirmond published at Paris in 1643, also began to be attributed to Vincent. But apart from a slight similarity of name in the one case and of doctrine in both cases to the suspicion of Semi-Pelagianism concerning Vincent, all the other arguments fail [Note: On these matters Oudinus should also be consulted, chapters 4 and 5].

## III. Editions, Translations, and Manuscripts of the Works of Vincent of Lérins

### Editions

As soon as Vincent’s *Commonitorium* came forth from its author’s hands, it immediately found numerous readers, and thereafter throughout every age frequent readers and admirers among those readers. Not without reason. For this author possesses a certain acumen—although at times false and foolish—and a concise style of expression, vivid through frequent questions and a certain confidence in teaching and answering. This could easily hold the attention of many people, each of whom brought his own opinion to the reading.

This was doubtless also why, in more recent times, it found admirers and praisers among learned men of both the highest and lowest ranks in both Churches, and why it was employed by each side to convict the other of error. Since it first appeared in print in 1528, issued by Johann Sichard in the *Antidote against All Heresies*, though it is uncertain from what source, it was printed so frequently throughout that century and nearly half of the next that the rivalry of readers seems to have destroyed the desire—which could not fail to arise among many somewhat more learned men—to read it in an emended form.

Indeed, from the immense multitude of editions printed almost every year until 1663, especially at Basel [Col. 0631B], Paris, Cologne, Louvain, and other places and countries, only a few deserve mention for the critical or other editorial work applied to them. Two were based on a more accurate text: one by Pierre Pithou, produced at Paris in 1586, in quarto; the other by Bartholomew Peter, issued at Douai in 1611, in sextodecimo, with notes by the same author. Besides these were the Costerian edition, published at Louvain in 1552, in quarto, because of its brief commentary; that of Johann Filesac, Paris, 1619, in quarto; and the Calixtine edition, Helmstedt, 1629 and 1655, because of the policy of its editor, famous in many respects.

I call these editions notable, of course, in honor of their editors, who were certainly not to blame if later editions failed to profit from them. We know of no one of these that was reprinted with a particular purpose, and only the Costerian edition—or rather Coster’s commentary—was repeated ten or more times.

Far more distinguished was the work of Stephen Baluzius, who presented Vincent, revised against the manuscripts of the Royal Library of Paris and supplied with learned notes, to the republic of letters together with Salvianus in 1663, again in 1669, and for the third time, revised and enlarged, in 1684. The Baluzius edition was reprinted at Cambridge in 1687, Bremen in 1688, Rome in 1709, and more recently by Gallandius. Nor does Salinasius’s edition of 1731 contain anything praiseworthy apart from the Baluzius text.

The evidence may be taken from the following chronological list of editions.

### The Sixteenth Century

**1528.** Basel, printed by Heinrich Petri; folio. *Vincent of Lérins, a Gaul, Concerning the Antiquity and Universality of the Catholic Faith, against the Profane Innovations of All Heresies*, in Johann Sichard’s *Antidote against the Diverse Heresies of Nearly All Centuries*, fols. 202–214.

**1543.** Lyon, at the house of Jacques Gazel; octavo. The same book. Benedictines, in *Hist. litt. Galliae*.

**1544.** Paris, at the same bookseller; octavo. *The Book of Vincent of Lérins, a Gaul, Concerning the Antiquity and Universality of the Catholic Faith, against the Profane Innovations of All Heresies; also One Book of Quintus Septimius Florens Tertullian, Concerning the Prescriptions against Heretics*. Second edition. Catalogue of the Royal Library of Paris.

**1547.** In the same place, at the same bookseller; octavo. *The Book of Vincent of Lérins concerning the Catholic Faith …* The Benedictines’ catalogue, at the cited place, reports it as printed at Venice by Jacques Gazel. In one or the other account there must be an error, either in the place or in the bookseller’s name. The same catalogue, when it adds that it was first published at Venice—whether on its own authority or, more probably, from the title of the book—misled the Benedictines into inventing a first edition of Vincent produced at Venice in an uncertain year.

**1552.** Venice, at the Sign of Hope; octavo. *The Little Book of Vincent … Concerning the Truth and Antiquity of the Catholic Faith*, etc. Catalogue of the Royal Library of Paris. The Benedictines say that Johann Cochlaeus’s dissertation *Concerning Vows* was included with it.

**1552.** Louvain, at the house of Anthony Maria Bergagne; quarto. *The Most Elegant Book of Vincent of Lérins, a Gaul, Concerning the Antiquity and Truth of the Catholic Faith, against the Profane Innovations of All Heresies, Written by the Author a Thousand Years Ago*. A brief commentary was added, chiefly for the benefit of those less practiced in the divine writings, by Johann Costerus. The image of a leopard on the title page is undoubtedly the printer’s device.

**1554.** Reims, at the house of Nicholas Bacnetius; quarto. The same book. Catalogue of the Tellier Library, at the cited place.

**1554.** Cologne … twenty-fourmo. The same book with the same commentary. Catalogue of the Baluzius Library, vol. II, p. 1001.

**1556.** Basel, at the house of Heinrich Petri; folio. *Vincent … Concerning the Antiquity and Universality of the Catholic Faith*, etc., in Johann Herold’s *Hæresiologia*, pp. 643–663.

**1560.** Paris, at the house of Johann Foucher, Jacobaea Street, under the shield of Florence; sextodecimo. *The Most Elegant Book of Vincent … Concerning the Antiquity and Truth of the Catholic Faith, against the Profane Innovations of All Heresies, Written by the Author a Thousand Years Ago*. With a brief commentary added at the end by Johann Costerus. The catalogue of the Barberini Library mentions an edition of this year produced at Cologne, in duodecimo.

**1561.** Paris, at the house of … Buon; duodecimo. *Vincent … Concerning the Antiquity of the Catholic Faith*, etc., together with Cardinal Stanislaus Hosius’s dialogue *Concerning Communion in the Eucharist under Both Species; the Marriage of Priests; and the Celebration of the Mass in the Vernacular*. The Benedictines praise this edition, though I do not know how accurately. Certainly some error has arisen from confusion with the following edition.

**1562.** Paris, at the house of Johann Foucher; duodecimo. *The Book of Vincent … Concerning the Antiquity of the Catholic Faith*, etc. Reprinted from the 1560 edition. In the same place and year, in the same format, but not printed together with Vincent, was Stanislaus Hosius’s *Little Book Concerning the Express Word of God*, newly enlarged and revised, together with the little books named shortly before.

**1562.** Louvain; duodecimo. The same book with the same commentary. Catalogue of the Baluzius Library, vol. II, p. 1000.

**1568.** Louvain, at the house of Johann Bogard; duodecimo. The same book, and perhaps also the commentary. Benedictines and Ceillier, vol. XIII, p. 582.

**1569.** Cologne, at the house of Maternus Cholinus; duodecimo. The same book with Coster’s commentary. Possevinus, appendix, vol. III, p. 353.

**1569.** Paris, at the house of Michael Julianus; octavo. The same book, undoubtedly with the same commentary. Catalogue of the Bodleian Library.

**1575.** Paris, at the house of Michael Sonnius; folio. *Vincent … Commonitorium for the Catholic Faith against Heresies*, in the fifth volume of the *Library of the Fathers* published by Bigne. I cite the title from Ittigius.

**1585.** Lyon, at the house of Guillaume Roville; duodecimo. *Vincent … The Book Concerning the Catholic Faith*, with the works of Dionysius the Areopagite and the letters of Saints Ignatius, Polycarp, and Martial. Benedictines.

**1586.** Paris, at the house of Sebastian Nivellius; quarto. *Two Commonitories of Peregrinus Concerning the Antiquity and Universality of the Catholic Faith against the Profane Innovations of All Heretics*, in *The Writings of Several Ancient Theologians of Gaul* edited by Pithou, pp. 1–76. The title adds that, among the little works contained in this volume, some are printed more accurately from ancient books and some for the first time [Col. 0633B]. Since there is no room in the volume for a preface or other declaration, these notices must serve, together with the author’s name, as a recommendation.

**1589.** Cologne, at the house of … Herstius; duodecimo. *Vincent … The Book Concerning the Antiquity of the Catholic Faith*, etc. Benedictines, from Possevinus.

**1589.** Paris; folio. *Vincent of Lérins, Concerning Heresies*, in volume IV of the second edition of Bigne’s *Library of the Fathers*.

**1591.** London; octavo. *Vincent … The Book Concerning the Antiquity of the Catholic Faith*, etc. Catalogue of the Bodleian Library.

**1591.** Prague, printed by Michael Petrelius; duodecimo. *Vincent’s Little Book Concerning the Antiquity and Truth of the Catholic Faith, against the Profane Innovations of All Heresies*, with the marginal notes of Johann Langius. Catalogue of the Bunau Library.

**1594.** Cologne; duodecimo. *Vincent … The Book Concerning the Antiquity of the Catholic Faith*, with Various Notes by Learned Men. Catalogue of the Barberini Library.

**1600.** Cologne, in the Birkmann printing house; duodecimo. *The Little Book of Saint Vincent of Lérins against the Profane Innovations of Heresies*, with the scholia and commentaries of Johann Costerus; also Edmund Campion’s ten reasons for the proposed disputation in the cause of the faith, delivered to the academicians of England, by Edmund Campion, S.J., who was killed in England for the Catholic religion. Catalogue of the Royal Library of Paris.

### The Seventeenth Century

**1605.** Kraków; sextodecimo. *The Truly Golden Little Book of Vincent of Lérins, a Gaul, against the Profane Innovations of Heresies*, divided into chapters and illustrated with brief notes from the commentaries of Johann Costerus.

**1611.** Douai, at the house of Marcus Wyon; sextodecimo. *Vincent … against the Profane Innovations of Heresies*, with a brief commentary by Johann Costerus, brief notes by Bartholomew Peter, and an apologetic dissertation concerning Vincent and his writings. Cave, vol. I, p. 425, new Oxford edition.

The Benedictines note that Bartholomew Peter supplied a text of Vincent revised against two ancient manuscripts for transcription.

**1613.** Cologne; sextodecimo. The same book with the commentaries of Johann Costerus. Cave.

**1613.** Lyon … *Vincent of Lérins, Concerning the Antiquity of the Catholic Faith, against the Innovations of Heresies*, with the notes of Johann Costerus, in *Chronology of the Saints and Other Illustrious Men and Abbots of the Holy Island of Lérins*, compiled into one volume by Vincent Barrali, a monk of Lérins from Salerno.

**1618.** Cologne, at the house of Anthony Hierat; folio. *Vincent of Lérins, Concerning the Profane Innovations of Words*, in the *Great Library of the Fathers*, vol. V, part II.

**1619.** Paris, at the house of Dionysius Langlois; quarto. *Two Commonitories of Vincent of Lérins, a Monk, or Peregrinus*, with the commentaries of Johann Filesac. Catalogue of the Royal Library of Paris.

**1622.** Lyon, at the expense of Claude Landry; duodecimo. *Vincent … Concerning the Antiquity and Universality of the Catholic Faith*, etc., pp. 65–131, in a book entitled *Sandapila Silicernio*—“a bier for a funeral feast”—for bearing the Fifth and Sixth Gospel on the shoulders and by the exertions of four most powerful bearers. The first two bearers are Tertullian, in his book *Concerning Prescriptions*, and Vincent of Lérins, in his *Commonitorium against Heresies*. The other two are Edmund Campion of the Society of Jesus, the most glorious martyr of Christ, in his *Book of Reasons Offered to the Academicians of Oxford*, and Leonard Lessius of the same Society, in his *Consultation Concerning Religion*.

The preface to this little work explains the subtleties of the title at greater length and readily reveals from what school the editor drew these elegant conceits.

**1624.** Paris; folio. The same book of Vincent, in volume IV of the *Library of the Fathers*.

**1629.** Helmstedt, at the Julia Academy, from the Calixtine press, printed by Henning Müller; octavo. *The Commonitorium of Vincent of Lérins*, revised and published by George Calixtus, together with Augustine’s four books *On Christian Doctrine* and *On Faith and the Creed*. Its particular title is: *The Two Commonitories of Peregrinus, or Vincent of Lérins, Concerning the Antiquity and Universality of the Catholic Faith against the Profane Innovations of All Heresies*, though the latter of them has been lost for the greater part.

Most of the preface to the reader concerns Vincent’s book. It carefully explains his opinions and rule, and chiefly endeavors to show what ought to be understood by the term heresy and what constitutes the agreement of the Churches in one doctrine. From this standpoint he directs his pen against Catholic teachings concerning tradition and also concerning authority and infallibility [Col. 0634D], and concludes by explaining how the Jesuits had then begun to abuse these matters to the detriment of the commonwealth and of all authorities.

**1631.** Oxford; twenty-fourmo. *Two Commonitories of Peregrinus—that is, as he is commonly called, Vincent of Lérins—against Profane Heresies*. Augustine’s book *Concerning Heresies* is added, in a purified edition more accurate than the others. Catalogue of the Royal Library of Paris.

**1644.** Paris; folio. *Vincent of Lérins, Concerning Heresies*, in volume IV, part I, of the *Library of the Fathers*. As we have often noted, this edition differs from that of 1654 only in its title.

**1655.** Helmstedt, from the Calixtine press, through the work of Henning Müller; quarto. *The Commonitorium of Vincent of Lérins*, revised and published by George Calixtus. Second edition.

At the end of this edition there was added a new discussion by the editor, entitled *Admonition to the Reader*. At the beginning he explains how, twenty-six years earlier, he had first been led to publish Vincent:

“Since at that time the papists were occupying the monasteries and ecclesiastical benefices in this and the neighboring provinces, expelling our people and attempting to implant their new doctrines in the minds of certain persons willing to lend them their ears, it occurred to me that Vincent’s *Commonitorium*, published under the name of Peregrinus, seriously and sternly rejects every novelty concerning doctrines necessary for salvation and judges that only what rests upon the testimony of antiquity should be admitted—that is, what, as he says, was received universally in ancient times. It also occurred to me that the more recent papist writers whom I remembered having read, and who were among the principal ones, highly praised and approved Vincent’s doctrine. Accordingly, I thought I would act rightly if I opposed papist innovations with this work, so firmly attached to antiquity and so greatly approved by its adversaries.”

How he did this has been explained above.

**1663.** Paris, at the house of François Muguet; octavo. *The Commonitorium of Vincent of Lérins*, emended by Stephen Baluzius according to the evidence of manuscripts and illustrated with notes, together with Salvianus.

He used two manuscripts of the Royal Library of Paris and added a few notes; concerning these, see the notes to Salvianus.

**1664.** Ratzeburg, through Nicholas Nissen; duodecimo. *Vincent of Lérins, Concerning the Antiquity of the Catholic Faith*, etc. Catalogue of the Bunau Library.

**1669.** Paris, at the house of François Muguet; octavo. *The Commonitorium of Vincent of Lérins from the Second Edition of Baluzius*.

**1677.** Lyon, at the house of the Anissons; folio. *Vincent’s Commonitorium against Heresies*, in volume VII of the *Greatest Library of the Fathers*, pp. 249–263.

**1684.** Paris, at the house of François Muguet; octavo. *The Commonitorium of Vincent of Lérins from the Third Edition of Stephen Baluzius*, together with Salvianus.

He revised and frequently altered the text of the earlier editions and added fuller notes.

**1687.** Cambridge, from the press of John Hayes, at the expense of William Graves; duodecimo. *The Commonitorium of Vincent of Lérins against the Profane Innovations of All Heretics*, with the notes of the learned Stephen Baluzius. Augustine’s *Book Concerning Heresies* is added.

A very long preface precedes it. An appendix of the acts against Pelagius and Coelestius is added to the notes. See Salvianus.

**1688.** Bremen, at the expense of Hermann Braver; quarto. *The Commonitorium of Vincent of Lérins, revised and illustrated by Baluzius of Tulle according to ancient manuscript codices*. A dissertation by George Calixtus concerning Vincent, etc., precedes it, together with the works of Salvianus.

Calixtus’s dissertation was taken from his preface.

### The Eighteenth Century

**1709.** Rome, from the printing house of the Sacred Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith; octavo. *The Commonitorium of Vincent of Lérins*, in the first volume of Joseph Tommasius’s *Theological Institutions of the Ancient Fathers*, pp. 193–275. The same books were reprinted there in 1746 in the same number of volumes.

The late C. A. Heumann added several remarks to our library’s copy, among which the following are worth noting:

“In this little book Vincent endeavors with all his strength to establish a prejudgment in favor of authority and strives to deprive human beings of every use of reason in sacred matters, commending altogether an ἄλογος λατρεία, an irrational worship. He therefore acts here not as a defender of truth but of error. It belongs to error to seek concealment beneath the shadow of authority and antiquity. Truth shines by its own light and offers itself to be seen and examined by everyone at every time. If you examine good gold six hundred times, you will always find it good gold. So too, after a thousand examinations, truth remains truth; and just as an arithmetician never proves the truth of his calculation by the agreement of other arithmeticians, but cries out, ‘Prove it, examine it,’ so also does truth.”

He likewise noted how greatly Daniel Whitby despised this work in the preface to his book *Concerning the Commentaries of the Fathers on Holy Scripture*.

**1731.** Rome, printed by Johann Zempel near the Jordan Gate; octavo. *The Works of Saints Vincent of Lérins and Hilary of Arles, Revised against Distinguished Manuscript Codices and Editions and Illustrated with Notes and Observations, by Don Johann Salinas of Naples, Canon Regular of the Lateran and Lecturer in Sacred Theology, addressed to the Most Holy Father Clement XII, Supreme Pontiff*.

He did not, strictly speaking, revise Vincent’s work anew, but reproduced the Baluzius edition of 1669. For he did not know the third edition, nor had he any knowledge of the other editions except through Labbeus and Cave. Indeed, he explicitly cites more than one edition in whose year there is an error.

“We have added,” he says, “notes and observations of such a kind as required labor and diligence [sic]. Whether they may afterward be of any use, I do not dare to say, and I willingly submit them to the judgment of the fair-minded reader. Although the division into chapters was removed by Baluzius, it appeared just and reasonable to retain it with the other editors [sic], and in my judgment not entirely useless. Concerning the doctrine of the holy man,” he continues, “with regard to traditions, we shall discuss elsewhere against Johann Dallaeus and George Calixtus, a man of the Lutheran family, who died at Helmstedt!”

In the same style and spirit he composed the notes immediately following.

**1774.** Venice, at the house of Johann Baptist Albritius; folio. *The Commonitorium of Vincent of Lérins, reproduced according to the third edition of Stephen Baluzius with the notes of the same*, in volume X of Andrea Gallandi’s *Library of the Fathers and Holy Writers of the Ancient Church*, pp. 103–121.

He added a few observations of his own at the bottom margin of the page and prefixed a dissertation concerning Vincent in the *Prolegomena*, chapter II, pp. IV–VI.

### Translations

No less energetically than learned and unlearned men in the preceding two centuries had labored to multiply Vincent’s text in print did others labor to teach him to speak in some more modern language. The first example, as far as I know, was English; but the French produced the greatest number and the best translations, as the following list will show.

#### 1. English

**1554.** London, by Robert Caly; octavo. *The Way Home to Christ and Truth, Leading from Antichrist and Error, Made and Set Forth in the Latin Tongue by That Famous and Great Scholar Vincent.* Or: *The Return to Christ, Composed by Doctor Vincent of Lérins, a Frenchman by Nation, and Translated into English*. Catalogue of the Royal Library of Paris, from which the following entries were also taken.

#### 2. French

**1560.** Paris, at the house of M. Vascosan; octavo. *Treatise of Vincent of Lérins Concerning the Truth and Antiquity of the Catholic Faith against the Profane Innovations of All Heresies, Translated from Latin into French by G. Ruzé*.

**1580.** Paris, at the house of Federic Morel; octavo. The same translation.

**1615.** Paris, at the house of Jean de Heuqueville; octavo. *Vincent of Lérins against Heresies, with Two Letters, One of Saint Cyprian and the Other of Saint Jerome; All Translated into French by Monsieur de la Brosse*.

**1684.** Paris, at the house of Christophe Journel; duodecimo. *The Admonitions of Vincent of Lérins Concerning the Antiquity and Universality of the Catholic Faith against the Profane Innovations of All Heretics, Translated into French with Remarks by de Frontignières*.

#### 3. Italian

**1565.** Mondovì, at the house of Leonardo Torrentino; octavo. *The Book of Vincent of Lérins against the Profane Innovations of All Heresies, Translated into Italian by Girolamo Muzio of Justinopolis*. Argelati, *Library of Vernacular Translations*, vol. IV, p. 109.

### Manuscripts

From what has been noted above, it will be clear that only four editors of Vincent consulted manuscript copies: Johann Sichard, Pierre Pithou, Bartholomew Peter, and—about the first three of whom we have no further information—Baluzius, who was the last. Baluzius possessed two: one from the Colbert Library, the same manuscript that had belonged to Pithou, and the other from the monastery of Corbie.

[Col. 0637]

# TWO COMMONITORIES [C]

## THE FIRST COMMONITORIUM OF SAINT VINCENT OF LÉRINS

*(From the edition of Baluzius)*

### THE TREATISE OF PEREGRINUS BEGINS [Note: Baluzius and Joseph Antelmius report that this heading was found in three manuscripts of the Royal Library, with the words “a Gaul by nation” removed, although these appear in the older editions. I suspect, with Costerus, that the title prefixed to the work by Lérins was: *The Commonitorium of Peregrinus against the Heretics*, just as Tertullian entitled his golden work—on which Vincent drew no little—*Concerning Prescriptions against Heretics*. Gennadius supports this view when he says that Vincent “composed a disputation which he entitled, concealing his name,” or, as the Corbie Codex reads, “entitled *Peregrinus against the Heretics*.” This is especially likely because, among the ancients, the term *treatise* generally referred not to disputations against heretics but to sermons delivered to the people. Thus our author says in chapter 40 of the *Commonitorium*: “Thirdly he appointed teachers, who are now called Treatise-writers, because through them the mysteries of the prophets are opened to the people.”]

Concerning the Antiquity and Universality of the Catholic Faith against the Profane Innovations of All Heretics.

## I

Scripture says and admonishes us: “Ask your fathers, and they will tell you; your elders, and they will declare it to you” (Deut. 32); likewise, “Incline your ear to the words of the wise” (Ecclus. 6); and again, “My son, do not forget these sayings, but let your heart keep my words” (Prov. 3).

It seems to me, Peregrinus, the least of all the servants of God, that it would be no small and useful undertaking, with the Lord’s help, to commit to writing the things that I have faithfully received from the holy Fathers. This would certainly be very necessary for my own weakness, since it would provide a ready means by which the frailty of my memory might be restored through continual reading.

I am encouraged to undertake this task not only by the fruit of the work itself but also by consideration of the time and the suitability of the place.

The time: because, since all human things are carried away by time, we too ought in return to snatch from it something that may advance us toward eternal life. Especially since the terrifying expectation of the approaching divine Judgment demands that our religious efforts be increased, and the deceitfulness of the new heretics calls for great care and attention.

The place [Note: The island of Lerina, or Lirinus, lies at latitude 43° 30′ 6″ and longitude 24° 42′ 55″. Lerina is now called the island of Saint Honoratus, who was the founder and originator of the once most famous monastery in all Gaul situated on that island]: we inhabit a more remote little settlement and, in it, the secluded dwelling of a monastery, avoiding the crowds and commotion of cities. There, without great distraction, what is sung in the Psalm can be carried out: “Be still, and know that I am God” (Ps. 45).

The nature of our purpose also agrees with this. For after we had for some time been tossed about by the various and sorrowful storms of worldly service, at last, with Christ breathing upon us, we cast anchor in the harbor of religion, always the most trustworthy of all harbors. There, laying aside the winds of vanity and pride, and appeasing God with the sacrifice of Christian humility, we may avoid not only the shipwrecks of the present life but also the fires of the age to come.

But now, in the name of the Lord, I shall undertake what lies before me: namely, to describe what has been handed down by our ancestors and entrusted to us, with the faithfulness of a reporter rather than the presumption of an author. I shall observe this rule of writing, however: I will not touch upon everything, but only upon what is necessary; nor will I do so in an ornate and polished style, but in an easy and ordinary manner, so that most things may appear indicated rather than explained.

Let those write elegantly and accurately who are led to this task either by confidence in their abilities or by the requirements of their office. For myself, it will be enough, for the sake of relieving my memory—or rather my forgetfulness—to prepare this *Commonitorium* [Note: In Vincent’s time the word *Commonitorium* was in use both for written instructions given to envoys—for example, the *Commonitorium* given by Theodosius to Count Elpidius when he was going to Ephesus for the synod, and another entrusted by Zosimus to Faustinus when he was sent to Africa—and, more frequently, for a rule prescribed by one giving orders, which the recipient was to carry out, as is clear from Pope Innocent’s letter concerning John Chrysostom. Here, as Baluzius correctly observes in his notes, it signifies a kind of writing such as memoranda, intended to assist the memory]. I shall nevertheless try, day by day, with the Lord’s assistance, gradually to correct and complete it by recalling what I have learned.

I have given this warning beforehand so that, if what has escaped me should come into the hands of the holy, they may not rashly criticize anything in it that they still see requires polishing in accordance with the promised revision.

## II

Often, therefore, as I sought with great zeal and the utmost attention to learn from very many men distinguished in holiness and learning how I might distinguish, by some definite and as it were general and regular method, the truth of the Catholic faith from the falsehood of heretical depravity, I almost always received from them an answer of the following kind:

Whether I or anyone else wished to detect the frauds of rising heretics, avoid their snares, and remain sound and whole in the sound faith, we ought, with the Lord’s help, to fortify our faith in two ways: first, by the authority of the divine law, and then by the tradition of the Catholic Church.

Someone may perhaps ask: Since the canon of the Scriptures is perfect and more than sufficient in itself for every matter, what need is there to add to it the authority of ecclesiastical interpretation?

Because, owing to the very loftiness of Holy Scripture, not everyone understands it in one and the same sense. One person interprets its words one way, another differently, so that almost as many opinions seem capable of being drawn from it as there are people. Novatian explains it one way, Sabellius another, Donatus another; Arius, Eunomius, and Macedonius each in another way; Photinus, Apollinaris, and Priscillianus in another; Jovinianus, Pelagius, and Caelestius in another; and finally Nestorius in another.

For that reason, amid so many winding paths of such varied error, it is greatly necessary that the line of prophetic and apostolic interpretation be directed according to the standard of ecclesiastical and Catholic meaning.

Within the Catholic Church itself, we must take the greatest care to hold what has been believed everywhere, always, and by all. For this is truly and properly Catholic, as the force and meaning of the name itself indicate, since it embraces almost everything universally [Note: The Fathers used the distinctive meaning of the name “Catholic” to refute heretics, since according to the prophecies the Church was to be spread throughout the world and not confined to a corner of a small region or to a fragment of the earth. Otherwise, as Optatus rightly argues in book 2, chapter 1 of *Against the Donatist Schism*: “Where will the distinctive character of the name Catholic be, since it was called Catholic because it is rational and spread everywhere?” Because this name is honorable and embraces the hope of salvation, the heretics begrudge it to us and attempt to take it away, just as the apostate Julian once begrudged Christians the name Christian. Augustine sharply demonstrates from the very mind of the heretics that it belongs to the sons of the Roman Church, in book 75 of the *Unfinished Work*: “The Arians,” he says, “call the Athanasians, or Homousians, Catholics; other heretics do not. But you are called Pelagians not only by Catholics but also by heretics who disagree with you and resemble you, just as the Arians are called so not only by Catholics but also by heresies. You alone call us Traducians, just as they call us Homousians, the Donatists call us Macarians, the Manichaeans Pharisees, and the other heretics call us by different names. Nor should it be surprising that the new heretics impose a new name on the Catholics from whom they depart—as has also pleased the vanity of the heretics of our own age. For others did the same when they similarly departed.”]

But this will happen only if we follow universality, antiquity, and agreement.

We shall follow universality in this way: if we confess that this faith alone is true which the Church throughout the whole world confesses.

We shall follow antiquity in this way: if we in no respect depart from those understandings that it is clear our holy ancestors and fathers upheld.

We shall follow agreement in this way: if, within antiquity itself, we follow the definitions and opinions of all, or certainly almost all, priests and teachers alike.

## III

What, then, will a Catholic Christian do if some portion of the Church cuts itself off from communion with the universal faith? What else, surely, than prefer the health of the whole body to a diseased and corrupted limb?

What if some new contagion attempts to defile not merely a small part but the whole Church at once? Then likewise he will take care to cling to antiquity, which can no longer be seduced by any fraud of novelty.

What if, within antiquity itself, an error is discovered belonging to two or three men, or certainly to a single city or even a province? Then he will take every care to set against the rashness or ignorance of the few, if such there be, the universally ancient decrees of the universal Church [Note: The ancient Royal Codex reads, “the decrees of the Universal Council.” Baluzius].

What if something of this kind should arise in a matter for which no such precedent can be found? Then he will make every effort to consult and question the opinions of the ancestors, at least those who, although living at different times and in different places, remained in the communion and faith of the one Catholic Church and proved themselves approved teachers.

Whatever he discovers that not merely one or two, but all alike, with one and the same agreement, have clearly, frequently, and steadfastly held, written, and taught, he should understand that he too must believe without any hesitation.

## IV

But in order to make what we are saying clearer, these matters must be illustrated individually with examples and developed somewhat more fully, lest the weight of the subject be carried away by the rapidity produced by excessive brevity.

In the time of Donatus [Note: Here Vincentius means Donatus Magnus, from whom the Donatists were named; this is proved by the clear testimony of Optatus in the Life of Saint Possidius. The reader should consult that passage. It must nevertheless be observed that, long after the schism had begun, his followers were called Donatists, whereas at first they were called followers of Majorinus. Thus, in the report of Anulinus, Proconsul, to Constantine, we read: “A libellus of the Catholic Church accusing Caecilianus was delivered by the party of Majorinus.” Likewise, when Augustine speaks of the libellus, he says that it was brought by the party of Majorinus. But since around A.D. 370 people were already speaking of “the party of Donatus”—“as though,” says Optatus, “he had divided the people from God, so that he might boldly call it his party”—this holy man, in book 3 of On the Donatist Schism, no. 3, discussing the libellus that Capito, Nasucius, Dignus, and the other bishops gave to Constantine, calls them “of Donatus’s party,” not “of Majorinus’s,” perhaps substituting the better-known name for the older one. Nevertheless, we must honestly acknowledge Optatus’s mistake: from that libellus he infers that Donatus Magnus was proscribed at Rome by Miltiades and at the council celebrated by him, although at the Conference the Catholic bishops admitted that Donatus had been condemned at Casae Nigrae. See Augustine, Brief Account of the Conference, day 3, chapters 12 and 17, and Retractions, chapter 21.] [Note: [Cols. 0641–0642] In the fourth century, according to Optatus, the Catholics were more numerous in Africa; for in book 2, no. 1, he scarcely grants the Donatists even a small portion, saying: “Therefore, if the Church can be among you in a small part of Africa, in a corner of a small region, will it not be among us in another part of Africa?” Yet as that century declined and drew to its close, the schismatics were far more numerous, as Possidius reports in chapter 7 of the Life of Augustine: “Through that holy man the Catholic Church in Africa began to lift its head, though it lay deceived and oppressed by Donatus’s rebaptizing party, which comprised the larger multitude of Africans.” I suspect that the faction grew in this way because, within the space of a century, scarcely one or two men—namely Optatus and Augustine—were found to expose their frauds and deceits in writing and to convict their stratagems, while meanwhile the Donatists in every place made a great clamor with abusive voices, as Optatus says in book 1, no. 4; he himself answered them when an occasion presented itself. “How,” asks Optatus, “will satisfaction be given even to the desires of certain persons? For many have often desired that, in order to bring out the truth, the conflict of the parties should be conducted by some defenders; and this could be done.”]—when a large part of Africa was rushing headlong into the madness of its error, and, forgetful of its name, religion, and profession, was placing the sacrilegious rashness of one man above the Church of Christ—then all those established throughout Africa who, abhorring the profane schism, joined themselves to all the churches of the world, were the only ones among them all who could remain safe within the sanctuaries of the Catholic faith. They left to posterity an outstanding example of how, thereafter, in accordance with good custom, the soundness of all should be preferred to the madness of one or, at most, a few.

Likewise, when the poison of the Arians had contaminated not merely some small portion but almost the entire world, so that nearly all the bishops of the Latin-speaking world, deceived partly by force and partly by fraud, were covered by a kind of darkness of mind, what ought chiefly to be followed amid such great confusion? Whoever then proved to be a true lover and worshipper of Christ escaped defilement by that contagion when he preferred the ancient faith to the novel treachery.

The danger of that period sufficiently and abundantly demonstrated how much calamity is brought in by introducing a new doctrine. For not merely small things but even the greatest were shaken. Not only relationships, kinships, friendships, and households, but also cities, peoples, provinces, nations, and finally the entire Roman Empire were utterly convulsed and displaced.

For when that profane novelty of the Arians, like some Bellona or Fury, after first capturing the Emperor himself [Note: He means Constantius, about whom Hilary of Poitiers complains most bitterly in the book published against him in A.D. 360. Yet one must candidly admit that another man of equal distinction, Gregory of Nazianzus, entirely excuses the Emperor in Oration 1 against Julian, written at the same time, and instead sharply blames the courtiers, directing all the resentment against them.] had then subjected all the heights of the palace to new laws, it did not thereafter cease to throw everything into confusion and affliction, private and public, sacred and profane alike. It made no distinction between good and true things, but struck whomever it pleased, as though from a position of superiority.

Then wives were violated, widows stripped of their dark garments [Note: [Col. 0642] So the older editions, except the Douai edition, which reads “widows plundered.” It is known that no distinctive garments were imposed on widows, virgins, and penitents. In book 3, no. 11, of the Gallican Liturgy, the Missal of the Franks contains a blessing of a widow’s garments, which also appears in the Roman order. Hence Saint Asterius, bishop of Amasea, metropolis of the Hellespont, says in his Oration on Saint Euphemia, no. 3: “A virgin stands there in a dark garment and mantle, professing philosophy”; and again, in no. 4: “A chaste virgin, sitting alone in dark garments, stretches both hands toward heaven.” Asterius flourished near the end of the fourth century under the Emperor Arcadius. As the Arians took dark garments from widows, so the Donatists took head-coverings from virgins consecrated to God. “You took away,” says Optatus, book 6, no. 4, “not ornaments of the head, but tokens of good will. You scattered with unclean ashes hair already consecrated to God, and even ordered it to be drenched with false water. Would that you had at least quickly restored what you took away! You prolonged the delay, so that some, returned to their former dress, might remain longer with the signs withdrawn by which they had long defended themselves against suitors and ravishers. When these men saw that the bar long set against them had been removed by you, they became ravishers of brides; and no one seemed to himself to have sinned when he carried off one whom he had seen in the condition in which she had appeared when he sought her as a wife.”], virgins profaned, monasteries demolished [Note: [Col. 0643] The Royal manuscript reads “monasteries torn apart.” Baluzius.], clergy disturbed, Levites beaten, priests driven into exile, penal workhouses, prisons, and mines filled with holy men [Note: Lucifer of Cagliari, in his book On Dying for the Son of God, blames Constantius because, as he says, “you filled all the mines and all the places called exiles—with the number of those whom you thought worthy to resist your craft—by banishing the innocent and tormenting them with hunger, thirst, and nakedness.” He also restored the custom abolished by Constantine, according to law 2, On Punishments, in the Theodosian Code: “If anyone has been condemned to the gladiatorial school or the mines, he must not be branded on the face … so that the face, which is formed in the likeness of heavenly beauty, may not be defiled.” Hilary testifies to this in numbers 5 and 11 of his book against Constantius: “It is a notorious grievance,” he says, “that bishops whom no one dared to condemn were ordered by you not to exist, and that even now they are listed on ecclesiastical faces under the title of condemnation to the mines.”]; most of whom, expelled from the cities and driven into exile, were afflicted, crushed, and wasted amid deserts, caves, wild beasts, rocks, nakedness, hunger, and thirst.

And did all these things happen for any other reason than this: that human superstitions were being introduced in place of heavenly doctrine; that a well-established antiquity was being overthrown by wicked novelty; that the institutions of earlier times were being violated; that the decrees of the Fathers were being rescinded; that the decisions of our ancestors were being torn up; and that the appetite of profane and novel curiosity refused to confine itself within the most chaste boundaries of sacred and incorrupt antiquity?

## V

But perhaps, someone may say, we invent these things out of hatred of novelty and love of antiquity. Whoever thinks this should at least believe blessed Ambrose, who, in the second book addressed to the Emperor Gratian, lamenting the bitterness of the times, says:

“But now, almighty God, we have sufficiently washed away, by our exile and our blood, the slaughter of the Confessors, the exiles of priests, and the wickedness of such great impiety. It has become sufficiently clear that those who violate the faith cannot be safe.”

Ambrose, On the Faith, book 2, chapter 4, elsewhere 16.

Likewise, in the third book of the same work:

“Let us therefore preserve the precepts of our ancestors, and let us not, with the rashness of inexperience, dare to violate the hereditary seals. That prophetic sealed book neither Elders, nor Powers, nor Angels, nor Archangels dared to open; the privilege of explaining it was reserved for Christ alone. Who among us would dare to unseal the priestly book, sealed by the Confessors and already consecrated by the martyrdom of so many? Those who were compelled to unseal it [Note: Ambrose means the bishops who fell at Rimini in A.D. 359, whom Constantius compelled to renounce the faith on October 10 of that year, when he refused to allow bishops worn out by poverty and age to return home. Severus Sulpicius reveals the cause of such great evils in book 2, chapter 41 of his Ecclesiastical History, discussing the envoys sent to the Emperor: “On our side,” he says, “young men were sent, poorly educated and insufficiently cautious; by the Arians, however, elderly men, crafty and talented, steeped in the torpor of treachery, who easily prevailed before the Emperor.” Once the deception was recognized, the bishops of Rimini protested that they had suspected no evil concerning the body of the Lord or anything holy in the Church. They declared this amid tears and were ready to condemn both their former subscription and all the blasphemies of the Arians, as Jerome says in his Dialogue against the Luciferians.] nevertheless afterwards signed it when the fraud had been condemned; those who did not dare to violate it became Confessors and martyrs. How can we deny the faith of those whose victory we proclaim?”

The same, book 3, chapter 7, elsewhere 15.

“We proclaim it indeed,” I say, “venerable Ambrose; we proclaim it indeed, and we praise and admire it. For who is so mad that, even if he cannot attain to them, would not desire to follow those whom no force drove from defending the faith of their ancestors—neither threats, nor flatteries, nor life, nor death, nor the palace, nor guards, nor the Emperor, nor the empire, nor men, nor demons?

“Those, I say, whom the Lord judged worthy of so great a privilege because of their steadfastness in religious antiquity” [Note: These holy men, through whom God performed such wonders, were Athanasius, Hilary, Eusebius, and Ambrose. Hence Jerome says in his Dialogue against the Luciferians: “Then Egypt received its victor Athanasius; then the Church of Gaul embraced Hilary returning from battle with the heretics; then Italy changed its mourning garments at the return of Eusebius.” Concerning Ambrose, Prosper, after Jerome, speaks under the eleventh year of Gratian in his Chronicle: After the “late death of Auxentius, when Ambrose had been appointed bishop of Milan, all Italy was converted to the true faith”—that is, the portion of those regions subject to the Vicar of Italy, namely Insubria, Aemilia, and Liguria. By his preaching Ambrose joined and bound the divided churches to the summit and guardian of the faith, the Roman Pontiff. Thus, in his Commentary on Luke, written at that time, book 9, chapter 20, he rejoices over the defeat of heresy at the beginning of his episcopate, saying: “The storm of all dissensions has subsided. All the fires and heats of worldly desire, all the passions by which the people of Italy had once been scorched through the conflagrations of the Jewish and almost Arian savagery, are now tempered by a serene breath.” Hence Felix Ennodius sang his praises in book 1 of his Poems, number XV, hymn VI:

“Joined to the Apostles here,
He restored the banished faith,
He proclaimed the triumphs of the martyrs
With the laurel of his flourishing tongue.”

This preaching of the true faith, with the assent of the Roman Pontiff, was the reason that the Church of Milan began to be regarded as metropolitan. Benedict Bacchinius recognized this learnedly and carefully in his dissertation On the Origins of the Church’s Hierarchy, part 2, no. 10.]
