“so that through them he might restore the prostrate churches, give life to peoples whose spiritual life had been extinguished, restore the crowns of priests that had been cast down, and, by a fountain of the faithful’s tears poured from heaven upon the bishops, erase those wicked things of novel impiety—not letters, but blottings.” Finally, he might recall the whole world, already almost struck by the savage storm of sudden heresy, from novel treachery to the ancient faith, from the madness of novelty to ancient soundness, and from the blindness of novelty to the ancient light.”

But in this divine virtue of the Confessors [Note: [Col. 0644] The Royal manuscripts read “of the Confessors,” whereas the editions read “of the Confessions.” Baluzius.] we must especially consider that, at that time, the defense undertaken by them on behalf of the Church’s antiquity was not that of some part but of the whole.

For it was not right that such great and such men should, with so much effort, defend the wandering and mutually contradictory suspicions of one or two men, or fight on behalf of one province through some rash conspiracy. Rather, following the decrees and decisions of all the priests of the holy Church, heirs of apostolic and Catholic truth, they preferred to betray themselves rather than the faith of the ancient whole.

Thus they deserved to attain such glory that they are rightly and deservedly regarded not only as Confessors but as princes of the Confessors.

## VI

This, then, is the great and plainly divine example of those same blessed men, an example that all true Catholics should recall through unwearied meditation. Radiating with the sevenfold light of the Holy Spirit, like the seven-branched lampstand, they set before posterity a most brilliant model of how, thereafter, the authority of sacred antiquity should crush the insolence of profane novelty in each of its empty errors.

Nor is this really something new. For this custom has always flourished in the Church: the more religious a person was, the more readily he opposed novel innovations.

Everything is full of such examples. But, so that this may not become lengthy, we shall take one example, and especially one from the Apostolic See, so that everyone may see more clearly than daylight with what force, zeal, and determination the blessed succession of the holy Apostles has always defended the integrity of the religion once received.

Once, then, Agrippinus of venerable memory, bishop of Carthage [Note: He was the second of the Carthaginian bishops whose memory has come down to us. Under him two councils of Carthage were held. The first concerned the baptism of heretics by the bishops of Proconsular Africa and Numidia, at the beginning of the third century. Tertullian, who is said certainly to have fallen into error concerning the baptism of heretics, wrote in his book On Baptism, published after A.D. 200: “Concerning heretics, let anyone suitably reconsider what must be observed; for a decision has been issued to us.” An impartial reader will admit that by these words he was referring to Agrippinus’s decree. P. Hardouin therefore dated this council incorrectly to A.D. 215, especially since Cyprian, in Letter 73 to Jubaianus, written in A.D. 254, says: “Among us it is not a new or sudden matter that we judge those who come to the Church from heretics ought to be baptized, since many years and a long time have passed since, under Agrippinus, a man of good memory, many bishops met together and decreed this.” The second council, at which the canon was enacted that no cleric should undertake guardianship or administration, was held around A.D. 215.], was the first of all mortals to judge that heretics ought to be rebaptized—against the divine Canon, against the rule of the universal Church, against the mind of all his fellow priests, and against the custom and institutions of our ancestors.

This presumption introduced so great an evil that it provided not only all heretics with a model of sacrilege but also certain Catholics with an occasion for error.

When everyone everywhere was therefore protesting against the novelty of the matter, and all the priests in every direction were, each according to his own zeal, holding their ground, then Pope Stephen, of blessed memory [Note: After Cyprian had celebrated the third Council of Carthage on the question of rebaptism in A.D. 255 or 256, on the Kalends of September, with eighty-seven bishops from Proconsular Africa, Numidia, and Mauretania, Stephen, who had shortly before succeeded Lucius, was deeply angered. Thus, in A.D. 256, he convened a synod at Rome and sent sharp and pointed letters to Africa, Firmilianus, Helenus of Tarsus, and others. If we accept Dionysius of Alexandria in his Letter to Xystus, Stephen determined “that communion must not be held with those who rebaptize, but that the gravity of the matter must be considered, because those who have judged this to be right are not just anyone, but very great and distinguished bishops.”], bishop of the Apostolic See, resisted, together indeed with his other colleagues but more than the rest, judging, as I think, that he ought to surpass the others in devotion to the faith as much as he surpassed them in the authority of his position.

Finally, in the letter that was then sent to Africa [Note: [Col. 0646] Though the letter has been lost, its ruling is preserved in Cyprian’s Letter 74 to Pompeianus. When consulted by Pompeius, bishop of Sabrata, he excerpted these words from Stephen’s letter: “If, therefore, anyone comes to us from any heresy, let nothing be innovated except what has been handed down: let hands be imposed upon him for penance; since heretics themselves, when persons come to them from one another, do not baptize them but merely admit them to communion.” That the pontiff did not err in the matter of rebaptism is proved by the very great light of the arguments in the learned Father D. Coustant, vol. 1, Letters of the Pontiffs, p. 2217; anyone not persuaded by them is excessively slow or malicious.], he decreed in these words:

“LET NOTHING BE INNOVATED EXCEPT WHAT HAS BEEN HANDED DOWN.”

For that holy and prudent man understood that piety’s reason admitted nothing other than that all things received from the Fathers in faith should be entrusted to their sons in the same faith; that we ought not to lead religion wherever we wished, but rather to follow wherever it led; and that this is proper to Christian modesty and seriousness: not to hand down our own inventions to posterity, but to preserve what we have received from our ancestors.

What, then, was the outcome of the whole affair? What else, surely, than the usual and customary outcome? Antiquity was retained, novelty rejected.

But perhaps at that time the novel invention itself lacked supporters? On the contrary, there was such force of intellect, such rivers of eloquence, such a multitude of advocates, such plausibility, and such oracles of divine law—though understood in an entirely new and evil manner—that it seems to me that the whole conspiracy could not have been overthrown in any way except that the very profession of novelty, undertaken, defended, and praised as the cause of so great an effort, finally abandoned it.

What, finally, was the force of the African Council—or decree [Note: He means the third universal council of Africa, which Augustine refutes with singular moderation in books 2 and 3 of On Baptism against the Donatists.]? By God’s gift, none. Everything was abolished, antiquated, and trampled underfoot as though it were dreams, fables, and superfluities [Note: I suspect that the author had in mind these words of Jerome in the Dialogue against the Luciferians: “Blessed Cyprian tried to flee from broken cisterns and not drink from foreign water. Therefore, rejecting the baptism of heretics, he sent a letter on this subject to Stephen, then bishop of the city of Rome, for the African synod; but his attempt was unsuccessful. Finally, those very bishops who had determined with him that heretics should be rebaptized returned to the ancient custom and issued a new decree.” Baluzius observes that Jerome said that a new decree had been issued by the African council in this sense because he saw the crime of rebaptizing heretics condemned by the better and larger part of the Donatists. Whatever may be made of Jerome’s report, it is certain that after Stephen’s death, when Xystus was seated in the See and Dionysius of Alexandria served as mediator, peace was restored between the Roman and African Churches. Hence Pontius, in the Life of Cyprian, no. 14, calls Xystus “a good and peace-loving priest.” Cyprian, in Letter 80, elsewhere numbered 82, reports the succession of Xystus’s martyrdom and says that “messengers whom he had sent to Rome so that he might learn the truth had informed him of the most severe persecution and of the Pope’s martyrdom.” This peace may have been the reason why many Africans understood the truth, especially since, according to Cyprian, some shared Stephen’s opinion.]

And, O wondrous reversal of affairs! Catholics who held the same opinion as the authors of that decree are judged heretics; the teachers are acquitted, the disciples condemned; those who wrote the books will be sons of the kingdom, while their advocates will be received by hell.

For who is so mad as eternally to doubt that the most blessed light of all the saints, Cyprian, together with his other colleagues, will reign with Christ forever? Or who is so sacrilegious as to deny that the Donatists and the other plagues who boast that they rebaptize on the authority of that council will burn forever with the devil?

## VII

This judgment seems to me to have been divinely proclaimed especially because of the fraud of those who, while plotting to construct a heresy under another man’s name, commonly seek out the writings of some ancient man, composed in a somewhat obscure manner, so that by their very obscurity they may seem to correspond to their own doctrine. Thus, whatever they produce, they do not appear to be the first—or the only ones—to hold it.

I judge their wickedness worthy of a double hatred: first, because they do not fear administering the poison of heresy to others; and second, because they stir up the memory of each holy man with profane hands, as though fanning smoldering ashes, and spread abroad by reviving an opinion what ought to have been buried in silence.

They entirely follow the footsteps of their ancestor Ham, who not only neglected to cover the nakedness of venerable Noah but also announced it to the others for ridicule. Therefore he deserved so great an offense against piety that even his descendants were bound by the curse of his sin.

How different from those blessed brothers who did not wish either to violate the nakedness of their revered father with their own eyes or to expose it to the eyes of others, but, turning away, as Scripture says, covered him. This means that they neither approved nor disclosed the holy man’s error [Note: They covered their father’s nakedness by placing a cloak upon their backs and, while turned away, covering him. As Gregory says in Moralia 25, chapter 22, good subjects should be displeased by the faults of their superiors while nevertheless concealing them from others: “They carry the covering while turned away, because, judging the deed and revering the office, they do not wish to see what they cover.” This prudent admonition of the excellent Pope and of Vincentius is strongly commended by the celebrated Protestant editor of Cyprian, John Fell, Bishop of Oxford. Others, however, prefer to chastise the errors of the Fathers; among them Clericus readily professed his own name. For this reason, in Letter 6 of his Critical and Ecclesiastical Works, he condemns all concealments in ecclesiastical history as unlawful. Let us grant that the sins of great men should be chastised, lest the unwary follow them. Yet the manner in which some have done this is fitting neither for a Christian nor even for a gentleman: with bitterness, rage, and acrimony; magnifying slight errors through spiteful language while passing over and concealing enormous merits. Clericus himself was severely accused of such great injustice by men distinguished for integrity and learning. It was necessary to take notice of this, following his own practice, so that nothing worthy of record might be concealed in ecclesiastical history.]; and for this reason they were blessed with a blessing upon their descendants.

But let us return to the subject.

We must therefore fear with great dread the sacrilege of changing the faith and violating religion. From this we are restrained not only by the discipline of the Church’s constitution but also by the judgment of apostolic authority.

For it is known to all how gravely, severely, and vehemently blessed Paul the Apostle inveighs against certain people who, with astonishing fickleness, had been transferred too quickly from the one who had called them into the grace of Christ to another Gospel [Note: This apostolic testimony is cited in the same form by Tertullian in book 4 against Marcion and by Jerome in his Commentary on this epistle, although Erasmus resisted it.]—which is not another Gospel; 2 Timothy 4.

They accumulated teachers for themselves according to their desires, turning their hearing away from the truth and turning instead to fables; 1 Timothy 5.

They incurred condemnation because they had made their first faith void.

Those who deceived them are the people of whom the same Apostle writes to the Roman brothers:

“I urge you, brothers, to watch those who create dissensions and scandals contrary to the doctrine that you have learned, and avoid them. For such people do not serve Christ the Lord but their own belly, and by smooth speech and blessings they deceive the hearts of the innocent”; Romans 16.

“They enter houses and lead captive little women weighed down by sins, driven by various desires, always learning and never arriving at knowledge of the truth”; 2 Timothy 3.

“They are empty talkers and deceivers who overturn entire households, teaching what ought not to be taught for the sake of shameful gain”; Titus 1.

“They are corrupt in mind and disqualified concerning the faith”; 2 Timothy 3.

“They are proud and know nothing, but are sick over questions and disputes about words. They have been deprived of the truth, supposing that godliness is a means of gain. At the same time, being idle, they learn to go around the houses; and not only idle but also talkative and inquisitive, speaking things that ought not to be spoken”; 1 Timothy 5.

“By rejecting a good conscience, they have suffered shipwreck concerning the faith”; 1 Timothy 1.

“Their profane empty talk advances greatly toward ungodliness, and their word spreads like a cancer”; 2 Timothy 2.

Yet it is rightly written of them as well:

“But they will progress no further. For their folly will be evident to everyone, just as theirs also was”; 2 Timothy 3.

## VIII

When certain such people were therefore traveling through provinces and cities, carrying around their errors for sale, and had even reached the Galatians [Note: These false brothers taught that a person was justified by works of the Law. They deceived the Galatians into observing circumcision and the other ceremonies of the Law together with the law of Christ as necessary for salvation. For this reason they disparaged Paul among the Apostles, accusing him of contradicting the others. While Paul was staying at Ephesus, he learned of the situation and treated the Galatians’ sick minds by means of this letter: first, he restrained the audacity of the wicked by defending the dignity of his apostleship; second, he proved the agreement of his teaching with that of the other Apostles by showing that he had conferred with them; third, by adducing arguments and testimonies from the ancient Scripture, he recalled those who had been led astray from their error. He wrote the epistle around A.D. 56, twenty-three years after Christ’s death.], and when, after hearing these things, the Galatians, seized by a kind of nausea toward the truth, vomited up the manna of apostolic and Catholic doctrine and delighted in the filth of heretical novelty, the authority of apostolic power displayed itself so severely that it decreed:

“But even if we,” he says, “or an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel contrary to what we preached to you, let him be accursed”; Galatians 1.

What does he mean by “even if we”? Why does he not say instead, “Even if I”? This is what he means: Even if Peter, even if Andrew, even if John, even if finally the entire company of the Apostles should preach to you a gospel contrary to what we preached, let him be accursed.

A terrifying strictness! In order to assert steadfastness in the original faith, he spared neither himself nor his fellow Apostles.

It is not enough. “Even if an angel from heaven,” he says, “should preach to you a gospel contrary to what we preached, let him be accursed.” For the protection of the faith once handed down, it was not enough to mention the nature of human beings unless he also included the excellence of angels.

“Even if we,” he says, “or an angel from heaven.”

Not because holy and heavenly angels could now sin, but because this is what he means: If even what cannot happen should happen, whoever he may be who attempts to change the faith once handed down, let him be accursed.

But perhaps he merely uttered these words in passing and poured them forth in a human impulse rather than decreeing them by divine reason. Far from it. He continues and, by repeating the same warning with great force, impresses it upon us:

“As we have said before, and now I say again: If anyone preaches to you a gospel contrary to what you received, let him be accursed.”

He did not say: If anyone announces to you something contrary to what you received, let him be blessed, praised, and received. Rather, he says, “Let him be accursed”—that is, separated, set apart, and excluded, lest the dreadful contagion of one sheep infect Christ’s unharmed flock through poisonous mingling.

## IX

But perhaps these instructions were given only to the Galatians. Then the commands mentioned later in the same Epistle were also imposed only upon the Galatians, such as these:

“If we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit. Let us not become desirous of empty glory, provoking one another and envying one another”; Galatians 5; and what follows.

But if that is absurd, and these commands were imposed equally upon everyone, it remains that, just as these moral commandments apply to all, so too all must equally understand those precautions concerning the faith. Just as no one is permitted to provoke or envy another, so no one is permitted to receive anything beyond what the Catholic Church everywhere proclaims.

Or perhaps it was then commanded that if anyone announced something different from what had been announced, he should be anathematized, but that this is no longer commanded. Then the statement made there as well—“I say, walk by the Spirit, and you will not fulfill the desire of the flesh”—was commanded only then and is no longer commanded.

But if it is equally impious and harmful to believe this, it necessarily follows that, just as these commands must be observed in every age, so too those decrees concerning the faith’s not being changed were imposed for every age.

Therefore, to announce anything to Catholic Christians beyond what they received was never permitted, is nowhere permitted, and never will be permitted. And to anathematize those who announce anything beyond what was once received was always right, is always right, and will always be right.

Since this is so, is there anyone either so audacious as to announce anything beyond what has been announced in the Church, or so fickle as to receive anything beyond what he has received from the Church?

That man—the chosen vessel, the teacher of the nations, the trumpet of the Apostles, the herald of the earth, the initiate of heaven—cries out and cries out again, in all his letters, to everyone, always, and everywhere, that if anyone announces a new doctrine, he must be anathematized.

And against him certain frogs, gnats, and dying flies [Note: P. Macedo suspects that Pope Gelasius had Vincentius’s passage in mind when, in his Letter to the Bishops established throughout Picenum, he calls a certain Pelagian old man “a dying fly,” whereas the common reading, as Gelasius says, has “dying flies.” Hence, in Ecclesiastical Controversy, chapter 11, he concludes that Lirinensis was not infected with the Pelagian plague. He could have added that Gelasius also calls him a frog: “A miserable old man named Seneca was brought before us, imprudently immersed in the mire of the Pelagian abyss, like one of the frogs of which we read in the Apocalypse.” I do not believe that Gelasius knew Vincentius’s work; otherwise, he would have paid him the honor he deserved in his catalogue of books. He may perhaps have read the testimony of Ecclesiasticus 10:1 concerning dying flies in Optatus of Milevis, book 7, no. 4, or in Augustine, book 2 against the Letter of Petilianus, chapter 10, where Augustine says: “Because of their number, I think they may be compared to flies; but those who look not to God’s grace itself but to human behavior destroy the oil of sweetness.”], such as the Pelagians, croak back to Catholics:

“On our authority, under our leadership, and through our interpretation, condemn what you held; hold what you condemned; reject the ancient faith, the institutions of the Fathers, and the deposit of our ancestors; and receive—what, finally? I shudder to say it. For their claims are so arrogant that it seems to me not only that they cannot be asserted without some sacrilege, but that they cannot even be refuted without one.”

### X

But someone may say: Why, then, are certain eminent persons established in the Church so often permitted by divine providence to announce novelties to Catholics? The question is rightly put and deserves to be treated more carefully and fully. Yet it must be answered not by our own ingenuity but by the authority of divine law and the teaching of the Church’s magisterium.

Let us therefore hear the holy Moses; let him himself teach us why learned men—men whom the Apostle even calls prophets because of their knowledge—are sometimes permitted to bring forward new doctrines, which the Old Testament habitually calls “foreign gods” in allegorical language, because heretics observe their opinions just as the nations observe their gods.

Blessed Moses writes in Deuteronomy: “If there arises in your midst,” he says, “a prophet, or one who claims to have seen a dream” (Deut. 13)—that is, a teacher established in the Church whom his disciples or hearers suppose to be teaching from some revelation. What next? “And he predicts,” he says, “a sign or portent, and what he has spoken comes to pass.” A great teacher indeed is being indicated—I scarcely know whom—of such knowledge that he seems able to know in advance for his followers not only what is human but even what is beyond humanity; such, for example, as his disciples boast Valentinus, Donatus, Photinus, Apollinaris, and others of that sort to have been.

What follows? “And he says to you,” he says, “Let us go and follow foreign gods whom you do not know, and let us serve them.” Who are the foreign gods except alien errors which you did not know—that is, new and unheard-of errors? And “let us serve them,” that is, let us believe them and follow them.

What finally? “You shall not listen,” he says, “to the words of that prophet or dreamer.” And why, I ask you, is one forbidden by God to teach what he is forbidden by God to hear? “Because,” he says, “the Lord your God is testing you, to make plain whether you love him or not with all your heart and with all your soul.”

The reason is clearer than daylight why divine Providence sometimes allows certain teachers of the Churches to preach novel doctrines: “To test you,” he says, “the Lord your God.” And truly it is a great temptation when the person whom you think a prophet, a disciple of prophets, a teacher and defender of truth, whom you have embraced with the highest veneration and love, suddenly and secretly introduces harmful errors—errors which you cannot quickly detect because you are led by the prejudice of his former teaching, nor easily condemn because your affection for the old teacher holds you back.

### XI

At this point someone may perhaps demand that the things asserted in the words of holy Moses be demonstrated by examples from the Church. The demand is fair and should not be long postponed. To begin with the recent and obvious, what greater temptation can we suppose there was than when that wretched Nestorius, suddenly changed from a sheep into a wolf, began to tear Christ’s flock, while those very people who were being gnawed still largely believed him to be a sheep and therefore suffered his bites all the more?

For who would easily suppose that he could be in error when he saw him chosen with such careful imperial judgment, pursued with such zeal by the priests, and celebrated with the great love of the saints and the highest favor of the people? Every day he openly discussed the divine Scriptures and refuted the harmful errors of Jews and Gentiles.

[Note: After Sisinnius had been removed from the living and disputes had arisen among the clergy, Nestorius, who had been living at Antioch under the habit and profession of a monk, was appointed bishop of the Church of Constantinople by the younger Theodosius. As Socrates relates (book 7, chapter 29), he was ordained in the year of Christ 428, on the fourth day before the Ides of April, with all good men applauding and congratulating one another, as though he were destined to be another Chrysostom. The reader should consult Celestine’s letter to him in part 1 of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 17, and Cyril’s letter to Theodosius in part 3 of that same council.]

[Note: Scarcely had he entered the city and Church when, in his first sermon, he addressed Theodosius with that celebrated saying which, as it pleased some, so appeared savage and arrogant to others: “Give me, Emperor, a land purged of heretics, and I in return will give you heaven; overthrow the heretics with me, and I will overthrow the Persians with you.” Hence he began sharply to persecute, by word and deed, people of every sect, relying on the power of the city prefects. And, if Gothofredus is to be believed after Baronius, the extensive law of Theodosius enacted against all heretics, issued in the year of Christ 428 about the end of May, was promulgated at Nestorius’s instigation. See Gothofredus’s commentary on Law 65 of the Theodosian Code, and Socrates, book 7, chapter 28 and following.]

How, then, could he fail to persuade anyone that he was teaching, preaching, and thinking rightly, when, in order to gain a hearing for his one heresy, he attacked the blasphemies of all heresies?

But this was precisely what Moses meant: “The Lord your God is testing you, to see whether you love him or not.”

Let us pass over Nestorius, in whom there was always more to provoke admiration than to produce benefit, more reputation than experience—whom popular opinion for a time made great by human favor rather than divine grace—and let us instead recall those who, endowed with many accomplishments and great diligence, became no small temptation to Catholic people.

Thus, in Pannonia, the memory of our ancestors records that Photinus tested the Church of Sirmium. When he had been called to the priesthood with the great favor of everyone and had administered his office for some time as a Catholic, suddenly, like the evil prophet or dreamer signified by Moses, he began to persuade the people of God entrusted to him to follow foreign gods—that is, alien errors which they had previously not known.

But that was commonplace. What was pernicious was that he employed no ordinary resources in pursuing such great wickedness. For he was strong in intellectual powers and outstanding in the resources of learning and eloquence,

[Note: Concerning Photinus, a Galatian by nation, Jerome’s expanded version of Eusebius’s Chronicle, under the year 379 and according to the edition of Arnoldus Pontacus, bishop of Bazas, says: “Photinus died in Galatia. From him the doctrine of the Photinians was introduced; he lost many good qualities of self-restraint and intellect through the single evil of pride.” But Jean Le Clerc, in the preface to the German edition of the *Ars Critica*, p. 15, assigns the words “who lost many good qualities of self-restraint and intellect through the single evil of pride” to Basil in the following passage. He supports this from manuscripts “which,” as he says, “did not permit the rash correction,” and from Nazianzenus. I am surprised that these things escaped a man who everywhere professes and boasts of his love of truth and candor. Pontacus certainly examined six Vatican manuscripts: only two, both more recent and of inferior quality, attribute the words to Basil, while the other four, superior in authority and antiquity, consistently assign to Photinus the praise of intellect and the evil of pride. To these may be added two others: Vatican Library, Palatine Codex no. 818, and another in the Library of Cardinal Ottoboni, shelfmark G. IV, 1. There are also two copies of Eusebius’s Chronicle expanded by Jerome in the Christian Library, nos. 553 and 560; yet the words do not appear in Basil there either, although those manuscripts have undergone no rash correction. Indeed, Scaliger, in his notes on this passage, testifies that the words were added by someone in the margin as foreign to the text.

“What we have said is also confirmed by the authority of the Fathers. On Photinus’s intellect and pride, it is enough to hear Epiphanius in *Heresy* 71, where he says: ‘Photinus, lifted up by no small madness and having become more frenzied than all others, and so forth, was talkative and sharp-tongued, and could deceive many by his delivery and readiness of speech.’

“The Fathers’ judgments concerning Basil are altogether different. The Council of Ephesus called him ‘Great and Most Holy, the glory of the Church and truly a servant of God.’ Athanasius, in his letter to John, called him ‘the light of the world, the voice and trumpet of the world’; Gregory Nazianzen called him ‘the palace of doctrine’ in Letter 10. Augustine, in book 1 of *Against Julian*, chapter 5, no. 18, called him ‘an eminent man endowed with conspicuous holiness,’ whose immense merit was divinely shown to blessed Ephrem in the following way. When Ephrem asked God to show him what kind and how great a man Basil was, ‘God granted his request, and while Ephrem was praying, the appearance of an immense column was presented opposite the altar, so great that it seemed to join heaven to earth; and voices sounded these words: “As you have seen the fiery column, so believe Basil to be.”’ This weighty testimony is found in vol. 1 of the *Bibliotheca Orientalis*, p. 39, no. 11, published for the great benefit of the Church and the republic of letters by the distinguished Joseph Simon Assemani.

“Nor does it matter that Basil was accused of arrogance not only by heretics but also by Catholics; he answered them in Letter 164, and the devout seriousness of Nazianzenus marks them as unjust and bitter judges of affairs. In his oration in praise of Basil, Nazianzenus also left it recorded for posterity that ‘this man abhorred both ambition and a certain theatrical display of intellect.’”]

for he argued and wrote copiously and forcefully in both languages; this is shown by the monuments of his books, which he composed partly in Greek and partly in Latin.

But it was fortunate that the sheep of Christ entrusted to him, greatly watchful and cautious on behalf of the Catholic faith, quickly turned their attention to the words of Moses, who had given them warning. Though they admired the eloquence of their prophet and shepherd, they did not fail to recognize the temptation. They had previously followed him as though he were the ram of the flock; afterward they began to flee from him as though he were a wolf.

[Note: Besides Apollinaris of Hierapolis, a bishop of great renown who flourished under Marcus Antoninus, there were, about the middle of the fourth century, two Apollinarises, father and son, both Alexandrians by birth. Each moved to Laodicea under Theodotus, bishop of the city, and they remained there under his successor George. But they were removed from communion by him, although the father had been admitted to the order of presbyters and the son to that of readers. For what reason is uncertain, since the ancient writers disagree. Some say it was because both were bound by a very close friendship with Epiphanius the Sophist, a pagan; others, such as Sozomen, because they had communicated with Athanasius when he passed through Laodicea on his return from exile to Alexandria, since the Apollinarises knew that George was not very steadfast in his profession of the Trinity. However the matter occurred, the son Apollinaris, bearing the injury inflicted on him with indignation, relying on confidence in his skill and eager for revenge, devised a new heresy. Nor did he cease to spread it shortly afterward, when the bishop of Laodicea was announced. And because, before he fell into misfortune, he had been especially dear to holy men—Epiphanius, Athanasius, Basil, Serapion, and other defenders of the faith—his fall proved more disastrous for the Church and drew more abundant tears from Epiphanius and Basil, who lamented the unhappy end of so great a man. The reader should consult Dionysius Petavius, vol. 5 of *Dogmatic Theology*, book 1, chapter 6, nos. 2 and 3.]

From the example of Apollinaris as well as Photinus we learn the danger of this ecclesiastical temptation, and at the same time we are warned to guard the faith more carefully. For Apollinaris himself generated great agitation and great distress among his hearers, since the authority of the Church drew them in one direction while the habit of their teacher drew them back in another; and, wavering and drifting between the two, they could not determine what they ought to choose.

[Note: This is the reading of the Royal manuscript. It confirms the conjecture of Bartholomew Peter of Douai, who noted in the margin of his edition that *aestus* should be read here instead of *actus*, which the editions had. Baluze.]

But perhaps that man was the sort who deserved to be easily despised. On the contrary: he was so great and of such a kind that people in many respects believed him far too quickly. For what was superior to him in acuity, training, and learning? How many heresies he crushed in many volumes, how many errors of the enemies of the faith he refuted, is shown by that work of no fewer than thirty books—famous and immense—in which he overwhelmed the insane calumnies of Porphyry with a great mass of proofs.

It would take too long to recount all his works. In them he could surely have been the equal of the greatest builders of the Church, had he not, through that profane lust for heretical curiosity, devised some new thing by which he both stained all his labors, as though by the admixture of a kind of leprosy, and caused his teaching to be called not so much ecclesiastical edification as ecclesiastical temptation.

### XII

At this point I may perhaps be asked to explain the heresies of those whom I mentioned above—namely, Nestorius, Apollinaris, and Photinus. This does not properly belong to the matter now before us. Our purpose is not to pursue the errors of individuals but to offer a few examples by which it may be clearly and plainly demonstrated that, whenever some ecclesiastical teacher, himself a prophet in interpreting the mysteries of the prophets, attempts to introduce something new into the Church of God, divine Providence permits it to happen for our testing, as Moses says.

It will nevertheless be useful, in passing, to explain briefly what the heretics mentioned above—Photinus, Apollinaris, and Nestorius—believed.

This, then, is the sect of Photinus. He says that God is single and solitary and must be confessed in the Jewish manner. He denies the fullness of the Trinity and thinks that there is no person of God the Word and no person of the Holy Spirit. He asserts that Christ is merely a solitary man, assigning his beginning to Mary; and he dogmatizes in every way that we ought to worship only the one person of God the Father and Christ as merely human.

That is Photinus.

Apollinaris, however, pretends that he agrees in some way concerning the unity of the Trinity—and even this without the full soundness of faith—

[Note: I am surprised that the most learned Dionysius Petavius, in vol. 5 of his *Dogmatic Theology*, book 1, chapter 6, no. 15, read the opposite, as though Vincentius had said “and this with full soundness of faith,” contrary to the editions and to the context itself. This is especially surprising because a man of such universal learning could not have been unaware that Apollinaris was reproved by Basil in Letter 293 and by Gregory Nazianzen in Letter 1 to Cledonius, p. 744, as inclining toward the error of Sabellius; the latter even cites Apollinaris’s books as witnesses to this. Thus Leontius should by no means be heeded in book 4 of *On the Sects*, vol. 11 of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, when he asserts that Apollinaris did not err concerning the Trinity: “Although,” he says, “both Gregories also accuse him of error in this respect.” Besides the two Gregories, Basil and the author of Lérins also stand as witnesses, to say nothing of others. I therefore suspect that Apollinaris’s books, in which Nazianzenus detected his error, did not reach Leontius—unless someone would rather say that Apollinaris published contradictory doctrines, which could have happened while “in treating theology he drew his arguments not from the Scriptures but from human inventions,” as Basil says.]

but in the incarnation of the Lord he openly blasphemes. For he says that in the very flesh of our Savior there was either no human soul at all, or at least one without mind and reason. He also said that the Lord’s flesh was not taken from the flesh of the holy Virgin Mary but descended from heaven into the Virgin; and, always wavering and uncertain, he proclaimed it now coeternal with God the Word, now made from the divinity of the Word.

For he did not want Christ to possess two substances, one divine and the other human, one from the Father and the other from the mother. Rather, he thought that the very nature of the Word had been divided, as though one part of it remained in God while another had been changed into flesh. Thus, while the truth says that Christ is one from two substances, he, contrary to the truth, asserts that two substances had been made from Christ’s one divinity.

This, then, is Apollinaris.

Nestorius, however, through an illness opposite to that of Apollinaris, while pretending to distinguish two substances in Christ, suddenly introduces two persons and, with unheard-of wickedness, wants there to be two sons of God, two Christs: one God and the other man; one from the Father and the other generated from the mother. For this reason he asserts that holy Mary should be called not *Theotokos*—“God-bearer”—but *Christotokos*—“Christ-bearer”—because from her was born not that Christ who is God, but that one who was man.

If anyone thinks that in his writings Nestorius speaks of one Christ and proclaims one person of Christ, let him not believe this rashly. Either he contrived this by an artifice of deception, so that through good things he might more easily persuade people of evil things, as the Apostle says: “Through what was good he worked death in me” (Rom. 7); or, as we have said, he boasts in certain passages of his writings that he believes in one Christ and one person of Christ for the sake of fraud. Or else, after the Virgin’s birth, he claims that two persons came together into one Christ in such a way that, nevertheless, at the time of the Virgin’s conception and birth, and for some time afterward, there were two Christs: namely, when Christ as a common and solitary man was first born, not yet joined to the person of God the Word by unity of person, and afterward the person of the assuming Word descended upon him. Although he now remains assumed into the glory of God, for a time he appears to have had nothing distinguishing him from other human beings.

### XIII

Thus Nestorius, Apollinaris, and Photinus bark like rabid dogs against the Catholic faith: Photinus by refusing to confess the Trinity; Apollinaris by saying that the nature of the Word was convertible, by refusing to confess two substances in Christ, by denying either the whole soul of Christ or at least mind and reason in the soul, and by asserting that the Word of God took the place of the mind’s faculty; Nestorius by affirming that there are, or for some time were, two Christs.

The Catholic Church, however, thinking rightly both about God and about our Savior, blasphemes neither in the mystery of the Trinity nor in Christ’s incarnation. It venerates one divinity in the fullness of the Trinity and the equality of the Trinity in one and the same majesty; and it confesses one Christ Jesus, not two, the same both God and man.

It believes that in him there is one person but two substances; two substances but one person: two substances, because the Word of God is not mutable, so that it could be changed into flesh; one person, lest, by professing two sons, it appear to worship a quaternity rather than a Trinity.

It is worthwhile to unfold this matter again and again, more distinctly and explicitly.

In God there is one substance but three persons; in Christ there are two substances but one person. In the Trinity there is one distinct from another, not one thing distinct from another; in the Savior there is one thing distinct from another, not one person distinct from another.

How is there in the Trinity one distinct from another, not one thing distinct from another? Because the person of the Father is one, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another; yet the nature of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is not one thing and another, but one and the same.

How is there in the Savior one thing distinct from another, not one person distinct from another? Because one substance is divine and the other human; yet divinity and humanity are not one person and another, but one and the same Christ, one and the same Son of God. The person of the one and same Christ and Son of God is one and the same—just as in a human being flesh is one thing and soul another, yet soul and flesh constitute one and the same human being.

In Peter and Paul there is one thing, soul, and another thing, flesh; yet there are not two Peters, flesh and soul, nor is one Paul the soul and another the flesh. Rather, there is one and the same Peter and one and the same Paul, subsisting from the two diverse natures of soul and body.

Thus in one and the same Christ there are two substances: one divine, the other human; one from God the Father, the other from the Virgin mother; one coeternal and equal with the Father, the other existing in time and lesser than the Father; one consubstantial with the Father, the other consubstantial with the mother. Yet there is one and the same Christ in both substances.

Therefore Christ is not one as God and another as man; not one uncreated and another created; not one impassible and another passible; not one equal to the Father and another lesser than the Father; not one from the Father and another from the mother. Rather, there is one and the same Christ, God and man; the same both uncreated and created; the same immutable and impassible, the same changed and suffering; the same both equal to and lesser than the Father; the same begotten from the Father before the ages, the same born in the age from the mother; perfect God, perfect man.

As God, he possesses supreme divinity; as man, complete humanity. Complete humanity, I say, since he possesses both soul and flesh—true flesh, ours, maternal flesh, and a soul endowed with understanding, possessing mind and reason.

Thus in Christ there are Word, soul, and flesh; yet this whole is one Christ, one Son of God, and one Savior and Redeemer of ours. He is one—not through some corruptible confusion of divinity and humanity, but through the complete and singular unity of person.

For that union did not convert or change one into the other—which is the particular error of the Arians—

[Note: So that the Arians might more easily persuade the unwary that the Word was of a substance different from the Father, they asserted that he suffered in the flesh; and they said that the divinity of the Word was, as it were, secondary to the body, in the manner of a soul. In their view, therefore, divinity had been in some sense converted into humanity, since it occupied in Christ the place of the substantive form of a human being.

Besides the author of Lérins, Leontius in *On the Sects*, Act 2, Athanasius in *On the Saving Advent* and in another work *On the Incarnation of Christ*, and especially Hilary throughout book 10 of *On the Trinity*, condemn this error, which destroys faith in the assumed humanity. Hilary says in section 9: “Many of them wish him, because of fear of suffering and the weakness of being able to suffer, not to have been in the nature of the impassible God . . . but to have trembled in fear of human suffering as one of a nature inferior to God the Father, and to have groaned beneath the cruelty of bodily punishment.”

Since this is so, the entire controversy raised against Hilary by Claudianus Mamertus, Berengarius, and a certain John before Philip, abbot of Bonne-Espérance, is easily settled without any ambiguity: they accused Hilary of denying human sufferings in Christ at section 23 of the same book, where he says: “The Lord Jesus Christ did indeed suffer when he was beaten, when he was hung, when he was crucified, when he died; but the Passion rushing upon the Lord’s body was indeed a Passion, yet it did not exercise the nature of Passion, while it raged through the ministry of punishment and the power of the body received in itself the force of the punishment raging against it without experiencing the pain of punishment.”

The meaning, therefore, is this: the Passion by which Christ was beaten belonged to the body, or to the humanity assumed by the Word, which was altered through sensation, pain, and endurance; but it did not truly belong to the Word, which remained untouched by the effects of alteration. This is what Hilary means when he says that the Son of God received the force of the punishment raging against him without experiencing the pain of punishment.

The reader should consult the general preface prefixed to the works of St. Hilary in the edition of P. Coustant, section III.]

but rather joined both together into one, so that, while the singularity of one and the same person always remained in Christ, the proper character of each nature might likewise remain forever. Thus God never begins to be body, nor does body ever cease to be body.

This is also demonstrated by the example of human condition. For not only in the present but also in the future each human being will consist of soul and body; yet body will never become soul, nor soul become body. Rather, while each human being lives forever, the difference between the two substances will necessarily remain forever in each human being.

So also in Christ the proper character of each substance must be retained forever, while the unity of person remains intact.

### XIV

But since we so often use the word “person” and say that God became man through person, we must take great care lest we seem to mean that God the Word assumed only the imitation of actions that belong to us, and performed everything belonging to human conduct as though he were merely shadowed or disguised, not as a true man—just as happens in the theater, where one person suddenly represents several characters while himself being none of them.

Whenever an imitation of another’s action is undertaken, the duties or works of others are performed in such a way that those who perform them are nevertheless not themselves the persons whom they portray. For, to use the examples of secular persons and Manichaeans, when a tragic actor represents a priest or a king, he is not a priest or a king. When the performance ends, the character he had assumed ends with it.

[Note: Baluze thinks that the word “Manichaeans” was added by some ignorant person. The latter, not understanding Vincentius, thought that the comparison was taken from the Manichaeans. He then says that, at the words “he represents a priest,” tragedians and comedians publicly assumed the role of a bishop, just as they assumed the roles of other men.]

Far be such a wicked and criminal mockery from us. Let that madness belong to the Manichaeans, who, as preachers of phantasy, say that the Son of God, though God, existed as a human person not in substance but by a certain supposed action and simulated conduct.

The Catholic faith, however, says that the Word of God became man in such a way that he assumed what belongs to us not deceitfully or in mere semblance but truly and explicitly; and that what was human he did not imitate as something foreign, but rather carried as his own. What he did, he truly was.

We too, in what we speak, understand, live, and subsist, do not imitate human beings but are human beings. Peter and John, to name them above all, were not human beings by imitation but by subsistence. Paul did not pretend to be an apostle or fabricate a Paul; he was an apostle, and Paul subsisted as Paul.

So also God the Word, by assuming and possessing flesh, by speaking, acting, and suffering through the flesh, while undergoing no corruption of his own nature, deigned to accomplish this completely: not to imitate or fabricate a perfect man, but to present one; not merely to seem or be thought a true man, but to be and subsist as one.

Therefore, just as a soul joined to flesh, yet not changed into flesh, does not imitate a human being but is a human being—a human being not by pretense but by substance—so also God the Word, without any change in himself, became man by uniting himself to man, not by confusing or imitating but by subsisting.

Let the whole notion of that kind of person be entirely rejected which is assumed through fabrication and imitation, where one person is always present and another is merely represented, where the one who acts is never the one whom he portrays.

Far be it from us to believe that God the Word assumed a human person in this deceptive manner. Rather, while his substance remained immutable and he assumed within himself the nature of a perfect man, he himself existed as flesh, as man, and as a human person—not in pretense but in truth, not imitatively but substantially, and not as a character that ceased with the action, but as one that remained wholly in substance.

### XV

This unity of person in Christ was not joined and perfected after the Virgin’s birth but in the very womb of the Virgin. We must take the greatest care to confess Christ not only as one but as always one. For it is intolerable blasphemy to concede that he is now one while maintaining that at some earlier time he was not one but two: one after the time of baptism, but two at the time of his birth.

We can avoid this immense sacrilege only by confessing that man was united to God by unity of person—not from the time of the ascension, resurrection, or baptism, but already in the mother, already in the womb, already in the very virginal conception. Because of this unity of person, what properly belongs to God is indiscriminately and interchangeably attributed to man, and what properly belongs to flesh is attributed to God.

Hence it is divinely written both that the Son of Man descended from heaven and that the Lord of glory was crucified on earth (John 3; 1 Cor. 2). Hence also, when the Lord’s flesh was made and created, the Word of God himself is said to have been made, the very Wisdom of God to have been fulfilled, and knowledge to have been created; likewise, in foreknowledge, his hands and feet are said to have been pierced.

Through this unity of person, I say, the following mystery was also accomplished: when the flesh of the Word was born from an intact mother, God the Word himself is most properly believed to have been born from the Virgin, though this is most impiously denied.

Since these things are so, let no one attempt to deprive holy Mary of the privileges of divine grace and her special glory. By a singular gift of the Lord and our God, who is also her Son, she must most truly and blessedly be confessed as *Theotokos*, “God-bearer.” But she is not *Theotokos* in the manner imagined by a certain impious heresy, which asserts that she should be called the mother of God only by designation, because she gave birth to a man who afterward became God—just as we speak of the mother of a priest or the mother of a bishop, not because she gave birth to a priest or bishop as such, but because she generated a man who later became a priest or bishop.

Holy Mary is not *Theotokos* in that way. Rather, she is so called because, as was said above, in her consecrated womb that most sacred mystery was already accomplished: by the singular and unique unity of person, just as the Word in flesh is flesh, so man in God is God.

### XVI

Let us now briefly and concisely repeat, for the sake of renewing our memory, what was said above about the heresies mentioned and about the Catholic faith, so that it may be understood more fully through repetition and retained more firmly through renewed emphasis.

Anathema to Photinus, who does not receive the fullness of the Trinity and preaches Christ as merely a solitary man.

Anathema to Apollinaris, who asserts the corruption of a divinity changed in Christ and removes the proper character of complete humanity.

Anathema to Nestorius, who denies that God was born from the Virgin, asserts two Christs, and, having rejected faith in the Trinity, introduces a quaternity among us.

But blessed is the Catholic Church, which venerates one God in the fullness of the Trinity and likewise the equality of the Trinity in one divinity, so that neither the singularity of substance confuses the distinctness of the persons nor the distinction of the Trinity separates the unity of the Godhead.

[Note: Although there formerly were—and still are—so many and such great idle deceits of heretics against the mysteries of the Trinity and the Incarnation, the integrity of the Catholic faith nevertheless stands like a strong and immovable rock against all winds, rains, and torrents. For, as Hilary says in book 2 of *On the Trinity*, no. 22: “Just as certain kinds of medicines are prepared so that they are useful not merely for individual illnesses but heal all illnesses in common and possess within themselves the power of a general remedy, so the Catholic faith grants the help of a common cure not against individual plagues only but against all diseases; it is not weakened by kind, defeated by number, or deceived by diversity, but stands one and the same against each and against all. For it is a great thing that there should be as many remedies in one faith as there are diseases, and as many teachings of truth as there are pursuits of falsehood. Let the names of the heretics be brought together; let all the schools come forward. Let them hear of one unbegotten God the Father and one only-begotten Son of God, the perfect offspring of the perfect Father,” and so forth.]

Blessed, I say, is the Church that believes in Christ two true and perfect substances but one person of Christ, so that neither the distinction of natures divides the unity of person nor the unity of person confuses the difference between the substances.

Blessed, I say, is the Church which, in confessing that Christ is and has always been one, confesses that man was united to God not after the birth but already in the very womb of the mother.

Blessed, I say, is the Church which understands God made man not through a conversion of nature but through the reality of person—and understands the person not as a simulated and transitory one but as substantial and permanent.

Blessed, I say, is the Church which proclaims that this unity of person has such power that, because of it, through a wondrous and ineffable mystery, it attributes what is divine to man and what is human to God. For because of it, it does not deny that man, according to his divinity, descended from heaven; and it believes that God, according to his humanity, was made, suffered, and was crucified on earth. Finally, because of it, it confesses both the man as Son of God and God as Son of the Virgin.

Blessed, therefore, venerable, blessed, and most holy is that confession, wholly comparable to the heavenly praise of the angels, which glorifies one Lord God with a threefold sanctification. For this very reason above all it proclaims the unity of Christ, lest it exceed the mystery of the Trinity.

Let these remarks have been made in passing; on another occasion, if God wills, they may be treated and explained more fully.

Now let us return to our subject.

### XVII

We said above that in the Church of God the people’s temptation was the error of a teacher, and that the temptation was all the greater when the one who went astray was himself more learned. We taught this first by the authority of Scripture and then by ecclesiastical examples—namely, by recalling those who, although for a time they were regarded as holding sound faith, nevertheless in the end either fell into a foreign sect or founded a heresy of their own.

This is certainly a great matter, useful for learning and necessary for remembrance, which we ought repeatedly to illuminate and impress upon minds by a mass of examples, so that all who are truly Catholic may know that they ought to receive teachers together with the Church, not abandon the faith of the Church together with its teachers.

But I judge that, although we can produce many examples in this kind of temptation, scarcely anyone can be compared with Origen’s temptation. In him there appeared so many things of such excellence, uniqueness, and wonder that, at the beginning, anyone might easily have judged his every assertion worthy of acceptance.

For if life confers authority, he possessed great diligence, great chastity, patience, and endurance.

> **[Note: [Col. 0660]]** Out of love for chastity he dared to emasculate his own body—not so much by cutting out his genitals with a knife as by applying hemlock to them, as he himself testifies in book 7 *Against Celsus*, saying that the Athenians had used it on the Hierophants to restrain lust. Although even the ancient Fathers differ in their opinions on this matter, it was proper to acknowledge this candidly. He himself later condemned this grave deed, even though belatedly, and strongly warned others against it in volume 15, on Matthew 19:12, both by the authority of Scripture and by the force of his arguments, so that they might not offer themselves to all as objects of insult and disgrace. He appropriately reproves Philo and Sextus in these words:
>
> “But,” he says, “no credence should be given to those who have entirely failed to understand the meaning of the sacred writings concerning that matter. For since chastity is numbered among the fruits of the Spirit, together with love, joy, patience, and the others, one ought rather to produce it as a fruit and preserve the masculine body given by God than dare anything else, so that one may not transgress, by applying to the matter under discussion this commandment: ‘You shall not damage the appearance of your beard,’ Leviticus 19:27 . . . . .”
>
> And after citing several passages of Scripture, he addresses young men endowed with fervent faith as follows:
>
> “Let the person who is about to commit such a deed consider in his heart what he will have to endure from those who, assailing him with reproaches and insults, will address him in these words: ‘A eunuch with bruised or amputated testicles shall not enter the Church of the Lord’; and they will count this man among the castrated.”
>
> A little later he adds:
>
> “What heaviness of the head do they suffer, what dizziness, and what disturbances that sometimes even invade the mind and trouble the soul’s power of forming images, as it invents for itself new and unusual forms from this material”—that is, semen.
>
> If we add to this what Augustine sharply observed in book 6, chapter 14, no. 41, of his earlier work *Against Julian*: eunuchs too are driven by the goads of carnal desire,
>
> “though with less labor, lest,” he says, “the unsuccessful attempt at intercourse itself should fall into that disgrace for which we know Calligonus, the eunuch of the younger Valentinian, to have been punished by the avenging sword after being convicted by the confession of a prostitute. Otherwise, in the *Ecclesiastical Book*, a comparison would not have been applied from this circumstance, and it would not have been said: ‘Seeing with his eyes and groaning, like a eunuch embracing a virgin and sighing,’ unless they too were moved by the effects of carnal desire, although deprived of the effects of the flesh.”
>
> If, I say, what the holy Doctor says is true, then certainly it is of no help to emasculate one’s own body by drying it up or cutting it off. Let the reader consult Baronius under the year 230 and Huet, book 1, chapter 1, no. 13, of *Origen*, against Halloix, who undertook to excuse Origen’s act in book 4 of *The Defense of Origen*.

If nobility of birth or learning confers authority, who was more distinguished than he? He was first born into a household ennobled by martyrdom and then, for Christ’s sake, deprived not only of his father but also of every resource. He advanced so greatly amid the straits of holy poverty that, for the sake of confessing the Lord’s name, he was, as they say, frequently afflicted.

> **[Note: [Col. 0661]]** He was an Egyptian by birth, born at Alexandria in the year of Christ 185, in the sixth year of Commodus and the ninth of Pope Eleutherus, when Friarius Maternus and Marcus Attilius Bradua were consuls. His father was Leonides the Martyr, who suffered capital punishment on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, when Laetus governed Egypt and raged savagely against the children of the Church.

> **[Note: [Col. 0661]]** The most learned Bishop Huet, book 9, chapter 1, no. 9 of *Origen*, citing Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* 64.1, records this remarkable and extraordinary deed performed by Origen at the age of eighteen, when Demetrius, bishop of the Alexandrian Church, had entrusted him with the care of the catechumens. In that deed he confessed the Lord’s name with the highest praise, and thereafter the pagans never spared him.
>
> For since it was customary for the ministers of the Egyptian gods, with their heads shaved, to address the people on the steps of the profane Serapis, carrying palm branches so that they might ascend to perform the sacred rites—a custom by which their most solemn ceremonies were conducted—he took palm branches and, with upright and courageous spirit, addressed the bystanders in a loud voice:
>
> “Come, take a branch, consecrated not to the idols of a temple, but to Christ.”
>
> Consequently, when the minds of the pagans were stirred against him, he was forced to flee, hide, and change his hiding places. These events occurred under Aquila, prefect of Alexandria.

Nor were these the only qualities in him that would later become occasions of temptation. He also possessed such power of intellect—so profound, penetrating, and elegant—that he surpassed nearly everyone by a great distance. His learning and the magnificence of his entire erudition were so extensive that there were few areas of divine knowledge, and perhaps none of human philosophy, which he did not thoroughly master. When the Greek sciences yielded to him, Hebrew learning too was cultivated.

> **[Note: [Col. 0661]]** The severe critic of learned antiquity, John Clericus, attempts in his second *Hieronymian Question* to argue that Origen was extremely ignorant of Hebrew, despite the opposition of Tillemont, Montefalconius, and Fabricius. There is neither time nor inclination here to examine Clericus’s arguments, since the narrow limits of these notes do not permit it. It is enough to observe that Origen consulted Jews about more difficult passages in such a way that not only Jerome but Origen himself bears witness to it. At times he even publicly disputed with them and defeated the wisest of the Alexandrian Jews from Scripture according to the Hebrew truth. He reports this himself in book 1 of *Against Celsus*:
>
> “I remember,” he says, “that I pressed these words vigorously upon a Jew who was considered wise among his own people; and when he could not explain himself, he replied as a Jew ought to have done.”
>
> Moreover, Origen himself frequently states that he carefully examined Hebrew manuscripts in order to correct the editions of Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, and the Seventy wherever they had been corrupted.
>
> Thus, in volume 8 of Huet’s edition of his *Commentary on John*, page 130, when discussing the pigs thrown headlong from the cliff and drowned in the sea by demons, he observes that the reading “in the country of the Gerasenes” or “Gadarenes” is incorrect:
>
> “Gergesa,” he says, “from which come the Gergesenes, is an ancient city beside the lake that we now call Tiberias. Near it there is a cliff adjoining the lake, from which it is shown that the pigs were driven headlong by the demons . . . . .”
>
> A little later he adds:
>
> “A similar error concerning names in the Law and the Prophets may be observed, as we learned by careful investigation from the Hebrews, when we compared our copies with theirs—copies that bear witness to the editions of Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion, which are not corrupted.”
>
> Let the reader consult Fabricius, volume 5, book 5, chapter 1, pages 223–224; Tillemont, in his discussion of Origen in the *Ecclesiastical Memoirs*; and D. Bernard of Montefalcon in the preface to Origen’s *Hexapla*.

And what should I say of his eloquence? His speech was so pleasant, so smooth, and so sweet that it seems to me that not words but a kind of honey flowed from his mouth. What difficult matters did he not clarify by the power of argument? What things arduous to accomplish did he not make appear easy?

But perhaps he merely wove his assertions together with chains of arguments? On the contrary: never was there a teacher who made use of more examples from the divine Law. But, I suppose, he wrote little? No mortal wrote more, so that all his works seem to me not merely impossible to read in their entirety, but scarcely even possible to find. And, so that nothing might be lacking from the instruments of his knowledge, he enjoyed an abundance of years as well.

> **[Note: [Col. 0662]]** He lived sixty-nine years. When labor had worn down this great man, death overtook him at Tyre in the year after Christ’s birth 254, in which year Gallus and Volusianus were killed at Interamna. He was buried in that same city. Those who visited those places report that traces of his tomb still survive today; Huet records this in book 1, chapter 4, nos. 7 and 9 of *Origen*.

But perhaps he was unsuccessful with his disciples? Who was ever more successful? From his bosom arose countless teachers, countless priests, confessors, and martyrs.

And who could recount how great his admiration, glory, and favor were among all people? Who did not hasten to him from the remotest parts of the world, somewhat more religiously inclined? Which Christian did not venerate him almost as a prophet, or which philosopher did not revere him as a teacher?

That he was revered not only in private life but even by imperial power itself is shown by histories, which relate that he was summoned by the mother of the Emperor Alexander—certainly on account of his heavenly wisdom, for which he burned with favor and she with love.

> **[Note: [Col. 0662]]** The mother was Mammaea, who, while staying at Antioch, summoned Origen. After Severus’s death he came to Rome under Zephyrinus, not, as Baronius judged, out of a desire to court Mammaea, but from the desire to know more deeply the Roman Church, the most ancient of all, as Eusebius testifies in book 6, chapter 10, of his *Ecclesiastical History*.

The histories also attest that he wrote letters to the Emperor Philip, who was the first of the Roman emperors to be Christian, with the authority of Christian teaching.

> **[Note: [Col. 0662]]** Eusebius of Caesarea, in the *Chronicle* expanded by Jerome under the year of Christ 247, writes:
>
> “Philip, the twenty-third Roman emperor, reigned for seven years. Philip made his son Philip his partner in the rule and was the first of all the Roman emperors to be Christian.”
>
> Under the year 254 he says that they were killed by Decius out of hatred for the Christian religion. Orosius, book 7, chapter 20 of his *History*, and others agree with Eusebius; I shall pass over their testimonies.
>
> In the acts of Saint Pontius the Martyr, published by Baluzius from ancient manuscripts, it is said that these men were converted to the faith by this holy man. Pagi, however, in a lengthy dissertation proves that everything reported about the Philips’ embracing Christianity is fictitious. He relies on the testimony of Ambrose, Sulpicius, and others, who say that Constantine was the first Christian emperor. Petavius, volume 2, book 11, chapter 27 of *On the Doctrine of Time*, following Baronius and citing Zonaras, observes from the coins, on which clear signs of the Philips’ paganism are found, that some people, deceived by the similarity of the name, applied to the Emperor Philip what properly belongs to Philip the Augustal of Egypt. He makes this assertion especially concerning Origen’s letters.
>
> Huet, book 1, chapter 2, no. 12 of *Origen*, says that Philip was secretly initiated by Fabian at Antioch under Babylas; hence Catholics celebrated the event, while the pagans did not criticize it because they were unaware of it. I suspect that Philip embraced Christianity because some people reproached him with doing so as a way of concealing his crimes. Besides those cited above, this is attested by Leontius of Antioch, Chrysostom, and the author of the *Alexandrian Chronicle*—though not completely. For this reason he retained many pagan practices and did not transmit the faith to the emperors who followed him. This suspicion could be strengthened by many pieces of evidence.

If anyone does not accept Christian testimony from those who report his extraordinary knowledge, let him at least accept the pagan confession of the philosophers who testify to it. For that impious man Porphyry says that, stirred by Origen’s fame, he went to Alexandria when he was almost a boy and saw him there already an old man, but plainly a man of such character and greatness that he had established the citadel of all knowledge.

> **[Note: [Col. 0663]]** Valesius, and after him Huet, infer from this testimony of Porphyry that there were two Origens, both disciples of Ammonius. One was our Origen, commonly called Adamantius, of whom Porphyry says that he won great glory among later generations through his writings and that he was well known to Porphyry when the latter was a young man. The other was the fellow student of Herennius and Plotinus, frequently mentioned in the life of Plotinus written by Porphyry. According to Longinus, he left to posterity nothing except a little book on demons. If Eunapius is to be trusted, this man was Porphyry’s fellow student and contemporary at Rome. To make the great difference between the two Origens clear, one must observe that, according to Eusebius, Adamantius died under Gallus and Volusianus, whereas according to Porphyry, in the life of Plotinus, the other Origen was still alive under Gallienus and produced a certain book.

My day would sooner end than I could even briefly touch upon the things that were outstanding in that man. Yet all these things belonged not only to the glory of Religion but also to the magnitude of the temptation. For how many people could easily reject a man of such intellect, learning, and favor, rather than adopt the opinion that they would prefer to err with Origen than to hold the truth with others?

And what more need be said? Matters came to such a point that a temptation so great—not human, but, as the outcome showed, exceedingly dangerous—drew many away from the integrity of the faith because of such a person, such a teacher, such a prophet.

Accordingly, this great and remarkable Origen, while abusing God’s grace with excessive boldness, while indulging his intellect too freely and trusting himself too much, while setting little value on the ancient simplicity of the Christian Religion, while presuming that he knew more than everyone else, and while despising ecclesiastical traditions and the teaching of the ancients, interpreted certain passages of Scripture in a novel manner.

> **[Note: [Col. 0663]]** Epiphanius explains which passages of Scripture these were in *The Anchor* 54 and 62—namely, the opening passages of Genesis:
>
> “Many,” he says, “discuss Paradise allegorically; and among them the madman Origen introduced into the world, in place of truth, some shadowy form—I do not know what.”
>
> In the later section he says again:
>
> “I return to Origen—may God forgive him—who proposed another utterly absurd story and allegory for deceiving people, and so forth.”
>
> See the holy man in the cited passage. It must nevertheless be observed here that, although Origen sinned through his frequent use of allegory, among the ancients no one explained the literal sense of Scripture more accurately than he did, as is well known to those who have examined his works. It is therefore greatly to be wished that some of the ancients had been somewhat fairer toward Origen: after making vigorous use of his labors, they later raised serious disputes against him.

Thus he deserved that what was said concerning him should also be said concerning the Church of God:

> “If a prophet arises in your midst,” Deuteronomy 13.

And shortly afterward:

> “You shall not listen,” he says, “to the words of that prophet. For,” he says, “the Lord your God is testing you, to see whether you love him or not.”

Truly it was not merely a temptation but a great temptation that a Church devoted to him and dependent upon him—suspecting and fearing nothing concerning him—should be gradually and little by little led, through admiration for his intellect, knowledge, eloquence, conduct, and favor, from the ancient Religion into a new profaneness.

Someone may say that Origen’s books were corrupted. I do not resist this claim; indeed, I prefer it. For this has been handed down and written by certain people—not only Catholics but also heretics. But what we must now observe is that, even if the man himself was not responsible, the books published under his name were nevertheless a great temptation. They are filled with many wounds of blasphemy, yet they are read and loved not as the works of another but as though they were his own. Thus, even if Origen did not possess the intention of conceiving error, Origen’s authority appears capable of persuading people to accept error.

### XVIII

The same account applies also to Tertullian. For just as Origen is easily judged the foremost of all our writers among the Greeks, so Tertullian is easily judged the foremost among the Latins.

What man was more learned than he, or more practiced in divine and human matters? With extraordinary intellectual capacity he embraced the whole of philosophy and all the philosophical schools, their founders and defenders, all their teachings, and every variety of history and scholarship.

And did he not excel in intellect so grave and forceful that he scarcely ever had anything proposed for conquest which he did not either penetrate by sharpness or crush by weight?

Who could recount the praises of his speech? It was composed with such an indescribable necessity of reasoning that it drives those whom it cannot persuade toward agreement. Almost every word of his is a judgment, and every meaning a victory.

The Marcionites, Apelles, Praxeas, Hermogenes, the Jews, the Gentiles, the Gnostics, and others know this. He overturned their blasphemies with the great and massive volumes of his works, like thunderbolts.

Yet even after all this, this Tertullian—who was insufficiently steadfast in Catholic doctrine, that is, in the universal and ancient faith, and much more eloquent than fortunate—later changed his position and finally did what blessed Hilary the Confessor writes of him in one passage:

> “By the error that followed,” he says, “he deprived his credible writings of authority.”  
> Hilary, *On Matthew*, chapter 5.

He too was a great temptation in the Church. But I do not wish to say more about him. I shall mention only that, by affirming as true prophecies the novel frenzies of Montanus that arose in the Church against Moses’ command, and those insane dreams of insane women belonging to the new doctrine, he deserved that it should also be said of him and his writings:

> “If a prophet arises in your midst.”

And immediately afterward:

> “You shall not listen to the words of that prophet. Why? Because,” he says, “the Lord your God is testing you, to see whether you love him or not.”

> **[Note: [Col. 0664]]** He means Priscilla and Maximilla, noble and wealthy women who first corrupted several Churches with gold and then with wicked doctrines. Prosper discusses them and Montanus in his *Chronicle*, under the consulship of Cethegus and Clarus, which falls in the year of Christ 170:
>
> “At this time the false prophecy called Cataphrygian prophecy began, with Montanus as its author and Prisca and Maximilla as its mad prophetesses. The province of Phrygia gave its name to the error, because its inventors first arose and lived there, and even now have peoples in those same regions. They assert that the coming of the Holy Spirit promised by the Lord occurred in themselves rather than in the Apostles. They regard second marriages as fornication, and therefore say that the Apostle Paul permitted them because he knew in part and prophesied in part; for what is perfect had not yet come. They deliriously claim that this perfection came upon Montanus and his prophetesses.”
>
> Tertullian lived until the middle period of the Church as a presbyter:
>
> “Later,” says Jerome in chapter 53 of the *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, “because of envy and insults from the clergy of the Roman Church, he fell into the doctrine of Montanus. In many books he mentions the new prophecy; specifically, against the Church he composed volumes *On Modesty*, *On Persecution*, *On Fasting*, and *On Monogamy*, six books *On Ecstasy*, and a seventh composed against Apollonius.”
>
