> His fall is truly to be lamented, since, as Jerome himself testifies in his letter to Magnus, among the Latins there was no one more learned or more acute than Tertullian, whose *Apology* and books *Against the Gentiles* contain the entire discipline of the age. He is said to have lived to an advanced old age.

### XIX

From these many and great examples of ecclesiastical men, and from others of the same kind, we must clearly take notice and understand, more plainly than daylight and in accordance with the laws of Deuteronomy, that whenever an ecclesiastical teacher has strayed from the faith, Divine Providence permits this to happen as our temptation: to test whether we love God with all our heart and with all our soul.

### XX

Since this is so, the true and genuine Catholic is the person who loves the truth of God, the Church, and the body of Christ; who places nothing before divine Religion and the Catholic faith—not the authority of any human being, nor affection, nor intellect, nor eloquence, nor philosophy—but, despising all these things and firmly, steadily, and permanently established in the faith, determines that he must hold and believe only what he knows the Catholic Church universally held from ancient times.

Whatever he later perceives to have been introduced by one individual, apart from or against all the saints, as something new and unheard-of, he understands as belonging not to Religion but rather to temptation. He is especially instructed by the words of the blessed Apostle Paul.

For this is what Paul writes in the First Epistle to the Corinthians:

> “There must also be heresies,” he says, “so that those who are approved may become manifest among you.”  
> 1 Corinthians 11.

It is as though he were saying: the authors of heresies are not immediately uprooted by divine action for this reason—that those who are approved may become manifest, that is, so that it may be revealed how steadfast, faithful, and firmly devoted each person is to the Catholic faith.

And indeed, whenever some novelty boils up, the heaviness of the grain and the lightness of the chaff are immediately seen. Then, without great exertion, what was held within the threshing floor by no weight is shaken out of it.

Some fly away at once and entirely. Others are merely shaken out: they fear perishing and are ashamed to return, wounded, half-dead, and half-alive. They have swallowed such a quantity of poison that it neither kills nor can be digested, neither forces them to die nor allows them to live. Wretched condition! Through how many waves of anxiety and storms are they driven?

Now, wherever the wind has pushed them, they are swept along by accelerated error. Now, returning to themselves, they are dashed back like opposing waves. Now, with reckless presumption, they approve what seems uncertain; now, through irrational fear, they dread even what is certain. They are unsure where to go or return, what to seek or avoid, what to hold or abandon.

This affliction of a doubtful and badly suspended heart is a medicine of divine mercy toward them, if only they understand it. For this reason they are shaken, beaten, and almost destroyed by storms of various thoughts outside the safest harbor of the Catholic faith: so that, once the sails of their exalted minds have been struck down—sails they had wrongly spread to the winds of novelty—they may return and remain within the most trustworthy anchorage of a peaceful and good mother, and first vomit up those bitter and turbulent waves of error, so that thereafter they may drink the streams of living and springing water.

Let them unlearn what they had learned badly, and from the whole doctrine of the Church let them grasp what can be understood by the intellect and believe what cannot.

### XXI

Since this is so, as I turn the same matters over and over again with myself and reflect upon them, I can scarcely marvel enough at the madness of certain people, the impiety of minds blinded, and finally the sheer desire to err. They are not satisfied with the rule of belief handed down once and received from antiquity; instead, day by day they seek something new and are always eager to add to, alter, or subtract from Religion—as though it were not a heavenly doctrine, for which revelation once given ought to be sufficient, but an earthly institution incapable of being perfected except through continual correction, or rather criticism.

Yet the divine oracles proclaim:

> “Do not move the boundaries established by your fathers.”  
> Proverbs 22.

And:

> “Do not judge one who is already judging.”  
> Ecclesiasticus 8.

And:

> “Whoever breaks through a hedge will be bitten by a serpent.”  
> Ecclesiastes 10.

There is also that apostolic saying by which the wicked novelties of all heresies are repeatedly cut down, and must always be cut down, as though by a spiritual sword:

> “O Timothy, guard the deposit, avoiding profane novelties of words and oppositions of falsely named knowledge. By professing this, some have fallen away from the faith.”  
> 1 Timothy 6.

And after all this, there are people with such hardened faces from long habit, such an anvil of shamelessness, and such diamond-like obstinacy that they do not yield to such great masses of heavenly words, grow weary under such weights, break beneath such hammers, or finally crumble beneath such thunderbolts.

He says: “Avoid profane novelties of words.” He did not say “antiquities”; he did not say “old things.” Rather, he clearly showed what follows in the opposite direction. For if novelty must be avoided, antiquity must be held; and if novelty is profane, antiquity is sacred.

And he says: “Oppositions of falsely named knowledge.” Truly, among the doctrines of heretics there is a false name, by which ignorance is disguised as knowledge, darkness as brightness, and shadows as light.

“By professing this,” he says, “some have fallen away from the faith.” What did they profess and thereby fall away, unless it was some new and unknown doctrine?

For you may hear some of them say:

> “Come, you foolish and wretched people who are commonly called Catholics, and learn the true faith, which no one understands except us. It lay hidden for many centuries but has recently been revealed and displayed. Learn it secretly and in private, for it will delight you.”

And again:

> “Once you have learned it, teach it secretly, so that the world may not hear and the Church may not know. For only a few have been granted the ability to grasp the secret of so great a mystery.”

Are these not the words of that prostitute who, in Solomon’s Proverbs, calls to herself passersby who are directing their way?

> “Whoever among you is most foolish, let him turn aside to me,” she says.

She encourages those who lack understanding, saying:

> “Gladly partake of hidden bread and secretly drink sweet water.”

What follows?

> “But he does not know,” it says, “that the earthborn perish there.”  
> Proverbs 9.

Who are these earthborn? Let the Apostle explain:

> “Those who have fallen away from the faith.”  
> 2 Timothy 2.

### XXII

It is worthwhile to examine more carefully the Apostle’s entire passage.

> “O Timothy,” he says, “guard the deposit, avoiding profane novelties of words.”

“O!” This exclamation expresses both foreknowledge and love. He foresaw the errors that were to come, and he already grieved over them.

Who is Timothy today, unless it is either, in general, the whole Church, or, in particular, the entire body of its overseers, who ought either to possess the complete knowledge of divine worship themselves or to pour it into others?

What does “guard the deposit” mean?

Guard it, he says, because of thieves and enemies, lest, while people sleep, they sow weeds over the good seed of wheat which the Son of Man had sown in his field.

“Guard the deposit,” he says.

What is the deposit? It is what has been entrusted to you, not what you have discovered; what you received, not what you devised; something belonging not to personal ingenuity but to teaching, not to private usurpation but to public tradition; something brought to you, not produced by you.

In this matter you must not be the author but the guardian; not the founder but the follower; not the leader but the one who follows.

“Guard the deposit,” he says. Preserve the treasure of the Catholic faith inviolate and undefiled. What was entrusted to you—let that remain with you and be handed on by you.

You received gold; return gold. I do not want you to substitute one thing for another. I do not want you to put down shameless lead or fraudulent bronze in place of gold. I do not want merely the appearance of gold, but its true nature.

O Timothy, O priest, O interpreter, O teacher—if the divine gift has made you capable through intellect, practice, and learning—be a Bezalel of the spiritual tabernacle. Carve out the precious jewels of divine doctrine; fit them together faithfully; adorn them wisely; add brilliance, grace, and beauty.

Let what was previously believed obscurely be understood more clearly through your explanation. Let posterity rejoice that, through you, it has understood what antiquity previously revered without understanding.

Nevertheless, teach the same things that you learned, so that when you speak in a new way, you do not speak new things.

### XXIII

But perhaps someone says: “Then will there be no development of religion in the Church of Christ?” Certainly there will be—and a very great one. For who is so envious of human beings, so hostile to God, as to try to prevent it? Yet only in such a way that it is truly a development of the faith, not an alteration. For development belongs to a thing when each thing is enlarged within itself; alteration, however, occurs when something is transformed from one thing into another.

Therefore, intelligence, knowledge, and wisdom ought to increase and advance greatly and vigorously—both in individuals and in all, both in one person and in the whole Church, through the stages of ages and centuries—but only within their own kind: that is, within the same doctrine, the same meaning, and the same judgment.

Let religion of the soul imitate the development of bodies. Although bodies unfold and extend their proportions as the years pass, they nevertheless remain the same as they were. There is a great difference between the bloom of childhood and the maturity of old age; yet the very same people who were adolescents become old men. Thus, although the condition and appearance of one and the same person change, there nevertheless remains one and the same nature and one and the same person. The limbs of infants are small, those of young people large, but they are nevertheless the very same limbs. As many joints as infants have, so many do adults; and whatever is born in the more mature stages of life already lies, in seed-form, prefigured, so that nothing new is later produced in the elderly that had not already been hidden in children.

Hence there is no doubt that this is the legitimate and correct rule of development, this the proper and most beautiful order of growth: that the increase of age should always disclose in adults those parts and forms that the Creator’s wisdom had prefigured in children. But if the human form should thereafter be changed into some figure not belonging to its own kind, or if something should be added to or taken away from the number of its limbs, the whole body must either perish, become monstrous, or at least be weakened.

So too the doctrine of the Christian religion ought to follow these laws of development: it should be consolidated by the years, expanded by time, elevated by age, yet remain incorrupt and undefiled; and it should be full and complete in all the measures of its parts and in all, so to speak, its proper limbs and senses, admitting no further alteration, suffering no loss of its distinctive character, and tolerating no variation in its definition.

For example: our ancestors long ago sowed in this ecclesiastical field the seeds of a wheat-like faith. It would be most unjust and incongruous if we, their descendants, were to reap, instead of the genuine truth of wheat, the spurious error of weeds. Rather, this is right and fitting: that, with the first and the last not differing from one another, we should harvest the fruit of a wheat-like doctrine from the growth of a wheat-like instruction. Thus, when something develops over time from those first beginnings of the seeds, and now flourishes and is cultivated, nothing in the character of the shoot should nevertheless be changed. Its appearance, form, and distinctions may be added, but the nature of each kind must remain the same.

For heaven forbid that those rose-colored plantations of Catholic understanding should be changed into thistles and thorns. Heaven forbid, I say, that in this spiritual paradise tares and aconites should suddenly grow from shoots of cinnamon and balsam. Whatever has been sown in this cultivation of the Church of God by the faith of the fathers, the same ought to be cultivated and guarded by the diligence of the children; the same ought to flower and mature; the same ought to develop and reach perfection.

It is lawful, indeed, for those ancient doctrines of heavenly philosophy to be worked over, smoothed, and polished in the course of time; but it is unlawful for them to be changed, unlawful for them to be cut down or mutilated. They may receive clarity, light, and distinction, but they must retain fullness, integrity, and their proper character.

For if this license of impious fraud is once admitted, I shudder to say how great a danger of cutting away and abolishing religion will follow. Once any part of Catholic doctrine has been rejected, another and then another, and thereafter still others, will be rejected as though this were customary and permitted. When the parts have been rejected one by one, what else will ultimately follow except that the whole too will be rejected?

Conversely, if new things begin to be mixed with old, foreign things with those belonging to the household, and profane things with what has been consecrated, this practice must spread everywhere, until thereafter nothing remains untouched, undefiled, whole, or unblemished in the Church. The shrine of chaste and incorrupt truth will become a brothel of impious and shameful errors.

But may divine mercy turn this abomination away from the minds of His own, and may such madness belong rather to the impious. The Church of Christ, however, a diligent and watchful guardian of the doctrines entrusted to her, never changes anything in them, diminishes nothing, adds nothing; she does not cut away what is necessary, does not append what is superfluous, does not lose what is her own, and does not seize what belongs to another. With every effort she attends to this one thing: by treating the ancient faithfully and wisely, to refine and polish whatever has long been formed and begun; to consolidate and strengthen whatever has already been expressed and clarified; and to guard whatever has already been confirmed and defined.

In short, what else has she ever striven for through the decrees of Councils except that what was formerly believed simply should afterward be believed more carefully; what was formerly preached more slowly should afterward be preached more insistently; and what was formerly observed more securely should afterward be cultivated with greater diligence?

This, I say, and nothing more, is what the Catholic Church, stirred up by the novelties of heretics, has accomplished through the decrees of her Councils: what she had previously received from the ancestors by tradition alone, she later committed also to posterity in the written record of Scripture, gathering a great body of matters into a few writings and, generally for the sake of clarity of understanding, marking an ancient meaning of the faith with the precision of a new designation.

[Note: [Col. 0669] It pleased the Church, and all good people, to prevent desperate men from laying a stain upon the truth, so that at times the ancient meaning of the faith might be marked by the precision of a new designation. Some, however, took offense, among them John Clericus in the first volume of his *Art of Criticism*, where he censures terms consecrated by the Church—namely, *Transubstantiation*, *Consubstantial*, and similar expressions—as though they were meaningless words. But the criticism is unjust, and he behaves as though someone were to say—as Hilary says in Book 1 *Against the Emperor Constantius*, no. 16—“I do not want new comparisons of medicines against new poisons; I do not want new wars against new enemies; I do not want recent Councils against new ambushes . . . .” The Apostle commands us to avoid profane novelties of words; why then do you exclude pious ones, especially when it has been said: “Every Scripture inspired by God is useful”? You have never read the word *Innascibilem* [“unbegotten”] in Scripture; must it therefore be denied because it is new? You define the Son as like the Father. The Gospels do not proclaim this; why do you not reject the expression? In one case novelty is chosen, in another it is removed. Where there is an occasion for impiety, novelty is admitted; but where “the greatest and sole safeguard of religion” exists, it is excluded. Why, then, when Clericus is discussing words that signify nothing, does he cite as examples those terms consecrated by the Church? No prudent person can understand, since a legitimate meaning has already been attached to those words by the Church’s sense and intention. This has always been lawful and will remain so, despite the growling of savage—and perhaps insane—critics, as the poet says: “It has always been permitted, and always will be, to coin a marked name with the current stamp.”]

### XXIV

But let us return to the Apostle. “O Timothy,” he says, “guard the deposit, avoiding profane novelties of words.” Avoid them, he says, as a viper, as a scorpion, as a basilisk, lest they strike you not only by touch but also by sight and breath.

What does “avoid” mean? It means not even to take food with such a person, as in 1 Corinthians 5. What does “avoid” mean? “If anyone comes to you,” he says, “and does not bring this doctrine” (2 John). What doctrine, unless the Catholic and universal doctrine, remaining one and the same through the succession of every age by an incorrupt tradition of truth, and destined to remain forever without end?

What then? “Do not receive him into your house,” he says, “nor say to him, ‘Hail.’ For whoever says to him, ‘Hail,’ shares in his evil works.”

“Profane novelties of words,” he says. What does “profane” mean? Things possessing nothing sacred, nothing religious, wholly alien to the inner sanctuaries of the Church, which is the temple of God. “Profane novelties of words,” he says: novelties of words—that is, of doctrines, matters, and judgments—which are contrary to antiquity and the ancient tradition.

If such novelties are received, the faith of the blessed fathers must necessarily be violated, either entirely or at least to a considerable extent. It must be declared that all the faithful of every age, all the saints, all the chaste, continent, and virginal, all clerics, Levites, and priests, so many thousands of confessors, such armies of martyrs, so many cities and peoples, so many islands, provinces, kings, nations, kingdoms, and peoples—in short, nearly the whole world, incorporated into Christ the Head through the Catholic faith over so long a span of centuries—were ignorant, mistaken, blasphemous, and unaware of what they ought to believe.

“Avoid,” he says, “profane novelties of words”—novelties which it has never belonged to Catholics to receive and follow, but which has always belonged to heretics. Indeed, what heresy has ever erupted except under a definite name, in a definite place, and at a definite time? Who has ever instituted a heresy except one who first separated himself from the consensus of the Catholic Church in its universality and antiquity?

Examples demonstrate that this is so with the greatest clarity. For who before that profane Pelagius presumed such power for free choice that he did not think God’s grace necessary to assist it, through each act, in good things? Who before his monstrous disciple Caelestius denied that the whole human race was bound under the guilt of Adam’s transgression?

[Note: [Col. 0670] He was noble by birth, but, through a defect of nature, was born a eunuch from his mother’s womb. Whether Lirinensis calls him “monstrous” for this reason is uncertain; nevertheless, the Fathers of Saint-Maur, following Garnerius, consider it probable. Certainly, in the *Commonitorium* of Marius Mercator, presented to the Church of Constantinople and to Theodosius, these words appear at its beginning: “Caelestius, indeed, was born a eunuch from his mother’s womb.”]

Who before the sacrilegious Arius dared to divide the unity of the Trinity? Who before the wicked Sabellius dared to confuse the Trinity with unity? Who before the most cruel Novatian called God cruel because He preferred the death of the one who dies to his return and life?

[Note: [Col. 0671] Let no one infer from Vincentius’s words that Novatian said that no indulgence or forgiveness had been reserved for sinners. His error was the following, which Tertullian had earlier defended: he denied that the Church had been granted the power to forgive those grave sins—namely apostasy from the faith, murder, and fornication—by herself, since pardon for such offenses had been reserved to God alone. Hence he maintained that perpetual penance should be performed for them. For lesser sins, however, he acknowledged that the Church possessed the power of forgiving. See Petavius, vol. IV, *Theological Dogmatics*, Book 3, *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, chapter 12, no. 6.]

Who before the magician Simon, struck down by apostolic severity—from whom that ancient abyss of shameful things flowed by continuous and hidden succession down to the latest Priscillian—dared to call God the creator of our evils, that is, of our crimes, impieties, and disgraceful acts?

[Note: [Col. 0671] Simon’s impure and abominable doctrines, described at length by Irenaeus, Epiphanius, and Theodoret, acquired many disciples and defenders, including Saturninus, Basilides, and Basilides’ sons Epiphanes and Isidore. Their unfortunate heirs were Cerdon and Marcion, and, in the third century of the Church, the Manichaeans. The Priscillianists succeeded them; Saint Leo calls them kindred to the Manichaeans in Letter 93 of the old numbering, now 15, chapter 4. Thus Prosper writes in his *Chronicle*, under the consuls Ausonius and Olybrius: “At that time Priscillian, bishop of Gallaecia, founded a heresy bearing his own name from the doctrine of the Manichaeans and Gnostics.” That the Gnostics originated with Simon is attested by Irenaeus.]

[Note: [Col. 0671] Irenaeus, Book 1 *Against Heresies*, chapter 20 in Erasmus’s edition, testifies that Simon wished to be glorified by everyone as a god and was regarded as such by many. Hence it is not easy to explain how he could have said that human beings are driven toward evil by the impulse and necessity of the creator God. From Irenaeus, however, we have the following account. When the impious man professed himself to be the highest power, he said that a certain Helen—the first conception of his mind—was the means through which angels and archangels had been created. They fashioned and perversely governed the world, and compelled him to come for its correction. Hence, as Irenaeus says, he added that “the prophets, inspired by the angels who fashioned the world, uttered their prophecies.” Therefore he warned those who placed their hope in him and in his Helen not to heed them [the prophets] any longer, and to act freely as they wished. Human beings, he said, are saved according to his grace, but not according to righteous works. For righteous works do not exist by nature, but accidentally, as the angels who made the world established them, bringing human beings into slavery through such commandments. Perhaps for this reason Lirinensis said that, according to Simon’s view, human beings are driven by necessity toward evil.]

He asserted that the creator God made human nature by His own hands such that, through a particular movement of its own and the impulse of a necessary will, it could do and desire nothing other than sin, because, driven and inflamed by the furies of every vice, it was swept by inexhaustible desire into every abyss of disgrace.

There are countless examples of this kind, which we omit for the sake of brevity. Yet all of them demonstrate sufficiently and clearly that among almost all heresies it is as though a customary and established practice prevails: they always delight in profane novelties, despise the decrees of antiquity, and suffer shipwreck in the faith through the opposition of falsely named knowledge.

The truly distinctive practice of Catholics, by contrast, is to preserve the deposit entrusted by the holy fathers, to condemn profane novelties, and, as the Apostle said and said again, if anyone announces anything other than what was received, let him be accursed (Galatians 1).

### XXV

Here perhaps someone will ask whether heretics also make use of testimonies from divine Scripture. They certainly do—and very vigorously. You may see them flying through every volume of the holy law, through the books of Moses and of Kings, through the Psalms, the Apostles, the Gospels, and the Prophets.

Whether among their own people or among strangers, privately or publicly, in speeches or books, at banquets or in the streets, they scarcely ever produce anything of their own that they do not also attempt to shade with the words of Scripture.

[Note: [Col. 0672] What Lirinensis says here and in the following sections, at length, about the abuse of Scripture among heretics is taken from Tertullian’s *On Prescription Against Heretics*, especially chapters 38–40. See below.]

Read the little works of Paul of Samosata, Priscillian, Eunomius, Jovinian, and the remaining plagues; you will see an infinite heap of examples, with scarcely a page omitted that has not been painted and colored with statements from either the Old or the New Testament.

But the more secretly they hide beneath the shelter of divine law, the more they must be avoided and feared. For they know that their foul odors will scarcely please anyone if they are exhaled naked and unadorned. Therefore they sprinkle them, as it were, with the aroma of heavenly speech, so that one who would easily despise a human error may not easily disregard divine oracles.

Thus they do what those people customarily do who prepare harsh drinks for children: first they smear the rims with honey, so that, when the unsuspecting age senses sweetness, it will not recoil from the bitterness.

The same is done by those who give harmful grasses and poisonous juices the outward coloring of medicinal names, so that almost no one, when he has read the remedy described above, suspects poison.

[Note: [Col. 0672] I do not dare determine whether Lirinensis took this from the fourth book of Lucretius’ *On the Nature of Things*, concerning little children who unwisely swallow harsh cups. Nevertheless, the following lines are similar to what Lucretius sings, while he raises himself beyond his deserts:

“Whenever physicians try to give children  
the bitter wormwood, they first touch the rims  
of the cups all around with sweet, yellow honey,  
so that the thoughtless age of children may be deceived  
at the lips’ edge, while meanwhile they drink down  
the bitter juice of wormwood and, having been deceived,  
may not be trapped, but rather, refreshed by such a device,  
may recover and grow strong.”

But since one who drinks a bitter and obscene error does not become strong, however much color may cover it, Saint Vincentius deliberately presents the example of those who pre-color harmful medicinal juices with the names of medicines, from which certain and deadly death arises.]

Hence the Savior also cried out: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves” (Matthew 7).

What is “sheep’s clothing” except the sayings of the Prophets and Apostles, which they themselves, with a certain sheepfold-like sincerity, wove as fleeces around that spotless Lamb who takes away the sin of the world?

Who are the ravenous wolves except the savage and rabid ideas of heretics, who always attack the sheepfolds of the Church and tear apart Christ’s flock wherever they can?

But in order to creep more deceptively among unsuspecting sheep, while retaining the ferocity of wolves they lay aside the appearance of wolves and wrap themselves in the sayings of divine law as though in fleeces, so that, when someone senses the softness of the wool, he will not at all fear the fangs of their teeth.

But what does the Savior say? “You will know them by their fruits.” That is: when they begin not merely to utter those divine words but also to explain them, and not merely to boast of them but also to interpret them, then their bitterness, their harshness, and their madness will be understood; then the new poison will exhale; then profane novelties will be revealed. Then you will first see the hedge being cut apart, the boundary stones of the fathers being moved, the Catholic faith being beaten, and ecclesiastical doctrine being torn to pieces.

Such were those whom the Apostle Paul strikes in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, saying: “For such men,” he says, “are false apostles, deceitful workers, disguising themselves as apostles of Christ” (2 Corinthians 11).

What does “disguising themselves as apostles of Christ” mean? The Apostles produced examples from divine law, and so did they. The Apostles produced the authority of the Psalms, and so did they. The Apostles produced statements of the Prophets, and they likewise produced them.

But when they began to interpret the things they had similarly produced in a dissimilar manner, then the simple were distinguished from the deceitful, the unpainted from the painted, the upright from the perverse, and finally the true Apostles from the false Apostles.

“And no wonder,” he says. “For Satan himself disguises himself as an angel of light. Therefore it is no great thing if his ministers also disguise themselves as ministers of righteousness.”

According to the teaching of the Apostle Paul, therefore, whenever false apostles, false prophets, or false teachers produce statements of divine law by which they attempt, through bad interpretation, to support their errors, there is no doubt that they are following the crafty devices of their author. He would certainly never have contrived them unless he knew that there is no easier way to deceive than to place the authority of divine words wherever the fraudulence of a wicked error is being introduced.

### XXVI

But someone may say: “How is it proved that the Devil is accustomed to use examples from the sacred law?”

Let him read the Gospels, where it is written: “Then the Devil took Him”—that is, the Lord and Savior—“and set Him on the pinnacle of the temple, and said to Him: ‘If You are the Son of God, throw Yourself down. For it is written that He has commanded His angels concerning You, that they should guard You in all Your ways; they will lift You up in their hands, lest You strike Your foot against a stone’” (Matthew 4).

What will he do to wretched human beings, when he attacked the Lord of majesty himself with testimonies from Scripture?

“If You are the Son of God,” he says, “throw Yourself down.” Why? “For it is written,” he says.

We must attend very carefully to and retain the teaching of this passage, so that, following so great an example of evangelical authority, whenever we see someone producing apostolic or prophetic words against the Catholic faith, we may have no doubt that the Devil is speaking through him.

For just as then head spoke to Head, so now members speak to members: the Devil’s members to Christ’s members, the faithless to the faithful, the sacrilegious to the religious, and finally heretics to Catholics.

But what do they say? “If You are the Son of God, throw Yourself down.” That is: if you wish to be a son of God and receive the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom, throw yourself down; that is, lower yourself from the teaching and tradition of this exalted Church, which is also regarded as the temple of God.

And if someone asks a heretic who is persuading him of such things: “Where do you prove, where do you teach, that I ought to abandon the universal and ancient faith of the Catholic Church?” he immediately replies: “For it is written.” And at once he prepares a thousand testimonies, a thousand examples, a thousand authorities from the law, the Psalms, the Apostles, and the Prophets. Interpreted in a new and evil manner, these cause the unhappy soul to plunge from the citadel of Catholicism into the abyss of heresy.

Heretics are also accustomed to deceive unsuspecting people in a marvelous way by the promises that follow. For they dare to promise and teach that in their Church—that is, in the assembly of their communion—there is a great, special, and entirely personal grace of God, so much so that, without any labor, study, or diligence, even if they neither ask, seek, nor knock, all who belong to their number are nevertheless so divinely provided for that, carried by angelic hands—that is, preserved by angelic protection—they can never strike their foot against a stone; that is, they can never be scandalized.

### XXVII

But someone may say: “If both the Devil and his disciples use divine utterances, judgments, and promises—some of them false apostles, others false prophets and false teachers, and all entirely heretics—what are Catholic Christians, the children of Mother Church, to do? How will they distinguish truth from falsehood in the sacred Scriptures?”

They will take the greatest care to do what, at the beginning of this *Commonitorium*, we wrote that holy and learned men handed down to us: they must interpret the divine Canon according to the traditions of the universal Church and according to the rules of Catholic doctrine. In that same Catholic and apostolic Church they must necessarily follow universality, antiquity, and agreement.

Whenever a part rebels against universality, novelty against antiquity, or the disagreement of one or a few erring persons against the agreement of all, or at least of a far greater number, of Catholics, they should prefer the integrity of universality to the corruption of the part.

Within that universality, they should prefer the religion of antiquity to the profanation of novelty; and within antiquity itself, they should first of all prefer the general decrees of a universal Council, if any exist, to the rashness of one or of very few.

Then, if this is insufficient, they should follow what comes nearest to it: the concordant judgments of many and great teachers.

If these principles are faithfully, soberly, and carefully observed with the Lord’s help, we shall detect the harmful errors of every rising heresy without great difficulty.

### XXVIII

It now seems appropriate to me to demonstrate by examples how the profane novelties of heretics are both detected and condemned by presenting and comparing the mutually harmonious judgments of the ancient teachers.

This ancient agreement of the holy fathers, however, is not to be sought and followed with great diligence in every minor question of divine law, but only—and certainly above all—in the rule of faith.

Nor are all heresies always to be attacked in this way, but only recent and newly arising ones, specifically when they first emerge, before the constraints of the time prevent them from falsifying the rules of the ancient faith, and before, as the poison spreads more widely, they attempt to corrupt the books of the ancestors.

Established and long-standing heresies, on the other hand, should by no means be attacked by this method, since over the long course of time they have had abundant opportunity to enjoy the truth. Therefore, whatever ancient profanations of schisms or heresies there may be, we ought in no way to confront them except either by the authority of Scripture alone, if necessary, or by avoiding them as already convicted and condemned long ago by universal Councils of Catholic priests.

Accordingly, as soon as the corruption of any evil error begins to burst forth and it steals certain words of sacred law for its own defense, interpreting them falsely and fraudulently, the judgments of the ancestors must immediately be assembled as an interpretive canon. By these judgments, whatever novelty arises may be exposed as profane without any ambiguity and condemned without any reconsideration.

But only the judgments of those fathers should be compared who, living, teaching, and remaining holy, wise, and steadfast in the Catholic faith and communion, deserved either to die faithfully in Christ or to be killed happily for Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0675] From this passage Dallaeus infers, in his book *On the True Use of the Fathers*, that the Fathers were inconsistent in the doctrine of faith. But Lirinensis means this: since he had shown above, by many examples, that through divine judgment and human weakness it sometimes happens that ecclesiastical men of great merit and learning fall and announce new doctrines contrary to the Apostle—something he had demonstrated through the examples of Photinus, Apollinaris, Nestorius, Origen, and Tertullian—no one should follow their perverse doctrines under the pretext of their authority. Thus, at the end of section 24, he says: “For this reason he wisely warns here that those who did not consistently teach and live in the Church should not be heeded.” Hence, in section 45, speaking of the priests who had assembled at Ephesus, he says: “It seemed best to bring forward the judgments of the holy Fathers; some of them were Confessors, and all were known to have been and to have remained Catholic priests, so that the ancient doctrine might be properly and solemnly confirmed by their agreement and decree.”]

These fathers are to be believed under this condition: whatever all, or the greater number, have clearly, frequently, and perseveringly received, held, and transmitted with one and the same meaning, as though through a Council of teachers agreeing among themselves, should be regarded as indubitable, certain, and established.

But whatever anyone—even if he is holy and learned, even if he is a Confessor and Martyr—has thought apart from all or even against all, let it remain separated from the authority of the common, public, and general judgment, as his own hidden and private little opinion. Otherwise, at the greatest peril to eternal salvation, we might abandon the ancient truth of universal doctrine and, following the sacrilegious custom of heretics and schismatics, pursue the novel error of one man.

Lest anyone perhaps rashly suppose that the holy Catholic agreement of these blessed fathers may be despised, the Apostle says in the First Epistle to the Corinthians: “Some indeed God has appointed in the Church: first, Apostles”—of whom he himself was one—“second, Prophets”—such as Agabus, whom we read about in the Acts of the Apostles—“third, Teachers,” who are now called interpreters; the same Apostle sometimes also calls them Prophets, because through them the mysteries of the Prophets are opened to the people.

Whoever despises these men, divinely distributed through times and places in the Church of God, while they agree in one thing according to the meaning of Catholic doctrine in Christ, does not despise a human being but God.

To prevent anyone from differing from their truthful unity, that same Apostle earnestly exhorts us, saying: “I beseech you, brothers, that you all say the same thing, and that there be no schisms among you, but that you be perfect in the same meaning and in the same judgment” (1 Corinthians 1).

If anyone withdraws from communion with their judgment, he will hear the same Apostle say: “God is not the God of dissension but of peace” (1 Corinthians 14)—that is, He is not the God of one who has departed from unity in agreement, but of those who remain in the peace of agreement—“as I teach in all the churches of the saints,” that is, of Catholics. They are holy because they persist in the communion of faith.

And lest anyone, neglecting all the others, arrogate to himself the right to be heard alone and believed alone, the Apostle says shortly afterward: “Did the word of God proceed from you, or did it come to you alone?”

And lest this be received as though casually, he adds: “If anyone thinks that he is a prophet or spiritual, let him acknowledge that the things I am writing to you are the Lord’s commandments.”

What commandments are these, unless that, if someone is a prophet or spiritual—that is, a teacher of spiritual matters—he should be a devoted guardian of equality and unity, so that he neither places his own opinions above those of others nor departs from the understanding of all?

“He who is ignorant of this,” he says, “will be ignored.” That is: the person who either does not learn what he does not know or despises what he does know will be ignored—that is, regarded as unworthy of being divinely esteemed among those united in faith and equal in humility. I do not know whether anything more bitter than this evil can be imagined.

Yet we see that this happened, in accordance with the Apostle’s threat, to that Pelagian Julian who neglected either to incorporate himself into the judgment of his colleagues or dared to separate himself from it.

[Note: [Col. 0676] Among the heretics who attempted to disturb the Church and to attack its judgments with the pen of faith, Julian was especially prominent, particularly after he was deposed from the bishopric of Eclanum under Zosimus in A.D. 418, indeed expelled from Italy, wandering and exiled, with no fixed place of residence. He first fled to Constantinople, but in A.D. 431 or 432, after the Synod of Ephesus, he was expelled and moved to Gaul. In A.D. 439, during the pontificate of Pope Sixtus, whether by fraud or under the appearance of a desire to defend himself from error, he attempted to vindicate himself; but Leo’s prudence and insight resisted his schemes, as Prosper testifies in his *Chronicle*: “At that time Julian of Eclanum, a most boastful defender of the Pelagian error, whom the unrestrained desire for his lost bishopric was driving on, attempted by many arts of deception to insinuate himself into the communion of the Church, presenting the appearance of correction. But Pope Sixtus, alertly confronting these ambushes at the urging of the deacon Leo, allowed no access to his poisonous efforts. Thus he caused all Catholics to rejoice at the rejection of the deceitful beast, as though the Apostolic sword had then for the first time cut down the most arrogant heresy.” Since the deceitful heretic was stirring up new disturbances around A.D. 444, when Leo was already Pope, Leo therefore took up arms against the wounded enemy of the faith, already weakened by many blows, as Prosper’s other work, *On the Promises and Predictions of God*, chapter 6, part 4, testifies.

Vignerius adds, following the Fathers of Saint-Maur, that after long wanderings here and there—for which Fulgentius calls him another Cain, a fugitive and exile—this unhappy heretic finally occupied, as a last refuge, a certain village in Sicily. There he taught the people of his sect and, having been a bishop, became a schoolmaster. Augustine had long before assigned him this occupation as fitting his character and learning, in Book 2 of *The Unfinished Work*, no. 51: “You speak of homonyms and equivocal terms. How, then, will even the Pelagians themselves understand you unless they are first sent to the schools of dialecticians, wherever they may be found throughout the world, for the purpose of discussing these things? Or perhaps, while explaining Aristotle’s categories to your followers before they read your books, you will yourself read them? Why not do this as well, most ingenious man, since you live in idleness at the expense of the poor wretches whom you have deceived?” Thus Jerome said of the pseudo-deacon Annianus of Celeda: “He is abundantly nourished, so that he may supply frivolous words to another’s blasphemy.”]

But now it is time to present the promised example: where and how the judgments of the holy fathers were assembled, so that, according to them, the rule of ecclesiastical faith might be established by the decree and authority of a Council.

To make this more convenient, let this be the conclusion of this *Commonitorium* here, so that we may begin the remaining matters from another starting point.

## THE SECOND COMMONITORIUM

[Col. 0677]

It has been lost, and nothing more remains from it than the final portion—that is, the sole recapitulation, which is set out below.

[Note: [Col. 0677] These two lines, by which the reader is warned of the loss of the second *Commonitorium*, are found in the ancient editions and likewise in the more recent edition based on the Royal manuscripts, according to which Baluzius corrected Lirinensis’s work. It seemed best to retain them along with all the rest.]

[Col. 0677] **XXIX.** Since these things are so, it is now time to recapitulate, at the end of this second *Commonitorium*, what was said in these two *Commonitoria*. In the preceding discussion we said that this always had been, and is still today, the custom of Catholics: to establish the true faith in two ways—first, by the authority of the divine Canon, and then by the tradition of the Catholic Church—not because the Canon alone is not sufficient in itself for every matter, but because many people, interpreting the divine words according to their own preference, conceive various opinions and errors. It is therefore necessary that the understanding of heavenly Scripture be directed by one rule of ecclesiastical interpretation, especially in those questions on which the foundations of the whole Catholic doctrine rest.

We also said that within the Church itself one must look equally to universality and antiquity, lest we be torn from the integrity of unity into some part of schism, or be driven from reverence for antiquity into the novelties of heresies. We further said that, within the antiquity of the Church, two matters must be observed with the utmost care, to which all who do not wish to be heretics ought wholly to adhere: first, if something had been decreed in ancient times by all the Catholic Church’s priests through the authority of a universal council; and then, if some new question arose for which no such decision could be found, recourse should be had to the judgments of the holy Fathers—only to those who, each in his own time [Col. 0678] and place, remaining in the unity of communion and faith, had proved themselves approved teachers. Whatever they were found to have held with one mind and agreement should be judged, without any hesitation, true and Catholic by the Church.

Lest we seem to bring forward this point more from our own presumption than from ecclesiastical authority, we offered the example of the holy Council held almost three years ago [Note: [Col. 0678] The Synod was held in the year of Christ 431, in the church called Mary. Prosper says of it in his *Chronicle*: “A Synod of more than two hundred priests having been assembled at Ephesus, Nestorius was condemned, together with the heresy bearing his name and with many Pelagians who supported a doctrine akin to his error.” See also the same author in *Against the Collator*, 21, chapter 2.] in Asia, at Ephesus, during the consulship of Bassus and Antiochus: when the rules of faith were being discussed, lest some profane novelty should perhaps creep in there under the guise of the perfidy of Rimini, it seemed most Catholic, most faithful, and most expedient to all the priests who had gathered there—nearly two hundred in number [Note: [Col. 0678] In the first act of the Council, after the bishops’ subscriptions, we read: “After all these men had subscribed to the deposition of Nestorius, other bishops came to the holy Synod, and they too subscribed to the condemnation already pronounced. Thus the bishops who deposed Nestorius numbered more than two hundred; for some took the place of other bishops who had been unable to come to the metropolitan city of Ephesus.”]—that the judgments of the holy Fathers should be brought forward publicly. It was evident that some of these Fathers had been martyrs, others confessors, and all Catholic priests and had remained so; [Col. 0679] thus, properly and solemnly, on the basis of their agreement and decree, the reverence due to the ancient doctrine might be confirmed and the blasphemy of profane novelty condemned.

When this had been done, that impious man Nestorius, contrary to Catholic antiquity [Note: [Col. 0679] Although this is true, it did not deter men of hardened conscience from undertaking the defense of the impure Nestorius and from assailing holy Cyril with dreadful calumnies. Not to mention that impostor who sold Nestorius as a saint and Cyril as though he were a restorer of the Apollinarian heresy, though the most learned Petavius convicted him by a great mass of evidence in volume 5 of *On the Incarnation*, it is certainly astonishing that the author of *Critical and Ecclesiastical Letters*, letter 6, should have uttered such unseemly things about Cyril as that, in the Ephesian Synod, he had shown little concern for either justice or injustice.

And since he misuses the letters of the holy ascetic Isidore of Pelusium in order to dispel the darkness cast over the truth, it seems worthwhile to note the following few points. Four letters of Isidore to Cyril survive, namely letters 310, 323, 324, and 370. In the first he certainly draws a comparison between Theophilus and Chrysostom: just as Theophilus oppressed Chrysostom, so Cyril oppressed Nestorius. Yet he says this not so much in his own voice as from the opinion of others: “Many of those who have been compelled to go to Ephesus denounce you as one pursuing private hostility rather than seeking what is right according to Christ’s judgment. They say: He is the son of Theophilus’ sister and imitates his disposition; for just as Theophilus openly poured out his fury against the religious and God-loving John, so this man too desires to act arrogantly.”

A critical light ought to have been applied to these complaints. For if they were fabricated by impious men—as indeed the Council itself testifies in its letter to the clergy of Constantinople, where it says that many charges were brought by the heretics not only against Cyril but also against Memnon—then the order of reason required that the accusations of enemies of the faith be regarded as worthless. For, as Augustine wittily says in book 1, chapter 6, number 11 of *Against Parmenian*, the man most justly defeated murmurs against an innocent judge with the same blindness with which he litigated against an innocent adversary.

Indeed, the Pelusiot deliberately adds to what has been quoted: “although there is a great and wide difference between those who are judged.” The excellent man well knew that Cyril, as he himself says in letter 370, followed and held only the doctrine of Saint Athanasius, while Nestorius openly professed and pursued an impious doctrine opposed to it. For this reason, in the same honored letter, he wonderfully exalts the holy man as one displaying the appearance and bearing of that great Mark; and in letter 324 he calls him an admirable man, while in the preceding letter, 323, he praises him most highly because he vigorously followed and defended the mind of the holy Fathers, especially Athanasius, concerning the mystery of the Incarnation.

It is therefore neither surprising nor novel that Cyril resisted Nestorius because of the perversity of his doctrine, after he had omitted no service or act of kindness by which he might recall that ruined man from error. This is clear from the letters addressed to him and from the letter sent to the Egyptian monks. When the poison of Nestorius’ homilies had reached the monks, Cyril warned them in a serious letter, lest simple people should be infected by the plague. In it he taught them the true faith; when copies of it were brought to Constantinople, many were strengthened in the ancient faith. For this reason the leaders and magistrates thanked Cyril in letters addressed to him.

Nestorius’ mind was consequently inflamed against the Alexandrian bishop, and he attempted everything in order to avenge himself on him. Abusing the Emperor’s favor, he stirred up accusations against Cyril, as is shown by the sharp and threatening letters sent to Cyril, in which Nestorius is blamed as shameless, restless, and eager for disturbances. Yet shortly afterward, when the clouds had been dispelled, the serene face of truth appeared: Nestorius was recognized as a heretic and impious man, while Cyril, by the agreement of the whole world, was judged a man of the highest integrity and, as our Vincentius puts it, in harmony with sacred antiquity.

For these immense services to the Catholic faith, and so that he might act with greater authority as the Apostolic See’s legate at the Synod, he was given a *phrygium*—that is, a mitre—by Pope Celestine. Cardinal de Noris, in book 2, chapter 12 of his *History of the Pelagian Controversy*, thinks it was called a *phrygium* because it was a distinctive head-covering used by the Phrygians. Hence the Latin poet, in Virgil’s *Aeneid* 9.616, reproaches the Phrygians, Aeneas’ companions, because they wore mitres on their heads:

> “And tunics with sleeves, and they wear the bands of a mitre—  
> O truly Phrygian women—for indeed you are not Phrygian men!”

The reader should consult the honored Cardinal and will find in him many ancient testimonies illuminating the matter.] while blessed [Col. 0680] Cyril was judged to be in harmony with sacred antiquity.

And so that nothing should be lacking for the certainty of the facts, we published the names and number—although we had forgotten the order—of those Fathers alongside whose harmonious and concordant judgment the statements of sacred law were there explained and the rule of divine doctrine firmly established. It is by no means superfluous to list them here also, in order to reinforce the memory.

**XXX.** These, then, are the men whose writings were read aloud at that Council, either as judges or as witnesses. Saint Peter [Note: [Col. 0680] The holy man forgot not less the order than the number. He forgot the order because, after Peter and Athanasius, Julius and Felix ought to have been mentioned; after Theophilus, Cyprian and then Ambrose; after them, Nazianzenus, Basil, and Nyssenus, without omitting Atticus, bishop of Constantinople, and Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium, whose testimonies were cited last at the Synod.

It follows that he also forgot the number, because there were not ten, as he says shortly afterward, but twelve who were introduced at the Synod as witnesses, judges, and advisers. Father Hardouin has shown, on the basis of manuscript codices and of Marius Mercator, that the testimonies of Amphilochius and Atticus ought certainly to be retained, in volume 1 of the *Councils*, page 147. One may add the very ancient codex of the Vatican Library, no. 1342, which likewise contains those testimonies and which Baronius frequently cites in his *Annals*.] Alexandrian bishop [Note: [Col. 0680] Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* 8.13, Valesius’s edition, lists those who had suffered noble martyrdom at Alexandria and throughout Egypt and the Thebaid: “The first of all to be named,” he says, “is Peter, bishop of the Alexandrian Church, an outstanding teacher of the Christian religion.” His book *On the Divinity* was commended not only at the Ephesian Synod but shortly afterward at Chalcedon as well.

His martyrdom occurred in the year 311, the ninth year of the persecution under the Emperor Maximian, if Diocletian’s persecution began in the year of Christ 302 rather than 303, as the most expert chronologists nevertheless believe.] an outstanding teacher and most blessed martyr.

Saint Athanasius, bishop of that same city, a most faithful teacher and most eminent confessor.

Saint Theophilus [Note: [Col. 0680] Prosper says the following about Theophilus and John Chrysostom in his *Chronicle*, under the consulship of Vincentius and Fravitus, which fell in the year of Christ 401: “John of Constantinople and Theophilus of Alexandria were regarded as illustrious bishops. But discord darkened both of them; it proceeded so far that John, oppressed by Theophilus, was compelled to go into exile in Pontus, although the greater part of the bishops, following the example of the Roman Pontiff, preserved communion with him.”], likewise bishop of that city, a man sufficiently distinguished in faith, life, and knowledge. His successor was the venerable Cyril, who now adorns the Alexandrian Church.

[Col. 0681] And lest this doctrine perhaps be thought to belong to only one city and province, those lights of Cappadocia were also brought forward: Saint Gregory, bishop and confessor of Nazianzus; Saint Basil, bishop and confessor of Caesarea in Cappadocia; and likewise the other Saint Gregory, bishop of Nyssa, who, by his faith, conduct, integrity, and wisdom, was fully worthy of his brother Basil.

And lest it be demonstrated that only Greece or the East had always held this view, certain letters of Saint Felix [Note: [Col. 0681] At the Ephesian Synod the words of Julius were read first and those of Felix afterward. But in the *Commonitorium* of Lirinensis and Hypatius, bishop of Ephesus, against the Acephali, Felix is placed before Julius, in accordance with chronological order. He was certainly not the Felix who was substituted by Constantius for Liberius, but the first of that name, ordained on 27 December 269 and deceased on 22 December 274.

This is clear from the name of Maximinus, bishop of Alexandria, to whom the Pontiff’s letter cited by the Synod was addressed on the occasion of Paul of Samosata’s expulsion from his Church. The encyclical letter of the Council of Antioch was addressed to Dionysius of Rome and to Maximinus; hence it may be inferred that Maximinus was a contemporary and equal of Felix I, the successor and heir of Dionysius of Alexandria.

Michael Le Quien proves that Felix’s testimony cited at the Synod was spurious. Yet from Liberatus and Hypatius, Father Constant, in volume 1 of *Pontifical Letters*, section “On the Writings of Pope Felix,” shows that it is wholly genuine, although he readily concedes that false or adulterated letters of Felix were circulated by the Acephali.

Both these highly learned men, however, compelled by a great mass of arguments, maintain with Leontius of Byzantium—who flourished under Justinian, in book 8 of *On the Sects*—that the fragment read at the Council of Ephesus was not by Pope Julius but rather by Apollinaris or by some Timothy infected with the same disease. They do not say this because anything contrary to orthodox faith appears in the letter, especially in the fragment used by the Council, as Leontius says, but because the Apollinarists circulated it under Julius’ name; therefore it should be treated as worthless.

These are the arguments that move learned men:

1. Nyssenus, in his work against Apollinaris, reports many things contained in this letter and refutes them as erroneous.
2. Leontius, relying on several copies, asserts in the cited passage that the letter belonged not to Julius but to Timothy, who had Apollinaris as his teacher.
3. Another opponent of the Severians, who advances the same point as Leontius, says that the phrasing is not appropriate to Julius as a translation from Latin, since it is excessively Greek.
4. At its beginning it bears the inscription, “To my most desired lord,” which certainly also appears in another letter falsely attributed to Julius.
5. Prosdocius, to whom the letter was sent, is not called either presbyter or bishop, contrary to the custom of Roman prelates.
6. Beneath Catholic words lie seeds of an impious doctrine. For when it speaks of the body, it never calls it endowed with a mind or animated; indeed, the words found in number 4 reveal an Apollinarian: “But whoever proclaims the body divine because of its union with the uncreated God, and worships both together as one uncreated God according to their composition, in which both are one, shall be blessed.”

Nevertheless, these careful scholars did not believe that this brought any reproach upon the holy Synod. Since a letter circulated under the name of Julius through the hands of many people, and since nothing openly false appeared in it, there was no reason for the Synod to distrust the inscription. But when several others emerged from the same workshop, which the Eutychians vigorously exploited, lovers of the faith were compelled to devote themselves to uncovering the author. The letter seems to have been composed after the heresy of Macedonius, and therefore after the year of Christ 260.] of the martyr and Saint Julius, bishops of the city of Rome, were read there as well.

And so that not only the head of the world but also its flanks might bear witness to that judgment, [Col. 0682] from the south there was brought forward blessed Cyprian, bishop of Carthage and martyr; from the north, Saint Ambrose, bishop of Milan.

These, then, are all the teachers, advisers, witnesses, and judges brought forward at Ephesus in the sacred number of the Decalogue. Holding their doctrine, following their counsel, believing their testimony, and obeying their judgment, that blessed Synod pronounced on the rules of faith without weariness, presumption, or favoritism.

A much larger number of our ancestors could have been brought forward, but it was not necessary. For the time of the proceedings ought not to have been occupied by a multitude of witnesses, and no one doubted that those ten had truly held the same view as all their other colleagues.

**XXXI.** After all this we also added the judgment of blessed Cyril, which is contained in the ecclesiastical acts themselves. For when the letter of Saint Capreolus [Note: [Col. 0682] Capreolus succeeded Aurelius, though the year is uncertain; he appears to have held office around the year of Christ 430. Theodosius invited him by letter to the Synod together with the African bishops, specifically naming Augustine.

But since Augustine had gone to heaven about nine months before the Council’s celebration, and since, owing to the severity of the times, the Vandals under their leader Geiseric were laying waste and depopulating everything, the Primate could not summon a Synod so that delegates—or at least an honorable and solemn embassy—might be sent from it to Ephesus. Nevertheless, in observance of ecclesiastical discipline, he wished to send Besula, a Carthaginian deacon, to the Synod. Capreolus himself mentions this embassy in his letter to Vitalis and Tonantius, which Sirmond published from a manuscript codex.] bishop of Carthage had been read—a bishop who intended and requested nothing other than that, once novelty had been defeated, antiquity [Note: [Col. 0682] Capreolus’ words are these: “I wish your holiness to be asked again and again that, with the Holy Spirit cooperating—of whose presence in your hearts, in everything you are about to undertake, I have no doubt—you may, furnished with the strength of ancient authority, drive from your midst new doctrines, previously unheard by ecclesiastical ears, and thus resist every novel error.” Ferrandus quotes a fragment of this letter in his letter to Pelagius and Anatolius, deacons of the Holy Roman Church, though in a different Latin version.] might be defended, Bishop Cyril spoke and gave his decision as follows. It does not seem out of place to insert it here also.

At the end of the acts he says:

“And this letter of the venerable and most religious bishop of Carthage, Capreolus, which has been read, shall be inserted among the records of the faith. Its clear meaning is this: he wishes the dogmas of the ancient faith to be confirmed, but those that are novel, needlessly invented, and impiously promulgated to be rejected and condemned.”

All the bishops cried out:

“These are the voices of all; this is what we all say; this is the wish of all.”

What, finally, were those voices of all, or what were the wishes of all, except that what had been handed down from ancient times should be retained, while what had recently been invented should be rejected?

After this we admired and proclaimed how great were the humility and holiness of that Council: so many priests, almost all of them metropolitans, of such learning and doctrine that nearly all could have debated about dogmas, and therefore might have seemed, by their very gathering together, to possess the confidence to propose and establish something of their own—yet they innovated nothing, presumed nothing, [Col. 0683] and arrogated nothing to themselves. They took every precaution not to hand on to posterity anything they had not received from the Fathers. They not only ordered the matter well in the present, but also provided an example for the future, so that later generations too might revere the dogmas of sacred antiquity and condemn the inventions of profane novelty.

We also attacked Nestorius’ criminal presumption: he claimed that he alone and for the first time understood sacred Scripture [Note: [Col. 0683] This is clear from interrogation 23, whose words are also quoted by Marius Mercator in the version of the acts of the sixth session of the Council of Ephesus, though somewhat differently: “I observe,” Nestorius says, “that our people possess much religion and the greatest zeal for piety; yet, because they are ignorant of the knowledge of the dogmas, they greatly err and go astray. This, however, should not be counted as a fault of the people themselves, but of their teachers—though I say this with what measure of modesty is appropriate—for they too lack the ability to propose to you anything concerning the more exact dogmas.”

After these words had been read in the Synod, Peter, an Alexandrian presbyter and chief secretary, said: “Here he plainly declares that none of the teachers who existed before him had spoken to the people about those things that he himself has spoken.” The same man who persuaded his disciples to show no reverence to the Church spread throughout the world was Montanus, as Apollinaris and Eusebius testify. See Melchior Cano, book 3 of *On Theological Places*, at the beginning.] and declared that all who before him had been endowed with the office of teaching and had interpreted the divine utterances were ignorant of them: all the priests, all the confessors and martyrs—some of whom had explained God’s law, while others had agreed with or believed those who explained it. Finally, he asserted that the whole Church, even now, was in error and had always been in error, since, as it seemed to him, the Church had followed and continued to follow ignorant and mistaken teachers.

**XXXII.** Although all these points, taken together, were more than sufficient to overwhelm and extinguish every profane novelty, nevertheless, lest anything seem lacking to such fullness, we added at the end the twofold authority of the Apostolic See: one belonging to the holy Pope Sixtus [Note: [Col. 0683] Cardinal Thomasius rightly writes “Xystus” in volume 1 of his *Theological Institutes*, whereas Baluzius writes “Sixtus.” For, according to Father Coustant, the name appears in this form in less ancient copies, contrary to the testimony of the Greeks and of ancient monuments.

Xystus succeeded Celestine in the year of Christ 432, during the consulship of Aetius and Valerius. Prosper says of him in his *Chronicle*: “Xystus, the forty-second bishop, is placed over the Roman Church for eight years and nineteen days, with peace throughout the city and remarkable agreement.” Thus, when Vincentius was writing in the year of Christ 434, he rightly said that Xystus was then illuminating the Roman Church.

When he was formerly a presbyter of the Roman Church, the Pelagians falsely represented him as a defender of their error. But when the diligence of the Africans exposed the Pelagians’ schemes, he was the first, after Pope Zosimus, to pronounce an anathema against the Pelagians before the Roman people. He did so by sending letters to Augustine and Alypius, in which the grace of God was wonderfully commended. Thus Augustine, rejoicing with him in his reply, says: “How much do you think we rejoiced while reading those longer writings of yours, or while offering them, as we were able, to others for reading, and still offering them to those whom we can? For what can be read or heard more agreeably than so pure a defense of God’s grace against its enemies, from the mouth of one who had previously been falsely represented as a powerful patron of those same enemies?” See the present letter 191.

Saint Leo seems to be speaking of Xystus III in sermon 82, chapter 5, when discussing the dedication of a church, perhaps Saint Mary Major. The *Liber Pontificalis* reports, as does Pope Adrian in his letter to Charlemagne, that this church was built or restored by the excellent Pontiff: “You venerate with fitting honor the martyrs and the mother of the martyrs, and also the memory of him who on this day doubled the ancient festival by consecrating this place: a magnificent builder of walls, but a more magnificent builder of souls, extending works of piety beyond the boundaries of his age, so that devoted posterity might enjoy the benefits of his institutions even in its own time, both by inhabiting what he founded and by doing what he taught.”] who now venerably [Col. 0684] illuminates the Roman Church; the other belonging to his predecessor, Pope Celestine of blessed memory, which we likewise judged necessary to insert here.

Thus Saint Pope Xystus says in the letter he sent to the bishop of Antioch concerning the case of Nestorius [Note: [Col. 0684] That is, to John. The letter was sent on 17 September, during the consulship of Theodosius for the fourteenth time and Maximus, in the year of Christ 433, after peace had been made between Cyril and John, as is clear from another letter sent to Cyril on the same day.]:

“Therefore, since, as the Apostle says, there is one faith, let us believe what has manifestly prevailed and let us say what must be held.”

What, then, are those things that must be believed and said? He continues:

“Let nothing further be permitted to novelty, since nothing should be added to antiquity. Let the clear faith and belief of our ancestors not be disturbed by any admixture of mire.”

This is entirely apostolic. He adorns the belief of the ancestors with the light of clarity, while describing novel profanities as an admixture of mire.

But holy Pope Celestine likewise speaks in the same manner and with the same judgment. In the letter he sent to the priests of Gaul, rebuking their connivance because, by abandoning the ancient faith to silence, they allowed profane novelties to arise, he says:

“Rightly does the matter concern us if we foster error by silence. Therefore let such men be corrected; let them not be free to speak according to their own will.”

Here someone might perhaps wonder whom he forbids to speak freely according to their own will: the preachers of antiquity, or the inventors of novelty. Let him speak for himself; let him himself remove the readers’ doubt. He continues:

“Let novelty cease”—that is, if the matter is as it is alleged before me, namely, that you make your cities and provinces consent to certain novelties through a culpable dissimulation—“let novelty cease, then, if this is so, from assailing antiquity.”

This, therefore, was the blessed judgment of blessed Celestine: not that antiquity should cease from overwhelming novelty, but rather that novelty should cease from attacking antiquity.

**XXXIII.** Whoever resists these apostolic and Catholic decrees must first insult the memory of Saint Celestine, who decreed that novelty should cease from attacking antiquity. He must then mock the decisions of Saint Xystus, who judged that nothing further should be permitted to novelty, since nothing ought to be added to antiquity. He must also despise the decrees of blessed Cyril, who praised the zeal of the venerable Capreolus with great commendation because he desired the ancient dogmas of the faith to be confirmed and novel inventions condemned.

He must trample upon the judgments of the Ephesian Synod—that is, of almost the entire East’s holy bishops—who, by divine inspiration, resolved that posterity should believe nothing other than what the sacred antiquity of the Fathers, [Col. 0685A] united with itself and agreeing in Christ, had held. They too, crying out and acclaiming with one voice, testified that these were the voices of all, that this was what all desired, and that this was what all judged.

Thus, just as nearly all heretics before Nestorius had been condemned because they despised antiquity and asserted novelty, so Nestorius too—the author of novelty and attacker of antiquity—was condemned.

If anyone dislikes their agreement, inspired by the gift of sacred and heavenly grace, what else follows except that he asserts that Nestorius’ profaneness was not justly condemned? Finally, he must despise as mere refuse the whole Church of Christ and its teachers, the Apostles and prophets, especially blessed Paul: the Church, because it has never departed from the reverence due to the faith entrusted to it once for all, to be cultivated and developed [Col. 0685B]; Paul, because he wrote:

> “O Timothy, guard the deposit, avoiding profane [Col. 0686A] novelties of words,”

and likewise:

> “If anyone announces to you anything other than what you received, let him be anathema.”

If neither apostolic decisions nor ecclesiastical decrees are to be rashly violated—decrees by which, in accordance with the sacred agreement of universality and antiquity, all heretics, and finally Pelagius, Caelestius, and Nestorius, were rightly and deservedly condemned—then all Catholics thereafter who strive to prove themselves legitimate children of the Church their mother must necessarily cling to, adhere to, and devote themselves unto death to the faith of the holy Fathers; but they must detest, dread, attack, and persecute the profane novelties of profane men.

These are almost all the matters discussed at greater length in the two *Commonitoria* and now compressed into a somewhat shorter recapitulation, so that the memory for whose support [Col. 0686B] I composed this work might be restored by repeated reminder and not be overwhelmed by weariness at excessive length.

**In the year of the Lord 449. Saint Eucherius, bishop of Lyons.**

# Prolegomena

[Col. 0685]

## Historical-Literary Notice on Saint Eucherius

*(From Schoenemann’s* Historical-Literary Library, *Leipzig, 1794, volume II.)*

### § I. Life

[Col. 0685C]

Eucherius was a Gaul, descended from senatorial blood, and his father was Valerianus, whom most people identify with Priscus Valerianus, who obtained the prefecture of Gaul around the same time and was related to the Emperor Avitus.

He married Galla, a woman of equal nobility, and had by her two sons. One of them, Salonius, later presided over the Church of Geneva; the other, Veranius, succeeded his father in the bishopric of Lyons.

Around the year 409 or 410, while he was still vigorous and in the prime of life, he withdrew to Lérins. From there he went with his wife and sons to the nearby island of Lerona, now Saint Margaret’s Island, and lived as an anchorite. Nevertheless, he devoted his chief care to the education of his children, and entrusted Salonius [Col. 0685D] for some time to the instruction of the Lérins teachers Honoratus, Salvianus, and Vincentius.

[Col. 0686C] Hardly any other of the more distinguished members of the Gallican Church acquired such esteem among the best and most learned men of the age as Eucherius. He lived familiarly with many people, maintained literary correspondence with most of them, and was honored by all with immense praise.

At length this reputation led to his elevation, around the year 434, to the bishopric of Lyons, an office which is generally thought to have been held by him until the year 450 [Note: [Col. 0685D] This was a different Eucherius from the Gallic bishop who lived in the sixth century and signed various Gallican councils, such as the Fourth Council of Arles in 425, the Council of Carpentras in 527, and the Councils of Orange and Vaison in 529. Nor was that man bishop of Lyons, as certain people [Col. 0686D] falsely persuaded themselves. Josephus Antelmius learnedly and perceptively refutes them in his *Assertion for the Uniqueness of Saint Eucherius, Bishop of Lyons*, which his brother Carolus Antelmius published after his death at Paris, by Claude Briasson, 1726, quarto.].

### § II. Writings

The following writings of Eucherius of Lyons are currently in circulation:

1. A letter *On the Praise of the Desert*, addressed to Hilary of Arles, written in the year 428.

2. A *Paraenetic Letter* to his kinsman Valerianus, *On [Col. 0686D] Contempt for the World and Secular Philosophy*, written in the year 432.

[Col. 0687A] 3. The *Book of Forms of Spiritual Understanding*, addressed to his son Veranius. It is also otherwise entitled *On the Form of Spiritual Understanding*.

4. Two books of *Instructions*, addressed to his son Salonius. One treats questions concerning the more difficult passages of the Old and New Testaments; the other contains explanations of Hebrew names and bears that title.

5. The *History of the Passion of Saint Maurice and His Fellow Martyrs of the Fortunate Theban Legion at Agaunum*, which some deny to Eucherius and attribute to a later author.

6. Homilies, namely those recognized by everyone as genuine.

7. The first of three *Exhortations to Monks* which Holstenius published under Eucherius’ name in his *Code of Rules* [Col. 0687B].

8. An *Epitome of the Works of Cassian*.

Several homilies of Eucherius have been lost, unless others perhaps survive in the collection of homilies which, in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, bears the name of Eusebius Emissenus, or of Eusebius Gallicanus.

The following works are attributed to Eucherius, but falsely:

1. A commentary on Genesis.
2. Four books of commentaries on the Books of Kings, first published by Johannes Alexander Brassicanus.
3. A letter to Faustinus, published by Labbe.
4. A letter to a certain Philo, which Baluzius printed at the end of Agobard.
5. A twofold rule for monks in Holstenius’ *Code of Rules*.
6. The entire collection of homilies circulated under the name of Eusebius Emissenus.

### § III. Editions
[Col. 0687C] A complete collection of all Eucherius’s minor works does not yet exist. The first worklet to see the light of day through the printing press was the *Passion of Saint Maurice and His Companions*, but in an interpolated form and without his name, in Mombritius’s *Lives of the Saints*.
