Not long afterward, in 1516, there appeared at Basel, from the revision of Beatus Rhenanus, a letter bearing the author’s name on its title page, addressed to Valerian; it was quickly reprinted there in 1520 with Erasmus’s notes, and again at Paris in 1525. Shortly afterward, at Basel, apud Cratander, in 1530—or somewhat earlier at Paris, apud Claude Chevallon, without a date—there appeared the *Formulae of Spiritual Understanding* and the two books of the *Instructions*. In the following year, John Alexander Brassicanus added two spurious works from the remains of the Buda Library, the *Commentaries on Genesis* and on the *Books of Kings*, and at the same time carefully corrected the book of the *Formulae* from a manuscript codex. All these works were reprinted together at Rome by Paulus Manutius in 1564, under the care of Petrus Galesinius, and through the care of Andreas Schottus in 1618, in volume V of the Cologne *Bibliotheca Patrum*.

Meanwhile, a letter *On the Praise of the Desert* addressed to Hilary was discovered and published at Paris in 1578 by Gilbert Genebrard—or rather by Dionysius Faucherius. The genuine homilies, rescued from obscurity and published, appeared through Johannes Livineius together with Theodore the Studite at Antwerp in 1602. Thereafter, with the homilies omitted, Eucherius’s genuine works—namely, the *Formulae of Spiritual Understanding*, the two books of the *Instructions*, and the letters to Valerian and Hilary—were presented together at Lyon in 1613 in Vincentius Barralis’s *Lérins Chronology*. Finally, with the *Passion of Saint Maurice* and those spurious commentaries on Genesis and the Books of Kings added, they were reprinted in the *Maxima Bibliotheca Patrum* at Lyon in 1677.

After this, the individual works—especially the ascetic ones—were printed either separately or together with other works. To prevent the following chronological catalogue of all the editions from becoming burdensome, it is useful to summarize them briefly here.

Thus, after the editions of Mombritius, Surius, and Stevartius, the *Passion of Saint Maurice* was published in a more authentic form by Chiffletius in his *Pauline Illustrated* in 1662; it was thereafter reprinted in the *Maxima Bibliotheca Patrum* at Lyon in 1677, volume XXVII, and again by Ruinartus and in the *Acta Sanctorum* of the Bollandists.

The letter to Valerian was reprinted at Lyon in 1541 and 1627; with the notes of Heribert Rosweyd at Antwerp in 1621, at Munich in 1635, at Genoa in 1644, and at Paris in 1646; under the care of Philip Labbe, together with the letter to Hilary and other ascetic works, at Vienna in Austria in 1670, Brussels in 1671, Paris in 1673, and Venice in 1726. It was also quite often translated into the vernacular languages of more recent peoples.

The *Formulae of Spiritual Understanding* was included by Flacius Illyricus in the *Key of Sacred Scripture*, Basel, 1580, and was frequently reprinted in various places together with that work.

The letter to Hilary, with the notes of Heribert Rosweyd, appeared at Antwerp in 1621; it was thereafter transferred into the Cologne *Bibliotheca Patrum* of 1618, volume XV, and was copied together with the letter to Valerian at Lyon in 1627, Genoa in 1644, and Paris in 1673.

The homilies published by Livineius were included in the Paris *Bibliotheca Patrum* of 1624, 1644, and 1654, volume II, and migrated into Combefisius’s *Preaching Library*.

[Col. 0688C] Moreover, in 1657, in the *Library of Manuscripts*, he published under Eucherius’s name a letter to Faustus or Faustinus. In 1661 Lucas Holstenius produced in the *Code of Rules* three rules of Eucherius for monks—one genuine, but two falsely bearing his name. A letter to a certain priest Philo, falsely bearing Eucherius’s name, was found by Baluzius and published by him at the end of Agobard’s works at Paris in 1665.

Finally, Montefalco provided a specimen of the *Epitome of Cassian*, translated into Greek, in his edition of Athanasius’s works; I remember having spoken of this in the discussion of Cassian.

The chronological index follows.

## Sixteenth Century

**Without year, place, or printer (Milan); folio.** [Col. 0688D] *The Passion of Saint Maurice and His Fellow Soldiers*, in volume II of Boninus Mombritius’s *Lives of the Saints*, folios CLIII–CLV.

This is the first edition of this work, but, as noted earlier, it is not authentic.

**1516. Basel; quarto.** *The Paraenetic Letter of the Lord Eucherius to His Kinsman Valerian, on Contempt of the World* (from the revision of Beatus Rhenanus). Catalogue of the Bunau Library.

**1520. Basel; apud Andreas Cratander; quarto.** *The Paraenetic Letter of the Illustrious and Eloquent Man Eucherius, Bishop of Lyon, to His Kinsman Valerian, Calling Him Away from Love of the World and Devotion to Profane Philosophy toward Devotion to Piety and True Wisdom, with Notes by Desiderius Erasmus.*

[Col. 0689A] The letter of Erasmus that was prefixed to this little book in the Basel edition of 1531 undoubtedly belongs to this edition. It is addressed to Alard of Amsterdam, professor of the liberal arts, from whom he seems to have received a manuscript copy without the author’s name:

> “Although the little book you sent pleased me wonderfully in every respect through its own merits, it pleased me especially because I remember having read it and liked it when I was a boy. If you attribute anything to my judgment, I see nothing produced by men of our religion who have also flourished in the glory of eloquence that can be compared with this style. Everywhere it displays an outstanding craftsman, whether one considers its arrangement, its frequent new transitions, or its unusual opening, such as the threshold of an argument. It treats every part of the persuasive genre. Nowhere does it loiter among commonplaces. It presses and insists upon its arguments; it pierces wonderfully with its emphatic conclusions; it delights and moves equally through its aphorisms. What is even more remarkable is that the discourse is so modulated, constructed, and adorned with the figures of Isocrates that it nowhere grows cold or becomes inept. It is so pointed that it is meanwhile vigorous; so carefully wrought that it is nevertheless clear; so novel that it is free from the tedium of affectation; so lively that it is nonetheless grave and serious; so rhetorical that it is nevertheless genuinely Christian (*γνησίως*, genuinely). Finally, it is so sharp and vehement that it remains everywhere like itself, hastening with equal intensity all the way to the final line—a sign, evidently, of a sound and vigorous intellect. When Gennadius attributes a scholastic style to this work, if I am not mistaken, he found it somewhat deficient in esoteric learning. Otherwise, the style itself sufficiently proves that this little book was not translated by Rudolph Agricola, especially since it contains certain figures that could not possibly correspond to Greek discourse. Gennadius indicates that it belongs to Eucherius, bishop of the Church of Lyon. He immediately recalls this letter, which he had written to his kinsman Valerian, on contempt of the world and on abandoning devotion to profane philosophy. And would that the rest of this author’s works still existed—either the book in which he explained, in excerpts, the more obscure chapters of the divine volumes, or the one in which he condensed Cassian’s lengthy works into an epitome.”

**1525. Paris, apud Jodocus Badius; octavo.** *Eucherius’s Letter to Valerian; also Distichs of a Certain Ancient Philosopher*, etc. Beneddictines, in the *Literary History of France*.

**Without year. Paris, through Claude Chevallon; octavo or duodecimo.** *The Formulae of Spiritual Understanding of Eucherius, Archbishop of Lyon; the Two Books of the Instructions, Now Published for the First Time; the Paraenetic Letter to His Kinsman Valerian, with the Notes of Desiderius Erasmus; the Consolatory Letter of Saint Basil, Bishop, against the Troubles of the World, Now Published for the First Time; and Something Concerning the Resurrection of the Flesh from the Letter of the Blessed Jerome to Pammachius against the Errors of John of Jerusalem: All Published through the Efforts of Petrus Gerardus.* Catalogue of the Royal Library of Paris and Baluzius, volume II, p. 641.

Although this edition lacks a date, since its age cannot be uncertain on account of the printer or bookseller, and since it seemed appropriate not to interrupt the sequence of these editions that present several of Eucherius’s works together, it has been placed here.

Petrus Gerardus prefixed a letter dated at Paris on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of November, without a year, to William the Small, bishop of Troyes and auditor of the royal confession. Since, as he says, he had obtained these otherwise rare works of Eucherius through William’s favor, he says that he would be ungrateful and shameless unless he dedicated them to his name:

> “Moreover, what is being sent into public view has been industriously printed and prepared by Claude Chevallon, a man most devoted to the theological doctorate, who labored strenuously so that, as far as possible, the copy he had obtained through his own generosity might be cleansed of the many errors by which it had almost been destroyed. For this purpose he also consulted the most ancient Septuagint interpreters and the translations of other codices to which that age was accustomed. He adopted them without reluctance, so that in this way he might demonstrate his diligence to you and contribute in this respect also to sound studies.”

The Lyon edition of 1613 provides us with a copy of this letter.

It should be noted, however, that Casimir Oudinus (*Commentary on the Sacred Writers of the Church*, volume I, p. 1220), who places the origin of this edition around the year 1520, compared its first work, the *Formulae of Spiritual Understanding*, with the manuscript codices of the Paris libraries—Royal Library 3795, Colbert Library 1893, and Saint-Germain 250—and rightly judged this first edition to be the only genuine one and to conform to these codices, which were six or seven hundred years old.

He observes that the later editions—for example, the Basel edition of 1531, which he calls the second, the Roman edition of 1564, and the Lyon edition of 1677—are twice as large and contain countless additions drawn from authors later than Saint Eucherius, especially Saint Gregory the pope, so that the genuine work of Eucherius scarcely constitutes half of what was printed in the latest editions of this book.

**1530. Basel, apud Andreas Cratander; quarto.** *The Book of the Formulae of Spiritual Understanding of the Blessed Eucherius, Bishop of Lyon; His Book on Difficult Questions of the Old and New Testament; An Interpretation of Hebrew Names and of Other Things Contained in Sacred Scripture; and His Letter to Valerian on Contempt of the World: From the Edition and with the Notes of Desiderius Erasmus.* Catalogue of the Royal Library of Paris.

**1531. Basel, in the Frobenian workshop; folio.** *The Most Learned Works of the Blessed Eucherius, Bishop of Lyon, No Less Pious than Learned, Newly Revised through the Care and Assistance of John Alexander Brassicanus, Jurist*, whose contents are as follows:

- Three books of commentaries on Genesis;
- Four books of commentaries on the Books of Kings;
- One book of the *Spiritual Formulae*, carefully revised, with all the material that had been greatly lacking in the earlier edition added;
- Questions on the Old and New Testament;
- An interpretation of Hebrew names and also of other names found in sacred Scripture;
- The paraenetic letter to his kinsman Valerian, on contempt of the world, with the notes of Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam.

At the end: Basel, in the workshop of Froben, through Jerome Froben and Nicholas Episcopius, in August (on the title page, September), 1531.

Concerning the editor John Alexander Brassicanus, see what we discuss below under Salvianus. He first dedicated the first work to the same man to whom he dedicated Salvianus, Christoph Stadion, bishop of Augsburg. His letter, dated at Vienna in Austria, from the royal college, on 20 December 1530, is full of praise for Eucherius but contributes little to the present matter.

The second work, which bears a separate title, and the third, were dedicated to Janus a Sivolla, knight and jurist, in letters written there in the same year and month. In these letters there are pleasant and noteworthy remarks about the varied fate of ancient books within and outside the city of Vienna while it was besieged by the Turks.

Brassicanus praises divine care and providence for the preservation of the writings of ancient authors, especially those that expound sacred subjects, and takes Eucherius as an example:

> “For in the preceding year, when the most savage Turks were pressing Vienna with an unheard-of siege, and were laying waste with iron and fire everything around it—namely, cities, fortresses, monasteries, villages, hamlets, fields, vineyards—they also overran this royal monastery of the Order of Saint Bernard, which they had chosen to call the Monastery of the Holy Cross after Saint Leopold, archduke of Austria. Although they had treated it so miserably that one might now search for the monastery within the monastery, they nevertheless left all the books, both ancient and still entirely unpublished, unharmed and undiminished in any respect. Thus the fire seems to have spared them no otherwise than it spared Anchises when Aeneas carried his father on his shoulders; neither the force of the flames nor the hostile and disastrous encounter could harm him, just as the fire of Etna allowed those pious young men, who sheltered their parents at their sides, to depart safe and sound. This most savage fire therefore spared Eucherius, and the Turks abstained from exercising every right of war against all the books there. Meanwhile our own soldiers, within the walls, were scattering all the books and corrupting every volume. They were scarcely prevented by force or removed by authority from plundering even the public libraries. You see, excellent man, how these beasts differ from the Turks in name alone and not even in conduct. Certainly there was no less danger from the garrison installed within than from the external enemy, and that one particularly destructive.”

Brassicanus himself first produced the first two works from the parchment or paper manuscripts of the monastery just mentioned. The third, as the title itself states, he once again revised against a manuscript copy from the same monastery.

Concerning this labor of his he writes to the same Janus a Sivolla:

> “You yourself, my Janus, are an eyewitness of how much labor I had to expend—or, to speak more truly, how much tedium I had to swallow—in restoring and cleansing those *Spiritual Formulae* of Eucherius. The recently published copy was not merely mutilated but also extraordinarily corrupt. So far am I from blaming the man who first gave us this copy that I consider the generosity and openness of this learned man worthy of praise: he preferred to offer scholars what he had conveniently acquired rather than allow it to perish. But we used a copy that was both complete and exceptionally authentic, which the Reverend Father Lord John Hartmann, abbot of the Holy Cross in Austria, a unique patron of learning and of learned men, and my chief honor and support, willingly and wholeheartedly shared with me. First we supplied what was lacking, and we conscientiously corrected what had been corrupted. So that scholars may recognize this more clearly, I shall offer only two examples, from which they may easily estimate the rest, as one judges a lion from its claws.

> “The first chapter, on divine names, which had been entirely missing, has now been restored from an old and no less authentic copy. I deliberately pass over how much was added in all the chapters. In Eucherius’s preface it reads: ‘But according to allegory, baptism; according to anagogy, angels’; whereas it should read: ‘Waters, according to allegory, baptism; according to anagogy, angels.’ Hence the passage: ‘And let the waters that are above the heavens praise the name of the Lord,’ and so forth. I do not begrudge anyone who brings ancient writers into the light; but I am more astonished if anyone devotes all his effort to publishing them in a corrected form.”

The sixth work, namely the paraenetic letter to Valerian, was copied from Erasmus’s edition, with his notes and his letter to Alard added. The Frobenian press, moreover, took care that the volume should be printed both conveniently and handsomely.

**1541. Lyon, apud Sebastian Gryphius; octavo.** *Eucherius’s Letter to His Kinsman Valerian on Contempt of the World.* Beneddictines, in the *Literary History of France*.

**1564. Rome, apud Paulus Manutius; folio.** *The Works of the Blessed Eucherius, Bishop of Lyon, or Commentaries on Genesis and the Books of Kings, etc., from the edition of Petrus Galesinius.* Catalogue of the Royal Library of Paris and Pinellius. If only they had supplied the complete title!

**1574. Cologne, apud Gervinus Calenus and the heirs of Quentel; folio.** *The Martyrdom of the Most Courageous Martyrs Maurice and His Companions, Written by Eucherius of Lyon, with His Letter to the Bishop Silvius (so);* in volume V of Laurentius Surius’s *Lives of the Saints*, pp. 325–330.

**1578. Paris, apud Aegidius Gorbinus, under the sign of Hope; octavo.** *Saint Eucherius, Bishop of Lyon, to Hilary of Arles, on the Praise of the Desert, Now Published for the First Time from the Lérins Library; with the Funeral Oration of Hilary of Arles for Saint Honoratus.* Cinelli, *Flying Library*, volume II, p. 265.

This edition is generally said to be Gilbert Genebrard’s. Genebrard, however, prefixed the dedication, while Dionysius Faucherius wrote the preface. I remember that it was reprinted in the *Lérins Chronography*, although that work maintains a profound silence concerning the copy from which this little book was published. For the other works contained in this volume, see under Hilary of Arles.

[Col. 0693A] **1580. Basel, from the workshop of Hervagius, through Eusebius the bishop; folio.** *The Book of the Formulae of Spiritual Understanding of Eucherius, Bishop of Lyon*, at the end of Matthias Flacius’s *Key of Sacred Scripture*.

Flacius appended it as an appendix to his *Explanation of Individual Words and Names*, so that readers might learn the opinion of the ancients on this subject. I do not doubt that this is the first edition of the work that we have mentioned. It was reprinted frequently in various places—for example, at Basel in 1609, Frankfurt in 1659, and Copenhagen in 1695. In the last edition Eucherius’s book appears on pp. 1345–1372.

## Seventeenth Century

**1602. Antwerp; octavo.** *The Homilies of Eucherius, Bishop of Lyon*, from the edition of Johannes Livineius of Antwerp, canon, at the end of Theodore the Studite’s *Catechetical Sermons*, beginning on p. 372.

As we have shown above, this is the first edition of the sermons that are truly regarded as Eucherius’s and that differ from those circulating under the name of Eusebius Emissenus or Gallicanus.

**1613. Lyon, at the expense of Petrus Rigaud; quarto.** *The Formulae of Spiritual Understanding of Eucherius, formerly Archbishop of the Church of Lyon, a most learned theologian; the Two Books of the Instructions; his Paraenetic Letter to Valerian* [from the edition of Petrus Gerardus]; *together with his Letter to Hilary, with a preface by Dionysius Faucherius, monk of Lérins, and annotations by Vincentius of Salerno;* in Vincentius Barralis Salernus’s *Chronology of the Saints and Other Illustrious Men and Abbots of the Holy Island of Lérins*, compiled into one work by Vincentius Barralis Salernus, monk of Lérins.

We noted above that Gerardus’s preface is reproduced here.

**1617. Ingolstadt, from the Ederian press; quarto.** *Saint Maurice, Leader of the Theban Legion, or the Martyrdom of Saint Maurice, Written by Saint Eucherius, Bishop of Lyon, Now Published Again, with Notes and Observations through the Care and Labor of Petrus Stevartius.* The *Office of Saint Maurice* is also added. Catalogue of the Royal Library of Paris.

**1618. Cologne, at the expense of Antonius Hierat; folio.** *All the Extant Pious Works of the Blessed Eucherius, Bishop of Lyon, Concerning Sacred Scripture.*

1. *The Formulae or Phrases of Sacred Scripture.*
2. *Questions on the Old and New Testament.*
3. *Interpretation of Hebrew Names.*
4. *On the Solitary Life, to Valerian*, illustrated, revised, and corrected through the efforts of Andreas Schottus of the Society of Jesus.

The commentaries on Genesis and the Books of Kings, attributed to Eucherius, are also added; in volume V, part I, of the *Great Library of the Fathers*, pp. 739–918. The preface of Alexander Brassicanus is included.

In the preface Schottus discusses Eucherius’s writings, both genuine and spurious. There also, from p. 543 to p. 738, are inserted the homilies of Eusebius Gallicanus, newly revised by Andreas Schottus after the edition of Johannes Gaigneius and enriched with sermons.

**1618. Cologne, at the expense of Joannes Kreps and Hermann Mylius; folio.** *The Martyrdom of Saints Maurice and His Companions, the Agaunian Martyrs, Written by Eucherius, Bishop of Lyon*, in the second edition of Surius’s *Lives of the Saints*, volume II, for 22 September, pp. 220–223.

**1621. Antwerp, from the Plantin press, apud Balthasar Moretus, the Widow of Joannes Moretus, and Joannes Meursius; octavo.** *The Paraenetic Letter of the Blessed Eucherius, Bishop of Lyon, to His Kinsman Valerian, on Contempt of the World.* The *Life of Saint Paulinus of Nola, a True Contemner of the World*, is added.

The editor is Heribert Rosweyd, who scattered several brief notes throughout the work and dedicated it, as well as the following work, to Henricus Vander Heyden, abbot of Villers.

**1621. Antwerp, in the same place and from the same booksellers; octavo.** *The Little Book of the Blessed Eucherius, Bishop of Lyon, on the Praise of the Desert, to Hilary, Monk of Lérins*, with the brief notes of Heribert Rosweyd.

**1622. Cologne, at the expense of Antonius Hierat; folio.** *The Little Book of the Blessed Eucherius, Bishop of Lyon, on the Praise of the Desert, with the Brief Notes of Heribert Rosweyd*, in volume XV, whether called a supplement to or an appendix of the *Great Cologne Library*.

**1624. Paris …; folio.** *The Homilies of Eucherius, Bishop of Lyon, with the Catechetical Sermons of Theodore the Studite, Printed According to the Edition of Johannes Livineius*, in the fourth edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum* of Bignius, volume II, beginning at column 767.

**1626. Lyon, at the expense of Ludovic Prost, heir of Rovillius; folio.** *The More Difficult Questions of Saint Eucherius on the Old and New Testament; and His Interpretation of Hebrew Names*, in chapter 115, pp. 204–219, and chapter 164, pp. 423–426, of Ludovic de la Cerda’s *Sacred Adversaria*. Fabricius is mistaken when he counts chapter 159 among these, for it has nothing whatever to do with Eucherius but belongs to La Cerda himself.

**1627. Lyon, apud François de la Bottière; duodecimo.** *The Ascetic Works of Saint Eucherius, together with Other Works of Dorotheus*, edited by the priest Turrianus. The Benedictines in the *Literary History of France* do not praise this work in detail but note that it contains two letters of Eucherius, to Hilary and to Valerian.

**1635. Munich; twenty-fourmo.** *On True Wisdom, True Virtue, and Tranquility of Mind*, by Saints Eucherius of Lyon, Martin of Braga, and Magnus Wigo, bishops. See the Brussels edition of 1671.

**1644. Genoa, apud Joannes Maria Pavoni; octavo.** *The Genuine Letters of the Divine Eucherius, Bishop of Lyon, Which Many Desired to Possess at the Encouragement of an Excellent Preacher, Though Hardly Any Could Obtain Them; Most Recently Arranged for Printing by the Members of the Society of Jesus Established at the College of Genoa.* Cinelli, *Flying Library*, with Sancassani’s continuation, volume II, p. 265; Baluzius’s library, volume II, p. 1002.

**1644. Paris, apud three booksellers; folio.** *The Homilies of Eucherius, Bishop of Lyon*, in volume II of the *Bibliotheca Patrum* of Bignius, at the very end, after the sermons of Theodore the Studite. Copies bearing the year 1654 belong to the same edition.

**1646. Paris; duodecimo.** *The Paraenetic Letter of Saint Eucherius to His Kinsman Valerian*, edited by Philip Labbe. Fabricius, *Bibliotheca of Medieval and Modern Latin Authors*, Padua edition, volume I, p. 116.

[Col. 0695A] **1657. Paris, apud Sebastian and Gabriel Cramoisy; folio.** *The Letter of Eucherius, Bishop, to Faustus or Faustinus, Priest of the Island, on the Site of the City of Jerusalem and of Judea Itself*, in volume I of Philip Labbe’s *New Library of Manuscript Books*, p. 665 ff.

**1661. Rome, printed by Vitale Mascardo; quarto.** *The Exhortation of Saint Eucherius to Monks; His Saying to Monks; His Admonition to Virgins*, published by Lucas Holstenius from two manuscript codices of Floriacum belonging to the Queen of Sweden, in the appendix to the *Code of Rules*, p. 89 ff., in the Paris edition, pp. 55–62.

**1662. Paris, at the expense of Antonius Bertier; folio.** *Several Homilies of Saint Eucherius, Bishop of Lyon*, in François Combefis’s *Preaching Library*, distributed in eight volumes. The latest edition is the Venetian one of 1749, in seven volumes. The editor took from Livineius all the homilies that he inserted into this collection under Eucherius’s name.

**1662. Dijon; quarto.** *The Passion of the Agaunian Martyrs, by Saint Eucherius, Bishop of Lyon*, in Petrus Franciscus Chiffletius’s *Pauline Illustrated*, part I, pp. 86–92.

**1665. Paris, apud François Muguet; octavo.** *The Letter of Saint Eucherius, Bishop of Lyon, to Philo the Priest*, published by Stephanus Baluzius from an old manuscript codex belonging to Petrus Marnaesius, senator of Grenoble, in the notes to Saint Agobard’s works, volume II, pp. 155–156.

**1670. Zwickau; octavo.** *A Fragment of a Homily of the Blessed Eucherius on the Conception of the Blessed Virgin*, in Christian Daumius’s *Homilies of the Fathers on the Nativity of Jesus Christ*, pp. 213–255. From Livineius.

**1670. Vienna in Austria, from the press of Matthias Cosmerovius; octavo.** *The Paraenetic Letter of the Divine Eucherius, Bishop of Lyon, to the Lord Valerian, His Kinsman, Calling Him from Love of Profane Philosophy to the Study of True Wisdom.* Also a practical letter of Blessed Francis Borgia, formerly duke of Gandía and later superior general of the Society of Jesus, offered as a New Year’s gift in 1671 to the most illustrious confraternity of gentlemen under the title of the Assumption of the Mother of God, established in the professed house of the Society of Jesus at Vienna.

**1671. Brussels, apud Francis Foppens; twenty-fourmo.** *On True Wisdom, True Virtue, and Tranquility of Mind*, by Saints Eucherius of Lyon, Martin of Braga, and Magnus Wigo, bishops. A new edition according to the copy printed at Munich in 1635.

The work contains Eucherius’s paraenetic letter to Valerian. A certain priest of the Society of Jesus, director of the Latin confraternity established in the Jesuit college at Brussels under the title of the Blessed Virgin Mary of the Visitation, who wished to remain hidden under the initials G. H., arranged for a reprint of the edition of these little books made at Munich in 1635, which, as he says, was immediately sold out.

**1673. Paris, apud Sebastian Cramoisy; duodecimo.** *The Way to Eternity, or Three Little Works of Saints Eucherius of Lyon and Hilary of Arles: 1. On the Praise of the Desert; 2. On Contempt of the World; 3. On the Life of Saint Honoratus.* Catalogue of the Teller Library, p. 34a.

**1677. Lyon, apud the Anissons; folio.** *All the Extant Pious Works of the Blessed Eucherius, Bishop of Lyon, Concerning Sacred Scripture*, illustrated, revised, and corrected through the efforts of A. Schottus of the Society of Jesus, in volume VI of the *Greatest Library of the Fathers*, pp. 822–1014.

Printed according to the Cologne edition; but after the fourth work there were inserted the *Letter to Hilary on the Praise of the Desert* and the *Acts of the Holy Agaunian Martyrs* (from Chiffletius), followed by the letter to the bishop Salvius. In the same work, volume XXVII, p. 180 ff., one reads the *Exhortation of Eucherius to Monks* and his *Saying to Them*, from the edition of Lucas Holstenius.

**1689. Paris; quarto.** *The Passion of Saints Maurice and His Companion Martyrs, by Eucherius, Bishop of Lyon*, from Chiffletius’s *Pauline Illustrated* and various manuscript codices of the Royal Library and other libraries, with a preliminary notice by Theodorus Ruinartus; in his *Acts of the Martyrs*, p. 289 ff.; in the second edition, revised by the author himself, which appeared at Amsterdam from the Wetstein press in 1713, folio, p. 271; and in the Verona edition, from the Tumermann press, 1731, folio, pp. 237–243.

## Eighteenth Century

**1726. Venice, apud Bartholomeus Giavarina, in the district of Saint John Chrysostom; sixteenths.** *The Works on True Wisdom, True Virtue, and Tranquility of Mind of Saints Eucherius of Lyon, Martin of Braga, and Magnus Wigo, Bishops*, dedicated to the most illustrious and reverend Lord Marcus Gradenicus, patriarch of Venice and primate of Dalmatia, etc. The *Flying Library* of Cinelli, cited above.

**1747. Venice …; folio.** *The Letter of Eucherius, Bishop of Lyon, to Faustus, Priest of the Island, on the Site of the City of Jerusalem and of Judea Itself* (wrongly attributed to him), in Blasius Ugolini’s *Treasury of Sacred Antiquities*, volume VII, column 1201.

**1757. Antwerp, apud Bernhard Albert van der Plassche; folio.** *The Passion of Saints Maurice and the Other Martyrs of the Theban Legion, Published by Peter Francis Chiffletius, S.J., and by Ruinartus, Collated with Other Manuscripts.* Also *The Interpolated Passion from the Manuscript of Saint Maximinus of Trier, Collated with the Editions of Surius and the Manuscripts of Fulda, Saint Salvator of Utrecht, and Marchiennes, with Notes by John Stilting*, etc., in the Bollandist *Acta Sanctorum*, September, volume VI, pp. 342–349.

A preliminary commentary was added, in which everything relating both to the history itself and to the authenticity of the acts is illuminated with uncommon learning and skill. Other documents relevant to the same acts are also interspersed.

## Translations

Of all Eucherius’s works, almost only the letter to Valerian has been translated into a modern language. If I am not mistaken, we owe the first undertaking of this kind to the French. The Italians did not neglect it, and Spanish and English translations are also said to exist. We have been able to gather the following.

### I. Letter to Valerian

**1552. Lyon, chez Mace Bonhomme; quarto.** *Saint Euchier to Valerian, a Rational Exhortation, Withdrawing Him from Worldliness and Profane Philosophy [Col. 0697A] to God and the Study of Sacred Letters, Translated into French Verse, with Annotations, by Barthélemy Aneau.* Catalogue of the Royal Library of Paris.

**1659. Lyon; octavo.** The same work, together with the *Letter to Hilary on the Praises of the Desert*, by an anonymous translator [Note: Fabricius counts Canagium and Antonius Godellus among the French translators], in a French book entitled *Christian Solitude*, volume I, p. 137 ff. A third edition of this work in 1662 is recorded by the Benedictines in the *Literary History of France*.

**1672. Paris, chez Pierre le Petit; duodecimo.** *Saint Eucher, On Contempt of the World*, translated into French by Robert Arnauld d’Andilly, with the Latin following. The same work appears in his *Works*, volume I, Paris, 1675, p. 24 ff.

**1609. Venice.** *The Letter of Saint Eucherius, Holy Bishop of Lyon, etc.*, translated from the Spanish (of Ludovicus of Granada) into Italian by Giovanni Giolito. It appears together with *The Book of Spiritual Grace*, etc., by Giovanni Lanspergius, p. 210 ff.

[Note: This Spanish translation is praised in the catalogue of the Barberini Library, volume I, p. 382, but the place and year are not mentioned.]

**1715. Milan, through Giuseppe Pandolfo Malatesta; octavo.** The same work, translated from the Latin by Don Carlo Giacinto Gariboldi, together with the Latin text.

### II. The Passion of the Holy Agaunian Martyrs

**1705. Amsterdam; duodecimo.** *A Historical and Critical Dissertation on the Martyrdom of the Theban Legion, with the History of the Martyrdom of This Legion Attributed to Saint Eucher.*

The original of this dissertation by John Dubourdieu, a Calvinist minister of the Savoyard congregation in London, appeared in English around the year 1696 [Note: Christoph Saxius, *Literary Onomasticon*, volume V, *Analecta*, p. 652]. But the French translation is more commonly available. The Antwerp editors of the *Acta Sanctorum* attempt to refute him assiduously and not without bitterness.

**1778. Rome, in the printing house of Saint Michael at Ripa; quarto.** *The Passion of Saints Maurice and His Companion Martyrs, Written by Saint Eucherius, Bishop of Lyon*, in the *Authentic Acts of the First Martyrs of the Catholic Church*, collected by Father Ruinartus and translated by Francesco Maria Luchini, volume II, pp. 457–467. An introduction precedes it, written not by Ruinartus but by the translator himself.

[Col. 0697]

# ANDREAS SCHOTTUS’S PREFACE TO THE WORKS OF SAINT EUCHERIUS

[Col. 0697B] To the Pious Reader, Andreas Schottus of the Society of Jesus.

Here, pious reader, we present the works of the Blessed Eucherius, Bishop of Lyon, hitherto scattered and published in various forms—first by Johannes Sichardus, and afterward with some improvements through the work of Alexander Brassicanus, a man exceptionally diligent in gathering the writings of the ancients from their shipwreck. Concerning these writings of Eucherius I shall now briefly disclose my judgment.

First I shall discuss these legitimate little works of the bishop, useful—and I might almost say necessary—for understanding Sacred Scripture; then I shall speak of the illegitimate or spurious works falsely attributed to him. For I have always considered it of the greatest importance to distinguish true things from false by the proper art of discrimination, and likewise to be able to distinguish the genuine (*γνήσια*, genuine) writings of the ancient Fathers from the counterfeit (*νόθα*, spurious), lest anyone misuse them.

Bede frequently employs the work of the *Spiritual Formulae*, just as he transcribed many works of the ancients, especially Augustine’s, without naming them. For that reason, however, the work should not, with Sixtus of Siena, be taken away from Eucherius and attributed to Bede.

Here too one finds the mystical significance of the members of God and of other things pertaining to human form that are attributed to God in the sacred Scriptures. These are also read in the little book *On the Essence of the Trinity*—which is falsely ascribed to the Blessed Augustine in volume IV—as Conrad Brunus observed in chapter 4 and John Molanus in book II, chapter 3, both while discussing images.

For this reason we have taken care to assign throughout the entire work the passages of Sacred Scripture cited here and there in individual lines, so that we might carry before the reader, as it were, a torch in the darkness.

The Blessed Augustine also wrote *Questions on the Old and New Testament* in three books, as did other Greek Fathers. But Alphonsus de Castro, in his book *On Heresies*, teaches that the work is not Augustine’s legitimate offspring. Julian of Toledo likewise wrote a work entitled *Antikeimena* (*Contradictions*), which was vindicated for him in the catalogue of the Blessed Ildephonsus; because, through the injury of time, they could not summon their father, these works often went forth into Germany without an author’s title.

That letter to Valerian, his kinsman, *On Contempt of the World and on Abandoning Devotion to Profane Philosophy*, as Gennadius praises it in chapter LXIII, is altogether golden and honey-sweet. He also sent to the bishops Uranium and Salonius a work explaining the more obscure chapters of the holy Scriptures.

Here you have the testimony of Claudianus Mamercus, bishop of Vienne, from his book *On the State of the Soul*. “I would certainly not pass over Eucherius,” he says, “who, though now alive for me in his teaching and known to me through face-to-face discussions, was plainly a man of vigorous age and mature mind, despising earth and aspiring to heaven, humble in spirit, ardent in merit, and likewise exceedingly subtle in intellect, full of knowledge, fluent in speech, by far the greatest of the eminent bishops of his age. Having published many volumes of diverse works for the advancement of the faith, he also preached much and nobly to the people concerning the state of the soul.” Thus far he.

I shall also produce the testimony of the critic of this vigorous age concerning Eucherius’ almost unique eloquence: “I see nothing produced by men of our religion who have also flourished in the glory of eloquence that can be compared with this style. In every respect it displays outstanding artistry, whether one considers its arrangement, its frequent new transitions, or its unconventional opening, as though it were the threshold of an argument. It handles every part of the persuasive genre. Nowhere does it languish in commonplaces. It presses and insists more forcefully through its arguments; it pierces wonderfully with its emphatic conclusions; it delights and moves at once through its maxims. And what is even more remarkable, the speech is so modulated, constructed, and adorned with the figures of Isocrates that nowhere does it grow cold or become inept. It is so pointed that it is nevertheless sinewy; so elaborately wrought that it is nevertheless lucid; so novel that it remains free from the tedium of affectation; so lively that it is nonetheless grave and serious; so rhetorical that it is nevertheless genuinely Christian. Finally, it is so sharp and vehement that it remains everywhere like itself, hastening with equal intensity to the very last step—a sign, plainly, of a sound and vigorous intellect.”

If only there still existed the *Epitome of Eucherius* by John Cassian, which I see mentioned in the catalogues of ecclesiastical writers. It would doubtless bring some light to obscure passages and some assistance to corrupt ones. I have now reviewed what survives and what has perished.

I now come to those works which I believe are falsely attributed to Eucherius. Three books on Genesis and a Commentary on the Four Books of Kings were published long ago at Basel by Andreas Cratander and Johannes Frobenius under Eucherius’ name. The latter work was excessively enlarged—almost like a *Stromateus* or miscellany—by Angelomius of Lisieux, of the Benedictine order. So that we might more readily believe it to be Eucherius’, the bold title was added: “To Uranus and Salonius, brother bishops”—plainly the men to whom Eucherius had also addressed other short works: to the former, the *Questions on Both Testaments* and the *Interpretation of Hebrew Names*; to the latter, the *Spiritual Formulas*. Away with it! Let us expose the deception by stripping off its mask. The following arguments will show that this work is not by the blessed Eucherius.

First, its date refutes the attribution. For, according to Gennadius, Eucherius died while the emperors Valentinian and Marcian were ruling, around the year 440 of the world redeemed by Christ. In that famous letter to Valerian he himself testifies that he had flourished five years earlier, that is, in the year 1185 after the founding of Rome, or 435 after Christ. He was a contemporary of Petronius, bishop of Bologna, who was illustrious in the twenty-seventh year of that century. But the author of that Commentary on the Books of Kings—whoever he may be—repeatedly cites Pope Gregory I, who lived almost two centuries later, and transcribes him word for word on nearly every page. Indeed, it is not so much a commentary on Gregory’s Books of Kings as on his truly golden *Moralia on Job*. At the end of the first book of the *Exposition of Gregory’s Moralia*, the reader is referred there.

Furthermore, if it is permissible to investigate by conjecture, he was not a Gaul but a Briton. For in the third Commentary on the Books of Kings, chapter 22, he says:

“The wheels placed beneath the bases lifted the laver of the temple from the ground for transport, while in our own recent times the blessed pope Gregory, strengthened by evangelical utterances, governed the Roman Church. Those same wheels, supporting the chariots of God, carried it far away when the most reverend Fathers Augustine, Paulinus, and their other companions, strengthened by those same evangelical utterances and sent by him, came to Britain and entrusted the word of God to peoples who had long been unbelieving.”

Since this is so, it follows that this writer was a contemporary—σύγχρονος, that is, of the same time—as the blessed Gregory, through whose work Britain was first illumined by the light of Christ’s Gospel; and that he was an Englishman, not the Gallic Eucherius, who shared a homeland with Paulinus, the disciple of Ausonius.

“But why,” you will say, “should we not assert that Bede the Venerable was the author?” This is also the judgment of Sixtus of Siena, that most learned Dominican, in book four of the *Sacred Library*. Moreover, a large part of this commentary is found in Bede’s *Questions on the Books of Kings*, and it may be observed that he published almost two commentaries on the sacred books.

My answer is readily available: Bede’s date stands in the way, since he lived almost an entire century after the blessed Gregory. Indeed, he himself declares that Britain was converted to the faith of Christ in his own time. But let the more learned decide these matters. For my part, I willingly and gladly submit and dedicate my efforts to illuminating the genuine Eucherius and placing him in the hands of the Roman Church, the mother of the faith.

[Col. 0699]

## Letter of Alexander Brassicanus on Saint Eucherius

[Col. 0699C] To the most honorable man, Lord Janus of Suolla, knight and jurist, Johannes Alexander Brassicanus sends his greetings.

You yourself, my dearest Janus, have witnessed how much labor I had to expend—or, to speak more accurately, how much tedium I had to swallow—in restoring and purifying those *Spiritual Formulas* of Eucherius. The recently published copy was not merely mutilated but exceptionally full of errors. I am far from assigning the blame for this to the man who first gave us the work; rather, I think the kindness and candor of that learned man deserve praise, since he preferred to present scholars with what he had conveniently acquired rather than allow it to perish.

We, however, used a copy that was both complete and remarkably accurate, which the Reverend Father Lord Johannes Hartmann, abbot of the Holy Cross in Austria—a unique patron of learning and of students, and my chief distinction and support—generously and wholeheartedly shared with me. First, we supplied what was missing; then we carefully corrected what had been corrupted. So that scholars may recognize this more clearly, I shall offer only two examples, from which they may easily estimate the rest, as one may judge the lion from its claws.

The first chapter, on the divine names, which was entirely missing, has now been restored from an old and no less trustworthy copy. I shall say nothing for the moment about how much was added throughout all the chapters.

In Eucherius’ preface it reads:

“But according to allegory, baptism; according to anagoge, angels.”

It should read:

“Waters, according to allegory, signify baptism; according to anagoge, angels.”

Hence the passage: “And let the waters that are above the heavens praise the name of the Lord,” and so forth.

I do not begrudge anyone who brings ancient writers to light; but I am more astonished if someone devotes all his effort to publishing them correctly. But enough of this.

What Eucherius accomplished among the Latins, that Theodoret, the bishop of Cyrus, accomplished most exactly among the Greeks. From his distinguished work, which has been copied for us in ancient manuscripts, I would like to set down here several exceptionally learned passages, from which the dignity and usefulness of the entire work will shine forth.

“Wine signifies divine punishment. Thus David says: ‘A cup is in the hand of the Lord, full of unmixed wine and mixture’” (Ps. LXXIV, 8).

Likewise:

“Hair is a symbol of mortality; for, being dead, it does not receive the sensation of pain. Therefore he commands those who serve God to possess true life and to have nothing mortal or foul. The divinely inspired Paul also teaches us this when he says: ‘I have been crucified with Christ; yet I live, no longer I, but Christ lives in me’; as though he were saying that he had devoted himself to sacred offices and divine actions.”

The Greek reads:

> οἴνος ἐπὶ Θεοῦ ἡ τιμωρία, Δαβὶδ, ὅτι ποτήριον ἐν χειρὶ Κυρίου οἴνου ἀκράτου πλήρες κεράσματος

That is: “Wine signifies divine punishment. Thus David says: ‘A cup is in the hand of the Lord, full of unmixed wine and mixture.’”

Likewise:

> αἱ τρίχες τὸν νεκρώσεως σύμβολον· νεκραὶ γὰρ αὗται, καὶ ὀδύνης αἴσθησιν οὐ δεχόμεναι· τὴν ἀληθῆ τοίνυν ζωὴν ἔχειν κελεύει τοὺς τῷ Θεῷ λειτουργοῦντας, καὶ μηδὲν ἔχειν νεκρὸν, μήδε δυσῶδες τοῦτο, καὶ ὁ θεσπέσιος ἡμᾶς διδάσκει Παῦλος. Χριστῷ, φησίν, συνεσταύρωμαι· ζῶ δὲ οὐκ ἔτι ἐγώ· ζῇ δὲ ἐν ἐμοὶ Χριστός· ταῖς μετὰ θείαις ἐνεργείαις ἐμαυτὸν ἀφιέρωσα.

That is:

“Hair is a symbol of mortality; for, being dead, it admits no sensation of pain. Therefore he admonishes and commands those who have devoted themselves to God’s service to live a true life and to possess nothing mortal or foul. The divine Paul also teaches us this when he says: ‘I have been crucified with Christ; yet I live, no longer I, but Christ lives in me’—as though he were saying that he had devoted himself to sacred offices and divine actions, and so forth.”

Such *Formulae* have something in common with the Hebrew Kabbalah, which the Greeks of old, paying too little attention to it, called κόβαλλα—“frauds”—after changing only a few letters, although it is highly suited to extracting secret meanings.

For thus the scholiast of Gregory the Theologian writes. And since our own countrymen—namely, Johannes Picus of Mirandola, Paulus Ritius, and Johannes Reuchlin, men who rival all antiquity—have written sufficiently about this matter, I shall say nothing more at length here. I commend to you only my own zeal and my ready willingness to promote every sound pursuit.

Whenever I mention you, I wish it understood that, in a single word and only once, I have meant all those who excel in intellect, virtue, good character, and complete learning.

Farewell, most noble man, and one whom I love in every way.

Vienna in Austria, from the Royal College, in the year 1530 after the birth of Jesus, in the month of December.

[Col. 0701]

## Letter or Short Treatise of Saint Eucherius, Bishop of Lyon, *On the Praise of the Desert*, to Hilary, Presbyter of Lérins (C, S)

[Col. 0701C] To the holy, most blessed in merit, and most glorious in Christ, Hilary: Eucherius sends greetings.

### 1

With great courage you once left your home and your family and penetrated as far as the distant solitudes of the desert, reaching the great sea. Yet you returned to the desert with greater virtue than you had first sought it. For when you initially entered it as a stranger, you had a guide, as it were the leader of your journey, whom you later made the teacher of your heavenly warfare. Following him then, and leaving your parents, you nevertheless followed a parent.

But now, when you thought that you should accompany the same man after he had been summoned to the pontifical dignity, love brought you back to the familiar solitude of the desert. Therefore you are now nobler and greater in example. Previously, when you sought the desert, you seemed to be accompanying a brother; now, when you have returned to the desert, you have left even a father behind.

But what sort of father, and how great? With what constant devotion of affection did you honor him? With what singular love were you bound to him? You could prefer nothing to his love, unless perhaps the love of the desert alone. When you rightly place the latter before him, you have shown that you loved him not a little, but loved this more. You have also shown how great the love of solitude was in you, since even the greatest love yielded to it.

What else is this love of the desert in you to be called except the love of God? You have therefore preserved the order of charity prescribed by the law, loving your God first and then your neighbor.

### 2

Yet I think that he, considering only your advancement—as I infer from my own mind—did not oppose your journey and purpose. Rather, in an unusual manner between persons bound together, he wished to release you no less than you wished to depart. For he also loves you greatly in return; yet in his love for you he considered your advantage. Although his love for you is abundant and supreme, its highest point nevertheless reaches toward your benefit.

### 3

And although long ago you poured out all your wealth, rich in Christ, for Christ’s poor; although you are young in years and old in character; although you are distinguished in intellect and distinguished in eloquence—nevertheless there is nothing in you that I have admired and loved more than this: that you so ardently desired a dwelling in solitude.

Since you often ask me to answer your very extensive and eloquent letters more fully, you must bear with my foolishness for a little while, although you yourself are wise, while I recall the manifold grace of the Lord toward this very desert that you love.

I would therefore rightly call the desert the unbounded temple of our God. For since it is certain that he dwells in silence, we must believe that he delights in solitude. More than once he has shown himself there to his saints and, making the place favorable, has not disdained human intercourse.

In the desert Moses sees God with his face glorified (Exod. III); in the desert Elijah, fearing to see God, covers his face (III Kings XIX, 13). And although God himself revisits all things as his own and is absent nowhere, nevertheless—as one may judge—he grants a more special visitation to the desert and to the solitude of heaven.

### 4

Some tell of a man who, when another asked in what sort of place he believed God to be present, replied that one should follow God diligently wherever he led. Then, with that same person accompanying him, he came to the solitudes of the widely extending desert. Pointing out the recess of the vast solitude, he said: “Behold, there is God.”

And not without reason is he more readily believed to be there where he is more easily found.

[Col. 0703B]

### 5

For even in the beginnings of creation, when God made all things in wisdom and distinguished each thing according to its future uses, he did not leave this part of the earth useless and dishonored. Rather, creating all things with regard not only to their present magnificence but also to his foreknowledge of the future, he prepared the desert, as I believe, for the saints who were to come.

I believe that he wished to make it rich in fruits for them and, in place of a more indulgent nature, to make it fruitful for the saints, so that the boundaries of the desert might grow fertile, and, while he watered its mountains from above, the valleys too might abound in multiplied harvests. Thus he would compensate for the deficiencies of the places by enriching a sterile habitation with its inhabitant.

### 6

The possessor of paradise and transgressor of the commandment, although he dwelt in a place of pleasure, could not keep the fixed law given him by God. For the more delightful that place was in its attractions, the more prone he was to fall there.

Therefore God not only subjected him to his laws, but also extended that same goad of his—the punishment of death—even to us. Let the one who desires life cultivate the desert, because the inhabitant of a pleasant place prepared death.

But let us now come to later examples of the desert, which has always been pleasing to God.

### 7

When Moses had driven the flock into the inner desert, he saw God shining from afar in harmless fire. He not only saw him but also heard him speaking. At that moment, when the Lord warned him to cast off the bonds of his feet, he declared the desert’s ground holy, saying: “The place on which you stand is holy ground” (Exod. III, 5). By this evident judgment he expressed the worth of its hidden honor.

The holiness of the place was confirmed by God through the holiness of his testimony. In this, as I think, he also secretly and simultaneously declares that whoever approaches the desert should release himself from the former obligations of his cares and proceed freed from his earlier bonds, lest he pollute the place.

There Moses is first employed as the familiar interpreter of divine conversation. He receives words and in turn reports them; he both asks about what must be said or done and is instructed; and in the accustomed exchange of conversation he speaks with the Lord of heaven.

There he takes up again the staff powerful for the performance of signs. Entering the desert as a shepherd of sheep, he returns from the desert as a shepherd of peoples.

### 8

What of the people of God, who were to be liberated from Egypt and released from earthly labors? Did they not seek byways and flee into solitudes (Exod. XIV), approaching God in the desert, from whose servitude they had been freed?

Under Moses as guide, they moved toward the desert, terrifying in its vast extent. “How great is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord!” Moses entered the desert and had seen God. Behold, he returns again to see him.

The Lord himself plainly led his people as their guide on the journey into the deserts, drawing out for the travelers a pillar for the use of both times: now red with flame, now shining white with cloud. Thus, for those who pleased him, he gave from heaven a sign that stretched out in a milky mass and gleamed by turns with fiery rays.

Israel, fixing its gaze upon the light, followed the beam glowing red from afar with flashing fire, so that the Lord, as he showed the way to those journeying toward the solitudes of the desert, might fittingly go before them with light.

### 9

Did not the barriers of the impassable sea open before this same people as it journeyed toward the deserts (Exod. XIV, 22)? As it made its way between steep whirlpools, its dusty procession of footprints crossed the shores of the Red Sea. Looking up from the deep valley at the towering mountains of suspended waters, the guardian of the nation conveyed them across the sea’s pools.

### 10

Nor did the power of this divine work end there. For, covering them again with the returning sea, it destroyed their road together with the enemy and set the entire sea back in its place—so, I believe, that Israel would not return from the desert.

He opened a way among the waters and afterward covered it with the surrounding waters, so that he might open the passage to those seeking the desert and close the return (Exod. XIV, 27).

[Col. 0704C]

### 11

Thus endowed with this power of grace, that people, while journeying toward solitude, received even more blessings when it possessed them. There the Lord refreshed the same people by an unexpected miracle, when he provided water overflowing from struck rock for the thirsty. Drawing streams as from a natural spring from inhospitable rocks, his hidden hand imposed a sudden nature upon concealed veins (Exod. XVII, 6).

Nor did he merely pour a river into the dry rock’s interior. He also restrained bitter draughts from mournful waters by adding sweetness to them (Exod. XV, 25). He drew forth the former and pacified the latter. It was no greater miracle to bring water from rocks than to produce other waters from water. The entire people marveled, sensing the aid of heavenly assistance no less in the waters that existed than in those that had not yet existed.

[Col. 0704D]

### 12

There too the same people gathered food sent down from heaven upon the whitish ground, when the Lord cast down bread from the clouds in a dry rain (Exod. XVI, 14). In the tents and throughout the surrounding camps, manna fell through the snowy air, and there human beings ate the bread of angels.

And because each day has enough trouble of its own, divine indulgence provided daily nourishment, already prescribing by its law that they should not think about the next day. Thus, when the people were once established in the desert and the earth could not provide food, heaven supplied it.

### 13

Did not the same Hebrew, an inhabitant of the desert, also receive the law and heavenly decrees, when he was brought near and deserved to inspect the signs impressed upon the tablets by the divine finger (Exod. XX)? Led out from the camp to meet the Lord, he stood face to face at the foot of the mountain.

Struck with fear, he saw the summit of Sinai, upon which the visible majesty had settled in great terror. Astonished, he looked at the mountain smoking from afar amid the fire that passed through it; afterward the thickest cloud covered the whole mountain far and wide.

Then he was terrified by flashing lightning expressed in fiery bursts and by thunder reverberating in repeated crashes mingled with the blast of trumpets. Thus, while the children of Israel dwelt in the solitudes, they deserved to see the dwelling of God and hear his voice.

### 14

That nation once made use of and was sustained by such miracles and others like them (Deut. XXIX, 5), when it was an inhabitant of the desert; when an extraordinary food, a sudden drink, and clothing that did not wear out nourished it; and when even those things that surrounded the body externally remained in an unfailing state.

Whatever the character of the place had not supplied for their needs, the manifest magnificence of God provided. One of the saints, scarcely having reached these gifts of heavenly grace, said concerning this people: “He has not dealt so with every nation” (Ps. CXLVII, 20). He bestowed special things and granted unheard-of gifts when he refreshed the people in the desert with divine provisions.

### 15

Although these events are handed down as figures of our own condition, and although the appearance of these events flourishes with hidden mysteries, and all who were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea are said to have eaten spiritual food and drunk spiritual drink (I Cor. X, 2), nevertheless all these things contain the faith of future events in such a way that they preserve the truth of what happened.

Nor is the praise of the desert diminished on this account, even if the events that occurred there are to be referred to the profundity of the sacraments. Nothing is therefore taken away from grace, even if the condition of their bodies at that time and the preservation of their garments from decay offered a model of the life to come.

For great is the grace of the place if the desert already possesses such people here as the blessedness of that age will make them.

### 16

What shall we say of the fact that the children of Israel reached that desirable land only by dwelling in the desert? And so that the same nation might afterward possess that land flowing with milk and honey, it first possessed this dry and uncultivated land.

The entire journey toward the true homeland is always opened through dwelling in the desert. Let the one who wishes to see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living inhabit an uninhabitable land; let the one who strives to be a citizen of that homeland be a guest in this one.

### 17

But, leaving these matters aside, David himself escaped the snares of the hostile king only when he sought the desert (I Kings XXIII). Dwelling in the arid regions of Idumea, he thirsted for the Lord with all his heart, so that, thirsting in a desert and trackless, waterless place, he might at last appear before God in the sanctuary, and thereafter, as a holy man, behold both God’s power and his glory.

### 18

Elijah, the greatest inhabitant of solitude, shut the heavens against rain and opened them by fire; he received food from a ministering bird; he recalled the fixed laws of death; he crossed the divided Jordan after interrupting its stream; and he ascended to heaven, carried away in a fiery chariot (III Kings XVII, 18; IV Kings II).

### 19

What of Elisha, the pursuer of this life and virtue? Did he not likewise become renowned through divine works of miracles? He was made famous now by the divided torrent, now by iron floating, now by the raising of the dead, now by the increase of oil. After countless other deeds, he finally proved that a doubled portion of his master’s power rested in him by this also: whereas Elijah, while still alive, raised the dead, Elisha raised the dead after he himself had died (IV Kings II, 4, 6).

### 20

The sons of the prophets, too, left the cities and sought the Jordan, flowing in a double stream. They built tents in hidden places beside the remote torrent. A holy company kept watch on the banks of the secluded river, scattered as though among separate tents, and in dwellings suited to them that excellent character preserved the spirit of their father (IV Kings VI).

### 21

What of the man greater than whom no one born of women has arisen (Matt. III)? Did he not live in the desert, crying out in the desert? In the desert baptism is bestowed by him; in the desert repentance is preached; in the desert the kingdom of heaven is first proclaimed.

There he first impressed these teachings upon his hearers, where each person seeking them more quickly attained them. And not without reason was this future lofty inhabitant of the desert sent as an angel before the face of the Lord: he opened the way into the heavenly kingdom. He was both forerunner and a worthy witness, hearing the Father speak from heaven and touching the Son in baptism, and seeing the Holy Spirit descend.

### 22

Our Lord and Savior himself, immediately after being baptized—as Scripture says (Matt. IV, 1)—was led by the Spirit into the desert. Who, then, is this Spirit? There is no hesitation: he is the Holy Spirit.

Since the Holy Spirit then draws him into the desert, surely he dictates this, silently inspires this, and the desert becomes a worthy prompting for the Holy Spirit who suggests it. Thus, immersed in the mystical stream, he considers nothing more important to do than hasten to the solitudes.

Yet he had already sanctified the waters that always sanctify, and he had been cleansed and washed of no sin; for he had neither committed sin nor feared it. Nevertheless he burned with love for the desert and, in all things the author of a saving example, desired this place as not unworthy of us.

If it was desirable for God to one free from error, how much more necessary is it for a human being subject to error? If it was sought by one who did not sin, how much more ought it to be desired by one who sins?

### 23

There, too, once the surrounding crowds had been removed, the silent ministries of divine power followed in the service of the Lord. Established in the desert, as though already carried back into heaven, he was received by the services of the angels who came to him (Matt. IV, 11).

There he refuted that ancient enemy who was tempting him with the snares of his familiar art; and the new Adam repelled the supplanter of the old Adam.

O great praise of the desert: the devil who had conquered in paradise was conquered in the desert!

### 24

That place was also a desert in which our Savior fed, satisfied, and filled five thousand men with only five loaves and two fish (Mark VIII). Always in the desert Jesus feeds his own with bread.

Formerly he had set before his own the manna as proof of the divine gift; now the fragments testified to it. By the same miracle, food fell then for the hungry, while now it increased for those who were eating. The feast, enlarged by his gift for all, was greater than the food that had been brought to the banquets.

Let us, I say, assign the causes of so many signs to the deserts, to the deserts! Nor would the power have displayed its might if the place had possessed abundance.

### 25

Then also the Lord Jesus withdrew to the more remote parts of a lofty mountain, when, taking only three chosen companions with him, he shone with an extraordinary brightness of face. Although he openly displayed the humanity he had assumed, he entrusted the sign of his majesty to solitude.

There the chief of the apostles said: “It is good for us to be here” (Matt. XVII, 4), clearly admiring the greatness of the sign in the remoteness of the desert.

### 26

The same Lord Jesus also, as it is written, went into a deserted place and prayed there (Luke V, 16). Let that place therefore already be called a place of prayer, which God the author showed to be suitable for entreating God. He taught from where the cloud of a prayer that humbles itself might more easily penetrate, aided by the place because honored by solitude.

And by praying there while he made his requests, he demonstrated where he wished us to pray when we make our requests.

### 27

Why should I now mention John, Macarius, and many others, whose dwelling, while it is in the deserts, has become heavenly? They approached the Lord as closely as it is permitted for a human being to approach God; and they were admitted to the works of divine things as far as those clothed in flesh could be admitted.

They fixed their minds on things above and joined them to heavenly solitudes. Here they displayed the grace accompanying them either through silent revelations or through signs that cried out. With solitude assisting them, they advanced so far that, while their bodies still touched the earth, they already possessed heaven in spirit.

### 28

This dwelling of the desert, therefore, I would not unjustly call a seat of faith, an ark of virtue, a sanctuary of charity, a treasury of devotion, and a storehouse of justice.

For just as in a great house valuable objects are kept under seal in remote places, so that magnificence of the hidden saints is deposited in the desert, which nature has enclosed with its difficulties, within a kind of chamber of solitude, lest it fade through the habits of human society.

Appropriately, therefore, this precious store of riches belonging to the Lord of the world is not only kept in that part of the worldly house but, whenever there is need, is also brought forth from its hidden places.

[Col. 0707D]

### 29

Once there was supreme and greatest divine providence toward the desert, but even now it is not small. For even now, when food arrives unexpectedly to the inhabitants of the desert through a divinely granted abundance, what else is it than something falling and flowing down from heaven?

These people too have their manna in this munificence, and the Lord no less scatters nourishment for them from his hidden store through the secret work of his arm.

And when, after the rocks have been pierced, waters finally flow from the stones in answer to the divine gift, what else are they than waters emerging as though from a rock struck by Moses’ staff?

The condition of clothing for those living in the vastness of the desert likewise does not fail even now. Since it continually follows by free divine provision, it remains by continuing to follow.

The Lord once nourished his people in the desert, and he nourishes them now; he nourished the former for forty years, and these for as many years as there shall be.

### 30

Rightly does the saint, inflamed by divine fire, leave his own dwelling and choose this as his dwelling; rightly does he prefer it to relatives, children, and parents, and purchase it at the price of fellowship with all his own people.

Rightly does this place, for those who abandon their native homeland, obtain the name of a temporary homeland, from which neither fear, longing, joy, nor grief can call them back.

Rightly, indeed, is it alone the price of every affection.

### 31

For who could worthily enumerate the benefits of the desert and the advantages of virtue for those who dwell there? Although placed in the world, they withdraw in a certain manner outside the world, “wandering,” as the Apostle says, “in deserts, and mountains, and caves, and caverns of the earth” (Hebr. XI, 38).

And not without reason does the Apostle declare the world unworthy of such people: they are strangers to the tumult of human society, set apart, quiet, and silent. They are no farther from the will to sin than from the ability to sin.

### 32

Among the ancients, distinguished men of this age, exhausted by the labors of their affairs, withdrew into philosophy as into their own home. How much more beautifully do these people turn to the studies of manifest wisdom and withdraw more magnificently into the freedom of solitudes and the recesses of deserts, so that, devoting themselves only to philosophy, they may exercise themselves in the walks of that desert [Vulg.: “waste”] as in their own gymnasia?

Where, I ask, can Easter be observed more freely than in a dwelling of the desert? But it is observed through virtues and self-restraint—self-restraint, I say, which is like another desert of the heart.

For Moses devoted himself to fasting in the desert for forty continuous days (Exod. XXIV, 18), and Elijah afterward did the same there for an equal number of days (III Kings XIX, 8). Both extended their abstinence beyond the powers of human endurance.

Then the Lord likewise spent the same period of abstinence in the desert (Matt. IV, 2). Nor do we read anywhere else that equal spans of time were spent in fasting, so that it must be thought that the Lord granted those places a special strength as well.

### 33

Where, I ask, does it happen more fully that one may devote oneself to leisure and see how sweet the Lord is? Where is the path more open to those striving toward perfection? Where is a greater field opened for virtues? Where is the mind’s vigilance easier, so that it may look around? Where is the heart’s intention freer, so that it may strive to cling to God, than in those solitudes where it is not only easy to find God but also to keep him?

### 34

Although the thin dust of the soil often appears in the desert, nowhere nevertheless are the foundations of that evangelical house laid more firmly (Matt. VII, 24).

Even if someone wishes to stand upon those sands, he does not build his house upon sand. Nowhere more than there is that foretold building placed upon rock; founded with immovable stability, it will endure with an unshaken mass, so that when storms break in it will not be overthrown by blowing winds or rushing torrents.

Thus the inhabitants of the desert construct such buildings within their hearts: they seek what is highest from what is lowest; they pursue lofty things with humility; they are unconcerned and forgetful regarding earthly matters because of their hope and desire for heavenly things.

They cast away riches while choosing to be needy; they hasten to be needy while desiring to be rich. By day and by night they contend through labor and vigils to seize the beginning of that life whose end they will not find.

Thus the desert, with its maternal bosom, holds those who are rightly greedy for eternity and commendably prodigal of transience; unconcerned with the present age and certain of the future. Through this they attain that ages without end may be theirs, upon whom the ends of the ages have come.

### 35

There the health-giving laws of the inner person, written within, burn brightly, and the ordinances of the eternal age more keenly. Human regulations concerning crimes and offenses do not there resound with their force, nor do the avenging laws concerning capital offenses assert themselves.

The laws of the inhabitants make the heart guilty unless it is perfectly pure. The inner movement of the mind itself is restrained with every effort within the boundaries of justice; and, with that same judge, even the beginnings of slight thoughts are punished.

Among others, it is evil to have done evil; among these people, it is evil not to have done good.

### 36

But how could I honor, in a commemoration worthy of them, the inner institutions of the desert? Yet I cannot silently pass over this: in its inhabitants, the power of virtue is hidden from all and nevertheless almost as well known.

For although they withdraw themselves into remote places, rejecting the world and human society, they desire indeed to remain hidden, but they cannot hide their merit. To the extent that their life drives itself inward, their glory thrusts itself outward.

God, as I think, so moderates the two that the inhabitant of the desert is hidden from the age but not hidden in example.

This is the lamp that illuminates the whole world, placed upon the lampstand of the desert. From here its blazing light spreads through the dark limbs of the world.

This is the city that cannot be hidden, built upon a mountain in the desert; by its image it has given the heavenly Jerusalem to the earth.

Therefore, if anyone is in darkness, let him approach this light so that he may see; if anyone is exposed to danger, let him hasten to this city so that he may be safe.

### 37

O how delightful, even to those thirsting for God, are those pathless solitudes amid the remote groves! How pleasant, to those seeking Christ, are those retreats stretching far and wide while nature keeps watch over them!

Everything is silent. Then the joyful mind is aroused toward its God by certain goads of silence; then it is invigorated by ineffable transports.

No intrusive sound is heard there; there is no voice except perhaps the voice of God. Only that exceedingly sweet sound of silence intervenes in the secrecy of the station and interrupts it: a noise sweeter than repose, the holy tumult of the most modest way of life.

Then the fervent choirs strike the heights themselves with hymns that resound sweetly, and one reaches heaven almost no less through voices than through prayers.

### 38

Then the adversary, circling around, rages in vain, like a wolf among sheep enclosed within their folds. Indeed, the spacious choir of rejoicing angels visits the desert, and, passing along that ladder of Jacob, they illuminate the wilderness with the abundance of their hidden visitation (Gen. 28:12). And lest those who guard the city keep watch in vain, it is especially fortified by Christ as its defender. Just as an obstacle of walls drives enemies away, so he keeps his foes at a distance by the circuit of the desert, so that the people adopted by God are as exposed to the open spaces of solitude as they are shut off from their enemies. In that same noonday the bridegroom reclines, and the inhabitants of the desert, wounded by love, contemplate him, saying: “We have found him whom my soul loves; I will hold him and will not let him go” (Song 3:4).

### 39

That desert soil is not unfruitful, as it is thought to be; nor is that ground sterile, nor are the dry rocks of the wilderness barren. There it puts forth manifold growth and yields its inhabitants a hundredfold harvest. The seeds sown there do not easily fall beside the road for the birds to consume; nor do they readily slip among the rocky places, where, having no depth of soil, they would be scorched and wither; nor do they easily escape into the thorn bushes, where they would be overwhelmed by already-grown briars. There the farmer will reap a harvest with abundant yield; from these rocks that crop is produced by which even the bones grow fat. There too is found the living bread that descended from heaven. In those crags, welling springs and living waters burst forth—waters able not merely to satisfy, but even to suffice for those who are being saved. Here is the meadow [Vulgate: pasture] and delight of the inner person; here is an uncultivated desert, yet there it is rendered joyful by wondrous loveliness. The same place is a desert for the body and a paradise for the soul.

### 40

Now let no land, however fertile, boast of itself in comparison with the soil of the desert. Is there some land rich in crops? In this land above all is produced that grain which satisfies the hungry with its fatness. Is another land joyful with heavy vineyards? In this one above all is brought forth that wine which truly gladdens the human heart. Is another excellent for its pastures? In this one those sheep are most healthfully pastured of whom it is said, “Feed my sheep” (John 21:17). Is another adorned with blooming flowers? In this one above all shines that true flower of the field and lily of the valleys. Finally, is one more splendidly radiant with metals, while another gleams with its gold? In this one the varied splendors of the stones sparkle with flashing light. Thus this land, greater than each land in each individual respect, far surpasses all of them in every good.

### 41

Rightly, therefore, O venerable land, you have been worthy of reverence to saints either established in you or dwelling not far from you; you have long been either habitable or desirable, because you are fruitful in every good in which all things are found. You seek this cultivator, who cultivates his own land, not yours. You are barren of the vices of those who inhabit you; fertile in virtues. Whoever among the saints sought intimacy with you found God; whoever cultivated you found Christ in you. The one who inhabits you rejoices in the Lord who inhabits him. He is at once your possessor and the divine possession. Whoever did not reject your dwelling-place has himself become the temple of God.

### 42

Indeed, I owe reverence to all the places of the desert that are illumined by the retreat of the devout; yet I embrace my own Lirinus [Vulgate: Lerina] with particular honor. It receives in its most pious arms those cast out by the shipwrecks of the stormy world as they come; it gently leads them, burning with the world’s heat, beneath its shades, so that there they may recover their breath beneath that innermost shadow of the Lord. Abounding in waters, green with grasses, gleaming with vines, pleasing to the eyes and to the sense of smell, it presents itself as paradise to those who dwell there. It is worthy to have been founded for heavenly disciplines with Honoratus as its founder; worthy, through such institutions, to have obtained so great a Father, radiant with the vigor of an apostolic spirit and the dignity of his countenance. Worthy to receive him, it was thus worthy to send him forth [Port. cod.: bring him forth]; worthy to nourish outstanding monks and to produce priests worthy of being sought.

Now it holds his successor, Maximus by name, renowned because he deserved to be appointed after him.
