It possessed Lupus, of revered name, who brought him back to us as the wolf from the tribe of Benjamin. It had his brother Vincentius, a jewel clearly visible through his inward splendor. It possesses Caprasius, venerable for his gravity and equal to the ancient saints. It now has those holy old men who, in separate cells, have brought the Egyptian Fathers to our Gauls.

### 43

What gatherings and assemblies of holy men I saw there, good Jesus! In these men alabaster breathed forth fragrance with precious, sweet ointment; everywhere the scent of life was exhaled. In the habit of the outward man they displayed the face of the inner man: bound by charity, cast down in humility, most gentle in compassion, most steadfast in hope, modest in their walk, prompt in obedience, silent when they met others, serene in countenance. At once, by the very contemplation of them, they plainly displayed a company of angelic peace.

They desire nothing, long for nothing except him whom alone they desire in their longing. While they seek the blessed life, they live it; and while they are still striving after it, they already attain it. Thus they wish to be separated from sinners? They are already separated. They wish to possess a chaste life? They possess it. They desire to spend all their time in the praises of God? They do. They desire to rejoice in the assemblies of the saints? They rejoice. They wish to enjoy Christ? They enjoy Christ. They ardently long to attain the life of the desert? They attain it in their hearts.

Thus, through the most abundant grace of Christ, they already merit in the present many of the things they hope for in the future. They already grasp the reality while following hope. They possess no small reward of their labor even in the labor itself, because what will be the reward is almost already present in the work.

### 44

By being restored to and inserted into their fellowship, my dearest Hilary, you have benefited yourself greatly and have benefited them also, for they now rejoice with lively exultation at your return. With them, I beg you, do not forget the memory of my sins and of my intercession; with them, I say—though I do not know whether you have brought them more joy or have found greater joy yourself.

You are now a truer Israel: with your heart you behold God; long freed from the darkness of the Egypt of this world, you have crossed the saving waters while your enemy was submerged; in the desert you have followed the fire kindled by faith; what was once bitter you now experience as sweet through the wood of the cross. You draw from Christ waters springing up into eternal life; you feed the inner man with heavenly bread; in the Gospel you receive the divine voice of your throne (Matt. 19:28). As you dwell with Israel in the desert, you will enter the promised land with Jesus.

Farewell in Christ Jesus our Lord.

---

## [Col. 0711] Letter of Saint Eucherius, Bishop of Lyons, an exhortation to Valerian, his kinsman, concerning contempt for the world and secular philosophy (C)

Those who are joined by the bond of love are well bound by the bond of blood. Thus we too may rightly glory greatly in this very gift of God: love binds us together just as kinship does, and two relationships draw us into one affection—one we received from the parents of our flesh, the other we have taken upon ourselves. This twofold bond, by which we are joined, united on one side by birth and on the other by affection, has compelled me to write to you at somewhat greater length, so that I might commend to your mind the cause of your soul and that true blessedness capable of possessing eternal things, and assert it as the work of our profession.

For since I love you as much as I love myself, I must desire that you attain the highest good as though you were another self. Indeed, you are not opposed in disposition to the profession of a holy life; rather, with a devout character, you have anticipated in many respects what sacred teachings instruct, through the precocious excellence of your morals. Thus it seems to me that, by a provident natural inclination, you have already taken possession of certain duties of religion, through the indulgence toward you of our Lord and God—a grace by which divine teaching can find some of its goods already present in you and confer others upon you.

Although your father and father-in-law have raised you to the highest summits of the world and you are surrounded by distinguished titles from both sides, I nevertheless desire for you the heights of a far superior honor. I call you not to earthly dignity but to heavenly dignity; not to the dignity of this age but to that of the ages. For this glory is certain and indelible: to glory in eternity.

I shall speak to you not of the wisdom of this age, but of that secret and hidden wisdom which God ordained before the ages for our glory (1 Cor. 2). I shall speak with you with great zeal, having taken little thought for myself, since I have considered more what I want for you than what I can accomplish for myself.

The first duty of a human being, formed and brought into the light, is to recognize his own author and, having recognized him, to receive him; and to turn life—that is, the divine gift—into divine service and worship. What he received through God’s gift must be completed through devotion to God, and what he unworthily received from him must be offered back to him in submission. We are guided by the sound conviction that, just as he brought us forth from himself, so we should regard ourselves as brought forth for him. Whoever understands that God made us both for himself and as his own clearly and magnificently perceives the intention of our Creator in forming humanity.

Next, it is best to devote principal care to the soul, so that what is superior in usefulness may not be inferior in consideration. Let the first concerns among us hold the first place; let the highest portion of our solicitude be claimed by salvation, which is supreme. Let salvation occupy us in its defense and protection—not merely as the first concern, but as the only one. Let it conquer everything through a zeal that places it above all.

We owe God the highest observance, and the greatest care to the soul; yet the matter stands thus: although each is of supreme importance, neither seems capable of being observed without the other. Thus whoever has satisfied God must necessarily already have cared for the soul; and, conversely, whoever has cared for the soul must necessarily already have satisfied God. In this way the matter concerning both supreme goods is settled among us through a useful economy: if someone diligently fulfills one, he contributes both, because, through divine goodness beyond words, that very usefulness becomes a sacrifice to God.

Much attention is devoted to the body’s treatments; much effort is expended in the hope of healing it [perhaps: for the appearance of healing]. Does the soul not deserve medicine? And if various remedies are applied to the body with care for preserving health, it is not right for the soul to lie abandoned as though excluded, to waste away as though neglected amid its diseases, and to be the one thing banished from its proper remedies. Rather, more must truly be given to the soul if so much is given to the body.

For if some have rightly called the flesh a servant and the soul its mistress, we ought not to place the mistress in a secondary position and unjustly prefer the servant. The better part rightly demands greater attention, because all our care must look toward the place where the more abundant dignity of our substance has been established. It is not fitting that, in this honor of our solicitude, we subject the soul to what is worse.

The flesh, inclined toward vices, calls us back to the earth as to its origin (Gen. 8); but the soul, coming from the Father of lights, strives upward, as iron is accustomed to be drawn toward fires. It is the image of God in us; it is the precious pledge of the divine gift. Let us protect it with every resource and with all our strength. If we govern and preserve it, we guard God’s deposit (2 Tim. 1).

What place is there for building unless you have first laid foundations? For one intending to build up the remaining advantages, salvation is the foundation. Otherwise, how can anyone add what follows if he has not possessed what comes first? How will increase grow through what succeeds if the beginnings of what precedes fail? How can he think himself partaking of blessedness when he lacks even salvation? Lacking life, how can he abound in a happy life? Or what benefit is it if he adds to his food while lacking what is needed to care for the soul?

Our Lord Jesus Christ says of this: “For what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul?” (Matt. 16). Therefore no reason for profit can stand if it is certain that loss has intervened for the soul. Where there is damage to salvation, there is plainly no profit at all; for where can profit be obtained unless the place in which it is obtained remains secure? And therefore, while there is time, let us hasten toward that true profit, that holy and desirable exchange (Gal. 6).

A few days can produce eternal life; yet even if those days possessed the blessedness of life unharmed and undefiled, they would still be valued little because they were few. Nothing is great in reality if it is small in duration; nor is anything enclosed within a narrow limit extended by long joys.

The brief advantages of this age have brief benefits. Therefore, even for the good of a brief life, the benefit of eternal life would rightly seem preferable, because the former is temporal, the latter eternal happiness; because it is fragile to enjoy brief goods, but secure to rejoice in perpetual ones.

Now, however, eternal life is supremely blessed. For what can be called more blessed than eternal life? This present life, by contrast, is brief—so exceedingly brief that it is full of misery. It is pressed on every side by the inconveniences of surrounding sorrows and is worn down by evils as they fail, while it is tossed about by the injuries of unforeseen events.

For what course of life is as untrustworthy, changeable, and wretched as this one? It is full of labor, full of anxiety, full of cares, and even full of dangers themselves. Scattered through uncertain accidents, it is restless through bodily sufferings, anxious through the anguish of the mind, and unsettled amid the whirlwinds of dangers.

What advantage or reason is there, then, not to seek eternal goods but to pursue temporal ones—even evils? Do you not see how, even in this life, every prudent person stocks with abundant expenditure the place or estate in which he thinks he will remain longer? Where he will be for a short time, he makes short preparations; where for a longer time, he arranges greater ones.

Since our present time is exceedingly brief, confined by straitening troubles, while in the future ages await us, let us enlarge eternal life with suitable resources and furnish our brief life with suitable provisions, lest through a perverse policy we devote our greatest care to a brief time and brief care to the greatest time.

I scarcely know what ought to urge us more swiftly or effectively toward this supremely blessed life: the advantages of the future life that are promised, or the inconveniences of the present life that are visible. The former attract us most gently; the latter drive us out forcefully. Therefore, since even the worst things cooperate for the better, if we are not enticed by good things, let us be expelled by evils. For the best things join in urging us on through the inferior, and different things converge toward the same advantage. While some invite us and others drive us away, both together urge us toward what is better.

If some distinguished and wealthy person were to call you to be adopted in place of his children, would you go through opposing difficulties and hasten along whatever journey, however long the retreat, carried by the road? God, the Lord of the universe and of all things, calls you to adoption, granting you—if you wish—the gracious name of son, by which he calls our God his only one [the wording is textually uncertain] (Rom. 8; Gal. 4; Eph. 1). Will you not be inflamed and carried away? Will you not be urgently hastened, lest swift death snatch away so great a condition before your speedy arrival?

To obtain this adoption, will you not penetrate the trackless solitudes of the earth or the uncertain expanses of the distant sea? Whenever you wish, this adoption is with you. Will this reality make us sluggish and idle simply because it is as immediate as it is great? The more readily available this condition is, the more harshly those who ignore it will experience it. For it is all the more destructive to the unwilling the more readily available it is to the willing.

Certainly, the desire for life is what has bound us to the pleasure of present things. Therefore, loving life, we exhort you to life. It is a true method of persuasion to ask you for what you desire. We act as ambassadors among you on behalf of the life you love (2 Cor. 5:20; Eph. 6:20), and we commend this life, which you all love as brief, so that you may love it as eternal.

I do not know how we can love it unless we desire that the life we love be as beautiful as possible. Therefore, let what pleases us because it is confined please us more if it can be perpetual; and let what has value among us because it has an end be beyond value for us if it can be without end.

It is right, therefore, to have looked after the lesser life for the sake of the greater, so that a passage to the other may be constructed for us—but through this one. It is certainly not fitting that this life should interfere with the interests of its companion through misguided counsels. It must not oppose it so as to hinder or harm it.

For it is absurd and contradictory that love of life should bring about the loss of life. Therefore, whether you think this life should be despised or embraced, my case is easy in either respect. If it is despised, there is only one reason for despising it: so that a better life may be sought. And if it is loved, the greater life must be loved all the more.

For my part, I would wish you to regard this life as a test of itself, to judge it—as it is—as most burdensome and troubled by uncertain fatigue, and to despise and reject it together with its occupations.

Let that endless chain of secular affairs be broken, and that single labor of necessity which extends throughout the whole of life. Let us tear apart the bonds of empty cares, whose interwoven links succeed one another and in which our occupation always seems to be beginning anew. Let those causes be removed, as empty as they are mutually connected, in which, as long as one lives, the zeal of mortals, continually beginning new business, is never finished.

The tireless concentration upon these matters has made life, already brief and confined in itself, even more confined. From them come now empty joys, now bitter sorrows, now anxious wishes, now fearful apprehensions. Finally, let all those things be cast away that make this present life brief in occupation but long in sorrow.

Let us reject the world’s untrustworthy life, suspect in both circumstances, in which high and low alike are scarcely safe. Low things are crushed by their abasement; high things totter at their summit. Choose whatever condition you wish: neither among the lowest nor among the highest is there rest. Neither condition escapes the burdensome lot of the whirlwind. The lesser is subject to insult; the greater to envy.

There are, I think, two principal things that hold people most tightly bound in the affairs of this age and, having beguiled their senses, constrain them with seductive love: the pleasure of wealth and the dignity of honors. Of these, the former ought to be called not pleasure but want; the latter not dignity but vanity.

Both, entangled in alternating knots, impede one’s steps, their deceptive embrace binding the pair together. These vices, deadly to human hearts and flattering to their desires, breathe themselves into them; they entice the exhausted minds of mortals with an easy sweetness.

For what is more destructive than those riches—to speak of them first—which are rarely amassed except with justice? Such a matter is acquired under such an administrator and preserved under such a guardian. For, he says, “the root of all evils is greed” (1 Tim. 6:10). There is almost a fellowship even of name between these two things, vices and riches.

Are not these riches also a kind of material for insults? Like prizes exposed for the wicked, do they not provoke the eyes and minds of factions, display their very proscriptions in a way, and invite them? But suppose such things do not happen: can we be certain that, after we have wandered and fled, they will migrate with us? “He amasses wealth,” it says, “and does not know for whom he gathers it” (Ps. 38:7).

But suppose an heir comes according to our wish: does the heir not often intercept the estate, and does not the accumulated wealth disappear through a badly raised son or a badly chosen son-in-law? What pleasure do these riches possess in themselves, when their possession is miserable and their transmission uncertain?

To what crooked and headlong course is the love of human beings carried? You know how to love the things that come to you, but do not know how to love yourself. What you love is outside; what you desire is beyond you. Return instead into yourself, so that you may be dearer to yourself than your possessions.

Certainly, if some person knowledgeable about worldly affairs approaches you, you would prefer that he love you yourself rather than the things that are yours; and you would choose that he direct his affection toward your life rather than your riches. You want him to keep faith with a human being, not with possessions. What you would wish another to grant you, grant to yourself—you who are your own most faithful companion. Let us love ourselves rather than what is ours.

Let these remarks suffice concerning possessions.

As for the honors of this world, to say nothing of the rest, what dignity can be attributed to things when the ambition of the wicked rises indiscriminately with the good into this position, and one honor embraces men of unequal merit, so that dignity no longer distinguishes the worthy from the unworthy but confounds them? Thus what ought to prefer the better to the worse has begun to make them equal; and, in a new way, there is almost nowhere less distinction between the best and the worst men than in honor.

Is it not a greater honor to prefer being without honor of this sort, and to be judged more by one’s own character than by indiscriminate honors?

Moreover, however they may be, how fleeting and perishable are these very honors! Recently we saw men conspicuous for honor seated upon the summits of lofty dignities, with patrimonies spread throughout the world through their widely dispersed wealth. They had overcome their desires through success and surpassed their wishes through their possessions.

I recall only private fortunes. Kings themselves, raised high by great power, shone with jewels; their coverings glittered with gems. Strange to say, woven fabrics flashed with metals; a diadem [perhaps: the diadem flashed with metals] sparkled with separated trees [perhaps: the house with trees]; a palace hall equipped with courtly splendors shone; roofs with gilded beams glowed. Their wishes were called the rights of men; their words were called laws.

Who can flee above the summit of humanity into temporary happiness? Behold, their magnificence is nowhere; even their most abundant riches have departed, and the masters themselves of such great wealth have passed away (Job 14; Wis. 5).

The recent and illustrious kingdoms among us are now almost a fable. All those things that were great here are now nothing. They carried away none of those riches, honors, and kingdoms with them, as I think—or rather, as I know with certainty—except, if any such substance was found among them, the substance of faith and devotion.

These alone accompany them, deprived as they are of all other things; these alone follow them, inseparable and like faithful companions as they depart. By these resources they are now nourished; in these riches, in these honors alone, they now find rest. These goods they now possess in the form of rewards.

Therefore, if we are captivated by honors and riches, let us be awakened by true riches and true honors. Every excellent person transfers earthly honors and earthly riches into heavenly honors and heavenly riches—there, certainly, where the full and unconfused distinction between good and evil exists; where what we once attain we hold forever; where, if there is any place for obtaining, there is none for losing.

But since we have spoken of the fragile possession of temporal goods, we must say something also about the condition of this brief life itself.

What is this, I ask? What is it? Nothing do human beings see so daily as death; nothing do they forget so completely as death. The human race is carried onward by swift mortality toward its setting, and every generation runs its course under the law of succeeding ages.

Our fathers have passed away; we shall depart; those who come after us will follow. Like waves cast from the deep, breaking one after another upon the farthest edge of the shore, so generations are dashed against the boundary of death in their decline.

Let this reflection, let this memory of our condition, surround us day and night. Let us think that the appointed end of life is already, already at hand; it will approach us all the more closely the longer it has been delayed. Let us expect the day as near; we do not know it to be far away. As it is written, let us prepare our ways for departure (Mal. 3:1).

If we think and meditate upon these things, we shall not fear death by fearing it. Blessed are those who have already reconciled themselves to Christ. Great fear of death does not harass those who already desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ (Phil. 1); who, already prepared and already at rest, await in silence the final day of this life.

For it makes little difference when those who pass into eternity bring their temporal life to an end.

Let not the crowd of the negligent persuade us to neglect life, nor let us be led by the errors of others toward the loss of our own salvation. What will the multitude profit us in that judgment of God, where individuals will be judged, where the examination of merits alone will take place, and where each person’s conduct, not the people, will acquit him?

Let the comforters who give bad counsel in danger cease—let them cease. Surely it is better to prolong life with the few than to lose it with the many. Let the mere multitude of sinners not draw us into carelessness about sins; let the fact that others take little care of themselves never become for us a kind of authority.

I beg you always to regard another’s sin as a disgrace, never as an example. But if you wish to turn your eyes toward examples, look rather toward that side where, although there are fewer, they are nevertheless numerous in their own order. Look, I say, toward those who wisely understand why they were born and, while they live, conduct the business of their life.

Distinguished by useful work and outstanding in virtue, they cultivate the present life and sow the future. Nor are there lacking not only abundant examples among them but also great ones. For what nobility of the world, what honors, what dignity, what wisdom, what eloquence, what literary learning has not already devoted itself to this military service of the heavenly kingdom (Matt. 11:30)? What exalted rank has not now submitted itself, in surrender, to this light heavenly yoke?

And indeed it is beyond every error and ignorance for anyone to neglect the business of his salvation. I could, if it were not too long, name many from among countless others—men illustrious in the world who pursued this stricter observance of divine worship and this way of life. Yet, so as not to omit everything entirely, I shall briefly append a few examples.

Clement, of an ancient senatorial family and even descended from the stock of the Caesars, filled with every kind of knowledge and highly skilled in all the liberal arts, passed over to this path of the just. He flourished in it so excellently that he even became the successor of the chief of the apostles.

Gregory, a priest from Pontus, foremost in philosophy in the world and outstanding in eloquence, later became still greater and more excellent in virtues. Thus, as the trustworthiness of our history tells of him, among the other marvelous signs of his merits, a mountain is said to have withdrawn and a lake to have dried up at his prayers and supplications.

There was also another holy man named Gregory, equally devoted to letters and philosophy, who desired this heavenly philosophy. What concerns the matter at hand must not be left unmentioned: when Basil, formerly familiar to him through secular studies and still devoted to the profession of rhetoric, entered his lecture hall, Gregory took him by the hand and led him away from the school, saying, “Leave these things and devote yourself to salvation.”

Later, both memorable priests left in the books of our Church splendid monuments of their talent.

Paulinus also, bishop of Nola, a distinctive and blessed example for our Gaul, once possessed an immense wealth of resources and an abundant fountain of eloquence. He passed over to our conviction and purpose in such a way that he sprinkled nearly every part of the world with his eloquence and works.

Hilary recently, and Petronius, now a bishop in Italy, both came from that seat of worldly power which, as they say, was filled to overflowing. One ascended into the name of religion, the other into that of the priesthood.

And when shall I unfold from that vast volume of names the most renowned for eloquence—Firmianus, Minucius, Cyprian, Hilary [Erasmus thinks Evagrius should be substituted for Hilary], John [clearly Chrysostom], Ambrose?

I believe that these men too had said to themselves what one of our own people said when he urged himself away from the world into this happier life with that sort of goad: “What does this mean? The uneducated rise up and seize heaven, while we, with our learning—behold where we roll about in flesh and blood!” (Matt. 11).

Had they said this? And for that reason they later did violence to the kingdom.

Having cited in part those whom a greater ardor of our faith possessed, though they had passed through the philosophy, eloquence, and honors of the world, I shall now come to the kings themselves and to that head of the world.

Nor will I now think it necessary to recall all those earlier men devoted to religion and possessing royal dignity. From the memory of revered annals, I shall mention only the distinguished: David for devotion, Josiah for faith, Hezekiah for humility.

There have also been some among more recent generations, princes in our own time, who drew nearer to the knowledge of the true King and confessed that supreme Lord of lords with the deepest contrition of heart. Both sexes in the palace displayed attentive reverence before the divine majesty.

These, I think, are more suitable to be proposed for imitation. Their examples possess salvation concerning future things and authority concerning present things.

You see how even the days and years, and all these ornaments of heaven, preserve God’s word and command through tireless observance and maintain service to his precepts under an unremitting law. Shall we, for whose use these things were fashioned and into whose service their lights were pressed, ignorant neither of the heavenly commandments nor of the divine will, pass over God’s command with deaf ears?

To these aforesaid instruments of the world it was commanded once and for all what they were to observe throughout the ages. But to us the commands of the divine law are repeated in so many volumes, so that at least in this respect—assigned to humanity itself—we may learn to obey the will of the author and devote ourselves to his precepts, since all this, while providing service, also provides an example.

Yet if some refuse to return to their author, can they for that reason avoid their Lord? Or where is there a place for those who turn away from God to flee? Let holy David hear them; let them hear you saying: “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present. If I take my wings at dawn and dwell at the ends of the sea, even there your hand will lead me, and your right hand will hold me” (Ps. 138).

Therefore, whether they wish it or not, they cannot withdraw themselves from the Lord of the universe. If they remove themselves by their will, they do not withdraw themselves by right. They are absent in affection, but he is present in dominion. Thus, in a state that is thoughtless and utterly ill-advised, they live as wanderers shut away from consideration of the Lord but within his power.

If each person pursues a fleeing servant with threatening investigation and, as the servant avoids him, the one asserting his legal authority follows him, why does a person not render to the heavenly Lord the right that belongs to him concerning himself? Why does he not, as soon as possible, offer himself voluntarily into his service, acting with justice toward himself as well as serving as judge in his own case?

Why are we fixed upon the pleasurable appearance of present things? Why do we devote ourselves so wholly to what we see? Do we live only for these lights, or do we carry eyes merely for use? [Perhaps: merely for the sun’s use.]

We live also by our ears, so that we may yearn for the promises. Great emotions draw us through this part of the body as well. Let us await with fervent vows and urgent desires the things that are promised and proclaimed. That faithful author, that faithful one, impresses upon us the reliability of his promises. Let us strive toward the best things that are promised.

Although, if we also wish to use our eyes well and profitably, through them too we are carried forward in large part by great desire for the future—if only we turn back toward the author of so great a structure the admiration that we receive from contemplating the world.

Or let us consider how great a splendor of light may meet our eyes in the future, since so great a splendor now enters them: how magnificently will the form of everlasting things shine, since it is now so beautiful in things destined to perish?

Therefore we must not urge the functions of our members toward the worse direction; rather, let them be suitably balanced toward both lives. Let them preserve the use of temporal things in such a way that they do not reject the service of eternal things.

And if this diversion and love delight us, if pleasure stimulates the senses themselves, then here plainly is the love of supreme delight: here is not only what may be loved with the fullest outpouring, but also what above all ought to be loved—a joyful, splendid, unique, eternal good.

Our God, I mean, for whom you can burn with as great a fire as with a devout one, if precious desires once again take the place of your former cravings. If the dignity of so magnificent a reality captivated you in any way, nothing is more magnificent than that. If something carried you away as though suited and adapted to glory, nothing is more glorious than that. If your sight led you toward splendid and shining things, nothing is brighter than that. If your gaze drew you toward beautiful things, nothing is more beautiful than that. If you thought you were embracing truth in anything, nothing is truer than that. If you believed that generosity deserving admiration existed anywhere, nothing is more munificent than that. Do you marvel at what is pure and simple? Nothing is more sincere than that goodness. Are you concerned with the abundance of things that overflow? Nothing is more abundant than that abundance. Do you love something as trustworthy? Nothing is firmer in faith than this. Do you love something as useful? Nothing is more beneficial than love of this very thing. Is there something that attracts you either by the appearance of severity or of delight? Nothing is either more terrible or more gracious than that greatness and that condescension. Kindness is needed in adversity, sweetness in prosperity: from that one source there is either joy amid gladness or consolation amid grief. Therefore it is entirely reasonable to love above all else the one in whom you possess everything. Riches, and whatever else it is that now holds you by its pleasures, are possessed not only within him but also by him. Let love, hitherto scattered, henceforth be devoted to divine vigils. Let affection, still wandering among its desires, now chaste, be recalled to sacred uses; and correct and direct your love, which strays among opinions, by restraining its error, and turn it toward God: for whatever you now love is his—his, I say, entirely his. For he is so great that those who do not love him can indeed love nothing except what belongs to him, though they do so unjustly.

Yet let the just judge consider whether it is right to love the work while neglecting and abandoning its maker, the creator of all things; to rush everywhere, indiscriminately and heedlessly, upon the object of one’s desires, when God ought surely to have been drawing us to love him precisely through this affection for his works. And now man turns himself against the desires and services of merely unworthy creations, and, with souls incongruously divided, he pursues the product while abandoning the craftsman; he embraces the beauty whose author he does not admire. And what have we said about that vast multitude of his sweetness? Or what have we said about the great and ineffable pleasantness of that good, about the holy and profound treasure of his love? Or when can anyone, speaking about him, ever attain in words to the dignity of the reality itself? Let us therefore judge that loving him is not merely a matter of pleasure but also of necessity. For it is impious not to love him whom, even after loving him, you could not repay. It is supremely unjust that you should be unwilling to give him what you can give, when even if you wished to repay him, you could not. For what shall we render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to us (Ps. 115 [116])? What shall we render even for this alone: that through faith he gave salvation to humanity and ordained that the means by which he would spread hope through the world and life among mortals should be as easy as possible?

And, to descend to these matters, do you think that all those external things—namely, nations and kingdoms—submitted to Roman authority and jurisdiction for any other reason, or that a large part of the human race became one people for any other reason, than so that faith might more easily penetrate, like medicine through one body, when infused through one nation, and so that, having been introduced into the head, it might swiftly spread through the limbs? Otherwise, it would not have converged among nations numerous in their customs and languages and differing from one another, nor would it have crossed such great distances over the obstacles of ever-new stages. Finally, blessed Paul, distributing the faith through this same people, writes that from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum he had filled everything with the gospel of Christ (Rom. 15:19). When would this have come to pass among nations either “numberless in multitude” (Cicero, *For Marcus Marcellus*) or barbarous in savagery? Hence it is that now the earth resounds with Christ from the rising and setting of the sun, from the north and from the sea; hence it is that every region of the world converges upon life, while the Thracian receives the faith, the Libyan receives the faith, the Syrian receives the faith, and the Spaniard receives the faith. A great proof of divine compassion, therefore, is furnished by the fact that under Caesar Augustus, when Roman power had reached its summit, God then gave himself to the world. Thus, to present what is in your own sphere, since approximately the one thousand one hundred and eighty-fifth year has now turned since the beginning of this kingdom, anyone competent to make the case can show that whatever came to the Roman empire either under that ancient rule of kings or later under that twofold administration of consuls was all prepared for Christ’s coming and provided for the spreading of the faith.

Let us return to our subject. “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world” (1 John 2), because all these things flatter our sight with deceptive colors. Let the power of vision granted to the light not be applied to error; and, while it is available for the uses of life, let it not admit the causes of death. “The desires of the flesh,” as the distinguished Apostle says, “wage war against the soul” (1 Pet. 2:11); and all their array is prepared for our destruction and ruin. When they rise against us, they maintain a watchful position, plainly like external enemies, acquiring as much strength for themselves as they take away from us. Thus I have spoken at length about the inextricable attractions of the world lying in wait, about honors and riches, as though the world, pleasant in its flatteries, were flourishing. Whatever appearance those things possess, once polished by deceptive splendors, has now grown worn, and all its painted brilliance has perished. The world scarcely retains even the power to deceive. That image of things, once beautiful enough to deceive, has disappeared. Previously it tried to seduce us with its true radiance; it could not. Now it is scarcely able even to corrupt us through its false display. It lacked solid goods; behold, it is failing even in its perishable ones. Neither do temporary beauties adorn it, nor do lasting ones confirm it for the future; unless we deceive ourselves, the world can scarcely deceive us.

But why do we conceal matters that are stronger still? We speak of the world’s dissipated riches when the world itself, moving toward its end, is already being driven through its final spans. How much greater and more serious is the fact that it itself will soon no longer exist? Why recall its worn-out property and furnishings? Nor is it without reason that, its strength consumed by age, it is pressed toward decline and deprived of its supports, since, already tottering beneath its burden, it collapses into old age. The final age of the world is filled with evils, just as old age is filled with illnesses. Famine, pestilence, devastation, wars, and terrors have long been seen and are still seen in this ancient age. These are now its illnesses in its final years. Hence signs in the sky are often observed, together with earthquakes, altered cycles of the seasons, and monstrous fertility among living creatures: all these are portents of a time that is still advancing, but already failing. And this is confirmed not only by the words of our weakness but also by the declarations of apostolic authority. For there we read: “The ends of the ages have come upon us” (1 Cor. 10). Since this was said long ago, why do we delay, and what are we waiting for? That day presses upon us, now belonging not only to us but also to the age itself. Every hour reminds us that the appointed time of dissolution is near, when the alternating end, with its twofold danger, and the twofold crisis threaten one death to all. The mortality of the world already bears down upon me, wretched as I am, as though my own mortality were not enough to terrify me. Why do we grope after our fears? There is no room for security when the end hangs impartially over all of us, each and every one. All the more pitiable, therefore, is the condition of human beings amid this—not merely the end of the age, but even the decline of its present order—since they lay up for themselves no hope of future joys while they do not enjoy present pleasures. They do not attain the pleasure of this brief life, and they cannot hope for the everlasting one. They do not make use of temporal goods; no, they will not make use of eternal ones. Here there is little possession; there, no hope at all. This condition of humanity is altogether deserving of grief and pity—unless, perhaps, it turns bitter necessity into a fitting response; unless, for this very reason, it reforms itself toward better remedies for its welfare and strives toward the hopes of a healthier counsel, especially since the affairs of the present age have been so torn apart that whoever loses the benefit of one future age will have lost the benefit of both.

Every intention of the soul must be directed toward hope for the future. To help you attain this hope more fully and clearly, I shall not refuse to disclose it under the form of an example. If someone today offered a person five bronze coins but promised five hundred gold coins for tomorrow, and offered him the choice of whether he preferred to take the bronze immediately or the gold later, would there be any doubt that he would choose those great gifts, with only a short delay? You too, when you have considered the condition of this brief life and the eternal one, should not choose to seize worthless things when you can hope for precious ones. It is not worth as much to take small things as it is to await what is great. And if we both see and grasp everything fragile that exists in the world—and “hope” receives its name from hoping—it is clear that hope cannot at all be possessed in this age, in which we enjoy the things we behold. For “hope that is seen is not hope. For who hopes for what he sees?” (Rom. 8:24). Therefore, whatever hope is mixed with human affairs must be sought in the future; otherwise it cannot be called hope if it is not hoped for.

Accordingly, we pursue the reality of hope more clearly in the future than we experience the hope of a reality in the present. Behold, we do not look upon the things brought directly before our eyes as though our vision were overwhelmed; rather, with our sight unimpeded, we focus much more certainly on the things presented at a distance. The same, almost certainly, has happened with present and future things. For present things, as though thrust into our eyes, are not seen correctly; future things, as though withdrawn from our eyes, are perceived with the greatest clarity. Nor do we assume this confidence in future things from an uncertain guarantor, but from our Lord Jesus Christ, the truest sponsor of truth, who promises the righteous an endless kingdom and the ample rewards of blessed eternity; who also, through the ineffable mystery of the flesh he assumed, being both human and God, reconciled humanity to God; and who, through the great and hidden mystery of his passion, absolved the world from sin. Thus “he was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, appeared to angels, was preached among the nations, was believed in the world, was taken up in glory”; therefore “God exalted him,” so that all might now confess in heaven, on earth, in the sea, and in the abysses that “the Lord Jesus is in glory, King and God before the ages” (Phil. 2).

Why not, then, rejecting those precepts of the philosophers to whose reading you devote your effort and talent, apply your mind to absorbing the teachings of Christian doctrine? There too you will find material with which to exercise your eloquence and talent, and it will soon become clear to you how much these our teachings—that is, the precepts of piety and truth—owe to those of the philosophers [perhaps: *quam non haec*, “than not these”]. In their precepts there is either virtue cast in shadow or false wisdom; in ours there is perfected justice and solid truth. Hence one may rightly say that others have appropriated the name of philosophy, while we possess its life. For what kind of precepts for living can be given by them? They do not know the cause. Since they are ignorant of God and turn aside from justice at the very outset, they proceed into all the rest through consequent error. Thus the end of such studies is vanity. If some among them define more honorable principles, they serve and labor for this boastfulness; thus among them abstinence from vices is not free from vices. They are therefore, as it is written, those “who set their minds on earthly things” (Phil. 3:19). From this it is plainly shown that they do not see true justice or true wisdom. Will someone from the school of Aristippus see the truth, when by his own reasoning he differs in nothing from swine or cattle, since he places blessedness in bodily pleasure—whose god is the belly, and whose glory is in his shameful parts (ibid.)? Will he teach what is honorable and just, in whose company the prodigal, the shameless, and the adulterer philosophize? But let another occasion be reserved for speaking against the philosophers; I shall come to the matters about which I am speaking with you.

Set aside now those highly general opinions of theirs, which delight you, gathered briefly from every kind of disputation, and turn yourself toward our studies and writings. There, my excellent friend, you will satisfy your heart with instruction of many kinds. There, to instill faith, these things will be said to you—not indeed in these words, but with this meaning: “Whoever does not believe the Word of God does not understand.” There you will be admonished: “Because you call him Lord, fear the Lord; because you call him Father, love him.” There you will learn the true sacrifices by hearing: “The sacrifices most acceptable to God are justice and mercy.” There this will be impressed upon you: “If you love yourself, love your neighbor; you will give nothing more beneficial to your own interests than what you confer upon another’s.” There you will be instructed to consider no cause so worthy that it makes the death of a human being justifiable to you. There you will be warned against unlawful things: “Resist lust as the most bitter enemy, which rejoices in insulting the defeated, even through the humiliation of the body.” There you will be taught this concerning not coveting: “It is better not to want what you do not have than to have what you want.” There, concerning not becoming angry, this will be impressed upon you: “One who becomes angry when provoked does not become angry only when he is not provoked.” There too you will hear about enemies: “Love the one who does not love you, because scarcely anyone fails to love one who loves.” There this will often be repeated to you: “The one who stores up treasure well is the one who distributes it to the needy. For he can no longer lose what he has placed securely by giving it away.” There too you will be urged toward better things when it is said: “The fruit of faithful marriages is continence.” There you will learn to distinguish things when you hear: “The evils of this age are common to the just and the unjust.” There this will be offered for you to hear: “It is a greater illness for the soul to languish under vices than for the body to suffer from diseases.” There, to commend peace, this will be declared: “Similarity of character among the impatient is the cause of discord.” There, so that you do not follow the wicked, you will hear: “The prudent and wise person instructs, and so does the fool: the former teaches what should be imitated, the latter what should be avoided.” There these things too are proclaimed: “Many things benefit those who do not know; therefore God’s kindness is no less in secret than in what is open.” There you will be admonished: “Give thanks to God no more in prosperity than in adversity; and when things go well, acknowledge that you have not deserved it.” There more remote matters will also be disclosed to you when these things are proclaimed: “That fate does not exist—let the nations ask their own laws, which certainly punish no one except for the will behind deeds.” There you will hear these instructions for preserving purity: “If you wish to be truthful, you will not be suspicious. For we suspect only what we do not know.” There you will hear this also concerning higher matters: “When one is fixed in mind upon God and is tickled by passions, he falls from heaven to earth.” There these things too will be recalled to you: “When the wicked sometimes receive good things here, and the good are afflicted by evils, those who do not believe in God’s future judgment judge God to be unjust—which God forbid.” There you will be advised: “Do not do even in secret what you would not want people to know; and do not think what you would not want God to know.” There you will be told, against every kind of fraud: “It is more wretched to deceive than to be deceived.” There, against boastfulness, these completing instructions will be given to you: “Flee vanity all the more as you become better. For other vices grow through vices, but vanity grows through virtues.” These few matters, then, have been briefly and selectively previewed from the studies.

But if you approach as an investigator the very sources of sacred eloquence, there you will marvel not more at the external than at the internal things. Thus Scripture, while shining within, like a precious gem, sends the eyes of those who contemplate it down into the depths of its radiance. Accustom yourself without resistance to this light, which at first dims the mind’s vision; learn through this inner and health-giving food to nourish the soul’s hunger. Through the work of the merciful Lord, we do not doubt that this will happen: that, desiring what is ours and disregarding what is yours, you will grow disgusted with empty things and desire what is solid. It is most foolish that, when God has done so many things for us, we ourselves have done nothing for ourselves; and that, while he has looked to human welfare in his works, a human being should refuse to look after his own welfare. We look after ourselves when we restore ourselves to the worship and love of God. For true blessedness is to despise the blessedness of the age and, neglecting earthly things, burn with desire for divine things. Therefore, direct all your words and actions now toward God or for God’s sake. See to it that innocence is always your companion, and it will be your guardian. Innocence is indeed trustworthy. It is a great thing to follow virtue and to contribute to it something according to one’s strength. Nor need we fear that the soul will be unable, through a better life, to free itself from those things that habit has made familiar. The same one to whom we offer ourselves for healing and protection grants strength to our desire. But from where? So that anyone may be able to grasp, even by estimation, the reward of future goods. Behold, as we can see, divine munificence has granted to all alike the common use of the most precious light. The pious and the impious alike are allowed to behold the sun; creation preserves its service to all through kindly acts; the good and the wicked alike possess the whole world without distinction.

Since God therefore grants such splendid things here equally to the just and the unjust, what must we think of the things he reserves for the just? Let us consider what he will restore, since he has given so much; how great he will be in rewards, since he is so great in gifts. If the kindness of the giver is so beyond estimation, what will that of the rewarder be? “What God has prepared for those who love him” is ineffable, rightly and plainly so, because it is truly immeasurable how great are the things he will repay to the good, who bestows such great things even upon the ungrateful. Look around you, and from the sea of your occupations, look out as though toward a certain harbor of our profession, and turn your prow toward it. This is the one harbor to which we may return from all the tossing of the wavering age, which weary we may seek amid the world’s rushing storms; here all who are battered by the tempest of the roaring age must take refuge. Here is the most trustworthy anchorage and assured rest. Here a broad retreat, shut off from the waves, lies silent. Here a soothing tranquility smiles serenely. When you have been carried here, your ship, safely anchored at the cross after its empty labors, will remain secured here. But now the length of the written page demands a limit. Receive, for the honor of God, the force of the heavenly precepts, gathered together in a compact and brief summary. These are all the commandments. Forgive me, and acknowledge me.

[Col. 0727]

ONE BOOK OF THE FORMULAS OF SPIRITUAL UNDERSTANDING OF SAINT EUCHERIUS, BISHOP OF LYONS, ADDRESSED TO URANIUS (C)

Preface

[Col. 0727A] I have judged it appropriate, out of the paternal concern I have for you, to compose and send you formulas of spiritual understanding for Latin names. Once these have been grasped, the understanding of all the divine writings and the meaning of the remaining passages may most easily be sharpened. For since “the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3:6), it is necessary to penetrate by the life-giving Spirit into the inner realities of those spiritual utterances.

Moreover, the whole of Scripture, both of the Old Instrument and of the New, teaches us that an allegorical understanding must be adopted, either through what we read in the Old Testament: “I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter ancient things in riddles” (Ps. 77 [78]:2); or through what is likewise written in the New Testament: “Jesus spoke all these things to the crowds in parables, and without parables he did not speak to them” (Mark 4:16).

Nor is it surprising that the divine word, uttered through the mouths of prophets and apostles, departed greatly from the customary manner of writing among human beings, having easy things readily at hand but containing great things in its depths. For it was truly fitting that sacred words spoken by God should be distinguished from other writings not only in worth, as they deserved, but also in appearance, lest the dignity of heavenly mysteries become exposed indiscriminately and openly to everyone, and lest one “give what is holy to dogs and cast pearls before swine” (Matt. 7:6); lest the consecrated vessels of the temple, wrapped up, be carried by the common people without their seeing them (Num. 4:15, 20); and so that, truly in the manner of “that silver-colored dove” (Ps. 68 [67]:14), whose hindparts shine with the appearance of gleaming gold, the first things in divine Scripture might shine with silver, while its more hidden things might glow with gold.

It was therefore rightly arranged that the purity of those utterances should be concealed from the common gaze of all beneath its hidden veil, as though beneath a veil of modesty; and divine providence most appropriately ensured that the writings themselves should be covered, shaded by heavenly mysteries, just as divinity itself concealed its own nature in secrecy.

Since, therefore, the holy books contain references to the eyes of the Lord, the mouth of the Lord, the womb of the Lord, the Lord’s hands and feet, and even the Lord’s weapons, while it is entirely contrary to the Catholic faith of the Churches to define God as corporeal—for he is invisible, incomprehensible, immutable, and infinite—we must inquire how these things are disclosed figuratively through the Holy Spirit. Here are found the inner parts of the Lord’s temple (Ezek. 40); here are those mysteries of the holy of holies, with the riddles unveiled.

The body of sacred Scripture, as it is traditionally understood, is in the letter, or history; it is the soul in the moral sense, which is called tropology; and it is the spirit in the higher understanding, which is called anagogy. This threefold rule of the Scriptures is fittingly observed by the confession of the Holy Trinity, sanctifying us in every respect, so that our spirit, soul, and body may be preserved blameless at the coming and judgment of our Lord Jesus Christ (1 Thess. 5:24).

The wisdom of this world, however, divided its philosophy into three parts: physics, ethics, and logic—that is, natural, moral, and rational philosophy. Natural philosophy concerns the causes of nature, which contains all things; moral philosophy concerns conduct; rational philosophy, discussing higher matters, affirms that God is the Father of all. This threefold division of teaching is not entirely unlike the distinction made by our own learned writers in their discussions, according to which this heavenly philosophy of the Scriptures is to be interpreted according to history, according to tropology, and according to anagogy.

History therefore impresses upon us the truth of events and the reliability of the account. Tropology refers mystical meanings to the correction of life. Anagogy leads us to the more sacred secrets of heavenly figures. There are also those who think that allegory should be added as a fourth category in this field of knowledge, affirming that it sets forth the narrative of past events as a shadow of future things.

To make these matters clearer through the examples that follow: according to history, heaven is what we behold; according to tropology, it is heavenly life; according to allegory, the waters are baptism; according to anagogy, they are angels. Hence the passage: “And let the waters that are above the heavens praise the name of the Lord” (Ps. 148:4).

The whole discipline of our religion flowed from that source of twofold knowledge, whose first part they called *praktikē* and the second *theōrētikē*—that is, active and contemplative. One completes active life through the correction of conduct; the other is occupied with contemplation of heavenly things and discussion of the divine Scriptures. Active knowledge, therefore, is dispersed among various studies; contemplative knowledge branches into two parts, consisting in historical discussion and the interpretation of spiritual understanding.

But setting these matters aside for now, let us present the formulas of spiritual understanding that we promised, proceeding through the figures of individual names by which these things are customarily understood when inserted into the text of divine reading. Let us therefore pray to the Lord that he may disclose the hidden things of his Scriptures, and let us set forth how their more secret matters ought to be understood.

I. On divine names.  
II. On those things that are called the Lord’s members, or that are signified concerning him.  
III. On heavenly creatures.  
IV. On earthly things.  
V. On living creatures.  
VI. On various names and designations of things.  
VII. On the inner human being.  
VIII. On things that are in use and commonly present.  
IX. On various meanings of words or names.  
X. On Jerusalem, or its adversaries.  
XI. On numbers whose meanings are drawn into allegory.

Let us now explain the meanings of the names and words themselves, according to which they are most especially drawn into allegory, insofar as God’s gift may suggest.

CHAPTER I. On Divine Names

Almighty God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, is one and threefold. He is one in nature, plainly, and threefold in persons. He alone is invisible, immeasurable, and incomprehensible. He alone is uncircumscribed, immutable, incorporeal, and immortal; everywhere present and hidden; everywhere entire and immeasurable.

He is invisible because in his essence he cannot be seen at all, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “Whom no human being has seen, nor can see” (1 Tim. 6:16). And in the Gospel: “No one has ever seen God” (John 1:18).

He is incorporeal because he does not exist composed or joined together out of any bodily contours of limbs. Thus the truth says in the Gospel: “God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth” (John 4:24).

He is immeasurable because his quantity or quality cannot be measured by any created thing. Solomon, beseeching him in his prayers, says: “If heaven and the heaven of heavens do not contain you, how much less this house that I have built?” (1 Kings 8:27).

He is uncircumscribed because he cannot be circumscribed.

He is not confined to a place because he does not pass from place to place, nor is he held in any particular place. He himself bears witness concerning himself through Isaiah, saying: “Heaven is my throne, but the earth is the footstool for my feet” (Isa. 66:1). And through Jeremiah: “Do I not fill heaven and earth?” (Jer. 23:24). The prophet, confessing his immeasurability in a psalm, says to the Lord himself: “If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present” (Ps. 138 [139]:8). Of his immeasurability it is written in the Book of Job: “He is higher than heaven—what can you do? Deeper than the abyss—what can you know? Its measure is longer than the earth and broader than the sea” (Job 11:8). For he who fills heaven and earth is unquestionably absent from no place in his essence. He is above all things by ruling and commanding; beneath all things by sustaining and carrying them—not through the burden of labor but through tireless power, since no creature created by him can subsist by itself unless it is sustained by the one who created it. He is outside all things, but not excluded.

He is immutable because he cannot in any way be changed from what he is, as he himself says through the prophet Malachi: “I am the Lord, and I do not change” (Mal. 3:6). God is called immutable because anger, wrath, repentance, forgetfulness, remembrance, and other things of this kind do not occur in his soul. For he is a simple, immutable, and undisturbed nature. He himself is not one thing and what he possesses another; rather, he is himself what he possesses and what he is.

He is immortal because he cannot die in any way, as the Apostle testifies, saying: “He alone possesses immortality, dwelling in inaccessible light, whom no human being has seen nor can see” (1 Tim. 6:16).

Whenever sacred Scripture, scattered throughout the divine books, describes movements of the soul or human limbs in God—that is, a head, hair, eyes, eyelids, ears, and other members, or movements of the soul such as anger, wrath, forgetfulness, repentance, remembrance, and similar things—those who understand rightly must not take them carnally according to the historical sense, as do the Jews and many heretics who think carnally and suppose that God is corporeal and confined to a place. Rather, all these things concerning him must be understood and confessed spiritually. If anyone believes that God possesses human limbs or movements of the soul in a human manner, he unquestionably fashions idols in his heart.

Therefore, as has been said, we read figuratively that God has a head, and we must understand by it the very essence of his divinity, which precedes all things and to which all things are subject (1 Cor. 11:3).

The hairs of his head should typically be understood as the holy angels or virtuous elect. Concerning this it is written symbolically in the Book of Daniel: “I watched until thrones were placed, and the Ancient of Days sat. His clothing was white as snow, and the hair of his head like pure wool” (Dan. 7:9). For the white garments of God signify the same thing as the hairs of his head, namely, the holy angels and the multitude of saints made white. Or certainly the hairs are compared to pure wool so that by this the Ancient of Days may be understood.

God is said to have eyes because he sees everything and nothing is hidden from him. In his sight, as the Apostle says, no creature is invisible: “All things are naked and open to his eyes” (Heb. 4:13). In another sense, they signify the regard of his grace, as in the psalm: “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous” (Ps. 33 [34]:16). In yet another sense, the eyes of the Lord are understood as his commandments, through which the light of knowledge is supplied to us, as in the psalm: “The commandment of the Lord is lucid, enlightening the eyes” (Ps. 18 [19]:9).

The eyelids of the Lord signify his hidden and incomprehensible judgments, or the spiritual speech of the divine books. Concerning these hidden and incomprehensible mysteries and judgments, the psalm says: “His eyelids examine the children of men” (Ps. 10 [11]:5)—that is, they test them.

God is said to have ears because he hears everything and nothing is hidden from him in silence. Concerning this it is written in the Book of Wisdom: “The ear of heaven hears all things, and the tumult of murmuring will not be hidden” (Wis. 1:10).

The nostrils of God signify his inspiration into the hearts of the faithful, as in the Book of Kings: “Smoke rose from his nostrils” (2 Kings 22:9)—that is, his inspiration produces the tearful contrition of those who repent.

The face of God is the knowledge of his divinity communicated to all. Concerning this knowledge it is written in the Psalms: “Show us your face, and we shall be saved” (Ps. 79 [80]:4)—that is, grant us your knowledge. This knowledge he made known to humanity through the Son of Man, who himself says in the Gospel: “No one knows the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wishes to reveal him” (Matt. 11:27). In another sense, the face of God signifies the invisible essence of the divinity of the Son of God. Concerning this the Lord himself answers Moses through the angel, saying: “You shall see my back, but you cannot see my face” (Exod. 33:23), as though he were saying: “You cannot see my divinity.”

The mouth of God is the Son of God the Father, that is, the Lord Christ; concerning this the prophet Isaiah spoke in the person of the Jews: “Because we provoked his mouth to anger” (Isa. 1:20). In another sense, his mouth is understood as his word or command. Concerning this word of the Lord the aforementioned prophet says: “The mouth of the Lord has spoken this.”

The Word of God is the Son of God the Father, through whom all things were made. Concerning him the psalm says: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established” (Ps. 32 [33]:6). And elsewhere: “He sent his Word and healed them” (Ps. 106 [107]:20). And in the Gospel according to John: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1).

The tongue of God mystically signifies the Holy Spirit, through whom God the Father disclosed his secret to human beings. Hence the psalm: “My tongue is the pen of a ready writer” (Ps. 44 [45]:2).

The lips of God are mystically understood as the harmonious utterance of the two Testaments. Concerning these two Testaments it is written in Proverbs: “His mouth shall not err in judgment” (Prov. 16:10).

The arms of God the Father are understood as his Son and the Holy Spirit, as in Isaiah: “And my arms shall judge the peoples” (Isa. 51:5). The arm of God, in the singular, is understood as the Son. Concerning him Jeremiah says to the Lord himself: “And now, Lord God, you who led your people out of the land of Egypt with a strong hand and an outstretched arm” (Jer. 32:21). The Son of God the Father is therefore called the arm because the elect creation is held together by him.

[Col. 0732A] The right hand of God the Father is understood as his only-begotten Son. Concerning him the psalm says in the person of the assumed human being: “The right hand of the Lord has done mighty things” (Ps. 117 [118]:16). In another sense, the right hand of the Lord signifies the glory of the Father and eternal blessedness. Concerning this, the psalm says in the person of the Father to the Son: “Sit at my right hand” (Ps. 109 [110]:1). The right hand of God is also said to be every elect creature in heaven and on earth; just as by his left hand the rejected creation is understood, namely, all demons and impious people, who, placed on the left, will endure eternal punishments (Matt. 25:33).

The hand of God the Father is understood as his Son, because all things were made through him, as in Isaiah: “All these things my hand has made, and all things came to be” (Isa. LXVI, 2). In another sense, the hand of God is understood as his power [Col. 0732B], concerning which power the prophet says in the Book of Jeremiah: “As clay is in the hand of the potter, so are you in my hand, house of Israel” (Jer. XVIII, 6). The hand of the Lord is also understood as a scourge; concerning its striking, it is written in the prophet Zephaniah: “I will stretch out my hand over Judah and over the inhabitants of Israel, and I will destroy from this place the remnant of Baal” (Zeph. I, 4), and so forth. For this striking of the Lord, blessed Job says of himself: “The hand of the Lord has touched me” (Job XIX, 21).

The finger of God is understood individually as the Holy Spirit, by whom the Law is related to have been written on two stone tablets on Mount Sinai (Exod. XXXII, 16). He himself wrote who dictated what was to be written—that is, the Holy Spirit. Concerning him the Lord says in the Gospel: “If I cast out demons by the finger of God” (Luke XI, 20). [Col. 0732C] For just as a finger with the hand, and the hand or arm with the body, are one in nature, so the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are indeed three persons, but one substance of divinity.

The fingers of God, in the plural, are understood as the holy prophets, through whom the Holy Spirit, by his inspiration, set down the books of the Law and the Prophets. Concerning them it is written in the psalm: “I will see the heavens, the works of your fingers” (Ps. VIII, 4). Through the heavens, therefore, the books of the Law and the Prophets are mystically indicated; through the fingers, as has been said, the holy prophets.

The image of the invisible God the Father is his only-begotten Son, concerning whom the Apostle says: “The image of the invisible God” (Col. I, 15). For in one sense there is the image of God the Father in his Son, whom he begot not from elsewhere but from himself—that is, [Col. 0732D] from his own substance—making him in every respect like and equal to himself. In another sense there is the human soul, which he did not beget from himself, that is, from his substance, as many heretics have supposed, but created from nothing. It is like the image of any king in his son, whom he begot from himself in his own likeness—that is, a human being from a human being. In another sense there is the image on his ring, as his image impressed in wax, which is not what he himself is, unlike the Son, who by nature is what the Father is.

The heart of God the Father mystically signifies the secret of his wisdom, from which he impassibly begot his Word, that is, his Son, without beginning. He himself says through the prophet: “My heart has uttered a good word” (Ps. XLIV, 2).

[Col. 0733A] God is said to have wings because, like a bird, he gathers his chosen beneath himself as chicks, cherishes them, and protects them from the snares of the devil and of evil people. Hence the prophet says: “Protect me under the shadow of your wings” (Ps. XVI, 8).

God is said to have shoulders because he carries the weak members of the Church, as it were, upon his shoulders. Concerning this the psalm says: “He will overshadow you with his shoulders” (Ps. XC, 4).

The belly is understood as the hidden origin of his substance. Hence the psalm says: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Ps. CIX, 3). In another sense, his womb mystically signifies his incomprehensible judgments, which cannot be investigated. Concerning this hidden judgment of his it is written in the Book of blessed Job: “From whose womb did the ice come forth, and who begot the frost from heaven?” (Job XXXVIII, 29).

[Col. 0733B] The posterior parts are understood as the incarnation of the Son of God. Concerning these posterior parts the Son, speaking to Moses on Mount Sinai through an angel, says: “You shall see my posterior parts, but you cannot see my face” (Exod. XXXIII, 23).

The feet of God are the foundation of his power, because he is present everywhere and all things are subject to him. He himself says through Isaiah: “Heaven is my throne, but the earth is the footstool of my feet” (Isa. LXVI, 1). In another sense, the feet of the Son of God signify his incarnation, which is subject to divinity as feet are subject to the head. Just as the head expresses divinity, so the feet express his humanity. Concerning this humanity it is written in Exodus: “They saw the Lord Jesus—this is Moses and Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy of the elders—beneath his feet, as it were, something like sapphire stones, and as it were the sky when it is clear” [Col. 0733C] (Exod. XXIV, 10). Just as by the sapphire stone he wished to signify heavenly creatures, or holy angels, so by the clear sky he wished to indicate symbolically the holy Church gathered from human beings. Over these two creatures the assumed human being, the Son of God, reigns forever. Concerning him the psalm says: “You have subjected all things under their feet” (Ps. VIII, 8). In another sense, the feet of the Lord, that is, of Jesus Christ, signify the holy preachers, concerning whom it is written in Deuteronomy: “Those who approach his feet shall receive his teaching” (Deut. XXXIII, 3).

The garment of the Son of God is sometimes understood figuratively in the divine books as his flesh, which was assumed by divinity. Concerning this garment of flesh Isaiah prophesies: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with garments dyed [Col. 0733D] from Bozrah?” (Isa. LXIII, 1). Again, the garment of the same Lord is understood as the holy Church, which is joined to him through faith and love. Concerning this it is written in the psalm: “The Lord has reigned; he has clothed himself with beauty” (Ps. XCII, 1). And in another psalm, addressed to the Lord himself: “You have clothed yourself with confession and beauty, wrapped in light as in a garment” (Ps. CIII, 2).

The cloak of Christ is understood as the Church already mentioned. Concerning it, it is written in the Book of Genesis: “He washed his robe in wine” (Gen. XLIX, 11)—that is, his flesh in the blood of his passion, and his cloak, that is, his Church, in the blood of the grape.

The footwear of the Lord Jesus Christ mystically signifies his incarnation, which he deigned to assume from the mortality of the human [Col. 0734A] race. Concerning this incarnation of his he says through the prophet in the psalm: “I will extend my shoe over Edom” (Ps. LIX, 10)—that is, “I will manifest my incarnation among the people of the Gentiles.”

The steps signify the coming of the Son of God into the world and his return to the Father. Concerning them the psalm says: “Your steps were seen, O God, the steps of my God, my King who is in the sanctuary” (Ps. LXVII, 25). He came from heaven into the Virgin’s womb; from the womb, by being born, he was placed in a manger (Luke II, 7). After he had fulfilled everything for which he had come, sent by the Father, he was hung upon the wood of the cross. After being taken down from the cross (Acts XIII, 29), he was buried bodily; in soul, however, he descended to the underworld. On the third day, by the power of his divinity, he raised his flesh from the [Col. 0734B] tomb; and on the fortieth day after his resurrection, in the sight of the Apostles, he ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father (Acts I, 9; Mark XVI, 19), that is, in his glory. These are the steps of the Son of God: this is his descent and ascent, which are frequently read of in the sacred Scriptures.

God is said to ascend when the Son led into heaven, as captive, the flesh assumed from us, leading captivity captive (Ps. LXVII, 19). For, having assumed the nature of the human race, which in this world was held captive by the devil, he carried it with him into heaven, where it had never previously been, transporting it as a captive.

God is said to hide his face (Deut. XXXII, 20) when, on account of certain sins among the Gentiles, he hides his knowledge from them. We now see this fulfilled among the Jewish [Col. 0734C] people, because, by denying the Son of God, they have so lost knowledge of the true God that they have become like the Gentiles, who did not know the Lord.

God is said to show his face (Ps. LXXIX, 4) when, by the regard of his grace, he reveals himself to whomever he wishes—namely, to his chosen—by secretly inspiring their hearts, and pours his love into them so that they may love him.

God is said to sit, not bodily in the human manner, but in the sense that he presides rationally over every creature in his power, as in the psalm: “The Lord has reigned over all the nations; God sits upon his holy throne” (Ps. XLVI, 9). God is also said to sit upon the Cherubim [Col. 0734D] (Ps. XCVIII, 1), a name interpreted as “multitude” or “fullness of knowledge.” By this are signified holy angels or the minds of spiritual men, in whom God invisibly presides and reigns. He sits in those who are filled with his knowledge and love. For in the Proverbs of Solomon it is written: “His soul is the seat of wisdom”; and the wisdom of God the Father is Christ (1 Cor. I, 24), who is said to sit in the souls of the saints.

God is said to descend into the world when he works something new in human creation that had not previously existed. Thus the Son of God is said to have descended when, for our redemption, he assumed true flesh from the Virgin Mary and deigned to become truly human—not by losing what he was, but by assuming what he was not. Concerning this descent, that is, [Col. 0735A] his incarnation, it is written in the psalm: “He inclined the heavens and descended, and darkness was beneath his feet” (Ps. XVII, 10). He inclined the heavens because, before his coming, he sent angels or prophets as heralds to announce his coming to human beings. Darkness was beneath his feet because impious people, on account of their wickedness, could not recognize his incarnation, nor can they even now.

God is said to stand when he patiently bears with us in our weakness—that is, with his creature—for repentance and conversion, as in the prophet Habakkuk: “He stood and measured the earth, and it was dissolved” (Hab. III, 6). That is, he stood ready to intervene, and he dissolved those who believe in him from the bonds of sins.

God is said to pass over when he departs from the hearts of certain [Col. 0735B] people in whom he had previously been believed through faith, after unbelief or some other sin has crept in, and passes over to others—as from the Jews to the Gentiles, from heretics to Catholics, or from any irreligious people to the religious.

God is said to withdraw and pass over to others, not locally or visibly, but because he habitually does so invisibly, by a hidden and just judgment.

God is said to walk, not by passing from place to place—for it is impious to believe this—but because his walking is his delight in the hearts of the saints, as it is written: “I will dwell in them and walk among them, and I will be their God” (2 Cor. VI, 16). Or certainly, God’s walking means his passing from place to place in his holy preachers.
