[Col. 0735C] God’s speaking means that, invisibly and without the sound of a voice or any noise, he secretly inspires the minds of the saints with his will and correct understanding, or reveals the future, as he does in the holy prophets. This speech of God, as some maintain, is understood in three ways. First, through an assumed creature, as when he appeared to Moses in the bush (Exod. III, 2), or to Abraham (Gen. XVIII), Jacob (Gen. XXXII, 24), and the other saints to whom he deigned to appear in angels. Second, in dreams, as to Jacob (Gen. XXVIII, 12), the prophet Zechariah (Zech. IV, 1), Joseph, the husband of Mary (Matt. I, 20), and other saints to whom he wished to reveal his secret. Third, neither through a visible creature nor through a human being, but by touching [Col. 0735D] the hearts of his own invisibly through hidden inspiration alone, he makes them speak, as is written in the books of the prophets, when the prophets themselves, suddenly filled with the divine Spirit, exclaimed: “Thus says the Lord” (Isa. VII, 7).

God’s seeing means approving good deeds, as in Genesis: “God saw all that he had made, and it was very good” (Gen. I, 31)—that is, he showed it to be good to those who understood. In another sense, God’s seeing means rejecting the evils of human beings by knowing them, as in the prophet Isaiah: “God saw, and it appeared evil in his eyes” (Isa. LIX, 15). Again, God’s seeing means making us see, as in the psalm: “Test me, O God, and know my heart” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 23), and so forth: “and see whether there is any way of iniquity in me.” This manner of speaking is likewise found in the Book of Blessed Job, where, having spoken of the wisdom of God the Father in many notable ways, he adds concerning the Father: “Then he saw it, and declared it, and investigated it, and prepared it” [Col. 0736A] (Job XX, 27)—that is, he made people see, proclaim, investigate, and announce it to others.

God’s knowing means making people know, as he said to Abraham: “Now I know that you fear the Lord” (Gen. XXII, 12). For he did not come to know this in time, since he knows everything before it happens. Rather, God is said to know when he makes people know, so that those who had previously been unknown to themselves as to what sort of people they were might, through his questioning, become manifest to themselves by being tested. Such is the passage in the Law of Moses concerning the people of Israel: “I will test them,” he says, “whether they will keep my commandments or not” (Exod. [Col. 0736B] XVI, 4).

God’s not knowing means rejecting certain reprobates, as in the Gospel: “I do not know where you are from; depart from me, you workers of iniquity” (Luke XIII, 27).

God is said to be jealous when he frequently chastises, rebukes, and scourges his creature, whom he does not wish to perish, and by scourging brings him back to himself. Or God is said to be jealous when he wishes to leave no sin unpunished. For he is just, and therefore every injustice is detestable to him; as has been said, he in no way allows it to go unpunished.

God is said to be angry, not because of a movement of the soul or any disturbance—for nothing of this kind can happen to him—but because he is said to inflict a just vengeance upon the offending creature, that is, upon impious people and sinners. This means that he repays them what they deserve; and this [Col. 0736C] divine vengeance is called his anger (Ps. VI, 1).

God is said to repent, not because he repents, in the human manner, of deeds already completed—for he who knows before they happen cannot repent of acts committed—but because God’s repentance means changing his decrees, changing what previously had been one way into something else. This may be from good to evil because of sins that merit it, as the Lord is read to have repented that he had made Saul king (1 Sam. XV, 12); or as we now see happened among the Jewish people, who, although they had been God’s people, on account of their impiety became a synagogue of Satan (Rev. II, 9). From evil to good, it occurs among the people of the Gentiles, who formerly were not God’s people but have now, through the grace of Christ, become God’s people (Rom. IX, 26). In this way, by the hidden judgment of God, Judas the betrayer fell from the rank of the apostles [Col. 0736D] (Acts I, 18) and was plunged into the abyss of hell, while the thief, previously engaged in the crime of robbery, was transferred from the cross to paradise (Luke XXIII, 43). This change also—from good to better, as has been said, or from good to evil, or from evil to good—which takes place by God’s hidden and just judgment, whether through the severity of his justice or through his mercy, we call God’s repentance. This is expressed more clearly in the Book of Jeremiah (Jer. XVIII, 8).

God’s not repenting means changing his decrees in no way, as in the psalm: “God swore, and it did not repent him”—that is, the Father said to the Son: “You are a priest forever, [Col. 0737A] according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX, 4). Yet the Son of God is called the priest of the Father not according to his divinity but according to his humanity, in which he offered himself for us, through his passion and death, as an acceptable sacrifice to God the Father, so that he himself might be both the sacrifice and the priest.

God is said to forget when he does not have mercy on certain impious people and sinners. He does not do this through cruelty, which is not in God, but through his hidden and just judgment.

God is said to harden the hearts of certain evil people, as it is written concerning Pharaoh, king of Egypt (Exod. VII, 3). This does not mean that almighty God hardens their hearts [Col. 0737B] by his power—for it is impious to believe this—but that, their sins demanding it, he does not remove the hardness of heart by which they themselves, perpetrating every evil, distort everything. He is said to harden those whom, by a just judgment, he permits to be hardened.

God’s sleeping occurs when the only-begotten Son of the Father deigned to die for us in the flesh he had assumed. His death is rightly called a sweet sleep, as he himself says through the prophet Jeremiah: “Therefore, as if awakened from sleep, I arose; and I saw, and my sleep was sweet to me” (Jer. XXXI, 26). In another sense, God is said to sleep when faith in him does not remain vigilant amid the prosperities of this world and in the hearts of certain believers, but sleeps. Jesus himself signified this sleep when he slept on the sea amid the waves of the sea (Mark IV, 38). Or certainly, God’s sleeping means delaying to help the distressed, as in the psalm: “Arise; why do you sleep, O Lord?” (Ps. XLIII, 23), and so forth.

[Col. 0737C] God’s keeping watch means making himself manifest in the defense of his chosen.

**CHAPTER II. Concerning those things that are called the Lord’s members, or that are signified by them**

The eyes of the Lord are understood as divine inspection. In the psalm: “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous” (Ps. XXXIII, 16). The eyelids of God are his judgments, which test the children of human beings; the latter are neither wearied by the obscurity of things but exercised by it, nor puffed up by knowledge but strengthened. The ears of the Lord are understood when he deigns to hear. In the psalm: “And his ears are attentive to their prayers” (ibid.).

The mouth of the Lord is speech addressed to human beings. In the prophet: “The mouth of the Lord has spoken” (Isa. I, 20).

[Col. 0737D] The Word of the Lord is the Son. In the psalm: “My heart has uttered a good word” (Ps. XLIV, 2).

The arm or hand of the Lord is the Son, through whom he has worked all things. In the prophet: “And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isa. LIII, 1). The right hand of the Lord means the same as above, in the psalm: “The right hand of the Lord has done mightily” (Ps. CXVII, 16). The finger of God is called the Holy Spirit because of the distribution of the good things that are given by him individually to each person, whether human or angelic. For in none of our members does division appear so clearly as in the fingers. Nor should the diversity of the members scandalize you, since the unity of the body builds you up. The womb of the Lord is the secret place from which he brought forth the Son. In the psalm: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Ps. CIX, 3). The feet [Col. 0738A] of the Lord are the stability of eternity. In the psalm: “And darkness was beneath his feet” (Ps. XVII, 10). The footprints of the Lord are signs of hidden works. In the psalm: “And your footprints will not be known” (Ps. LXXVI, 20). The steps of the Lord are the Lord’s coming or visitation. In the psalm: “The entrances of the steps of the Lord were seen” (Ps. LXVII, 25).

The weapons of the Lord are his assistance to the saints. In the psalm: “Take hold of weapons and shield” (Ps. XXXIV, 2). The shield is the Lord’s protection. In the psalm: “Lord, you have crowned us with the shield of your good will” (Ps. V, 13). The broadsword (*framea*) is divine vengeance against the impious. In the psalm: “Bring out the broadsword and shut it in” (Ps. XXXIV, 3). The bow is the intention of divine threat. In the psalm: “He bent his bow and prepared it” (Ps. VII, 13). The arrows are divine commandments, apostles, or prophets. In the psalm: “He sent his arrows [Col. 0738B] and scattered them” (Ps. XVII, 15). Again: “Arrows in the hand of the mighty” (Ps. CXXVI, 4; CXIX, 4). The sword is vengeance, or the word of the Lord. In the Apostle: “For the word of God is living and effective, and sharper than any two-edged sword” (Heb. IV, 12). The rhomphaia is the same as above. The trumpet of the Lord is the Lord’s manifest voice. In the Apostle: “At the command, and at the voice of the archangel, and at the trumpet of God” (1 Thess. IV, 15). The chariot of God is the seat of God, or the fourfold character of the Gospels. In the psalm: “The chariot of God is manifold, ten thousand times over” (Ps. LXVII, 18). The rod of the Lord signifies the kingdom, or correction through discipline. In the psalm: “A rod of equity, the rod of your kingdom” (Ps. XLIV, 7). The hand of the Lord signifies his threats or vengeance. The staff of the Lord is the support of the Lord’s consolation. In the psalm: “Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me” (Ps. XXII, 4). In another sense, the staff of the Lord signifies the holy cross or the discipline of the holy Church. A staff is also any support [Col. 0738C], as in the Book of Tobit: “The staff of our old age” (Tob. V, 23).

**CHAPTER III. Concerning the heavenly creatures**

Coals are the fire of charity, or of examples, or of repentance. In the psalm: “With desolating coals” (Ps. CXIX, 4). Smoke is the beginning of future compunction, or of God’s own threat. In the psalm: “Smoke rose up in his anger” (Ps. XVII, 9). In another sense, as smoke is harmful to the eyes, it signifies vanity. Fire is the Holy Spirit. In the Acts of the Apostles: “And there appeared to them divided tongues, as it were of fire, and it rested [Col. 0738D] upon each of them; and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit” (Acts II, 3). Heaven signifies the apostles or saints, because the Lord dwells in them. “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps. XVIII, 2). In Holy Scripture, the heavens sometimes signify the higher bodies of the world, whose manner of distinction is unknown to us and concerning which it is quite difficult, though not impossible, to discuss for one to whom God grants understanding—as he granted it to the Apostle, who was caught up to the third heaven (2 Cor. XII, 2)—apart from those material heavens. The holy apostles, preachers of the word of truth, are called heavens; through these heavens, watered as though by rain, we have been refreshed, so that the Church’s harvest might sprout throughout the whole world. All holy and righteous souls are also heavens, in whom [Col. 0739A] God dwells in the temple of faith and works. In another sense, heaven is Holy Scripture, from which the sun of wisdom, the moon of knowledge, and, from the ancient fathers, the stars of examples and virtues shine for us. This heaven is stretched out like a skin (Ps. CIII, 2), because through its writers it is formed from fleshly language and expounded before our eyes through the words of teachers.

Clouds are prophets or saints, who rain down the word of the Lord. In Isaiah: “I will command the clouds above not to rain” (Isa. V, 6). In another sense, clouds signify the times of the wicked, as in: “Like a cloud my salvation has passed away” (Job XXX, 15). Thunderclaps are the voices of the Gospel, because they thunder from heaven through the sayings of God. In the psalm: “The sound of your thunder is in the wheel” (Ps. LXXVI, 19)—that is, throughout everything. Lightning-flashes are the splendors of the Gospel. In the psalm: “Your lightning-flashes shone upon the world” (ibid.). Flashes of lightning are the powers or words of Jesus Christ. In the psalm: “He multiplied his lightning-flashes and troubled them”—that is, the enemies or the Jews.

[Col. 0739B] In Holy Scripture, the name “angels” designates the Lord, as Isaiah testifies: “And his name shall be called the Angel of Great Counsel.” Sometimes it designates the angelic choir, as when Christ says to Peter: “Do you think that I cannot ask my Father, and he will provide me with more than twelve legions of angels?” (Matt. XXVI, 53). Sometimes it designates the citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem taken from human beings, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “For in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like the angels of God in heaven” (Matt. XXII, 30). Sometimes it designates the people of the faithful, as in: “He established the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the children of Israel” (Deut. XXXII, 8), or “of the angels of God.” By this name any righteous person is also designated, as the Lord says concerning John the Baptist: “Behold, I send my angel before [Col. 0739C] your face” (Matt. XI, 10). Sometimes it designates preachers or priests, as it is written: “The lips of the priest guard knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. II, 7). And the Apostle says: “A woman ought to veil her head in the church because of the angels” (1 Cor. XI, 10)—that is, the bishops. Every believer who announces good things claims for himself the name “angel” if he lives well. Finally, the devil and his fellow apostates are called evil angels. Although they have lost their angelic dignity, they have not lost the subtlety of their angelic nature. Through these evil angels, the sending of adversities or illnesses takes place by God’s permission, whenever and wherever he wills (Ps. LXXVII, 49).

[Col. 0739D] Thrones are angels, or saints, or the very power of reigning. In the psalm: “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever” (Ps. XLIV, 7). In another sense, concerning the devil: “I will set my throne toward the north” (Isa. XIV, 13). Seats mean the same as above—angels or saints—because the Lord sits in them and through them decrees his judgments. In the psalm: “God sits upon his holy seat” (Ps. XLVI, 9).

The sun is the Lord Jesus Christ, who shines upon the earth. In Solomon, this is what the reprobates are to say at the end: “Therefore the sun of justice did not shine for us” (Wis. V, 6). In another sense, it signifies persecution, as in: “When the sun rose, they were scorched” (Matt. III, 6). The moon is the Church, because it shines in this night of the world. In the psalm: “He made the moon for the appointed time” (Ps. CIII, 19). It is also used for the defect of our flesh, because, as it wanes at monthly intervals, it signifies the decline of our mortality.

[Col. 0740A] The stars are saints, or learned people, or those who instruct others in righteousness. In Daniel: “Those who are learned shall shine like the stars” (Dan. XII, 3). Mists are the veil of God’s mysteries, and sometimes also God’s angels. In the prophet: “And the mist is the dust beneath his feet” (Nahum I, 3). In another sense, they signify the wiping away of sins, as Isaiah says: “I have blotted out your iniquity like a cloud, and your sins like a mist” (Isa. XLIV, 22). Darkness is the covering of divine secrets. In the psalm: “And darkness was beneath his feet” (Ps. XVII, 10).

The abyss is the depth of the Scriptures. In the psalm: “Deep calls to deep” (Ps. XLI, 8). The name “abyss” also signifies the depth of the Old and New Testaments. Hence, “Deep calls to deep,” when the Old Testament announces the New. Or the abyss is the human mind [Col. 0740B], which cannot comprehend itself. Hence the prophet says: “The abyss gave forth its voice from the height” (Hab. III, 10) of its imagination, because, since the human mind does not penetrate itself, by comparison with itself it praises more humbly the power of the divine nature, which it is not sufficient to comprehend. Or certainly, the abyss signifies the judgments of God. “Deep calls to deep” (Ps. XXXV, 7; XLI, 8) when, by God’s hidden judgment, the sinner passes from present evils to eternal evils, and from the heat of desires into the flames of Gehenna.

Dew is the word of the Lord, because it moistens human hearts, as in: “Rain down, you heavens, from above” (Isa. XLV, 8). And in the psalm: “Like the dew of Hermon, which descends upon Mount Zion” (Ps. CXXXII, 3). Rain is the Lord’s precepts or commandments, [Col. 0740C] or the words of the holy apostles, because it waters the earth—that is, human beings. In the psalm: “You will set aside a voluntary rain for your inheritance” (Ps. LXVII, 10).

Snow signifies the whiteness of righteousness and baptism. In the psalm: “You will wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow” (Ps. L, 9). Hail signifies the Lord’s threats, with which he strikes the obstinate. In the psalm: “Hail and coals of fire” (Ps. XVII, 13). In another sense: “And he killed their vineyards with hail” (Ps. LXXVII, 46). In the coldness of snow and the hardness of hail, the life of the wicked is understood, since it grows cold through numbness and perishes through the malice of hardness.

Frost signifies abstinence, because through it the body’s heat grows cold. In the psalm: “I have become like a wineskin in the frost” (Ps. CXVIII, 83). A storm is the force of persecutions or tribulations. [Col. 0740D] In the psalm: “He saved me from faintheartedness of spirit and from the storm” (Ps. LIV, 9). Ice is the hardness of sins. In Solomon: “As ice in clear weather, so your sins shall be dissolved” (Eccl. III, 17).

Winds are the souls of the saints. In the psalm: “He flew upon the wings of the winds” (Ps. XVII, 11). In another sense, they signify evil, as in Matthew: “The winds blew” (Matt. VII, 2).

The north wind is the devil, or unbelieving or evil people, or the coldness of sins. In the prophet: “From the north the evils will blaze forth over the earth.” And elsewhere: “From the north the evil will be opened” (Jer. I, 14). And elsewhere: “Rise up, north wind” (Song IV, 16)—that is, “Depart.” The right [wind] is the same as above. In Solomon: “The north is a harsh wind” (Prov. XXV, 23). It is called “north” because the devil presumptuously claims for himself the name of the right side, as though he were good; or because, to those who look toward the west—that is, toward sin—it becomes the right side.

[Col. 0741A] The south wind is the warmth of faith. In the psalm: “As a torrent in the south” (Ps. CXXV, 4). It is also the Holy Spirit, as in: “Rise up, north wind, and come, south wind” (Song IV, 6)—that is, “Depart, devil, and come, gracious Spirit.”

Air signifies the utterance of emptiness. In the Apostle: “So I fight, not as one beating the air” (1 Cor. IX, 26)—that is, “not pursuing empty things.”

Times are the fitting distribution of the divine will. In the psalm: “He made the moon for the seasons” (Ps. CIII, 19). Spring is the renewal of life, either through baptism or through resurrection. In the psalm: “You made summer and spring” (Ps. LXXIII, 17). Summer is a prefiguration of the joy to come. In the psalm, as above.

Winter is the present life, persecution, or tribulation. In the Gospel: “So that your flight may not occur in winter or on the Sabbath” (Matt. XXIV, 20). Years are sometimes understood as eternity [Col. 0741B], as in: “Your years shall not fail” (Ps. CI, 28). Sometimes they signify the brevity of this life, as here: “Our years shall be considered like a spider’s web” (Ps. LXXXIX, 3).

By the name “months,” which are gathered into days, collections of souls or the perfection of the saints are signified, as in: “It shall be month after month” (Isa. LXVI, 23)—namely, for those who are now perfected in their works and will be in rest.

Day and night signify righteousness and iniquity, faith and unbelief, prosperity and adversity. In the psalm: “By day the Lord commanded his mercy, and by night he declared it” (Ps. XLI, 9). The name “days” also signifies the illumination of divine grace through the various gifts of virtues. In another sense, “day” designates the apostate angel [Col. 0741C], when Job says: “Let those curse it who curse the day” (Job III, 8).

By the name “night,” either the blindness of the error of ignorance or the bitterness of death is understood. Light and darkness are understood chiefly in the same way as day and night. In the Epistle of John: “Whoever loves his brother remains in the light, but whoever hates his brother is in darkness” (1 John II, 10). Through light the disposition of the heart is also revealed.

Shadow is divine protection. In the psalm: “Protect me under the shadow of your wings” (Ps. XVI, 8). In another sense, it is forgetfulness or sins, as in: “Sitting in darkness and in the shadow of death” (Ps. CVI, 10). Sometimes shadow is the delight of sins, as in Job: “Under the shadow he sleeps in secret” (Job XL, 16). Again, shadow signifies forgetfulness of the mind, or death of the flesh, or imitation of the devil.

[Col. 0741D] By the name “light,” the Lord or any righteous person is understood, as in the Gospel: “He was the true light which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John I, 9). And the Apostle says: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. V, 8). It is also used for the illumination of faith and for life.

An hour is five hundred years, as some think, whenever “day” is understood as the whole age of this world. In the Epistle of John: “My little children, it is the last hour” (1 John II, 18).

The East, because light rises from that direction, signifies the Savior, especially in Luke: “The Dawn from on high has visited us” (Luke I, 78). And in Zechariah: “Behold, a man whose name is Dawn” (Zech. VI, 12).

The West signifies the decline of the better life. In the prophet: “The sun shall set for you at midday” (Zech. VI, 12).

The northern region is always placed in an adverse sense, as the prophet says concerning the devil: “I will set my seat toward the north” (Amos VIII, 9); and elsewhere: “From the north the evil will be opened” (Jer. I, 14).

[Col. 0742A] Morning is the light of good deeds, or baptism, or the Lord’s resurrection. In the psalm: “In the morning I shall stand before you, and I shall see” (Ps. V, 5); and elsewhere: “From the morning watch until night, let Israel hope in the Lord” (Ps. CXXIX, 6)—that is, from the Lord’s resurrection our hope lasts until the end of the age, that is, the day of judgment.

By “morning” or “early morning,” the prosperity of the present life is also signified, as in: “Woe to you, land, whose king is a child, and whose princes eat in the morning” (Eccl. X, 16). They eat in the morning who are lifted up by the prosperity of this world, when they ought to await its end and enjoy eternal blessings.

[Col. 0742B] Midday is the clear and evident brilliance of teachings and deeds. In Solomon: “Where do you lie at midday?” (Song I, 6). In an adverse sense, in the psalm: “From the demon of midday” (Ps. XC, 6)—that is, from the manifest demon.

Evening is the end of life, or of the world, or punishment. In the psalm: “In the evening weeping will remain, and in the morning joy” (Ps. XXIX, 6).

By the name “dawn,” the mind of the righteous is understood: leaving behind the darkness of its sin, it breaks forth into the light, illuminated by the sun of justice (Song VI, 9).

By the name “Arcturus,” which is set in the axis of heaven and shines with the rays of seven stars, the universal Church is expressed. In the Apocalypse of John it is represented by the seven churches and seven lampstands (Rev. I, 20).

The Orions, rising amid the weight of winter, designate the holy martyrs, because they endured the weight of persecutors and of those who love this life, and came, as though in winter, to the face of heaven.

The Hyades, named from the Greek letter υ, [Col. 0742C] from whose shape they do not differ in appearance, and whose rising brings rain, signify the holy preachers, because they rain through their words and beneficially water human hearts. For ὑετός in Greek means “rain” in Latin.

**CHAPTER IV. Concerning earthly things**
Earth means the human being himself. In the Gospel: “Some seed fell on good earth” (Mark 4:8). Likewise: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:19). Also, in the negative sense, concerning the sinner: “You shall eat earth all the days of your life” (Gen. 3:14). In another sense, “earth” means those who, occupied with earthly activities, attain eternal life through almsgiving and tears; hence the Psalm: “He summoned heaven above and earth, to distinguish his people” (Ps. 49:4).

Dry ground means unfruitful people: in Solomon, “To cover dry ground with malice and deceit” (Eccl. 37:3). [Col. 0742D]

Dust means sinners, or the vanity of the flesh: in the Psalm, “Like dust that the wind drives away” (Ps. 1:4).

Mud means the adhesive mire of sins: in the Psalm, “Deliver me from the mud, lest I become stuck” (Ps. 68:15). In another sense, in John: “He made mud and spread it on my eyes” (John 9:11).

Mountains mean the Lord, the Church, the apostles, or the saints, because of the height of their virtues: in the Psalm, “He who descends upon Mount Zion” (Ps. 132:3). Likewise in the Prophet: “The mountain of the house of the Lord shall be established above the tops of the mountains” (Isa. 2:2). Again, in another Prophet: “Lest your feet stumble against the dark mountains” (Jer. 13:16), that is, heretics.

Hills mean the saints, but those of lesser merit: in the Psalm, “Mountains and all hills” (Ps. 148:9). In another sense, [Col. 0743A] in the Gospel: “Every mountain and hill shall be brought low” (Luke 3:5).

Valleys mean the contrition of a humble heart: in the Psalm, “And the valleys shall abound with grain” (Ps. 64:14). In another sense, in the Prophet: “The valley of the sons of Hinnom” (Jer. 19:2).

Rock means Christ, because of his firmness: in the Apostle, “The rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4).

Stones sometimes mean Christ or the saints: in the Psalm, “The stone which the builders rejected” (Ps. 117:22). Likewise: “A stone was cut from the mountain without hands and filled the whole earth” (Dan. 2:35). Likewise: “You too, like living stones, are being built up” (1 Pet. 2:5). In another sense, concerning the foolish and hard-hearted: “God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Matt. 3:9). And elsewhere: “I shall take the heart of stone from your flesh” (Ezek. 36:26).

Field means this world: [Col. 0743B] in the Gospel, “The field is this world” (Matt. 13:38). Elsewhere, a field is the discipline of heavenly study, in which a treasure is hidden (ibid., 44), that is, heavenly desire.

Fields mean the saints or the divine Scriptures, because they provide nourishment for souls: in the Psalm, “And your fields shall be filled with abundance” (Ps. 64:12). In another sense, in the negative: “In the field of Tanis” (Ps. 77:43). Fields are also called so because of their evenness, and thus signify righteous peoples.

Pastures mean spiritual refreshment: in the Psalm, “He has placed me in a place of pasture” (Ps. 22:2).

Cultivation means the saints, who are cultivated by God: in the Apostle, “You are God’s cultivation” (1 Cor. 3:8).

Farmer means God: in the Gospel, “I am the true vine, and my Father is the farmer” (John 15:1).

Furrows mean the hearts of the saints: in the Psalm, “Watering its furrows” (Ps. 64:11).

Seed means divine preaching: [Col. 0743C] in the Gospel, “The sower went out to sow his seed” (Luke 8:5).

Harvest means the abundance or multitude of the faithful: in the Gospel, “Lift up your eyes and see the regions, for they are white for harvest” (John 4:35). In another sense: “The harvest is the consummation of the age, and the reapers are angels” (Matt. 13:39).

Sheaves mean the fruits of righteousness: in the Psalm, “Carrying their sheaves” (Ps. 125:6).

Stubble means those who are dry with respect to faith, or empty people: in the Apostle, “Wood, hay, and stubble” (1 Cor. 3:13). And in the Prophet: “Woe is me, for I have become like one gathering stubble at harvest” (Mic. 7:1), that is, I have found no fruits of good work. And elsewhere: “Stubble gathered is the congregation of sinners” (Eccl. 21:10).

Threshing floor means the Church: in the Gospel, “He will thoroughly cleanse his threshing floor” (Matt. 3:12).

Winnowing shovel means God’s judgment of justice: in the Gospel, “Whose winnowing shovel is in his hand” (ibid.).

[Col. 0743D] Wheat means the word of God, or the saints and elect of God: in the Gospel, “He will gather his wheat into the barn” (ibid.).

Barley means the letter of the Law: in the Gospel, “There is a boy here who has five barley loaves” (John 3:10), that is, the letter, the five books of Moses.

Chaff means sinners: in the Gospel, “But the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire” (Matt. 3:10); and in Jeremiah, “What has chaff to do with wheat? says the Lord” (Jer. 23:28).

Weeds mean scandals or those who live wickedly: in the Gospel, “The enemy came and sowed weeds among the wheat” (Matt. 13:25).

Vineyard means the Church or the people of Israel: in the Psalm, “You brought a vine out of Egypt” (Ps. 89:9). In another sense, negatively: “For their vine is from the vine of Sodom” (Deut. 32:52).

Vine means Christ: in the Gospel, “I am [Col. 0744A] the true vine” (John 15:1). In another sense, in the Song of Deuteronomy, the passage cited above.

Branches mean the apostles or the saints: in the Gospel, “I am the true vine, and you are the branches.” In the negative sense, in the passage cited above: “And their branch is from Gomorrah.”

Grapes mean the fruits of righteousness: in Isaiah, “I expected it to produce grapes” (Isa. 5:4). In the negative sense, in the passage cited above: “Their grape is a grape of gall” (Deut. 32:32).

Cluster means the Church or the body of the Lord. In Numbers: “Because the sons of Israel had carried a cluster from there” (Num. 13:24).

Vintage means the consummation of the age or vengeance upon the people: in the Psalm, “All who pass by the way strip it bare” (Ps. 79:13); and in Joel, “Send in the sickles and harvest the vineyard of the earth, for its grapes are ripe” (Joel 3:13).

Winepress means the altar, because offerings are brought there as [Col. 0744B] fruits; thus in Isaiah: “And I dug a winepress in it” (Isa. 5:2). In another sense, the winepress means the pressure of tribulations in the holy Church, in which the faithful are tested. In the title of the Psalm: “For the end, concerning the winepresses” (Ps. 8:1).

Hay means the people, the flesh, or empty glory. In Isaiah: “All flesh is hay, and all its glory is like the flower of hay” (Isa. 40:6).

Grass means joyfulness, or certain first beginnings of a soul making progress. In Genesis: “Let the earth bring forth green grass” (Gen. 1:11). In the negative sense: “In the morning let it pass away like grass” (Ps. 89:6).

Flowers mean Christ, or the appearance of righteousness, or the beginning of those who do good works; thus in the Song of Songs the bridegroom says: “Strengthen me with flowers” (Song 2:1).

Lily means Christ, or the angels in the whiteness of righteousness. In Solomon: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (ibid.).

Roses mean martyrs, [Col. 0744C] because of the redness of their blood. In Solomon: “As a rose springs up beside moist streams.”

Violets mean confessors, because of their resemblance to bruised bodies. In the Song of Songs: “The flowers have appeared in the land” (Song 2:12).

Forests mean the nations. In the Psalm: “We found it in the fields of the forest” (Ps. 131:6). From these forests came the two bears—namely, Vespasian and Titus, kings of the Romans—who, represented at the command of Elisha, devoured the Jewish boys forty-two years after his ascent into heaven (2 Kings 2:24).

Thickets mean the obscure, shadowed, or covered parts of divine Scripture. In the Psalm: “And he revealed the thickets” (Ps. 28:9).

Wood means sinners destined for the fire. In Ecclesiastes: “Whoever cuts wood will be endangered by it” (Eccl. 10:9). In the positive sense: “And he shall be like a tree planted” (Ps. 1:3). Elsewhere, under the name of wood, the holy cross is signified; thus the Prophet: “Let us put wood in his bread” (Jer. 11:19), that is, let us suspend Christ upon the cross in his flesh. Likewise: “Behold, I am gathering two pieces of wood” (1 Kings 17:12). [Col. 0744D] Wood also signifies the righteous and sinners, as Solomon says: “If a tree falls toward the south or toward the north, wherever it falls, there it shall remain” (Eccl. 11:3): for on the day of death the righteous falls toward the south and the sinner toward the north. The righteous, through the fervor of the spirit, is led to joy; the sinner, with the apostate angel, is rejected in a cold heart.

Root means origin: in the Apostle, “But if the root is holy, so are the branches” (Rom. 11:16). In the negative sense, in the Psalm: “He will uproot your root from the land of the living” (Ps. 51:7).

[Col. 0745A] Tree means the human being, judged by the fruit of his works: in the Gospel, “Either make the tree good and its fruit good” (Matt. 12:33); and in the negative sense, “Or make the tree bad and its fruit bad.” Some think that in this passage “tree” should be understood more as the human will than as the human being himself.

Christ was also a tree when he rose again; when he died, he was a grain.

Branch means succession: in the Apostle, “But if the root is holy, so are the branches” (Rom. 11:16). In another sense, in Daniel: “Cut off its branches” (Dan. 4:11). Branches are also the judgments of the holy Fathers: in the Gospel, “Others were cutting branches from the trees” (Matt. 21:8).

Leaf means the word of doctrine: in the Psalm, “And its leaf shall not fall” (Ps. 1:3). In another sense, a leaf means clothing and beauty together with the protection of divine [Col. 0745B] grace. In the negative sense: “He found no fruit on it because of the leaves” (Matt. 21:19), that is, words without fruit. Hence the Apostle urges us to love not in word or tongue, but in deed and truth (1 John 3:18). The human being is also compared to a leaf that fell from the tree in paradise.

Fruit means the fruits of the saints in virtues: in the Song of Songs, “Let him eat the fruit of his trees” (Song 5:1).

Palm means perfection or victory: in the Psalm, “The righteous shall flourish like a palm tree” (Ps. 91:13). The palm tree makes progress slowly, but remains green for a long time. So too the holy Church, after coming to the condition of faith through many difficulties, desires to stand longer in the glory of that same faith for the sake of gathering many.

Below, the palm is constricted by the coils of its bark, but above [Col. 0745C] it spreads out in the breadth of its beautiful greenness. Thus the life of the elect is despised below but beautiful above.

The palm also has another characteristic by which it differs from all other kinds of trees. Every tree that stands broadly near the ground in its strength becomes narrower as it grows upward; the taller it becomes, the thinner it grows toward the height. The palm, however, begins from its base and rises with greater strength toward its branches and fruits. What grows slender from below becomes broader as it grows toward the top.

To whom, then, are such trees found to be similar except to earthly minds—broad below and narrow above? For all the loves of this age are strong in earthly matters but weak in heavenly ones. They desire to toil until death for temporal glory, yet do not persevere even a little in labor for eternal hope. For earthly profits they endure every kind of injury, but for heavenly reward they refuse to bear even the slightest insult of a single word. [Col. 0745D] They are strong enough to stand all day before an earthly judge, but in prayer before the Lord they grow weary in the space of even one hour. They often endure nakedness, vigils, and hunger in order to acquire wealth and honors, and torment themselves with much abstinence.

But, by contrast, the evenness of the palms represents the life of the righteous who are making progress. They are not strong in earthly pursuits and weak in heavenly ones; rather, they show themselves more earnest toward God, and at greater distance from worldly concerns, than they remember ever having been toward the world.

Thus it is rightly written, as I have said: “The righteous shall flourish like a palm tree,” and so forth.

Cedars mean men of exalted power: [Col. 0746A] in the Psalm, “He shall multiply like a cedar of Lebanon” (Ps. 91:15). In the negative sense, they mean the proud and exalted: thus in the Psalm, “And the Lord will break the cedars of Lebanon” (Ps. 28:5).

Olive means the saint abounding in the fruits of mercy: in the Psalm, “But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of the Lord” (Ps. 51:10).

Wild olive means a fruitless person or a Gentile: in the Apostle, “But if you were cut from the natural wild olive” (Rom. 11:24).

Fig tree sometimes means the synagogue: in the Gospel, “The fig tree immediately withered” (Matt. 21:19); and in Habakkuk, “The fig tree shall not bear fruit” (Hab. 3:17). The fig tree is understood both positively and negatively, as in Isaiah: “He showed me figs, very good and very bad” (Jer. 24:3). And the Lord said to Nathanael: “When you were under the fig tree”—that is, under original sin—“I saw you,” in order to redeem you (John 1:48).

The fig tree [Col. 0746B] also signifies human nature or the unbelieving synagogue. Though well established, it fell of its own accord and produced neither the fruit of God’s commandment nor that of good works. Therefore the Lord sought fruit from it for three years and did not find any, because he admonished, visited, and examined it during three periods (Luke 13:7): before the Law, under the Law, and under grace. Before the Law he patiently endured it by sparing it; under grace, he manifested himself by presenting the presence of his incarnation; under the Law, he taught by commanding. Yet throughout these three periods it remained fruitless and withered from its roots.

Sycamore is called a foolish fig tree. Little Zacchaeus climbed it (Luke 19:4) and saw the Lord, because those who humbly choose the wisdom of the world themselves perceive the wisdom of God subtly. We wisely climb the sycamore [Col. 0746C] if we deliberately hold fast to the praiseworthy and wise “foolishness” prescribed by God.

For what is more foolish in this world than not to seek what has been lost; to give away what one possesses; to release those who rob; to return no injury for injuries received; but, according to the Lord’s commandment, to show patience in all things? Hyssop is a lowly herb, attached to the stone on which it grows; its roots are said to penetrate the rock. It is especially beneficial for the lungs. Pride is marked by the lungs: there is swelling there, there is panting. Hyssop therefore signifies humility and patience.

[Col. 0746D] Buckthorn, nettles, thistles, briars, and paliurus are herbs full of prickles. They signify the harsh, deceitful, proud, and all wicked people whom none of the good or gentle can touch or chastise without the sting of pain. They also signify vices and the assaults of temptations, as in Genesis: “It shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Gen. 3:18).

Pomegranates mean the Church composed of many nations, or possessing diverse graces: in the Song of Songs, “Your plants are a paradise of pomegranates with the fruit of trees” (Song 4:3). Elsewhere, apples (*mala*) mean the fruits of good works accompanied by a good fragrance—that is, the grace of a good reputation and the fruits of virtuous conduct.

Reed means a sinner, or one fragile in faith or in some temptation: in the Gospel, “He will not break a bruised reed” (Matt. 12:20). Reed also means weak assistance: in Isaiah, “Why do you trust in this staff of the Egyptian reed? If anyone leans upon it, it will break and pierce his hand …” (Isa. 36:6).

[Col. 0747A] Bush, as some think, prefigures the Virgin Mary, because from the thornbush of the human body she brought forth the Savior like a rose, or because she endured the force of the divine radiance without the intervention of a man. In Exodus: “The Lord appeared to him in a flame of fire from the midst of the bush; and he saw that the bush was burning, yet was not consumed” (Exod. 3:2). Elsewhere, the burning bush that was not consumed signified the Jewish people, because it prescribed the flame of God’s Law, yet did not escape the punishment of sin.

Thorns sometimes mean the harmful cares of riches, choking the soul, and the anxieties of this world: in the Gospel, “Other seed fell among thorns” (Luke 8:6); and again, “Those who are choked by anxieties, riches, and pleasures” (ibid., 14).

Thistles mean the prickles of vices or temptations: in Genesis, “It shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Gen. 13:18).

[Col. 0747B] Springs mean baptism: in the Psalm, “As the deer longs for the springs of water” (Ps. 41:2). The spring is also Christ, as in the Psalm: “My soul thirsted for God, the living fountain” (ibid.); and Isaiah: “On that day there shall be an open spring for the house of David” (Zech. 13:1), and so forth. In the negative sense, as the Apostle says: “Springs without water” (2 Pet. 2:17).

Waters mean temptations: in the Psalm, “Perhaps the waters would have swallowed us” (Ps. 123:4). Likewise: “The waters have entered even to my soul” (Ps. 68:2). In the positive sense, in Jeremiah: “They have abandoned me, the fountain of living water” (Jer. 2:13); and in Isaiah: “You who thirst, go to the water” (Isa. 55:1), that is, to doctrine.

In Holy Scripture, the name “water” sometimes signifies the Holy Spirit. Thus the outpouring of the Holy [Col. 0747C] Spirit is represented: in the Gospel, “Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly” (John 7:38).

Water also expresses the angelic choir, as in the Psalm: “And the waters that are above the heavens, let them praise the name of the Lord” (Ps. 148:4).

It also signifies sacred knowledge, as in the Book of Wisdom: “He will give them water to drink, the water of wisdom” (Eccl. 15:3). And again: “Deep water is the word from the mouth of a man” (Prov. 18:4).

Perverse knowledge is likewise called water. Thus the woman who represents heresy, through cunning persuasions, entices people by saying through Solomon: “Stolen waters are sweeter” (Prov. 9:17).

Water also signifies the prosperity of this world: in the Psalm, “We passed through fire and water, and you brought us out into refreshment” (Ps. 65:12). Fire and water are both dangerous. [Col. 0747D] Thus in the Gospel: “He often threw him into the fire and into the water, in order to destroy him” (Mark 9:21). When circumstances are difficult and there are various misfortunes in this world, it is as though there were fire. When circumstances are prosperous and worldly abundance flows around us, it is as though there were already water.

Through water, peoples are also signified, as in the Apocalypse: “The many waters are many peoples” (Rev. 17:15). Water indicates not only the course of peoples flowing along, but also the minds of good people who follow the proclamations of faith, as in Isaiah: “Blessed are you who sow beside all waters” (Isa. 32:20).

Water also indicates baptism, as the Evangelist John says: “There are three that bear witness on earth: the spirit, the water, and the blood” (1 John 5:8). [Col. 0748A] The Spirit made us children of God by adoption. The water of the sacred font washed us. The Lord’s blood redeemed us.

Torrent means the assault of persecution or the passing away of death. In the Psalm: “He shall drink from the torrent on the way” (Ps. 109:7). Likewise: “My soul has passed through the torrent” (Ps. 123:5). In the positive sense: “You shall give them drink from the torrent of your delight” (Ps. 35:9).

Torrents are also called the holy preachers, who, while in the present life, pour divine words upon us. They are gathered like a multitude of waters in winter, because when the summer sun arrives they withdraw; for when the light of the eternal homeland shines forth, they will cease to preach.

Rivers mean the peoples of unbelievers. In the Psalm: “By the rivers of Babylon” (Ps. 136:1). In the positive sense: “From his belly shall flow rivers of living [Col. 0748B] water” (John 7:38), that is, diverse gifts of the Spirit. Thus in the Psalm: “The rush of the river gladdens the city of God” (Ps. 45:5).

Lake means hell. In the Psalm: “They placed me in the lower lake” (Ps. 87:7), that is, in that place of hell where sinners alone are held in punitive custody.

Sea means the world or peoples. In the Psalm: “This sea, great and spacious” (Ps. 102:25). “Sea” also means the sacred Scriptures, as in Ezekiel: “The appearance of the wheels and their workmanship was like the appearance of the sea” (Ezek. 1:16). The sacred utterances are rightly compared to the vision of the sea, because the meanings of their speech are confirmed by the sacrament of baptism.

Fish mean the saints, and sometimes sinners. In the Gospel: “They drew up a net full of large fish” (John 21:11). In the negative sense: “They threw the bad ones outside” (Matt. 13:48).

[Col. 0748C] Again, under the name of fish, unfeigned faith is expressed. Just as a fish is born, lives, and is nourished beneath the covering of the waters, so faith in God generates within the heart, through present lamentations and unceasing tears, the joys of the life to come. It is consecrated by the invisible grace of the Spirit through the water of baptism; it is nourished by the invisible help of divine protection so that it does not fail; and, through the invisible vision of rewards, it performs whatever good it is able to perform, mindful of the Apostle’s saying: “The things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal” (2 Cor. 4:18).

A roasted fish signifies the Passion.

Waves mean temptations. In the Psalm: “All your heights and your waves have passed over me” (Ps. 41:8). Waves also signify fear of God, as in the Book of Job: “As swelling waves over me, so I have always [Col. 0748D] feared the Lord” “As swelling waves over me, so I have always feared the Lord” (Job 31:23). Hence, likewise, in the Song cited above: “The waves froze in the midst of the sea” (Exod. 15:8).

Islands mean souls or the Churches of God, which are battered by the diverse waves of temptations. In the Psalm: “Let the many islands rejoice” (Ps. 96:1).

Shore means the end of the age. In the Gospel: “They sat beside the shore and selected the good into vessels” (Matt. 13:48).

The sand of the sea means the countless multitude of the nations. In Genesis: “I shall multiply your seed”—that is, the saints—“like the stars of heaven and like the sand”—that is, sinners—“which is on the seashore” (Gen. 22:17).

## CHAPTER V. On Living Creatures

Birds mean the saints, because in [Col. 0749A] heart they fly upward. In the Gospel: “It made great branches, so that the birds of heaven could dwell under its shade” (Mark 4:32).

Birds are also understood as superfluous thoughts, as is shown by Abraham, who, when he offered sacrifice to God, had to drive away the birds that settled upon it (Gen. 15:11). For when importunate thoughts intrude upon the sacrifice of prayer and, arising within them, pollute the hearts of the righteous, they must be quickly driven away by the hand of discernment. In this way one acts joyfully, lest the darkness of temptation cover the face of the heart, which had already been touched by illicit pleasure.

Flight means the saints’ elevation toward God, or understanding in the Scriptures. In the Psalm: “I shall fly away and rest” (Ps. 54:7).

Winged creatures are understood positively, as we have said of birds. In the negative sense, however, they signify proud demons, as the Lord says in the Gospel: [Col. 0749B] “Other seed fell beside the way, and the birds of heaven ate it” (Luke 8:5). The malignant spirits that besiege human minds, by introducing harmful thoughts, tear the word of life from the memory.

Wings mean the two Testaments. In Ezekiel: “Each one covered his body with two wings” (Ezek. 1:23). Wings also mean the virtues of the saints, by which they fly toward contemplation or heavenly things, or they mean divine protection.

Feathers mean the Scriptures. In the Psalm: “The silvered feathers of the dove” (Ps. 67:14).

Nest means the Church, or the exalted repose of the saints. In the Psalm: “And the turtledove has found for herself a nest where she may place her young” (Ps. 83:4). In another sense, a nest means a good conscience, in which the offspring of good thoughts are nourished and brought forth in action, so that afterward they may be called children. [Col. 0749C] In the Psalm: “Your children are like young olive trees around your table” (Ps. 127:3).

Young birds mean the saints. In the Psalm, as above. Likewise in the Book of Job: “Her young ones lick up blood” (Job 39:30), which is said of the children of the holy Church who drink Christ’s blood. In the negative sense, in Solomon: “Let the young of eagles devour him” (Prov. 30:17).

Eagles mean the saints. In the Gospel: “Wherever the body is, there the eagles will be gathered” (Matt. 24:28), because holy souls, departing from the body, are gathered to Christ, who became a corpse by dying for them.

The eagle also signifies Christ, as Solomon says: “The way of an eagle in the heavens” (Prov. 30:19), that is, Christ’s ascension. In the negative sense: “Let the young of eagles devour him.” Thus in Jeremiah, concerning malignant spirits: “Our pursuers were swifter than eagles” (Lam. 4:19).

[Col. 0749D] The eagle also signifies an earthly tempest.

Ostrich means any heretic, philosopher, or hypocrite who, as though possessing the feathers of wisdom, nevertheless does not fly. In Isaiah: “It shall be a lair of dragons and a pasture for ostriches” (Isa. 34:13). The ostrich lays eggs but does not nourish its young from them, because although the hypocrite may preach correctly, he generates no children through the example of a good life. Thus in the Book of Job: “The ostrich leaves her eggs upon the earth and forgets that a foot may trample them” (Job 39:14).

Pelican means the Lord Christ in his Passion, or a holy man devoted to solitude. In the Psalm: “I have become like a pelican of the wilderness” (Ps. 101:7).

Raven means the blackness of sins or demons. In Solomon: “Let ravens dig him out from the torrent or from the rocks” (Prov. 30:17). In the positive sense, in the Song of Songs, concerning the bridegroom: “His locks are like fir trees, black as ravens” (Song 5:11).

[Col. 0750A] Partridge means the devil. In the Prophet: “The partridge cried out; it gathered what it did not hatch” (Jer. 17:11).

Dove means the Holy Spirit. In the Gospel: “And I saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove” (John 1:32). In the negative sense, in the Prophet: “Ephraim became like a senseless dove, without understanding” (Hos. 7:11).

Turtledove means the Holy Spirit, or a holy man, or spiritual understanding. In the Song of Songs: “The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land” (Song 2:12). The Holy Spirit is called a dove when the sacred Scriptures are being openly expounded. The Holy Spirit is understood as a turtledove when the Scriptures are raised to their lofty and obscure [Col. 0750B] mysteries.

The dove also indicates simplicity; the turtledove, chastity, because after losing its first mate it does not seek another companion.

Kite, I think, signifies a rapacious or exalted person. In the Psalm, according to the Hebrews: “The fir tree is the house of the kite.”

Hawk sometimes means a saint, as I think, who seizes the kingdom of God. Renewed by changing its old feathers, it casts off the worn-out habits of deceitful action and assumes the simple practices of a good life. In Job: “Does the hawk grow feathers by your wisdom?”

Night-raven means Christ, or a holy man despised by unbelievers. In the Psalm: “I have become like a night-raven in a dwelling” (Ps. 101:7).

Sparrow sometimes means the Lord or a holy man. In the Psalm: “For even the sparrow has found a house for itself” (Ps. 83:4). Elsewhere it means any Christian to whom heretics say that they alone possess Christ, who is called a mountain in the [Col. 0750C] Scriptures: “Move to the mountain like a sparrow” (Ps. 10:2).

Rooster means the Lord, as I think, or a saint. In Solomon: “And a rooster walking among the hens, cheerful” (Prov. 30:31). And in Job: “Who gave the rooster understanding?” (Job 38:36). In another sense: “I shall carry you away as a rooster is carried away” (Isa. 22:17).

Under the name of roosters are signified the holy preachers who, amid the darkness of the present life, strive to announce the coming light by preaching, as though by singing. For they say: “The night has passed, and the day has drawn near.” The rooster is also written as walking with girded loins (Prov. 30:31), because the holy preachers, announcing the true morning amid the darkness of this night, restrain the loose impulses of lust in their bodies. To them the Lord says: [Col. 0750D] “Let your loins be girded” (Luke 12:35).

Understanding is also attributed to the rooster from above, because the power of discernment is divinely supplied to the teacher of truth, so that he may know to whom, what, when, and how he should impart it. For the same exhortation does not suit everyone, since not everyone is constrained by the same quality of character.

Hen means wisdom, or the Church, or the soul. In the Gospel: “As a hen gathers her young under her wings” (Matt. 23:37).

Bats mean the monsters of idols devoted to darkness. In the Prophet: “That you may worship moles and bats” (Isa. 2:20). They also mean impure thoughts that enter through demons.

Scarab means the Prophet. “And the scarab will cry out from the wood,” as some think, concerning the Lord.

[Col. 0751A] Locusts mean peoples. In the Gospel: “His food was locusts” (Matt. 3:4). Under the name of locusts are sometimes signified the people of the Jews, sometimes converted Gentiles, sometimes the tongue of flatterers, sometimes—by comparison—the Lord’s resurrection, and sometimes the life of preachers.

Bee represents virginity or wisdom. In Solomon: “Go to the bee and learn how industrious she is” (Prov. 6:6). In the negative sense, in the Prophet: “And the bee that is in Assyria” (Isa. 7:18). And: “They surrounded me like bees” (Ps. 117:12), that is, malicious and angry people.

Bees also signify, by their name, all who flatter with the tongue but secretly strike out of malice. They offer the sweetness of honey in speech, but inflict a wound by their sting. The sayings of the wise may also be signified by this [Col. 0751B] name, as in the saying: “Good words are a honeycomb” (Prov. 16:24).

Fly means the devil, or his minister, or the uncleanness of idolatry. In Solomon: “Dead flies destroy the sweetness of the oil” (Eccl. 10:1).

Beasts mean the devil or savage people. In the Psalm: “Do not hand over to beasts the souls confessing you” (Ps. 73:19).

Lion means the Lord, as the Apostle says: “The lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered” (Rev. 5:5). In the negative sense: “Lest he seize my soul like a lion” (Ps. 7:3). Likewise: “Our adversary the devil prowls around like a lion” (1 Pet. 5:8).

Lioness signifies the proud or reckless.

Leopard means the devil or a sinner with varied morals. In the Prophet: “As the Ethiopian cannot change his skin, nor the leopard his spots” (Jer. 13:23).

Elephant means an enormous sinner. [Col. 0751C] In Kings: “And they brought to Solomon apes and elephants” (1 Kings 10:22).

Bear means the devil, or savage leaders, or ambushers. In the Book of Kings: “Two bears came out and devoured them” (2 Kings 2:24), because Vespasian and Titus, Roman emperors, destroyed the Jews.

Deer means Christ or the saints. In the Psalm: “As the deer longs for the springs of water” (Ps. 41:2). And again in the Psalm: “The high mountains are for the deer; the rock is a refuge for the hedgehogs” (Ps. 103:18), for here those devoted to the contemplative life are signified.

Wolf means the devil or a heretic. In the Gospel: “Within are ravenous wolves” (Matt. 7:15). In the positive sense: “Benjamin is a ravenous wolf” (Gen. 49:27), signifying the Apostle Paul.

Boar means the devil. In the Psalm: “The boar from the forest will ravage it” (Ps. 79:14).

Tiger sometimes means feminine arrogance. In the Book of Job, according to the [Col. 0751D] Hebrew: In the Book of Job, according to the Hebrew: “The tiger perished because it had no prey” (Job 4:11).

Monoceros, that is, unicorn, means: in the Psalm, “And the beloved like the son of unicorns” (Ps. 28:6), that is, one of singular power, or the saints who hold fast to the one word of God. In another sense: “And from the horns of unicorns, my humility” (Ps. 21:22). In the negative sense, it is used for any proud and violent person, or one who holds only one Testament, as the Psalmist speaks in the person of the Lord who was to suffer: “Deliver me, Lord, from the horns of unicorns.”

Rhinoceros means any strong person, either in the positive or negative sense. In the Book of Job, according to the Hebrew: “Will the rhinoceros be willing to serve you?” (Job 39:9).

Wild ass means a hermit, or those who live apart from the crowds of the people. [Col. 0752A] In Job: “Who sets the wild ass free?” (Job 39:5). The Jewish people may also be called a wild ass, because the same book continues: “And who loosens its bonds?”—meaning, certainly, the bonds of the commandments.

Fawn means Christ or the saints, on account of the variety of graces. In Solomon: “You are like my brother, like a gazelle or a fawn of the deer” (Song 2:9).

Gazelle means the same as above.

Hare means one who fears God. In the Psalm: “The rock is a refuge for hares and hedgehogs” (Ps. 103:18).

Hedgehog means the same as above. “And the race of hedgehogs” means the weak, who made houses for themselves in the rocks.

Fox means a heretic, or the devil, or a crafty sinner. In the Gospel: “Go and tell that fox” (Luke 13:32).

Animal means a carnal person. [Col. 0752B] In the Apostle: “The animal person does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 2:14).

Beast of burden means one lacking understanding or eloquence, and sometimes those who are obedient. In the Psalm: “I became like a beast of burden before you” (Ps. 72:23). Sometimes it means the lustful, as in the saying: “The beasts of burden rotted in their dung” (Joel 4:17).

Horse means a holy man. In Habakkuk: “You who ride upon your horses” (Hab. 3:8). In the negative sense: “A horse is deceitful for salvation” (Ps. 32:17), meaning anyone irrational. In the Psalm: “Do not become like horse and mule, which have no understanding” (Ps. 31:9).

Ass means the human body or the people of the Gentiles. In the Gospel: “They brought to Jesus a she-ass and her colt, and made him sit upon them” (Matt. 21:7). Under the name of asses, the laziness of fools is signified, as Moses testifies: “You shall not plow with an ox and an ass together” (Deut. 22:10), that is, in preaching, do not yoke the prudent [Col. 0752C] together with the foolish.

Under this name the simplicity of the faithful is also expressed, and Christ, ruling and presiding over it, leads it to Jerusalem—that is, to the vision of peace. Hence it is said: “The ox knows its owner, and the ass its master’s manger” (Isa. 1:3).

Again, the ass signifies the unrestrained lust of the wanton, as the Prophet says: “Their flesh is like the flesh of asses” (Ezek. 23:20).

**She-ass** signifies the flesh or the populace lacking knowledge of God. In the Gospel, it has the same meaning as above.

**Camel** signifies the rich, weighed down by the things of the world, or those distorted in their morals. In the Gospel: “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XIX, 24). The Lord himself is also signified by the camel, as in: “Straining out the gnat but swallowing the camel” (Matt. XXIII, 24). Here the Lord is clearly indicated, [Col. 0752D] who willingly humbled himself, bore the burdens of our weakness, and endured the piercing of the needle and the narrowness of the opening in the suffering of his Passion. The gnat wounds by buzzing, whereas the camel willingly bends itself to receive burdens. Thus the Jews strained out the gnat because they asked that the seditious robber be released; but they swallowed the camel because by their cries they attempted to destroy him who had willingly descended to bear the burdens of our mortality.

**Bulls** signify the rulers of peoples. In the Psalm: “Fat bulls surrounded me” (Ps. XXI, 13).

**Oxen** signify the apostles, who, having taken upon themselves Christ’s yoke, plowed the world with the plowshare of the Gospel. In the Psalm: “I will offer you oxen with goats” (Ps. LXV, 15). Oxen also signify the senselessness of fools, as it is rightly said through [Col. 0753A] Solomon: “And immediately she follows him, like an ox led to the slaughter” (Prov. VII, 22). By the name of oxen, too, the life of each person who labors is expressed, as through Moses: “You shall not muzzle an ox while it is threshing” (Deut. XXV, 4); and the Lord says: “The laborer is worthy of his food” (Matt. I, 10).

**Cows** signify those filled with carnal vices. In the Psalm: “Among the cows of the peoples” (Ps. LXVII, 31). Cows also designate all the faithful in the Church, who, while they consider the commandments of sacred speech, carry upon themselves, as it were, the ark of the Lord. Many of them are bound outwardly by carnal desires, but they do not turn aside from the right path, because they carry the Lord’s ark in their minds (I Kings VI, 12).

**Calf** signifies Christ or the saints. In the [Col. 0753B] Psalm: “Then they will place calves upon your altar” (Ps. L, 21). In another sense: “Many calves surrounded me” (Ps. XXI, 13), that is, the wanton ones.

**Swine** signify unclean sinners. In Peter’s Epistle: “And the washed sow returns to wallowing in the mud” (II Peter II, 22).

**Rams** signify the apostles or the leaders of the Churches. In the Psalm: “Bring to the Lord the sons of rams” (Ps. XXVIII, 1).

**Sheep** signify faithful peoples. In the Gospel: “My sheep hear my voice” (John X, 27).

**Cattle** signify the more simple, those less endowed with subtle powers of reasoning. In Solomon: “Take care of the souls of your cattle” (Prov. XXVII, 23).

**Goats** signify sinners or the Gentiles. In Daniel: “And behold, a he-goat was coming from the west over the face of the whole earth” (Dan. VIII, 5). In another, favorable sense: “I will offer you oxen with goats” (Ps. LXV, 15).

**She-goats** sometimes signify the righteous who come from the Gentiles. In Solomon: “Your hair is like a flock of goats [Col. 0753C] that have come down from Gilead” (Song VI, 4). Just as goats seek their pasture especially in high places, so the saints, cleansed through baptism and repentance, desire pasture in heavenly places. Hence the Apostle says: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III, 20).

**Roe deer** signify souls made more savage through the vain teaching of philosophers, but now brought within the holy Church through the holy Gospel.

**Lambs** signify Christ, or the apostles, or the saints. In the Gospel: “Feed my lambs” (John I, 15).

**Kids** signify sinners or the movements of the flesh. In the Gospel: “The kids on the left” (Matt. XXV, 33).

**Moles** signify idols or heretics who do not see the truth. In Isaiah: “That you may worship moles and bats” (Isa. II, 20).

**Dog** signifies the devil, or the Jew, or the Gentile. In the Psalm: “And from the hand of the dog my only one” (Ps. [Col. 0753D] XX, 21). In another sense, in Ecclesiastes: “Better is a living dog than a dead lion” (Eccl. IX, 4). Here they think that the lion should be understood as the devil, and the dog as the Gentile or the sinful person: the latter can come to faith or repentance, whereas the former does not come. The dog also designates sluggish preachers, as there: “Dumb dogs unable to bark” (Isa. LVI, 10).

**Frogs** signify demons. In the Apocalypse: “And I saw three unclean spirits like frogs coming from the mouth of the dragon. They are spirits of demons” (Apoc. XVI, 13). Frogs also signify heretics who dwell in the mire of the basest opinions and do not cease to bark with empty chatter.

**Ant** signifies the provident or industrious person. In Solomon: “Go to the ant, you sluggard” (Prov. VI, 6).

[Col. 0754A]

**Worm** signifies Christ because of the humility of the humanity he assumed. In the Psalm: “But I am a worm and not a man” (Ps. XXI, 7). In another sense, in Isaiah: “Their worm shall not die” (Isa. LXVI, 24), that is, either the worm itself, or the consciousness of sin, or the restlessness of an evil thought.

**Spider** signifies human frailty. In the Psalm: “And you have made my soul waste away like a spider” (Ps. XXXVIII, 2). Spiderwebs are the works of temporal desire, which are made firm by no subtle strength and which mortal wind carries away.

**Serpent** signifies the devil or evil men. In the Gospel: “Serpents, offspring of vipers” (Matt. XXIII, 33). In another sense, in the Gospel: “Just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness” (John III, 14). The serpent also signifies the prudent, as there: “Be wise as serpents” (Matt. [Col. 0754B] X, 16).

**Dragon** signifies the devil or an open persecutor. In the Psalm: “You crushed the head of the dragon; you gave him as food to the people of Ethiopia” (Ps. LXXIII, 14).

**Scorpion** signifies the devil or his ministers. In the Gospel: “I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions” (Luke X, 19).

**Viper** has the same meaning as above. In the Gospel: “Offspring of vipers” (Luke III, 7).

# CHAPTER VI. On the Various Designations of Names

**Man** signifies either the whole man or the mind. In Genesis: “God made man in his own image and likeness” (Gen. I, 26). In an unfavorable sense, in the Psalm: “Arise, O Lord; let man not prevail” (Ps. IX, 20), that is, the flesh or the devil. Does it not also designate blameworthy man, as in this saying of the [Col. 0754C] Apostle: “Since there is jealousy and contention among you, are you not carnal, are you not human?” (I Cor. III, 4). And elsewhere: “An enemy has done this” (Matt. XIII, 28), that is, the devil. The Apostle also speaks of “the man of sin and the son of perdition” (II Thess. II, 3), that is, the Antichrist. But human beings are also signified by the name “flesh”; hence: “And all flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Luke III, 6).

**Soul** is spoken of both human beings and animals. Thus in Job: “The soul of every living thing and the spirit of all flesh are in the power of the Almighty” (Job XII, 10). He raises the rational soul of human beings up to spiritual understanding, but gives the soul of irrational creatures life only up to bodily sensation.

**Man (vir)** signifies the spirit, that is, the mind. In the Apostle: “The head [Col. 0754D] of the woman is the man” (I Cor. XI, 3). In an unfavorable sense, man appears in Genesis: “A virgin of very beautiful appearance, whom no man had known” (Gen. XXIV, 16), that is, the devil, who often corrupts the mind through thought.

**Woman** signifies the soul or human flesh. In the Apostle: “The head of the woman is the man.” “Woman” may refer to sex, as in: “God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the Law” (Gal. IV, 4); or to weakness, as in the Wise Man: “Better is the iniquity of a man than a woman doing good” (Eccl. XLII, 14).

**Virgin** signifies the Church or holy souls. In the Apostle: “For I betrothed you to one man, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (II Cor. XI, 12). In an unfavorable sense: “Come down, sit in the dust, virgin daughter of Babylon” (Isa. XLVII, 1), that is, a soul barren of goodness, which through hypocrisy or malice [Col. 0755A] becomes a daughter of confusion.

**King** signifies the Lord. In the Apostle: “King of kings and Lord of lords” (I Tim. VI, 15). In an unfavorable sense, it refers to the devil: “He is king over all the sons of pride” (Job XLI, 25).

**Queen** signifies the Church. In the Psalm: “The queen stood at your right hand” (Ps. XLIV, 10). Again, queen signifies the soul ruling the body.

**Father** signifies the Lord. In the prophet: “I will be a father to you, and you shall be sons and daughters to me, says the Lord Almighty” (Jer. XXXI, 9); and in the Gospel: “For you have one Father, who is in heaven” (II Cor. V, 18). It may also refer to the devil: “Because he is a liar and its father” (Matt. XXIII, 9), the father of falsehood and of all who have not remained in the truth.

**Mother** signifies the Church or the heavenly Jerusalem. In the Apostle: “But the Jerusalem above is free, [Col. 0755B] and she is our mother” (John VIII, 44). Those who, by speaking rightly, beget and nurture the faithful for Christ exist as mothers in either sex, as Christ himself bears witness (Gal. IV, 26).

**Brother** signifies Christ or one’s neighbor. In the Psalm: “I will declare your name to my brothers” (Ps. XXI, 23); and he himself says: “Go, announce to my brothers” (Matt. XXVIII, 10).

**Sister** signifies the Church, the Synagogue, or the soul of Christ. In the Song of Songs: “My sister, my bride” (Song IV, 9).

**Man and wife** signify Christ and the Church, and spiritual understanding and the historical sense of the Scriptures. In the Apostle: “Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ also loved the Church” (Eph. III, 25).

**Bridegroom** signifies Christ, because he was promised by the Father from the beginning. In the Psalm: “And he himself, like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber” [Col. 0755C] (Ps. XVIII, 9). In the Gospel: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom” (John III, 29).

**Bride** signifies the Church, which has been promised through divine pledges. In the Song of Songs: “Come from Lebanon, bride; come from Lebanon” (Song IV, 8).

**Son** signifies the people of believers. In the Apostle: “You are no longer a slave but a son; and if a son, also an heir through God” (Gal. IV, 7). “Son” may also signify the Lord, as in: “If the Son makes you free” (John VIII, 36).

**Daughter** signifies the faithful soul or the Church. In the Psalm: “Hear, daughter, and see” (Ps. XLIV, 11). In an unfavorable sense: “Set a guard over a wandering daughter” (Eccl. XLII, 11), that is, over the levity of the soul.

**Neighbors** signify those close in faith and those who show mercy to the needy. In Solomon: “Come, eat and drink, and be drunk, [Col. 0755D] neighbors” (Song V, 1).

**Friends** signify those in harmony with God. In the Gospel: “You are my friends” (John XV, 14).

**Old men** signify those perfected in righteousness. In Genesis: “And Abraham died old and full of days” (Gen. XXV, 8). In Solomon: “Gray hair is a person’s understanding, and the age of old age is an undefiled life” (Wis. IV, 9). In an unfavorable sense, Solomon says: “When he had grown old, his heart was perverted” (III Kings XI, 4).

**Young men** signify those eager for God. In John’s Epistle: “I write to you, young men, because you are strong, and the word of God remains in you, and you have conquered the Evil One” (I John II, 14). In an unfavorable sense, in the Book of Kings concerning Rehoboam: “Abandoning the counsel of the elders, he spoke according to the counsel of the young men” (III Kings XII, 14). Also [Col. 0756A] there: “Woe to you, land whose king is a boy” (Eccl. X, 16).

**Little one** signifies the humble and simple in mind. In the Gospel: “You have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Mark XI, 25). And in the Gospel: “Unless you become like little ones, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XVIII, 3). The Apostle likewise says: “In wickedness be little ones, but in understanding be mature” (I Cor. XIV, 20). In another sense, in the Apostle: “When I was a little one, I spoke as a little one” (I Cor. XIII, 11). “Little one” also signifies Christ, who humbled himself even unto death (Phil. II, 8).

**Prostitute** signifies the sinful soul which, having abandoned her heavenly husband, that is, Christ, conceived adulterous fruits of iniquity from the devil. In Jeremiah: “The face of a prostitute has become yours” (Jer. III, 3).

**Laborers** signify the apostles or preachers of the Gospel. In the Gospel: “The harvest is indeed abundant, but the laborers are few” (Matt. IX, 37).

**Shepherd** signifies the Lord: “I am the good Shepherd” (John X, 11). It also signifies the [Col. 0756B] Apostle, in the Gospel: “Feed my sheep” (John XXI, 17). In an unfavorable sense: “And he went away to feed pigs” (Luke XV, 15), that is, those who are filled with unclean thoughts.

**Hirelings** signify those who serve the Lord not solely out of divine love but also for temporal reward. In the Gospel: “How many hired servants of my father have an abundance of bread!” (Luke XV, 17).

**Fishermen** signify the apostles or teachers. In the Gospel: “I will make you become fishers of men” (Matt. IV, 15).

**Physician** signifies Christ or a learned person. In Solomon: “A gentle-hearted man is a physician.” Also: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Luke V, 31).

**Rich** signifies a believer abounding [Col. 0756C] in spiritual goods. In the Apostle: “Because in him you have become rich in every kind of knowledge and in every word” (I Cor. I, 5). Christ is also rich, as in: “Rich toward all who call upon him” (Rom. X, 10). In another sense, in the Gospel: “Woe to you who are rich” (Luke VI, 24).

**Poor** signifies the humble. In the Gospel: “There was indeed a poor man named Lazarus” (Luke XVI, 24). Again: “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matt. V, 3). Christ is also poor, as the Apostle says: “Christ became poor for our sake, although he was rich” (II Cor. VIII, 9). In an unfavorable sense, in the Psalm: “For we have become exceedingly poor” (Ps. LXXVIII, 8).

**Clothed** signifies one possessing the integrity of baptism or faith, or the garment of righteousness. In the Gospel: “And he saw there a man not clothed in a wedding garment” [Col. 0756D] (Matt. XXII, 11). The Apostle says: “All of you who have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. III, 27).

**Naked** signifies one lacking the sacrament of Baptism [possibly: “garment”], or divine assistance, or good works. In the Apocalypse: “But you are naked and wretched” (Apoc. III, 17). In a favorable sense, in the Gospel: “And, he says, casting aside the linen cloth, he fled from them naked” (Mark XIV, 52), that is, naked of earthly possessions.

**Living** signifies the righteous. In the Psalm: “I will please the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. CXIV, 9). In another sense, in Solomon: “And I praised the dead more than the living” (Eccl. IV, 2).

**Dead** signifies sinners or unbelievers. In the Gospel: “Let the dead bury their own dead” (Matt. VIII, 22). In a favorable sense: “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord” (Apoc. XIV, 13). Also: “You have died, [Col. 0757A] and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. III, 3).

**Corpses** signify the bodies of unbelievers. In the prophet: “And I will fill the valley of Jehoshaphat with the corpses of the dead.” In another sense: “They have laid out the corpses of your servants” (Ps. LXXVIII, 2). Also: “They shall see the corpses of men who were unbelieving, cast out” (Isa. LXVI, 24).

**Tomb** signifies the body of a sinner, retaining within itself a soul dead through vices. In the Gospel: “You are like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful to men, but inwardly are full of the bones of the dead” (Matt. XXIII, 27). Conversely, the prophet speaks of the Lord’s tomb: “And his tomb shall be glorious” (Isa. XI, 10).

# CHAPTER VII. The Inner Man

[Col. 0757B]

**The inner man** signifies the rational soul. In the Apostle: “That Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts in the inner man” (Eph. III, 16).

**His head** is Christ. In the Apostle: “The head of the man is Christ” (I Cor. XI, 3).

**Crown of the head** signifies the summit of righteousness. In Solomon: “For your crown will receive a crown of graces” (Prov. IV, 9). In another sense: “The crown of the hair of those walking in their sins” (Ps. LXVII, 22), that is, the height of wickedness.

**Hair** signifies the adornment of righteousness or understanding. In the Gospel: “Even the hairs of your head are all numbered” (Matt. X, 30).

**Neck** signifies Holy Scripture, as in the Song of Songs: “Your neck is like the tower of Lebanon, from which hang a thousand shields, [Col. 0757C] all the armor of the mighty” (Song IV, 4), that is, the testimonies of the Holy Scriptures. In another sense it signifies pride: “The daughters of Zion walked with outstretched neck” (Isa. III, 16).

**Nape** signifies pride, as in: “Stiff-necked” (Acts VII, 51).

**Eyes** signify faithful and simple understanding. In the Gospel: “Blessed are your eyes because they see” (Matt. XIII, 16). Elsewhere: “The eyes of the wise man are in his head,” that is, understanding is in the heart of the prudent (Eccl. II, 14). In an unfavorable sense, in the Gospel: “If your eye is evil” (Matt. VI, 23).

**Ears** signify faithful obedience. In the Gospel: “And your ears because they hear” (Matt. XIII, 16).

**Nostrils** signify the breath of faith and of good virtues. In Job: “And the divine spirit is in my nostrils” (Job XXVII, 3). Also: “Your nose is like the tower that is in Lebanon” (Song VII, 4). In an unfavorable sense: “Smoke comes forth from his [Col. 0757D] nostrils” (Job XLI, 11), that is, from the devil.

**Throat** signifies the judgment of understanding. In the Book of Job: “And does not my throat meditate wisdom?” In an unfavorable sense: “My throat has become hoarse” (Ps. LXVIII, 4).

**Mouth** signifies speech itself. In the Psalm: “The mouth of the righteous shall meditate wisdom” (Ps. XXXVI, 30).

**Tongue** has the same meaning as above. In the Psalm: “And his tongue shall speak judgment” (ibid.). It may also signify Scripture, as in: “My tongue is the pen of a ready writer” (Ps. XLIV, 2).

**Teeth** signify holy preachers who give right instruction and live as they teach.
