Thus it is said to the bride: “Your teeth are like flocks of shorn sheep, which have come up from the washing; all of them bear twins, and none is barren among them” (Song IV, 2). Teeth also signify the inner senses, as through Jeremiah: “He broke my teeth one by one” (Lam. III, 16). Teeth also signify the inner senses, [Col. 0758A] for the teeth, as it were, eat and grind each individual thing they think, and send it into the stomach of memory.

**Armpits**, which are the beginnings of the arms, signify the beginning of good works. Scripture imputes to the sluggard that he does not move them: “The sluggard hides his hand under his armpit” (Prov. XIX, 24).

**Shoulders** signify the strength of one who bears. The prophet speaks of the Lord who was to bear the cross: “Authority is upon his shoulder” (Isa. IX, 6).

**Hands** signify work. In the Psalm: “I have washed my hands among the innocent” (Ps. XXV, 6). They also signify power, as in: “Your hands made me” (Ps. CXVIII, 73).

**Right hand** signifies good works. In the Gospel: “Let your left hand not know what your right hand is doing” (Matt. VI, 3).

**Left hand** signifies none-good works, as above. The right hand also signifies eternal life, while the left signifies the present [Col. 0758B] life, as in: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me” (Song II, 6).

**Breast** signifies the secret place of understanding. In the Gospel: “The disciple whom Jesus loved greatly was reclining upon the Lord’s breast” (John XIII, 23).

**Belly** signifies the capacity of reason. In Habakkuk: “My belly was troubled within me” (Hab. III, 16). Belly also signifies the mind, as in Jeremiah: “I am in pain in my belly” (Jer. IV, 19). He said this of a spiritual, not bodily, belly, and adds: “The senses of my heart are troubled” (ibid.). The Lord likewise says in the Gospel: “Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John VII, 38).

**Kidneys** signify the inner parts of understanding. In the Psalm: “Even until night my kidneys have reproved me” (Ps. XV, 7). Nothing in a person is more hidden than the heart and kidneys; hence Scripture says: “God searches hearts and kidneys” (Ps. VII, 10).

**Loins** signify strength of spirit. In the [Col. 0758C] Apostle: “Gird up the loins of your mind” (Eccl. VI, 14). They also signify lust, as in the Gospel: “Let your loins be girded” (Luke XII, 35); and in Job: “Gird your loins like a man” (Job XXXVIII, 3).

**Navel** signifies the appetite of desire. In Job: “And his strength is under the navel of his belly” (Job XL, 11), meaning that this signifies female genitalia, just as it signifies male genitalia in the loins.

**Fat** signifies the richness of divine grace or the fullness of heavenly wisdom. In the Psalm: “That my soul may be filled with fat and richness” (Ps. XXVI, 6). In an unfavorable sense, fat signifies the thickness of wickedness. In the Psalm: “They have closed up their fat” (Ps. XVI, 10).

**Bones** signify firmness of spirit. In the Psalm: “All my bones shall say, O Lord, who is like you?” (Ps. XXXIV, 10). In an unfavorable sense, [Col. 0758D] in Job: “His bones are like tubes of bronze” (Job XL, 13). Bones also signify the deceitful counsels of the ministers of the Antichrist, as in the Psalm: “God has scattered the bones of those who please men” (Ps. LII, 6).

**Marrow** signifies the infusion of charity and other virtues, as in the Psalm: “I will offer you burnt offerings full of marrow” (Ps. LXV, 15).

**Bowels** signify affections of piety and mercy. In the Apostle: “If there is any affection of compassion” (Phil. II, 1). In another sense, in the Acts of the Apostles concerning Judas: “And all his bowels were poured out” (Acts I, 18).

**Skin** signifies mortality. In Genesis: “And he made them tunics of skin” (Gen. II, 21).

**Hide** signifies those who attend only to external things and wither inwardly.

**Hairs** signify the thoughts of the old life, which must be cut off. Hence Moses commands: “Let the Levites shave all the hair of their flesh” (Num. VIII, 7).

**Blood** signifies carnal activity. In the Psalm: “Deliver me from bloodshed, O God, God of my salvation” [Col. 0759A] (Ps. L, 16). Also: “Flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God” (I Cor. XV, 50). And Isaiah: “Blood has touched blood” (Hos. IV, 2). In a favorable sense, the Apostle says: “The blood of Jesus Christ cleanses us from every sin” (Heb. IX).

**Flesh** signifies the outward human being. In the Apostle: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. V, 17). Flesh according to nature is meant in: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh” (Gen. II, 23), and in: “The Word became flesh” (John I, 14). Hence the Apostle says: “But you are not in the flesh, but in the spirit” (Rom. VIII, 9). Flesh according to guilt is meant in: “My spirit shall not remain in these human beings, because they are flesh” (Gen. VI, 3).

**Knees** signify confession of humility. In the Canticles: “And now I bend the knees of my heart” [Col. 0759B] (Eph. III, 14); and in the Psalm: “My knees have grown weak from fasting” (Ps. CVIII, 24). Sometimes they signify the strength of faith, as in the prophet: “I have left myself seven thousand men who have not bent the knee before Baal” (III Kings XIX, 18).

**Feet** signify the course of life, or stability of mind, or faith. In the Psalm: “Our feet were standing” (Ps. CXXI, 2). In an unfavorable sense, in the prophet: “Why do you limp on both feet?” (III Kings XVIII, 21). Also: “Their feet are swift to shed blood” (Ps. XIII, 3).

**Heel** signifies the overthrow of vices. In Genesis: “He shall watch your head, and you shall watch his heel” (Gen. III, 15). It also signifies the end of an action, as in the Psalm: “They themselves will watch my heel” (Ps. LV, [Col. 0759C] 7). (Ps. LV, 7).

**Steps** signify progress in works. In the Psalm: “Perfect my steps in your paths” (Ps. XVI, 5).

**Footprints** signify the signs of virtues. In the Psalm: “So that my footsteps may not be moved.” In another sense, in Solomon: “And the life of the ungodly shall pass like a footprint of the sea.”

**Robe** signifies the garment of baptism or faith. In the Gospel: “Quickly bring out the first robe” (Luke XV, 22).

**Haircloth** signifies a testimony of repentance. In the Gospel: “Long ago they would have repented in ashes and haircloth” (Matt. XI, 21).

**Belt** signifies being girded for spiritual work. In the Psalm: “And you girded me with gladness” (Ps. XXIX, 12).

**Girdle** signifies purity of heart. The Apostle: “Girded around the loins with golden girdles” (Apoc. XV, 6).

**Footwear** signifies preparation for peace. In the Apostle: “With your feet shod in preparation for the Gospel of peace.”

**Armor of the inner man** is described by the Apostle: “Clothed with the breastplate of righteousness, the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. VI, [Col. 0759D] 15).

# CHAPTER VIII. On Things That Are in Use and at Hand

**Bread** signifies Christ or the word of God. In the Gospel: “I am the living bread” (John VI, 41). Elsewhere: “Let us put wood into his bread” (Jer. XI, 19), that is, the cross into his body. Bread can signify doctrine, and likewise evil doctrine, as in: “Hidden bread is sweeter” (Prov. IX, 17).

**Wine** has the same meaning as above. In Solomon: “Drink the wine that I have mixed for you” (Prov. IX, 5). Wine also signifies the security of uprightness, as [Col. 0760A] in: “Pouring in oil and wine” (Luke X, 34), so that the wounds may be bitten by the wine and soothed by the oil.

**Oil** signifies mercy or the Holy Spirit. In the Psalm: “I have anointed you with my holy oil” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 21). In another sense: “But let the oil of the sinner not fatten my head” (Ps. CXL, 5), that is, flattery.

**Pork** signifies sins. In the Psalm: “I have been filled with pork.”

**Unleavened bread** signifies sincerity of heart, without the leaven of malice. In the Apostle: “In the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (I Cor. V, 8).

**Egg** signifies the sure hope of the faithful. In an unfavorable sense: “Whoever eats of their eggs shall die” (Isa. LIX, 5), referring to the wicked and badly instructed.

**Fine flour** signifies purity of mind and the strength of charity. In Leviticus: “But if a soul offers a sacrificial gift to God, let his offering be fine flour” (Lev. II, 1).

**Ash-cake** signifies an offering of humility. In Genesis: “Quickly mix three measures of fine flour and make ash-cakes” (Gen. XVIII, 6). In an unfavorable sense: “Ephraim has become an ash-cake” [Col. 0760B] (Hos. VII, 8).

**Milk** signifies sincerity of mind. In Peter’s Epistle: “Desire rational, guileless milk” (I Peter II, 2). In another sense, concerning the inexperienced in the Church: “I gave you milk to drink, not food, for you were not yet able” (I Cor. III, 2). Here milk signifies a limited understanding.

**Curdled milk** signifies something congealed by vices. In the Psalm: “Their heart has curdled like milk” (Ps. CXVIII, 70).

**Salt** signifies the seasoning of wisdom. In the Gospel: “You are the salt of the earth” (Matt. V, 13), and: “Have salt in yourselves” (Mark IX, 49).

**Honey** signifies the sweetness of God’s commandments. In the Psalm: “How sweet are your words to my throat, O Lord, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth” (Ps. CXVIII, 103). In another sense, in Solomon: “When you find honey, eat what is sufficient, lest, having been filled, you [Col. 0760C] vomit it out” (Prov. XXV, 18), that is, “Do not seek what is beyond you” (Eccl. III, 22).

**Gall** signifies the bitterness of malice. In the Psalm: “They gave me gall for food” (Ps. LXVIII, 22).

**Vinegar** signifies the harshness of a corrupted mind. In the Psalm: “In my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Ps. LXVIII, 22). Vinegar also signifies the correction of teachers, whence Solomon says: “Vinegar on soda is one who sings songs with a wicked heart” (Prov. XXV, 20).

**Pitch** signifies the defilement and blackness of sins. In Solomon: “Whoever touches pitch will be defiled by it” (Eccl. XIII, 1).

**Strong drink** signifies a certain concoction of malice and wickedness. In the Gospel: “He shall drink neither wine nor strong drink” (Luke I, 15).

**Cup** signifies the Lord’s Passion. In the Psalm: “I will take the cup of salvation” (Ps. CXV, 13). The Lord himself says: “Father, take this cup away from me” (Mark XIV, [Col. 0760D] 36). (Mark XIV, 36). In an unfavorable sense: “The golden cup of Babylon” (Jer. LI, 7).

**Pure wine** signifies the sincerity of judgment or truth, or the fervor of faith. In the Psalm: “A cup full of pure wine mixed” (Ps. LXXIV, 9).

**Dregs** signify the final judgment. In the Psalm: “Yet its dregs have not been emptied.” They also signify those who rest securely in their sins; hence the prophet: “He has rested upon his dregs” (Jer. XLVIII, 11).

**Food** signifies the word or will of the Lord. In the Gospel: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me, the Father” (John IV, 34).

**Drink** has the same meaning as above. In the Psalm: “You will give them drink from the torrent of your delight” (Ps. XXXV, 9), that is, from the Holy Spirit. The Psalmist also says: “In my sorrow I mixed my drink with weeping” (Ps. CI, 10). In another sense: “The kingdom of God is not food and drink” [Col. 0761A] (Rom. XIV, 17).

**Storehouses** signify receptacles of the heart. In the Song of Deuteronomy: “In their storehouses, fear.”

**Bag** signifies concern for sustenance and the impediments of the world. In the Gospel: “No bag for the journey” (Matt. X, 9).

**Purse** signifies storing up treasure in God. In the Gospel: “Make for yourselves purses that do not grow old” (Luke XII, 33). In another sense: “Let us possess a common purse” (Prov. I, 14), that is, greed.

**Money** signifies divine words. In the Gospel: “Therefore you ought to have put my money with the money-changers” (Matt. XXV, 27). It also signifies wisdom, as Solomon says: “Hidden wisdom and an unseen treasure—what benefit is there in either?” (Eccl. XX, 32).

**Fleece** signifies the people. In the Psalm: “And he descended like rain upon the fleece” (Ps. LXXI, 6).

**Flax** signifies spiritual strength, brightness, or the subtlety of the Scriptures. In Exodus: “Moreover, you shall prepare linen tunics for the sons of [Col. 0761B] Aaron” (Exod. XXVIII, 30). In an unfavorable sense: “You shall not wear a garment woven of wool and linen together” (Deut. XXII, 11).

**Wineskins** signify vessels of the human body. In the Gospel: “New wine must be put into new wineskins” (Luke V, 38).

**Flour** signifies good works or knowledge. In the Gospel: “The woman hid it in three measures of flour” (Luke XIII, 21). In an unfavorable sense it signifies vain thoughts, as the prophet says: “Take the millstone and grind flour” (Isa. XLVII, 2).

**Millstone** signifies the conduct of life. In the Gospel: “Two women grinding at the mill” (Matt. XXIV, 41). The two Testaments may also be signified by the two stones of the mill, through which, by the labor of interpreters, the wheat of the Old Testament is transformed into the flour of the Gospel.

[Col. 0761C]

When these names occur in the text of sacred reading, they are to be understood above all in the more obvious senses in which they are expressed, although they often extend into different meanings according to the person, time, or place, and emerge into figures appropriate to particular passages according to the logic of allegorical interpretation. Thus **abyss**, as we said above, signifies the depth of the Scriptures; and likewise the abyss signifies the immensity of the waters: “And the fountains of the great abyss were broken open” (Gen. VII, 11). Again, abyss signifies the ineffable judgments of God. In the Psalm: “Your judgments are a great abyss” (Ps. XXXV, 7). Again, abyss signifies hell: “Or who descended into the abyss?” (Rom. X, 7), that is, to bring Christ back from the dead. Again, abyss signifies the hearts of human beings darkened by crimes: “The abyss said: ‘It is not with me’” (Job XXVIII, 14), that is, wisdom.

**Fire**, as we mentioned above, is understood as the Holy Spirit, as Paul says: “Our God is a consuming fire” [Col. 0761D] (Heb. XII, 29). Again, fire signifies charity: “its enclosures are enclosures of fire, its flames” [materially uncertain]. Fire signifies tribulation. In the Psalter: “You tested us by fire, as silver is tested by fire” (Ps. LXV, 10–11). Also: “We passed through fire and water.” Fire signifies anger: “And I will consume them in the fire of my anger,” says the Lord. Fire signifies pleasure: “They all commit adultery like an oven; their hearts.” Fire also signifies the malice of the mind, as in: “Then fire consumes the adversaries” (Heb. X, 27). It also signifies the power of charity, as in: “The chariot of God is a flame of fire; its wheels are burning fire” (Dan. VII, 9).

**Shadow**, as we indicated, signifies divine protection. At times shadow signifies sins: “Sitting in darkness and in the shadow of death” (Ps. CVIII, 10). At times shadow signifies punishment, in [Col. 0762A] Job: “A land of darkness and the shadow of death, and no order” (Job X, 22). Since a shadow is not far from the thing of which it is the shadow, so death is not far from the punishment that inflicts death. At times shadow signifies the pleasure of sinners, as Job says of the devil: “He sleeps under the shadow in the secret place of the reed, in moist places” (Job XL, 16). Again, certain forms signify many things by means of a single form.

We have mentioned the **two Testaments**, since they can signify the two millstones. [Col. 0762B] Likewise, the two Testaments signify the two cherubim in Exodus (Exod. XXV, 20); the two animals in Habakkuk; the two rocks in Exodus (Exod. XVII, 6) and in the Song of Songs (Song II, 14), under whose covering the bride and Moses are protected; and the two bronze mountains in Zechariah, from whose myrtle thickets and obscure shade the chariots emerge with red, black, white, and variegated horses (Zech. VI, 1). But to pursue such manifold meanings in each individual name seemed to us not only an immense labor but also impossible. Let us therefore now return to that method and order of interpretation which, because of the necessity of our discussion, we interrupted for a little while.

**Baskets** signify the apostles. In the Gospel: “And they took up twelve baskets full of the fragments that remained” [Col. 0762B] (Matt. XIV, 20). In another sense: “His hands served in the basket” (Ps. LXXX, 7), that is, in the slavery or tribulation imposed by the Egyptians.

**Chair** signifies doctrine. In the Psalm: “And let them praise him in the chair of the elders” (Ps. CVI, 32). [Col. 0762C] (Ps. CVI, 32). In another sense: “He did not sit in the chair of pestilence” (Ps. I, 1), that is, in the doctrine of heretics.

**Footstool** signifies the subjection of those who have been humbled. In the Psalm: “Until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet” (Ps. CIX, 1). It also signifies Christ’s humanity, as in the Psalm: “Worship his footstool” (Ps. XCVIII, 5).

**Scales** signify equity or the power of divine governance. In Isaiah: “And he weighed the mountains in the balance and the hills on the scales” (Isa. XL, 12).

Ashes: the emptiness of human frailty. In Solomon: “Why are you proud, earth and ashes?” (Eccl. X, 9).

Pot: lineage. In the psalm: “Moab is the pot of my hope” (Ps. LIX, 10), that is, the lineage of Christ according to the flesh descended from Ruth the Moabite woman.

In another sense, pot means the baking of tribulation; in the prophet: “And I saw a pot boiling from the face of the north” (Jer. I, 13).

Lamps: souls shining with righteousness. In the Gospel: “And they prepared their lamps” (Matt. XXV, 7). In another sense, the brightness of miracles, or the words of preachers, which fools despise, as in Job: “A lamp despised in the thoughts of the fool” (Job XII, 5).

Darkness: pleasures or wicked teachings, as in the psalm: “They walk in darkness” (Ps. LXXXI, 5). In another sense, the hidden judgments of God, as in the psalm: “He made darkness his hiding place” (Ps. XVII, 12). In another, chastisement or adversity, as Isaiah says: “I am the Lord, forming light and creating darkness” (Isa. XLV, 7).

Lamp: the Church or the soul. In the Gospel: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning” (Luke XII, 55). Sometimes lamps mean good works: “Let your light shine, so that they may see your good works” (Matt. V, 16).

Bushel: the human body, or the letter of the law, or the people of the Jews. In the Gospel: “No one lights a lamp and places it under a bushel” (Matt. V, 15). In another sense, just judgment or the weighing of the mind in an equal balance toward God and one’s neighbor. Hence Moses says: “Let your bushel be just” (Lev. XIX, 36).

Lampstand: the Church, or the Lord’s body, or holy Scripture. In the prophet: “And I saw two burning lampstands on the right side of the altar” (Zech. IV, 2–3).

Table: the altar, or spiritual nourishment. In the psalm: “You have prepared a table before me” (Ps. XXII, 5).

Key: the opening of spiritual knowledge. In Luke: “Woe to you lawyers, because you have taken away the key of knowledge: you yourselves have not entered, and you have hindered those who were entering” (Luke XI, 12)! In another sense, keys mean the virtues of justice, mercy, and piety. In the Gospel: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XVI, 19).

Nail: the fear of God, as in the psalm: “Fasten my flesh with your fear” (Ps. CXVIII, 120). In another sense, nails mean strong teachers of knowledge, as Solomon says: “The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails driven deeply” (Eccl. XII, 11).

Bars: barriers against the impious, consisting of the divine commandments. In the psalm: “For he has strengthened the bars of your gates” (Ps. CXLVII, 12).

Axe or hatchet: the persecution of the wicked. In the psalm: “With the double axe and the hatchet they cut it down” (Ps. LXXIII, 6).

Double axe: doubled affliction, in the psalm, as above.

Spear: the soul of the righteous. [The following printed clause is uncertain:] “Therefore let the righteous abound and the spear be poured forth.” It also means death, as in the psalm: “Deliver my soul, O God, from the spear” (Ps. XXI, 21).

Sword: the word of God. For the Apostle says: “The sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. VI, 17). In another sense, the tongue of a false witness, as in the psalm: “Their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword” (Ps. LVI, 5).

[Col. 0763C]

Ship: the Church. In the Gospel: “The little boat was being tossed by waves in the middle of the sea” (Matt. XIV, 24). A human being is also sometimes called a little boat, so that sailors may be understood as guiding human thoughts.

Nets: preaching. In the Gospel: “Put out the nets for a catch” (Luke V, 4).

Beam: a more serious sin. In the Gospel: “First remove the beam from your eye” (Matt. VII, 5).

Splinter: a lesser sin. In the Gospel: “And then you will see to remove the splinter from your brother’s eye.”

Noose: deceit. In the psalm: “They prepared a noose for my feet” (Ps. LVI, 7).

Ropes: lot or inheritance. In the psalm: “The ropes have fallen to me in pleasant places” (Ps. XV, 6). In another sense, ropes mean sins: “Woe to those who drag sins as though they were a long rope” (Isa. V, 18). And again: “The ropes of sinners have entangled me” (Ps. CXVIII, 61).

Wheel: the world, or human life. In the psalm: “The sound of your thunder is in the wheel” (Ps. LXXVI, 19). Again: “My God, make them like a wheel” (Ps. LXXXII, 14), that is, make them rolling or unstable in their wickedness. In another sense, it means both Testaments, as in Ezekiel (Ezek. I, 16).

Sponge: the hollow unbelief of the Jews. In the Gospel: “But they placed a sponge full of vinegar around hyssop and offered it to his mouth” (John XIX, 29).

Ladder: the progress of the saints. In Genesis: “And he saw in a dream a ladder standing on the earth, with its top touching heaven, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon it” (Gen. XXVIII, 12).

Brooms: the care of superstition through vainglory. In the Gospel: “And coming, he found it empty, swept with brooms and adorned” (Matt. XII, 4).

[Col. 0764A]

Tow: a gathering of the wicked through vices and sins, as the prophet says: “Gathered tow is an assembly of sinners” (Eccl. XXI, 10).

Pearl: evangelical teaching, or hope of the kingdom of heaven. In the Gospel: “When he had found one precious pearl, he went away and sold everything he had and bought it” (Matt. XIII, 46).

Ring: the seal of faith. In the Gospel: “And put a ring on his hand” (Luke XV, 22). Concerning this also in the psalm: “The light of your face has been marked upon us, O Lord.”

Cloak: the adornment of praise. In Solomon: “She made cloaks for her husband” (Ps. IV, 7), that is, a garment composed of two colors, as though of the two Testaments (Prov. XXXI, 22).

Gold: the inner meaning of the Scriptures. In the psalm: “And the back parts of his back in the appearance of gold” (Ps. LXVII, 14). In another sense, Christ’s divinity, as it is said of the bridegroom in the Song of Songs: “His head is finest gold” (Song V, 11). In another, the splendor of the heavenly city Jerusalem, which John testifies that he saw: “The city itself was pure gold” (Rev. XXI, 18). In another, wisdom, as Solomon says: “A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise.” In another, the splendor of holiness, which Jeremiah laments as suddenly changed: “How the gold has become dim, how the finest color has been changed” (Lam. IV, 1).

Silver: the divine utterances, or the understanding of the letter or of history. In the psalm: “The utterances of the Lord are pure utterances, silver tested by fire” (Ps. XI, 7). In a negative sense: “Their gold and silver have rusted” (James V, 3). Dross—foam or rust, which silver deposits in the furnace—will be such as sinners when the furnace of Gehenna receives them.

[Col. 0764C]

Precious stones: the apostles or the saints, or the works themselves of the virtues. In the Apocalypse: “All the foundations of the city wall were adorned with every precious stone” (Rev. XI).

Bronze: vanity or emptiness of faith. In the Apostle: “I have become like sounding bronze” (I Cor. XIII, 1). In another sense: “You have made my arms like a bronze bow.” Here “bronze” means strong or firm.

Iron: tribulation, or the human being himself. In the psalm: “Iron passed through his soul” (Ps. CIV, 18).

Lead: the weights of sins. In the prophet: “And I saw iniquity upon a talent of lead.”

Clay: the frailty of the flesh. In the Apostle: “We have this treasure in clay vessels” (II Cor. IV, 7).

## CHAPTER IX. On the Various Meanings of Words Expressed by the Infinitive

[Col. 0764D]

To build: to do good works, or to teach well. In the Apostle: “But if anyone builds upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones” (I Cor. III, 12), that is, works of various virtues.

To destroy: to practice evil works, or to teach badly. In Solomon: “One builds, and another destroys” (Eccl. XXXIV, 28).

To cleanse: to purge from vices. In the Gospel: “Jesus touched him, saying, ‘I will; be cleansed,’ and immediately his leprosy was cleansed” (Matt. VIII, 3).

To stand: to stand firm in faith. In the Apostle: “Stand firm in the faith” (I Cor. XVI, 13).

To walk: to strive toward God. In the psalm: “And I walked in a broad place” (Ps. CXVIII, 45).

To sit: to rest humbly in God. In the Gospel: “But you, remain in the city” (Luke XXIV, 49).

To lie: to succumb either to vices or to temptations. In the Gospel: “And he found her lying in bed” (Mark VII, 30).

To run: to hasten in good works. In the Apostle: “Run in such a way that you may obtain” (I Cor. IX, 24).

To keep watch: to guard the heart, or to rise toward God. In the psalm: “From the morning watch until night” (Ps. CXXIX, 6). And the Apostle says: “Awake righteously, and do not sin” (I Cor. XV, 34). Elsewhere: “Keep watch, stand firm in the faith, act courageously” (I Cor. XVI, 13).

To sleep: after passing away, to rest with God. In the psalm: “Will the one who sleeps not continue until he rises?” (Ps. XL, 9). In another sense, to sleep means to grow numb in the stupor of sins. In the Apostle: “Rise, you who sleep” (Eph. V, 14).

To be ashamed: in evil, something excellent; in good, something deplorable. Hence it is said: “There is a shame that brings sin, and a shame that brings glory” (Eccl. IV, 25).

Ascent: progress toward God. In the psalm: “The ascent is in his heart” (Ps. LXXXIII, 6).

Descent: falling away from God. In the Gospel: “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho” (Luke X, 30).

Way: Christ. In the Gospel: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV, 6). In another sense, the way means human life. In the psalm: “I have declared my ways, and you have heard me” (Ps. CXVIII, 26). And Solomon says: “They shall eat the fruit of their ways” (Prov. I, 3).

Broad: widened by the enticements of vices. In the Gospel: “Broad is the gate and spacious the way that leads to destruction” (Matt. VII, 13).

Narrow: strict, or pressed by tribulations, which leads to life. In the Gospel: “How narrow the gate and confined the way that leads to life” (ibid.).

[Col. 0765C]

Straight: ordered according to God’s commandments. In Isaiah: “Make his paths straight” (Isa. XL, 3).

Crooked: deviating from God’s commandments. In Isaiah: “And the crooked ways shall become straight, and the rough places into level roads” (ibid.).

Level: obedience to the commandments made even and smooth. In Isaiah, as above.

Rough: made harsh and fearful by the harshness of disobedience, as above.

At the right hand: on the side of righteousness. In the Gospel: “He will place the sheep at his right hand, but the goats at his left” (Matt. XXV, 33).

At the left hand: on the side of unrighteousness. In the Gospel, as above.

Pit: deceit, or a fall into death. In the psalm: “They dug a pit before my face” (Ps. LVI, 17).

Well: the devil or hell. In the psalm: “Nor let the well close its mouth over me” (Ps. LXVIII, 16). In a positive sense, in Genesis: “To the well of the oath” (Gen. XLVI, 1), that is, to the water of faith.

In another sense, the beginning of faith, as in the Song of Songs: “A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters” (Song IV, 15).

Spring: Christ, as in the psalm: “My soul thirsted for God, the living spring” (Ps. XLI, 3). In another sense, the gifts of God, as in the psalm: “And the springs of waters appeared” (Ps. XVII, 16). In a negative sense, teachers of perverse doctrines and evildoers, as Peter says: “These are waterless springs” (II Peter II, 17).

Torrent: the force of temptations driving the mind onward, as in the psalm: “Our soul has passed through the torrent” (Ps. CXXIII, 5). In another sense, the coldness of sins, from which David desires to be freed when he says: “Restore our captivity, O Lord, like a torrent in the south” (Ps. CXXV, 6).

Health: soundness of mind. In the psalm: “I cried to you, and you healed me” (Ps. XXIX, 3).

Sickness: the disease of vices. In the psalm: “Who heals all your sicknesses” (Ps. CII, 3). And in the Gospel: “He himself bore our sicknesses” (Isa. LIII, 4).

Leprosy: the contamination of sins. In the Gospel: “And immediately his leprosy was cleansed” (Matt. VIII, 3).

## CHAPTER X. On Jerusalem and Its Adversaries

Jerusalem: the Church or the soul. In the psalm: “Praise Jerusalem” (Ps. CXLVII, 12). It should also be noted that whatever applies generally to the Church can be referred to the soul.

Zion: the same as above. In the psalm: “Praise your God, Zion” (ibid.).

Sons of Zion: the sons of the Church. In the psalm: “And the sons of Zion rejoiced over their king” (Ps. CXLIX, 2).

Daughters of Jerusalem: the same as above, that is, souls devoted to the heavenly life. Sometimes daughters are souls belonging to the lower realm, as in the Book of Wisdom: “You have daughters; preserve their bodies” (Eccl. VII, 26).

Tabernacle: the Lord’s body or the Church. In the psalm: “He placed his tabernacle in the sun” (Ps. XVIII, 6). In another sense, the heavenly homeland, as in the psalm: “I shall enter the place of the tabernacle” (Ps. XLI, 5).

Ark: the Lord’s flesh, or the hearts of the saints filled with God. In the psalm: “You and the ark of your sanctification” (Ps. CXXXI, 8). In another sense, the ark means the Church, within which those who are to be saved are enclosed. In Genesis: “Only Noah remained, and those who were with him in the ark” (Gen. VII, 23).

Two stone tablets: as I think, because of the two Testaments, or because of the two commandments of love of God and neighbor. In Exodus: “And the Lord said to Moses: ‘Cut for yourself two tablets’” (Exod. XXXIV, 1).

Law: the divine commandments. In the psalm: “The law of the Lord is spotless” (Ps. XVIII, 8).

Handwriting: the written contract of a sinful human being with the devil, made through the hand of iniquity. In the Apostle: “The handwriting of sin that was against us” (Col. II, 14).

Covenant: the alliance of divine grace with humanity. In the psalm: “I saw those who do not keep the covenant.”

Testament: the confirmation of the divine will. In the prophet: “And I will confirm my testament over the house of Judah” (Heb. VIII, 8).

Iron stylus (Job XIX, 24): the firm sentence of the divine word.

Foreskin: Gentile life. In the Apostle: “Was anyone called in uncircumcision? Let him not be circumcised” (I Cor. VII, 18), that is, even one who comes from the Gentiles to faith in Christ need not be circumcised in the body.

Circumcision: the stripping away of vices. In the Apostle: “You were circumcised with a circumcision not made by hand, in the stripping away of the body of the flesh” (Col. II, 11).

Horn: strength or kingship. In I Kings: “And he exalted the horn of his Christ” (I Reg. II, 10).

Purple: the form of martyrdom through blood. In Exodus: “Everyone whose heart moves him shall bring firstfruits to the Lord: gold, silver, bronze, violet, purple, scarlet yarn, and linen” (Exod. XXXV, 5).

Fringes: words of faith to be carefully retained, as in the psalm: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within, in the fringe” (Ps. XLIV, 14).

Scarlet: the same as above; or the ardor of charity; or reference to the cross. In Exodus, as above.

Linen: the whiteness of chastity or continence. In Exodus, as above.

Violet: the bruises of confessors. In Exodus, as above.

Ephod: a sign of works proceeding from the shoulders. In Exodus: “And they made the ephod of gold, violet, purple, scarlet yarn, and twisted linen” (Exod. XXXIX, 2).

Breastpiece: the manifestation of teaching or reason from the breast. In Exodus: “And they made the breastpiece of woven work, according to the work of the ephod” (Exod. XXX, 8).

Poderis: a more secret and more perfect teaching. In Exodus: “And they made the long robe beneath the boss, wholly of violet, woven work” (Exod. XXXIX, 20).

Golden plate on the forehead: a prefiguration of the cross. In Exodus: “And they made a golden plate, and inscribed on it letters formed as the seal of the holiness of the Lord” (Exod. XXXIX, 29), that is, the name of the Lord, the Tetragrammaton.

Temple: the Lord’s body, or the saints. In the Apostle: “For you are the temple of the living God” (II Cor. VI, 16). And he himself says: “Destroy this temple” (John II, 19).

Altar: the height of faith. In the psalm: “Then they shall place calves upon your altar” (Ps. L, 21).

Sacrifice: an offering of righteousness. In the psalm: “Offer the sacrifice of righteousness” (Ps. IV, 6). In another sense, praise of God, as in the psalm: “The sacrifice of praise will honor me” (Ps. XLIX, 23).

Burnt offering: one wholly inflamed by faith. In the psalm: “I will offer you marrow-filled burnt offerings” (Ps. LXV, 15).

Victim: Christ, or a soul dedicated to God. In the Apostle: “An offering and sacrifice to God, for a fragrant aroma” (Eph. V, 2).

Myrrh: an indication of mortality. In the psalm: “Myrrh, drops, and cassia are from your garments” (Ps. XLIV, 9).

[Col. 0767C]

Incense: the power of prayer, as in the psalm: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight” (Ps. CXL, 2).

Ointment: the grace of Christ’s name spread abroad. In Solomon: “Your name is poured-out ointment” (Song I, 3).

Holy of holies: the innermost mysteries of the Lord, or the kingdoms of heaven. In the Epistle to the Hebrews: “For Jesus did not enter into man-made holy places, representations of the true ones, but into heaven itself, to appear now before the face of God on our behalf” (Heb. IX, 24).

Sabbath: spiritual rest. In Genesis: “And the Lord rested from all his works” (Gen. II, 2). Also Isaiah: “If you turn your foot away from the Sabbath” (Isa. LVIII, 12). In a negative sense: “The enemies saw her and mocked her Sabbaths” (Lam. I, 7), and so forth.

Lent: a figure of the present life and its labor. In the Gospel: “And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights” (Matt. IV, 2).

Passover: a foretelling of the Lord’s passage. In the Gospel: “Before the feast-day of Passover, Jesus, knowing that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father” (John XIII, 1).

Fiftieth day: the manifestation of future blessedness or forgiveness. In Leviticus: “You shall count seven full weeks until the following day” (Lev. XXIII, 15), and below, that is, fifty days.

Jubilee: a sign of the rest to come. In Leviticus: “It is a year of remission; it shall be a holy sign for you” (Lev. XXV, 10).

City of God: the Church or the soul. In the psalm: “In the city of our God” (Ps. XLVIII, 2).

Citizens: the faithful. In the Apostle: “But you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household” (Eph. II, 19).

Walls: the defenses of divine Scripture, or the prophets, or the saints. In the psalm: “Let the walls of Jerusalem be built” (Ps. L, 20). In another sense: “In my God I shall leap over a wall” (Ps. XVII, 30).

Towers: the apostles or all who are perfect. In the psalm: “And abundance in your towers” (Ps. CXXI, 7).

Gates: holy Scriptures, or righteousness, or the apostles, or angels. In the psalm: “Lift up, eternal gates” (Ps. XXIII, 7). In another sense: “Because broad is the gate and spacious the way that leads to death” (Matt. VII, 13).

Streets: the broadened spaciousness [variant: blessedness] of the saints. In the Apocalypse: “And the streets of the city were pure gold, like transparent glass” (Rev. XXI, 21).

Foundation: Christ, or faith. In the Apostle: “No one can lay another foundation than the one that has been laid, which is Jesus Christ” (I Cor. III, 11).

Wall: the law, or the protection of angels. In Isaiah’s Song: “And I surrounded it with a wall, and fixed reeds, and planted a vineyard” (Isa. V, 2).

House: the soul in which Christ dwells, or the Church. In the psalm: “We shall go into the house of the Lord” (Ps. CXXI, 1).

Upper room: the height of merits, or of knowledge. In the Gospel: “And he will show you a large upper room” (Luke XXII, 12).

Door: the opening of faith. In the Apostle: “For a great and evident door has been opened to me” (I Cor. XVI, 9).

Doorkeeper: Christ, who says: “If anyone enters through me, he will be saved” (John X, 9).

Pillar: spiritual support or stability. In the Apostle: “James and John and Cephas, who were regarded as pillars” (Gal. II, 9).

Wall: sometimes the structure of good works. In the Song of Songs: “Behold, he stands behind our wall, looking through the windows” (Song II, 9).

Windows: sight and hearing, or the remaining senses, as above: “Looking through the windows.” In a negative sense: “Death entered through the windows” (Jer. IX, 12).

Steps: spiritual ascent. In the title of the psalms: “A Song of Steps” (Ps. CXIX, 1). “The saints shall go from strength to strength” (Ps. LXXXIII, 8).

Floor: humiliation or affliction of the soul, or its inclination toward earthly things. In the psalm: “My soul clings to the pavement” (Ps. CXVIII, 25).

Psaltery: good works. In the psalm: “A pleasant psaltery with the lyre” (Ps. LXXX, 3).

Lyre: a devoted breast, in which the virtues are like strings—that is, spiritual goods. In the psalm: “Rise up, psaltery with the lyre” (Ps. XCVI, 9), that is, works together with faith; or, concerning the Lord himself, the resurrection of the flesh with divine power.

Ten-stringed instrument: the ten commandments, or the five external human senses doubled with the inner sense. In the psalm: “On the ten-stringed psaltery, with song and lyre” (Ps. XCI, 4).

Organ: the human being, or the one who was assumed by the Lord. In the psalm: “Praise him with strings and organ” (Ps. CL, 4).

Timbrel: the body weakened by fasting. In the psalter: “Praise him with timbrel and chorus” (ibid.).

Chorus: concord. In the psalm, as above.

Trumpet: the raising of the voice in divine preaching. In the prophet: “Raise your voice like a trumpet” (Isa. LVIII, 1).

Cymbals: lips confessing the Lord, or love of God and neighbor. In the psalm: “Praise him with well-sounding cymbals” (Ps. CL, 5).

Jubilation: a cry expressed with greater spiritual fervor. In the psalm: “Praise him with cymbals of jubilation” (ibid.).

Egypt: this world, or the people of the Gentiles. In the psalm: “Envoys shall come from Egypt” (Ps. LXVII, 32).

Ethiopia: the Church from the Gentiles. In the psalm: “Ethiopia shall stretch out her hands to God” (ibid.). In another sense, in the psalm: “You gave him as food to the people of Ethiopia” (Ps. LXXIII, 14).

Babylon: either the world or Rome. In the Apocalypse: “And Babylon the great came into remembrance before God, to give her the cup of the wine of the indignation of his wrath” (Rev. XVI, 19).

Enemies: the devil or vices. In the psalm: “He shall not be ashamed when he speaks with his enemies in the gate” (Ps. CXXVI, 5).

[Col. 0769B]

Thieves: heretics and false prophets. In the Gospel: “All who came before me were thieves and robbers” (John X, 8).

Nations: vices. In the Pentateuch: “When the Lord your God brings you into the land which you are entering to possess, and destroys many nations before you” (Deut. VII, 1). In another sense: “All nations, clap your hands” (Ps. XLVI, 2).

Battle: combat against spiritual wickedness, or conflict against vices. In the Apostle: “So I fight, not as one beating the air” (I Cor. IX, 26).

Peace: the agreement of the flesh, for good, with the spirit. In the psalm: “Pray for the things that make for the peace of Jerusalem” (Ps. CXXI, 6). In another sense, peace means Christ. In the Apostle: “For he himself is our peace” (Eph. II, 14).

Victory: triumph over the devil or over adversities. In the Apostle: “But thanks be to God, who has given us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” (I Cor. XV, 57).

Prize: the reward of completed merits. In the Apostle: “I press on toward the goal, toward the prize of the heavenly calling of God” (Phil. III, 14).

Crown: the reward of eternal glory for righteousness. In the Apostle: “From now on the crown of righteousness is laid up for me” (II Tim. IV, 8).

Since the completion of spiritual progress leads onward to the crown, the crown rightly completes the spiritual interpretation of these names as well. Nevertheless, we have thought it difficult to encompass all these names, just as it is difficult to bring forward everything whose meaning extends in two directions.

## CHAPTER XI. On Numbers

[Col. 0769D]

Now that these names have finally been completed, let us also briefly arrange the numbers, which the mystical logic of examples has made especially prominent among sacred subjects.

**I.** This number refers to the unity of the Godhead. In the Pentateuch: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one” (Deut. VI, 4). And the Apostle: “One God, one faith, one baptism” (Eph. IV, 5). Noah’s ark, which signifies the holy Church, is completed in one cubit (Gen. VI, 16), because eternal rest is perfected in contemplation of the one God.

**II.** Two refers to the two Testaments of divine law. In Kings: “And he made in the inner sanctuary two cherubim, ten cubits in height” (III Kings VI, 23). It also refers to the two commandments of charity, namely love of God and neighbor. “Two in the field, two at the mill, two in bed” (Luke XVII, 34) are read in the holy Gospel.

**III.** Three refers to the Trinity. In John’s Epistle: “There are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit; and there are three who bear witness on earth: spirit, water, and blood” (I John V, 7). And in Genesis: “Three branches” (Gen. XL, 10).

**IV.** Four refers to the four Gospels. In Ezekiel: “And from the midst of them came the likeness of four living creatures” (Ezek. I, 5). Likewise to the four rivers of paradise (Gen. II, 10). The name Tetragrammaton is written with four Hebrew letters. The holy cross is marked by four horns, as Habakkuk says: “Horns are in his hands” (Hab. III, 4).

**V.** Five refers to the five books of Moses, the five porticoes (John V, 2), the five loaves (John VI, 9), and the five wounds in the Lord’s body (John XX, 25). The Apostle says: “In the Church I wish to speak five words with my understanding” (I Cor. XIV).

**VI.** Six refers to the sixth day, on which the Lord made the human being together with all the animals of the earth. In Genesis: “Let us make the human being according to our image and likeness” (Gen. I, 26). A little later: “And evening came and morning came, the sixth day” (ibid., 31).

Perfection is comprehended in the number six. Therefore God is described as having perfected the world in six days, and one is added to the five so that the law may be fulfilled through the Gospel.

There are six ages of the world: five have passed; the sixth runs from John the Baptist and Christ’s incarnation to the end of the age. Thus on the sixth day God made the human being according to his image, because in this sixth age the reformation of our mind according to the image of the one who created us is manifested through the Gospel.

Those six ages are signified by the six water jars that the Lord commanded to be filled with water, and in which the water was changed into wine (John II, 6), so that we may understand Christ, already manifested in the law and the prophets. Those six periods, then, distributed and distinguished as though by joints, would be empty vessels unless they were filled by Christ. The periods of time would pass uselessly unless the Lord Jesus Christ were preached in them. The jars were therefore filled—that is, the prophecies were fulfilled.

**VII.** Seven refers to the seventh day, on which the Lord rested after completing everything. In Genesis: “And God rested on the seventh day from all the work that he had done” (Gen. II, 2).

This number signifies the highest perfection for the purposes of human reasoning, because it consists of the first even number and the first odd number: of the first number that can be divided and the first number that cannot be divided. Hence the Jubilee, which expresses perfect rest, consists of seven weeks. Hence the seven spirits who stand before the throne of God (Rev. I, 4). And the seven loaves with which Christ fed four thousand men signified the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit (Matt. XV, 34).

**VIII.** Eight refers to the Lord’s resurrection day, that is, the eighth day. In the title of the psalm: “For the end, for the eighth” (Ps. VI, 1).

**IX.** Nine refers to the mystery of the ninth hour, at which the Lord gave up his spirit. In the Gospel: “And about the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice” (Matt. XXVII, 46). There are also nine names of precious stones, and nine orders of angels.

**X.** Ten refers to the Decalogue, that is, the ten words written on the two tablets. In the psalm: “On the ten-stringed psaltery I will sing to you” (Ps. CXLIII, 9).

**XI.** Eleven refers to the apostles. In the Gospel: “The eleven disciples went to Galilee” (Matt. XXVIII, 16). The number eleven, when it exceeds ten by one, is also used for transgression and rebuke. Therefore the Apostle Peter did not allow the number of the apostles to remain at eleven, but chose Matthias as the twelfth in their order (Acts I, 26).

Hence eleven goats’ hair curtains are commanded to be made in the Old Law (Exod. XXVI, 7), signifying the acts of penitents for sins committed. Finally, the eleventh hour (Matt. XX, 6) refers to the Gentiles and to old age.

**XII.** Twelve refers to the apostles in the Gospel: “These are the names of the twelve apostles” (Matt. X, 2). By this number the whole multitude of those who judge is signified (Matt. XIX, 28), because the two parts of seven often signify universality. Those two parts—three and four—multiplied one by the other make twelve.

**XIV.** Fourteen refers to the mystery of the Lord’s birth. In the Gospel: “From Abraham to David there are fourteen generations” (Matt. I, 17).

**XV.** Fifteen refers to the fifteen steps of the temple made by Solomon. According to this number, fifteen psalms were composed that are entitled “A Song of Steps,” namely from the psalm “When I was in distress I called upon the Lord” (Ps. CXIX, 1) through “Praise the name of the Lord.”

**XVI.** Sixteen refers to the number of the prophets.

**XXII.** Twenty-two refers to the mystery of the divine books, according to the letters of the Hebrews.

**XXIV.** Twenty-four refers to the mystery of the number of elders. In the Apocalypse: “And upon thrones were twenty-four elders” (Rev. IV, 4). King David also distributed the priests into twenty-four divisions for the service of the temple (I Chron. XXIV, 7).

**XXX.** Thirty refers to the fruit of faithful marriages. In the Gospel: “They will bear fruit, one a hundredfold, another sixtyfold, another thirtyfold” (Matt. XIII, 8). The thirtyfold refers to married people, the sixtyfold to widows, and the hundredfold to virgins.

**XXXIII.** Thirty-three refers to the mystery of the age during which the Lord lived in the flesh. In the Apostle, as it seems to some from this passage: “Until we all attain to the unity of faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to a perfect man, to the measure of the fullness of the age of Christ” (Eph. IV, 13).

[Col. 0772A]

**XL.** Forty refers to the mystery of Lent. In the Gospel: “He was led by the Spirit in the wilderness for forty days” (Luke IV, 2).

The power of the Decalogue is fulfilled through the four books of the Gospel. We fulfill the commandments of the Decalogue if we perfectly observe the four books of the holy Gospel. Thus, through continence, vigils, prayers, and the other things that the Apostle mentions as weapons of righteousness (II Cor. VI, 7), we reach the rewards of immortal life.

**XLII.** Forty-two refers to the number of encampments in the wilderness, or to the number of generations from Abraham to the Lord Jesus Christ (Matt. I).

**XLVI.** The temple was built over forty-six years (John II, 20), after the Jews had returned from the exile, in a second building after Solomon. This number of years corresponds most fittingly to the perfection of the Lord’s body.

**L.** Fifty refers to Pentecost. In the Acts of the Apostles: “And when the days of Pentecost were fulfilled” (Acts II, 1).

**LX.** Sixty refers to the fruit owed to widows or to those living in continence. In the Gospel: “They will bear fruit, another sixtyfold” (Matt. XIII, 8).

**LXXII.** Seventy-two refers to the number of Moses’ elders (Num. XI, 24), or of the disciples whom the Lord chose. In the Gospel: “After this the Lord appointed another seventy-two and sent them two by two before his face into every city” (Luke X, 1).

**C.** One hundred refers to the fruit of martyrs or virgins. In the Gospel: “They will bear fruit, another a hundredfold” (Matt. XV, 8). This number signifies absolute perfection, as it is said of the elect: “Whoever has left house, or brothers, or sisters,” and the rest that follows, “will receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life” (Matt. XIX, 29).

One hundred also indicates an amount of time, as Isaiah says: “The child of a hundred years shall die,” and so forth (Isa. LXV, 20). In the Gospel there is also the hundredth sheep (Luke XV, 4), which Christ placed upon his sacred shoulders and carried to the heavenly homeland.

**M.** One thousand is used for the perfection of all numbers and for the perfect practice of every good. Thus Peter says in his Epistle: “Let this one thing not escape you, beloved, that one day with the Lord is like a thousand years” (II Peter III, 8). For in the knowledge of God, past, present, and future are equally present; and the long or short courses of time that seem so to us are equal in duration with God.

We have therefore brought forward these certain and sacred numbers merely as examples. Besides them there are very many, indeed almost all numbers are sacred; how they become so, you yourself, the investigator of divine reading, will discover.

[Col. 0773]

# TWO BOOKS OF INSTRUCTIONS TO SALONIUS BY SAINT EUCHERIUS, BISHOP OF LYONS (C)

## BOOK ONE

### PREFACE TO SALONIUS

[Col. 0773A]

You often ask me to resolve many matters that require an interpreter in the divine books. I shall collect, as they return to my memory, the things that you, my Salonius, have diligently and abundantly brought forward in your eagerness to know, and I shall answer them not from my own ingenuity but from the judgment of illustrious teachers, not with personal presumption but on the authority of others. I shall pursue not so much the scope of exuberant eloquence as the measure of necessary brevity.

In this way I shall be able both to satisfy your countless inquiries and to have the freedom to insert from elsewhere whatever I judge useful to your understanding—for example, what “Alleluia,” “Diapsalma,” and “Amen” signify; what the Cidaris, Ephod, Siclus, and the rest are. These terms, frequently encountered in the sacred books or especially established in the usage of the Church, require interpretation.

Since they repeatedly present themselves to readers throughout the whole body of Scripture, I have thought it worthwhile to display them to you in this work, gathered together with their meanings. For it is worthy of all my care to restore and strengthen your intellect, you who, scarcely ten years old when you entered the wilderness, were not merely instructed but also nourished among those hands of the saints by Father Honoratus—first, I mean, the teacher of the islands and later also of the churches.

There, the teaching of the most blessed Hilary—then a novice of the island, but now the supreme Pontiff—formed you in every discipline of spiritual matters; and afterward the holy men Salvianus and Vincentius, preeminent alike in eloquence and wisdom, completed your education. Having used so many such teachers, you will also hear from me, the least of all, the things you have asked. In them recognize now both you as the questioner and me as the respondent.

Farewell in Christ.

### CHAPTER ONE. On More Difficult Questions of the Old Testament

## IN GENESIS

**Question.** By what testimonies of Scripture is the Trinity proved?

**Response.** This is declared and made manifest in many ways and with many meanings throughout nearly all the sacred books; but let us briefly demonstrate it at the very beginning of the divine Scriptures. “In the beginning,” he says, “God made heaven and earth. And below: ‘The Spirit of God was borne over the waters’” (Gen. 1:2). “In the beginning”—that is, in the Son—because God the Father made heaven and earth through the Son. To him the Father also says: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26). For he accomplished everything through the Son: “For all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3). “The Spirit of God was borne over the waters” (Gen. 1:2)—that is, the Holy Spirit. Behold: God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Again, elsewhere: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their power” (Ps. 32:6). Behold God, and the Word, who is the Son, and his Holy Spirit.

Again, in the Gospel: “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19). But the Father is unbegotten, the Son begotten, and the Holy Spirit neither begotten nor unbegotten. For if we call him unbegotten, we may seem to be saying that there are two Fathers; and if begotten, two sons. Rather, he proceeds from the Father and the Son, as a kind of concord of the Father and the Son. Nor can there be among us a right concord without the Holy Spirit. The same Spirit is called love and the gift of God. He is also the distributor of graces (1 Cor. 12:4). Therefore, the Father is the one from whom all things are, the Son the one through whom all things are, and the Holy Spirit the one in whom all things are, just as the Apostle also says: “For from him and through him and in him are all things; to him be glory for ever and ever” (Rom. 11:36).

**Question.** How was the Spirit of God borne over the waters?

[Col. 0774C] **Answer.** Not by wandering about, but by power, since in the authority of his governance he rises above his creature.

**Question.** Where do we read that God made the waters?

**Answer.** Although the text of the divine reading does not clearly state that they were made at the beginning of creation, nevertheless they were made by God. For the way in which certain other things that are not written are to be understood from what is written is also shown. Thus the Apostles are to be understood as having been baptized, even though the clearer meaning of Scripture does not expressly state that they were baptized. Some, however, want this to be understood from the testimony in which the Savior says: “The one who has bathed does not need to wash” (John 13:10).

Nevertheless, the testimony that says, “Let the waters be gathered into one place, and let the dry land appear” (Gen. 1:9), can instruct us to some extent that the waters were made by God. For he would not have commanded the waters to be separated from the earth that he had made unless he himself had also made the waters. Nor would he subsequently have ordered something to be distinguished in the order of creation that he had not previously created. We draw this conclusion because Genesis does not explicitly mention his creation of the waters. More clearly, however, that psalm designates God as the author of this creature when it says: “For the sea is his, and he made it” (Ps. 94:5).

**Question.** What is meant by: “And God saw that they were very good” (Gen. 1:31)?

**Answer.** “Saw” means approved—that is, not through ignorance, but through manifestation.

**Question.** What is the etymological connection implied when it is written: “She shall be called woman, because she was taken from man” (Gen. 2:23)?

[Col. 0775B] **Answer.** The etymology, which does not sound in Latin, is preserved in the Hebrew language. For *vir* (“man”) is called *ish*, and this woman *ishshah*. The translation has most beautifully preserved this point in saying: “She shall be called *virago* [woman], because she was taken from man” (ibid.).

**Question.** In what respect do we retain the likeness of God?

**Answer.** In the mind.

**Question.** Where is Paradise held to be located?

**Answer.** There are various opinions on this matter. Some nevertheless define it as being on earth, so that an earthly being could dwell only on earth; yet they affirm that it was made inaccessible to humanity by divine power.

**Question.** What are we to understand by Eden in Genesis (Gen. 4:16)?

[Col. 0775C] **Answer.** That most sacred place toward the east of Paradise.

**Question.** What should be understood concerning that tree of the knowledge of good and evil (Gen. 2:9)?

**Answer.** First of all, one must not conclude from this, as certain heretics interpret it, that God is likewise the creator of evil. Whatever that tree was, the commandment of God is to be understood in it: in keeping the commandment there was knowledge of good; in transgressing the commandment there was knowledge of evil. Thus, after tasting the tree—that is, after violating the law of the commandment—there was knowledge of evil, because punishment followed the transgression of the commandment and the law.

**Question.** If God made man immortal (Wis. 2:23), how could he die?

[Col. 0775D] **Answer.** Man was not made by God wholly immortal. Rather, by keeping the commandment he would grow into eternity, while by transgressing he would fall into hell. This was so lest those living according to their own law should think themselves like God, or possess an everlasting Paradise without any merits. For both angel and human being are protected by divine favor only so long as each fulfills the duty assigned to him.

**Question.** How should we understand what Scripture reports about God walking in Paradise (Gen. 3:8)?

**Answer.** God’s presence in that place is made manifest by the expression “walking.” Scripture’s custom is, so that it may more readily become clear to human understanding, to show divine movements and emotions through human expressions. Thus, when it speaks of God’s arm (Isa. 53:1), it signifies his power and strength; when it speaks of his ears (Ps. 33:16), it signifies that he hears everything without doubt; when it speaks of his eyes (Isa. 1:14), it signifies that he observes all things without distinction; when it speaks of his soul, it signifies that he lives perpetually and eternally, or that all things are given life by their author himself.

**Question.** Since God made all things good, and nothing was made except by him, whence comes evil?

**Answer.** From the deprivation of good: what the good Creator produced for good is corrupted into evil by those who use it badly. In the substance of creation itself there is nothing that can rightly be called evil. As for the things thought to be evil—such as serpents and the other animals and beasts—what makes them harmful is an unsuitable condition of nature. For poison, which brings death to a human being, is the life of a serpent. If man had remained perpetually immortal, he would not have feared suffering the destruction caused by poison. In the same way, some creatures live in water and die when exposed to the earth; conversely, others live on earth and perish when immersed in water.

**Question.** Since the whole substance of creation proceeded from God the Creator, what are we to think about darkness?

**Answer.** Some argue as follows: silence is said to exist where there is no sound, although we know of no substance belonging to silence. Likewise, since there is no darkness where the presence of light exists, darkness is rightly understood as the absence of light. Others think this opinion accords poorly with the testimony that says: “The day is yours, and the night is yours” (Ps. 73:16).

**Question.** Since there can be no ignorance in God, how is it that, at the beginning of the book of Genesis, the Lord says: “Adam, where are you?” (Gen. 3:9)?

**Answer.** This means: “Adam, from where have you fallen?” These words are therefore not spoken as though someone were asking out of uncertainty, but as an interrogator’s rebuke. Alternatively: this statement does not show that God was ignorant of the truth or of where Adam was; rather, it shows that everyone who sins, as though already led astray by his errors and withdrawing from God’s presence through transgression, becomes unworthy of his knowledge. Alternatively: he asks so that each person may be convicted by his own answer. For although he does not fail to know what he wishes to have indicated, he nevertheless wishes the offender to be established as guilty by the testimony of his own response. While he asks, he judges.

**Question.** What is meant by: “Cursed is the earth in your works” (Gen. 3:17)?

**Answer.** Some think that here “works” should be understood not so much as cultivation and labor as sins.

**Question.** How should we understand the statement: “And he dwelt in the land of Naid,” or, as the Hebrew has it, Nod (Gen. 4:16)?

**Answer.** *Naid* means “unstable.” Thus it is the name of a land, but it declares that Cain, in accordance with the divine punishment and sentence, was a wandering exile.

[Col. 0777A] **Question.** Since above he had designated the man and the woman each by their own names, what does it mean that he subsequently added: “He made them male and female, and blessed them, and called their name Adam” (Gen. 5:2)?

**Answer.** *Adam* is interpreted as “human being.” It is clear from the name “human being” that both male and female can be so called.

**Question.** What is the meaning of the fact that, in the years of Methuselah, careful calculation finds fourteen years extending beyond the Flood, although only eight persons are reported to have been in the ark (Gen. 5:22)?

**Answer.** There is an error in the number. For the Hebrew books read in such a way that this number of fourteen years is completed within the time of the Flood.

[Col. 0777B] **Question.** Since the Lord says, “Their days shall be one hundred and twenty years” (Gen. 6:3), how did the lifespans of Abraham and many others subsequently extend beyond this period (Gen. 25:7; 35:28)?

**Answer.** Because this number of years was assigned rather for the performance of repentance than for the duration of human life: within the prescribed number they were to devote themselves to confession, so that they would not perish in the Flood. Or, if one prefers to refer that number to human life: even now no one is permitted to live more than one hundred and twenty years. The statement, “Their days shall be one hundred and twenty years,” was not pronounced concerning those who immediately followed at that time, but concerning their descendants, because he did not say, “They are,” but “They shall be.”

**Question.** What is meant by: “May God enlarge Japheth, and may he dwell in the tents of Shem” (Gen. 9:27)?

**Answer.** From Japheth, whose name in our language signifies “breadth,” arises the multitude of the nations; from Shem, the Hebrews. This therefore signifies that, after Israel had been cast out, the knowledge of God and of the Scriptures was to be claimed by our people. It should also be noted that Noah’s three sons occupied three parts of the earth after the Flood. The descendants of Shem extended into Asia, or the East; Ham into Africa, or the South; and Japheth, together with part of Asia, into Europe and the West.

**Question.** What is meant by the statement in Genesis: “From that land went forth Asshur, and he built Nineveh and Rooboth, the city” (Gen. 10:11)?

**Answer.** It does not signify two cities. *Rooboth* means “streets.” The sense is therefore: “He built Nineveh and the streets of the city.”

**Question.** How should we answer those who criticize Abraham for taking his brother’s daughter Sarah as his wife (Gen. 20:12)?

**Answer.** What had not yet been forbidden by the Lord’s law was not yet considered illicit.

**Question.** Why was the sign placed among the Jews on that more private part of the body, concerning which we too do not ask without embarrassment (Gen. 17:11)?

**Answer.** The depth of such questions, my Salonius, would indeed demand that we satisfy the matters proposed with an ordered and extended discussion and assign each, according to its merits, a kind of dignity that would require us to linger. But what are we to do? Since those who are hurrying need answers and are hastening toward so many matters, we must offer, in response to the subjects you have brought forward, a bare and circumcised answer. Recognize, then, in response to what you now ask, that nothing shameful can be seen in the very creation of the human being, since God fashioned the whole structure of his limbs and the entire person (Job 10:8). Moreover, it was not inappropriate that that generation should receive a sign on the part of the genital member through which the beginnings of generation itself were brought forth. In accordance with the inner meaning, however, this circumcision of the body’s more private part prefigured the need for a more inward circumcision—that is, of the heart.

**Question.** It is written in Genesis: “God tested Abraham,” as though the Lord did not know whether Abraham would be faithful unless he tested him by putting the matter to proof.

**Answer.** God did not test Abraham by investigating the truth because he was ignorant of his faith. He was tested so that, having been tested, he might be justified and set before others as an example for imitation.

**Question.** How does Jacob say, “I saw the Lord face to face, and my soul was saved” (Gen. 32:30), when the Gospel says, “No one has ever seen God” (John 1:18)? Or how is Moses said to have spoken with God face to face, as with a friend (Exod. 33:11)? And again he says to the Lord: “Show me your glory” (Exod. 33:18).

**Answer.** Jacob and Moses had not seen God in the glory of his very majesty, but through a visible form of created being subject to divine power, which could appear to human sight. As for the substance of the majesty in which God exists, how could it be seen by a mortal human being while he is still mortal, when God himself says to Moses: “You cannot see my face; for no human being shall see me and live” (Exod. 33:20)? For this reason both testimonies are true.

**Question.** What is meant by: “He is Ana, who found Jamin in the wilderness while he was pasturing the asses of Sebeon his father” (Gen. 36:24)?

**Answer.** *Jamin* is interpreted in Latin as *maria*, “seas,” that is, a gathering of waters, because he undoubtedly found a pool in the wilderness, a difficult thing to find there. Jamin also denotes asses that are born from wild asses through his contrivance. Some think that he was the first to discover the interbreeding of different animals with one another, so that mules or female mules might be born.

**Question.** What was the birthright that Esau sold to his brother Jacob (Gen. 25:33)?

**Answer.** The first and greater portion belonged to the firstborn, whether in honor, hereditary succession, or the favor of the father’s blessing. Thus Jacob himself says: “Reuben, my firstborn, first in gifts, greatest in authority” (Gen. 49:3). And in the book of Deuteronomy it is written concerning the firstborn: “He shall give him”—that is, the father shall give him—“a double portion of all that he possesses. For he is the beginning of his children, and the birthright belongs to him” (Deut. 21:17). For this reason Isaac had thought that his blessing should be conveyed to Esau by the right of the firstborn (Gen. 27).

[Col. 0779A] **Question.** What should be said in response to those who think that, because of their many wives, our fathers or patriarchs should be accused of unchastity?

**Answer.** First, what had not yet been forbidden by law could not be a crime, since it was customary. Further, at that time such things were not unacceptable to God, either because of the place or because of the time. Because of the place: just as, in one house, a master may command something to be done in one corner that he by no means permits in another. Because of the time: in an as-yet-undeveloped world the command had been given, “Increase and multiply” (Gen. 1:28). Now, however, those who have wives are commanded to be as though they had none. This is not because justice varies, but because times change; they cannot all proceed in the same way, and different things are appropriate to different times and places. Finally, it is necessary to recognize that in these matters, by the will of the Lord and under the appearance of present events, a certain foretelling of future things was taking place.

**Question.** What is meant by: “And behold, a vine was before me, and behold, three branches were on the vine” (Gen. 40:10)?

**Answer.** Under the threefold mention of the branches, three shoots or branches are indicated.

## IN EXODUS

**Question.** God speaks to Abraham, saying that Israel’s sons would return from the land of Egypt in the fourth generation (Gen. 15:16). How, then, does Moses later write: “But in the fifth generation the sons of Israel went up from the land of Egypt”?

**Answer.** If you seek the genealogy according to the tribe of Levi, you will count four generations in the succession of sons. If the order of the tribe of Judah is reviewed, you will find the succession of five generations. Nevertheless, in Hebrew, as the edition of Aquila, that most careful translator, indicates, it does not read, “In the fifth generation they went up,” but: “Armed, the sons of Israel went up from the land of Egypt” (Exod. 13:18).

**Question.** We frequently read in Scripture: “And the Lord said.” How should this speaking of the Lord be understood?

**Answer.** The Lord is said to speak or talk whenever he makes a sound of words reach the ears of the saints in an articulated form, though it is often not heard by others; or when God speaks through the appearance of whatever body he has assumed; or when someone is instructed by the warning or revelation of a nocturnal vision; or, certainly, when the Lord inspires the hearts of the saints to do what he wishes to be done, in accordance with: “I will hear what the Lord God speaks within me” (Ps. 84:9).

**Question.** The Lord says to Moses: “You shall see my posterior parts” (Exod. 33:23). What should be understood here?

**Answer.** He would see, either in the spirit or in his descendants, the latter works of God that were to be revealed in Christ in the final times.

**Question.** What answer should be given to those who ask why God gave the Law through Moses to only one nation, and why he gave it only after so many ages of the world had already passed?

[Col. 0780A] **Answer.** That Law was not given only to the Jews, since the law that arises naturally in all nations through the establishment of natural law is also confirmed by the Apostle, who says: “When Gentiles, who do not have the law, by nature do what the law requires, these, though they do not have the law, are a law to themselves. They show the work of the law written in their hearts” (Rom. 2:14–15). Therefore the Lord did not gather the law of innocence into ten words too late, since its origin, implanted in human hearts, had preceded it. Nor did he inscribe late on tablets of stone what he had already engraved on the pages of the heart. For before this Law of Moses, nature had its own law, by which it was readily possible both to recognize and therefore love God, the author of the world and of life, and to maintain justice and love toward one’s neighbor. “On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets.” (Matt. 22:40.)

They also already knew the following: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, you also do to them; for this is the law and the prophets” (Matt. 7:12). And, to prove this by examples: before the written Law, through that law of nature, Abel is recognized as righteous (Gen. 4:4), Enoch is taken away (Gen. 5:24), Noah is chosen (Gen. 6:8), and Abraham is called the father of nations (Gen. 17:4). Therefore, the preceding law of nature made it clear that the Law of Moses had not been given too late, since through it many had already proved acceptable to God.

**Question.** Who is the finger of God by which the two tablets of the Law are said to have been written (Exod. 31:18)?

**Answer.** The finger of God is to be understood here as the Holy Spirit.

## IN LEVITICUS

**Question.** Why is honey forbidden to be offered in sacrifices (Lev. 2:11)?

**Answer.** Because, according to the inner meaning, those dissolved by the allurements of luxuries or by the sweetness of pleasures cannot share in the mysteries of God. Hence it is also commanded that the Lord’s Passover be eaten with bitterness (Exod. 12:8), because the discipline of truth must always be austere. Therefore, without any harmful honey of flattery or pleasure, we must always offer God saving sacrifices and say: “Have I then become your enemy by telling you the truth?” (Gal. 4:16.) Conversely, salt is commanded to be added to every sacrifice (Lev. 2:13), so that everything we offer for the honor and worship of Christ may always receive the salt of reason and discernment.

**Question.** What among the things offered by the people belonged specifically to the use of the priests, and what to the Levites?

**Answer.** The firstfruits of crops and of other things were assigned to the priests, while tithes were assigned to the Levites. From these tithes, however, a tenth was owed to the priests (Num. 18:19, 21, 26).

**Question.** Everything God created is very good (Gen. 1:31). How, then, are certain animals called unclean in the Law (Lev. 11)?

**Answer.** To say nothing of the other points that can be made from this, they were called unclean with respect to eating, not with respect to creation. Their use as food was forbidden by the divine Law on account of certain figures.

[Col. 0781A] **Question.** Since clean and unclean animals were distinguished by the divine Law through Moses, how is it that even before the Flood the animals that were to be received into the ark are called clean and unclean (Gen. 7:8)?

**Answer.** Moses, inspired by the Holy Spirit, is the writer and author of the Pentateuch. Since the distinction between clean and unclean animals was to be set forth in Leviticus, in Genesis also—because the same author composed both books—he called the animals by the same terms, “unclean.”

**Question.** What should we abandon from the Old Testament, and what should we observe?

**Answer.** We should observe the commandments that concern the correction of life and conduct. We should abandon the ceremonies and rites of sacrifices, which at that time presented figures and a shadow of future realities.

[Col. 0781B] **Question.** What shall we answer those who object that, after rejecting the ancient sacrifices, God took pleasure in new ones? They maintain that nothing is corrected unless it is thought to have been done wrongly.

**Answer.** This is a broad question, but we shall answer briefly as necessity requires: God cannot therefore be considered changeable simply because these things were changed according to the appropriateness of the times. The year also varies according to its seasons, and the span of life according to its ages. Yet the reason of divine providence that established these things does not thereby vary. Nor does the principle of agriculture change if a farmer orders one thing to be done in summer and another in winter in the cultivation of the field. It is not that the one who acts appears different from himself, but that the time in which he acts is different.

God therefore commanded what was suitable to each particular time. Thus, in the matter of sacrifices as well, he commanded not for his own pleasure but, as with the other things, for human benefit. Hence the Lord is true, because he has no need of our goods (Ps. 16:2). But this very change in the sacraments, so that it should not be thought to have been adopted as something new and sudden, had long before been foretold by prophetic and divine utterances, in which it is said: “I will not accept calves from your house, nor goats from your flocks” (Ps. 50:9).

Finally, to conclude briefly: God willed different sacrifices to be offered because Christ had to be foretold by some sacraments when he was still to come, and proclaimed by others when he had come.

## IN NUMBERS

[Col. 0781D] **Question.** What are we to make of the fact that that gentile Balaam is shown by the trustworthy history of Scripture to have prophesied (Num. 24:17)?

**Answer.** It was so that the matter might become known in many ways, since, when it was proclaimed everywhere, it was announced even through unbelievers. And it was so that a sign might be given to the nations through a prophet from the nations, for the nations that would believe. For Elihu also, in the book of Job, undoubtedly foretold certain future things (Job 32:5 and following); and Caiaphas prophesied in the Gospel concerning the Lord and our Savior (John 11:50).

## IN DEUTERONOMY

**Question.** Since Deuteronomy records that only seventy persons entered Egypt with Jacob (Deut. 10:22), how does the Acts of the Apostles later report that seventy-five persons entered Egypt (Acts 7:14)?

[Col. 0782A] **Answer.** It is established that, at the time when Jacob entered Egypt with Joseph and his sons Ephraim and Manasseh, there were only seventy persons. But where the number of seventy-five persons is given, the writer seems, by anticipation, to have counted also the sons and grandsons of Ephraim and Manasseh, whom the account of the divine reading shows were later born in Egypt.

**Question.** What should be said to the Jews who object with the testimony: “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree” (Deut. 21:23)?

**Answer.** The person who hangs on a tree is called accursed, but one who is guilty, not one who is innocent. The punishment of sin cannot be a curse upon innocence. For if Mordecai, having been hanged on the prepared tree (Esth. 7:9), had fulfilled the sentence of the king’s cruelty, would these people now judge him worthy of this curse? Or would they regard the Maccabees and the others, whom Scripture (2 Macc. 7) attests to have been most undeservedly afflicted by a similar death, as accursed?

Therefore our Savior, when he was about to redeem humanity from death, did not shrink from the cross any more than from death.
