Let them not make accusations over lesser matters, since in greater matters we glory in the Lord’s endurance. Nor is it surprising if he is said to have undergone the gallows, whom we also confess to have descended to the underworld: although he had no sin of his own, he nevertheless accepted the death that came from the curse of sin. For this reason he hung on the tree (Gal. 3:13), so that, by hanging on the tree, he might absolve us from the sin committed on the tree of destruction.

**Question.** How is God said to have been jealous in Deuteronomy (5:9), when no disturbance can befall God?

**Answer.** God cannot be disturbed, as you yourself say, but he is jealous with tranquil goodness, lest the soul, which owes chastity to the one God, be defiled and prostituted by many false gods.

## IN JOB

**Question.** How should we understand what Scripture mentions in Job (28:15), “gold of Ophir”?

**Answer.** Ophir is a region extending toward India; therefore the gold of that region is indicated. Others affirm that Ophir gold is extremely precious; among the Latins it is called *obryzum* [refined gold].

**Question.** What is intended by the fact that, following the custom of secular authors, we read there of the Pleiades, Orion, and Arcturus (Job 9:9)?

[Col. 0782D] **Answer.** It is not that these objects are known among the Hebrews by those names, but that, so that the meaning of these stars might be clearer among us, the translator wished to call them what usage among the nations had established. This general point should also be observed: the Apostles and apostolic men, when writing in their letters to peoples, sometimes make use of testimonies that appeared to have been widely circulated among the peoples (Titus 1:12).

**Question.** In the same book, what is meant by the statement concerning that dragon: “Even if all the ships come together, they cannot bear the skin of his tail”?

[Col. 0783A] **Answer.** The ships are called Churches. Harassed by temptations and tribulations, they will scarcely endure Antichrist at the end of the world. He rightly calls Antichrist the tail of that dragon—that is, of the devil—from whom the final persecution will come.

## IN THE BOOKS OF KINGS

**Question.** What is meant by the fact that the Lord later rejects Saul as king, although earlier he had judged him fit to be chosen for the kingdom (1 Kings 13:14)?

**Answer.** God brings forth his just and incorruptible judgment from equity, not from foreknowledge. He chooses someone (1 Kings 10:1) when he deserves it, and rejects him when he becomes unworthy of the choice. Otherwise it would by no means accord with the sacred truth and justice of God for an offense to precede the sin.

**Question.** How should we understand the fact that the Lord is often said in Scripture to repent? Thus he also says concerning Saul: “I repent that I made Saul king” (1 Kings 15:11).

**Answer.** The Lord’s “repentance” means a change in things established by him, which follows according to the changing circumstances of events or according to the arrangement of what is right. For divine arrangements must be indicated through expressions belonging to the human mind, so that they may become clearer to those who hear them.

**Question.** We read that “a wicked spirit from the Lord was suffocating Saul” (1 Kings 16:14). How can it be from the Lord if it was wicked?

[Col. 0783C] **Answer.** Because everything brought forth by the Lord the author is subject to divine power. Therefore the devil himself, although not as he now is but once created good by the Lord, and always subject to God under the dominion of the Almighty, belonged to the Lord.

**Question.** What is the meaning of the fact that, although the Lord avenges certain things here, he does not avenge everything?

**Answer.** He avenges some things so that it may be understood that he cares for human affairs. He does not avenge everything so that it may be recognized that a terrible judgment still awaits all.

**Question.** How could the Pythoness summon Samuel’s shade (1 Kings 28:12)?

**Answer.** Either the devil at that time showed a false shade to those who saw it; or, if it was genuine, we must believe that he was permitted to do only as much as was granted by the Lord’s permission. Nor is it surprising that, for certain hidden and secret reasons, or for the manifestation of trials, such things were permitted to the devil, since he both set the Savior on the pinnacle of the Temple and requested and received permission to test Job (Matt. 4:5; Job 1:11).

**Question.** Since there is no fate, how are fifteen years added to Hezekiah’s life, as though to a predetermined term, when he prayed (2 Kings 20:6)?

**Answer.** Hezekiah was indeed being pressed at the point of death, not by a decree of fate, but by God’s summons and judgment. His years of life had not previously been fixed to such an extent that they could not be understood as added through supplication.

## IN MICAH

[Col. 0784A] **Question.** How should we understand what the prophet Micah says: “Behold, the Lord goes forth from his holy place, and descends, and walks upon the heights of the earth” (Mic. 1:3)?

**Answer.** The Lord is said to descend when he shows, through unmistakable signs of most gracious mercy, that he cares for human frailty. Thus also the angels ascending and descending by that ladder of Jacob (Gen. 28:12) indicate a visitation of earthly things, not the fall of the descending angels. Likewise, men superior in righteousness are thought to descend whenever, moved by holy love, they accommodate themselves to those below.

## IN ISAIAH

[Col. 0784B] **Question.** What should be understood in the song of the prophet Isaiah when he says: “I shall sing to my beloved a song of my cousin concerning his vineyard: A vineyard was made for my beloved on a horn, the son of oil” (Isa. 5:1)?

**Answer.** Some think that this song is sung by the Holy Spirit; others, by the prophet, who likewise was not without the Holy Spirit. He sings it as a lament over his vineyard, which is the house of Israel. The Beloved is Jesus Christ. To him it was said: “You are my beloved Son” (Matt. 3:17). He also calls him his cousin because he was born from the same stock.

This vineyard, therefore, was planted for him “on a horn,” that is, in exaltation and power. He is the beloved and the son of oil because he was anointed, from which he is also called Christ; or because he shone upon the whole world like a brilliant light. In this song he calls the grape righteousness and the thorns iniquity.

**Question.** In Isaiah’s vision, when he saw the Lord seated upon a throne, what should be understood by the statement: “Seraphim stood above it; each had six wings, and each had six wings. With two they covered his face, with two they covered his feet, and with two they flew; and they cried out to one another and said: ‘Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of hosts’”?

**Answer.** In this vision the Evangelist John testifies that Isaiah saw the Lord Jesus Christ, saying: “Isaiah said this because he saw his glory and spoke of him” (John 12:41). The first question, then, is how the seraphim are said both to stand around the Lord’s throne and to fly. The prophet expresses this well in mystical language: for with God “to stand” is the same as to fly and to rise on high; the one who hastens to appear before the divine gaze will sit.

As for the indication that the seraphim cover their faces with their wings, this is because neither any human being nor any creature can contemplate the light of the divine majesty as it truly is. They therefore cover their faces and feet because what occurred before the world and what will occur after the world are hidden from us. The wings of the seraphim also indicate the swiftness of divine service. They have six wings each because we see only those things in the world that were made in six days. Their crying out to one another and saying, “Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of hosts,” reveals one divinity in the mystery of the Trinity.

**Question.** What should be said to those who ask us: “What did the Jews do if they could not believe? For it was necessary that the word of the prophet Isaiah be fulfilled, when he says: ‘He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, lest they see with their eyes, understand with their heart, and be converted, and I heal them’” (Isa. 6:10)?

**Answer.** The prophet foretold this because God foreknew that it would happen. For God, to whom sin cannot be pleasing, cannot compel anyone to sin. In these matters, therefore, divine predestination is not to be understood, but foreknowledge.

It is written about this in the Gospel: “Therefore they could not believe, because Isaiah said again: ‘He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart,’” and so forth (John 12:39–40). “They could not believe” is said in the same way that we often say that we cannot do something because we do not wish to. And concerning Pharaoh it is written: “For this very purpose I raised you up, to show my power in you” (Exod. 9:16). He did not say, “For this purpose I made you, so that you would be such,” but, “For this purpose I chose and raised you up,” when he had already made himself such.

Thus here too their eyes are said to have been blinded and their heart hardened because they had already made themselves worthy of this blindness. The Lord blinds and hardens the sinner by abandoning him and withholding his help. If this meaning of so profound a question is insufficient for anyone, let him tremble with me and say: “The judgments of the Lord are a great abyss” (Ps. 36:6), because God’s judgments are always just, but frequently hidden.

[Col. 0785C] **Question.** What is meant by what is written: “As a bridegroom he placed a headdress upon me, and as a bride he adorned me with an ornament” (Isa. 61:10)? How can the same person be both bridegroom and bride?

**Answer.** He has passed from the head to the body. For Christ is the head, and the body is the Church (Eph. 5:23); nevertheless, it is clear that both are in Christ. This rule, which frequently occurs in the prophets and generates obscurity for the uninstructed, must be noted and retained: the prophetic order shifts from the head to the body, or from the body to the head.

**Question.** “Heaven is my throne, and the earth is the footstool of my feet” (Isa. 66:1). How can this be understood, since we believe that God is incorporeal?

[Col. 0785D] **Answer.** According to our customary manner of speaking, this appears to designate the state of one who reigns, so that God may be understood either to dwell in the heavenly realms or to have earthly things subject to him.

## IN EZEKIEL
**Question:** For what reason is it written: “On that great day of tribulation no one will be delivered except Noah, Daniel, and Job” (Ezek. 14:14), when, plainly, at the time the prophet Ezekiel said this, perhaps only Daniel was still alive, while the other two were already sleeping in peace or released from the bonds of the flesh?

**Answer:** These three holy men appear to signify three classes of human beings who are promised deliverance from dangers on that great day of tribulation. In Noah, the governors of the Church are prefigured; in Daniel, those who pursue holiness and continence; in Job, married persons who love righteousness.

**Question:** What does that saying in the prophet mean: “I will take the stony heart from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh” (Ezek. 11:19; 36:26)?

**Answer:** By the image of stone he demonstrates a hard and disobedient heart; by the image of flesh he shows a tender and teachable heart, one capable of receiving the compunction that is imparted.

## IN THE BOOKS OF CHRONICLES

**Question:** What is meant by what is written in Chronicles: “Who dwelt in Jerusalem in the second” (2 Kings 22:14)?

**Answer:** “In the second,” that is, in the second section. Hezekiah made a second wall around Jerusalem, and his son Manasseh a third. Therefore she of whom it is written dwelt in the second part of the city.

**Question:** Where should we believe the ark of the Lord, in which were the two tablets of the Testament, was taken?

**Answer:** We read in Chronicles that Josiah, king of Judah, when he was celebrating the Passover for the Lord in Jerusalem, said to the Levites: “Put the ark in the sanctuary of the temple which Solomon, son of David, king of Israel, built. You shall no longer carry it” (2 Chron. 35:3). Some wish this passage to be understood as meaning that Josiah, foreseeing the captivity, arranged for the Lord’s ark to be hidden in some secure place.

**Question:** What is the difference between a burnt offering and a sacrifice?

**Answer:** In sacrifices the priests ate a portion; a burnt offering, however, was a whole and complete victim, because it was entirely given to the fire in the offering of sacrifice. Peace offerings were also called sacrifices, and the people customarily ate of them.

## IN THE BOOK OF PSALMS

**Question:** Since the first psalm distinguishes the impious man, the sinner, and the heretic in its opening verses, what is the meaning of the conclusion at the end of the psalm, where it says: “Therefore the impious do not rise in judgment” (Ps. 1:5)?

**Answer:** The beginning of this psalm concerns the distinction of merit, and its conclusion the distinction of judgment. It shows that every human being will undoubtedly rise: the righteous, in order to judge; the sinner, in order to be judged; and the impious, in order to be punished. For one who has already been judged will not then be judged again, according to what is written: “Whoever does not believe has already been judged” (John 3:18).

**Question:** Since passion cannot be attributed to God, what does it mean when Scripture often speaks of God’s anger and fury (Ps. 6:2)?

**Answer:** It is the custom of Scripture to use “anger” for vengeance. It is anger according to human terminology, vengeance according to God, and fury according to the disposition of the one who suffers, not according to the justice of the judge. Hence also the saying in the prophet: “The Lord creates evils” (Isa. 45:7). Evils, therefore, are so called according to the feeling of the one who endures them, not according to the equity of the one who decrees them.

**Question:** What is meant by what is frequently inscribed in the titles of the psalms: “For the end, a psalm of David” (Pss. 4, 5, 6, and others)?

**Answer:** It means either that the psalms look toward the promise of good things at the end of the world, or that we attain in Christ—whom we confess to have come at the end—what the Jews at the beginning believed they could obtain.

**Question:** How should we understand what is written: “The utterances of the Lord are pure utterances, silver tested by fire, proved in the earth, purified sevenfold” (Ps. 12:7)?

**Answer:** The utterances of the Lord are called pure because they have not been adulterated by any falsehood; and, corresponding to silver tested by a sevenfold fire, spirits are cleansed by fire.

**Question:** “I will not gather their assemblies from bloods” (Ps. 16:4): since Latin would plainly have sounded more natural with *de sanguine*, “from blood,” for what reason is *sanguinibus*, “from bloods,” written contrary to the rule of Latin?

**Answer:** In Greek, αἱμάτων (*haimatōn*) is read in the plural, signifying “blood.” The translator expressed the force of this usage in Latin as well by employing the plural.

**Question:** Since Psalm 16:10 says, “You will not permit your holy one to see corruption,” how is it that another psalm says: “What profit is there in my blood, when I descend into corruption?” (Ps. 30:10)?

**Answer:** The Savior declares through the prophet’s voice that he descends into corruption when he is pierced by the penetration of the nails that fasten him. Again, the Lord did not allow his holy one to see corruption, because Christ forestalled the corruption of the flesh by a swift resurrection.

**Question:** What does the prophet mean when he says of his enemies: “They have enclosed their fat” (Ps. 17:10)?

**Answer:** The fat of the impious is enclosed when, fattened in understanding and made thick by iniquity, they depart either from righteousness or from God’s commandments. Therefore he says elsewhere: “Their iniquity will go forth from their fatness” (Ps. 73:7). Manna, however—that is, heavenly food—is fine and suited to the nourishment of those who are vigorous in the subtlety of their understanding.

**Question:** What should we understand by what is written: “Their belly has been filled from your hidden things; they have been satisfied with swine’s flesh, and they have left what remained for their little ones” (Ps. 17:14)?

**Answer:** Above, he asked that the Jews be separated from the few—that is, from the righteous—because “many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 20:16). Now he says that these same people, first instructed by the hidden things of the divine law, were later filled with their swine’s flesh—that is, with the uncleanness of their doctrines—when they denied Christ, and that they also transmitted the same impiety to their descendants.

**Question:** How should we understand: “Day pours forth the word to day, and night gives knowledge to night” (Ps. 19:3)?

**Answer:** Day pours forth the word to day when the apostles announce the Savior to believers. Night gives knowledge to night when Judas pours the teaching of a perverse understanding into the Jews. Or certainly, day pours forth the word to day and night gives knowledge to night when, every day and night, the word and knowledge are spread through the proclamation of the faithful.

**Question:** “Your rod and your staff, they themselves have comforted me” (Ps. 23:4): what distinction is intended here?

**Answer:** Correction is signified by the rod, consolation by the staff.

**Question:** Since animals are not without sensation, how does the psalm say: “Do not become like the horse and the mule, in which there is no understanding” (Ps. 32:9)?

**Answer:** Because animals possess sensation, whereas human beings possess understanding.

**Question:** Since God does not care for beasts, just as he does not care for oxen (1 Cor. 9:9), how does the psalm say: “And you will save beasts, O Lord” (Ps. 36:7)?

**Answer:** He calls those capable of reason “human beings,” and those without reason “beasts.” He confirms that the former are to be saved through a present conversion, and the latter through a future conversion.

**Question:** How should we understand what is written: “Spare me, that I may recover before I depart and exist no more” (Ps. 39:14)?

**Answer:** The meaning is made clear by the preceding verses. Above he had said: “For I am a sojourner with you and a pilgrim, like all my fathers.” “Spare me, that I may recover before I depart and exist no more” means, by implication, “before I depart as a pilgrim,” as he said earlier. Otherwise, it is clear that he will exist, since by calling himself a pilgrim above he declares that he has a homeland in which he will be.

**Question:** What does the saying in the psalm indicate: “In the head of the book it is written concerning me” (Ps. 40:8)?

**Answer:** This is said in the person of the Savior, concerning whom it is written: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1:1)—that is, in the Son. Or certainly it refers to: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1).

**Question:** “Deep calls to deep in the voice of your cataracts” (Ps. 42:8): how should this be understood?

**Answer:** The depth of the divine Scriptures is rightly called “the deep.” Therefore deep calls to deep in the voice of the cataracts when the Old Testament announces the New, or the New Testament calls the Old to bear witness in the voices of the prophets.

**Question:** What should be understood from what is written: “In place of your fathers sons have been born to you” (Ps. 45:17)?

**Answer:** It means that, through the succession of times, apostles or evangelists have been given in place of patriarchs or prophets.

**Question:** “A brother does not redeem; a man will redeem” (Ps. 49:8): what should we think about this?

**Answer:** What Moses did not redeem, Christ will redeem.

**Question:** How should we understand what David cries out to the Lord, saying: “Against you alone I have sinned” (Ps. 51:6)?

**Answer:** Sin is committed against God alone because he alone is without sin. Thus, when he is judged, he is nevertheless shown to be righteous—that is, either Christ in his passion, or according to what the prophet says: “Come, and let us be judged,” says the Lord.

**Question:** “Men of blood and deceit will not halve their days” (Ps. 55:24): what should we understand here?

**Answer:** Those who are seized by premature death do not complete half their days. By this reasoning we can also understand: “Do not take me away in the midst of my days” (Ps. 102:25). Alternatively, they do not complete their days because they do not devote even a portion of their life to satisfying God.

**Question:** What does the inner sense convey concerning what is written: “Before your thorns produce the bramble” (Ps. 58:10)?

**Answer:** It means: before your sins consume you.

**Question:** How does the righteous man wash his hands in the blood of sinners (Ps. 58:11)?

**Answer:** This occurs when vengeance is inflicted upon the impious, without the saints bringing it about; and after the crimes and destruction of sinners, the life and works of the righteous shine more brightly.

**Question:** How should we understand what is written in the psalm: “Do not have mercy on all who work iniquity” (Ps. 59:6)?

**Answer:** This is said less in the spirit of one pronouncing a curse than of one desiring the correction and amendment of sinners: namely, that, corrected in the present life, they should not abuse divine patience until the future severity of punishments.

**Question:** “God has spoken once; I have heard these two things” (Ps. 62:12): what should be understood here?

**Answer:** Here “once” does not refer to number but to firmness. What are the two things that belong to the Lord? That he can do all things and that he wills to show mercy. Alternatively: “God has spoken once,” that is, in the Law. For he commanded nothing different in the Gospel, since he said: “I have not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it” (Matt. 5:17).

**Question:** What is meant by what is written: “We passed through fire and water, and you brought us into refreshment” (Ps. 66:12)?

**Answer:** Fire and water signify persecution and martyrdom. Some think that water here should be understood as baptism, and fire as the Holy Spirit, who, when poured out, burns away sins like fire. Hence it is written: “The Lord your God is a consuming fire” (Deut. 4:24).

**Question:** What does the saying mean: “Make a way for him who ascends over the setting sun; the Lord is his name” (Ps. 68:5)?

**Answer:** Prepare a way of good works for him who has overcome the setting of the sun by conquering death.

**Question:** “You will set apart, O God, a voluntary rain for your inheritance, and it was weakened; but you perfected it: your animals will dwell in it” (Ps. 68:10): what is the meaning of this passage?

**Answer:** Literally, the rain here is manna; according to the allegorical sense, it signifies the commandments. Although those commandments, or the Law, may seem weakened by the transgressions of the Jews, they are shown to have been completed by the grace of the Gospel. In this inheritance now the animals—that is, the nations—dwell and abide.

**Question:** What interpretation is contained in what we read: “If you sleep among the midst of the lots, the wings of the dove are silvered, and the hind parts of its back are like the appearance of gold” (Ps. 68:14)?

**Answer:** In this passage the prophet prays concerning the apostles that they may persevere to the end, believing in the two Testaments. The dove signifies the Holy Spirit; its hind parts, a more hidden interpretation. Silver signifies the shining historical sense of the Scriptures, while gold signifies the inner or more precious sense.

**Question:** The Lord said: “I will turn back from Bashan; I will turn back into the depth of the sea, so that your foot may be dipped in blood, the tongue of your dogs from the enemies, from him” (Ps. 68:23–24): what interpretation should we follow here?

**Answer:** *Bashan* means “confusion” in Latin. Therefore the Lord turns us away from the confusion that is in his cross. On that cross he dipped his foot in blood, while the Jews, prompted by his enemies—that is, by demons—cried out that he should be crucified. But the whole matter came from the Savior himself, because he endured all these things of his own will.

**Question:** Whom should we understand by the princes of Zebulun and the princes of Naphtali (Ps. 68:28)?

**Answer:** The apostles Peter or Andrew, who were called from those same tribes. Likewise, above, the apostle Paul should be understood under the name Benjamin.

**Question:** What does the saying indicate: “They set up their signs as signs, and they did not know, as in the way, above at the summit” (Ps. 74:5)?

**Answer:** The Babylonians, made insolent by victory, displayed their standards in the temple of God just as standards are customarily set up on triumphal arches and at the entrances of gates.

**Question:** What is meant by what is written: “But God our king before the ages worked salvation in the midst of the earth” (Ps. 74:12)?

**Answer:** He means Judea, in which Christ liberated the world through the cross; some think that it should be called the navel of the earth. Alternatively, “he worked salvation in the midst of the earth” means in the virginal womb.

**Question:** What do we read here: “For the cup in the hand of the Lord is full of unmixed wine mingled; he inclined from this to that; nevertheless its dregs have not been emptied” (Ps. 75:9)?

**Answer:** The Lord’s cup is mingled with mercy and judgment. It is inclined from this to that when, through divine severity, there is a transition from mercy to judgment. Its dregs are not emptied because the final judgment is still being reserved.

**Question:** What is signified by what is written: “And the remnants of thoughts will keep feast for you” (Ps. 76:11)?

**Answer:** The passage beautifully shows that God rejoices in purity of mind as in a kind of festival.

**Question:** “The voice of your thunder is in the wheel” (Ps. 77:19): what should we understand here?

**Answer:** By “the wheel” he means the orb of the earth, because thunderclaps carry their rumbling within the wheel of that same orb.

**Question:** What should be understood by what is written: “And he struck his enemies on their backsides” (Ps. 78:66)?

**Answer:** According to the literal sense, the passage recalls the tumors with which the Philistines were struck on their backsides. According to the inner sense, God’s enemies are struck on their backsides when they are punished at the final judgment of the Lord.

**Question:** Whom does he signify when he says: “The boar from the forest has ravaged it, and the solitary wild beast has devoured it” (Ps. 80:14)?

**Answer:** By the boar, some say, he wishes Vespasian to be understood, since he devastated the Jews in war. By the solitary wild beast, Titus, Vespasian’s son, who consumed Jerusalem by his assault.

**Question:** We read in the psalm: “Israel, if you listen to me, there will be no new god among you” (Ps. 81:9). How should we understand this?

**Answer:** He declares that idols or the Antichrist must be rejected. Christ, however, was not a new god, although he shone upon the world in our times through the flesh. For “in the beginning the Word was with God, and the Word was God,” himself creating humanity in the likeness of God (John 1:1; Gen. 1:26); and he appeared continually, at different times, to Abraham and to our fathers (Gen. 18:1).

**Question:** How should we understand what the psalm says: “God stood in the assembly of gods” (Ps. 82:1)?

**Answer:** That is, in the assembly of the saints. Our Lord has granted his saints participation not only in his kingdom but also in his name. Hence he says to Moses: “I have appointed you as a god to Pharaoh” (Exod. 7:1). They are therefore called by the name of God because they are also called sons of God. Nor is it surprising, in view of that ineffable indulgence of divine kindness, if he wished a human being to be called god, since God himself has been called man.

**Question:** What should we understand here: “Righteousness and peace have kissed one another” (Ps. 85:11)?

**Answer:** It means that the Law and grace have been joined through our mediator, the Lord Jesus Christ, “who made both one” (Eph. 2:14).

**Question:** How should we understand what we read: “The Lord loves the gates of Zion above all the tents of Jacob” (Ps. 87:2)?

**Answer:** It means that the Lord has preferred the fortifications of the Church to the shelters of the synagogue.

**Question:** “A man will say, ‘Mother Zion’; and a man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her” (Ps. 87:5): what interpretation should we follow?

**Answer:** Some wish “Mother Zion” to signify Mary, in whom the man Christ was born, he who was also the creator of his mother. It should nevertheless be known that it is better, and truer according to the Hebrew, to say: “Will a man say, ‘Zion’? And was a man born in her? And did the Most High himself found her?” The meaning is: Who among human beings could announce this? Just as in the saying: “Or to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isa. 53:1). Thus he says that no human being could announce to her that Zion would be saved in the man who was born in her. He himself is the Most High man who founded her. It should also be noted that the Son is called “the Most High.”

**Question:** What should be understood where it is written: “I became like a man without help, free among the dead” (Ps. 88:5)?

**Answer:** Christ was indeed free among the dead, because he appeared among sinners without sin.

**Question:** What is that land of forgetfulness of which it is said: “Will your wonders be known in darkness, and your righteousness in the land of forgetfulness?” (Ps. 88:13)?

**Answer:** The flesh of the impious, abandoned by the Lord, is most rightly called the land of forgetfulness. Alternatively, the land of forgetfulness may also be understood in the saying: “For there is no one in death who remembers you; and in hell, who will confess to you?” (Ps. 6:6).

**Question:** How is the youth of the eagle renewed, according to what we read: “Your youth will be renewed like that of the eagle” (Ps. 103:5)?

**Answer:** Eagles are said, through the force of extreme old age, to become featherless; when carried back to the nest, they are fed in turn by their young until, after the decay of old age has been rubbed away, they recover the use of flight with their feathers. According to the allegorical sense, our youth is renewed either through baptism or through the resurrection.

**Question:** “The deep, like a garment, is its covering” (Ps. 104:6): what interpretation should we follow?

**Answer:** Many wrongly think that the deep is here called God’s garment, whereas the order of the preceding verses itself makes clear that it should rather be called the garment of the earth, since the earth itself is covered by the deep as though enveloped in a kind of cloak.

**Question:** How do waters stand above the mountains? For it is written: “Above the mountains the waters will stand.”

**Answer:** Certainly, when clouds full of water hang over the mountains, or when waves are raised in the sea like mountains.

**Question:** What should we understand by what we read: “This dragon, whom you formed to play with him” (Ps. 104:26)?

**Answer:** This dragon is the devil, but he was formed by the Lord before, through the prompting of voluntary wickedness, he passed into the name of devil. The prophet Isaiah describes him as being played with by little children (Isa. 11:7).

**Question:** How should we understand what is written: “Iron passed through his soul” (Ps. 105:18)?

**Answer:** Christ is most clearly signified here, since by rising again he overcame the pain and torment of the nails that afflicted him. “Iron” may also be understood as the tribulation of harsh necessity, because he said “soul.” At times, however, Scripture uses “soul” for the present life, as in the Gospel: “Is not the soul more than food?” (Matt. 6:25).

**Question:** What is the difference between a psalm and a song?

**Answer:** Psalms are so called from the psalter, whereas a song is produced by the voice; and a song is understood with reference to knowledge, while a psalm is understood with reference to action. A psalm therefore pertains to practical activity—that is, to *praxis*—whereas a song pertains to theory, that is, to contemplation.

**Question:** “The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent” (Ps. 110:4): how has the Lord sworn?

**Answer:** For the Lord to swear is to promise immutably. Thus this change of expression is rightly used, because his promise possesses the firmness of an oath.

**Question:** What does the saying indicate: “He drank from the torrent on the way; therefore he will lift up his head” (Ps. 110:7)?

**Answer:** This should be referred to the person of Christ, because he drank from the torrent—that is, from suffering—on the way, that is, in the world. Therefore God, exalting his head, gave him the name that is above every name (Phil. 2:9; Ps. 105 and following).

**Question:** For what reason are those fifteen psalms prefaced with the title “A Song of Ascents”?

**Answer:** As the historical account shows, people formerly ascended to the temple by fifteen steps. Therefore these fifteen psalms are marked by the inscription “Song of Ascents,” because through certain stages of progress they lead us upward to the heights of spiritual realities.

**Question:** “The sharp arrows of the mighty one, with destructive coals” (Ps. 120:4): what is the meaning of this verse?

**Answer:** The arrows of the mighty one are the words of the Lord, which pierce our hearts with his charity. The destructive coals are those that dissolve sins, according to the coal of the prophet Isaiah (Isa. 6:6), which was brought to his lips to cleanse the faults he had contracted either by speaking or by remaining silent through fear.

**Question:** What is meant by what is written: “Behold, he will neither slumber nor sleep who guards Israel” (Ps. 121:4)?

**Answer:** In Scripture the Lord is sometimes said to sleep when, rather, faith in us is asleep and he leaves the unbeliever to slumber. But he does not fail those who seek him, nor does he know how to sleep for those who keep watch.

**Question:** We read in the psalm concerning Jerusalem: “Its participation is in the same thing” (Ps. 122:3). What interpretation should we follow?

**Answer:** It means that different parts constitute one city, or that different members form one body of the Lord.

**Question:** What should we understand by what is written: “Perhaps our soul would have passed through an immense water” (Ps. 124:5)?

**Answer:** In Greek it is written ἅρα (*ara*), which is more clearly translated in Latin as *putas*, “do you suppose?” The meaning is therefore: “Do you suppose our soul would have passed through an immense water, unless the Lord had been with us?”

**Question:** What is meant by what is written: “Turn back our captivity, O Lord, like a torrent in the South” (Ps. 126:4)?

**Answer:** It is the voice of a rejoicing soul returning from the bonds of vices to freedom and conversion. It asks that, through the inspiration of divine mercy, it may be released from the captivity of sins just as torrents bound by ice are released by the warmth of the South.

**Question:** How should we understand: “Behold, the inheritance of the Lord: sons are the reward, the fruit of the womb; like arrows in the hand of the mighty, so are the sons of those who have been shaken” (Ps. 127:3–4)?

**Answer:** The prophet shows that he is speaking there of future things, since after that sitting he declares the time of rising. Later, after saying that the Lord will give sleep to his beloved, he shows what that resurrection of the saints will be, when he says: “Behold, the inheritance of the Lord: sons are the reward, the fruit of the womb.” The Lord’s inheritance, therefore, consists in sons, whom he has obtained as the reward of the fruit of the womb, because the Savior is the fruit of the womb; his reward is that the nations should be his inheritance, since through faith he generates them as sons.

The apostles are rightly called arrows: traversing the orb of the earth as though in flight, they pierced the hearts of unbelievers with their teaching. The prophet very aptly designates them as “sons of those who have been shaken,” that is, of the prophets. For when the prophets are shaken out in their prophecy, what else is revealed in them except the apostles? Since apostles were generated when the prophets had been shaken out, they are rightly called the sons of those who were shaken out.

**Question:** What do we read in the saying: “As a weaned child upon his mother, so you repay my soul” (Ps. 131:2)?

**Answer:** The weaning of our soul occurs when, by the maturity of understanding, it is raised from the ignorance of infancy to the perfect nourishment of life. Therefore he had said above: “If I did not think humbly,” that is, if I thought about humble and earthly things, “but raised my soul,” that is, if I directed my mind toward heavenly things: “let this be my recompense,” that the completion of understanding may overtake my soul.

**Question:** “Blessed is he who will repay you with what you repaid us” (Ps. 137:8): who should be understood here?

**Answer:** This psalm may be understood both of the captivity of the Jews when they were led away to Babylon and of sinners who, expelled from the Church, are handed over to shame. According to the historical sense, as some think, King Cyrus is signified here, since after Babylon had been overthrown he restored this restitution and raged there with complete destruction even against its little ones. According to the inner sense, the one who repays Babylon in kind is he who takes captive the one that had previously held itself captive under the law of sin, and brings forth the beginnings of vices upon the rock, which is Christ.

**Question:** Scripture often says: “I will confess to you, O Lord.” How should this be understood?

**Answer:** Confession does not always seem to signify repentance. For *I will confess* is sometimes used for “I will praise,” or “I will give thanks,” or “I will glorify the Lord.”

**Question:** “Your eyes saw my imperfect state, and in your book all will be written” (Ps. 139:16): what is signified here?

**Answer:** The eyes of the Lord see our imperfect state because God knows a human being even before he is formed. Alternatively, the eyes of God see our imperfection because he observes our thoughts even before they are completed. “All will be written in his book” because no human beings are born without his will, or because all our intentions are fully recorded with him. The passage continues: “By day they will be completed, and no one will be among them.” “By day,” that is, by Christ, they will be filled, and apart from Christ no one will be in them; those who are filled with God cannot receive what is not of God.

**Question:** Who are the young ravens of which it is written: “And the young ravens that call upon him” (Ps. 147:9)?

**Answer:** He signifies faithful children begotten from unbelievers.

**Question:** What is indicated by what we read: “Who will stand before his cold?” (Ps. 147:17)?

**Answer:** Through this cold he shows temptation.

**Question:** For what reason are those two-edged swords of the saints so called, of which it is written: “And two-edged swords in their hands” (Ps. 149:6)?

**Answer:** They are called two-edged swords because in judgment they can punish body and soul simultaneously. Alternatively, because they punish both by the penalty of present punishment and by fear of the future one. Hence the song in the same psalm: “Sing to the Lord a new song” (v. 1), since those believed to be the refuse of the world will judge nations and kings.

## IN THE PROVERBS OF SOLOMON

**Question:** “Let the stag of friendship and the young one of graces converse with you” (Prov. 5:19): what should we understand here?

**Answer:** Some think that the stag of friendship should here be understood as Christ, the teacher of all love and charity. The young one of graces signifies the Holy Spirit, who is the distributor of all graces, that is, spiritual gifts. We are therefore admonished by this passage always to seek the consolations of Christ or of the Holy Spirit.

**Question:** What is meant by what is written: “The righteous man falls seven times and rises again” (Prov. 24:16)?

**Answer:** He falls either in speech or in thought when he slips, or certainly within the grace of the sevenfold Spirit when he sins. Some affirm that “seven times” is said because of the seven days through which the course of human life revolves, since the course of this life cannot be without sin.

## IN ECCLESIASTES

**Question:** What do we read in Ecclesiastes: “The almond tree will blossom, the locust will grow fat, and the caper will be scattered, because the human being will go to the house of his eternity” (Eccl. 12:5)?

**Answer:** They hand down that these expressions signify the members of the human body. In the blossom of the almond tree he shows white hair; in the fattening of the locust, the swelling of the feet; and in the scattering of the caper, the cooling of desire. When these things come upon an old man at the end of life, then he must return to the earth, as though to the house of his eternity. Nevertheless, this house of eternity may also rightly be understood as that future land of which it is written: “I will please the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 116:9).

## IN THE SONG OF SONGS

**Question:** What is meant by what is written concerning the Church: “I am dark and beautiful, daughter of Jerusalem” (Song 1:4)? If she is dark, how is she beautiful?

**Answer:** Before her self-examination, the Church is divided according to the diversity of those who belong to her: she is beautiful in the saints and dark in sinners. Thus Scripture sometimes calls Jerusalem a holy city (Matt. 4:5), and sometimes a sinful one (Matt. 24:37).

**Question:** What is meant by the name “cousin” in the Song of Songs?

**Answer:** The Church, in whose name those words are spoken there to the Savior, calls Christ “cousin,” because he is the son of the synagogue. And because some have wished the Church to be understood as the sister of the synagogue in the saints among us, Christ is therefore called, according to a certain expression of Scripture, both the Church’s cousin and her bridegroom.

## CHAPTER II  
### On the More Difficult Questions of the New Testament

## IN THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW

**Question:** For what reason are the four evangelists represented by four different kinds of animals in the prophet (Ezek. 1:5)?

**Answer:** Matthew retains the form of a man because he begins with the birth of a human being, saying: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham” (Matt. 1:1). Mark is prefigured in the form of a lion, because, like a lion, he begins with a mighty voice: “The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord” (Mark 1:3). Luke is represented by a calf because he begins from sacrifices or from the priesthood, saying: “There was in the days of Herod, king of Judea, a certain priest named Zechariah” (Luke 1:5). John is marked by an eagle because, flying upward in spirit toward heavenly things, he speaks from on high as follows: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1).

**Question:** How should we understand that the Lord Jesus Christ is called the son of David (Matt. 1:1), when he plainly was not born from Joseph, who descended from the line of David?

**Answer:** At that time the Jews, according to the Law, took close blood relatives in marriage. There is no doubt that for this reason Mary too, coming from the same tribe, descended—or rather proceeded—from the line of David, just as Joseph did. Mary’s origin is therefore indicated through Joseph’s genealogy because it is the custom of Scripture to weave the line of men rather than of women into a genealogy. Since Mary’s kinswoman, as we read, was Elizabeth (Luke 1:36), who is recorded as having been one of the daughters of Aaron (Luke 1:5), it is completely clear that in Christ, according to the flesh, the succession of both families converged: that of kings and that of priests.

**Question:** The evangelist Matthew says that Joseph was begotten from Jacob (Matt. 1:16), whereas Luke records that he was from Heli (Luke 3:23). How can this be?

**Answer:** It is because one was his father by nature and the other became his father according to the Law. Among the Jews, there was a legal custom that a surviving brother should take the wife of a deceased brother in order to raise up offspring. Jacob and Heli were therefore uterine brothers; when the elder died, the younger entered into marriage according to the Law. In recording them, Matthew traced Joseph’s ancestry through royal descent, whereas Luke derived his genealogy through priestly succession. Joseph’s natural father, however, was undoubtedly Jacob.

**Question:** Why is Mary called Joseph’s wife in the Gospel (Matt. 1:20)?

**Answer:** It is the custom of Scripture to call even betrothed women wives.

**Question:** What is meant by what we read: “He himself will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire” (Matt. 3:11)?

**Answer:** Through the Holy Spirit, either sins are burned away in us, sanctification is bestowed, or the ardor of charity is kindled for enduring sufferings. Alternatively, those baptized with the Spirit will be tested by divine judgment. Some say that the apostles were baptized with the Holy Spirit when fire appeared over them (Acts 2:3).

**Question:** How should we understand the body of that dove in which the manifest descent of the Holy Spirit upon the Savior became visible (Matt. 3:16)? Had it existed previously, or did it suddenly appear, being made for that occasion?

**Answer:** It was certainly displayed for that occasion. In order that a visible sign of the invisible Holy Spirit might be shown, one should believe that a real body of a dove was made by divine power for that moment, appeared for an hour, and then ceased to exist. When angels present themselves to human eyes, some think that they assume a body for the moment from the denser air—that is, from the air close to the earth. Moreover, they are thought to produce a voice in this way: when a blow strikes the air, it returns a sound like the palate producing words.

**Question:** The kingdom of heaven is promised to the righteous; how, then, is this also said: “For they will possess the earth” (Matt. 5:4)?

**Answer:** Because a new heaven and a new earth (Rev. 21:1) are promised to the righteous in the future, so that then, together with God like the angels, they may possess both.

**Question:** Since the Savior says that Tyre and Sidon could have repented (Matt. 11:21) if signs of divine powers had appeared among them, why were those signs not performed there, since they would have brought salvation to those who believed?

Because the Lord and Savior, in accordance with the divine dispensation, had come only for the sheep that had perished from the house of Israel (Matt. 15:24). And why had he come only for the sheep of the house of Israel? Because, among all the other nations, Israel alone had worshiped God with particular devotion. It had once been God’s own special people (Deut. 7:6), on account of the merits of Abraham (Gen. 22:18), the patriarchs, and David (Ps. 131:11). Christ had been promised specifically to them, and, descending from their stock, he assumed from them the very flesh (Rom. 1:3) in which he appeared on earth. Yet because signs of divine power were later performed among the Gentiles as well, this testimony may be understood so that when he says, “I came only,” we should supply “first”: thus both the truth of the testimony and the readiness of God’s mercy toward all may be made clearer.

**Question.** In the Gospel our Lord and Savior says, “My yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matt. 11:30); how, then, is it written in the Psalm, “Because of the words of your lips I have kept to difficult ways” (Ps. 16:4)?

**Answer.** It is indeed evident that all who wish to live devoutly in Christ suffer persecution (2 Tim. 3:12). Yet for those who love God, what is difficult in the circumstances of the present becomes light in the hope of the future.

**Question.** What should be understood in the passage where it is written: “Pray that your flight may not be in winter or on the Sabbath” (Matt. 24:20)?

**Answer.** According to the historical sense, it should be understood thus: “that your flight may not be in winter”—that is, lest the hardship of the season be added to the tribulation of flight. “That your flight may not be on the Sabbath”—that is, lest it occur on the very day on which you are accustomed to have rest and leisure. According to the higher interpretation, however, “that your flight may not be in winter or on the Sabbath” may be understood as: lest that flight find you either chilled by sins or idle with respect to good works.

**Question.** In the same Matthew (26:29) it is written: “But I say to you, from now on I will not drink of this fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new with you in the kingdom of my Father.” What interpretation should we follow here?

**Answer.** The kingdom of God, as learned interpreters explain it, is the Church. In it Christ daily drinks his own blood through his saints, as the head in his members.

**Question.** What is the reason for the statement: “From now on you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming in the clouds of heaven” (Matt. 26:64), when elsewhere it is said that they will not see him coming in the clouds of heaven except on the last day, when all the tribes of the earth will mourn and then see the Son of Man in the clouds of heaven (Matt. 24:30)?

**Answer.** Because in this first coming of the body—that is, of the Church—his coming is announced through the manifestation and splendor of signs; the other coming is that of the Head, namely Christ himself. In that coming Christ comes through his members; in this one, through himself.

## IN MARK

**Question.** What does the Gospel signify when it says: “For whoever has, to him shall be given; and whoever does not have, even what he has shall be taken away from him” (Mark 4:25)?

**Answer.** For example, if someone has faith but does not have love, he will lose even the faith that he seemed perhaps to possess. Thus the Jews, failing to understand Christ through the divine Scripture, lost even the knowledge of God that they thought they possessed; and, refusing to receive the Son, they did not have the Father either.

**Question.** The evangelist Mark indicates that the Lord was crucified at the third hour of the day (Mark 15:25); how, then, does another evangelist state that the sixth hour was when he was crucified (Luke 23:44)?

**Answer.** The former reported in his writings almost the hour at which he was truly crucified. The other, however, thought that the earlier time should be recorded, when judgment concerning him was pronounced at the Jews’ demand—as though, by anticipation in the narrative, he had been crucified at the hour at which he was ordered to be crucified. Nevertheless, in this very passion of his we must hold that the man who was assumed endured it according to his will in such a way that the Word who was in the beginning with God the Father remained inviolate and undefiled. Thus it was that which he had assumed on account of human weakness that was exposed to insult; but that which divine eternity possessed remained incorrupt.

## IN LUKE

**Question.** What does Luke’s statement about the priest Zechariah mean, that he was “of the division of Abijah” (Luke 1:5)?

**Answer.** The priests had been distributed into twenty-four courses for the service of the Temple (1 Chron. 24:7), so that each might perform the priestly office in the order of his course. In this order, therefore, Abijah held the eighth course, and the priest Zechariah belonged to that course.

**Question.** Who are those who received names in the sacred Scriptures before they were born?

**Answer.** In the New Testament, besides the Savior, we read only of John the Baptist. In the Old Testament there are four: Isaac (Gen. 17:19), Ishmael (Gen. 16:11), Solomon, or Josiah (3 Kings 13:2), who appear by their birth to be younger than they are by name.

**Question.** At the arrival of the Lord’s mother, how could John, while still without understanding in the womb, leap for joy in his mother’s womb (Luke 1:44)?

**Answer.** Some think that this occurred through the mother’s own perception or joy, so that he could even leap for joy in her inward womb. Or, if one prefers to refer it to John himself, it should be counted among the divine miracles, just as when the voice of a she-ass broke forth into the sound of speech (Num. 22:28).

**Question.** In the same Gospel, what is meant by the statement: “It happened on the Sabbath, the second-first, that as he passed through the grainfields, his disciples were plucking the ears of grain and eating them, rubbing them in their hands” (Luke 6:1)?

**Answer.** Some think that the Lord’s Day was called by this name because it appears to be second in relation to the legal observance of the Sabbath, while being first in the celebration of evangelical grace. If this seems insufficient to someone who argues that the day itself was more properly a Sabbath, because it is written concerning it, “Why are you doing what is not lawful on the Sabbaths?” (Luke 6:1), perhaps the Sabbath day may nevertheless be understood in this way: according to our observance it is now second, whereas formerly it was first according to Jewish observance. For the first day is most correctly reckoned as the Lord’s Day.

**Question.** How should we understand the vision in which the Lord was glorified after taking three disciples with him, when Luke records that it occurred after eight days, while the other evangelists say after six days (Luke 9:28; Matt. 17:1; Mark 9:1)?

**Answer.** Luke, who writes that this vision was shown to the disciples after eight days had passed since the Lord’s discourse among them, included both the day on which the Lord spoke and the day on which Jesus appeared glorified. Those who thought that six days should be specified counted only the intervening complete days and, as it were, left uncounted the partial first and last days.

**Question.** Again, in the same Gospel he says: “For from now on there will be five in one house divided, three against two and two against three; father against son and son against his father; mother against daughter and daughter against her mother; mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law and daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law” (Luke 12:52). Since he seems above to have set down five persons, why does he subsequently introduce six with the indication of the persons?

**Answer.** The mother and the mother-in-law may be understood as the same person, addressed by two names through “daughter” and “daughter-in-law.” Accordingly, the number of persons may still be seen to be five in what follows.

**Question.** In the parable of Lazarus and the rich man, how many questions arise! How can the rich man be in torment before the judgment (Luke 16:19)? How can Lazarus’s finger be mentioned (Luke 16:24)? Are there bodies in the underworld? Or does he himself desire water? Was he experiencing bodily thirst?

**Answer.** He speaks of all these things according to the emotions that he had once experienced through the needs of the body. As for the rich man’s awareness of torment before the judgment, it should be understood as corresponding to the place of custody in which he was. For those awaiting judgment, custody itself is not without torment even before the judgment. In the further point, that he saw Abraham as being in the underworld, some think the explanation is that all the saints are said to have descended into the underworld before the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, though into a place of refreshment. Others suppose that the place where Abraham was had been established in a higher region, separate from those places of the underworld; this is why the Lord says of the rich man: “Lifting up his eyes while he was in torments, he saw Abraham from afar.” They understand Abraham’s bosom to designate the repose of that region.

**Question.** How should we understand what we read: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke 17:21)?

**Answer.** In each person, according to the difference between good and evil actions, either God reigns or the devil; for the one whose will someone carries out in deed must necessarily be regarded as exercising authority over him. Thus, if some are righteous, God is said to reign in them; if they are unrighteous, the devil is. Faith may also be called the kingdom of God, since through it one goes to the kingdom, because “the righteous lives by faith”; and through it Christ dwells in the hearts of his saints (Heb. 2:4; Eph. 3:17).

**Question.** In Luke, how does the Savior say to the thief, “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43), when on that very day, according to his humanity, he was bodily on earth and his soul was in the underworld?

**Answer.** Perhaps “paradise” here may be understood as the place of the repose bestowed where the Savior shows Abraham to have been with Lazarus in the Gospel (Luke 16:22). Or it should be understood in this way: the Lord fulfilled this promise according to the effect of his divine power, since we must recognize that God is everywhere.

## IN JOHN

**Question.** The Jews state that forty-six years had been spent in building the Temple according to John’s Gospel (John 2:20). How are these years to be understood?

**Answer.** It is sufficiently clear from Scripture that Solomon built the house of the Lord in only seven years, as it says: “He built it in seven years” (1 Kings 6:38). The forty-six years are assigned to the restoration of the Temple, which took place in the days of Ezra, after the destruction of Jerusalem and the captivity of the Jews. The rebuilding itself, however, was prolonged for a long time, because the surrounding nations continually hindered the work by their attacks.

**Question.** How did the Savior lead the assumed man into heaven? Or how is heaven promised to the saints, when he says: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3:13)? Or how was he in heaven while he was still on earth?

**Answer.** According to the flesh he was on earth; according to his divinity he was not absent from heaven. Therefore the one who descended also ascended, because although he assumed a man, yet man and God—that is, Christ—are one person. And since he is the Head while the saints are members, the members must necessarily follow where the Head has gone before, so that the fullness of Christ’s body may be in heaven.

**Question.** How should we understand what is written: “For God does not give the Spirit by measure” (John 3:34)?

**Answer.** Some affirm that this should be understood specifically of the Son, because human beings, while receiving more or less than one another, appear to receive the Spirit according to measure, in accordance with the Apostle’s statement: “Having gifts that differ according to the grace given to us, whether prophecy, according to the measure of faith” (Rom. 12:6), and so forth. But to Christ, his only-begotten Son, who also gives the Spirit, the Spirit was not given by measure, because “in him dwells all the fullness of divinity” (Col. 2:9).

**Question.** The Savior says: “You go up to this feast; I am not going up to this feast” (John 7:8). How, then, is it subsequently written of him: “But when his brothers had gone up, then he also went up to the feast” (John 7:10)?

**Answer.** Truth cannot speak falsehood. Therefore Jesus did nothing other than what he had declared he would do. The Jewish feast of Booths, or Tabernacles (*Scenopegia*), did not comprise only one day, but several days of celebration, just as the feast of Passover does. Therefore, because he had said, “I am not going up to this feast,” he certainly did not go up on that particular feast day, as he had foretold. For the Gospel continues: “When he had said these things”—that is, the Savior—“he remained in Galilee.” We are to understand that although he was present during the same celebration, it was not the same day of the feast of which it is later written: “But when his brothers had gone up, then he also went up to the feast.” This feast day may also be understood figuratively as the feast to which the Savior declared that he would not ascend, in order to teach that the celebration was to be changed in himself.

**Question.** How should we understand the passage written about Jesus Christ our Savior: “No one laid hands on him, because his hour had not yet come” (John 7:30)?

**Answer.** This hour should not be understood according to the astrologers or mathematicians, but rather as the hour at which he himself willed to be crucified and to suffer. Therefore his hour had not yet come because he had not yet completed everything, because he had not yet fulfilled all the work he had undertaken, for the sake of which he had visited humanity and the earth.

**Question.** How should we understand the Savior’s statement: “When he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own things, because he is a liar and its father” (John 8:44)?

**Answer.** The Lord had earlier said to the Jews: “If God were your Father, you would surely love me”; and afterward: “You are from your father the devil, and you wish to do your father’s desires. He was a murderer from the beginning and did not stand in the truth, because there is no truth in him.” In the phrase, “When he speaks a lie,” we should supply “each one of you speaks from his own things,” because he is a liar and his father—that is, the devil. Some argue in this way: “When he speaks a lie”—that is, when the devil speaks—“he speaks from his own things, because he is a liar, and its father,” that is, the father of the lie itself, because the lie appears to have originated from him. Thus, just as God begot the Son, who is truth, so the devil begot a son, falsehood.

**Question.** How should we understand the statement: “Abraham your father rejoiced that he might see my day; he saw it and was glad” (John 8:58)?

**Answer.** Prophets were called “seers” (1 Sam. 9:9), because by the gift of the Holy Spirit they saw things hidden from others, as though they were conscious of future events. Among them, Abraham also saw Christ in the spirit.

**Question.** The Gospel says: “We know that God does not hear sinners” (John 9:31). How, then, does the Savior say elsewhere: “Everyone who asks receives” (Matt. 7:8)?

**Answer.** Some understand this passage as follows: “The one who said that sinners are not heard,” they say, “was blind and, as though his eyes had only just been treated with eye-salve, was not yet able to see the truth fully.” It is certain, however, that the ear of divine mercy is open to those who knock. It may also be understood in this way: God does not hear sinners even if they are heard when they ask for their own salvation; they are not heard in the working of signs.

**Question.** What does God and Savior mean when he says in John’s Gospel: “For judgment I came into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9:39)?

**Answer.** This is no small question, but, as necessity requires, we shall briefly present what the learned have thought about it. “So that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind”: that is, so that those who confess that they do not see and seek a physician may see, while those who think they see and do not seek a physician may remain in their blindness. Thus he said that he had come for judgment in order to distinguish the case of believers from that of unbelievers. Therefore, “so that those who do not see may see” may be understood of the Gentiles, who were to see through faith; and “those who see may become blind” may be understood of the Jews, who were blinded through their own unbelief.

**Question.** How can the Savior say, “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28), while elsewhere he says, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30)?

**Answer.** The Lord Jesus, true man just as he is true God—God from God the Father, man from his human mother—is believed to have spoken the former according to his humanity and the latter according to his divinity. In accordance with this distinction between divinity and humanity, the meaning of the other passages that express either equality with the Father or his humility will also readily become clear.

**Question.** What mystery is contained in the passage where the Lord washed the disciples’ feet (John 13:5)?

**Answer.** In that passage the curse of the heel is washed away, the curse into which the steps of our soul had fallen through the instigation of the devil (Gen. 3:15). At first our heel was exposed to his bites. But when it was said, “Behold, I have given you authority to tread upon serpents and scorpions” (Luke 10:19), that curse was abolished.

## IN THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

**Question.** (Rom. 3:5.) What is the meaning of the passage in which the Apostle begins: “But if our iniquity commends the righteousness of God, what shall we say? Is God unrighteous who inflicts wrath? I speak according to human terms. Certainly not. Otherwise, how will God judge the world? For if the truth of God has abounded through my lie to his glory, why am I still judged as a sinner, and why not”—as we are slanderously accused, and as some claim that we say—“do evil so that good may come”? Their condemnation is just.

**Answer.** This is an extremely obscure and complicated passage in the Apostle, requiring many words for its discussion and exposition; nevertheless, because our discourse must be brief, we shall compress it. Above he had said: “But God is truthful, and every human being is a liar, as it is written: ‘So that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged.’” He now adds: “But if our iniquity commends the righteousness of God, what shall we say?” Here he raises a question arising from the testimonies he had previously cited and adds: “Is God unrighteous who inflicts wrath”—that is, vengeance? “I speak according to human terms”: that is, according to human speech, since he had seemingly called God unrighteous. Or he may have spoken of God’s wrath, although passion cannot be attributed to God. “Certainly not”: that is, we must not believe it in such a way as to say that God is unrighteous, since, if these things are so, he inflicts wrath on the sinner. Otherwise, how would God judge the world, unless with perfect equity and justice?

Then follows: “For if the truth of God has abounded through my lie to his glory.” He proposes this as a refutation, not as an approval: for if God’s truth needed human falsehood, then the sinner would not be judged as a sinner, and the things slanderously said against the apostles would appear true. What, then, does he mean? Even if righteousness shines more clearly by comparison with injustice, a person nevertheless ought not to be unjust so that God may appear just. The condemnation of those who claim that we say such things is just. What things? “Let us do evil so that good may come.” The apostles were thought to say this by those who misinterpreted the apostolic statement: “Where sin abounded, grace abounded still more” (Rom. 5:20).

**Question.** What does the passage mean: “For while we were still weak, Christ died at the appointed time for the ungodly. For scarcely will anyone die for a righteous person; perhaps someone might even dare to die for a good person” (Rom. 5:6)?

**Answer.** This is what he intends to mean: He died for the ungodly, although scarcely anyone is found willing to die for a righteous person. But for the good person—that is, for Christ—perhaps someone might dare to die. Here he also modestly indicates with regard to himself that he might be able to die for Christ. Or otherwise: “Scarcely will anyone die for a righteous person.” Under the Old Covenant, in which justice is demanded by the severity of the commandments, scarcely a few martyrs were found; but under the New Testament, in which goodness is demanded by the piety of the commandments, countless martyrs have appeared.

**Question.** The Apostle says of God the Father: “But he delivered him up for us all” (Rom. 8:32)—that is, the Son. What does this signify?

**Answer.** He consented to the handing-over. For in the sacred books God is sometimes said to do things in whose execution he appears to provide endurance. There are, after all, things that God wills to be done and things that he permits to be done. He wills those things to be done that prove to be better once accomplished. But he permits worse things to occur so that the freedom of the human will may remain, and in that freedom a just recompense of merits may be displayed by divine judgment to those who pursue good or evil.

**Question.** In this same Epistle, what should be understood by what we read: “Who will bring an accusation against God’s elect? God, who justifies. Who is the one who condemns? Christ Jesus, who died, indeed who was raised, who is at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us” (Rom. 8:33)?

**Answer.** These words, in which he answers himself, should be read, as it were, *eirōnikōs*—ironically. The sense is this: Surely neither God, who justifies his elect, nor Christ, who died for them, will condemn them. Certainly not, since he also intercedes for us. This is what he means: No one will condemn the elect.

**Question.** What should we think about the passage in which the Apostle says: “For I myself was wishing to be anathema from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh, and so forth” (Rom. 9:3)?

**Answer.** “Anathema” sometimes, as here, signifies slaughter and death. Thus the Apostle here wishes to perish in the flesh so that others may be saved in the spirit. Or otherwise: Here the Apostle expressed the force of an exceedingly great love, wishing, if it were possible, to be anathema from Christ for the sake of his brothers, just as Moses, when he was entreating God on behalf of his people, said: “And now, Lord, if you will forgive their sin, forgive it; but if not, erase me from your book which you have written” (Exod. 32:31).

**Question.** He says the same concerning God: “Therefore he has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens” (Rom. 9:18). What interpretation should we follow here?

**Answer.** The heart is hardened by God when the punishment of sins is delayed.

**Question.** Again he himself declares: “What Israel was seeking it did not obtain; but the election obtained it, while the rest were blinded” (Rom. 11:7). What is the meaning of this?

**Answer.** It is not that God strikes with blindness anyone who wishes to see, since, as it is written, he wishes all to be saved (1 Tim. 2:4). Rather, those who had blinded themselves are said to have been handed over [variant: “to hand over”] in recompense for their wickedness, when he abandons them. For to hand over is the Lord’s way of leaving someone.

**Question.** How should we understand what is written: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink; for by doing this you will heap burning coals upon his head” (Rom. 12:20)?

**Answer.** This means that you will heap up the fire of remorse when you return good for evil. Or otherwise: It does not mean that the enemy should be fed with the intention that burning coals be heaped upon his head while he is being fed. Rather, when that enemy receives good for evil, if he is moved by no repentance for his wickedness, he himself instead heaps burning coals upon his own head.

**Question.** Since there is no authority except from God, as the Apostle says (Rom. 13:1), why are not all those who administer it found to receive it well?

**Answer.** Because all alike receive this life from God, yet not all live equally well.

## I TO THE CORINTHIANS

**Question.** He says: “Every sin that a person commits is outside the body; but the one who commits fornication sins against his own body” (1 Cor. 6:18). What should we think about this?

**Answer.** Other sins are committed externally through the body, whereas fornication alone is carried out in the body’s passions.

**Question.** How should the passage be understood in which it is written: “Do you not have houses in which to eat and drink? Or do you despise the Church of God and shame those who have nothing?” (1 Cor. 11:22)?

**Answer.** Among the Corinthians, as some assert, a corrupt custom had once become prevalent: they dishonored the churches everywhere with banquets at which they ate before the Lord’s offering, which they brought in at night after the meal. When the wealthy came to the Eucharist drunk, the poor were troubled by hunger. This custom, it is reported, came from the continuing superstition of the Gentiles. Hence in certain places throughout the countryside of Egypt and Syria people are also said to gather at the church on Saturday night after the meal.

**Question.** What kind of prophecy is meant by the statement: “But if all prophesy, and an unbeliever or an unlearned person enters, he is convicted by all and judged by all; the secrets of his heart become manifest” (1 Cor. 14:24)?

**Answer.** There are two kinds of prophecy: one of teaching and another of prediction. Prediction was more prevalent in former times; teaching is more prevalent in the present. “The secrets of his heart become manifest” when, as the teacher prophesies in the Church, the conscience of the listener is pierced.

**Question.** What does it mean that it is written: “He will hand over the kingdom to God the Father” (1 Cor. 15:24)?

**Answer.** He will indeed hand it over, but not in such a way that he will be deprived of it. The handing over of the kingdom is our advancement, when we shall have come to be wholly the Son’s in the Father’s kingdom.

**Question.** What is meant by the statement: “We shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed” (1 Cor. 15:51)?

**Answer.** That is, not all will be changed into glory, because resurrection and incorruption are common to everyone, whereas transformation into glory belongs properly to the righteous.

## II TO THE CORINTHIANS

**Question.** The Apostle says: “We entreat you on behalf of Christ: be reconciled to God. He made him who knew no sin to be sin for us, so that we might become the righteousness of God in him” (2 Cor. 5:20). What interpretation should we follow?

**Answer.** “Be reconciled,” he says, “to God, who made Christ an offering for sin.” If you search the Old Testament, you will find that the offering itself is called “sin.” This may also be understood in the following way: Christ was made an offering for sin because God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh.

**Question.** He says: “A thorn in my flesh was given to me, an angel of Satan, to strike me with blows” (2 Cor. 12:7). How should this be understood?

**Answer.** Some say that the Apostle was often afflicted by headache. I think it better understood in this way: he was struck by blows in those sufferings which he himself enumerated when he said: “Three times I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned,” and so forth (2 Cor. 11:25). Therefore he calls the tribulation of the flesh a “thorn in the flesh,” and he shows that the angel of Satan was the one through whom, as an instigator, he suffered such great things.

## TO THE EPHESIANS

**Question.** How should we understand what the Apostle writes: that the Lord had purposed, in the dispensation of the fullness of times, to restore in Christ all things, those in heaven and those on earth, in him (Eph. 1:10)?

**Answer.** It is truly remarkable what is now being restored in heaven. According to the opinion of some, that portion of the angels which fell with its prince is restored through the increase and fellowship of the saints, of whom it is written: “But they are like the angels in heaven” (Matt. 22:30). All things on earth are also restored when believers from the Gentiles are admitted in place of the Jews who have fallen away. Or otherwise: The things on earth are restored when we are reconciled and restored through the blood of our Mediator. The heavenly things are restored when joy concerning our salvation arises among the angels.

**Question.** What does the Apostle mean when he says of God the Father: “From whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named” (Eph. 3:15)?

**Answer.** Because although he is our first and true Father, it is from his name that others are called fathers.

**Question.** How does the Apostle say, “Honor your father and mother, which is the first commandment” (Eph. 6:2), when, according to the arrangement made by some, it is fourth in the commandments?

**Answer.** Some discuss this as follows: The three commandments above it all pertain to God, while the following seven pertain to human beings. The three that pertain to God were contained on one tablet of the Law, while the other tablet contained the commandments that pertained to human beings. Accordingly, this commandment is the first among the seven commandments that concern one’s neighbor.

Others, who affirm that this commandment is not fourth but fifth—and this is what we approve—argue as follows: The entire Decalogue, because it was written in that first Law, may rightly be called the first commandment; the order itself makes it first, followed by the other commandments in the Law.

Again, it may be understood in another way: “Honor your father and mother, which is the first commandment,” and he adds, “with a promise.” What promise? “So that it may be well with you and you may live long upon the earth” (Exod. 20:12). Therefore, among the commandments this is the first commandment that has the promise we mentioned above.

**Question.** What is meant by the statement: “Do not extinguish the Spirit” (1 Thess. 5:19)?

**Answer.** To extinguish means to drive away through works of iniquity. David says: “Do not take your Holy Spirit from me” (Ps. 50:13).

**Question.** A little later in the same Epistle it says: “May your spirit, soul, and body be preserved blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Thess. 5:23). What should be understood here?

**Answer.** Here “spirit” certainly means the Holy Spirit, of whom he had said above: “Do not extinguish the Spirit.” Although he cannot be extinguished in his own substance, he is extinguished in us when he is taken away from us.
