For his gift or grace in human beings is kindled by their virtues and extinguished by their vices.

Others assert that “spirit” here should be understood as the soul’s intellect and wisdom. Concerning this the same Apostle says elsewhere: “The Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God” (Rom. 8:16). That is, the Holy Spirit bears witness to this intellectual and spiritual part of ours that we are children of God. Elsewhere also the Apostle says: “I will sing praise with the spirit; I will sing praise also with the mind” (1 Cor. 14:15). Here he uses “spirit” for the voice and says that praise should be sung equally with voice and mind.

## TO THE COLOSSIANS

**Question.** What should be understood in the passage written to the Colossians: “If you have died with Christ to the elements of the world, why, as though you were living in the world, do you submit to regulations?” (Col. 2:20), and what follows?

**Answer.** Let us summarize, as we can, a passage wrapped in profound obscurity. He argues against those who, having become Christians from Judaism, insisted on clinging to their own ceremonies. For above he had spoken of their unacceptable observance concerning food and drink, and that their new moons and Sabbaths had set forth a shadow of things to come (Col. 2:16).

Again, in what follows, he says: “If you have died with Christ to the elements of the world, why, as though you were living in the world, do you submit to regulations?” That is, why do you judge by saying: “Do not touch, do not taste, do not handle”—things that all perish in their very use, that is, while they are being consumed—“according to the commandments and teachings of human beings”? He calls them human teachings because they understand the commandments themselves carnally, prescribing in the Law that what is forbidden must not be eaten. But, as he himself adds, this is superstition and needless humility, an affliction of the body in which the body is not spared, either through such abstinence or through circumcision.

He continues: “Not in any honor, for the satisfying of the flesh.” This, then, is what he intends to mean: All those observances, although in their practice they may seem to display some figure of wisdom, because they are thought to preserve the Law’s commandments, are nevertheless superstition. They are not directed toward any honor of God, but toward satisfying the will of a carnal observance.

## I TO TIMOTHY

**Question.** What distinction should be understood among the individual things the Apostle sets forth when he says: “Therefore, first of all, I ask that supplications, prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings be made” (1 Tim. 2:1)?

**Answer.** Supplications are made for past and present sins; prayers for obtaining what we hope for; petitions when we intervene on behalf of others; thanksgivings when we obtain what we ask for, or certainly when we render thanks and praise for God’s immense benefits.

**Question.** How should the passage be understood in which it is written: “The sins of some people are manifest, going before them to judgment, while some people are also followed by them” (1 Tim. 5:24)?

**Answer.** Above he had said that an accusation against a presbyter should not be received except on the testimony of two or three witnesses (1 Tim. 5:19). A little later he added: “The sins of some people go before them to judgment”—that is, when they are known to everyone—“while some also follow them”—that is, when they are subsequently proved in judgment.

If some think that this should rather be understood of God’s judgment, it may be interpreted as follows: The sins that each person committed here beforehand go before him to judgment; those that follow are sins for which we indeed gave the causes, but which are understood to have been completed after our departure. Such sins, then, follow us into judgment if, for example, someone to whom we had caused poverty was consumed by hunger and want after our death.

## II TO TIMOTHY

**Question.** The Apostle says: “Alexander the coppersmith showed me many evils; the Lord will repay him according to his works” (2 Tim. 4:14). And again: “The Lord will strike you, whitewashed wall” (Acts 23:3). How should these statements be understood?

He will strike you, he says, not “may he strike you”; and again, “he will repay,” not “may he repay.” Hence the words appear to have been spoken not so much in a spirit of cursing as of announcing God’s judgment and vengeance. Alternatively: if, in the exercise of the prophetic office, the prophet curses with an unwavering spirit—as in, “Let their eyes be darkened, so that they may not see” (Ps. 68:24)—he declares what was owed according to their merits. For every transgression and disobedience receives a just recompense of deed and reward (Heb. 2:2).

## TO THE HEBREWS

**Question.** How are we to understand what the Apostle says here: “By faith Jacob, when dying, blessed each of Joseph’s sons, and worshiped the top of his staff” (Heb. 11:21)?

**Answer.** By “staff” (*virga*) one must understand the meaning of a scepter; and by this summit of royal power and authority, Christ is understood to have been worshiped, since he was destined to be the head of the Hebrew kingdom.

## IN THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES

**Question.** What does the passage we read indicate: “Having a Sabbath day’s journey” (Acts 1:12), that is, one thousand paces?

**Answer.** For on the Sabbath the Jews were permitted to go as far as the Mount of Olives; or, wherever they happened to be, they presumed to have permission to walk that distance.

**Question.** How was the Holy Spirit breathed upon the apostles by the Savior before the Ascension, according to the evangelist John (John 20:22), when, according to the Acts of the Apostles, he was sent upon them after the tenth day following the Ascension (Acts 2:1)?

**Answer.** There are many gifts of the Holy Spirit’s grace, in accordance with what the Apostle says: “To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another gifts of healings in the one Spirit,” and so forth (1 Cor. 12:8). Therefore, before the Ascension they received the grace of the Holy Spirit by which they could forgive sins, baptize, and pour the Spirit of adoption into believers, in accordance with what was then said when the Savior breathed the Spirit upon them: “Whose sins you forgive, they shall be forgiven; and whose you retain, they shall be retained” (John 20:22).

But after the Ascension they received a much greater grace of the Holy Spirit in the working of miracles, the grace of healings, and the reception of various languages, in keeping with what had been promised to them on that same day: that they would be baptized with the Holy Spirit and clothed with power (Acts 1:5), by which they could preach the Gospel of Christ to all nations.

In this reception of the Holy Spirit, therefore, the apostles’ progress is demonstrated according to the distribution of the Lord’s grace, not any contradiction among the Scriptures. Alternatively, why the Holy Spirit was given twice has been excellently explained by a certain teacher, who spoke of the Spirit whom the Savior first gave here through himself and later sent from heaven, so that the love of neighbor and the love of God might be signified—love which is poured into the hearts of the saints through the Holy Spirit (Rom. 5:5), who was given for proclaiming God’s word.

Through this proclamation the apostles spread themselves throughout the regions of the world, as history relates: Bartholomew went to India; Thomas made his way to the Parthians; Matthew subdued the Ethiopians by his preaching; Andrew softened the Scythians; John corrected Asia through his divine message; Peter traveled through Cappadocia and Galatia, likewise Bithynia and Pontus and the neighboring provinces, while preaching to the Jews; and finally he came to enlighten Rome. Paul, after filling the region from Jerusalem to Illyricum with the Gospel (Rom. 15:19), subdued countless and diverse nations by his commandments as though by weapons of war.

**Question.** In the Acts of the Apostles we first read: “The men who were accompanying him”—that is, the Apostle—“stood amazed, hearing the voice but seeing no one” (Acts 9:7). How, then, does the Apostle later say: “Those who were with me saw the light, but they did not hear the voice of the one speaking with me” (Acts 22:9)?

**Answer.** Above, where they are said to have heard the voice from God, they received not an articulate voice but the unformed sound of a voice. Thus he later says that they did not hear the voice—that is, the clearly expressed meaning of the words, by which they could understand what was being uttered. Accordingly, they are reported on the one hand to have heard and on the other not to have heard because, insofar as sound is concerned, they heard; but insofar as words are concerned, they did not hear.

**Question.** Why was ordinary food previously called “common,” as though it were unclean?

**Answer.** Because what was then forbidden by God was open in common to the other peoples, who did not observe the Law’s distinctions among foods, by which the Jews claimed to be God’s portion. It was also purified when the Lord said to Peter: “What God has purified, do not call common” (Acts 10:15).

**Question.** What is meant by the passage in the Acts of the Apostles in which those twelve who had been baptized with John’s baptism are baptized by Paul (Acts 19:4)?

**Answer.** This was because they had not been baptized in the name of the Trinity. Although John’s baptism baptized people into the one who was to come, it was properly called John’s baptism. Hence those who come from heretics are not rebaptized by us if it is established that they were baptized in the name of the Trinity; only the laying on of hands is applied to those converted to the right faith, so that through it they may receive the infusion of the Holy Spirit.

## IN THE EPISTLE OF JAMES

**Question.** How can it be said, “God is not a tempter of evil, and he himself tempts no one” (Jas. 1:13), when nevertheless it is written: “The Lord your God is testing you” (Deut. 13:3)?

**Answer.** The Lord’s testing is called a proving. For he does not tempt anyone through sufferings; rather, that temptation comes from our desires, when, having been humbled, we are cast down. The temptation is from the Lord when he tests us and we are glorified. Therefore the Lord is not a tempter of evil.

## IN THE EPISTLE OF JOHN

**Question.** How does perfect love cast out fear (1 John 4:18), when it is again written: “The fear of the Lord is pure, enduring forever and ever” (Ps. 18:4)?

**Answer.** Whoever loves God certainly fears being without God. This is the fear of God that endures forever and ever. Thus this fear proceeds from perfect love of the Lord. But the other fear arises from temporal things, whose loss we often dread. The perfection of divine love casts out this fear.

**Question.** Again, in his Epistle John states: “There are three that bear witness: water, blood, and spirit” (1 John 5:8). What is indicated by this?

**Answer.** A similar passage seems to me to be the one in which he himself speaks in his Gospel about Christ’s passion, saying: “One of the soldiers opened his side with a lance, and immediately blood and water came out; and the one who saw it bore witness” (John 19:34). Earlier in the same Gospel he had said of Jesus: “He bowed his head and gave up his spirit” (John 19:30).

Accordingly, some argue as follows: water appears to indicate baptism, blood martyrdom, and the Spirit is the one who passes through martyrdom to the Lord. Many, however, understand this passage in a mystical interpretation as referring to the Trinity, since the Trinity itself in its perfection bears witness to Christ: water indicating the Father, because he himself says, “They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water” (Jer. 2:13); blood demonstrating Christ, plainly through the blood of his passion; and spirit manifesting the Holy Spirit.

These three therefore bear witness to Christ, as he himself says in the Gospel: “I am the one who bears witness concerning myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness concerning me” (John 8:18). And again: “When the Paraclete comes, whom I shall send to you—the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father—he will bear witness concerning me” (John 15:16).

The Father therefore bears witness when he says, “This is my beloved Son” (Matt. 3:17); the Son, when he says, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30); and the Holy Spirit, when it is said of him: “He saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming upon him” (Matt. 3:16).

**Question.** What does John again present in his Epistle as a sin for which one ought not to pray—that is, sin unto death (1 John 5:16)?

**Answer.** The sinner sins unto death when, throughout the course of this temporal life, he does not repent. For the same reason, the following must also be understood: “Whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come” (Matt. 12:32). A person blasphemes when, not believing at all in the divine promises or in the Holy Spirit, in whom there is forgiveness of sins, he refuses to be reconciled to God in this life through works of satisfaction.

**Question.** What does it mean when we read in the same Epistle that “the world lies in the evil one” (1 John 5:19)?

**Answer.** It does not mean that the world has been placed by God in evil, but that the vices of human beings living in the world are evil. In this way it will also become clear what is written: “Because the days are evil” (Eph. 5:16).

## IN THE APOCALYPSE

**Question.** Who are the seven spirits of God mentioned in the Apocalypse (1:4)?

**Answer.** They are those whom the prophet Isaiah also enumerates: “The spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and piety, the spirit of knowledge and truth, the spirit of the fear of God” (Isa. 11:2). Yet these signify spiritual operations. “All these things are worked by one and the same Spirit” (1 Cor. 12:11).

These matters I have presented to you at your request from the opinions of the most learned men. If, however, anyone should bring forward in the discussions of the questions mentioned above arguments that are more convincing, and should criticize the obstinacy that is customary in many people, I do not refuse to follow what is better.

# BOOK TWO

[Column 811]

## PREFACE TO SALONIUS

[Column 811C]

Since, dearest son, in the preceding book a frequent response followed upon your questions, and I fear that continual interrogations, as usually happens, may produce satiety and disgust in the reader, I shall now, under my own name, vary the work by adding the matters I had promised. I shall divide each item according to its categories, so that the very order may make them clearer, and place each under its proper heading. First I shall come to the interpretation of Hebrew names, of which, for the sake of brevity, I shall set down the more certain and famous ones.

## CHAPTER ONE  
### Interpretation of Hebrew Names

Adonai means “Lord” in Latin. Sabaoth means “of armies” or “of powers”; or, as some wish, “almighty Jesus, the Savior.” Nazarenus means “holy” or “pure.” Messias means “anointed,” that is, “Christ.” Michael means “Who is like God?” Gabriel means “strength of God.” Raphael means “medicine of God.” Adam means “man” or “earth-born.” Eve means “life” or “calamity.” I wonder why among the Hebrews the interpretation of this name is so different, unless perhaps it is because she brought life to the man by eating, and calamity by transgressing; or because a woman is sometimes life to some and calamity to others.

Abel means “mourning” or “miserable.” Cain means “possession” or “lamentation.” Enoch means “dedication.” Methuselah means “he sent his death.” Noah means “rest.” Shem means “named.” Ham means “cunning.” Japheth means “breadth.” Lot means “declining” or “anointed.” Melchizedek means “righteous king.” Abram means “exalted father.” Abraham means “father seeing the people,” or “father of many,” namely, of nations.

Sarai means “my princess.” Sarah means “princess.” It should be noted that in both names, namely Abraham’s and Sarah’s, the Lord added only the letter *a*, although among the Hebrews it is pronounced with *e*. Hagar means “stranger” or “converted.” Ishmael means “hearing of God.” Isaac means “laughter,” not, as some think, because Sarah laughed, but because Abraham, who is clearly indicated to have laughed first, did so. Rebecca means “patience” or “she who has received much.” Jacob means “supplanter.” Israel means “a man seeing God,” but better, “a prince with God.”

Leah means “laborious.” Rachel means “ewe” or “seeing God.” Reuben means “seeing sons” or “seeing in the midst.” Simeon means “hearing sorrows.” Levi means “opposed” or “added.” Judah means “confessing” or “glorifying.” Zebulun means “dwelling of beauty.” Issachar means “there is a reward.” Dan means “judgment” or “judging.” Gad means “temptation.” Asher means “breadth” or “blessed.” Naphtali means “those conducting themselves.” Benjamin means “son of the right hand.”

Ephraim means “fruitful,” or “abundance,” or “increased” in Latin. Manasseh means “forgotten.” Esau means “red” or “heap of stones.” Kedar means “darkness” or “sorrow.” Job means “magician” or “suffering.” Amalek means “people licking” or “extinguishing.” Moses means “taking up” or “anointing.” Aaron means “mountain of strength.” Pharaoh means “uncovering him” or “his destroyer.” But Pharaoh is not the name of a man, but of an office, just as among us kings are called Augusti while being known by their proper names. That Pharaoh, however, who was drowned in the Red Sea was called by his proper name Centres.

Joshua means “savior.” Othniel means “his time is God” or “answer of God.” Ehud means “glorious.” Shamgar means “an arriving name” or “a settler there.” Barak means “flashing.” Deborah means “bee” or “talkative.” Gideon means “the temptation of their iniquity.” Abimelech means “my father is king.” Tola means “a worm for dyeing” or “scarlet.” Jair means “illuminating.” Jephthah means “opening” or “opened.” Heshbon means “thought” or “belt of sorrow.” Achilon means “living to God” or “seeing God.” Abdon means “his servant.” Samson means “their sun” or “strength of the sun.” Delilah means “little poor woman” or “bucket.” Eli means “my God.” Samuel means “his name is God.” Saul means “prepared” or “request.” Jesse means “island of holocaust” or “sacrifice.” David means “desirable” or “strong of hand.”

Jonathan means “gift of a dove” or “gift of the Lord.” Absalom means “father of peace.” Solomon means “peaceful.” He is also Ecclesiastes, that is, “preacher”; and likewise Idida, that is, “beloved of the Lord.” Rehoboam means “breadth of the people.” Abijah means “the Lord is father.” Asa means “taking” or “lifting up.” Jehoshaphat means “judgment of the Lord.” Joram means “he who is exalted,” but better, “raised up.” Ahaziah means “grasping the Lord.” Athaliah means “time of the Lord.” Joash means “hoping” or “temporal.” Amaziah means “lifting up the people.” Uzziah means “strength of the Lord.” Azariah means “help of the Lord.” Jotham means “perfect.” Ahaz means “grasping.” Hezekiah means “strength of the Lord.” Manasseh means “forgetful,” or “because he forgot.” Amon means “faithful” or “nourishing.” Josiah means “where incense is” or “salvation of the Lord.” Jehoahaz means “strong.” Jehoiakim means “whose is the preparation.” Eliakim means “resurrection of God.” Jeconiah means “preparation of the Lord.” Zedekiah means “righteous of the Lord.” Jeroboam means “judging the people” or “judging those above us.” Nave means “barking.”

Baasha means “fatness.” Elam means “of the age” or “of the world.” Zimri means “psalm” or “my song.” Omri means “my curling.” Ahab means “brother of the father.” Jezebel means “flowing with blood” or “dung.” Jehu means “he himself” or “he is.” Joah means “strong.” Zechariah means “fear of the Lord.” Shallum means “his shadow” or “request.” Menahem means “comforting.” Pekah means “opening.” Elijah means “God the Lord.” Elisha means “salvation of my God.” Hosea means “savior.” Joel means “with God beginning” or “God is.” Amos means “powerful,” or “strong,” or “subduing the people.” Obadiah means “servant of the Lord.” Jonah means “dove” or “suffering.” Micah means “Who is this?” Nahum means “sprout” or “consolation.” Habakkuk means “embracing.” Zephaniah means “hiding her.” Haggai means “festive” or “solemn.” Malachi means “my angel.” Isaiah means “salvation of the Lord.” Jeremiah means “exalted of the Lord.” Ezekiel means “strength of God.” Daniel means “judgment of God.”

Judith means “praising” or “Jewess.” Joseph means “increased.” Mary means “illumined” or “star of the sea”; but in the Syriac language, “lady.” Simon means “put away sorrow” or “obedient.” Peter means “recognizing.” Bar-Jonah means “son of a dove,” in both Syriac and Hebrew. Cephas means “Peter” and is Syriac. Paul means “wonderful.” Saul means “the tester of the one who looks back” or “security of testing.” Andrew means “manly” and is Greek. James means “supplanter.” John means “grace of the Lord.” Philip means “mouth of lamps.” Bartholomew means “son of the one who suspends waters.” Thomas means “abyss” or “twin”; hence in Greek he is also called Didymus. Matthew means “gift.” He was also called Levi. Lebbaeus means “little heart,” that is, “from the heart.” He is also Thaddaeus; he is Judas of James. Cananaeus means “possessing” or “possession.” Simon was so called from the village of Cana; he is also called the Zealot. Iscariot means “memorial of the Lord” or “memory of death.” Judas was called by this name from the village in which he was born.

Mark means “exalted in command.” Luke means “he himself rising” or “he himself lifting up.” Stephen means “your standard”; in Greek, “crowned.” Augusti means “standing solemnly.” Caesar means “principal possession.” Cyrenians means “heirs.” Bethsaida means “house of fruits.” Bethphage is Syriac for “house of the valley.” Bethany means “house of affliction.” Gennesaret means “birth of a prince.” Emmaus means “rejected people.” Capernaum means “field of consolation.” Sarepta means “burned” or “distress of bread.” Gethsemane means “valley of fatness.” Golgotha means “skull.” Nazareth means “flower of purity” or “a young shoot.” Ninevites means “born beautiful.” Sidon means “hunting.” Zacchaeus means “justified.” Idumea means “rose.” Lisama means “birth of temptation.” Jordan means “descent.”

Martha means “provoking God.” Magdalena means “tower.” Susanna means “lily.” Sheba means “captivity.” Caiaphas means “investigator” or “vomiting from the mouth.” Pontius means “turning aside counsel.” Pilate means “mouth of a hammerer.” Herod means “leathery.” Barabbas means “son of the father,” or “of their master”—plainly, the master of the Jews, who is the devil.

Eden in Genesis means “delights.” Judea means “confession.” Jerusalem means “vision of peace.” Zion means “watchtower,” and rightly so, for this city of David was built on a mountain. Babylon means “confusion” or “transference.” Ethiopia means “darkness.” Egypt means “tribulation” or “darkness.” Tyre means “distress.” Romans means “exalted” or “thunderers.” Sinai means “measure,” or “commandment,” or “temptation,” or “my amphora.” Gehenna means “free valley.” Some think it was named from the valley of Hinnom, which lies beside the wall of Jerusalem. Hebrews means “those who cross over.” Sadducees means “justified.” Pharisees means “divided.” Galileans means “rolling about.” Samaritans means “guardians,” because they were placed there by the Babylonians to keep watch over the Jews.

In this matter, as in many others, it becomes abundantly clear how truly divine and full of mysteries all Holy Scripture is, since names correspond so aptly to realities and answer to their qualities. Thus David is rendered in Latin as “strong of hand,” for he proved exceedingly strong in nearly all his wars. Solomon means “peaceful,” for he governed the kingdom in peace. Daniel means “judgment of God,” for in the judgment of the elders he displayed the sentence of divine deliberation. Why, then, is it surprising if these men proclaimed the future, when even their names, as events demonstrate, sound forth prophecy? But let us now set down the interpretation of various terms.

## CHAPTER TWO  
### Various Terms

Alleluia means “praise the Lord” in Latin; for *ia* is one of the ten names of God recognized among the Hebrews. Amen means “truly” or “faithfully.” *Diapsalma* means “always,” because it confirms that the things to which it is attached are everlasting from God. It does not signify, as some think, a change of meter or a restoration of the prophetic spirit. There are also those who think that *diapsalma* is written so that from it a change of persons or meanings may be understood.

Hosanna means “save” or “save me.” For *osi* is interpreted as “save,” while *anna* is an interjection of one making supplication. Thus the complete form is *osianna*. But when shortened or corrupted, it sounds *hosanna*. The meaning is “save”—with “the people of Israel” or “the whole world” understood.

Rama means “exalted.” In the Gospel: “A voice was heard in Rama,” that is, “in the heights.” There is also a city called Rama. Raca means “vain” or “empty.” Rabbi means “teacher” and is Syriac. *Man* means “What?” *Manna* means “What is this?” Abba means “father” and is also Syriac. Anathema means “destruction.” Maranatha means “Our Lord has come” and is Syriac. But *anathema maranatha*, as some say, means “destruction at the Lord’s coming.” Mammon means “wealth.”

Teraphim means “figures” or “images,” preferably rather than “fires.” Seraphim, or seraphin, means “burning” or “kindling,” in accordance with: “Who makes his angels spirits and his ministers a burning fire.” Thus seraphin confirms that there are powers in heaven who praise God and are sent on various ministries.

Cherubim means “abundance of knowledge.” Moreover, the cherubim themselves signify only two living creatures in the Holy of Holies. In other places where this name is read, it either indicates some painting or signifies variety.

## CHAPTER THREE  
### The Interpretation of Various Things

Mandrake, in Genesis, is a kind of fruit very similar in appearance or smell to a small melon. *Mazaroth* is the zodiac, which mathematicians assert consists of twelve signs. *Fath* means “climate,” that is, the southern or western region. *Rhamnus* in the Psalter is not a bramble but a kind of thorn exceedingly troublesome because of its prickles.

*Rhomphaia* means “sword” in Latin. For where Genesis says, “a flaming and revolving sword,” the Greek has *rhomphaia*. *Frameae* are very long spears. Some assign this name even now to those who use them as weapons. Others also think that swords are signified by it.

*Capparis* in Solomon denotes in the East a kind of shrub resembling the mastic tree. *Palathae* in the Books of Kings are masses made by pressing together fresh figs. *Palathae* is Greek. In the prophet Hosea, *debelaim* is said to mean *palathae*.

*Dabir* in the Books of Kings is the oracle that was made in the innermost central part of the Temple, where the Ark of the Lord also was; this was called the Holy of Holies. *Byssus* is a kind of coarser and stronger silk. Some think that *byssus* is also a kind of linen. *Phoenicium* in Isaiah means “scarlet.”

*Luteres* in the Books of Kings means “shells” or “water jars.” But *cantharus* is also a Greek word. *Latomi* in the Books of Kings means “stonecutters,” and this too is Greek. *Creagrae* in Chronicles means “hooks” used to remove meat from cauldrons; it is Greek.

*Sambuca* in musical terminology is a kind of harmony. *Nablum*, which in Greek is called *psalterium* and derives its name from plucking, resembles a barbarian harp shaped like the Greek letter delta, Δ. A *tympanum* is made with stretched skin or hide. *Cinari*, as some think, are cymbals which, when struck, set rhythms in motion. *Thyina* means “woods.” From these Solomon made steps in the house of the Lord—woods unknown even to the more learned Jews.

*Sethim* is a kind of thorny growth in the desert, from which incorruptible wood is obtained. *Sabeth* is the Hebrew name for a shrub in Genesis: “Behold,” it says, “a ram was caught behind its back in a Sabeth shrub.”

*Lebetae* are small bronze vessels prepared for cooking. In Chronicles: “They cooked the peace offerings in cauldrons, pans, and pots.” *Cophinus* means “basket.” *Hydria* means “water vessel.” *Condi* in Genesis means “cup” or “goblet.” *Lecythus* in the Books of Kings means “oil flask.” *Lenticula* in the Book of Kings is a small bronze vessel containing oil with which kings were anointed.

*Paropsis* means a larger dish. Some also think that a platter is called by this name. *Epistylia* in the Books of Kings are the structures placed above the capitals of columns; it is Greek. *Mechonoth* in the Books of Kings means “supports,” which we call bases. *Topazion* is a precious stone in which, as some assert, the colors of all stones shine.

*Corbana* means “treasury.” *Corbona* means “offering.” *Chasma* in Luke means “chasm”; it is Greek. *Erysibe* in the prophet means “verdigris,” that is, rust affecting crops; it is Greek. *Zizania* means “weeds” or “darnel.” *Sicera* is juice made from dates; and every liquid other than wine that is prepared for drinking from fruits or from any other substance is called *sicera*.

*Nardum pisticum* means “trustworthy nard,” that is, nard without adulteration; it is Greek. *Nardum spicatum* means “spikenard,” because the form of the nard itself resembles a spike, into which it is infused and prepared. *Alabastrum* is a kind of precious marble, from which the vessel of the Gospel ointment was made. A *stadium* in the Gospel is a definite measure of distance. Eight stadia make one thousand paces.

The names that follow are found in Exodus or in the Books of Kings in passages dealing with the Ark, the tabernacle, or the Temple of the Lord. The terms for these names that are more obscure are found in the old translation; those that appear clearer are contained in the text of the new translation. Thus the old translation has *sperateres*; the new, *ferulae*.

*Calamiscos*: reeds. *Troiscos*, or *cariscos*: things fashioned approximately in the shape of a nut. *Anconiscos*: fittings or sockets. *Aspidiscas*: hooks. *Fimbrias*: chains. *Scitalas*: bars. *Acrotomis lapidibus*: stones cut smooth. *Degrapidem*: engraving. *Petalis*: plates. *Perimentum*: line. *Spiras*: the capitals of columns, or, as I think, their construction. *Elam*: portico; but it is better interpreted as “before the doors” or “vestibule.” Thus *Elam* is Hebrew. The remaining terms above are for the most part Greek.

Likewise, in the final part of Ezekiel, in the vision of the city, the old translation has *pastophoria*, while the new has *gazophylacia*, that is, “small chambers.” *Thee*: chambers. *Aileu*: forehead. *Aelaucooth*: vestibule. *Polyandron*: multitudes. *Spitamis*: palm’s breadth. *Gissus*: definition. *Manaa*: sacrifice. In the Books of Kings, *cenotaphia* means images, which in Greek are *μορφώματα* (*morphōmata*).

But enough of this. Now also receive the following: certain names were first used by Scripture, and this is what they are called now.

## CHAPTER FOUR  
### Peoples

Gomor in Genesis means the Galatians, that is, the Gauls, who were first called Galatians because of the whiteness of their bodies. Some of these peoples once migrated to the distant regions of the East and were first called Gallo-Greeks; now, under the ancient name of the Gauls, they are called Galatians.

Magog means Scythians. Some think that Gog and Magog are the Goths. Jubal means Iberians, who are also Spaniards.

Thiras means Thracians. Togarmah means Phrygians. Madai means Medes. Javan means Ionians, who are also Greeks; hence the Ionian Sea. Cethim means Citians, that is, Cypriots, among whom the city of Citium is also so called. Dodanim means Rhodians. From these Greek peoples arose those who occupied the coastal region from Mount Taurus to the Western Ocean. All these nations descend from the stock of Japheth.

Cush means Ethiopia. Mizraim means Egypt. Casluhim are those who later became the Philistines, now called Palestinians. They are also called Allophyli and foreigners. Their city is Ashkelon. Sheba means Arabia. Sheba is also the name of the region where the Sabaeans now live. Havilah means Getulians. Labain means those now called Libyans, formerly called Putheans. Tarshish, or Carchedon, is Carthage. Some think Tarshish is Cilicia, because the city of Tarsus is situated there.

Africa was named from one of Abraham’s descendants by Keturah, who was called Apher. Ishmaelites were named from Ishmael, Abraham’s son. They are also called Saracens, from Sarah, and Hagarenes, from Hagar. Nabataeans were named from Nabaioth, Ishmael’s son; they extend from the Euphrates to the Red Sea.

Canaanites were named from Canaan, the son of Ham. After expelling its inhabitants, the Jews possessed their land. All these peoples descend from the line of Ham.

Asshur means Assyrians, from Asshur, the son of Shem. They founded the city of Ninum, named after King Ninus, which is now called Nineveh. Some maintain that the Syrians were named from Asshurim, Abraham’s son by Keturah. Uz, which is also the region of Ausitis around Coelesyria, was named from Uz, the great-grandson of Shem. Elamites means Persians, from Elam, the son of Shem. Hebrews were named from Eber, who was Shem’s great-grandson. Chaldeans, now called Chaldaeans, were named from Chesed, the son of Nahor, Abraham’s brother. All these peoples proceed from the descendants of Shem.

## CHAPTER FIVE  
### Places

Jebus is Jerusalem; it is also Salem, where Melchizedek reigned. It is now called Aelia by Hadrian. Babel in Genesis is now called Babylon. At this place, when human beings once undertook to build a tower against heaven, they were scattered by an immense divinely imposed confusion of languages.

Achar is now called Nisibis. Reblatha is now called Antioch. It is also Epiphaneia. Shechem is also Sichem; it is now the city of Neapolis belonging to the Samaritans. Oholibamah in the prophet is the city in which the princes of Edom lived.

Ariel in Isaiah is thought by some to be Ariopolis, named after the idol of Mars, Ariel, which is located there. But Ariel means “lion of God,” figuratively signifying Jerusalem. Ararat means Armenia, in whose mountains the Ark came to rest after the Flood, so that some traces of it are said still to remain there.

Arba, which is corruptly read as Arbos in our manuscripts, is the place where the three patriarchs—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—and, in addition, Adam himself, were buried. It is also Hebron, where David reigned. Lod is Lydda; it is also Diospolis.

Decapolis in the Gospel is a region containing ten cities. Ekron is a city of Palestine. Antilebanon is the name given to the places above Mount Lebanon that face the eastern region. Ephrathah is the city of Bethlehem. The Euphrates, however, is a river from Paradise.

Mesopotamia is so called because it is surrounded by the rivers Tigris and Euphrates. Samaria is now called Sebaste. Emmaus in the Gospel was once the name of a fortified town; it is now a city called Nicopolis. Calvary is so called because, according to custom, those condemned were beheaded at that place. Areopagus is the name of the court among the Athenians, which received its name from Mars.

## CHAPTER SIX  
### Rivers and Waters

Geon is a river of Ethiopia emerging from Paradise; by its customary name it is called the Nile. Pishon is a river of India, likewise flowing from Paradise; some call it the Ganges.

Siloam is a spring in Jerusalem that bubbles up from the root of Mount Zion. It does not flow constantly, but emerges at particular hours and on particular days, running through caves and over rocks.

Jordan is so called because two springs flow together into one; one is called Jor and the other Dan. The Sea of Galilee is also the Sea of Tiberias, the Lake of Gennesaret, and the Lake of Genesareth. The Salt Sea is also called the Dead Sea or the Asphalt Sea—that is, the Sea of Bitumen—and lies not far from Jericho.

Bethsaida is a pool in Jerusalem to which the sick were also carried. Hence it is called Probatica, that is, “belonging to sheep,” because the priests once washed sacrificial victims in it.

## CHAPTER SEVEN  
### Months

Nisan in the Book of Ezra is the month called March, and in Scripture it is called the first month. Elul in the Book of Maccabees is August, which among us is called the sixth month. Kislev in the prophet Zechariah is November, which is the ninth month. Tebeth in the Book of Esther is December, which is the tenth month. Shebat in the prophet Zechariah is January, which among us is the eleventh month. Adar in the Book of Ezra is February, which among us is the twelfth month.

If you also wish to know the remaining Hebrew names of the months, which I have not found in the canon: Iyar is called the second month; Sivan, the third; Tammuz, the fourth; Ab, the fifth; Tishri, the sixth; Marcheshvan, the seventh.

## CHAPTER EIGHT  
### Festivals

The jubilee year is the fiftieth year, the year of remission, in which, in Israel, whatever one had sold returned to its owner, even without payment.

Passover (*Pascha*) means “crossing over”; it is Hebrew, not Greek. It is called “crossing over” because the Hebrews crossed over from Egypt into the land of promise. Certainly our Passover is so called because the Savior, rising from the dead, crossed over into the kingdoms of heaven.

*Phase* likewise means Passover, “crossing over” or “passage.” Some maintain that it was called “crossing over” or “passage” rather because on that same night the Lord passed through Egypt, when he struck down all the firstborn of the Egyptians (Exod. 13:15).

Pentecost means “fiftieth”; it is Greek. The jubilee year bore the figure of this fiftieth year, and now again prefigures the eternal rest of the future promise.

*Scenopegia* is the setting up of booths by the Jews, in memory of the tabernacles. For *σκηνή* (*skēnē*) means “tabernacle” in Greek. This Jewish festival is celebrated in the month of September.

*Encaenia* means the observance or dedication of a new building. For *καινόν* (*kainon*) means “new” in Greek. Thus, in this festival, the Jews celebrated the day of the Temple’s dedication in the month of October.

Epiphany is Greek and means “appearance” or “manifestation”: either because on that day the Lord and Savior was manifested to the peoples in his baptism; or because the star was manifested to the Magi; or because at the Lord’s first sign, when water was changed into wine, it then appeared.

*Neomenia* means what among us is called the kalends. But since the Hebrews calculate the months according to the courses of the moon, and *μήνη* (*mēnē*) means “moon” in Greek, *neomenia* may therefore be understood as “new moon.”

*Parasceve* means “preparation” and is Greek. For Friday is called *parasceve*, the sixth day of the week. It is called “preparation” because on that day the Jews prepare the things necessary for the Sabbath.

Sabbath means “rest” and is Hebrew. It is called “rest” because on that day the Lord rested from his work, after all things had been completed and finished.

## CHAPTER NINE  
### Idols

Idols means “images”; it is Greek. Baal-peor, interpreted as “image of shame,” is an idol of Moab. The Latins call him Priapus. Bel, interpreted as “old age,” is a Babylonian idol. This same Bel was the father of Ninus, king of the Assyrians.

Adrammelech is an idol of the Assyrians, which the Samaritans also worshiped. Astarte, which in Latin means “superfluous workmanship,” is said to be an idol of the Sidonians. Beelzebul means “man of flies.” The Devil means “flowing downward”; in Greek he is called “the accuser.” Satan means “adversary” or “transgressor” in Latin.

Sirens in Isaiah are demons, or great dragons, both crested and winged, as some think.

[Column 819D] Owls in Isaiah are called *Iim* by the Hebrew name itself in every translation. Only the Seventy translators rendered this term as *onocentaurs*. Some think that owls are nocturnal birds, named from the howling sound they make; in common speech they are called cavanni. *Lamia* is a kind of monster, as some assert. The hairy ones in Isaiah are kinds of demons. Some of the most learned men have thought that these are incubi, satyrs, or certain wild men.

## CHAPTER TEN  
### Garments
Ephod: a priestly garment, which is called an overgarment or shoulder-piece. It is shaped somewhat like a [Col. 0820A] *caracalla*, but without a hood. This garment is of two kinds: one is linen and plain, which the priests wore; the other was woven of gold, purple, fine linen, hyacinth-colored material, and gems of various colors, and was worn only by the high priests. *Poderis*: a linen priestly garment tightly fitted to the body and reaching to the ankles, whence it is called *poderis*; it is also called a tunic. *Logion*, also called the breastpiece, is a small cloth made of gems, gold, and various colors, which was fastened to the shoulder-piece opposite the high priest’s breast.

*Cidaris*: a priestly cap made of fine linen. The Greeks and our own people call it a tiara; some also call it a miter. *Petalum*: a golden plate on the high priest’s forehead, bearing written upon it in four Hebrew letters that ineffable name of God, the tetragrammaton. *Penula*, in the Apostle, [Col. 0820B] is a Latin word. It is like a cloak with hanging bands (*clavi*). *Baddim*, in Daniel, means linen garments, by which, I think, undergarments are signified. Among the Hebrews *badenim* means “linen”; hence in some places one reads *Ephod bad*, that is, “linen ephod,” and not *Ephod barud*, as some incorrectly read. *Diplois*, in the Books of Kings, is a cloak or mantle, from ἀπὸ τῷ διπλόῳ, “from being doubled”; and every garment with which we are wrapped double may be called *diplois*. *Melotae*, in the Book of Kings, is a simple skin, which the Egyptian monks still use, hanging down on one side. *Theristrum*, in Genesis, is, among the Arabs, a kind of woman’s cloak. *Periscelides*, in Isaiah, according to some, are among women ornaments for the legs.

## CHAPTER XI. On Birds or Flying Creatures

[Col. 0820C]

*Pelicanus*: a small bird that delights in solitude. There is also another kind of pelican on the Nile, almost like swans, except that they are somewhat larger. Some call these *onocrotali* as well. *Nycticorax*: an owl; many insist that it is a horned owl. There are also those who assert that it is an eastern bird called the night-raven. *Ibis*, in the Pentateuch, is an Egyptian bird rendered unclean by the obscenity of its mouth, with which it is accustomed to cleanse its bowels. *Herodius*, in the psalm (Ps. 103:17), is thought by some to mean a heron. *Larus*, in the Pentateuch (Lev. 11:16; Deut. 14:15), signifies a seagull.

*Coenomyia* is not to be understood in the psalm (Ps. 77; 104) as a dog-fly, as some think, but as a fly of every kind; and therefore it ought to be written not with the Greek letter *y*, but with the diphthong *oe* (Deut. 14:15). *Ciniphes*: a kind of gnat, extremely troublesome because of its stings.

## CHAPTER XII. On Beasts or Reptiles

*Rhinoceron*: a terrifying wild beast bearing two horns on its nostrils. *Monoceron*, in the psalm, is called a unicorn. *Tragelaphus*, in Deuteronomy, is *platoceros*, that is, “broad-horned.” *Erinacii* are called *chirogrilli*; they are nearly the size of medium-sized rabbits and emerge in groups from rocky caves. In the wilderness opposite the Dead Sea they graze. *Hericii*, also called hedgehogs, are so protected by a covering of spines that they cannot even be touched. *Bruchus*, in the psalm (Ps. 77; 104), is a locust that does not yet fly, which is commonly called an *olba*.

## CHAPTER XIII. On Weights

A *talent* weighs 62 pounds, which make 80 Attic pounds. A *mina* is one pound and a half-ounce. A talent contains 60 minas. In Greek, *mna*; in Latin, *mina*. A *drachma* contains three scruples [alt. *scripula*]. A *didrachma* is two drachmas. Hence I wonder how, in the Book of Hebrew Questions, a half-ounce is written. A *stater* is a coin weighing, as some assert, one ounce—that is, six gold pieces; others think three. For in the Gospel a stater is given for two didrachmas. A *sicle*, which in Latin is incorrectly called *siclus*, [Col. 0821B] as is indicated in the Questions mentioned above, weighs an ounce; elsewhere, as I have found written, it weighs ten scruples [alt. *scripula*], which is also my own opinion. For *siclus* itself, or *sicel*, because of the closeness of its weight, sounds rather like *sicilicus*. An *obol* is half a scruple, making three carats, in Ezekiel. A sicle contains twenty obols.

## CHAPTER XIV. On Measures

A *corus* is 30 modii. A *bath* is one amphora, that is, three modii. A *cadus* is a Greek amphora and contains three urns. An *ephah*, or *opha*, is three modii. The ephah has the same measure for dry goods as the bath has for liquids. One *metreta*, according to some, contains one hundred sextarii. In Greek, measure is called *metron*, whence *metreta* derives its name. It should be noted, however, that “measure” is a Hebrew name. *Artabae*, in Isaiah, is an Egyptian measure, three of which make ten modii. *Sata* are the same as ephah, that is, three modii. A *gomer* is an Attic measure containing, as some suppose, three *choenices*, that is, twelve sextarii. Others say that a gomer is somewhat less than five sextarii; this is also my own view, because a gomer is a tenth of an ephah. Some think that a *nebel* is three modii. A sextarius is half a cotyla when used for liquids. A *cotyla* is a hemina. In Ezekiel: “Ten cotylae are a gomer.”

## CHAPTER XV. On Greek Names

Now receive the meanings of the remaining names, [Col. 0821D] which, celebrated in the speech of the Church, are converted from Greek into our language.

*Theos*: God. According to the opinion of some, *theos* derives from ἀπὸ τοῦ θεάομαι, that is, “from seeing,” meaning “because he sees all things.” *Homoousion*: of one substance. *Homoiousion*: of similar substance. *Christus*: anointed. *Paracletus*: comforter or advocate. *Hagios*: holy. *Angelus*: messenger. *Thronus*: seat or throne. *Apostolus*: one sent, because they were sent by the Lord to evangelize. *Propheta*: one who foretells. *Martyres*: witnesses. *Episcopus*: overseer; hence the prophet says, “I have appointed you as a watchman over the house of Israel.” *Presbyter*: elder. *Diaconus*: minister. *Clerus*: lot. *Ecclesia*: calling or assembly. *Catholica*: universal, ἀπὸ τοῦ καθ’ ὅλον, that is, “according to the whole.”

*Synagoga*: assembly or congregation. *Ethnicus*: gentile. *Hypocrita*: pretender. *Haeresis*: sect. *Monachus*: solitary. *Eremus*: desert. *Paroecia*: an adjoining house, namely, of God. *Dioecesis*: administration; this is not according to the proper meaning and power of the word, but according to its effect. *Laicus*: belonging to the people, ἀπὸ τοῦ λαοῦ, that is, “from the people.” *Catechumenus*: instructed or hearing. *Neophytus*: a newly planted shoot. *Baptisterium*: a dyeing-place. *Holocaustum*: wholly burned; because the entire victim was handed over to the fire and consumed. *Chrisma*: anointing. *Eucharistia*: grace. *Symbolum*: contribution, agreement, or an arrangement made between a human being and God. *Hymnus*: a song in praise of God. *Antiphona*: a responsive voice. *Pentateuchus*: five volumes, that is, the five books of Moses; concerning them the Apostle says that he wishes to speak five words in the Church. *Exodus*: departure or going out, namely, of the people of Israel. *Deuteronomium*: second law, in which there is a foreshadowing of the evangelical law. *Paralipomenon*: of things passed over or remaining; that is, because it contains histories omitted in the Books of Kings. *Evangelium*: good announcement or good news. *Apocalypsis*: revelation. *Gazophylacium*: treasury of riches, a compound word from the Persian and Greek languages. *Synodus*: assembly or gathering. *Canon*: rule. *Teuchos*: volume. *Apocrypha*: hidden or concealed things. *Hexapla*: sixfold things. *Apologia*: excuse, whence *apologeticus* is derived; or, as some think, purification or defense. *Anagoge*: higher meaning. *Tropologia*: moral understanding. *Parabola*: likeness or parable. *Anacephaleosis*: recapitulation.

You have here, my dearest son, a little work serving as a kind of seedbed of understanding for almost the whole body of the Scriptures. In two volumes I have gathered together, from various necessary matters, a not inconsiderable amount of instruction, as I think, for teaching you.

[Col. 0821]

## RUINART’S PREFACE TO THE PASSION OF THE SAINTS MAURICE AND HIS COMPANIONS, MARTYRS

[Col. 0821D]

### 1

Long ago the Acts of the holy Maurice and his companions had been published by Lawrence Surius under the name of Saint Eucherius, bishop of Lyons; but they were so internally inconsistent that learned men were rightly inclined to regard them as false and spurious. They also existed in Mombritius, somewhat more corrected, but so interpolated that they could not be attributed to Eucherius of Lyons. Consequently, more discerning men deeply lamented that the genuine Acts of such illustrious martyrs had either been lost or had at least been so corrupted and mutilated that they deserved no credence among sensible people.

At last, however, these long-desired Acts were discovered by the Reverend Father Pierre-François Chifflet, a Jesuit priest, in an ancient manuscript of the celebrated monastery of the Jura; he published them in the first part of his *Pauline Illustrated*. We publish the same text, collated with several manuscript codices, and indeed with very ancient ones, among them one deriving from the remains of the Fossatensis library and approaching nine hundred years of age. The name of Eucherius is prefixed indiscriminately in the manuscript codices both to the interpolated and to the genuine Acts, and indeed more rarely to the genuine ones. The same is true of the letter of Eucherius to Silvius or Salvius, which we found joined to the genuine Acts in a single codex of the Royal Library.

Since this codex is nevertheless of excellent quality, and since it is also found in the codex used by Chifflet, we have retained the letter and present it after comparison with several manuscript codices. Eucherius, the author of this Passion, presided over the Church of Lyons at the beginning of the fifth century. If you desire further information about him, consult, besides those who have compiled catalogues of ecclesiastical writers, Chifflet, in *Pauline Illustrated*, part I, chapter 14 and following. There he argues that only one Eucherius presided over the Church of Lyons. By contrast, Theophilus Raynaldus in his *Catalogue of the Saints of Lyons*, Cardinal Baronius—who had earlier argued for the contrary position—and Mabillon in his notes to the *Life of Saint Consortia*, along with other learned men, admit two Eucheriuses, bishops of Lyons. The elder, a contemporary of Hilary of Arles and praised by him in his sermon on Saint Honoratus, died in 454; the younger, mentioned in the *Life of Saint Caesarius of Arles*, only after the Second Council of Orange II, which he is said to have subscribed in 529.

### 2

Moreover, the Gallican Fathers seem to have used Eucherius’s narrative in composing the office that was read on the feast day of these martyrs. This is clearly indicated by the Gothic Missal, whose passage we shall transcribe below. It also seems to be the Passion that Saint Avitus, bishop of Vienne, testifies was read according to customary obligation in the homily he delivered on these martyrs. For what is set out more fully in Eucherius’s narrative, Avitus expresses in a few words in the fragment of that homily that survives for us.

He acknowledges that these martyrs, whom he calls the “fortunate army,” were decimated once and again by lot and were finally entirely destroyed. The complete fragment ought to be presented; it was copied by James Sirmond, a most devoted student of sacred antiquity, from very ancient sheets written on bark in the Thuane Library. The most expert men who examined these sheets—which are now preserved in the Royal Library—assert that they were written while Avitus was still alive, or at least shortly after his death.

The title of the homily is as follows:

**“Delivered in the Basilica of the Saints of Agaunum, at the Renewal of the Monastery itself or on the Passion of the Martyrs.”**

The homily begins as follows:

“The proclamation of the fortunate army, in whose most blessed company no one perished, though no one escaped, when it judged the unjust death of the holy martyrs as though by the justice of the lot—by which, twice dispersed over the gentle battle-line, a hundredfold harvest increased from the decimated ranks, and, with hatred lending its support to the favorable outcome, individuals were selected until the chosen were gathered together—the sequence of the Passion read according to customary obligation set forth.”

Marius, bishop of Avenches, mentions the monastery of Agaunum more than once, especially in his *Chronicle* under the year 515, during the consulship of Florentius and Anthemius. He says that in that year the monastery at Acaunum was constructed by King Sigismund. This seems to refer to the renewal of which we are speaking. For even if the monastery had stood previously, it was so enlarged through the generosity of this pious prince that he may rightly be called its founder.

### 3

Although most of the names of these martyrs are unknown, their memory has nevertheless always been celebrated throughout the Church. This is evident not only from what we have cited but also from other ancient authors, who honored them under the name of the saints of Acaunum, after the place of their martyrdom, or under the name of the Theban Legion.

Gregory of Tours calls it the Fortunate Legion in Book I of *The Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 75. There he reports that Sigismund, king of the Burgundians, enriched the Church of Agaunum most lavishly with territories and other possessions and established there continual psalmody. In the following chapter the same author reports several miracles of these martyrs. In Book X of his *History*, however, he says that he found relics of the blessed martyrs of Agaunum both in the principal church of Tours, over which he presided, and in the basilica of Saint Martin.

In honor of these same martyrs, Venantius Fortunatus composed the fifteenth poem of Book II, and in Book VIII, poem 4, he lists them among the more celebrated martyrs and calls the legion the Fortunate Legion of Agaunum. From this it may be conjectured that in ancient times these martyrs were commonly called the **Fortunate Legion**. Saint Avitus supports this conjecture in the passage cited above, where they are called the Fortunate Army.

I pass over Walafrid Strabo and countless other authors of various periods who celebrated the martyrs of Agaunum. It is impossible, however, to omit the testimony of the ancient Gallican liturgy, taken from the Gothic-Gallican Missal. Joseph Maria Thomasius and our own John Mabillon published this Missal from a very ancient manuscript, written in square letters more than nine hundred years ago, in Book III of the *Gallican Liturgy*.

In this Missal, at number 64, there is a Mass of Saint Maurice and his companions, in which a narrative of their history appears, undoubtedly taken from our Eucherius, as will become clear when the two are compared. For the sake of making that comparison more convenient, it is useful to reproduce the entire Preface, which there is called the *Immolatio Missae*:

“It is truly fitting and just that we give you thanks, holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God. For you, Lord, recalled the army of the Thebans, destined for the punishment of your people, by the sudden grace of your command, so that they chose rather to be slain through vigilant devotion than to be sated with the blood of Christians; nor, when they took upon themselves the burden of persecution with so many [the text reads *ut te*; I think it should read *nec cunctantes, te*], you helping them, did they bend their necks to their persecutors.

“And when the enemy’s rage decreed that the people of God should perish through the urgency of repeated counting, the tenth man was seized, so that by anticipating martyrdom he might become the firstfruits. A cry arises in the camp; the courage to fight is rejected; a difficult contest over the acceptance of martyrdom is stirred up. The people of God are pierced with the sword, the blood of the innocent is poured out, and faith is preserved undefiled.

“Thus, Lord, you protect your soldiers, so that neither patience is lacking in suffering nor steadfastness in confession. Amid the battles of the blessed and the blessed struggles, glorious confession deserved more to be divided from the company of fellow soldiers than for the executioner’s hand to boast. For the whole people of God burned with such ardent faith and eagerness that, if persecution of the body were delayed, the devotion of suffering would go before it.

“For such was the steadfastness of the people and [lacuna] of the enemy that afterward neither fury found anything to kill nor anything glorious remained to perish. That sacred place of Agaunum became, through the intercessions of the martyrs, the salvation of those present and the protection of those to come. The wave of blood poured over it, and the fellowship of precious bodies consecrated it. Therefore, rightly, to you, Lord, and so forth.”

In the collects these same martyrs are called the holy Acaunenses. From this it is clear that the cult of these martyrs, whom our ancestors esteemed so highly, is ancient in our Gaul.

Two metropolitan churches, those of Vienne and Tours, and likewise two cathedral churches, namely Angers and Mirepoix, have been consecrated to God under the name of Saint Maurice. To say nothing of the others, among the ancient churches that once existed in the city of Reims there is listed a church of Saint Maurice, which Sonnatius and Lando, bishops of that city, mention in their wills, as recorded by Marlot in volume I of the *Metropolis of Reims*.

### 4

Fewer statements are found concerning the number of these martyrs. The liturgy cited above designates them by the name of “the people.” In the Preface—which, according to ancient custom, is called the Admonition—they are also said to have numbered six thousand six hundred. It reads as follows:

“Dearest brothers, let us implore the mercy of almighty God on the solemnity of this day of the six thousand six hundred martyrs, so that he who granted such a multitude of his people the glory of martyrdom may likewise grant us, and so forth.”

The number seems to be given there because Eucherius said that the legion at that time consisted of six thousand six hundred men. The author of the *Life of Saint Romanus*, abbot of the Jura, who was himself a contemporary of Romanus and flourished toward the end of the fifth century, likewise says that there were just as many martyrs of Agaunum.

Such a slaughter of soldiers, moreover, was not without precedent. I shall give one example from Xiphilinus’ epitome of Dio Cassius, in the *Life of Galba*, where he reports that seven thousand Praetorian soldiers were killed and that the rest were decimated.

### 5

Except for those listed by Eucherius, the names of these martyrs are entirely unknown to us. Most writers, however, add Innocentius or Innocent and Vitalis to the names given by Eucherius. These men are mentioned in the most ancient Martyrologies and in the Gregorian Sacramentary from Ratold’s Corbie codex, as our own Hugh Menard observes in his notes, page 180; they also occur in an ancient manuscript of the metropolitan Church of Reims and in several others.

Orderic Vitalis certainly reports, in Book XIII of his *Ecclesiastical History*, that he was named after this holy martyr Vitalis. “The name Vitalis,” he says, [Col. 0825B] “was given to me in place of an English name, which the Normans considered harsh; it was borrowed from one of the companions of Saint Maurice the martyr, whose martyrdom was then being celebrated.”

Various churches also celebrate other martyrs of the same legion, who perhaps were absent from the army at that time or had certainly already been brought to completion before that general destruction. Gregory of Tours says in Book I of *The Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 62, that fifty of them suffered at Cologne, and he notes that their basilica was once called “of the Golden Saints.”

The widely circulated Martyrologies commemorate Gereon and three hundred eighteen others as having suffered in the same city on October 10; Ado says that they were believed to have belonged to the legion of blessed Maurice. Some think that the martyr Mallosus, whom Gregory says in the following chapter was buried with the martyr Victor in the town of Bertuna, belonged to the Theban Legion.

On October 10, Usuardus confuses this man with Gereon in these words: “In the city of Cologne, Saint Gereon the martyr, surnamed Mallosus, with three hundred eighteen others, who …”

The martyrs of Turin are commonly counted among the same group: Octavius, Adventitius, and Solutor. Saint Maximus, bishop of Turin, delivered two homilies on them, which are preserved in volume V, part I, of the *Library of the Fathers*. They are also praised by Ennodius of Pavia in poem I.

There are other celebrated martyrs in various Italian cities: Maximinus of Milan; Maurice, George, and Tiberius of Pinerolo; Sebastian and Alverius of Fossano in Liguria; and Alexander of Bergamo, about whom Ughellus gives further information.

If we are to believe Notker and others, the legion also included female martyrs. Notker mentions among them Regula, who, together with her brother Felix, was beheaded after enduring various tortures on September 11. He had reported more about the virgin Verena under the first day of the same month.

Other martyrs, completed elsewhere, are encountered throughout the Martyrologies and in the particular records of churches; there is no time to discuss them more fully. It has never entered my mind to defend as certain and indisputable everything that some authors have casually related about these martyrs without legitimate foundation.

But to call into question the martyrdom of that most celebrated legion, which unquestionable testimonies of such authority and antiquity affirm, is not the act of an honest mind, nor of a person who, rejecting every partisan inclination, loves to embrace the truth wherever it shines forth.

### 6

The ancient and more recent Latin Martyrologies commemorate the feast of Saint Maurice and his companions on September 22. I have not, however, been able to find any memory of them among the Greeks. For the Maurice whom the Greeks celebrate with seventy soldier-companions on February 21 is plainly different from our Maurice; apart from the name, scarcely anything is common to the two.

Our Maurice suffered in Gaul with an entire legion. The other suffered at Apamea in Syria, after his son Photinus had gone before him to the palm of martyrdom. Having endured intolerable tortures with his companions for ten days and nights, he brought his life to an end with them amid prayers.

Theodoret praises this martyr Maurice in sermon 8 of *The Cure of Greek Affections*. His complete Acts, taken from Symeon Metaphrastes, are found under February 21 in the Bollandists.

### 7

Cardinal Baronius assigns the Passion of the martyrs of Agaunum to the year 297. We think, however, that it should rather be referred to the beginning of the reign of the emperors Diocletian and Maximian. We infer that it may be assigned to the year 286 from the fact that Maximian Herculius—whom, as the learned Baluze observes in his notes to Lactantius’ *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, Diocletian had taken into partnership in the imperial power the preceding year—was at that time in Gaul with the army.

We do not deny, however, that this Passion of the martyrs may also be assigned to the following years.

### 8

The place at Agaunum where this slaughter occurred thereafter became famous among Christians, both because of the memory of so many martyrs and because of the remarkable monastery built there. It has continued to the present day and is widely known under the name of Saint Maurice.

It is situated in the diocese of Sion, at the foot of Mount Saint Bernard. It was first established under a private rule, later passed to Benedictine monks, and finally came into the possession of Augustinian canons regular.

Our Mabillon proves in volume I of the *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order*, page 568, that this monastery existed before the year 515. It was therefore enriched, and perhaps restored, by Sigismund, king of the Burgundians, but was not originally constructed by him; this is certain from the title of the fragment of the homily of Avitus of Vienne cited above.

How famous this monastery once was is shown by the fact that it was regarded as a model for the establishment of others, especially because of its unbroken psalmody, commonly called “Perpetual Praise.” This practice of singing continually in the churches of monasteries was received from the Greek monks called the *Acoemetae* and was once observed in many monasteries of our holy Benedictine order, as the ancient charters published in various collections demonstrate. On this practice, see Mabillon’s preface to the second part of the fourth century of the Benedictine order, no. 204 and following.

[Col. 0827]

# THE PASSION OF THE MARTYRS OF AGAUNUM, OF SAINTS MAURICE AND HIS COMPANIONS, BY SAINT EUCHERIUS, BISHOP OF LYONS

*(From Theod. Ruinart’s Acts of the Martyrs.)* (C, S)

## Preface

**Eucherius to Salvius, bishop,**

[Note: In the manuscripts of Saint-Remi, Saint-Thierry, and others, “Silvius.” In the codex of Saint-Maur-des-Fossés there is another letter of Eucherius to all the faithful, but it does not possess the character of antiquity. In the codex of the monastery of the Jura, more than nine hundred years old, this letter appears as follows: “Eucherius to his son Veranus in Christ, greetings. I send and commend to you the formulas of spiritual understanding, out of the zeal of my fatherly concern for you,” and so forth.]

[Note: [Col. 0828A] There also and in the editions: “I have sent . . . the written account of our [martyrs],” etc.]

I send to your blessedness the Passion of our martyrs. For I feared that, through negligence, the passage of time might erase from human memory the deeds of so glorious a martyrdom.

I sought the truth of the matter from reliable authorities, namely from those who affirmed that Saint Isaac, bishop of Geneva, [Note: His bare name is listed among the bishops of Geneva by the Sammarthani, *Gallia Christiana*, volume II.] had learned the sequence of the Passion which he related; and I believe that he had in turn received it in earlier times from the most blessed Bishop Theodore, a man of an earlier age. [Note: Theodore was bishop of Octodurum, or Sion, in whose diocese Agaunum is situated. He subscribed to the Council of Aquileia in the year 381.]

Thus, while others from various places and provinces offer gifts of gold, silver, and other things in honor and service of the saints, we reverently offer you this written work of ours, asking in return their intercession for all my sins and, in the future, their perpetual protection, since they are always my patrons.

Remember us also before the Lord, always cleaving to the service of the saints, holy lord and deservedly most blessed brother.

# THE PASSION OF THE MARTYRS OF AGAUNUM

[Col. 0827]

### I

We set forth in writing, for the honor of their deeds, the Passion of the holy martyrs who have made Acaunum illustrious with their glorious blood, with that faithfulness with which the order of their martyrdom has come down to us. Through the testimony passed down from one generation to another, forgetfulness has not yet interrupted the memory of what happened.

Although individual places possessing them, or individual distinguished cities, are honored on behalf of individual martyrs—and not without reason, since they poured out their precious souls for the supreme God [Note: Thus the Floriac manuscript. Others read: “they pour out the precious souls of the saints.”]—with what reverence ought that sacred place of the Acaunenses to be honored, where so many thousands of martyrs are reported to have been struck down by the sword for Christ?

Let us now speak of the very cause of that most blessed Passion.

### II

Under Maximian, who held imperial power together with Diocletian as his colleague in governing the Roman state, peoples of martyrs were tortured or killed throughout nearly every province. This same Maximian, just as he raged while possessed by avarice, lust, cruelty, and the other vices, was also devoted to the accursed rites of the pagans. Profane toward the God of heaven, he had armed his impiety to extinguish the Christian name.

At that time, if anyone dared to profess the worship of the true God, troops of soldiers were scattered everywhere to drag them either to punishment or to death. As though permission had been granted to barbarian peoples, he had directed his weapons entirely against the religion.

At the same time there was in the army a legion of soldiers called Thebans. A legion was then called a force that had six thousand six hundred men under arms. [Note: Vegetius, *On Military Affairs*, Book II, chapter 2: “The Romans have legions in which they customarily serve six thousand men each, sometimes more.” Certainly, from various passages of Livy and other authors, it seems possible to infer that the number of soldiers was not fixed: sometimes there were more, sometimes fewer in a legion. See Florentinius’ notes on the *Hieronymian Martyrology*.]

These men had been summoned from the regions of the East to assist Maximian. They were brave in military affairs and noble in valor, but nobler still in faith. They competed in courage toward the emperor and devotion toward Christ.

Even under arms they did not forget the evangelical commandment: they rendered to God the things that were God’s and restored to Caesar the things that were Caesar’s. Therefore, when they, like the other soldiers, were assigned [Col. 0828C] to drag away the multitude of Christians [Note: The Sorbonne and German manuscripts read “to tear apart.”], they alone dared to refuse the service of cruelty [Note: The same manuscripts read “to withdraw themselves from the ministry of cruelty”] and declared that they would not obey commands of this kind.

Maximian was not far away; he was resting at Octodurum, exhausted by the journey. [Note: The German manuscript corruptly reads: “For he was keeping himself exhausted by an eight-day journey.” Octodurum is the town commonly called Martinach or Martigny, in Valais in Switzerland, not far from Sion and Agaunum.] When word was brought to him that this legion had halted in the narrow passes of Acaunum in rebellion against the imperial commands, he burst into a rage, provoked by indignation.

Before I relate the rest, however, it seems necessary to insert a description of the site into the narrative.

### III

Acaunum lies approximately sixty miles from the city of Geneva and fourteen miles from the head of Lake Geneva, into which the Rhône flows. The place itself is situated among the Alpine ridges, in a valley. For travelers proceeding toward it, a difficult passage opens up, a rough and narrow road.

The hostile Rhône leaves travelers scarcely any passable embankment at the foot of a rocky mountain. Having overcome and crossed the constricted defiles, a sudden and not insignificant plain opens between the mountain crags. [Col. 0829B] The holy legion had taken up its position there.

Therefore, as we said above, when Maximian learned the response of the Thebans, burning with impetuous anger because his commands had been neglected, he ordered every tenth man from that same legion to be struck down with the sword, so that the others might more easily be frightened by fear and yield to the royal commands. [Note: Decimation was a punishment customary among the Romans. Baronius gives several examples in his notes to the Martyrology under September 22.]

After renewing his commands, he ordered that the survivors be compelled to persecute the Christians. When the repeated order reached the Thebans and they learned that profane executions were again being imposed upon them, an outcry and tumult arose throughout the camp. They declared that they would never submit to such sacrilegious duties; that they would always detest the profanities of idols and devote themselves to the worship of the sacred and divine religion; that they worshiped the one God of eternity; and that it was better to undergo the utmost sufferings than to act against the Christian faith.

When Maximian learned this, more bloodthirsty than any beast, he returned again to the savagery of his nature. He ordered that a second tenth of them be put to death and that the others nevertheless be compelled to do what they had rejected.

When these orders had once more been carried into the camp, the man who had been selected as the tenth was separated from the others and struck down. The remaining multitude of soldiers, however, encouraged one another in conversation to persevere in so glorious a work.

### IV

At that time the greatest stimulus to faith was Saint Maurice, who, as tradition relates, was then the *primicerius* of that legion. [Note: Cangius says in his *Glossary*: “The *primicerius* is a military rank, close to that of tribune.” Jerome, in his letter to Pammachius, writes: “But first a *primicerius*, then a senator, a ducenarius, a biarchus, a *cirmicitor*, a horseman, and finally a recruit.” These ranks are discussed in various authors.]

Together with Exsuperius, the army’s *campiductor* (field-leader), and with Candidus, the military senator, he inflamed the soldiers by exhorting and admonishing each one to faith. [Note: The Royal and German manuscripts read: “Candidus, the military senator, came forward to exhort and admonish each one, and the faithful fellow soldiers …” The same reading occurs in the Fossatensis manuscript; but instead of “to exhort … and admonish,” it has “by exhorting … and admonishing.”]

He also placed before them the examples of their fellow soldiers who had become martyrs, persuading all that, for the covenant of Christ and the divine laws, they must die if necessity required it, and reminding them that those companions and comrades of theirs who had already gone before them into heaven were to be followed.

For even then the glorious ardor of martyrdom was burning in those most blessed men. Thus encouraged by these leaders and instigators of theirs [Note: The Sorbonne manuscript reads “encouraging them”], they sent a message to Maximian, who was still seething with madness—a message at once pious and courageous, which is said to have been as follows.

We are soldiers, emperor, of yours; yet we are servants—this we freely confess—of God. To you we owe military service; to Him, innocence. From you we have received the pay of our labor; from Him we have received the beginning of life. We cannot in any way follow you as emperor so as to deny God, our author—indeed, our author, Lord, whether you wish it or not, and yours as well. If we are not compelled to such atrocious acts as would offend Him, we shall continue to obey you, as we have done until now; but if otherwise, we shall obey Him rather than you.

We offer our hands against any enemy; but we consider it unlawful to stain them with the blood of the innocent. These right hands know how to fight against the impious and the enemies; they do not know how to tear apart the pious and our fellow citizens. We remember that we took up arms for our fellow citizens rather than against our fellow citizens. We have always fought for justice [Note: Sorbonic manuscript: “for the province.”], for piety, for the safety of the innocent: these have hitherto been the rewards of our dangers [Note: Regius manuscript: “the chief rewards.”]. We fought for the faith; but how shall we preserve it for you if we do not show it to our God? First we swore allegiance to the divine sacrament; afterward we swore allegiance to the imperial sacrament. You must not think that anything is owed to the second if we violate the first.

You order Christians to be sought out for punishment through us. From this point onward you need seek no others: here you have us, confessing God the Father, author of all things, and believing that His Son, Jesus Christ, is God [Note: In Chifflet’s edition, “Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit” is added. In the German manuscript, however, neither “and in the Holy Spirit” nor “we believe God” is found.]. We saw our companions in labors and dangers slaughtered by the sword, while we too were sprinkled with their blood; and yet we did not weep or grieve over the deaths of our most holy fellow soldiers and the funerals of our brothers. Rather, we praised them and accompanied them with joy, because they had been deemed worthy to suffer for the Lord their God.

And now even this final necessity of life has not driven us into rebellion; even despair itself—which is strongest in dangers—has not armed us against you, emperor. Behold, we hold weapons, yet we do not resist, because we greatly prefer to die rather than to kill, and we desire that the innocent perish rather than that the guilty live. If you decide anything further against us, if you give any further order, if you inflict anything further upon us, we are ready to undergo fire, torments, and the sword. We confess that we are Christians; we cannot persecute Christians.

[Col. 0830D]

V. When Maximian had heard these things and perceived that their minds were steadfast in the faith of Christ, despairing of being able to recall their glorious constancy, he decreed that they should all be killed by a single sentence. He ordered the deed to be carried out after surrounding them with ranks of soldiers. When those who had been sent came to the most blessed legion, the impious men drew their swords against the saints [Note: The Fossat manuscript and Chifflet’s edition, together with the Sorbonic manuscript, read “the impious sword.”], who did not refuse to die out of love for life.

Thus they were cut down everywhere with swords. They did not even cry out or resist; instead, laying down their arms, they offered their necks to their persecutors and presented their throats—or their uncovered bodies—to the persecutors. They were not elated even by the number of their own men or by the protection of their weapons so as to attempt to establish the cause of justice by the sword. They remembered only that they confessed Him who, when led to slaughter, did not protest and, like a lamb, did not open His mouth. They too, like a flock [Note: Thus the Sorbonic manuscript.
