Other manuscripts read “of the Lord’s sheep.”] of the Lord’s sheep, allowed themselves to be torn apart as though by attacking wolves.

The earth there was covered by the bodies of the pious as they fell to their deaths, and streams of precious blood flowed. What madness ever, without a war, produced such a slaughter of human bodies? What savagery ever ordered so many guilty men to perish at once merely by its own decision? The crowd did not prevail so that the just might not be punished, although what a crowd commits usually goes unpunished. Thus, by the cruelty of that most savage tyrant, that holy people was destroyed: the people who despised present things because of their hope in things to come. Thus that wholly angelic legion was killed, which, as we believe, now continually praises the Lord God Sabaoth in heaven together with those legions of angels.

VI. Victor, however, was neither of that same legion nor a soldier, but a veteran who had already completed his military service. While traveling, he suddenly came upon men who were feasting merrily on the spoils of the martyrs. Invited by them to join the meal, he learned in due order from the rejoicing men the reason for their celebration. He detested the banqueters and detested the banquet, and withdrew. When they asked whether he too perhaps was a Christian, he replied that he was a Christian and would always remain one. He was immediately killed by those who attacked him, and was joined to the other martyrs in that same place both in death and in honor.

Of that number of martyrs we have learned only these names: the most blessed Mauritius, Exsuperius, Candidus, and Victor. The others, indeed, are unknown to us, but they are written in the book of life. The martyrs Ursus and Victor are also said to have belonged to this same legion; tradition confirms that they suffered at Salodorum [Note: On these men, see Surius under September 30. Fredegar describes the translation of Ursus, carried out by Oecunius, bishop of Maurienne, in the year 602, in his Chronicle, chapter 22.].

Salodorum still survives today as the chief town of one of the Catholic cantons of the Helvetians; in French, *le canton de Soleure*, and to its inhabitants, Solothurn [Note: Salodorum]. It is a fortress above the River Aare, situated not far from the Rhine.

VII. It is also worth indicating what end subsequently overtook Maximian, the savage tyrant. When he was plotting the death of his son-in-law Constantine, who at that time held the imperial power, his deception was discovered. He was captured near Massilia and not long afterward strangled. Having suffered this most hideous punishment, he ended a life worthy of such an impious death [Note: Eusebius reports that, after being discovered plotting against Constantine, he died by a most shameful form of death, in *Ecclesiastical History*, book VIII, chapter 13, and in *The Life of Constantine*, book I, chapter 47. Paulus Orosius, book VII, chapter 28, reports that this occurred at Massilia, as does our Eucherius. Lactantius gives a fuller account in his notable work *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, sections 29 and 30. The learned Antonius Pagi proves that he was not killed before the year 311, under the years 307 and 310.].

But the bodies of the most blessed martyrs of Agaunum are said to have been revealed, many years after their passion, to Saint Theodore, bishop of that place. When a basilica was being built in their honor, lying not merely adjacent to but sloping toward a vast cliff, I thought that I ought not to remain silent about the miracle that then appeared.

Among the other craftsmen who seemed to have gathered, having been invited to undertake that work, there happened to be a certain smith who was clearly still a pagan. On the Lord’s Day, when the others had departed to await that day’s festivities, he remained alone at the construction site. Then, when the saints suddenly revealed themselves in that solitude by a bright light, the smith was seized and stretched out for punishment or torment. He visibly saw a crowd of martyrs, and was also beaten and rebuked because, whether for being the only one absent from the church on the Lord’s Day or for daring as a pagan to undertake that sacred work of construction, he had offended. It became clear that the saints had acted with such mercy that the smith, overwhelmed and terrified, asked that the saving name be given to him, and immediately became a Christian.

VIII. Nor will I omit from the miracles of the saints another event that is equally famous and known to everyone. The wife of Quincius, an outstanding and honored man, had been so bound by paralysis that she had even lost the use of her feet. She asked her husband to have her carried to Agaunum, across the considerable distance of the journey. When she arrived there, carried by the hands of those serving the basilica of the holy martyrs, she returned to the lodging on foot. Restored to health in limbs that had been as good as dead, she now carries her own miracle about with her.

I have thought that only these two miracles should be inserted into the account of the saints’ passion. There are, however, many others through which the power of the Lord works there by means of His saints, whether in the expulsion of demons or in other healings.

[Col. 0833]

SOME HOMILIES OF SAINT EUCHERIUS, BISHOP OF LYONS. (C,G)*

HOMILY I. To the Monks.

[Col. 0833A]

The divine word exhorts us to run while we have the light, before the darkness overtakes us. We have the light if we run, if we advance the step of faith; we remain in darkness if we cease to advance. May the final necessity find us ready, for it often overtakes the unprepared. Let our uncertain condition impose a definite anxiety upon us; let there be a daily fear of that danger whose arrival is unknown.

How slowly will the wretched soul repent of its evils when, with the final day approaching, it sees itself separated from its body; when, as it closes its eyes at the end, eternal night begins to grow black and dreadful for it; when it sees lying before it, empty of salvation and light, its unhappy fellow soldier, both instigator and deceiver, with whom it departed defeated from the arena of this world through its wickedness?

What will happen when, already separated from that companion, it begins to utter enormous and empty lamentations over him and say: “Where are your spirited impulses and your desires, for which you burned impatiently until now and gathered things destined to burn continually?” Behold, all those things have passed like a shadow; pleasures have gone away, and only reproaches and crimes have remained forever. Woe is me, O soul! Willingly or unwillingly, I am returning to such a ruined vessel, and because of fleeting pleasures I shall be burned together with it by vapors from which I can never escape.”

What will happen amid these things when the importunate exactor of the deposit begins to drag it toward a fixed sentence, established by immovable law, and the dreadful faces of infernal ministers begin to taunt and press upon it from every side [Note: Perhaps “to leap upon it.”]?

What will happen when it begins to be separated by the officers of death and led away through this vast air, along the paths of darkness, beyond the day; when it travels a road from which there is no return, through those regions where the light itself fails; when that alien soul, accompanied everywhere by the mournful procession of its evils, sees itself falling out of the world through the farthest boundaries of the earth into that emptiness and void, entering the great chaos that distinguishes the region of life from that of death, and, exiled from its own nature, losing the vital airs?

When, saying its final farewell to human affairs, with death before it and life left behind, it is dragged into that dreadful depth, scarcely reachable by the eyes, chained by various crimes of avarice and wickedness—the measure of the reward it has lost, such punishment will it receive.

When, therefore, it has reached those places of cruel custody, where the expectation itself of the coming judgment of punishments will already rage against it, to say nothing else, grief alone will torture the soul deprived of every consolation; thought alone will torment the despairing soul; fear alone will examine the stunned soul. And because there will then be no concern about preparing food or clothing, no occupation with laboring, serving as a soldier, or conducting affairs, no ambition for wealth or honor, the terror of giving an account will alone fill the mind, empty of every other concern and made intolerable; the entire weight of judgment will hang over its captive senses.

What, moreover, will happen when it is ordered to return to the prison of its body and, through the resurrection, to receive it again for companionship with its evils? What will it do when it must be presented before the sight of the chaste angels with the foul marks of its wounds, and must render an account of each matter before the King of the ages? If these things were now, without doubt, brought before us, the soul could not bear the guilt within itself, crushed beneath the shame of great confusion.

What frame of mind will it then have when it sees the Lord bestowing upon others there the reward of uninjured and complete faith, the treasure of radiant chastity, the fruits of mercy, and the talents of justice? When it sees the last becoming first and the first last by an undeserved reversal of fortune; the poor glorified above the rich, servants above masters; each person, according to his merits, flooded with the light of immortality, raised from humanity into the state of angels; once clothed in an earthly body, now placed above the heights of the heavenly kingdom; enriched among the children of majesty by the abundant inheritance of God the Father; while it itself, left among these things with its sins, bears away from the spectacle of another’s happiness only the defects that produce sorrow?

What afterward [Note: Perhaps “What will it do afterward?”], when in its pitiable condition it sees itself stripped of every consolation, cast into the outer darkness, excluded from that Church of the blessed by perpetual excommunication, and cut off from the very root of life [Note: Perhaps “condition”]?

But how will the trembling and guilty speech be able to explain what will happen when the unexpiated flesh and the marrow infected with sins begin to be penetrated by the savage heats of Gehenna; when, in the manner of glowing and melting metals, the entire substance of the human being is infused within by an unquenchable burning; and when the consuming flames partly consume bodies and souls, yet partly nourish them, so that condemned nature, amid the masses of fire, both supplies fuel and receives increase?

If that vice once sprinkled into consciences—the adulterine mixture of bronze and lead—should at some time be burned away among the boiling pools of the panting torrent, then, for those passing through the fiery channels, the magnitude of the sin will be the duration of the punishment. Crimes will supply food to the flames, and this command of both the author and the judge will remain: that fire, having consumed the entrails subject to pain and consecrated solely to torments, should not devour them, but should burn [the text reads “perish”] for this purpose: always to destroy.

Thus the work and formation of our body, dead in ancient crimes and revived only for torments, will not find an end at the very boundary of destruction; rather, when its strength to endure has already been emptied, it will perish in such a way that it may rise again. For that burning is not accidental but rational and punitive: because it is ordered to seek out guilt, it does not know how to consume the substance. And because, as with linen cloth [Note: Perhaps “as in punishments”], a light, passing burning runs through it, that flame is itself a purification; it pursues not so much the guilty person as the guilt. If there has been a measure of offenses, there will also be a measure of torments. But if the excesses of capital crimes have occupied and enveloped the whole nature at once, because the case admits no remedy, the punishment will have no end.

When punishment kills and the sentence gives life, the matter capable of restoration will stand throughout the ages, and it will never reach the goal because the end of evils continually flees. Even while it is unable to promise itself any hope, not even after immense ages, the torments of the ages that follow will already be felt in the present; and thus the immortality imposed upon consciousness will increase the pain of death.

Woe to those who reckon these things, which are to be mourned in the future, as matters for laughter now! Woe to those for whom these things must first be experienced rather than believed!

Therefore, dearest brothers, all these things that cannot be ended there can here be redeemed through amendment of one’s former life, through almsgiving, through tears, through humility of heart, through chastity of body, and through the practices of justice and mercy. Since this is so, we hasten through so many errors toward death, though we have received so many paths to salvation.

Through Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

HOMILY II. To the Monks.

We ought to know how much benefit, even in the present life, holy occupations confer, dearest brothers. Sacred reading has handed down that the animals which ruminate are clean. What it means to ruminate, however, the divine word clearly teaches when it says: “His delight is in the law of the Lord, and on his law he meditates day and night” (Ps. I, 2); and again: “The meditation of my heart is always in your sight” (Ps. XLVIII, 4).

Thus, while we spiritually ruminate the food of salvation, we exclude evil thoughts by closing our senses. Then we delight in the praises of God, and through holy practices we perceive our inner self becoming a clean animal. While we fortify our inward parts against rejected desires, we satisfy our souls with heavenly foods, so that the prophetic saying may also be spoken of us: “He gave them the bread of heaven; man ate the bread of angels.” The bread of angels is Christ, and we too share in His food when we occupy our minds with His praises.

Behold the true food, which refreshes and does not fail, but through its use increases, and grows through the expenditure it requires. By this bread we are refreshed through hunger, and nourished through fasting, inflicting a kind of violence upon our vices and desires, so that it may be said of us: “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. XI, 12).

We must know who the violent are. We know that the human mind, softened by the various allurements and desires of the world, flees labor and seeks pleasure, and is scarcely persuaded to exclude from itself the habit of its former life. But when it begins to consider the necessity of the final day, driven and goaded toward the weight of the coming judgment, either by hope of reward or by fear of punishment, it declares voluntary war on its passions, does violence to its former pursuits, and strives violently to conquer itself by changing to a better life.

For it cannot happen without violence that someone passes from abundance and riches to hunger and thirst, to abstinence and the cross; that he breaks down the flesh, previously a friend to sleep and leisure, through hardship and vigils. Nor, I say, can it happen without violence that each person exchanges anger for patience, pride for humility, overcomes abundance through love of poverty and sufficiency, commends drunkenness through sobriety and lust through chastity, and that a person is suddenly transformed into another man—somehow made other from what he was before. In this way the heavenly kingdom is seized by such people through violence.

There are two kinds of abstinence and the cross: one bodily, the other spiritual. The first is to abstain from drink and banquets, to restrain the appetite of the stomach from pleasures and the softest delights, and to withdraw and forcibly drag back the senses from those things that deceive through touch, taste, and sight.

The second and more precious kind of abstinence and the cross is to govern the movements of the soul, to calm its disturbances through the tranquility of moderation, to restrain the assaults of pride like a wild beast, to contend daily against one’s vices, to rebuke oneself with the censorial severity of virtue, and, in a certain sense, to engage in combat with the inner person.

This is what the one who breaks through the wall of the passions does, violently ascending to the kingdom of heaven. May He who reigns forever and ever deign to lead you there as you live in His fear. Amen.

HOMILY III. To the Monks.

The divine word instructs and exhorts us concerning how we ought to gird ourselves to seek its promises and to obtain those good things that cannot be grasped by sight, perceived by hearing, or comprehended by thought. “Ask,” it says, “and you will receive; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you” (Luke XI, 9). That is: let us ask by praying; let us seek by laboring; let us knock by desiring, by making progress, and by persevering. Let us be stirred toward the hope of heavenly promises with such zeal and burn with such affection that the greatness of our desires may correspond to the worthiness of the rewards.

Our God does not wish His good things to become cheap through excessive ease of discovery. A precious and desirable reward requires an eager lover and an avid merchant.

Therefore, He who promises such great gifts does not want you lukewarm in your work; He despises the disdainful, rejects the compelled, and refuses the halfhearted. To seek the grace of a divine gift sluggishly and with little gratitude is the greatest insult to the one who bestows the reward.

Therefore, even if we sweat through all the labors of soul and body, even if we exercise ourselves with all the strength of obedience, we shall still be unable to compensate for or offer anything worthy in exchange for heavenly goods. The services of the present life cannot be balanced against the joys of eternal life. Let our limbs grow weary through vigils, let our faces grow pale through fasts; nevertheless, “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that is to be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII, 18).

Let us knock, then, dearest brothers, as much as we can, because we cannot knock as much as we ought. Future blessedness can be acquired, but it cannot be measured. Unless we perform God’s works eagerly, with good will and joy, let us recognize that we are perishing before God.

Do we suppose that the soul truly seeks and knocks so that it may be opened to it when, in response to a light command from an elder, it presumes to say: “Are we perhaps your servants? I have already done my part; let him do his”? How can this be said by one who has been commanded: “Do not seek what is your own”? And again: “Not considering each one his own interests” (Phil. II, 4). From him is required not merely that he fulfill his own reward, but that he undertake, anticipate, and seize the tasks of others.

Do we suppose, I say, that someone asks so that he may receive, seeks so that he may find, and knocks so that it may be opened to him, when, corrected for some negligence and chastised according to the order of discipline, he does not turn toward amendment or satisfaction, but instead toward such insolence as to say: “I am leaving and departing; I cannot endure this. I am a freeborn man”?

First, when someone boasts before a superior or abbot that he is freeborn, I think he still does not know that he has been bought. One who has been enlisted in the Christian army and presumes to call himself freeborn comes close to denying that he was purchased by Christ’s blood. What else is “I am free” than to cry out to the Lord Himself, “I owe nothing”? Of such people the Apostle said: “When you were servants of disobedience, you were free from righteousness” (Rom. VI, 20).

A man is not rightly proved freeborn if he is oppressed by slavery to vices. In contempt of discipline and in sin against his own soul, he cries out: “I would rather depart than amend, rather depart than make satisfaction, rather depart than fulfill what you command.” What else is this than to shake Christ’s yoke from his rebellious neck?

Such people do not know what they know; they have forgotten why they came here. Such people do not ask rightly, but are wrongly pursued by their vices. They do not knock in faith, but are battered by faithlessness. What benefit is it that you depart when you are bound on every side by the chains of your passions, when your vices surround you and fortify themselves against you from every direction? What benefit, I ask, is it that you depart when, wherever you go, you carry yourself with you? You would rightly depart if you could flee somewhere. Someone has departed rightly if he can go where the devil cannot find him.

Let no one deceive himself: do not flee the adversary from place to place, but from vice to virtue, from passion to amendment. For if you flee him in this way, he will follow you. Amend yourself, and he will flee from you, as the Apostle says: “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you” (James IV, 7).

But not to obey and to wish to depart is to do the devil’s will in two ways; it is voluntarily to bring condemnation upon oneself even in the present life. For those who commit more serious offenses among us, we can find no sadder or harsher sentence than that they be cut off from the body of the congregation and depart without peace. Is it not madness for someone to seek as a remedy what even a superior cannot impose except for the gravest crime?

Let us understand, then, dearest brothers, that these indignities and contradictions arise through the enemy’s activity and design. Because he cannot openly shake someone from the place of salvation, he first introduces occasions and causes; he introduces the passion of disobedience, which is always accompanied by faithlessness. Once this has ensnared the mind and taken it captive, it immediately makes even small and light things seem intolerable and impossible.

And indeed there is no doubt that divine strength is withdrawn from the disobedient. Just as the one who did not possess within himself the necessary devotion of faith had even what he possessed taken away from him, so disobedience hardens the mind it has once seized, so that it cannot be bent toward accepting commands either by authority or by reason.

But what is worst is that such a person believes only himself, follows his own intentions as though they were the whole of reason, and considers right only what he has conceived with a hardened heart. He becomes like the one of whom the divine word declares: “The ways of fools are right in their own eyes” (Prov. XVI, 25); and again: “There are ways that seem right to men, but their end comes into the depths of hell” (Prov. XIV, 12).

Finally, something like this will happen to such souls as happened to the house built upon sand (Matt. VII, 26). This parable refers especially to the disobedient. For we read: “Everyone who hears these words and does not do them will be like a foolish man who built his house upon sand: the floods came,” and so forth (ibid.). That is, when the showers of passions pour in, when the torrents and assaults of tribulations arrive through the multitude of negligences, when the winds blow—those, certainly, that fly about in this air, ready to winnow Christ’s threshing floor wherever they find chaff to seize and scatter for their sport—then they will rush upon that house which has been built without the foundation of obedience, and its fall will be great.

But perhaps someone will say: “Is departing from this place immediately to be called a fall?” I say, dearest brothers, that there is not much hope if a ship stands amid the waves: even if it does not itself perish, it may nevertheless suffer the greatest loss in its cargo and merchandise, and may reach the harbor empty and bare.

So it is no great joy if someone, returning to the waves of the world, appears to preserve the name and habit of his profession, while his soul wastes away and ebbs through negligence. And what is more serious than that you should suddenly be uprooted like a swift bird from the place to which your Lord had called you, in which He had first enlightened you, and into which He had brought you after the evils of the world, as into a harbor from a severe storm?

To forget suddenly the brotherhood, fellowship, and consolation; to forget that place in which you first removed your former habit and worldly name! Birds themselves love their nests; wild beasts love the places in which they were raised; they love their lairs and pastures. Although by their natural freedom they may be carried away by disorderly attacks in every direction, they nevertheless return more often to places dear to them, driven by a certain desire for food.

And you, endowed with understanding and fortified by reason, sometimes become so estranged from your senses that you prefer your own wishes or intentions to God’s gifts and follow your own thoughts—even when they drag you toward harsh labors, toward the shipwreck of salvation, and toward the ruin of your soul. Yet, because of your heart’s excessive indignation, you do not perceive any of this.

The divine word says this: “At the time of departure the enemy makes many promises. He persuades himself that he will find greater progress, abundant grace, and an abundance of all things in the place toward which he is heading, and that he will be received as though he were an angel.”

Afterward, when filled with anxiety and stripped of peace, he remembers how he abandoned his pursuit of progress and the sacred sheepfold. Then he takes notice; as though the storm of his time had subsided, he sees what evil he has done to himself. Then he recognizes what danger he incurred when he departed from the place to which he had come with joy, without peace and with scandal.

Then, in delayed repentance, he repents and mourns over his ruins—like certain birds said to weep in grief over those whom they have killed. All these injuries to the soul arise from the evil of disobedience. Obedient and humble souls, however, overthrow many tribulations and all labors, and reduce them to a manageable measure.

For it must be understood that the humbler and more obedient we are, the more lightly and sweetly we shall feel the Lord’s yoke upon us. The more obedient we are to our superiors and fathers, the more God will obey our prayers.

Let us see how acceptable to the Lord are the works or fasts [the text adds “and”] of those who obey their own wishes rather than those of their elders. They cry out: “Why have we fasted, and you did not know? We humbled our souls, and you did not look upon us?” And He replies: “Because on the days of your fasts your own desires are found” (Isa. LVIII, 3).

We see that through disobedience the works of souls are not regarded, their fasts are not heard, and their vows are not received. Therefore let us follow all the more closely the commands of Him who descended to us from heaven for this purpose: not only to redeem us at the price of death, but also to build us up by the example of His life. Let us say with Him: “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of Him who sent me, the Father” (John VI, 38).

To follow one’s own wishes is so harmful that the Lord, afterward in anger as a condemnation of sin, imposes this upon the guilty, saying: “And I gave them over to the desires of their hearts” (Ps. LXXX, 13).

Therefore, whoever wishes his works to be safe or right in the sight of God must prefer nothing to obedience and place absolutely nothing before it, whether he is senior or junior. Indeed, the older he is, the more he ought to devote himself to edification and perfection. Let him set no end to his progress and establish no limit to his acquisition, since he hears it said: “Prepare your works for the end”; and again: “Do not fear to be justified unto death” (Ecclus. XVIII, 22). And again: “Wisdom will be proclaimed at the end” (Prov. I, 20).

The more we progress, therefore, the more let us humble ourselves; for the more we have been humbled, the more we shall progress. Let no senior there appear so learned that he thinks obedience unbecoming to him, although obedience was becoming to God.

Humility and obedience are still a necessity in the young, but in the old they are an honor. He progresses well, he completes his course well, who acts each day as though he were always beginning.

Therefore, increases in merit ought to be incentives to progress. Scripture, speaking of those who overlook their first negligences and continually fall into others, says: “The sinner adds to sinning” (Ecclus. III, 29) [Col. 0840A]. Of progress it says: “And let the holy be sanctified still” (Rev. XXII, 11).

Let us first see what “the sinner adds to sinning” means. For example, some vice or passion of slander begins to attack me. If repentance in this life does not immediately sting me, tomorrow the ease of this vice—and, so to speak, a certain sweetness—will come upon me in such measure that I shall be unable either to recall myself from it or to restrain myself. Thus it happens that one who did not wish to amend at first begins afterward neither to wish nor to be able to do so.

For example, I began to yield to pride, violated the rule, injured an elder, and brought down a junior. If I did not immediately repent that I had been overtaken so gravely, then from day to day the very force of habit and the impulse of passion will most willingly carry me away, so that I will no longer understand that I am doing wrong or feel that I am sinning.

The burden of wrongdoing and the continual practice of sin obscure and overwhelm the understanding. The heart becomes so hardened by negligences that, unless a person humbles himself and makes satisfaction to his superior [Note: Perhaps “to his superior,” rather than “to his purpose”], he thinks that he is doing harm; moreover, he insults him and says: “How firmly I resisted him! How well I refused to yield! With what authority I answered him! He thought I ought always to humble myself before him.”

It is clear that one who does this has handed himself over captive to the devil, who rejoices in the vices, passions, and destruction of human beings. Such a soul will experience the sentence: “The sinner adds to sinning” (Ecclus. III, 29).

Let us, dearest brothers, flee this sentence and instead hold fast to the one that says: “And let the holy be sanctified still” (Rev. XXII, 11). Let us add daily to our merits and presume nothing about ourselves, because everything we can do belongs to God. Let us therefore be brothers unceasing in the work of God, for the sake of eternal recompense, and let us strive daily toward better things.

For the very eagerness to seize what lies ahead, and the very practice of progress, will always call us on toward greater things. When God sees a more ardent devotion of soul, He will inspire affection; as much as we add to our zeal, so much will He add to our assistance; as much as we add to diligence, so much will He add to glory.

“To him who has, it will be given, and he will abound” (Matt. XIII, 12). And in another place he says: “I have placed help upon the mighty” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 20).

Thus grace is born from grace, and progress serves progress; gains make gains, and merits make merits profitable [Note: Perhaps “make room”], so that the more someone begins to acquire, the more he strives and delights in seeking, and the gain of acquisition nourishes the appetite for acquiring.

The more eagerly someone draws from the goods of wisdom, the more he desires to draw, just as Wisdom herself says concerning herself: “Whoever eats me will hunger still.”

Let us therefore press forward, dearest brothers, along our course, so that our life may grow at its end. Let us seek to the end the means by which we may deserve to rejoice without end.

But suppose that we cannot perform bodily labors. Let us devote ourselves to the desire for spiritual goods, to an increase of compunction and charity. If we arrange ascents in our hearts daily, no weakness and no age can weary us, so that we may deserve to ascend by these spiritual steps to the promises of the Lord Jesus Christ.

HOMILY IV. To the Monks.

Since the Lord requires from us the duty of speaking because of the office we have undertaken, so from you, dearly beloved, he requires the disposition to listen. Thus, I say, it is fitting for your charity to obey what we say for your salvation, just as it is incumbent upon us not to remain silent. For if we fear offending through silence, how much more ought you to dread the same offense through contempt? If, I say, it is a great danger for us not to reprove what belongs to others, how much more dangerous is it not to correct what belongs to ourselves?

The blessed Apostle says in one place: “Consider your calling, brothers” (1 Cor. 1:26). Therefore, beloved, [Col. 0841C] let us also consider our calling. It is of no sufficient benefit that we have sought this place if here we are such as we could have been in the world. For if we look carefully, not only does this solitude compel us toward perfection, but the very multitude of the community also binds us to it. For just as it is precious and exceedingly important to live well in the midst of many and to stir many toward progress by the example of good works, so it is dangerous and destructive to break the faith of many and corrupt the souls of many by acting carelessly and lukewarmly. Just as it is fruitful to live commendably when placed among so many, so it is dangerous to have done anything destructive.

[Col. 0841D] Why do I say this? Because—and this is worse—we more easily find people who follow what is worse than what is better; for human weakness is more readily drawn to imitate evil. Therefore, let us not think it sufficient that we see ourselves gathered into this school, unless the perfection we have professed condemns our negligences in us all the more severely, since the profession we have undertaken does not excuse them. For, according to the testimony of Scripture, those who make many promises must necessarily be called to account for many things.

Oh, for how many this opportunity of the place and the suitability of this dwelling will be beneficial, and for how many, on the contrary, harmful! It is not living in this place that deserves praise, but acting well in this place. For what benefit does the seclusion of this dwelling provide when wickedness reigns in us with tyrannical domination, when anger rides over us, when the human eye sees us as fearing it more than the divine eye; [Col. 0842A] when we, those admirable hermits who believe ourselves to be outside the world, keep the world enclosed within us through the vices of various passions, so that although we thought that by our prayers we could come to the aid of the world itself, we almost find that we need the world’s intercessions more?

There is no doubt that the soul which, through desire for worldly pleasures, becomes the possession of worldly conduct cannot become the kingdom of Divinity. Therefore, brothers, consider your calling. To come to the desert is indeed the highest perfection; but not to live perfectly in the desert is the highest condemnation.

[Col. 0842B] What benefit is it if a place of rest is occupied only bodily, while unrest dwells in the heart? What, I ask, does it profit if there is silence in the dwelling, but among its inhabitants there is the tumult of vices and the conflict of passions? If serenity possesses our outward selves, but tempest our inward selves? We have not come together in this place so that the world might serve us, or so that, abounding in all things, we might enjoy complete repose. We have come here not for rest, not for security, but for battle; we have advanced to the contest; we have hastened to wage war against our vices: so that we may blunt the swords of our tongues, not merely refrain from inflicting injuries upon one another, but not even feel those inflicted upon us.

[Col. 0842C] More particularly, this belongs to our profession: to seek no consolation in this life, no rest; not to wish to receive good things during one’s lifetime, but to flee honors, to rejoice in submission and lowliness, to seek poverty deliberately, and to eradicate from our hearts not only possessions but even desires themselves. For sometimes to possess nothing is a matter of necessity; to desire nothing, however, is a matter of virtue. Therefore the religious person must especially impose this rule upon himself: to possess as much as necessity demands, not as desire craves.

For unless the love of possessing is cut away completely, it burns more fiercely in small matters, and people are tormented more over the least things. And unless you are poor in heart and in desire, poverty itself must be judged not a virtue but a misery.

Let us therefore understand, brothers, that it is of no benefit if we afflict our flesh with fasts and vigils but do not amend our minds or care for what is within. For what does bodily affliction profit if we defile our tongue with wickedness and slander? [Col. 0842D] Are not all our labors reduced to nothing? Does not our work vanish like smoke and shadow, and is it not reduced to nothing like the ash of stubble? Oh, how many and how prolonged labors suddenly perish! How much good, frequently already acquired and stored up, is snatched from our hands while we neglect to guard what we strive to acquire!

Therefore we flatter ourselves in vain about the cross and bodily affliction if our exterior is exercised by holy labors while our interior is not cared for in relation to the passions. It is like someone making a statue golden on the outside but earthen within; or like a house built with magnificent skill, appearing on the outside painted in the most beautiful colors, but within full of serpents and scorpions.

[Col. 0843A] What does it profit that you afflict your body when your heart makes no progress? It is an extremely harsh and deeply lamentable condition to devote every effort to labor and receive no fruit after the labor; to fast and keep vigil and not correct one’s conduct. It is like someone who clears and cultivates the ground outside or around a vineyard but leaves the vineyard itself deserted and uncultivated, so that it produces thorns and thistles, although, if the cultivator had tended it, it could have brought forth from itself the most delightful fruits.

Recognize, therefore, dearly beloved, that bodily abstinence alone is not sufficient for obtaining eternal salvation, unless the soul’s fasting also has been satisfied [possibly: joined] through abstinence from vices. For what does it help if someone is chaste in body but polluted in mind? [Col. 0843B] If malice deforms him, if the fury of anger drives him with torches, if pride strips him of every grace of God, if his tongue stains him with lies or curses—is he not deceiving himself, mocking himself, and deluding himself if he believes that he can be sanctified by fasts and vigils alone?

Therefore, beloved, let us exercise the body with fasts in such a way that we cleanse the mind from vices. Let us continually contemplate the coming of that Judge—may he find us prepared in the manner in which no one can doubt that he will come. And if you ask how he will come: he will come in that very body which he assumed for our salvation, which was handed over on account of our crimes, condemned for our acquittal, and pierced with spear and nails as the remedy for our wounds.

For the first intolerable sentence against the guilty will be the presence of the revered scars. What, then, shall we do at that time, when the marks of our sins and the stains of our lusts are brought forward against those bruises of the crucified Lord? Or with what expression, do you think, will our redemption look upon our destruction? Human offenses will be all the more serious insofar as divine benefits have shown themselves to be greater.

[Col. 0843C] We must fear that he will also bring forth in his judgment that voice of the resurrection, bearing witness to the precious traces of the cross, and say to the vessels of iniquity: “Put your finger here, and see my hands; and bring your hand and put it into my side” (John 20:27), and recognize what I, human impiety, endured for you and from you.

[Col. 0843D] Those marks of the nails—salutary to the good, terrifying to the wicked—which do not cause pain until the day of judgment, are undoubtedly being kept to be brought forward. And what follows after this except that dreaded chaos interposed between the living and the dead, that vast separation: the outer darkness, shut out from the nature of the living; harsh separation from the sweet vision of the saints and from the fellowship of the faithful [possibly: blessed]; and, on the other side, amid the tearful groans and laments of mourners, the sad company of the wretched and eternal exile from the blessed homeland into the most terrible night?

How mournful it will be for a human being to see God, and lose him, and perish before the sight of his own price! Therefore, dearly beloved, while there is time, considering these things, let us labor with tireless zeal, so that the Judge, when he comes to judge, may find intact in us what he bestowed upon us when he was judged.

## HOMILY V. To the Monks

[Col. 0844A]

We certainly know that a great reward is laid up in the future for the spiritual warfare to which we have devoted ourselves. But if we look carefully, even in the very work that we are doing [possibly: that we do], we possess, in a certain way, a share of the reward already in the present. It is plainly a great fruit of life to have been able to despise the world and to have begun to serve God; to have escaped the most wretched domination of vices and fled the foulest slavery of gluttony and luxury.

[Col. 0844B] What, then? Is it not already a great part of the reward to have nothing in common with the world, not to be tormented by desires for vain things, not to be mixed up in crimes, to spend the day in innocence, to devote oneself to blessed chastity, and to possess, with fear of the Lord, the sufficiency of glorious poverty? Concerning this Wisdom says: “Better is a little portion with fear of the Lord than great treasures without fear” [cf. Prov. 15:16].

Let us therefore understand how much the Lord has bestowed upon us through his gracious calling. Let us count, if we can, from the time when we seem to have been preserved here, how much profit we have gained: from how many frauds, how many adulteries, robberies, perjuries, and sacrileges we have been freed. Then we shall see how much we also owe the Lord for his present benefits.

[Col. 0844C] If we were now in the world, what else would we be doing than rolling about in our evils and daily defiling our souls with stains, being daily pierced by wounds—and doing so without even perceiving it? For sinful habit has this unhappy character: the more someone sins, the less he understands his sins, and the more he takes pleasure in sinning. Thus what the prophet cries to sinners comes to pass: “There is no God” [possibly: “There is no Lord”] “before his eyes; your judgments are removed from his sight” (Ps. 9:26). For when the pleasure of sinning steals upon a person, forgetfulness immediately conceals the day of future judgment.

On the contrary, the more concerned someone is about himself, the more he fears, as Scripture says: “The wise man, by fearing, turns away from evil” (Eccl. 1:16). The wise person, therefore, is always in compunction and always in fear. Just as he sighs over past evils, so he trembles with vigilant concern over future dangers. He who is anxious about the past reflects and turns this over within himself: perhaps he has not sufficiently mourned his past; perhaps he has not yet made satisfaction for his countless debts; perhaps he has placed new wounds upon his former iniquities; perhaps he has stamped still more recent crimes upon the ancient stains of his conscience; perhaps he assumed the name of this way of life in order to sin more grievously under a sacred profession.

[Col. 0844D] Some of us think it sufficient that we have climbed to this secluded place, changed our location and manner of life, and lived here for some time, placing all our hope in the number of years. And so, deceiving ourselves by a destructive persuasion, we think that we have settled all our debts; we think that our evils have vanished through the passage of time. And because we have forgotten them, we believe that they have escaped the memory of divine severity.

[Col. 0845A] But it is not so. Everything is collected with him; everything is stored up and marked with him. Let us hear what blessed Job says, he who fought hand-to-hand in single combat with the devil himself: “You have sealed up my sins as in a bag” (Job 14:17). And again the Lord himself says: “Are they not gathered together and sealed up in my treasuries?” (Deut. 32:34).

Let us not think that crimes once branded upon the soul and impressed by a deep wound into its very inmost parts can be forgiven so easily. Much weeping, much groaning, and much sorrow of heart are needed to heal the pains of the heart itself. We must devote ourselves entirely to contrition of spirit, so that ancient evils may be driven from the conscience like arrows.

It is not sufficient to say with one’s lips alone: “I have sinned; spare me; forgive me.” Saul also said, “I have sinned” (1 Sam. 26:21), but [Col. 0845B] he did not obtain the forgiveness which David merited by a single utterance of repentance. Why was this? Because that confession was expressed more by bare words than by genuine groaning. His cheerful humiliation as a suppliant did not correspond to the magnitude of his crime.

We must not act with a light contrition, as though those debts for which eternal death is owed could be redeemed by it. Nor is a passing satisfaction sufficient for those evils on account of which eternal fire has been prepared.

If we wish to understand how seriously our Judge regards the sins of human beings, let us look to the punishments. As patient as our God now is in bearing our offenses, so severe will he be in examining them. And just as he has prepared immeasurable glory for the just, so he has prepared immeasurable punishment for the wicked. Therefore, let us infer the severity of punishments from the greatness of the rewards themselves. For the one who knows how to reward merits also knows how to punish offenses.

[Col. 0845C] The remembrance of future judgment, the recollection of past offenses, and the lamentation of sins are therefore most healthful and greatly necessary. But if there is someone who flatters himself with the merits of an unharmed past life, and thinks that he came into the Lord’s service still innocent, and therefore believes that he ought to be secure, let such a person consider how uncertain and slippery are the ends of life, concerning which it is said: “Do not praise anyone during his lifetime” (Ecclus. 11:30). And when he has considered this, even if he thinks that he has nothing in the past for which to mourn, he will find in the future something to fear.

[Col. 0845D] Let no one, therefore, be secure about the past. So many snares are set before the feet of our soul; so countless are the enemies who watch and guard our path; so many are the pits and precipices; so many difficulties of circumstance lie between us and our end. The road itself, which is narrow and steep by nature, is besieged by so many ambushes of spiritual robbers. We must cross and face so many reefs and waves before we may finally cast our anchor on the desired shore. Yet we think that we ought to be secure about the past and pass our day without daily care, without daily fear and trembling!

Who, while crossing the depths of a river over the narrow span of a very narrow bridge, would think himself already out of danger, even if he had traversed most of it with an untroubled step, when in the final stretch of the bridge, if he wavered even slightly, he would suffer the fall he had feared in the middle of the crossing? [Col. 0846A] So even if a large part of this life seems to have been passed successfully, let us not therefore presume upon confidence, since danger still threatens in the final portion.

Who, stationed in battle, lays down his arms before the end of the contest or before the security of victory? Let no one, therefore, judge himself secure before he reaches the end in a happy completion.

Nor should we think this sufficient for complete salvation: that we are counted among God’s servants by our dwelling or reckoned among them by name; that we seem to live on an island and to flourish among monks. For our God cries out to us: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 7:21). Why is this? Because “it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law will be justified” (James 1:22; Rom. 2:13).

[Col. 0846B] Therefore, even if we have lived well, we must commend our course by steadfastness and perseverance, remaining and progressing in the place of our calling. I tell you truly: even if we had devoted twenty or thirty years to the Lord here—and we certainly know that we owe him entirely whatever life we possess—and even if we spent only one year adequately in the world, it would be immeasurable how much we would defraud ourselves of the joys of eternal life. For all our hope rests upon completion and the end.

What does it profit me if my green crops, standing in the grass, show me the hope of a harvest, yet at the very time of harvest deceive me through a sudden change of weather or an inundation of rains? What will it profit me if a vineyard promises all its hope in its blossom, but either the attack of wild animals or the destruction caused by hail removes all hope before completion? Therefore every success, and the whole outcome of labors, rests upon the end.

[Col. 0846C] But if those are to be mourned who, after many wages of labor and some progress over the years, are drawn away from here by certain desires, what will become of those who think four or five years here an extremely long time and spend the entire course of the rest of their life in the vanity of the world? A single year in the world can consume the labors acquired in the desert just as the great sea might receive and swallow up a tiny stream within itself, leaving it not even its name.

I do not know for what gains we wish to live in that world. For where it is considered a great loss not to acquire something every day, there it must be considered a great gain not to lose what has been acquired. Where, I say, it is considered serious damage not to make progress every day, there the highest virtue is not to perish.

[Col. 0846D] Therefore, if we are still weak and poor, let us labor here to acquire something. But if we have acquired something, let us take care here to preserve it. This alone will be our advantage and joy: that we have lived here for the Lord.

Therefore, as long as we remain here, it is within our choice when we wish to turn toward the world. But once we have turned away, it will already be difficult, almost impossible, to look back in thought toward this place.

If someone therefore thinks himself secure because he can someday leave this place, since he has run well here and labored much here, such a person acts as though someone were to release a ship laden with merchandise from the harbor, hand it over to storms, and steer it toward reefs and rocks.

[Col. 0847A] The more we labor, therefore, the more cautious we must be. For the enemy lies in wait for those who are making progress. Wherever he sees some hope, some grace, there, like a roaring lion prowling around to attack its prey, he concentrates all his strength. And because he cannot prevail against those established here, he wishes through thoughts and various temptations to lead some who are less cautious out of this place, as though outside the camp, and to cast them down from a most strongly fortified citadel. Once he has cast them down, he fights them as if from a higher position, so that even if he cannot sink the ship, he may at least carry away a most delightful prey from the losses and damages that abound in the world.

First he will inject various intentions, resentments, and hostile feelings, so that while a person strives to carry out what he once resolved and determined in anger, he does not consider his loss or look toward his ruin. And once he has cast him down [possibly: cast him down with that], remorse no longer follows in any way.

[Col. 0847B] Here we are, but we are not wholly here. For either we are driven by diverse, evil, and shameful thoughts of the heart, or we are wounded by the poisonous swords of the tongue; we take offense at the smallest and most insignificant matters; sometimes even—we who are monks ought not do this—we break out into quarrels and disputes. Sometimes we violate our profession by transgressing the rule, not fearing to commit theft against our superiors—or rather, to commit it against our own souls under the eyes of God. What we are ashamed to do in the presence of our superiors, we are not afraid to commit under the eyes of God.

[Col. 0847C] We are not content with necessities, but, through the lukewarmness of our hearts, we again desire the abundance we left in the world. Thus it is not enough that we have excluded from ourselves whatever possessions we may have had, when the desires themselves have remained within us.

This is why we are sometimes aroused by the smallest things and stir up the basest intentions for the appetite of worthless objects. Why is this? Because although we have left external goods in outward possessions, we still retain interior evils in our hearts. And how our adversary rejoices when he sees us despising the greatest things only to be defeated more shamefully in the smallest!

Therefore it is of no benefit to cast away what was placed outside unless what has adhered within the very inmost parts of the soul is also torn out by the roots.

[Col. 0847D] Thus the Apostle did not say that gold or silver is the root of all evils, but rather “the desire for riches” (1 Tim. 6:20); and not only the rich, but also “those who desire to become rich,” fall into temptation and a snare (1 Tim. 6:9). The Apostle therefore attacks not only those who possess, but the very will to possess.

Consequently, a person makes no progress by abandoning what is outside himself [possibly: what he has outside himself] if he keeps vices within himself. Therefore, as I said, brothers, we are here, but we are not wholly here. If we scarcely resist when placed within these walls, what will we do when exposed in the world? How will those be able to stand amid the waves, in the very assault of contending storms, who are in such grave danger in the harbor?

[Col. 0848A] Therefore, insofar as we can, let us be steadfast. In this most tranquil harbor, no matter how negligent or lukewarm he may have been, whoever reaches the palm of completion through perseverance has not run in vain.

## HOMILY VI. To the Monks

We have come together in this place, brothers, so that we may be free for our Lord, not for those things in which our enemy takes pleasure. It is certain that whenever we speak of matters belonging to the world, or bite one another with excessive murmuring and slander, he rejoices that our hours are being taken away from God and acquired for himself.

What does it profit that we wear ourselves out with precious vigils and labors while we do not possess what our God desires above all? That is, a pure heart, free from these petty negligences; for anyone who does not guard against them gradually falls away and slips into greater things.

[Col. 0848B] Let us therefore strive above all to possess what our Lord expects in us: gentle and kind speech; a mind free from every curse and every malice; and, while avoiding those things by which the Holy Spirit is offended, devotion to humility, quietness, and charity [alternative: “devoting himself”]. These are the chief sacrifices, these the rich holocausts that ascend before the Lord as an odor of sweetness.

Let us also take the greatest care that whatever we do in honor of our Lord, we do with a clear mind, with the joy of faith, and with the good and devout affection of the will.

[Col. 0848C] Whatever we do unwillingly and under compulsion, let us understand that from it we not only gain no fruit, but incur the greatest loss. Suppose we were to offer service to some powerful man, as people of superior rank are accustomed to expect from their clients. If that man were to see us performing the service owed to him with an unwilling and forced spirit, and even displaying a certain disdain, would he not judge that an injury had been done to him? Would he not declare that he had been dishonored rather than honored, and believe that such negligent and undevoted conduct deserved offense rather than gratitude?

If, then, the worship and honor of a human being require devotion, faith, and cheerfulness, then sometimes the one who offers the worship is better than the one who is worshiped, where the service itself produces no fruit but only this fruit: that the recipient may be deemed worthy to receive it.

How much more must we observe ourselves in honoring our God, so that we do not come to his service undevoted and compelled, sad, ungrateful, and unwilling; and so that God may not look upon gifts offered with a negligent and base spirit!

[Col. 0848D] For our faith has promised service not to a human being, but rather to him. To serve him even unto death, or to expend one’s very soul, ought to seem little in his sight; yet even the angels themselves confess that they are unequal to his services and benefits.

Although everything is owed to him in the end, nothing is nevertheless paid without recompense. As though he himself had in turn become a debtor, he returns a reward for the discharge of debts, and for small things he will restore immeasurable things.

[Col. 0849A] In exchange for this miserable life, full of labors and pains, in which use is brief and even that brevity uncertain—a life which, even if the devotion of our will hesitates to offer it to its author, the law of death will immediately exact from us; and what is not given by choice is paid by debt—in exchange for this life, he will give that life which cannot be seen by the eye or reached by the silent thought of the mind.

To attain this life is easier than to describe it. Its course will be without end, its use without weariness, its refreshment without need of assistance from itself, its rest without the inactivity of night, its age without old age, its unfailing brightness beneath the face of God, and, amid ancient and everlasting joys, a delight always new, a secure happiness without any danger of loss.

[Col. 0849B] Let us therefore now strive to taste in advance, even in this body, the sweetness of that life by thinking daily about those future ages. Having expelled from our senses the bitterness of worldly conversations and desires, let us draw toward ourselves with our whole hearts a certain fragrance of that blessedness. Casting off all torpor and all sluggishness, whose mother is unbelief, let us serve the Lord our God with that cheerfulness and that eagerness, and with that joy with which, at his invitation, we shall come to his gifts.

## HOMILY VII. To the Monks

Those who have decided to live among many people do so either with great benefit or with great danger, whether they are diligent or negligent. Therefore happy is the soul which, while living well in the community, becomes the joy of many, and through which very many are either built up or enlightened. For when many share in its goodness, that goodness increases.

[Col. 0849C] The saying of that wise man also refers to this: “My son, if you are wise, you will be wise for yourself and for your neighbors” (Prov. 9:12).

Therefore, if someone placed in the community has maintained obedience and shown himself humble and patient, how many he has built up, to so many has he lent at interest; and as much good as he has bestowed upon his neighbors from himself, so much has he converted into his own gain.

But if, on the contrary, through his disobedience or pride he has driven others toward defilement [alternative: evil]—as more easily tends to happen—how many has he destroyed, from so many does he incur the danger of condemnation; to as many as he was a loss, from so many does he contract losses. And the sin that once proceeded from him has returned upon him many times over.

Therefore, just as the person whose course is the progress of many is greatly to be admired and praised, so the person whose life is the ruin of many is rightly to be mourned.

[Col. 0849D] Therefore, dearly beloved, let us strive, when placed among others, to do those things that pertain to edification: lest our vices harm the virtues of others; lest our lukewarmness weaken the fervor of others; lest our anger violate the patience [of their virtues] of others; lest our pride corrupt the humility of others; lest our weakness corrupt the health of others; lest our ugliness defile the beauty of others; lest we extinguish the burning lamps of others if we cannot light our own.

[Col. 0850A] Those foolish virgins, foolish though they were, nevertheless did not wish to extinguish the lamps of others but to light their own. Therefore, in imitation of them, if any one of us lacks the richest grace—humanity, the fire of faith, the flame of fervor, the oil of charity, or the light of discernment—let him go to those whom he sees to possess these more abundantly, and let him transmit the grace of his neighbor to himself not by taking it away, but by imitating it; let him seize the good belonging to another without harming its possessor, indeed with the possessor’s profit.

For what benefits another through you will never be lacking to you. A fire kindled for many has never felt the loss of its light, nor has the multitude of those who gaze upon it diminished the sun’s light. As many as look toward it, so many receive its gifts, while it itself always remains whole.

[Col. 0850B] Blessed by God is that soul whose humility confounds another’s pride; whose patience extinguishes the anger of a neighbor; whose obedience silently reproves another’s laziness; whose fervor arouses the inertia of another’s lukewarmness; and which illuminates, by the grace of consolation and edification, the eye of the heart troubled by anger in a neighbor.

Better is this person than the one who, when a brother has been slightly saddened by someone, not merely raises him up by extending a hand, but rather assists him in falling, like a leaning wall, by pushing him with evil speech; and, when he has been rebuked for the sake of discipline, urges him on by evil counsels so that he may strike him down, arms him so that he may destroy him.

Therefore, brothers, if a person’s own evils are not sufficient for him, let him act in such a way that he also incurs judgment for another’s destruction.

It is certain, dearly beloved, that unless we daily cut off and circumcise our passions here, we will become far worse than we were when we lived in the world, so that our last state will be worse than the first.

## HOMILY VIII. To the Monks

[Col. 0850C]

If at any time a farm laborer and cultivator of the countryside prepares his field with seeds, he does not think it enough to have broken up the rough ground with the plow, subdued the hard clods with the continual plow, and finished it with frequent furrows. Rather, he additionally strives to cleanse that field of unfruitful shoots [Alternative reading: grasses], to empty it of the harmful rubble of thorns, and to tear out the sources of growth by shaking them loose from the root, knowing that his soil cannot be fertile in good produce without the purging of harmful growth. He considers that saying addressed to the spiritual farmer to apply to him: “Break up new ground for yourselves, and do not sow upon thorns” (Jeremiah 4:3; Hosea 10:12).

So also we, who have become God’s field [Col. 0850D], who do not entrust the hope of our fruits to the earth but have it stored up in heaven, must not think it enough to subdue the soil of our body by exercises of vigils or to exhaust it by the labor of fasts. Rather, let us strive above all to cleanse the mind by uprooting vices, to prune our habits, cut away our passions, eradicate pride, plant humility, dig out anger, establish patience, amputate envy, graft in benevolence, and by virtues of this kind make the field of the heart fertile, as it were, with seeds of good harvest.

Otherwise, if the flesh is worn down but the soul bears no fruit, it is as though the field never ceased to be plowed, yet a harvest never appeared. Therefore, if we are not cleansed inwardly while being afflicted outwardly [Col. 0851A], then, as far as I can see, we undertake hostilities against both. We impose so much labor upon ourselves for the sake of the soul, yet expend no effort upon the soul itself. We have forbidden ourselves the various pleasures of the world and the diverse flavors of delights, in which there was some enjoyment and sweetness; yet now we cannot abstain from pride, anger, and the poisonous passions of envy, in which there is nothing except whatever bitterness and rancor consist of.

For love of our Lord we were exceedingly brave in abandoning sweet affections and beloved pledges. We fled from the most delightful and most pious faces of our parents as though we hated them. In a way, we declared war upon piety itself; yet now, when it comes to avoiding negligence and conquering the lightest [Alternative reading: gentlest] vices, we are weak and sluggish. In renouncing the world’s pleasure [Col. 0851B] we undertook great things, and now we think it impossible—and beyond human strength—to overcome cursing, slander, anger over trivial matters, anger even against another person, and the taking of offense.

Yet we do not blame our own vices for the fact that we now yield in lesser matters. For we demonstrate that whatever we are doing now is not a matter of inability but of sluggishness. Therefore, brothers, let us look back to that faith and fervor with which we began, and, at least in adorning the practice of our way of life, let us take an example from our beginnings. If it is dangerous not to have added something every day, how much more dangerous is it even to have retreated from our beginnings?

It is therefore necessary that spiritual fruit—that is, the correction of conduct—follow bodily labor. The vices that attack both the inner and outer person [Col. 0851C] must be conquered and defeated by each person’s labor. Bodily mortification accomplishes little if there is no concern for the heart and attentiveness of the mind.

But if the body alone labors while our spirit resists, what benefit is there in passions being attacked by a servant-girl who is found to be at peace with her mistress? It is less serious if the flesh alone is sometimes harassed by various assaults—for example, if the appetite is disturbed by the goads of gluttony and lust. It can happen that the danger does not reach the whole person, if the mind rejects the pleasure.

But if the desire for sin occupies the citadel of the mind, what benefit is it to me if the outward person still appears undefiled, while the better part of him has been corrupted? For if the inner person has been conquered, both are already captive.

[Col. 0851D] What benefit is there if we wage war outside the city while suffering destruction within? Therefore, if, when I return from the vigils, the passion of disobedience receives me; if the spirit of envy receives me; if the habit of slander receives me; if furtive presumption urges me toward transgression of the rule; and if I have mixed weeds with the wheat, dispersing what I seemed to have gathered, then I have handed over the hope of the harvest to birds and wild beasts. Thus, in a single moment I have poured out the labor of the whole night—and, what is worse, I have not even realized that I poured it out.

Such is the condition of spiritual goods: although they are acquired with the greatest labor, they perish so easily that scarcely anyone can understand it. Hence it is that we sometimes consider ourselves holy, because we reckon the gains from our labors but are unable to detect the subsequent losses. [Col. 0852A]

Oh, how often we incur, without noticing it, the evil of judgment and the disease of vanity and boasting! How often we are burned by the spirit of envy, or are confounded by dishonorable and obscene thoughts even while they are present, and no awareness of pain follows our perception of the wound, no contrition of compunction! But why am I speaking of these hidden things, which, penetrating into the very soul by a kind of serpentine slipping, strike the unaware and ignorant with a poisonous tooth?

Sometimes we are struck by open battles of scandals arising from ourselves; we are stabbed by the slanders and evil words of our own tongue as though by our own sword. At times we are defiled even by vices directed against our superiors, and in their injuries we in a way strike the Lord Christ in the face, who said: “Whoever despises you despises me” [Col. 0852B] (Luke 10:16). Yet no prick of conscience, no medicine of compunction follows.

But why do I seek in us the medicine of repentance [Alternative reading: seek the groans of repentance]? Would that sometimes, after hoping for pardon, we did not regret it! Would that those who do not regret being anticipated did not regret being humbled! Let that soul answer me which was ashamed to acknowledge its sin before the brothers with a deadly shame, although it ought to have been ashamed to avoid the sin: what will it do when it has been brought before the divine tribunal, before the assembly of the heavenly host?

When it begins to be pressed from every side as though by the most powerful witnesses, surrounded by the ancient evils that it refused to cure through the remedy of humility and compunction while there was still time—evils that, by concealing and hiding them from its superiors [Col. 0852C], it reserved intact for the eternal examination and the eternal Judge [Alternative reading: will reserve them intact]—then what will it do?

Therefore, whoever weeps over and exposes his faults and negligences, even those considered small, in the present accusation should know that he has passed swiftly out of eternal punishment.

If, then, we wish the most anxious vanity of the flesh, the hidden obscenity of dishonorable thought, the silent pleasure of the mind, and the irreverence of an unwary heart never to deceive or mislead us, let us first hasten to cut away from our conduct those things that are manifest: the appetite of gluttony, the movements of anger, the assaults of pride, swollen contradictions, and shameless slanders.

For how will we be able to foresee the hidden enemy if here we have not been able to avoid him when he fights us in open combat? Therefore, beloved [Col. 0852D], our warfare demands this of us: that we fight daily not against others but against ourselves, and that, constantly pursuing all our enemies within ourselves, we obtain from the Lord the palm of spiritual triumph.

Indeed, as long as we belonged to the world and were engaged in those acts and occupations of which we are now ashamed, our adversary did not hinder us; rather, he agreed with us, because, with regard to our wretched and ruined life, he found no occasion to exercise his envy. Our actions pleased him; our crimes were sufficient for him by themselves. Who would undertake war against his own soldier? Who would wish to attack his own subordinate? Beyond every misery was the life of one whom the enemy did not [Col. 0853A] deign to harm.

But now, after we have renounced his pleasures, he sees his worshipers returning to the service of their former master. He sees his idols in a way being changed into temples of God. Gnashing his teeth and roaring like a lion, the ever-watchful ambusher examines every avenue of attack against us (1 Peter 5). He directs against us the forces of visions, bringing with him seven spirits more evil than himself, in case he should find our house empty and vacant of spiritual goods and be able to occupy it with his throngs, preparing a dwelling for himself there by placing former vices ahead of him like advance scouts.

For this reason, beloved, he employs a thousand devices against us. He attacks the younger and more foolish either with the shameful flatteries of gluttony or with the goads [Col. 0853B] of an untamed flesh, if he can pollute their understanding or honorable thoughts and carry off an ignoble [Alternative reading: noble] triumph through a wound to chastity.

But he tries to conquer the better and older by the evil of pride and boasting, through their very progress and merits, so that, by thrusting their years and merits before them, he may cut humility out of their hearts through the foulest vanity and—what is dangerous—persuade a person that he is pleasing to God.

There is, moreover, that common and familiar evil which arms against us the swords of our own tongues and inflames the goads of anger. In this way he intoxicates the mind with various passions, so that, when we are angry, slander, or curse, we think that we are harming others.

But it is not so, beloved [Col. 0853C], for the evil of every vice rebounds upon its own author. The evil-speaker stains his own tongue; the slanderer festers his own heart; the angry person blinds the light of his own mind; the envious person sprinkles his own soul with the poison of resentment. In this the saying of Solomon is also fulfilled: “My son, if you are wicked, you alone will bear the evil” (Proverbs 9:12).

Hence it happens, beloved, as I said, that we sometimes feel ourselves worse than we were in the world, because in the struggle we become instigators of evil, because in the midst of combat we give our hands to the enemy whom we ourselves procured [Alternative reading: provoked] by our way of life. We do not persevere in the fervor with which we began, but, overcome by sluggishness, we fall.

Therefore, the name of our great profession must be defended with great strength. Great indeed is what we promised [Col. 0853D] God by coming to the desert, however much we may hope to receive from God. Let us therefore examine all sluggishness, all weariness of mind, and let us practice this precious military service with precious devotion.

Let us not wait to be compelled to the service of our Lord like hired laborers and slaves, nor be content for another person to demand from us whatever we recognize as belonging to our salvation and glory. Above all, let us beware of doing unwillingly what we must do. Let us neither contradict before the work begins, nor murmur during the work, nor take pleasure in the completed work, with boasting deceitfully flattering us.

Above all, brothers, let us examine our negligences daily with the watchful eye of the heart, and, after dispelling the cloud of sluggishness, set them before our eyes, saying: “I acknowledge my sin, and my offense is always before me” (Psalm 50).

[Col. 0854A] It is a crime that the very habit of sinning sometimes makes our sins seem light and trivial to us, when it is certain that just as we are increased by the smallest good deeds, so we ought to be pierced with compunction over the smallest negligences. For it is no small thing to neglect small faults in human life [Alternative reading: among human vices].

I do not know what offenses people ought to feel secure about, since they will be judged even for sins of ignorance and will have to give an account of idle words and thoughts. I do not know what faults they ought to neglect, when the Lord himself declares with a certain definition: “Amen, I say to you, if anyone says to his brother, ‘Fool,’ he will be liable to the fire” (Matthew 5:22).

[Col. 0854B] Who could hope for any indulgence amid these things, unless our Lord’s mercy were as rich in forgiving as human beings are inclined to sin?

Let us therefore look back, brothers, to our calling. Let us walk in humility, in all patience, and in all gentleness. Let us set a guard over our mouths; let fear of the future judgment moderate anger; let thought of the final day break pride.

Let us consider what mourning will belong to the negligent soul departing from this body, what distress, what darkness, what gloom, when its own conscience, surrounded by various crimes, begins to come forward first from that number of adversaries. For it itself, once all other proofs have been removed, must be brought before our eyes, so that the proof may convict us and the recognition may shame us.

[Col. 0854C] No one will be allowed either to conceal or deny anything there, where the accuser and witness will proceed not from somewhere far away but from within.

Therefore, to infer that future shame from the present shame that commonly occurs among human beings, let us imagine that the offenses and hidden deeds of one of us were brought forward among us—things that are known inwardly to the heart. Truly, I say, he could not endure the faces of us all. What, then, will the wretched soul do when it is brought with its reproaches and foulness before the sight of the angels?

But the soul that has directed its course well, that has obeyed Christ in its superiors, and that has guarded its profession in every respect, will not fear the necessity of that final hour. To leave the dwelling of this body will seem to it as though, after long darkness in prison, it were led out into the light; as though [Col. 0854D] it were brought from some most obscure cavern into a royal hall; as though, drawn out of the pit of misery and the mire of filth, it were clothed in beautiful and splendid garments and placed amid the sweetness of flowers and perfumes, to be refreshed by marvelous fragrances.

Let us remember how pleasant rest is, how delightful repose is, after laying down the burden of some very heavy load. How sweet it is, after the chains of a long captivity, to return to one’s beloved homeland in recovered freedom. How precious it is, after the dangers of a long voyage, to reach the desired land and the wished-for harbor.

From these examples let us gather and understand how delightful it will be, accompanied by a good conscience, to pass into true and solid joys and into the fellowship of the angels, and to ascend to that life [Col. 0855A] where there will be no labors, no pains, no losses, no hardships—and, above every good, no sins; but eternal innocence, inviolate justice, unshaken security, and everlasting happiness.

## HOMILY IX. To the Monks

“See your calling, beloved brothers” (1 Corinthians 1:26). To come to the desert is the height of perfection; not to live perfectly in the desert is the height of condemnation.
