What benefit is there if quiet is maintained in the place while unrest moves within the heart? If there is silence in the dwelling but in the inhabitants there is a tumult of vices and a struggle of passions? If outwardly there is serenity while inwardly there is a storm? [Col. 0855B]

We are accustomed to count our years and the periods of time in which we now live. Whoever you are, do not let the number of days you have spent here after physically leaving the world deceive you.

Count yourself to have lived only that day on which you denied your own wishes and resisted evil desires. Count yourself to have lived the day that you conducted without any transgression of the rule; the day that malice, envy, and pride did not stain; that the fault of lying or perjury did not bespatter; that did not yield to sin and resisted the devil.

Count yourself to have lived the day that possessed the light of equality [possibly: parity] and holy meditation, the day that a dark way of life did not change into night. Apply that day, I say, to your life—the day whose use reached your soul.

[Col. 0855C] We are also accustomed to flatter ourselves about the constancy of bodily fasts and visible vigils, although after the vigils, and perhaps because of the vigils themselves, we go out into the evil of slander, loquacity, and murmuring.

The person who withdraws from the choir of those singing psalms [Alternative reading: from care] to shameful feasts and secret drinking—not only by a blameworthy transgression but also with contemptible baseness—would fare much more lightly if he slept while sobriety ruled him.

The person who fasts while carrying a chest burdened and weighed down by anger and the tension of indignation; who abstains from wine yet is troubled in his thoughts by the bitter drunkenness of discord; who, I say, torments himself outwardly by a salutary moderation in drinks while his inward heart belches forth the deadly poison of hatred from infected vitals [Col. 0855D]—does he not understand that the prophetic words are already directed against him in this present life, as one condemned beforehand: “I have not chosen such a fast, says the Lord” (Isaiah 58:5)?

Or again: “For from the vine of Sodom is their vine, and their vines are from Gomorrah. Their grape is a grape of gall, and their cluster is bitterness in them” (Deuteronomy 32:32).

Sometimes, then, when the devil notices a soul empty of faith and stripped of the fear of God, he intoxicates the mind with various passions, so that, when we curse, become angry, or slander, while doing these things we think that we are harming others.

But it is not so. For the evil of every vice returns upon its own author, as the divine word says: “My son, if you are wicked, you alone will bear the evil” [Col. 0856A] (Proverbs 9:12). The evil-speaker stains his own tongue; the slanderer festers his own heart; the angry person blinds the light of his own mind; the envious person corrupts his own soul, as though with a kind of rust, through poisonous resentment.

And just as vipers are said to be born from wounded parents, just as, I say, the offspring of vipers are said to be born by tearing apart their mothers’ wombs, so the human inward parts are first torn apart by the very passions they have conceived. Those inward parts, I say, from which the serpentine generation of vices is brought forth, are themselves first violated by the monstrous fertility of the birth [Alternative reading: by the offspring of the birth].

Of such a birth the divine word says: “Behold, he is in labor with injustice, he has conceived sorrow, and he has given birth to iniquity. His pain will return upon his own head, and his iniquity will descend upon his own crown” (Psalm 7).

After hearing these things, the spirit of our fervent charity [Col. 0856B] toward you, as it ought, was tormented by prolonged grief over certain negligences. [Alternative: After expressing this affection,] and having discharged some of the burdens of our troubled hearts, we command, admonish, and also beg you on your own behalf—if indeed you do not disdain to hear the affection of one giving commands—that from now on we correct our conduct and amend our negligences, lest later we come here not with the rod of tongue and speech but with those scourges that hardened [Alternative reading: stopped-up] hearts demand.

Rather, work from now on so that among yourselves you may contend in commendable rivalry and, at last, in a better emulation. Let each one of you be more prompt in God’s work, more fervent in prayer, more attentive in reading, purer in chastity, more sparing in sobriety [Col. 0856C], more lavish in the abundance of tears, more honorable in body, more sincere in heart, milder in anger, more moderate in gentleness, rarer in laughter, more fervent in compunction, more firmly grounded in seriousness, and more joyful in charity. [Alternative readings: “who among you”; “whoever in prayer”; “whoever”; the variants affect the syntax but not the exhortation.]

Therefore, let us ourselves discipline ourselves; let each of us daily reckon with himself concerning his daily conduct. Let each soul address itself in the secrecy of its heart and say:

“Let us see whether I have passed this day without sin, without envy, without slander and murmuring. Let us see whether today I have done anything that contributed to my own progress or to the edification of others. I think that today I destroyed a beginner; today I was disobedient to my elder; I lied; I swore falsely [Alternative reading: committed perjury]; I was overcome by anger or gluttony; today I laughed too much [Col. 0856D]; I indulged more than was fitting in food and drink, in idleness and sleep; I read less and prayed less than I ought.

“Who will give me back this day, which I have lost in empty tales?”

And so, brothers, let us be pierced with compunction over all our negligences in our beds (Psalm 4), that is, in our hearts. If you act in this way, we will indeed rejoice [Alternative reading: be made joyful] over your progress, but you will rejoice over the salvation you have gained; and you will make us your debtors for the acquisition of your salvation.

May his goodness grant that you profit so greatly from our speech that, in turn, you may assist us by your merits, and may be our adornment in the present [life] and our protection in the future [Alternative reading: in the future].

## HOMILY X. To the Monks

[Col. 0857A]

The divine word says in one place: “On the days of your solemnities, afflict your souls” (Leviticus 16:29; 23:27). Why did he say this? Because fasts, vigils, and holy afflictions weaken humbled bodies but purify stained hearts. They take strength away from the limbs but add brightness to consciences; for by contrition crimes of pleasure are redeemed. Through the exercises of the hard cross, the joys of the flesh that formerly deceived us are punished.

Thus, by present mortification, the sentence of future death is anticipated; while the author of the fault is humbled, the fault is consumed; and while outward affliction of voluntary severity is imposed, the offense of the fearful judgment [Col. 0857B] is appeased. A small labor pays immense debts that eternal fire would scarcely have consumed.

Therefore, as we consider the matter of our salvation, let us do within ourselves what physicians ordinarily do around us. If some injury or complaint is felt on the outermost skin of the body, a gentler medicinal treatment is applied. But if a wound has been hidden in the bones or has sunk deep into the viscera, the concealed force demands a harsher and more powerful medicine, so that the magnitude of the ulcer may be healed either by cauterization, or pain driven out by pain.

A similar method must be applied to the sickness of the inner person. If the offenses are perhaps light—for example, if someone has sinned in speech, or in some blameworthy intention, with the eye or with the heart—the stains of words and thoughts must be cured by daily prayer and wiped away by private compunction. [Col. 0857C]

But if anyone, examining his conscience within, has committed some capital crime; or if he has attacked and betrayed his faith by false testimony; if he has violated the sacred name of truth through the recklessness of perjury; if he has stained the veil of baptism or the tunic, and then also the beautiful silk garment of virginity, with the filth of defiled modesty; if he has killed the new person in himself—[the text is materially uncertain here: “hece hominis” is corrupt in the supplied text]; if through augurs, diviners, and enchanters he has handed himself over captive to the devil—such offenses and those like them cannot be completely expiated by ordinary and moderate satisfaction, or by private satisfaction. They require serious, more serious, and harsher public remedies, so that one who destroyed himself along with the destruction of many may redeem himself in a similar manner through the edification of many.

[Col. 0857D] A person deceives himself if, while feeling disease burning in his marrow, he applies a soft ointment over the surface of the body.

These principal evils therefore require a great roar, groan, and fountain of tears; and after weeping one must say with the prophet: “I roared from the groaning of my heart; every night I wash my bed” (Psalm 6). And again: “But I ate ashes like bread, and mixed my drink with weeping” (Psalm 101).

Let no one despise this humility. It was the supreme king who said these things; it was the supreme king who did these things.

Therefore, just as lamentation is raised over the dead, so great mourning must be offered over a soul that has been extinguished. And just as a bereaved mother [Col. 0858A] commonly laments the loss of her only child with a broken heart, so it is fitting to be afflicted over one’s only soul, but with hope of restoration.

Concerning this only one, the prophetic word says: “Deliver my soul from the sword, and my only one from the hand of the dog” (Psalm 21:21). Why did he say “only one”? Either because it must be loved as an only child, or because it alone and singly will render an account before the heavenly tribunal, with every other support removed.

Thus, I say, it is necessary to pour out the entire weight of sorrow over this only soul, pierced by the sword of crimes, if perhaps it may be revived by the warmth of faith through the life-giving fountains of tears. Compunction must be kindled; prayers must be strengthened by remembrance of the future judgment; they must be assisted by works of mercy.

The prophet’s pronouncement must be heard, but heard with the ear of obedience: “Receive my counsel, O king,” he says, “and redeem your sins with almsgiving” [Col. 0858B] (Daniel 4:24).

The example of that Gospel man must also be heard as though it had truly been written for our redemption: “Behold, Lord, I give half of my possessions to the poor” (Luke 19:8).

Of these matters we have heard the Lord say in the Gospel, with ineffable condescension and charity: “Whoever did it for one of these least ones did it for me” (Matthew 24). These words commend to us the effectiveness of almsgiving by heavenly authority.

But perhaps, when we speak of almsgiving, august poverty is afraid. It is not so, beloved. Rather, let it remember that the small coins were preferred to the treasures of the rich. For our God is nourished not only by the abundance of the gift but also by the goodwill of the giver.

I think, beloved, that our Lord allowed the poor to exist in this world so that he might test the faith of the rich through the poor [Col. 0858C], or might show mercy to the rich through mercy toward the poor. Thus, while good works abounded, this opportunity for redemption would not be lacking; the goodwill of the wealthy person might even be enriched by another’s poverty; and the richer person might receive immense profits from the needy.

By a wondrous and supreme exchange, while temporal generosity grants mercy to the needy, an eternal treasure is repaid to the giver.

Let us direct our actions, and whatever we can and whatever strength we possess, let us devote to exercises of good will and to the pursuits of justice and mercy. Let us run while we have the light, before darkness overtakes us (John 12:35), because in that world it will no longer be possible to provide for amendment and redemption.

As the divine word says: “For in death there is no one who remembers you” [Col. 0858D] (Psalm 6). Therefore, just as there will then be no fear of losing merits, so no forgiveness of sins will be granted. No opportunity to practice good works will be granted there.

Will anyone be able there to feed the hungry, where there will be no need to eat and drink; where neither the impious amid the flames of hell nor the righteous amid the delights of paradise will need food and drink?

Will anyone there be able to clothe the shivering, where all care for covering the body will cease; where, beneath that cold of which the prophet says, “Before his face, who can endure the cold?” [Alternative reading: “who can stand?”] (Psalm 147); where forever naked will be the one who here lost the wedding garment; where the wicked person will be clothed in the darkness of a stained conscience, but the good person in the cloak of immortality and blessedness? [Col. 0859A]

There garments will be merits, as the Lord says: “Then the righteous will shine”; and again: “Let your priests be clothed with righteousness” (Psalm 131); or as it says elsewhere: “The queen stood at your right hand in a garment of gold” (Psalm 44).

Where, therefore, eternal light will shine in place of a tunic for the bodies of the saints, there clothing will be transformed into the body, never to be removed throughout any ages; there a garment will become a reward; there that angelic robe will no longer be an outer covering or an attire, but nature itself.

Will the greedy or grasping person there be able to do good to another from his abundance, where he will not find even a single drop for himself in the midst of the burning pool?

For he will carry nothing with him of those things he believed he possessed, as the prophet said: “For when he dies, he will take nothing with him, nor will his glory descend [Col. 0859B] with him” (Psalm 48:18). He will hear amid his exhausted punishments: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food; I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink” (Matthew 25:42).

Let us understand what condemnation it will be to have stripped the poor person whom it is the highest crime not to have fed.

To the person who now oppresses the weak and needy without any consideration of the future judgment, to him, I say, as someone has said: “The time will come when he will wish that the poor man he hated had remained untouched by him and not been stripped.” And how intolerable will the pain be if someone incurs the causes of death from the very source from which he could have obtained the joys of life?

Therefore, do not despise the needy person who, although poor for himself, can make you rich. Let us seize from the present world, with fervent devotion, whatever we can.

Our days pass quickly [Col. 0859C]; may they pass well! Let us therefore seize whatever we can from this world, giving thanks to him who so ordered both lives that the times of labor and struggle would quickly end, while the joys of honors and rewards would last without end.

## HOMILY. On Saint Blandina of Lyons.

[Col. 0859D]

Even if we were to render to martyrs from a foreign region the pious dues of our vows, we would be shown to be consulting our own interests and advantages; faith would make them ours, and, however distant their boundaries, they would obtain for us the patronage we hoped for. Such intercessions belong to devotion, not to places; therefore, among God’s household, you will merit as much intercession as you have offered veneration. It is therefore necessary that religious devotion should win strangers for us, rather than, perhaps, the negligence of irreligious apathy estrange our own.

Let us recognize, dearest brethren, the richer abundance of divine gifts bestowed upon our Church. The peoples of individual cities rejoice even if they are fortified by the relics of a single martyr; but behold, we possess peoples of martyrs. Let our land rejoice, the nurse of heavenly soldiers and the fertile mother of such great virtues. Behold, the profane enemy could never have benefited it as much by his service as he has by his sword. For, as the festivals of this most sacred day plainly show, as much as iniquity abounded against it, so much grace and blessing now overflow within it.

[Col. 0860A]

We read that at Bethlehem, while Herod was persecuting Christ, thousands of blessed infants were slain, as the prophet says: “Rachel weeping for her children, and she refused to be comforted, because they are not” (Jer. XXXI, 15; Matt. II, 18). Thus this blessed mother, that illustrious homeland of triumphant warriors, rich in the merits of so many pledges, although she seemed to have been deprived of them in the sight of those who looked upon the monument, nevertheless has no need to be comforted and does not weep for her children: for, while losing them amid the sight of mourning, she acquired them.

Confidently, O land of Bethlehem of Judah, I would contend with you—you who endured Herod’s savagery in the slaughter of infants, and who, at a single time, were permitted to offer to God a radiant people of unwarlike infancy—and, worthy of the contest, our Lugdunum would contend with you and, as though in a conversation held with you, compete with you over the divine benefits bestowed upon both, saying:

[Col. 0860B]

“O Bethlehem, perhaps you surpass me in number in the records of our martyrs; I surpass you in merit. In yours there was slaughter, not confession; in mine there was the struggle of suffering. In yours, there was only the opportunity and occasion of blessedness; your end enriched you with blessing, mine with virtue. You were able to see the little ones perishing in their blood, but you could not await those who were struggling. Innocence crowned you through the dying; glory crowned me through the triumphant. Yours reached the reward of the kingdom without awareness of martyrdom; mine, afflicted by tortures, tested by punishments, and boiled in savage fires after the manner of sacrifice, received in the body as many punishments as they received crowns in the spirit. Thus, through the wounds of their torments and the delays of their torturers, they were consecrated before they were slain.

[Col. 0860C]

“You offered infants in years; I offered those perfected also in merits. I offered those who would conquer through their torments, though they could have been placed in danger concerning the faith; you offered those who could possess the fruit of dying, but could not fear the danger of denial. You offered a weak people, lest the sacrilegious persecutor find Christ; I offered a strong multitude, through whose example Christ might also gain sacrilegious men by saving the persecutors’ servants.

“Finally, in that blessed death by which Herod, while seeking the sacred child alone, sacrificed so many children, one sex earned your triumph, but both sexes earned mine. My struggle brought back the palm from the ruler of the world even among women. My choir could have your innocent children; your choir could not have my Blandina.”

[Col. 0860D]

Amid these events divine providence arranged that, in such sacrifices of the homeland, a bishop should not be absent. Our blessed Father Focinus, venerable with age and full of days, bishop of this Church, is dragged to an impious interrogation; and, as we believe, because of the merit of his learning, he is joined to his flock. After the sacrifice of the Lord’s body, he is brought before profane tribunals to offer Christ a new victim from himself. His aged weakness, through the outrages and afflictions inflicted by raging attendants, meets so swift an end that one would understand him to have been reserved for that moment solely by martyrdom. Blessed is he who, standing at the very threshold of life, was granted to owe his end not so much to nature as to glory.

[Col. 0861A]

Here devout minds are strengthened by the example of so great a father, and they receive the punishments prepared for them—or rather, they rush upon them. Diverse contrivances of manifold cruelty expend new tortures upon the invincible breasts of the saints; by despising the unbearable weight of evils they conquer it, and by experiencing them they obtain the power not to feel them. Fires are applied, but are found capable only of consecrating them; beasts are provoked, but their unfed ferocity marvels at [or: threatens] its prey. Limbs torn apart by various kinds of torture are sanctified by the flames, which do not know how to feed upon them; they are honored by the beasts, which do not know how to rage against them.

[Col. 0861B]

Where are those who say that veneration ought not to be offered to the sacred bodies of martyrs? Behold the savagery of bloody ferocity, which does not admit the meaning of religion, nevertheless offering the service of veneration; and, ignorant of rational discernment and therefore not receiving it, nevertheless recognizing, for the condemnation of evils, what honor is owed to the saints. Thus, in a wondrous manner, the ministry or instrument of punishment becomes a testimony to their merits; and, while showing reverence to piety, it pronounces a silent judgment upon impiety.

Since, then, dearest brethren, our Church is adorned with such trophies of faith, the law of iniquity was striving to surpass itself through the novelty of its crimes. Depriving the sacred bodies of the honor of burial, they committed them to the flames and, after the death of human beings, continued to wage war against humanity itself. Although the cause of their rage had already perished, they did not put an end to their cruelty; nevertheless, whether they wished it or not, they were witnesses of the blessedness of those whom they envied even after death.

[Col. 0861C]

How is malice always joined to folly? They reduced the venerable bones to ashes, as though merits could be consumed by flames and virtues burned up together with ashes. What confused madness! By those means through which the martyrs were acquiring heaven, they denied them earth.

Therefore, unheard-of savagery, you accomplished nothing. In vain did you believe that you could extinguish the memory of those whose glory you extended. You scatter the dust of the saints into the streams of the Rhône so that it may not rise again; but resurrection is not consumed by waters, since it is celebrated also through the gift of water by the grace of regeneration. You entrust relics to be worshiped to the Rhône: the force of the river does in the dissolution of the body what time does. Whatever a bird carries away from human substance, whatever a beast devours, whatever a wave swallows—even if it is not enclosed in a tomb—is contained within the bosom of the world.

[Col. 0861D]

For the restoration of man does not consist in the constitution of the earth, but in the nature of the law and in the power of the Restorer. For he himself testified with truthful mouth: “I am the resurrection and the life” (John XI, 25), who lives for ever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY. On the holy martyrs Ephipodius [Epiphodius, Martyrology, 22 April] and Alexander

It is indeed a great thing to offer vows at public and common solemnities, but a certain festival ought to be judged more excellent when the people rejoice in the virtues of their own offspring. Therefore, just as the worship and honor of native martyrs and special patrons provide a particular joy, so they demand a distinctive affection.

For if we ought to venerate foreign [Col. 0862A] palms, victories from abroad, crowns, and overseas triumphs with such devoted care that, by our religious service, we make what is foreign in place our own, and that what is not enclosed in tombs becomes common through our prayers, how much more zealously ought we to burn at the celebration of those to whom religion owes manifold devotion, the Church honor, and the homeland affection?

Thus, just as by right of birth we are related to them through the womb of one parent, so let us claim for ourselves toward them the privilege of piety and gratitude. Let us approach them first through the devotion of faith, so that, rejoicing that we are their fellow citizens on earth, we may deserve to possess citizenship with them in heaven [Greek: πολίτευμα, “citizenship”; Phil. III, 20; the Vulgate has conversationem, “conduct” or “way of life”].

[Col. 0862B]

Accordingly, the faith of our Church celebrates the twin trophies of Ephipodius and Alexander, with an interval of two or three days between them—not festivals made by relics brought in from elsewhere, but festivals of the undefiled monuments of our native soil. Many Churches of the peoples are content even with that sanctification which they have snatched by touching sacred vestments taken from angelic limbs, or hard links of chains, so that what was an instrument of punishment may be a testimony of glory, and the material of sufferings may pass into a mark of merits.

But we possess wholly and intact the illustrious gift of the blessed. What could suffice for the whole world, we hold specially enclosed within the bosom of this city. We raise up within the City two palms of triumph, rivals of the apostolic ones; and, possessing our own Peter and Paul, we contend with that exalted see, having two intercessors.

[Col. 0862C]

Indeed, the blessed martyrs, whose precious dust is scattered everywhere through different regions for the salvation of peoples, receive wherever they are a full worship through the religious devotion offered to God in their honor; and the richer the faith with which they are celebrated, the more acceptable to them will be the grace of the celebration. But without doubt it is much more pleasing and much more joyful to them if the fervor of piety honors them especially where the fury of persecution fell upon them; if sacrifices of supplication are offered to them there where they fell as a sacrifice to God; if posterity, destined to praise them, pours out vows there where savage brutality shed their innocent blood; finally, if there the enemy of the Christian name sees them consecrated where he believed that he had slain them.

[Col. 0862D]

Their service, I say, is sweeter to them if blessing in praise celebrates them there where the magnitude of tribulations raged against them; if they are invoked for assistance from the place from which they will first be called forth to their reward at the sign of the resurrection.

Since these things are so, dearest brethren, in order to hold fast the faith and cultivate religion, we need not await examples from far away. We are instructed by the teachings of our fathers and admonished by examples from our own household. Does not the living voice of kindred blood cry out to our hearts? “Learn from us,” it says, “to acquire faith by seeking it, to cultivate it by living, and to preserve it by dying. Learn to fear sin more than the sword; learn, for the sake of life, to love justice more than life itself, and to love faith and the fear of God.

[Col. 0863A]

“Keep the fear of God, which we preserved amid the tribulation of war, lest you lose it in peace or in the security of peace. Take care lest you lose in the harbor the anchor of hope and religion that we guarded amid the waves. Take care lest, when you see the good life subjected to afflictions, you judge it miserable. Take care lest, in the arena of the world, into which we were sent to undergo struggles, you think that any happiness is to be expected.

“Blessedness can be prepared here; it cannot be acquired here. Do not seek here what no saint who completed his labor here, and no confessor, has obtained here. Do not seek here what even Christ did not find here. If the world had peace, the martyrs would not have glory; if testing did not precede, the opportunity for tribulation would disappear.”

[Col. 0863B]

These, therefore, dearest brothers, are those who passed through great tribulations, who washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb (Rev. VII, 14). These are the fellow soldiers of those who, according to the Apostle, “were stoned, were sawn apart, were tested, died by the slaughter of the sword; they went about in poverty, distress, and affliction—of whom the world was not worthy” (Heb. XI, 37).

But amid these things, dearest brethren, when the good and holy suffer such great evils here, someone may think within himself and say: “It is clear that the Lord of all does not regard what concerns us, neglects human affairs, and does not care for earthly matters.”

O whoever you are, how do you regard the labors of the saints, but not their rewards? Behold, throughout the whole world, in the holy apostles and martyrs, adversity made a path for blessedness, destruction served salvation, and, while closing the door on life, opened one to glory. [Col. 0863C]

While God withheld the earth from those who placed their trust in him—or, according to the variant, despised the earth—he prepared heaven for them.

Divine providence therefore set this before the human race as an example of patience. Since these things are so, the man who is not injured in virtue is wrongly thought miserable. Let no one, therefore, among Christians and the faithful call poverty, the affliction of labor, the injustices of tribulation, unhappiness, or misery. When these things happen to the good, let us understand that they are not inconveniences of distress but exercises of virtue.

When the worshiper of God is permitted to labor under adversity, he is not abandoned but tested. Therefore the divine word says: “Blessed is the one who endures temptation; for when he has been tested, he will receive the crown of life, which God promised to those who love him” (James I).

[Col. 0863D]

In this world, where wickedness prevails and iniquity dominates, the poor man is afflicted and the rich man multiplies his wealth. Do you call powerful the man who is strong for his own death, for whom the deceptive shadow of present gains gathers the causes of eternal evils? Who would call blessed the strong right hand raised against its own throat? Who would reasonably praise the swift man hurrying toward steep precipices? Who would marvel at the ascent of one whom he sees from the summit about to fall?

It is the same if you marvel at someone who acts impiously and unjustly through wealth and riches as if you saw someone mixing poisons for himself in a gilded and jeweled cup. Do you call happy the man who, faithless, obscene, greedy, and bloodstained, is allowed to go his own ways because he scorns the ways of the Lord; who, offended by the narrowness of the right hand and delighted by the breadth of the left, is entangled in crimes, stained by wickedness, polluted by plunder, and amid all this considers himself supremely blessed—more wretched for this very reason, that he does not understand himself to be wretched?

[Col. 0864A]

What can the medicine of heavenly commandments do for such people, since it heals only those who are willing? Thus, sluggish in seeking salvation but eager for the warfare and captivity of death, as it is said, they “rejoice in doing evil” (Prov. II, 14) and delight in their own destruction, like those who, perhaps taking deadly juices of herbs, are said to perish with laughter.

But amid these things someone thinks within himself and says [variant: “may say”]: “The God of power, the God who dwells in the fortress of justice—if he does not condemn sins, he is ignorant of them; or, if he refrains from condemning them, he favors sins.”

[Col. 0864B]

First, there can be no doubt that he knows all things—he who enters, fills, and exceeds all things, before whose eyes everything is exposed and naked; of whom it is said: “For God’s wisdom is great, and he is mighty in power, seeing all things without ceasing.” There can therefore be no doubt that he knows all things and is near: he who commanded you, when you pray, to enter the chamber of your conscience; who hears in thought and hears in the heart.

That he condemns offenses and crimes is clearly testified by the warnings of the prophets, the teachings of the apostles, and the declarations of the evangelists. Meanwhile, while he announces a grievous punishment and threatens eternal fire, here he gives sentence but reserves the punishment for there. Here he brandishes the sword; there he will bring destruction to completion.

“Why,” someone asks, “does he not immediately punish the sinner who is guilty?” What mind could endure such an error? He complains of God’s patience, though he does not deserve indulgence. [Col. 0864C]

The justice of the one who condemns would not be perfect unless the mercy of the one who reproves went before it. Throughout the entire sequence of Scripture, God kindly makes patience known to us; and what the Lord proclaims in the servant, how does the servant rebuke in the Lord?

Do we not sometimes see even administrators of human laws—who are worthy of praise no less for moderation than for strictness—anticipating postponed judgments by many preliminary decisions and edicts? The guilt is already proved, yet anger is still delayed. Thus they display movement toward severity without neglecting deliberation in their restraint.

So too our Lord does not ignorantly disregard what is done on earth, but patiently waits. He first examines the works and intentions of human beings; then he judges, weighs, and considers merit in their conduct [or conversion]; he moderates judgment through delay. Gradually he orders human affairs through the delays of time, the dispenser of eternities. Here he threatens the blow; there he will complete destruction.

[Col. 0864D]

But if God did not know human affairs, who would assist the blessed martyrs through the immediate conduct of the battle? Or how would the death of the saints be precious in God’s sight (Ps. CXV, 13)? Or from where would the salvation of the righteous come from the Lord, unless they received protection in the time of tribulation? All these things show, to those who fight the battles of faith for religion and justice, the presence of the Lord who waits and protects.

Therefore let us also confidently entreat the Son, our helper and protector of martyrs, to strengthen our hands for spiritual combat against that enemy who, if he is feared, must be driven back; but if he is not recognized, will enter. He loses much of his strength when he becomes manifest to consciences, since he conquers only by ambushes.

[Col. 0865A]

Our fathers fought against the harshest pains; let us, in contrast, fight against the softest pleasures. They conquered the torments of flames; let us conquer the fiery darts of vices. They trampled on the devil and carried spoils away from death; let us beware lest we strip Christ in the poor. They were expended as a sacrifice to God through the strength of faith; let us take care lest one of us become a victim of the enemy through the wound of sin. They died in punishment in their outward limbs; we have something within ourselves that we ought to kill.

Thus let us contemplate the battles of those illustrious warriors through our private struggle with our passions. For since we know that there can be a battle without a persecutor, God can also grant martyrdom without bloodshed.

## FRAGMENT OF A HOMILY CITED BY MAMERTUS CLAUDIANUS, *On the State of the Soul*, Book II, chapter 9

[Col. 0866A]

Some people ask how man and God could be joined in Christ. They also ask for an explanation of this mystery, which happened only once, although they are entirely unable to explain how something that happens continually takes place—namely, how the soul is joined to the body so that a human being comes into existence.

Therefore, just as a corporeal and an incorporeal thing are joined, and the soul is mingled with the body so that a human being may be formed, so man was joined to God and Christ came into being. Yet, for Christ to come into being, those two incorporeal realities—that is, soul and God—could be joined and mingled more easily than one incorporeal and another corporeal reality are mingled, namely soul and body, so that the person of a human being may exist.

[Col. 0865]

## EXHORTATION TO MONKS OF SAINT EUCHERIUS, BISHOP OF LYONS

(From the *Codex Regularis* of Marianus Brockie, vol. I.) (C, G, S)*

[Col. 0865B]

### 1

What can we present to you, dearest brothers, that would be worthy both for us to say and for you to hear? How dare we speak to you, whom we regard even with silent admiration? How can we build you up by our word, when you build us up by your example? Shall we teach you what you should do, when we already marvel at what you do?

What, then, shall we say? That you should abandon the world, which you have already abandoned? That you should despise riches, which many of you have already despised? That you should flee desires, which you have already fled? That you should choose what is healthier, which you have already chosen?

Let me therefore open my mouth amid the common rejoicing, with him fulfilling his promise who said: “Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Ps. LXXX, 11). I shall speak among you, beloved, without fear; let there not be the embarrassment of one where there is the joy of many.

[Col. 0865C]

The work in which we rejoice is divine. May you learn for a long time what you may teach well. Would that our mouth could preach to you worthily according to your merit. What others preach correctly, you fulfill; what others say, you do, because you display the life of angels while you are still human beings placed on earth.

For that heavenly way of life, although few will see it there, you already make visible here. You are, as the Savior says, “the light of this world” (Matt. V, 14), the lamp placed upon a lampstand. If anyone is distant from this lamp, he must be enveloped in the darkness of the world. Whoever approaches this light will certainly have eyes for seeing, just as he has had ears for hearing.

[Col. 0865D]

This lamp, therefore, so that it may possess the brightest light, must always be filled with the oil of mercy, piety, gentleness, humility, obedience, and love.

### 2

[Col. 0866B]

Humility, however, must be cultivated above all. It makes us equal to the just, joins us to the angels, and enables us to draw near to God. It is humility that fears neither ruin, nor a precipice, nor a fall, because humility has no place from which to fall.

Do you wish not to fall? Do not exalt yourself. Do you wish not to become puffed up? Do not puff yourself up. For someone rightly said: “Whatever swells is not healthy.” Pride, which is opposed to humility, is nothing other than swelling. But just as the body has no health with swelling, so the soul has no health with pride.

“Humble yourself, therefore, and do not seek what is higher than you” (Eccl. III, 22). Yet if someone wishes to be proud, he has within himself a place in which to exercise his pride. Let him be proud against the world; let him despise worldly conduct; let him regard its desires as nothing; let him rise up against vices; let him be proud against pride itself; and let him hold beneath his feet power, riches, desires, and all the other things that dominate the world.

[Col. 0866C]

Whatever is considered great and magnificent here, let him despise as refuse and dung with a praiseworthy strictness. He will satisfy his pride when he sees himself in spirit even above kings. Yet, if he wishes to be holy in this pride, he will indeed be a despiser of the world, but he will be humble toward Christ. There he will be chosen, but here he will be subject. For he raises himself against those things in order more easily to humble himself before these.

### 3

If, therefore, we guard this humility attentively, true obedience will also be preserved without difficulty. In this obedience, dearest brethren, contrition is plainly manifested. For the person contrite in heart is the one who judges himself least.

When would such a person dare to carry out his own wishes? [Col. 0866D]

When would he dare to resist the authority of the one who has commanded him? Hence the Apostle says: “Obey those set over you,” and so forth (Heb. XIII, 17).

[Col. 0867A]

But is only the one who commands worthy of praise? Nor, dearest brethren, will the one who obeys be without praise. The one deserves glory by governing, the other by obeying. Thus both strive toward great honor and reward: one gives good counsel, and the other obeys good counsel.

Our Savior especially impressed this obedience upon us. He wished to save us not only when he redeemed us, but also when he taught obedience. For, being equal to the Father, he obeyed the Father. And how did he obey? Did he obey in an easy matter? “Unto death”—and what kind of death? “The death of the cross” (Phil. II, 8).

He not only obeyed, but also made the Father’s will his own. We can do what we are commanded even unwillingly; true obedience exists when the person who obeys begins to will what the one who commands wills.

[Col. 0867B]

Holy Scripture says: “It is good for a man when he has borne the yoke from his youth; he will sit alone and be silent” (Lam. IV, 27). Let us therefore, with Christ helping us, place a door and bolts upon our mouth, and a scale upon our words. For the Apostle says: “The one who ministers well acquires a good standing for himself” (1 Tim. III, 13).

### 4

And these things, dearest brethren, I do not say in order to instruct you, but so that in my words you may recognize the goods of humility and obedience that you practice. We desire you to possess these goods continually, since they draw you toward the eternal kingdom of God.

“For it is not the one who has begun, but the one who has persevered, who will be saved” (Mark 10, 12). The one who wishes to be saved must struggle here. If someone withdraws from his place in a battle when the line is drawn up and stands against its adversaries, he is thereafter regarded as cowardly and a deserter.

[Col. 0867C]

In this place too, the soldiers of Christ appear to stand arrayed as though in battle formation against the devil. To abandon the struggle and withdraw from here is not only inglorious but dangerous. We must remain in this same place, so that, while we hold what we hold, [Col. 0868A] others may not receive our crowns.

We must remain and persevere, so that, fighting here most gloriously and sailing most peacefully, we may spend our lives in the safest manner amid spiritual pursuits and seize eternal life, for which we have been called.

### 5

Our Savior says: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden; nor do they light a lamp and place it under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, so that it may give light to all who are in the house” (Matt. V, 14).

Rightly, therefore, so illustrious a lamp, placed beneath the monastery’s bushel, has been transferred to the lampstand of the Church. Indeed, this evangelical bushel is well suited to the monastery, where nothing is done without measure. Everything there has been measured; all things done or said are maintained as being expressed with the most equitable reason, according to the measure of a bushel.

[Col. 0868B]

Therefore, in a spiritual interpretation, we rightly understand by this figure the monastery, which, in the likeness of a bushel, is accustomed to contain nothing mixed within itself. For just as wheat is separated from chaff, so it is accustomed to receive those separated from the world. Then, after the Lord’s winnowing fan has cleansed his threshing floor, once the refuse has been cast outside, it contains within itself his chosen ones as purer grains.

Accordingly, just as the bushel is compared with the monastery, so the lampstand is compared with the Church. Since the Church is established in a high or conspicuous place, raising before the eyes the brilliance transferred to it, it displays to all the light placed upon it.

A fire that has been kindled is reasonably brought forth so that it may shine; hidden goodness is of little benefit, and concealed light shines little.

[Col. 0868C]

Exalt your voice, most blessed bishop, and proclaim it from heaven to the peoples like a trumpet. Reveal the treasure you have dug out in secret. Scatter the riches you have gathered. Pour out openly to the hungry the wealth you prepared in the wilderness, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with God the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0867]

## TWO BOOKS OF THE EPITOMES OF THE WORKS OF CASSIAN, BY SAINT EUCHERIUS, BISHOP OF LYONS, FOR CASTOR, BISHOP OF APT

(C, G, S)*

## BOOK ONE. ON THE CANONICAL INSTITUTES OF MONASTERIES

[Col. 0867D]

### 1

(Cassian, *Institutes*, preface and Book II, chapters 7–11.)

When you, most blessed Father Castor, ordered me to explain to you the canonical regulations of the monasteries of the East, and especially those of Egypt, which I myself saw with my own eyes, I obeyed your command and sent you these few words, so that from them a provision for virtue might be available to those who, with God’s help, have been gathered into your new monastery. I also sent the canons of blessed men and several others.

[Col. 0868D]

It is therefore necessary that before everything else I speak about prayer, the source of all good things: namely, how and in what excellent order it is performed in the monasteries of Egypt and the Thebaid.

When they have gathered in the same place at the time of the synaxis, after the psalm has been completed, they do not immediately proceed to kneeling. [Col. 0869A]

Before bending their knees, they first pray for a short time while standing with their hands extended. Then, prostrating themselves on the ground and saying a brief prayer while kneeling, they all rise together. Again, with hands extended, they offer supplications for a longer time and with greater fervor. No one kneels or rises from kneeling until the one reciting the prayer has first knelt or first risen.

As has been said, whenever they gather for such a synaxis, such silence is observed by everyone that, in so large and almost innumerable an assembly, no one seems to be present. Above all, this is so during the prayers, when neither spitting is heard nor coughing. There is no sign of laziness, dozing, yawning, or audible groaning.

[Col. 0869B]

They say that the person who prays aloud because of nausea or weakness of spirit commits a double sin: first, because he prays sluggishly; second, because with that undisciplined voice he deafens the ears of his neighbor and distracts his mind. At the same time, evil spirits attack; when they see us standing in prayer, they burden our soul with indecent thoughts, nausea, and disgust.

For this reason they recite the psalms neither with tumult and agitation nor in haste, nor do they take pleasure in the number of verses, but in the mind’s attentive reflection, obeying the one who says: “I will sing with the spirit; I will sing also with the mind” (1 Cor. XIV, 15). They consider it more useful to sing ten verses attentively than the entire Psalter with a confused mind.

### 2

(Cassian, *Institutes*, Book II, chapter 15.)

[Col. 0869C]

When the psalms and the office have been completed, as we mentioned above, none of the brothers dares to remain even for a moment or to speak with another. Nor does he dare to leave his cell or abandon the work he is handling, in accordance with the apostolic command, unless the occasion of some necessary task requires everyone to come together.

When they leave, they carry out their work so that there is not even the slightest conversation among them. Each devotes himself to meditation of mind and to the psalm, and fulfills what has been commanded him.

They take great care that no brother, especially a novice, should ever be left alone with another, or dare to touch or embrace anyone with outstretched hands. If anyone is discovered to have transgressed this rule, he is subjected to the most severe correction.

[Col. 0869D]

### 3

(Cassian, *Institutes*, Book IV, chapters 1–6.)

We have now said enough about the canonical practice, whether of prayers or of psalms—namely, how they ought to be observed in the daily assemblies. We must next discuss those who have renounced the world: how they enter these monasteries and remain in them in humility and obedience until extreme old age.

Among them there is such obedience and such humility even into old age as is not found in our monasteries even during the first year among those who have renounced the world. Therefore, the person who wishes to be a monk is not admitted into the monastery before he has given, through the fullest obedience, a [Col. 0870A] kind of proof and trial of his love toward God, his humility, and his equanimity.

Once he has been tested in this way and is regarded by them as ready for admission, he is taught not to keep anything of his possessions hidden with him. For they know that one who retains anything of his possessions cannot long remain in the obedience of the monastery, nor persevere to the end, because of weakness and weariness of spirit.

Whenever even the smallest occasion or affliction moves his mind, the hope of the hidden treasure, like a slingstone, casts him out of the monastery. Therefore, each person is stripped of his former possessions, so that he is not even permitted to use the garment in which he arrived.

When all the brothers have assembled, he is brought into their midst and stripped of his own clothing. In its place he is clothed by the abbot’s hands in the monastery’s garments, so that by this form he may recognize [Col. 0870B] that he has been stripped of all worldly things, as well as of arrogance and pride, and has put on the poverty of Christ. Without shame, he is to count and equal himself with the body of the brotherhood.

The steward of the monastery receives and preserves the garments he has removed, setting them aside until he himself has made progress and has given proof of endurance in his way of life and patience amid various temptations.

If he is found capable of persevering in these things and of remaining with the same zeal and fervent purpose with which he began, they number him among the other brothers. But if they discover in him the offense of murmuring or any sin of disobedience, they strip him of the monastery’s garments, clothe him again in worldly garments, and expel him from the monastery.

Thus, after such careful testing, it is not easy for someone who wishes to do so to enter or withdraw from the monastery at his own [Col. 0870C] discretion. Rather, whoever declares that he does not wish to remain must be completely stripped of the monastery’s garments.

4. (Cass. *Institutes*, Book II, chapters 7–9.) When, therefore, the man who has been received has been tested with the thoroughness we have described and has been found blameless, he is not immediately permitted to join the company of the brothers. Instead, he is entrusted to the man charged with the care of guests and is ordered to devote himself entirely to serving and attending to them. After he has received guests blamelessly for a full year, and has thereby been formed in humility and equanimity, he is finally enrolled among the company of the brothers and entrusted to one of the elders, who is responsible for this duty, so that he may teach the disciple by what paths he can arrive at the perfection of the virtues.

[Col. 0870D] First, he teaches him the discipline of overcoming his own desires and pleasures, ordering him to do what is contrary to his will. For the Fathers say that no one can otherwise restrain pleasures, anger, or sadness; attain true humility; or ultimately be properly perfected together with the brothers in the coenobium, unless he has first mortified his own will through obedience.

When they have brought the disciple to a higher condition through these constitutions and teachings, as through certain elements and syllables, they then teach him this: not to conceal his thoughts, but, whenever they arise, to reveal them at once to his father; not to entrust anything to his own heart concerning their judgment and examination, but to know that something is good or evil according to what his father, having examined the matter, has declared it to be. In this way, anyone being trained in virtue can avoid all the deceptions of the enemy, since, being inexperienced, he does not know the enemy’s snares.

For the holy Fathers say that it is a conspicuous sign of the devil’s art and ambushes when he persuades disciples to hide their thoughts from their fathers—either from a movement of pride, as though they themselves were capable of forming suitable counsel about the matter on their own, or from empty glory, because they are ashamed, naturally enough, to make their thoughts public.

5. (Cass. *Institutes*, Book IV, chapters 10–12.) Their obedience, moreover, is so great that no one dares to leave even his own cell, in which he is sitting, without the abbot’s command; and they fulfill his orders with as much zeal as they would if God himself had commanded them.

While they are sitting in their cells, occupied with manual work, meditation, and prayer, and devoting themselves diligently to these things, if they hear someone knocking at the door of the cell who is summoning them either to the common prayer or to manual work, they immediately abandon everything and hasten to the task assigned to them, practicing the virtue of obedience with the utmost devotion. They place it before not only manual work, reading, and quiet residence in the cell, but also before every virtue, and they put everything else second.

6. (Cass. *Institutes*, Book IV, chapters 13–16.) It is superfluous to mention that none of them possesses anything other than a *colobium*, a *hemiphorium*, a sandal, a *melotes*, and a mat; they consider it shameful if anyone says, “my book,” “my pen,” or anything else “of mine.”

Yet each of them brings such proceeds to the monastery from his work and labor that they suffice not only for their own needs but also for the service of guests and the poor. While they labor in this way, they are not puffed up or swollen with pride, and no one, on account of his own work and sweat, asks for more than the abbot grants according to necessity. No one acquires possession of anything for himself, since he considers himself a stranger and exile in the whole world; rather, he regards himself as the brothers’ servant and minister than as the master of any earthly thing.

If anyone breaks or loses any vessel, he confesses the mishap caused by his negligence to the abbot, and thus, with the humility of repentance, receives pardon. But if anyone, summoned to some work or to the assembly, arrives late out of contempt, or answers more harshly and insolently; or if he completes the assigned task negligently or with murmuring; or if, preferring reading to manual work and obedience, he completes the work assigned to him late; or if, having been dismissed from the assembly, he does not hurry quickly to his task; or if he has conversed with someone without necessity; or if he has touched another’s hand with familiarity; or if he has visited relatives without the abbot’s permission and blessing; or if he has dared to receive a letter from someone or write to someone without the abbot’s consent—in short, if he has committed any such offense, he is subjected to the following punishment: when the brothers are gathered in the assembly, he throws himself to the ground and, after confessing, asks pardon for his sin.

[Col. 0872A] But if anyone is found to have committed more serious offenses—such as contempt, resistance accompanied by pride, leaving the monastery without the abbot’s permission, intercourse with a woman, anger, fighting, hostility toward anyone, remembrance of injuries, love of money, which is leprosy of the soul, possession of any object except those given by the abbot, secretly eating food without the abbot’s blessing, or anything similar—he does not undergo the punishment described above, but a more severe and much harsher one. If he does not repent, he is expelled from the monastery.

7. (Cass. *Institutes*, Book IV, chapters 17–18.) As for the fact that in certain coenobia there is reading during the meal, this is observed not according to the rule of the Egyptians but according to that of the Cappadocians, who established it not so much for spiritual exercise as for the sake of quiet and avoiding conversation.

Among the Egyptians, however, and especially among the Tabennesiots, such silence is maintained by everyone when that great multitude of brothers gathers at table during the meal that scarcely anything similar can be found elsewhere. Indeed, no one dares even to spit, except the person in charge of the table, who, if anything is needed, indicates it by a knock rather than by his voice.

They also wear their cowls lowered even below their eyelids, so that they may not inspect others too inquisitively with wandering eyes; they devote their attention only to the table and to giving thanks to the God who nourishes them. They take great care that none of them should eat food outside the table.

8. (Cass. *Institutes*, Book IV, chapters 19–21.) But lest we seem to omit anything concerning the rules of the coenobites, we must also mention the regulations handed down in other regions.

Throughout Mesopotamia, Palestine, Cappadocia, and the whole East, during the assemblies of the third, sixth, and ninth hours, if anyone has not arrived before the first psalm has been completed, he does not dare to enter the oratory or join those singing the psalms; instead, he stands outside the doors and waits for the dismissal of the brothers. When everyone has gone out, he prostrates himself on the ground and, performing penance, asks pardon for his negligence.

At the nocturnal assemblies, however, permission is granted to those who arrive late up to the second psalm. The brothers take turns by weeks in the kitchen and in the other duties, both to lighten one another’s labor and to fulfill the law of charity through mutual services. They perform these ministries with such humility and care that even servants do not show as much toward their masters.

When the week has ended, on Sunday, after the morning hymns, as others enter to take their turn at serving, they hand over to them the vessels of their office, marked with identifying signs. Those who receive them guard them with such care and attention that nothing is broken or lost, just as a person entrusted with sacred vessels dedicated to God would do.

For they prepare themselves to give an account not only to the steward in the present time but also to God in the future, if anything should be lost through their negligence or sluggishness.

To give greater credibility to what I have said, I shall relate what I myself saw with my own eyes. During a certain brother’s week of service, the steward passed by and saw a few lentils scattered on the ground. He did not disregard them as something worthless; instead, he rebuked the brother to whom that week had been entrusted and imposed a penalty on him, as though he had been negligent with things dedicated to God and had trampled upon his own conscience.

For they preserve and administer everything with such care and concern that they guard with great attention things that seem worthless and contemptible to us. Thus they move a vessel that has been put down improperly, gather up what has been thrown away, and believe that they will receive from the Lord God a reward even for such things.

We have found these weekly regulations observed throughout the entire East. Among the Egyptians, however, the rotation of weekly service is not maintained in this way. Instead, responsibility for the kitchen is entrusted to one of the most proven brothers for as long as his virtue continues to increase, his bodily strength remains sufficient for the performance of the duty, and old age or illness does not prevent him.

Since we are speaking about obedience and humility, by which we can reach the highest summit of virtue, I think it worthwhile to add to our account, as examples, a few of the many remarkable deeds performed by the holy Fathers who shone in the coenobia.

9. (Cass. *Institutes*, Book IV, chapters 27–28.) There was a certain father named Muthius [variant: Patermuthius]. When he wished to renounce the world, he approached a coenobium and remained for a long time before the monastery gates. Because of his exceptional patience, he was admitted, contrary to the monastery’s customary rule, together with his young son.

After he had entered following many hardships, the two were assigned not only to various kinds of work but were also separated in their lodging, so that through that separation they might gradually be freed from the natural affection they had for one another. By God’s grace, the father was likewise freed from it through extensive discipline.

To test and prove his virtue, the abbot would sometimes pretend to be angered against the boy and ordered his father, the man mentioned above, to pick him up and throw him into the river. The father then, as though God were commanding him to take up his son, hurried to the riverbank. As he hastened to fulfill the command out of ardent faith and the fervor of obedience, he was stopped by the brothers, who had gone ahead of him and rescued the boy.

His faith and obedience were so acceptable to God that it was revealed by God to the abbot that he had completed the deed of Abraham. After a short time, when the abbot of that coenobium died, he left him as his successor.

10. (Cass. *Institutes*, Book IV, chapter 29.) We knew another brother who renounced the world. He had also been prominent in secular life—for his father was a count engaged in warfare and was wealthy—and he was by no means uneducated, being devoted to reading.

After abandoning secular pride, he therefore embraced the monastic life. To test his faith and humility, the abbot ordered him to carry ten baskets and sell them in his own city, not all together but one at a time. He fulfilled this with complete patience and humility, placing the baskets one by one on his shoulders and selling them. He did not consider the lowliness of the merchandise or the nobility of his family, for he was striving to become an imitator of Christ’s humility.

[Col. 0874A] 11. (Cass. *Institutes*, Book IV, chapters 30–32.) We also saw another abbot from among the Fathers, Pinophan [Cassian: Pinufius], a man adorned with every virtue. He was an old man and abbot of a great coenobium situated in Egypt near the city of Panepho.

When he saw that everyone praised and celebrated him both because of his way of life and because of his old age and position of authority, and that he could no longer exercise himself in the discipline of humility as he had at the beginning of his conversion, he was moved by his desire for the subjection to which he had been called. He secretly fled from his own coenobium and withdrew alone to the remotest parts of the Thebaid.

After removing his monastic clothing and putting on secular garments, he sought a coenobium of the Tabennesiots, thinking that he could remain hidden there, both because of the multitude of brothers and because it was far from the region in which his own coenobium was situated.

After he had made his request there for many days, he was received by the archimandrite, who, considering him an old man useful for nothing else, entrusted him with the care of the garden. He assigned another brother to him as well; by remaining subordinate to that brother, he practiced the humility and obedience he desired.

Nor was he satisfied with that service alone. Whatever tasks seemed hard and difficult to the others, he completed cheerfully.

After he had thus spent three years in concealment, his disciples searched for him throughout all Egypt. At last he was scarcely recognized by a certain brother who had come there. When that brother saw him and recognized the features of his face, he was still doubtful and tried to hear his voice. He was not certain from sight alone, having seen an old man digging the earth with a mattock and carrying manure on his shoulders to place it at the roots of the vegetables.

When, by attending to the sound of his voice, he discovered who he was, he threw himself at his feet. This caused the onlookers great astonishment, because he had behaved in this way toward a man who, among them, was regarded as the lowest of the novices, having only recently abandoned the world.

They were even more amazed when they learned his name, for he had previously been held in great esteem among them. They asked his pardon because, in ignorance, they had placed him among the newest novices.

After urging him with many words, they unwillingly sent him back to his own coenobium, while he lamented that he had not been permitted to practice the humility and obedience he loved.

After spending a short time in his monastery, burning again with a desire for humility and obedience, he fled at night when the opportunity arose. This time he went no farther to a foreign region; rather, he boarded a small boat and came to the parts of Palestine, hoping to remain hidden there until the end.

When he arrived in Palestine, he sought a monastery situated near the cave in which the Lord Christ was born, and he stayed in that monastery. Yet he could not remain hidden there, in accordance with the Lord’s saying: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matt. 5:15).

When brothers came from Egypt to worship at the holy places, they recognized him and, after many entreaties and tears, persuaded him to return once more to his own coenobium.

I lived with this holy man in Egypt for a short time. I shall conclude my account by relating what I heard from him when, in my presence, he admonished a brother whom he had admitted.

[Col. 0875A] 12. (Cass. *Institutes*, Book IV, chapters 33–35.) “You know, brother,” he said, “how many days you spent before the monastery gate before being admitted today. If you learn the reason for this difficulty, it can benefit you on the path you wish to enter and make you a faithful servant of God.

“For just as glory and honor are promised in the future to those who serve the Lord faithfully, so the gravest punishments threaten those who approach that promise softly and sluggishly. For, according to Scripture, it is better not to make a vow than to make one and fail to fulfill it. It is said again: ‘Cursed is the one who performs the work of the Lord negligently’ (Jer. 48:10).

“For this reason we rejected you and hesitated to admit you—not because we do not earnestly desire your salvation and that of all who believe in Christ, but lest, by admitting you rashly and without difficulty, we ourselves should incur from God, even while praying, the punishment for excessive leniency, and make you liable to a more severe punishment. This would happen if we admitted you too easily, before you had learned the gravity and thoroughness of the promise, and you later became soft and sluggish.

“Therefore, as has been said above, you must learn the reason for your renunciation—that is, what you must do. Renunciation, then, is nothing other than a promise of the cross and of death.

“Know, therefore, that from this day you are dead and crucified to the world, and that, according to the Apostle, the world is dead to you. Learn what the power of the cross is, since you no longer live, but the one who was crucified for you lives in you.

“Just as the Lord was suspended for us in this form, so we must live in the coenobium, as blessed David, fearing the Lord, asks that his flesh be pierced” (Ps. 118:120). For just as a person whose body is fastened to a piece of wood is unable to move toward any action, so one whose mind is pierced by divine fear is unmoved by every carnal desire.

“And just as the person fastened to the cross no longer thinks about present things, is not directed by his own will, is not disturbed by desire, is not held back by concern for possession, is not inflated by pride, does not burn with contention or envy, does not grieve over present insult, and does not remember past injuries—for after a short time he awaits the end of his life through the cross—so the person who has sincerely renounced the world and is, as it were, fixed upon the cross through the fear of God, awaiting the end of this life each day, keeps all desires and carnal affections immobile and powerless.”

13. (Cass. *Institutes*, Book IV, chapters 36–37.) Take care, therefore, never to desire to take up again what you abandoned in your renunciation. For according to the Lord’s saying, “The one who puts his hand to the plow and turns back is not fit for the kingdom of heaven” (Luke 9:62). Whoever descends from a lofty way of life to the worthless and earthly things of this world acts against the Lord’s command, when he comes down from the house and tries to carry something away from it.

Take care, then, lest, remembering your former affection for your carnal relatives and turning back to the cares of this age, you are found, according to the Lord’s word, unfit for the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 5:19).

Take care lest you stir up again within yourself the pride that at the beginning you trampled down through the fervor of humility. Once you have learned the Psalter or something from Scripture, do not, in the Apostle’s words, rebuild the things you destroyed and thus show yourself to be a transgressor. Rather, as you began and professed humility, preserve it before God and his angels to the end.

Similarly, the humility you displayed in the monastery, when you remained for many days weeping and pleading before the monastery gate, must be increased. It would be a thoroughly miserable thing if, when you ought daily to add to your fervor and ascend through continual progress toward perfection, you diminished it and returned to lower things.

For the blessed person is not the one who begins to do good, but whoever perseveres in it to the end. The serpent that is dragged along the ground always watches our heel—that is, it lays ambushes for our death and tries to trip us until the end of our life.

Therefore, it will be of no benefit to have begun well, nor will an ardent beginning of obedience avail anything, unless the end likewise follows. Nor will the humility that is according to Christ, which you have now promised, be made firm unless you display it to the end.

Therefore, so that you may possess it perfectly and crush the dragon’s head (Gen. 3:15), whenever thoughts attack you, reveal them promptly from the very beginning. For if from the outset you disclose the dragon’s destructive thoughts, and are not ashamed to declare them to your father, you will crush his head.

Indeed, according to divine Scripture, ‘If you approach to serve God, prepare yourself’ (Sir. 2:1)—not for carelessness or idleness, but for temptations and afflictions. For ‘through many afflictions we must enter the kingdom of heaven’ (Acts 14:22), and ‘the gate is narrow and the way is constricted that leads to life, and few are those who find it’ (Matt. 7:14).

Direct your attention, therefore, to those few good people, and form your life according to their example. Do not attend to the lazy and contemptuous, however numerous they may be. For he says: ‘Many are called, but few are chosen’ (Matt. 20:16), and ‘it is a little flock to which the Father has been pleased to give the kingdom’ (Luke 12:32).

Do not consider it a small sin to promise perfection and imitate those who are more negligent and sluggish. If you wish to be able to arrive at perfection, follow this discipline and ascend these steps.”

14. (Cass. *Institutes*, Book IV, chapters 39–40.) The first step of virtue and the beginning of our salvation is the fear of God. Through it the cleansing of sins is accomplished, the guarding of virtues is obtained, and the way to perfection is secured. For when the fear of God enters the soul, it persuades us to despise all worldly things; from this arises forgetfulness of relatives and of the whole world.

From these things humility, the head of all virtues and the completion of all good things, is practiced, since humility comes from contempt for and deprivation of all things.

Humility, moreover, is confirmed by these signs: first, if a person has mortified his own wills within himself; second, if he hides nothing from his father, not only of his actions but also of his thoughts; third, if he does not trust his own judgment, but relies in everything upon his father’s discernment, and always thirsts for, desires, and listens willingly to his admonitions; fourth, if he carries out all his father’s commands without shame; fifth, if he not only does not dare to insult another but also receives insults from others with joy; sixth, if he undertakes nothing new that neither the common rule nor the examples of the Fathers permit; seventh, if, content with every lowly condition, he gives thanks for the things given to him and considers himself unworthy of them; eighth, if he considers himself altogether inferior to everyone and is not rash in speech [Cassian, at this point: “Ninth, if he restrains his tongue or is not loud in his voice”]; tenth, if he is not free in conversation or hasty with his tongue.

Humility is recognized by these and similar signs. When these have genuinely been displayed, they quickly lead to the summit of love, in which there is no fear of Gehenna and through which everything is accomplished no longer from necessity and with toil, but from fervent love and desire for the good.

To help you attain this virtue more easily, let the words of the brothers who strive alongside you and possess devotion be your model, not those who are greater in number and lead their lives more carelessly and sluggishly. For those who wish to strive toward perfection gain immense benefit from imitating and emulating the saints.

15. (Cass. *Institutes*, Book IV, chapters 41–43.) If you wish, therefore, to have the ability to carry out all these things and to persevere under them to the end in the spiritual contest of the coenobium, you will need, for your preservation in the company of the brothers, what David says: “But I, like a deaf man, did not hear, and like a man who does not hear and has no reproofs in his mouth” (Ps. 37:14).

Whenever, therefore, you see anything foreign to edification and usefulness, be as though blind. If you hear anything of this kind, become as though deaf and mute, with no reproofs in your mouth. Do not imitate those who are faithless, disobedient, insolent, buffoonish, or abusive; but, like someone mute and unable to hear, pass over these things.

If anyone brings reproaches, insults, or abuse against you, remain unmoved, as though restrained and mute. Repeat constantly to yourself this verse of the Psalm: “I said, ‘I will guard my ways, so that I may not sin with my tongue. I have set a guard over my mouth, while the sinner stood against me. I was silent and humbled myself’” (Ps. 38:1).

In addition to these things, meditate above all on a fourth principle, which can adorn the three mentioned earlier: namely, that, according to the Apostle’s command, you should make yourself foolish and ignorant in this age, so that you may be wise (1 Cor. 3:18)—that is, neither judging nor doubting anything among the commands given to you, but instructed in the simplicity and faith of obedience.

Among all holy things, believe that only that is holy, wise, and useful which has been commanded to you by your father. If you establish your heart in this purpose, you will be able to bear Christ’s yoke of obedience to the end, and none of the devil’s temptations or devices will be able to shake you from the knowledge of life.

Do not wait to establish your patience, humility, and equanimity through the virtue of others—that is, by having no one provoke you, despise you, or dishonor you. This is neither proof of your virtue nor within your power. But if you willingly endure insults, abuse, and contempt, that is within your own choice.

To summarize what we have discussed more fully above, so that you may remember it more easily, listen again to how you can arrive at perfection in order. The beginning of our salvation is the fear of God; from it good obedience is born; from this arise submission and contempt for worldly things; from these humility is born; from humility comes the mortification of one’s own wills; from the mortification of one’s own wills the roots of pleasure are dried up; through these all the imperfections of the soul are eliminated; through their expulsion the virtues grow and bear fruit; from the increase of the virtues purity of heart is born; and purity of heart is followed by apostolic perfection, through the grace and help of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.

# BOOK TWO. ON THE EIGHT THOUGHTS OF WICKEDNESS

[Col. 0877]

[Col. 0877D] 1. (Cass. *Institutes*, Book V, chapters 1 and following.) Having previously spoken about the constitution of the coenobia, and relying upon your prayers, we now undertake to write about the eight thoughts of wickedness: gluttony, fornication, avarice, anger, sadness, sloth, vainglory, and pride.

We shall speak first about abstinence, which is opposed to gluttony; we shall also discuss the proper measure of fasting and the quality and quantity of food. We shall not speak about these matters from our own resources, but about what we received from our holy Fathers.

They did not hand down one rule of fasting, one manner of eating, or the same measure for everyone, because not all possess the same strength or age, and because some suffer from bodily weakness while others have a more delicate constitution.

They did, however, hand down one objective for all: that they should flee surfeit and shun fullness of the belly. They also declared, as experience has shown, that daily fasting is more beneficial and contributes more to purity than fasting prolonged for three or four days, or even for an entire week.

For they say that someone who prolongs a fast immoderately often uses food beyond the proper measure afterward. Thus it frequently happens that at one time, because of excessive abstinence, the body falls into weakness and becomes less capable of spiritual duties; while at another time, burdened by an abundance of food, it generates sluggishness and softness of spirit.

Again, the use of vegetables is not suitable for everyone, nor legumes for everyone, and dry bread cannot suffice as food for everyone. Some, after eating two pounds of bread, are still hungry; others are satisfied with one pound, or even with six ounces.

Thus, as has been said, they handed down one objective of abstinence for everyone: not to be deceived by fullness of the belly and not to be dragged along by the pleasure of the appetite.

For not only a difference in quality but also a large quantity of food commonly kindles the fiery weapons of sin. Whatever food fills the belly, it generates the seeds of lust.
