Likewise, not only the satiety produced by wine but also an excess of water and an abundance of any food weigh a person down and make him sluggish and drowsy.

It was not satiety from wine or from various foods that caused the overthrow of the Sodomites, but satiety from bread, according to the prophet (Ezek. 16:49).

Bodily weakness is not opposed to purity of heart. Therefore, give the body what its weakness requires, not what pleasure demands. Food should be used to the extent necessary to sustain life, not to serve the impulse of desire. Moderate and rational consumption of food brings bodily health and does not take away holiness.

This is the precise norm and rule of abstinence handed down by the holy Fathers: the person eating should stop taking food while appetite is still present.

When the Apostle says, “Do not make provision for the flesh in its desires” (Rom. 13:14), he did not prohibit the necessary care of life but forbade care directed toward nourishing pleasure.

For the rest, abstinence from food alone is not sufficient for perfect purity of soul unless the other virtues cooperate as well. Humility, therefore, through obedience in action and through bodily affliction, confers great benefits upon us.

To be free from avarice means not only not to possess money but not even to desire possession of it. Restraint of anger, sadness, vainglory, and pride brings the soul to purity. All these things produce the complete purity of the soul.

But that particular purity of soul which is obtained through self-control is produced above all by abstinence and fasting. For it is impossible for one whose belly is full to fight in spirit against the spirit of fornication.

Our first contest, therefore, must be to command the belly and bring the body into subjection—not only through fasting but also through vigils, labor, reading, and by conceiving in the mind fear of Gehenna and desire for the heavenly kingdom.

## 2. (Cassian, *Institutes*, Book VI, chapters 1 and following)

Our second struggle is against the spirit of fornication and the desire of the flesh, a desire that begins to trouble human beings from their earliest age. It is a great and arduous struggle, consisting of a double contest; for it is waged both in body and in soul. Therefore, one must fight against it with a twofold battle. Bodily fasting alone is not sufficient for possessing perfect self-control and true chastity, unless there is also constant prayer to God, frequent meditation on the divine Scriptures, and manual labor and work, which are able to restrain the restless impulses of the soul and recall it from obscene thoughts. Humility of soul contributes especially to this, without which no one will be able to overcome either fornication or the other passions.

Above all, therefore, we must guard the heart with every care from filthy thoughts (Prov. IV, 23). For from it, according to the Lord’s word, proceed evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, and the rest (Matt. XV, 19). Fasting has indeed been imposed upon us not only for the affliction of the body, but also for the discipline of the mind, so that, not clouded by an excess of food, it may be able to guard against thoughts. We must therefore devote our entire attention not only to bodily fasting, but also to attentiveness to our thoughts and to spiritual meditation; without these it is impossible to ascend to the summit of true chastity and purity.

It is therefore fitting, according to the Lord’s word, that we cleanse the inside of the cup and dish, so that the outside may be clean (Matt. XXIII, 26). Accordingly, if we are concerned, in the Apostle’s words, to struggle lawfully and receive the crown (II Tim. II, 5), once the impure spirit of fornication has been defeated, let us not trust in our own strength or our own ascetic practice, but in the assistance of the Lord God. No one’s struggle with such a demon ever ends until he truly believes that he is freed from such a disease and ascends to the highest summit of chastity not through his own zeal or labor, but through God’s impulse and help.

Indeed, the person who has trampled underfoot the goads of the flesh and its pleasures is doing something beyond nature and, in a certain sense, exists outside the body. Therefore it is impossible for a human being, on his own “wings,” so to speak, to fly up to this summit and to the prize of holiness and become an imitator of the angels, unless God’s grace raises him from earth and filth. For no virtue makes human beings bound to the flesh more like the heavenly angels than self-control: through it, while they still dwell on earth, they have, according to the Apostle, their citizenship in heaven (Phil. III, 20).

An indication that this virtue has been acquired by us is that no image of an obscene fantasy enters the mind of a sleeping person. Even if such movements are not counted as sin, they are nevertheless a sign of a soul that is sick and not yet freed from such a passion. Therefore we must judge that those obscene fantasies which occur during sleep are evidence of preceding negligence [Col. 0880D] and of our weakness; and the cessation of sleep upon awakening reveals the disease lying hidden in the secret recesses of our heart.

For this reason the physician of souls placed the remedy in the inner chambers of the soul, knowing that the causes of the disease are located there, when he says: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. V, 28). He said this not merely to correct lustful and inquisitive eyes, but much more to correct the soul within, which has dishonestly misused the eyes given to it by God for a good purpose. This is why the Wise Man says, not “Guard your eyes with every care,” but “Guard your heart with every care” (Prov. IV, 23). He applies the remedy of the strictest guard especially to that which uses the eyes according to its own will.

Let this, then, be the first guard of our purification: when the memory of a woman enters our mind through the devil’s activity—even if she is our mother, sister, or another pious woman—let us promptly cast it out of our heart. Otherwise, if we linger too long on such a thought, the deceiver and author of evil may, from the imagined appearance of such faces, bring and plunge the mind into obscene and harmful thoughts.

This is what is commanded in the order given by God to the first human being: namely, that he should watch the serpent’s head—that is, the beginning of the harmful thought by which it attempts to creep into our soul—so that, once the head has been admitted, that is, the first incursion of the thought, we do not admit the rest of the serpent’s body, namely, the consent of pleasure, and thus allow it finally to cast the mind into a wicked deed.

Rather, as it is written, we must “kill all the sinners of the earth in the morning” (Ps. C, 8)—that is, by the light of knowledge distinguish and destroy the thoughts that lead to sin, “from the earth,” namely, from the heart, according to the Lord’s word. And while the children of Babylon (Ps. CXXXVI, 9), that is, evil thoughts, are still little, we must level them with the ground and dash them against the stone, which is Christ. For if they reach maturity through our consent, they will not be overcome without great sighs and labors.

To what has been said above from sacred Scripture, the sayings of the holy Fathers should be added. Thus Saint Basil, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, is reported to have said: “I do not know a woman, yet I am not a virgin.” He understood this so clearly that he recognized that the gift of virginity is not rightly possessed merely through bodily self-control regarding a woman, but is possessed much more through holiness and purity of soul and the fear of God.

The Fathers likewise say that we cannot possess the virtue of perfect chastity unless we first possess true humility in our heart, nor can we be regarded as worthy of true knowledge so long as the desire for fornication lies in the inner recesses of the soul.

To make this great virtue publicly evident from the Apostle himself, let us recall one of his statements, with which we shall bring our speech to an end: “Pursue peace with all people, and holiness, without which no one will see the Lord” (Heb. XII, 14). That he is speaking about this matter is clear from what he adds: “Let there be no fornicator or profane person, like Esau” (ibid.).

The more heavenly and angelic the virtue of chastity is, therefore, the more grievous are the ambushes with which it is attacked by the enemy. Accordingly, we must take care not only to preserve bodily self-control, but also to maintain contrition of heart and pour out frequent prayers with sighs, so that the furnace of our flesh, which the Babylonian king kindles daily with the goads of desire, may be extinguished by the dew of the Holy Spirit’s presence.

Moreover, we have a very great weapon against such an enemy: namely, vigils kept in God’s service. For just as chastity and daytime watchfulness prepare holiness for the night, so nighttime vigils kept in God prepare it for the day. . . .

## 3. (Cassian, *Institutes*, Book VII, chapters 1 and following)

Our third struggle is against the spirit of avarice. This kind of war is foreign and contrary to nature, and it comes upon the monk through the occasion of unbelief. The goads of the other passions—anger and desire, for example—appear to derive their opportunity from the body; they are, in a certain sense, implanted in it and have their beginning from birth. This is why they are overcome only after a long period of time.

The disease of avarice, however, comes from outside and can be cut away more easily, provided that care and attentiveness of mind are present. But if it is neglected, it becomes more destructive than the other passions and turns into something accursed, for, according to the Apostle, it is “the root of all evils” (I Tim. VI, 10).

Let us consider the matter in this way. Natural movements of the body are seen not only in children, who do not yet possess discernment between good and evil, but even in the smallest and nursing infants [Col. 0882B]. Although they possess not even a trace of carnal pleasure, they nevertheless display movement in the flesh. The impulse of anger likewise appears in infants, when we see them becoming agitated against those who cause them annoyance.

I say this not to reproach nature as the cause of sin—far from it—but to show that, although anger and desire have been bestowed upon human beings by God the Creator for a good purpose, nevertheless through the nature of the body a person may, in a certain sense, through his own negligence, fall into things contrary to nature.

The movement of the body was given by the Creator for the procreation of children and the continuing succession of the human race, not for fornication. The movement of anger was implanted in us for salvation, so that we might be angry against sin, not so that we might be stirred by fury against one of our own kind.

If, therefore, we misuse these things, nature is by no means thereby guilty, nor should we accuse the Maker—just as we would not accuse the one who gave iron for a necessary and useful purpose if the person who received it were to use it for committing murders.

We have said this to show that the passion of avarice does not originate from a natural movement, but from sheer wickedness and a corrupt purpose. For when this disease finds a soul tepid and unbelieving at the beginning of its withdrawal from the world, it presents certain plausible, and in appearance rational, reasons, persuading the monk to retain something from his possessions.

It brings before the monk’s mind the prospect of a long old age and bodily infirmity; it suggests that what is provided in the monastery for necessity is not sufficient for consolation, not only for the sick but not even for the healthy; that proper care is not given there to the sick, but that they are greatly neglected, so that, unless some gold is secretly available, one must perish miserably.

Finally, it suggests that he will not be able to persevere long in the monastery because of the hardship of the tasks and the severity of the superior. Once it has armed his mind with such thoughts so that he retains even a single coin, it then persuades him to learn, secretly from the abbot, a craft by which he can diligently increase the money he has saved.

At last it deceives the wretch with a hidden hope, suggesting that profit will come from his craft and that from this there will be quiet and a mind free from cares. Bound at length by the thought of profit, he considers nothing adverse: neither how great his anger and fury will be if he happens to suffer some loss, nor how great his grief and pain will be if he is deprived of the profit from his work. But just as the belly is the god of others, so gold is his god.

Therefore, since blessed Paul knew this well, he called avarice not only “the root of all evils,” but also idolatry. Let us consider, then, into what great wickedness this disease drives a human being, since it casts him into idolatry.

After the avaricious person has torn his mind away from the love of God, he loves images of human beings engraved in gold. The monk, darkened by such thoughts and receiving further increase toward worse things, can no longer possess any humility or obedience. He becomes angry and indignant, murmurs against every task, resists, and, with no sense of shame remaining, is carried headlong like an utterly unbridled horse.

Not content with his daily food, he finally declares that he can endure no longer. He says that God is not present only there and that his salvation is not confined to that place, but that God is found everywhere by those who seek him. He declares that he will perish unless he leaves that monastery.

Thus, when hidden money is available to assist his corrupted mind, he seems to have been lifted on certain wings and, while planning his departure from the monastery, thereafter answers every command proudly and harshly. Considering himself a stranger and an outsider, if he sees anything in the monastery worthy of correction, he does not care about it—indeed, he despises it.

Next he seeks occasions for anger or complaint, so that he may not appear to leave the monastery lightly and without cause. He does not hesitate to conduct himself in such a way as to find someone to assist him in his wrongdoing.

Thus deceived and inflamed by the fire of his money, the avaricious person can never rest in the monastery or live under its rule. When the demon has snatched him from the fold like a wolf, separated him from the fold, and taken him for its own devouring, it then makes him carry out in his cell, both night and day and with great eagerness, the tasks which he had neglected at their appointed hours in the monastery.

It does not allow him to observe his customary prayers, the practice of fasting, or the rule of vigils. Rather, once he has been bound by the madness of avarice, it persuades him to devote all his zeal and all his labor to his own work.

This disease has three forms, equally prohibited by the divine Scriptures and by the teaching of the Fathers.

The first, about which we wrote above, seeks to make wretched people acquire and accumulate things that they did not possess even in the world. The second acts so that those who have renounced money may repent of what they have done, and persuades them to seek again what they offered to God. The third, after binding the monk at the beginning with the tepidness of unbelief, does not allow him to renounce worldly things completely, placing in his mind fear of poverty and distrust of God’s providence. It makes him a violator of the promises he professed when he renounced the world.

We find examples of these three forms hidden in divine Scripture. Gehazi, because he desired money that he had not previously possessed, was deprived of the prophetic grace which his master wished to leave him as an inheritance; and instead of a blessing, through the prophet’s curse he possessed eternal leprosy (IV Kings V).

Judas, however, when he wished to recover the money that he had previously cast aside in order to follow the Lord, was not only expelled from the company of the Apostles after he had turned his mind toward betraying the Lord, but also ended his bodily life by a violent death (Matt. XXVII, 5).

Ananias and Sapphira, when they kept back some of what they had consecrated to the Lord, paid the penalty of death by the apostolic word (Acts V).

But that great man Moses, in Deuteronomy, gives a mystical command to those who are about to renounce the world and who, through a certain fear of distrust, still cling to earthly things: “If any man is timid and fearful in heart, he shall not go out to war; let him return home and live softly there, lest he perhaps make the hearts of his brothers fearful” (Deut. XX, 8).

Is anything more secure and clearer than this testimony? Do we not learn from these words that those who renounce the world must renounce it completely and proceed to war, lest through a soft and corrupted beginning they turn others away from evangelical perfection?

Since it is clearly said in Scripture, “It is more blessed to give than to receive” (Acts XX, 35), some people interpret it badly, do violence to the force of the wording, and twist the meaning of the saying toward their own fraud and desire for money. They likewise distort the Lord’s teaching, which says: “If you wish to be perfect, sell everything you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me” (Matt. XIX, 21).

They judge that the possession of wealth is more fortunate than poverty, and that from such abundance they can distribute gifts to those in need. Such people should know that they have not yet renounced the world and are not walking in monastic perfection, so long as they are ashamed to embrace with the Apostle, for Christ’s sake, glorious poverty, and to support themselves and the needy by the work of their hands.

If they wish to fulfill their monastic promise in practice and to receive glory with the Apostle, let them distribute their former wealth and, in hunger, thirst, and nakedness, struggle with Paul in the good struggle (II Tim. IV, 7).

For if the Apostle himself had regarded possession of his former wealth as necessary for perfection, he would certainly not have despised his earlier status. For he testifies that he was distinguished and a Roman citizen (Acts XXII, 25).

Those who sold their houses and fields in Jerusalem and laid the proceeds at the feet of the Apostles (Acts IV, 35) would certainly not have done so if they had thought that the Apostles were more fortunate when supplied with money than when supported by their own labor and the work of their hands.

The Apostle teaches the matter even more clearly in his Epistle to the Romans: “But now I am setting out for Jerusalem to minister to the saints. For Macedonia and Achaia have decided to make some contribution for the poor among the saints who are in Jerusalem” (Rom. XV, 25).

He himself, however, often imprisoned and subjected to the hardships of travel, and hindered from providing by his own hands the necessities he had previously been accustomed to provide, teaches that he received these necessities from the brothers who came from Macedonia and who had come to meet him, saying: “For the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied what I lacked” (II Cor. XI, 9).

And to the Philippians: “In the beginning of the Gospel, when no church shared with me in the matter of giving and receiving except you alone—for even in Thessalonica you sent something for my needs once and twice” (Philipp. IV, 15).

Let the avaricious, then, according to their own judgment, be happier than the Apostle, since their necessities are supplied from their own substance. Yet no one but someone who had fallen into the extremity of madness would dare to say this.

If, therefore, we wish to follow the evangelical and apostolic command, and the entire Church founded upon the Apostles from the beginning, let us not obey our own opinions, nor misunderstand what has been properly said. Let us reject that tepid and unbelieving disposition of soul and attain to a careful zeal for the Gospel.

In this way we shall be able to follow in the footsteps of the holy Fathers, never depart from the knowledge and discipline of the coenobium, and truly renounce this world.

It will be worthwhile at this point to recall sayings of the holy Fathers. The following saying is attributed to Saint Basil, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, addressed to a certain senatorial man who had tepidly renounced the world but had kept back something from his money: “You have lost your senatorial rank, and you have not become a monk.”

We must therefore cut away from our soul with every care the root and source of all evils, namely, avarice, knowing with complete certainty that, so long as the root remains, branches will sprout, and that it is difficult to practice virtue unless we live in a coenobium; for there we do not even concern ourselves with necessary things.

Keeping before our eyes the condemnation of Ananias and Sapphira (Acts V), let us shudder at reserving anything for ourselves from our former possessions. Let us likewise fear the example of Gehazi (IV Kings V), who because of avarice was handed over to eternal leprosy.

Let us beware of accumulating for ourselves the money of this life, which we did not possess even in the world. Let us also fear, remembering Judas perishing by the noose, lest we preserve anything from all those things to which we renounced ourselves with contempt.

And, always keeping before our eyes the uncertain hour of death, let us beware lest the Lord come at an hour when we do not expect him and find our conscience stained with avarice, and say to us what was said to that rich man in the Gospel: “Fool, this night they demand your soul from you; and the things you have prepared—whose will they be?” (Luke XII, 20).

## 4. (Cassian, *Institutes*, Book VIII, chapters 1 and following)

Our fourth struggle is against the spirit of anger, so that with God we may cut this deadly poison out from the innermost part of our soul. Once it has been placed within our heart and has blinded the eye of the mind with dark disturbances, we can no longer possess discernment concerning anything appropriate to us, nor attain an understanding of spiritual knowledge, nor become participants in true life; nor will our mind be capable of divine and true light.

For it is written: “My eye has been troubled by fury” (Ps. VI, 8).

Nor shall we share in wisdom, even if we appear wise to ourselves, since it is written: “Fury will dwell in the bosom of fools.” Nor can we attain the salutary rays of discernment, even if people regard us as exceedingly wise, for it is written: “Anger also destroys the prudent.” Nor can we hold the helm of justice with a watchful heart, since it is written: “The anger of man does not accomplish the justice of God” (James I, 20). Nor can we obtain the modesty and propriety celebrated by everyone, since it is written: “An angry man is not modest” (Prov. XI, 25).

Whoever therefore wishes to reach perfection and desires to engage lawfully in spiritual combat must be free from every fault of anger and fury, and must listen to what that chosen Vessel commands: “Let all bitterness and anger and indignation and clamor and blasphemy be removed from you, together with all malice” (Eph. IV, 31).

When he says “all,” he leaves us no occasion for indignation, whether supposedly necessary or supposedly justified.

Whoever therefore wishes to rebuke an erring brother or impose correction upon him should take care to keep himself free from agitation and disturbance, lest, while he wishes to heal another, he acquire the disease himself, and the evangelical saying be spoken to him: “Physician, heal yourself” (Luke IV, 23); and again: “Why do you see the splinter in your brother’s eye but do not notice the beam in your own eye? Or how will you say to your brother, ‘Let me remove the splinter from your eye,’ while you have a beam in your own eye covering it?” (Mark VII, 23).

For whatever the cause from which the movement of anger boils up, it blinds the eyes of the mind and does not allow a person to look upon the Sun of justice. Just as someone who places gold or lead before his eyes is equally prevented from seeing, and the value of the gold makes no difference to the blindness, so, whatever the cause from which the movement of anger is kindled, it darkens the soul’s faculty of sight.

We use indignation according to nature only when we arouse it against vicious and pleasure-seeking thoughts. The prophet David teaches this when he says: “Be angry and do not sin” (Ps. IV, 5); that is, arouse anger against your own passions and against perverse thoughts, and do not sin by doing what they suggest to you.

The interpretation is made entirely clear by what follows: “What you say in your hearts,” he says, “be pierced in your beds” (ibid.); that is, when perverse thoughts rise into your heart, drive them out by stirring up your anger against them. Once they have been expelled, then, as though upon a bed or in a place of rest, be pierced with repentance.

Blessed Paul agrees with this, using the testimony of this saying and adding: “Let not the sun go down upon your anger; do not give place to the devil” (Eph. IV, 26). That is: by consenting to perverse thoughts, do not provoke Christ, the Sun of justice, so that he may set in your hearts, and so that, when he has departed, the devil may find a place in you.

God speaks of this Sun through the prophet: “For those who fear my name, the Sun of justice shall rise, and healing shall be in his wings” (Mal. IV, 2).

But if we take the Apostle’s saying literally, we are not permitted to preserve anger even until sunset. What, then, shall we say of those who, corrupted by savagery and madness, preserve their anger not merely until this sun has set, but prolong it for many days, abstaining from mutual conversation? They no longer express their anger in words, but by maintaining silence toward one another, they inflame the poison of remembered injuries to their own destruction.

They do not understand that one must abstain not only from the sin committed in deed, but also from the sin conceived in the mind, lest the mind, darkened by the shadows of remembered injuries, fall away from the light of knowledge and discernment and be deprived of the indwelling of the Holy Spirit.

For this reason the Lord commands in the Gospels that the gift be left upon the altar and that one be reconciled with one’s brother (Matt. V, 24). A gift cannot be acceptable while we are occupied by anger and the memory of injuries.

When the Apostle says that we must pray without ceasing and lift up holy hands in every place (I Thess. V, 17), he teaches that this must be done without anger, even if the anger exists only in thought.

It remains, therefore, either that we never pray and thus become liable to the apostolic command, or that, if we are concerned to obey the command, we pray without anger and without remembrance of injuries.

But since it often happens that, when our brothers are saddened or disturbed, we disregard the matter and say that we are not responsible for their sadness, the physician of souls, in order to uproot the occasions of anger from our heart, commands not only that, if we are saddened or angry against our brother, we leave our gift and be reconciled with him (Matt. V, 24), but also that, even if he is angry with us justly or unjustly, we calm his anger by our excuse, and then offer our gift.

But why should we linger longer over evangelical and apostolic commands, when we can learn this also from the ancient Law? Although it seems to turn away from its former severity and to moderate itself, it says: “You shall not hate your brother in your heart” (Lev. XIX, 17); and again: “The ways of those who retain the memory of injuries lead to death” (Prov. XII, 25).

In this passage it prohibits and condemns not only the anger that breaks out into action, but also the anger retained in the mind.

Therefore, clinging to the divine laws, we must struggle with all our strength against the spirit of anger and against that disease located within us. We must not stir up anger against human beings and therefore pursue solitude and withdrawal, imagining that, because no one is present there to provoke us to anger, the virtue of equanimity can easily be practiced in solitude.

For this desire to be separated from our brothers arises both from pride and from our unwillingness to accuse ourselves and to attribute the causes of anger to our own negligence. As long as we attribute the causes of our weakness to others, it is impossible for us to attain the perfection of equanimity.

The sum of our correction is not obtained from our neighbor’s equanimity toward us, but from our own patience toward our neighbor and our forgetfulness of injuries.

When we flee the struggle for equanimity and seek the desert and solitude, we must consider that whatever passions we bring there, still unhealed and unquieted, remain hidden rather than destroyed. The desert and withdrawal know how not only to preserve imperfections in those who are not yet free from passions, but also to conceal them.

It does not even allow such people to recognize what passions they are subject to. On the contrary, through the fantasies it suggests, it persuades them that they have attained equanimity and humility, so long as no one is present to provoke and test them.

But when an occasion arises in which they are provoked and put to the test, the passions hidden and concealed for so long immediately burst forth like unbridled horses breaking out of their stalls. Fed by long rest and idleness, they hurl their rider into destruction with greater violence and savagery.

For passions that remain idle and are not stirred up by human beings become more savage within us. The very shadow of patience and equanimity that we possess only in fantasy and opinion is lost, through the idleness of solitude and our negligence in exercising it, if we mix with our brothers.

Just as poisonous animals lying in the desert and in their lairs display their fury only when they seize someone who approaches, so people subject to passions, who are at rest not through a love of virtue but through the necessary condition of a deserted place, vomit forth the poison of their soul when they seize someone who approaches and provokes them.

Therefore, those who seek the perfection of gentleness must not only avoid becoming angry against human beings, but also against animals, and even against inanimate things.

I remember that when I was living in the desert, I became angry against a reed because I disliked either its thickness or its thinness; against a piece of wood because, when I wished to cut it, I could not do so quickly; and again against a flint for striking fire, because, while I was hurrying to produce fire, the spark did not leap out immediately [Col. 0888C]. Such is the extent to which anger rages that it extends even to insensible and inanimate things.

If, therefore, we wish to attain the blessedness of Christ, we must restrain not only the anger that breaks out into action, as was said above, but also the anger conceived in the mind.

For it is not nearly as beneficial to restrain one’s mouth and refrain from uttering some furious word as it is to cleanse the heart from the memory of injuries and not nourish perverse thoughts.

Evangelical teaching teaches that the roots of sins must be cut out rather than merely their branches. Once the root of anger has been cut from the heart, no hatred or envy will be carried into action. For “whoever hates his brother is a murderer”; in the affection of hatred, he has killed him.

God sees the one who has been killed. Human beings do not see his blood poured out by a sword, but he has been killed through the affection of hatred.

God therefore will recompense each person with crowns or punishments not only for deeds, but also for thoughts and intention, just as he says through the prophet: “I am coming to gather their works, thoughts, and meditations.”

Again the Apostle says: “Their thoughts alternately accusing or even defending them, on the day when God will judge the hidden things of human beings” (Rom. II, 15).

The Lord himself, teaching that we must lay aside all anger, says in the Gospels: “Whoever is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment” (Matt. V, 22).

Thus the accurate copies read; for the word “without cause” is an addition. This is evident from the preceding clause of Scripture. The Lord’s intention is entirely to cut away the root and spark of anger and not to preserve within us even the smallest occasion of anger, lest, if we arouse anger for a supposedly justified reason, we finally fall into the fury of a brute animal.

The perfect cure for this disease is therefore to be convinced that we are permitted to stir up our indignation for neither a just nor an unjust cause. For if the spirit of anger darkens the mind, neither the light of discernment nor the guidance of right counsel and justice will be found in us. While the spirit of anger rules, our soul cannot become a temple of the Holy Spirit.

Finally, keeping before our eyes the uncertain hour of death, we must guard ourselves from anger and know that neither ascetic discipline, nor self-control, nor renunciation of every material possession, nor fasts and vigils will benefit us if, seized by anger and hatred, we are liable to judgment.

From this may we be freed by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever.

## 5. (Cassian, *Institutes*, Book IX, chapters 1 and following)

Our fifth struggle is against the spirit of sadness, which darkens our soul so that it cannot devote itself to any spiritual contemplation, and restrains it from every good work.

When that wicked spirit has seized the soul and wholly darkened it, it does not allow it to pour out prayers with eagerness, to devote itself to receiving benefit from sacred readings, or to be gentle and accommodating toward the brothers. It suggests hatred of every serious activity and of the very profession of this life.

Finally, while sadness confuses all the soul’s salutary counsels [Col. 0889C], dissolves its firmness and perseverance, and makes it, as it were, foolish and stunned, it binds the soul at last with thoughts of despair.

Therefore our single aim must be to wage the spiritual struggle, to conquer the spirit of wickedness with God’s help, and to guard our heart with every care from the spirit of sadness (Prov. IV, 23).

For just as the moth consumes clothing and the worm wood, so sadness gnaws at a human being’s soul. It persuades him to withdraw from every good association, does not allow him to receive counsel from true friends, or to give them a gentle and peaceful answer. Instead, it wholly disturbs the soul and fills it with carelessness, and finally persuades it to flee from human beings, as though they had been responsible for its disturbance.

It does not allow the soul to recognize that the sickness is located not externally but internally [Col. 0889D], and that it becomes apparent when the assaults of temptation reveal it by experience.

For no human being will ever be harmed by another unless he has the disease within himself—namely, the causes of the passions. For this reason God, the Maker of all things and the physician of souls, who alone knows the wounds of the soul accurately and thoroughly, does not command us to abandon human society, but to cut away the causes of wickedness within ourselves. He knows that the soul’s health is obtained not in separation from human beings, but in interaction with them and through exercise.

Therefore, when we leave our brothers because of certain supposedly justified occasions, we do not cut off the occasions of sadness at all; we have merely changed them, since the disease located within us moves them according to circumstances [Col. 0890A].

Our entire battle must therefore be against the inner passions. Once these have been expelled with God’s help, we shall live easily not only with human beings but even with wild beasts, according to the saying of blessed Job: “The savage beasts will be at peace with you” (Job V, 23).

We must first fight against the spirit of sadness, which casts the soul into despair, so that we may drive that evil from our heart. For it did not allow Cain to repent after the murder of his brother, nor Judas after the betrayal of the Lord.

Let us consider as sadness alone that which concerns repentance for sins, joined with good hope, and which obtains possession of heavenly goods. Of this the Apostle said: “The sadness that is according to God” (II Cor. VII, 10). [lacuna]

That sadness, therefore, which nourishes the soul with the hope of repentance is mingled with joy. Consequently, it makes a person eager and ready for every good work, and also approachable and humble.

### Editorial note

Here one leaf is missing—namely, the remainder of what is said against the spirit of sadness and the beginning of what is said about the spirit of torpor.

### 6. (Cassian, *Institutes*, Book X, chapters 13 and following)

…Let them eat bread.

Let us hear how wisely the Apostle shows us the causes of this torpor. He calls those who do not work “disorderly” (II Thess. 3:6), revealing much wickedness in that single word. For whoever is idle is also reckless in speech, ready to abuse others, ultimately unfit to lead a quiet life, and a slave of torpor. He therefore commands us to withdraw from such a person—that is, to separate ourselves from him—as from a pestilential disease.

Then what does he say? “And not according to the tradition which they received from us” (II Thess. 3:6). By this statement he shows them to be proud, contemptuous, and violators of the apostolic traditions. And again: “Nor did we eat bread from anyone without paying for it, but in labor and toil, working night and day, so as not to burden any of you” (ibid., 8).

That teacher of the Gentiles, preacher of the Gospel, who was caught up to the third heaven (II Cor. 12:2), who says that the Lord commanded those who proclaim the Gospel to live from the Gospel (I Cor. 9:14), worked in labor night and day so as not to burden anyone. What, then, should we do, who through torpor shun work and seek bodily ease, to whom neither the preaching of the Gospel nor the care of churches has been entrusted, but only concern for our own soul falls upon us?

Then, showing more clearly how much harm arises from idleness, he adds: “Doing nothing, but being busybodies” (II Thess. 3:11). From idleness disorder arises, and from disorder every form of wickedness. Then, preparing a remedy for this, he says: “But such persons we command and exhort, that, working quietly, they eat their own bread” (ibid., 12). And with a strong rebuke he adds: “If anyone does not wish to work, neither let him eat” (ibid., 10).

Instructed by these apostolic commands, the holy Egyptian fathers do not allow monks to be idle even for the shortest time, especially younger monks, knowing that through perseverance in work they drive away torpor, obtain their own nourishment, and become a help to those in need. For they work not only for their own necessities, but also supply from their labor what is necessary to strangers, the poor, those handed over to prison, and all who are needy. They believe that such service is a sacrifice acceptable to God.

The Fathers also say this: the person who works fights with one demon and is often troubled by him; the idle person, however, is held captive by countless demons.

It will be worthwhile to recall a saying of Abba Moses, one of the most esteemed among the Fathers, which he spoke to me. When I had been sitting in the desert for a short time, torpor afflicted me. I approached him and addressed him as follows:

“Afflicted and greatly weakened by torpor, I was not freed from it until I went and met Abba Paul.”

Abba Moses answered me:

“I see clearly that you have not freed yourself from it at all until now; rather, you have surrendered yourself to it and handed yourself over as its captive and slave. Know, therefore, that you must fight against it all the more severely, as a deserter, unless henceforth you strive to oppose it through perseverance, prayer, and manual labor.”

### 7. (Cassian, *Institutes*, Book XI, chapters 1 and following)

Our seventh contest is against the spirit of vainglory, that manifold and extremely subtle passion which is not even perceived by the person who is being tempted by it. The attacks of the other passions are more obvious, and it is easier to fight against them: when the soul recognizes the battle, it overcomes them by resistance and prayer.

But since the wickedness of vainglory is manifold, as was said above, it is difficult to defeat. It presents itself in every human activity: in clothing, appearance, gait, speech, vigils, fasts, prayer, reading, quietness, and equanimity. Through all these things it attempts to stab Christ’s soldier.

When it cannot deceive someone through costly clothing and turn him toward vainglory, it tempts him through the cheapness of his clothing. One whom it could not inflate through honor, it inflates through patiently enduring dishonor, even to the point of folly. One whom it could not lead to vainglory through knowledge, it tries to deceive through silence, as though he were a quiet person. One whom it could not draw toward softness through luxurious foods, it leads through fasting to a desire for praise.

In short, every work and every pursuit offers this demon an occasion for battle. Moreover, the person attacked by it sometimes imagines for himself the ranks of the sacred ministry.

I remember a certain old man who, when I was living at Scetis, went to the cell of a brother in order to visit him. As he approached the cell door, he heard the man speaking inside. Since the old man thought that he was reciting something from Scripture, he stood listening. He realized, however, that the brother was raving under the influence of vainglory and was ordaining himself deacon and dismissing the catechumens.

When the old man heard this, he finally opened the door and entered. The brother came to meet him, greeted him as usual, and asked whether he had been standing at the door for a long time. The old man then calmly replied:

“I arrived just now, when you were dismissing the catechumens.”

When the brother heard this, he fell at the old man’s feet and asked him in prayer to free him from such an error.

I recall this event to show into what great folly this demon casts a person.

Whoever, therefore, wishes to fight perfectly and be crowned with righteousness should strive by every means to overcome this many-shaped beast, always keeping before his eyes the saying of holy David: “The Lord has scattered the bones of those who please men” (Ps. 52:6). Let him do nothing with a view to human praise, but seek his reward from God; let him always cast away from his heart the thoughts of his own praise that invade it, and let him despise himself in the sight of God.

By this means, with God’s help, he will be able to escape the demon of vainglory, through the grace of our Lord Jesus, to whom be glory forever. Amen.

### 8. (Cassian, *Institutes*, Book XII, chapters 1 and following)

Our eighth contest is against the spirit of pride. This is more serious and more fierce than all the others; it is especially against the perfect that it wages war, and it attempts to overthrow those who have almost reached the summit of virtue. Like a pestilential disease, it destroys not merely one part of the body but the whole.

The other passions, each individually, although they disturb the soul, nevertheless fight only against the one virtue opposed to them and try to overcome it; thus they obscure and trouble the soul only in part. The passion of pride, however, covers the whole soul with darkness and leads it to utter ruin.

To understand more clearly what has been said, let us consider the matter in this way. The vice of gluttony strives to corrupt abstinence; fornication, chastity; avarice, poverty; anger, gentleness; and the remaining forms of wickedness, the virtues opposed to them. But when the wickedness of pride dominates the wretched soul, it acts like some most savage tyrant who, after capturing a spacious and lofty city, destroys it entirely and overturns it from its foundations.

The angel who fell from heaven because of pride is a witness to this. Created by God and adorned with every virtue and wisdom, he did not wish to attribute these things to God’s grace but to his own nature. Hence he thought himself equal to God. Rebuking this thought, the prophet says: “You said in your heart: ‘I will sit upon the lofty mountain; I will set my throne above the clouds, and I will be like the Most High’” (Isa. 14:13). “But you are a man, and not God” (ibid., 31:3).

Another prophet says: “Why do you boast in wickedness, you who are mighty?” And shortly afterward: “You loved all words of destruction, and a deceitful tongue. Therefore God will destroy you forever; he will pluck you up and remove you from your tent, and your root from the land of the living. The righteous will see and fear, and they will laugh at him and say: ‘Behold the man who did not set God as his helper, and prevailed in his vanity’” (Ps. 51).

Knowing these things, let us fear and guard our heart with every care (Prov. 4:23) against the deadly spirit of pride. When we have accomplished some work of virtue, let us recite to ourselves the Apostle’s words: “Yet not I, but the grace of God which is with me” (I Cor. 15:10); and what was spoken by the Lord: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5); and what the prophet said: “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain” (Ps. 126:1); and again: “It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Rom. 9:16).

For even if someone is ardent in zeal and diligent in purpose, yet bound by flesh and blood, he cannot attain perfection unless he places his hope for all these things in the mercy and grace of Christ. For, according to the divine James: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (James 1:17). And Paul says: “What do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (I Cor. 4:7). Yet you exalt yourself over another’s gifts as though they were your own.

That salvation comes to us through the grace and mercy of God is shown by that thief who obtained the kingdom of heaven not as the reward of virtue, but through the grace and mercy of God (Luke 23:43).

Since our fathers knew these things well, they all taught with one accord that we cannot lay a firm foundation for the perfection of virtue unless we do so through humility, which proceeds from faith, gentleness, and perfect poverty. Through these, perfect love is obtained by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be glory forever. Amen.

# Appendix to the Works of Saint Eucherius, Containing Writings Doubtfully or Falsely Attributed to the Holy Father

## Commentaries on Genesis, Divided into Three Books (C, G, S)*

## Book One

### [Column 893B]

Since we fear piling up too much, lest the stomachs of readers, once filled, should not only refuse what is offered but also reject what has been swallowed, before speaking about the origin of the world we must respond to those who attempt to argue about God with sacrilegious speech, saying: “Why did God make heaven and earth? What was God doing before he made heaven and earth? Why did a new will arise in God, so that he should create the world?”

They should be answered as follows: No new will arose in God. For although the world did not exist in reality, it always existed in the eternal will. Therefore it is said in vain: “Why, while God remained inactive for so many ages in the past, did a new thought of making the world arise?” The construction of the world always remains in his eternal plan. There was not time before the beginning, but eternity; for time began with the establishment of creation, not creation with time.

### (Chapter 1.—Verse 1)

“In the beginning God made.” This meaning may be understood in two ways without difficulty: either that he made it first of all things, or that he made it “in the Beginning,” which is Wisdom—that is, in his Word. For he is the Son, through whom all things were made (John 1); he is the Beginning in which all things were made.

### (The same passage)

“Heaven and earth.” If heaven and earth were made first of all, then the angels were made afterward; but if the angels were made beforehand, God did not make heaven and earth first of all.

Some judge that by the name “heaven” the heavenly—that is, the angelic—creation is meant, in comparison with which this corporeal heaven is called “earth.” By the name “earth,” however, he indicates that formless matter from which this visible heaven and earth, and the entire mass of this world, was formed. Of it it is written: “You made the world from formless matter.”

But matter was made from nothing, whereas the appearance of the world was made from formless matter, which was called by the names “heaven” and “earth”—not because it already was this, but because this could already come to be from it.

At first, therefore, he wished to speak of heaven and earth as a kind of spiritual and corporeal matter, and then to weave the sequence according to which they were made individually.

We read how the creation of heaven and earth was historically established from the beginning of the beginning; but let us understand how it is received spiritually by teachers in the Church.

“In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” Christ is the Beginning, as he himself says in the Gospel: “I am the Beginning, who also speak to you” (ibid., 8). In this Beginning, therefore, God made heaven—that is, spiritual people who meditate on and seek heavenly things. In him he also made the carnal, who have not yet laid aside the earthly human being.

### (Verse 2)

“Now the earth was formless and empty.” That is, the matter itself was still formless, because heaven and earth had not yet been made from it, nor had all the things that remained to be formed yet been formed.

For this matter, made from nothing, nevertheless preceded the things made from it—not in eternity or in time, just as wood precedes a chest, but only in origin, as a voice precedes a word, or sound a song. For he who lives eternally created all things simultaneously.

The earth of our flesh was formless and empty before it received the shape of instruction.

“And darkness was over the face of the abyss.” This dark abyss signifies the obscurity of the still-formless matter itself, because as yet no form could be seen or handled. For “abyss” is the name given to an immense depth of waters, because the blindness of sins and ignorance covered our hearts with profound darkness.

“And the Spirit of God was borne over the waters.” By the name “waters” he likewise indicates that same formless matter which lay subject to the Creator’s will, so that all things might be established according to their kinds. For whether you call it empty earth, dark abyss, or water, the names are different, but the matter is one and the same.

It is called empty earth because it was not yet filled with the totality of created things. It is called dark abyss because it did not yet possess the appearance of light. It is called water because whether flesh or all things that are generated, they are moist and formed from moisture.

For this corporeal heaven also, which is called the firmament, was made on the second day after the establishment of light; and this earth then received its form when the abyss was distinguished. The waters themselves then assumed their form when they were gathered together in one place beneath the firmament.

Accordingly, by “heaven” we are not to understand this corporeal heaven, but the spiritual creation of the angels; nor by “earth” or “abyss” these visible elements, but the formless and dark matter of the world.

“And darkness was over the face of the abyss.” Some customarily ask: “Whence was there darkness before light existed? Who had made it? Or, if no one had made it, is it eternal?”

They should be answered as follows: Darkness is not something in itself; rather, the absence of light received this name. Just as silence is nothing, but where there is no voice it is called silence, so darkness is nothing, but where there is no light it is called darkness.

“And the Spirit of God was borne over the waters.” The Holy Spirit is God, who is not contained or extended in a place, nor subject to changes of time, but is everywhere present and wholly present.

The Spirit of the Lord is said to be borne over the waters not by wandering about, but by power; not locally, but potentially; not through the spaces of places, as the sun is borne over the earth, but through the power of his sublimity.

For God did not make his works from need, but from benevolence and omnipotence. Though needing nothing, he creates all things; in mercy he gives life to all; and he remains in holy fullness. He is not enlarged by our praises, but is made known and praised through his works, for he does not need the things he makes.

For needy and impoverished love is subjected to the things it loves; therefore love that is not needy is borne above the things it loves. Thus the Holy Spirit is said to be borne over creation because he did not operate in creating creation from need.

In place of what is written in our codices as “was borne,” the Hebrew has [Hebrew term missing in the supplied text], which we may render “brooded” or “warmed,” in the manner of a bird giving life to eggs through heat.

From this we understand that the passage does not speak of the spirit of the world, as some suppose, but of the Holy Spirit, who from the beginning is likewise called the vivifier of all things. He is a vivifier in the same way as he is Creator and God. For Scripture says: “Send forth your Spirit, and they will be created” (Ps. 104).

It should be noted that at the very beginning of heaven and earth the entire Trinity of the Creator is indicated: the Father is understood in the name “God,” the Son in “Beginning,” and the Holy Spirit in the one who was borne over the waters.

The Holy Spirit was borne over the waters.

The Holy Spirit was already borne over our dark and unstable heart as over the waters, so that we might rest by abiding in him, be given life by his breath, and be washed by his wave.

### (Verse 3)

“God said, ‘Let there be light.’ And there was light.”

If he spoke in the day, he spoke temporally; if he spoke temporally, he spoke through some creature. Therefore light is not the first creature, since there already existed something through which he could say, “Let there be light.”

In truth, he neither spoke in the day nor spoke temporally, because before every creature he begot his Word.

The speech of God, therefore, is the Word of God. But divine Scripture, accommodating itself to little ones and in a certain way nursing them so that they may progress and receive spiritual food, chose throughout the formation of every creature to call God’s act of speaking “speech.”

For example, if you ask how light was made, you hear: “It was in the Word of God that it should be made.” How was heaven made? “It was in the Word of God that it should be made.” And so with the rest in order: if you ask how they were made, the answer is: “They were in the Word of God so that they should be made.”

This is what “God said, ‘Let there be light’” means. The writer used “said” in place of “made,” to show the speed or ease of God’s work. For the divine nature does not speak in bodily ways, nor did it form words each time it spoke. It begot one Word, coeternal and consubstantial with itself, in which it spoke all things ineffably and outside time.

Such speech by God is not a sound passing away in time, but the mere expression of reason.

“God said, ‘Let there be light.’” Historically, the creation of the angels is recapitulated in this light. Because they participate in eternal light, they are called light and day. To show their unity, it is not said “the first day,” but “one day.”

A question arises concerning the angels: why are they passed over in the creation of the six days, as though they were not among God’s works?

That the angels are God’s work is attested by the hymn of the three young men. For after it had said, “Bless all the works of the Lord, O Lord” (Ps. 102), in the execution of those same works it also named the angels. And in the Psalms, after saying among other things, “Praise the Lord, all his angels,” it added: “For he spoke, and they were made” (Ps. 116).

By these examples it is demonstrated that the angels were made by God, but nowhere does Scripture indicate on what day they were created.

Yet since it is written in Holy Scripture that God said, “When the stars were made, all my angels praised me,” the angels already existed on the fourth day, when the stars were established. Therefore they were not made on the third day either. It is obvious that on that day the earth, separated from the waters, produced the grass of pasture.

Nor were they made on the second day, for then, when the firmament had been made, there was a division between the waters above and the waters below.

There is nothing surprising, then, if the angels of light are understood to have been created in the works of the six days. For they were made before every creature, since Wisdom was created before all things. They are therefore called wisdom because they cleave to eternal Wisdom.

But were they also made before time, since Wisdom was made before all things—that is, before everything, including time?

It was fitting that a creature cleaving immovably to its Creator, although not equal to its Creator, should at least be prior and superior to every other creature. Although they are mutable by nature, everlasting grace makes them immutable and incorruptible.

For if they were by nature unchangeable, the devil would certainly not have fallen. The contemplation of the Creator, however, supports the mutability of their nature. Hence the apostate angel was deprived of grace, because he wished his strength to consist not in God but in himself.

The angels possess such great grace that neither their coming nor their departure has been subject to the succession of times. For it is established that there are two things among created beings whose change cannot be encompassed by time.

First are the angels, because they cleave immutably to the Creator. Second is that formless matter, because its prior state cannot be encompassed by time before all these things that move temporally were formed from it.

God also said, “Let there be light”—that is, “Let the illumination of faith appear.” On the first day he gave the light of faith, because faith is first in conversion.

Hence this is also the first commandment in God’s precepts: “The Lord your God is one God” (Deut. 6). Because of this faith, the Lord himself also wished to appear visibly in the world.

### (Verses 4 and following)

“And God saw the light, that it was good.”

God did not suddenly see that the light was good, as though the sight had given him knowledge. In us, every work is preceded by our will, when we think about what we ought to do. No one who is ignorant does something while considering how to accomplish what he has decided through thought should be done.

If it cannot happen to a human being that he does something in ignorance, how much less can it happen to God, who does everything according to his eternal and unchanging counsel?

Therefore he does not learn, but teaches what has been made in the art of what was to be made. He did not see things after they were made in one way and before they were made in another. He saw them made in the same manner in which he had seen them to be made.

Thus it is that Scripture says, “God saw that it was good”: that is, it pleased him that what he had made should remain in that goodness in which it had pleased him that it should be made.

“And he divided the light from the darkness.” The division of light from darkness signifies the separation of the good angels from the evil. Because he foreknew that some of them would fall through pride, by the immutability of his foreknowledge he divided the good from the evil.

Calling the evil “darkness” and the good “light,” he says of the latter, “God saw that they were good,” but he does not say this of the former, as he does concerning all God’s works, “God saw that it was good,” lest he appear to approve the evil of the transgressing angels.

“And he divided the light from the darkness.” Then God, according to the grace of his foreknowledge, divided between light and darkness—that is, between the children of God and the lights, and sinners as darkness. He called the righteous day and the others night.

Since the righteous are called “light” in the Church, hear the Apostle: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5).

It follows: “There was evening and there was morning.” Evening is the limit of created creation; morning is the beginning of another creation to be made.

Some ask why Scripture mentions evening first and then morning, lest it seem to signify night before day. They do not notice that it first mentioned day, saying: “God called the light day, and the darkness he called night.”

Therefore evening is the end of day, and morning the end of night. Thus, in order to give the benefit of precedence and the primacy of birth to the day, it first indicated the end of day, after which night would follow. Then it added the end of night, saying: “And there was evening and there was morning, one day.”

This one day was made first. Because of the harmony of the remaining angels it was called “one,” rather than “the first day,” and for this reason it is repeatedly mentioned in the execution of creation.

For that day—that is, the nature of the angels—grew evening, in a certain manner, when it contemplated the creation which God was making. Yet because it did not remain fixed upon the contemplation of that creation, but referred its praise to God and thereby saw it more perfectly in the divine reason, it immediately became, as it were, morning.

If it had remained in the contemplation of creation while neglecting the Creator, it would certainly have become not evening but night.

It follows: “God also said, ‘Let there be a firmament.’” By the name “firmament” he signified heaven, because it was composed strongly and firmly; and it was especially called firmament because of the firmness, support, and impassable boundary of the waters above.

### (Verse 7)

“And God made the firmament, and he divided the waters from the waters which were beneath the firmament.”

Since he added, “And he divided the waters from the waters,” it must be asked whether he calls this cloudy air the firmament—the air which divides the waters above, namely those of the clouds, from the waters below that flow upon the earth.

This air itself is also called heaven, as we read: “The birds of heaven” (Ps. 8), although the reference is not to that higher heaven but to this one in which birds fly.

It may therefore be asked how the element of water can be above the heavens. Water yields to earth, air yields to water, and fire yields to air. Thus it seems impossible that the second element, water, should be above the fourth, fire.

But whatever those waters are, and of what kind, which Scripture says are above the heavens, we do not doubt that they are there—not because of their position in space, but because of the dignity of their nature. For just as these clouds, which are everywhere, are borne above the air, the third element, so I think it possible that thin and subtle waters are borne above the heaven.

From the weight of the elements many philosophers mock the resurrection of the flesh, saying that it cannot happen that a human being, who was certainly made from earth, should be in heaven.

But truth refutes them: the power of God makes many earthly animals fly through the air, makes water exist above the air, and makes fire—which is certainly the fourth element—exist in the earth.

Therefore the power of God, which is shown to accomplish these things, also makes it possible for both human beings and water to be above heaven.

Some impiously deny that these visible waters were made by God because Genesis does not mention where they were made, since it is not written: “God said, ‘Let the waters be made.’”

They should be answered as follows: when it was said, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” the waters are to be understood there as well. For both are included under one name, by a metonymic figure, as when what contains is used for what is contained. For the sea is his, and he made it.

It follows: “And God called the firmament heaven” (Ps. 99).

What does it mean that he says heaven was made, and that this is afterward called the firmament? It means that the angelic nature, which had first been wondrously created, was afterward confirmed even more wondrously, so that it could never fall.

“Firmament,” that is, “solid foundation”: the firmament is understood in the Church as the divine Scriptures, as it is written: “Heaven will be folded up like a book.”

“And he separated the waters above this firmament”—that is, the heavenly peoples of the angels, who have no need to receive this firmament in order to hear the word of God by reading. For they always see him and love him.

But he placed the firmament of his law above the weakness of the lower peoples, so that, looking up to it, they might learn how to distinguish between carnal and spiritual things, as between the waters above and the waters below.

It follows: “God also said, ‘Let the waters beneath heaven be gathered into one place.’”

If everything was full of waters, how could the waters be gathered into one place? But it was already said above that the Spirit of God was borne over the water, from which God was going to form all things.

Now, when it says, “Let them be gathered into one place,” this means that the incorporeal matter should be formed into the appearance possessed by these visible waters. For the waters gathered into one place are themselves the formation of the waters which we see and touch.

“Let the dry land appear.” What else should be understood here except that the matter should receive the visible form which we now see this earth possessing?

Earlier, when it was called “earth,” formless and empty, the matter of things was being named, not yet filled with the bodily kinds of creatures. And when it was called “water,” over which the Spirit of God was borne, the same matter was again being named.

Now this water and earth are formed from that matter, which had been called by those names before it received the form of the waters that we now see.

“And he called the dry land earth.” Earth is therefore called dry because, just as fire naturally possesses heat and water moisture, earth naturally possesses dryness.

“And he called the gatherings of waters seas.” It should be noted that in Hebrew usage every gathering of waters is called “seas.”

### (Verses 10ff.)

“And God saw that it was good.” He teaches that what he made is good; he does not learn this. “Let the earth bring forth green vegetation, producing seed, and fruit-bearing trees producing fruit.” He blessed the green vegetation and the fruit-bearing tree. The dry and fruitful earth, cursed because of human sin, produced thistles and thorns.

Hence a question arises: Since God rested on the seventh day from all his work, how did he afterward create these new things? Although these are said to have been created because of human sin, nevertheless nothing new was created afterward, as though some new thing had been created after humanity’s sin as its punishment. This is especially clear because the same passage does not say, “Let the earth produce thorns and thistles,” but, “The earth shall produce for you,” as if it said: “What was once created as food for animals will now begin to grow for you, to bring your labor to an end.”

Although poisonous plants were created for the punishment or destruction of mortals, they themselves nevertheless possess certain remedies that promote health. Those that do not provide food supply medicine; those that are harmful for human use provide harmless nourishment for beasts and birds.

“According to its kind.” This was so that each thing coming forth might possess a generative power, and that things like it might be born according to its kind, distinguished by likeness just as by origin.

After this, on the third day, he gathered together the lower, salt waters: that is, unbelieving people, who are shaken by the storm of desires and the waves of carnal temptations, and who contain bitterness within themselves, as it were. “And he separated the dry land from them”: namely, the people thirsting for the fountain of faith. Then he fixed the boundaries of the proud and restrained them, so that they would not disturb the dry land—that is, the soul thirsting for God—with the turbulent waves of their iniquities. Thus it might bring forth the fruits of good works according to its kind.

Loving one’s neighbor in the necessities of bodily need, one has within oneself seed according to likeness, so that from one’s own weakness one may suffer with others and come to the aid of the needy. Bringing forth also a tree strong in its timber and fruitful—that is, a benefaction by which one rescues the person suffering injustice from the hand of the powerful [Col. 0899A] and provides a form of protection through a sturdy shelter, by the strength of righteous judgment.

It follows: “And God said: Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven.” If the lights were made on the fourth day, how had three days already passed? Unless we understand that, at that very point in time, the distinctions among the works were named in this way: evening, because the completed work had been brought to an end; morning, because the future day was beginning. This was in the likeness of human works, since most people begin in the morning and finish in the evening.

“And let them divide the day and the night.” It is as if he said: “Let them divide day and night in such a way that day is assigned to the sun, while night belongs to the moon and the other heavenly bodies.”

“And let them be for signs and seasons, for days and years.” For signs, namely, in the way that certain signs are gathered from the sun and moon, in accordance with what the Lord also says: “There will be signs in the sun, and in the moon, and in the stars.” By this the time of the future consummation would be signified. They are called signs because they signify something future, or because the divisions of time are marked by the courses of the heavenly bodies. But these are not the signs by which some have attempted to determine human births and qualities.

And he added: “Let them be for signs and seasons”—that is, so that the seasons might be distinguished by alternating changes: winter, spring, summer, and autumn. In these seasons the sun’s passage is either faster, slower, or equal. For one season it merely grazes with its rays, another it inflames with heat, and another it fosters with temperate warmth.

“For signs and for days.” So that the sun might hold authority over the day.

“For years.” For the moon, running twelve times through thirty days, completes a year. The sun, however, after completing its circuit through all the signs, returns to the same starting point of its course. “Signs” and “seasons” therefore pertain to all the heavenly bodies; “day” to the sun alone; and “year” to the course of the sun and moon.

“The greater light, to rule the day.” Certainly, because during the day the sun holds authority.

“The lesser light, to rule the night, and the stars.” Because the moon holds authority during the night, although the other heavenly bodies shine together with it.

On the fourth day the lights flashed forth, fixed in the firmament of the Law: that is, the Evangelists and teachers of Holy Scripture, joined to it by their exposition and displaying the light of wisdom to all below [Col. 0899C]. At the same time he also brought forth the remaining multitude of shining stars: that is, the abundance of diverse virtues in the Church, shining in the obscurity of this life as in night. These divide within the firmament of Scripture sensible and intelligible things, as it were between the light of the perfected and the darkness of the wicked.

“And they are for signs”—of virtues and miracles, because preachers live according to their own times, whereas the word of the Lord remains forever.

But why did the earth first bring forth vegetation, and only afterward were the lights made? Was it not because illumination by light for contemplating the appearance of heavenly virtue comes after good works?

It follows: “And God also said: Let the waters bring forth the creeping creature possessing a living soul, and the winged creature above the earth.” The reason that birds are recorded as having been produced from the waters is that the air in which birds fly is reckoned by the wise together with the waters, since it grows dense through the moist dissolution of water so that it can support the flight of birds. For this reason fish and birds are rightly said to have been born from the waters, because the nature of air and water is one. But whatever is wavy and fluid in the waters is assigned to creeping creatures, whereas whatever is suspended in the manner of vapor is assigned to birds.

### (Verses 21ff.)

“According to their kinds, according to their kind.” They were created in such a way that others would be generated from them, preserving the form of their posterity while being distinguished in appearance from the rest.

Among these, on the fifth day, creatures creeping in the waters and possessing living souls were made: namely, human beings renewed to life through the sacrament of baptism. Birds were also made—that is, holy souls flying toward heavenly things.

It follows: “And God said: Let the earth bring forth a living soul according to its kind: cattle, creeping things, and beasts of the earth.” He distinguishes these three generally. By “cattle” he means animals that serve human uses; by “creeping things,” serpents; by “beasts,” lions, leopards, tigers, and whatever rages with mouth and claws.

Since everything is read to have been created good by God, why are some things found to be harmful [Col. 0900A]? Or were they perhaps made harmless in the beginning and began to cause harm after sin? They were created good, but were given to those who act wickedly as a scourge. Hence it is said through the prophet: “I am the Lord, making peace and creating evil” (Isaiah 45). The Lord indicates that he creates evils when he turns good things that were created into a scourge for sinners, so that they are evil to the transgressors through the pain by which they strike, but good through the nature by which they exist.

The question is asked again: If they harm us because of sin, why do they harm one another? The answer is that some were given as food for others. All things are beautiful in their own kind, although because of our sins they appear hostile to us.

It must be believed that whatever minute animals now arise from the waters or the earth were created at the first formation of things. Other creatures, however, which arise from the decay of bodily growths, trees, or corpses, were not then created in their visible form; rather, the origin of their seed was already present in their bodies, so that afterward they might emerge from their corruptions, each according to its kind.

After this, on the sixth day, the earth brings forth a living soul, when our flesh, abstaining from dead works, gives birth to living shoots of virtues, according to its kind—that is, imitating the life of the saints, as the Apostle says: “Be imitators of me” (1 Corinthians 11). We live according to our kind when, in good works, we imitate holy men as our neighbors.

Then the earth brought forth beasts: human beings in the exercise of power over things, or in the ferocity of pride. Likewise it brought forth cattle: the faithful living in the simplicity of life. It also brought forth harmless serpents: holy men who, with the alertness of cunning, distinguish good from evil and, insofar as is permitted, investigate earthly things by creeping upon them, through which they understand eternal things. These are not the venomous serpents that establish themselves in the earthly desires of this world.

It follows.

### (Verse 26)

“Let us make humanity in our image and likeness.” Why is it said only of humanity, “Let us make humanity,” whereas of the other creatures we read, “God said that they should be made, and they were made”? Clearly, this is because a rational creature was being established, so that it might appear to have been made with deliberation, and so that its nobility might be displayed.

Was it said to the angels, “Let us make humanity”? But since it follows, “in our image,” it is impious to believe that humanity was created in the image of angels rather than in the image of God. It is therefore rightly understood as the plurality of the Trinity. Yet because this Trinity is one God, even when he had said, “Let us make,” he added: “And God made humanity in his image; in the image of God he created him.” He did not say, “They made.”

Therefore, since humanity was made in the image of God—that is, of the Trinity—it was said: “In our image and likeness.” But the image of its Creator is in the inner human being: the image consists in immortality, the likeness in moral character.

Again, lest those who believe in the Trinity should suppose that there are three gods, since the same Trinity is one God, he says: “And God made humanity in his image”—as if he were saying, “in the image of God.”

There is this difference between likeness and image: the image of God belongs to all, likeness to few. For this image of God differs from the excellence of divine likeness in that a sinful soul ceases to be the image of God; but it does not attain to the likeness of God unless it has become holy. The former image was created by nature; the latter will be brought to completion by grace. For if the image of God is nothing other than the mind naturally bestowed upon the human soul, what else will likeness be except blessedness happily conferred?

It is therefore a great thing that the human mind was given by nature made in the image of God, a privilege from which the other animals are excluded. But it is much more excellent that the likeness of its Creator should be granted to it in glory, so that it may be like its Creator there where it will be equal to the holy angels.
