It may also be asked why humanity was created on the sixth day, although it is clear that, because of its understanding, it is nobler than the other creatures made during the six days. The answer is that the Creator first prepared the world like a house and then introduced its inhabitant, the master of the house [Col. 0901A].

“God made humanity in his image and likeness.” Humanity was not made in the image of God according to the form of the body, but according to the rational mind, in accordance with what the Apostle says: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new human being, who was created according to God” (Ephesians 4). And elsewhere he says: “Having put off the old human being, put on the new, who is renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of him who created him” (Colossians 3).

From this it is clear that humanity was made in the image of God not according to the body but according to the understanding of the mind. Nevertheless, our body itself was fashioned in such a way as to show that we are better than the beasts and therefore unlike them. All those creatures are bent down toward the earth, whereas the human body is upright. This signifies that our soul should always be upright in heavenly things—that is, toward spiritual realities.

### (Verse 27)

“In the image of God he created him.” Here this human being, according to the soul, is created according to a causal principle. For it still follows that he is to be formed from the dust.

“Male and female he made them.” Eve has not yet been described as having been made, so how is the human being here called male and female? The answer is that, since the woman was to proceed from the same side, she is already counted in him according to substance, from whom she was to be produced in form. Thus, according to origin, Adam and Eve were made together; but according to the visible form of their bodies, the woman was afterward formed from the man’s side.

### (Verse 28)

“And God blessed them and said: Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Psalm 137).

Some of our people do not wish this to be understood according to bodily fertility but according to the soul, as in the saying: “You will multiply strength in my soul.” Thus they understand what follows, “And fill the earth,” as referring to the flesh, which the soul fills and rules when it multiplies in virtue. They also hold that bodily offspring could not then have been born in paradise, but that they would have procreated outside it, as in fact happened.

We, however, do not doubt that, according to God’s blessing, they could have multiplied bodily in paradise. If they had not sinned, they would have united without any disturbance of lust, so that the members would have been moved by the will alone, not by lust.

Nevertheless, it must be believed that so great a multitude of human beings could have been born that the number of the predestined saints might be completed, as even now they are gathered by God’s grace.

“And rule over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of heaven, and over all the animals.” Apart from the meaning by which humanity rules all living creatures, all the spiritual affections and movements of the soul that we possess in likeness to these animals would be subjected to us, and we would rule them through temperance.

How did humanity receive power over beasts, when we see that many people are killed by them? After sin, the first human being, having been condemned, lost the perfection in which he had been made in the image of God, so that he might rule over all things. It was deservedly brought about by sins that things naturally favorable became hostile to humanity.

[Col. 0901D]

### (Verse 31)

“God saw everything that he had made, and it was very good.” Observe that creation as a whole is called very good, whereas each individual thing is called merely good. Why is this so, unless because all beauty that consists in parts is less praiseworthy in a part than in the whole? Thus the individual members of the body are each good, but together they produce a greater good when they form one very good body and contribute their beauty to the whole.

Before this, the individual things were good; because of humanity, everything was very good, since everything was created for humanity’s adornment. Humanity, however, was made for the glory and praise of its Creator.

It follows.

### (Chapter II, verse 1)

“Thus the heavens and the earth were completed.” He rightly used the plural “heavens,” whether referring to that spiritual heaven which we do not see, by which the angels are signified, or to this bodily heaven which we see and which was called the firmament.

“And all their adornment.” The adornment of the spiritual heaven is the angels and principalities. The adornment of this bodily heaven is the stars, the sun, and the moon. The adornment of the earth is the seas, the rising mountains, the sunken valleys, the dense fields, the courses of the rivers, the abundance of springs, the jewels of the meadows, the variety of crops, the shade of trees, the kinds of seeds, and the diversity of animals differing from one another in appearance and kind.

The fact that the creation of humanity was completed on the sixth day corresponds to the number six. The number six is the perfection of the world, because on that day the sum of the whole kind and work was completed. Hence the perfection of this number possesses a certain special dignity: one, two, and three make six. For it has three such parts: a sixth, a third, and a half. Its sixth is one, its third is two, and its half is three. These three parts, added together—one, two, and three—together complete and perfect the same number, six. This is the principle governing the number of the remaining parts. Thus the division of two is into one; the division of three is into one.

What else does this number indicate except the Trinity, which is God? Although there are three persons, they are nevertheless believed to exist in the unity of one nature. One, two, and three therefore make six. For this reason, because of the perfection of that number, he worked on the six days to create the whole of creation.

These three parts of the number six show us that the Trinity of the Lord made all creation according to the Trinity of number, measure, and weight. He ordered everything in number, measure, and weight, because he ordered all things in himself; and everything that he made possesses number, measure, and weight.

After this, God made humanity in his image, namely a perfect man. Such a person does not act justly by imitating any individual holy man, but by contemplatively gazing upon Truth itself, so that he may understand and follow the very Truth in whose image he was made.

This person also receives power over the fish of the sea and the birds of heaven, over cattle and serpents as well. Anyone who has become spiritual and like God, according to the Apostle, “judges all things, but is himself judged by no one” [Col. 0902C] (1 Corinthians 2).

As for what follows, “Male and female he made them,” he shows the spiritual and obedient within the Church. Just as the woman is subject to the man, so one who is less perfect is obedient to a spiritual and perfect man, as the Apostle says: “We ask you, brothers, to acknowledge those who labor among you and preside over you in the Lord” (Romans 16).

For it is said to them: “Increase and multiply,” whether in languages or in the degrees of spiritual understanding, so that through the understanding of reason they may rule over all carnal disturbances, as over irrational animals.

“Every seed-bearing plant and every fruit-bearing tree,” which was given to human beings for food, signifies the faithful who share in the offerings of the saints (Romans 15). Hence the Apostle says: “For if the Gentiles have come to share in their spiritual goods, they ought also to minister to them in material goods.” These are the fruit-bearing trees.

In these stages, therefore, as in certain days, there is evening: the completion of each individual work; and morning: the beginning of what follows.

It follows.

[Col. 0902D]

### (Verse 2)

“And God completed on the seventh day his work that he had made.” The Jews, who boast of the leisure of the Sabbath, are refuted, since even then, at the beginning, the Sabbath was dissolved when God worked on the Sabbath, completing his works in it.

“And God rested from all his work.” Either, by a transferred manner of speaking, he is believed to rest when he makes us rest in him; or because he, through whom all things were made, rested in the tomb on that day; or because he completed the origin of all creatures within those six days in such a way that afterward he created no new creature.

But how is this compatible with what the Lord says in the Gospel: “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5), together with the statement that “God rested from his works”? He rested, certainly, because from then on he created no new kind of creature. Yet he works until now because he makes everything from the things that he made in those six mystical days.

Thus he rested from creating the kinds of creatures [Col. 0903A], but he did not cease from the work of governing or administering all that he created.

### (Verse 3)

“And he blessed the seventh day and sanctified it.” Why did the Lord sanctify the day of his rest, unless because he set himself before the creature he had made as one to be loved? He did not sanctify the day on which he began making these things, nor the day on which he completed them, lest it seem that he rejoiced in them either as things to be made or as things already made and in their increase. Rather, he sanctified the day on which he rested from them in himself.

After these works of six days, which were, as it were, very good, humanity hopes for rest of mind, established in a spiritual paradise signifying the blessed life. There the fountain of wisdom is divided into four streams of virtues; there one may eat the grace of the tree of life and gather useful moral disciplines, as it were, the fruits of trees.

Paradise is the life of the blessed. Its four rivers are the four virtues; its trees are all useful disciplines; the fruits of its trees are the conduct of the devout. The tree of life is Wisdom itself, the mother of all good things, concerning which Solomon says: “She is a tree of life to those who take hold of her, and blessed is the one who holds her” (Proverbs 3).

The tree of the knowledge of good and evil is the transgression of the commandment.

The works of the six days have now been explained as to how they are spiritually understood in the Church. Next it must be set forth what they signify figuratively with respect to the world.

God completed all his works in six days and rested on the seventh. The six ages of the human race in this world, through the succession of times, signify God’s works. The first is from Adam to Noah; the second from Noah to Abraham; the third from Abraham to David; the fourth from David to the deportation to Babylon; the fifth from then until the humble coming of our Lord Jesus Christ; the sixth, which is now taking place, until the world comes to an end, when the Most High comes for judgment. The seventh is understood as the rest of the saints; it has no evening, because no limit now closes it.

Let us therefore proceed briefly through all the ages of the world, reviewing their sequence of times [Col. 0903C] and distinguishing their differences mystically.

In the first age, humanity was made like light in paradise. In that age God separated the sons of God, under the name of light, from the sons of human beings, as from darkness. The evening of this day was the Flood.

The second age was made like the firmament between water and water. It was that ark which floated amid the rainwater, brought an end to the earlier peoples because of the enormity of their crimes, and gave a beginning to those who came afterward, after Noah and his sons. The evening of this age was the confusion of languages.

The third age came about when, through Abraham, God separated his people from the nations, as from salty and bitter waters, like dry land from the waters, so that it might bring forth the shoots of plants and trees—that is, saints and the fruits of the Holy Scriptures. The evening of this age was the sin and wickedness of the evil king Saul.

From there the fourth age began with David, when God placed lights in the firmament of heaven: namely, the splendor of the kingdom, like the excellence of the sun; the synagogue, obedient like the moon; and its rulers, like the stars. The evening of this age occurs in the sins of the kings, because of which that people deserved to be taken captive.

In the fifth age, that is, in the Babylonian deportation, creatures in the waters and birds of heaven were made, as it were, because at that time the Jews began to live among the nations as in the sea. They had no stable place, like flying birds. The evening of this day was the multiplication of sins among the Jewish people, when they were so blinded that they could not even recognize the Lord Jesus.

The sixth age now takes place with the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. For just as on that sixth day the first human being, Adam, was formed from the dust of the earth in the image of God, so in this sixth age of the world the second Adam, that is, Christ, was born in the flesh from the Virgin Mary: the former into a living soul, the latter into a life-giving spirit.

And just as on that day a living soul was made, so in this age those desiring eternal life are made. And just as on that sixth day the earth produced kinds of serpents and beasts, so in this sixth age of the world the Church has generated nations desiring eternal life. The same interpretation was also revealed by the vessel shown to Peter.

And just as male and female were created on the sixth day, so in this age of the world Christ and the Church are manifested.

And just as humanity was placed above cattle, serpents, and the birds of heaven on that day, so Christ is placed in this age of the world above peoples and nations, so that they may be ruled by him—whether they are devoted to carnal desire like cattle, obscured by earthly curiosity like serpents, or lifted up by pride like birds.

And just as on that day humanity and the animals with it were fed with seed-bearing plants, fruit-bearing trees, and green vegetation, so in this sixth age of the world the spiritual person, who is a good minister of Jesus Christ, is spiritually nourished together with the spiritual people by the food of the Holy Scriptures and by divine law, so as to desire the fruitfulness of meanings and words.

This nourishment is like seed-bearing plants, partly for the usefulness of moral human conduct, like fruit-bearing trees, and partly for the vigor of faith, hope, and charity unto eternal life, like green plants that do not wither in the heat of tribulations. With these spiritual foods and nourishments he is fed so that he may understand many things.

Carnal people, however—that is, little ones in Christ—are like God’s cattle, so that they may believe many things which they are not yet able or capable of understanding. Nevertheless, they possess all the same foods.

May the evening of this age not find us! For it is the evening of which the Lord says: “Do you think that when the Son of Man comes, he will find faith upon the earth?” (Luke 18). After that evening there will be morning, when the Lord himself will come in glory.

Then those who were told, “Be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect” (Matthew 5), will rest with Christ from all their works. Such people perform very good works; after such works, rest is to be hoped for on the seventh day, which has no evening.

It follows.

[Col. 0904C]

### (Verse 4)

“These are the generations of heaven and earth, when they were created, on the day when God made heaven and earth.”

Since above he reported distinctly that everything was established on separate days, he now added how all things were created together on one day, so that he might at some point show that all creation existed together in substance, but did not come forth together in visible form.

The origin of things was created together, but was not formed together in appearance. What existed together through the substance of matter did not appear together in the form of visible things. For when heaven and earth are written to have been made together, this indicates that spiritual and bodily things were made together; everything that arises from heaven was made together, and everything produced from the earth was made together.

The stars are said to have been made in heaven on the fourth day. But what came forth in visible form on the fourth day existed on the first day through the establishment of its substance. The same applies to the rest.

For it is written: “He who lives forever created all things together” (Ecclesiasticus 18).

### (Verse 5)

“On the day when he made every shrub of the field, before it arose upon the earth, and every plant of the region, before it sprouted.”

How were the grass and green plants of the field established before they arose? And if they had not arisen, how had they been made? The answer is that, causally, on the day when it was said, “Let the earth bring forth green vegetation,” the earth received the power to bring it forth. In that power, as in its roots, so to speak, were made the things that were to come forth through future ages.

“For the Lord God had not caused it to rain upon the earth, and there was no human being to work it.” Why does he recall here, by recapitulation, what had already been made on the sixth day? It is because, when God made the green plants of the field, it had not yet rained and the human being had not yet been made.

### (Verse 6)

“But a fountain rose from the earth, watering the whole surface of the earth.”

He used the singular “fountain” instead of the plural, as if he were saying: “There was not yet rain, but fountains, bursting forth in their several places throughout the whole earth, watered their respective regions.”

He did not wish to call them fountains but fountain, because of the unity of their nature. Or certainly he did so so that we might understand how different the first generation of the earth is from the later one. The latter is completed slowly and belatedly through the watering of rains, whereas the former appeared immediately at the command of the one ordering it.

“These are the generations of heaven and earth, when they were created, on the day when God made heaven and earth, and every shrub of the field and every plant of the region, before it existed upon the earth.”

Above, seven days were counted. Now one day is mentioned, on which he made heaven and earth, every shrub of the field, and every plant of the region.

Under the name of this day, according to the prophet, the whole time of this life is signified—the time in which heaven and earth were made, that is, in which visible creatures are arranged.

But what does it mean that, after naming heaven and earth, he now added, “the shrub of the field and the plant of the region,” while remaining silent about the other things that are in heaven and earth, or even in the sea? It means that by “the shrub of the field” he indicates the invisible creature, such as the soul.

It is called a shrub because of the vigor of life, and a plant because of that same life, which never withers.

Then, when he added, “before it existed upon the earth,” this is understood as “before the soul sinned.” Once stained by earthly desires, it is rightly said to have been born upon the earth, or to exist upon the earth.

Hence he added: “For the Lord God had not yet caused it to rain upon the earth.” It is as if he were saying openly: Before the soul sinned, the Lord had not yet granted the rain of teaching from the clouds of Scripture to water the soul. On account of the human being, who is earth, our Lord had not yet assumed a cloud of flesh, through which he poured out the most abundant rain of the holy Gospel.

But when he added, “And there was no human being to work the earth,” this means that no human being worked the Virgin from whom Christ was born. He is the stone cut from the mountain without hands (Daniel 2): that is, without sexual union and human seed, cut from the virginal womb as from the mountain of human nature and the substance of flesh.

“But a fountain rose from the earth, watering the whole surface of the earth.” The earth is most rightly understood as the Virgin, the Lord’s mother, Mary, concerning whom it is written: “Let the earth open, and bring forth the Savior” (Isaiah 45).

The Holy Spirit watered this earth; in the Gospel he is signified under the name of fountain and water.

It follows.

### (Verse 7)

“Then the Lord God formed man from the dust of the earth.” According to the causal account, he was made in the works of the six days; but according to the origin of temporal things, he was formed at this point. For when it was said that man was made, God had already made the cause from which man was to come in his own time; and the cause from which he would subsequently be formed—that is, the earth—had preceded him.

Again, some understand the passage in this way: after it says, “God formed man from the dust of the earth,” the words “in his own image” are not added, because the reference is to the formation of the body. The inner man, however, was signified when it was said, “in his image and likeness.”

It is asked whether man was formed with the stature of an adult, or whether he grew through the successive intervals of time; and whether God made him a keeper of his will. Yet, if this was done for the sake of future human beings—whose causes were implanted and pre-established on the day when heaven and earth were made, when God created all things together—we understand Adam to have been made from the dust only as a fully developed man. It is not credible that he was made as small as our infants, since he was already constituted in those causes where God made man in the works of the six days.

“And God made man from the dust of the earth.” The mortal body that had already been made was not of the same kind as the body apparently created for the first man before the sin. If the body in which we now live is of the same kind as that body either was or will be, then the body of the first man, although by nature it possessed the capacity not to die, also possessed the capacity, if he sinned, to be dissolved by death.

But the body whose corruption arose from sin, and whose mortality leads to death, after it fell into this necessity of dying, was so changed from the creation of that first man’s body that it cannot pass into immortality except through death. The body that we believe will exist in the resurrection, once made immortal, will no longer be able to die. When it has become the immortal body of the soul, the condition of dying will never again be restored to it, just as it will never again be restored to the soul.

If the body of the first man was living in such a way that it could also not die, this present body is mortal, since the necessity of dying has been imposed upon it. The body that will be immortal in the future will no longer be able to die at all. Thus that body possessed by nature the capacity not to die; this mortal body possesses, as punishment, the condition of dying; and that immortal body possesses in glory the blessedness of never dying.

It follows:

“And he breathed into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul.”

By “the breath of life” we understand, in this passage, the soul joined to the body. If that man, when he was made from the dust, was already body and soul, then his soul itself was now added to this breathing, when he became a living soul. When it is said, “He breathed into him the spirit of life, and man became a living soul,” we must not believe that a part of God’s nature was changed into the human soul, so that we would be compelled to say that God’s nature is changeable, like the soul, which at one moment advances and at another declines, at one moment understands and at another is foolish.

Therefore the soul, which is changeable, must not be believed to be God’s nature or a part of God, as the prophet bears witness when he says, “He who formed the spirit of man knows all things”; and the Evangelist bears witness concerning the soul that Christ received in the flesh, when the Lord said, “I have power to lay down my soul” (John 10)—which he laid down when, bowing his head, he gave up his spirit.

Thus there is no doubt that the spirit is the soul. God made it neither from himself nor from any underlying matter of the elements, but from nothing. For if he had made it from himself, it could never have become faulty, changeable, or miserable. If, however, it had been made from the visible elements, it would possess either solidity from earth, moisture from water, breath from air, or heat from fire. But since it lacks all these things, it is evident that it does not come from them, because it is shown to have nothing in common with them.

For this reason the soul is called “breath”: having been made from nothing, it was breathed into the body that it was to animate. It is called “the breath of life” because air itself is often called spirit; yet air is not called the spirit of life, because it lacks life.

It is asked whether God made the soul by breathing it in, or whether, having already made it, he rather breathed it into the body by giving it to the body. I think both statements are true, and that there is no real difficulty in asking how he either made the soul by breathing or gave it by creating it. He created it or breathed it into the body neither from some breath of his own nor from himself, but from nothing. This does not mean that the breath was changed into a living soul, but that he brought about a living soul.

We must not yet understand man to have been spiritual merely because he became a living soul; he was still animal. He became spiritual when he was placed in paradise and received the commandment of perfection. Therefore, after he sinned and was expelled from paradise, he remained animal. For this reason all of us who were born from him after the sin first bear the animal man, until we attain the spiritual Adam, that is, Christ. Thus the Apostle says: “Not first what is spiritual, but what is animal” (1 Corinthians 15).

“Therefore God formed man from the dust of the earth”: that is, Christ was made, according to what the Apostle says, “from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Romans 1), as though from the dust of the earth.

“And he breathed into his face the breath of life”: namely, the infusion of the Holy Spirit, who brought about the human Christ.

“And man became a living soul”: that is, so that he who was perfect God might also be believed to be perfect man.

It follows:

### (Verse 8)

“Now the Lord God had planted a paradise of delight from the beginning, in which he placed the man whom he had formed.”

“Paradise” is interpreted as a garden, or delight, or pleasures. There are three opinions concerning paradise: one held by those who understand paradise only in a bodily sense; another held by those who understand it in both ways. “From the beginning” signifies the time from which it is made clear that God had established paradise beforehand, as though before he made heaven and earth.

### (Verse 9)

“And God brought forth from the ground every tree beautiful to the sight and pleasant for food.”

This does not mean that he created some new kind of tree. Rather, trees arose afterward from those kinds that the earth had already brought forth on the third day, and from the power of reproduction that the earth had already received.

Some wish the tree of life, which was in the middle of paradise, to be understood only allegorically, as signifying wisdom, which is the tree of life. But just as the struck rock gave forth water, although it signified Christ and was nevertheless historically a rock, so also the tree of life, although it signified Christ, was also bodily and most clearly a tree. It was called the tree of life because, when those men tasted from it, they would not fail through illness or old age.

In the other trees there was nourishment; in this one there was a sacrament.

“And the tree of the knowledge of good and evil”—not because the tree itself was rational by nature or possessed knowledge of good and evil, but because it was called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil since, through experience of it, man learned what was good in obedience and what was evil in disobedience.

It follows:

### (Verses 10ff.)

“And a river went out from the place of delight to water paradise, and from there it divides into four heads. The name of one is Pishon. It is the Ganges, which is now called the Nile and waters the regions of Ethiopia. The Tigris and the Euphrates still retain the same names. The Euphrates, however, is a river of Mesopotamia. The Tigris flows toward the Assyrians and, after making a great circuit, empties into the Red Sea. It is called by this name because of its speed, like a beast running with extreme swiftness.”

“Now the Lord God had planted paradise from the beginning.” Paradise is the Church. Thus we read of it in the Song of Songs: “My sister is a garden enclosed” (Song of Songs 4).

Paradise is planted from the beginning because the Catholic Church is known to have been founded by Christ, the beginning of all things. The river flowing out from paradise bears the image of Christ flowing from the Father’s fountain, watering his Church with the word of preaching through the gift of baptism.

The four rivers of paradise are the four Gospels, sent forth for the preaching to all nations. The fruit-bearing trees are all the saints; their fruits are their works. The tree of life is the Holy of Holies, namely Christ. Whoever reaches out his hand toward him will live forever.

The tree of the knowledge of good and evil is the freedom of the will itself, which has been placed in the middle for discerning good and evil. Whoever, abandoning God’s grace, tastes from it will die by death.

It follows:

### (Verse 15)

“Therefore the Lord God took the man and placed him in the paradise of delight, so that he might work it and guard it.”

Here, by way of recapitulation, he relates how God placed man in paradise so that he might work it and guard it. What was he to work, when there was no weariness from labor? What was he to guard, where there was no assailant or plunderer?

He was to guard that same paradise for himself, lest he commit something by which he might deserve to be expelled from it; or, certainly, he was to work so that he might be just, and guard so that he might be safe.

“Therefore God took the man and placed him in paradise.” God assumed flesh and became the head of the Church.

“So that he might work it and guard it”: that is, by the will of the Father he might fill the Church from all the nations.

It follows:

### (Verses 16–17)

“And he commanded him, saying.”

It may be asked how God spoke to Adam: whether, as he now speaks to angels, through a heavenly substance; or as he spoke to the patriarchs, through a bodily appearance assumed from heavenly air; or as he spoke to the prophets, in the mind, as it is written: “And the angel who spoke in me said to me” (Zechariah 1).

It follows:

“You shall eat from every tree of paradise; but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat.”

This is not because the tree itself was rational by nature or possessed knowledge of good and evil, but because through it man could experience and know what lay between the good of obedience and the evil of disobedience. For this reason he was forbidden to eat from it: so that he might observe the commandment and know himself to be obedient under God’s dominion. It was for this reason that the tree received such a name.

He used the tree of life as a medicine, so that he might be incorruptible; the tree of the knowledge of good and evil he used as poison, so that he might die. He was also forbidden so that he would not become excessively exalted by such great dominion, but would know himself to be subject to his Creator in the observance of the commandment.

It follows:

“On whatever day you eat from it, you shall die by death.”

Thus we should understand that the Lord announced death in saying, “On whatever day you eat from it, you shall die by death,” as though he were saying: “On the day you abandon me through disobedience, I will abandon you through justice.”

How could he fear a death that he had never experienced? Just as we know the resurrection, although we have never experienced or seen it, so he knew death—not yet by experience, but by knowledge. He knew what it was: through the deprivation of life he knew that the departure of the soul from the body brings about death, and that when the soul returns to the body it brings about resurrection. In the same way, he knew death through the deprivation of life.

He speaks of the death of the soul, not of the body, because they did not die at the very time when they ate. Therefore we must not understand the death that God then threatened man to be only that by which the flesh is separated from the soul. We must also understand it as the death by which these are alienated from God, who is their life.

For just as the body lives from the soul, so the soul, in order to live blessedly, lives from God. Therefore the soul, when abandoned by God, is rightly called dead. From this, three deaths subsequently followed: the first in the soul, the second in the flesh, and the third in condemnation. But for these to follow, God’s abandonment came first.

It follows:

### (Verse 18)

“God also said: It is not good for man to be alone; let us make him a helper like himself.”

At the first creation of things it had been said: “He made them male and female; and he blessed them, saying: Increase and multiply, and fill the earth.”

That blessing of the marriage of the first human beings—that they should increase, multiply, and fill the earth—although it remained even in those who sinned, was given before they sinned, so that it might be understood that the procreation of children belonged to the glory of marriage, not to the punishment of sin.

Although they are said to have begotten children after they had been expelled from paradise, we nevertheless believe that they could have produced children in paradise without any heat of lust or pain of childbirth. By drawing the strength of immortality from the tree of life, they would have been brought to the number of the saints that the fullness of the predestined awaits.

Nor is it surprising that, if they had not sinned, they could have lived forever, since Enoch and Elijah, although they died in Adam, are nevertheless believed still to be alive in the body.

“God also said: It is not good for man to be alone.”

Heretics are refuted here: they think that Christ is merely man and not also God.

“Let us make him a helper like himself.”

For in the man whom he assumed, the Church was joined to God.

It follows:

### (Verses 19ff.)

“Therefore, after the Lord God had formed from the ground all the animals of the earth and all the birds of heaven, he brought them to Adam, to see what he would call them. For whatever Adam called each living creature, that was its name. And Adam gave names to all the animals, to all the birds of heaven, and to all the beasts of the earth.”

To show by how great a privilege man surpasses the animals—since by his reason he could distinguish all things and separate them by name—God willed the animals to be brought to Adam, not by physical movement through space but by a hidden divine command. Man was to understand how much better he was than the beasts, since he assigned names based on their etymologies; and he was to love his Creator all the more, knowing himself to be better than all the living creatures to which he had given names.

Adam gave names to all the animals, the birds of heaven, and the beasts of the earth, signifying the nations that would be saved in the Church and would receive, through the same Lord, the name “Christianity,” which they had not previously possessed, as it is written: “And I will call my servants by another name” (Isaiah 65).

It follows:

“But for Adam no helper like him was found.”

For among all the animals of the earth no rational creature was found except Adam alone.

“Therefore the Lord God cast a sleep upon Adam, and when he had fallen asleep, he took one of his ribs and filled up flesh in its place.”

This sleep is understood to have been sent for the purpose that Adam’s mind, through ecstasy, might become a participant in the angels; and, entering into the sanctuary of God, might understand the last things. Awakening as though filled with prophecy, he might pour forth the sacrament commended by the Apostle: “He took one of his ribs and filled up flesh in its place” (Ephesians 5).

All these things were accomplished in Christ and the Church, and they are full of mysteries and sacraments, which must be discussed in their proper place.

“But for Adam no helper like him was found.” This is because, however faithful or just anyone may be, no one can be equal to Christ, since no one among the sons of God is like him. No one but Christ could free the human race from death and overcome death itself.

It follows:

### (Verse 22)

“And the Lord God built the rib that he had taken from Adam into a woman.”

How did God create the female, when above he had rested from every work? He did not create her in matter, but expressed her in form. She had first been made originally in the man’s side; afterward, when his rib was removed, the woman was made from it.

It is asked whether the woman, formed from the man’s side, received her soul from his soul; and whether, just as the flesh of those being born comes from flesh, souls are produced from souls, or whether God always creates new souls from nothing. This question is difficult to settle, because nothing has been stated more clearly by the lives of the saints or by the authority of Scripture.

Adam slept, and a woman was made for him from his side. Christ suffers, and as he dies the Church is made from the sacrament of the blood that flowed from the side of the dead man.

It follows:

“And he brought her to Adam to see what he would call her.”

### (Verse 23)

“And Adam said: This is now bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh. She shall be called Woman, because she was taken from Man.”

He called the woman “life,” for thus Eve is interpreted: “life,” or “calamity”—life for some, but calamity for others.

“She shall be called virago [man-woman], because she was taken from vir [man].” For virago has a likeness to vir; mulier [woman] does not.

“And he put flesh in its place.”

So also Christ, by dying on the wood of the cross, gave his flesh for the Church.

“And Adam said: This is now bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh.”

Whether they are spiritual saints, very strong in temptations, or less perfect, both are one body of Christ and one Church.

“She shall be called Woman, because she was taken from Man.”

So also Christ gave the Church the name “Christian,” since she was taken from his side.

All these things, therefore, were done in figure: they were destined to come forth in the Church.

It follows:

### (Verse 24)

“For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh.”

The blessed Apostle Paul explains this passage in this way, saying: “This mystery is great, but I am speaking of Christ and the Church” (Ephesians 5).

But how did Christ leave the Father, since he is of one substance with the Father? Or where could the Father be without the Son, when it is said of the Son himself, who is the Father’s Wisdom, that “he reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly” (Wisdom 8)?

Wherever the Son is, the Father also is. The Father cannot be without the Son, nor the Son without the Father, because just as they are inseparable in nature, so they are inseparable in person. Thus the Son himself says of the Father in the Gospel: “He who sent me is with me” (John 8).

How, then, did he leave the Father in order to cling to his wife, that is, to his Church? Only in the manner in which the Apostle says: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2).

The taking of the servant’s form is therefore an emptying; and this emptying, although it is not the abolition of divinity or the loss of nature, is nevertheless rightly said to be a leaving of the Father because of the servant’s form in which he is recognized to have appeared.

He also left his mother, namely the synagogue, which clung carnally to the Old Testament. And he clung to his wife, that is, to the holy Church, so that in the peace of the New Testament the two might be one flesh.

It follows:

### (Verse 25)

“Now both were naked, Adam and his wife, and they were not ashamed.”

This does not mean that they were unaware of their nakedness. Rather, the shamefulness of nakedness had not yet been recognized, because lust did not yet move those members against their will. They had not yet felt any law in their members resisting the law of their mind.

They thought that nothing needed to be covered, because they had felt nothing that needed to be restrained. It was as a punishment for sin that man’s own flesh became rebellious against him, because he himself had become rebellious against his Creator in his actions. For this reason he later became ashamed of his body.

It follows:

### (Chapter 3, Verse 1)

“But the serpent was more subtle than all the animals of the earth that the Lord God had made.”

This subtlety was not from its own nature, but from the inflation of the devilish spirit that was in it and through it carried on its deceit. The devil used the serpent as an instrument to accomplish the malice of his cunning.

When he says, “more than all the animals of the earth,” he shows that although the transgressing angels had been cast out through pride, they were nevertheless by nature superior and more cunning than all the animals of the earth. That angel fell only from the spiritual paradise; man fell from both the spiritual and the bodily paradise.

There was a bodily paradise, which man enjoyed through the external sense of the body; and there was also a spiritual paradise, in which he rejoiced inwardly through contemplation of the mind.

The command given to him is therefore: “You shall eat from every tree of paradise, but you shall not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.”

We are commanded to enjoy every tree of paradise, by which spiritual delights are signified, concerning which the Apostle says: “The fruit of the spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, gentleness, self-control, chastity” (Galatians 5).

We must not touch the tree planted in the middle of paradise, the tree of the knowledge of good and evil—that is, we must not wish to become proud of the nature of our free will, which occupies the middle place, lest, deceived through knowledge, we experience evil.

That serpent, wiser than all the beasts, indicates the devil. He is called a serpent because he moves about in winding cunning.

It follows:

“He said to the woman: Why did God command you not to eat from every tree of paradise?”

It may be asked whether the serpent could understand the sounds of the words through which the devil was speaking by means of it. For it is not credible that the serpent could understand what the devil was doing through it.

The serpent therefore did not understand the sounds of the words that came from it to the woman. Its soul should not be thought to have been changed into a rational nature, since even human beings, whose nature is rational, do not know what they are saying when a demon speaks in them and they are questioned by an exorcist. A person possessed in this way does not know what he is saying.

So also the serpent uttered words that it did not understand. Through it the devil persuaded the woman to disregard the divine will and retain her own will.

It follows:

### (Verses 2ff.)

“We eat of the fruit of the trees that are in paradise. But concerning the fruit of the tree that is in the middle of paradise, God commanded us not to eat from it and not to touch it, lest perhaps we die.”

“But the serpent said to the woman: You shall certainly not die. For God knows that on whatever day you eat from it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil.”

Why did the woman, when questioned by the serpent, answer, unless it was so that her transgression would be inexcusable? She could not in any way claim that she had forgotten the divine command. Thus, by keeping the divine command through the voluntary freedom of her will, she might have appeared praiseworthy, while in despising it she would be condemnable.

By saying, “Your eyes will be opened,” the serpent persuaded them not to remain under God but to become like him, no longer needing his inward light, but living by their own prudence in order to distinguish good and evil, which he had forbidden.

It follows:

### (Verse 6)

“Then the woman saw that the tree was good for food, beautiful to the eyes, and pleasing to look at.”

How could the woman believe the serpent, which promised her divinity? Perhaps there was already in her mind a certain love of her own power and a proud presumption concerning herself, which was to be overcome and humbled through that temptation.

“Then the woman saw that the tree was good.”

How could they see if they had closed eyes? She considered the tree after the serpent’s persuasion, to test whether there was anything deadly in it. When she saw nothing of the kind in it, she tasted from it with greater confidence, ate, and gave some to her husband.

The slippery animal, moving through winding coils, was fittingly chosen for the devil’s work and for the one through whom he would speak. Through an angelic presence and a superior nature, spiritual wickedness had subjected the serpent to itself and used it as an instrument. Speaking deceitfully to the woman, the devil began with the lower part of the human union, so that he might gradually reach the whole.

He did not suppose that the man would be easily credulous or that he could be deceived through error, but that he would yield to another’s error. Aaron, for example, was not persuaded to consent to the erring people when they made an idol, but yielded under constraint. Nor is it credible that Solomon considered error to be good.

So we must believe that the man, as one with his woman, and a human being with his spouse, did not believe her as one speaking the truth and thus become seduced into transgressing God’s law. Rather, he obeyed her out of their bond of companionship.

The Apostle did not say without reason, “Adam was not deceived, but the woman, having been deceived, was in transgression” (1 Timothy 2). She accepted what the serpent said to her as though it were true; he, however, did not wish to be separated from his one companion, either in the communion of sin or in the social bond. Yet he was no less guilty, since he sinned knowingly and deliberately.

It follows:

### (Verse 7)

“And the eyes of both were opened.”

They were not born blind, as the unlearned masses suppose. Adam saw the animals to which he gave names, and it is written of the woman: “The woman saw that the tree was good.”

Their eyes were open, but they were not open to this—to attend to what garment of grace had been given them, when their members did not know how to resist their will. When that grace was removed, so that disobedience might be punished by a corresponding punishment, a certain shameless novelty arose in the movement of the body. From this came indecent nakedness, which made them attentive and rendered them confused.

It follows:

“When they had recognized that they were naked.”

They were naked, that is, of the grace by which the nakedness of their bodies had not caused their minds to be confused through resistance under the law of sin.

But why does the devil deceive through the woman and not through the man? Because our reason cannot be seduced into sin unless pleasure first arises in the feeling of carnal weakness, which ought to obey reason as a woman obeys a ruling man. This takes place in every human being in a hidden and secret marriage.

We understand the suggestion as the serpent, the bodily animal sense as the woman, and reason as the man. When an evil suggestion arises, the serpent speaks, as it were.

But if thought alone takes pleasure in that suggestion and reason restrains it so that consent to carry out the act does not follow, the woman alone seems to have eaten the forbidden food. If the mind itself also decides that the sin should be committed, then the man has been deceived; then the woman seems to have given the food to the man. To consent to what is forbidden is to eat from the prohibited tree.

At that point man is rightly expelled from blessed life, as from paradise, and sin is imputed to him even if the act does not follow. For although guilt is not present in the deeds, the conscience is nevertheless held guilty in its consent.

This is according to the anagogical interpretation. According to the metaphorical interpretation, however, this cunning serpent can signify the craftiness of heretics. Some of them, with excessive loquacity and subtlety, promise the opening and knowledge of forbidden secrets, and attempt to display their own discernment in the human being, as in a tree planted in the middle of paradise.

Against this serpent the Apostle cries out when he says: “I fear that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by its cunning, so your minds may be corrupted” (2 Corinthians 11).

Our carnal desire is seduced by the words of this serpent, and through it the Christian Adam—not Christ—is deceived.

This serpent says to the woman: “Why did God command you not to eat from every tree of paradise?” In this way the curious desire of heretics and wicked preachers inflames the carnal hearts of their hearers to love the deception of error, saying: “Why do you avoid possessing hidden knowledge? Always seek new things; penetrate the knowledge of good and evil.”

Hence the saying in Solomon, where that woman, representing heretics, says: “Stolen waters are sweeter, and hidden bread is more pleasant” (Proverbs 9).

Then the same serpent added: “On whatever day you eat, your eyes will immediately be opened, and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil.”

So also all heretics profess the privilege of divinity. Through the promise of knowledge they deceive and criticize those whom they find to be simple believers. And because they persuade people toward wholly carnal things, they attempt to lead them toward the opening of carnal eyes, so that they may darken the inward eyes.

“Then the woman saw that the tree was good, and she took of its fruit and ate.”

The woman ate first, not the man, because carnal people are more easily persuaded to sin, while spiritual people are not so quickly deceived. “And she gave it to her husband, and he ate”: that is, after the pleasure of our carnal desire, our reason also becomes subject to sin.

It follows:

“They sewed fig leaves and made loincloths for themselves.”

We may call these “breeches” or “coverings of the loins.” After they had miserably recognized that they had been stripped of the grace by which the nakedness of their bodies did not cause their minds to be confused under the law of sin, they came to know what it would have been happier for them not to know, if they had obeyed and believed God rather than committing the act that forced them to experience it.

Therefore, confused by the disobedience of their flesh, which testified against them as punishment for their disobedience, they sewed fig leaves and made loincloths for themselves—or “breeches,” which we may also call girdles.

These are called “breeches” because young men who exercised naked in the field covered their private parts with them. Hence the common people call those who are so girded “breeched.”

“When they had recognized that they were naked, they sewed fig leaves to cover themselves.”

Those who embrace the harshness of the world, who are constrained in the name of religion by carnal pleasure, and who, deceived by heretical perversity and stripped of God’s grace, gather coverings of lies like fig leaves, make girdles of vanity for themselves when they lie about the Lord or the Church.

It follows:

### (Verse 8)

“And when they heard the voice of God walking in paradise at the breeze after midday.”

What does it mean that, after man’s sin in paradise, the Lord no longer stands but walks? It means that, when guilt invaded their hearts, he showed himself to have withdrawn from them, since he no longer found them steadfast in his command.

What does “at the breeze after midday” mean? It means that the more fervent light of truth had departed from them, and the chill of unbelief was constricting their sinful souls.

“Adam and his wife hid themselves from the face of the Lord God in the middle of the tree of paradise.”

This folly came upon him as a punishment for sin: he wished to be able to hide from the one whom nothing can escape.

Therefore the Lord rebuked Adam while walking, so that he might reveal the wickedness of blind minds not only through words but also through events. The sinful man was to hear through the words that had been spoken; through the walking, he was to perceive the instability of his mutability after losing the state of eternity; through the breeze, with the warmth of charity driven away from him, he was to recognize his torpor; and through the sun’s decline, he was to understand that he was approaching darkness.

It follows:

### (Verse 9)

“And the Lord God called Adam and said to him: Adam, where are you?”

This is the voice of one rebuking, not of one who does not know. He did not ask because he was ignorant, but admonished him by rebuking him, so that he might attend to where he was and from where he had fallen—as though he were saying: “What sort of man were you when you walked simply in obedience, and what sort of man do you now appear to be, since you have become a transgressor?”

Although perhaps he had previously spoken with them as with angels, he must now be believed to have appeared to them through a subordinate creature. He says, “Adam, where are you?” He saw him fallen under guilt and now, through his sin, hidden as it were from the eyes of truth, because he did not approve the darkness of his error.

By calling him and saying, “Where are you?” he gives a sign that he is recalling him to repentance. By seeking him, he openly indicates that sinners are justly condemned.

It follows:

### (Verse 10)

“He said: I heard your voice in paradise, and I was afraid because I was naked, and I hid myself.”

Now, in a most wretched error, he answered evasively, as though he could displease God precisely because he was no longer what he had been. Yet he would have pleased God if he had remained as God himself had made him.

“And I was afraid.” This is what is written: “You turned your face from me, and I became troubled.” It was because he was naked. Before the sin, he did not recognize himself as naked because his attention was directed toward higher things.

“And I hid myself.” Why? Because in that nakedness he no longer dared to appear, since he had begun to be ashamed of it.

It follows:

### (Verse 11)

“Who told you that you were naked, unless you have eaten from the tree concerning which I commanded you not to eat?”

Then Adam did not attribute the fault to himself, but to the woman whom the Lord had given him. He indirectly turned his guilt back upon the author, who had given him a woman who would persuade him to do such a thing. To add to his sin, he answered proudly rather than humbly, as though directing a complaint against God: why had he given him such a companion, from whom an occasion of sin would arise?

Likewise the woman referred the cause of her fault back to the Creator, asking why he had created the serpent by which she would be deceived in paradise, or why he had permitted it to enter.

The serpent, however, was not questioned, because its repentance was not being sought. Those who were questioned, being summoned to repentance, offered a defensive response against just correction.

Thus, even to the present day, the practice of sinners is perpetuated: when guilt is being addressed, it is defended, and the very means by which guilt ought to have been ended cause it to increase.

The serpent was not questioned because it could neither confess its sin nor find a means of excusing itself. Nevertheless, it received its punishment first—not the punishment reserved for it and its angels at the final judgment. Its punishment is said here to consist in its having power over those who despise God’s commandments. This is a greater punishment for it because it rejoices in such misery.

It follows:

### (Verse 14)

And the Lord God said to the serpent:

“Because you have done this, you are accursed among all cattle and all the beasts of the earth. You shall go upon your breast, and you shall eat earth all the days of your life.”

Now what is said to the serpent is understood also to apply to the one who acted through the serpent, not to the irrational animal, since the animal did not do this by its own nature or will; rather, the devil acted through it and by means of it. “You shall go upon your breast, and you shall eat earth”: by “breast” is indicated the cunning of his wickedness; and he devours earth when he feeds and delights upon the luxury and lust of sinners.

When they heard the voice of the Lord God walking in the garden in the breeze after midday, God “walks” in those who do not remain steadfast and persevere in his command—he does not stand. And appropriately it says, “in the breeze after midday,” because that more fervent light of truth is already being taken away from them as the darkness of error draws near.

“They hid themselves from the face of God in the midst of the tree of the garden.” For the one who has turned away from the command of the Creator and lives amid the pleasures of error and of his own will hides himself in the midst of the tree.

“And God called Adam and said, ‘Adam, where are you?’” Here he shows that, if some fall from faith or good works into their own lies and desires, God does not despise them; rather, he still calls them to return to repentance, because he does not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live (Ezek. XVIII). Therefore one must not despair of any sinners, since even the ungodly are summoned to the hope of pardon.

After this, however, he says to the serpent: “You shall be accursed among all cattle; upon your breast and belly you shall go.” By “breast” is signified pride of mind; by “belly” are signified the desires of the flesh. For by these two things the devil creeps against those whom he wishes to deceive: either by earthly desire and lust, or by the insane ruin of pride.

“And you shall eat earth”—that is, those whom you have deceived through earthly desire shall belong to you. “All the days of your life”—that is, throughout the whole time during which you exercise this power, before that final punishment of judgment.

It follows:

### (Verse 15)

“I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed. She shall crush your head, and you shall lie in wait for her heel.”

The seed of the woman is the entire human race; the seed of the serpent is carnal desire. These two seeds ought to maintain continual hatred between themselves, so that we do not do what the devil wishes.

What does he mean by saying, “She shall crush your head, and you shall lie in wait for her heel”? The serpent’s head is the thought of unlawful suggestion. We ought with all our attention to crush it and dash it against the rock, which is Christ. The woman’s heel is the final period of our life, when the devil strives to attack us more fiercely. If we resist him courageously, we shall receive the victory of perseverance together with our salvation.

“I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed.” The seed of the devil is perverse suggestion. The seed of the woman is the fruit of the good work by which perverse suggestion is resisted. She crushes his head when the mind excludes him at the very beginning of the evil suggestion; he lies in wait for her heel because he strives to deceive at the end the mind that he did not deceive in the first suggestion.

Some, however, have understood the words “I will put enmity between you and the woman” of the virgin from whom the Lord was born, since at that time the Lord, who was destined to be born from her in order to defeat the enemy and destroy death, whose author he was, was promised. They understand what follows—“She shall crush your head, and you shall lie in wait for her heel”—of the fruit of Mary’s womb, which is Christ: that is, you will trip him up so that he dies, but he will rise victorious and crush your head, which is death.

David had likewise said, speaking in the person of the Father to the Son: “You shall tread upon the asp and the basilisk, and you shall trample upon the lion and the dragon” (Ps. XC). He called death the asp, sin the basilisk, Antichrist the lion, and the devil the dragon.

It follows:

### (Verse 16)

“You shall be under the power of the man, and he shall rule over you.”

When he says, “You shall be under the power of the man,” it is asked whether, if the woman had not sinned, she would have been under the man’s power. She certainly would have been, but under that servitude which operates through love and casts out fear. After sin, however, there came the fear of conditional servitude, which operates through discipline: it came as the punishment of the curse, not from an equality of nature.

The man therefore has her desire subjected to him, so that according to this law he may impose a measure upon the woman.

But what does the punishment of the woman signify when it is said to her, “In pain you shall bear children,” except that when the carnal will wishes to overcome some evil habit, it suffers pains at the beginning and thus, through a better habit, gives birth to a good work as to children?

What he added—“And your turning shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you”—signifies that the carnal pleasure which had struggled in pain in order to establish a good habit, now instructed by those very pains, becomes more cautious. So that it may not fall, it obeys reason and willingly serves, as though a husband were giving orders.

It follows:

### (Verse 17)

“But to Adam he said: ‘Because you listened to the voice of your wife.’”

He therefore blames the man because, anticipating God’s command, he preferred the will of his wife, over whom he ought to have ruled:

“And you ate from the tree concerning which I commanded you not to eat.”

Again he is accused of the desire of the appetite, which is the second punishment in the fall of transgression after pride.

“Cursed is the earth in your work.” Here “work” does not refer to the cultivation of the soil, but signifies sins, as it is found in the Hebrew. Aquila likewise does not differ, saying, “Cursed is the ground because of you.” “It shall produce thorns and thistles for you”: incentives, as it were, to vices, which would in no way exist in us if the first man had not lost the happiness of paradise.

It follows:

### (Verse 19)

“By the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread, until you return to the earth from which you were taken.”

He wished that the bread which testified that it had descended from heaven and gives life to the world might be understood here (John VI). Penitents therefore receive this bread with the greatest toil and the satisfaction of repentance.

When God had said, “Adam, where are you?”, he signified the death of the soul, which occurred when Adam deserted God. By saying, “You are dust, and to dust you shall return,” he signified the death of the body, which comes to him when the soul departs.

For this reason one should not think that he said nothing about the second death, because he wished it to remain hidden on account of the dispensation of the New Testament, in which the second death is most openly declared. The first death, which is common to all, had to come first; the second death, however, is certainly not common to all.

It follows:

### (Verse 21)

“And the Lord God made tunics of skins for Adam and his wife, and clothed them.”

In the tunics of skins the condition of death is to be understood: those who, through disobedience to God, did not wish to retain the likeness of God—that is, immortality—received through the condition of death the likeness of animals and cattle.

They themselves made loincloths for themselves from fig leaves, and God made tunics of skins for them. That is, they desired the lust of lying, abandoning the face of truth, while God changed their bodies into this mortality of the flesh. When man, through pride, desired to be God, he was cast down as far as the mortality of beasts.

It follows:

### (Verse 22)

“Behold, Adam has become like one of us.”

That is, as though he himself were the Lord and creator of Adam: this belongs to the mockery of one who taunts. “Like one of us” serves as an example of fear, since Adam not only did not become what he wished to become, but did not preserve even what he had been made.

What he added—“Like one of us”—was said on account of the Trinity, just as was the statement, “Let us make man in our image and likeness.”

It follows: “Knowing good and evil.” This means that he himself would learn evil by experience, whereas God knows it through wisdom.

It follows: “Now therefore see, lest he perhaps put out his hand and also take from the tree of life, and eat, and live forever.”

Truly, as the most merciful Lord, he deemed it right to provide for their salvation, lest, having already become unworthy through transgression, they presume to eat from the tree of life and live forever in torment. They were therefore temporarily excluded from eating it, so that through an appropriate satisfaction of repentance they might return again to the place from which they had been expelled.

It may therefore be understood that man was sent into the labor of this life for the following reason: that at some time he might stretch out his hand toward the tree of life.

### (Columns 0915D–0916B; Verses 23–24)

“And the Lord God sent him out from the garden of delight, to work the earth from which he had been taken.”

That is, to labor in this body, and there to establish for himself a merit by which he might return.

“And he placed him before the garden.” This too was done symbolically, so that the sinner might live in misery opposite the garden in which blessed life was also signified spiritually.

“And he appointed the cherubim and the flaming sword, which turns, to guard the way of the tree of life.”

This must certainly be believed to have been done visibly in paradise through the heavenly powers, so that there might be there, through angelic ministry, a certain fiery guard. Yet it was not done without reason, since there can be no doubt that something concerning the spiritual paradise is also signified.

But the Hebrew has a different sense from what is read here. It says: “He expelled Adam”—clearly meaning the Lord—“and caused the cherubim and the flaming sword, which turns, to dwell before the garden of delight, to guard the way of the tree of life.” This does not mean that God caused Adam himself, whom he had expelled, to dwell opposite the garden of delight; rather, after expelling him, he placed the cherubim and the flaming sword before the gates of paradise to guard its entrance, so that no one could enter.

From then on she is called Eve, “mother of the living”—that is, of those who act rightly. Opposed to these are sins, which are signified by the name “the dead.”

Now, through the sentence imposed upon the man, our reason is reproved. Having been seduced above by the desire of sin and removed from the paradise of blessedness, it has the curses of earthly labor and the pains of temporal cares, like thorns and thistles.

Nevertheless, he is dismissed from the paradise of blessedness in such a way that he may work the earth—that is, labor in this body—and establish for himself a merit by which he may return to the blessed life signified by the name “paradise.” He may at some time stretch out his hand toward the tree of life and live forever.

The stretching out of the hand appropriately signifies the cross, or the torment of repentance, through which eternal life is recovered.

He also receives a tunic of skins by divine judgment. In the historical sense, this name signifies the mortality of the body; in the allegorical sense, it signifies pleasures withdrawn from carnal perceptions, which pursue and cover the person living according to the flesh under divine law.

If such a person at some time turns to God, then, through the flaming sword—that is, through temporal tribulations—he acknowledges and mourns his sins; and through the cherubim—that is, through the fullness of knowledge, which is love—he reaches the tree of life, Christ, and lives forever.

“Cherubim” is interpreted as “fullness of knowledge.” The revolving sword placed to guard the way of the tree of life signifies temporal punishments. No one can reach the tree of life except through these two things: endurance of afflictions and fullness of knowledge, that is, through love of God and neighbor. For love is the fullness of the law.

It follows:

### (Chapter IV, verse 1)

“Now Adam knew Eve his wife, and she conceived and bore Cain, saying, ‘I have acquired a man through God.’”

Cain is interpreted as “possession.” Hence, when he was born, she said, “I have acquired a man through God.” Adam would not have said, as he is reported to have said, “I have acquired a man through God,” unless, by his birth, this first man had been added to those two.

Cain was therefore born first from those two parents of the human race, belonging to the city of men; afterward Abel, belonging to the city of God.

For in one man we experience what the Apostle said: “Not the spiritual first, but the natural, and afterward the spiritual” (1 Cor. XV). Therefore, since everyone arises from a condemned stock, it is necessary that each person first be evil and carnal from Adam. But if he progresses by being reborn in Christ, he can become good and spiritual.

Thus, in the whole human race, when these two cities first began to proceed through birth and death, the citizen of this world was born first, while afterward came the one who is a stranger in this world and belongs to the city of God.

It follows:

### (Verses 2 and following)

“Now Abel was a shepherd of sheep, and Cain was a tiller of the soil. And it came to pass, after many days, that Cain offered gifts to the Lord from the fruits of the earth. Abel also offered from the firstborn of his flock and from their fat; and God looked upon Abel and his gifts, but upon Cain and his gifts he did not look. Cain was therefore greatly angered, and his face fell.”

How could Cain have known that God had accepted his brother’s gifts and rejected his own, unless that interpretation is true which Theodotion gives: “And the Lord was inflamed over Abel and over his sacrifice; but over Cain and over his sacrifice he was not inflamed”?

We read that fire ordinarily came from heaven to consume sacrifices both at the dedication of the Temple under Solomon and when Elijah built an altar on Mount Carmel.

It follows:

### (Verses 6–7)

“And the Lord said to him, ‘Why are you angry, and why has your face fallen? If you do well, will you not receive? But if you do evil, will your sin not immediately be at the door? Yet its desire shall be under you, and you shall rule over it.’”

This means: Why are you angry, and why are you tortured by the envy and bitterness you feel toward your brother? Why do you cast an angry face toward the ground? If you do well, will not every offense be forgiven you? Or, as Theodotion says, “Will it not be acceptable?”—that is, I shall accept your gift just as I accepted your brother’s.

But if you have done evil, your sin will immediately sit before your threshold, and will you be accompanied by such a doorkeeper? Yet because you possess free will, I warn you: do not let sin rule you; rather, rule over your sin.

The birth of Adam’s two sons resembles the two peoples who, at different times, were destined to come to faith—equal in work but unlike in love before God.

“Abel was a shepherd of sheep, and Cain a tiller of the soil.” But just as Cain’s sacrifice from the fruits of the earth is rejected, while Abel’s sacrifice from sheep and their fat is accepted, so the faith of the New Testament, praising God through innocence, is preferred to the earthly works of the Old Testament.

It follows:

### (Verses 8 and following)

“And Cain said to Abel his brother, ‘Let us go out into the field.’ And when they were in the field, Cain rose up against his brother and killed him.

“And the Lord said to Cain, ‘Where is Abel your brother?’ He answered, ‘I do not know.’”

He asks not as one ignorant, but as a judge who is about to punish the guilty.

“The voice of your brother’s blood,” he says, “cries to me from the earth.”

Abel’s blood is said to cry to the Lord not with a voice, but by its cause.

To this Cain, adding deceitfully and proudly to his sin, answered, thinking that God did not know what he had done: “I do not know. Am I my brother’s keeper?”

God said to him: Do you suppose that I do not know what you have done? I looked upon the thought you had impiously conceived and warned you not to carry it out in deed. But lest you complain that I unjustly pronounce a sentence against you, I do not bring an accusation against you myself. There is a witness who accuses you: namely, the voice of your brother’s blood, which cries to me from the earth.

It follows:

### (Verses 13 and following)

“And Cain answered the Lord, ‘My iniquity is greater than that I may deserve pardon.’”

That is: I have sinned more than I deserve to be acquitted.

“Behold, today you cast me away from your face, and I shall be hidden from your face so that I may lie concealed; and I shall be groaning upon the earth, and everyone who finds me will kill me.”

“I am cast away,” he says, “from your sight. Since I cannot endure even the light itself because of the consciousness of my crime, I added, ‘I shall be hidden so that I may lie concealed; and everyone who finds me will kill me.’”

As he is agitated by trembling of body and madness of mind, he understands that he is one who deserves to be killed.

But God, unwilling to end his torment by the shortcut of death or to hand him over to the punishment by which he had condemned himself, said: “Not so.” That is: You will not die as you think, nor will you receive death as a remedy. Rather, you will live until the seventh generation and be tormented by the fire of your conscience, so that whoever kills you will, according to the twofold interpretation, either do so in the seventh generation or free you from great torment.

This does not mean that the one who struck Cain would himself be subjected to seven punishments. Rather, the killer releases the seven acts of vengeance that continued against Cain for so long a time, by killing the man who had been left alive for punishment.

To make what we are saying clearer, let us give an example from everyday usage.

A servant speaks to his master amid blows: “Because I burned down your house and destroyed all your property, kill me.” The master replies: “No. You will not die as you wish and end your punishments by death. Rather, you will be guarded alive for a long time, and you will live so unhappily in this light that whoever kills you will do a favor to the man killed, since he frees you from so many torments.”

This, at least, seems to be the sense for us according to the Septuagint.

As for the reading Aquila gives, “sevenfold,” and Symmachus gives, “a hebdomad,” or “the seventh shall avenge,” this is the opinion of our predecessors: they think that Cain was killed by Lamech in the seventh generation.

Adam begot Cain; Cain begot Enoch; Enoch begot Irad; Irad begot Maviahel; Maviahel begot Matusahel; and Matusahel begot Lamech, who is the seventh from Adam.

According to what is written in a certain Hebrew volume, Lamech did not kill Cain intentionally, as he himself later confesses: “For I have killed a man by my wound, and a young man by my bruise.”

Others speculate in various ways about Cain’s seven acts of vengeance. They assert that his first sin was that he did not divide rightly; the second, that he envied his brother; the third, that he acted deceitfully when he said, “Let us cross over into the field”; the fourth, that he killed him; the fifth, that he denied it insolently; the sixth, that he condemned himself when he said, “My guilt is greater than I deserve to be forgiven”; and the seventh, that even after being condemned he did not repent.

They say that the most merciful God therefore delayed him until seven generations, so that at least through these evils and through the sorrow of a long life he might be compelled to repent and deserve to be pardoned.

Some interpret the number seven as complete and perfect, collecting testimonies from many passages of Scripture. They say that this is the sense we touched on above: whoever killed Cain freed him from the great punishment of every temporal penalty, since Cain would be avenged sevenfold, but Lamech seventy-sevenfold.

The Hebrews report that seventy-seven persons descended from Lamech were found and were destroyed in the Flood. They say that vengeance was carried out against Lamech in this number, because his race continued until the cataclysm. Others maintain, on the authority of the evangelist Luke, that there were seventy-seven generations from Adam to Christ.

Therefore, just as Cain’s sin was dissolved in the seventh generation—for the Lord did not exact vengeance twice for the same matter, and one who received his evils once in life will not suffer the same torments in death that he suffered in life—so also Lamech’s sin, that is, the sin of the whole world and of the blood that was shed, will be dissolved by the coming of Christ. He bore the sins of the world, washed his garment in the blood of the grape, trod the winepress alone, and at his ascension displayed a marvel to the angels.

### (Verse 15)

“And the Lord placed a sign upon Cain, so that no one who found him would kill him.”

This sign itself was that, trembling and groaning, wandering and fugitive, he should live forever and be unable to find anywhere on earth a settled place of rest. Therefore, so that he might be preserved, he built a city.
