God said to Cain: “If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, you have sinned.” This means that although the Jews had earlier done those things rightly, they are nevertheless guilty of unbelief because, when Christ came, they did not distinguish the time of the New Testament from the time of the Old Testament.

If Cain had obeyed when God said, “Be still; your desire shall be under you, and you shall rule over it,” he would have turned his sin back upon himself, attributing it to himself and confessing it to God. Thus, aided by the grace of pardon, he himself would have ruled over his sin; he would not have been its servant while it ruled him, and he would not have killed his innocent brother.

So also the Jews, in whose figure these things were taking place: if they had ceased from their disturbance and, recognizing the time of salvation through grace for the forgiveness of sins, had listened to Christ saying, “I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Matt. IX), then they would have turned their sin back upon themselves in confession, as it is written in Psalm XL. They would have said to the physician, “I said, Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against you” (Ps. XL). As long as that sin still remained in their mortal body, they would have ruled over it freely through the hope of grace.

But now, because they did not know the righteousness of God and wished to establish their own, exalted by the works of the law and not humbled by their sins, they did not remain still. Rather, they stumbled against the stone of stumbling and blazed with anger against Christ, whose works they saw and grieved that they were pleasing to God.

It follows:

After this, Abel, the younger brother, is killed by his elder brother Cain. Christ, the head of the younger people, is killed by the Jewish people, the elder: the one in the field, the other at the place of Calvary.

God asks Cain, not as one ignorant from whom he might learn, but as a judge questioning a guilty man whom he is about to punish. He asks where his brother is. Cain answers that he does not know and that he is not his brother’s keeper.

What do the Jews answer us even now when, with the voice of the holy Scriptures, we question them about Christ? They answer that they do not know Christ. The deceitful ignorance of Cain is the false denial of the Jews.

They would in some sense be keepers of Christ if they had wished to accept and preserve the Christian faith.

It follows:

God said to Cain: “What have you done? The voice of your brother’s blood cries to me from the earth.”

Thus the divine voice accuses the Jews in the holy Scriptures. For the blood of Christ has a loud voice on earth. When, after receiving the sacrament, all the nations answer, “Amen,” this is the clear voice, the voice of the blood, which that blood expresses from the mouths of the faithful redeemed by the same blood.

God said to Cain: “You shall be accursed from the earth, which has opened its mouth and received your brother’s blood from your hand.”

The unbelieving Jewish people is accursed from the earth—that is, from the Church, which opened its mouth in confession of sins to receive the blood of Christ, poured out for the remission of all sins, from the hand of the persecutor who did not wish to be under grace but under the law. He was therefore accursed by the Church—that is, the Church showed him to be accursed, as the Apostle testifies: “For all who rely on works of the law are under the curse of the law” (Gal. III).

“When you work the earth, it shall not give you its fruits.”

For upon the very earth which Christ bore—that is, in his flesh—they worked our salvation by crucifying Christ, who died for our sins (Rom. IV). Yet that same earth did not give them its power, because they were not justified by the power of his resurrection, of him who rose for our justification. Although he was crucified from the weakness of our condition, he lives by the power of God (2 Cor. XIII).

This, then, is the power of that earth, which he did not show to the ungodly and unbelieving. Hence, when he rose, he did not appear to those by whom he had been crucified, just as Cain worked the earth so that that grain might be sown.

“Wandering and fugitive,” or, as it is written in the Septuagint, “Groaning and trembling you shall be upon the earth.”

Now who does not see, who does not recognize, throughout the whole earth wherever that people has been scattered, how it is wandering among the nations and a fugitive from Jerusalem; how it groans in sorrow over the loss of its kingdom and trembles with fear among innumerable Christian peoples?

Therefore he answered, saying:

“My iniquity is greater than I deserve to be forgiven. Behold, today you cast me away from the face of the earth, and I shall be hidden from your face; and I shall be wandering and fugitive upon the earth. Therefore everyone who finds me will kill me.”

Truly, as a wanderer and fugitive, he groans and trembles lest, after losing his earthly kingdom, he also be killed by visible death.

He calls this the greater cause than the one by which our earth does not give its power, lest he die spiritually. For he has a carnal understanding and hides himself from the face of God—that is, he does not consider it a serious matter to have God angry with him. But he fears that he may be found and killed. He has a carnal understanding, as one working the earth, whose power he has not received.

To understand according to the flesh is death. Not understanding this, he groans over the loss of his kingdom and trembles at bodily death.

But what did God answer him?

“By no means shall this happen; rather, whoever kills Cain shall be punished sevenfold.” Or, as the Septuagint translated it, “He shall pay seven acts of vengeance.”

That is: It will not happen as you say. The impious race of carnal Jews will not perish by bodily death. Whoever destroys them in this way will pay seven acts of vengeance—that is, he will remove from them the seven acts of vengeance to which they are bound because of the guilt of Christ’s death.

Throughout this entire period, which turns according to the number seven of the days, it is especially clear to faithful Christians that the Jewish nation has not perished, but has deserved only dispersion, in accordance with what Scripture says:

“Do not kill them, lest my people forget your law; scatter them by your power and bring them down” (Ps. LVIII).

“And the Lord placed a sign upon Cain, so that no one who found him would kill him.”

This is truly marvelous: all the nations that were subdued by the Romans passed into the Roman rite of sacrifices and accepted those sacrileges for observance and celebration.

But the Jewish nation, whether under pagan kings or under Christians, did not lose the sign of its law and circumcision, by which it is distinguished from the other nations and peoples. Every emperor or king who found them in his kingdom found them with that sign and did not kill them.

Therefore he went out from the face of the Lord and dwelt in the land of Nod, which is interpreted as “commotion,” or “unstable,” “wavering,” and “of uncertain dwelling.” Against this evil God is invoked in the psalm:

“Do not let my feet be moved, and do not let the hands of sinners move me” (Ps. XXXV).

Now the Jews and all who, through various errors, stubbornly resist the truth go out, sold away, from the face of God—that is, from the mercy of his love, or from participation in his light. They dwell as fugitives in the land of commotion—that is, in carnal disturbance—against the delight of God, which is Eden, interpreted as “feasting,” where paradise was planted.

It follows:

### (Verse 17)

“Now Cain knew his wife, and she conceived and bore Enoch. And he built a city and called its name after the name of his son Enoch.”

It does not necessarily follow that Enoch should be believed to have been his first son. This should not be inferred merely because it is said that he knew his wife, as though he had intercourse with her for the first time only then.

For even concerning Adam, the father of all, Scripture does not say this only when Cain was conceived, whom he appears to have had as his firstborn. Later the same Scripture says: “Adam knew Eve his wife, and she conceived and bore a son, and called his name Seth.”

Hence it is understood that Scripture is accustomed to speak in this way—although not always—when it says that people were conceived: it does not do so only when the two sexes first joined.

Nor is it necessary to suppose from this argument that Enoch was his father’s firstborn, because the city was called by Enoch’s name. It is not impossible that, for some reason, although he had other children, the father loved him more than the others. Judas, after all, was not the firstborn, yet Judea and the Jews were named from him.

But even if this son, who founded the city, was born first, it should not therefore be thought that the city was given his name by his father at the time of his birth. A city could not then have been established by one person, since a city is nothing other than a multitude of people bound together by some bond of association. Rather, when that man’s family had grown to such numbers that it also possessed the size of a people, it could certainly have happened that he established a city and gave the city he founded the name of his firstborn.

For this reason no prudent evaluator of affairs will doubt that Cain could have founded not merely some city but even a great city, since the life of mortals was prolonged for so long a time.

It follows:

### (Verses 18 and following)

“Moreover, Enoch begot Irad; and Irad begot Maviahel; and Maviahel begot Matusahel; and Matusahel begot Lamech. Lamech took two wives: the name of one was Ada, and the name of the other Sela. Ada bore Jabal, who was the father of those who dwell in tents and of shepherds. Sela also bore Tubal-cain, who was a hammerer and craftsman in every work of bronze and iron. The sister of Tubal-cain was Naamah.”

I do not think it was written without reason that, in those generations descended from the one called Seth, although sons and daughters are said to have been born, no female child born there is specifically named. In the generations descended from Cain, however, at the very end, where they reach their conclusion, the last woman born is named.

For it is read as follows: “Matusahel begot Lamech. And Lamech took two wives: the name of one was Ada, and the name of the second was Sela, who bore Jabal. He was the father of those who dwell in tents and of shepherds, and the name of his brother was Tubal. He was the father of those who play the lyre and the pipe. Sela also bore Tubal-cain, who was a hammerer and craftsman in every work of bronze and iron. The sister of Tubal-cain was Naamah.”

Here the generations from Cain extend. There are eight generations in all from Adam, counting Adam himself: seven, namely, up to Lamech, who was the husband of two wives, and the eighth generation is found in his sons, among whom a woman is also mentioned.

This elegantly signifies that the earthly city, throughout its entire course to the end, will have carnal generations arising from the union of males and females. Hence, these women themselves—something never found before the Flood except in the case of Eve—are expressed by their proper names: the wives of that man who is here called the last father.

Although Adam was the father of both lines—that is, both of the line belonging to the earthly city and of the line belonging to the heavenly city—after Abel was killed, and after the wondrous mystery was commended in his killing, two fathers of the two lines arose in Cain and Seth.

In their sons it was appropriate that the generation of these two cities should be recorded, and the clear signs of mortal beings began to become more evident.

Cain begot Enoch. Enoch is interpreted as “dedication.” The earthly city is dedicated here, where it is founded, because here it possesses the end toward which it directs itself and which it desires.

After him Abel, whom his elder brother killed, first displayed a certain prefiguration of the city of God as a pilgrim: that it would suffer persecutions from the impious, and, in a sense, from earthborn people—that is, those who love an earthly origin and rejoice in the earthly happiness of the earthly city.

But how many years old Adam was when he begot them is not apparent.

From that point onward, some generations from Cain and others from him whom Adam begot as his successor—the one whom his brother killed and whose name he called Seth—are set out. As it is written:

“For God has raised up for me another seed in place of Abel, whom Cain killed.”

Among Cain’s descendants, although Adam is mentioned and the reckoning extends to the eighth generation, the age of none of them is stated when he begot the one mentioned after him. For the Spirit of God did not wish to mark the periods of the earthly city’s generations before the Flood; rather, he preferred to do so in the case of the heavenly city, as though they were more worthy of remembrance.

It follows:

## (Verses 25–26)

Adam again knew his wife, and she gave birth to a son and called his name Seth, saying, “The Lord has appointed for me another offspring in place of Abel, whom Cain killed.” [[Col. 0921C]]

Seth also had a son, whom he called Enosh: he began to call upon the name of the Lord.

Adam, divinely admonished, could indeed have said after Seth was born, “God has raised up for me another offspring in place of Abel, whom Cain killed,” since he was destined to be one who would fulfill Abel’s holiness. Seth also had a son, whom he called Enosh: he began to call upon the name of the Lord. [[Col. 0921D]]

For from those two men—Abel, whose name means “mourning,” and his brother Seth, whose name means “resurrection”—the death of Christ and his life from the dead are prefigured. From this faith the city of God is born, that is, the human being who began to call upon the name of the Lord. “For by hope we were saved,” as the Apostle says (Rom. 8).

Who, indeed, would think that this has nothing to do with the depth of the mystery? Did Abel not begin to call upon the name of the Lord God—or, as it is found in the Septuagint, “He hoped to call upon the name of the Lord God,” whose sacrifice Scripture records as having been so acceptable to God? Did Seth himself not begin—or hope—to call upon the name of the Lord God, concerning whom it was said, “God has raised up for me another offspring in place of Abel”?

Why, then, is what is understood to be common to all the devout attributed specifically to this man? It is because it was necessary that, in the one who is first recorded as having arisen from the father of the generations toward the better part—that is, toward the heavenly city—there should be prefigured the human being, or human society, which does not live according to humanity in the pursuit of earthly happiness, but according to God in hope of eternal happiness.

The very statement, “And he called his name Enosh”—which means “human being”—followed by “He hoped, or began, to call upon the name of the Lord God,” sufficiently shows that a human being ought not to place hope in himself. “For cursed is everyone,” as we read elsewhere, “who places his hope in a human being” (Jer. 17); consequently, he should not place hope even in himself, so as to be a citizen of the other city, which is not dedicated according to the son of Cain at this time—that is, according to this mortal age—but in that immortality of everlasting blessedness. [[Col. 0922A]]

This lineage, whose father is Seth, also has the name of dedication in the generation that is seventh from Adam, counting Adam himself. For the seventh born from him was Enoch, whose name means “dedication.” He is the one who was translated, because he pleased God, and he occupies a distinguished place in the order of the generations, in the number in which the Sabbath was consecrated, being seventh from Adam.

From the father of these generations, which are distinguished from the offspring of Cain—that is, from Seth—Enoch is sixth, corresponding to the sixth day on which the human being was made and God completed all his works.

But Enoch’s translation prefigured the delay of our dedication, which has already taken place in Christ our head: he rose in such a way that he would never again die, and what went before in the head is hoped for in the body.

It continues:

## (Chapter 5—Verses 1–2)

“This is the book of the generation of Adam. On the day when God created the human being, he made him in the likeness of God. Male and female he made them, and God blessed them and called their name Adam on the day when they were created.” [[Col. 0922B]]

Why, then, does the narrative return here to this recapitulation after the son of Seth has been mentioned, the one who began—or hoped—to call upon the name of the Lord God?

We should understand that Enosh, the son of Seth, means “human being,” but not in the same way as Adam. That name too means “human being,” but in that language—that is, in Hebrew—it is said to be a common term for male and female. Thus it is written concerning them: “Male and female he made them, and he blessed them, and he called their name Adam” (Gen. 1:5). Hence there is no doubt that the woman was called Eve by her proper name, while Adam, which means “human being,” was the name of both.

Enosh, however, means “human being” in such a way that those skilled in that language assert that a woman cannot be called by it—as though he were the son of the resurrection, where “they will neither marry nor be given in marriage.” For in the resurrection there will be no generation, since regeneration will have brought them there.

It continues:

## (Verses 3 and following)

“Adam lived one hundred and thirty years and begot a son in his own image and likeness, and called his name Seth. Seth also lived one hundred and five years and begot Enosh. Enosh lived ninety years and begot Cainan.” [[Col. 0922C]]

Someone may say: Should we believe that a human being who was going to father children, without having adopted a purpose of continence, did not cease from intercourse for one hundred years or more—or, according to the Hebrews, for not much less, namely eighty, seventy, or sixty years—or, if he did not abstain, that he could have fathered no offspring?

This question is resolved in two ways. Either puberty lasted proportionately longer because the whole span of life was longer; or—and this seems more credible to me—the firstborn sons are not mentioned here, but those whom the order of succession required to be mentioned, so that the narrative might reach Noah, from whom we see that it proceeded again to Abraham, and then onward to a definite point in time. The course of the most glorious city, which journeys in this world and seeks its heavenly homeland, had to be marked out, including the generations that were necessary for this purpose.

What cannot be denied is that Cain was born first of all from the union of male and female. He was followed by Abel, whom his older brother killed. But how many years old Adam was when he fathered them does not appear.

When Seth was born, however, the years of his father are not withheld; yet Adam had already fathered others. Whether these were only Cain and Abel is uncertain. The fact that only they are named does not mean that, for the sake of the order of the generations that had to be recorded, they were the only children then born to Adam.

For, although all the names of the others are covered in silence, we read that Adam fathered sons and daughters. If someone avoids the fault of rashness, who would dare assert what place this offspring occupied among them? [[Col. 0922D]]

Adam, then, when he was one hundred and thirty years old, begot Seth. Seth, when he was one hundred and five years old, begot Enosh. Who could thoughtlessly assert that Enosh was his firstborn, so that we should rightly wonder how he had remained free from [[Col. 0923A]] marriage for so many years without any purpose of continence, or, if married, had not fathered children? For concerning Seth himself we read: “And he begot sons and daughters, and all the days of Seth were nine hundred and twelve years, and he died.” The same is said in succession of those whose years are recorded, and whose fathering of sons and daughters is not omitted.

Therefore it is not at all apparent whether the one said to have been begotten was himself the firstborn.

Indeed, since it is not credible that those fathers, given their long lifespans, were either still immature or without wives or children, neither is it credible that the sons named were their first children. Rather, when the sacred historian intended to reach Noah—at whose time the Flood occurred—through the succession of generations whose times were marked, he recorded not those who were first born to their parents, but those who entered into the order of descent.

To make this clearer, I shall insert an example from which no one will doubt that what I am saying could have happened. [[Col. 0923B]] The Evangelist Matthew, wishing to preserve the generation of the Lord’s incarnation through a sequence of ancestors, began from Abraham and David and directed the order toward its completion. He says, “Abraham begot Isaac” (Matt. 1), and does not mention Ishmael, who was the firstborn. “Isaac begot Jacob,” and he does not mention Esau, who was his firstborn, because the line could not reach David through them.

Then follows: “Jacob begot Judah,” who was not his firstborn. “Judah,” he says, “begot Perez,” although he had already fathered three sons before him. Matthew therefore retained the one through whom the order of generations reached David and, from there, the destination toward which it was directed.

From this it may be understood that the ancient people before the Flood likewise had not their firstborn recorded, but those through whom the order of successive generations was led to Noah the patriarch.

This was also the purpose of the author of this history in recording the generations from Adam through his son Seth: to reach Noah through them, under whom the Flood took place.

Through Seth, from Adam to Noah, the legitimate number ten is indicated. [[Col. 0923C]] To Noah are added three sons. When one fell and two were blessed by their father, the rejected one being removed and the approved sons being added to the number, the number twelve is also signified. This number is distinguished both among the patriarchs and among the Apostles because of the parts of seven, each multiplied by the other.

Nor is it surprising that, with varying numbers of years interposed, the two lineages did not have an equal number of generations over so long a period from Adam to the Flood: Cain has seven, whereas Seth has ten.

For Lamech is seventh from Adam, as I have already said, and Noah is tenth. Therefore, unlike the others mentioned earlier, not one son but several are recorded for Lamech, because it was uncertain who would succeed him after his death if time for ruling had remained between him and the Flood.

Since Lamech was found to be seventh from Adam, his children are counted until the number eleven, by which sin is signified, is completed; three sons and one daughter are added. 

Since the Law is proclaimed through the number ten, from which [[Col. 0923D]] the memorable Decalogue derives, the number eleven, because it exceeds ten, signifies transgression of the Law and therefore sin.

Thus the offspring from Adam through Cain, the criminal murderer, ends with the number eleven, by which sin is signified. This number is closed by a woman, from whose sex the beginning of sin arose, through which we all die.

It also happened that the pleasure of the flesh, which would resist the spirit, followed. For Lamech’s daughter, Noema, means “pleasure.” Consequently, it could have happened that the Flood occurred while Lamech was still alive and ruling, so that it would find him, together with all the other human beings except those who were in the ark, and destroy him, fulfilling what he himself said: “Sevenfold vengeance shall be taken for Cain, but for Lamech seventy-sevenfold.”

For it was necessary to set forth these two cities: one from murderer to murderer—for Lamech himself confesses to his two wives [[Col. 0924A]] that he committed murder—and the other through the one who hoped to call upon the name of the Lord God. 

It continues:

## (Verses 21 and following)

“Enoch lived sixty-five years and begot Methuselah.”

This is a famous question, debated throughout all the Churches: according to a careful calculation, Methuselah is said to have lived fourteen years after the Flood, whereas above he is said to have lived nine hundred and sixty-nine years. And how can it be true that only eight persons were saved in the ark?

It remains, therefore, that here too, as in many other places, there is an error in the number. For in both the Hebrew and the Samaritan books the text is found as follows:

“Methuselah lived one hundred and eighty-six years and begot Lamech; and Methuselah lived seven hundred and eighty-two years after he begot Lamech; and all the days of Methuselah were nine hundred and sixty-nine years.”

“And Lamech lived one hundred and eighty-two years and begot Noah.”

From the day of Methuselah’s birth to the day of Noah’s birth there are therefore three hundred and sixty-nine years. Add Noah’s six hundred years, because [[Col. 0924B]] the Flood occurred in the six hundredth year of his life, and it follows that Methuselah died in the nine hundred and sixty-ninth year of his life, namely in the year in which the Flood began. 

It continues:

“Lamech said to his wives Adah and Zillah: ‘Hear my voice, wives of Lamech; listen to my speech: for I have killed a man for my wound, and a young man for my bruise. Sevenfold vengeance shall be taken for Cain, but for Lamech seventy-sevenfold.’”

Elsewhere, according to the historical sense, it has been said that seventy-seven generations are found from Adam to Christ. In these generations the sin of Lamech—that is, of the whole world—was dissolved through the shedding of Christ’s blood.

Likewise, among the Jewish people, seventy-seven punishments were appointed because of the killing of Christ, in accordance with the Gospel saying addressed to the Apostle Peter: “Not seven times, but seventy-seven times,” if he repents, forgiveness is to be granted to one’s brother (Matt. 18). That is, the Jew who returns after the seventy-seven appointed punishments is to be received into Christ’s forgiveness.

[[Col. 0924C]] ## (Chapter 6—Verses 1 and following) 

“Now when Noah was five hundred years old, he begot Shem, Ham, and Japheth. When human beings began to multiply upon the earth and had begotten daughters, the sons of God, seeing that the daughters of human beings were beautiful, took wives for themselves from all whom they chose.”

Here divine Scripture wished, though silently, to indicate the stock of Cain—that is, the sons of possession. Whose possession, if not that of the earthly city, which was founded in the name of the one called Enoch?

Enoch means “dedication,” because he has the end that he intends and desires.

When Scripture adds, “and had begotten daughters,” it shows that evil was again discovered through the female sex—not, indeed, in the same manner as at the beginning. For those women did not then persuade men to sin through any deception of their own. Rather, women who had been of depraved character from the beginning, in the earthly city—that is, in the society of those born of the earth—were loved by the sons of God because of the beauty of their bodies.

This is a good that is indeed God’s gift, but for that very reason he grants it also to the wicked, [[Col. 0924D]] lest it appear to be a great good to the good. 

Another translation reads as follows:

“And it happened, after human beings began to become numerous upon the earth and daughters were born to them, that the angels of God, seeing that the daughters of human beings were good, took for themselves wives from all whom they chose.”

Thus, abandoning the great good and their proper good, they fell toward the least good—a good that was not proper to the good, but common to both the good and the wicked. In this way the sons of God were captivated by love for the daughters of human beings, and, so that they might enjoy them as wives, they descended into the customs of the earthly society, abandoning the piety they maintained in the holy society.

For bodily beauty, although made by God, is a temporal, carnal, and inferior good.

When the order of this affection—that is, of devotion and love—was disturbed, the sons of God, that is, the sons of Seth and the sons of resurrection, neglected God and loved the daughters of human beings, that is, the daughters of Cain.

Certainly, those who were sons of Seth and were called sons of God were also called angels of God. By nature they were sons of human beings, [[Col. 0925A]] but by grace they had begun to bear another name. For in the same Scripture in which they are called sons of God, they are also called angels of God.

It may be asked how angels could have intercourse with the daughters of human beings, from whom giants are said to have been born. We believe that these were human beings who were righteous and who could even be called by the name “angels.” For concerning the human being John it is written: “Behold, I send my angel before your face, who will prepare your way” (Mal. 3).

But this raises the question how giants could have been born from intercourse between human beings, or how they could have mingled with women, if they were not human beings but angels.

Nevertheless, I do not believe that the holy angels of God could have fallen in that way at that time, nor that the Apostle Peter spoke of them when he said: “For God did not spare the angels when they sinned, but thrust them into the prisons of darkness and delivered them to be kept for judgment and punishment.”

As for the giants—that is, those who were exceedingly large and strong—I think there is no reason to wonder that they could have been born from human beings, since even after the Flood some such people are found to have existed.

[[Col. 0925B]] It is therefore more credible that human beings who were righteous, called either angels or sons of God, fell through desire and sinned with women, than that angels without bodies could have descended to that sin. 

It continues:

## (Verse 3)

“God also said: ‘My spirit shall not remain in human beings forever, because they are flesh; their days shall be one hundred and twenty years.’ The giants were on the earth in those days.”

They had been made by the Spirit of God as angels and sons of God, but by turning toward lower things they are called human beings by the name of nature, not of grace. They are also called flesh: deserters from the spirit, and, by deserting, themselves deserted.

When God said, “Their days shall be one hundred and twenty years,” this should not be understood as though it had been foretold that thereafter human beings would not exceed one hundred and twenty years of life, since even after the Flood we find some who lived beyond five hundred years.

Rather, we should understand God to have said this when Noah was near the end of his five hundredth year—that is, when he was four hundred and eighty years old—[[Col. 0925C]] whom Scripture, according to its custom, calls five hundred, often designating the greater part by the name of the whole. 

For the Flood occurred in the six hundredth year of Noah’s life, in the second month. Thus the one hundred and twenty years were foretold for the future life of human beings who were going to perish; when those years had elapsed, they would be destroyed by the Flood.

Or alternatively, as it is found in Hebrew:

“My spirit shall not judge righteous human beings forever, because they are flesh.”

That is: because the human condition is fragile, I shall not preserve them from eternal punishment; rather, here I shall repay them according to what they deserve.

Thus the statement, as it appears in our books, does not express God’s severity but his clemency, since the sinner is punished for his crime in this life.

Moreover, lest God seem cruel for not having given sinners an opportunity for repentance, he added: “But their days shall be one hundred and twenty years”—that is, they shall have one hundred and twenty years in which to practice repentance.

Human life, therefore, is not confined to one hundred and twenty years, as many mistakenly think. Rather, one hundred and twenty years were given to that generation for repentance, since we find that after the Flood [[Col. 0925D]] Abraham lived one hundred and seventy-five years.

God did not choose to wait for the appointed period. Instead, cutting twenty years from it, he brought on the Flood in the six-hundredth year, which had been set apart for repentance. 

It continues.

## (Verse 4)

“The giants were on the earth in those days.”

These words of the divine book clearly indicate that giants were already on the earth in those days when the sons of God took wives from the daughters of human beings.

It continues:

“For after the sons of God had gone in to the daughters of human beings, and they had borne children, these were the mighty men from of old, famous men.”

After this had happened, the giants were born. For Scripture says: “The giants were on the earth in those days,” when they loved the women because they were beautiful. Another translation calls them not beautiful but good—that is, good in bodily appearance—and calls them “good.”

When Scripture says, “And they generated,” or “begot for themselves,” it sufficiently shows that before the sons of God fell in this way, they generated for God, [[Col. 0926A]] not for themselves; that is, not under the domination of the lust for intercourse, but in the service of the duty of propagation. They were not producing a family for their own pride, but citizens of the city of God. 

Nor is it surprising that giants could also be born from them. For not all people were giants, but there were certainly more of them at that time than in the later periods after the Flood. The Creator chose to create them so that it might also be shown by this example that the beauty, size, and strength of bodies are not to be highly valued by the wise.

## (Verses 5 and following)

“God saw that the wickedness of human beings was great upon the earth and that every intention of their heart was directed toward evil at all times. The Lord regretted that he had made human beings upon the earth, and, touched inwardly by grief of heart, he said: ‘I will destroy the human being whom I created from the face of the earth, from human being to animals, from creeping things to the birds of the sky; for I regret that I made them.’”

For God does not regret any of his works in the same way as a human being, since his judgment concerning all things is as fixed as his foreknowledge is certain. [[Col. 0926B]] Nevertheless, Scripture also says, in figurative language, that God regretted something.

It speaks according to what human hope had expected, or what the order of natural causes was carrying toward completion, not according to what the Almighty had foreknown that he would do.

If Scripture did not use such expressions, it would not in a certain sense make itself more familiar to every kind of human being. Scripture wishes to provide for them: it punishes the proud, arouses the negligent, exercises those who seek, and nourishes those who understand. It would not do this unless it first bent down and, in a manner of speaking, descended to those who lie below.

“God saw,” it says, “that the wickedness of human beings had multiplied upon the earth and that every thought of their heart was directed toward evil at all times. The Lord regretted that he had made the human being upon the earth.”

God’s regret is the unchanging reason for changing things. 

When he announces the destruction of all terrestrial animals and birds, he is expressing the magnitude of the future disaster. He is not threatening irrational creatures with destruction as though they themselves had sinned. 

It continues:

[[Col. 0926C]] ## (Verses 8 and following)

“But Noah found grace before the Lord. Noah was a righteous and perfect man in his generations.”

If no one is without sin, how can anyone be perfect? Only because some are called perfect here, not in the way the saints will be perfected in that immortality in which they will be made equal to the angels of God, but in the way that perfection can exist in this pilgrimage through sin.

“He walked with God”—that is, he followed God’s footsteps.

God said to Noah: “The end of all flesh has come before me; for the earth is filled with iniquity.”

This signifies the destruction of all mortals except those who were to be saved in the ark. They were therefore preserved as the seedbed of a second origin.

Nor is it without reason that the Flood is believed to have occurred when no one remained on earth who was not worthy of dying such a death, by which vengeance was taken upon the wicked. This is not because such a death could harm the good, who would in any event die, after death; nevertheless, none of those whom Holy Scripture records as descended from Seth died in the Flood.

[[Col. 0926D]] When God says, “And I will destroy them with the earth,” how are human beings said to have perished with the earth, since, once they had perished, the material of the earth remained afterward? The statement must mean that the appearance, vigor, or fertility of the earth was left far inferior after the Flood to what it had possessed before.

Perhaps this is why permission was later granted to human beings to eat meat, since before the Flood they lived only on the fruits of the earth. 

It continues:

## (Verse 14)

“Make an ark for yourself from smoothed wood.”

What is meant by the smoothed wood from which the ark is commanded to be made, if not strong and durable wood? Hence another translation commands that it be made not from smoothed wood but from squared wood, so that the ark could not be broken apart or overturned either by the force of winds or by the inundation of waters.

It continues:

“And you shall coat it with bitumen.”

Bitumen is an extremely hot and powerful adhesive. Its virtue is such that wood coated with it cannot be eaten by worms, nor dissolved by the heat of the sun, the blowing of winds, [[Col. 0927A]] or the continual action of water. 

It continues:

## (Verse 15)

“The length of the ark shall be three hundred cubits, its width fifty cubits, and its height thirty cubits.”

We should understand the shape of the ark in this way: its four sides rose from the bottom toward the top, gradually narrowing until they were gathered at the summit into a space of one cubit. At the foundation it was three hundred cubits long, fifty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high. It narrowed toward the top so that the uppermost point was one cubit in length and width.

No shape could have been more suitable and appropriate for an ark. From its narrow summit, like a roof with a peaked ridge, it could disperse the force of the rain. At the bottom, resting upon the waters with the stability of a square foundation, it could neither be tilted nor submerged by the force of winds, the violence of waves, or the restlessness of the animals inside it.

Some also customarily object that the ark could not have held [[Col. 0927B]] so many kinds of animals in both sexes—two of the unclean and seven of the clean. They seem to count only three hundred cubits in length and fifty in width, without considering that there was an equal amount above, and yet another equal amount above that.

Thus, with those cubits reckoned threefold, the height becomes ninety cubits and the width one hundred and fifty.

If we consider what Origen constructed with some elegance—namely, that Moses, a learned man of God, “instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians” (Acts 7), who loved geometry, intended to indicate geometrical cubits, each of which, they assert, was equal to six of ours—who cannot see how much that enormous structure could contain?

Those who argue that an ark of such a size could not have been joined together make a most foolish objection, since they know that immense cities have been built. They also fail to consider the one hundred years during which that ark was constructed. 

Unless, perhaps, stone can adhere to stone, joined only by mortar, [[Col. 0927C]] so that a wall may extend around through many thousands, while wood cannot adhere to wood when cemented and fastened with nails and bitumen in order to construct an ark extending far and wide in straight rather than curved lines. 

No human effort launched it into the sea. Rather, the waves lifted it when, according to the natural order of weights, it came upon them, and divine providence governed it as it floated more than human skill could have done, so that it would not suffer shipwreck anywhere.

It continues:

## (Verse 16)

“You shall make a window in the ark, and you shall complete it to a cubit at the top. You shall place the door of the ark in its side below. You shall make compartments and three tiers in it.”

He commands that a window be made at the top of the ark so that Noah would have a means by which he could send out birds to investigate whether the earth had become dry.

The door of the ark, which is said to have been made in its side, should be understood to have been placed in such a way that it provided access to the lower sections, which he called two-compartment sections. The upper sections, which he called three-compartment sections, were named from the location of the door.

All the animals entered through the door and were separated into their respective places according to an appropriate arrangement of compartments and tiers. 

[[Col. 0927D]] Another translation wished to call these structures “two-compartment” and “three-compartment,” so that we understand there to have been five distinct dwelling places in the ark:

1. the lower places, assigned to excrement, so that the animals—and especially human beings—would not be troubled by the stench of dung;

2. the section above and adjoining these, divided into two compartments and assigned to the preservation or stabling of the animals;

3. the upper sections, divided into three compartments and assigned first to wild beasts, fiercer animals, or serpents;

4. the appropriate places above these, which served as stalls for gentler animals;

5. the highest place, assigned to birds and human beings.

Thus, just as wisdom surpasses everything, so the human being would surpass all animals. We are therefore to understand that there were five dwellings in the same ark: the first for excrement, the second for storage, the third for wild animals, the fourth for tame animals, and the fifth for human beings. 

[[Col. 0928A]] ## (Chapter 7—Verses 1 and following)

God commands Noah to bring into the ark pairs of clean and unclean animals, male and female; pairs of birds according to their kinds; pairs of cattle according to their kinds; and pairs of every creeping thing of the earth according to its kind.

Afterward he adds:

“Of the clean animals you shall take seven and seven, male and female; but of the animals that are not clean, two and two, male and female; and of the birds of the sky, seven and seven, male and female.”

He does not say two and two on account of the number four, but only two on account of male and female. And he says seven of the clean animals alone.

He placed the unclean in an even number for the preservation of their kind, but the clean in an odd number so that Noah would have animals from which to offer sacrifices to God. Or perhaps there were more clean animals than unclean because of the future use owed to humanity by the clean animals, so that there would be more that benefited than harmed.

A question is often raised with great precision concerning [[Col. 0928B]] the smallest creatures—not only such as mice and geckos, but also locusts, beetles, flies, and even fleas. Were there more of them in the ark than the number defined when God gave this command?

Those troubled by this question should first be advised to understand the statement, “Whatever creeps upon the earth,” in such a way that it was not necessary to preserve in the ark creatures that can live in water—not only when submerged, like fish, but also when floating upon it, like many winged creatures. 

Further, when it says, “Male and female shall be,” it clearly means that they were to be brought in for the renewal of the species. Consequently, it was not necessary for those creatures to be there that can be born without intercourse from the corruption of various things.

If creatures commonly found in houses were present, they could have been there without any fixed number. Or, if the most sacred mystery then being enacted, and so great a figure, could not otherwise be fulfilled through the reality of the event unless everything that could not live in water were present in that definite number, [[Col. 0928C]] this was not the concern of Noah or of human beings, but of God.

Noah did not capture these creatures and bring them inside. He merely allowed them to enter when they came. This is the force of the statement, “They shall enter to you”: not by human action, but by God’s will.

It should nevertheless be understood that creatures lacking sex were not to be believed to have been there, since it is prescribed and defined: “Male and female shall be.”

Some creatures are born from various things without intercourse in such a way that afterward they themselves engage in intercourse and reproduce, like flies. Others contain nothing of male and female, like bees.

As for creatures that have sex but do not produce offspring, such as mules, it is surprising if they were there. Would it not have been enough for their parents to be there—the horse and ass kinds—and any other animals that produce a kind through the mixing of different species? But if this too belonged to the mystery, they were there, since this kind too has male and female.

Some people are also troubled by the kinds of food the animals could have had there, [[Col. 0928D]] especially those thought to live only on meat. Were provisions for them included beyond the prescribed number, without violating the command, because the need to feed other animals required their presence? Or, as should rather be believed, could there have been foods other than meat that suited them all?

We know how many animals whose food is flesh also eat grain and fruit, especially figs and chestnuts. What wonder is it, then, if that wise and righteous man, divinely instructed about what was suitable for each creature, prepared and stored appropriate food for every kind without meat?

What is there that hunger could not compel an animal to eat? Or what could God not make pleasant or healthful, since by divine power he could even have enabled them to live without food—unless the fact that they were fed also served to fulfill the figure of so great a mystery?

Some think that so great a Flood could not have occurred that the waters rose fifteen cubits above the highest mountains, [[Col. 0929A]] because of the summit of Mount Olympus, above which clouds are said not to be able to form. They say that the heavens are already so high there that the denser air in which winds, mists, and fires are generated is absent.

They fail to consider that the thickest of all the elements, earth, could have been present there. Or do they perhaps deny that there is earth on the summit of a mountain?

Why, then, do they contend that earth could be raised through those regions of the sky but that water could not, when these measurers and weighers of the elements declare that water is above earth and lighter than earth?

What reason, then, do they offer for saying that heavier and lower earth invaded the place of the calmer sky through the passage of so many years, while lighter and higher water was not permitted to do this, at least for a short time?

It may also be asked why, when the human beings entered the ark, the men and women are mentioned separately, whereas when they left the ark God said to Noah:

“Go out, you and your wife, your sons and your sons’ wives with them.”

The reason is perhaps that, while the world had been condemned and the entire race of mortals was perishing, those alone who had been delivered from danger ceased from intercourse [[Col. 0929B]] until the ark came to rest and the destructive waters subsided. Then they returned again to what marriage owes to the body, so that they might increase and multiply upon the earth. Thus, at their entrance they are named separately, but at their departure they are named as joined in marriage.

From Adam to the Flood, according to the edition of the Septuagint translators, 2,262 years are calculated; according to the Hebrew text, 1,656.

It continues:

## (Chapter 8—Verse 1)

“God remembered Noah, and all the animals and all the cattle that were with him in the ark.”

There is never forgetfulness in God, so that he should remember something he had forgotten. Rather, the writer used “remembered” to mean “showed mercy.”

It continues:

“He brought a spirit over the earth, and the waters diminished.”

This may properly be understood of the spirit concerning which it was said: “The Spirit of God was borne over the waters” (Gen. 1). Then the Spirit was borne over them so that, when the waters had been gathered into their place, the earth might appear. Now the spirit is said to have been brought forth so that, [[Col. 0929C]] when the waters of the Flood had been removed , it might reveal the face of the earth.

The word “spirit” may also be understood as “wind,” in accordance with the Psalmist’s statement: “He spoke, and the spirit of the storm stood still” (Ps. 106). Through its repeated gusts, the water was forced to withdraw from the earth.

It continues:

(Vers. 3.) The waters returned from the earth, going and returning. Where did the waters return, going and returning, except that all the courses of rivers and streams return through the hidden veins of the earth to the womb of the abyss, according to Solomon’s statement: “The rivers return to the place from which they flow, so that they may flow again” (Eccles. 1). But one may ask why the dove brought back in its beak, toward evening, an olive branch with green leaves, unless it was because, after the crimes of the world had in some manner been expiated by the flood, it displayed the grace of the divine gift through an outpouring likeness, and by the olive branch announced that peace had been restored to the earth through refreshment and light.

Behold, as we have been able and as the Lord has granted, we have attempted to explain something about the construction of the ark according to the historical sense. Now, however, let us spread the sails of spiritual understanding, and let spiritual [Col. 0929D] understanding raise above heaven what the water lifted from the earth.

God commands Noah to make an ark from incorruptible wood; so also the Church is built by Christ from all the nations that are destined to live forever. For that ark signified the Church, which floats upon the waves of this world. Thus Noah, together with all his own—namely, his wife, sons, and daughters-in-law—and with the animals that, at God’s command, entered the ark with him in order to be delivered from the devastation of the flood, is without doubt a figure of the pilgrim City of God in this world, that is, the Church, which is saved through the wood on which hung the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus.

The fact that the same ark was made from squared timbers signifies on every side the steadfast life of the saints, prepared for every good work; for wherever you push a square object, you find it standing firm. Its length being six times its width and ten times its height displays the likeness of the human body, because Christ appeared in a human body. Indeed, the very measure of its length, height, and width signifies the human body, in the reality of which he was foretold as coming to human beings, and did come. For the length of the human body from the crown of the head to the feet is six times as great as the width from one side to the other, and ten times as great as the height, the measure of which is taken from the back to the belly. Thus, if you measure a person lying on his back or front, he is six times as long from head to feet as he is wide from right to left or from left to right, and ten times as long as he is high above the ground.

The fact that its width is extended to fifty cubits signifies, as the Apostle says, “Our heart has been enlarged” (2 Cor. 6)—by what, except spiritual charity? For this reason he likewise says, “The love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5). On the fiftieth day after his resurrection Christ sent the Holy Spirit, by whom he enlarged the hearts of believers.

Thus the ark was made three hundred cubits long, fifty [Col. 0930A] wide, and thirty high. Its length is three hundred cubits so that six times fifty may be completed, just as the whole period of this world extends through six ages, in all of which Christ never ceased to be proclaimed: in the first five he was foretold through prophecy, and in the sixth he was proclaimed through the Gospel.

That its height rises to thirty cubits, a number contained ten times in the three hundred cubits of its length, signifies that Christ is our height. At the age of thirty he consecrated the teaching of the Gospel, testifying that he had not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it (Matt. 5). The heart of the Law is recognized in the Ten Commandments. Hence the length of the ark is completed by ten times thirty cubits. For this reason Noah himself is counted as the tenth from Adam.

The fact that the ark’s timbers were joined on the inside with bitumen signifies the endurance of charity in the bond of unity, so that, when scandals assail the Church—whether from those within or from those outside—the fraternal joint may not give way and the bond of peace be broken. Bitumen is a very hot and forceful adhesive, signifying the ardor of love, which, through the great strength of fortitude, endures everything in order to preserve spiritual fellowship.

The fact that every kind of animal was enclosed in the ark signifies likewise all the nations, which are also represented by that sheet shown to Peter and contained by the Church. The fact that clean and unclean animals were there signifies that both good and evil people are found within the Church’s sacraments. The fact that there were seven of the clean and two of the unclean does not mean that the wicked are fewer than the good, but that the good preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.

Holy Scripture commends the Holy Spirit in a sevenfold operation: wisdom and understanding, counsel and strength, knowledge and piety, and fear of God. Hence that number of fifty days associated with the coming of the Holy Spirit is completed in seven times seven, which makes forty-nine, with one added. For this reason it is said, “Strive to preserve the unity in the bond of peace” (Eph. 4).

The wicked, however, are shown by the number two to be prone to schisms and, in a certain sense, divisible. Noah himself is counted as the eighth with his companions, because in Christ the hope of our resurrection appeared. He rose from the dead on the eighth day—that is, after the seventh day of the Sabbath, on the first day—although this was the third day after his passion; in the sequence of days that revolve throughout all time, it is both the eighth and the first.

The fact that the ark, gathered together above, was completed at one cubit signifies likewise that the Church, which is the body of Christ, is exalted and perfected when gathered into unity. Hence he says in the Gospel, “Whoever does not gather with me scatters” (Matt. 12).

The fact that it received a door in its side clearly signifies the wound made when Christ’s side was pierced by the lance. Through this opening those who come to him enter, because from it flowed the sacraments by which believers are initiated. No one enters the Church except through the sacrament of the forgiveness of sins, which flowed from Christ’s opened side.

The fact that the lower parts of the ark were constructed with two and three chambers, so that a third habitation rose upward from the bottom, has this meaning: it is called two-chambered because of the two kinds of people, namely circumcision and uncircumcision, whom the Apostle elsewhere calls Jews and Greeks (Rom. 1). It is called three-chambered because all the nations were restored after the flood from Noah’s three sons.

Here too those three things commended by the Apostle may be understood: faith, hope, and charity. More suitably still, the three evangelical yields may be understood: thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and a hundredfold, so that in the lowest place conjugal chastity dwells, above it widowhood, and higher still virginity.

For this reason the lower parts of the ark are so called: in this earthly life there is a diversity of nations, but at the summit all are perfected into one, and there is no diversity, because “Christ is all and in all,” perfecting us in one cubit above through heavenly unity.

The fact that the flood occurred seven days after Noah entered the ark signifies that we are baptized in the hope of the future rest, which was signified by the seventh day.

The fact that, apart from the ark, every living creature sustained by the earth was consumed by the flood signifies that, outside fellowship with the Church, the water of baptism, although it is the same water, not only does not avail for salvation but rather avails for destruction.

The fact that it rained for forty days and forty nights signifies that every guilt of sin admitted against the Ten Commandments throughout the whole world—which is contained in four regions, since ten multiplied by four makes forty—is washed away by the sacrament of heavenly baptism. Whether that guilt belongs to the days, contracted through prosperity, or to the nights, contracted through adversity, it is washed away.

The fact that Noah was five hundred years old when the Lord spoke to him and ordered him to make an ark, and was six hundred years old when he entered it, indicates that the ark was built over one hundred years. What else do these hundred years seem to signify except the individual ages of the world? Thus this sixth age, represented by the period from the completion of five hundred years to six hundred, is understood to be built through the manifestation of the Gospel.

Therefore, whoever takes thought for his salvation should be like a squared [Col. 0931C] piece of wood, prepared for every good work, and should enter the holy structure. For the second month of the six-hundredth year, in which Noah entered the ark, signifies the same sixth age. Two months are contained in the number sixty; from the number six come sixty, six hundred, six thousand, sixty thousand, six hundred thousand, six hundred times, and whatever further numbers rise through the same progression in infinite increase.

The fact that twenty-seven days of the month are mentioned pertains to the significance of that same squareness, already explained through the squared timbers. Here it is clearer still, because the Trinity makes us ready for every good work—that is, in a certain sense, makes us square—in memory, by which we remember God; understanding, by which we know him; and will, by which we love him. For three times three, and that again three times, makes twenty-seven, which is the square of the ternary number.

The fact that the ark came to rest in the seventh month—that is, rested—points back to that seventh rest in which the perfected rest. There too the number of that squareness is repeated. For on the twenty-seventh day of the second month this mystery was commended, and again on the twenty-seventh day of the seventh month the same commendation was confirmed when the ark came to rest. What is promised in hope is displayed in reality, because that seventh rest is joined to the eighth resurrection. Rest does not end when the body is restored, for after this life it receives the saints; rather, the whole person—no longer in hope but already in reality, perfected in every part of spirit and body—is renewed in immortal salvation and received into the gift of eternal life.

Since, then, the seventh rest is joined to the eighth resurrection, this is a deep and profound mystery in the sacrament of our regeneration, that is, in baptism. The fact that the water rose fifteen cubits, exceeding the height of the mountains, signifies that this sacrament transcends all the wisdom of the proud. For seven and eight joined together make fifteen. And because seventy is named from seven and eighty from eight, when both numbers are joined the water was raised for one hundred and fifty days, commending and confirming for us the same height of baptism, in consecrating the new person for holding fast the faith of rest and resurrection. It is too lengthy to touch upon everything, even as briefly as I have hurried through these matters: why in the six-hundred-first year of Noah’s life, that is, after six hundred years had been completed, the roof of the ark was opened, as though the hidden mystery were being revealed; why on the twenty-seventh day of the second month the earth is said to have dried, [Col. 0932C] as though the necessity of baptism had ended, in the number of days fifty-seven—for that is the twenty-seventh day of the second month, a number composed of seven times eight, with one added because of the bond of unity; and why those who entered separately, men separately and women separately, emerge from the ark joined together.

Noah and his wife, his sons and the wives of his sons, emerge; males and females are now mentioned together because at the end of the world, and in the resurrection of the righteous, the body will cling to the spirit in complete and perfect peace, with no need or desire of mortality resisting.

The sequence follows:

(Vers. 20, 21.) “Noah built an altar to the Lord, and taking from all the clean cattle and clean birds, he offered burnt offerings upon the altar, and the Lord smelled the fragrance of sweetness.”

If God had made everything good, and even very good, what does it mean that Noah took from all the clean cattle and birds and offered burnt offerings? Nothing was created unclean in its nature; rather, by comparison with something better, what is good in its own nature is considered, as it were, unclean.

The construction of the altar is to be understood as a confession of the holy Trinity, concerning which the Lord, ascending to heaven, instructed the apostles, saying, “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you” (Matt., end).

Upon this altar of faith he took from every clean animal and every clean bird and offered holy sacrifices pleasing to the Lord, the rational service of the saints. By the clean animal are signified those who live simply in the Church and retain a sense of innocence, possessing no bite of malice. By the clean bird are understood those who meditate on the law of the Lord day and night (Ps. 1), who can say with the Apostle, “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3). This does not mean that they were naturally clean, since they were conceived in iniquities and born in sins, but that, having been reborn from water and the Holy Spirit, they are rightly called clean; and thus afterward they were offered to God the Father upon the altar of faith, having been put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit.

“And the Lord smelled the fragrance of sweetness.” God is not pleased by the smell of flesh or by the irrational blood of animals—for he plainly testified through the prophet Isaiah that he had never sought such things—but “he smelled” means that he was pleased by the conversion of the human race to him and by the salvation of believers.

The sequence follows:

“Never again will I curse the earth because of human beings, for the sense and thought of the human heart are inclined to evil from his youth. Therefore I will never again strike every living creature as I have done.”

For after the resurrection, vices and sins will no longer rule over bodies, nor will bodies be subject to corruption and death. After the resurrection they will be changed for glory and will receive incorruption and immortality.

The sequence follows:

(Cap. IX.—Vers. 1 ff.) “And God blessed Noah and his sons, and said to them: Increase and multiply, and fill the earth; and let your terror and dread be upon all the animals of the earth and upon all the birds of heaven, together with everything that moves upon the earth.”

Since terror and dread of them are commanded to be upon the animals of the earth, they are certainly forbidden to be upon human beings. Human nature has been placed above brute animals, not above other human beings; and therefore he is told to be feared by animals, not by human beings. For it is contrary to nature to be arrogant, to wish to be feared by one’s equal.

The sequence follows:

“All the fish of the sea have been delivered into your hand, and everything that moves and lives shall be food for you. Just as I gave you all the green plants, so I give you everything, except that you shall not eat flesh with its blood.”

He did not permit carrion as food for human use, because the flesh of animals that have not been killed but have died is diseased and unsuitable for the health of the body, for whose sake we take nourishment.

But the command imposed by the apostles upon the Gentiles in the Acts of the Apostles—that the Gentiles should abstain only from fornication, from things sacrificed to idols, and from blood (Acts 15)—means that they should not eat flesh whose blood had not been poured out. Others understand it differently: namely, that no one should defile himself by homicide. In any case, whether by this interpretation or by another, Christians could not exist merely by observing these matters. For who does not know that Noah and his sons signified Jesus Christ and his preachers, who received from God the Father a blessing in the heavenly places, with every spiritual blessing?

They were commanded to increase and multiply when, as if emerging from the ark, they were dispersed from Jerusalem and Judea and commanded, as it were, to enter the earth, while they were ordered to go into the world and preach the Gospel to every creature. Then they increased spiritually through sons, namely holy disciples and a large multitude of other believers.

Their terror and dread were upon all the animals of the earth—that is, upon the nations, which lived in the world in the manner of irrational cattle or animals—and upon all the [Col. 0933D] birds of heaven, namely the wise men of the world, who, while trying to debate about the creatures or elements of heaven and earth, seemed, like birds, to fly into heaven.

At that time the fish of the sea were also delivered into their hand, when all who were curious and pursued worldly actions, and who, while stripping the weak and little ones who could not defend themselves, devoured them as fish do, later, at the preaching of the apostles, began to give even their own possessions, although previously they had seized those belonging to others.

That saying was fulfilled which the prophet had earlier sung concerning them: “He subjected peoples to us, and nations beneath our feet.” And, “Everything that moves and lives shall be food for you; just as I gave you all the green plants” (Ps. 46): that is, the one who is from circumcision will be received into the faith in the same way as the one who is from the nations, just as it was also said to Peter: “Rise, Peter; kill and eat” (Acts 10).

When he refused, saying that he had never eaten anything common or unclean, he was told: “What God has purified, you must not call common.” That is, those whom God, through the Spirit of sanctification, by remitting their former sins, has transformed by free mercy from vessels of wrath into vessels of mercy—you must not reject as though they were unclean.

“Except that you shall not eat flesh with its blood”: that is, you must not receive them into the faith together with their former sin. Rather, like water, they must pour it out through confession in the sight of the Lord, or at least hide it in the earth—in their own flesh, namely, from which it arose—and put it to death.

But because, while they were doing these things among the nations, they were destined to suffer persecution from unbelievers, words of consolation immediately follow:

“For I will require the blood of your lives from the hand of every beast.” The soul, which is incorporeal by nature, does not have blood, nor will brute and irrational beasts at some time render an account to God for every deed. By “the blood of the soul,” therefore, he wished to indicate the life of the flesh.

Here we should understand the beasts as persecutors from the nations, who exercised their malice like beasts against the saints of God. By adding, “from the hand of man,” he wished to indicate the same persecutors both from the Jews and from the nations, since by nature they are human beings but by their savagery they are beasts.

Then he continues: “From the hand of man and of his brother I will require the life of man.”

Without abandoning the historical meaning, according to which God the just judge repays each person according to his works, and following the allegorical order begun above, we should understand by the human being, as a rational man and brother of the holy preachers—that is, of the apostles and their companions—the Jews, who came from one father and descended from Abraham’s lineage. They cast those same holy preachers out of the synagogue, and, while killing or persecuting them, thought that they were rendering service to God.

To them the Lord promises—that is, to the persecutors from the nations, like irrational beasts, and to the human beings, namely the Jews, who, as though using reason, seemed to themselves to persecute the apostles according to the Law—that although both persecuted them unjustly, both would be punished by a just judgment.

(Vers. 6.) “Whoever sheds human blood, his blood shall be shed.”

Here he wished to indicate the saints by “human beings,” since they are rational. For what else does it mean to say, “Whoever sheds human blood, his blood shall be shed,” than this? It is as though he were saying plainly: Whoever unjustly inflicts temporal death upon them will be punished by eternal death, that is, condemnation.

“For human beings were made in the image of God.” Indeed, those were created in the image of God who strive each day to put to death their members that are upon the earth (Col. 3) and to be renewed in the spirit of their mind, which was created according to God (Eph. 4); they put away falsehood and speak truth to their neighbors, with whom they are members of one another.

The sequence follows:

(Vers. 7.) “But you, increase and multiply, enter upon the earth, and fill it.”

These are words of exhortation to the same holy preachers, that, setting aside the fear by which the body is killed while the soul suffers no harm, they may increase either in virtues or by multiplying the number of believers; that they may enter upon the earth by preaching, fill it by teaching, and make the marvelous name of Christ known throughout the whole earth. For when the knowledge, faith, or worship of God did not yet exist among human beings, the earth was like a deserted and uninhabitable place without a cultivator.

The sequence follows:

(Vers. 12.) “And God said: This is the sign of the covenant that I establish between me and you: I will place my bow in the clouds, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and the earth. When I cover the sky with clouds, my bow will appear in the clouds, and I will remember my covenant that I made with you.”

The bow was placed in the sky as a sign of security, so that it could be seen by everyone. This sign itself is displayed in fire and water, because part of it is blue and part red, since it bears witness to both judgments: one already enacted and the other yet to be enacted.

God established this covenant between himself and human beings, and every living soul, so that he would not destroy it by a flood. The bow that appears in the clouds shines only from the sun. Those who recognize Christ’s glory in the prophets and in all the divine Scriptures, as in the clouds of God, and do not seek their own glory, do not perish in the flood, though separated from the Church.

Human life is completed in six ages: the first is infancy, the second childhood, the third adolescence, the fourth youth, the fifth old age, and the sixth extreme old age, which alone is terminated by death. Thus this world too is to be completed in six ages. Its first age was from Adam to the flood, corresponding to infancy, which was so called because one cannot yet speak. That age is the first to be submerged in forgetfulness, just as the first age of the human race was blotted out by the flood. Thus now the book of our work must also be brought to an end.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 0935]

[Col. 0935A] The second age of the world, from Noah to Abraham himself, was like childhood. After the flood a new world appeared, as it were the second age of the human race; so also, with God’s help, a second book must now be begun.

The sequence follows:

(Vers. 20, 21.) “And Noah, a man who cultivated the earth, began to work the soil, and he planted a vineyard. When he drank wine, he became drunk, and he was uncovered in his tent.”

Why was the righteous man drunk, unless perhaps he did not know that one could become drunk from wine? For before the flood human beings are not recorded as using wine. Therefore it is specifically written of Noah: “Noah planted a vineyard.”

“The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel.” He drank from its wine. Or perhaps the cup should be understood here, concerning which the same Lord says, “Can you drink the cup that I am about to drink?” (Mark 10), and, “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. 26), by which he undoubtedly signifies his passion.

Or, since wine is the fruit of the vine, this rather was signified by it: that from that very vine—that is, from the race of the Israelites—he assumed flesh and blood for us, so that he could suffer. “And he became drunk,” that is, he suffered. There he was uncovered, that is, his weakness appeared, concerning which the Apostle says, “And although he was crucified from weakness” (2 Cor. 13). Hence he likewise says, “The weakness of God is stronger than human beings, and the foolishness of God is wiser than human beings” (1 Cor. 1).

When it had been said, “And he was uncovered,” Scripture added, “In his house,” elegantly showing that he was destined to suffer crucifixion and death from the people of his own flesh and from his own blood relations, namely the Jews.

The sequence follows:

(Vers. 22, 23.) “When Cham, the father of Canaan, saw that the nakedness of his father had been exposed, he reported it outside to his two brothers. But Sem and Japhet placed a cloak upon their shoulders, and, walking backward, covered the nakedness of their father; their faces were turned away, so that they did not see their father’s private parts.”

Accordingly, in the two sons, the eldest and the youngest, two peoples are represented: circumcision and uncircumcision. Carrying one garment behind them—the sacrament, namely, of the Lord’s passion, which had already taken place—they do not look upon their father’s nakedness, because they do not consent to Christ’s death; yet they honor him by the covering, as though they knew from whom they had been born.

The middle son, however—that is, the Jewish people—is called middle because it held neither primacy among the apostles nor the last place in believing among the nations. He saw the nakedness of his father because he consented to Christ’s death, and he reported it outside to his brothers. Through him what had been hidden in prophecy was made known and, in a certain sense, made public. Therefore he becomes the servant of his brothers.

For what else is that nation even today except a kind of archive of the Christians, carrying the Law and the Prophets as testimony to the Church’s claim, so that we honor them through the sacrament that it announces through the letter?

The sequence follows:

(Vers. 24 ff.) “But Noah awoke from the wine. When he learned what his younger son had done to him, he said: Cursed be Canaan; he shall be a servant of servants to his brothers. And he said: Blessed be the Lord, the God of Sem; let Canaan be his servant. May God enlarge Japhet, and may he dwell in the tents of Sem.”

It is asked why Cham, who sinned by offending his father, is cursed not in himself but in his son Canaan. The reason is that it was prophesied that, after the Canaanites had been expelled from that land and defeated, the sons of Israel, who came from the seed of Sem, would receive it. This was seen and foreseen as something that would happen far in the future.

Hence it also came about that he cursed the middle son—the younger than the firstborn but older than the last—who had sinned against his father, not in the son himself but in his son, his grandson, with these words: “Cursed be Canaan; let him be a servant to his brothers.”

Canaan had been born from Cham, who had not covered the nakedness of his sleeping father but rather [Col. 0936B] exposed it. Therefore he immediately adds the blessing of the two sons, the eldest and the youngest, saying: “Blessed be the Lord, the God of Sem; Canaan shall be his servant. May God enlarge Japhet, and may he dwell in the tents of Sem.”

Although God is the God of all nations, in a certain sense he is nevertheless called “Israel” by a proper name even among those nations. And whence did this come except from the blessing of Japhet? For in the people of the nations the Church has occupied the whole world.

This was precisely foretold when it was said: “May God enlarge Japhet, and may he dwell in the tents of Sem.” Sem, from whose seed Christ was made incarnate, is interpreted as “named” or “renowned.” And what is more renowned than Christ, whose name now resounds everywhere, so that in the Song of Songs, even in the prophecy that precedes it, he is compared to poured-out ointment (Song 1)? In his houses, that is, in the churches, the breadth of the nations dwells, for Japhet is interpreted as “breadth.”

Behold how God enlarges Japhet and makes him dwell in the tents of Sem—that is, in the churches that the apostles, the sons of the prophets, built.
