Accordingly, the Apostle Paul says to the faithful from the nations: “At that time you were without Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, strangers to the covenants and to the promise, having no hope of the promise and being without God in this world” (Eph. 2).

These words show that Japhet did not yet dwell in the houses of Sem. But let us observe how he concludes shortly afterward: “Therefore,” he says, “you are no longer strangers and sojourners, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household, built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the chief cornerstone” (ibid.).

Cham, whose name is interpreted as “cunning,” the middle son of Noah, as though distinguishing himself from both and remaining between them, belonging neither to the first fruits of the Israelites nor to the fullness of the nations—what does he signify except the cunning class of heretics, not endowed with the spirit of wisdom, by which the beginnings of heretics are wont to burn and disturb the peace of the saints? [The transmitted wording is syntactically uncertain.]

Many matters pertaining to the Catholic faith, while they are attacked by the cunning restlessness of heretics so that they may be defended against them, are considered more diligently, understood more clearly, preached more earnestly, and, when an adversary raises a question, become an occasion for learning.

Although not only those who are most openly separated, but all who boast of the Christian name while living destructively, may not unreasonably be seen as figured by Noah’s middle son: they proclaim by confession the passion of Christ, signified by that man’s nakedness, but dishonor it by their evil conduct.

Of such people it was said: “You will know them by their fruits” (Matt. 7). Therefore Cham is cursed in his son, as in his fruit, that is, in his work. Accordingly, his son Canaan is also suitably interpreted as “their movement.” For what else is this than their work?

Sem and Japhet, then, as circumcision and uncircumcision—or, as the Apostle calls them in another way, Jews and Greeks (Rom. 1)—but called and justified, recognizing in a certain sense the nakedness of their father, by which the Savior’s passion was signified, took a garment, placed it upon their backs, and entered turned away; they covered their father’s nakedness and did not see what they had covered out of reverence.

In Christ’s passion, in a certain sense, we honor what was done for us and turn away from the crime of the Jews. The garment signifies the sacrament; the backs signify the memory of past events, because, at the time when Japhet dwells in the houses of Sem and the evil brother is among them, the Church celebrates Christ’s passion as something completed and does not yet look toward what is future.

The evil brother, in his son—that is, in his work—is a child, or servant, of his brothers when the good, for the exercise of patience or the advancement of wisdom, knowingly make use of the wicked.

The sequence follows:

(Vers. 28, 29.) “Noah lived 350 years after the flood, and all the days of his life were 950 years, and he died.”

(Cap. X.—Vers. 1 ff.) “These are the generations of the sons of Noah: Sem, Cham, and Japhet. Sons were born to them after the flood.

“The sons of Japhet were Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Mosoch, and Thyras. These seven sons of Japhet possessed the land in Asia, from Amanus and the Taurus, the mountains of Coelesyria and Cilicia, as far as the river Tanais.

“The sons of Gomer were Aschenez, Riphat, and Togorma. The sons of Javan were Elisa, Tharsis, Cethim, and Dodanim. From these the islands of the nations were divided into their regions, each according to its language and its families in its nations.”

Leaving aside the names of the places and nations, many of which were later changed while the rest remain as they were, these are: Gomer, the Galatians; Magog, the Scythians; Madai, the Medes; Javan, the Ionians, who are also the Greeks, from whom the Ionian Sea is named; Tubal, the Iberians, who are also the Spaniards, from whom the Celtiberians were later named; Mosoch, the Cappadocians, whose city is still called Mazecha among them; and Thyras, the Thracians, whose name has not been greatly altered.

These seven nations, which I have said came from the stock of Japhet, inhabit the northern region.

“The sons of Gomer: Aschenez, Riphat, and Togorma.” Aschenez is what the Greeks call the Rheginians; Riphat, the Paphlagonians; Togorma, the Phrygians.

“The sons of Javan: Elisa, Tharsis, Cethim, and Dodanim.” Cethim are the Cittians, from whom the city of Cyprus is still called Cittium; Dodanim are the Rhodians.

Almost all the islands, the shores of the whole world, and the lands near the sea were occupied by Greek settlers. As we said above, from the mountains of Amanus and Taurus they possessed all the coastal regions as far as the British Ocean.

The sequence follows:

### (Verses 6–7)

The sons of Ham were Cush, Mesraim, Put, and Canaan. Cush is still called Ethiopia by the Hebrews; Mesraim is Egypt; Put is Libya, from whom the river of Mauretania is still called Put, and the whole surrounding region is called Putensis. Yet now the ancient name Libya remains only in one part of that climatic region, while the rest of the land is called Africa. Canaan, moreover, occupied the land which the Jews thereafter possessed, after expelling the Canaanites.

The sons of Cush were Seba, Havilah, Sabtah, Raamah, and Sabteca. Seba gave his name to the Sabaeans; Havilah to the Getulians, in the more remote part of Africa, adjoining the desert; Sabtah to the Sabatheni, who are now called Astavari. Raamah and Sabteca gradually lost their ancient names, and it is unknown what names they now bear in place of the old ones.

The sons of Seba are from the one from whom, as we said, the Sabaeans were named. Seba is now interpreted as Arabia. In Psalm 71, where we read, “The kings of the Arabians and of Seba shall offer gifts,” the Hebrew has, “The kings of Seba.” Dadai is a people of Ethiopia, in the western region. It follows:

### (Verses 8ff.)

Cush fathered Nimrod. He began to be powerful upon the earth, and was a mighty hunter before the Lord. From him arose the proverb: “Like Nimrod, a mighty hunter before the Lord.” Thus this giant is to be understood as a hunter against the Lord. What, then, is signified by the name “hunter,” except a deceiver, oppressor, and destroyer of the souls of earthly human beings? Therefore he is called a mighty hunter against the Lord, because he was drawing people away from the worship of God.

It follows: “The beginning of his kingdom was Babylon, and Erech, and Accad, and Calneh, in the land of Shinar.” Nimrod, the son of Cush, was the first among the peoples to seize the unprecedented power of tyranny, and he ruled in Babylon. It was called Babel because there the languages of those building the tower were confused. Babel means “confusion.”

Erech is the city of Edessa. Accad is now called Nisibis. Calneh was later renamed Seleucia after King Seleucus.

It follows:

### (Verses 11–12)

“From that land Assur went out and built Nineveh, and the streets of the city, and Calah; and Resen also, between Nineveh and Calah: this is the great city.”

The statement that Assur went out from the land of Shinar—which belonged to Nimrod’s kingdom—and built Nineveh and the other cities he constructed refers to something that happened much later. The author briefly introduced it on account of the renown of the Assyrian kingdom, which Ninus, son of Belus, greatly enlarged. Ninus was the founder of the great city Nineveh, whose name was derived from his own, so that it was called Nineveh from Ninus.

Assur, from whom the Assyrians took their name, was not among the sons of Ham but is found among the sons of Shem, who was Noah’s eldest son. It is therefore evident that those who later obtained that giant’s kingdom and proceeded from it, founding other cities, arose from the progeny of Shem.

It follows:

### (Verses 13–14)

“Mesraim fathered Ludim, Anamim, Lehabim, Naphtuhim, Pathrusim, and Casluhim, from whom came the Philistines and the Caphtorim.”

Except for the Lehabim—from whom the Libyans were later called, whereas previously they were called Putites—and the Casluhim, who thereafter were called Philistines, whom we incorrectly call Palestinians, the other six peoples are unknown to us. They were destroyed in the Ethiopian war and passed into oblivion together with their former names.

They occupied the land from Gaza to the farthest borders of Egypt.

It follows:

### (Verses 15ff.)

“Canaan fathered Sidon, his firstborn, and the Hittite, the Jebusite, the Amorite, the Girgashite, the Hivite, the Arkite, the Sinite, the Arvadite, the Zemarite, and the Hamathite.”

The firstborn of Canaan was Sidon, from whom the Phoenician city was called Sidon. The Arkite founded Arca, a town situated at the foot of Lebanon. The Arvadites are those who occupied the island of Aradus, separated from Phoenicia by a narrow strait. The Zemarites gave their name to Emesa, a renowned city of Coelesyria. The Macedonians who ruled after the death of Alexander called it Epiphanea.

“The territory of the Canaanites extended from Sidon as far as Gerar, and, going toward Gaza, as far as Sodom and Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim, as far as Lesha.” The other cities—namely Sidon, Gerar, Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim—are known by their own names.

Thus all the sons of Ham—that is, the middle son of Noah—amount to four, with five grandsons from one of his sons, and two great-grandsons from one grandson; their total is therefore eleven. After these have been enumerated, the account turns back to another son of Ham, called Mesraim, and lists those whom he fathered—not as individual men, but as seven peoples. From the sixth, as though from a sixth son, it records the people called the Philistines, making eight in all.

Then it turns back again to Canaan, in whom Ham was cursed, and names the eleven whom he fathered. Afterward, having mentioned the regions to which they extended, it says that, counting sons and grandsons, thirty-one descendants are recorded from the line of Ham.

It follows:

### (Verse 21)

“Children were also born to Shem, the father of all the sons of Eber and the elder brother of Japheth.”

It remains to commemorate the sons of Shem, Noah’s eldest son. The account, proceeding gradually through these generations, has reached him from the youngest branch. But the point at which Shem’s sons begin to be listed contains a certain obscurity, which must be clarified by explanation, since it is also highly relevant to the matter under consideration. The text reads:

“And to Shem was born Eber; Shem was the father of all the sons, the elder brother of Japheth.”

The order of the words is: “And Shem fathered Eber, who was the father of all the sons.” Thus Scripture intended Shem to be understood as the patriarch of all those who arose from his stock, whom it is about to mention, whether sons, grandsons, or great-grandsons.

It follows:

### (Verse 22)

“The sons of Shem were Elam, Assur, Arphaxad, Lud, and Aram.”

These peoples occupied the region from the Euphrates River through part of Asia as far as the Indian Ocean. Elam was the ancestor of the Elamites, the rulers of Persia. Assur has already been discussed.

It follows:

### (Verse 23)

“The sons of Aram were Uz, Hul, Gether, and Mash.”

But Arphaxad fathered Shelah, from whom Eber arose. Arphaxad was the ancestor of the Chaldeans; Lud of the Lydians; and Aram of the Syrians, whose capital is the city of Damascus.

The sons of Aram were Uz, Hul, Gether, and Mash. Uz held the region of Trachonitis and founded Damascus, exercising authority between Palestine and Coelesyria. For this reason, in the Book of Job, where the Hebrew has “the land of Uz,” the translators of the Septuagint rendered the region as Ausitis. Hul was the ancestor of the Armenians; Gether of the Carmanians or Carians.

It follows:

### (Verses 24ff.)

“Arphaxad fathered Shelah, from whom Eber arose.”

Eber was not directly fathered by Shem; rather, he is found fourth in the succession of firstborn descendants. Shem fathered Arphaxad among his other sons. Arphaxad fathered Shelah, from whom Eber arose.

He was therefore not without reason born first in the genealogy proceeding from Shem and given precedence even over sons, although he was a fourth-generation descendant. The reason is that the tradition is true which says that the Hebrews were named from him, as though they were called Ebereans. Another opinion is possible, namely, that they appear to have been called Abraheans from Abraham. Yet surely the former is correct: they were called Ebereans from Eber and thereafter, with one letter removed, Hebrews.

This was the language which only the people of Israel could preserve. In that people the city of God both sojourned among the saints and was prefigured in all things through the sacrament.

Thus the sons of Shem are named first; afterward four grandsons are born from one of them. Again, another of Shem’s sons fathered his grandson, and from that grandson came a great-grandson, Eber. Eber fathered two sons, one of whom he called Peleg (1 Chronicles 1), which means “dividing.” Scripture then adds the reason for the name: “For in his days the earth was divided.” What this means will appear later.

The other son born from Eber fathered twelve sons. Thus all those born from Shem number twenty-seven. In total, therefore, all the descendants of Noah’s three sons amount to seventy-three: fifteen from Japheth, thirty-one from Ham, and twenty-seven from Shem.

Then Scripture continues:

### (Verse 31)

“These are the sons of Shem, according to their tribes, according to their languages, in their lands and among their nations.”

And concerning them all:

“These are the tribes of the sons of Noah, according to their generations and according to their nations. From these the islands of the nations were dispersed over the earth after the flood.”

From this it is inferred that there were seventy-three—or rather, as will later be demonstrated, seventy-two—nations at that time, not seventy-three individual men. Earlier too, when the sons of Peleg had been mentioned, the conclusion was:

“From these the islands of the nations were separated in their lands, each according to its language, in its tribes and among its nations.”

In the case of the sons of Ham, this is mentioned even more explicitly, as I showed above: “Mesraim fathered those who are called Ludim,” and similarly the others, making seven nations. After all have been counted, Scripture concludes:

“These are the sons of Ham, according to their tribes, according to their languages, in their lands.”

This is why the sons of many others were not mentioned: as they were born, others joined existing nations, but they themselves were unable to establish nations. For what other reason, when eight sons of Japheth are enumerated, are the sons of only two of them mentioned? And when four sons of Ham are named, are descendants added from only three? And when six sons of Shem are named, is the posterity of only two attached to the account? Did the others remain without children? Far be it from us to believe this.

They simply did not produce nations for which they would have deserved mention, because, as they were born, they were added to other nations. Although these nations are therefore said to have existed in their own languages, the narrator returns to the time when all had one language and then explains what happened so that the diversity of languages arose.

It follows:

### (Chapter 11, verses 1ff.)

“Now the earth had one language and the same speech. As they journeyed from the east, they found a plain in the land of Shinar and settled there. And one said to his neighbor, ‘Come, let us make bricks and bake them with fire.’ They used bricks for stone and bitumen for mortar. And they said, ‘Come, let us build ourselves a city and a tower whose summit may reach heaven; and let us make our name renowned before we are scattered throughout all the lands.’”

This city, which was called Confusion, is Babylon itself, whose extraordinary construction is also praised in the histories of the nations. Babylon means “confusion.” From this it is inferred that the giant Nimrod was its founder, as had been indicated above.

When Scripture spoke of him, it said: “The beginning of his kingdom was Babylon”—that is, Babylon held primacy over the other cities and served as the royal residence, as though it were the capital. Yet it was not completed to the extent that arrogant impiety had imagined, for an excessive height had been planned, one that was to be raised to heaven—or at least the tower that they were constructing was intended to be preeminent among the others.

Pride is commonly followed by folly, and humility by wisdom.

It follows:

### (Verses 5–6)

“The Lord descended to see the city and the tower which the sons of Adam were building, and he said, ‘Behold, they are one people, and they all have one language. They have begun to do this, and they will not desist from their plans until they accomplish them in deed.’”

“The Lord descended to see the city and the tower which the sons of Adam were building”—that is, not the sons of God but the sons of human beings: the society living according to humanity, which we call the earthly city.

God, who is wholly present everywhere at all times, does not move from place to place. He is said to descend when he does something on earth which, because it occurs wondrously beyond the ordinary course of nature, displays his presence in a certain manner. He does not learn by seeing at a particular moment, since he can never be ignorant of anything. Rather, he is said to see and know at a particular time what he causes to be seen and known.

That city was not seen in the same way when God made it visible to himself—that is, when he showed how displeasing it was to him. Yet it may be understood that God descended to that city because his angels descended, and he dwells in them. He descended through the angels, while himself being present in the descending angels.

It is fitting that he did not say, “Come, let us descend and confuse them,” but rather, “Let us confuse their language there,” showing that he works through his ministers in such a way that they too are God’s fellow workers.

God does not speak to angels as we speak to one another, or to God, or to angels; nor as angels speak to us, or the Lord through them speaks to us. He speaks in his own ineffable manner. To us, however, this is reported according to our manner of understanding.

God’s sublime speech before the accomplishment of his work is the immutable reason of the work itself. It has no resounding and passing sound, but an everlasting power that remains and acts in time. In this manner he speaks to the holy angels; to us, who are far removed, he speaks through angels according to the measure of our capacity. When we too grasp something of this kind of speech with our inner ears, we draw near to the angels.

The statement, “They will not desist from their plans until they accomplish them in deed,” was not spoken as a confirmation but as a question, in the manner commonly used by those who threaten. It should therefore be understood as though he had said: “Will none of the things they have attempted to do fail?” If it is phrased in this way, however, it does not express the threatening tone, since we cannot write down the voice of the speaker.

It follows:

### (Verses 7ff.)

“Come, therefore, let us descend and confuse their language there, so that each may not hear the voice of his neighbor.”

“And so the Lord scattered them from that place over all the lands, and they ceased building the city. Therefore its name was called Babel, because there the language of the whole earth was confused. From there the Lord scattered them over the face of all the regions.”

The evil intention is rightly punished even when its intended result does not follow.

What was the nature of this punishment? Since the authority of a commander resides in language, pride was condemned precisely there, so that the person who had refused to understand God’s command and obey it would not be understood when giving commands to another human being.

Thus that conspiracy was dissolved: each person withdrew from the one whom he did not understand and joined himself only to someone with whom he could speak. The nations were divided by languages and scattered over the lands, as God pleased, accomplishing this through hidden and incomprehensible means.

From those three men, the sons of Noah, seventy-two languages began to exist throughout the earth, and as they increased they reached the islands. The number of nations, however, became far greater than the number of languages.

The first among human beings after the flood to seize tyranny was Nimrod, the son of Cush, driven by a new desire for imperial power. He ruled in Babylonia, which was called Babel because there the languages were confused; Babel means “confusion.” Nimrod himself was the author of the tower’s construction.

Because he attempted to penetrate the heights of heaven beyond the limits of his nature, he may appropriately be compared with the devil. The devil, swelling with the thought of his heart, wished to exalt himself above the stars—that is, above every angelic power—and intended to make himself equal to God, saying: “I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High.”

When he is called a hunter, what is signified by that name except a deceiver of earthly souls, capturing human beings for death?

His tower is the pride of this world, or the impious doctrines of heretics. After they moved away from the east—that is, withdrew from the true light—and came to the mountain of Shinar, whose name means “shaking of the teeth,” they immediately built a tower of their impiety against God and fashioned, with wicked audacity, the pride of their doctrines. They sought through unlawful curiosity to penetrate the heights of heaven itself.

But just as those people were divided through pride from one language into many, so heretics, separated from the unity of faith and confession, are divided among themselves by the diversity of error, as though by the discord of language. Those whom the destructive agreement of an exalted conspiracy arms against God are again divided when the discord of their doctrines produces a sudden confusion.

The Trinity itself condemns them, since they offend against it; it itself scatters them when it says: “Come, let us descend and confuse their languages”—that is, into the variety of error or schism.

At the time when the diversity of languages arose, the language which had previously existed remained in the house of Eber alone. So also now, in the Church alone, which is the house of Christ, the peace of a unified confession and faith remains, while all the condemned are divided.

After Noah’s two sons had been blessed and one in their midst had been cursed, Scripture is silent until Abraham about certain righteous people who worshiped God devoutly. I do not believe that such people were absent. But if all had been mentioned, the account would have become excessively long, and its concern would have been historical diligence rather than prophetic providence.

The sacred writer of these books—or rather, the Spirit of God speaking through him—pursues what is appropriate not merely for narrating past events but also for announcing future ones, insofar as they pertain to the city of God. For whatever is said here about people who are not citizens of that city is said so that the city of God may, by contrast with them, either advance or stand forth more clearly.

Not everything that happened should be thought to signify something. But events that signify something are joined to events that signify nothing, for the sake of those that do signify. The earth is plowed only by the plowshare; yet for this to be possible, the other parts of the plow are also necessary. Likewise, only the strings of a lyre or similar musical instrument are fitted to produce song, but in order that they may be fitted, the other parts of the instrument’s framework—which are not struck by the musicians—must be joined to those that sound when struck.

Similarly, prophetic history includes some things that signify nothing, but these are attached to, and in a certain way bind together, the things that do signify.

For this reason, after divine Scripture had displayed the earthly city in Babylon—that is, in confusion—it returns by recapitulation to the patriarch Shem and orders the generations from him to Abraham, also recording the number of years: how old each person was when he fathered the son relevant to this succession and how long each person lived.

Here we must recognize what I promised to explain earlier: why it is said of Eber’s son that his name was Peleg, because “in his days the earth was divided.” What else should be understood by the division of the earth except the diversity of languages?

The other sons of Noah, who are irrelevant to this matter, are therefore omitted, and those are linked in the genealogical succession through whom it is possible to reach Abraham, just as before the flood those were linked through whom it was possible to reach Noah, through the generations descended from Adam’s son who was called Seth.

Thus the succession of these generations begins.

It follows:

### (Verses 10ff.)

“These are the generations of Shem. Shem was one hundred years old when he fathered Arphaxad, two years after the flood. Arphaxad, when he was thirty-five years old, fathered Shelah. Shelah, in the thirtieth year of his life, fathered Eber.”

As I mentioned above, when the sons of Shem began to be enumerated—each of whom produced a separate nation—Eber was given first prominence, although he was Shem’s great-grandson, the fourth in descent from him.

Because this language remained in Eber’s family while the other nations were divided among different languages—and because it is reasonably believed to have been the language formerly common to the human race—it was thereafter called Hebrew. It was then necessary to distinguish it from the other languages by a proper name, just as the others too were called by their proper names.

When there was only one language, it was called nothing other than human language or human speech, because the whole human race spoke only it.

It follows:

### (Verse 16)

“Eber lived thirty-four years and fathered Peleg.”

Someone might say: If the earth was divided by languages—that is, if the people who then lived on earth were divided—in the days of Eber’s son Peleg, that language which had previously been common to all should rather have been named from him.

But it must be understood that Eber gave his son the name Peleg, meaning “division,” because the boy was born at the time when the earth was divided by languages. Thus the statement, “In his days the earth was divided,” means “at that time.” For unless Eber were still alive when the multitude of languages arose, the language that remained with him could not have received its name from him.

It must therefore be believed that this was the first language, the one that had previously been common to all. The multiplication and alteration of languages came as a punishment, and the people of God ought surely to have existed apart from this punishment.

Nor is it without significance that this is the language Abraham preserved. He could not transmit it to all his sons, but only to those who could be propagated through Jacob and, growing together more distinctly and prominently into the people of God, could possess God’s covenants and the stock of Christ.

Eber himself did not pour this language into all his descendants, but only into that line whose generations are carried forward to Abraham.

Therefore, even though it is not expressly stated that there was a pious race of human beings when Babylon was being founded by the impious, this obscurity was not intended to deprive the inquirer of an answer but rather to exercise his attention.

When, then, we seek the city of God among those seventy-two nations, we cannot assert that, at the time when they had one language—that is, one form of speech—the human race had already become alienated from the worship of the true God, so that true piety remained only in those generations descended from Shem through Arphaxad and reaching toward Abraham.

Rather, from the pride involved in building a tower up to heaven—by which impious exaltation is signified—the city, that is, the society of the impious, became manifest.

Whether it had previously been hidden, whether it had existed, or whether both societies had continued—namely, the pious society in the two sons of Noah who were blessed and in their descendants, and the impious society in the one who was cursed and in his progeny, from whom the giant hunter against the Lord also arose—is not easy to determine.

Perhaps—and this is certainly more credible—even among the sons of those two blessed men there were already despisers of God before Babylon began to be established, while among the sons of Ham there were worshipers of God. In any case, both kinds of human beings must be believed never to have been absent from the earth.

Therefore, just as the fact that there was one language common to all did not mean that there were no sons of perdition—for before the flood there was also one language, yet all except the one righteous household of Noah deserved to be destroyed by the flood—so, when the nations were punished and divided through the diversity of languages because of their deserved pride, and the city of the impious received the name of confusion, that is, was called Babylon, the house of Eber was not absent, and in it the language that had previously belonged to all remained.

When we read that originally there was one language shared by all, and that Eber is commended before all the sons of Shem, although he was fourth from him, and when that language is called Hebrew—the language which the authority of the patriarchs and prophets preserved not only in speech but also in the sacred writings—then, when we ask where the language that had previously been common could have remained after the division of languages, and when we recognize without doubt that wherever it remained there the punishment of the changed languages was absent, what else presents itself except that it remained among the people from whose ancestor it received its name?

This was no small indication of the righteousness of that people: while the other nations were punished by the alteration of their languages, such a punishment did not reach them.

It follows:

### (Verses 27–28)

“These are the generations of Terah. Terah fathered Abram, Nahor, and Haran.”

A human being begins to be capable of fathering children from adolescence. For this reason Matthew took his beginning from Abraham and proceeded as far as David. The evangelist did not recall the generations in this way without reason, so that the first interval might be marked by fourteen generations, from Abraham to David.

A human being indeed begins to be capable of fathering children from adolescence. Therefore the order of the generations begins with Abraham, who was also established as the father of nations when he received his changed name.

Now let us consider the progress of the city of God, beginning from that moment which took place in the person of Abraham. From this point its identity becomes more evident, and the divine promises are read more clearly—promises which we now see fulfilled in Christ.

As we have learned from the indication of divine Scripture, Abraham was born in the region of the Chaldeans, a land belonging to the Assyrian kingdom. Among the Chaldeans, impious superstitions already prevailed, as they did among the other nations.

There was therefore one household of Terah, from whom Abraham was born, in which the worship of the one true God was preserved and, as is credible, in which alone the Hebrew language had also remained. Yet even they, like the people of God who were later manifest in Egypt, are reported by Joshua to have served foreign gods in Mesopotamia, as Abraham’s descendants gradually flowed into different languages and different nations from the stock of Eber.

Thus, just as during the flood of waters Noah’s one household remained for the restoration of the human race, so amid the flood of many superstitions throughout the world one household remained—that of Terah—in which the planting of the city of God was preserved.

Accordingly, just as, after the preceding generations had been enumerated up to Noah together with the numbers of their years and the cause of the flood had been explained, before God began speaking to Noah about the construction of the ark, it is said, “These are the generations of Noah,” so here too, after the generations had been enumerated from Shem, who was called Noah’s son, to Abraham, the same formula is placed at the several stages:

“These are the generations of Terah: Terah fathered Abram, Nahor, and Haran.”

It follows:

“Now Haran fathered Lot. Haran died before his father Terah in the land of his birth, in Ur of the Chaldeans.”

Where we read “in the land of his birth,” the Hebrew has “in Ur of the Chaldeans,” that is, “in the fire of the Chaldeans.” The Hebrews tell the following story on this occasion: Abraham was thrown into the fire because he refused to worship fire; surrounded by a Babylonian blaze, he was rescued by God’s help and fled from the fire of idolatry.

This is what is said later, when Terah is reported to have gone out with his descendants from the region of the Chaldeans. The Hebrew has “from Ur,” that is, “from the fire of the Chaldeans.” It is also understood to be the meaning of the statement now made: “Haran died before Terah his father in the land of his birth, in the fire of the Chaldeans”—namely, that because he refused to worship fire, he was consumed by fire.

It follows:

### (Verse 29)

“Abram and Nahor took wives. The name of Abram’s wife was Sarai, and the name of Nahor’s wife was Milcah, the daughter of Haran, the father of Milcah and the father of Iscah.”

Haran, the son of Terah and the brother of Abram and Nahor, fathered two daughters, Milcah and Sarai, also called Iscah. Nahor took Milcah as his wife, and Abram took Sarai.

At that time marriages between uncles and their brothers’ daughters had not yet been prohibited by law, just as at the beginning marriages had even been contracted between brothers and sisters.

It follows:

### (Verses 30–31)

“Sarai was barren and had no children. Terah therefore took Abram his son, and Lot the son of Haran, his son, and Sarai his daughter-in-law, the wife of Abram his son, and led them out of Ur of the Chaldeans to go to the land of Canaan. They came as far as Haran and settled there.”

The account tells how Terah left the region of the Chaldeans with his household, came to Mesopotamia, and settled there.

It is silent, however, about one of his sons, who was called Nahor, as though Terah had not taken him with him. But later, when Abraham sent his servant to obtain a wife for his son Isaac, we read:

“The servant took ten camels from his master’s camels with him, and he arose and went to Mesopotamia, to the city of Nahor.”

This and other testimonies of this sacred history show that Nahor too went out from the region of the Chaldeans and established a dwelling in Mesopotamia, where Abraham had lived with his father.

Why, then, did Scripture not mention him when Terah departed from the Chaldean nation with his household and settled in Mesopotamia, where it records not only Abraham his son but also Sarai his daughter-in-law and Lot his grandson, saying that he took them with him?

What else are we to suppose except that Nahor had departed from his father’s and brother’s piety and adhered to the superstition of the Chaldeans, and that afterward he migrated from there either in repentance or because he was suspected and suffered persecution?

It follows:

### (Verse 32)

“All the days of Terah were two hundred and five years, and he died in Haran.”

Another translation commonly calls this place Carrhae. The statement should not be understood as though Terah spent all these years there, but rather that he completed there all the days of his life, which amounted to two hundred and five years.

Otherwise we would not know how many years Terah lived in Carrhae, since Scripture does not say in what year of his life he came to Carrhae. It is absurd to suppose that, in this succession of generations—where the number of years each person lived is carefully recorded—the number of years of this one man’s life was omitted from memory.

The years of certain people mentioned by the same Scripture are indeed not given, but they do not belong to this sequence, in which the reckoning of time is woven together through the departure of those who beget and the succession of those who are begotten.

This sequence, which runs from Adam to Noah and from Noah to Abraham, contains no one without the number of the years of his life.

After Terah’s death is mentioned, we then read:

“The Lord said to Abraham, ‘Go out from your land, and from your kindred, and from your father’s house,’” and so forth.

But blessed Stephen, recounting this in the Acts of the Apostles, says among other things:

“The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham when he was in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Carrhae, and said to him: ‘Go out from your land, and from your kindred, and from your father’s house’” (Acts 7).

According to the words of blessed Stephen, God did not speak to Abraham after his father’s death. His father died in Carrhae, where Abraham himself had lived with him and had sons; rather, God spoke to Abraham before he lived in that city, although he was already in Mesopotamia. He had therefore already left the Chaldeans.

When blessed Stephen adds, “Then Abraham went out from the land of the Chaldeans and lived in Carrhae” (Acts 7), this does not mean that it happened after God spoke to him. Abraham did not leave the land of the Chaldeans after those divine words, since Stephen says that the Lord spoke to him while he was in Mesopotamia.

Rather, the word “then” refers to the entire period beginning when he left the Chaldeans and lived in Carrhae. The following statement has the same meaning:

“After his father died, he settled him in this land in which you now dwell, and your fathers.”

Stephen does not say that Abraham left Carrhae after his father died. Rather, after taking him from there and settling him in this land, Abraham’s father died.

We must therefore understand that God spoke to Abraham while he was in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Carrhae; that Abraham reached Carrhae with his father while retaining God’s command; and that he left Carrhae in the seventy-fifth year of his own life and the one hundred forty-fifth year of his father’s.

Stephen says that Abraham’s settlement in the land of Canaan, not his departure from Carrhae, occurred after his father’s death, because his father had already died when Abraham purchased the land and began to possess it as his own property.

Although God says to Abraham, already established in Mesopotamia—that is, already gone out from the land of the Chaldeans—“Go out from your land, and from your kindred, and from your father’s house,” this does not mean that he was to remove his body from that place, since he had already done so. It means that he was to detach his mind from it.

He had not left in spirit if he was held by the hope and desire of returning. That hope and desire had to be cut away at God’s command and with God’s help, through Abraham’s obedience.

It is not implausible to suppose that, when Nahor later followed his father, Abraham then fulfilled the Lord’s command by leaving Carrhae with his wife Sarah and Lot, his brother’s son.

The promises made by God to Abraham must now be considered. In them the oracles of our God—that is, the true God—concerning the people of the pious begin to appear more clearly, as prophetic authority foretold. The first of these is read as follows:

### (Chapter XII—verses 1ff.)

And he said to Abraham: “Go out from your land, and from your kindred, and from your father’s house, and come into the land that I shall show you; and I shall make you into a great nation, and I shall bless you, and I shall magnify your name, and you shall be blessed. I shall bless those who bless you, and curse those who curse you; and in you all the kindreds of the earth shall be blessed.”

It must therefore be noted that two things were promised to Abraham: [Col. 0945D] one, namely, that his offspring would possess the land of Canaan. This is signified where it is said: “Go into the land that I shall show you, and I shall make you into a great nation.” The other was far more excellent: not concerning carnal but spiritual offspring, through which he is father not of one nation, Israel, but of all the nations that follow the traces of his faith. This began to be promised in the words: “And in you all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed.”

Eusebius thinks that this promise was made in the seventy-fifth year of Abraham’s life, as though Abraham had left Carran immediately after it was made, because Scripture cannot be contradicted where it reads: “Abraham was seventy-five years old when he went out from Carran.” But if this promise was made in that year, Abraham was certainly already dwelling in Carran with his father; for he could not go out from there unless he had first lived there. Is Stephen, then, contradicted when he says: “The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham when he was in Mesopotamia, before he lived [Col. 0946A] in Carran”?

It must instead be understood that everything happened in the same year: God’s promise before Abraham lived in Carran, his residence in Carran, and his departure from there. This is so not only because Eusebius, in his *Chronicle*, reckons from the year of this promise and demonstrates that the departure from Egypt occurred four hundred and thirty years later, when the Law was given, but also because the apostle Paul recalls this.

Abraham therefore went out from Carran in the seventy-fifth year of his life. Ninus, king of the Assyrians, had then been reigning for forty-three years, and Abraham was born approximately twelve hundred years before the founding of Rome, which was like another Babylon in the West. In the one hundred and forty-fifth year of his father’s life, Abraham went into the land of Canaan with Lot, his brother’s son, and Sarah his wife, and reached Shechem, where he again received a divine oracle.

But who else went out in Abraham from his land and from his kindred in order to become enriched among the other nations and become a great nation, except Christ, who, after leaving the land and [Col. 0946B] kindred of the Jews, now prevails among the nations?

The moral interpretation is also as follows: We go out from our land when we despise the riches and resources of this world; and from our kindred—that is, from our former vices, which cling to us from our birth and are joined to us as though by a certain affinity and blood relationship; and from our father’s house—that is, from every memory of this world that presents itself to our eyes.

The text continues:

### (Verses 5–6)

“And they went out to go into the land of Canaan. When they had entered it, Abraham passed through the land as far as the place of Shechem and as far as the illustrious valley.”

Shechem is the same place as Salem, which in Latin and Greek is called *Sicima*: the city of Jacob, situated in the territory of the tribe of Ephraim. The son of Hamor was also called Shechem, from whom the place received its name. There was also another Shechem on Mount Ephraim, a city of fugitives.

The text continues:

### (Verse 7)

“And the Lord appeared to Abraham and said [Col. 0946C] to him: ‘To your offspring I shall give this land.’ And he built there an altar to the Lord, who had appeared to him.”

Nothing here is promised concerning that offspring through which he became the father of all nations, but only concerning the offspring through which he is the father of the one Israelite nation. This offspring possessed the land itself.

Then, after building an altar there and calling upon God, Abraham departed from that place and lived in the wilderness.

The text continues:

### (Verses 10ff.)

“There was a famine in the land, and Abraham went down into Egypt to sojourn there, for the famine had become severe in the land. When he was near entering Egypt, he said to Sarai his wife: ‘I know that you are a beautiful woman. When the Egyptians see you, they will say, “She is his wife,” and they will kill me but preserve you. Say, I beg you, that you are my sister, so that it may go well with me because of you, and my life may be preserved on your account.’”

Because, among strangers, Sarah’s outstanding beauty and chastity placed both her and her husband’s life in danger, and Abraham could not protect both, he entrusted the preservation of his wife’s chastity [Col. 0946D] to God while, as a human being, taking precautions against human schemes. For if he failed to avoid a danger that could be avoided, he would be tempting God rather than hoping in God. He did what he could; what he could not do, he entrusted to God.

God was certainly able to avert from him the death that he feared and to guard him and his wife from every danger during that sojourn, so that no one would desire his wife, however beautiful she was, and so that he would not die because of her.

If Abraham, when questioned, had declared that the woman was his wife, he would have entrusted two things to God’s protection: his own life and his wife’s chastity. He did not, however, answer that she was not his wife when he was asked about her. Rather, when he was asked what relationship the woman had to him, he identified her as his sister; he did not deny that she was his wife. She was indeed also his sister, because she was related to him by blood. Thus he kept silent about her as wife, but did not deny it.

The text continues:

### (Verses 14ff.)

“When Abraham had entered Egypt, the Egyptians saw that the woman was [Col. 0947A] exceedingly beautiful. They reported this to Pharaoh’s princes, and they praised her before him; and the woman was taken into Pharaoh’s house. They treated Abraham well because of her. But God struck Pharaoh and his household with very great plagues because of Sarai, Abraham’s wife. Pharaoh summoned Abraham and said to him: ‘What have you done to me? Why did you not tell me that she was your wife? Why did you say that she was your sister, so that I might take her as my wife? Now, then, here is your wife: take her and go.’”

Thus what Abraham had expected from the Lord came to pass. Pharaoh, king of Egypt, who had taken her as his wife, was severely afflicted and returned her to her husband. Far be it from us to believe that she had been defiled by another’s intercourse, because it is much more credible that Pharaoh was not permitted, amid the great afflictions, to do this.

The matter can nevertheless be excused in another way. According to the book of Esther, among the ancients any woman who pleased the king was anointed for six months with myrtle oil, and for six months was treated with various perfumes and women’s preparations; only then did she enter the king’s [Col. 0947B] presence. It may therefore be that, after Sarai had pleased the king, while her entry to the king was being prepared over the course of a year, Pharaoh gave Abraham many gifts and was subsequently struck by the Lord, while she still remained untouched by his intercourse.

The text continues:

### (Chapter XIII—verses 1ff.)

“So Abraham went up from Egypt, he and his wife and everything he possessed, and Lot with him, toward the south. He was exceedingly rich in the possession of gold and silver. Lot also, who was with Abraham, had flocks of sheep and herds, and the land could not contain them so that they might dwell together, for their possessions were abundant.”

When Abraham had returned from Egypt to the place from which he had come, Lot, his brother’s son, separated from him and went into the land of Sodom, while preserving their affection. They had become rich, and had begun to have many herdsmen of their livestock. When these men quarreled with one another, Abraham and Lot avoided in this way a contentious conflict between their households. For, as human affairs go, some quarrel might otherwise have arisen even between them.

[Col. 0947C] Accordingly, Abraham’s words to Lot, by which he took precautions against this evil, were: “Let there be no quarrel between me and you, and between my herdsmen and your herdsmen, for we are all brothers. Is not the whole land before you? Separate from me, I beg you: if you go to the left, I shall go to the right; or if you go to the right, I shall go to the left.”

Perhaps from this arose among human beings the peaceful custom that, whenever something belonging to the earth must be divided, the elder divides and the younger chooses.

When they had departed and Abraham and Lot were living separately—not because of the disgrace of discord, but because their households had to be supported—Abraham began to dwell in the land of Canaan, while Lot began to dwell in Sodom.

Abraham, whose name means “exalted father,” whom else does he signify but the Lord Jesus Christ? Through the prophet he says: “You will call me Father, and you will not cease to follow after me”; and all the faithful beseech him, saying: “Our Father, who are in heaven” (Matthew 6). He is rightly called exalted because he dwells in heaven, as the Psalmist testifies concerning him: “To you I lifted up my eyes, who dwell in heaven” (Psalm 122).

Lot, however, [Col. 0947D] whose name means “one who declines,” signifies the Jewish people, who declined from him who is the way, the truth, and the life, and stumbled away from his paths.

Abraham’s herdsmen signified the holy apostles; the sheep, the rest of the multitude of the faithful. Concerning these he himself says: “My sheep hear my voice”; and again: “I have other sheep that are not of this fold” (John 10).

Lot’s herdsmen, on the other hand, prefigured the scribes and Pharisees—not because they truly were shepherds, but because they falsely boasted that they were. The Lord calls them not shepherds but thieves and robbers.

What else did the quarrel of the herdsmen signify except the conflict between the two parties, the devout and the impious? Their possessions signified the multitude of the faithful and the unfaithful, the devout and the impious.

But when Abraham said to Lot, “Please, let there be no quarrel between me and you, and between my herdsmen and your herdsmen; separate from me, I beg you; behold, the whole land is before you: if you go to the left, I shall hold to the right; if you choose the right, [Col. 0948A] I shall go to the left,” what is signified by the right and the left except both Testaments? Concerning them the Church says in the *Song of Songs*: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me” (Song of Songs 2).

The Jews, as it were, declined toward the right when, ignorant of God’s righteousness and wishing to establish their own, they were not subject to God’s righteousness. But he, as it were, chose the left when he said: “I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners” (Luke 15); and again: “Amen, I say to you, there will be such joy in heaven over one sinner doing penance as over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of penance.”

Again, they chose the left when they said: “This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath” (John 9); and to Pilate: “If he were not a criminal, we would not have handed him over to you” (John 18).

But the Lord again chose the right in his preachers when, after his resurrection, he commanded them, saying: “Go into the whole world and preach the gospel to every creature” (Matthew, final chapter); and again: “For judgment I came into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9).

The fact that Lot departed from the east and chose for himself the region around the Jordan signified nothing else, surely, than that the carnal Jewish people, [Col. 0948B] abandoning the promise of heavenly things, fixed all their hope upon love of temporal things. And afterward, by dwelling in Sodom, he signified that the Jewish people became worse than the nations that were ignorant of God: for while those nations were ignorant of the one whom they did not know, these blasphemed him. What the Psalmist sang concerning them was fulfilled: “And I gave them over to the desire of their flesh; they went according to their own inventions” (Psalm 80).

The text continues:

### (Verses 14ff.)

“And the Lord said to Abraham, after Lot had separated from him: ‘Lift up your eyes and look from the place where you now are, toward the north and the south, toward the east and the west. All the land that you see I shall give to you and to your offspring forever; and I shall make your offspring like the dust of the earth. If anyone [Col. 0948C] can count the dust of the earth, he will also be able to count your offspring. Rise, walk through the land in its length and breadth, for I shall give it to you.’”

Abraham therefore moved his tent and came to dwell beside the valley of Mamre, which is Hebron, and there he built an altar to the Lord.

Whether this promise also includes the one through which he became the father of all nations does not clearly appear. It may seem to refer to this in the words, “I shall make your offspring like the dust of the earth,” expressed in the figure that the Greeks call *hyperbole*—a figurative, not literal, expression. No one who has learned Scripture doubts that it regularly uses this and other figures of speech.

This figure, that is, this manner of expression, occurs when something is said to be far greater than what the words signify. Who does not see that the number of grains of sand is incomparably greater than the entire human race from Adam himself to the end of the age? How much more, then, does this apply to Abraham’s offspring—not only to what belongs to the Israelite [Col. 0948D] nation, but also to what is and will be found throughout the whole world among all nations according to the imitation of faith?

Compared with the multitude of the impious, this offspring is certainly few, although even these few become innumerable in view of their own immense multitude, which is signified figuratively by the sand of the earth.

Certainly, the multitude promised to Abraham is not innumerable to God, but to human beings; to God, not even the sand of the earth is innumerable.

Therefore, since not only the Israelite nation but Abraham’s entire offspring—where the promise exists not according to the flesh but according to the spirit of many sons—is more appropriately compared with the multitude of sand, it can be understood from this that a promise concerning both was made. We said, however, that this does not appear clearly because the multitude of that one nation, born according to the flesh from Abraham through his grandson Jacob, grew so greatly that it nearly filled all the regions of the world. It too could [Col. 0949A] therefore be compared figuratively with the multitude of sand, since even this one nation is innumerable to human beings.

No one doubts that the land signified is specifically the land called Canaan. But the statement, “I shall give it to you and to your offspring forever,” may trouble some if “forever” is understood as “for eternity.” If, however, they understand “age” in this passage as we faithfully hold it—that the beginning of the future age starts from the end of the present one—nothing will trouble them. For although the Israelites have been expelled from Jerusalem, they nevertheless remain in the other cities of the land of Canaan and will remain there until the end; and when that entire land is inhabited by Christians, it too is Abraham’s offspring.

After receiving this answer concerning the promise, Abraham moved and remained in another place in the same land, beside the oak of Mamre, which was in Hebron.

Hebron was once called Arbe, but is corruptly written *Arboch* in our manuscripts, whereas in Hebrew it reads *Arbe*, meaning “four,” because three patriarchs—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—were buried there, together with the great Adam, [Col. 0949B] as is written in the book of Joshua, although some suppose that Adam was buried at the place of Calvary.

This same Hebron was formerly the metropolis of the Philistines and the dwelling place of giants; afterward it was the royal city of David in the tribe of Judah, a priestly city and a city of fugitives. It lies approximately twenty-two miles south of Jerusalem.

Abraham’s oak, which is Mamre, remained until the reign of King Constantius, and his little dwelling can still be seen today. Although our people have already built a church there, all the surrounding nations superstitiously venerate the place of the terebinth, because Abraham once received angels as guests beneath it.

It was the metropolis of the Anakim, whom we should understand as giants.

The text continues:

### (Chapter XIV—verses 1ff.)

“It came to pass at that time that Amraphel, king of Shinar, Arioch, king of Pontus, Chedorlaomer, king of the Elamites, and Tidal, king of nations, made war against Bera, king of Sodom, [Col. 0949C] and against Birsha, king of Gomorrah, and against Shinab, king of Admah, and against Shemeber, king of Zeboiim, and against the king of Bela, which is Segor.

All these gathered in the wooded valley, which is now the Salt Sea. They served Chedorlaomer for twelve years, and in the thirteenth year they revolted from him. In the fourteenth year Chedorlaomer and the kings who were with him struck down the Rephaim in Ashtaroth-karnaim, the Zuzim with them, the Emim in Shaveh-kiriathaim, and the Horites in the mountains of Seir, as far as the plain of Paran, which is in the wilderness. They turned back and came to the spring of Mishpat, which is Kadesh, and struck down the giants in Ashtaroth-karnaim and the strong nations with them, and all of them in Shaveh, the city, before they reached Sodom.”

The four kings who departed from Babylonia killed the giants, that is, the Rephaim, the strongest men of Arabia, and the Zuzim and Emim in the city of Shaveh, which is still called by that name today. *Zuzim* and *Emim* are interpreted as “terrible” and “horrible.”

### (Verse 7)

“And returning, they came to the spring of Mishpat, [Col. 0949D] which is Kadesh.”

This name is spoken by anticipation, because it was called this only afterward. It signifies the place beside the rock called the Spring of Judgment, because God judged the people there.

“And they struck down the whole region of the Amalekites, and the Amorite who dwelt in Hazazon-tamar.”

This is the town now called Engaddi, fertile in balsam and palms. *Hazazon-tamar* in our language sounds like “City of Palms”; for *tamar* means “palm.”

Ashtaroth is part of the wilderness where Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses, formerly the city of Og, king of Bashan. Karnaim is a large village of Ashtaroth beyond the fords of the Jordan; tradition says that Job’s house was there.

### (Verses 11ff.)

“And they took all the cavalry of Sodom and Gomorrah, as well as Lot and his people of the suburbs.” And behold, one who had escaped reported this to Abraham the Hebrew, who was dwelling beside the valley of Mamre the Amorite, the brother of Eshcol and the brother of Aner.”

This shows that Mamre, [Col. 0950A] Eshcol, and Aner were Amorites and Abraham’s kinsmen and allies.

“And they struck them as far as Dan, the Phoenician town now called Paneas.”

Dan is one of the sources of the Jordan. The other is called Jor, which is interpreted as *Rithron*, that is, “stream.” When the two sources, which are not far from one another, join into one stream, it is thereafter called the Jordan.

After those who had invaded Sodom had carried away its inhabitants, while five kings were waging war against four and Lot too had been captured with the Sodomites, Abraham rescued him. He took with him into battle three hundred and eighteen of his household-born servants and won the victory for the kings of Sodom. He did not wish to take any of the spoils, although the king for whom he had won the victory offered them to him.

But what did Abraham’s victory over the five kings signify? Abraham conquered them through the mystery of faith, the father of which he was. It signified that our faith has been so strengthened in the ruling spirit that it subdues the same number of bodily senses by the word of God. For just as Abraham, coming from near at hand, was victorious over the kings, so faith, victorious through the soul, triumphs over the outward human being.

Moreover, the fact that Abraham defeated the opposing princes not by a multitude or the strength of legions, but with only three hundred and eighteen companions, [Col. 0950B] already signified the figure of the holy cross. This number is expressed by the Greek letter *tau* (*T*) and by the name of Jesus, which is written in Greek characters as *iota* and *theta*, and is interpreted as “Savior.” Thus the passion of Christ was prefigured as freeing us from the domination of the five carnal senses, which had previously taken us captive through various vices and overcome us.

The text continues:

### (Verses 18ff.)

“But Melchizedek, king of Salem, brought out bread and wine, for he was priest of God Most High. And he blessed him and said: ‘Blessed be Abraham by God Most High, who created heaven and earth; and blessed be God Most High, by whose protection your enemies are in your hands.’ And he gave him tithes of everything.”

The Hebrews say that this man was Shem, Noah’s first son. At the time of Abraham’s birth, they say, Shem was three hundred and ninety years old, reckoned as follows.

In the second year after the Flood, [Col. 0950C] when Shem was one hundred years old, he fathered Arphaxad. After Arphaxad’s birth he lived five hundred years, making six hundred years altogether. In his thirty-fifth year Arphaxad fathered Shelah. Shelah, in turn, fathered Eber when he was thirty years old. We read that Eber fathered Peleg at the age of thirty-four. Peleg, after completing thirty years, fathered Reu. Reu, after thirty-five years, produced Serug. When Serug reached the age of thirty, Nahor was born. Nahor, at the age of thirty-nine, fathered Terah. We read that Terah, at the age of seventy, fathered Abram, Nahor, and Haran.

Add up the years of each generation, and you will find three hundred and ninety years from Shem’s birth to the birth of Abram. Abraham died in the one hundred and seventy-fifth year of his life. By this calculation, Shem is found to have outlived his tenth-generation descendant Abraham by thirty-five years.

They also relate concerning Shem that, until the priesthood of Aaron, all the firstborn of his line—whose succession and order are [Col. 0950D] described—were priests and offered sacrifices to God. They say that these were the birthrights that Esau sold to his brother Jacob.

It is not surprising, then, if Melchizedek came out to meet Abraham after his victory and brought bread and wine for the refreshment both of Abraham himself and of his warriors, and blessed him, since he owed this right to his tenth-generation descendant. He also received from him tithes of the spoils and victory—or, since the matter is uncertain, perhaps Melchizedek gave Abraham tithes of his property and thereby demonstrated his generosity toward his descendant.

Both interpretations can be understood, according to the Hebrew text and the Septuagint translators: Melchizedek both received tithes of the spoils and gave Abraham tithes of his property. Nevertheless, the Apostle in the Epistle to the Hebrews states most clearly that Abram did not receive tithes of Melchizedek’s wealth, but that the priest received a portion from the spoils of the enemies (Hebrews 3).

Salem is not, as [Col. 0951A] Hegesippus and all our writers suppose, Jerusalem, a name composed from Greek and Hebrew. The mixture of a foreign language demonstrates that this is absurd. Rather, it is a town near Scythopolis that is still called Salem today.

There too the palace of Melchizedek is displayed, its vast ruins revealing the magnificence of the ancient structure. Concerning it, it is also written elsewhere in Genesis: “Jacob came to Succoth”—that is, “to tents”—“and made houses and tents for himself there. And he crossed over to Salem, a city of the region of Shechem, which is in the land of Canaan” (Genesis 33).

It must also be considered that when Abraham returned from slaughtering the enemies whom he had pursued as far as Dan, now called Paneas, he was traveling not from the direction of Jerusalem but from the town of the metropolis of Shechem. Of this place we read in the Gospel: “John was baptizing in Aenon near Salim, because there was much water there” (John 3).

It makes no difference whether it is called Salem or Salim, since the Hebrews [Col. 0951B] very rarely use vowels in the middle of words, and pronounce the same words with different sounds and accents according to the will of the readers and the customs of the regions.

We learned these things from the most learned members of that nation. They so entirely reject the idea that Melchizedek was the Holy Spirit or an angel that they even assign him the most certain name of a human being.

Indeed, it is foolish to refer some things to allegory in such a way that the historical truth is removed, claiming that he was not a king but that an angel was represented in the image of a human being. The Hebrews strive so earnestly to show that Melchizedek, king of Salem, was Shem, the son of Noah, that they even place this earlier in their account.

“Now the king of Sodom went out to meet him”—there is no doubt that this occurred after Abraham had returned from the slaughter of Chedorlaomer and the kings who were with him in the Valley of Shaveh, which is the [Col. 0951C] King’s Valley. Immediately afterward the text says: “And Melchizedek, king of Salem, brought out bread and wine,” and the rest.

If this is the king’s city and the King’s Valley—or, as the Septuagint translated it, the plain that the Palestinians today call the *Aulon*—then *Aulon* is not a Greek word, as some suppose, but a Hebrew term. It is called a great and level valley, extending to an immense length and surrounded on every side by mountains that follow and join one another. These mountains begin at Lebanon and beyond it and extend as far as the wilderness of Paran.

In this Aulon, that is, in the level valley, are famous cities: Scythopolis, Tiberias, the lake of Gennesaret, Jericho, the Dead Sea, and the surrounding regions through which the Jordan flows. It rises from the springs of Paneas and empties into the Dead Sea.

It is therefore clear that Melchizedek was a human being who ruled over an earthly valley and city.

This Melchizedek, whose name is interpreted as “king of righteousness,” was king of the city Salem, which is interpreted as “peace,” and priest of [Col. 0951D] God Most High. He offered bread and wine as a sacrifice, and Abraham the patriarch is read to have offered him tithes from the chief spoils; he was also blessed by him. For the one who blesses is greater than the one who is blessed.

Thus the priests born from Abraham’s offspring blessed their brothers, that is, the children of Israel, who gave them tithes according to the command of the Law, truly giving them to those greater and more eminent than themselves—“without father,” as the Apostle says, “without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life” (Hebrews 7). This cannot properly apply to any human being except the Lord alone.

For Melchizedek’s name is introduced suddenly, and the family from which he was born is not indicated at all. Nothing is reported either before or afterward about the beginning or end of his life. In this respect he is made like the Son of God our Lord.

He alone was born from a Father without a mother according to his divinity; he alone was born from a mother without a father according to his humanity. He is also the eternal priest, to whom it is said: “You are a priest [Col. 0952A] forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 109). He is righteousness and peace, king and priest: king from God the Father, priest from the Virgin mother.

That he was without a mother is clear in relation to the Father, when the Evangelist says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1).

That he existed without a father from his mother is proclaimed by the Evangelist when the angel speaks to Mary: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1).

He also existed as a human being from human beings without any priestly genealogy, since he was not born from the tribe of Levi but from the tribe of Judah. From that tribe he received nothing concerning the priestly ordinance. This was in accordance with the mystery of the sacrament that Christians are commanded to celebrate: not, according to Aaron, offering the sacrifices of animals, but offering as a sacrifice the offering of bread and wine—that is, the sacrament of his body and blood.

There [Col. 0952B] the sacrifice that is now offered to God by Christians throughout the whole world first appeared. The statement spoken much later through the prophet to Christ, who was still to come in the flesh, is fulfilled: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 109). This is not according to Aaron, whose order was to be removed when the realities that had been indicated by those shadows began to shine forth.

The fact that the great patriarch gave tithes of all his substance to Melchizedek the priest after receiving his blessing shows that he knew spiritually that a better priesthood would arise among the Gentiles than the Levitical priesthood that was to be born from him in Israel. It also signified that the priesthood of the Church, possessing the foreskin, would bless in circumcised Abram the priesthood of the Synagogue.

The text continues:

### (Chapter XV—verses 1ff.)

“After these things, the word of the Lord came to Abram in a vision, saying: ‘Do not fear, Abram; I am your protector, and your reward is [Col. 0952C] exceedingly great.’ And Abram said: ‘Lord God, what will you give me? I shall depart childless, and this Eliezer of Damascus, the steward of my house, will be my heir.’ Abram added: ‘You have not given me offspring, and behold, my household-born servant will be my heir.’”

A promise had already been made to Abram concerning offspring and an abundant, innumerable multitude. It had not yet been revealed, however, in what manner the promise concerning that offspring would be fulfilled: whether from Abraham’s flesh, if he were to beget it himself, or from his will, if he were perhaps to adopt someone.

Thus, when Abram saw that no children were being born to him but nevertheless understood that a promise had been made concerning his offspring, he first considered adoption. This is indicated when, speaking with God, he says concerning his household-born servant: “He will be my heir,” as though he were saying: “Since you have not given me offspring from myself, fulfill in this man what you promised concerning my offspring.”

For if no one’s offspring were called his except that which was born from his flesh, the Apostle would not call us Abraham’s offspring (Romans 11; Hebrews 2). Certainly we do not derive the origin [Col. 0952D] of our flesh from him; rather, through imitation of faith we became his offspring by believing in Christ, whose flesh was propagated from his flesh.

Then Abram heard from the Lord: “This man will not be your heir; but the one who will come out from your own body will be your heir.”

Now that the thought of adoption had been removed, and Abram hoped for offspring from himself, it remained uncertain whether the child would come from Sarah or from another woman. God wished to conceal this from him until the old covenant had first been prefigured through her.

The text continues:

### (Verses 5–6)

“And he led him outside and said to him: ‘Look up at the sky and count the stars, if you are able.’ And he said to him: ‘So shall your offspring be.’ Abram believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness.”

Again an innumerable offspring is indicated—not like the sand of the earth, but like the stars of heaven. Here it seems to me that offspring raised to heavenly blessedness is more especially promised. For in respect of number, what are the stars of heaven compared with the sand of the earth?

Unless someone says that this comparison is similar precisely to the extent that the stars too cannot be counted, since it should be believed that not all of them can be seen. The more sharply anyone looks, [Col. 0953A] the more stars he sees. Accordingly, those who see most keenly rightly suppose that some stars remain unseen, apart from the heavenly bodies said to rise and set in the part of the world most remote from us.

The text continues: “Abram believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Romans 4).

Here, certainly, that statement is inserted which the Apostle recalls in order to commend God’s grace, lest circumcision should boast and refuse to admit uncircumcised nations to faith in Christ. For when this occurred—when faith was counted as righteousness for Abraham who believed—he had not yet been circumcised.

The text continues:

(Verses 7ff.) And the Lord said to him, “I am the Lord who brought you out from Ur of the Chaldeans, to give you this land and that you might possess it.” When he asked what basis he would have for knowing that he would possess it, the Lord answered him, “Take for me,” he said, “a three-year-old heifer, a three-year-old she-goat, and a three-year-old ram, as well as a turtledove and a pigeon.” [Col. 0953B] Taking all these, he divided them through the middle and placed the two halves opposite each other; but he did not divide the birds.

For he did not say, “How shall I know?” as though he still did not believe; rather, he said, “By what shall I know?” so that some likeness might be applied to the matter he had believed, by which its mode might be understood. Thus there is no distrust in the Virgin Mary when she says, “How will this happen, since I do not know a man?” (Luke 1). She was certain that it would happen; she was asking how it would happen. When she had asked this, she received an answer.

Accordingly, here too there is a likeness drawn from the animals—the heifer, the she-goat, the ram, and the two birds, the turtledove and the pigeon—so that he might know, through these, what would happen, although he did not doubt that it would happen.

By the heifer the people themselves are signified, placed under the yoke of the law; by the she-goat, those same people as destined to be sinful; by the ram, those same people as destined to reign. These animals are called three-year-old because, as the notable divisions of time extend from Adam to Noah, from Noah to Abram, and from Abram to David—David being the first, after Saul was rejected, to be established by the Lord’s will in the kingship of the Israelite nation—in this third order, extending from Abram to David, that people grew to maturity as though it were passing through a third age.

In the turtledove, we should understand those whom the Apostle says wandered in deserts and mountains, in caves and holes in the ground, people of whom the world was not worthy (Heb. 11). In the pigeon the prophets were prefigured: filled with the Holy Spirit, they announced future events to the peoples.

Alternatively, through the turtledove and the pigeon, spiritual people in that nation were prefigured—the undivided children of the promise and heirs of the future kingdom. Their temporal age is not stated because, meditating on eternal things, they have passed beyond temporal desires. Hence it is said, “But he did not divide the birds,” because carnal people are divided among themselves, whereas spiritual people are in no way divided, whether they withdraw from the busy dealings of human beings, like the turtledove, or live among them, like the pigeon. Yet each bird is simple and harmless, signifying that even within the Israelite people, to whom the land was to be given, there would be undivided children of the promise and heirs of the kingdom, destined to remain in eternal happiness.

It follows:

(Vers. 11.) And birds of prey descended upon the carcasses, and Abram drove them away. By his merit the Israelite people were often delivered and defended from the attacks of various nations. The birds descending upon the divided bodies signify not something good, but certain spirits of this air seeking their nourishment from the division of carnal people. Abram’s driving them away signifies that, even amid those divisions of the carnal, true believers would persevere to the end.

It follows:

(Vers. 12.) And when the sun was setting, a deep sleep fell upon Abram, and a great and dark terror seized him. This signifies the great disturbance and tribulation that will come upon the faithful near the end of this age, concerning which the Lord says in the Gospel, “For then there will be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning” (Matt. 24).

It follows:

(Verses 13–14.) And it was said to him, “Know beforehand that your offspring will be strangers in a land not their own, and they will subject them to slavery and afflict them for four hundred years. Yet I shall judge the nation to which they will be enslaved, and after this they will go out with great wealth.”

He prophesied most openly about the people of Israel, who were destined to be enslaved in Egypt—not that the people would spend four hundred years in that slavery under the Egyptians who afflicted them, but that this future event was foretold within those four hundred years. It is like what is written concerning Terah, Abraham’s father: “And the days of Terah in Harran were two hundred and five years”—not because all those years were spent there, but because they were completed there. So here also the statement is inserted, “They will reduce them to slavery and afflict them for four hundred years,” because that number was completed in the same affliction, not because the whole period was spent there.

Four hundred years are mentioned because of the completeness of the number, although the actual period is somewhat longer—whether one counts from the time when these things were promised to Abraham, or from the birth of Isaac, on account of the offspring of Abraham concerning whom these things were foretold.
