As we have already said above, the period from Abraham’s seventy-fifth year, when this promise was made to him, until Israel’s departure from Egypt amounts to four hundred and thirty years. The Apostle refers to them as follows: “This is what I mean: the law, which came four hundred and thirty years afterward, does not annul a covenant previously ratified by God, so as to invalidate the promise” (Gal. 3).

Those four hundred and thirty years could therefore be called four hundred, since they are not very much more; how much more so when several years of that number had already passed at the time when those things were shown and spoken to Abraham in the vision—or when Isaac was born to his father at the age of one hundred, twenty-five years after the first promise, when four hundred and five years remained of the four hundred and thirty. The Lord wished to call these four hundred.

It follows:

(Verses 15–16.) “But you shall go to your fathers in peace; you shall be buried in a good old age. And in the fourth generation they shall return here. For the iniquities of the Amorites have not yet been completed up to the present time.”

Let us review Levi’s genealogy: Levi fathered Kohath; Kohath fathered Amram; Amram fathered Aaron; Aaron fathered Eleazar; Eleazar fathered Phinehas. Kohath entered Egypt with his father Levi. From Kohath to Eleazar there are four generations, although some wish to begin with Amram and reach Phinehas, just as we have reached Eleazar.

If you wish to demonstrate a different number, namely how the children of Israel came out of the land of Egypt in the fifth generation, let the genealogy of the tribe of Judah be counted for you: Judah fathered Perez; Perez fathered Hezron; Hezron fathered Aram; Aram fathered Amminadab; Amminadab fathered Nahshon; Nahshon fathered Salmon (Matt. 1). Perez entered Egypt with his father Judah. Nahshon is described as the leader of the tribe of Judah in the wilderness, and his son Salmon entered the promised land. Count from Perez to Nahshon, and you will find five generations.

It follows:

(Vers. 17.) When the sun had set, a dark gloom arose; and behold, a smoking furnace and a fiery torch passed between those divisions. This signifies that at the end of the age carnal people will be judged by fire. For just as the affliction of the city of God—such as has never before occurred, and which is expected to come under Antichrist—is signified by Abraham’s dark fear around sunset, that is, as the end of the age already approaches, so at sunset, that is, at the very end, the day of judgment is signified by this fire. It will divide carnal people: some will be saved through fire, others condemned in fire.

It follows:

(Verses 18ff.) On that day the Lord made a covenant with Abram, saying, “To your offspring I shall give this land, from the river of Egypt to the great river, the Euphrates: the Kenites, the Kenizzites, the Kadmonites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, [Col. 0955A] the Rephaim also, and the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Girgashites, and the Jebusites.”

The covenant made with Abram then specifically reveals the land of Canaan and names eleven nations in it, from the river of Egypt to the great river Euphrates. It is therefore not from the great river of Egypt, namely the Nile, but from the small one that divides Egypt from Palestine, where the city of Rhinocorura is situated.

It follows:

(Chapter 16.—Verses 1ff.) Now Sarai, Abram’s wife, had not borne children, but she had an Egyptian maidservant named Hagar. She said to her husband, “Behold, God has closed me off, so that I cannot give birth; go in to my maidservant, perhaps I may at least receive children through her.” When he agreed to her request, she took Hagar the Egyptian, her maidservant, ten years after she had begun to dwell in the land of Canaan, and gave her to her husband as a wife; and he went in to her. When she saw that she had conceived, she despised her mistress.

As for the event itself, Abraham must in no way be accused on account of this concubine. Once the thought of adoption had been set aside, and Abram hoped for offspring from himself, it remained uncertain whether the child would come from Sarah or from another woman. God wished to conceal this from him until the Old Testament had been prefigured through the maidservant.

What is surprising, then, if, seeing a barren wife who desired offspring—offspring which she herself could not bear, but which could come from her maidservant and her husband—he did not yield to his own desire but obeyed the authority of his wife? Abram used her for producing offspring, not for satisfying lust; not insulting her, but rather obeying; he believed that she could be a consolation to his wife in her barrenness, if, according to the womb of the maidservant, he made the child his by will, since nature could not do so. He thereby acted according to the principle stated by the Apostle: “Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does” (1 Cor. 7). He used the maidservant for giving birth through another woman to what he could not produce from his wife herself.

There is here no desire for wantonness, no disgrace of wickedness. The maidservant is handed over by the wife to the husband for the sake of offspring; she is accepted by the husband for the sake of offspring. From both, not the guilt of luxury but the fruit of nature is sought.

It follows:

(Vers. 5.) And Sarai said to Abram, “You act unjustly against me. I gave my maidservant into your embrace, and when she saw that she had conceived, she holds me in contempt. May the Lord judge between me and you.” Abram answered her, “Behold, your maidservant is in your hand; use her as you please.”

Thus, when the pregnant maidservant was behaving arrogantly toward her barren mistress, and Sarah, with a woman’s suspicion, attributed this rather to her husband, Abram demonstrated even to her that he was not a servile lover but a free father, and that in Hagar he had guarded the chastity of Sarah his wife, fulfilling not his own will but hers: he had accepted, not requested; approached, not yielded; sown, not loved.

For he says, “Behold, your maidservant is in your hands; use her as you please.” O man making manly use of women: temperately of his wife, obediently of his maidservant, and intemperately of none!

It follows:

(Verses 6–7.) Since Sarai was afflicting her, she fled. When the angel of the Lord found her beside a spring of water in the wilderness, which is on the road in the desert of Shur, [Col. 0955D] the Egyptian woman was naturally hurrying along the road to Shur, which leads through the desert to Egypt. Shur, where the angel found Sarah’s maidservant Hagar, lies between Kadesh and Barath. The desert extends as far as the Red Sea, which reaches the borders of Egypt. Kadesh, moreover, is a wilderness above the city of Petra. Scripture also records that the wilderness of Kadesh extends opposite Egypt.

It follows:

(Verses 9ff.) And the angel of the Lord said, “Return to your mistress and humble yourself under her hand. I shall multiply,” he said, “your offspring exceedingly, and it shall not be counted because of its multitude. Behold,” he said, “you have conceived and shall bear a son, and you shall call his name Ishmael, because God has heard your affliction. He shall be a wild man; his hand shall be against everyone, and everyone’s hand against him, and he shall pitch his tents opposite his brothers.”

Ishmael is interpreted as “hearing of God.” “He shall dwell opposite his brothers” signified that his offspring would dwell in the wilderness—that is, the wandering Saracens, with uncertain settlements, who attack all the nations adjoining the desert and are attacked by all.

It follows:

(Chapter 17.—Verses 1ff.) Hagar bore Abram a son, and he called his name Ishmael. He was seventy-six years old when Hagar bore Ishmael to him.

After Ishmael had been born from Hagar, Abram might have thought that what had been promised was fulfilled, when he had wished to adopt his household servant, until God said, “He shall not be your heir, but the one who shall come from you shall be your heir.” Therefore, lest he think that this promise had been fulfilled in the son of the maidservant, when he was already ninety-nine years old God appeared to him and said, “I am God Almighty; walk before me and be perfect. And I shall establish my covenant between me and you, and I shall multiply you exceedingly.”

Abram fell facedown, and God said to him, “I am he, and my covenant is with you, and you shall be the father of many nations. No longer shall your name be called Abram, but you shall be called Abraham, because I have made you the father of many nations. And I shall make you grow exceedingly.”

The Hebrews say that in his name God added the letter he to Abraham and Sarah—the divine name among them being the tetragrammaton. At first he was called Abram, which is interpreted “exalted father”; afterward he was called Abraham, which is translated “father of many.” For the following word, “nations,” is not contained in the name but is understood.

Nor is it surprising that, although among the Greeks and among us an a seems to have been added, we say that the letter he was added to Abraham. It is a peculiarity of that language to write with he but read with a, and conversely: they often pronounce the letter a as he.

It follows:

(Verses 7–8.) “And I shall establish kings among the nations who shall come forth from you. And I shall establish my covenant between me and you, and between your offspring after you throughout their generations, as an everlasting covenant, to be God to you and to your offspring after you. And I shall give to you and to your offspring after you the land of your sojourning, the whole land, as an everlasting possession, and I shall be their God.”

If anyone is troubled by the statement, “I shall give to you and to your offspring after you the land of your sojourning as an everlasting possession,” and asks how this may be understood as fulfilled—or as still awaiting fulfillment—since no earthly possession can be everlasting for any nation, let him know that what our translators render as “everlasting” is, in Greek, αἰώνιον (*aiōnion*), and means either that which has no end or that which extends to the end of this age.

It follows:

(Verses 9ff.) Again God said to Abraham, “And you shall keep my covenant, you and your offspring after you throughout their generations. This is the covenant that you shall keep between me and you, and your offspring after you: every male among you shall be circumcised, and you shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin, so that it may be a sign of my covenant between me and you. A child eight days old shall be circumcised among you. Every male throughout your generations, whether born in your household or bought, and whoever is not of your lineage, shall be circumcised. And my covenant shall be in your flesh as an everlasting covenant. The male whose foreskin has not been circumcised shall be cut off from his people, because he has broken my covenant.”

It should be noted that wherever we read “testament” in Greek, the Hebrew reads “covenant” or “pact.” For many things are called God’s testaments, apart from those two great ones, the Old and the New, as anyone may learn by reading.

The first testament, made with the first human being, is certainly this: “On the day you eat from it, you shall die” (Gen. 2). For although the law was later given more explicitly, and the Apostle says, “Where there is no law, there is no transgression” (Rom. 4), how can what is read in the psalm be true—“I have considered all sinners of the earth transgressors” (Ps. 118)—unless all are guilty of transgressing some law, since they are bound by some covenant?

Therefore, if even infants, as true faith holds, are born sinners—not properly, but originally—why do we confess that they need the grace of the remission of sins? Surely, in the same way that they are sinners, they are also recognized as transgressors of that law which was given in paradise, so that both statements written in Scripture may be true: “I have considered all sinners of the earth transgressors,” and, “Where there is no law, neither is there transgression.”

Consequently, because circumcision was a sign of regeneration, and because, on account of original sin, by which God’s first covenant was broken, generation would destroy the child unless regeneration set him free, these divine words must be understood as though they said: “Whoever has not been regenerated, that soul shall perish from his people, because he has dissolved God’s testament.” This would seem to compel us to understand the statement as referring only to this circumcision.

But now, since it expressly states what kind of covenant the child would have broken, it is permissible to understand it as referring to a covenant whose violation could pertain to a child. If, however, someone insists that it was spoken only of this circumcision—that the child broke God’s covenant in it because he was not circumcised—let him seek some mode of expression by which it may reasonably be understood that he broke the testament because, although it was not broken by him, it was broken in him.

Even so, it must be observed that the uncircumcised child’s soul does not unjustly perish through any negligence of its own, except by the obligation of original sin.

God also said to Abraham, “You shall not call your wife Sarai; rather, her name shall be Sarah. And I shall bless her, and from her I shall give you a son, whom I shall bless.”

Those are mistaken who think that she was first called *Sarra*, written with one r, and that another r was later added; and because r is the number one hundred among the Greeks, they imagine many absurd things about her name. However her name may have been changed, its explanation must be Hebrew, not Greek, since the name itself is Hebrew. No one, when calling someone by a name in another language, derives the etymology of that name from a different language.

Sarai was therefore first called with the letters sin, resh, yod. When the yod, that is, the i, was removed, the letter he was added, which is read as a; and she was called *Saraa*. The reason for the change of name is that previously she was called “my princess,” the mother of a household belonging to one person only; afterward she was called simply “princess,” since she was now destined to be the princess of all nations.

It follows:

(Vers. 16.) “And she shall become nations of peoples, and kings of nations shall arise from her.” How is the statement to Abraham concerning his son—“And kings of nations shall be from him”—to be understood? Is it because it was fulfilled according to earthly kingdoms, or should it be understood according to the Church? Or did it also come about literally on account of Esau?

It follows:

(Vers. 17.) Abraham fell facedown and laughed, saying in his heart, “Will a son be born to a man who is one hundred years old, and will Sarah, who is ninety, give birth?” For both were elderly, as Scripture testifies; but she was also barren and deprived of menstrual blood, and therefore could no longer give birth, even if she had not been barren.

Furthermore, if a woman of such advanced age that her customary menstruation still flows can bear a child from a young man but not from an old man, although an old man may still beget a child from a young woman—as Abraham was able to do with Keturah after Sarah’s death, because he found her of vigorous age—then this is what the Apostle emphasizes as remarkable when he says that Abraham’s body was already dead (Rom. 4). He means that, at that age, Abraham could not beget a child from every woman who still had some final period in which she could bear children.

We must understand the body as dead in relation to something, not in relation to everything. For if it were dead in relation to everything, then old age would no longer be the old age of a living person but the corpse of a dead one.

The question may also be resolved in this way: Abraham later fathered children by Keturah because the power of begetting that he had received from the Lord remained even after his wife’s death. Nevertheless, the solution we have followed seems preferable to me, because a hundred-year-old man in our time cannot beget a child from any woman, whereas at that time people lived so long that one hundred years did not yet make a man decrepit with old age.

It follows:

(Verses 18ff.) And Abraham said to the Lord, “If only Ishmael might live before you!” And the Lord said to Abraham, “Sarah your wife shall bear you a son, and you shall call his name Isaac; and I shall establish my covenant with him as an everlasting covenant, and with his offspring after him. I have also heard you concerning Ishmael. Behold, I shall bless him and increase him and multiply him exceedingly. He shall beget twelve leaders, and I shall make him into a great nation. But I shall establish my covenant with Isaac, whom Sarah shall bear to you at this time next year.”

It should nevertheless be known that four people in the Old Testament were called by their names before they were born, without any veil or concealment: Ishmael, Isaac, Samson, and Josiah.

Here the promises concerning the calling of the nations are clearer in Isaac, that is, in the son of promise, by whom grace rather than nature is signified. For a son is promised from an old man and a barren old woman. Although God also brings about the natural process of procreation, wherever God’s work is evident—when nature is impaired and has ceased—there grace is understood more clearly.

It follows:

(Verses 22ff.) When he had finished speaking with him, God went up from Abraham. Abraham took his son Ishmael, all the male servants born in his household, everyone he had bought, and every male among the men of his household, and he circumcised the flesh of their foreskins that very day, just as God had commanded him. He was ninety-nine years old when he circumcised the flesh of his foreskin, and his son Ishmael had completed twelve years at the time of his circumcision. On the same day Abraham was circumcised, and his son Ishmael, and all the men of his household—both those born in the household and those bought, as well as foreigners—were circumcised together.

For if Adam had kept God’s covenant, Abraham would not have received this covenant. But because Adam first acknowledged the guilt of disobedience in this member, it was fitting that Abraham should receive in this member the sign of obedience a second time, so that it might be shown that the obedient would one day beget children for life, whereas formerly transgressors had begotten children for death.

And because this was to take place not through generation but through regeneration, circumcision was now commanded when a son was promised from Sarah. Moreover, the command that not only sons but also household servants and purchased servants be circumcised testifies that this grace pertains to everyone. For what else does circumcision signify but nature renewed from its old condition? And what else does the eighth day signify but Christ, who, when the week was complete—that is, after the Sabbath—rose again?

The names of the parents are changed; everything resounds with newness; and in the Old Testament the New is overshadowed. For what else is called the Old Testament but concealment? And what else is called the New but revelation of the Old?

Abraham’s laughter was the exultation of one rejoicing, not the mockery of one doubting. His words in his heart—“If a son is to be born to me at one hundred, and if Sarah at ninety is to give birth”—are not words of doubt but of astonishment. Therefore, because Abraham laughed for joy, the son was called Isaac, that is, “laughter.” This laughter must be understood in a good sense.

It follows:

(Chapter 18.—Verses 1ff.) God appeared to him in the valley of Mamre, as he was sitting at the entrance of his tent in the heat of the day. When he lifted his eyes, three men appeared to him standing near him. When he saw them, he ran to meet them from the entrance of the tent, bowed to the ground, and said, “Lord, if I have found favor in your eyes, do not pass by your servant. Let me bring a little water and wash your feet; rest under the tree. I shall set out a morsel of bread, and strengthen your hearts; afterward you shall pass on, since you have turned aside to your servant.” They answered, “Do as you have said.”

There is no doubt that the three men who came to him were angels, although some think that one of them was the Lord Christ, asserting that he was visible even before he put on flesh. It certainly belongs to the nature of divine power—an invisible, incorporeal, and immutable nature—to appear even to mortal eyes without any change in itself, not through what it is but through something subject to it. And what is not subject to it?

Nevertheless, if they confirm that one of these three was Christ because, when Abraham saw three, he addressed God in the singular, why do they not also consider that two of them came so that the Sodomites might be destroyed, while Abraham was still speaking to one, calling him Lord and interceding that he should not destroy the righteous together with the impious Sodomites? Lot likewise received those two in such a way that, in speaking with them, he too called them Lord in the singular.

For although he had said to them in the plural, “Behold, my lords, turn aside into the house of your servant,” and other words recorded there, it is nevertheless afterward written: “And the angels took his hand, and the hand of his wife, and the hands of his two daughters, because the Lord spared them.”

It follows:

[Col. 0959B] (Verses 6ff.) Abraham hurried into the tent to Sarah and said to her, “Quickly, mix three measures of fine flour and make cakes baked under the ashes.” He himself ran to the herd, took from it a tender and choice calf, and gave it to the servant, who hurried and cooked it. He then took butter and milk, and the calf he had cooked, and set them before them; while he himself stood beside them under the tree.

Three measures are three jars, so that we may recognize the same mystery here and in the Gospel, where the woman is said to leaven three measures.

It is asked: if he understood them to be angels, how could he invite them to this human nourishment, which is necessary for the refreshment of mortal flesh but not for the immortality of angels? Because, clothed with the certain and altogether inviolable gift of immortality, they ate not from necessity but from possibility, if they wished. They did so not because they needed food but because they wished, in a certain humanity, to conform themselves to human beings.

Nor should we believe that they appeared as phantoms when human beings received them as guests. Such bodies are deprived not of the power but of the need to eat and drink.

Abraham’s tent, moreover, bore the type of earthly Jerusalem: there the prophets and apostles dwelt for a time; there also, when the Lord first came, he was received by believers and hung upon the wood by unbelievers.

In the three men who came to him, the advent of the Lord Christ was foretold, accompanied by two angels. Most people understand these two as Moses and Elijah: one, the lawgiver of the ancient law, who indicated the Lord’s coming through that same law; the other, the one who will come at the end of the world to announce Christ’s second coming and preach his Gospel to the Jews. Hence, on the mountain, when the Lord had been transfigured, these two—Moses and Elijah—were seen with him by the apostles (Mark 9).

That Abraham, seeing three, worshiped one, namely the Lord and Savior, showed that he was awaiting his coming, in accordance with what the Lord says in the Gospel: “Abraham your father rejoiced that he might see my day; he saw it and was glad” (John 8). At that time he saw beforehand the future mystery of the sacrament. Hence he washed their feet, signifying the washing and purification that would occur at the end of the world; for feet signify the last things.

He also prepared a banquet, namely a fattened calf. This tender and fattened calf is the body of the Lord Jesus Christ. It is also the Lord’s calf, sacrificed for the salvation of believers upon the tree of the cross. It is the calf of the Lord’s body that is killed in the Gospel for the sinful son.

He also set out butter and milk with the flesh of the calf. The Apostle announces that milk represents the law when he says, “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food, for you were not yet able to receive it; indeed, even now you are not able” (1 Cor. 3). He had handed on to them the commandment of the law, like milk pressed from the breasts of the two tablets, that is, the covenant of faith. Because of their immature understanding, they were not yet able to receive the solid and robust food of evangelical teaching.

The tenderest and richest butter, however, is the testimony of the Gospels, which is given to believers like oil as a sign. Thus Abraham set out the calf with milk and butter to be eaten, because the body of the Lord, which is the calf, cannot exist without the milk of the law, nor the milk of the law without butter, that is, without the testimony of the Gospel.

The three measures from which Sarah made cakes baked under the ashes signified the three sons of Noah, from whom the whole human race was born. Believing in the divine Trinity, they were to be kneaded through the water of baptism by the Church, of which Sarah was an image, and brought together in the one bread of Christ’s body. These are the three measures that the woman in the Gospel is said to have leavened.

The cakes were unleavened because the unity of believers must be without the leaven of malice, without the illness of wickedness, and without the leaven of doctrine. They were baked under the ashes so that, having been cooked by the heat of the Holy Spirit through repentance for former sins, they might become acceptable, like food pleasing to God. Their sitting under the tree was a sign of the Lord’s Passion, whose preachers they are.

It follows:

(Verses 9ff.) When they had eaten, they said to him, “Where is Sarah your wife?” He answered, “Behold, she is in the tent.” He said to him, “I shall return to you at this time, with life as companion, and Sarah your wife shall have a son.”

When Sarah heard this, she laughed behind the door of the tent, for both were old and advanced in age, and Sarah’s customary menstrual flow had ceased. She laughed secretly, saying, “After I have grown old, and my lord is elderly, shall I give myself to pleasure?”

The Lord said to Abraham, “Why did Sarah laugh, saying, ‘Shall I truly give birth, an old woman that I am?’ Is anything difficult for God? At the appointed time I shall return to you, with life as companion, and Sarah shall have a son.”

It is asked why the Lord rebuked Sarah when Abraham also laughed. The answer is that Abraham’s laughter was one of astonishment and joy, whereas Sarah’s was one of doubt. This could be judged by the one who knows human hearts.

It follows:

(Vers. 15.) Sarah denied it, saying, “I did not laugh,” because she was terrified. How did Abraham understand that the one speaking with him was God, when Sarah even dared to deny that she had laughed? Perhaps Sarah thought that they were human beings, whereas Abraham understood them to be God because certain signs of divine majesty were present and visible?

It follows:

(Verses 16–17.) When the men had departed from there, they directed their eyes toward Sodom; and Abraham walked with them, escorting them. The Lord said, “Can I hide from Abraham what I am about to do, since he shall become a great nation, and all the nations of the earth shall be blessed in him?”

Here those two promises are expressed very briefly and yet completely: Israel according to the flesh, and all nations according to faith.

“For I know that he will command his sons and his household after him to keep the way of the Lord and to do justice and judgment, so that the Lord may bring upon Abraham all that he has spoken to him.”

Behold, here the Lord promises Abraham not only rewards but also the obedience of justice by his children, so that the promised rewards may likewise be fulfilled concerning them.

It follows:

(Verses 20 ff.) Then the Lord said, “The outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah has become great, and their sin has become exceedingly grave. I will go down and see whether they have actually done according to the outcry that has come to me, or not, so that I may know.” We must understand these words not as those of one uncertain which of the alternatives will occur, but of one angry and threatening. Sin accompanied by a voice is guilt in action; sin accompanied by an outcry is guilt combined with license and boastfulness.

But since he said, “I will go down and see,” and similar things, why does the omnipotent Lord, who knows everything, seem to doubt before making an investigation, unless it is to set before us an example of gravity, so that we do not presume to believe evil about people before we have established it? And behold, through the angels he descended to learn of their wickedness; immediately afterward he struck the criminals down. [Col. 0961A] Yet he who is patient and gentle, he of whom it is written, “But you, Lord, judge all things with tranquillity,” when he found them involved in so great a crime, as if he had set aside his patience, anticipated the day of the final judgment.

Behold, he believed the evil only with difficulty when he heard of it, yet he struck without delay when he discovered it through investigation, so that he might evidently give us an example: greater crimes are to be believed only slowly when they are reported, but are to be punished more swiftly when they are truthfully recognized.

And they turned away from there and went toward Sodom, while Abraham still stood before the Lord. Drawing near, he said: “Will you indeed destroy the righteous with the wicked? If fifty righteous are found in the city, will they perish together? Will you not spare that place for the sake of the fifty righteous, if they are in it? Far be it from you to do such a thing, to kill the righteous with the wicked.”

It is commonly asked whether what God said concerning Sodom—that he would not destroy the place if ten righteous were found there—was a particular sentence applying to that city, or whether it is to be understood generally of all places: that God spares a place in which even ten righteous are found. In this question, it is not necessary that we be compelled to interpret it of every place. Nevertheless, it could be said in this way concerning Sodom because God knew that not even ten righteous were there. Thus he answered Abraham in order to signify that so many could not even be found there, thereby emphasizing the magnitude of their wickedness. For God was not obliged to spare such wicked people, nor to destroy the righteous along with them, since he could free the righteous from their midst and inflict on the wicked the punishment they deserved.

But, as I have said, to display the malignity of their multitude he said, “If I find ten there, I will spare the whole city”—as though he were saying: “Certainly I can neither destroy the godly with the wicked nor, for that reason, spare the wicked, since, after freeing and separating the godly from them, I can repay the wicked with what they deserve.”

Why did Abraham call himself dust and ashes, although he had received such great promises from God? It was so that he might temper the loftiness of the promises by submitting himself in humility. For it is clearly understood in what position he placed himself: even while speaking with God, he considered himself dust and ashes. If, then, he so despised himself, although he had risen to the honour of divine conversation, it must be weighed with careful attention by what punishment those will be struck who make no progress toward the highest things and yet exalt themselves over the smallest.

But what does it signify that the Lord said that Sodom would be saved if anywhere from fifty righteous down to ten were found there? He placed the number fifty as a sign of repentance, in case they should turn and be saved; for the number fifty is always related to repentance. Hence David also composed a psalm of repentance in that number.

Therefore, when God sees that the life of sinners is wholly unwilling to return to repentance—the repentance signified by the number fifty—he immediately restrains the heat of immoderate lust with the fire of Gehenna. But he said that Sodom would not perish if there were as many as ten righteous, because if the name of Christ is found in anyone through the observance of the Ten Commandments, that person does not perish. [Col. 0961D] For the figure of the number ten points to the cross of Christ.

It follows:

(Cap. XIX.—Verses 1 ff.) Two angels came to Sodom in the evening, while Lot was sitting at the gate of the city. When he saw them, he rose and went to meet them; bowing face-down to the ground, he said, “I beg you, my lords, turn aside into your servant’s house and stay there. Wash your feet, and in the morning continue on your way.” They said, “Not at all; we shall spend the night in the square.” But he pressed them strongly, and they turned aside to him.

When they had entered his house, he prepared a feast for them, baked unleavened bread, and they ate. For it is entirely credible that Abraham, in the three men, and Lot, in the two men, recognized the Lord. They addressed them using the singular number even when they supposed them to be human beings. They would not have received them in any other way—serving them as mortals in need of human refreshment—unless there was in them something that distinguished them, even though they appeared as human beings: something of divine radiance, such as is usually found in prophets, so that those who offered them hospitality could not doubt that there was something divine in them. Therefore, they sometimes worshiped them in the plural and at other times worshiped the Lord in them in the singular.

Scripture testifies that they were angels, not only in this book of Genesis, where these events are related, but also in the Epistle to the Hebrews, where hospitality is praised: “Through it,” he says, “some, without knowing it, received angels as guests” (Heb. 13).

The angels are therefore said to have been compelled, as guests, to enter Lot’s house so that Lot’s charity might be tested, proved, and rewarded, and so that the greatness of hospitality might be demonstrated. The angels entered the hospitable house in order to rescue. But into houses closed to guests, fire entered in order to destroy the sinners. Therefore guests are not to be avoided but willingly invited.

It follows:

(Verses 4 ff.) But before they went to bed, the men of the city surrounded the house, from boy to old man, the entire people together. They called Lot and said to him, “Where are the men who came in to you during the night? Bring them out to us, so that we may know them.”

Lot went out to them, shutting the door behind him, and said, “Do not, I beg you, my brothers; do not commit this evil. I have two daughters who have not yet known a man. I will bring them out to you, and you may abuse them as you please, provided that you do nothing evil to these men, for they have entered beneath the shelter of my roof.”

It is rightly asked why he wished to prostitute his daughters as a compensation, so that his guests would suffer nothing of this kind from the Sodomites: whether compensation for crimes or for sins of any kind is to be admitted, so that we may do something evil lest another do something worse; or whether this should rather be attributed to Lot’s disturbance, not to his considered judgment, since he said this. Such compensation is admitted only with extreme and dangerous error. If, however, it is attributed to human disturbance and to a mind so deeply agitated, it is in no way to be imitated.

It follows:

(Verses 9 ff.) They pressed Lot with the greatest violence. They were already close to breaking down the doors. And behold, the men stretched out their hands, brought Lot inside to them, and shut the door. They struck those who were outside with blindness, from the least to the greatest, so that they could not find the door.

It is not without reason that the question is raised how they could have become incapable of finding the door: if they had been struck with such blindness that they could see absolutely nothing, then, disturbed by their misfortune, they would no longer have continued searching for it. Those who were seeking Elisha were also struck with this aorasia, that is, blindness.

It follows:

(Verses 12 ff.) They said to Lot, “Do you have here anyone belonging to you—a son-in-law, or sons, or daughters? Bring out from this place all who belong to you. For we are going to destroy this place, because their outcry has grown great before the Lord, who sent us to destroy them.”

Because the outcry of sinners is said to have risen to heaven, they were therefore to be punished from heaven.

Lot went out and spoke to his sons-in-law, who were going to take his daughters, and said, “Rise and leave this place, because the Lord is going to destroy this city.” But he seemed to them to be speaking as one who was joking.

When morning came, the angels urged him, saying, “Rise, take your wife and your two daughters whom you have, lest you too perish together in the wickedness of the city.”

A question arises from the statement, “He spoke to his sons-in-law, who were going to take his daughters,” since afterward Lot’s two daughters are said to have been virgins, and earlier he himself had said to the Sodomites, “Behold, I have two daughters who have not known a man.” Yet now Scripture mentions that he had sons-in-law. Some think that the daughters who had husbands remained in Sodom, while those who were virgins went out with their father.

But since Scripture does not say this, the Hebrew truth must be explained. In it we read: “Lot went out and spoke to his betrothed sons-in-law, who were going to take his daughters.” His virgin daughters, therefore, had not yet been joined in marriage.

It follows:

[Col. 0963A] (Verses 16 ff.) While he hesitated, they seized his hand and the hand of his wife and of his two daughters, because the Lord was sparing him. They brought him out and placed him beyond the city. There they said to him, “Save your life. Do not look behind you, and do not remain anywhere in the surrounding region. Save yourself on the mountain, lest you too perish.”

Lot said to them, “I beg you, my lord: since your servant has found favour before you, and you have magnified your mercy, which you have shown me by saving my life, I cannot be saved on the mountain, lest evil overtake me. There is a city nearby to which I can flee. It is small, and I shall be saved there. Is it not a little one? Then my life will live there.”

He said to him, “Behold, I have also granted you this request, so that I will not overthrow the city on whose behalf you have spoken.”

To flee from burning Sodom is to avoid the unlawful fires of the flesh. The height of the mountains is the purity of those who practise continence. Or certainly, those who remain attached to carnal intercourse are, as it were, on a mountain, provided that they are not dissolved by any pleasure of the flesh beyond the proper union for the begetting of children. For what does it mean to stand on a mountain except not to seek the fruit of propagation in the flesh? To stand on a mountain is not to cling carnally to the flesh.

But because there are many who abandon the crimes of the flesh and yet, once placed in marriage, preserve only the rights of lawful intercourse, Lot did indeed leave Sodom, but did not immediately reach the mountains. The condemnable life has been abandoned, but the height of conjugal continence has not yet been carefully maintained.

There is, however, in the middle, the city of Segor, which saves the weak fugitive. For when spouses are joined to one another through incontinence and flee the downfall of crimes, they are nevertheless saved through forgiveness. They find, as it were, a small city in which they are defended from the fires, because married life is not remarkable for its virtues, yet it is secure from punishments.

Thus Lot says to the angel, “There is a city nearby to which I can flee; it is small, and I shall be saved there. Is it not a little one? Then my life will live there.” It is said to be nearby, yet it is declared safe for salvation, because married life is neither far removed from the world nor excluded from the joy of salvation.

Spouses preserve this life of theirs, as though in a small city, in their conduct when they intercede for one another through continual prayers. Hence the angel rightly says to that same Lot, “Behold, I have also granted you this request, so that I will not overthrow the city on whose behalf you have spoken,” because when supplication is poured out before God, the life of such spouses is by no means condemned.

Then the Lord rained upon Sodom and Gomorrah sulphur and fire from the Lord out of heaven, and overthrew those cities and the entire surrounding region, all the inhabitants of the cities, and everything living on the land.

Why were they punished with sulphurous fire, unless it was so that the most foul heat of lust might be punished by the most foul heat of flames? When fiery rain came from heaven, that entire region was turned to ashes, where the practice of sexual offences against males had grown so strong that in our own time we see impious nations committing such acts openly.

Their punishment was also an image of the future divine judgment. It may further be asked why, in the days of Noah, God avenged the sin of the world with water, while here the Sodomites were punished with fire. Was it not because the natural sin of lust with women is condemned by a milder element, whereas the unnatural sin of lust with men is avenged by the burning of a harsher element? There the earth, washed by waters, grows green again; here, burned by flames, it withers in eternal sterility.

Those who were delivered were forbidden by the angels to look back, evidently because, if we hope to escape the final judgment, we must not return in our hearts to the former life from which we have been stripped by grace. Thus Lot’s wife, when she looked back, remained behind and was changed into salt, providing all the faithful with a certain seasoning by which they may gain wisdom and avoid that example.

It follows:

(Verses 27 ff.) Abraham rose early in the morning and went to the place where he had previously stood with the Lord. He looked out over Sodom and Gomorrah and over the whole land of that region, and saw smoke rising from the earth like the smoke of a furnace. When God overthrew the cities of that region, he remembered Abraham and rescued Lot from the overthrow of the cities in which he had lived.

Scripture attributes Lot’s deliverance more particularly to Abraham’s merits, so that we may understand that Lot was called righteous in a certain sense—especially because he worshiped the one true God and, in comparison with the crimes of the Sodomites, among whom he lived, could not be bent toward a similar life.

It follows:

(Verses 30.) Lot went up from Segor and settled on the mountain, and his two daughters with him, for he was afraid to remain in Segor. He himself and his two daughters lived in a cave.

It is strange if this is the very mountain to which he went up of his own accord, although, when the Lord advised and commanded him to do so, he had refused to go there. It is asked why, after initially preferring Segor to a flight into the mountains and wishing to be delivered there as his dwelling place, he now migrated from Segor to the mountain.

We shall answer that the Hebrew conjecture concerning Segor is true: frequently damaged by earthquakes, it was first called Vala and afterward Salisa. It is the same place as Vala, which is now called Zoara. It lies near the Dead Sea, and balsam and palm-fruit grow there, signs of its ancient fertility.

No one should be troubled by the fact that Segor is called Zoara, since both names mean “little” or “smaller.” Segor is called Zoara in Hebrew and Syriac; Vala, however, is interpreted as “swallowed up.” Lot was afraid, saying, “Lest evil overtake me there,” because if, while the other cities were still standing, that city had often been overthrown, how much more could it fail to be preserved now in the general ruin? This occasion of unbelief also led to intercourse with his daughters. For after seeing the other cities overthrown while this one remained standing, and after being rescued by God’s help according to what he had heard promised to him, he should certainly not have doubted God.

It follows:

(Verses 31 ff.) The elder daughter said to the younger, “Our father is old, and no man remains in the land who can come in to us according to the custom of the whole earth. Come, let us give our father wine to drink, and let us sleep with him, so that we may preserve offspring from our father.”

They gave their father wine to drink that night. The elder entered and slept with her father; but he did not know when she lay down or when she arose. The next night the elder said to the younger, “Behold, I slept yesterday with my father. Let us give him wine to drink tonight also, and you shall sleep with him, so that we may preserve offspring from our father.”

It appears that Lot’s daughters had heard something about the consummation of the age, which was to come through fire, but, as girls, did not fully understand what they had learned. They did not know that, after the Sodomites had been destroyed by fire, a great period of time still remained for the world. They suspected that something like what they had heard had happened in the days of Noah, and that, in order to restore the human race, they alone had been preserved with their aged father.

Thus they thought that their desire to restore the human race and renew the age must have its beginning from themselves. Although it seemed to them a great crime to steal intercourse with their father, they considered it a still graver impiety if the hope of what they supposed to be the human race’s continuation were destroyed through the preservation of chastity.

For this reason they formed their plan, as I judge, with lesser guilt but greater hope and purpose: they softened and relaxed their father’s grief or severity with wine; entering separately on separate nights, they conceived by a father unaware of the conception, and did not repeat the act.

Where is the guilt of lust here, where the crime of incest? How, then, can that be attributed to vice which was not repeated in the deed? Since they sought offspring for the preservation of the race, moved by a human and natural affection, and believed that they could find no other men—as though the whole world had been consumed in that conflagration—they slept with their father.

Yet they perceived that their father shrank so greatly from the act that they did not believe they could accomplish it unless they arranged for him to be unaware, as it is written: “They gave him wine to drink, and while he was unaware they lay with him.” [Col. 0965A]

He is therefore indeed to be blamed, though not to the extent of their incest, but to the extent deserved by his drunkenness. For the eternal law also condemns this, since it permits food and drink according to the natural order only for the preservation of health.

Although there is a great difference between a habitual drunkard and a drunken person—for a drunkard is not always drunk, nor is everyone who is occasionally drunk consequently a drunkard—nevertheless, in the case of a righteous man, the cause of this condition must be sought, even if it was not habitual drunkenness but certainly drunkenness.

What finally compelled him to consent to or believe the repeated serving of wine by his daughters, or perhaps to receive wine that they had not even mixed but repeatedly offered to him, unless the pain of his desolation and maternal mourning was driven from the thought of his drunken mind? He evidently supposed that they too were drinking, and we cannot see how it was fitting for a righteous man to provide such consolation for the three of them while they acted by some deception so that he would drink.

Or were they able, by some exceedingly evil Sodomite art, to make their father so drunk with only a few cups that they could commit that sin with him, or rather concerning him, while he was unaware? We, however, defend the holy Scriptures, not the sins of human beings.

It follows:

(Verses 36 ff.) Thus both daughters of Lot conceived from their father. The elder gave birth to a son and called his name Moab; he is the father of the Moabites to the present day. The younger also gave birth to a son and called his name Ammon; he is the father of the Ammonites to this day.

Moab is interpreted as “from the father.” Ammon, however—whose name is explained as meaning “son of my kindred” or “son of my people”—is derived in such a way that part of the sense is supplied by the name’s meaning and part by the word itself. Ammon, from whom the Ammonites were named, is called “my people.”

Thus God, who knows how to make good works even from an evil human deed, brought forth from that origin the nations he willed. He reported these things through his Scriptures; he did not command them to be done, but warned that they were to be avoided, and did not present them as objects of imitation.

For the five cities that were consumed by fiery rains signify, unless I am mistaken, that all who have handled the five bodily senses lustfully will be burned in that future conflagration.

Lot, however, Abraham’s brother, righteous and hospitable in Sodom, pure and undefiled by every contamination of the Sodomites, who deserved to escape safely from that fire which was an image of the future judgment, represented the type of the body of Christ. That body, present in all the saints, now groans among the wicked and impious, does not consent to their deeds, and at the end of the age will be delivered from their association, while they are condemned to the punishment of eternal fire.

But another kind of human beings is represented in Lot’s wife: those who, although called by God’s grace, look backward, unlike Paul, who forgets what lies behind and stretches forward to what lies ahead (Phil. 3). Hence the Lord himself says, “No one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of heaven” (Luke 9).

Nor did he leave unmentioned that example by which he might season us, as it were, with salt, so that we would not foolishly neglect this evil but wisely beware of it: “Remember Lot’s wife.”

Likewise, in Lot himself, when his daughters lay with him, not the fact that he was delivered from Sodom but something else was signified. At that time Lot himself appears to have represented the future Law: certain people begotten from it and placed under the Law, by understanding it wrongly, in a certain sense intoxicate it and, by failing to use it lawfully, produce the works of unbelief.

“For the law is good,” the Apostle says, “if one uses it lawfully” (1 Tim. 1). Nevertheless, we do not thereby justify this deed, whether of Lot or of his daughters, because it signified something that foretold the future perversity of certain people. They intended one thing when they did this, while God, who permitted it to happen, intended something else, so that he might also display through it a sign of future things.

Therefore, when this deed is narrated in Holy Scripture, it is prophecy; but when it is considered in the lives of those who committed it, it is a crime.

It follows:

[Col. 0966A] (Cap. XX.—Verses 1 ff.) Abraham departed from there toward the southern land and lived between Kadesh and Shur. He sojourned in Gerar. He said of his wife Sarah, “She is my sister.” Therefore Abimelech, king of Gerar, sent for her and took her.

But God came to Abimelech in a dream by night and said to him, “Behold, you are going to die because of the woman whom you have taken, for she has a husband.” Abimelech, however, had not touched her. He said, “Lord, will you destroy an ignorant and righteous nation? Did he not himself say, ‘She is my sister,’ and did she herself not say, ‘He is my brother’? In the integrity of my heart and purity of my hands I have done this.”

It may be asked how Abraham, even at that age, was still afraid of being endangered because of Sarah’s beauty. Rather, the power of her appearance is remarkable: she was still capable of being loved. Therefore, in Gerar, before King Abimelech, he did with his wife what he had done in Egypt, and she was likewise returned to him untouched.

It follows:

(Verses 6, 7.) God said to him, “I know that you did this with an upright heart. Therefore I guarded you, so that you would not sin against me, and I did not permit you to touch her. Now, therefore, return the man his wife, for he is a prophet, and he will pray for you, and you will live. But if you do not return her, know that you will certainly die, you and all that is yours.”

When God said to Abimelech concerning Sarah, “I spared you so that you would not sin against me,” and warned him that she was Abraham’s wife although he thought she was Abraham’s sister, we must observe and note that people sin against God when they commit such acts, thinking that sins of the flesh of this kind are to be regarded lightly.

When he said to him, “Behold, you are going to die,” this too must be noted: God speaks as though predicting something that will certainly happen, while his warning is intended to prevent sin by inducing him to abstain from it.

It follows:

(Verses 8 ff.) Abimelech immediately rose during the night, called all his servants, and told them all these words in their hearing. All the men were very much afraid.

Abimelech also called Abraham and said to him, “What have you done to us? What have we done against you, that you have brought upon me and upon my kingdom such a great sin? You have done to us what you ought not to have done.”

Abraham replied, “I thought to myself, ‘Perhaps there is no fear of God in this place, and they will kill me because of my wife.’ Besides, she truly is my sister: she is the daughter of my father, though not the daughter of my mother.”

Sarah was Abraham’s sister by his father, and therefore his relative—his brother’s daughter, not his sister. At that time such marriages had not yet been prohibited by law; men took their sisters as wives. But the more ancient such a practice was, compelled by necessity, the more blameworthy it became afterward, when religion prohibited it.

Then Abimelech took sheep and cattle, male and female slaves, and gave them to Abraham. He also returned his wife Sarah to him and said, “Behold, my land is before you; dwell wherever it pleases you.”

To Sarah he said, “Behold, I have given your brother a thousand pieces of silver. Let this be for you a covering for the eyes of all who are with you, and wherever you go, remember that you have been exposed.”

Faustus the Manichaean calls the righteous and faithful man the most infamous trafficker in his own marriage. He claims that Abraham, out of greed and concern for his belly, at different times sold his wife Sarah—who, because she was very beautiful, falsely said that she was his sister—to the two kings, Abimelech and Pharaoh, for intercourse.

With a lying mouth he does not separate honesty from shame, but with a slanderous mouth turns everything into a crime. Abraham’s action seems similar to pandering, but such people are unable, in the light of the eternal law, to distinguish righteous deeds from sins. To them steadfastness may appear obstinacy, and the virtue of confidence may be judged the vice of rashness. Whatever similar accusations are brought forward arise from people who do not see rightly against those who are not acting wrongly.

Abraham did not consent to his wife’s dishonour or sell her adultery. Just as Sarah had not given her servant to her husband’s lust but voluntarily brought her forward for the duty of bearing children—without disturbing the natural order, commanding one who obeyed rather than yielding to one who desired—so Abraham kept silent about his chaste wife, who was joined to him with a chaste heart. He had no doubt that the virtue of chastity dwelt in her soul. He called her his sister rather than his wife so that, if he were killed by foreigners and impious men, she would not be held captive by them, being confident in his God that he would not permit her to suffer anything shameful or criminal.

His faith and hope did not deceive him. Pharaoh, terrified by prodigies and afflicted with many evils because of her, learned by divine revelation that she was Abraham’s wife and restored her unharmed and with honour. Abimelech, similarly warned and instructed in a dream, did the same.

Now, in this event, recorded and faithfully narrated in the divine books, who would not delight in investigating the prophetic meaning and knocking with devout faith and zeal at the door of the sacrament, so that the Lord might open it and show who was then represented by that man, and whose wife she is who, during this pilgrimage and among foreigners, is not permitted to be polluted or stained, so that she may be presented to her husband without spot or wrinkle?

The Church rightly lives in the glory of Christ, so that her beauty may be an honour to her husband. Thus, because of Sarah’s beauty, Abraham was honoured among foreigners, and to him of whom it is said in the Song of Songs, “O beautiful among women” (Song 1), kings offer gifts because of the excellence of that beauty.

King Abimelech offered gifts to Sarah, marvelling in her at the beauty of a form that he could love but could not violate. The holy Church too is secretly the wife of the Lord Jesus Christ. For secretly, inwardly, in the hidden spiritual sanctuary, the human soul clings to the Word of God, so that “the two become one flesh.” The Apostle commends this great sacrament of marriage in Christ and in the Church (Eph. 5).

Therefore the earthly kingdom of this age, represented by the kings who were not permitted to violate Sarah, did not experience or find the Church as Christ’s wife—that is, as one who faithfully clings to him in submission as to her chief husband—except when it attempted to violate her and, on divine testimony, yielded in faith to the marriage. Corrected also in later kings, it honoured with gifts her whom, in earlier kings, it had not been able to subject to its corruption.

For what was then represented first and afterward in the same king is fulfilled in this kingdom through its earlier and later kings.

When the Church is said to be a sister from the father, not from the mother, the relationship of heavenly grace, which will remain forever, is commended—not the earthly generation that will be abolished. According to this grace we will no longer be a mortal race, but, having received the power to be called and to be the children of God, we will truly be so. We did not receive this grace from the mother Synagogue of Christ according to the flesh, but from God the Father.

Christ taught us to deny and not acknowledge this earthly relationship, which gives birth temporarily unto death, when he called us into another life where no one dies. He said to his disciples, “Do not call anyone your father on earth, for one is your Father, who is in heaven” (Matt. 23).

He provided an example of this when he said, “Who is my mother? Or who are my brothers?” Then, stretching out his hand over his disciples, he said, “These are my brothers” (Mark 2). And lest anyone think of earthly kinship in this designation, he added, “Whoever does the will of my Father, that person is my brother and sister and mother” (ibid.).

It was as though he were saying: “I call this relationship one that comes from God the Father, not from the mother Synagogue. For now I call people to eternal life, where I was born immortal, not to temporal life, for the sake of which I became mortal.”

Why, then, is it concealed from foreigners whose wife the Church is, while it is not concealed whose sister she is? The reason readily presents itself: it is hidden and difficult to understand how the human soul is joined or united to the Word of God—or, if something better and clearer can be said, how the bridegroom and bride, or husband and wife, are called Christ and the Church, although one is God and the other is a creature.

But by what relationship Christ and all the saints are joined—namely, divine grace, not earthly blood relationship—is expressed as being from the father and not from the mother. This is more easily spoken and heard with greater safety. All the saints are brothers to one another through the same grace; but none of them is the bridegroom within their fellowship.

Thus foreigners believed much more easily and readily that Christ was a man of the highest righteousness and wisdom—not falsely, since he was a man—but they did not understand how he was also God. Hence Jeremiah says, “He is a man, and who will know him?” (Jer. 17). “He is a man,” because it is disclosed that he is a brother; “and who will know him?” because it is concealed that he is the bridegroom.

(Cap. XXI.—Verses 1 ff.) The Lord visited Sarah as he had promised, and fulfilled what he had spoken. She conceived and bore a son in her old age, at the time that God had foretold. Abraham called the name of his son whom Sarah bore to him Isaac, and he circumcised him on the eighth day, as God had commanded him, when he was one hundred years old.

Isaac was born at this age of his father. He was born to Abraham, according to God’s promise, as a son from Sarah, and he named him Isaac. His father had laughed when he was promised, marvelling with joy; his mother had also laughed when he was promised again through the three men, doubting with joy, although the angel reproved her. Although that laughter was laughter of joy, it was not yet accompanied by complete faith; afterward she was confirmed in faith by the same angel. From this, therefore, the child received his name.

A great sacrament was signified in Abraham’s two sons. One, Ishmael, was born according to the flesh from the slave woman called Hagar; the other was born from the free woman Sarah according to the promise. Both were from Abraham’s seed, but the one was begotten by the customary course of nature, while the other was given by the promise signifying grace. In the former, human practice is displayed; in the latter, divine beneficence is commended.

But since what was to be signified was God’s gift, freely bestowed by grace upon ungrateful people, it was fitting that the son be given in a way that nature’s ordinary course did not allow. Nature no longer promised children through such a union of male and female as could have existed between Abraham and Sarah at that age, especially since the woman was also barren. Nor could she give birth even then, when it was not age that lacked fertility but fertility that was lacking to age.

Therefore, since the fruit of posterity was not owed to nature in this condition, it signifies that human nature, corrupted by sin and therefore condemned by right, deserved no true happiness in the future. Isaac, rightly born through the promise, signifies the children of grace, citizens of the free city, companions of eternal peace.

It follows:

(Verses 6, 7.) Sarah said, “God has made laughter for me; everyone who hears will laugh with me.” And again she said, “Who would have believed Abraham that Sarah would nurse a son, whom she bore to him when he was already old?”

Isaac is interpreted as “Laughter.” It referred not to the disgrace of mockery but to the celebration of joy, which Sarah expressed when Isaac was born and was given this name. For she said, “The Lord has made laughter for me; whoever hears will rejoice with me.”

It follows:

(Verses 8.) The child grew and was weaned, and Abraham held a great feast on the day of his weaning.

Why did Abraham hold a feast neither on the day his son was born nor on the day he was circumcised, but on the day he was weaned? Unless this is referred to some spiritual signification, there is no solution to the question. The great spiritual joy ought to occur, namely, when a person has become spiritually mature and has become a new human being—not one of the kind of whom the Apostle says, “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food; for you were not yet able. Indeed, even now you are not able, for you are still carnal” (1 Cor. 3).

It follows:

### (Verses 9 ff.)

When Sarah saw the son of Hagar the Egyptian playing with Isaac, she said to Abraham, “Cast out this maidservant and her son, for the son of this maidservant shall not be heir with my son Isaac.” Abraham took this very hard because of his son. But God said to him: “Let it not seem harsh to you concerning the boy and concerning your maidservant. In everything that Sarah has said to you, listen to her voice, because in Isaac shall your offspring be called.”

The Hebrews explain this in two ways: either that he had made idols out of clay, or that, against Isaac, as though claiming for himself the position of the elder, he had asserted his primogeniture through play. Thus it appears that the play had been a quarrel. When Sarah heard of this, she could not tolerate it; this is also confirmed by her words: “Cast out this maidservant and her son, for the son of this maidservant shall not be heir with my son Isaac.”

But why was Abraham saddened, since these things were prophecy—which Abraham himself ought certainly to have understood better than Sarah? We must understand either that Sarah said this by revelation, because it had first been revealed to her, while he, whom the Lord subsequently instructed concerning it, was moved by paternal affection for his son; or that both of them initially did not know what this signified, and that, through Sarah—who herself did not understand—he was taught this prophecy when she had been stirred by a woman’s feelings because of the maidservant’s arrogance. It continues:

### (Verse 13)

“But I shall also make the son of the maidservant into a great nation, because he is your offspring.”

It should be noted that Ishmael too is called by God the offspring of Abraham; but Ishmael is one thing and Isaac another, because of what the Apostle teaches: “In Isaac shall your offspring be called”—that is, not the children of the flesh, but the children of the promise, are counted as offspring (Romans 9).

### (Verses 14 ff.) [Col. 0969B]

So Abraham rose early, and taking bread and a skin of water, placed them on her shoulder. He handed over the boy to her and dismissed her.

When Isaac was born, Ishmael was thirteen years old. After Isaac’s weaning, Ishmael was expelled with his mother, at the time fixed as the fifth year after the weaning. We therefore calculate that Ishmael was expelled with his mother eighteen years later; it is no longer plausible that a young adolescent sat upon his mother’s neck. After doing this, Abraham gave the boy to his mother—that is, he handed or entrusted him to her—and so dismissed him from the household.

When she had departed, she wandered in the wilderness of Beersheba. When the water in the skin had been exhausted, she cast the boy under one of the trees that were there, and went away. She sat opposite him at a distance, as far as a bow can shoot, for she said, “I shall not see the death of the boy.” Sitting opposite him, she raised her voice and wept. But God heard the voice of the boy.

It is customary to ask how, when the boy was eighteen years old, his mother could have cast him under a tree and gone as far away as a bow can shoot so that she would not see him dying. For the wording seems to suggest that she had thrown down someone whom she had been carrying, especially since it follows: “The boy wept.” But we must understand that he was cast down not by someone carrying him, but—as happens—as though he were already dying, in the anguish of her heart. For when Scripture says, “I have been cast away from before your eyes,” the speaker was not being carried; and it is common in daily speech to say that someone has been cast away by a person with whom he had been, so that he will neither be seen by that person nor remain with him.

We must understand that Scripture has omitted the detail that the mother withdrew from her son in such a way that the boy did not know where his mother had gone, and that she hid among the wooded growth so that she would not see her son dying and wasting away from thirst. Even at that age, what wonder is it if, after not seeing his mother for some time and supposing her lost, he wept in the place where he had been left alone?

Therefore, when it is said afterward, “Take up the boy,” this does not mean that he was to lift him from the ground as though he were lying there. It means that she was to join him, take him by the hand, and thereafter have him as her companion, as people of any age commonly do when walking together.

We must now ask why Sarah had earlier wanted her husband to receive a son from the maidservant, or why she now ordered that he be expelled from the household with his mother. She did not do this because she had been inflamed by jealousy, but because she had been compelled by the mystery of prophecy.

For Hagar, as the Apostle says, bore a carnal people into slavery; Sarah, however, being free, bore a people who are not according to the flesh but were called in freedom—the freedom with which Christ set them free. By this mystery it was signified that the former people, generated in the slavery of sins, would not remain forever in the house of Israel, that is, in the Church; nor would it be heir or partner with the worshipers of Christ, nor possess the kingdom of heavenly glory with the noble son, that is, with the faithful people.

When Abraham therefore expelled Hagar from the household, he took bread and a skin of water, placed the child upon Hagar’s shoulders, and dismissed her. As Hagar went out, she wandered in the wilderness; and when she had cast her son, dying of thirst, under a tree, the angel of the Lord appeared to her, showed her a spring of water, and gave her son drink.

What, then, does it signify that, as Hagar went out, she placed the child upon her shoulders, except that the sinful and foolish people burdened the neck of its mother, the Synagogue, when it said, “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matthew 7)? The bread signified that the old priesthood carried with it the bread of the Presence, as it is written, and that this bread would grow old. The skin of water, which failed, signified that Jewish purification would fail—or else their carnal teaching, enclosed in dead skin, that is, in the flesh of the old person condemned by the sentence of transgression. It provides neither refreshment nor satisfaction for thirst, but produces vomiting through its tepid heat.

That Hagar wandered in the wilderness with her son signifies that the Synagogue, expelled from its land with its people, is without priesthood and sacrifice throughout the whole world and is utterly ignorant of the life that is Christ. That her son was wasting away from thirst shows that this same people possessed no spiritual purification.

[Col. 0970B] That she cast her son, dying of thirst, under a tree, and then, when the angel showed her, saw a spring, signifies that certain people from that very nation would flee for refuge to the shadow of the wood of the cross.

That the boy cried out in tears, that God heard him, and that, when the angel showed her, she saw a spring, is said concerning those Jews who are converted to Christ. They weep over their former errors, and their cries are heard; with the eyes of their hearts opened, they see the spring of living water, that is, Christ the Son of God, who says, “I am the spring of living water; let the thirsty person come and drink.” Hence Ishmael is interpreted as “hearing of God.”

This angel is a likeness of Elijah, through whom this people will come to believe, as it is said through Malachi: “Behold, I shall send you Elijah, who will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children” (Malachi 4).

The fact that the angel of the Lord immediately called to Hagar, saying, “Rise, take up the boy, for I shall make him into a great nation,” signified either that the people of the Jews would rule more abundantly throughout the age, or that those among them who believed in Christ would attain the glory of the heavenly kingdom.

The same angel who speaks to Hagar is first called an angel by Scripture and afterward God, the Son of God. We must believe that he was the one who always spoke through the Law and the Prophets. He is called an angel because of his obedience to the Father’s will, but God according to the nature of the Father, since he too is truly God, just as the Father is. It continues:

### (Verses 22 ff.) [Col. 0970C]

At that time Abimelech and Phicol, the commander of his army, said to Abraham: “God is with you in everything that you do. Therefore swear by the Lord that you will not harm me, my descendants, or my stock, but that, according to the mercy that I have shown you, you will act toward me and toward the land in which you have lived as a stranger.”

And Abraham said, “I shall swear.”

Then Abraham reproached Abimelech concerning the well of water which his servants had seized by force. Abimelech answered: “I did not know who had done this thing; moreover, you did not tell me, and I did not hear of it until today.”

So Abraham took sheep and cattle and gave them to Abimelech, and the two of them made a covenant. Abraham set apart seven ewe lambs of the flock. Abimelech said to him: “What do these seven ewe lambs mean, which you have set apart?”

He replied: “You shall accept these seven ewe lambs from my hand, so that they may be a witness for me that I dug this well.”

Therefore that place was called Beersheba, because there the two of them swore an oath. And they made a covenant concerning the well of the oath.

Where the text reads “the well of the oath,” the Hebrew has *Beersheba*. There are two reasons why it was called this: either because Abimelech received the seven ewe lambs from Abraham’s hand—for seven is called *sabee*—or because they swore an oath there, since an oath is likewise called *sabee*.

If we read this name above, before this event, we should know that it was spoken by anticipation, just as with Bethel and Gilgal, which certainly had other names until the time when they were so called.

How, then, could Hagar have been unaware of the well that Abraham had dug, if it had been dug before she was expelled? It could easily have happened that, for the sake of his livestock, he dug a well far from the house in which he lived with his household, and that she did not know of it. It continues:

### (Verses 33–34) [Col. 0971A]

Abraham planted a grove at Beersheba, and there he called upon the name of the Lord, the eternal God. He lived as a settler in the land of the Philistines for many days.

It may be asked how Abraham planted a grove beside the well of the oath—or, as another translation says, a field—if, in that land, as Stephen says, he had not received even a foot’s breadth as an inheritance. But this should be understood as the inheritance that God was going to give by his gift, not one purchased at a price.

The area around the well is understood to belong to that purchased tract in which the ewe lambs had been given, when Abimelech and Abraham also swore an oath to one another. It continues:

### (Chapter 22, verse 1) [Col. 0971B]

God tested Abraham and said to him, “Abraham, Abraham.” He replied, “Here I am.”

It is customary to ask how this can be true, since James says in his Epistle that God tests no one. The answer is that, according to the language of Scripture, he is said to test for what is meant by “prove.”

The temptation of which James speaks is understood as that by which a person becomes entangled in sin. Hence the Apostle says, “Lest the tempter tempt you” (1 Thessalonians 3). Elsewhere too it is written, “The Lord your God tests you, to know whether you love him” (Deuteronomy 13).

Here also the expression “to know” is used as though it said, “to make you know,” since the strength of a person’s love remains hidden from him unless it becomes known to him through experience. It continues:

### (Verse 2)

“Take your son, your beloved Isaac, and go into the land of Vision, and offer him there as a burnt offering upon one of the mountains that I shall show you.”

It should be noted, both from the preceding passages and from the present one, that Isaac was not born at the oak of Mamre but in Gerar, where the town of Beersheba still exists today. Scripture bears witness to this when it says: “Abraham lived as a settler in the land of the Philistines for many days.” Then God said to him, “Take your only-begotten son, whom you love, Isaac.”

The Hebrews say that this mountain was Moriah, where the Temple was later built, on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, as it is written in Chronicles: “They began to build the Temple in the second month, on the second day of the month, on Mount Moriah” (2 Chronicles 3). It is interpreted as “illuminating” and “shining” because there is the *Dabir*, that is, the oracle of God, and the Law and the Spirit that teaches a person the truth and inspires the prophets.

When he says, “Offer him as a burnt offering,” the weight of the test was increased by the reminder of love and of the name, and paternal affection was tormented by the memory of the promise, since God had previously said to him, “In Isaac shall your offspring be called,” as though, if Isaac were killed, the entire hope of the promises would be frustrated.

Abraham certainly would never have believed that God delighted in human victims, although, when a divine command thunders forth, it must be obeyed, not debated. Nevertheless, Abraham is to be praised because, when he was about to sacrifice his son, he immediately believed that he would rise again: for the promises of God had to be fulfilled through the one whom God commanded to be killed. It continues:

### (Verses 3 ff.) [Col. 0971D]

So Abraham rose during the night, saddled his donkey, and took with him two young men and his son Isaac. When he had cut wood for the burnt offering, he went to the place that God had commanded him.

On the third day, he lifted his eyes and saw the place from a distance. He said to his young men: “Wait here with the donkey. I and the boy will hurry there; after we have worshiped, we shall return to you.”

It should be noted that the journey from Gerar to Mount Moriah, that is, to the site of the Temple, takes three days, so that the text appropriately says that he arrived on the third day. Those are therefore wrong who think that Abraham lived at that time near the oak of Mamre, since from there to Mount Moriah the full journey is scarcely one day.

He was commanded to take the boy with him for a three-day journey so that the test might be increased through the length of time.
