For the journey was prolonged over three days, and throughout the entire period the father’s inward parts were tormented by ever-growing anxieties, so that during all that extended time he would see his son eating food with him; through so many nights the boy would hang upon his father’s embraces, cling to his breast, and lie in his lap. Thus, at every moment, the pain of killing his son was accumulated within his paternal affection. It continues:

### (Verses 6 ff.) [Col. 0972A]

He also took the wood for the burnt offering and placed it upon his son Isaac. He himself carried fire and a sword in his hands.

As the two of them went on together, Isaac said to his father, “My father.” He replied, “What do you want, my son?”

“Behold,” he said, “the fire and the wood. Where is the victim for the burnt offering?”

Abraham said, “God will provide himself with a victim for the burnt offering, my son.”

So they went on together and came to the place that God had shown him. There he built an altar and arranged the wood upon it.

If Abraham was firmly and unhesitatingly resolved to slaughter the boy as a burnt offering to the Lord, why did he say to his young men, “You wait here; I and the boy, after we have worshiped, shall return to you”? He truly believed without hesitation that the boy would rise again, and therefore he is to be praised both for his constancy in offering and for his faith in the resurrection.

He knew with absolute certainty that God could not be deceived. Even if the boy were killed, God’s promise would nevertheless remain intact. Hence the Apostle Paul, taught by the Spirit of God what Abraham held in his heart, praises his faith, saying: “By faith Abraham did not hesitate” (Romans 4), when he offered his only son, the one in whom he had received the promises, considering that God was able to raise him even from the dead. It continues:

### (Verse 9)

When he had bound his son Isaac, he placed him on the altar upon the pile of wood, stretched out his hand, and seized the sword to sacrifice his son.

He did not hesitate, because the one who had been given without hope could be restored after being sacrificed. It continues:

### (Verses 11–12) [Col. 0972C]

And behold, the angel of the Lord called to him from heaven, saying, “Abraham, Abraham.” He replied, “Here I am.”

And he said to him: “Do not stretch out your hand against the boy, and do nothing to him. Now I know that you fear God.”

This means, “Now I have made you know that you fear the Lord.” It continues:

### (Verses 13–14)

Abraham lifted his eyes and saw behind him a ram caught by its horns among the thorns. He took it and offered it as a burnt offering in place of his son. He called the name of that place, “The Lord sees.” Hence, to this day, it is said on the mountain, “The Lord will see.”

This manner of expression is clearly evident where it says, “Abraham called the name of that place, ‘The Lord sees.’” “He saw” is used for “he appeared,” that is, “he caused himself to be seen,” signifying through the agent what is accomplished. It continues:

### (Verses 15 ff.) [Col. 0972D]

The angel of the Lord called Abraham a second time from heaven, saying: “By myself I have sworn, says the Lord: because you have done this thing and have not spared your only-begotten son for my sake, I shall bless you and multiply your offspring like the stars of heaven and like the sand on the shore of the sea. Your offspring shall possess the gates of their enemies, and all the nations of the earth shall be blessed in your offspring.”

Did Abraham spare his son for the sake of an angel, and not rather for the sake of God? Therefore, under the name of the angel, the Lord Jesus Christ is signified. He is unquestionably God, and the prophet explicitly calls him the Angel of Great Counsel.

Or else God was in the angel, and the angel spoke in the person of God, as also often happens in the Prophets. This seems even clearer in what follows, where it is written: “The angel of the Lord called Abraham again from heaven, saying: ‘By myself I have sworn, says the Lord.’”

He had often made promises, but had never sworn an oath. What, then, is the oath of the true and truthful God except confirmation of the promise and a kind of rebuke of unbelievers?

Let us now see what mystery lies hidden within this sacrament. When Abraham brought his only son to be sacrificed, he represented God the Father on high. But what does it mean that he is portrayed as an old man? God does not grow old; rather, the prophecy concerning Christ had already, in a certain sense, grown old when Christ was born.

It began with Adam, where it was said, “The two shall be one flesh” (Genesis 2)—that great mystery concerning Christ and the Church (Ephesians 5). It was completed in the sixth age of the world, which is signified by Abraham’s old age, because this mystery of God was already ancient. Sarah’s old age likewise signifies the people of God, that is, the multitude of the prophets, because at the end of the ages Christ was born from that people of holy souls.

Her barrenness indicates that in this world we have been saved in hope, and that in Christ, as in Isaac, we have all been born. This birth of the Church at the end of the ages was foretold by the wondrous grace of God, not by natural fertility.

We must now examine what the mystery of the subsequent history figuratively foretold. Who, therefore, was represented in Abraham through that sacrifice, as has been said, except the exalted Father? Who in Isaac except Christ?

For just as Abraham offered his only and beloved son as a victim to God, so God the Father handed over his only Son for us all. And just as Isaac himself carried the wood upon which he was to be placed, so Christ carried upon his shoulders the wood of the cross on which he was to be crucified.

The two servants who were left behind and were not brought to the place of sacrifice represented the Jews. Living as slaves and understanding things carnally, they did not understand the humility of Christ or the passion of Christ; therefore they did not reach the place of sacrifice.

Why were there two servants? Because the people itself was to be divided into two parts. This happened when Solomon sinned, when the same people was divided with respect to the kingdom, not through an error of impiety. To these two parts the prophet also often says: “Israel the adversary and Judah the transgressor” (Jeremiah 3).

The donkey represented the senseless folly of the Jews. This senseless folly carried all the mysteries but did not know what it was carrying.

As for what was said to them, “Wait here with the donkey; after we have worshiped, we shall return to you,” hear the Apostle saying: “A partial blindness has happened in Israel” (Romans 11).

What is this blindness? “Wait here with the donkey,” until, he says, the fullness of the nations should enter—that is, “after we have worshiped,” when the sacrifice of the Lord’s cross has been fulfilled and proclaimed among the nations; that is, until the fullness of the nations should enter.

What does “we shall return to you” mean? “And thus all Israel would be saved.”

The three days in which they came to the place of sacrifice signify the three ages of the world: one before the Law, another under the Law, and a third under grace.

Before the Law extends from Abraham to Moses; under the Law, from Moses to John. From that point onward—from the Lord and through everything that remains—is the third day, the day of grace. In this third age, as after three days, the mystery of Christ’s sacrifice was completed.

Then Isaac is placed upon the altar with his feet bound, and the Lord is hung upon the wood and fastened to the cross.

But what was figuratively represented in Isaac was transferred to the ram. Why, except because Christ is the sheep? He is both son and lamb: son because he was born; ram because he was sacrificed.

But what does it mean that the ram was caught among the thorns? The cross has horns, for the two pieces of wood are joined together so as to produce the form of a cross. Hence it is written concerning him: “Horns are in his hands” (Habakkuk 3).

The ram caught by its horns therefore signifies Christ crucified. The brambles, however, are thorns. The thorns signify the wicked and sinners who hung the Lord upon the cross.

Thus the Lord was suspended among the thorns of the sinful Jews, as he says through Jeremiah: “This people surrounded me with the thorns of their sins.”

Others understood this ram, bound by its horns among the thorns, as signifying the same Christ before he was sacrificed, crowned with thorns by the Jews.

After the sacrifice had been completed, Abraham was told: “In your offspring all the nations shall be blessed.” When did this happen except when that ram says: “They pierced my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones” (Psalm 21)?

When this sacrifice was accomplished in the Psalms, it was then said in that same Psalm: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship in his presence,” because the kingdom belongs to the Lord, and so forth.

After Abraham had sacrificed the ram in place of his son Isaac, he called the name of that place, “The Lord sees,” in the sense that “the Lord caused himself to be seen,” namely, through the Incarnation. It continues:

### (Verses 20 ff.) [Col. 0974A]

After these things, Abraham was told that Milcah too had borne sons to his brother Nahor: Uz his firstborn, and Buz his brother, and Kemuel, the father of the Syrians, and Chesed, and Hazo, and Pildash, and Jidlaph, and Bethuel, from whom Rebekah was born.

Milcah bore these eight sons to Nahor, Abraham’s brother.

From Milcah, the wife of Nahor and daughter of Haran, Uz was born. Job descended from his stock, as it is written at the beginning of this book: “There was a man in the land of Uz whose name was Job” (Job 1).

Some therefore wrongly think that Job was descended from Esau. For what is found at the end of the book itself—that it was translated from the Syrian language, that he was the fourth generation from Esau, and the other details contained there—is not found in the Hebrew books.

Buz was the second born of Milcah. According to the Hebrews, that diviner Balaam was descended from his line. In the Book of Job he is called Elihu: first a holy man and prophet of God, but afterward, through disobedience and desire for gifts, when he wished to curse Israel, he was deprived of the divine title.

It is said in that same book: “Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite became angry” (Job 31). He descended, that is, from the root of this Buz.

Kemuel was the father of Damascus. The same region is called Aram, which is here written for Syria; it is also read under that name in Isaiah.

Those who reported this could not have announced him as the father of the Syrians, since the Syrian race was propagated from his origin much later. Rather, this was said from the perspective of the writer, who narrated these events in writing after all those times had passed.

Chesed was the fourth, from whom the Chaldeans, called *Casdaim*, were later named. It continues:

### (Chapter 23, verses 1–2) [Col. 0974B]

Sarah lived for one hundred and twenty-seven years and died in the city of Arbe, which is Hebron in the land of Canaan.

In the Hebrew language, *Arbe* means “four,” because Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob were buried there, as well as Adam himself, the first father of the human race, as is shown more clearly in the Book of Joshua. It continues:

### (Verses 3 ff.)

Abraham came to mourn and weep for her. When he had risen from the funeral rites, he spoke to the sons of Heth, saying: “I am a stranger and sojourner among you. Give me the right to a burial place among you, so that I may bury my dead.”

The sons of Heth answered Abraham: “Hear us, my lord. You are a prince of God among us. Bury your dead in the choicest of our tombs. No one will be able to prevent you from burying your dead in his tomb.”

Abraham rose and bowed to the people of the land, namely, the sons of Heth (Deuteronomy 6).

It is asked how it can be written, “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve,” when Abraham honored a certain people of the nations in such a way that he even bowed down to them.

It should be observed that the same command does not say, “You shall worship the Lord your God alone,” as it says, “You shall serve him alone.”

Nor should one be troubled by the fact that, in another passage of Scripture, an angel forbids people to worship him and admonishes them to worship the Lord instead. The angel had appeared in such a form that he could be worshiped in place of God, and therefore the worshiper had to be corrected.

Then Abraham bought the field in which he buried his wife Sarah. Thus, according to Stephen’s account, he was established as a possessor in that land when he began to possess it—namely, after the death of his father Terah, who is reckoned to have died two years before Sarah.

But what does it mean that Sarah was buried in a double tomb, except that the soul which dies to the world in order to live for God is received into a twofold rest of life: the practice of good works and contemplation of divinity?

### (Chapter 24, verses 1 ff.) [Col. 0974D]

Abraham was old and advanced in years, and the Lord had blessed him in all things.

He said to his senior servant, the steward of his household who was in charge of all that he possessed: “Place your hand under my thigh, so that I may make you swear by the Lord, the God of heaven and earth, that you will not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites among whom I dwell, but that you will go to my land and to my kindred.”

The Hebrews report that Abraham’s servant swore by the sanctification of Abraham, that is, by his circumcision. We, however, say that he swore by the offspring of Abraham, that is, by Christ, who was to be born from him, according to the Evangelist Matthew: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham” (Matthew 2). It continues:

### (Verses 12 ff.) [Col. 0975A]

“O Lord, God of my master Abraham, meet me, I pray, today, and show mercy to my master Abraham. Behold, I stand beside the spring of water, and the daughters of the inhabitants of this city will come out to draw water.

Therefore, let the girl to whom I say, ‘Incline your jar, so that I may drink,’ and who answers, ‘Drink—and I shall also give your camels drink,’ be the one whom you have prepared for your servant Isaac.”

There is a difference between asking for something extraordinary, where the very miracle is to be a sign rather than an omen, and observing things that happen in such a way that they are not extraordinary but are interpreted by diviners through superstitious vanity.

But even the request for something extraordinary, by which what someone wishes to know may be signified, is not a minor question as to whether it should be accepted. This relates to the statement that those who do such things improperly are said to test the Lord.

For when the Lord himself was tested by the devil, he brought forward the testimony of Scripture: “You shall not test the Lord your God” (Matthew 4). The devil was suggesting to him, as though he were merely a human being, that he should test by some sign how great he was—that is, how much power he possessed with God. This is done wrongly when it is done for that purpose.

What Gideon did is distinguished from this, since he was facing the danger of battle. That was consolation more than testing. It continues:

### (Verses 40–41) [Col. 0975B]

“He said, ‘The Lord, in whose presence I walk, will send his angel with you and direct your way. You shall take a wife for my son from my kindred and from my father’s house.

You shall be innocent of my curse when you come to my relatives and they do not give her to you.’”

How could that adjuration be understood as a curse, unless he would have been accursed if he acted against the adjuration? It continues:

### (Verse 50)

Laban and Bethuel answered: “The word has come forth from the Lord; we cannot speak anything else to you outside his pleasure.

Behold, Rebekah is before you. Take her and go, and let her be the wife of your master’s son, as the Lord has spoken.”

It is asked when the Lord spoke, unless they either knew Abraham to be a prophet and recognized as prophetically spoken by the Lord what had been spoken through him, or called the sign that his servant had reported to them the speech of the Lord. It continues:

### (Verse 59)

So they sent her away, along with her nurse, Abraham’s servant, and his companions.

It was fitting that, since the young woman was departing for her wedding without her parents, she should have the assistance of her nurse. It continues:

(Vers. 60.) “You are our sister; may you grow into thousands upon thousands, and may your offspring possess the gates of their enemies.” They were not prophets, nor did they make so great a wish out of vanity; rather, what God had promised Abraham could not have been hidden from them.

What is the meaning of Abraham’s commanding the boy to place his hand under his thigh and swear by the God of heaven, unless it is that the flesh of the one who was both Abraham’s son according to his humanity and Lord according to his divinity was to descend through that member? Thus the boy is told: “Place your hand under my thigh, and swear by the God of heaven.” It is as though he were being told plainly: “Touch my son, and swear by my Lord.” Hence he is commanded to place his hand not upon the thigh but under the thigh, because the one who was to descend from that thigh would come as a human being, yet above all human beings. It was therefore not fitting that he place his hand upon the thigh, since no flesh is above that flesh which the Only-Begotten of the Father united to himself for our redemption.

What is the meaning of Isaac’s being forbidden to take a wife for his beloved son from the daughters of the Canaanites, unless it is that no rejected souls are joined to the one of whom it is written, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III)? The servant is commanded to bring a wife for his son from his kindred, because only the holy Church of the elect was to be joined to the Only-Begotten Son; and the Only-Begotten himself, by predestination and foreknowledge, did not regard her as a stranger.

But who is the boy sent to bring the wife, unless it is the order of the prophets and apostles, and of all teachers? When they bring the word of preaching to good minds, they become, as it were, agents appointed to join each soul to the Only-Begotten Son. He went forth carrying all his master’s goods, because, in the things they speak concerning the Lord, they display within themselves the riches of virtues, so that they draw their hearers more swiftly to follow God precisely because they show in themselves what they proclaim.

The same boy stood beside the spring and, according to the predetermined judgment, proposed which girl should be chosen, because holy preachers consider the streams of sacred eloquence and from them discern to whom, and to what sort of people, they should entrust the words of their preaching, and from which hearers they may gain the confidence of certainty.

He asked for a drink, because every preacher thirsts for the soul of his hearer. Rebecca, however, offered him a drink, because the holy Church of the elect satisfied the desire of her preachers through the faith of her virtue. For, by confessing the God whom she had heard, she offered her preacher water for refreshment and cooled his spirit.

It should be noted that she moved the jar from her shoulders to her arms, because that confession is pleasing which proceeds from good works. Or certainly she offered water because she did not remain empty in what she believed: immediately she strove to preach what she had heard, and by teaching she produced many preachers from herself.

The water in the jar is knowledge of preaching held in measure, because the holy Church strives not to know more than one ought to know, but to know with sobriety (Rom. III). The water of the jar in the arm is the doctrine of preaching expressed in works: she offered it as drink not only to the boy’s companions but also to the camels, because she preaches the word of life not only to the prudent but also to the foolish, according to Paul’s saying: “I am debtor both to the wise and to the foolish” (Rom. I).

Or certainly water is also given to beasts when it is determined how care for the flesh is to be exercised, so that it must not be expended upon pleasure, yet must not be denied in necessities, as it is written: “Do not make provision for the flesh in its desires” (Rom. XIII). For whoever forbids such provision in desires plainly allows it in necessity, in accordance with what is said again: “No one ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it” (Eph. V).

The boy gave Rebecca earrings and bracelets, because every preacher adorns the hearing of the holy Church through obedience, and her hands through the merit of good works. The earrings are worth two shekels, while the bracelets are worth ten shekels, because the first virtue of obedience is charity, and this charity is distinguished in two commandments, namely, that God and one’s neighbor be loved. Right action is perfected through the completion of the Decalogue, so that once good works have begun, no evil is thereafter committed.

Rebecca said that there was ample space in her father’s house for lodging, because the holy Church showed that she had learned the law of nature from the earlier people, and received the words of preaching in the broad bosom of charity. For the teacher, the heart of the hearers is an ample place for dwelling, in the breadth of truth. Hence it is said to certain people: “Receive us; we have wronged no one, we have corrupted no one” (II Cor. VII); and, “You are not restricted by us, but you are restricted in your own affections” (II Cor. VI). It is as though they were being told plainly: “Make a spacious place in your mind for receiving doctrine, but remain narrow in entertaining carnal thoughts.”

Her indication that she had an abundance of straw and hay signifies that the holy Church, hearing the words of life, returned earthly provisions to the preachers. Paul said that he accepted these as though they were nothing: “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great matter if we reap your carnal things?” (I Cor. IX).

Rebecca’s brother was Laban, who hurried out, saw his sister’s earrings and bracelets, and brought the boy inside. For there are carnal people joined to the faithful who, when they see the gifts of spiritual things, are filled with wonder and admit the word of preaching into their souls so as to receive the faith, even if they do not proceed all the way to works. Since they often see good people shining with miracles, they do not reject what they hear about eternity, although they remain in carnal practice because they do not follow the holy Church of the elect in their conduct.

Laban offered straw, hay, water, and bread, but the boy refused to accept them unless he first obtained the matter of the marriage. For there are many who are ready to sustain their teachers with temporal provisions, but holy preachers refuse to receive temporal things unless they first obtain eternal things. If they find no fruit in the animals, they disdain to accept provisions for their bodies; nor do they wash their feet with water, because they relieve the labor of their desire with no consolation.

As soon as the boy obtained the matter of his master’s marriage, he brought out golden and silver vessels and garments and gave them to Rebecca, because the teachers of the holy Church provide as many ornaments as they have taught gifts of virtue. She had first received earrings and bracelets, but now she received golden and silver vessels and garments, because the holy Church, having first received faith, works, and obedience, later grows strong in spiritual gifts as well. Filled with the spirit of prophecy and the grace of virtues, she increases as her gifts are enlarged.

The boy also offered gifts to her mother and brothers, because, from the time the Church came to faith, the Gentiles grew strong in temporal glory after her conversion. We see this even now: Christians everywhere experience affliction, while the Gentiles glory in earthly power.

Her brothers also receive gifts, because those who hold the faith in words only, yet live carnally without following their profession in their conduct, are often honorably treated by the faithful because they appear to be faithful.

The mother and brothers therefore receive gifts but are excluded from the lot of the inheritance, because whether unbelievers or carnal people who remain within the profession of faith, they do not attain the lot of the eternal inheritance, although they temporarily obtain the glory of heavenly generosity.

Rebecca with her maidens signifies that the holy Church has with her souls of lesser merit as her companions. For although some do not possess contemplation in its fullness through the perception of the mind, such souls are like Rebecca’s maidens: they follow her in their conduct. Nevertheless, these souls ascend toward contemplation. The boy had some of them in his company because among the holy prophets there were certain people who lived well but did not possess the spirit of prophecy; and among the blessed apostles and teachers there were many who maintained a good life in their conduct but did not utter the preacher’s words.

The boy hastens back to the house because holy preachers, when by preaching they have obtained the life of their hearers, immediately return thanks to the one from whose gift they received this. They attribute nothing of it to themselves in that work, but to its author.

(Vers. 62.) At that time Isaac was walking along the road that leads to the well whose name is “The Well of the Living One Who Sees.” Who is the living and seeing one except almighty God, of whom it is written: “I live forever, says the Lord”? Of him it is said again: “All things are naked and open to his eyes.”

The well of the Living One Who Sees is the depth of sacred Scripture, which almighty God has given us for the watering of the mind. What is the road that leads to the well of the Living One Who Sees except the humility of the Only-Begotten’s passion? Through it what the streams of sacred Scripture had previously spoken obscurely was opened to us. For unless the Only-Begotten Son of God had become incarnate, been tempted, seized, struck with blows, mocked with spittle, crucified, and killed, the depth of this well—that is, of sacred Scripture—would not have been open to us.

What, then, did the humility of his passion become for the faithful except the key to opening, by which we find the well of God’s mysteries and drink the water of knowledge from its depths? The pages of sacred eloquence bear witness to his incarnation, passion, death, resurrection, and ascension. Because we know that these things have happened, we now understand what we had heard. They could indeed be read before, but because they had not yet occurred, they could not be understood.

Hence John says: “The Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered so as to open the book and loose its seals” (Apoc. V). He opened the book and loosed its seals by being born, dying, rising again, and ascending to heaven, thereby revealing to us the mysteries of sacred Scripture.

It should be noted that it does not say, “He walked along the road that leads to the well,” but, “He walked back and forth.” For one walks back and forth when, by going and returning, he treads repeatedly upon the road along which he walks.

The Lord walked back and forth in the humility of his passion when he endured from the Jews, in turn, insults in words, false testimony against him, slaps, spitting, a crown of thorns, and the cross. To have walked back and forth in the humility of his passion, therefore, is to have endured so many adversities and insults by repeating them in various forms.

When Rebecca came, Isaac was living in the southern land, because the Only-Begotten Lord and our Redeemer, when the Church came to him, dwelt in the minds of those born from the Jews whom not the cold of sluggishness but the warmth of charity possessed. From that people came the prophetess Anna, and from it came Simeon, who took the Lord into his arms (Matt. XIII).

He had gone out to meditate in the field, because the field is understood to be the world; the Lord himself explains this, saying: “The field is the world.” He went out into it because he deigned to appear visibly, as it is written: “You went forth for the salvation of your people, to save your anointed ones.”

Young men commonly practice the use of weapons. Isaac therefore went out to meditate in the field because our Redeemer, offering those who follow him a pattern of humility, displayed in himself examples of endurance and patience through the exercise of his long-suffering passion.

Meditation upon weapons is the repeated experience of sufferings. For the one who endured blows from hands, the lance, and the cross endured the repetition of his passion in himself all the way to death. We call sufferings weapons because through them we are freed from the hidden adversary.

He went out to meditate in the field when the day was already declining because he accepted the exercise of his sufferings near the end of the world, as he speaks through the Psalmist of the passion of his crucifixion: “The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice” (Ps. CXL).

What does it mean that Rebecca was brought to Isaac upon the back of a camel except that, as we have already said, Rebecca signifies the Church, while the people of the Gentiles, upon the camel on which she rides, are signified by their twisted conduct and shameful worship of idols? For those who invented gods for themselves to worship had, as it were, a burden grown upon their backs from themselves for them to carry.

Rebecca, therefore, coming to Isaac, is brought upon the back of a camel because the Church, hastening from among the Gentiles to Christ, is found still entangled in the distorted and vicious ways of her former life.

When she saw Isaac, she descended from the camel, because the more subtly the holy Church recognizes her Redeemer, the more humbly she abandons the practices of carnal life, and within herself resists the strength of vice. Thus, having seen Isaac, she descended: once the Lord was known, the Gentiles abandoned their vices and sought the depths of humility from the height of pride.

What does it mean that Rebecca saw Isaac sitting upon the camel except that the Church coming from the Gentiles recognized her Redeemer while she still leaned upon vices and clung not yet to spiritual but to animal impulses?

Nor should it trouble us that the boy also came with camels carrying his master’s riches. For holy preachers, although they already shine in understanding and life as they grasp and set forth higher things, nevertheless still feel within themselves the constraint of the flesh. They see another law in their members, warring against the law of their mind and leading them captive in the law of sin (Rom. VII). They carry riches upon camels because, lest the greatness of revelations should exalt them, a stimulus of the flesh is given to them.

They have this treasure in earthen vessels, so that the excellence may belong to the power of God and not to them. For those who speak heavenly things through the flesh, yet still feel within the flesh the contradiction arising from vice—what are they doing except sitting upon the crooked backs of camels?

When Rebecca saw Isaac, she asked the boy who the man was and learned his identity, because every day the holy Church continues to understand through the words of the prophets and apostles what she ought to believe concerning her Redeemer.

She immediately covered herself with a cloak, because the more subtly she penetrates the mysteries of her Savior, the more deeply she is ashamed of her former life and blushes because she acted perversely. She took care to cover herself with a cloak because, when she saw the Lord, she was ashamed of the deeds of her weakness. She who had previously been carried openly upon the camel was afterward covered by modesty when she descended.

Hence, through the apostolic voice, the same Church, converted from her former election, is addressed like Rebecca descending from the camel and covering herself with a cloak: “What fruit did you have then in those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Rom. VI).

Isaac brought her into the tent of his mother and took her as his wife, because, in place of the Synagogue from which he was born according to the flesh, the Lord loves the holy Church and joined her to himself in love and contemplation. She had previously been near to him by kindred—that is, related by predestination—but afterward, once joined to him, she became his wife in enduring love.

He loved her so greatly that he lessened the grief caused by his mother’s death, because our Redeemer wiped away the sorrow that could come from the destruction of the Synagogue by the gain of the holy Church. When Rebecca is joined to him, grief for the mother’s death is removed, because, when the holy Church coming from the Gentiles is brought as far as the bridal chamber of contemplation, the Jews are regarded as nothing.

If we also interpret the meanings of their names, Isaac is called “Laughter,” while Rebecca is called “Patience.” Laughter arises from joy, while patience arises from tribulation. Although the holy Church is already suspended in contemplation of heavenly joy, she still has something sorrowful to endure from the burden of mortal flesh.

Isaac and Rebecca are joined—that is, laughter and patience are mingled—because in the holy Church there comes to pass what is written: “Rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation” (ibid., XII). Thus prosperity arising from contemplation makes her joyful, while adversity arising from tribulation still disturbs her.

(Cap. XXV.—Vers. 1.) “Abraham took another wife, whose name was Keturah.” A question would arise here if this were a sin, especially among the ancients, who devoted themselves to the propagation of offspring. Nor should the incontinent behavior of so great a man be suspected, particularly at that age. Why he had sons by her, although he had already had a son from Sarah by a miracle, has been stated above: what if it too was provided for in the father of many nations—that after his wife’s death he should marry again, so that it might be shown not to be a sin?

Nevertheless, this deed of Abraham, by which he fathered sons from Keturah after Sarah’s death, should not be understood as though it had been done merely according to human custom and thought for the replacement of his earlier offspring with a more numerous progeny. For in that case people could also understand what happened with Hagar in the same way, unless the Apostle warned them (Gal. IV) that those events had occurred prophetically in the persons of both women, and that their sons prefigured the two testaments through allegorical symbolism, as a prediction of things to come.

Therefore something of this kind must also be sought in Abraham’s deed, even if it does not readily present itself. For the moment, the gifts received by the sons of the concubines seem to me to signify certain gifts of God, whether in the sacraments or in various signs, given also to the carnal people of the Jews and to heretics, as to the sons of concubines. The gift of the inheritance, however, which is charity and eternal life, belongs only to Isaac—that is, to the sons of promise.

(Vers. 7.) “The days of Abraham’s life were one hundred and seventy-five years, and, failing, he died in a good old age.” Thus Abraham left his son Isaac seventy-five years old; he had begotten him when he was one hundred. From this point, let us examine through Abraham’s descendants—Isaac and Jacob—how far the times of the city of God extend.

(Vers. 12.) “These are the generations of Ishmael, the son of Abraham, whom Hagar the Egyptian, Sarah’s servant, bore to him; and these are the names of his sons according to their names and their generations.” It is not sufficiently clear why the phrase “according to the names of their generations” was added, since only those whom he himself begot are named, not those who were begotten by them. Unless perhaps it signifies that the nations descended from them were called by their names, when it says, “according to the names of their generations.” Even so, in this expression those nations are described according to the names of these men, not these names according to those nations, since the nations came into existence later.

The expression should therefore be noted, because later it is also said of them: “Twelve princes according to their nations,” as though it had said, “according to the names by which their nations were called.”

(Vers. 16 ff.) “Twelve princes of their tribes. And the years of Ishmael’s life were one hundred and thirty-seven years; and, failing, he died and was gathered to his people. He dwelt from Havilah as far as Shur, which faces Egypt as one enters Assyria; he died in the presence of all his brothers.”

Havilah is the region around which the river Pishon flows as it comes forth from Paradise; it was named Havilah after a certain descendant of Noah. There is also another Havilah, a wilderness opposite Egypt. Shur likewise is a wilderness between Kadesh and Barath, extending the desert as far as the Red Sea and the borders of Egypt.

Twelve sons were born to Ishmael. The firstborn was Nebaioth, after whom the entire region from the Euphrates to the Red Sea has been called Nabataea down to the present day; it is part of Arabia. For their families, towns, fortified settlements, and tribe are also celebrated under this name.

What is written at the end of this account, “He died in the presence of all his brothers,” means that he died in the hands of all his sons, with his children surviving him and none having been taken by death before him.

That brothers are called sons is also demonstrated by Jacob in his words to Laban: “What is my sin, that you pursued me, and that you searched through all my vessels? What have you found of all the goods of your house? Place it before my brothers and your brothers, and let them judge between us” (Gen. XXXI). For we cannot believe that Jacob, apart from his children, had other brothers with him, as Scripture relates.

(Vers. 21 ff.) “He entreated the Lord for his wife, because she was barren. He heard him and granted conception to Rebecca. But the children struggled in her womb. She said, ‘If this was to happen to me, why was it necessary for me to conceive?’ And she went to consult the Lord.”

It is asked where she went, for at that time there were no prophets or priests according to the order of the Lord’s tabernacle or temple. Where, then, she went is rightly questioned, unless perhaps to the place where Abraham had built an altar. But how answers were given there Scripture is entirely silent: whether through some priest—which is incredible, if one existed, since he would not have been named—or whether even at that time there were certain men of God in whom God could be consulted.

Whatever the case, and whatever else there may be that I have perhaps failed to mention, Scripture nevertheless cannot lie. It says that Rebecca went to inquire of God, and that he answered her: “Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples shall be divided from your womb; one people shall overcome the other people, and the elder shall serve the younger.”

According to a spiritual understanding, carnal people in the people of God are signified by the elder son, and spiritual people by the younger, because, as the Apostle says, “The spiritual was not first, but the animal; afterward the spiritual” (I Cor. XV).

This passage is also commonly understood in this way: Esau figures the elder people of God, namely, the Israelite people according to the flesh; while Jacob figures Jacob himself according to spiritual descent.

Historically as well, this answer is found to have been fulfilled when the people of Israel—that is, Jacob, the younger son—overcame the Idumeans, the nation descended from Esau. David made them tributary for as long as they remained under the king, until the Idumeans rebelled and cast the yoke of the Israelites from their neck, in accordance with the prophecy of Isaac himself, when he blessed the younger in place of the elder. For he had said this to the elder when he afterward blessed him as well.

I think that this can also be said concerning each one of us, because there are two nations and two peoples within us. For there is within us both a people of virtues and a people of vices. From our heart proceed evil thoughts, adulteries, thefts, false testimonies, deceit, disputes, heresies, envy, and revelries (Matt. XV; Mark VII; Gal. V), and things like them. You see how great a people of evils exists within us.

But if we deserve to utter the words of the saints, “Because of your fear, O Lord, we conceived and gave birth; we brought forth the spirit of your salvation upon the earth” (Isa. XXVI), then another people is also found within us, generated in the spirit. For the fruit of the spirit is charity, joy, peace, long-suffering, patience, goodness, gentleness, self-control, and chastity (Gal. V), and things like them.

You see another people, which is also within us. But this one is the younger, and the other the elder. For the wicked are always more numerous than the good, and vices more numerous than virtues. But if we are like Rebecca and deserve to conceive from Isaac—that is, from the word of God—then even in us one people will overcome the other, and the elder will serve the younger. The flesh will serve the spirit, and vices will yield to virtues.

(Vers. 24 ff.) “The time for giving birth had come, and behold, twins were found in her womb.” This expression, “the completion of the time,” is never written except concerning holy women, as concerning this Rebecca, Elizabeth the mother of John, and Mary the mother of our Lord Jesus Christ. Thus something extraordinary and surpassing other human beings is shown by such a birth, and the fulfillment of the days indicates the birth of perfect offspring.

“The first who came forth was red and entirely hairy like a pelt, and his name was called Esau. Immediately afterward the other came forth, holding his brother’s heel with his hand, and therefore he was called Jacob.”

Everything that we read in the holy Scriptures was written before the Lord’s coming for no other reason than to commend the Lord’s coming and to foreshadow the future Church, that is, the people of God among all nations, which is his body, with all the saints joined and counted among it, including those who lived in this world before his coming, believing that he would come just as we believe that he has come.

For just as Jacob first sent out his hand from the womb as he was being born, and that hand held the foot of his brother who was being born before him, then the head necessarily followed, and only afterward the remaining limbs, so the head nevertheless surpasses in dignity and power not only those limbs that followed but also the very hand that preceded it in birth. Although it is not prior in the time of appearing, it is prior in the order of nature.

So also the Lord Jesus Christ, although, before he appeared in the flesh and in a certain manner came forth from the womb of his mystery before human eyes as the mediator between God and human beings, the human being “who is God over all, blessed forever” (I Tim. II), sent ahead in the holy patriarchs and prophets a certain part of his body. Through it, as through a hand, he foretold that he would be born, and he supplants the people who proudly preceded him with the five fingers of the bonds of the law.

For through the five divisions of time he did not cease to be foretold and prophesied as the one who was to come; and he composed five books consonant with this matter, through which the law was given. Those who were carnally proud in their wisdom and wished to establish their own righteousness were not filled with the blessing of Christ’s open hand, but were held back by a hand bound and closed.

Thus they were bound by the foot and fell, whereas we rose and were set upright.

Although, as I have said, the Lord Christ sent ahead a certain part of his body in the holy ones who preceded him in the time of his birth, he himself is nevertheless the head of the body, the Church. All those saints adhered to the same body, of which he is the head, by believing in the one whom they foretold. They were not torn away by running ahead, but rather joined to him through obedience. For although a hand may be sent ahead of the head, its connection remains beneath the head.

Therefore everything written beforehand was written to instruct us; it was our foreshadowing, and it happened to them in figure. It was written for us, upon whom the end of the ages has come.

“The first who came forth was red and entirely hairy like a pelt, and his name was called Esau. Immediately afterward the other came forth, holding his brother’s heel with his hand, and therefore he was called Jacob.”

The Apostle Paul wishes this to be understood as a great testimony to grace. Why was he entirely red and hairy, unless because the earlier people, the people of the prophets and of Christ, were stained with blood and surrounded by the roughness of sin and wickedness?

For this reason the younger held his heel: mystically, the younger was destined to overcome the elder. The heel of Esau foreshadowed the final period of the Israelite people, in which our Lord deigned to come to them to bring them salvation.

But in the type involving the Ninevites, the people of the Gentiles, as Jacob, condemned Esau, Israel in its unbelief. Hence Jacob received his name from wrestling or supplanting.

It follows: “Isaac was sixty years old when the children were born.” In the sixth age of the world we see the Jewish people rejected because of pride and unbelief, while the people of the Gentiles were recalled to faith in Christ.

It follows: “When they had grown up, Esau became a man skilled in hunting and a farmer; Jacob, however, was a simple man who dwelt in tents. Isaac loved Esau because he ate of his hunting, while Rebecca loved Jacob.”

In the type, therefore, Esau signifies the carnal people of Israel. As it is read concerning Nimrod, he was a hunter and a farmer: that is, abandoning the true God, he offered sacrilegious worship to the gods of foreign nations and devoted himself to earthly desires and passions.

But the fact that Jacob dwelt in the house as a simple and guileless man means that he did not receive the blessing of the firstborn through deceit, nor steal it by fraud. Rather, he received it as something owed to him, having purchased it from his brother with lentils, with his brother’s consent.

It follows: “Jacob cooked a stew. When Esau came to him from the field, exhausted, he said, ‘Give me some of this red stew, for I am exceedingly weary.’ Therefore his name was called Edom. Jacob said to him, ‘Sell me your birthright.’ He replied, ‘Behold, I am dying; of what use is my birthright to me?’ Jacob said, ‘Swear to me, then.’ Esau swore to him and sold his birthright. Having received bread and the dish of lentils, he ate and drank and went away, thinking little of having sold his birthright.”

The Hebrews transmit that all the firstborn exercised the priestly office before Aaron was chosen for the priesthood, and that they possessed priestly clothing in which they, dressed as they were, offered victims to God. They say that this was the birthright—that is, the garments of Esau—which he sold to his brother Jacob.

For the fact that Esau sold his birthright for food to his younger brother and afterward was deprived of his father’s blessing signifies the same Israelite people, who, as the book of Exodus indicates, were called God’s firstborn son. For the sake of the profits of the present age, they not only lost the honor of their primacy but also did not deserve to obtain the prepared reward of the heavenly kingdom, when the Lord reproaches them in a certain manner, saying: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matt. XXI).

The birthright itself, as has already been said above, was priestly clothing, which the elder sons, clothed in it with their father’s blessing, wore when they offered victims to God as though they were high priests. Through their desire for earthly love, the Jews lost this gift together with the glory of the future kingdom.

It follows:

### (Chapter XXVI—verses 1 and following) [Cols. 0983A–D]

When a famine arose in the land, after the barrenness that had occurred in the days of Abraham, Isaac went to Abimelech, king of the Philistines, at Gerar. The question arises when this happened: whether after Esau sold his birthright—for it is after that account that this narrative begins—or whether, as often happens, the narrator returned by recapitulation to an earlier event when, proceeding from the account of his sons, he had reached the passage concerning the lentil stew. The difficulty is that this is the same Abimelech who had also desired Sarah; for his intermediary and the commander of his army, who are mentioned there, are mentioned here as well. Could he have lived so long? When he became Abraham’s friend, Isaac had not yet been born, although he had already been promised. Let us suppose that this occurred one year before Isaac was born. Isaac then fathered his sons when he was sixty years old; they were young men when Esau sold his birthright. Let us suppose that they were about twenty years old: Isaac’s age at the time of this event involving his sons would then have been about eighty. Let us suppose that Abimelech was a young man when he desired Isaac’s mother and became Abraham’s friend. He could therefore already have been nearly one hundred years old if Isaac went into that land because of the famine after the event involving his sons. Necessity, then, does not force us to think that Isaac’s journey to Gerar is narrated by recapitulation. But since Isaac is said to have remained there for a long time, to have dug wells, to have disputed over them, and to have become wealthy, it is remarkable unless these matters are recalled by way of recapitulation. They had been omitted so that the narrative might first proceed from the account of his sons to the passage concerning the lentil stew. The narrative continues:

“And the Lord appeared to him and said: ‘Do not go down into Egypt, but remain in the land that I shall tell you, and dwell there as a stranger. I will be with you and bless you; for to you and to your offspring I will give all these regions, fulfilling the oath that I swore to Abraham your father. I will multiply your offspring like the stars of heaven, and I will give your descendants all these regions; and all the nations of the earth shall be blessed in your offspring, because Abraham obeyed my voice.’”

This patriarch had neither another wife nor a concubine; nevertheless, we should not for that reason prefer him to his father. The merits of his father’s faith and obedience were undoubtedly greater, so much so that, because of him, God says that he is doing for Isaac the good things that he does, when he says to him: “I am the God of Abraham your father. Do not be afraid, for I am with you; I have blessed you, and I will multiply your offspring.” Thus we understand how chastely Abraham acted—something that seems to those who are impure and who seek from the Holy Scriptures defenses for their wickedness to have been done lustfully.

The narrative continues:

“So Isaac remained in Gerar. When the men of that place questioned him about his wife, he replied, ‘She is my sister,’ for he had been afraid to confess that she was joined to him in marriage, thinking that perhaps they would kill him because of her beauty.”

Isaac pretended that Rebecca, who was his wife, was his sister. Rebecca’s lineage is not concealed, and it is clear that she was his sister through a well-known relationship. But as for his concealing that she was his wife, what is surprising or wrong if he imitated his father, since the same justice defends him by which his father was found blameless when accused in a similar matter?

The narrative continues:

“When many days had passed and he had remained there, Abimelech, king of the Philistines, looked out through the window and saw him playing with Rebecca his wife. He summoned him and said, ‘It is obvious that she is your wife. Why did you say that she was your sister?’ He replied, ‘I was afraid that I might die because of her.’”

The same arguments that apply to Abraham in this matter also apply to Isaac his son, and it is not difficult to review them. Unless, perhaps, one of the diligent wishes to ask in what figurative sacrament we should understand the fact that the foreign king recognized Rebecca as the wife of her husband when he saw him playing with her—something he would not have recognized unless he was playing with her as one ought not to play with a woman who was not his wife. When holy married men do this, they do not do it pointlessly but prudently: they descend, in a certain sense, to the weakness of the female sex, so that with gentle cheerfulness they may say or do something, not weakening but tempering masculine vigor.

What does it signify, in the sacrament of Christ and the Church, that so great a patriarch played with his wife, and that their marriage was recognized on that account? Surely anyone who carefully examines this man’s secret in the Holy Scriptures, lest he sin through error in the Church, will find that he briefly concealed his majesty—by which, in the form of God, he is equal to God—in the form of a servant, so that human weakness might be capable of receiving him; and in this way he suitably adapted himself to his wife.

For what is absurd—or rather, what is not fittingly adapted to the foreshadowing of future things—if God’s prophet played in a bodily manner so as to win his wife’s affection, when the Word of God himself became flesh in order to dwell among us?

The narrative continues:

### (Verses 12–13) [Cols. 0984A–D]

“Isaac sowed in that land and received a hundredfold in that same year. The Lord blessed him, and the man became wealthy; he continued to prosper and grow until he became exceedingly great.”

The following words show that Isaac’s wealth is being spoken of in terms of earthly prosperity. The narrator explains the same riches by which he became great, and this moved Abimelech. He was afraid that Isaac’s presence there might be dangerous to his own power. Although these things signify something spiritual, nevertheless, in accordance with what actually happened, the words “The Lord blessed him” were placed beforehand. Thus sound faith may understand that even temporal gifts can neither be given nor hoped for—although they are sought by the weak—unless they are granted by the one God; and that the person who is faithful in little should also be faithful in much, and that whoever is found faithful in unrighteous mammon may also deserve to receive what is true, as the Lord says in the Gospel (Luke 16).

Isaac is the word of the Lord. In the Law of God this word sows barley, while in the Gospels it sows wheat: the former food it prepares for the more perfect and spiritual, the latter for the imperfect and natural, because it is written: “You will save both human beings and animals, O Lord” (Psalm 35).

Isaac, therefore—that is, the word of the Law—sows barley, and yet in that barley he finds a hundredfold harvest. You also find in the Law martyrs, whose fruit is a hundredfold.

But our Lord Isaac—the more perfect things of the Gospels—spoke everything to the apostles, while speaking plainly and commonly to the crowds. Do you wish to see that he himself also offers barley food to beginners? It is written in the Gospels that he fed the crowds a second time, but he fed those whom he had first fed; afterward, when they had already advanced in word and teaching, he offered them loaves of wheat.

But afterward, the Lord, it says, blessed Isaac, and he became very great. Isaac was small in the Law, but with the passage of time he becomes great in the Prophets. For while he is only in the Law, he is not yet great, since the Law is also covered by a veil. He therefore grows in the Prophets. When he has reached the point at which the veil is removed from the letter, then he will be exceedingly great, when the letter of the Law begins to be separated from him like barley straw and what is spiritual in the Law appears. Then Isaac will be magnified and become exceedingly great.

Consider how the Lord also breaks a few loaves in the Gospels and feeds so many thousands of people, while so many baskets of leftovers remain. As long as the loaves remain whole, no one is satisfied and no one is refreshed; nor do the loaves themselves appear to increase. Consider, then, how we now break a few loaves in the divine Scriptures. We take a few words, and how many thousands of people are fed!

The narrative continues:

### (Verses 14 and following) [Cols. 0985A–C]

“He possessed flocks of sheep and herds of cattle, and a very large household. He began to dig the wells that the servants of his father Abraham had dug; but the Philistines, envying them, filled them with earth, and so forth.”

Who is this Isaac if not our Savior? Who is the one who, having descended into this torrent of Gerar, first wishes to dig those wells that his father’s servants had dug? Moses had dug the well of the Law; David, Solomon, and the Prophets, who wrote the books of the Old Testament, had dug them also. Yet they had been filled with the earthly and sordid understanding of the Jews.

When Isaac—that is, our Lord and Savior, whose figure Isaac represented—wished to cleanse these wells, he showed that whatever the Prophets said, they said about him. The Philistines—that is, the Jews, alienated from the kingdom of God—quarreled with him. But he departs from them, for he cannot be with those who did not wish to have water in the wells but earth. He says to them: “Behold, your house will be left to you desolate” (Matthew 23).

Isaac therefore dug a new well. Indeed, Isaac’s servants dug it. Isaac’s servants are Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. His servants are Peter, James, and Jude; the apostle Paul is also his servant. All of them dig the wells of the New Testament.

But those who think in earthly terms quarrel on their behalf. They neither allow new things to be established nor cleanse the old; they oppose the Gospel wells and resist the apostolic ones. Since they contradict and quarrel in everything, it is said to them: “Since you have judged yourselves unworthy of the grace of God, behold, we are turning to the Gentiles” (Acts 13).

After this Isaac dug a third well and called the name of that place “Broadness,” saying: “Now the Lord has enlarged us and made us increase upon the earth.” Truly Isaac has now been enlarged, and his name has increased throughout the whole earth, when he fulfilled in us the knowledge of the Trinity. At that time he was known only in Judea, and his name was proclaimed in Israel (Psalm 75); but now “their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Romans 10).

For Isaac’s servants—that is, the apostles of the Lord and Savior—went out through the whole world, dug wells, and revealed living water to everyone, baptizing all nations in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

But what does it mean that Isaac called the wells that Abraham had opened by the same names as his father? He did not change the names of the wells. It is remarkable that Moses among us is still called Moses, and that each prophet is called by his own name. Christ did not change their names but their understanding.

This is the mystical interpretation.

Morally, however, Isaac is described as digging wells among a foreign people. By this example we learn that, placed in the hardship of this pilgrimage, we should penetrate the depths of our thoughts; and, until the water of true understanding answers us, the hand of our inquiry should never grow sluggish in drawing out the inner things of the heart.

Yet these wells are filled by the allophyli—that is, unclean spirits lying in wait—because unclean spirits, when they see us digging with greater diligence, plunge troublesome thoughts of temptation into us.

The narrative continues:

### (Verses 23 and following) [Cols. 0985D–0986A]

“From there he went up to Beersheba, where the Lord appeared to him that very night and said: ‘I am the God of Abraham your father.’”

This continues up to the point where it says: “They rose early and swore an oath to one another, and he sent them away in peace.”

The apostle Paul explained two figures to us in Isaac. First, he said that Ishmael, the son of Hagar, represented the people according to the flesh, while Isaac represented the people who are of faith. Second, he said: “He does not say, ‘And to seeds,’ as though referring to many, but ‘And to your seed,’ as referring to one, who is Christ.”

Isaac therefore represents both the people and Christ. It is certain that Christ, as the Word of God, speaks not only in the Gospels but also in the Law and in the Prophets. In the Law he teaches beginners; in the Gospels, the perfect. Isaac therefore now represents the Word that is in the Law and the Prophets.

Isaac therefore went up to the well of the oath, and the Lord appeared to him. We call the ascent of the Law the adornment of the Temple and the services of the divine things carried out there. The increase of the Prophets can also be called the ascent of the Law. Perhaps for this reason he is said to have gone to the well of the oath, and the Lord appeared to him there. For through the Prophets the Lord swore, “and he will not repent,” that he himself would be a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek (Psalm 109).

God therefore appeared to him at the well of the oath, confirming the promises that had been made concerning him.

“And he built an altar there to the Lord; and, having invoked the name of the Lord, he pitched his tent there, and commanded his servants to dig a well.”

Isaac also builds an altar in the Law and pitches his tent. In the Gospels, however, he does not pitch a tent but builds a house and lays a foundation. Hear Wisdom speaking about the Church: “Wisdom,” it says, “built herself a house and set up seven pillars.”

Hear Paul also speaking about this: “For no one can lay any foundation other than the one that has been laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 3).

Where there is a tent, even if it is pitched, it must undoubtedly be taken down. But where there are foundations and a house is built upon a rock, that house is never taken down, for it has been founded upon the rock.

Yet Isaac also digs a well there, and he never ceases digging wells until a spring of living water rises and the rushing river gladdens the city of God.

The narrative continues:

“But that same Abimelech, who had previously honored Abraham, now came with his friends from Gerar to Isaac. Isaac said to them, ‘Why have you come to me? You hate me and drove me away from you.’ They replied, saying, ‘Indeed, we have clearly seen that the Lord is with you. And we said, Let there be an oath between us and you, and let us make a covenant with you, so that you will do us no harm.’”

[Cols. 0986B–D]

This Abimelech does not always have peace with Isaac. Sometimes he disagrees with him; sometimes he seeks peace. This Abimelech represents the learned and wise men of the world, who through philosophical education have grasped many things even from the truth.

We can understand how this Abimelech relates to Isaac, who represents the Word of God that is in the Law. He cannot always be in disagreement with him, nor can he always be at peace. The philosophy of the world is neither contrary to the Law of God in everything nor harmonious with it in everything.

Many philosophers have written that there is one God who created all things. In this they agree with the Law of God. Some have also added that God made and governs all things through his Word, and that the Word of God is the means by which he orders everything. In this they write things consonant not only with the Law but also with the Gospels.

Moral and natural philosophy, as it is called, agrees with nearly everything that belongs to us. It disagrees with us when it says that matter is coeternal with God; it disagrees when it denies that God cares for mortal things and restricts his providence to the regions above the sphere of the moon. They disagree with us when they make the lives of those who are born depend upon the courses of the stars; they disagree when they say that this world is eternal and will never be brought to an end. There are also many other matters in which they either disagree or agree with us.

For this reason Abimelech, according to this figure, is sometimes described as disagreeing.

Nor do I think it was without purpose that the Holy Spirit, who wrote these things, took care to mention that two others came with Abimelech: Ochozath, his friend, and Phicol, the commander of his army.

Ochozath is interpreted as “holding,” and Phicol as “the mouth of all”; Abimelech himself means “my father is king.” These three represent the whole of philosophy, which among them is divided into three parts: logic, physics, and ethics—that is, rational, natural, and moral philosophy.

Rational philosophy is the one that confesses God as the Father of all; it is represented by Abimelech. Natural philosophy is the one that is fixed and holds all things, relying, as it were, upon the powers of nature itself; it is represented by Ochozath, whose name means “holding.” Moral philosophy is in everyone’s mouth, belongs to everyone, and circulates in everyone’s speech through the common likeness of its precepts; it is represented by Phicol, whose name means “the mouth of all.”

All those, therefore, who have been trained in such disciplines come to the Law of God and say: “Indeed, we have clearly seen that the Lord is with you. And we said, Let there be an oath between us, and let us enter into a covenant, so that you will do us no harm, just as we have touched none of your possessions and have done nothing that would injure you, but sent you away in peace, increased by the blessing of the Lord.”

These three, who seek peace from the Word of God and wish to anticipate through a covenant their fellowship with it, can also represent the Magi who came from the eastern regions, instructed by the books of their ancestors and by the teaching of their forebears. They say: “We have clearly seen that the king has been born, and we have seen that God is with him, and we have come to adore him” (Matthew 2).

And if anyone has been trained in such disciplines, seeing that God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, and astonished by the greatness of his works, should say: “We have clearly seen that the Lord is with you, and we said, Let there be an oath between us.” For when he approaches the Law of God, he necessarily says: “I have sworn and determined to keep your judgments” (Psalm 118).

But what do they ask? “Do not do us any harm, just as we have touched none of your possessions, nor have we done anything that would injure you, but sent you away in peace, increased by the blessing of the Lord.”

By this they appear to ask for the remission of sins, so that they may not receive evils; they ask for blessing, not recompense.

[Cols. 0987A–B]

Finally, see what follows:

“Isaac made a great feast for them, and they ate and drank. After eating and drinking, they rose and swore an oath to one another, and Isaac sent them away in peace to their own place.”

It is certain that the one who ministers the Word is a debtor both to the wise and to the foolish. Because here he provides a feast for the wise, it is therefore said that he made not a small but a great feast.

The narrative continues:

“Behold, on that same day Isaac’s servants came and reported to him concerning the well that they had dug, saying, ‘We have found water.’ Therefore he called it Abundance; and the name of the city was called Beersheba.”

This signifies that they found water, and that the well was therefore called “the Well of Satiety”; and the city was called Beersheba, that is, “the Well of Satiety.”

Although above we may assert that Beersheba was named either from the word “oath” or from the number seven of the sheep—for *Sabee* means “seven”—nevertheless, here, because water was found, Isaac, alluding to the name of the city that already existed, slightly altered the letter. Instead of the hissing Hebrew *sin*, with which *Sabee* begins, he used the Greek sigma—that is, the Hebrew *samekh*.

Otherwise, according to the rule of allegory, after so many wells it would not at all be fitting that, at the end of his virtues, Isaac should fail to find water.

The narrative continues:

### (Chapter XXVII—verses 1 and following) [Cols. 0987C–D]

“Isaac grew old, and his eyes became dim, so that he could not see. He called Esau his elder son and said to him, ‘My son.’ He answered, ‘Here I am.’ His father said to him, ‘You see that I have grown old and do not know the day of my death. Take your weapons, your quiver and bow, and go out. When you have caught something by hunting, prepare for me from it the kind of dish you know I like, and bring it to me so that I may eat, and my soul may bless you before I die.’”

There are too many examples for us to demonstrate by examples that holy men and those dear to God knew only what had been revealed to them by the Lord, while they were ignorant of what had not been revealed to them. Isaac too was a just man and dear to God, yet through error he blessed not the one he wished to bless but the one he did not wish to bless.

It is therefore not surprising that Isaac, especially when his own interests were involved, did not know what he was doing. He was all the more mistaken at the time when he wished to elevate a bloodthirsty son, devoted to pleasure and later willing to kill his brother, while passing over the one who lived innocently at home, and to carry out his own will rather than God’s.

Thus, by the dispensation of divine judgment, he was made blind in his eyes. Although he himself said, “The voice is Jacob’s voice, but the hands are Esau’s hands,” he nevertheless came to understand that the younger son was the one who had remained after taking away his brother’s blessing. From this we should understand that a spiritual admonition was given in this event, so that he might confirm his blessing upon the younger son, with whom he ought rather to have been angry because he had deceived his father.

Isaac bears the image of God the Father; Rebecca, of the Holy Spirit; Esau, of the earlier people and of the devil; Jacob, of the Church or of Christ.

Isaac’s old age indicates the consummation of the world. His eyes becoming dim signifies that faith had failed and perished from the world, and that the ancient light of religion had been neglected.

The elder son’s being called the elder signifies the Jews’ acceptance of the Law. The father’s love of his food and his catch signifies human beings saved from error, whom every just person hunts through teaching.

The Word of God is the promise of blessing and the hope of the future kingdom, in which the saints will reign with Christ and celebrate the true Sabbath.

The narrative continues:

### (Verses 5 and following) [Cols. 0988A–C]

“When Rebecca heard this, and he had gone into the field to fulfill his father’s command, she said to her son Jacob: ‘I heard your father speaking with your brother Esau and saying to him, “Bring me some of your game and prepare food for me to eat, and I will bless you before the Lord before I die.” Now therefore, my son, obey my advice. Go to the flock and bring me two excellent young goats, so that I may prepare from them food for your father, of the kind he gladly eats. When you bring it to him and he has eaten, may he bless you before he dies.’”

Rebecca, full of the Holy Spirit and knowing what she had heard before she gave birth—“The elder shall serve the younger”—but especially representing the form of the Holy Spirit, who knew beforehand what was to come in Christ, was already meditating upon Jacob.

“Bring me two young goats,” she says, prefiguring the Savior’s coming in the flesh, in which he would especially free those who were held liable for sins. For throughout the Scriptures young goats are understood as representing sinners.

The command to bring two signifies the assumption of two peoples; the fact that they are young and good signifies docile and innocent dispositions.

Or, alternatively, the flesh of the goats from which Isaac’s food was prepared should be understood as the conversion of sinners coming from two peoples, namely the Jews and all the nations.

The bread signifies the faith of the apostles and of those from the Jewish people who believed at Pentecost when the Holy Spirit came. In the wine, the blood of the martyrs is to be understood. God is understood to take delight in such food and drink.

The narrative continues:

“She then clothed him in Esau’s very fine garments, which she had with her at home, and wrapped the skins of the young goats around his hands and covered his bare neck.”

At this point the Hebrews relate that the firstborn exercised the priestly office and possessed priestly clothing, in which they clothed themselves to offer sacrifices to God before Aaron was chosen for the priesthood.

Esau’s garment signifies the faith and Scriptures of the Hebrews, with which the people of the nations have been clothed; or it should be understood as the faith of the patriarchs.

The skins of the young goats with which Jacob’s hands and neck were covered signify the sins of both peoples, which Christ affixed with himself to the cross in the extension of his hands.

The fact that she covered his bare neck with the same skins signifies that, because he assumed their person, he also lamented their weaknesses and wept for their sins in his own voice.

The narrative continues:

“‘How were you able to find it so quickly, my son?’ he asked. He replied, ‘It was God’s will that what I wanted should quickly come to me.’”

When Isaac asks Jacob why he has come so quickly, he marvels at the swift faith of believers. The offering of delectable food signifies a sacrifice pleasing to God and the salvation of sinners.

The narrative continues:

### (Verses 21 and following) [Cols. 0988D–0989A]

“Isaac said, ‘Come closer, so that I may touch you, my son, and test whether you are my son Esau or not.’ He approached his father; and when Isaac had felt him, he said, ‘The voice is Jacob’s voice, but the hands are Esau’s hands.’ He did not recognize him, because his hairy hands resembled those of his elder brother.”

Here Isaac prefigured the Jewish people, and his son Jacob, the Lord Jesus Christ. Isaac was dim-sighted in his eyes and prophesied, yet in the present he did not see the son for whom he foresaw so many things in the future. For the Jewish people, filled with the spirit of prophecy and yet blind, did not recognize in the present the one about whom they foretold so much in the future.

The narrative continues:

“As soon as he perceived the fragrance of his garments, he blessed him and said: ‘Behold, the fragrance of my son is like the fragrance of a full field which the Lord has blessed. May God give you of the dew of heaven and of the richness of the earth, abundance of grain, wine, and oil. May peoples serve you, and tribes bow down to you. Be lord over your brothers, and may the sons of your mother bow before you. Let the one who curses you be cursed, and let the one who blesses you be filled with blessings.’”

Jacob’s blessing is the preaching of Christ among all the nations. This is being accomplished and is taking place; this is the Law and the Prophecy.

Isaac represents the Jewish people, by whom Christ is blessed as though by one who does not know him, because he is not known by that people. By the fragrance of Christ’s name, the world is filled as a field is filled. Or certainly, the fragrance of a full field should be understood as the deeds of good works.

His blessing comes from the dew of heaven, that is, from the rain of divine words; and from the richness of the earth, that is, from the gathering of peoples or from apostolic teaching.

His are the abundance of grain and wine, that is, the multitude that gathers grain and wine in the sacrament of his body and blood. The abundance of grain and wine can also be understood as the multitude of holy martyrs and virgins.

The nations serve him, and rulers worship him. He is the Lord of his brothers, because his people rules over the Jews.

The sons of his father worship him, that is, the sons of Abraham according to faith, since he himself is also the son of Abraham according to the flesh.

The one who curses him will be cursed, and the one who blesses him is blessed.

Our Christ, I say, is blessed by the mouth of the Jews—although they are in error, they nevertheless sing the Law and the Prophets—that is, he is truly proclaimed. Another is thought to be blessed, the one whom those erring people expect.

The narrative continues:

### (Verses 30 and following) [Cols. 0989B–C]

“Isaac had scarcely finished speaking when Jacob went outside and Esau came in. He brought food prepared from his hunt to his father and said, ‘Rise, my father, and eat from your son’s game, so that your soul may bless me.’”

In the prefiguration of these two brothers, what the Gospel reading relates is very aptly applicable. It says: “A certain ruler of the synagogue came to Jesus and said to him, ‘My daughter has just died; but come, lay your hand upon her, and she will live’” (Matthew 9).

As the Lord went to raise her, behold, a woman who suffered from a flow of blood came and represented the type of the Church. She approached from behind, as though the Lord did not know, and touched the fringe of his garment, and was immediately healed.

The Lord said to her: “Go, daughter, in peace; your faith has saved you.”

The narrative continues:

“Isaac said to him, ‘Who are you?’ He replied, ‘I am your firstborn son, Esau.’ Isaac was struck with great astonishment and, marveling beyond what can be believed, said: ‘Who, then, was the one who brought me his captured game earlier, and I ate from everything before you came? I blessed him, and he shall be blessed?’”

Behold, when the elder son asks for the promised blessing, Isaac is astonished. Recognizing that he had blessed one person in place of another, he marvels and asks who that person was. Yet he does not complain that he has been deceived. Rather, as soon as the great mystery has been revealed to him inwardly in his heart, he avoids anger and confirms the blessing rather than pronouncing a curse.
