Rather, he would have been astonished in anger if these things had happened according to earthly custom rather than through heavenly inspiration.

These are events, but prophetic events; events on earth, but from heaven; through human beings, but by divine action. If each detail were examined, so richly fertile in mysteries, many volumes would have to be completed. But a moderate limit must be imposed upon this work, and it compels us to hasten on to other matters.

The narrative continues:

### (Verses 34 and following) [Cols. 0989D–0990A]

“When Esau heard his father’s words, he cried out with a great cry and, dismayed, said, ‘Bless me too, my father.’ He replied, ‘Your brother came deceitfully and took your blessing.’ He added, ‘He was rightly named Jacob, for he has supplanted me twice. First he took away my birthright, and now for the second time he has stolen my blessing.’”

Here again Jacob is interpreted as “supplanter.” By referring to the fact that he had deceived his brother through craft, Isaac alluded to Jacob’s name. He had previously been called Jacob because at his birth he grasped his brother’s heel.

The narrative continues:

“He said again to his father: ‘Have you not reserved a blessing for me also?’ Isaac replied, ‘I have made him your lord, and I have subjected all his brothers to his service. I have established him with grain and wine; what more can I do for you now, my son?’ Esau said to him, ‘Do you have only one blessing, father? I beg you, bless me also.’ And when he wept with a great wail, Isaac was moved and said to him: ‘Your blessing shall be in the richness of the earth and in the dew of heaven from above. You shall live by the sword, and you shall serve your brother. But the time will come when you shall shake off and break his yoke from your neck.’”

This signifies that the Idumeans would serve the Jews, and that a time would come when they would cast off the yoke of servitude from their neck and resist their rule.

For we do not see that the elder son was entirely despised. Rather, as the Apostle says: “When the fullness of the nations has entered, then all Israel will be saved” (Romans 11).

The prophecy of this second blessing is nevertheless as follows: “Your blessing shall be in the richness of the earth and in the dew of heaven from above.” This means in the fertility of possessions and the power of the kingdom that existed among that people.

Or certainly, “in the richness of the earth and in the dew of heaven from above” means that Israel will be blessed in confession of the Lord’s incarnation and in faith in his divinity.

Or again, “in the dew of heaven shall be his blessing,” that is, in the utterances of God. For to them the utterances of God and the covenants of the Law were first entrusted.

“You shall live by the sword”: that people, being devoted to bloodshed, carried out death against Christ and the Prophets.

“And you shall serve your brother,” namely, the Christian people.

“The time will come when you shall shake off and break the yoke from your neck,” when, through knowledge of the faith, you turn to the grace of Christ and lay down the burden of the Law; when you will no longer be called the servant of the lesser people but, through faith, their brother.

The narrative continues:

### (Verses 41 and following) [Cols. 0990B–C]

“Esau always hated Jacob because of the blessing with which his father had blessed him. He said in his heart, ‘The days of mourning for my father will come, and then I will kill my brother Jacob.’”

Because iniquity is hostile to righteousness, Esau is stirred to discord and deceitfully devises murder, saying in his heart: “The days of mourning for my father will approach, and I will kill my brother Jacob.”

So too the devil, who had earlier prefigured the fratricidal Jews in Cain, confesses it most plainly in Esau. He also indicates the time of the killing and the wickedness that the Jews exercised against Christ.

The narrative continues:

“Rebecca sent and called for Jacob her son and said to him: ‘Behold, your brother Esau is threatening to kill you.’”

How were Esau’s words reported to Rebecca—that he had threatened to kill his brother—when Scripture says that he spoke this in his own thoughts? It is because we are thereby given to understand that everything was revealed to her divinely. Hence this too belongs to the great mystery: she wished her younger son to be blessed in place of the elder.

The narrative continues:

“Now therefore, my son, listen to my voice. Arise and flee to my brother Laban in Aram. You shall dwell with him for a few days, until your brother’s fury subsides, his anger ceases, and he forgets what you have done to him. Then I will send for you and bring you back from there.”

(Cap. XXVIII.—Verses 1 ff.) Isaac called Jacob and blessed him, and commanded him, saying: “Do not take a wife from the stock of Canaan; but go and depart to Mesopotamia of Syria, to the house of Bethuel, your mother’s father, and take for yourself from there a wife from the daughters of Laban, your maternal uncle. May almighty God bless you and make you grow and multiply, so that you may become a multitude of peoples; and may he give you the blessings of Abraham, and to your offspring after you, so that you may possess the land of your sojourning, which he promised to your grandfather.”

Here we now understand that Jacob’s offspring was separated from Isaac’s other offspring, which came through Esau. For when it was said, “In Isaac shall your offspring be called” (Gen. XXI), referring even to the city of God, another offspring was separated from it: the one that was in the son of the slave woman, and the one that was destined to be in the sons of Keturah. But it was still uncertain, concerning the two twin sons of Isaac, whether that blessing pertained to both or to one of them; and, if to one, which one it was. This has now been made clear, when Jacob is prophetically blessed by his father and is told, “May you become a multitude of peoples, and may you possess the blessings of your grandfather Abraham.”

Just as Jacob, fleeing his brother’s deceit, made his way to Mesopotamia, so Christ too, compelled by the unbelief of the Jews, departed for Galilee, intending from there to take the Church as a bride from the Gentiles. And just as Jacob, fleeing his brother’s deceit, left his house, homeland, and parents and went to a distant region in order to take a wife for himself, so Christ, leaving his parents according to the flesh—that is, the people of Israel—and his homeland—that is, Jerusalem and all the regions of Judaea—went to the Gentiles, taking the Church for himself, so that what was spoken through the prophet might be fulfilled: “The people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me” (Ps. XVII).

Yet we say that the Lord came only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, and that he did not wish to take the children’s bread and give it to dogs; and that he first brought the blessing to the Jewish people, to whom the utterances of God, the promise, the giving of the law, and the making of the covenant had been entrusted. But because they were unwilling to believe, we see that the blessing was transferred to Jacob—that is, to the younger people. Nevertheless, we do not see the elder son as wholly rejected, because “when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved” (Rom. XI).

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 0991]

[Col. 0991A] God of supreme goodness, from whom every good and every perfect gift is given, descending from above, from the Father of lights (Jas. I), from whom and through whom good will is prepared in human beings—he who gave me the beginning of this work—may he himself also grant me to provide well-sounding speech. And I shall say to my Lord what the holy patriarch Jacob also said: “If the Lord my God is with me in the work that I have now undertaken, and guards me” (Gen. XXVIII), “he shall be my God”; and this holy Scripture, which I hold in my hands, shall be for my benefit. I shall offer him tithes, sacrifices, and firstfruits—that is, I shall consecrate to his holy name both the beginning of good will and the perfection of good work.

(Verses 10 ff.) Jacob therefore departed from Beersheba and proceeded toward Haran. When he had come to a certain place and wished to rest there after sunset, he took one of the stones lying there, placed it beneath his head, and slept in that same place. And he saw in a dream a ladder standing upon the earth, whose top touched heaven; and he also saw the angels of God ascending and descending upon it, and the Lord leaning upon the ladder and saying to him:

“I am the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac your father. The land on which you sleep I will give to you and to your offspring. Your offspring shall be like the dust of the earth; you shall spread toward the east and the west, the north and the south; and all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed in you and in your offspring. I will be your guardian wherever you go, and I will bring you back to this land. I will not abandon you until I have fulfilled everything that I have said.”

This sleep of Jacob is the death or passion of Christ. The stone at his head, which is in a certain sense also expressly called “anointed,” signifies Christ: for “the head of the man is Christ”; and who does not know that Christ is named from anointing?

The house of God signifies that Christ was born there, in Bethlehem. The gate of heaven signifies that there he descended to earth and from there ascended again to heaven. The raising up of the stone is the resurrection of Christ.

Moreover, the ladder is Christ, who said, “I am the way” (John XIV). Upon this ladder the angels ascend and descend; in them the evangelists, the preachers of Christ, are signified. The two Testaments may also be understood through the ladder, or certainly faith and works, through which the Gentiles have become heirs of the heavenly kingdom. For through these there is ascent to God and descent of God to human beings.

The angels—that is, the messengers of the Church—are to be understood as its teachers. They ascend when, in order to understand his utterly transcendent divinity, they rise above the whole of creation, so that they may find him “in the beginning, the Word, God with God, through whom all things were made” (John I). They descend when they find him “made of a woman, made under the law, in order to redeem those who were under the law” (Gal. IV).

For on that ladder, from earth to heaven and from flesh to spirit, carnal people, advancing as though ascending, become spiritual. The spiritual themselves descend in a certain way to nourish them with milk, when they cannot speak to them as spiritual people but as carnal people. He himself is above in his head, and he himself is below in his body, which is the Church.

We therefore understand him himself to be the ladder, because he said, “No one can come to the Father except through me” (John XVI). One therefore ascends to him so that he may be understood in the heights; and one descends to him so that the little one may be nourished in his members. Through him they raise themselves up so that they may await him in sublime fashion; through him they also humble themselves so that they may announce him with sublimity and moderation. It follows:

(Verses 18 ff.) Rising in the morning, therefore, Jacob took the stone that he had placed beneath his head and set it up as a pillar, pouring oil over it. And he called the name of that city Bethel, which previously had been called Luz.

And he called the name of that place Bethel, although previously Luz had been the name of the ancient city. This signifies nothing other than “before” or “previously,” or “vestibule,” “threshold,” or “doorposts.”

But when he says, “The Lord is in this place, and I did not know it,” and, “How awe-inspiring is this place! This is nothing other than the house of God and the gate of heaven,” these words pertain to prophecy, because there the tabernacle that God established among human beings in his first people was destined to be. We should understand the gate of heaven as the entrance by which believers gain access to obtain the kingdom of heaven.

When Jacob set up the stone that he had placed at his head and made it into a pillar, pouring oil over it, he did nothing resembling idolatry. For neither then nor afterward did he frequent the stone by worshiping or sacrificing to it. Rather, it was an unmistakable prophetic sign, pertaining to anointing; hence Christ’s name comes from chrism.

As for the vow he made—that, if his journey there and back prospered, he would give tithes to the house of God that was to be established in that place—this is a prophecy of the house of God. On returning, he sacrificed to God there also, not calling that stone God, but calling it the house of God, because the house of God was destined to be in that place. It follows:

(Cap. XXIX.—Verses 1 ff.) Jacob departed from there and came to the land of the East. He saw a well in a field, and three flocks of sheep lying beside it, for the animals were watered from it; and its mouth was closed with a large stone. It was customary that, after all the sheep had been gathered, they would roll away the stone, and, when the flocks had been refreshed, they would place it again over the mouth of the well.

The eastern land to which our Lord departed signifies those who, leaving behind the darkness of vices, were seeking works of light. For God was known only in Judaea. The well that he found there is to be understood as the Mosaic law. Beside it the three flocks are said to have lain: namely, the scribes, the Pharisees, and the Sadducees, whom the Lord is read to have reproved.

The sheep of Laban, whom the Lord watered after removing the large stone with which the mouth of the well was closed: this happened when he spoke separately to the disciples and separately to the crowds. At that time he removed the shadows and images with which the history of the law had been covered, when he allowed everything that had been written about him to be fulfilled in himself, or showed that it had been fulfilled. From the Lord’s passion onward, the law is open to all the faithful through spiritual understanding.

For previously, although during the festival of Booths, when peoples gathered from everywhere, the book of Deuteronomy was read aloud by the priests, it was nevertheless closed again, because the one in whom everything was fulfilled in truth had not yet come. It follows:

(Verses 6 ff.) “Look, Rachel was coming with her father’s sheep, for she herself tended the flock.” When Jacob saw her and knew that she was his cousin, and that they were the sheep of Laban, his maternal uncle, he removed the stone with which the well was closed. After watering the flock, he kissed her; then, raising his voice, he wept and told her that he was her father’s brother’s son and the son of Rebekah.

The meaning is that those with whom Jacob had previously been speaking, when asked who the woman was who was coming with the sheep, had told him that she was Laban’s daughter, whom Jacob of course did not know. Scripture placed their question and answer beforehand in order to make this understood.

What is written—“Jacob kissed Rachel; and crying out with his voice, he wept and told her that he was her father’s brother’s son and the son of Rebekah” (Gen. XXIX)—belonged to the custom of the simplicity of the ancients, in which relatives kissed their female relatives; this is still done today in many places. But it may be asked how she accepted a kiss from a stranger, if Jacob only afterward revealed their relationship.

It must therefore be understood either that he, who had already heard who she was, confidently rushed to kiss her, or that Scripture later narrated by recapitulation what had happened first—that is, it subsequently indicated who he was. It follows:

(Verses 13 ff.) When Laban had heard the reasons for Jacob’s journey, he answered him, “You are my bone and my flesh.” After a full month had passed, he said to him, “Because you are my brother, are you going to serve me for nothing? Tell me what your wages will be.”

He had two daughters: the name of the elder was Leah, while the younger was called Rachel. Leah, however, was bleary-eyed; Rachel had a beautiful face and an attractive appearance. Jacob loved her and said, “I will serve you for Rachel, your younger daughter, for seven years.”

Laban answered, “It is better that I give her to you than to another man.” Jacob therefore served for Rachel for seven years, and they seemed to him like a few days because of the greatness of his love.

It must be asked how it was said that they seemed to him like a few days, when even a short period of time usually seems long to lovers. It was said, therefore, with reference to the labor of servitude, which love made easy and light.

Jacob said to Laban, “Give me my wife, for the time has been completed, so that I may go in to her.” Laban summoned a great crowd of friends to a banquet and held the wedding. In the evening he brought his daughter Leah to Jacob, giving her a maidservant named Zilpah. When Jacob had gone in to her according to custom, morning came and he saw that it was Leah. He said to his father-in-law, “What is this that you have done to me? Did I not serve you for Rachel?”

Laban answered, “It is not customary in our place to give the younger in marriage before the elder. Complete the week of this marriage, and I will also give you this one for the work by which you will serve me for another seven years.”

Jacob agreed to the arrangement. After the week had passed, he took Rachel as his wife; her father had given her Bilhah as a maidservant. Finally, preferring the marriage he had desired, he placed the love of the later wife before that of the first.

If the account of this matter is not carefully considered, it will be thought that after Jacob took Leah as his wife, he then served another seven years for Rachel and only afterward took her as his wife. But this is not what happened. Rather, Laban said to him: “Complete the week of this marriage, and I will give you this one also for the work by which you will serve me for another seven years.”

By this he meant: “Complete the seven days of the wedding, which pertain to the woman you have taken, and I will give you this one also in return for working for me for another seven years.” Then it follows: “Jacob did so; he completed the week, and he took Rachel as his wife. Laban gave his daughter Rachel his maidservant Bilhah, and Jacob went in to Rachel. He loved Rachel more than Leah, and he served another seven years.”

It is plainly apparent that after he had taken Rachel as his wife, he then served another seven years for her. For it would have been excessively harsh and exceedingly unjust for him, after being deceived, to be made to wait another seven years and only then to receive the woman whom he ought to have received first.

That weddings were customarily celebrated for seven days is also shown by the book of Judges in the case of Samson, when he made a vow for seven days; Scripture adds that young men customarily did this. It follows:

(Verses 31 ff.) When the Lord saw that Leah was despised, he opened her womb, while her sister remained barren. She conceived and bore a son, and called his name Reuben, saying, “God has seen my humiliation; now my husband will love me.”

Reuben is interpreted as “son of vision.” Again she conceived and bore a son, and said, “Because the Lord heard that my husband hated me, he has given me this one also.” And she called his name Simeon. From the expression “she was heard,” she gave the son the name Simeon. Simeon is interpreted as “hearing.”

She conceived a third time and bore a son, saying, “Now too my husband will be joined to me, because I have borne him three sons.” Therefore she called his name Levi. Levi is interpreted as “assumption.”

She conceived a fourth time and bore a son, and said, “Now I will confess to the Lord.” For this reason she called him Judah. Judah is interpreted as “confession.” His name was therefore derived from confession. Here, however, “confession” is understood as thanksgiving or praise, as it frequently is in the Psalms and in the Gospel: “I confess to you, Lord, Father of heaven and earth” (Matt. XI)—that is, “I give you thanks,” or “I glorify you.” It follows:

(Cap. XXX.—Verses 1 ff.) Rachel, seeing that she was barren, envied her sister and said to her husband, “Give me children, or else I shall die.” Jacob, becoming angry with her, answered, “Am I in the place of God, who has deprived you of the fruit of your womb?”

She said, “I have Bilhah, my maidservant. Go in to her, so that she may give birth upon my knees, and I may have children through her.” And she gave Bilhah to him in marriage. When the man had gone in to her, she conceived and bore a son.

Rachel said, “The Lord has judged in my favor and has heard my voice, giving me a son.” Therefore she called his name Dan. She called his name Dan because she expressed the reason for the name: since the Lord had judged, she gave the son of the maidservant that name. Dan is interpreted as “judgment.”

Again Bilhah conceived and bore a son. Rachel said of him, “God has compared me with my sister, and I have prevailed.” And she called his name Naphtali. Here another explanation of the name Naphtali is given than the one written in the book of the Hebrews. Why? From “conversation” or “comparison,” because the name Naphtali conveys both comparison and conversation. It follows:

(Verses 9 ff.) When Leah realized that she had stopped giving birth, she gave her maidservant Zilpah to her husband. After she had conceived and borne a son, Leah said, “Fortunate!” And for this reason his name was called Gad.

We may understand this as “ungirded.” For Gad can also sound like a preposition, and it derives from “event” or “girding,” which is called *gad*. Zilpah bore another son, and Leah said, “This is for my happiness; women will indeed call me happy.” Therefore she called his name Asher.

Asher therefore means not “riches” but “blessed,” at least in this passage. In other passages, because of the ambiguity of the word, riches may also be called by this name. It follows:

(Verses 14 ff.) Reuben went out during the wheat harvest and found mandrakes in the field, which he brought to his mother Leah. Rachel said, “Give me some of your son’s mandrakes.”

She answered, “Is it not enough that you have taken my husband from me, unless you also take my son’s mandrakes?” Rachel said, “Let him sleep with you tonight in exchange for your son’s mandrakes.”

When Jacob returned from the field in the evening, Leah went out to meet him and said, “You shall come in to me, because I have hired you with my son’s mandrakes.” He slept with her that night, and God heard her prayers. She conceived and bore a fifth son, and said, “God has given me my wages, because I gave my maidservant to my husband.”

And she called his name Issachar. The whole name is interpreted as “there is a reward”: *is* means “there is,” and *sachar* means “reward.” This was because, with the mandrakes of her son Reuben, she purchased for herself her husband’s access, which was owed to Rachel. It follows:

(Verses 19–20.) Again Leah conceived and bore a sixth son, and said, “God has endowed me with a good dowry; even this time my husband will remain with me, because I have borne him six sons.” Therefore she called his name Zebulun. The meaning is: “Because I have borne Jacob six sons, I am now secure, for my husband will dwell with me”; hence her son is called “dwelling.”

After this she bore a daughter and called her name Dinah. This is translated as “cause” or “quarrel,” for she became the cause of the quarrel at Shechem.

After the sons, the names of the parents should be set forth. Leah is interpreted as “one who labors”; Rachel as “sheep,” whose son is Joseph, from the fact that his mother wished another to be added to her.

Now Jacob, against whom four wives are brought as a grave accusation, is cleared by a general statement: when a custom existed, it was not a crime; and now it is a crime precisely because it is not customary. For some sins are against nature, others against custom, and others against a commandment. Since this is so, what crime is there in the charge brought against the holy man Jacob for having several wives at the same time? [Col. 0995A] If you consult nature, he used those women not for wantonness but for begetting children; if custom, this was regularly practiced at that time and in those lands; if commandment, no law prohibited it.

But now why is it a crime if someone does this, except that both custom and law forbid it? If anyone disregards these two, even if he can use several women solely for the purpose of begetting children, he nevertheless sins and violates human society itself, for which the propagation of children is necessary.

But because people, now that customs and laws have changed, cannot take pleasure in a multitude of wives except through the magnitude of lust, they err and suppose that it would have been altogether impossible to have many wives without the burning of carnal desire and sordid pleasure. They compare themselves—not with others whose spiritual virtue they are wholly unable to know—but, as the Apostle says, “do not understand themselves in relation to themselves” (I Tim. I). For they themselves, even if they have only one wife, approach her not merely manfully, moved by the duty of begetting children, but are often dragged weakly onward, overcome by the urge to intercourse. [Col. 0995B]

Therefore, just as the holy apostles rejoiced together with their hearers, who admired their teaching—not through eagerness to obtain praise, but through love for sowing the truth—so the holy patriarchs mingled with their wives as they received their seed, not from lust for pleasure, but from concern to propagate their succession.

For as to the charge that Faustus brought forward with utterly false accusation—that the four women had competed among themselves like prostitutes over which of them should drag him to intercourse—I do not know where he read this, unless perhaps in his own heart, as in a book of wicked deceptions, where he himself truly prostituted himself with that serpent, of whom the Apostle was afraid for the Church, which he desired to present as a chaste virgin to one husband, Christ (II Cor. XI), lest, just as the serpent had deceived Eve by its cunning, it should corrupt their minds by turning them away from Christ’s chastity. For these men are so friendly to that serpent that they maintain that it did good rather than harm.

That serpent plainly persuaded Faustus’ adulterated heart, pouring into it seeds of falsehood, so that it gave birth through its most filthy mouth to these badly conceived slanders and, with its most audacious pen, committed them also to memory. For none of the maidservants dragged Jacob away from the other; none quarreled with the other over intercourse with him.

That is why there was all the more order, because there was no lust; and the rights of conjugal authority were preserved all the more firmly because the injury of carnal desire was avoided more chastely. For the fact that he was hired by a wife makes our contention especially clear; there the truth itself cries out on its own behalf against the curses of the Manichaeans. What need was there for one wife to hire him unless it was the other’s turn for her husband to enter her? He would never have approached the other unless she had hired him; but he approached her in due and just alternation—her by whom he had fathered so many sons and whom he had obeyed, so that he might also father children by her maidservant, and by whom he later fathered children without her hiring him.

At that time Rachel had the night assigned to her, so that she might remain with her husband; the authority about which the Apostle spoke belonged to her—certainly the voice of the New Testament did not remain silent when it said, “Likewise, the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does” (I Cor. VII). She had therefore already made an agreement with her sister, becoming indebted to her and handing over to her own debtor the man whom she owed; for the Apostle calls it by this name: “Let the husband render the due to his wife” (ibid.). The husband was already her sister’s debtor; Rachel had received from her sister what the latter had voluntarily chosen, so that she might give her what was in her power.

But this man whom Faustus, with closed—or rather extinguished—eyes, accuses as shameless: if he had been a servant of lust rather than of justice, would he not have spent the whole day burning with desire for that night’s pleasure, when he was going to lie with the more beautiful woman, whom he certainly loved more and for whom he had freely expended twice seven years of labor? Once the day had ended and he went into her embrace, when would he have turned away, if he had been the sort of man the Manichaeans, understanding nothing, imagine him to be?

Would he not, disregarding the agreement with the women, have entered instead the beautiful woman, who owed him that very night not only by the custom of a wife but also by the right of their arrangement? He would have used his marital authority, since “the wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband” (ibid.), and since at that time the exchange of their service was being made in return for him.

He would therefore have used conjugal authority much more forcefully if he had been conquered by desire for her beauty. But the women would have proved better if they had competed for conceiving children, while he competed for intercourse and pleasure. Thus the man, temperate in every respect—and truly a man, because he used the women so manfully that he did not become subject to carnal pleasure but ruled over it—paid attention more to what he ought to do than to what was owed to him. He did not wish to abuse his authority for his own desire; he preferred to be the fulfiller of the debt rather than its exactor.

It therefore followed that he should render himself to the one whom she, for her own sake, had chosen—the one to whom he was indebted. When he suddenly and unexpectedly was called away from his most beautiful wife, and summoned to the less attractive one, he did not blaze with anger, was not clouded by sadness, and did not, in weakly coaxing fashion, strive to make Rachel give him the night instead. [Col. 0996B]

Rather, as a just husband and provident father, seeing that they were concerned with the care of offspring and that he sought nothing else from intercourse, he judged that he ought to obey their wishes. Each of them desired sons for herself, while nothing was diminished for him, since both bore children to him. It was as though he were saying: “Among yourselves, yield and concede as you wish, so that one of you may become more of a mother; why should I contend, when, whether from one side or the other, the child being born will have no other father?”

If Faustus had been sharp-minded in those writings, he would both have understood and praised this modesty, this restraint of desire, and the single aim of human posterity in the joining of conjugal bodies. But his intellect had been corrupted by a detestable sect; he looked for something to criticize and regarded as the greatest crime the honorable union of man and woman in marriage, by which they are joined for the purpose of begetting children.

Now that the patriarch’s conduct has been defended and the crime rejected which wicked error brought against him, let us proceed as best we can to examine the secrets of the mysteries. Let us knock with the devotion of faith, so that the Lord may open to us what these four wives of Jacob prefigured—two free women and two slave women.

We see that the Apostle understands the free woman and the slave woman whom Abraham had as the two covenants; but there it is easier to see the meaning of “one and one,” whereas here there are “two and two.” Moreover, there the slave woman’s son is disinherited, while here the sons of the slave women, together with the sons of the free women, receive the land of promise. Thus something else is certainly signified here.

Although I think that Jacob’s two free wives belong to the New Testament, through which we have been called into freedom, they are nevertheless not two without reason—unless perhaps because Scripture teaches and proclaims to us two lives in the body of Christ: one temporal, in which we labor; the other eternal, in which we contemplate the enjoyment of God. The Lord revealed the former through his passion and the latter through his resurrection.

The women’s names also urge us to understand this. Leah is interpreted as “one who labors”; Rachel as “the beginning seen,” or “the word from which the beginning is seen.” The activity of human and mortal life, in which we live by faith, performing many laborious works whose outcome is uncertain but which are undertaken for the benefit of those for whom we wish to care, is Leah, Jacob’s first wife. Accordingly, she is also said to have had weak eyes: the thoughts of mortals are timid, and our foresight is uncertain.

But the hope of eternal contemplation of God, possessing a certain and delightful understanding of the truth, is Rachel. Hence she is beautiful in face and beautiful in appearance. Every devout student loves her, and for her sake serves the grace of God, by which our sins, even if they were like scarlet, will be made white as snow (Isa. I).

Laban, moreover, is interpreted as “whitening,” and Jacob served him for Rachel. No one turns under the grace of the remission of sins to serve righteousness unless he wishes to live peacefully in the Word from whom the beginning is seen, who is God.

Therefore one serves for Rachel, not for Leah. For who would ever love the labor of actions and sufferings in works of righteousness? Who would desire that life for its own sake, just as Jacob did not desire Leah for her own sake? Yet when she was placed with him at night for the purpose of begetting children, he embraced her and experienced her fruitfulness.

For the Lord, because she could not be loved for her own sake, first caused her to be endured so that Rachel might be reached; afterward he commended her because of her children. Thus every useful servant of God, established under the grace of the whitening of his sins, what else has he contemplated in his conduct, what else has he carried in his heart, what else has he loved in his heart, except the teaching of wisdom?

Many think that they will immediately acquire and receive this teaching as soon as they have practiced the seven commandments of the law concerning love of neighbor, so that no harm is done to anyone: “Honor your father and mother”; “You shall not commit adultery”; “You shall not kill”; “You shall not steal”; “You shall not bear false witness”; “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife”; “You shall not covet your neighbor’s property” (Exod. XX). [Col. 0997B]

After these have been observed as far as possible, once a person has clung through various trials—as through the night of this age—to the labor of endurance, in exchange for the beautiful delight of the teaching he has desired and hoped for, Leah is unexpectedly joined to him as though in place of Rachel. He endures her in order to reach the other. If he perseveringly loves her, after receiving the other seven commandments it is as though he were told: “Serve another seven years for Rachel”: to be poor in spirit, meek, mourning, hungering and thirsting for righteousness, merciful, pure in heart, and a peacemaker.

A person would wish, if it were possible, to reach immediately, without any endurance of labor—which must be embraced in action and suffering—the delights of beautiful and perfect wisdom. But this cannot happen in the land of the dying. This seems to be signified by what was said to Jacob: “It is not customary in our place for the younger to marry before the elder.” For it is not absurd that the one who is earlier in time is called “elder.” In the proper education of a human being, the labor of doing what is just comes before the will to understand what is true.

This is the force of what is written: “Have you desired wisdom? Keep the commandments, and the Lord will grant it to you” (Ecclus. I). The commandments certainly pertain to righteousness—the righteousness that is from faith, which moves amid the uncertainties of trials—so that by devoutly believing what he does not yet understand, a person may also obtain the merit of understanding.

For just as the passage I have now recalled is valuable—“Have you desired wisdom? Keep the commandments, and the Lord will grant it to you”—so I think this passage is valuable as well: “Unless you believe, you will not understand.” It shows that righteousness pertains to faith, while understanding pertains to wisdom.

Accordingly, among those who burn with an immense love of manifest truth, zeal should not be condemned but brought back into proper order, so that they may begin from faith and strive through good morals to reach their goal. In what opposes the desired end there is laborious virtue; in what is desired there is luminous wisdom.

“What need is there,” someone says, “to believe? Why is no manifest word shown to me by which I may see the beginning of the knowledge of all things?” For this is what the rational mind, if it is devoted, first and most intensely burns to attain. The answer should be: “What you desire is indeed beautiful and worthy of the greatest love; but Leah must marry first, and Rachel afterward.”

Let this ardor therefore serve the purpose that the proper order is not rejected but rather endured. Once the goal has been reached, both beautiful understanding and laborious righteousness will be possessed in this age. However sharply and sincerely mortals may perceive the unchangeable good, “the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks on many things” (Wis. IX). To hold fast to one thing, many things must therefore be endured.

Thus Jacob has two free wives. Both are daughters of the remission of sins—that is, of whitening, which is Laban. Nevertheless, one is loved and the other endured; but the one who is endured is the first and more abundantly fruitful, so that, if not for her own sake, at least for the sake of her children, she may be loved.

For the labor of the righteous bears its greatest fruit in those whom they beget for the kingdom of God by preaching the Gospel amid many temptations and tribulations. For their sake they have “more abundant labors, imprisonments beyond measure, deaths frequently”; for their sake they have “battles outside and fears within,” and they call them their joy and crown.

They are born to them more easily and more abundantly from that word of faith by which they preach Christ crucified, and whatever of his humanity is more readily grasped by human thought—something that does not disturb even Leah’s weak eyes.

But Rachel, clear in sight, goes beyond herself in the mind toward God and sees “in the beginning the Word, God with God” (John I). She wishes to give birth but cannot, “for who shall declare his generation?” Therefore the life belonging to the pursuit of contemplation, so that it may behold what is invisible to the flesh through what has been made, not with the weak eyes of the mind, and may gaze ineffably upon the eternal power of God, wishes to be free from every occupation and is therefore barren.

By seeking the leisure in which the pursuits of contemplation find release, it does not accommodate itself to the weakness of people who, amid various pressures, have entrusted themselves to be helped. But because it too burns with the love of begetting, it wishes to teach what it knows. It does not waste away with envy when it sees its sister abounding in children through the labor of action and suffering; rather, it grieves that people run toward the virtue by which their weaknesses and necessities are served rather than toward the virtue by which something divine and unchangeable is learned.

This grief appears to be represented in what is written: “Rachel was jealous of her sister.” Since clear and pure understanding of that substance which is not body does not belong to the sense of the flesh and cannot be expressed in words produced by the flesh, wisdom chose to convey divine things, insofar as they can be contemplated, through every sort of bodily image and likeness rather than cease from the duty of teaching such things.

Rachel therefore chose to receive children from her husband through her maidservant rather than remain altogether without children. For Bala is said to be interpreted as “grown old.” Rachel had her as a maidservant. From the old life devoted to bodily senses, bodily images are conceived, even when something concerning the spiritual and unchangeable substance of divinity is heard.

Leah also received sons from her maidservant, inflamed by love for a greater number of children. We find that her maidservant Zilpah is interpreted as “gaping mouth.” Therefore, whenever we observe in Scripture those preachers of evangelical faith whose mouth gapes open while their heart does not, this is understood as Leah’s maidservant.

For it is written of certain people: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. XXIX). And to such people the Apostle says: “You who preach that one should not steal, do you steal? You who say that one should not commit adultery, do you commit adultery?” (Rom. II).

But so that the free wife Jacob, the one who labors, might even through this condition receive children as heirs of the kingdom, the Lord says: “Do what they say, but do not do what they do” (Matt. XXII). Hence the apostolic life, amid the labor of its bonds, says: “Whether in pretense or in truth, Christ is proclaimed, and in this I rejoice, and I will rejoice”—as though the maidservant too were giving birth to a greater number of children.

Leah’s affection was indeed gladdened by the favor that came through Rachel, when Rachel, having received the mandrakes from Leah’s son, allowed her husband to sleep with her sister on the night assigned to him.

I know that some people hold the opinion concerning this kind of fruit that, when eaten, it produces fertility in barren women. For this reason they think that Rachel insisted on receiving it from her sister’s son because she desired to bear children. I would not think so, even if she had conceived at that time. But since, after Leah’s two subsequent children, the Lord granted Rachel offspring after that night, there is no reason for us to suspect of the mandrake anything such as we have experienced in no woman.

I shall therefore say what I think; perhaps those more learned than I will say something better about it. When I myself had seen these fruits and, because of this very passage of sacred reading, congratulated myself that they had come into my possession—for the object is a rare one—I carefully investigated their nature as far as I could. I did not do so by means of some more recondite science, such as teaches the properties of roots and powers of herbs, but only as sight, smell, and taste reported to me and to any other person.

I found, therefore, that the object was beautiful and fragrant, but tasteless. Thus I confess that I do not know why the woman desired it so greatly, unless perhaps because of the rarity of the fruit and the pleasantness of its scent.

But why sacred Scripture did not wish to leave the deed itself unmentioned—since it would surely not take pains to present to us such desires of little women as something important unless it were urging us to seek something important in them—I cannot conjecture beyond what common sense suggests to me.

I understand that mandrake fruit to represent good reputation—not the reputation bestowed when a few just and wise people praise someone, but the popular reputation by which broader and more illustrious recognition is acquired. This reputation is not to be sought for its own sake, but is highly necessary to the intention of the good, by which they care for the human race.

Hence the Apostle says: “He must also have a good testimony from those who are outside” (I Tim. III). Although such people may possess little wisdom, they nevertheless often repay the labor of those who care for them with the splendor of praise and the fragrance of a good reputation.

The members of the Church who first attain this popular glory are not those who are at rest, but those who are engaged in the dangers and labor of action. Therefore Leah’s son found the mandrake fruit when he went out into the field—that is, when he walked honorably among those who are outside.

That teaching of wisdom, however, which is far removed from the clamor of the crowd and is fixed in the contemplation of truth with sweet delight, would not attain even a small measure of this popular glory except through those who preside over peoples amid the crowds, acting and persuading—not so that they may rule, but so that they may benefit others.

For when these active and occupied people, through whom the welfare of the multitude is administered and whose authority is dear to the people, also bear witness to a life more remote from the world because of their devotion to seeking and contemplating truth, the mandrakes come, as it were, at leisure through Leah to Rachel.

They come to Leah herself through her firstborn son—that is, through the honor of her fruitfulness, in which lies the entire fruit of action that is laborious and exposed to danger amid the uncertainties of temptations. Many people who possess good natural ability and burn with zeal, although they may be capable of governing peoples, nevertheless avoid this because of its turbulent occupations and enjoy the embraces of beautiful Rachel in the leisure of teaching.

But since it is good that this life too, becoming more widely known, should earn popular glory, and since it is unjust for it to attain that glory if it keeps in leisure the person suited and capable of administering ecclesiastical responsibilities, and does not share him with the governance of the common good, Leah therefore says to her sister: “Is it not enough that you have taken my husband, but you also want to take my son’s mandrakes?”

By the one husband she signifies all those who, although capable of action and worthy to be entrusted with the government of the Church for the administration of the sacrament of faith, are inflamed by zeal for teaching and for investigating and contemplating wisdom and wish to withdraw from all the burdens of action, hiding themselves in the leisure of learning and teaching.

Thus the words mean: “Is it not enough that you have taken my husband, but you also want to take my son’s mandrakes?” It is as though she were saying: “Is it not enough that the life of students keeps in leisure people necessary for the conduct of affairs, but it also seeks popular glory?”

Therefore, in order to acquire it justly, Rachel shares her husband with her sister for that night, so that those who are suited by their laborious virtue to govern peoples—even if they had chosen to devote themselves to knowledge—may undertake the experience of temptations and the burden of responsibilities for the common good. Otherwise the teaching of wisdom to which they had decided to devote themselves would be blasphemed and would not acquire among unlearned peoples the good reputation signified by those fruits, which is necessary for the encouragement of learners.

But they are plainly compelled by force to undertake this care. This too is sufficiently signified by the fact that when Jacob was coming from the field, Leah met him and detained him, saying: “You shall enter in to me, for I have hired you with my son’s mandrakes.” It is as though she were saying: “You wish to confer a good reputation upon the teaching that you love; do not flee the labor of duty.” [Col. 1000A]

Anyone who observes these things taking place in the Church sees them clearly. We experience in examples what we understand in books. Who does not see this happening throughout the world: everyone comes from the works of the age and goes into the leisure of recognizing the truth, as though into Rachel’s embrace, and is intercepted by ecclesiastical necessity and appointed to labor, as Leah says, “You shall enter in to me”?

When such people chastely administer the mystery of God, so that in the night of this age they may beget children of God for God, they are praised by the peoples even in the very life whose love led them to abandon hope in the world, and from whose profession they were taken up for the ministry of governing the people.

For this is what they do amid all their labors: they seek to make that profession from which they had turned away more widely and more gloriously honored, because it has given such leaders to the peoples. This is like Jacob’s not refusing Leah’s night, so that Rachel may enjoy the mandrakes, fragrant and brightly shining.

At times Rachel herself also gives birth independently, by the mercy of God—only after great delay, since it is exceedingly rare that “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word,” and that anything wisely said about this subject is grasped, even in part, without the phantasm of carnal thought and in a way conducive to salvation.

(Verses 26 ff.) “Give me my wives and my children, for whom I served you, so that I may depart; you know the service with which I served you.” Laban said to him, “Let me find favor in your sight; I have learned by experience that God has blessed me because of you. Set your wages, which I shall give you.”

But he replied: “You know how I have served you and how great your possession has been in my hands. You had little before I came to you, and now you have become rich; God has blessed you at my arrival.”

The meaning of Scripture deserves careful attention and consideration, lest, whenever someone speaks in this way, he appear to be boasting. For it makes a great difference that he added, “God has blessed you at my arrival.” He intended his entrance to be understood and was thereby giving thanks to God.

(Verses 31 ff.) Laban said, “What shall I give you?” He replied, “I want nothing. But if you do what I ask, I will again pasture and guard your flock. Go through all your flocks and separate every sheep that is variegated and speckled; and whatever is tawny, spotted, or variegated, among both the sheep and the goats, shall be my wage.

“Tomorrow my righteousness will answer for me, when the time of the agreement comes before you. Everything that is not variegated, spotted, or tawny, among both the sheep and the goats, will accuse me of theft.”

Laban said, “I gladly accept what you ask.” On that day he separated the goats, sheep, he-goats, and rams that were variegated and spotted. But he handed over the entire flock of a single color—that is, with white and black fleece—to his sons’ keeping, and placed a distance of three days’ journey between himself and his son-in-law, who was pasturing the rest of his flocks.

Jacob then took green poplar rods, almond rods, and rods from plane trees, and peeled them in part. When the bark had been stripped away, whiteness appeared in the places that had been stripped; but the portions that remained intact stayed green. In this way the color became variegated.

He placed them in the channels where the water flowed, so that when the flocks came to drink they would have the rods before their eyes and conceive while looking at them. It happened, at the very heat of mating, that the sheep looked at the rods and gave birth to spotted and variegated young, dappled with different colors.

In Jacob’s action, when he stripped the rods so that white appeared in variegated form, the animals’ offspring were similarly varied before their eyes when the mothers drank at the watering troughs. Seeing the rods, they conceived that variegation, so that, while they eagerly drank and were mounted by the males, they conceived such offspring as the shadows of the rams mounting above them appeared in the water’s mirror. For the color of the images was also varied by the rods placed in the channels.

It is not surprising that this should be the nature of females, that whatever they have seen or conceived in their minds at the final heat of pleasure in which they conceive, they should produce as offspring. It is said that this very thing also happens among herds of mares in Spain.

Many similar things are said to occur in the offspring of animals. Quintilian too, in the controversy in which a matron was accused because she had given birth to an Ethiopian, argues in her defense that this is the nature of women who conceive, as we have described above.

It is also reported to have happened to a woman, and is found written in the books of the ancient and most skilled physician Hippocrates, that a woman who was about to be punished on suspicion of adultery had given birth to a child exceptionally beautiful but unlike both parents and the whole family. The physician resolved the question by advising them to inquire whether there might perhaps be some such picture in the bedroom. When one was found, the woman was freed from suspicion.

But as to what benefit the combination of rods from three different trees, which Jacob made, contributed to multiplying variegated animals, this is not at all apparent. Nor does it make any difference for this purpose whether the rods were varied from one kind of wood or whether several kinds of wood were used, since only the variety of the wood is at issue.

Accordingly, he understood that this action was meant to signify some prophecy. Jacob undoubtedly performed it as a prophet, and therefore he should not be accused of fraud. For it must be believed that he did such a thing only through spiritual revelation.

The poplar and almond rods, or those from plane trees, should be understood as testimonies from the Law, the Prophets, and the Hagiographa. Our Lord stripped some of them and left some in their proper color.

He stripped them when he said: “It is written, ‘An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth’; but I say to you, do not return retaliation at all to your adversary” (Matt. V).

Or when, being asked by the Jews whether a man ought to dismiss his wife for any reason in accordance with the commandment of Moses, he is recorded to have replied that Moses gave this commandment because of the hardness of their hearts, for “from the beginning it was not so” (Matt. XIX; Mark X).

Again: “For it is written, ‘You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy’; but I say to you: Pray for your enemies and do good to those who persecute you” (Matt. XXII; Luke X; Mark X), and so forth. He appeared to strip this verse in part when he said that an enemy ought to be loved; but in part he left it in its proper color, namely, what he had stated earlier about loving one’s neighbor.

The sheep are to be understood as those who come to the faith of Christ; the rams as the blessed apostles or ministers of the Churches; the channels as the books of the Gospels; and the rods as the testimonies of the Old Testament, which are known to be woven together with the Gospels.

The first time of conception should be understood either as the day of Pentecost, on which, through the preaching of the apostles, some three thousand men are recorded to have conceived the divine word together, as it were the firstfruits; or the time of Lent or Easter, during which, according to the measure of their understanding, testimonies of Scripture are presented either spiritually to penitents and catechumens, or, certainly according to the historical text, in a form suited to both, so that by hearing they may conceive and produce the fruit of good works.

The rods are stripped together when testimonies of Scripture that do not at all seem to stand according to the historical sense are explained spiritually by priests, as in what is written in Leviticus concerning the leprosy of a wall and the skin of the warp and the weft.

But when Jacob says that, as his wages, he is to receive the variegated, tawny, and spotted animals, both sheep and goats, this signifies what he is read to have answered the scribes and Pharisees in the Gospel: “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Matt. IX).

When he says, “Tomorrow my righteousness will answer for me,” he indicates the time of judgment, when he will give the faithful the eternal reward of blessedness and bring the vengeance of punishment upon the unfaithful and transgressors.

The meaning of sacred speech must be weighed between the text and the mystery with such balance that, with the scales of both sides kept in due measure, neither the weight of excessive investigation depresses one side nor, conversely, the torpor of negligence leaves it empty. [Col. 1002A]

Many of its statements are pregnant with the conception of allegories, so that whoever tries to hold them only according to the historical sense is deprived of their meaning through his own negligence. Others, however, serve external commandments in such a way that, if anyone wishes to penetrate them more subtly, he finds nothing within—and even conceals from himself what they say outwardly.

Hence, also in the historical narrative, it is appropriately said through signification: “Jacob took green poplar and almond rods, and rods from plane trees, and stripped them in part,” and so forth.

What does it mean to place green poplar and almond rods, and rods from plane trees, before the eyes of the flocks, except to offer the lives and teachings of the ancient Fathers to peoples as an example through the sequence of Scripture? Since these are straight according to the examination of reason, they are called rods.

He removes the bark from them in part, so that in what is stripped the inner whiteness may appear; and in part he preserves the bark, so that outwardly they may remain green as they had been. The color of the rods becomes variegated when the bark is partly removed and partly retained.

Before the eyes of our consideration, therefore, the teachings of the preceding Fathers are set forth like variegated rods. In some cases we flee from the literal meaning and, as it were, remove the bark; in others we follow the literal meaning and, as it were, preserve the bark. When the bark of the letter is withdrawn, the inner whiteness of allegory is revealed; when the bark is retained, the verdant examples of outward understanding are displayed.

Jacob rightly placed these rods in channels of water, because our Redeemer fixed them in the books of sacred knowledge, by which we are inwardly nourished.

The rams look on while they mate with the sheep, because our rational spirits, when fixed upon their meaning, are mingled with each of our actions, so that they produce offspring of deeds corresponding to the examples of those who preceded us, which they see in the words of the commandments. The offspring have a varied color because at times, when the bark of the letter has been removed, a person considers the inner meaning more deeply, while at other times, when the covering of the history has been preserved, he forms himself well in outward matters.

### (Verse 41)

Therefore, when the sheep first began to mate, Jacob placed the rods in the water channels before the eyes of the rams and ewes, so that they might conceive while looking at them, up to the passage: “When you changed my wages ten times.” Scripture does not say when or how this happened; but certainly what he recalls did happen. For he also said this to his wives when he summoned them in the field. Complaining about their father, he said, among other things: “He changed my wages ten times,” or “ten lambs.”

It is therefore understood that, at each season when the sheep gave birth, whenever Laban saw that offspring had been born of the kind that he had agreed should belong to Jacob, he fraudulently changed the agreement and said that in the future Jacob was to have other colors of livestock as his wages. But whenever Jacob did not place the variegated rods beneath them, variegated offspring were not born; rather, they were of one color, and Jacob took them away under the new agreement. When Laban saw this, he again [Col. 1002D] fraudulently changed the agreement, so that the variegated animals would belong to Jacob. Then, when the variegated rods were placed beneath them, variegated offspring were born.

Thus, when Jacob said to his wives, “He changed my wages ten times,” and later said the same to Laban, he did not speak as though the fraud itself had benefited his father-in-law. On the contrary, he said that God had been with him against Laban so that the fraud would not benefit him.

He called ten occasions “ten times,” referring to the ten periods during which the sheep he tended gave birth over the six-year period. For they gave birth twice a year. It happened that in the first year, when they had made the agreement and he undertook to tend them in return for this wage, they gave birth once at the end of the year: when he arrived, they had already given birth once. Likewise, in the sixth, that is, the final year, after they had given birth once, the need to depart arose, and he left before they gave birth again. Thus, since the first and final years together contained two births of the sheep under his care—that is, one each—while the four middle years contained two births each, the total is [Col. 1003A] ten.

Nor is it surprising that he called these ten periods by the name “occasions,” since the animals were born during those same periods. It is as though someone were to speak of so many grape harvests or so many grain harvests, by which a number of years is understood. The fertility of the livestock in that region is said to be as great as that of Italian livestock, so that they give birth twice a year.

The text continues:

### (Chapter 31—verses 17 ff.)

So Jacob arose, placed his children and wives upon camels, and departed. He took all his property, his flocks, and everything he had acquired in Mesopotamia, and went to his father Isaac in the land of Canaan. At that time Laban had gone to shear the sheep, and Rachel stole her father’s idols. Jacob did not wish to tell his father-in-law that he was fleeing. After he had departed, both he and everything that belonged to him, and had crossed the river, he proceeded toward Mount Gilead.

It is not that the mountain was called Gilead at that time; rather, by anticipation, as we have often said, it is called by the name it was later to bear. Laban was informed on the third day that Jacob had fled. Taking his [Col. 1003B] brothers with him, he pursued him for seven days and caught him at Mount Gilead. In a dream God said to him: “Beware of speaking anything harsh against Jacob.”

Jacob had already pitched his tent on the mountain when Laban caught up with him and his brothers. He too pitched his tent on the same mountain and said to Jacob: “Why did you wish to flee secretly from me and not tell me, so that I might have escorted you with joy, with songs, tambourines, and lyres? You did not allow me to kiss my sons and daughters. You have acted foolishly. It is indeed within the power of my hand to repay you with evil; but the God of your father said to me yesterday, ‘Beware of saying anything harsh to Jacob.’ Granted: you wished to go to your own people, and you longed for your father’s house. But why did you steal my gods?”

It should be noted that, from the beginning of the book, we encounter the gods of the Gentiles here for the first time. In the earlier passages of Scripture, they called him God.

The text continues:

### (Verse 45)

So Jacob took a stone and set it up as a monument. We must carefully observe how [Col. 1003C] they established such monuments as witnesses to particular matters—not in order to worship them as gods, but so that something might be signified by them.

The text continues:

### (Verse 47)

Laban called it “The Mound of the Witness,” and Jacob called it “The Heap of Testimony,” each according to the character of his own language.

Those who knew both the Syrian and Hebrew languages report that this was done on account of the particular character of each language. It often happens that what is expressed in one language by a single word is not expressed in another by one word, and that something is named according to a neighboring meaning. Laban was a Syrian and had not altered the ancient language of his ancestors in the region where he lived. This expression was placed midway between the two, so that it suited both the one who had said “Heap of Testimony” and the one who had said “Mound of the Witness.”

The text continues:

### (Verses 49 ff.)

“May the Lord look upon us and judge between us when we have departed from one another, if you afflict my daughters or bring other wives in addition to them.”

“There is no witness to what we say except God, who is present and watches.” When Laban says, “There is no witness to what we say except God, who is present and watches,” he means that there was no outsider besides the testimony of God, whom they ought to regard as though no one were with them whom they could associate with his testimony.

After Jacob had endured a long period of servitude with his father-in-law, serving as a hired man for the sake of his wives, the Lord commanded him to return to his native land. Then he hastened away with his wives and company, without his father-in-law’s knowledge. Laban pursued him furiously to Mount Gilead and searched for the idols that Rachel had stolen, but did not find them.

Let us therefore inquire what this very event signifies allegorically. Although Laban previously represented another person, he now figures the devil. Laban means “whitening.” “Whitening” may appropriately be understood as the devil, who, though dark by merit, disguises himself as an angel of light (2 Corinthians 11).

Jacob served him as the Jewish people, descended from the father of the reprobate, from whose flesh the Lord [Col. 1004A] came incarnate. Laban may also represent the world, which pursues Jacob furiously because it attempts to crush by persecution the elect, who are members of our Redeemer.

Jacob took away Laban’s daughter—that is, either the world’s daughter or the devil’s—when Christ joined the Church from among the Gentiles to himself. He also drew her away from her father’s house, because through the prophet he says to her: “Forget your people and your father’s house” (Psalm 44).

What else is signified by the idols except avarice? Hence Paul says: “And avarice, which is the service of idols” (Ephesians 5).

When Laban therefore came to Jacob, he did not find the idol, because, after displaying the treasures of the world, the devil found no trace of earthly desire in our Redeemer. But what Jacob did not possess, Rachel covered by sitting upon it.

Through Rachel, who is also called “sheep,” the Church is signified. To sit means to seek the humility of repentance, as it is written: “Rise after you have sat” (Psalm 126). Rachel therefore covered the idols by sitting upon them because the holy Church, following Christ, covered the vice of earthly desire through the humility of [Col. 1004B] repentance.

The prophet David speaks of this covering: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered” (Psalm 31). We are signified by that Rachel when, by repenting, we condemn the faults of avarice and press down the idols by sitting upon them.

This impurity of avarice does not hinder those who run courageously, to whom it is said: “Act courageously, and let your heart be strengthened” (Psalm 30). Rather, it especially hinders those who, walking as though with a woman’s languid step, are weakened by the blandishments of the world. Hence the following words of that same Rachel occur there: “According to the custom of women, it has now happened to me”—that is, she revealed herself as though she had behaved in a womanly manner.

After Laban had pursued Jacob, found him, and spoken with him, they made a covenant. Jacob then took a stone and set it up as a monument, and said to his brothers: “Bring stones.” They gathered them and made a mound. Laban called it “The Mound of the Witness,” and Jacob called it “The Heap of Testimony.”

Among the faithful, both Jews and Gentiles, the prominent stone is a witness [Col. 1004C] in the likeness of Christ, and the heap of stones is the multitude of believers.

The text continues:

### (Chapter 32—verses 1–2)

Jacob also went on by the road he had begun. Angels of God met him, and when he saw them he said: “These are the camps of God.” He called the name of that place Mahanaim, that is, “camps.”

There is no doubt that the camps of God Jacob saw on his journey were a multitude of angels. In Scripture this multitude is called the army of heaven. Beautifully, as he goes to his hostile brother, he is received by choirs of accompanying angels.

### (Verses 3 ff.)

Jacob sent messengers ahead of him to his brother Esau, into the region of Edom, and commanded them: “Speak this way to my lord: ‘Your brother Jacob says this: I have lived as a resident alien with Laban and have remained there until the present day. I have oxen, donkeys, sheep, male servants, and female servants. I am sending an embassy to my lord, so that I may find favor in your sight.’”

The messengers returned to Jacob and said: “We came to your brother Esau, and behold, he is hastening to meet you with four hundred [Col. 1004D] men.”

Jacob was greatly afraid and, terrified, divided the people who were with him, as well as the flocks, sheep, oxen, and camels, into two groups.

It may be asked how he retained faith in God’s promise when he said: “If my brother comes against the first group and strikes it, the other group that remains will be saved.” But it could also have happened that Esau turned his camp away, and that God nevertheless came to his aid after that affliction, in order to rescue him and fulfill what he had promised.

We are also admonished by this example that, although we believe in God, we should nevertheless do what human beings must do as a safeguard for salvation, lest by neglecting such measures we appear to tempt God.

Finally, we must consider what Jacob himself says afterward:

“O God of my father Abraham, and God of my father Isaac, who said to me, ‘Return to your land and to the place of your birth, and I will do good to you’: I am less than all the mercies and the faithfulness that you have shown your servant [Col. 1005A]. With my staff I crossed this Jordan, and now I return with two groups. Deliver me from the hand of my brother, because I fear him greatly, lest he come and strike the mother together with her children. You said that you would do good to me and make my offspring like the sand of the sea, which cannot be counted because of its multitude.”

In these words both human weakness and faith in divine goodness are plainly evident.

The text continues:

After he had slept there that night, he separated from what he possessed gifts for his brother Esau: two hundred she-goats and twenty he-goats, two hundred sheep and twenty rams, thirty nursing camels with their young, forty cows and twenty bulls, twenty female donkeys and ten of their young. He sent the separate flocks one by one through the hands of his servants.

He said to his servants: “Go on ahead of me, and let there be a space between one flock and the next.” He commanded the first, saying: “If you meet Esau my brother and he asks you, ‘Whose are you?’ or ‘Where are you going?’ or ‘Whose are these animals following you?’ you shall answer: ‘Your servant Jacob’s. He has sent gifts to my lord Esau; he himself is also coming behind us.’”

He gave the same instructions to the second and third servants, and to all who followed [Col. 1005B] the flocks, saying: “Speak to Esau in these same words when you meet him. You shall also add: ‘Your servant Jacob himself is following our journey.’”

For he said: “I will appease him with the gifts that go before me, and afterward I will see his face; perhaps he will receive me favorably.”

So the gifts went ahead of him, while he himself remained in the camp that night. For he said: “I will appease his face with the gifts going before him.”

The writer of the book is speaking about Jacob, for he says: “I will appease his face.”

Up to this point, Jacob is understood to have spoken. The remaining words—“with the gifts going before him”—are the writer’s addition, as though he were saying: “With the gifts that went before Jacob, I will appease the face of my brother.”

The order of Jacob’s words is: “I will appease his face, and afterward I will see his face; perhaps he will receive my face”—that is, receive me favorably. The writer’s words, “with the gifts going before him,” have been inserted between them.

The text continues:

### (Verses 22 ff.)

When he had risen early, he took his two wives and his two female servants, together with his eleven sons, [Col. 1005C] and crossed the torrent of Jabbok. After he had brought across everything that belonged to him, he remained alone. And behold, a man wrestled with him until morning.

When the man saw that he could not overcome him, he touched the sinew of his thigh, and it immediately shriveled. He said to him: “Let me go, for dawn has risen.”

He replied: “I will not let you go unless you bless me.”

He said: “What is your name?”

He answered: “Jacob.”

Then the other said: “Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel, because if you have been strong against God, how much more will you prevail against human beings?”

Jacob asked him: “Tell me by what name you are called.”

He replied: “Why do you ask my name, which is wonderful?”

And he blessed him there. Jacob called the name of that place Peniel, saying: “I have seen the Lord face to face, and my soul has been saved.”

The meaning, therefore, is this: “Your name shall not be called Supplanter”—that is, Jacob—but “Prince with God”—that is, Israel. Just as I am a prince, [Col. 1005D] so you, who were able to wrestle with me, shall be called a prince.

But if you were able to fight with me, who am God—or an angel, since many interpret the passage in different ways—how much more will you prevail against human beings, that is, against Esau, whom you should not fear?

The interpretation found in the Book of Names, however, which explains Israel as “a man seeing God,” or “a mind seeing God,” seems to me to have been worn down by nearly everyone’s repeated usage and interpreted more violently than accurately. Although those interpreters possess great authority and their eloquence overshadows us—since they translated Israel as “a man” or “a mind seeing God”—we are guided more by the authority of Scripture and of the angel, or of God, who himself called him Israel, than by that of any secular eloquence.

The name given to him by the angel who wrestled with him as he returned from Mesopotamia and traveled with him most clearly bears the figure of Christ. For the fact that Jacob prevailed over him, since the angel willed it, signifies the passion of Christ, in which the Jews appeared to prevail over him. Yet Jacob obtained a blessing from the same angel whom he had overcome [Col. 1006A]; thus the imposition of this name was itself a blessing.

Israel is interpreted as “prince with God,” or, as others prefer, “a man seeing God,” which will be the final reward of all the saints.

Moreover, that same angel touched the breadth of his thigh, as though Jacob had prevailed, and in this way made him lame. Thus Jacob was one and the same person, both blessed and lame: blessed in those from the same people who believed in Christ, and lame in the unbelievers. For the breadth of the thigh is the multitude of the race. There are many in that lineage of whom it was prophetically said: “And they limped from their paths” (Psalm 17).

The text continues:

### (Chapter 33—verses 1 ff.)

Jacob lifted his eyes and saw Esau coming, with four hundred men. He divided the children of Leah and Rachel and those of both female servants. He placed each female servant and her children in front, Leah and her children in the second position, and Rachel and Joseph last. He himself went ahead and bowed to the ground seven times, until he approached his brother.

Running to meet his brother Esau, [Col. 1006B] he embraced him, clasping his neck and kissing him, and they wept. When Esau lifted his eyes and saw the women and their children, he said: “What do these groups mean, and do they belong to you?”

He answered: “They are the little ones whom God has given your servant.”

The female servants and their children approached and bowed. Leah also came with her children, and they likewise bowed. Rachel and Joseph, at the rear, bowed.

Esau said: “What are these groups that I met?”

He answered: “So that I might find favor before my lord.”

Esau said: “I have very much, my brother. Let what is yours be yours.”

Jacob replied: “Do not do this, I beg you. But if I have found favor in your eyes, accept this little gift from my hand. For I have seen your face as though I were seeing the face of an angel of God.”

What does Jacob’s statement to his brother mean: “For this reason I have seen your face, as when someone sees the face of God”? Did the words of a frightened and troubled mind burst forth into such flattery? Or can they be understood as spoken without sin according to some interpretation?

Perhaps, because the gods of the Gentiles are also mentioned—gods who are demons—these words should not be held against the man of God. For he did not say, “As though I were seeing the face of God,” but, “As when someone sees.” It is uncertain whom this “someone” might signify. [Col. 1006C]

Perhaps the words were moderated in such a way that Esau himself would gratefully accept the great honor shown to him, while anyone who understood them differently would not accuse the speaker of any impiety. The words were spoken by a brother with a kindly disposition, since after the favorable reception even the fear itself had passed.

It could also have been said in the same sense in which Moses was called “God” to Pharaoh, according to what the Apostle says: “And if there are those who are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth, just as there are many gods and many lords” (1 Corinthians 8). This is especially so because the Greek was written without the article, by which the one true God is most clearly indicated. For he did not say, *πρόσωπον τοῦ Θεοῦ*—“the face of God”—but *πρόσωπον Θεοῦ*—“face of God.”

Those who are accustomed to hearing and understanding Greek easily perceive the distinction in how the expression is used. [Col. 1006D]

The text continues:

### (Verses 13–14)

Esau said to Jacob: “Let us travel together, and I will accompany you.”

Jacob said: “You know, my lord, that I have tender little children, and sheep and cattle with young beside me. If I make them labor too much in walking, all the flocks will die in one day. Let my lord go ahead of his servant, and I will follow little by little in his footsteps, as I see that my children can manage, until I come to my lord in Seir.”
