According to the account of divine Scripture, Jacob did not do this—he did not come to Esau in Seir—but went by the road that led toward his own people. Or perhaps he had promised this sincerely but later chose another course after reconsidering.

The text continues:

### (Verses 17 ff.)

Jacob came to Succoth, where he built a house and pitched tents. He therefore called the name of that place Succoth, that is, “booths.” He then crossed to Salem, the city of the Shechemites, which is in the land of Canaan, after returning from Mesopotamia of Syria. He settled near the [Col. 1007A] town and bought from the sons of Hamor, the father of Shechem, a portion of the field where he had pitched his tents, for one hundred lambs. There he erected an altar and invoked upon it the most mighty God of Israel.

There is still today a city across the Jordan with this name, Succoth, among the regions of Scythopolis.

Jacob came to Salem, the city of Shechem, in the land of Canaan, when he had come from Mesopotamia of Syria. A difficulty arises: how can Salem be the name of the city of Shechem, when Jerusalem, where Melchizedek reigned, was earlier called Salem?

Either both cities have the same name—a situation that we can also find in several places in Judaea, where the same name belongs to a city and a place in different tribes—or else we should say that this Salem, which is now identified with Shechem, is interpreted here as “complete” or “perfect,” while the one later called Jerusalem is translated in our language as “peaceful.” Both meanings are conveyed by the word with a slightly different accent.

The text continues:

### (Chapter 34—verses 1 ff.)

Dina, the daughter of Leah, went out to see the women of that region. When Shechem, the son of Hamor the Hivite, the prince of that land, [Col. 1007B] saw her, he fell in love with her, seized her, and slept with her, violating the virgin by force. His soul was joined to her, and he soothed her distress with blandishments. Then he went to his father and said: “Take this girl for me as a wife.”

If he had already slept with her and violated her, how does he later call her a virgin? Perhaps “virgin” is a term for age according to the Hebrew language. Or is what happened first recalled afterward by recapitulation? For he could first have turned his attention to her soul, fallen in love with the virgin, and spoken according to the meaning of “virgin,” and then slept with her and violated her.

Dina goes out to see the women of a foreign region when any mind, neglecting its own pursuits and attending to the actions of others, wanders outside its proper condition and order. Shechem, the prince of the land, saw and loved her because the devil corrupts her when he finds her occupied with external concerns. Her soul was joined to his [Col. 1007C] because he makes her united with himself through iniquity.

And because, when the mind sees that it has sinned, it tries to grieve over what it has done, corrupt hope summons empty assurances before its eyes in order to remove the benefit of sorrow. It says that the deeds of others are worse, that what has been done is nothing, that God is merciful, and that there is still time ahead for repentance. Thus, while the deceived mind is led along by these notions, it is suspended from the resolve to repent, so that it accepts no good at that time because no evil now causes it grief, and is then more fully besieged by punishments because it now rejoices even in its sins.

The text continues:

### (Verses 25 ff.)

On the third day, when the pain of the wounds is most severe, two of Jacob’s sons, Simeon and Levi, Dina’s brothers, took their swords and entered confidently. They killed every male, and slew Hamor and Shechem together, taking their sister Dina from Shechem’s house.

After they had gone out, the other sons of Jacob entered upon the slain and plundered the city [Col. 1007D] in revenge for their sister’s violation.

These words therefore show that Jacob did not remain there merely in passing, as a traveler ordinarily does. Rather, he bought a field, established a tent, built an altar, and thus remained for a longer time at Shechem, which is also called Salem and is in the land of Canaan.

His daughter, when she had reached the age at which she could already have companions, wished to see the daughters of the city’s inhabitants. Thus the bloody slaughter and plunder occurred on her account. As I think, this no longer presents a problem: the population was not small, since Jacob had become very wealthy. His sons are named in this deed because they were its leaders and authors.

The text continues:

### (Chapter 35—verse 1)

Meanwhile God spoke to Jacob: “Rise and go up to Bethel, and dwell there. Make an altar to the God who appeared to you when you were fleeing from your [Col. 1008A] brother.”

Why did he not say, “Make an altar there to me, who appeared to you,” but rather, “Make there an altar to the God who appeared to you”? Did the Son appear there, and is God the Father saying this? Or should this be included among a certain kind of expression, such as: “The Lord rained from the Lord” (Genesis 19)?

### (Verses 2 ff.)

He said: “Throw away the foreign gods that are among you, purify yourselves, and change your garments. Rise, and let us go up to Bethel, and let us make there an altar to the Lord, who heard me in the day of my distress and was my companion on the journey.”

So they gave him all the foreign gods they possessed, as well as the earrings that were in their ears. He buried them beneath the terebinth that is behind the city of [Col. 1008B] Shechem.

It is asked why the earrings were included, since they were ornaments and did not belong to idolatry, unless we are to understand that they were amulets of demons. Scripture testifies that Rebecca received earrings from Abraham’s servant; this would not have happened if earrings were impermissible as ornaments. Therefore those earrings that were handed over along with the idols were, as has been said, amulets of idols.

The text continues:

### (Verse 5)

When they had departed, the terror of the Lord seized all the surrounding regions, and they did not dare pursue those who were leaving.

Let us begin to observe how God works in the minds of human beings. From whom did the fear of God arise in those cities, except from the one who was protecting his promises to Jacob and his sons?

The text continues:

### (Verse 6)

Jacob therefore came to Luz, which is in the land of Canaan and is surnamed Bethel—he and all the people with him. He built an altar there and called the name of the place “House of God,” because God had appeared to him there when he was fleeing from his brother.

Here it is most clearly confirmed that Bethel was formerly called Luz, not Ulamma, as the Seventy translators said. Luz means “almond.” This should not seem surprising, since it has happened in many places—in cities, rivers, and various localities—that names were added or changed for different reasons, just as happens with human beings.

The text continues:

[Col. 1008C]

### (Verse 8)

At that time Deborah, Rebecca’s nurse, died and was buried at the foot of Bethel, beneath an oak. The name of that place was called “The Oak of Weeping.”

Deborah represented the Mosaic Law, which, like a bee, offered the peoples the honey of divine knowledge and worship. For this reason she was also the Lord’s nurse, because, as the Apostle says: “Born of a woman, born under the law” (Galatians 4).

The shadows and images of the Law are born dead and buried when the Lord is read as having cried out in his passion: “It is finished.”

The oak beneath which Deborah is said to have been buried is to be understood as the Lord’s cross. It was called the Oak of Weeping because upon it was suspended the life that brought perpetual mourning upon the unbelieving Jews.

The text continues:

### (Verses 9–10)

God appeared again to Jacob after he had returned from Mesopotamia of Syria, and he blessed him, saying: “You shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name.” And he called him Israel.

Earlier the name was by no means imposed upon him by the angel; rather, it was foretold that God would impose it. What is therefore promised as future [Col. 1008D] there is here shown to have been fulfilled.

Thus God repeats this statement to him in the blessing. The repetition confirms the great promise contained in this name. For this is remarkable: those to whom it was once said that they would no longer be called by the name they had borne, but that a new name would be imposed upon them, were never afterward called by anything except the name given to them.

This man, however, was called Jacob throughout his entire life, even though God had once said to him: “You shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name.”

Clearly, then, this name should properly be understood as referring to that promise in which God will be seen in a way in which he was not previously seen by the patriarchs. There the old name will no longer exist, because nothing of old age will remain even in the body itself, and the vision of God will be the supreme reward.

The text continues:

### (Verse 11)

“I am God Almighty. Grow and multiply. [Col. 1009A] Nations and peoples of nations shall come from you, and kings shall come forth from your loins.”

Does “nations” refer to those according to the flesh, and “peoples” to gatherings of nations according to faith? Or was both said on account of the faith of the nations? For Israel according to the flesh, being one nation, cannot be called “nations.”

The text continues:

### (Verse 14)

He set up a stone monument in the place where God had spoken to him, pouring libations over it and pouring oil upon it, and calling the name of that place Bethel.

Was what had been done earlier done again at this place, or is it merely recalled again? Whichever is the case, Jacob poured a libation over the stone, not to the stone—not as idolaters customarily set up altars before stones and pour libations to stones as though they were gods.

The text continues:

### (Verses 15 ff.)

Departing from there, he came in the springtime to the land that leads to Ephrathah. While Rachel was giving birth there, she began to be in danger because of the difficulty of the birth. The midwife said to her: “Do not be afraid, for you will have this son also.”

As her soul was departing because of the pain [Col. 1009B] and death was already approaching, she called the name of her son Ben-oni, that is, “son of my sorrow.” But his father called him Benjamin, that is, “son of the right hand.”

Rachel therefore died and was buried on the road that leads to Ephrathah, which is Bethlehem. Jacob set up a monument over her tomb.

Ephrathah and Bethlehem are names for the same city, with similar interpretations. One is translated as “fruitful,” the other as “house of bread,” on account of that bread which is read as having descended there from heaven.

But what does it mean that, when Rachel gave birth to this same Benjamin, she called his name “son of my sorrow,” except that she was prophetically foretelling Paul, who would arise from his tribe and afflict the children of the Church during the time of his persecution?

Or, in another interpretation, earthly Jerusalem was represented by Benjamin. Jerusalem lies in the territory of that same Benjamin, whose people caused their mother deep sorrow by shedding the blood of the prophets and, in addition, by crying out with impious voices for the death of Christ: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Mark 7).

The text continues:

### (Verse 21)

Departing from there, he pitched his tent beyond the torrent of the flock [Col. 1009C]. Another translation says: “Beyond the torrent of Hader.”

The Hebrews believe that this was the place where the temple was later built, and that the Tower of Hader signifies the Tower of the Flock—that is, of the gathering and assembly. The prophet Micah bears witness to this when he says: “And you, Tower of the Flock, daughter of Zion” (Micah 4), and so forth. At that time Jacob had his tents beyond the place where the temple was later built.

But let us follow the order of the text. The Way of the Shepherds near Bethlehem is the place where the flock of angels sang at the Lord’s birth. Alternatively, Jacob may have pastured his own animals there and given the place its name. Or, what is more accurate, the mystery that was to come was already being revealed at that time through prophecy.

The text continues:

### (Verse 22)

While he was dwelling in that region, Reuben went and slept with his father’s concubine Bilhah, and Israel learned of it.

Reuben, moved by the desire of lust, rushed headlong into passion for his father’s concubine. This crime of incest would not have been written unless it foretold the future [Col. 1009D] perversity of the Israelite people.

Although the disgrace of the individual who committed this act may also be considered, Scripture nevertheless contains a prophecy of future events. For through Reuben, the firstborn, the firstborn people of Israel according to circumcision is signified. He polluted the bed of the concubine—that is, he repeatedly defiled the law of the Old Testament by transgression.

That the Old Testament is represented in the concubine was taught by the Apostle Paul, who says: “Abraham had two sons, one by the slave woman and one by the free woman; these are the two covenants” (Galatians 4), and so forth. In this passage Hagar, who was a concubine, is placed as a type of the Old Testament.

There is one perfect dove of her mother, the Church, which is joined through the Gospel as the chaste virgin, queen, and bride of Christ.

The text continues:

## (Verse 23 and following)

Now Jacob had twelve sons. The sons of Leah: the firstborn, Reuben; then Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun. The sons of Rachel: Joseph and Benjamin. The sons of Bilhah, Rachel’s maidservant: Dan and Naphtali. The sons of Zilpah, Leah’s maidservant: Gad and Asher. These are Jacob’s sons who were born to him in Mesopotamia. How are the twelve sons of Israel counted as having been born, and how is it said, “These are the sons of Israel who were born to him in Mesopotamia,” when Benjamin was born much later, after he had already passed Bethel and was approaching Bethlehem?

For this reason some, attempting in vain to solve the problem, have said that one should not read “were born,” as most Latin manuscripts have it, but “came into being”; for in Greek it is written ἐγένοντο (*egenonto*, “came into being”). They therefore wish it to be understood that Benjamin, although he was not born there, nevertheless came into being there, because he had already been conceived in the womb, so that Rachel may be believed to have left that place pregnant.

But even if one read “were born,” they could say that he had already been born in the womb because he had been conceived, just as it was said to Joseph concerning holy Mary: “For that which is born in her is of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 1). Yet another consideration prevents this solution of the problem: if Benjamin had already been conceived there, when Jacob’s other sons departed from that place as grown men, they could scarcely have been twelve years old. For Jacob completed twenty years there, during the first seven of which he was unmarried, until he obtained his wife by serving. Thus, if a son was born to him in the first year after he took a wife, the firstborn could have been twelve years old when he departed from that place.

Therefore, if Benjamin had already been conceived, the whole journey, together with everything recorded as having occurred along the way, would have been completed within ten months. It would then follow that his sons, being so young, carried out such a slaughter on behalf of their sister Dinah, killed so many people, and conquered the city so completely. Among them Simeon and Levi, who were the first to enter armed with swords and kill the men, would have been found to be eleven and ten years old respectively—even if she had given birth every single year without interruption. It is plainly incredible that boys of that age could have done all these things, when Dinah herself was scarcely six years old.

The problem must therefore be solved in another way: namely, it is to be understood that, after the twelve sons had been mentioned, it was said, “These are the sons of Jacob who were born to him in Mesopotamia of Syria,” because, among all the many sons, only one had not been born there. Nevertheless, he had obtained the cause of his birth there, since his mother had been joined to his father there.

This solution to the problem, however, still needs at some point to be supported by an example of similar expression. Yet no easier solution to this question exists than to understand it by synecdoche. Wherever the greater or more important part is present, it is customary for what belongs to that designation also to be included under its name. Thus Judas no longer belonged to the twelve apostles—and had even died by the time the Lord rose from the dead—yet the Apostle retained the name of that twelvefold number in his Epistle when he said: “When he appeared to the twelve.” The Greek manuscripts have the article here, so that it could not be understood as merely any twelve, but as those distinguished within that number.

I think the Lord’s statement is expressed in the same way: “Did I not choose you twelve, and one of you is a devil?” (John 6), so that the latter might not be understood as belonging to the election. Likewise, because the number twelve was more appropriate to the sons of Jacob who had been born in Mesopotamia, Scripture, in mentioning them, included Benjamin as well, although he had not been born there, and said: “These are the sons of Jacob who were born to him in Mesopotamia of Syria.”

It follows:

## Chapter 36 — (Verses 1 and following)

These are the generations of Esau; he is Edom. Esau took wives from the daughters of Canaan: Adah, the daughter of Elon the Hittite; and Oholibamah, the daughter of Anah, son of Zibeon the Hivite; and Basemath, the daughter of Ishmael, sister of Nebaioth. Adah bore Eliphaz; Basemath bore Reuel; and Oholibamah gave birth to Jeush, Elon, and Korah. These are the sons of Esau who were born to him in the land of Canaan.

The fact that, after the account of Isaac’s death, it is narrated which wives Esau took and which sons were born to him must be understood as a recapitulation. It did not begin to happen after Isaac’s death, since Esau and Jacob were already one hundred and twenty years old by then. Isaac had begotten them when he was sixty, and he lived to be one hundred and eighty-five. This is the Eliphaz whom Scripture mentions in the Book of Job.

It follows.

### (Verses 6 and following)

Esau took his wives, his sons and daughters, every person belonging to his household, his property, his livestock, and everything he could possess in the land of Canaan. He departed for another region and withdrew from his brother Jacob, for they were exceedingly wealthy and could not dwell together; the land of their sojourn could not support them because of the abundance of their flocks. Esau dwelt on Mount Seir; he is Edom.

Esau, Edom, and Seir are names belonging to one man; why he is called by different names has been explained above. But a question arises concerning how Scripture can say that, after the death of his father Isaac, Esau departed from the land of Canaan and dwelt on Mount Seir, when it is read that, by the time his brother Jacob came from Mesopotamia, he was already living there.

It is therefore easy to consider what may have happened, so that Scripture is not thought either to have been mistaken or to have misled us. Namely, after his brother Jacob had departed for Mesopotamia, Esau did not wish to live with his parents—whether because of the agitation in which he grieved that he had been deprived of the blessing, or for some other reason, perhaps because of his wives, whom he saw to be displeasing to his parents, or for any other cause—and he began to live on Mount Seir.

Then, after his brother Jacob’s return, when peace had been made between them, Esau himself returned to his parents. After they had buried their father together, because that land, as Scripture says, could not contain them, being greatly enriched, he again departed for Seir and there propagated the nation of the Idumaeans.

It follows.

### (Verses 31 and following)

These are the kings who reigned in the land of Edom before the sons of Israel had a king: Bahale son of Beor, whose city was named Denaba. Bahale died, and Jobab son of Zerah from Bozrah reigned in his place.

Some suspect that this man was Job, as was added at the end of his book. The Hebrews, however, assert that he was descended from the line of Nahor, as was stated above.

As for what is written—“These are the kings who reigned in Edom before a king reigned in Israel”—it should not be understood as though all the kings had been named up to the time when the kings of Israel began, the first of whom was Saul. There were many kings in Edom up to the time of Saul, including those who ruled during the period of the judges, whose time preceded that of the kings. But among those many, Moses could mention only those who lived before his own death.

Nor is it surprising that, when one counts from Abraham through Esau, the father of the Idumaean nation, and through Reuel, Esau’s son, and Zerah, Reuel’s son, and Jobab, Zerah’s son—Jobab being succeeded in the kingship by Balak, who is first mentioned as having been king in the land of Edom—up to the last king whom Moses could name, more generations are found than are counted from Abraham through Jacob to Moses. In the former line nearly eleven generations are found; in the latter, up to Moses, about seven. It could have happened that more were named in the former line because, by dying sooner, more succeeded one another.

The same thing occurred when Matthew, following a different order, counted forty-two generations from Abraham to Joseph (Matt. 1), while Luke, counting the generations in another order—not through Solomon as Matthew did, but through Nathan—listed fifty-five generations from Abraham to Joseph (Luke 3). In the line in which more are counted, they died sooner than in the line in which fewer are counted.

Lest anyone be troubled by the fact that Balak son of Beor is listed among the kings of Edom and, because of the similarity of the names, suppose that he was Balaak, who resisted Moses when he was leading the people of Israel, let him know that that Balaak was a Moabite, not an Idumaean; he was the son of Zippor, not the son of Beor. At that same time there was also a son of Beor, namely Balaam, not Balaak. Balaak himself hired Balaam to curse the people of Israel.

## Chapter 37 — (Verses 2 and following)

When Joseph was sixteen years old, he was tending the flock with his brothers, still a boy, and he was with the sons of Bilhah and Zilpah, his father’s wives. He accused his brothers before his father of a very serious offense.

Israel loved Joseph more than all his sons, because he had begotten him in his old age, and he made him a multicolored tunic. When his brothers saw that their father loved him more than all his brothers, they hated him and could not speak peacefully to him.

If Joseph was sold into Egypt in his sixteenth year, he is found to have been sold thirteen years before his grandfather died. For he could not have been sixteen unless, thirteen years before Isaac’s death, he was in the one hundred and seventh year of his father Jacob’s life. When we add to this the twenty-three years Joseph spent in Egypt before his father’s arrival, Joseph’s age becomes thirty-nine, while Jacob’s becomes one hundred and thirty, and there is no difficulty.

But because Scripture narrated these events after Isaac’s death, it is thought that Joseph was sixteen years old after the death of that same father of his. We should therefore understand that, when Scripture was speaking of Jacob and his sons, it was silent concerning Isaac’s life, as though he were a very aged man. Nevertheless, Joseph began to be sixteen years old while Isaac was still alive.

It happened also that Joseph related a dream to his brothers, and this became the cause and seed of even greater hatred. He said to them: “Hear my dream, which I dreamed. I thought that we were binding sheaves in the field, and that my sheaf, as though rising, stood upright, while your sheaves stood around it and bowed down to my sheaf.”

His brothers answered him: “Will you perhaps be our king, or shall we be subjected to your authority?” This, therefore, furnished fuel for envy and hatred—the dreams and the words that accompanied them.

He saw another dream as well. When he related it to his brothers, he said: “I saw in a dream that the sun, the moon, and eleven stars were bowing down to me.” When he had related it to his father and brothers, his father rebuked him and said: “What does this dream that you dreamed mean? Shall I, your mother, and your brothers indeed come and bow down to you upon the earth?”

His brothers therefore envied him, but his father silently considered the matter.

When Jacob said to Joseph, “What is this dream that you have dreamed? Shall I, your mother, and your brothers indeed come and bow down to you upon the earth?”—unless this is understood as having been said with reference to some mystery, how can it be understood of Joseph’s mother, who was already dead?

Nor should it be thought that this was fulfilled in Egypt when Joseph was exalted, since neither did his father bow down to him when he came to him in Egypt, nor could his mother, who had long been dead, do so. It can therefore easily be understood in relation to Christ, even concerning the dead, according to what the Apostle says: “He bestowed upon him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. 2).

It follows:

Joseph therefore went after his brothers and found them at Dothan. When they saw him from a distance, before he approached them, they plotted to kill him and said to one another: “Behold, the dreamer is coming. Come, let us kill him and throw him into an old cistern, and we shall say: ‘A most savage beast has devoured him.’ Then it will become clear what his dreams profit him.”

When Reuben heard this, he tried to rescue him from their hands and said: “Let us not kill him, nor shed his blood. Instead, throw him into this cistern, which is in the wilderness, and keep your hands innocent.” He said this because he wished to rescue him from their hands and return him to his father.

As soon as he came to his brothers, they stripped him of his long, multicolored tunic and threw him into a cistern that had no water. Then they sat down to eat bread and saw Ishmaelites coming from Gilead, their camels carrying spices, resin, and stacte on the way to Egypt.

Judah said to his brothers: “What profit is there for us if we kill our brother and conceal his blood? It is better that he be sold to the Ishmaelites and that our hands not be defiled; for he is our brother and our flesh.”

His brothers agreed with his words. As the Midianite merchants passed by, they drew Joseph out of the cistern and sold him to the Ishmaelites for thirty pieces of silver [the Vulgate has: twenty].

The question is asked why Scripture calls those to whom Joseph was sold by his brothers Ishmaelites and also calls them Midianites, since Ishmael was the son of Abraham by Hagar, whereas the Midianites descended from Keturah. Is it because Scripture had said of Abraham that he gave gifts to the sons of his concubines—namely Hagar and Keturah—and sent them away from his son Isaac toward the land of the East, so that they should be understood to have formed a single nation?

It follows.

### (Verses 28 and following)

They brought him into Egypt.

When Reuben returned to the cistern and did not find the boy, he tore his garments and went to his brothers, saying: “The boy is gone, and where shall I go?”

They took Joseph’s tunic, dipped it in the blood of the goat they had killed, and sent someone to carry it to their father and say: “We found this. See whether it is your son’s tunic or not.”

When the father recognized it, he said: “It is my son’s tunic. A most savage beast has eaten him; a beast has devoured Joseph.” He tore his garments, put on sackcloth, and mourned his son for a long time.

When all his children gathered to lessen their father’s grief, he refused to accept consolation and said: “I shall go down to my son, mourning, into the underworld.”

It is often a major question how “the underworld” is to be understood: whether only the wicked, or also the righteous, customarily descend there when they die. If only the wicked do so, how can this man say that he wishes to descend to his son in mourning? He did not believe that his son was in the punishments of the underworld; rather, these are the words of a troubled and grieving man, intensifying his misfortunes even further by this expression.

It follows.

### (Verse 36)

The Midianites sold Joseph in Egypt to Potiphar, a eunuch of Pharaoh and commander of the army.

The question is asked how this same eunuch is later said to have had a wife. The Hebrews relate that Joseph was purchased by him because of his extraordinary beauty for a shameful service, and that, after his male organs had been dried up by his master, he was later chosen, according to the custom of the hierophants, for the priesthood of Heliopolis. They say that Asenath was his daughter, whom Joseph later took as his wife.

Joseph, one of Jacob’s twelve sons, whom his father loved more than the other sons, prefigured Christ the Lord. God the Father preferred him, born according to the flesh, to the other brothers descended from the line of Abraham.

Thus it is also said there: “Jacob loved him because he had begotten him in his old age.” As the world grew old, the Son of God, dawning through the birth of the Virgin Mary, came late, as a son of old age, and according to the mystery assumed a body, while in the substance of his divinity he had always been with the Father.

The multicolored tunic that his father made for him signified the diversity of peoples gathered from all nations into the body of Christ.

The dream in which his brothers’ sheaves bowed down to his sheaf is what was fulfilled in Christ: “All the kings of the earth shall adore him; all nations shall serve him” (Ps. 71), namely, through faith, bringing forth the fruit of good works.

He is the one whom the sun and moon adore, concerning whom it is said of the sun: “Praise him, sun and moon; praise him, all stars” (Ps. 148). The excellence of the saints adores him under the name of the sun, the splendor of the Church under the image of the moon, and the multitude of all peoples under the figure of the stars.

Therefore his father rebuked him, saying: “Shall I, your mother, and your brothers bow down to you?” This rebuke by his father signifies the hardness of the people of Israel, because they recognize that Christ was born from them yet disdain to adore him.

Jacob sends his son Joseph to inquire after his brothers; God the Father sent his only-begotten Son to visit the human race, weakened by sins. He was sent by that Father of whom it is written: “God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh” (Rom. 8), to see whether the sheep were faring well. And the Lord says in the Gospel: “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. 15).

Joseph therefore found his brothers at Dothan. Dothan is interpreted as “defection.” Truly they were in great defection, since they were plotting the murder of their brother.

When Joseph’s brothers saw him from a distance, they plotted to kill him. And when the Jews saw the true Joseph, the Lord Jesus Christ, they all together formed a plan to crucify him, saying: “Crucify him” (Luke 23).

“A most savage beast has devoured him”—that is, the Jewish people killed him, concerning which the Lord says in the Gospel: “Behold, I am sending you as sheep among wolves” (Matt. 10).

Joseph’s brothers stripped him of his multicolored and long tunic; and the Jews, through the death of the cross, stripped Christ of his bodily garment. The multicolored tunic, that is, adorned with the diversity of all virtues, signified this.

They sprinkled the tunic with the blood of a goat, because, accusing him with false testimonies, they delivered him over to the envy of the people, although he was granting forgiveness of all sins.

Then he was thrown into a cistern—that is, into a pit—and Christ, stripped of human flesh, descended into the underworld.

He was also lifted from the cistern and sold to the Ishmaelites, that is, to the Gentiles. Christ, after emerging from the underworld, was purchased by all the nations in the commerce of faith.

Through Judah’s counsel, Joseph was sold for thirty pieces of silver; and Christ, through the counsel of Judas Iscariot, was sold for the same number.

Then Jacob, mourning the loss of his descendants, grieved as a father over his lost son, and as a prophet lamented the destruction of the Jews.

Finally, he tore his garment, as we read that the high priest did during the Passion (Matt. 26); and the veil of the temple was also torn (ibid., 27), so that the prophet might show both that his people had been stripped bare and that the kingdom had been divided.

## Chapter 38 — (Verses 1 and following)

At that time Judah went down from his brothers and turned aside to a man from Adullam named Hirah. There he saw the daughter of a Canaanite man named Shua. He took her as his wife and went in to her; she conceived and bore a son, and he called his name Er.

Again she conceived and bore a son, whom she named Onan. She also bore a third, whom she called Shelah. After his birth she ceased bearing children.

Judah gave Tamar as a wife to his firstborn son Er. But Er, Judah’s firstborn, was wicked in the sight of the Lord, and the Lord killed him.

Then Judah said to his son Onan: “Go in to your brother’s wife, so that you may raise up offspring for your brother.” But Onan knew that the children would not be regarded as his. When he went in to his brother’s wife, he spilled his seed upon the ground, so that children would not be born in his brother’s name.

For this reason the Lord struck him, because he had committed a detestable act.

Therefore Judah said to his daughter-in-law: “Remain a widow in your father’s house until my son Shelah grows up.” For he was afraid that Shelah too might die, as his brothers had died.

The question is asked how these things could have happened. If they occurred after Joseph came into Egypt, how could they have taken place within approximately twenty-three years? For after that length of time they are understood to have come to Joseph, their brother, in Egypt with their father.

It could have happened that Judah and his sons, given their ages, were able to take wives. After the death of her firstborn, Judah gave his daughter-in-law Tamar to another son; when that son also died, he waited for the third to grow up, and when he had grown up, he did not give him to her, fearing that he too might die. Thus it happened that she offered herself to her father-in-law.

How, then, could all these events have occurred within so few years? The question rightly causes difficulty, unless, as Scripture sometimes does, it is understood by recapitulation that this began several years before Joseph was sold, since the narrative is arranged so as to say: “It happened at that time.”

Yet one may still ask how old Judah could have been when Joseph was sold, if Joseph was sixteen years old. His firstborn brother Reuben could at most have preceded Joseph by five or six years.

Scripture clearly says that Joseph was thirty years old when he became known to Pharaoh. If, therefore, he is believed to have been sold in the sixteenth year of his life, he had spent fourteen years in Egypt unknown to Pharaoh. To these fourteen years were added seven years of abundance, making twenty-one years. Two more were added, because Jacob entered Egypt with his sons in the second year of the famine; thus there are found to be twenty-three years during which Joseph was absent from his father and brothers.

During that interval, how all the things narrated concerning Judah’s wife, sons, and daughter-in-law could have occurred is difficult to investigate—unless perhaps we believe, for this too could have happened, that as soon as Judah began to reach adolescence, he fell in love with the woman whom he married, before Joseph was sold into Egypt.

It follows.

(Verses 12 ff.) After many days had passed, Shuah, Judah’s wife, died. When he had received consolation after his mourning, he went up to the shearers of his sheep, he and Hirah, the Adullamite shepherd of the flock, to Timnah. And Tamar was told that her father-in-law was going up to Timnah to shear his sheep. She removed her widow’s clothing, took a veil, and, changing her appearance, sat at the crossroads on the road that leads to Timnah, because Shelah had grown up and she had not taken him as her husband.

When Judah saw her, he supposed that she was a prostitute; for she had covered her face so that she would not be recognized. He approached her and said, “Let me come in to you,” for he did not know that she was his daughter-in-law. When she replied, “What will you give me, so that you may enjoy intercourse with me?” he said, “I will send you a young goat from the flock.” Again she said, “I will allow it, if you give me a pledge until you send what you promise.” Judah said, “What do you want me to give you as a pledge?” She answered, “Your ring, your bracelet, and the staff that you hold in your hand.”

Thus, after one act of intercourse, the woman conceived. She rose and went away, and, laying aside the clothing she had assumed, put on her widow’s garments. For if a man and wife, as the Lord says, are no longer two but one flesh, a daughter-in-law must be reckoned no differently from a daughter. Nevertheless, there is no doubt that, so far as it depended on him, Judah shamefully lay with a prostitute.

But she who deceived her father-in-law did not sin out of desire for his flesh or from greed for a prostitute’s payment. Seeking offspring from the very bloodline from which she had been married to two brothers, and from which she had been unable to have children because a third husband was denied her, she fraudulently offered her father-in-law, their father, a body to beget children. It would indeed have been better for her to remain without children than to become a mother without the right of marriage. Yet she sinned with a very different intention: she provided her father-in-law as a father for her children, rather than desiring him as an adulterer.

Finally, when, by his order, she was being led out to death, she brought forth the staff, necklace, and ring, saying that she had been made pregnant by the man whose pledges these were. When he recognized what he had given her, he replied that she was more justified than he, because he had not given her his son as her husband. Compelled by that refusal, she had sought offspring in that manner rather than not at all, and from no other source than the same family line.

In this statement, when he says that she was justified—not merely justified, but more justified than he—he did not praise her in herself, but preferred her in comparison with himself. That is, he judged less blameworthy the desire to have offspring, which had led her to submit to her father-in-law, than the ardor of lust by which he himself, overcome as though by a prostitute, had entered her chamber. This is like the statement addressed to certain people, “You have justified Sodom,” that is, “You have sinned so greatly that, by comparison with you, Sodom appears righteous.” Yet this woman may also be understood to have been judged less blameworthy, not merely in comparison with a worse deed, but to have been wholly praised by her father-in-law.

Nevertheless, when judged by that eternal law of justice which forbids the natural order to be disturbed—not merely the order of bodies, but especially and primarily that of souls—she is rightly found blameworthy, because she did not preserve an ordered union in begetting children.

What is surprising if a sinner is praised by a sinner? Faustus, or the very perversity of the Manichaeans, considers this to be opposed to us, as though, in our true and worthy exposition of this Scripture, we were compelled to approve the vices of the people whose deeds it records. On the contrary, the more reverently we accept it, the more confidently we must condemn those things which, through its truth, we have learned ought more certainly to be condemned. For in it fornication and every illicit intercourse are condemned by divine law.

Accordingly, when it records the deeds of certain people while at that point keeping its own judgment silent, it allows us to indicate that judgment; it does not prescribe that we praise them. Hence it appears more clearly here that the prophecy spoken by the patriarch Jacob under the name of Judah does not pertain to Judah himself, but to Christ, who was foretold as destined to come in the flesh from Judah’s tribe.

For this reason divine Scripture ought not to have concealed Judah’s disgrace, just as it did not conceal it in the words of his father, by which he was praised after that dishonor. Since he himself is not recognized in the prophecy, another must be sought. For when Judah entered Tamar’s presence, overcome by desire, he had no intention that anything should be signified through him which would contribute to the salvation of humanity. Nor did that other Judas who betrayed God intend that something should happen through his deed which would contribute to the same salvation.

Moreover, if the Lord brought so great a good from that Judas’s very evil deed that he redeemed us by the blood of his own Passion, what is surprising if his prophet—of whom the Lord himself says, “For he wrote about me” (John 5)—signified something good through this Judah’s evil deed, so that by its mystery he might instruct us?

The prophet-narrator, under the direction and inspiration of the Holy Spirit, gathered together those human deeds whose insertion was not without purpose, since they prefigured the events he intended to prophesy. To signify certain good things, it makes no difference whether the deeds by which they are signified are good or evil. What difference would it make, if I wished to learn something by reading, whether I found black Ethiopians written in vermilion and white Gauls in ink? Yet if I saw, not things written, but writing of that kind, I would unquestionably criticize it.

Thus, in human deeds that are set before us for imitation or avoidance, it matters greatly whether they are good or evil. But when deeds are written or spoken for the purpose of signifying something, it is irrelevant, with respect to the morals of those who perform them, what praise or blame they deserve—provided only that they possess some necessary correspondence with the matter being prefigured.

For example, the words of Caiaphas in the Gospel were evil insofar as they pertained to his harmful and destructive intention, and even with respect to the words themselves, if one attends to the speaker’s will: he was saying that the just man should be unjustly killed. Nevertheless, without his knowing it, they signified a great good when he said, “It is expedient for you that one man should die and that the whole nation should not perish.” It was said of him: “He did not say this of himself, but, because he was high priest, he prophesied that Jesus was to die for the nation” (John 11).

So Judah’s deed was evil according to his lust; but without his knowing it, it signified a great good. He did evil of himself, but did not signify good of himself.

What I have necessarily set forth in advance should apply not only to this deed of Judah, but also to any other evil deeds of human beings that may arise, through which the narrator prophetically signified something good.

In Tamar, Judah’s daughter-in-law, the people of the kingdom of Judah are understood, to whom kings from the tribe of Judah were given as husbands. Her name is rightly interpreted as “Bitterness,” for she gave the Lord a cup of gall.

The two kinds of rulers who did not govern the people rightly are signified in Judah’s two sons: one consisted of those who acted wickedly, the other of those who did nothing useful. One was a violent man before the Lord; the other poured his seed upon the ground so that he would not provide offspring for Tamar.

There are no more than two kinds of people who are useless to the human race: those who do harm, and those who refuse to be of benefit. If they possess anything good in this earthly life, they lose it, as though pouring it upon the ground. Since the one who harms is worse than the one who is of no benefit, the elder is called “Malignant,” while the younger, who poured his seed upon the ground, is called “Their Sorrow.”

The name of the elder, who was called Er, is interpreted as “Clad in skins,” such as the tunics with which the first human beings were clothed in punishment for their condemnation after they had been expelled from paradise. The name of the younger, who was called Onan, is interpreted as “Their Sorrow.” Whose sorrow, if not that of those who are of no benefit, although they possess the means by which they could be useful, but squander it upon the earth?

The greater evil is life taken away, signified by skin, than life not possessed, signified by “their sorrow.” Yet God is said to have killed both of them, signifying that he removed the kingdom from people of this kind.

Judah’s third son, who is not joined to that woman, signifies the time from which kings of the Jewish people began no longer to come from the tribe of Judah. He was indeed Judah’s son, but Tamar did not receive him as her husband, because the tribe of Judah still existed, but no one from it was any longer reigning among the people.

Hence his name, Shelah, is interpreted as “His Dismissal.”

Holy and righteous men do not belong to this interpretation. Although they lived at that time, they belonged nevertheless to the New Testament, for they were knowingly useful to it through prophecy, as David was.

At the time when the Jews had already begun to have no kings from the tribe of Judah, the elder Herod must not be counted among its kings as Tamar’s husband. He was a foreigner, and he was not joined to the people by the sacrament of mystical anointing as by a marital covenant. Rather, he ruled as an outsider, having received that power from the Romans and from Caesar. The same applies to his sons, the tetrarchs, one of whom was called Herod after his father and agreed with Pilate in the Lord’s Passion.

These foreigners were so far from being counted as belonging to that mystical kingdom of the Jews that the Jews themselves publicly cried out, gnashing their teeth against Christ, “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19). This was not true except under that universal Roman dominion, since Caesar was also a king, though not properly the king of the Jews. But in order to deny Christ and flatter Caesar, they condemned themselves with that utterance.

At the time, therefore, when the kingdom had already departed from the tribe of Judah, it was necessary for Christ, the true Savior and our Lord, to come—one who would not harm but would greatly benefit. For it had been prophesied:

> “The prince shall not fail from Judah, nor the ruler from his loins, until he comes to whom it has been promised; and he shall be the expectation of the nations” (Genesis 49).

By that time, all Jewish teaching had also failed, as had the mystical anointing from which they were called “anointed.” In accordance with Daniel’s prophecy, the one to whom the promise had been made then came: he is the expectation of the nations, and he was anointed, the Holy of Holies, with the oil of gladness above his companions.

He was born during the time of the elder Herod, but he suffered during the time of the younger Herod.

Judah himself, when he went to shear the sheep at Timnah—which is interpreted as “Failing”—prefigured this one who came to the sheep that had perished, the house of Israel. For the prince had already failed from Judah, as had all Jewish teaching and anointing, so that the one to whom the promise had been made might come.

He came with his shepherd, the Adullamite, whose name was Hirah. “Adullamite” is interpreted as “Testimony in water.” The Lord plainly came with this testimony. He did indeed have testimony greater than John’s, but, because of the weak sheep, he used this testimony in water.

Hirah, the name of that shepherd, is interpreted as “The Vision of My Brother.” John truly saw his brother: his brother according to the seed of Abraham, and according to the kinship of Mary, his mother, and Elizabeth, John’s mother. He saw the same one as his Lord and God, since, as John himself says, he received from his fullness.

John truly saw him, and therefore no one born of women has arisen greater than he (Matthew 11). For among all those who foretold Christ, he saw what many righteous people and prophets desired to see but did not see (Matthew 13). He greeted him from the womb; he recognized him perfectly from the dove. Therefore, as an Adullamite, he truly bore witness in water.

The Lord came to shear the sheep—that is, to relieve them of their burdensome loads—of which the Church is told in the Song of Songs: “Your teeth are like a flock of shorn sheep” (Song of Songs 6).

Now let Tamar change her clothing. For Tamar is also interpreted as “Changing,” but let the name “Bitterness” remain in her completely—not the bitterness by which she gave the Lord gall, but that by which Peter wept bitterly (Luke 22). For Judah in Latin means “Confession.”

Let bitterness, therefore, be mingled with confession, so that true repentance may be prefigured. By this repentance the Church, established among all nations, is made fruitful. For it was necessary that Christ should suffer, rise on the third day, and that repentance and the forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem (Luke 24). The prostitute’s clothing itself is also a confession of sins.

Tamar already bears the figure of the Church, called from the nations. Sitting in this clothing at the gate of Enaim, or Henaim, which is interpreted as “Fountains,” she hastened like a deer to reach the fountains of water, to come to the seed of Abraham. There she is impregnated by one who does not recognize her, because it was foretold of her: “A people whom I did not know served me.”

She receives the ring, necklace, and staff in secret: by calling she is marked, by justification adorned, and by glorification exalted. “Those whom he predestined, he also called; those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified” (Romans 8). But these things, as I said, are still hidden, where the conception of holy fruitfulness also takes place.

The promised young goat is sent to her as though to a prostitute: the goat is a reproach for sin, sent through the same Adullamite, as though he were rebuking her and saying, “Brood of vipers” (Matthew 12). Yet the reproach for sin did not find her, because the bitterness of confession had changed her.

Later, when the signs—the ring, necklace, and staff—had been made public, she overcame the Jews who judged rashly. Judah himself will now bear their role: even today they say that this is not the people of Christ and that we do not possess the seed of Abraham. But when the most certain proofs of our calling, justification, and glorification are brought forward, they will undoubtedly be confounded and confess that we have been justified more than they.

(Verses 27 ff.) When the time came for her to give birth, twins appeared in her womb. During the very delivery, one put out his hand, and the midwife tied a scarlet thread around it, saying, “This one will come out first.” But when he withdrew his hand, the other came out. The woman said, “Why has the wall been divided because of you?” For this reason she called his name Perez. Afterwards the other came out, on whose hand was the scarlet thread, and she called him Zerah.

Why is the patriarch Judah recorded as having sought intercourse with his own daughter-in-law after the death of his son, through which the birth of twins was brought about, unless it was so that a figure might precede concerning the two Testaments of the Lord Jesus: one founded in the type of his future death, the other in the truth of the Gospel, showing that two peoples were to be generated, the later of whom, in the sign of the cross, would often break through the whole fortification of the earlier people?

This is the people whose hand came first but whose birth came later. The Lord Jesus himself, born from the tribe of Judah, sent his works ahead before he was born to us from the Virgin.

Or, alternatively, works are signified by the hand. Zerah is interpreted as “Rising,” and signified the ancient Israelite people established under the Law. It put out its hand first, as it were, when, through prophetic utterances and legal sacrifices, it announced the Lord’s birth and Passion in the flesh. But, when the time of delivery came, it withdrew its hand, because, when the fullness of time arrived, it refused to believe in the Son of God and despised him when he was present—the one about whom it had later foretold so many things.

Perez, however, who is interpreted as “Dividing,” came out first, because, after blindness had occurred in Israel, the fullness of the nations entered, and afterward Israel will be saved (Romans 11).

[Col. 1018D] (Chapter 39—Verse 1.) “Joseph was therefore brought down to Egypt.” Scripture returns to the order from which it had departed, in order to relate the matters arranged above.

“And Potiphar, a eunuch of Pharaoh, commander of the army, an Egyptian man, bought him from the hand of the Ishmaelites, by whom he had been brought there. And the Lord was with him, and he was a man prospering in all things.”

Just as Joseph descended into Egypt, so Christ descended into the world. A eunuch bought him—that is, a Christian people chaste in the discipline of the Gospel.

“Joseph was beautiful in face and handsome in appearance.” Thus David says concerning Christ: “You are beautiful beyond the sons of men; grace has been poured upon your lips” (Psalm 44).

After many days, his master’s wife cast her eyes upon Joseph and said, “Lie with me.” But he by no means consented to the wicked deed and said to her:

> “Behold, my master, having entrusted everything to me, does not know what he has in his house. There is nothing that is not in my power or that he has not handed over to me, except you, who are his wife. How, then, can I do this and sin against my master?”

With such words, day after day, the woman harassed the young man, while he refused adultery.

Whoever is lifted up by the successes of this world, and feels himself tempted by the goadings of lust while the joy of his heart acts as a procurer, should recall Joseph’s deed and preserve himself in the stronghold of chastity. When he saw his mistress persuading him to sacrifice his purity, he said to her:

> “Behold, my master, having entrusted everything to me, does not know what he has in his house. There is nothing that is not in my power or that he has not handed over to me, except you, who are his wife. How, then, can I do this evil and sin against my master?”

These words show that he suddenly recalled the good things he had acquired, drove away the evil that was assaulting him, and, remembering the grace he had received, broke the force of the impending sin.

For when slippery pleasure tempts a person amid prosperity, that very prosperity must be pressed down by the goad of adversity, so that we may blush to commit wicked deeds precisely because we remember that we have received gratuitous benefits from God. We must turn the grace bestowed upon us in outward things into weapons of virtue, so that what we have received may stand before our eyes and we may subdue whatever entices us.

Since pleasure arises from prosperity, it must be struck by consideration of that same prosperity, so that our enemy may die from the very source from which it arose. We must take care not to turn a gift we have received into a vice, lest the abyss of wickedness swallow us through the favor of this life. We also kindle the anger of the heavenly Judge against ourselves without end if, contrary to his kindness, we fight against him even by means of his own generosity.

The narrative continues:

(Verses 11.) It happened one day that Joseph entered the house to carry out some task without anyone else present. She seized the edge of his garment and said, “Lie with me.” But he left his cloak in her hand, fled, and went outside.

When the adulterous woman wished to misuse Joseph, he left his cloak and fled outside. So, when the synagogue, believing the Lord to be merely a man, wished to bind him in an adulterous embrace, he left only the letter of his Law before its eyes and presented himself openly to the nations so that they might recognize the power of his divinity.

Hence Paul says: “To this day, whenever Moses is read, a veil lies over their heart” (2 Corinthians 3). The adulterous woman kept the cloak with herself and lost naked the one whom she had held wrongly.

The narrative continues:

(Verses 13 ff.) When the woman saw the cloak in her hands and that she had been despised, she called the men of her household and said to them:

> “Look, he has brought in a Hebrew man to me to mock me. When I cried out, and he heard my voice, he left the cloak that he was holding and fled outside.”

As evidence of her story, she displayed the cloak she had retained to her husband when he returned home.

This woman, as I have already said, was a figure of the synagogue, which, as it is written, often prostituted itself after foreign gods. In the same way, she wished to retain Christ in the crime of her adultery, so that he would deny that he was God and observe the commands of the Pharisees and scribes rather than those of the Law, which was like her husband.

But Christ, refusing the unlawful doctrine—that is, the adultery of the adulterous synagogue—when the garment of his body had been seized in her hand, stripped himself of the flesh and, free from death, ascended to heaven.

(Verses 19 ff.) When his master heard these things, and was excessively credulous toward his wife’s words, he became very angry. He handed Joseph over to the prison where the king’s prisoners were kept, and there he was confined. But the Lord was with Joseph and had mercy on him. He gave him favor in the sight of the prison commander, who placed all the prisoners in his charge. For the Lord was with him and directed all his works.

Potiphar’s wife prefigured the Jewish people, whom Pilate had undertaken to govern under the Roman authorities. That people, relying on the traditions of the Law temporarily handed down to it, wished to make the Lord agree that the rest of the Sabbath should be observed and that a wife might be dismissed by her husband for any reason.

When the Lord refuted these positions with definite answers, they handed him over to Pilate the governor, declaring him in a sense a malefactor and claiming that he ought to be punished according to the Law, because he called himself the Son of God and declared himself equal to the Father.

Because of these accusations, he was handed over to the prison of death. But neither the prison terrified him nor the underworld held him. Even when he had descended there as one who was apparently to be punished, he freed others from it.

The narrative continues:

(Chapter 40—Verses 1 ff.) After these things had happened, it came about that two eunuchs offended their master, the king of Egypt: the king’s cupbearer and the baker. Pharaoh was angry with them. One was in charge of the cupbearers, the other of the bakers. He sent them to the prison of the commander of the army, where Joseph was.

The keeper of the prison handed them over to Joseph, who also served them. Thus Joseph found two eunuchs from the king’s household bound in prison. They bore the figure of the two peoples, believers and unbelievers, who, shut up under Adam’s sin and liable because of transgression, were being held captive.

Whether because of original sin or because of their own offenses—for all are debtors to God, and no one is exempt who does not need his grace, according to the Apostle’s statement, “All have sinned and lack the grace of God”—all the saints also were liable by condition to the debt of death. The Apostle proclaims this when he says: “Death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who had not sinned in the likeness of Adam’s transgression” (Romans 5).

Both peoples are therefore called, or understood to be, eunuchs because they had received a chaste rule of discipline. “The words of the Lord are pure words” (Psalm 11).

The narrative continues:

(Verses 4 ff.) Some time had passed, and they were being held in custody. In one night they each saw a dream with an interpretation appropriate to themselves.

When Joseph entered to them in the morning and saw that they were sad, he asked them, saying, “Why is your face sadder today than usual?” They answered, “We have seen a dream, and there is no one to interpret it for us.” Joseph said to them, “Tell me what you have seen.”

The chief cupbearer replied:

> “I saw before me a vine, on which were three branches. It gradually grew into buds, and after the blossoms, the grapes ripened. Pharaoh’s cup was in my hand. I took the grapes, pressed them into the cup that I held, and gave the drink to Pharaoh.”

The three branches signify either the three days of the Lord’s Passion and Resurrection, during which the souls of the saints are said to have been brought out of the underworld by the Lord; or certainly three periods are to be understood: before the Law, under the Law, and under evangelical grace.

In the first period the buds were enclosed, because Scripture does not report who else pleased God besides Abel, Seth, Enosh, Enoch, Noah, and Melchizedek, who are mentioned in it.

In the second period, that is, under the Law, the blossoms of the saints burst forth, because those who pleased God under the Law are displayed in the sacred books.

In the third period, under evangelical preaching, the grapes in a certain sense reached maturity. This happened when the faith of those believing in Christ grew so strong that they did not shrink from having their blood poured out by persecutors for confession of the divine name. Or, for love of Christ, they crucify the members of their body with harsh chastisement, together with their vices and desires, castrating themselves, so to speak, from the pleasures of the world and carnal longings.

Always remembering the cup of the Lord’s Passion, and proclaiming his words in the world, they offer the drink to Pharaoh.

The narrative continues:

(Verses 12–13.) “This is the interpretation of the dream: The three branches are three more days, after which Pharaoh will remember your service and restore you to your former position. You will give him the cup according to your office, as you used to do before.”

After the threefold light, when the Lord rose from the underworld and revealed the obscure things of the Law, as Joseph interpreted the dreams, the people of believers were released from sins, freed from the prison of hell and from the power of demons, and restored to the service of divine Law.

Just as the cupbearer, who was brought out of prison and restored to his office, signified the gentile people, so the chief of the bakers undoubtedly signifies the Jewish nation.

The three baskets upon his head, and the fact that in the uppermost basket he carried all the foods made by the baker’s art while birds ate from it, signify nothing other than the threefold utterances of the divine Law granted to that people: the Law, the Prophets, and the Hagiographa. He carried them all upon his head because the fullness of spiritual knowledge had risen above their understanding.

The loaves baked by the baker’s art signify nothing other than that the Law of the Old Testament was not invented by human cleverness, as the impious Marcionites and Manichaean heretics assert, but was entrusted by the authority of the Holy Spirit to the ancient patriarchs and holy prophets.

For we read in many places in divine Scripture that the Holy Spirit is signified by fire. The one basket that was higher than the others is clearly to be understood as the Mosaic Law, because of the density of its mysteries and its shadowy meanings. From it the birds of heaven receive food, while holy souls, signified by the birds of heaven, are spiritually nourished as they meditate day and night on the Law of the Lord. They can say with the Apostle: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3).

There is no doubt that Pharaoh, who brought Joseph out of prison, gave him power over the whole land of Egypt, restored his cupbearer to his former office, and hanged his baker on the third day, bore the figure of God the Father. He raised Jesus Christ our Lord from the underworld and freed the faithful people of the New Testament from the bonds of the first transgression and from all other chains.

But the unbeliever, with his head cut off—that is, with Christ, who is the head of the Law and the Prophets—and on the third day, that is, in the third period, he hanged him. For on the cross of our Savior, where the faithful were released from the bonds of sins, those impious Jews and the other nations, whose figure was borne by Pharaoh’s baker, were condemned because they despised the Lord when he was placed in the humility of the flesh.

The fact that the birds of heaven tore his flesh was a foreshadowing of what happened forty-two years after the Lord’s Resurrection and Ascension into heaven. Peoples came from every part of the world with the Roman commanders Titus and Vespasian. They afflicted the Jews not only with devastation and famine but also inflicted many forms of mockery upon them.

They were worthy to suffer such things, since they had done such things to God’s prophets and to the Lord himself. Those among them who escaped famine and the sword they scattered throughout the whole world, leaving them by perpetual right as servants to themselves and their descendants, until the fullness of the nations enters and afterward they too are saved—not by their own merit but by God’s grace.

At the first coming of our Savior, they did not know God’s righteousness and sought to establish their own; therefore they did not submit to God’s righteousness. The statement spoken by the blessed patriarch Jacob in the person of Esau his son will be fulfilled:

> “You shall live by the sword, and you shall serve your brother; but the time will come when you shall loosen and shake off the yoke from your neck” (Genesis 27).

The narrative continues:

(Chapter 41—Verses 1 ff.) After two years Pharaoh saw a dream. He thought that he was standing beside the river, from which seven cows, beautiful and exceedingly fat, came up and fed in the marshes. Then seven other cows emerged from the river, ugly and utterly wasted by emaciation, and fed on the very bank of the river, in green places. They devoured the first cows, whose appearance and bodily form had been remarkable.

Pharaoh thought that he was standing above the river, just as Abraham’s servant said: “Behold, I am standing beside the spring of water.” If this expression is understood in this way, it agrees with what is written in the Psalm: “He founded it above the waters of the earth” (Psalm 23).

According to this expression, it is rightly understood that the earth is higher than the water; for it is raised above the waters, where earthly animals dwell.

The narrative continues:

(Verses 4 ff.) Pharaoh awoke and slept again, and saw another dream: Seven ears of grain were sprouting on one stalk, full and beautiful. Then seven other ears, thin and scorched by blight, were growing up and devouring all the beauty of the first ears.

When he awoke after his rest and morning came, he was terrified with fear. He sent for the diviners of Egypt and all the wise men. When they had been summoned, he told them the dream, but there was no one who could interpret it.

Then, at last, the chief of the cupbearers remembered and said:

> “The king was angry with his servants and ordered me and the chief baker to be confined in the prison of the commander of the army, where, in one night, both of us saw dreams foretelling the future. A Hebrew boy was there, a servant of the same commander of the army. When we told him our dreams, we heard from him what later proved true by the outcome. I was restored to my office, and he was hanged on a cross.”

Pharaoh’s dream prefigured the figures of the Law and the Prophets, in which, by the revelation of the Holy Spirit, they spoke about the conversion of all nations and the persecutions of Antichrist.

The former was shown in the seven full ears of grain or in the seven fat cows, because there are seven gifts of spiritual charisms, through which the abundance of faith overflows in the generous grace of the New Testament.

The week of fertility is to be understood as the period during which, among all nations, faith in the confession of Christ’s name and knowledge of the Trinity were received. Concerning this the prophet says: “The earth has been filled with the knowledge of the Lord, as the waters cover the sea” (Isaiah 11).

The word of divine preaching advanced so greatly throughout all the regions of the world and among all nations, and the grace of the faith they had received strove toward perfection through holy conduct, that they became suitable not only for the heavenly granary but also, by their example, urged others to imitate them.

By contrast, the seven years of famine signified the famine of truth and justice in the last times, which will consume the multitude of believers during the time of Antichrist.

The narrative continues:

(Verses 29 ff.) “Behold, seven years of great fertility will come throughout the whole land of Egypt, followed by seven other years of such great sterility that all the former abundance will be forgotten. For famine will consume the whole land, and the magnitude of scarcity will destroy the magnitude of fertility.”

The meaning is this: During the famine signified by the evil cows and ears of grain, people will forget the abundance that the good cows signified as future.

The seven years may also signify the present and future ages. Those who labor faithfully and piously in this present world will obtain in the future what leads to the blessedness of eternal life. But those who are faithless, think nothing of the future, and grow sluggish in the leisure of the present world will find the end of their sterility in the future.

The narrative continues:

(Verses 33 ff.) “Now, therefore, let the king provide a wise and industrious man and place him over the land of Egypt. Let him appoint overseers throughout the various regions and collect a fifth part of the produce during the seven years of fertility that are now about to come. Let him gather it into storehouses, and let all the grain be stored under Pharaoh’s authority and kept in the cities. Let provision be made for the future seven-year famine that will oppress Egypt, so that the land may not be consumed by scarcity.”

The advice pleased Pharaoh and all his ministers. He said to them, “Can we find such a man, one who is filled with the spirit of God?”

Behold, unless I am mistaken, this is the third time that this book indicates to us that the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of God. First, where it is said, “The Spirit of God was moving over the waters” (Genesis 1); second, where God said, “My spirit shall not remain in these people, because they are flesh” (Genesis 6); and third, here, when Pharaoh says that the Spirit of God is in Joseph.

We have not yet read the words “Holy Spirit.”

(Verses 39–40.) Pharaoh said to Joseph: “Since God has shown you all that you have spoken, can I find anyone wiser and like you? You shall be over my house, and at the command of your mouth all the people shall obey you. Only by the throne of the kingdom will I precede you.”

The same thing is said by the Father to the Lord in the [Col. 1023A] second Psalm: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession the ends of the earth.” The Lord himself also says to the disciples in the Gospel: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. 28). Authority was given, of course, to the man who was assumed, not to the Word of God, the Son coeternal with the Father and the Spirit, through whom all things were created. The Father precedes the Son by one thing only: namely, by the title of the paternal name, so that in confession or praise the name “Father” is always placed first. For in dignity and power, nature and virtue, eternity and origin, they are one—of one Godhead and substance; they are distinguished only by their names.

It follows:

(Verses 41ff.) Pharaoh said again to Joseph: “Behold, I have appointed you over the whole land [Col. 1023B] of Egypt.” And he took the ring from his hand and gave it into Joseph’s hand; he clothed him in a linen robe and placed a golden chain around his neck. He made him mount his second chariot, with the herald proclaiming that all should bend the knee before him, and that he had been appointed ruler throughout the land of Egypt.

Joseph, who assumed the role of Christ, deserved to mount the chariot; the herald proclaimed before him, and Pharaoh appointed him over the whole land of Egypt. So also, after our Lord had been sold by Judas, as Joseph was sold by his brothers, and had risen from the prison of the underworld, he mounted the chariot of the heavenly kingdom, of which it is said: “The chariot of God is ten thousandfold” (Ps. 67); and he received authority to preach and to judge, as the apostle Paul says: “He gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. 2).

He also received the ring, that is, the priesthood of faith, by which the souls of believers are marked for the Savior, and by which the figure of the eternal King is expressed upon our foreheads and hearts through the sign of the cross. He is clothed in the linen robe, that is, in holy flesh brighter than linen, and in the robe of immortality. He also received the golden chain, that is, good understanding.

The herald goes before him—that is, John the Baptist, who, preceding his way [Col. 1023C], proclaimed, saying: “Prepare the way of the Lord” (Matt. 3; Mark 1). For we have learned of Christ’s labors throughout the world of the nations, signified by Egypt, through the various sufferings of the martyrs; and now we see Christ’s honor in that same world, subjugating all things through the distribution of grain, that is, through the preaching of the divine word.

It follows:

(Verses 44–45.) The king said to Joseph: “I am Pharaoh; without your authority no one shall move hand or foot throughout the whole land of Egypt.” And he changed his name and called him in the Egyptian language “Savior of the world.”

What could be clearer concerning Christ, when under the figure of Joseph the Savior is revealed—not merely of the one land of Egypt, but of the whole world?

It follows:

(Verse 45.) And he gave him as wife Asenath, daughter of Potiphera, priest of Heliopolis. It is usually asked whose daughter Joseph took as his wife: whether the daughter of the man whose slave he had been [Col. 1023D], or of another. Let each believe what he wishes. The question of who he was is not decisive: whether he was one man or two, whichever view someone holds is not dangerous to the faith, nor contrary to the truth of the Scriptures of God.

For just as Joseph received a wife from among the nations, so also Christ received the Church. From her he begot two sons, that is, two peoples gathered from Jews and nations.

Joseph was thirty years old when he stood before Pharaoh the king. Christ likewise is read to have been that age when, under Pharaoh’s type, he appeared revealed before the world.

Then came the abundance of the seven years, and the gathered crops were collected into the granaries of Egypt. All the abundance of produce was stored in the individual cities, and there was so much grain that it equaled the sand of the sea and exceeded all measure. It is said that no number was assigned to it because that abundance exceeded the familiar names of number, and no designation for it could be found. For it can [Col. 1024A] happen that an immense and infinite multitude has no number, as Joseph gathered the whole abundance of produce during the seven years.

This means that he stored the grain of the saints’ faith in granaries through the seven gifts, as through seven years. When the seven years of scarcity begin—that is, when iniquity arises in the form of the seven capital crimes under Antichrist, and there is a famine of faith in the Savior—then the saints and the faithful together will possess an abundant harvest of righteousness, so that their faith, weakened in the works of discourse or preaching, may not fail.

It follows:

(Chapter 42.—Verses 1ff.) When Jacob heard that food was being sold in Egypt, he said to his sons: “Why are you negligent? I have heard that grain is being sold in Egypt. Go down and buy what we need, so that we may live and not perish from scarcity.”

So Joseph’s ten brothers went down to buy grain. They entered the land of Egypt, and Joseph was governor of the land of Egypt; at his command grain was sold to the people. When his brothers had bowed before him and he recognized them, he spoke harshly to them as though they were strangers, [Col. 1024B] asking them: “Where have you come from?” They answered: “From the land of Canaan, to buy grain.” Yet although he recognized his brothers, he was not recognized by them.

After the years of abundance, famine prevailed throughout the whole world, rightly so, because there was no one who did good. After this Joseph saves Egypt from the shortage of grain, and Christ frees the world from hunger for the word of God. For Christ opened his granaries throughout the whole world, and through the distribution of his grain subjected all things to himself. If Joseph’s brothers had not sold him into Egypt, Egypt would have perished; and if the Jews had not crucified Christ, the world would have perished.

Joseph is interpreted as “Increase” or “Enlargement.” But in that Joseph only Egypt received enlargement; in our Joseph the whole world was worthy to receive increase. He distributed wheat; our Joseph distributed the word of God.

Jacob says to his sons: “There is grain in Egypt.” God the Father also says: “Out of Egypt I called my Son” [Col. 1024C] (Matt. 2).
