The ten older brothers therefore descend, that is, the Jews, as though constituted under the Decalogue of the law and its number. He himself recognizes them, but is not recognized by them. The Hebrews are recognized by Christ, but they themselves do not recognize him.

It follows:

(Verses 9ff.) Remembering the dreams that he had once seen, he said: “You have come to inspect the weaker places of the land.” They said: “It is not so, my lord; your servants have come to buy food. We are all sons of one man, and your servants are plotting no evil.”

He said to them: “It is otherwise; you have come to inspect the undefended places of this land.” They replied: “We, your servants, are twelve brothers, sons of one man in the land of Canaan. The youngest is with our father, and another no longer exists.”

He said: “This is what I said: you are spies. Now you shall be tested. By the life of Pharaoh, you shall not leave this place until your youngest brother comes. Send one of you to bring him. You, however, shall remain in bonds until what you have said is tested, whether it is false [Col. 1024D] or true. Otherwise, by the life of Pharaoh, you are spies.”

What are we to make of the fact that Joseph, a man so wise, praised not only by the people among whom he lived but also by Scripture itself, swears by the life of Pharaoh that his brothers will not leave Egypt unless their younger brother comes? Was Pharaoh’s life of such little value even to a good and faithful man who first preserved loyalty in all things toward his master—and all the more toward Pharaoh himself, who had placed him in such honor—if he preserved it toward the man who possessed him as a purchased slave? And if he did not care about Pharaoh’s life, ought he not to have avoided perjury even for the life of any human being? Or is this not perjury?

He detained one of them until Benjamin came, and what he had said proved true: “You shall not leave this place unless your youngest brother comes.” The statement could indeed apply to all of them. They could not properly be said to return to their father while their brother was being held captive in Egypt, since they too were bound to him in mind and spirit, [Col. 1025A] as though by certain bonds of affection. For how would he come unless some of them returned to bring him?

But what follows presses the question more forcefully, when he swore again, saying: “Send one of you and bring your brother; but you shall remain in bonds until what you have said is tested, whether it is true or false. Otherwise, by the life of Pharaoh, you are spies.”

He inserted an oath into this statement because, if they had not spoken the truth, they would be spies—that is, they would deserve the punishment of spies. Yet he knew that they were speaking the truth, as though he had said: “You are spies; you will deserve the punishment of spies.”

It follows:

(Verses 17ff.) He handed them over to custody for three days. On the third day, after bringing them out of prison, he said: “Do what I have said, and you shall live, for I fear God. If you are peaceful men, let one of your brothers remain bound in custody. You go, carry the grain you have bought to your households, and bring your youngest brother to me, so that I may test your words and you may not die.”

[Col. 1025B] They did as he had said and spoke to one another: “We deserve this, because we sinned against our brother. We saw the distress of his soul when he entreated us, but we did not listen to him. That is why this tribulation has come upon us.”

One of them, Reuben, said: “Did I not tell you, ‘Do not sin against the boy’? But you did not listen to me. Behold, his blood is being demanded.”

They did not know that Joseph understood, because he spoke to them through an interpreter.

Why, when the sons of Israel were repenting among themselves and speaking about their brother Joseph—confessing that they had treated him wickedly and that this was being repaid to them by divine judgment—does Scripture add: “They themselves did not know that Joseph understood, for there was an interpreter between them”?

This is to be understood as meaning that they thought he did not understand what they were saying. They thought an interpreter had been employed for no other reason than that Joseph did not know their language. Nor was it the interpreter’s concern to tell Joseph what they were saying to one another rather than addressing him.

It follows:

[Col. 1025C] (Verse 24.) He turned away from them for a little while and wept; then he returned and spoke to them. Scripture does not add what he said to them. Hence it is understood that he said the same things he had said before.

It follows:

(Verses 25ff.) Taking Simeon and binding him in their presence, he ordered his servants to fill their sacks with grain and to return each man’s money to his sack, while also giving them provisions for the journey. They did so.

They carried the grain on their donkeys and departed. When one of them opened his sack at the lodging place to give fodder to his animal, he saw the money at the mouth of the sack and said to his brothers: “My money has been returned; behold, it is here in the sack.” They were astonished and troubled and said to one another: “What is this that God has done to us?”

If we examine the matter more carefully, we shall find that almost no one is said to have descended to a holy place without being remembered as having ascended to a blameworthy one. These observations show that divine Scripture was not composed, as many suppose, in an uneducated and rustic style, but was shaped according to the discipline of divine learning [Col. 1025D]. Nor does it serve merely historical narratives as much as it serves mystical events and meanings.

Thus, when Simeon had been detained in Egypt and his brothers had been sent away to return to their father, it is not written that they ascended from Egypt. Rather, it says: “They placed the grain upon their donkeys and departed.”

But when, after receiving their brother and recognizing Joseph, and after Benjamin had also been presented before him, they returned with joy, then it says: “They ascended from Egypt and came into the land of Canaan to Jacob their father” (Gen. 45).

It follows:

(Verses 29ff.) They told him everything that had happened to them, saying: “The lord of the land spoke harshly to us and thought us spies of the province. We answered him: ‘We are peaceful men and are plotting no ambush. We are twelve brothers, born of one father; one no longer exists, and the youngest is with our father in the land of Canaan.’

“He said to us: ‘This is how I shall test whether you are peaceful men: leave one of your brothers with me, take the provisions necessary for your households, and depart. Bring your [Col. 1026A] youngest brother to me, so that I may know that you are not spies, and so that I may return to you the one who is being held in bonds. After that you shall have permission to buy whatever you wish.’”

When they poured out the grain, each one found the money tied up at the mouth of his sack. They had indeed given him money, but Joseph—that is, Christ the Lord—gave grain and bestowed silver, because Christ is not bought with silver but with grace.

It follows:

(Verse 36.) Jacob said to his sons: “You have deprived me of my children. Joseph is no more; Simeon is held in bonds; you will take Benjamin away, and you will bring my gray hairs down with sorrow to the underworld.”

Is it to the underworld because of sorrow? Or would he descend there by dying even if sorrow were absent? There is a major question concerning the underworld, and we must observe what Scripture means by it wherever it may have mentioned it.

It follows:

(Chapter 43.—Verses 8ff.) Judah also said [Col. 1026B] to his father: “Send the boy, so that we may depart and live—we and our little ones.”

They went down to Egypt and stood before Joseph. When he saw them, and Benjamin with them, he ordered his steward: “Bring the men into the house, slaughter victims, and prepare a feast, for they shall dine with me at noon.”

They approached the steward and said: “We ask you, sir, to listen. We came down here previously to buy food. After buying it, when we reached the lodging place, we opened our sacks and found money at the mouths of the sacks. We have now brought it back in the same weight.”

He answered them: “Your God and the God of your father has given you treasures in your sacks. I have the money you gave me, which has been tested.”

What they hear from the master of the house—“Your God and the God of your fathers gave you money in your sacks, but I have your silver, which has been tested”—appears to be a lie. Yet we must believe that it signifies something. The silver that is given and does not diminish, and that is called “tested,” evidently refers [Col. 1026C] to what we read elsewhere: “The sayings of the Lord are pure sayings, silver tested by fire, proven on the earth, purified sevenfold” (Ps. 12)—that is, perfected.

It follows:

(Verses 24ff.) He brought Simeon out to them. After bringing them into the house, he gave them water, and they washed their feet; he also gave fodder to their animals. They prepared their gifts until Joseph came at noon, for they had heard that they were to eat bread there.

Joseph entered his house, and they offered him gifts and bowed prostrate to the ground. He greeted them graciously and asked: “Is your aged father well, of whom you spoke to me? Is he still alive?” They bowed and worshiped him.

They had cunningly dared to sell their brother so that God’s plan might be altered. But by divine judgment, they served the very thing they had tried to avoid; they were compelled to carry out God’s will from the point at which they had cunningly attempted to oppose it.

Thus the divine plan is fulfilled while it is being avoided; thus human wisdom is caught while it resists. The brothers [Col. 1026D] feared that Joseph would rise above them, but what had been divinely arranged was accomplished through their very attempt to prevent it. Human wisdom was therefore caught in itself: the point from which it intentionally resisted God’s will became the means by which it served its fulfillment.

Often, when some people are puffed up with human wisdom and see that divine judgments oppose their desires, they try to resist them by cunning devices. To bend the force of the heavenly disposition to their wishes, they apply themselves to crafty thoughts and seek subtler plans. But they carry out God’s will precisely where they strive to change it; while attempting to resist the plan of the Almighty, they obey it. For it often serves his disposition appropriately that which human effort foolishly throws back against it, as it is written: “He catches the wise in their craftiness” (Job 5).

He catches the wise in their own craftiness when human actions suitably serve his plans even while they resist them. Hence [Col. 1027A] the Psalmist says: “The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings, that they are futile” (Ps. 94).

Let us therefore consider the order of what happened; let us consider how divinity catches human thoughts within the very act of its providence. Joseph had been sold by them so that he would not be worshiped; but he was worshiped because he had been sold.

It remains, therefore, that in everything we do we should seek the force of the heavenly will. Once we know it, our action ought to serve it and follow it as the guide of its journey, lest it serve that will unwillingly if it proudly avoids it. For the force of the heavenly plan cannot be escaped. But the person who restrains himself beneath its commands tempers it for himself with great strength, and lightens its burdens for himself by willingly carrying them upon the obedient shoulder of his heart.

It follows:

(Verses 29ff.) Joseph lifted his eyes and saw Benjamin, his maternal brother, and said: “Is this your youngest brother, of whom you spoke to me?” Then he said: “May God have mercy on you, my son.”

He hurried away because his compassion had been stirred for his brother [Col. 1027B]; his tears were bursting forth. He entered his chamber and wept. Then, after washing his face, he came out again and controlled himself.

Joseph saw Benjamin, his little brother. Mystically, the Lord Jesus also saw Paul when light shone around him. Paul is called “the least” because he had not yet reached maturity in the flesh of faith. Thus he is read to have been a young man when he guarded the garments of those stoning Stephen.

Joseph wept over Benjamin; Paul’s blindness is Christ’s weeping. Joseph washed his face so that the lost light might be restored to him. Christ washed his face when Paul was baptized, through whom our Lord Jesus Christ was to be seen by many.

It follows:

(Verses 31ff.) He said: “Set out the bread.” When it had been served, Joseph sat separately, his brothers separately, and the Egyptians who were eating likewise separately—for it is unlawful for Egyptians to eat with them, and they regard such a meal as profane.

They sat before him: the firstborn according to their birthright, and the youngest according to his birthright [Col. 1027C]. They were greatly astonished when they received portions from him. Benjamin’s portion was greater, exceeding the others by fivefold. They drank and became filled with him.

Drunkards often use this passage as a defense—not on account of the sons of Israel, but on account of Joseph, who was commended as exceedingly wise. But anyone who pays close attention will find that this word is also commonly used in Scripture for satiety.

Thus we read: “You visited the earth and made it drunk; you multiplied and enriched it” (Ps. 65). Since the expression occurs in the praise of blessing and refers to God’s gift, it is evident that this “drunkenness” signifies fullness. For to become drunk as drunkards do is useful neither to the earth nor to anyone else.

It follows:

(Chapter 44.—Verses 1–2.) Joseph commanded the steward of his house: “Fill their sacks with grain, as much as they can hold, and place each man’s money at the top of his sack. Put my silver cup, together with the price paid for the grain, at the mouth of the youngest one’s sack.” And it was done.

The question arises why Joseph did this—why he repeatedly [Col. 1027D] deceived his brothers and kept them in suspense until he revealed who he was. Although the story is all the sweeter to read because it is so unexpected for those involved, nevertheless, given the gravity of his wisdom, he would not have done this, nor would Scripture have preserved it—with its great authority of holiness and its profound purpose of prophesying future things, which we have now undertaken to expound—unless something important were signified by this apparent game.

It follows:

(Verses 9ff.) “With whichever of your servants the object you seek is found, let him die, and we shall be slaves to my lord.”

He said: “Let it be according to your word. The one with whom it is found shall be my slave, but you shall be innocent.”

So they quickly lowered their sacks to the ground and opened each one. He searched them, beginning with the eldest and ending with the youngest, and found the cup in Benjamin’s sack.

But what does it mean that Joseph’s cup was found in Benjamin’s sack, except [Col. 1028A] that in Paul’s body the eloquence of heavenly doctrine was already shining while he was learned in the Law? But because he was not yet subject to divine grace, the cup was inside the sack: doctrine was within the Law, a lamp beneath a bushel.

Yet Ananias was sent, placed his hand upon him, and loosed the purse. When the purse was loosed, the silver shone forth; and when the scales fell away, like certain cords of the sack, the sack was opened—that is, the veil of the Law was set aside. He attained the freedom of grace, and with unveiled face he preached the words of the Gospel.

It follows:

(Verses 13ff.) They tore their garments, loaded their donkeys again, and returned to the town. Judah entered first with his brothers to Joseph, who had not yet left the place, and they all fell together before him upon the ground.

He said to them: “Why did you wish to act in this way? Do you not know that there is no one like me in the knowledge of divination?”

Judah said: “What shall we answer my lord? What shall we say? Or how can we justly defend ourselves? God has found the iniquity of your servants. Behold, we are all my lord’s slaves—we and the one with whom [Col. 1028B] the cup was found.”

An oracle lay in his heart. They had come as strangers, fleeing the danger of famine and seeking grain; they had not taken it, and now they saw themselves exposed to the accusation of a crime.

In the midst of all this they were led to prison. After three days they were brought out, yet they were still terrified by the same severity. Their hearts now returned to them; the memory of their guilt struck their minds, and they said to one another: “We deserve this, because we sinned against our brother, seeing the anguish of his soul when he entreated us, and we did not listen to him.”

At these words Joseph’s heart withdrew; by weeping he discharged what he owed to affection, then returned to his brothers with severity, so that the anguish of their minds might free them from guilt.

After this one brother is bound, while the others are sent away with grain, so that the one whom they had said was their youngest brother might come. When the brother later came, affection overcame his mind, since the brother appeared innocent; yet severity remained in outward appearance, so that the guilty brothers might be purified.

Grain is given; the cup is hidden in the sack [Col. 1028C] of the younger brother; a severe inquiry is raised against them; they are sent for and brought back; it is decreed that the one with whom the cup was found shall be enslaved; it is found in the sack of the youngest brother; Benjamin is brought back, and all the afflicted brothers follow.

O torments of mercy! He tortures, and he loves.

They returned, therefore, prostrated themselves on the ground with tears, and asked pardon. Remembering what they had promised their father concerning him, they wasted away in intolerable grief. Then, no longer able to restrain himself, the affection that had been enclosed burst forth into their midst and drew tears of love from a face of serenity.

The severity that appeared arose from terror, but it was not truly there, because mercy was present even though it did not appear. Thus the holy man both forgave and punished his brothers’ crime; thus he restrained clemency upon his lips, so that toward his offending brothers he would be neither merciful without vengeance nor strict without compassion.

It follows:

(Verse 17.) Joseph answered: “Far be it from me to do this. The one who stole the cup shall be my slave; but you go free to your father.”

Surely we should [Col. 1028D] consider with compassion the great misery of his brothers amid this turmoil: Joseph held them as long as he wished and prolonged the delay as much as he wished. Yet he was not making them suffer unjustly, since he was contemplating the outcome of their future joy. Everything he did to delay their happiness he did in order that the same delay might increase it—as though all their sufferings throughout the time in which they were troubled were not worthy to be compared with the future glory of exultation that would be revealed in them when they recognized the brother whom they thought they had lost.

It follows:

(Verses 18ff.) Judah drew nearer and said confidently: “I beg you, my lord, let your servant speak a word in your ears, and do not be angry with your servant. You previously questioned your servants: ‘Do you have a father or a brother?’ We answered you: ‘We have an aged father and a young boy, born in his old age. His [Col. 1029A] maternal brother is dead, and he alone remains to his mother; his father loves him tenderly.’

“You said to your servants: ‘Bring him to me, and I will set my eyes upon him.’ We told my lord: ‘The boy cannot leave his father. For if he leaves him, his father will die.’

“Then you said to your servants: ‘Unless your youngest brother comes with you, you shall not see my face again.’”

Many things are reported differently in Judah’s account from the way Joseph had dealt with them, although he was speaking in Joseph’s presence. It is not clear whether the omission of the pretense that they were spies was deliberate, or whether it resulted from forgetfulness caused by their distress.

It is also remarkable that they said Joseph himself had questioned them about their father and brother, and that they had given him the information when he asked. The narrative could scarcely be brought into agreement with the facts so as to prove entirely truthful. Yet even if some things in it are false, Judah could have been mistaken through forgetfulness rather than daring to lie—especially before one to whom they were speaking not as though he were ignorant, but even of things which they knew that he knew, inserting them into their account in order to move his mercy.

It follows:

(Verse 33.) “Therefore your servant shall remain in place of the boy as my lord’s servant, and let the boy go up with his brothers.”

(Chapter 45.—Verses 1ff.) Joseph could no longer restrain himself. He raised his voice with weeping, which the Egyptians heard, and said to his brothers: “I am Joseph. Is my father still alive?”

His brothers could not answer him, for they were terrified by great fear. He said to them kindly: “Come closer to me.” When they had drawn near, he said: “I am Joseph, your brother, whom you sold. For God sent me before you into Egypt for your preservation, so that you might be preserved upon the earth and have food to live.”

What does Joseph mean when he says, “God sent me before you into Egypt for your preservation, so that you might have food to live,” unless he signifies another and hidden mystery—what the Apostle says: “A remnant has been saved according to the election of grace” (Rom. 11)? For [Col. 1029C] the prophet had foretold: “If the number of the children of Israel should be like the sand of the sea, a remnant will be saved” (Hos. 1).

For this reason Christ was killed by the Jews and handed over to the nations, as Joseph was handed over to the Egyptians by his brothers, so that the remnant of Israel might also be saved. Hence the Apostle says: “For I too am an Israelite,” and “so that the fullness of the nations might enter, and thus all Israel might be saved” (Rom. 11).

That is, Israel consists of the remnant of Israel according to the flesh and the fullness of the nations who, according to the spirit, are Israel through faith in Christ. Or, if the fullness of faith still remains for that Israelite people from which the remnant came—and among that remnant the Apostles were then saved—this signifies the fullness of Israel’s deliverance by which they were freed from Egypt through Moses.

It follows:

(Verses 21ff.) Joseph gave his brothers wagons according to Pharaoh’s command, together with provisions for the journey. He ordered two garments to be brought for each of them. To Benjamin he gave three hundred silver pieces and five finest garments. He sent his father the same amount of money and clothing, adding ten donkeys to carry all [Col. 1029D] the riches of Egypt, and as many she-donkeys carrying grain and bread for the journey.

Anyone who preaches the Trinity or the cross of Christ has received thirty pieces of silver from Christ. Therefore Paul says: “I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Cor. 2).

He received five garments—that is, wisdom and the manifold discipline in the Law of all the senses. Paul’s portion therefore excels and overflows in merit. Yet the brothers, that is, the other preachers, also receive by their own grace two garments: namely, that they confess Christ to be both God and man, according to what is read in Proverbs: “All her household are clothed with double garments” (Prov. 31)—that is, with mystical and moral understanding.

Gifts are also sent to the father. The Son honors his Father, and Christ invites his people to promised gifts. Those gifts are carried by those Gentile donkeys, once useless and laborious; now useful, as a type of Christ, they carry [Col. 1030A] gifts and bear in the Gospel the giver of gifts.

It follows:

(Verse 25.) They went up and came into the land of Canaan to their father Jacob. They announced to him: “Joseph is alive, and he rules over the whole land of Egypt.”

If Joseph had been overcome by lust and had sinned with his master’s wife, I do not think the patriarchs would have announced to his father Jacob that he was alive. For if he had done this, he would certainly not have been alive: “The soul that sins shall die.”

This passage also seems to indicate something similar in Jacob. As long as he was far from Joseph and had not been told of his life, his spirit seemed to have failed within him, and the light that was in him, deprived of nourishment, had already been darkened. But when those who announced his life came to him—that is, those who said that “the life was the light of human beings” (John 1)—he rekindled his spirit within himself. The radiance of true light was restored in him, and the one who seemed dead was brought to life by faith in the resurrection.

For [Col. 1030B] us also, to trample down lust, flee luxury, and suppress and restrain all bodily pleasures is to exercise dominion over the whole of Egypt. This is what is considered great and held in admiration among Israel.

But if someone subdues some bodily vices while yielding and becoming subject to others, it cannot be said of him in full that he rules the whole land of Egypt. He will appear to rule perhaps one, two, or three cities.

It follows:

(Verse 26.) When he heard this, he seemed to awaken from a deep sleep, yet he did not believe them. They, in turn, reported the sequence of events.

Thus the unbelieving people—that is, Jacob—are summoned by their sons, Peter, Paul, and John, while the Jewish people are invited to grace.

It follows:

(Verses 27–28.) When he saw everything that Joseph had sent, his spirit revived, and he said: “It is enough for me if my son Joseph is still alive. I will go and see him before I die.”

This too should not be passed over carelessly: Scripture says that not his soul but his spirit, as the [Col. 1030C] better part of him, was revived.

The splendor of the light within him had not been utterly extinguished when his sons presented Joseph’s tunic stained with the blood of a kid and deceived him by their lie, so that he tore his garments, put sackcloth around his loins, and mourned his son. He refused all consolation and said: “I shall go down to my son mourning into the underworld.”

Even then, as we have said, the light within him was not entirely extinguished, but it had been darkened to a great extent. He could be deceived; he could tear his garments; he could mourn falsely; he could invoke death; he could desire to descend into the underworld in mourning.

For these reasons his spirit is now revived and comes back to life, because it was fitting that the hearing of truth should rekindle and nourish the light that the deceit of falsehood had darkened.

It follows:

### Chapter XLVI

**Verses 1ff.** Israel departed with all that he had and came to the Well of the Oath. After sacrificing victims there to the God of his father Isaac, he heard God calling him in a vision by night and saying to him, “Jacob, Jacob.” He answered, “Here I am.” God said to him:

“I am God, the mighty God of your father. Do not fear going down into Egypt, because there I shall make you into a great nation. I shall go down there with you, and I shall bring you back when you return.”

Who is it who became a great nation in Egypt and was brought back at the end? If this is understood of that Jacob of whom it is thought to have been said, it will not appear true; for he was not brought back at the end from Egypt, since he died in Egypt. It would be absurd if someone said that Jacob was brought back by God because his body was transported elsewhere. Even if this is accepted, it will not be true, because God is not the God of the dead but of the living. These words cannot be understood of a dead body, but must be demonstrated concerning the living and concerning the nations.

Let us therefore consider the Lord’s descent into this world and into a great nation—that is, into the Church formed from the nations—and his return to the Father after all things had been completed. In him, then, rather than in Jacob, what was said will be fulfilled: “For I shall bring you back from there at the end.” But each one of us also enters Egypt and its struggles in the same order and by the same path, if he is found worthy that God should always remain with him and make him into a great nation. For the great nation is the multitude of virtues and the abundance of righteousness, in which all the saints are said to multiply and grow.

That other saying is also fulfilled in him: “For I shall bring you back at the end.” For “the end” is understood as the perfection of things and the completion of virtues.

It follows:

**Verse 4.** “Joseph also shall place his hand upon your eyes.”

For the true Joseph, our Lord and Savior, just as he placed his bodily hand upon the eyes of the blind man and restored both his sight and the vision he had lost, so also placed his spiritual hands upon the eyes of the Law, which had been blinded by the bodily understanding of the scribes and Pharisees. He restored its sight, so that for those to whom the Lord opens the Scriptures, spiritual vision and understanding may appear in the Law.

Would that the Lord Jesus might also place his hands upon our eyes, so that we too might begin to see—not the things that are seen, but those that are unseen—and that he might open for us those eyes which do not look upon present things but future ones, and reveal to us the sight of the heart by which God is seen in the spirit.

It follows:

**Verses 5–6.** Jacob rose from the Well of the Oath, and his sons carried him, together with the children and their wives, in the wagons that Pharaoh had sent to transport the old man, along with everything that he had possessed in the land of Canaan. He came into Egypt with all his offspring: his sons and grandsons, his daughters and granddaughters, and all his descendants together.

It must be asked how the text can say, “his daughters with him,” when he is read to have had only one daughter. Earlier we said that “his daughters” could be understood as his granddaughters, just as all the sons of Israel are also called the entire people descended from him. But here, when it says “the daughters of his daughters,” apart from Dinah alone, the plural has been used for the singular, just as the singular is sometimes used for the plural. Unless someone should maintain that his daughters-in-law could have been called his daughters.

It follows:

**Verse 15.** “These are the sons of Leah, whom she bore in Mesopotamia of Syria, together with Dinah her daughter; all the persons of her sons and daughters were thirty-three.”

Were all these thirty-three persons born from Leah in Mesopotamia of Syria? Certainly six sons and one daughter were born there, and their grandsons are then included. If, therefore, a question had arisen concerning the one son Benjamin, when Jacob’s twelve sons had been counted and named and the text said, “These are the sons of Jacob who were born to him in Mesopotamia of Syria,” how much greater is the present question: how could thirty-three persons have been born from Leah in Mesopotamia of Syria? It can only be because that expression is confirmed as though they had all been born there.

Furthermore, it is now beyond doubt that daughters are named in the case of one daughter, with the plural used for the singular. Yet we must still see what answer should be given to those who try to confirm from this testimony that persons are propagated from parents together with bodies. No one doubts that “persons” are named for human beings, in an expression in which the whole is signified by a part. But how can we separate that very part from which the whole is recalled—namely, the soul, by whose name the whole human being is signified—from what is said, “They came forth from his loins,” as though only flesh had been born from him, although only souls are named?

It follows:

**Verses 26–27.** “All the persons who entered Egypt with Jacob and who came forth from his loins, apart from the wives of his sons, were sixty-six. The sons of Joseph who were born in the land of Egypt were two persons. All the persons of the house of Jacob who entered Egypt were seventy.”

The statement that sixty-six persons entered Egypt with Jacob, excluding Joseph’s sons, and that afterward, once they had been added, it is stated that there were seventy persons with whom Jacob entered Egypt, must be understood in this way: they were in Jacob’s household when he entered Egypt. Those whom he found there certainly did not enter with him. Yet, upon a more careful examination of the truth, it is found that two had already been born when he entered—Ephraim and Manasseh. This is said to be found not only in the Hebrew copies; the translation itself according to the Septuagint makes it clear in Exodus (Exod. 1).

Nor do the Seventy Translators seem to me to have erred when they say that seventy-five persons entered Egypt with Jacob. Because of some mystical significance, they wished, with a kind of prophetic freedom, to complete this number: if, while Jacob was still alive, descendants had been produced from his two sons Manasseh and Ephraim, they indicated that these too should be added to the same number of Jacob’s household.

But since Jacob is found to have lived seventeen years in Egypt, it cannot be discovered how Joseph’s sons could have had grandsons while he was alive. Jacob entered Egypt in the second year of the famine, whereas Joseph’s sons were born during the years of abundance. However many years of prosperity one supposes them to have been born in, from the first year of abundance until the second year of famine, when Jacob entered Egypt, there were nine years. When the seventeen years that Jacob lived there are added, twenty-six years are found. How, then, could young men less than twenty-six years old have had grandsons?

Nor is this question resolved by the Hebrew truth. For how could it have been fulfilled that Jacob should receive so many grandsons before entering Egypt, even from Benjamin, who came to his brother at that age? Scripture not only records that he had sons, but also grandsons and a great-grandson; all of them are counted among the sixty-six persons with whom Jacob is said to have entered Egypt even according to the Hebrew truth.

We must also consider what is meant by the fact that, although Joseph and his sons are counted as no more than eight, Benjamin and his sons together are found to number eleven, yet the total is reported as eighteen rather than nineteen, which would be the sum of eight and eleven. Later Joseph and his sons are said to have been not eight but nine persons, although eight are found.

All these matters, which appear impossible to resolve, undoubtedly contain a profound meaning. Yet I do not know whether everything can be reconciled literally, especially in the case of numbers which, as we rightly believe from certain things we have been able to learn from Scripture, are most sacred and filled with mysteries.

It follows:

**Verses 28–29.** Judah he sent before him to Joseph, to announce his arrival so that Joseph might meet him in Goshen. When he arrived there, Joseph harnessed his chariot and went up to meet his father at the same place. When he saw him, he fell upon his neck and wept in his embrace.

Judah, that is, Confession, met him. For confession now goes before those whom unbelief formerly possessed, and in this way they met Christ. In this way Joseph—that is, the true Christ—met them by imparting faith to them. Who else at this late age receives the Jewish people in the last times—not according to their merits, but according to the grace of their election—and places his hands upon their eyes and removes their blindness? He delayed removing their blindness for this reason: so that they might believe last, because earlier they did not think that one should believe in Christ.

Thus the Apostle says: “For blindness in part has happened to Israel until the fullness of the nations should enter, and so all Israel should be saved” (Rom. 11).

It follows:

**Verses 31ff.** Joseph spoke to his brothers and to all his father’s household:

“I shall go up and announce it to Pharaoh, and I shall say to him: ‘My brothers and my father’s household, who were in the land of Canaan, have come to me. They are shepherds of sheep and take care of feeding flocks. They have brought with them their sheep, cattle, herds, and everything they have been able to possess. When Pharaoh calls you and says, “What is your occupation?” you shall answer: “Your servants are shepherds, from our infancy until now, both we and our fathers.”’”

The patriarchs are commended because from their youth and through their fathers they were keepers of animals—and rightly so. For this is without doubt just servitude and just dominion: when animals serve human beings and human beings rule over animals. Thus it was said when the human being was created: “Let us make man according to our image and likeness, and let him have power over the fish of the sea, the birds of the air, and all the animals that are upon the earth” (Gen. 1). This intimates that reason ought to rule irrational life.

That one human being should be the servant of another was caused either by iniquity or by adversity. Iniquity, as it was said: “Cursed be Canaan; he shall be a servant to his brothers” (Gen. 9). Adversity, as happened in Joseph’s case, so that, after being sold by his brothers, he became the servant of foreigners.

Thus wars made the first servants, to whom this name was given in the Latin language. For a man who had been overcome by another man could lawfully be killed by the law of war; because he was spared, he was called a servant. Hence they are also called *mancipia*, because they were taken by hand.

There is also a natural order among human beings: women serve men, and children their parents, because in that too there is justice—that the weaker reason should serve the stronger. This, then, is the clear justice found in condemnations and servitudes: that those who excel in reason should excel in dominion.

When this order is disturbed in the present age by human iniquities or by the natural adversity of carnal conditions, the righteous endure temporal inequality, destined at the end to possess an exceedingly glorious and eternal happiness.

The patriarchs and prophets therefore reigned here, so that it might be shown that God grants and removes earthly kingdoms. The apostles and martyrs did not reign here, so that the kingdom of heaven might be revealed as something to be desired. The patriarchs waged royal wars, so that it might be evident that such victories too are granted by God’s will. The apostles and martyrs were killed without resisting, so that they might teach that it is a better victory to be killed for the faith of truth, although even there the prophets knew that one should die for the truth.

“You shall say these things so that you may dwell in the land of Goshen.”

Goshen is interpreted as “nearness” or “proximity.” This shows that even if Israel dwells in Egypt, it is not far from God but is near and joined to him, just as he himself says: “I shall go down with you into Egypt, and I shall be with you.”

Even if we seem to have descended into Egypt, even if, placed in the flesh, we endure the struggles and contests of this world, even if we dwell among those who serve Pharaoh, nevertheless, if we are near God, if we occupy ourselves with meditation on his commandments and seek out his precepts and judgments—for this is what it means to be near God, always to think about the things of God and seek the things of God—then God will always be with us.

It follows:

“For all the shepherds of sheep are detestable to the Egyptians. For every shepherd of sheep is an abomination to the Egyptians.”

It is fitting that to the Egyptians, in whom the figure of the present age is represented, an age in which iniquity abounds, every shepherd of animals should be an abomination. For a righteous man is an abomination to the unrighteous.

### Chapter XLVII

**Verses 1ff.** Joseph entered and announced to Pharaoh:

“My father and my brothers, their sheep and cattle, and everything they possess, have come to me from the land of Canaan. Behold, they are staying in the land of Goshen.”

He also placed the five last of his brothers before the king. Pharaoh questioned them: “What is your occupation?” They answered:

“We are shepherds of sheep, both we and our fathers. We have come to reside in your land, because there is no pasture for the flocks of your servants in the land of Canaan, as the famine has grown severe. We therefore ask that you allow us to live in the land of Goshen.”

It may be asked: if Joseph was gathering grain by which human beings might live, where did the animals live, while so great a famine was increasing? This is especially difficult because Joseph’s brothers said to Pharaoh, “There are no pastures for the flocks of your servants in the land of Canaan,” and identified the lack of pasture as the reason for their coming.

If the pastures had failed in the land of Canaan because of that famine, why had they not failed in Egypt when the same famine was increasing? For, as those who know those regions report, in many of the marshes of Egypt pasture could remain abundant even when there was a famine of grain, which usually grows through the inundation of the Nile. Indeed, those marshes are said to produce pasture more abundantly when the water of the Nile rises less.

It follows:

**Verses 5–6.** The king said to Joseph:

“Your father and your brothers have come to you. The land of Egypt is before you. Settle them in the best place, and give them the land of Goshen.”

After this Joseph settled his parents and brothers in the best land of Goshen.

So too the Lord, choosing a better land for his parents—that is, for the prophets and patriarchs, from whom he deigned to be born according to the flesh—or for all the saints, of whom he says in the Gospel, “These are my brothers, who do the will of my Father” (Matt. 12), will give them the promised land of the kingdom of God, concerning which the prophet says, “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.”

It follows:

**Verses 7ff.** After this he brought his father in to the king and set him before him. Jacob blessed Pharaoh, and when Pharaoh asked him, “How many are the days of the years of your life?” he answered:

“The days of the years of my pilgrimage are one hundred and thirty years. Few and evil have been the days of my life, and they have not reached the days of the years of my fathers’ pilgrimage.”

We say that it is not so much the age itself, which proceeds through days and nights, years and months, that is called evil, as the things that take place in the age. Just as it is said, “Its own evil is sufficient for the day,” so Jacob’s days are also called few and evil, because the things he endured exercised him through various trials.

Thus John says: “The world is set in the evil one” (1 John 5)—not because the world itself is evil, but because evil things are done in the world by human beings.

It follows:

**Verse 12.** “He fed his entire father’s household, providing food for each one.”

Yet Jacob neither worshiped Joseph when he saw him nor when he received grain from him. How, then, shall we think that Joseph’s dream was fulfilled, rather than that it contained a prophecy of something greater?

It follows:

**Verse 13.** In the whole world there was no bread, and famine had oppressed the land, especially Egypt and Canaan. From these regions Joseph gathered all the money and brought it into the king’s treasury.

In this matter too Scripture was concerned to commend the faithfulness of God’s servant. Joseph therefore bought the whole land of Egypt, as each person sold his possessions because of the severity of the famine, and subjected it to Pharaoh, together with all his people, from the remotest borders of Egypt to its farthest limits.

Look back to the origin of the race, and you will find that their father Ham, who had laughed at his father’s nakedness, deserved this kind of sentence: that his son Canaan should be a servant to his brothers. In him, the condition of servitude would expose the wickedness of his character. Therefore it is not undeserved that an ignoble posterity imitates the dishonor of its race.

If we understand these matters spiritually, we recognize what the servitude of the Egyptians is: to serve the Egyptians is nothing other than to be subject to carnal vices and enslaved to demons. No external necessity compels a person into this condition; rather, sluggishness of spirit and the lust and pleasure of the body subdue him, and through negligence the mind submits itself to them.

But the person who cares for the freedom of the soul and ennobles the dignity of the mind through heavenly contemplation belongs to the sons of Israel. Even if he is violently oppressed for a time, he does not lose his freedom forever.

It follows:

**Verse 22.** “Except the land of the priests, which had been given to them by the king, and for whom appointed provisions were supplied from the public storehouses; therefore they were not compelled to sell their possessions.”

Do you wish to know what difference there is between the priests of God and the priests of Pharaoh? Pharaoh grants land to his priests, but the Lord grants his priests no portion in the land. Instead he says to them: “I am your portion” (Num. 18:20).

Consider this, all you priests of the Lord who read these words, and see what the difference between priests is, lest those who possess a portion in the land and devote themselves to earthly worship and pursuits appear to be priests not of the Lord but of Pharaoh. For it is he who wishes his priests to possess earthly estates and to cultivate the soil rather than the soul, to devote themselves to farming rather than to the laws.

But let us hear what Christ our Lord commands his priests:

“Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple.”

I tremble as I say this. For I myself am, above all, my own accuser; I speak my own condemnations. Christ denies that the person whom he sees possessing anything is his disciple—he denies that the one who does not renounce everything he possesses is his disciple.

What shall we do? How can we either read these words ourselves or preach them to the people, when we not only do not renounce what we possess but wish to acquire things that we never had before we came to Christ? Can we hide what conscience reproves us for and not bring forth what has been written? If we do so, can we avoid being guilty of a doubled crime?

I confess openly, and I confess before the listening people, that these things have been written, even though I know that I have not yet fulfilled them. But let us at least, having been admonished, hasten to fulfill them. Let us hasten to pass over from the priests of Pharaoh, who possess earthly property, to the priests of God, who have no portion in the earth and whose portion is the Lord.

It follows:

**Verses 23–24.** Joseph said to the people:

“Behold, as you see, both you and your land belong to Pharaoh. Take seed and sow your fields, so that you may have crops. You shall give a fifth part to the king; I permit you to keep the remaining four parts for seed and for food for your servants and children.”

We have compared priests with priests. Now, if you wish, let us also compare the Egyptian people with the Israelite people. For it is said in what follows that, after the famine and servitude, the Egyptian people offered a fifth part to Pharaoh, whereas the Israelite people, by contrast, paid tithes to the priests.

Observe here too the divine Scripture supported by the meaning of numbers. Observe the Egyptian people paying tribute according to the number five. For they are marked by the five bodily senses, by which a carnal people is enslaved; the Egyptians always serve visible and bodily things.

But the Israelite people honor the number ten, the number of perfection. They received the ten words of the Law, and, bound by the power of the Decalogue, received through divine generosity mysteries unknown to the world.

In the New Testament too the number ten is similarly venerable. The fruit of the Spirit is described as flourishing through divine virtues; the faithful servant offers the Lord ten minas from his business profits and receives authority over ten cities.

Yet because there is one author of all things, one source, and one beginning—Christ—therefore the people indeed offer tithes to ministers and priests, but first offer the firstborn of every creature and the first fruits to the Beginning of all, concerning whom it is written: “Who is the beginning, the firstborn of every creature” (Col. 1).

Observe, then, from all these things the difference between the people of the Egyptians and the people of Israel, and the difference between Pharaoh’s priests and the Lord’s priests. Examining yourself, foresee to which people you belong and which priestly order you hold.

If you still serve carnal senses, if you still pay tribute according to the number five, if you look upon visible and temporal things and do not look upon invisible and eternal things, recognize that you belong to the Egyptian people.

But if you always keep before your eyes the Decalogue of the Law and the tenfold number of the New Testament, which we have explained above, and offer tithes from these things, and sacrifice the first fruits of your understanding in faith to the Firstborn from the dead, and refer your beginnings to the Beginning of all, then you are a true Israelite, in whom there is no deceit.

It follows:

**Verse 29.** When Israel saw that the day of his death was approaching, he called his son Joseph and said to him:

“If I have found favor in your sight, place your hand under my thigh and deal with me in mercy and truth.”

By this oath he binds his son in the same way that Abraham had bound his servant: Abraham, when he instructed him from where he should take a wife for his son; Jacob, when he entrusted to him the burial of his body.

In both matters, however, those two things are named which must be regarded and valued as great throughout all the Scriptures, wherever they are scattered: mercy and justice, or mercy and judgment, or mercy and truth. Thus it is written: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. 24).

These two things, therefore, having been commended, must be considered very carefully. Abraham’s servant had said, “If you will deal with my master in mercy and justice” (Gen. 24), while Jacob says to his son, “That you may deal with me in mercy and truth.”

It follows:

**Verse 30.** “Do not bury me in Egypt, but I shall sleep with my fathers. Carry me away from this land and bury me in the tomb of my ancestors.”

What does it mean that so great a man was so concerned about the disposition of his body, asking not to be buried in Egypt but in the land of Canaan beside his fathers? It seems strange and almost absurd, and scarcely fitting for so lofty a prophetic mind, if he was concerned about this merely according to human custom. But if mysteries are sought in all these things, the person who discovers them will experience a joy of far greater wonder.

It is beyond doubt that the sins of the dead are signified by dead bodies, since people are commanded to be purified as from uncleanness after touching them in any manner. Hence the saying: “Whoever is baptized from a dead body and again touches it, what does his washing profit him?” (Eccl. 34).

The burial of the dead therefore signifies the remission of sins, referring to what was said: “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered” (Ps. 31).

Where, then, should the corpses of the patriarchs—whose burial signified this—have been buried, except in that land where the one who brought about the remission of sins was crucified? Other matters concerning so great a subject may also be understood in this way or in a more exalted manner.

Yet we must not suppose without reason that such great men took such great care concerning the burial of their bodies. The security of the faithful is and ought to be that wherever their bodies are buried—or even if, through the rage of enemies, they are left unburied or torn apart and consumed according to their enemies’ will—we do not for that reason believe their resurrection will be either less complete or less glorious.

It follows:

**Verse 31.** Joseph answered, “I shall do what you have commanded.” Jacob said, “Then swear to me.” When Joseph had sworn, Israel worshiped God, turning toward the head of the bed.

It is rightly asked what is meant by the statement, “Israel worshiped God, turning toward the head of the bed.” The old man was lying there, and his head was positioned in such a way that he could pray there without difficulty whenever he wished. Thus, after his son had sworn, assured that the request he had made would be granted, he worshiped God toward the head of his bed.

For the holy man, devoted to God and weighed down by old age, had his bed arranged so that his posture while lying down was prepared for prayer without any difficulty.

### Chapter XLVIII

**Verses 1ff.** After these things had taken place, Joseph was told that his father was ill. He took his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim, and went to him. The old man was told, “Behold, your son Joseph is coming to you.” Strengthened, he sat up on his bed, and when Joseph had entered, he said:

“Almighty God appeared to me at Luz, which is in the land of Canaan, and he blessed me. He said, ‘I shall increase you and multiply you, and I shall make you into multitudes of peoples. I shall give this land to you and to your offspring after you as an everlasting possession.’”

Here too Jacob recalls the promises of God made to him, and says that it was told him, “I shall make you into multitudes of peoples.” By these words he signifies the calling of the faithful more than the propagation of a carnal race.

It follows:

**Verse 5.** “Therefore your two sons, who were born to you in the land of Egypt before I came to you here, shall be mine: Ephraim and Manasseh shall be reckoned to me as Reuben and Simeon.”

If anyone doubts that seventy persons of the sons of Israel entered Egypt, and that Joseph, at the time Jacob entered, had not nine sons but only two, the present chapter confirms it. Jacob himself says that Joseph had two sons, not nine.

But if, by contrast, we are confronted with the statement that in the Acts of the Apostles, in Stephen’s speech to the people, it is said that seventy-five persons entered Egypt (Acts 7), the explanation is easy. Saint Luke, the author of that history, should not have issued the immense volume of the Acts of the Apostles to the nations while writing something contrary to the Scripture that had already been disseminated among the nations. At that time, the authority of the Seventy Translators was certainly held in greater esteem than that of Luke, who was unknown and insignificant and not regarded by the nations as possessing great authority.

This should be observed generally: whenever the holy apostles or apostolic men speak to the peoples, they usually employ testimonies that had already been disseminated among the nations.

When he says, “Ephraim and Manasseh shall be to me as Reuben and Simeon,” this means that, just as Reuben and Simeon would become two tribes and be called by their own names, producing two peoples and inheriting the promised land, so too would Ephraim and Manasseh, like the rest of his sons.

It follows:

**Verse 6.** “But the others whom you beget after them shall be yours, and they shall be called by the name of their brothers in their possessions.”

They shall not, he says, receive land separately or have their own portions, as the other tribes do. Rather, within the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh they shall be mingled as additions to the people.

It follows:

**Verse 7.** “When I was coming from Mesopotamia, Rachel your mother died in the land of Canaan, on the very journey. It was springtime, and I was entering Ephrath. I buried her beside the road to Ephrath, which is otherwise called Bethlehem.”

Jacob wished to tell his son Joseph, as though he did not know, where and when he had buried his mother, although Joseph himself had been with his brothers at the time. Yet even if he had been there, he was so young that he could neither attend to the matter nor retain it in his mind.

This circumstance compelled Jacob to mention it now—unless perhaps it was relevant to recall that Joseph’s mother had been buried where Christ was destined to be born.

Just as Isaac’s two sons, Jacob and Esau, represented two peoples, the Jews and Christians—although, insofar as bodily descent is concerned, the Jews did not come from Esau’s seed but from the Idumaeans, and the Christian nations did not come from Jacob but rather the Jews—so the figure applies only to the saying, “The elder shall serve the younger.”

The same thing also happened in the case of Joseph’s two sons. The elder bore the type of the Jews, and the younger that of Christians.

When Jacob blessed them, placing his right hand upon the younger, who was at his left, and his left hand upon the elder, who was at his right, this seemed serious to their father. He admonished Jacob as though correcting his error and showing which of them was the elder.

But Jacob refused to change his hands and said, “I know, my son, I know. He too shall become a people and shall be exalted; but his younger brother shall be greater than he, and his seed shall be a multitude of nations.”

Here too he demonstrates those two promises: the one in a people, the other in a multitude of nations. What could be clearer than that these two promises contain the people of Israel and the whole world in the seed of Abraham—one according to the flesh, the other according to faith?

It follows:

**Verses 21–22.** Jacob also said to his son Joseph:

“Behold, I am dying, and God will be with you and will bring you back to the land of your fathers. I give you one portion beyond your brothers, which I took from the hand of the Amorite with my sword and bow.”

*Sichym* is declined according to Greek and Latin usage; in Hebrew it is called *Shechem*, as the evangelist John also testifies, although an erroneous usage has become established in which it is called *Sychar*. It is now Neapolis, a city of the Samaritans.

Since *Shechem* is translated from the Hebrew language as “shoulder,” he fittingly alludes to the name by saying, “I shall also give you one shoulder.” “One” is used here to mean “the chief” or “the principal.”

When he says that he possessed it with bow and sword, he calls the bow and sword justice, by which he deserved to be delivered from danger as a foreigner and sojourner after the killing of Shechem and Hamor. For, as we said above, he feared that the neighboring towns and fortified places might rise up against him because of the destruction of the allied city. But the Lord did not allow them to harm him.

Or it must be understood in this way: “I shall give you Shechem, which I bought through my strength”—that is, with money that I acquired through much labor and sweat.

When he says, “Beyond your brothers,” he shows that he gave it to the tribe of Joseph apart from the lot. Joseph was buried in that place, and his mausoleum can still be seen.

Without doubt, then, a prophetic mystery lies hidden here. For Joseph, through a certain special significance, prefigured Christ, and that land is given to him where Jacob had destroyed and buried foreign gods. Thus Christ is understood to possess the nations that renounce the gods of their fathers and believe in him.

The holy Joseph was therefore chosen before the others as heir of good works, whose works his brothers could not equal. Accordingly, by heavenly words and a spiritual sword he took possession of a place that had been devoted to fornications and crimes, so that where formerly inhabitants of wantonness and princes of luxury had lived, where there had been incentives to lust and fuel for wickedness, holy priests might now teach the disciplines of chastity, and many examples of virginal integrity might shine with a kind of radiance from above.

It follows:

### Chapter XLIX

**Verses 1–2.** Jacob called his sons and said to them:

“Gather together, so that I may announce to you what will happen to you in the last days. Gather together and hear, sons of Jacob; hear Israel your father.”

The one who had earlier preferred the younger to the elder began with the firstborn, so that in the former he might display the priority of the mystery’s grace, while in the latter he might preserve the order of age.

It follows:

**Verses 3–4.** “Reuben, my firstborn, you are my strength and the beginning of my sorrow, first in gifts, greater in authority. You have poured yourself out like water; you shall not increase, because you went up upon your father’s bed and defiled his couch.”

The meaning is this: You are my firstborn, greater in children. According to the order of your birth and the inheritance that belonged to the firstborn by right, you ought to have received the priesthood and the kingdom. This is demonstrated by the burden you carried and by your great strength.

But because you sinned, and like water that cannot be held in a vessel you poured yourself out in the rush of pleasure, I therefore command you not to sin any longer. You shall remain among your brothers, paying the penalty for your sin because you lost the order of the firstborn.

According to the mystical understanding, Reuben seems to bear the person of the former people. Therefore he appears to be rebuked rather than blessed. He is the firstborn, just as the prophet says, “Israel is my firstborn.” For, according to what was due to the firstborn, it belonged to him to receive the priesthood and the kingdom.

The words “You are my strength” are added because from that people came the foundation of faith, and from that people came the power of God, which is Christ.

But how is he himself “the beginning of sorrow”? It was because he continually inflicted injury upon God the Father, turning his back toward him and not his face.

He is “first in gifts” because to them first were entrusted the words of God, to them first the giving of the Law and the covenant, or the promise.

He is “greater in authority,” meaning greater in the abundance of his strength, because that same people reigned more extensively than the others in this world.

But he poured himself out by sinning against Christ, like water that cannot be held in a vessel; he poured himself out in the rush of pleasure. Therefore he added, “You shall not increase,” because after that people was scattered throughout the whole world, it was greatly diminished and reduced.

But why did it deserve such things? He adds: “Because you went up upon your father’s bed and defiled his couch.” For he proclaims the passion of the Lord and the audacity of the firstborn people: it went up upon the bed of God the Father and defiled his couch when it seized the Lord’s body, in which the fullness of divinity rested, hung it upon the cross, and stained it with iron.

It follows:

### (Verses 5ff.)

“Simeon and Levi are brothers; weapons of iniquity are instruments of warfare. Let my soul not enter into their council, nor let my glory be united with their assembly, for in their fury they killed a man, and in their self-will they undermined [Col. 1039A] a wall. Cursed be their fury, because it was obstinate, and their indignation, because it was harsh. I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel.”

He signifies that it was not according to his own counsel that they killed Shechem and Hamor, men bound to them by treaty, and shed innocent blood contrary to the law of peace and friendship—as though, seized by a kind of fury, they had cruelly and obstinately destroyed the walls and guests of the city. Hence he continues and says: “Cursed be their fury, because it was obstinate, and their indignation, because it was harsh: I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel.”

Levi did not receive a distinct inheritance, but throughout all their settlements he had only a few cities in which to dwell. Concerning Simeon, it is written in the Book of Joshua that he too did not obtain his own territory, but received certain possessions from the tribe of Judah. In the Book of Chronicles it is written more explicitly that, when he had multiplied and had no place for a possession, he went out into the desert.

By Simeon and Levi are understood the scribes and priests of the Jewish people. The scribes of the Jews are meant by Simeon; [Col. 1039B] by the tribe of Levi, the chief priests. Of them it is written that they took counsel to deliver Jesus to death (Matt. 26). Of that council the patriarch, who already saw God in spirit, says: “Let my soul not enter into their council.” For already at that time the holy patriarch shuddered at the sight of the crime of such great wickedness, which the Jews were to commit in the last days.

It continues:

“For in their fury they killed a man”—that is, the Lord Jesus Christ—“and in their anger they undermined a wall,” when they pierced with a spear that spiritual and most powerful bulwark which guards Israel.

“Cursed be their fury, because it was obstinate”—obstinate in the perpetration of so great a crime—when, inflamed by fury and anger, they handed Christ over to Pontius Pilate, saying to him, “Crucify, crucify him” (Luke 23), and, “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend” (John 18). “And their indignation, because it was harsh,” when they asked that the robber Barabbas be released and demanded that the Prince of Life be crucified.

[Col. 1039C] “I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel.” Here two things are named: division and dispersion. This is because some of them believed in the Lord, while others remained in unbelief. Those who separate from them and come to faith are said to be divided; those whose homeland and Temple were destroyed, and whose unbelieving race was scattered throughout the world, are said to be dispersed.

It continues:

### (Verses 8ff.)

“Judah, your brothers shall praise you. Your hand shall be upon the necks of your enemies; the sons of your father shall worship you. Judah is a lion’s cub; you have gone up to the prey, my son; reclining, you have lain down like a lion and like a lioness—who will rouse him? The scepter shall not be taken away from Judah, nor a ruler from his loins, until he comes who is to be sent; and he shall be the expectation of the nations, binding his foal to the vine, and his ass, my son, to the vine. He shall wash his robe in wine and his cloak in the blood of the grape. His eyes are more beautiful than wine, and his teeth whiter than milk.”

[Col. 1039D] Although this passage contains a mystery concerning Christ, nevertheless, according to the literal sense, it was prophesied that kings would arise from Judah through the line of David and that all the tribes would worship him. For he does not say, “The sons of your mother,” but, “The sons of your father.”

What follows, “You have gone up from the offspring, my son,” has in Hebrew, “You have gone up from captivity, my son,” to show that he would lead captive peoples. Here no one doubts that the person of the prophet has been clearly disclosed. Let us therefore hear what he says to his son Judah, from whose tribe Christ came according to the flesh, from the seed of David, as apostolic teaching testifies (Rom. 1).

“Judah, your brothers shall praise you.” Through this Judah, Christ is represented as the true confessor, because according to the flesh he was born from Judah’s tribe. His brothers praise him—namely, the apostles and all his co-heirs—for those who have been made sons of God the Father by adoption are, through grace, Christ’s brothers, while he is their Lord by nature.

“Your hand shall be upon the necks of your enemies.” With these same hands, and by the same trophy of the cross, he both stripped his own people and dealt with his enemies and the opposing powers, [Col. 1040A] in accordance with the Father’s promise to him: “Sit at my right hand, until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet” (Ps. 109).

“The sons of your father shall worship you,” because many of Jacob’s sons worshiped him—those who were saved through the election of grace.

“Judah is a lion’s cub,” because by being born he became small, as it is written: “A little child is born for us” (Isa. 9).

“You have gone up to the prey, my son”—that is, ascending the cross, you redeemed captive peoples, and those whom the hostile lion had attacked, you rescued by dying. Finally, returning from the underworld, you ascended on high and led captivity captive.

“Reclining, you have lain down like a lion.” Christ most clearly reclined in his Passion when, bowing his head, he handed over his spirit (John 19), or when, secure in the tomb, he rested as though in a kind of sleep of the body.

But why “like a lion” and “like a lion’s cub”? In his sleep he was a lion because he fulfilled this not by necessity but by power, according to what he himself had said: “I have power to lay down my life, and no one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord” (John 10).

[Col. 1040B] What he added, “And like a lion’s cub, Judah,” means that he died from the same source from which he was born. Natural philosophers write of a lion’s cub that, after being born, it sleeps for three days and three nights; then, awakened by its father’s roar or growl, as though the place of its bed were shaken, it is said to rouse from sleep.

This is very appropriately applied to Christ’s death and Passion: lying for three days and three nights in the bed of the tomb, he completed the sleep of death. Christ therefore rested like a lion, because he did not fear the bitterness of death but, even in death itself, conquered death’s dominion. Again, he was like a lion’s cub because he rose on the third day. Hence the account of his resurrection is added: “Who will rouse him?” That is, no human being will do so; he will raise himself, in accordance with what he said concerning his body: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2).

“The ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor the leader from his loins, [Col. 1040C] until he comes who is to be sent, and he shall be the expectation of the nations.”

This passage most clearly refers to Judah. For as long as Christ remained to be born of a virgin for the redemption of the world, an unbroken succession of royal rule from his seed continued among the Jews. The histories of the Jews prove this, showing that Herod was the first foreign king among the Jewish people, at the time when Christ was born.

If the Jews think that Christ has not come, then the kingdom of the Jews from the tribe of Judah must remain even to this day. Thus neither a leader nor a ruler from the seed of Judah was lacking until he came for whom it had been reserved.

But because he who was to be sent benefited not only the Jews, it follows: “And he shall be the expectation of the nations.”

“Binding his foal to the vine”: evidently the foal of the ass upon which Jesus sat—the people of the Gentiles—was joined to the vine of the apostles who are from the Jews, a people upon whom the burden of the Law had never yet been imposed. For the Lord’s vineyard is the house of Israel.

“And to the vine, my son, his ass.” By saying “my son,” he addresses Judah directly, indicating that Christ would accomplish all these things. For he himself said, “I am the true vine” (John 15). To this vine, therefore, he bound his ass upon which he sat—that is, the Church gathered from the Gentiles.

[Col. 1040D] He bound it to the vine of his body by the bond of love and by the union of evangelical discipline, so that, living in imitation of him, it might become an heir of God and a co-heir of Christ. Others interpret this ass as the synagogue—slow-footed and weighed down by the heavy burden of the Law.

“He shall wash his robe in wine.” Christ’s flesh is a good robe: it covered the sins of all, took upon itself the offenses of all, and concealed the errors of all. It is a good robe that clothed everyone in a garment of joy. He washed it in that wine which was poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins.

“And his cloak in the blood of the grape”—that is, in the Passion of his body he cleansed the Gentiles with his blood. His cloak is the Gentiles, whom he covered with his body, as it is written: “As I live, says the Lord, unless I clothe all these as with a garment.” He therefore cleansed not his own sins—for he had none—but the sins we committed.

[Col. 1041A] He rightly spoke of the grape, because, like a grape, he hung upon the wood. He is himself the vine; he is himself the grape: the vine, because he clung to the wood; the grape, because, when the soldier’s spear opened his side, he poured forth water and blood—water for washing, blood as the price. The water cleansed us; the blood redeemed us.

“His eyes are more beautiful than wine.” Christ’s eyes are the apostles and evangelists, who provide the light of knowledge to the entire body of the Church. They are proved more beautiful than wine because their teaching surpasses the austerity of old wine—that is, the tradition of the ancient Law. The commandments of the Gospel are far clearer than the ordinances of the Old Testament.

“And his teeth whiter than milk.” The teeth are the holy preachers, who cut people away from error and, as though grinding them, transfer them into the body of Christ. By the name “milk” the teaching of the Law is signified. It nourished the carnal people as infants with milk. The teachers of the Church have become whiter than this milk because they chew and distribute the strong and solid food of the word. Concerning them the Apostle says in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “Solid food belongs to the mature” (Heb. 5).

[Col. 1041B] He rightly says that the teeth are whiter than milk. All who are mature, and who, by explaining the nourishment of Scripture, supply the body with the subtle and finely divided understanding called spiritual, ought to be white and pure, free from every stain.

It continues:

### (Verse 13)

“Zebulun shall dwell on the shore of the sea and at the station of ships, reaching as far as Sidon.”

Zebulun, whose name is interpreted as “Dwelling of Beauty,” signifies the Church, most powerful in enduring every kind of suffering. It dwells on the shore of the sea so that it may observe the shipwrecks of others. Free from danger, it awaits those tossed upon the strait of this world, who are carried about by every wind of doctrine. It remains immovable, rooted in faith, awaiting the storms and shipwrecks of heretics and of the Jews, because they have denied the helmsman whom they had.

[Col. 1041C] It therefore dwells beside the waves but is not shaken by the waves. It is more ready to offer help than exposed to danger, so that if those driven by severe storms wish to flee to the harbor, the Church may be present as a harbor of salvation. With outstretched arms she calls those in peril into the peace of her embrace and shows them the station of faith.

Thus, in this world, the Church, like a maritime harbor extended along the shore, meets those who labor and tells believers that a refuge has been prepared where ships shaken by the winds may be drawn ashore.

In these Churches are the princes of Zebulun and the princes of Naphtali, as David teaches in the Psalm (Ps. 67). Some of them are deliverers, crying out amid the night storm, “Let us cast off the works of darkness, and let us put on the armor of light.” Others are the apostolic expanses, who can say: “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians; our heart is enlarged” (2 Cor. 6).

These are the very people who, while they were in darkness, saw a great light, as the prophet testifies, saying: “The land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, the way of the sea beyond the Jordan, the people who sat in darkness saw a great light; for those dwelling in the region and shadow of death, a light has risen” (Isa. 9).

[Col. 1041D] Our Lord God therefore appointed the heirs of this patriarch as scouts beside the ascent of ships. Their ever-watchful care and spiritual succession extends as far as Sidon—that is, it reaches the Gentiles—so that the mercy of the Lord might wash away the sins of the nations.

For Sidon was the firstborn son of Ham, that is, of the one who was condemned by a curse because of his irreverence toward his father’s piety. The father’s nighttime deliverance, like a spiritual bulwark stationed on watch, so that no one might strike the reefs of this life, extends even to sinners guilty of the gravest crimes, including the Sidonians themselves. Formerly, as their name is interpreted, they were called hunters of crimes. Now, once the inheritance of the accursed has been released, he frees the inheritance given to the curse, so that where guilt was greater, grace may now be more abundant.

[Col. 1042A] “Issachar is a strong ass, lying down between the boundaries. He saw that rest was good and the land that it was excellent; he placed his shoulder under the burden and became a servant of tribute.”

Since he had said above that Zebulun would possess the shores of the great sea and would reach Sidon and the other cities of Phoenicia, he now returns to the Mediterranean province. Issachar, who was to possess the most beautiful region of Galilee near Naphtali, is made by his blessing its inhabitant.

He calls him a strong ass, devoted to bearing the burden, because he had labored greatly in cultivating the land and transporting to the sea all that was produced within his borders, and also in carrying tribute to the kings.

The Hebrews say that all this is metaphorical: whoever meditates on the Holy Scriptures day and night applies himself to labor, and therefore all the tribes serve him, bringing gifts as to a teacher.

To lie down between the boundaries means to await rest at the end of the world and to seek nothing of the things now occurring in the interval, but to desire the last things.

[Col. 1042B] The strong ass sees good rest and an excellent land when the simple Gentile raises himself to the strength of good works because he is journeying toward the homeland of eternal life.

He also places his shoulder beneath the burden because, having seen the heavenly rest, he submits himself in action even to difficult commandments. Whatever weakness declares intolerable, the hope of reward shows to be light and easy.

It continues:

### (Verses 16ff.)
