“Dan shall judge his people, as also the other tribes in Israel. Let Dan be a serpent on the way, a horned serpent on the path, biting the horse’s heels so that its rider may fall backward. I shall await your salvation, Lord.”

Samson, the judge of Israel, was from the tribe of Dan. Jacob therefore says this while seeing in spirit that Samson the Nazarite would grow his hair and triumph over blinded enemies. He would resemble a serpent or horned serpent lying in ambush along the roads, allowing no one to pass through the land of Israel. If anyone, relying on his own strength as though on the speed of a horse, [Col. 1042C] rashly wished to ravage that land like a plunderer, he would not be able to escape.

Everything is nevertheless spoken metaphorically through the serpent and the horse. Seeing such a powerful Nazarite, and then seeing that he himself died because of a prostitute and, by dying, killed our enemies, I thought, O God, that he was your true Christ, your Son. But because he died and did not rise again, and because Israel was once more led away captive, another savior of the world and of my race must be awaited: he must come for whom it has been reserved, and he shall be the expectation of the nations.

What is signified here by the name “horse” except the present age? In this testimony we shall show more clearly what the horse signifies, whose heels the serpent bites (Gen. 49), if we explain somewhat more carefully the matters surrounding the passage.

Some say that the Antichrist will come from the tribe of Dan, because in this passage Dan is called both a serpent and one who bites. Hence, not without reason, when the Israelite people were receiving their lands as the portions of their camps, Dan was encamped first toward the north. He signified the one who had said in his heart: “I will sit on the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north; I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14).

[Col. 1042D] He is called not only a serpent but also a horned serpent. “Horned” is the meaning of *cerasta*, and this serpent is said to have horns. Through it the coming of the Antichrist is fittingly signified, because he comes against the life of the faithful armed not only with the bite of poisonous preaching but also with the horn of power.

Who does not know that a path is narrower than a road? Dan therefore becomes a serpent on the road because, in the breadth of the present life, he urges those to walk whom he flatters as though sparing them. But he bites on the road because he consumes with the poison of his error those to whom he grants liberty.

He becomes a horned serpent on the path because those whom he finds faithful, constraining themselves to the narrow ways of the heavenly commandment, he not only obstructs by the wickedness of crafty persuasion but also crushes with the terror of power. After the benefits of feigned sweetness, he exercises the horns of his power upon them amid the anguish of persecution.

[Col. 1043A] In this passage the horse also signifies this world, which, through its pride, foams as it runs along the course of passing time. Because the Antichrist strives to seize the world’s final period, this horned serpent is said to bite the horse’s heel. To bite the horse’s heel means to reach the world’s extremities by striking them.

“So that its rider may fall backward.” The rider of the horse is whoever is exalted in the honors of the world. He is said to fall backward, not forward, as Saul is recorded to have fallen.

To fall forward means for each person in this life to acknowledge his sins and mourn them in repentance. To fall backward means to fall suddenly from this life, which is unseen, and not to know to what punishments one is being led.

Because Judea, caught in the snares of its error, awaits the Antichrist instead of Christ, Jacob rightly changes at that very point into the voice of the elect, saying: “I shall await your salvation, Lord.” That is: I do not, like unbelievers, await the Antichrist; rather, I faithfully believe in the true Christ, who will come for our redemption.

It continues:

[Col. 1043B] “Gad, girded, shall fight before him, and he himself shall be girded behind.”

This entire passage refers to the event when, after fourteen years, returning to the sons whom he had left in possession beyond the Jordan, before Reuben and half the tribe of Manasseh, he found a great battle against them from the neighboring nations and fought bravely after defeating the enemies.

This Gad, girded, expresses the person of the Lord, who, in the humility of his first coming, goes forth to fight before the coming of the Antichrist. He is girded most powerfully with the sword of his word around his thigh, by which he divided—that is, son from father, daughter from mother, daughter-in-law from mother-in-law—according to what is read in the Gospel: “I have not come to bring peace, but a sword.”

When he says, “And he himself shall be girded behind” (Mark 10), the glory of our Lord in his second reign is shown. When the Antichrist comes, Christ will again meet him from behind—that is, following in his tracks—advancing swiftly in order to kill him with the sword of his mouth.

[Col. 1043C] Hence Gad is also rightly interpreted as “raider,” because afterward—that is, close behind his feet—he will spring forth like a raider with a swift and unexpected coming against the Antichrist’s open attack.

Christ is therefore written as fighting against the Antichrist both before and behind: before him in the hidden coming of humility, and behind him as manifest in the glory of majesty.

“Aser—his bread is rich, and he shall provide delights for kings.”

Aser, whose name signifies “delights” or “riches,” is Christ himself, whose height is the riches of wisdom and knowledge (Rom. 11), who, though he was rich, became poor for our sake (2 Cor. 8). His bread became rich: namely, his flesh, which is the holy food of holy things. Whoever eats it will live forever.

He also provides the delights of wisdom to kings—that is, to those who rule their own minds well, who exercise dominion over their vices, who chastise their bodies and subject them to the service of their souls.

It continues:

“Naphtali is a swift deer, giving beautiful words.”

This signifies either that warm waters arise in that very tribe, or that it is watered by Lake Gennesaret and the streams of the Jordan.

[Col. 1043D] The Hebrews, however, wish “an irrigated field and beautiful words” to be prophesied on account of Tiberias, which appears to possess knowledge of the Law. “A swift deer” may be interpreted as indicating the speed of seasonal crops and the fertility of the land. But it is better if we refer it to the teaching of the Savior.

Naphtali, whose name is interpreted as “breadth,” signifies the apostles and preachers, whose teaching has been spread throughout the breadth of the whole world. From this tribe came the apostles, who are the princes and leaders of the Churches—the princes of Zebulun and Naphtali. These unquestionably refer to the persons of the apostles.

They are the sons of those who have been shaken out—that is, of the prophets—who have been placed in the hand of the mighty God and, like arrows shot forth, have reached the ends of the earth.

[Col. 1044A] Hence Naphtali is rightly written here as a swift deer, because the apostles or preachers of the Gospel, leaping forth with the speed of deer, pass beyond the entanglements of this world. Meditating on what is lofty and exalted, they give beautiful words—that is, they preach to all nations the teaching of the Lord and Savior.

It continues:

### (Verses 22ff.)

“Joseph is a growing son, a growing and handsome son to look upon; the daughters ran upon the wall, but they embittered him and quarreled with him, and they envied him, carrying weapons. His bow sat firmly, and the bonds of his arms and his hands were loosened by the hand of the Mighty One of Jacob; from there the shepherd, the stone of Israel, went forth.”

According to the literal sense, this is the meaning of this passage:

O Joseph, who are so called either because the Lord has added you to me, or because you are destined to become greater than your brothers. The tribe of Ephraim was indeed the strongest, as we read in the Books of Kings and Chronicles.

O, I say, my son Joseph, who are so beautiful that the entire crowd of the girls of Egypt looks upon you from walls, towers, and windows: they envied you, and your brothers provoked you to anger, carrying the arrows of jealousy and wounded by the darts of envy. [Col. 1044B] But you placed your bow and weapons for battle in God, who is a strong defender. The bonds with which your brothers bound you were loosened and broken by him, so that from your seed the tribe of Ephraim might arise—strong, stable, more invincible than a stone—and might rule over the ten tribes of Israel.

In prophecy the father presented all this after the Lord’s Passion in the likeness of the Father’s voice. When Christ returned to heaven after his victory, the Father addresses him, saying:

“Joseph is a growing son, a growing son”—growing, certainly, among the Gentiles, because, when the Synagogue’s unbelief had caused him to abandon the people, he increased for himself an innumerable people of the Church from all the nations. David also sang this, saying: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord” (Ps. 21).

“A growing and handsome son to look upon.” His beauty surpasses all others, according to what the psalmist also testifies of him: “Beautiful beyond the sons of men.”

“The daughters ran upon the wall” (Ps. 44)—that is, the nations, or the Churches that believed in Christ. [Col. 1044C] Inflamed by love of Christ’s beauty, they run upon the solidity of faith as upon a wall, so that by contemplation they may behold the man and bridegroom, and may be joined and attached to him by the kiss of love.

“But they embittered him”—Christ being understood—when the peoples of the synagogues, accusing him with false testimony, attempted to destroy the Holy One of the Lord.

“And they envied him, carrying weapons.” No one actually shot an arrow at Joseph or hurled any weapon of wounding against him; this happened specifically in the case of Christ.

“His bow sat firmly.” Christ placed his bow and weapons for battle in God, who is a strong defender. By his power all the wickedness of the faithless is overthrown.

“And the bonds of his arms were loosened”—the bonds by which his brothers, that is, the Jews, bound him and handed him over to Pontius Pilate, or by which they suspended him on the wood of the cross. They were cut by the hands of the omnipotent Jacob—that is, by the hands of the omnipotent God of Jacob—from whose mouth Christ himself, the good shepherd, went forth as the stone and firmness of believers in Israel.

[Col. 1044D] “The God of your father shall be your helper.” Who helped the Son except the Father alone, who said: “Jacob is my servant; my soul shall receive him”?

“And the Almighty shall bless you with the blessings of heaven above, with the blessings of the abyss lying below.” For he subjected everything to him: heavenly things through the blessing of heaven, and earthly things through the blessing of the abyss lying below, so that he might rule over all angels and human beings.

“With the blessings of the breasts”—that is, of the two Testaments, in one of which he was announced and in the other revealed. Or these are the blessings of Mary’s breasts, she who was truly blessed because that holy Virgin gave the Lord drink of milk.

Hence the woman in the Gospel says: “Blessed is the womb that bore you and the breasts that you sucked” (Luke 11).

“With the blessings of the breasts and of the womb.” Here too the womb of the same mother is blessed—the virginal womb, certainly, which gave birth to Christ the Lord for us. This is clear from Jeremiah, who assumed the person of the same mother and heard, under her figure, these words spoken to him: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you, and before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you” (Jer. 1).

[Col. 1045A] “The blessings of your father have been strengthened by the blessings of your ancestors.” The blessings, he says, of your heavenly Father, which were given to you by the highest heaven and the abyss, have been strengthened—that is, they have prevailed over the blessings of your fathers. For the blessing of the omnipotent Father in the Son prevailed beyond all the merit of the saints, prophets, and patriarchs, so that no saint could be made equal to him.

“Until the desire of the eternal hills comes.”

These hills are the saints who, prophesying Christ’s coming, awaited his incarnation with great desire. Concerning them the Lord says: “Many righteous people and prophets desired to see what you see” (Matt. 13).

These saints are called hills because of the excellence of their holiness. They are also called eternal because they attain eternal life and do not perish with the world, but are believed to be eternal.

“Let them come upon the head of Joseph.” All these blessings are placed upon Christ’s head, which he received when he became incarnate, and upon the crown of the Nazarite, of whom it is written [Col. 1045B]: “He shall be called a Nazarene” (Matt. 2)—that is, the holy one of God.

“Among his brothers,” because he is the head, standing above all the saints, whom he also calls his brothers in the Psalms.

It continues:

“Benjamin is a ravenous wolf; in the morning he shall eat the prey, and in the evening he shall divide the spoils.”

The Hebrews explain this passage by saying that the altar on which sacrifices were offered and at whose base the blood of the victims was poured stood within the territory of the tribe of Benjamin.

This, they say, signifies that the priests offered sacrifices in the morning and in the evening divided among themselves what had been granted to them by the people according to the Law. They interpret the bloody or ravenous wolf as the altar, and the spoils as the priests, who served the altar and lived from the altar.

“Benjamin is a ravenous wolf; in the morning he shall eat the prey, and in the evening he shall divide the spoils.” In these words the Apostle Paul is represented, descended from the stock of Benjamin. In the morning he seized the prey—that is, at the beginning he ravaged as many of the faithful as he could. In the evening he divided the spoils because, [Col. 1045C] after becoming faithful, he dispensed the sacred utterances to those who heard them with marvelous discernment.

We read of one of the teachers referring to the city of Jerusalem what is written about Benjamin. “Benjamin,” he says, “is interpreted as ‘son of pain.’ By lot he received the place where the earthly Jerusalem is situated, which now, because of its unbelief, has been rejected and cast away. This is signified in its children under the person of Benjamin.

“For just as Benjamin received the final blessing, so also this people will be saved last, after the fullness of the Gentiles has entered. For he says: ‘Benjamin is a ravenous wolf’—a wolf, certainly, because this people shed the blood of the prophets. It is called ravenous because of its greed; from great hunger for the word of God and deprivation it will become ravenous, because it too will violently seize the kingdom of God.

“Now, ‘in the morning he shall eat the prey.’ The morning is believed to signify the time when he received the Law; for then the first illumination of knowledge was given. He shall eat in the morning because he still consumes, meditates upon, and reads the Law which he received in the morning. [Col. 1045D] He follows the righteousness of the Law but does not attain the law of faith.

“But ‘in the evening he shall divide the spoils.’ The evening will be that final time when he is converted. Then he will divide the spoils—that is, then he will understand that the letter must be divided from the spirit, and then he will recognize that ‘the letter kills, but the spirit gives life’ (1 Cor. 3).

“Because, already illumined by the grace of the Lord, he begins to divide and separate the spiritual things of the Law from its bodily forms, it is therefore said: ‘In the evening he shall divide the spoils,’ or the food, because, although he meditated on the Law throughout the entire day, he had not previously done so.”

The question is asked why Jacob made all those whom he fathered by free women and maidservants sons and heirs with equal honor. The answer is that he wished to show that Christ the Lord grants heavenly rewards to all nations who are reconciled to his body through faith, holding all in equal honor and glory. There is no distinction whether one is Jew or Greek, Barbarian or Scythian, slave or free (Col. 3), because Christ is all and in all.

[Col. 1046A] For this reason our Savior and Lord assumed the form of a servant and served both free and slave, so that he might grant all who believe in him an equal gift of heavenly blessings. In his presence it does not matter who is nobler according to the flesh. Whoever wins the Lord’s approval through faith is not darkened by any stain of carnal birth.

The prophet also promises that this will indeed happen, when the Lord says: “In the last days I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh” (Acts 2).

It continues.

Source/review notes: One printed Latin clause is materially corrupt; the edit preserves it as an explicitly marked fragment rather than inventing a completion.

(Cap. L.—Vers. 1 ff.) When he had finished the commands with which he instructed his sons, he drew up his feet upon the bed, died, and was gathered to his people. When Joseph saw this, he fell upon his father’s face, weeping and kissing him.

We should consider how Scripture habitually speaks of the dead: “And he was gathered to his fathers,” or, “He was gathered to his people.” Thus Jacob is said to have been gathered, already dead but not yet buried. Yet to what people he was gathered is not immediately clear. From him was born the people later called the people of Israel. Those who preceded him were so few righteous men that we hesitate to call them a people. For if it had said, “He was gathered to his fathers,” there would be no difficulty.

Or perhaps the people is not only the people of holy human beings but also of the angels—the people of that city of which Hebrews says: “You have approached Mount Zion and the city of Jerusalem and thousands of rejoicing angels.” Those who finish this life pleasing to God are gathered to this people. They are said to be gathered then, when no anxiety from temptations and no danger from sins remains.

It follows: “And he commanded his servants, the physicians, to embalm his father. When they had fulfilled the command, forty days passed; for this was the customary period for embalmed corpses. And Egypt mourned him for seventy days.”

The forty days of burial which Scripture mentions perhaps signify something concerning repentance, by which sins are buried. For it was not without reason that forty days of fasting were appointed: during that period Moses, Elijah, and the Lord himself fasted, and the Church calls its principal observance of fasting the Quadragesima, or Lent. The prophet Jonah also preached to the Ninevites: “Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown,” so that through the appointed number of days the humiliation of penitents and the forgiveness they receive may be understood.

It follows: “When the time of mourning was over, Joseph spoke to Pharaoh’s household: ‘If I have found favor in your sight, speak in Pharaoh’s ears, because my father made me swear, saying, “Behold, I am dying. In my tomb, which I dug for myself in the land of Canaan, you shall bury me.” Therefore I will go up and bury my father, and I will return.’ Pharaoh said to him, ‘Go up and bury your father.’ When he had gone up, all the elders went with him.”

Joseph’s instruction to the powerful men of Egypt—that they should say to Pharaoh in his name, “My father made me swear, saying, ‘In my monument, which I dug for myself in the land of Canaan, there you shall bury me’”—raises the question how this can be true, since these words of his father, when he gave instructions about his burial, are not recorded. But we must refer the words to the sense, as we have similarly pointed out above concerning repeated words and narratives elsewhere.

That Jacob dug a tomb for himself is nowhere previously recorded in this Scripture. Yet unless this had happened while he was in those same lands, it would not now be said.

It follows: “And they came to the threshing floor of Achar, which is beyond the Jordan.”

What is meant by the fact that, when they were proceeding to bury Jacob, Scripture says, “They came to the threshing floor which is beyond the Jordan”? They passed the place where the dead man was to be buried by many miles—more than five hundred, according to those who know the region. For that is roughly the distance from the place where the patriarchs were buried to the place where they are said to have arrived. After mourning and lamenting there with great grief, they returned to the place they had passed, crossing the Jordan again.

Unless, perhaps, someone says that they came with the body through the wilderness in order to avoid certain enemies, taking the route by which the people of Israel was also led when Moses liberated it from Egypt. Along that route there is a very long detour, and one comes by way of the Jordan to Abramium, where the bodies of the patriarchs are located—that is, to the land of Canaan.

But why they went so far beyond those places toward the east and then came from there to them by way of the Jordan should be understood as having occurred for the sake of its significance: Israel was later to come to those lands through the Jordan in its descendants.

It follows: “There they celebrated the funeral rites and, with great and vehement mourning, completed seven days. When the inhabitants of that land—that is, of Canaan—saw this, they said, ‘This is a great mourning for the Egyptians.’ And therefore they called the name of that place ‘The Mourning of Egypt.’ Thus the sons of Jacob did as he had commanded them; and, carrying him into the land of Canaan, they buried him in the double cave.”

I do not know whether anyone can find in Scripture that mourning was observed for nine days, which among the Latins is called a novendium. It is therefore evident that Christians were forbidden by this custom to preserve this number in mourning for the dead, since it belongs more properly to pagan practice.

The seventh day, however, has authority in Scripture. Thus it is written elsewhere: “The mourning of the dead is seven days, but for the fool, all the days of his life.” The number seven, because of the mystery of the Sabbath, is especially an indication of rest. Therefore it is rightly offered to the dead as to those who are resting. Yet the Egyptians multiplied this number tenfold in Jacob’s mourning, for they mourned him for seventy days.

It follows: “Joseph lived one hundred and ten years, and saw the sons of Ephraim to the third generation. The sons also of Machir, the son of Manasseh, were born upon Joseph’s knees. And Joseph died when the one hundred and ten years of his life had been completed, and, having been embalmed with spices, was buried in Egypt.”

Since Scripture says that Joseph lived to see these sons of sons, or grandsons, how does it join them to those seventy persons with whom Jacob is said to have entered Egypt, when Joseph had grown old before he saw these children born? When Jacob entered Egypt, Joseph was still young; and his father, when he died, left him nearly fifty-six years old. It is therefore clear that Scripture wished to commend that number—the number seventy—for a particular mystery.

But if someone demands how it can also be true according to the historical sense that Jacob entered Egypt with seventy souls, his entry should not be understood as occurring on the one day when he arrived. Rather, since Jacob is often named in his sons—that is, in his descendants—and since it is clear that he entered Egypt through Joseph, his entry should be understood to have continued as long as Joseph lived, through whom it came about that he entered.

Throughout that entire period all those who are mentioned could have been born and lived, so that the seventy souls—or, according to the Septuagint translators, seventy-five souls—might be completed, down to Benjamin’s grandsons.

For Scripture says: “These are the sons of Leah, whom she bore to Jacob in Mesopotamia of Syria,” speaking even of those who had not yet been born. Since their parents, from whom they were born, had borne them there, it declares them to have been born there, because the cause of their birth arose there—that is, their parents, whom Leah bore there.

So, since Jacob had in Joseph the cause of entering Egypt, the whole time that Joseph lived in Egypt was Jacob’s entry into Egypt through his offspring, which was propagated during Joseph’s lifetime, through whom it came about that Jacob entered.

[Col. 1047]

# COMMENTARIES ON THE BOOKS OF KINGS (C, G, S)*

## BOOK ONE

[Col. 1047C] The periods of the kings begin after the judges, when David, after Saul had been rejected, began to reign. Hence the book in which their deeds are contained—the book we are now undertaking—is called *Malachim*, that is, “Kings,” since it is contained in the third and fourth volumes. It is much better to say *Malachim*, “Kings,” than *Malachot*, “Kingdoms.” For it does not describe the kingdoms of many nations, but of the one Israelite people, which consists of twelve tribes. Nevertheless, in earthly Jerusalem the tribe of Judah, one of the twelve, ruled for a long succession. In that city David first reigned after Saul had been rejected.

In these events many varied mysteries of Christ and the Church are represented. For at the very beginning of the Books of Kings, when the priesthood is changed in Samuel after Heli has been rejected, and the kingship is changed in David after Saul has been rejected, it cries out that a new priesthood and a new kingship are being foretold: the old having been rejected, it was a shadow of what was to come in the Lord Jesus Christ.

Was it not David himself who, when he ate the bread of the Presence—which no one was permitted to eat except the priests—represented in one and the same person what was to come, namely, kingship and priesthood in the one Jesus Christ?

And observe the periods of the kings: first the judges, then the kings; so there will be first judgment and afterward the kingdom.

The beginning of this book is as follows:

## I. Concerning Elkanah

### Chapter I

“There was a certain man from Ramathaim-zophim, from the hill country of Ephraim, and his name was Elkanah, son of Jeroboam, son of Elihu, son of Tohu, son of Zuph, an Ephrathite.”

Elkanah was not descended from Amram but from Izhar, who himself was the son of Kohath, and Kohath was the son of Levi. This Izhar was the father of Korah; after Korah perished, his sons remained. Samuel was descended from his line, and later, in the days of David and Solomon, his descendants were singers and prophets among the people and in the temple of God.

The families of this Kohath received cities and their surrounding lands for habitation, as the Book of Joshua testifies, in the hill country of Ephraim, where were the cities of Shechem, Gezer, Chethsaïn, and Beth-horon.

Elkanah was the son of Jeroboam, son of Elihu, son of Tohu, son of Zuph, son of Elkanah, son of Joel, son of Azariah, son of Zephaniah, son of Tahath, son of Assir, son of Abiasaph, son of Korah, son of Izhar, son of Kohath, son of Levi, son of Israel, as the Book of Chronicles relates.

“And he had two wives: the name of one was Hannah, and the name of the second was Peninnah. Peninnah had children, but Hannah had no children,” and so forth.

This admirable man, then, had two wives: the name of one was Hannah and the name of the second Peninnah. He had children from the second, Peninnah, while the first, who was also the nobler, was barren.

You will find similar things in Genesis, for divine Scripture is related to itself. There you will find (Chapter XVI) that Abraham’s first wife, Sarah, was the nobler, while the second, the Egyptian Hagar, was of low status; and Abraham became a father from the lowly wife before he did from the noble one. Yet afterward he also became the father of a child by his noble wife.

So now too Elkanah—whose name means “possession of God”—first becomes a father by his second wife, because God had closed Hannah’s womb, just as earlier he had closed Sarah’s womb. But after Peninnah had borne many children, Hannah’s womb too is opened through prayers and petitions, and she herself also becomes the mother of a son, whom she offers to God.

Let us see what mystery these things contain.

Peninnah is interpreted as “conversion,” while Hannah is interpreted as “grace.” Therefore let each one of us who wishes to become God’s possession join these two wives to himself and celebrate marriage with them. Let him first join to himself the nobler and more distinguished one, grace. For grace is joined to us first through faith, as the Apostle also says: “By grace you have been saved through faith” (Eph. II).

We are joined second to Peninnah, that is, to conversion, because after the grace of believing comes the amendment of conduct and the conversion of life.

But although this is the order of marriage, the order of procreation is different. Peninnah first bears children for us, because we produce the first fruits from conversion and beget the first shoots of righteousness through actions and works. For the first work of righteousness is to turn away from sins. Unless we first turn and decline from evil, we cannot become fathers through Hannah, nor generate children through grace.

Let us therefore now consider the differences among them.

Peninnah has children, but they do not stand beside God. For such children cannot belong to conversion in such a way that they stand beside and cling to God. Yet they are not empty or wholly alien to the things of God: they receive portions from the divine sacrifices and eat from God’s offerings.

Thus each of us first turns away from sin and, from conversion, produces works of righteousness. afterward Hannah, awakened within us through zeal and emulation of the good, pours out a prayer to God, so that she herself may bear children.

What sort of children, then, does Hannah, who is grace, bear—children who stand beside God? For “grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.”

This, then, is the son of grace, who is free for the Word of God and for God.

## II. Concerning Hannah’s Song

### Chapter II

“After this Hannah prayed and said:

‘My heart is established in the Lord,
and my horn is exalted in my God and Savior.
My mouth is enlarged over my enemies;
I have rejoiced in your salvation,’”

and so forth.

Can these words really be thought to belong to one little woman rejoicing over the son born to her? So far is the human mind turned away from the light of truth that it does not perceive that the words poured forth by this woman transcend the measure of a woman.

But one who is rightly moved by the realities themselves—which had already begun to be fulfilled even in this earthly pilgrimage—does he not attend, look, and recognize that through this woman, whose name Hannah is interpreted to mean “his grace,” the Christian religion itself, the city of God whose king and founder is Christ, and finally the grace of God itself spoke in the prophetic Spirit?

By that grace the proud are alienated so that they may fall, and the humble are filled so that they may rise. This is what the hymn chiefly resounds.

Unless, perhaps, someone will say that this woman prophesied nothing, but merely praised God with exultant thanksgiving on account of the son whom she had prayed for and obtained.

What, then, does she mean by saying:

“The bow of the mighty has been overcome,
and the weak have been girded with strength;
those who were full of bread have become diminished,
and the hungry have passed over the land,
because the barren woman has borne seven,
while she who had many children has grown weak”?

Had she herself borne seven? Although she had been barren, she had one son when she said this. Nor afterward did she bear seven—or six, with Samuel as the seventh—but three sons and two daughters.

Moreover, while that people still had no king, what does the final statement mean: “He gives strength to our kings, and exalts the horn of his Christ”? From where did she speak this, unless she was prophesying?

Let the Church of Christ, the city of the great King, full of grace and fruitful in offspring, speak. Let it say of itself what it recognizes as having been prophesied so long before through the mouth of this devout mother.

“My heart is established in the Lord,
and my horn is exalted in my God.”

The heart is truly established and the horn truly exalted because they are not established or exalted in oneself but in the Lord, one’s God.

“My mouth is enlarged over my enemies.”

For even amid the straits of persecution the word of God is not bound, nor is it bound in those who proclaim it while themselves confined.

“I have rejoiced,” she says, “in your salvation.”

This is Christ Jesus, whom Simeon, as we read in the Gospel, an old man embracing the little child and recognizing the greatness within him, said:

“Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, in peace,
for my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke II).

Let the Church therefore say: “I have rejoiced in your salvation.”

“For there is no one holy like the Lord,
and there is no one righteous like our God.”

He is holy and makes holy; righteous and makes righteous.

“There is none holy apart from you,” because no one becomes holy except through you.

Then it follows:

“Do not boast, you proud,
and do not speak lofty things.
Let no grandiloquence come out of your mouth,
for the Lord is a God of knowledge.”

He knows you—even where no one else knows. For “whoever thinks that he is something, when he is nothing, deceives himself” (Gal. VI).

These words are addressed to the adversaries of the city of God, those who belong to Babylon, who presume upon their own strength and boast in themselves rather than in the Lord. Among them are also the carnal Israelites, earthly citizens of Jerusalem, earthborn people who, as the Apostle says, “being ignorant of the righteousness of God”—that is, the righteousness God gives to a human being, who alone is righteous and makes righteous—“and seeking to establish their own”—as though prepared by themselves for themselves, not imparted by him—“have not submitted to the righteousness of God” (Rom. X).

They are proud, thinking that they please God by what is their own rather than by what is God’s. He is the God of knowledge and therefore, I think, also the judge of consciences. There he sees human thoughts, because they are empty if they are human and do not come from him.

“And he prepares,” she says, “his designs.”

What designs can we think these are, except that the proud may fall and the humble rise?

She carries out these designs, saying:

“The bow of the mighty has been weakened,
and the weak have been girded with strength.”

The bow has been weakened—that is, the intention of those who seem so powerful to themselves that, by human sufficiency and without God’s gift and assistance, they think they can fulfill divine commands. The weak are girded with strength, those whose voice on earth is: “Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am weak.”

“Those who were full of bread,” she says, “have become diminished; the hungry have passed over the land.”

Who are to be understood as those full of bread except those same apparently powerful people—that is, the Israelites—to whom the utterances of God were entrusted?

But in that people the children of the handmaid have become diminished. Although the wording is somewhat abbreviated, it is nevertheless well expressed: those who were greater have become lesser. For even in those loaves—that is, in the divine words, which at that time the Israelites alone of all the nations received—they have an earthly understanding.

But the nations, to whom that law had not been given, after they came through the New Testament to those divine utterances, crossed over the land in great hunger, because in them they understood not earthly but heavenly things.

And as though someone might ask why this happened, she adds:

“Because the barren woman has borne seven,
and she who had many children has become weak.”

Here the whole prophecy shone forth for those who recognized the number seven, by which the perfection of the universal Church is signified.

For this reason the Apostle John also writes to seven churches, thereby showing that he is writing to the fullness of one Church. Solomon likewise prefigured this earlier in Proverbs: “Wisdom built herself a house and set up seven pillars.”

The city of God was barren among all the nations before this offspring, whom we behold, arose.

We also see that earthly Jerusalem, which had many children, has now become weak. For whoever among the children of the free woman belonged to it was its strength. But now, because the letter is there and the spirit is not, it has lost its strength and become weak.

“The Lord puts to death and gives life;
he leads down to the underworld and brings back.”

He put to death the one who had many children and gave life to this barren woman who bore seven.

Although it can more suitably be understood that he gives life to the very ones whom he has put to death, for he repeated the thought, adding: “He leads down to the underworld and brings back.”

To those to whom the Apostle says, “If you have died with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God” (Col. III), the Lord brings a salutary death. He adds to them: “Set your minds on the things that are above, not on the things that are on earth.” They are the ones who, being hungry, have passed over the land.

“For you have died,” he says.

See how God gives them a salutary death.

Then it follows:

“And your life is hidden with Christ in God.”

See how God gives life to these same people.

But did he lead these same people down to the underworld and bring them back? Without controversy among the faithful, we see both fulfilled rather in that one who is our Head, with whom the Apostle said that our life is hidden in God (Col. III).

For “he did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all” (Rom. VIII). In this way he put him to death; and because he raised him from the dead, he again gave life to the same one. And because his voice is recognized in prophecy—“You will not abandon my soul in the underworld”—he led the same one down to the underworld and brought him back.

By his poverty we have been enriched. For “the Lord makes poor and makes rich” (James IV).

But so that we may know what this means, let us hear what follows:

“He humbles and exalts.”

Certainly he humbles the proud and exalts the humble. For what is read elsewhere—“God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble”—is contained in its entirety in the speech of this woman, whose name is interpreted as “his grace.”

Now, when it adds, “He raises the poor from the earth,” I understand this of no one better than of him who became poor for us, though he was rich, so that by his poverty we might be enriched, as was said shortly before (II Cor. VIII). He raised him from the earth so quickly that his flesh did not see corruption.

Nor will I detach from him what is added: “And he lifts the needy from the dung heap.” The needy, who is the same as the poor, and the dung heap from which he was lifted are most rightly understood as the persecuting Jews. Among them the Apostle said that he had persecuted the Church, and he continues:

“The things that were gains to me, these I have regarded as losses for Christ. Indeed, I regard everything as loss—and even as dung—in order that I may gain Christ.”

From the earth, then, he was raised—the poor man above all the rich; and from that dung heap he was lifted above all the wealthy—the needy one.

“And he seats him with the princes of the people.”

To them he says: “You shall sit upon twelve thrones,” giving them a seat of glory as their inheritance.

Those powerful men had said: “Behold, we have left everything and followed you.” The most powerful among them made this vow. But from where did they receive it, except from the one of whom it is immediately said: “He gives a vow to the one who vows”?

[The text is corrupt: “Something from those mighty ones whose bow has been weakened.”]

“He gives,” he says, “a vow to the one who vows.”

No one would vow anything rightly to the Lord unless he received from him what he was to vow.

It follows:

“And he blesses the years of the righteous.”

He blesses them so that the righteous person may live with him without end. It was said to him: “Your years shall not fail.” There the years stand; here they pass—or rather, they perish. Before they come, they do not exist; when they have come, they will no longer exist, because they arrive together with their end.

Of these two things—“He gives a vow to the one who vows” and “He blesses the years of the righteous”—one is what we do, the other what we receive. But the latter is not received from God the giver unless, with him as helper, the former is first accomplished.

For “a man is not strong by his own strength” (Jer. IX).

The Lord makes his adversary weak—namely, the one who envies the person making a vow and resists him so that he cannot fulfill what he has vowed.

The Greek may also be understood ambiguously as “his adversary.” For when the Lord begins to possess us, the adversary who had been ours becomes his, and he is conquered by us—not by our strength, since “a man is not strong by his own strength.”

Therefore the Lord, the Holy One, will weaken his adversary, so that he may be conquered by the saints whom the Lord, the Holy One of holy ones, makes holy.

Accordingly, let the wise man not boast in his wisdom; let the powerful man not boast in his power; let the rich man not boast in his riches. Rather, let the one who boasts boast in this: understanding and knowing God, and practicing judgment and righteousness in the midst of the earth.

He understands and knows the Lord in no small measure who also understands and knows that this very ability to understand and know the Lord is given to him by the Lord.

For what does the Apostle say? “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (I Cor. IV)—that is, as though you had from yourself the source of your boasting.

He practices judgment and righteousness who lives rightly. He lives rightly who obeys God when he commands.

And the end of the commandment—that is, the goal toward which the commandment is directed—is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith.

This love, as the Apostle John testifies, is from God (I John IV). Therefore to practice judgment and righteousness is from God.

But what does “in the midst of the earth” mean? Surely those who live at the ends of the earth are not required to practice judgment and righteousness? Who could say that?

Why, then, was “in the midst of the earth” added? If it were not added, and it merely said, “To practice judgment and righteousness,” the command would apply more broadly to both kinds of people, those living inland and those living by the sea.

But lest anyone suppose that after the end of the life conducted in this body there remains time for practicing judgment and righteousness—which he did not practice while he was in the flesh—and that he might thereby escape divine judgment, the phrase “in the midst of the earth” seems to me to have been said with reference to the time when each person lives in the body.

For in this life each person carries his own earth, which, when the human being dies, the earth receives, in order to return it when he rises.

Therefore judgment and righteousness must be practiced in the midst of the earth—that is, while our soul is enclosed in this earthly body—for this will benefit us in the future, when each person receives according to the things he did through the body, whether good or evil.

The Apostle said “through the body,” meaning through the time during which he lived in the body. For if someone blasphemes with an evil and impious mind, and does not carry out the blasphemy through any bodily members, he will not for that reason be guiltless, since he did it during the time in which he also possessed a body.

In this way we can suitably understand what is also read in the Psalm:

“But God our King before the ages worked salvation in the midst of the earth” (Ps. LXXIII).

The Lord Jesus is understood as our God, who existed before the ages, because through him the ages were made. He worked salvation in the midst of the earth when the Word became flesh and dwelt in an earthly body.

After Hannah’s words had prophesied how the one who boasts should boast—not in himself but in the Lord, because of the recompense that will come on the day of judgment—it says:

“The Lord has ascended into the heavens and thundered;
he himself will judge the ends of the earth, because he is righteous.”

It follows the order of the confession of the faithful exactly. The Lord Christ ascended into heaven, and from there he will come to judge the living and the dead.

For who ascended, as the Apostle says, except the one who descended into the lower parts of the earth? “He who descended is also the one who ascended above all the heavens, that he might fill all things” (Eph. IV).

Therefore he thundered through his clouds, because, after he had ascended, he filled them with the Holy Spirit.

Through Isaiah the prophet he threatened these things to that Jerusalem—that is, to the ungrateful vineyard—so that he would not cause rain to fall upon it.

The words are: “He himself will judge the ends of the earth” (Isa. V), as though it said, “even the ends of the human being.” For the one who will certainly judge all human beings will not fail to judge the other parts as well.

But “the ends of the earth” are better understood as the ends of the human being. For judgment will not be passed upon those things that are changed for better or worse in the middle of the earth, but upon the condition in which the one being judged is found at the end.

For this reason it is said: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. X).

Whoever therefore perseveringly practices judgment and righteousness in the midst of the earth will not be condemned when the ends of the earth are judged.

“And he gives strength,” she says, “to our kings,” so that he may not condemn them when judging them. He gives them strength by which, as kings, they may rule their flesh and, in him who shed his blood for them, conquer the world.

“And he has exalted the horn of his Christ.”

How has Christ exalted the horn of his Christ? The one of whom it was said above, “The Lord has ascended into the heavens,” was understood to be the Lord Christ. He himself, as it is said here, “will exalt the horn of his Christ.”

Who, then, is the Christ of Christ? Or will he exalt the horn of each of his faithful, just as this same woman said at the beginning of this hymn: “My horn has been exalted in my God”?

All those anointed with his chrism may rightly be called *Christoi*, “anointed ones,” or “Christs.” Yet the whole body, together with its head, is one Christ.

These things were prophesied by Hannah, the mother of Samuel, a holy and greatly praised man. In him the change of the old priesthood was then represented in figure; and now it has been fulfilled, when she who had many children has become weak, so that the barren woman might bear seven and a new priesthood might exist in Christ.

We were compelled to insert this song according to the translation of the Septuagint interpreters, as it was set forth by the blessed Augustine, because that translation contains a fuller and truer narrative.

Meanwhile Samuel was ministering in the temple of God, girded with an *ephod*. But the sons of Heli sinned by violating the divine sacrifices, and through them many mocked the sacrifices of the Lord. Thus the priest Heli was condemned because of their iniquity, since he punished their sins with insufficient severity.

He did restrain them; he did rebuke them. But he did so with the gentleness and mildness of a father, not with the severity and authority of a high priest.

By this sentence priests should learn how they themselves are punished even for the crimes of their sons, and how, though they may be holy, the fault of their subordinates is imputed to them if they do not restrain them.

## III. Concerning the Prophecy to Heli and His Sons

### Chapter II

After this, a man of God sent to Heli the priest speaks more explicitly to Heli himself. His name is not given, but from his office and ministry it is undoubtedly understood that he was a prophet. For it is written:

“A man of God came to Heli and said to him:

‘Thus says the Lord: Was I not openly revealed to the house of your father when he was in Egypt, in Pharaoh’s house? And I chose him from all the sons of Israel for myself as priest, so that he might ascend my altar, burn incense for me, wear the *ephod* before me, and I gave to the house of your father all the sacrifices of the sons of Israel.

Why have you kicked away my victim and my offerings, which I commanded to be offered in the temple? And why have you honored your sons more than me, so that you might eat the first portions of every sacrifice of my people Israel?

Therefore the Lord, the God of Israel, says: I explicitly said that your house and the house of your father would minister in my presence forever.

But now the Lord says: Far be this from me. Rather, whoever glorifies me, I will glorify; but those who despise me will be held of no account.

Behold, the days are coming, and I will cut off your arm and the arm of your father’s house, so that there will be no old man in your house. You will see your rival, the Christ, in the temple, amid all the prosperity of Israel, and there will be no old man in your house for all your days.

Nevertheless, I will not utterly remove a man from you from my altar. But your eyes will fail and your soul will waste away, and a great part of your house will die when it reaches manhood.

This will be a sign for you concerning what will happen to your two sons, Hophni and Phinehas: on one day both will die.

And I will raise up for myself a faithful priest, who will act according to my heart and my soul.’”

It cannot be said that this prophecy, in which the change of the old priesthood was foretold with such clarity, was fulfilled in Samuel. For although Samuel belonged to a tribe that had been appointed by the Lord to serve at the altar, he was not descended from the sons of Aaron, whose lineage had been designated to produce the priests.

Thus in this historical event too the same change that was to come through Christ Jesus was foreshadowed. In its literal sense it belonged to the Old Testament, but figuratively it belonged to the New. The event itself was a prophecy—not in words but in deed—signifying by what happened what the prophet had said in words to the priest Heli.

For afterward, while David reigned, there were priests from the line of Aaron, such as Zadok and Abiathar, and others thereafter, before the time arrived when what had been foretold so long before concerning the change of the priesthood had to be accomplished through Christ.

But who, now looking upon these things with faithful eyes, did not see that they had been fulfilled, since no tabernacle, no temple, no altar, and no sacrifice—and therefore no priest—remains among the Jews, for whom it had been commanded in God’s law that priests should be appointed from the seed of Aaron?

This too is recalled here, when the prophet says:

“Thus says the Lord God of Israel: I explicitly said that your house and the house of your father would minister in my presence forever.

But now the Lord says: Far be this from me. Rather, whoever glorifies me, I will glorify; but those who despise me will be held of no account.”

When he names the house of his father, he is not speaking of Heli’s immediate father. The preceding words show that he is speaking of Aaron, who was the first priest appointed and from whose descendants the others were to follow. He says:

“I was openly revealed to the house of your father when he was in Egypt, in Pharaoh’s house, and I chose him from all the tribes of Israel for myself as priest.”

Which of Heli’s fathers was in that Egyptian servitude? When the Israelites had been liberated, who was chosen for the priesthood except Aaron?

It is therefore from Aaron’s line that he says in this passage that priests would no longer exist—a fact that we already see fulfilled.

Let faith keep watch: the three things are present, visible, tangible, and thrust before the eyes of those who refuse to see.

“Behold,” he says, “the days are coming, and I will cut off your arm and the arm of your house, so that there will be no old man in your house, and you will see your rival, the Christ, in the temple, amid all the prosperity of Israel.”

Behold, the days that were foretold have now come. There is no priest according to the order of Aaron. Whenever a man from his lineage sees the sacrifice of Christians prevailing throughout the world while that great honor has been taken away from him, his eyes fail and his soul wastes away from the decay of grief.

What follows applies specifically to the house of this Heli, to whom these words were addressed:

“And a great part of your house will die when it reaches manhood. This will be a sign for you concerning what will happen to your two sons, Hophni and Phinehas: on one day both will die.”

This sign was therefore given to the house as an indication that the priesthood would be changed. By this sign it was signified that the priesthood of Aaron’s house would be changed. The death of Heli’s sons signified not the death of individual men but the death of the priesthood itself, which had descended from the sons of Aaron.

## IV. On the Faithful Priest

What follows now pertains to that priest whose figure Samuel represented by succeeding him [Col. 1054B]. Accordingly, what follows is said of Christ Jesus, the true priest of the New Testament:

> “I will raise up for myself a faithful priest, who shall act according to my heart and my soul.”

Under the figure of Samuel, this must be understood of the Lord and Savior, the supreme and true high priest, who, just as Samuel succeeded the deceased Eli in the priesthood, was chosen not from the stock of Aaron but from another family of Levi. For, as we have already recalled above, he was the son of Elkanah, son of Jeroboam, son of Thau, son of Suph, son of Elkanah, son of Joel, son of Azariah, son of Zephaniah, son of Thahath, son of Assir, son of Abiasaph, son of Korah, son of Izhar, son of Kohath, son of Levi, son of Israel (1 Kings I; 1 Chronicles VI), as the Books of Chronicles relate.

Thus the mediator of God and human beings, in order to be our high priest, took the origin of his flesh not from Levi but from another tribe, namely from Judah; he offered the Father on our behalf another sacrifice than the legal one—that is, his own flesh; and he left as heirs of his priesthood others than those descended from Aaron, namely the sons of the grace of the New Testament, gathered from every nation of the Gentiles.

But when God speaks, as though in human fashion, saying, “who shall act according to my heart and my soul,” this can rightly be understood of Samuel, in that as a human being he obeyed God’s will in everything; and of the Lord and Savior, in that, as the only-begotten Son, he is in all things aware of the Father’s hidden purposes, according to what he himself plainly testifies concerning himself:

> “Of myself I do nothing, but as the Father taught me, so I speak; and he who sent me is with me, and he has not left me alone, because I always do what pleases him” (John VIII).

But when God says that he does everything that is in his heart and in his soul, we do not think that God has a soul, since he is the creator of the soul. Rather, this is said figuratively, not literally, of God, just as “hand,” “foot,” and the other bodily members are said of him. And lest anyone should therefore believe that the human being was made in the image of God according to the likeness of this flesh, wings are also attributed to him, which human beings certainly do not possess; thus it is said to God:

> “Protect me beneath the shadow of your wings” (Psalm XVI),

so that people may understand that such things are said of that ineffable nature not by proper but by transferred terms.

> “And I will build for him a faithful house, and he shall walk before my Christ all his days.”

This is the house that the Father builds, of which the Apostle says:

> “We are that house, if we hold firmly to the end the confidence and glory of hope” (Hebrews III).

And this house shall walk before his Christ, namely before the supreme high priest himself. He said “shall walk,” that is, “shall live and conduct itself,” just as he had earlier said concerning the house of Aaron:

> “I spoke and indeed declared that your house and the house of your father should minister in my sight forever.”

But when he says, “It shall walk before my Christ,” this must certainly be understood of the house itself, not of that priest who is Christ, the mediator and Savior. His house, therefore, shall walk before him.

“Shall walk” may also be understood as passing from death to life throughout all the days during which this mortality is carried on, until the end of the present age. Otherwise, how can it be understood of Samuel that a faithful house was built which would proceed before Christ the Lord—that is, before Samuel himself—throughout all days, when we read later that his sons turned aside from his ways, followed greed, and perverted judgment? Unless perhaps by his house here we understand the Israelite people, which throughout all the days of his priesthood served the Lord. Of this it is written:

> “And all the house of Israel rested after the Lord”;

and shortly afterward:

> “The children of Israel removed the Baals and the Astartes, and served the Lord alone.”

But what is added—“It shall come to pass that whoever remains in your house shall come, so that he may be prayed for”—is not said literally of the house of this Eli, but of that of Aaron, from which people remained until the coming of Jesus Christ and from which some still remain even now. For concerning the house of this Eli it had already been said above:

> “Everyone who survives from your house shall fall by the sword of men.”

How, then, could it truly be said here, “He who remains in your house shall come, so that he may be prayed for,” if it is true that no one would survive from it under the avenging sword? It is because he wished those people to be understood who belong to the stock of that entire priesthood according to the order of Aaron.

Therefore, if these are the predestined remnants of which another prophet said, “The remnants shall be saved” (Isaiah X)—whence the Apostle also says, “So therefore, at the present time also remnants have been saved according to the election of grace” (Romans XI)—then it is rightly understood of such remnants that it was said, “He who remains in your house.” Certainly, he believes in Christ, just as in the time of the apostles many from that people believed, and even now there are some, though very few, who believe. In him is fulfilled what this man of God immediately added:

> “And he shall offer a silver coin and a round loaf of bread, and shall say, ‘Dismiss me, I beg you, to one priestly portion, so that I may eat a morsel of bread.’”

What is signified by the silver coin, if not the confession of the mouth, which is made by believers for salvation? Silver is ordinarily used for speech, as the Psalmist testifies where it is sung:

> “The sayings of the Lord are pure sayings, silver tested by fire, proved, purified from the earth” (Psalm XI).

But when the one who comes says, “Dismiss me, I beg you, to one priestly portion, so that I may eat a morsel of bread,” he calls the priestly portion the body of Christ, that is, the Church, whose priest is that mediator of God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus. To this people the apostle Peter says:

> “A holy people, a royal priesthood” (1 Peter II).

He asks to eat a morsel of bread in this priestly portion. In these words the sacrifice of Christians is elegantly expressed, concerning which the priest himself says:

> “The bread that I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world.”

This is the sacrifice—not according to the order of Aaron, but according to the order of Melchizedek.

## V. On the Dimness of Eli’s Eyes

### Chapter III

> “It came to pass one day that Eli was lying in his place, and his eyes had grown dim, and he could not see the lamp of God before it was extinguished.”

In the tabernacle of the covenant there was a lampstand whose lamps, prepared outside the veil, burned continually from evening until morning, with the high priest arranging them each evening, as the Lord had commanded. When this priest entered the tabernacle, already worn down by advanced old age, his eyes had grown so dim that he could not even look at a lighted lamp—how much less at an extinguished one?

Figuratively, Eli had been the lamp of God when, possessing the dignity of the priesthood, he shone with the justice of brightness. The prophet declares that this lamp was extinguished when, on account of his sons’ crimes, he lost the power of the priesthood and the light of his merits.

> “But Samuel grew, and the Lord was with him, and none of all his words fell to the ground.”

This signifies that nothing of what he said was ineffectual, but everything he declared was fulfilled in events. For empty words fall to the ground: they are to be regarded as nothing and trampled under universal contempt, just as blessed Job also said:

> “The light of my face did not fall to the ground.”

He was accustomed to hold his face with such gravity that he was never relaxed by contemptible merriment; but whenever he displayed himself as more cheerful to those present, he always did so for some definite reason connected with their benefit.

## VI. On the Captivity of the Ark

### Chapter IV

After these things had been foretold by that prophet to Eli as a figure of the change of the Old Testament, Israel having offended the Lord, the Philistines drew up their battle line against them. The Israelites brought the ark to their position, but the ark was captured by the enemies; they themselves were not merely defeated and put to flight, but a great slaughter of the slain also took place.

This event signifies certain future things. For in prophecy the ark captured by foreigners indicated that God’s covenant would pass to the Gentiles. When Eli the priest was told that the ark of the Lord had been captured, he fell from his seat and died. When the ark of the Lord passed to the Gentiles, the Jewish priesthood perished and came to an end.

The two sons of Eli also fell; one wife was widowed and soon afterward died in childbirth because of the same upheaval. This was prefigured by a clear sign: after the Jewish priesthood had been extinguished, the carnal Synagogue, which clung to it carnally, would perish. When Eli was thrown from his seat, the Jewish high priests had their seat left vacant, and the glory of the priesthood and of the kingdom was extinguished.

But what does it mean that, when the Philistines had placed the ark of the Lord in the temple of their god Dagon, they entered the temple and found their god thrown down and shattered, with his head and both his hands cut off? As soon as the Lord’s covenant reached the Gentiles, the idols that had possessed the deceived world were immediately destroyed, and all the error of images collapsed, unable to endure the presence of God. In Dagon’s severed hands, the end of idolatry can be recognized; for the threshold signifies the end of a journey.

The following also pertains to a profound significance in the very fall and breaking of Dagon their god: they found only his back, all his other limbs having been broken. The back signifies flight, for those who flee turn their backs to their pursuers. Hence it is written concerning the enemies:

> “You shall make them turn their backs” (Psalm XX).

Where idols have perished, even if some remain hidden by certain people, they have fled.

But the fact that those who captured the ark of God were struck in their hind parts seems to have been signified by this punishment: if some receive the covenant of God yet love the things behind them, they will be tortured most justly by those very things which, according to the Apostle, they ought to regard as refuse. Those who receive the divine covenant in such a way that, looking back, they do not strip off their old vanity are like those enemies who placed the ark of the covenant beside their idols.

Those things, however, truly fall, even though those attached to them are unwilling, because:

> “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass. The grass withered, and the flower fell” (Isaiah XL).

But the ark of the Lord remains forever: namely, the hidden covenant of the kingdom of heaven, where the word of God remains.

## VII. On the Return of the Ark

### Chapter VI

When the ark of the Lord returned from the land of the Philistines to the land of the Israelites, it was placed upon a cart, and cows were yoked to the cart. They are said to have been cows that had calved, whose calves they had shut up at home, as it is written:

> “The cows went straight along the road that leads to Beth-shemesh; they proceeded along one path, going and lowing, and they did not turn either to the right or to the left.”

What, then, do the cows signify except the faithful in the Church, who, when they attend to the precepts of sacred discourse, carry the ark of the Lord as though it had been placed upon them?

It should also be noted concerning them that they are said to have been cows that had calved, because there are many who, though placed inwardly on the way of God, are bound outwardly by carnal affections. Yet the one who carries the ark of God in his mind does not turn aside from the straight path. Behold, the cows proceed to Beth-shemesh.

Beth-shemesh means “house of the sun.” The Prophet says:

> “But for you who fear the Lord, the sun of righteousness shall rise.”

If, then, we are striving toward the dwelling of the eternal Sun, it is certainly fitting that we should not turn aside from God’s path on account of carnal affections. For we must consider with all our strength that the cows yoked to God’s cart proceed and groan. They utter lowings from their inmost depths, yet do not turn their steps back from the road. They feel love through compassion, but do not turn their necks backward.

So preachers, and so all the faithful within the holy Church, ought to be: they should sympathize with their neighbors through charity, yet not deviate from God’s way through compassion.

For the ark placed upon the cart proceeding to Beth-shemesh means advancing with heavenly knowledge toward the dwelling of inward light. But we truly strive toward Beth-shemesh when, walking along the way of uprightness, we do not turn toward the neighboring paths of error because of affection for our loved ones.

This is how, indeed, those who have been placed under sacred obligations and now carry the ark of the Lord through inward knowledge must walk: they should grieve over the needs of their relatives, yet not turn aside from the path of uprightness once they have entered it. Their example ought to govern our mind, so that this same mind may be neither hard if it is not touched by affection nor lax if it is bent by being touched too deeply.

## VIII. On the Slaughter of the Men of Beth-shemesh

He struck the men of Beth-shemesh because they had looked upon the ark of the Lord; he struck seventy men of the people and fifty thousand of the populace.

“People” and “populace” are used indiscriminately for one and the same thing, for both are commonly translated from the one Greek word λαός (*laos*). But there appears to be a distinction in this respect: in the first clause of the verse the word “men” has been added, and “men” signifies those of more advanced age, that is, elders. The meaning, then, is: seventy of the leaders of the people were struck, but fifty thousand of the common crowd.

So that the people would not suffer this in Exodus, they stood at a distance and prayed, while Moses alone went up to the Lord. These men were struck by God because they not only approached but also, as another translation has it, “looked with contempt”—which is more consistent with reason.

For in Exodus they saw and heard, they perceived the manifest displays of divine power, and they did not perish. Therefore these men were punished not for seeing but for contempt and presumption.

## IX. On the Statement, “From the Day …”

### Chapter VII

> “It came to pass that from the day when the ark of the Lord remained in Kiriath-jearim, the days multiplied. It was already the twentieth year, and all the house of Israel rested after the Lord.”

This should not be understood as though the twenty years during which the ark remained in Kiriath-jearim were to be counted up to the eighth year of David’s reign, when he brought it to Jerusalem with a great gathering of the people.

For it is found later that, in the time of Saul, it was carried from this city and brought into the camp while he was fighting against the Philistines. Thus it is written:

> “And Saul said to Ahimelech, ‘Bring the ark of God.’ For the ark of God was with the children of Israel on that day.”

And since it is established that David brought it to Jerusalem from the house of Abinadab, into which it is now said to have been brought, it remains to be understood that in Saul’s days it was brought back from the camp and carried into the aforesaid city, from which it was again brought to Jerusalem during David’s reign.

The meaning of this obscure statement, then, is that from the time when the ark remained in Kiriath-jearim, it was the twentieth year when it happened to be moved from there in Saul’s time on account of the war. Or certainly, it was the twentieth year while all the house of Israel still rested after the Lord, having cast away their idols and serving him alone.

No diligent student of sacred history is unaware that Israel did this throughout the entire period of Samuel’s leadership—which, according to Josephus, lasted twelve years—and during the first period of Saul’s reign, which, according to the same historian, lasted twenty years. For afterward, when the Spirit of the Lord had departed from Saul and an evil spirit troubled him, especially to persecute David, who was innocent and just, it was necessary that some portion of his army or people should have become accomplices in his wickedness.

Kiriath-jearim is the same city that is also called Kiriath-baal, “city of forests.” It was one of the cities of the Gibeonites, belonging to the tribe of Judah, for those traveling from Jerusalem to Diospolis at the ninth milestone. Uriah the prophet, whom Jehoiakim killed in Jerusalem, came from this place, as it is written.

Samuel, however, governed Israel after Eli’s death.

## X. On Samuel’s Prayers for the People

### Chapter VIII

When all the people had been gathered, he cried out to the Lord for Israel, and the Lord heard him. When he was offering a burnt offering, as the foreigners advanced to battle against the people of God, the Lord thundered against them; they were thrown into confusion, fell before Israel, and were defeated.

Then Samuel took one stone and placed it between Mizpah and Shen. As the translators of the Septuagint rendered it, he placed it between “new Mizpah and old Mizpah,” and he called its name “Stone of Help,” saying:

> “Thus far the Lord has helped us.”

Mizpah means “watchfulness” or “intentness.” That Stone of Help is the mediator, the Savior, through whom one must pass from the old Mizpah to the new: from the expectation directed toward a carnal kingdom, which was a false blessedness, to the expectation directed through the New Testament toward the kingdom of heaven, where the truest spiritual blessedness is found. Since nothing is better than this, God helps us to this point.

This Samuel, having called upon the name of the Lord, was heard by God, and at the time of harvest he obtained rain. For in the sacred Scriptures rain signifies the words of the Gospel or of the Law, just as Moses says:

> “Let my discourse be awaited like rain, and let my words descend like dew” (Deuteronomy XXXII).

Christ therefore gave this rain to the world at the time of harvest, that is, when the Gentiles had to be gathered, so that, like grain in granaries, they might be gathered into the bosom of the Church.

Samuel judged Israel throughout all the days of his life, and judges and leaders were over Israel down to his time.

## XI. On Samuel’s Sons

### Chapter IX

Samuel’s sons turned aside after greed and accepted gifts. They became such unjust judges that the people, unable to endure them, requested a king for themselves in imitation of the other nations. The Lord gave them Saul as king while he was seeking his father’s donkeys and came to Samuel at Ramah.

Among the other things they said, Samuel also foretold to him the signs that would happen to him that day when he departed from him. After he had left him, he came to the hill of God, where there was a Philistine garrison; the first event had already taken place, just as the man of God had said.

And behold, a band of prophets met him, and the Spirit of God rushed upon him, and he prophesied in their midst. When all who had known him yesterday and the day before saw that he was with the prophets, they said to one another:

> “What has happened to the son of Kish? Is Saul also among the prophets?”

I do not think there is anything difficult about this. For:

> “The Spirit breathes where he wills” (John III),

and no contact with any soul can defile the spirit of prophecy. Because of its purity, it touches everything everywhere. It affects everyone in different ways: some through the shaping of their own spirit, where images of things are displayed; others through the mind’s fruition in understanding; others through both kinds of inspiration.

It also affects some who are unaware, through the shaping of their spirit, in two ways: either through dreams, as not only many holy people but also Pharaoh and King Nebuchadnezzar saw what none of them could understand, although both could see it; or through a manifestation in ecstasy. Some Latins interpret this as “terror,” which is surprising if taken strictly, though it is related in meaning.

In ecstasy there is an alienation of the mind from the bodily senses, so that the human spirit, seized by the divine Spirit, is free to receive and contemplate images, as was shown to Daniel, who did not understand what was shown to him. Likewise, the vessel descended to Peter from heaven by its four corners (Acts X); he too later came to know what that manifestation signified.

Through the mind’s fruition in understanding, prophecy occurs in one way when the meaning and purpose of the very things displayed in images are revealed. This is the more certain form of prophecy. The Apostle more particularly calls this prophecy, just as Joseph was granted understanding of what Pharaoh could only see, and Daniel explained to the king what the king perceived but did not know.

But when the mind is affected in such a way that it understands not the images of things through conjectural examination but the things themselves, as wisdom and justice are understood, then every unchangeable and divine reality does not belong to the prophecy of which we are now speaking.

Those who are endowed with both gifts of prophecy see images of things in the spirit and understand at the same time what they signify; or else they are instructed through clear utterances within the manifestation itself, as certain things are explained in the Apocalypse.

The spirit of prophecy also affects those who are unaware, as when Caiaphas, being high priest, prophesied about the Lord that it was expedient for one man to die for the whole people, while he had something else in mind in the words he spoke and did not know that he was speaking them not from himself. Examples abound in the holy books.

By the expression “the spirit rushed upon him,” a sudden inspiration is signified, as though arising from the hidden secrecy of divinity.

Which of these modes, then, should we understand Saul to have experienced? This is sufficiently clear from what is written there:

> “God changed Saul’s heart into another heart.”

For by changing it, God signifies that he produced a different affection of the heart, so that Saul might become capable of prophetic divination through images that signified and prefigured things.

There is as much difference between the prophecy of prophets such as Isaiah, Jeremiah, and the others of that kind, and the passing prophecy that appeared in Saul, as there is between human speech when human beings speak and that same speech when, through a necessary prodigy, the she-ass on which the prophet Balaam was sitting spoke (Numbers XXII). That animal received this ability for that moment so that God might reveal what he had determined, not so that the beast might speak by a permanent habit.

Or, if this example is too remote because of the greater difference involved, it is even less surprising that a reprobate man was given prophecy for a moment through a passing experience, since the one who gave it also made the she-ass speak when he wished. A beast is farther removed from a human being than a reprobate human being is from elect human beings.

For if someone says something pertaining to wisdom, he is not immediately to be considered wise. Likewise, if someone prophesies on one occasion, he is not thereby counted among the prophets, since the Lord also says in the Gospel that some receive the word with joy but have no depth of root and are temporary.

Therefore, as the subsequent reading indicates, it happened “in a proverb”:

> “Is Saul also among the prophets?” (1 Samuel X).

Let us cease, then, to marvel when something divine appears in human beings that exceeds either their merit or their habitual condition, whenever God wishes something of a particular significance to be revealed through it.

If it troubles anyone that Saul was later seized and strangled by an evil spirit, although he had earlier received the spirit of prophecy, this too should not be surprising. The former occurred as part of a providential arrangement for signifying something; the latter occurred as a merited punishment.
