Nor should these alternations in the human mind—that is, in a mutable creature—trouble us, especially while the corruptible and mortal flesh is being carried. Do we not see in Peter himself, as the Gospel indicates, such a great confession that he deserved to hear:

> “Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew XVI)?

And shortly afterward did he not think so carnally about the Lord’s passion that he immediately heard:

> “Get behind me, Satan; you are a stumbling block to me, for you do not understand the things of God but those of human beings” (ibid.)?

Perhaps, for those who understand somewhat more deeply, this difference between those visions of the mind is as significant as the distinction between the vision that Peter understood when God the Father revealed that he was the Christ, the Son of God, and the later vision in which he feared that he should die. It corresponds to the distinction between the visions that occur imaginatively in the human spirit when the mind is alienated, the prophetic revelation with which Saul was first inspired, and the mingling of the evil spirit by which he was later oppressed.

## XII. On Saul’s Anointing

### Chapter X

After this, at the Lord’s command, the first king was anointed by the prophet for the kingdom. In what he was anointed for, he himself also bore an image of Christ. Hence blessed David, who was himself also called “Christ,” said to the man who falsely claimed to have killed Saul:

> “How were you not afraid to raise your hand against the Lord’s Christ?”

This is why Saul towered above everyone from the shoulders upward: our head is above us, raised up, and this is Christ.

But in the fact that, after being rejected, he was later displaced when David succeeded him in the kingdom, he represented the person of the people of Israel. That people had obtained a kingdom which it was destined to lose when Christ our Lord came to reign through the New Testament, not carnally but spiritually.

Saul was the son of one year when he began to reign, and he reigned over Israel for two years. For one year after he had been chosen king by Samuel, he sat in his domestic house and concealed the fact that he was king. During the remaining two years he publicly judged all Israel, maintaining obedience with humility. This was the period before he transgressed the Lord’s commandment concerning Amalek. Throughout the remaining time of his life and reign, he was a transgressor of the Lord’s commandment.

After this, Saul waited for Samuel at Gilgal. When he saw that Samuel was late, he offered the burnt offering. When Samuel came, he said among other things to Saul:

> “You have acted foolishly and have not kept the commandment of the Lord, which he commanded you. If you had not done this, the Lord would by now have established your kingdom over Israel forever. But your kingdom shall certainly not continue. The Lord has sought for himself a man according to his heart, and he has appointed him leader over his people, because you have not kept what the Lord commanded you.”

This should not be understood as though God had prepared Saul himself to reign forever and later refused to preserve this arrangement when Saul sinned. For God did not fail to know him; rather, he had prepared Saul’s kingdom as a figure of the eternal kingdom.

Therefore he added:

> “And now your kingdom shall not stand for you.”

What was signified in Saul stood and shall stand, but it does not stand for Saul, because he was not destined to reign forever, nor was his offspring, so that the statement “forever” might at least appear to be fulfilled through descendants succeeding one another.

> “And the Lord will seek for himself a man,”

he says—whether David, or the mediator of the New Testament himself, who was prefigured in the anointing, by which David himself and his descendants were also anointed.

God does not seek a man as though he were unaware of these things; rather, he speaks to human beings in human fashion, because by speaking in this way he seeks us. For not only were we known to God the Father, but also to his only-begotten Son, who came to seek what had been lost, so fully were we already known to him that we had been chosen in him before the foundation of the world.

“Will seek for himself,” he said, meaning “will have his own.” Hence in the Latin language this verb takes a preposition and becomes *acquirit* (“acquires”), whose meaning is quite clear. Yet even without the added preposition, *quaerere* (“to seek”) can be understood as “to acquire”; hence profits and gains are so called.

Moreover, no blacksmith was found throughout all Israel, for the Philistines had taken precautions lest the Hebrews make swords or spears.

Just as the Philistines had then taken precautions lest the Hebrews make swords or spears and lest they have blacksmiths to produce weapons for resistance, so the Chaldeans, after destroying Jerusalem and laying waste the whole land of promise, endeavored to leave no craftsman there, no metalworker who could either repair the defiled walls of the city or mend what had been torn apart. Rather, whatever craftsmanship they found among the exterminated people, they transferred entirely to Babylon, so that it might either be rendered useless thereafter or serve the needs of that city.

What are the weapons with which, while fighting against the devil, we defend the freedom granted to us by the Lord, if not the sayings of the Scriptures? In them we learn with the greatest clarity, from the examples of the Lord himself and of his saints, by what order the battles against vices are to be overcome.

But the Philistines deprive the children of Israel of weaponsmiths when evil spirits burden the minds of the faithful with such great crimes that they are utterly ashamed to speak the good things they had learned. They insert worldly occupations into them and thus delay them from meditating on sacred reading, so that they may neither gain confidence through the exercise of resistance nor perhaps kindle others who do not know how to read by exhorting or correcting them toward resistance to vices.

## XIII. On the Fast Proclaimed by Saul

### Chapter XIV

They remove the weaponsmiths when they overwhelm those who know the sacred utterances with such great crimes that they become completely ashamed to say the good things they had learned.

After this, as Saul was proceeding to fight against the Philistines, he proclaimed a fast for the entire army until they returned from battle. But Jonathan, his son, saw honey upon the surface of the field; he extended the tip of his staff, dipped it into the honeycomb, and tasted it, and his eyes were enlightened.

They were not enlightened so as to see, since he had seen before, but so as to discern, because he had touched what was forbidden. That fall, like Adam’s, made him attentive and rendered him ashamed. By this we were all admonished that those who strive to serve God must despise the allurements of pleasures in the world. For one who still neglects to avoid the sweetness of this world cannot contend with the spiritual foreigners—that is, against the rulers of darkness—with the strength of the mind.

> “The lips of the adulterous woman drip honey” (Proverbs III),

which signifies the delight of carnal pleasure. According to mystical interpretations, Jonathan is thought to have tasted this honey, and perhaps, after being discovered, to have been freed only through the prayers of the people.

## XIV. On Saul’s Battle against Amalek. Chapter XV

Saul again entered into battle against Amalek, killing all the enemies from Havilah to Shur. There is one Havilah, a region around which the river Phison flows as it issues from Paradise; today it is called India. It was called Havilah after a certain grandson of Noah. There is also another Havilah, a wilderness facing Egypt; the latter should be called *Havila*, the former *Havilah*. Shur too is a wilderness between Kadesh and Bered, extending the desert as far as the Red Sea and the borders of Egypt.

After striking this region, Saul spared Agag the king and was unwilling to destroy everything according to the Lord’s command; and the Lord became angry with him. The word of the Lord came to Samuel, saying: “I repent that I made Saul king, because he has forsaken me and has not fulfilled my words in action.”

[Col. 1061C] For God does not repent of any deed of his in the same way as a human being does; his judgment concerning all things is as fixed as his foreknowledge is certain. Yet when we hear this said of God in the divine Scriptures, we consider it unworthy to think this about him. Something must therefore be said by which this may in some fashion be demonstrated.

Since his eternal power and divinity wonderfully and unmistakably surpass all the words by which human conversations are carried on, whenever something is said of him in human terms—even something that human beings themselves would regard as objectionable—human weakness is thereby reminded that even those things which it considers appropriately spoken of God in the holy Scriptures are more suited to human capacity than to divine sublimity. For this reason, even these expressions must themselves be transcended by a sounder understanding, just as they have been transcended in whatever way is possible here.

Who is there among human beings to whom it would not occur that, since God foreknows everything, repentance cannot exist in him? Yet there are these two words, “repentance” and “foreknowledge.” Because we believe that one of them—foreknowledge—can properly be applied to God, we deny that repentance exists in him.

[Col. 1061D] But when another person, examining these matters with clearer consideration, asks how foreknowledge itself can properly be attributed to God, and discovers that even the meaning of this word is surpassed far and high by his ineffable divinity, he will not be surprised that both expressions could be used of him for the sake of human beings, although neither could appropriately be used of him in relation to himself.

For what is foreknowledge except knowledge of future things? But what is future for God, who transcends all times? If God’s knowledge possesses the things themselves, and they are not future for him but present, then it may no longer be called foreknowledge but knowledge. If, however, just as things are not yet present in the order of temporal creatures, so also they are not yet present for him, but he anticipates them by knowing them, then he experiences them twice: once according to foreknowledge of future things, and again according to knowledge of present things.

[Col. 1062A] Something temporal would therefore happen to God’s knowledge, which is utterly absurd and false. For he could not know what he foreknows will come unless he knew it when it came—unless it became known to him twice: first by foreknowing it before it existed, and then by knowing it when it already existed. Thus something temporal would happen to God’s knowledge, although this is far removed from the truth: temporal things that are foreknown are later experienced as present, though they were not previously experienced as present.

If, however, when the things foreknown to come have arrived, nothing new happens to God’s knowledge, but that foreknowledge remains as it was even before the foreknown things came, how could it still be called foreknowledge when the things are no longer future? What he saw as future is now present, and shortly afterward will be past. Yet the knowledge of past things, just as of present things, cannot in any way be called foreknowledge.

We are therefore brought back to the conclusion that what was foreknowledge when things were future becomes knowledge when those same things are present. And if what was previously foreknowledge later becomes knowledge in God, this admits change and makes him temporal, although God truly and supremely is, is in no respect changeable, and does not become temporal through any novel movement.

[Col. 1062B] It is therefore preferable not to speak of foreknowledge, but only of knowledge. Let us ask how even this is possible. We customarily speak of knowledge in ourselves only when we retain through memory what we have sensed and understood, when we remember having sensed or understood something so that we may recall what we wish.

If this is the case in God—if it can properly be said that he understands and has understood, senses and has sensed—then time is admitted, and that changeability which must be removed far from God’s substance enters as well. Yet God both knows and foreknows in an ineffable manner; in an ineffable manner, therefore, he also repents.

For God’s knowledge is so far removed from human knowledge that the comparison itself deserves ridicule, yet both are called knowledge. Human knowledge is such that the Apostle even says of it, “Knowledge will be destroyed” (1 Cor. XIII). This cannot rightly be said of God’s knowledge.

Similarly, human anger is turbulent and not without mental anguish. But God’s anger, of which it is said in the Gospel, “But the wrath of God remains upon him” (John III), and which the Apostle describes thus: “For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness” (Rom. I), exercises vengeance upon the subjected creature with marvelous equity while God himself remains perpetually tranquil.

[Col. 1062C] Human mercy too is accompanied by a certain misery of the heart; hence it even received its name in Latin. This is why the Apostle exhorts us not only to rejoice with those who rejoice but also to weep with those who weep (Rom. XII). Yet who in his right mind would say that God is touched by any misery? Nevertheless, Scripture everywhere testifies that he is merciful.

Thus we understand human jealousy as inseparable from the disease of envy, but God’s jealousy otherwise: the same word, but not the same manner.

It would take too long to go through the remaining examples. There are countless cases showing that many divine realities are called by the same names as human realities, although they are separated from them by an incomparable difference. Yet the same names have not been given to both kinds of things without reason. These familiar realities, which occur in daily life and become known through ordinary experience, provide some sort of path toward understanding those sublime realities.

[Col. 1062D] If I remove from human knowledge the changeability by which we recall certain transitions from thought to thought, so that the mind sees what was not present in its contemplation a moment earlier, and by frequent acts of recollection leaps from one part to another—on which account the Apostle also says that our knowledge is “in part”—then, when I have removed all these things and retained only the vitality of certain and unshaken truth, illuminating by one eternal contemplation—indeed, when I have not retained it, since human knowledge does not possess this, but have thought about it as far as my strength permits—God’s knowledge is somehow disclosed to me.

This name could nevertheless be common to both realities because, through knowing, something is not hidden from a human being. Even among human beings, knowledge is usually distinguished from wisdom, as the Apostle also says: “To one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom, to another a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit” (1 Cor. XII).

[Col. 1063A] In God, however, these are not two things but one. Among human beings they are commonly and plausibly distinguished in such a way that wisdom concerns the understanding of eternal things, while knowledge concerns what we experience through the bodily senses.

But although someone may propose another distinction, unless the two were different the Apostle would not distinguish them in this manner. If, however, the word “knowledge” must be assigned to things that we experience through bodily sensation, then God has no knowledge at all; for God does not consist, as a human being does, of body and soul.

It is better, then, to say that God’s knowledge is different and not of the same kind as that which is called human knowledge. Even the thing called “God” is something altogether different from the meaning intended when it is said that he “stood in the assembly of gods.” Nevertheless, the shared word in both cases has to do in some way with not being hidden.

In the same way, from human anger I remove turbulent movement, leaving the force of vengeance; thus I rise, as best I can, toward an understanding of what is called God’s anger.

[Col. 1063B] Again, from mercy, if you remove compassion for the one whose misery you pity—your participation in his misery—what remains is the tranquil goodness of helping and freeing from misery; and this gives some sort of understanding of divine mercy.

Nor should we reject or disdain jealousy when we find it written in Scripture. Let us instead remove from human jealousy the pale wasting of grief and the diseased disturbance of the mind. Let only that judgment remain by which corruption of chastity is not allowed to go unpunished; then we rise toward beginning, in some fashion, to grasp God’s jealousy.

Therefore, when we read God himself saying, “I repent” (Gen. VI), let us consider what the act of repentance ordinarily is among human beings. It certainly involves the will to change, but in a human being it is accompanied by mental anguish, because he reproaches himself for having acted rashly.

Let us remove, then, those features that arise from human weakness and ignorance, and let only the willing remain: that something should not be as it was. In this way our mind can to some extent be instructed by what rule we should understand God’s repentance.

[Col. 1063C] When it is said that God repents, he wills that something not be as it was when he had made it to be. Yet while it was such that it ought to be such, once it is no longer permitted to be such, it ought no longer to be such. This occurs according to that perpetual and tranquil judgment of equity by which God, through an unchangeable will, orders all changeable things.

Just as we habitually speak of foreknowledge and knowledge with praise when referring to human beings, and the human race tends to fear anger itself in great authorities rather than reproach it, we think that such expressions can appropriately be used of God.

But one who is jealous, or whom something causes to repent, is ordinarily either blamed or corrects some fault in himself. For this reason, when such expressions are used of human beings, they carry reproach; and this is why we are disturbed when we read that something of this kind exists in God.

Yet Scripture, caring for everyone, includes these expressions precisely so that those which please us may not be understood in God in the manner in which they are customarily understood among human beings. Through the things that displease us—when we do not see them understood in the way in which they are found in human beings—we learn also to seek those things which we had thought suitable and fitting in a different way.

[Col. 1063D] For if something should not be said of God because it is objectionable in a human being, then we should not call God unchangeable, since “there is no change” among human beings was spoken with reproach (Ps. LIV).

There are also certain things that are praiseworthy in a human being but cannot exist in God, such as shame, which is a great ornament of vigorous youth, and the fear of God. The latter is praised not only in the ancient books; the Apostle also says, “Perfecting holiness in the fear of God” (2 Cor. VII). Yet there is no fear of God in God himself.

Thus certain things that are rightly praised in human beings are rightly understood in God—not in the same way as in human beings, but merely under the same names and with an utterly different reason and manner.

[Col. 1064A] A little later, the same Samuel, to whom the Lord had said, “I repent that I made Saul king,” says to Saul concerning God: “For he is not like a human being, that he should repent.” Here he plainly shows that even when God says, “I repent,” it must not be understood according to human custom, as far as we have been able to explain.

## XV. On Samuel’s Rebuke of Saul. Chapter XV

When Samuel came to Saul … he said to Saul: “Wait, and I will tell you what the Lord spoke to me during the night.” He replied, “Speak.” And Samuel said: “Were you not small in your own eyes when you were made head over the tribes of Israel?”

A person is “small in his own eyes” when, considering himself, he judges himself inferior to the merits of others. Whoever stretches himself above the merits of others through the arrogance of his thoughts regards himself as great.

Saul, however, did not remain in the goodness with which he had begun, because he swelled with pride at the power he had received. David, by contrast, always thinking humbly of himself and placing himself below Saul by comparison with him, spared him when he found an opportunity to strike him. He humbled himself before that raging adversary, saying: “Whom are you pursuing, king of Israel? Whom are you pursuing? A dead dog and a single flea.”

He had certainly already been anointed king. [Col. 1064B] Samuel had already made supplication, and, pouring oil from the horn upon him, had taught him that divine grace was preserving him to govern the kingdom after Saul had been rejected. Yet David humbly subjected himself in spirit to the adversary who pursued him, although he knew by divine judgment that he had been placed above him.

He therefore humbly placed himself below the man whom he knew himself, by the grace of election, to be incomparably better than.

Samuel rebuked Saul for not listening to the Lord’s voice but turning to the spoil and doing evil in the Lord’s sight by sparing Amalek and not killing him. Samuel said: “Does the Lord desire burnt offerings and sacrifices, and not rather that the Lord’s voice should be obeyed? For obedience is better than sacrifices, and to listen better than to offer the fat of rams. For rebellion is like the sin of divination, and refusal to comply is like the crime of idolatry. Because you have rejected the word of the Lord, he has rejected you from being king.”

Obedience is rightly placed before sacrifices, because through sacrifices another’s flesh is slaughtered, but through obedience one’s own will is sacrificed. [Col. 1064C] Therefore, a person appeases God all the more quickly as, having suppressed the pride of his own will before God’s eyes, he offers himself with the sword of the commandment.

Disobedience is called like the sin of divination in order to show how great is the virtue of obedience. Its praise is therefore made clearer by contrast. If rebellion is like the sin of divination, and refusal to comply like the crime of idolatry, then obedience alone possesses the merit of faith; without it, anyone is proved unbelieving, even if he appears faithful.

Hence Solomon says in praise of obedience: “An obedient man speaks of victories” (Prov. XXI). An obedient man speaks of victories because, when we humbly submit to another’s voice, we conquer ourselves in our hearts.

For this reason Truth says in the Gospel: “The one who comes to me I will certainly not cast out, because I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will but the will of him who sent me” (John VI).

What if he had done his own will? He would have driven away those who came to him. Yet who does not know that the Son’s will does not differ from the Father’s will? But because the first human being, who wished to do his own will, departed from the joy of Paradise, the second, coming for the redemption of human beings and showing that he did the Father’s will rather than his own, taught us to remain within.

When, therefore, he does not his own will but the Father’s, he does not cast out those who come to him, because by subjecting us to obedience through his example, he closes the way by which we might depart.

[Col. 1064D] Samuel then turned to leave. But Saul seized the edge of his cloak, and it was torn. Samuel said to him: “The Lord has torn the kingdom of Israel from you today and has given it to your neighbor, who is better than you.”

We are compelled to include this statement according to the translation of the Seventy, because it contains much more there. It is written there as follows:

“I will not return with you, because you have rejected the word of the Lord, and the Lord will reject you, so that you may not be king over Israel.” And Samuel turned his face to leave, and Saul seized the edge of his double cloak and tore it. Samuel said to him: “The Lord will tear the kingdom of Israel from your hand today and give it to your good neighbor, one better than you. [Col. 1065A] Israel will be divided in two, and he will not turn back, nor will he repent, because he is not like a human being, that he should repent. He threatens, but does not remain”—that is, a human being threatens but does not remain.

This is the one to whom it is said: “The Lord will reject you, so that you may not be king over Israel,” and: “The Lord will tear the kingdom of Israel from your hand today.”

Saul reigned over Israel for forty years, for as long a period of time, that is, as David himself did, and he heard this at the beginning of his reign. We should therefore understand it as having been said because no one from his lineage was destined to reign. We should turn our attention to the lineage of David, from which arose according to the flesh “the mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus” (1 Tim. II).

Scripture does not contain what is read in many Latin manuscripts: “The Lord will tear the kingdom of Israel from your hand,” as we have given it and as it is found in the Greek manuscripts. Rather, it says: “The Lord will tear the kingdom from Israel from your hand,” so that “from your hand” is understood to mean “from Israel.”

This man therefore figuratively bore the person of the people of Israel. That people was destined to lose its kingdom, while Christ Jesus our Lord would reign through the New Testament—not carnally but spiritually.

[Col. 1065B] When it says, “He will give it to your neighbor,” this refers to kinship according to the flesh. For Christ is from Israel according to the flesh, as was Saul. But the addition, “to your good neighbor,” can indeed be understood as “to one better than you”: because he is good, he is therefore above you, in accordance with the prophetic statement, “Until I place your enemies beneath your feet” (Ps. CIX). Among these enemies is Israel, from whom Christ took away the kingdom, although there too there was an Israel “in whom there was no deceit,” a kind of grain among that chaff.

For the apostles came from there, as did so many martyrs—Stephen first among them—and so many churches, which the Apostle Paul mentions as glorifying God at his conversion.

I have no doubt that the following words must be understood in relation to this: “Israel will be divided in two”—namely, into the Israel hostile to Christ and the Israel belonging to the slave woman, and the Israel belonging to the free woman. [Col. 1065C] At first these two groups were together, as if Abraham were still clinging to the slave woman, until she who had been barren and was made fruitful through Christ’s grace cried out: “Cast out the slave woman and her son.”

Because of Solomon’s sin, when his son Rehoboam reigned, we know that Israel was divided in two. The division continued in this way, with each part having its own kings, until the entire nation was overthrown and deported by the Chaldaeans in a vast devastation.

But what has this to do with Saul? If something of this kind had to be threatened, it should rather have been threatened to David, whose son Solomon was. Finally, the Hebrew nation is not now divided among itself but scattered throughout the lands indiscriminately in fellowship of the same error.

The division that God, under the person of Saul—who bore the figure of that people and kingdom—threatened against the same kingdom and people is shown to be eternal and unchangeable by the words added: “And he will not turn back, nor will he repent, because he is not like a human being, that he should repent. He threatens, but does not remain.” That is, a human being threatens but does not remain; God is not so.

[Col. 1065D] God does not repent as a human being does. Where it is read that he repents, a change in things is signified while divine foreknowledge remains unchangeable; where he is said not to repent, he is understood not to change.

We plainly see that through these words a divinely uttered judgment has been pronounced concerning this division of the people of Israel, and that it is wholly perpetual. Whoever has passed over to Christ, or is passing over, or will pass over, did not belong to that people except according to God’s foreknowledge, not according to the single and common nature of the human race.

Absolutely all Israelites who cling to Christ and persevere in him will never be numbered with those Israelites who persist in being his enemies to the end of this life. They will remain perpetually in the division that was foretold.

For the Old Testament, which generates slavery from Mount Sinai, is of no benefit except insofar as it bears witness to the New Testament. Otherwise, as long as Moses is read, a veil lies over their hearts; but whenever anyone turns to Christ, the veil is removed.

[Col. 1066A] The intention of those who turn is changed from the old covenant to the new, so that each person no longer seeks to receive carnal happiness but spiritual happiness.

Samuel therefore took a sword and cut Agag into pieces (1 Kings XV). By doing this Samuel did not merely avoid sin; if he had not done it, he would have sinned. For the Lord had commanded the Amalekites to be killed. He certainly knew not only their deeds but also, according to the human heart, what each person deserved to suffer and through whom he deserved to suffer it.

Saul was therefore worthy to receive such commands, and the Amalekites worthy to suffer such things, because they had not honored the divine name but had sought to kill the people of God, who had crossed the sea on dry ground.

Since the Lord had departed from Saul on account of his disobedience, he was seized by an evil spirit from the Lord, and the evil spirit of the Lord rushed upon him.

The fact that this spirit of the Lord is also called evil is understood in the same way as the statement, “The earth is the Lord’s”: it is so called as a creature placed under his power.

[Col. 1066B] If this example of speech seems inappropriate because the earth is not evil—for every creature of God is good—then the following example may be appropriate: Saul himself, already rejected and wicked, angry with holy David, and persecuting him while driven by the flames of the fiercest envy, was nevertheless still called “the Lord’s anointed.” David himself called him this when he avenged the man who had killed him.

I am more inclined to think that the evil spirit by whom Saul was tormented was called the Lord’s because it tormented Saul by the Lord’s hidden judgment. God uses even evil spirits as ministers, either to avenge the wicked or to test the good—one spirit for one purpose, another for another.

Although a spirit is evil because by its will it seeks to harm, it does not receive the power to harm except from him under whom all things have been ordered by fixed and just degrees according to their merits. For just as an evil will is not from God, so power is not except from God (Rom. XIII).

[Col. 1066C] Although it is in each person’s power what he wills, it is not in each person’s power what he can do—whether to do something to anyone or to suffer something from anyone. Even the only-begotten Son of God, destined to suffer for a time, said humbly to the man who spoke arrogantly and claimed to have power to kill or release him: “You would have no power over me unless it had been given to you from above” (John XIX).

The devil, wishing to harm the righteous man Job, was a devil in his will to harm; yet he asked the Lord God for the power, saying: “Stretch out your hand and touch his flesh” (Job II). Even if permitted, he himself would have done this. He was asking for that permission in this manner, and called the hand of the Lord the hand permitted by the Lord—that is, the very power he wished to receive.

The corresponding passage in the Gospel is where the Lord says to his disciples: “This night Satan asked to sift you like wheat” (Luke XXII).

The spirit of God was therefore called evil—that is, God’s minister for doing in Saul what the most just judge, the Almighty, judged that he should suffer. The spirit was not God’s in the will by which it was evil; but because it had been created and made, it was God’s creature. The power, however, which it had received not from itself but from the Lord of all through his equity, was God’s power.

[Col. 1066D] The very words of Scripture are as follows:

## XVI. On Saul’s Demon. Chapter XVI

“Samuel set out and went to Ramah. The Spirit of the Lord departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from the Lord seized him and suffocated him. Saul’s servants said to him: ‘Behold, an evil Spirit of the Lord is suffocating you.’”

How this was said by his servants—“the evil Spirit of the Lord”—is indicated by the preceding words of the narrating Scripture, which says: “An evil spirit from the Lord.”

Accordingly, the spirit is called the Lord’s because it is from the Lord. By itself it had the will to kill Saul, that is, to seize him, but it did not have the power unless it were permitted by supreme justice.

For if God justly avenges—as the Apostle himself says, when God gives people over to the desires of their hearts (Rom. I)—it is not surprising that, in justly avenging, he also gives them over to the desires of others who wish to harm them, while his own unchangeable equity is always preserved.

[Col. 1067A] It should certainly be noted that the expression says, with an addition, “the evil Spirit of the Lord.” When only “the Spirit of the Lord” is said, even if “good” is not added, the spirit is understood to be good. From this it appears that God’s spirit is called good according to substance but evil according to ministry.

Nevertheless, it may still be asked whether, when “the Spirit of God” is said, and even without an addition the good Spirit is understood from the expression itself, this refers to the Spirit who is consubstantial with the Father and the Son, the Holy Spirit.

Of him it is said: “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (1 Cor. III); and again: “But God has revealed them to us through his Spirit” (1 Cor. II); and: “So also no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God.” In many ways the Spirit of God is spoken of here and the Holy Spirit is understood, even when nothing is added, because the surrounding words sufficiently indicate whom the passage concerns.

[Col. 1067B] Sometimes even “of God” is not added, and yet that Spirit is understood—principally the Holy Spirit. For whom else does the Apostle mention when he says: “The Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God” (Rom. VIII); “The Spirit himself helps our weakness”; “All these things the one and same Spirit accomplishes, distributing to each one as he wills”; and: “There are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit” (1 Cor. XII)?

In all these statements neither “of God” nor “holy” is added, yet the same Spirit is understood.

I do not know whether any clear example can be found in which the Spirit of God is mentioned without an addition and does not signify the Holy Spirit, but rather some good created and made spirit. Matters that are presented as doubtful require clearer evidence.

Consider the statement: “The Spirit of God was moving over the waters” (Gen. I). I find nothing preventing us from understanding there the Holy Spirit. For when the name “waters” indicated that formless matter which had been made from nothing so that all things might be made from it, what prevents us from understanding the Holy Spirit of the Creator, who was moving over this matter?

[Col. 1067C] This movement was not by degrees of place or intervals of space—for such a statement cannot rightly be made of anything incorporeal—but by the excellence and eminence of a will that rules over all things, so that all things might be created.

This is especially so because the expression, in accordance with the custom of those Scriptures, also gives forth a certain prophetic mystery, by which the people who would later be baptized in water and the Holy Spirit were prefigured.

The statement “The Spirit of God was moving over the waters” therefore does not compel us to understand that spirit, as some do, by which the whole corporeal mass of the world is, as it were, animated for the service of whatever things are generated and for preserving corporeal creatures in their proper forms. Whatever is of this kind is a creature.

It is also written: “For the Spirit of the Lord has filled the inhabited world” (Wis. I). Some wish to understand this same spirit as an invisible creature that gives life to and sustains all visible things by a kind of universal inspiration.

[Col. 1067D] But here too I see nothing preventing us from understanding the Holy Spirit, since God himself says through the prophet: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. XXIII). God does not fill heaven and earth without his Holy Spirit.

What is surprising, then, if it is said of his Holy Spirit, “He has filled the inhabited world” (Wis. I)?

He also fills in another way by sanctifying, as it is said of Stephen, “He was filled with the Holy Spirit,” and of other such people in another way: he fills them by sanctifying grace, as he does certain holy persons; in another way, by his presence standing by and ordering, as he does all things.

Therefore, I do not know whether any definite scriptural evidence can show that, when “the Spirit of God” or “the Spirit of the Lord” is said without any addition, anything other than the Holy Spirit is meant.

Even if there is perhaps some example that does not presently occur to me, I think it can certainly be said without rashness that whenever the Spirit of God is mentioned in the holy writings without an addition, whether the consubstantial Spirit with the Father and the Son is understood, or some invisible creature, evil cannot be understood unless “evil” is also added.

[Col. 1068A] For because God makes good use of an evil spirit for the ministry of his judgment, that spirit too is called the Spirit of God when it is used to avenge the wicked and discipline or test the good.

Nor should the later statement disturb us, that Saul prophesied after the Spirit of God came upon him. How can there be an evil spirit after the good Spirit, and again a good spirit after the evil one?

This does not happen through any changeability in the Holy Spirit, who is unchangeable with the Father and the Son, but through the changeability of the human mind, while God distributes everything either to the wicked according to the merit of their condemnation or correction, or to the good according to the generosity of his grace.

It may perhaps be thought that the Spirit of God was always in Saul, but was evil to him because he was not capable of that Spirit’s substance. Yet this is not rightly thought. The safer and truer interpretation is that, according to the changeability of human disposition, the good Spirit of God makes a person well disposed either for prophecy or for any work in the divine service.

The evil spirit, however, affects a person adversely; because of the mystery of divine equity—which distributes everything and uses everything rightly—it too is called the Spirit of God.

[Col. 1068B] This is especially clear because it is said: “The Spirit of God departed from him, and an evil spirit from the Lord seized him.” It is in no way possible to regard the same spirit as having both departed and seized him.

Moreover, in some copies, especially those that appear to have been rendered word for word from the Hebrew language, “the Spirit of God” is found without an addition, and it is understood to be evil from the fact that it seized Saul, while David refreshed him by playing the harp.

It is nevertheless clear why “evil” was not added: it had already been said shortly before, and from the proximity of the scriptural passage it could be supplied and understood. Thus those copies read:

“Whenever the Spirit of God seized Saul, David took the harp and played it with his hand; Saul was refreshed and felt better, for the evil spirit departed from him.”

Either because what is said here is not “the Spirit of God” but only “the evil spirit,” what had been said less fully there appears, as it were, to be supplied; or because the earlier passage had said:

[Col. 1068C] “Saul’s servants said to him: ‘Behold, an evil Spirit of God is troubling you. Let our lord command his servants who are before you to seek a man skilled in playing the harp, so that whenever the evil Spirit of God seizes you, he may play with his hand and you may feel better.’”

there was no need, when the text said again, “Whenever the Spirit of God seized Saul,” to add “evil,” because it was known which spirit was meant at that point.

[Col. 1068D]

## XVII. On David’s Anointing. Chapter XVI

Thus, after Saul had been rejected because of his disobedience, the Lord sent Samuel to Jesse. Samuel took a horn of oil and anointed David king.

Let us see how David prophetically signified Christ. David is interpreted as “strong of hand” or “desirable.”

What is stronger than that lion from the tribe of Judah, who conquered the world? What is more desirable than the one of whom it is said, “The Desired One of all the nations will come” (Haggai II)?

This David was anointed as the future king, announcing Christ through that anointing. Christ is named from *chrism*—anointing. David was transferred from pastoral office to rule over human beings.

But our David, Jesus himself, was taken away from the sheep of the Jewish people and transferred to the kingdom of the nations. For Christ has now been taken away from the Jewish people, and therefore he now feeds the flocks of the nations.

David was also skilled in music and learned in songs. The rational and measured harmony of diverse sounds, joined together in harmonious variety, signifies the unity of the ordered Church, which daily resounds in marvelous ways and sings with mystical sweetness.

While still a boy, David sang sweetly—indeed, powerfully—on the harp and restrained the evil spirit that was at work in Saul. This was not because the harp itself possessed such great power, but because it mystically represented the cross of Christ, which was made of wood and the stretching of strings; the Passion itself was also sung through it.

At the same time, this provides a moral example: by humble speech we should invite the pride of the rich toward some good. [Col. 1069A] A proud rich person often has to be appeased by the gentle charm of exhortation, because hard wounds are often softened by soothing applications, and the fury of the insane is frequently restored to health when the physician uses gentle persuasion.

When we accommodate ourselves to such people with sweetness, the sickness of their madness is eased.

We should not overlook the significance of the fact that, when the hostile spirit invaded Saul, David took up the harp and calmed his madness. What is indicated by Saul if not the arrogance of the powerful? And what is signified by David if not the humble life of the saints?

When Saul is therefore seized by the unclean spirit, his madness is moderated as David plays; for when the understanding of the powerful is turned toward frenzy through arrogance, it is fitting that it should be recalled to mental health, as if by the sweetness of a harp, through the calmness of our speech.

### XVIII. Concerning David’s Contest with Goliath. Chapter XVII

After this David defeated the giant in battle, when foreigners were fighting against the people of God. The devil challenged Christ; holy David took up weapons of war in order to advance against Goliath. Because of his age and the smallness of his stature, he was unable to carry these weapons; he cast off the burdensome armor, took five stones from the stream, and placed them in the shepherd’s pouch. Armed with these, he advanced and conquered.

This was indeed that David. But if we search out the mysteries, Christ is understood in David. Foreseeing the time of the revelation of the New Testament, when grace would be disclosed and bestowed, he laid aside the armor and took five stones. He therefore laid aside the bodily sacraments of the Law, which were not imposed upon the nations. He laid aside those things that we do not observe: for we read the ancient Law and do not observe it, yet we understand that its prescriptions and institutions were set forth for a certain signification.

Finally, he laid aside these weapons as burdens of the sacraments of the ancient Law, and took up the Law itself. For the five stones signify the five books of Moses. He therefore took those five stones from the stream—that is, from the world. The mortal world flows onward, and whatever enters the world passes away. The stones had been in the stream, as it were, in that original people: they were there useless and unoccupied; they profited nothing and passed away like the river.

But what did David do so that the Law itself might become useful? He took grace. For the Law cannot be fulfilled without grace: “the fullness of the Law is love” (Romans XIII). Since grace causes the Law to be fulfilled, grace is signified by milk. For milk is something freely given by the flesh, where the mother does not seek to receive but strives to give. A mother gives this freely and is distressed if there is no one to receive it.

How, then, did David show that the Law cannot operate without grace, unless by taking those five stones, which signified the Law in the five books, and joining them to grace by placing them in the shepherd’s pouch, with which he was accustomed to milk? Armed with these, he advanced against proud Goliath, who boasted and relied upon himself. He took one stone and cast down the devil; he struck him in the forehead, and he fell from that part of the body where he did not have the sign of Christ.

You may also observe this. He set down five stones and sent one. There are five books of the Law, but unity conquered: “the fullness of the Law is love,” as the Apostle says (ibid.); “bearing with one another in love, eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Ephesians IV).

Then, after striking and casting him down, he took away his sword and afterward cut off his head. This is also what our David does. He cast down the devil from among those who are his own, who believe more in him—the very ones whom the devil had held in his hand and from whom he slaughtered certain souls. They turn their tongues against the devil, and thus Goliath’s head is cut off by his own sword.

This also applies to the man who is filled with right faith, which is ordinarily reckoned to the saints as righteousness, when he gathers together the very testimonies of Sacred Scripture that a heretic brings forward and uses them to refute the obstinacy of his error. For when they bring against us the testimonies of the sacred Law, they bring with them the means by which they themselves may be defeated.

Thus David, whose name means “strong of hand,” signifies the Lord, while Goliath signifies the pride of heretics. These figures spoke through events what we disclose in words. Goliath came to battle with a sword, but David with a shepherd’s staff; yet David, after overcoming that same Goliath, killed him with his own sword.

This too is what we do, since by the Lord’s gracious appointment we have been found to be members of the David who preceded us. When we defeat proud heretics who bring forward sentences from Sacred Scripture by the very words and sentences that they themselves produce, we cut down the raised-up Goliath, as it were, with his own sword.

### XIX. Concerning the Matter in Which Saul Took David as His Son-in-Law in Exchange for the Philistines’ Foreskins. Chapter XVIII

Meanwhile David’s victory offended the spirit of King Saul, who was indignant that the mouths of the people, resounding with public rejoicing, proclaimed Saul in thousands and David in tens of thousands. From this arose Saul’s envy and the beginning of his hatred against David. Cunningly pretending friendship, Saul decided to bind David to the marriage of his daughter Michal, provided that David brought him, as a victor, one hundred foreskins of the Philistines. For the hundred requested, David gave two hundred.

Thus, from the very thing by which he was thought likely to perish according to the king’s wish, he increased his more glorious trophy. So also, while the Jews sought to kill Christ against the will of God, through the very deed by which they believed they were extinguishing him they brought about the salvation of the nations.

That David first brought the foreskins of foreigners and only afterward became joined in marriage to Saul’s daughter signified that Christ would not first betroth the Synagogue to himself in marriage until he had previously become glorious among the nations. First, among the nations, he cut away the pollution of the flesh, and afterward he was joined to the Synagogue. For when, as it is written, “the fullness of the nations has entered, then all Israel will be saved” (Romans XI).

He brought twice as many—namely, two hundred foreskins—either because he acquired both Jews and gentiles, or because the number of the people acquired from the nations is greater than that of believing Jews.

Saul then increased his hatred against David to such an extent that, when David was customarily playing music to cure the king’s spirit, Saul attempted to pin him with a spear. But what does it mean that, when an evil spirit attacked Saul, David took up the lyre and soothed his madness? Saul signifies the pride of the Jews, while David signifies the humility of Christ. When, therefore, Saul is seized by an unclean spirit, his madness is calmed by David’s playing, because when the minds of the Jews are turned to fury through blasphemy, it is fitting that they should be recalled to the salvation of their minds by the tranquility of evangelical speech, as though by the sweetness of a lyre.

### XX. Concerning David’s Flight. Chapter XIX

Saul sent guards to David’s house to keep watch over him and kill him. But David departed by night and fled, and so was saved. When Saul’s messengers came, they found a statue placed in David’s bed, with a goatskin at its head.

Let us therefore hear what this signifies: that Saul sent to guard David’s house in order to kill him. This does not refer to the Lord’s cross, but nevertheless concerns his passion; for Christ was crucified, died, and was buried.

That burial was therefore like a house, and to it—to guard it—the kingdom of the Jews sent guards, when guards were assigned to Christ’s tomb. How, then, was the house guarded, if David represented Christ, so that Christ might be killed, when Christ was killed not in the burial place but on the cross?

It refers, then, to Christ’s body, because to kill Christ meant to remove the name of Christ. For no one would have believed in Christ if the lie of the guards who had been bribed had prevailed—the lie that “while we were sleeping, his disciples came and stole him.” To wish to kill Christ is therefore to extinguish the name of his resurrection, so that the lie might be placed before the Gospel.

But just as Saul could not accomplish the killing of David, so the kingdom of the Jews could not erase the memory of Christ. Those who, relying on Saul’s power—that is, on the kingdom of the Jews—sought to act against Christ stumbled upon the stone of stumbling, as upon a statue. A kid seemed to them to be a lamb, because they persecuted as a sinner the one in whom they found no sin.

### XXI. Concerning David’s Flight to Samuel. Chapter XIX

Thus David, avoiding the stroke of the royal hand and escaping his persecution, fled and came to Samuel. Saul sent messengers to seize David. Samuel was among the prophets and the assembly of prophets who were prophesying at that time.

The messengers who were sent, having received the same spirit, prophesied. The same thing happened when others were sent, and likewise when a third group was sent. But afterward, when Saul himself also came, the Spirit of the Lord came upon him, and he walked along as he entered and prophesied.

Here the Spirit cannot be understood as anything other than the good Spirit, through whom the holy prophets perceived images and visions of future things—not merely because it is said, “and he prophesied.” For in copies that derive from the Hebrew, this is also found said of an evil spirit: “On the following day the evil Spirit of God came upon Saul, and he prophesied in the midst of his house.”

It is also often found in other places in Scripture that prophecy is said not only of good things but also of evil things; and prophets were called “Baalim,” while certain men who prophesied in Baal were reproached. It is therefore not necessary to understand that the Spirit who afterward came upon Saul was good merely because it is said, “he walked along as he entered, and he prophesied.” Rather, it is good because the text says without qualification, “the Spirit of God came upon him.” It does not say, as it did in that other passage, “the evil Spirit of God,” so that this might be understood from what follows. Indeed, the preceding statements testify more and more strongly that this was the good and truly prophetic Spirit.

David was with Samuel, and Saul sent messengers to seize David. But how was Samuel among the prophets and the assembly of prophets who were prophesying at that time, and how did the messengers who were sent, having received the spirit from him, prophesy—then others, and likewise a third group? Afterwards, when Saul himself came, the Spirit of God came upon him, and he walked along as he entered and prophesied.

For when it is said, “The Spirit of the Lord came upon them also, and they too prophesied,” it was plainly the same Spirit who was in the prophets, among whom Samuel was found. From this it must necessarily be understood that the Spirit was good. Therefore the question must be carefully examined: how did those men, when sent to hold a man and lead him to his death, deserve to be affected by such a Spirit? And how did Saul himself, who had sent them, come there seeking to shed innocent blood, yet deserve to receive that Spirit and prophesy?

Here there comes to mind what the Apostle Paul explains when he points out the way that surpasses all others: “If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but do not have love, I have become like sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal. And if I have prophecy and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so that I move mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing. And if I distribute all my possessions, and if I hand over my body to be burned, but do not have love, it profits me nothing” (1 Corinthians XIII).

Here it is clear that he was listing those gifts which are given through the divisions of the Holy Spirit, as he says above: “To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for usefulness. To one is given through the Spirit a word of knowledge, to another a word of wisdom according to the same Spirit, to another faith in the same Spirit, to another gifts of healings in the one Spirit, to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another the discernment of spirits, to another kinds of tongues. But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing what is proper to each one as he wills” (1 Corinthians XII).

It is therefore sufficiently evident that prophecy is among the gifts of the Holy Spirit; yet if someone has it and does not have love, he is nothing. From this it is understood that certain people who are unworthy of eternal life and the kingdom of heaven may nevertheless be sprinkled with certain gifts of the Holy Spirit, without having love. Without love those gifts are not nothing in themselves, but they profit such people nothing. For prophecy without love, as has already been shown, does not lead to the kingdom of God.

Love without prophecy, however, certainly does lead there. When, speaking of the members of Christ, he says, “Are all apostles? Are all prophets?” (ibid.), he clearly shows that even one who does not have prophecy can be numbered among the members of Christ. Where would a person have a place among those members without love, without which a human being is nothing, if he did not possess love?

He would certainly not say, when speaking of the members by which Christ’s body is fulfilled, “Do all have love?” in the same way as he says, “Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all workers of miracles? Do all have gifts of healings?” and the rest of this kind.

Someone may say that it is indeed possible for a person not to have prophecy. A human being who has prophecy without love is nothing. This may perhaps be said in the same way that we can say that a human being possessing a soul without a mind is nothing—not because a human being can be found who has a soul but no mind, but because, if such a person could be found, he would be nothing.

Similarly, it may be said that if a body had shape but no color, it could not be seen—not because there is a body lacking color, but because, if color were absent, it could not be perceived. In the same way, it may have been said that if someone has prophecy but does not have love, he is nothing: not because prophecy can exist in anyone without love, but because, if it did exist, it could not profit him.

To resolve this question, therefore, we must show that some reprobate person possessed the gift of prophecy. If we could find no such person, this Saul himself would make the matter sufficiently clear. Yet that Balaam was also reprobate is apparent. Scripture does not fail to say that he was condemned by divine judgment; nevertheless, he had prophecy, because he lacked love. He possessed the will to curse the Israelite people—a will that the enemy had purchased when he hired him for payment to curse.

Yet by the gift of prophecy with which he was sprinkled, he blessed unwillingly. The words written in the Gospel also bear strong witness to this interpretation: many will say on that day, “Lord, Lord, in your name we ate and drank, and in your name we prophesied; in your name we performed many mighty works.” Yet he will say to them, “I do not know you; depart from me, workers of iniquity” (Matthew VII; Luke XIII).

We will not suppose that they are lying when they say these things at that judgment, where there will be no opportunity for deception. Nor do we read that any such people say, “We loved you.” They may therefore say, “In your name we prophesied,” while being wicked and reprobate; but they will not be able to say, “We kept the love that you commanded.” For if they say this, the answer will be given to them: “I do not know you.” “By this,” he says, “it is known that you are my disciples, if you love one another” (John XIII).

This example of Saul therefore stands against certain proud heretics who deny that anything good from the gifts of the Holy Spirit can be given to those who do not belong to the lot of the saints, when we tell them that they can possess the sacrament of baptism, which, when they come to the Catholic Church, must in no way be violated in them or administered as though they did not possess it.

Nevertheless, they must not for that reason place their confidence in salvation, because we do not reject what we acknowledge that they received. Rather, they must recognize that fellowship in unity is to be entered through the bond of love. Without it, whatever they may have been able to possess—although holy and worthy of reverence in itself—makes them themselves nothing. The more they have misused the gifts that they received in this life, which is passing away, the more unworthy they have become of the reward of eternal life.

No one makes proper use of anything except through love. Love endures all things, and for that reason does not divide unity, of which it is the strongest bond. Did that servant not also receive a talent? Or does a talent signify anything other than some divine gift? “To the one who has, more will be given; but from the one who does not have, even what he has will be taken away” (Luke VIII).

What he does not have cannot be taken away; rather, he lacks something else, so that what he does have may rightly be taken away. He lacks the love by which he might use it, and thus whatever else he possesses, which is unprofitable without love, is taken away.

It is therefore not surprising that King Saul received the spirit of prophecy at the time when he was first anointed, and that later, after he had been rejected because of disobedience and the Spirit of God had departed from him, he was seized by an evil spirit from the Lord. That spirit itself was called the Spirit of the Lord because of its ministry, since the Lord makes good use even of evil spirits—either for the condemnation of some or for their testing. Although wickedness is not from God, power nevertheless exists only from God.

The “sleep of the Lord” is also mentioned, which had overcome Saul’s soldiers when David took the spear and the cup from beside the head of the sleeping man. This does not mean that the sleep was then in the Lord, so that he himself was sleeping, but that the sleep which at that time seized the men had been infused by God’s command, so that David and his servants’ presence would not be perceived in that place.

Nor is it surprising that the same Saul again received the spirit of prophecy when he was pursuing the righteous man and came to the place where the assembly of prophets was, intending to seize and kill him. Thus it has been sufficiently demonstrated that no one ought to feel secure because of such a gift, as though he were especially pleasing to God, if he does not have love. For that gift could be given to Saul because of the hidden purpose of some sacrament; yet it could be given to one who had been rejected, envious, ungrateful, repaying good with evil, and who, even after receiving the Spirit, was not corrected or changed for the better.

### XXII. Concerning the Covenant between David and Jonathan. Chapter XX

Jonathan went to David, grieving that he was being wearied by the unjust persecutions of his father. “If I live, you shall show me the mercy of the Lord; but if I die, you shall not remove your mercy from my house forever, when the Lord has eradicated David’s enemies, each one from the earth.”

When Scripture added, “Jonathan therefore made a covenant with the house of David,” it immediately continued by saying, “And the Lord required it from the hand of David’s enemies.” It did this by anticipation, inserting into the history beforehand what happened much later, when, after Saul had been killed, the kingdom was transferred to the house of David, and those who had unjustly persecuted him were justly punished by divine vengeance.

Then the Lord required it from the hand of David’s enemies: he required an account of why they had afflicted the holy man; then they were compelled to give an account of the hatred with which they had raged against him for so long. The same may equally be understood of Absalom, Sheba son of Bochri, and David’s other enemies.

Alternatively: if you wish to know what the Lord required from the hand of David’s enemies, you may, unless I am mistaken, derive it from the preceding sentence in which it was said that Jonathan had made a covenant. He required to know why they too had not been willing to enter into a covenant of peace with the one with whom they had seen that the Lord was.

Scripture seems to insert this sentence here in anticipation for this reason: so that Jonathan’s testimony—when he said that the Lord would eradicate David’s enemies, each one from the earth—might show that David himself would not avenge himself upon his adversaries, but that the Lord would judge on his behalf.

Well, then, it is added:

> “And Jonathan made David swear again, because he loved him as his own life; for he loved him as his own soul.”

Thus that man who embraced David with such a perfect love according to the Law of God appeared to be exempt from the destruction of his enemies. Although he was taken away by death so that he could not share the kingdom with David as he had hoped, nevertheless he received, without any contradiction, a share in the heavenly kingdom with the one whom he had loved so greatly for the glory of his virtues, since he himself too was a man of virtue.

### XXIII. Concerning David’s Coming to Abimelech. Chapter XXI

David therefore arose again to flee on that day from the face of Saul, and he came to the priest Abimelech. From him he took Goliath’s sword and received the bread of the Presence. As a result, he brought death upon the priest and punishment upon the religious city.

This is the factual account of what happened. But as far as the prophetic mystery is concerned, it was fulfilled in Christ our Lord. When he had been placed in the flesh and was avoiding Jewish persecution, he passed over to the apostles, with whom he took the food he desired. “With desire,” he says, “I have desired to eat this Passover with you” (Luke XXII). From them he took the weapons of Goliath—that is, of the devil—for he himself, being strong, plundered the strong man’s goods.

Against those by whom Christ was received, the devil therefore brought tribulations and death. For, as the Apostle says, “All who wish to live devoutly in Christ suffer persecutions” (2 Timothy III). And the Lord says, “If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you” (John XV).

As for the fact that in the Gospel the Lord calls Abiathar, the chief priest, Abimelech, there is no inconsistency. Both of them were there when David came and asked for and received the bread: Abimelech, namely, the high priest, and Abiathar, his son.

After Abimelech was killed by Saul, Abiathar fled to David with eighty-five men of his priestly family. He became the companion of David’s entire exile. Later, when David was reigning, Abiathar himself received the rank of high priest, and he continued in the priesthood throughout the whole period of David’s reign. He became much more distinguished than his father, and therefore was worthy for the Lord to mention him as high priest even while his father was still alive.

In Doeg the Idumean, who betrayed the priests of the Lord, the person of Judas the betrayer is signified. Through him the devil brought these things about, so that after his betrayal the Church would suffer persecution in Christ, and many disciples and priests would be killed and suffer destruction for his name.

Some say that Doeg signified the Antichrist, of whom Judas was a member: for just as Doeg killed eighty priests, so the Antichrist will kill the martyrs who hold to faith in the resurrection.

### XXIV. Concerning David’s Flight to Achish. Chapter XXI

Meanwhile, while David was fleeing from Saul, he wanted to hide with a certain king of Gath named Achish. But when David’s glory had been mentioned, lest the king to whom he had fled should contrive something against him out of jealousy, he pretended madness. As though seized by a frenzy, he altered his mouth; saliva ran down his beard, he collapsed in their hands, and he fell at the doors of the gate.

King Achish said to his servants, “Why have you brought this man to me? Were madmen lacking among us?” And so he dismissed him.

Achish is interpreted as “How is it?” By this are signified ignorance and the speech of one who wonders without recognizing. This was fulfilled among the Jewish people: when they saw Christ, they did not recognize him. Before them he altered his mouth and departed.

The commandments of the Law had been carnal, and there had been a sacrifice according to the order of Aaron; afterward he himself established a sacrifice from his body and blood according to Melchizedek. He therefore altered his mouth in the priesthood; he altered it in the commandments, giving another covenant after abolishing carnal observance.

From there he collapsed in their hands when they seized and crucified him. And he fell at the doors of the gate: that is, he humbled himself; this means falling at the door of our faith. The door of the gate is the beginning of faith. From there the Church begins and advances to vision, so that when it believes what it does not see, it may deserve to enjoy it once it has begun to see those things face to face.

As for the fact that, in that apparent madness, saliva flowed down over his beard, the Apostle explains it by saying: “Jews seek signs, and Greeks seek wisdom; but we preach Christ crucified, to the Jews a stumbling block and to the gentiles foolishness, but to those who are called, Jews and Greeks alike, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God. For what is foolish in God is wiser than human beings, and what is weak in God is stronger than human beings” (1 Corinthians I).

Saliva signifies weakness, but “what is weak in God is stronger than human beings.” Do not consider only the saliva; consider that it flows down over the beard. Just as weakness is shown in the saliva, so strength is shown in the beard. He therefore concealed his strength beneath the body of his weakness. What appeared outwardly as weakness was like saliva, while the divine power within was covered as though by the beard.

### XXV. How in the Cave David Cut off a Portion of Saul’s Cloak. Chapter XXII

Afterward, in the wilderness of Engedi, when Saul was seeking to pursue David, David entered a cave and hid there. The king, however, unexpectedly caught in the ambush that he had prepared for the innocent man, fell into what he had contrived. For it is written, “Whoever digs a pit will fall into it.”

David, repaying good for evil, did not kill his enemy. Instead, as evidence, he cut off the edge of the royal cloak, although it would have been easier to destroy an adversary caught in an ambush than merely to deceive him.

What, then, does it mean that David, fleeing from the face of Saul, hid in a cave? Why did he hide, unless so that he might be concealed and not found? What does being covered by a cave mean except being covered by earth? For one who flees into a cave is covered by earth so that he may not be seen.

Jesus carried the earth—the flesh that he had received from the earth—and in it he concealed himself, so that God would not be found by the Jews. “For if they had understood, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians II).

Why, then, did they not find the Lord of glory? Because he had hidden himself in a cave: that is, he exposed only the weakness of the flesh, and concealed the majesty of his divinity beneath the covering of the body, as in the recess of a cave.

Not recognizing him, they therefore persecuted a human being. He could not die except as a human being, nor could he be crucified except as a human being, because he could not be seized except as a human being.

Thus he placed earth before those who sought him wrongly, but preserved life for those who sought him rightly. According to the flesh, he therefore fled from Saul’s face into a cave, because he suffered, concealing himself from the Jews to such an extent that he died.

But why did he wish to remain patient unto death, fleeing from Saul’s face into a cave? A cave may be understood as the lower part of the earth. Certainly, as is clear and known to all, his body was placed in a tomb that had been cut out of rock.

That tomb was therefore the cave. Our David fled there from the face of Saul, for the Jews persecuted him until he was placed in the cave.

But what does it mean that Saul the persecutor entered the cave to relieve his bowels? It means that the Jews emitted, as a foul odor, the malice conceived in their minds against Christ. They revealed their harmful thoughts through worse deeds when they killed Christ.

Nevertheless, David did not wish to kill Saul. Although he had him in his power while hidden in the recess of the cave, he preferred to spare him rather than kill him. So also Christ, while he was in the cave of the flesh, had the persecuting people in his power and did not kill them. For it had been written concerning them by the prophet, “Do not kill them.”

Finally, David silently cut off the edge of Saul’s cloak, to show through prophecy that Christ did not kill the Jews, but nevertheless took away the glory of their kingdom, leaving them, through their persecution, bereft of seat or dominion. The cutting off of the cloak signifies the cutting off of the kingdom.

In the fact that David himself revered Saul so greatly that his heart struck him with remorse when, hidden in the dark cave into which Saul too had entered because of the needs of nature, he secretly cut off a small piece of Saul’s garment from behind, so that he would have something by which to show how he had spared him although he could have killed him, and thus remove from Saul’s mind the suspicion that had led him, thinking holy David his enemy, to persecute him so fiercely—in this there was a shadow of the future kingdom that would remain in eternity.

For that oil with which Saul had been anointed made him a *christus*, that is, an anointed one. David therefore feared that he would be guilty of violating so great a sacrament in Saul, since he had even touched his garment. Thus it is written: “David’s heart struck him because he had cut off the edge of Saul’s cloak.”

The men who were with him advised him to kill Saul, who had been delivered into his hands. But David said, “May the Lord forbid that I should do this thing to my lord, the Lord’s anointed, and lay my hand upon him, because he is the Lord’s anointed.”

Such reverence was shown to this shadow of the future not for its own sake, but because of what it prefigured.

In the moral sense, whom does Saul signify except evil rulers, and whom does David signify except good subjects? Saul’s relieving his bowels therefore means that wicked superiors extend the malice conceived in their hearts into deeds of miserable odor, and reveal their harmful thoughts by carrying them out in worse actions.

David feared to strike him because the minds of subjects, abstaining from every pest of detraction, do not strike the lives of their superiors with the sword of the tongue, even when they criticize their imperfections.

If, because of weakness, they can scarcely restrain themselves and therefore speak of certain extreme and outward faults of their superiors—provided that they speak humbly—they silently cut off a portion of the cloak, as it were. For when they detract, at least harmlessly and secretly, from the dignity placed over them, they stain the garment of the king set above them.

Nevertheless, they return to themselves and rebuke themselves most severely even for the slightest tearing of a word. Thus it is rightly written there as well: “After this David’s heart struck him because he had cut off the edge of Saul’s cloak” (1 Samuel XXIV).

The deeds of superiors are not to be struck with the sword of the mouth, even when they are rightly judged worthy of reproof. But if the tongue at any time slips against them, even in the smallest matter, the heart must be pressed by the affliction of repentance, so that the person may return to himself. When he has offended against the authority placed over him, he must dread the judgment of the one by whom that authority was placed over him.

For when we sin against our superiors, we oppose the order of the one who placed them over us. Thus Moses too, when he learned that the people were complaining against him and Aaron, said, “What are we? Your murmuring is not against us but against the Lord” (Exodus XVI).

### XXVI. Concerning David’s Coming to Nabal. Chapter XXV

After this David descended into the wilderness of Aon [the Vulgate reads *Maon*], where Nabal lived; his wife’s name was Abigail. David sent his young men to him, asking him to send David and his young men whatever his hand might find.

Nabal foolishly rejected them, and they reported this to David. Then David girded himself with weapons and wished to plunder him. But Abigail went to meet David and pleaded for herself and for her household. Her husband, stupefied by foolishness and drunkenness, had offended him.

> “If a man should ever rise up pursuing you and seeking your life, the life of my lord shall be kept as in a bundle of the living with the Lord your God. But the lives of your enemies shall be whirled about as in the motion and circle of a sling.”

By a most beautiful comparison she distinguishes the condition of the righteous from the lot of the reprobate. She calls the souls of the former “living,” thereby indicating conversely that the souls of the latter have been overtaken by spiritual death, in accordance with the prophet’s saying: “The soul that sins, it shall die.”

She compares the righteous to a bundle and the wicked to a stone in a sling. A bundle is bound together so that it may remain whole and be preserved; a stone is placed loose in a sling so that it may be cast away.

So in this world the elect are constricted by the pressures of tribulations, so that, admonished by them, they may bind themselves more closely to one another by the hand of their Redeemer and be preserved forever. But the more freely the reprobate are released in this life into the pleasures proper to them, as though unrestrained, the farther they are cast away in the future from the glory of the divine vision, so that it may rightly be said of them, “Indeed, they have been driven away from your hand” (Psalm XXVII).

She wonderfully describes the omnipotent providence of the heavenly protector when she says that the soul of the holy man is kept by him as in a bundle of the living. Just as it is very easy for anyone to preserve a bundle of grass or hay held in his hand, so the power of our Lord and Savior effortlessly protects all the elect throughout the world, from the beginning to the end of the age, so that none of them may perish in any way.

This agrees with what he himself says about them in the Gospel under the figure of sheep: “They follow me, and I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them from my hand” (John X).

Just as a single bundle is tied together by various bonds, so the whole assembly of the saints is bound together by one and the same faith, hope, and love, and is surrounded by the one protection of God.

The literal meaning is also clear: David’s soul, although enemies were pursuing him, was always kept among the living. His enemies, however, beset by adversities, were like a stone whirled about in a sling; they were to be disturbed by unstable motion and driven from their own boundaries, or even removed from human affairs.
