In this action of Abigail, what does her yielding suggest to us except that we correct angry people more effectively if, in their very anger, we withdraw from admonishing them? When people are disturbed, they do not know what they are hearing. But once restored to themselves, they receive words of exhortation all the more willingly because they are ashamed to find that they have been endured so calmly.

To a mind drunk with fury, everything right that is said appears perverse. Thus Nabal rightly and commendably kept silent about his fault while drunk, and commendably spoke of it once the wine had been digested. For he was able to recognize the evil he had done precisely because he had not heard it while drunk.

## XXVII. How David Took the Spear and Cup from the Sleeping Saul. Chapter XXVI

Again, while David was fleeing from Saul, he entered the king’s camp and, finding him asleep, did not strike or kill him, but took only the spear that was fixed beside his head and the cup of water that was at his head. With everyone asleep, he went out from the camp and crossed over to the summit of the mountain.

What, then, does this signify? The Jews were pursuing Christ, but in pursuing him they were asleep, because they were not watchful in heart; for hardness of heart is a kind of sleep. They sleep in the old life and do not awaken to the new. Christ came and did not kill them, but [Col. 1077B] took from them the cup of water—that is, the grace of the Law. He also took away the royal scepter, that is, the power of the kingdom, which they regarded as a great possession and by which they protected themselves temporally, and which, through unbelief, they wielded against God. Then our victorious David, returning from their camp, rose up to the height of the heavenly mountain.

## XXVIII. David’s Battle against Amalek. Chapter XXVII

Meanwhile, while David was fleeing and proceeding to Achish, king of the Philistines, the Amalekites rose up for battle against Israel. They attacked Ziklag, destroyed it, and took captive everything belonging to David and his young men. [Col. 1077C] When David returned to pursue the Amalekites, he found an Egyptian boy exhausted; the Amalekites had left him sick on the road. David restored him with food and made him the guide of his journey. Thus he pursued the Amalekites, found them feasting, and utterly destroyed them.

What does it mean that the Egyptian Amalekite boy, exhausted on the road, sits there, except that the lover of the present age, covered by the blackness of his sin, is often left behind by that same world, weak and despised, so that he is entirely unable to run along with it but, broken by adversity, grows numb? God therefore chooses those whom the world despises, because very often that very contempt brings a person back to himself. The one who had left his father and squandered prodigally the portion of property he had received, after he began to hunger, came to himself and said: “How many hired servants of my father have bread in abundance!” (Luke 15). He had indeed departed far from himself when he sinned; and if he had not hungered, he would not have returned to himself.

After he had come to need earthly things, he began to consider what he had lost of spiritual things. The weak and despised in this world often hear God’s voice all the more quickly because they have nothing in this world in which to delight. This is well represented by that aforementioned boy of the Amalekites. While the Amalekites were plundering and running about, he remained sick on the road; he wasted away from hunger and thirst. Yet David [Col. 1077D] found him, gave him food and drink, and he immediately recovered. He became David’s guide, found the Amalekites feasting, and with great strength struck down those who had abandoned him in his weakness.

The Amalekites are called a “licking people.” What, then, is signified by a “licking people” except a worldly mind? It surrounds and, as it were, licks all earthly things while delighting only in temporal matters. A “licking people” makes plunder, as it were, when those who love earthly things gather profits from the losses of others.

But the sick Egyptian boy is left on the road, because whenever any sinner begins to grow weak from the condition of this world, he immediately becomes despised by worldly minds. Yet David found him and gave him food and drink, because the Lord, mighty in hand, does not despise those cast aside by the world. Often he turns to the grace of his love those who are entirely unable to follow the world, as though they had remained on the road; he offers them the food of his word and, as it were, sends them forward as guides for himself along the way, making them his preachers. [Col. 1078A]

For when they bring Christ into the hearts of sinners, they lead David against his enemies, as it were. They strike the feasting Amalekites with David’s sword, because by the Lord’s power they cast down the proud who had despised them in the world. Thus the Egyptian boy who had remained on the road killed the Amalekites, because often those who were previously unable to run through this world with worldly people overcome worldly minds by preaching.

## XXIX. Saul Consults the Witch. Chapter XXVIII

After Samuel’s death, the Philistines gathered against Israel, and Saul consulted the Lord, but he did not answer him. Saul then sought out a witch who would raise Samuel for him; and when he had immediately been raised, he said to Saul: “Why have you disturbed me so that I should be raised?”—and so forth.

According to the historical sense, the question is whether the witch actually summoned the prophet himself from the underworld, or whether it was some imaginary apparition fabricated by the deceit of demons. On this question blessed Augustine of holy memory wrote as follows to Simplicianus, bishop of Milan: [Col. 1078B]

“You ask, I say, whether the unclean spirit who was in the witch could have acted so that Samuel would be seen by Saul and speak with him. Yet it is a much greater miracle that Satan himself, the prince of unclean spirits, could speak with God and ask that Job, a most righteous man, be put to the test—just as he also asked that the apostles be tested.

“Or, if this does not present a difficult question because present Truth speaks everywhere through whatever creature he chooses to whatever creature he chooses, and because it is not therefore a matter of great merit for the one to whom God speaks—for what matters is what he says, since an emperor does not speak with many innocent people for whom, with the greatest foresight, he provides salvation, while he speaks with many guilty people whom he orders to be killed—then, if for this reason there is no question here, there should likewise be no question about how an unclean spirit could speak with the soul of a holy man. For God, the Creator and Sanctifier, is certainly far greater than all the saints.

“But if it is troubling that an evil spirit was [Col. 1078C] permitted to raise the soul of a righteous man and, as it were, summon it back from the hidden receptacles of the dead, is it not more astonishing that Satan took up the Lord himself and set him upon the pinnacle of the temple (Matthew 4)? However he did this, the manner in which it happened to Samuel—that he should be raised—likewise remains hidden, unless someone should say that the devil had easier permission to take up the living Lord from wherever he wished and set him wherever he wished than to raise the spirit of dead Samuel from its dwelling.

“If the Gospel does not disturb us in that matter because the Lord willed and permitted it to happen, without any diminution of his power or divinity—for he permitted himself to be seized, bound, mocked, crucified, and killed by the Jews themselves, although they were perverse and unclean and were doing the works of the devil—then it is not absurd to believe that, by some dispensation of the divine will, it was permitted that the spirit of the holy prophet should consent to be shown to the king’s eyes, not unwillingly or under the domination and subjugation of magical power, but willingly and in obedience to God’s hidden dispensation, which was concealed from both the witch and Samuel, in order that he might strike the king with the divine judgment. [Col. 1078D]

“For why should the soul of a good man, if summoned by wicked people who are alive and should come, seem to lose its dignity, when good people who are alive are often summoned to wicked people and act toward them as the duty of righteousness requires, preserving and undiminished the dignity of their virtue, while dealing with their vices according to the use or necessity of present circumstances?

“Nevertheless, there may be another easier solution and more straightforward understanding: namely, that we should not believe that Samuel’s spirit was truly raised from its rest, but that it was some phantasm and imaginary apparition produced by the devil’s machinations. Scripture therefore calls it Samuel by name because images are customarily called by the names of the things whose images they are. Thus everything painted or fashioned from some portion of metal or wood, or from any material suitable for such works, and everything seen in dreams—in fact, almost all images—are usually called by the names of the things whose images they are. [Col. 1079A]

“For who is there who would hesitate to call a painted man a man? When we look at pictures of individual persons, we quite properly and without hesitation apply their names, as when, looking at a panel or wall, we say, ‘That is Cicero; that is Sallust; that is Achilles; that is Hector; this is the river Simois; that is Rome,’ although they are nothing other than painted images.

“Likewise, although the cherubim are heavenly powers, those images fashioned from metal at God’s command over the Ark of the Covenant, for the sake of signifying a great reality, are also called cherubim. Again, whoever sees a dream does not say, ‘I saw an image of Augustine or Simplicianus,’ but, ‘I saw Augustine or Simplicianus,’ although at the time when he saw such a thing we were unaware of it. So evident is it that it is not the people themselves but their images that are seen.

“Pharaoh likewise said that in his dream he had seen ears of grain and cattle, not images of ears of grain or cattle. If, therefore, it is clearly established that images are called by the names of the things whose images they are, it is not surprising that Scripture says that Samuel was seen, even if perhaps an image of Samuel appeared through the contrivance of him who transforms himself into an angel of light and his ministers into ministers of righteousness (2 Corinthians 11). [Col. 1079B]

“But if it is troubling how true predictions were made by the evil spirit to Saul, it may likewise seem astonishing how the demons recognized Christ, whom the Jews did not recognize. When God wishes someone to know something through even the lowest or highest spirits—provided it concerns temporal matters and things belonging to this mortal life—it is easy and not unfitting for the omnipotent and just God, for the punishment of those to whom such things are foretold, so that they may suffer in advance by knowing the evil that threatens them before it arrives, to impart by the hidden arrangement of his ministers some power of divination even to such spirits, so that they may announce to human beings what they hear from the angels.

“Yet they hear only as much as the Lord and Ruler of all either commands or permits. Hence the pythonic spirit in the Acts of the Apostles also bore witness to the apostle Paul (Acts 16) and attempted to preach the gospel.

“Nevertheless, these spirits mix in deceptions, and they announce what they were able to know as truth not so much for the purpose of teaching as of deceiving. Perhaps this is why, when that image of Samuel foretold to Saul that he would die, it also said that he would be with him—which is certainly false. [Col. 1079C]

“For in the Gospel we read that the good are separated from the wicked by a great interval after death (Luke 9), when the Lord testifies that a great chasm was fixed between that proud rich man, who was already suffering torments in the underworld, and the man who had lain ulcerated at his gate and was now established in rest.

“Or, if Samuel said to Saul, ‘You will be with me,’ so that this refers not to equality of blessedness but to a similar condition of death—so that both were human, both could die, and one, already dead, foretold death to the living—your prudence, I think, perceives that, under either interpretation, the passage already admits a conclusion that is not contrary to the faith.

“Unless perhaps, through a deeper and more intricate inquiry—one that exceeds either my powers or the limits of the present time—it may be discovered with certainty whether or not a human soul, after departing this life, can be summoned by magical incantations and appear before the eyes of the living, bearing even the features of its body, so that it can not only be seen but recognized; and, if this is possible, whether even the soul of a righteous person might not indeed be compelled by magic but consent to be shown, obeying the more hidden commands of the highest law.

“If it becomes clear that this cannot happen, then both interpretations should not be admitted in the treatment and exposition of this passage; rather, once the interpretation that Samuel himself appeared has been excluded, the imaginary imitation of Samuel produced by a diabolical rite should be understood. [Col. 1079D]

“Since, however, whether this can happen or cannot happen, Satan’s deception and his cunning activity in fabricating appearances are continually and variously at work to deceive human senses, let us proceed cautiously—not prescribing limits to more diligent inquiry—but nevertheless let us rather suppose that something of this kind was done through the service of that witch’s evil spirit, so long as we are not granted the ability to devise and explain anything more.” [Col. 1080A]

## XXX. Saul’s Slaughter. Chapter XXVIII

When the battle had begun, the Philistines struck Israel with a great slaughter, and Saul and his son Jonathan were killed. A certain man who had escaped came to David at Ziklag and announced to him the great slaughter that had taken place among the people. He also added falsely that he himself had killed Saul. But David, avenging the Lord’s anointed, ordered him to be killed.

David then sang this lament over Saul and over his son Jonathan, and commanded that they teach it to the sons of Judah, as it is written in the Book of the Upright. He did this because he already knew that the Philistines abounded in archers, and Saul had perished especially from their arrows; therefore he wanted his own soldiers to learn the same art of warfare so that they might defeat them in turn.

As for what follows—“as it is written in the Book of the Upright”—they affirm that this very book can now be found nowhere, not even among the Hebrews. The same is true of the Book of the Wars of the Lord, which is mentioned in the Book of Numbers; of Solomon’s songs; of his most wise discussions concerning the nature of trees and all herbs, and likewise of animals, birds, reptiles, and fish; and of what is said in the Book of Days. The remaining accounts of Solomon’s earlier and later works, they say, were written in the words of Nathan the prophet, of Ahijah the Shilonite, and also in the vision of Iddo the seer concerning Jeroboam son of Nebat. [Col. 1080B]

There are many volumes of this sort, which Scripture certainly commends but which plainly do not exist today. For when Judaea was devastated by the Chaldeans, the library gathered in ancient times, together with the other wealth of the province, was consumed by enemy fire. The few books that are now contained in Holy Scripture were later restored through the efforts of Ezra, the priest and prophet. Hence it is written of him: “Ezra went up from Babylon, and he was a ready scribe in the law of Moses” (1 Esdras 7) [Col. 1080C]—“ready,” that is, because he discovered more efficient forms of writing than the Hebrews had possessed up to that time. And in the letter of the Persian king Artaxerxes: “To Ezra, the priest, the most learned scribe of the law of the God of heaven, greetings.”

“Mountains of Gilboa, let neither dew nor rain come upon you, nor fields of firstfruits, because there the shield of the mighty was cast away, the shield of Saul, as though he had not been anointed with oil.”

You should understand that Saul, who truly deserved to be killed after the anointing of the holy chrism—from which he was also called “the Lord’s anointed”—signifies the death of the true Christ, which he deigned to undergo without guilt. The mountains of Gilboa, where he perished, signify the proud efforts of the Jewish people, by which they rebelled against the author of life.

Accordingly, Gilboa is rightly interpreted as “Rolling” or “Descent.” For they rolled about in the filth of sins, in accordance with the proverb: “And the sow that has been washed returns to wallowing in the mire” (2 Peter 2). Straying from the straight path of a life that brings salvation, they were already rushing downward—that is, toward the lowest desires of this age. Because of that desire, they did not hesitate to hand over the King of heaven and earth to death. [Col. 1080D]

For this reason it is deservedly wished for them that they receive neither dew nor rain from heaven. We see this fulfilled in the facts of the present day, in that, after heavenly grace abandoned them, it was transferred to the people of the nations.

Isaiah also threatened that this would happen to them under the figure of a vineyard, speaking in the person of the Lord: “I will command the clouds not to rain upon it” (Isaiah 5). This means plainly: “I will command the apostles and all apostolic men no longer to preach the word of life to them, but to leave them, unworthy and empty in their barrenness, to be burned by everlasting fire, because in their arrogance they rejected the watering of the heavenly word that came from me.”

Of these people it is also said that they should not be fields of firstfruits. The proud minds of the Hebrews do not bear the first fruits, because, remaining for the most part in unbelief at the Redeemer’s coming, they refused to follow the beginnings of faith.

Holy Church, fruitful in its beginnings through the multitude of the nations, scarcely receives the Jews whom it finds at the end of the world; gathering the last, it places them like gleanings of the harvest. Concerning these remnants Isaiah says: “Though the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant will be saved” (Isaiah 9; Romans 9). [Col. 1081A]

Nevertheless, the mountains of Gilboa may be cursed by the prophet’s mouth for this reason: while no fruit, withering before it rises from the earth, is produced, the owners of the land may be struck by the harm of sterility, so that they themselves receive the sentence of the curse who, because of their wickedness, had deserved to suffer the death of the king among them.

Nor should it seem absurd to you that the evil deeds of the reprobate should signify something good, or, conversely, that the good works of the righteous should be placed in an opposing signification. Read the *Moralia* of holy Pope Gregory, where he explained how blessed Job cursed his own day, saying, “Let the day perish on which I was born,” and so forth (Job 3). You will see that it is entirely customary in Scripture for good things to be understood as signifying evil things, and conversely.

Thus they interpret Uriah, the most faithful soldier of King David, [Col. 1081B] together with his most pious and innocent deeds and words, in an evil signification; and, conversely, David himself, in his greatest crime, as signifying something good. Otherwise, if evil could not be signified by good things, and good by evil things, it would never be permissible to write the name of God in black ink; it would always have to be written in shining gold, because God is light and there are no shadows in him. Nor, conversely, should the names Absalom and Doeg, wicked men, be written in the bright red pigment used in the titles of the Psalms, but only in ink. [Col. 1082A]

Therefore, just as both evil and good things can be represented without reproach on the pages of books in any color, so too, in the realm of signification, both good and evil can rightly be expressed through any human deeds. Yet it happens much more often, and is heard much more sweetly, that good things are represented by good things and evil things by evil things.

Just as in a wall painting it would be unfitting to depict a dark-skinned Ethiopian in white, or a Saxon with a white body or hair in ink, so in the distribution of merits each person will receive according to his own work, and whatever he is in deed, such will he also appear in countenance at the judgment. It will not matter at all what each person represented, but what he did.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 1081]

[Col. 1081B] The city of God, advancing through the succession of the ages, has shown how the promises of God made to Abraham—whose seed, God promising it, we have learned was to include both the Israelite nation according to the flesh and all nations according to faith—are fulfilled.

Since, therefore, the preceding book came to an end with the kingdom of David, we now take up, beginning from that same kingdom, the remaining matters that follow, insofar as they seem sufficient for the work undertaken.

The period beginning when the holy Samuel began to prophesy and continuing until the people of Israel were led captive into Babylon, and from there, according to the prophecy of the holy Jeremiah, until the Israelites returned after seventy years and the house of God was restored, is entirely the period of the prophets. [Col. 1081C]

Although we can rightly call the patriarch Noah himself, in whose days the whole earth was destroyed by the Flood, and others both before and after him up to the time when kings began to exist among God’s people, “prophets,” because of certain things that they either signified in some manner or foretold concerning the future and pertaining to the city of God and the kingdom of heaven—especially since we read that some of them were more explicitly called prophets, such as Abraham and Moses—nevertheless, the days of the prophets are chiefly and especially said to begin when Samuel began to prophesy.

Samuel first anointed Saul, and, after Saul had been rejected, anointed David himself as king at God’s command; from David’s stock the others were to proceed, in succession, for as long as it was necessary for them to follow one another.

If I wished to recall everything that the prophets foretold concerning Christ while the city of God passed through these ages, its members departing through death and succeeding one another through birth, the task would extend without limit. [Col. 1081D]

First, the very Scripture that, in setting forth in order the kings and their deeds and events, appears to be occupied with narrating historical matters with painstaking diligence will be found, if considered with the assistance of God’s Spirit, to be concerned no more—or certainly not less—with announcing future things than with recounting past things. Who does not know, if he gives even moderate thought to it, how laborious and extensive it is to investigate this by careful searching and demonstrate it through exposition, and how many volumes it would require?

Then, the very passages that are undoubtedly prophetic contain so much concerning Christ and the kingdom of heaven, which is the city of God, that a fuller discussion would be needed to disclose this than the scope of this work demands. Accordingly, if I can, I shall so moderate my style that, with God’s will, in completing this work I shall neither say what is unnecessary nor omit what is sufficient.

The seed of Abraham—that is, the people of Israel according to the flesh—was already in the promised land. It had begun to reign there not only by holding and possessing the cities of its adversaries, but also by having kings. A large part of God’s promises concerning that people had already been fulfilled—not only those made to the three patriarchs, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and whatever other promises had been made during their times, but also those made through Moses himself, through whom that people was freed from Egyptian servitude and through whom all the earlier events were revealed in his time, when he led the people through the wilderness. [Col. 1082B]

[Col. 1082C] Yet neither through the illustrious leader Joshua son of Nun, through whom that people was brought into the promised land and, after conquering the nations, divided it among the twelve tribes to whom God had commanded it to be given, nor after any judge, had God’s promise concerning the land of Canaan been fulfilled for so long a period—from a certain river of Egypt to the great river Euphrates. Nor was it yet being prophesied as something future; it was awaited as something still to be fulfilled.

It was fulfilled through David and his son Solomon, whose kingdom was extended over as great a territory as had been promised. For they subdued all those peoples and made them tributary.

Thus the seed of Abraham had been established in the promised land according to the flesh—that is, in the land of Canaan—under kings, so that nothing remained by which that earthly promise of God would not be fulfilled, except that the Hebrew nation might remain in that same land, in an unshaken succession of generations, as far as temporal prosperity was concerned, until the end of this mortal age, if it obeyed the laws of the Lord its God.

But because God knew that it would not do this, he also used its temporal punishments to discipline the few faithful among it and to warn those who would later exist among all the nations—those whom he was to admonish and to whom, through the incarnation of Christ, he was to fulfill another promise by the revelation of the New Testament. [Col. 1082D]

Therefore, just as those divine oracles made to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and all the other prophetic signs or words given in the earlier sacred Scriptures, were made, so also the other prophecies from this period of the kings partly concern the nation descended from Abraham according to the flesh, but partly concern that seed of his in which all nations, as co-heirs of Christ through the New Testament, will be blessed to possess eternal life and the kingdom of heaven.

Some, then, concern the slave woman who gives birth in slavery—that is, earthly Jerusalem, which is in slavery with her children. Others concern the free city of God, that is, the true and eternal Jerusalem in heaven, whose children, all living according to God, are pilgrims on earth. Some passages are understood to pertain to both: properly to the slave woman, figuratively to the free woman.

The sayings of the prophets are therefore found to be threefold: some concern earthly Jerusalem, some the heavenly Jerusalem, and some both. [Col. 1083A]

## I. David’s Anointing. Chapter II

After Saul’s death, the men of Judah came and anointed David in Hebron, so that he might reign over the house of Judah. David was then told that the men of Jabesh-gilead had buried Saul. David therefore sent messengers to the men of Jabesh-gilead and said to them:

“Blessed are you by the Lord, because you have shown this kindness to your lord Saul and have buried him. And now the Lord will indeed repay you with kindness and faithfulness.”

Why, then, are those who buried Saul and his son said to have shown kindness, and why are they blessed for this by a pious king, unless because the hearts of compassionate people are rightly moved when they grieve over the bodies of the dead—bodies not their own—which they [Col. 1083B] wish, with the affection by which no one has ever hated his own flesh, to be treated after their death, and which they take care to treat, while they are alive, as they wish to be treated when they themselves will no longer feel?

## II. The Anointing of Ishbosheth as King Produced Sedition. Chapter III

After David had been anointed king over the house of Judah, Abner son of Ner made Ishbosheth son of Saul king over all Israel. Abner son of Ner went out from the camp at Gibeon with the servants of Ishbosheth. Joab son of Zeruiah, with David’s servants, went out from Hebron; they stirred up a battle beside the pool of Gibeon, and Asahel pursued Abner.

Abner said to Asahel: “Turn aside; do not follow me, lest I be forced to strike you down upon the ground.” But Asahel despised this warning and refused to turn aside. Abner therefore struck him in the groin with the butt end of his spear, pierced him through, and he died.

Whom did Asahel symbolize except those whom violent fury seizes and drives headlong? The more madly they are carried away, the more cautiously they must be avoided.

Hence Abner, whose name in our language means “Lamp of the Father,” fled. For the tongue of teachers, which points to the light of God above, sees someone’s mind being carried over the precipices of fury; and when it refrains from returning verbal darts against the angry person, it is unwilling, as it were, to strike its pursuer. [Col. 1083C]

But when angry people do not calm themselves through any reflection, and, like Asahel, do not cease pursuing and raging, those who attempt to restrain the furious must not raise themselves in anger but must display whatever tranquility they possess. They should also bring forward certain words subtly, by which they may wound the mind of the furious person indirectly.

Thus, when Abner stood against his pursuer, he pierced him not with the point of the spear but with its butt end. To strike with the blade is to meet someone with the force of open reproof; to strike a pursuer with the butt end of the spear is to touch the enraged person calmly in certain respects and, as it were, to overcome him by sparing him.

Asahel immediately fell dead, because when agitated minds perceive that they are being spared, yet are touched inwardly with calm reasoning in the words spoken to them, they immediately fall from the position to which they had raised themselves. Those who recoil from the force of their own passion under the blow of gentleness die, as it were, without iron. [Col. 1083D]

## III. Baanah and Rechab, Commanders of the Soldiers, Kill Ishbosheth in His Sleep. Chapter IV

The sons of Rimmon, the Beerothite—Rechab and Baanah—came and entered Ishbosheth’s house at the heat of the day, while he was sleeping upon his bed at noon. They entered the house while the woman who guarded the house was cleaning wheat and had fallen asleep. Taking ears of wheat, they entered secretly and struck him in the groin.

The woman cleans wheat when the vigilance of the mind separates virtues from vices by discernment. If she falls asleep, she admits assassins against her own lord, because when the care of discernment ceases, it opens a path for evil spirits to kill the soul.

They enter and take away the ears of grain because they immediately remove the sprouts of good thoughts. They strike in the groin because they kill the virtue of the heart through the pleasure of the flesh. To strike in the groin is to pierce the life of the mind with the pleasure of the flesh. [Col. 1084A]

This Ishbosheth would never have succumbed to death if he had not assigned a woman—that is, a soft and feeble guard—to the entrance of the house, the access to his mind. A strong and watchful understanding ought to stand as guard at the gates of the heart; it should be overcome neither by the sleep of negligence nor deceived by the error of ignorance.

Thus Ishbosheth was rightly named, since he was stripped by the swords of enemies while a woman kept watch. Ishbosheth means “man of confusion.” A man of confusion is one who is not fortified by the strong guard of the mind, because while he thinks he is practicing virtues, vices that enter secretly kill him without his knowing.

The entrance to the mind must therefore be fortified with every virtue, lest at any time enemies lying in wait penetrate it through the opening of neglected thought.

## IV. David Brings the Ark. Chapter VI

Now David gathered all the chosen men of Israel, thirty thousand. He arose and departed, and all the people who were with him from the men of Judah, to bring up the ark of God, over which the name of the Lord of hosts had been invoked, who sits upon the cherubim.

David gathered all the chosen men of Israel, thirty thousand, because the Lord established the primitive Church from Israel—not indeed from all Israel, but joining to himself those who were chosen. For not all who are from Israel are Israelites; rather, the children of the promise are counted as the offspring (Rom. 9). They are reported to have numbered thirty thousand, that is, perfected in the steadfastness of faith, works, and hope. Three pertains to faith because of the confession of the Holy Trinity; ten pertains to the works of the law because of the Decalogue; a thousand pertains to hope because of its perfection in eternal life, beyond which nothing higher exists, just as no number is greater than a thousand when counted as a single unit. For when you say ten thousand, thirty thousand, or even a million, you do not surpass that thousand by counting beyond it, but multiply it by repeatedly applying it to itself or to smaller numbers. Therefore multiply three by ten, lest faith without works be dead. Likewise multiply thirty by a thousand, so that faith, which works through love, may hope for its reward nowhere other than in heaven. Thus the chosen from Israel signify peoples who rightly believe, work, and hope.

The men of Judah who were with David signify those same peoples and their teachers, who clung more familiarly to Christ’s side. Accompanied by this twofold army, he rejoices in bringing up the Lord’s ark—that is, in extending the Church and implanting it in the hearts of those who had not believed.

The ark is placed upon a new cart, so that the grace of the New Testament may be poured into minds renewed in baptism, and new wine may be stored in new wineskins. Previously the ark had been in the house of Amminadab, which was in Gabaa, because the faith of the Church that is now preached had already flourished before the time of the Lord’s incarnation among those who followed the devotion of the patriarchs and prophets. Amminadab, whose name means “My spontaneous father,” signifies either Abraham, the father of faith, or Moses, the lawgiver. Each of them guards the ark in Gabaa, because by the lofty example of his virtue he fortifies the breasts of believers. Hence Gabaa is also interpreted as “Hill”; it is a place in the city of Cariathiarim.

When the ark had been brought out, David and all Israel danced before the Lord to various kinds of musical instruments, because, as soon as the proclamation of the new grace began, the Lord invited everyone to offer praises to God the Father in humility, saying, “Whoever serves me, let him follow me” (John 12); “to one the word of knowledge through the Spirit, to another kinds of tongues, to another the grace of healings,” and so forth (1 Cor. 12).

As the ark advanced—that is, as the primitive Church grew—they came to the threshing floor of Naor, that is, to a prepared threshing floor, namely, the Church of the Gentiles, which was to be consecrated by the truth of faith. Concerning it John says, “And he will thoroughly cleanse his threshing floor” (Matt. 3). There the priest who imprudently touched the ark, as though to steady it, was immediately struck down by the Lord and died. This signifies that the Jewish people, while envying the Gentiles, deprive themselves of the gift of salvation; and while wishing to mix the law with the Gospel, lose the grace of both for themselves.

“And he held it,” it says, “because the oxen were kicking.” For oxen kicking signifies the preachers of the Gospel acting with greater freedom concerning the faith, not entering according to the custom of the law, but interpreting the Sabbaths, new moons, circumcision, and sacrifices spiritually. Those who came down from Judea and taught the brothers that they could not be saved unless they were circumcised according to the custom of Moses (Acts 15) attempted to correct them as though they were straying. These are also the men concerning whom James said to Paul: “You see, brother, how many thousands there are among the Jews who have believed, and they are all zealous for the law” (Acts 21).

Therefore, because the priest had been killed, David did not wish to turn the Lord’s ark aside to himself, into the city of David; instead he diverted it to the house of Obededom the Gittite. This signifies that, when the Jews rejected the word, the apostles were taken away from them and sent to instruct the Gentiles, lest preaching that was heard but not received should cause further harm.

Hence the place of the threshing floor of Naor, which signifies the faith of the Gentiles prepared for the Lord’s grace, is called “the striking of Uzzah,” because salvation came to the Gentiles through the sin of those men. Obededom is interpreted as “Serving man.” He is the one of whom the Lord says to the Father: “You will appoint me as head of the nations; a people whom I did not know has served me” (Ps. 17). There, anticipating the rejection of the Jews as though it were the death of Uzzah, he says: “You will deliver me from the contradictions of the people” (ibid.).

The name of the city also corresponds to this meaning, for it is interpreted as “Winepress,” signifying the cross, on which the true vine deigned to be trodden and pressed. From this, the entire people of the Gentiles may rightly be called Gittite, since it is said: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. 6).

The three months during which the ark remains there signify faith, hope, and love. Just as a month is completed by its days, so each virtue advances toward perfection by its own stages. These months do not cease to run until the fullness of the Gentiles enters.

At last David will return and bring the ark into the city of David, because the Lord, with Enoch and Elijah preaching, will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children. By sacrificing oxen and rams—that is, crowning with the blood of martyrdom those who thresh the Lord’s threshing floor and exercise leadership over his sheep—and by openly displaying the example of his own incarnation and passion, which the unbelieving Jews had hitherto not acknowledged, he signifies this also: David himself was girded with a linen ephod. Linen, produced from the earth and brought to the whiteness of a garment through manifold labor, displays the truth of human flesh triumphing amid scourges.

But while everyone rejoiced and hymns resounded at the entrance of the heavenly ark, Michal, the daughter of Saul, alone was absent from those who led the ark. Indeed, she despised David, humbled, through a window. This signifies that, when the Jews believe at the end of the world, some will follow Christ in profession but the Antichrist in conduct. It is fittingly said of them that Michal herself—whose name, signifying the instability of the carnal, is interpreted as “Every water”—is called not David’s wife but Saul’s daughter. Those who serve Christ only as far as faith is concerned will not be crowned in his kingdom; rather, they will be condemned by the anathema of his persecutors, whom they imitated.

But if they despise the humility of the Church, they are condemned. Nevertheless, the Lord’s ark enters its place and is set in the middle of the tabernacle that David had pitched for it. This means that the faith of the Church is preached, advances, and is implanted in the hearts of all whom the Lord had predestined for eternal life.

David offers holocausts and peace offerings before the Lord. Christ, who is at the right hand of God and also intercedes for us, commends to the Father the faith and devotion of the Church. Following David’s example, he blesses the faithful and humble, feeds them with the nourishment of saving mysteries, and distributes to each one a single round loaf of bread—namely, the bread that descended from heaven and gives life to the world.

He also distributes one portion of roasted beef, namely, that fatted calf which was slaughtered for the younger son returning to his father and roasted in the fire of passion, saying: “My strength has dried up like a potsherd” (Ps. 21).

He distributes fine flour fried in oil, namely, flesh utterly cleansed from the stain of sin but tortured in the frying-pan of the cross because of its abundant love for human salvation.

It is rightly said that one round loaf of bread and one portion of meat are given, because there is “one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all” (Eph. 4).

The faithful receive these gifts in another sense when, although many, we are one bread and one body in Christ. Each individual chastises the wantonness of his own flesh and subjects it to service; they cook it in the fire of the Holy Spirit. They also make the fruits of good works, exceedingly rich with the oil of mercy, boil with compassion for their neighbor.

But, by contrast, the daughter of Saul enters the king’s chamber in vain and bears no offspring from the seed she conceived. Those who receive the word of God only through the ear, without the offspring of good works, await the day of everlasting death.

In this history of the blessed king and prophet David, in which he is said to have brought up the ark of God, humility is morally approved, pride condemned, and presumption punished. David himself was not ashamed humbly to dance before the Lord’s ark, and soon deserved to receive the promise of the Son of God who would be born from his line. His wife, who despised that same humility, was not worthy to be made fertile by his seed and paid the penalty of perpetual barrenness.

It is delightful to consider how many gifts of virtue David had received, and how firmly he preserved humility amid them all. Who would not be lifted up by having broken the mouths of lions, torn apart the limbs of bears, been chosen over his older brothers, anointed to govern the kingdom after the king had been rejected, struck down Goliath—terrible to everyone—with a single stone, brought back numerous foreskins after destroying the Philistines at the king’s command, finally received the promised kingdom, and possessed the entire Israelite people without opposition? (From Gregory, *Moralia*, book 27, chapter 26.)

And yet, when he brought back the ark of God to Jerusalem, as though forgetting that he had been set above other men, he danced before the ark among the people. Since dancing before the ark was, as is believed, the custom of the common people, the king whirled about in the service of God through his dancing.

Behold the man whom the Lord had singularly preferred to all others: he so humbled himself beneath the Lord, both lowering himself to the level of the lowly and displaying himself as rejected. He did not call to mind the power of his kingdom; he did not fear becoming contemptible in the eyes of his subjects by dancing; he did not recognize himself as superior to the others before the ark of the one who had granted him honor. Before God he performed what was weak and lowly, so that by humility he might strengthen what he had done bravely before men.

I do not know how others judge his deeds; I am more astonished by David dancing than by David fighting. By fighting he subjected an enemy; by dancing before the Lord he conquered himself.

Michal, the daughter of Saul, still insane with the swelling pride of royal descent, despised him when he had humbled himself, saying: “How glorious was the king of Israel today, uncovering himself before the servant-girls of his servants, and being naked as one of the buffoons is naked!” At once she heard him reply: “Before the Lord, who chose me rather than your father.” A little later he said: “I will play, and I will make myself even more contemptible than I have been, and I will be humble in my own eyes.”

It is as though he plainly said: “I desire to become contemptible before men, because through humility I seek to be noble before God.”

There are some who think humbly of themselves because, although placed in positions of honor, they recognize that they are nothing but dust and ashes. Yet they refuse to appear lowly before men and, contrary to what they think inwardly about themselves, conceal themselves outwardly beneath a rigid dignity.

There are others who desire to appear lowly before men and, by displaying themselves as rejected, despise everything that they are. Yet inwardly, within themselves, they swell with pride as though because of the very merit of their displayed lowliness. They are all the more lifted up in heart the more they suppress pride in outward appearance.

David detected and overcame both these battles of pride with great vigilance and marvelous strength. Because he thought humbly of himself inwardly and did not seek honor outwardly, he says: “I will play, and I will make myself more contemptible.” And because, by presenting himself as lowly outwardly, he did not swell inwardly, he adds: “And I will be humble in my own eyes.” It is as though he said: “I regard myself inwardly as the kind of person I display outwardly by despising myself.”

What, then, will those who are elevated by learning do, if David knew that the Redeemer was to come from his flesh and announced his joys prophetically, yet nevertheless pressed down the neck of his heart within himself with the strong heel of discernment, saying: “And I will be humble in my own eyes”?

The priest who touched the ark with inconsiderate presumption cleansed the guilt of his daring by an untimely death. He demonstrates that those who are lesser and worse are unable to understand and despise either the deeds or the words of their superiors. Yet the latter should not be rashly censured by them precisely because they cannot truly grasp them.

Often something is done by superiors as a matter of prudent administration which is judged an error by inferiors. Often many things are said by the strong which the weak condemn for the very reason that they do not understand them. The ark of the covenant, which was tilted when the oxen kicked, aptly signified this: the Levite, believing it was about to fall, tried to raise it and immediately received the sentence of death.

For what is the mind of the righteous except the ark of the covenant? It is carried by oxen and becomes tilted when sometimes even one who governs well, shaken by the confession of subject peoples, is moved by love alone to accommodate himself to their weakness. But what is done as a matter of administration is regarded by the inexperienced as the collapse of strength. Hence some subjects stretch out against it the hand of criticism, but through their own presumption fall into the very vices they condemn.

The Levite therefore stretched out his hand as though to assist, but, by his transgression, lost his life. Thus, while the weak reproach the deeds of the strong, they themselves are rejected from the company of the living.

At times holy men, accommodating themselves to the lowly, say certain things, while contemplating higher realities they express other things. Since fools do not understand either the force of accommodation or that of loftiness, they criticize these statements boldly.

What is it to wish to correct a righteous man for his accommodation except to raise up the tilted ark with the proud hand of criticism? What is it to criticize his unpolished speech except to regard a movement of his strength as a fall?

But the one who presumptuously raises God’s ark loses his life, because no one would dare to correct the righteous acts of the saints unless he had first thought himself better than they. Hence that Levite is rightly called Uzza, which is interpreted as “Strong of the Lord.” For presumptuous people would never judge the deeds or words of their betters to be weak unless they believed themselves strong in the Lord through an audacious mind.

## V. David Is Forbidden by the Prophet to Build the Temple. Chapters VII–VIII

After this, when many successes had come to King David, he considered making a house for God—namely, that most magnificent temple whose fame spread widely and which was later built by his son King Solomon.

While he was considering this, the word of the Lord came to Nathan the prophet, who was to convey it to the king. The Lord said that a house would not be built for him by David, and that for so long a time he had not commanded anyone among his people to build a cedar house for him. Then he said:

“And now you shall say this to my servant David: Thus says the Lord: When your days are fulfilled and you sleep with your fathers, I will raise up your offspring after you, who shall come forth from your womb, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever. I will be his father, and he shall be my son.”

Anyone who thinks that this great promise was fulfilled in Solomon is greatly mistaken. He notices what was said—“He shall build me a house,” since Solomon built that famous temple—but he does not notice: “His house shall be faithful, and his kingdom shall endure forever before me.”

Let him therefore observe and consider Solomon’s house, filled with foreign women who worshipped false gods, and Solomon himself, once a wise king, at some point seduced and cast down by them into that same idolatry. Let him not dare to suppose either that God promised this falsely or that he could not have foreseen such a Solomon and such a house.

We should not doubt this; nor, if we did not already see these things fulfilled in Christ Jesus our Lord, who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh (Rom. 1), should we vainly and pointlessly seek another person here, as the carnal Jews do. Indeed, they say that the son whom they read as promised in this passage to King David was not Solomon, to such an extent that, although the promised one has already been revealed with such clarity, they still profess to hope for another with marvelous blindness.

Some image of the future reality was certainly present in Solomon: he built the temple, had peace in accordance with his name—for *Solomon* means “Peaceful” in Latin—and was remarkably praiseworthy at the beginning of his reign. But his very person, through the shadow of what was to come, also foretold Christ the Lord; it did not present him.

Thus certain things are written about him as though they had been predicted about Christ himself. Holy Scripture, by the events it narrates, also acts prophetically, in a certain manner sketching the outline of future things in him. Apart from the books of the sacred history, where Solomon is said to have reigned, Psalm 71 is also inscribed with his name as its title. In that psalm many things are said which cannot at all apply to him but apply with the greatest clarity to Christ the Lord. It therefore plainly appears that in Solomon some kind of figure was shadowed, while in Christ the truth was presented.

It is known within what limits Solomon’s kingdom had been confined; yet in that psalm we read, to say nothing of other passages: “He shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth” (Ps. 71). We see this fulfilled in Christ.

He took the beginning of his rule from the river, where, after being baptized by John and pointed out by him, he began to be recognized by the disciples, who called him not only Teacher but also Lord.

Nor was there any other reason why Solomon began to reign while his father David was still alive—something that happened to none of those kings—except that this too might make sufficiently clear that Solomon himself is not the one whom the prophecy foreshadows. The prophecy speaks to his father:

“And it shall be, when your days are fulfilled and you sleep with your fathers, I will raise up your offspring after you, who shall come forth from your womb, and I will prepare his kingdom.”

How, then, because of what follows—“He shall build me a house”—will Solomon be thought to have been the one prophesied, and not rather, because of what precedes—“When your days are fulfilled and you sleep with your fathers, I will raise up your offspring after you”—will another peaceful one be understood to have been promised, one who, unlike Solomon, was foretold as rising after David’s death?

For when Jesus Christ came after a long intervening period, undoubtedly he had to come after the death of King David, to whom he had been promised, in order to build a house for God—not from wood and stones, but from human beings, such as we rejoice that he builds.

To this house the Apostle says, that is, to Christ’s faithful: “For the temple of God is holy, which you are” (1 Cor. 3).

For this reason, in Psalm 88, whose title is “Understanding, for Ethan the Israelite,” the promises of God made to King David are recalled, just as they are set forth in this Book of Kings. Similar things are also said there, including: “I swore to David my servant: Forever I will prepare your offspring,” and so forth.

But when it says, “If he commits any iniquity, I will rebuke him with the rod of men and with the blows of the sons of men; but I will not remove my mercy from him, as I removed it from Saul, whom I took away from before my face,” it does not say “from them” but “from him.” For no sins can be found in Christ himself, who is the head of the Church, which would need to be restrained by divine discipline while mercy was preserved; rather, these words apply to his body and members, which is his people.

The word that God spoke through Nathan to David must by no means be passed over. He said:

“I will appoint a place for my people Israel, and I will plant him there. He shall dwell apart and shall no longer be troubled, and the son of iniquity shall not again humble him as at the beginning, from the days when I appointed judges over my people Israel.”

Whoever hopes for this great good in this age and on this earth acts foolishly. Or will someone think that it was fulfilled in the peace of King Solomon? Scripture commends that peace in an excellent proclamation as a shadow of what was to come.

But this suspicion is carefully forestalled. After it says, “The son of iniquity shall not again humble him,” it immediately adds, “as at the beginning, from the days when I appointed judges over my people Israel.”

Before kings began to exist there, judges had been appointed over that people from the time when it received the promised land. Certainly the son of iniquity—the foreign enemy—humbled it at intervals, during which they are recorded to have alternated peace with war. Longer periods of peace are found there than Solomon possessed, although he reigned forty years. Under the judge called Ehud, eighty years of peace occurred.

Therefore, far be it from us to believe that Solomon’s time was predicted in this promise, much less the time of any other king. None of them reigned in such peace as Solomon did; nor did that nation ever hold its kingdom in such complete security that it was not anxious about being subjected to enemies. For amid the great instability of human affairs, no people has ever been granted such security that it need not fear the hostile attacks belonging to this life.

The place promised as a habitation so peaceful and secure is therefore eternal, and is owed to the eternal in that free Jerusalem where Israel will truly be the people. For this name is interpreted as “Seeing God.” In hope of that reward, a life devoted to God must be led through faith in this troubled pilgrimage.

When Nathan announced these words to David, “King David entered and sat before the Lord.” What should be understood by this sitting except that he sat in the presence of the Lord—either where the ark of the covenant was, through which a more secret and honored presence of the Lord could already be understood; or because he sat in order to pray, which is not rightly done except in the presence of God, that is, in the innermost heart?

The words may be understood in this way: “Before the Lord,” where no human being would be present to hear him praying. Whether, therefore, because of the ark of the covenant, because of the secrecy of being away from witnesses, or because of the innermost heart where the affection of the one praying was found, it was fittingly said: “He sat before the Lord”—unless perhaps the fact that he prayed while sitting is meant to teach us something, since holy Elijah also did this when he obtained rain through prayer.

By these examples we are reminded that no particular bodily posture has been prescribed for prayer, so long as the mind, present to God, carries out its intention. We pray standing, as it is written: “But the tax collector stood at a distance” (Luke 18). We pray on bended knees, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 20). We pray sitting, as David and Elijah did.

And if we also prayed lying down, it would not have been written in the Psalms: “Every night I wash my bed; I water my couch with my tears” (Ps. 6).

When someone seeks prayer, he places his limbs as circumstances and the position of his body at that moment suggest, in order to move his mind. But when he is not seeking it, but the desire to pray comes upon him, and something suddenly enters his mind by which his affection is moved to supplication, prayer must not be postponed, with inexpressible groanings, in whatever posture it finds the person, in order that he may seek a place of retreat, or where to stand, or where to prostrate himself. The mind’s concentration creates solitude for itself, and often even forgets which part of the heavens it was beneath or in what bodily posture that moment found its limbs.

David also made a name for himself when, after capturing Syria in the Valley of Salt, he returned, having killed one hundred twenty thousand [Vulgate: eighteen thousand].

What is signified by the multitude struck down by David in the Valley of Salt except that our Redeemer, by the judgment of his discernment, extinguishes the folly of immoderate taste in those who hold perverse opinions about him?

## VI. The Insult to David’s Envoys by the Ammonites. Chapter X

After this it happened that the king of the Ammonites died, and his son Hannon reigned in his place. David said: “I will show mercy to Hannon son of Nahash, as his father showed mercy to me.” David therefore sent his servants to console him concerning his father’s death.

When David’s servants had come into the land of the Ammonites, the princes of the Ammonites said to Hannon their lord: “Do you think that David has sent you consolers out of regard for your father’s honor, and not rather to investigate and explore the city and overthrow it—that David has sent his servants to you for this reason?”

So Hannon seized David’s servants, shaved off half of each man’s beard, cut their garments in half up to their buttocks, and dismissed them.

When this was reported to David, he sent to meet them, for they were exceedingly shamefully disgraced. David commanded them: “Remain in Jericho until your beards grow, and then return.”

Just as Hannon, king of Ammon, disfigured the servants of David who had been sent to him and sent them back to David in shameful mockery, so the devil, the prince of this world, is accustomed to disfigure many religious people through creeping vices.

When he exposes their hidden evils in open and shameful acts and completed lust, he leaves them naked of the dignity of chastity, as though their garments had been cut away up to their buttocks. And when he takes away their former strength, he shaves them as though he were cutting off their beards.

Yet the true David—namely, our Lord and Savior—does not, in his merciful regard, exclude them from the forgiveness of repentance. He commands them to remain in Jericho, that is, under the anathema of repentance, until by making satisfaction they recover the spiritual mysteries and strength of mind that they lost through sinning, and thus at last become able to stand in his presence.

### VII. Concerning David’s Adultery. Chapter XI [Cols. 1090C–1092B]

Now it happened that, when David rose from his bed after midday and was walking on the roof of the royal house, he saw a woman washing herself. He sent for her and took her, and slept with her, and she conceived. When David learned this, he sent to Joab, saying: “Send Uriah the Hittite to me.” When Uriah came to David, David sent a letter by Uriah to Joab, instructing him to place Uriah where the fiercest battle was, and Joab did so; and Uriah the Hittite died.

Very often a thing is a virtue in its historical sense but a fault in its symbolic meaning; sometimes an event that, considered as an act, is condemned becomes, in writing, a prophecy of virtue. We shall demonstrate both points more readily when we bring forward the testimony of this Holy Scripture to establish each.

For who, hearing this—not only among the faithful but even among unbelievers—would not utterly detest the fact that David, walking on the roof, desired Bathsheba, Uriah’s wife? Yet when Uriah returned from battle, David urged him to go home and wash his feet. He immediately replied: “The ark of the Lord is under coverings, and shall I rest in my house?” David received him at his own table and handed him the letter by which he was to die.

Whom, then, did David represent while walking on the roof, if not the one of whom it is written: “He has placed his tabernacle in the sun” (Ps. XVIII)? What does it mean to bring Bathsheba to oneself, if not to join the law of the letter, united to the carnal people, to oneself through spiritual understanding? Bathsheba is said to mean “the seventh well,” because through knowledge of the law, perfect wisdom is supplied to us by the infusion of spiritual grace.

Whom, then, does Uriah signify, if not the Jewish people, whose name is interpreted as “The Lord is my light”? The Jewish people, being lifted up by the knowledge of the law it has received, boasts as though of the light of God.

But David took this man’s wife from him and joined her to himself, because our Redeemer—whose name David means “strong of hand”—appeared in the flesh and, when he revealed that the law was to be understood spiritually, showed that, as it was held according to the letter, it was foreign to the Jewish people; and he joined it to himself because he continually explained it by his preaching.

Yet David urged Uriah to go home and wash his feet, because the incarnate Lord, coming among the Jewish people, commands them to return to the conscience and to wipe away the dirt of their deeds with tears, so that they may understand the commandments of the law spiritually; so that, after such hardness of precepts, finding the fountain of baptism, they may run to the water after their labor.

But Uriah, remembering that the ark of the Lord was under coverings, replied that he could not enter his house. It was as though the Jewish people were saying: “I see the commandments of God in carnal sacrifices, and I do not seek to return to the conscience through spiritual understanding.” For he says, as it were, that the ark is under coverings because he understands the commandments of God as requiring no service other than that of carnal sacrifice.

Nevertheless, David calls him to his table even though he refuses to return home, because although the Jewish people scorns returning to the conscience, the Redeemer who comes nonetheless preaches spiritual commandments to it, saying: “If you believed Moses, you would perhaps believe me also, for he wrote about me.” Thus the Jewish people holds the law, which speaks of his divinity, while that same people disdains to believe in him.

Therefore Uriah is sent to Joab with the letter by which he is to be killed, because that same Jewish people carries the law by which it is convicted and must die. For while it retains the commandments of the law and tries to fulfill them, it itself carries the judgment by which it is condemned.

What, then, could be called more wicked than this David, or more pure than Uriah? Yet again, in the mystery, who is found more sacred than David, or more unbelieving than Uriah, when the one, through the fault of his life, signifies innocence in prophecy, while the other, through the innocence of his life, expresses guilt in prophecy?

For sacred eloquence narrates past events in such a way as to express things to come; it approves them as accomplished facts while contradicting them in the mystery; it condemns deeds as performed while urging that they be performed mystically.

For this reason the sins of such men in Holy Scripture—namely, David and Peter—were recorded, so that the fall of the great might serve as a warning to the lesser. For this reason also the repentance and pardon of both are revealed there, so that the recovery of the lost might be the hope of those who are perishing. Let no one, then, grow proud because David fell from his standing; let no one despair because David rose again after his fall.

Behold how wonderfully Holy Scripture presses down the proud by the same word with which it lifts up the humble. It recounts one and the same event in different ways: it recalls the proud to fear through humility, but the humble to confidence. O immeasurable medicine of a new kind, which, set forth in one and the same order, both dries up swollen things by pressing them down and pours moisture into parched things by raising them up! It frightened us by the fall of the great, but strengthened us by their restoration.

Thus, always thus, the mercy of the divine dispensation restrains us when we grow proud and supports us lest we fall into despair.

But since, compelled by the occasion, we have brought David forward and recalled so great a crime, the reader’s mind may perhaps be troubled by the question why almighty God does not preserve from bodily vices those whom he has chosen forever and whom he has raised even to the summit of spiritual gifts.

Since we believe that a sufficient answer can be given quickly, we shall reply briefly. Some people, after receiving the gift of virtues, fall through the abundant grace of good works into the vice of pride, yet do not recognize how they have fallen. Therefore the ancient enemy, who already rules within them, is also permitted to rage against them outwardly, so that those who are exalted in thought may be cast down through the lust of the flesh.

We know, however, that it is sometimes less serious to fall into bodily corruption than to sin silently in thought through deliberate pride. But because pride is believed to be less shameful, it is avoided less; whereas people are more ashamed of lust because everyone recognizes its shamefulness.

It therefore often happens that some who fall through pride into lust become ashamed of their hidden fault because of their open fall, and then correct greater faults when, cast down in lesser matters, they are more deeply confounded. They see themselves guilty in lesser things who had believed themselves free in greater ones.

For by the merciful dispensation of the Lord, the evil spirit is sometimes released to draw a person from one fault to another; and while striking him more severely, it thereby loses the one whom it had seized. By the very means through which it appears to have conquered, it is overcome.

It is worth considering within what fortified bosom of grace God holds us by the favor of his mercy. Behold: the one who exalts himself because of virtue returns through vice to humility; and the one who is lifted up by the virtues he has received is wounded not by a sword but, so to speak, by a medicine. For what is virtue but a medicine, and what is vice but a wound?

Because we make a wound out of medicine, he makes medicine out of a wound, so that we who are struck by virtue may be healed by vice. We turn the gifts of virtues toward the use of vices; he takes up allurements in the stronghold of virtues and strikes the condition of salvation in order to preserve it, so that we who flee the humility of the one who heals us may cleave to the saving benefit of yielding.

Yet among these things we must know that many people, the more they fall in numerous ways, become more tightly bound. When the ancient enemy strikes them with one vice so that they collapse, he also binds them with another so that they cannot rise.

Let a person therefore consider against what adversary he is waging war. If he realizes that he has already committed some fault, let him at least fear being dragged from fault to fault, so that he may diligently avoid the wounds by which people are often killed. For it is very rare that our enemy preserves the salvation of the elect even through wounds. As we have said, the Lord often subjects his elect to the tempter in order to educate them.

Thus, after the barriers of paradise and after the third heaven’s secrets, lest Paul become exalted by the greatness of his revelations, an angel of Satan was given to him. But, as we said earlier, by this very temptation it is arranged that those who could have perished through exaltation may be saved from destruction through humility.

Therefore, by the secret order of the divine dispensation, from the very place where the devil’s wickedness is permitted to rage, the goodness of God is piously brought to completion. Our adversary obeys the commands of heavenly grace precisely where he exercises the anger of his wicked will.

When these things had taken place, the Lord sent Nathan to David.

### VIII. Nathan Sent to David. Chapter XII [Cols. 1092C–1093B]

Nathan came and proposed a parable about a rich man and a poor man: one had sheep and cattle, while the other had only a single ewe. The rich man took this one ewe from the poor man.

When David heard this, he became indignant against that man and said: “As the Lord lives, the man who has done this is a son of death.” But Nathan said to David: “You are that man.”

And David said to Nathan: “I have sinned against the Lord.” Nathan said to David: “The Lord has also taken away your sin; you shall not die.”

If the Lord took away David’s sin, detestable as it was, what does it mean that he afterward endured all that the Lord had said to him through the prophet concerning that same sin? Without doubt, the Lord does not leave a sin without punishment. Either the person himself punishes it in himself through repentance, or God strikes him, taking vengeance together with the person.

He therefore does not spare the sin at all when he never dismisses it without vengeance. Thus, after his confession, David deserved to hear: “The Lord has taken away your sin”; yet afterward, afflicted by torments and fleeing, he paid the debt of guilt for what he had committed.

So the water of salvation absolves us from the guilt of our first parent; nevertheless, while cleansing away the guilt of that same sin, we who have been absolved still die bodily, because he cuts away our sins—whether through us or through himself—even when he releases them. For he strives to cleanse the stains of iniquity from his elect through temporal affliction, though he does not wish to punish them forever.

When it says: “There were two men in one city,” Uriah and David are understood. And learn to distinguish their persons.

He calls the poor man’s ewe better—that is, his wife, who was violated, who ate from his table, drank from his cup, and lay in his bosom. Consider that the poor man possesses the supports that encourage compassion, whereas the rich have great pride.

Among the poor, the wife is both servant and attendant; she bears children and is herself both mother and nurse. Among the rich it is not so: as soon as a woman has borne a child, she immediately hands him over to others, and pride cuts away the marks of affection. She is ashamed to become a nurse, though she has become a mother.

Thus the ewe lay in his bosom. He enlarged the parable by his account of affection.

A traveler came to that king. Who, then, is the traveler? Concupiscence, plainly. In order to show that the man’s chastity was intact, he called the desire foreign; for he had never violated another man’s marriage, nor looked upon it with wicked eyes. But, struck by that woman, he lost his chastity because, through the security of peace, he had made himself somewhat more relaxed.

The foreigner—an evil and savage desire—came to that rich man. He came, and the rich man did not take from his own flocks or herds to prepare a feast for the traveler; instead, he sent and seized the poor man’s ewe, which lay in his bosom and ate from his table.

When David heard this, he became exceedingly angry against that man and said to Nathan: “As the Lord lives, the man who has done this is a son of death. He shall restore the ewe fourfold, and he himself shall be punished by the sword.”

O justice overflowing beyond measure in its judgment! There was no thread of love in him that would have prevented him from speaking justly. He commands a fourfold restitution according to the law, for the law ordered a thief to be bound to fourfold repayment; but this man went beyond the law. He commands that the man himself be killed and also held liable for fourfold restitution.

Thus he pronounced the sentence, and the judgment was refined.

When the prophet heard this, he casts away every shadow of the image and brings forth the sword; boldly he says: “You are the king who has done this deed.”

O incision that cuts not the sensation of pain with a sword but, through the brevity of the accusation, cuts it away! When the time required it, he concealed the narrative; but when the moment came, he immediately struck and severed it, without the wound of a great blow, saying only this: “You are the king.”

But David quickly returned to his conscience and, like a faithful and capable servant, simply confessed his guilt, saying: “I have sinned against the Lord.” The prophet replied: “And the Lord has taken away your sin.”

A swift confession, a swifter cure. He sinned by deed; he repented by word. God gave assent, and correction was made; the wound appeared, and health returned.

But the prophet was not content with this. After the correction, after the repentance, after the absolution of sins, he wrote a psalm for this reason, so that his suffering might become a medicine even for later generations, his shipwreck a harbor for others, and those who fall into the same things by which he was wounded and reformed might be able to use that very medicine and be healed through reformation.

### IX. Concerning David Driven into Exile by His Son. Chapter XV [Cols. 1093C–1094C]

When David was fleeing from his son Absalom and walking barefoot, he crossed the brook Kidron, with all the people accompanying him, and they reached as far as Bahurim. And behold, Shimei, the son of Gera, from the family of Saul’s household, came out, throwing stones and cursing the king, saying: “Go away, go away, man of blood and man of Belial.”

Whoever among the faithful is pierced by the illumination of divine grace and, with holy desire, hastens from the depths toward the heights on the wing of heavenly contemplation should place before the eyes of his mind these deeds of blessed David and of the other holy fathers who preceded us, whenever they suffered something unjustly. By exercising himself in imitation of them, let him advance; and whatever presently pricks him through vice, let him restrain either by remembering former evils, quench by the consolation of former gifts, or blunt, as has been said, by imitating the fathers who preceded him.

This must be demonstrated by clearer examples, as we proposed. To speak of one among many, so that the diligent reader may understand many things in one, whoever is oppressed by insulting words and is unable to preserve patience with virtue should call David’s conduct to mind.

When Shimei was pressing him with so many insults and the armed nobles were eager to take revenge, David said: “What have I to do with you, sons of Zeruiah? Leave him, that he may curse. For the Lord commanded him to curse David.”

Who would dare ask why he did this? A little later David says: “Leave him, that he may curse according to the Lord’s command, if perhaps the Lord will look upon my affliction and repay me good for this cursing today.”

By these words he clearly indicates that, because of the crime committed against Bathsheba, he recalled to mind, while fleeing from the son rising against him, the evil he had committed. He considered the insulting words not so much reproaches as aids, by which he believed he could be cleansed and receive mercy.

We tolerate insults well when, in the secrecy of our mind, we return to the evil deeds we have committed. For the injury by which we are struck will seem light when, in our conduct, we understand that what we deserve is worse. Thus it happens that insults deserve gratitude rather than anger, since through their intervention we trust that a heavier punishment can be avoided before God the judge.

But what does it signify that the parricidal son Absalom pursued his father, while his father first withdrew and fled before his face, secure of victory; that David saw the wicked man perish, yet mourned him greatly and lamented the death of the parricide?

For it is written that David fled from the face of his son who was waging war against him. And since it is written concerning the people of Jerusalem: “I nourished and exalted sons, but they contemptuously rejected me” (Isa. I), his son is signified tropologically—that is, the Jewish people, which handed him over.

Absalom, as some interpret it, is understood to mean “the Father’s peace.” This seems remarkable in the historical account: how can “the Father’s peace” be understood of one who pursued his father in war?

But those who attend carefully to the allegory perceive that Absalom is Jerusalem, because Jerusalem itself is interpreted as “Peace.” Christ fled from its face when, abandoning it through his suffering, he succeeded among the Gentiles through faith.

Others understand Absalom as Judas the traitor, whom Christ endured with such great and extraordinary patience as though he were good, even though he was not ignorant of his thoughts. Christ admitted him to the meal at which he entrusted to the disciples the figure of his body and blood, and Judas betrayed him.

Finally, the fact that, even in the betrayal itself, Christ received a kiss is rightly understood as showing that he offered peace to his betrayer, although Judas was ravaged by the inward warfare of so wicked a purpose. Absalom is therefore called “the Father’s peace” because the Father possessed the peace that Absalom did not possess.

But perhaps someone may say: If David bore the image of Christ, how is it written that he had many wives and concubines, when Christ both abhors and condemns such things?

This occurred in prophecy. David’s many wives indicated the image of the many peoples and nations that would be joined to Christ through faith.
