His concubines, however, signify the churches of heretics, which boast that they remain under the title of Christ’s name; but because they follow Christ for carnal profits, they are called not wives but concubines.

Thus, nowadays, if kings have several wives or concubines, it is a crime, because the figures have now passed away for which permission regarding wives or concubines was granted. But now that the figures have passed away, no permission is given.

After Absalom had been struck down and David had returned to Jerusalem, he told Amasa to gather all the men of Judah by the third day and appointed him commander in place of Joab. When Amasa delayed beyond the appointed time, David ordered Joab and Abishai to go and seize Sheba, the son of Bichri.

When Joab came to Gibeon, Joab took Amasa by the chin with his right hand, as though kissing him; secretly moving his left hand toward the sword, he struck him in the side, and Amasa died.

What does it mean that Joab held Amasa’s chin with his right hand and, secretly moving his left hand toward the sword, spilled out his entrails, if not what is plainly understood? To hold with the right hand is, as it were, to flatter with apparent kindness; but he moves his left hand toward the sword who secretly strikes out of malice.

### X. David’s Song. Chapter XXII [Cols. 1094D–1098D]

The seventeenth psalm follows. And it is rightly asked why this psalm alone is found written in the Books of Kings.

Nor is it without reason that this psalm alone is found in the Books of Kings, because it signifies that kingdom in which we shall have no adversary. For its title is: “On the day when the Lord delivered him from the hand of his enemies and from the hand of Saul.”

Who is prefigured in David if not the one who came according to the flesh from David’s seed? He still suffers enemies in his body, which is the Church. Hence, to that persecutor whom he overthrew by his voice and, in a certain sense, consumed by transferring him into his own body, a voice sounded from heaven: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts IX).

When does this body deserve to be delivered from the hand of its enemies, if not when that last enemy, death, is destroyed, so that it may arrive at the kingdom of God?

“I will love you, O Lord, my strength.” I will love you, Lord, through whom I am strong.

“O Lord, my firmament and my refuge, my deliverer.” Lord, who strengthened me because I took refuge in you; I took refuge in you because you delivered me.

“My God, my helper, and I will hope in him.” My God, who first granted me the help of your calling, so that I might be able to hope in you.

“My protector, and the horn of my salvation, and my deliverer.” My protector, because I did not presume upon myself, as though raising against you the horn of pride; instead, I found you yourself to be the horn—that is, the firm height—of salvation, and in order that I might find it, you redeemed me.

“Praising, I will call upon the Lord, and I shall be saved from my enemies.” Seeking not my own glory but the Lord’s, I will call upon the Lord, and there will be no source from which the errors of iniquity can harm me.

“The pains of death surrounded me”—that is, the pains of the flesh.

“And torrents of iniquity troubled me.” Unrighteous crowds, stirred up for a time like rain-swollen rivers soon to dry up, acted in such a way as to trouble me.

“The pains of hell surrounded me.” Among those who surrounded me in order to destroy me were the pains of envy, which bring about death and lead to the hell of sin.

“The snares of death went before me.” They went before me because they wished to harm me first, so that what they did might later be repaid to them. Such people are caught for destruction: they have persuaded themselves to do evil by boasting of a righteousness in whose name, though not in reality, they glory against the nations.

“And in my distress I called upon the Lord, and I cried to my God. And he heard my voice from his holy temple.” He heard the voice of my heart, in which he dwells.

“And my cry was in his presence.” My cry, which I hold not in the ears of human beings but inwardly before him, entered his ears.

“And the earth was shaken and trembled.” When the Son was thus glorified, sinners were shaken and trembled.

“And the foundations of the mountains were troubled.” The hopes of the proud, which were fixed in this world, were troubled.

“And they were shaken because the Lord was angry with them”—namely, so that hope in temporal goods would no longer have a foundation in human hearts.

“Smoke rose in his anger.” The tearful prayer of penitents rose when they learned what God threatens the wicked.

“And fire blazed from his face.” After repentance, the burning of charity arising from knowledge of him will blaze.

“Coals were kindled by him.” They had already died, abandoned by the fire of good desire and the light of righteousness; they had remained cold and dark. Then they were kindled and illuminated again, and revived.

“And he inclined the heavens and descended.” He humbled the righteous person so that he might descend to human weakness.

“And darkness was beneath his feet.” Darkness is beneath his feet because he is not seen by those below with the brightness that rules above. For the wicked, who think earthly thoughts, did not know him because of the darkness of their wickedness; the earth is beneath his feet, as a footstool for his feet.

“And he mounted upon the cherubim and flew.” Cherubim is said to mean “fullness of knowledge.” Therefore he is said to have mounted and flown above the fullness of knowledge, because no knowledge comprehends the height of his majesty.

He flew, therefore, who carried himself far above the reach of our understanding, so that no one might reach God except through love; for the fullness of the law is love. He quickly showed himself incomprehensible to his lovers, lest they imagine that he could be grasped by bodily images.

The Lord mounted and flew above the cherubim because he graciously exalted the glory of his incarnation above the fullness of knowledge that could exist in human beings. His flying therefore means that the mystery of his power was withdrawn from human understanding.

For however brightly the spiritual life may shine with the fullness of knowledge, it cannot grasp how it came about that the one who existed was conceived, and that the creator of human beings before the ages was born as a human being at the end of the ages—God became flesh, and the Word became an infant.

Therefore it is rightly added there:

“He flew above the wings of the winds.” For he surpassed every understanding of souls. We may appropriately understand the soul to be represented by wind because of the speed of its thought. That swiftness by which he showed himself incomprehensible is above the virtues of souls, which, as though on wings, raise themselves into the airs of freedom through eternal fears.

“And he made darkness his hiding place.” He made the obscurity of the mysteries and the hidden hope in the hearts of believers his hiding place, where he might remain concealed without abandoning them. For while we are obscured by the darkness of our weakness, he is hidden from us through our ignorance, lest we see him now in eternal and unchanging brightness.

In this darkness also, where we still walk by faith and not by sight, as long as we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience. Since our creator has taken away the light of his vision from us, cast down as we are in this exile, he has hidden himself from our eyes as though in hiding places of darkness.

When we diligently contemplate the darkness of our blindness, we are recalled to lamentation. If the mind humbly remembers the inner light from which it has been deprived, it weeps over the blindness it suffers outwardly.

When it looks upon the darkness by which it is surrounded, it torments itself with ardent desire for the inner splendor; with every act of attentive vision it shakes itself and seeks, though rejected, the heavenly light from which it departed when it was created.

It therefore often happens that, within those very devout tears, the brightness of inward joy breaks forth, and the mind, which had previously lain blind in the body, is strengthened and revived above for the contemplation of its inner radiance.

“His tabernacle is around him.” Those who believe in him, though converted to him, surround him because he is in their midst, favoring all equally, dwelling in them as in a tabernacle during this present time.

“Dark water in the clouds of the air.” For this reason no one who rightly understands the Scriptures should imagine that he already possesses that light which is to come, when we shall pass from faith to sight.

For in the prophets and in all preachers of the divine word, teaching is obscure, because before the Lord’s coming, while they carried the table of the mysteries hidden within their ministries, the eyes of those who looked upon them were darkened in their understanding.

“Before the brightness in his presence.” In comparison with the brightness that exists in the presence of his manifestation.

“His clouds passed over.” The preachers of his word are no longer confined within the borders of Judea but have passed over to the Gentiles and traverse the whole expanse of the world with the brightness of miracles.

“Hail and coals of fire.” These are figurative rebukes by which hard hearts are struck as though by hail. If the hard and gentle earth—that is, a devout mind—receives them, the hardness of the hail—that is, the terror of a rebuke flashed forth and, as it were, frozen—is dissolved into water, that is, into nourishing instruction. Hearts kindled by the fire of charity revive.

All these things passed over in his clouds to the Gentiles, because holy men both strike terror into the hearts of their hearers and pour in consolation through their gentleness.

The prophet testifies to how they strike, saying: “They will proclaim the power of your terrors, and they will tell of your greatness” (Ps. CXLIV). And he added how they refresh through gentleness: “They will pour forth the memory of the abundance of your sweetness, and they will exult in your righteousness.”

“And the Lord thundered from heaven.” The trumpet of the Gospel sounded from the heart of the righteous.

“And the Most High gave his voice.” He gave it so that we might possess it and hear heavenly things in the depths of human affairs.

“And he sent out arrows and scattered them.” He sent out evangelists, flying along straight paths on the wings of virtues—not their own wings, but those of the one by whom they were sent—so that for some they might be the fragrance of life leading to life, and for others the fragrance of death leading to death.

“And he multiplied flashes of lightning, and troubled them, and the springs of waters appeared.” Those who had become springs of water in the preachers appeared, springs leaping up into eternal life.

“And the foundations of the world were revealed.” The prophets were brought forward, though they had not been understood, as the foundation on which the world believing in the Lord would be built.

“At your rebuke, O Lord.” At the cry: “The kingdom of God will draw near to you” (Luke X).

“At the inspiration of the breath of your anger.” At the words: “Unless you repent, you will all likewise perish” (Luke XIII).

“He sent from on high and took me.” Calling from the Gentiles the Church, a glorious inheritance without spot or wrinkle (Song IV; Eph. V).

“He took me up from the multitude of waters.” He took me up from the multitude of peoples.

“He delivered me from my strongest enemies.” He delivered me from my enemies who had prevailed in afflicting and corrupting this temporal life of mine.

“And from those who hated me, because they were strengthened against me.” From those who hated me because they were strengthened against me as long as I remained beneath them, ignorant of God.

“They went before me on the day of my affliction.” They harmed me first during the time in which I bear a mortal and laborious body.

“And the Lord became my firmament.” Since the firmament of earthly pleasure had been afflicted and shaken by the bitterness of miseries, the Lord became my firmament.

“And he led me out into a broad place.” Because I was suffering carnal confinement, he led me out into the spiritual breadth of faith.

“He delivered me, because he desired me”—because he desired me before I desired him.

“He delivered me from my most powerful enemies, who already envy me because I desire him.”

“And from those who hate me, because I desire him.”

“And the Lord will repay me according to the righteousness of my good will.” He who first supplied mercy before I possessed good will.

“And according to the purity of my hands he will repay me.” According to the purity of my deeds he will repay me, he who granted me the ability to do good by leading me into the breadth of faith.

“Because I have kept the ways of the Lord.” I have kept the ways so that the breadth of good works, which come through faith, may be accompanied by the length of perseverance.

“And I have not acted wickedly against my God.” For all his judgments are always before my eyes: all his judgments—that is, the rewards of the righteous, the punishments of the wicked, the chastisements of those being corrected, and the temptations of those being tested—I consider with persevering contemplation.

“And I have not cast his righteousness away from me.” This is what those do who fail under the burden of righteousness and return to their vomit.

“And I shall be blameless before him, and I shall keep myself from my iniquity.” And the Lord will repay me according to my righteousness. Therefore the Lord will repay me not only because of the breadth of faith, which works through love, but also because of the length of perseverance.

“And according to the purity of my hands he will repay me in the sight of his eyes.” Not according to what human beings see, but in the sight of his eyes, because the things that are seen are temporal, while the things that are not seen are eternal. To this belongs the height of hope.

“With the holy one you will be holy.” There is also a hidden depth in which you are understood: with the holy one you will be holy because you sanctify.

“And with the innocent man you will be innocent.” You harm no one; rather, each person is bound by the cords of his own sins.

“And with the chosen one you will be chosen.” You will be chosen by the one whom you choose.

“And with the perverse you will be overturned.” With the perverse you appear perverse, because you do not favor them; you appear perverse to them because they say: “The way of the Lord is not straight,” while their own way is not straight.

“For you will save the humble people.” This appears perverse to the perverse: that you save those who confess their sins.

“And you will humble the eyes of the proud.” You will humble those who, ignorant of God’s righteousness, wish to establish their own.

“For you illuminate my lamp, O Lord.” Our light does not come from ourselves; you illuminate my lamp, O Lord.

“My God, you will illuminate my darkness.” We are darkness in our sins, but my God will illuminate my darkness.

“For I shall be delivered from temptation by you.” Not by myself, but by you I shall be delivered from temptation.

“And in my God I shall pass over a wall.” Not in myself, but in my God I shall pass over the wall that sins have raised between human beings and the heavenly Jerusalem.

“My God, his way is spotless.” My God does not come to human beings unless they have cleansed the way of faith by which he is to come to them, because his way is spotless.

“The words of the Lord are tested by fire.” The words of the Lord are proved by the fire of testing.

“He is the protector of all who hope in him.” All who hope not in themselves but in him are not consumed by the same tribulation, for hope follows faith.

“For who is God besides the Lord whom we serve?”

“And who is God besides our Lord?” Who is God besides the Lord whom, after good service, we shall possess as sons who hope for him as an inheritance?

“God who girded me with strength.” God who girds me so that I may be strong, lest the folds of desire, falling loose, impede my works and my steps.

“And he made my way spotless.” He made spotless the way of my charity by which I shall come to him, just as the way of faith by which he comes to me is spotless.

“Who made my feet like those of a deer” (Ps. XVII). He perfected my love so that I might rise above the thorny and shadowy entanglements of this world.

He calls spiritual men “deer” because of the joyful swiftness of their course. For minds firmly fixed in God despise every adversity all the more because they see that whatever grows contrary to the commands of the Creator is destined to perish.

While they await the rewards of eternity, they draw strength from adversities, because as the battle increases, they do not doubt that a more glorious victory remains for them.

Thus the desires of the elect, while pressed by adversity, advance, just as fire is pressed by the breath that makes it grow; from the very point where it seems to be extinguished, it gains strength.

For we show how great is the desire with which we burn for God if we pass to him not only through tranquil and pleasant things but also through harsh and difficult ones.

The psalmist therefore rightly says: “Who made my feet like those of a deer.” When a deer climbs the ridges of mountains, it leaps over whatever is rough and whatever obstructs it, even when entangled with thorns; without any obstacle to its course, it rises to the heights.

So too the minds of the elect, when they see the things of this world standing in their way and opposing them, transcend them with a leap of contemplation and, like deer, despising the thorns of earthly things, raise themselves to the heights above.

“And he set me upon high places.” He will fix my attention upon the heavenly dwelling, so that I may be filled unto all the fullness of God.

He who teaches my hands for battle, who teaches me to act so as to overcome the enemies who try to bar the heavenly kingdoms to us.

And you made my arms like a bronze bow, and you established an unfailing resolve for good works.

And you gave me the protection of your salvation, and your right hand received me—that is, the favor of grace received me.

And your discipline directed me toward the end. Your correction, not allowing me to go astray, directed me so that whatever I do I may refer it to the end that is joined to me.

And your discipline itself will teach me, and that same correction of yours will itself teach me to arrive where it directed me.

[Col. 1099A] You enlarged my steps beneath me; the constrictions of the flesh will not impede me, because you made my charity broad, so that I might work cheerfully even with regard to the mortal things and members that are beneath me. And my footsteps have not been weakened. Neither my paths nor the signs that I have impressed for those who follow to imitate have been weakened.

I will pursue my enemies and crush them. I will pursue my carnal affections, lest I be seized by them; rather, I will seize them so that they may be consumed.

And I will not turn back until they fail. I will not turn from this resolve to rest until those who oppose me have failed.

And I will break them, and they will not be able to stand; I will break them, and they will not endure against me.

They will fall beneath my feet; I will set beloved loves before them, with which I walk forever.

And you girded me with strength for battle; you restrained with strength the flowing desires of my flesh, so that I would not be hindered in such a struggle. [Col. 1099B]

You brought low beneath me those rising up against me; you caused those who pursued me to be deceived, so that they became beneath me, though they wished to be above me.

And you gave me the backs of my enemies; you turned my enemies around and made them my back—that is, so that they would follow me. And you destroyed those who hated me; you destroyed those of them who persisted in hatred.

They will cry out, and there will be no one to save them. For who would save those whom you would not save?

They cried out to the Lord, and he did not hear them; they cried not to just anyone but to the Lord, and he judged them unworthy of being heard because they did not withdraw from their wickedness.

And I will crush them like dust before the face of the wind; I will crush them, for they are dry, receiving none of the rain of God’s mercy, so that, lifted up and swollen with pride, they may be snatched away from firm and unshaken hope, as though from the solidity and stability of the earth.

Like the mud of the streets I will wipe them away. Along the broad roads of perdition, on which many [Col. 1099C] walk, I will wipe away those who live luxuriously and slip easily into sin.

You will rescue me from the disputes of the people; you will rescue me from the disputes of those who said: “If we let him live, the world will follow him.”

You will establish me as head of the nations. A people whom I did not know will serve me; the people of the nations whom I did not visit in bodily presence served me, though they did not see me with their eyes; receiving my preachers, they obeyed me when they heard.

The sons of strangers lied to me; sons who should not be called mine but rather strangers, to whom it was rightly said, “You are of your father the devil,” lied to me.

The sons of strangers grew old, and they limped from their paths; like men weak in one foot, because they clung to the old and rejected the new. The sons of strangers, to whom I brought the New Testament so that they might be renewed, remained in the old man. They also became lame within the old law itself, following their own traditions rather than those of God. For they reproached him concerning unwashed hands, although such were their paths, as though they themselves had established and sanctioned the custom by straying from the path of God’s commandments.

[Col. 1099D] The Lord lives, and blessed is my God. To set one’s mind on the flesh, however, is death; the Lord lives, and blessed is my God. And let the God of my salvation be exalted, and let me not think of the God of my salvation according to earthly custom, but hope in him above for that salvation itself, which is eternal. O God, who gives me vengeance; O God, who avenges me by subjecting peoples beneath me.

My deliverer from my enraged enemies—those who cried, “Crucify him, crucify him.” From those rising up against me you will exalt me; from the Jews rising up against me you will exalt me as I rise from the dead. Rescue me from an iniquitous man; from their iniquitous kingdom you will deliver me.

Therefore I will confess you among the nations, O Lord. Therefore through me the nations will confess you, O Lord. [Col. 1100A] And I will sing psalms to your name, and you will become more widely known through my good works.

Magnifying the salvation of his king. God magnifies the salvation that his Son gives to believers, making it worthy of love.

And showing mercy to his Christ. God shows mercy to his Christ, David, and to his offspring forever: to that deliverer by a powerful hand, who conquered this world, and to those whom he begot as believers in the Gospel forever. Whatever has been said in this psalm that cannot properly be applied to the Lord himself—that is, to the head of the Church—must be referred to the Church; for the whole Christ speaks here, in whom all his members are present.

Now these are the last words spoken by David son of Jesse. He calls David’s last words not words to be ended but to be completed—not words to be consumed, but words that confer the fullness of perfection upon all the faithful. The Spirit of the Lord has spoken through me, and his word has been upon my tongue. By the Spirit of the Lord he means the Holy Spirit; by the word of God, Christ [Col. 1100B], the Son of God, is understood; for he is the Christ of the God of Jacob.

But all the transgressors will be plucked out like thorns. The transgressors—the Jews and heretics—will be plucked out like thorns from the Church, which is the land of the living, and, burned in the eternal fire, will perish.

[Col. 1100C] These are the names of David’s mighty men: seated in the chair, most wise, chief among the three. He is like the tenderest worm of wood, who killed eight hundred in a single attack. He is not Jesbaa, as some think, but David himself is called the tenderest worm of wood. By this the man’s military strength and restrained civility are signified: for just as a worm of wood appears tender and fragile throughout its body, and also very small, yet it consumes the strongest wood and reduces it to dust—and from wearing away wood it receives the name of woodworm—so he seemed gentle toward everyone at home, quiet and humble, yet in public battle he showed himself strong and intolerable to his enemies.

It is not absurd to understand these three mighty men—David, Eleazar, and Shammah—as the Trinity: God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. The remaining mighty men did not attain to their equality.

### XI. David’s Thirst. Chapter XVII

David himself, while engaged in battle against the Philistines and suffering thirst, sought water in the war. “Who will give me a drink,” he said, “from the reservoir [cistern, II Kings 23] that is in Bethlehem?” The road to the cistern was near the gates. David was surrounded by enemies and had penetrated to the middle of the enemy camp. Three men cut through the multitude of adversaries, drew water from the cistern that was in Bethlehem, and offered it to the king to drink. But the king refused to drink it and poured it out to the Lord, saying: “Far be it from me to do this: that I should drink the blood of men who went at the risk of their lives.”

Thus he overcame nature: although thirsty, he did not drink, and he provided an example by which the whole army might learn to endure thirst. But if you wish to look more deeply and examine the mystery, David thirsted [Col. 1100D] not for the water that was in Bethlehem, but in spirit foresaw Christ, born in that same Bethlehem from the Virgin. Therefore he wished to drink not the water of a stream but the bath flowing from Christ’s side. He did not thirst for the element of water but for the blood of Christ. Hence he did not drink the water offered to him but poured it out to the Lord, signifying that he thirsted for a sacrifice—not the flow of nature, but that sacrifice in which there would be remission of sins; he thirsted for that eternal fountain, not one sought through the dangers of others, but one that would erase the dangers of others.

In this deed, one must consider very carefully what concerns human conduct: whoever remembers that he has committed illicit acts should strive to abstain even from certain licit acts, so that by this he may satisfy his Creator. Whoever has committed what is forbidden ought to cut off from himself even what is permitted, and should reproach himself in small matters if he remembers that he has sinned in great ones.

[Col. 1101A] Certainly, the law of the Old Testament forbids coveting another man’s wife, but it does not prohibit a king, under penalty, from commanding brave deeds of soldiers or desiring water. We all know that David, pierced by the sword of desire, both coveted and took another man’s wife; worthy scourging followed his guilt, and he corrected the evil he had committed through the lamentations of repentance.

Long afterward, when he engaged the ranks of the enemy, he wished out of desire to drink water from the cistern. His chosen soldiers broke through the middle of the opposing forces and brought back unharmed the water he had desired. But the man of the Lord, instructed by the scourges he had received, immediately reproached himself for desiring water at the risk of his soldiers; pouring it out to the Lord, he offered it as a libation, as it is written: “He poured it out as a libation to the Lord.” For the water poured out was transformed into the Lord’s sacrifice, because through the repentance of his self-reproach he slaughtered the guilt of his desire.

Therefore, he who once had no fear of coveting another man’s wife afterward became afraid even because he had coveted water. For he remembered that he had committed illicit acts, and so he was now strict with himself and abstained even from [Col. 1101B] licit things.

Three mighty men rushed to draw this water: Abishai, the brother of Joab; Asahel; and Benaiah son of Jehoiada. This Benaiah struck down two lions of Moab. He also descended and struck a lion in the middle of a cistern on snowy days.

Josephus explains more clearly how this happened: the cistern was exceedingly deep, and in winter, when everything was full of snow, it too had been leveled by a great accumulation of snow. When a lion, unaware of the danger, fell into it and, trapped there, cried out with a great roar, people ran to see what had happened. When Benaiah arrived with others to watch the spectacle, he immediately leapt into the cistern, attacked the lion amid the snow, and struck and killed it.

After this follows a catalogue of mighty men as figures of the saints. Strengthened by the courage of virtuous deeds and by knowledge of the divine Trinity, they not only defend themselves from evil enemies but also protect the weak.

[Col. 1101C] ### XII. David’s Sin in Numbering the People. Chapter XXIV

After this David sinned by numbering the people. For David commanded Joab to travel throughout all Israel and bring back the number of the people. Scripture says that this happened because the anger of the Lord began to burn against Israel.

What else is demonstrated in this deed except that the actions of rulers are arranged according to the qualities of their subjects, so that often, because of the evil of the flock, even good men sin in their pastoral office? This David, praised by God’s testimony, this prophet David, acquainted with heavenly mysteries, swollen by the sudden tumor of exaltation, sinned by numbering the people; yet while David sinned, the people received the punishment.

Why was this? Because the hearts of rulers are arranged according to the merit of the people. The just Judge corrected the ruler’s fault through the punishment of those because of whom he had sinned. But because David himself, growing proud by his own will, was not free from guilt, he too received the punishment of his fault. For the raging anger that struck the people bodily also struck down the ruler of the people through the inward pain of his heart.

It is certain that the merits of rulers and those of the people are so bound together that often, through the guilt of shepherds, the life of the people becomes worse, and often, through the merit of the people, the life of the shepherds is changed.

[Col. 1102A] But because rulers have their own Judge, it is a matter of great caution for subjects not rashly to judge the lives of those who govern. For the Lord did not in vain himself pour out the coins of the money changers and overturn the seats of those selling doves, clearly signifying that the life of the people is indeed judged through teachers, but that he himself examines the deeds of teachers. The faults of subjects, moreover, which are either overlooked by teachers or cannot now be judged by them, are undoubtedly reserved for his judgment.

Therefore, while the matter is conducted in sound faith, it is a mark of virtue to endure whatever belongs to one’s predecessor. Yet one should humbly suggest a correction if what is displeasing in one’s superior can perhaps be amended. Above all, however, care must be taken lest the disordered defense of justice pass into pride, and lest, while rectitude is loved without caution, humility—the teacher of rectitude itself—be lost.

[Col. 1102B] No one should despise the person placed over him merely because he happens to find him blameworthy in some action. Against this swelling of pride, the mind of subjects is subdued to guard humility if it continually considers its own weakness. For we neglect to examine our strength truthfully, and because we believe ourselves capable of great things, we judge those placed over us severely. The less we know ourselves, the more we see in those whom we strive to criticize.

These are individual evils that are often committed by subjects against superiors and by superiors against subjects. Those who preside think that all their subjects are less wise than they themselves are; and those who are subject judge the actions of their rulers and, if they happened to hold authority themselves, think they could act better.

Hence it often happens that rulers [Col. 1102C] see less wisely what ought to be done, because the very cloud of exaltation darkens their eyes. And sometimes the person who is subject, once he becomes a superior, does what, while subject, he used to accuse others of doing. Since he commits what he had judged, he should at least be ashamed that he judged it.

Therefore, just as superiors must take care lest the higher position of authority exalt their hearts through an estimation of their singular wisdom, so subjects must take care lest the actions of their rulers displease them. If the life of teachers is rightly reproved, subjects ought nevertheless to honor them with discipline.

But this must be observed carefully: do not seek to imitate one whom it is necessary to honor, nor refuse to honor one whom you despise imitating. A subtle path must be maintained—the path of rectitude and humility—so that the blameworthy deeds of teachers may displease the mind of subjects without causing them to depart from preserving reverence for the teaching office.

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 1101]

[Col. 1101D] ### I. Solomon’s Succession. Chapter I

David grew old, and Solomon was anointed king over Israel at Gihon, so that the promise made to David might be fulfilled in him: “You shall not build a house for me, but your son who will come forth from your womb.”

In this event an image of what was to come was formed: Solomon built the temple and had peace according to his name. For Solomon is interpreted as “Peaceful,” and therefore that name most truly suits him through whom, having received the remission of sins from our enemies, we are reconciled to God. For while we were enemies, having received forgiveness of sins, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son.

He himself is the peaceful one who made both into one and [Col. 1102D] broke down the middle wall of enmity in his flesh, annulling the law of commandments by decrees, so that he might create the two in himself as one new man, making peace for those who were far away and peace for those who were near. In the Gospel he says: “I give you my peace; I leave you my peace” (John 14).

By these and many other testimonies the Lord Christ is shown to be peaceful. For the fact that he built the most excellent temple for the Lord also signifies Christ, who built a dwelling for God in the heavens—not from wood and stones, but from all the saints, that is, the faithful, to whom the Apostle says: “The temple of God is holy, and you are that temple” (1 Cor. 3).

[Col. 1103A] The Scriptures clearly teach that Solomon was called by three names: Peaceful, that is, Solomon; Jedidiah, that is, “Beloved of the Lord”; and Qoheleth, that is, Ecclesiastes. In Greek, Ecclesiastes is the one who gathers an assembly—that is, a church. We may call him a preacher, one who speaks to the people, whose speech is directed not particularly to one person but generally to all.

The names “Peaceful” and “Beloved of the Lord” were given to him because there was peace in his kingdom and the Lord loved him. Psalms 44 and 71 are also prefaced by the title “Beloved” and “Peaceful.” Although, as pertaining to the prophecy of Christ and the Church, they surpass Solomon’s happiness and strength, nevertheless, according to the historical sense, they were written concerning Solomon.

### II. The Wisdom Granted to Solomon and His Judgment. Chapter III

Solomon went to Gibeon and offered a burnt offering there to the Lord. The Lord appeared to him by night, heard the prayer that he requested, and gave him wisdom and knowledge, so much so that [Col. 1103B] no one like him had existed before him or would arise after him.

After receiving wisdom from God, he was immediately tested in judgment because of wicked women. Here it should be noted that after the Lord illumines the darkness of our error with the knowledge of his light, he immediately tests us by visiting us with the goad of temptation. By drawing near, he advances our hearts toward virtues; by withdrawing, he permits us to be shaken by temptation.

For if the mind were shaken by no temptation after receiving the gifts of virtue, it would already boast that it possessed these things from itself. Therefore, so that it may possess the gifts of weakness and humbly acknowledge its weakness, it is lifted up to higher things through the approach of grace, and through grace’s withdrawal it is shown what it is of itself.

This is well suggested to us by the history of this sacred reading: Solomon is remembered as having received wisdom from God, yet, after receiving that same wisdom, he was immediately troubled by the question of the prostitutes. As soon as he received the grace of so great a revelation, he endured the contest of wicked women. For whenever [Col. 1103C] the inward brightness of divine regard illumines our mind through virtues granted to us, slippery thoughts immediately disturb it, so that the mind which rejoices at being raised up by an immense gift may discover what it is when struck by temptation.

Thus Elijah, visited from above, opened the heavens by his word, yet, suddenly tested and made weak, he fled through the wilderness and was exceedingly afraid of a woman. Thus Paul was taken up to the third heaven and saw the secrets of paradise, yet, returning to himself, he struggled against the battle of the flesh and endured another law in his members, grieving in spirit because he was wearied by the law of that battle.

Therefore, even after the gift has been bestowed, God tests a person because, by granting the gift, he raises him up, and by withdrawing it for a little while, he shows the person to himself. We undoubtedly endure this until we are completely reshaped from earth and the stain of sin into the substance of the incorruption that has been promised.

[Col. 1103D] In Solomon’s judgment, where he is first described as judging between two women contending over compassion—love burning in one and deceit stealing into the other—there was a figure of Christ. The wicked people, namely the synagogue or the heretics, desired the son of the true mother, that is, the Church; but they desired him not to preserve him, rather truly to kill him.

But just as, when Solomon divided with the sword, this true offspring was revealed through the grief of his own mother, so, taught by the Spirit of Jesus Christ, those who have been seduced and captured by the error of heretics sometimes deserve to recognize the Church, their mother, grieving on their behalf.

Thus it is sufficiently clear that this woman represented the impiety of the heretics or of the synagogue. They wickedly kill their own children by nurturing them, and entice and persuade others until they destroy them.

In the moral sense, however, what else is signified by the mothers nursing their children except the order of teachers, and by their sons except the persons of disciples? Teachers who are vigilant in knowledge but asleep in life, while neglecting to do what they say, kill through the sleep of their sluggishness those [Col. 1104A] hearers whom they nourish through the vigils of preaching. By their negligence they crush those whom they seemed to feed with the milk of words.

Hence, when they themselves live reprehensibly and cannot have disciples whose lives are praiseworthy, they often try to attract the disciples of others, so that by displaying good followers they may excuse the evils they commit in the judgment of people and, as it were, cover their own mortal negligence with the life of their subjects.

Thus the woman who had killed her own son sought another’s. Nevertheless, Solomon found the true mother, because the strict Judge’s final examination reveals whose fruit lives and whose perishes.

Here it should also be carefully observed that the living son is first ordered to be divided, so that afterward he may be returned to his sole mother. For in this life the disciple’s life is, as it were, permitted to be divided, since it is sometimes permitted to have merit before God in one respect and praise before human beings in another.

But the false mother did not fear to have the one she had not borne killed, because arrogant teachers, ignorant [Col. 1104B] of charity, if they cannot obtain the fullest name of praise through the disciples of others, cruelly pursue those disciples’ lives. Inflamed by the torch of envy, they do not want others to live whom they see themselves unable to possess.

Hence the perverse woman cries: “Let him be neither mine nor hers.” As we have said, they begrudge others the life in truth of those whom they do not see obeying them for the sake of temporal glory.

But the true mother strives that her son may at least be with another woman and live. For faithful teachers allow their disciples to bring praise for teaching to others, provided that those same disciples do not lose the integrity of their lives. By this compassionate affection the true mother is recognized, because every teaching office is approved in the examination of charity. Only she deserved to receive the child because she, as it were, conceded everything: faithful superiors do not merely begrudge others the praise arising from their good disciples, but even pray for their greater usefulness; and they receive their sons whole and living [Col. 1104C] when, in the heavenly examination, they obtain the joys of perfect recompense through their lives.

### III. Solomon’s Parables, Songs, and Discussions. Chapter IV

Solomon spoke three thousand parables, and his songs numbered five thousand. What else is signified by the three thousand parables except the fullness of the faith delivered by Christ in the Law and the Gospels? Since the whole of this faith is discussed in many ways through the sense of allegory under the mystery of the Trinity, it is, as it were, called three thousand parables.

His five thousand songs are understood through the five bodily senses. Whoever uses these well in various virtues is blessed, and through them sings, as it were, five thousand songs to the Lord.

Solomon also discussed matters from the cedar to the hyssop. By the cedar is understood the height of grace in the elect, as the prophet also testifies: “The righteous will flourish like a palm tree and grow like a cedar of Mount Lebanon” (Ps. 91).

Hyssop, however, is a lowly herb clinging to a rock, by which Christ’s humility is signified. Our [Col. 1104D] Redeemer discussed matters from the cedar to the hyssop, because he descended from the excellence of heavenly glory to the humility of the flesh.

Indeed, by the cedar is also signified the proud exaltation of the wicked, as David says: “The voice of the Lord breaking the cedars” (Ps. 28). Thus Christ discusses matters from the cedar to the hyssop because he himself judges both the hearts of the wicked and those of the humble.

He discussed matters concerning wood when he hung upon the cross. For then he bent down the arrogance of the world in the cedar and brought it down to the humility of hyssop—that is, to the foolishness of the cross and to the faith despised by the world.

### IV. How Hiram Helps Solomon in the Work of the Temple. Chapter V

The history next relates how Solomon, intending to build a house for the Lord, sought assistance from Hiram, king of Tyre. Hiram had always been a friend of David, and after Solomon gained the kingdom he had begun to live at peace with him. Hiram immediately proved ready [Col. 1105A] to help him in every way, giving him craftsmen, wood, and gold as the work required. In gratitude for this favor, Solomon gave him every year many kors of wheat and barley as food for his household.

There is no doubt that Solomon, whose name means “Peaceful,” signifies by both his name and the peaceful condition of his reign the one of whom Isaiah said: “His government will be multiplied, and there will be no end of peace” (Isa. 9).

Hiram, whose name in Latin means “Living on high,” figuratively represents believers from the nations, glorious in both life and faith. Nor does anything prevent us from understanding Hiram, because he was a king and assisted Solomon in building the house of the Lord with royal power, as typologically indicating those converted to the faith who are themselves rulers of earthly affairs. Through their help the Church is known to have been often assisted and nobly increased, and heretics, schismatics, and pagans have been raised up by the decrees of rulers.

Solomon therefore seeks Hiram’s assistance in the work of the temple because, when the Lord came in the flesh and planned to build the house beloved by him—that is, the [Col. 1105B] Church—he chose assistants for the work not only from the Jews but also from the nations. From both peoples he appointed ministers of the word.

Hiram sent Solomon cedar and fir logs cut from Lebanon, to be placed in the house of the Lord. This signifies that the converted Gentiles sent to the Lord men who had once been distinguished in the world but had already been cast down and humbled from the mountain of their pride by the axe of the Lord’s rebuke. Trained according to the rule of evangelical truth, each would be placed in the building of the Church according to his merit and his time.

He also sent craftsmen, because the Gentiles offered to the Lord philosophers converted to true wisdom, who, by the grace of their learning, could rightly be placed in charge of governing peoples. Such were Dionysius the Areopagite in the times of the apostles, and afterward the most eloquent teacher and courageous martyr Cyprian, along with many others.

He also sent gold, which is understood in the same sense, since it signifies men distinguished by wisdom and [Col. 1105C] talent. In return for these offerings, the whole Gentile world awaits gifts of heavenly grace from the Lord: namely, the wheat of God’s word, the oil of charity and anointing, and the illumination of the Holy Spirit.

It aptly accords with the affairs of the Church that Solomon, asking Hiram for assistance in the holy work, says:

“Therefore command them to cut cedars for me from Lebanon, and let my servants be with your servants.”

Hiram’s [Col. 1105D] servants, who cut cedars for Solomon from Lebanon, are chosen teachers from the nations. Their duty is to correct and bring low those who rejoiced in worldly possessions and glory because of the arrogance of pride, and to transfer their desires to this purpose according to those of their Redeemer.

These servants were at once Hiram’s servants and Solomon’s servants, and together they labored at the work mentioned. For the first teachers from the nations necessarily had to be instructed in the word of faith by the apostles themselves, who had learned from the Lord. If they had begun to teach without teachers, they would have become teachers of error.

Solomon therefore wanted Hiram’s servants to cut the wood for him from Lebanon because they were more learned than his servants at cutting it. But he also wanted his own servants to be present at the same time, so that they might show the cutters what dimensions the wood ought to have.

The meaning of this figure is clear: the apostles knew the word of the Gospel more certainly, because they had learned to hear it from the Lord; but the Gentiles who had been converted from error and transformed into the truth of the Gospel knew the errors of the nations better. The more certainly they knew them, the more skillfully they learned to attack and destroy them.

Paul knew the mystery of the Gospel, which he had learned through revelation, better; but Dionysius could refute the false doctrines of the pagans more effectively, since from childhood he had known all their syllogisms and arguments together with their errors.

This meaning accords well with what follows: “For you know that there is no man among my people who knows how to cut wood like the Sidonians.”

There was no man among the Jewish people, where the Lord was bodily present and teaching, who [Col. 1106A] knew how to refute the errors of the Gentiles as learnedly as those Gentiles themselves who had been converted to the faith and had become Christians from among the nations. Since the Sidonians and Tyrians were peoples of the Gentiles, they are rightly understood as figures of the nations.

### V. The Number of Those Who Cut, Those Who Carried Burdens, and Others. Chapter VI

That our Solomon sent his servants to this work is designated in mystical language in what follows, where it is said:

“Solomon chose laborers from all Israel, and the levy was thirty thousand men. He sent ten thousand to Lebanon each month in rotation, so that they would be at home for two months.”

First it should be noted that Solomon did not choose laborers from all Israel without reason, nor was there any part of the people from which men worthy of so great a work were not taken. For now priests are not to be chosen from one lineage of Aaron; rather, those who are sufficient to build the house of the Lord either by their example or by their word are to be sought from the whole Church. Wherever they are found, they are immediately advanced to the office of [Col. 1106B] teachers without respect of persons.

When such men are appointed to instruct unbelievers and call them into the fellowship of the Church, they are sent like vigorous and chosen men to cut the materials for the temple in Lebanon.

The number thirty thousand, by which these woodcutters were counted, can aptly be referred as a figure to those who are perfected in faith in the Holy Trinity, something especially appropriate to teachers.

But because the thirty thousand were arranged so that ten thousand at a time would devote themselves to their work each month, we should weigh more carefully the mystery of the number ten. Ten thousand men from Israel are sent to cut wood for the work of the house of the Lord because all teachers and instructors of the ignorant who are to be appointed must observe the ten commandments of the Law in every respect and show them to their hearers by observing them. They must also hope for the future rewards in heaven, which are commonly signified by the number ten, and continually declare them as objects of hope to their hearers.

[Col. 1106C] [Col. 1106C] The three-month intervals assigned to each group of woodcutters figuratively announce the perfection of the three evangelical virtues: almsgiving, prayer, and fasting.

When the Lord had said in the Gospel, “Take care not to practice your righteousness before people in order to be seen by them,” in explaining the same statement he mentioned nothing other than almsgiving, prayer, and fasting. These are to be practiced not for the display of human beings but for the glory of the one who sees within; otherwise they would remain empty of the fruit of eternity.

By these words he plainly taught that all the fruits of virtue are suggested through these three branches, as though growing from one root of charity. Through almsgiving are understood all the things we accomplish out of love for our neighbor, working benevolently for our brothers and sisters. Through prayer are understood all the things by which, through inward contrition, we are joined to our Creator. Through fasting are understood all the things by which we guard ourselves from the contagion of vices and the enticements of the world, so that with a free mind and [Col. 1106D] chaste body we may cling to love of both our Creator and our neighbor.

These, then, are the three months of the temple’s laborers. Since a month is completed by the fullness of the days of the lunar cycle, it displays the fullness of each spiritual virtue, in which the mind of the faithful is regarded by the Lord through daily illumination, as the moon is regarded by the sun.

One month, during which the wood was cut for the work of the temple, is almsgiving—that is, works of mercy—which advance beneficially toward the salvation of one’s neighbor and toward the unity of the holy Church: teaching, correcting, providing temporal goods, and displaying examples of life.

The other two months, during which they were permitted to remain in their homes and attend to their own needs, are prayer and fasting. Through these, in addition to the works we perform outside for the needs of our brothers and sisters, we care within for our own salvation, turning our minds toward the Lord.

And because only those care perfectly for their own salvation and that of their brothers and sisters who humbly submit themselves to the contemplation of divine grace, it rightly follows:

“And Adoniram was over this levy.”

[Col. 1107A] Adoniram, whose name in Latin means “My exalted Lord”—whom does this name better suggest than the Lord Savior himself? Adoniram is placed over the temple’s laborers so that, through his provision, it may rightly be arranged in which months each group should go out to work and in which months they should return again to care for their own household.

This occurs when our Lord and Savior, through his more intimate illumination, instructs the minds of the holy preachers to discern when it is fitting to begin the work of building the Church by preaching or by performing other duties of piety, and when it is again appropriate to return, as if to inspect their own house, in order to examine their consciences and make them worthy, through prayers and fasts, of the heavenly inspector and visitor.

## VI. On the Number of the Temple Workers. Chapter V

Thus Solomon had seventy thousand men who carried burdens, and eighty thousand stonecutters [Col. 1107B] in the mountain, besides the overseers who directed each particular task, numbering three thousand three hundred, who commanded the people and those who performed the work.

By “stonecutters” he means cutters of stones. These same cutters of stones, figuratively considered together with the cutters of wood, signify the holy preachers: they labor upon the minds of the foolish through the word of God, strive to transform them from the disgrace and deformity with which they have been stained, and take care to make them, once regularly instructed, suitable for the unity of the faithful—that is, for the building of the house of God.

The fact that both wood and stones are cut in the mountain, and that both materials, once cut and prepared, are transferred to the mountain of the Lord’s house, makes the meaning clear: all human beings are born on the mountain of pride, because we have derived the origin of our flesh from the transgression of the first man, which pride caused. But whenever, by grace and predestination, we are cut out for life, we are transferred through catechesis, so that we may receive the sacraments of faith, from the mountain of pride to the mountain of the Lord’s house. Once rescued from the power of darkness, we arrive at the citadel of virtues, which exists in the unity of the holy Church [Col. 1107C].

It should be noted, however, that these same workers were distributed in such a way that some cut stones in the mountain, while others carried burdens. For the gifts of the Spirit are diverse. Some possess greater steadfastness in speaking and rebuking the obstinate; others are gentler in consoling the fainthearted and supporting the weak; others, endowed with both virtues, come together for the work of the Lord’s house. Such are the people whom the Apostle wished those he addresses to become, when he says: “Reprove the restless, console the fainthearted, support the weak, be patient toward all” (I Thess. V).

The overseers who directed the individual tasks are the authors of Sacred Scripture. Through their teaching we are instructed in every respect: how it is fitting to teach the uninstructed and rebuke the contemptuous, and how we should bear one another’s burdens, so that we may fulfill the law of Christ. The more each person labors either in supporting the needs of his neighbors or in correcting their errors [Col. 1107D], the more certain are the rewards he awaits in the future—whether the rest of souls after death or the blessed immortality of bodies.

Hence the aforesaid workers are rightly said to have numbered seventy thousand and eighty thousand: seventy thousand on account of the sabbath of souls, since the seventh day was consecrated as a sabbath, that is, as rest; and eighty thousand on account of the hope of resurrection, which took place in the Lord on the eighth day, that is, after the sabbath, and which is also hoped for in us on the eighth day and in the eighth age.

The overseers numbered three thousand three hundred, clearly on account of faith in the holy Trinity, which the sacred writings preach to us. But the fact that, instead of three thousand three hundred overseers, the Book of Chronicles records three thousand six hundred refers entirely to the same perfection of exalted men. For since the Lord completed the adornment of the world in the number six, good works are rightly accustomed to be represented as perfect by that number. And because Holy Scripture teaches that works of justice are to be joined with faith in the truth, the overseers of the temple works are rightly said to have numbered three thousand six hundred.

Nor should it be passed over that these seventy thousand and eighty thousand burden-bearers and stonecutters, together with their overseers, were not Israelites but proselytes—that is, resident foreigners who lived among them. For it is written in the Book of Chronicles:

“Solomon therefore counted all the proselyte men who were in the land of Israel, after the census which David his father had taken, and they were found to number one hundred fifty thousand and three thousand six hundred. Of these he made seventy thousand to carry burdens, etc.” (II Chron. II).

Proselytes were so called in Greek: they were people born of other nations who, having received circumcision, had passed over into the faith and fellowship of the people of God.

Thus the workers of the Lord’s house came from the children of Israel, from the proselytes, and from the nations. From the children of Israel there were thirty thousand, who were sent to cut cedars from Lebanon; from the proselytes there were those whom we have discussed, the cutters of stones [Col. 1108B]; and from the nations there were Hiram himself and his servants, who cut wood from Lebanon together with Solomon’s servants.

Therefore every class of human beings through whom the Church was to be built preceded it in the building of the temple. For Jews, proselytes, and Gentiles converted to the truth of the Gospel build one and the same Church of Christ, whether by living rightly or also by teaching.

## VII. On the Stones. Chapter V

And the king commanded them to take large stones, precious stones, for the foundation of the temple, and to square them.

Mystically, no other foundation of the temple is to be understood than the one Paul points out when he says: “For no one can lay any other foundation than that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (I Cor. III). He can rightly be called the foundation of the Lord’s house because, as Peter says: “There is no other name under heaven given among human beings by which we must be saved.”

Large and precious stones are placed upon this foundation when men distinguished for their deeds and holiness, by the familiar holiness of their minds, adhere to their Creator, so that the more firmly they place their hope in him, the more strongly they may be able to direct the lives of others—that is, to bear what is high.

The stones that were placed in the foundation of the temple to bear the entire building are properly the prophets and apostles, who received the word and sacraments of the truth from the Wisdom of God itself, whether visibly or invisibly. Hence the Apostle says that we too, insofar as we strive to imitate their life or teaching, have been “built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets.”

More generally, all the perfect who have faithfully learned to cling to the Lord himself and courageously bear the burdens imposed upon them by their brothers may be represented by the large and precious stones. They are rightly commanded first to be squared and then placed in the foundation, for whatever direction a square object is turned, it customarily stands firm.

The hearts of teachers are appropriately likened to this figure. They have learned to stand so firmly in the constancy of faith that no adversity among the events that befall them—not even their own death—can bend them from the rectitude of their position. The Church has received many such teachers not only from Judea but also from the nations.

Thus, concerning such large, precious, and squared stones, it is suitably added:

“Which the masons of Solomon and the masons of Hiram hewed.”

Precious stones are hewn when each of the elect, through the instruction and diligence of the saints who preceded them, casts away whatever harmful and useless thing they possess, and displays before the sight of their Creator only the rule of innate righteousness, like the stable form of squareness.

The stones were hewn not only by Solomon’s masons but also by Hiram’s masons, because teachers of the holy Church came from both peoples. Indeed, some men of such eminence came from both peoples that they rightly became teachers even of those exalted teachers themselves, preparing them, as it were, by squaring them, to support the building of the Lord’s house [Col. 1109A].

For it was not only Jeremiah and Isaiah and the other prophets from the circumcision, but also blessed Job with his sons, who were from the nations, who supplied teachers of later ages with the greatest pattern of patience in life and the most extensive proclamations of saving doctrine. Thus, after casting away superfluous words, deeds, and thoughts, they were found worthy and suitable to bear the burden of the holy Church.

Moreover, the Byblians prepared wood and stones for building a house for the Lord.

Byblus is a city in Syria Phoenicia, from which the Byblians received their name. Ezekiel mentions it when he says: “Your wise men, O Tyre, have become pilots; your governors are the elders of Byblus and its wise men” (Ezek. XXVII).

In Hebrew the name is Gobel or Gebal, which is interpreted as “Defining” or “Determining.” This name suits those who prepare human hearts for the spiritual building constructed from the virtues of the soul. They are able to teach their assistants faith and works of righteousness only because they themselves, first instructed by the sacred pages, have learned by a firm definition of the truth what faith must be held and by what path of virtue one must walk [Col. 1109B].

For one who does not know the exposition of the Catholic faith vainly assumes the office of teacher. Nor do those build a sanctuary for the Lord, but rather a ruin for themselves, who try to teach others a rule that they themselves have not learned.

In building the Lord’s house, wood and stones must first be cut from the mountain, because those whom we seek to instruct in the faith of the truth must first be taught to renounce the devil and, by being reborn, to be rescued from the condition of the first transgression in which they were born.

Next, precious and large stones must be sought and placed in the foundation of the temple, so that, once their former way of life has been rejected, we may remember to examine their life and conduct in every respect and propose for imitation by our hearers those whom we know to cling spiritually to the Lord through the virtue of humility. We observe them enduring with invincible firmness of mind, as though squared and immovable against every assault of temptation; and for this reason we rightly learn from their reputation that they are precious and large [Col. 1109C].

After the foundation has been composed of such great stones, the house must be built with wood and stones carefully prepared and placed in fitting order, materials that had once been removed from their former condition or root. For after the first beginnings of faith have been established in us according to the example of exalted men through humility, the wall of good works must be raised upward, as though with successive courses of stones placed upon one another, by walking and advancing from virtue to virtue.

Or certainly, the large, precious, squared stones of the foundation are, as we said above, the first teachers of the Churches, who heard the word of salvation from the Lord himself. The courses of stones or wood placed above them signify, each in its own succeeding age, the priests and teachers whose preaching and ministry cause the structure of the Church either to grow or to be ordered through virtues.

What color the stones were with which the temple was made is clearly declared in the Book of Chronicles, where David says to Solomon, when he showed him the resources he had prepared for the temple: “I have prepared in the greatest abundance every precious stone and Parian marble” (I Chron. XXIX).

Parian marble is called white marble, such as that island customarily produces. Hence the poet writes of it:

“Olearos, and snowy Paros, and the Cyclades scattered across the sea,

and the straits stirred by frequent winds, we read.”

(Virgil, *Aeneid* III.)

Paros is therefore called snowy because it sends forth marble of the whitest kind. It is one of the Cyclades, and Josephus indicates that the temple was made from this stone when he says: “He raised the temple up to the vaulted roof, constructed of white stone. Its height was one hundred and twenty cubits.”

The mystical meaning is not hidden. It is evident to everyone that the white marble from which the Lord’s house was constructed signifies the clean action of the elect and, at the same time, their conscience disciplined from every blemish of corruption [Col. 1110A]. The wise architect wished those whom he placed as precious stones upon the foundation of Christ to be such—redeemed with gold and silver. “Beloved,” he says, “let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God” (II Cor. VII).

## VII. When and Where the Temple Was Built. Chapter V

It came to pass, then, in the four hundred and eightieth year after the children of Israel had come out of the land of Egypt, in the fourth year, in the month Zio—which is the second month—of Solomon’s reign over Israel, that he began to build the house for the Lord.

The house of the Lord that King Solomon built in Jerusalem was made as a figure of the holy universal Church. From the first elect person to the last, who will be born at the end of the world, it is built daily by the grace of its peaceful king, namely the Redeemer. Part of it still journeys away from him on earth; part, having escaped the hardships of pilgrimage, already reigns with him in heaven, where, after the final judgment, the whole will reign with him.

The elect angels belong to this house; their likeness is promised to us in the life to come, as the Lord says: “Those who are deemed worthy to attain that age and the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage; for they cannot die any longer, because they are equal to the angels, and are sons of God, being sons of the resurrection” (Matt. XXII).

The Mediator of God and human beings himself also belongs to it, the man Christ Jesus, as he himself testifies when he says: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John II). Explaining this, the Evangelist added: “But he was speaking about the temple of his body” (I Cor. III).

The Apostle says of us: “Do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” If, then, he became the temple of God through the humanity he assumed, and we become his temple through his Spirit dwelling in us, it is plainly established that the material temple represented all of us—namely, the Lord himself and his members, which we are: the Lord as the uniquely chosen and precious cornerstone, founded in the foundation [Col. 1110C]; and us as living stones built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, that is, upon the Lord himself.

This will become clearer when the construction of the temple is considered in order. In some respects its figure refers to the Lord himself, and in others to all the elect; in some it describes the undefiled blessedness of the angels in heaven, and in others the unconquered endurance of human beings on earth; in some it demonstrates the assistance of angels granted to human beings, and in others the struggles of human beings rewarded together with the angels.

The same spiritual house of the Lord is also represented by the tabernacle once made in the wilderness through Moses. But that house was built on the journey by which they were coming to the promised land, whereas this one was built in the promised land itself and in the city of Jerusalem. The former was frequently carried from place to place through the ministry of the Levites, until at last it was brought into the land of the promised inheritance [Col. 1110D]; the latter, constructed immediately in the homeland itself and in the royal city, was to stand forever on an inviolable foundation until it fulfilled the heavenly function of the figures imposed upon it.

The labor and exile of the present Church may therefore be represented in the former, and future rest and blessedness in the latter. Or, since the former was made by the children of Israel alone, while this one was also made by proselytes and Gentiles, the fathers of the Old Testament and that ancient people of God may chiefly be expressed figuratively in the former, while the Church gathered from the nations may be expressed in the latter. Nevertheless, when the construction of both houses is more fully examined in a spiritual sense, it is shown in many ways to signify the daily labors of the present Church, the eternal rewards and joys of the heavenly kingdom in the future, the election of the first Church from Israel, and the salvation of all nations in Christ.

When it says, “In the fourth year, in the month Zio, which is the second month of Solomon’s reign over Israel,” the order of the sense is: “In the fourth year of King Solomon, in the month Zio, which is the second month.” By the second month it means May. For April, in which Passover is celebrated, was the first month of the year among the Hebrews. From this it is plainly evident that, immediately after Passover had been completed, he began to build the house of the Lord, and that the people, consecrated by the mystical solemnity, applied their hands to the mystical work.

The exodus from Egypt is mentioned, when the tabernacle began to be built, so that the reader may be reminded how many years passed between the building of the two houses and may recognize the spiritual mystery of this total span of time.

For four times one hundred and twenty make four hundred and eighty. Four appropriately corresponds to evangelical perfection because of the number of Evangelists; one hundred and twenty corresponds to legal teaching because of the same number of years belonging to the lawgiver. In this number too the grace of the Holy Spirit was received by the first Church, plainly showing that those who use the law lawfully—that is, those who recognize and embrace the grace of Christ in it—are rightly filled with the grace of his Spirit, because they burn more ardently in his charity [Col. 1111B].

We have said that the tabernacle made by Moses and the children of Israel in the desert can signify the Synagogue, while the temple constructed by Solomon and the children of Israel with the assistance of proselytes and Gentiles can signify the Church of the nations.

The worship and religion of the tabernacle continued for four hundred and eighty years, and then the temple began to be built, because the Scripture of the Old Testament abounds in such perfection that, if someone understands it well, it contains within itself all the mysteries of the New Testament. The fathers of the Old Testament also held the citadel of perfection with such excellence that they are in no respect to be considered inferior to the apostles and apostolic men.

The tabernacle remained among the people of God until the construction of the temple for four hundred and eighty years, that is, one hundred and twenty multiplied by four. For from the time the law was given until the Lord’s incarnation and the time when grace was revealed, there were men living under the law who maintained evangelical perfection in every respect by mind and deed [Col. 1111C]. There was also Scripture that announced the grace of the New Testament in the prophetic utterances of the Old.

That the house of the Lord began to be built in the fourth year of King Solomon can be referred mystically to the fact that, after the dispensation of the Lord’s incarnation had been completed—an incarnation recorded in the four books of the Gospel—the structure of the Church began when the Holy Spirit was sent from heaven. It can also refer to the fact that, in the second month, after the building of Israel, the Church of the nations received the Creator within itself.

Hence the second month was also permitted in the law for celebrating Passover by those who were unclean in soul or far away on a journey and could not come to celebrate Passover in the first month. Here we are very clearly represented: unclean because of the death of our soul and still far away from the people of God, we could not celebrate the first Passover, which took place in the flesh and blood of the lamb. But we celebrate this second Passover, which was accomplished in the body and blood of our Redeemer, by whom we were sought out and cleansed [Col. 1111D].

The place where the temple was built is shown more clearly in the Book of Chronicles, where it is written:

“Solomon began to build the house of the Lord in Jerusalem, on Mount Moriah, which had been shown to David his father, at the place that David had prepared on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite” (II Chron. III).

The Lord’s house is therefore built in the vision of peace, because the Church, spread throughout the world, stands in one and the same faith and fellowship of Catholic truth. For God is not in the division of minds; rather, “his place has been made in peace, and his dwelling in Zion.”

It is built on a mountain—namely, on the Lord and Savior himself—of whom Isaiah says: “In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the summit of the mountains” (Isa. II). He himself says in the Gospel: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matt. V). For he is the mountain of mountains, who arose from the earth through the origin of the flesh he assumed, yet surpasses the power and holiness of all earthly beings by the singular height of his dignity [Col. 1112A].

The city or house of the Lord was constructed on this mountain because, unless our hope and faith fix their root in him, they are nothing. He is rightly called Mount Moriah, that is, “of Vision,” because he deigns to see and assist in this present life those of his elect whom he preserves for the eternal vision of his glory.

This is the place where Abraham offered his son Isaac to the Lord and, through the devotion of his obedience, merited to be seen by him. Hence it received its name, about which the Lord says: “Take your only-begotten son, whom you love, Isaac, and go into the land of Vision, and offer him there as a burnt offering” (Gen. XXII). In place of “land of Vision,” the Hebrew has “land of Moriah.”

And because Isaac’s sacrifice was a type of the Lord’s passion, the temple is rightly built at the place of that sacrifice, because, dedicated through faith in and the mystery of the Lord’s passion, the Church grows into a holy temple for the Lord.

Concerning this mountain it is suitably added: “Which had been shown to David his father.” The Lord who was to come in the flesh had been shown to David, as also to the other prophets. Through the sacraments of that same incarnation he would wash the Church called from the nations from its sins and consecrate it as a faithful and beloved house for himself [Col. 1112B].

It is rightly added: “At the place that David had prepared.” David prepared the place by singing psalms; the other prophets prepared it by prophesying. They prepared a place for the Lord, the true Solomon, in which he would build the house, because they instructed the hearts of their hearers in the faith of the truth, diligently warning them to receive with faithful and devoted minds the Son of God coming in the flesh.

For this reason the Lord says to his disciples concerning the peoples prepared to believe in him: “Lift up your eyes and see the regions, for they are already white for harvest; and the one who reaps receives a reward and gathers fruit for eternal life, so that the one who sows may rejoice together with the one who sends” (John IV).

As though speaking in other words about the building of the temple, he said: “Lift up your eyes and see the place, for it is already prepared for building the house of the Lord; and the one who builds, by teaching, receives a reward and gathers precious stones for eternal life, so that the one who prepares the place may rejoice together with the one who builds; that is, so that the prophet who foretells the Lord’s coming and the apostle who preaches the Lord who has come may together receive their reward in him” [Col. 1112C].

The same place was rightly the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, because the Church is customarily signified by the word “threshing floor.” John says of the Lord: “His winnowing fork is in his hand, and he will thoroughly cleanse his threshing floor” (Matt. III).

Ornan, whose name is interpreted as “Illuminated,” was by nation a Jebusite. His nation signifies the Gentiles, while his name shows that these same people would be enlightened by the Lord and transformed into children of the Church. To them the Apostle rightly says: “Once you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (I Thess. V).

Jebus is the same city as Jerusalem. Jebus is called “Trampled,” whereas Jerusalem is called “Vision of Peace.” As long as Ornan the Gentile ruled in it, it was called Jebus; but when David bought the place of the burnt offering there, and Solomon built the temple for the Lord there, it was no longer called Jebus but Jerusalem [Col. 1112D].

For as long as the Gentiles remained ignorant of divine worship, they were trampled and mocked by unclean spirits, following mute idols wherever they were led.
