But when the grace of their Creator looked upon them, they immediately found both peace and a name for that peace within themselves, as the Lord says of them: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matt. V).

Thus, while Ornan still held royal power in that city, it was called Jebus. But when he sold the place of his threshing floor, together with its oxen and threshing sledges, to King David, it received the name Jerusalem. For while the Gentiles persisted in their obstinacy, they were trampled as worthless and rejected by the evil spirits. But when they learned to sell all that they possessed and offer it to the true king, they could no longer be trampled by demons and vices; rather, they became more fully established in the inner peace they possessed with their Creator.

## VIII. On the Measurements of the Temple. Chapter VI

The house that Solomon built for the Lord was sixty cubits long, twenty cubits wide [Col. 1113A], and thirty cubits high.

The Book of Kings says in describing the construction of the temple that it was thirty cubits high, while the Book of Chronicles states: “The height was one hundred and twenty cubits.” These accounts should not be considered contradictory; rather, both should be understood as true.

For, as Josephus’s history reports, there were thirty cubits from the pavement to the middle story, and another thirty from the middle story to the third, up to which point reached the height of the porticoes attached to the temple on its southern, western, and northern sides—that is, sixty cubits in all. Then there were another sixty cubits up to the highest roof of the house. Thus its total height amounted to one hundred and twenty cubits.

The length of the house signifies the long-suffering of the holy Church, which patiently endures every adversity in the exile of this pilgrimage until it reaches the homeland for which it waits.

Its breadth signifies charity, which, with the bosom of the mind enlarged, rejoices to love not only friends in God but also enemies for God’s sake, until the time comes when, either with those converted to its peace or with those utterly destroyed, it may rejoice in God with friends alone [Col. 1113B].

Its height declares the hope of future recompense. With its gaze fixed upon this hope, it willingly disregards all that is lowly, whether what delights or what opposes, until, having passed beyond both, it deserves to see only the goodness of the Lord in the land of the living.

Hence the length of the house is appropriately encompassed by the number sixty. For the number six, in which the world was made, customarily signifies the perfection of good works. We must endure the troubles of our pilgrimage through long-suffering in such a way that, by the merit of good works, we may be able to enter the promised homeland when it appears.

The breadth is determined by the number twenty, on account of the twofold distinction of that charity by which we love God and neighbor. The height is represented by thirty because of faith in the holy Trinity, which is one God, in the vision of whom all the desires of our hope are suspended.

Thus six pertains to the perfection of work, two to love of God and neighbor, and three to hope for the vision of God [Col. 1113C]. Each number is rightly multiplied by ten, because our patience is profitably exercised, our charity usefully increased, and our hope sublimely carried toward eternal desires only through faith and observance of the law’s Decalogue.

There was also a portico before the temple, twenty cubits long, corresponding to the breadth of the temple, and ten cubits wide before the front of the temple.

Concerning this portico the Book of Chronicles says: “The portico before the front extended lengthwise according to the breadth of the house, twenty cubits” (II Chron. III).

It is therefore evident that this portico was built on the eastern side of the temple. For the temple faced east, as did the tabernacle, and the door of the portico stood before the door of the temple. The Jewish historian Josephus teaches this most clearly (*Jewish Antiquities*, Book VIII, chapter 3), so that the equinoctial sun, rising, could pour its rays in a straight line through the three doors—the portico, the temple, and the sanctuary—and reach the ark of the covenant [Col. 1113D].

Since the temple signifies the holy Church, and the portico before the temple was accustomed to receive the sunlight first, what could it more aptly announce figuratively than that part of the Church that preceded the times of the Lord’s incarnation? In it are the patriarchs and prophets, who first received the Sun of Righteousness rising for this world and bore witness to the Lord born in the flesh—by living, preaching, being born, and even dying.

The door of the temple is therefore the Lord, because no one comes to the Father except through him; and elsewhere he says: “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved” (John X).

The door of the portico is prophetic speech, which led those entering, as though along a straight path, to the door of the temple and proclaimed the grace of the Lord and Savior by which he was to redeem the world.

The entire structure of the portico therefore signifies the faithful of that time. The door within the portico represents the teachers who opened to others the light of life and the entrance to the Lord. There was rightly one door, on account of the harmonious faith in and love of the truth found in all the saints [Col. 1114A].

This portico was twenty cubits long, corresponding to the breadth of the temple, because the ancient righteous waited for a long time, with great patience and long-suffering, for the Lord to appear in the flesh and bring the new grace of the Gospel to the world. They did not receive the promises themselves, but saw and greeted them from afar.

Thus its length equaled the breadth of the temple, because with the long-suffering of devoted minds they desired to see the Church enlarged in the charity that is in Christ Jesus our Lord. Although they were still separated in time from the sacraments of the Lord’s incarnation, they were near through faith and preaching.

At the first outer front of this most sacred portico were blessed Abel, the first martyr, and Seth, and Enos, and the other righteous people of the original world. In its innermost recess, as though near the mystical wall of the temple, Simeon and Anna, the parents of the blessed Forerunner of the Lord, and the others who, although they were worthy to see his birth, could not attain to hearing his teaching or receiving his sacraments, held their place [Col. 1114B].

The portico was rightly ten cubits wide, because although such people had not yet received the words or mysteries of the Gospel that were to be handed down by the Lord, they nevertheless preserved the commands of the Decalogue, which they had received, enlarged in the Lord through perfect love.

## IX. On the Windows and Chambers of the Temple. Chapter VI

And he made slanting windows in the temple.

The windows of the temple are the learned teachers and all the spiritual people in the Church. Because, in their minds being lifted beyond themselves toward God, they are granted a more special vision than others of the secrets of heavenly mysteries, and because they openly disclose to the faithful what they see in secret, the windows, as though receiving the sun’s light, fill all the inner parts of the temple.

Hence the same windows are rightly said to have been slanting—that is, wider within and narrower outside—because whoever has received even for a moment the radiance of heavenly contemplation must immediately enlarge the bosom of the heart through greater discipline and prepare it through diligent practice to undertake greater things [Col. 1114C].

And he built structures around the wall of the temple, around the walls of the house on every side of the temple and of the inner sanctuary, and he made side-chambers all around. The upper structure had a width of five cubits, the middle structure a width of six cubits, and the third structure a width of seven cubits. In the Gospel, where the Lord is tempted by the devil, these structures are called the pinnacles of the temple (Matt. 4). We have also heard that James, the apostle and brother of the Lord, was raised onto the pinnacle of the temple, from which he might preach to the people. Whether, however, it was customary for teachers to sit on these structures and address the crowd standing below, we nowhere find stated in Scripture.

The sacramental meaning is therefore clear: these three structures signify three corresponding ranks of the faithful—married people, the continent, and virgins. They are distinguished by the height of their profession, but all belong to the house of the Lord through the fellowship of faith and truth and [Col. 1114D] cling to it with steadfast mind. Thus it is beautifully said that the upper structure had a width of five cubits, the middle one six, and the third seven. The highest structure was therefore narrower than the others, because a higher profession of virtue must surely follow a loftier way of life.

For all who, having renounced the marital bond, have consecrated their virginity to the Lord ought also to display conduct worthy of virginity. They should abstain from idle speech, anger, quarrels, slander, immodest dress, feasting, drinking, rivalry, and jealousy; and conversely they should devote themselves to holy vigils, prayers, sacred readings and psalms, teaching, almsgiving, and the other holy fruits, so that those who hold in their profession the condition of the future life—in which they will neither marry nor be given in marriage, but will be like the angels in heaven (Matt. 22)—may strive, insofar as is possible for mortals, to imitate that condition in the present.

The lowest structure, on the other hand, was broader, because God did not say to the married, “Go and [Col. 1115A] sell what you have and give to the poor,” but, “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments: You shall not murder, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal, you shall not bear false witness,” and so forth (Matt. 19). Between these two stand the continent: as much lower than virgins, so much higher than married people. In Jerusalem the blessed Luke records that the most glorious first Church was built from such people, because “the multitude of those who believed were of one heart and one soul,” and so forth (Acts 4). The history of Saint Stephen testifies that most of them had left behind marital embraces; there it calls women pursuing the same religious devotion their widows, not their wives.

Each structure had side-chambers all around—that is, protective parapets—so that no one standing or sitting on those structures could fall to the lower level. We read that this happened to King Ozias in Samaria. These parapets, appropriately enough, signify the daily protections of divine guardianship toward us. Of these the psalmist says: “The angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear him, and he will deliver them” (Ps. [Col. 1115B] 33).

King Ozias of Samaria, who had separated himself from the house of David, did indeed ascend to the upper chamber, but he fell through the latticework. For although heretics or schismatics may appear to climb some height of good action, they do not possess the structure of the Church’s unity; as though their parapet defenses were open and unsolid, they continually fall back to the depths of vices, and, deprived of divine help, perish through the arrogance of their obstinacy.

By what method the structures mentioned above were attached to the walls of the temple is made clear when the text continues: “He placed beams around the house on the outside, so that they would not be attached to the walls of the temple.” The beams that strengthened and adorned the house within were of such length that their ends projected outside: in the lowest tier seven cubits, in the middle six, and in the highest five. The structures were assembled upon these projecting ends, not fixed into the walls of the temple, but placed beside the walls upon the beams that extended from them.

What, then, are the beams of the house that carried the structures typologically meant to signify, if not preachers? While they themselves hold a lofty and honorable place in the Church of God, through their preaching they lift the weaker and more fragile above the craving for inferior things and suspend them in the desire and hope of heavenly things; they also help them through their intercessions to persevere in what they have begun.

We read in the Book of Chronicles that the beams of the temple, like its other interior parts, were covered with gold. This was surely done in such a way that those parts of the beams that were inside the temple were covered with golden plates, while those exposed outside were not gilded at all, but displayed to everyone the appearance and form of cedar. [Col. 1115C] Upon them, nevertheless, they carried the structures placed on them.

What projected outward from the beams signifies the life of the saints that could become known to us on earth; what shone within the temple, covered with gold, announces the glory in which the righteous rejoice in the heavenly homeland in the presence of their Creator. That glory of the golden beams was disclosed only to those who entered the temple, [Col. 1115D] because only those who have deserved to enter the heavenly kingdom know how great is the abundance of God’s sweetness, which he has hidden for those who fear him (Ps. 30), and perfected for those who hope in him.

Yet when, seeing or reading in Scripture the life, sufferings, and teachings of the saints, we are stirred by their example to do good, we are lifted from the earth as though upon the visible ends of the beams. For although we are not yet able to behold the saints’ inward glory, nevertheless, from what we have been able to see outwardly, we cling faithfully to the exalted members of the Church.

We may also understand these things of the saints who are still placed in this life. We cannot see the purity of their love, by which they shine before the Lord in the secrecy of their hearts; nevertheless, from what they display outwardly by speaking, acting, or suffering, we find assistance for our salvation.

The house, when it was built, was constructed of dressed and [Col. 1116A] perfected stones; and no hammer, axe, or any iron tool was heard in the house while it was being built. These words properly concern that part of the Church which, after the labors and struggles of this age, has deserved to be brought into eternal rewards. There, as John wrote in the Apocalypse, nothing defiled will enter, nor anything that practices abomination and falsehood (Rev. 21).

The hammer, axe, and every iron tool are not heard there, because here we are beaten by adversities and trained by the discipline of truth, so that there we may be arranged in places corresponding to our merits. When correction has ceased, we shall be joined to one another only by the bond of love and filled and suffused with one Spirit. Here we are beaten outside so that there we may be found without reproach.

Here are the hammer, the axe, and all the ringing instruments of blows; but in the house of God none of these is heard, because in the eternal homeland every noise of striking has already fallen silent. There the hammer does not strike, because no punishment afflicts anyone; the axe does not cut, because no [Col. 1116B] sentence of severity casts out those received within. The tools do not clang there, because no one thereafter feels even the smallest scourges.

The stones were therefore struck outside so that they might be placed in the construction of the Lord’s temple without the sound of a hammer. For now we are beaten outside by scourges so that afterward we may be arranged within the temple of God without the blows of discipline. In this way the blow may now cut away whatever is superfluous in us, and then only the harmony of love may bind us in the building. Thus a person, bruised and purified here outside by various adversities from the errors of his merits, may there, already pure, see the pure God, and may deserve to be attached to the adornments of that city, having after his passage a place prepared for him by the Lord alone.

### X. On the Spiral Staircase of the Temple. Chapter VI

The entrance of the middle side-chamber was on the right side of the house, and by a spiral staircase one ascended to the middle upper chamber, and from the middle one to the third.

Some people, misunderstanding this passage, think [Col. 1116C] that the entrance of the temple was on the south, not observing that, if Scripture had intended to signify this, it would not have said, “The entrance of the middle side-chamber was on the right side of the house,” but would rather have said simply, “The house had an entrance toward the south.” The passage now signifies something quite different.

It calls the right side of the house the southern side of the temple. On its eastern part there was an entrance made at the very corner, near the ground; those entering it immediately ascended gradually to higher levels, having their way and ascent through the inner parts of the wall. Consequently it adds: “And by a spiral staircase they ascended to the middle upper chamber, and from the middle one to the third.”

Nor should we doubt that, although Scripture does not say so, those who ascended in this way had very numerous windows on the southern side. By their light they certainly made their whole journey safely and without stumbling.

The entrance by which they entered for the daily services of the temple was toward the east, as we have already recalled, according to Josephus; and there was a portico in front of it, itself also open toward the east. Thus the rising equinoctial sun could send its rays without any obstacle through the doors of the temple and of the inner sanctuary into the ark itself, [Col. 1116D] which was in the Holy of Holies.

The ascent that led into the upper house, and from the upper house into the third, was on the southern side of the temple. Its arrangement commends to us a very memorable mystery. It is clear that this temple, which Solomon built, figuratively indicates the body of Christ, the peaceful King—not only that body which is his whole Church, but also that body which he received from the Virgin, holy and most sacred, in order to be the head of the Church.

“There was the entrance of the middle side-chamber in the wall of the right side of the house” (John 19). Through it one ascended secretly from below into the middle upper chamber, and from the middle one into the third, because, when the Lord had suffered on the cross, one of the soldiers opened his side with a spear.

It was rightly on the right side of the house, because the holy Church believes that his right side was opened by the soldier. The evangelist also used an appropriate word: he did not say, “He struck his side,” or “He wounded it,” but “He opened it,” [Col. 1117A] as though it were the entrance of the middle side-chamber through which a way to heavenly things might be opened for us.

Finally he added: “And immediately blood and water came out”—water, by which we are cleansed in baptism, and blood, by which we are consecrated in the holy chalice.

Through this entrance we ascend into the middle upper chamber, and from the middle one into the third. Through faith and the mysteries of our Redeemer, we ascend from our present life in the Church to the rest of souls after death; and again, on the coming day of judgment, from the rest of souls to the immortality of bodies, as though into a third upper chamber, entering by a loftier progress. From there we shall live forever in the great blessedness of both body and soul.

This journey was made invisibly, so that only those who entered knew it, although those standing outside could also see the entrance itself. For the actions of the faithful in this age and the celebrations of the sacraments can even be observed by the reprobate; but no one recognizes the secrets of faith and the innermost grace of love except the one who, guided by the Lord through these things, is led [Col. 1117B] to heavenly realities. “Whoever says that he knows God but does not keep his commandments is a liar” (John 2).

It should also be noted that the thirty cubits of height mentioned above reached as far as the middle upper chamber. Then another thirty cubits were added up to the third upper chamber, until the porticoes around the temple, on the south, north, and west, reached the roof, as we learn from Josephus. From there another sixty cubits were measured up to the highest roof of the temple; thus the entire height of the house, according to the Book of Chronicles, was completed at one hundred and twenty cubits.

The portico in front of the façade of the temple toward the east, according to the testimony of the aforementioned book, had the same total height. That book calls the porticoes around the temple, of which we spoke above, storerooms and chambers: “David gave Solomon his son the plan of the portico, the temple, the storerooms, the upper chamber, the inner chambers [Col. 1117C] and the house of atonement” (1 Chron. 28). It also mentions the outer houses that were outside the priests’ court around the temple, when it immediately adds: “And likewise the plan of all that he had considered: the courts, the chambers around them, and the treasuries of the holy things.”

The fact that the entire height of the temple was one hundred and twenty cubits refers to the same mystery as the primitive Church in Jerusalem after the Lord’s passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven, when it received the grace of the Holy Spirit in this number of men.

Fifteen, which is composed of seven and eight, is sometimes taken as a sign of the life now lived by the souls of the faithful in sabbath-rest; that life, however, will be perfected at the end of the age by the resurrection of immortal bodies. When fifteen is multiplied into a triangle—that is, when all its parts are added together—it produces one hundred and twenty. Therefore the great blessedness of the elect in the future life [Col. 1117D] is appropriately signified by the number one hundred and twenty.

Appropriately the third upper chamber of the Lord’s house is completed in this number, because through the present labors of the faithful, after the future rest of souls has been received, the full happiness of the entire Church will be completed in the glory of the resurrection.

The same mystery is equally involved, as we said, in the fact that, rising from the dead and ascending into heaven, the Lord sent the Holy Spirit in fiery tongues to this number of men. Through the diversity of languages he caused them to possess a common speech in the knowledge of words and in praise.

In the same way, when the Church in its own time rises from death and ascends into heaven in incorruptible flesh, it will be fully and perfectly illuminated by the gift of the Holy Spirit, when, according to the Apostle’s promise, God will be all in all. Then there will be a complete uniting of languages in everyone for proclaiming the mighty works of God, because all, with one mind and voice, will praise together the glory of the divine majesty, since they behold it present.

### XI. On the Inner House of the Oracle, into the Holy of Holies. [Col. 1118A] Chapter VI

“And he built the house and completed it, and covered the house with cedar ceilings.” The ceilings are structures that, arranged and adorned with great beauty, are attached by nails to the beams on their lower side.

Because the house of the Lord had three corresponding levels of height, it had three ceilings: the first after thirty cubits from the pavement, the second after sixty cubits, opposite the top of the porticoes, and the third after one hundred and twenty cubits, at the summit of the entire house.

What could more appropriately be signified by the ceilings than the more exalted righteous in the holy Church? Their work and teaching, set before everyone as an example, stand out as though raised higher in the distance; and through their intercessions and exhortations they protect the minds of the weak, lest they fail in temptations.

These ceilings are rightly described as cedar. Cedar is a tree entirely imperishable by nature, pleasant in scent, bright in appearance, driving away and killing snakes when its fragrant resin is kindled. These qualities correspond to the perfect: their endurance is unconquerable, [Col. 1118B] the fame of their virtues exceptional, their goodness more pleasing than all others’, and their authority most steadfast in defeating and refuting those who resist the truth. In this life and in the future they shine with a distinction surpassing that of the other saints.

“And he built a structure over the whole house, five cubits high.” This is what Moses commands in Deuteronomy to be made on every house that anyone builds: “When you build a new house,” he says, “you shall make a wall around the roof, lest blood be shed in your house and you become guilty if someone falls from it and plunges headlong” (Deut. 22).

This structure, erected around the highest roof of the house at the outer edge of the walls, served as a lattice or parapet, so that when someone climbed to the upper parts and reached the edge of the roof, he would not carelessly fall to the depths. King Ozias is found in what follows to have suffered this fate: falling through the lattice of the upper chamber, he contracted a deadly illness.

When such structures, walls, or lattices are placed for the protection [Col. 1118C] of a walkway, the common people have given them the name *luriculae*—little parapets. Above, these structures were called side-chambers. When it was said, “He built structures around the wall of the temple, around the walls of the house on every side of the temple and of the inner sanctuary,” it was immediately added, “And he made side-chambers all around.”

In these side-chambers we understood divine protections to be signified. While we still labor in this age and strive upward according to our capacity, they help us daily not to fail. We should understand this passage in accordance with that pattern, but with this distinction: in the present life, amid frequent and implacable assaults from the enemy and obstacles arising from our own frailty, we are frequently—or rather continually—defended from falling by the gift of heavenly mercy.

In the future life, which the highest roof of the temple, as we have shown above, indicates, we shall be so fortified by the abundant grace of the present God that we shall neither wish nor be able to sin any longer, nor shall we be afflicted by any fear of death, pain, or a tempting [Col. 1118D] adversary.

Of the Lord’s present helps, as of the side-chambers of the structures, the Lord himself says concerning his people: “He will call upon me, and I will answer him; I am with him in tribulation, I will deliver him and glorify him” (Ps. 90).

Of his future grace, by which that heavenly city is illuminated, the prophet says to the same city: “Praise the Lord, Jerusalem; praise your God, Zion. For he has strengthened the bars of your gates; he has blessed your children within you; he has established peace as your boundary” (Ps. 147).

It is appropriately recalled that this structure on the roof of the Lord’s house was five cubits high, because in that homeland the presence of the divine glory so fills us that our sight, hearing, smell, taste, and every faculty find nothing sweet except this: “To love the Lord our God with all our heart, with all our soul, and with all our strength, and our neighbor as ourselves” (Deut. 6).

“And he covered the house with cedar wood.” This signifies the covering at the summit of the entire structure of the house—that [Col. 1119A] is, the structure placed above those beams to which the highest ceilings mentioned earlier were attached beneath.

The temple did not have a peaked roof above, any more than the tabernacle did, but was level, as is customary among all who build houses in Palestine and Egypt, since such roofs are constructed for sitting or walking upon. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “What you have heard in the ear shall be proclaimed upon the roofs” (Luke 12). Such a place was especially suitable for a preacher to speak from, whether to those standing with him or to hearers situated below.

Solomon says the same in Proverbs: “It is better,” he says, “to live in the corner of a roof than with a quarrelsome woman in a common house” (Prov. 21). What is called a roof in Latin is called *doma* in Greek.

The porticoes themselves around the temple also had three ceilings: the first after twenty cubits from the ground, the second after forty, and the third after sixty, for their roofs too were flat. There were thirty porticoes below, thirty in the middle, and thirty [Col. 1119B] above. They were separated from one another not by walls but by structures, so that each of the ninety porticoes had five cubits in width and length and twenty cubits in height.

These porticoes are frequently mentioned in the Book of Chronicles, but Josephus explains more fully in what arrangement they were placed.

This same structure by which the house was covered, like the ceilings, signifies the most eminent men in the glory of the resurrection, those who reach the very summit of virtue through singular holiness. Of one of them it is said: “Among those born of women no greater has arisen than John the Baptist” (Matt. 11). If you wish to know the measure of his greatness, hear what the angel said to his father: “He himself will go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah” (Luke 1).

“And he built the walls of the house within with cedar structures, from the pavement of the house to the summit of the walls, and he covered the interior with wood up to the ceilings.”

What does it mean that the house was clothed with cedar? On the outside, the stone of which it was built [Col. 1119C] shone with such brilliance that it seemed to be covered with a white pebble-stone. According to the mystical senses, however, the walls of the temple are the faithful peoples, from whom the holy universal Church is constituted. The breadth of the walls signifies their extension throughout the world; their height signifies their entire hope and intention, raised toward heavenly things.

Or certainly the height of the wall, which consists of rows of stones placed one above another, signifies the present condition of the Church. Here the elect, all built upon Christ the foundation, succeed one another in order through the cycles of time; bearing one another, they fulfill the law of Christ, which is love.

Those who are now instructed by teachers who preceded them themselves in turn instruct others, like successive rows of five living stones placed one upon another in the house of God. They are so firmly supported by others that they too are able to support others, down to the last righteous people who will be born at the end of the world. These are placed, as it were, at the summit of the house of God; they are taught and supported by others, but have no one whom they themselves may teach or whose frailty they must endure. [Col. 1119D]

The inner walls are covered with cedar structures when the hearts of the faithful overflow with the love of virtues. For just as the nature of cedar, as we have explained above, typologically announces perfect human beings, so in suitable places it also appropriately signifies the height of the virtues by which one reaches the same perfection.

Everything is covered with wood from the pavement of the house to the summit of the walls and to the ceilings when the elect, from the first beginnings of faith to the perfection of good action and to entry into the heavenly homeland, do not cease to labor at good works. From the first righteous people to the last at the completion of the age, all strive after virtues, so that they may rightly proclaim: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God in every place.”

“And he covered the pavement with fir structures.” The Book of Chronicles explains more fully how this was done, where it is written: “He also laid the pavement of the temple with the most precious [Col. 1120A] marble, with great beauty” (2 Chron. 3).

It is therefore clear that he did not place the fir boards with which he was to cover the pavement directly on the ground. First he covered it with marble, then placed the boards above it, and afterward added a third covering of gold over both, as is read below.

Just as the height of the wall, rising upward and reaching to the ceilings, signifies the progress of virtues by which the elect attain the heavenly kingdom—or, certainly, the choirs of the elect themselves succeeding one another through changing times—so the levelness of the pavement appropriately demonstrates their concordant humility, by which, while still placed in temporal life, they live together according to the command of love.

That pavement was laid with the most precious marble and great beauty, and this marble was immediately covered with fir boards, because the life of the righteous must first be fortified in the heart by the firmness of faith and then adorned in action by the breadth of spiritual virtues. Otherwise, what benefit would there be in the beauty of the most precious marble [Col. 1120B] covered by wooden boards, if it did not silently signify something mystical and teach that the abundance of good works must be supported by the strength of undefiled faith?

Fir, because of its height and lasting strength, appropriately signifies the mind of the elect, which scorns the lowest desires, is always intent upon heavenly contemplation, and is especially excellent in the virtue of patience.

The golden plates placed above the marble and the fir boards signify the breadth of love proceeding from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith. Just as gold is more precious than other metals, so in the temple of God love shines with a singular light, surpassing the other virtues.

Thus the Apostle, when he enumerated many good virtues to be preserved by the humble in heart, as though listing the adornment of the pavement, said: “Clothe yourselves, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, with compassion, kindness, humility, patience, and gentleness; bearing with one another and forgiving one another, if anyone has a complaint against another. [Col. 1120C] As Christ forgave you, so also do you” (Col. 3). Then, as though adding a golden covering from above, he suddenly continued: “Above all these things have love, which is the bond of perfection.”

### XII. On the Measurement of the Temple and the Inner Sanctuary. Chapter VI

“He also built twenty cubits at the rear of the temple, with cedar structures from the pavement to the rear, and he made the inner house, the inner sanctuary, the Holy of Holies.”

By the rear part of the temple he means the western side. The temple had its entrance from the rising of the sun, while at the setting of the sun it had the inner house—that is, the Holy of Holies.

When it is said that the structures separating the inner house from the outer house were built from the pavement up to the upper parts, this does not mean up to the ceilings, which were suspended thirty cubits above the pavement, as was stated earlier, but up to a height of twenty cubits, as is made clear below. Above these structures there remained an open and empty space up to the ceilings, ten cubits high and twenty cubits long [Col. 1120D], corresponding to the width of the house.

In this distinction within the house of the Lord the figure of the mystery is evident, and, when explained by the Apostle, it is clearer than light. The first house, into which the priests continually entered to complete the duties of sacrifice, is the present Church, where we daily persist in pious works and offer sacrifices of praise to the Lord.

The inner house, which was made at the rear of the temple, is the life promised to us in heaven. It is removed from the way of life of our exile and is perpetual in the presence of the supreme King, where the solemn assembly of the blessed, both angels and human beings, takes place. Hence it is rightly said to the faithful servant concerning it: “Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. 25).

The rear part, however, signifies the time when, after the labors of this age, we are led into entry there.

The structures dividing the two houses from one another are the barriers of heaven. We sigh daily for their opening, and, as much as the Lord grants, [Col. 1121A] we knock with continual pious persistence until they are opened and entry is allowed. Although we are not yet permitted to enter before the dissolution of our bodies, we nevertheless have an open door of divine mercy through which we may send ahead the incense of our prayers, almsgiving, fasting, and other good works.

The inner house was appropriately made twenty cubits long, because of the mystery of the twofold love of which we spoke above. In the present life this love illuminates the minds of most of the elect in part; in that homeland, when the works of the other virtues have ceased, it alone will reign forever.

The temple itself, in front of the entrance to the inner sanctuary, was forty cubits long. We said that the temple itself, in front of the entrance to the inner sanctuary, bore the type of the present Church. It was therefore rightly forty cubits, since this number is often used to signify the present labor of the faithful, just as fifty signifies future rest and peace.

The commandments are contained in the number ten, by whose observance one comes to life. The number ten likewise signifies the very [Col. 1121B] eternal life that we desire and for which we labor. The world in which we struggle to obtain that life is four-sided. Thus the psalmist, foreseeing the Church gathered from the nations, said: “He gathered them from the lands, from the rising and the setting of the sun, from the north and from the sea” (Ps. 106).

Ten multiplied by four makes forty. Accordingly, the people liberated from Egypt were exercised for forty years in the wilderness by many labors, while also being refreshed by heavenly bread; and at last they reached the homeland promised long before.

They are exercised by temptations for forty years, signifying the labors of the Church, by which it toils throughout the whole world in observing God’s law. It is fed with manna from heaven through the same forty years, showing that the sufferings endured by the Church are to be lightened by hope of the heavenly ten—that is, of eternal blessedness.

There those who now hunger and thirst for righteousness will be filled (Matt. 5); and, as the same Church [Col. 1121C] sings to its Redeemer: “But I shall appear in righteousness before your sight; I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed.”

The people of God are therefore afflicted by adversities and refreshed by manna at the same time, so that the Apostle’s words may be fulfilled: “Rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation” (Rom. 12).

In this figure our Lord fasted for forty days before the death of his flesh, and for forty days after the resurrection of his flesh he feasted with his disciples, appearing to them with many proofs, speaking about the kingdom of God, and eating with them.

By fasting he showed our labor in himself; by eating with his disciples he showed his consolation in us. Fasting, as it were, he cried out: “Take heed lest your hearts be weighed down with excess, drunkenness, and the cares of this life” (Luke 21). Eating and drinking, he seemed to cry out: “Behold, I am with you all days, until the completion of the age” (Matt. 28); and again: “I shall see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and your joy no one will take from you” [Col. 1121D] (Matt. 28).

As we travel the Lord’s way and fast from the vanity of the present age, we are refreshed by the future promise. Here we do not lay up for ourselves, because there we shall feast; our heart is above.

“And the whole house within was clothed with cedar, having its turned moldings, its skillfully made joints, and its projecting carvings.”

We have said that cedar signifies the invincible beauty of the virtues. The whole house of the Lord is clothed with this wood within when the hearts of the righteous shine only through their love of good works.

The house has its turned moldings and skillfully made joints in the cedar boards when the elect connect themselves to one another by the most beautiful bond of love, so that, although the multitude of the faithful is countless, they are rightly said to have one heart and one soul because of their fellowship in common faith and love.

The turned moldings placed at the joints of the boards, so that one structure might be made from all of them, are the ministries of love by which the holy brotherhood is joined together and formed into one house of Christ throughout the entire [Col. 1122A] world.

This house also has projecting carvings when the saints do not conceal their works of virtue in secrecy, but disclose outwardly, in manifest expression, what kind of people they are and what they do as an example of living.

The apostle Paul did this. Not only did he preach Christ to the nations and show by suffering for Christ how greatly he excelled; in letters sent to the Churches he also declared, with joyful glorification, how many dangers he had endured for Christ and by how many revelations he had been exalted by Christ.

When he did not hesitate to say to his hearers, “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Cor. 11), what else did he display in the house of the Lord but projecting carvings? By the singular height of his virtue he offered himself to everyone as worthy of imitation.

### XIII. That the house was clad in cedar and gold. Chapter VI

Everything was covered with cedar boards, and no stone could at all be seen in the wall. The stone of the wall or pavement, the boards, and the gold all signify the life of the saints in the Church; but with this distinction, when they are placed together: the living stones are the saints, cemented to one another by the strength of faith according to one and the same rule; the cedar or fir boards are the saints, broad in the variety of their virtues, joined to one another in one and the same faith according to the gifts of the Holy Spirit; the sheets of gold are the saints who possess a surpassing love of knowledge—those who rejoice with one another in most gracious radiance. Blessed Paul gathered these three into a single statement when he said: “For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision avails anything, nor uncircumcision, but faith which works through love” (Gal. V).

The stone represented unconquerable faith, the cedar fragrant holiness, and the gold love transcending all things. The stone wall is clothed with cedar boards when the profession of faith is adorned with good works, lest it be judged idle or dead without works. Yet because the law was written on stone, while the teaching of the Gospel was confirmed through the wood of the Lord’s Passion—hence the people circumcised in the foreskin with a stone, while we are consecrated on the forehead by the sign of the cross—the stone walls of the temple, or the pavement laid with most precious marble, may appropriately represent those who lived faithfully and perfectly under the law. The cedar or fir boards, however, may signify the righteous of the New Testament, who, wishing to come after the Lord, deny themselves and take up their cross daily and follow him (Luke IX).

And because the righteous of both periods await the common reward of heavenly glory, there is a third kind, alongside the precious stones and woods: the sheets of gold. Conversely, what we said above should be understood in another way. The portico that stood before the temple should bear the figure of the ancient faithful; the temple itself, of those who came into the world after the time of the Lord’s Incarnation. The inner house, moreover, represented the joys of the heavenly kingdom, which are granted to the righteous of both groups.

Now, however, let us say that the stone walls signify the ancient people of God, the cedar boards the new people, and the golden sheets the rewards of both in heaven, since the same walls of the temple—in the portico, in the temple itself, and in the Holy of Holies—were alike constructed of stones, wood, and gold. For the repetition of the same figures in different matters is manifold.

But this must be said: under the law and even before the law was written, there were many who served the Lord according to the law—not killing, not committing fornication, not stealing, not bearing false witness, honoring father and mother, and loving their neighbors as themselves. These belonged to the stone walls of the portico.

There were others who, with greater perfection, abandoned the affairs of the world, took up their cross, and followed the Lord—those of whom the Apostle writes: “They experienced mockeries and scourging, and moreover bonds and imprisonment; they were stoned, they were sawn in two, they were tempted, they died by the sword. They wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins, needy, afflicted, tormented—of whom the world was not worthy” (Hebr. XI). These, who led an evangelical life before the times of the Gospel were revealed, what were they but cedar boards shining in the portico before the entrance?

Since the same heavenly kingdom received both groups into distinct dwelling places, the portico of the temple was, as it were, covered within with gold after the stone and cedar. Even now there are very many who are content with the legal commandments mentioned above and believe that it is enough for them if they should deserve to attain life. There are others who strive toward perfection, selling all that they possess and remembering that promise by which he foretold that such people would receive in the resurrection not only life but also a special honor:

> “Amen, I say to you, that you who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. XIX).

These belong figuratively to the temple walls made of white stone; the others to the cedar boards. And because both await from the Lord the rewards of perpetual light, like sheets of gold with which they may be adorned, there are precious stones in the hidden places of the temple, and there are boards of aromatic wood, both covered with gold: for those who walked blamelessly in the law of the Lord and those who perfectly received the grace of the Gospel alike enjoy eternal life.

He had made the inner sanctuary in the middle of the house in order to place there the ark of the Lord’s covenant. This was explained above in anticipation: namely, the inner house signifies the hidden homeland of heaven; the ark of the covenant signifies the Lord and Savior, in whom alone we have a covenant of peace with the Father. After his resurrection, ascending into heaven, he placed at the Father’s right hand the flesh that he had assumed from the Virgin.

The inner sanctuary was twenty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and twenty cubits high. The statement that it was twenty cubits high signifies the cedar wall that separated the sanctuary—that is, the Holy of Holies—from the outer building, as we said above. Thus the sanctuary where the ark was situated had twenty cubits in length, breadth, and height—that is, it was square—because in that heavenly homeland, where the eyes of the saints behold Christ the King in his beauty, only the grace of divine and fraternal love shines everywhere. This is also established by the words that follow, when it is said:

### XIV. That the altar was clothed with cedar and gold. Chapter VI

“And he covered it and clothed it with the purest gold.”

This plainly means that the walls of the heavenly city were filled with the grace of love. But he also clothed the altar with cedar. He means the altar of incense, which was within the sanctuary. Concerning it he adds shortly afterward: “And he covered the whole altar of the sanctuary with gold.” From this it may be understood that the same altar was made of stone, clothed with cedar, and then covered with gold.

Typologically, it signifies the life of the perfect righteous, who are placed, as it were, in the sanctuary because, having abandoned lowly pleasures, they devote all their concern to the entrance into the heavenly kingdom. Hence it was fitting that not the flesh of victims but incense alone was burned on this altar, because such people no longer need to slaughter within themselves the sins of the flesh and the enticements of thought; rather, through the fire of love they offer before their Creator only the fragrances of spiritual prayers and heavenly desires.

What the stone, cedar, and gold signify on such an altar can easily be understood from what was said above.

He also covered the house before the sanctuary with the purest gold and fastened sheets of gold with golden nails. We have said that the house before the sanctuary represents the present Church, where we burn with love for our Redeemer, yet are not able to see him face to face. Hence this house was appropriately covered with the purest gold, but a middle wall intervened because of the hidden character of the sanctuary.

The sanctuary is so called when a divine or angelic address to human beings, or the revelation of any secrets, is granted. Thus it was fitting that the sanctuary was made in a hidden place—that is, in the inner house—because in the heavenly homeland both the vision and address of the angels and the very presence of God will be revealed to us, according to what Truth itself promises those who love him, saying:

> “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him” (John XIV).

And again:

> “The hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in figures, but will announce to you openly concerning the Father” (John XVI).

The house before the sanctuary, therefore, was covered with gold because the perfect righteous in this life—where they cannot yet hear openly concerning the Father, that is, cannot yet see him openly—adorn faith and the work of righteousness with divine love, through which we may deserve the full knowledge of God.

The golden sheets with which the house was covered are the manifold works of piety that chaste love offers in service to its Creator or to the needs of the brethren. The golden nails by which the golden sheets were fastened are the commandments of love, or the promises of eternal glory, by which, through the grace of Christ, we are held firm in the practice and pursuit of virtue so that we do not falter.

Hence it is fittingly written of these same nails in the book of Chronicles:

> “He also made golden nails, so that each nail weighed fifty shekels.”

The number fifty commonly signifies in Scripture the forgiveness of sins, the grace of the Holy Spirit, and eternal life. The fiftieth Psalm concerns repentance and forgiveness; the fiftieth year is the jubilee; on the fiftieth day after Easter, the Holy Spirit came and consecrated the primitive Church. Each nail weighed fifty shekels, and by these nails the golden sheets were fastened to the walls of the house of the Lord, because the heavenly words by which we advance and are preserved in the love of good works promise us forgiveness of sins through the grace of the Holy Spirit and promise eternal rest in the future.

These, indeed, are the nails of love. But there are other nails of fear, by which those who are beginning and have not yet arrived at perfection mortify the enticements of carnal vices and pleasure, through that saying of Truth whose instruction teaches us to crucify our flesh with its vices and desires. The prophet desired to possess these when he said:

> “Nail my flesh with the nails of your fear, for I have feared your judgments” (Ps. CXVIII).

Then, advancing to greater perfection, he says concerning the nails of love:

> “But for me, it is good to cling to God.”

“Nothing in the temple was not covered with gold; and he also covered the whole altar of the sanctuary with gold” (2 Chron. III). We have spoken above about the altar. These matters are explained more fully in the book of Chronicles, where it is also reported that the portico before the front of the temple was gilded within and that the upper chambers were likewise covered with gold.

Here the figure of the mystery is clear: the whole Church, both in this age and in the age to come, abounds above all other virtues pleasing to God in the gift of love; and love alone, standing out as if in singular eminence, seems to adorn the others.

The portico before the temple was gilded because the fathers of the Old Testament pleased God through love. The temple was gilded because that same love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us. The inner house was gilded because in the heavenly homeland love alone reigns. There it reigns more truly and securely because God himself, who is love, is seen; there more certainly because the Mediator of God and human beings, who alone knows the Father’s secrets, is always seen like the ark of the covenant.

The fact that the upper chambers were covered with gold refers to the same meaning. Just as the inner house of the Holy of Holies, where the ark was located, signifies the eternal life of the saints in the presence of their Creator and Redeemer, according to the Psalmist:

> “You will hide them in the secrecy of your face, away from the disturbance of men” (Ps. XXX),

so the upper chambers signify that this same life is in heaven and not in this world, as the Apostle says:

> “Seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God. Set your minds on the things that are above, not on the things that are on earth.”

### XV. Concerning the making of the cherubim. Chapter VI

“And he made in the sanctuary two cherubim of olive wood, ten cubits high.”

Cherubim, as the prophet Ezekiel clearly declares, is the name of an angelic dignity; in the singular it is Cherub, in the plural Cherubim. Hence, in the figures of the cherubim made in the sanctuary, the angelic ministries that always stand before their Creator in heaven may appropriately be understood.

They are rightly said to have been made of olive wood, because the angelic powers have been anointed by the grace of the Holy Spirit so that they may never wither away from the love of God. They are participants with us in that same grace, concerning whom the prophet says in praise of Christ:

> “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. XLIV).

Figuratively, they were rightly made of olive wood because the one who created them immediately filled them with the light of heavenly wisdom. Hence he wished them to be called Cherub, which in Latin is interpreted as “multiplied knowledge” or “a multitude of knowledge.”

They are ten cubits high because they enjoy the denarius of eternal life, possessing within themselves the inviolate image of their Creator, with the holiness, righteousness, and truth that they received at their first creation preserved forever. For the denarius consists of obols and customarily contains within itself the name and image of the king. Therefore it most aptly corresponds to the figure of the heavenly kingdom, where the holy angels always remain in the image of their Creator, in whose likeness they were made, and where the elect receive his image, which they had lost through sinning.

“For we know,” he says, “that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John III).

“One wing of one cherub was five cubits, and the other wing of the cherub was five cubits”—that is, together they measured ten cubits from the tip of one wing to the tip of the other.

When wings are presented as figures of holy human beings, they signify their virtues, by which they continually fly toward heavenly things and delight to have their way of life in them. When wings are presented as figures of angels, what do they demonstrate more clearly than the grace of their perpetual and unfailing blessedness, since they always remain in the heavenly places in the service of their Creator? Or perhaps they signify that the angels possess the lightness of spiritual nature, so that wherever they wish, they arrive immediately, as if flying. Thus both they and the prophets are represented with wings.

It is rightly said that one wing of one cherub was five cubits and the other wing five cubits, because the angelic powers guard with tireless devotion the law of God, which was written in five books: loving God and their Lord with all their strength, and loving their neighbors as themselves. “Love is the fullness of the law.”

Their neighbors are the angelic spirits and elect human beings themselves, who are equally their fellow citizens. Hence each wing is said to be of the same measurement, because with the same devotion with which they love one another in God, they also desire our fellowship as we ascend to them. Thus the two wings together complete ten cubits, when, in the twofold manifestation of love, the angels rejoice in the presence of their Creator.

“One cherub was ten cubits,” the measure of the wall, “and the work was one in the two cherubim.”

Two cherubim were made to signify the fellowship of that same love of which we are speaking, because love cannot exist with fewer than two. Hence the Savior also took care to send his disciples out to preach two by two (Luke X), silently teaching that those who preach the word of faith must hold the virtue of love before all works.

The two cherubim had one measurement and one workmanship because there is no inequality of wills or thoughts in the heavenly homeland, where all are illumined by one and the same vision and glory of the present God.

“And he placed the cherubim in the middle of the inner temple. The cherubim stretched out their wings, and one wing touched one wall, while the wing of the second cherub touched the other wall. The other wings touched one another in the middle of the temple.”

It is clear from what has already been said why the cherubim were placed in the middle of the inner temple, since their dwelling is in heaven. The cherubim stretched out their wings as if to fly, because angelic spirits always have their minds prepared for the service of the divine will.

The wing that touched one wall refers to that ministry of love which the angels extend to us. The other wings touching one another in the middle of the temple express the grace of love with which they embrace one another.

It fittingly follows: “He also covered the cherubim with gold,” because the Creator both exalted their nature with immortal radiance and filled their minds with the light of true love and humility.

It should certainly be noted that when Moses made the tabernacle, he also made two golden cherubim, which he placed upon the mercy seat above the ark. Solomon added two others, much larger, to place in the temple; beneath their wings he would place the ark in the middle, together with the mercy seat and the earlier cherubim. Thus there were two cherubim in the tabernacle, but four in the temple.

Both groups belong to one and the same meaning. But the work was repeated in a more august form through Solomon, so that it might be shown figuratively that, after the Lord’s Incarnation, the holy Church, multiplied and spread among the nations, would reveal more broadly the dignity of the citizens of heaven. These citizens praise their Creator for the blessedness bestowed upon them in such a way that they also rejoice in our deliverance and introduction into the same blessedness.

They stretch out their wings toward one another over the ark when they refer every good they have received to the praise of the Lord and Savior. They stretch out their other wings toward the walls of the sanctuary when they rejoice to see holy human beings with them and touch, as it were with the tips of their wings, those whom they celebrate as having been their companions and imitators in purity during this life.

They touch two opposite walls with their wings because they have with them as possessors of the heavenly court the faithful of both peoples, Jews and Gentiles. For in that homeland there is a local distinction between the two peoples. But because the inner festival of blessedness is made greater by the fellowship of united brotherhood, the cherubim stretch their wings toward both walls of the sanctuary. Rejoicing in the heavenly homeland at the sight of the righteous of both peoples, they also rouse them by the vision of their own glory to praise the Creator.

The heavenly hosts rejoice not only in the blessedness of those righteous human beings whom they have with them inside; they also keep diligent watch over us, who are still placed outside and cry to the Lord from the depths. Hence it is fittingly written of these same cherubim in the book of Chronicles:

> “They stood with their feet upright, and their faces were turned toward the outer house” (2 Chron. III).

The cherubim stood with their feet upright because the angels have never strayed from the way of truth in which they were placed as soon as they were created. Their faces are turned toward the outer house because they desire us, once rescued from the misery of this pilgrimage, to come into their fellowship.

Thus they stand with straight feet and extend their wings covered with gold toward the walls of the sanctuary, while their faces are turned toward the outer house, because the angels preserve their own innocence forever and rejoice in the blessedness of holy souls in heaven, yet do not cease to bring help to those elect whom they see still wandering on earth, until they introduce them into the heavenly homeland. For all are “ministering spirits sent out for service on behalf of those who are to inherit salvation.”

The two cherubim may also signify the two Testaments. These cherubim were made in the sanctuary because, in the counsel of the divine promise—which was arranged for us before the ages, inaccessible and incomprehensible to us—it was determined when, how, and through which authors the sacred Scripture would be composed.

They were made of olive wood because the divine books were written through men of mercy, whose strength did not fail their piety, enlightened by the anointing of the Holy Spirit. They were made of olive wood because they give us the light of knowledge with the help of the flame of the love of God, which is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit.

They are ten cubits high because they proclaim that God must be served through observance of the Decalogue and show that those who faithfully serve God will be rewarded with the denarius of the everlasting kingdom.

They have two wings because the Testaments declare that, through hardships and prosperity alike, they have always pressed toward and reached heavenly things with tireless purpose, and they demonstrate that their hearers must do the same.

“One wing of one cherub was five cubits, and the other wing of the cherub was five cubits,” because amid every changing condition of transitory things, the saints extend all the senses of their body in the service of their Creator: they keep their eyes always upon the Lord; they desire to hear the voice of his praise; they declare all his wonders; they hold his sayings sweet in their throats, sweeter to their mouths than honey and the honeycomb; they run in the fragrance of his ointments; and, while breath remains in them and the spirit of God is in their nostrils, they do not speak wickedness with their lips or sound folly with their tongue. Thus, advancing with the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left, they reach the heavenly denarius that the supreme householder promised to the laborers in his vineyard.

“The work was one in the two cherubim,” because the writers of both Testaments served God with one and the same purity of conduct and devotion of love. With one harmonious voice and faith they proclaim God, because what the New Testament narrates concerning the Lord’s Incarnation, Passion, Resurrection, Ascension, the calling of the Gentiles, the rejection of the Jews, and the manifold tribulation of the Church, the Old Testament, if rightly understood, proclaimed beforehand as truly destined to occur.

Both Testaments likewise confirm with harmonious truth the coming of the Antichrist, the end of the world, the peril of the final judgment, and the eternal glory of the good and punishment of the wicked.

The inner wings of the cherubim touched one another over the ark because both Testaments agree in equal testimony concerning the Lord. With their outer wings, one touched one wall and the other the other wall, because the Old Testament was written specifically for the ancient people of God, while the New was written for us, who came to faith after the Lord’s Incarnation.

We are rightly compared with the second wall—that is, the northern one—because after the cold and darkness of idolatry we were granted knowledge of the light of truth. For although the primitive Church especially blossomed from the Jews, and it is believed that all Israel will be saved near the end of the world, very many of the faithful of this body are gathered to receive the sacraments of the Gospel. To them it has also been divinely granted, with the eyes of their hearts unveiled, to recognize clearly that the letter of the Old Testament is full of the mysteries of evangelical grace.

The cherubim have their faces turned toward the outer house because the divine books were composed for us, who still stand outside and have not yet been saved in reality but in hope. Their writers, now reigning with the Lord and praising him in heaven, care for our salvation and intercede for our errors before his mercy.

The cherubim are surrounded with gold because the authority of the Testaments is confirmed by the glorious works of their writers and by the knowledge of the divine Scriptures now revealed throughout the world, or by the inner glory of the heavenly hosts. For, as we said, each cherub signifies both angels and the Testaments, when many begin to be converted to the faith and to abound in good works.

Hence it is appropriately added:

> “And he carved all the walls of the temple around with various engravings and with turning-work.”

“All the walls of the temple around” are all the peoples of the holy Church. Set upon the foundation of Christ, it has filled the entire circuit of the world and does not cease daily to enlarge the building of faith by a new generation of its members, as if by the addition of precious stones.

These walls are carved with various engravings when “to one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith in the same Spirit, to another gifts of healing in the one Spirit, to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another the discernment of spirits, to another kinds of tongues, to another the interpretation of tongues” (1 Cor. XII).

And, to come to those virtues that we can all possess—“love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, modesty, self-control” (Gal. V), and the other fruits of the Spirit—what are these but the engravings of the temple walls, the adornments of the minds of God’s people?

The same walls are also carved with turning-work when the faithful possess a ready spirit for doing everything that the Lord commands and enduring everything that he permits, saying from the heart in every circumstance that arises:

> “I will bless the Lord at all times” (Ps. LXII).

And:

> “My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready; I will sing and make melody to the Lord” (Ps. CVII).

They are carved with turning-work when they devote themselves so greatly to virtue that no opposition from surrounding circumstances and no enticements can turn them from its path. Because turning-work surpasses other arts in speed and preserves for itself the rule by which the work may be completed without error, the holy life of the saints is aptly signified by it: it is always ready for the service of the divine will, and through long practice in virtue it has learned to fulfill that will without wandering into error.

Hence the holy Church, admiring the virtues of her Bridegroom and Redeemer, said in the Song of Songs:

> “His hands are turning-work, gold, full of hyacinths” (Song V).

His hands are indeed turning-work because, appearing in the flesh, the power and wisdom of God accomplished whatever healings and miracles he wished without any delay or winding paths of error. They are golden because what he commanded outwardly by his word he granted inwardly, full of divine power. They are full of hyacinths because he referred everything he did to the glory of the Father, and through the works he performed he lifts our senses toward the pursuit of heavenly things.

### XVI. Concerning the carving of the walls. Chapter VI

All the walls of the temple around are carved with various engravings and turning-work when the whole Church throughout the world applies itself to the practice of spiritual virtues with ready devotion and without any error at all.

Here it is fittingly added:

> “And he made in them cherubim and palm trees and various images, as though projecting from the wall and emerging from it.”

Solomon makes cherubim on the walls of the temple when the Lord grants his elect to direct their lives according to the rule of the holy Scriptures, in which there is a multitude of knowledge. He makes cherubim when he teaches them, according to their capacity, to imitate in this world the chastity of an angelic way of life, which is practiced above all through vigils and divine praises and through sincere love of the Creator and of one’s neighbor.

He makes palm trees when he fixes the memory of eternal recompense in their minds, so that they may be less able to slip from the citadel of righteousness because they always have the reward of righteousness before the eyes of their hearts.

He makes various images projecting from the wall and emerging from it when he grants the faithful manifold works of virtue—for example, compassionate hearts, kindness, humility, patience, bearing with one another, forgiving one another, and, above all these, possessing love, which is the bond of perfection.

When these virtues have become such a settled habit in the elect that they seem naturally implanted in them, what are they other than the images of the Lord’s house projecting outward, as if emerging from the wall? For they no longer learn the words and works of truth from others externally; rather, as things rooted within them, they always bring forth from the depths of their hearts what must be done or taught.

“He also covered the pavement of the house with gold within and without, in the sanctuary and in the temple itself.”

We said above that the evenness of the pavement signifies the humble concord of holy brotherhood. Although there are Jews and Gentiles, barbarians and Scythians, free and enslaved, noble and ignoble, all glory in being brothers in Christ and in having one and the same Father in heaven. No one may doubt the supremely harmonious humility of the citizens of heaven.

## XVII. On the Entrance to the Inner Sanctuary. Chapter VI

Solomon therefore covered the floor of the house with gold, inside and out, because our peaceful King filled both the angels and the souls of the righteous in heaven perfectly and completely with the gift of love, and separated those who dwell as pilgrims in this world, citizens of the same heavenly homeland, from the baseness of the rest of mortals by the mark of love: “By this,” he says, “everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13).

At the entrance to the inner sanctuary he also made little doors of olive wood, with five-sided doorposts at the corners, and two doors of olive wood. What he had first said—“He made little doors of olive wood”—he seems to have wished to explain more clearly when he added, “And two doors of olive wood.” There was indeed one entrance to the inner sanctuary, but that same entrance was closed by two doors and, when they were opened again, was made accessible, just as the temple was, and as the portico before the temple was. They had no more than one entrance, certainly for a definite symbolic reason: because there is “one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God” (Ephesians 4); one entrance into the present Church through baptism, and one entrance into the heavenly kingdom through the works of faith, must be hoped for.

That the inner sanctuary had one entrance is attested by what is written below concerning the ark: “When the poles projected, and their ends appeared outside the sanctuary before the inner sanctuary, they were no longer visible outside.” Here, unless I am mistaken, it is plainly shown that there was one entrance to the inner sanctuary, and that this was made directly opposite the ark, which stood in the middle of that same inner sanctuary.

The entrance and its little doors can be understood symbolically in many ways. They most appropriately signify the angelic spirits, by whose ministry we are introduced into the habitation of the heavenly homeland; and they also represent the apostles and apostolic men. To these the keys of the kingdom of heaven have been given. Having received from the Lord the authority to bind and loose, they admit the worthy within the gate of the kingdom, while by excommunicating or anathematizing the obstinate, the impure, and the proud, they exclude them from the entrance to eternal life.

The works of righteousness, by whose merit one reaches the heavenly kingdom, may also rightly be symbolized by the doors through which one entered the Holy of Holies, in accordance with what is written in the Book of Wisdom: “The keeping of the laws is the completion of incorruption; and incorruption brings one near to God. Therefore the desire for wisdom leads to the everlasting kingdom.” All these things aptly agree with the fact that the little doors themselves were made of olive wood. For angels and perfect human beings alike display themselves gloriously in God’s house through the fruit of mercy and works of light; indeed, all the elect open for themselves the entrance to the heavenly homeland through the weapons of light and piety.

There are two little doors, either because angels and holy human beings love the Lord and their neighbors, and no one can enter the gate of life except through this twofold love, or because the same gate of life is opened to the faithful of both peoples, namely Jews and Gentiles.

The doorposts are five-sided because the court of heaven receives not only the souls of the elect but also opens its gates at the judgment to bodies endowed with immortal glory. For there are five senses of our body, as we have mentioned above: sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch.

Certainly, each of the two doorposts of the inner sanctuary was also five cubits high, because access to the heavenly homeland is opened only to those who have striven to serve the Lord with all the senses of their body and heart. With the senses of the body, when through those same senses they do something for him; with the senses of the heart, when they think soberly, justly, and piously about the things they resolve to do through those bodily senses.

“And he carved upon them figures of cherubim and palm trees, and very prominent reliefs, and covered them with gold; he overlaid both the cherubim and the palm trees and the rest with gold.” *Anaglypha* in Greek are called *caelaturae* in Latin, “engravings.” Vessels of gold or silver are engraved when figures in higher relief are represented on their inner and outer surfaces. These are also called “carved” by another name; they are called *anaglypha* because they are carved above. For the Greeks call *ana* “upward” and *glyphē* “carving”—that is, “carved upward.”

All these things, placed above those same cherubim in the decoration of the temple walls, have been explained according to our capacity; there is no need to labor over a further demonstration. Rather, those who have been entrusted with the care of the faithful and have been given the keys of the kingdom of heaven ought to devote themselves with every diligence to the works of virtue that the Church throughout the whole world practices in her holy and perfect members, so that, to the degree that they excel others in rank, they may also surpass them in the merit of good action.

They have within themselves a carved image of cherubim when, as far as is possible for mortals, they imitate an angelic life on earth both in mind and in action. They have figures of palm trees when, with steadfast intention, they continually meditate on the gifts of heavenly recompense. For the palm is the ornament of a victorious hand. They have very prominent reliefs when they display before all who look upon them the most certain evidence of good works—works that no one can interpret in a sinister sense.

All these works are covered with plates of gold when, as has often been said and must always be said, the radiance of love rises above the other flowers of virtue with particular brilliance in the great members of the Church.

The Book of Chronicles reports that a veil was added to these doors: “He also made a veil,” it says, “of violet, purple, scarlet, and fine linen, and embroidered cherubim upon it.” This was certainly made for the sake of adornment, so that it might shine among the gilded walls and the *holosericum*—silk cloth; but it was hung before the ark and the entrance to the inner sanctuary as a sign of the same mystery as the doors. Just as the doors were opened at appointed times, so the veil was revealed whenever the one who was to enter the Holy of Holies arrived.

The diligent revealing of this veil signifies the diligent opening of the kingdom of heaven, which has been granted to us through the incarnation of our Lord and Savior. Hence, when he was baptized, the heavens were opened, so that it might be shown that through the baptism which he himself consecrated for us we ought to enter the gate of the heavenly homeland.

When he died upon the cross, the same veil was torn in the middle from top to bottom, openly teaching that the legal figures had then reached their end, and that the truth of the Gospel, the heavenly mysteries, and entrance into heaven itself were no longer to be foretold and signified figurally, but were already about to be opened to all those who, from the beginning of the world up to that time, had passed from the world in faith in the truth.

For on the fortieth day after the Lord’s resurrection, all went up to heaven with him; every veil having been removed, each received in the house of the Lord the many dwellings according to their merits. At that same hour, the entrance into that heavenly city and the house of the Father was also opened for us, who were still to come.
