One ascends into that city only through inward desires for eternal goods, through faith and the sacraments of the Lord’s Passion, through words of sincere love, through the mortification of carnal desire, and through the daily assistance of the angels.

Thus the same veil, beneath which one entered the inner sanctuary, was appropriately made of violet, purple, scarlet, and fine linen, and cherubim are recorded as having been woven into it.

Violet, which imitates the color of heaven; purple, which is made from the blood of shellfish and displays a blood-red appearance—this not improperly signifies the sacrament of the Lord’s Passion, which we must imitate by carrying our cross.

Scarlet, which blazes with a red color, fittingly expresses the virtue of love, concerning which the disciples who walked with the Lord said in wonder: “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke to us on the way and opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24).

Fine linen, which grows from the earth by means of a green shoot, and through the long labor of craftsmen loses its natural greenness and is brought to a white appearance, fittingly suggests the chastity of our flesh. The Apostle commands that its inborn moisture, as it were, be dried up, saying: “Put to death your members that are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil desire, and avarice, which is idolatry” (Colossians 3).

He shows to what glory of whiteness he wishes this chastity to be brought when he says elsewhere: “I beseech you, brothers, by the mercy of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God, your rational service” (Romans 12).

He wove cherubim into the veil, and these same cherubim were made with four distinguished colors, when, in everything we piously do, we are protected, by the Lord’s gift, from the poisonous darts of demons through angelic defenses.

Again, he wove cherubim into the veil when, in the good things we do, we continually employ an abundance of knowledge, always attending to the divine words and, lest we stray from the path of virtue, constantly directing our footsteps by their guidance.

“And he made four-sided doorposts at the entrance of the temple, and two doors of fir wood on the interior; each door was double, and they opened by holding one another.”

Just as the entrance to the inner sanctuary, by which one reached the ark of the Lord and the cherubim, signifies the entrance into the heavenly kingdom, where we hope and desire to be brought into the vision of the Creator together with the citizens above, so the entrance into the temple typologically demonstrates the beginnings of our conversion to God, when we enter the present Church.

The former signifies our entrance into faith; the latter, our entrance into vision. Accordingly, the doorposts of this entrance were appropriately made four-sided, on account of the four books of the holy Gospel, whose teaching instructs us in the faith of truth; or on account of the same number of principal virtues—prudence, fortitude, temperance, and justice—upon which, as upon a most firm foundation, the whole structure of good actions rests.

Prudence is the virtue by which we learn what we ought to do and how it is fitting for us to live. Fortitude is the virtue by which we carry out what we have learned ought to be done. The prophet briefly gathers these virtues into one verse when he says: “The Lord is my light and my salvation” (Psalm 26). “Light,” that he may teach us what we ought to do; “salvation,” that he may strengthen us to do it.

Temperance is the virtue by which we discern whether we are found to devote more or less attention than is right to prudence or fortitude. Whoever makes use of prudence, fortitude, and temperance will, without any contradiction, be shown to be just. Justice follows as the fourth virtue after prudence, fortitude, and temperance.

The two doors made for this entrance are the love of God and of one’s neighbor. They are rightly said to have been made on opposite sides, because they face one another, so that one can in no way be possessed without the other: “Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God; and everyone who loves the one who gave birth loves the one born from him.” And again it is said: “Whoever does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” (1 John 4).

Accordingly, the outer door is rightly understood as brotherly love, and the inner one as divine love: the former is earlier in time, while the latter is higher in dignity. Through the former one enters into the latter, because in love of one’s neighbor one learns how the Creator ought to be loved.

Each door was double, and they opened by holding one another, because in both kinds of love there are two things that we must chiefly observe.

In the love of God, we must have the faith of truth and the purity of good action. For without faith it is impossible to please God, and faith without works is dead.

In brotherly love, patience and kindness must be preserved, as the Apostle says: “Love is patient; love is kind” (1 Corinthians 13). Patient, in order to endure the troubles and injuries of one’s neighbors; kind, in order to forgive from the heart and do good to those whose injuries one bears.

This is the kind of love the Lord wished us to have when he said: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven.” Forgive the injuries of those who hurt you; give assistance in compassion to those whose injuries you release. This is the love he desires us to offer—the one who commanded us to say in prayer: “Give us this day our daily bread, and forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew 6).

Each door, therefore, was double, because each love is perfected in a twofold order; and they opened by holding one another, because the virtues are joined together and cannot be separated from one another. Faith without works cannot please God, nor can good works please him without faith. Likewise, it is not enough to endure injuries if the person whom one tolerates is denied the things he needs, even though one is able to provide them. Nor is it enough for someone who possesses the goods of the world to give from them to a needy neighbor if he does not also forgive from a sincere heart the injuries that neighbor may have inflicted upon him.

What is said of both doors—that they opened by holding one another—does not signify the separation of spiritual virtues from one another. Rather, it indicates that after these virtues have been joined together, the entrance into the holy Church becomes increasingly open to us, so that the more abundantly we possess them, the more truly we may be associated with the assemblies of the saints.

Likewise, the division of the Red Sea, by which the people of God escaped the pursuing Egyptians, signified not the division of the one baptism but rather the opening by which, after all sins have been extinguished, we cross over to the shore and the desert of virtues.

Alternatively, the door that holds the other is opened when, after the ministry of the preacher, one discerns what properly pertains to knowledge of the faith and what pertains to purity of life. Yet neither of these can be separated from its connection with the other, because there is no difference between enduring the evils of one’s neighbors and supplying them with good things, since these two qualities most certainly remain inseparable in one and the same perfect person.

It should certainly be noted that at the entrance to the inner sanctuary two doors are mentioned, but they are not said to have been double. In the temple—that is, at the entrance of the earlier house—the two doors were such that each was double. For in the present Church it is necessary for us to enter and lead a life in which we preserve the love of God and neighbor through faith and action, through patience and kindness.

In the future life, however, where we shall see the Lord and our neighbors in the inward light of blessedness, we shall enjoy this same twofold love without any labor at all, indeed in a great abundance of divine sweetness.

Accordingly, the inner entrance of the house appropriately had two doors, but these were single. Faith is not necessary there, where we shall see in manifest light all the things that we now believe and hope. The labor of works is not necessary there, where we shall be given the everlasting reward of the things for which we labor here. Patience is not necessary there, where no one inflicts anything adverse. The generosity of kindness is not necessary there, where no one lacks what is needed.

We have discussed the symbolic meaning of the doors according to our limited ability, following in the footsteps of the Fathers.

In accordance with the practical form of the building, however, it was provided for the sake of beauty that there should be two doors in one and the same entrance to the temple. The walls of the house, which were one hundred and twenty cubits in length, necessarily had some thickness; the doors were fixed in the outer part of that thickness, so that each door was aligned with the wall. Whether someone stood inside or outside the temple and looked at the door, it appeared to him to be in every respect one continuous wall.

Likewise, since the cedar wall was twenty cubits in length and height, it too necessarily had considerable thickness. Therefore, two doors were also made at its entrance, so that from either side—inside and outside—the door might open in alignment with the wall.

Since the door and the wall had the same pictures, so that they genuinely appeared to be one continuous wall extending without interruption, one projected forward for the sake of beauty, while the other prefigured the mystery through its symbolic arrangement.

What follows the description of the temple doors—“And he carved cherubim and palm trees, highly raised engravings, and covered everything with gold plates, worked in squares according to the rule”—has already been explained above. The same pictures or engravings were made on the walls of the house and on the inner doors.

It is clear why the very same pictures and engravings, and the same cherubim, were received by the first door of the temple as by the inner door: because the same mysteries of faith, hope, and love that the highest and most perfect grasp in an exalted manner, and that all the elect fully perceive in heaven through the divine vision, are also handed down to the unlearned who are being instructed, so that, having been initiated into the sacred mysteries, they may eventually attain to receiving the things they have piously believed.

Where our translation has, “And he covered everything with gold plates, worked in squares according to the rule,” the Septuagint has: “He spread over them plates and gilded them with gold laid over the carving.”

## XVIII. On the Courts of the House of the Lord. Chapter VI

“He built the inner court with three courses of hewn stones and one course of cedar beams.”

He speaks briefly of the inner court and seems entirely to pass over the outer one. Yet in the Book of Chronicles both are mentioned, where it is written: “He also made the court of the priests and the great basilica, and doors for the basilica, which he covered with bronze.”

The inner court, which is called the court of the priests because the priests and Levites ministered there, was enclosed by the temple on every side from the east. Hence the entrance to the temple was placed much farther from the temple on that side than on the other three sides, because the sacred services were performed there, that is, at the front of the temple. There stood the bronze altar for offering sacrifices to the Lord; there were the ten basins for washing those same sacrifices; and there was the bronze sea for washing the hands and feet of the priests when they entered to minister.

This court was three cubits high, as Josephus reports (*Jewish Antiquities*, Book 8, chapter 3), so that it might keep the rest of the people from entering the temple and signify that this was permitted to priests alone. There was a gate on the eastern side, as far as which the people brought their sacrifices; the priests received them there and carried them to the altar.

Concerning the outer court, which the Book of Chronicles calls the great basilica, Josephus wrote as follows:

> “Outside this temple he built another court, made in the form of a square, raising very large and broad porticoes and high, spacious gates on the four regions of the world, assigning each of them to one of the winds at the four corners, where he placed bronze doors.”

A little later he says:

> “All the peoples entered this sanctuary who possessed purification and observance of the lawful rites.”

Cassiodorus the senator distinguished these porticoes in three rows in the picture of the temple that he placed on a wall, as he himself records in his exposition of the Psalms. He placed the first row outside the court of the priests, square on every side; the second, in the same manner, outside the innermost porticoes; and the outermost, extending all around, likewise on every side beyond the earlier porticoes.

Thus the temple was fortified on every side by a threefold protection of buildings. The pavement under the open sky between the individual buildings was made of marble. The inner walls of the buildings—that is, those facing the temple—were constructed with columns, while the outer walls were solid. In this way the entire structure of the temple was rationally differentiated by stages through its variety.

The high priest entered the Holy of Holies; purified priests entered the temple itself; purified and unpurified priests, together with Levites and singers, entered the court of the priests; purified Jewish men stood in the innermost court of the great basilica and prayed in the open air if the weather was clear, but withdrew into the nearest porticoes if there was a storm. Purified Jewish women occupied the outer court; in the extreme court were Gentiles and Jews who had recently come from among the Gentiles, until the sixth day of purification.

We found these distinctions represented in Cassiodorus’s picture and have taken care to note them briefly, supposing that he learned these things from ancient Jews and that an educated man would not have wished to present as a model for reading anything that he himself had not first learned accurately.

These are the places mentioned by the last of the Songs of Ascents, which begins:

> “Behold, now bless the Lord, all servants of the Lord,  
> who stand in the house of the Lord,  
> in the courts of the house of our God” (Psalm 133).

In these porticoes Jeremiah and the other prophets preached the word to the people; in these the Lord and the apostles preached. In one of them the Lord sat teaching when the woman accused of adultery was brought to him for judgment by the Pharisees who were testing him.

In these he found those selling and buying sheep, oxen, and doves, and expelled them with their merchandise from the temple (Mark 11; Luke 19). In these Peter and John found and healed a lame man, and led him inside with them to pray. In these the whole multitude of the people prayed for as long as the angel appeared at the altar of incense to Zechariah, who was offering incense, and instructed him fully concerning the birth of the Lord’s forerunner.

These courts with their porticoes could conceal the sight of the temple from those looking at it from far away, because the place where the temple stood was much higher than the place where the porticoes had been founded. For, as Josephus writes, the outermost structures of the courts, although raised to a height of four hundred cubits, reached only as far as the summit of the mountain on which the temple had been built.

We have thought that these details concerning the structure of the temple should be made known to the diligent reader. In whatever matters Scripture has chosen to report them as useful, let us seek the figures of the mysteries; in the rest, let us use them simply for historical knowledge.

The building of the temple within the court of the priests expresses the life of perfect and exalted men in the holy Church—those who both draw near to the Lord through the excellence of their virtues and regularly offer others the leadership of salvation by word and deed.

The word “priest” (*sacerdos*) receives its Latin name from the fact that one ought to provide sacred leadership to those of lesser rank. In the Scriptures this name is understood mystically to refer not only to ministers of the altar, namely bishops and presbyters, but to all who excel in the height of upright conduct and saving doctrine, benefiting not themselves alone but many others, while presenting their bodies as a living, holy, and pleasing sacrifice to God.

For the apostle Peter was not speaking only to bishops and presbyters but to the whole Church of God when he said: “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people of possession” (1 Peter 2).

The ancient people of God were also marked with the honor of this dignity, when he himself said to Moses: “Thus you shall say to the house of Jacob and proclaim to the children of Israel” (Exodus 19); and a little later: “You shall be to me a priestly kingdom and a holy nation.”

The great basilica, which stood outside the court of the priests and in which the whole multitude of the people regularly gathered either to worship or to hear the word, figurally indicates the life and behavior of carnal people in the holy Church. To them the Apostle says: “And I, brothers, could not speak to you as spiritual people but as carnal, as infants in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not food” (1 Corinthians 3).

They are appropriately represented by the great basilica because, without any doubt, the number of such people in the holy Church is much greater than the number of the perfect. But to the extent that they surpass them in number, to that same extent they fall short in merit.

Accordingly, although this great basilica receives very many people, it does not admit them into the inner parts of the gilded temple, nor to the service of the altar, nor even into the court of the priests. For although all who are carnal and weak in the Church belong, through the merit of a chaste faith and piety, to the lot of the elect, they are nevertheless far from equaling those who can confidently say: “I will not dare to speak of anything except what Christ has accomplished through me for the obedience of the Gentiles by word and deed” (Romans 15).

And again: “I have fought the good fight; I have finished the course; I have kept the faith. From now on there is laid up for me the crown” (2 Timothy 4).

The common people did indeed come as far as the court of the priests. They carried their sacrifices to its gate, followed with their eyes what the priest received and offered upon the altar, and, when the temple was opened, directed their gaze from afar even into the temple itself. Yet they did not have the opportunity to enter the court of the priests; instead, from the lower places they cried out to the Lord.

For the simplicity of the carnal in the Church is not despised by the Lord when they faithfully offer the vows of piety that they are able to offer. They direct their sight from afar toward the temple of God when they gladly and attentively learn and admire the life of the exalted. Those whom they cannot follow by imitating their virtues, they embrace with the affection of pious reverence.

They see the sacrifices of the priests consumed upon the altar by sacred fire because they recognize that the great works of great men are graciously accepted by the Lord through the Holy Spirit.

They also bring their own sacrifices to the court of the priests to be offered to the Lord through them, when, doing the good things of which they are capable, they are strengthened by the exhortation of their elders and teachers and commended through their intercession.

They likewise offer their sacrifices to the priests to be commended by them to the Lord when, for the sake of the highest reward, they give to the holy needy the necessities of this world in which they themselves abound, as the Lord admonishes and says: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that when it fails you, they may receive you into eternal dwellings” (Luke 16); and, “Whoever,” he says, “gives one of these little ones a cup of cold water in the name of a disciple, truly I tell you, he will not lose his reward” (Mark 19).

Thus the one and same person receives the sacrifices of both upon the altar of God, when the Lord judges the almsgiving of the wealthy, by which they have ministered to the saints, worthy of his regard and recompense together with the great virtues of those same saints.

The multitude of believers who, after abandoning their possessions, served the Lord with one heart and soul is itself the temple of God, and the place specially consecrated to it within the court of the priests.

The great basilica, and those praying in it around the court of the priests, represent those who entered this same temple from the Gentiles in Syria, Antioch, and the other provinces and cities. The apostles and the elders who were in Jerusalem imposed no greater burden upon them than that they should abstain from idols, from what had been sacrificed and strangled, from blood, and from fornication.

Yet they wished the poor among the saints who were in Jerusalem to be supported by their offerings, so that, by ministering their material goods to them, they might become participants in their spiritual goods.

Barnabas and Paul with their companions, who received the offerings of these people and carried them to Jerusalem, are themselves the priests who, receiving the sacrifice, brought it to the altar of the Lord to be consecrated. These were the gifts of their devotion, which they brought to the saints who were to pray for them.

The court placed between the place of the common people and that of the priests, lying midway between them, signifies the separation that distinguishes carnal people in the holy Church, who have recently begun the way of righteousness, from the stronghold of the perfect—not in the lot of election, but in the measure of their merits.

The carnal believe that it is sufficient for them to possess faith, hope, and love, together with purity of works. The perfect possess these things as well, but in addition labor in preaching the word, give all their possessions to the poor, devote themselves to vigils, fasts, hymns, spiritual songs, and sacred readings, endure persecutions and dangers for the sake of righteousness, and carry out with ready devotion the other things that Paul boasts of having done with his companions.

Thus the court of the priests is appropriately said to have been built with three courses of hewn stones and one course of cedar beams.

The three courses of hewn stones are faith, hope, and love. They are rightly called “hewn” or “polished,” because it is certainly necessary, through the diligence of learning, for each person to discern how one ought to believe, what one ought to hope for, and what one ought to love.

The one course of cedar beams is good action displayed without the corruption of pretense. Without its addition, faith, hope, and love cannot be genuine. For it has often been said that cedar wood, on account of its fragrance and the enduring strength of its incorruptible nature, signifies the perseverance and good reputation of pious action.

All the elect who desire to please God through faith, hope, love, and action ascend as far as this court. The perfect rise above it through the high grace of their merits when they advance to such a summit of virtue that they can say to their hearers: “Be imitators of us, as we also are of Christ” (1 Corinthians 4). They also glory and say: “Do you not know that we shall judge angels, to say nothing of worldly matters?” (2 Corinthians 6).

XIX. In the fourth year the temple was built. Chapter VI.—In the fourth year the house of the Lord was founded, in the month Ziv; and in the eleventh year, in the month Bul—that is, the eighth month—the house of the Lord was completed in all its work and in all its furnishings. He built it over seven years.

The allegorical meaning of why the house of the Lord was built over seven years is evident: namely, that holy Church is constructed from elect souls throughout this entire age, which proceeds in a cycle of seven days, and at the end of the age brings its own growth to completion. Or certainly it is built over seven years to signify the spiritual grace which the Church alone receives in order to be the Church. Isaiah enumerates seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, without which no believer can either preserve faith or attain, by the merit of faith, the crown of righteousness.

But the fact that in the seventh year, and in its eighth month, the house was completed in all its work and furnishings pertains to the age to come and to the day of judgment, when holy Church will have reached such perfection that nothing can be found which could be added to it. For then it will possess what that pious suppliant desired and asked of the Lord, saying: “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us” (John XIV). It is established that the day of judgment is often represented typologically in Scripture by the number eight, because it follows this age, which runs through seven days. Hence the prophet placed the title of a psalm “for the eighth day,” which he sang because of the severity of that same judgment, beginning thus: “O Lord, rebuke me not in thy indignation, nor chastise me in thy wrath” (Ps. VI).

But a question naturally arises which must not be disregarded: how can the house of the Lord be said to have been completed in the eighth month in all its work and furnishings, when it is subsequently read that its dedication was completed in the seventh month? It is not credible that Solomon, having built the temple over seven years, held its dedication in the eighth month of the eighth year, but delayed it until the seventh month of that eighth year. It therefore seems more likely to me that the house was built over seven years and seven months, so that in that same seventh month the solemnity of the dedication was celebrated, and on the twenty-third day of that month, as the Books of Chronicles relate, Solomon dismissed the people to their tents. Thus, after one week had passed, when the eighth month arrived, the house of the Lord was found to be complete—in all its works, that is—and its dedication itself had already been completed.

Unless perhaps one should suppose that, after the dedication, some furnishings were still added for its ministry up to the beginning of the eighth month, because the king hastened to have the temple dedicated entirely within the seventh month, which was wholly solemn. In this way both statements would prove true: that the temple was completed in the eighth month in all its work and furnishings, and that it was dedicated in the seventh month.

[Col. 1136B] King Solomon also sent for Hiram and brought him from Tyre: the son of a widow, from the tribe of Naphtali, with a Tyrian father, a worker in bronze, full of wisdom, understanding, and knowledge, to perform every kind of work in bronze. When he came to King Solomon, he performed all his work.

This too was done for the sake of a mystery. For the Tyrian craftsman whom Solomon took as an assistant in his work signifies the ministers of the word chosen from the Gentiles. He is fittingly called a craftsman because he was the son of an Israelite widow, in whose person the Church of the present age is sometimes represented. Her husband, that is, Christ, after tasting death, rose again and ascended into heaven, leaving her meanwhile on earth pregnant by him.

There is no need to labor over explaining how the holy preachers are sons of this widow, since all elect men acknowledge that they are sons of the Church. Indeed, a special promise is made concerning these same preachers of the New Testament, when the prophet says: “In place of your fathers, sons have been born to you,” and so forth (Ps. XLIV).

[Col. 1136C] Hiram performed all Solomon’s work because holy teachers, while faithfully devoting themselves to the ministry of the word, truly perform God’s work. By speaking outwardly, they open the way of truth to those whom God himself, by illuminating them inwardly, has predestined to eternal life. “I planted,” he says, “Apollo watered, but God gave the growth” (I Cor. III).

He performed work in bronze because the energetic teacher seeks to entrust the word to those who desire either to receive it piously or to preserve it perseveringly, and who also strive to spread more widely, by preaching to others, what they themselves have rightly learned. For bronze is known to be highly durable and thoroughly sonorous.

XX. Concerning Solomon’s palace. Chapter VII.—He also cast two bronze columns, each column being eighteen cubits high. These are the columns of which Paul says: “James, and John, and Cephas, who were reputed to be pillars, gave to me and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship, so that we should go to the Gentiles, and they to the circumcision” (Gal. II).

By these words he seems almost to explain the mystery of the material columns: what they represented and why two were made. The Apostle and all spiritual teachers are signified by them—those who are strong in faith, action, and contemplation, and raised upright toward heavenly things. There are two so that by preaching they may bring both the Gentiles and the circumcision into the Church.

They stood in the portico before the doors of the temple and wonderfully adorned its entrance on either side with their splendor and beauty. The Lord is the door of the temple, because “no one comes to the Father except through him” (John XIV); and as he says elsewhere: “I am the door. If anyone enters through me, he will be saved” (John X).

The columns stand before this door on both sides when the minister of the word shows both peoples the entrance to the heavenly kingdom, so that whether someone comes to the faith of the Gospel from the light of legal knowledge or from the rigor of paganism, he may find ready guides who show him the way of salvation both by word and by example.

Or certainly, because it is written of these columns in the Book of Chronicles: “He placed the columns in the vestibule of the temple, one on the right and the other on the left” (II Chron. III), the two columns were made and arranged in such a way as to teach us that, in prosperity as well as adversity, we must keep the entrance to our heavenly homeland before the eyes of our mind.

For this reason Paul, surely the most excellent column of the house of the Lord, earnestly urges by his own diligent example and that of his companions that we must be fortified by the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left, so that neither delighted by prosperity nor broken by adversity, we may deviate in any respect from the royal way of life by which we must journey toward the promised inheritance of our heavenly homeland.

It should be carefully noted in the passage from Chronicles that I have cited that the same portico of the temple was also called the vestibule of the temple. And where we read in the prophets that the priests prayed between the vestibule and the altar, we must understand “between the portico and the altar of burnt offerings.”

It is fittingly recorded that each column was eighteen cubits high. Three times six makes eighteen: that three pertain to faith because of the Holy Trinity, and six to works, because the world was made in that number of days, is clearer than light. The three are multiplied by the six when the righteous person lives by faith and increases the knowledge of pious belief through the execution of good action.

A column before the doors of the temple is eighteen cubits high when every distinguished preacher openly declares to all that we can reach the joys of the heavenly life only through faith and works of righteousness.

Yet this may also be understood in a higher sense, since the name JESUS among the Greeks begins with this number. The first letter of the name Jesus signifies ten among them, and the second signifies eight. The columns of God’s house are appropriately eighteen cubits high because holy teachers—or rather, all the elect—direct their good lives toward this end: that they may deserve to see their Creator face to face. For when they reach him who is above all things, they will have nothing further to seek.

And a line of twelve cubits surrounded each column. The twelve-cubit line is the standard of apostolic instruction. It surrounds both columns when a teacher sent to preach either to Jews or to Gentiles takes care to do and teach only what the holy Church received and learned through the apostles.

For if anyone should wish to live or preach otherwise, either rejecting apostolic decrees or choosing to establish new things according to his own will, he is not a column suitable for the temple of God. Since he disdains to follow apostolic statutes, he does not fit the twelve-cubit line, as though because of the thinness of his inertia or the bulk of his swollen pride.

[Col. 1137D] The Lord surrounded the columns of his temple with these lines when he said to the disciples whom he sent to teach and baptize all nations: “Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you” (Matt. XXVIII).

Whoever therefore observes and teaches all things that the Lord commanded the apostles, adding nothing else and passing over none of them, is truly a column in the house of God, which is the Church and the pillar of truth, such as the Apostle Paul declared Timothy would be (I Tim. III).

But because the life and speech of teachers cannot be firm without knowledge of the Scriptures, it is appropriately added: “He also made two capitals, cast in bronze, to be placed upon the tops of the columns; one capital was five cubits high, and the other capital was five cubits high.”

The tops of the columns—that is, their uppermost part—are the hearts of faithful teachers. Just as the limbs are directed by the head, so all their works and words are directed by thoughts devoted to God.

The two capitals placed upon these heads are the two Testaments, to whose meditation and observance teachers submit themselves in soul and body.

Thus it is fitting that each capital was five cubits high, because the Mosaic Law is contained in five books, and the whole series of the Old Testament encompasses five ages of the world.

The New Testament proclaims nothing else to us except what Moses and the prophets foretold was to be proclaimed. Hence the Lord said to the Jews who clung uselessly to the letter of the Old Testament and rejected the grace of the New: “If you believed Moses, you would perhaps believe me also; for he wrote about me” (John V).

For Moses wrote about the Lord both many things figuratively and one thing most openly, when he recounts the promise made by the Lord to Abraham: “In your seed all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. XXII). And Moses himself says to the children of Israel: “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers; you shall listen to him as to me, according to all things whatsoever he shall speak to you” (Deut. XXVIII).

The voice of the Father from heaven warned the disciples concerning the fulfillment of this prophecy, when the Lord appeared to them in glory on the holy mountain between Moses and Elijah and thundered forth, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Matt. III).

With an admirable harmony of divine action, at first the grace of the New Testament was hidden under the veil of the Old; and now the mysteries of the Old Testament have been revealed through the light of the New. Thus the capital of each column is five cubits high, because it is clear that in the Old Testament all its mysteries were more fully contained, whether prefigured in the five books of the Law or in the five ages, and that the grace of evangelical perfection was also implanted there.

Thus every distinguished preacher, whether sent to the Jews or to the Gentiles, preserves without error the rightness of faith and action, confirmed by the harmonious testimony of the divine utterances, and knows how, while teaching, to bring forth from his treasure things new and old.

The two Testaments not only agree with one another through the relation of their divine mysteries; all the elect whose names are contained in the books of those same Testaments also possess one faith and are joined to one another by the same charity.

Hence it is appropriately added concerning the construction of the capitals: “And, as if in the form of a net and chains woven together with wondrous workmanship, each of the two capitals was cast” (II Chron. III).

This is written in the Book of Chronicles as follows: “And also chains like little chains for the inner sanctuary, and he placed them upon the heads of the columns.”

The appearance of the virtues and their likeness in the capitals signifies the variety of spiritual virtues in the saints. Of this the Lord is sung in the psalm: “The queen stood at your right hand, clothed in gold, surrounded by variety” (Ps. XLIV)—that is, in the garment of radiant love, clothed all around with the variety of differing spiritual gifts.

Or certainly, the multiple weaving of the chains and the spreading of the net suggests the many kinds of persons among the elect. When they cling to the words of the holy preachers by faithfully listening and obeying, they are like nets and chains placed upon the heads of the columns, presenting to all who look upon them the wonder of their connectedness.

For those chains are woven together with wondrous workmanship because it was accomplished through the utterly marvelous grace of the Holy Spirit that the lives of the faithful—though widely separated from one another in place, time, rank, condition, sex, and age—should be joined together by one and the same faith and love.

That this fraternal union of the righteous, separated both by places and by times, is brought about through the unifying gift of the Spirit is also shown by the words that follow, when the construction of the capitals is further described: “Seven rows of network were on one capital, and seven networks on the other capital.”

The number seven customarily signifies the grace of the Holy Spirit, as John testifies in the Apocalypse. After saying that he had seen a Lamb having seven horns and seven eyes, he immediately explained: “These are the seven spirits of God sent forth into all the earth” (Rev. V).

The prophet Isaiah explains this more clearly when, speaking of the Lord who was to be born in the flesh, he says: “And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. XI).

There were therefore seven rows of network on each capital because the fathers of both Testaments received, through the grace of the one and the same sevenfold Spirit, the gift of becoming elect.

And he completed the columns and two rows around the network of each, so that they covered the capitals. There were indeed two rows of network around the capital, but each row proceeded in a sevenfold number of courses until, having encircled the capital, it returned again to itself like a circle.

The hidden mystery of this figure is why there are two rows of network, since it is clear that the virtue of love is twofold, when we are commanded to love God with our whole heart, whole soul, and whole strength, and our neighbor as ourselves.

Each row, however, has seven networks of courses because neither God nor our neighbor can be loved without the grace of the Holy Spirit. The truthful saying remains: “The charity of God is poured forth in our hearts,” not by our merit, but “through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Rom. V).

And wherever the love of God is present, there the love of our neighbor is certainly poured into the hearts of the faithful, because one cannot in any way be possessed without the other.

These networks were made to cover the capitals—that is, to surround them on every side in a circle—because every page of Holy Scripture, when rightly understood, proclaims throughout the grace of charity and peace. The capitals are the volumes of the divine utterances; the networks are the bonds of mutual love. The capitals are covered with networks when the sacred utterances are, so to speak, shown to be clothed on every side with the gift of charity. For even in those things that we do not understand in Scripture, charity lies broadly manifest.

It is fittingly added concerning these networks or capitals: “They were above the top of the pomegranates.”

Pomegranates, whose nature is to enclose many seeds within a single outer rind, are aptly placed as a figure of holy Church, which customarily encloses innumerable ranks of the elect within the catholic protection of one faith.

They can also signify the life and conduct of each righteous person, as though a single rind enclosed a great many seeds: the firm protection of faith and humility surrounds many signs of spiritual thoughts and virtues, lest they disperse.

And with wholly appropriate symbolism the tops of the columns were surrounded by pomegranates in a circle, because holy teachers must recall the lives of the faithful to their memory and always fortify their own actions and words on every side by their examples, lest they err if they should live or teach otherwise than those examples prescribe.

Just as the marvelous interweaving of the networks signifies the unity of the faithful, which exists in the bond of peace, so also the pomegranate typologically indicates that same unity, which restrains innumerable peoples throughout the world within the one rule of the catholic faith.

Or certainly, the marvelous concatenation of the networks demonstrates the manifest concord of all the faithful. The arrangement of the pomegranates, however, expresses the inward virtues of the soul, which cannot be seen by others at all: patience, humility, kindness, modesty, and other qualities of this kind.

The beautiful outer surface of fruits appears, but the abundance of seeds enclosed within is not visible; so, when the pious activity of the saints is displayed openly to all, the grace of faith, hope, love, and the other good qualities of the soul that exist within cannot be seen.

When it is said that the networks covered the capitals which were above the tops of the pomegranates, it seems, according to the order of the work itself, that the pomegranates were made around the capitals on their lower side, and that from those same pomegranates the networks arose, by which the capitals were partly covered.

The symbolic figure is clear: why networks were made, and why the capitals were attached to pomegranates. These belong almost to one meaning, whether of spiritual persons or of spiritual virtues. For we know that virtues arise from virtues, and that the saints walk from virtue to virtue, until “the God of gods is seen in Zion”—a virtue greater than which none can be granted.

Hence the Apostle says: “Knowing that tribulation works patience, and patience probation, and probation hope” (Rom. V).

But within the universal company of the elect, the persons of the righteous succeed one another in various ways. The lesser rejoice faithfully to cling to the footsteps of their elders and predecessors, and to rely upon their sayings or writings, lest they should slip into error.

The networks are placed above the tops of the pomegranates when the concord of charity has been added to perfected works. And when the life of the saints shines through both gifts of virtue—namely, through action and charity—the concatenation of networks added above accompanies the circle of pomegranates on the capitals of the column.

And because all the present gifts of virtue look toward the glory of eternal recompense, which has been promised and bestowed upon us through the Gospel, it is appropriately added: “The capitals which were upon the heads of the columns were made as lily-work, in the portico, four cubits.”

What is signified by lilies except the homeland of heavenly brightness and the delight of paradise, fragrant with the flowers of immortality? What is signified by four cubits except the evangelical word, which promises us entrance into the blessedness of eternal life and shows the way by which it may be reached?

Therefore, when the holy teachers show us the promised thresholds of the heavenly kingdom in the four books of the holy Gospel, the work of the lily on the heads of the columns displays four cubits in itself.

Here it should be noted according to the literal sense that when the lily-work on the capitals is said to be four cubits, and neither its width nor its height is added, it is left to the judgment of the reader whether it should be understood in height or in width.

It is established, however, without any doubt whatsoever, that the column which a twelve-cubit cord surrounded was four cubits thick. For every circle has three times as much circumference as it has space across its diameter. Indeed, the bronze sea, which was ten cubits in diameter, as is read below, consequently had thirty cubits in circumference.

But since the lily-work is said to have been four cubits, whether it indicates width or height, the logic of the figure is nevertheless clear: for only through the Gospel did that most desirable voice resound throughout the world: “Do penance, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand” (Matt. III).

What follows—“And again there were other capitals at the top of the columns above”—means that the network was made according to the measurement of the column, that is, of such a height as the column itself had. Yet how great that height was is not reported.

Whatever the nature and size of these capitals may have been—for Scripture does not explicitly specify their measurement—they seem to have been added in the manner of lilies. If one takes pleasure in seeking a mystical meaning in their construction, they may not unfittingly signify that exaltation of the everlasting kingdom “which eye has not seen,” and so forth, through “those who love him” [cf. I Cor. II].

After the lilies of four cubits, other capitals were added, whose height is not stated, because we read many things in the Gospel about heavenly blessedness: that there the pure in heart will see God (Matt. V); that they will be equal to the angels of God; that they will neither marry nor be given in marriage (Luke XX), because they will no longer be able to die (John XII); that wherever Christ is, his ministers will also be (John XIV); that he will reveal himself to them, as he announced plainly to them concerning the Father (John XVI); and that no one will take the joy of his vision from them (ibid.).

But the actual appearance of these things we have mentioned, and the nature of the condition and society of that heavenly homeland, are evident only to those who have deserved to enter it, its own citizens.

Thus it is fitting that the construction or height of these capitals was above the lily, so that the incomprehensible nature of the heavenly dwelling might be indicated to earthly beings.

Yet this is by no means hidden from us: all there enjoy the common happiness of the divine vision, each one more sublimely according as he has possessed purer eyes of the heart with which to see him. For the one who said, “All who fear the Lord, both small and great” (Rev. XIX), also said, “You will render to each according to his works” (Rom. II).

The blessing of all the elect will therefore be common there; nevertheless, according to the distinct quality of their works, there are many dwelling places of the blessed in the one and same eternal house of the Father in heaven.

I think this is mystically signified also in the construction of these columns, when it is said: “And again there were other capitals at the top of the columns above.” The capitals are made above according to the measurement of the column when holy teachers—or rather, all the elect who follow in the footsteps of those teachers—receive the rewards of heavenly recompense according to the merits of their pious activity.

Networks also are made according to the capitals, because, according to the measure of the love by which holy fraternity joined them to one another in this life, they are also joined in heaven to the fellowship of the citizens above, in the presence of their Creator.

But because that same heavenly fellowship of citizens is granted to the faithful of both peoples, it is rightly added: “There were two hundred rows of pomegranates around the second capital.”

We have said that the pomegranates represent the whole of holy Church. The number one hundred, which first reaches the right hand, is sometimes customarily used as a figure of eternal blessedness.

This number is doubled in the circle of the second capital, to indicate mystically that the people of both Testaments, to be united in Christ, are to be brought into the crown of eternal life.

This figure corresponds to what is written about the apostles fishing after the Lord’s resurrection, when they saw him standing on the shore: “For they were not far from the land, but about two hundred cubits,” drawing the net full of fish (John XXI).

Through two hundred cubits the disciples draw the net full of large fish to the Lord, who was already displaying the effect of his resurrection on the shore. So holy preachers entrust the word of faith both to Jews and to Gentiles, and lead the elect of both peoples, drawn out from the waves of the present age, to the glory of future peace and immortality.

The circuit of the second capital therefore has two hundred rows of pomegranates when the sublimity of the heavenly kingdom gathers the elect of both peoples into one citadel of blessedness.

And he set up two columns in the portico of the temple. When he had set up the column on the right, he called it by the name Jachim, “Firmness.” Likewise, he raised the second column and called its name Booz, “In strength.”

The right-hand column, as we said above, represents the teachers who established the primitive Church in Jerusalem; the second represents those who were sent to preach to the Gentiles.

Or certainly, the right-hand column signifies those who foretold by prophecy that the Lord would come in the flesh; the second signifies those who testify that he has already come and redeemed the world by his blood.

Both columns were appropriately designated by similar names, since one was called “Firmness” and the other “In strength,” so that one strength of faith and action might be shown to belong to all teachers, while the inertia of silence might be marked in those of our own times.

Some wish to be seen and called teachers, priests, and columns of the house of God, although they possess no firmness of God within themselves for despising the pomps of the world and desiring invisible goods; no strength for correcting the errors of those placed under their authority; and not even enough diligence to understand those errors.

## XXI. On the Bronze Sea. Chapter VII

He also made a cast sea, ten cubits from rim to rim, circular all around. This cast sea was made as a figure of the saving bath, by which we are cleansed for the remission of sins. For priests were washed in it, as the Books of Chronicles plainly testify. In Scripture, all the elect are understood typologically to be called priests, since they are members of the supreme Priest, the Lord Jesus Christ.

And rightly did Scripture give this vessel the name [Col. 1142B] “sea,” namely in remembrance of the Red Sea, in which, through the destruction of the Egyptians and the liberation of God’s people, the figure of baptism first went before us. The Apostle explains this when he says: “For our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea” (1 Cor. 10).

The sacrament of baptism requires from us the purity of life in this present age and promises us the glory of eternal life in the future. Both of these are indicated in a single statement concerning this bronze sea, when it is said to have been ten cubits from rim to rim. For by the Ten Commandments the Lord expressed everything that we ought to do in the law; and likewise he signified the reward of good works by the number ten, when he foretold that this sum would be given to those laboring in the vineyard.

The sea, therefore, was ten cubits from rim to rim because, from the first person baptized to the last, who will be baptized and will believe in the name of Jesus Christ at the end of the age, the whole company of the faithful must enter upon one and the same way of truth [Col. 1142C] and hope together for the common crown of righteousness from the Lord.

It was circular all around, so that the whole world, encircled in its circuit, might be shown to require cleansing from the filth of sins by the bath of life. Concerning this it is appropriately added: “Its height was five cubits.” For whatever we sin by sight, hearing, smell, taste, or touch—all this the grace of God forgives us through the washing of the life-giving font.

But forgiveness of past sins is not sufficient if each person does not thereafter strive to devote himself to good works. Otherwise, when the devil who has gone out from a person sees that he is idle in good deeds, he returns more abundantly and makes the final condition of that person worse than the first. Hence it is appropriately added: “And a cord of thirty cubits encircled it.”

By the cord may aptly be signified the discipline of the heavenly commandments, by which we are bound back from our pleasures, as Scripture says: “A threefold cord is not easily broken” (Eccles. 4). For the observance of God’s commandments, which is secured in the hearts of the elect by faith, hope, [Col. 1142D] and love of the heavenly reward, cannot be undone by any obstacle of temporal things.

The cord encircles the sea when we strive to strengthen the sacrament of baptism that we receive with pious works. This cord is appropriately said to have been thirty cubits long: five times six makes thirty. The number six, in which the Lord both made the human being when he did not yet exist and remade him after he had perished, rightly represents our good work. Six is multiplied by five to reach thirty when we humbly subject all the senses of our body to the divine commands.

We may also, not improperly, understand this number thirty in the sea mystically in another way. Three times ten makes thirty, and after the Flood the human race, descended from the three sons of Noah, filled the breadth of the whole world. The descendants of Shem possessed Asia, the descendants of Ham Africa, and the offspring of Japheth Europe and the islands of the sea. [Col. 1143A] Thus, since the mystery of baptism, together with the practice of good works and hope of heavenly rewards, was to be administered to all nations, appropriately did a cord of thirty cubits encircle that sea in which the water of baptism was prefigured.

It should also be said that the Lord was thirty years old when he came to the Jordan to be baptized by John. Since by his baptism, which he received at the age of thirty, he consecrated for us the water of the saving bath, rightly did a cord of thirty cubits encircle the sea that prefigured our baptism. This signified that, by the gift of him who underwent baptism without sin, baptism is dedicated for the remission of sins to all of us who believe in him.

“And a carved work ran beneath the rim, encircling it; it encompassed the sea for ten cubits, and there were two rows of carved work, cast in strips.” Since it was stated above that a cord of thirty cubits encircled the sea, and it is now added that this carved work, placed beneath the rim, encompassed it for ten cubits, it is clear from both statements that the vessel was shaped like a bowl, flaring and spreading outward. [Col. 1143B] Its circumference at the rim, which was thirty cubits, narrowed toward the lower part to ten cubits.

Carved work is that which imitates certain scenes or representations of things. Accordingly, the carved strips with which the sea was surrounded properly signify examples of former times. We must carefully contemplate these examples so that we may see by what works the holy pleased God from the beginning; with what obstinacy the wicked persisted in crimes and with what iniquity the reprobate perished because of their crimes; how, at the beginning of the world’s origin, Cain was condemned for the malice of envy, while Abel was crowned for the merits of righteousness; how Lamech was cursed for adultery and murder, while Enoch was led to paradise through the grace of his piety; how, after the Flood, Ham was denounced by his father for impiety, while Shem and Japheth were granted perpetual blessing for their dutiful reverence; how Abraham, through the merit of faith, became heir of the divine promise, while the countless multitude of the nations was left in unheard-of unbelief; how, when the Lord came in the flesh, [Col. 1143C] Judea was rejected because of the guilt of unbelief, while the Gentiles were brought back to salvation through the grace of faith; and other matters of this kind, which, when attentively and devoutly considered in both Testaments, greatly benefit all who are diligent.

For this reason, perhaps, there were two rows of carved strips made on the bronze sea: so that those who had been instructed in the baptismal font might diligently listen to the histories of both Testaments. They were ten cubits around so that, when people saw in these histories those who were devoted to the heavenly commands and wholly intent upon the rewards above, they might strive to imitate them.

Well, then, it follows: “And it stood upon twelve oxen, three of which looked toward the north, three toward the west, three toward the south, and three toward the east.”

We understand by the oxen the apostles and evangelists, indeed all ministers of the word, as the Apostle teaches. Explaining the command of the law that says, “You shall not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain” (Deut. 25), he asks: “Is it oxen that God is [Col. 1143D] concerned about? Or does he surely say this for our sake? Indeed, it was written for our sake, because the one who plows ought to plow in hope, and the one who threshes ought to partake of the fruit of his hope” (1 Cor. 9).

The twelve oxen, therefore, are the twelve apostles and all those who, in their place, have undertaken to govern the Church in Christ. These oxen carry the sea placed upon them when the apostles and their successors strive to fulfill with ready devotion the duty of evangelizing entrusted to them.

Three look toward the north, three toward the west, three toward the south, and three toward the east when they preach the faith of the Holy Trinity throughout the regions of the four-cornered world. The apostles, too, were chosen in the mystery of this number—twelve, that is, four groups of three—so that, by evangelizing the faith and confession of the Holy Trinity throughout the four parts of the world, they might baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

We can readily see, either at present or by reading, the words, deeds, and sufferings of those apostles and of their successors [Col. 1144A] but what glory of reward awaits them in the future we are not yet able to see. Hence it is appropriately added: “Their hindquarters were all hidden inside.” For all the future rewards of the good are hidden within, since the reward with which holy preachers will be endowed forever has already been established in the judgment of the inner Judge. But to us, who are still outside, that which then cannot in any way remain hidden is now wholly concealed.

Everyone who has received the bath of baptism for salvation and life must possess faith, hope, and love; without these three virtues no one can either perform any good work or enter into life. Hence it is rightly added: “The thickness of the basin was three handbreadths.”

The thickness of the basin signifies the strength of virtue in baptism. Its thickness is three handbreadths when the reception of baptism is strengthened by the power of faith, hope, and love. Nor is baptism shown to be beneficial to those who receive it in any other way, unless the firm certainty of these virtues simultaneously confirms the minds and the works of those receiving it.

[Col. 1144B] The bath of baptism is received and celebrated as an example of the Lord’s passion and resurrection from the dead, according to the Apostle’s explanation: “All of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death. Therefore we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life. For if we have been united with the likeness of his death, we shall also be united with that of his resurrection” (Rom. 6).

This too was typologically marked in the construction of the bronze sea, when it is subsequently added: “Its rim was like the rim of a cup, and like the leaf of an open lily.”

By the rim of the cup is expressed the taste of the Lord’s passion; by the leaf of the open lily, the revealed brightness of the resurrection. For that the cup signifies the drink of the passion is attested by the Lord himself, who, as he approached his passion, prayed to the Father, saying: “Father, if you are willing, take this cup from me” (Mark 14).

The lily, which, accompanied by the grace of a most pleasing fragrance, appears white on the outside [Col. 1144C] of the cup and golden within, appropriately suggests the glory of his resurrection. For he showed his disciples the immortality of his body outwardly, and taught that within himself there was also a soul shining with divine light.

The open lily may also, not improperly, be understood as the Mediator between God and human beings, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death. Before his passion he was, as it were, still a closed lily, although he shone as a glorious man through the signs of the miracles he performed. But after his resurrection and ascension he displayed himself as an open lily to the citizens of the heavenly homeland, revealing in the humanity he had assumed the power of divine glory that he had with the Father before the world existed.

Thus, in the Song of Songs, he wished to designate himself by the name of lily, saying: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song 2).

The rim of the sea, in which the priests were washed, was therefore like the rim of a cup and the leaf of an open lily, because the saving bath by which we become members of the supreme Priest cleanses us through faith in his most holy passion from every stain [Col. 1144D] of sin, and admits those who have been cleansed to the sight of his everlasting glory.

In this bath the two peoples—the people of the circumcision and the people of the foreskin—are made one in the Lord through faith, hope, and love. He himself attests this when, after speaking of the circumcision, he says, among other things: “I have other sheep that are not of this fold; I must bring them also, and they will hear my voice, and there will be one flock and one shepherd” (John 10).

This too was typologically represented in the sea, for it is added: “It held two thousand baths.”

The number one thousand is customarily used in Scripture as a sign of perfection, because the number ten makes a solid square. Ten multiplied by ten makes one hundred, a figure that is already square but still flat. But for it to rise in height and become solid, one hundred multiplied by ten makes one thousand. By this number the stable, unconquerable, and, as it were, squared conscience of the righteous [Col. 1145A] is signified: for a square stands whichever way one turns it, and so the mind of the elect does not know how to be bent from the uprightness of its position by any assault of temptations.

The bath is a Hebrew measure, which they call *bath*, containing four *modii*. It is the same as the *ephah*, which they call *epha*. But the *ephah* concerns the measurement of various crops—wheat, barley, and legumes—whereas the *bath* concerns liquid substances, wine, oil, and water.

Thus the bath, which is a fixed standard of measurement, signifies the works of equity and righteousness by which those who are baptized for the remission of sins must necessarily be formed.

The sea held that one thousand baths when, washing the people of the Jews with the water of baptism, it conveyed them to the heavenly kingdom. It received another thousand when it also made the crowds of the nations, reborn from the same font and strengthened by works of righteousness, participants in that same everlasting kingdom.

## XXII. On the Ten Bases. Chapter VII

“And he made ten bronze bases, each base four cubits long, four cubits wide, and three cubits [Col. 1145B] high.”

The one and the same mysteries of our salvation are prefigured in many ways and by many means. The same apostles and apostolic men who are signified by the oxen carrying the sea are also signified by the bases prepared for carrying the basins. The basins themselves, like the sea, bore the type of the same spiritual bath, since, as the Books of Chronicles relate, everything that they were going to offer as a burnt offering was washed in them.

The Lord’s burnt offering may, in a general sense, be understood as the entire multitude of the elect, which, according to the word of the Forerunner, was baptized by him in the Holy Spirit and fire (Matt. 3). Just as the priests who were washed in the sea express the form of those who through baptism are made sharers in the supreme priesthood that is in the Lord Jesus Christ, so also the burnt offerings most suitably foreshadow their figure, when through the washing of baptism the grace of the Holy Spirit is bestowed.

The victim is washed in the basin when one of the faithful is drenched with the water of baptism; [Col. 1145C] but it is offered as a burnt offering when, through the laying on of the bishop’s hands, that person receives the gift of the Holy Spirit.

When the evangelist Philip was preaching in Samaria, what else was he doing but washing the Lord’s victims in the basin of the temple? But because the Holy Spirit had not yet descended upon any of them, and they had only been baptized in the name of Jesus, the washed victims had not yet reached the sacred fire of the altar.

When Peter and John were sent there, however, and laid hands upon those who had been baptized, and they received the Holy Spirit and spoke in tongues, the victims had already reached the fire of the altar, so that they might become a burnt offering—what is called in Latin *totum incensum*, “wholly burned.” For the grace of the Holy Spirit filled their consciences and made them burn with divine love.

The fact that ten bases were made for carrying the basins could be interpreted mystically in this way: the ministers of the life-giving bath call those whom they instruct to the joys of eternal blessedness, which is customarily represented by the number ten.

But since it is written distinctly below concerning these same basins that five of them were placed [Col. 1145D] on the right side of the temple and five on the left, we should rather discern in them the mysteries of the number five. Bases for the basins were placed on both sides of the temple so that it might be signified that the grace of the sacred font was to be opened to both peoples of God. There are five on each side so that, as we already said in the exposition of the sea, which is five cubits high, it might be shown typologically that everything in which the faithful had sinned through the five senses of the body is remitted through the bath of baptism.

Thus, just as in the one sea placed upon twelve oxen the unity of baptism is expressed—a unity that was to be preached throughout the whole world by the apostles—so by the two rows of basins it is mystically shown that the Gentiles, together with the Jews, were to be gathered into one fellowship of faith after the water of baptism.

For although victims were washed in twin basins, some on the right side of the court and others on the left, they were nevertheless consumed in one fire of the altar, so that they might become a burnt offering. [Col. 1146A] For whether someone receives the bath among the circumcision or among the uncircumcision, all are sanctified by one Spirit so that they may become children of God.

Hence the Apostle says: “But you have received the Spirit of adoption as children, by whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Rom. 8). You have received one Spirit, he says, so that all of you may become children of adoption, in that Spirit in which we cry, “Abba, Father.” “Abba” signifies those of us who came to faith from the Hebrews; “Father” signifies those who came from the Gentiles, invoking one and the same God the Father in various languages according to the diversity of nations, but through the gift of the one Spirit.

The fact that each base was four cubits long, four cubits wide, and four cubits high is to be understood as follows. Length pertains to the patience of endurance; width to the widening of love; height to hope of heavenly reward.

There are four principal virtues on which the whole structure of the virtues rests: prudence, fortitude, temperance, and justice. Therefore the bases were four cubits in length and width, because [Col. 1146B] holy preachers—whether they endure the adversities of the world, the length of exile, and the evils of present labors, or enlarge their hearts in love of their Creator and their neighbors with inward joy—continually devote themselves to the virtues: discerning good and evil with prudent care, enduring adversity bravely, restraining the heart from the desires of pleasure, and maintaining justice in their actions.

The bases are three cubits high when, through the exercise of the virtues that they practice with patience in adversity and love of the good, they strive with continual attention to reach the vision of the Holy Trinity.

“The work of the bases itself was in openwork, with carved figures between the joints.” By “joints” he seems to mean the places by which the boards of the basins themselves were joined to one another, so that one base was made from four or five boards. What sort of carvings they had between these joints—that is, on their very sides, front and back, right and left, and also above—is disclosed by what follows [Col. 1146C]:

“Between the crowns and the festoons were lions and oxen and cherubim, and likewise above, at the joints.”

The surfaces of the bases were therefore not flat on any side, but were carved with mystical figures that displayed the minds of the saints, indeed all their actions, as endowed with the grace of the virtues in every respect. No hour passed for them empty and vacant, in which they ceased to devote themselves to pious works, words, or at least thoughts.

They have little crowns carved upon them when they long for entry into eternal life with tireless desire. They have festoons when, amid their desires for the heavenly life above, they never dissolve the bonds of fraternal fellowship that is near at hand.

They have lions between the little crowns and festoons when they raise their minds toward hope of heavenly things and enlarge them toward love of their neighbors in such a way that they do not delay exercising the fervor of severe rebuke against sinners entrusted to their care.

They have oxen together with lions when they offer the very rebuke of correction in a spirit of gentleness [Col. 1146D]; when, in the fervor of admonition, they never cease to maintain the tireless vigilance of disciplined action and speech; and when they never cease turning over the words of divine reading in their mouths, as if ruminating upon them.

The blessed Stephen, an eminent base of the Lord’s temple, seemed to display the teeth and claws of a savage lion when he said to his persecutors: “You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit. Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute?” and so forth.

Yet by saying this he showed how much, if I may so put it, of the gentleness of an ox he carried within his heart, when, kneeling, he said concerning those same persecutors who raged against him even to his death: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them” (ibid.).

But because we cannot possess either hope of eternal things in heaven, love of our neighbors on earth, the fervor of biting zeal, or the gentleness of compassionate modesty without knowledge of the Holy Scriptures, it is appropriately remembered that [Col. 1147A] after the little crowns and festoons, after the lions and oxen, cherubim were carved.

It is clear that the cherubim hold the type of Sacred Scripture: either because the two cherubim on the mercy seat of the ark were fashioned as a figure of the two Testaments singing harmoniously of Christ, or because this name signifies an abundance of knowledge.

The more diligently a person applies himself to reading the pages of the divine utterances, the more necessarily he fears in all that he does or judges the scrutiny of the inward witness or Judge. He fears lest, either by exacting punishment from sinners more severely than justice permits, or conversely by forgiving without the restraint of just discernment, he incur the anger of the just Judge. “Whoever increases knowledge increases sorrow.”

Hence, because of the carvings of the cherubim, it is appropriately added here: “And above the lions and oxen were bronze straps hanging down like reins.”

Reins hang above the lions and oxen when holy teachers, both in the severity of strictness with which they judge sinners and in the gentleness of mercy with which they forgive the penitent, fear the judgment of their Author, lest perhaps, by binding [Col. 1147B] unjustly, they themselves deserve to be bound by him whose judgment cannot err.

“And there were four wheels for each base, and bronze axles on the four sides, like shoulder-pieces cast beneath the basin, facing one another.”

The four wheels are the four books of the Gospels. They are most suitably compared with wheels because, just as the revolving wheel runs with very swift motion wherever it is driven, so the evangelical word, with the Lord’s help, quickly filled all regions of the world through the apostles.

Just as a wheel lifts the chariot placed upon it from the ground and carries it once lifted wherever the charioteer directs, so evangelical preaching raises the minds of the elect from earthly desires toward heavenly longings and leads them, once elevated, toward progress in good works or toward the ministry of preaching, wherever the assisting grace of the Spirit wills.

For it says below: “The wheels were of such a kind as wheels are usually made for a chariot.” We read concerning the saints: “The chariot of God is tens of thousands, thousands upon thousands rejoicing” (Ps. 68).

[Col. 1147C] What, then, does it mean that the wheels of the bases are compared with the wheels of chariots, except that the one and the same evangelical word makes some of those whom it instructs into the chariots of God and others into the bases of God’s temple?

All those teachers who were sent throughout the world, far and wide, to evangelize the word were certainly chariots of God, and very swift ones, because, running through all places, they brought God into the hearts of believers.

But those who remained in one place and announced the word of salvation to their neighbors, kindling them toward the bath of life, which is celebrated either in baptism or in contrition accompanied by tears, are like the bases of the temple that carry the basins for washing the victims. They provide the ministry of salvation to the faithful placed under their care, but do not undertake the labors of traveling farther afield to acquire new peoples.

The wheels of the bases are therefore like the wheels of chariots because the same books of the Gospels that send some teachers to preach the faith to those who do not know it command others to remain in order to strengthen the faith more fully among those already instructed and imbued with the heavenly sacraments. [Col. 1147D]

The four wheels supported the base of the basin when the Gospels commanded James, the brother of the Lord, to remain in order to preserve the Church in Jerusalem.

Their wheels, made ready for running like those beneath the chariot of God, supported them when the same Gospels wished Paul and Barnabas to travel everywhere preaching to the Gentiles.

The wheels placed beneath the bases lifted the basin of the temple from the ground when, in our own recent times, the blessed Pope Gregory, strengthened by evangelical utterances, governed the Roman Church.

The same wheels, supporting the chariots of God, carried them far away when the most reverend fathers Augustine, Paulinus, and their other companions, likewise strengthened by evangelical utterances, came to Britain at Gregory’s command and entrusted the word of God to peoples who had long been unbelieving.

If, then, the bases of the basins are holy teachers who minister to us the bath of life, and if the four wheels of the bases are the four books of the Gospels, what are the axles [Col. 1148A] of the wheels that carry the bases except the hearts of those same teachers? While their hearts are diligently intent upon the commands of the Gospel, they lift the teachers away from the pursuit of lowly things, just as axles fitted with wheels raise the base higher from the ground.

The shoulder-pieces placed before the wheels, preventing them from slipping away from the axles, are the proclamations of the prophets. Through these the evangelical and apostolic Scripture is confirmed, so that it may not fall into doubt for any reader. The Apostle Peter, speaking of the Lord, says: “We have the prophetic word made more certain, and you do well to attend to it” (2 Pet. 1).

All the evangelists and apostles likewise were accustomed to mention the law and the prophets in what they wrote. Thus Mark begins: “The beginning of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, as it is written in Isaiah the prophet” (Mark 1). Matthew says: “All this took place so that the Scripture of the prophets might be fulfilled” (Matt. 1), and other passages of the same kind.

It is appropriately said that the shoulder-pieces were placed beneath the basin on its four sides and faced one another, because all prophetic [Col. 1148B] Scripture agrees with itself, having been composed by the one Spirit of God.

There were four shoulder-pieces for each base, corresponding to the number of wheels—not because there are only four prophetic books, but because in everything the prophets and Moses spoke, they supplied testimony to the words of the four evangelists.
