Thus, through the agreement of both, one faith and love of Christ may strengthen the hearts of us all.

“The opening of the basin was within, at the top of its head; and what appeared outside was wholly circular, one cubit, and it also had one and a half cubits.”

The opening of the basin was one cubit because of the unity of confession and faith: all of us are baptized in the confession of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, as the Apostle says: “One Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all” (Eph. 4).

The opening itself was at the top of the head so that it might teach that the way to the heavenly kingdoms has been opened to us through baptism. The basin itself had a breadth of one and a half cubits because of the [Col. 1148C] perfection of action and the beginning of contemplation.

The complete cubit in the basin signifies the perfection of good action, which that man undoubtedly possessed concerning whom the Lord said to the ancient tempter: “Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on earth, a blameless and upright man, fearing God and turning away from evil?” (Job 1).

The remaining half-cubit signifies divine vision, which is customarily granted in some measure even in this life to the faithful who still remain here. Thus Job, after overcoming his adversary, says while speaking with the Lord: “I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear” (Job 42).

So Moses saw the Lord face to face; Isaiah saw him seated upon the throne of his kingdom, with the citizens of heaven standing around him and offering due praise; the other prophets also often saw him; the glory of God was shown to the blessed Stephen when the gates of heaven were opened at the moment of his passion; and the mysteries of paradise and the third heaven were disclosed to Paul.

Yet all these things are only partial in comparison with the glory that is to be revealed in the future. Therefore, after the cubit of good action that can be perfected in the saints in this life [Col. 1148D], there begins the cubit of heavenly contemplation, which, in the future, will plainly be perfected in all the elect.

This measure of one and a half cubits was present not only in the basins but also in their wheels and bases. For it is written below: “One wheel had a height of one and a half cubits”; and shortly afterward: “At the top of the base there was a rounded section of one and a half cubits, so fashioned that the basin could be placed upon it.”

The basins measured one and a half cubits because we are washed in the font of life by that faith through which, by works of righteousness, we deserve to enter eternal life, although, while we live here, we cannot be without sin. We can taste and love the sweetness of heavenly life in part during the present life, but we cannot in any way see it perfectly until the future.

The wheels are measured at one and a half cubits because the Scripture of evangelical teaching shows how those who wish to be perfect ought to live [Col. 1149A] and, in the present, displays to us the hope of eternal reward. It promises that the nature of that reward will be revealed and bestowed upon us in the future.

The bases themselves also had a breadth of one and a half cubits at their top, where they received the basins, because those teachers and ministers of the supreme saving bath shone in this life as perfect in action, but enjoyed the light of contemplation only in part.

Hence they say: “We know in part and we prophesy in part; but when the perfect comes, the partial will pass away” (1 Cor. 13).

In this manner he made ten bases, of one pattern, with the same measurements and similar carving. “He also made ten bronze basins.”

Why ten bases were made, and an equal number of basins placed upon them, has already been explained. But the fact that all the bases and basins had one pattern, one measurement, and similar carving was not done to signify that all the merits of teachers can be equal. Rather, it signifies that there is one faith of the Gospel by which they are instructed, one [Col. 1149B] baptism by which they are washed, and one and the same Spirit by whom all the elect are consecrated—although they possess different gifts in that same Spirit, who distributes to each as he wills.

“One basin held forty baths.”

The number forty customarily bears the type of great perfection, because four times ten makes forty. There are ten commandments by which the activity of all of us is prescribed in the divine law. There are four books of the Gospels, in which, through the dispensation of the Lord’s incarnation, the entrance into the heavenly homeland has been opened to us.

Since all who belong to the ministry of sacred baptism must, together with faith and the sacraments of the Gospel, produce the fruit of right action, appropriately did each basin in which the burnt offerings were washed hold forty baths.

What follows—“It was four cubits,” whether in height or in breadth—signifies that the meaning of the mystery is readily apparent. A single basin was four [Col. 1149C] cubits either because of the four books of the Holy Gospel, in which the form of baptism has been prescribed for us; or because of the four cardinal virtues by which every believer ought to be formed; or, certainly, because of the four regions of the world in which the bath of salvation is administered, as the psalmist says: “Those whom he redeemed from the hand of the enemy, and gathered from the lands, from the rising and setting of the sun, from the north and from the south” (Ps. 107).

When he said above, “It also had one cubit and a half,” without indicating whether this referred to height or breadth, he seems to have been describing the breadth of the bottom of the basin. From this measurement, if I am not mistaken, anyone can easily infer the size of the base upon which the basin was placed. It is described in this way: “At the top of the base there was a rounded section of one and a half cubits, fashioned so that the basin could be placed upon it.”

The breadth of the bottom of the basins was therefore one and a half cubits; the capacity of the basins themselves was four cubits. But whether he means four cubits in height, in breadth, or in both—who can know?

[Col. 1149D] “And he placed ten bases, five on the right side of the temple and five on the left.”

By the right and left side of the temple he does not mean inside the temple itself, but in front of the temple, namely on the eastern side, in the inner court, which was properly called the court of the priests.

He placed five on the right side of the temple because of the Jews, who in ancient times were accustomed to use the southern side because of the teaching of the law; and five on the left because of us, who for a long time had clung in blind-hearted servitude to him who says, “I will set my throne in the north.”

This is plainly to say: “I desire to rest in the hearts of those whom I see to be alienated from the light of truth and from the flame of divine love.”

The Sea he placed on the right side of the temple, facing east toward the south. It too was placed in the same court, toward the east. As for “on the right side of the temple,” this is what he repeats when he says “toward the south”: for those entering the court from the east had first [Col. 1150A] to turn toward the south, where the Sea stood in the very corner, prepared for the priests’ washing. Then, as they proceeded farther inside, the basins set on both sides for washing the sacrificial victims met them. Between these was a bronze platform, five cubits long, five cubits wide, and three cubits high, on which Solomon stood when he dedicated the temple. Proceeding farther, one encountered the altar of burnt offering, opposite the southern side of the court; then the portico of the temple, or vestibule, in which the bronze columns stood around the entrance to the temple.

That he placed the Sea on the right side of the temple signifies that, through the washing of baptism, we must arrive at the heavenly kingdom, which is rightly represented by the term “right,” for “whoever believes and is baptized will be saved.” Whenever “right” and “left” are both understood positively, they signify either the Jews and the Gentiles, as we said above in the exposition of the bases; or the present life of the Church and the future life; or joy and sorrow; or something similar. But whenever “right” is used absolutely in a positive sense, it more often [Col. 1150B] indicates eternal joys. That he placed the Sea facing east refers properly to the same meaning: namely, that through the washing of the holy font the radiance of inward brightness is opened to us. That it was placed on the southern side of the court signifies that the faithful, through receiving the Holy Spirit, are accustomed to be kindled with the fervor of true charity. For in Scripture the heat of the noonday sun commonly signifies the ardor of love and the illumination of the Holy Spirit, through whom that same love is poured into the hearts of the elect.

## XXIII. That the temple vessels were made in the region of the Jordan. Chapter VII

All the vessels that Hiram made for King Solomon in the house of the Lord were of orichalcum; the king cast them in the clayey ground of the region of the Jordan.

Appropriately, the vessels of the house of the Lord were cast in the region of the Jordan, in that river in which our Lord was willing to be baptized; and, once he had been immersed in its waters, he turned the element of water into a washing away of sins for us. For every baptism of the faithful, by which they are consecrated to the Lord, is celebrated as an imitation [Col. 1150C] of that baptism by which he himself sanctified the waters. Rightly, then, the vessels of the house of the Lord were made in the region of the Jordan. For we cannot otherwise become vessels of election and mercy unless, looking to his baptism, which he underwent in that river, we too strive to be washed in the river of life.

It should be noted, however, that he says these same vessels were made not only in the region of the Jordan but also in its plain, signifying the multiplication of the faithful, who were destined to exist not only in Judea but throughout the breadth of all nations, in fulfillment of the prophecy: “The plains will rejoice, and everything in them” (Ps. XCV). Similar is what the same psalmist says when, speaking of the mysteries of the Lord’s incarnation in the person of those who came to faith after the secrets of his incarnation had been accomplished:

> “Behold, we heard of them in Ephrata;  
> we found them in the fields of the wood” (Ps. CXXXI).

We heard of them in Ephrata—that is, in Bethlehem—the mysteries of the Lord, because we read that it had been promised to the patriarch David, who came from that same city, that Christ would come in the flesh from the fruit of his womb. We found [Col. 1150D] them in the fields of the wood, because, once they had been revealed throughout the breadth of the nations across the world, we ourselves came to know them, we ourselves saw them, and we ourselves became participants in them.

Thus the king cast the vessels of the house of the Lord in the plain of the Jordan, because the Lord filled the whole breadth of the world in order to make vessels of mercy through the baptism of salvation. But what is the clayey earth from which the molds for casting the vessels of the Lord were made better understood to be than holy Scripture, from which we receive the rule of right living? Like clay hardened by fire, it displays the form of the vessels of the Lord—how great and of what kind they ought to be—when it shows us the rule of righteousness that we are to follow. It also sets before us the examples of the saints who endured invincibly in the fire of tribulations, examples to be followed in all things if we desire to be chosen as precious vessels of the house of the Lord.

Bronze, melted by fire, enters the clay molds so that the vessel may be made suitable for heavenly ministries. Likewise, when we have been salutarily humbled and softened by the flame either of divine love or of human adversity, [Col. 1151A] we enter the way of the fathers by doing good, so that by running well we may reach the rewards of the fathers. For we do not always need to be shaped by rules of good action; once good action has been completed, the palm of blessed recompense is to be hoped for. The vessels, too, were not always held enclosed in the clay molds; once they had reached their perfection, they were brought into the light when the restraints of the molds were broken, and each was placed in its proper location in the temple of the Lord.

We say this not because the works of the saints will ever perish, but because, once they have received the crown of righteousness that they earned by doing good, all the duties of laborious action will cease. For who in that life will suffer martyrdom for the faith of Christ, when, after their adversaries have been driven out, all the elect rejoice in the presence of Christ? Who will bury the dead there, where the earth belongs only to the living? Who will console the grieving, where God will wipe every tear from the eyes of the saints? Who will prepare a house for the stranger and the guest, where all [Col. 1151B] the elect together have from God a dwelling, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens? Who will bring bread to the hungry or drink to the thirsty, where “the Lord is my shepherd, and I shall lack nothing”?

Once the molds formerly necessary for the vessels have therefore been broken apart, the vessels themselves now shine splendidly in the house of the Lord. For at the end of the world, when not only the persecutions that the elect endure for righteousness but also the laborious works of righteousness by which they willingly toil for eternal blessedness have ceased, they will rejoice in the sole vision of their Creator, having received the splendor of immortality.

## XXIV. Concerning the altar. Chapter VII

Solomon also made all the vessels in the house of the Lord, and the golden altar.

The golden altar signifies the hearts of the perfect righteous, gleaming with the light of inward love and chastity. The location of that altar is also appropriate for signifying their exalted state: it stood before the entrance to the holy of holies, as we read clearly in the account of the tabernacle. On that altar no blood of victims, nor libations, [Col. 1151C] were burned, but only incense, whose smoke, rising upward, covered the ark and the sanctuary and filled it with a fragrance of sweetness.

In this it expressed a figure of the saints. While they disregard desires for temporal things and seek heavenly things with their whole attention, they are placed, as it were, within, near the sanctuary. They are not far removed from the veil that separates the temple from the holy of holies, because in body alone do they inhabit the earth; in all other respects, according to the inward person, their entire way of life is in heaven.

The smoke of incense rises from such an altar into the holy of holies where the ark is hidden, when the prayers of the saints, stirred by the flame of love, reach as far as heaven, where Christ sits at the right hand of God. For on this altar the blood of victims is not burned, but only incense, because such men do not have works of flesh and blood to sacrifice upon the altar of their hearts. Rather, they offer to him only the vows of tears and prayer, out of desire for the heavenly kingdom.

Yet because no one [Col. 1151D] suddenly becomes supreme, but ascends carefully toward heavenly desire through the offering of carnal pleasures, Scripture did not omit, in the mystical construction of the house of the Lord, to place there also a figure of those who still labor to kindle within themselves the carnal desires that wage war against the soul with the flame of heavenly fear. Once these have been uprooted from heart or body, they may consequently ascend to greater things and offer to God the spiritual incense of prayers and compunction.

Another altar was made for offering sacrifices. It was much larger, but insofar as it surpassed the other in size, it was inferior in the position of its location and in the appearance of its metal. It was made of bronze and placed before the doors of the temple. In it, figuratively, are represented those who serve the Lord with such devotion that their flesh still desires against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh. They are accustomed to say: “In mind we serve the law of God, but in flesh the law of sin.” [Col. 1152A] When they strive to rise worthily to the tranquility of chastity before God by subduing the incitements of the flesh, restraining the excesses of lust through frequent fasts and prayers, vigils and almsgiving, and the other fruits of the Spirit, what do they sacrifice to him but the victim of their devotion, fulfilling the Apostle’s appeal, by which he implores us through the mercy of God to present our bodies as a living, holy, acceptable sacrifice to God (Rom. XII)?

Because such men burn with the fervor of spiritual love but do not yet stand out in the triumph of conquered carnal desire, the altar of burnt offering indeed has the holy fire from heaven, but displays the appearance of bronze rather than gold. Since, however, there are more carnal people in the holy Church than spiritual people—more who restrain and curb the enticements of vices than those who, having overcome and quieted the struggle with vices, rejoice in the security acquired through the virtues—it was rightly asserted that the altar of burnt offering was much larger than the altar of incense.

It is written of it in the book of Chronicles:

> “He also made a bronze altar twenty cubits long, and twenty [Col. 1152B] cubits wide, and ten cubits high.”

Moses made the altar of incense in the wilderness, having a cubit in length and width and two cubits in height. Scripture does not say how large Solomon made this altar, but only says that he made a golden altar. It is clear, however, that he could not have made it as large as the altar of burnt offering. For if it had been made twenty cubits long and wide, it would have filled the entire width of the temple.

Thus, to the extent that the altar of burnt offering was placed farther outside than the altar of incense, and to the extent that it was more inferior in the kind of offering and in the baseness of its metal, it surpassed the other in the size of its measurements and in the frequency of its sacrifices. For there are far more to whom it is said, “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments” (Matt. XIX), than there are who delight to hear, “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell what you possess” (ibid.), and what follows.

Nor is the measurement of this altar without a mystical significance based on number. It was twenty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and ten [Col. 1152C] cubits high. We spoke above, in the exposition of the temple and its vestibule, about this number; but it should also be discussed briefly now.

If the altar of burnt offering represents in the Church those who seek to consecrate their body and soul to God through the fire of his love, their perseverance in good action is signified by the altar’s length; their breadth in the love of God and neighbor by its width; and their hope in awaiting the divine vision by its height.

The fact that the altar’s length and width were each twenty cubits clearly signifies the great perfection of that indefatigable patience and sincere love which is granted to us through observance of both Testaments. Four times five makes the number twenty: five books of the Mosaic law and four of evangelical freedom. When, enlightened by the grace of the Gospel, we arrive at the understanding and observance of the spiritual law, we complete the number twenty.

The same number twenty is formed in the length and width of the altar when [Col. 1152D] the hearts of the elect, taught by both Testaments and aided by the one author of both Testaments, preserve perseverance in good action even amid persecutions and display the cheerfulness of love toward those who persecute them.

The number ten commonly signifies hope of heavenly rewards, as the Lord affirms when he declares that those who labored in the vineyard of the great householder would be rewarded with a denarius. And rightly is eternal reward represented by this number, in which our nature is joined forever to the divine vision, because in this number the divine and human natures are mystically signified together.

God is Trinity, while man is comprehended by the number seven: by four because of the body, which consists of four elements, and by three because of the threefold distinction of the inward person that holy Scripture shows us when it commands us to love the Lord with all our heart, all our soul, and all our strength.

Hence, in the Ten Commandments [Col. 1153A] of the law, three commandments arouse us to the worship of divine love, while seven commend love of neighbor. Those who keep the Ten Commandments of the law in the love of God and neighbor rightly receive the reward of this observance in the vision of both God and neighbor. Those who in this life love both the neighbor whom they see and God whom they do not see will in the future life see both God the King in his beauty and their neighbor glorified and adorned in God.

Therefore the altar made as a figure of the elect was ten cubits high, to signify their perpetual life.

When it had been said that Solomon made a golden altar, it was immediately added:

> “And a golden table on which they would place the bread of the Presence.”

The table is holy Scripture, rich in the brightness of spiritual understanding. Concerning it the psalmist says to the Lord: “You have prepared a table before me, against those who afflict me” (Ps. XXII). So that adversaries who afflict us might not bend us into error, our Creator has prepared for us a table of knowledge, through which we confess [Col. 1153B] him in the faith of truth.

The bread of the Presence is the holy teachers, whose works or salutary words, set before us as an example of life, anyone who seeks will always find in the divine writings. Hence, appropriately, these same loaves were commanded to be made twelve in Exodus (Chapter XXV), on account of the twelve apostles, through whose ministry the writing of the New Testament was composed and the mysteries of the Old Testament were revealed by the Lord’s gift.

By this number not only the apostles themselves were signified, but also all who, by preaching the word, minister the nourishment of life to the faithful, since they all follow the same form of teaching that the apostles received from the Lord.

We read of these loaves in Exodus (ibid.) that they were to be changed each Sabbath, with new ones placed on the Lord’s table in place of the old, and that they were always to be prepared from fine flour in a single measure. From all these details the mystical meaning concerning inward nourishment shines forth more brightly than light.

The old loaves are removed and new ones are [Col. 1153C] restored when, after some faithful teachers have been taken from this life, holy Church appoints others in their place. This occurs only on the Sabbath, because whoever has fought the good fight, completed the course, and kept the faith enters the rest of blessed perpetuity at the time of his departure.

The loaves were always made from fine flour in one measure and were not unequal, because there is one and the same form of truth and faith which the apostles first displayed to their hearers, and which their successors and all pious teachers in the Churches of Christ throughout the world continue to preach without ceasing until the end of the age.

## XXV. Concerning the ten tables. Chapter VII

As for what we read in the Chronicles, that Solomon made ten tables and placed them in the temple, five on the right and five on the left, as well as one hundred golden bowls (II Chron. IV), it is credible that these tables were made both for the bread of the Presence and for carrying the vessels of the Lord. The bowls, namely, are reported by Scripture [Col. 1153D] to have been made at the same time, along with the incense vessels, censers, mortars, and so forth, which are read of below.

For when the same book of Chronicles shortly afterward adds, “Solomon made all the vessels of the house of the Lord, and the golden altar, and the tables, and upon them the bread of the Presence,” he either used the plural number instead of the singular, in the very common manner of Scripture—as in Joshua: “But the children of Israel transgressed the commandments concerning the devoted thing” (Josh. VII), when Achan alone, and not several children of Israel, had done this—or, certainly, because the bread of the Presence used to be baked before the Sabbath so that it could immediately be placed upon the table of the Presence on the Sabbath, it could have happened that freshly baked loaves were immediately placed on those tables and kept covered there during that night, until early morning, when the old loaves were removed and the warm ones placed upon the table of the Presence.

These ten tables do not differ in their figurative meaning from the table of the Presence. Just as one table laden with twelve loaves signifies the unity of the whole of Scripture, and its harmony united [Col. 1154A] by apostolic authority, so the ten golden tables not inappropriately figuratively proclaim the words of the divine law and the prophets. These either offer us the refreshment of the word of God, like the bread of the Presence, or set before us the examples of the faithful, like vessels of the Lord placed upon them, together with their splendor and miracles.

The tables are rightly twice five, not only because the lawgiver wrote five books, but also because the entire sequence of the Old Testament embraces five ages of the world. The number five is doubled, and five are placed on the right and five on the left, when, after the Lord’s incarnation, the same Scripture is entrusted either to both peoples of God—the Jew and the Gentile—or is shown to be filled with evangelical figures, whereas formerly it was thought that the ancient people of God were to understand it according to the letter alone.

When, for example, in holy Scripture we read of Abel crowned with martyrdom; Enoch taken from the world; Noah marvelously saved while the world perished; Lot’s hospitality sublimely remunerated after [Col. 1154B] the wicked had been destroyed; Abraham, on account of his obedience, established as the father of all nations; and Joseph, after his sale, exalted as an example of chastity and innocence (Genesis, passim)—when we take up these and countless other examples of virtue, what do they do but open for us, as five golden tables, or vessels of the Lord, or loaves of the Presence still on the left side of the temple, the divine writings according to their historical meaning, together with the door to right living and the eternal rewards to be hoped for from the Lord?

But when, understanding the same Scripture more deeply, we perceive it to proclaim either the dispensation of the Lord’s incarnation or any other mysteries of the holy Church, we find, as it were, another five tables on the right side of the temple for carrying vessels of election and providing spiritual nourishment. We recognize that the very words of sacred history open for us an entirely new splendor of heavenly wisdom and new meanings from old things.

In the same figure, five lampstands were also made in the temple. For when Scripture had said that King Solomon made a table on which the bread of the Presence was to be [Col. 1154C] placed, it added immediately:

## XXVI. Concerning the ten lampstands. Chapter VII

And five golden lampstands on the right and five on the left, opposite the sanctuary, of purest gold, with what were like lily flowers and golden lamps above.

Just as tables are rightly placed as a type of holy Scripture, because they both provide the hungry with the bread of the word as nourishment in righteousness and carry vessels of heavenly ministry—that is, they set before us the deeds of the righteous as examples—so the same divine words are most appropriately represented by lampstands, because they bring the light of wisdom to those who are wandering. Hence the psalmist says, “Your word is a lamp to my feet,” and so forth (Ps. CXVIII). Solomon likewise says: “For the commandment is a lamp, and the law is light” (Prov. VI).

He appropriately added “opposite the sanctuary” when he said that there were five on the right and five on the left. The sanctuary, where the ark was, as has often been said, clearly represents the heavenly homeland, where Christ sits at the right hand of God, [Col. 1154D] conscious, of course, of the Father’s mysteries. The golden lampstands of the temple are placed opposite the sanctuary when the divine words look toward the dwelling of the heavenly city, so that they may infuse our hearts with knowledge and desire for it and kindle those who have their bodily origin from the earth to seek and merit an everlasting dwelling in heaven.

Some think that the statement concerning the lampstands—five on the right and five on the left—is to be understood as meaning that five stood on the right of the lampstand that Moses made in the desert and five on its left, although both groups were toward the southern side, where the one lampstand that Moses made was commanded to stand. They understand the same arrangement concerning the ten tables: all were placed toward the northern side, but five on the right of that Mosaic table and five on the left.

Yet if one considers the words of holy Scripture, which say, “And five golden lampstands on the right and five on the left, opposite the sanctuary,” [Col. 1155A] it is clear, I think, that both groups of five faced the sanctuary equally, being placed lengthwise along each side of the temple. For if all the lampstands had been placed lengthwise along the southern side of the temple, they would not be said to have been placed opposite the sanctuary, but rather opposite the north, or opposite the tables, if the tables also stood there.

This is what is said in Exodus concerning the one lampstand which without any doubt stood toward the south: “He also placed the lampstand in the tabernacle of the testimony, opposite the table, on the southern side” (Exod. XL). Likewise, in the book of Numbers: “When he has placed the seven lamps opposite the side toward which the lampstand gives light” (Num. VIII).

Thus there were lampstands on both sides of the temple, and tables on both sides, because divine Scripture was composed for the illumination and refreshment of both peoples of God. It is accustomed to refresh us in prosperity and adversity, in sorrowful and joyful circumstances, so that we may not faint and may not remain blind.

The vessels of mercy are also placed above them—that is, Scripture sets before both of us in itself the works of the righteous, through which we too may be strengthened in the practice [Col. 1155B] of righteousness.

If you ask what typological difference there is between the lampstands and their lamps, we can rightly understand the lamps to be holy men, who, filled with the oil of the Holy Spirit, themselves burn with the fire of love in their hearts and bring forth the light of knowledge through their tongues. The lampstands that raise these lamps aloft, so that they may be seen far and wide in the Church, are holy Scripture, which by its reading displays to us the virtues and examples of the saints.

The Lord’s saying about John supports this interpretation: “He was a burning and shining lamp” (John V).

We may also most appropriately say that the lamps are the divine words, in accordance with the psalmist’s statement quoted above: “Your word is a lamp to my feet” (Ps. CXVIII). The lampstands of these lamps, however, are all the saints, who humbly submit their hearts and bodies to bearing the Lord’s commandments.

For whoever takes care in no matter what to follow his own will, but attends to all that holy [Col. 1155C] Scripture says and strives to subject himself to its commandments, carries its golden lamps like a golden lampstand of the house of God. He strives to submit the chaste members of his body and the chaste thoughts of his mind to doing what God commands, with as firm an intention as a lampstand must be firmly erected toward heaven in order to preserve the lamps placed upon it not only without falling but also without any alteration in its position.

When he had said, “And five golden lampstands on the right and five on the left, opposite the sanctuary, of purest gold,” he added, “And what were like lily flowers, and golden lamps above.” Literally, it appears that the uppermost part of the lampstands was formed in the shape of an open lily. We read that this was done in the lampstand of the tabernacle, whose central stem and branches proceeding from it are said to have had many lilies along with cups and spheres.

The flowers of the lily, as has often been said, always signify the beauty of the ever-green land of the living, of which blessed Peter says: “He has regenerated us into a living hope, [Col. 1155D], into an incorruptible, undefiled, and unfading inheritance, kept in heaven” (I Pet. I).

The golden lily flowers were appropriately made in the lampstand of the house of God, because divine Scripture, spurning temporal joys, customarily urges us to seek the good things of the heavenly homeland. And just as the lampstand, erected on high, has golden lily flowers and golden lamps at its head, so all the elect contained in that same sacred Scripture are shown, with their minds raised toward heavenly things, to have sought and received heavenly goods from the Lord.

He also made golden tongs, as well as pitchers, forks, bowls, mortars, and censers of purest gold.

The various vessels made for offering libations are the various distinctions of divine speech suited to the differing capacities of those who hear. For one and the same teaching cannot suit everyone. Accordingly, we should understand the different vessels of the altar either as different persons among the faithful or, certainly, as the many kinds of their actions or thoughts [Col. 1156A] arranged for the service of their Creator.

The tongs, as may be believed, were made for tending the fire of the altar. Hence they rightly signify holy preachers, who customarily kindle in us the fire of love, as though on the altar of God, through their exhortations. Like the two teeth of a pair of tongs, they arrange the logs on the altar to kindle this fire when they instruct us with harmonious pages from both Testaments and place the words of truth in our hearts, so that we may be more greatly inflamed with desire for eternal things.

The forks—which in Greek are called κρεάγραι, that is, “meat-hooks”—were kept for the service of the altar so that the flesh of the victim, cooked in cauldrons, might be brought out on them and carried for the consumption of those who were to be refreshed by it.

Their use also figuratively suits holy preachers, whose ministry is to refresh the souls of the faithful with the word of faith and, according to the rule of apostolic discernment, to provide still inexperienced disciples with the rational and guileless milk of simple teaching, while supplying the more perfect with solid food of higher [Col. 1156B] teaching.

For all who know how to receive the mysteries of Christ in imitation of him are satisfied as though refreshed by the flesh of a saving victim. It belongs to spiritual teachers most diligently to discern which mysteries should be entrusted to each person to hear. Solomon rightly introduced forks for the priests in the house of the Lord, with which they could arrange the flesh of the victims as appropriate, offering some portions for human consumption, clean ones, but leaving others to be consumed by the fires of the altar.

For there are certain things in the words of God that he has deigned to reveal to our humility and grant as food for our refreshment. There are also others of such depth that they are disclosed only to the knowledge of the Holy Spirit and entirely exceed the measure of our capacity.

For what is meant by the bowls except the measure of preaching, by which the grace of exhortation ought to be imparted to each person according to the capacity of his understanding? The teacher must carefully discern that he not strive to preach [Col. 1156C] more than the hearer can grasp. He must contract himself and condescend to the weakness of his hearers, lest, while speaking lofty things to the lowly and therefore things that will not benefit them, he care more to display himself than to benefit his hearers.

We have spoken more fully about the table and the lampstand, and about both altars and the vessels of the house of the Lord, in the books that we wrote concerning the construction of the tabernacle and the priestly vesture. Therefore, if anyone desires to know about these matters according to the capacity of our understanding, derived from the tradition of the Fathers, let him seek it in that work.

The text continues:

## XXVII. Concerning the hinges. Chapter VII

And the hinges of the doors of the inner house of the holy of holies, and of the doors of the house of the temple, were of gold.

If the doors of the inner house of the holy of holies are the angelic ministries that open the entrance to heavenly life for us when we depart from the body, and if the doors of the house of the temple are the holy teachers and priests who, by instructing, baptizing, and communicating the mysteries of the Lord’s body and blood, open for us the first thresholds of the present Church, then what are the hinges of both sets of doors except the minds and [Col. 1156D] hearts of those same angels or saints? By these they cling immovably to the embrace and love of their Creator, so that they may rightly fulfill the ministry divinely assigned to them.

When they minister according to his will, they never turn their eyes away. The doors are opened and closed at the appropriate time, but they never leave the temple’s hinge, because angels and holy men, whether they receive the faithful and elect into this life of faith or into that life of vision, always keep their minds fixed in the root of love.

Hence the same hinges are rightly said to have been made of gold, on account of the merit either of their own radiance or of the love that they possess for God.

And Solomon completed all the work that he was doing in the house of the Lord.

This occurs when our peaceful King, on the last day, glorifies all the elect with the immortality of the resurrection. Otherwise, so long as the present condition of the world continues, Solomon does indeed carry out the work of the house of the Lord, but he does not yet [Col. 1157A] complete it. For the Lord inspires and assists the hearts of the elect so that they may do good, but he does not grant anyone who remains in this life to be without sin. That gift he reserves for the blessedness of the future life.

He completes every work of his temple and makes it fit for dedication when he brings his elect, transferred from this life, into the eternal kingdom. This is well signified by the fact that the temple was built in seven years but completed and dedicated in the eighth. For the whole of this work unfolds through seven days; the eighth is the day of judgment and the future resurrection, concerning which Psalms VI and XI were given their titles.

What follows is appropriately suited to that time:

And he brought in the things that David his father had consecrated—silver, gold, and vessels—and placed them in the treasuries of the house of the Lord.

Silver pertains to the brilliance of eloquence, gold to the splendor of wisdom, and vessels in general to rational creatures. David, the father of Solomon, sanctifies silver when God the Father strengthens those who are eloquent with the grace of the Holy Spirit to speak [Col. 1157B] the word of the Gospel. He sanctifies gold when, filling those endowed with natural intelligence with his Spirit, he enlightens them to consider his wondrous works in the law. He sanctifies the vessels when, in general, he grants all the children of the Church the grace of the same Spirit and kindles them to desire the gifts of perpetual salvation.

Solomon brings this silver, this gold, and these sanctified vessels into the temple when our Lord, after the universal judgment has been completed, introduces all the elect—the assembly both of teachers and of the rest of the faithful—into the joy of the heavenly kingdom.

He places vessels of various kinds, whether silver or gold, in the treasuries of the house of the Lord when he hides those who have merited to enjoy the abundance of his sweetness in the secret place of his face, away from the disturbance of human beings.

There are appropriately many treasuries in which the vessels of election are stored, but one house of the Lord in which those treasuries have been made, because there is one Church in which all the elect are contained, however much they differ in merits. There is also one [Col. 1157C] and not a different heavenly homeland, which is promised to all, although “as star differs from star in glory, so also is the resurrection of the dead.”

The Judge and distributor of rewards himself demonstrated both truths in a single statement when he said: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places” (John XIV).

Solomon therefore made one house of the Lord, but prepared many treasuries within it to receive vessels of different kinds, all sanctified by one blessing. For there is indeed one house of the Father, not made with hands, eternal in the heavens, but in it there are many dwelling places for receiving all who fear him and love him.

The Lord will bless the little ones together with the great.

## XXVIII. On the Ark Brought into the Inner Sanctuary. Chapter VIII

And all the elders of Israel came to King Solomon in Jerusalem, to bring up the ark of the covenant of the Lord from the City of David—that is, from Zion. The priests carried the ark of the covenant of the Lord and brought it into its place, into the inner sanctuary of the temple, into the Holy of Holies, beneath the wings of the cherubim. For the cherubim spread their wings over the place of the ark and covered the ark and its poles from above [Col. 1157D]. And when the poles projected, and their ends appeared outside the sanctuary before the inner sanctuary, they did not appear farther outward. And they have remained there to the present day (2 Chronicles V).

This is written more explicitly in the book of Chronicles:

> The ends of the poles with which they carried the ark, because they were somewhat longer, appeared before the inner sanctuary; but if anyone had been a little farther outside, he could not see them.

Here it should be noted that, although the ends of the poles appeared before the inner sanctuary to those who looked ahead and observed more attentively, it could not actually be that the ends of the poles themselves projected before the inner sanctuary. For, once the inner sanctuary had been closed and a veil hung before its doors, the poles also, together with the ark and the cherubim, necessarily had to be concealed inside. This could not happen if the poles projected too far and left no room for the doors to be extended and closed. Scripture took such care to explain the placement of the poles not without reason, but with regard to a great mystery [Col. 1158A]. For it is clear that the outer house of the temple signifies the Church journeying on earth, while the Holy of Holies signifies the inward blessedness of the heavenly homeland.

Likewise, the ark brought into the Holy of Holies typologically announces the humanity assumed by Christ and led within the veil into the heavenly royal palace. The poles by which that ark was carried signify the preachers of the word, through whom he himself was made known to the world. Their ends appeared outside, before the inner sanctuary—not always, but whenever it happened that the doors of that inner sanctuary were opened; nor did they appear to everyone, but only to those who approached more closely and strove to observe more attentively the things within.

The ark itself—what it was like and how it had been placed—could be seen only by those who had entered the inner sanctuary. For no saint placed in this life, however greatly he may raise himself in the height of contemplation, sees the glory of his Redeemer there plainly; only the citizens of that homeland behold it. The poles, moreover, were hidden with the ark in the inner sanctuary, because all the perfect elect who have gone before us from the world are even now hidden in the secret place of the face of God, away from the disturbance of human beings [Col. 1158B].

Yet the ends of those poles are sometimes seen by those who draw near when the inner sanctuary is opened, whenever divine grace grants the more perfect, and those who cleanse the eye of their heart with complete devotion, the opportunity to contemplate something at the extremity of the joy of the heavenly citizens. This contemplation, however, is not granted to those who have withdrawn somewhat farther away, because the more they remain outside with wandering minds, the less they see what the inward joys are.

Then follows:

## XXIX. On the Stone Tablets Enclosed in the Ark. Chapter VIII

Now there was nothing in the ark except the two stone tablets which Moses had placed in it at Horeb, when the Lord made a covenant with the children of Israel as they came out of the land of Egypt.

It may be asked how he can say here that there was nothing in the ark except the two tablets of the testimony, when the Apostle Paul, the teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth, writes to the Hebrews—that is, to the children of Israel—as follows:

> For the first tabernacle was made, in which there was a golden urn containing manna, and Aaron’s rod that had blossomed, and the tablets of the covenant (Hebrews IX).

Behold, on the testimony of the Apostle, we have learned that these things too were there. For he would not have dared to write anything else to them except what they held with certainty: that all these things had been in the very ark. Yet it does not appear more fully when they were brought into it, except that it is written in the book of Numbers:

> Moses brought out all the rods from before the Lord to all the children of Israel; and they saw them, and each one received his rod. And the Lord said to Moses, “Bring Aaron’s rod back into the tabernacle of the testimony, to be kept there as a sign for the rebellious children of Israel, so that their complaints may cease from me, lest they die” (Numbers XVII).

Finally, concerning the manna, it is written in Exodus:

> And Moses said to Aaron, “Take one vessel and put there as much manna as a gomor can hold, and place it before the Lord, to be kept for your generations, as the Lord commanded Moses.” And Aaron placed it in the tabernacle, to be preserved (Exodus XVI).

There was therefore in the ark a golden urn containing manna, because in the man Christ all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily (Colossians II) [Col. 1158D]. There was Aaron’s rod, which, after being cut off, blossomed again, because all power of judgment belongs to him whose judgment appeared to have been removed in the humility of his passion. There were also the tablets of the covenant, because in him all the treasures of wisdom are hidden.

The poles by which it was carried were attached to it, because the teachers who once labored in the word of Christ now rejoice in Christ’s glory through his present vision. What one of them said—“I desire to depart and be with Christ”—he left us to understand of all his fellow workers.

## XXX. On the Cloud in the Temple. Chapter VIII

Now when the priests had come out of the sanctuary, a cloud filled the house of the Lord, and the priests could not stand because of the cloud. For the glory of the Lord had filled the house of the Lord.

The glory of the Lord is understood as Christ, whose faith has filled the whole world. Concerning this glory, when Moses was praying to the Lord on behalf of the sinful people, asking him to spare them after the worship of the calf, the Lord answered:

> I will be merciful to them; nevertheless, as I live, and as my name lives, the whole earth shall be filled with my glory.

And the seventy-first Psalm sings:

> The whole earth shall be filled with his glory.

Therefore the angels also cried out to the shepherds:

> Glory to God in the highest, and peace on earth to people of good will (Luke III).

But the fact that the cloud filled the house of God, and that the priests could not minister because of the cloud, signifies the proud chief priests and teachers of the Jews. While they disdain to investigate the mysteries of Christ’s birth, they lost the ministry required by their faith through the cloud of error. For the darkness of unbelief filled their minds so completely that, as their own merits demanded, they did not recognize the worship of belief.

## XXXI. On Solomon’s Fleet. Chapter IX

After the whole work of the Lord had been completed, after Solomon’s lengthy prayer and the divine oracles addressed to him, Scripture reports among other things that King Solomon made a fleet of ships at Ezion-geber [Col. 1159B].

Ezion-geber is a harbor of the Red Sea, and it was the thirty-first encampment of the children of Israel when they departed from Egypt. At that same place, at a later time, Jehoshaphat’s fleet was battered by the violence of a storm, as Scripture testifies.

*Classes* are ships of the sea; *classis* is also the name given to a multitude of ships. Scripture subsequently reports again that the servants of Hiram went with Solomon’s servants in those same ships to Ophir, and that they brought from there four hundred and twenty talents of gold to King Solomon in Jerusalem.

Ophir, from which, as we have already said, gold was brought to Solomon, was one of the descendants of Eber, named Ophir. Josephus reports that people descended from his line lived from the river Cophene as far as the region of India called Hieria; from him that region itself received its name. Hence the Seventy translators, deriving the name, translated it not as *Ophir* but as *Ophiram*.

## XXXII. On the Queen of Sheba. Chapter X

The queen of Sheba also, having heard of Solomon’s fame, came in the name of the Lord to test him with riddles. Just as this queen came from the ends of the earth—that is, from India, as some say—to hear Solomon’s wisdom, so the Church came many ages later to her Redeemer and teacher, in order that, after the folly of error, she might receive the teaching of truth.

She is that queen of whom it is said to the Lord:

> The queen stood at your right hand in a garment of gold, surrounded by variety (Psalm XLIV);

that is, surrounded by the precious beauty of diverse virtues. For she is the mother of all believers: she gives birth again to those born for death, bringing them to salvation. Through her Christ restored more in grace than was lost in nature; from the race of Adam the transgressor he took offspring into adoption as sons of divine paternity, and he made those who had been disinherited from paradise citizens of heaven.

She was called after the Synagogue, but promised before the Synagogue. For she was already prefigured in the first human being: just as Eve was fashioned from Adam’s side, so the Church, redeemed from Christ’s body and wound, grew forth.

When the queen of Sheba entered Jerusalem with a great retinue [Col. 1159D] and riches, with camels carrying spices, an exceedingly vast quantity of gold, and precious gems, she came to Solomon and spoke to him about everything that was in her heart.

Thus, in the figure of this queen, the Church comes from the Gentiles, from the ends of the earth, putting an end to earthly desires and vices, to hear the wisdom of Solomon—that is, of our Lord Jesus Christ, the man of peace, who made both one, abolishing enmity between God and humanity in his flesh. After the ancient and profane superstitions, she comes to hear and learn about the illumination of faith and the future judgment, the immortality of the soul, the hope of resurrection, and glory.

She therefore comes to Jerusalem with a great retinue—that is, no longer with only one Jewish people, as the Synagogue formerly possessed Hebrews alone, but with the Gentiles and diverse nations of the whole world.

She comes, then, bringing gifts worthy of Christ: gold and precious gems, and this with camels carrying spices. These camels signify people coming from the Gentile population, people who had previously been distorted by the foulness of vices, bent beneath the burden of evils, and deformed by the crookedness of sins.

With these as though they were gifts, this queen enters before Christ, the peaceful king. She brings with her the gold of faith, the purity of understanding, the precious gems of radiance—that is, the notable ornaments of virtuous conduct. And she spoke to him of what was in her heart: she opened her heart to him and disclosed her hidden conscience in confession and repentance for her former offenses.

Let us see what this queen does.

When the queen of Sheba saw all Solomon’s wisdom, and the house that he had built, and the food of his table, and the holocausts that he offered in the house of the Lord, she was no longer able to contain her spirit.

What reason was there for so powerful a queen to marvel so greatly at the house, the expenses, and the royal foods? We must therefore seek greater things in this passage.

The Church gathered from the Gentiles saw the wisdom of Christ. After the carnal institutions of the Gentiles, after the human and animal-like teaching of the philosophers [Col. 1160B], she received the understanding of salvation and life. She looked upon the wonders of spiritual goods; she recognized the man who fashioned heaven and earth and the most powerful Creator of the human race.

Of his wisdom it is said:

> You have established all things by measure, number, and weight (Wisdom XI).

She also saw the house that he had built—that is, the incarnation of the human being, in whom all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily.

She saw Solomon’s foods, namely those of which he said:

> My food is to do the will of my Father (John IV).

The food of Christ is our salvation; he is refreshed by heavenly banquets, by our progress. We are his food when, acquired by the Church, we pass into his members and body. Or his food is the heavenly sacrament of the altar, concerning which it is said:

> He gave them the bread of heaven; human beings ate the bread of angels (John VI).

She also saw his holocausts—without doubt, the mysteries of prayers and supplications—and she was astonished. There she saw the immeasurable riches of her Lord.

And she said to the king:

> The word is true that I heard in my land concerning your words and your wisdom. I did not believe those who told me until I came myself and saw with my own eyes, and proved that they had not told me even half. Your wisdom and works are greater than the report that I heard.

When either the Church or any holy soul reaches the eternal Jerusalem—that is, the Vision of Peace—and enters the blessed rest and glory of the heavenly promises, it will perceive things far greater and more magnificent than were announced to it in this life through the sacred writings, through the prophets and apostles.

For now it sees as though in a mirror and in a riddle; then it will see with its eyes, that is, face to face. When, I say, each faithful and holy soul in that age has been presented before the divine sight, full of the fruits of good works, presenting within itself an immense gift for its God, offering itself to him, and bringing gifts worthy of heaven and capable of possessing heaven—gems of mercy, pearls of justice, ornaments of diverse merits, that is, spices of compunction and sweet-smelling balsams of chastity—then, as I have said, it will bring exceedingly abundant gold.

It will restore in itself an undivided offering for the immeasurable price paid to the Redeemer, pleasing him with spiritual offerings of heart and body. Joined to the wonders of heaven, it will be able to take up the voice of prophetic rejoicing:

> I will enter your house with holocausts (Psalm LVI).

Then the blessed and illustrious soul, placed amid the astonishing riches of its Requiter, will be able to address God with the ineffable words of this queen, saying:

> The word is true that I heard in my land concerning your words; your works are greater than the report that I heard.

This means:

> O Lord, I presumed, indeed, to hope for great things amid my tribulations, but I have received a greater forgiveness, made manifest. The reward exceeds the understanding of my thought by the greatness of its sweetness.

And truly, what God prepares for those who love him cannot be comprehended by faith, reached by hope, or grasped by charity; it surpasses desires and prayers. It can be acquired, but it cannot be measured. A person will see his merits increase through the unlooked-for abundance of rewards; he will have the fruit of receiving, but will not have weariness from satisfaction.

## XXXIII. On Solomon’s Throne and the Abundance of Gold. Chapter X

King Solomon also made a great throne of ivory and overlaid it with exceedingly pure gold. It had six steps, and the top of the throne was rounded at the back.

There is no doubt that the ivory throne bore the figure of the power of eternal judgment, shining with the gold of divinity, which the human being belonging to the Lord received from the Father.

The six steps of this throne typologically signified every visible and invisible creature, which was made in six days and subjected by the Father to Christ the Lord.

The fact that the throne itself is described as rounded at its rear undoubtedly signifies that the present world, which revolves through the limits of time, is to be judged by the Lord at its end.

The twelve young lions, standing in pairs on the six steps, represented the authority of the holy apostles, to whom the Lord said:

> You will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel (Luke XXII).

After some further material, Scripture again reports that Solomon made the following:

> There was as much silver in Jerusalem as stones.

This is a figurative expression, not a literal one. It is like what we read in Genesis, where God said to Abraham:

> I will make your offspring like the dust of the earth (Genesis XIII).

That statement uses the figure that the Greeks call *hyperbolē*—hyperbole—which is figurative, not literal. No one who has learned Scripture doubts that it regularly uses this and the other figures of speech.

This figure, that is, this mode of expression, occurs when what is said is far less than what is signified by the statement. For who does not see that the number of stones in the city of Jerusalem was incomparably greater than the weight of silver?

## XXXIV. On Solomon’s Fall. Chapter XI

King Solomon loved many foreign women, including the daughter of Pharaoh, Moabite women, Ammonite women, Edomite women, Sidonian women, and Hittite women from the nations. Concerning them the Lord had said to the children of Israel:

> You shall not enter in to them, nor shall they enter in to you; for they will certainly turn your hearts away, so that you follow their gods.

Solomon was joined to these women in the most ardent love. He had seven hundred wives who were like queens and three hundred concubines, and the women turned his heart away.

Those to whom this world prospers must be warned. They are struck by none of the adversities of this world, yet Solomon is described as having fallen into idolatry after receiving wisdom. For it is recorded that before his fall he had suffered no adversity in this world. But the wisdom granted to him abandoned him entirely, because no discipline of even the smallest tribulation guarded him, until he abandoned God and realized that he had been abandoned by God.

As for the rest of his deeds, Scripture vehemently accuses and condemns him, and it makes absolutely no mention of his repentance or of God’s pardon toward him. Nor does it at all occur what good his later evil deeds might signify, even allegorically, or what good his grievous submersion might represent—unless perhaps someone should say that the foreign women whose love deceived him signified the elect Churches from the Gentiles.

This could perhaps be understood without absurdity if, because of Solomon, those women had abandoned their gods and worshiped his God. But when he offended his God on their account and worshiped their gods, nothing good can be inferred from it. Nevertheless, it should not be thought that it could have signified nothing at all, but rather evil. For in the person of this Solomon there appears a remarkable excellence and a terrible overthrow.

Thus, what existed in him at different times—good first and evil afterward—is displayed in the Church in this present age simultaneously and at one time. I think that his goodness signifies the good people of the Church, while his evil signifies the evil people of the Church, as in the unity of a threshing floor: in that one man, the good are as grains and the evil as chaff; or, certainly, in the unity of one field, the good are as wheat and the evil as weeds.

It happened, then, at that time that Jeroboam went out from Jerusalem and met the prophet Ahijah the Shilonite on the road, covered with a new cloak. They were alone in the field. Ahijah seized the new cloak with which he was covered, tore it into twelve pieces, and said to Jeroboam:

> Take ten pieces for yourself. For thus says the Lord God of Israel: “Behold, I will tear the kingdom from Solomon’s hand and give you ten tribes. One tribe, however, shall remain to him on account of my servant David, and another tribe on account of Jerusalem, which I chose from all the tribes of Israel.”

The fact that after Solomon’s death ten tribes were separated from the temple and two remained sufficiently indicates what the Apostle said concerning that entire people:

> The remnant has been saved through election (Romans XI).

But the fact that the prophet’s single cloak was torn into twelve pieces, from which Jeroboam received ten, appears to have prefigured this: the harmony of the Church, torn apart by heretics, is divided by the very teachers of error; and they tyrannically hold under their control the deceived people whom they separate from Catholics by their error.

After many other matters, Scripture reports and says:

> The rest of Solomon’s words, and everything that he did, and his wisdom—behold, are all written in the Book of the Words of Solomon.

In the book of Chronicles, which we call by this Greek name and which we can call *Of Past Events* in Latin, it is written about Solomon as follows:

> The rest of Solomon’s first and last deeds are written in the words of Nathan the prophet, and in the books of Ahijah the Shilonite, and also in the vision of Iddo the seer concerning Jeroboam (2 Chronicles IX).

They assert that these books can now be found nowhere, not even among the Hebrews themselves. The same is true of the Book of the Wars of the Lord, which is mentioned in the Book of Numbers; the Book of the Just; Solomon’s songs; and his most wise discussions concerning the nature of trees and all plants, as well as animals, birds, reptiles, and fish.

The same is true of what we have already brought forth from the Book of Days, where it says:

> The rest of Solomon’s earlier and later works are written in the words of Nathan the prophet, and in the books of Ahijah the Shilonite, and also in the vision of Iddo the seer concerning Jeroboam the son of Nebat.

And there are many volumes of this kind, which Scripture indeed attests to, but which plainly do not exist today. For when Judea was devastated by the Chaldeans, the library gathered in ancient times was also consumed by hostile fire along with the other wealth of the province. From it, the few books that are now contained in Holy Scripture were later restored through the diligence of Ezra, the high priest and prophet.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 1161]

After the division of the kingdom of Israel between Rehoboam and Jeroboam, after Israel withdrew from the house of David, Scripture continues and says:

## I. On the Prophet Deceived by a False Prophet

Now when all Israel heard that Jeroboam had returned, they sent for him and summoned him. After assembling an assembly, they appointed him king over Israel.

There is therefore no doubt that human wills cannot resist the will of God, who does everything whatsoever he wills in heaven and on earth, and who has also made the things that are to come, so as to prevent him from doing what he wills. For even with regard to the wills of human beings themselves, he does what he wills and when he wills.

Unless perhaps—as these many considerations concerning Jeroboam are sufficient—when God wished to give him the kingdom on account of Solomon’s sin, it was within the power of the Israelites either to submit to that king or not to submit. This was plainly placed within their will, so that they might even have been able to resist God. Yet God did not wish to do this except through the wills of those people, undoubtedly possessing the power to bend human minds in whatever direction pleased him.

Thus, when God wishes to establish kings on earth, he has human wills more within his power than they have their own wills.

Scripture then reports that a prophet came from Judah to Bethel, to the sacrilegious king Jeroboam, and rebuked him for the sacrileges of the idols that he had made, by which he had turned the children of Israel away from the Lord, the God of their fathers. The prophet was commanded not to eat or drink there. Because he was deceived by a false prophet and disobeyed the word of the Lord, he was killed by a lion on the road (1 Kings XIII).

Indeed, whatever a person’s merit may be, if he is abandoned by the protection of his Creator—and this protection is thought less necessary if it is always possessed, but is often beneficially withdrawn so that a person may be shown to be nothing without it—then the hand of the Lord sometimes reveals us to ourselves through adversities, though it also carries us, unknowingly, through prosperity.

When deprived of that protection, we begin to fall; yet, while we are helped, we are restrained. Instruction is thus produced by the trembling we experience in falling, and guardianship by the fact that we remain standing.

Let no one therefore consider himself to possess any virtue, even when he is able to act bravely in some matter. If divine protection abandons him, he is suddenly overwhelmed weakly precisely where he boasts that he stands firmly.

What was it, after all, that enabled the man of God, sent to prophesy against the altar of Samaria, to exercise the authority of a free voice in the presence of the king, and miraculously to stiffen the king’s outstretched arm into rigidity, yet afterward mercifully to restore it to health? What was it that enabled him, when invited into the king’s house, to refuse to eat there because he had observed the Lord’s command forbidding him to eat on the road—yet on that same road he was deceived, ate, and died?

What do we gather from this by careful reflection? What, so to speak, do we suspect with fear, except perhaps that he had silently congratulated himself inwardly for having despised the king on account of the Lord’s commands? Then, shaken from his inward firmness, he incurred guilt in his deed at the very point from which glory had crept into his heart. Deceived by the false words of the prophet, he would have said that what he had done in resisting the king’s words had not at all been a matter of his own strength.

He rightly received from the mouth of the one whose deception caused him to depart from the command of life the sentence of death, so that he might truly receive punishment from the place where he had negligently incurred guilt.

Then follows:

> Thus says the Lord: “Because you were disobedient to the mouth of the Lord and did not keep the commandment that the Lord your God commanded you, but turned back, ate bread, and drank water in the place where he commanded you not to eat bread or drink water, your corpse shall not be placed in the tomb of your fathers,” and the rest.

How great this punishment should be considered, if we think according to the Gospel, where we have learned that after the body has been killed there is nothing to fear—that the lifeless limbs may suffer—so that it cannot even be called a punishment.

But if we consider the human affection a person has for his own flesh, the living man could have been frightened or saddened by what he would not himself experience as punishment, because his mind grieved that this would happen to his body, although when it happened he would not feel pain.

The Lord wished to chastise his servant only to this extent. The servant had not refused to fulfill the command through his own defiance; rather, deceived by another’s falsehood, he believed that he was obeying when he was not. Nor should we think that he was killed by the beast’s bite in such a way that his soul was then carried off to Tartarus as punishment. For the lion that had killed him guarded his body; the animal on which he had been riding remained unharmed; and it stood fearlessly, together with that savage beast, present at the funeral of its master.

By this wonderful sign it is clear that the man of God was disciplined temporarily, even unto death, rather than punished after death [Col. 1164A].

Concerning this, the Apostle, after mentioning the illnesses of many on account of certain offenses, says:

> If we judged ourselves, we would not be judged by the Lord. But when we are judged by the Lord, we are disciplined, so that we may not be condemned with the world (1 Corinthians XI).

The man who had deceived him buried him quite honorably in his own tomb, and arranged to be buried beside his bones. He hoped in this way that his own bones might be spared when the time came when, according to the prophecy of that man of God, King Josiah of Judah would bring forth the bones of many dead people in that land and defile with those bones the sacrilegious altars that had been established for carved images.

He spared the tomb in which the prophet lay—the prophet who had foretold these things more than three hundred years earlier—and on his account the burial of the man who had deceived him was not violated either.

For the one who had killed him by a lie, moved by that affection by which no one ever hates his own flesh, had provided for his own corpse. From the fact that everyone naturally loves his own flesh, it was punishment for the one man to learn that he would not be placed in the tomb of his fathers; and it was a matter of concern for the other to ensure that his bones would be spared if he lay beside the one whose tomb no one would violate.

The martyrs of Christ, striving for the truth, conquered this affection. Nor is it surprising that they despised what they would not feel after death, since they could not be overcome by the torments of those whom they felt while still alive.

God could certainly have prevented the dogs from touching the bodies of his servants who had been killed, just as he did not allow the lion to touch the prophet’s body—the body of the man whom the lion itself had killed—and made the killer into its guard.

God could, I say, have restrained the dogs from the bodies of his servants, to whom those bodies had been thrown. He could also have terrified the savagery of those people in countless ways, so that they would not dare to burn the corpses or scatter them into the air.

But this trial too had to be added to the varied forms of temptation, so that the strength of confession—which would not yield to the violence of persecution for the sake of preserving the body—would not tremble before the honor of the grave, and finally so that faith in the resurrection would not fear the destruction of bodies.

These things therefore had to be permitted, so that after such examples of horror the martyrs, fervent in confessing Christ, might also become witnesses to this truth: that those by whom their bodies were killed afterward had nothing they could do to them—indeed, could do nothing—since the one who had departed from the flesh, devoid of all life, could feel nothing, and the one who had created it could lose nothing from it.

Yet it had accordingly grown, as Isaiah says, from head to foot.

## II. On the Most Impious King Ahab. 1 Kings XVI

Passing over much of the history in the Books of Kings, we hasten briefly to the times of Ahab, that most wicked king, and of his sacrilegious wife Jezebel, in order to say at least something, however slight, about the virtues of the holy prophets Elijah and Elisha.

Meanwhile, Scripture reports that Ahab, son of Omri, after his father’s death reigned over Israel in Samaria for twenty-two years, and did evil in the sight of the Lord more than all who had been before him. Nor was it enough for him to walk in the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat: he further took as wife the daughter of Ethbaal, king of the Sidonians; he went and served Baal in the temple which he had built in Samaria; he planted a grove there; and Ahab added to his deeds by provoking the Lord God of Israel more than all who had been before him [Col. 1164D].

A *lucus* is a thick wooded place, so called because it has little light: a pleasant place clothed with many trees, where there are many trees. It is called a *lucus* by antiphrasis, because it lacks light owing to the excessive shade of its groves, enclosed by dense trees and shutting out the sunlight. Or it may be called so from being illuminated by frequent lights, which were set there for the religion and worship of the Gentiles. The pagans used to consult demons in groves and receive answers from them, not by signs but by voices; hence also temples (*fana*) were named from speaking (*fari*).

Now when, in Elijah’s days, the people of the Jews had already been divided into two parts, Ahab held the sovereignty of the Israelites by succession to the kingdom. He took as wife Jezebel, a woman of a foreign people and a profane mind; through her care and insistence the worship of idols had advanced, so that king and people alike were drawn into the sacrilegious rite [Col. 1165A].

The devil, artificer of ancient tyranny, was raging to the injury of God, striving to destroy God’s manifold worship. He was raging in the heart of a woman, at whose prompting the divine law and its priesthood were despised, the prophets were killed, and the altars were removed. All things stood aghast and shuddered at so great a crime—by “all things” I mean the world wasting away in all its members and forms, because human error ascribed to them the name of the Creator.

But perhaps you ask that it be proved to you whether the elements fear when human beings sin. Hear the illustrious prophet Jeremiah crying out with a divine voice: “Heaven was appalled at this,” he says, “and the earth was shaken, because my people committed two evils: they forsook me, the fountain of living water, and dug for themselves broken cisterns which cannot hold water” (Jeremiah II).

The elements, therefore, were troubled—not in their function, but in their feeling—because, as I have said, human error imposed on them the unique name of deity and, in blind devotion, rendered them the service due to the Creator [Col. 1165B].

Elijah stood in the midst of so great a peril to souls; he stood amid the very shipwreck of the world, which not a flood of waters but the punitive and blind rivalry of the devil had brought upon the earth. Alone, while the rest lay hidden, like a burning lamp he offered himself to those whom he saw submerged in the darkness of profound night—now warning, now rebuking, now healing, now even threatening. But light does not benefit the blind, nor speech the deaf.

Day by day the disastrous error increased and the shadow of death covered every creature. Wretched humankind bowed down to every form and every appearance. What need I say of the sun, moon, and stars, of earth and sea, the principal and most splendid elements? Before all living creatures—birds, quadrupeds, reptiles, even flies and worms—the image of the eternal and unique God was prostrated.

How, then, could that mind wholly devoted to piety and faith—I mean the mind of the prophet Elijah—endure so great a ruin and destruction of souls [Col. 1165C]? The body of that people lay bound by a deep sickness, and, as though already lifeless and without feeling, with its limbs torn apart and cast over crags and rocks, through woods and groves, it possessed no remnant in itself of the divine image.

No draught and no kind of medicine, even if administered, could benefit it, because its limbs rejected whatever was applied. The knife had to be used; the wound had to be healed by blood; it had to be treated with a violent cautery. Yet it had accordingly grown, as Isaiah says, from head to foot.

During the days of Ahab’s reign, Hiel of Bethel rebuilt Jericho; he laid its foundations at the cost of Abiram, his firstborn, and set up its gates at the cost of Segub, his youngest son (Isa. LVI). The meaning is clear: when the aforementioned founder of the city began to lay its foundations, his firstborn, named Abiram, died; and when, after the city had been built, he attempted to fortify its gates, he lost the youngest of his sons, whose name was Segub. Joshua had foretold that this would happen when, after destroying it, he delivered it over to the ban: “Cursed before the Lord be the man who shall rise up and rebuild this city of Jericho. At the cost of his firstborn shall he lay its foundations, and at the cost of his youngest child shall he set up its gates” (Josh. VI).

Since Hiel means “Living for God,” and Bethel is interpreted as “House of God,” Hiel of Bethel restores the walls of Jericho, which Joshua had destroyed and placed under the ban, whenever one of those who had assumed the religious habit in the Church returns to the crimes from which the Lord Jesus had freed him on the day of baptism, and, living wantonly, takes up again the pomps of the devil, which he himself had renounced, and prefers the teachings of error or the tales of the pagans to the ecclesiastical truth in which he had been instructed. As though departing from Bethel, he revives the ruins of Jericho. Such a man is deservedly accursed before the Lord, and loses both his firstborn in the foundation of the wicked city and his youngest in the setting up of its gates, because he has lost both the foundations of faith, from which good buildings should begin, and the barriers of good conduct, by which the work ought to have been brought to completion.

I have also explained these matters in an allegorical sense, so that you may remember the truth of the Apostle’s saying: “All these things happened to them figuratively, but they were written for our sake” (1 Cor. X). The text continues:
