And Elijah the Tishbite, from the inhabitants of Gilead, said to Ahab: “As the Lord, the God of Israel, lives, in whose sight I stand.” It should be understood that we come into the sight of the Lord in two ways. In one way, we carefully examine our sins here, place ourselves in his sight, and judge ourselves with tears. In the other way, we come into the sight of the Lord when, at the final judgment, we stand before his tribunal. For whenever we bring the power of our Creator back to our awareness, we stand in his sight. Thus it is rightly said now through Elijah, the man of God: “As the Lord, the God of Israel, lives, in whose sight I stand.”

He now approaches Ahab, the very head of the body, no longer as he was accustomed to do—gentle and mild—but harsh and severe, and says to him: “As the Lord lives, the God of hosts, the God of Israel, in whose sight I stand, there shall be neither dew nor rain during these years, except at my word.” Great is the power of prophetic dignity: the speech is human, but the effect is divine. A man speaks on earth, and the heavenly powers obey his command. One utterance of the prophet disturbed all creation; and, in a wondrous manner, as it sounded upon the ground, it shook the air and heaven. The order of human service was thrown into confusion, and the harmony of the elements established from the beginning withered away, when moisture was denied to dryness and cold to heat. Yet the elements gladly receive their punishment, provided that it advances either the salvation of human beings or the honor of the Creator.

Elijah is commanded to withdraw and hide; birds provide him with food from heaven. Then the torrent dries up, and his drinking vessels fail. For, advancing like fire, the sentence itself somehow penetrated the vital parts of the earth and immediately dried everything up. There was no charm in the fields, no beauty in the meadows; even the riverbanks, once clothed with flourishing shrubs, languished beneath the most wretched squalor, when springs were deprived of their waters and rivers of their courses.

From there the prophet moves on and, at God’s command, goes to prepared storerooms. Forgetful of all the affliction, he thinks only of himself. He is not moved by humanity, nor bent by any compassion. He does not look to the very laws of nature; he does not see the little child panting beneath its mother’s dry breast. With a troubled expression he passes by old and young alike, exhausted by the profound death of hunger—no longer bodies, but corpses. He does not answer the pleading farmer or respond to the supplicating cultivator; becoming more cruel than wild beasts and fiercer than animals, he despises the whole human race.

### III. Elijah Is Fed by Ravens. 3 Kings XVII

“And the word of the Lord came to Elijah, saying: ‘Depart from here, go toward the east, and hide yourself in the torrent Cherith, which is opposite the Jordan. There you shall drink from the torrent, and I have commanded the ravens to feed you there.’ He went, therefore, and acted according to the word of the Lord. The ravens also brought him bread and meat in the morning, and likewise bread and meat in the evening, and he drank from the torrent. After some days the torrent dried up, for it had not rained upon the earth.”

Elijah, therefore, is rightly likened to the Son of God, with whom both his authority and his name correspond in truth. Elijah is interpreted as “My God,” a name that belongs substantially to the Son of God, who originally claims for himself the authority to do whatever he wills, since he testified that everything belonging to the Father is also his.

Tishbite is interpreted as “Captivating” or “Converting.” For concerning the Lord the Psalmist says: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive” (Ps. CXLV); and again: “Convert our captivity, O Lord, like a torrent in the south” (Ps. LXVII).

And lest anyone perhaps be disturbed that I have compared Elijah with the Son of God, let him read the Epistle to the Hebrews, and he will find that the Apostle made this very comparison, saying in effect: “This Melchizedek, likened to the Son of God, remains a priest forever; without father, he says, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end” (Heb. VII). This can certainly apply to no human being except the Son of God alone, whose origin, whether from whom or from where, Scripture nowhere indicates.

Scripture likewise bears witness to the same thing concerning Elijah, when it suddenly introduces his name without at all stating from what tribe or family he arose.

The torrent Cherith, which is interpreted as “Division” or “Cutting off,” most certainly corresponds to the Jewish people. That people is rightly compared to a torrent, because what had been divinely entrusted to it for observance through the Law was destined to be brought to an end at the appointed time of the Lord’s incarnation, when the shadows and images of the Law were recognized as fulfilled.

Elijah is then fed during the famine by ravens, which bring bread in the morning and meat in the evening. The Manichaeans understand Christ in those books, to whom, as though hungering for our salvation, they confess sinners—now possessing the first fruits of faith, but at the end, as at the evening of the world, receiving also the resurrection of the flesh.

The bread and meat that Scripture says the ravens brought to Elijah morning and evening may also be understood in this way: in the bread, works of piety, which the Lord testified are given to himself in strangers and the needy; in the meat, the disciplining or suffering of the body, which all the saints are read to have imposed upon themselves or endured from persecutors for the sake of divine love or worship, morning and evening—that is, under the Old Testament and under the preaching of the Gospel.

### IV. Elijah Is Fed by the Woman of Zarephath, Whose Jar of Flour and Jug of Oil Do Not Diminish. 3 Kings XVII

After the torrent had dried up, the Lord said to Elijah: “Arise and go to Zarephath of the Sidonians, and remain there. For I have commanded a woman there to feed you.” He arose and went to Zarephath. When he had come to the gate of the city, a widow appeared to him, gathering sticks. He called her and said to her: “Give me a little water in a vessel, that I may drink.” As she was going to fetch it, he called after her: “Bring me also, I beg you, a morsel of bread in your hand.”

She answered: “As the Lord your God lives, I have no bread, except as much flour as a handful can hold in a jar, and a little oil in a jug. And now I am gathering two sticks, so that I may go in and prepare it for myself and my son, so that we may eat and die.”

To her Elijah said: “Do not be afraid, but go and do as you have said. Nevertheless, first make for me from that little flour a small cake baked under the ashes, and bring it to me; afterward you shall make something for yourself and your son. For thus says the Lord, the God of Israel: The jar of flour shall not fail, nor shall the jug of oil diminish, until the day on which the Lord gives rain upon the face of the earth.”

She went and did according to Elijah’s word, and he and she and her son ate. From that day the jar of flour did not fail, and the jug of oil did not diminish, according to the word of the Lord that he had spoken through Elijah.

For the moment, let us omit what sacramental meaning lies hidden in the fact that he is sent from the land of Israel to the region of Sidon, from which Jezebel, the source and cause of all evils, had arisen. Let us briefly consider that he goes to a widow struggling with poverty and abandoned at the very boundary between life and death. She had gone out to gather wood and to secure for herself and her children their last means of sustenance.

But Elijah sees the woman worn out by the squalor of hunger. He is not moved, he does not hesitate, he does not turn back his steps; rather, he thrusts himself upon her and plunges into her affairs. He makes himself even more burdensome to her than hunger itself and says: “Give me a little water to drink.”

O, blessed man, if the widow had answered you and, driving you away with a just reproach, had said: “Why do you ask from me what you have taken away from everyone? Why do you seek from a woman what you have denied to the world? This universal need and poverty has been brought about by the authority of your own mouth. I ought to be refreshed by you; I ought to be filled by you. You come to me!”

But the woman neither did nor said any of these things. Instead, her devoted mind, not unworthy of an evangelical reward, immediately brought a cup of cold water to the thirsty prophet.

Elijah adds and says: “Bring me also a morsel of bread in your hand.” But she replied: “As the Lord your God lives, I have no bread, unless it be a handful of flour in the jar. Behold, I am gathering two sticks, so that I may go in and prepare it for myself and my son; we shall eat and die.”

But what does Elijah say to this? “Have confidence,” he says, “and go in, and do according to your word; but first make me a small cake from it under the ashes; afterward you shall make one for yourself and your son.”

O magnificent spirit of the woman! O unchangeable resolve of her mind! O deed truly worthy of veneration throughout the ages! He asks for a drink, and she immediately offers it. What perhaps was already lacking to kings, what the rich did not possess, the widow distributed from her abundance.

She feeds with bread the one who, together with her son, was to die the next day. She does not deny that she possesses it but simply confesses the truth, nor does she fear to reveal it. She lays the whole matter before the one who is not so much asking as, in a sense, demanding: the quantity of food and the number of persons, as though she wished to have not so much a guest as a judge.

She did not say: “I cannot do what you command.” Nor did she say: “Consider the widow, wasting away not so much from concern for herself as for her son. Consider the chorus of little children; do not take me away from them, and do not abandon a mother deprived of so many children.”

She did not say: “You are surely the one who condemned the whole earth to the sentence of famine; the entire human race has perished because you were angry. Then you crossed through your homeland and traversed almost the entire land and province of your people. Nowhere did a rich man meet you, nowhere did a wealthy person encounter you who would receive the hungry man and refresh the fasting one.

“I alone have met you—or perhaps I alone remain—the one who, in addition to the destitution of poverty, is also weighed down by a multitude of children, suffering in this very plague a burden made heavier by so many offspring. I go out of the house not to gather ears of grain but sticks; not to bring back food but fuel. Since I cannot free those whom I cannot save from hunger, I try at least to protect them from the cold.

“Certainly, since you are so cruel that you do not consider what you command, you ought at least to have been content to eat with us the little that remains; or first allow the children to be satisfied, and then let what remained be offered to you. But you command that food be prepared for you alone; and not only alone, but you want to be satisfied first. You show no concern for the wretched, nor does the very reverence owed to nature move you. You want to take away from the children and nursing infants the last morsel of food from their very teeth.”

But she neither did nor said any of this. On the contrary, she ran without fear and completed what had been commanded.

At that time there was a spectacle most pleasing to angels and human beings: in a profane land among the nations, a widowed woman was already a daughter of Abraham, much more hospitable than her forefather and much more humane than the father of the faithful.

Abraham was indeed hospitable and held in great affection those who came from abroad; but he was truly prosperous, he was rich. He possessed the ability to do whatever he wished, since his spirit was no smaller than his resources, and his wealth did not exceed his courage.

This woman, however, who had been deprived not only of her husband but also of her resources, who was poor not only by birth but also constrained by the misfortune of the times, had fallen into such poverty that she could possess in her house nothing except what increased her hunger—namely, a crowd of children more burdensome than hunger itself. Yet amid all these evils her generous and devoted spirit remained steadfast. She went and, as the man of God had commanded, faithfully completed the task; she welcomed the prophet and received him.

With what words, then, and with what voice should I praise this woman? Nothing worthy occurs to me that could match such a spirit of virtue. I consider how, through her devotion to hospitality, she disregarded every force of natural affection—not for herself, not for her children. Nothing recalled her from her resolve: neither the weakness of her sex nor the maternal tenderness of her heart toward her children.

For the sake of hospitality she killed within herself the duties of nature, and the mother’s devotion toward her guest became the cruel grave of her children. So far as she was concerned, the children were dead, strangled and buried, as it were, by their mother’s own hands. But as far as God’s mercy was concerned, they were not truly dead, nor consumed by hunger or starvation, because, while the others perished, they alone recovered.

Immediately the prophet, rewarding her faith with a divine recompense, said: “As the Lord lives, your jar of flour shall not fail, and your vessel of oil shall not diminish.”

The widow’s hand thus became an everlasting oil press and a mill continually pouring forth its produce. Why do I speak of the woman’s hand? At the prophet’s word, the widow’s whole house became a storehouse of the pious. There was no dew there, no rain, no breeze of spring, no warm sunlight, no needed cloud, no plow, no farmer, no cultivator; but the prophet’s word supplied the widow abundantly with everything in every respect.

It should nevertheless be understood that, according to the Septuagint translators, this widow is said to have had not one son but several.

The woman who is said to have lived in Zarephath bore the figure of the Church. For a long time abandoned by her Creator, she did not know the people of true faith. She nourished them on a meager allowance—that is, she taught the word without fruit—until the prophetic word arrived. Israel’s fleece having been dried up, as though heaven’s door were closed, Judea was suffering from famine. She was called a widow because, being a Gentile, she had not yet been dedicated to divine worship and did not possess knowledge of the sacred Law.

The city of Zarephath, which is interpreted as “Fire,” or “Tribulation of bread,” or “Bread of distress,” should be understood as the present world. In it the fire of the worst desire burns fiercely; there, care was devoted to acquiring superfluous possessions, as though to the capture of birds; there, the fire was truly fierce and spiritual bread had previously become a source of distress.

Therefore, as Scripture declares concerning Elijah, when our Lord came to the Church of the nations and found it outside the gate of the city—that is, in the ancestral error of paganism—he did not summon it to confess his name through signs, miracles, and great wonders, as he had done for Israel. Instead, he commanded it only by his word, saying: “Give me a little water in a vessel, that I may drink, and a morsel of bread in your hand.”

The water in the vessel is to be understood as faith of the heart, by which one believes unto righteousness. The morsel of bread in the hand is to be understood as the work of mercy. Faith and works are joined to one another by an indissoluble bond; for where one is absent, the other cannot stand at all. As the Apostle James says: “Faith without works is dead” (Jas. II), and works without faith are rendered empty and futile.

The Church, therefore, under the figure of that widow, goes at the Lord’s command to bring him water and, in a certain sense, displays to the Lord the faith prepared in her heart. She confesses that she does not yet have bread—that is, works worthy of divine worship—but testifies that she has a little flour in the jar and a little oil in the jug.

The handful of flour in the jar signifies the natural law, which by divine generosity has been implanted in human nature. Through it one distinguishes good from evil and learns that one must not do to another what one does not wish done to oneself.

The little oil in the jug is to be understood as rational understanding, through which creation understands the Creator and strives to please him through pious works. She said that she possessed only a little of it because she had not yet received the gift of spiritual grace through the sacrament of baptism.

There, however, the flour and oil are blessed by the prophetic word—that is, the fruit and joyfulness of charity, or the grace of the Lord’s body and the anointing of chrism—so that they are made fruitful by the unfailing gift of the heavenly word. In these vessels the oil of spiritual joy and the flour of blessing have never since failed, while the other nations, which do not believe, are given over to the poverty of divine bread, misery, and useless pursuit.

As for her statement that she was gathering two sticks, from which she would bake the little flour she possessed and eat it with her children while awaiting death, it should be understood in this way: in the two sticks—not only in the name “wood” but also in the number of the pieces of wood—she prefigured the mystery of the cross. Through it she believed that the bread of eternal life would be given to herself and her children, that is, to the people who would believe in Christ, and that they would die to past sins through the washing of baptism, in accordance with the saying the Lord proclaimed in the Gospel: “Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed” (John XX).

By the small cake baked under the ashes she already prefigured that small provision which the Gentiles are read to have resolved, at the beginning of their faith, to observe through the Apostle’s letter: that they should abstain only from the worship of idols, from fornication, and from things strangled. These practices, granted by the Apostles through wise counsel to people still crude and wild, are known to have been very limited and small in comparison with the preaching of the Gospel, into which they were later introduced.

When he says, “Make it for me first,” he intended this for all believers from the Gentiles: they should not ascribe to their own merits the fact that they were saved while Israel had become hardened and was rejected. Rather, they should ascribe it to him who, in his mercy, enabled them to believe. For, as it was said to Cain, “He does not offer rightly who does not divide rightly” (Gen. III). That is, he does not divide rightly who ascribes to himself rather than to God all the good that he possesses.

Or, alternatively: the cake baked under the ashes is to be understood as the history of the Law, which contained spiritual understanding hidden beneath the letter. By fermented bread, however, the preaching of the Gospel is to be understood, because testimonies were inserted into the Old Testament like leaven.

As for the fact that Elijah fed the woman who fed him, it should be understood in this way: although all the faithful feed God through their faith and pious works, nevertheless the fact that they possess these things is granted to them by him. For, as it is written, “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (Jas. I). Divine gifts are never wholly diminished for those who fear God.

Again, in another sense, what else should be understood by the cake baked under the ashes that the true Elijah, our Lord, commands the Church of the nations to offer him, except the satisfaction of penitents? The Psalmist sings the same thing in the person of a penitent when he says: “For I ate ashes like bread and mingled my drink with weeping” (Ps. CI). By such satisfactions the Lord urges that he be fed.

### V. The Son of the Woman of Zarephath Is Raised through Elijah’s Prayer. 3 Kings XVII

After these words the son of the woman, the mother of the household, became ill, and his sickness was so severe that no breath remained in him. She said to Elijah: “What have I to do with you, man of God? You came to me so that my iniquities might be remembered and you might kill my son.”

Elijah said to her: “Give me your son.” He took him from her bosom, carried him to the upper room where he lived, and laid him upon his bed. Then he stretched himself out and measured himself over the child three times. The child’s soul returned to him, and he revived. He brought him down from the upper room, gave him to his mother, and said: “Behold, your son lives.”

She answered: “Now I know that you are a man of God and that the word of the Lord in your mouth is true.”

The statement that the woman’s son was held by an excessive illness and brought even to the point of death is understood to have this meaning. After receiving a command, and divine knowledge or the preaching of the Gospel, and after tasting good works, a person must languish under the most severe affliction because of committed crimes and past errors. For, as it is written, “He who increases knowledge also increases the salutary pain of repentance” (Eccl. I), and through continual discipline he does violence to his own destruction, so that he may escape eternal death and attain the life of everlasting blessedness.

The Apostle Paul confirms this very thing when he says that he is not worthy to be called an apostle because he persecuted the Church of God and attacked it (1 Cor. XV).

In descending into the font, the one who has believed in Christ dies through baptism to original sin and former vices. Then, lifted up to the upper room of the sacred altar through the anointing of chrism, the invocation of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and communion in the Lord’s body and blood, he is clearly given life. Then from the whole Church, whose figure was borne by the child’s mother, comes that confession: the Lord Jesus is the true Son of God and is seated in the bosom or at the right hand of the Father. Once more, having been taken down from the altar, he is restored alive to the assembly of the faithful as to his mother.

Or, alternatively: after a believer has put to death his former vices in his members through the satisfaction of repentance, and after he has been lifted above earthly desires and carnal longings through meditation on the Law and the Prophets and through the preaching of the Gospel, he deserves to be given life and becomes a temple of God. He directs the intention of his mind there where Christ sits at the right hand of the Father, and, while still dwelling in the flesh, he already strives to live in heaven.

Yet however much a person may strive to raise his mind toward God and, through a certain ecstatic vision, rejoice in clinging to Christ the Lord in the heights, the nature of the body, to which the soul is joined, nevertheless compels him to be drawn back once more from the heights to the lower things.

As for Elijah’s stretching himself over the child and measuring himself over him three times, it is clear that the Lord fulfilled this very thing when, through the Law and the prophecies of the Prophets, as well as through his own preaching, he brought salvation to the people of the nations.

The words of Elijah concerning the widow, already explained figuratively above, are found in a much different form in the ancient translations. In them Elijah implores the Lord, saying: “O Lord, witness of this widow with whom I dwell in her house, have you done evil by killing her son?”

Nothing in this statement would trouble the mind if the correct pronunciation were preserved. It is the voice of someone asking whether God would act so wickedly toward that widow who had received the prophet so piously, especially at the time when he was staying there and she had offered him her entire, exceedingly small livelihood in the midst of such great and extreme poverty.

Thus it should be understood as though he had said: “O Lord, witness of this widow with whom I dwell in her house, have you done evil by killing her son?” The implication is that the Lord, who was witness to the woman’s heart, saw how great her piety was. For this reason he had sent Elijah to her; and he had not killed her son in order to do harm, but to display a miracle for the glory of his name, by which he would commend so great a prophet both to those living at that time and to posterity. Thus the Lord says that Lazarus had not died for death’s sake, but so that God might be glorified in his Son.

The following words prove this as well. For from the very confidence he possessed, Elijah believed that this had not happened so that his hostess might be afflicted with bitter mourning, but rather so that God might show the widow more magnificently what kind of servant of God she had received.

Scripture continues and says:

“He breathed upon the child three times, and called upon the Lord and said: ‘O Lord my God, let the soul of this child return into him now.’ And it happened so.”

This prayer, by which Elijah asked so briefly and faithfully that the child be raised, sufficiently indicates with what feeling the preceding words were spoken. The woman herself also showed that her son had been put to death for the purpose Elijah had presumed, when she had rejected those words rather than confirmed them. For when she had received her son alive, she said: “Now I know that you are a man of God, and that the word of God in your mouth is most certain.”

There are many passages in Scripture which, unless they are pronounced in this way, fall into the opposite meaning. Such is the statement: “Who shall bring an accusation against God’s elect? God, who justifies.” If you answer as though this were a confirmation, you see what great perversity arises. It must therefore be pronounced as though it said: “Is it God who justifies?” The implied answer is, “Certainly not.” Thus I think Elijah’s meaning is clear; an unobserved manner of pronunciation had made it obscure.

### VI. Elijah Obtains Rain from God. 3 Kings XVIII

“And the word of the Lord,” it says, “came to Elijah: ‘Go, show yourself to Ahab, so that I may give rain upon the face of the earth.’”

He went, and on the way Abdias, the steward of King Ahab, met him and said: “Go, announce to Ahab: ‘Elijah is here.’” He went and announced it to him. Ahab came to meet him and said to Elijah: “Are you the one who troubles Israel?”

Elijah answered: “I have not troubled Israel, but you and your father’s house, because you abandoned the commandment of the Lord and followed the Baals. Nevertheless, send now and gather all Israel to me on Mount Carmel, and the four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal, and the prophets of the sacred groves who eat at Jezebel’s table.”

Ahab sent to all the children of Israel and gathered them on Mount Carmel. Elijah approached all the people and said: “How long will you limp between two sides? If the Lord is God, follow him; but if Baal is God, follow him.” The people did not answer him a word.

Elijah said to them again: “I alone remain a prophet of the Lord, while the prophets of the Baals number four hundred and fifty men. Let two oxen be given to us. Let them choose one ox, cut it into pieces, and place it upon the wood, but let them not put fire beneath it. I too shall prepare the other ox and place it upon the wood, but I shall not put fire beneath it. Let them call upon the names of their gods, and I shall call upon the name of the Lord. The one who answers by fire, he shall be God.”

All the people answered and said: “This is an excellent proposal.”

Elijah said to the prophets of Baal: “Choose one ox and prepare it first, because you are the greater number.” They did so, and called upon Baal from morning until midday. There was neither voice nor anyone who answered. They cut themselves with knives and lances according to their rite until they were covered with blood.

When midday had passed and the time had already come at which the sacrifice ought to be offered, Elijah said to the people: “Come to me.” When the people had come to him, he repaired the altar of the Lord that had been destroyed. He took twelve stones according to the number of the tribes of the sons of Jacob, and built an altar to the Lord in the name of the Lord. He made a channel around the altar, large enough for two measures of seed, and placed the wood there. He divided the ox and laid it upon the wood, and said: “Fill four jars with water and pour it over the burnt offering and the wood.”

When they had done this, he ordered the same thing to be done a second and a third time, and the channel was filled with water.

See why Elijah does this also, and pay close attention. Blessed Elijah possessed, both because of the grace of his prophetic dignity and because of his zeal for divine worship, knowledge of everything that was done in the temples of demons. Among their other inept inventions, he knew of a crafty fraud of this kind, devised so that the souls of the wretched might more easily be ensnared.

Their altars were not simply set before the feet of the shrine. Instead, a projecting ledge, upon which the altars were constructed, was supported by a subterranean pyre beneath a vaulted passage. From the opposite side, through a hollow wall, one descended by a concealed entrance; and through open cavities a servant of the deception secretly supplied prepared fires at the time of the sacrifice by hidden means. Thus the minds of the wretched, astonished when they saw no flames applied from above but observed the victim suddenly consumed, believed that fires had been brought from heaven by invisible power.

Therefore, lest unbelieving minds suspect this concerning the divine altars, he ordered the trench that he had commanded to be made to be filled with water, so that if there were any pit beneath the altar it might be exposed, or so that the water descending downward would certainly extinguish any hidden fires. Nor was it enough to soak the place once; this was done three times. But the prophet was not satisfied even with that: he ordered the wood of the altar itself to be drenched, so that, once every suspicion of fraud had been removed, neither the king, nor the people, nor the priests themselves could doubt that the power belonged to God.

When it was now time for the burnt offering to be presented, Elijah approached the altar and cried out, saying:

“Lord God, hear me today by fire, as you heard me by water, so that this people may know that you are the Lord God of Israel, and that I am your servant, and that I have done all these things because of you. Hear me, Lord, hear me by fire, so that this people may know that you are the Lord God, and that you have turned the heart of this people back again.”

Behold, while he was crying out, fire fell from heaven and consumed the burnt offering, the wood, and the stones, as well as the dust; and it licked up the water that was in the trench. When all the people saw this [Col. 1172D], they fell on their faces and said, “The Lord himself is God.”

Then Elijah said to them, “Seize the prophets of Baal, and let not one of them escape.” So they seized them, and Elijah immediately led them down to the torrent Kishon, where he ordered them to be slaughtered.

For the most merciful God, who does not forget to show pity, nor in his anger restrain his mercies, once again deigned to send his Son to Israel, so that he might grant them the rain of evangelical preaching. The three years of famine prefigured that the knowledge of the holy Trinity had been lacking among the Jewish people, or indeed throughout the whole world.

Ahab, whose name is interpreted as “Brother of the father,” and of whom Scripture also declares that he killed the prophets of God, bore the figure of the chief priests. When Ahab said to Elijah, “Are you the one who troubles Israel?” the same words are read as having been spoken by the chief priests about the Lord to Pilate: “We found this man subverting, or troubling, our nation” (Luke [Col. 1173A] 23). For they were, as the Lord is read to have reproached them, sons of their father the devil, whose works they desired to do, so that they impiously proclaimed the author of their life worthy of crucifixion.

“For you,” says the Lord, “are of your father the devil, and you wish to do your father’s works; for he was a murderer from the beginning and a liar, and he never stood in the truth” (John 8).

Obadiah, whose name is interpreted as “Servant of the Lord,” and who, at the very time when Ahab had ordered the Lord’s prophets to be slaughtered, had hidden one hundred prophets in caves and supplied them daily with food, prefigured in a certain way those who, from among the Jewish leaders, were secretly disciples of the Lord—namely, Nicodemus and the others whom the Evangelist mentions.

The prophets of Baal and the prophets of the sacred groves bore the figure of the scribes and Pharisees, who, neglecting the commandments of the sacred law, perverted the people through their own traditions (Matthew 21); against them the Lord is read to have foretold that there would be a “Woe” (Luke 11).

Mount Carmel, whose name is interpreted as “Knowledge of circumcision,” represented the Church of Christ [Col. 1173B], in which we are commanded to know not the circumcision of the foreskin, but how circumcision is to be understood. By circumcision of the flesh’s foreskin, one must understand that lust and wantonness are to be cut away; by circumcision of the heart, that impure thoughts are to be amputated.

The ox that Elijah slaughtered as a burnt offering and cut into pieces is to be understood as the Old Testament. From it, in order to refute Jewish superstitions, the things written there are shown to have been drawn out in many places through evangelical preaching, as when he is recorded to have said: “Have you not read what was said, ‘The stone which the builders rejected has become the cornerstone’?” And, he says, “the scribes and Pharisees understood that he was speaking about them” (Matthew 23), and so forth, as these things are found in the Gospel.

The other ox chosen by the false prophets signifies the reprobate people, offered by the Pharisees and scribes—or by heretics—not to God but to their author, the devil. The passing time of midday signified the course of the pressing world, toward whose evening the Lord Jesus Christ offered himself to the Father as the true sacrifice—which he himself is—for the removal of the sins of the human race.

The altar repaired by Elijah and restored with twelve stones is to be understood as the confession of the holy Trinity, which had formerly been destroyed among the Jews and among the heretics, but was reestablished by the Lord through the apostles in the Church.

The wood arranged upon the altar prefigured the cross’s instrument of execution, to which the Lord’s body was fastened—a true and acceptable burnt offering to God the Father.

The four jars filled with water signified, in their number, the four Gospels, in which the sacrament of baptism, administered in the name of the holy Trinity, is commanded.

The fire that devoured the altar stones, everything that was upon it, and also the water prefigured the Holy Spirit, who consumes and sanctifies not only the apostles but all believers, through the bath of regeneration, as a sacrifice to God.

The false prophets who are read to have been killed by Elijah [Col. 1173D] are to be understood as the hostile powers, concerning whom the Apostle declares that the Lord triumphed over them on the cross. Alternatively, they are to be understood as those who are read to have impiously cried out against the Lord: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matthew 27). Anyone who reads Josephus the historian will not doubt that this was fulfilled in the times of Vespasian and Titus.

Then the narrative continues and says:

“Now Elijah went up to the summit of Carmel and, bending down to the earth, placed his face between his knees. He implored the Lord and said to his servant, ‘Go up and look toward the sea, seven times.’ When he had done this, on the seventh occasion a small cloud appeared, like a man’s footprint, rising from the sea; and suddenly the heavens were darkened, and there was a great rain.”

What Elijah implored—that rain should be granted by God—the Evangelist also declares that the Lord did for his disciples and for those who were to believe through their word.

There is no doubt that Elijah’s servant, who was ordered to look toward the sea, bore the figure of all the prophets who lived before the Savior’s coming. By the grace of the Holy Spirit, throughout the entire period preceding the Savior’s coming, they were granted to await his incarnation.

The small cloud that is described as rising from the sea like a footprint is to be understood as our Lord and Redeemer. For just as a footprint is the extremity of a bodily member, so also the Lord Jesus wished to exist in the world as humble, small, and childlike, in order to cleanse us from sin.

The heavens were darkened because the holy preachers of the divine word are filled with hidden mysteries. There was a great rain because the evangelical shower watered the boundaries of the whole world through the apostles’ preaching.

Ahab’s chariot, which Elijah preceded with his loins girded, is to be understood as the power of the devil, to whom the Lord says, “Go behind me, Satan; you shall not tempt the Lord your God” (Matthew 5). For at the Lord’s coming the devil’s power became so empty and weak that it did not even have permission to enter the pigs unless this had been granted to it [Col. 1174B].

## VII. On Jezebel’s hatred of Elijah. III Kings XIX

“Everything Elijah had done,” it says, “and how he had killed the prophets of Baal, was reported to Jezebel. Immediately she sent a messenger to him, saying: ‘May the gods do these things to me and add these things, unless by this time tomorrow I make your life like the life of one of them.’”

When Elijah heard this, he was very afraid and went wherever his will led him. He came to Beersheba of Judah, left his servant there, and himself went on into a day’s journey through the wilderness. When he had arrived there and sat beneath a juniper tree, he said, “It is enough for me, Lord; take my life.”

Holy men who, lifted up by the Spirit, are carried to the heights are restrained by certain temptations as long as they remain in this life, lest they become proud through some elevation. Thus they are never able to advance as far as they wish; rather, lest they be raised up by pride, a certain measure of virtues is established in them.

This is why Elijah [Col. 1174C], although he had advanced to great heights through so many virtues, was held back by a certain measure when he later fled Jezebel—although she was a queen, she was still merely a little woman.

I consider this man of extraordinary virtue drawing fire from heaven, suddenly burning up, by a sudden petition, two captains of fifty with all their men, closing the heavens with a word and opening them to rain with a word, raising the dead, and foreseeing all future things. Yet behold, my mind again encounters the fear with which he fled from one woman.

Consider a man struck by fear: he asked death from the hand of the Lord and did not receive it, while fleeing from death at the hand of a woman and thereby escaped it. For while fleeing he sought death, saying, “It is enough for me; take my life,” since “I am no better than my fathers.”

How, then, was he so powerful that he could perform all those virtues, and so weak that he feared a woman in this way? Only because, by the will of the heavenly steward, they are weighed according to a hidden balance, so that the holy men of God are both greatly empowered through God’s power and, in turn, moderated by a certain measure through their own weakness.

In those virtues Elijah recognized what he had received from God; in these weaknesses he recognized what he could be in himself. In the former, there was the virtue of power; in the latter, weakness was the guardian of virtue. Through those virtues he displayed what he had received; through his weaknesses he preserved what he had received. Elijah was revealed in the miracles; he was preserved in his weaknesses.

After this the narrative continues:

“He threw himself down and slept in the shade of the juniper tree. And behold, an angel of the Lord touched him and said to him, ‘Rise and eat.’ He looked, and behold, at his head was a hearth-baked loaf and a vessel of water. He ate and drank, and again fell asleep. The angel touched him a second time and said, ‘Rise and eat, for a great journey remains before you.’ He rose, ate, and drank, and walked in the strength of that food for forty days and forty nights, as far as Horeb, the mountain of God.”

What, then, of Jezebel? “May the gods do these things to me and add these things, unless I take your life.” Elijah heard this and fled a journey of forty days [Col. 1175A].

O the violence of the word! O the enormity of the fear! At the word of a woman Elijah fled; and he fled not for one, two, or three days. Rather, the woman’s speech entered into him, and he did not know what he was doing, driven and tossed by fear through so great a stretch of travel. It was as when a violent contrary wind seizes the mast of a ship driven forward by favorable breezes and reverses its course and momentum. Thus the woman’s speech struck the prophet’s mind, which had been sailing under the canvas of his virtues, and tossed his whole ship through every wave of fear, while its helmsman was thrown into confusion.

What, then, is this, Elijah? You are the one who by a word had closed the heavens and withheld the rains; who had commanded the air and brought forth divine fires; who had rightly ordered the false priests to be killed; who had boldly reproached the king to his face because he and his house were overthrowing the people of Israel; who had said, “As the Lord lives, there shall be neither rain nor dew except at the word of my mouth”; who had made the widow’s house into a threshing floor for grain and a winepress for oil; who had commanded all the elements—and now, hearing the speech of a prostitute, you were terrified, and one little woman made you a fugitive [Col. 1175B] and captive of fear.

O astonishing thing! Look at these two men, Peter and Elijah, magnificent and more illustrious than the rest, like two citadels of cities raised up on high, worn down by women: Peter fears a young girl, and Jezebel terrifies Elijah.

And because both were subject to the fault of the same weakness, their natural frailty found one betrayer for each. Elijah therefore fled a journey of forty days.

Where is the unchecked ardor of your zeal? Where is the flame of your steadfastness? Where is the authority of your freedom when you said, “As the Lord lives, there shall be rain upon the earth”? Or when you confronted the king and reproved him, and brought down avenging flames from heaven, performing such great and numerous wonders—could you not endure one adulteress’s word?

But consider what is shown in these events: as long as the grace of the Lord cooperates with a person, everything goes well for him and everything is secure; the elements serve him, rulers are overthrown, kings worship, and peoples venerate him. But if, once, the heavenly assistance withdraws from a person, whether for the sake of perfection or correction, the frailty of nature is immediately revealed. At once those things that had seemed subject rise up; those that previously feared him as their lord begin to become a terror to him.

Jezebel, whose name is interpreted as “Vain Flow,” bore the figure of the Synagogue. Serving vain superstitions, it refused to believe in evangelical preaching, and, persecuting the author of life, preferred to extinguish him rather than believe, just as Jezebel preferred to destroy Elijah rather than believe him.

Elijah’s servant, who was left at Beersheba—interpreted as “Well of the oath”—is to be understood as the priestly ministry that was offered to the Lord’s temple in Jerusalem through divine worship.

The wilderness to which Elijah is read to have come after a day’s journey, and beneath whose juniper tree he rested, is to be understood as the whole world, which had been placed in wickedness because of the worship of demons. To this world the Lord deigned to pass through his preachers, having left Judea; and there he seems to sleep, while he rests by faith in the hearts of the faithful.

The wild and uncultivated juniper tree prefigured the Church from the Gentiles [Col. 1175D], which had not been cultivated by the commandments of the sacred Scriptures. The Evangelist declares that the Lord foretold that the kingdom of Israel would pass to it: “The kingdom,” he says to the Jews, “will be taken from you and given to a nation producing God’s will” (Matthew 21).

The one-day journey that Elijah is read to have made is to be understood as the unity of the Trinity, which evangelical preaching introduced to all nations.

What else do the hearth-baked bread and the vessel of water indicate except the repentance of the Gentiles and the pouring out of tears, by which the Lord is greatly refreshed?

## VIII. On Elijah’s coming to Horeb. III Kings XIX

“After this,” it says, “Elijah came to Horeb, the mountain of God, and remained in a cave. And behold, the word of the Lord came to him and said: ‘What are you doing here, Elijah?’”

He replied, “I have been zealous with zeal for the Lord God of hosts, because the children of Israel have abandoned the Lord’s covenant. They have destroyed your altars and killed your prophets with the sword. I alone have been left, and they seek my life in order to take it” [Col. 1176A].

Elijah, then, fleeing, came to a certain place and slept there. The Lord came to him—the Lord, that is, to his servant—and said, “What are you doing here, Elijah?” It was as though he were reproaching him for his fear and flight.

“What are you doing,” he says, “Elijah? Do you think you fled, and that the fury of one little woman made you a fugitive? Where is that steadfastness? Where is that freedom? Learn henceforth not to trust in yourself, nor to attribute to your own virtue those things that go well.”

Yet Elijah replies, retaining one thing in his mind but bringing another forth from his mouth: “Lord, they have killed your prophets, destroyed your altars, and I alone have been left, and they seek my life.”

This thought, which had cast so great a prophet down from the very height of his merits, showed him to be an ordinary human being. Accordingly, the divine word immediately rebukes him.

“Not so,” it says, “Elijah; you are mistaken and caught in the snares of human thought. You did not flee for that reason, nor did the queen terrify you because you were alone. For you are not the only one who has not worshiped Baal. I have faithful servants; I have many friends, seven thousand men of the highest virtue, whom neither human error could bend nor the thought of empty glory elevate. All these have not bent their knees before Baal, but with steadfast knees, after the likeness of the heavenly host, they continually worship me.

“You fled, then, not because the adulteress’s fury raged against you alone, but because the greatness of your virtues produced this exaltation in you, so that you pronounced so arrogant a judgment upon the human race. For a little while you were to be abandoned by my grace; and unless I had loosened the reins of such great exaltation for you, you would have fallen into a more serious fall and learned to attribute good deeds not to your own virtue but to the divine.

“You fled, therefore, for no other reason than that, when my grace withdrew, the woman frightened you with her threatening speech.”

Let us consider, then, how great was the force of the adulteress’s speech when grace had withdrawn, and how great the magnitude of the fear: for forty days Elijah wandered in flight through trackless places and deserts, and, shaken with fear by so long a fast, did not feel hunger.

What are you doing, Elijah? Where is that confidence, so often mentioned, which astonished everyone? Where is that dreadful mouth? Where is that terrible tongue commanding the elements in turn [Col. 1176C]?

But, as I said, this stood firm for you while grace supplied its aid. See, therefore, how through the lightness of his fault so great a prophet is permitted to fall, so that, corrected and rebuked for his exaltation, he may be clothed in the complete garment of moderation and mercy.

We have now been instructed and taught through Peter and Elijah how the Lord, for our sake, permitted them to be encompassed by sin; how he allowed those standard-bearers of faith and devotion and pillars of the human race to be shaken by fear’s domination. This was so that they might be an example to peoples: God had by no means granted them the grace not to sin, lest, while they themselves were free from faults and vices, they should prove harsh and cruel toward sinners. Rather, when someone happens to be overtaken by sin, they should not immediately reject him or condemn the feeling of one lying fallen, but should extend the inner compassion of charity, offer a hand, raise up the fallen, promise him hope in divine mercy, and thus commend themselves as teachers by the example of those men.

We have said these things not to blame the righteous, but to raise sinners toward hope. First we exalted their virtues; now we have presented their faults, so that we might show the righteous a pattern of caution and sinners a most reliable harbor of salvation.

It is rightly asked how Elijah could lawfully offer sacrifice outside God’s temple, when he both obtained fire from heaven and convicted the prophets of demons. This seems to me defensible by no other argument than the one by which Abraham’s action is defended when, at God’s command, he wished to sacrifice his son. When the one who established the law commands something to be done that he prohibited in the law, the command itself is held in place of the law, since he is the author of the law. For there could have been other miracles, apart from the sacrifice, by which the prophets of the sacred groves might be overcome and convicted; but the Spirit of God who was in Elijah could not, in whatever he did in this matter, act against the law, because he is the giver of the law.

Another question still troubles the mind: why did Elijah appeal to God because Israel, having abandoned God, had killed his prophets and destroyed his altars, when the law had formerly commanded that they could no longer have more than one altar—first in the tabernacle, and afterward in the temple?

The explanation is that, after the ten tribes had been cut off from the house of David and separated from the temple and Jerusalem, those among the ten tribes called Ephraim who worshiped the divine name—and, as must be supposed, resorted to those altars that the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob had once erected in suitable places where God had appeared to them—went back to those altars.

The worshipers of the divine name resorted to these altars, if not to sacrifice, at least to worship the God of their fathers. The sacrilegious Israelites and worshipers of idols saw this and destroyed them, so that there would be no place where true worshipers could pray to the Lord. This is what was already stated above: Elijah restored the Lord’s altar because it had been destroyed.

[Col. 1177B] “And the Lord said to Elijah, ‘Go out and stand on the mountain before the Lord.’ And behold, the Lord passed by, and a great and powerful wind, overturning mountains and shattering rocks before the Lord.”

The statement that a great wind went before the Lord, and the rest, signifies that his coming would benefit the hearts of believers through certain hidden and ineffable signs. For when it says, “overturning mountains and shattering rocks before the Lord,” this is what the Apostle says: “The weapons of our warfare are not carnal but spiritual, for the destruction of strongholds and of every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God” (2 Corinthians 10).

“The Lord was not in the wind, and after the wind an earthquake; the Lord was not in the earthquake, and after the earthquake a fire; the Lord was not in the fire, and after the fire the sound of a gentle breeze.”

The wind before the Lord overturns mountains and shatters rocks because the terror that descends from his coming casts down the height of our hearts and melts their hardness.

But he says that God was not in the wind of the earthquake or in the fire, while he does not deny him in the sound of the gentle breeze. For plainly, when the mind is suspended in the sublimity of contemplation, God is not whatever it is able perfectly to discern. But when it perceives something subtly, it receives what it hears concerning the incomprehensible substance of eternity as though it were the sound of a gentle breeze.

We perceive the sound of a gentle breeze when, through sudden contemplation, we subtly taste the savor of uncircumscribed truth. Then what we know of God is true, when we recognize that we cannot fully know anything about him.

Accordingly, it is rightly added there: “When Elijah heard this, he covered his face with his cloak, went out, and stood at the entrance of the cave.”

Why does the prophet, when he hears the voice of the Lord speaking with him, stand at the entrance of his cave and veil his face? Because, while through the grace of contemplation the voice of heavenly understanding arises in the mind, the whole person is no longer within the cave, since concern for the flesh does not possess the mind; but he stands at the entrance because he is contemplating how to go out from the narrow confines of mortality.

But since he stands at the entrance of the cave and perceives God’s words in the ear of his heart, it is necessary for him to veil his face. For while through heavenly grace we are led to higher understanding, the more sublimely we are raised, the more we must always press ourselves down through humility before our own understanding, lest we attempt to know more than we ought, but know with sobriety. Otherwise, while we investigate invisible things too intently, we may go astray, seeking something corporeal in that incorporeal nature.

To incline the ear and cover the face is to hear the voice of the inner substance through the mind, while turning the eyes of the heart away from every corporeal appearance, lest the mind imagine anything bodily in that nature which is wholly everywhere and everywhere uncircumscribed.

## IX. Elijah’s return to Damascus. III Kings XIX

“And the Lord said to Elijah: ‘Go, return on your way through the wilderness to Damascus. When you arrive there, anoint Hazael as king over Syria, and Jehu son of Nimshi as king over Israel; and anoint Elisha son of Shaphat, who is from Abel-meholah, as prophet in your place. And whoever escapes the sword of Hazael, Jehu will kill; and whoever escapes the sword of Jehu, Elisha will kill.’”

Abel-meholah is one of the principal cities of Solomon. It is now a village, as we read in the Book of Places, in the plain, ten miles from Scythopolis toward the southern region, and it is now called Bethulia.

Damascus, whose name is interpreted as “Drinking blood” or “Offering blood to drink,” bore the figure of the whole world. It is beyond doubt that its inhabitants, by sacrificing their sons to demons, drank and offered blood to drink. For in Scripture blood stands for sin and death, which the wretched seemed to inflict not only upon themselves but also to offer as drink to their imitators.

Hazael, whose name is interpreted as “Work of God,” contained the figure of all the nations. The interpretation “work of God” suits him very well. For it was the work of God that, when Israel had been hardened and had refused utterly to believe in the Lord’s signs and virtues, the peoples of the nations should believe in the Crucified One with complete eagerness of mind.

Alternatively, no one can doubt that “work of God” means “image of God,” restored to the nations through faith in Christ.

For just as a figure had gone before in Jacob and Esau, when the birthright and blessing of the elder son were once transferred to the younger brother, so also in these two—namely, Hazael and Jehu—we understand that, by divine dispensation, the people of the nations, who had been younger, are placed before Israel, the firstborn, in the person of Jehu. As Scripture testifies, the people who had been at the head, because of their continual transgressions and the offense they committed against the Lord, became the tail. When the kingdom was transferred from them, as the Lord had declared, it was given to the people of the nations, who carried out God’s will.

But because it is an expression of divine mercy that all people should be saved, just as Esau, although subjected to his younger brother, was not deprived of blessing, so also here God foretells to Elijah: “I will leave for myself seven thousand men whose knees have not bent before Baal.”

By “I will leave,” he wished it to be understood that this referred to the future; and it is clear that it was fulfilled at the Lord’s coming. These are to be understood as those who, from the whole of Israel, received the faith of Christ through the apostles and possess the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit.

Jehu, whose name is interpreted as “He himself” or “He is,” son of Nimshi, whose name is interpreted as “Touching” or “Handling,” spiritually prefigured the person of the apostles. The interpretation of these names suits them very well.

The blessed apostles truly are always “He is,” because, for their confession of the Trinity and truthful preaching, they live perpetually for God and for the whole world. John also, when writing in his Epistle about the Word of life—that is, the Son of God who assumed flesh—spoke as follows: “Him whom we saw with our eyes, heard with our ears, and our hands touched.”

When it is said to Elijah, “Anoint Elisha son of Shaphat of Abel-meholah as prophet in your place,” it is to be understood as follows: Elisha is interpreted as “Salvation of my God,” Shaphat as “Judging,” and Abel-meholah as “Lament bearing labor.”

The Son of God, who is the true salvation of the faithful and to whom the Father has entrusted all judgment—a judgment in which there will be lament bearing labor for the impious and unbelieving, namely, the torments of Gehenna—could not be contemplated by human beings in the splendor and power of his divinity. Therefore, as the Apostle says, he emptied himself of majesty and, in the prefiguration of Elisha, deigned to assume the form of a servant. He was true man, born from the Virgin’s womb and anointed by the Holy Spirit.

When the narrative says, “Whoever escapes the sword of Hazael, Jehu will kill him; and whoever escapes the sword of Jehu, Elisha will kill him,” this may be understood in the following way.

The sword of Hazael the Syrian is to be understood as the teaching of those who, from among the nations, became divinely inspired witnesses of the Lord’s incarnation, passion, and resurrection, in order to refute the Jewish teachers who concealed this mystery from the peoples.

The sword of Jehu, who was anointed over Israel, is to be understood as the preaching of John, the Lord’s forerunner. Rebuking the Sadducees and Pharisees who came to his baptism, he is recorded to have said: “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath?” (Luke 3).

The sword of Elisha, moreover, is to be understood as evangelical preaching, concerning which it is written that he said: “I have not come to bring peace, but a sword” (Matthew 10), because it in a certain way divides and separates the faithful and righteous from the unfaithful and unjust, and because it kills harmful desires and all vices and sins in the hearts of believers.

Meanwhile the Lord says to Elijah: “I have left for myself seven thousand men who have not bent their knees before Baal, and every mouth that has not worshiped him by kissing his hand.”

It is certain that the one who, while acting rightly, neglects to consider the merits of those who are better extinguishes the eye of his heart through the darkness of pride. Conversely, he greatly illuminates himself through an example of humility when he carefully weighs the good deeds of others. For when he sees externally, and in others, the deeds that he himself has done, he restrains the swelling of pride that strives to break out from his inward sense of uniqueness.

This is why the Lord’s voice says to Elijah, who thought himself alone: “I have left for myself seven thousand men who have not bent their knees before Baal.” When he learned that he was not the only one remaining, the glory of exaltation that had arisen in him from his supposed uniqueness was brought low.

He was a prophet and had often understood heavenly mysteries. How, then, was it difficult for him to recognize that faithful servants of God and others had remained in this world? But here one must carefully observe how wickedly exaltation closes the eye: the man who, while humble, knew God’s hidden things, when exalted did not know even what was manifest.

## X. Elijah calls Elisha to himself. 1 Kings 19

“After this,” it says, “Elijah found Elisha son of Shaphat plowing with twelve yokes of oxen, and he himself was one of the twelve at the plowing. When he came, he threw his cloak over him. He immediately left the oxen, ran after Elijah, and said, ‘Please let me kiss my father and my mother, and then I will follow you.’

“Elijah said to him, ‘Go back; for what was mine, I have done for you.’

“So Elisha returned, took a pair of oxen, and slaughtered them. He cooked their flesh on the plow of the oxen and gave it to the people to eat.”

The twelve yoke of oxen are to be understood figuratively as the twenty-four books of the Old Testament. The twelve plowmen are to be understood as the twelve apostles. Yet the Lord deigned to be the worker among them all, saying, “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15).

The kiss of the father is recognized as a sign of reconciliation.

In the two oxen, the law and the prophecy are to be understood. Through the mystery of his incarnation and passion, our Lord killed their shadows and images in the letter, cooked them on the plow of his cross, and also offered them to the faithful for eating, so that they might now live not according to the letter but according to the spirit.

After this Scripture relates that King Ben-hadad of Syria, besieging Samaria and beginning to attack it, said: “May the gods do these things to me and add these things, if the dust of Samaria will suffice for handfuls for all the people who follow me.”

The meaning is this: Samaria, according to the custom of cities, had earth inside, near the walls, almost level with the walls themselves, so that frequent blows from a battering ram, driven by an enemy’s hand, might knock them down without the support of the adjoining earth. Outside, however, the height of the walls rose far above the surface of the ground, especially since, as Scripture reports, the city itself was situated on the summit of a mountain.

The arrogant king therefore frightened the besieged city by claiming that his army was so numerous that, even if each of his soldiers brought only a stone, a clod of earth, or a piece of wood to construct a mound against the city, a mound could rise from these materials so high that it would appear level with the surface of the city within the walls, enabling the attackers to hurl weapons or torches against the city from equal height.

The king of Israel restrained this presumptuous arrogance with a measured saying: “Tell him, ‘Let not the one who is girded boast as though he were ungirded.’”

There is a difference between one who is girded, one who is ungirded, and one who is not girded. The girded man is one who walks wearing a belt. The ungirded man is one who has just removed his belt—for example, in order to enter a bath, climb into bed, or perhaps put on another tunic. The not-girded man is one who has recently put on his tunic but has not yet secured himself by wrapping a belt around it.

Thus, in a military expedition, the man who has been stationed is rightly called girded—that is, dressed in arms. The man who has completed the battle and returned home victorious is properly called ungirded, because, having laid down his arms, he enjoys the leisure of the desired peace. But one who has not yet begun to fight or to prepare himself for battle is rightly said to be not girded.

The king of Israel therefore said to the king of Syria, who was boasting as though he had already captured Samaria, although he had only begun to besiege it: “Let not the one who is girded boast as though he were ungirded.”

It was as though he plainly said: “Do not boast as though you were already victorious in the hazard of war, when you are still stationed in the battle line and do not know whom victory will follow.”

And he was certainly speaking the truth. For as soon as the battle began, Ben-hadad did not triumph over defeated enemies; rather, after his army had been slaughtered, he fled and returned home.

There is no doubt that Ben-hadad, king of Syria, bore the figure of the devil, who is the prince of this world. Together with thirty-two kings—that is, with all his vices—he does not cease to fight against the human race.

Ahab, whose name is interpreted as “Brother of the father,” bore here the person of the Jews, with whom the devil had previously engaged in conflict.

## XI. On Micaiah’s Vision. 3 Kings 22

Meanwhile Scripture proceeds to recount the vision of the prophet Micaiah, where he says to Ahab:

“I saw the Lord seated upon his throne, and all the army of heaven standing at his right and at his left. And it was said: ‘Who will deceive Ahab, so that he may go up and fall at Ramoth-gilead?’ And one spoke words of one kind, and another of another kind. Then a spirit came forth and said, ‘I will deceive Ahab.’ And it was said to him, ‘By what means will you deceive him?’ He answered, saying, ‘I will go forth and be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.’”

What are we to understand by the Lord’s throne except the angelic powers, presiding upon whose wings, he disposes all things below? What is meant by the army of heaven except the multitude of ministering angels? What, then, does it mean that the army of heaven is said to stand at his right and at his left?

God, who is within all things and also outside all things, and who is unbounded—the truth, eternal blessedness, which is called his right hand—has no left hand, because there is nothing displeasing to him and because he beholds all things together and sees everything at once. But those things in which both a good spirit and an evil spirit dwell are described as having the army of heaven at their right and at their left: by the right, we are to understand the elect angels, and by the left, the reprobate spirits.

For it is not only the good who minister to God—those who help—but also the evil, who test; not only those who raise up people returning from guilt, but also those who burden those unwilling to return.

Nor should it trouble us that even the rejected angels are called the army of heaven. Although they have been expelled from the ethereal heaven, they nevertheless still dwell in the aerial heaven. We know that the waters are suspended in the air, and we call the birds “of heaven”; and concerning these same spiritual beings Paul says: “Against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 6). In announcing their head he says: “According to the prince of the power of this air.”

The army therefore stands at the right and at the left, because the will of the elect spirits agrees with divine mercy, while the understanding of the reprobate, serving wickedness, obeys the judgment of God’s severity.

Hence the spirit is immediately described as springing forth into their midst, through whom King Ahab was to be deceived in accordance with his deserving. For it is not right to believe that a good spirit wished to serve deception by saying, “I will go forth and be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.” Rather, because King Ahab was worthy, by his preceding sins, to be condemned through such a deception, so that he who had often fallen willingly into guilt might at last be seized unwillingly for punishment, by a hidden justice permission is granted to evil spirits: those whom they strangle willingly in the noose of sin, they also drag unwillingly into the punishment of sin.

But how God accomplishes these things while being everywhere present, wholly present everywhere, and always present; how the holy angels and all the lofty and most pure spirits created by him consult his simple, unchangeable, and eternal truth; how they carry out temporally, in accordance with the circumstances of the things to be brought about, what they see to be eternally just in him; and how the fallen spirits, who did not remain in the truth, unable because of the uncleanness and weakness of their desires and punishments to behold and consult the truth present within, await outward signs through creation and are moved by them, whether to do something or not to do it; and how they are compelled by the eternal law by which the universe is governed—bound and constrained either to act when God permits it or to yield when he commands it—would be difficult to embrace and exceedingly lengthy to explain.

## XII. On the Death of Ahab. 3 Kings 22

After the death of Ahab, his son Ahaziah began to reign in his place. Scripture reports concerning him that he fell through the lattice of his upper chamber, which he had in Samaria, and became ill.

Ahaziah, king of Samaria, had separated himself from the house of David. His falling through the lattice appears to signify that heretics or schismatics, even if they seem to climb some height of good action, nevertheless, because they do not possess the structure of the unity of the Church, continually fall back into the weakness of vices, as though relying on the exposed and unsolid supports of their sides; deprived of divine help, they perish through the arrogance of their obstinacy.

## XIII. On the Soldiers Who Were Consumed by Fire. 4 Kings 1

Next the same Scripture relates that Ahaziah sent two commanders of fifty to Elijah. Because they insolently called him a man of God, they were consumed by heavenly fire while he prayed; but a third man who was sent was saved.

Figuratively, the number fifty is a confession of repentance, through which the remission of sins is signified. For the Jews, unwilling to acknowledge Christ as true God and as the prince who bestows forgiveness, say to him: “You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?” (John 8). Such people are extinguished in the burning of the future divine fire.

But the third commander of fifty, because he turned to faith in the Trinity, signifies the mysteries of repentance and therefore deserved to attain forgiveness.

It must be understood that Holy Scripture speaks of a curse in two ways: one which it approves and another which it condemns. A curse is uttered in one way by the judgment of justice, and in another by the spite of vengeance.

A curse by the judgment of justice was pronounced when the first man sinned, when he heard: “Cursed is the earth in your work” (Genesis 3). A curse by the judgment of justice is pronounced when it is said to Abraham: “I will curse those who curse you” (Genesis 12).

Again, because a curse is uttered not by the judgment of justice but by the spite of vengeance, we are admonished by the voice of the preaching Paul, who says: “Bless, and do not curse” (Romans 12); and again the same apostle says: “Nor will the cursers possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 6).

God, therefore, is said to curse, and yet he forbids a human being to curse, because what a human being does through the malice of vengeance, God does only after examination and by the power of justice. Even holy men, when they pronounce a sentence of cursing, do not burst forth into it from a desire for vengeance, but from the judgment of justice. Within themselves they behold God’s subtle judgment, and they recognize what evils arising outwardly ought to be struck by a curse. Thus they do not sin in cursing, because they do not disagree with the inward judgment.

For this reason Peter directed a sentence of cursing against Simon, who offered him money, saying: “May your money be with you for destruction” (Acts 8). By saying not “It is,” but “May it be,” he indicated that he spoke these words not in the indicative but in the optative mood.

For this reason Elijah said to the two commanders of fifty who came to him: “If I am a man of God, let fire come down from heaven and consume you.” The outcome of the case showed how strongly their sentence was confirmed by the reason of truth: Simon perished in eternal destruction, and fire coming down from above consumed the two commanders of fifty.

The virtue that followed therefore testifies with what intention the sentence of cursing was pronounced while the innocence of the one who pronounced it remained intact: the curse absorbed the one who was cursed, even unto destruction.

Thus, from the end of both parties it is gathered that the sentence was hurled against the guilty by one inward judge.

The fact that Elijah, before being taken away and lifted up to heaven, commanded Elisha to remain in Bethel, or at Jericho, or at the Jordan, while Elisha continually swore by the Lord that he would not leave him, appears to have signified that Elisha bore the figure of the apostles. Beginning from the very revelation of faith—for Galgala is interpreted as “revelation”—they clung inseparably to Christ the Lord and did not withdraw from his company until the day of his ascension into heaven.

When they had crossed the Jordan, Elijah said to Elisha: “Ask what you wish me to do for you before I am taken away from you.” Elisha said: “I ask that your spirit become double in me.”

According to the literal meaning of the narrative, Elijah’s spirit was bestowed doubly upon Elisha, because Elisha performed many more mighty works than Elijah. Tropologically, however, Elijah’s spirit was attributed doubly to Elisha because, after the Lord’s ascension, through the coming of the Holy Spirit, a twofold gift of understanding—that is, of the New and Old Testaments—was bestowed upon the apostles.

## XIV. On Elijah’s Being Taken Up. 4 Kings 2

As they went on and walked while conversing, behold, a fiery chariot and fiery horses divided the two, and Elijah went up into heaven in a whirlwind. Elisha saw it and cried out: “My father, my father, the chariot of Israel and its charioteer!” And he saw him no more.

“The chariot of Israel”—that is, the mind of those who see God—may appropriately be understood as the Lord Jesus Christ, who patiently bearing with his elect carries them as though in a chariot, and by his preaching and discipline moves them as a charioteer.

Morally, what does it mean that Elijah is called both chariot and charioteer, except that the charioteer drives and the chariot carries? A teacher, therefore, who both supports the character of the people through patience and instructs them by the words of sacred eloquence is called both charioteer and chariot: chariot, because he carries them by bearing with them; charioteer, because he exercises the peoples through good admonitions.

What, then, does it mean that Elijah is said to have been taken up to heaven? Do we believe that, while he was still placed in this corruptible flesh, he was brought to the rest of that highest peace before the resurrection and ascension of the Lord?

But one heaven is the aerial heaven, and another is the ethereal. The aerial heaven is close to the earth; hence we speak of the birds of heaven, because we see them flying in the air.

Elijah was lifted up into the aerial heaven, so that he might suddenly be led into a certain hidden region of the earth, where he might already live in great rest of body and spirit until he returns at the end of the world and pays the debt of death.

By being lifted up, Elijah signified the Lord’s ascension: Elijah postponed death but did not escape it; our Redeemer, however, did not postpone death but conquered it, destroyed it by rising again, and revealed the glory of his resurrection by ascending.

It should also be noted that Elijah is read to have ascended in a chariot, so that it might plainly be shown that a mere human being needed help from another. Those aids were accomplished and displayed through angels, because he could not even ascend to the aerial heaven by himself, weighed down as he was by the weakness of his nature.

Our Redeemer, however, is not read to have been lifted up by a chariot or by angels, because he who had made all things was, surely, above all things carried by his own power. He was returning to where he was and coming back from where he remained, because through his humanity he had ascended into heaven, while through his divinity he simultaneously contained both earth and heaven.

Nor should it be supposed that Elijah is either in the condition in which the saints will be when, after the day of their labor is completed, they will receive the denarius together, or in the condition of human beings who have not yet departed from this life—although he did depart from it not by death but by translation.

He therefore now possesses something better than he could have possessed in this life, although he does not yet possess what he will rightly possess at the end as a result of the good things done in this life. For they provided something better for us, so that they might not be perfected without us.

Or, if anyone thinks that Elijah could not have merited this if he had taken a wife and fathered children—for it is believed that he had none because Scripture did not say so, although it also said nothing about his celibacy—what will he answer concerning Enoch, who, after fathering children and pleasing God, did not die but was translated?

Why, then, if Adam and Eve had lived justly and chastely fathered children, could they not have yielded their place to those who would follow them by translation rather than by death?
