For if Enoch and Elijah, having died in Adam and carrying in the flesh the succession of death—which they are believed to return to this life in order to discharge, and to die after it has been delayed for so long—are nevertheless now in another life, where before the resurrection of the flesh, before the animal body is changed into a spiritual one, they do not waste away through sickness or old age, how much more justly and plausibly might this have been granted to the first human beings, living without any sin of their own or of their parents, so that, after fathering children, they might pass into some better condition, from which, when the age had ended, they would be changed, together with all the prosperity of the saints, into the evangelical form—not through the death of the flesh, but through the power of God—and much more happily!

He seized his garments and tore them into two parts, and Elisha lifted up Elijah’s cloak that had fallen from him.

Elisha bore the figure of our Lord and Redeemer. His garments are to be understood as the writings of the Old Testament, which were then torn—that is, revealed to human beings—when they were fulfilled through his passion, resurrection, or ascension into heaven.

The cloak of Elijah collected by Elisha is to be understood as the power of the Word, which he left to the world for the glorification of his flesh.

## XV. The Waters Healed by Elisha. 4 Kings 2

While Elisha was living in Jericho, the men of the city came to him and said: “Behold, the dwelling-place of this city is very good, as you yourself, lord, see; but the waters are bad, and the land is barren.”

He said: “Bring me a new vessel and put salt in it.” When they had brought it, he went out to the spring of the waters, threw salt into it, and said: “Thus says the Lord: I have healed these waters, and there will no longer be death or barrenness in them.” So the waters were healed to this day, according to the word that Elisha spoke.

The city of Jericho prefigured the figure of this world. Its dwelling-place, according to the creation of the Creator, is not merely good but, as can be seen, very good in every respect.

Its bad waters are to be understood as the teaching of philosophers and poets, which provokes human minds to the worship of demons, lust, and luxury. The barren land indicates the whole human race, which, having abandoned God the Creator and having its perceptions darkened, served all created things.

Whom else did this miracle prefigure except the Lord Jesus Christ? After the Word became flesh (John 1) and deigned to be baptized by his minister in the Jordan River, he changed the barren waters of Jericho—that is, of this world—into the fruitfulness of the laver, so that whatever was regenerated from them might receive the spirit of life.

In the salt, wisdom is understood; in the vessel, the Lord’s unformed flesh.

## XVI. On the Children Cursed by Him. 4 Kings 2

“He went up,” it says, “to Bethel. And as he was going up by the way, little children came out of the city and mocked him, saying: ‘Go up, baldhead! Go up, baldhead!’ When he had cursed them in the name of the Lord, two bears immediately came out of the forest and tore forty-two of the children. Then he departed from there for Mount Carmel.”

There is no doubt that Elisha, whose name is interpreted as “salvation of God,” bore the person of the Savior.

The Savior, ascending to Bethel—that is, to the heavenly house of God—was mocked by the Jews as by foolish children, those same Jews crying out: “Go up, baldhead! Go up, baldhead!” and, at the place of Calvary, “Crucify, crucify!” (John 19).

Because of this crime of sacrilege, after forty-two years had passed from the Savior’s resurrection and ascension into heaven, the Jewish people were consumed by the Roman commanders, Vespasian and Titus, as though by two bears.

Mount Carmel is to be understood as the Church, to which the Lord transferred his kingdom after rejecting Israel.

## XVII. On the Widow’s Sons Rescued from Slavery. 4 Kings 4

“A certain woman,” it says, “from the wives of the prophets came to Elisha and said: ‘Your servant, my husband, is dead, and you know that he feared God. Now the creditor has come and wishes to take my two sons as his slaves.’”

Elisha said to her: “What do you have in your house? Tell me.” She answered: “A little oil, with which I anoint myself.”

Elisha said to her: “Go and ask your neighbors for not a few vessels. Enter your room, take the oil you have, and pour it into the vessels; you pour, and your sons shall offer the vessels. When they are full, sell the oil and pay your creditor; you and your sons shall live on what remains.”

She went away and did as the man of God had commanded her.

This widowed woman signified the Church of the ancient holy fathers who were under the law. At the Savior’s coming, deprived of the legal commandment as though of a lawful husband, she was left with two surviving sons—that is, with a twofold people.

The creditor of this Church is to be understood as the devil, who before the Savior’s coming held the human race under obligation through original sin and daily sins.

This Church kept a little oil in a small vessel, because she held within the letter of the law and the prophecy of the Old Testament, unrevealed, the grace of evangelical preaching.

But after she was worthy to attain knowledge of the true Elisha—that is, of our Savior—at his direction she asked her neighbors for many empty vessels, because through the preaching of the apostles she gathered into the house of faith a multitude of believers from the various nations.

She also poured into the other vessels the oil she had, because through the mouths of preachers she spread spiritual grace among all nations. By that oil—that is, by the divine oil—she redeemed her sons, because through the gift of the Holy Spirit and the anointing of charity she set herself and all the faithful free from the perpetual slavery of sin.

## XVIII. On Elisha’s Hosts. 4 Kings 4

It happened that Elisha passed through, and there was a prominent woman there who detained him so that he might eat bread. Whenever he passed by, he would turn aside to her to eat bread.

She said to her husband: “I perceive that this is a holy man of God who frequently passes by us. Let us make a small upper room for him, and place in it a bed, a table, a chair, and a lampstand, so that whenever he comes to us, he may stay there,” and so forth.

This Shunammite woman represented the type of the Church. Before she received the true Elisha—that is, our Savior—through faith, she was barren. But after she was worthy to receive the same Lord as a guest in the dwelling-place of her heart, she gave birth to a faithful people as to an only son.

In the upper room, the height of faith is prefigured; in the bed, spiritual rest and the leisure of contemplation. In the table, the unity of faith and harmony of preaching are indicated; in the chair, the authority to teach; in the lampstand, the illumination of faith or the splendor of virtues is expressed.

## XIX. On the Child Who Was Raised. 4 Kings 4

After this Scripture recounts the son of the Shunammite woman, whom Elisha’s servant, sent with a staff, does not raise. But Elisha himself came, stretched himself over the dead child, gathered himself over his limbs, walked back and forth, and breathed seven times into the mouth of the dead child. Through the mystery of compassion he immediately restored him to living light.

This was because God, the author of the human race, grieved as over a dead child when, in pity, he looked upon us extinguished by the sting of iniquity.

And because he brought forth the terror of the law through Moses, he sent the rod as though through a child. For through the law the Lord had held the rod when he said: “If anyone does this or that, let him die.”

The fear of sin, therefore, was unable to raise us from the death of sin; but the grace of gentleness, breathed upon us, lifted us to the condition of life.

The child, however, did not wish to raise the dead with the staff, because, as Paul testifies, “the law brought nothing to perfection” (Hebrews 7).

But Elisha himself came, stretched humbly over the corpse, and gathered himself to equal the limbs of the dead, because, although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings, and found in appearance as a human being (Philippians 2).

He walked back and forth because he calls both the Jews nearby and the nations situated far away.

He breathed seven times over the dead because, through the opening of the divine majesty, the sevenfold grace of the Spirit breathes upon those lying in the death of sin. Immediately the living child began to stir, because the one whom the rod of terror could not raise returned to life through the spirit of love.

## XX. On Naaman Cleansed of Leprosy. 4 Kings 5

Now the narrative of Naaman the Syrian must be continued.

Above we showed that Elisha bore the figure of the Lord and Savior. Naaman, the commander of the Syrian army, who had been a leper and came to be healed by the blessed Elisha at the suggestion of a young maidservant, represented the people of the nations.

The little girl who had been captured from the land of Israel by the Assyrians and taken to Syria, where she served Naaman’s wife, and who told her mistress that if her husband went to the blessed Elisha he would obtain health, is to be understood as the report of the law.

She was called “little” for this reason: as the Apostle says (Hebrews 7), the law was able to bring no one to perfection. For all perfection is in the Lord Jesus Christ.

The report of those things contained in the law concerning chastity and sobriety, patience, justice, hospitality, piety, and the other virtues had reached all nations. Although at that time prophecy flourished in Judea alone, it could not have happened otherwise than that its blessed reputation should also reach those neighboring peoples.

Although they attempted to observe it, it nevertheless served them as though captive, because they were devoted to the worship of idols.

Naaman listened to the girl and came to Elisha to be cleansed of leprosy; the people of the nations heard the report of the law and prophecy and came to Christ to be cleansed from the leprosy of all sins.

But let us see what the blessed Elisha said to Naaman through a messenger. He said to him: “Go and wash seven times in the Jordan.”

When Naaman heard this—that he should merely wash seven times in the Jordan—he became indignant and wanted to refuse. But after receiving counsel from his friends, he agreed to wash, and he was cleansed.

This signified that the people of the nations, before Christ was crucified, did not believe Christ speaking by himself; afterward, however, when the apostles taught, they faithfully came to the mystery of baptism.

Elisha, in the prefiguration of future things, did not wish to see Naaman the Syrian, and yet he did not despise him at all. In the same way, the Lord Jesus Christ did not exclude from his salvation the people of the nations, who did not see him with bodily eyes.

Elisha therefore told Naaman to wash seven times in the Jordan. It should be noted that Elisha sent Naaman to the Jordan River; so Christ was going to send the people of the nations to baptism.

But the fact that Elisha did not himself touch or baptize Naaman signified that Christ did not come to the people of the nations in person, but through his apostles, because he said to them: “Go and baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28).

This also deserves attention: Naaman, who represented the people of the nations, received health in that river which Christ afterward consecrated by his baptism.

When Naaman heard that he should wash seven times in the Jordan, he became indignant and said: “Are not the rivers of my country better—the rivers of Damascus, Abana and Pharphar—so that I may wash in them and be cleansed?”

When he said this, his servants advised him to comply with the prophet’s counsel.

What this signifies must be considered. As we have said, the holy Elisha bore the type of the Lord and Savior, and Naaman represented the people of the nations.

Naaman’s belief that he would receive health from his own rivers indicated that the human race presumed upon free will and its own merits.

But merits of their own, without the grace of Christ, may possess freedom; they cannot receive healing at all.

Therefore, unless the human race, following the example of Naaman, had listened to the counsel of Elisha—that is, had humbly received the gift of baptism through the grace of Christ—it could not have been freed from original and actual leprosy.

Alternatively, the rivers of Damascus, whose waters Naaman the Syrian thought better than the waters of the Jordan, signify the wisdom of this world. Before the people of the nations received faith in Christ, they esteemed this wisdom highly, despised the evangelical commandments, and rejected them.

“Wash seven times,” he said, because of the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, which rested in Christ the Lord. Indeed, when the Lord was baptized in that river, the Holy Spirit came upon him in the form of a dove.

When Naaman therefore descended into the river as a figure of baptism, Scripture says: “His flesh became like the flesh of a little child” (4 Kings 5).

We see this likeness fulfilled in the Christian people, because all who are baptized—whether old or young—are nevertheless called infants. Through Adam and Eve they are born old; through Christ and the Church they are regenerated new.

The first generation leads to death; the second generation leads to life. The first generation produces children of wrath; the second, vessels of mercy, as the Apostle says: “In Adam all die, in Christ all will be made alive” (1 Corinthians 15).

Just as Naaman, an old man, became like a child by washing seven times, so the people of the nations, although old through ancient sins and covered as though with leprosy by many stains of iniquity, are renewed through the grace of baptism, so that no leprosy of either original or actual sin remains in them.

The one who had been bent beneath the weight of crimes is renewed, after the example of Naaman, by the saving bath, like a little child, and is clothed in the first robe. Concerning this the Apostle says: “All of you who were baptized in Christ have put on Christ.”

In Naaman the Syrian’s cleansing, the tenth virtue of Elisha is placed. For the number ten signifies completion or perfection, because the Lord is read to have come at the end of the world, in whom salvation is recognized as having been granted to all sprinkled with the leprosy of unbelief.

But the fact that, after Naaman had been cleansed, he offered gifts to the blessed Elisha, who refused to accept them, signifies the grace of Christ. It is called grace because it is given freely. Thus the Lord himself said to his disciples in the Gospel:

“Heal the sick, raise the dead, cast out demons; you have received freely, give freely” (Matthew 10).

Meanwhile Naaman said to Elisha: “I ask you to grant your servant that I may take a load of earth carried by two mules. For your servant will no longer offer a burnt offering or sacrifices to foreign gods, but to the Lord alone.”

The load of earth carried by two mules prefigured the mystery of Christ’s incarnation. The two peoples—namely, from circumcision and from uncircumcision—did not refuse to carry its mystery in hope of eternal blessedness.

After this the same Scripture relates that Elisha questioned his servant Gehazi:

“Where have you come from, Gehazi?”

He answered: “Your servant did not go anywhere.”

Elisha said: “Was not my heart present when the man turned back from his chariot to meet you? Now, therefore, you have received silver, and you have received garments, so that you may buy olive groves and vineyards, sheep and oxen, male servants and female servants. Moreover, the leprosy of Naaman will cling to you and to your offspring forever.”

Thus the prophet Elisha, although absent in body, saw his servant Gehazi receiving the gifts given to him by Naaman the Syrian, whom the prophet had cleansed from the deformity of leprosy. That wicked servant had thought that he had secretly done this while his master did not see him. How much more will the saints, in that spiritual body, see everything—not only when they close their eyes, but even things from which they are bodily absent?

Then that statement of the Apostle will be perfected: “We know in part and we prophesy in part; but when the perfect comes, the partial will be abolished” (Hebrews 13).

Then, to show by some likeness how far this life is from the life that is to come—not merely the life of ordinary people, but even of those distinguished here by exceptional holiness—the Apostle says:

“When I was a child, I understood as a child, I spoke as a child, I thought as a child; but when I became a man, I abolished the things of a child. Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face; now I know in part, but then I shall know even as I am known” (Hebrews 13).

If, therefore, in this life, where the prophecy of marvelous human beings must be compared with that future life as a child is compared with a young man, Elisha nevertheless saw his servant receiving gifts where he himself was not present, when the perfect comes and the corruptible body will no longer weigh down the soul, but the incorruptible will impede nothing, will the saints need bodily eyes to see what must be seen, when Elisha did not need them to see his absent servant?

For, according to the interpreters of the Septuagint, these are the prophet’s words to Gehazi: “Was not my heart with you when the man turned from his chariot to meet you, and you received money?” and the rest. But the presbyter Jerome translated it thus from the Hebrew: “Was not my heart,” he says, “present when the man turned back from his chariot to meet you?” The prophet therefore said that he saw this with his heart, aided, beyond doubt, in a wonderful manner by God. Yet how much more will all then abound in this gift, when God will be all in all. Nevertheless, those bodily eyes will also have their own function, and each spirit will be in its own place for them through the spiritual body. For the prophet, although he did not need them to see one absent, nevertheless used them to see things present; yet he could have seen those things by the spirit even had he closed them, just as he saw absent things where he himself was not.

Far be it, therefore, for us to say that those saints in that life will not see God with closed eyes, whom they will always see by the spirit; but whether they will also see him through the eyes of the body when they have them open is the question.

For if, in a spiritual body, they will have only as much power as these eyes of ours now possess, then those eyes, without doubt, will not be able to see God in that way. They will therefore have a power of an altogether different kind, if through them that incorporeal nature is to be seen which is not contained in any place but is wholly everywhere.

Gehazi, Elisha’s servant, who, deceived by desire for silver, accepted money from Naaman the Syrian and shortly afterward was struck by the contagion of leprosy, undoubtedly bore the type of Judas the betrayer.

For just as Gehazi served the blessed Elisha in order to acquire money, so Judas clung to the Lord and Savior in order to commit fraud and gather earthly wealth. Thus it is written of him in the Gospel: “Because he was a thief and had the money box, he used to carry off what was put into it” (John 12).

Gehazi, who could have obtained the grace of his master, just as his master had obtained that of the blessed Elijah, was overcome by greed and deserved to be covered forever with a cruel leprosy.

Judas, however, through love of money, lost the grace of the apostleship and ended his life by a noose.

Thus we understand that all wicked priests within the Church are inwardly covered in their souls with the leprosy of sin. Against the Lord’s commandments, they do not administer freely the ministry they received freely; for every work they perform in the Church they seek not future reward but present payment.

Gehazi can also represent the Jewish people, who are struck by the leprosy of sin at the time when the people of the nations are freed from it.

Thus the unbelieving Jews cried out during the Passion: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matthew 27). They deserved to be covered with the leprosy of sin at the very time when, with sacrilegious mouths, they cried out against the heavenly physician: “Take him away, take him away, crucify him!” (John 19).

At that time, therefore, the leprosy remained in them, while grace passed over to us.

Thus also the Apostle Paul spoke to them, saying: “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you first, but since you judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the nations” (Acts 13).

When the teaching of the apostles passed to the nations, the leprosy of sin remained in the wretched Jews.

## XXI. Concerning the Iron Floating. 4 Kings 6

After this, Scripture relates that, when blessed Elisha was going with the sons of the prophets to the Jordan River, and they were cutting wood for themselves, an axe-head fell into the water. The man from whose hand it had fallen cried out to blessed Elisha: “Alas! alas! And this one I had borrowed.” After this, at the place where the axe had fallen, blessed Elisha threw in a piece of wood, and the iron floated.

The Lord Jesus Christ, whose figure Elisha represented, wished to cut down the impiety of the Jews like a fruitless tree through the presence of his body, since John says of him: “Behold, the axe is laid at the root of the trees” (Matt. 3). When the Passion intervened, he left the body itself, as though it were a handle, and descended into the depths of hell; the body, deposited in the tomb, rose to life when the spirit returned to it, as to its own handle.

Or otherwise: We have frequently said above that Elisha bore the type of the Lord Savior. But in that boy, the son of the prophet, from whose hand the axe fell, Christ may also appropriately be understood. The axe that fell appears to signify Adam, or the entire human race. The prophet’s son was therefore holding the axe in his hand, and our Lord and Savior was holding in the hand of his power the human race whom he had created. But just as that axe fell from the prophet’s hand into the depths, so the human race, through pride, shook itself from the hand of almighty God, fell into the river of lust, and submerged itself in the whirlpool of every sin.

That axe therefore lay in the depths because the human race had fallen through an unhappy ruin into the abyss of every crime, as it is written: “I am sunk in the mud of the deep” (Ps. 68). Again: “I have come into the depths of the sea, and the storm has submerged me” (ibid.). For the river in which the axe fell signifies the course of this world, which flows past, flees away, and descends into pleasure or lust. The river received its name from flowing; and because all sinners, clinging to transitory pleasures, are said to flow away, that axe therefore lay oppressed in the river’s mud.

Elisha then came, threw in the wood, and the iron floated. What is it to throw in wood and bring the iron into the light, if not to ascend the gallows of the cross, rescue the human race from the depths of hell, and free it from the mud of every sin through the mystery of the cross?

After the iron had floated, the prophet stretched out his hand, took it, and restored it to its useful service for its master. The same has happened to us: we had fallen from the Lord’s hand through pride, but through the wood of the cross we have returned to the Lord’s hand, or power.

Morally understood, the iron in the handle signifies the gift of understanding in the heart. To cut wood with it signifies rebuking those who act wrongly. Sometimes, when one acts carelessly, when the fall of vainglory is not avoided in the knowledge one has received, the iron is lost in the water, because understanding grows foolish through undisciplined conduct. We know that understanding is given precisely for this purpose: that, through good action, it should be restored before the eyes of the giver.

Hence the man who had lost the iron rightly cried out: “Alas! alas! alas! my lord, and this one I had borrowed.” The elect possess this characteristic: whenever the fault of vainglory furtively steals away their knowledge, they quickly return to their heart; and whatever they find in themselves to be condemnable before the eyes of the strict Judge, they pursue with tears. In their weeping, they carefully examine not only the evils they have committed, but also the good things they ought to have returned from the gift they received. For they recognize themselves as sinners all the more deeply because, through the good things they neglected—things they were able to do—they remain debtors.

Rightly, therefore, the man who had lost the iron cried: “Alas! alas! alas! and this one I had borrowed.” It is as though he said: “Through the dissipation of negligence I lost what I had received from the creditor’s grace in order to return it through good works.”

God never abandons the mind that truly recognizes itself in sin. Hence Elisha immediately came, threw the wood downward, and brought the iron to the surface [Col. 1188D–1189A]. Our Redeemer, looking upon us with mercy, humbles the sinner’s heart and restores to him the understanding he had lost. He submerges the wood and raises the iron, because he afflicts the heart and repairs knowledge.

Thus, in another translation, it is rightly said that he broke the wood and threw it in, and so lifted up the iron. To break the wood is to crush the heart’s arrogance; to throw the wood downward is to humble the elevated heart into recognition, as we have said, of its own weakness. Immediately the iron returns to the surface, because understanding returns to its former use in practical exercise.

Since the gift of understanding, once received, is scarcely preserved amid so many difficulties, we must take great care lest it grow sluggish through idleness, and lest the impulses toward action vanish through the vice of elation. Holy men do not rejoice merely when they understand what they do, but when they do what they have understood. Although, through understanding, they rejoice together in the greater abundance received from the giver’s gift, they nevertheless sorrowfully consider the obligation of action, so that by their conduct they may repay what has been extended to them in thought.

A debtor is foolish who gladly accepts borrowed money but does not consider the time when he must repay it. The joy of receiving is properly moderated when, with diligent foresight, the appointed time for repayment is also kept in mind.

Now the king of Syria was warring against Israel, and he took counsel with his servants, saying: “In such-and-such a place let us set an ambush,” and so forth.

The king of Syria, besieging Samaria, represented the devil, who before the Savior’s coming had shut in the Jewish people through his siege. His cruelty and the hidden ambushes that he displayed against the human race were frustrated by the foreknowledge and power of the true Elisha, that is, the Lord Savior.

The army of the king of Assyria, which he himself sent to capture Elisha, represented the scribes and Pharisees, who were incited by the devil to persecute God. Through the power of that same Lord and Savior, they were blinded by a just judgment; and then, through his mercy, they were fed with the bread of the word of God [Col. 1189B–C] and refreshed with the water of knowledge.

It is reasonably asked how these Syrians could have gone into Samaria if they had been struck with such blindness that they saw absolutely nothing. Those who sought Lot’s door were also struck with this *aorasia* (“blindness”). In the same way, these men, confused by their misfortune, became deranged until they reached Samaria, and thereafter they no longer sought to capture the prophet in this manner.

## XXII. Concerning the Siege of Samaria. 4 Kings 6

After this, Ben-hadad, king of Syria, gathered his entire army, went up, and besieged Samaria. A great famine arose in Samaria, and the city was besieged until a donkey’s head was sold for eighty pieces of silver, and a quarter of a cab of dove’s dung for five pieces of silver, and so forth.

The famine brought upon Samaria signifies the scarcity of the word of God, or the poverty of faith, through which the devil had shut in God’s people before the Savior’s coming.

The donkey’s head sold for eighty pieces of silver signifies pride, which is the beginning of every sin. For it is beyond doubt that, through the donkey—an unclean animal—all the vices of the devil were prefigured, and, as has been said, their head is pride.

All the reprobate preferred to consume this as food, neglecting the Decalogue of the Law and the Gospel’s ogdoad, in which the image of God is present, rather than the bread of the word of God.

The quarter of a cab of dove’s dung, which is said to have been purchased for five pieces of silver and eaten as food, seems to signify that the reprobate people, having abandoned the worship of God and become subject to the five bodily senses, fed themselves through the worship of idols and pretense as though on a certain stench of sins, thereby satisfying the devil.

There is no doubt that the two women, one of whom, compelled by the scarcity of the famine, ate her own son, signified the reprobate multitude among the Jews. Through the poverty of faith, it consumed every good thing that it originally possessed within itself. The other woman, who refused to consent to such a crime, clearly represented the elect people.

[Col. 1190A] There were therefore four lepers near the entrance of the gate, who said to one another: “Why should we remain here until we die?” and so forth.

The four lepers placed outside the city, who announce Israel’s future deliverance, seem to signify those among the Jewish people who first confessed the uncleanness of their sins before the others and were deemed worthy to attain such great grace that they might announce to the rest the devil’s defeat and flight through the victory of Christ’s cross.

The five horses said to have remained in Samaria because of the extreme scarcity of the famine certainly represented the carnal Jewish people, abandoned under the five books of the Law.

That commander who, hearing that an abundance of grain would come through Elisha, refused to believe, represented the scribes and Pharisees. He saw the fertility divinely bestowed upon the Church, but because he refused to believe, he died in this impiety and was trampled underfoot by the faithful.

The Shunammite woman, who, because of the scarcity of the famine and on Elisha’s advice, went from Judea to the land of the Philistines, prefigured the primitive Church, which through the apostles believed in Christ from among the circumcised. Because of the Jews’ unbelief and the poverty of the word of God that had overtaken them, this Church, when the divine Spirit revealed it to her, migrated to the people of the Gentiles.

At the end of the world, after the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, she will return to the former people. When Elijah preaches, she will receive the elect from that same people as though reclaiming, under her own right, their former paternal possession; and then “all Israel will be saved” (Rom. 11).

This is what the high priest Jehoiada said to the priests and Levites in the temple when he brought forth Joash, the son of Azariah, whom he had secretly nourished in the temple for the six years during which Athaliah reigned.

## XXIII. Concerning Joash Anointed King. 4 Kings 11

“Let a third of you enter on the sabbath and keep watch over the king’s house; let another third be at the Gate of Sur; and let another third be at the gate that is behind the dwelling of the shield-bearers. You shall keep watch over the house of Messa; and the two divisions among you, all who go out on the sabbath, shall keep watch over the house of the Lord around the king, and you shall surround him, holding weapons in your hands,” and so forth.

The things that are said or done there are better understood if something more is said about the places in the temple where the events occurred.

The temple itself, apart from the porticoes that surrounded it and were attached to it on every side, had the following dimensions within its walls. This is the first measurement named by the Books of Chronicles: sixty cubits in length and twenty in width. Its entire circuit was surrounded by a court three cubits high, with an entrance on the eastern side. Scripture refers to this in the Book of Kings as follows: “He built the inner court with three rows of dressed stone and one row of cedar timber.” It calls this the inner court because other outer courts were made around it.

The Books of Chronicles say: “He also made the court of the priests, and the great basilica, and doors in the basilica, which he overlaid with bronze” (2 Chron. 4). It calls it the court of the priests because it had been made to keep the others from entering the temple and to indicate that only priests were permitted there.

This same court was closer to the temple wall on the southern, western, and northern sides. On the eastern side, toward the Gate of the Sun, from which it also had an entrance by steps, it extended a great distance away from the temple. In that part it had the altar of burnt offering; in another, ten basins in which the sacrifices were washed; in another, the bronze sea in which the priests entering upon their ministry washed; and in another, the choirs of the Levites who slaughtered the sacrifices and sang psalms.

This court was surrounded on every side by a long building extending greatly in a square. Its inner wall—that is, the wall facing the temple from the four regions of the world—was constructed below throughout in arches, while the outer wall was founded in solid masonry and had bronze doors, as we recalled above: “doors in the basilica, which he overlaid with bronze.” Reinforced by porticoes, it was divided into very large and suitable upper chambers.

Outside this building, another was constructed in a circle according to a similar design; and, around that one, a third was likewise made in the same arrangement, enclosing all the inner areas far and wide. It differed from the earlier buildings only in this: its eastern and northern walls had no doors, because each belonged to the city walls.

These are the courts of which it is sung in the Psalms: “You who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God” (Ps. 133).

Since the house of the Lord had been constructed on moderately level ground, the courts became higher in their walls the farther outward they were. Their foundations were lower, so much so that the outermost courts were four hundred cubits high, yet did not come close to equaling the height of the temple.

The Book of Chronicles makes a general reference to all these structures as follows: “David gave Solomon his son the description of the portico, the temple, the storerooms, the upper chamber, the rooms in the inner sanctuaries, and the house of propitiation, and also of all the courts and chambers around, for the treasuries of the house of the Lord and for the treasuries of the holy things” (1 Chron. 28).

The writing of Josephus—or the picture made by the ancients after it—distinguishes more fully the order in which these things were constructed (Josephus, *Jewish Antiquities*, book 8, chapter 3).

When these arrangements had been made, only the high priest was permitted to enter the Holy of Holies once a year, with the blood of sacrifices. Only purified priests entered the sanctuary before the oracle. All the priests and Levites entered the inner court. Around this court, in the open air—or, if bad weather prevented it, in the surrounding buildings—the Israelite men gathered to pray or to hear the word of God.

In the third order of courts, Israelite women stood in prayer under the open sky; or, if the weather did not permit it, they went beneath the roofs of the nearest surrounding buildings.

In the last order of courts, Gentiles who happened to have gathered for prayer entered. After the times of the dispersion, Gentiles who had recently become Israelites also entered there; after being purified for seven days, they finally proceeded into the inner sanctuaries.

The pavements within or among the courts were all laid with various-colored stone. The doors in the buildings were positioned opposite one another, so that even those standing in the outermost areas could see the temple.

There were twenty-four divisions of priests, Levites, and doorkeepers, which succeeded one another in order over an equal number of weeks. A new company entered upon its service on the sabbath, and after the sabbath the company that had ministered during the preceding week returned home.

But here the high priest proposes the necessity of increasing the forces around the new king. He received into the ranks those whose week of service was beginning, and retained those who had already completed their week of service, preventing them from departing. He had also gathered other Levites from all the cities of Judah, together with the heads of Israelite families, sending centurions for this purpose to Jerusalem, as the Books of Chronicles relate.

When he was about to bring out the king’s son, he divided them in this way: all those who had completed their sabbath service and were about to leave were divided into two groups and, armed, surrounded the king in the inner parts of the court. The remaining multitude—that is, those who were not of the tribe of Levi—guarded the outer doors of the courts against the queen’s fury, should she attempt any hostile action.

The priests, Levites, and doorkeepers who had recently come for the sabbath were divided into three groups. They were to watch over the king’s house—that is, the palace—lest the queen, having gathered an army, defend it against the king; and they were to guard the Gate of the Dwelling of the Shield-bearers, through which one descended from the temple to the palace, as is said below (2 Chron. 12).

They led the king from the house of the Lord and went by way of the Gate of the Shield-bearers into the palace, and he sat upon the royal throne. The Gate of Sur and the House of Messa, mentioned together with the Gate of the Shield-bearers, appear to have been located there.

He calls the shield-bearers the king’s guardians. The Book of Chronicles bears witness to this: after recounting that Rehoboam had made bronze shields in place of gold ones, it adds: “And he gave them to the commanders of the shield-bearers, who guarded the entrance of the palace” (2 Chron. 23).

In that book all these matters are repeated more distinctly:

“A third of you who come on the sabbath, of the priests, Levites, and doorkeepers, shall be at the gates; another third shall be at the king’s house; and another third at the gate called the Foundation. Let all the remaining people be in the courts of the house of the Lord, and let no one else enter the house of the Lord except the priests and those Levites who minister; they alone shall enter, because they have been sanctified. Let all the remaining people keep watch over the Lord’s guards. Let the Levites surround the king, each holding his weapons,” and so forth.

The passage that follows concerning the same matter says: “He brought out the king’s son and placed upon him the diadem and the testimony.” The diadem is the royal insignia worn on the head; by the testimony he signifies the decrees of God’s Law, which prescribe what a king ought to do and how he ought to live.

The Books of Chronicles express this more clearly: “They placed the diadem upon him and gave him the Law to hold in his hand.” It was certainly a matter of great and salutary wisdom that, when the son of the legitimate king succeeded to the throne after the death of the tyrannical and impious queen, observance of God’s Law should accompany him together with the trappings of kingship. Seeing himself set over others in ruling, he should remember that he himself ought to be subject to divine laws and to be ruled by them.

It is said that the temple of the Lord was restored during the reign of the aforementioned King Joash. The statement that no accounting was made with the men who received the money in order to distribute it to the craftsmen, but that they dealt with it faithfully, displays the devotion of those under discussion. They showed such zeal for religion that no one doubted they would handle the Lord’s money without any suspicion of fraud and faithfully bring it, taken from the treasury, to the craftsmen for the fortification of the house, according to each man’s need.

After this, it says, Elisha died, and they buried him. Bands of Moabites came into the land in that same year. Some people were burying a man when they saw the bands; they threw the corpse into Elisha’s tomb. When it touched Elisha’s bones, the man came to life at once and stood upon his feet.

The Moabite bands are to be understood figuratively as demons, who drive the unhappy minds of men toward incest and every detestable work through the goads of vice.

Those who were burying the dead are to be understood as those who, as the apostle James says, turn the impious and sinners from the error of their way to the path of piety and chastity through continual exhortation; they save their souls from perpetual death and cover a multitude of sins.

Or otherwise: Those burying the dead and fleeing the bands should rightly be called those who, wishing to live piously in Christ, flee and avoid every vice and sin, because these produce death. They throw the bodies into the font of baptism, in which, according to the Apostle, believers are buried with Christ, so that thereafter, through communion in his body and blood, they may live with Christ.

## XXIV. Concerning King Amaziah. 4 Kings 12

Regarding Amaziah, king of Judah, it is said: “He struck Edom in the Valley of Salt, ten thousand men, and captured the Rock in battle, and called its name Joktheel.”

The Valley of Salt was the place where salt was made, either from salt-bearing grass that was cut, dried, and burned in many places; or from the waters of salt wells, heated and boiled until they acquired the solidity of salt; or by some other method by which salt is customarily made. It was also in this place that Joab is read to have struck twelve thousand Idumeans.

It should not be passed over that, in place of “the Valley of Salt,” the old edition gives what appears to be the name of a region, “Gemela.”

The Rock is a famous city of Arabia in the same land of Edom. In the Book of Numbers it is called Rekem, and it is still called by this name by the Syrians.

Jectehel, the name that Amaziah the victor imposed upon it, is interpreted as “Assembly of God” or “Help of God.” He acted faithfully so that it might be committed to perpetual memory that he had captured it either through the assembly of God’s people or with God’s help.

## XXV. Concerning King Jeroboam. 4 Kings 14

Regarding Jeroboam, king of Israel, it is said: “He restored the boundaries of Israel from the entrance of Hamath to the Sea of the Wilderness.”

Hamath, now called Epiphaneia, was Israel’s northern boundary. The Sea of the Wilderness, which in Hebrew is called *Arabah*, designates the Dead Sea. In length it extends for 580 stadia as far as Zoar of Arabia, and in width for 1,150 as far as the vicinity of Sodom.

## XXVI. Concerning the Colonists Brought into Samaria by the Assyrians. 4 Kings 17

Regarding those nations brought into Samaria by the king of Assyria, it is said: “Each nation made its own god, and they placed them in the shrines on the high places that the Samaritan people had made; each nation did so in its cities in which they lived. The men of Babylon made Succoth-benoth; the men of Cuth made Nergal; the men of Hamath made Ashima; and the Avvites made Nibhaz and Tartak.”

In the Book of Places it is written that Benoth and Nergal were cities that the Samaritans who had crossed over from Babylonia built in the region of Judea. Ashima was also a town built by those who had come from Hamath. Nibhaz and Tartak were likewise cities that the Avvites established in the same land of Judea.

Nevertheless, according to the sequence of the passage, the names of the idols that these nations had previously worshiped in their own land may also be understood here. For after it had said, “Each nation made its own god,” the statement “The men of Babylon made Succoth, that is, the tabernacles of Benoth,” seems to have been added to complete the thought.

If I am not mistaken, the interpreter would have done better to translate *Succoth* into Latin as “tabernacles” and to set down the name of the idol, *Benoth*, by itself. The same is plainly said later: “Those who were from Sepharvaim burned their sons in the fire to Adrammelech and Anammelech, the gods of Sepharvaim.” There it is shown that Adrammelech and Anammelech were idols of the city of Sepharvaim. Accordingly, it seems to follow that Nergal was the idol of the Cuthites, Ashima the idol of the Hamathites, and Nibhaz and Tartak the idols of the Avvites.

[Col. 1193C] ## XXVII. Concerning Sennacherib. 4 Kings 19

“In the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah, Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, came up against all the fortified cities of Judah and captured them,” and so forth.

The history is clear and needs no interpretation. In the words of the Rabshakeh, however, we must consider his arrogance, which imitates, as though in opposition, a certain prophetic practice. What prophets usually place in their prologues—“Thus says the Lord”—to display the authority and greatness of the speaker, this man now says: “Thus says the great king, the king of the Assyrians.”

Let us consider the Rabshakeh’s words, beginning with what he says: “You trust in that broken reed-staff, in Egypt.” This is false, for no history relates that Hezekiah sent to the Egyptians and sought Pharaoh’s aid.

What he adds—“If you say to me, ‘We trust in the Lord our God’”—is true. But again he joins a lie to the truth, claiming that Hezekiah had removed the Lord’s high places and altars. He had done this not against the Lord but for the Lord: after destroying idolatry and the ancient error, he commanded that the Lord be worshiped in Jerusalem, where his temple was.

When, wishing to demonstrate the smallness of the besieged, he promises two thousand horses for which Hezekiah could not provide riders, this does not arise from the weakness of the Jews, who lacked knowledge of riding. Rather, it arises from their observance of God’s commandments. Through Moses, God had commanded concerning the king of Israel: “He shall not multiply horses for himself, and he shall not have very many wives” (Deut. 17).

To what he had said—“If you say to me, ‘We trust in the Lord our God’”—he craftily and prudently replied that he had come not by his own will but at the Lord’s command.

And Eliakim and the others said to the Rabshakeh:

“Speak to your servants in the Syrian language, if we understand anything,” and so forth.

The Rabshakeh’s accusation is a testimony to Hezekiah: after all the cities of Judea had been captured, he had trusted in the Lord God and had said to the people: “Do not fear or be afraid of the king of Assyria and all the multitude that is with him, for more are with us than with him. With him is an arm of flesh, but with us is the Lord our God, who is our helper and fights for us.” And, it says, “the people were strengthened by these words of Hezekiah” (2 Chron. 32).

Therefore the Rabshakeh wishes to destroy what Hezekiah had built, and he says to the people: “Let not Hezekiah deceive you, and let him not give you confidence in the Lord God” (Isa. 36).

Then, adding threats and terror, he says: “That you may eat your own dung and drink the urine of your feet with you.” By these words he shows that they are to be overcome by hunger, want, and thirst. At the same time, he joins enticement to fear, so that those whom he had not conquered through terror he might deceive through promises and persuasion, saying:

“Do what is beneficial with me.”

The meaning, therefore, is: “Do,” he says, “what benefits you and turns to your blessing.” Or he means this: “Bless the king of Assyria and praise him as lord; confess him, so that you may obtain rewards.”

“Until I return from Egypt, or return after capturing Libnah, live in your city and enjoy your possessions. Afterwards I shall come and transfer you to a land like your own.”

Some think that the land of Media was promised to them, since it resembled the land of Judea both in location and in its produce.

When he adds, “Where is the god of Hamath, and of Arpad, and of Sepharvaim? Did they deliver Samaria from my hand?” he shows that the Samaritans had served the gods of all those cities or nations. Since they were not gods but idols, he rightly shows that the worshipers of vanity had, as was fitting, been overwhelmed.

Hamath is a city of Coelesyria, now called Epiphaneia, near Emesa, as we noted above. Arpad is a city of Damascus, which Jeremiah also records as having been conquered by the king of Assyria.

Sepharvaim, which in the plural signifies “books” or “letters,” is the name of the places from which the Assyrians migrated and settled in Samaria, as we find in the Books of Places. In Isaiah, however, this also appears to be the name of a city, where it plainly says: “Where is the god of the city of Sepharvaim?” Although it is expressed in the plural, as with Thebes and Athens.

In place of Ana and Ava, the old edition gives what appears to be the name of a single city, “Ana and Ava”; and this is indeed how it is written in Hebrew. But because the syllable *v*, placed in the middle of the name, signifies a conjunction among them, it can also be divided so as to read “Ante and Gave,” as Aquila translated it, or “Ana and Ava,” as our translator rendered it.

All the people were silent and did not answer him a word, for they had received the king’s command that they should not answer.

Hezekiah was truly acting justly, doing everything faithfully and with deliberation. For this reason he had ordered that the blaspheming Assyrian should not be answered, lest he provoke him to greater blasphemies.

Eliakim and the others with him entered Hezekiah with their garments torn.

Leaving aside what is obvious, let us discuss only what contains a hidden meaning. They tore their garments because they had heard the Rabshakeh blaspheming. The king himself also tore his garments because he believed that it was on account of his own sins and those of the people that the Rabshakeh had come as far as the gates of Jerusalem and had spoken such things against the Lord.

He was therefore wrapped in sackcloth instead of royal attire. Going from the palace to the temple, he sent Eliakim the high priest, Shebna the scribe, and the elders among the priests to Isaiah the prophet, son of Amoz.

Here we should consider the king’s humility and prudence. He himself went to the temple, while he sent the leaders of the people and the elders of the priests to Isaiah the prophet, son of Amoz, clothed not in priestly robes but in sackcloth.

“They said to him,” it says: “Thus says Hezekiah: This is a day of tribulation, destruction, and blasphemy”—a day of our tribulation, of God’s destruction, and of the enemies’ blasphemy.

He compares it to a woman in labor and suffering, because the children have come to the time of birth, but the woman in labor has no strength. In the literal sense, we see this occurring through sins: when enemies attack, our defenders are prepared, but they are in no way strong enough to carry out what has been prepared.

For it is written: “The spirit of counsel and fortitude shall rest upon him.” These two are necessarily joined together, because neither strength without counsel can be useful nor counsel without strength.

What benefit, then, do those prepared by counsel provide when they do not proceed to battle through strength?

King Hezekiah, therefore, afflicted and troubled, says: “This is a day of tribulation and blasphemy; the children have come to the time of birth, but the woman in labor has no strength.”

The children come to the time of birth when suitable counsels advance as far as the desire to carry out the work. But the woman in labor has no strength when a weak person does not bring such counsels to any useful result through the birth of action.

The passage continues:

“Perhaps the Lord your God will hear all the words of the Rabshakeh, whom his master, the king of Assyria, has sent.”

We do not dare call the Lord of us all “our Lord,” since, while he is angry, we suffer such things; rather, we call him “your Lord.” Yet we possess this confidence in vengeance: that the living God is being blasphemed by a worshiper of dead idols.

When the servants of King Hezekiah came to Isaiah, Isaiah anticipated them. He had heard even the absent king, and he told them what they should say to their master, with humility joined to the confidence of a clear conscience.

“Say,” he says, “to your master, who is your Lord—for my Lord says this: Do not fear the words with which not you but I have been blasphemed. Behold, I shall send him a spirit, and he shall hear a report, return to his own land, and I shall strike him down with the sword in his own land.”

Thus Hezekiah would hear both the things he desired: that he would be delivered from the siege and danger, and that the hostile and enraged king would die in his own land.

When the Rabshakeh returned, he found the king of Assyria attacking Libnah, and so forth.

Herodotus relates that Sennacherib, king of Assyria, fought against the Egyptians and besieged Pelusium; when the earthworks had already been constructed and the city was about to be captured, Tirhakah, king of the Ethiopians, came to its aid, and in one night 185,000 men of the Assyrian army fell from pestilence near Jerusalem. Berossus, the Chaldean writer of history, gives the fullest account.

[Col. 1195C] When Hezekiah had received the letters from the messengers’ hands and read them, he went up into the house of the Lord and spread them out before the Lord, and so forth.

Against the blasphemies of King Sennacherib, Hezekiah took up solid weapons. He went again to the temple and spread the letters before the Lord, boldly entreating him. He asserts that the one God is living; by this we understand the idols to be images of the dead.

Isaiah sent to Hezekiah, saying: “Thus says the Lord God of Israel: I have heard what you prayed to me concerning Sennacherib, king of Assyria. This is the word that the Lord has spoken concerning him:

‘The virgin daughter of Zion has despised you and mocked you; the daughter of Jerusalem has shaken her head behind you.’”

Because Hezekiah had prayed to the Lord so boldly and had not sent for Isaiah as he had done before, the prophet himself did not go to him. Instead, he sent messengers to speak God’s word to him.

The following judgment of the Lord concerns Sennacherib, against whom Hezekiah prayed: “The virgin daughter of Zion and the daughter of Jerusalem.” She is called both virgin and daughter because, while all the nations worship images, she alone preserves the chastity of the worship of God and the service of the one divinity.

“She mocked you and despised you.” Since she had not answered you in person, lest she provoke you to greater blasphemies, after you depart she will shake her head, confident of vengeance and secure in punishment.

And this is what she has said: “You have acted proudly not against me but against the Lord; nor did you do this through yourself, but through your servants, so that the arrogance of the blasphemer might be greater. For you said that you had ascended the heights of the mountains with the multitude of your chariots and had cut down the peaks of Lebanon, its cedars and fir trees.”

These words should be understood either metaphorically of all the nations and their rulers; or of Jerusalem, which is interpreted as “Lebanon,” so that its cedars and fir trees refer to the powerful and nobles, its lofty summit to its highest point, and the forest of Carmel to the temple.

When he adds, “I dug and drank water, and with the sole of my foot I dried up all the channels of the embankments,” this may be understood historically to mean that, because of the multitude of his army, he dried up all the streams and was compelled to dig wells for himself. According to the translation, it may mean that he devastated with his army all the peoples who are sometimes represented under the name of waters.

Did you not hear what I did long ago, from ancient days? I fashioned it, and now I have brought it about. The fortified cities of warring hills shall be reduced to a heap; and those who dwell in them, weakened in hand, trembled and were put to shame. They became like the grass of the field and the green growth of the rooftops, which withers before it reaches maturity. Your dwelling and your going out, and your way, I knew beforehand, as well as your fury against me. You raged against me, and your arrogance rose into my ears.

These words are to be understood as spoken by the Lord against the Assyrian’s statements: the Lord answered his blasphemy in this way: “Do you not know that you did these things by my will, and that I foretold these future events and commanded that they be carried out through you? Therefore, what I had once decreed has now been fulfilled: the hills—that is, the rulers who fought among themselves—and the most strongly fortified cities, when I withdrew my hand and gave them no customary aid, were uprooted, trembled, and perished. They were compared not to fruitful olive trees, vineyards, or other productive trees, but to hay, grass, and the plants of rooftops, which hinder crops and wither before reaching maturity.

“Therefore I knew beforehand your sitting, your going out, and your coming in; I spoke through the prophets about the madness with which you were to rage against me. Through them I knew that long ago you would say: ‘I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of heaven I will set my throne, and I will be like the Most High’ (Isa. XIV). Thus your fury and your arrogance have reached my ears, and I will no longer endure you, so that you may understand that, although you were able to do these things, you were not able to do them by your own strength, but by my decision. For the impious nations and unfruitful trees deserved to be cut down and fall through you, as through my axe and saw.

“Therefore I will put a ring in your nostrils and a bit in your lips, so that I may restrain the mouths of blasphemers and you may no longer dare to speak such things; I will place a bridle on your lips, one that will tame your ferocity and lead you back to Assyria.”

But for you, Hezekiah, this shall be the sign: Eat this year what you find growing, and in the second year what grows of its own accord; but in the third year sow and reap, plant vineyards, and eat their fruit.

The prophet speaks all these words to Hezekiah through messengers. What Sennacherib said and what the Lord answered him do not belong directly to the present discourse, lest he perhaps doubt the future events that had been foretold. The prophets therefore had all the greater credibility among the people because they recalled not only things that would happen many centuries later, but also things that would be fulfilled immediately or after no very long interval: namely, that within two years the king of the Assyrians would perish and security would be restored to Jerusalem. [Col. 1196B]

“This shall be the sign of the things I announce as future: this year you shall eat what you find; in the second year, what grows of its own accord; but in the third year, once the Assyrian has been driven away and the siege lifted, sow and reap, plant vineyards, and eat their fruits. For the survivors of this city, now surrounded by the enemy army and not believing that they will escape, will receive such abundance and prosperity in all things that they will be filled with the densest fruits, like a tree firmly established by a deep root.

“And whatever remains of the house of Judah shall send its root downward and produce fruit upward.”

What else should we understand by “roots” in this passage except hidden thoughts, which emerge secretly but rise openly in the display of action? To send a root downward, therefore, is to multiply a good thought in hidden places. To produce fruit upward is to demonstrate through the effectiveness of a right action what one has conceived. Thus it sends its root downward so that it may produce fruit upward, as though it were said openly: “In the depths the thought is born, so that in the heights the recompense may be given.”

For from Jerusalem and from Mount Zion survivors shall go out, and they shall fill the land of Judah, not by their own merit but by the mercy of God—indeed, by the zeal with which he was zealous for his people against the impious. When the passage finally adds, “For my sake and for the sake of David my servant,” it signifies that they are preserved not by their own merit but by God’s clemency—or rather, by the memory of their father David. Through him they are reminded both of their own negligence and of his faith and righteousness. God loves righteousness so greatly that even the descendants of holy people are protected, not because of their own merit, but because of the virtue of their ancestors. [Col. 1197A]

It happened, therefore, on that night that the angel of the Lord came and struck the camp of the Assyrians—185,000 men. Concerning this also we read in Chronicles: “And the Lord sent an angel who struck every mighty man and warrior and leader of the army of the king of Assyria; and he returned with shame to his own land” (2 Chron. XXXII).

One hundred and eighty-five thousand of the strongest men were slain by one angel in a single night. Savage death swept through them without wounds, separating their souls from their bodies at the Lord’s command. The king of the Assyrians himself was spared for this reason: so that he might recognize the power of God and silence his blaspheming mouth, and become a witness to the majesty of the one whom he had shortly before despised.

The almighty God accomplishes many such things through angels—not so that he may learn from them, but so that they may act or announce through his word what he wishes, even without bodily sound. Sent by him to whomever he wills, they hear everything from him through that word of his—that is, in his truth they discover what they must do, and what must be announced, to whom, and when.

Nevertheless, God does not make human beings blessed through the angels, but from himself he makes both angels and human beings blessed. Nor did he learn anything at any point from anyone, whether angels or human beings, so that he might know it. Rather, before the beginning, he foreknew all future temporal events and, within them, what we would ask of him and when, and whom and concerning what matters he would hear or not hear. He foreknew this without beginning. He knows all his creatures, spiritual and bodily, not because they exist, but because he knows them and therefore they exist.

When he rose at dawn, he saw all the bodies of the dead, and, gnashing his teeth, he departed. Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, returned and remained in Nineveh. While he was worshiping in the temple of Nesrach, his god, Adrammelech and Sharezer, his sons, struck him with the sword and fled to the land of Armenia; and his son Esarhaddon reigned in his place.

When this king had returned to Nineveh, the seat of his kingdom, and worshiped in the temple of his god Nesrach as though he had carried off victory over his enemies, and entered the shrine of his idol in triumph and rejoicing, the one who had despised the true God was slaughtered in the sanctuary of a false deity. He did not perish by an angel’s sword, which would have been common to many, but by the murder committed by his sons, who fled to the land of Ararat. Scripture testifies that Esarhaddon, his son, who reigned in his place, sent inhabitants of Samaria there so that the land would not remain uncultivated. [Col. 1197D]

Ararat is a region of Armenia, a plain through which the river Araxes flows. It is extraordinarily fertile and lies at the foot of Mount Taurus, which extends as far as that place. Therefore the ark in which Noah and his children were rescued, after the flood had ceased, was not carried generally to the mountains of Armenia called Ararat, but to the highest mountains of Taurus, which overlook the plains of Ararat.

## XXVIII. On Hezekiah’s Illness

*4 Kings XX*

“In those days Hezekiah became sick unto death, and Isaiah the son of Amoz the prophet came to him and said: Thus says the Lord: Set your house in order, for you shall die and not live.”

“The Lord disciplines the one he loves, and chastises every son whom he receives” (Heb. XII).

So that Hezekiah’s heart would not be lifted up after his unbelievable triumphs and victory in the midst of captivity, he was visited by bodily illness and heard that he was going to die, so that, turning toward the Lord, he might move him to change his sentence.

Yet nothing that happens to human beings in this world occurs without the hidden purpose of almighty God. For God, foreknowing all future events, decreed before the ages how they would be ordered throughout the ages. It has already been determined how much worldly prosperity will accompany each person, and how much adversity will strike each one, so that neither excessive prosperity may lift up his chosen nor excessive adversity weigh them down.

It has likewise been determined in eternal truth how long each person will live temporally in this mortal life. For although the almighty God added fifteen years to King Hezekiah’s life, when he allowed him to die, he nevertheless foreknew that he would die at that time.

Here a question arises: How could the prophet say to him, “Set your house in order, for you shall die and not live,” when a sentence of death had been pronounced upon him, but life was immediately added in response to his tears? Through the prophet the Lord announced the time at which he was to die; but by the generosity of his mercy he postponed his death until the time that he had foreknown before the ages. The prophet was therefore not false, since the time of death was made known at which that man deserved to die; nor were the Lord’s decrees overturned, since it had also been fixed before the ages that, through God’s generosity, the years of his life would be increased. The span of life unexpectedly added outwardly had been established inwardly without any alteration in God’s foreknowledge. [Col. 1198B]

Hezekiah turned his face toward the wall. Since he could not go to the temple, he turned toward the wall of the temple, beside which Solomon had built the palace; or simply toward the wall, so that he would not appear to be displaying his tears to those sitting with him.

And he said: “I beg you, Lord; remember, I pray, how I have walked before you in truth and with a perfect heart, and have done what was pleasing in your sight.”

He now calls his heart perfect because he had destroyed the idols, opened the doors of the temple, crushed the bronze serpent, and done the other things that Scripture records in the Books of Kings and Chronicles.

And he wept with great weeping because of the Lord’s promise to David, which he saw would perish with his own death. At that time Hezekiah had no children; only after the third year of the life granted to him did he father Manasseh.

Thus all his weeping arose from the fact that he had despaired that Christ would be born from his offspring. Often righteous people, afflicted by certain necessities, are compelled to confess their own deeds; but when the wicked hear their words, they judge that they were spoken through pride rather than truth. They weigh the words of the righteous from their own hearts and do not believe that good things can be spoken humbly.

For just as it is a grave fault for someone to claim arrogantly what he is not, so it is often no fault at all to speak humbly of the good that one possesses. Hence it frequently happens that the righteous and the wicked have similar words, though their hearts are always entirely different. Through the very words by which the Lord is offended by the wicked, he is also pleased by the righteous.

For when the Pharisee entered the temple, he said: “I fast twice a week; I give tithes of all that I possess.” Yet the tax collector went away more justified than he (Luke XVIII). Likewise King Hezekiah, afflicted by bodily suffering and having reached the point of death, said in compunction during his prayer: “I beg you, Lord; remember how I have walked before you in truth and with a perfect heart.”

The Lord nevertheless did not despise or reject this confession of his perfection, but immediately heard him in his prayers. Behold: the Pharisee justified himself in his actions, while Hezekiah asserted himself to be righteous even in his thoughts. The one displeased the Lord by this; the other pleased him by it. Why was this so, except that almighty God weighs the words and thoughts of each person, and that what is spoken with a humble heart is not arrogant in his ears? [Col. 1198D]

And the word of the Lord came to Isaiah, saying: “Return and say to Hezekiah, the leader of my people: I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears. Behold, I have healed you, and on the third day you shall go up to the temple of the Lord.”

He is also called Hezekiah, leader of the people and son of David, whose works he followed, for he had done what was right according to all that David his father had done. His prayer was heard; his tears were seen—how he had walked before the Lord in truth and with a perfect heart, had wept with great weeping, and had done what was pleasing in his sight. [Col. 1199A]

“And I will add fifteen years to your days. I will also deliver you and this city from the hand of the king of Assyria, and I will protect this city for my sake and for the sake of David my servant.”

According to certain causes belonging to future events, Hezekiah was going to die; God added fifteen years to his life, doing precisely what he had foreknown before the foundation of the world that he would do and had preserved in his will.

He therefore did not do something that was not going to happen. Rather, what he foreknew that he would do was more truly destined to happen. Nevertheless, those years would not properly be called “added” unless they were added to something that had been otherwise determined according to other causes.

According to certain lower causes, then, he had already completed his life; but according to those causes that lie in the will and foreknowledge of God—who from eternity knew what he would do at that time, and what truly was going to happen—he was to end his life when he did end it. For although it was granted to him when he prayed, God nevertheless foreknew that he would pray in such a way that such a prayer ought to be granted. His foreknowledge could not be deceived, and therefore what he foreknew necessarily came to pass.

The fifteen years granted to King Hezekiah’s life through God’s mercy mystically signify that whoever preserves the fullness of both Testaments attains the reward of eternal salvation and, through the completion of the Law and the fullness of the Gospel, passes into the blessedness of eternal life.

And Isaiah said: “Bring me a cake of figs.” When they had brought it and placed it upon his ulcer, he was healed. From this we learn that medicine grounded in use and experience is not to be despised, since God also made use of it.

Afterward Isaiah said: “This shall be the sign from the Lord that the Lord will perform the word he has spoken. Do you want the shadow to advance ten lines, or to return ten steps?”

And Hezekiah said: “It is easy for the shadow to advance ten lines. I do not want that; let it return backward ten steps.”

Then the prophet Isaiah called upon the Lord, and he brought the shadow back through the lines by which it had already descended on the sundial of Ahaz—ten steps.

The name “steps” has the same meaning as “lines”: namely, the divisions of the hours, which we customarily mark as twelve during the day on a sundial. The steps had been constructed by mechanical art in such a way that, as the shadow descended through each one, it marked off the intervals of the hours.

It was the tenth hour of the day when he said these things to the king. “Do you want,” he said, “the shadow to advance ten lines as the sun proceeds over the earth through the northern regions toward the east, following the course it habitually makes beneath the earth; or do you want the shadow to return backward by the same number of steps, with the sun itself also returning eastward through the southern region?”

The king replied: “It is easy for the shadow to advance ten lines. I do not want that; let it return backward ten steps.”

He saw that it might be a greater miracle if the sun followed a course contrary to its own, than if, proceeding along its customary path—although much higher, that is, carried above the earth toward the east—it flew onward as though it were bringing the morning of a second day without the intervention of night.

Those who live on the island of Thule, which lies beyond Britain at the furthest boundaries of Scythia, see this happen for several days every summer. While the sun is at setting and beneath the earth for the rest of the world, it nevertheless appears above the earth throughout the entire night; and one can clearly see how, after setting openly, it returns low toward the east, until at the appropriate time it is restored to the whole world by its common rising. Both the histories of the ancients and people of our own age who come from those regions report this most abundantly.

Those who inhabit the interior southern regions, however, can never see the sun return from west to east through the southern skies.

To give readers a clearer understanding of the matter—since the sign was both of the present time and a type of the future—just as the sun returned to the beginning of its course, so that years were added to Hezekiah’s life, may the spans of life also be extended for us, who live in the week and the eighth day, through Christ’s resurrection.

Or certainly, the ten steps of the sun’s descent represent the successive periods through which the shadow of Christ descended; and through those same steps Christ, the Sun of righteousness, rose again through the resurrection. [Col. 1200A]

The first step of the descent was in the angels, in whom he deigned to appear to the ancient fathers, because he was the messenger of the great counsel. Thus he also speaks to Jacob: “And the angel of God said, ‘I am the God to whom you anointed a pillar and made a vow’” (Gen. XXXI), so that he might show himself both as an angel and as God.

The second step of the descent was in the patriarchs, because, as the Apostle says, he himself worked in them all.

The third was in the giving of the Law, because he himself also spoke in the Law.

The fourth step was in Joshua, who introduced the people into the promised land.

The fifth was in the judges, because through them he himself ruled the same people.

The sixth was in the kings of the Jews, because he himself reigned in them.

The seventh was in the prophets, because through them he was announced.

The eighth was in the high priests, because he himself is the Father’s supreme Priest.

The ninth was in the human being.

The tenth was in the Passion.

Through these ten steps Christ descended through the shadow of the Law; and after his resurrection Christ, the Sun of righteousness, ascended to heaven by those same steps, illuminating all that shadow of the Law with the rays of truth, revealing what was obscure, opening what was closed, and laying bare everything that was straight.

At that time Merodach-baladan, king of Babylon, sent letters and gifts to Hezekiah, for he had heard that he had been sick.

“At that time”—that is, in the same year in which the events related above took place—Merodach-baladan, king of Babylon, sent books and gifts to Hezekiah. Among them the observation of the stars was practiced, and the courses of the heavenly bodies were known through long use and training, as is also shown in the account of the Lord’s birth.

They understood that the sun had turned back and that the length of the day had been doubled, and they recognized that it served the one whom they believed to be God alone. When they investigated the cause and explanation of this miracle, rumor flying throughout all the nations, they learned that even the course of the most conspicuous heavenly sign had been changed because of the illness of the king of Judah. [Col. 1200C]

The Book of Chronicles also testifies to this most fully, saying: “This is Hezekiah, who carried out prosperously in all his affairs whatever he wished; nevertheless, when the Babylonian princes who had been sent to him came to inquire about the sign that had occurred over the earth, God left him so that he might be tested and that everything in his heart might become known” (2 Chron. XXXII).

He was left to temptation because, after such a great victory, the return of the sun, and the congratulations of the most powerful kingdom, his heart was lifted up. Accordingly, the same book says: “Many brought victims and sacrifices to the Lord in Jerusalem, and gifts to Hezekiah king of Judah, and he was exalted before all the nations. In those days he became sick unto death, and he prayed to the Lord, and he heard him and gave him a sign; but he did not repay according to the benefits he had received, because his heart was lifted up, and wrath came against him and against Judah and Jerusalem” (ibid.).

Again, Holy Scripture speaks of the lifting up of his heart and adds that it was mitigated by repentance: “Afterward he humbled himself because his heart had been lifted up, both he himself and the inhabitants of Jerusalem; and therefore the wrath of the Lord did not come upon them.”

In those days Hezekiah rejoiced at the arrival of the envoys of Merodach-baladan, whom the Hebrews claim to have been the father of Nebuchadnezzar, and at the offering of gifts and the congratulations on his recovery.

## XXIX. On Hezekiah’s Wealth Displayed in Boasting

*4 Kings XX*

“He showed them the house of his spices, the treasuries of silver and gold, the spices and finest ointment, and all the treasuries of his vessels. There was nothing that he did not show them in his house and throughout all his dominion.”
