For this reason he most justly deserved God’s anger: he showed them not only his own treasures and the treasures of his palace, but also those of the temple. Certainly that was within his authority, since he had previously removed the golden plates from its doors.

The prophet Isaiah then entered King Hezekiah’s presence. [Col. 1201A]

Again, after his bodily recovery and the greatness of the sign, we see another opportunity for pride presented to him—an opportunity that a prudent worshiper of God ought to have avoided. He should not have displayed to foreigners the riches he possessed through God’s gift. From this we learn, according to the tropological interpretation of the Law, that pearls should not be cast before swine, nor what is holy given to dogs (Matt. VII).

The one who is faithful in spirit conceals his affairs; whoever fails to do this weakens all his virtue, and his posterity perishes. When manly strength has been lost, he is reduced to feminine softness.

Isaiah therefore entered the king’s presence and, as though ignorant, asked: “What did these men say, and from where did they come?”

He asked two questions: what they had said and from where they had come. He answered one and omitted the other:

“They came to me from a distant land, from Babylon”—the farther the land was from which they had come, the more glorious, he implied, was the king for whose sake they had come.

“And they came to me,” he said. He should instead have said: “They came to glorify God, because of the greatness of the sign, from Babylon, the most powerful city in the whole world.”

Again Isaiah asked: “What did they see in your house?”

He answered partially and truthfully: they had seen everything in his house, and there had been nothing that he had not shown them among his treasures. But he kept silent about the other matter, for fear of causing offense: that he had shown them everything under his authority—without doubt, including the temple vessels.

Because of these things, Isaiah pronounced the sentence in the word of God:

“Hear the word of the Lord of hosts: The time will come when everything that is in your house—and not yours alone, but acquired through the labor of your fathers—will be carried away to Babylon, and some of your descendants will become eunuchs in the palace of the king.”

From this the Hebrews wish to infer that Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, who were of royal descent, were made eunuchs. There is no doubt that they served Nebuchadnezzar; but we must not believe that they were eunuchs. If they had been, that ruler who instructed them while they were still boys would not have feared their physical beauty and appearance, since the appearance of the face in boys who have been castrated normally deteriorates.

Among the ancients it was also customary to call chamberlains and palace guards “eunuchs,” even when they had wives and had not been physically castrated. [Col. 1201C]

And Hezekiah said: “The word of the Lord that he has spoken is good; let there only be peace in my days.”

For this the Hebrews criticize him, asking why he did not imitate the goodness of Moses, who said to God: “Either forgive them this offense, or, if you will not, erase me from the book that you have written” (Exod. XXXII).

What does the prophet’s judgment against King Hezekiah signify here except the thoughts of arrogant hypocrites, who seek the admiration of human beings? In everything hypocrites do, they seek human praise through hidden thoughts. When they are about to act, they think of their own praise; when praised, they silently turn over in their thoughts the fact that they have appeared distinguished in their deeds while wearing the costume of piety.

When they swell with favor and grow proud within themselves, they often silently marvel even at their own greatness. They wish to appear greater to themselves day by day and expand their deeds through remarkable inventions. For just as virtues weaken every vice, arrogance strengthens it: it compels the mind to renew its youth and to be strong beyond its powers, since the love of praise commands what the strength of health refuses.

Hence, as we have said, they seek witnesses for their deeds. If witnesses to the deed happen to be lacking, they themselves recount what they have done. When they begin to be carried away by praise, they often add something false to the very deeds they report themselves to have performed.

But even when they speak the truth, by speaking it they make those deeds alien, because, having been rewarded with the praise they sought, they are deprived of the true and inward reward. In revealing their good deeds, they show the evil spirits, lurking like enemies, what they may plunder.

Thus the well-known fault of Hezekiah represented the life of all such people. After he had cast down 185,000 enemies through one prayer and in the space of a single night, with an angel striking them; after he had brought the sun, already near its setting, back into the higher regions of heaven; and after he had prolonged a life already contracted by the approach of death into a longer span of time, he received the messengers of the Babylonian king and showed them all the good things he possessed. But immediately he heard the prophet’s voice:

“Behold, days are coming, and everything that is in your house will be carried away to Babylon; nothing will be left, says the Lord.”

In the same way hypocrites, after they have grown through great virtues, neglecting to beware of the snares of evil spirits and unwilling to conceal those virtues, make their good deeds the property of their enemies by displaying them. By betraying them, they suddenly lose whatever they have labored for so long to accomplish.

Hence the Psalmist says: “He delivered their strength into captivity, and their beauty into the hand of the enemy” (Ps. LXXVII). The strength and beauty of the arrogant are delivered into the enemy’s hands because every good that is displayed through the desire for praise is handed over to the power of the hidden adversary.

Those who expose their riches to the knowledge of their enemies provoke them to plunder. For as long as we are separated from the security of our eternal homeland, we walk along the road of robbers lying in wait. Whoever fears being robbed on the journey must necessarily conceal the good things he carries.

Wretched are those who, desiring human praise, dissipate within themselves the fruits of their labors! When they desire to display themselves to foreign eyes, they condemn what they do. When evil spirits provoke them to boast, they strip them of their works by taking those works captive, as we have said.

For this reason Truth says through the Gospel: “Let your left hand not know what your right hand is doing, so that your alms may be in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will reward you.”

For this reason it is said of the Church of the elect through the Psalmist: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within” (Ps. XLIV).

For this reason Paul says: “Our glory is this: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. I). The Church, the daughter of kings, which was generated in good works through the preaching of spiritual rulers, has glory within, because what it does is not found in ostentatious display.

Paul calls the testimony of his conscience his glory because, since he does not seek the approval of another’s mouth, he does not know how to place the joys of his life outside himself.

What we do must therefore be concealed, lest, carrying these things carelessly along the road of this life, we lose them through the attack of plundering spirits. [Col. 1202C]

## XXX. On King Manasseh

*4 Kings XXI*

“Manasseh was twelve years old when he began to reign, and he reigned fifty-five years in Jerusalem. He did evil in the sight of the Lord, according to the idols of the nations whom the Lord had destroyed from before the children of Israel. He turned back and rebuilt the high places that Hezekiah his father had destroyed. He raised altars to Baal and made sacred groves, as Ahab king of Israel had done; he worshiped all the army of heaven and served it. He built altars in the house of the Lord, concerning which the Lord had said: ‘In Jerusalem I will place my name.’ He built altars for the whole army of heaven in the two courts of the temple. He passed his son through the fire; he practiced divination and observed omens; he made spirit-mediums and multiplied diviners, so that he might do evil in the sight of the Lord and provoke him.”

I have no doubt that all these practices—whether divination, the taking of auspices, any kind of sacrifice, the casting of lots, any movement of birds or animals, the inspection of entrails, or anything else that appears to reveal the future—are carried out through the operation of demons, by those who carefully observe the movements of birds, animals, entrails, or lots according to the signs which those same demons have taught to be observed by the people to whom they handed down knowledge of this art.

The person who is a man of God and counted among God’s portion must be entirely separate from all these things. He must have nothing in common with what demons carry out through hidden mechanisms, lest through these practices he again become associated with demons, be filled with their spirit and power, and be restored once more to the worship of idols. [Col. 1203A]

## XXXI. On King Josiah

*4 Kings XXI*

After some intervening material it is said that Josiah sent messengers to Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum, who lived in the Second Quarter of Jerusalem, because of the book of the divine Law that had been found.

What does it mean that she lived “in the Second Quarter”? Earlier in this book, concerning King Hezekiah, it is written: “He also repaired the entire wall that had been destroyed, built towers, and constructed another wall on the outside” (2 Chron. XII).

Zephaniah also mentions this place, saying: “A cry from the Fish Gate, and a howling from the Second Quarter” (Zeph. I). For this phrase the Old Edition translated the place-name almost as though it were a favorable name, rendering it *Masana*. For *Masana* means “Second.”

Therefore, when it is said that this prophetess lived in the Second Quarter, we should understand that she lived in the section of the second wall.

To King Josiah, who sent you to consult the Lord, you shall say this: “Thus says the Lord God of Israel: Because you heard the words of this volume, and your heart was terrified, and you humbled yourself before the Lord when you heard the words concerning this place and its inhabitants—that they would become an object of astonishment and a curse—and because you tore your garments and wept before me, I too have heard, says the Lord. Therefore I will gather you to your fathers, and you will be gathered into your tomb in peace, so that your eyes may not see all the evils that I am going to bring upon this place.”

Terrified by these threats of God, Josiah had wept and torn his garments; and by a prepared death he is made secure against all the future evils, since he would rest in peace in such a way that he would not see any of them. The spirits of the dead, therefore, are there where they do not see whatever is done or happens in this life of human beings. How, then, do they see their own tombs or their bodies—whether they lie cast aside or buried? How do they take part in the misery of the living, when either they themselves are suffering their own evils, if they have incurred such merits, or are resting in peace, as was promised to this Josiah, where they endure no evils by suffering them—freed from all the evils that, while they lived here, they endured by suffering and sharing in the suffering of others?

Someone might say: “If the dead have no concern for the living, how did the rich man who was being tormented in the underworld ask Abraham his father to send Lazarus to his five brothers, who were not yet dead, and warn them so that they too would not come to the same place of torment?” But surely, because that rich man said this, he therefore knew what his brothers were doing or what they were suffering at that time? Thus he had concern for the living, although he had no knowledge at all of what they were doing—just as we have concern for the dead, although we certainly do not know what they are doing. For if we had no concern for the dead, we would certainly not beseech God on their behalf.

In the end, Abraham neither sent Lazarus nor complied with the request; instead, he replied that they had Moses and the prophets here, whom they ought to hear so that they would not come to those punishments. Here again the question arises: How did Abraham himself, the father, know what was being done, when he knew that Moses and the prophets were present—that is, their books, by obeying which people might avoid infernal torments? In the end, he knew that the rich man had lived in luxury, while poor Lazarus had lived in hardship; for he also said to him: “Remember, son, that you received good things during your life, while Lazarus received evil things” (Luke 16). He therefore knew these things, which had certainly taken place among the living; but he did not know them while they were occurring among the living. Rather, once they were dead, he was able to learn them from Lazarus, lest the prophet’s statement be false: “Abraham did not know us.”

Accordingly, we must acknowledge that the dead do not know what is being done here while it is happening; afterward, however, they hear from those who, by dying, pass from here to them—not everything, certainly, but whatever they are permitted to disclose—and they remember only those things which it is appropriate for those to hear to whom they disclose them. The dead may also hear something from the angels who are present at the affairs taking place here, whenever he who has all things subject to him judges that each of them ought to hear it. For if there were no angels who could be present both in the places of the living and in those of the dead, the Lord Jesus would not have said: “Now it happened that the poor man died and was carried by the angels into Abraham’s bosom.” Thus those who carried away from here the man whom God willed could be here at one time and there at another.

The spirits of the dead may also come to know certain things happening here which it is necessary for them to know—not only present or past things, but also future things—by the revelation of God’s Spirit, just as, while they lived here, not all human beings but the prophets knew such things; and even they did not know everything, but only what God’s providence judged should be revealed to them.

Scripture also testifies that some of the dead may be sent to the living, just as, conversely, Paul was caught up from among the living into paradise. For the deceased prophet Samuel foretold the future to the living king Saul, although some think that it was not Samuel himself, who could have been summoned by magical arts, but some spirit corresponding to such wicked deeds that assumed his likeness.

We have introduced these matters by way of digression so that people may know that those who wish to be saved must seek the eternal truth—from whom we were created, in whom we live, through whom we move and exist. As for holy souls, let us believe them to be holy and not involved in human miseries, as Isaiah says to God, who was Abraham’s son: “You, Lord, are our father; Abraham did not know us, and Israel did not recognize us.”

After this comes the history of Josiah’s deeds, as follows:

“He also defiled Topheth, which is in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, so that no one might consecrate his son or daughter through fire to Molech.”

These places are frequently mentioned in Scripture, especially in the Book of Kings and by the prophet Jeremiah. The Valley of Hinnom, or of the Son of Hinnom, lies beside the wall of Jerusalem toward the east; in it a beautiful grove is watered by the springs of Siloam. Topheth was a place in the same valley, near the Fullers’ Pool, which Scripture mentions, beside the field of Acheldemach, which to this day is shown on the southern side of Mount Zion.

In Topheth, because it was a most pleasant place—so that even today it offers the delights of gardens—they used to set up an altar and sacrifice to demons, and by a criminal fire consecrate their children or offer them as a burnt offering. Thus it is written in the Book of Chronicles concerning King Ahaz: “He is the one who burned incense in the Valley of Ben-Hinnom and purified his sons in the fire of Ben-Hinnom” (2 Chronicles 28); for Ben-Hinnom signifies the son of Hinnom.

The Valley of Hinnom is called in Hebrew גֵּיא־הִנֹּם (*Gehennom*), from whose name the punishment of the underworld is called *Gehenna* in the New Testament. For just as those who served idols perished in the Valley of Hinnom, as the prophets bear witness, so sinners are punished with eternal condemnation because of the things they have committed.

Accordingly, when Jeremiah reported that the Lord had commanded him and said this to the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, which is beside the entrance of the Potsherd Gate, he shortly afterward added: “And this place shall no longer be called Topheth or the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, but the Valley of Slaughter; and I will destroy the counsel of Judah and Jerusalem in this place, and I will overthrow them by the sword” (Jeremiah 19).

Isaiah also most explicitly calls Topheth the underworld. When he described the everlasting destruction of the devil under the name Assyria, saying, “For at the voice of the Lord Assyria will be terrified; he will be struck with the rod, and there will be a passage of the rod firmly established, which the Lord will cause to rest upon him,” he immediately added how and where he would perish, saying: “For Topheth has been prepared from yesterday, prepared by the king, deep and broad.” He aptly says “broad,” because *Topheth* is said to mean “breadth.” “Its nourishment,” he says, “is fire and abundant wood; the breath of the Lord, like a torrent of sulphur, sets it ablaze” (ibid.).

Josiah defiled Topheth either with the bones of the dead there, as we read that he did with other places of idols below, or by scattering various other unclean things over it, so that the place might appear suitable to all who saw it for abomination rather than for delight.

What is said shortly afterward about the same King Josiah—“He also removed the horses that the kings of Judah had given to the sun at the entrance of the temple of the Lord”; and a little later, “He burned the chariots of the sun with fire”—shows that at that time the Jews were enslaved to the superstition of all idolatrous nations. Thus, in veneration of the sun, which they believed, after the manner of the Gentiles, to be a god, they had subjected horses and chariots to the image of the sun that they had made, and had placed these in the courts of the temple of the Lord.

For the Gentiles customarily paint or fashion an image of the sun by placing a beardless boy in a chariot and yoking horses to him, as though they were carrying the chariot toward heaven. They attach the image of a boy to it for this reason: the sun, as though born each day with a new rising, never suffers old age throughout the ages.

John, bishop of Constantinople, believes that the attribution of chariots and horses to the sun was taken from the miracle of the prophet Elijah, because he was carried up to heaven in a fiery chariot and with fiery horses. For since the sun is called *helios* (ἥλιος) in Greek, as Sedulius also showed when he sang of Elijah’s ascent, saying:

> How well the shining path of lightning-bright heaven  
> Suits Elijah, radiant both in merit and in name!

He was worthy of this assistance; for if one letter of this expression were changed by an accent, it would mean “sun.” The Greeks, hearing from the Israelites—who were reputed to possess the divine writings—that Elijah had been carried to heaven in a fiery chariot and with fiery horses, or perhaps seeing this very event depicted among other scenes on a wall, were deceived by the similarity of the name and believed that the passage of the sun through the heavens was being represented here. They changed a miracle divinely performed into an argument for error, commended by human folly. The Jews themselves, imitating them, took pains not to appear in any respect less foolish than the most foolish of the Gentiles.

What is said shortly afterward about the same king is as follows:

“He also polluted and crushed the high places that were in Jerusalem, on the right side of the Mount of Offense, which King Solomon had built for the idol Ashtoreth of the Sidonians, for Chemosh, the offense of Moab, and for Milcom, the abomination of the children of Ammon; he cut down the groves and filled their places with the bones of the dead.”

It is clearer than daylight that Scripture customarily calls “high places” locations situated on leafy hills, where people either sacrificed to demons or, attracted by the beauty of the places, offered victims to the Lord contrary to the prohibition, having abandoned the altar that was in the temple. Hence, in this book, it is repeatedly said of kings who were not perfectly just: “Nevertheless, he did not remove the high places.”

It calls the Mount of Offense the mountain of an idol, because it is the custom of Scripture to call idols “offenses”: either God is offended by them, or they bring offense and ruin upon their worshipers. This is made clear in the very sentence that follows, when it says: “Which King Solomon of Israel had built for Ashtoreth, the idol of the Sidonians, and for Chemosh, the offense of Moab, and the mountain for the abomination of the children of Ammon.”

Here too, unless I am mistaken, it is plainly shown—would that it had not been shown!—that Solomon never fully repented of the crime of idolatry he had committed. For if he had brought forth worthy fruits of repentance, he would have taken care above all that the idols he had built should be removed from the holy city, rather than leaving, as though wisely and rightly made, those things that he himself, although he had been the wisest of men, had wrongly constructed as a stumbling-block to the foolish.

Scripture mentioned this place above as well, saying: “Then Solomon built a shrine for Chemosh, the idol of Moab, on the mountain that is opposite Jerusalem, and for Molech, the idol of the children of Ammon.” It should not seem contradictory that there the mountain on which these idols were made is said to be opposite Jerusalem, while here it is asserted to be in Jerusalem. It was evidently situated so near the city that it seemed to belong to it, and that the defilements heaped upon it also seemed to reach the city itself.

### XXXII. Concerning Nebuchadnezzar  
*2 Kings 24*

In reporting concerning Nebuchadnezzar that he had carried all Jerusalem into exile, together with all the princes and all the warriors, ten thousand in number, Scripture added: “And every craftsman and smith.” This is what is reported above as having been done to the same people of Israel by the Philistines when it says: “Now no smith was found throughout all the land of Israel, for the Philistines had taken precautions lest the Hebrews make a sword or a spear” (1 Samuel 13).

For just as at that time the Philistines took care that the Hebrews should not have ironworkers who could make weapons for resistance, so now the Chaldeans, after Jerusalem had been destroyed and the entire Promised Land devastated, took pains that no craftsman and no smith should remain in it—someone who could either restore the defiled walls of the city or repair what had been broken. Rather, whatever skill they found among the exterminated nation, they transferred entirely to Babylon, so that it might thereafter be useful for nothing, or might benefit the needs of that city.

I do not think that the allegory of this deeply lamentable history, which corresponds so closely to the negligence of our own time, should be left unmentioned. For it is clear that Jerusalem and the land of Israel signify the city of Christ, that is, the holy Church; while Babylon and the Chaldeans—or the Philistines—signify the city of the devil, that is, the entire multitude of evil spirits, whether human or angelic.

Israel serves the Philistines or Chaldeans when the faithful, remaining in the Church in name only, deceived either by unclean spirits or by unclean human beings, submit the necks of their minds to avarice, lust, or any other sin.

Nebuchadnezzar carries Jerusalem away, together with all the princes and the ten thousand warriors, when he carries off the teachers of peoples and those who seemed to serve the Lord with unconquerable spirit and faithfully preserve the law’s Decalogue in love of God and neighbor—when, suddenly overcome either by the attractions of the world or by adversities, they defile themselves with greater crimes or, turning aside into heresy, incur the mark of open apostasy.

What are the weapons with which, while resisting the devil, we defend the freedom given to us by God, except the words of Scripture? In them we learn with the greatest clarity, through the examples both of the Lord himself and of his saints, in what manner the battles against vices should be overcome.

The Philistines deprive the children of Israel of weaponsmiths when evil spirits delay the minds of the faithful from meditation on sacred reading by bringing secular affairs upon them, so that they may neither gain confidence for resistance through this exercise nor perhaps kindle others who do not know how to read by exhorting or correcting them to resist vices.

They remove the weaponsmiths when they so overwhelm with crimes those who know the sacred words that they become utterly ashamed to speak the good things they have learned.

They transfer every craftsman and smith from Jerusalem to Babylon when they turn away from their purpose those who used to benefit many through the manifold practice of virtues and fortify the city of God against the assaults of temptations, compelling the skill that they ought to have devoted to the protection of the holy Church instead to serve the will of the king of vices.

If, however, we wish to understand “smith” here not as a maker of doors or walls but rather as a worker in gold and jewels, the spiritual interpretation still points to one and the same conclusion. For it is said of wisdom that it is gold and an abundance of precious stones; therefore we can understand no others more suitably as the workers of these things than teachers, who, as long as they live and teach rightly, devote the industry of their skill to the adornment of the holy city.

But if they should happen to go astray, what are they except captives carried away by the king of the Chaldeans to Babylon? For a craftsman and smith to migrate from Jerusalem to Babylon means that a talent of the word received from heaven is buried in the earth—that is, that spiritual wisdom is turned toward the works of sinners.

After this Scripture relates that King Zedekiah, while fleeing from the Chaldean army, was captured and brought to the king of Babylon at Riblah, where the latter pronounced judgment upon him; that he killed Zedekiah’s sons before his eyes, put out his eyes, bound him in chains, and led him away to Babylon.

While sacred Scripture recounts Zedekiah’s captivity, it announces the order of inward captivity. The king of Babylon is the ancient enemy, the possessor of inner confusion, who first slaughters the sons before the eyes of the one who is looking on, because he often kills good works in such a way that the captive himself sees with grief that he has lost them. For the soul often groans and yet, overcome by the pleasures of its flesh, loses the good works it produced and loved. It considers the losses it suffers, but nevertheless does not raise the arm of virtue against the king of Babylon.

But while it is struck by the sight of wickedness being committed, it is eventually led by sin to the point where it is deprived even of the light of reason. Hence the king of Babylon first destroys Zedekiah’s sons and then tears out his eyes, because the evil spirit first removes good works and afterward takes away the light of understanding.

Zedekiah rightly suffers this at Riblah. For *Riblah* is interpreted as “many things.” The light of reason is eventually closed to the person who is weighed down by the multitude of his iniquity through the perverse practice of it.

For just as on the fourth day, at the beginning of creation, the heavens were adorned with lights, so in the fourth age of the world the Israelite people, renowned for heavenly faith, illuminated by the prophets as by stars, glorious under the kingdom of David and Solomon, and made famous throughout the world even by the height of the temple, received its evening when, as sins multiplied, that kingdom was destroyed by the Chaldeans, the temple was demolished, and the entire people was transferred to Babylon.

This fourth age of the world, from David to the Babylonian captivity, comprises, according to the Hebrew truth, 483 years; according to the Seventy Interpreters, somewhat more; and, according to the books of both versions, seventeen generations, which the evangelist Matthew nevertheless sets at fourteen for the sake of a certain mystery. From this age, as from the youthful age, the periods of the kings began among the people of God. For this is ordinarily the age in human beings suited to governing.

The aforementioned Zedekiah, son of Josiah, reigned for eleven years. In his eleventh year, and in the eighteenth year of the king of Babylon, on the fourth month according to lunar reckoning, on the fifth day of the month—or, according to solar reckoning, on the eighth day before the Kalends of July, with the moon on the fifth day, which they count as the fifth day, a seventh day of the week—the city was opened. All the princes of the king of Babylon entered, took possession of the city, and led the people captive into Babylon.

Afterward, in the fifth month, on the tenth day of the lunar month—or, according to solar reckoning, on the fifth day before the Kalends of August, with the moon on the tenth day, which the Hebrews call the tenth day of the fifth month—the walls of the city were destroyed, and the temple likewise burned and devastated, in the 430th year from the time when it had begun to be founded.

If I am asked how I know this, or how it could have happened that the city was captured or burned on those particular days, I reply that in that year the beginning of the year and the beginning of the first month occurred, according to lunar reckoning, on the tenth day before the Kalends of April.

As for the migration itself into Babylon—concerning which the Spirit of God, through the prophet Jeremiah, commands them to carry out their affairs and pray for those among whose kingdom they were living as strangers, since their peace would also be their own peace, and to build houses, renew vineyards, and plant gardens—who would fail to recognize what this prefigured, if he considers the true Israelites, in whom there is no deceit, migrating through apostolic dispensation, together with the mystery of the Gospel, into the kingdom of the Gentiles?

Therefore the Apostle, repeating the words of Jeremiah as it were, says to us: “I desire, then, first of all, that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all people, for kings and for all who are in high positions, so that we may lead a quiet and peaceful life in all piety and chastity. For this is good and acceptable before God our Savior, who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Timothy 2:1ff.).

Through this, dwellings of peace have also been built for those who believe: the basilicas of Christian assemblies; vineyards of faithful peoples have been renewed; and gardens have been planted, where, among all the vegetables, that mustard seed reigns beneath whose far-stretching shade the lofty pride of the Gentiles also finds refuge and rest, like the birds of heaven.

And since, according to the prophecy of the same Jeremiah, the return from captivity occurs after seventy years and the temple is restored, what faithful Christian would not understand that, after the periods have passed which run their course through the repetition of the number seven in days, we too—that is, the Church of God—must return from our pilgrimage in this world to that heavenly Jerusalem?

Through whom else than Jesus Christ, truly the great priest, whose figure was borne by that Jesus, the great priest of the time when the temple was built after the captivity? The prophet Zechariah saw him in filthy clothing; after the devil, who stood accusing him, had been defeated, his filthy garment was removed and a garment of honor and glory was given to him. In the same way, the body of Jesus Christ, which is the Church, after the adversary has been overcome at the end of time through judgment, will be taken from the mourning of pilgrimage into the glory of everlasting salvation.

This is also sung most openly in the psalm of the dedication of the house: “You have turned my mourning into joy for me,” and so forth (Psalm 29:12).

Who could, taking the occasion of another work, touch upon all the things in those ancient books of the Law and the Prophets that announce Christ, however briefly, lest someone suppose that it is merely a product of ingenuity to turn into signs of Christ, through interpretation, those events that unfolded in their own times according to the order of events?

Jews or pagans may perhaps say this; but for those who wish to be regarded as Christians, apostolic authority presses upon their necks, saying: “All these things happened to them in figure, and all these things were figures for us” (1 Corinthians 10).

[Col. 1207]

## A SENTENCE FOR MONKS  
*(C, G, S)*

[Col. 1207C] In this manner, roughly speaking, God, the Maker of the world, having commanded that the other animals be formed with their faces bent toward the earth, made man alone upright and raised, and by the posture of his body summoned him to contemplation of God himself. Not to understand this is to injure him. We understand it if we bring observance to his commandments.

The greatest commandments are these: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your mind, and with all your soul” (Deuteronomy 6:5; Matthew 22:37). Is anything intolerable or burdensome being commanded, I ask? He commands us to love the one whose gift is everything that is in us and everything within us that belongs to us. He grants immortality; he restored that same immortality to the one who had been deceived; he established the law for us; he sent the prophets; finally, for our sake, he allowed his only Son to descend from heaven, to be born, to be touched, and to die.

Does he not compel us to love him—even if he does not urge us by commandments—by his benefits? “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?” (Psalm 115:12). I shall love him with all my heart, with all my mind, and with all my soul.

The next commandment is: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Leviticus 19:18; Matthew 22:39). We are led to obedience to this commandment not so much by precept as by nature. For what is so common to all as loving one’s neighbor? Or what is so proper to the human race as this humanity, which is derived even from the name itself? What else, more than this affection, distinguishes us from beasts? Thus, without reserved love, there is savagery.

And yet in this matter, as in many others, we do not merely confer a benefit; through the reciprocal duties of joined love, we give its fruit no more than we receive it. For while we love our neighbor, it is necessary that we be loved by our neighbor. Let us therefore love with all our heart the one who established the law that we should love one another in return.

The remaining commandments of the Lord are contained in these precepts. For these are of such a kind that if someone keeps only these, he fulfills them all.

These commandments were observed even before the advent of God our Savior. We, however, who came later, must moreover cling to the commandments and to Christ, to whom we belong, as the Apostle says: “For we are not our own, and you are not your own; for you were bought at a great price: glorify and bear God in your body” (1 Corinthians 6:20). He gave us the price—that is, he who himself is the price—so that we should now obey not our own will but his.

Hence our Redeemer says to his chosen ones: “You are not of this world” (John 15:19). Hence also the command: “Come out from among them and be separate” (2 Corinthians 6:17). Following these words and withdrawing, we have left the world, together with its vices, as though behind our backs.

The price of this withdrawal is indicated by our Lord Jesus Christ himself when he says: “If anyone comes to me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matthew 16:24). Let us therefore carry our cross, resisting the desires of the flesh—that is, vices—and indulging none of its perverse pleasures.

The one who does not live for the body has crucified the body. “Make no provision for the flesh in its desires” (Romans 13:14), because through its enticements it is no less hostile and dangerous to us than that prince of this air, our tireless enemy, who strives to drag us back from our effort toward the kingdom of heaven.

Indeed, this very thing is often his device for deceiving human beings. Since we ourselves are constituted in the soul and the body is external, the body was given to us by God to be left here for the time being, until the day of resurrection arrives. Is it doubtful that we ought to guard more carefully what is proper to us than what is external to us? Let us care for ourselves rather than for the body, which must plainly be abandoned no less than riches and the other things that we once called our own.

Let us put our members to death so that we may live the life that proves this present existence to be not so much life as the price of life. We are not now emerging for the first time from the mire of this troubled age. To what period, indeed, can the art of these commandments seem to belong? Nevertheless, we must continually impress upon ourselves that the empty joys of this world—all those empty things that have always deprived us, willingly or unwillingly—must, in piety, be returned to God as things owed to mortality.

Narrow and low is the spirit that does not extend its hopes beyond this age. Therefore, stretching ourselves toward the future, let us forget past possessions and pleasures. The wife of Lot remains an eternal witness that the one who looks backward cannot escape to what lies above (Genesis 19).

What difficulty is there in turning back to things that one has once rejected? Yet if we consider the matter, and ensure that there is no room even here for empty glory, we did not reject or cast them away; rather, we exchanged them for a greater return. We would indeed have despised what we left behind if we did not hope for the heaven of heavens.

Nevertheless, even those things we left behind are not our own. For since we ourselves belong to the one by whom we appear to have been created, we must recognize that both what we left behind and what we desire belong to him.

With these rejected things therefore blotted out from our minds, let us pursue justice, benevolence, piety, gentleness, faith, and charity. Let us guard the treasure that Christ’s poor carry, and keep it deposited in earthen vessels.

We must stand firmly in the footprints, because the path we are climbing is slippery; and the more difficult it is to be free from sin, the greater must be our vigilance there.

But lest there be uncertainty concerning the hope of this labor and faith, let us hear what reward awaits the just and the unjust. “The one who believes in me has eternal life,” says the Lord (John 8:24). What end, then, awaits those who believe in or fear God, for whom eternal life will be the end?

Conversely, what outcome does he announce for those who do not obey the Lord’s commandments? “Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire that has been prepared for the devil and his angels,” says the Lord (Matthew 25:41). You see what end follows each kind of merit.

If, from what is promised—punishment or glory—one thing alone were removed from us while the other were declared endless, even so I would think that incentives to live well had been set before us. But now, when on one side there are great punishments and on the other great rewards, should we not flee the one more earnestly and seek the other more eagerly?

And yet, even if no reward worthy of our merits followed, what could a human being do more rightly than live chastely and piously the life that has been granted, and imitate the holiness of the one whose image he bears?

Add to this that, through the ineffable mercy of our Lord, we are urged toward the blessed life both by threats and by rewards. O how beautiful will be the reward that comes after the Lord’s faithful recompense, when, having faithfully rejected the affairs of this world, we shall follow the true Son of God, the Lamb, mingled with the choirs of the saints in that shining seat of glory! And having been buried with Christ in this life, we shall likewise rejoice and reign with him in that life.

“The sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Romans 8:18). For this reason, let us ensure that we are not deprived of that glory by being captivated by the pleasure of this life. Our life is hidden in heaven. Let us hope for nothing in this world. “Hope that is seen is not hope.”

Let us not take refuge in the example of the multitude: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matthew 22:14). Let us not grow weary in a beginning effort; for it is not the one who has begun, but the one who has persevered, who will be saved (Mark 10:12).

Continence is the one conqueror of the many crimes of gluttony, lust, avarice, anger, vanity, and pride. Its best guardian will be fear, if we remember that we are always placed in the sight of the Lord.

Let us make our neighbors’ joy and sorrow our own, especially when they are theirs. In matters of slander, let the itch of both tongue and ears be equally detestable to us.

These things, my sons, entrust to memory and observance; nor will the labor of guarding them be long. For how few are the days of this life that we possess? Since, as it is written, the ends of the ages have run their course (1 Corinthians 10:11), it cannot be long before either the common or at least our individual release transfers us to our judge and the Lord who rewards our merits.

Hearing these things, they moisten their silent faces with tears; so great is their affection for future blessedness in response to such exhortations. Thus the most blessed Paul, imbued with mystical teachings and devoting his service to God, the King of the ages, pursues eternal rewards through the wages of an innocent life.

[Col. 1209]

## AN EXHORTATION TO VIRGINS  
*(C, G, S)*

[Col. 1209D] 1. If you attend carefully, venerable daughters, you clearly recognize that no human being lives for himself alone, and no human being dies for himself alone. For everyone who offers an example of holy conduct will arrive at eternal rewards with as many people and on behalf of as many people as he has influenced. Conversely, whoever displays an example of an evil life and perverse conduct will endure everlasting punishments with as many people and on behalf of as many people as he has provoked by his evil habits to wicked deeds.

Let us, then, not only refrain from offering others an example of evil living, but also continually urge them by holy and salutary admonition toward humility, charity, and obedience.

Let us not be among those who, whenever certain sisters are angry or raging, habitually provide fuel for pride by evil counsel, saying that they should not for so long abase themselves through rejected humility or endure such harsh or foolish commands.

Let us not be among those who, through their most bitter tongues, not only refuse to heal the wounded but also strive to wound those who are healthy—those who, by murmuring, slandering, disobedience, or anger, are accustomed not to serve Christ but to serve and fight for the devil.

For the cunning and cruel devil, through the craft of his ancient art and his manifold ingenuity, compels the souls whom he has once made sluggish, lukewarm, and negligent through his most wicked persuasion to serve him even in the overthrow of others. Of such souls it is written: “Would that you were hot or cold! But because you are lukewarm, I am beginning to vomit you out of my mouth” (Revelation 5:15).

The devil blinds such souls, prepared for disobedience or pride, to every light of truth and charity. Like a very powerful hunter and an exceedingly crafty fowler, he fashions and prepares them as decoys for himself, if possible, to capture even holy souls. This is how bird-catchers act: they blind and deafen the doves they have first caught, so that when the other doves gather around them, they may be caught in the nets prepared for them.

Thus the ancient enemy is also accustomed to act through lukewarm clerics, negligent monks, and sluggish virgins. Once he has closed the eyes of their patience, extinguished the fire of compunction and the flame of true charity, and persuaded them to take pride merely in the religious habit, as I have already said, he sets them forward and prepares them as decoys for the destruction of others and as examples, so that while the simple and less vigilant imitate them, they may be caught in various snares and nets.

Such people will have to render an account on the day of judgment not only for themselves but also for those whom, by the example of their evil conduct, they have drawn back from the good of humility and obedience.

2. For the ancient enemy, who has always been accustomed to envy the good, first persuades the servants or handmaids of God whom he discovers to be lukewarm and negligent to occupy themselves with idle tales, to provoke others to obstinacy by grumbling or slander, and to become exceedingly slow in listening to reading. When he has introduced into their hearts, as it were, a callus—and, so to speak, a crust of lukewarmness—he prepares them for every evil work and unhappily compels them to serve every vice and negligence. Thus says the Truth: “Whoever commits sin is the slave of sin” (John 8:34); and “by whatever a person is overcome, of that he is made the slave” (2 Peter 2:19).

For just as holy and spiritual souls, kindled by the fervor of charity, are moved by the Holy Spirit and continually prepared for every good work, according to the Apostle’s saying, “All who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God” (Romans 8:14), so, conversely, [Col. 1211C] the negligent and lukewarm are possessed by that contrary spirit of which it is written: “When the unclean spirit has gone out from a person, it passes through dry places, seeking rest, and does not find it. Then, returning, it finds its house empty and swept clean, and it brings with it seven other spirits more wicked than itself; and the last state of that person becomes worse than the first” (Luke 11:44).

Without doubt this is what clerics, monks, or proud, disobedient, and lukewarm virgins suffer. For when, at the beginning of their conversion, they have abandoned worldly conduct and fled with fervent spirit to the service of holy religion, by God’s grace they are emptied of all evil. Afterwards, however, when through negligence and sloth they do not apply themselves diligently to being filled, with God’s help, with spiritual goods, the vices that [Col. 1211D] had departed find them and return with multiplied wickedness, compelling them to return to their vomit. In them is fulfilled what is written: “As a dog, when it returns to its vomit, becomes hateful, so also a sinner, when he returns to his sin.” Concerning such people the Apostle Peter cries out terribly:

“For if,” he says, “after escaping the defilements of the world, they are again entangled in them and overcome, their latter condition has become worse than their former. Better,” he says, “would it have been for them not to know the way of righteousness than, after knowing it, to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them. For what has happened to them accords with the truth of the proverb: ‘The dog has returned to its vomit,’ and ‘the washed sow to wallowing in the mire’” (2 Peter 2:20).

This happens to those who, after abstinence, return to gluttony; after vigils, to drowsiness; [Col. 1212A] after humility, to pride; after obedience, to obstinacy; and after patience, to anger—returning like a dog to its vomit and like swine to the mire of lust.

3. Therefore, whoever recognizes that he is such a person should, while there is still time for correction, strive with groaning and lamentation to apply the medicine of humility to the wound of pride. Against the poison of grumbling or anger, let him hasten to receive the antidote of obedience. Before his soul, burdened with many sins, departs from this light, let him acquire for himself a remedy for the day of necessity. Let him strive, while there is still time to gather and purchase it, to prepare for his lamp—extinguished through pride—the oil of humility and charity, so that, with the lamp of virginity burning among the holy virgins, the oil of charity may overflow in the vessel of his soul. For bodily virginity will be of no benefit at all if charity or humility has departed from the heart.

These things holy souls observe, and those who desire to be like them do not cease to practice them.

[Col. 1212B] 4. Others, however, who live not spiritually but carnally, submit their unhappy necks not to humility but to pride. They do not gather spiritual honey like bees; rather, like wasps, they spread cruel poisons. This occurs when they are disobedient to their elders; when they are kindled by the flames of anger; when they store hatred in their hearts; and when, through their grumbling, they cause both themselves and others—shaken by the wind of pride from the harbor of obedience and driven from the calm of patience—to suffer shipwreck.

At the beginning of their religious life, they abandoned the waves of the world and fled to the quiet of the monastery. Now, however, through the excessive fury of pride, they are shown to suffer shipwreck in the very harbor amid the storms of anger. Such women are worse than those who appear to serve the world, for humble marriage is far better than proud virginity. More praiseworthy, too, are those who, with God’s help, preserve themselves in the midst of the open sea than those who, through excessive negligence or security, are drowned in the harbor.

5. Blessed, therefore, are those souls who strive, with Christ’s gift, to fill their hearts with the various fragrances of the virtues, so that nothing but charity and humility, and never anything but chastity, gentleness, or obedience, proceeds from their mouths. Thus they provide both themselves with eternal rewards and others with examples of holy conduct.

Conversely, unhappy and wretched—and deserving of mourning with every fountain of tears—are those who are so corrupted by evil behavior that from their mouths, or from their unworthy conduct, proceed not Christ’s medicines but the devil’s poisons. Although outwardly they are covered with religious dress, as though with sheep’s skins, inwardly they are known to be ravenous wolves. Like serpents or vipers, they appear to display a feigned humility in their bodily bearing only so long as they are corrected by no disciplinary rebuke. But whenever even a slight admonition is given, their false humility removed, the fury of pride breaks forth. Then it becomes clear that one thing was uttered by the mouth and another concealed in the heart: false humility was feigned in the body, while the poison of pride was hidden in the mind.

6. Fearing all these things rather than supposing anything unfavorable about you, we have offered this admonition to your charity with complete humility and paternal concern. For this reason we wished to place before your eyes the negligence of the lukewarm, so that, spiritually rejoicing in the good things bestowed upon you by divine grace, you might give thanks to God, and continually implore God’s mercy for me and for those like me, who are still oppressed by many negligences.

Thus, when before the tribunal of Christ a crown is granted to you for perseverance in good works, may forgiveness of sins also be granted to us through your intercession, by the favor of our Lord, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 1213]

## Letter Said to Be by St. Eucherius, Bishop of Lyon, to Philo, His Presbyter

Published by Baluze in the appendix to the works of St. Agobard. (C, G, S)

[Col. 1213A] Eucherius the bishop sends greetings in the Lord to his holy and venerable brother and fellow presbyter, Philo.

I ask your charity and affection, which you possess perfectly in the Lord, that you would be willing to undertake the journey as far as the monastery of the Island of Barbara, and visit and encourage our brother Maximus, the abbot who presides over that monastery. We have learned that he wishes to leave it and abandon his brothers because many, out of fear of the heathen, have withdrawn the offerings which they had been accustomed to give for God’s sake.

But if we live and return in good health, we intend, in God’s name, to provide either him [Col. 1214A] or his monks with so much that they will seem to lack nothing. I ask this especially of our brother: that he prepare for us the suspended house which we ordered to be built, and parchment. For, if God permits, we intend to keep Lent there with him, so that, residing together in that place, we may complete the work already begun.

Meanwhile, arrange for three hundred modii of grain, two hundred modii of wine, two hundred pounds of cheese, and one hundred pounds of oil to be given to him, so that, when he and his congregation are refreshed by our little offering, we may receive from the Lord, through their prayers, a safe return in good health.

## In the Year of Our Lord 449: St. Hilary, Bishop of Arles

## Prolegomena

[Col. 1213]

## Historical and Literary Notice on St. Hilary

(From Schoenemann’s *Bibliotheca Historico-Litteraria Patrum Latinorum*, vol. I)

### I. Life

[Col. 1213B]

Hilary of Arles, a Gaul, of distinguished birth and liberally educated, while still a young man, at the urging of Honoratus, abbot of the monks of Lérins, abandoned his family and the worldly advantages dependent upon it, and under that same leader and patron devoted himself to the monastic life. His sole concern was to reproduce his master’s example in himself and to reflect it in mind and spirit.

Accordingly, for as long as Honoratus presided over Lérins, Hilary always remained attached to him and followed his instruction. When Honoratus was summoned in 426 to govern the Church of Arles, Hilary accompanied him; soon, however, he returned to his island and did not leave it again until he had to exchange the leisure of the monastery for episcopal care. For after Honoratus died, Hilary was appointed in his place at the beginning of 429.

[Col. 1213C] The episcopate of Arles, which in the Gallican Church—especially since the time of Patroclus, when, through the favor of the Roman see, metropolitan rights over the provinces of Vienne and Narbonne had been transferred to it—was the principal summit of honor, could not fail to make conspicuous and widely known whatever virtues might be worthy of a bishop who held it. Hence his life was greatly commended by everyone, not only throughout Gaul, and after his death his memory was honored.

Yet that same position also became the cause of great [Col. 1214B] difficulties and serious grief for him. For when, about the year 444, he had deposed, by common judgment, a certain Chelidonius, bishop of Besançon, whom his people had accused before him and whose case, apparently, had been examined rather hastily in a certain synod, Chelidonius went to Rome and complained to Bishop Leo that he had been condemned with unjust severity.

Hilary himself immediately hastened to Rome and presented himself before Leo, though he openly indicated that he had come for the sake of official duties, not to plead a case. But when he saw the whole matter being retried by the Roman bishop and himself being treated as though he were guilty of an unjust judgment, and when he realized that he could neither overthrow by himself nor refute the documents produced by Chelidonius in defense of his innocence, he indignantly endured in his heart [Col. 1214C] the reversal of the judicial procedure. On the other hand, he spoke much more freely and incautiously than the ambition and by then undisputed power of the Roman bishop could tolerate. It could hardly remain uncertain in which direction Leo’s judgment would incline.

Hilary therefore departed from Rome without Leo’s knowledge and returned to Arles. Soon afterwards, however, as the author of his life relates, he turned wholly to appeasing Leo’s mind, with humility inclined toward reconciliation. First he sent the holy Ravennius, then a presbyter and later his successor; afterwards he sent [Col. 1215A] Nectarius and Constantius, distinguished priests.

But all was in vain. The sentence had already been pronounced: Chelidonius had been acquitted at Rome, and the judgment delivered by Hilary in the case had been annulled. Moreover, so that Hilary would not go unpunished for his audacity toward the apostolic see, he was not only deprived of metropolitan authority over the province of Vienne, which was meanwhile restored to the bishop of Vienne, but was entirely stripped of the exercise of that authority. The right to summon synods of the various provinces was transferred to the senior bishop, Leontius.

Leo also arranged for these measures to be strengthened and carried out by imperial authority. In the edict of the emperors Theodosius and Valentinian III, dated 8 July, during the consulship of Valentinian Augustus for the sixth time and Nonius, illustrious men (445), it was commanded, among other things, that for all Gallican bishops and everyone else [Col. 1215B] whatever the authority of the apostolic see had decreed should have the force of law. Thus, if any bishop summoned to the judgment of the Roman bishop neglected to appear, he was to be compelled to attend by the governor of the same province.

Hilary died not long afterwards, in 449.

Modern writers have judged Hilary and his dispute with the Roman bishop very differently, according as they were more or less favorable to the Roman Curia or more hostile to it. Hilary’s reputation among all his contemporaries was certainly great. The author of his life adorns him with exceptional praises, and Leo the Great himself calls him, after his death, a pope of holy memory.

Thus the superstitious defenders of the rights of the Roman see deny that these facts can be reconciled with his rashness toward the pontiff unless he seriously repented and obtained pardon from him. Opponents of Roman authority, by contrast, believe that Hilary did nothing other than defend what he owed to the rights of his own Church; that his case lacked neither legal merit nor prudence in its defense.

Indeed, they insist that Hilary recognized no authority whatsoever of the Roman bishop in the Gallican Church, and that for this reason he rejected Leo’s judgment and continued to exercise the rights of a metropolitan in both provinces until the end of his life, in contempt of Leo’s sentence.

[Col. 1215C] This was also the position of Paschasius Quesnellus in the apology which he composed for Hilary on the occasion of his edition of the works of Leo the Great. In it he strives no less to diminish the authority of the Roman bishop than to extol Hilary’s actions and virtues: his courage in defending the rights of his [Col. 1215D] Church, his gentle disposition and love of peace, and his steadfastness and perseverance in his office, unshaken by Leo’s threats.

But whatever Quesnellus may argue, I cannot recognize prudence in Hilary, nor does any consistent policy at all emerge from his actions. Nor are the claims by which Quesnellus attacks the power of the Roman bishops in the Gallican Church so well founded that one would not prefer, [Col. 1216A] in many respects, to agree with his most recent opponents, the Ballerini, although they were devoted to the Roman Curia, rather than to share Quesnellus’s judgment.

Furthermore, from Prosper we learn that Hilary, together with many other bishops of Gaul, by no means approved Augustine’s then-recent opinion concerning predestination and grace.

[Note: [Col. 1215D] In the *Letter to Augustine*, if the reading is certain. For some have judged that Hilary’s name has intruded into that passage. See Oudinus, chapter 1, p. 1224.]

From this arose the question of his Semipelagianism—a minor matter, certainly, but one treated seriously even by learned men—and in which same question Quesnellus was seriously mistaken. See Oudinus, *Dissertation on Hilary of Arles*, chapter 3, vol. I, pp. 1227–28.

### § II. Writings

Honoratus, or whoever may have been the author of Hilary’s life, lists the following writings by him: namely, the *Life of Honoratus the Bishop*, homilies for the festivals of the entire year, an exposition of the Creed, a large number of [Col. 1216B] letters, and poems.

Of these, only the following are certainly and genuinely extant today:

1. The *Life of St. Honoratus, Bishop of Arles*; and  
2. The *Letter to Eucherius, Bishop of Lyon*.

The rest have perished, unless perhaps some of them survive among the homilies published under the name of Eusebius of Emesa or of a Gallican author.

Oudinus, who had persuaded himself that all those homilies were by one author, once thought that they belonged to Hilary, following, among other arguments, the authority of learned men, especially Cumdius and Mosanus, the editors of the *Bibliotheca Concionatoria*. But after considering the matter more carefully, he judged that they could in no way belong to Hilary; rather, he concluded that their author lived certainly after the Council of Chalcedon, celebrated in 451, and after the condemnation of Eutyches.

[Note: [Col. 1215D] Many writers have discussed these homilies: Baronius, who attempted to claim them for Eucherius, under the year 441 of the *Annals* and in his commentary on the Roman Martyrology for 16 November; Combefisius, Labbeus, Dupinius, and Tillemontius. But Oudinus treated the question of their author most thoroughly, vol. I, pp. 390–425. See Fabricius, *Bibliotheca Mediae et Infimae Latinitatis*, under “Eusebius of Emesa.”]

[Col. 1216C] This, however, does not prevent the opinion from being true which Combefisius and not a few learned men with him maintained: namely, that the collection was selected from preachers of various cities and provinces, especially those of Arles and Lyon, and that among many homilies by other authors it also contained some by Hilary.

A number of poems composed in hexameter verse are additionally attributed to Hilary: for example, the *Poem on the Seven Maccabean Brothers*, killed by Antiochus Epiphanes, which is otherwise commonly circulated under the name of Victorinus Afer; the *Poem on the Providence of God*; and the *Poem on Genesis* addressed to Pope Leo. On these works, the judgments of scholars differ very widely.

The manuscripts have no authority in this matter, since they consistently attribute the third poem, the one addressed to Leo, to Hilary of Poitiers. The Maurist Fathers made the same attribution in their edition of the works of that Hilary.

[Col. 1216D] Nevertheless, because of the testimony of those same scholars, Oudinus has no doubt that the true author of the poem on the Maccabees was Hilary of Arles. As for the other poem, on Providence, he adopts the judgment of Norisius, who assigned it to Hilary of Arles on the basis of traces of Semipelagianism which he thought he had detected in it.

[Col. 1217A] For he believed that Prosper, in his poem *Against the Ungrateful*, had undertaken to refute this poem. But Antelmius and the most recent editor of the works of Prosper of Aquitaine long ago weakened that opinion.

Salinasius, however, infers from the poem’s mention of incursions by Vandals and Goths that it was written around the year 416, and therefore could hardly have been composed by Hilary, who was then scarcely fifteen years old. Although he did not venture to decide anything about the remaining two poems, he nevertheless considers it probable that their author was Hilary.

But it is perhaps more correct to agree with those who think that none of these poems belongs to our Hilary. Among them are the very careful and acute authors of the *Literary History of France*.

Finally, there remains the account of the miracle performed by the blessed martyr Genesius, which is likewise attributed to Hilary of Arles [Col. 1217B] in certain manuscripts and by the judgment of learned men, especially the Benedictines in the aforementioned *Literary History of France*. But most scholars, together with Quesnellus, consider this work also foreign to Hilary.

Finally, the two letters to Augustine on this subject plainly belong not to this Hilary but to another Hilary, a friend of Prosper, or even to two different men, both defenders of Augustine’s doctrine of grace.

### § III. Editions

Among Hilary’s genuine writings, the *Life of St. Honoratus* was first published by Genebrard at Paris in 1578, from which edition Surius took it. Not long afterwards Vincentius Barralis produced the same work from Lérins manuscripts, and Bollandus followed him, himself also collating manuscript copies.

[Col. 1217C] Quesnellus’s edition followed, formed from Bollandus’s text and Arles manuscripts. The most recent editor, Joannes Salinasius, departs from it in most places.

The letter to Eucherius appeared for the first time, if I am not mistaken, in the *Chronology of Lérins*. It was soon inserted in the Cologne and Lyon *Bibliothecae Patrum*, in Quesnellus’s edition, and in the latest edition, reprinted in 1731.

All these publications will be set before the reader in the following catalogue. From it we have separated works of doubtful authenticity or those falsely attributed to Hilary, thinking that we have sufficiently met the reader’s wishes if we briefly indicate where and under whose name they occur.

The *Poem on the Maccabees* was first published under the name of Victorinus Afer by Joannes Sichardus in the *Antidote against All Heresies* in 1528. From there it passed into the Bignean [Col. 1217D] *Bibliotheca Patrum* in 1575 and into all subsequent editions. According to the Benedictines in the *Literary History of France*, it was also inserted in the *Collection of Christian Poets* at Lyon in 1605 and in Joannes a Bosco’s *Bibliotheca Floriacensis*, vol. II, pp. 198–210.

The *Poem on Providence* was frequently copied together with the works of Prosper of Aquitaine. The *Poem on Genesis* was first published under the name of Hilary of Poitiers by Ludovicus Miraeus, with the works of Hilary of Poitiers, in 1544, and was thereafter repeated in all, including the most recent, editions of those works.

Morellus also published it separately at Paris, by Guillot, in 1559, in quarto. Soon afterwards, in 1560, it appeared again at Paris in octavo, together with poems on Genesis by Claudius Victor and others; in the same year it was published at Antwerp with the poems of Paulinus of Nola, edited by Pulmannus.

[Col. 1218A] It was subsequently included by Georgius Fabricius among the Christian poets and in the *Bibliothecae Patrum*, and was illustrated by a separate commentary by Joannes Weitzius, Frankfurt, 1625, in octavo.

The *Miracle of Genesius* appeared in Surius and in the Bollandists under 25 August.

The two letters to Augustine will be discussed below.

Finally, the homilies which some have attributed in their entirety to Hilary, while we have indicated that some portion of them may indeed be his, were published more than once. After the *Ten Homilies to Monks* first appeared at Cologne in 1531, in duodecimo, the forty-six *Homilies to the People* under the name of Eusebius of Emesa were joined to them by Joannes Gagneius at Paris in 1547, in octavo.

They were later reprinted at Antwerp in 1555 and at Paris in 1561, and, after Andrea Schottus’s recension, in [Col. 1218B] volume V of the Cologne *Bibliotheca Patrum* in 1618 and volume VI of the Lyon edition in 1677. Cumdius and Mosanus published them under Hilary’s name, whereas Combefisius transferred them to the *Bibliotheca Concionatoria* as the works of different authors.

## Sixteenth Century

1578. Paris, apud Aegidium Gorbinum; in octavo. *The Funeral Oration of D. Hilary, Bishop of Arles, on St. Honoratus, and D. Eucherius, Bishop of Lyon, on the Praises of the Desert, now first brought forth from the Lérins library.* See Eucherius, *Catalogue of the Royal Library of Paris*, vol. I, pp. 383 and 364, no. 465.

This catalogue also adds the *Instruction to Monks* of Faustus, bishop of Riez, which certainly occurs in this book but is not indicated in the title, as Sancassani teaches in the *Continuation of Cinelli’s Bibliotheca*.

## Seventeenth Century

[Col. 1218C] 1613. Lyon, in quarto. *The Distinguished Sermon of St. Hilary, Archbishop of Arles, on the Life of St. Honoratus, His Predecessor and First Founder of the Holy Monastery of Lérins, and Also His Letter to Eucherius*, in Vincentius Barralis’s *Chronology of the Saints of the Island of Lérins*, pp. 1–15 and 126.

1618. Cologne, Agrippina, at the expense of Antonius Hieratus; in folio. *The Minor Works of St. Hilary of Arles*, namely, the *Letter to Eucherius*, the *Letter to Augustine*, and the *Poem on Genesis*, in the major *Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. V, part II.

1618. Cologne, Agrippina; in folio. *The Sermon of St. Hilary, Bishop of Arles, on the Life and Death of the Most Blessed Father Honoratus, Chief of the Monks of Lérins and Bishop of Arles*, in the final edition of Laurentius Surius’s *Lives of the Saints*, under 16 January, pp. 252–258.

[Col. 1218D] 1643. Antwerp, apud Joannem Meursium; in folio. *The Sermon of St. Hilary, Bishop of Arles, on the Life of St. Honoratus*, in the *Acts of the Saints* of Joannes Bollandus, January, vol. II, pp. 11–24.

It was revised against the editions of Surius and Barralis and the manuscripts of St. Mary of Ripatorio and of Canon Preudhomme of Cambrai, and was furnished with marginal notes, biblical references, and a preface.

1673. Paris, apud Sebastianum Cramoisy; in duodecimo. *The Life of St. Honoratus by St. Hilary of Arles*, together with Eucherius of Lyon’s books *On the Praise of the Desert* and *On Contempt of the World*. These three minor works were given the title *The Way to Eternity*. See Eucherius of Lyon.

1675. Paris, at the expense of Joannes Baptista Coignard; in quarto. *The Minor Works of St. Hilary, Bishop of Arles*, [Col. 1219A] *Life and Apology*, or, as the interior title says, or, as the interior title says, *The Life of St. Hilary of Arles and What Remains of His Minor Works*, collated by Paschasius Quesnellus with printed copies and the manuscript of the holy Church of Arles; appended to volume I of the works of Leo the Great edited by him, pp. 729–776.

In these minor works Quesnellus included nothing except the *Life of Honoratus*, reread against the Arles manuscript and the Bollandist edition; the *Poem on Genesis*; and the *Letter to Eucherius of Lyon*.

He writes that the account of the miracles of Genesius, which is read under Hilary’s name in Surius, is foreign to Hilary’s eloquence and rather suggests the style of Honoratus of Marseille.

[Col. 1219B] The *Apology for St. Hilary and the Ancient Rights of the Church of Arles*, appended to the *Dissertations on the Works of Leo* in volume II, is the fifth dissertation. It concerns Leo’s Letter X—elsewhere numbered XLIX—to the bishops of the province of Vienne.

1677. Lyon, apud the Anissons; in folio. *The Minor Works of St. Hilary of Arles*, namely, the *Letter to Eucherius*, the *Brief Letter to Augustine*, and the history of Genesis described in heroic verse, in the *Maxima Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. VII, pp. 1228–1230.

1700. Lyon, apud Joannem Certe; in folio. *The Life, Minor Works, and Apology of St. Hilary, Bishop of Arles*, edited together with the works of Leo the Great by Paschasius Quesnellus, vol. I, pp. 361–386.

## Eighteenth Century

1731. Rome, printed by Joannes Zempel; in octavo. *The Minor Works of St. Hilary, Bishop of Arles, Revised against the More Important Manuscript Codices and Editions [Col. 1219C] and Illustrated with Notes by D. Joannes Salinas of Naples*, etc., together with Vincentius of Lérins.

[Col. 1220A] He separated Hilary’s genuine writings from those whose authenticity was less certain or which were falsely attributed to him. He judged that only two belonged to the former class: the *Life of Honoratus* and the *Letter to Eucherius*. From the latter class he reproduced three works: the *Poem on Genesis*, the *Poem on the Maccabean Brothers*—both of which he considers rightly attributable to Hilary of Arles—and the *Miracle of Genesius*.

The text of the *Life of Honoratus* is based on the Bollandist recension; readings from Quesnellus were rarely admitted. Salinasius himself also consulted the manuscripts in the library of the Queen of Sweden, nos. 645 and 1025, ancient and of excellent quality, but chiefly to defend the Bollandist readings rather than to introduce new ones.

For he testifies that, relying on the authority of the manuscripts and other considerations, he restored sparingly and cautiously certain passages which [Col. 1220B] Bollandus had fortunately corrected by his acumen, but which had been disfigured rather than emended in subsequent editions.

Nor did he wish to disturb the division of chapters and numbers introduced by Bollandus, lest readers and writers should be needlessly wearied by a variety of citation systems. Bollandus also contributed much to the notes and observations, for which Joannes Barralis had already prepared abundant material.

As for the *Letter to Eucherius*, Salinasius declares that he revised and corrected it with the aid of a manuscript codex. The works which we have indicated that he separated from the genuine writings he reproduced according to the authority of the best editions, such as those of Weitzius, Quesnellus, the Maurist Fathers, and Rosweydus.

The *Poem on Providence*, which he denies can be attributed to Hilary on any plausible grounds, he intended to publish in an appendix [Col. 1220C] to an apologetic dissertation which he was planning. In it, among other matters, he intended to examine more carefully the teaching of this poem.

[Col. 1219]

## The Life of St. Hilary of Arles, Written by a Disciple of St. Hilary Himself

[Note: [Col. 1219C] Those who consider Honoratus, bishop of Marseille, to have been the author of the following *Life* rely on the authority of no manuscript. [Col. 1219D] They rely only on the testimony of the commonly circulated Gennadius, chapter 99, where it is written of St. Honoratus of Marseille: “He also adapted the lives of the holy Fathers for the edification of posterity, arranging them to be read, especially the life of his teacher” (Barralis reads “benefactor”) “Hilary of Arles.”

It is now generally agreed among scholars that chapter 99 is not by Gennadius but was attached to his work as a later addition. For it is absent from several manuscripts, as Petrus Franciscus Chiffletius, Miraeus, Suffridus Petrus, and Ernestus Salomon Cyprianus observed. Moreover—and this is especially significant—it is absent from certain ancient copies which contain other additions that are nowhere found in the older or more reliable codices.

For this reason the eulogy of St. Honoratus is also omitted by St. Isidore, St. Ildefonsus, Honorius of Autun, and Sigibert, the last of whom copied chiefly from Gennadius.

In manuscript 100 of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme, Gennadius’s catalogue ends with John of Antioch. [Col. 1220C] The same is found in Vatican manuscript 551 and in the earlier editions of Gennadius, which Aleriensis printed from another codex. [Col. 1220D]

A very old copy belonging to the cathedral chapter of Verona likewise carries the catalogue only as far as John of Antioch and then, after his eulogy, adds only two additions: one concerning Pope Gelasius and the other concerning Gennadius himself. This alone may be believed to be an addition deriving from Gennadius after the first edition of his work.

The other eulogies—that is, those of Caesarius of Arles, Eugenius of Carthage, Julianus Pomerius, and Gennadius of Marseille—which do occur in printed editions but are absent from the ancient copies mentioned above, must be attributed to later additions by uncertain or unknown writers.

This is even more evident in the case of the eulogy of St. Honoratus, since it is absent from some of the manuscripts which contain the other additions as far as Pomerius, as Petrus Chiffletius observed.

Accordingly, when Ernestus Salomon Cyprianus passed judgment on this chapter 99 in Fabricius’s edition, he wrote: “Some utterly incompetent little fellow [Col. 1221B] has attributed this description of the *Life of Honoratus* to Gennadius. Its style is plainly different from the manner of writing of our Gennadius, and it is absent from our manuscripts.”

Although Gennadius is not the author of this chapter, since it is found in certain not recent manuscripts of Gennadius, it cannot be denied [Col. 1221C] that it was written and added by some ancient unknown author who attributed the *Life of Hilary* to Honoratus of Marseille.

Nor does this make the *Life* certainly attributable to that same Honoratus. The author of this *Life* was present at Hilary’s funeral, as is clear from chapter 22, where he also names Basil, then a presbyter and later, when the work was written, a bishop. This is not incompatible with the dates of Honoratus of Marseille. But it does not therefore establish that he was the author.

Of the three manuscript copies known to date, two—the Lérins manuscript and Vatican Queen Christina manuscript 645—give no author’s name. The third, the Arles manuscript, although it belongs to the same Church over which Hilary presided, gives not Honoratus but Reverentius as the author, as Petrus Saxius and Quesnellus himself attest.

This inscription in the Arles manuscript is generally rejected because Saxius thought that the name Reverentius referred to Ravennius of Arles, who immediately succeeded Hilary. But the *Life* cannot have been written by Ravennius, as is shown by the fact that Ravennius is twice named with praise in the same work, and in chapter 23 Hilary’s successors are called by a plural name.

[Col. 1221D] Chapter 24 makes it clear that the *Life* was written many years after Hilary’s death, that is, toward the end of the fifth century, when Ravennius had long since departed this life.
