Quesnellus suspects that Honoratus of Marseille wished to conceal himself under the name Reverentius, as seemed pleasing to other writers of the same age and region. But there is no reason why Honoratus, if he was the author of the *Life*, should have wished not merely to conceal himself but to place a fictitious name at the head of the work, especially since this was a *Life* written at venerable commands, as the preface relates—a circumstance that would not permit the true author, known to others, to be concealed under another name.

Hence Cardinal Baronius, Miraeus, and Papebrochius perhaps rightly suspected that the *Life* bearing the name Reverentius was different from the one which an ancient author, in the commonly circulated Gennadius, attributed to Honoratus of Marseille. They judge that it should be attributed, on the authority of the Arles manuscript, to a Reverentius unknown [Col. 1222B] to us.

This author is believed to have been a bishop because of the words at the end of the final chapter, in which he calls himself a priest. But apart from the fact that this chapter is absent from Vatican Queen Christina manuscript 645, the word “priest” is not always used for a bishop; sometimes it also means a presbyter, as could be demonstrated by many examples. [Col. 1222C]

But without wandering into external matters, the same author of the *Life*, in chapter 8, when recounting Hilary’s episcopal duties, says that he kindled the priests of the Lord not only by words but by deeds, consecrated worthy priesthoods, and ordained bishops. By distinguishing priests from bishops, he clearly understood by “priests” presbyters—especially since instruction not merely by words but by deeds is appropriate to those presbyters who lived together with Hilary.

Tillemontius inferred from other passages of the same *Life* that its author, although called a priest, was a presbyter, not a bishop, when he wrote it; see note 6 on Hilary.

If he is believed to have been a bishop, there is nothing to prevent our believing that an unknown bishop of an unknown see named Reverentius was the author of the *Life*, without having recourse to Honoratus of Marseille.

Whoever this author may be judged to have been, our observations in Quesnellus’s fifth dissertation, [Col. 1222D] part I, chapter 1, no. 3, make it easy to understand that he was certainly not free from a desire to defend Hilary, at least in those matters in which Hilary incurred Leo’s censure.

Barralis published this *Life* from an ancient codex of the monastery of Lérins, and it was subsequently inserted into the final edition of Surius. The Bollandists reprinted it with corrections from the manuscript of the Queen of Sweden, which Father Possinus sent to them. Quesnellus used the Arles manuscript in his edition.

We owe much to the diligence of D. Joannes Salinas, a canon regular of the Lateran, who printed the same *Life* at Rome in 1732. He not only consulted the editions mentioned above but also examined with the greatest care Vatican Queen Christina manuscript 645. Whether this is the same manuscript which Father Possinus found with the queen, who was then still alive, or a different one is unknown.]

Published from the Ballerini edition of the works of St. Leo the Great, vol. II. (C, S)*

## Preface

[Col. 1219C]

1. Conscious of my lack of competence and not unaware of my sluggishness, while I hesitantly wished to conceal the tender brow of my modesty in the hiding places of silence and to hide it beneath a veil of reticence, I resisted the venerable commands for a very long time. But the merit of the present lords and bishops prevailed—provided, that is, that the rashness of one who obeys does not diminish the judgment of such exalted priests. For when one lacks the ability to speak with fluent abundance, and is weighed down by unlearned rusticity, he is wrongly summoned to account if he cannot cultivate the proposed subject with barren speech. The magnitude of its burden chokes the narrow mind at the very beginning of the preface, while it surveys on every side the innumerable palms of his virtues: it can neither begin what it attempts to undertake nor prevail to complete what it has begun.

[Note: Quesnellus reads, “so that he may prudently take care not to begin … to complete.” We have followed the Vatican Regina manuscript and the Bollandists.]

## CHAPTER ONE. The nobility of Hilary’s birth, and of the author of his Life, set aside

[Col. 1221B]

2. Wishing, therefore, to present the Life of the most blessed Hilary—my special father, singular monk, supreme bishop, outstanding teacher, and devout instructor—in poor language and with modest understanding, I judge it wholly inappropriate, in the rhetorical manner, to recount his homeland and parents. For even he himself, in praising his venerable kinsman, preferred to ennoble the exalted stem of his birth by rejecting it, to commend it by passing it over, and to enlarge upon it by despising it.

I think, so to speak, that I may rightly suffer some loss in this matter when there is such an overflowing abundance of lofty praises. It is like craftsmen who, when they are preparing a precious diadem, select genuine gems so carefully that nevertheless they are known deliberately to omit some. So too, where the pearls of his virtues overflow, I shall necessarily pass over certain things, so that the most precious necklace of his Life—adorned not with human gems but radiant with heavenly virtues—may be commended by its own preciousness, without the hand of an artificer.

Accordingly, the beginnings of his infancy, the character of his childhood, and what followed even then—the whiteness of his snow-bright countenance, the torches of his shining eyes, the modest gait of one who walked, the fire of his burning intelligence, the inexhaustible spring of his eloquence, and the inner and true teaching of philosophical doctrines—are briefly conveyed in summary; the splendid memorials handed down to posterity through his eloquence bear witness to them.

[Note: The manuscripts of Lérins and Vatican Regina read, “the brightness of his snow-white countenance.”]

[Note: The Lérins manuscript reads, “the earlier [teaching].”]

I define these matters as things to be sought in persons in whom such distinguished qualities cannot bear the fruit of virtue. But I, who proclaim grace in humility, wisdom in contempt of the world, justice in love of the author, prudence in the mortification of the flesh, and courage in the acquisition of eternal rewards, pass over all these things with necessary restraint. I shall attempt, with a fitting judgment, to offer as the beginning of my narrative what he himself judged worthy to be the beginning of his way of life: how he entered the harbor of true salvation after overcoming the shipwreck of this life.

## CHAPTER TWO. Honoratus visits Hilary in order to convert him to God

3. Therefore, while the father Honoratus of blessed memory desired to regenerate him, through the compassionate womb of piety, for the immortality of a new life, he briefly left behind the community he had gathered for the Lord by his own efforts.

[Note: The Lérins manuscript reads, “a little acquired.” A little later, that manuscript and Vatican Regina read *heavenly* instead of *of heavenly things*.]

The affection he bore for so great a son recalled him to the homeland from which love of heavenly things had driven him away. Weak in body but strong and vigorous in mind, conceiving a new offspring through spiritual exhortation, forming it by instruction, and bringing it forth through prayers, he, like a skilled farmer, cast holy seed into the heart of a noble field, to be refined by the plow of faith; he watered it with the perennial gifts of prayers and the flowing streams of tears.

But that generous soul, which had conceived the false and deceptive happiness of the world through the immense labor of learning, did not receive an easy or slight proposal when it was summoned to the service of the heavenly kingdom. For the sweetness of present things subtly insinuated itself, so as to draw him away from the true fruit and glory of the future.

But the devout father longed to release from the bonds of worldly prosperity the mind that was constrained by these enticements:

> “My son, inflamed by heavenly inspiration, I am compelled to return for your sake to the very places from which I have long since determined, as you see, that I ought healthfully to flee, so that you may attain the glory of eternal life. I shall provide for you forever—not earthly things but heavenly; not things that perish with the world but things eternal with Christ, who is both the guarantor and the giver of the gift.
>
> “Death can cut off everything that you pursue and have conceived in your mind, at whatever stage of life. But the things I urge you not to abandon prepare riches—not riches that are lost, but those that remain; not temporal advantages but eternal ones; not the titles of vanishing honors but the everlasting glory of the angels.
>
> “In the fleeting conduct of the world, which prophetic Scripture judged comparable to a visible shadow that immediately vanishes, saying, ‘My days pass away like a shadow’ (Psalm 143:4), everything that is seen is rightly judged deceptive.”

[Note: Vatican Regina reads, “deception.”]

And therefore, whether bodily strength, the resources of inheritances, increases of prosperity, or the distinctions of various successes, they scarcely begin to please their possessor through any use before they pass away, even before the joy they produce has matured.

[Note: The Roman edition of 1732 reads, “indications.”]

[Note: The Lérins manuscript adds *lightly*.]

Yet these things torment their lover more through fear of losing them than they delight their possessor through the scope of their prosperity. They are constantly suspect, yet do not remain; like a treacherous enemy offering a small prize in order to hold the soul captive forever.

And so, kindled not by human affection but by divine prompting, because he who said inwardly does not deceive: “I promise to reap great things from you, beyond what can be believed; I shall provide for you in the present things that you do not expect, and in the future things that cannot yet be imagined”—

## CHAPTER THREE. Hilary resists Honoratus. His urgent supplication. Hilary’s deliberation giving birth to his conversion

4. But when blessed Hilary, with the exceptional discipline in which he excelled, the forcefulness by which he surpassed others, and the fountain of eloquence that flowed more abundantly than that of his own instructors, was dismantling these arguments, believing that what he saw through the highest insight of the mind ought not easily to be undertaken, blessed Honoratus turned his whole strength of soul toward God.

By doing so, he won not only the assent of one who was reluctant, but also, by Christ’s agency, a man humbled and made subject to Christ through tears and groans. The man whom gentle exhortation had not bent, he overcame by urgent supplication: prostrate before the Lord so that he might exalt him more highly, and pouring forth streams of tears so that he might free him from tears concerning the future.

At once a storm of new thought boiled up in his breast. Different counsels of contending wills were aroused against one another, and while the rewards of the inviting Lord were being pressed upon him, the obstacles of the world were nevertheless set against them. Thus, stirred to undertake the first service of the heavenly army, he deliberated with himself as follows:

> “When engaged in the studies of the world, we have sometimes undertaken the deliberation of persuasion and, after a salutary examination, distinguished the just from the unjust and the useful from the useless. Sometimes, flattering human ears, we have concealed the appearance of justice beneath the beauty of rhetorical art.
>
> “What must be done here, where the matter concerns eternal salvation, where the condition of the soul and the security of the infinite heavens must be weighed? These matters must be considered with profound maturity, since in them neither reason nor recourse to the harbor of repentance remains.
>
> “Everything must be weighed on the scales of equity, so that, by the weight of usefulness, they may fill the measure on the balance of justice. Everything sought by mortals, although desired as precious beyond comparison, becomes cheap as soon as it is obtained. Human nature, insolent in the harmful appetite of its vices, is not content with what it wanted, is not satisfied with what it coveted; like a flame, it grows through new fires of desire to its own detriment, while diminishing through the taking in of fuel. It does not understand that sometimes, in the very attempts themselves, it is compelled by premature death to undergo eternal death.
>
> “Therefore let us consider, as we ought, what justice, prudence, courage, and temperance customarily demonstrate.”

5. Justice persuades us that nothing should be preferred to the Author and Redeemer, because the Godhead descended in humility to us for this very reason: to make us reach the heavenly kingdoms. Life is rightly assigned to the one who gave it. Service is owed to the Redeemer. We must embrace the devotion that produces the glory of angelic dignity.

Prudence likewise teaches that we ought to follow the examples of those who pleased the Lord. Let us choose one who may strengthen our uncertainty. Abraham first presents himself: compelled to leave his homeland, he turned the command into a reward. Ordered to look upon the stars, he believed what eternity promised contrary to nature. He turned the promise into a debt.

[Note: The Arelate codex, Quesnellus notes, has *aetatis* (“of age”) above the line in another hand; apparently this is the best reading.]

It is fitting to imitate this man, made fruitful in comparison with the countless stars, who became a glorious guest of the heavenly kingdom, whose bosom is rightly called the paradise of souls.

[Note: The Lérins and Vatican Regina manuscripts read, “everlasting.”]

Courage of heart permits a generous soul to grasp nothing humble, nothing base. It makes one pursue lofty things, climb difficult heights, and overcome adversities, permitting despair in no way to present itself as a trial to the brave.

Temperance urges that a temple be prepared for the King of heaven: when the darkness of vices has been driven away, it must be filled with the most splendid light of purity; when the foul odors of pleasures have been cast aside, it must breathe forth the incense of chastity.

Therefore, since justice persuaded us to hand ourselves over to the Creator, prudence to follow the examples of our elders, courage to overthrow opposing powers, and temperance that a temple ought to be prepared for the Author, let us amend our former contempt by a willing encounter. For we shall offend not this one but the one by whom he was sent if we believe that the cause of salvation should be diminished by any evasion or worldly occupation. And since heavenly power has summoned him to this labor, let him himself, as victor, receive the spoils of the devil.

[Note: Quesnellus, drawing on the Arelate and Lérins manuscripts, noted *laetandum* (“to be rejoiced in”), and observed that another hand in the Arelate manuscript had *latendam* (“to be concealed”). Vatican Regina also reads *laetandum*. The Bollandists and the Roman edition of 1732 read *levandam* (“to be lightened”), which seemed preferable.]

[Note: Quesnellus writes in the margin: “Perhaps *incitavit* [‘stirred up’].”]

## CHAPTER FOUR. Hilary yields and sends the world away. Grace precedes free will

6. Blessed Hilary himself bears witness to our assertion, saying:

[Note: Quesnellus has, “my hesitation.” The reading of the Bollandists, approved by the two manuscripts of Lérins and Vatican Regina, seemed preferable.]

> “While the compassionate Lord invited me amid my hesitation, the whole world, with its pleasures, stood before me. My mind debated what seemed worth abandoning and what worth pursuing, as though arguments had been exchanged in the presence of a friend. How often did willing and unwilling succeed one another in my mind? And what more need I say? In his absence Christ carries out his part in me.”

Strengthened by such a decision, he came forward with serene appearance, secure mind, and submissive speech. He demonstrated how human choice is changed for the better by preceding divine grace, through a worthy way of life, speech, mind, and appearance. At once he was about to place his hand upon the plow of the Gospel, so that he would not look back even in thought.

After an assessment had been made of all his estates and of his entire property, he assigned the money received from his brother either to the needs of the poor or to the refreshment of monks.

I cannot adequately estimate or express how the pleasure of the world—which ordinarily deceives human frailty by the slippery age and alluring bait of pernicious delight—was cast away from this blessed man’s soul, condemned by a salutary judgment as he rejected it, avoided by rational flight, and how the desired desert was glorified in its seclusion.

He surpassed that evangelical questioner in merit, defeated him in virtue, and transcended him through perfect completion.

[Note: The Arelate manuscript reads, “sinner”; the Lérins manuscript reads *meritis* (“in merits”) instead of *merito* (“in merit”).]

The other man refused to sell; this one sold everything. The other departed sadly; this one, made joyful, hastened to enter the paradise of the world.

[Note: Quesnellus writes in the margin: “That is, of this life; or read ‘of the desert.’” Dom Salinas rightly observed that the paradise of the world here means the island of Lérins, as it is called by Eucherius in his book *On the Praise of the Desert*, sent to Hilary, from which the author of the Life drew material. This is confirmed even more strongly by the following chapter, where the island of Lérins is called paradise.]

Blessed Eucherius bears worthy witness to our assertion, saying:

> “And although you have poured out your entire wealth upon Christ’s poor, rich in Christ; although in years you surpass the young and in character the old, still greater is the fact that you desired the desert.”

[Note: The Lérins manuscript deletes *Christo* (“to Christ”).]

## CHAPTER FIVE. Hilary withdraws to the monastery of Lérins. He leaves the desert for a time

7. Having therefore broken the chains of worldly occupations and handed over his resources to the Author, under so great a guide he entered the earthly paradise of the island of Lérins—not from there to be sent, like the first Adam, into the exile of this life, but from there later to be carried, as a victor, by right into the heavenly kingdoms.

From this point onward the glory of his pontificate, well known to the world and more than sufficiently demonstrated, showed how that sharpness of mind already known to all, that burning soul, and that contrite mind pervaded each of the servants of God with eager attention; how he absorbed perseverance, surpassed vigils, seized upon abstinence, went beyond the gentleness of humility, exceeded persistence in prayer, merited streams of tears, claimed for himself the gratitude of all, drew forth the virtues of contrition, and violently seized the kingdom of heaven.

[Note: The same manuscript deletes the following nine words.]

For how much contrition he acquired at that time is clearly recognized from this: afterward, in the midst of the eremitical city, he caused the institutions he had established to flourish.

8. He drank in love of solitude so deeply and implanted it so thoroughly that, when he believed that he would accompany his guide and father in spiritual progress, now placed upon the priestly height, at the beginning of his ordination, he immediately resolved to leave him.

How great was his love of the desert, if the affection of blessed Honoratus could be diminished by zeal of love?

[Note: The same manuscript reads, “could not.” These words receive their illumination from Eucherius’ letter *On the Praise of the Desert*, an excerpt from which the Author inserted here. “Previously,” Eucherius writes to Hilary, “when you sought the desert, you appeared to have Honoratus as your companion. Now, when you have returned to the desert, you have left even your father behind. Yet what sort of man was he, and how great, and with what measure of loving devotion was he always honored by you, how uniquely bound to you in affection—that you could prefer nothing to his love, unless perhaps only the love of the desert itself.”]

But, O most ardent flame of contrition, I cannot behold your radiance with a wounded gaze. Why do you flee so intensely? Why do you abandon him? As though you could prepare the light elsewhere than where the Author has chosen.

Although you may wish to enjoy your own solitude, although, leaving your father, you may be carried away by your accustomed affection for the desert, you will later return as one who has become a father. The writings of blessed Eucherius provide testimony to this account; addressed to him, they attest:

> “With great courage, long ago you went out from your house and from your kindred and penetrated the remote solitudes of the desert as far as the great sea. Yet with greater virtue the desert was revisited by you than it had been sought.
>
> “For you entered as a guest with a guide, as though he were the leader of your journey, and afterward even the master of your heavenly service. When you thought that he should be followed in the priestly height, love brought you back to the familiar solitude of the desert.”

And since we must confirm the narrative of the work we have undertaken with the testimony of many, whoever wishes to know these things more fully should read that work in which they have been worthily set forth.

[Note: That is, the letter of Eucherius mentioned above.]

## CHAPTER SIX. He visits Honoratus as he lies at the point of death. Honoratus designates Hilary as his successor. Hilary is carried off to the episcopate

9. After two years had passed, when blessed Bishop Honoratus was summoned from the uncertain course of this life to receive the reward of his own merit, he sent letters warning Hilary that he ought to be present at his final moments.

[Note: Barralis suspected that the reading should be *triennio* (“after three years”), because he assigned Honoratus’ death to the year 430. But from Prosper’s letter to Augustine it is clear that Saint Hilary, who succeeded Saint Honoratus, was already bishop in 429. In the Bollandists this passage is given as follows: “Groaning for two years, when … in order to receive the reward due to his own merit, from the course of his own life,” and so forth.]

Hilary hastened to fulfill his command as though he were being recalled to the desert. And when frequent throngs of distinguished men came to so great a man in order to receive his blessing, they began to demand an answer concerning the successor of blessed Honoratus. Their minds, stirred from above, were proceeding to the judgment of the bishop’s election and requested a testimony; with his final breath he pointed out with his finger the bishop supreme in merits.

After the final acts of service had been performed, holy Hilary again hastened to the solitude of the desert. But that divine power which, by hidden means, accomplishes its will through human ministries suddenly kindled the mind of the illustrious Cassius, who at that time was in command of the soldiers, so that he passionately desired, forcefully detained, and violently dragged away a man unknown to him, far distant, and finally hastening toward the desert.

He sent a chosen number of citizens with a considerable force of soldiers. They arrived successfully. Spiritual prey stood before the eyes of those seeking him, and yet remained unknown. Eventually, disclosed by the indications of certain persons, he was seized.

And O unheard-of dispensation of heavenly grace! There the sheep performed the duties of a shepherd, and not without reason he later drove away the wolf from the place where the sheep had first performed the duties of a shepherd.

While he was being guarded by an anxious troop of the flock, his mind was more concerned with the manifestation of divine judgment than occupied with the burden of undertaking the office. By day and by night he earnestly begged that the Lord’s will be made known to him through tears.

[Note: The Lérins manuscript reads, “earnestly”; a little later, the Arelate manuscript reads, “of anxious expectation.”]

When the fear of judgment, as he remained on the road in anxious expectation, wearied him, he also disclosed aloud to everyone what he was turning over inwardly:

> “Although you hold me firmly bound by the bond of charity, and although the violent hands of my guards encircle and fasten me with chains, unless the Lord gives me a sign of his will, I shall in no way undertake the office of the priesthood.”

Thus, after he had wounded the wishes and minds of all by such a declaration and had been surrounded by the sorrowful troop of those leading him, as he was descending from the fortress of Alamannicum, a snow-white dove came from above and settled upon his head. As though he had been confirmed by a divine touch, it cut away every uncertainty.

Neither the numerous crowds of citizens and soldiers nor the guards could drive it away or frighten it into separating, so that, resting securely upon the blessed head, it most clearly demonstrated the Lord’s will.

Thereafter no trace of doubt remained. By divine command the appearance of the dove—which had already been likened to the Holy Spirit when it came upon Jesus’ head at his baptism—designated with special distinction the dignity of the future bishop.

[Note: The Lérins manuscript reads, “designated … a special dignity …”]

It was, of course, the dove that had carried heavenly blessing to the earth on swift wings and with shrill flight, more quickly than any human voice, so that the worthy bishop might be proclaimed by heavenly favor before he was proclaimed by human speech.

The grandeur of the subject demanded that we linger longer over so illustrious an honor and so new a miracle, had not the order of the narrative compelled us to explain what we had begun.

## CHAPTER SEVEN. Hilary reaches Arles. The episcopal seminary, or ecclesiastical community, under the bishop’s direction

[Col. 1228C]

10. When, therefore, all arrived at the city of Arles, eager in their will and even more joyful both because their common resolve had been confirmed and because the merit of the supreme pontiff had been revealed, they hurried to meet him. He offered to those arriving the first delights of his countenance through the splendor of his face, and displayed the merits of the inner man through the beauty of the outer.

[Note: The same manuscript together with Vatican Regina reads, “Therefore, by the Lord’s will …”]

Displaying the preeminent dignity of the priesthood and the new privilege of holiness in an angelic countenance, he was recognized and he recognized. In that in which he was recognized, he was great; in that which he recognized, he appeared greater.

Just as he was supreme in the rank of the priesthood, so through his descent into humility he attained the summit of lofty exaltation. O truly perfect disciple of Christ, who followed the ways of his teacher and practiced through teaching what he had learned!

He was consecrated in the priesthood, having long since been consecrated by the merits of his virtues. He embraced the ministry of consecration, which increased the merits of those who consecrated him. He became a priest in name, though long before he had been adorned with the insignia of virtue.

He began and carried through to the highest perfection what he undertook with such ardor and energy, so that amid the uncertain turmoil of that time, which a long peace had nurtured, he suddenly established a community eager for solitude and growing through the virtue of continence. He imbued it almost as much by his example as he formed it by his eloquence.

I confess that my affection is ready but my speech unequal to the task, so that I hardly dare begin to describe with what piety he supported the weak and with what teachings he instructed the unlearned. Whatever was supreme in virtue, difficult in loftiness, harsh in bodily mortification, most contemptible in disdain of the world, precious in the equity of justice, provident in correction, eminent in the consideration of wisdom, and eternal in heavenly desire—he practiced, fulfilled, and displayed.

Having himself attained heavenly glory, he made others attain it through his example. He advanced freely toward the teachings of heavenly philosophy and inflamed others also to walk in them. He lived the temporal life at the smallest expense—indeed, at none—and thus taught how the course of each day should be spent in order to obtain future rewards.

He always burned with renewed zeal, and compelled others to burn with prayer and exhortation.

## CHAPTER EIGHT. Having become a bishop, he becomes an example to all. He gives the churches’ ornaments to the poor

11. As soon as he assumed the office of watchman, he first demonstrated in himself how the community should despise the world, disdain the body, overcome vices, be wearied by labors, and be afflicted even by continuous work of the hands; how it should cling to the sacred pages, devote itself to fasts and vigils, endure the heat of summer and the harshness of winter content with the covering of a single tunic, and complete journeys on foot.

He impressed such lessons upon himself and his followers:

> “The necessity of eating presses upon us; let us sow seeds. The consumption of wine must be anticipated; let us cultivate vineyards.”

He fulfilled the apostolic injunction, taking account of his own livelihood lest he burden anyone by idleness. If any work remained over, he assigned it to the expenses of mercy.

[Note: The same manuscript, together with the Bollandists, reads, “he assigned it to the poor.”]

He remained constantly in meditation, devoted himself without interruption to the ministry of the word, nourished himself on the manifold mysteries of heavenly wisdom, loved God and his neighbor, kindled the priests of the Lord not only by words but by deeds, burned with emulation of heavenly zeal, established monasteries, built temples, worthily consecrated priests, and spared neither his own hands nor dangers.

[Note: Lérins reads, “temples worthy of the priesthood, with his own …” From the words “with his own” through “to spare,” the Arelate manuscript is defective.]

He received orphans, strengthened monks, summoned laypeople through his instruction, ordained bishops, and examined the account of his daily conduct so carefully that he sought to present himself to the heavenly Judge as though he were offering a talent of stewardship multiplied many times over.

Thus compassion and piety shook his inmost being, as though he alone had been urged by the heavenly writings to redeem the captives. He considered, deliberated with himself, and brought it about that the sacred vessels should offer captives consolation rather than provide churches with ornaments.

[Note: The Lérins manuscript adds, “and he did it.”]

What should I say, being eager? What should I omit, being ignorant? Should I be judged negligent by those who know greater things? Whatever silver all the basilicas possessed, he immediately assigned to the redemption of captives. And when he had learned that everything had been spent, he rejoiced and offered congratulations because, through his administration, he saw the faithful’s vows sent ahead to heaven as to its seat.

Can it be estimated how deeply piety dwelt in his heart, when he believed that everything should be sold until one came even to glass patens or chalices?

He kindled the zeal of those making offerings through praiseworthy administration. He did not reject what they offered so that they might become weary; rather, he encouraged them to offer more abundantly a second time. The devotion of the offerers gladly desired that their offering should first serve the sacred altars and afterward the redemption of Christ’s members.

## CHAPTER NINE. How he conducted himself toward the servants of God

12. He did not deny to later generations a salutary example, through spiritual instruction, of how the servants of God ought also to be honored.

When he learned through reliable messengers that the holy Caprasius—who, as he himself used to say, lived an angelic life in the islands—was weakened by bodily illness, he hurried swiftly to meet him. Sitting at his feet, he humbly and earnestly begged him to remember him, with submissive humility and illustrious virtue.

In this way, while he rendered service to so great an inhabitant of the desert and displayed an exceptional affection of humility, he skillfully discovered how to exalt the dignity of the priesthood all the more.

[Note: Vatican Regina and Lérins read, “through the dignity of the priesthood.”]

At the same place and at that time he honored Saint Faustus, both presbyter and abbot, with such foreknowledge of the future that he compelled him to sit between himself and the holy priests Theodore and Maximus.

[Note: Lérins reads, “he compelled.”]

It is therefore clear that he acquired the summit of humility through his own self-contempt and consequently merited the lofty height of virtues.

But perhaps such great and manifold examples of true humility produced some proud arrogance, rather than winning the lofty praises of humility.

[Note: The same manuscript and the Bollandists read, “danger.” A little later, the Lérins manuscript has *sublimibus* (“lofty”), while the Bollandists have *sublimis* (“lofty,” singular).]

He was severe, but toward the proud; he was terrifying, but toward those swollen with the wickedness of the world and puffed up with the vanity of vainglory. Toward the holy community and perfected men, however, he most readily prostrated not only his heart and mind but also his body.

## CHAPTER TEN. What he was like toward the powers of the world

[Col. 1230D]

13. How strict he was in the cause of justice he demonstrated most clearly, so that he did not even spare the dignity of the prefecture.

When he had repeatedly admonished the prefect of that time in private to refrain from unjust judgments, and the man was being carried headlong by his customary fall, it happened that, while sacred solemnities were being celebrated in the basilica of Constantia and Hilary was watering the hearts of the faithful with streams of heavenly teachings, the prefect suddenly entered with the insignia of his office.

When Hilary saw him lingering there, he stopped preaching, saying that it was not fitting for one who had despised his admonitions concerning his own salvation to receive nourishment from spiritual food.

But when the prefect, covered with due shame, had gone out, Hilary again began, with renewed zeal, to offer the feast of spiritual delights and food most abundantly to the gathered crowds of the people.

He left behind an example of how worldly powers ought to be despised through the virtue of steadfastness.

## CHAPTER ELEVEN. What he was like in preaching the word

[Col. 1231B]

14. But what his preaching in his own time possessed in the way of a river of eloquence; what gems of thought it carved; what gold of heavenly meanings it discovered; how abundantly it produced the silver of resplendent speech; what varied pictures of description and rhetorical colors it displayed; how it wielded the iron edge of the spiritual sword in cutting away the poisonous errors of heretics—I declare that I am unable not merely to discuss these things, but even to conceive them.

> **Note:** [Col. 1231C] The next eight words are absent from the Arelate manuscript.

With seats prepared for those fasting, he fattened the people with spiritual banquets from the sixth hour of the day until its tenth; by feeding them, he compelled them to hunger, and he never ceased feeding those who were hungry.

> **Note:** [Col. 1231C] Quesnell, in the margin: “That is, tables prepared for taking food.” But the learned Salinas rightly observed that these should be understood as seats prepared for fasting hearers who were about to listen to the word of God. Although in many places sacred sermons were heard by the faithful while standing—as is clear from Optatus, book IV, chapter 5, where he denies that the people had permission to sit in church—nevertheless, as Saint Augustine reports in *On Catechizing the Uninstructed*, chapter 13: “It is much more advisable that in certain overseas churches not only do the bishops speak to the people while seated, but seats are also provided for the people themselves, lest anyone weakened by standing should be distracted from the most health-giving attentiveness, or even be forced to leave.” This danger was much greater during the time of fasting, when Masses were celebrated toward evening while the people were still fasting, and Hilary kept them from the sixth hour until the tenth in preaching the word of God. A few words before *voces*, Quesnell inserted the particle *ut* (“so that”); we thought it better deleted, following the Vatican, Reginensis, and Lirinensis manuscripts, as well as Bolland.

I do not know whether the fullness of satisfaction provoked the hunger of the faithful more, or whether by feeding the people he compelled them to hunger more, fulfilling that prophetic saying: “Those who eat me will still hunger, and those who drink me will still thirst” (*Ecclesiasticus* 24:29).

> **Note:** [Col. 1231D] The Lirinensis manuscript: “The saying of Wisdom.”

If a crowd of learned men was absent, he nourished the hearts of country people with simple speech; but whenever he saw instructed men arrive, he was stirred by an unusual grace both in speech and countenance, appearing greater than himself. Thus the distinguished authors of that age, who deservedly attained renown through their writings—Silvius, Eusebius, and Domnulus—were inflamed with admiration and burst out with these words: “He has attained not learning, not eloquence, but I know not what beyond human beings.”

> **Note:** [Col. 1231D] Quesnell: *prolati* (“uttered”). The Lirinensis and Vatican-Reginensis manuscripts have *praelati* (“prelates”). We prefer the reading of Bolland. Shortly afterward, where the text has *pro meritis claruerunt* (“who became renowned for their merits”), the Vatican-Reginensis manuscript reads *meritis summi* (“of supreme merit”); Bolland has *meriti summi* (“of supreme merit”).

> **Note:** [Col. 1231D–1232D] Bolland’s continuator did not discover who these three authors were. John Salinas observed that Domnulus was commended by Sidonius Apollinaris in book IV, letter 25, and book IX, letters 13 and 15; from these testimonies it is learned that he was an African by birth, a highly educated man, and a quaestor on account of his literary attainments. We find Silvius mentioned in Prosper of Aquitaine’s *Chronicle*, published under the name of Prosper Tiro, under the fifteenth year of Theodosius the Younger, after the death of Honorius—that is, in the year 439: “Silvius,” he says, “after the duties of military service in the palace, being greatly disturbed in mind, wrote something about religion.” He is also the author of the *Calendar* published by the Bollandists in volume VI of the June saints, part II, page 182, and dedicated to Eucherius, bishop, in the year 449, as is evident from Bolland’s notes in volume I of the January saints, preface, chapter 4, section 3. From Silvius’s dedicatory letter it also appears that he was the author of other works, which he had sent to the same Eucherius for reading. We know nothing about Eusebius.

What more can I say? Unless a pause in speaking had come to him from above, he could not have brought his sermon to an end, so abundantly did grace overflow, and so greatly did wonder and astonishment increase, that his speech then drove the most learned authors of his age to despair—so much so that Livius, a celebrated poet and author of that time, publicly declared: “If Augustine had lived after you, he would have been judged inferior.”

> **Note:** [Col. 1232D] The Arelate manuscript has *ex stupore* (“from astonishment”), and shortly afterward *auditoribus* (“hearers”) instead of *auctoribus* (“authors”).

Although his grace can readily be recognized from the works which, in the same surge of speech, he conceived, produced, adorned, and brought forth—namely, the *Life of Bishop Honoratus*, homilies prepared for the festivals of the entire year, an exposition of the Creed, and a very large number of letters, as well as the poem *The Burning Fountain*—I thought it right to add the testimony of blessed Eucherius, bishop, lest anyone think that I might be asserting falsehoods. After receiving one of his works, written in prose and verse, he replied:

> “Although you are distinguished in eloquence and distinguished in talent; although in years you surpass a young man, yet in character you are an old man.”

And Auxiliaris, an author of Roman eloquence, wrote:

> “It is difficult to say how precious to me were the letters of Your Holiness, in which I recognized eloquence expressed in such a way that, in your other works of modesty and character, you hold the highest rank. Forgive me for speaking deliberately of lesser things concerning you, since virtue always blushes when it praises itself; and this very kind of modesty is a great part of virtue.”

> **Note:** [Col. 1232D] The same manuscript has *quia semper in precatione virtus sit* (“because virtue is always in prayer”); the present reading is *praedicatione* (“in self-praise”).

## CHAPTER XII. His Conduct at Table and in Manual Labor

15. I might perhaps seem to be repeating unheard-of things, unless I supported them by the sayings, writings, and testimonies of great men. When a seat and table had been set out, a book was brought, and also nets, while a notary stood by. The book supplied food to his mind; his hands moved swiftly in the work of knotting; the notary’s pen moved along at the same time, and his eye ran over the page.

> **Note:** [Col. 1232D] The learned Salinas gives another reading and punctuation: “A book was thrust before him; and, with Titius the notary standing by, the book was offered,” and so forth. We have not altered the received reading, which is also that of the manuscripts, because the verb *nectendi* (“of knotting”) which follows requires nets to be understood.

When the holy Edesius arrived, a man highly skilled in rhetorical eloquence and metrical art, he poured forth the following lines in joy, astonishment, and admiration:

> I saw it myself, though unworthy to bear witness to such praises:  
> The long days of summer yielding continually to labor.  
>   
> The art of knotting had appointed many hours,  
> Nor had the altered task brought his prayers to an end.  
>   
> I can scarcely believe that anyone could at the same time  
> Knot while dictating, reread what had been read, and speak it aloud,  
> Working at this with mouth and hand together, attending and speaking.

> **Note:** [Col. 1233C–D] Quesnell has *Plexos sole jugi digitos cessisse labori* (“I saw fingers joined in labor yield to the unceasing sun”), and noted that the Lirinensis manuscript reads *Prolixos soles* (“the long days of summer”). The same reading is found in the Vatican manuscript and in Bolland, and should have been preferred, since the first syllable of *jugi* is long. Shortly afterward, instead of *Nectendi ratio* (“the method of knotting”), the Vatican-Reginensis manuscript and Bolland have *Nectendi operatio* (“the work of knotting”), which is inferior.

> **Note:** [Col. 1233D] That is, “by speaking”; hence in the following line *fari* means “to speak.”

He never took food without reading. This custom was first introduced into the cities by him.

> **Note:** [Col. 1233D] The Lirinensis manuscript has *inventa* (“devised”). The statement that this custom of reading at table was first introduced “into the cities” should be understood to mean into Gaul, for Augustine too used reading at table in the city of Hippo, as Possidius testifies in his *Life*. The monks of Lérins, who likewise read at table, lived outside the city.

His life was sustained with such frugality that he rarely invited any secular person. In every action and every place, whatever could contribute to spiritual progress, he habitually sought eagerly, practiced energetically, and completed skillfully.

How, while journeying toward Salinas, he made automata with his own hands and sweat, how, after completing a full week, he would rise at midnight on Sunday, travel thirty thousand paces on foot, then attend the sacred rites and feed the people until the seventh hour—I cannot explain as it deserves, nor could the eloquence of the ancients adequately express it.

> **Note:** [Col. 1233D] Quesnell, in a marginal note: “I think that town was the place now called Salon, lying between Arles and Aquae Sextiae, about five leagues from the latter city and approximately seven from the former. It is commonly called Salon; on Hondius’s geographical map it is Salins, corresponding to Honoratus’s *Salinae*.”

> **Note:** [Col. 1233D–1234C] The Arelate manuscript, and partly the Lirinensis, have this marginal note: “Automata are instruments in mechanical art that move without labor, as though by their own power. From these words one may conjecture that Saint Hilary made these instruments with his own hands for the benefit of those laboring at Salinas.” Quesnell: “Some think these automata were machines by which water was channeled into the saltworks.”

## CHAPTER XIII. His Conduct in the Tribunal of Penance. The Form of a Penitential Supplication. The Solemn Reading of the Lessons

16. Whenever he imposed penance, a varied crowd often flocked to him on Sunday. Whoever wished to be present hastened to his correction and washed himself in showers of tears, terrified by heavenly judgments and inflamed by the promises. Such groans and weeping arose among those standing by that the dwelling-place of the present life seemed dreadful.

Who has displayed the tribunal of the future judgment in this way? Who has so terribly made known the dark fire? Who has so vividly portrayed the river of torments that both burns and carries away? Who has brought the wounds of conscience back before the eyes for inspection in such a manner?

> **Note:** [Col. 1234D] The Lirinensis and Vatican-Reginensis manuscripts have *fluvii* (“of the river”).

When his admonition was complete, he began supplications with tears, so that through prayer he might strengthen the fruit of penance which he had bestowed by admonishing. For a certain blind woman, while she was being blessed by the laying on of his hands, declared that she had received her sight. I think that what he had previously granted to the inner person, he afterward obtained for the outer one.

> **Note:** [Col. 1234D] The Arelate manuscript has *imperavit* (“commanded”).

Once she had received the light, she no longer sought a guide for the road. I have no doubt that through his prayers it was obtained that so great a miracle should come to the attention of very few.

Also on Sunday, while the solemn readings of the lessons were being recited, a certain man held fast by a phantom cried out publicly: “Holy Hilary, why are you tormenting me?” Then blessed Hilary constrained and entreated the Lord with whatever force he could. When he perceived that he had obtained his request, he said: “Jesus commands you not to mention this man.”

> **Note:** [Col. 1234D] The Lirinensis manuscript has *nomine* (“by name”).

At this supplication the spirit fell silent, as though bound by chains, and departed.

> **Note:** [Col. 1234D] The same Lirinensis manuscript omits “and departed,” as do Bolland and the Vatican-Reginensis manuscript, which immediately adds that he rejoiced because he had obtained more.

He rejoiced more that the spirit had fallen silent, because the man’s merit could remain concealed, than in the preservation of a living body.

## CHAPTER XIV. He Drives Out the Python. He Detains Those Leaving the Basilica

17. Nor will I pass over in silence how he extinguished the sacrilege which the spirit of Python, having taken possession of a woman, had introduced into the city through the skillful art of spiritual counsel. He ordered the woman to be seized and, after the readings of the Old Testament had been recited, placed in the public enclosure of the church. In flowing speech he demonstrated what the Law commanded and how much evil the craft of diabolical perversity poured into Christian minds.

And so that no one thereafter, while seeking the responses of demons, might voluntarily submit to so great a sacrilege, he taught the necessary instruction fully, leaving no excuse even for the negligent. He had done this publicly for the very purpose that it could not afterward be claimed that the matter was unknown.

He commanded the evil spirit to depart. Then, because it saw that it had been openly exposed and would no longer be able to deceive souls by secret fraud, it said: “Where shall I go?” The holy man, perceiving how much the grace of God had accomplished through his ministry, joyfully exclaimed:

> “It is the greatest sign of purification to be ignorant of where you will return.”

> **Note:** [Col. 1234D] Quesnell has *Maximum purgati orbis* (“the greatest sign of a purified world”). Bolland’s reading is preferable and is confirmed by the Vatican-Reginensis manuscript.

18. After the Gospel reading, he also recalled the people as they were leaving with this cry: “Go out, go out, for you will not be permitted to do this in hell.”

> **Note:** [Col. 1235D] The same abuse continued under Saint Caesarius, Hilary’s successor, as may be gathered from his sermons 280 and following in the appendix to Augustine, and from Cyprian’s *Life*, book I, section 14.

Then the singular rivalry of spiritual zeal exacted a terrible punishment in vengeance for the injury they had done. For when a crowd of people, easily stirred up, heedless, unaccustomed, and deceived, had come to him and provoked his spirit, the greater part of the city was suddenly consumed by a dreadful fire sent from above. Even those who had been afflicted by no small losses recognized in their own words that it had come as vengeance on his behalf, and, throwing themselves sorrowfully at his knees, cried out and begged for mercy.

> **Note:** [Col. 1235D] Perhaps *inconsulta* (“heedless”). Quesnell.

But he, intent upon reading, devoted to vigils, and continually given over to prayer and fasting, wore down his emaciated body with the harshness of the hair shirt. Not even in the cold of winter, when rushing rivers are usually bound by icy frost, did he cover his feet with any additional garment, never allowing linen or wool.

> **Note:** [Col. 1235D] The Lirinensis manuscript and Bolland have *rigore* (“with the severity”), and afterward *algore* (“with the chill”). The Lirinensis manuscript has *numquam sinum lanamine concedens* (“never allowing a fold of wool”); perhaps this should read *contegens* (“covering”).

## CHAPTER XV. His Zeal for Souls and an Example of a Compassionate Spirit. The Bishop of the Chief See of Gaul Living Together with His Clergy in a Seminary

19. While the mysteries of the Psalms were sung in sweet modulation, he added abundant weeping; he doubled his prayer with indescribable groans, never ceasing from his work even in the darkness of night. His hands were known to be carried along swiftly in knotting; his mind was exercised by the diligence of recollection. Once awakened, he spared neither his eyes nor laid his limbs down to rest, doing nothing else except ensuring that the spiritual armies of his enemies would find him both occupied and armed.

20. While he was established in these pursuits, a sudden ardor kindled him to seek out the mother of Heliodorus, bound in the chains of the Arian heresy, to enlighten and draw her, and, intending to offer her forever in the presence of God, consecrate her.

He displayed the insignia of his compassion toward those whom he sent ahead to the heavenly kingdom with such inward merciful tenderness that no one can imitate him. At the death of even the least reader, his spirit was wounded inwardly in such a way that he was shaken by sobs and poured forth the most abundant tears, as though he had been deprived of the comfort of an only child. The misfortunes and illnesses of his own people he counted as his own wounds.

This was plainly demonstrated in the case of Saint Cyril, then a deacon. He had been placed in charge of constructing basilicas and was removing marble facings and the lofty stage-fronts of a theater, stripping places of luxury in the service of faith. What he was preparing as a sacred place, he was adorning with ornaments; suddenly, when the ropes of the hoisting-machines broke, the force of the marble falling from above struck and crushed the foot of the man standing there, together with the ends of his toes.

> **Note:** [Col. 1235D] The Lirinensis manuscript has *fideli* (“faithful”) and shortly afterward *sanctum* (“holy”) instead of *sacrum* (“sacred”).

> **Note:** [Col. 1235D] The Lirinensis manuscript has *itantis*; Quesnell has *statim* (“immediately”). Our reading is that of the Vatican-Reginensis manuscript and Bolland.

Because of the deacon’s groaning and pain, the blessed man suffered no less a wound in his heart than the crushed man endured in his body. And when the immense wound of the servant drew continual and tireless groans from the priest—for his cell was adjacent to that same chamber—the holy man, as was his custom, earnestly sought remedies through supplication.

> **Note:** [Col. 1235D] The Lirinensis manuscript has *reverentem* (“a reverent person standing”), and shortly afterward *justitiae* (“of justice”) instead of *tristitiae* (“of sorrow”).

Overcome by sleep for a little while, he saw a venerable figure standing at a distance, anxiously asking the cause of his grief. He indicated that the deacon’s crushed foot had caused him not merely sorrowful grief but a wound of the spirit.

The figure asked: “Do you wish all the pain to depart?”

He replied that he desired this with every longing.

“Stretch out your substitute foot to be cut off,” the figure said, “and all the servant’s pain will immediately flee.”

Without hesitation he extended his foot, willingly received the blow of the one striking, and such pain came upon him that the magnitude of the pain drove out the sweetness of relief.

> **Note:** [Col. 1236D] The printed editions have *vicario* (“substitute”); the reading of the Arelate manuscript seemed better. We believe that “substitute foot” means Hilary’s own foot, which he is asked to have cut off in place of the deacon’s foot.

When he awoke, he did not doubt that what had been promised should be fulfilled. He sent someone to the aforementioned cell to inquire and immediately report how the deacon was feeling. The messenger reported that all the pain had departed and that rest had also been granted.

> **Note:** [Col. 1236D] The Arelate manuscript has *repromissum* (“promised”).

He is rightly believed to have been healed through Hilary’s compassion, since the one who inquired after him was found to be in complete repose.

He who, in the revelation concerning his neighbor, believed that the loss of his own limb should be accepted, fulfilled the divine command—or rather, he surpassed it happily—for the Lord says: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (*Matthew* 22:37). Here this blessed man is found to have loved his neighbor more than himself: insofar as his mind’s resolve extended, he offered his own limbs to be cut off in order to heal another’s.

> **Note:** [Col. 1236D] The Lirinensis manuscript has *supra se ipsum* (“more than himself”).

## CHAPTER XVI. He Removes Celidonius

21. But who can adequately explain, during his journeys, how much benefit his presence brought to the cities of Gaul, when he repeatedly sought out Saint Germanus, with whom he discussed the care and life of priests and ministers, as well as their progress and failures?

When his arrival became known, the fervent zeal of nobles and commoners alike rushed toward both men, asserting that Celidonius had taken an unmarried woman into his companionship—something prohibited by the authority of the apostolic see and the decrees of the canons—and at the same time alleging that, after holding secular office, he had condemned certain people to capital punishment.

Moved by the novelty of so serious a matter, they ordered witnesses to be prepared. Highly respected priests gathered from different places. The matter was examined with every consideration of reason and prudence. The accusation was confirmed by testimony. A true and simple judgment was pronounced: the man whom the rule of Scripture excluded should, by his own decision, withdraw himself.

> **Note:** [Col. 1236D] The Lirinensis manuscript has *impetrant* (“they obtain”). Jacobus Cujacius, *Observations*, book XV, chapter 38, reads *permutus … imperat* (“moved … he orders”).

Celidonius believed that Rome should be sought, and there asserted that he had been condemned with unjust severity. When the blessed man learned this, with what ardor of zeal and what heavenly fervor he was inflamed! He did not consider the harshness of winter, the roar of the Alps, or the cold; he did not immediately recoil from the spikes of the glasslike icy crust hanging above, resembling sword blows, imitating a brandished hand through the deadly terror of frozen frost.

But, steadfastly encouraged by the unshaken root of faith—especially since he had voluntarily come to such poverty that he did not fear undertaking the journey on foot—he entered the city of Rome fearlessly and swiftly, without a horse, without a pack animal, or even a cloak, having overcome every difficulty.

> **Note:** [Col. 1237C] The Lirinensis manuscript has *fragores* (“crashes” or “roars”).

> **Note:** [Col. 1237C] The Lirinensis manuscript has *voluntarie* (“voluntarily”).

> **Note:** [Col. 1237C] The same manuscript has *saginario*. A *sagmarius* is a mule or packhorse.

## CHAPTER XVII. What Hilary Did at Rome. What Hilary Did after Returning to Arles

22. After visiting the apostles and martyrs, he immediately presented himself to blessed Pope Leo, offering reverent service and humbly requesting that he regulate the condition of the churches according to customary practice. He asserted that certain men in Gaul had rightly received a public sentence, yet were attending the sacred altars in Rome.

He begged and urged Leo that, if he willingly received his petition, he should secretly order matters to be corrected, and that Hilary had come for service, not for litigation; he proposed to report what had occurred in the manner of a protest, not an accusation. If Leo wished otherwise, however, Hilary said that he would not be troublesome.

Since I especially do not dare to debate in this account the judgments of such great men, already called to heavenly grace, it is enough to touch briefly upon the fact that Hilary alone endured so much; that he was not at all frightened by threats; that he instructed those who questioned him; that he defeated those who argued with him; that he did not yield to the powerful; and that, when placed in danger of his life, he refused in any way to be joined in communion with the man whom he had condemned together with such great men; and that, guards having been set over him while winter raged, he thought that those whom he had not swayed by reason should be left behind.

> **Note:** [Col. 1237C–D] The Vatican-Reginensis manuscript has *positum* (“placed”). Two incredible matters are related here by the author of the *Life*. We observed in our notes on Quesnell’s fifth dissertation, part I, chapter 1, that the author, writing about events at Rome from popular report, may in good faith have been mistaken in some details. It is incredible that Saint Hilary was in danger of his life at Rome and that guards were assigned to him, whether to prevent his escape or to protect him from harm by someone else. For if he had anything to fear in the city from Celidonius’s friends, he would have had far more to fear on the journey, when he departed Rome on foot, alone or with only a few companions. If Saint Leo, forgetting his own gentleness, had thought that force should be used against him, once Hilary’s flight was known he could easily have ordered some men to pursue him immediately and bring him back to the city. Such violence was wholly foreign to the customs of that age and to the character of the pontiff; they appear to have been invented only so that Hilary’s flight from the Roman judgment might be excused under some specious pretext. Shortly afterward, we have restored *communioni ejus* (“to his communion”) from the two manuscripts, Lirinensis and Vatican-Reginensis, instead of *communioni suae* (“to his own communion”). The reference is to the Roman affair: Hilary had complained that certain men who had deserved a public sentence in Gaul were attending the sacred altars in Rome, and he did not agree to be joined there in communion with Celidonius, whom he considered to have been rightly and properly condemned by him in the Gallic synod. Referring to this, Saint Leo, letter 10, chapter 7, declared Hilary excluded from apostolic communion because he preferred to flee from Rome rather than attend the sacred rites there together with Celidonius.

Returning to the city, although weakened by bodily illness, yet holy in perfection and most ready in compassion, he turned his whole self, with humbled humility, toward appeasing the mind of Saint Leo.

> **Note:** [Col. 1237D] “In the withdrawal from the city,” according to the Lirinensis manuscript.

He first sent Saint Ravennius, then a priest and later his own successor; afterward he sent Saint Nectarius and Saint Constantius, distinguished priests.

> **Note:** [Col. 1237D–1238C] This is taken from Cujacius’s emendation. The Lirinensis, Arelate, and Vatican-Reginensis manuscripts incorrectly read: “Having first sent Saint Ravennius,” and so forth.

> **Note:** [Col. 1238C–D] It is clear from Valentinian’s Novel, which we printed as Letter 11, that Leo’s judgment in the case of Celidonius, by which Hilary’s sentence was annulled, occurred in 445. Albinus, who was prefect of the praetorium of Italy for the second time in 443, according to Valentinian’s Novel 22, still held that prefecture on 13 Kalends of July 445, according to Novel 2, concerning the Manichaeans; likewise in 446, according to Novels 1 and 2 concerning testaments, and in 447, according to other Novels. Some have therefore wrongly supposed that Auxiliaris was prefect of the praetorium of Italy at the time when, before Leo’s judgment, he wrote to Hilary. We learn from the Novel concerning the Corporati, title 26, that Auxentius administered the prefecture of the City on 18 Kalends of May 445. Unless the name Auxiliaris entered the Life of Hilary through scribal error in place of Auxentius, it is more credible that this Auxiliaris—who, from a still-extant inscription at Arles, was prefect of the praetorium of Gaul about 435 (see Maffei, *Antiquities of Gaul*, letter 1, p. 38), and resided at Arles, as is inferred from the *Life of Saint Germanus of Auxerre*, no. 34, where he had formed a friendship with Hilary—preceded Auxentius in the prefecture of the City rather than succeeded him. For when he wrote at Rome about Hilary’s affair, he held the prefecture there. What he did for Hilary preceded Leo’s letter and Valentinian’s Novel issued on 8 Ides of July. Perhaps, however, Auxiliaris, though living at Rome at this time, was neither prefect of the praetorium of Italy nor prefect of the City, but was again administering the prefecture of the praetorium of Gaul after Marcellus in this year 445, and had gone to Rome for some unknown reason, as we find sometimes happened to other prefects.

Since I cannot in any way connect with this work everything he dictated in this matter, I thought it right to insert the judgment of Auxiliaris, then prefect, whose words are these:

> “I received Saints Nectarius and Constantius, priests who came from Your Beatitude’s side, with worthy admiration. I have often spoken with them about strength of spirit, steadfastness, and contempt for human affairs, by which you are always blessed amid our frailties. For what can there be in this bodily life that is secure, when, although wretched, it cannot be everlasting?
>
> “I also spoke with holy Pope Leo. At this point, I think, you shudder somewhat in spirit; but since you are firm in your purpose, always even-tempered, and never carried away by the gall of agitation—just as you are not lifted up by any allurements of joy—I remember no deed of Your Beatitude stained even in the least by the contagion of arrogance.
>
> “But people impatiently endure it if we speak as we know ourselves to be conscious. Moreover, Roman ears are drawn by a certain tenderness; if Your Holiness occasionally lowers yourself to this, you will gain much while losing nothing. Grant me this, and restrain the small clouds with the serenity of a slight change.”

> **Note:** [Col. 1238D] In the margin of the Arelate manuscript, another hand adds: “To be inserted.”

> **Note:** [Col. 1238D] The same manuscript, in another hand in the margin, has *securum* (“secure”).

## CHAPTER XVIII. He Devotes Himself Entirely to Pastoral Duties and Penance

23. Hearing such words, he devoted his whole self, as though beginning anew, to prayer, preaching, and action: strict in discipline, inclined toward mercy, and most ready in generosity. He was not content merely to distribute what was available unless he also heaped up consolations with streams of tears.

> **Note:** [Col. 1239D] This is based on the Vatican-Reginensis manuscript and Bolland. Quesnell has, less correctly, *inhibebantur* (“were restrained”).

Thus the holy Edesius continues, speaking poetically:

> I saw him anticipated by tears,  
> By tears more abundant still;  
> What had increased through coins, he wished to increase through prayers.  
> How spontaneously mercy flourishes, how swiftly grace comes with gifts!  
> You were not generous only in presents:  
> Greater riches accompany you, supplied by compassion.

> **Note:** [Col. 1239D] The Lirinensis manuscript has *magno ubere fletus* (“with a great abundance of tears”). The Bollandists print these verses according to an emendation by Father Possini, who believed that he could restore them from the marks written on the parchment of the Regina manuscript:

> I saw him anticipated by tears, by tears more abundant still;  
> What he gave in coins, he wished to increase through prayers.  
> How ready mercy flourishes, how swiftly grace comes with gifts!  
> Nor was he generous only in presents;  
> With eager compassion he supplied greater riches.

> John Salinas preferred this reading.

24. By abstaining from food, persisting in work, and completing journeys on foot, he so weakened, wearied, and exhausted himself that he scarcely completed the circle of his forty-eighth year. For that lofty perfection of virtues, which had prepared for him not merely a place but a worthy dwelling in heaven, could no longer endure delays on earth.

But the faithful servant, fulfilling the command and desiring the promise, subjected his body to various illnesses, so that, like refined gold of the heavenly mint, purified in the furnace of sickness, he might be stored away in eternal treasuries.

> **Note:** [Col. 1239D] The same Lirinensis manuscript has *verum* (“true”), and shortly afterward *calculo exortum* (“arisen from a calculus”) instead of *caliculo excoctum* (“refined in a little furnace”).

## CHAPTER XIX. He Is Refreshed by a Heavenly Vision, through Which He Also Foreknows His Successor

25. When, therefore, as his illness increased, not the strength of his mind but the very substance of his body was consumed, I cannot explain with what eager purpose and exhortation he strengthened everyone, compelled them to persevere in their resolve, and supported them by eloquent and necessary persuasion.

Thus, standing at the final uncertain point, he received no slight consolation from a clear revelation. His mind was loosened in sleep for this purpose: the greatness of his singular reward disclosed to him and depicted the ornaments of his virtues.

He saw himself participating in the sacred mysteries. He beheld himself adorned with the covering of the tunic of Aaron, once the high priest, which by divine command through Moses had been woven with marvelous variety of workmanship. His breast was adorned with the manifold and diverse brilliance of twelve gems, and his shoulders were clothed with the same snow-white radiance. A robe, glittering with varied distinctions, encircled his limbs; its precious fabric, woven of linen, scarlet, hyacinth, and gleaming gold, had been skillfully fashioned by the hands of spiritual craftsmen in contrasting colors.

> **Note:** [Col. 1240D] The same manuscript has *croco* (“saffron-colored”).

The bells—ornaments more precious in beauty than those we have described, because God himself had formed and fashioned them—were shaken by the walker’s steps and, struck within by the pomegranates, sounded outwardly with clear strokes and a life-giving ringing.

> **Note:** [Col. 1240D] The Lirinensis manuscript has *tinniola*, and the Vatican-Reginensis *tinnivola*, that is, bells hanging from the garment and shaken as the wearer walked. In Sidonius one reads *tinnibulatas*; perhaps *tinnibula* should be read here. Shortly afterward, where the text has *claris* (“clear”), the Lirinensis manuscript has *clarum* (“clear,” singular).

When he saw himself adorned with the gifts, rewards, and honors of everlasting merits, in human affection he urgently asked that garments of every kind also be added to him from above. When he learned that this request had been denied, and saw his son, Saint Ravennius, brought forward to be consecrated for the celebration of the divine mysteries, he understood that he was about to depart.

How blessed, then, and how renowned was the Father, who, while still established in this world, received the reward of that true priest, whom not a figure but the reality of his merits properly adorned in manifold variety of colors.

> **Note:** [Col. 1240D] Quesnell, from the Lirinensis and Arelate manuscripts, has *viri* (“of the man”), and noted in the margin that perhaps *veri* (“of the true [priest]”) should be read. We have preferred the reading found in the Roman edition.

Why should it not have been shown to him in the covering of that tunic what he possessed in every diversity of virtue? Why should it not have been revealed to him in the beauty of that garment what was to be repaid to him in an everlasting robe?

Since he had been adorned with a purity of mind untouched by corruption, and authority shone in him through an immaculate conscience, the plate of shining gold rightly covered the mirror of his modest brow. He whom the primacy of virtue had always exalted was adorned by the fabric of precious stones.

> **Note:** [Col. 1240D] The Lirinensis manuscript has *exaltarat* (“had exalted”); the Arelate has *principalitas* (“primacy”).

Why should he not be surrounded with linen, whom the girdle of chastity had bound?

> **Note:** [Col. 1240D] The Lirinensis manuscript adds *zeli* (“of zeal”).

For, to speak truly, his principal plate gleamed with the authority of faith and the radiance of fiery flame. The gems, too, shone with the starry splendor of every virtue: the breastpiece upon his breast gleamed; the emblem of piety shone; the linen of justice, the girdle of continence, and the bell of preaching resounded; the pomegranates of good hope continually rang out in deed and word.

> **Note:** [Col. 1240D] The Arelate manuscript has *logium* (“breastpiece”); afterward the Lirinensis has *tinniolum* (“little bell”).

## CHAPTER XX. Hilary’s Exhortation to His People as He Was About to Die
26. When, then, he had been raised up and suffused with such great consolation, he addressed the congregation in an eager discourse, both for their comfort and as an example, and spoke to them all in these words:

“We have completed the course of life up to this point; now we are summoned to that dread judgment of the heavenly Majesty. Having entered upon the way of this flesh and the uncertain life of the present age, we obeyed the commands of the Creator; and, having fulfilled the duties of our own servitude, we shall migrate, with consolation placed before us, to the true and everlasting homeland. Up to now we have served in spiritual warfare. With the harshness of the hair shirt we have confronted the goads of our treacherous body. With the austerity of abstinence and the weariness of vigils, we have overcome every struggle against vices, with help implored from above. By holy meditation we have broken the snares of our thoughts. Occupied with the study of heavenly teaching, we have never ceased to distribute the talent of eternity among the faithful. We have sailed across the sea of this life and, with the Lord’s help, have received various profitable goods of virtue, to be returned to God with the interest of a saving usury. Under the Lord’s guidance, we have begun to draw near to the harbor of rest.

“We have fought against the princes of this world, with whom the Apostle describes an unceasing war, a war that no one will escape who wishes to reach blessedness, with heavenly grace going before and diligence following after. I believe that, once absolved and freed, I shall come into the sight of my Lord, with him showing mercy. To obtain those rewards, you must carry on the struggles with persevering course.

“That one, certainly, who destroyed himself through his own envy, who smells out war from afar [Job 39:28], crafty through long antiquity, deceitful in subtlety, skilled through constant practice and art in deceiving—he who feeds upon chosen foods and fattens himself on the destruction of the perfect, who regards his own punishment as salvation when it belongs to another—considers it no small consolation if he can capture those striving toward the things above in snares of sins and cords of destruction. The prophet, sighing, said of these: ‘The cords of sinners have entangled me’ [Psalm 118:51].

“This enemy of human salvation must be guarded against; he must be opposed and resisted in every way. For how can one already bound advance, or how will a captive dare to fight back? Beyond doubt, he will have as a companion in infernal punishment the one whom he has held as his companion in worldly pleasure.

“Showing the strength of this enemy to blessed Job, the Lord says: ‘He regards gold as mud; he thinks that he can greedily drink down the bed of the Jordan’ [Job 41:21–22]. What does ‘he regards gold as mud’ mean, except that he thinks he can trample the life of the saints as though it were mud, as the prophet proclaims: ‘Draw my feet out of the mire of mud’ [Psalm 39:3]? And what are the streams of the Jordan except the sacrament of baptism, which he believes must be swallowed up by his attack?

“The muddy structure cannot overcome his antiquity and power without God’s grace; nevertheless, his ambushes must be endured in unceasing struggle and continual conflict. The calm Spectator of human combat looks upon the daily training-ground of the contest. He sees flaming arrows directed, but causes them to be quenched in a fountain of tears. He sees snares being prepared, but rescues those who pray and those who weep, so that they may sing with true exultation: ‘My eyes are always toward the Lord, because he himself will draw my feet out of the snare’ [Psalm 24:15]; and thus, freed, they may become precious for announcing peace.

“And therefore whatever in the present can separate one from love of the Creator must be considered an enemy. If human illusion does not deceive me, a great storm threatens this city; an affliction not moderate but exceedingly grave is impending. Prepare yourselves continually for every contrary and adverse circumstance. Hold immovably to faith in the Trinity. Penetrate the inner meaning of the Scriptures, so that, calling upon the abyss through the voice of the waterfalls—that is, of believers—you may never cease in every way to water the earth with the gift from above.

“Let your clothing be rougher, your bread coarser, your food harder. Nevertheless, let the journey be completed with unencumbered feet, lest sudden necessity bring ruin upon those made delicate by new labor; for just as exercise makes one strong, so idleness will make one sluggish.”

*Note:* The manuscripts of Lérins and Arles read “all.”  
*Note:* “And”: added from the Roman edition.  
*Note:* The Lérins manuscript reads “unfaithful.”  
*Note:* Don Salinas added “rewards” from the Roman edition.  
*Note:* The Lérins manuscript reads *iras* (“wraths”), and then *vestitus* (“clothed”), in place of *vestis* (“garment”).

## CHAPTER XXI. He foretells his death and dies

27. When this exhortation had been completed, he ordered the sorrowful congregation to offer the sacrifice of evening praise and to take food according to their customary refreshment, saying: “At the eleventh hour of the day my soul, freed from the dwelling of the body, will hasten to the heavenly Judge.”

When he had begun eagerly to offer the customary offices of praise to the Creator with the usual modulation of the psalms, and was already returning and departing, he said: “Holy voices, voices that reach the ears of the Creator, commend me also to the Lord.”

After the brethren had finished their meal, he fortified his eyes and mouth with the sign of the Lord’s cross, continued in prayer, and, secure and joyful, departed for the heavenly homeland as innumerable choirs of saints came to meet him.

*Note:* The Lérins manuscript adds “holy.”

28. From this point, who could adequately explain how the whole city gathered, or how each person mourned him not as a father or mother or only child, but as the singular parent of all the religious and orphans? No one ceased from weeping; no one ceased from groaning. Universal love imposed equal mourning upon all, and the common grief of everyone who loved him was like a nursery of tears.

When the venerable body had been brought into the basilica of blessed Stephen, the protomartyr, one voice of the entire people rose amid weeping. “This day,” he said, “has forever cut off the complaints of unjust accusation, so that we may say no more than is sufficient in preaching.” The people, inflamed with excessive fervor for the faith, nearly tore apart the holy limbs while trying to touch them.

*Note:* The Arles manuscript reads “more quickly.”

## CHAPTER XXII. The funeral of Saint Hilary

29. Through the congregation’s diligence it was arranged that blazing columns of candles would drive back the crowds rushing in from every side during the night. When the vigils had been completed, and the brightness of the sun itself was considered dim in comparison with the venerable funeral rites, large companies gathered, not only of the faithful but also of Jews.
