Each person’s tears strove to surpass the others. As the voice failed, the groans increased. I remember hearing the Hebrew language of those singing at the funeral rites in his honor. For grief had so overwhelmed our people that the magnitude of their pain prevented them from carrying out the customary office.

Then, when they were bringing the holy body in before the altar of blessed Genesius, such a shout arose amid the tears of both sexes that the very stars seemed to have been struck and to have returned an unusual echo from heaven, reverberating with a roar comparable to thunder.

Again, new love inflamed hearts with heavier weeping, as each person wished to tear away a fringe and touch the body. Saint Basil—then a presbyter, now the supreme bishop—devised a means of seizing with both hands the greater part of the covering in which the body had been wrapped, tearing it apart and, withdrawing farther away, distributing it among the people by dividing it.

While he delighted the people by his zeal to distribute so great a gift, they withdrew a little from the tomb; and thus that venerable and beautiful body was secretly placed in the tomb, lest it again be injured by the devoted attentions of the faithful. When the people realized that it had been buried, they all suddenly uttered such a shout, with their own groaning, that one would have thought the roof of the basilica itself had been torn apart, collapsed, and buried the people.

*Note:* The Salinas edition reads “those rushing in. During the night vigils.”  
*Note:* The Lérins and Bollandist editions read, “Finally, before the blessed …”  
*Note:* The Bollandists read “with a sound.”  
*Note:* The Lérins manuscript reads “seized it.”  
*Note:* Quesnel reads “would be restored.” The correction was supplied by the Vatican Regina manuscript.

## CHAPTER XXIII. How precious Saint Hilary’s memory is, and how abundant the fruit of his life

30. At his death his life becomes precious in the minds of all, and desire for so heavenly a bishop is reborn in praise. Once he had been buried, his teaching began to be recounted with applause and his memory proclaimed with glory: contempt of the world, the feeling of compunction, a river of tears, the onset of temporality, the treasure of piety, the summit of justice, and the moderation of temperance were all drawn forth as examples.

What more is there to say? Whatever the entire city wished to confirm by oath, it brought forward his name, asserting that no one like him would arise thereafter. But this is the greatest thing: while he himself prayed, true love managed, in some fashion, to have falsehood. For it has not ceased to be reborn not only in his successors but also in the growing number of many bishops. As he labors with them here and shares in temporal fruits, he undoubtedly becomes a companion of eternal joys—like a fruitful tree of paradise, which never ceases to produce, with singular fertility for posterity, both what it may offer in the present and what it may leave behind by producing thereafter.

However many priests have been appointed, whether through him by heavenly ordinance or after him through God’s providence, they strive, with grace helping and merits increasing, to correspond to his intercession through learned instruction.

Happy is he who provided not only for his own city through his formation, but also arranged to illuminate diverse places by lighting countless lamps with the warmth of faith and placing them upon the lampstand. Thus his grace, growing warm in each person, is reborn through daily progress; for whatever is produced from his formation is most deservedly assigned to him. Whatever the members receive through abundant cultivation is credited to the gains of the head.

Concerned for all who are engaged in the contest of this life, he supplied the comfort of prayers, granted the presence of his visitation, and sowed countless and venerable commands of holy correction or rebuke, like a spiritual and skilled farmer—now threatening and grieving, rejoicing and sorrowful, glad and anxious, troubled and patient, calm and terrible, stern and gentle, lenient and strict; now groaning with a sigh, yet pouring forth abundant tears with joy.

From the overflowing river of his breast and the well-watered spring of charity, each person drew whatever he wished and was able to receive, so that holy generosity felt no loss; rather, by distributing, the lender of the heavenly treasure received an increase. For this is the nature of heavenly gifts: that through more lavish interest they continually increase within themselves; and when they are thought to have failed, they seem always to begin again. Descending into the poverty of diminution, the divine steward always obtains a certain increase from loss.

*Note:* The Lérins manuscript reads “laboring with temporal fruits.”  
*Note:* Four following words are missing in the Vatican Regina manuscript and in the Bollandist edition.  
*Note:* The Lérins manuscript reads “divine”; the Arles manuscript later reads “having been kindled.”  
*Note:* The Lérins manuscript reads “are assigned to his merits.”  
*Note:* The same manuscript reads “of prosperity.”  
*Note:* The same source reads “in the strengthening.”

## CHAPTER XXIV. A eulogy of Hilary

31. O great, lofty, and singular host of graces! Presented to the eyes in venerable remembrance, and perceived through your benefits, you are recognized as still serving our progress. After so many years have passed, you do not cease to be reborn and renewed in the honors of your children.

You are rightly honored by perpetual titles of praise: you are invoked and hear, interceding for those who supplicate and answering them; you are constrained, and you accomplish what is requested so that their petitions may be obtained; you are entreated, and, with God granting it, you do not cease to secure what is sought.

Behold the precious title of praise after the surpassing of sanctity’s appointed course. Behold the head crowned with green laurels and the emblem of the cross, woven with the fruit of virtues and the foliage that never withers. Behold the proclamation to be set forth after death by triumphal merits.

His body lies enclosed in the tomb—he whose prayers unlock the kingdoms of heaven. The insignia of your merits do not cease to be renewed in the various summits of virtue. Why should your soul, established in the blessedness of paradise, not accomplish greater things than when it was engaged in the struggle of this world—the soul whose virtue prayer obtained that signs should not reveal?

The unique pledge and glory of the priesthood, and the treasures of all heavenly knowledge, continually flowed from your heart. Your lamp, shining with the light of faith, also permitted the other lamps placed upon the Church’s lampstand to shine.

Called by the Creator to the fruit of labor and everlasting refreshment, you have happily arrived there, received into that most blessed fellowship of the patriarchs. Now you behold the singular ornaments of your soul, which have grown so greatly through the assistance of divine grace that they are eternally adorned and made conspicuous by the precious hands of the virtues.

32. You made the temple of your heart and body blaze with the purity of continence and the incense of all the Scriptures, and prepared it by the vigilance of unceasing diligence so that the Creator might rest in it. You nourished your mind and affection with love of solitude. You joined rivers of tears to the melody of the psalms. On the ten-stringed instrument of the commandments you excelled alike in conduct and in speech; by guarding the difficult ways, you preached them through life and teaching.

With the sweet-sounding song of the spiritual instrument and heavenly harmony, you resounded with the varied sweetness of melody. By the sacrifice of fasting, restraining the outward person, you did not cease, through the customary assiduity of vigils, to delight the inward person in an energetic course.

Nor did I think that this should be passed over: before the day of resurrection, while you traversed the regions of Campilapide, you regenerated each shepherd by the water of baptism, baptizing them and teaching those who had been baptized to live rightly.

Therefore, we ask, cause us who rejoice that you have happily come to Christ and reign with him without end to be fortified by your continual prayers, protected through your intercession, and allowed to enjoy the glory with Christ in which you rejoice.

*Note:* Quesnel inserted the particle “or,” which we judged redundant and removed. The Bollandists also omit the words “even before the day of restoration,” although they occur in the manuscripts and therefore had to be retained.  
*Note:* The Vatican Regina manuscript omits “you baptized.”  
*Note:* Here the Vatican Regina manuscript ends, as does the manuscript used by Father Possinus, according to the continuation of the Bollandist edition. From this indication, this manuscript seems to be the same as the Vatican Regina manuscript.  
*Note:* The Lérins manuscript reads “with a different sweetness of melody”; afterward the Arles manuscript reads “sacrifices” instead of “sacrifice.”

33. Since the merits of so great and so eminent a man have borne witness to him and have worthily praised his deeds, I dared to hope for pardon because, forgetful of my own ability and impelled by love, I rashly sprang forward to so great a panegyric. May he, established in that glorious summit of his merits, not cease to intercede even for me; and, joined to those venerable assemblies of the patriarchs, may he enlist that company of pious fellowship for our protection. May he obtain that he not be saddened by my conduct or slothfulness. Therefore, may his intercession fortify me, and may his patronage cause the merit of a priest to be found acceptable at that dread judgment—our Lord Jesus Christ reigning, to whom are honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

*Note:* Quesnel reads “of solidity.” From Bolland and Salinas we have corrected it to *sodalitatis* (“fellowship”), as the manuscripts read.

## Epitaph of Saint Hilary

On a marble tablet fixed into the wall in the church of Saint Honoratus.

Hilary, the Lord’s bishop, who,  
Preferring love of poverty to gold, seized the heavenly kingdoms;  
To whom death was victory and Christ was life;  
Despising the fragile use of an earthly body,  
Here left the spoil of the flesh and flew to the stars.

He spurns wealth while seeking wealth, exchanging mortal things;  
With earthly gifts he purchased everlasting heaven.  
The jewel of priests, and teacher of people and world.

Even undertaking rustic duties for Christ,  
He did not disdain to enter upon servile service.  
He lived least in office, but highest in rank.

Nor is it surprising that afterward he deserved your threshold, Christ,  
And entered angelic dwellings and golden kingdoms,  
Your riches, paradise, your ever-fragrant  
Grasses and gardens breathing forth divine flowers,  
And sees the clouds below and the stars of heaven.

*Note:* The Arles manuscript reads “spurned”; shortly afterward the Lérins manuscript reads “avoiding” instead of “exchanging.”  
*Note:* The Bollandist edition reads “in service.”

Inscription carved on Saint Hilary’s own tomb:

**HILARY, BISHOP OF THE MOST HOLY LAW, RESTS HERE.**

## Notice concerning the minor works of Saint Hilary of Arles

1. We assign the first place to Saint Hilary’s sermon on the Life of Saint Honoratus, bishop of Arles. Father Rosweyde published it in 1620 in a more corrected and annotated form; John Bolland published it again in volume II of the *January* collection, on January 16, using two manuscript copies, one from Saint Mary of Ripatorium and the other belonging to Preuhdomius, canon of Cambrai. With their aid he applied a correcting hand to not a few corrupt and obscure passages.

In 1673, John Adam of the Society of Jesus printed the same sermon again together with Eucherius’s little works *On the Praise of the Desert* and *On Contempt of the World*. Quesnel’s edition followed, in which the same sermon was revised against an Arles manuscript. Most recently, Don John Salinas, a regular canon, having obtained two manuscripts of excellent quality—the Vatican Regina 645 and 1025—carefully reprinted it at Rome in 1731. He stated that from these manuscripts he had successfully restored certain passages corrected through Bolland’s insight but distorted rather than corrected in subsequent editions.

With these aids it was possible for us in some places to supplement and correct Quesnel’s edition. This sermon was delivered by Saint Hilary, the immediate successor of Saint Honoratus, in the church of Arles itself, on the anniversary of Honoratus’s death and before the death of Leontius, bishop of Fréjus, who is mentioned as living in chapter 15. It must therefore date between 430 and 432: Honoratus died in 429, on January 16, whereas Leontius died in 432. More probably, Saint Hilary delivered this sermon in the first year of his episcopate, on the anniversary itself, January 16, 430.

2. This first sermon will be followed by a narrative of the miracle of Saint Genesius the martyr, which Surius published under Hilary of Arles’s name on August 25. Quesnel omitted it because he thought it unlike Hilary’s eloquence and believed its style rather to resemble that of Honoratus of Marseille. We, however, detected no such great difference of style and found nothing in the whole sermon unworthy of Hilary.

The author certainly witnessed the miracle himself. Since it occurred while Saint Honoratus was living bishop of Arles, in 427 or 428, it suits our Hilary, but cannot suit Honoratus of Marseille, who flourished toward the end of the century. For this reason the continuators of Bolland, under August 25, and Tillemont, in article 22 of his *Life of Hilary*, attack Quesnel. Consequently, this narrative could not be omitted from Hilary’s minor works.

3. These two minor works of Hilary will be followed by his letter to Saint Eucherius, bishop of Lyon and his dearest friend. Antelmius thinks it was written between 435 and 440; but the aforementioned John Salinas prefers approximately 435, since the mention of youth suits that year better, when Hilary had scarcely reached his thirty-fourth year, than 440, when he was entering manhood. He was born in 401.

The edition of Don Salinas was especially helpful, for it was prepared against the very ancient and excellent manuscript of Santa Croce in Jerusalem, no. 186. Salinas received its variant readings, which supplied distinctive corrections, from Joachim Besozzi, then abbot and now most eminent cardinal, who has always favored, and continues to favor, learned men.

4. We shall insert among Hilary’s works a poem on the seven Maccabean brothers. Although some editions attribute it to Marius Victorinus the African, most manuscripts vindicate it for Hilary. Father Labbe, in his historical dissertation on Victorinus, mentions certain manuscripts that prefer Hilary.

Oudin also, in volume V of *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, page 1230, lists four manuscript copies assigning the same poem to Hilary: three Colbert manuscripts, numbers 1512, 3898, and 4734, and one among his own manuscripts. John a Bosco likewise testifies that another old manuscript from Fleury prefixed Hilary’s name, in volume II of his *Fleury Library*, page 198.

On the authority of so many manuscripts, this poem seems more properly to be attributed to Hilary than to Victorinus. Since the author of the Life of Saint Hilary of Arles testifies that Hilary wrote verses on the “burning fountain,” the poem may be attributed to him, unless someone prefers to believe that another, unknown Hilary was its author.

The common editions present the poem in an extremely corrupt state, so that it appears unworthy of our Hilary. Yet Oudin stated that, with the support of his manuscripts, he had corrected the poem so thoroughly that it might seem an entirely new work. Although Oudin’s manuscripts and corrections were unavailable to us, John a Bosco was at hand: he inserted the poem, with Saint Hilary’s name prefixed, as though it were unpublished, from the aforementioned Fleury manuscript in the volume already cited. From this edition, which served in place of the manuscript, it was possible to correct the common reading, corrupted in many places, so that the poem may be recognized as almost another poem, and one not unworthy of Saint Hilary.

5. A poem on Genesis addressed to Pope Leo will follow—not because it certainly belongs to Hilary, but because Quesnel published it among his minor works. According to Father Coustant, in the manuscripts it is attributed not to Saint Hilary of Arles but to Hilary of Poitiers; its attribution to the latter prevailed in printed editions until Sixtus of Siena and Gillotius of Campania assigned it to Hilary of Arles. On what authority, however, is not apparent.

On the sole authority of these men, Quesnel added the poem to Hilary of Arles’s minor works, appending this note: “On the authority of printed manuscripts, we assign this meter to Hilary of Arles. Whether it truly belongs to him, we dare neither assert nor deny, since no manuscript copies were available from which anything might be extracted.”

Whatever may be the case concerning its author, it seems to me to be a beginning rather than a finished poem—a poem not so much written as contemplated. Everywhere it bristles with the ugliest errors, errors that would deserve no pardon even in a beginner. Scarcely any laws of meter are observed; many verses are incomplete; scarcely even the subject matter has been touched upon.

Nevertheless, however poor the work may be, I did not think it should be withheld from the reader, lest something bearing the name of Hilary of Arles be missing here. Coustant, approving Quesnel’s judgment of the poem, says: “If for this reason it is unworthy of Hilary of Poitiers, no reason presents itself why it should be attributed to Hilary of Arles—especially since, so far as we know, no manuscripts prefer the Arlesian.”

Coustant used three manuscript copies in correcting this poem—the Lyon, Colbert, and Victorine manuscripts—and made such progress from them that we have arranged for his edition, together with its notes, to be reprinted here.

6. Some attribute two other minor works to Hilary: the poem *On Providence*, published among Prosper’s works, and the *Life of Saint Genesius*. That the poem *On Providence* cannot belong to Hilary is clear from the fact that it was written in 416, when Hilary had scarcely entered his fifteenth year.

Only Hadrian Valesius, in his *Account of the Gauls*, thought that the *Life of Saint Genesius* should be assigned to Hilary. The manuscripts, no less than the printed editions, attribute it to Bishop Paulinus, as may be seen in Ruinart’s *Acts of the Martyrs*. Therefore, just as Quesnel rightly omitted these two minor works, so we willingly omit them as well.

7. The author of the *Literary History of France*, volume II, page 265, thinks that the homily on Saint Genesius printed by Surius on August 25—the fiftieth among the homilies of Eusebius of Emesa—may be attributed to Hilary.

It was certainly recited at Arles; and since its style is not unworthy of that bishop, he thinks this sufficient to make it more readily attributable to Hilary than to Saint Eucherius, Saint Paulinus, Saint Patient, bishop of Lyon, or the others to whom some have conjectured that it should be assigned.

This opinion does indeed seem probable. Since, however, no manuscripts have so far been found that attribute this discourse to Hilary, we have also refrained from adding it here.

# Genuine minor works of Saint Hilary, bishop of Arles

## Sermon on the Life of Saint Honoratus, Bishop of Arles

*Note:* In the Vatican Regina manuscript 645 this title reads: “Here begins the Life of Saint Honoratus, bishop of Arles, whose deposition is celebrated on January 16.” At the end, however, it is called a sermon and Saint Hilary is named as its author as follows: “Here ends the sermon on the Life of Saint Honoratus, bishop, published by Saint Hilary, bishop of Arles, on the day of his deposition. Successfully completed.” Another, more recent Vatican Regina manuscript, 1025, reads: “February 17. Sermon of Saint Hilary on the deposition of the holy memory of the Lord Honoratus, bishop.” The words “Delivered on the same day” have visibly been erased; and rightly, says Don John Salinas, for Hilary delivered the sermon one year after Honoratus’s death, namely in 430.

*Note:* We have retained the Bollandist division into chapters and numbers, although a more accurate division could have been made, so that the variety of citations might not weary writers and confuse readers. — Quesnel.

### Preface

*Note:* The Ripatorium manuscript used by Bolland reads: “Recognize, most beloved.”

1. You recognize, dearest brothers, the day consecrated to the public mourning of the faithful. As long as the Lord grants me these fleeting days of this life, it will always come to me weighted with bitterness, yet full of dignity. For today that bishop of this Church, Honoratus in virtue, priesthood, and name, has been stripped of his body, in blessed memory.

Whatever I may add to conclude my speech could be judged absurd. If I say, “He has migrated to the stars,” he was already numbered among those most splendid stars of God even while he dwelt on earth. Shall I add, “He stands beside Christ”? When did he not stand beside him during his life? His whole life embodied that saying of Elijah: “The Lord lives, before whom I stand today” [1 Kings 18:15].

Shall I say, “He has abandoned earthly things,” when, as the Apostle says, “his citizenship was always in heaven” [Philippians 3:20]? Thus, whatever my mind can summon to be said about such a man lacks a fitting conclusion by the very magnitude of its subject. Joys contend with sorrows. It is sweet to remember such a man; it is punishment to be deprived of him.

2. Twofold, then, is the subject that summons me. On one side, the grace of his praises draws me toward speech; on the other, our common loss pulls me back toward sobs. Forgive me, therefore, if, while these two emotions tear my mind in opposite directions, the duty of my mouth, serving two masters, fails to respond appropriately.

Whatever memory supplies in the realm of praise, grief claims all of it for itself, counting it among our losses. Yet even if serenity of mind were present to me, and my tongue served my mind with fitting obedience, could his praise be expressed more abundantly in my words than it remains in your hearts? No one, I think, fails to perceive in that man a grace greater than the most eloquent speech of anyone could convey.

Since, therefore, as Scripture says, “the memory of the righteous is always with praises” [Proverbs 10:7], and no one can remember men of illustrious merits without praising them, I shall bring forward, as far as I am able, some of the things that your loving hearts meditate upon concerning him. Your perceptions will assist my efforts; and whatever is difficult for my speech to express, your hearts will articulate for themselves through their own thoughts.

*Note:* Some witnesses read “commemorations.”  
*Note:* Quesnel, together with certain printed editions, reads: “Full of consolatory praise, full also of dignity he will come.” The words we have removed are absent from the Bollandist manuscript and from both Vatican Regina manuscripts.  
*Note:* The two Vatican Regina manuscripts and another Bollandist manuscript read “draw back.”  
*Note:* The Bollandist edition reads, “Scripture contains in a certain passage,” in agreement with both Vatican Regina manuscripts.  
*Note:* One Vatican Regina manuscript and the Bollandist edition read, “at the end of the completion.”  
*Note:* The same manuscripts add “especially.”  
*Note:* The Vatican Regina 645 manuscript adds “God.”  
*Note:* Quesnel reads “that which belongs to the sermon.” The reading of the three manuscripts mentioned above seemed preferable.  
*Note:* Quesnel correctly reads *tepentis* (“lukewarm”), from the Arles, Lérins, and Surius manuscripts; Bolland and the cited Vatican Regina manuscript read *repentis*.

3. It is written: “Wisdom is praised at its departure”; that is, the conduct of the wise person is praised at the end of his life. Hence, in another place: “Do not praise a man during his life.” And again: “Before death, praise no one” [Sirach 11:30]—as though it said: Praise him after death. For in praising the living, an opportunity for empty exultation is offered both to the one praised, and a mark of flattery is attached to the one who praises.

In many ways, however, it is useful to praise the dead. First, because when the person whom we might please by praise is absent, all praise must necessarily be referred to the giver of grace. Then, because only admiration for virtue remains when suspicion of flattery has been removed.

The praise of the deceased, spoken in the holy congregation of the faithful, is full of edification and empty of boasting. His merits also increase in this respect: many people advance through his praise. Nor will I fear that I may be thought to speak too favorably of my own concerns, since, apart from the fact that nothing can be said about his virtues that is not inferior to them, there is no one who does not count him as his own, feel him as his own, and believe him to be his own.

Yet I do not undertake to touch upon the life of so great a man through confidence in my talent or reliance upon eloquence. If an author of ancient eloquence attempted it, his speech would not merely fail to adorn the subject; overcome by its mass, it would collapse beneath it.

Your love summons me; your affection supplies the confidence to say something about him. We believe that his merits will animate the discourse, even though my talent is lukewarm; what lies low in words will be lifted up by realities; and the discourse, poured forth upon him, will be seasoned in the dwelling of your hearts by the love that fills them.

## CHAPTER I. The consular nobility of Honoratus. He is baptized as a young man

4. It is known to all trained in oratory that those who undertake to praise someone’s life first proclaim his homeland and origin, so that whatever is lacking in his own virtues may seem to have preceded him in the glory of his ancestors.

But we are all one in Christ, and the height of nobility is to be counted among the children of God. The splendor of earthly origin cannot add anything to our dignity except by being despised. No one in heaven is more glorious than the person who, rejecting the lineage of his fathers, chooses to be known solely by the fatherhood of Christ.

I therefore pass over the insignia of his ancestral worldly honors, and the nobility of his family, advanced even to the consulship—something the world possesses as desirable and almost supreme—but which he disdained with the greater nobility of his heart. He did not please himself with the superfluous honors of his family, for through love of the truth he no longer desired what had once been his own.

*Note:* The Lérins, Arles, and Surius manuscripts read this way. Bolland reads “servants,” less appropriately.

[Col. 1251C] 5. Rather, my account hastens to explain with what faith, of his own accord, he desired baptism during the years of adolescence, and how, while sound in judgment, he feared death with mature deliberation; [Note: [Col. 1251D] Bollandus and one Vaticanus Reginensis, who had perceived that he would die before baptism.] how he foresaw that he would die before baptism; with what thirst he desired his life to be renewed; how sweet his infancy was; how well-disciplined his boyhood; how serious his adolescence; how, throughout all the stages of life, he always surpassed others in grace and virtue, and was always found greater than himself, so that you would think he had been educated under some divine tutelage. He was instructed without any urging from his family. With God’s help he preserved his baptism without any human concern; and, greater still, while the radiance of the font was still fresh and undefiled, he turned away without an adviser [Note: Lirinensis: “to the fonts,” less well; for the subject is flight from the world, not haste toward baptism. Quesnel.]. I said, “without an adviser”; but what of the obstacle presented by his homeland, the resistance of his father, the opposition of all his relatives [Note: Bollandus: “held him back.”]? For his charm had entered the minds of all; and when Christ claimed him for himself, the world held him fast in all those who belonged to him. Some had been bound by affection for him; others were fettered by the allurements of companionship; still others were held by admiration for worldly accomplishments in the various pursuits of young men. As many attractions from his former life as he had, so many bonds drew him back from conversion. Everyone feared that a common ornament of the family would be carried away. And indeed, who ever failed to receive his bearing as though it were his own? What clothing did he not adorn? Thus his homeland, his friends, and his parents alike thought that they were losing him as a most splendid gem and the common glory of all; for they did not believe that all these things were to be changed and reformed for the better, as we saw them changed, but almost that they were going to die. Hence, because his father saw that he diligently carried out everything he undertook, he kept him away from baptism as long as he could, fearing that he would be wholly swept away, as indeed happened, by love of religion. Yet the desire for and love of Christ prevailed, and, once his father’s evasions had been dispelled, faithful boyhood rushed upon baptism. For while still a catechumen he had so shaped himself amid the first rudiments of faith that he rejected wantonness in exchange for the reverence due to the baptism he would one day receive, honored the clergy as fathers, and at times, with a child’s resources, helped the poor. Whatever that age could still possess, and whatever it could love all the more because possessing it was new, he offered generously out of compassion: already then rehearsing, in small things, the contempt of everything and the distribution of all that was his.

6. Through these and similar exercises, therefore, the catechumen’s sturdy faith hurried him toward baptism. From this point his prudent father, troubled by a suspicion of tender, earthly affection [Note: Bollandus: “tender.”], tried to entice him with various pleasures, lure him into youthful pursuits, ensnare him in the diverse vanities of the world, and grow young again, as it were, in fellowship with his adolescent son; [Col. 1252C] he occupied him with hunting and various games and armed himself with every sweetness of this world to subdue that age. Nor was it without reason that his worldly father feared he would be carried away from him by Christ [Note: [Col. 1252D] Salinas adds: “from him to Christ.”], for he embraced him as unique among the other most distinguished young men.

7. Yet amid all this his greater concern was to preserve his baptism. The adolescent grew weary of what delighted his aged father, always exhorting himself as follows:

“This life is pleasant, but it deceives. In the churches other precepts are recited; in my ears other commands have sounded. There modesty, continence, tranquility, and shame are taught; here unrestrained luxury is nourished. There piety flourishes; here bodily exercise. There Christ invites us to an eternal kingdom; here the devil solicits us toward what is temporary. Everything that is in the world is vanity and the desire of the eyes, and the world is passing away, together with its desire; but whoever does the will of God remains forever, just as he himself remains forever. Let us therefore hurry to be torn away from these snares while we are still held less tightly. [Note: [Col. 1252D] One Vaticanus Reginensis: ‘Things long tied are loosened more slowly.’ Another, with Bollandus: ‘Things long tied are loosened with difficulty.’] Things long bound are loosened with difficulty. It is easier to uproot tender growth than to cut down what has grown strong. Save your life on the mountain, [Col. 1253A] lest evil thoughts seize you [Note: [Col. 1253D] Bollandus: ‘the evils of this way of life.’ One Vaticanus Reginensis and the editions before Quesnel read likewise, except Surius.]. The poison of pleasure spreads quickly; the freedom received through his grace must be preserved for Christ. Let others marvel at gold and silver. As I see it, metals rule those who rule. Let others possess estates and slaves, not without the captivity of their own souls. Let others rejoice in honors and crush within themselves the honor of the divine image. For me it is enough not to be a slave of vices; for me salvation is joy; for me wisdom is a spouse; for me pleasure is in the virtues [Note: [Col. 1253D] This is better according to Vaticanus Reginensis 1025 and according to Bollandus, Joannes Adam, and Joannes Salinas. Quesnel reads ‘will.’]; let Christ be my treasure, who will weigh against my fleeting joys better things, and will grant that in this life I may both take delight in and be adorned by devotion to discipline, and amid these things become worthy of the heavenly kingdoms.”

8. Such meditation did not produce long delays; rather, the spark, nourished by such fuel, immediately burst into the flame of conversion [Col. 1253B] [Note: [Col. 1253D] The same Vaticanus, with Bollandus: “burst forth.”]. Submitting his neck to the yoke of the Lord’s service, he shook off the yoke of freedom, understanding that the greatest form of captivity is the license of youth. His luxuriant hair was reduced to short locks. The splendor of his clothing was transferred to the radiance of his mind. The beauty of his milk-white neck was covered by stiff cloaks. Joy passed into serenity [Note: [Col. 1253D] Thus the Arelatensis manuscript and one Vaticanus Reginensis. Another, with Bollandus, reads “gravity”; Lirinensis, “severity.”], and the vigor of his limbs was changed into vigor of spirit. The strength of his body migrated into strength of spirit. His handsome face grew pale through fasting and, though formerly full of color [Note: [Col. 1253D] Bollandus: “cosmetics.”], became full of gravity. And why say more? He suddenly appeared wholly other, changed from one person into another, so that his father lamented him no otherwise than as a father bereaved of his son. Truly, his body was completely mortified; but for him the spirit was life. From this point the whole persecution of his parents was aroused. He was contumacious toward his father only then and for the first time, when he strove to be a son of God the Father, with that love already ordered within him, as Solomon commanded. Thus the prophet mentioned above declares under God’s voice: “Order love within me” (Song of Songs II, 4). He certainly ordered it, and under the arrangement of love perceived that God was to be loved first, and then one’s neighbor. The father’s old age therefore believed that it was being condemned by the conversion of that young man [Note: [Col. 1253D] Salinas: “by his way of life.”]. It confronted him, resisted him, threatened him; yet none of this shook the boy, who trusted in God.

## CHAPTER II. He travels abroad with his brother Venantius.—The latter’s death.—Honoratus and Venantius leave their homeland.—Pilgrimages to holy places.

9. The Lord, the consoler, stands beside his young recruit and does not fail to raise up one of his own brothers to join him. Called to conversion by his example, and with the elder following the younger, he accompanied him during the brief time he lived, both in their fellowship and in virtue. From this arose among them agreeable contests over their chosen way of life: whose mind was more inclined toward piety [Note: Salinas adds “was”; and, shortly afterward, “was able.”], whose food more austere, whose speech gentler, whose clothing rougher; who spoke less often, who could pray more frequently; whom bed detained less, whom reading held more; whom injury moved less, whom compassion moved more; who more promptly gave away what he had taken from himself; who more willingly offered a guest a bed of haircloth and the pillow of the customary stone; who more readily refreshed a traveler with tears before distributing alms, and fed Christ in the guest first through affection before feeding the stranger at table; in whose mouth the world was rarer, in whose mouth Christ was more frequent; who, amid that height of virtues, seemed smaller to himself, and the more meritoriously he ascended, the more he diminished through compunction. A certain private episcopate was then exercised in their way of life [Note: Salinas adds “already then.”]. I am mistaken unless many bishops learned from them, while being received, how to receive; for if some were not frightened by the rigor of their discipline, they carried away from there more humanity in the soul than refreshment in the body [Note: Vaticanus Reginensis 1025 reads “of the soul,” and later “of the bodies.”]. Thus together they adorned the whole homeland; and, as long as their memory remains in the minds of many, they guarded the bodies of some and the spirits of others, clothing, feeding, and instructing each according as he lacked clothing, teaching, or resources. No one who had been exhausted by the labor of travel arrived there without feeling that he had reached his homeland and the fields of his patrimony; no one departing from there toward farther places moved his foot without feeling as though he had left his own house again, and once again left his fellow citizens and relatives [Note: Quesnel’s edition omitted, by a leap, the following seven words.].

10. Meanwhile everyone’s love for them grew, multiplied, and spread, and their fame was carried into every farther region; by now the whole homeland vied in service, love, and honor toward them. It was impossible for them to attain obscurity and poverty: the more their life was hidden, the more their fame shone forth, and each exposed the other to praise and glory, referring everything to one common virtue [Note: Quesnel’s edition reads “summit of virtues,” less well.]. But while each wished to be obscured beneath the other’s shadow, like reflected brightness [Note: The Vaticanus Reginensis manuscripts: “shone upon both.” Bollandus and Joannes Adam: “shone from both sides.”] illuminated them both. What gravity they possessed, what elderly maturity, how rare the visits of women, even of those closest to them, and what flight from every vanity amid so many virtues! How gentle their consolation, and how vigilant their care for the salvation of those who had entrusted themselves to their teaching! They led an angelic life on earth, in great patience, in vigils, in fasts, in chastity, in knowledge, in long-suffering, in gentleness, in the Holy Spirit, in unfeigned love, in the word of truth, and in the power of God. Meanwhile they were afraid of their own glory and of the fragrance of their good way of life, spread far and wide. Although they referred it to the praise of God, they nevertheless feared that it would bring them the danger of vanity; they considered that they had received their reward during their own lifetime, and, disdaining human companionship, burned with love for the desert.

11. Having therefore taken counsel, and in a way suffered persecution because of their honor, they set out for foreign lands. Again the homeland rose up; again their relatives resisted. [Note: Thus both Vaticanus Reginensis manuscripts, Bollandus, and others. Quesnel’s version reads: “They all fear being deprived at once of this light of their own.” But the better reading of the text indicates that their fear was now sounder, since it arose not, as before, from love of the world but from love of the virtues shining in Honoratus and his brother.] They feared losing their own light, but now with a sounder fear. What a contest of faith and love there was then, good Jesus! What efforts of counsel, prayers, and tears! Who there did not claim for himself the duty of a relative, or whose tears did not compete with those of their father? The whole homeland felt that it was losing fathers in those young men. And truly, their old age was gray not with years but with graces; not wrinkled in their limbs but beautiful in their conduct [Note: Thus both Vaticanus Reginensis manuscripts, with the Arelatensis and Ripatensis; Bollandus Al. reads “ancient,” while Bollandus and Surius read “venerable.”].

O what a great dispensation of your administration, Lord! You do not permit your lamps, shining with the fire of faith, to remain fixed in one place, but you carry them before the illumination of different places [Note: The Ripatensis manuscript, in Bollandus: “you carry them forth for the illumination.”], inspiring the desire to migrate and to flee glory. That glory was indeed to be multiplied by the very increase of virtue gained through their pilgrimage. Their estate, long worn down by varied works of mercy yet still ample, was broken up; and relative and stranger alike were admitted as purchasers of the patrimony [Note: Another reading: “a neighbor.”]. There was no consideration for the parents’ profits, as though they were selling what was not their own. The property that had served the poor ever since it had been possessed by them was now sold for distribution to the poor. The homeland received their overflowing mercy and repaid it with overflowing tears.

12. “They went out from their land, their household, and their kindred,” and by an equal example they were shown to be true sons of Abraham [Note: The Ripatensis manuscript reads “of their father,” and shortly afterward “truly” instead of “of the true.” Bollandus.]. Yet, so that no one would think that they had begun this venture rashly in youthful daring, they took with them an old man of perfect and consummate gravity [Note: Quesnel: “of age.” The correction introduced from Vaticanus Reginensis 1025 is confirmed by Joannes Salinas from Eucherius, On the Praise of the Desert, where he calls Caprasius “venerable in gravity.”], whom they had always called their father in Christ: the holy Caprasius, who was still living an angelic life in the islands. Although your affection has hitherto been unaware of his name and still does not know his life, Christ counts him among his friends. They took him as the organizer and guardian of their life in the Lord—men whom a great many young people had already chosen as their guardians. Thus a hiding place for their pilgrimage was sought, and the fame of their virtue was fled; but wherever they went, another fame arose there, whether they wished it or not. [Col. 1256A] Happy lands and blessed shores that a pilgrim thirsting for the heavenly homeland makes illustrious! Others approach the shores of the East and whatever other places are filled with saints, in order to receive the grace of example; these men arouse whatever places they approach by their good examples. Their substance was scattered everywhere, and at every arrival the good fragrance of Christ burned brightly.

13. At that time the Church of Massilia almost snatched from this city the very man whose memory nourishes us today, at the urging of that city’s bishop, who rejoiced greatly in having him as a companion. But what could that fervor not overcome through a contest of tears and a struggle of entreaties? Therefore, more eagerly, warned by this new danger [Note: Salinas adds “as if.”], they crossed the seas [Note: Another reading: “they crossed over.” Quesnel.] and sought shores for which even that Roman eloquence, so abundant in them, would be barbarous [Note: Salinas adds “even.”]. It would take too long to recount what benefit each place derived from their departure, how much health they brought to the churches without any clerical office, and how many teachers they silently became for teachers.

14. It is enough to recall that, undaunted by their desire for Christ, they endured the sea’s swell; they sought the squalor and barrenness of the Achaean shore; and, delicately and softly raised [Note: The Ripatensis manuscript: “nobly.”] as they had been, they contended against such great variations of waters and winds. How burdensome and intolerable this was to their tender constitution was shown by the passing there of their most blessed brother in Christ, the man Venantius, and by their own illnesses and those of their companions. What he thought he had done or received at that funeral in Methone [Note: There are several cities of this name. Here the one situated at the mouth of Messenia in the Peloponnese seems to be intended. Bollandus.] was made clear by the many ranks of those singing psalms. Here Hebrew, Greek, and Latin speakers rejoice; even the Jew, while rejecting Christ, admires Christ’s faithful servant. The fervent choirs themselves strike the stars, and, as we believe, angelic choirs sing together with human voices; Christ comes to meet his faithful servant.

“Well done, Venantius, good and faithful servant; and when you hear, ‘Enter into the joy of your Lord’ (Matthew XXV, 21), remember us, whom the joys of this world still assail.”

The struggles of flesh and soul come to an end; eternal life and glory begin [Note: Quesnel adds “Amen,” absent from Bollandus and our manuscripts.].

## CHAPTER III. After his brother’s death, Honoratus comes to Italy and lodges with bishops.—Leontius, bishop of Fréjus.—He enters the island of Lérins.

15. From there Christ now restores your Honoratus to you and, by a hidden hand, tempers the healing brought by his return [Note: Thus the Vaticanus Reginensis 1025 manuscript, with Bollandus. Quesnel: “the healthfulness of his return.”]. For whatever he touches in passing, he illuminates. [Col. 1257A] Italy rejoices to be blessed by his arrival. Tuscany, having revered him, embraces him and, through its priests, binds him with the most affectionate delays. But God’s providence, looking ahead for us, broke through every obstacle, and Christ invited into a desert near this city the man whom the desire for the desert had drawn from his homeland. He therefore sought an unoccupied island, deserted because of its excessive wildness and inaccessible through fear of poisonous animals, situated under a mountain ridge of the Alps not far away. Besides the convenience of solitude, he was attracted by the proximity and bound by the affection of the holy and most blessed man in Christ, Leontius the bishop, while many others were also trying to draw him back by a new undertaking [Note: Thus the manuscripts and editions, except Quesnel, who reads: “while many, trying to prolong their thirst by a new draught.”]. The surrounding inhabitants considered that terrible wasteland their own and competed in their eagerness of faith to occupy him within their borders. But he, unable to endure human society and desiring to be cut off from the world even by the barrier of the sea [Col. 1257B], carried this in his heart and on his lips, saying now to himself, now to his companions:

“You shall walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and you shall trample the lion and the dragon” (Psalm XC, 13);

and the promise made by Christ in the Gospels to his disciples:

“Behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions” (Luke X, 19).

Thus he entered fearlessly and dispelled the fear of his companions by his own security. The horror of the solitude fled; the multitude of serpents yielded. But what darkness did that light not drive away? What poisons did not yield to that remedy? I judge that this must truly be counted among his unheard-of and plainly miraculous merits [Note: Thus from the same Vaticanus Reginensis manuscripts, Salinas, Quesnel, and other editions: “remarkable.”]: although, as we saw, encounters with serpents were so frequent in those arid places, especially when stirred up by the heat of the sea, they were never a source not only of danger but even of fear to anyone.

16. Why delay longer? With Christ cooperating, so to speak, and every adversity that had previously inspired terror overcome, your Honoratus [Note: Thus Salinas, as also above: “your Honoratus.” Quesnel: “our.”] establishes there a kind of camp of God. The place that had formerly driven human beings away from dwelling there is illumined by angelic services. The hiding place is illuminated while the light remains hidden. The darkness of the previously unknown exile yields to the radiance of the voluntary exile. What, then, does that addition or improvement contribute? Wherever Honoratus goes, honor must necessarily be present there [Note: Salinas adds “also.”]. Here he is first bound to the office of the clergy, which he had long avoided; here the priestly fillet binds the man who had fled from it; and he who had refused to go to ecclesiastical dignity finds dignity coming to him [Note: The Vaticanus Reginensis manuscripts and Bollandus read “to come.”]. There appeared a priest worthy of not merely double but manifold honor, before whom episcopacy acknowledged no difference of priesthood and no privilege of title [Col. 1257D]. No bishop ever claimed so much for himself as to recognize, before that priest, any distinction of priestly rank or any privilege of the episcopal title, or to count himself that priest’s companion [Note: The Arelatensis manuscript reads “join himself.” Shortly afterward, instead of “in the priesthood,” Quesnel notes in the margin: “Perhaps, ‘into the priesthood.’”]. Yet he preserved the monk’s humility in the priesthood as completely as, as a monk, he fully possessed the merits of the priesthood.

17. Through his own industry, a church worthy of God’s chosen is built there; roofs suitable for monastic dwellings rise; waters denied for centuries flow abundantly [Note: Salinas, who used the Vaticanus Reginensis manuscripts, reads thus. Quesnel: “waters denied for centuries flow in rivalry.”], bringing forth, at their single source, two miracles of the Old Testament. For when they burst from the rock, they flowed sweet amid the bitterness of the sea. [Note: Thus from the same Salinas. Quesnel: “Now the whole region, seeking God, was eagerly making its way there,” and so forth.] By now the whole region was eagerly directing thither those who sought God. Whoever desired Christ sought Honoratus; and plainly, whoever sought Honoratus found Christ. For Christ lived wholly in him; Christ had taken up residence in his breast as though in a lofty citadel and most splendid temple. There dwelt chastity, which is holiness, faith, wisdom, and virtue; there justice and truth shone. Thus, as though with outstretched and open arms [Note: Quesnel: “with veins poured forth and arms extended.” We have preferred the reading of the other editions and of Vaticanus Reginensis 1025.], he invited everyone into his embrace—that is, into the love of Christ—and people from every direction flocked eagerly to him.

For what land, what nation does not yet have citizens in his monastery? What barbarism did he not soften? How often did he make doves, as it were, from savage beasts [Note: One manuscript: “how he made them gentle.”]? How he sprinkled bitter dispositions, at times, with the sweetness of Christ! Those whose depravity had previously been painful to themselves later became a delight to everyone through their grace; and once they had tasted the sweetness of goodness, they could not help hating more and more what they had been. For, as though led into a new light, they detested that ancient prison of errors long dwelling within them [Note: Quesnel: “of errors long compressed within them.” We have followed the reading of the other editions and manuscripts.]. Through his exhortation, the various plague of souls was driven away [Col. 1258C]. Bitterness, harshness, and rage gave way to the freedom that Christ had offered and which brought delight [Note: In Quesnel: “and he rejoiced.”]; and rest after long and heavy Pharaonic servitude brought pleasure.

A wondrous and astonishing transformation: not, as they say, by Circe’s cup turning human beings into beasts, but by the word of Christ, with Honoratus serving it as the sweetest cup, making human beings out of beasts. For what would that persistence, joined with zeal, not accomplish [Note: Vaticanus Reginensis 1025: “would obtain.”]? Or what stones would it not turn into sons of Abraham? There was such a workshop of virtues for polishing minds [Note: Vaticanus Reginensis 645: “there were such services.” Shortly afterward Salinas reads “and if it were less.”] that, if he did not advance a person toward salvation by living exhortations, he constrained God through prayer.

He took everyone’s sufferings as his own and wept over them as though they were his own; he counted everyone’s progress and labors as his own. Knowing how to rejoice with those who rejoice and weep with those who weep, he transferred both everyone’s vices and virtues into the accumulation of his own merit. For just as virtue stimulates virtue, so compassion bestowed upon the suffering bears fruit. [Col. 1259A] [Note: Quesnel, from the Arelatensis manuscript: “For he heals each person more than each person heals himself.” The reading of the other editors, which is also found in the Vaticanus Reginensis manuscripts, seemed preferable and appears to explain the verb “bears fruit,” insofar as Honoratus reaps more glory from compassion bestowed on many than each individual who attains salvation through his work.] For he would reap more from each person than each person would reap for himself. The salvation of each person built up one glory for him [Note: Vaticanus Reginensis 1025: “builds one glory for him.”].

He persisted industriously, promptly, and tirelessly, according as he had perceived each person’s nature and character. He approached one in secret, another publicly; one sternly, another gently; and, in order to alter the correction, he often altered the very appearance of the correction. Hence it was that we have not easily seen anyone so greatly loved or feared: he placed these two emotions of his in each of his people in such a way that his love introduced fear of sin, and his fear of discipline introduced love.

## CHAPTER IV. The illustrious formation of the people of Lérins.—The virtues of Honoratus.—Honoratus kind and generous toward guests.—Eucherius writes to Honoratus.

[Col. 1259B] 18. It is incredible how concerned he was that no one should be afflicted by sadness and that no worldly thought should oppress anyone. How readily he perceived what troubled each person, as though he carried the minds of individuals within his own mind [Note: This reading is better in Salinas, who used the Vaticanus Reginensis manuscripts. Quesnel: “how, in his mind, he carried the minds of individuals.”], and with what thoughtful administration of compassion he took care that no one should be burdened by excessive labor or grow sluggish through excessive rest. With pious affection he measured, if one may say so, the sleep of each of the brothers [Note: Quesnel: “of each of the fathers.”]. He was always shaking the physically strong out of idleness, while compelling those fervent in spirit to rest. I believe that by divine prompting he knew everyone’s strength, everyone’s spirit, and everyone’s appetite, having truly become the servant of all for the sake of Jesus Christ.

It is astonishing how one man fulfilled so many duties at once, especially while afflicted by such varied weakness. Though unequal in strength, he accompanied the strongest, still robust from their recent conversion, in fasts and vigils under the same rule [Col. 1259C]. He visited the sick, himself even weaker; he provided refreshment for souls and bodies alike; and, lest anything be given less attention than it deserved, he was always reviewing matters in his mind:

“This one is cold; this one is thinking; that man finds the labor difficult; this one cannot tolerate this food; that man has been injured by another; what this one inflicted is serious, and no less serious is what that one suffered” [Note: Salinas adds “the injury”; shortly afterward he prefers the singular, “the insult inflicted,” and likewise in what follows.].

Great diligence was needed for the offended party to obtain reconciliation, while he counted the insults inflicted upon himself as light or nonexistent, and the other person sighed that he had inflicted very serious ones. This was his continual work and constant concern: to lighten Christ’s yoke for everyone; to avert whatever the devil had introduced; to disperse the cloud of faults and restore the clear skies of graces; to implant, by loving, love of Christ and of neighbors; and to cultivate everyone’s minds as though they were his own breast [Col. 1260A]; to renew their joys and always burn with desire for Christ as though it were the first day of their conversion.

19. Hence it was that the whole congregation, eager for divine service and gathered to his name from different parts of the earth, diverse in both customs and languages, conspired in love for him. Everyone called him lord; everyone called him father, counting that in him they had been given a homeland, relatives, and everything at once [Note: Quesnel adds “or.”]. All had learned, because he suffered with them, to count his sorrows as their own. Thus the distinguished and most blessed man in Christ, the presbyter Salvianus, one of his beloved companions, rightly said in his writings that, just as the sun changes the appearance of the sky through its own obscurity or brightness [Note: Salinas: “just as the sun changed the face of heaven by its own obscurity or brightness,” and so forth.], so that congregation, thirsting for heaven and devoted to heavenly pursuits, received from him either the cloudiness or the serenity of their minds, as though from a special Sun in Christ; when he was afflicted, they too were afflicted, and when he breathed freely, they recovered.

Hence there was—and still remains through his prayers—spread throughout his monastery the grace of the Holy Spirit, established by the example and instruction of so great a teacher in a variety of gifts of grace, in humility and gentleness, in unfeigned love, and in the one glory of the head amid the diversity of the members [Note: Thus Vaticanus Reginensis 1025 and most editions. Quesnel: “in the division.”].

20. Amid all this he showed great care for visitors and guests. Who ever passed him by? Who, in longing for such a great man and disregarding his own convenience, did not at once abandon however prosperous a voyage and however pleasant the winds [Note: Salinas, from the same Vaticanus Reginensis: “and did not refuse whatever favorable winds, out of longing for such a great man and disregard for his own convenience?” Bollandus has “or” instead of “did not.”]? Or, if it was not possible to reach the island, who did not count the violent assistance of a favorable voyage the bitterest storm? No one approached there without haste; no one felt his stay there prolonged; no one departed from there without the greatest security, escorted by his love, resources, and prayers, and sent away as one newly recognized yet as though long his own. In the squalor of the desert he supplied delights by his presence [Note: In Quesnel the words “by his presence” are omitted.], receiving everyone with such joy and love as though he had been expecting him. His resources were equal to his generosity of spirit, and were administered with equal faith.

For he who had gladly heard, “Sell all that you have, give to the poor, and come, follow me” (Matthew XIX, 21), gladly accepted from each person whatever he had devoted in his heart to an act of mercy, so that it might be distributed. Everyone entrusted all his possessions to him without fear, since he had followed his example in leaving everything. Hence there was a frequent gathering to him from the devastation of various regions [Col. 1261A] [Note: In the same author, “captivity” is less suitable.]. Truly he was not like a stingy or timid steward who, out of regard for the congregation entrusted to him and growing daily, would distribute some things and preserve more [Note: Salinas: “one who regarded.”]. But what would he not do daily with another’s property, when he had once done it with his own? That is, he reserved nothing for himself or his people except the food and clothing of the present day [Note: Some editions: “he would reserve clothing.”].

21. Once the material available for distribution was exhausted; faith never was. On one occasion, when his free-flowing treasury retained a single gold coin from many thousands [Note: The Lérins manuscript: “eager.”], he gave that very coin with unwavering resolve to a poor man passing by, even though many necessities were lacking, and said to me and to the others standing there:

“It is certain that the one who will provide is already approaching, if our generosity has nothing to bring forth” [Note: Quesnel adds “Christ.”].

Scarcely three or four hours had passed as the day advanced when the man who would confirm his words immediately appeared [Col. 1261B] [Note: We have added, with Salinas, the words found in both Vaticanus Reginensis manuscripts.]. O happy generosity, which faith served! O happy faith, which generosity never delayed! Indeed, however much his faith supplied [Note: Another reading: “however much was available to him.”], he could not distribute it all with his own hand alone. He had many highly trusted men in many places, through whose hands he always spent what was brought to him. Thus, by the grace of one steward, he had many stewards; and his faith, like a common spring, flowed out to many givers and receivers. No hardship reached him that extended beyond him or failed to find its limit in him [Note: Salinas adds “almost.”].

22. From all sides, then, the services of letters were eagerly brought to him, whom people thought—or at least hoped—was hidden away. What novel emotions marked the replies he sent: how weighty, how gentle, how sweet! Hence the blessed Eucherius, splendid in the world and more splendid in Christ as an emulator of Honoratus’s virtue, while living on an island near him, received Honoratus’s letter from the desert, written as usual on wax-covered tablets, and said:

“You have returned your honey to the wax.”

Who therefore did not consider himself blessed, his house blessed, and his writing cases blessed, enriched by a great blessing through a small gift from his mouth? And indeed there was so much salt and sweetness in his writings that they deserved to be stored not in writing cases or cupboards but in the treasury of the breast. Hence many carry them inscribed upon their minds and gladly bring them forth as testimony to their love [Note: Quesnel: “carry them forward.” Later Salinas: “such great friends for themselves.”]. Finally, who ever bound so many friends to himself by the services of his presence as he had unknown people who loved him and desired him most eagerly?

## CHAPTER V. Saint Hilary Is Converted by the Exhortations of Honoratus. The Efficacy of Christ’s Grace in Hilary.

### 23.

Meanwhile, while I recall his abundant kindness toward everyone [Note: Salinas reads *multimodam*, “manifold,” instead of *multam*, “great.”], I pass over his infinite concern for me—for his concern for my salvation in Christ certainly brought me no less benefit than his love left among you as a source of honor and affection. For my sake, so far as concerns his merit and my own judgment, he did not disdain to approach the homeland he had despised; nor did he shrink from the labor of so long a journey [Note: Salinas likewise reads *tanti itineris*, “of so great a journey.”], burdensome especially because of his many illnesses already long endured [Note: Quesnellus, placing a full stop earlier, inserted *Venit* (“He came”) and omitted *illic* (“there”). We have followed the reading of the manuscripts and other editions.]. There, although I was already in those years excessively attached to the world and rebellious against God, he gently sought to lead me, as both a deceiver and a man of truth, toward the love of Christ.

It would take too long to introduce the force of his eloquence in exhortation. In those exhortations, after he had already been able to apply to himself the sharpest spurs toward conversion, he poured himself forth in many ways, having long drunk from the springs of wisdom [Note: Quesnellus reads “to remove the sharpest spurs toward his way of life from himself.”]. But when his words of piety descended only slightly into my ears, he turned to the customary defenses of prayer [Note: The Vatican manuscript, Reg. 1025, reads: “and thus, driven by the fruit of his labor, my hardness…”]. The cry of his affection, repulsed by my hardness, beat upon and penetrated the most compassionate ears of God, even unto mercy [Note: Thus in certain printed editions and the Vatican manuscript, Reg. 1025; Quesnellus reads this way through “merciful.”].

Indeed, while I resisted him and sometimes bound my obstinacy by an oath through that excessively dangerous worldly habit, he had earlier promised, in what I may call a prophetic spirit [Note: Salinas adds *jam*, “already”]: “What you do not grant me, God grants.” And oh, how long he strove to soften my hardness with a rain of tears! With what devout kisses and embraces he struggled with me for my salvation! Yet for the moment, as that man says, “I won”—a most wretched victory [Note: Quesnellus reads “the most wretched victory.” Shortly afterward, instead of *Exagitandum*, Salinas reads *Sed agitandum*, “But I had to be driven.”].

Then the right hand of God undertook to drive me from there and tame me; for to Him Honoratus had entrusted me in prayer. What waves then arose in my heart! What storms of different and mutually opposing wills were stirred up! How often did willing and unwilling succeed one another in my mind!

And why say more? In his absence Christ carried out His work in me. After two days [Note: Thus with Quesnellus, the manuscript Vaticanus Reginensis 645. Salinas and Bollandus, with another Vatican manuscript, Reginensis, read “after three days.”], through the mercy of God, my stubbornness was subdued by his prayers. Thought had driven away sleep, and, when the devout Lord invited me, the whole world with its pleasures stood before me at a distance. My mind debated with me what should be sought and what should be abandoned [Note: In the *Life of Saint Hilary*, chapter 4, where this testimony is quoted, we read *videretur*, “might seem.” Salinas omits “what should be sought,” using instead “what should be desired” in the *Life* cited.], as though we were discussing matters with a friend.

Thanks be to You, good Jesus; thanks be to You, who, moved by the devout supplication of Your servant Honoratus, broke my chains and placed upon me the chains of Your love. If I am bound by these, the chains of sin will never regain their strength. Therefore I come obedient, I who had departed proud; laying aside every resistance, I approach as a new petitioner.

Thus, thus the prayer of a holy man brings back his fugitives; thus it subdues the obstinate; thus it overcomes the rebellious.

### 24.

With what tears did he then sprinkle my dryness [Note: Thus Bollandus, Salinas, and both Vatican manuscripts, Reginenses. Quesnellus reads “he watered.”], and with what devout weeping did he also draw me into tears! He received me with such humility and gentleness, as though he himself were being rescued by me. Immediately every reason for delay was removed.

Then, for the first time, he recognized that homeland which he had long believed must be fled [Note: Salinas adds *esse*, “to be,” and notes that Honoratus and Hilary were from the same homeland]. He led me away with him as his spoil; he rejoiced, triumphed, and exulted. Yet, following his own example, he hastened to enclose me in the desert, since I desired solitude. First he nourished me with milk, and afterward with solid food. He also gave me to drink from that overflowing fountain of heavenly wisdom which was within him.

Would that my spirit’s narrowness had received as much as he strove to pour into it [Note: Salinas reads *studebat*, “he strove,” instead of *studuit*, “he strove” in the completed form]! He would surely have prepared me for you and given you someone worthy of your desire; and, without knowing it, he would have educated a suitable successor to himself [Note: The next six words are absent in Quesnellus; we have supplied them from other editions and manuscripts.].

Moreover, how much he had increased in me that overflowing love of his for all people—something I may say without envy—and how much lighter he had made Christ’s light yoke for me by his gentleness! [Note: Salinas has this form. Quesnellus instead reads: “How often did he name my mind, how often my soul, how often my tongue!”] How often did he call me his mind, how often his soul, how often his tongue! How impatient he was of my absence, how constantly he desired my presence, considering it most unworthy that I should be absent! What shall I say about all these things except that prophetic saying which the Lord fulfilled for him on my behalf?

## CHAPTER VI. Honoratus Becomes a Bishop and Lives as a Bishop. — Almsgiving as Refreshment for the Dead.

### 25.

Meanwhile, beloved ones, touching upon everything briefly rather than recounting it, I have repeated concerning your most diligent shepherd things that were known more to others than to you [Note: Quesnellus reads *refricari*, “to be refreshed,” perhaps through a typographical error, instead of *refricavi*, “I have recalled.”]. We saw his priesthood increased in dignity in this Church, while in holiness and conduct it had already been supreme.

But why, I ask, is one so far away and previously unknown so eagerly desired? Who impressed upon your hearts the grace of one who was absent and whom you had not previously seen? Who awakened that longing, so that when you had been deprived of those whom the Lord had granted you in the desert, such a longing for him was born among you? It was certainly He who orders all things: He who granted him to his homeland for as long as He saw it fitting, and who led this great grace of His servant across seas and lands for the benefit of those who saw him.

### 26.

In short, from that brief period during which he was brought to you, it is easy to measure how much more or less I may say about him. For you saw, beloved ones, that watchfulness of concern, that devotion to discipline, those tears of piety, and that constant and perpetual serenity of mind, whose testimony was an unchanging countenance [Note: Quesnellus reads “his countenance was almost unchanging,” while the other printed editions and the Vatican manuscripts read “the rest being penitent.”].

You also heard that mouth, harmonious with his life, in which there was a purity of heart corresponding to it [Note: Thus with Quesnellus and Salinas, manuscript Vaticanus Reginensis 645. Bollandus, with other manuscripts, reads: “in which there was the consciousness of a heart made golden.”], and a clarity of speech.

You saw that breadth of charity which was so great in him that, not without reason, the same holy man whose nearby saying I quoted declared that, if charity itself had to be represented in a face, it would seem that it ought most especially to be painted in the face of Honoratus [Note: Salinas reads: “if it had to be expressed in a face, it would seem that it should be painted above all in the face of Honoratus.”].

Who, then, ever thought that he had seen him sufficiently? To whom was he not all things in place of every affection? Who joined gentleness with severity in such a way? Who administered discipline so mingled with joy [Note: Salinas, with most printed editions and one Vatican manuscript, reads *hilaritate*, “joy,” rather than Quesnellus’s *laetitiae*, “gladness”]? Whom did he correct without sharing in the joy of the person being corrected? When did his joy ever smell of frivolity? When was his sorrow not salutary? When did his groaning arise except from grief over another’s sin?

Who did not find him greater than he had previously seen him? Always placed at the summit of the virtues, he always found some way in which he might grow.

### 27.

Moreover, under his exhortation, what anxious person did not despise his own grief? What person of savage character did not curse his own madness? What arrogant person did not loathe his own pride more than anyone else? What wanton person did not detest his lust?

And why say more? He had become all things to all people, as the Apostle says (1 Cor. II, 22), and was a common medicine for everyone. He possessed scarcely any grace that was not so full in him that he seemed specially to cultivate and possess it as though it were his one special quality. In no condition of life did he fail to flourish so greatly that he seemed especially suited to it.

### 28.

Finally, as soon as he received the governance of this Church of Arles [Note: Salinas adds *sanctae*, “holy,” and omits *Arelatensis*, “of Arles,” although he notes that this word is found in one Vatican manuscript], his first concern was concord, and his chief labor was to join together in mutual love the brotherhood, still heated by disagreements over the appointment of a bishop [Note: Salinas reads *fraternitatis*, “of the brotherhood,” and shortly afterward *dissidentes*, “disagreeing.” Quesnellus had *de assumendo episcopatu erat*, “there was [disagreement] concerning the assumption of the episcopate.” Salinas’s reading is preferable, since the disagreements mentioned here arose on the occasion of choosing a bishop to succeed Patroclus, who had been killed in 426, or rather Euladius, who is listed in the ancient diptych of Arles, published by Mabillon in the *Analecta*, between Patroclus and Honoratus. Since it is certain that Honoratus was elected bishop late in 426 or early in 427, Euladius is understood to have held the episcopate for only a few months.].

Like a proven leader of Israel, he knew well that it is not easy to command anything among people who are in disagreement. He also strove to rule by love rather than to dominate by fear, so that voluntary correction rather than compelled correction might add this honor to his subjects, and they might not seem to have been forced into their duty [Note: Salinas reads “might think,” instead of “might seem.”].

Therefore, once discord had been expelled, it immediately gave place to charity, which is the mother of all virtues. Thus Christ’s Church flourished under him, just as the monastery had flourished earlier [Note: Salinas and Quesnellus read “under him.”]. It increased in graces and diminished in worldly wealth. When discipline entered, it expelled from his house, as from the house of the Lord, the mammon of iniquity [Note: Quesnellus omitted the next five words; we have restored them from other printed editions and Vatican manuscripts. The “mammon of iniquity” here refers to the monies amassed by Patroclus, Honoratus’s predecessor, who had shortly before been killed and who, as Prosper Tiro says in his *Chronicle*, had accumulated them through infamous commerce by selling priestly offices.].

Those things which had long been accumulated in idleness he finally assigned to worthy uses. He sent his treasures to those who had long since died; and again those who had made the offerings felt the refreshment of their offerings. He kept back only what was sufficient for his ministry. But if necessity had demanded it, I think he would not even have spared what was needed for his ministry. He made the desires of another age the object of his stewardship.

## CHAPTER VII. The Illness, Death, and Burial of Honoratus. — The Saints Pray in Heaven for Mortals.

### 29.

He did not cease to labor even amid his final sufferings. From his sickbed he enriched many through the dispensation of the word. But how long did the bed hold him—him who had already become accustomed to overcoming even the wearinesses neighboring upon death [Note: Salinas reads *mortis*, “of death,” and shortly afterward *conflictante*, “struggling,” instead of *pro colluctante*, “instead of struggling.”]?

Finally, when his pains were already resisting him, he delivered a sermon in the church on the day of Epiphany. Although he had never allowed the faith struggling with infirmities to yield more to the heat of bodily pain than to that of the spirit, he served your desires beyond his strength.

For no illness arriving from outside overwhelmed him, nor did a sudden fever consume him. Rather, an illness long delayed—contracted earlier through excessive strictness of purpose and growing worse because he still yielded too little to rest—gradually weakened and exhausted him on the eighth or ninth day after the solemnity mentioned above [Note: Thus he died one or two days earlier than the date recorded in the Roman Martyrology, says Quesnellus in the margin. But the day of burial is sometimes recorded in Martyrologies as the day of death.].

Nevertheless, he denied us his presence in works of charity for scarcely four days, undoubtedly fearing that the nearness of his passing would grieve his own people. No one ever found him burdensome amid his most serious illnesses. His illnesses never caused anyone, as usually happens, any horror. And in this manner that dwelling-place of the Holy Spirit came to rest [Note: Salinas reads “receptacle,” instead of “dwelling-place.”].

### 30.

Moreover, it is incredible how intact he preserved the vigor of that undefiled mind right up to the end. First, he always consoled his people most abundantly, and feared nothing so much as that they should be consumed by prolonged despair [Note: Quesnellus reads “Or first.” Salinas then reads: “lest he consume us by prolonged despair.”]. He understood that the end is almost easier to endure than uncertainty.

With well-composed speech he continually wiped away the tears of those standing around him; yet the more he wiped them away, the more he provoked them [Note: This is better according to Salinas. Quesnellus reads: “he wipes away, he provokes.” He counted our greater grief as his own pain.]. From this he reckoned our sorrow heavier than his own.

No one easily endured with such a strong heart whatever was harsh and difficult to bear [Note: Thus the Vatican manuscript Reginensis 645 with Salinas. Earlier printed editions read “long endured.” Quesnellus reads “endured difficulties.” Shortly afterward Salinas has: “For he who did not shrink from living amid any grave circumstances…”]. He neither desired death nor feared it. For he who had not been reluctant to live amid every hardship in Christ’s service did not fear passing through that common gateway of new life into a new life.

The final necessity of human beings had come to him as something contemplated beforehand, not as something sudden. Therefore, with the end already before his eyes, as though he were departing, as though he were saying farewell, he asked each of us questions and urged us to suggest anything that might have escaped his memory, so that he would leave nothing unfinished and arrange nothing less fully than he had intended.
