Meanwhile he confirmed everything by his signature and compelled us, though we spared his weariness, to undertake everything that had to be done—yet he compelled us with that gentle authority which was always his.

### 31.

On one occasion, when I was trying to restrain the storm of my tears and break off the streams of my weeping, he said: “Why are you crying? Over the unavoidable necessity of the human race? Should my passing have found you unprepared, when it has not found me unprepared?”

While I, impeded by sobs, was somehow joining his words to my own as best I could, I said that I was grieving not now over my abandonment—for I trusted that the protection of his prayers would never fail me, and indeed I anticipated that it would be stronger after his passing—but that I was being gravely afflicted by a single wound of grief and by the difficult struggles of his final sufferings.

“And what,” he said, “do I, the least of all, endure compared with what many of the saints bore in their final hours, in the utmost bitterness?” After recalling several examples, he added what I believe he had read somewhere: “Great men suffer many things, and they were born as examples so that they might teach others to suffer.”

### 32.

When officials, the prefect, and men who had held prefectural office gathered around him, what fervent commands he delivered even while death’s chill was upon him, taking from his very departure the sharpest beginning for exhortation! It was entirely fitting that he who had always offered examples in life should also call his own death forth as an example.

“You see,” he said, “how fragile is the lodging in which we dwell. However high we may have climbed in life, death will drag us down from there. From this necessity no honors free anyone; no treasures ransom anyone [Note: Thus with Quesnellus, manuscript Vaticanus Reginensis. Other printed editions, with another Vatican manuscript, Reginensis 1025, read “no riches free anyone.”].

“This is common to the just and the unjust, to the powerful and the humble. We owe great thanks to Christ, who by His own death and resurrection enlivened our death with the hope of resurrection, offering eternal life and dispersing the horror of eternal death [Note: The next four words are absent from printed editions before Quesnellus but are found in both Vatican manuscripts, Reginenses.].

“Therefore live in such a way that you do not fear the end of life, and await what we call death as though it were a migration. Death is not a punishment if it does not lead to torments. The separation of flesh and soul is indeed harsh; but it will be far harsher to have flesh and soul together in the flames of Gehenna, unless throughout life the spirit, recognizing its own nobility, declares war upon the body and engages in battle with bodily vices, and, happily separated from the filth of the flesh [Note: The printed editions read *a carnali*, “from the carnal,” while Quesnellus alone has *a carnis*, “from the flesh.”], preserves both substances undefiled for eternal peace, there to be joined happily, where the saints will exult in glory and rejoice in their chambers—that is, in their bodies as in their own receptacles [Note: Quesnellus omitted the words “that is, in their bodies,” which we have restored from the other printed editions and manuscripts.]—when they recognize, as their familiar dwellings, the members they had dedicated to righteousness [Note: Quesnellus reads “will recognize.”].

“Do this, then. Your Honoratus leaves you this inheritance; with his final breath he invites you to inherit the heavenly kingdom. Let no one be held too tightly by love of this world. It is best to despise it willingly when you see that necessity will deprive you of it. Let no one overflow with riches; let no one serve money; let no one be corrupted by the empty display of wealth. It is a crime to take the price of salvation and turn it into the material of destruction, and to be caught by that by which one can be redeemed [Note: Quesnellus likewise reads *in illo*, “by that.”].”

Meanwhile, he admonished us more by his face, more by his eyes, and more by the feeling that shone upward toward heaven. The speech of the one reporting is unequal to his fiery discourse; yet words were no less unequal to the spirit of the one who was admonishing. With such an exhortation, therefore, and with an unusual gesture [Note: Thus Arles, Lérins, Surius, Quesnellus, and Salinas with one Vatican manuscript, Reginensis. Bollandus and another Vatican manuscript read “with an unusual nod.”], he poured forth his prayer and bestowed an extraordinary gift of blessing.

### 33.

As the service of his limbs failed, a new grace of mind was continually springing forth. When everything had been put in order—for little remained incomplete in his actions—he reviewed all his beloved people in his mind. His weariness did not prevent him from naming as many as he could, and through those who stood by he enriched them with a greeting [Note: Quesnellus omitted “his own.”].

But to me, in my ear, he said: “Make my excuses to that holy man for not being able to do what he wished.” What great and admirable foresight it was, amid those grave constraints of death, to ensure that he did not leave the sorrow of anyone whom he could not, so far as lay within him, wipe away—at least not without an explanation.

What, I ask, was the reason that, although he was about to leave behind all his people whom his love had drawn to this city, amid a foreign land, he commended no return to anyone, entrusted no companionship to anyone, and assigned no settled places of residence—as though he truly foresaw that none of his people would be scattered except those who, even while he was still alive, had already departed in the determination of their minds? And indeed we know that scarcely anyone will be absent from our fellowship except one whom he himself foretold would be absent—someone who had judged either his homeland dearer than his presence or discipline more burdensome [Note: Quesnellus reads “who would be absent.”].

Meanwhile, a heavier sleep pressed upon him. When we occasionally interrupted him anxiously, he said: “I am surprised that, after the long sleeplessness that preceded it, my heavy sleep seems heavy to you, given the gravity of my weariness.”

And when all of us, suspicious, complained that he had been sitting up too long toward the end [Note: Thus Quesnellus with one Arles manuscript and another Vatican manuscript. Others read “we prevented him”], he answered with the playful gentleness customary to him and with his habitual serenity of mind, saying that he found us troublesome in this aspect of our anxiety.

Thus almost before his life, his sweetness was exhausted [Note: Quesnellus reads “his own life.”].

### 34.

Then, received by his final sleep, he passed into the repose of death, sleeping without any struggle, as the circumstances of his end were [Note: Salinas reads this way. Quesnellus has “as is characteristic of the final struggle.”]. He experienced none of the difficult delays of dying. That holy, noble, sincere soul, undefiled by every contact with the world, was received by angelic choirs.

Meanwhile, sleep was disturbed for many by various visions; yet all had one appearance: namely, that the offices of the saints were coming to meet that holy man. And indeed, at that very moment in the middle of the night, the assembly filled the church to meet the holy body, so that one might think it had been awakened only by angelic messengers.

The body, always invigorated by the spirit and full of grace, was left lifeless; for the face preserved intact the beauty of his countenance, which was pleasing to everyone [Note: Salinas reads “preserved.” Shortly afterward we have restored from Salinas “this” in place of “thus,” which Quesnellus preferred.]. You know these things well, and in the meditation of your hearts you describe them much more fully than speech can express.

### 35.

Nor did anyone fail to think himself greatly harmed if he was deprived of the sight of his body [Note: Quesnellus reads “of his body”], if he did not, as reverence or love moved each person, impress a kiss upon his mouth or upon any of his limbs [Note: Quesnellus omits “of his”; shortly afterward Bollandus and Salinas, with two Vatican manuscripts, omit *in quo*, “in which,” and read: “That holy body was clothed with great eagerness of faith; afterward, with even greater faith, while it was brought to the tomb, it was almost stripped bare.”], or if he did not place his hand upon the bier or submit his neck to it. That holy body was clothed with great eagerness of faith and afterward, while it was being brought to the tomb, almost stripped bare by even greater faith.

For faith, which regarded it as a precious gift, did not spare the cloaks sanctified by his clothing; it considered it a privilege to tear away some fringe of his garments [Note: Salinas reads “some of his coverings.”].

Your affection contended in his funeral rites. At his burial you refreshed my pilgrimage, which still remained hidden among you. You nourished me with such an outpouring of love for him. Whom did his own roof shelter on that day? Or whom did not the walls of this city give to this basilica as though overwhelmed by a private grief?

It was considered a great gift to lay a hand upon his bier or to place one’s neck beneath it [Note: Thus from the same Salinas, better than Quesnellus’s reading “or a shoulder.”]. You saw his glory, not without glory for yourselves. For that religious devotion at his funeral was devotion of faith; and it was as joyful to have possessed such a man as it was grievous to have lost him.

Nor does the grace of his tomb give us little confidence: for since we have buried his bones here, we confidently anticipate his intercession in heaven. Then we saw perfumes and incense carried before his bier; but God received greater fragrances from your hearts, in view of your love for so great a shepherd.

The glory of God leapt for joy in his glory, and amid discordant choirs of different languages, love was harmonious.

[Note: In the funeral of Venantius Methona, Hebrews, Greeks, and Latins are said in this very discourse, §14, each to have sung psalms in his own language. Similarly, the author of the *Life of Saint Hilary of Arles*, printed above, ch. 22, records: “I remember hearing the Hebrew language of those singing in the honored funeral rites.”]

## CHAPTER VIII. Hilary, the Successor and Relative of Honoratus. — Honoratus Is Invoked as Patron.

### 36.

The merciful Lord, who, by stirring your hearts toward the election of my littleness, granted that I should not be far from his tomb, will also grant, as you pray, that I may not depart far from his ways [Note: In Quesnellus, less correctly, if I am not mistaken, “that I may not depart.” But also, “whatever I may learn that he did, may I act on it without any investigation, or reasoning, or discussion.” We have followed the reading of the other editions.].

Rather, may He grant that I hasten to do whatever I learn that he did, without any investigation or discussion of his actions. For, as I see, God already fathered me for you through him. He prepared me for you, unworthy though I am [Note: The following four words, perhaps omitted through a saut du même au même in Quesnellus’s edition, have been restored from other editions and manuscripts.].

Without knowing it, he sought me for you with such great labor. With such devoted concern and care he educated me as best he could, seeking in me a vein of faith, as of his own blood. Through letters, with such labor, and through his journey, with such effort, he strove to bring me from the island to which, after abandoning the beginnings of his episcopate, I had returned in my love of solitude [Note: Bollandus reads “by letters sent.” Quesnellus’s reading from the Lérins and Arles manuscripts is also confirmed by Salinas with the Vatican manuscripts.].

I do not dare say it, since he did not know it, but perhaps he foresaw it: he strove to move me away so that he might establish my homeland in your love beside the site of his tomb [Note: Bollandus reads “to bring near”; the Arles manuscript reads “he was bringing near,” as though to place me …].

But what are we doing, since he handed me over to you before my maturity, by a mature departure? It is not ours to accuse, even slightly, the secret judgment of the eternal King. You would scarcely have realized how much good you had lost if your good had been restored to you [Note: Salinas reads “how much.”].

### 37.

O great and renowned is your glory, Honoratus! Your merit did not need to be proved by signs. Your very way of life, full of virtues and exalted by the novelty of its excellence, supplied a kind of perpetual sign.

We who stood nearer to you know that many things were granted to you divinely [Note: Salinas adds “in the form of signs.”]; but you counted these as the smallest part, and you took greater joy in Christ’s recording your merits and virtues than in people’s noting signs.

And yet what greater sign of virtue can there be than to flee from signs and conceal one’s virtues? Indeed, your prayer was in a certain way so familiar to the ears of Christ that I think you obtained, through your most earnest prayers, that signs should not proclaim your virtue.

Peace also has its martyrs. For you were Christ’s perpetual witness for as long as you remained in the body.

There is also this astonishing fact: the strength of your youth, weakened by the constant rigor of abstinence and reduced to the slenderness we saw, though your beauty was preserved, was surely consumed by a daily cross. Yet you always bore it without any conspicuous superstition, fleeing every excess and every related desire for glory.

Never was there anything in your mouth except peace, chastity, piety, and charity. Never did anything dwell in your heart except Christ, the fountain of all these things. Through you He supplied to many the fruits of charity, joy, peace, patience, goodness, kindness, faith, gentleness, and self-control [Note: Thus Lérins, Bollandus, and Salinas. Quesnellus reads “overflowing … of many.”], abounding in manifold fullness for the salvation and joy of many, so that you not undeservedly sang to Him: “Those who fear You will see me and rejoice” (Ps. CXVIII, 74). To Him you always ascribed every good thing in your way of life, constantly impressing upon yourself and your people: “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (2 Cor. IV, 7). Yet the good of your life was all the more yours because you denied that it was yours.

### 38.

In you there was comfort for all who desired the common Lord. Some boast in the prosperity of this life; you, on the contrary, urged them to exult in God, murmuring your affection with the voice of gentle song: “Let the hearts of those who seek the Lord rejoice” (Ps. CIV, 3).

You never had greater pleasure than in prayers and psalms [Note: Some manuscripts read “desire”]. Christ had taken His seat so deeply in your inmost being that sometimes—even though I speak from experience—while your limbs were bound in peaceful sleep, your tongue would resound with Him even in dreams. Often while sleeping you uttered words of the soundest exhortation, often words filled with the deepest feeling of prayer.

The body rested in its little bed; the mind was occupied with Christ. Indeed, all of us who were present experienced these things, each according to his opportunity [Note: Quesnellus reads “each person.”].

Yet you, the one repose of all, how eagerly and how often you reported your dreams! They did not foretell anything, nor were they troubled by any anxiety about the future; rather, they were aroused by the restless desires of your soul [Note: Bollandus and Surius read “of your troubled spirit.” The Vatican manuscript Reginensis 1025 reads: “But you bore the martyrdom of a troubled spirit, namely …” Another Vatican manuscript supports the reading adopted here.].

You were undergoing the martyrdom which you always carried in meditation, I believe, when the Lord sometimes alluded to and provoked your desire, as though persecution had been stirred up against your faith. And indeed, I think no one would deny that for martyrdom you lacked torturers, not courage [Note: Thus with Quesnellus and Salinas, Vatican manuscript Reginensis 645. Other manuscripts read “you lacked time”].

For every day, in your most sincere discussions, you were a witness to the confession of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit [Note: Bollandus reads “in confession”; the Arles manuscript, “of confessions.”]. No one easily spoke so openly and so clearly about the Trinity of the Godhead, distinguishing the persons while joining them in the eternity and majesty of their glory [Note: Bollandus reads “glory.”].

### 39.

Remember us, then, friend of God; remember us continually, standing undefiled before God, singing that new song and following the Lamb wherever He goes. You are His attendant; you are our patron, an acceptable interpreter and powerful advocate of our prayers. Carry the prayers of your fostered flock, poured out at your tomb [Note: Quesnellus reads “bring forth.” We have preferred Salinas’s reading.].

Obtain for us that, in common agreement, priest and people together may deserve in some measure to attain what you commanded and what you taught [Note: This conclusion is absent from both Vatican manuscripts, Reginenses].

Through our Lord Jesus Christ, who has taken you into His glory and, with His Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 1271]

[Note: This letter was revised and corrected by Father John Salinas from manuscript 186 of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme.]

## LETTER OF SAINT HILARY, BISHOP OF ARLES, TO SAINT EUCHERIUS, BISHOP OF LYONS. (C, S)

[Col. 1271B]

[Note: This title was absent from Quesnellus’s edition. We supplied it from the Lyons edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum* and from the manuscript of Santa Croce, which also contains Eucherius’s books of *Instruction*. In this codex the reading is *devictissimo* rather than *devinctissimo*.]

To the most blessed lord, deservedly welcomed and worthy of welcome, and most closely bound in Christ, Pope Eucherius, bishop, Hilary, bishop.

When I had indicated in my preceding letter that I would bring your little books back with me, I was wholly unable to delay the urgency and insistence of the boy whom you had sent. [Note: [Col. 1271C] Thus from the same manuscript of Santa Croce, according to D. Salinas; the printed editions instead read: “When the demand of the boy whom you had sent was pressing, I could not read at all.”] [Note: [Col. 1271C] “I should prefer to read: ‘I sent back.’” Salinas likewise.] Accordingly, I sent forth the flower-laden works of your blessedness, being not a little anxious lest, since they had not yet been copied, such continuous and heavy rains should damage them as they fell. [Note: [Col. 1271D] These words are absent from the manuscript of Santa Croce up to “I marvelled.”] I read through them only once, marvelling at them all. May the Lord grant that, with you as my guide in your pages, I may someday read through in full these beautiful works in Christ—the glory of our Instructions—which are your work. [Note: [Col. 1272C] From this very brief letter written by Hilary, we possess an excellent testimony affirming that Eucherius had composed two books of Instructions, or Institutions. No one can doubt that these are the works indicated here; and he suggests that they were written by Eucherius for both his sons, although the printed copies of the Instructions name only Salonius. — Quesnell.] [Note: [Col. 1272C] Thus the manuscript of Santa Croce and Salinas from it. Other editions read *persentiam*. A little later we wrote *Instructionibus*, following the same manuscript; *Institutionibus* in another.] This one request I make: do not allow me to be deprived for long of these Instructions. Rather, since you have me as one of your young men, for whose instruction you arranged these works, [Note: [Col. 1272C] We followed the reading of Salinas from the same manuscript. Another edition reads: “whom you adorned with this learning.” After several words we added this reading from the manuscript mentioned above.] I ask you to let me have them all the more urgently, inasmuch as the snares of youth press upon me more heavily. [Note: [Col. 1272D] The same manuscript reads: “the old age of life oppresses the inexperience of youth.”] May the Lord preserve you, most blessed father, mindful of me for the advancement of his Church, for a long time.

# Doubtful Minor Works of Saint Hilary, Bishop of Arles

[Col. 1273]

## Sermon, or Narrative, on the Miracle of Saint Genesius, Martyr of Arles

*(From Surius, 25 August.) (C, G, S)*

[Col. 1273A]

It is an honourable thing to recount the works of God; therefore it is worthwhile to narrate the miracles of that work, to be related for the glory of the holy martyr Genesius. For on his birthday, that crowded gathering in the city of Arles, endangered by the breaking of a bridge, shook the whole city with extraordinary terror; and when their minds had been shaken by the peril of sudden fear, the joy of the festival, through the recovery of safety, was made more joyful still, its gladness doubled.

For when the people of Arles had drawn together in this celebration crowds even larger than their own citizens, people whose joy on that day made the city itself too small, the paths and open spaces of the fields became crowded as the procession rose and everyone struggled under the pressure of the throng. They were making their way toward the farther bank of the river, Christ’s devoted army, with beloved wives and cherished children, hastening to receive several blessings at once in honour of the martyr.

Not content to pour out their vows in one place, they kept vigil in the church and, before dawn, hurried to the place of the slaughter and the shedding of blood; then, offering sacrifices again at the tomb of joy, they hastened as though they were about to gain access to the martyr’s ears. They did not even wait for the solemnly ordered services of the clergy, or finally for the proper time of day. For the splendour of the festival, the whole city shining with light, had in every way driven away the horror of night.

Meanwhile that naval passage, by which the backs of the dreadful Rhône are crossed between allied cities, suddenly—whether under an unjust burden, or because of the excessive weight of the materials, or because the current had slipped obliquely beneath it—sagged downward and spread open. It is uncertain by what accident; yet it is certain through whose treachery the precious burden, namely, the throng of the faithful, was deposited in the midst of the waves by the treacherously swaying bridge. I was present, and I speak truthfully, having, so to say, withdrawn my foot from the bridge itself.

At once there arose a great crash from the falling crowd and from those standing around; terror ran through the whole city. One person feared for his wife, another for his children, others for relatives, others for friends; all at once feared amid differing attachments—[the supplied text breaks off here: *qui parum, civibus*].

Amid these events the whole weight of the disaster fell upon Honoratus, the bishop of holy memory, whose shepherding delighted that people at the time: he alone feared on behalf of all. What goads that devotion then received! With what sudden anguish of spirit did he stand beside those in distress! Immediately raising his eyes to heaven, his inward concentration matching the brightness of his eyes, he withdrew wholly from us who stood around in an ecstasy of mind, so that no one doubted that he was standing before the tribunals of Christ together with Saint Genesius, seeking assistance in the present evil.

Meanwhile, amid great tumult, pitiful shipwrecks were taking place. Horses adorned with trappings were mixed with human beings; indignant at being hindered in their swimming, they showed their legs above the deep water with their chests raised high. Whatever lay in their way, whether warned by the danger or driven by frightened instinct, they trampled underfoot with fearful courage. Servants were entangled with the beloved burdens of their mothers’ arms; attendants were pressed beneath the matronly litters; and the whole solemn procession was mingled with the fragments of its own journey.

Let no malicious interpreter appear here; let no one obscure so great a glory of the martyr by spiteful detraction; let no one claim that the crowd was close to the bank, or assert that those people were saved by standing in shallow water. Divine power openly saved them.

Daily, vessels bearing loads of priceless merchandise are brought alongside these same banks, weighed down with merchants’ goods. At that place an ancient arrangement had installed a vessel to bear the bridge structures, as though it despaired of laying a foundation with embankments. Over that vast gulf it exposed as great a weight of packed people as it had received upon its very long and strong beams, which were now broken.

Let the minds and eyes of those who recall this scene now confront it: the whole Rhône together with the collapse, the shipwreck, the diverse crowd of wretched people entangled with one another, and the destruction piled into one mass by the devil’s snares. Nothing was lacking to the danger, so that nothing might be lacking to the martyr’s glory. For how could the river drown his foster children on the very day which he had consecrated through a holy birth?

O great glory of God! A glorious army burst forth from the vast whirlpool. You might have believed that the Jordan had once again been opened, the river divided by divine power; or that once again the seas had provided the people of God with a solid path through the waters, as once under Moses’ leadership, at the command of the rod.

The collapse shook no one; the river enfolded no one burdened by his clothing; the river’s draught overwhelmed no one. The familiar, native bank received them all unharmed and safe. The entire procession emerged just as it had entered.

The mother of a household saw the privacy of her movable chambers on the shoulders of her servants rise from the depths. The virgins adorned in honour of God suffered no loss of their floating necklaces; the pins themselves, so to speak, remained fixed just as they had been fastened in their mothers’ hands. No one suffered damage to his property; no one suffered loss of life.

Beloved children met beloved children. Each person joyfully embraced the one nearest to him, for whom he had been most afraid.

[Col. 1275A]

Who but Christ, through the intercession of his martyr, brought about this present power? The bishop certainly encountered the martyr, and the martyr encountered the Lord. The service of the faithful people was shown worthy of salvation.

Finally, many of them—as perhaps you acknowledge along with me, you who were present—immediately, lest the enemy be allowed even slightly to disturb their holy devotion, boarded the boats while still wearing their wet clothes and, with fervent hope, disregarded the morning chill of the river. Hurrying toward the place for which they had set out, namely, the place of the slaughter, they arrived with victorious hearts, intending to pour out their vows with even greater eagerness after their recent danger.

O prayers worthy to be heard! They were not broken by injuries, and they did not know how to reproach God for having been endangered; they knew how to give thanks because they had escaped. Everyone rejoiced and exulted; at last they attended the solemn rites in happiness. It was a joy to have been present at the dangers, because it was a visible joy to have been present at the miracles. For each person’s doubt about his safety was so great that he acquired his safety wondrously.

The shepherd Honoratus rejoiced, with all his people still numbered among the living. He could indeed have committed these events to writing in a more polished hand and with greater grace, in words destined to endure forever, had he not feared to exult too boldly, conscious that he had been appointed a participant in the embassy of the holy martyr and that the Lord had bestowed these things while he was bishop.

In fact, blessings spread among many reach us as well. But how many private blessings do people recognize in themselves? We ascribe all these to God alone, who is worshipped as the creator and knower of all things, and who lives with the Son and the Holy Spirit for endless ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1275]

## Verses for the Birthday of the Maccabean Martyrs

*(C, G)*

[Col. 1275B]

Antiochus was once a very wealthy king of Syria.

In his reign, so report declares, a mother and her seven sons

Were born of the holy race;

And the care of their excellent lineage urged them

To remember it and to serve the law that had been given.

Thus, willingly, they held the ordinances of God

As members of his better people.

The king, eager to change their faith and alter their reverence,

Wanted to corrupt the righteous and mix them with the wicked.

He promised the mother rewards; he promised gold,

And whatever he might obtain throughout his kingdom,

If only she would change her former character and convictions

And compel her sons to adopt other customs for himself.

She refused and suppressed her silent grief within her heart.

When he could corrupt her by no words,

He first tried to conquer her by savage tortures.

Yet she endured her heavy groans

And did not fear the king’s grievous blows.

When he saw himself defeated, he said:

“Alas, what am I to do?

You conquer a king, though you are a woman!

Yet you will not escape: you will suffer still more severely.

I shall rage against your sons, even if you persist in your wickedness;

By this means at least I shall heal my grief.”

She raised her hands and looked up to heaven;

She uttered groans and spoke these words:

“Though you offer treasure and kingdoms, tyrant,

We are not ensnared by the gifts of kings,

Nor will earthly presents tear from the holy

The promises of God.

That hope is more certain

Which promises us life through the long ages.

I follow it; I have learned to follow it.

For it is easy to touch slippery gifts,

To take riches, and to lose one’s life.

But even if you threaten flames after savage blows,

You cannot change what we began in our earliest years.

I am certain that I shall overcome it through the virtue

Given to me together with the law.

What do you command now, savage king?

What harsh threats do you make against my sons?

By this alone you will be able to trouble their mother with grief.

For I have God as my hope, and concern for my children;

Because of that concern I trust that you can conquer none of them.

May you, Power of heaven, favour us,

Because our requests are just.”



Antiochus raged, his heart disturbed by turmoil.

He could not endure it; his savage face bore witness to his anger,

And he wondered for a long time that a woman could accomplish so much.

“Come,” he said, “soldier, obey! You too, attendant, obey the king.

You servants, obey me; give a furious king

Tortures worthy of a woman’s evil.

A woman forces me to rage; what is more,

A woman conquers the commands of her own king.

But she shall not have spoken with impunity.

I shall destroy, one by one, the seven sons

Whom that treacherous woman holds within herself.

Let the one counted first perish first;

Thus I shall destroy them all in order.”



Let her see her sons laid upon the supporting grates

And burned in the flames; let her see, harsh woman,

Her own sons in this way.

“But the punishment remains,” he said.

“Ministers, you ought to be swift.”

Meanwhile the fruitful mother, her hair already loosened,

Stood there, extending her breasts,

As though exhorting them, baring her maternal nourishment,

The food of her sons.

When she saw her son proceeding boldly and steadfastly toward the fire,

She said:

“You, my offspring, you are the first;

Look upon your mother.

You are certainly mine; now, my son, remember us.

I gave birth to you first; now imitate your mother.

Take on my character and conquer the king by silence.

You will be able to endure for a long time

If you overcome these treacherous times,

So that the king’s violence may not overcome the holy.

Follow your mother’s counsel, and you will fear no loss.

Be stronger than bronze and than the stone itself.”

[Col. 1277B]

“Go forward like a young man; conquer suffering patiently.”

He looked now toward his mother, now raised his eyes above.

While he remained silent and silently asked whom he ought to fear,

He climbed upon the flames laid beneath the grates.

His lifeless body slipped away; the mother herself, burdened with grief, sprang forward,

And said: “I have conquered; I shall conquer if I pray more often.

Let the courage of my sons, unknown to the king

But already known to God, remain firm—

To God who knows the hearts of the people.”

She had finished the grief of her first childbirth,

But, with fear remaining for the others, the mother was anxious.

Nevertheless she concealed it, lest the king’s joy be touched.

Antiochus was astonished and did not believe

That the others could overcome such a form of punishment

With the same courage.

He ordered the undertaking to continue.

The mother did not remain terrified;

Yet when she saw her son standing there pale,

She revolved these thoughts within herself

And was already somewhat relieved:

“Behold, the second stage of my childbirth is brought forth.

How like your brother’s form you are!

If only you harden your heart

And follow the path of my first child.

You can be mine; you can recover the salvation

Which your brother already possesses,

Because he followed his mother’s commands.

Lay aside your fears and scorn the threats of the raging king.

As for kingdoms, to which fleeting times are granted,

This king will not be able to harm you after these things.

Rather, after this, you, my son, will be able to harm the king.

Look: you are being forced to climb the light fire of time;

You need courage—put away your languishing fear.

Remember our lineage, if its meaning remains with you.

This man who holds the sceptre and rages in this kingdom

Deems his time empty; he will be deprived of kingdom and life,

And, condemned in his guilt, will feel eternal fires.

You will be secure, accompanied by the multitude of the righteous.

Look upon my face, my son, and raise your eyes to heaven

And to God the Creator, through whom life is prepared for you.

Tread in this better path, following the footsteps of your brother.

Do not listen to what this man commands,

But to what God orders.”

As he had been instructed, he stood looking at his mother and heaven.

With joyful face he began to scorn the king,

And, as though laughing, rushed into the burning flames.

Falling down, he rested, his soul prevailing.

When his mother saw this, she spoke with a steadfast face:

“In some measure I am already blessed;

you are now no longer able, savage tyrant,

to overcome all my sons by slaughtering them.

A more grievous punishment awaits you soon,

Cruel and wicked man, which you will suffer shortly;

For God sees all these things.”

Now two remained secure, having scorned the king.

The mother’s hope was now better; the third son stood before her.

“Behold the place of punishment, if it is punishment to conquer the king;

To serve God is praise, not the punishment of a madman.”

The third youth was dragged forward,

While the tyrant growled in anger.

He was not yet satisfied. Fury and anger raged together within him,

Because he had seen the brave hearts of the brothers

Fearlessly overcome the king’s rage.

The youth stood before him, in the flower of his years,

Outstanding in appearance, worthy to possess kingdoms,

More worthy than Antiochus,

Because he followed better kingdoms,

At God’s summons.

To him the mother spoke:

“Receive, my son, without fear, the words of your mother;

Receive them, lest through sluggishness you lose the honour of courage.

Your brothers are already dwelling in a seat of holiness,

In a place better than the king’s fleeting kingdoms.

If you touch their true convictions with your heart,

You will be proclaimed a victor among the peoples,

As report has already sent your brothers to the heights.

Come to them, I beg you; these are gifts

Most suitable for one who suffers.

It would be wicked to despise them

And to abandon the laws of the unconquered king,

After whom no pleasure remains.”

But the youth sent forth words in a quiet murmur,

As though praying; he stretched his hands upward,

And, supported on his mother’s knee, hung upon her words,

So far as the crowd allowed him to see her,

Though he did not himself press his body against her.

As soon as he was summoned, he climbed upon the grate

And fearlessly placed his limbs in the fire,

With steadfast faith.

The flames closed over him, while warm ash remained,

And the earth, opening, received his uninjured body.

His holy soul likewise departed unharmed to the heights.

But the mother, uncertain whether to take up groans or joys,

Hesitated and spoke in complaining words:

“What are you preparing now, cruel man?

Are we all to obey your commands?

But let no guard remove any one from the number of my children.

And even if you yourself wish it, tyrant,

I will not suffer all my children to perish in this contest.

This is the punishment of your own time;

Even if you change it, it remains a dreadful punishment,

And the same sentence is imposed upon condemned sons.

If you think of something worse, if there is something worse, threaten it.

And because, when you see my face, you are held by horror,

We rejoice together whenever you rage against them.”

But the king himself burned more fiercely,

Driven by raging anger.

He thought himself being tested, lest they endure punishments like the rest of their brothers’ company,

And perceived that the mother was asking this of him.

He endured it for destruction and soon wanted to consign the fourth son to punishment.

For the exhausted ministers could bear neither the king’s fury nor the king himself.

Shame! The son blushed to show his face to his mother

And began to confuse her troubled mind.

When she saw him standing there with lowered eyes,

She addressed him with such words, intending to instruct him in his fear:

“You are the fourth child of three births;

You are the fourth infant for me.

What words can I now speak to you?

What can I say except that heaven’s enduring power and strength may be with you,

And that we owe to that King the origin of our holy lineage, whatever we refuse?

He gave us Abraham together with his holy seed,

Through whom nobility and every lineage are established,

Which abides in the Lord;

To him holy Isaac was born,

At the time when old age could by no natural power

Hope for any child,

Because Sarah remained barren.

Yet when she gave birth and the propagation of the lineage began,

Sarah left you descendants beyond expectation:

Esau and Jacob, brought forth from their ancestral origin,

Whom we know Rebecca bore as twins.

From them we arise; from them we are born.

This is the lineage you must seek, my son.

Open a path for yourself; approach the fathers of old.

Their descendants, scattered throughout the whole world,

Suffer hatred because they alone worship the almighty Lord

In their minds and do not mingle with the wicked crowd.

Why do you wear a sorrowful expression?

Why do you keep your eyes fixed upon the ground?

Look instead upon heaven and the Father of heaven.

Do not hesitate: your mother, wishing you well, points him out to you.

Bear patiently whatever is involved,

And bravely join my crowd, my son;

Encourage the number that follows.”

[Col. 1281A]

Thus the beloved mother, mingling grief and joy,

Had finished her noble exhortation.

Then he himself raised his eyes

And began to direct them toward his mother.

He showed by his bearing and expression

That he now felt no sadness,

Except for the mother’s grievous wounds,

Divided among her children.

Then, slipping from the hands of those who held him,

He rushed toward the flames.

I shall speak of wonders:

The flame did not touch his face.

His body, lifeless, overcame the flame and the fires;

Yet with open mouth, silently,

He breathed out the spirit through the passage

From which it had been received,

And it departed together with his blood.

The mother rejoiced at this:

The son who had just stood there with a sorrowful face

Now, trusting with his whole heart,

Had obeyed her commands and scorned the king’s anger.

Yet she began in this way, while the king hesitated before those who still remained:

The pious crowd groaned, and the ministers,

Cursing the king, asked in silent speech:

“Why do you delay? Why do you hesitate?

You must now spare no one.

Even if you wish to do so, you cannot break your decree.

I appeal to the King who governs the whole world,

To whom the sea, the heaven, and the stars of heaven obey.

If you do not bring them forth, it is fear;

You are now pressing your attack too sluggishly.

Already you perceive what kingdoms they seek,

And what glory remains for us on both sides

If you do not spare them.

For all whom you ordered to depart from your kingdom

Have conquered your fury, whether through some accompanying fault;

They are yours, and they remain joyfully in the dwelling of the righteous.

Perhaps you believe this to be death, mad tyrant?

It is a longer life, more powerful than this kingdom

That you rule, whose final portion you now inhabit.

You are mortal nevertheless, and will not rule forever.

But carry out your command and do not divide our children.

Give these also to the flames, those who are younger in age

But surpass you; use the rights of your kingdom.

These too will conquer your kingdoms, proud man.”



Antiochus conceived fresh madness, and the savage tyrant

Boiled with rage, turning groans over in his breast.

His complexion agreed with his mind;

He raised his sorrow-laden face and spoke these words:

“This is your freedom, and this the harsh power of your tongue;

And this haughtiness which you carry on your swollen neck

Will learn what the blows of an angry king can do,

If you are not yet satisfied with misfortunes

And try to fashion joy,

Turning your griefs into celebrations.

I shall not change the death. Rejoice, be glad, triumph—

Provided that you conquer in such a way

That you are supreme among your children.

Thus, with maddened spirit, she rejoices in the death of her sons.

I give these also to the flames; no power can change this.

The decrees stand. Rejoice, surviving,

Bereft of your sons.

And let the order complete its course,

So that my commands may not be delayed.

Bring forth the sons.

Let the flames spare no one.

I do not think that a king may appear doubtful after this;

Certainly, woman, fear is entirely absent from me.

You are brought forward as the foremost of your race,

remarkable boy, in face and appearance,

In whose breast firm courage remains.

From this point you might even have conquered the king.”

To him the mother spoke in a calm voice:

“If it were permitted you, my son, to give your mother an embrace,

I confess that, after your wounds,

I alone would have given it to you.

But the harsh and gloomy power of the king forbids me.

Let him deny the embrace, so long as our voice remains free

And we are allowed to remember God

And keep the law—not one given by the king,

But one which God, arbiter and ruler of the world, handed down, and which Moses received after seeking it, and gave to the people,

Whose greatest glory is to know God,

To whom we owe the honour due.

Only do not hesitate to obey your mother’s commands.

Let there be strength and courage;

Let your mind remain wholly full of God.

Let your youth be stronger

Than the king, in ordering your defeat, could have hoped.

O how great is courage! How great is the confidence of the brave!

But now do not hesitate to overcome the flames in their midst.

Believe me, boy: you will be victorious,

And victorious you will return.

The bones and strong sinews will again mingle with bodies,

And the souls that have been preserved will once more be restored

To new limbs.

Yet lest the swift fire frighten you,

Take courage from your brothers

And look upon the eternal Godhead.”

He carried out the commands; silently he bore witness to God and prayed

With whatever murmur he was able to utter.

His youth did not hinder the boy.

He did not fear the grate set before him,

But obeyed his mother’s desire,

And sooner than words can say rushed upon the flames.

The flames yielded; all pain yielded.

Body and fire became one,

Yet the body overcame the fire,

And the spirit had already overcome the peaceful air.

The joyful mother suffered silently,

And, suppressing her grief,

Turned her sadness and mourning into joy.

Meanwhile she trembled and revolved anxieties in her heart,

Not about what had already happened,

But about the sons who remained in their childish years—

Lest they perhaps refuse,

Lest they perhaps conceive fear in their minds

And prefer to approach the king.

And the younger each one was, the greater was the fear.

Anxiously she carried her cares within herself;

Hope and fear struggled together,

And passed through the breast of the pious mother.

Yet her hope was stronger.

When she saw her son advancing

And, rejoicing, saw him from afar,

She said:

“I see what hope can bring me through this boy.

He must recognize our faces

And, here also, obey his brothers

And their number.”

Perhaps this boy’s childish heart alone

Will be touched,

And he will feel indignation

At being offered up like a sacrificial victim.

I shall address him

And try to say in a few words

That he should remember his lineage

Rather than his present age.

“If the nobility of your lineage moves you,

If your origin touches you,

Look upon your ancestors, my son,

And look upon us also, my son.

Do not count your years, boy.

Begin, with a brave heart,

To bear God within you.

The ages will hand this on from generation to generation.

## Editorial Apparatus to the Maccabean Verses

The following notes translate the complete supplied apparatus in source order. Latin lemma anchors identify each note’s position; fragmentary and corrupt readings remain explicit.

- **Title, [Col. 1275C], before *Versus in natali Machabaeorum martyrum*.** We give the title found in the Fleury manuscript.
- **1. [Col. 1275C], after *Antiochus Syriae ditissimus olim, In cujus regno mater*.** Thus in the same codex; the other editions wrongly read *fuisse* (‘had been’).
- **2. [Col. 1275C], after *fama refert, de sancta gente creati; Quos cura*.** The printed editions read *assidui* (‘constant’). We preferred the cited manuscript, which shortly afterward reads *videbat* (‘saw’) for *jubebat* (‘ordered’).
- **3. [Col. 1275C], after *jura tenebant. Rex avidus mutare fidem, mutare timorem*.** Thus in the same codex. The printed editions wrongly read *Voluit*, and ‘and so that he might mingle [them] equally with the wicked people.’
- **4. [Col. 1275D], after *populo ut misceret iniquo Praemia promittit matri, promittit*.** The printed editions read ‘and to them’; later, ‘to search the whole kingdom, if she changed their minds.’ The Fleury manuscript is better.
- **5. [Col. 1275D], after *negat, tacitumque premit sub corde dolorem. Hanc postquam*.** Thus in the same codex. The printed editions read ‘no booty could compel [her].’
- **6. [Col. 1275D], after *verbis, Tentavit primum tormentis vincere saevis. Pertulit illa*.** The Fleury manuscript reads ‘heavy groans.’
- **7. [Col. 1275D], after *tamen gemitus, et tristia regis Verbera non timuit*.** The same codex reads ‘But when he saw himself defeated.’
- **8. [Col. 1275D], after *se vidit ut ille: Heu! quid agam? dixit*.** The printed editions read ‘I am conquered; why more? by grieving.’ The Fleury manuscript has the better reading.
- **9. [Col. 1275D], after *femina regem! Non tamen effugies: plus est quod*.** The same printed editions read ‘more.’
- **10. [Col. 1275D], after *tuos, licet improba perstes: Hac certe ratione meum*.** The Fleury manuscript reads ‘I shall satisfy.’
- **11. [Col. 1275D], after *Flor., satiabo.] sanabo dolorem. Sustulit illa manus, coelumque*.** The printed editions read ‘he looked upward, uttering groans.’
- **12. [Col. 1275D], after *nobis promittit tempore longo. Hanc sequor, hanc didici*.** The printed editions read ‘not to touch slippery kingdoms.’
- **13. [Col. 1275D], after *est, et perdere vitam. Sed licet et flammas*.** We supplied *post* (‘after’) from the Fleury manuscript, which has *vulnera* (‘wounds’) for *verbera* (‘blows’).
- **14. [Col. 1276C], after *verbera.] post verbera saeva mineris, Nil mutare potes*.** We followed the Fleury manuscript. The printed editions omit this, and another reading gives: ‘We received in our earliest years / virtue together with the law: I am resolved to abandon / whatever you command, savage man. The harsh threat you make against my sons / alone will be able to trouble their mother with fear.’
- **15. [Col. 1276D], after *dolore. Est mihi namque Deus spes, est mihi*.** The printed editions read ‘certain of my children, through whom I now hope that he [or: you] can conquer none.’
- **16. [Col. 1276D], after *Per quam spero equidem te nullum vincere posse*.** The printed editions read ‘Look favorably, Father of heaven, upon the just things we ask.’ The Fleury manuscript is somewhat less faulty, although *justa* had to be supplied from the printed editions. The meter requires our correction of *fave* to *faveas* (‘may you favor’).
- **17. [Col. 1276D], after *faveas Numen, quia justa rogamus. Rex furit Antiochus*.** The printed editions read ‘and troubled hearts swelled’; then ‘he shakes, and savage…’
- **18. [Col. 1276D], after *lumine vultus, Miraturque diu possit quod femina tantum*.** There the reading is ‘Soldier, he says, obey the king; and you, attendant, obey.’
- **19. [Col. 1276D], after *quoque pare, minister. Vos famuli, parete mihi, date*.** There the printed text reads ‘kingdoms.’
- **20. [Col. 1276D], after *jussa sui: sed non impune locuta est. Membratim*.** The printed text reads ‘let them perish, for the treacherous woman holds seven sons within her realm.’
- **21. [Col. 1276D], after *retinet: quorum qui primus habetur, Hic primus pereat*.** There: ‘so let them all perish in order.’
- **22. [Col. 1276D], after *pereant sic ordine cuncti.] perdam sic ordine cunctos*.** The following two verses are absent from the Fleury manuscript.
- **23. [Col. 1277C], after *ut ipsa suos, sic cernat ut aspera natos*.** The printed text reads ‘or what punishment awaits him.’
- **24. [Col. 1277C], after *esse ministros. Interea fecunda parens, jam crine soluto*.** There: ‘He stood by while she exhorted.’
- **25. [Col. 1277C], after *nudo Ubera protendens, natorum alimenta suorum Non confusa*.** The printed editions read ‘he stood,’ and then ‘to the fires.’
- **26. [Col. 1277C], after *ad ignes.] aperit; natumque ut vidit ad ignem*.** The printed editions give the opposite and false sense: ‘to advance timidly with an unsteady step.’
- **27. [Col. 1277C], after *dixit: Tu, mea progenies, tu primus respice matrem*.** There: ‘You now are surely mine, son of your mother.’
- **28. [Col. 1277C], after *es, nunc nostri, nate, memento. Te primum peperi*.** We followed the printed editions. The Fleury manuscript reads ‘now, now imitate.’
- **29. [Col. 1277C], after *et regem vince tacendo. Tu poteris durare diu*.** The printed editions read ‘thus the times.’
- **30. [Col. 1277C], after *Perfida, ne superet sanctos violentia regis. Utere consilio*.** There: ‘do not fear the king’s losses.’
- **31. [Col. 1277C], after *ne damna timeto.] matris, nec damna timebis, Fortior*.** The printed editions are metrically better with *isto, saxoque* (‘than that, and than stone’), but the codex is better in sense, although *aere* (‘bronze’) indicates some error in the verse. Jean du Bois notes in the margin: perhaps *armis* (‘arms’).
- **32. [Col. 1277D], after *in altum: Dumque tacet tacitusque rogat quem debet*.** The printed editions read ‘and he prays. He did not feel the swift…’ The codex is better here too; perhaps the author originally wrote *debe timetque*, omitting the final *t* of *debet* before the same letter beginning the next word, an ancient practice used to preserve the meter.
- **33. [Col. 1277D], after *timetque, Conscendit rapidos subjectos cratibus ignes. Corpus inane*.** The printed editions read ‘it happened; the mother rejoiced in grief.’
- **34. [Col. 1277D], after *fluit: mater gravis ipsa resultat, Et dixit: Vici*.** We preferred the printed reading. The Fleury manuscript has ‘Thus, unconquered, I pray more often.’
- **35. [Col. 1277D], after *tamen, ne regem gaudia tangant. Rex stupet Antiochus*.** The Fleury manuscript reads ‘he himself [could] the following…’; *posse* (‘to be able’) is better from the printed editions, which then read ‘to conquer sons like [him].’
- **36. [Col. 1277D], after *assistere natum, Haec secum volvens, aliqua jam parte*.** The printed editions read ‘relieved.’
- **37. [Col. 1277D], after *Ecce secunda mihi partus producitur aetas. Quam similis*.** The printed editions read ‘hard in heart toward his handsome brother.’
- **38. [Col. 1278C], after *sequeris primi partus vestigia nostri! Esse meus poteris*.** There: ‘and thus to recover salvation.’
- **39. [Col. 1278C], after *secutus. Pone metus, regisque minas contemne furentis, Regnaque*.** The printed editions read ‘which are granted to those dwelling for a short time.’
- **40. [Col. 1278C], after *Non poterit post ista tibi rex iste nocere*.** This verse is supplied by the Fleury manuscript and is absent from the printed editions.
- **41. [Col. 1278C], after *haec tu regi, nate, nocere Temporis ecce levis*.** The printed editions read ‘the fire is kindled; there is room for courage; [put away] your languishing…’
- **42. [Col. 1278C], after *ignes, Sed virtute opus est, languentem pone timorem*.** There: ‘Take courage, if the sense of our lineage remains [with you].’
- **43. [Col. 1278C], after *tenet, regno qui saevit in isto, Tempus inane*.** The printed editions read ‘he rules; [he will lose] kingdom and life, and, guilty, be condemned.’
- **44. [Col. 1278D], after *Auctoremque Deum, per quem tibi vita paratur Hac*.** The Fleury manuscript is better. The reading of the printed editions was preferred.
- **45. [Col. 1278D], after *lectio magis placuit.] melior, fratrisque tui vestigia calca*.** The printed editions read ‘not what the king ordered, but…’
- **46. [Col. 1278D], after *rigido sic ore locuta est: Felix parte aliqua*.** The same editions read ‘since now you wish it, yet cannot [destroy] them all.’
- **47. [Col. 1278D], after *sum, jam non potis omnes Saeve tyranne, meos*.** Thus from the printed editions, as the meter requires. The Fleury manuscript reads *cremando* (‘by burning’); *urendo* (‘by consuming with fire’) is better, as Jean du Bois noted in the margin.
- **48. [Col. 1278D], after *Jo. a Bosco.] trucidando vincere natos. Te gravior*.** The printed editions read ‘now the punishment,’ and shortly afterward *in igne* (‘in the fire’) for *inique* (‘wickedly’).
- **49. [Col. 1278D], after *poena manet, crudelis inique, Quam patiere brevi: Deus*.** The Fleury manuscript reads *namque haec*, which mars the meter; the printed editions have *hic namque*. We expressed the true reading from the two.
- **50. [Col. 1278D], after *laus est, non poena furentis. Tertius attrahitur juvenis*.** The printed editions read ‘while [God] commands.’
- **51. [Col. 1278D], after *Constitit ante pedes juvenis florentibus annis, Egregius forma*.** There: ‘who [is] savage…’
- **52. [Col. 1278D], after *diro qui.] dignus qui regna teneret, Dignior Antiocho*.** There: ‘and thus better things.’
- **53. [Col. 1278D], after *Ibid., et sic meliora.] verum meliora secutus Regna*.** The Fleury manuscript reads ‘with God willing.’ We preferred the printed reading.
- **54. [Col. 1279C], after *honorem. Sunt tibi jam fratres pietatis sede manentes*.** The printed editions read: ‘Now there is a place better than the king’s fleeting realms.’
- **55. [Col. 1279C], after *] Inque loco meliori quam labentia regna; Quorum*.** The Fleury manuscript reads ‘your own [brothers]’ and, in the next verse, *ferentes* for *fereris*, then ‘into all things’ for ‘into hardships.’ The printed reading pleased us more.
- **56. [Col. 1279C], after *Sicut fama tuos jam misit in ardua fratres*.** The printed editions read: ‘Come here, I beg you: these, these are fitting gifts for one who suffers.’
- **57. [Col. 1279C], after *similis, palmas tendebat in altum, Subnixoque genu matris*.** There: ‘He fixed [his gaze] upon her face, / as far as the crowd that held him allowed his body to see [her].’
- **58. [Col. 1279C], after *non ipsa premebat. Qui simul admonitus cratem conscendit*.** The printed editions read ‘and into the fire.’
- **59. [Col. 1279C], after *in igne Intrepidus certaque fide sua membra locavit*.** The printed editions give the following three verses thus: ‘And the holy soul that remained departed unharmed. / The flames had fallen, while warm ash remained; / the opened earth received the uninjured body.’
- **60. [Col. 1279D], after *est sermone locuta: Quid nunc, dire, paras? Jussis*.** The printed editions read: ‘Let us obey, all of us. / But let no guard remove any gift of childbirth. / Yet although…’
- **61. [Col. 1279D], after *Ac licet ipse velis, non sum passura, tyranne*.** The same printed editions read: ‘For let all perish alike in so great a contest; / although you may change, dreadful man, the punishment of your own time, / the same harsh sentence remains for the holy sons. / But you prepare worse things—if there are worse things, you threaten them— / and because you see my face held by horror, / you would rejoice whenever you decree a part for that side.’
- **62. [Col. 1279D], after *quoties desaevis in istos. Ardet at ipse magis*.** The printed editions read ‘swift.’
- **63. [Col. 1280C], after *magis [Note: Vulg., rapida.] rabida rex concitus ira*.** There: ‘and he thinks [them] despised.’
- **64. [Col. 1280C], after *putat, ne sicut caetera fratrum Turba ferant poenas*.** There: ‘He perceives that the mother seeks this also, / and almost wished with his own hand to bring the fourth son forth / to harsh exile.’ A little later those same printed editions read *volebant* (‘wished’) for *valebant* (‘were able’).
- **65. [Col. 1280C], after *Proh pudor! erubuit vultus ostendere matri Natus, et*.** Jean du Bois reads ‘with an astonished mind,’ wrongly.
- **66. [Col. 1280C], after *submisso lumine vidit, Talibus aggreditur dictis monitura timentem*.** The printed editions read: ‘From the first, the fourth birth for me; fourth from the lowest.’
- **67. [Col. 1280C], after *tibi, quae possum dicere, nate? Hoc nisi quod*.** Thus from the printed editions. The Fleury manuscript reads only ‘hardened.’
- **68. [Col. 1280C], after *coeli durata potentia tecum Sit simul et virtus*.** The printed editions read: ‘And the holy author of [our] origin. / To that King we owe whatever we are asked.’ The passage is difficult in both readings and appears corrupt.
- **69. [Col. 1280C], after *quem genus omne probatur, Quod manet in Domino*.** The Fleury manuscript reads ‘holy when he is born to him.’ The printed reading pleased us more.
- **70. [Col. 1280D], after *quia Sarra manebat; Illaque cum peperit, generisque propagine*.** Jean du Bois reads *septa* (‘enclosed’). We corrected from the printed editions, which read: ‘Yet she gave birth to these, and the propagation of the lineage began.’
- **71. [Col. 1280D], after *coepta, Ex insperato remanent tibi Sarra nepotes, Esau*.** The printed editions read: ‘And Jacob, led into one fatherland, / whom it is certain [she bore] in childbirth.’
- **72. [Col. 1280D], after *scimus partu geminos peperisse Rebeccam. Hinc sumus, hinc*.** Thus from the printed editions; Jean du Bois wrongly has ‘we die.’ A little later the printed editions read ‘open the path of the lineage, which [leads] into the citadel of the righteous,’ and then ‘nor did he join the mixed crowd.’
- **73. [Col. 1280D], after *Parentem Conspice, ne dubites, mater tibi prospera monstrat*.** The printed editions read: ‘Whatever it is, endure it patiently; by your assent increase / my crowd, son … of those who follow.’
- **74. [Col. 1281C], after *comitare valenter Turbam, nate, meam, numerumque hortare sequentem*.** Those same editions read: ‘Nor did the parent complete [her speech], mingling grief and joy.’
- **75. [Col. 1281C], after *monitus, cum luminis orbes Ipse levat, matremque oculis*.** There: ‘to attend’; and shortly afterward, ‘his bearing and expression confess [it].’
- **76. [Col. 1281C], after *nisi tristia vulnera matris Per partus divisa suos*.** There: ‘But he too, in a swift course, / slipped from their hands and climbed upon the fires.’
- **77. [Col. 1281C], after *Elapsus manibus, cursu contendit in ignes. Mira loquar*.** There: ‘the flame touched neither his hair nor his face.’
- **78. [Col. 1281C], after *non contigit ora.] flamma illius non contigit ora*.** The Fleury manuscript reads ‘the body as though lifeless.’ We emended from the printed editions, where the next three verses nevertheless read: ‘When the fire had overcome the lifeless body, / yet, with mouth open, silently, by the way through which the spirit might go, / he poured it forth, from where it had been received, together with the blood.’
- **79. [Col. 1281C], after *gavisa parens, quod qui modo tristi Constiterat vultu*.** The printed editions read: ‘Trusting with a secure heart / that he had obeyed the commands, despising the king and his anger, / the mother began thus, while the king…’ A little later: ‘They curse the king, complaining in so long a speech.’
- **80. [Col. 1281D], after *cui sidera parent: Quod nisi producis, timor est*.** The Fleury manuscript reads ‘now an heir follows.’ The printed editions are better; later they read: ‘Now you perceive whom punishment seeks; now glory remains for us / on either side, though none may be brought forth’; and then, ‘whom you ordered to leave your kingdom.’
- **81. [Col. 1281D], after *parcere nolis. Nam quoscumque tuo jussisti excedere regno*.** The following two verses are absent from the printed editions. Whether the transmitted *seu vitio comitante* (‘whether with fault accompanying it’) should read *saevitia comitante* (‘with savagery accompanying it’) is for others to judge.
- **82. [Col. 1282C], after *est longa magis, regnoque potentior isto Quod regis*.** The Fleury manuscript reads ‘and in whose final part’; the printed editions, ‘now in the final part of this.’ We expressed a more probable reading from both faulty texts. The printed editions then give: ‘If you also fear these, though younger in age, / they surpass you and likewise conquer your kingdoms by their contempt, proud man. / But carry out your command, and do not divide our offspring. / Give these also to the flames, and exercise the powers of your kingdom. / Yet you are mortal and will not hold kingdoms forever.’
- **83. [Col. 1282C], after *gemitus inter sua pectora volvit. Consentit cum mente*.** Thus from the printed editions. The Fleury manuscript reads ‘grief.’
- **84. [Col. 1282C], after *et talia verba profatur: Haec tua libertas et*.** The printed editions read ‘dreadful.’
- **85. [Col. 1282C], after *tumida portas cervice rigorem, Sentiet irati regis quid*.** The same printed editions read ‘wounds.’
- **86. [Col. 1282C], after *fingere tentas Laetitiam, luctusque tuos in gaudia vertis*.** The Fleury manuscript has the copyist’s error ‘Do not change: it is well; rejoice.’
- **87. [Col. 1282D], after *triumpha; Dummodo sic vincas, ut sis suprema tuorum*.** The printed editions read: ‘Thus, utterly maddened, you rejoice in the death of your sons.’
- **88. [Col. 1282D], after *do flammis, hoc nec mutare potestas Ulla potest*.** There: ‘the decrees [stand]; only you live on, surviving.’
- **89. [Col. 1282D], after *ne mea jussa morentur, Ordo suos peragat cursus*.** The printed editions read: ‘Bring forth the son; / let the fires spare none. Do I think the king / appears doubtful after this? It is fear.’
- **90. [Col. 1282D], after *mihi, femina, nullus. Praecipuus de gente tua produceris*.** The printed editions read *index* (‘discloser’), and ‘whom in appearance…’
- **91. [Col. 1282D], after *specie, mirande puer, cui pectore virtus Firma manet*.** There: ‘Now she who was able…’
- **92. [Col. 1282D], after *dedissem. Sed me dura vetat, tristisque potentia regis*.** The Fleury manuscript reads ‘denies’; the printed editions, ‘but let him deny.’ We presented a more probable reading from the two.
- **93. [Col. 1282D], after *et mundi rector, Moysesque petitam Accepit, populoque dedit*.** The printed editions read ‘which’; and shortly afterward, ‘to whom we should deservedly give honor.’
- **94. [Col. 1283C], after *honorem. Tu modo ne dubites monitis parere parentis*.** The same printed editions read ‘But vigor…’
- **95. [Col. 1283C], after *maneat jam plena Deo; sit fortior aetas, Quam*.** There: ‘than the king had reason to hope—had reason to hope when he commanded.’
- **96. [Col. 1283C], after *O quanta est virtus, quanta est fiducia fortis!*.** The printed editions read ‘But why do you hesitate to conquer amid [the flames]?’; then ‘believe me’; and later, ‘the sinew will join the bodies, and the preserved [souls]…’
- **97. [Col. 1283C], after *tamen rapidus te terreat ignis, Fratrum sume animos*.** The Fleury manuscript reads ‘and invoke the eternal name.’ The printed editions are better, and we followed them.
- **98. [Col. 1283C], after *orat Murmure quo poterat: puerum non impedit aetas*.** The printed editions read ‘He no longer fears death, and [turns] to his mother…’
- **99. [Col. 1283C], after *tamen placidas superaverat auras. Laeta dolet tacite mater*.** There: ‘and joy suppressed the grief, and mourning…’
- **100. [Col. 1283C], after *pressoque dolore Tristitiam luctusque suos in gaudia vertit*.** This verse is supplied by the Fleury manuscript.
- **101. [Col. 1283D], after *superant; ne forte negent, ne forte timorem Concipiant*.** Thus from the printed editions. The Fleury manuscript reads ‘in spirit.’ Soon the printed editions wrongly read ‘The younger the age…’
- **102. [Col. 1283D], after *quo quis minor est, major metus, anxia secum*.** The printed editions read ‘It divides both cares and hopes, and fear along with them.’
- **103. [Col. 1283D], after *matrisque piae per viscera currunt. Spes tamen est*.** We supplied the better word from the printed editions, which read ‘she saw [him] brought forth and entering from afar: Let me see…’
- **104. [Col. 1283D], after *mihi, vultus agnoscere nostros Debet et hic, fratrum*.** The word ‘and’ is absent from the Fleury manuscript.
- **105. [Col. 1283D], after *numero parere suorum. Forsitan hunc solum puerilia pectora*.** Thus from the printed editions. The Fleury manuscript reads ‘they touch,’ and soon afterward ‘may bear.’
- **106. [Col. 1283D], after *nobilitas generis, si tangit origo, Respice, nate, tuos*.** The Fleury manuscript reads ‘Israel also.’ The printed reading is better.
- **107. [Col. 1283D], after *respice, nate: Noli annos numerare tuos, puer: incipe*.** The printed editions read ‘but to bear God in the heart.’

Let not the deceit of the foolish king trouble you.

Thus, growing stronger, he now conquered what opposed him;  
Thus the spirit extinguished the flames; thus afterward the summoned body  
Was received back by the opened earth, which had given it,  
And the sacred soul that remains withdrew inviolate.

Although the mother was weary, victorious through so many wounds,  
She fell forward upon her face, and with hands raised upward  
She uttered these words and spoke as follows:

You who rule the sovereignty of heaven, earth, and sea,  
You who give the stars to heaven and living creatures to the earth,  
Fish to the waters, and birds to the air—  
To you, O great One, the confidence of my mind rises;  
You who divide the immense chaos mixed with blind darkness  
Into parts, and give both night and day,  
The moon and sun, which you always command at varying times  
To provide light throughout the world by night and day.

After this you give humankind, from whose seed the mortal race fills the world; its tongue begins to speak in differing languages among the nations, though all share the same taste.

But to recount what changed the merit of humankind and their speech  
Would require a long delay; I am resolved to continue what I began.

We confess that you held the divided sea with your staff,  
While the people crossed the waters on dry ground,  
Fleeing the death and king of Egypt, Pharaoh,  
Who commanded the number of the saints to serve him,  
Whom Moses, guided by your majesty, led across in its entirety,  
And, once preserved, released safely through your power.

The earth produced the fruits that it bore at your command,  
And thirst sought water hidden in secret places.  
There was no moisture; all, crying aloud,  
Asked Moses to give water to the thirsty.  
To them he spoke these brief words:

“Believe that you can obtain from God whatever you ask of him,  
Who by this staff can make a river flow from the rock,  
So that springs, denied throughout the whole region, may come forth.”

He struck it, and, swifter than any word,  
The rock poured forth springs with their first sweetness.

I confess that the whole world is indebted to you:  
Whatever the nations can do, you alone can do entirely,  
And whatever the nations cannot comprehend, you alone comprehend.

You burden and relieve mortal humanity of its cares.  
I beseech you, while I fear with an apprehensive yet steadfast mind,  
That my youngest child may not be absent from the number of his brothers,  
The child unaware of himself, whom I now see being held at a distance,  
With a great crowd gathered around him.  
For his sake alone my age arouses tears in me;  
Only one remains, and for him I have my greatest concern:  
That the tender child may not be ignorant of the people from whom he was born.

If I could take him aside alone,  
I would comfort him and teach him his father’s race and homeland.  
Yet I shall send whatever consolations I can.

Little boy, dearer to me than your tender years,  
You are dearer to me than kingship, dearer even than life itself.  
You can make your mother, victorious in all things, completely victorious;  
You are the end of childbirth and the end of future sorrows.

If concern for me touches you, if in a pious mind  
You retain the honor of your mother, although you are [lacuna] and a child,  
Pay all the more attentive ear to your parent’s words.

First learn, boy, what you will become after these things,  
If you are patient; what you will become for me, dear child,  
Your deeds themselves teach. You will remain among the company  
Of the holy brothers, and will be secure in rest while the ages  
Complete their savage courses after the long span of time has ended.  
You will return to this light and see eternal kingdoms,  
Unstained by evils and nowhere opposed to the saints.  
There will be no place for death, nor will wars  
Be waged by swift horses; eternal peace will remain.

[Col. 1286A] Believe your mother, who always desires you to be safe.

Alas! Why do you reject my words with a sorrowful face?  
Why do you shrink back? Have pity on me, have pity on yourself.  
If it were permitted, I would wish to go first—but I am forbidden; nevertheless I shall go,  
When I have seen you, my son, conquer these evils.

What do you command me to hope for? Are you alone delaying my words?  
Are you alone, my son, still calling back my grief?  
Do you nod assent, or condemn me, your brothers, and your race?  
Whatever you may wish, I beg and implore you: listen.

With these breasts I nourished you when you were small, my son,  
And for your sake I shed these tears as well.  
Do not wish to remain: you will remain alone and orphaned.  
You have no brother left: who will give you the consolations of life?  
Alas! Alone you try to disgrace your mother, your race,  
And your homeland, if you refuse words such as these.

[Col. 1286B] O how much better you will preserve your life forever  
If you do before God whatever those who came before have done.  
Boldly lay aside your fears; lay aside your dread.  
Conceive God in your mind; he will give you manly strength.

While the mother was doing this, the boy looked toward his mother’s commands.  
When he saw that he alone had been left,  
He raised his face and uplifted hands to heaven,  
And, with a powerful voice, adored the eternal God,  
Whom in his mind and likewise by his gesture he entreated  
To conquer the king and to conquer the savage flames.

And so, neither sluggish nor restrained by his childish years,  
He leapt fearlessly into the midst of the flames.  
He overcame everything, until, victorious, his spirit  
Returned on high and sought the hidden dwelling of his former brothers.

While the boy was doing these things, joy released his mother.

[Col. 1286C] Now, exhausted by suffering and deprived of speech,  
She breathed out triumphantly and, collapsing among the hands of her own,  
Fell lifeless; her loosened limbs came to rest.



Thus she herself, like her sons, was received among the company of the saints.

[Col. 1287]

## THE METER ON GENESIS, TO POPE LEO

Which Quesnel appended to the minor works of Hilary, bishop of Arles. (C, G, S)

[Col. 1287A]

We have obeyed your instructions, following your sweet commands,  
O bishop of Christ, which you gave with pious lips.  
Would I not sing the praises of so great a Father,  
The work and gift of God, while I still possessed a tongue?  
My voice is hoarse and harsh, worthy of no crowns,  
And my talent lies inert; yet I desire to speak of lofty things.

It is worthy and just always to give you thanks,  
Almighty Father of the world, under whose rule all things  
Received their day of birth, and, suddenly arising,  
Saw the light beneath a heaven astonished after the darkness.

The race of humankind, cattle, wild beasts, a thousand birds,  
And the hosts that move across the flowing fields—  
All things are through you, from you, who create the greatest things;  
From you, Father, existing from yourself, and there is no other father of the Father.

[Col. 1287B]

You are the head of the first Head, the source of the fountain,  
The first summit of things, the first sower, creator of all.  
Yet you derive your lineage from no other: yourself the everlasting Spirit,  
Living through the ages in ancient motion,  
You will always be, because you always were, needing no death,  
Without a birthday and knowing no end of time.



From himself comes the beginning; no other remains to him as author.  
Chance presses upon things as they are born, and their end constrains them.

When black chaos covered everything, and the shapeless mass  
Pressed from above upon the bodies of the world,  
And late darkness weighed upon it,  
When there was neither appearance nor form, you, God, were working within,  
A hidden power mingled with bodies concealed from view.



Already you were arranging the newborn walls of the world,  
Its various forms and the souls that were to be.

And when you first brought forth its head from conquered night,  
Raising your lofty face, the darknesses perceived it.



Soon the Lord of things dispelled sluggish sleep,  
And inert matter, driven by the divine power, trembled,  
Stirred at once by its ripeness and conscious of childbirth.  
The body of the immense mass is split into many limbs;  
At the command, seeds are measured out into their places,  
And the confused entrails of the mass descend together,  
Pieces cut apart by sections and looking toward their forms;  
Already color nourishes within and awakens them with gentle fire.









[Col. 1288A]

First the expanse of heaven, opened wide, embraces  
All the spaces of the world and is suspended in its lofty sphere.  
Heavy earth descends to the bottom under its sluggish weight,  
And, fixed in place, settles upon the sea as its foundation.  
It was to be an open space for the empty region,  
Where the tender ether, moving through it, might nourish mortals,  
And through which so many gifts of the Father might emerge  
And, once born, be carried effortlessly through the void.

The waters are forced apart; then, within a definite boundary,  
The seas melt together, and the wave does not pass beyond its limit.

Then the nourishing light arises, the day commanded to be called.  
It floods the newborn world with tender brightness,  
Revealing your gift and work, your greatest gifts,  
Which the Father was preparing to create in his native love,  
So that human life might shine forth skillfully  
Through heavenly arts capable of guiding all the lights.  
It rejoices and exerts its intelligence in diverse praise.

Night follows, black, and dense darkness,  
Bringing sleep and leisure to weary bodies,  
And giving all things one face and a similar appearance.  
For day distinguishes the faces of changing things,  
And, once night has been scattered, gives each its own color;  
It stirs minds glowing for greater labor,  
Sharpening mortal hearts with various cares.  
Thus the form of day is life, while night is an image of death.

Then the Father, creating the stars in the heavens and living by light,  
Distinguishing the constellations with various patterns across the sky:  
The rosy Morning Star rises, radiant in face;  
Evening appears, and dawn scatters its purple hair.

The Serpent brings clear weather; the Pleiades bring rain.

[Col. 1288C]

There are mountains, there are wagons, and crowns glittering with flowers;  
There are signs that turn the year through twelve forms.  
And many other ornaments of the lofty dwelling,  
By these signs the world is sustained, and the highest royal palace,  
Its painted parent, gleams with the varied light of the stars.



But greater light belongs to the sun, whom the Father, adorned with lavish generosity,  
Deigns to honor with full distinction.  
That fiery radiance raises itself upon its lofty crown,  
Carrying its red face through the open structures of heaven;  
The guide of the stars, it flourishes as lord of the world and of the elements.

Behold another marvel, a marvelous glory: see, the moon changes its course.  
The fires it loses it gathers again,  
And, extinguishing its horns, disturbs the light upon its brow.  
Yet soon, when its circle is complete, it blazes again  
And the night-shining moon feeds the sown stars with light.



Nor is the mechanism that revolves in the eternal ether  
Merely a painting of the sky, nor is there only lofty will;  
Mind and reason lie beneath it, and a useful order governs things.



Hence instruction comes to the earth; hence, finally,  
Guidance comes to farmers and to those who traverse the deep sea,  
So that they may predict how the lights will move,  
Know the coming rains and the dry clear weather,  
Know the season in which the ploughman should lead oxen into the fields,
