And the sailor may safely attempt the uncertain sea.

With the fires set in the heavens, O best Father,  
You undertake to cultivate the earth and enrich it with a lavish gift.



[Col. 1289B]

The plains spread level as realms for humankind,  
A home for cattle and a resting place for birds;  
The hills raise their lofty swell,  
The valleys sink, the flowering meadows grow green,  
The rocks harden, and the rich soil loosens;  
Springs burst forth, the lofty source from which rivers arise;  
Varied grasses of herbs spring up across the fields.



Already the tender ear was pouring forth its grain,  
Although there were no yokes and no ploughshare of any plough,  
And no bull lowed in furrowed fields.  
Behold also the vine, already full of its moist cluster,  
Still untouched by the sickle and ignorant of hard iron,  
Casting the shade of its leaves over the lofty hills.

The various forms of different wild animals arise,  
Four-footed creatures, and also those that crawl upon the earth.

[Col. 1289C]

Birds are born through the clouds on colorful wings.

When the Father had completed these things, and now, in a world rich with abundance,  
Saw that everything required the care of a great king—  
One who would govern the sea, the lands, and all created things,  
Who would look upon the high heaven and praise the mighty gifts  
Of the powerful God, lest these things have been created in vain—

“Let us make a human being,” you say. Tell us, best of all, with whom?



Now you speak? It is clear: even then your Son  
Sits beside you on the lofty throne and looks upon the friendly earth.



“But let us make a human being,” you say, “whose face will be our image,  
And who will proceed into eternity from my hands.”

Then you, the maker of things, take the soft substance of earth  
And form the man, from whose side, in answer to his desire,  
The woman is made in face; the woman is made from the man’s side,  
So that she might be dearer to the man and suited to be the companion of his side.



O happy creature, whose father is the right hand of the highest Thunderer!  
O exceedingly happy one, who derive from heaven  
Both your race and your form! If the harmful vices of earth  
Do not deceive you, and flattering error does not overthrow you,  
You will be divine, and, restored to heaven, will marvel at the kingdoms  
Which the Father promises to the good with faithful speech.

For at your birth God freely bestowed many things upon you:  
First, a heavenly face and a fatherly countenance,  
An upright gait, and a lofty neck,  
So that no hindrance would prevent your eyes from looking toward heaven;  
Then active and ready hands, ministers of life,  
And, in your breast, the dwelling of divine reason and the seat  
Of lofty counsel, together with the honor of a voice ready to be poured forth.



These things were granted to human beings alone; for the rest, the beast is mute.  
It received a belly, internal organs, sinews,  
The channels of its veins, and blood scattered through its body,  
Together with sensations—of what is just and what is slight—and pains [the supplied line is textually difficult].



But you, Almighty One, lavish in your private gift toward humanity,  
Applying your hands and work with loving care  
To cultivate the pledge of the Father’s affection,  
So that nothing would be lacking from the divine countenance,  
Breathe into it the fire of heaven  
And bestow upon it an abundant share of the sacred mind,  
Mingled throughout the whole body.



Then it is permitted to remember ancient things and to know the present,  
And the soul is allowed to see what is to come.



Hence we speak and sing of God; hence all the stars  
And the cultivation of the earth flourish, and the sea is set in motion.  
Hence come the arts, a name, modesty, prudence, and justice;  
Hence strong souls arise, hence honor proceeds,  
And the path that leads the chaste to the thresholds of heaven.



Therefore, Father, you place human beings, perfected by your full gift,  
Above the earth and entrust them with the reins of things.  
So that they might possess everything and subject it to themselves,  
Become lords of the earth while remaining your servants,  
And possess all the world, provided that they serve you, their one Lord.



After the first human being did not fear to feed upon the forbidden tree  
And, captured by the serpent’s deceptions, gave himself over to it,  
He stands guilty and naked, with his eyes cast down,  
Begging for clothing; he flees the Lord and hides his face.  
Guilt follows as his companion; life, made subject to sin,  
Weakens its powers and the gifts descending from heaven.

The heavenly fire gradually grows faint when sent down from the ether;  
Hearts numbed by the cold of sin grow stiff.  
Concern for food and the belly entered, along with concern  
For covering the body, and mortal cares entered the sacred breast.



From this offspring of sin is born; from it grows  
A much worse and more evil descendant than the first.  
Generation follows generation, growing by degrees toward crimes—  
Crimes that sharpen deranged hearts with their goads  
And arm you, Father, with various weapons.



Then for the first time untimely rain came down from the clouds  
To fall upon the earth with violence;  
Then for the first time lightning was hurled from the serene sky;  
Then dreadful hail beat upon the troubled fields,  
And the ether, unbroken, rumbled with loud thunder.

Yet these things do not recall the wicked. Impious frenzy  
Occupies the world, and madness runs loose with slackened reins.  
Wars are pleasing, and slaughter as well, perjuries and frauds;  
They delight in lying, love to seize, and conceal their thefts.  
There is no loyalty among the peoples; there is no truth anywhere now.

The crime of the earth is washed away by the Flood and its waters,  
And one man remains, the renewer of the race and the people.

[Col. 1291B]

The ark shelters a few, preserving the seeds of the righteous.  
Already then the form of the coming cleansing was revealed.

[Col. 1292A]

And one man, through whom those reborn after receiving the light  
Are preserved by the faithful Church, which guards her adopted offspring.



After the swelling of the Flood subsided and the waters withdrew,  
The dove carried a leaf of the peace-bearing olive,  
And, flying back on dry wings, gave signs of peace.

Then a better people rises, purer after the waters,  
A race of human beings destined to produce great descendants on earth.



From then on, hearts devoted to heaven belonged to the priesthood;  
From then on, boys prepared to sing amid the flames;  
And the unfed boy whom the lions did not touch;  
Then kings sang of God; then the true mouths of the prophets  
Sounded forth, the offspring of heaven shining upon the earth.

Although all things served God once sin had been defeated,  
Nevertheless, even now an ancient drop of poison  
Was scattered among the peoples, and traces of fraud remained—  
Traces which a good teacher would wash away with better waters.



## IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 450. PASCHASINUS, BISHOP OF LILYBAEUM

[Col. 1291]

## HISTORICAL-LITERARY NOTICE ON PASCHASINUS

(From Schoenemann’s *Bibliotheca historico-litteraria*, volume II.)

### § I. Life

[Col. 1291C]

Paschasinus was a distinguished citizen and bishop, especially renowned for the embassy undertaken by order of Leo I to the Council of Chalcedon in the year 451, together with Lucentius, bishop of Asculum, and the presbyter Boniface. Among them, however, he held the first place in rank and honor, and he was the first to sign the acts of the council in Leo’s name.

Nor was this the only testimony Leo gave to the learning and prudence of this man. Even earlier, Paschasinus had deserved to be consulted by him about the calculation of Easter for the year 444, a matter that was then no light question.

During that period he also suffered many serious hardships with his church at the hands of Genseric, about which he complains to Leo in a letter. The final circumstances of his life are uncertain.

### § II. Writings

There survives his letter to Leo concerning the Easter question, written in the year 443, in which he replies to a letter of Leo that has perished. In Marianus Scotus it was wrongly divided into two letters, and by others it is also often cited under two inept titles, namely “On the Miracle of the Font” and “On Vandal Captivity.”

The other letter of Paschasinus concerning the condemnation of Dioscorus, which is reported to survive in the third session of the Council of Chalcedon, is not a letter but the judgment against Dioscorus pronounced by Paschasinus before the council itself in Leo’s name. Anyone who wishes to inspect the acts themselves can see this. It is readily accessible in Labbe’s *Councils*, volume IV, pages 419–421; Hardouin’s volume II, pages 343–346; and Mansi’s volume VI, pages 1046–1048.

### § III. Editions

Paschasinus’s letter was preserved not only by many manuscript copies of the letters of Leo the Great, but was also transmitted by the eleventh-century chronicler Marianus Scotus in his *Chronicles*, book II, act 6, under the year 444, in the Basel edition printed by Oporinus in 1559, pages 344–346, and in Pistorius’s *Scriptores rerum Germanicarum*, Regensburg, 1726.

It was chiefly corrected through the work of Petavius and Bucherius. The former made several emendations according to the manuscripts of Jacques Sirmond in his work *On the Doctrine of Times*; the latter transcribed the whole letter, expanded and polished, from other manuscript copies in his *Commentary on Victorius of Aquitaine* (Antwerp, Plantin press, printed by Balthasar Moretus, 1634), pages 75–77.

Quesnel next included it among the Leonine works after Letter II and added learned annotations, pages 425 and following, in the Lyon edition. Finally, the Ballerini brothers, having reread it against Vatican manuscript Regina Suecorum no. 586, of the eleventh century, in which it was inserted among Paschasinus’s works, reproduced it among the Leonine letters as no. III, with extensive notes and variant readings of their own, without omitting Quesnel’s notes in volume III. See also Mansi’s *Councils*, volume III, page 1222.

[Col. 1293]

## PASCHASINUS’S LETTER

See below among the letters of Leo the Great, no. III, volume 54.

## AT THE SAME TIME. P. ANNAEUS SYLVIUS, BISHOP OF OCTODURUM

[Col. 1293]

## HISTORICAL-LITERARY NOTICE ON SYLVIUS

(From Schoenemann’s *Bibliotheca historico-litteraria*, volume II.)

### § I. Life

[Col. 1293B]

Polemius, or Sylvius or Salvius , bishop of Octodurum—which place is now called Martignac and is situated on the Rhône in the Valais district of Switzerland—if he was indeed the same person to whom Eucherius of Lyon dedicated the *Passion of the Martyrs of Agaunum*. Certainly nothing beyond this connection with that most celebrated man, to whom he in turn dedicated his own works, preserves the memory of his life.

### § II. Writings

There survives his *Laterculus*, or index of feast days customarily celebrated in each month, both among Christians and among pagans. It was written under the consuls Flavius Zeno and Porthumianus, that is, in the year 448.

### § III. Editions

[Col. 1294B]

Bollandus first published part of this *Laterculus*, namely the month of January and excerpts from other months, in the general preface to the *Acts of the Saints*, volume I, January, pages 44–45.

His continuators subsequently published it in full in volume VII of June, pages 178–481, together with a preface concerning the manuscript from which it derives, as well as its age, author, and character. To illustrate these matters further, they also published alongside it another calendar, the *Calendar of Furius Dionysius Philocalus*, which had previously been published by Bucherius in his *Commentary on Victorius of Aquitaine*.

Nevertheless, this *Laterculus* is defective in many places and very often differs even from the excerpts that Bollandus had earlier published, as the Benedictine authors of the *Literary History of France*, volume II, pages 295–296, observed long ago, and Mansi more recently remarked in his annotations to Fabricius’s *Bibliotheca Latina Mediae et Infimae Aetatis*.

[Col. 1293]

## THE CALENDAR OF SYLVIUS

See above, reader, volume XIII of our *Patrology*, column 676, where the closeness of the subject matter already gave us reason to publish the work of Sylvius.

## AT THE SAME TIME. TURRIBIUS, BISHOP OF ASTORGA

[Col. 1293]

## HISTORICAL-LITERARY NOTICE ON TURRIBIUS

(From Schoenemann’s *Bibliotheca historico-litteraria*, volume II.)

### § I. Life

[Col. 1293D]

Turribius, bishop of Astorga in Hispania Tarraconensis, was a most ardent opponent and persecutor of the Priscillianists. After returning from travels through various regions of Spain and perhaps also foreign provinces, and recognizing how widely this evil had spread while creeping in darkness, he first stirred up his friends Idacius and Ceponius, bishops, and then Leo of Rome, once and again, to provide assistance against it. He also made himself the agent of Leo’s instructions and letters to the bishops of Tarraconensis, Carthage, Lusitania (Baetica), and Gallaecia concerning the celebration of a general council.

A synod was also held in this matter, not only in Gallaecia but in four other provinces as well ; but nothing concerning the outcome of either council has reached our memory.

### § II. Writings

There remains a letter of Turribius to Idacius and Ceponius, concerning the exclusion of apocryphal writings from the authority of the faith and concerning the sect of the Priscillianists. It was written about the year 447, when he had not yet attained the dignity of bishop.

His letter to Leo and other writings have perished; Leo explicitly mentions them in his reply, which in editions produced before Quesnel is numbered 93, and in the Quesnel and Ballerini editions 15.

### § III. Editions

The letter mentioned above was first published by Ambrosius de Morales in his *History of Spain*, book XI, chapter 26, from a manuscript of St. Emilianus preserved in the Library of St. Laurence at the Escorial.

Baronius thereafter inserted it in his *Annals* under the year 447 (Roman edition of 1607, volume VI, pages 43–44; Cologne edition of 1624, page 50; Mansi edition, volume VII, pages 604–606), as did Franciscus Bivarius in his *Commentaries on the Chronicle of Maximus’s Continuator, Pseudo-Dexter* (Madrid, 1651), under the year 445, no. 6, pages 137–159, where he discusses Turribius at length.

It was soon incorporated into the *Councils of Spain* of Cardinal de Aguirre and furnished with his notes in the first edition (Rome, printed by Jo. Jac. Komareck, 1694), volume II, pages 218–222, and in the new edition (Rome, from the printing house of Antoninus Fulgentius), volume III, pages 108–111.

Paschasius Quesnel first inserted it among the Leonine letters after Leo’s letter to Turribius, which is numbered XV. Most recently the Ballerini brothers reprinted it after the same letter of Leo, volume I, column 711. It occupies that position, however, not so much by the editors’ intention as through a typographical error by those who had been given Quesnel’s copy to transcribe. It ought to have been placed in the appendix to volume I, page 1478. They did not wish to repeat it twice.

Quesnel’s observations on the aforementioned letter of Leo, Lyon edition, page 445, shed considerable light on this letter; these should be joined with the Ballerini brothers’ notes on the same observations, volume III, columns 1362–1386.

Baluzius had cast suspicion on this letter in the preface to his *New Collection of Councils*, but the Ballerini brothers demonstrated that it is sufficiently vindicated by the antiquity of the Aemilianus manuscript. Ambrosius de Morales did indeed provide information about that manuscript, though not with adequate precision. But Leo’s editors affirm, on the basis of the Book of Canons that Joannes Baptista Perez had compiled from Spanish manuscripts before Ambrosius, in 1575, at the command of Cardinal Quiroga, and sent to Rome to Gregory XIII for use in correcting Gratian, where it is now preserved in the Vatican Library as no. 4887, that the signs of the antiquity and excellence of this Aemilianus manuscript—one of the Spanish collection’s manuscripts used in that work—are so evident that they completely remove every suspicion of interpolation or forgery.

[Col. 1295]

## TURRIBIUS’S LETTER

It is found below in the cited volume 54 of our edition, among the Leonine letters, where it has been assigned number XV. See it there, benevolent reader.

## INDEX OF NOTABLE SUBJECTS AND TERMS OCCURRING IN THE TEXT OF CASSIAN

The Roman numeral indicates the book or conference; the Arabic numeral indicates the chapter.

## Complete Editorial Apparatus

These notes translate the supplied apparatus in source order. Latin lemma anchors preserve their scope.

- **1. [Col. 1283D], after **.** The Fleury manuscript reads: ‘May your vigorous age give examples to future times. Give yourself—and this is what I pray, beyond which there is nothing more. Consider what you should flee.’
- **2. [Col. 1283D], after *fugias, et quam meliora petantur. Non te sollicitet*.** The printed editions read ‘the wretched king’s deceit,’ then ‘but may you now grow for him’; soon afterward, ‘His spirit, extinguished by the flames, then departed thus.’
- **3. [Col. 1284C], after *quae superest anima inviolata recessit. Quamvis lassa parens*.** The Fleury manuscript reads *perque et sua*. The printed editions: ‘Through all his wounds he endured the king, yet likewise in spirit…’
- **4. [Col. 1284C], after *habuit voces et talia verba locuta est: Qui*.** The Fleury manuscript reads *tenes, male* (‘you hold, badly’).
- **5. [Col. 1284C], after *qui coelo, qui das animalia terris, Aequoribus pisces*.** The printed editions: ‘[You] who beat the winds through the air, to you the first eager confidence of my mind rises.’
- **6. [Col. 1284C], after *te, magne, meae mentis fiducia surgit; Qui chaos*.** There: ‘mingling the chaos wrapped in blind darkness.’
- **7. [Col. 1284C], after *Dividis in partes, et das noctemque diemque, Lunamque*.** There: ‘and the swift sun, which preserve the times’; afterward ‘then humankind,’ with the intervening verse omitted.
- **8. [Col. 1284D], after *orbem. Post haec das hominem, cujus de semine*.** The printed editions read *mundus* (‘world’), then ‘the tongue melts.’
- **9. [Col. 1284D], after *per gentes, sapor est tamen omnibus unus. Sed*.** The printed editions read ‘which changed by merits, and of humankind…’
- **10. [Col. 1284D], after *est, coeptis insistere certum est. Te mare divisum*.** There: ‘with the rod you roll and hold.’
- **11. [Col. 1284D], after *pede per siccum populus transcenderet aequor, Aegypti fugiens*.** Thus from the printed editions; the Fleury manuscript reads ‘mountains.’
- **12. [Col. 1284D], after *servire jubebat, Quem tua majestas Moses duce transtulit*.** The Fleury manuscript reads ‘river.’ We preferred the printed editions, which later read ‘redeemed the whole by power.’
- **13. [Col. 1284D], after *diremit. Terra dabat fructus, quos te cogente ferebat*.** The printed editions: ‘And water takes possession of him, sought through all its hiding places.’
- **14. [Col. 1284D], after *sic est sermone locutus: Credite posse Deum quidquid*.** Perhaps *poscetis* (‘you will demand’) should be read for *petetis* (‘you will seek’), the Fleury reading. The printed editions: ‘You will have sought him; yet this rod [will be able] to split the hard rock.’
- **15. [Col. 1285C], after *amnem diffundere saxo, Ut veniant fontes tota regione*.** The printed editions read *morati* (‘having delayed’).
- **16. [Col. 1285C], after *orbis, Tu quidquid possunt gentes, potes omnia solus*.** This verse is absent from those printed editions.
- **17. [Col. 1285C], after *Tu mortale genus curis onerasque levasque, Te precor*.** The Fleury manuscript wrongly reads ‘with an astonished mind strengthen the fearful one.’ We retained the printed reading.
- **18. [Col. 1285C], after *Conspicio, turba circumveniente frequenti Hunc propter solum lacrymas*.** The printed editions read ‘which she moves.’
- **19. [Col. 1285C], after *potes in totum victricem reddere matrem, Tu finis*.** There: *parvus* (‘small’); afterward ‘if, created [son], you retain in mind the scent of your mother.’
- **20. [Col. 1285C], after *tangit, si matris honorem Mente pia retines, quamvis*.** The printed editions read ‘both dear and an infant.’ In the lacunose Fleury manuscript, *parvus* (‘small’) would be the preferable supplement. Soon the printed editions read ‘with a pious ear.’
- **21. [Col. 1285C], after *quid sis post ista futurus, Si patiens fueris*.** The printed editions read ‘then you.’
- **22. [Col. 1285C], after *chare futurum Facta docent. Fratrum sanctorum in parte*.** There: ‘placed.’
- **23. [Col. 1285D], after *dum saecula cursus Saeva suos peragunt, finito tempore*.** There: ‘certainly.’
- **24. [Col. 1285D], after *lucem repetes, aeternaque regna videbis Non maculata malis*.** The printed editions read ‘but there will be concord among the saints.’
- **25. [Col. 1285D], after *Nec morti locus ullus erit, nec bella citatis*.** There: ‘they are exercised.’ The Fleury manuscript reads ‘they are mingled’; the context requires the future tense.
- **26. [Col. 1285D], after *requisivit contextus.] Committentur equis, sed pax aeterna manebit*.** The printed editions: ‘Believe that your mother is always eager for your salvation.’
- **27. [Col. 1285D], after *Quid refugis? Miserere mei, miserere tuique. Si liceat*.** There: ‘I would wish to go first; behold, I am forbidden.’ We retained the last words; the Fleury manuscript less correctly reads ‘behold, he forbids.’
- **28. [Col. 1285D], after *velim, vetor ecce; sed ibo, Tunc cum victorem*.** The printed editions read ‘I shall see you.’
- **29. [Col. 1285D], after *sperare jubes? solus mea dicta moraris? Solus adhuc*.** There: ‘you renew what is right for me.’
- **30. [Col. 1285D], after *etiam revocas, mi nate, dolorem? Annuis, an damnas*.** There: ‘me also.’
- **31. [Col. 1285D], after *audi. His ego te parvum nutrivi, nate, papillis*.** The printed editions: ‘By my breast, I beg you, and by the weeping and tears of my children, / be willing to return; you will return alone, and your brothers / will no longer have given you consolation in this life. / You dishonor the most holy names of your brothers, your mother, / and your race.’
- **32. [Col. 1286C], after *Et genus, et patriam! si talia dicta recusas*.** There: ‘Alas! when…’; shortly afterward, ‘if at last you do whatever…’
- **33. [Col. 1286C], after *agit, puer ad praecepta parentis Respicit, et solum*.** There: ‘when he saw that he alone had been left.’
- **34. [Col. 1286C], after *supinas, Et sic voce potens, aeternum Numen adorat*.** There: ‘and thus, at once in feeling within himself and by a nod, he asked.’
- **35. [Col. 1286C], after *puerilibus annis Prosilit intrepidus medios delapsus in ignes*.** The printed editions: ‘He conquered whatever there was, so that he went into the life on high.’
- **36. [Col. 1286D], after *fratrum peteret secreta priorum. Dum puer ista gerit*.** Second Maccabees 7:41 says only: ‘Last of all, after the sons, the mother too was consumed.’ Accounts differ about her death. Josephus says she threw herself on the pyre lest a man touch her. Some, following the old Latin translator of Josephus, think she underwent a most severe martyrdom. Sorionides and the Arabic account say that after her sons’ deaths she prayed for God to remove her from this life and died fallen upon them. Others say joy at all her sons’ constancy took her life; our author belongs among these.
- **37. [Col. 1286D], after *Jamque ut erat lassata malis, jam voce negata*.** The printed editions read ‘sighing, and amid…’
- **38. [Col. 1286D], after *manus collapsa suorum Concidit exanimis, resolutaque membra quierunt*.** The Fleury manuscript reads *Sic ipsas nati*; the printed editions *Sic ipsa et nati*. We emended here as the sense requires.
- **39. [Col. 1287C], after *monitis, tua dulcia jussa secuti, Antistes Christi, quae*.** Quesnel emended *dabat* for meter, but the sense requires *dabas* (‘you were giving’).
- **40. [Col. 1287C], after *stupido spectarunt lumina coelo. Gens hominum, pecudesque, ferae*.** Quesnel likewise reads ‘and a thousand’ for meter.
- **41. [Col. 1287C], after *temet, ex te, qui maxima condis, Ex te*.** Quesnel conjectures *nata* (‘daughter’), also favored elsewhere by Veitz. With all manuscripts we retain *nate* (‘son’), as though meaning ‘existing from you and deriving origin from no other.’ — Coustant.
- **42. [Col. 1287D], after *nate Pater; nec jam patris est pater alter*.** Another reading: ‘You are the head, and of the first…’ — Quesnel, margin.
- **43. [Col. 1287D], after *egenus, Qui natalis inops, nec finem noveris aevi*.** Another reading: ‘From you.’ — Quesnel, margin.
- **44. [Col. 1287D], after *Deus intus agebas, Corporibus tectis mixtus, secreta potestas*.** The printed editions read *Jam tumiti ponens*. This is emended from the Laon manuscript. — Coustant.
- **45. [Col. 1287D], after *Et varias rerum facies animasque futuras, Utque caput*.** Another reading: ‘he brought [it] forth, the darkness itself having been conquered.’ — Quesnel, margin.
- **46. [Col. 1287D], after *Dominus rerum somnos discussit inertes, Pigraque materies trepidavit*.** Thus with the Laon manuscript, says Quesnel; other books read *nomine* (‘name’). — Coustant.
- **47. [Col. 1288C], after *vero libri, nomine. COUSTANT.] numine pulsa Commotaque simul*.** Veitz reads *maturo* (‘mature’); the Colbertine manuscript supports *natura* (‘nature’). — Coustant.
- **48. [Col. 1288C], after *partus, Scinditur ingentis cumuli per plurima corpus Membra*.** Veitz’s *locosque* (‘and places’) is not displeasing. — Coustant.
- **49. [Col. 1288C], after *COUSTANT.] locusque simul metantur semina jussu, Et confusa*.** We added *simul* (‘together’) from the Laon manuscript. Quesnel reads ‘And unconfused entrails descend’; Veitz, ‘And the entrails of the mass, formerly confused, descend.’ For *descendunt* (‘descend’), *discindunt* (‘split apart’) would be attractive. — Coustant.
- **50. [Col. 1288D], after *nullo per inane labore, Diffusae coguntur aquae; mox*.** The Victor and Colbertine manuscripts read *limine* (‘threshold’). — Coustant.
- **51. [Col. 1288D], after *cunctis unam faciem similemque figuram. Namque dies varia*.** Veitz’s ‘various faces’ is unsatisfactory, for *os* here means form and appearance. — Coustant.
- **52. [Col. 1288D], after *dat cuique suum disjecta nocte colorem, Instigatque animos*.** The printed editions read *opera* (‘works’), against the manuscripts. — Coustant.
- **53. [Col. 1288D], after *imago. Tunc condens Pater astra polo, ac lumine*.** Quesnel reads *vivo* (‘living’); the Laon manuscript *videns* (‘seeing’).
- **54. [Col. 1288D], after *annum volventia formis. Multaque praeterea celsae domus ornamenta*.** Quesnel reads *Qui* (‘which’).
- **55. [Col. 1289D], after *suum, quos perdit colligit ignes, Cornuaque exstinguens perturbat*.** Thus the Laon manuscript; the printed editions read *limite* (‘boundary’). — Coustant.
- **56. [Col. 1289D], after *sidera luce. Nec tamen aeterno, quae machina volvitur*.** Veitz reads *axe* (‘axis’) and soon *volanti* (‘flying’), not *voluntas* (‘will’). — Coustant.
- **57. [Col. 1289D], after *ignes coelo, Pater optime, terras Excolere aggrederis, et*.** For meter Quesnel reads *donas munere opimo* (‘you bestow with a rich gift’).
- **58. [Col. 1289D], after *Saxaque durantur, pinguis se gleba resolvit, Rumpuntur fontes*.** Veitz restores ‘whence is the origin of all rivers,’ but misses the author’s meaning: rivers have a lofty origin because their springs are usually in high places. — Coustant.
- **59. [Col. 1289D], after *omnia nata gubernet, Quique altum spectet coelum, laudetque*.** Coustant reads *potenter* (‘powerfully’).
- **60. [Col. 1289D], after *Dei, ne sint haec condita frustra. Tunc faciamus*.** Quesnel’s text has *ait* (‘he says’), his margin *ais* (‘you say’).
- **61. [Col. 1289D], after *Alias, ais.] ais, hominem. Dic, optime, cum quo?*.** Thus the Colbertine manuscript with Veitz. Elsewhere: ‘You do not speak clearly; now…’ — Coustant.
- **62. [Col. 1289D], after *tibi Filius alto Assidet in solio, et terras*.** A metrical foot now seems lacking, but not by ancient practice, under which *exspectat* was read accordingly. — Coustant.
- **63. [Col. 1289D], after *rerum, assumis mollia terrae Atque virum formas, cujus*.** Veitz soon reads ‘the desired rib,’ and then *nam costa* for *de costa* (‘from the rib’). — Coustant.
- **64. [Col. 1290D], after *domum divae pectus rationis, et alti Sedem consilii*.** The Laon manuscript reads ‘of eloquent speech’; in the next verse another reading has ‘the rest in motion.’ — Coustant.
- **65. [Col. 1290D], after *praecordia, nervos, Venarum rivos, et sparsum corpore sanguen*.** Veitz reads ‘the bosoms of joy and the sensation of hard pain.’ A second hand in the Victor manuscript partly supports it. Perhaps ‘in life and death’? — Coustant.
- **66. [Col. 1290D], after *Aetheris inspiras, et sacrae mentis opimam Indulges partem*.** Veitz alone reads ‘mingling’; then with the Victor and Colbertine manuscripts ‘the whole [share] in the body’; he alone later adds ‘hence to remember.’ — Coustant.
- **67. [Col. 1290D], after *permixtus corpore toto, Tunc meminisse licet veterum, praesentia*.** Quesnel has *menti* (‘to the mind’) for *nosse* (‘to know’).
- **68. [Col. 1290D], after *cuncta Terrarumque viget cultus, pontusque movetur; Hinc artes*.** Quesnel prints *manantque* (‘and flow’), with *nomenque* (‘and a name’) in the margin; we retained the latter with the other editions and manuscripts.
- **69. [Col. 1290D], after *et rerum tradis habenas: Cuncta habeat subdatque sibi*.** The Colbertine manuscript reads ‘and he would conquer all’; a later Victor correction, ‘and live forever.’ — Coustant.
- **70. [Col. 1290D], after *Frigore peccati torpentia corda rigescunt, Cura cibi ventrisque*.** Quesnel alone reads ‘enters, and concern.’
- **71. [Col. 1291B], after *stimulis acuunt dementia corda, Teque, Pater, variis armant*.** A second Victor hand adds ‘with deeds [fitting] for thunderbolts’; Veitz reads ‘to punish by dangers,’ then ‘then evils first began.’ — Coustant.
- **72. [Col. 1291B], after *facies monstrata lavacri, Atque unus multis, per quem*.** Following Zeliner, Veitz reads ‘the Church gives [it] to those reborn in light, preserving the children she received.’ Other editions read ‘reborn by the given lance, but received … the Church preserving by childbirth.’ We follow the Laon manuscript. — Coustant.
- **73. [Col. 1292B], after *pennis dedit omina pacis. Tum populus surgit melior*.** Quesnel reads ‘than the former in the waters,’ and later ‘Hence priests…’
- **74. [Col. 1291], after *vestigia fraudis, Quae bonus ablueret doctor melioribus undis*.** The preceding Prolegomena show that Quesnel appended these minor works of Hilary of Arles, with an extensive dissertation, to his edition of Leo the Great. Though styled an apology for Hilary, that dissertation pertains so extensively to Leo that it cannot be moved without disrupting the order. We therefore omit it here, reserving it for Quesnel’s elucidations on Leo in volume 55 of this Patrology. — Editor.
- **75. [Col. 1293C], after *§ I. Vita. Polemius sive Sylvius aut Salvius*.** Bollandus wrote ‘P. Annaeus Silvius.’
- **76. [Col. 1295], after *in Gallaecia solum, sed et aliarum quatuor provinciarum*.** Antonio, *Bibliotheca Hispana Vetus*, book 3, chapter 4, §104.
- **77. [Col. 1295], after *benevole lector. Volume back matter INDICES IN CASSIANUM*.** The following indices apply only to the works of John Cassian in volume 49 and volume 50, columns 0009–0372.

[Col. 1295]

A certain abbot, when dying, chose a successor because of the merit of obedience, *Institutes* IV, 28. What an abbot ought to be, *Institutes* II, 3. Abraham the anchorite: his virtues and miracles, *Conferences* XV, 4–5. What renunciation is, *Institutes* IV, 34. Three kinds of renunciation, *Conferences* III, 6. These three correspond to the three books of Solomon, *Conferences* III, 6. External renunciation is useless without interior renunciation, *Institutes* IV, 36; *Conferences* III, 7. Evil renunciation, and those who renounce wrongly, are described, *Conferences* IV, 20. See *Renunciation*. The abstinence of the ancient Fathers, *Institutes* IV, 11. It must be joined to the other virtues, *Institutes* V, 10–11. What abstinence ought to be for overcoming the spirit of fornication, *Institutes* VI, 7–8. The measure of abstinence is not uniform for everyone, *Institutes* IV, 5. The purpose of bodily abstinence, *Institutes* V, 22. The abstinence of a certain old man who ate six times and was still hungry, *Institutes* V, 25. That of Abbot Paesius until sunset, *Institutes* V, 27. [Col. 1296] How moderation in abstinence is to be maintained on Sundays and feast days, *Conferences* XXI, 23. See *Fasting*. Acedia is described, *Institutes* X, 1 ff. It is related to sadness, *ibid.* It especially attacks solitaries around midday, *ibid.* Hence it is called the “noonday demon,” *ibid.* How it afflicts monks, *Institutes* X, 2–3. How it is to be overcome, *Institutes* X, 25. From where it arises, *Conferences* V, 3, 9. Its two kinds and its twofold temptation, *Conferences* V, 11. The active life consists in two things, *Conferences* XIV, 3. The actual life is exercised only in the present, *Conferences* I, 10. It must end after this life, *Conferences* I, 10. The many works of the active life, *Conferences* I, 4. To what extent recollection of past actions is useful or harmful, *Conferences* XX, 19. Whether Adam’s sin was lighter or graver than Eve’s, *Conferences* XX, 11. The punishment of both sins, *Conferences* XX, 11. Adversity is endured more easily than prosperity, *Conferences* VI, 9; *Institutes* XI, 11. What the aerial powers are, *Conferences* VIII, 12.

[Col. 1297]

The disposition of the agent, not the effect or outcome of the work, must be considered, *Conferences* VI, 8–9. An excessive affection, even for the most worthless things, contrary to the pursuit of perfection, *Conferences* I, 6, 9. The afflictions of the righteous are justly inflicted by God, *Conferences* VI, 2 ff. The different kinds and causes of afflictions, *Conferences* VI, 11. How ἀγάπη (*agapē*, love) and διάθεσις (*diathesis*, disposition) differ, *Conferences* XVI, 14. What *agape* is, *Conferences* XXIV, 12. Comparison of the spiritual contest with the external and worldly contest, *Institutes* V, 12. The foundation of the spiritual contest lies in the chastisement of the body, *Institutes* V, 17. The use of allegory in the sacred Scriptures, *Conferences* VIII, 3; XIV, 8. The allegory of the foreign nations expelled from the Holy Land, *Conferences* V, 16 ff. How a lover and one who fears differ, *Conferences* XI, 9–10. Who are called ambidextrous in Scripture, *Conferences* XVI, 10. Ambition is censured in monks, *Conferences* I, 20; IV, 20; *Institutes* X, 2; XI, 14–15; XII, 30. The ambitious do not acquire true and solid knowledge, *Conferences* XIV, 9–10. Encomium of Ambrose, *On the Incarnation* VII, 26. The various kinds of friendship, *Conferences* XVI, 2. From what friendship becomes indissoluble, *Conferences* XVI, 3, 6. True friendship rests on virtue, *Conferences* XVI, 3. Perpetual friendship can exist only among the perfect, *Conferences* XVI, 4, 24, 28. Private friendships contracted by oath are disapproved, *Conferences* XVI, 28. The life and conduct of anchorites, *Institutes* V, 36. From where anchorites arose and received their name, *Conferences* XVIII, 6. The holiness of anchorites shining forth in their very faces, *Conferences* XI, 2. What places they ought to seek, *Conferences* XXIV, 3. What the pursuits of anchorites ought to be, *Conferences* XXIV, 4. God does not allow anchorites to remain unknown even in the most remote places, *Conferences* XXIV, 19. What *anagoge* is in Scripture, *Conferences* XIV, 8. Why angels are called Principalities and Powers, *Conferences* VIII, 18. Whether they were created before the visible world, *Conferences* VIII, 7. From where their names were given them, *Conferences* VIII, 15. The stability of angels proceeds from God’s grace, *Conferences* VI, 16. The fall of the angels, *Conferences* VIII, 8 ff. Abbot Serenus thinks that evil angels have been assigned to individual human beings, *Conferences* VIII, 17. Evil angels fight among themselves, *Conferences* VIII, 13. The three states of the soul, *Conferences* IV, 19. The human soul is immortal, *Conferences* I, 14. After this life it will lack neither sensation nor understanding, *Conferences* I, 14. It is never idle, *Conferences* VII, 4 ff. It is like a watermill, *Conferences* I, 18; likewise like a feather or flying little plume, *Collect.* IX, 3. In what the soul’s beauty and ugliness consist, *Conferences* III, 8. Its mobility, *Conferences* VII, 3. Its perfection, *Conferences* VII, 3–4. Its threefold faculty, *Conferences* XXIV, 15. The seeds of the virtues naturally exist in the soul, *Conferences* XIII, 12. The higher part of the soul must be cared for first, *Conferences* XXIV, 16. The threefold disease of the mind, *Conferences* XXIV, 15. The anniversary of the burial of the deceased is celebrated, *Conferences* XIX, 1. The heresy of the Anthropomorphites, *Conferences* X, 2 ff. The ancient use of antiphons, *Institutes* II, 2. The faith of the Antiochene creed and its exposition, *On the Incarnation* VI, 3 ff. Praise of Antony the Hermit, *Conferences* XVIII, 6. His notable saying about perfect prayer, *Conferences* IX, 3; likewise about discretion, or prudence, *Conferences* II, 2; likewise about loving and imitating examples of the virtues, *ibid.* What “to appear” means, *On the Incarnation* II, 5. What the appetite for food ought to be, *Institutes* V, 8–9. The industry of bees, *On the Incarnation* VII, 5. The drinking of water must also be moderate, *Conferences* XII, 11, 15; XXII, 3. The commendation and recollection of the virtues of the anchorite Archebius, *Institutes* V, 37–38. His call and advancement to the episcopate, *Conferences* XI, 2. Every art has its proper end, *Conferences* I, 2. Cham was the author of magical art, *Conferences* VIII, 21. Encomium of Athanasius, *On the Incarnation* VII, 30. Avarice is the service of idols, *Conferences* XII, 2. See *Love of Money*. God adapts the teacher’s discourse to the capacity and merits of the hearers, *Conferences* I, 23. Commendation of Augustine, *On the Incarnation* VII, 28. Why the Egyptian monks carried a staff, and what it signified, *Institutes* I, 9. The use of staffs was formerly familiar to monks, *Conferences* XI, 3. Basil the Great’s statement about his own virginity, *Institutes* VI, 19. His statement about a monk who does not perfectly renounce temporal goods, *Institutes* VII, 19. The blasphemer is handed over to a most unclean spirit, *Institutes* XII, 20. What are properly called goods, *Conferences* VI, 3; XXI, 12, 16.

[Col. 1298]

Virtue is the principal good, *Conferences* XXI, 12. How it is distinguished from other goods, *Conferences* XXI, 16. The good which the Apostle testifies that he cannot perfect, *Conferences* XXIII, 3. Why Egyptian monks did not use shoes, *Institutes* I, 10. Canonical prayers at night, *Institutes* II, 1 ff. The canonical manner of singing psalms and the number of psalms handed down by an angel, *Institutes* III, 4–5. Canonical daytime prayers among the Egyptian monks, *Institutes* III, 1 ff. The word “flesh” is used in various senses in Scripture, *Conferences* IV, 10. The struggle of flesh and spirit has usefully been left within us, *Conferences* IV, 7. How the desires of the flesh are restrained, *Conferences* XII, 5. Carnal vices differ from spiritual ones, *Conferences* V, 4. Cassian was ordained deacon by Chrysostom, *On the Incarnation* VII, 32. Reprobate men are unworthy of temporal correction, *Conferences* VII, 31. Commendation of chastity, *Institutes* VI, 15–17. Chastity is called holiness by the Apostle, *Institutes* VI, 15. It makes human beings in a certain way equal to angels, *Institutes* VI, 6. The ways in which it is compared, *Institutes* VI, 9–10, 12; *Conferences* XI, 14; XII, 11 ff. How it is preserved, *Conferences* XII, 21. By what arguments it is tested, *Conferences* XIX, 16. It is acquired especially through fasts and prayers, *Conferences* VII, 2. The reward of chastity, *Institutes* VI, 17. It is a particular gift of God, *Institutes* VI, 6; *Conferences* XII, 4, 15–16. It differs from continence, *Institutes* VI, 4; *Conferences* XII, 10–11. Chastity rests upon humility and knowledge of chastity, *Institutes* VI, 18. How the perfection of chastity is recognized, *Institutes* VI, 10, 20, 22. Chastity must be carefully preserved, *Conferences* XII, 16. Patience promotes chastity, *Conferences* XII, 6. The degrees and differences of chastity, *Conferences* XII, 7. Great sweetness is joined to chastity, *Conferences* XII, 13. Only those who experience it recognize it, *Conferences* XII, 13. The imaginary or feigned chastity of pagan philosophers, *Conferences* XIII, 5. Bodily chastity is nothing without purity of heart, *Institutes* VI, 12, 20. The exceptional chastity of Abbot Serenus, *Conferences* VII, 1; of Abbot Paul, *Conferences* VII, 16; of St. Basil, *Institutes* VI, 19; of Abbot Theonas, *Conferences* XXI, 8–9; of a certain rustic or farmer, *Conferences* XIV, 7. The stirring of the flesh in dreams does not harm chastity, *Conferences* XII, 10. Nor does relaxing a fast at the time prescribed by the Church, provided frugality is maintained, *Conferences* VI, 22. The letter of Castor to Cassian, *Conferences* 53. The usefulness of the cell and solitude, *Conferences* XXI, 22. Archebius yielded his cell to guests and pilgrims, *Institutes* V, 37. How harmful it is for a monk to abandon his cell or wander outside it, *Conferences* VI, 15. What *cenodoxy* is, *Institutes* XI, 1 ff. It is manifold and multiform, *Institutes* XI, 3 ff. It is compared to bulbs, *Institutes* XI, 5. It lies in wait for all the virtues, *Conferences* V, 10. It is difficult to cure, *Institutes* XI, 6 ff. How it is to be cleansed, *Institutes* XI. The two kinds of cenodoxy, *Conferences* V, 11. It is sometimes useful, *Conferences* V, 12. Ecclesiastical censures are also customary among monks, *Institutes* II, 15–16. What it means to receive a hundredfold in this life, *Conferences* XXIV, 26. The Gospel centurion as a type of the perfect soul, *Conferences* VII, 5. Cham, son of Noah, before the Flood engraved magical arts on bronze tablets and very hard stones, *Conferences* VIII, 21. The threefold classification of divine charisms, *Conferences* XV, 1. Charity is not only a thing belonging to God but also God himself, *Conferences* XVI, 13. It must be embraced above all, *Conferences* XVI, 7. It even prays for enemies, *Conferences* XI, 10. Its comparison with faith and hope, *Conferences* XI, 6. Blessedness is specially promised to its works, *Conferences* II, 2. The degrees of charity, *Conferences* XVI, 14. Its dignity is commended, *Conferences* XI, 6 ff. Nothing is to be preferred to charity, *Conferences* XI, 7. The land of the Canaanites was first assigned to the sons of Shem and usurped by the Canaanites, *Conferences* V, 24. Abbot Chaeremon is praised, *Conferences* XI, 4. Christ alone is free from every sin, *Conferences* XXII, 9–10. He alone came in the likeness of sinful flesh, *Conferences* XXII, 11–12. He alone was tempted without sin, *Conferences* V, 5. He was tempted by the devil in the same ways as Adam, *Conferences* XXII, 6. How Christ’s three-day death is to be understood, *On the Incarnation* VI, 23. Christ’s name was made illustrious by miracles, *On the Incarnation* II, 19. Christ ascended into heaven by his own power, *On the Incarnation* II, 23–24. Christ is not merely θεοφόρος (*theophoros*, “God-bearing”) but also God, *On the Incarnation* V, 1 ff., 16. It is impious to divide Christ or distinguish two persons in him, *On the Incarnation* V, 7. What it means to “loose” Christ, *On the Incarnation* V, 12. Christ alone is the author of our salvation, *On the Incarnation* V, 17. Christ is one, not two, *On the Incarnation* VI, 13, 15–16. Christ is not merely our teacher but also our liberator, *On the Incarnation* VI, 14. Christ’s temporal birth took nothing away from his divinity, *On the Incarnation* VI, 19. Their condition is described, *Conferences* I, 17. Their origins and beginnings must be carefully examined, *Institutes* VI, 13; *Conferences* I, 20–21. Their mutability and inconstancy, *Institutes* VI, 16; *Conferences* X, 12. The fourfold examination, or discernment, of thoughts, after the manner of money-changers, *Conferences* I, 21–22. Thoughts must not immediately be put into action, *ibid.* How we ought to exclude evil thoughts, *Institutes* VI, 13. Monks should reveal their thoughts to the elders, *Institutes* IV, 9; *Conferences* II, 11–13. The great usefulness of this, *ibid.* Whether and how demons know our thoughts, *Conferences* VII, 15. How good and spiritual thoughts are to be guarded, *Conferences* X, 11, 13. Why Egyptian monks wore *colobia*, *Institutes* I, 5. They frequently received holy Communion every Sunday, *Conferences* XXIII, 21. Holy Communion is not prevented by venial sins, *ibid.* nor by involuntary pollution, *Conferences* XXII, 4 ff.; nor is it denied even to the possessed, *Conferences* VII, 30. How it benefits us, *Conferences* IV, 13, 15–16. How useful confession and acknowledgment of one’s sin are, *Conferences* II, 11. How dangerous it is to rely on one’s own counsels, *Conferences* II, 21; XVI, 11–12. Evil counsels must be carefully avoided, *Conferences* VIII, 11. The customs of one’s ancestors must not be despised, *Conferences* XXI, 12. The contemplative life. See *Theoria*. How continence differs from chastity, *Institutes* VI, 4; *Conferences* XII, 10. Monks’ disputes over worthless matters are censured, *Conferences* I, 6. What the body of sin is, *Conferences* XXIII, 16. Bodily weakness does not prevent the virtue of continence or abstinence, *Institutes* V, 7. The various kinds and methods of monastic correction, *Institutes* IV, 16. How one’s neighbor is to be corrected, *Institutes* VIII, 5; XI, 16. Correction must be moderate, *Conferences* II, 13. What it means to be spiritually crucified, *Institutes* IV, 34. Our cross is the fear of the Lord, *Institutes* IV, 34. The power and effectiveness of the Lord’s cross against demons, *Conferences* VII, 23; VIII, 18. The hoods of the Egyptian monks, *Institutes* I, 4. Why lighter offenses are sometimes punished more severely, *Conferences* VI, 11. A monk ought to flee worldly cares, *Conferences* IX, 5–6. For many reasons he recognized Christ as God, *On the Incarnation* VII, 21. He is the author and instigator of idle talk and stories, *Institutes* V, 21. The demon openly confessed that he had spread heresies through Arius and Eunomius, *Conferences* VII, 32. Demons cannot harm anyone without divine permission, *Conferences* VII, 22. They are ignorant of the inner thoughts of human beings, *Conferences* VII, 15. Abbot Serenus found that they do not fight with human beings without difficulty, *Conferences* VII, 21. Different demons preside over different vices, *Conferences* VII, 17. Demons generally besiege and possess souls before bodies, *ibid.* They possess souls more dangerously than bodies, *Conferences* VII, 28. They are subjected to human beings in two ways, *Conferences* VIII, 19. The powers of demons have been weakened through Christ, *Conferences* VII, 23. In attacking human beings they maintain a certain order and harmony, *Conferences* VII, 19. They are not all equally savage, *Conferences* VII, 20. The various kinds of demons, *Conferences* VII, 32. Their powers and abilities also differ, *Conferences* VII, 20. The ruin and fall of demons, *Conferences* VIII, 8 ff. Some demons are subjected to others, *Conferences* VIII, 16. Demons occasionally fight among themselves, *Conferences* VIII, 13. The air is full of a multitude of demons, *Conferences* VIII, 12. See *Devil*. Praise of Abbot Daniel, *Conferences* IV, 1. Archebius paid his creditors’ debt in place of his mother, *Institutes* V, 38. The offering of tithes and firstfruits is pleasing to God, *Conferences* XXI, 2. What the offering of tithes and firstfruits was like among the Jews, *Conferences* XXI, 3. The punishment of the deceiver and the deceived is distinguished, *Conferences* VIII, 11. A monk must carefully avoid the delights of food and drink, *Conferences* V, 11. It is harmful to listen to a slanderer, *Institutes* V, 29. God created nothing evil by its nature, *Conferences* VIII, 6. God alone perfectly knows divine things, *On the Incarnation* VII, 7. God is more concerned for us than we are for ourselves, *Conferences* IX, 20. God wills all human beings to be saved, *Conferences* XIII, 7. The force of “God, come to my assistance,” *Conferences* X, 10. God alone is incorporeal, *Conferences* VII, 13. He must be loved for his own sake, *Conferences* XI, 8. God judges human beings according to present justice, *Conferences* XVII, 26. God’s omnipotence is infinite, *On the Incarnation* VI, 1. God’s works are wondrous, *Conferences* XII, 14. What God’s anger is like, *Institutes* VIII, 23. God often draws the unwilling to salvation, *Conferences* XIII, 6. Human emotions and bodily members are metaphorically attributed to God, *Institutes* VIII, 4. No one seeks to avenge injuries done to God, but rather injuries done to oneself, *Conferences* IX, 22. To abandon God is the death of the soul, *Conferences* IX, 6; XXIII, 9. It is sometimes beneficial to be abandoned by God, *Conferences* IV, 6. “To be” is most properly attributed to God, *On the Incarnation* V, 6. Human beings are called gods, *On the Incarnation* III, 2. Everything occurs by God’s will or permission, *Conferences* III, 20. The devil is to be feared more than an external enemy, *Institutes* V, 21. He perceived the hidden operation of Christ’s divinity, *On the Incarnation* VII, 13. The ways in which he tempted Christ, *Conferences* V, 5. By sin, the human being sold to the devil was not removed from divine power, *Conferences* XXIII, 12. The devil’s illusions by which he deceives the unwary, *Conferences* I, 21 ff. How the devil is called a liar and the father of lies, *Conferences* VIII, 25. See *Demon*. The supervision or administration of the monastery’s property or alms was entrusted to a highly approved elder, *Conferences* XXI, 1. The supervisor of the administration received the people’s offerings, *Conferences* XXI, 1–2. Diogenes’ opinion that adultery should not be punished, *Conferences* XIII, 5. Diolcos, a town of Egypt, *Institutes* V, 36; likewise the Desert, *Conferences* XVIII, 1. Those who had previously sinned were justly punished by the Flood, *Conferences* VIII, 24. The rigor of discipline in monasteries, *Institutes* IV, 16, 20. The virtue of discretion, or prudence, is called the eye and lamp in the Gospel, *Conferences* II, 2. It is to be preferred to all virtues, *ibid.* The Apostle counts it among the noblest gifts of the Holy Spirit, *Conferences* II, 2, 4. Its usefulness and necessity are commended, *Conferences* I, 22–23; II, 1 ff. It is given by God alone, *Conferences* II, 1. Saul and Ahab were deceived through lack of discretion, *Conferences* II, 3. Many anchorites shamefully fell through lack of discretion, *Conferences* II, 5 ff. How the virtue of discretion is acquired and possessed, *Conferences* II, 9–10. The threefold division of riches in Scripture—good, evil, and intermediate, *Conferences* III, 9. What riches are properly called ours, *ibid.* What the use of riches ought to be, *Conferences* VI, 3. No one should readily consider himself fit to teach others, *Institutes* X, 2; *Conferences* XIV, 10, 17. Those who presume to teach others while themselves unlearned are censured, *Institutes* II, 3; *Conferences* XXIV, 13, 16. The twofold benefit of those who teach others, *Conferences* XXII, 1. The office of a teacher, *Conferences* XI, 4.

Changing one’s clothing at entry into and profession of the religious life, *Institutes* I, 3; IV, 5; *Conferences* XVIII, 2. See *The Monks’ Clothing*. Christ’s humanity is asserted, *On the Incarnation* III, 5. Humility is the teacher of all virtues, *Conferences* XV, 7; XIX, 1; XXIV, 16. From where inequality and division of goods among human beings arose, *Conferences* I, 10. Explanation of the Lord’s Incarnation, *On the Incarnation* V, 13 ff. Everyone is more eager to avenge personal injuries than injuries done to God, *Conferences* IX, 22. What those provoked by injuries ought to do, *Conferences* XVI, 26. The disease of envy is difficult to cure, *Conferences* XVIII, 17. Demons are expelled through invocation of the saints, *Conferences* XIV, 7. Even brief anger must be avoided, *Institutes* VIII, 12. We ought to be angry with ourselves and with our vices, *Institutes* VIII, 8. Spiritual Israel, *Conferences* XII, 11. Spiritual Jacob, *Conferences* XII, 11.
