The human mind is never idle, Collation VII, 4. The reasons why our mind is weighed down, Collation IX, 6. The inconstancy of the human mind, Collations VI, 14; IX, 4. Abbot Chaeremon held that lying is sometimes permissible and praiseworthy, Collation XVII, 17 and following. The memory of God must be retained constantly, Collation XXIII, 9. The monks serve one another at table, Institutes IV, 19. What the desire for the Messiah was like among the holy Fathers, On the Incarnation V, 15, 17. Among the monks, “mine” and “yours” were not heard, Institutes IV, 13. “Man’s life is a warfare upon earth,” Institutes V, 17. No one’s merit should be judged by miracles, Collation XV, 6, 11. It is a greater miracle to drive away from oneself the fuel of lust than to drive demons from other people’s bodies, Collation XV, 8 and following. Humility outweighs miracles, Collation XV, 7. The miracles of Abbot Abraham, Collation XV, 4, 5. The merit of mercy, Collation II, 2.

How a monk should order his life from the beginning, Institutes V, 41. What the monk’s end should be, Collation IX, 3. What food a monk should have, Institutes V, 23. A monk’s renunciation of himself and temporal things is necessary, Collations II, 3; XXIV, 2. A monk should flee worldly concerns, Collation IX, 5, 6. He should always pursue purity of heart, Institutes V, 15. Gentleness especially adorns a monk, Institutes VIII, 5. From what the monks derive their name, Collation XVIII, 5. Their origin is from the apostles, ibid. Monks were established at Alexandria by Saint Mark, Institutes II, 3. Some monks exist only in habit and name, Collation IV, 20. Monks have always abstained from marriage, Collation XVIII, 5. From where they conceive the plague of avarice, or private ownership, Institutes I, 1. In former times they were tested and approved for a long time before being admitted, Collations IV, 3, 7, 27, 36 and following; XX, 1. They change their clothing upon entering the religious life, Institutes I, 3; IV, 5; XVIII, 2. They must renounce their own will, Institutes IV, 8; V, 28. Nor should they scrutinize the actions or commands of their superiors, Collation XVIII, 2. How they should guard their thoughts, Collation XXIV, 6. The younger monks should disclose their thoughts to their elders, Institutes IV, 9. See Novice. Lukewarm monks are worse than secular people, Collation IV, 19. The Tabennesiot monks brought nothing into the monastery, Institutes IV, 5. Monks who seek prefectures or the office of teaching are censured, Institutes X, 2; XI, 14, 15; Collations I, 20; IV, 20. Three kinds of monks in Egypt, Collation XVIII, 4. A fourth kind, more recent, ibid., 8. The faults of monks were also punished severely, Institutes IV, 16, 20. The monks’ mutual and reciprocal services, Institutes IV, 19 and following. The monks’ manual labor. See Manual labor. The obedience of the Egyptian monks was most perfect, Institutes IV, 1, 10, 12. How the monks’ vices should be corrected, Collation XIX, 13 and following. Everything is common among monks; nothing is private, Collation XXIV, 26. Philargyria, or the vice of private ownership, must be detested above all by monks, Institutes VII, 7 and following. Monks must avoid singularity within the community, Institutes I, 3; XI, 18. The association of monks with bishops, just as with women, was disapproved by the elders, Institutes XI, 17. How a monastery differs from a coenobium, Collation XVIII, 9, 10. The monastic life is a perpetual struggle, Institutes IV, 38. Private assistance from parents is incompatible with monastic perfection, Collation XXIV, 10 and following. Those who seek the care of nuns are censured, Collation I, 20. The threefold disease of the soul, Collation XXIV, 21. Death lies in wait for every age, Collation XXI, 8. The constant remembrance of death must be maintained, Institutes V, 41; Collation XVI, 8. The mortification of Abbot Apollo, Collation XXIV, 9. The raising of a dead man, Collation XV, 3. Offerings for the dead, Collation II, 5. The annual anniversary of the day of the dead person’s burial was celebrated, Collation XIX, 1. Abbot Moses, Collations I and II. Abbot Mucius, Institutes IV, 17.

How novices are to be tested, trained, and instructed in monasteries, Institutes IV, 6 and following; XII, 26, 27. Obedience and silence are commended to novices, Institutes II, 15; V, 28. Novices laid aside their secular clothing and were clothed in monastic garments by the abbot, Institutes IV, 5. See Monks. Novices must not conceal their thoughts, Institutes IV, 9. What the nakedness of monks consists in, Collations II, 2; XXIV, 2; Institutes VII, 24 and following. The commendation of obedience, Institutes I, 3; XVI, 23. Obedience must be simple and blind, Institutes XI, 33; Collation XVIII, 3. Monastic obedience is founded upon Christ’s example, Collation XIX, 6. The obedience of Abbot Mucius, Institutes IV, 17; of the Tabennesiot monks, Institutes IV, 1, 10, 12; of the monk John, Institutes IV, 23 and following; of certain younger monks, Institutes IV, 10; of two monks carrying figs, Institutes V, 4; of another monk dividing baskets, Institutes IV, 29; of Abbot Pynuphius cultivating a garden, Institutes IV, 30. Obedience is preferred to all virtues, Institutes IV, 13.

[Col. 1305]

Offerings customarily made for the dead, Collation II, 5. What supplication is, Collation IX, 11, 15. The eight principal vices, Collation V, 18; Institutes V and following. The greatness of divine omnipotence, On the Incarnation VI, 1. It cannot be grasped by human reason, On the Incarnation VII, 2, 3. Not everything suits everyone, Collation XXIV, 8. God’s works in the saints are worthy of admiration, Collation XII, 12, 13. Manual labor is extremely useful and necessary for monks, Institutes II, 3; V, 37 and following; X, 8 and following; Collation XXIV, 11, 12. Manual work prevents and removes many evils, Institutes X, 14. Manual labor was prescribed for the Egyptian monks, Institutes X, 22. The apostle Paul lived by the work and labor of his hands, Institutes X, 9, 10. Manual labor does not hinder private prayer, Institutes III, 2. Abbot Paul burns the manual work of an entire year, Institutes X, 24.

What prayer is, Collation IX, 12, 15. How attention and devotion are maintained in prayer, Collations X, 12 and following; IX, 26. The impediments to prayer and attention, and how they are excluded, Collations XIV, 12, 13. Short and frequent prayer is acceptable to God, Institutes II, 11; Collations IX, 36; X, 6. Prayer requires the deepest silence, Institutes II, 10. How prayer is to be made secretly and in private, Collation IX, 24. What prayer should be according to the judgment of Saint Antony, Collation IX, 31. Prayer requires attention, Collation XXIII, 7. Prayer that is merely vocal is censured for two reasons, Institutes II, 10. Prayer is a sacrifice, Institutes II, 12. How prayer can be continual, Collation X, 10. How pure and sincere prayer is obtained, Collations IX, 16; X, 8 and following. It is not hindered by manual labor, Institutes III, 2. An exposition of the Lord’s Prayer, Collation IX, 18 and following. One often sins in prayer, Collation XXIII, 20. The priest concludes the public prayer, Institutes II, 10. Perseverance, or constancy, is required in prayer, Collations IX, 3; X, 10 and following. By what sign one can know that a prayer has been heard, Collation IX, 32 and following. Those who came late to prayer were excluded from the oratory, Institutes III, 7. Canonical prayers. See Hourly prayers. Why prayers were instituted in the Church at fixed hours, Institutes III, 2 and following. Why our prayers are not always heard, Collation XIII, 7. Private prayers must be joined to public prayers, Institutes II, 12 and following. Four kinds of prayer, Collation IX, 8, 9. Understanding of the Scriptures is reached more by prayer than by study, Institutes V, 31, 34. What should be asked of God in prayer, Collation IX, 24. What the orders of angels signify, Collation VIII, 15.

Idleness is the fuel of many evils, Institutes X, 8, 10, 20 and following. See Acedia. The condition of the idle and lazy is described, Institutes X, 6. The praise of Abbot Paesius, Institutes V, 27. The praise of Abbot Paphnutius, Collation III, 1. His patience, Collation XVIII, 15. The surname “Buffalo” given to him, ibid. What barley loaves signify, On the Incarnation V, 2. Why the remembrance of parents must be excluded from monks, Institutes V, 22. The celebration of Easter, Collation X, 2. The book of the Shepherd cited, Collations VIII, 17; XIII, 12. Patience is so called from suffering, Collations XVIII, 12, 13. It must be shown to everyone, Collation XVI, 17. It is necessary for monks, Institutes IV, 41. How it can be acquired and retained, Collations XVIII, 12, 13, 16. It must be hoped for not from another’s restraint but from one’s own will, Institutes, chapter 42. It extinguishes the ardor of fornication, Collation XII, 6. Feigned patience, Collations XVI, 20, 22. The patience of a certain devout woman, Collation XVIII, 14; of Abbot Paphnutius, ibid., 15; of a certain devout young man, Collation XIX, 1. The encomium of Paul the Hermit, Collation XVIII, 6. Evangelical poverty, Collation X, 11.

Every sin is voluntary, Collation XXIII, 1. Sins are expiated in many ways, Collation XX, 8. Public sin must be washed away by public satisfaction, On the Incarnation I, 4, 5. How venial sins are committed, Collations XX, 11; XXII, 13. Few understand the magnitude and foulness of sins, Collation XXIII, 8. The roots of sins must be uprooted, Collation XXIX, 2. How far remembrance of sins is useful, Collation XX, 6, 7, 9, 11. The body of sin and its members are described, Collations XII, 2; XXIII, 16. No one is free from sin, Collation XXXIII, 6, 7, 17, 18. What it means to lend money at interest, Collation XIV, 17. The desire for money is foreign to monks, Collations IV, 20; V, 11. See Philargyria.

The errors of the Pelagians, On the Incarnation I, 3. The renunciation of Pelagianism made by Leporius and others, On the Incarnation I, 4. The pouch and staff are customary possessions of the Egyptian monks, Institutes I, 8, 9; Collation XI, 3. What perfection consists in, Collation I, 6. How it is acquired, Institutes IV, 30 and following; XII, 13, 15, 23, 31, 32; Collations I, 7, 8; XIX, 9; XXIII, 10. Not everyone understands the doctrine of perfection, Collation I, 1. Different kinds of perfection, [Col. 1306] Collation XI, 12. Examples of perfection should be sought from the few, Institutes V, 4. A perfect man is called ambidextrous, Collation VI, 10. One must persevere in one’s vocation, Collation XIV, 5 and following. Perseverance in the religious life is necessary, Institutes IV, 36, 37. The apostle Peter, shepherd of the Church, On the Incarnation I, 12.

What philargyria is and from where it arises, Institutes VII, 11. It is not money but love of money that produces it, Institutes VII, 21, 22. It is a destructive disease of the soul, Institutes VII, 20; Collation V, 8. Why it is difficult to cure, ibid. It is the begetter of many evils, Institutes VII, 7, 23, 26 and following. Its three kinds, Institutes VII, 14; Collation V, 11. It is a shameful and disgraceful vice, Institutes VII, 3 and following, 20. How it may be overcome, Institutes VII, 21, 30, 31. It was unknown before the Flood, Collation V, 8. The philargyria of Judas the betrayer, Institutes VII, 23, 24, 25; of Gehazi, Institutes VII, 14; of Ananias and Sapphira, ibid.

Definition of repentance, Collation XX, 5. Its various fruits, Collation XX, 8. In what its perfection and penitence consist, Collations X, 3, 5. Its necessity, On the Incarnation VI, 18. Various instruction is given to penitents, Collation XX, 8 and following.

The causes from which nocturnal pollution proceeds, Institutes VI, 11; Collation XXII, 3 and following. When it constitutes guilt, Collation XXII, 6. It is often brought about by the devil, ibid. It does not always prevent reception of the Eucharist, ibid., 4 and following. Involuntary pollution does not harm chastity, Collation XII, 9, 10. How it may be prevented or avoided, Institutes VI, 13; Collation XXII, 6. What petition is, Collation IX, 13, 15. What are called aerial powers, Collation VIII, 12. Why they are called powers and principalities, ibid., 14.

Practice: what it consists in, Collation XIV, 2 and following. How it is acquired, ibid., 3. Through it one reaches theory, ibid., 2. The difference between evangelical and legal precepts, Collation XXI, 33. What the spiritual firstfruits are, Collation XXI, 16. The offering of firstfruits and tithes in the Old Testament, ibid. The testing of monks. See Novice. The antiquity and obligation of the monastic profession, Institutes IV, 36, 37. How prophetic imprecations are to be understood, Collation VII, 21. The death of the deceived prophet because of disobedience, Collation VII, 15.

Private ownership is a grave crime in a monk, Institutes XII, 26, 27; I, 6; IV, 21; XVIII, 7; XXIV, 26. The vice of private ownership and its description, Institutes II, 3; IV, 13, 14, 15; Collation VII, 7. See Philargyria. How harmful it is to rely on one’s own judgment and counsel, Collation II, 11. Prosperity is more harmful than adversity, Collation VI, 9. God’s providence in all things, Collation XXIII, 20. The manner and discipline of psalmody, Institutes II, 7; Collations X, 14; XVII, 3; XVIII, 2. The angel’s teaching of the number twelve for the psalms, Institutes II, 5, 6. How we can attain understanding of the Psalms, Collation XI, 8. Purity of heart is to be pursued above all, Institutes V, 15. How purity of heart and body is acquired, Institutes VI, 9, 10, 12, 20. The judgment of perfect purity, Institutes VI, 10. How purity is guarded, Institutes VI, 15; Collation I, 7. The humility and concealment of Abbot Pynuphius, Institutes IV, 30 and following; Collation XX, 1.

The observance of Lent, Collations VII, 2; X, 2. Its differing practice in different regions, Collation XXI, 24, 25 and following. Its fast as the equivalent of a tenth of the year, Collation XXI, 25. To whom the law of Lent was imposed, Collation XXI, 29. Why Lent is so called, Collation XXI, 28. The monk is especially tempted during Lent, ibid. The perfect go beyond the law of Lent, Collation XXI, 29. During Pentecost, that is, the Easter season, there is no fasting, Collation XXI, 11, 19, 20. Nor are the knees bent during the canonical hours, Institutes II, 18; Collation XXI, 11, 19, 20. The type of Pentecost in the old law, Collation XXI, 20.

What monks’ rebrachiatoria (arm-coverings) are, Institutes I, 6. To depart from God is death for the soul, Collations IX, 6; XXIII, 9. When and how reconciliation with a brother is to be made, Institutes VIII, 12, 13; IX, 2; Collations VI, 15, 16, 18. The redemption of the human race could be accomplished only through Jesus Christ, On the Incarnation IV, 12. The time and measure of meals, Collation XXI, 23. Eating outside the proper hour and the common table is forbidden to monks, Collations II, 2, 17; V, 11; XXIII, 22. Sacred reading is to be used during meals, and which authors are to be read, Institutes IV, 17. Silence is to be maintained, ibid. The kingdom of God, Collation IX, 18. The kingdom of God and the kingdom of the Devil are described, Collation I, 13. The kingdom of heaven is understood in three ways, Collation I, 13.

[Col. 1307]

Veneration of holy relics, Collations VI, 1; VII, 26. Relaxation and relief of the mind are occasionally necessary, Collation XXIV, 20, 21. The renunciation of all possessions is confirmed by Scripture, Institutes VII, 16 and following. It is necessary for monks, Collation XXI, 1. It leaves nothing under one’s private ownership, Collation VII, 7. Once made, it must be pursued throughout one’s entire life, Institutes IV, 18; Collation XXIV, 1. It must be made not so much with the voice as with the mind and affection, Collation III, 7. Improperly made renunciation, Institutes VII, 15. See Abrenunciation and Philargyria. Three kinds of renunciation, Collation III, 6. The resurrection of the dead is a kind of generation, On the Incarnation V, 7. The praise of Rufinus, On the Incarnation VII, 28.

Among Eastern Christians, Saturday is free from fasting, Institutes III, 9. Why the Saturday fast was instituted in the Roman and Western Church, Institutes III, 10. Saturday vigils, Institutes III, 8, 9. The office of priests, Collation IV, 1; On the Incarnation VI, 11. The sacrifice of the Lord’s Supper, Institutes III, 3. Solomon’s three books correspond to the three kinds of renunciation, Collation III, 6. How “holy” differs from “spotless,” Collation XXII, 9. Even in this life the saints profess themselves sinners and unclean, Collations XXIII, 17 and following; XXII, 12. The afflictions of the saints are just, Collation VI, 2 and following. The saints of the Old Testament went beyond God’s commandments, Collation XXI, 4. The origin and way of life of the Sarabaites, Collation XVIII, 7. Satiety from food and drink must be avoided, Institutes V, 6; Collation II, 1, 22, 23. Satiety after abstinence and fasting must be avoided, Institutes V, 9. The sign of perfect satisfaction, Collation XX, 5, 7, 10, 11.

What spiritual knowledge is, Collation XIV, 8. Knowledge of divine law is a gift from God, Collation III, 14. Knowledge rests upon chastity, Institutes VI, 18; Collation XIV, 14. The ambitious do not attain true knowledge, Collation XIV, 9. What the goal of our actions should be, Collation VII, 6. How the mysteries of the sacred Scriptures should be expounded, Collations VIII, 3; XIV, 17. Their understanding is acquired more through prayer than study, Institutes V, 34. Some have attained the meaning of Scripture in dreams, Collation XIV, 10. By what steps it is reached, ibid., 9. The various meanings of Scripture, ibid., 8. Why God wished Scripture to be obscure, Collation VIII, 3. Sacred Scripture is compared to a fertile field, ibid. Constant reading of Scripture is commended, Collation XIV, 10. Demons are driven away by the authority of sacred Scripture, Collation XXII, 10. Many distort it toward meanings belonging to others, Collation I, 20.

The grounds on which old age is commended, Collation II, 13. The old are to be imitated, but not all of them, ibid. One must submit to the counsels and teaching of elders, ibid., 15. The commendation of Abbot Serenus, Collation VII, 1. What it means to serve the law of sin, Collation XXIII, 15. The deepest silence during the divine office among the Egyptian monks, Institutes II, 10. Silence at the monks’ table, Institutes IV, 17. The commendation of silence, Institutes II, 15; Collation XIV, 9. Singularity within the community must be avoided, Institutes XI, 18. Spiritual Zion, Collation XII, 11. The continence of Socrates, Collation XIII, 5. For whom the solitary life is to be sought, Institutes VIII, 17; Collation XIX, 10 and following. Solitude is to be sought and loved, Institutes II, 15. The commendation of solitude, Institutes IV, 10 and following; Collations I, 20; II, 2; VI, 15; XI, 2; XIX, 20; XX, 1. The prescribed time for sleep must neither be exceeded nor anticipated, Collations II, 17; V, 11. Moderate sleep is necessary, Institutes III, 8. Eunuchs are generally lukewarm, Collation IV, 17.

Hope is compared with faith and charity, Collation XI, 6. The proud wish to rule over others, Institutes XII, 30. Pride destroyed Lucifer and our first parents, Institutes XII, 4. Pride is twofold, spiritual and carnal, Institutes XII, 2; Collation V, 12. Whom spiritual pride attacks, Institutes XII, 4. Whom carnal pride attacks, ibid., 24, 25. Pride destroys all virtues, ibid., 3. It lies in wait for every virtue, Collation V, 10. The deformity and ruinous power of pride are described, Institutes V, 1, 3, 5, 7, 20, 21, 22, 27, 28; Collation IV, 16. It grievously attacks even the perfect, Collation V, 6. By what signs and indications it is recognized, [Col. 1308] Institutes XII, 29. Pride divinely punished, ibid., 20 and following. How many evils and vices spring from pride, ibid., 27. How it can be overcome, ibid., 9, 31, 32, 33. A monk must not say “mine,” Institutes IV, 13.

Why the Creed is so called, On the Incarnation VI, 3. The Creed conforms to the divine Scriptures, ibid., 8. An exposition of the Antiochene Creed, ibid., 3 and following. The authority of the Creed, ibid., 4. Synaxis (assembly), Institutes II, 19. Synecdochic speech is familiar to Scripture, On the Incarnation VI, 23. Those admitted to the Tabennesiot monastery brought nothing of their possessions with them, Institutes IV, 4. The obedience of the Tabennesiot monks, ibid., 1, 10, 12. Taciturnity. See Silence. Nothing should be decided rashly, Collation XVII, 8. No temptation can be overcome without God’s grace, Collations II, 13; III, 17. Endurance of temptations or afflictions is granted by God, Collation III, 17. The usefulness of temptations, Collation XXIV, 25. The order and reason of Christ’s temptations, Collation V, 6. The commendation of Abbot Theonas, Collation XXI, 1, 8, 9. Lukewarm monks are censured, Collations IV, 12, 19.

What the theoretical life is and what it consists in, Collation XIV, 1 and following. How it is acquired, ibid., 10. It is apprehended only by pure minds, ibid., 10, 14, 15, 16. Its parts and kinds, ibid., 8. The theoretical, or contemplative, life is praised, Collation I, 8. All pursuit of virtue is placed after theory, that is, contemplation of God, Collation XXIII, 3. To devote oneself constantly to theory in this life is impossible, Collation XXIII, 5, 13. The Virgin Mary, Theotokos, that is, “God-bearer,” On the Incarnation II, 2, 4. What holy fear is, Collation XI, 13. The fear of the Lord is the beginning and advancement of salvation, Institutes IV, 39. The difference between fear and love, Collations XI, 9, 10. The traditions of the elders must be observed, Collation II, 15.

From where sadness arises, Institutes IX, 4. It is a destructive disease of the soul, ibid., 1, 2, 3. Two kinds of sadness, Collation V, 11. Which sadness is salutary and which deadly, Institutes IX, 10 and following. How sadness is to be driven away, ibid., 13. Sadness sometimes induces despair, ibid., 9. Sadness and acedia (spiritual listlessness) also afflict solitaries, Collation V, 9. What tropology is, Collation XIV, 8. Vainglory. See Cenodoxia (vainglory).

Venial sins cannot be avoided in this life, Collations XI, 10; XXII, 7, 8, 9; XXIII, 7, 8. Venial sins do not remove the designation of justice and holiness, Collation XXII, 13. Nor do they prevent holy communion, Collation XXIII. They must not be regarded as insignificant, Collation XXIII, 7. See Sins. The Word is rightly called flesh because of the one hypostasis in Christ, On the Incarnation IV, 5 and following; V, 7; VI, 22. How truth is to be sought, Collation XVI, 10. The clothing of monks. See Habit. Vigils celebrated on Saturday, Institutes III, 8, 9. The monks’ private vigils, Institutes II, 12 and following.

Virgins in the Old Testament: Elijah, Jeremiah, and Daniel, Institutes VI, 4; Collation XXI, 4. In the New Testament: John the Baptist and the Evangelist, ibid. The commendation of virginity, Collation XXII, 6. Virtue is acquired through difficult things, Collation IV, 12. Virtue is the principal good in itself, Collation VI, 3. Virtues are implanted with greater difficulty than vices are uprooted, Collation XIV, 3. Each person must chiefly attack the vice by which he feels himself most strongly attacked, Collation V, 27. The principal, or capital, vices are eight, Institutes V, 1; Collation V, 18. Some vices are carnal, others spiritual, Collation V, 5. Vices are expelled more easily than virtues are implanted, Collation XIV, 3. Those vices that are outside nature are almost incurable, Institutes VII, 3 and following. The causes and roots of vices must be uprooted, Institutes XI, 15. How vices are to be resisted, Collation V, 14. How vices and defects are to be recognized and corrected, Collation XIX, 12 and following. There are more kinds of vices than of virtues, Collation V, 16.

Three kinds of vocation, Collations III, 3, 4. The diversity of vocations, Collation XIII, 15. To subject one’s own will to another’s is the mark of a strong man, Collation XVI, 23. One must renounce one’s own will, Institutes IV, 8; V, 28. The beginning and completion of a good will are from God, Collations III, 19; XIII, 3. God examines the will, and not merely the deed, Collation XVI. The abundant fruit of a hospice, Collation XXIV, 8. Xerophagy (a diet of dry food), Institutes IV, 21.

[Col. 1309]

# Index of Matters and Terms Explained in the Commentaries and Notes
[Col. 1309]

Abbot: what sort should be elected, I, 82. Most abbots, even among the Egyptians, were priests, 190. Called elders, 481. Abraham’s sacrifice not to be imitated rashly, I, 534. Abraham the anchorite, I, 999. “The abomination of desolation” foretold by Daniel, I, 727. Renunciation, I, 194. See Renunciation. Apse, or apsis, I, 1294. Abstinence from meat commended, I, 217. Necessary for restraining lust, 225. Its necessity, 551 ff. Singular example of abstinence, 958. Acedia: what it is, I, 361. A Greek term, 359. A capital vice, ibid. Its daughters and effects, 361 ff. When it is mortal, ibid. How it differs from sadness, 363. Its two kinds, 370. Especially afflicts solitaries around midday; hence the Fathers called it also the “noonday demon,” 364, 367. It is conquered not by fleeing but by resisting, 368. The vices of acedia and their antidotes, 370 ff. Ahab, king of Israel, I, 528. Achan and his punishment, I, 515. Whether he was condemned, ibid. Feverish attacks, I, 364. Ἀκρότητες ἰσότητες [extremities, equalities], I, 554. Ἀκτημοσύνη [freedom from possessions], I, 1105. Three kinds of human actions, I, 1186. Two duties of the active life, I, 956. Works of the active life necessary in this age, 493. Threefold kind of actions of the active life, ibid. See Life. Adam: whether he was deceived, I, 612, 738. How he sinned and in what ways he was tempted by the devil, 612. Adam, Eve, and the Serpent punished in different ways, 737. The advents of Christ, several in number, I, 233. Punishment of adultery, I, 906. Egypt divided into two parts, I, 79. Irrigated by the overflow of the Nile, 997. Ἀγάπη, Agape [love/charity], I, 1028, 1299. Agatho, I, 968. Ἄγνος [chaste tree], I, 271. Comparison of the spiritual and worldly contest, I, 276. Customs of contestants, I, 276. Agonothetes [judge or director of contests], I, 277, 695. Ehud, ambidextrous, I, 657. King Agrippa, II, 56. Albert the Great, I, 968. At what times the Alleluia is sung, I, 101. Who the allophyli [foreign peoples] are, I, 514. Ἀλύς [chain/bond], I, 627. The disease of ambition, I, 777. St Ambrose, II, 252. Definition of friendship, I, 1011. Its division, ibid. What is required for it to be firm, 1017. How it is preserved, 1019. How it is dissolved, 1038. What perfect friendship is, 1014. Particular friendships in monasteries rejected, 1041. Conspiratorial friendships, ibid. Whether one may at times sin for a friend’s sake, I, 1019. Ammonius, I, 968. The prophet Amos, I, 643. Ἀμφιδέξιοι, or ἀμφοτεροδέξιοι [ambidextrous], I, 657. Ἀναβολή [delay/postponement], I, 71. Ἀναχώρησις [retirement/withdrawal], I, 97. Anchorites, I, 97, 477. Long-lived, 559. Analabus, that is, scapular, I, 71. Ananias and Sapphira, leaders of the Sarabaites, I, 1103. Their destruction, 315, 663. Monks warned by their example, 320. Anathema, I, 514 ff. How the Apostle wished to become one for the sake of his brothers, 790. Abbot Andronicus, I, 710. “Angel” is a name not of nature but of ministry, I, 746. The angel, prince of the Persians, in Daniel, 741. All angels created by God in a state of grace, I, 729. Whether they were created before the corporeal world, 730. Whether they are immutable by nature, 601, 667. They preside over nations, 743. In what sense they are said to fight among themselves, ibid. Guardian angels assigned to individual human beings, 748. Whether two are assigned by God to each person, ibid. and 929. They are incorporeal, 601. Whence their names are derived, 745. Why their fall is irreparable, 602. Their three hierarchies, 733. Angels also fell from the first orders, 603, 733. “He has commanded his angels concerning you,” 515. The rational soul is created by God and infused into the body, I, 756. What the soul does when separated from the body, 500. Threefold will of the soul, 597. Three states, 605. Comparison with a millstone, 507. With a feather, 774. Three faculties, 1306. Three errors concerning the human soul, 499.

[Col. 1310]

The *xenodochium* and its ancient institution, I, 958. *Xerophagia*, that is, the eating of dry foods, I, 181, 182, 211. The practices of heretics are rejected, 181.

[Col. 1323]

The Devil, I, 499, 517. Good and evil zeal, I, 753.

[Col. 1324]

The monks’ belt. See Girdle. Several persons named Zoroaster, I, 758.

### CASSIAN (continued)

Preface to Leo, bishop of the city of Rome, on the books *On the Incarnation*. 9

## ON THE INCARNATION

### BOOK ONE. 11

**Chapter 1.** He compares heresy with the poetic Hydra. Ibid.

**Chapter 2.** He describes the various monsters of heresies, sprouting one from another. 14

**Chapter 3.** He points out the pestilential error of the Pelagians. 20

**Chapter 4.** Leporius, together with several others, recants Pelagianism. 23

**Chapter 5.** He confirms by the example of Leporius that public sin must be washed away by public confession. 24

**Chapter 6.** The harmonious doctrine of Catholics must be embraced as orthodox faith. 29

### BOOK TWO. Ibid.

**Chapter 1.** The errors of later heretics have been condemned and refuted in their authors themselves. Ibid.

**Chapter 2.** He demonstrates that the Virgin Mother of God is not only *Christotokos* (Χριστοτόκος, “Bearer of Christ”), but also *Theotokos* (Θεοτόκος, “Bearer of God”), and that Christ is truly God. 31

**Chapter 3.** He pursues the same argument with testimonies from the Old Scripture. 37

**Chapter 4.** He adduces testimonies of the same doctrine from the Apostle. 40

**Chapter 5.** From the gifts of divine grace that we receive through Christ, he concludes that Christ himself is truly God. 42

**Chapter 6.** The capacity to confer divine grace did not come to Christ with the progress of time, but was congenitally his from his very origin. 44

**Chapter 7.** In Christ, divinity, majesty, power, virtue, and the like were, are, and will be perfect from eternity. 48

### BOOK THREE. 49

**Chapter 1.** Christ, the same person both human and divine, was born according to the flesh from Israel and from the Virgin Mary. Ibid.

**Chapter 2.** The designation “God” is attributed to Christ in one way and to human beings in another. 50

**Chapter 3.** He explains the Apostle’s statement: “From this point onward we know no one according to the flesh.” 52

**Chapter 4.** From the Epistle to the Galatians he adduces testimony by which he proves that the weakness of the flesh in Christ was absorbed by divinity. 54

**Chapter 5.** Just as it is blasphemy to take divinity away from Christ, so it is also blasphemous to deny that he is truly human. 55

**Chapter 6.** From the appearance of Christ that was granted to the Apostle while he was persecuting the Church, he demonstrates that both natures were in Christ. 56

**Chapter 7.** Again, from other testimonies of the Apostle, he declares that Christ is God. 58

**Chapter 8.** In confessing Christ’s divinity, the confession of the cross must not be suppressed in silence. 60

**Chapter 9.** The apostolic preaching was rejected by Jews and Gentiles because it confessed that the crucified Christ was God. 62

**Chapter 10.** How the Apostle asserts that Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God. 63

**Chapter 11.** He strengthens the same doctrine with testimonies from the Gospels. 66

**Chapter 12.** From the most celebrated confession of Blessed Peter, he proves that Christ is God. Ibid.

**Chapter 13.** The confession of Blessed Peter received from Christ himself the testimony of truth. 69

**Chapter 14.** The confession of Blessed Peter is the faith of the whole Church. Ibid.

**Chapter 15.** The same faith of Peter was also professed by Saint Thomas after the Lord’s resurrection. 70

**Chapter 16.** He adduces the testimony of God the Father concerning the divinity of the Son. 73

### BOOK FOUR. 75

**Chapter 1.** Before assuming flesh, Christ was God from eternity. Ibid.

**Chapter 2.** From what he has said, he concludes that the Virgin Mary bore a Son older and greater than herself. 77

**Chapter 3.** From the Epistle to the Romans he proves Christ’s divinity from eternity. 78

[Col. 1324]

**Chapter 4.** From elsewhere he adduces testimonies of the same doctrine. 79

**Chapter 5.** Because of the hypostatic union of both natures in Christ, he is rightly called both the saving Word, or incarnate human being, and the Son of God. 80

**Chapter 6.** There is one hypostasis in Christ. 81

**Chapter 7.** He returns to the earlier consideration, to show against the Nestorians that things belonging to the divine nature are said of the human being as of the hypostasis of the divine nature. 84

**Chapter 8.** This variety of designations does not prejudice divine power in any way. Ibid.

**Chapter 9.** He strengthens this position by the authority of the ancient prophets. 85

**Chapter 10.** He proves Christ’s divinity both from the faithlessness of the Judaizing Jews and from the confession of those who are converted to faith in Christ. 89

**Chapter 11.** He returns to Isaiah’s prophecy. 90

**Chapter 12.** The designation “Savior” is attributed to Christ in one way and to human beings in another. 91

**Chapter 13.** He explains whose person Isaiah represented in the words, “You are our God, and we did not know.” 94

### BOOK FIVE. 95

**Chapter 1.** He attacks most vigorously the error of the Pelagianists, who asserted that Christ was a solitary human being. Ibid.

**Chapter 2.** The doctrine of Nestorius is connected and closely related to the Pelagian error. 98

**Chapter 3.** The participation in divinity that the Pelagians and Nestorians attribute to Christ is common to all holy men. 101

**Chapter 4.** The difference between Christ and the saints. 103

**Chapter 5.** Before his temporal birth, Christ was always called God by the prophets. 106

**Chapter 6.** He illustrates the same doctrine with testimonies from the New Testament. 109

**Chapter 7.** Again he shows that, because the two natures in Christ are united in one person, things belonging to the divine nature may rightly be attributed to the human being, and things belonging to the human nature to God. 111

**Chapter 8.** He confirms the apostolic judgment by the authority of the Lord. 113

**Chapter 9.** Since those miraculous works that had been foretold concerning the children of Israel from the time of Moses are attributed to Christ, it is also inferred that he existed long ago, before his temporal birth. 120

**Chapter 10.** He explains what it means to confess Jesus and what it means to loose him. 124

**Chapter 11.** The mystery of the Lord’s incarnation clearly demonstrates Christ’s divinity. 126

**Chapter 12.** He explains at greater length what that mystery is which is signified under the names of husband and wife. 130

**Chapter 13.** With what longing the ancient patriarchs desired to see the revelation of this mystery. 132

**Chapter 14.** He refutes the impious and blasphemous opinion of the heretics who said that God had dwelt and spoken in Christ as in an instrument or statue. 133

**Chapter 15.** What the wishes of the saints concerning the coming of the Messiah contained, or what kind of desire that was. 134

### BOOK SIX. 135

**Chapter 1.** From the miracle of the multitude’s being fed with five barley loaves and two fish, he demonstrates the immensity of divine power. Ibid.

**Chapter 2.** The author applies the mystery of this number—five loaves and two fish, making seven—to his work. 137

**Chapter 3.** He refutes his adversary by the testimony of the Antiochene synod. 149

**Chapter 4.** The creed possesses divine and human authority. 149

**Chapter 5.** He argues with the finest proofs against his adversary and shows that the religion received from the forefathers must be held to with utmost firmness. 150

**Chapter 6.** Again he challenges him to the profession of the Antiochene creed. 152

**Chapter 7.** He persists in the same argument drawn from the Antiochene creed. 157

**Chapter 8.** How Christ is said to have come and to have been born of the Virgin. 158

**Chapter 9.** Again he refutes his adversary from the latter’s own confession of his pestilential error. 160

[Col. 1325]

**Chapter 10.** He attacks him because, although a deserter of the Catholic religion, he had nevertheless dared to teach, celebrate sacrifice, and administer justice in the Church. 163

**Chapter 11.** He dissolves the objection of the heretics who wish to recant the profession of their faith made in childhood. 168

**Chapter 12.** Christ crucified is a stumbling block and folly to those who assert that he was a solitary human being. 169

**Chapter 13.** He responds to the objection that the birth must be *homoousios* (“of the same substance”) with the one who gives birth. 170

**Chapter 14.** He compares this error with the doctrine of the Pelagians. 171

**Chapter 15.** He shows that those who support this error acknowledge two Christs. 172

**Chapter 16.** He further shows that this doctrine overturns the confession of the Trinity. 173

**Chapter 17.** Whoever goes astray in one article of the Catholic religion nullifies the whole faith and the merit of faith. 176

**Chapter 18.** He turns his speech directly to the adversary against whom he is arguing and invites him to come to his senses. The sacrament of reconciliation is necessary for the salvation of those who have fallen. 178

**Chapter 19.** Christ’s temporal birth took nothing away from the honor or virtue of his divinity. 181

**Chapter 20.** He teaches that his statements do not entail that God is said to have been mortal or fleshly before the ages, even though it is the same Christ who was God from eternity and became human in time. 183

**Chapter 21.** The authority of the divine Scriptures hands down that Christ existed from eternity. 184

**Chapter 22.** The hypostatic union causes things belonging to the flesh in Christ to be attributed to God. Ibid.

**Chapter 23.** This synecdochic manner of speaking, by which the whole is understood from a part, is exceedingly familiar in the sacred writings. 188

### BOOK SEVEN. 195

**Chapter 1.** About to respond to his adversaries’ slanders, he implores the aid of the divine Majesty, so as to teach that those who approach a disputation with heretics must begin with prayer. Ibid.

**Chapter 2.** He dissolves the objection drawn from the words: “No one gives birth to one older than himself.” 199

**Chapter 3.** He responds to the words: “The birth must be *homoousios* with the one who gives birth.” 201

**Chapter 4.** God, as in all other matters, displayed his omnipotence in his temporal birth. 203

**Chapter 5.** From arguments drawn from nature itself, he teaches that the adversaries’ rule—that the birth must be *homoousios* with the one who gives birth—fails in many cases. 205

**Chapter 6.** He refutes another argument of Nestorius, by which Nestorius tried to make Christ equal to Adam in every respect. 212

**Chapter 7.** Heretics are accustomed to cloak their doctrines with the mantle of divine Scripture. 214

**Chapter 8.** Heretics attribute to Christ only an image of divinity and therefore assert that he should be honored together with God, not as God. 215

**Chapter 9.** They are mistaken who said that Christ’s origin was hidden, since it was also plainly demonstrated to the patriarch Jacob. 216

**Chapter 10.** He gathers several further testimonies to the same matter. 223

**Chapter 11.** The devil was impelled by many reasons to suppose that Christ was God. 224

**Chapter 12.** He compares this supposition and plausible suspicion of the devil with the adversaries’ obstinate and stubborn position. 229

**Chapter 13.** Because of Christ’s hidden activity, which the devil perceived, he retained this supposition of Christ’s divinity continuously, up to Christ’s very cross and death. 230

**Chapter 14.** He shows that the heretics distort sacred Scripture, responding to the argument drawn from the Apostle’s words: “Without father, without mother,” and so forth. 232

**Chapter 15.** In what sense Christ is said by the Apostle to be without genealogy. 234

**Chapter 16.** By the example of the devil tempting Christ, he shows that the heretics mutilate and distort sacred Scripture. Ibid.

**Chapter 17.** Christ’s glory and dignity must not be ascribed to the Holy Spirit in such a way that they are denied to have proceeded from Christ himself, as though all the excellence that was in him had come from elsewhere. 235

**Chapter 18.** How the Apostle’s statement is to be understood: “He appeared in the flesh, he was justified in the Spirit.” 238

**Chapter 19.** Christ made himself feared not only through the Spirit but also by himself. 239

**Chapter 20.** He endeavors to invalidate that position with weightier and more compelling arguments. 241

[Col. 1326]

**Chapter 21.** It must be attributed to Christ no less than to the Holy Spirit that his flesh and humanity became the temple of God. 242

**Chapter 22.** Christ’s elevation into heaven must not be attributed to the Holy Spirit alone. 244

**Chapter 23.** He persists in the same argument, to show that Christ did not need glory belonging to another but possessed glory of his own. 247

**Chapter 24.** He confirms this doctrine by the authority of Blessed Hilary. 250

**Chapter 25.** He shows that Ambrose supports Blessed Hilary. 252

**Chapter 26.** He adds to the preceding the testimony of Blessed Jerome. 256

**Chapter 27.** To the foregoing he adds Rufinus and Blessed Augustine. 258

**Chapter 28.** About to produce testimonies of Greek, or Eastern, bishops, he first brings forward Blessed Gregory Nazianzen. 263

**Chapter 29.** In the next place he sets forth the authority of Blessed Athanasius. 265

**Chapter 30.** He also adds Blessed John Chrysostom. 266

**Chapter 31.** He laments the unhappy fall of the city of Constantinople because of the defeat it suffered at the hands of this heretic, and at the same time exhorts its citizens to persevere in the ancient Catholic religion of their forefathers. 269
